title.en: Prometheus and the Theft of Fire
title.zh: 普羅米修斯與盜火

region.en: Mount Olympus / Caucasus
region.zh: 奧林匹斯山／高加索山

period: c. 8th–5th c. BCE

source.work: Bulfinch, Age of Fable; Aeschylus, Prometheus Bound

summary.en: The Titan Prometheus defies Zeus by stealing fire from Olympus in a fennel stalk and giving it to humankind; as punishment he is chained to a Caucasus peak, where an eagle eats his ever-regenerating liver.
summary.zh: 泰坦普羅米修斯違抗宙斯，以茴香莖自奧林匹斯盜取火種贈予人類；因而被縛於高加索山崖，白晝有鷲鷹啄食其不斷重生之肝臟。

passages.text: Prometheus took fire from the forge of Hephaestus and from the hearth of Zeus, hid it in a hollow fennel stalk, and carried it down to mortals. With flame came warmth, metalwork, sacrifice, and all the arts of civilization. Zeus commanded that Prometheus be bound in unbreakable chains to a crag of the Caucasus, where an eagle should feed upon his liver, which grew again each night; so the benefactor of mankind suffered for his gift.

title.en: Deucalion and Pyrrha
title.zh: 丟卡利翁與皮拉

region.en: Delphi / Mount Parnassus
region.zh: 德爾斐／帕納索斯山

period: c. 7th–2nd c. BCE

source.archive: Project Gutenberg (eBook #21765, H. T. Riley, trans.)
source.work: Ovid, Metamorphoses, Book I, Fables VII-X (Riley 1851); passage 1 derives from the original sample corpus (Bulfinch/Apollodorus-based)

summary.en: Zeus destroys the Bronze Age with a flood; Deucalion and Pyrrha survive in a chest, land on Parnassus, and repopulate the earth by throwing 'the bones of the mother' — stones that soften into people.
summary.zh: 宙斯以洪水毀滅青銅時代；丟卡利翁與皮拉乘匣倖存，擱於帕納索斯山，並擲下「大地之母的骨骼」——石頭——使石塊化為人，重新繁衍大地。

passages.text: Deucalion, son of Prometheus, built a chest and embarked with his wife Pyrrha; the sea rose and drowned all else. When the waters fell, an oracle bade the pair to 'throw the bones of your mother behind you' — the bones of Earth, that is, stones.

And at the last, Jupiter bade the seas retire; the god-given Triton blew on his shell-wrought trumpet; the sea had a shore again, the channels received the rivers, and the hills put forth their tops. Then Deucalion led the tears from Pyrrha and fell upon her husband, and both of them were at a loss how to re-people the desolate earth: They were the last of mankind, weeping at the prospect of being left too few. Yet this pair had understanding of the will of the god.

They drew near to the temple of Themis, the daughter of Uranus, and leaning upon their head, kissing the cold pavement, they cried out: 'If the gods still rule, unfold by Thymia, or by whatever art the mortal race may be restored.' The goddess, moved, said: 'go beyond the roof of this temple; draw your garments loose, and throw behind your backs the bones of your great mother.' Then Pyrrha broke the silence first: 'Leave her bones unviolated', she said, 'I am not qualified to do the will of an offended mother, who gave me my bones.' And Pyrrha, after they had for a long time weighed the words in secret, begged, 'I begin to suspect our discernment is fallacious, and the oracles are just and advise no sacrilege; the earth is the great mother — the stones are the bones she bids us cast.' So they threw stones behind their backs. And every stone did grow — as successive — into a man, for those Deucalion had thrown; and into a woman, for those Pyrrha had thrown: and thus sprang up a race of hard-working men, hardened and patient, from the nature of the stone from which they came.

sensitivity.note: [Merged 2026-11-11: the entry 'greek-ovid-deucalion-flood' (Ovid, Metamorphoses Book I, verbatim from the Riley translation, 1851) was folded in as passages 2-3; the original entry's 31-word second passage was dropped as redundant with the Ovid stone-passage, and the duplicate entry removed. Motif world-renewal comes from the folded material.]

title.en: Orpheus Descends to the Underworld
title.zh: 俄耳甫斯下冥府

region.en: Pieria / Lower Olympus
region.zh: 皮埃里亞／奧林帕斯山下

period: c. 6th c. BCE onward

source.work: Virgil, Georgics; Ovid, Metamorphoses; in Bulfinch

summary.en: Orpheus' music charms Hades; he may lead Eurydice from the dead if he does not look back. He looks back; she returns forever to the shades.
summary.zh: 俄耳甫斯的音樂迷住哈迪斯；若不回頭，便可領歐律狄刻出冥府。他回頭了——她便永遠歸於幽冥。

passages.text: Orpheus sang so that in Hades the wheel of Ixion stood still, the vulture left Tityos' liver, and for the first time the Furies wept; Hades and Persephone granted Eurydice's return on one condition. 'Do not look back,' the lovers were warned. At the threshold of the upper world, fearing for her and longing to see her, Orpheus turned — and Eurydice sank back, a phantom, into the deep.

title.en: Ymir and the World from the Giant's Body
title.zh: 尤彌爾與巨軀造世

region.en: Ginnungagap (symbolic: Iceland)
region.zh: 金倫加鴻溝（象徵位置：冰島）

period: c. 13th c. CE (Prose Edda)

source.work: Snorri Sturluson, Prose Edda; Poetic Edda (Völuspá)

summary.en: From the meeting of fire and ice in the void Ginnungagap arises the frost-giant Ymir; Odin and his brothers slay him and build the world from his flesh, blood, bones, and skull.
summary.zh: 火與冰於鴻溝金倫加相遇，霜巨人尤彌爾由此而生；奧丁與其兄弟誅之，以其血肉骨骼與頭顱造成世界。

passages.text: In Ginnungagap, where the heat of Muspelheim met the rime of Niflheim, Ymir the frost-giant took form, and from his sweat came other giants; a cow fed him, licking the first gods from the salt stones. Odin, Vili, and Vé slew Ymir and flung him into the void: of his flesh they made the earth, of his blood the sea, of his bones the cliffs, of his skull the heavens, and of his brains the drifting clouds.

title.en: Odin Sacrifices for Wisdom
title.zh: 奧丁犧牲求智

region.en: Mímir's Well (symbolic: Uppsala)
region.zh: 密米爾之泉（象徵位置：烏普薩拉）

period: c. 13th c. CE (Prose Edda; Hávamál)

source.work: Prose Edda; Poetic Edda (Hávamál 138–139)

summary.en: Odin pledges one eye to Mímir's well for sight of fate, and hangs nine nights on Yggdrasil, wounded by his own spear, to win the runes.
summary.zh: 奧丁以一隻眼睛換取密米爾之泉中的智慧，又自縛於世界樹九夜、以己矛傷己，終得盧恩符文。

passages.text: Odin gave an eye of his for a drink from Mímir's well, wherein lies wit and understanding; the well's ward kept it at its deep root, and from the pledge Odin gained sight of what was to come. Nine nights I hung on the windy tree, wounded with a spear, given to Odin, myself to myself; no bread nor horn did men give me; down I peered, took up the runes, screaming I took them, and fell back thence.

title.en: Ragnarök and the World Serpent
title.zh: 諸神黃昏與世界蛇

region.en: Vígríðr plain (symbolic: Iceland)
region.zh: 維格利德平原（象徵位置：冰島）

period: c. 13th c. CE (Prose Edda; Völuspá)

source.work: Prose Edda; Poetic Edda (Völuspá)

summary.en: The world ends in fire and water: Jörmungandr rises, the sea floods the land, Surtr burns the world; a green earth rises again, and two humans survive to begin anew.
summary.zh: 世界終於火與水：耶夢加得巨蛇騰起，海水淹沒大地，蘇爾特焚盡世界；其後新地自海中再起，二人倖存，人類重新開始。

passages.text: The serpent Jörmungandr, furious, waded ashore, spitting venom; the sea rushed over the land, for the serpent was writhing in giant rage and made waves high as mountains. Surtr flung fire over the world and burned it all. Yet afterward the earth rose again from the sea, green and fair; two of mankind, Líf and Lífþrasir, woke in Hoddmímis wood, and from them come the folk of the new age.

title.en: Manu and the Great Fish
title.zh: 摩奴與大魚

region.en: Sarasvati river banks (symbolic pin at the Vedic river's course)
region.zh: 薩拉斯瓦蒂河畔（象徵性定位於吠陀河流故道）

period: Shatapatha Brahmana 1.8.1, c. 8th-6th c. BCE (Eggeling translation, 1882)

source.archive: Internet Archive (Sacred Books of the East, vol. 12)
source.work: The Satapatha-Brahmana, Part I, trans. Julius Eggeling (SBE 12, 1882), Kanda I, Adhyaya VIII, Brahmana 1

summary.en: Washing at morning in the river, Manu finds a tiny fish in his joined hands. The fish begs to be reared - 'rear me, I will save thee' - and grows through jar, trough, pit and ocean until it is mountain-sized. When the deluge comes, Manu builds the ship, ties its rope to the fish's horn, and is towed through the drowning world to the northern mountain. From his sacrifice, and the waters' deposit, a woman arises: 'in her the race was born.'
summary.zh: 清晨於河中沐浴時，摩奴合掌得一小魚。魚懇求飼養——『養我，我將救你』——經罐、槽、坑、海而成山岳般巨獸。洪水來時，摩奴造舟，以繩繫於魚角，被拖曳過滅世之水，抵北方之山。由其祭祀與水中沉積，一位女子生於其間：『族類由她而生。』

sensitivity.note: Living tradition: Manu is the named progenitor in ritual law and the flood story is retold in Matsya imagery. Classified 'myth'.

passages.text: There was a rishi called Manu, son of Vivasvat, famed in austerity. One morning, bringing water for the oblation in his joined hands, he found a small fish in his palms. The fish spoke: 'Rear me, I will save thee.' Manu asked where it came from; the fish answered only that it was in his hands - nourish it, for a flood would carry off all creatures, and it would save him from the flood.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Shatapatha Brahmana 1.8.1 (Eggeling 1882); not verbatim.

passages.text: The fish asked in what vessel it should be reared. Manu said 'in a jar'; the fish outgrew the jar and asked for a trough, outgrew the trough and asked for a large pit, outgrew the pit and asked for the ocean - Manu carried it to the sea. The fish then told him the year of the flood and the means: 'Build a ship; bring in it the seven seers; stow the seeds of all things, pair by pair; and when the waters rise, fasten the ship to me - I will have a horn, and thou shalt tie the rope to it.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Shatapatha Brahmana 1.8.1 (Eggeling 1882); not verbatim.

passages.text: And in that same year, as the fish had foretold, Manu built the ship, paid homage to the fish, and loaded it with the seeds. The flood arose and swept away all creatures; Manu alone was left, in his ship tethered to the fish's horn. The fish swam - across the drowned earth, through waters rolling like the sea - northward to the northern mountain, and said: 'I have saved thee. Fasten the ship to this tree; descend thou gently, slowly, as the water subsides.' Manu descended - and therefore the northern slope is called 'the descent of Manu'.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Shatapatha Brahmana 1.8.1 (Eggeling 1882); not verbatim.

passages.text: The flood had carried off every living being; Manu alone was left. Desiring offspring, he sacrificed diligently: butter, milk, whey and curds he offered in the waters. In the first year a woman arose from them, wet, ointment trickling from her; Mitra and Varuna passed by and claimed her, but she went to Manu. 'From the very seed thou hast begotten in the waters,' she said, 'thou hast placed me in the waters. Make me thy mate; in me the race shall be born.' Manu was unwilling at first; they sacrificed together - and 'in her, this race was born': she is Ida, the mother of this offspring.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Shatapatha Brahmana 1.8.1 (Eggeling 1882); not verbatim.

canonical_translation: Julius Eggeling, The Satapatha-Brahmana, Part I (Sacred Books of the East, vol. 12), Oxford, 1882 (public domain)

narrative.en:
The flood of Manu - in the Shatapatha Brahmana, the oldest continuous telling of the deluge in Indian literature - is the Vedic ritual corpus' own Noah story, told inside a manual of sacrifice to explain a rite: why morning oblations begin with water held in the joined hands.

The beginning is almost domestic. Manu, son of Vivasvat (the Sun), a seer 'famed in austerity', brings water for his morning oblation with cupped hands, and finds in his palms a small fish that speaks. 'Rear me, I will save thee' - the fish does not explain at first, only repeats that a flood will carry off all creatures. Manu, courteously incredulous, asks what will become of it; the fish's answer escalates with its body. Reared in a jar, it outgrows the jar; moved to a trough, it outgrows the trough; a large pit suffices briefly; then the sea. Manu carries it - the story's quiet comedy is that the future savior of the world must be carried in ever-larger household vessels - and the fish, grown vast, gives the logistics: in such-and-such a year the flood will come; build a ship; load the seven seers; stow the seeds of all things, pair by pair; when the water rises, tie the ship's rope to the horn I will have grown.

The flood comes 'in that same year'. It is total: 'the flood swept away all creatures; Manu alone was left'. The fish tows the tethered ship through rivers, across the drowned earth, northward to the northern mountain - where it tells Manu he is saved, to fasten the ship to a tree, and to descend slowly as the water falls. (The Brahmana adds the aition: the mountain's northern slope is called 'Manu's descent' - the landscape remembers.)

The rebeginning is the strangest part. The flood has left Manu alone and - the text is careful - desiring offspring. He sacrifices: butter, milk, whey, curds, offered into the waters. In the first year, from the sacrifice, a woman arises, dripping; the gods Mitra and Varuna pass by and claim her for themselves, but she comes to Manu. Asked for whom she was born, she answers that she is made from the very seed Manu poured into the waters - his sacrifice made flesh. 'Make me thy mate; in me the race shall be born.' After a joint sacrifice, they unite, and the Brahmana concludes: 'in her this race was born' - she is Ida, mother of humanity.

Function and lineage: the story does double duty as flood myth and sacrifice charter - the deluge is survived by ritual, and the new humanity is generated by an offering rather than by the survivor's children alone. The Puranic versions expand it into the Matsya avatar: Vishnu himself is the fish, warning Manu (Vaivasvata) and preserving the Vedas as well as the seeds; the Mahabharata retells it in the Markandeya section; the iconography is the temple panel of Vishnu-fish towing the boat. In the cross-tradition flood cluster, this is the Vedic-Hindu anchor: survival by animal guide, rescue of the seeds of life, landing on a mountain - with the distinctive Hindu signature that the rescuer is the god who will be worshipped forever after, and that a sacrifice, not a family, restarts the world.
narrative.zh: 摩奴洪水——見於薩塔帕塔梵書，印度文獻中最古老的連貫洪水敘事——是吠陀祭祀文獻自身的『挪亞』故事，嵌於祭祀手冊之中，用以解釋一項儀式：為何晨祭以合掌捧水開始。開端近乎家常。摩奴，毗首竭之子（日神之子），『以苦行聞名』的仙人，清晨合掌捧祭水，於掌中得一小魚，魚能言語：『養我，我將救你』——魚起初不作解釋，只重申洪水將席捲一切眾生。摩奴禮貌地半信半疑，問其何往；魚的回答隨其身軀而升級：養於罐中，罐不足以容；移於槽，槽不足；掘大坑，坑不足；直至入海。摩奴以越來越大的家用器皿搬運這位未來的世界救主——神話的靜默喜劇——而後長成的魚交付後勤細節：某年洪水將至；造舟；載七仙人；貯藏萬物之種，一對一對；水漲時，以繩繫舟於我所生之角。洪水『於同年』而至，且是全然的：『洪水捲走一切眾生；唯摩奴存焉。』魚拖曳繫舟渡河、越滅世大地、北行至北方之山——在那裡告訴摩奴：你得救了；把船繫於樹；水退時緩緩下行。（梵書補充詞源：山之北坡名『摩奴降處』——地貌記得。）重生之部分最奇特：洪水後摩奴獨存且——經文審慎地說——渴望後嗣。他祭祀：酥油、乳、乳清、凝乳，祭入水中。第一年，自祭中生一女子，滴著水；密多羅與伐樓那經過欲納之，她卻走向摩奴。問她為誰而生，她答：由你親自祭入水中的種子所造——你的祭祀成為肉身。『使我為伴；族類將由我而生。』二人合祭之後結合，梵書結語：『族類由她而生』——她即伊陀，人類之母。功能與譜系：故事兼任洪水神話與祭祀憲章——倖存於洪水者靠儀式，新人類由祭品而非倖存者之子女獨自生成。往世書版本擴充為摩蹉化身：毘濕奴親為魚，警示摩奴（婆藪瓦陀），並保存吠陀與萬物之種；摩訶婆羅多於摩根德耶章重述；廟宇浮雕為拖舟的毘濕奴魚。在跨傳統洪水母題群中，此為吠陀-印度之錨：動物嚮導之救、生命之種之存、泊於山巔——帶著鮮明的印度印記：救者正是其後永受崇拜之神，且重啟世界的是一場祭祀，而非一個家族。

functions: Flood myth of the Indian tradition - survival by divine fish, seeds of life, mountain landing
Charter of morning water-oblations (the cupped-hands rite re-enacts Manu's finding)
Foundation of human descent from Manu, progenitor named in later law and ritual
Matrix of the Matsya avatar (Puranic expansion) and temple iconography

variants.name: Matsya avatar version (Vishnu Purana; Bhagavata 8.24)
variants.summary: The fish is Vishnu's first avatar, and the cargo expands: the Vedas (stolen and hidden by a demon) are recovered as well as the seeds; Manu Vaivasvata is a king - deluge, scripture-rescue and incarnation fused.

variants.name: Mahabharata retelling (Markandeya section)
variants.summary: The epic retells the Brahmana story with Markandeya as witness, aligning the historical flood with the cosmic dissolution and adding Manu's descendants as the lineage of kings.

variants.name: Utnapishtim's flood (Gilgamesh XI)
variants.summary: The closest Mesopotamian parallel: divine warning, a vessel with the seed of life, an animal guide, mountain landing, and a post-flood rite - the shared ancient flood grammar.

variants.name: Noah's flood (Genesis 6-9)
variants.summary: Parallel cluster member: divine warning, vessel with animal pairs, mountain landing, covenant rite - with the moral-theological frame of human wickedness and a binding covenant.

primary_sources.citation: Madhyandina recension, SBE 12 (Eggeling 1882), pp. 240-253. English: Eggeling 1882 (public domain).

secondary_sources.work: Wendy Doniger O'Flaherty, Hindu Myths

sensitivity_guidance: The story is retold in living religious education and Matsya imagery remains in temple art; quote public-domain translations; note which version (Brahmana vs Purana avatar) is meant, as they differ on who the fish is.

title.en: The Churning of the Ocean of Milk
title.zh: 攪拌乳海

region.en: Mount Mandara (symbolic)
region.zh: 曼陀羅山（象徵位置）

period: Mahābhārata / Purāṇas, c. 4th c. BCE–4th c. CE

source.work: Mahābhārata, Ādi Parva (trans. K. M. Ganguli)

summary.en: Gods and demons churn the milk-ocean with the serpent Vāsuki as a rope around Mount Mandara; from the waters emerge the elixir of immortality and wonders, including Lakṣmī.
summary.zh: 諸神與阿修羅以巨蛇伐蘇吉纏繞曼陀羅山為攪棒，攪動乳海；自海中湧出不死甘露與諸般異寶，吉祥天女亦隨之而生。

passages.text: They took Mount Mandara for the churning-staff and the serpent Vāsuki for the churning-rope; the gods pulled at the tail, the demons at the head, and the ocean began to foam like milk over fire. From the ocean arose, among many treasures, the amṛta, the drink of immortality, and Lakṣmī herself, lotus-borne; then Viṣṇu, taking the form of Mohinī the enchantress, divided the elixir to the gods alone.

title.en: Pangu and the Cosmic Egg
title.zh: 盤古開天闢地

region.en: Pangu Mountain, Biyang, Henan
region.zh: 河南泌陽盤古山

period: c. 3rd c. CE (Xu Zheng, Sanwu Liji)

source.work: Xu Zheng, Sanwu Liji; Wuyun Linian Ji

summary.en: Pangu breaks the cosmic egg: light yang rises as sky, heavy yin settles as earth, and Pangu grows between them for 18,000 years; when he dies his body becomes the world.
summary.zh: 盤古破混沌如破雞卵：清陽上浮為天，濁陰下沉為地，盤古居中而長，歷萬八千歲；及其死，身化萬物。

passages.text: The heavens and earth were once chaos like a hen's egg, and Pangu was born within; in eighteen thousand years the clear and light rose to be heaven, and the heavy and murky settled to be earth. When Pangu neared death, his breath became wind and cloud, his voice thunder; his left eye the sun, his right eye the moon; his limbs the four poles, his blood the rivers, his flesh the fields, his hair the stars.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Xu Zheng, Sanwu Liji; not verbatim.

license: Public domain (original Chinese texts); modern English paraphrase

title.en: Nüwa Mends the Sky and Molds Humans
title.zh: 女媧補天摶土

region.en: Kunlun Mountains (symbolic)
region.zh: 崑崙山（象徵位置）

period: Huainanzi / Fengsu Tongyi, c. 2nd c. BCE–2nd c. CE

source.work: Huainanzi, Lanming Xun; Fengsu Tongyi

summary.en: When the four pillars collapse and floods rage, Nüwa smelts five-colored stones to mend the sky, cuts turtle legs as new pillars, and molds humans from yellow clay.
summary.zh: 四極傾折、洪水氾濫之際，女媧煉五色石補蒼天，斷鰲足立四極，摶黃土以造人。

passages.text: The four poles collapsed; heaven broke in the northwest and earth sank in the southeast. Nüwa smelted stones of five colors to patch the azure sky, cut the legs of the great tortoise to stand as pillars, and gathered ashes of reeds to stop the deep floods. Nüwa took yellow earth and molded human figures with her hand; the work was great and she had no leisure, so she drew a cord through the mud and flung it, and the drops that fell became human beings.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Huainanzi, Lanming Xun; not verbatim.

license: Public domain (original Chinese texts); modern English paraphrase

title.en: Rangi and Papa, Sky and Earth
title.zh: 天父蘭基與地母帕帕

region.en: Lake Taupō, Aotearoa
region.zh: 紐西蘭陶波湖

period: Oral tradition; recorded 19th c.

source.work: John White, Ancient History of the Maori; Grey, Polynesian Mythology

summary.en: Sky-father Ranginui and Earth-mother Papatūānuku lie locked in embrace; their children, cramped in darkness, separate them — the primordial act that lets light and life into the world.
summary.zh: 天父蘭基與地母帕帕緊擁不分；其子女困於黑暗之中，遂分開雙親——此為光與生命入世之原初舉動。

passages.text: In darkness the children of Rangi and Papa were crowded between their parents; they consulted together how they might sever them, for only in separation would light be, and life. Tāne thrust between earth and sky and pushed his parents apart with his legs; the sky wept for the earth in rain, and mist rose from the earth's sighs for her husband.

title.en: Māui Snares the Sun
title.zh: 毛伊縛日

region.en: East Cape, Aotearoa
region.zh: 紐西蘭東角

period: Oral tradition; recorded 19th c.

source.work: Grey, Polynesian Mythology; White, Ancient History of the Maori

summary.en: The days are too short; Māui plaits ropes, lies in wait at the sun's rising, and beats and binds Te Rā until he agrees to travel slower across the sky.
summary.zh: 白晝太短；毛伊編繩埋伏於日出之處，痛毆並捆綁太陽特羅，使其允諾緩行天空。

passages.text: Māui said to his brothers: 'The sun goes too fast; his food is not cooked before he sets.' So they plaited ropes of flax, and in the morning crept to the pit by which the sun climbed into the sky. Māui snared the sun's rays with the ropes and beat him till he cried out; then Māui unloosed him on his promise to crawl slowly across the heaven, and so the days grew long.

title.en: Māui and Hine-nui-te-pō
title.zh: 毛伊與夜之大地

region.en: Waitomo, Aotearoa
region.zh: 紐西蘭懷托莫

period: Oral tradition; recorded 19th c.

source.work: Grey, Polynesian Mythology

summary.en: To win immortality for humankind, Māui must enter the night-goddess Hine-nui-te-pō through her body while she sleeps; the birds laugh, the goddess wakes, and Māui is crushed — death keeps humankind.
summary.zh: 毛伊欲為人類奪得永生，須趁夜之女神海因努伊特波熟睡時自其身體進入；眾鳥發笑，女神驚醒，毛伊被夾斃——死亡從此常駐人間。

passages.text: Māui said: 'Let us enter the great woman of night, that death may have no more power over men.' The birds feared; the small birds accompanied him to the place where Hine-nui-te-pō slept. When Māui crept into Hine-nui-te-pō, the little tiwakawaka laughed aloud, the goddess awoke, closed upon him, and Māui died; so death remains for humankind to this day.

title.en: Obatala Forms the Land and Humankind
title.zh: 奧巴塔拉造陸塑人

region.en: Ile-Ife, Nigeria
region.zh: 奈及利亞伊費

period: Oral tradition; recorded 19th–20th c.

source.work: Yoruba oral tradition, Ifa corpus

summary.en: Obatala descends on a chain from the sky with earth and a cockerel to spread land over primeval waters, and molds human figures from clay, which Olodumare breathes life into.
summary.zh: 奧巴塔拉攜泥土與公雞沿天鏈而下，將土撒於原初之水成陸；又摶土塑人，奧洛杜馬雷吹入生命。

passages.text: Obatala carried a snail-shell of earth, a hen, and a palm-nut down a chain from the sky; he cast the earth upon the waters and the hen scattered it with her feet, until land lay far and wide. Obatala molded figures of clay; Olodumare breathed life into them, and men dwelt in the town of Ife, from which the rivers of humankind flow forth.

title.en: Shango, King of Thunder
title.zh: 珊戈，雷霆之王

region.en: Oyo, Nigeria
region.zh: 奈及利亞奧約

period: Oral tradition; recorded 19th–20th c.

source.work: Yoruba oral tradition, Shango cult narratives

summary.en: Shango, king of Oyo, masters lightning and the thunder-stones; after his fall his cult endures, and the axe of thunder still marks the houses struck by the sky's anger.
summary.zh: 奧約之王珊戈掌閃電與雷石；其沒後崇拜猶存，雷斧至今標記遭天之怒擊中之屋舍。

passages.text: Shango reigned at Oyo; he had power over lightning and the thunder, and his followers bore him the thunder-stones that fell from the sky. When lightning struck a house, the priests of Shango sought the axe of thunder at its foot; the king went into the sky, and his voice is the thunder still.

title.en: Izanagi and Izanami Stir the Sea
title.zh: 伊邪那岐與伊邪那美

region.en: Izumo, Japan
region.zh: 日本出雲

period: Kojiki 712 CE; Nihon Shoki 720 CE

source.work: Kojiki (trans. Basil Hall Chamberlain)

summary.en: The sibling deities stir the brine with the jeweled spear to raise Onogoro and beget the islands of Japan; when Izanami dies bearing fire, Izanagi follows her to Yomi and flees back, sealing death's door.
summary.zh: 兄妹二神以天沼矛攪海，凝成淤能碁呂島並生下日本諸島；伊邪那美因產火神而死，伊邪那岐追至黃泉，終逃歸並封死泉戶。

passages.text: They dipped the jeweled spear of heaven and stirred the brine; drops from its point piled up and became the island Onogoro, and there the two deities came together and begat the islands. Izanagi followed his dead wife to Yomi; but seeing her changed, he fled, and at the pass he rolled a great boulder; from the darkness she vowed to strangle a thousand of his people each day, and he vowed to build fifteen hundred birthing huts.

title.en: Amaterasu and the Rock Cave
title.zh: 天照大神與岩戶

region.en: Ise, Japan
region.zh: 日本伊勢

period: Kojiki 712 CE; Nihon Shoki 720 CE

source.work: Kojiki (trans. Basil Hall Chamberlain)

summary.en: When storm-god Susanoo's fury drives sun-goddess Amaterasu into a cave, the world goes dark; the gods' mirrored festival lures her out, and light returns to heaven and earth.
summary.zh: 暴風神素盞嗚尊之暴行使天照大神匿於岩戶，世界遂暗；諸神以鏡與祭典誘其出，天 地復明。

passages.text: Amaterasu hid in the heavenly rock-cave, and the plain of high heaven went dark, as did the central land of reed plains; constant night fell upon the world. The gods set a mirror before the cave and laughed at the dancing of Uzume; Amaterasu, wondering that there should be laughter in the dark, came to the door, saw her own radiance in the mirror, and the world had light again.

title.en: The Hero Twins in Xibalbá
title.zh: 英雄兄弟下希巴爾巴

region.en: Guatemalan highlands
region.zh: 瓜地馬拉高地

period: Popol Vuh, c. 1554–58 (copy of older traditions)

source.work: Popol Vuh (trans. various)

summary.en: Hunahpú and Xbalanqué are summoned to Xibalbá, survive its houses of night and blades by cunning, are slain and reborn as entertainers, and end the lords of death — becoming sun and moon.
summary.zh: 烏納普與斯巴蘭克被召至希巴爾巴，以機智度過黑夜之屋與刀刃之屋；死而復生為巡遊藝人，終結死神諸君——化為太陽與月亮。

passages.text: The lords of Xibalbá summoned the twins to play ball in the place of fear; through the river of blood and the houses of blades and darkness the twins passed by cunning. They died in the ovens and rose again as wandering performers, diving to the bones of the lords; thus they defeated One Death and Seven Death, and rose as the sun and the moon.

title.en: The Flood and the People of Wood
title.zh: 洪水與木人

region.en: Chichicastenango, Guatemala
region.zh: 瓜地馬拉奇奇卡斯德南哥

period: Popol Vuh, c. 1554–58 (copy of older traditions)

source.work: Popol Vuh (trans. various)

summary.en: The gods' first humans of wood lack souls and memory; a resinous rain and a great flood destroy them, and even the tools turn upon their makers.
summary.zh: 神所造之木人無魂無記；樹脂之雨與大洪水滅之，就連器物也起而攻其造主。

passages.text: The wooden people spoke, multiplied, and had faces; but there was no heart in them, no memory of their maker, and they walked without purpose. There came a rain of resin and a great flood upon the heads of the wooden people; their griddles, bowls, and dogs rose against them, and darkness at dawn destroyed those that remained.

title.en: Osiris Slain, and Risen
title.zh: 歐西里斯之死與復生

region.en: Abydos, Egypt
region.zh: 埃及阿拜多斯

period: Plutarch, De Iside; Egyptian sources c. 2400 BCE–2nd c. CE

source.work: Plutarch, De Iside et Osiride; Pyramid Texts (selections)

summary.en: Set tricks Osiris into a chest and scatters his body; Isis gathers and revives him long enough to beget Horus; Osiris becomes king and judge of the dead, and Egypt's hope of rebirth.
summary.zh: 塞特以匣計殺歐西里斯並散其屍；伊西斯尋屍復活之並得霍霍魯斯；歐西里斯遂為亡者之王與審判者，成為埃及人之復生希望。

passages.text: Set measured Osiris with a chest and at the feast offered it to him who fit; Osiris entered, the lid was sealed with lead, and the chest was cast upon the Nile to the sea. Isis sought her husband among the reeds of the Delta, gathered the scattered body, and by her charms raised Osiris to life; he thereafter ruled the realm of the dead, where every Egyptian hoped to flourish eternally.

The gods gathered at Teotihuacan to cast themselves into the fire, that a fifth sun might rise; and the lowly god who leaped first became the sun that now moves, which feeds on the hearts of men and cannot go on forever.

On the way out Quetzalcoatl stumbled and fell upon the bones, and they broke; and he gathered them up, and mixed them with his own blood, and from them the people of this sun were made â€” therefore all men are bent and varied.

When Perun struck Veles down, the waters that he had stolen behind the clouds ran free again over the fields, and the people called it rain sent by the thunderer.

She said: 'It is well, Lord,' and went from house to house. At every door they said: 'The dead are many here'; and when the day was spent, she thought: 'The dead are many everywhere' â€” and she laid her child away in the forest, and returned to the Master as his disciple.

passages.text: Hwanung said to the bear and the tiger: 'Eat this mugwort and this garlic, stay in the cave a hundred days, and you shall become human'; before twenty-one days the tiger broke the rule and went out, but the bear endured and became a woman. The bear-woman had no husband, and prayed under the sandalwood tree; and Hwanung made her his wife, and she bore a son called Dangun Wanggeom, who came to Pungsan, made the city, and called the country Joseon.

In her jealousy Pele burned the forests of her friend Hopoe to ashes; but HiÊ»iaka returned, and called the burned land to remember, and the lehua stood red again on the mountains.

summary.en: Sedna is given to a bird-spirit; her father rescues her by kayak, and to save himself cuts off her fingers as she clings to the gunwale â€” the severed fingers become the seals, whales, and walrus, and Sedna becomes their keeper beneath the sea.

passages.text: The bird-spirit had said he was a man and built her a house of fish-skins; when her father came in his kayak she climbed in and fled across the water, and the bird raised a storm against them. Lest the kayak sink, the father cut her fingers joint by joint; the first joints became seals, the second the whale, and Sedna went down to the house under the sea, where the shaman must comb her tangled hair before the beasts may be taken.

summary.en: Corruption fills the earth, and God tells Noah to build an ark; the fountains of the deep and windows of heaven open, everything outside the ark perishes, and the ark rests on Ararat â€” the dove brings the olive leaf, and God sets the rainbow as a covenant.

passages.text: The waters prevailed, and were increased greatly upon the earth; and the ark went upon the face of the waters; and all in whose nostrils was the breath of life, of all that was in the dry land, died. And the dove came in to him in the evening; and, lo, in her mouth was an olive leaf pluckt off: so Noah knew that the waters were abated from off the earth; and the bow was set in the cloud, for a token of a covenant.

passages.text: Loki found that mistletoe had been passed over in the oaths, for it seemed too young; he put the sprig in the hand of the blind Hodr, and guided his aim, and Baldr fell dead on the field. Hermod rode nine nights through dark valleys to the river Gjoll, and Hel said: 'If all things in the world, quick and dead, weep for him, then he shall go back to the Aesir; but if one word is spoken against him, he shall remain with me.'

summary.en: Each night the sun god Ra sails the underworld river in his barque; the great serpent Apophis lies in wait to swallow the waters and stop the boat, and the gods and the justified dead strike it down â€” until dawn, when the sun emerges again.

passages.text: Apophis turned his face against the barque of Ra, that he might swallow the waters and stay the boat; and Set struck at him with the spear, and the crew of Ra cut him with knives, and he could not come. The dead who were justified stood at the mooring posts and speared the serpent each night, for if the serpent prevailed, the sun would not rise and the world would stand in darkness.

summary.en: Sixty thousand princes burn to ash under a sage's curse; only the heavenly river Ganga, falling from the sky, can wash their bones â€” but her fall would shatter the earth, so Shiva receives the whole river in his matted hair and lets her down gently to the sea.

passages.text: Bhagiratha stood on one foot for a thousand years, that the Ganga might come down; and Ganga said: 'Who shall bear my fall? The earth would be split by me, and heaven shaken.' Shiva said: 'Let her fall on my head'; and the river of heaven fell upon his matted hair and wandered in it a season, and then came down to the earth in seven streams, and washed the bones of the sons of Sagara, and they ascended to heaven.

title.en: The Nativity of Jesus (Luke)
title.zh: 耶穌降生（路加福音）

region.en: Bethlehem, Judea
region.zh: 伯利恆（猶太地）

period: Gospel of Luke, c. 80–110 CE (KJV, 1611)

source.work: Gospel of Luke 2, King James Version

summary.en: A Roman census brings Mary and Joseph to Bethlehem, where Jesus is born and laid in a manger; angels announce the birth to shepherds in the field, who spread the word — for Christians, God taking human form, the turning point of salvation history.
summary.zh: 羅馬戶籍令使馬利亞與約瑟前往伯利恆，耶穌降生於馬槽；天使向野地牧羊人報喜，牧羊人傳揚此事——基督宗教視之為道成肉身、救恩史之轉捩點。

sensitivity.note: Presented as a comparative text alongside other miraculous-birth narratives — a scholarly framing, not a claim about religious truth.

passages.text: And she brought forth her firstborn son, and wrapped him in swaddling clothes, and laid him in a manger; because there was no room for them in the inn. And there were in the same country shepherds abiding in the field, keeping watch over their flock by night: and, lo, the angel of the Lord came upon them, and the glory of the Lord shone round about them; and the shepherds said one to another, Let us now go even unto Bethlehem, and see this thing which is come to pass.

title.en: Moses and the Burning Bush (Exodus)
title.zh: 摩西與焚而不燬的荊棘（出埃及記）

region.en: Mount Horeb (Sinai), Egypt
region.zh: 何烈山（西奈，埃及）

period: Exodus, compiled c. 6th-5th c. BCE (KJV, 1611)

source.work: Exodus 3, King James Version

summary.en: Moses keeps the flock of Jethro beyond the wilderness and comes to Horeb, the mountain of God; the angel of the Lord appears in a flame out of the bush that burns yet is not consumed, and God, speaking from the bush, sends Moses to bring Israel out of Egypt and reveals the name I AM THAT I AM.
summary.zh: 摩西牧羊至何烈山——神的山；耶和華的使者於荊棘火焰中顯現，荊棘被火燒著卻不燬壞。神自荊棘中呼召摩西領以色列人出埃及，並啟示聖名：「我是自有永有的。」

sensitivity.note: Living tradition of Judaism. Included as a comparative text in a digital-history corpus — a scholarly framing, not a claim about religious truth.

passages.text: And the angel of the LORD appeared unto him in a flame of fire out of the midst of a bush: and he looked, and, behold, the bush burned with fire, and the bush was not consumed. And Moses said, I will now turn aside, and see this great sight, why the bush is not burnt. And when the LORD saw that he turned aside to see, God called unto him out of the midst of the bush, and said, Moses, Moses. And he said, Here am I.

And God said unto Moses, I AM THAT I AM: and he said, Thus shalt thou say unto the children of Israel, I AM hath sent me unto you. And God said moreover unto Moses, Thus shalt thou say unto the children of Israel, The LORD God of your fathers, the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob, hath sent me unto you: this is my name for ever, and this is my memorial unto all generations.

title.en: Ezekiel's Vision of the Divine Chariot
title.zh: 以西結見神之御座車

region.en: River Chebar, Babylonian Exile (Iraq)
region.zh: 迦巴魯河畔（巴比倫之囚，伊拉克）

period: Ezekiel, c. 593-571 BCE (KJV, 1611)

source.work: Ezekiel 1, King James Version

summary.en: By the river Chebar in exile, the priest Ezekiel sees the heavens open: a whirlwind out of the north, four living creatures, and above the firmament the likeness of a throne of sapphire — the appearance of the glory of the Lord, at which he falls upon his face.
summary.zh: 被擄至迦巴魯河畔的祭司以西結見天開：北方颶風挾大雲與火，四活物自火中而出；穹蒼之上彷彿藍寶石寶座，其上有彷彿人的形狀——耶和華榮耀之形，以西結俯伏在地。

sensitivity.note: Living tradition of Judaism; a foundational text of later Merkabah mysticism. Included as a comparative text — a scholarly framing, not a claim about religious truth.

passages.text: And I looked, and, behold, a whirlwind came out of the north, a great cloud, and a fire infolding itself, and a brightness was about it, and out of the midst thereof as the colour of amber, out of the midst of the fire. Also out of the midst thereof came the likeness of four living creatures. And this was their appearance; they had the likeness of a man.

And above the firmament that was over their heads was the likeness of a throne, as the appearance of a sapphire stone: and upon the likeness of the throne was the likeness as the appearance of a man above upon it. And I saw as the colour of amber, as the appearance of fire round about within it, from the appearance of his loins even upward, and from the appearance of his loins even downward, I saw as it were the appearance of fire, and it had brightness round about. This was the appearance of the likeness of the glory of the LORD. And when I saw it, I fell upon my face, and I heard a voice of one that spake.

title.en: Pentecost and the Coming of the Spirit (Acts)
title.zh: 五旬節聖靈降臨（使徒行傳）

region.en: Jerusalem, Judea
region.zh: 耶路撒冷（猶太地）

period: Acts of the Apostles, c. 80-90 CE (KJV, 1611)

source.work: Acts 2, King James Version

summary.en: When the day of Pentecost is fully come, a sound as of a rushing mighty wind fills the house, cloven tongues like fire sit upon the disciples, and all are filled with the Holy Ghost and speak with other tongues; Peter declares it the Spirit poured out, as the prophet Joel had promised.
summary.zh: 五旬節那日，天上有響聲如大風充滿屋子，火焰之舌分落門徒頭上，眾人皆被聖靈充滿、說起別國的話來；彼得宣告此乃先知約珥所預言：神要將祂的靈澆灌凡有血氣的。

sensitivity.note: Living tradition of Christianity. Included as a comparative text alongside other spirit-pouring and possession narratives — a scholarly framing, not a claim about religious truth.

passages.text: And suddenly there came a sound from heaven as of a rushing mighty wind, and it filled all the house where they were sitting. And there appeared unto them cloven tongues like as of fire, and it sat upon each of them. And they were all filled with the Holy Ghost, and began to speak with other tongues, as the Spirit gave them utterance.

But this is that which was spoken by the prophet Joel; And it shall come to pass in the last days, saith God, I will pour out of my Spirit upon all flesh: and your sons and your daughters shall prophesy, and your young men shall see visions, and your old men shall dream dreams: and on my servants and on my handmaidens I will pour out in those days of my Spirit; and they shall prophesy.

title.en: A New Heaven and a New Earth (Revelation)
title.zh: 新天新地（啟示錄）

region.en: Patmos, Aegean Sea (symbolic: New Jerusalem)
region.zh: 拔摩島（象徵位置：新耶路撒冷）

period: Revelation, c. 95 CE (KJV, 1611)

source.work: Revelation 21-22, King James Version

summary.en: John sees a new heaven and a new earth, the holy city new Jerusalem coming down from God out of heaven as a bride adorned for her husband, and the river of the water of life flowing from the throne with the tree of life whose leaves are for the healing of the nations — where there shall be no more night.
summary.zh: 約翰見新天新地，聖城新耶路撒冷由神那裡從天而降，如妝飾整齊等候丈夫的新婦；又有生命水之河自寶座流出，兩岸生命樹月月結果，其葉可醫萬民——那裡再無黑夜。

sensitivity.note: Living tradition of Christianity. Included as a comparative text alongside other world-renewal narratives — a scholarly framing, not a claim about religious truth.

passages.text: And I saw a new heaven and a new earth: for the first heaven and the first earth were passed away; and there was no more sea. And I John saw the holy city, new Jerusalem, coming down from God out of heaven, prepared as a bride adorned for her husband. And I heard a great voice out of heaven saying, Behold, the tabernacle of God is with men, and he will dwell with them, and they shall be his people, and God himself shall be with them, and be their God.

And he shewed me a pure river of water of life, clear as crystal, proceeding out of the throne of God and of the Lamb. In the midst of the street of it, and on either side of the river, was there the tree of life, which bare twelve manner of fruits, and yielded her fruit every month: and the leaves of the tree were for the healing of the nations. And there shall be no night there; and they need no candle, neither light of the sun; for the Lord God giveth them light.

title.en: The First Revelation: 'Read!' (Surah al-Alaq)
title.zh: 首次啟示：「你讀！」（古蘭經·血塊章）

region.en: Cave of Hira, Jabal al-Nur, Mecca, Saudi Arabia
region.zh: 希拉山洞（麥加，沙烏地阿拉伯）

period: Qur'an, Surah al-'Alaq 96:1-8, c. 610 CE (trans. Sale, 1734)

source.work: The Koran (Al-Qur'an), trans. George Sale, ch. 96

summary.en: In the cave of Hira above Mecca the angel commands the Prophet to read — the first revealed words of the Qur'an; God, who made man from congealed blood and taught the use of the pen, teaches man what he did not know, and unto the Lord shall be the return of all.
summary.zh: 在麥加希拉山洞中，天使命令先知「你讀！」——此為《古蘭》最早啟示的經文；那造人於血塊、教人用筆的主，教人所未知的道理，萬物終必歸於主。

sensitivity.note: Sacred text of a living tradition, presented as a public-domain eighteenth-century translation for comparative study — a scholarly framing, not a claim about religious truth.

passages.text: READ, in the name of thy LORD, who hath created all things; who hath created man of congealed blood. Read, by thy most beneficent LORD; who taught the use of the pen; who teacheth man that which he knoweth not. Verily man becometh insolent, because he seeth himself abound in riches. Verily unto thy LORD shall be the return of all.

title.en: Joseph Cast into the Well (Surah Yusuf)
title.zh: 約瑟被投井（古蘭經·優素福章）

region.en: Canaan to Egypt (symbolic: Nile Valley)
region.zh: 迦南至埃及（象徵位置：尼羅河谷）

period: Qur'an, Surah Yusuf 12, c. 610-632 CE (trans. Sale, 1734)

source.work: The Koran (Al-Qur'an), trans. George Sale, ch. 12

summary.en: Cast into a well by jealous brothers who show their father Jacob a blood-stained garment and cry that a wolf has devoured Joseph, the boy is drawn up by travellers and sold as merchandise — the Qur'anic retelling of the Joseph story, which it calls the best of narratives.
summary.zh: 忌妒的兄長將約瑟投入井中，向父親葉爾孤白展示染血的長衫，哭稱惡狼吞之；旅人汲水時救起童子，轉手賣為奴僕——《古蘭》重述約瑟故事，稱之為最優美的敘事。

sensitivity.note: Sacred text of a living tradition, presented as a public-domain eighteenth-century translation for comparative study — a scholarly framing, not a claim about religious truth.

passages.text: And when they had carried him with them, and agreed to set him at the bottom of the well, they executed their design: and we sent a revelation unto him, saying, Thou shalt hereafter declare this their action unto them; and they shall not perceive thee to be Joseph.

And they came to their father at even, weeping, and said, Father, we went and ran races with one another, and we left Joseph with our baggage, and the wolf hath devoured him; but thou wilt not believe us, although we speak the truth. And they produced his inner garment stained with false blood. Jacob answered, Nay, but ye yourselves have contrived the thing for your own sakes: however patience is most becoming, and GOD'S assistance is to be implored to enable me to support the misfortune which ye relate.

And certain travellers came, and sent one to draw water for them; and he let down his bucket, and said, Good news! this is a youth. And they concealed him, that they might sell him as a piece of merchandise: but GOD knew that which they did.

title.en: Noah Warns His People (Surah Nuh)
title.zh: 努哈警告族人（古蘭經·努哈章）

region.en: Mesopotamia (symbolic: Baghdad region, Iraq)
region.zh: 美索不達米亞（象徵位置：伊拉克巴格達一帶）

period: Qur'an, Surah Nuh 71, c. 610-632 CE (trans. Sale, 1734)

source.work: The Koran (Al-Qur'an), trans. George Sale, ch. 71

summary.en: Sent to warn his people before a grievous punishment overtakes them, Noah calls them night and day; they put their fingers in their ears; and their chiefs refuse to forsake the idols Wadd, Sowa, Yaghuth, Yauk, and Nesr — so the Qur'anic Noah pleads against the unbelievers who were drowned for their sins.
summary.zh: 努哈奉命警告族人重罰將至；他晝夜呼喚，眾人卻以指塞耳、以衣蒙首；諸酋長拒絕捨棄瓦德、素瓦、雅巫斯、葉歐克、奈斯爾諸偶像——悖逆者因罪而溺亡。

sensitivity.note: Sacred text of a living tradition, presented as a public-domain eighteenth-century translation for comparative study — a scholarly framing, not a claim about religious truth.

passages.text: VERILY we sent Noah unto his people, saying, Warn thy people, before a grievous punishment overtake them. Noah said, O my people, verily I am a public warner unto you; wherefore serve GOD, and fear him, and obey me; he will forgive you part of your sins, and will grant you respite until a determined time: for GOD'S determined time, when it cometh, shall not be deferred; if ye were men of understanding, ye would know this.

He said, LORD, verily I have called my people night and day; but my calling only increaseth their aversion: and whensoever I call them to the true faith, that thou mayest forgive them, they put their fingers in their ears, and cover themselves with their garments, and persist in their infidelity, and proudly disdain my counsel.

And they devised a dangerous plot against Noah: and the chief men said to the others, Ye shall by no means leave your gods; neither shall ye forsake Wadd, nor Sowa, nor Yaghuth, and Yauk, and Nesr. And they seduced many; (for thou shalt only increase error in the wicked:) because of their sins they were drowned, and cast into the fire of hell; and they found none to protect them against GOD.

title.en: Krishna's Cosmic Form (Bhagavad Gita 11)
title.zh: 黑天的宇宙本相（薄伽梵歌·十一章）

region.en: Kurukshetra, India
region.zh: 庫魯克謝特拉（印度）

period: Bhagavad Gita 11, c. 2nd c. BCE-2nd c. CE (trans. Arnold, 1885)

source.work: The Song Celestial, trans. Sir Edwin Arnold, ch. 11

summary.en: Arjuna asks to see Krishna's universal form; the vision shows countless eyes, mouths, and celestial ornaments gathered into one blazing Body — as if a thousand suns should rise at once — and the Lord declares Himself Time, the slayer who brings all to doom, before whom the hosts of battle already stand destroyed.
summary.zh: 阿周那求見黑天的宇宙本相；異象中無數眼目、面孔與天飾匯於一體熾然之軀——如千日齊昇——主自稱為「時」，誅滅萬物之時，戰場之眾在他眼中業已不存。

sensitivity.note: Living tradition of Hinduism. Included as a comparative text alongside other divine-manifestation narratives — a scholarly framing, not a claim about religious truth.

passages.text:
Out of countless eyes beholding,
Out of countless mouths commanding,
Countless mystic forms enfolding
In one Form: supremely standing
Countless radiant glories wearing,
Countless heavenly weapons bearing,
Crowned with garlands of star-clusters,
Robed in garb of woven lustres,
Breathing from His perfect Presence
Breaths of every subtle essence
Of all heavenly odours; shedding
Blinding brilliance; overspreading--
Boundless, beautiful--all spaces
With His all-regarding faces;
So He showed! If there should rise
Suddenly within the skies
Sunburst of a thousand suns
Flooding earth with beams undeemed-of,
Then might be that Holy One's
Majesty and radiance dreamed of!

Thou seest Me as Time who kills,
Time who brings all to doom,
The Slayer Time, Ancient of Days, come hither to consume;
Excepting thee, of all these hosts of hostile chiefs arrayed,
There stands not one shall leave alive the battlefield! Dismayed
No longer be! Arise! obtain renown! destroy thy foes!
Fight for the kingdom waiting thee when thou hast vanquished those.
By Me they fall--not thee! the stroke of death is dealt them now,
Even as they show thus gallantly; My instrument art thou!

title.en: The Hymn of Creation (Nasadiya Sukta)
title.zh: 無有歌（創造頌）

region.en: Punjab, Indus plains (India/Pakistan)
region.zh: 旁遮普（印度河平原）

period: Rigveda 10.129, c. 1500-1200 BCE (trans. Griffith, 1896)

source.work: The Hymns of the Rigveda, Book 10, Hymn 129 (trans. Ralph T. H. Griffith)

summary.en: The celebrated 'Hymn of Creation' asks what was before being and non-being: no death, no sign of day and night, darkness wrapped in darkness — until Warmth begot the One and Desire arose, the first seed of mind; even the gods are later than this creation, and perhaps the highest overseer knows not how it came to be.
summary.zh: 著名的「無有歌」追問存在與非存在之先：無死無不死、無晝夜之分，黑暗為黑暗所蔽——熱力生「太一」，愛欲初起為心之種子；諸神晚於此造，究極之主或亦未知世界何自而生。

sensitivity.note: Living scriptural tradition of Hinduism. Included as a comparative text — a scholarly framing, not a claim about religious truth.

passages.text:
THEN was not non-existent nor existent: there was no realm of air, no sky beyond it.
What covered in, and where? and what gave shelter? Was water there, unfathomed depth of water?
Death was not then, nor was there aught immortal: no sign was there, the day's and night's divider.
That One Thing, breathless, breathed by its own nature: apart from it was nothing whatsoever.

Darkness there was: at first concealed in darkness this All was indiscriminate chaos.
All that existed then was void and formless: by the great power of Warmth was born that Unit.
Who verily knows and who can here declare it, whence it was born and whence comes this creation?
The Gods are later than this world's production. Who knows then whence it first came into being?
He, the first origin of this creation, whether he formed it all or did not form it,
Whose eye controls this world in highest heaven, he verily knows it, or perhaps he knows not.

title.en: Nachiketas and Death (Katha Upanishad)
title.zh: 那啟凱多與死神（加陀奧義書）

region.en: Yama's realm (symbolic: North India)
region.zh: 閻摩之境（象徵位置：北印度）

period: Katha Upanishad, c. 5th-1st c. BCE (trans. Müller, 1884)

source.work: Sacred Books of the East, Vol. 15: Katha-upanishad (trans. F. Max Müller)

summary.en: Vagashravasa surrenders all he possesses at a sacrifice, and when the boy Nachiketas presses him — 'To whom wilt thou give me?' — the father answers in anger, 'Unto Death I give thee.' Three nights a guest in Yama's house, Nachiketas is granted three boons; the third is the question whether a man who is dead still is.
summary.zh: 婆遮沙瑞士行祭許獻所有，童子那啟凱多再三追問「父親將把我給誰？」父怒答「給死神！」那啟凱多入閻摩之宮三夕為客，獲三項恩賜——最後一問：人死之後，存耶？亡耶？

sensitivity.note: Living scriptural tradition of Hinduism. Included as a comparative text — a scholarly framing, not a claim about religious truth.

passages.text: Vagasravasa, desirous (of heavenly rewards), surrendered (at a sacrifice) all that he possessed. He had a son of the name of Nakiketas. When the (promised) presents were being given (to the priests), faith entered into the heart of Nakiketas, who was still a boy, and he thought: Unblessed, surely, are the worlds to which a man goes by giving (as his promised present at a sacrifice) cows which have drunk water, eaten hay, given their milk, and are barren. He said to his father: Dear father, to whom wilt thou give me? He said it a second and a third time. Then the father replied (angrily): I shall give thee unto Death.

The son said: I go as the first, at the head of many (who have still to die); I go in the midst of many (who are now dying). What will be the work of Yama (the ruler of the departed) which to-day he has to do unto me? Look back how it was with those who came before, look forward how it will be with those who come hereafter. A mortal ripens like corn, like corn he springs up again.

Nakiketas said: There is that doubt, when a man is dead, — some saying, he is; others, he is not. This I should like to know, taught by thee; this is the third of my boons. Death said: On this point even the gods have doubted formerly; it is not easy to understand. That subject is subtle. Choose another boon, O Nakiketas, do not press me, and let me off that boon.

Nakiketas said: These things last till tomorrow, O Death, for they wear out this vigour of all the senses. Even the whole of life is short. Keep thou thy horses, keep dance and song for thyself. No man can be made happy by wealth. Shall we possess wealth, when we see thee? Shall we live, as long as thou rulest? Only that boon (which I have chosen) is to be chosen by me.

title.en: The Parable of the Burning House (Lotus Sutra)
title.zh: 火宅之喻（法華經）

region.en: Vulture Peak, Rajagriha, India
region.zh: 靈鷲山（王舍城，印度）

period: Lotus Sutra 3, c. 1st-2nd c. CE (trans. Kern, 1884)

source.work: Sacred Books of the East, Vol. 21: The Lotus of the True Law, ch. 3 (trans. Hendrik Kern)

summary.en: The Buddha teaches with the parable of the burning house: an old man's children, playing heedless within a tottering mansion all ablaze, will not come out until he promises them three toy-carts — the three vehicles by which the Tathagata, father of the world, lures beings from the triple world aflame with birth, age, disease, and death.
summary.zh: 佛陀以火宅喻說法：老父宅邸朽壞、四面起火，諸童子嬉戲其中不肯出；父許以三種玩具之車誘之——如來為世間之父，以三乘引渡眾生，出離為生老病死所焚之三界火宅。

sensitivity.note: Living scriptural tradition of Buddhism. Included as a comparative text — a scholarly framing, not a claim about religious truth.

passages.text: In a certain village, town, borough, province, kingdom, or capital, there was a certain housekeeper, old, aged, decrepit, very advanced in years, rich, wealthy, opulent; he had a great house, high, spacious, built a long time ago and old, inhabited by some two, three, four, or five hundred living beings. The house had but one door, and a thatch; its terraces were tottering, the bases of its pillars rotten, the coverings and plaster of the walls loose. On a sudden the whole house was from every side put in conflagration by a mass of fire.

He, the Tathagata, endowed with Buddha-knowledge, forces, absence of hesitation, uncommon properties, and mighty by magical power, is the father of the world, who has reached the highest perfection in the knowledge of skilful means, who is most merciful, long-suffering, benevolent, compassionate. He appears in this triple world, which is like a house the roof and shelter whereof are decayed, (a house) burning by a mass of misery, in order to deliver from affection, hatred, and delusion the beings subject to birth, old age, disease, death, grief, wailing, pain, melancholy, despondency, the dark enveloping mists of ignorance, in order to rouse them to supreme and perfect enlightenment.

Do not delight in this triple world, which is like a burning house, in these miserable forms, sounds, odours, flavours, and contacts. For in delighting in this triple world ye are burnt, heated, inflamed with the thirst inseparable from the pleasures of the five senses. Fly from this triple world; betake yourselves to the three vehicles: the vehicle of the disciples, the vehicle of the Pratyekabuddhas, the vehicle of the Bodhisattvas.

title.en: Ifa, the Great Oracle of the Yoruba
title.zh: 伊法：約魯巴大神諭

region.en: Yoruba country (symbolic: Ile-Ife, Nigeria)
region.zh: 約魯巴之地（象徵位置：奈及利亞伊費）

period: Yoruba oral tradition; recorded 1906 (Johnson, in Dennett)

source.work: At the Back of the Black Man's Mind, Appendix: 'Yoruba Heathenism' (Rt. Rev. James Johnson, in R. E. Dennett, 1906)

summary.en: Ifa, the great oracle of Yoruba country, speaks through sixteen palm nuts whose grasp and mark combinations name the Odu — 256 principal signs, each connected with sixteen subordinates, 4,096 in all; from each sign and its traditional stories the babalawo takes and delivers divination, with the aid of lot casting and the opele.
summary.zh: 伊法為約魯巴之大神諭：以十六枚棕櫚果仁的執取與刻痕組合命名「奧杜」——主卦二百五十六，每卦又轄十六，合計四千零九十六卦；巴巴拉沃（占卜師）依卦象及其傳統故事，配合擲占與奧佩勒鏈為人占問。

sensitivity.note: Living religious system of the Yoruba. Recorded here from a 1906 public-domain publication by a Yoruba-born bishop; presented as an archival record, not as permission to speak for Ifa practitioners.

passages.text: The great Oracle of the Yoruba country is Ifa. He is represented chiefly by 16 palm nuts each having from four to 10 or more eyelets on them. Behind each one of these representative nuts are 16 subordinate Divinities. Each one of the whole lot is termed an Odu - which means a chief, a head. This makes the number of Odu altogether 256. Besides these, there are 16 other Odus connected with each of the 256, and this makes the whole number of Odus 4,096. Some increase this large number still by an addition of 16 more to each of the last number of Odus, but the 16 principal ones are those more frequently in requisition.

Divination is taken by a Babalawo on a highly esteemed broad circular bowl or four cornered fan of a moderate size, which is generally covered with white flour from a dry tree, and upon which he works, and with one of the fingers of the right hand imprints certain signs, representing such Ifa representatives as may be left in the palm of his left hand, after he has attempted with one grasp of the palm of his right hand to take up all the 16, where they were all held.

title.en: Obatala, Owner of the Best Clay
title.zh: 奧巴塔拉：得美土之主

region.en: Ile-Ife, Nigeria
region.zh: 奈及利亞伊費

period: Yoruba oral tradition; recorded 1894 (Ellis)

source.work: A. B. Ellis, The Yoruba-speaking Peoples of the Slave Coast of West Africa (1894), ch. 2

summary.en: In the priests' doctrine recorded by Ellis, Olorun made Obatala and handed over to him the management of the firmament and the world; Obatala — 'Owner of the best clay,' 'the Orisha who kneads clay' — made the first man and woman out of clay, and forms every child in the mother's womb, so that women who desire to become mothers address their prayers to him.
summary.zh: 埃利斯所錄祭司教義：奧洛倫造奧巴塔拉，並將蒼穹與世界交其掌理；「得美土之主」「摶土之神」奧巴塔拉以土造首對男女，且於母腹中塑造每一嬰孩——求子之婦皆向其祈禱。

sensitivity.note: Living religious system of the Yoruba. Recorded from an 1894 colonial-era collection; presented as an archival record, not as permission to speak for Orisha worshippers.

passages.text: Obatala, say the priests, was made by Olorun, who then handed over to him the management of the firmament and the world, and himself retired to rest. Obatala is thus also a sky-god, but is a more anthropomorphic conception than Olorun, and performs functions which are not in the least connected with the firmament. According to a myth, which is, however, contradicted by another, Obatala made the first man and woman out of clay, on which account he has the title of Alamorere, 'Owner of the best clay;' and because he kneaded the clay himself he is called Orisha Iyokpo, 'The Orisha who kneads clay' (kpo, to knead or temper clay). Though this point is disputed by some natives, all are agreed that Obatala forms the child in the mother's womb, and women who desire to become mothers address their prayers to him.

title.en: Shango in His Brazen Palace of Clouds
title.zh: 珊戈：雲端銅宮中的雷神

region.en: Oyo, Nigeria
region.zh: 奈及利亞奧約

period: Yoruba oral tradition; recorded 1894 (Ellis)

source.work: A. B. Ellis, The Yoruba-speaking Peoples of the Slave Coast of West Africa (1894), ch. 2

summary.en: Ellis records the priests' account of the thunder-god: Shango dwells in the clouds in an immense brazen palace with a great retinue, hurling red-hot chains of iron forged by his brother Ogun upon those who offend him; and a later myth makes him an earthly king of Oyo whose tyranny ended in flight — after which the people proclaimed that Shango was not dead, but had become an orisha.
summary.zh: 埃利斯錄雷神祭司之說：珊戈居雲中廣大銅宮，侍從車馬甚眾，以兄長奧貢鍛造之赤熱鐵鏈擊罰冒犯者；晚出神話則謂其本為奧約人王，因暴虐遭逐出逃——族人遂宣告：珊戈未死，已升為歐里沙（神）。

sensitivity.note: Living religious system of the Yoruba. Recorded from an 1894 colonial-era collection; presented as an archival record, not as permission to speak for Orisha worshippers.

passages.text: He dwells in the clouds in an immense brazen palace, where he maintains a large retinue and keeps a great number of horses; for, besides being the thunder-god, he is also the god of the chase and of pillage. From his palace, Shango hurls upon those who have offended him red-hot chains of iron, which are forged for him by his brother Ogun.

This Shango was King of Oyo, capital of Yoruba, and became so unbearable through rapacity, cruelty, and tyranny, that the chiefs and people at last sent him a calabash of parrots' eggs, in accordance with the custom that has already been mentioned; with a message that he must be fatigued with the cares of government, and that it was time for him to go to sleep. On receiving this intimation, Shango, instead of allowing himself to be quietly strangled by his wives, defied public opinion and endeavoured to assemble his adherents; and, when this failed, sought safety in flight.

title.en: The Vaudoux Ceremony at the Serpent's Box
title.zh: 伏都儀式：靈蛇之匣

region.en: Port-au-Prince, Haiti
region.zh: 海地太子港

period: Haitian Vodou; recorded 1884 (St. John, after Moreau de St. Méry)

source.work: Sir Spenser St. John, Hayti; or, The Black Republic (1884), ch. 5

summary.en: A nineteenth-century diplomatic record of a Vaudoux gathering: worshippers gathered in a secure place adore the serpent kept in a box upon the altar, renew the oath of secrecy holding the hands of the king and queen of the order, and fall into a contagious frenzy that shakes the whole circle until some fall senseless to the ground.
summary.zh: 十九世紀外交官所錄伏都聚會：信眾於隱密之地環繞祭壇膜拜匣中之蛇，執該會王與后之手重申守密之誓，繼而全圈陷入相互感染之癲狂痙攣，直至有人昏厥倒地。

sensitivity.note: Colonial-era source strongly shaped by hostile outsider framing. Recorded here as an archival account of Haitian Vodou; the details reflect what its opponents reported, not the self-understanding of the living religion.

passages.text: The King and Queen place themselves at one end of the room, near a kind of altar, on which is a box where the serpent is kept, and where each adept can see it through the bars of its cage. When they have verified that no curious stranger has penetrated into the place, they commence the ceremony by the adoration of the serpent, by protestations of being faithful to its worship and entirely submissive to its commands. They renew, holding the hands of the King and Queen, the oath of secrecy, which is the foundation of the association, and it is accompanied by everything horrible which delirium could imagine to render it more imposing.

This ceremony over, the King places his hand or his foot on the box in which the serpent is confined, and soon becomes agitated. This impression he communicates to the Queen, and from her it gains the whole circle, and every one commences certain movements, in which the upper part of the body, the head and shoulders, appear to be dislocated. The Queen above all is a prey to the most violent agitation. From time to time she approaches the serpent in order to add to her frenzy; she shakes the box, and the hawkbells attached to it sound like a fool's bauble, and the excitement goes on increasing.

title.en: The Voodoo Dance and Chant of Louisiana
title.zh: 路易斯安那伏都舞歌

region.en: New Orleans, Louisiana, USA
region.zh: 美國路易斯安那紐奧良

period: Louisiana Voodoo; recorded 1886 (Cable)

source.work: George W. Cable, 'Creole Slave Songs,' The Century Magazine, XXXI (Apr. 1886)

summary.en: Cable's magazine account of Louisiana Voodoo: worship is paid to a snake kept in a box; a queen presides over a midnight forest gathering around the unseen living serpent; and the chant alternating between king and chorus — 'Eh! eh! Bomba, honc! honc! Canga bafio tay...' — drives the ring of dancers till the novice falls in convulsions.
summary.zh: 凱布爾所錄路易斯安那伏都信仰：信眾膜拜匣中之蛇；王與后主持林中夜會，祭壇上靜臥未見之活蛇；王與眾合唱之咒歌——「欸！欸！邦巴，哄！哄！崗加巴菲奧泰……」——令舞圈狂轉，新手痙攣倒地。

sensitivity.note: Colonial-era source written for a popular magazine, framed by hostile stereotypes. Recorded here as an archival account of Louisiana Voodoo and of a chant as transcribed in 1886; not representative of the living religion.

passages.text: The worship of Voodoo is paid to a snake kept in a box. The worshipers are not merely a sect, but in some rude, savage way also an order. A man and woman chosen from their own number to be the oracles of the serpent deity are called the king and queen. The queen is the more important of the two, and even in the present dilapidated state of the worship in Louisiana, where the king's office has almost or quite disappeared, the queen is still a person of great note.

When the queen decides that such a celebration shall take place, she appoints a night for the gathering, and some remote, secluded spot in the forest for the rendezvous. Thither all the worshipers are summoned. The silence of midnight is overhead, the gigantic forms and shadows and still, dank airs of the tropical forest close in around, and on the altar, in a small box ornamented with little tinkling bells, lies, unseen, the living serpent.

But the dance goes on about the snake. The contortions of the upper part of the body, especially of the neck and shoulders, are such as threaten to dislocate them. The queen shakes the box and tinkles its bells, the rum-bottle gurgles, the chant alternates between king and chorus —

"Eh! eh! Bomba, honc! honc!
Canga bafio tay,
Canga moon day lay,
Canga do keelah, Canga li —"

title.en: The King of the Congo Nation in Brazil
title.zh: 巴西剛果族王加冕禮

region.en: Itamaraca, Pernambuco, Brazil
region.zh: 巴西伯南布哥伊塔馬拉卡

period: Afro-Brazilian brotherhood rite; recorded 1816 (Koster)

source.work: Henry Koster, Travels in Brazil (1816), ch. 12

summary.en: Koster describes the yearly festival of Our Lady of the Rosary, directed by negroes, at which the Congo nation of slaves and freedmen elects a king and queen and crowns them before the vicar in the church — an African nation-rite carried across the Atlantic and woven into Brazilian Catholic brotherhood worship.
summary.zh: 科斯特記玫瑰聖母年度慶典：由黑人主持，巴西的黑人「剛果族」——奴隸與自由民——選立王與后，於教堂中跪在本堂神父前加冕——非洲族群儀式橫渡大西洋，與巴西天主教善會崇拜合流。

sensitivity.note: Colonial-era source; the term 'mock jurisdiction' is Koster's own framing. Recorded here as an archival account of an Afro-Brazilian coronation rite, not as representative of the participants' own understanding.

passages.text: In March took place the yearly festival of our Lady of the Rosary, which was directed by negroes; and at this period is chosen the King of the Congo nation, if the person who holds this situation has died in the course of the year, has from any cause resigned, or has been displaced by his subjects. The Congo negroes are permitted to elect a king and queen from among the individuals of their own nation; the personages who are fixed upon may either actually be slaves, or they may be manumitted negroes.

About eleven o'clock I proceeded to the church with the vicar. We were standing at the door, when there appeared a number of male and female negroes, habited in cotton dresses of colours and of white, with flags flying and drums beating; and as they approached we discovered among them the king and queen, and the secretary of state. Each of the former wore upon their heads a crown, which was partly covered with gilt paper, and painted of various colours. The king was dressed in an old fashioned suit of divers tints, green, red, and yellow; coat, waistcoat, and breeches; his sceptre was in his hand, which was of wood, and finely gilt.

title.en: The Sixteen Lands of Ahura Mazda
title.zh: 阿胡拉·馬茲達的十六國土

region.en: Airyanem Vaego (symbolic: Arran, Caucasus)
region.zh: 雅利安維耶迦（象徵位置：高加索阿蘭）

period: Vendidad, Fargard I; Avestan, c. 1000-600 BCE (trans. Darmesteter, 1895)

source.work: Sacred Books of the East, Vol. 4: The Zend-Avesta, Part I, The Vendidad, Fargard I (trans. James Darmesteter)

summary.en: Ahura Mazda enumerates to Zarathustra the sixteen good lands he created, each marred in its turn by the counter-creations of Angra Mainyu, 'who is all death': the first, Airyanem Vaego by the Vanguhi Daitya, receives the serpent in the river and ten months of winter; and in four-cornered Varena was Thraetaona born, who smote the dragon Azi Dahaka.
summary.zh: 阿胡拉·馬茲達向瑣羅亞斯德細數所造十六善土，而「即死亡」的安格拉·曼紐逐一以反造毀之：首土雅利安維耶迦臨達伊提亞河，得河中之蛇與十月寒冬；四角之瓦雷納生了誅龍者特勞塔奧納。

sensitivity.note: Living scriptural tradition of Zoroastrianism. Included as a comparative text — a scholarly framing, not a claim about religious truth.

passages.text:
Ahura Mazda spake unto Spitama Zarathustra, saying: I have made every land dear (to its people), even though it had no charms whatever in it: had I not made every land dear (to its people), even though it had no charms whatever in it, then the whole living world would have invaded the Airyana Vaego.
The first of the good lands and countries which I, Ahura Mazda, created, was the Airyana Vaego, by the Vanguhi Daitya. Thereupon came Angra Mainyu, who is all death, and he counter-created the serpent in the river and Winter, a work of the Daêvas.
There are ten winter months there, two summer months; and those are cold for the waters, cold for the earth, cold for the trees. Winter falls there, the worst of all plagues.

The fourteenth of the good lands and countries which I, Ahura Mazda, created, was the four-cornered Varena, for which was born Thraetaona, who smote Azi Dahaka. Thereupon came Angra Mainyu, who is all death, and he counter-created abnormal issues in women and barbarian oppression.

title.en: Yima and the Vara Against the Deadly Winter
title.zh: 伊瑪與避冬之瓦拉

region.en: Airyanem Vaego (symbolic: Samarkand, Uzbekistan)
region.zh: 雅利安維耶迦（象徵位置：撒馬爾罕）

period: Vendidad, Fargard II; Avestan, c. 1000-600 BCE (trans. Darmesteter, 1895)

source.work: Sacred Books of the East, Vol. 4: The Vendidad, Fargard II (trans. James Darmesteter)

summary.en: The fair Yima, the good shepherd, refuses to preach the Religion but agrees to nourish the world, where for his sway there is 'neither cold wind nor hot wind, neither disease nor death'; warned of deadly winters to come, he builds the Vara and brings into it, two of every kind, the seeds of men, cattle, trees, and fires, to live the happiest life until the earth is renewed.
summary.zh: 美裔牧者伊瑪拒傳其教，卻允養育世界——其治下「無寒風無熱風，無病無死」；得預警毀滅性寒冬將至，遂築地下瓦拉，攜人畜樹火之種各二入內，安居極樂，以候大地更新。

sensitivity.note: Living scriptural tradition of Zoroastrianism. Included as a comparative text — a scholarly framing, not a claim about religious truth.

passages.text: Ahura Mazda answered: The fair Yima, the good shepherd, O holy Zarathustra! he was the first mortal, before thee, Zarathustra, with whom I, Ahura Mazda, did converse, whom I taught the Religion of Ahura, the Religion of Zarathustra. Unto him, O Zarathustra, I, Ahura Mazda, spake, saying: 'Well, fair Yima, son of Vivanghat, be thou the preacher and the bearer of my Religion!' And the fair Yima, O Zarathusra, replied unto me, saying: 'I was not born, I was not taught to be the preacher and the bearer of thy Religion.'

O fair Yima, son of Vivanghat! Upon the material world the evil winters are about to fall, that shall bring the fierce, deadly frost; upon the material world the evil winters are about to fall, that shall make snow-flakes fall thick, even an aredvi deep on the highest tops of mountains. Therefore make thee a Vara, long as a riding-ground on every side of the square, and thither bring the seeds of sheep and oxen, of men, of dogs, of birds, and of red blazing fires.

Thither thou shalt bring the seeds of men and women, of the greatest, best, and finest on this earth; thither thou shalt bring the seeds of every kind of cattle, of the greatest, best, and finest on this earth. Thither thou shalt bring the seeds of every kind of tree, of the highest of size and sweetest of odour on this earth; thither thou shalt bring the seeds of every kind of fruit, the best of savour and sweetest of odour. All those seeds shalt thou bring, two of every kind, to be kept inexhaustible there, so long as those men shall stay in the Vara.

title.en: The Bundahishn: The Covenant of the Two Spirits
title.zh: 邦達希申：二靈之約

region.en: Fars, Persia (symbolic: Pars, Iran)
region.zh: 法爾斯（波斯帕薩，伊朗）

period: Bundahishn, Pahlavi, c. 7th-9th c. CE (trans. West, 1880)

source.work: Sacred Books of the East, Vol. 5: Pahlavi Texts, Part I, The Bundahis, ch. 1 (trans. E. W. West)

summary.en: The Zoroastrian cosmology opens with the two spirits: Auharmazd in endless light, omniscient and good; Aharman in the endlessly dark abyss, 'with backward understanding and desire for destruction.' Foreseeing the end, Auharmazd recites the Ahunavar that confounds the evil spirit, and creates within his confusion the sky, water, earth, plants, animals, and mankind.
summary.zh: 祆教宇宙論開篇即二靈：奧哈爾馬茲達居無盡光明，全知至善；阿哈爾曼居無盡黑暗之淵，「悟性倒錯，志在毀滅」。奧哈爾馬茲達預知終局，誦阿胡納瓦爾咒使惡靈昏亂，並於其昏亂中造天、水、地、植、獸與人。

sensitivity.note: Living scriptural tradition of Zoroastrianism. Included as a comparative text — a scholarly framing, not a claim about religious truth.

passages.text: As revealed by the religion of the Mazdayasnians, so it is declared that Auharmazd is supreme in omniscience and goodness, and unrivalled in splendour; the region of light is the place of Auharmazd, which they call 'endless light,' and the omniscience and goodness of the unrivalled Auharmazd is what they call 'revelation.' Revelation is the explanation of both spirits together; one is he who is independent of unlimited time, because Auharmazd and the region, religion, and time of Auharmazd were and are and ever will be; while Aharman in darkness, with backward understanding and desire for destruction, was in the abyss, and 'it is he who will not be; and the place of that destruction, and also of that darkness, is what they call the 'endlessly dark.' And between them was empty space, that is, what they call 'air,' in which is now their meeting.

Auharmazd also knew this, through omniscience, that within these nine thousand years, for three thousand years everything proceeds by the will of Auharmazd, three thousand years there is an intermingling of the wills of Auharmazd and Aharman, and the last three thousand years the evil spirit is disabled, and they keep the adversary away from the creatures. Afterwards, Auharmazd recited the Ahunavar thus: Yatha ahuv vairy ('as a heavenly lord is to be chosen'), &c. once, and uttered the twenty-one words; He also exhibited to the evil spirit His own triumph in the end, and the impotence of the evil spirit, the annihilation of the demons, and the resurrection and undisturbed future existence of the creatures for ever and everlasting. And the evil spirit, who perceived his own impotence and the annihilation of the demons, became confounded, and fell back to the gloomy darkness.

Auharmazd created his creatures in the confusion of Aharman; first he produced Vohuman ('good thought'), by whom the progress of the creatures of Auharmazd was advanced. Of Auharmazd's creatures of the world, the first was the sky; the second, water; the third, earth; the fourth, plants; the fifth, animals; the sixth, mankind.

title.en: The Tao Before Heaven and Earth (Tao Te Ching 25, 42)
title.zh: 道在天地之先（道德經·二十五、四十二章）

region.en: Hangu Pass, Shaanxi (traditional), China
region.zh: 函谷關（陝西，傳統說法）

period: Tao Te Ching, c. 4th-3rd c. BCE (trans. Legge, 1891)

source.work: The Tao Teh King, trans. James Legge, chs. 25 and 42

summary.en: Two cosmological chapters of the classic of the Way: before Heaven and Earth there was something undefined and complete — the Mother of all things, whose law is simply being what it is; and the Tao produced One, One produced Two, Two produced Three, and Three produced all things, harmonised by the Breath of Vacancy.
summary.zh: 《道德經》兩章：有物混成，先天地生——可以為天下母，其法自然；又道生一，一生二，二生三，三生萬物，沖氣以為和。

sensitivity.note: Living tradition of Taoism. Included as a comparative text — a scholarly framing, not a claim about religious truth.

passages.text: There was something undefined and complete, coming into existence before Heaven and Earth. How still it was and formless, standing alone, and undergoing no change, reaching everywhere and in no danger (of being exhausted)! It may be regarded as the Mother of all things. I do not know its name, and I give it the designation of the Tao (the Way or Course). Making an effort (further) to give it a name I call it The Great. Great, it passes on (in constant flow). Passing on, it becomes remote. Having become remote, it returns. Therefore the Tao is great; Heaven is great; Earth is great; and the (sage) king is also great. In the universe there are four that are great, and the (sage) king is one of them. Man takes his law from the Earth; the Earth takes its law from Heaven; Heaven takes its law from the Tao. The law of the Tao is its being what it is.

The Tao produced One; One produced Two; Two produced Three; Three produced All things. All things leave behind them the Obscurity (out of which they have come), and go forward to embrace the Brightness (into which they have emerged), while they are harmonised by the Breath of Vacancy. What men dislike is to be orphans, to have little virtue, to be as carriages without naves; and yet these are the designations which kings and princes use for themselves. So it is that some things are increased by being diminished, and others are diminished by being increased.

title.en: The Leviathan, the Butterfly, and the Death of Chaos (Zhuangzi)
title.zh: 鯤鵬、蝶夢與混沌之死（莊子）

region.en: Meng, Song state (Anhui/Henan, China)
region.zh: 宋國蒙（今安徽／河南一帶）

period: Zhuangzi, c. 4th-3rd c. BCE (trans. Giles, 1889)

source.work: Chuang Tzu: Mystic, Moralist, and Social Reformer, trans. Herbert A. Giles, chs. 1, 2, 7

summary.en: Zhuangzi's Taoist allegories from the canonised Nanhua zhenjing: the Leviathan of the northern ocean changes into the Rukh bird that mounts a typhoon ninety thousand li towards the southern lake; the sage dreams he is a butterfly and wakes unsure which he is; and the rulers of south and north bore seven holes in primal Chaos — who died on the seventh day.
summary.zh: 莊子寓言（《南華真經》）：北冥鯤魚化為大鵬，乘颶風九萬里而南徙天池；莊周夢蝶，醒後不知人耶蝶耶；南海之帝與北海之帝為中央混沌日鑿一竅——七日而混沌死。

sensitivity.note: Canonical text of the Taoist canon (Nanhua zhenjing, canonised 742 CE). Included as a comparative text — a scholarly framing, not a claim about religious truth.

passages.text: In the northern ocean there is a fish, called the Leviathan, many thousand li in size. This leviathan changes into a bird, called the Rukh, whose back is many thousand li in breadth. With a mighty effort it rises, and its wings obscure the sky like clouds. At the equinox, this bird prepares to start for the southern ocean, the Celestial Lake. And in the Record of Marvels we read that when the rukh flies southwards, the water is smitten for a space of three thousand li around, while the bird itself mounts upon a typhoon to a height of ninety thousand li, for a flight of six months' duration.

Once upon a time, I, Chuang Tzu, dreamt I was a butterfly, fluttering hither and thither, to all intents and purposes a butterfly. I was conscious only of following my fancies as a butterfly, and was unconscious of my individuality as a man. Suddenly, I awaked, and there I lay, myself again. Now I do not know whether I was then a man dreaming I was a butterfly, or whether I am now a butterfly dreaming I am a man. Between a man and a butterfly there is necessarily a barrier. The transition is called Metempsychosis.

The ruler of the southern sea was called Shu. The ruler of the northern sea was called Hu. The ruler of the central zone was called Hun Tun. Shu and Hu often met on Hun Tun's territory, and being always well treated by him, determined to repay his kindness. They said, 'All men have seven holes,--for seeing, hearing, eating, and breathing. Hun Tun alone has none. We will bore some for him.' So every day they bored one hole; but on the seventh day Hun Tun died.

title.en: The Thai-Shang Tractate of Actions and their Retributions
title.zh: 太上感應篇

region.en: The Supreme Empyrean (symbolic: Wudang, Hubei, China)
