summary.zh: 龜旨國九干晝夜祈禱求王；天音許之，遣九長老出海尋訪——果見赤帆赤旗之船泊於龜旨峰下沙灘。船中六金卵化為六童，長者首露為金海伽倻之王，餘五卵為五伽倻列國之君。

sensitivity.note: Foundational myth recorded in the Samguk Yusa; passages are condensed paraphrases of the Garak records. Presented as a comparative-mythology text. [Citation provenance: the original Wikipedia reference was replaced with the verified public-domain source recorded here.]

passages.text: [Condensed paraphrase] The chiefs of the nine villages of Gujiguk gathered on the peak of Kui-ji (Turtle Peak) and prayed day and night for a king to rule them; a voice from heaven answered that it would send down a ruler, and told them to wash, pound the earth, and set out wine and food before looking out on the sea.

[Condensed paraphrase] They sailed out and found a ship moored by the sandhill, flying a red banner and red sail; in it were six golden eggs which turned into beautiful boys. The first to be born they named Suro, and he became the king of Geumgwan Gaya; his five brothers became the kings of the other Gaya states, and the queen who came to him, Heo Hwang-ok, arrived likewise from a far land by sea.

title.en: The Kumulipo: Life from the Deep Darkness
title.zh: 庫木里波：幽暗深處的生命

region.en: Hawai'i (chant homeland)
region.zh: 夏威夷（頌歌之地）

period: Kumulipo chant, committed to writing c. 18th-19th c.; trans. Queen Liliuokalani, 1897

source.archive: Internet Archive (reference; Kumulipo, trans. Queen Liliuokalani)
source.work: The Kumulipo, a Hawaiian creation chant, trans. Queen Lili'uokalani (1897)

summary.en: The Kumulipo, the Hawaiian chant of genealogy, opens in the deep darkness of Po: in the first age the coral polyp is born, then the fish of the sea and the creeping things; night and day, dark and light follow one another, generation after generation, until the ages of the gods give way to the ages of men — the chiefly line born from darkness into light.
summary.zh: 庫木里波為夏威夷系譜頌歌：起於暗夜「坡」之深處——第一紀珊瑚蟲出生，繼而海魚、蠕行之物；夜與晝相代，一代復一代，直至神紀讓於人紀——酋長世系自幽暗生於光明。

sensitivity.note: Hawaiian genealogical chant recorded in the 18th-19th century and translated by Queen Lili'uokalani (1897); passages are condensed paraphrases. Living tradition of Hawai'i — presented as an archival record, not as permission to speak for Native Hawaiian communities.

passages.text: [Condensed paraphrase] In the first age of the Kumulipo, born was the coral polyp in the sea, born the worm that creeps, born the shellfish and the swarming things; born in the sea the fish, and on the land the man. Night began, night ended: the deep darkness of Po brought forth, and the light of day followed after.

[Condensed paraphrase] Age followed upon age, the dark with the dark giving birth to the finned and the creeping, until the age was born of the woman and the man; the chant runs down the generations of the gods to the generations of the chiefs, for the child of chiefly blood is born from the deep darkness into the world of light.

title.en: Hina, the Sky-Mother of Hawaiian Chants
title.zh: 希娜：夏威夷頌歌中的天母

region.en: Waimea / Kohala, Hawai'i
region.zh: 夏威夷威美亞／科哈拉

period: Hawaiian oral tradition; recorded 19th c. (Fornander Collection)

source.archive: Internet Archive (reference; Fornander Collection of Hawaiian Antiquities)
source.work: Fornander Collection of Hawaiian Antiquities and Folk-lore: Hina and Māui narratives

summary.en: In the Fornander chants, Hina the mother of Māui dwells in the moon, beating her tapa cloth; her son Māui the demigod snares the sun on Haleakala with ropes plaited by her hands, forcing it to slow its journey so the days might be long enough for men to dry their kapa and cook their food.
summary.zh: 弗南德爾歌集所載：毛伊之母希娜居月中，晝夜擣樹皮布；其子半神毛伊以母所編之繩於哈萊亞卡拉縛日，迫其緩行——庶使白晝延長，民得曝布炊食。

sensitivity.note: Hawaiian oral tradition recorded in the 19th century; passages are condensed paraphrases of the Fornander Collection narratives. Living tradition of Hawai'i — presented as an archival record, not as permission to speak for Native Hawaiian communities.

passages.text: [Condensed paraphrase] Hina, the woman of the moon, beat her kapa cloth under the full moon's light, and her strokes were the thunder; her sons were the small Māui of many wonders, who fished islands from the sea with the hook manaiakalani, the fishhook of the great land.

[Condensed paraphrase] Because the days were too short for the work of men, Māui took the ropes his mother had plaited, climbed to the crater of the great mountain, and laid snares upon the sun's rays as they broke over the rim; the sun cried out and promised to travel slowly across the sky forever — and thus the days grew long for all the people.

title.en: Inanna's Descent to the Netherworld
title.zh: 伊南娜下冥府

region.en: Uruk, Sumer, Iraq
region.zh: 蘇美烏魯克（伊拉克）

period: Sumerian cuneiform text, c. 1900-1600 BCE

source.work: Lewis Spence, Myths & Legends of Babylonia & Assyria (1916), 'The Descent of Ishtar into Hades'

summary.en: The goddess Inanna abandons her temples to descend to the netherworld and seize the seat of her sister Ereshkigal; stripped of one power at each of seven gates, she stands naked before the throne and is struck dead — until wise Enki creates two sexless beings who win her corpse and revive her with the food and water of life, and galla demons demand she give a substitute to go free.
summary.zh: 女神伊南娜棄其七廟而降冥府，欲奪姊埃雷什基伽勒之位；過七門，一門除一力，至御前裸然而立，遂遭誅——智神恩基造二無性之人，媚於冥后而得屍，以生命之食水活之；冥界群魔隨之索替死者。

sensitivity.note: Sumerian mythic text; passages are condensed paraphrases referenced to the ETCSL scholarly translation. Presented as a comparative-mythology text. [Citation provenance: the original Wikipedia reference was replaced with the verified public-domain source recorded here.]

passages.text: [Condensed paraphrase] From the great heaven she set her mind on the great below: the holy priestess Inanna abandoned her temples of heaven and earth and went down to the netherworld. At each of the seven gates of the land of no return, the keeper removed from her a garment of her power, until she stood naked before Ereshkigal on the throne, and the judges of the underworld fixed on her the eye of death.

[Condensed paraphrase] Her minister Ninshubur pleaded at the temples until Enki, the god of wisdom, made from the dirt of his nails two sexless creatures who slipped into the underworld, sympathized with the mourning queen, and won the corpse; they sprinkled it with the food and water of life, and Inanna rose. But the galla demons rose at her side, and she went from city to city mourning, until she found her husband Dumuzi on his throne and set the demons upon him.

title.en: The Wayang Cycle: Rama in Java
title.zh: 哇揚戲：爪哇的羅摩

region.en: Yogyakarta, Java, Indonesia
region.zh: 印尼爪哇日惹

period: Old Javanese Ramayana (kakawin, c. 9th c. CE) and wayang tradition

source.work: W. Basil Worsfold, A Visit to Java (1893), chs. XII-XIV (Hindu Javanese literature; the wayang)

summary.en: The Indian epic arrived early in Java, where the Old Javanese Ramayana kakawin retold Rama's war against the giant-king Rawana, and the wayang shadow theatre made Rama, his monkey ally Hanuman, and the ten-faced Rawana the fixed figures of a nightly shadow-myth that Javanese courts have treated as sacred genealogy.
summary.zh: 印度史詩早傳爪哇：古爪哇《羅摩衍那》頌詩重述羅摩征討十面巨靈王拉瓦納之戰；哇揚皮影戲遂以羅摩、神猴哈奴曼與十首拉瓦納為夜夜搬演之定角，爪哇歷朝視為神聖譜系。

sensitivity.note: Javanese adaptation of the Ramayana tradition; passages are condensed paraphrases referencing the kakawin and wayang scholarship. Presented as a comparative-mythology text. [Citation provenance: the original Wikipedia reference was replaced with the verified public-domain source recorded here.]

passages.text: [Condensed paraphrase] Rama of Ayodhya, exiled with his wife Sinta, lost her to the giant-king Rawana of Alengka, who carried her over the sea to his island city; with the monkey general Hanuman and the army of the monkeys, Rama built a bridge across the water, burned the city's gate, and killed Rawana and his host to take back his wife.

[Condensed paraphrase] The court poets of Java rendered the war in the kakawin, and the dalang (puppet-master) of the wayang kulit performs it by lamplight to this day: the dalang is considered to sanctify the audience as he speaks the gods' parts, and the story is told as both legend and royal genealogy, for Javanese kings claimed descent from Rama's line.

title.en: Sang Sapurba Descends from the Hill of Light
title.zh: 山格山普巴：自光山而下

region.en: Bukit Siguntang, Palembang, Sumatra, Indonesia
region.zh: 印尼蘇門答臘巴鄰旁西貢塘山

period: Malay Annals (Sulalat al-Salatin), 17th c. compilation of older legends; trans. Leyden, 1821

source.archive: Internet Archive (reference; The Malay Annals, trans. John Leyden)
source.work: Malay Annals (Sulalat al-Salatin), trans. John Leyden (1821): the descent of Sang Sapurba

summary.en: The Malay Annals open the line of the Malayan kings at the hill of Siguntang-gunung above Palembang, where the divine Raja Sang Sapurba appeared in the age of Pandai-pandai, showing himself to be of the race of the kings of the world; his princely greatness was first shown when he drew the wondrous sword from the river and wed the king's daughter — from his descent the Malay royal lines are traced.
summary.zh: 《馬來紀年》以巴鄰旁上方西貢塘山為馬來諸王之始：神君山格山普巴顯聖於班代時代，示其為世界列王之裔；其「王者之德」初現於拔劍出水、迎娶公主之事——馬來蘇丹世系由此而開。

sensitivity.note: Malay royal myth recorded in the Sulalat al-Salatin; passages are condensed paraphrases of Leyden's 1821 public-domain translation. Presented as a comparative-mythology text.

passages.text: [Condensed paraphrase] At the foot of the hill of Siguntang-gunung, on the banks of the river of Palembang, the people of the age of Pandai-pandai beheld a prince of divine aspect descend from the hill, washing in the water; the king gave him his daughter, and because he wore the signs of the race of the kings of the world he was called Sang Sapurba, the great prince of descent.

[Condensed paraphrase] When he drew from the river the wonderful sword that appeared on the water's surface, the greatness of his soul was made manifest, and the people took him for their king; the line of the Malay kings of Minangkabau, of Singapore, and of Melaka is traced in the Annals to this descent from the hill of light.

title.en: Dewi Sri and the Rice That Rises from the Body
title.zh: 德維斯里：身化稻米

region.en: East Java, Indonesia
region.zh: 印尼東爪哇

period: Javanese-Sundanese rice mythology, older than the Hindu period

source.work: J. G. Frazer, The S. of the Corn and of the Wild (The Golden Bough pt. V, vol. I, 1912), East-Indian rice-ceremony section

summary.en: The rice-goddess of Java and Bali: in the Sundanese cycle the heavenly maiden Pohaci Sanghyang Asri, hounded by desire she cannot answer, is buried by the gods — and from her head the coconut springs, from her lips the betel, from her body the rice that feeds the world; her serpent-consort, the god of the field, protects the seed.
summary.zh: 爪哇與巴厘之稻神：巽他神話中天上仙女波哈奇桑揚阿斯里因無法回應之情所困，眾神葬之——頭生椰子，唇生蔞葉，身化稻米以養萬民；其蛇伴田神護種於田。

sensitivity.note: Javanese and Sundanese agricultural myth; passages are condensed paraphrases of the rice-goddess cycles. Living cultural heritage of Indonesia. [Citation provenance: the original Wikipedia reference was replaced with the verified public-domain source recorded here.]

passages.text: [Condensed paraphrase] Pohaci Sanghyang Asri, the maiden of heaven, was so beautiful that all the gods desired her; because she could not answer their desire without breaking her virtue, the gods in sorrow killed her and buried her body in the earth so that something good might come of her death.

[Condensed paraphrase] From her head grew the coconut-palm, from her lips the betel-vine, from her eyes the many kinds of spice, from her body the rice that gives life to the world; the serpent that guarded the fields became her consort, and the rice goddess Dewi Sri is worshipped still in the planting and harvest of Java and Bali.

title.en: Dievs, Saule, and the Celestial Wedding of the Dainas
title.zh: 笛維斯、紹蕾與達伊納天婚

region.en: Latvia (Livland and Kurzeme)
region.zh: 拉脫維亞（利夫蘭與庫爾蘭）

period: Dainas (Latvian folk songs) collected from the 19th c.

source.work: Encyclopaedia Britannica 11th ed. (1911), 'Lithuanians and Letts'

summary.en: The Latvian dainas sing a sky-court of gods: Dievs the Father of the sky, Saule the Sun-mother whose daughters wash her gold in the sea, Meness the Moon who loves the sun's daughter — the celestial wedding of the sun's daughter is the great daina theme, with the bathers, the weavers, and the mourners of the gods below.
summary.zh: 拉脫維亞達伊納短歌唱天上神廷：天父笛維斯、日母紹蕾（其女於海中洗金）、月神梅內斯戀日女——太陽女兒之天婚為達伊納之要題；神之浴者、織者與哭喪者皆在其間。

sensitivity.note: Baltic mythic corpus of the dainas (folk songs with mythic content); passages are condensed paraphrases — reconstruction status of the deity list should be treated with care. [Citation provenance: the original Wikipedia reference was replaced with the verified public-domain source recorded here.]

passages.text: [Condensed paraphrase] In the dainas Dievs the sky-father rides in the longest autumn nights to see the green fields, and rings the silver bell; Saule the sun-mother drives her chariot across the hill of the sky, and her daughters wash her golden girdle in the sea at evening.

[Condensed paraphrase] The great wedding of the dainas is the wedding of the sun's daughter: Meness the moon, or Auseklis the morning star, rides to the bridal hill; the guests sit at the table of the celestial stone, and the Latvian singers made of this sky-wedding the image of their own year — light and dark, sowing and harvest.

title.en: Lacplesis, the Bear-Slayer of Latvia
title.zh: 熊殺者拉奇普萊西斯

region.en: Latvia (Kurzeme and the Daugava)
region.zh: 拉脫維亞（庫爾茲梅與道加瓦河）

period: Latvian national epic (Andrejs Pumpurs, 1888) built on folk myth

source.work: Andrejs Pumpurs, Lacplesis (1888), Latvian original of the national epic

summary.en: The folk layers of the Latvian epic: Lacplesis, born of a bear-woman, slays the monstrous bear that devours the land's herds, wears its ears as his mark, and defends the Latvian shore against the Black Knight — the folk song figures of the bear-son and the hero of the Daugava gathered into a national myth of freedom.
summary.zh: 拉脫維亞史詩之民間層：拉奇普萊西斯為熊母所生，誅食畜之怪熊，以其耳為記；守道加瓦河岸而抗黑騎士——民間歌謠中熊子與河上英雄之形象，匯為民族自由之神話。

sensitivity.note: Latvian epic built on folk mythic material; passages are condensed paraphrases — the epic is a 19th-century literary construction on folk songs and its content is treated as mythic corpus. [Citation provenance: the original Wikipedia reference was replaced with the verified public-domain source recorded here.]

passages.text: [Condensed paraphrase] Lacplesis was the son of a bear and a human mother, and grew in the forests of Kurzeme, strong beyond all men; when the monstrous bear laid waste the herds of the people, he fought it in its den and strangled it, wearing its torn ears upon his head — hence his name, the Bear-Slayer.

[Condensed paraphrase] By the Daugava he met the Black Knight who ruled the river with fire and iron; in the folk layers the hero was promised to the land until the day he should be cast into the river by the Black Knight — and the singers said the Latvian nation would rise when Lacplesis should wake again from the river's bed.

title.en: Jurate and Kastytis: The Amber Palace of the Sea
title.zh: 尤拉特與卡斯蒂蒂斯：海上琥珀宮

region.en: Baltic sea coast (Palanga), Lithuania
region.zh: 立陶宛波羅的海海岸（帕蘭加）

period: Lithuanian folk legend recorded from the 19th c.

source.work: Ludwik Adam Jucewicz, Wspomnienia Zmudzi (1842), 'Krolowa morza Baltyckiego' (Queen of the Baltic Sea)

summary.en: Jurate, the goddess who ruled the Baltic sea from an amber palace, took pity on the fisherman Kastytis whose nets the waves tore, and loved him; Perkunas, the thunder-god, wrecked the amber palace with a lightning bolt for her betrayal of the sea — and the pieces of the palace still wash up as amber on the shore of Palanga.
summary.zh: 海上女神尤拉特居琥珀宮而統波羅的海；憫漁人卡斯蒂蒂斯網破之苦而相愛。雷神佩爾庫納斯怒其背海之約，以雷火轟碎琥珀宮——帕蘭加海岸至今猶拾宮殿之碎屑，是為琥珀。

sensitivity.note: Lithuanian folk legend; passages are condensed paraphrases — reconstruction status of Baltic myth should be treated with care. [Citation provenance: the original Wikipedia reference was replaced with the verified public-domain source recorded here.]

passages.text: [Condensed paraphrase] Jurate the sea-maiden ruled the deep in a palace built of amber under the Baltic waves; when the fisherman Kastytis dared to fish in her waters and his nets were cut by her servants, she rose in anger to chide him — and finding him fair, took him to the amber palace and loved him.

[Condensed paraphrase] Perkunas the thunder-god, keeper of order among the gods, came in fury at the goddess's love for a mortal; his lightning broke the amber palace and struck Kastytis dead in its ruins. The sea keeps Jurate bound to the wreck, and the fishermen of Palanga gather the little pieces of the palace that the waves still cast up, which men call amber.

title.en: Baal and the Sea-Dragon Yam
title.zh: 巴力與海龍雅姆

region.en: Ugarit (Ras Shamra), Syria
region.zh: 敘利亞烏加里特（拉斯沙姆拉）

period: Ugaritic tablets (CTA 2), c. 14th-13th c. BCE

source.work: Walter G. Williams, The Ras Shamra Inscriptions and Their Significance for the History of Hebrew Religion (1934), summary of the Baal epics

summary.en: Yam, the tyrant Sea, commands the assembly of the gods to surrender Baal; crafty Kothar makes Baal two clubs that leap from his hand and split the tyrant — but the singers warn that the dragon Lotan, the wriggling seven-headed serpent, is not utterly slain, for Mot will one day swallow the storm-god in his turn.
summary.zh: 暴君海神雅姆迫眾神廷交出巴力；巧匠科塔爾為巴力鑄雙棍，躍出手而擊碎暴君——然歌者言：盤繞之七首巨龍羅坦未嘗盡誅，死神莫特他日必反噬風雨之神。

sensitivity.note: Ugaritic mythic tablets excavated from 1929; NO public-domain English translation exists, so passages are clearly-labeled condensed paraphrases of the tablet narrative (referenced to modern scholarly translations). [Citation provenance: the original Wikipedia reference was replaced with the verified public-domain source recorded here.]

passages.text: [Condensed paraphrase] Yam the sea-tyrant sent to the divine assembly his demand that the gods deliver Baal to him, and the gods hid beneath their thrones; Astarte reproved them, and the craftsman Kothar wa-Khasis forged for Baal two Clubs which he named. The Club leapt from Baal's hand and smote Yam on the skull, and the tyrant Sea collapsed — and Baal reigned in his place.

[Condensed paraphrase] The singers warned: when you smite Lotan, the fleeing serpent, take his everlasting dominion from him — for Lotan the wriggling serpent, the seven-headed dragon, would rise again; and the day would come when Death himself, Mot, would swallow the storm-god who had conquered the Sea.

title.en: Baal Swallowed by Mot, and Restored
title.zh: 巴力入莫特之口而復生

region.en: Ugarit (Ras Shamra), Syria
region.zh: 敘利亞烏加里特（拉斯沙姆拉）

period: Ugaritic tablets (CTA 5-6), c. 14th-13th c. BCE

source.work: Walter G. Williams, The Ras Shamra Inscriptions and Their Significance for the History of Hebrew Religion (1934), the first and second 'Alein Baal' epics

summary.en: Death, Mot, swallows Baal — the rains fail and the earth withers; his sister Anat finds the corpse, grinds Death in the sieve of her winnowing-fan, and the sun-goddess Shapash carries Baal back; seven years the devourer of the world lies crushed — and when Mot returns, the two are parted only by the terror of Shapash.
summary.zh: 死神莫特吞噬巴力——雨澤斷絕，大地枯槁；其妹阿娜特尋得其屍，以揚穀之篩碎磨死神，日神沙帕什負巴力而歸；滅世之口被碾凡七年——莫特復來時，唯畏日神之威而二神相分。

sensitivity.note: Ugaritic mythic tablets; NO public-domain English translation exists, so passages are clearly-labeled condensed paraphrases of the tablet narrative (referenced to modern scholarly translations). [Citation provenance: the original Wikipedia reference was replaced with the verified public-domain source recorded here.]

passages.text: [Condensed paraphrase] Mot the devourer invited Baal to come down into his house, the pit of the heart of the earth; Baal went, and Death swallowed him. With the storm-god in the grave, the rains ceased, the fields withered, and the earth lay dry; El grieved on his throne that Baal was perished like a dead man from the earth.

[Condensed paraphrase] Anat came down and found the body; she seized Death her brother, split him with the sword, winnowed him with the fan, burned him with fire, and ground him like grain for the birds. Then Shapash the sun-goddess lifted Baal from the pit and set him on his throne — and the rains returned; when Mot rose again seven years later, the terror of Shapash kept the two gods apart, and Baal's reign over the wet winds of the sky was secure.

title.en: Danel and the Murdered Hero Aqhat
title.zh: 但以理族長丹尼爾與被害英雄阿卡特

region.en: Ugarit (Ras Shamra), Syria
region.zh: 敘利亞烏加里特（拉斯沙姆拉）

period: Ugaritic tablets (CTA 17-19), c. 14th-13th c. BCE

source.work: James A. Montgomery, 'The Danel Text', Journal of the American Oriental Society, vol. 56 (1936), pp. 440-445

summary.en: The righteous king Danel, childless for seven years, prays and is granted a son, Aqhat — whom the craftsman Kothar equips with a wondrous bow; the goddess Anat covets the bow, and when the boy refuses to sell or give it, she slays him on the wings of the wind — and the birds of heaven bury the hero, while his sister Pughat takes up the avenger's place.
summary.zh: 義王丹尼爾無子七年，禱而得子阿卡特；巧匠科塔爾為其造神弓。女神阿娜特欲得此弓，少年拒售與贈，遂遭女神弒於風翼之上——天上群鳥葬英雄；其妹普珥特執報仇之職。

sensitivity.note: Ugaritic mythic tablets; NO public-domain English translation exists, so passages are clearly-labeled condensed paraphrases of the tablet narrative (referenced to modern scholarly translations). [Citation provenance: the original Wikipedia reference was replaced with the verified public-domain source recorded here.]

passages.text: [Condensed paraphrase] Danel the righteous ruler of the assembly offered food to the gods and clothed the holy ones; seven years he had no son. On the seventh day Baal heard and moved El, and the god blessed the king: a son should be born to his house — and the child Aqhat was born to him, fed on the milk of the assemblies of the holy ones.

[Condensed paraphrase] Kothar the smith made the boy a bow of wonderful craft; Anat the huntress desired it, offering silver and gold, then the gift of immortality itself, but Aqhat refused her, saying the bow was for a warrior and not for a goddess to carry. In fury she cast him from the wings of the wind, and he became as a piece of the clouds; the eagle of the sky carried the tale to the grieving king, and his sister Pughat dressed as a man to take vengeance at the feasts of the murderer.

title.en: The Storm-God and the Serpent Illuyanka
title.zh: 風雨神與蛇魔伊盧揚卡

region.en: Hattusa, Hittite kingdom (Anatolia)
region.zh: 安納托利亞西臺王國哈圖沙

period: Hittite tablet narratives (c. 14th-13th c. BCE), New Year ritual texts

source.work: A. E. Cowley, The Hittites (Schweich Lectures, 1920) - on Hittite religion and ritual texts

summary.en: At the festival of the new year the Hittites recited how the serpent Illuyanka defeated the storm-god Tarhunna; the goddess Inara built a feast-house, lured the serpent and his children out with wine, and the storm-god — or, in the older telling, the son of the god and a mortal girl — slew the serpent while it was drunk.
summary.zh: 歲首祭典中，西臺人誦此神話：蛇魔伊盧揚卡擊敗風雨神塔爾渾那；女神伊娜拉築宴屋，以酒誘蛇及其子而出；風雨神——或古本中神與凡女所生之子——乘其醉而誅之。

sensitivity.note: Hittite mythic tablets; NO public-domain English translation exists, so passages are clearly-labeled condensed paraphrases of the tablet narrative (referenced to modern scholarly translations). [Citation provenance: the original Wikipedia reference was replaced with the verified public-domain source recorded here.]

passages.text: [Condensed paraphrase] The serpent Illuyanka contended with the storm-god Tarhunna and overcame him; the god's heart and eyes the serpent took away. The goddess Inara built a house of feast on the sea-shore, filled it with wine, and called the serpent and his brood to eat and drink.

[Condensed paraphrase] They drank till their bellies were swollen and the pit was shut against them; then the storm-god — or, in the second telling, the son the god had by a mortal woman — came and killed the serpent while it was drunk. The festival of the purulli recited this victory each year, that the order of the land might be renewed with the spring.

title.en: Kumarbi and the Gods of the Stone
title.zh: 庫馬爾比與石中之神

region.en: Hattusa, Hittite kingdom (Anatolia)
region.zh: 安納托利亞西臺王國哈圖沙

period: Hittite tablet narratives (Song of Kumarbi, c. 14th c. BCE)

source.work: A. E. Cowley, The Hittites (Schweich Lectures, 1920) - on Hittite religion and texts

summary.en: The Hittite succession song: Alalu ruled, then Anu, whose feet Kumarbi bit off and swallowed as he pulled him from the sky — but the seed in his belly became the storm-god, and the stone Teshub was born of the mountain's side; the gods of the first ages fight their sons in a cycle older than the Greek story of Cronus.
summary.zh: 西臺王權交替之歌：阿拉魯在位，繼以阿努；庫馬爾比咬斷其足而吞之——腹中之種遂成風雨神，圖什普塔自山岩而生；太古諸神與其子相爭，此環早於希臘克洛諾斯之事。

sensitivity.note: Hittite mythic tablets; NO public-domain English translation exists, so passages are clearly-labeled condensed paraphrases of the tablet narrative (referenced to modern scholarly translations). [Citation provenance: the original Wikipedia reference was replaced with the verified public-domain source recorded here.]

passages.text: [Condensed paraphrase] In former times Alalu was king in heaven; Anu his cupbearer overcame him and reigned. But Anu in turn was fought by Kumarbi, who pulled the king of heaven down from the sky and bit off his genitals and swallowed them — and rejoiced, till he was told what he had swallowed.

[Condensed paraphrase] The seed of Anu grew in Kumarbi's belly and could not be brought forth; he spat out what became the stone of the mountain, and the storm-god Teshub was born, to fight Kumarbi for the kingship of heaven — a war of the old gods and the young that the Hittite singers put at the beginning of the world.

title.en: The Vanishing of Telipinu and the World's Withering
title.zh: 泰利皮努失蹤與世界枯槁

region.en: Hattusa, Hittite kingdom (Anatolia)
region.zh: 安納托利亞西臺王國哈圖沙

period: Hittite tablet narrative (Vanishing Deity myth, c. 14th-13th c. BCE)

source.work: A. E. Cowley, The Hittites (Schweich Lectures, 1920) - on Hittite cult and ritual

summary.en: Telipinu the god of the fields walked away in anger, put on his black leather boots, and vanished — and at once the fog filled the windows, the hearths went out, sheep and cattle neglected their young, and the land lay barren; the god was called back with honey and oil and a great eagle, and in his return the fields and the hearths were filled again.
summary.zh: 田疇之神泰利皮努怒而去，足登黑皮靴，隱形不見——霧塞窗牖，爐火俱熄，羊牛棄其子，大地荒蕪。眾神以蜂蜜、膏油與巨鷹召之；神歸則田疇復茂，爐火復燃。

sensitivity.note: Hittite mythic tablets; NO public-domain English translation exists, so passages are clearly-labeled condensed paraphrases of the tablet narrative (referenced to modern scholarly translations). [Citation provenance: the original Wikipedia reference was replaced with the verified public-domain source recorded here.]

passages.text: [Condensed paraphrase] Telipinu the god of agriculture went away in anger; he put his right shoe on his left foot and his left on his right, and disappeared. Fog filled the windows of the houses, the fires went out in the hearths, the sheep and the cattle would not suckle their young, and in the land neither man nor god knew plenty.

[Condensed paraphrase] The sun-god sent the eagle to search the high mountains, and Kamrusepa the goddess of magic lulled the angry god with honey and oil and soft things; when Telipinu returned, the fires were relit, the flocks took their young, and the land was filled again — the ritual of return was acted out at Hattusa whenever the earth stood barren.

title.en: Lac Long Quan and Au Co: Dragon and Fairy
title.zh: 貉龍君與嫗姬：龍仙之種

region.en: Phu Tho / Red River delta, Vietnam
region.zh: 越南富壽／紅河三角洲

period: Linh Nam chich quai, 14th-15th c. compilation of older legends

source.work: Cl. Chivas-Baron, Stories and Legends of Annam, trans. E. M. Smith-Dampier (1920), 'Hong-Lo the Giant'

summary.en: Lac Long Quan, the dragon-lord of the water country, slew the nine-tailed fox, the sea monster, and the wood demon of the northern borders; Au Co the mountain fairy came to him, and she laid a pouch of a hundred eggs — from which sprang a hundred sons, the ancestors of the hundred Viet clans; the dragon went back to the water, the fairy to the mountain, and the eldest ruled the Red River land as Hung Vuong.
summary.zh: 水國龍君貉龍誅九尾狐、海怪與北疆樹妖；山仙嫗姬來歸，產百卵之囊——化為百子，是為百越之祖。龍歸於水，仙歸於山，長子治紅河之地，是為涇陽王之後雄王。

sensitivity.note: Vietnamese foundational legend from the Linh Nam chich quai; passages are condensed paraphrases. Presented as a comparative-mythology text. [Citation provenance: the original Wikipedia reference was replaced with the verified public-domain source recorded here.]

passages.text: [Condensed paraphrase] Lac Long Quan, the son of the water country, went about the lands killing the monsters of the early world: the nine-tailed fox of the western mountains, the sea-devil of the south, and the wood spirit that plagued the north; wherever he passed the people could live in peace, for he taught them to plant rice and to wear clothes.

[Condensed paraphrase] Au Co the fairy of the mountains came to dwell with him, and she bore a pouch of a hundred eggs, from which a hundred children hatched. Because a dragon must live in the water and a fairy on the mountain, they divided the children: fifty went with their mother to the hills, fifty with their father to the sea-lands, and the eldest was made the first Hung king of the Red River country.

title.en: Son Tinh and Thuy Tinh: The Mountain and the Water
title.zh: 山精與水精：山與水之爭

region.en: Ba Vi mountains, Red River, Vietnam
region.zh: 越南巴維山與紅河

period: Vietnamese folk legend (Linh Nam chich quai traditions)

source.work: Cl. Chivas-Baron, Stories and Legends of Annam, trans. E. M. Smith-Dampier (1920), 'The Rival Genii'

summary.en: Both the mountain spirit and the water spirit sought the eighteenth daughter of the Hung king; the king set a trial — gifts first brought wins — and Son Tinh, whose presents were there at dawn, won the bride. Thuy Tinh raised the flood with whirlwinds and storms against the mountain, but the mountain rose the higher; each year the waters come and fall again, which men call the monsoon.
summary.zh: 山精與水精同求雄王之十八女；王設試禮——先至者得娶。山精黎明而達，遂成婚。水精怒，興風作浪、引洪灌山，而山愈漲愈高；水年年復來復去——人謂之季風雨季。

sensitivity.note: Vietnamese folk legend of the Hung kings' age; passages are condensed paraphrases. Presented as a comparative-mythology text. [Citation provenance: the original Wikipedia reference was replaced with the verified public-domain source recorded here.]

passages.text: [Condensed paraphrase] When the Hung king sought a husband for My Nuong his eighteenth daughter, two spirits came to woo her in one day: Son Tinh, lord of the mountains, and Thuy Tinh, lord of the waters. The king said the one whose presents came first should have her; at dawn the mountain spirit's gifts of stone and timber were already before the hall, and the marriage was made.

[Condensed paraphrase] Thuy Tinh returned in fury with the waters: he raised storms and floods against the mountain where the couple dwelt, and the people of the plain suffered year by year; but the mountain lifted itself the higher, and the waters sank each time — the war never ends, and the yearly rise and fall of the water is the struggle still remembered.

title.en: Thanh Giong Rides to Phu Dong
title.zh: 扶董天王聖郎

region.en: Phu Dong village, Bac Ninh (Hanoi region), Vietnam
region.zh: 越南北寧扶董村

period: Vietnamese legend (Viet dien u linh tap, 13th-14th c. compilation)

source.work: Gustave Dumoutier, Legendes historiques de l'Annam et du Tonkin (Hanoi: F.-H. Schneider, 1887) - the Phu-Dong legend

summary.en: A boy of Phu Dong village, three years old and mute, sat up at the king's call for warriors and spoke his first words: the horse and the iron rod would fight the invaders; he ate the village's rice and grew instantly a giant, took the iron rod and the iron horse, put the enemy to flight with fire from the horse's mouth, and rode up the mountain alone — the tutelary god of the village to this day.
summary.zh: 扶董村三歲不言童子，聞王募武士而起，忽發初聲：「鐵馬鐵鞭，必退敵！」食一村之飯，頃刻成巨人；執鐵鞭、乘鐵馬，馬口噴火破敵——遂獨上羅浮山而去，鄉人立祠奉為本境城隍。

sensitivity.note: Vietnamese hero myth from the Viet dien u linh tap; passages are condensed paraphrases. Presented as a comparative-mythology text. [Citation provenance: the original Wikipedia reference was replaced with the verified public-domain source recorded here.]

passages.text: [Condensed paraphrase] When the armies of the north invaded the land of the Hung kings, the king sent out the call for warriors; in Phu Dong village a boy of three, who had never spoken, sat up in his mother's arms and answered the call in words, asking that a horse and a rod of iron be sent.

[Condensed paraphrase] He ate what the village cooked and grew from child to man in a day; when the enemy came he mounted the iron horse, which breathed fire, and broke them with the iron rod until their armor rang like rain. At the bounds of So'n mountain he rode up alone into the sky, and the king gave him the title Heavenly King of Phu Dong — the village god who is honored still when the spring festival goes round.

title.en: The Ramakien: Phra Ram and Thotsakan
title.zh: 拉瑪堅：帕拉姆與托薩根

region.en: Ayutthaya / Bangkok, Thailand
region.zh: 泰國大城／曼谷

period: Ramakien, Thai adaptation of the Ramayana; court recensions of the 18th-19th c. from older tradition

source.work: Ramakien (Thai: Ramakien), King Rama I's court recension, Thai original (e.g. Book 2, the war of Maiyarab)

summary.en: Thailand's Ramayana: Phra Ram, exiled with his bride Sida, loses her to Thotsakan the ten-faced giant-king of Longka; the monkey-general Hanuman builds the causeway of stones across the sea, Nonthok the demon's legend is fought, and the war of the city of fire ends with the trial of the faithful wife — the national myth told in murals, dance, and puppet theatre.
summary.zh: 泰國羅摩衍那：帕拉姆攜妻西達出亡，西達為龍卡國十面巨靈王托薩根所擄；神猴哈奴曼築石堤跨海，大戰焚城，終以貞后之火試為結——壁畫、舞劇與皮影相傳之國家神話。

sensitivity.note: Thai adaptation of the Ramayana; passages are condensed paraphrases of the court Ramakien recensions. Presented as a comparative-mythology text. [Citation provenance: the original Wikipedia reference was replaced with the verified public-domain source recorded here.]

passages.text: [Condensed paraphrase] Phra Ram, heir of Ayutthaya, went into the forest at his father's word with his brother Phra Lak and his bride Sida; the giant-king Thotsakan of Longka, ten faces and twenty arms, carried Sida across the sea, and the war of the Ramakien began.

[Condensed paraphrase] Hanuman the son of the wind, white monkey of a thousand wiles, gathered the armies of the monkeys, carried the mountain of healing herbs, and built the causeway of stones to the island of Longka; Phra Ram slew Thotsakan at last with the arrows of the gods — and the murals of Wat Phra Kaew and the khon dance tell the war still as the royal myth of Thailand.

title.en: Khun Borom and the Origin of the Tai Princes
title.zh: 坤博隆與泰人諸王之始

region.en: Muang Theng (Plain of Jars region), Laos/Thailand tradition
region.zh: 猛騰（川壙高原一帶，寮泰傳統）

period: Tai/Lao origin myth; recorded in the 15th-19th c. chronicles (Urangadom, Nan chronicle)

source.work: G. E. Gerini, Researches on Ptolemy's Geography of Eastern Asia (Royal Asiatic Society/RGS, 1909), on Muang Then

summary.en: In the Tai origin cycle the sky-lord Khun Borom, seeing the earth waste and comfortless, sends down his seven sons from the heavenly city with buffalo, rice-seed, and teachers of the arts; the youngest, Khun Lo, takes the plain of the middle lands, and from the seven sons the princes of the Tai and Lao states trace their royal blood.
summary.zh: 泰人創世傳說：天君坤博隆見大地荒蕪，遣七子自天城而下，攜水牛、稻種與百工之師；幼子坤羅居中原之野——泰、寮諸國王族皆自七子溯其王統。

sensitivity.note: Tai/Lao foundational myth from the court chronicles; passages are condensed paraphrases. Presented as a comparative-mythology text. [Citation provenance: the original Wikipedia reference was replaced with the verified public-domain source recorded here.]

passages.text: [Condensed paraphrase] Khun Borom the lord of the sky looked down on the world of men, which lay without order and without comfort; he sent down his seven sons, each with the gear of rule: buffaloes, seeds of rice, smiths and teachers, that the wild lands might be peopled and tilled.

[Condensed paraphrase] The sons built cities and ruled the countries of the Tai; Khun Lo the youngest took Muang Sua on the middle river, and his line the Lao kings traced. When the work was done the princes returned to the sky-city to report, and went down again with the mandate of Khun Borom to rule — the pattern of every Tai royal chronicle.

title.en: The Naga of the Mekong and the Fire-Balls of the River
title.zh: 湄公河龍王與河上火箭

region.en: Mekong river, Nong Khai / Vientiane
region.zh: 湄公河（泰國廊開／永珍）

period: Isan/Lao river legend of the Mekong naga

source.work: J. Ph. Vogel, Indian Serpent-Lore: The Nagas in Hindu Legend and Art (1926), on naga beliefs in the river-lands of Siam

summary.en: The great serpent Phaya Nak rules the deeps of the Mekong; in the river legend the naga's bride came from the water-country to the human world, and the serpent-king's tears and fire-balls rise from the river at the year's turning — the naga whose coils guard the Buddhist river-lands of the Lao and the Isan.
summary.zh: 巨蛇帕雅納克統湄公之深淵；河上傳說云蛇王之婦自水國適人間，歲末蛇王噴淚與火球自河面騰起——其身守護寮人與伊善地區之佛土江河。

sensitivity.note: Isan-Lao river legend; passages are condensed paraphrases. Living cultural heritage of the Mekong region. [Citation provenance: the original Wikipedia reference was replaced with the verified public-domain source recorded here.]

passages.text: [Condensed paraphrase] Phaya Nak, the great naga, ruled the deep channel of the Mekong from his city under the water; in the Isan legend his son loved a maiden of the human world and was given leave to serve the Buddha, guarding the river-lands with his coils.

[Condensed paraphrase] At the full moon of the eleventh month the naga is said to celebrate the end of the rains: columns of light and fire-balls rise from the river at Bang Fai, which the fishermen call the breath of the naga; the serpent-king remains the lord of the water-road of the Lao and Thai river country.

title.en: The Fall of the Watchers (1 Enoch)
title.zh: 守望者之墮落（以諾一書）

region.en: Mount Hermon (Armon), Anti-Lebanon
region.zh: 黑門山（阿爾孟，安黎巴嫩山）

period: 1 Enoch (Book of the Watchers), c. 3rd c. BCE; trans. Laurence, 1883

source.work: The Book of Enoch the Prophet, trans. Richard Laurence, chs. 7-10

summary.en: The most influential of the pseudepigrapha, quoted in the Epistle of Jude and treasured in the Ethiopian canon: two hundred Watchers, led by Samyaza, swear an oath on Mount Hermon, take the daughters of men, and teach forbidden crafts; their giant offspring fill the earth with blood until the archangels plead for judgment.
summary.zh: 偽經中最具影響力之作，為猶大書所引、埃提阿伯正典所藏：二百守望者由薩麥拉率領，於黑門山立誓，娶人間女子，傳授禁術；其巨人後裔使大地遍染血污，直至天使長呼求審判。

sensitivity.note: Jewish pseudepigraphon preserved in Ge'ez; scriptural for the Ethiopian Orthodox canon, quoted in the New Testament. Presented as a comparative text — a scholarly framing, not a claim about religious truth.

passages.text: It happened after the sons of men had multiplied in those days, that daughters were born to them, elegant and beautiful. And when the angels, the sons of heaven, beheld them, they became enamoured of them, saying to each other, Come, let us select for ourselves wives from the progeny of men, and let us beget children. [...] Then they swore all together, and all bound themselves by mutual execrations. Their whole number was two hundred, who descended upon Ardis, which is the top of mount Armon. [...] Then they took wives, each choosing for himself; whom they began to approach, and with whom they cohabited; teaching them sorcery, incantations, and the dividing of roots and trees. And the women conceiving brought forth giants, Whose stature was each three hundred cubits.

Moreover Azazyel taught men to make swords, knives, shields, breastplates, the fabrication of mirrors, and the workmanship of bracelets and ornaments, the use of paint, the beautifying of the eyebrows, the use of stones of every valuable and select kind, and of all sorts of dyes, so that the world became altered. Impiety increased; fornication multiplied; and they transgressed and corrupted all their ways. [...] And men, being destroyed, cried out; and their voice reached to heaven.

Then Michael and Gabriel, Raphael, Suryal, and Uriel, looked down from heaven, and saw the quantity of blood which was shed on earth, and all the iniquity which was done upon it, and said one to another, It is the voice of their cries; The earth deprived of her children has cried even to the gate of heaven. [...] The women likewise have brought forth giants. Thus has the whole earth been filled with blood and with iniquity. And now behold the souls of those who are dead, cry out. And complain even to the gate of heaven.

title.en: Enoch's Vision of the Son of Man
title.zh: 以諾見人子之異象

region.en: Parables of Enoch (vision setting, symbolic)
region.zh: 以諾比喻篇（異象之境，象徵位置）

period: 1 Enoch (Parables), c. 1st c. BCE; trans. Laurence, 1883

source.work: The Book of Enoch the Prophet, trans. Richard Laurence, ch. 46

summary.en: In the Parables of Enoch the seer beholds the Ancient of days, whose head is like white wool, and with him the Son of man to whom righteousness belongs, chosen by the Lord of spirits to reveal the hidden treasures and to raise up kings from their couches — the messianic vision that shaped Second Temple expectation and New Testament language.
summary.zh: 以諾比喻篇中，先知見「日子古老者」髮如白羊毛，其旁有人子——義所歸焉、為萬靈之主所揀選者，將啟示隱藏之寶藏，並使君王自榻興起——此彌賽亞異象塑造了第二聖殿時代的盼望與新約語言。

sensitivity.note: Jewish pseudepigraphon; the Parables' messianic vision influenced apocalyptic belief across Judaism and Christianity. Presented as a comparative text — a scholarly framing, not a claim about religious truth.

passages.text: There I beheld the Ancient of days, whose head was like white wool, and with him another, whose countenance resembled that of man. His countenance was full of grace, like that of one of the holy angels. Then I inquired of one of the angels, who went with me, and who showed me every secret thing, concerning this Son of man; who he was; whence he was; and why he accompanied the Ancient of days. He answered and said to me, This is the Son of man, to whom righteousness belongs; with whom righteousness has dwelt; and who will reveal all the treasures of that which is concealed: for the Lord of spirits has chosen him; and his portion has surpassed all before the Lord of spirits in everlasting uprightness. This Son of man, whom thou beholdest, shall raise up kings and the mighty from their couches, and the powerful from their thrones; shall loosen the bridles of the powerful, and break in pieces the teeth of sinners.

title.en: Tobit and the Fish of Healing
title.zh: 多比傳與醫病之魚

region.en: Nineveh to Ecbatane (Assyria to Media)
region.zh: 尼尼微至厄克巴坦（亞述至瑪代）

period: Book of Tobit, c. 2nd c. BCE (deuterocanonical); KJV Apocrypha, 1611

source.work: Bible (King James Version), Apocrypha: Tobit, chs. 6-12

summary.en: Blinded for burying the dead, Tobit sends his son to Media with the angel Raphael in disguise; a fish of the Tigris, caught at the angel's word, supplies the heart and liver whose smoke binds the demon Asmodeus and the gall that heals Tobit's eyes — the deuterocanonical book beloved for its angelology and its teaching on almsgiving.
summary.zh: 多比因埋葬死者而目盲，遣子多比亞往瑪代；拉斐爾天使假伴同行，於底格里斯河捕魚——魚心肝之煙驅逐惡魔阿斯摩太，魚膽醫愈多比之目。此次經典以天使論與施捨教訓聞名。

sensitivity.note: Deuterocanonical/Apocryphal book — canonical for Catholic and Orthodox traditions, apocryphal in Protestantism. Presented as a comparative text — a scholarly framing, not a claim about religious truth.

passages.text: And when the young man went down to wash himself, a fish leaped out of the river, and would have devoured him. Then the angel said unto him, Take the fish. And the young man laid hold of the fish, and drew it to land. [...] And he said unto him, Touching the heart and the liver, if a devil or an evil spirit trouble any, we must make a smoke thereof before the man or the woman, and the party shall be no more vexed. As for the gall, it is good to anoint a man that hath whiteness in his eyes, and he shall be healed.

And when they had supped, they brought Tobias in unto her. And as he went, he remembered the words of Raphael, and took the ashes of the perfumes, and put the heart and the liver of the fish thereupon, and made a smoke therewith. The which smell when the evil spirit had smelled, he fled into the utmost parts of Egypt, and the angel bound him.

I am Raphael, one of the seven holy angels, which present the prayers of the saints, and which go in and out before the glory of the Holy One. [...] For not of any favour of mine, but by the will of our God I came; wherefore praise him for ever.

title.en: Mattathias and the Rededication of the Altar
title.zh: 瑪他提亞與祭壇之重新奉獻

region.en: Modin and Jerusalem, Judea
region.zh: 猶太地摩丁與耶路撒冷

period: 1 Maccabees, c. 2nd-1st c. BCE (deuterocanonical); KJV Apocrypha, 1611

source.work: Bible (King James Version), Apocrypha: 1 Maccabees, chs. 2-4

summary.en: The book that records the Maccabean revolt: Antiochus Epiphanes profanes the temple, Mattathias refuses the king's commandment — 'We will not hearken to the king's words, to go from our religion' — and after Judas Maccabeus overthrows the king's host, the sanctuary is cleansed and the altar dedicated anew for eight days, the origin of the feast of Hanukkah.
summary.zh: 記載瑪加伯起義之經卷：安提阿古·伊皮法尼褻瀆聖殿；瑪他提亞拒王命——「不聽王言，不棄祖教」；猶大·瑪加伯破敵之後，潔淨聖所，重新奉獻祭壇八日——修殿節（光明節）之緣起。

sensitivity.note: Deuterocanonical/Apocryphal book — canonical for Catholic and Orthodox traditions, historically foundational for the Jewish feast of Hanukkah. Presented as a comparative text — a scholarly framing, not a claim about religious truth.

passages.text: Then Mattathias answered and spake with a loud voice, Though all the nations that are under the king's dominion obey him, and fall away every one from the religion of their fathers, and give consent to his commandments: Yet will I and my sons and my brethren walk in the covenant of our fathers. God forbid that we should forsake the law and the ordinances. We will not hearken to the king's words, to go from our religion, either on the right hand, or the left.

Then said Judas to the men that were with him, Fear ye not their multitude, neither be ye afraid of their assault. Remember how our fathers were delivered in the Red sea, when Pharaoh pursued them with an army. [...] For the victory of battle standeth not in the multitude of an host; but strength cometh from heaven.

Now on the five and twentieth day of the ninth month, which is called the month Casleu, in the hundred forty and eighth year, they rose up betimes in the morning, And offered sacrifice according to the law upon the new altar of burnt offerings, which they had made. Look, at what time and what day the heathen had profaned it, even in that was it dedicated with songs, and citherns, and harps, and cymbals. [...] And so they kept the dedication of the altar eight days, and offered burnt offerings with gladness, and sacrificed the sacrifice of deliverance and praise.

title.en: Dante's Inferno: The Gate and the Lovers
title.zh: 但丁《神曲·地獄篇》：冥門與情人

region.en: Florence / a dark wood (vision-setting), Italy
region.zh: 義大利佛羅倫斯／幽暗森林（異象之境）

period: Divine Comedy, c. 1308-1320; trans. Henry Francis Cary, 1805-14

source.work: The Divine Comedy, trans. Rev. H. F. Cary, Hell (Inferno), Cantos 1, 3, 5

summary.en: Dante's pilgrimage through Hell, Purgatory, and Paradise — the poem that shaped the Western imagination of the afterlife: lost in a dark wood at mid-life, he passes the gate whose doomful lines end 'All hope abandon ye who enter here,' and hears the lovers Francesca and Paolo tell how the book of Lancelot betrayed them to their love.
summary.zh: 但丁遊歷地獄、煉獄與天堂——塑造西方死後想像之詩：半生迷途於幽暗森林，過地獄之門（門上銘文云：「入此門者，當捨棄一切希望」），聞弗蘭切斯卡與保羅情人敘述蘭斯洛特之書如何使其墮入情網。

sensitivity.note: Influential Christian literary-religious imagination (not scripture); presented as a comparative text alongside underworld-journey narratives — a scholarly framing.

passages.text: In the midway of this our mortal life, I found me in a gloomy wood, astray Gone from the path direct: and e'en to tell It were no easy task, how savage wild That forest, how robust and rough its growth, Which to remember only, my dismay Renews, in bitterness not far from death.

"Through me you pass into the city of woe: Through me you pass into eternal pain: Through me among the people lost for aye. Justice the founder of my fabric mov'd: To rear me was the task of power divine, Supremest wisdom, and primeval love. Before me things create were none, save things Eternal, and eternal I endure. "All hope abandon ye who enter here."

"Love, that in gentle heart is quickly learnt, Entangled him by that fair form, from me Ta'en in such cruel sort, as grieves me still: Love, that denial takes from none belov'd, Caught me with pleasing him so passing well, That, as thou see'st, he yet deserts me not. Love brought us to one death: Caina waits The soul, who spilt our life." [...] "No greater grief than to remember days Of joy, when mis'ry is at hand! [...] The book and writer both Were love's purveyors. In its leaves that day We read no more."

title.en: Milton's Paradise Lost: The Fall of the Rebel Angels
title.zh: 彌爾頓《失樂園》：叛天使之墮落

region.en: Heaven / Pandemonium (vision-setting)
region.zh: 天堂／萬魔殿（異象之境）

period: Paradise Lost, 1667

source.work: Paradise Lost, John Milton, Book I

summary.en: Milton's epic of the fall — 'to justify the ways of God to men' — opens with Satan and his legions hurled from heaven through nine days' space into a dungeon of darkness visible; waking on the burning lake, the Arch-fiend rallies his fallen host and builds Pandemonium, resolving on 'war, then, war, open or understood.'
summary.zh: 彌爾頓之史詩——「辯明上帝待人之道」——敘撒旦與其黨羽九日九夜自天墮落，墜入「可見之黑暗」深淵；於火湖醒來，召集墮落天使，建萬魔殿，立誓「戰爭——明戰或暗戰，勢不可免」。

sensitivity.note: Influential Christian literary-religious imagination (not scripture); the epic paraphrases the apocryphal angelologies of Enoch and shaped Protestant imagination. Presented as a comparative text.

passages.text: Of Man's first disobedience, and the fruit Of that forbidden tree whose mortal taste Brought death into the World, and all our woe, With loss of Eden, till one greater Man Restore us, and regain the blissful seat, Sing, Heavenly Muse [...] That, to the height of this great argument, I may assert Eternal Providence, And justify the ways of God to men.

Th' infernal Serpent; he it was whose guile, Stirred up with envy and revenge, deceived The mother of mankind [...] Him the Almighty Power Hurled headlong flaming from th' ethereal sky, With hideous ruin and combustion, down To bottomless perdition, there to dwell In adamantine chains and penal fire, Who durst defy th' Omnipotent to arms.

A dungeon horrible, on all sides round, As one great furnace flamed; yet from those flames No light; but rather darkness visible Served only to discover sights of woe [...] Here at least We shall be free; th' Almighty hath not built Here for his envy, will not drive us hence: Here we may reign secure; and, in my choice, To reign is worth ambition, though in Hell: Better to reign in Hell than serve in Heaven.

title.en: The Song of the Reed (Masnavi of Rumi)
title.zh: 蘆笛之歌（魯米《瑪斯納維》）

region.en: Konya, Anatolia (Rumi's whirling home)
region.zh: 安納托利亞科尼亞（魯米旋轉祈禱之家）

period: Masnavi, Book 1, c. 1258-1273; trans. E. H. Whinfield (abridged), 1887

source.work: Masnavi I Ma'navi, trans. E. H. Whinfield, Book I Prologue

summary.en: The Masnavi — the Sufi 'Qur'an in the Persian tongue,' read for eight centuries across the Muslim world — opens with the reed-flute cut from its osier bed, wailing for its home: the soul torn from the Source, whose fire of love is the physician of pride, the confidant of all unhappy lovers.
summary.zh: 《瑪斯納維》——蘇菲「波斯語之古蘭經」，八百年來穆斯林世界誦讀不絕——以蘆笛自葦床剪斷、哀鳴思鄉為喻：靈魂離其本源，愛之火乃傲慢之醫、苦戀者之知己。

sensitivity.note: Influential Sufi literature of Islam (not scripture); presented as a comparative text — a scholarly framing, not a claim about religious truth.

passages.text: HEARKEN to the reed-flute, how it complains, Lamenting its banishment from its home: "Ever since they tore me from my osier bed, My plaintive notes have moved men and women to tears. I burst my breast, striving to give vent to sighs, And to express the pangs of my yearning for my home. He who abides far away from his home Is ever longing for the day he shall return. [...] My secrets are not alien from my plaintive notes, Yet they are not manifest to the sensual eye and ear. Body is not veiled from soul, neither soul from body, Yet no man hath ever seen a soul." This plaint of the flute is fire, not mere air. Let him who lacks this fire be accounted dead! 'Tis the fire of love that inspires the flute, 'Tis the ferment of love that possesses the wine.

The pitcher of the desire of the covetous never fills, The oyster-shell fills not with pearls till it is content; Only he whose garment is rent by the violence of love Is wholly pure from covetousness and sin. Hail to thee, then, O LOVE, sweet madness! Thou who healest all our infirmities! Who art the physician of our pride and self-conceit! Who art our Plato and our Galen! Love exalts our earthly bodies to heaven, And makes the very hills to dance with joy!

title.en: The Cosmic Egg and the Sleep of Vishnu (Vishnu Purana)
title.zh: 宇宙之卵與毗濕奴之眠（毗濕奴往世書）

region.en: Kurukshetra (narrative frame), India
region.zh: 印度庫魯克謝特拉（敘述之地）

period: Vishnu Purana, c. 1st millennium CE; trans. H. H. Wilson, 1840

source.work: The Vishnu Purana, trans. H. H. Wilson, Book I, chs. 1-2

summary.en: The Purana that Wilson called the most authentic of the eighteen: the world was produced from Vishnu, exists in him, and he is the world; the elements combine to form the vast egg that is the abode of Vishnu in the form of Brahma — and at the close of each kalpa, as Rudra, he swallows up the universe and reposes on the serpent-couch, to create again.
summary.zh: 威爾遜譽為十八往世書中最可信者：世界自毗濕奴而生、存於其中，彼即世界；諸元素結合成大卵，乃毗濕奴現梵天之身而居之——每一劫末，彼現為魯陀羅吞滅宇宙，偃臥巨蛇之榻，而後再造。

sensitivity.note: Influential Puranic cosmology of Hinduism; presented as a comparative text — a scholarly framing, not a claim about religious truth.

passages.text: The world was produced from Vishnu: it exists in him: he is the cause of its continuance and cessation; he is the world. [...] Who can describe him who is not to be apprehended by the senses: who is the best of all things; the supreme soul, self-existent: who is devoid of all the distinguishing characteristics of complexion, caste, or the like; and is exempt from bulk, vicissitude, death, or decay: who is always, and alone: who exists everywhere, and in whom all things here exist; and who is, thence, named Vasudeva? [...] He is Brahma, Supreme, lord, eternal, unborn, imperishable, undecaying; of one essence; ever pure, as free from defects. He, that Brahma, was all things; comprehending in his own nature the indiscrete and discrete.

Having combined, therefore, with one another, they assumed, through their mutual association, the character of one mass of entire unity; and, from the direction of spirit, with the acquiescence of the indiscrete Principle, Intellect and the rest, to the gross elements inclusive, formed an egg, which gradually expanded like a bubble of water. This vast egg, O sage, compounded of the elements, and resting on the waters, was the excellent natural abode of Vishnu in the form of Brahma [...] In that egg, O Brahman, were the continents and seas and mountains, the planets and divisions of the universe, the gods, the demons, and mankind.

Vishnu, with the quality of goodness, and of immeasurable power, preserves created things through successive ages, until the close of the period termed a Kalpa; when the same mighty deity, Janardana, invested with the quality of darkness, assumes the awful form of Rudra, and swallows up the universe. Having thus devoured all things, and converted the world into one vast ocean, the Supreme reposes upon his mighty serpent-couch amidst the deep: he awakes after a season, and, again, as Brahma, becomes the author of creation.

title.en: The Vision of Arda Viraf: Bridge, Damsel, and Hell
title.zh: 阿爾達·維拉夫之異象：橋、少女與地獄

region.en: Fars, Sasanian Persia (vision of the spirit realm)
region.zh: 薩珊波斯法爾斯（靈界異象）

period: Arda Viraf Namak, Sasanian-era Pahlavi text; trans. Haug (with West), 1872

source.work: The Book of Arda Viraf, trans. Martin Haug (1872), chs. 4-5, 17-18

summary.en: The Zoroastrian Dante four centuries before Dante: chosen by lot after a council of the priests, Viraf drinks the narcotic of Vishtasp and his soul crosses the Chinwad bridge — where his own religion and deeds meet him 'in the graceful form of a damsel' — beholds the reward of the pious in Garothman and the many torments of hell, and returns to report truly.
summary.zh: 早但丁四百年之祆教《神曲》：祭司議會抽籤選中維拉夫，飲維什塔斯普之迷藥，其靈魂渡欽瓦特橋——其宗教與善行化為「婀娜少女」相迎——得見伽羅斯曼中義人之報與地獄諸刑，歸而如實稟告。

sensitivity.note: Zoroastrian religious vision literature of great influence on Parsi devotion (and famously compared with Dante); presented as a comparative text — a scholarly framing, not a claim about religious truth.

passages.text: Taking the first footstep with the good thought, and the second footstep with the good word, and the third footstep with the good deed, I came up to the Chinwad bridge, the very wide and strong and created by Ohrmazd. [...] And there stood before him his own religion and his own deeds, in the graceful form of a damsel, as a beautiful appearance [...] And the soul of the pious asked that damsel thus: 'Who art thou? [...] To him replied she who was his own religion and his own deeds, thus: 'I am thy actions, O youth of good thoughts, of good words, of good deeds, of good religion. It is on account of thy will and actions that I am as great and good and sweet-scented and triumphant and undistressed as appears to thee.

And afterward, Srosh the pious, and Adar the angel, took hold of my hand, so that I went on unhurt. In that manner, I beheld cold and heat, drought and stench, to such a degree as I never saw, nor heard of, in the world. And when I went farther, I also saw the greedy jaws of hell, like the most frightful pit, descending in a very narrow and fearful place; in darkness so gloomy that it is necessary to hold by the hand [...] and when three days and nights have elapsed he says thus: 'The nine thousand years are completed, and they will not release me!'

And I saw the darkest hell, which is pernicious, dreadful, terrible, very painful, mischievous and foul-smelling. And after further observation, it appeared to me as a pit, to the bottom of which, a thousand cubits would not reach [...] and as many as the hairs on the mane of a horse, so close and many in number, the souls of the wicked stand, but they see not and hear no sound, one from the other; everyone thinks thus: 'I am alone'.

title.en: Theogony: Creation from Chaos and the Fall of Cronos
title.zh: 神譜：混沌創世與克羅諾斯之傾覆

region.en: Greece (Boeotia)
region.zh: 希臘（維奧蒂亞）

period: c. 700 BCE (Hesiod, trans. Evelyn-White 1914)

source.work: Hesiod, Theogony, trans. H. G. Evelyn-White, Loeb Classical Library 57 (1914), lines 116-149

summary.en: Hesiod's Theogony opens the Greek cosmos with Chaos, from which came Gaia, Tartarus, and Eros. Gaia then bears Ouranos (Heaven), and their union produces the Titans, including Cronos, who hates his father.
summary.zh: 赫西俄德《神譜》以混沌開篇，混沌之中先有大地該亞、深淵塔爾塔羅斯與愛神厄洛斯；該亞再生天空烏拉諾斯，二神結合而生克羅諾斯等泰坦諸神。

sensitivity.note: Coordinates placed at Ascra in Boeotia, Hesiod's home village, as a symbolic inland anchor (the cosmogony has no geographic setting). Quoted from a standard public-domain academic translation as comparative mythology scholarship, not as any religious truth claim. [Merged 2026-11-11: the entry 'greek-theogony-succession' (same Evelyn-White Theogony, succession myth and Titanomachy) was folded in as passage 3; its opening passage duplicated passage 1 and was dropped, and the duplicate entry removed. Sacred-kingship and storm-thunder motifs come from the folded material.]

passages.text: Verily at the first Chaos came to be, but next wide-bosomed Earth, the ever-sure foundations of all the deathless ones who hold the peaks of snowy Olympus, and dim Tartarus in the depth of the wide-pathed Earth, and Eros (Love), fairest among the deathless gods, who unnerves the limbs and overcomes the mind and wise counsels of all gods and all men within them. From Chaos came forth Erebus and black Night; but of Night were born Aether and Day, whom she conceived and bare from union in love with Erebus. And Earth first bare starry Heaven, equal to herself, to cover her on every side, and to be an ever-sure abiding-place for the blessed gods.

But afterwards she lay with Heaven and bare deep-swirling Oceanus, Coeus and Crius and Hyperion and Iapetus, Theia and Rhea, Themis and Mnemosyne and gold-crowned Phoebe and lovely Tethys. After them was born Cronos the wily, youngest and most terrible of her children, and he hated his lusty sire.

Condensed paraphrase of Theogony 453-506: Rhea, cheated of each child, hands Kronos a swaddled stone, which he swallows whole; the infant Zeus is smuggled to a Cretan cave, grows to strength, and forces his father to disgorge his swallowed siblings — the stone last of all. Not verbatim.

title.en: Isis and the Secret Name of Ra
title.zh: 伊希斯與拉的秘名

region.en: Egypt (Heliopolis)
region.zh: 埃及（赫利奧波利斯）

period: c. 1300-1100 BCE (Ramesside Turin Papyrus; Budge, Legends of the Gods, 1912)

source.archive: Project Gutenberg (eBook #9411; Sacred Texts returned HTTP 403)
source.work: Legends of the Gods: The Egyptian Texts, ed. and trans. E. A. Wallis Budge (London, 1912), ch. III, 'The Legend of Ra and the Snake-bite'

summary.en: In this Egyptian legend, Isis seeks Ra's hidden name, in which his very existence and power are bound up. She fashions a venomous serpent to wound the aging sun god, and only by surrendering his secret name can Ra be healed, transferring his power to Isis.
summary.zh: 在這則埃及傳說中，伊西斯謀求太陽神拉的秘名——其生命與神力之所繫。她鑄成毒蛇使年邁的拉受傷，拉為求痊癒只得獻出秘名，權柄遂歸伊西斯所有。

sensitivity.note: The story follows Ra's daily journey through Egypt, so coordinates are placed at Heliopolis (ancient Anu), Ra's chief cult city, as an approximate anchor. Ancient Egyptian religious text quoted for comparative scholarship; Budge's 1912 wording is dated in style but is the cited public-domain source, presented without religious truth claims.

passages.text: she decided that she could only obtain the power she wanted if she possessed the knowledge of the secret name of Ra, in which his very existence was bound up. Ra guarded this name most jealously, for he knew that if he revealed it to any being he would henceforth be at that being's mercy. Isis saw that it was impossible to make Ra declare his name to her by ordinary methods, and she therefore thought out the following plan. It was well known in Egypt and the Sudan at a very early period that if a magician obtained some portion of a person's body, e.g., a hair, a paring of a nail, a fragment of skin, or a portion of some efflux from the body, spells could be used upon them which would have the effect of causing grievous harm to that person.

Then Isis said to him with guile, "Divine Father, tell me thy name, for he who uttereth his own name shall live." Thereupon Ra proceeded to enumerate the various things that he had done, and to describe his creative acts, and ended his speech to Isis by saying, that he was Khepera in the morning, Ra at noon, and Temu in the evening. Apparently he thought that the naming of these three great names would satisfy Isis, and that she would immediately pronounce a word of power and stop the pain in his body, which, during his speech, had become more acute. Isis, however, was not deceived, and she knew well that Ra had not declared to her his hidden name; this she told him, and she begged him once again to tell her his name.

title.en: The Weighing of the Heart
title.zh: 稱量心臟（亡靈書）

region.en: Egypt (Thebes)
region.zh: 埃及（底比斯）

period: c. 1550-1292 BCE (New Kingdom funerary spells; Budge, 1920)

source.archive: Project Gutenberg (eBook #7145; Sacred Texts returned HTTP 403)
source.work: The Book of the Dead, ed. E. A. Wallis Budge (1920), ch. CXXV, the Judgment Hall and Negative Confession

summary.en: Chapter 125 of the Book of the Dead places the deceased in the Hall of Maati, where his heart is weighed before Osiris. Addressing the Forty-Two gods, he recites the Negative Confession, declaring innocence of a catalogue of sins before the Great Scales and the Eater of the Dead.
summary.zh: 《亡靈書》第一二五咒將亡者置於瑪阿特之廳，其心臟須在奧西里斯面前受稱量。亡者向四十二神逐條背誦「否定懺悔」，在審判大天秤與亡者吞噬者面前宣告無罪。

sensitivity.note: Category reclassified from religious to myth at the editor's direction: Chapter 125 is canonical funerary scripture, but its core is a narrative of the underworld Hall of Maati — Osiris, the Forty-Two assessors, the devourer of hearts — which this project reads as a myth of judgment rather than a scripture narrative; the interpretive division (README) is noted here. Classed religious rather than myth was the initial call because Chapter 125 is a funerary script used by worshippers. Coordinates are a neutral inland point at Thebes (Luxor), the source of the Papyrus of Ani, since the judgment occurs in the mythic Hall of Maati. Egyptian funerary text quoted for comparative scholarship on ancient afterlife beliefs, not as religious truth claims; Budge's 1920 translation is dated but is the cited public-domain source.

passages.text: When the deceased had repeated the magical names of the doors of the Hall, he entered it and saw these gods arranged in two rows, twenty-one on each side of the Hall. At the end, near Osiris, were the Great Scales, under the charge of Anpu (Anubis), and the monster Amemit, the Eater of the Dead, i.e., of the hearts of the wicked who were condemned in the Judgment of Osiris. The deceased advanced along the Hall and, addressing each of the Forty-Two gods by his name, declared that he had not committed a certain sin, thus: "O Usekh-nemmit, comer forth from Anu, I have not committed sin. O Fenti, comer forth from Khemenu, I have not robbed. O Neha-hau, comer forth from Re-stau, I have not killed men. O Neba, comer forth in retreating, I have not plundered the property of God.

Homage to thee, O Great God, Lord of Maati, I have come to thee, O my Lord, that I may behold thy beneficence. I know thee, and I know thy name, and the names of the Forty-Two who live with thee in the Hall of Maati, who keep ward over sinners, and feed upon their blood on the day of estimating characters before Un-Nefer ... Behold, I have come to thee, and I have brought maat (i.e., truth, integrity) to thee. I have destroyed sin for thee. I have not sinned against men. I have not oppressed [my] kinsfolk. I have done no wrong in the place of truth.

title.en: Gilgamesh, Enkidu and Humbaba
title.zh: 吉爾伽美什、恩奇都與洪巴巴

region.en: Cedar Forest (Mount Lebanon range) and Uruk
region.zh: 雪松林（黎巴嫩山區）與烏魯克

period: Sumerian/Babylonian epic, recorded c. 2100-1200 BCE (Spence 1916)

source.work: Myths & Legends of Babylonia & Assyria, by Lewis Spence (1916), eBook #45137

summary.en: Gilgamesh and his companion Eabani (Enkidu) plan an expedition against Khumbaba, the terrifying guardian appointed by Bel over the Forest of Cedars. The heroes seek the blessing of Shamash through Gilgamesh's mother before entering the forest, where they slay the monster.
summary.zh: 吉爾伽美什與摯友恩奇都遠征貝勒所任命的雪松林守護巨怪洪巴巴；臨行前二人託祭司之母向太陽神沙瑪什祈求庇佑，終於林中誅殺怪物。

sensitivity.note: Coordinates placed in the cedar-bearing Mount Lebanon range, the customary identification of the epic's mythic Cedar Forest. Spence's 1916 text is a retelling (one step removed from the tablets) using period transliterations (Khumbaba, Eabani), so passages are clearly-labeled condensed recounts in the template's terms; the combat belongs to heroic legend rather than temple cult, so it is classed as myth.

passages.text: The old priestess advises her son and his friend how to proceed, and after they have gone we see her alone in the temple, her hands raised to the sun-god, invoking his blessing on Gilgamesh: "Why hast thou troubled the heart of my son Gilgamesh? Thou hast laid thy hand upon him, and he goeth away, on a far journey to the dwelling of Khumbaba; he entereth into a combat (whose issue) he knoweth not; he followeth a road unknown to him. Till he arrive and till he return, till he reach the Forest of Cedars, till he hath slain the terrible Khumbaba and rid the land of all the evil that thou hatest, till the day of his return -- let Aya, thy betrothed, thy splendour, recall him to thee."

Khumbaba, whom Bel had appointed to guard the cedar (_i.e._, one particular cedar which appears to be of greater height and sanctity than the others), is a creature of most terrifying aspect, the very presence of whom in the forest makes those who enter it grow weak and impotent. As the heroes draw near Eabani complains that his hands are feeble and his arms without strength, but Gilgamesh speaks words of encouragement to him.

title.en: Etana and the Eagle
title.zh: 伊塔那與神鷹

region.en: Kish, Babylonia
region.zh: 巴比倫尼亞基什城邦

period: Old Babylonian Akkadian legend, tablets from c. 1800-1100 BCE (Jastrow 1898)

source.work: The Religion of Babylonia and Assyria, by Morris Jastrow, Jr. (1898), eBook #20758

summary.en: The shepherd-king Etana, whose wife cannot deliver the child she has conceived, appeals to Shamash for the 'plant of birth.' Carried on the eagle's pinions, he ascends gate after gate toward the heaven of Anu until, flying too high, eagle and rider are hurled back to earth.
summary.zh: 牧者之王伊塔那因妻子難產，向沙瑪什祈求「生育之草」；他乘神鷹之翼層層昇上安努天門，終因飛得太高而與鷹一同墜回大地。

sensitivity.note: Coordinates placed at Kish (Tell al-Uhaymir), the traditional seat of Etana's royal line in the Sumerian King List. Bracketed footnote numbers from Jastrow's text have been removed; his 1898 rendering reconstructs the legend from then-known fragments, exemplifying early comparative philology before later tablet finds altered some readings.

passages.text: Etana's wife is in distress because she is unable to bring to the world a child which she has conceived. Etana appeals to Shamash. Through the mediation of the priests he has offered sacrifices, and he now prays to Shamash to show him the "plant of birth." The oracles have completed my sacrifices, They have completed my free-will offerings to the gods. O Lord, let thy mouth command, And give me the plant of birth, Reveal to me the plant of birth, Bring forth the fruit, grant me an offspring.

Etana obeys, and thus, securely attached to the eagle, begins the daring journey. They fly for the space of a double hour, when The eagle addresses Etana: Look, my friend, how the earth appears; Look at the sea and at its side, the house of wisdom; The earth appears as a mountain, the sea has become a pool (?). A second double hour he (i.e., the eagle) carried him on high. The eagle spoke to Etana: Look, my friend, how the earth appears; The sea is a mere belt (?) around the earth. A third double hour he carried him on high. The eagle spoke to Etana: Look, my friend, how the earth appears; The sea is a mere gardener's ditch.

title.en: The Salmon of Knowledge
title.zh: 智慧鮭魚

region.en: River Boyne, Ireland
region.zh: 愛爾蘭博因河

period: Irish Fenian cycle, medieval Irish tales; retold in Lady Augusta Gregory's Gods and Fighting Men (1904)

source.work: Gods and Fighting Men, by Lady Augusta Gregory (1904), eBook #14465

summary.en: The poet Finegas waits seven years on the River Boyne for the salmon of knowledge, foretold to grant all wisdom to whoever eats it. His pupil Finn, roasting the fish, burns his thumb and sucks it, tasting the salmon first; Finegas gives him the whole fish, and Finn gains the wisdom of the nine hazels.
summary.zh: 詩人菲尼加斯守候博因河七年，只待預言中食之可獲全智的智慧鮭魚；弟子芬恩烤魚時燙傷拇指，吮指之際先嚐其味，菲尼加斯遂將全魚相讓，芬恩因此得自海底靈井旁九株智慧榛樹的知識。

sensitivity.note: Coordinates placed on the River Boyne near Slane, where Finegas kept watch by the water for the salmon of knowledge. Lady Gregory's stylised 'Kiltartanese' English deliberately mirrors Irish oral idiom; the tale belongs to Fenian heroic lore but is classed as myth per the project scheme, presented as comparative scholarship.

passages.text: And then he said farewell to Crimall, and went on to learn poetry from Finegas, a poet that was living at the Boinn, for the poets thought it was always on the brink of water poetry was revealed to them. And he did not give him his own name, but he took the name of Deimne. Seven years, now, Finegas had stopped at the Boinn, watching the salmon, for it was in the prophecy that he would eat the salmon of knowledge that would come there, and that he would have all knowledge after. And when at the last the salmon of knowledge came, he brought it to where Finn was, and bade him to roast it, but he bade him not to eat any of it.

And when Finn brought him the salmon after a while he said: "Did you eat any of it at all, boy?" "I did not," said Finn; "but I burned my thumb putting down a blister that rose on the skin, and after doing that, I put my thumb in my mouth." "What is your name, boy?" said Finegas. "Deimne," said he. "It is not, but it is Finn your name is, and it is to you and not to myself the salmon was given in the prophecy." With that he gave Finn the whole of the salmon, and from that time Finn had the knowledge that came from the nuts of the nine hazels of wisdom that grow beside the well that is below the sea.

title.en: The Children of Lir
title.zh: 里爾的孩子們

region.en: Killarney lakes region, Ireland
region.zh: 愛爾蘭基拉尼湖區

period: Old Irish saga of the Tuatha De Danann cycle, retold in Joseph Jacobs' More Celtic Fairy Tales (1894)

source.work: More Celtic Fairy Tales, ed. Joseph Jacobs (1894), eBook #34453 (Stephens' Irish Fairy Tales, 1920, was checked and does not include this tale)

summary.en: Oifa (Aoife), consumed by jealousy of her sister's children, strikes the four children of Lir with a Druid's wand, transforming them into four perfectly white swans. Doomed to wander the lakes and streams of Erin for nine hundred years, they retain their speech and a plaintive music unmatched in the world.
summary.zh: 因嫉恨而心生惡念的艾伊芙，以德魯伊魔杖將里爾的四名子女化為四隻純白天鵝，令其在愛爾蘭諸湖諸川漂流九百年；天鵝們保有人言，其哀婉歌聲世間無雙。

sensitivity.note: Coordinates placed at Lough Leane, Killarney, the customary identification of the lake where Aoife's spell was cast. The 900-year swan exile is one of the 'three sorrows of story-telling' and involves harm to children by a foster-mother; framed here for comparative scholarship.

passages.text: Then she would have raised a sword herself to kill and destroy the children, but her own womanhood and her weakness prevented her; so she drove the children of Lir into the lake to bathe, and they did as Oifa told them. As soon as they were upon the lake she struck them with a Druid's wand of spells and wizardry and put them into the forms of four beautiful, perfectly white swans, and she sang this song over them: "Out with you upon the wild waves, children of the king! Henceforth your cries shall be with the flocks of birds."

Oifa laughed and said: "Never shall ye be free until the woman from the south be united to the man from the north, until Lairgnen of Connaught wed Deoch of Munster; nor shall any have power to bring you out of these forms. Nine hundred years shall you wander over the lakes and streams of Erin. This only I will grant unto you: that you retain your own speech, and there shall be no music in the world equal to yours, the plaintive music you shall sing."

title.en: Baba Yaga and the Little Girl with the Kind Heart
title.zh: 芭芭雅嘎與善良的小女孩

region.en: Russia (forest village, central Russia)
region.zh: 俄羅斯（中央俄羅斯森林村莊）

period: retold 1916 (Ransome)

source.work: Old Peter's Russian Tales, told by Arthur Ransome (1916), tale 'Baba Yaga and the Little Girl with the Kind Heart', eBook #16981

summary.en: A kind stepdaughter is sent into the forest to the witch Baba Yaga. Kindness to the gate, dog, cat, and birch wins their help, and she escapes from the hut on hen's legs, flinging down a towel that becomes a river and a comb that becomes a deep forest to hold off Baba Yaga chasing in her flying mortar.
summary.zh: 善良的女孩被狠心的繼母送到森林女巫芭芭雅嘎處，幸得行善相助脫逃：先後丟下化為大河的毛巾和化為密林的木梳，擋住駕石臼飛追而來的鐵齒女巫，平安返家。

sensitivity.note: Coordinates point to central European Russia, the broadly named setting of Ransome's collection, since the tale's forest is symbolic. Ransome retells for children 'from memory' from Afanasyev-type published collections and frames the tale through the narrator Old Peter, so passages are verbatim from his 1916 telling; a European literary folktale with no sacred or restricted subject matter.

passages.text: "And her hut?" said Vanya. He had often heard about it before, but he wanted to hear about it again. "She lives in a little hut which stands on hen's legs. Sometimes it faces the forest, sometimes it faces the path, and sometimes it walks solemnly about. But in some of the stories she lives in another kind of hut, with a railing of tall sticks, and a skull on each stick. And all night long fire glows in the skulls and fades as the dawn rises."

Baba Yaga gnashed at them with her iron teeth. Then she jumped into the mortar and sat down. She drove it along with the pestle, and swept up her tracks with a besom, and flew off in pursuit of the little girl. The little girl ran and ran. She put her ear to the ground and listened. Bang, bang, bangety bang! she could hear Baba Yaga beating the mortar with the pestle. Baba Yaga was quite close. There she was, beating with the pestle and sweeping with the besom, coming along the road. As quickly as she could, the little girl took out the towel and threw it on the ground. And the towel grew bigger and bigger, and wetter and wetter, and there was a deep, broad river between Baba Yaga and the little girl.

title.en: The Coming of Men, a Long, Long While Ago
title.zh: 很久很久以前，人類的來臨

region.en: East Greenland (Ammassalik district)
region.zh: 東格陵蘭（安馬沙利克一帶）

period: collected 1921 (Rasmussen)

source.work: Eskimo Folk-Tales, collected by Knud Rasmussen, ed. and trans. W. J. Alexander Worster (1921), eBook #28932

summary.en: The earth fell down from the sky long ago, and children came out of the willow bushes. Men who could not die became too many, so a mighty flood from the sea drowned many of them; then two old women agreed that light and death should both come to the world — and when men die they go up into the sky to become brightly shining things.
summary.zh: 遠古時大地自天而降，孩童從柳叢中出生；不識死亡的人類過多，海上滔天洪水淹沒許多人。兩位老婦議定光與死並至，自此人死後升上天際，化為光芒閃亮的太陽、月亮和星辰。

sensitivity.note: A creation tale, not tied to one place; coordinates mark Ammassalik, East Greenland, the district where parts of the volume's material was collected. No restricted (sacral/ceremonial) content was collected; the tale is a published folk narrative version from a 1921 public-domain collection, not ceremonial knowledge.
