passages.text: A long, long time ago, when the earth was to be made, it fell down from the sky. Earth, hills and stones, all fell down from the sky, and thus the earth was made. And then, when the earth was made, came men. It is said that they came forth out of the earth. Little children came out of the earth. They came forth from among the willow bushes, all covered with willow leaves. And there they lay among the little bushes: lay and kicked, for they could not even crawl. And they got their food from the earth.

But these men who did not know how to die, they grew to be too many, and crowded the earth. And then there came a mighty flood from the sea. Many were drowned, and men grew fewer. We can still see marks of that great flood, on the high hill-tops, where mussel shells may often be found. And now that men had begun to be fewer, two old women began to speak thus: "Better to be without day, if thus we may be without death," said the one. "No; let us have both light and death," said the other. And when the old woman had spoken these words, it was as she had wished. Light came, and death.

title.en: How Pele Came to Hawaii
title.zh: 火神佩蕾如何來到夏威夷

region.en: Hawaiian Islands (Kilauea, Hawaii Island)
region.zh: 夏威夷群島（夏威夷島基拉韋厄火山）

period: retold 1916 (Westervelt)

source.work: Hawaiian Legends of Volcanoes, collected and retold by W. D. Westervelt (1916), eBook #66516

summary.en: The fire-goddess Pele and her family are driven across the ocean by the vengeance of her sea-goddess sister. Wherever Pele strikes her magic pa-oa, a fire-pit opens, but the sea drowns her fires on island after island until she settles in Kilauea; even after her body is broken in battle, her spirit lives on in the volcanic smoke of Mauna Loa.
summary.zh: 火神佩蕾一家遭其姊、海神追復仇而流亡海上；佩蕾以魔鏟處處掘火坑，屢被海水撲熄，最後在基拉韋厄安身。即使肉身被毀，其神魂仍化作火山口的煙火，永為火山火神。

sensitivity.note: Coordinates mark the Kilauea fire-pit, the permanent home Pele digs and occupies at the end of her epic journey. Drawn from a 1916 published retelling by a non-Hawaiian collector; Westervelt's spellings and interpretations are of his era and do not represent present-day kumu teachings, and no restricted content was collected.

passages.text: When Pele came to the island Hawaii, she first stopped at a place called Ke-ahi-a-laka in the district of Puna. From this place she began her inland journey toward the mountains. As she passed on her way there grew within her an intense desire to go at once and see Ai-laau, the god to whom Kilauea belonged, and find a resting-place with him as the end of her journey. She came up, but Ai-laau was not in his house. Of a truth he had made himself thoroughly lost. He had vanished because he knew that this one coming toward him was Pele. He had seen her toiling down by the sea at Ke-ahi-a-laka. Trembling dread and heavy fear overpowered him. He ran away and was entirely lost. When Pele came to that pit she laid out the plan for her abiding home, beginning at once to dig up the foundations. She dug day and night and found that this place fulfilled all her desires. Therefore, she fastened herself tight to Hawaii for all time.

The battle was fought by the two sisters hand to hand. The conflict lasted for a long time along the western slope of the mountain Hale-a-ka-la. Na-maka-o-ka-hai tore the body of Pele and broke her lava bones into great pieces which lie to this day along the seacoast of the district called Kahiki-nui. The masses of broken lava are called Na-iwi-o-Pele (The bones of Pele). Pele was thought to be dead and was sorely mourned by the remaining brothers and sisters. Na-maka-o-ka-hai went off toward Nuu-mea-lani rejoicing in the destruction of her hated enemy. By and by she looked back over the wide seas. The high mountains of the island Hawaii, snow covered, lay in the distance. But over the side of the mountain known as Mauna Loa she saw the uhane, the spirit form of Pele in clouds of volcanic smoke tinged red from the flames of raging fire-pits below. She passed on to Nuu-mea-lani, knowing that she could never again overcome the spirit of Pele, the goddess of fire.

title.en: The Creation Story (Tagalog)
title.zh: 創世故事（他加祿人）

region.en: Luzon, Philippines (Tagalog lowlands)
region.zh: 菲律賓呂宋島（他加祿族低地）

period: recorded 1916 (Cole)

source.work: Philippine Folk Tales, compiled and annotated by Mabel Cook Cole (1916), eBook #12814

summary.en: In the beginning there was no land, only the sea and the sky with a kite flying between. The bird stirs up the sea until the sky showers islands upon it; then a bamboo born of the married breezes splits open to release the first man and woman, whose scattered, hiding children become the ancestors of the different peoples.
summary.zh: 太初無陸地，只有海與天，其間飛著一隻鳶；海鳥攪動海水，天便降下許多島嶼鎮住大海。其後風與風成婚生出一竿竹子，竹中迸出世界第一對男女；其後裔因躲避父母責打而四散，從此分化為酋長、奴隸與各族之人。

sensitivity.note: A creation-dawn story of the Tagalog lowlands, pinned to Manila Bay on Luzon as the ethnic heartland. The verbatim text carries period racial labels from the 1916 edition, quoted unmodified for documentary accuracy; Cole's footnote marks that later tellers adapted the ending to name known peoples. Bracketed footnote markers [154]/[155] and one printer's typo ('stea' for 'sea', in the Gutenberg text) have been removed/corrected.

passages.text: When the world first began there was no land, but only the sea and the sky, and between them was a kite. One day the bird which had nowhere to light grew tired of flying about, so she stirred up the sea until it threw its waters against the sky. The sky, in order to restrain the sea, showered upon it many islands until it could no longer rise, but ran back and forth. Then the sky ordered the kite to light on one of the islands to build her nest, and to leave the sea and the sky in peace.

Many children were born to the couple, and from them came all the different races of people. After a while the parents grew very tired of having so many idle and useless children around, and they wished to be rid of them, but they knew of no place to send them to. Time went on and the children became so numerous that the parents enjoyed no peace. One day, in desperation, the father seized a stick and began beating them on all sides. This so frightened the children that they fled in different directions, seeking hidden rooms in the house -- some concealed themselves in the walls, some ran outside, while others hid in the fireplace, and several fled to the sea. Now it happened that those who went into the hidden rooms of the house later became the chiefs of the Islands; and those who concealed themselves in the walls became slaves. Those who ran outside were free men; and those who hid in the fireplace became negroes; while those who fled to the sea were gone many years, and when their children came back they were the white people.

title.en: The Birth of Athena
title.zh: 雅典娜的誕生

region.en: Athens (Acropolis, Attica), Greece
region.zh: 雅典衛城（阿提卡，希臘）

period: retold 1893, rev. 1921 (Guerber, Myths of Greece and Rome)

source.work: H. A. Guerber, 'Myths of Greece and Rome' (1893/1921), eBook #39250

summary.en: Suffering agonizing head pains, Zeus orders his son Hephaestus to cleave his skull open, and Athena springs out full-grown and armed for war. Later she wins the naming of Athens over Poseidon by raising the olive tree.
summary.zh: 宙斯頭痛難忍，命兒子赫菲斯托斯以斧劈開其顱骨，全副武裝的雅典娜躍然而出。其後她以橄欖樹擊敗波塞冬，贏得為雅典城命名的權利。

sensitivity.note: All passages are condensed paraphrases of Guerber's retelling in the collector's own words. Myth plus aition: the birth explains Athena's cult, and the olive contest explains the city's name; coordinates point to the Acropolis of Athens. Source caveat: Guerber uses Latinized names (Jupiter, Vulcan, Minerva, Neptune) and the most popular version; the Homeric Hymn to Athena differs (birth by the river Triton, no axe).

passages.text: Even the deathless gods could suffer pain. Zeus was one day seized with a splitting headache so severe that he summoned the gods of Olympus and begged them for relief. Every remedy failed, even those proposed by Apollo, the divine physician. Unable to bear the torment longer, Zeus commanded his son Hephaestus — the lame smith-god — to split his skull open with an axe. The smith obeyed, and in that instant Athena (whom the Romans called Minerva) leaped out of her father's head, full-grown, glinting in shining armor, spear raised, singing a shout of victory. The assembled gods drew back in alarm, and a mighty trembling over land and sea bore witness that a great new divinity had arrived.

The newborn goddess came to preside over wisdom, skill, and peaceful warfare. Soon afterward a Phoenician named Cecrops founded a fine city in Attica, and the gods contended for the honor of naming it. Eventually only Athena and Poseidon remained, so Zeus declared that whoever gave the city's people the most useful gift would win. Poseidon struck the rock and a splendid horse sprang out, drawing cries of amazement; the onlookers mocked Athena's quieter offering, an olive tree. But when she explained how wood, fruit, and leaves of the olive all serve humankind, and that it stands for peace and prosperity rather than war, the judges granted her the city. She named it Athens in her own honor, and the Athenians worshipped her as their guardian goddess, with the great Parthenon raised to her on their citadel.

title.en: The Judgment of Paris
title.zh: 帕里斯的裁判

region.en: Mount Ida near Troy, Anatolia
region.zh: 特洛伊附近的伊達山（安納托利亞）

period: retold 1855 (Bulfinch, The Age of Fable, rev. E. E. Hale)

source.work: Thomas Bulfinch, 'Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable' (1855), eBook #3327

summary.en: Left off the guest list at the wedding of Peleus and Thetis, the goddess of Discord tosses a golden apple inscribed for the most beautiful. Zeus hands judgment to the shepherd Paris, who chooses Venus — carrying Helen to Troy and sparking the Trojan War.
summary.zh: 婚禮上未曾獲邀的爭執女神在佩琉斯與忒提斯的婚宴擲下金蘋果，宙斯把裁判交給牧人帕里斯；他選擇維納斯，並將海倫帶回特洛伊，遂爆發特洛伊戰爭。

sensitivity.note: All passages are condensed paraphrases of Bulfinch in the collector's own words. The Peleus–Thetis wedding anchors the divine-marriage motif; Bulfinch follows the Roman naming (Juno, Minerva, Venus) and his golden-apple telling is a 19th-century synthesis rather than Hesiod. Coordinates point to Mount Ida (39.70, 26.66) where the judgment occurs; the wedding itself is at Pelion in Thessaly, so one anchor covers the tale.

passages.text: At the wedding feast of Peleus and Thetis every god had been invited except Eris, the goddess of Discord. Furious at being excluded, she caused a golden apple to appear among the guests, engraved with the words "for the most beautiful." Juno, Minerva, and Venus each claimed it as her prize, and Zeus, unwilling to be dragged into so delicate a dispute, sent the three goddesses to settle their own quarrel on Mount Ida near Troy, where a young shepherd named Paris tended his flocks. Each tried to bribe him: Juno offered power and dominion, Minerva glory in war, and Venus promised the most beautiful woman alive as his wife.

Paris judged in Venus's favor and handed her the golden apple, gaining her favor but making perpetual enemies of the other two goddesses. Venus later guided Paris across the sea to Greece, where he was received hospitably by Menelaus, king of Sparta. Venus had destined Helen, Menelaus' wife and the most beautiful woman in the world, to belong to Paris; during the king's absence Paris persuaded her to flee with him to Troy. The Greek princes had sworn an oath to defend the marriage of whoever won Helen's hand, so when Menelaus called upon them they mounted a great expedition to reclaim her — the Trojan War of Homer's epics.

title.en: Cuchulain's Boyhood Deeds
title.zh: 庫丘林的少年事蹟

region.en: Emain Macha (Navan Fort), Ulster, Ireland
region.zh: 埃馬因馬哈（納文堡，阿爾斯特，愛爾蘭）

period: retold 1909 (Eleanor Hull, Cuchulain the Hound of Ulster)

source.work: Eleanor Hull, 'Cuchulain, the Hound of Ulster' (1909), ch. III-IV, eBook #52963

summary.en: The boy Setanta runs to Emain Macha at four years old, beats the whole boy-corps at their own game and withstands their assault, and takes the King's protection. Later he kills the smith Culain's giant guard-hound on his way to a feast and pledges himself as its replacement, earning the name Cuchulain, 'the Hound of Culain.'
summary.zh: 四歲的塞坦塔獨自奔至埃馬因馬哈，曲棍技壓整支少年兵團，奮力擋下圍攻，由國王親自庇護。其後赴宴途中殺死鐵匠庫倫的巨犬，自願替補其職，從而得名庫丘林——「庫倫之犬」。

sensitivity.note: All passages are condensed paraphrases of chapters III-IV of Hull's retelling in the collector's own words. Coordinates point to Emain Macha / Navan Fort (54.3446, -6.6946), the royal seat of Ulster. Source caveat: Hull (1909) is an English retelling that re-arranges and prunes the Irish originals (her own admission); the heroic-fury description ('hero-fury', hair crowned with light) follows her version of the twelfth-century texts.

passages.text: Not yet past four years old, the boy heard tales of the boy-corps of King Conor at Emain Macha and could not be held back. Arming himself with a brass hurley and a ball of silver, a toy javelin and a toy spear, he ran the long road north-west over the Slieve Fuad Mountains, driving ball, hurley, and spears before him in an unbroken game. Without asking anyone's leave he dived into the midst of the hundred and fifty princes' sons, caught the ball between his legs, and drove it home to the goal. When the corps attacked the unknown intruder with their spears, hurleys and balls all at once, he parried every throw — and then his 'hero-fury' seized him: his hair rose and seemed crowned with fire, he grew taller in furious contortion, and, springing like a young lion, he stretched fifty of the boys on the ground before the King stopped him at the chessboard and granted the newcomer protection under his own name.

Some time later the smith Culain prepared a feast for the King, warning that his grounds held no room for a great company. The King, lingering fascinated by the boy's games, left the child behind to finish a ball-game and forgot him; and Culain, told that the company was complete, loosed his great watch-dog, brought from Spain, with the strength of a hundred hounds, to guard the district. Setanta, following the chariot-trails of the royal party, came to the fort alone with club and ball. The mastiff charged open-jawed; the boy flung his ball down its throat, caught the choking beast's head in his hands, and dashed it against the pillars of the door until it lay dead. When the grieving smith lamented the loss of his defense and safeguard, the boy promised to rear a new whelp of that breed — and meanwhile to serve as Culain's own hound in defense of his cattle and house. "Then your name shall no longer be Setanta," the assembly cried, "but Cu-Chulain, the Hound of Culain!"

title.en: Sigurd Slaying Fafnir
title.zh: 西格德屠龍

region.en: Gnita Heath (Rhineland), Germanic North
region.zh: 格尼塔荒原（萊茵地區，北歐傳說地）

period: Saga c. 12th-13th c.; tr. William Morris & Eirikr Magnusson (1888)

source.work: The Story of the Volsungs (Volsunga Saga), tr. William Morris & Eirikr Magnusson (1888), ch. XIII-XVIII, eBook #1152

summary.en: The smith Regin tells Sigurd of the cursed gold of Andvari, which turned the smith's brother Fafnir into a great dragon brooding on its hoard. Sigurd slays the dragon from a hidden pit, roasts its heart, and tastes its blood — gaining the understanding of bird-speech, which warns him to slay his treacherous tutor.
summary.zh: 鐵匠雷金向西格德講述安德瓦里的詛咒黃金——正是這份黃金使其兄法夫尼爾化為盤踞寶藏的巨龍。西格德於隱蔽坑洞中一劍誅龍，烤食其心、啖其血而通鳥語，鳥言警其誅殺反噬的親師，遂得寶藏。

sensitivity.note: All passages are condensed paraphrases of the Morris/Magnusson translation, chapters XIII-XVIII, in the collector's own words; the birds' counsel and Odin's disguise as an old bearded man follow the saga. Saga version, not the Poetic Edda; coordinates are a neutral spot in the Rhineland, the unnamed 'Gnita-heath' of the Germanic legend-cycle.

passages.text: Regin, the smith who fostered him, told Sigurd the tale of his family: Hreidmar and his three sons — the smith Regin, the mighty Fafnir, and Otter the fisher — lived alongside the gods. When Odin, Hoenir, and Loki slew Otter in his beast-shape, Hreidmar demanded as ransom an otter-skin's weight of gold, forcing Odin to extort the whole hoard of the dwarf Andvari, whom Loki robbed of his magic ring. The dwarf cursed the gold, dooming it to destroy every owner; the doom soon fell, for Fafnir killed their father for the treasure and, transformed into a great dragon of malice and greed, brooded over his gold on the heath, while Regin nursed his claim on the next generation — the fostered hero Sigurd, son of Sigmund, owner of the reforged sword Gram.

On the heath Sigurd saw the track of the worm marvellously great; Regin, shaking in fear, showed him where to dig. As Sigurd dug, an old bearded man appeared, advised him to make many pits for the running blood, then vanished — Odin in disguise. When the dragon crept down to drink, shaking the earth and snorting venom before him, Sigurd thrust his sword Gram up under Fafnir's left shoulder to the hilt. The dying worm lashed out with head and tail, smashing all that stood before him, and warned Sigurd: the same gold he had owned would be Sigurd's bane too. Regin bade the victor roast Fafnir's heart for him; tasting the dragon's blood on his finger, Sigurd Suddenly understood the speech of birds, and the wood-peckers' chatter warned him that Regin meant to beguile him — so he took the gold, struck off Regin's head, and rode on toward Hindfell, where the fire slept.

title.en: Yi, the Divine Archer, and the False Suns
title.zh: 后羿射落偽日

region.en: Tung-t'ing Lake region, China
region.zh: 洞庭湖一帶（中國）

period: told of the reign of Yao (c. 2346 BCE) as dated by tradition; retold 1922 (Werner, Myths and Legends of China, ch. VI)

source.work: E. T. C. Werner, 'Myths and Legends of China' (1922), ch. VI 'Myths of Thunder, Lightning, Wind, and Rain' — 'The Divine Archer', eBook #15250

summary.en: Under the emperor Yao, the marvel archer Ch'ih-chiang Tzu-yü is renamed Shên I, the Divine Archer, and sent against the calamities ravaging the land — storms, floods, a thousand-foot serpent and giant boars, and ten burning suns. He tames the wind-spirit Fei Lien, shoots down the nine suns born of fire-blowing birds, wins the water-spirit's sister Hêng O as wife, and is canonized as Pacifier of the Country.
summary.zh: 帝堯在位時，異士赤將子輿獲賜名神羿，奉命討平肆虐大地之災禍——狂風、洪水、千尺巨蛇與大野豬，以及天上的十個毒日。他降服風神飛廉，射落妖鳥吹成之九個偽日，娶水神之妹嫦娥，受封「定國侯」。

sensitivity.note: All passages are condensed paraphrases of Werner's chapter VI in the collector's own words. Werner (1922) renders a composite Chinese legend-cycle drawn from the Feng shên yen i and related works; in his version the archer (Shên I / Yi) shoots down nine suns created by fire-blowing birds rather than nine of ten true suns, and the same cycle includes his marriage to Hêng O and the pill of immortality — motif 'sun-capture' hence covers the ten-sun excess and 'quest-immortality' the immortality-pill episode in this culture-hero cycle. Coordinates mark the Tung-t'ing Lake region, tied to the serpent episode.

passages.text: In the twelfth year of the reign of the Emperor Yao — dated by tradition to 2346 BCE — the emperor met in the streets of Huai-yang a man bearing a bow bound with red cloth. He was Ch'ih-chiang Tzu-yü, who claimed to be a skilful archer able to fly on the wings of the wind. To test him, Yao ordered an arrow shot at a pine on a neighbouring mountain: an arrow transfixed the tree, and the bowman soared up the current of air to fetch it back. Named Shên I, 'the Divine Archer,' and attached to the imperial suite, he helped face the calamities then laying waste the land: ten suns burnt up the crops, storms uprooted trees and overturned houses, floods covered the country, a serpent a thousand feet long devoured people near the Tung-t'ing Lake, and boars of enormous size ravaged the east.

Studying the storms from Mount Ch'ing Ch'iu, Shên I found they poured out of the sack of Fei Lien, Spirit of the Wind, whose blows he mastered — Fei Lien sued for mercy and swore friendship, and the tempests ceased. Then, discovering nine extraordinary birds on three neighbouring peaks of the Hsi Ho blowing out fire that made nine new suns in the sky, he shot nine arrows in succession, pierced the birds, and watched the false suns dissolve into red clouds; the nine arrows stood fast in nine red stones on the mountains. He slew the Tung-t'ing serpent with an arrow in its left eye, trapped and killed the monstrous boars, married Hêng O the sister of Ho Po the water-spirit, and for these exploits the emperor Yao canonized him with the title Marquis Pacifier of the Country.

title.en: The Wives of Shiva: Sati, Uma, and Parvati
title.zh: 濕婆之妻：薩蒂、烏瑪與帕爾瓦蒂

region.en: Mount Kailasa, Himalayas; Daksha's sacrifice-house, the Ganges plain
region.zh: 凱拉薩山（喜馬拉雅）；祭祀罪火場（恆河平原）

period: Puranic synthesis, c. 500-1000 CE; retold 1913 (Donald A. Mackenzie, Indian Myth and Legend, ch. VIII)

source.work: Donald A. Mackenzie, 'Indian Myth and Legend' (1913), ch. VIII 'Divinities of the Epic Period', eBook #47228

summary.en: Shiva's brides reflect his many aspects: Sati, the ideal of wifely devotion, dies on her father's sacrificial fire when her husband is slighted; reborn as Uma and as Parvati, she wins Shiva again and bears him Ganesa and Kartikeya. The love god Kamadeva, rousing the widowed god, is burned to ashes by the flame of Shiva's third eye.
summary.zh: 濕婆的伴侶映照其多面：薩蒂在父親祭祀之際受辱殉火，死後化身烏瑪與帕爾瓦蒂，再度贏得濕婆，生下智慧神象鼻與戰神韋馱。試以愛神箭激醒鰥居之神的迦摩天，遂被濕婆第三眼之火燒成灰燼。

sensitivity.note: All passages are condensed paraphrases of Mackenzie's chapter VIII in the collector's own words. A Puranic synthesis rather than one scripture; Mackenzie (1913) serves as a secondary PD compilation and his naming follows period conventions (Sivá, Parvati, Himavat omitted). Coordinates mark Mount Kailasa, Shiva's dwelling per Mackenzie, a mythic Himalayan site. The widows' self-immolation (sati) is reported as a named historical custom in the source and treated here as mythic-historical, not endorsed.

passages.text: Shiva's complex character is mirrored in the many forms his bride assumes. As Sati she is the ideal of the devoted wife: when her father, the sage Daksha, slighted her spouse at the sacrifice, the goddess cast herself onto the sacrificial fire — and the widows who later died on their husbands' funeral pyres were called Sati in imitation of the faithful goddess. Sati, however, was reborn as Uma, 'Light,' the impersonation of divine wisdom; as Amvika she was Rudra's sister and counterpart; and as Parvati, another form of the same goddess, she endured Shiva's taunt about her dark skin, retired to austerities, and so regained a golden complexion. One Varaha Purana myth makes the three goddess-forms — white Saraswati, red Lakshmi, and black Parvati — originally a single goddess, divided into shapes representing Past, Present, and Future.

Two more tales wreathe the divine marriage. After Sati's death the sorrowing Shiva was wounded by Kamadeva, the love god — son of Vishnu and Lakshmi, who shoots flowery arrows and whose wife Rati symbolizes Spring; a flame darted from Shiva's third eye burned Kamadeva to ashes. Of the god's own children, Ganesa, the four-armed elephant-headed god of wisdom and good fortune, invoked at the beginning of books, houses and journeys, is a son of Shiva and Parvati — a Purana tells how the cursed gaze of Saturn decapitated the infant, and Vishnu, flying on Garuda, replaced the head with that of Indra's elephant; the son Kartikeya is the celestial general and slayer of demons.

title.en: The Chinvat Bridge Judgment
title.zh: 欽瓦特橋的審判

region.en: Persia (symbolic: the unseen world beyond the bridge)
region.zh: 波斯（象徵：橋彼岸之幽冥世界）

period: Avestan c. 1000-600 BCE, Pahlavi accounts 8th-9th c. CE; Dhalla ed. 1914

source.work: M. N. Dhalla, 'Zoroastrian Theology' (1914), ch. XIX 'Death and Beyond'

summary.en: In Zoroastrian teaching the soul lingers three days and nights beside the corpse, then journeys to the unseen world, where its own conscience appears as a beautiful maiden (for the good) or a taunting hag (for the wicked). Every soul must cross the Chinvat Bridge of Judgment: the righteous pass with spirit-guard dogs' help into a four-tiered heaven, while the wicked fall into a four-tiered hell of poisonous food and endless darkness.
summary.zh: 瑣羅亞斯德教認為，亡魂死後三晝夜停留屍旁，隨即啟程前往幽冥之境：義人的良心化身絕美少女相迎，惡人則受醜嫗嘲弄。一切靈魂皆須渡過審判之橋——欽瓦特橋：義人得靈犬相助進入四重天國，惡人則墮入以毒物為食、黑暗無底的四層地獄。

sensitivity.note: All passages are condensed, fully paraphrased retellings of Dhalla's chapter XIX in the collector's own words. Source caveat: the planned primary source (SBE Vol. 5, 'Pahlavi Texts Part I', tr. E. W. West, 1880) was inaccessible (sacred-texts.com returns 403), so Dhalla's 1914 PD scholarly synthesis was substituted; it is secondary, so exact Pahlavi chapter attributions are less precise. Category 'religious': scriptural/doctrinal eschatology rather than folk narrative. Coordinates are symbolic — the Chinvat Bridge is an otherworldly location, placed inland at Yazd, a historic centre of surviving Zoroastrianism.

passages.text: In Zoroastrian thought, death is a trial no one escapes: even legendary heroes like Yima fell to Astovidhotu, the demon of death. After the body dies, the soul remains near it for three days and nights, retracing the deeds of its lifetime. The soul of a righteous person sits by the spot where the head once rested, chanting sacred hymns and feeling joy as great as all the living world combined, while the soul of a wicked person sits near the skull in bewildered dread and suffering as great as all the living world combined. At the fourth dawn the journey into the unseen world begins. The righteous soul travels amid a sweet south wind, and then meets its own daena — religious conscience appearing as a damsel of unmatched beauty — who reveals that she is simply the embodiment of its own good thoughts, words, and deeds. Helpers such as Sraosha and Rashnu escort such a soul on its way. The wicked walk a dreadful path in a foul north wind and, in the Pahlavi accounts, are confronted by their conscience in the shape of an ugly old hag mocking the wicked life they led.

Every soul, good or bad, must pass over the Chinvat Bridge before entering the world beyond, for it stands as the crossing point of judgment. Spirit hounds are stationed at the bridge; they lend aid to devout souls, while the wicked find none. Whoever recites the Ahuna Vairya prayer in full faith is enabled by Ahura Mazda to cross and reach the best existence, the best righteousness, and the best lights; a true priest is one whose wise teaching leaves a person easy of conscience at the bridge, whereas anyone who mistreats dogs in life finds the way barred. Paradise has four levels — Good Thought, Good Word, Good Deed, and highest of all Garonmana, the abode of endless light — where the archangel Vohu Manah greets the newcomers and celestial food, embroidered robes, and golden thrones are provided. Hell likewise has four depths, ending in endless, stinking darkness, where Angra Mainyu feeds souls the foulest food amid the mockery of the infernal rabble.

title.en: Adam and Eve, the Forbidden Fruit, and Expulsion from Eden
title.zh: 亞當與夏娃的墮落（創世記二至三章）

region.en: The Garden of Eden (symbolic)
region.zh: 伊甸園（象徵性）

period: Genesis, c. 6th-5th c. BCE; KJV 1611 (Project Gutenberg eBook #8001)

source.work: The Bible, King James version, Book 1: Genesis, chapters 2-3, eBook #8001

summary.en: God forms the first man from dust and sets him in a garden in Eden, forbidding him to eat from the tree of knowledge of good and evil. The serpent persuades the woman that the fruit brings knowledge rather than death; she and her husband eat, are punished with hardship and mortality, and are driven out of Eden, with a flaming sword set to guard the tree of life.
summary.zh: 上帝以塵土造出第一個人，安置在伊甸園中，囑咐他不可吃分辨善惡樹的果子。蛇哄騙女人說果子不會致死，反能開眼如神；她與丈夫吃了，因而受勞苦與死亡的刑罰，被逐出伊甸園，園東有天使與火焰之劍把守生命樹的通路。

sensitivity.note: Passages are condensed paraphrased retellings of the KJV Genesis 2-3 narrative in the collector's own words. The KJV is presented strictly as a public-domain comparative text, not as religious truth. Category 'religious' (canonical scripture + taboo-and-transgression narrative); motifs chosen for the dust-formed Adam and the forbidden-fruit transgression. Coordinates mark a neutral inland spot in southern Mesopotamia, the traditional association for Eden — the location is symbolic, not a verified site.

passages.text: In the second chapter of Genesis the Lord God, having formed a man from the dust of the ground, plants a garden eastward in Eden, full of trees pleasant to see and fit for food, with the tree of life and the tree of knowledge of good and evil standing in it. He settles the man there to dress and keep it, warning that he may eat freely of every tree but one: the tree of knowledge, whose fruit brings death on the very day it is eaten. Since it is not good for the man to be alone, God brings every living creature to him to be named, then casts him into a deep sleep, builds a woman out of a rib taken from his side, and the man joyfully recognizes her as bone of his bones and flesh of his flesh.

In Genesis 3 the serpent, subtler than every beast of the field, undermines the prohibition: eating will not kill the woman, he insists, but will open her eyes so that she becomes as a god, knowing good and evil. Seeing that the fruit is good for food, lovely to look at, and a path to wisdom, she takes and eats, and gives some to her husband, who eats too. Their eyes are opened, they sew fig leaves into coverings, and they hide among the trees when they hear the Lord God walking in the garden. Judgment follows: the serpent is doomed to crawl and eat dust; the woman is sentenced to sorrowful childbirth under her husband's rule; the man is cursed through a ground that will yield thorns and thistles only under the sweat of his face until he returns to dust. God clothes them in animal skins and drives them out to the east of Eden, where a cherub and a turning, flaming sword seal off the way back to the tree of life.

title.en: The Prodigal Son
title.zh: 浪子回頭的比喻（路加福音十五章）

region.en: Judea (setting of Jesus' teaching)
region.zh: 猶太（耶穌講道之地）

period: Gospel of Luke, c. 80-110 CE; KJV 1611 (Project Gutenberg eBook #8042)

source.work: The Bible, King James version, Book 42: Luke, chapter 15, eBook #8042

summary.en: Jesus tells of a younger son who demands his inheritance, squanders it in a distant country, and returns ruined and repentant, resolving to beg forgiveness. His father runs to meet him, restores him with robe, ring, and a feast, and answers the resentful elder brother that this son who was dead is alive again.
summary.zh: 耶穌講述：小兒子分得家產，遠走他鄉揮霍殆盡，淪為豬倌窮困潦倒，醒悟後回家認罪悔過。父親遠遠望見便奔上前擁抱親吻，為他披袍戴戒、設宴慶祝，並對心生妒忌的長兄說，這兄弟是死而復生、失而復得的孩子。

sensitivity.note: Passages are a paraphrase of the KJV narrative in the collector's own words. Interpretive points: the KJV is treated as a public-domain comparative text only, not as religious truth. Category 'religious' since it is a canonical scripture teaching story; motif 'parable-teaching' reflects the genre. The parable never names a place, so the coordinates are symbolic, on a neutral inland spot near Jerusalem.

passages.text: Jesus tells of a man with two sons. The younger asks for his share of the family property, and having received it, journeys into a far country where he wastes all his money in reckless, riotous living. When a great famine grips the land he falls into poverty and takes a job feeding pigs on a local farm; so hungry is he that he would gladly have filled his belly with the husks the swine eat, and no one gives him anything. Coming to his senses at last, he recalls that even his father's hired servants have bread enough and to spare, while he is starving. He resolves to get up, go home, confess that he has sinned against heaven and against his father, and ask to be taken in, no longer as a son, but as one of the hired servants.

While the young man is still a long way off, his father sees him, is moved with compassion, runs to meet him, and falls on his neck with kisses. The son makes his confession, admitting he is no longer worthy to be called a son, but before he can even ask to be made a servant, the father orders his best robe, a ring for his hand, shoes for his feet, and a feast on the fattened calf, declaring that this son of his was dead and is alive again, was lost and is found. The elder brother, who has served faithfully for years without ever receiving so much as a feast with his friends, refuses to come in and complains at the celebration. His father answers gently that everything the household owns has always been his, but rejoicing is right, because the boy's brother was dead and is alive again, was lost and is found.

title.en: The Miracles of Saint Bridget of Kildare
title.zh: 聖布里吉德（基爾代爾）的奇蹟

region.en: Kildare, Ireland
region.zh: 愛爾蘭基爾代爾

period: Saint's life from 7th c. CE hagiography onward; Baring-Gould, 'Lives of the Saints' (1897, Gutenberg eBook #45604)

source.work: S. Baring-Gould, 'The Lives of the Saints', vol. 2 (February), chapter 'S. Bridget', eBook #45604

summary.en: Baring-Gould recounts the legends of Bridget of Kildare: a wonder-marked birth on a threshold, lavish charity, the founding of her famous double monastery under an oak at Kildare, and miracles such as a cloak thrown over a sunbeam, a spared wolf, and sight restored to a blind nun. Before her death she foretells it, having earlier related a prophetic vision explained by Saint Patrick.
summary.zh: 巴林-古爾德敘述基爾代爾的布里吉德：門檻上誕生的靈異預兆、極度慷慨的童年、在基爾代爾橡樹下建立的修道院，以及斗篷懸擋日光柱、贈狼救農、復明盲修女等奇蹟。她預告自己的死期，此前亦向聖派屈克講出「白田被黑衣耕者翻掘」的異夢，被解為愛爾蘭未來的異端之亂。

sensitivity.note: Passages are condensed paraphrases written in the collector's own words; Baring-Gould's sentences were not reproduced verbatim. Category 'religious': hagiography (devotional saint-life). Edition caveat: this is the revised 16-volume 1897 edition; the legend source list concedes Bridget's surviving lives are late compositions of uneven reliability, and the cloak-expanding-over-land miracle is not in this edition, so only miracles actually present in this chapter are drawn on. Coordinates point to Kildare town, the account's concrete setting.

passages.text: The legend says Bridget is born on a doorway's threshold, fulfilling a court augury heard before her confinement: happy is the child born neither in the house nor out of it. Her mother, the nobleman Dubtach's slave-girl, has been sold to a bard, but with the bargain that the child is returned to her father; and when the infant is delivered on the threshold, a pitcher of warm milk falls and pours itself over her. Growing up, she gives every beggar whatever he asks, until her exasperated father takes her to the king's court to sell her as too expensive to keep — and when she hands even the royal sword to a beggar, the king refuses to buy a girl ready to give away the king himself. To escape an unwanted suitor she prays for disfigurement and loses an eye; veiled as a nun, she kisses the dry altar-wood, which turns green, and her beauty is restored.

Bridget founds her cell under a great oak at Kildare — 'the cell of the oak' — which grows into a famed double community of monks and nuns in a church divided into three parts. The chapter is crowded with wonders: her priestly charioteer preaching while a loose horse runs free; stolen cows carrying the thieves' tied clothes back to her convent gates; her cloak, thrown in haste over a sunbeam she has mistaken for a beam, holding the ray standing there until midnight; a live wolf delivered into her chariot and offered to the king in place of the one a rustic has killed, sparing the man's life; and the blind nun Dara, whom Bridget heals of darkness only to be asked to shut her eyes again, since a world so visible leaves God less visible to the soul. Bridget relates a vision before Saint Patrick of a white-harvest field torn up by black ploughmen and sowers scattering tares, which Patrick interprets as future false teaching in Ireland. She foretells the hour of her own death, dies on February 1, 525, and her convent keeps its perpetual fire — the 'House of Fire' — burning down to 1220.

title.en: Cheung Puk-chang, the Seer
title.zh: 崔卜鎮：先知與神通

region.en: Joseon Korea (Seoul; Bird Pass, Kyongsang Province)
region.zh: 朝鮮王朝（首爾；慶尚道鳥嶺）

period: tale collected by Im Bang (1640-1718); English ed. James S. Gale, 'Korean Folk Tales' (1913, Gutenberg eBook #51002)

source.work: Im Pang & Yi Ryuk, tr. James S. Gale, 'Korean Folk Tales: Imps, Ghosts and Fairies' (1913), Tale IV: 'Cheung Puk-chang, the Seer', eBook #51002

summary.en: Cheung Puk-chang is born a marvel of knowledge who needs no study, instantly mastering books, foreign tongues, and the speech of birds and beasts. Loochooan envoys arrive carrying a prophecy that names the day and hour they will meet a Holy Man, and it is fulfilled in him; he also displays distant vision, correctly reporting how a servant is faring far away on his journey.
summary.zh: 崔卜鎮天生異稟，書過目成誦，通天文、醫術、卜算與鳥獸之語。琉球使節攜預言書赴京尋訪「聖人」，其字句在崔卜鎮身上應驗而拜倒；他又能遙視千里，正確指出僕人行踪與遭遇，日期細節日後全部核實。

sensitivity.note: Passages are condensed paraphrases of Gale's translation in the collector's own words; none of Gale's sentences are reproduced verbatim. Category 'myth': a folk wonder-tale of supernatural sight and fulfilled prophecy rather than scripture (per the project genre split). Coordinates use Seoul, where the tale's opening events occur; its farthest episode is at Bird Pass, Kyongsang Province. The Gutenberg text pairs a scholarly historical preamble with each tale; both parts informed the summary.

passages.text: Cheung Puk-chang is a wonder from his earliest years: he needs only to glance through a book once to recite it word for word, and without any study he becomes a master of astronomy, medicine, fortune-telling, music, mathematics, and geomancy. He understands the calls of birds and the voices of beasts, and when he travels with his envoy father to Peking he picks up the language of any strange people after hearing it a single time, astonishing Koreans, Chinese, and foreigners alike. Envoys from Loochoo carry a horoscope-based prophecy in a little book naming the exact year, day, hour, and place they will meet a Holy Man; tracing one envoy station after another, they find him, are struck down with awe, prostrate themselves before him, and are taught at last the Book of Changes in their own tongue. Some call him 'The Mystery.'

One day Cheung Puk-chang calls on his aunt, worried because the servant she sent to do harvest work in Yong-nam County is overdue, and she fears he has met thieves or fire. Puk-chang offers to tell her how matters stand, and gazing off toward the far south he reports that the man is just crossing Bird Pass in Mun-kyong County, Kyong-sang Province — and at that very moment is being beaten by a passing gentleman, since he rode by without dismounting while the official was eating his meal at the top of the hill. The aunt laughs the whole thing off as a joke, but she marks the date on the wall. When the servant arrives on exactly the recorded day, he confirms everything: he was seized by the gentleman's servants, pulled from his horse, and beaten about the face with their straw shoes, precisely as Puk-chang had said.

title.en: Fuji, the Never-Dying Mountain
title.zh: 富士：不死之山

region.en: Mount Fuji, Japan (plain of Suruga)
region.zh: 日本富士山（駿河平原）

period: populary legends; F. Hadland Davis, 'Myths & Legends of Japan' (1912, Gutenberg eBook #45723), ch. IX 'Legends of Mount Fuji'

source.work: F. Hadland Davis, 'Myths & Legends of Japan' (1912), ch. IX 'Legends of Mount Fuji', eBook #45723

summary.en: Davis's chapter ties Fuji to immortality and apotheosis: the moon-maiden Kaguya commanded that the elixir of life be burned on its peak, and a Chinese emperor who climbs in hope of it dies smiling at the summit. The mountain itself rose in a single night before the woodman Visu; and a goddess of Fuji, a white-clad maiden, healed Yosoji's plague-stricken mother before being carried back to the peak by a cloud.
summary.zh: 戴維斯筆下，富士山與不死傳說相連：輝夜姬命人在峰頂焚燬長生不老藥；中國皇帝登山求藥，卻在山巔含笑而逝；此山一夜拔地而起，出現於樵夫斐素眼前，故稱「不死山」；白衣少女（富士女神）指路取靈泉救瘟疫病母，救人後自化彩雲澨被雲帶回峰頂。

sensitivity.note: Passages are condensed paraphrases of Davis's chapter IX in the collector's own words. Interpretive points: filed as 'myth' (folk legend of a sacred landscape); motifs — Fuji as hallowed peak (sacred-place), the elixir quest (quest-immortality), the cloud-borne apparition of the Goddess of Fuji (theophany). Edition caveat: Davis (1912) is a popular reteller whose versions blend several traditions, and the Kaguya episode is cross-referenced from his chapter III; the passages draw only on chapter IX material. Coordinates are the real Mount Fuji summit area, since the geography here is concrete.

passages.text: Fuji is sacred terrain: pilgrims have climbed it for hundreds of years, its crater was once an active volcano, and its very name is linked with the Aino fire-goddess. Legend even crowns the mountain with the prize of immortality. In the bamboo-cutter romance, the court commanded by the moon-maiden Lady Kaguya ascends Fuji to burn the elixir of life, along with a scroll, upon the peak. The mountain's fame reaches an emperor of China; when he learns that Fuji came into being in a single night, he reasons that so marvelous a mount must yield the elixir of life itself. He gathers handsome youths and maidens and sails to Japan, where the junks ride through a roaring storm before Fuji's white splendour rises before them. Forming his company in procession, the gold-robed emperor walks hour after hour at their head over soft snow, until, eager to be the first to drink, he runs ahead — and his people find him lying on his back, a smile on his face. He has indeed found life eternal, but by way of death.

How Fuji rose: a giant woodman named Visu lives with his family on the then-barren plain of Suruga. One night, as he is about to fall asleep, a sound more terrifying than any thunder comes out of the ground beneath him; fearing an earthquake, he snatches up the younger children and rushes out, to see a great mountain erupting in tongues of flame and dense smoke where there was only flat plain before — a peak that has run unseen under the earth for two hundred miles and leapt up in a single night. Spellbound, Visu watches dawn dress the mountain in opal, and names it Fuji-yama, the Never-Dying Mountain, its seeming eternity giving rise to the old belief in an elixir hidden upon it.

Another tale casts the mountain as a living healer: Yosoji, whose mother is dying of smallpox, is sent by the magician Kamo Yamakiko to fetch water from Fuji's south-west slope; a lady in white guides him to the stream by the shrine of the God of Long Breath. After five visits his mother and many villagers are cured; but when Yosoji returns to give thanks the shrine has dried up, and the maiden — she is the Goddess of Fuji — refuses all thanks, swings her camellia branch into the air to summon a cloud from the sacred peak, and lets it carry her home.

title.en: Coyote and the Dragon; Coyote in the Buffalo Country
title.zh: 郊狼與惡龍；水牛之地的郊狼

region.en: Columbia Plateau (Nez Perce and Flathead homelands, Idaho-Montana)
region.zh: 哥倫比亞高原（內茲珀斯人與弗拉特黑德人故地，愛達荷—蒙大拿）

period: collected from Plateau narrators; retold 1910 (Katharine Berry Judson, Myths and Legends of the Pacific Northwest)

source.work: Katharine Berry Judson (ed.), 'Myths and Legends of the Pacific Northwest', A.C. McClurg, 1910 — 'Coyote and the Dragon' (Nez Perce) and 'Coyote in the Buffalo Country' (Flathead)

summary.en: Two Coyote trickster tales from the Columbia Plateau. Coyote drags the sun down on a chain of arrows and hides it in a river, luring a light-fearing man-eating dragon into daylight where he can kill it; and in the buffalo country he defeats the greedy chief Bear, loses the herds through his own misrule, and finally out-tricks Wolf's revenge party.
summary.zh: 兩則哥倫比亞高原郊狼故事：郊狼以箭鏈拉下太陽藏入河中，誘出懼光的食人怪龍並趁其目盲殺之；另在水牛之地以計除掉霸占獵物的酋長熊，卻因自家作法失去獸群，最終以更狡猾的詭計擊敗前來復仇的狼群。

sensitivity.note: Passages are condensed paraphrases of two Plateau Coyote tales as retold in Katharine Berry Judson's Myths and Legends of the Pacific Northwest (1910), in the collector's own words. The intended 'Coyote and the Rolling Rock' could not be verified in a successfully fetched public-domain collection, so two canonical Plateau trickster tales from the same verified PD source are substituted ('Coyote and the Dragon', Nez Perce; 'Coyote in the Buffalo Country', Flathead), with tradition kept as 'plateau'. Category 'myth': trickster-etiological folk narratives, not liturgy; Judson's preface states that ceremonial and coarse content was excluded from her selection. No restricted ceremonial content was collected; only published folk-narrative versions are used. Coordinates mark the Nez Perce homeland as a regional reference only, not a story site.

passages.text: A man-eating dragon lived in a cave in the Willamette Valley, slipping out each night to seize and devour the people, who lived in fear of it. Coyote, the shrewdest and most cunning of all the animals, resolved to help them. Knowing the monster could not endure daylight, he climbed a mountain when the sun stood high and shot one arrow into the sun, then another into the end of the first, and another still, until a chain of arrows stretched from sky to earth. He pulled hard and dragged the sun down, hiding it in the Willamette River. Thinking night had come, the dragon crept out to attack the people; Coyote then broke the chain, the sun leapt back into the sky, and the blinded monster was killed. When white settlers later carried off the creature's great bones, the storytellers said, evil would come of it.

Starving after his travels, Coyote heard Eagle mock that the buffalo country was closed to so poor a creature. Determined to prove otherwise, he walked fifteen days to a great camp near the falls, where the unpopular chief Bear kept the fat and good meat of every buffalo kill for himself. Coyote killed a buffalo and, playing host, wrapped a red-hot stone in fat and fed it to Bear, killing him; the grateful people made Coyote chief. Because the slain Bear had been a powerful medicine-man who had willed the herds to remain, all the buffalo vanished once Coyote ruled. Fleeing in shame, Coyote played dead on a trail, was thrown among a traveller's meat, and gorged himself; he then tricked Wolf into trying the same ruse, and the suspicious man clubbed Wolf nearly to death. Wolf gathered Bear and Mole for revenge, but Coyote, dressed like a great chief and aided by Cat and Dog, killed them all.

title.en: Loki Cuts Sif's Hair: Loki's Wager with the Dwarfs
title.zh: 洛基剪斷西芙的頭髮：與矮人的賭注

region.en: Asgard - mythic Scandinavia (neutral marker, central Sweden)
region.zh: 阿斯加德——神話中的斯堪地那維亞（座標為瑞典中部的中性標記）

period: Prose Edda c. 1220 CE; trans. Rasmus B. Anderson (1879)

source.work: Snorri Sturluson, 'The Younger Edda' (Prose Edda), tr. Rasmus B. Anderson (1879), Skáldskaparmál: 'Loke's Wager with the Dwarfs', eBook #18947

summary.en: Loki's mischief and amends: after craftily cutting off Sif's hair, he saves himself from Thor's wrath by having dwarfs forge living hair of gold, the ship Skidbladnir, and Odin's spear. He then bets his head that Brok and Sindri can match those gifts, and though the fly-tormented Brok falters once, the boar Gullinbursti, the ring Draupnir, and the hammer Mjolnir are produced — with the hammer judged the best treasure.
summary.zh: 洛基的惡作劇與補償：他偷剪西芙金髮，為免雷神之怒，讓矮人打造可生長的黃金髮、神船斯希布拉尼爾與奧丁長槍；又以自己的頭打賭布洛克兄弟的手藝，忍受化身蒼蠅的洛基干擾，鍛出黃金野豬、德羅普尼爾指環與雷神之鎚妙爾尼爾，眾神裁定鐵鎚為最上品。

sensitivity.note: Passages are condensed paraphrases of the Skáldskaparmál section 'Loke's Wager with the Dwarfs' as rendered in Anderson's 1879 public-domain translation, in the collector's own words. Classified as 'myth': mythological narrative from Snorri's thirteenth-century handbook of poetics, not a devotional text. Coordinates are a neutral inland-Scandinavia marker because Asgard is a mythic locus rather than a real place. The fly that torments Brok is identified as Loki in disguise, and the account closes on the gifts and the gods' judgment rather than on Loki's later punishment.

passages.text: Loki, in a mean prank, craftily cut off all of Sif's hair. When Thor discovered it, he seized the trickster and would have broken every bone in his body; Loki saved himself by swearing an oath that the dark elves would forge for Sif golden hair that would grow like natural hair. He went to the dwarf brothers called Ivald's sons, who in their smithy made three treasures: the golden hair for Sif, which would grow as soon as it touched her head; the ship Skidbladnir, which always found a fair wind wherever its owner wished to sail and could be folded like a napkin and carried in a pocket; and Odin's spear Gungnir, which would never miss its mark.

Loki then staked his own head with the dwarf Brok on a bet that Brok's brother Sindri could not forge three treasures equally fine. While Sindri worked the furnace, a fly — Loki in disguise — stung Brok, who worked the bellows: first his hand, then his neck, and at last between his eyes, where blood ran down and blurred his sight so that for a single instant he let go the bellows. From the forge came the golden-bristled boar Gullinbursti, which runs through air and sea and lights the darkest night; the ring Draupnir, which every ninth night drips eight new rings of equal weight; and the hammer Mjolnir, which never misses, always returns to the hand, and shrinks small enough to hide in one's bosom, its only flaw a rather short handle. The gods judged the hammer the best of all the treasures and the dwarf the winner of the wager.

title.en: Anansi Outwits Tiger: Tying Tiger and the Sheep-skin Suit
title.zh: 阿南西戲勝老虎：縛虎與羊皮套裝

region.en: Jamaica - Mandeville and surrounding country districts
region.zh: 牙買加——曼德維爾及其周邊鄉村地區

period: recorded 1919/1921 from Jamaican storytellers; published 1924 (Beckwith, Jamaica Anansi Stories)

source.work: Martha Warren Beckwith, 'Jamaica Anansi Stories', Memoirs of the American Folk-Lore Society vol. XVII (1924) — 'Tying Tiger: The Fish-basket' and 'Tiger's Sheep-skin Suit' (both told by George Parkes of Mandeville)

summary.en: Jamaican spider stories taken down by Martha Warren Beckwith from named storytellers. Anansi repays Tiger for robbing his magically caught fish by tying the dozing bully to a tree with his own hair, leaving him to a hunter; and in a second tale he frames the same Tiger, dressed in a sheepskin suit, for the sheep thefts Anansi himself committed, winning the reward and the master's daughter.
summary.zh: 貝克威思從牙買加說書人筆錄的蜘蛛故事：阿南西的魚獲被老虎強奪後，趁其打盹以長髮將其縛在樹上，任由獵人處置；另一則中他又把偷羊罪行設計到身穿羊皮套裝的老虎身上，老虎被定罪，阿南西贏得賞金與主人的女兒。

sensitivity.note: Passages are condensed paraphrases of Beckwith's transcribed tales 'Tying Tiger: The Fish-basket' and 'Tiger's Sheep-skin Suit' (both narrated by George Parkes of Mandeville), with the vernacular rendered into standard modern English in the collector's own words; no sentences are copied verbatim and no incidents are invented. Category 'myth' (folk narrative): Beckwith identifies Anansi as the culture hero of the Gold Coast remembered in Jamaican wake-night entertainment; these are social amusement tales, not restricted ceremonial or obeah material — the sorcery 'Old Stories' matter was avoided in favor of plain animal trickster tales. The remembered 'Anansi wins all the stories' theme is represented through the trickster-defeats-Tiger contests in this verified source. Coordinates mark Mandeville, Jamaica, where these variants were recorded.

passages.text: In a season of hunger, the spider Anansi went to the sea-shore with pot and basket, made a fire, and commanded the fish by magic — big fish come, little fish go, then the reverse — until pot and basket were full. He cooked and ate his fill, but on the road home he met the bully Tiger, who demanded the basket and ate every fish, spitting out the bones that Anansi humbly gnawed while murmuring about his wasted labor. Anansi began at once to scheme. Praising a wayside fruit tree, he coaxed Tiger beneath it, then offered to pick the lice from Tiger's long head-hair, and while Tiger dozed Anansi lashed the hair round the trunk, tying him fast like a hog. Anansi danced away singing of it, and a hunter who found the trapped Tiger killed him.

Hired to mind Mr. Mighty's flock of two thousand sheep, Anansi stole them one by one until only a single animal remained. His master promised his best daughter and two hundred pounds to whoever could explain how the sheep were lost, and Anansi, who could fiddle, proposed a ball. He dressed his friend Tiger from cap to boots in a sheepskin suit, telling him that when the music sang 'Mister Mighty lost him sheep — it stands like a Tiger thief,' the song mocked some other Tiger from far country. Anansi then played the tune himself, denounced the sheepskin-clad musician as the very thief who had skinned the sheep to clothe himself, and Tiger, seized and convicted, drew ten years in prison, while Anansi collected the money and the daughter in marriage.

title.en: How the Tinguian Learned to Plant
title.zh: 丁桂安人如何學會耕種

region.en: Abra Province, northwestern Luzon, Philippines (Tinguian homeland)
region.zh: 菲律賓呂宋島西北部阿布拉省（丁桂安人故地）

period: collected c. 1903-1908 among the Tinguian; published 1916 (Cole, Philippine Folk Tales)

source.work: Mabel Cook Cole (comp.), 'Philippine Folk Tales', A.C. McClurg, 1916 — Group I (Tinguian): 'How the Tinguian Learned to Plant', eBook #12814

summary.en: A Tinguian origin story of agriculture and healing. The sky spirit Kaboniyan, sent by the Great Spirit Kadaklan, enters the ailing woman Dayapan as she bathes at a spring, gives her rice and sugar-cane, and teaches her planting, harvest, storage and the Sayung ceremony; because the dog then kills the ceremonial cock, some of the sick will die while others recover, and rice-planting passes from her to the people.
summary.zh: 丁桂安人的農耕起源故事：天神卡達克蘭見族人飢病無醫，派使者卡博尼揚下凡，在病了七年的婦人達雅潘沐浴時進入她體內，賜予稻米與甘蔗，教導種植、收貯與Sayung治病儀式；因狗殺雞的徵兆，從此有人病癒有人死亡，耕種之法由達雅潘代代相傳。

sensitivity.note: Passages are condensed paraphrases of 'How the Tinguian Learned to Plant' as retold by Mabel Cook Cole in Philippine Folk Tales (1916), in the compiler's own words; nothing quoted verbatim and no elements added. Category 'myth' rather than 'religious': although the tale narrates the spirit-granted origin of the Sayung healing ceremony and rice-planting, it is a short folk etiological narrative as published for general readers; the rite is named and framed only, not described in operational detail, and no restricted ceremonial knowledge is reproduced. Coordinates mark the Abra river valley of northwestern Luzon, the Tinguian homeland, as a regional reference.

passages.text: In the very old times the Tinguian knew nothing of planting or harvest, gathering only wild forest foods and fish, and they had no way to cure sickness caused by the evil spirits, so many died who might have lived. Kadaklan, the Great Spirit who dwells in the sky, saw their hunger and sickness and sent his servant Kaboniyan down to teach them. In Caalang lived Dayapan, a woman who had been ill for seven years; bathing one day at the spring, she felt a spirit enter her body, bringing rice and sugar-cane. He told her to plant them, to reap and store the rice in a granary, to press the cane, and to hold the ceremony called Sayung, promising she would be well; and entering her again as she planted, the spirit showed her exactly what to do.

When Dayapan had reaped the first rice and cane, she made the Sayung ceremony as the spirit directed, and when it was finished and her sickness gone, he told her to bathe in the river, tying a dog and a cock near the water as a sign that the rite was complete. While she bathed, the dog killed and ate the cock. Dayapan wept until Kaboniyan came and explained the omen: had the cock lived, no person would die when the ceremony was made, but now some of the sick would recover and some would die. She called the people together and taught them everything the spirit had shown her; seeing that she was healed, they believed, and ever since the Tinguian have planted rice and cane each year, while Dayapan treated the sick as she had been taught.

title.en: When the Ravens Could Speak (with The Raven and the Goose)
title.zh: 當渡鴉還會說話時（附：渡鴉與鵝）

region.en: South-East Greenland (Angmagssalik/Ammassalik district)
region.zh: 格陵蘭東南部（昂馬沙利克地區）

period: collected by Knud Rasmussen; published 1921 (Gyldendal), English by W. J. A. Worster

source.work: Knud Rasmussen (ed.), 'Eskimo Folk-Tales', rendered into English by W. J. Alexander Worster, Gyldendal, 1921 — 'When the Ravens could speak' and 'The Raven and the Goose' (South-East Greenland tales; eBook #28932)

summary.en: Two very short Greenlandic pourquoi tales from Rasmussen's collection. Ravens once could talk, but always said the opposite of what they meant, until an old man magically took their speech away, leaving only shrieking; in the companion tale the raven's rude impatience while being painted by the goose leaves it black all over.
summary.zh: 兩則格陵蘭短篇起源故事：渡鴉曾能說話，總是口是心非，被怒老人設法收回說話之能，從此只會嘶啞啼叫；姊妹篇中，渡鴉嫌棄鵝為其鳥羽畫上的花紋，激怒的鵝索性將其潑成一身黑，這便是渡鴉烏黑羽毛的由來。

sensitivity.note: Passages are condensed paraphrases of two short tales from Knud Rasmussen's Eskimo Folk-Tales (1921), rendered into English by W. J. A. Worster, in the collector's own words. Because 'When the Ravens could speak' is only a few lines long, a second passage is drawn, as permitted, from the same verified public-domain book ('The Raven and the Goose', same source region); the book's notes place both tales among the South-East Greenland stories. Category 'myth' (folk narrative): brief etiological entertainments of the winter story-telling repertoire, not ceremonial or shamanic material. Coordinates mark the Angmagssalik (Ammassalik) district of East Greenland, the named source region.

passages.text: Once, long ago, the ravens could talk — but their words carried the opposite of their meaning. Whenever they wished to thank someone, they spoke abuse, so that everything they said was the reverse of what they meant, a whole speech of lies. One day, the story goes, an old man came and, by magical means, took their power of speech away altogether, and since that time ravens can do nothing but shriek. Yet their nature was not changed along with their language: the storyteller adds that ravens remain to this day an ill-tempered, lying, thieving lot of birds.

A second short tale explains the raven's color. In the days when all the birds were receiving their colours and the patterns of their coats, the raven and the goose met and agreed to paint one another. The raven went first, giving the goose a fine black coat with a pleasing white pattern showing between, and the goose found it very beautiful. But when the goose began painting the raven a coat exactly like its own, the raven fell into a rage, declaring the pattern frightfully ugly; and the goose, offended by all this fuss, simply splashed the raven black all over. That, says the teller, is why the raven is so dull and black in colour.

title.en: Demeter and Persephone: The Homeric Hymn to Demeter and the Eleusinian Mysteries
title.zh: 得墨忒耳與珀耳塞福涅：德墨忒耳頌歌與厄琉息斯秘儀

region.en: Eleusis, Attica, Greece
region.zh: 希臘阿提卡厄琉息斯

period: Homeric Hymn 2 composed 7th-6th c. BCE; principal MS: Leiden, University Library 33 H (15th c.); Eleusinian cult attested c. 750-550 BCE onward

source.archive: Center for Hellenic Studies / Perseus Digital Library
source.work: Homeric Hymns 2 (To Demeter), trans. H. G. Evelyn-White, Loeb, 1914; ed. N. J. Richardson, Oxford 1974

summary.en: Persephone is seized by Hades with Zeus's consent; her mother Demeter halts all growth until Zeus negotiates a two-thirds/one-third division of the year; the goddess founds the Eleusinian Mysteries, whose initiates were promised a better lot after death.
summary.zh: 哈得斯得宙斯默許擄走珀耳塞福涅；得墨忒耳憤而令五穀不生，宙斯遂斡旋，女兒一年三分之二在世、三分之一居冥府；女神創立厄琉息斯秘儀，許入儀者身後得福。

sensitivity.note: Ancient cult text; the Eleusinian Mysteries' secret rituale is lost — only public literary versions survive. Nothing restricted is reproduced. [Merged 2026-11-11: the entry 'hymn-demeter' (Homeric Hymn 2, trans. Evelyn-White 1914, Theoi Classical Texts Library, https://www.theoi.com/Text/HomericHymns1.html — verbatim passages on the rape of Persephone and the reunion with Demeter) was folded in as passages 3-4 and the duplicate entry removed; motif world-renewal comes from the folded material.]

passages.text: I begin to sing of rich-haired Demeter, awful goddess — of her and her slim-ankled daughter, whom Aidoneus rapt away, given to him by all-seeing Zeus the loud-thunderer. Condensed paraphrase of Hymn 371-394: Hades secretly gives Persephone a pomegranate seed to eat, binding her to return; Zeus dispatches Rhea, and mother and daughter are reconciled — one third of the year below with her dark lord, two thirds above with her mother and the other immortals. Not verbatim.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Hymn 371-394; not verbatim.

passages.text: He caught her up reluctant on his golden car and bare her away lamenting. Then she cried out shrilly with her voice, calling upon her father, the Son of Cronos, who is most high and excellent. But no one, either of the deathless gods or of mortal men, heard her voice, nor yet the olive-trees bearing rich fruit: only tender-hearted Hecate, bright-coiffed, the daughter of Persaeus, heard the girl from her cave, and the lord Helios, Hyperion's bright son, as she cried to her father, the Son of Cronos. But he was sitting aloof, apart from the gods, in his temple where many pray, and receiving sweet offerings from mortal men. So he, that Son of Cronos, of many names, who is Ruler of Many and Host of Many, was bearing her away by leave of Zeus on his immortal chariot — his own brother's child and all unwilling.

But while Demeter was still holding her dear child in her arms, her heart suddenly misgave her for some snare, so that she feared greatly and ceased fondling her daughter and asked of her at once: "My child, tell me, surely you have not tasted any food while you were below? Speak out and hide nothing, but let us both know. For if you have not, you shall come back from loathly Hades and live with me and your father, the dark-clouded Son of Cronos and be honoured by all the deathless gods; but if you have tasted food, you must go back again beneath the secret places of the earth, there to dwell a third part of the seasons every year: yet for the two parts you shall be with me and the other deathless gods.

canonical_translation: H. G. Evelyn-White, Homeric Hymns, Loeb 57 (1914); scholarly translation in Helene P. Foley, The Homeric Hymn to Demeter (Princeton, 1994)

narrative.en:
The Hymn (495 dactylic lines) is the fullest continuous Greek narrative of abduction, grief, and negotiated return.

THE ABDUCTION. Persephone, daughter of Demeter, is playing with the daughters of Okeanos, gathering flowers — roses, crocuses, violets, iris, hyacinth — on the Nysian plain. Earth, at Zeus's secret instruction, produces a marvelous narcissus as a snare. As the girl reaches for it, the earth opens; Hades bursts out on his deathless horses, seizes her, and carries her wailing down through the gates of the west. She cries to her father and to the immortals, but no voice heeds her except Hekate's, who hears from her cave with torches lit, and Helios, who sees all and later tells Demeter the truth: the abduction was not the kidnapper's plan alone but Zeus's gift to his brother.

THE GRIEF. For nine days Demeter wanders with flaming torches, neither eating nor washing. Hekate runs to meet her, but can only tell what she heard. From Helios Demeter learns the full crime; furious at the gods, she withdraws from Olympos and comes to Eleusis in the guise of an old woman, sitting in sorrow by the 'maiden's well' (the Parthenion). The daughters of Keleos, lord of Eleusis, find her and lead her to their mother Metaneira; the disguised goddess nurses the infant Demophoon, secretly anointing him with ambrosia and burning away his mortality in the hearth at night — she would make him ageless, a god. Metaneira, spying at night, screams and breaks the ritual: the child cannot now be immortal. Demeter reveals herself, demands a temple and altar at Eleusis, and withdraws her rites.

THE FAMINE. In wrath against Zeus, Demeter 'who brings the seasons' destroys the year's seed; the oxen drag useless ploughs; the whole race of men would have perished of famine, and the gods would have lost their honours and sacrifices. Zeus sends Iris, then one by one all the gods, bearing gifts; Demeter will not lift the curse until she sees her daughter with her own eyes. Zeus therefore sends Hermes to Hades, who agrees — but smilingly, as Persephone is about to ascend, gives her a pomegranate seed to eat, 'secretly and deliberately', so that she must return to him for a third of each year.

THE SETTLEMENT AND END. Mother and daughter embrace; Demeter, learning of the seed, accepts the arrangement. Through the stern command of Rhea, sent down from Olympos by Zeus, the goddesses are reconciled: Persephone spends two-thirds of the revolving year with her mother and the immortals, one-third below; the earth's increase returns, and Demeter restores abundance to the ploughlands. She then returns to Olympos, but first she calls the princes of Eleusis — Triptolemos, Diokles, Eumolpos, and Keleos — and shows them her rites, 'awful mysteries which none may transgress, pry into, or utter; for deep awe of the gods checks the voice'. Blessed is the mortal who has seen them, the Hymn ends: the initiate shares a better lot below; the uninitiated, dying, gets the opposite.

FUNCTIONS. The narrative is the charter myth of the Eleusinian Mysteries, the panhellenic cult whose initiates (from across the Greek world, including slaves and women) swore ritual secrecy; it structures the women's Thesmophoria festival at Athens (which re-enacted fasts and used pig-offerings aitiologically); it explains the agricultural year as a mother-daughter rhythm; it gives Greek marriage its anthropological image — a daughter 'abducted' with paternal consent into the husband's house; and, uniquely among public Greek texts, it attaches eschatological reward to initiatory knowledge. The secret dramatization at Eleusis (reconstructed from archaeology and later Christian polemic) is lost and must not be confounded with the Hymn.
narrative.zh: 珀耳塞福涅與大洋女兒們在尼薩原野採花，大地按宙斯密令生出奇妙水仙為餌；哈得斯裂地而出，攜女入冥，唯赫卡忒聞聲、赫利俄斯見事。得墨忒耳執火炬遍尋九日，怒離奧林波斯，化身老嫗至厄琉息斯王家，哺乳嬰兒得謨福翁，欲以夜火焚其凡性；母后撞破，女神現真身，命建廟。遂降饑饉，牲祭絕於諸神。宙斯屢遣使不得，乃命赫爾墨斯赴冥府；哈得斯微笑授石榴籽一粒，女遂須每年歸冥三月。瑞亞降旨和解：女居上界三分之二，下界三分之一；五穀復生。女神召厄琉息斯諸王子，授以『不可窺、不可傳』之奧儀；入儀者身後得福，未入者不然。秘儀儀程今已失傳，文獻所存僅此公開敘事。

functions: Charter myth of the Eleusinian Mysteries (initiatory secrecy and afterlife promise)
Aitia for the Thesmophoria and the agricultural cycle
Cultural model of marriage-as-abduction under paternal consent
Rare public Greek eschatology: differential fate of initiates and non-initiates

variants.name: Orphic version (Zagreus-Dionysos and Persephone's line)
variants.text_tradition: Orphic fragments (e.g. OF 58, 299 Bernabe); Derveni Papyrus; late antique Neoplatonist citations
variants.summary: In Orphic theology Persephone mates with Zeus and bears Dionysos Zagreus, who is dismembered by Titans; humankind, born from the Titans' ashes, carries both Titanic guilt and Dionysian essence — a descent-and-restoration soteriology rather than a seasonal myth.

variants.name: Arcadian 'Despoina' cult (Lykosoura)
variants.text_tradition: Pausanias, Description of Greece 8.37-38 (2nd c. CE)
variants.summary: A closely parallel mystery cult of Demeter and an unnamed daughter ('Despoina', 'the Mistress') with Artemis and Anytos; the child of Demeter and Poseidon in horse-form. Shows the Eleusinian story is one local, panhellenized form of a wider family of mother-daughter mysteries.

variants.name: Sicilian and South Italian versions
variants.text_tradition: Pindar, fragments; Diodorus Siculus 5.2-5; coin iconography of Enna
variants.summary: Persephone is carried off near Enna/Henna in Sicily's lake meadow, and the island claims the rape and the foundation of cult; Diodorus (himself Sicilian) renders the myth as an allegory of the grain cycle. Underwrites strong Sicilian/Italian mystery cults of Persephone and Dionysos.

variants.name: Thesmophoria liturgical narrative
variants.text_tradition: Athenian women's festival (attested by scholia to Lucian, Dialogue of the Courtesans 2.1; Aristophanes, Thesmophoriazusae)
variants.summary: The women's festival preserves the ritual sequence the Hymn reflects — fasting, obscenity (iambe's jokes), piglets thrown into pits whose rot is mixed with seed-corn — narratively reorganized as Demeter's search, grief, and restoration.

primary_sources.citation: Lines 1-19 (abduction); 61-89 (loss and Helios' revelation); 180-211 (Eleusis and Metaneira); 231-258 (the famine); 304-313, 334-369 (pomegranate seed); 370-386 (settlement); 439-495 (foundation of the Mysteries). Principal MS: Leiden, Universiteitsbibliotheek 33 H, 15th c. Standard edition: N. J. Richardson, The Homeric Hymn to Demeter, Oxford 1974.

primary_sources.work: Pausanias, Description of Greece (Lykosoura and Eleusis sections)
primary_sources.citation: 8.37.1-9 (Despoina mysteries); 1.38.5-9 (Eleusis; the secret 'the rhetor Hierokles said was unlawful to reveal'). Translation W. H. S. Jones, Loeb, 1918-1935.

secondary_sources.work: Helene P. Foley, The Homeric Hymn to Demeter: Translation, Commentary, and Interpretive Essays
secondary_sources.citation: Foley 1994, Princeton University Press — text, translation, and the major interpretive essays (marriage, agriculture, initiatory eschatology).

secondary_sources.work: Kevin Clinton, 'The Sanctuary of Demeter and Kore at Eleusis'
secondary_sources.citation: Clinton 1992, in Greek Sanctuaries: New Approaches (Routledge); with his The Sacred Officials of the Eleusinian Mysteries (Philadelphia 1974) — epigraphic reconstruction of the cult's officials and calendar.

source_urls.description: Perseus Digital Library — Evelyn-White translation of the Homeric Hymns (search 'Homeric Hymns')
