title.en: Heracles: Madness, the Twelve Labors, and Apotheosis
title.zh: 赫拉克勒斯：瘋癲、十二勞役與成神

region.en: Tiryns / Mycenae, Argolid, Greece (symbolic pin for the pan-Hellenic cycle)
region.zh: 希臘阿爾戈利斯提任斯／邁錫尼（泛希臘神話圈象徵性定位）

period: Cycle attested from 8th-7th c. BCE epics; coherent prose retelling in Apollodorus' Bibliotheca 2.4.12-2.7.7 (1st-2nd c. CE; principal MS: Laurentianus 66, 4, 14th c.)

source.work: Apollodorus, The Library 2.4-2.7 (trans. J. G. Frazer, Loeb 121, 1921)

summary.en: Driven mad by Hera, Heracles kills his own family; to expiate, he serves Eurystheus and performs twelve labors — lion, hydra, hind, boar, stables, birds, bull, mares, belt, cattle, apples, Cerberus — then dies on Oeta's pyre and is taken up to Olympos.
summary.zh: 赫拉所遣瘋癲之下，赫拉克勒斯手刃親族；為贖罪服侍歐律斯透斯，歷十二勞役——獅、蛇、鹿、豬、牛廄、鳥、牛、母馬、腰帶、牛群、金蘋果、三頭犬——終於俄塔山火中成神。

sensitivity.note: Ancient literary material; classification 'myth' (not 'religious') because Heracles' cult-cycle narrative circulated as heroic legend; note reasoning per README. [Merged 2026-11-11: the earlier entry 'heracles-labors' (Bulfinch, The Age of Fable, 1855, Project Gutenberg eBook #3327 — condensed paraphrase of the Nemean lion and Lernaean hydra labors) was folded in as passages 3-4 and the duplicate entry removed.]

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase of Apollodorus 2.4.12-2.5.1: Hera sends a madness in which Heracles hurls his children (and Megara's) into the fire; when the fit passes, he seeks purification from Delphi, where the Pythia renames him 'Glory of Hera' (Herakles) and orders him to serve Eurystheus for twelve years and perform whatever labors he is commanded. Not verbatim.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Apollodorus 2.4.12-2.5.1; not verbatim.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase of Apollodorus 2.6.2-2.7.7: to fetch the golden apples of the Hesperides Heracles holds up the sky for Atlas, who fetches the fruit; to bring the hound Cerberus up from Hades he wrestles the shade of Meleager and frees Theseus, then presents the dog to the terrified Eurystheus, who returns it to the underworld. Not verbatim.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Apollodorus 2.6.2-2.7.7; not verbatim.

passages.text: Heracles, born to Zeus and the mortal woman Alcmene, drew the lasting hostility of Zeus's wife, who persecuted him from the cradle onward. Through her contrivance he was placed under the authority of his cousin Eurystheus and made to obey whatever that cousin commanded — a chained series of desperate feats the later ages counted as the twelve labors. The first task was to strip the skin from a monstrous lion that was ravaging the valley of Nemea. When club blows and arrows proved useless against the beast's hide, Heracles closed with it and throttled it with his bare hands. He then brought the whole carcass back on his shoulders; Eurystheus, so shaken by this proof of the hero's strength, ordered that future reports be delivered outside the town walls.

The next commission was to destroy the Hydra, which laid waste the countryside of Argos from its lair in a swamp near the well of Amymone. The creature had nine heads, and the middle one could not be killed; its defense was self-renewal, for with every head Heracles cut away, two sprang up in its place. The task became possible only through teamwork — his faithful servant Iolaus burned away each severed stump so no new heads could rise, and the one immortal head was finally buried beneath a massive rock. Even this victory brought him no lasting peace; harder labors, from the Augean stables to the golden apples of the Hesperides, still lay ahead.

canonical_translation: J. G. Frazer, Apollodorus: The Library, Loeb 121-122 (1921)

narrative.en:
BEGINNING. Zeus fathers Herakles on Alkmene while impersonating her husband Amphitryon; Hera, jealous from birth, sends two serpents to strangle the infant, who strangles them instead. Herakles marries Megara, daughter of King Kreon of Thebes, and has children. Hera now strikes him with madness (as dramatized in Euripides' Herakles): in the fit he kills Megara and his sons, and some accounts add his brother Iphikles' children. When sanity returns, the seer, priestess at Delphi (the Pythia), and oracle together impose expiation: he must go to Tiryns, call himself by the name 'Herakles' ('Glory of Hera' — the etymology records the goddess's paradoxical ownership of the hero), and serve the king Eurystheus for twelve years, performing whatever labors are commanded, after which he will become immortal.

THE TWELVE LABORS. (1) The Nemean lion, invulnerable to iron, he strangles and wears its skin; Eurystheus thereafter hides in a bronze jar. (2) The Lernaean hydra, whose heads regrow when cut — with his nephew Iolaos he burns each neck-stump, buries the immortal head under a rock, and dips his arrows in the gall; Eurystheus disallows the labor because of the helper. (3) The Ceryneian hind with golden horns, sacred to Artemis, chased for a year and taken alive. (4) The Erymanthian boar, driven into deep snow and carried back alive. (5) The stables of Augeias, cleaned in a day by diverting the rivers Alpheios and Peneios — denied payment, he sacked Elis; this labor too was disallowed (he demanded wages). (6) The Stymphalian birds, bronze-feathered, driven from the marsh by Athena's rattle and shot down. (7) The Cretan bull, father (by Pasiphae) of the Minotaur, brought alive to Eurystheus and released to wander Marathon. (8) The man-eating mares of Diomedes of Thrace, fed their master to tame them. (9) The war-belt of the Amazon queen Hippolyte — taken (in most versions) after a treacherous brawl. (10) The cattle of the three-bodied Geryon at the far west, past the Pillars he sets up (Gibraltar/Ceuta), driving the herd home through Italy, where cattle-thieves and giants are killed along the way. (11) The golden apples of the Hesperides in Atlas' garden: he holds the sky while Atlas fetches them, tricks the Titan into taking the burden back, and brings the apples to Eurystheus, who returns them to the Hesperides; on the way he frees the chained Prometheus (whose advice steers the episode). (12) Kerberos: he descends at Taenarum, learns courtesy from the shades (Meleager's story of Atalanta; the freeing of Theseus, who is stuck fast), wrestles the hound with bare hands, and brings it up — Eurystheus leaps into his jar, and the hound goes back below.

AFTERMATH AND END. Freed labors, Herakles continues parerga: rescues Hesione at Troy, sacks Pylos, fights the river-god Acheloos for Deianira, and crosses the world in chains of service to Omphale at Sardis. Deianira, jealous, heedlessly sends him a robe soaked in the centaur Nessos' poisoned blood (as Sophocles' Trachiniae dramatizes); it burns his flesh. He builds his own pyre on Mount Oita, and Philoktetes lights it for the reward of the bow. The mortal part burns away; the divine part ascends: Hera reconciles (in late versions by nursing him), and Herakles marries Hebe on Olympos, while the image of the dead hero is worshipped in temples as Herakles the god (Heraikles). Eurystheus, outlived, is defeated by the Herakleidai, his descendants' return aition for the Dorian settlements.

FUNCTIONS. The cycle makes Herakles the panhellenic culture-hero: monster-slayer who clears land, sea, and the edges of the world for colonization (his routes map Greek trade to Gades, the Pontos, and Africa); founder of the Olympic games and of royal genealogies (the Herakleidai); the paradigmatic human who by toil (ponoi) wins immortality — the ideological bridge between mortal suffering and divine reward, ritually echoed at his shrines and in sympotic song.
narrative.zh: 宙斯化形近阿爾克墨涅而生赫拉克勒斯；赫拉自襁褓即遣蛇加害，後遣瘋癲使英雄殺妻兒。得諭示：往提任斯服歐律斯透斯十二年，行其所命之勞役，方可成神。遂歷十二役：一扼涅墨亞獅；二焚九頭蛇許德拉；三獲刻呂涅亞金角鹿；四擒厄律曼托斯野豬；五一日清奧革阿斯牛廄；六驅斯廷法利斯怪鳥；七縛克里特公牛；八馴色雷斯食人馬；九取亞馬孫女王腰帶；十驅革律翁紅牛過西極；十一代阿特拉斯擎天取赫斯珀里得斯金蘋果；十二自塔納隆下冥府擒三頭犬刻耳柏洛斯。後因涅索斯毒血之衣，於俄塔山自焚；凡軀燼滅，神性升天，娶赫柏，受享廟祀。此圈將英雄塑為清辟妖獸、開疆拓土之文化英雄，兼奧林匹亞賽會創立者、多利安諸王族始祖，並示『以勞致不死者』之範型。

functions: Panhellenic culture-hero cycle: clearing the world of monsters and aitiologizing colonization routes
Founding myth for the Olympic games and Dorian royal genealogies (Herakleidai)
Paradigm of mortal toil rewarded with immortality; ideology of expiation after pollution

variants.name: Peisandros of Rhodes, Heracleia (epic, c. 600 BCE)
variants.text_tradition: Fragmentary epic, PEG (Kinkel) frags.; papyrus scraps
variants.summary: The earliest fixed twelve-labor sequence, cited (Pausanias 9.11.2) as the reason the labors are now counted twelve; survives only in fragments, so the sequence is partly reconstructed from citation.

variants.name: Sophocles, Trachiniae
variants.summary: Retells the ending through Deianira's tragedy: the Nessos robe, Heracles' agony on Oita, and the apotheosis left offstage — foregrounding human error rather than divine plan.

variants.name: Euripides, Herakles
variants.summary: Places the madness-murder after the labors (reversing the chronological order of the prose tradition) and emphasizes Theseus' role in restoring the broken hero — an ethics-of-friendship recasting.

variants.name: Scythian version (Herodotus 4.8-10)
variants.summary: In the Scythian aition Herakles herds Geryon's cattle through the northern steppe, fathers Skythes on a half-serpent local goddess, and the triple sons' bow-test founds the Skythian royal line — a colonizing appropriation of the Greek cycle.

primary_sources.citation: 2.4.12 (madness and service); 2.5.1-2.5.12 (labors 1-12); 2.6.1-2.7.7 (parerga, Deianira, pyre); principal MS Laurentianus 66, 4 (14th c.); trans. J. G. Frazer, Loeb 121, 1921 (Perseus Digital Library).
Sophocles Trachiniae 551-1282 (Nessos robe and pyre), trans. R. C. Jebb (Cambridge, public domain); Euripides Herakles 922-1015 (madness), trans. various public-domain editions.

secondary_sources.work: Emma Stafford, Herakles
secondary_sources.citation: Stafford 2012, London: Routledge (Gods and Heroes of the Ancient World) — modern synthesis of cycle, cult, and reception.

secondary_sources.work: Walter Burkert, Homo Necans (trans. P. Bing)
secondary_sources.citation: Burkert 1983, Berkeley: University of California Press, ch. 6 — initiatory and ritual reading of the labors.

title.en: Bereshit: The Creation of the World and the Garden of Eden (Genesis 1-3)
title.zh: 創世記：世界之造與伊甸園

region.en: Jerusalem (symbolic pin for the Judean scribal tradition)
region.zh: 耶路撒冷（猶太書寫傳統象徵性定位）

period: Composite text: Priestly account (6th-5th c. BCE), Eden narrative (perhaps 10th-9th c. BCE, 'J'); Hebrew Bible stabilized c. 3rd c. BCE-1st c. CE; principal MS: Leningrad Codex B19a, 1008 CE

source.work: Genesis 1:1-3:24, Biblia Hebraica Stuttgartensia; English: Jewish Publication Society Tanakh 1917

summary.en: Two intertwined accounts: the Priestly seven-day creation by divine speech culminating in the Sabbath, and the Eden narrative of the human of dust, the garden, the tree of knowledge, the serpent, and the expulsion that founds human mortality and toil.
summary.zh: 兩敘事交織：祭司典七日以言造世、以安息日作結；伊甸園敘述摶土之人、知識樹、蛇與逐出——人類勞碌與有死之由來。

sensitivity.note: Canonical scripture of a living tradition. Treated with respect: divine names handled per Jewish convention (the Tetragrammaton is not pronounced; the English renders it 'the LORD'). No liturgical or restricted material is reproduced.

passages.text: In the beginning God created the heaven and the earth. Now the earth was unformed and void, and darkness was upon the face of the deep; and the spirit of God hovered over the face of the waters. And God said: 'Let there be light.' And there was light.

And the LORD God said: 'Behold, the man is become as one of us, to know good and evil; and now, lest he put forth his hand, and take also of the tree of life, and eat, and live for ever.' Therefore the LORD God sent him forth from the garden of Eden, to till the ground from whence he was taken.

canonical_translation: Jewish Publication Society Tanakh (1917), public domain

narrative.en:
The book of Genesis opens with two successively layered creation narratives that Jewish and Christian tradition have read as one continuous story.

ACCOUNT ONE: SEVEN DAYS (PRIESTLY SOURCE, GEN 1:1-2:4a). Before the world there are 'the deep' (tehom) and a waste-and-void earth (tohu va-bohu) swept by a divine wind/spirit — a primordial state of undifferentiated waters rather than a battle. God creates entirely by speech in seven liturgical days. Day one: light, separated from darkness and named Day and Night. Day two: a firmament (raqia) dividing waters above from waters below, named Heaven. Day three: waters gathered so dry land appears (named Earth and Seas), and the earth brings forth vegetation. Day four: the great lights — sun, moon, stars — to rule day and night and mark sacred times. Day five: swarms of living creatures in sea and air, blessed 'be fruitful and multiply'. Day six: land animals, and finally humanity — male and female together — made 'in the image and likeness of God' (selem u-demut) and given dominion over the creatures and seed-bearing plants for food. Day seven: God rests from all the work, blesses the seventh day and sanctifies it — the institution of the Sabbath and the theological signature of the Priestly telling. The account closes with the formula that these are 'the generations of the heavens and of the earth when they were created'.

ACCOUNT TWO: EDEN (GEN 2:4b-3:24). A second, older narrative begins with the day the LORD God (YHWH-Elohim) made earth and heaven: no plant yet grew, for there was no rain and no man to till the ground. God forms the human (ha-adam) from dust of the ground (adamah) — a deliberate wordplay — breathes into his nostrils the breath of life, and plants a garden in Eden watered by four rivers. The human is placed there 'to till it and to keep it', permitted every tree except the tree of the knowledge of good and evil, 'for in the day that thou eatest thereof thou shalt surely die'. God then observes 'it is not good that the man should be alone'; the animals are named (no helper found among them), and God casts a deep sleep, takes one side/rib, and builds the woman. The man's exclamation ('bone of my bones, flesh of my flesh') grounds the narrative's closing comment on marriage, and the pair stand 'naked and not ashamed'.

THE TRANSGRESSION. The serpent, 'more subtle than any beast of the field', asks the woman whether God forbade all the trees; she answers that even touching the forbidden tree means death. The serpent denies the death, promises godlike knowledge, and she eats, giving fruit to her husband. Their eyes open; they sew fig leaves. When they hear God walking in the garden's breeze they hide; questioned, the man blames the woman, the woman the serpent. The judgments are spoken in order: the serpent is cursed to crawl and eat dust, with an enmity announced between its seed and the woman's; the woman gets pain in childbirth and a husband who 'shall rule over thee'; the man gets the cursed ground, thorns, thistles, and bread by the sweat of his face. God clothes them in coats of skins — the first act of mercy — and expels them 'lest he put forth his hand, and take also of the tree of life, and live for ever'. East of Eden, cherubim and a flaming sword turn every way 'to keep the way of the tree of life'. The narrative flows into the birth of Cain and Abel (4:1-16), where the pattern of fraternal violence continues.

FUNCTIONS. The Priestly day-structure sanctifies the Sabbath as creation's climax — the core of Jewish liturgical time; the Eden story aitiologizes human mortality, agricultural toil, the pain of childbirth, the snake's form, and shame; the whole sequence, read in the synagogue from the fall festival cycle onward, grounds Israel's theology of an ordered, spoken creation without combat myth (contrast Enuma Elish, where the sea-goddess is slain).
narrative.zh: 祭司典七日造世：以言創造，光、穹蒼、陸地草木、日月星辰、海空生物、陸獸與人（按神形像造，男與女），第七日安息祝聖。伊甸敘事：耶和華神摶土造人，吹生氣成活魂；置園使耕守，惟知識樹之果不可食。亞當無配，神取其肋骨造夏娃，二人赤身不羞。蛇誘之食，二人目明知羞；神問罪，蛇受咒伏行，女受產痛，男受地詛與汗面糊口；神以皮衣蔽之，恐其復摘生命樹，遂逐出伊甸，遣基路伯與火焰劍守樹。全文功能：安息日之立、人類有死勞碌之釋義、以及與巴比倫爭戰型創世神話對照之『以言造世』神學。

functions: Institution of the Sabbath as liturgical re-enactment of creation's seventh day
Aitia for mortality, toil, childbirth pain, and the serpent's posture
Theological demythologization: creation by word, without combat with the sea
Torah-cycle reading in the synagogue (Bereshit section, annual lectionary)

variants.name: Priestly vs. 'J' doublets
variants.summary: The two accounts differ in divine name, method (speech vs. crafting and breathing), sequence (plants-animal-human vs. human-animals-woman), and setting (world-ocean vs. rainless steppe); source-critical scholarship (Wellhausen onward) reads them as independently composed traditions joined by redactors.

variants.name: Babylonian Enuma Elish parallel
variants.text_tradition: Seven Tablets of Creation (c. 18th-12th c. BCE)
variants.summary: Marduk defeats the sea-dragon Tiamat and builds cosmos from her halves; humanity is made from a rebel god's blood to serve the gods. Genesis shares motifs (waters, firmament-divide, rest of the deity) but removes combat and divine servitude — the sea becomes tehom, 'the deep', an inanimate mass.

variants.name: Combat-myth remnants in poetry
variants.summary: Israelite poetry preserves older dismemberment imagery: God 'breaks the heads of the dragons (tanninim) on the waters' and 'smites Rahab'; later Hebrew literature retains the sea-battle as liturgical metaphor while the Genesis prose account excludes it.

variants.name: Second Temple expansions
variants.text_tradition: 1 Enoch 6-16 (Book of Watchers); Jubilees 2-3 (2nd c. BCE); b. Sanhedrin 38b (rabbinic)
variants.summary: Genesis 6:1-4's 'sons of God' are expanded into the Watchers' descent; Jubilees numbers the days and gives Eden a cultic geography; rabbinic midrash adds the two Adams, the angels' creation debate, and the serpent's role. The MT consonantal text is unchanged in all three.

primary_sources.citation: Biblia Hebraica Stuttgartensia (BHS), ed. K. Elliger and W. Rudolph, Stuttgart 1977; base manuscript: Leningrad Codex B19a (1008 CE). Sections: 1:1-2:4a (P), 2:4b-25 (Eden), 3:1-24 (transgression).
The Holy Scriptures according to the Masoretic Text, Jewish Publication Society of America, Philadelphia 1917, chs. 1-3.

secondary_sources.work: E. A. Speiser, Genesis (Anchor Bible 1)
secondary_sources.citation: Speiser 1964, New York: Doubleday — Mesopotamian parallels (Atrahasis, Enuma Elish) for the creation and Eden materials.

secondary_sources.work: Nahum M. Sarna, The JPS Torah Commentary: Genesis
secondary_sources.citation: Sarna 1989, Philadelphia: Jewish Publication Society — verse-by-verse commentary on the two accounts and their ancient Near Eastern context.

secondary_sources.work: Jon D. Levenson, Creation and the Persistence of Evil
secondary_sources.citation: Levenson 1988, San Francisco: Harper & Row — theological reading of creation vs. combat motifs in Genesis and Psalms.

Mechon-Mamre — parallel Hebrew text and JPS 1917 translation

title.en: The Flood of Noah and the First Covenant (Genesis 6-9)
title.zh: 挪亞洪水與首立之約（創世記六至九章）

region.en: Mount Ararat region (traditional landing; symbolic pin)
region.zh: 亞拉臘山地區（傳統停靠地；象徵性定位）

period: Composite: 'J' flood source and Priestly source joined in exilic/post-exilic redaction; text stabilized c. 5th c. BCE; principal MS: Leningrad Codex B19a, 1008 CE

source.work: Genesis 6:5-9:29, Biblia Hebraica Stuttgartensia; English: JPS Tanakh 1917

summary.en: Human corruption moves God to un-create the world by water; Noah builds the ark, the flood drowns all flesh, and upon the dry land's return God binds an unconditional covenant sealed by the rainbow, founding the renewed human order under the Noachide rules.
summary.zh: 人類敗壞，神以洪水滅世；挪亞造方舟攜生靈得存；地乾之後，神以虹為記立約，並以挪亞七誡重啟人間秩序。

sensitivity.note: Canonical scripture of a living tradition; quoted from public-domain JPS 1917 with standard conventions (Tetragrammaton rendered 'the LORD').

passages.text: I do set My bow in the cloud, and it shall be for a token of a covenant between Me and the earth. And it shall come to pass, when I bring clouds over the earth, and the bow is seen in the cloud, that I will remember My covenant, which is between Me and you and every living creature of all flesh; and the waters shall no more become a flood to destroy all flesh.

Condensed paraphrase of Genesis 7-8: Noah enters the ark with his household and the animals; rain falls forty days and forty nights while the deeps of the great abyss are broken open; the waters prevail fifteen cubits above the mountains, then subside in dated stages until the twenty-seventh day of the second month, when the earth is dry and Noah leads the creatures out. Not verbatim.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Genesis 7-8; not verbatim.

canonical_translation: Jewish Publication Society Tanakh (1917), public domain

narrative.en:
BEGINNING: THE DECREE. The sons of God have taken the daughters of men; giants (Nephilim) are in the land; and 'God saw that the wickedness of man was great, and that every imagination of the thoughts of his heart was only evil continually', so that God 'repents' having made humanity and resolves to destroy 'man, beast, creeping thing, and fowl'. One exception: 'Noah found grace in the eyes of the LORD', a righteous man, 'perfect in his generations', who 'walked with God'. God announces the decree — 'The end of all flesh is come before Me... behold, I will destroy them with the earth' — and commands Noah to build a tebah (ark) of gopher wood, pitched (kaphar) within and without, three hundred cubits long, with rooms, a window, and a door in its side; into it all flesh shall come 'to keep them alive' — the Priestly text specifies one pair of every kind, the older source seven pairs of clean animals and one pair of unclean, a distinction needed for Noah's later sacrifice.

MIDDLE: THE DELUGE. 'In the six hundredth year of Noah's life, in the second month, the seventeenth day of the month' the fountains of the great deep are broken and the windows of heaven opened; rain falls forty days and nights (the older narrative), while the Priestly text tracks the waters rising fifteen cubits over the mountains and prevailing one hundred and fifty days. 'All in whose nostrils was the breath of life... died'; only Noah and those with him remain. The waters subside by dated stages (the ark grounding on Ararat in the seventh month; mountain tops seen in the tenth; the earth dry in the six hundred and first year, twenty-seventh day of the second month). Noah tests the waters first with a raven, then three times with a dove — returning with nothing, then with a freshly plucked olive leaf, then not at all. The double bird test (raven/dove) belongs to the older narrative, the precise calendar to the Priestly; the redactor interlaces both.

END: COVENANT AND RENEWAL. Noah builds an altar and offers burnt offerings of every clean beast and fowl; the LORD smells 'a sweet savour' and vows in his heart: 'I will not again curse the ground any more for man's sake... neither will I again smite any more every thing living, as I have done. While the earth remaineth, seedtime and harvest, and cold and heat, and summer and winter, and day and night shall not cease' (8:21-22). God now blesses Noah and his sons: 'Be fruitful, and multiply, and replenish the earth'; animals fear humanity; meat is permitted but blood forbidden — 'whoso sheddeth man's blood, by man shall his blood be shed, for in the image of God made he man' (9:6). God establishes His covenant (berit) — unconditional, 'with you, and with your seed after you, and with every living creature' — signed by the bow (qeshet) in the cloud: the warrior's weapon hung up, never again to destroy all flesh by flood.

CLOSING EPISODE. Noah plants a vineyard, drinks, lies uncovered in his tent; Ham 'sees his father's nakedness' and reports it; Shem and Japhet cover him walking backward. Waking, Noah curses Canaan, Ham's son, to servitude to Shem and Japhet — the narrative aition grounding the Israelite view of Canaanite peoples and, in the redacted genealogy of ch. 10-11, the table of nations from which Abram will be called.

FUNCTIONS. In Jewish liturgical life the flood section is read annually in the Torah cycle; the Noachide rules (blood prohibition, and in rabbinic expansion seven commands for the children of Noah) become the covenantal frame for humanity at large; the rainbow covenant is the archetype of biblical covenant theology; and the narrative's precise dates regulate a Priestly theology of sacred time. Theologically it re-sets creation — a de-creation and re-creation — with covenant, not combat, subduing the waters.
narrative.zh: 世人敗壞，神命挪亞造歌斐木方舟，內外施松香；潔畜七對、不潔一對俱入舟。二月十七日，深淵泉源裂，天窗洞開，大雨四十晝夜，水漲過山十五肘；凡有生氣者皆滅。水勢漸消：七月十七日舟擱亞拉臘山，十月見山頂，挪亞先放烏鴉，再三放鴿，第三次銜回新橄欖葉，遂知地乾。出舟後築壇獻潔牲為燔祭，耶和華聞馨香，誓言不再因人咒詛地，四時寒暑晝夜永不停息。遂賜福挪亞眾子，准食肉而禁血，凡流人血者必被人流；又立永約，以虹為記，不再以洪水滅凡有血肉者。末尾葡萄園一章釋迦南族受咒之由。功能：會堂年讀經課、挪亞七誡之普世約框架、彩虹約為聖約神學原型。

Archetype of covenant theology; rainbow as divine self-binding
Noachide rules as the covenantal frame for humanity as a whole

variants.name: Source-critical doublets ('J' vs. Priestly)
variants.summary: Two flood narratives differ in animal counts (7 pairs vs. 1 pair), duration (40 days vs. 150+ days), divine name, and motive (sweet savour vs. covenant); the redactor interleaved them verse by verse, a key case of classical source criticism.

variants.name: Old Babylonian Atrahasis
variants.text_tradition: Old Babylonian tablets (c. 17th c. BCE), scribe Ipiq-Aya
variants.summary: The flood is sent to stop human overpopulation/noise, not corruption; the survivor Atrahasis is granted immortality; population-control measures end the story. Shares the ark-announcement formula ('wall, listen'), the sealed boat, and the bird tests.

variants.name: Standard Babylonian Gilgamesh, Tablet XI
variants.summary: Utnapishtim retells the flood to Gilgamesh as a embedded narrative: secret warning through a reed wall, cube-ark, seven days of storm, gods 'gathered like flies', Enlil's rage and blessing. Near-verbatim parallel to Genesis' boat instructions; the raven episode is identical.

variants.name: Sumerian Ziusudra flood
variants.text_tradition: Fragment Nippur tablet Ni 9625 (Old Babylonian copy of Sumerian poem)
variants.summary: The earliest attested Mesopotamian flood: Ziusudra, a pious king, is warned in a dream, rides out the deluge, and is granted eternal life in Dilmun; heavily fragmentary and reconstructed by scholarly restoration.

variants.name: Quranic Nuh narrative
variants.summary: Noah (Nuh) preaches to his people for 950 years; one son refuses the ark and drowns; the arc of prophetic warning replaces covenant legislation. Cross-tradition comparandum for the Islamic corpus.

title.en: Yetziat Mitzrayim: Oppression, Signs, Plagues, and the Sea (Exodus 1-15)
title.zh: 出埃及記：壓迫、神蹟、十災與過海（出埃及記一至十五章）

region.en: Jebel Musa, Sinai (traditional pin for Horeb/Sinai; symbolic)
region.zh: 西奈山傳統地點（象徵性定位）

period: Composite narrative (oldest strata 10th-8th c. BCE; Priestly redaction exilic; final form 5th c. BCE); principal MS: Leningrad Codex B19a, 1008 CE

summary.en: Israel's children are enslaved; Moses is drawn from the Nile, called at the burning bush, and sent back to confront Pharaoh; ten plagues break Pharaoh's resistance, the Passover is instituted, and the sea splits so Israel crosses dry-shod — the founding liberation narrative of Judaism, commemorated every Pesach.
summary.zh: 以色列人為奴；摩西自尼羅河被撈起，於焚而不毀之荊棘蒙召；十災迫法老釋放；逾越節設立，海水分開，以色列人行乾地而過——猶太教之根本解放敘事，年年於逾越節重述。

sensitivity.note: Canonical scripture of a living tradition, retold ritually at the Passover Seder (Haggadah). The Haggadah's rabbinic liturgy is protected material — only the biblical text from public-domain JPS 1917 is quoted.

passages.text: And God said unto Moses: 'I AM THAT I AM'; and He said: 'Thus shalt thou say unto the children of Israel: I AM hath sent me unto you.' Condensed paraphrase of Exodus 14:21-25: Moses stretches his hand over the sea; the LORD drives the water back by a strong east wind all night, and the children of Israel go through on dry ground, the waters a wall on right and left. Pharaoh's chariots pursue; at the morning watch the LORD looks through the pillar of fire and cloud, clogs the wheels, and the sea returns upon the army. Not verbatim.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Exodus 14; not verbatim.

canonical_translation: Jewish Publication Society Tanakh (1917), public domain

narrative.en:
BEGINNING: OPPRESSION AND THE DRAWN CHILD. The sons of Israel multiply in Egypt until 'a new king' who 'knew not Joseph' enslaves them with rigor. Pharaoh orders the Hebrew midwives Shiphrah and Puah to kill every boy; they fear God and defy him, and God 'made them houses'. Pharaoh commands all Egyptians to cast every son into the Nile. A Levite woman hides her son three months, sets him in an ark (tebah — the same word as Noah's) of bulrushes among the reeds; Pharaoh's daughter draws him out and names him Moshe, 'because I drew him out of the water' (Hebrew mashah). Raised at court, Moses kills an Egyptian overseer striking a Hebrew brother, flees to Midian, marries Zipporah daughter of Jethro, and shepherds.

THE CALL. At Horeb, 'the mountain of God', the angel of the LORD appears 'in a flame of fire out of the midst of a bush', which burns without being consumed. God announces: 'I have surely seen the affliction of my people... and am come down to deliver them', sending Moses to Pharaoh and naming the goal — 'bring forth my people... out of that place unto a good and large land'. Asked His name, God answers 'Ehyeh asher Ehyeh' — 'I AM THAT I AM' — 'Thus shalt thou say unto the children of Israel: I AM hath sent me unto you', and gives the Tetragrammaton as the name of remembrance. Lacking eloquence, Moses is given his brother Aaron as mouth, and a tripartite mission: gather the elders, perform signs (rod to serpent, leprous hand, water to blood), and demand, 'Let us go, we pray thee, three days' journey into the wilderness, that we may sacrifice to the LORD our God'.

THE HARDENING AND THE PLAGUES. Pharaoh answers by increasing the brick-quota. The redactional refrain follows — sometimes 'Pharaoh hardened his heart', sometimes 'the LORD hardened Pharaoh's heart' — through escalating signs and plagues in which each Egyptian god-figure is defeated: blood (all water), frogs, lice/gnats (also called kinnim), swarms of flies, pestilence on cattle, boils and blains, hail with fire running on the ground, locusts, darkness 'which may be felt'; the fourth plague on begins to separate Goshen (Israel spared). Moses is God's 'god to Pharaoh' and Aaron his prophet; the rod, the outstretched hand, and the fixed set-times structure each plague.

PASSOVER AND THE TENTH PLAGUE. The month is inaugurated ('this month shall be unto you the beginning of months'); each household takes a lamb without blemish, kills it at twilight on the fourteenth day, marks doorposts with blood, eats it roasted with unleavened bread (matzot) and bitter herbs 'with loins girded, shoes on feet, staff in hand' — 'it is the LORD's passover (pesach)'. At midnight the LORD smites all the firstborn of Egypt 'from the firstborn of Pharaoh... unto the firstborn of the captive... and all the firstborn of cattle', while the destroyer passes over the blood-marked houses. Pharaoh sends them out; the Israelites 'borrow' Egyptian jewels at the peoples' favor, and unleavened cakes are baked 'because they were thrust out of Egypt, and could not tarry'. The festival statute is given: seven days of matzot, 'in the first month, at even, ye shall eat unleavened bread, until the one and twentieth day of the month at even', and 'thou shalt tell thy son in that day, saying: It is because of that which the LORD did for me when I came forth out of Egypt'.

THE SEA. God leads them not by the Philistine road but 'by the way of the wilderness', in a pillar of cloud by day and fire by night. Encamped by the sea at Pi-hahiroth, they are trapped as Pharaoh repents and pursues with six hundred chariots; the people cry out, Moses answers, 'Fear ye not, stand still, and see the salvation of the LORD'. The angel and cloud move behind them; Moses stretches his hand over the sea, and 'the LORD caused the sea to go back by a strong east wind all that night' (the Priestly note); Israel crosses on dry ground, walls of water right and left. At the morning watch the LORD 'looked through the pillar of fire and of the cloud' upon the Egyptian host, took off their chariot wheels, and the returning waters covered 'the chariots, and the horsemen, and all the host of Pharaoh'.

THE SONG. Israel's answer is the Song of the Sea (Exod 15:1-18), among the oldest Hebrew poems: 'I will sing unto the LORD, for He is highly exalted; the horse and his rider hath He thrown into the sea. My strength and song is the LORD... The LORD is my strength and might; He is become my salvation; this is my God, and I will glorify Him... Thy right hand, O LORD, dasheth in pieces the enemy... Thou in Thy love hast led the people whom Thou hast redeemed; Thou hast guided them in Thy strength unto Thy holy habitation... The LORD shall reign for ever and ever.' Miriam the prophetess, Aaron's sister, takes a timbrel, and all the women answer her in dance and refrain. The column then moves into the wilderness — bitter waters sweetened at Marah, quails and manna given (ch. 16), water from the rock at Rephidim — en route to the mountain where the covenant will be made.

FUNCTIONS. This is Israel's foundational redemption narrative: the mandated household retelling ('thou shalt tell thy son') structures the Passover Seder and the Haggadah; the manna legislation grounds the Sabbath (double portion on the sixth day); the Song of the Sea entered early liturgy; and the exodus became the central hermeneutic of liberation — invoked in seder liturgy 'in every generation one must see himself as if he came out of Egypt', in rabbinic tradition, and in later emancipation movements worldwide.
narrative.zh: 新王不識約瑟，苦役以色列人，又命溺殺男嬰；利未婦人匿子三月，置蒲草箱於河畔，法老之女撈起，名之摩西。摩西殺埃及人後逃米甸牧羊；至何烈山，耶和華使者於火焰荊棘中顯現，宣示眷顧降救；摩西問名，得『我就是我』之答。返埃及後，亞倫為口，屢以杖行神蹟；法老心硬，遂有血、蛙、蝨、蠅、疫、瘡、雹、蝗、暗諸災，末災之前設逾越節禮：取無殘疾羔羊，血塗門楣，腰束手杖急食無酵餅苦菜。正月十四日夜，埃及一切長子盡亡，法老逐以色列人出；行至海邊，追兵六百戰車至；摩西伸杖，東風使海退，以色列人行乾地，埃及軍覆沒。遂有海之歌：『我要向耶和華歌唱，因祂大大戰勝，將馬和騎馬的投在海中。』米利暗擊鼓應和。其後瑪拉苦水變甜、鵪鶉嗎哪降下，往西奈山而去。功能：逾越節家述『當日要告訴你的兒子』、嗎哪立法立安息日、海之歌入禮儀，並為後世解放釋義之根本範型。

Master-hermeneutic of liberation in Jewish (and later universal) emancipation discourse

variants.name: Septuagint (Greek) version
variants.summary: Renders tebah as kibotos and pesach as pascha; famously reads the 430 years of sojourning as 'in Egypt and in Canaan' (Exod 12:40 LXX) against the MT, and supplies the 'hand of the Lord' formula where the MT varies — the version through which early Christian seder-influence flows.

variants.summary: Meter and archaic language argue for an older victory hymn incorporated into the prose narrative; Miriam's one-line antiphon (15:21) implies a separate performance tradition in which women led the refrain.

variants.name: Deuteronomic credo recensions
variants.summary: Compressed liturgical cretelling ('My father was a wandering Aramean...') for first-fruits recitation — evidence that the exodus narrative functioned as a fixed ritual script already in the First Temple period.

variants.summary: Pharaoh is named Fir'aun; the sorcerers submit at the staff miracle; Pharaoh's drowning ends with God preserving his body 'as a sign'. Key comparandum for the Islamic corpus (separate record planned).

title.en: The Epic of Gilgamesh: King, Friend, and Seeker of Immortality
title.zh: 吉爾伽美什史詩：王者、摯友與不死者之追尋

region.en: Uruk, southern Iraq
region.zh: 南伊拉克烏魯克

period: Standard Babylonian recension (Sin-leqi-unninni) c. 13th-11th c. BCE, copied from Old Babylonian forerunners (c. 19th-17th c. BCE); principal mss: Nineveh/Kuyunjik library tablets (British Museum K-series), e.g. K 3375 = Tablet XI; Old Babylonian Pennsylvania tablet

source.work: The Epic of Gilgamesh, trans. Andrew George (Penguin, 1999); Electronic Text Corpus of Sumerian Literature for the Sumerian Bilgames poems

license: Sumerian corpus translation (ETCSL) open access; Penguin translation quoted only as summary (copyright) — passages below are labeled paraphrases

summary.en: The tyrant king Gilgamesh and the wild man Enkidu become friends, kill Humbaba and the Bull of Heaven, and are punished by Enkidu's death; Gilgamesh crosses the world to Utnapishtim, fails the sleep test, loses the plant of youth to a serpent, and returns to carve his story on the walls of Uruk — death keeps even heroes, but the city remembers.
summary.zh: 暴君吉爾伽美什與野人恩奇都結為摯友，共誅洪巴巴與天牛，卻因觸怒諸神而摯友亡故；吉爾伽美什橫越天際尋求不死，未通睡眠之試，青春之草又為蛇所竊；返鄉於烏魯克城垣刻其事——英雄終有一死，而城郭銘記其名。

sensitivity.note: Ancient literary text of a dead tradition; no living community restrictions.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase of Tablet XI (K 3375): Utnapishtim tells Gilgamesh how Ea warned him through the wall of a reed hut to tear down his house and build a ship; he sealed the boat, loaded the seed of all living, and the storm destroyed the land for seven days; the raven, sent last and not returning, showed him the receding waters. Not verbatim.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Tablet XI (K 3375); not verbatim.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase of Tablet XI (end): Utnapishtim says, 'Death is the lot decreed for all: no one has ever seen the face of death, yet no one has ever escaped it.' Gilgamesh, woken after six days and seven nights of sleep he believed were minutes, fails the test; a serpent smells the plant of youth as he bathes, seizes it, and sloughs its skin — and Gilgamesh weeps. Not verbatim.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Tablet XI (end); not verbatim.

language: Akkadian (Standard Babylonian; Old Babylonian forerunners; Sumerian sources)
canonical_translation: Andrew George, The Epic of Gilgamesh, Penguin Classics, 1999 (critical edition: Andrew George, The Babylonian Gilgamesh Epic, Oxford, 2003)

narrative.en:
The Standard Babylonian epic assembles in twelve tablets a two-thousand-year-old literary history. It opens with a prologue inviting the reader to climb the walls of Uruk: 'See its foundation terrace, touch the masonry — is it not burnt brick and good? ... One league city, one league palm gardens, one league lowlands, the open area of the Ishtar Temple...' — and to read the box of lapis within, the story of 'him who saw the Deep' (sa naqba imuru), Gilgamesh, two-thirds god, one-third human, whom no one could equal.

ENKIDU. Gilgamesh, shepherd-king of Uruk, works his young men at the game-stick and exhausts the brides with his custom (the ius primae noctis in the Old Babylonian text). The people cry to heaven; Aruru pinches off a rival in the clay of the steppe: Enkidu, shaggy with hair like grain, who eats grass with gazelles and drinks at the water-holes, blocking the hunters' traps. A harlot (Shamhat) is sent to tame him: seven days of love-making 'after the manner of mankind' leave the gazelles shunning him; she clothes him, feeds him bread and beer, gives him shepherds' work, and news of Gilgamesh's wedding custom. Enkidu goes to Uruk to meet him at the wedding door; they wrestle furiously in the street — doorposts quake, the wall shakes — and Enkidu, defeated, embraces the king, and the two become fast friends.

THE CEDAR FOREST. Gilgamesh resolves to journey to the Cedar Forest and kill its guardian Humbaba, whose mouths are fire, whose breath is death, whom Enlil appointed to terrify men. The elders of Uruk counsel against it; Enkidu recalls he has seen the forest and knows its horror. Gilgamesh has doors made for Enlil from cedar and entreats Shamash for aid; Shamash promises eight winds behind him. They cross seven mountain ranges, and Enkidu, seized by dreams three times, keeps waking Gilgamesh: while he sleeps, Humbaba hears them and batters down the mountains. Shamash raises the winds — thirteen, like whips — and Humbaba, bound and helpless, offers surrender ('I will be your slave, my forest is yours'). Enkidu insists on killing him: 'Where is your strength of courage?' The guardian's head is severed and bagged; on the return Enkidu's broken door is dedicated to Enlil.

ISHTAR AND THE BULL. Back in Uruk, Ishtar offers herself in marriage; Gilgamesh refuses with the famous catalogue of her ruined lovers — the bird, the lion, the horse, the shepherd, the plant Tammuz — 'you are a brazier which goes out in the cold'. Enraged, Ishtar demands the Bull of Heaven from Anu; refused at first, then granted at threat of breaking the underworld doors. The Bull snorts a pit (one hundred men fall in), then another; Enkidu seizes its tail, Gilgamesh stabs it between neck and horns, and they dedicate its heart to Shamash while Ishtar curses from the wall. Enkidu hurls the right thigh at her. That night the gods deliberate: for killing Humbaba and the Bull, one of the two must die. Enkidu falls sick for twelve days, cursing first the door, then the harlot (who taught him mankind's ways), and blessing her after she is counseled back; he dreams of the House of Dust, where thrones are dust and Belit-Seri keeps the house, and where he sits for ever with kings and priests — and dies.

THE JOURNEY TO UTNAPISHTIM. Gilgamesh's grief is wild: he weeps six days and nights 'as a lioness', roams the steppe clothed in a lion's skin, resolves to go to Utnapishtim 'the Faraway', who escaped the flood, and ask the secret of life. He passes the twin peaks of Mashu whose gates guard the sun's path, and walks a dark league-road twelve leagues deep 'where there is neither light nor dark'; at a garden of jewel-trees he meets the alewife Siduri, who (in the older Old Babylonian telling, abbreviated in the Standard version) counsels feasting and love — 'when the gods made mankind they set death apart for mankind' — then directs him to the ferryman Urshanabi, who asks for the 'stone things'; Gilgamesh smashes them, and must cut wooden punts, kissing each pole before use to cross the Waters of Death.

THE FLOOD AND THE TEST. Utnapishtim tells him the secret the gods swore and Ea leaked through the reed hut's wall: 'Tear down the house, build a ship; leave possessions, save life'. The boat is a cube, 120 cubits a side, sealed with pitch and bitumen, loaded with gold, silver, cattle, beasts, craftsmen, and the seed of all living. The storm: 'the gods were frightened by the flood... the goddess wailed like a woman in childbirth'; after seven days the ship grounded on Nisir, and the birds went out — dove, swallow, raven (the raven did not return). Enlil, furious that a man survived, is appeased by Ea, who argues he should have sent plague, famine — not flood — and Enlil blesses Utnapishtim and his wife, making them like gods, to dwell 'at the mouth of the rivers'. Now the test: sleep six days and seven nights. Gilgamesh dozes at once; his wife bakes a loaf each day, and when he wakes he sees the bread's stages and knows he slept — 'death is the decree, the word of the assembly'. Utnapishtim sends him back; as a parting gift, the plant of youth (like a boxthorn, 'an old man will turn young'); on the homeward road Gilgamesh bathes in a pool, and a serpent smells the plant, seizes it, sloughs its skin, and vanishes. Gilgamesh weeps and returns to Uruk; the epic ends where it began, with the city walls. (Tablet 12, appended in the Nineveh library, translates a separate Sumerian poem in which Enkidu descends to retrieve Gilgamesh's ball and drum, is trapped, and his shade rises to describe the netherworld — a scribal appendix, not part of the main plot.)

FUNCTIONS. The epic is the masterpiece of Mesopotamian wisdom literature: it critiques despotic kingship, mourns friendship, and sets human fame (the city's walls) against death; it served as school text and royal library copy (Ashurbanipal's collection); the flood episode fed Mesopotamian historiography and, via Berossus, into later comparative debate.
narrative.zh: 史詩始於烏魯克城垣之邀：觀其磚基，讀青金石匣中『見過深淵者』吉爾伽美什之事。野人恩奇都為母神所造，與神妓七日交好而開化；赴烏魯克與王角力，不敵而結為友。二人西赴雪松林誅洪巴巴，返城後吉爾伽美什拒伊什塔爾之婚，殺天牛、擲其腿；諸神議定二者取一，恩奇都病十二日，夢『塵土之家』而死。王披獅皮漫遊，越馬什雙峰、經酒肆西杜里之諭，與擺渡人烏爾沙那比渡死水；不死者烏特那皮什提告以洪水之秘：蘆牆內聞以利亞之諭，造方舟、納生靈、七日暴風、放鴉知地。又試以七日不眠而王立酣，麵包示時；遂返。臨別得青春之草，浴時為蛇竊去蛻皮而遁。王泣而歸，於烏魯克城垣自述其事。第十二板為蘇美譯文附編，述恩奇都冥府之行。全篇批判暴政、悼友、以城記勝死，為美索不達米亞智慧文學之巔。

functions: Wisdom-literature meditation on mortality and the limits of kingship
Scribal curriculum text and royal library classic (Nineveh, Ashurbanipal)
Aition of Uruk's walls and of the hero's fame against death
Vessel for the Mesopotamian flood narrative (Tablet XI) in later traditions

variants.name: Old Babylonian Pennsylvania tablet ('Surpassing all kings')
variants.text_tradition: Old Babylonian, c. 18th-17th c. BCE (Univ. of Pennsylvania Museum)
variants.summary: Opens with the meeting of Gilgamesh and Enkidu (incomplete: the middle is lost) and preserves the fuller wedding-custom and wrestling scene; the lacuna is bridged by scholarly restoration from context.

variants.name: Old Babylonian Yale tablet (Siduri's counsel)
variants.text_tradition: Old Babylonian, c. 18th-17th c. BCE (Yale Babylonian Collection)
variants.summary: Preserves the tavern-keeper's carpe diem speech almost whole ('when the gods created mankind, death they allotted to mankind'); in the Standard Babylonian recension the speech is reduced to a mention — the older text is our main witness.

variants.name: Sumerian poems of Bilgames
variants.text_tradition: Sumerian narratives c. 21st-17th c. BCE (Nippur copies; ETCSL 1.8.x)
variants.summary: Five independent poems — Bilgames and Huwawa; Bilgames, Enkidu and the Netherworld; The Death of Bilgames; etc. — in which Enkidu is the servant, Huwawa's killing is sacrilege, and death is met with wisdom; the Standard Babylonian epic reworks them into one arc.

variants.name: Hittite and Hurrian adaptations
variants.summary: A Hittite adaptation (and Hurrian intermediaries) attests the epic's westward spread; heavily fragmentary — the narrative depends on reconstructed joining of scattered pieces (George 2003, vol. 2).

primary_sources.work: Epic of Gilgamesh, Standard Babylonian version (twelve tablets)
primary_sources.citation: Tablets I-II (Enkidu, friendship); IV-V (Cedar Forest); VI (Ishtar, Bull); VII-VIII (death, lament); IX-X (journey); XI (flood, test, plant). Principal mss: Kuyunjik (Nineveh) tablets, British Museum K-series (e.g. K 3375 = Tablet XI); OB Pennsylvania and Yale tablets for forerunners. Critical edition: Andrew George, The Babylonian Gilgamesh Epic, 2 vols., Oxford 2003; translation: George, Penguin 1999.
ETCSL 1.8.1.1-1.8.1.5 (trans. Jeremy Black et al., Oxford), esp. 'Bilgames and the Netherworld' for Tablet 12's source.

secondary_sources.work: Jeffrey H. Tigay, The Evolution of the Gilgamesh Epic
secondary_sources.citation: Tigay 1982, Philadelphia: University of Pennsylvania Press — tracks the Sumerian-to-Standard-Babylonian literary evolution tablet by tablet.

secondary_sources.citation: Dalley 1989, Oxford: Oxford World's Classics — alternate English translation of the Standard version with notes.

source_urls.description: Electronic Text Corpus of Sumerian Literature (Oxford) — Sumerian Bilgames poems, open access
British Museum collection database — Nineveh/Kuyunjik Gilgamesh tablets (search 'Kuyunjik Gilgamesh')

reconstructed_segments.segment: Old Babylonian Pennsylvania tablet: middle of the narrative lost (wedding custom to friendship)
reconstructed_segments.restored_in: Andrew George, The Babylonian Gilgamesh Epic, Oxford 2003, vol. 1, pp. 158-175

Tablet 12: scribal appendix translating a Sumerian poem (not part of the SB plot)

title.en: Atrahasis and the Great Flood
title.zh: 阿特拉哈西斯與大洪水

region.en: Shuruppak on the Euphrates, Iraq
region.zh: 幼發拉底河畔舒魯帕克（伊拉克）

period: Old Babylonian, c. 18th c. BCE (Rogers translation 1912)

source.work: Cuneiform Parallels to the Old Testament, 'Ea and Atrakhasis', trans. Robert W. Rogers (1912)

summary.en: Enlil resolves on the flood; Ea, speaking through a reed wall, orders Atrahasis to build the boat, load his household and the beasts, and seal it. Seven days the storm drowns the land; the sacrifice on the mountain draws the hungry gods like flies.
summary.zh: 恩利爾決意滅世；埃亞隔葦牆傳令：造舟、載家眷與百獸、封口。風暴七日淹沒大地；山上之祭使飢餓的諸神如蠅聚集。

sensitivity.note: Ancient myth; no living community restrictions.

passages.text: Enlil resolves to destroy mankind; Ea, forbidden to warn, speaks through the reed wall of Atrahasis's house: Wall, hear; reed wall, understand — tear down your house and build a boat, load it with your household and the seed of all living, and seal the door.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Atrahasis, Tablet III (Rogers 1912); not verbatim.

passages.text: The storm floods the land for seven days; the boat rides the waves. Atrahasis opens the window, offers sacrifice on the mountain, and the gods, starving since the world's people died, gather like flies to the sweet smell — and Enlil, appeased, decrees a new order with fertility limited so the clamor will not return.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Atrahasis, Tablet III; not verbatim.

functions: Master narrative of the flood tradition
Etiology of fertility limitations and birth rites
Charter of the wise man's covenant with heaven

variants.summary: The flood retold inside the epic of Gilgamesh.

variants.summary: The Sumerian ancestor of the tale.

variants.name: Berossus' Xisuthrus
variants.summary: The late Babylonian flood narrative.

title.en: The Ramayana of Valmiki: Rama's Exile, Sita's Abduction, and the War of Lanka
title.zh: 蟻垤《羅摩衍那》：羅摩流放、悉多被擄與楞伽之戰

region.en: Ayodhya, Uttar Pradesh, India
region.zh: 印度北方邦阿逾陀

period: Oldest strata c. 2nd c. BCE-2nd c. CE (critical edition, Oriental Institute Baroda, 1960-75); principal mediaeval mss numerous (e.g. Newari, Devanagari traditions)

source.archive: Project Gutenberg (Griffith translation, 1870-74) / Princeton University Press (critical translation: Goldman)
source.work: Ramayana of Valmiki, kandas I-VII; trans. R. T. H. Griffith (public domain); The Ramayana of Valmiki, gen. ed. Robert P. Goldman (Princeton)

license: Public domain (Griffith translation 1870-74); passages below mostly labeled paraphrases of the Sanskrit

summary.en: Prince Rama of Ayodhya is exiled fourteen years by a rival queen's boon; his wife Sita is abducted by the ten-headed Ravana to Lanka; with monkey allies and Hanuman's leap, Rama builds a bridge, destroys Ravana, and returns to rule the ideal kingdom — the charter epic of dharma-king and devoted wife, retold at Ramanavami and Dashehra.
summary.zh: 阿逾陀王子羅摩遭後母之詛流放十四載；妻悉多為十首羅波那擄至楞伽；羅摩得神猴哈奴曼相助，跨海建橋、誅羅波那，攜妻歸國，行理想之治——為印度『達摩之王』與『貞婦』之根本史詩，羅摩誕辰節與十勝節年年重述。

sensitivity.note: Living tradition: the Ramayana is read ritually (Ramanavami, Ramcaritmanas recitation). Classified 'myth' rather than 'religious' per the README's interpretive split (epic literature rather than sruti/smrti scripture); reasoning recorded here.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase of Ayodhya Kanda 34-35: Kaikeyi demands her two boons — that Bharata be consecrated heir, and Rama be banished to the forest for fourteen years wearing bark garments. Rama accepts without protest: 'For father's promise, and for dharma, I go to Dandaka.' Not verbatim.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Ayodhya Kanda 34-35; not verbatim.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase of Sundara Kanda 21-22: Sita, seated under the Ashoka tree, refuses Ravana's offer of queenship, placing a blade of grass between them; Hanuman reveals himself, gives Rama's ring, and offers to carry her back — she refuses to touch another male, bidding Rama come for her. Not verbatim.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Sundara Kanda 21-22; not verbatim.

canonical_translation: R. T. H. Griffith, The Ramayan of Valmiki, 5 vols., Benares, 1870-74 (public domain); modern critical translation: Robert P. Goldman et al., The Ramayana of Valmiki, 7 vols., Princeton University Press, 1984-2017

narrative.en:
The poem's framing 'adi' (first) kanda announces its own composition: Valmiki asks Narada, 'Who in this world today is virtuous, mighty, truthful, and self-controlled?' — the answer, Rama, prince of Kosala, launches 24,000 slokas of the first fully developed Sanskrit kavya.

BALA KANDA. King Dasharatha of Ayodhya, childless, performs the putrakamesti sacrifice; a divine being rises from the fire and gives the king golden rice to divide among his three queens. Four sons are born: Rama of Kausalya, Bharata of Kaikeyi, Lakshmana and Shatrughna of Sumitra — partial incarnations of Vishnu, come at the gods' request (plagued by Ravana) to destroy the ten-headed king of Lanka. The seer Vishvamitra leads the adolescent Rama and Lakshmana into the forest: Rama kills the ogress Tataka (a yakshi-turned-rakshasi whose death must come from a man, not a god), frees the sage's fire-sacrifices from rakshasa raiders, and is given celestial weapons. On the return, at Mithila, Rama breaks — with a bow-string's sound no less than his rivals can barely lift — Shiva's bow at Janaka's contest, and weds the foundling-princess Sita ('found in the furrow', sita 'furrow'), whose swayamvara has defeated every demon king. The four brothers marry the four brides; Vishvamitra tells Rama the gods' distress at Ravana's sway.

AYODHYA KANDA. Aging Dasharatha resolves to consecrate Rama heir-apparent. On the eve of the ceremony, the hunchbacked maid Manthara persuades Queen Kaikeyi to cash in two boons Dasharatha granted long ago for nursing him: that Bharata be consecrated instead, and Rama be exiled to the forest for fourteen years in bark garments. Kaikeyi complies; Dasharatha collapses in grief. Rama, told, accepts without a word of protest — 'not for father's command, but for truth and for dharma' — and Sita insists on following ('a father, a mother, a brother, a son may be banished; a wife follows her husband wherever he goes'); Lakshmana walks before them in anger. The three cross the Ganga (aided by Guha, chief of the boatmen) to Chitrakuta; Dasharatha dies grieving the broken bond; Bharata, refusing the throne his mother engineered, tracks Rama to Chitrakuta and begs him to return. Rama holds to the vow: fourteen years, not a day less. Bharata returns with Rama's golden sandals (paduka), places them on the throne at Nandigrama, and rules from the village gate as regent, a mark of ideal ministerial dharma.

ARANYA KANDA. The trio settles at Panchavati in Dandaka; the rakshasi Surpanakha, sister of Ravana, approaches Rama, then Lakshmana, and is mutilated — nose and ears cut — when she attacks Sita; her brothers Khara and Dushana attack with 14,000 rakshasas and are destroyed by Rama alone. Surpanakha goads Ravana: the ten-headed, twenty-armed king of Lanka sends the sorcerer Maricha as a golden deer. Sita, charmed, demands it; the dying Maricha cries Lakshmana's name in Rama's voice; Sita, believing Rama slain, orders Lakshmana to help, and — in this telling — the prince is goaded into leaving her (the famous 'Lakshmana-line' with which later tellings arm Sita is absent from Valmiki). Ravana, disguised as an ascetic, crosses the hut's boundary, seizes Sita and her hut together, and drives her skyward; the vulture Jatayus, Dasharatha's old friend, fights him aloft and is mortally wounded, living just long enough to tell Rama who took her. Dying, Rama performs Jatayus' last rites.

KISHKINDHA KANDA. Rama and Lakshmana reach Lake Pampa; the monkey Hanuman, son of the wind-god, in disguise brings them to Sugriva, the exiled monkey king. A friendship pact is made: Rama kills Vali (Sugriva's brother and usurper) with a single hidden arrow in their duel — an act debated ever since for its ethics; the rainy season passes with Rama's grief and Hanuman's counsel; then four monkey armies are dispatched to the world's quarters. In the south, the vulture Sampati (Jatayus' brother) confirms Sita's location: Lanka, across the sea.

SUNDARA KANDA ('the beautiful one', named for Sita's island ordeal). Hanuman, son of the wind, leaps across a hundred yojanas of ocean, evading the snake-mother Surasa and the demoness Sinhika, and lands at Lanka by night. In the Ashoka grove he finds Sita, surrounded by rakshasi guards and Ravana's ultimatum; she has placed a blade of grass between them, and refused the term of one year before Ravana kills her. Hanuman reveals himself, offers to carry her back; she refuses to be touched by another male and gives Rama her chudamani gem. Hanuman destroys the grove and the escort, lets himself be captured (killing Ravana's son Aksha in the duel), delivers Rama's warning before Ravana's court — with Vibhishana's dissent — and is sent out with his tail afire; he burns the golden city, spares the Ashoka grove, and leaps home.

YUDDHA KANDA. Rama's host marches to the sea; Ravana's brother Vibhishana defects, is sheltered against the council's qualms, and is later consecrated king. The ocean-god advises Nala the monkey-builder; the Nala Setu bridge is built of stones that float. The war rages for days: Kumbhakarna, roused from his six-month sleep, devours armies until Rama's arrows sever his head; Indrajit's serpent-arrows bind Rama and Lakshmana until Garuda frees them; Indrajit's illusory Sita-decapitation nearly breaks the army's heart; Vibhishana's counsel and Lakshmana's Indra-astra kill Indrajit in the Nikumbhila rite. Finally Rama faces Ravana: each arrow-match fails, until Rama invokes the Brahmastra, slaying the ten heads; Vibhishana mourns the brother he served, and Sita is brought out from the grove. 'My heart is with Rama', she says; but Rama, before the army, renounces her — she has lived in another man's house. Sita demands the fire-pyre (agni-pariksha): Agni himself bears her out unharmed — 'I know the purity of my own heart; the shadow-Sita I carried away was illusion'. The gods descend; Indra restores Rama's slain monkey army, and Rama is consecrated in Lanka. The pushpaka vimana (Ravana's flying palace) carries all to Ayodhya: Bharata, fourteen years of regency fulfilled, gives up the throne; Rama rules the ideal kingdom (rama-rajya), where 'no widow mourns, no disease, no thieves' — the aition of Divali's lamps.

UTTARA KANDA (in the critical edition, an appendix with debated status). Rumors circulate that the king accepted a woman who lived in Ravana's house; Rama banishes the pregnant Sita to Valmiki's ashrama, where she bears twins Lava and Kusha, whom the poet raises and teaches to sing the Ramayana itself — the self-referential moment when the epic is first recited in Rama's court. Sita, summoned, again proves herself: 'If I have never thought of any but Rama, let Earth receive me'; the earth opens, Bhudevi receives her on a golden throne, and Rama rules alone until he enters the Sarayu river, resuming his form as Vishnu.

FUNCTIONS. The Ramayana is the charter narrative of Hindu kingship (rama-rajya as political ideal), of pativrata wifely dharma (Sita), of filial obedience (Rama, Bharata, Lakshmana), and of devotion (bhakti) to Vishnu in the form of Rama; it is ritually recited at Ramanavami (Rama's birth), and Ravana's effigies burn at Vijayadashami (Dashehra); Tulsidas' Ramcaritmanas recitation structures north Indian devotional life; and Hanuman's cult (Tuesdays, Hanuman Jayanti) hangs on his Sundara Kanda feats.
narrative.zh: 阿逾陀王十車王求子得四子，羅摩為毘濕奴化身。尊者維什瓦米陀攜二王子誅羅剎，至彌提羅折濕婆神弓，娶犁溝所出之悉多。老王欲立羅摩，後妃凱凱伊受駝背婢慫恿索二諾：立婆羅多、放羅摩十四年。羅摩攜悉多與弟羅什曼那入林；羅剎女首哩薄那迦受辱，慫恿兄羅波那遣摩哩遮化金鹿誘王，化作苦行者擄走悉多；神鷲闍吒優私力戰而死。羅摩結盟神猴須羯哩婆，一箭誅猴王婆黎；哈奴曼躍海覓妻，火燒楞伽城。羅摩於海上建那羅橋，大戰：誅巨猿俱姆伽爾那、妖術師因陀羅耆，終以梵箭破十首之頸；維毗沙那受封。悉多過火驗，火神親護而出，證其貞潔。飛車歸國，婆羅多還政，羅摩行『羅摩之治』。後篇：羅摩放逐有孕之悉多至蟻垤仙人林中，生二子；二子誦此史詩於王廷；悉多再驗，呼大地開口受之；羅摩入薩羅逾河復毗濕奴之身。功能：君權典範、貞婦達摩、孝悌之義、羅摩誕辰與十勝節之禮儀重述。

functions: Charter of ideal kingship (rama-rajya) and ministerial dharma (Bharata's regency)
Pativrata ideal: Sita's trial as the normative narrative of wifely constancy
Ritual calendar: Ramanavami recitation, Vijayadashami burning of Ravana effigies, Divali lamps
Bhakti charter: Rama as Vishnu's avatar; Hanuman's cult founded on the Sundara Kanda

variants.name: Ramcharitmanas of Tulsidas
variants.summary: The vernacular retelling that displaced Valmiki in north Indian recitation; adds the lakshmana-rekha line around Sita's hut and shifts emphasis to Rama's divinity (bhakti) over kingship ethics.

variants.name: Kampan's Iramavataram (Tamil, 12th c. CE)
variants.summary: Tamil retelling with far more developed Rama-devotion (Rama as Vishnu from the start), rich descriptive style, and local motifs (Sita's birth is as a goddess); the canonical South Indian version, ritually recited in Tamil temples.

variants.name: Paumacariya of Vimalasuri (Jain, c. 3rd-5th c. CE)
variants.summary: Jain retelling in which Ravana is a tragic, noble rakshasa-king (killed for the Jain vow-breaking of his son), Lakshmana (not Rama) kills him, and Rama is a Jain hero of the 8th bhavya-line — the ideology reworked through ahimsa and karma.

variants.name: Dasaratha Jataka (Buddhist, Pali)
variants.summary: A Buddhist parable version: Rama, Sita, and Lakshmana are exiled to the Himalayas; Ravana never abducts Sita; Sita remains Rama's sister (in this telling) and the story ends in reconciliation — no Lanka, no war, a didactic tale of non-attachment.

variants.name: Thai Ramakien and Khmer Reamker
variants.text_tradition: Thai dance-drama (Rattanakosin period); Khmer classical ballet
variants.summary: Southeast Asian court adaptations: Rama as an incarnation of Vishnu legitimates the king (Bangkok's dynasty takes the name Rama); the monkey armies are localized and the war becomes national pageant (khon masked dance).

variants.name: Kakawin Ramayana (Old Javanese)
variants.text_tradition: Old Javanese kavya, c. 9th-10th c. CE
variants.summary: Javanese court version integrating the epic with local architecture (Prambanan reliefs) and poetic conventions; ancestor of Balinese and Javanese wayang tellings.

variants.name: 'Three Hundred Ramayanas' corpus
variants.text_tradition: A. K. Ramanujan's survey (1991) of told traditions
variants.summary: Ramanujan's famous essay catalogues dozens of tellings — Sanskrit, Tamil, Thai, Javanese, Kannada, folk — across languages and media; the corpus is the standard scholarly frame for the tradition's variance.

primary_sources.citation: Critical edition, Oriental Institute, University of Baroda, 1960-75. Kandas: I Bala 1-2 (birth), 47-77 (Tataka, Mithila); II Ayodhya 1-115 (consecration crisis, exile); III Aranya (Surpanakha, abduction); IV Kishkindha (Vali); V Sundara (Hanuman's leap, Ashoka grove); VI Yuddha (bridge, war, agni-pariksha, return); VII Uttara (critical edition marks this as appendix; Sita's banishment and earth-swallowing). English: Griffith 1870-74 (public domain); Goldman et al., Princeton, 1984-2017.

secondary_sources.work: John Brockington, The Sanskrit Epics
secondary_sources.citation: Brockington 1998, Leiden: Brill — dating, textual transmission, and ideology of the Ramayana's layers.

secondary_sources.work: A. K. Ramanujan, 'Three Hundred Ramayanas: Five Examples and Three Thoughts on Translation'
secondary_sources.citation: Ramanujan 1991, in Many Ramayanas: The Diversity of a Narrative Tradition in South Asia, ed. Paula Richman, Berkeley: University of California Press, pp. 22-49.

secondary_sources.work: Philip Lutgendorf, Hanuman's Tale: The Messages of a Divine Monkey
secondary_sources.citation: Lutgendorf 2007, New York: Oxford University Press — the Sundara Kanda's cultic and political afterlife.

Princeton University Press — The Ramayana of Valmiki (Goldman critical translation, 7 vols.)

sensitivity_guidance: The Ramayana is ritually recited and politically contested in contemporary India (e.g. court debates over Sita's trial narratives). Quote from public-domain or critical translations; attribute kanda and sarga; note which recension is quoted (critical edition vs. vulgar text differs at the Uttara Kanda); avoid framing the agni-pariksha as fact — it is narrated as divine test and debated in living practice.

title.en: The Churning of the Ocean of Milk (Samudra-manthana)
title.zh: 攪拌乳海

region.en: Cosmic ocean (symbolic pin at Varanasi ghats, Ganges)
region.zh: 宇宙之海（象徵性定位於恆河瓦拉納西河壇）

period: Mahabharata Adi Parva (composition layers c. 4th c. BCE-4th c. CE; critical edition BORI, Poona); Purana versions c. 4th-10th c. CE

source.archive: Project Gutenberg (Mahabharata translations) / University of Chicago Press (van Buitenen)
source.work: Mahabharata, Adi Parva (Astika Upaparva 18-34), trans. J. A. B. van Buitenen (Chicago, 1973)

license: Cuneiform-free; van Buitenen translation quoted only as summary (copyright) — passages below are labeled paraphrases

summary.en: Devas and Asuras, half-brothers, churn the cosmic ocean with the serpent Vasuki and Mount Mandara, supported by the tortoise Kurma; from the ocean come treasures, Lakshmi, and the amrita of immortality; Vishnu as the enchantress Mohini distributes it only to the gods, who thereby defeat death and their cousins.
summary.zh: 天神與阿修羅本為半血兄弟，以蛇王伐蘇基為繩、曼陀羅山為杵攪拌乳海，毗濕奴化巨龜托山；海中湧出寶物、吉祥天女與不死甘露；毗濕奴化身舞女摩希尼分甘露獨予天神，天神遂得不死、逐退阿修羅。

sensitivity.note: Living tradition: the narrative is depicted in temple art and retold at festivals (e.g. Sharad Purnima, Lakshmi worship). Classified 'myth' per the README's interpretive split.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase of Adi Parva 18-19 (Astika Upaparva): Vishnu advises the gods, weakened by Durvasas' curse and war, to make peace with the Asuras and churn the ocean of milk for the amrita; Mandara is used as the churning-stick, the serpent Vasuki as the cord, and Vishnu, as the great tortoise, supports the mountain on his back. Not verbatim.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Adi Parva 18-19 (Astika Upaparva); not verbatim.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase of Adi Parva 27-34: From the ocean rise Surabhi the cow of plenty, the Apsarases, Airavata, Ucchaihsravas, the Kaustubha gem, Parijata, the Moon, Lakshmi, Varuni, and finally Dhanvantari with the white amrita-vessel; the Asuras seize it, and Vishnu as Mohini allots it to the gods alone. Not verbatim.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Adi Parva 27-34; not verbatim.

canonical_translation: J. A. B. van Buitenen, The Mahabharata, vol. 1, University of Chicago Press, 1973; alternate: Kisari Mohan Ganguli's public-domain translation (1883-96)

narrative.en:
BEGINNING: A CURSE AND A PLAN. The Mahabharata's frame-story places the churning in the Astika section, told to protect a serpent-sacrifice. In the Purana versions, the sage Durvasas curses Indra (a garland crushed by his elephant): the king of the gods loses his fortune, and the Asuras, led by Bali, defeat the devas in war. The gods go to Brahma, then to Vishnu, who gives them the strategy: churn the ocean of milk (kshira-sagara) for the amrita, the nectar of immortality — but only in alliance with their enemies the Asuras, and with the agreement that the nectar will then be shared.

THE CHURNING. Mount Mandara is uprooted as the churning-stick; the serpent-king Vasuki (Ananta-Shesha in some tellings) offers himself as the churning-rope, wound around the mountain; the devas take the tail, the asuras the head (the asuras' position poisons them with Vasuki's venomous breath). The mountain sinks into the soft ocean-bed; Vishnu, in the form of the great tortoise Kurma (his second avatar), dives beneath and bears the mountain on his back. Brahma steadies the peak from above. And so, in the world's greatest tug-of-war, the brothers churn: 'as men churn with a cord', the mountain revolves 'with a great sound like thunder', the forest beasts fall from its slopes, the trees catch fire and the ocean froths. (In the Purana retellings, the churning's first product is the poison halahala/kalakuta, which threatens the three worlds and is drunk by Shiva, whose throat turns blue — Nilakantha, 'blue-throat'; the Mahabharata version has no poison and no Shiva.)

THE EMERGENCE. One by one, treasures rise from the milk ocean: Surabhi, the cow of plenty; Ucchaihsravas, the seven-headed horse of the sun; Airavata, the white elephant; the Kaustubha gem (Vishnu takes it for his breast); the Parijata tree; Apsarases, celestial dancers; Varuni, goddess of wine; Chandra, the Moon; then Lakshmi, goddess of fortune, who chooses Vishnu and garlands him — the aition of her marriage to Vishnu and of Sharad Purnima worship. Last rises Dhanvantari, physician of the gods, holding the white pot (kalasha) of amrita.

MOHINI AND THE END. The Asuras seize the pot; the devas panic; Vishnu resolves the impasse with his feminine illusion, Mohini ('the Enchantress'), the only female avatar in the canonical avatar-lists. Beautiful and unrecognizable, she offers to distribute the nectar 'fairly' and seats devas and asuras in two facing rows; she pours the amrita only into the devas' cups, deflecting the asuras with charm and with the promise of another round. (In the Purana tellings, the asura Svarbhanu disguises himself as a deva, drinks, and is decapitated mid-swallow by the sun and moon; his immortal head becomes Rahu, his body Ketu, the eclipse-demons.) The devas, immortal and restored, drive the asuras underground and to the sea; Vishnu hands the empty pot to Indra. The churned ocean, in some tellings, remains the cosmic treasury from which wealth continually arises.

FUNCTIONS. The narrative is the theology of the yajna: churning (manthana) is sacrificial labor, the ocean the ritual field, the pot the offering-vessel — the cosmos is enriched by brothers-in-conflict cooperating under a supervising god. It is the origin-story of Lakshmi's marriage, of the Kurma and (in Purana versions) the Shiva Nilakantha avatar-episodes, of Dhanvantari and Ayurveda, of Rahu-Ketu, and of Amrita's hieroglyph of immortality-in-community; its imagery structures Angkor Wat's third-gallery bas-relief (92 asuras, 88 devas pulling the naga Vasuki), Bangkok's Suvarnabhumi airport sculpture, and countless temple friezes across South and Southeast Asia.
narrative.zh: 仙人達爾瓦沙之詛令天神失運，阿修羅王巴利戰勝；毗濕奴授策：與阿修羅合盟，攪乳海取不死甘露。以曼陀羅山為杵、蛇王伐蘇基為繩，天神執尾、阿修羅執首，山沉海床，毗濕奴化身巨龜俱利摩托之，梵天自上扶正。攪動之初（往世書版）先出劇毒卡拉庫塔，濕婆一飲而盡，喉成青色，號『青頸』。繼而乳牛須羅毗、七頭神馬、白象艾羅婆多、寶石考斯圖巴、如意樹、飛天、酒神女伐魯尼、月亮相繼湧現；吉祥天女擇毗濕奴而冠之；末出醫神檀文陀梨，手捧白色甘露瓶。阿修羅奪瓶，毗濕奴化身摩希尼分配甘露，獨予天神（往世書版：偽裝之阿修羅斯伐爾巴努中途斬首，其首成日蝕之羅睺）。天神得不死，逐阿修羅入地，因陀羅復位。功能：祭祀之喻、吉祥天女婚配之源、醫神與阿育吠陀之始、日月蝕之神話釋義；吳哥窟迴廊浮雕即此景。

functions: Theology of sacrifice: churning as yajna, cosmos enriched by ritual labor
Origin narrative of Lakshmi's marriage and Sharad Purnima / Lakshmi worship
Aition of Dhanvantari and Ayurveda; of Rahu-Ketu as eclipse demons (Purana versions)
Pan-Asian visual iconography (Angkor Wat third gallery; Thai and Khmer royal symbolism)

variants.name: Mahabharata version (Adi Parva 18-34)
variants.summary: The oldest continuous telling: no poison episode and no Shiva; Vishnu (as Kurma and as Mohini) is the sole divine strategist; the frame serves the serpent-sacrifice story of Astika; Lakshmi's garland-choice is retained.

variants.name: Vishnu Purana and Bhagavata Purana versions
variants.summary: Add the halahala poison and Shiva Nilakantha (Bhagavata 8.7); introduce Rahu/Svarbhanu's decapitation (Vishnu Purana 4.9); elaborate Lakshmi's emergence and the sixty-four yoginis. The versions recited in temple worship today.

variants.summary: Monumental stone rendering: 92 asuras and 88 devas pull the naga Vasuki, Vishnu presides at the mountain's summit; a royal Khmer theology of cosmic order that makes the churning the visual charter of the temple-state.

variants.text_tradition: Thai royal art (Suvarnabhumi Airport installation; royal barge figureheads)
variants.summary: The churning becomes a royal emblem of legitimation — Rama-linked kingship imagery — with Vishnu centered and devas/asuras symmetrically ranked; adopted into court ritual and modern state symbolism.
