passages.note: Paraphrase of Theogony, lines ca. 556-560 (Heumann 2021); not verbatim.

passages.text: In retaliation, Zeus withheld fire from the fire-trees of the earth so that mortals could not boil nor forge; but Prometheus stole the far-shining flame again in a hollow fennel stalk. Rage shook Zeus then: in reprisal for the stolen gift of fire he had Hephaestus mould a maiden out of earth and water, dressed her beautifully and crowned her, and had her sent down among men as a gift the likes of which Epimetheus took to his sorrow — the price of fire, Pandora, the mould-born evil who founded the whole race of womankind.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Theogony, lines ca. 560-616 (Heumann 2021); not verbatim.

title.en: The Ten-Year War of the Titans
title.zh: 十年提坦戰爭

region.en: Mounts Othrys & Olympus (mythic geography)
region.zh: 奧特里斯山與奧林波斯山（神話地理）

period: Composed c. 700 BCE (Heumann translation 2021)

source.work: Hesiod, Theogony, trans. Michael Heumann (2021), lines ca. 617-735

license: Poem public domain; translation CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 (Heumann 2021) — paraphrase only in this record

summary.en: For ten years the young gods from Olympus and the Titans on Othrys grind one another without result. Zeus frees the Hundred-Handed from their long prison in the deep, feeds them nectar and ambrosia, and turns the balance; three hundred stones thrown by three giants smash the Titans' hosts. Zeus hurls them down beneath the earth to Tartarus, guarded by his new allies.
summary.zh: 奧林波斯的新神與奧特里斯山的提坦纏鬥十年不分勝負。宙斯釋放長年囚於黑暗的百手三巨人，以仙食仙飲壯其氣力，戰局立轉；三百塊巨石接連砸下，提坦大軍潰敗，被宙斯投向大地深處的塔耳塔羅斯，由百手巨人看守。

sensitivity.note: Ancient literary source; no living community restrictions.

passages.text: Ouranos had long ago bound the Hundred-Handed — Cottus, Briareus, and Gyges — in strong chains for their reckless, terrifying size and hid them beneath the broad earth. But the sons of Cronos brought them up to the light at Gaia's own telling, having learned that with them the victory would be theirs against the Titans: the three sat sullenly below the earth's rim, suffering enormous grief, until the son of Cronos and the immortal gods set them free.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Theogony, lines ca. 617-635 (Heumann 2021); not verbatim.

passages.text: Then the two sides staked their strengths at war: the Titan gods on high Othrys, the younger gods gathered on Olympus, who were born to fair-haired Rhea after bed with Cronos; and for ten long years without end they fought one another, hearts and anger taut with fury, and the battle gave no decision to either side, since the victory was shared equally between the blowing thorns of the two proud families.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Theogony, lines ca. 635-655 (Heumann 2021); not verbatim.

passages.text: Then Zeus gave the Hundred-Handed nectar and ambrosia to eat and drink, the food of the undying, and their souls grew high; and the master of gods spoke to them: you, brightnesses from below, remember my kindness in freeing you from the stony prison and the grievous darkness; now with your untouchable hands stand against the Titans in their battles for us. And Cottus answered for them all: they knew his famous mind; with clear minds and quivering strength they would battle for his kingship in the fearsome war.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Theogony, lines ca. 655-685 (Heumann 2021); not verbatim.

passages.text: They armed that day and drew lines of battle, and with them Zeus from heaven hurled bolt after bolt, the crash of the sky, wrapped in a twisting flame; the life-bearing earth boomed and burned; the rivers, the streams of Oceanus, and the endless sea boiled, and the hot blast carried to the Aether of both sides; and blind-eyed Chaos reeled and shuddered. Then the Hundred-Handed rose from among the front lines and hurled hails of stones, three hundred boulders one after another; the Titans buried the sky no more, and were thrown under the whole earth and bound there; the drop to murky Tartarus is more than nine days' fall for a bronze anvil.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Theogony, lines ca. 685-730 (Heumann 2021); not verbatim.

title.en: Zeus and Typhon, the Last Challenger
title.zh: 宙斯戰堤豐

region.en: Arima, under the earth (mythic geography)
region.zh: 阿里馬亞，大地深處（神話地理）

period: Composed c. 700 BCE (Heumann translation 2021)

source.work: Hesiod, Theogony, trans. Michael Heumann (2021), lines ca. 820-880

license: Poem public domain; translation CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 (Heumann 2021) — paraphrase only in this record

summary.en: Gaia's comeback after the defeat of the Titans is a last child begotten on Tartarus itself: Typhon, whose shoulders sprout a hundred snake-heads with flickering tongues of fire, whose hundred voices bellow, roar, yelp and hiss. One day's contest would have ended with Typhon king over gods and men, had Zeus not watched: he leaps from Olympus and burns the heads away, hurls the monster lame into Tartarus, and settles forever the weather-winds that still wreck ships and harvests.
summary.zh: 提坦敗亡後，該亞的最後反撲是與塔耳塔羅斯所生的堤豐：肩上百顆蛇頭、吐信帶火，百聲齊鳴，可獅吼、牛吼、犬吠、蛇嘶。若非宙斯戒備，一日之戰堤豐便將稱王。宙斯自奧林波斯躍下，燒盡百顆頭顱，擊癱巨怪擲入塔耳塔羅斯；他化為的風暴狂風，至今仍是損毀船隻與莊稼的天災。

sensitivity.note: Ancient literary source; no living community restrictions.

passages.text: When Zeus had driven the Titans out of heaven, huge Gaia bore with Tartarus her youngest child, Typhon, whose hands were made for deeds of strength and whose feet were tireless. On his shoulders sat a hundred snake-heads of a fearsome dragon, each in its own pattern; his eyes flashed fire from every head, every head glared flame on every side, and fire darted from every one of all those glares and mouths.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Theogony, lines ca. 820-835 (Heumann 2021); not verbatim.

passages.text: Every voice in all the heads poured out voices unspeakable: sometimes such as the gods might understand, sometimes the bellow of a furious bull, sometimes like the proud roar of a lion, sometimes like whelps beneath their mother, wondrous to hear, sometimes hissing tall mountain-music, so that a terrible echo went round the rocks. Had not the father of gods and men been watching, that day would have ended with Typhon king over mortals and immortals alike.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Theogony, lines ca. 830-845 (Heumann 2021); not verbatim.

passages.text: Zeus thundered hard and mightily, and the earth about him, the sky above him, the sea, the courses of Ocean, and Tartarus itself shook. Great Olympus trembled under the immortal feet of the king as he came leaping in with his weapons, and all around him heat and flame and thunder exploded; the violet sea was consumed by the heat of the fire and flame and hasty wind and blazing lightnings, and the undying earth and sea and sky boiled over. The crash and the quaking came down deep into Tartarus, and Cronos and the Titans who lived there trembled with fear under the endless roar of the terrible combat-strife.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Theogony, lines ca. 845-860 (Heumann 2021); not verbatim.

passages.text: With thunder and lightning in his grip Zeus leapt out and burnt all the marvelous heads about the tremendous monster; and when he had beaten him down with blows, that huge thing fell lame, and the broad earth groaned. Flames went out from the thunder-lord into the cliff-girt dells below, burning much of the strange earth, melting it like tin in a skillful youth's crucible, or iron tamed in mountain dells by blazing fire: so the earth melted in the flash of the thunderbolt. With wrath in his heart Zeus threw him whole into wide Tartarus; and out of Typhon the strength of the wet, blowing winds is always blowing, useless winds whose storms toss ships and drown sailors and wreck the works of men upon the land.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Theogony, lines ca. 860-880 (Heumann 2021); not verbatim.

title.en: The Five Ages of Mankind
title.zh: 人類五大時代

region.en: Ascra, Boeotia (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 波厄提亞阿斯克拉村（象徵性定位）

period: Composed c. 700 BCE (Kelk translation 2020)

source.work: Hesiod, Works and Days, trans. Christopher Kelk (2020), lines ca. 106-210

license: Poem public domain; translation © 2020 Chris Kelk (free non-commercial use) — paraphrase only in this record

summary.en: A second story for Perses, 'which I will tell you skilfully': the gods made first a golden race under Cronus, then silver, then bronze, then a noble race of heroes swallowed up by war at Thebes and Troy, and finally the iron race — Hesiod's own — in which he wishes he had not been born.
summary.zh: 赫西俄德再講一則故事給佩耳塞斯：諸神先在克洛諾斯治下造黃金一族，其後白銀、青銅，再造亡於忒拜與特洛伊戰爭的英雄族，最後是鐵之族——詩人所在的當世，勞苦無休、父子相疏、義理蕩然，他寧願自己未生於此世。

sensitivity.note: Ancient literary source; no living community restrictions.

passages.text: The gods who dwell on Olympus first made a golden race of men who lived in the time of Cronus, when he ruled in heaven. They lived like gods with care-free hearts, remote from toil and misery; and dismal age did not abide with them, but they danced away from pain; and they rejoiced in festivals, with the dear gods nearby. Then in death they lay as if overcome by sleep; and all good things were theirs, for the fruitful earth unasked would bring forth for them fruits in their season, so that freely, in peace and quiet, they drove back the land with many flocks. This race was buried beneath the earth, but they became, by high Zeus's device, holy spirits upon the earth, guardians of mortal men — watching over judgments and wicked deeds, girded in mist, roaming everywhere over the earth, givers of wealth: this kingly office was theirs.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Works and Days, lines ca. 106-135 (Kelk 2020); not verbatim.

passages.text: Then they who dwell on Olympus made a second race, of silver, far inferior, in body and in mind. A child was bred up a hundred years at his mother's knee, playing about the house, a great bawling innocent; but when they grew up and came to their full measure, they lived but a brief time in suffering and sorrow, through their own foolishness; they could not hold back their own arrogance, and they were not willing to worship the blessed gods, nor to sacrifice upon the holy altars of the blessed ones, as is due law among men. Then Zeus, in wrath, hid them under the earth, because they gave no honour to the blessed gods who dwell on Olympus.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Works and Days, lines ca. 140-155 (Kelk 2020); not verbatim.

passages.text: Zeus the father made a third race, of bronze, in no wise like the ones of old: terrible and strong men, all their delight in works of war and violence; their food was not the grain of the earth, and their limbs and souls were of adamant; their weapons were bronze, their houses bronze, their tools of bronze, for as yet there was no black iron. They were brought down by their own hands, and went down nameless to the mouldy house of chill Hades, never seen again once black death had taken them.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Works and Days, lines ca. 155-170 (Kelk 2020); not verbatim.

passages.text: Then, upon the earth, Zeus son of Cronus made a fourth race, more just and better: the godly race of heroes, who are called half-gods, the race before ours on the boundless earth. But evil war and the dread battle-line destroyed some of them — some at seven-gated Thebes, in Cadmus' land, dying for the flocks of Oedipus; and others brought in ships over the great gulf of the sea to Troy for the sake of fair-haired Helen. There some were covered by the earth; but to others Zeus the father, son of Cronus, gave life and homes apart from men, at the ends of the earth, where they dwell with carefree hearts in the Isles of the Blessed by the deep-eddying ocean; and the earth bears them sweet fruit three times a year, while Cronus still rules among them.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Works and Days, lines ca. 170-190 (Kelk 2020); not verbatim.

passages.text: And Zeus made a fifth race, of men upon the bountiful earth, and I wish, he said, that I may not be among them; but either I had died before, or been born afterwards. For now the race is indeed one of iron; and never by day shall they rest from toil and sorrow, nor by night from being worn away; and the gods shall give them heavy troubles. Yet even so good shall be mingled with their evils. And Zeus shall destroy this race too, when children are born with grey hair on their temples. Nor shall the father be one with his children, nor children with their father, nor guest with host, nor comrade with comrade, nor shall brother be dear to brother as of old. Men shall dishonour their parents as soon as they are old, reviling them with hard words; and there shall be no grace for the man who keeps his oath, nor for the just, nor for the good: the devouring of wrong shall prosper, and shame shall no longer be. And at the last, from the broad-pathed earth, Majesty and Awe, wrapped in fair robes, shall leave the dwelling of men and go up to Olympus, forsaking mankind; and there shall be nothing left against the evil but sorrow.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Works and Days, lines ca. 190-210 (Kelk 2020); not verbatim.

title.en: The Hawk and the Nightingale
title.zh: 鷹與夜鶯

region.en: Ascra, Boeotia (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 波厄提亞阿斯克拉村（象徵性定位）

period: Composed c. 700 BCE (Kelk translation 2020)

source.work: Hesiod, Works and Days, trans. Christopher Kelk (2020), lines ca. 202-285

license: Poem public domain; translation © 2020 Chris Kelk (free non-commercial use) — paraphrase only in this record

summary.en: To his brother Perses, who has taken him to law before bribed judges, Hesiod tells a fable: a hawk gripping a nightingale in its talons mocks the small bird's crying — the strong can do what they like with the weak. But humans are not birds: for them Zeus has established Justice, which blesses the just city and ruins the extortionate.
summary.zh: 對已分產涉訟、賄賂法官的弟弟佩耳塞斯，赫西俄德講了一則寓言：高空中鷹爪抓住夜鶯，嘲弄其可憐哀鳴——強者可任意處置弱者。但人非鳥類：宙斯已為人類立下正義，公正之城因而興盛，貪暴之徒必遭現世報。

sensitivity.note: Ancient literary source; no living community restrictions.

passages.text: Hesiod told the lords and judges a fable that they, being wise, could read. A hawk had seized a speckled nightingale in its talons and was carrying it up through the clouds; the little bird hung there weeping out its piteous cry, pierced by the bent claws that held it fast.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Works and Days, lines ca. 202-215 (Kelk 2020); not verbatim.

passages.text: The hawk said to it scornfully: 'Wretched thing, why do you cry out? One far stronger than you holds you; you go wherever I take you. I will make you my dinner if I wish, or I may let you go. He is a fool who tries to contend against those stronger than himself: he loses the struggle and is insulted on top of it.' So spoke the swift-winged bird, the lordly one filled with pride.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Works and Days, lines ca. 215-231 (Kelk 2020); not verbatim.

passages.text: But Perses should listen to justice, and not exalt violence; this is the law the son of Cronus has made for men, for fish and beasts and winged birds eat one another, since there is no justice among them; but to men Zeus has given Justice, which is far the best. A man who knows and declares it, Zeus enriches; but a perjurer who deliberately does wrong has a descendant left to darkness, while his enemy's household prospers.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Works and Days, lines ca. 274-300 (Kelk 2020); not verbatim.

passages.text: Zeus sent thirty thousand watchers upon the earth, servants of the god, who oversee mankind, mixing unseen, over all the earth; and Justice, the daughter of Zeus, reports to him all crooked judgments. When judges swallow bribes, woe to the city: plague and famine come, women are barren, and houses dwindle. But when straight judgments are given, the city blooms, children grow, the earth yields acorns and honey, the sheep are heavy with wool, and there is abundance on the earth. So Hesiod warned the gift-swallowing lords to straighten the crooked decisions, for the watcher sees all, and the eye of Zeus observes all things.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Works and Days, lines ca. 240-285 (Kelk 2020); not verbatim.

title.en: Pandora and the Jar
title.zh: 潘多拉與罐中諸惡

region.en: Ascra, Boeotia (Hesiod's village; symbolic pin)
region.zh: 波厄提亞阿斯克拉村（赫西俄德故鄉，象徵性定位）

period: Composed c. 700 BCE (Kelk translation 2020)

source.work: Hesiod, Works and Days, trans. Christopher Kelk (2020), lines ca. 57-105

license: Poem public domain; translation © 2020 Chris Kelk (free non-commercial use) — paraphrase only in this record

summary.en: Because Prometheus stole fire, Zeus commissions a trap for men: Hephaestus fashions a maiden from clay, each god contributes an ornament or a flaw — beauty, weaving, lies, a shameless nature — and she is called Pandora. Hermes delivers her to Epimetheus, who forgets his brother's warning; she opens the great jar and scatters the whole race of ills upon mankind, keeping only Hope inside under the lid.
summary.zh: 因普羅米修斯盜火，宙斯設計陷害人類：赫菲斯托斯以黏土塑造少女，諸神各贈其一飾或一病——美貌、織布、謊言與羞怯——並名之潘多拉。赫爾墨斯將她送至厄庇墨透斯，他忘卻兄長的警告；她揭開大罐，人間從此疾病苦難橫行，唯希望獨存於罐中。

sensitivity.note: Ancient literary source; the myth carries Hesiod's misogyny and is presented as historical material without endorsement.

passages.text: In spite over the theft, Zeus prepared a second mischief to afflict mankind. He ordered the celebrated lame god, famed Hephaestus, to mix earth and water and to put in it the voice and strength of a human being, with the face of a goddess, a beautiful, sweet-looking girl. Athena was to teach her woman's skills, to weave richly-worked cloth of various kinds; golden Aphrodite was to pour grace about her head and painful desire and heavy-weariness that shakes the limbs; Hermes, the Argus-killer, was to add a dog's mind and a thieving disposition.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Works and Days, lines ca. 57-90 (Kelk 2020); not verbatim.

passages.text: At Zeus's word the famed lame god immediately moulded the likeness of a modest maiden from the earth, as Cronus's son had commanded. The grey-eyed queen Athena arrayed her and fastened her girdle; the divine Graces and our lady Persuasion hung golden necklaces upon her; the fair-tressed Hours crowned her with spring flowers; and Pallas Athena adorned her person fully. And in her breast the Argus-killer Hermes, by the contriving of loud-thundering Zeus, put lies and guile, a thieving nature, and a shameless spirit.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Works and Days, lines ca. 90-100 (Kelk 2020); not verbatim.

passages.text: Since all the Olympians had given a gift, her name was called Pandora, Bane of Men, on whose account the gods above all hatched this perfect snare in man's way, sending to Epimetheus the swift messenger of the gods, the Argus-slayer, with the gift. Epimetheus took no thought of the warning that Prometheus had given him — never to receive a gift from Zeus, but to send it back, lest some evil happen to men. He accepted her, and only when he had the evil did he see it at last.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Works and Days, lines ca. 90-105 (Kelk 2020); not verbatim.

passages.text: For before that no trouble, no disease, and no suffering had ever darkened this race's days: men used to live free of them. But the woman took off the great lid of the jar with her hands and scattered its contents; she dealt portentous griefs to men, and only Hope remained within the unbreakable jar beneath its rim, and did not fly out, because the lid stayed on it, by the will of Aegis-bearing Zeus. But other innumerable troubles wandered among men; the earth was full of evils, and the sea was full. So mankind had diseases to endure day and night of their own accord, in silence, since Zeus devised voicelessness for them. There is no way to escape the will of Zeus.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Works and Days, lines ca. 100-105 (Kelk 2020); not verbatim.

title.en: Heracles, the Wonderful Shield, and the Death of Cycnus
title.zh: 赫拉克勒斯神盾與刻克努斯之死

region.en: Grove of Apollo at Pagasae, Thessaly (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 色薩利帕加薩阿波羅聖林（象徵性定位）

period: Composed c. 6th century BCE (?), attributed to Hesiod (Evelyn-White translation 1914)

source.work: Ps.-Hesiod, Shield of Heracles, trans. Hugh G. Evelyn-White (1914), lines ca. 1-480

summary.en: Zeus comes by night to Alcmene, Amphitryon's faithful wife, while her husband is away burning the villages of the Taphians; she bears twins — Iphicles to her mortal husband, Heracles to the god. Years later Heracles and his charioteer Iolaus face Cycnus, the cruel son of Ares, and Ares himself in Apollo's grove: the god's new-made shield, emblazoned with Fear and battle-panic, cities and weddings and the Fates clawing at the fallen, protects the hero while he spears Cycnus through the neck and wounds Ares in the thigh, and Panic and Terror drive the raging war-god screaming back to Olympus.
summary.zh: 宙斯乘夜降臨安菲特律翁貞潔之妻阿爾克墨涅，其夫正赴塔福斯征戰；她產下雙胎：伊菲克勒斯屬凡父，赫拉克勒斯屬於神。日後赫拉克勒斯與御者伊俄拉俄斯在阿波羅聖林迎戰阿瑞斯之子刻克努斯及戰神本人：神匠特製的神盾滿怖恐懼與戰慄、城邦婚禮與抓拿亡者的命運女神，護著英雄以矛貫穿刻克努斯頸項，又刺傷阿瑞斯大腿；恐慌與恐怖二神架車，把咆哮的戰神送回奧林波斯。

sensitivity.note: Ancient literary source; no living community restrictions.

passages.text: Alcmena, daughter of Electryon, came to Thebes as the wife of Amphitryon, who had fled Tiryns after killing her father in a quarrel over oxen, and went suppliant to the shield-bearing men of Cadmus; until he had avenged her brothers and burned the villages of the Taphians and Teleboans, he might not go in to his wife, and the gods stood witness to the bargain. But Zeus, father of gods and men, was weaving another plan: to beget a defender who would keep both gods and bread-eating men from ruin. So one night he came down from Olympus and lay with Alcmene; and that same night her husband too, home from his heavy task, lay with her, rejoicing like a man escaped out of sickness or chains.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Shield of Heracles, lines ca. 1-56 (Evelyn-White 1914); not verbatim.

passages.text: She bore two sons in seven-gated Thebes, brothers unlike in spirit: Iphicles, weaker, of Amphitryon's fathering; and the terrible strong Heracles, the joy of Zeus of the dark clouds. Years on, with Alcmena's son grown, Zeus showered gifts upon him: the practice of killing Cycnus, the gallant son of Ares, in the close-grown grove of far-shooting Apollo — father and son stood in a chariot with armour like blazing fire, dust about their wheels; Cycnus wished aloud to strip their splendid armour, but Phoebus Apollo, who had stirred Heracles against him, would not listen.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Shield of Heracles, lines ca. 57-88 (Evelyn-White 1914); not verbatim.

passages.text: Heracles armed at the grove of Apollo: greaves, a golden breastplate of Athena's giving, a hollow quiver of death-bearing arrows, a spear, a close-fitted adamant helmet — and a shield the smith-god had made for him, a marvel no blow could break: in its centre Fear, unutterable, staring backward with eyes of fire, gnashing a white row of teeth; about him Strife, and Pursuit and Flight, and Panic, and Slaughter; deadly Fate dragging a newly-wounded man and casting behind him one already dead; twelve snake-heads on the rim to terrify the foes of the son of Zeus; and then the whole world by way of interleaf: boars and lions at battle, the Lapith spearmen against the Centaurs, Ares in his chariot and the drive of spoil-winning Athena, Olympus itself with Apollo playing the lyre and the Muses beginning their song, a tin-built harbour of darting dolphins and a watchful fisherman, Perseus flying with the winged sandals and the Gorgon's head in its silver bag while the immortal Gorgons storm after him on Adamantine paths, a city of dance and torchlight and festivals, ploughmen and vintage-men and boxers and wrestler, horse-race about a golden tripod, and Ocean flowing around the whole rim of the shield with swans above and fish below.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Shield of Heracles, lines ca. 139-326 (Evelyn-White 1914); not verbatim.

passages.text: Grey-eyed Athena came to the warriors' car and told Heracles the plan of battle: when Cycnus fell he was to leave the body and its armour, and watch only the man-slaying Ares, striking wherever he saw flesh uncovered beneath the cunning shield, then drawing back — it was not fated that he should take the god's horses or splendid armour. At her word they bore down; the earth rang; and Heracles called Cycnus to guide his car aside and yield the road, for he drove to Trachis, to Ceyx the king: already the war-god had thrice been dashed to earth by this spear at sandy Pylos, and the fourth thrust had cut his thigh and thrown him headlong. Cycnus heeded nothing: from their cars they sprang to the ground with a great shout, like two lions over a slain deer; Zeus thundered loud and rained drops of blood, the signal of battle for his dauntless son.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Shield of Heracles, lines ca. 327-401 (Evelyn-White 1914); not verbatim.

passages.text: Cycnus cast his brazen spear and could not break the bronze; but Heracles struck him in the neck beneath the chin, where the throat lies unguarded between helmet and shield, and the two sinews were cut through; Cycnus fell like a tall pine hit by Zeus's thunderbolt, his armour clashing about him. Then Ares came at him with grief for his dead son: he hurled his spear at the great shield, and Athena turned its force aside; and when the god drew his sword and leapt upon the son of Amphitryon, Heracles shrewdly wounded his bare thigh under the richly-wrought shield and tore deep into the flesh, and dashed him flat on the ground. Swiftly Panic and Terror drew near and lifted Ares into his chariot and lashed the horses to high Olympus. So Heracles and Iolaus stripped the armour from the dead Cycnus and drove their horses to Trachis; and Ceyx buried the fallen man — though a rain-swollen Anaurus later, on Apollo's orders, blotted out his grave and memorial, because he had been a plunderer of the rich hecatombs brought to Pytho.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Shield of Heracles, lines ca. 402-480 (Evelyn-White 1914); not verbatim.

title.en: The Children of Night
title.zh: 黑夜的兒女

region.en: Ascra, Boeotia (Hesiod's home; symbolic pin)
region.zh: 波厄提亞阿斯克拉村（赫西俄德故鄉，象徵性定位）

period: Composed c. 700 BCE (Evelyn-White translation 1914)

source.work: Hesiod, Theogony, trans. Hugh G. Evelyn-White (1914), lines ca. 211-232

summary.en: Born without a bedfellow, black Night brought forth the kindred of mortal fear: Doom, Death, Sleep and Dreams, the Hesperides, Blame and Woe, the Fates and the death-spirits, Nemesis, Deceit, Friendship, Old Age, and last of all Strife — whose own children are Toil, Forgetfulness, Hunger, Pains, Battles, Murders, Quarrels, Lies, Lawlessness, and Oath.
summary.zh: 黑夜無偶而生：命運、死亡、睡與夢、赫斯珀里得斯、譴責與悲苦、命運三女神與報應女神、欺瞞與友愛、老邁，最後是紛爭——紛爭復生勞苦、遺忘、飢餓、悲苦、戰陣、凶殺、口角、謊言、無法與誓言。

sensitivity.note: Ancient literary source; no living community restrictions.

passages.text: Hesiod's catalogue of the divine families reaches next to Earth's dark kin. From Chaos had come Erebos and black Night; and Night, without sleeping with any god, brought forth Doom and Death and sleep herself, and the race of Dreams; she bore too the Hesperides, who tend beyond glorious Ocean the golden apples and the trees that bear them.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Theogony, lines ca. 211-222 (Evelyn-White 1914); not verbatim.

passages.text: Night brought forth also the Moirai, the Fates, and the Keres, the death-spirits who pursue offenders: Clotho, Lachesis, and Atropos, who give men at their birth both good and evil, and who pursue the transgressions of gods and men — the goddesses whose wrath never ceases until they have punished the sinner with a heavy penalty. And Nemesis, that evil for mortals, is Night's child also, and after her Deceit and Friendship and cruel Old Age, and, strong-hearted Strife.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Theogony, lines ca. 217-226 (Evelyn-White 1914); not verbatim.

passages.text: Strife, in turn, had a brood of her own: Toil, Forgetfulness, Famine and grievous Pains; Combats, Battles, Manslaughters, Murders; Quarrels, Lying words, Disputes; Lawlessness and Ruin, all of one kin, and Oath, who brings men their greatest sorrow when they swear a false oath out of willingness. The night-brood is thus a map of the misfortunes that stalk human life.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Theogony, lines ca. 226-232 (Evelyn-White 1914); not verbatim.

title.en: Goddesses and Mortal Lovers
title.zh: 女神與凡人戀人

region.en: Crete to Troy (mythic geography)
region.zh: 克里特至特洛伊（神話地理）

period: Composed c. 700 BCE (Evelyn-White translation 1914)

source.work: Hesiod, Theogony, trans. Hugh G. Evelyn-White (1914), lines ca. 960-1018

summary.en: Now the Muses sing the race of goddesses who lay with men: Demeter with Iasion in a thrice-ploughed field, bearing Wealth; Eos with Tithonus, bearing Memnon of the gushing river Ethiope kingship; Thetis with Peleus, bearing single-hearted Achilles scatterer of men; Aphrodite with Anchises on Ida, bearing Aeneas; Circe and Calypso with Odysseus; and Medea, golden Aphrodite's kiss on Aeetes' daughter, wed to Jason.
summary.zh: 繆斯繼而歌詠與凡人交合的女神一系：得墨忒耳於三度新耕之田與伊阿西翁生財神普路托斯；厄俄斯與提托諾斯生門儂；忒提斯與珀琉斯生疏敵蕩手的阿基琉斯；阿芙洛狄忒於伊達山與安喀塞斯生埃涅阿斯；喀耳刻與卡呂普索皆戀奧德修斯；美狄亞為埃厄忒斯之女、得金劍之戀而下嫁伊阿宋。

sensitivity.note: Ancient literary source; no living community restrictions.

passages.text: Fair-cheeked Demeter lay with the hero Iasion in a thrice-ploughed fallow field in the fruitful land of Crete, and bore Plutus, the kindly god who walks the whole earth and the back of the sea; the man who meets him and takes him by the hand is enriched, for Wealth brims his hands with substance. And golden Aphrodite's daughter Harmonia, wed to Cadmus, bore Ino, Semele, fair-cheeked Agave, Autonoe, and Polydorus, in the fair-meadowed halls of Thebes.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Theogony, lines ca. 963-980 (Evelyn-White 1914); not verbatim.

passages.text: And Eos bore to Tithonus the bronze-helmeted Memnon, king of the Aethiopians, and lord Emathion; and to Cephalus a shining son, mighty Phaethon, a god among mortal men: while he was still a delicate youth in tender flower, laughter-loving Aphrodite seized him up and made him her nightly watchman of sacred temples, a shining guardian. And by the plan of the immortal gods the strong son of Aeson, Jason, bore off from Aeetes' halls the daughter of Zeus-honoured Aeetes — after the many grievous tasks set him by the wild king — and brought her home to Iolcus by night, on the swift ship, with rosy-cheeked Medea, child of golden Aphrodite's force upon Idyia's blood-line, and wed her: she bore Medus, whom the centaur Chiron reared in the mountains.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Theogony, lines ca. 984-1000 (Evelyn-White 1914); not verbatim.

passages.text: The daughters of the Old Man of the Sea came last: subtle-minded Psamathe bore to Aeacus the great Phocus; and silver-footed Thetis, wedding Peleus, bore the lion-hearted Achilles, the scatterer of ranks. And Cyprus-born Cytherea lay with Anchises on the peaks of windy Ida with its many glens, and bore Aeneas. Circe, child of Helios, bore to the enduring Odysseus Agrius and Latinus, lordly rulers of the far Tyrrhenian isles; and Calypso, nymph of Ogygia, bore him Nausithous and Nausinous: and so the line of heroes was braided into the dynasty of the gods.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Theogony, lines ca. 1010-1018 (Evelyn-White 1914); not verbatim.

title.en: Echidna's Brood: The Womb of Monsters
title.zh: 厄喀德那的子嗣：怪物之母

region.en: Arima caverns (mythic geography)
region.zh: 阿里馬亞洞窟（神話地理）

period: Composed c. 700 BCE (Evelyn-White translation 1914)

source.work: Hesiod, Theogony, trans. Hugh G. Evelyn-White (1914), lines ca. 295-338

summary.en: In a cave beyond the reach of gods and men lives Echidna, half nymph and half raw-flesh-eating serpent, mate of Typhon. She bears Orthrus the two-headed dog, Cerberus of Hades, the Lernaean Hydra, and the fire-breathing Chimera; and the Chimera, mated to Orthrus, in turn bears the Sphinx and the Nemean lion — the whole catalogue of heroes' monsters.
summary.zh: 厄喀德那半身仙子、半身食生肉之蛇，棲於人神難至的阿斯洞穴，配堤豐而生雙首犬俄耳托斯、冥府犬刻耳柏洛斯、勒拿九頭蛇與噴火奇美拉；奇美拉再配俄耳托斯，誕下忒拜的斯芬克斯與尼米亞獅——英雄們的怪物世界由此而出。

sensitivity.note: Ancient literary source; no living community restrictions.

passages.text: In a hollow cave beneath a great rock, far from immortal gods and mortal men, the gods keep the house of Echidna: a quick-glancing maiden above, a terrible snake below that eats raw flesh in hidden places under the earth. There, it is told, she lay with the violent and lawless Typhon, and, gotten with child, bore his fearsome brood.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Theogony, lines ca. 297-308 (Evelyn-White 1914); not verbatim.

passages.text: Her first-born was Orthrus, the herdsman-dog of Geryon; next Cerberus, devourer of raw flesh, the bronze-voiced dog of Hades, fifty-headed, pitiless and powerful; then the Lernaean Hydra of evil heart, whom white-armed Hera reared in wrath against Heracles — but Heracles, son of Zeus, slew it too with pitiless bronze, helped by Iolaus and Athena's cunning.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Theogony, lines ca. 309-318 (Evelyn-White 1914); not verbatim.

passages.text: Echidna bore the invincible Chimera, fire-breathing, huge and swift: three heads, lion and she-goat and serpent; lion before, goat behind, serpent at the tail, flame from each. Pegasus and noble Bellerophon destroyed her. And the Chimera mated with Orthrus and brought forth the doom-laden Sphinx to spite the men of Cadmus, and the Nemean lion, bane of mortals, whom Zeus's queen Hera raised and set in the Nemean valley to lay waste the tribes of men, until the strength of Heracles overcame it too.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Theogony, lines ca. 319-330 (Evelyn-White 1914); not verbatim.

title.en: Perseus and the Beheading of Medusa
title.zh: 珀爾修斯斬美杜莎

region.en: Beyond Oceanus, lair of the Gorgons (mythic geography)
region.zh: 大洋之外，戈耳貢巢穴（神話地理）

period: Composed c. 700 BCE (Evelyn-White translation 1914)

source.work: Hesiod, Theogony, trans. Hugh G. Evelyn-White (1914), lines ca. 270-287

summary.en: Phorcys and Ceto bore the immortal Gorgons beyond Ocean, and of them Medusa alone was mortal. Poseidon lay with her in a flowered meadow, and when Perseus cut off her head, great Chrysaor — wielder of the golden sword — sprang out, and the horse Pegasus, who flew up to the immortals and carries the thunderbolts of Zeus.
summary.zh: 福爾庫斯與刻托在大洋之外育出不朽的戈耳貢三姊妹，唯美杜莎為可死之身。波塞頓曾與她於花間草甸交歡；珀爾修斯斬下其首後，持金劍的克律薩俄耳與神馬珀伽索斯一齊躍出，神馬飛抵不死族，為宙斯馱運雷霆。

sensitivity.note: Ancient literary source; no living community restrictions.

passages.text: Sea's old man Phorcys wed the deep Ceto, and their children glittered at the edge of the world: the grey-haired Graiae, sisters born with grey from the womb, and the Gorgons who dwell beyond glorious Ocean at the edge of night where the clear-voiced Hesperides keep house — Sthenno and Euryale, immortal and ageless forever, and Medusa alone of the three was mortal.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Theogony, lines ca. 270-281 (Evelyn-White 1914); not verbatim.

passages.text: The dark-haired Poseidon had lain with Medusa in a soft meadow among the spring flowers; and so when the hero Perseus cut off her head, the Gorgon's death was also a birth-opening: out of her neck came the great Chrysaor and the foal Pegasus, the one named for the gold sword he bore, the other born by the water's edge.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Theogony, lines ca. 277-285 (Evelyn-White 1914); not verbatim.

passages.text: Pegasus left the earth, mother of flocks, and flew up to the immortals: he dwells thereafter in the house of Zeus, bringing to his king the well-woven thunder and lightning that the god hurls. Chrysaor, in turn, married Callirrhoe, daughter of Ocean, and she bore him the triple-headed Geryon, whom Heracles would one day kill for his shambling cattle on the far island of Erytheia.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Theogony, lines ca. 283-295 (Evelyn-White 1914); not verbatim.

title.en: The Marriages of Zeus
title.zh: 宙斯的婚姻

region.en: Mount Olympus (mythic geography)
region.zh: 奧林波斯山（神話地理）

period: Composed c. 700 BCE (Evelyn-White translation 1914)

source.work: Hesiod, Theogony, trans. Hugh G. Evelyn-White (1914), lines ca. 881-930

summary.en: After the wars, Zeus the king takes his wives in order, and each marriage brings an office into the settled world: Metis — whom he swallows outright, so that Athena may be born from his head; Themis, who bears the Seasons and the Fates; Eurynome the Graces; Demeter Persephone; Mnemosyne the nine Muses; Leto Apollo and Artemis; and Hera, queen and last, whose fury at Athena's head-birth brings forth Hephaestus without a father.
summary.zh: 戰事既畢，宙斯依次娶妻，每一樁婚姻都為新秩序帶來執掌：吞下智慧女神墨提斯，雅典娜自其首而出；忒彌斯生時序三女神與命運三女神；歐律諾墨生美惠三女神；得墨忒耳生珀耳塞福涅；謨涅摩敘涅生九繆斯；勒托生阿波羅與阿爾忒彌斯；末娶赫拉，竟因雅典娜降生而獨自生下赫菲斯托斯。

sensitivity.note: Ancient literary source; no living community restrictions.

passages.text: First Zeus took Metis, wisest of gods and men, for his wife. But when she was on the point of bearing Athena, the crafty king talked her round, and gulped her down into his belly — for Earth and starry Heaven had warned him that Metis was fated to bear children beyond his throne: first the flashing daughter equal to her father in mind and strength, and then a son, a king of gods and men with a proud heart. Zeus swallowed the danger, and his own belly became the child's chamber.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Theogony, lines ca. 881-900 (Evelyn-White 1914); not verbatim.

passages.text: Next he wedded shining Themis, who bore the Horae — Lawfulness, Justice and blooming Peace, who watch over the works of mortal men — and the Fates, Clotho, Lachesis and Atropos, whom the cunning Zeus honoured above all, for they allot mortal men good and evil alike. Then Eurynome, child of Ocean, bore the Graces — Aglae, Euphrosyne and Thalia — whose glances loosen desire and delight the eyes; and bountiful Demeter bore gleaming-armed Persephone, whom Hades stole from her mother with the nod of Zeus.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Theogony, lines ca. 901-915 (Evelyn-White 1914); not verbatim.

passages.text: Then Zeus loved the lovely-haired Mnemosyne, who bore the nine gold-banded Muses of Pieria, painters of laughter and sweet song; and Leto, who bore Apollo of the silver bow and Artemis of the arrow, dearest children of Heaven. Last of all he made his own flourishing queen Hera, who bore Hebe of the golden crown, Ares of the dreadful war-cry, and Eileithyia of childbed.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Theogony, lines ca. 915-922 (Evelyn-White 1914); not verbatim.

passages.text: But there was no joy even in its end: when Hera saw how Zeus — and Zeus alone, without a mother in the deed — had birthed grey-eyed Athena, terrible in arms and sacker of cities, anger came into her heart, and she conceived without mingling in love, and by her own device bore Hephaestus, the craftsman whose hands surpassed every son of Heaven; and thus the smith-god entered the world god-born differently from all his kin.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Theogony, lines ca. 925-930 (Evelyn-White 1914); not verbatim.

title.en: Lucky Days and the Thirty Thousand Watchers
title.zh: 吉日與三萬監神

region.en: Ascra, Boeotia (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 波厄提亞阿斯克拉村（象徵性定位）

period: Composed c. 700 BCE (Evelyn-White translation 1914)

source.work: Hesiod, Works and Days, trans. Hugh G. Evelyn-White (1914), lines ca. 240-285, 724-828

summary.en: The poem closes Hesiod's lesson in time: the days the gods have marked out are gods' gifts — a man must know them and teach his slaves, for the thirtieth is best for meting out rations, the first, fourth and seventh are sacred days, and none should urinate standing toward the sun nor cross a river with unpurged hands. Below it all runs the belief threaded through Works and Days: Zeus has thirty thousand watchers over men's deeds in the mist of earth, recording judgments and merciless acts.
summary.zh: 《勞作與時日》以時間之學收尾：諸神劃定的日子是神賜——須識而教僕，三十日宜分食舍，每月第一、四、七日為聖日；人們不該面向太陽撒尿，亦不可未洗手便過河。而貫穿全詩的信念是：宙斯派駐人間的三萬守望神，在塵霧中記錄每一樁審判與惡行。

sensitivity.note: Ancient literary source; no living community restrictions.

passages.text: Hesiod ends by teaching Perses the days Zeus has marked out on the month — folk should know and teach them to their household. The thirtieth day is best for the housekeeper's tasks of meting out and weighing; sacred are the first, the fourth, and the seventh, for on the seventh Leto bore Apollo of the golden sword; the eighth and the ninth are good for opening the jars and for work among men.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Works and Days, lines ca. 750-780 (Evelyn-White 1914); not verbatim.

passages.text: Around the calendar he hangs a body of household taboo: wash your hands before you pour the dark wine to Zeus, or the god will not heed your prayers when you call; never urinate standing toward the sun, nor on the road of wayfarers, nor in a river; do not cross a shining stream with hands and guilt unstained, for the gods visit it with pain; never leave the mixing-bowl and the cup at once, nor the ladle in the bowl — fatal blend; get no twelve-year-old boy to sit upon the funeral mound; nor will a widow's water-jar serve for washings without penalty. For so it is that even small talk is holy among the gods.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Works and Days, lines ca. 724-752 (Evelyn-White 1914); not verbatim.

passages.text: Under all runs one doctrine: men's sins bring their own revenge. When one does harm to a beggar's suppliant or to his guest, or, wrapt in shamelessness, goes in to his brother's wife or the mother's orphan child, or rails at the father old upon his sorrowful bed, and gives offence to the gods, then at once the avenging judges watch. Zeus, they warn, has thirty thousand immortal watchers: watchers of divisions and judgments all over the earth, clothed in the mist of air, ever looking upon men's wrongful doings — and the eye of Zeus, they say, notes all and does not accidentally miss.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Works and Days, lines ca. 250-280, 750-759 (Evelyn-White 1914); not verbatim.

title.en: The Short Road Down and the Long Road Up
title.zh: 捷徑與長路

region.en: Ascra, Boeotia (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 波厄提亞阿斯克拉村（象徵性定位）

period: Composed c. 700 BCE (Evelyn-White translation 1914)

source.work: Hesiod, Works and Days, trans. Hugh G. Evelyn-White (1914), lines ca. 287-320

summary.en: Hesiod sketches the two roads a man can walk: wickedness is close, flat, and easy to take in armfuls; the gods have set the road to virtue on the opposite side — long, uphill, rough at first, but easy once you stand on the summit. He grades three kinds of men by how they grasp the future, and warns Perses that Hunger walks close behind the idle.
summary.zh: 赫西俄德描畫兩條路：作惡之路近在咫尺，平坦易行，線路可大量批取；而眾神把通向德行的路置於其上——漫長、陡峭、開端崎嶇，但登頂之後反覺輕鬆。他依「如何對待未來」把人分為三等，並警告佩耳塞斯：懶惰者身旁總跟著飢餓。

sensitivity.note: Ancient literary source; no living community restrictions.

passages.text: Hesiod gave Perses rules for good living, and drew the map of conduct as two roads. The way to wickedness is short and smooth: she lives just around the corner, and you can take her in armfuls. But between us and goodness the immortal gods have set sweat: the road to virtue is long and climbs, rough at the top of the climb; yet once a man stands at the summit, easy becomes the going.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Works and Days, lines ca. 287-295 (Evelyn-White 1914); not verbatim.

passages.text: He then rated mankind by its use of the future: that man is best of all who takes thought for his own affairs, weighing how the later thing shall come out best; good also is he who takes another's advice; but a man with no wits about him, who neither plans nor listens, is useless, pointless as chaff.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Works and Days, lines ca. 295-315 (Evelyn-White 1914); not verbatim.

passages.text: And the wages of each road are plain. Do the work the gods have cut out for you, and lay it up safely; contentious Perses must work with boldness, so that Hunger come not and Demeter be glad: the man who labours finds the barn full of Demeter's grain; the idle man has Hunger close at hand — the gods and men alike despise him, a stingless drone that eats the toil of the bees. Work is no shame; it is the idle man who eats his shame.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Works and Days, lines ca. 315-320 (Evelyn-White 1914); not verbatim.

title.en: The Two Strifes
title.zh: 兩種紛爭

region.en: Ascra, Boeotia (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 波厄提亞阿斯克拉村（象徵性定位）

period: Composed c. 700 BCE (Evelyn-White translation 1914)

source.work: Hesiod, Works and Days, trans. Hugh G. Evelyn-White (1914), lines ca. 11-41

summary.en: Opening his case against Perses, Hesiod distinguishes two goddesses both called Strife: one cruel, fosterer of battle, whom no man loves; the other set by Zeus in the roots of the earth, the elder daughter of Night, who rouses even the lazy to work and is good for men. He tells his brother to choose only the second strife — the healthy envy that fills barns — and not the court-hall quarrels of ruined men.
summary.zh: 赫西俄德向佩耳塞斯陳情：世上原不止一種紛爭女神。其一殘忍好戰，人皆厭之；另一是黑夜的長女，宙斯親置於大地之根，專激懶人上進，對人有益。他勸弟弟只取後者——催人耕作、盈滿穀倉的良性競爭，別再去衙門打那傾家蕩產的官司。

sensitivity.note: Ancient literary source; no living community restrictions.

passages.text: Hesiod began his teaching to Perses by correcting a common belief: there is not one Strife in the world, but two goddesses wearing the same name. One is heavy and hateful, fosters evil war and battle, and no man loves her — yet, by the will of the deathless gods, mortals are forced to pay her their honours.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Works and Days, lines ca. 11-17 (Evelyn-White 1914); not verbatim.

passages.text: The other Strife is the elder daughter of dark Night; Zeus, who dwells in the aether, set her in the roots of the earth, and she is far kinder to men. She stirs the sluggish to labour: a man who notices his neighbour growing rich hurries to plough, to plant, to set his house in order — potter strives with potter, craftsman with craftsman, beggar envies beggar, and minstrel envies minstrel. This Strife, the poet says, is wholesome for men.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Works and Days, lines ca. 17-25 (Evelyn-White 1914); not verbatim.

passages.text: So Perses must not let the god-hated Strife drag his heart from work while he lounges about listening to quarrels at the courthouse. He reminds his brother: you had no livelihood, and so wrangled; but that grain-store is the true prize — lay it up betimes, so that you need not go bothering others, for friends may tide you over once or twice, but not for ever; third appeal answers nothing.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Works and Days, lines ca. 25-35 (Evelyn-White 1914); not verbatim.

title.en: Bellerophon and the Chimera
title.zh: 柏勒洛豐與奇美拉

region.en: Corinth to Lycia (mythic geography)
region.zh: 科任托斯至呂基亞（神話地理）

period: Compiled c. 1st-2nd century CE (attrib. Apollodorus; Frazer translation 1921)

source.work: Apollodorus, Library, trans. J. G. Frazer (1921), §§ 2.3.1-2.3.2

summary.en: Falsely accused by Proetus' wife, Bellerophon is sent to Lycia with a sealed letter ordering his own death. King Iobates, reluctant to kill a guest outright, tasks him to the Chimera — lion before, dragon behind, goat in the middle belching fire — and Bellerophon, mounted on Pegasus the winged horse, destroys it, then the warlike Solymi, then the Amazons, and finally the ambush meant to kill him, until the king recognizes him and gives him his daughter and his throne.
summary.zh: 珀羅埃圖斯之妻誣告柏勒洛豐後，他被遣往呂基亞，攜密令其死的書信。伊俄巴忒斯王不便直接殺害客人，便先後派他對付奇美拉——獅首、龍尾、中間羊身噴火；柏勒洛豐乘波塞冬與美杜莎所生之天馬珀伽索斯騰空以計射殺之；歷索呂米人與亞馬遜人及伏兵而不死，王遂認其勇、以女相許並傳王位。

sensitivity.note: Ancient literary source; no living community restrictions.

passages.text: Bellerophon, son of Glaucus, grandson of Sisyphus, killed a kinsman by accident and was purified by Proetus of Tiryns. But Proetus' queen Stheneboea fell in love with him; and, when her offers were refused, she told her husband that the stranger had tried to seduce her. Proetus believed her, and, being unwilling to kill within his own walls, sent his guest to Lycia to his own father-in-law Iobates with a folded letter which read: kill the man who brings this.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Apollodorus, Library 2.3.1 (Frazer 1921); not verbatim.

passages.text: Iobates read the letter, and, rather than strike a guest himself, ordered his visitor to kill the Chimera. It was more than one man's match, though one man alone had been commanded to face it: a single creature being three beasts at once — a lion's foreparts, a dragon's tail, and the goat in its middle out of which it belched fire; and it devastated the land and the herds. Homer said it was bred by Amisodarus; on Hesiod's account, it was Typhon's offspring, begotten on Echidna.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Apollodorus, Library 2.3.1 (Frazer 1921); not verbatim.

passages.text: Bellerophon mounted Pegasus, the winged steed born of Medusa and Poseidon when Perseus severed her neck; and, soaring above the Chimera's reach, shot it down from the height. Iobates then sent him to fight the Solymi, and when that, too, was survived, to combat the Amazons; then finally he picked out the most valiant of the Lycians and set them in ambush to slay the returning hero. Bellerophon killed them to a man.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Apollodorus, Library 2.3.2 (Frazer 1921); not verbatim.

passages.text: So Iobates, in admiration of his prowess, read him the letter himself and besought him to stay; gave him his daughter Philonoe in marriage, and left him the kingdom at his death. The tale leaves him, like Bellerophon in Homer's telling, at the height of his fame — victorious where ten deaths had been ordered for him.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Apollodorus, Library 2.3.2 (Frazer 1921); not verbatim.

title.en: Cadmus and the Serpent of Ares
title.zh: 卡德穆斯與阿瑞斯龍

region.en: Thebes, Boeotia (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 波厄提亞底比斯（象徵性定位）

period: Compiled c. 1st-2nd century CE (attrib. Apollodorus; Frazer translation 1921)

source.work: Apollodorus, Library, trans. J. G. Frazer (1921), §§ 3.4.1-3.4.3

summary.en: Sent off to find a runaway sister, Cadmus is told by the Delphic oracle to stop looking and follow a cow instead. Where she kneels he founds Thebes after killing the dragon of Ares' sacred grove and sowing its teeth, which spring up as armed men. Penned as a labourer, he gains Harmonia, the daughter of Aphrodite and Ares, to wife; the gods turn the pair into serpents at last.
summary.zh: 卡德穆斯奉命尋妹未果，得德爾菲神諭：勿再追尋，隨一母牛而行；牛跪臥處建城。他殺死泉水旁阿瑞斯聖園的巨龍，依雅典娜之計播龍齒於土，出土武士相互殘殺、剩下數人，助其築起底比斯；後娶阿芙洛狄忒與阿瑞斯之女和諧女神為妻。傳說晚年二位終變為蛇。

sensitivity.note: Ancient literary source; no living community restrictions.

passages.text: When Europa was carried off by the bull, her father sent her brother Cadmus in search of her, with orders not to return empty-handed if he could not bring her back. From the oracle at Delphi he received his strange founding-instruction: the sister would not be sought; he was to follow a cow he met, and build his city where she knelt down.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Apollodorus, Library 3.4.1 (Frazer 1921); not verbatim.

passages.text: The cow of Phoenicia led him into Boeotia and sank down by a spring guarded by a serpent, the child of Ares. When Cadmus sent his men to fetch water for the sacrifice, the dragon destroyed them; and the hero came up with the great beast and crushed its head with a heavy stone.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Apollodorus, Library 3.4.1 (Frazer 1921); not verbatim.

passages.text: By Athena's suggestion he sowed the dragon's teeth in the ploughed field, and armed men came up out of the earth, called Sparti. He cast stones in their midst until they turned on one another and fought until only a handful remained; those he spared helped Cadmus raise the walls of Thebes.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Apollodorus, Library 3.4.1 (Frazer 1921); not verbatim.

passages.text: Ares came to Cadmus afterwards in anger for his serpent's killing, and required his service in servitude to punish him; afterwards his new marriage was arranged to atone for the death: Aphrodite's daughter Harmonia. And at his wedding Zeus of the shining thunder gave away the bride; and the gods themselves, it is said, took seats there. But the old serpent answers in the end: gods, angry at Cadmus and his snake-brood, made serpents of the two in their old age, and sent them abroad to foreign acres.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Apollodorus, Library 3.4.2-3.4.3 (Frazer 1921); not verbatim.

title.en: Meleager and the Calydonian Boar
title.zh: 墨勒阿格號與卡呂冬野豬

region.en: Calydon, Aetolia (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 埃托利亞卡呂冬（象徵性定位）

period: Compiled c. 1st-2nd century CE (attrib. Apollodorus; Frazer translation 1921)

source.work: Apollodorus, Library, trans. J. G. Frazer (1921), §§ 1.8.2-1.8.3

summary.en: A forgotten sacrifice brings Artemis' great boar down on Calydon. Oeneus summons the noblest of Greece — Meleager, Atalanta, Theseus, Castor and Pollux, Jason among them — to destroy it. Atalanta draws first blood; Meleager gives her the skin from his own kill; his uncles dispute the prize, he kills them, and his mother Althaea, avenging her slain brothers by burning the brand his life hangs on, kills her own son.
summary.zh: 因一場遺漏的祭禮，阿爾忒彌斯放出巨豬毀壞卡呂冬。俄紐斯召集全希臘名士——墨勒阿格號、阿塔蘭忒、忒修斯、狄俄斯庫里、伊阿宋等——合蒐其獸。阿塔蘭忒首箭中的，墨勒阿格號補槍斃豬並將皮贈予她；其舅氏爭皮，他怒而殺之，母親阿爾泰亞為亡兄復仇而焚燬生命之柴枝，兒子當場喪命。

sensitivity.note: Ancient literary source; no living community restrictions.

passages.text: When Meleager was seven days old the Fates stood over his cradle and declared that he would live so long as a certain brand burning on the hearth remained unconsumed; his mother Althaea snatched it up and locked it in a chest. The boy grew invulnerable and heroic. But when King Oeneus of Calydon, offering the first-fruits of every crop to all the gods, forgot Artemis alone, she sent down on the Aetolian land a boar of extraordinary size and strength, a beast that trampled the corn, and killed cattle and the men who stood in its way.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Apollodorus, Library 1.8.2 (Frazer 1921); not verbatim.

passages.text: Oeneus called a hunt for the noblest men of Greece, promising the beast's skin to whoever killed it. The muster was nearly the whole Achaean age: Meleager; the Dioscuri; Theseus; Admetus; Peleus; Telamon; Jason; Iphicles; Pirithous; Amphiaraus; the Arcadian brothers Ancaeus and Cepheus; and Atalanta, daughter of Schoeneus, who came from Arcadia. When some of the lords refused to hunt alongside a woman, Meleager, who wanted Atalanta, compelled them to join; and the party feasted nine days and went out on the tenth.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Apollodorus, Library 1.8.2 (Frazer 1921); not verbatim.

passages.text: The hunt itself drew blood on all sides: Hyleus and Ancaeus were killed by the boar; Peleus, in a false throw, killed Eurytion. Atalanta was first to wound the beast with an arrow, in its back; Amphiaraus next, in the eye; Meleager drove in the killing thrust to the flank, and at once, though his uncles and a make-shift of men claimed the skin by birthright, he gave it to the woman herself.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Apollodorus, Library 1.8.2-1.8.3 (Frazer 1921); not verbatim.

passages.text: The brothers of Althaea, sons of Thestius, on hearing the prize was in a woman's hands, robbed her, and Meleager, enraged, cut them down. Althaea's grief at her brothers' slaughter overcame her — some say she put fire to the brand on the hearth, and Meleager straightway died. Other versions let war between Curetes and Calydonians end in the son's own death; but in all of them the tale is the same: the measure of a mother's grief that turned the great hunter into a life ruled by fire kept in a chest.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Apollodorus, Library 1.8.3 (Frazer 1921); not verbatim.

title.en: Daedalus and Icarus
title.zh: 代達羅斯與伊卡羅斯

region.en: Labyrinth, Crete to Sicily (mythic geography)
region.zh: 克里特迷宮至西西里（神話地理）

period: Compiled c. 1st-2nd century CE (attrib. Apollodorus; Frazer translation 1921)

source.work: Apollodorus, Library, trans. J. G. Frazer (1921), Epitome e.1.12-e.1.15

summary.en: Punished for leaking the Labyrinth's secret, Daedalus is shut up with his son Icarus. Father and son break out on feathered wings glued with wax: Icarus, flying too near the sun, melts his wings and drowns in the sea named after him. Daedalus keeps his wing and sails to Camicus in Sicily, and the hunting Minos dies at the bath there in a boiling-water trap built — ironically by the very man he hunted.
summary.zh: 因洩露迷宮之祕，代達羅斯與其子伊卡羅斯被囚迷宮。父子以鴿羽與蜂蠟製翼越獄：伊卡羅斯不聽告誡飛近太陽，蠟翼融化，墜海而亡，海即以其名命名。代達羅斯平安飛至西西里卡米科斯；追捕的米諾斯追至其地，卻被藏匿他的人物壁與滾水暗計所害，死於埃及公主希爾能浴池。

sensitivity.note: Ancient literary source; no living community restrictions.

passages.text: Minos learned that Daedalus had shown Ariadne the thread into the Labyrinth and its way out, and shut him up inside his giant stone warmongering along with his small son Icarus, who had been born to him overseas by a slavewoman of Minos' court. The ordinary walls of the builder could not hold the only truly clever of them both, however (in one of his own built walls).
passages.note: Paraphrase of Apollodorus, Library, Epitome e.1.12 (Frazer 1921); not verbatim.

passages.text: So Daedalus made wings of feathers fastened to frames with wax, and gave to his son as the one condition of flight: keep between the extremes; neither too near the sun, or the glue would soften; nor too near the sea, or the damp would loosen the feathers. The wings bore the two aloft and out.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Apollodorus, Library, Epitome e.1.12 (Frazer 1921); not verbatim.

passages.text: But the headstrong boy climbed higher and higher into his own horizon for love of the sun, until the wax melted and the pinions drooped turn away. He fell into the sea that is named after him, and perished; Daedalus flew on, safe, across the sea, and made land at Camicus in Sicily.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Apollodorus, Library, Epitome e.1.13 (Frazer 1921); not verbatim.

passages.text: Minos came searching for him, carrying a spiral shell about every coast and promising a reward to whoever could pass a thread through it, sure that only the inventor could do the trick with thread. At Camicus, King Cocalus took up the riddle, gave Daedalus the shell, who set a thread to a tiny ant, and passed it clean through the labyrinth of the shell.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Apollodorus, Library, Epitome e.1.14-e.1.15 (Frazer 1921); not verbatim.

passages.text: So Minos demanded back his prisoner, and in the bath of scalding water poured on the king Cocalus, he made his end. Daedalus the engineer, whose palace device had once invented such perfect mazes and the tale widely told, had engineered the only exit the father of the Labyrinth could not survive.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Apollodorus, Library, Epitome e.1.15 (Frazer 1921); not verbatim.

title.en: Jason and the Golden Fleece
title.zh: 伊阿宋與金羊毛

region.en: Iolcus to Colchis (mythic geography)
region.zh: 伊奧爾科斯至科爾基斯（神話地理）

period: Compiled c. 1st-2nd century CE (attrib. Apollodorus; Frazer translation 1921)

source.work: Apollodorus, Library, trans. J. G. Frazer (1921), §§ 1.9.10-1.9.27

summary.en: Cheated of his throne by Pelias, Jason is sent to fetch the Golden Fleece from a grove of Ares in Colchis, guarded by a sleepless dragon. With Athena's help he builds the Argo, assembles the nobles of Greece — Heracles, the Dioscuri, Orpheus, Peleus, Telamon and the rest — survives wedding-trap divinities in Denizli and all the rowed islands. His opening—and Ethiopia lie in wait; waging Medea and Aeetes, the ram gathers in return with a dragon that breathes fire and…
summary.zh: 佩利亞斯篡奪王位所害伊阿宋，遣其往科爾基斯取阿瑞斯聖林內不眠巨龍看守的金羊毛。雅典娜相助下，阿耳戈斯造五十槳快船阿爾戈號，希臘群英——赫拉克勒斯、狄俄斯庫里、俄耳甫斯、珀琉斯、忒拉蒙——齊聚其上。沿途除痺牛怪、食人哈爾庇厄等險阻；美狄亞鍾情於伊阿宋，以靈藥迷睡守護龍，取羊毛同返。歸國後，美狄亞又以妙計令佩利亞斯的女兒們剁父煮肉求還青春，事敗，伊阿宋與美狄亞被逐往科任托斯。

sensitivity.note: Ancient literary source; no living community restrictions.

passages.text: Pelias challenged the young Jason with what he thought was an impossible errand: fetch from Aeetes at Colchis the Golden Fleece, hanging on an oak in a grove of Ares and guarded by a sleepless dragon. Jason agreed to the far-spreading voyage. Argus, son of Phrixus, under Athena's advice built a fifty-oared ship, and named her the Argo after himself; and in the prow, Athena set a speaking timber cut from the oak of Dodona.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Apollodorus, Library 1.9.10-11 (Frazer 1921); not verbatim.

passages.text: The catalogue of the assembled nobles reaches from the steering pilot Tiphys, Orpheus son of Oiagrus, the two winged sons of Boreas Zetes and Calais, the divine Castor and Pollux, to the strongest and kindest of them, Heracles; and Peleus and Telamon, father of Ajax, went from their own Phthia and Salamis. And after shipwreck at Cyzicus and patiently mourned men, after the box of storms came to the prophecy and bull Boebianers: Pollux killed King Amycus with a blow, and the sailors leaped into the night's brand.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Apollodorus, Library 1.9.11-20 (Frazer 1921); not verbatim.

passages.text: At Salmydessus in Thrace they found the blind seer Phineus tormented by the Harpies, winged women who flew down on his meals and fouled what was left. Zetes and Calais, winged, pursued them until they gave up the toll; and Phineus, owing the crew advice, told them how to sail the Symplegades, the crashing clashing rocks. Then he came to Colchis, and the king Aeetes promised the fleece on conditions that could not be done: yoke the firebreathing bulls, sow the dragon's teeth, and overcome the men that sprang up from the furrows.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Apollodorus, Library 1.9.21-23 (Frazer 1921); not verbatim.

passages.text: Medea, daughter of Aeetes and a skilled herbalist, fell in love with Jason and, on his oath to take her to Greece, gave him the charmed salve that made flesh proof against fire and iron. He yoked the bulls, sowed the teeth, fought the springing men by hurling a stone among them that turned them against each other, and, when Aeetes turned on the Argonauts anyway, went with Medea by night to the grove of Ares: she threw the dragon into a sleep with her drugs, and Jason took the fleece.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Apollodorus, Library 1.9.23-24 (Frazer 1921); not verbatim.

passages.text: The return was again a tale of wonders: past the Sirens, past Charybdis and the Wandering Rocks with Thetis and the Nereids steering at Hera's call, to Corcyra, where Queen Arete married Jason and Medea speedily so that she could not be given back to Colchis; then the bronze giant Talos pelted the Argo from Crete until Medea drugged him mad, or drew the bronze nail that sealed the single vein with promising to make him immortal, and he bled out. In four months they came back to Iolcus. But the tale ended darkly: Medea tricked Pelias' own daughters into mincing their father and boiling him for a renewal she could not give. Acastus buried Papa Pelias and drove Jason and Medea into exile at Corinth.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Apollodorus, Library 1.9.25-27 (Frazer 1921); not verbatim.

title.en: Perseus: The Gorgon's Head and the Rescue of Andromeda
title.zh: 珀爾修斯：蛇髮女妖與安德洛墨達

region.en: Seriphos to Ethiopia (mythic geography)
region.zh: 塞里福斯至埃塞俄比亞（神話地理）

period: Compiled c. 1st-2nd century CE (attrib. Apollodorus; Frazer translation 1921)

source.work: Apollodorus, Library, trans. J. G. Frazer (1921), §§ 2.4.1-2.4.5

summary.en: Cast to sea with his mother in a chest, Perseus is raised on Seriphos and sent by King Polydectes to fetch the Gorgon's head. Guided by Hermes and Athena, armed with the winged sandals, the kibisis, the cap of Hades and a bronze mirror, he beheads the sleeping Medusa, rescues Andromeda from the sea monster, petrifies his enemies, and unknowingly fulfils the oracle against his grandfather Acrisius.
summary.zh: 達那厄與嬰兒被裝箱投海漂流至塞里福斯，珀爾修斯長成後被波呂得克忒斯王派往取蛇髮女妖之頭。在赫爾墨斯與雅典娜引導下，他持飛行涼鞋、神皮袋、冥王隱帽與青鏡，趁妖熟睡斬下美杜莎之頭；又救出被縛礁石上的安德洛墨達，石化仇敵；最後竟在運動會上不自知地以鐵餅擊斃祖父阿克里西俄斯，應驗神諭。

sensitivity.note: Ancient literary source; no living community restrictions.

passages.text: An oracle had warned Acrisius of Argos that his daughter's son would one day kill him; so the king shut Danae in an underground bronze chamber. Zeus came to her, in some tellings as a stream of gold poured through a chink in the roof, and she bore Perseus. Unbelieving and afraid, Acrisius put mother and child into a chest and cast it into the sea; it came ashore on Seriphos, where Dictys, a fisherman, took the boy up and reared him.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Apollodorus, Library 2.4.1 (Frazer 1921); not verbatim.

passages.text: Polydectes, king of Seriphos, wanted Danae and could not reach her while Perseus grew to manhood at her side. At a feast, feigning collection for Helios' wedding gifts, he pressed Perseus to buy horses or forfeit the ring; Perseus promised the young and reckless Gorgon's head instead. Under the guidance of Hermes and Athena he sought the sisters of the Gorgons, the three old Graiae, born grey-haired and sharing one eye and one tooth between them: he snatched it, and bought the way to the far nymphs with it.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Apollodorus, Library 2.4.2 (Frazer 1921); not verbatim.

passages.text: From the nymphs Apollo had given him nothing but their help: Perseus took from them his kit — winged sandals from Hermes, the kibisis wallet that carried heads and gear; the dark cap of Hades that made its wearer invisible; and an adamantine sickle-sword from Hermes. He flew with the storm-winds to the sea's edge and caught the three Gorgons asleep: Stheno and Euryale, ageless; and Medusa alone mortal. Guided by Athena's hand and looking only at her reflection in his bronze shield, he beheaded her; and out of her body sprang Pegasus, the winged horse, and Chrysaor, father of Geryon.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Apollodorus, Library 2.4.2-2.4.3 (Frazer 1921); not verbatim.

passages.text: Slung in the kibisis, invisible in the dark cap as the lion-like sisters hunted him with terrible gnashing of jaws, he flew back over the land and came to Ethiopia, where King Cepheus' daughter Andromeda was bound to a rock, exposed to a sea monster because her mother Cassiopeia had boasted that she was fairer than the Nereids. Perseus loved her at first sight, killed the monster, and got her to wife — then burned her rival Phineus and his fellow plotters with a look at the Gorgon's head.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Apollodorus, Library 2.4.3 (Frazer 1921); not verbatim.

passages.text: At Seriphos, his mother and Dictys sheltered at the altars from Polydectes' violence, so Perseus entered the assembled palace and with averted face lifted the head; Polydectes and his friends were turned to stone each in the posture he happened to hold. Dictys was set up as king; to Hermes the tools went back, and Medusa's head to Athena, who set it into the aegis. But the second oracle had not been forgotten: returning to Argos, Perseus could not face his grandfather; Acrisius fled to Larissa in Thessaly, where Perseus, competing at the games, threw his discus astray, and killed the old man who had feared his birth.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Apollodorus, Library 2.4.4-2.4.5 (Frazer 1921); not verbatim.

title.en: Theseus and the Minotaur
title.zh: 忒修斯與彌諾陶洛斯

region.en: Troezen to Crete (mythic geography)
region.zh: 特洛真至克里特（神話地理）

period: Compiled c. 1st-2nd century CE (attrib. Apollodorus; Frazer translation 1921)

source.work: Apollodorus, Library, trans. J. G. Frazer (1921), §§ 3.15.8-3.16.7 and Epitome e.1.1-e.1.11

summary.en: Theseus clears the Isthmus road of robbers, proves his sonship with the sword, drives out Medea, and sails as tribute to Crete where Ariadne helps him thread and end the Minotaur in the Labyrinth. Dionysus steals her on Naxos; Theseus forgets to hoist the white sail, and Aegeus leaps from the Acropolis.
summary.zh: 忒修斯途中剷除伊斯特摩斯路上的惡徒，以劍認父，逐走美狄亞，然後作為供奉少年前往克里特：依阿里阿德涅之線索深入迷宮，徒手擊斃彌諾陶洛斯。納克索斯島上酒神東京阿里阿德涅；忒修斯悲痛忘改白帆，黑帆入港，埃勾斯自城堡躍下身亡。

sensitivity.note: Ancient literary source; no living community restrictions.

passages.text: Aegeus of Athens had left childless by his wife Aethra until he prayed to Poseidon, and entrusted her with future care: under a heavy stone he laid a sword and sandals, and bade that their son lift both and claim them. Theseus came of age, and journeyed from Troezen to Athens the longer road for its hero-proof of evil monsters on it — Periphetes with the iron club, Sinis, the Pine-Bender, the wild sow of Crommyon, Sciron's robber cliff, Cercyon the wrestler-king of Eleusis and Damastus' two beds. He then was acknowledged in Athens, and drove out Medea's poison cup.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Apollodorus, Library 3.15.8-3.16.1 and Epitome e.1.1-e.1.6 (Frazer 1921); not verbatim.

passages.text: Androgeus, the son of Minos, was killed by the Athenians in Attica, and the Cretan tribute ran from Athens: at stated times seven youths and seven girls were shipped to Crete to be eaten by the Minotaur, the terrible warden of另一半圈 of Pasiphae the bull, and twin horns visible in the Labyrinth built by Daedalus. The third lot of tribute had fallen, and Theseus, of his own choosing, was numbered among the fourteen; or, as some tell it, he volunteered.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Apollodorus, Library 3.15.8 and Epitome e.1.7 (Frazer 1921); not verbatim.

passages.text: Aegeus charged his son what the fathers of the war sails said: if she came back safe, whiten the sail. And in Crete Ariadne, Minos' daughter, fell in love with him and promised her help for the pledge of taking her home to Athens in marriage. She begged the inventor Daedalus to teach her the way back from the Labyrinth, and he told her: Theseus unrolled a ball of thread at the door and drew it behind him as he walked the endless hollows.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Apollodorus, Library 3.16.2 and Epitome e.1.8-e.1.9 (Frazer 1921); not verbatim.

passages.text: The Minotaur was found at the utter end of the Labyrinth, and Theseus killed him with blows of his fists; and, drawing the clue after him, came out. By night he put to sea with Ariadne and her children, and at first anchored in Naxos; there Dionysus, who loved Ariadne, ran on them and snatched her away to Lemnos. Theseus in grief left sail dark, and Aegeus, watching the Acropolis, took the black sail as proof of his son drowned and pitched himself from the platform. Athens passed to Theseus' own hands.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Apollodorus, Library 3.16.7 and Epitome e.1.9-e.1.11 (Frazer 1921); not verbatim.

title.en: The Siege Ends: Penthesilea, Memnon, and the Death of Achilles
title.zh: 彭忒西勒亞、門儂與阿基琉斯之死

region.en: Plains of Troy (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 特洛伊平原（象徵性定位）

period: Composed from the lost epics (c. 7th century BCE; summary in Apollodorus; Frazer translation 1921)

source.work: Apollodorus, Library, trans. J. G. Frazer (1921), Epitome e.5.1-e.5.6

summary.en: Beyond the Iliad, the war found two last champions for Troy: the Amazon Penthesilea, whom Achilles kills and then mourns, and Memnon, son of Tithonus and the Dawn, killing Antilochus. Achilles is brought down in turn: Paris and Apollo with one arrow to the vulnerable ankle at the Scaean gates — a death that dismays the host and makes Ajax and Ulysses fight over his arms.
summary.zh: 《伊利亞特》之外，維繫特洛伊的最後兩位救兵為彭忒西勒亞（戰神亞馬遜女王，殺馬卡翁後被阿基琉斯所殺，英雄見其美貌心生哀念竟是掃興）與門儂（黎明的女神之子，殺安提洛科斯後為阿基琉斯所斃）、阿基琉斯命終於斯開亞門——帕里斯與阿波羅一箭射中易受傷的腳踵，全軍震動。繼而其甲胄懸花迎烏傑克斯與奧德修斯拚美，判定四人争甲，大埃阿斯憤怒屠牛亡己。

sensitivity.note: Ancient literary source; no living community restrictions.

passages.text: This champion Penthesilea, daughter of Otrere and of Ares herself, had accidentally killed the queen-Hippolyte in hunting and was purified by Priam at Troy. Then, driving against the Greeks in battle, she slew many of their men, among them the healer Machaon. Achilles killed her at last; and, seeing her dead beauty, fell in love with the Amazon, and, what still is told, killed the ugly Thersites for jeering at his grief.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Apollodorus, Library, Epitome e.5.1 (Frazer 1921); not verbatim.

passages.text: Memnon, the son of Tithonus and the goddess of Dawn, brought a great army of Ethiopians against the besiegers, and killed many of the Greeks, among them the young Antilochus, Nestor's son. Achilles killed him; and, as he drove the Trojans before him, Paris and Apollo beset him: at the Scaean gate, an arrow found the one spot on which Achilles was winnable — the ankle, which his mother Thetis had held him by when she dipped him as a baby.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Apollodorus, Library, Epitome e.5.3 (Frazer 1921); not verbatim.

passages.text: The host's grief at the death dismayed them; his body was rescued by Ajax under a rain of darts while Ulysses covered the foe; and his bones, mixed with Patroclus', were buried in a White Isle in an urn. For his funeral games, Eumelus won the chariot race, Diomedes the footrace, Ajax the quoit, and Teucer the archery.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Apollodorus, Library, Epitome e.5.4-e.5.5 (Frazer 1921); not verbatim.

passages.text: And his immortal arms, made by Hephaestus, were offered to the bravest of the living. Ajax and Ulysses came out as candiates, and the judgment fell — said Trojan prisoners or the allied kings — to Ulysses. Ajax was mad with chagrin: he planned a night-raid on his own allies, but Athena struck him mad, so that he believed the herds and the herdsmen were the Argive leaders, and he slew them in the dark. When he came back to himself, he fell on his own sword; Agamemnon forbade the customary burning of the body and buried him in a coffin at Rhoeteum.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Apollodorus, Library, Epitome e.5.6-e.5.7 (Frazer 1921); not verbatim.

title.en: Agamemnon's House: Clytemnestra, Aegisthus, and Orestes
title.zh: 阿伽門農家族：克呂泰涅斯特拉、厄癸斯托斯與俄瑞斯忒斯

region.en: Mycenae to Delphi (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 邁錫尼至德爾菲（象徵性定位）

period: Compiled c. 1st-2nd century CE (attrib. Apollodorus; Frazer translation 1921)

source.work: Apollodorus, Library, trans. J. G. Frazer (1921), Epitome e.6.23-e.6.29

summary.en: Apollodorus closes the Atreid saga with the murder of Agamemnon at his homecoming. Clytemnestra and Aegisthus cut the king down entangled in a garment woven without sleeves or neck; Cassandra dies too. Orestes, reared in exile by the Phocian Strophius beside Pylades, avenges his father at Delphi's command, is driven mad by the Furies, is tried at the Areopagus and acquitted, and is finally cured of his derangement after visiting the Taurian image, where the priestess turns out to be his sister Iphigenia.
summary.zh: 阿波羅多洛斯以阿伽門農歸家之死作結阿特柔斯家族悲劇：克呂泰涅斯特拉與厄癸斯托斯以無袖無領之衣縛王而弒之，卡珊德拉同死。俄瑞斯忒斯寄居福基斯之斯特羅菲俄斯家、與皮拉得斯為友，成年後依德爾菲神諭復仇弒母及其情人；復仇三女神使其狂亂，他至雅典戰神山受審獲釋；最後赴陶里安聖殿取像以愈狂疾，而祭司竟是失散的姊姊伊菲革尼亞。

sensitivity.note: Ancient literary source; no living community restrictions.

passages.text: Agamemnon returned to Mycenae with Cassandra in his train. But his wife had fitted herself a robe without sleeves or an opening for the neck; and while the king stood wrestling with the garment, she and her lover Aegisthus cut him down, and Cassandra also. Aegisthus reigned in his stead, and the death of the greatest of the Achaeans lay unavenged in his own house.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Apollodorus, Library, Epitome e.6.23 (Frazer 1921); not verbatim.

passages.text: Electra, the king's daughter, stole her little brother Orestes out of the house of his mother's new tenants and gave him to the Phocian Strophius to bring up with his own son Pylades. When Orestes was grown, he went to Delphi and asked the god whether he might take vengeance on his father's murderers, and the god gave him leave.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Apollodorus, Library, Epitome e.6.24 (Frazer 1921); not verbatim.

passages.text: He and Pylades, in company, made their way into Mycenae and killed both Aegisthus and their own mother. Then madness seized him, and beings called Furies pursued him over the land. In Athens he was tried before the Areopagus, and the votes came out equal, so that he was acquitted of the matricide and let go clean.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Apollodorus, Library, Epitome e.6.25 (Frazer 1921); not verbatim.

passages.text: The god also told him how he might be rid of his disorder: he must bring back to Greece the sacred image that stood in the land of the Taurians, a Scythian people who sacrificed strangers. Caught on arrival, Orestes and Pylades were bound and sent before King Thoas to be offered; but the priestess of the shrine recognized her brother, for the priestess was Iphigenia; and the three fled with the image, and Orestes came home cured, married Hermione, and lived to father Tisamenus, whose end was a serpent's bite at Oresteum in Arcadia.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Apollodorus, Library, Epitome e.6.26-e.6.28 (Frazer 1921); not verbatim.

title.en: Philoctetes and the Bow of Heracles
title.zh: 菲羅克忒忒斯與赫拉克勒斯之弓

region.en: Lemnos (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 利姆諾斯島（象徵性定位）

period: Composed from the lost Little Iliad (c. 7th century BCE; summary in Apollodorus; Frazer translation 1921)

source.work: Apollodorus, Library, trans. J. G. Frazer (1921), Epitome e.3.27, e.5.8

summary.en: On the way to Troy Philoctetes, keeper of the bow and arrows of the dead Heracles, is bitten in the foot by a water-serpent and carried so much pain on his cries that his comrades maroon him on Lemnos for ten years. When an oracle declares that Troy cannot fall without Heracles' weapons, Odysseus and Diomedes fetch the wounded man and the bow back to the camp; the physician cures him, and his arrow fells Alexander-Paris.
summary.zh: 赴特洛伊途中，攜赫拉克勒斯弓箭的菲羅克忒忒斯腳遭蛇咬，痛呼不止，同僚不堪其苦，將其棄於利姆諾斯島整整十年。神諭宣明：無赫拉克勒斯之弓則特洛伊不可破；奧德修斯與狄俄墨得斯遂迎其返營。醫者治其傷，菲羅克忒忒斯一箭射斃帕里斯，遂破十年之圍。

sensitivity.note: Ancient literary source; no living community restrictions.

passages.text: Philoctetes, son of Poeas, had lit the pyre of Heracles on Mount Oeta and been given the hero's bow and arrows in return. Sailing with the Greeks to Troy, the fleet put in first at Chryse, where he was bitten in the foot by a water-serpent. The wound would not close; it festered and stank, and the wounded man's cries of pain never ceased.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Apollodorus, Library, Epitome e.3.27 (Frazer 1921); not verbatim.

passages.text: The camp could not endure the noise and the stench beside them. So the Greeks marooned Philoctetes on Lemnos and sailed on, leaving him with rags, a hut of rock, and the bow of Heracles. He stayed ten years, hunting what he could and limping with pain through the rest.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Apollodorus, Library, Epitome e.3.27 (Frazer 1921); not verbatim.

passages.text: In the tenth year, with the war going nowhere, Calchas prophesied that Troy could not be taken unless the bow and arrows of Heracles were brought by them against Troy. Odysseus sailed for Lemnos with Diomedes, found the wounded man, got possession of the bow by cunning talk, and persuaded him to sail out for Troy.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Apollodorus, Library, Epitome e.5.8 (Frazer 1921); not verbatim.

passages.text: At the camp, Podalirius the physician treated the wound and healed it. Philoctetes took his place in the fighting and slew Paris with an arrow. With the bow's verdict delivered, the end of the war — the Wooden Horse — was soon to follow.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Apollodorus, Library, Epitome e.5.8 (Frazer 1921); not verbatim.

title.en: Telegonus: The Last of Odysseus
title.zh: 忒勒戈諾斯：奧德修斯的最後

region.en: Aeaea to Ithaca (mythic geography)
region.zh: 埃埃亞至伊薩卡（神話地理）
