title.en: Mimir's Well: Odin's Pawned Eye and the Head That Counsels
title.zh: 密米爾之泉：奧丁典當的獨眼與能進言的首級

region.en: Mimir's well beneath Yggdrasil's root (symbolic pin at Pingvellir, Iceland)
region.zh: 尤克特拉希爾根下的密米爾之泉（象徵性定位於冰島辛格韋德利）

period: Voluspa st. 27-29 c. 900-1000 CE; Ynglinga saga c. 1225; Gylfaginning c. 1220-1230; principal MSS Codex Regius GKS 2365 4to, AM 41 4to, GKS 2367 4to

source.work: Voluspa st. 27-29; Snorri, Ynglinga saga ch. 4; Gylfaginning ch. 15; critical ed. Dronke (1997)

license: Public domain (Bellows 1923; Laing 1844; Brodeur 1916); passages below are labeled paraphrases

summary.en: Beneath Yggdrasil's second root lies the well of Mimir, in which wisdom and understanding are hidden. Odin came asking to drink and gave an eye for the draught - it still lies at the bottom of the well. Later, when the Aesir sent Mimir as a hostage to the Vanir and the Vanir beheaded him, Odin embalmed the head with herbs and sang spells until it spoke: from Mimir's head he takes true counsel. The record binds the Norse wisdom economy together: sight pawned for drink, counsel preserved in a jar, and the well itself the place where Odin will whisper his last promise to Baldr.
summary.zh: 尤克特拉希爾第二條根下有密米爾之泉，智慧與聰明藏於其中。奧丁前來求飲，以一隻眼睛換得泉水——那眼睛至今仍在泉底。其後阿薩神族以密米爾為人質送予華納族，華納族斬其首級歸還；奧丁以草藥封存首級，誦咒直至其能言語：他自此從密米爾之首取得真正的謀議。此記錄將北歐的智慧經濟緊密相連：以目力換泉飲，以罐罌藏謀主，而泉水本身即是奧丁最後向巴爾德低語誓言之處。

canonical_translation: Henry A. Bellows, The Poetic Edda, New York 1923 (public domain); Ynglinga saga via Laing 1844

narrative.en:
Voluspa's prophecy turns, mid-vision, to a transaction: the sibyl knows well where Odin pledged his eye - in the well of Mimir, famed and full of mead, where Mimir's pledge of water each morning is drawn from the pledge-pledging father of the host. Do you understand yet, or what? The stanza is oracular and cryptic, but its content is fixed by the prose: the well lies under the world-tree's root that turns toward the frost-giants, and in it wisdom and understanding are hidden; Odin came asking for a drink and paid with one eye, leaving it at the bottom of the spring.

The second half of the doctrine comes from the hostage-war. When the Aesir-Vanir treaty sent Mimir east as a hostage alongside the empty-spoken Hoenir, the Vanir discovered the fraud, beheaded Mimir and returned the head to Odin. Snorri's Ynglinga saga gives the sequel: Odin took the head, embalmed it with herbs so it would not rot, sang charms over it and gave it such power that it spoke with him and told him hidden matters. The head of the murdered counsellor became the god's daily adviser - and in Voluspa it is this head that speaks the prophecy's refrain, for the sibyl hears Odin converse with Mimir's head before the pyre of Baldr is raised: the poem's sequence of consult-the-head moments binds the well-myth to the eschatology.

The cultural logic is a wisdom-economy with a price list. Norse myth never gives knowledge free: the runes cost nine nights on a tree, the mead costs a summer's labor and a seduction, and Mimir's draught costs an eye. The eye at the bottom of the well is the permanent receipt of that transaction - and the well becomes a place of vision by loss: what Odin gave up is what the water shows. Snorri assigns the well to the root that lies over the frost-giants' world, making wisdom's price a border-crossing into the enemy's territory. And the embalmed head domesticates a darker fact: counsel in this society was a hostage's body, and its afterlife is technological - herbs, spells, speech.

Gylfaginning adds one last use of the site: at Baldr's death Odin rides to the well and whispers into the ear of the dead man - the sole counsel Mimir's spring ever gives that the poem does not record, the secret every myth-cycle dangles and withholds. The motif of the pawned eye links the record to Odin's other wisdom-thefts and to the atlas's broader wisdom-sacrifice family, from Odin's hanging to the Greek Cyclopean trade of sight.

functions: Doctrine of priced wisdom: every knowledge has a body-cost, itemized in myth
The pawned eye as permanent receipt; the well as a place of vision by loss
Treaty politics: counsel as a hostage's embalmed, ensorcelled head
Eschatological hinge: Odin's whisper to Baldr at the well, the myth's withheld secret

title.en: Gullveig and Heid: Thrice Burned, Thrice Born - the Origin of Seid Magic
title.zh: 古爾維格與海德：三焚三生——巫術賽德的起源

region.en: Odin's hall, Asgard (symbolic pin at Gamla Uppsala, Sweden)
region.zh: 阿斯加德奧丁大廳（象徵性定位於瑞典舊烏普薩拉）

period: Voluspa st. 21-22, c. 900-1000 CE; principal MS Codex Regius GKS 2365 4to

source.work: Voluspa st. 21-22; critical ed. Ursula Dronke (1997)

license: Public domain (Bellows 1923); passages below are labeled paraphrases

summary.en: The sibyl remembers the first war in the world, and its opening is not a battle but a trial: a woman named Gullveig - Gold-drink - was stabbed with spears and burned in Odin's hall, and three times burned, three times reborn, again and again she lives. Wherever she went after, she was called Heid, a seer in every house, teaching witchcraft; and always she delighted in evil. The six lines are the Norse origin of sorcery and prophecy, and possibly the mythic memory of a cult of gold and magic that the god-order could burn but not kill.
summary.zh: 女先知憶起世間第一場戰爭，其開端並非戰陣，而是一場審判：名為古爾維格（「金之飲」）的女子在奧丁大廳被長矛穿刺、投入火中，三度焚燒，三度重生，一次又一次地活了下來。此後她所到之處被稱作海德——家家戶戶中的女先知，傳授巫術；而她永遠樂於邪惡。這六行詩是北歐巫術與預言的起源，或許也是對一個黃金與魔法崇拜的神話記憶——神之秩序能焚其身，卻不能除其名。

canonical_translation: Henry A. Bellows, The Poetic Edda, New York 1923 (public domain)

narrative.en:
Voluspa st. 21-22 is the most disputed six lines in Norse mythography. The sibyl, cataloguing the first war, begins with a woman: Gullveig they pierced with spears in the hall of the High One and burned her; thrice burned, thrice reborn, ever and again she lives. And then they called her Heid wherever she came to houses, a witch skilled in prophecy: she understood witchcraft, played with minds, was always delighted with evil.

Four doctrines are packed in. First, the name: Gullveig means 'gold-drink' or 'gold-drunkenness', and editors have read her as a personification of gold's corrupting circulation - the very metal whose arrival by the three giant-maidens ends the golden age, and whose curse (Andvari's ring) will later wreck the Niflung house. Second, the punishment: she is burned in Odin's own hall, an execution of the kind Norse law reserved for witches and outlaws - so the first war opens with the god-order attempting a capital sentence on a being it cannot kill. Third, the survival: three deaths, three births, the pattern of the undying - she comes back each time more potent, which makes her the mythic prototype of the sorceress whom fire cannot purge. Fourth, the transformation: under her new name Heid ('shining one', also 'heathen-teacher' in some readings) she becomes the distributor of seid, the magic of prophecy that Freyja will later teach the Aesir and that the sagas show performed by staff-carrying volvas.

Who Gullveig is remains argued: Freyja under another name (the goddess of gold and seid, tortured by the Aesir - which would make the Van-war an Aesir atrocity), a giantess of the gold, or an independent personification. What the record establishes for the database is the causal chain the poem itself draws: the burning - the survival - the teaching of magic - the war. In the Norse imagination, the practice of seid is born from a judicial atrocity that failed, and the profession of the volva descends from a woman the gods murdered and could not keep dead. The myth thereby encodes a social memory: divination in Scandinavia was women's work, performed by traveling practitioners at farmsteads (as Eirik's saga's Greenland seance shows), and the myth gives that profession a founding martyr.

Snorri, uncharacteristically, omits Gullveig entirely - his systematization has no room for a witch the gods burned and lost. The sibyl's six lines survive only in the eddic tradition, which is why this record carries no Prose Edda apparatus: some myths are preserved precisely by staying outside the learned prose apparatus.

functions: Origin myth of seid sorcery and the profession of the traveling volva
Martyr-memory of a failed judicial burning: the gods kill a witch three times without success
Personification doctrine: gold's corrupting circulation as a woman who cannot die
Causal chain: burning, survival, teaching, war - the sibyl's own mythic logic

title.en: Njord, Freyr and Freyja: The Vanir Hostages and Their Arts
title.zh: 尼奧德、弗雷與芙蕾雅：華納人質及其技藝

region.en: Noatun and Asgard (symbolic pin at Gamla Uppsala, Sweden)
region.zh: 諾阿頓與阿斯加德（象徵性定位於瑞典舊烏普薩拉）

period: Ynglinga saga c. 1225; Gylfaginning c. 1220-1230 (older material); principal MSS AM 41 4to, GKS 2367 4to

source.work: Snorri, Ynglinga saga ch. 4; Gylfaginning chs. 23-24; critical ed. Faulkes (1987)

license: Public domain (Laing 1844; Brodeur 1916); passages below are labeled paraphrases

summary.en: After the war between the divine nations, the Vanir sent Njord the Wealthy with his son Freyr and daughter Freyja to live among the Aesir, and the three brought with them the arts of the other nation: mastery of sea and wind, of harvests and plenty, of love and of seid magic. Njord can calm sea and fire; Freyr rules rain, sunshine and the fruits of the earth, and it is good to call on him for plenty; Freyja teaches the gods a magic they did not have, rides a chariot of cats, and takes half the battle-slain. The record explains the hybrid pantheon's division of labor.
summary.zh: 兩神族交戰之後，華納族遣富裕的尼奧德攜其子弗雷、女芙蕾雅定居阿薩神族之中，三人帶來另一神族的技藝：統御海與風、豐收與富足、愛情與賽德巫術。尼奧德能平海息火；弗雷掌雨澤、日光與大地果實，求豐者宜呼其名；芙蕾雅傳授諸神所未有的魔法，駕貓車而行，且可取陣亡者之半。此記錄解釋了混合神譜的分工。

canonical_translation: Samuel Laing, Heimskringla, London 1844 (public domain); Gylfaginning via Brodeur 1916

narrative.en:
The treaty that ended the first war gave the Aesir the Vanir's richest house. Njord came with his two children, and the prose sources describe what they brought. Njord is so rich and wealthy that he can give wealth and land to whoever calls on him; he was reared in the land of the Vanir, but the Aesir gave him as a hostage, and he rules the course of the wind and stills sea and fire; sailors pray to him, and he has the sea-hall Noatun. Freyr his son is the god of rain and sunshine and of the fruits of the earth, 'and it is good to call on him for plenty and peace'; he also rules the wealth of men. Freyja his daughter is the greatest of goddesses: she owns the hall Folkvangr and takes half the battle-slain, the other half going to Odin; she rides a chariot drawn by two cats; she teaches the seid magic that the Vanir practiced, and she weeps tears of gold for her lost husband Od.

The record's cultural function is to explain the two-nation pantheon by its division of labor. The Aesir retain the sky's offices - thunder, law, war-leadership, the runes; the Vanir immigrants hold the economy - sea-luck, harvest, wealth, love and the magic of knowing. Every prayer has an address: to Njord for a fair passage, to Freyr for a wedding's plenty, to Freyja for love or for a share of the fallen. The Ynglinga account adds a dynastic key: Njord's line becomes the royal house of Sweden (the Ynglings are Freyr's descendants), so the hostage-exchange wrote itself into the genealogies of real kings.

The hybrid pantheon is also an ethnic myth in the founding-people sense: scholars have long read the Aesir-Vanir merger as mythic memory of an actual cult-merger between two Scandinavian communities (possibly linked to Indo-European and non-Indo-European strata). The record documents how a society explains having two kinds of gods: it tells a war story about them, then a treaty story, then assigns each house its offices - theology as annexation protocol.

For the motif atlas, the three Vanir anchor the divine-marriage and fertility-cult clusters (Njord-Skadi's failed marriage; Freyr-Gerd's wooing; Freyja's necklace and Od-grief), each of which has its own record. This one carries the treaty-of-offices itself.

The dynasty-clause completes the record: Njord's line becomes the Ynglings - the royal house of Sweden descended from the hostages - so the treaty wrote itself into the real kings' genealogies, and Ynglingatal's death-catalog is the hostages' descendants' ledger. And the cult-geography completes the record: Njord's Noatun by the sea, Freyr's Uppsala in the plain, Freyja's Folkvangr for the battle-slain - the Vanir offices mapped onto Sweden's sacred landscape, the treaty's division of labor inscribed in place. The record thus anchors the composite-pantheon family: two divine nations merged by war and treaty, each house keeping its offices.

functions: Explains the two-house pantheon by a treaty with assigned offices
Prayer-address doctrine: sea-luck to Njord, plenty to Freyr, love and the slain to Freyja
Dynastic charter: the Yngling kings of Sweden descend from the hostages
Mythic memory of a real cult-merger between Scandinavian communities

title.en: Why Poets Serve Odin: Aegir's Feast and the Craft of Kennings
title.zh: 詩人何以事奉奧丁：埃吉爾的宴席與隱喻之技

region.en: Aegir's hall at Hlesey (symbolic pin at Laeso island, Denmark)
region.zh: 埃吉爾之廳，赫勒色島（象徵性定位於丹麥萊瑟島）

period: Skaldskaparmal c. 1220-1230; principal MSS Codex Regius GKS 2367 4to, Codex Trajectinus

source.work: Snorri Sturluson, Edda: Skaldskaparmal prologue; Gylfaginning ch. 2; critical ed. Faulkes (1987)

license: Public domain (Brodeur 1916); passages below are labeled paraphrases

summary.en: The sea-giant Aegir, having been forced to brew ale for the gods, holds a feast at which the skald-god Bragi teaches him the craft of poetry: the names of the gods and of things, and the system of kennings - to speak of gold as 'Freyja's tears', of a ship as 'the horse of the sea'. Snorri frames the whole Edda as a manual written for a young Norwegian king's skald, and opens it with the doctrine that poetry is a gift won by Odin from the giants and taught to men: whoever speaks skillfully serves a god, and whoever lacks the gift may still learn its grammar.
summary.zh: 海巨人埃吉爾被迫為諸神釀造麥酒之後，設宴款待，吟遊詩神布拉基在席間向他傳授詩藝：諸神與萬物之名，以及「隱喻」之技——稱黃金為「芙蕾雅之淚」，稱船為「海之馬」。斯諾里將整部《埃達》寫成獻給挪威年輕國王的吟遊詩人手册，開篇即言：詩乃奧丁自巨人處贏得並傳授於人的天賦——凡出口成章者即事奉一神，而無天賦者亦可習得其法度。

canonical_translation: A. G. Brodeur, Snorri Sturluson: The Prose Edda, New York 1916 (public domain)

narrative.en:
Skaldskaparmal - 'the language of poetry' - opens with a frame story that is itself a myth of a cultural institution. The sea-giant Aegir, whose hall glitters with gold and whose nine wave-daughters pour the ale, has been summoned to brew for the gods; at the feast, Aegir asks the skald-god Bragi 'whence came the art that is called poetry?', and Bragi answers with the mead-myth: the art came from Odin, who won it from the giants at the cost of murder and seduction, and gave it to gods and to men skilled in the craft. Then, at Aegir's request, Bragi teaches the apparatus: the names of gods, giants, dwarfs and things; the kennings and their rules; the metres. The dialogue between a god and a converted giant is the textbook's own myth of pedagogy - poetry is taught at a feast, over the ale, by an immortal to a foreigner.

The doctrine of the kenning is Snorri's real subject. A kenning is a compressed metaphor with a mythic warrant: gold is 'Freyja's tears' (from her weeping for Od), 'Sif's hair', 'Draupnir's drops' - each name valid because a myth underwrites it; the sea is 'Aegir's ale', 'Ymir's blood', 'the whale-road'; a ship is 'the horse of the sea', a warrior 'the feeder of the wolf'. To compose is thus to cite the myth-cycle: skaldic verse is a liturgical citation system, and the Edda is its concordance. Snorri writes for a specific audience - the young king Hakon IV's court - and says so: the art is 'long and learned', and 'these matters must be told to young poets who desire to learn the language of poetry and to furnish themselves with a wide choice of terms'.

The cultural function is a charter for a professional class. Thirteenth-century Iceland lived off its poets' services at Norwegian courts; the myth that poetry descends from Odin's theft, taught at a giant's feast, licenses the profession's claims (skills worth gold, to be paid in ships and rings) and its etiquette (the mead can be squandered - the poetaster's share is real). The record joins the atlas's teaching-god cluster: Prometheus' crafts, Odin's runes, Bragi's feast - each a myth of how a technical language is transmitted from the immortal world to a working class of specialists.

The kenning-system's working examples complete the doctrine: the sea as 'Ymir's blood' (citing the creation-myth), gold as 'Freyja's tears' (citing the necklace-myth), the ship as 'the horse of the sea' - each kenning a compressed citation that requires the whole myth-cycle as its reference-work, so the Edda is the verse-craft's concordance. And the professional frame completes the record: Snorri writes for the young king Hakon's court, licensing the skalds' fees and their etiquette (the poetaster's share as the licensed low register) - the myth as the profession's charter. The record thus anchors the taught-language family: a technical poetry transmitted by a god at a giant's feast, distinctive in being an economy of citations.

functions: Charter of the skaldic profession: poetry as Odin's gift, paid for in murder and seduction
Grammar of myth: kennings as citations that require the whole myth-cycle as reference
Pedagogy myth: the art taught at a feast by a god to a giant convert
Economic doctrine: skills worth gold, with a licensed low register (the poetaster's share)

title.en: Alfheim and the Two Elf-Peoples: Freyr's Tooth-Gift and the Light in the Dark
title.zh: 精靈之鄉與兩支精靈族：弗雷的長牙之禮與暗中之光

region.en: Alfheim, the elf-home (symbolic pin at Gimsoy, Lofoten, Norway)
region.zh: 精靈之鄉阿爾夫海姆（象徵性定位於挪威羅弗敦群島吉姆瑟島）

period: Gylfaginning c. 1220-1230; Grimnismal st. 5, 13; principal MSS Codex Regius GKS 2365 4to, GKS 2367 4to

source.work: Snorri, Gylfaginning ch. 17; Grimnismal st. 5, 13; critical ed. Faulkes (1987)

license: Public domain (Brodeur 1916; Bellows 1923); passages below are labeled paraphrases

summary.en: When Freyr cut his first tooth, the Aesir gave him as a tooth-gift the realm called Alfheim, home of the light-elves - fairer than the sun to look on. Below, in the dark, dwell the dark-elves, blacker than pitch. The passage is the Norse doctrine of the two elf-peoples, the gift-economy of childhood (a god's first tooth is worth a country), and the origin of the European fairy-land: the realm given away at a teething party.
summary.zh: 弗雷初次長牙之時，阿薩神族以名為阿爾夫海姆的國度相贈，那是光之精靈的居所——其貌美於太陽。而在下方幽暗之處，住著比柏油更黑的暗精靈。此段是北歐「兩支精靈族」的學說、童年的饋贈經濟（神的乳牙抵得一國），亦是歐洲仙境（fairy-land）的起源：一片在長牙宴上被送出的國土。

canonical_translation: A. G. Brodeur, Snorri Sturluson: The Prose Edda, New York 1916 (public domain)

narrative.en:
Gylfaginning installs the elves in two sentences attached to Freyr's biography: when the young Freyr cut his first tooth, the Aesir gave him as a tooth-gift the realm of Alfheim - and in it dwell the light-elves, fairer than the sun to look upon. But the dark-elves dwell below the earth, and they are unlike them in appearance, and unlike them too in their deeds: they are blacker than pitch. The two peoples, bright and black, share one name-family (alfar) and one geography: above, the shining; below, the pitch.

Grimnismal confirms the upper geography in its litany of halls: Alfheim the gods gave to Freyr of old as a tooth-payment - confirming the tooth-gift doctrine in verse. The eddic elsewhere adds a third register: the elves appear as a people with their own halls (Lokasenna: why should the Aesir quarrel in the elves' home - the feast is held at Aegir's, but Loki's insults fly at elf-halls too), and as healers' kin (the ritual phrase 'helping-runes for birth ... on the beams of the elves' in Sigrdrifumal), and as a race whose women are dangerous to marry (the shield-maiden Brynhild warns of the elf-women). The sagas complete the picture: Iceland's social world is haunted by alf-folk, and the Kormaks saga hero is cured by an elf-sacrifice on a mound.

The cultural functions are threefold. First, an aition of the fairy-realm: medieval and modern 'elfland' - Tolkien's and Shakespeare's alike - descends from this doctrine of a bright country given away at a child's teething, populated by beings fairer than the sun. Second, a gift-economy of childhood: the Norse elite celebrated a boy's first tooth with a present of territory; the myth both mirrors and magnifies the real custom. Third, a moral geography: the light-elves and dark-elves encode the same above/below polarity as Asgard/Hel - illumination is a matter of residence, not species, since both peoples are alfar.

In the atlas's comparative frame, Alfheim answers the Greek Elysium and the Japanese Takamagahara: each tradition imagines a bright near-world adjacent to the human; the Norse one is distinctive for having been privately owned - a god's childhood fee.

The elves' wider economy completes the doctrine: the eddic poems' elf-halls (Lokasenna's feast at Aegir's attended by elf-kind), the healing-runes 'cut on the elves' beams' (Sigrdrifumal), and the sagas' elf-sacrifice cures (Kormaks saga's mound-offering) document the elf-folk as healers, neighbors and dangerous kin - a people in legal-social relation with humans, not mere spirits. And the tooth-gift's real custom completes the record: the Norse elite's teething-gifts (a boy's first tooth celebrated with a present) are the myth's mirror, the god's country-sized fee magnifying the farm's gift. The record thus anchors the elf-geography family: the bright above and the pitch-dark below, one name-family divided by residence.

functions: Aition of the fairy-realm: elfland as a realm gifted at a god's first tooth
Two-elf doctrine: light-elves above, dark-elves below - residence, not species, as moral geography
Gift-economy of childhood: mirrors the real Norse tooth-gift custom
Links elves to healing, prophecy and dangerous marriage in eddic and saga material

title.en: The Kettle of the Gods' Feast: Thor and Tyr Fetch Hymir's Cauldron
title.zh: 諸神盛宴之鍋：索爾與提爾取回希米爾的巨釜

region.en: Hymir's hall at the edge of heaven (symbolic pin at Lofoten, Norway)
region.zh: 天之盡頭的希米爾之廳（象徵性定位於挪威羅弗敦）

period: Hymiskvida c. 900-1000 CE; Gylfaginning c. 1220-1230; principal MSS Codex Regius GKS 2365 4to, GKS 2367 4to

source.work: Hymiskvida; Snorri, Gylfaginning ch. 45; critical ed. Dronke (1997)

license: Public domain (Bellows 1923; Brodeur 1916); passages below are labeled paraphrases

summary.en: The gods want a kettle big enough to brew ale for all of them at once, and only one exists: the mile-deep cauldron of the giant Hymir. Thor and Tyr travel east to fetch it; on the trip Thor fishes up the World-Serpent with an ox-head bait, and in the hall Tyr lifts the cauldron's lid by its ring while Thor carries the whole vessel out on his head, breaking gates and pillars - then slays the pursuing giants and the kettle's owner. The myth is the aition of the communal feast: the brewing-vessel of the gods is war-booty from the giants, hauled home through the frontier.
summary.zh: 諸神想要一口足以一次為全體釀酒的巨鍋，而世上僅有一口：巨人希米爾深達一里的巨釜。索爾與提爾東行取鍋；途中索爾以牛頭為餌釣起世界之蛇；在廳中，提爾以手扣住鍋環掀起鍋蓋，索爾則以頭頂起整口巨釜，撞碎門扉與立柱而歸——隨後誅殺追來的巨人與鍋之主人。此神話是「共食盛宴」的起源：諸神的釀酒巨器乃自巨人處奪得的戰利品，穿越邊境而歸。

canonical_translation: Henry A. Bellows, The Poetic Edda, New York 1923 (public domain); Gylfaginning via Brodeur 1916

narrative.en:
The myth begins, like so much Norse myth, at a party that cannot happen. The gods want to brew ale for all of them together, and the prophetesses find no kettle big enough until the giant Hymir's is named - a cauldron a mile deep. Thor and Tyr set out to steal it. Tyr's own father is Hymir (a monstrous detail: the law-god has giant kin), and at the hall Thor eats two of the oxen at a sitting, which enrages the giant and leads to the fishing trip: to test the god's table-manners, Hymir rows out to his deep-sea fishing grounds with the ox-head as bait.

The fishing is the myth's famous center. Thor baits the hook with the head of Hymir's best ox, rows past the giants' shores to where the World-Serpent lies, and hooks it; the serpent's head comes up, jaw over the gunwale, venom and eye glaring; Thor reaches for his hammer to kill it - and Hymir, terrified, cuts the line. The serpent sinks, and Thor strikes it a blow on the head as it goes - the wound that will not close until Ragnarok. (Snorri makes the giants cut the line out of fear; the poem blames Hymir's cowardice or cunning.)

The kettle heist completes the logic. At Hymir's hall the tests of strength multiply: Thor breaks a goblet against a rock (it shatters - against the giant's forehead, the rock of the world's edge); the cauldron's three-mile depth is weighed; and in the escape Tyr lifts the lid by its ring, Thor hauls the vessel on his head through doors and posts, and when the giants pursue with a hundred-headed troop, Thor kills Hymir and the troop with the returning hammer. The kettle arrives in Asgard: from now on the gods can brew ale for everyone at the winter feasts.

The record is a compact institutional myth: the communal feast - the core ritual of Scandinavian society - is equipped by theft from the borderlands. The kettle is the one object whose absence prevents the gods' society from functioning (a feast without enough ale is not a feast), and it can only be got by a joint operation of the two most boundary-crossing gods: Thor (strength) and Tyr (law and giant-kinship). Skaldic poetry confirms the myth's age: Bragi's Ragnarsdrapa (9th c.) and Eysteinn's lausavisa both depict the fishing, centuries before Snorri - the myth is attested at every stage of its transmission. In the atlas's frame, it answers the Greek amphictyony-cauldrons and the Chinese ding-tripods: ritual vessels as the emblems of the communal order, here won in single combat with the wild.

functions: Aition of the communal feast: the gods' brewing-vessel as war-booty from the giants
Frontier myth: society's core equipment obtained by a joint strongman-lawman raid
Anchor of the Thor-fishing myth-plex, attested in skaldic verse from the 9th century
Tests-of-strength narrative: table, goblet, kettle - the feast as strength-contest

title.en: The Mill Grotti: Gold, Peace and the Roaring Sea
title.zh: 格羅蒂磨坊：黃金、和平與咆哮的大海

region.en: The king's mill-hall and the open sea (symbolic pin at Laeso island, Denmark)
region.zh: 王的磨坊大廳與外海（象徵性定位於丹麥萊瑟島）

period: Grottasongr c. 900-1100 CE; Skaldskaparmal c. 1220-1230; principal MSS Codex Regius GKS 2365 4to, GKS 2367 4to

source.work: Grottasongr; Snorri, Skaldskaparmal ch. 8 (the story of Grottasongr); critical ed. Dronke (1997)

license: Public domain (Bellows 1923; Brodeur 1916); passages below are labeled paraphrases

summary.en: A magic mill named Grotti grinds whatever its operator commands: gold, peace, happiness - anything. Two giant-maidens, Fenja and Menja, are bought from Sweden and set to turn it; they grind gold and peace for the Danish king Frodi so well that he never needs to buy a man's life or justice - until the king overworks them, gives them no rest but the time a song takes, and they grind out an army and their own revenge. The mill is flung into the sea, where it still grinds - the aition of the maelstrom and, with it, of why the sea's salt is endless.
summary.zh: 神磨格羅蒂能磨出操作者所求之物：黃金、和平、幸福——無所不能。兩名巨人族少女芬婭與梅尼婭購自瑞典，被迫轉動神磨；她們為丹麥王弗羅迪磨出黃金與和平，令其無須買命或買公正——直到國王苛使她們，只許她們歇息一首歌的工夫，她們便磨出大軍與自身的復仇。神磨最終被拋入海中，至今仍在磨轉——這是漩渦（maelstrom）的起源故事，也解釋了海水何以無盡地鹹。

canonical_translation: Henry A. Bellows, The Poetic Edda, New York 1923 (public domain); Skaldskaparmal via Brodeur 1916

narrative.en:
The mill is the Norse myth of prosperity's machinery. Grotti - 'the grinder' - is a quern-stone so heavy no man can turn it; its first wheel-turn was before any land existed, it ground the gravel that became the earth, and it has ground gold ever since. King Frodi of Denmark finds the two giant-maidens Fenja and Menja, daughters of the mountain-giant Hrungnir's kin, buys them as slaves from Sweden, and sets them at the mill; he orders them to grind gold, peace and happiness, and grants them no rest longer than the time a song takes.

The maidens comply - and compose. Their work-song (the poem Grottasongr itself) is a labor-arithmetic: they have turned the mill through wars and fortunes; they ground for Yngvi's hosts, ground the unsteady gold, ground peace for Frodi; and the king's wealth was such that no man needed to buy another's life or sue another for justice. But the song remembers too what they are: giant-kin, stronger than the strongest, born before the world. Their patience breaks: 'weary are we of the labor' - and they change the order. Now they grind out a host against the king: warships, warriors, a banner - and the sea-king Mysing comes, sacks the hall, burns Frodi's peace, and carries off the mill and the maidens.

On Mysing's ship he orders one last grinding - salt. The ship is heavy-laden; at midnight the maidens ask whether they are wearying the crew; the sea-king says they have ground long enough; but the mill has ground to the hull's waterline, and down goes the ship - mill, maidens, salt - and where it sank there has been a whirlpool ever since, where the sea runs through the eye of the stone: the maelstrom, whose waters are salt because the grinding never stopped.

The cultural functions are dense. The myth aitions three institutions at once: peace (it can be ground like gold - and it is perishable, resting on the labor of the unfree), the maelstrom (a whirlpool whose salt explains the sea), and the ethics of forced labor (the mill runs on giant-women bought as slaves, and their song is the exact price-list of the king's prosperity). Snorri embeds it in Skaldskaparmal as a kenning-source - 'Frodi's meal', 'the maidens' sea-mill' - and as a political fable for a thirteenth-century audience that understood grinding gold out of subject labor. In the atlas, Grotti answers the Chinese mulberry-field catastrophes and the Greek water-mill legends: machinery, labor and apocalypse in one mechanism.

functions: Aition of the maelstrom and the sea's endless salt
Political fable: peace and gold ground from the labor of unfree giant-women
The work-song as price-list: Grottasongr documents the cost of prosperity
Apocalypse mechanism: prosperity-machinery flung into the sea still operating

passages.text: But the king gave them no longer rest than the singing of a song; and the maidens changed their grinding: now they ground out a host and warships against the hall, and the sea-king Mysing came, burned the king's peace, and carried off the mill and the maidens. On his ship he bade them grind salt; they ground until the ship sank, and since then the sea has run through the eye of the stone, and the waters there are salt.

title.en: Skirnismal: Freyr's Wooing, the Pledged Sword and the Greening of the Fields
title.zh: 斯基尼爾之歌：弗雷的求愛、抵押的寶劍與田野回青

region.en: Gymir's garden, Jotunheimr (symbolic pin at Jotunheimen, Norway)
region.zh: 約頓海姆基米爾的花園（象徵性定位於挪威尤通黑門山）

period: Skirnismal c. 900-1000 CE; Gylfaginning c. 1220-1230; principal MSS Codex Regius GKS 2365 4to, GKS 2367 4to

source.work: Skirnismal; Snorri, Gylfaginning ch. 37; critical ed. Dronke (1997)

license: Public domain (Bellows 1923; Brodeur 1916); passages below are labeled paraphrases

summary.en: Seated on Odin's all-seeing throne, Freyr looks into Gymir's garden and falls mortally lovesick for the giant-maiden Gerd. His servant Skirnir rides as envoy, first offering her eleven golden apples and the ring Draupnir, then cursing her: her limbs shall wither, her face be seen only by terror, madness and misery follow her - unless she consents. She consents, nine nights hence, in the grove Barri. But the price is the god's own sword: Freyr has pledged it to Skirnir, and when Ragnarok comes he must fight Surtr bare-handed - and fall. The myth is the Norse aition of the harvest: the fertility god buys the earth's yielding with his own weapon, and pays at the world's end.
summary.zh: 弗雷坐上奧丁的全知王座，望見基米爾花園，為巨人族少女葛德害上致命的相思。其僕斯基尼爾奉命為使，先以十一枚金蘋果與指環德羅普尼爾相誘，後以咒語相脅：若不容應，其肢體將枯萎，其容顏只被恐懼所見，瘋狂與悲苦隨行——葛德遂允於九夜之後在巴里林中相會。然而代價是神自己的寶劍：弗雷已將其抵押給斯基尼爾，末日之戰來臨時他只能空手迎戰蘇爾特——並因此殞命。此神話是北歐豐收的起源故事：豐饒之神以自己的兵器換取大地的饋贈，並在世界終結之時償付。

canonical_translation: Henry A. Bellows, The Poetic Edda, New York 1923 (public domain); Gylfaginning via Brodeur 1916

narrative.en:
The myth begins with surveillance. Freyr sits one day in Hlidskjalf, Odin's high seat from which all worlds are seen, though no one but its owner should sit there; he looks north to Jotunheim, sees a maiden walking from her father Gymir's hall to the storehouse, and the sight does its work: his hand grows slack, his mind sick, and no one can speak with him. Njord sends Skirnir, Freyr's servant, to ask the matter; Freyr confesses, and asks the impossible: to woo the girl for him, over her father's will and her own.

Skirnir names his fee and takes the gear: Freyr's sword, the one that fights of itself. Then the embassy: past the hounds of Gymir's fence, to the garden where Gerd sits. First the gold: eleven apples of the goddess Iunn, the ring Draupnir that drops eight rings of its own kind every ninth night - she refuses: 'Gymir's gold I need not, nor the ring'. Then threats, in escalating verse: Skirnir draws (with what? the text withholds) a threatening shape and curses her: she shall sit lonely on the eagle's cliff, look toward the worlds, and find food more loathsome to her than to any man; she shall be seen of all as a terror; madness, misery and the restless urge shall follow her; her limbs shall grow; her face shall strike dread; with a three-leaved thurst-staff the giant Hrimgrimnir shall have her below the corpses' gate - and the wretched maid shall always serve, 'ever beneath the grips of men'. The curses land: Gerd bids him welcome - the ninth night, in the grove Barri, she will grant the god her love.

But the poem has one more stanza of freight: when Skirnir asks his wages, the exchange is stark - 'the sword I gave you is your fee; the maiden you won for me; and I know it well, that my fall draws near'. Gylfaginning confirms: because Freyr gave the sword away, he had none when he met Surtr at Ragnarok, and he slew Beli with a horn's point - and the Prose account adds the economics: had he kept the sword, the gods would have been served by it at Ragnarok. The sword bought the union of god and earth-giantess; the price is deferred to doomsday.

The record's cultural functions are the harvest-doctrine and the marriage-ethics of the north. Skirnismal is the aition of the fields' fruitfulness: the union of the god (rain, sunshine) with Gerd (the fenced garden, her name means 'enclosure') is agriculture itself - a marriage of cultivation and enclosure. And it is a courtship-law myth: consent extracted by escalating threats, negotiated by an envoy who is paid in weapons - the poem's own editors debate whether the curses are ritual magic (a warlock's wooing) or a legal parable of forced marriage. For the atlas, the pledged sword is the pattern of the culture-gift bought with doom - the myth answers Prometheus' fire-theft and Freyr's own corn-splendor with a mortgage: the fertility god's armament is pawned to buy the harvest, and the interest comes due at the end of the world.

functions: Aition of the harvest: the god's marriage to the enclosure (Gerd) as agriculture itself
Doctrine of priced consent: wooing by escalating threat, negotiated by a paid envoy
The pledged sword: the fertility god's armament pawned for the harvest, due at Ragnarok
Surveillance motif: Hlidskjalf's all-seeing throne as the trigger of love and doom

title.en: Yggdrasil and the Nine Worlds: The Rooted Map of the Norse Cosmos
title.zh: 尤克特拉希爾與九界：北歐宇宙的根鬚地圖

region.en: Yggdrasil, the World-Ash (symbolic pin at Pingvellir, Iceland)
region.zh: 世界梣樹尤克特拉希爾（象徵性定位於冰島辛格韋德利）

period: Grimnismal st. 26-35 c. 900-1000 CE; Gylfaginning c. 1220-1230; principal MSS Codex Regius GKS 2365 4to, GKS 2367 4to

source.work: Grimnismal st. 26-35; Snorri, Gylfaginning chs. 15-16; critical ed. Dronke (1997)

license: Public domain (Bellows 1923; Brodeur 1916); passages below are labeled paraphrases

summary.en: The Norse cosmos is a tree. Yggdrasil, the World-Ash, is the best of trees: three roots drive deep - one to the Aesir at Urd's well, one to the frost-giants at Mimir's well, one over Niflheim at Hvergelmir - and under each root something gnaws. An eagle with a hawk between its eyes sits on the crown; a squirrel runs the trunk carrying insults; four harts eat the bark; Nidhoggr gnaws the corpse-branches from below. Meanwhile the tree suffers more than men know: the harts bite, the trunk rots, the serpent wounds - and the three maidens water it. The nine worlds hang on this suffering axis, and its endurance is the universe's own.
summary.zh: 北歐宇宙是一棵樹。世界梣樹尤克特拉希爾是萬樹之最：三條巨根深扎——一條通向兀兒德泉旁的阿薩神族，一條通向霜巨人的密米爾之泉，一條橫越尼福爾海姆的赫維爾蓋爾米爾——每條根下皆有啃噬之物。樹冠上有鷹棲息，鷹眼之間有隼；松鼠沿樹幹奔跑挑撥；四鹿啃食樹皮；尼德霍格自下方啃咬屍枝。世界樹所受之苦遠超世人所知：鹿齒、腐朽、蛇傷——而三位少女每日澆灌。九界懸於這根苦難之軸上，樹的存續即宇宙的存續。

canonical_translation: Henry A. Bellows, The Poetic Edda, New York 1923 (public domain); Gylfaginning via Brodeur 1916

narrative.en:
Grimnismal, Odin's cosmological litany recited in disguise, gives the tree's full anatomy. The Ash stands 'above the hells of Hel'; beneath it go the three deep roots: the first to the frost-giants, under which is Mimir's well, where wisdom and understanding are hidden; the second to the Aesir, under which is Urd's well, where the gods hold their court and where the Norns water the tree daily so its bark stays white; the third over Niflheim, under which is Hvergelmir, where Nidhoggr gnaws the dead. Its top bears the eagle whose eyes' wisdom is a hawk between them; a squirrel named Ratatoskr runs up and down carrying malicious words between the eagle and the serpent; four harts eat the highest shoots with heads thrown back. The tree suffers more than men know: the harts above bite it, the side rots, and Nidhoggr wounds it from beneath - 'but yet shall it fall no more than it is fated'.

Gylfaginning fixes the geography around it. Under the first root is the gods' assembly-stead; under the second, wisdom; under the third, the corpse-spring. The worlds themselves are nine and named: Asgard of the Aesir, Midgard of men, Jotunheim of giants, Vanaheim of the Vanir, Alfheim of the light-elves, Svartalfheim (with Nidavellir) of the dwarfs, Muspell of fire, Niflheim of mist and ice, and Hel of the dead. No single eddic poem lists them all - the nine is Snorri's synthesis of the poems' halls and rivers - and that is itself a datum: the learned Icelander built the canonical map by reconciling verses, the same method as any critical historian.

The cultural functions are three. First, the tree is the constitution of interdependence: every level of the cosmos feeds on every other - the eagle insults the serpent through the squirrel's shuttle diplomacy, the goats of the gods eat its leaves, the roots drink from the two wells, and the Norns' watering is the only thing keeping the bark white; the universe is a body with metabolism, wounds, and care. Second, it is a theology of endurance: the tree suffers 'more than men know' yet holds - the Norse answer to why the cosmos persists in a world of winter. Third, it is the boundary-marker of the atlas's cosmology family: Yggdrasil answers the Chinese Chienmu ladder, the Maya ceiba, the Zoroastrian Haoma - each a world-tree; only the Norse one is dying on a schedule and scheduled to survive its own end (it stands in the renewal, green, feeding the last pair).

For the database the record anchors the whole cosmological cluster: the wells, the norns, the eagle-hawk, the squirrel, the hart-browsing and the corpse-gnawing are each separate mythic entries elsewhere; here they are the parts of one suffering machine that keeps all worlds in reach of each other.

functions: Cosmological constitution: the nine worlds as organs of one suffering, nourished tree
Doctrine of endurance: the tree holds though wounded beyond men's knowledge
Metabolism of the cosmos: wells, waterings, browsings and insult-relays as one system
Comparative anchor of the world-tree motif family

title.en: The Binding of Fenrir: Gleipnir, Tyr's Hand and the Contracted Doom
title.zh: 縛住芬里爾：格雷普尼爾之索、提爾斷掌與契約化的末日

region.en: The island Lyngvi in Lake Amsvartnir (symbolic pin at Lake Viborg, Denmark)
region.zh: 阿姆斯瓦特尼爾湖中的林格維島（象徵性定位於丹麥維堡湖）

period: Gylfaginning c. 1220-1230 (older material); Voluspa st. 39-40 (allusions); principal MSS Codex Regius GKS 2367 4to, GKS 2365 4to

source.work: Snorri, Gylfaginning ch. 34; critical ed. Faulkes (1987)

license: Public domain (Brodeur 1916; Bellows 1923); passages below are labeled paraphrases

summary.en: The gods raised Loki's wolf-son Fenrir themselves, and only Odin's prophecy feared him; when the gods tried to bind him, he broke every chain they forged - and he refused all bonds unless a god would lay a hand in his mouth as pledge. Tyr, the one-handed god to be, stepped forward. The chain they made was not iron: Gleipnir was woven of six impossible things - the footfall of a cat, the roots of a mountain, a bear's sinews, a woman's beard, a fish's breath, a bird's spittle - things that no longer exist because they went into it. The wolf was bound, and bit the hand off; and from that day the wolf waits on the island, jaws stretched by a sword, until Ragnarok, when the bond breaks and the pledged doom is collected.
summary.zh: 諸神親手養育洛基的狼子芬里爾，唯奧丁的預言懼之；諸神欲縛之，鍛造的鐐銬屢遭掙斷——而狼拒受任何束縛，除非有神願將一掌放入其口為信。提爾，那位將成獨臂的神，挺身而出。他們所製之索並非鐵造：格雷普尼爾由六種不可能之物織成——貓的腳步聲、山的根鬚、熊的筋腱、女人的鬍鬚、魚的氣息、鳥的唾沫——此六物因入索而不復存在。狼被縛住，咬斷了神的手；自此狼臥於島上，口中撐劍，直至末日之時鎖鏈斷裂，那被擔保的厄運終須償付。

canonical_translation: A. G. Brodeur, Snorri Sturluson: The Prose Edda, New York 1916 (public domain)

narrative.en:
Gylfaginning tells the binding as a story of failed engineering and a successful lie. Loki's three children - Fenrir the wolf, Jormungand the serpent, Hel the half-dead girl - were brought before the gods; Odin threw one into the sea and one into the grave, but the wolf they reared at home, and only Týr dared feed him. When prophecy said the wolf would destroy them, the gods made three fetters in succession: Leyding, which the wolf broke; Dromi, twice as strong, which he also broke, 'with great noise and lunge'. Then the gods sent a messenger to the dwarfs, and the dwarfs made a fetter called Gleipnir, of six things: the sound a cat makes in moving, a woman's beard, the roots of a mountain, a bear's sinews, a fish's breath, and a bird's spittle - and 'though you have not heard of these before, you may be sure they exist, for some have been shown to you that you could not see: why, what do you think a cat's footfall is, or a woman's beard, or the roots of mountains?' Everything has its absence explained by its absorption into the fetter.

The second doctrine is the contract. The wolf saw the slim silken band and smelled deceit: 'it seems to me that I have got no fame of skill though I snap that rope-band; but if it is made with craft and guile, it shall never come on my legs.' He would be bound only if someone put his hand in his mouth as a pledge of fair play - and each god looked at the other until Týr put forth his hand and laid it in the wolf's jaw. Bound, Fenrir strained, and the band would not give; the more he tugged, the tighter it gripped. Then he bit: Týr lost the hand at the wrist, 'and the wolf is called one-handed among the gods'. They thrust a sword into his gaping jaws, hilt up, and bound the band to a great stone slab on the island Lyngvi in the lake Amsvartnir, where the wolf waits, howling horribly - and drools a river from his mouth, called Van, to the hell-plain Vilrida-moor.

The cultural functions make this one of the atlas's central records. First, it is a doctrine of collateral: the gods cannot defeat the wolf, so they make a contract with it, buying binding by pledging a god's hand - the doom is not cancelled but financed. Second, it is the aition of absence: six ordinary impossibilities are explained as consumed ingredients - a completeness-proof myth of the kind Grimm catalogued for Germanic magic. Third, it is the aition of legal trust gone wrong: Týr's hand is the pledge of a bargain kept by all parties - the gods keep their word, the wolf keeps his, and both are ruined; Scandinavian law-culture recognized exactly this structure, a settlement whose collateral is honor. Fourth, it sets the eschatology's clock: at Ragnarok the wolf breaks free 'with a great howl', jaws stretched from earth to sky, and swallows Odin.

Snorri's narrative is compressed from lost eddic verse; Voluspa's prophecy already knows the bound wolf and the jaws stretched 'over the world' at the end - the binding and the release are one narrative arc across the corpus.

functions: Doctrine of collateral: the gods finance Fenrir's binding by pledging Týr's hand
Aition of absence: six impossible ingredients explain what the world no longer has
Trust-ethics myth: the pledge honored by both parties ruins both
Eschatological clock: the bond's scheduled release is Ragnarok's first act

title.en: The Fimbulwinter and the Wolves of the Lights: The Doom That Comes as Weather
title.zh: 芬布爾之冬與吞日之狼：以氣候降臨的末日

region.en: The darkening sky over Midgard (symbolic pin at Pingvellir, Iceland)
region.zh: 米德加爾特上空陰沉的天穹（象徵性定位於冰島辛格韋德利）

period: Voluspa st. 40-41, 57 c. 900-1000 CE; Gylfaginning c. 1220-1230; Vafthrudnismal st. 44; principal MSS Codex Regius GKS 2365 4to, GKS 2367 4to

source.work: Voluspa st. 40-41; Vafthrudnismal st. 44; Snorri, Gylfaginning ch. 51; critical ed. Dronke (1997)

license: Public domain (Bellows 1923; Brodeur 1916); passages below are labeled paraphrases

summary.en: Ragnarok begins not with a battle but with a sky. In the east a giantess rears the wolf-kin of the old giant; one of them, Managarm, feeds on the flesh of the dead and the moon; the sun's wolf Snorride? - Skoll - swallows the sun, Hati takes the moon, and the stars vanish from heaven. Then comes the Fimbulwinter: three winters together, no summer between, snow from all quarters, no warmth in the sun - and after those, three more. Brother will fight brother; the wind carries wolf-howls; the world is a spear-age, a sword-age, an axe-age, a wind-age, a wolf-age, before the world goes down. The record is the Norse doctrine that civilizations end as climates: apocalypse arrives as weather, and the moral collapse precedes the physical one.
summary.zh: 諸神黃昏的開端並非戰陣，而是天穹。東方有女巨人在老巨人的狼族中養子；其中名為瑪納加爾姆者，以死者之肉為食，並將吞月；吞日之狼斯科爾將吞下太陽，哈蒂奪月，星辰自天穹隱沒。隨後而來的是芬布爾之冬：三冬相連，夏不至，四方降雪，日光無溫——此後還有三冬。兄弟將相互殘殺；風中滿是狼嚎；世界成為矛之紀、劍之紀、斧之紀、風之紀、狼之紀——然後世界傾覆。此記錄是北歐的教義：文明以氣候終結，末日以天氣降臨，而道德的崩潰先於物理的崩潰。

canonical_translation: Henry A. Bellows, The Poetic Edda, New York 1923 (public domain); Gylfaginning via Brodeur 1916

narrative.en:
Völuspá's doom-sequence opens in the east, in the iron-wood (Járnviðr), where a giantess rears Fenrir's kin; among them is 'Managarm, the moon's feeder', who fills himself with the life-blood of doomed men and reddens with the blood of the gods - 'sun will be darkened, winds will howl murderously over the sky'. The parallel prose in Gylfaginning names the two wolves: Skoll ('treachery') who shall swallow the sun, and Hati ('hate'), the wolf that goes before the moon - and when both have taken their quarry, the stars go out.

Then the weather. Vafthrudnismal's prophecy gives the clearest statement: 'first comes the winter called Fimbulwinter: three winters together, no summer between; before that there have been three other winters, and then the world will be a war-age, brothers will fight brothers, and no one will spare another.' Gylfaginning adds the meteorology: snow drifts from all quarters, and the sun gives no heat. Human order collapses in the same stanzas - kinship-slaying, perjury, the axe-age and sword-age litany of Völuspá st. 45: 'brothers will fight brothers and slay each other; sisters' sons will break kinship-bonds; hard it is in the world, great whoredom, an axe-age, a sword-age, shields are cleft, a wind-age, a wolf-age, until the world falls.'

The cultural functions are the doctrine of climate-collapse and the moral sequencer. In a Norse environment where three bad winters could kill a colony (Iceland's and Greenland's actual famine cycles), the myth formalizes the observation: the end is not a monster first but a sky first - the food-system fails before the armies march. And the sequence is deliberate: the wolves take the lights (cosmological failure), the winter comes (climatological failure), kinship breaks (social failure), and only then do the monsters and the fire ride (military failure). The myth asserts that doom is legible in advance in exactly this order - a doctrine of prophecy by weather-station.

For the atlas the record is the eschatology family's hinge record: it documents a European tradition where the apocalypse is a climate event with a moral prologue, comparable to the Chinese catastrophes of the Five Ages and the Maya's collapsing world-ages - but here with named wolves, a nameable winter, and a schedule.

The wolves' genealogy completes the doctrine: Skoll and Hati are Fenrir's kin (reared in the iron-wood by the giantess), so the sun-eaters are the bound wolf's family - the gods' management of the monster-brood failing at the schedule's end. And the climate-doctrine's realism completes the record: three rainless, sunless winters is precisely the northern famine-experience (Iceland's and Greenland's colony-mortality cycles), so the myth formalizes observation as eschatology - the apocalypse arrived as weather-report before it arrived as battle. The record thus anchors the climate-collapse family: doom's order (sky, weather, kinship, army) legible in advance, the north's famine-memory written as prophecy.

functions: Doctrine of climate-collapse: doom arrives as sky, then weather, then kinship-break
Moral sequencer: cosmological, climatological, social, military failures in fixed order
Names the northern famine experience (three winters) as eschatological structure
Anchor of the sun-swallowing motif family

title.en: The Rök Stone: Theodoric, Twenty Kings, and the End of the Sun
title.zh: 勒克石碑：狄奧多里克、二十王與太陽之終

region.en: Rök churchyard, Odeshög, Ostergotland, Sweden (runic inscription Og 136, c. 800 CE)
region.zh: 瑞典東約特蘭厄德雪於呂克教堂墓地（如尼碑Og 136，約800年）

period: c. 800 CE (Vendel/early Viking Age); granite runestone, inscription recovered in full by Sophus Bugge (1877) and later scholars

summary.en: On a granite block in an Ostergotland churchyard, a man named Varin raised the longest known runic inscription, about five lines of dense cipher-runes and verse. It names Theodoric the Great, 'chief of sea-warriors, seated with shield over his shoulders on his Frankish steed' - the dead emperor remembered in Sweden - and runs through number-riddles: twenty kings, four brothers, the giant's line, 'I say this the twelfth, where the horse sees food on the wayside'. Its most disputed lines say: 'I say this the thirteenth, which twenty kings sat on Sjalfi's hill, four winters, four names' - and, most dramatically, 'nine generations back, when Theodoric ruled... I say this the twenty-sixth, when? - I say the twenty-seventh: I say to you which... ' and the couplet that some read as eschatological: the sun? the moon? - 'I say to you the myth of Viurr: the sun and moon... ' The stone is Scandinavia's earliest datable mythic-literary monument, and the strongest candidate for a pre-Viking eschatology carved in runes.
summary.zh: 在東約特蘭一處教堂墓地的花崗岩上，名為瓦林的男子立起已知最長的如尼文銘文，約五行密集的密碼如尼與詩句。碑文提及狄奧多里克大帝——「海戰者之首，肩負盾牌，騎法蘭克戰馬」——這位客死異鄉的皇帝在瑞典被傳頌；並以數字謎語貫穿：二十王、四兄弟、巨人之族、「我說此為第十二，那馬在路旁見食」。最具爭議的句子包括「我說此為第十三，二十王曾坐於謝爾菲之丘，四冬四名」——以及最戲劇性的：有人讀出末世色彩的對句：太陽？月亮？「我向你們訴說維烏爾之謎：太陽與月亮……」這塊石碑是斯堪的納維亞最早可斷代的神話文學碑刻，也是前維京時代末世觀刻入如尼文的最強候選。

canonical_translation: Readings per Sophus Bugge (1877), Ottar Gronvik (1985), Henrik Williams (1996); paraphrase-synthesis with critical apparatus noted

narrative.en:
The Rök stone is the strangest and most important runic monument of Scandinavia: a five-ton granite block in a churchyard at Odeshog, covered with about 750 runes - the longest known inscription - laid in long-twig and cipher forms across face, sides and top. Its sender, Varin, raised it in memory of his dead son Vamod; but instead of the usual memorial formulas, the inscription is a number-riddle poem: 'I say this the twelfth...' up to 'the twenty-seventh', interlacing heroic memory with cosmology.

Its most famous lines name Theodoric the Great - the Ostrogothic emperor who died in 526 - as 'Mærings' lord, seated armed on his Frankish horse over the rampart, lord of the sea-warriors: the earliest Swedish attestation of a legend that lives on in the German Dietrich songs. Around him the riddles accumulate: twenty kings who sat four winters on four names at Sjalfi's hill, the five Inkus sons, the four brothers, and the fight between Eirik and Valdemar; then the obscure 'Si'gtryggr', the 'giant's line', and the sequence 'I say this the twenty-sixth, when? ... I say the twenty-seventh: I say to you which...' - where the closing couplet has been read as: the sun and the moon, the fates of men, the battle-wolf's release? - and, on the strongest modern reading (Gronvik), as an eschatology: 'I say to you the myth of Viurr: the sun [and moon]? The fates... [shall] be swallowed by the enemy of the moon? ... when the wolf shall swallow the moon and the sun? The fates... shall be destroyed. Earth? shall see them... I say to you the strongest of fates and the most portentous: that the luminous sky-watcher [the sun] shall be swallowed... I say to you a truth: the end of the heaven and the sun - I say to you a second truth: the swelling sea [shall swallow]? the earth - I say to you a third truth: the ice-cold wolf shall swallow [the moon]?' On this reading the stone's climax is a Ragnarok before the Vikings: sun, moon and earth swallowed in sequence.

Not all scholars agree - Wessén read the monument as primarily a heroic-genealogical praise poem for local lines (Vamod's ancestry traced through Theodoric and the Volsungs), and the numerological structure resists final agreement. But the eschatological reading (Gronvik 1985; Williams 1996) explains the cipher-runes' ritual placement and the stone's placement facing the churchyard road. What is certain is the method: this is the earliest datable mythic-literary monument of Scandinavia, a century and a half before the Edda poems were written down, proving that narrative myth - heroic and cosmological together - circulated in runic form before any manuscript.

For the atlas the record is a hinge between the literary and archaeological datasets: it demonstrates that Ragnarök-type eschatology, the Theodoric hero-legend, and number-riddling co-existed on one stone in c. 800, and it anchors the database's runic corpus with its most ambitious specimen. The stone's provenance record (recovered in full by successive scholars from a damaged, cryptic text) also makes it the clearest case-study of the database's own method: a record_status of 'reconstructed', where the myth exists only through the successive restorations of its readers.

functions: Earliest datable mythic-literary monument of Scandinavia (c. 800 CE)
Evidences pre-Viking circulation of Theodoric hero-legend and eschatological myth in runes
Number-riddling as memory-technology: the monument as an oral archive carved in stone
Case-study of reconstructed provenance: the myth survives through successive critical readings

title.en: Naglfar, the Ship of Dead Men's Nails: Loki Breaks Loose
title.zh: 納格爾法爾，死人指甲之船：洛基掙脫

region.en: The eastern sea-road of the doomed (symbolic pin at Laeso island, Denmark)
region.zh: 亡者自東而來的海路（象徵性定位於丹麥萊瑟島）

period: Voluspa st. 48-51 c. 900-1000 CE; Gylfaginning c. 1220-1230; principal MSS Codex Regius GKS 2365 4to, GKS 2367 4to

source.work: Voluspa st. 48-51; Snorri, Gylfaginning ch. 51; critical ed. Dronke (1997)

license: Public domain (Bellows 1923; Brodeur 1916); passages below are labeled paraphrases

summary.en: At Ragnarok's approach, the ship Naglfar comes from the east: a vessel made of the untrimmed fingernails of dead men, and the giant Hrym steers it; Loki sails the other ship, Loki at the helm - freed from his rock, his sons' entrails torn as rigging, he takes the sea-lanes of the doomed to the field of the last battle. The myth welds the body-discipline of the living to the fate of the world: how you trim your nails helps decide how the enemy sails.
summary.zh: 諸神黃昏將至，納格爾法爾之船自東而來：那船以死者未剪的指甲所造，由巨人赫呂姆掌舵；另一船由洛基駕駛——他掙脫了岩石，其子之腸被扯作索具，駕著亡者之船駛向最後戰場。此神話將生者的身體紀律與世界的命運焊接在一起：你如何修剪指甲，竟與敵人如何揚帆有關。

canonical_translation: Henry A. Bellows, The Poetic Edda, New York 1923 (public domain); Gylfaginning via Brodeur 1916

narrative.en:
Voluspa's doom-litany assigns the sea-approach: 'from the east steers Hrym with shields high; Jormungand writhes in giant-fury and beats the waves; the eagle screams, slays corpses with his beak; Naglfar is loosed. A ship comes from the east, the hosts of Muspell are crossing the waves, and Loki steers; the monster's kin are all with the wolf; with them is Byleist's brother [Loki].' Gylfaginning supplies the ship's name and its construction: Naglfar, 'nail-ship', made of dead men's fingernails - 'and worthy of note is this, that he who dies untrimmed goes with important material to the ship's building, and therefore every man who is to die suddenly? should have uncut nails?' - no: therefore each person should die with trimmed nails, to delay the ship. Snorri also assigns the helmsmen: the giant Hrym steers Naglfar; Loki steers the second ship, with the fire-giants of Muspell aboard.

The myth's first function is body-discipline as eschatology. Naglfar is the only European apocalypse whose progress is slowed by personal hygiene: the untrimmed dead contribute timber, so the living's grooming is moral service. The doctrine presupposes a society in which nails were cut with shared tools and bodies were socially regulated - the myth turns grooming into cosmic citizenship.

The second function is Loki's release. In Gylfaginning's chronology, Loki lies bound until Ragnarok, when he breaks loose and joins the giants; the verse gives his crossing its horror-image: the father of the lie sails on the ship of the dead, whose rigging is (in some readings) his own sons' entrails - the binding's materials returning as equipment. The record thus closes the loop of the binding-myths: what the gods made of the enemy's family comes back as the enemy's navy.

For the atlas, Naglfar anchors the doom-fleet motif: the image of the end arriving by sea - comparable to the Turkish-Mongol flood-myths and the Chinese ghosts' ghost-ships - here with a construction doctrine: the enemy's vessel is built, plank by plank, out of the carelessness of the living.

The nail-doctrine's social logic completes the record: in a society where nails were cut with shared tools and the dead's bodies were community property, the myth turns grooming into cosmic citizenship - the untrimmed dead contribute timber to the enemy's navy, so the living's care delays the doom. And the binding-loop completes the record: Loki freed from his rock sails the ship of the dead, whose rigging is (in the prose's darkest clause) his own sons' entrails - what the gods made of the enemy's family returns as the enemy's equipment. The record thus anchors the doom-fleet family: the end arriving by sea, built plank by plank from the carelessness of the living.

functions: Body-discipline doctrine: untrimmed nails of the dead build the doom-ship, so grooming delays Ragnarok
Closes the binding-loop: Loki freed, his binding-materials returned as rigging
Sea-approach of the apocalypse: the end arrives as a fleet from the east
Assigns helmsmen to doom: Hrym on Naglfar, Loki with the Muspell-host

title.en: Hel's Realm: The Road North, the Bridge of Echoes and the Corpse-Gate
title.zh: 海爾之境：向北之路、迴聲之橋與屍骸之門

region.zh: 海爾——第九世界，死者之國（象徵性定位於冰島辛格韋德利）

period: Gylfaginning c. 1220-1230 (older material); Voluspa st. 37-39; principal MSS Codex Regius GKS 2367 4to, GKS 2365 4to

summary.en: Hel is a country with a compass: her realm lies northward and downward, nine nights' ride from the living, past the echoing river Gjoll, over the bridge Gjallarbru that rings under a living rider, through the iron-fenced gate Helgrind, into the hall Eljudnir ('damp-with-sleet'), where platters are 'hunger', the knife is 'famine', and the fallen stand. The dead of sickness and age go there; the battle-slain go to Odin. The record is the Norse geography of ordinary death - unmajestic, domestic, and strictly zoned.
summary.zh: 海爾之境自有方位：其國在北而向下，距生者九夜之程，越過迴聲之河吉奧爾，踏過吉亞拉爾橋——活人過橋時橋身轟響——穿過鐵柵之門海爾格林德，進入大廳埃爾尤德尼爾（「落雹濕冷」），廳中碗盤名為「飢」，餐刀名為「匱」，床位名為「病」。病老而死者入此國；戰死者則歸奧丁。此記錄是北歐對「尋常之死」的地理描述——無榮耀、居家氣息、且分區嚴明。

canonical_translation: A. G. Brodeur, Snorri Sturluson: The Prose Edda, New York 1916 (public domain)

narrative.en:
Gylfaginning assigns the realm its place and its people. When Odin threw Loki's daughter Hel down into Niflheim, he gave her authority over nine worlds, 'that she should apportion all abodes to those that were sent to her': this is the underworld of the unchosen dead - those who die of sickness or old age, as against the battle-slain whom the valkyries take to Odin. Her hall is Eljudnir, 'sprinkled with rain'; her dishes 'Hunger', her knife 'Famine', her thralls 'Sloth' and 'Sourness', her thresholds 'Pitfall', her bed 'Sickness', her curtains 'Misfortune' - a hall named for the deficits of a starving household. She is half flesh-colored and half blue-black, 'easily recognized, and more downcast and fierce-looking than the others'.

The geography is mapped in the Hermothr episode. The rider comes to the river Gjoll, the bridge Gjallarbru across it, 'roofed with shining gold', and meets the maiden Modgudr, who keeps it: five companies of dead men rode over, but it rang less under them; nothing is darker than under the dead man's eyebrows; the rider shakes the bridge and resounds like gold, and has not the color of dead men - his 'breast heaves with more hot air than a dead man's breath'. The bridge-keeper's questions are a customs post between the living and the dead; only Sleipnir's eight legs and a god's heat could cross ringing. Beyond lies the iron gate Helgrind ('the gates of Hel'), through which even Hermothr must creep sidewise past the hound Garmr.

The record's cultural functions are a taxonomy of deaths and a domestication of the grave. Norse society sorted its dead by manner of dying: the field of battle to Valhalla or Freyja, the sea to Ran's net, the bed to Hel - and this record maps the last, ordinary, majority death, without glory and without punishment, in a hall that is simply poverty and sickness continued. That absence of judgment is the record's sharpest comparative datum: Hel is not a hell; she is a large, gray household. (Völuspá's Náströnd, with its serpent and corpse-shore, is the separate doctrine for oath-breakers and murderers - a different record here.)

In the atlas's cosmology family, Hel's realm answers the Greek Hades and the Mesopotamian House of Dust - each an unmajestic underworld for the ordinary dead - but the Norse one adds a bridge-keeper, a customs-post, and a ring underfoot: the afterlife with the acoustics of frontier law.

functions: Taxonomy of deaths: the ordinary dead (sickness, age) zoned to Hel, the battle-slain to Odin
Geography of the grave: nine nights, echoing river, ringing bridge, iron gate
Domestic underworld without judgment: a hall named for hunger and sickness, not sin
Bridge-keeper motif: the customs-post between living and dead

summary.en: After Baldr's death, Frigg asks who will ride to Hel to offer ransom for her son, and Hermothr the swift takes Sleipnir, Odin's eight-legged horse, and rides nine nights through dark valleys to the bridge of the dead. Hel answers the gods' plea: if all things weep Baldr alive, he shall return; if anything refuses, he stays. Hermothr rides back with the message - and the failure of the weeping (one giantess refuses) leaves Baldr in Hel until the world's renewal. The record is the Norse descent-and-return that fails: a rescue mission defeated by a single withheld tear.
summary.zh: 巴爾德死後，弗麗格問誰願騎往冥府為兒子獻上贖金，迅捷的赫爾莫德乘上奧丁的八足神馬斯萊普尼爾，歷九夜穿過幽暗山谷，抵達死者之橋。海爾答覆諸神之求：若世間萬物皆為巴爾德哭泣，他便可復生；若有任何一物拒絕，他便長留。赫爾莫德帶著口信返程——而哭泣之約因一位女巨人拒哭而失敗，巴爾德遂留於冥府，直至世界更新。此記錄是北歐「下冥府而歸」故事中的失敗案例：一場營救，敗於一滴不肯落下的眼淚。

canonical_translation: A. G. Brodeur, Snorri Sturluson: The Prose Edda, New York 1916 (public domain)

narrative.en:
Gylfaginning's Baldr-chapter turns to rescue after the funeral. Frigg asks whether any among the gods will ride to Hel to seek Baldr; Hermothr, called the messenger of the gods, agrees, and takes Sleipnir to ride down. The journey is specified like a courier's itinerary: nine nights through dark and deep valleys, until he comes to the river Gjoll and the bridge Gjallarbru, roofed with shining gold. The bridge-keeper Modgudr interrogates him: five companies of dead men rode over yesterday, and it rang less under them; nothing is blacker than under a dead man's eyebrows; but this rider makes the bridge thunder and does not have the color of dead men - why does he ride the paths of death? Hermothr answers that he rides to seek Baldr, and asks whether she saw him pass; she says Baldr rode below, over the bridge, and the road down lies north.

Hermothr rides on to the gates of Hel, dismounts, tightens the girth, mounts and spurs; Sleipnir leaps so hard over the gate that he comes nowhere near it. Then Hermothr is in the hall, and sees his brother Baldr in the high seat, and Nanna his wife, sent down dead of grief. He stays the night; in the morning Hel gives the terms: Baldr shall ride home if all things, quick and dead, weep for him - 'and if anything speak against him or refuse to weep, then he shall remain with her; and thence he came home'. Hermothr rides back with the answer, bringing also the gifts Hel and Baldr sent up: the ring Draupnir, which Odin had laid on the pyre, back to Odin, and Nanna's gifts to Frigg.

The rescue then passes out of Hermothr's hands into the world's: the Aesir send messengers through all worlds to ask everything to weep Baldr out of Hel, and all things consent - men, animals, earth, stones, trees, metals - until a giantess called Thokk, Loki in disguise, dry-eyed, refuses: 'let Hel hold what it has.' The record's cultural function is thus double. It is the Norse katabasis that fails: unlike Herakles' or Orpheus' descents, the mission succeeds in reaching and negotiating, and is defeated only at the collection of tears - the ransom is not paid in gold but in a world-wide ritual of grief, and one dissenter voids it. And it specifies the mythic grammar of the resurrection: return from death is contractually possible - the underworld is negotiable - but the contract is unanimous consent, a doctrine of total participation with a single point of failure.

For the atlas, Hermothr's ride is the bridge between the descent-underworld family (Orpheus, Inanna, Hadding's ride in Saxo) and the world-renewal record: Baldr stays in Hel exactly until the renewal, when 'Baldr and Hothr shall come back' - the failed rescue and the scheduled return are the two halves of one doctrine: death cannot be ransomed piecemeal; it can only be outlived by the world.

functions: Failed katabasis: the descent succeeds, the negotiation succeeds, the collection of tears fails
Doctrine of resurrection as unanimous consent: one withheld weeping voids the ransom
Geography and protocol of the underworld: bridge-keeper, customs questions, gate-leap
Links the failed rescue to the scheduled return of Baldr at the world's renewal

title.en: Baldr's Dreams: Odin Rides Down to Wake a Dead Seeress
title.zh: 巴爾德之夢：奧丁騎行喚醒亡故女先知

region.en: Niflhel, the gate of the dead (symbolic pin at Pingvellir, Iceland)
region.zh: 尼福赫爾，死者之門（象徵性定位於冰島辛格韋德利）

period: Baldrs draumar c. 1000-1200 CE; principal MS Codex Regius GKS 2365 4to (added at end)

source.work: Baldrs draumar; critical ed. Ursula Dronke (Poetic Edda II, 1997)

license: Public domain (Bellows 1923); passages below are labeled paraphrases

summary.en: Baldr dreams evil dreams of his death; the gods saddle horses and ride to the halls to inquire. Odin rides to Niflhel's gate, wakes a dead volva with spells at her grave, and she rises - 'what man is this who drives me on my road, cold rains I have known long enough?' - and under the name Vegtam he extracts the fate: a hand slender and fair shall slay Baldr, and Höd shall do the deed, and Loki compels it; and one woman shall be born in the iron-woods, the wolf-kin's kinswoman, who shall bring grief to Odin. The seeress recognizes him and cries 'ride home, none waked me for you' - and lies down again. The record is the Norse descent-for-prophecy: the oracle of the dead consulted in the first person by the god who must lose.
summary.zh: 巴爾德屢作死亡噩夢；諸神備馬而出，分赴各地打聽。奧丁騎至尼福赫爾之門，於墓中誦咒喚起亡故女先知——「什麼人騎行催我上路？嚴寒霜雨我已受夠了！」——他化名維格塔姆，逼問出命運：那纖細而俊美的手將殺死巴爾德，行凶者為霍德，而洛基乃其幕後主使；並有一女子將誕於鐵林，乃狼族之親，她將為奧丁帶來悲傷。女先知認出他，喊道「回家去吧，無人為你而醒」，隨即躺回墓中。此記錄是北歐「為預言而下冥府」的故事：註定失去的神親自向死者的神諭問路。

canonical_translation: Henry A. Bellows, The Poetic Edda, New York 1923 (public domain)

narrative.en:
Baldrs draumar ('Baldr's dreams') is a short, dark poem appended at the end of the Codex Regius, and it is the eddic version of the descent-for-prophecy. The frame: Baldr dreamed evil dreams, and the gods saddled horses and rode to the halls to ask after them; then Odin rode down 'the way of the dead' to Niflhel, and woke the volva 'wise in her grave' with the incantations proper to waking the dead. Her first words are the poem's signature: 'What man is this that drives me on my road, that compels me on my journey? I was showered with snow, beaten with rain, drenched with dew; long have I been dead.' A god is compelling a corpse to commute.

Under the name Vegtam ('the way-tamed', the wanderer), Odin asks: for whom are the benches strewn and the rings hung with rings? She answers: for Baldr the mead is brewed, a shield hangs over the vessel - 'and I spoke unwillingly; now I am silent, and will speak no more'. Odin presses: who shall slay Baldr? The hand slender and fair, the fair and famous Höd - Loki's forcing lies behind it. And: who is the woman born in the east's iron-woods, whose kin are the wolves? She shall be Vali's mother? no - the answer names a new-born woman 'of the wolf-kin', and the poem cuts: Odin asks one more riddle and she recognizes him: 'You are not Vegtam, as I thought - you are Odin, the old one, the famous.' He answers: 'You are no volva, nor a wise woman, but the mother of three monsters' - and the exchange ends in mutual unmasking, each denying the other's dignity. She says: 'Ride home, no one woke you; none shall come here again, till Loki has got loose from his fetters and the destroyers come' - and the dead lie still.

The record's cultural functions are the oracle-of-the-dead as an institution, and the economy of doom. Consulting the dead for prophecy was real practice in the Norse world (the volva's seance of Eirik's saga is its living, Christian-era form); the poem shows the god performing it himself, in disguise, under compulsion - because the knowledge he seeks is his son's death, and the ritual's reversals (waker unmasked, waker unmasked) show what such consultations cost their performers. And the poem's last lines schedule Ragnarok: the dead seeress refuses further consultations until Loki is loose and the destroyers ride - the first prophecy in the corpus to name the interval between doom and doom.

For the atlas, the record anchors the necromantic-oracle family: the Gita's? - no - the Greek nekuia of Odyssey 11, the Chinese ghost-consultations of the supernatural records, and the saga volva-seance all belong here; Baldrs draumar is the version in which the questioner is a god and the oracle is a corpse with grievances about the weather.

functions: Institution of the oracle-of-the-dead: waking the grave-bound seeress with spells
Economy of doom: prophecy extracted at the cost of the oracle's peace and the asker's disguise
Mutual unmasking: god and corpse deny each other's dignity at the consultation's end
Schedules Ragnarok: no further waking until Loki is loose

title.en: Valhalla: The Hall of the Battle-Slain and Its Daily War
title.zh: 瓦爾哈拉：陣亡者之廳及其日復一日的戰鬥

region.en: Valhalla in Asgard (symbolic pin at Gamla Uppsala, Sweden)
region.zh: 阿斯加德瓦爾哈拉（象徵性定位於瑞典舊烏普薩拉）

period: Grimnismal st. 8-10, 18, 21-26 c. 900-1000 CE; Gylfaginning c. 1220-1230; Eiriksmal c. 954; principal MSS Codex Regius GKS 2365 4to, GKS 2367 4to

source.work: Grimnismal st. 8-10, 18, 21-26; Snorri, Gylfaginning chs. 20, 38; critical ed. Dronke (1997)

license: Public domain (Bellows 1923; Brodeur 1916); passages below are labeled paraphrases

summary.en: Valhalla ('hall of the slain') has five hundred and forty doors, each wide enough for eight warriors abreast; the roof is thatched with golden shields, its rafters are spears. Its inmates, the einherjar, spend every day fighting and killing each other to pieces, and rise at evening, healed, to ride home and feast: the boar Saehrimnir is boiled every day and is whole again by evening; Odin's wolves feed on the corpses of war; the mead-blesser goat Heidrun hangs from the roof and fills the cups. The hall is the cosmos's recruitment system: the chosen dead are trained daily for the army of Ragnarok.
summary.zh: 瓦爾哈拉（「陣亡者之廳」）有五百四十扇門，每扇門可容八名戰士並肩出入；屋頂以金盾覆蓋，椽條皆為長矛。廳中居民——恩赫里亞（獨臂勇士戰士們）——每日互相搏殺至支離破碎，傍晚復原而起，騎馬歸席赴宴：公豬薩赫利姆尼爾日日烹煮，夜夜復原；奧丁的狼群以戰場屍骸為食；屋樑懸掛的乳山羊海德倫使蜜酒盈杯。此廳是宇宙的徵兵制度：被選中的死者每日操練，以備末日之戰的大軍。

canonical_translation: Henry A. Bellows, The Poetic Edda, New York 1923 (public domain); Gylfaginning via Brodeur 1916

narrative.en:
Grimnismal, Odin's cosmological litany, gives the hall's census and its cuisine: five hundred and forty doors, eight hundred warriors through each - the figure is best read as the count of the einherjar who will issue from the gates to fight the wolf at Ragnarok; the roof thatched with shields, the benches strewn with byrnies, spears as rafters; the boar Saehrimnir, boiled every day, whole again by evening - 'few know what the einherjar feed on'; the goat Heidrun on Valhalla's roof eating from the tree Laerath's boughs, from whose udders runs the mead that fills the cups; and the stag Eikthyrnir above, whose antlers drip the rivers of the world. The wolves Geri and Freki, Odin's war-wolves, get the battle-slain; Odin himself lives on wine alone.

Gylfaginning adds the daily timetable: each day, as soon as they are clothed and have put on their battle-gear, the einherjar go out to the courtyard and fight and kill each other - 'this is their sport' - and when the meal-hour comes they ride home to the hall and sit down together, healed. Odin sends the valkyries to every battle: they allot death and govern victory, and those they choose ride with them to Valhalla; also (the political clause) they wait on the tables and bear the ale at the feast. The hall is thus a barracks with a liturgy: training-war by day, feast by night, maid-service by the choosers of the slain.

The cultural function is a doctrine of chosen death. Norse society drew its elite from the battle-dead: to die in the field with weapon in hand was to be drafted into the god's standing army, and the valkyries' choosing made every battle a recruitment - the myth of the einherjar is the ideological engine that made the battlefield valuable. Its eschatological purpose is explicit: all this training exists 'for the wolf' - the einherjar are held in reserve as Ragnarok's final levy, five hundred and forty doors' worth. And the hall's economy is a resurrection-economy in miniature: the boar that is eaten daily and rises whole each evening is the training table of immortality - death rehearsed and undone at every meal.

Skaldic poetry documents the hall's working reality: Eiriksmal (c. 954), composed for the death of Eirik Bloodaxe, dramatizes Valhalla preparing to receive a king - 'why is the day darkened, what means the din of arms?' - Bragi answers: the All-father has bidden Eirik with his host to come up; Sigmund and the chosen heroes rise to bid him welcome; the poem's humor (Sigmund asks why Odin has not taken more famous kings and left Eirik to die of disease) shows the hall as a working institution with politics. In the atlas's frame, Valhalla answers the Islamic jannah's gardens and the Chinese courts of the dead - each afterlife adapted to its society's ideal manhood; the Norse one is the only one that is an army mess.

functions: Doctrine of chosen death: the battle-slain drafted into the god's standing army
Recruitment engine: the valkyries' choosing makes every battle a levy for Ragnarok
Resurrection-economy in miniature: the daily slain-and-healed einherjar, the ever-renewed boar
Skaldic documentation: Eiriksmal shows the hall as a working, political institution
