summary.en: The most violent exploit in skaldic art: Loki, forced by Geirrod's capture of him, decoys Thor into the giant's land without hammer, belt or gloves; the giantess Grid lends the god her belt of strength, iron gloves and staff. At the Vimur river - swollen by the witch's incantations - Thor wades with the staff, 'and they say that the river rose highest at his shoulders', and he finds a stone and hurls it: 'and that stone stayed the stream, as if a rock had been set there' - the aition of a boulder-stopped river. In the hall, Geirrod's iron-hot wedge? - the giant hurls a molten iron wedge with tongs; Thor catches it in his iron gloves and hurls it back through pillar and giant. The skaldic Thorsdrapa, the corpus's most violent poem, tells the same with blood-drinking kennings.
summary.zh: 這是吟遊詩歌中最暴烈的神蹟：洛基被蓋爾羅德擒獲後受迫誘騙索爾——不帶錘、不帶腰帶與鐵手套——深入巨人之地；女巨人格里德借予雷神神力腰帶、鐵手套與木杖。在維穆爾河畔——河水因女巫咒語而暴漲——索爾執杖涉水，「據說河水最高漲至他的肩頭」；他拾起一塊巨石擲出：「那石頭便攔住了水流，如同天然巨岩立於河中」——這是巨石攔河的起源故事。在廳中，巨人以鐵鉗擲出熾熱的鐵楔；索爾以鐵手套接住，反擲回去，貫穿石柱與巨人。吟遊詩《索爾頌》——歌謠中最暴烈的作品——以嗜血的隱喻講述同一故事。

canonical_translation: Corpus Poeticum Boreale, ed. Vigfusson & Powell, Oxford 1883 (public domain); Skaldskaparmal via Brodeur 1916

narrative.en:
The tale's frame is a deception within a deception. Geirrod the giant captures Loki (in hawk-shape) and releases him only on his oath to bring Thor to the hall without his hammer or his strength-girdle; Loki decoys the god with a lying tale of hospitality. The journey is armed by a third party: the giantess Grid, mother of Vidar, warns Thor and lends him her belt of strength, her iron gloves and her staff Gridarvolr.

The river-crossing is the poem's physics-set-piece. The witch Gjalp, Geirrod's daughter, stands astride the Vimur and raises the water with incantations; Thor wades with the staff, 'and they say that the river rose highest at his shoulders'; he finds a stone in the riverbed and casts it, 'and that stone stayed the stream, as if a rock had been set there' - Snorri's aition for a river dammed by a thrown boulder - and then he wades out and grips a mountain-berry? - the prose: he seizes a rowan-tree (the famous 'Thor's salvation' of the rowan) and climbs out; whence the kenning that the rowan is 'Thor's salvation'. In the hall, the tests turn physical: Gjalp, hidden under Thor's chair, presses it up with her knees; the god breaks her back by seating himself hard. Geirrod, seeing the god's fury, hurls a wedge of molten iron with tongs; Thor catches it in the iron gloves and hurls it back 'so that it passed through the pillar and through Geirrod and through the wall, and so out? ' - and the giant's daughters, fleeing, are crushed.

The skaldic poem Thorsdrapa by Eilifr Godrunarson (10th c.) is the myth's oldest and most violent telling - so violent that the Edda-MSS preserve it 'because it is hard to understand? ' - Snorri says he quotes it 'because it is excellent and? ' - the prose says he includes it for its art. The poem's kennings drink blood: Geirrod's hall is 'the wolf-feeding hall? ', the wedge 'the reddening? iron of the giant', Thor 'the breaker of Geirrod's brain-pan'. Snorri retells it to explain the poem's obscure diction - the prose retelling exists for the verse, a case-study of the myth corpus's transmission: skaldic difficulty generating prose narrative.

The record's cultural functions are the river-as-attack doctrine (the frontier's waters weaponized by witchcraft, dammed by a god) and the counter-throw doctrine (the god defeats the giant's technology with the giant's own weapon, caught and returned). And the rowan-tree doctrine ('Thor's salvation') is an aition of folk botanical belief - the rowan's protective reputation in Scandinavian farm-culture descends from this river-crossing. In the atlas, the record anchors the duel-by-technology family: the Chinese Yi's archery, the Greek Heracles' poisoning? - no: the atlas frame is the hero armed by borrowed gear (Grid's belt answers the Greek Athena's aegis-loans), and the myth's weapons are industrial: molten iron against iron gloves.

functions: River-as-attack doctrine: frontier waters weaponized by witchcraft, dammed by a thrown boulder
Counter-throw doctrine: the giant's molten iron caught in iron gloves and returned
Aition of the rowan: 'Thor's salvation' as the tree's protective reputation in farm-culture
Transmission case-study: a violent skaldic poem generating its own prose retelling

title.en: The Utgard Contests: Drinking the Sea, Wrestling Old Age
title.zh: 烏特加德競賽：飲盡滄海、力戰暮年

region.en: Utgard, the giants' stronghold (symbolic pin at Jotunheimen, Norway)
region.zh: 巨人要塞烏特加德（象徵性定位於挪威尤通黑門山）

period: Gylfaginning c. 1220-1230 (older mythic material); principal MSS Codex Regius GKS 2367 4to, Codex Upsaliensis

source.work: Snorri, Gylfaginning chs. 44-47; critical ed. Faulkes (1987)

license: Public domain (Brodeur 1916); passages below are labeled paraphrases

summary.en: Thor, Loki and Thjalfi travel to the stronghold of Utgard-Loki and are set three contests. Thor must drain a drinking-horn (it is the sea, and he lowers it visibly), lift a grey cat (it is the Midgard-Serpent, and he raises one paw off the ground), and wrestle an old woman (she is Elli, Old Age itself, and he is forced to one knee). Thjalfi races a thought; Loki eats against fire itself. When the trickster-king reveals the illusions, he adds the cruelest doctrine of all: the giants had meant to kill them at the first tests - Skrymir's iron gloves were the mountain-range of the world, and the wrestling-match 'would never have been? ' - no man could stand before Old Age. The record is the Norse doctrine that strength has absolute rivals: the sea, the earth, and time.
summary.zh: 索爾、洛基與蒂亞爾菲前往烏特加德·洛基的要塞，被迫接受三項競賽。索爾須飲乾一隻號角（那是海洋，而他確實讓水位明顯下降），舉起一隻灰貓（那是環繞世界的大蛇，他抬起了它的一隻爪），並與一位老嫗角力（她是「暮年」本身，他只能單膝跪地）。蒂亞爾菲賽跑的對手是「思想」；洛基與火焰比賽吞食。當詭計之王揭穿幻象後，還補上一句最殘酷的教義：巨人們本想在第一輪就殺死他們——斯克利米爾的鐵手套原是世界的山脈，而那場角力「無人能敵」，因為無人能戰勝暮年。此記錄是北歐的教義：力量自有其絕對對手——海洋、大地與時間。

canonical_translation: A. G. Brodeur, Snorri Sturluson: The Prose Edda, New York 1916 (public domain)

narrative.en:
Gylfaginning's greatest adventure is a doctrine about the limits of strength, told as a tournament of illusions. Thor, Loki and the boy Thjalfi travel east into Jotunheim and spend a night in a vast hall - in the morning it is a glove: Skrymir's glove, the giant sleeping beside it. Skrymir travels with them, and his snoring, his stride and his food-sack test Thor three times on the road; each hammer-blow lands, and Skrymir only asks whether a leaf, an acorn or a bird has fallen on his head. At Utgard, the king sets the contests: Thjalfi races against Hugi (thought, unbeatable); Loki eats against Logi (fire, which consumes the trough, the bones and the table itself); and Thor must drink from a horn 'thought short by many' - and he drinks three deep draughts that lower the sea around the shore visibly; then lifts a cat off the ground with one paw - and the cat is Jormungand, arched, one foot raised; then wrestles the old nurse Elli - Old Age - and is brought to one knee.

The revelation is the myth's philosophy. Utgard-Loki confesses: 'I brought forth spells against you'; the horn was the sea; the cat was the Midgard-Serpent; Elli was Old Age, 'which no man can stand before, though he live to the world's end'. And the cruelest clause: 'I had purposed, had I known? ' - the text: 'had we known you were so mighty, you would never have come into the stronghold; for we had meant to destroy you with the first tests' - the giants' welcome was an execution, and the illusions were mercy. Then the giant offers to show Thor his match: two men who will fight him - 'and they were? ' - no one appears; the stronghold and its king vanish, 'and no castle and no king were to be seen'. Thor raises the hammer to strike and cannot find them; the record ends with the god swindled by geography.

The cultural functions are the doctrine of strength's absolute rivals and the theology of the borderline. In the Norse system, Thor's strength is the gods' insurance; the Utgard episode teaches what the insurance does not cover: the sea (drinkable only visibly), the earth's circumference (liftable only by a paw), and time (wrestled to one knee). It is a humility-doctrine delivered as comedy - the myth of a strongman beaten by the world's dimensions - and its politics are pointed: the giants' stronghold wins by wit and illusion, the same weapons Loki uses, so the frontier is shown as contestable by intelligence rather than muscle. And the wrestling-with-Old-Age is the myth-world's most precise existential statement: 'no man can stand before Old Age' - the sentence the whole Edda is written to prove.

For the atlas, the record anchors the impossible-contest family (the Greek labors' impossible tasks, the Chinese Sun Wukong's contests with Buddha's palm): each a hero tested by cosmic scale; the Norse one is unique in setting the tests against natural absolutes - sea, serpent, age - and in admitting defeat on the record.

functions: Doctrine of strength's absolute rivals: sea, serpent and Old Age
Humility-theology as comedy: the strongman beaten by the world's dimensions
Frontier politics: the giants win by illusion and intelligence, not muscle
Existential formula: no man can stand before Old Age

region.en: Asgard's orchard and Thjazi's eyrie (symbolic pin at Gamla Uppsala, Sweden)
region.zh: 阿斯加德果園與夏茲之巢（象徵性定位於瑞典舊烏普薩拉）

period: Haustlong (Thjodolfr of Hvinir, c. 900); Skaldskaparmal c. 1220-1230; principal MSS Codex Regius GKS 2367 4to

source.work: Thjodolfr of Hvinir, Haustlong; Snorri, Skaldskaparmal ch. 1-2; ed. Vigfusson & Powell, CPB 1883

license: Public domain (CPB 1883; Brodeur 1916); passages below are labeled paraphrases

summary.en: The gods' immortality is a produce-supply: Idunn the keeper keeps in her box the apples the gods bite when they feel age coming, and they grow young again. Loki, pressed by the eagle-shaped giant Thjazi, lures Idunn out of Asgard with a lie about apples better than hers - and the eagle carries her off. The gods age visibly; forced, Loki borrows Freyja's falcon-shape, flies to Thjazi's hall, turns Idunn into a nut and carries her back - pursued by the giant as an eagle; the Aesir set fire to the wood-shavings at the wall, and the burning eagle's wings drop him, and Thor kills him. The record is the aition of the gods' dependency on an orchard and the first dividend of the Skadi-feud: her father killed, she comes armed to Asgard.
summary.zh: 諸神的長生原來是一門農產品供應：看守者伊登在匣中保管那些蘋果，諸神感覺衰老將至時便咬上一口，重獲青春。洛基被化為巨鷹的巨人夏茲所迫，以謊言（外頭有更甜的蘋果）誘騙伊登離開阿斯加德——巨鷹遂將她擄走。諸神的容顏迅速衰老；被逼無奈，洛基借來芙蕾雅的游隼羽衣，飛至夏茲大廳，將伊登變作一顆核桃帶回——巨鷹窮追不捨；阿薩神族在牆邊點燃刨花，燒著鷹翼的巨人墜落，索爾隨即將其誅殺。此記錄既解釋了諸神對一座果園的依賴，也開啟了斯卡蒂世仇的序幕：父親被誅，她持械前來問罪。

canonical_translation: Corpus Poeticum Boreale, ed. Vigfusson & Powell, Oxford 1883 (public domain); Skaldskaparmal via Brodeur 1916

narrative.en:
Skaldskaparmal opens its treasure-chapters with a myth of divine logistics. Idunn, wife of Bragi the skald-god, 'keeps in her box those apples which the gods shall bite of when they begin to grow old; and then they all become young again, and so it shall be even unto the day of Ragnarok'. The supply-chain's weakness is Loki: the giant Thjazi (in eagle-shape) catches him in the flesh-pot trick? - the episode: Odin, Hoenir and Loki cook an ox in the wood; the eagle demands his share; Loki strikes the eagle with the staff, and the staff sticks to the eagle and Loki to the staff, and the eagle flies off with him, offering release only on his oath: he must bring Idunn out of Asgard with her apples.

The abduction is engineered by a lie: Loki tells Idunn that he has found apples better than hers, and she should come and compare; out in the wood, Thjazi in eagle-shape snatches her and flies to Thrymheimr. The gods age visibly - 'their beards? ' - the prose: 'the gods began to grow old' at council, asking where Idunn was gone; Loki confesses under threat of death and borrows Freyja's falcon-shape. The rescue is the myth's flight-comedy: Loki flies to Thrymheimr, finds Idunn alone, turns her into a nut, carries her in his claws and flies home 'with all his might'; the eagle pursues; the Aesir, seeing the flight, gather wood-shavings at the wall and set fire to them; the falcon clears the wall; the eagle, wings alight, drops, and Thor kills him inside the enclosure.

The aftermath founds a dynasty of feud: Thjazi's daughter Skadi comes armed to Asgard to demand atonement, and gets it - a husband (Njord, by feet-choice) and her father's eyes set as stars. The skaldic evidence: Thjodolfr's Haustlong (c. 900), a shield-poem, narrates the whole episode in kennings - Idunn's box, the eagle's claws, the burning wings - centuries before Snorri, and Snorri retells it to gloss the poem.

Cultural functions: the doctrine that divine immortality is agricultural (the gods' youth depends on an orchard and a keeper); the negotiation-with-hostage grammar (the eagle's oath extracted from a captured trickster); and the shapeshifting-rescue (nut, falcon, eagle). In the atlas, the record anchors the rejuvenation-produce family (the Greek ambrosia, the Chinese peaches of immortality, the Inca coca of the gods? - the frame is fruit-of-life myths): each an immortality-crop guarded by a keeper; the Norse one is distinctive in being portable, in a box, in a woman's keeping, and stealable by oath.

functions: Aition of divine youth: the gods' immortality as an orchard-supply with a keeper
Hostage-oath grammar: the eagle's release price extracted from a captured trickster
Shapeshifting-rescue: nut, falcon and eagle in the flight home
Feud-origination: Skadi's armed arrival and her settlement found the Njord-marriage

title.en: Njord and Skadi: A Marriage of Sea and Mountain, Settled by Feet
title.zh: 尼奧德與斯卡蒂：以雙腳擇定的山海聯姻

region.en: Noatun by the sea and Thrymheim in the mountains (symbolic pin at Lofoten, Norway)
region.zh: 海邊的諾阿頓與山中的特呂姆海姆（象徵性定位於挪威羅弗敦）

period: Skaldskaparmal c. 1220-1230 (older material); Grimnismal st. 11, 15; principal MSS Codex Regius GKS 2367 4to, GKS 2365 4to

source.work: Snorri, Skaldskaparmal ch. 3; Grimnismal st. 11, 15; critical ed. Faulkes (1987)

license: Public domain (Brodeur 1916; Bellows 1923); passages below are labeled paraphrases

summary.en: When the Aesir kill her father Thjazi, the giantess Skadi comes armed to Asgard for atonement. The settlement: she shall choose a husband from among the gods - by his feet. She picks the cleanest pair, believing them Baldr's; they are Njord's, and the marriage is made with the condition that each shall dwell nine nights in the other's home. The sea-hall deafens her with gulls; the mountain-hall wakes him with wolves; the compromise fails - and the myth of the failed divine marriage is also the aition of the shoreline's ecology: the place where sea-birds and wolves meet is the negotiated border between two households.
summary.zh: 阿薩神族誅殺其父夏茲後，女巨人斯卡蒂持械前來阿斯加德要求償付。和解條件是：她可從神族中自選一位丈夫——但只能看腳。她挑中雙足最潔淨者，以為是巴爾德，實則是尼奧德。婚約附加條款：夫妻須輪流在對方家中各住九夜。海邊大廳的海鳥鳴聲令她徹夜難眠；山中大廳的狼嚎又吵醒了海神。妥協失敗——而這則「失敗的神聖聯姻」神話，同時也是海岸線生態的起源故事：海鳥與狼群相遇之地，正是兩戶人家談判出的邊界。

canonical_translation: A. G. Brodeur, Snorri Sturluson: The Prose Edda, New York 1916 (public domain)

narrative.en:
The myth begins as a legal action. Skadi - 'the shining bride of the gods'? - the giantess, in helmet and byrnie and weapons of war, comes to Asgard to demand atonement for her father Thjazi, killed in the burning of the eagle. The Aesir offer compensation: she shall choose a husband from among them - 'but she shall choose by the feet only, and see nothing else of the man'. She finds one pair of feet passing fair and says: 'him I choose; little do I expect? ' - the text: 'there is little blemish, Baldr should be faultless in form' - and it is Njord of Noatun. The settlement also obliges the gods to make her laugh - Loki's trick (a goat's bait on his own beard, the rope tied to his testicles and to the goat's) does it - and to set her father's eyes as stars in the sky, which Odin does: 'the greatest memorials? ' - the two eyes thrown into the heaven as stars.

The marriage's terms are the myth's experimental clause: each shall dwell nine nights in the other's home. At Noatun, the sea-hall, the gulls' cries wake her: 'evil birds wake me that fly from the sea; every morning the gull wakes me'. At Thrymheim, the mountain-hall, the wolves' howls wake him: 'sick? ' - the prose: 'the wolves' howling wakes him, sick? ' - 'I was waked by the howling of wolves, he said? ' - the poem Grimnismal supplies the speeches in st. 11 and 15: each spouse testifies against the other's home. Neither can sleep in the other's world; the marriage dissolves by experiment, and Skadi returns to Thrymheim 'and abides there? ' - the text: 'she went up? ' - Snorri: 'Skadi then went up on the mountain and abode in Thrymheim, and often rides? ' - she keeps to the mountains, hunting on snowshoes with bow, and is called the snowshoe-goddess (ondurdís).

The record's cultural functions are the doctrine of habitat-marriage and the aition of the shore's ecology. The myth formalizes an observation about two landscapes - sea-shore and mountain - that cannot be inhabited by the other's household; the failed marriage is the boundary-negotiation of two ecological regimes, and the shoreline (where gull-cries and wolf-howls meet) is the myth's map of the compromise-point. And the feet-choice is the myth-world's theory of mate-selection: beauty is judged by its least poetic part, and the chooser guesses wrong - the doctrine that marriage by appearance mistakes its partner. Grimnismal's verse-argument (each spouse's testimony) is the poem's own trial-record, and Snorri's prose adds the judicial frame (atonement, choice, compensation, laugh-payment) that makes the whole episode read like a legal settlement of a feud.

In the atlas, the record anchors the divine-marriage family (Zeus-Hera's institution, the Izanagi-Izanami separation): each a marriage myth; the Norse one is distinctive in being failed by design - an experiment in cohabitation whose result is geography: the sea stays with the sea-folk, the mountain with the ski-goddess, and the boundary is the beach.

functions: Habitat-marriage doctrine: sea and mountain households cannot cohabit - the failed experiment maps the shoreline's ecology
Legal frame: the marriage as atonement, with feet-choice, laugh-payment and star-compensation
Mate-selection theory: beauty judged by feet, and the chooser guesses wrong
Skadi's office: the snowshoe-goddess of the mountains, bow and snowshoe as her cult-gear

title.en: Freyr of the Swedes: The God-King, Beli and the Mound at Uppsala
title.zh: 瑞典人的弗雷：神王、貝利與烏普薩拉的墳丘

region.en: Gamla Uppsala, Sweden (temple and royal mounds)
region.zh: 瑞典舊烏普薩拉（神廟與王家墳丘）

period: Ynglinga saga c. 1225 (older material); Gylfaginning c. 1220-1230; Adam of Bremen, Gesta c. 1070s; principal MSS AM 41 4to, GKS 2367 4to

source.work: Snorri, Ynglinga saga chs. 10-12; Gylfaginning ch. 37; Adam of Bremen, Gesta Hammaburgensis 4.26-27

license: Public domain (Laing 1844; Brodeur 1916); Adam of Bremen passages are labeled paraphrases

summary.en: Freyr, the Vanir hostage, becomes the first king of the Swedes and the god of their wealth: under his reign come the peace-froth? - the 'Frodi-peace'? - good seasons and peace. When he weds the giantess Gerd, he pledges his sword and later slays the giant Beli with a stag's antler, bare-handed. At his death his body is laid in a great mound at Uppsala, and the Swedes, still prospering, believe the god still alive beneath the barrow - offerings continue; the mound-cult of a buried god-king. Adam of Bremen, writing in the 1070s, saw the temple: Thor enthroned in the center, Wodan and Fricco (Freyr) with the enormous phallus on either side, sacrifices of nine males of every species hanging in the sacred grove. The record is the best-documented cult in the Norse corpus: god as king, king as buried god.
summary.zh: 華納人質弗雷成為瑞典人的開國之王，並成為其財富之神：其治下風調雨順、四海昇平。他娶巨人族女子葛德為妻時抵押了自己的寶劍，後來只能空手以鹿角誅殺巨人貝利。他死後，屍身被葬於烏普薩拉的巨大墳丘，而瑞典人見國運依舊昌隆，便相信神仍活在丘下——祭祀不絕。這是一座埋葬神王的墳丘崇拜。1070年代，不來梅的亞當親見其神廟：索爾居中而坐，沃坦與長著巨大陽具的弗里克科（弗雷）分列兩側，各種雄牲各九頭懸掛於神聖林中獻祭。此記錄是北歐文獻中記載最完備的崇拜：神即王，王即被葬之神。

language: Old Norse / Old Icelandic; Latin (Adam of Bremen)
canonical_translation: Samuel Laing, Heimskringla, London 1844 (public domain); Adam of Bremen via paraphrase per Tschan 1959

narrative.en:
The myth-histories fuse the god and the dynasty. In Ynglinga saga, Freyr (Frey) succeeds his father Njord as ruler of the Swedes and is called their king: 'in his days began the Fródi-peace' - good seasons and peace such that the Swedes attributed their wealth to him; he built a great temple at Uppsala and dedicated to himself? - the saga: he took up his dwelling at Uppsala 'and appointed? ' - the account continues that he established the great sacrifices there and the wealth of the Swedes was by his blessing. When he fell sick and died, his men buried him in a great mound 'in the Swedish manner'? - the text: 'and they laid him in a mound at Uppsala' - and because the good seasons continued, they believed he still lived beneath, and offerings were made to the mound 'as to a god': gold, rings and sacrifices poured into the barrow for three? years, until the Swedes understood he was dead - and then, the saga says, they burned him and worshipped him as a god still.

The prose Edda supplies the god's warrior-doctrine: Freyr, having pledged his sword for Gerd, meets the giant Beli and kills him bare-handed 'with a stag's horn' - Snorri's pointed economics: had Freyr kept his sword, 'then the giant would? ' - the text: 'the gods would be served by it at Ragnarok'; the god's martial poverty is the price of his marriage. Gylfaginning also names his gear: the ship Skidbladnir, folded like cloth in his purse, and the boar Gullinbursti with golden bristles that lights the dark.

The outsider's document fixes the cult's reality. Adam of Bremen, writing c. 1070s from the archbishopric's mission-station, describes the temple at Uppsala: 'the people? ' - the chronicle: a temple entirely of gold, in which three images stand - Thor, mightiest, enthroned in the center, with Wodan and Fricco on either side; Fricco (Freyr) is sculpted with an enormous phallus; the priests offer nine males of every species, male animals and men, and hang them in the sacred grove beside the temple; the grove's every tree is sacred, and a golden chain rings the temple's gable; sacrifices at nine-year intervals. The record is Europe's best-documented pagan cult-site, and its Fricco-phallus confirms the fertility-god's iconography that the sagas imply.

Cultural functions: the god-king doctrine (the deity as dynasty-founder, buried and worshipped in a mound - the mythic charter of Swedish sacral kingship); the naked-king economics (the fertility god fights without his sword because his marriage bought the harvest); and the mound-cult doctrine (offerings to a buried god whose prosperity proves his life - the mythic logic by which a barrow becomes a temple). In the atlas, the record anchors the god-king and mound-cult families (the Chinese sage-kings' temples, the Egyptian dead-god cults): each a ruler worshipped as god; the Norse one is distinctive in being a Vanir hostage whose marriage priced his arms.

functions: God-king doctrine: the deity as dynasty-founder, worshipped alive beneath the mound
Mound-cult charter: prosperity proves the buried god's life; offerings keep him fed
Naked-king economics: the fertility god fights bare-handed because his marriage bought the harvest
Outsider documentation: Adam of Bremen's temple description fixes the cult's reality

title.en: Freyja's Necklace: The Brisingamen, the Flea and the Duel
title.zh: 芙蕾雅的項鏈：布里辛嘉門、跳蚤與雙神決鬥

region.en: Folkvangr and the walls of Asgard (symbolic pin at Gamla Uppsala, Sweden)
region.zh: 弗爾克萬格與阿斯加德城牆（象徵性定位於瑞典舊烏普薩拉）

period: Skaldskaparmal c. 1220-1230 (older material); Sörla tháttr (14th c.); principal MSS Codex Regius GKS 2367 4to

source.work: Snorri, Skaldskaparmal (the theft of Brisingamen); Sorla thattr in Flateyjarbok; critical ed. Faulkes (1987)

license: Public domain (Brodeur 1916); passages below are labeled paraphrases

summary.en: The goddess Freyja owns the finest jewel of the gods, the necklace Brisingamen, bought from four dwarf-smiths at a night's price. Loki wants it: he turns himself into a flea, bites the sleeping goddess' cheek, and when she turns, steals the necklace from her neck. Heimdall, the watchman, sees him and pursues - both in seal-shape through the surf - and recovers it. The late Sörla þáttr variant darkens the doctrine: the necklace bought by promiscuity, a bargain with four dwarfs, and Odin's curse that she be war-stirred and never rest till a man is found to fight for it - the necklace as the engine of human war. The record is the aition of the gods' costliest possession and of watchman-theft: the finest object in Asgard is stolen by its own pest-control.
summary.zh: 女神芙蕾雅擁有諸神中最華美的寶物——布里辛嘉門項鏈，以一夜之價購自四位矮人工匠。洛基覬覦此物：他化作跳蚤，叮咬熟睡女神的臉頰；趁她翻身的瞬間，自其頸上偷走項鏈。守望者海姆達爾察覺並追擊——二神化作海豹穿越浪濤——終於奪回寶物。晚期《索爾拉短篇》將此教義染上陰影：項鏈以放縱為代價購得，是與四矮人的交易；奧丁更施以詛咒，令她為戰亂所擾、永無寧日，直到有人為此寶而戰——項鏈遂成為人間戰爭的引擎。此記錄解釋了諸神最昂貴財物的來歷，以及「守望者失竊」的主題：阿斯加德最珍貴之物，竟被自己的除蟲員偷走。

canonical_translation: A. G. Brodeur, Snorri Sturluson: The Prose Edda, New York 1916 (public domain); Sorla thattr per paraphrase

narrative.en:
The necklace-episode is preserved in two registers. The skaldic-prose register (Skaldskaparmal's kenning-apparatus) documents the theft and the duel: Freyja wears the necklace Bris (Brisingamen, 'the necklace of the Brisings'); Loki covets it, tells no one, and changes himself into a flea; he creeps into her chamber where she sleeps with the necklace around her neck, bites her cheek so that she turns over, unclasps the necklace and takes it - and does not return it. Heimdall, the watchman, has seen him; he changes into seal-shape and pursues; Loki, seeing himself caught, changes into seal likewise, and the two fight in the surf; Heimdall wins and brings back the necklace. The kenning-doctrine: gold is 'Freyja's tears' and 'the necklace's? ' - the prose lists the necklace among the kenning-bases for gold, evidencing the myth's poetic currency.

The late prose variant (Sörla þáttr, in the 14th-c. Flateyjarbok) darkens the economics: the four dwarf-smiths make the necklace and refuse gold; Freyja pays the price each demands - a night apiece - and Odin, told of it, orders the necklace taken (Loki steals it as a flea again), and imposes the curse: she shall have the necklace again only if she brings two kings to war eternally, each fighting for it - 'and she stirred up war between kings, and they fought on? ' - the tháttr makes the necklace the engine of a war that only the Christian king Olaf Tryggvason's coming ends. The variant is a converted Icelander's moralization: the love-goddess's jewel re-narrated as the cause of human war, and the myth's oldest stratum (theft and duel) preserved inside a Christian parable.

The record's cultural functions are the economics of the gods' jewelry and the watchman-theft doctrine. Brisingamen is the myth-world's costliest object - bought at a price the goddess alone could pay - and its theft by the flea is the trickster's signature: the finest possession of the order is stolen through its own smallest gap. The duel of the two shapeshifters in seal-form is the myth's image of law-enforcement: the watchman who never sleeps recovers the treasure in the border-medium (sea) between worlds. And the late variant's war-engine doctrine documents the conversion-era moralization of the fertility-cult: love's necklace becomes war's cause, until a king of the new faith shuts the story.

In the atlas, the record anchors the divine-ornament-theft family (the Greek Ares' belt? - the girdle of Aphrodite; the Chinese He Shi-bi jade): each a prized object circulating through theft; the Norse one is distinctive in being won by a flea and adjudicated by a watchman in seal-shape.

functions: Economics of the gods' jewelry: the costliest object bought at a price only the goddess could pay
Watchman-theft doctrine: the finest possession stolen through its own smallest gap
Border-medium duel: law-enforcement in seal-shape through the surf
Conversion-era moralization: the necklace re-narrated as the engine of human war

title.en: Tyr the One-Handed: The God of Oaths Who Fed the Wolf
title.zh: 獨臂的提爾：以誓言為職、曾餵養巨狼之神

region.en: Tyr's courts and the wolf's island (symbolic pin at Lake Viborg, Denmark)
region.zh: 提爾的法庭與巨狼之島（象徵性定位於丹麥維堡湖）

period: Gylfaginning c. 1220-1230 (older material); Lokasenna st. 37-40; Hymiskvida; principal MSS Codex Regius GKS 2367 4to, GKS 2365 4to

source.work: Snorri, Gylfaginning ch. 25; Lokasenna st. 37-40; Hymiskvida; critical ed. Faulkes (1987)

license: Public domain (Brodeur 1916; Bellows 1923); passages below are labeled paraphrases

summary.en: Tyr is the boldest and most courageous of the gods, and it is well for men of victory to call on him: 'it is proven that he rules over victory in battle'. His signature is his missing right hand - lost to the wolf Fenrir's bite when the other gods refused to pledge their own. In Lokasenna, when Loki taunts him - 'I have your hand, the wolf's snare' - Tyr answers with the oath-keeper's grief: 'I lost my hand, the wolf's snare, and grief have I got; the wolf stays bound, and I stay wretched'. And his deepest service is forgotten by all: he is Hymir's son, and it was Tyr who knew the giant's hall and led Thor to the mile-deep kettle. The record is the profile of law's god: the hand of the oath is the hand the wolf ate.
summary.zh: 提爾是諸神中最勇敢、最堅毅者，欲求戰勝者宜呼其名：「確切可知，他掌管戰鬥中的勝利」。其標誌是缺失的右手——當眾神皆不肯以手作保時，他的手被巨狼芬里爾咬去。在《洛基的吵罵》中，洛基譏諷他——「我握有你的手，那狼的鎖鏈」——提爾以守誓者的悲傷作答：「我失了手，成了狼的鎖鏈，我滿懷哀傷；狼被縛住，而我淒苦度日」。而他最深的功勞卻被眾神遺忘：他本是巨人希米爾之子，正是他知道巨人大廳之路，引索爾取回那口深達一里的巨釜。此記錄是法律之神的肖像：誓言之手，正是被狼吃掉的那隻手。

canonical_translation: A. G. Brodeur, Snorri Sturluson: The Prose Edda, New York 1916 (public domain)

narrative.en:
Gylfaginning's profile is brief and exact: Tyr is the boldest and most courageous of the gods, and he has great authority over victory in battle; 'it is well for men of valour to call on him'. His other name is 'the one-handed god', and the reason is the wolf: 'when the Aesir enticed Fenrir to let himself be bound with the chain Gleipnir, the wolf did not believe them to be minded to loose him till they laid Tyr's hand in his mouth as a pledge; and when the Aesir would not loose him, then he bit the hand off at the wrist - the place is called the wolf's joint? - and Tyr is one-handed and is not called a reconciler of men'. The prose adds the etymological point: the god of the oath is the god whose pledge-body is broken.

Lokasenna's flyting gives the grief its voice. Loki taunts: 'Be silent, Tyr! Thine hand? ' - the verses: 'I have thy hand, the snare of the wolf, and my son? ' - Loki claims credit for the binding and for the wolf's kinship? - the exchange: Loki says 'I was the father of the wolf? ' - no: Loki jeers 'thy hand could never hold aught', and Tyr answers: 'I lost my hand, the wolf's snare, and grief have I got; the wolf stays bound, and I stay wretched' - and then the second blow: Loki charges Tyr with cuckolding his wife, and Tyr falls silent - the oath-keeper's silence is the flyting's judgment that his private life cannot match his public honor.

The forgotten service is the kettle-quest's frame. In Hymiskvida, it is Tyr who offers to fetch the mile-deep kettle from the giant Hymir - 'for Hymir my father dwells there' - the law-god is the giant's son, and his kinship is the expedition's passport; he lifts the kettle-lid by its ring while Thor carries the vessel. The profile's cultural functions are the doctrine of pledged collateral (the god of oaths literally loses the body-part that secures them) and the paradox of law's kinships (the legal god is half giant - law's passport is a border-family). The etymology 'Tiwaz' ties him to the Indo-European sky-father (cf. Zeus, deus, Jupiter) - the oldest layer of the pantheon, and in the Norse material the god who has been overtaken by Odin and Thor in cult, surviving as the memory of what an oath costs.

For the atlas, the record anchors the sacrificial-office family: the god whose office is embodied (the hand as the pledge) - answering the Greek Zeus Horkios and the Roman Fides: each a deity of the sworn word; the Norse one pays for his office in flesh.

functions: Doctrine of pledged collateral: the oath-god's hand is the pledge the wolf ate
Office embodied in flesh: victory-law and oath-keeping carried on a one-armed body
Law's border-kinship: the legal god is the giant Hymir's son - law's passport is a border-family
Cult-history datum: the Indo-European sky-father (Tiwaz) demoted in Norse cult, surviving as oath-memory

title.en: Heimdall the White: Nine Mothers, Gold Teeth and the Horn That Wakes the Worlds
title.zh: 白神海姆達爾：九位母親、金齒與喚醒萬界的號角

region.en: Himinbjorg at Bifrost's edge (symbolic pin at Pingvellir, Iceland)
region.zh: 畢弗羅斯特橋頭的海姆比歐堡（象徵性定位於冰島辛格韋德利）

period: Gylfaginning c. 1220-1230 (older material); Vafthrudnismal st. 27-29, 39; Lokasenna; principal MSS Codex Regius GKS 2367 4to, GKS 2365 4to

source.work: Snorri, Gylfaginning ch. 27; Vafthrudnismal st. 27-29, 39; critical ed. Faulkes (1987)

summary.en: Heimdall is the white god, great and holy, born of nine mothers who are nine sisters - the wave-maidens, per Vafthrudnismal's riddle. His teeth are gold; he needs less sleep than a bird; he sees a hundred leagues by night as by day and hears the grass grow and the wool on the sheep. He guards the sky-bridge with the horn Gjallarhorn, whose blast wakes every world; he opposes Loki (and will kill him and be killed at Ragnarok); and in Rigspula he is the ancestor-father of the social estates. The record is the profile of the watchman-god: the senses of a frontier, the birth of nine waves, the horn of the last alarm.
summary.zh: 海姆達爾是白神，偉大而神聖，由九位彼此為姐妹的母親所生——據《瓦夫特魯德尼爾之歌》之謎，她們正是九位浪之侍女。他生有金齒；所需睡眠比鳥還少；晝夜皆能目視百里之遙，能聽見草的生長與羊背上的羊毛。他守護天橋，手持號角加拉德——其聲一響，萬界皆醒；他與洛基勢不兩立（末日之戰中二人同歸於盡）；在《里格詩篇》中他更是三階層的共同始祖。此記錄是守望之神的肖像：邊境的感官、九道浪濤的誕生，以及最後警報的號角。

canonical_translation: A. G. Brodeur, Snorri Sturluson: The Prose Edda, New York 1916 (public domain)

narrative.en:
The profile's strangest datum is his birth. Gylfaginning: 'nine mothers bore him, and all were sisters'; Vafthrudnismal's riddle supplies the identity: Odin asks 'whence came Heimdall, high-born, into the world?' and the giant answers in kenning-code - 'nine children the wave-maiden? ' - the verses: 'he was born of nine sisters, at the world's edge, of the wave-vaunted? one' - the nine sisters are the nine daughters of Aegir and Ran, the wave-maidens: the watchman is the sea's child, born at the world's rim, of the same water that rings Midgard.

The senses are his office: gold teeth; sleep less than a bird; sight of a hundred leagues night and day; hearing of the grass growing and the wool on the sheep's back; and the horn Gjallarhorn, kept in Himinbjorg at the bridge's edge, whose blast wakes every world - Snorri adds that Mimir's head? - no: the horn is also the trumpet of Ragnarok (Völuspá: 'Heimdall blows his horn aloft, men's road? - the sibyl hears it from the top of the tree'), and his counterpart is Loki: enmity between them is old (Lokasenna accuses Heimdall of drink-greed and back-stabbing prudence), and at Ragnarok the two kill each other - the watchman and the thief die in the same stroke.

His third office is social: in Rigspula he travels as Rig and fathers the three estates - thrall, freeman, noble - and the young king Kon, so that the class-system itself descends from the watchman's bed. The record's cultural functions are the frontier-senses doctrine (the guardian as a personified border-sensorium: sight, hearing, sleeplessness, teeth of gold - the god as infrastructure) and the wave-birth doctrine (the sea as the watchman's mother - the boundary made flesh). And his death at Loki's hand makes the profile eschatological: the alarm-system's final act is its own extinction, horn and thief dying together.

In the atlas, the record anchors the sentinel-god family (the Greek Hermes of the boundaries, the Chinese door-gods, the Roman Janus): each a guardian of crossings; the Norse one is distinctive in being born of the sea at the world's edge and in being scheduled to die with the very thief he watches.

The profile's nine-mothers doctrine completes the cosmology: the nine wave-maidens of Aegir and Ran as the watchman's mothers - the sea's daughters bearing the guardian of the sky-bridge - so the frontier between worlds is born from the sea itself. And the death-appointment completes the office: Heimdall and Loki, watchman and thief, kill each other at Ragnarok - the alarm-system's final act is its own extinction, the horn's last blast and the thief's last stroke in the same moment. The record thus anchors the sentinel-god family: the guardian born of the boundary's water, sensing the world's smallest motions, and scheduled to die with the boundary's breaker.

functions: Frontier-senses doctrine: the guardian as personified border-sensorium (sight, hearing, sleeplessness, gold teeth)
Wave-birth doctrine: nine wave-maiden mothers at the world's rim - the boundary made flesh
Watchman's eschatology: the horn of the last alarm, dying with the thief he watches
Social paternity: the class-system descending from the watchman's travels (Rigspula)

title.en: Loki's Kin: The Trickster's Family and the Monster Brood
title.zh: 洛基的親族：詭計者的家族與怪物之群

region.en: Asgard's walls and Jotunheim (symbolic pin at Pingvellir, Iceland)
region.zh: 阿斯加德城牆與約頓海姆（象徵性定位於冰島辛格韋德利）

period: Gylfaginning c. 1220-1230 (older material); Lokasenna st. 9; Hyndluljod st. 29-31; principal MSS Codex Regius GKS 2367 4to, GKS 2365 4to

summary.en: Loki is the son of the giant Farbauti ('dangerous striker') and Laufey ('leafy isle'), brother of Helblindi and Byleistr; Snorri calls him 'the calumniator and cheat of the gods', handsome and fair of face but evil in disposition, and 'the causer of? ' - the father of the lie. His children with Angrboda are the myth's doom-clock: Fenrir the wolf, Jormungand the serpent, Hel the half-dead girl; and by his wife Sigyn, the sons Narfi and Vali whose entrails bind him. And in Lokasenna's opening he is revealed as Odin's blood-brother - sworn in the morning of time, before the gods' order existed. The record is the genealogy of the trickster as the pantheon's internal border: kin to giants, brother to Odin, father to the world's end.
summary.zh: 洛基是巨人法爾鮑蒂（「危險的擊打者」）與勞菲（「繁茂之島」）之子，海爾布林迪與布萊斯耶爾的兄弟；斯諾里稱他為「諸神的誹謗者與欺詐者」，面容俊美而心地邪惡，是「謊言之父」。他與安格爾波達所生的子女是神話的末日時鐘：巨狼芬里爾、大蛇耶夢加得、半死的少女海爾；他與妻子西格恩所生的納爾菲與瓦利，其腸索日後成為捆縛他的繩索。而《洛基的吵罵》開篇揭示他竟與奧丁結為血盟兄弟——在遠古時光、神界秩序尚未建立之前。此記錄呈現詭計者的譜系：他既是神界的內部邊界——巨人一族之親、奧丁血誓之弟、末日之子的父親。

canonical_translation: A. G. Brodeur, Snorri Sturluson: The Prose Edda, New York 1916 (public domain)

narrative.en:
Gylfaginning's dossier opens with the parentage: Loki is the son of Farbauti the giant and Laufey, 'who is counted among the goddesses'? - the text: 'Laufey or Nal is his mother, and Byleistr and Helblindi are his brothers'; and the portrait: 'Loki is handsome and fair of face, but evil in disposition, and very changeable of mood? ' - the prose: 'he surpasses all men in the art of cunning, called the sly one? ' - the dossier reads: 'the calumniator and cheat of the gods, the father of the monster-fish? - the serpent? - Hel and the wolf and, further, the causer of all misfortune among gods and men'. The dossier's punch: Loki is the god-company's own member - 'he is counted among the Aesir' - because of his oath of blood-brotherhood: in Lokasenna's opening, Loki reminds Odin - 'remember, Odin, in the morning of time? we two mixed our blood together; then you said you would never taste ale unless it were brought to us both' - the blood-drinking pact that made the trickster a god's brother by the oldest ritual the north knows.

The brood is the myth's eschatology in genealogy. With the giantess Angrboda, Loki fathered the wolf Fenrir, the serpent Jormungand and Hel; Snorri's chapter reads the family as a prophecy: the three children are the materials of the doom (the wolf to swallow Odin, the serpent to kill Thor, Hel to keep Baldr). By his wife Sigyn he had the sons whose bodies become his binding - Narfi and Vali, one killed by the gods, the other's entrails made into the fetter that holds Loki to the rock. The genealogy thus runs from trickster to catastrophe in one generation: his love-life is the myth's weapon-manufacture.

The record's cultural functions are the internal-border doctrine (the pantheon's trickster is kin to its enemies and brother to its king - the oath-economy's cost made visible) and the lineage-of-doom doctrine (the myth-world's evil is familial, not foreign: the monsters are Loki's children, raised in Asgard itself). And the status is legally precise: Loki is not a giant among the gods nor a god among giants, but a sworn kinsman - the member whose membership is a contract, which is why the flyting is possible (a blood-brother may insult) and why the binding is a family matter (his wife Sigyn holds the bowl). In the atlas, the record anchors the trickster-kinship family (the Greek Hermes, son of Zeus; the Chinese Monkey, made a god by appointment): each a trickster inside the pantheon; the Norse one is unique in being bound by blood-oath to the king and in manufacturing the apocalypse as paternity.

functions: Internal-border doctrine: the trickster is kin to the enemies and blood-brother to the king
Lineage-of-doom: the monsters are Loki's children, raised in Asgard itself
Blood-oath economy: membership as contract - insultable, bindable, family-cared-for
Weapon-manufacture as paternity: his love-life produces the doom-clock

title.en: Hervor and Tyrfing: The Shieldmaiden Who Woke the Dead for a Sword
title.zh: 赫爾沃與提爾芬：為奪劍而喚醒亡者的女戰士

region.en: The mound of Angantyr on Samsø, Denmark
region.zh: 丹麥薩姆索島上的安甘提爾之墓

period: Hervarar saga ok Heidreks 13th century (older heroic material; verse Hervararkvida of older date); principal MS Hauksbok AM 544 4to; English: Nora Kershaw Chadwick, Stories and Ballads of the Far Past, 1921

source.work: Hervarar saga ok Heidreks (Hervararkvida); ed. C. C. Rafn, Fornaldar sogur; English trans. Nora Kershaw 1921; trans. Christopher Tolkien 1960

license: Public domain (Kershaw 1921); passages below are labeled paraphrases

summary.en: Hervor is the daughter of Angantyr, the berserk who died with his eleven brothers on the island of Samsø, buried in a mound with the cursed sword Tyrfing. Raised as a bondmaid in her mother's house, she learns her father's name, dresses as a man, and takes ship to the haunted island. Alone at night she walks the burning fire of the grave-mounds and calls the dead: 'Wake, Angantyr! Hervor wakes you, only daughter of Yngvi's kin!' The dead warn her; father Angantyr tells her the sword burns its holders; she persists, and the mound opens, and she takes Tyrfing from the dead man's hand - the only person to claim a cursed weapon from its own corpse. The record is the fornaldarsaga's signature descent: a living woman entering the world of the dead by command-voice, and winning its treasure against its own warning.
summary.zh: 赫爾沃是狂戰士安甘提爾之女——他與十一位兄弟死於薩姆索島，連同詛咒之劍提爾芬一同葬於墳丘。赫爾沃在母親家中被當作奴婢養大，得知父親之名後即改著男裝，乘船前往那座鬧鬼之島。夜深人靜，她獨自穿越墳墓間的鬼火，高聲呼喚亡者：「醒來吧，安甘提爾！喚你的是赫爾沃，英格維一族的獨女！」亡者出言警告；父親安甘提爾更告訴她，此劍必將反噬其主。她毫不退縮；墳丘終於開啟，她自死人手中取走提爾芬——唯一敢從詛咒武器的屍主手中將其奪走的人。此記錄是《上古傳說薩迦》的代表性冥府之行：一名生者女子以號令之聲踏入亡者世界，無視其警告，贏得其中寶物。

canonical_translation: Nora Kershaw Chadwick, Stories and Ballads of the Far Past, Cambridge 1921 (public domain); Christopher Tolkien, The Saga of King Heidrek the Wise, 1960

narrative.en:
The saga's first movement is Hervor's doubling. Her father Angantyr, berserk of the Arngrim-lineage? - of Arngrim's sons, died on Samsø in the berserk-duel with the Jomsviking? - with the brothers' enemy, all twelve brothers in one mound with the sword Tyrfing, forged by dwarfs and cursed to kill a man every time it is drawn. Her mother, fearing her lineage, has Hervor raised as a bondmaid with other women's children, unnamed; but the girl 'grew? ' - the saga: 'she was as strong as the men, and when she might? ' - she grew into a shieldmaiden's temperament, learned her father's name from an old woman, took weapons and men's clothes, joined a vikings-ship as Harv? - as Hervard, and commanded crews in raids - 'and when the ship's men knew she was a woman, they thought great things of her'? - the saga's note of collective respect.

The mound-raising is the saga's descent-scene, told in the verse of Hervararkvida. Hervor lands on Samsø alone at night while her crew stays aboard 'for fear of the ghosts' - the island's fires burn above the mounds, and none may land after sunset. She walks into the fire, 'and it did her no harm', and comes to the mound of her father and uncles, and calls the dead with the command-voice of the ritual waking: 'Wake up, Angantyr! Hervor wakes you, only daughter of Yngvi and Tota? - of Yngvi's kin; give me from the mound the dwarven sword!' The dead answer in fear - 'son, what has come to thee? ' - the dead Angantyr warns his daughter in the mound's voice: the sword will be her death, all its holders die; she answers with her lineage's logic: 'no one? ' - she will have the sword though it be her death. Angantyr then relents with the dead's only gift: 'the sword burns and is ruined? ' - he says the mound opens? - and the fire about the mounds is stilled, and she takes Tyrfing from the dead man's right hand - 'and she greeted her kin and went away with the sword', and the saga's verse closes: 'now fare I from the mounds? ' - she leaves the island as the dead quiet behind her.

The record's cultural functions are the descent-by-voice doctrine and the cursed-gift's claiming. Hervor's waking of the dead is the sagas' formalized necromancy: the living may enter the dead's world by speaking the lineage-code (her name and descent), and the dead may answer with warnings - the mound as a court of ancestors with jurisdiction over their own gear. Her victory is the cycle's hinge: the cursed sword enters the living world through a woman's claim, and its curse (to kill whenever drawn) will run through her son Heidrek and her grandson Angantyr - the saga's whole plot is the sword's biography, and this record is its first act. And the gender-doctrine is pointed: the lineage's weapon passes through a bondmaid raised in disguise - the fornaldarsaga's signature heroine, whose claim to arms outranks the dead's own caution.

For the atlas, the record anchors the descent-for-retrieval family (the Mesopotamian descent of Inanna, the Greek Herakles' Cerberus-fetch, the Japanese Okuninushi's underworld visit): each a living person entering the dead's realm for an object; the Norse one is distinctive in being performed by a woman in command-voice, at night, into a fire that does not burn her.

functions: Descent-by-voice doctrine: the living enter the dead's realm by speaking lineage-code
Mound as ancestor-court: the dead hold jurisdiction over their own gear and may warn
Cursed-gift claiming: the sword's biography begins with a woman's claim against the dead's warning
Gender-doctrine: the lineage's weapon passes through a bondmaid raised in disguise

title.en: The Riddle-Contest of Heidrek: Gestumblindi and the Riddles of the World
title.zh: 海德里克的謎語競賽：格斯圖姆布林迪與世界之謎

region.en: Heidrek's hall, Reidgotaland (symbolic pin at Dnieper region)
region.zh: 賴德戈塔蘭海德里克大廳（象徵性定位於第聶伯河流域）

period: Hervarar saga ok Heidreks 13th century (riddle-poem of older date); English: Nora Kershaw Chadwick 1921; Christopher Tolkien 1960

source.work: Hervarar saga ok Heidreks (Gatunor Heidreks konungs; the Heidrek riddles); ed. C. C. Rafn; English trans. Kershaw 1921; Tolkien 1960

license: Public domain (Kershaw 1921); passages below are labeled paraphrases

summary.en: King Heidrek, having outlawed the farmer Gestumblindi, receives from him (in truth, from Odin in disguise) a challenge: a riddle-contest, forfeit being the life of the loser. The riddles are the saga's cosmological catechism in verse-enigma form: who are the two that go to Mimir's well? (the sun and moon, pursued by the wolves); what drinks the dead and blows the slain? (the ravens? - Hugin and Munin, the ravens of Odin); what is the drink that is called 'ale of the dead'? ; what hangs above the king's head? (the sword of the gods? - the king's sky?); and thirty others on wind, ale, smithy, harlot, dwelling. The last riddle breaks the game: 'what did Odin whisper in Baldr's ear before he mounted the pyre?' - and the king, enraged, cuts down his opponent - who reveals himself as Odin: 'Fool, thou hast now? ' - the god promises to avenge himself on the king's head. The record is the fornaldarsaga's wisdom-contest at its most cosmological, and the myth corpus's last myth-riddle: the whisper that even a king may not know.
summary.zh: 海德里克國王宣布放逐農夫格斯圖姆布林迪之後，後者（實為喬裝的奧丁）向他發起挑戰：謎語競賽，輸者以性命為注。謎語以詩謎形式呈現整個北歐宇宙論的問答體系：誰是造訪密米爾之泉的兩者？（太陽與月亮，狼群所追）誰吞食死者、吹送亡魂？（奧丁的雙鴉）何謂「亡者之酒」？以及三十餘則關於風、麥酒、鐵匠鋪、屋舍的謎題。最後一謎令競賽崩盤：「巴爾德登上火葬堆之前，奧丁在他耳邊低語了什麼？」國王怒而斬之——對手現出奧丁真身：「蠢貨，你今日注定…」——神明宣告將以國王的性命復仇。此記錄是《上古傳說薩迦》中最具宇宙論色彩的智慧競賽，也是神話語料中最後一則神話謎語：連國王也不得知的低語。

canonical_translation: Nora Kershaw Chadwick, Stories and Ballads of the Far Past, Cambridge 1921 (public domain)

narrative.en:
The riddle-contest is the saga's intellectual set-piece and the myth corpus's catechism in disguise. The frame: Heidrek, the Tyrfing-cycle's most violent king, has outlawed Gestumblindi, who comes to Odin's temple to sacrifice; the god answers in his shape, goes to the king in his place, and - to save the life - challenges the riddle-contest: 'I will ask you riddles, and each that you cannot answer forfeits? ' - the forfeit is the king's judgment on the outlaw's case. The riddles run in sequence, and their content is the myth corpus's inventory: 'What drink is that which is called ale of the dead? ' - the ale in the mound? - the answers include: the two that go to Mimir's well (the sun and moon, that the wolves pursue); the one that drinks the dead and blows the slain? (the ravens Hugin and Munin); the four that hang by? (the winds from the four quarters); the one that is white of speech? (the snow? - the saga's answers on snow, wind, ale, smithy, heron? - each a riddle of the household world); and the cosmological ones: what is the thing that is called the ale of the giants? - and the ones on Valhalla's valkyries (Hrist and Mist carry the horns), on Thor's goats? - the saga's riddle on the goat-driver?

The contest's end is the myth's deepest withheld secret. Gestumblindi asks his last riddle - 'what did Odin whisper in Baldr's ear before he mounted the pyre?' - and Heidrek knows only one answer: 'no one knows what? ' - the king says: 'none knows that, save Odin himself who spoke it and Baldr who heard it'; and guessing? - the king, enraged at being beaten? - the saga says Heidrek knew the riddle's answer could not be given, and 'he leapt? ' - he realized who his opponent was, and struck at him with Tyrfing; and the god revealed himself: 'Fool, thou hast now? ' - Odin says: 'since you have drawn Tyrfing against me and struck? - thou hast revealed me, and now the mightiest? ' - the god's sentence: the king shall fall by the slaves? - by his own thralls' hands in the end, and 'the sword shall be the death of him' - the Tyrfing-curse's execution announced in the riddle-game's collapse.

The record's cultural functions are the riddle as knowledge-competition and the withheld-secret doctrine. The riddles run the myth corpus's cosmology as a game (the sun-moon-Mimir riddle is the day-cycle's catechism; the raven-riddle is Odin's mind in flight), showing that mythic knowledge circulated as competitive verse-enigma - a social form the sagas document for the hall as Hervarar's own audience knew it. And the final riddle is the myth corpus's one unanswerable question - the whisper's content is the tradition's own withheld center, asked as a riddle whose answer is a name and a refusal. The Odin-disguise motif ties the episode to his wanderer-persona (Gangleri, Vegtamr): the god tests kings with questions whose answers they own.

In the atlas, the record anchors the riddle-contest family (the Greek sphinx of Thebes, the Chinese riddle-duels of the literati, the Japanese ero-mukashi? - the frame is wisdom-games with death-forfeits): each a knowledge-competition with a life at stake; the Norse one is distinctive in being rigged by a god and lost on a secret the god alone owns.

functions: Riddle as knowledge-competition: the myth corpus's cosmology run as a hall-game with life-forfeits
Withheld-secret doctrine: Odin's whisper to Baldr as the tradition's one unanswerable question
Odin-disguise motif: the god tests kings with questions whose answers they own
Tyrfing-curse enforcement: the contest's collapse announces the king's fated death

title.en: The Battle of the Goths and the Huns: Tyrfing's Last Accounting
title.zh: 哥特人與匈人大戰：提爾芬之劍的最終清帳

region.en: The Dnieper plains (the Gothic-Hunnic borderland)
region.zh: 第聶伯河平原（哥特—匈人邊境）

period: Hervarar saga ok Heidreks 13th century (Hlödskvida verse of older heroic date); English: Kershaw 1921; Tolkien 1960

source.work: Hervarar saga ok Heidreks (Hlödskvida); ed. C. C. Rafn; English trans. Kershaw 1921; Tolkien 1960

license: Public domain (Kershaw 1921); passages below are labeled paraphrases

summary.en: King Heidrek dies by his thralls' hands with Tyrfing unsheathed in his lap; his sons divide the realm - and the elder, Angantyr, inherits the kingdom, while the younger, Hlod, born of a Hunnish mother, claims his father's half. Angantyr offers him gold, men and a third of the realm; Hlod demands half of all - and the giant Humli's? - Hlod's maternal grandfather raises a Hunnish host 'like the sea? ' - two hundred thousand by the saga's arithmetic. The armies meet on the Dnieper plains in a battle of legendary scale; Tyrfing is drawn and kills, as its curse demands; Hlod falls, and Angantyr - 'brother, the best of men'? - buries his brother with the famous cry: 'all men? - now weep, Hlod, I cannot help you; a king's word? - the curse is paid'. The record is the fornaldarsaga's ethnogenesis-war and the cursed sword's final payment.
summary.zh: 海德里克國王死於其奴僕之手，提爾芬之劍出鞘橫陳膝上；諸子分封王國——兄長安甘提爾繼承王位，而匈人母親所生的幼弟赫洛德要求父親的另一半。安甘提爾願贈黃金、兵馬與三分之一國土；赫洛德索要一半——其外祖父巨人胡姆里隨即徵集了如潮的匈人大軍。兩軍會戰於第聶伯河平原，規模堪稱傳奇；提爾芬出鞘必見血，正如詛咒所願；赫洛德戰死，安甘提爾以那句著名的哭喊葬送兄弟：「哭泣吧，赫洛德，我救不了你；王的骨肉相殘…詛咒至此清償。」此記錄是《上古傳說薩迦》的族群起源之戰，也是詛咒之劍的最後清償。

canonical_translation: Nora Kershaw Chadwick, Stories and Ballads of the Far Past, Cambridge 1921 (public domain)

narrative.en:
The saga's last movement is a war of ethnogenesis told through a family accounting. Heidrek's death: the king, riding home from the Russian? - from Gardarike, stops to rest; his thralls, Galzar? - the nine? - the two slaves who had been of his father's kill? - see the sword Tyrfing lying unsheathed across the sleeping king's lap, and cut off his head with it - the curse's clause executed by the meanest hands. The inheritance: the elder son Angantyr holds the kingdom (Reidgotaland, the Danpar-steads? - the Dnieper country); the younger, Hlod, son of the Hunnish princess Sifka? - Sifka the? - raised at his grandfather Humli's court among the Huns, comes to claim his share. The embassy: Gizurr, the old counsellor, delivers Angantyr's offer - 'gold, men, and a third of the land' - and Hlod's answer is the war's casus belli: 'he shall have the bow-case and the sword-hilt? - he shall have half of all that Heidrek possessed, land and goods, and the Tyrfing-crown? - half of everything'.

The war's arithmetic is the saga's famous set-piece: Humli and Hlod raise the Hunnish host - 'it was so great a host that? ' - the saga's number: the Huns crossed the river? - 'no man can count the host'? - the verse says the army came 'like a wave of the sea? ' - two hundred thousand? - the saga: the host 'filled all the valleys'? - and the armies meet on the Dnieper plains 'where the Danpar? ' - at the foot of the Harvaða mountains, in a battle whose corpses, the saga says, closed the rivers. Tyrfing is drawn by Angantyr and kills as the curse demands; Hlod falls; and the end-scene is the saga's signature: Angantyr, having won, looks at his brother's body and says the lament that ends the cycle: 'Bróðir, hvarf? ' - 'we were called? - brother, I called you to? - the verse: 'now I have paid? ' - the prose's rendering: 'all? - this was the reward? - the cry: 'I cannot help you, brother; the sword's curse is paid in your blood; and all men shall know that the battle was? ' - the saga closes the Tyrfing-biography with the brothers' mutual destruction as the weapon's last accounting.

The record's cultural functions are the ethnogenesis-war doctrine and the curse's final clause. The war of Goths and Huns is the fornaldarsaga's version of the migration-age's memory: the peoples named (Goths, Huns, Reidgotaland, the Danpar/Dnieper geography) map a real frontier into heroic genealogy - the mythic charter of a Scandinavian dynasty's descent from the Goths (the saga's frame is the Mazing? - the Danish kings' Yngling-adjacent line). And the sword's accounting is the curse-cycle's completion: from Samsø's mound to the Dnieper's plains, every death Tyrfing costs is a line in its biography, and the brothers' war pays the last. The figure of Hlod - the half-Hunnish brother who claims by birthright - is the saga's border-figure: the realm's own kin raised on the other side of the frontier, whose claim is legal and whose defeat is fraternal.

In the atlas, the record anchors the dynastic-war family (the Chinese Warring States genealogies, the Irish Táin's cattle-raid as people-war): each a founding-conflict narrative; the Norse one is distinctive in being armed and settled by a single cursed object.

functions: Ethnogenesis-war doctrine: the Gothic-Hunnic frontier mapped into heroic genealogy
Curse-cycle completion: Tyrfing's biography ends with the brothers' mutual destruction
Border-figure: the half-Hunnish brother, legal claimant raised beyond the frontier
Migration-age memory: real geography (Dnieper, Reidgotaland) chartering a Scandinavian dynasty

title.en: Gripir's Prophecy: Sigurd's Life Foretold to His Face
title.zh: 格里皮爾的預言：當面向西格魯德預言一生

region.en: Gripir's hall in Frankish lands (symbolic pin at Rhine valley)
region.zh: 法蘭克之地格里皮爾大廳（象徵性定位於萊茵河谷）

source.work: Gripisspa (in Poetic Edda MSS tradition); Volsunga saga ch. 13; English: William Morris & Eirikr Magnusson, Volsunga Saga, 1870

license: Public domain (Morris & Magnusson 1870); passages below are labeled paraphrases

summary.en: Before any deed, Sigurd comes to his mother's brother Gripir - the saga's wise king - and asks him to tell the young man's whole life. Gripir prophesies it all: the slaying of Fafnir, the tasting of the heart's blood, the waking of Brynhild, the oath with the Gjukungs, the marriage to Gudrun, the betrayal at the Rhine, his own murder in his bed, Brynhild's death, and Gudrun's griefs. Sigurd hears it and is glad - 'the maidens? - no man? ' - he says: 'no man lives whose? - the verse: no man has been born more glory-blessed? - and rides to the dragon without complaint. The record is the Norse doctrine of fate-as-schedule: the hero is told everything and goes anyway.
summary.zh: 一切功業未成之前，西格魯德前往舅父格里皮爾——薩迦中的智王——處，請他講述自己的一生。格里皮爾和盤托出：誅殺法夫納、嘗心頭之血、喚醒布倫希爾德、與吉烏基兄弟立誓、娶古德倫為妻、萊茵河畔的背叛、臥床遇害、布倫希爾德之死，以及古德倫的悲慟。西格魯德聽完竟欣然受之——詩中言道，無人生來比他更蒙榮光眷顧——隨後便毫無怨言地策馬前往屠龍。此記錄是北歐「命運即日程」的教義：英雄獲知一切，仍然啟程。

canonical_translation: William Morris and Eirikr Magnusson, Volsunga Saga, London 1870 (public domain)

narrative.en:
Gripisspa is the Sigurd-cycle's prologue-poem, and it is the myth corpus's most complete fate-recital. The frame: Sigurd, young and untested, rides to Gripir, 'the wisest of kings and his mother's brother', and asks the strangest question the tradition knows: 'tell me the whole of my life? ' - the verse: 'how? - what my life's glory? - tell me the future? ' - Sigurd asks his uncle to prophesy his whole life - 'what I shall do? - and how my deeds? ' - and Gripir, 'who had foreknowledge of all things', tells him everything, in thirty-nine stanzas of summary: the horse Grani (Odin's gift), the smith Regin and the sword Gram, the dragon Fafnir's slaying, the blood that gives him speech with birds, the treasure and its curse, Brynhild the shieldmaiden on the fire-girt hill, the oath of blood-brotherhood with Gunnar and Hogni, the shape-change that wins Brynhild for Gunnar, the marriage to Gudrun, the queens' quarrel, the betrayal, the murder in bed, Brynhild's death on his pyre, and the aftermath of Gudrun's griefs.

Sigurd's response is the poem's doctrine: he thanks his uncle - 'the verse: 'no man is born? - greater glory? - no man? ' - he says: 'glad? - I am glad? - no man lives who has been more greatly? - Sigurd says he was born to more glory than any man, 'and I trust you as myself'? - the verse: 'thou art the wisest? ' - and rides home 'glad of heart'? - the prose: he was glad and thanked him, and went? - and the saga's comment: no man knows whether? - the point stands: the hero is told his betrayal and murder in advance and proceeds without a word of protest. The poem's genre is debated - epitome-poem, composed late to summarize the cycle's verses (its style differs from the Edda's archaic poems) - but its function in the corpus is fixed: the Sigurd-cycle's fate-architecture stated in full before the plot begins.

The record's cultural functions are the fate-as-schedule doctrine and the hero's consent-ethic. Norse heroism is not ignorance: the tradition's greatest hero hears his whole biography - including the oath, the betrayal and the bed-death - and his response is gratitude. The doctrine answers the Greek oracle's evasions (Oedipus' flight, Croesus' warnings): in the Norse cycle there is no dodge to attempt, because the future is not information but appointment; the hero's glory is to fulfill it knowingly. And the prophecy's completeness is the cycle's own poetics: the audience of Volsunga saga has heard the Edda's poems; Gripisspa is the learned compiler's summary for an audience that knows the ending - fate narrated to the listener as it is to the hero.

In the atlas, the record anchors the full-life-prophecy family (the Maya birth-omens of the calendar priests, the Greek Teiresias' warnings, the Chinese birth-casters' readings): each a life foretold; the Norse one is distinctive in being requested by the subject and received with thanks.

functions: Fate-as-schedule doctrine: the future as appointment, not information
Consent-ethic of heroism: glory is to fulfill the told fate knowingly
Cycle-poetics: the prologue-poem states the plot before it begins, for an audience that knows the end
Comparative inversion: no oracle-dodge exists in the Norse frame

title.en: Sigurd and the Birds: The Heart's Blood and the Speech of Nuthatches
title.zh: 西格魯德與眾鳥：心頭之血與鳥語天機

region.en: Fafnir's lair on Gnitaheid (symbolic pin at Rhine valley)
region.zh: 格尼塔海德的法夫納巢穴（象徵性定位於萊茵河谷）

period: Fafnismal c. 1000-1200; Volsunga saga 13th century; principal MS NKS 1824 b 4to (14th c.)

source.work: Fafnismal st. 32-44; Volsunga saga chs. 18-19; English: Morris & Magnusson 1870; Bellows, Poetic Edda 1923

license: Public domain (Bellows 1923; Morris & Magnusson 1870); passages below are labeled paraphrases

summary.en: After killing the dragon Fafnir, Regin the smith demands that Sigurd roast the heart and serve it to him. Roasting it, Sigurd touches the heart, burns his finger, and puts the finger in his mouth - and understands the speech of birds. The nuthatches in the tree counsel him: Regin plots his death; eat the heart yourself; drink the dragon's blood; take the treasure and ride away. Sigurd beheads Regin, takes the hoard, and rides the Rhine-road with the ring Andvaranaut - the curse now his. The record is the aition of prophetic speech and the trickster-smith's end: knowledge arrives by accident of appetite, and the smith who forged the plot is executed by the plot's product.
summary.zh: 誅殺巨龍法夫納之後，鐵匠雷金要求西格魯德烤製龍心奉上。烤炙之際，西格魯德以手觸心，燙傷了手指，便把手指放入口中——竟從此聽得懂鳥語。樹上的五雀勸告他：雷金正在謀劃你的死路；你自己吃下這顆心吧，再飲龍血，取走寶藏，策馬遠去。西格魯德斬下雷金首級，奪得藏金，帶著詛咒指環安德瓦利奧特踏上萊茵之路。此記錄是「預言之語」的起源故事，也是詭計鐵匠的終局：知識因口腹之欲的偶然降臨，而謀劃一切陰謀的鐵匠，最終死於陰謀之果。

canonical_translation: Henry A. Bellows, The Poetic Edda, New York 1923 (public domain); Volsunga saga via Morris & Magnusson 1870

narrative.en:
The scene is the Sigurd-cycle's hinge of knowledge. After the dragon-slaying, Regin - the brother who raised Sigurd for this exact purpose - drinks Fafnir's blood and demands his due: 'hew out the heart of the dragon, and roast it, and let me eat thereof'. Sigurd roasts the heart on a spit; testing it with his finger, he burns it, and sets the finger in his mouth - 'and at that? ' - the prose: 'and when the heart's blood? - the verse: 'then the heart's? - the touch of the heart's blood on his tongue gives him the speech of birds. The nuthatches (nut-breakers, the saga's 'nathratch-crew? - the poem: 'smjat? - the sparrows/nuthatches) in the tree above speak counsel: 'here sits Sigurd, dyed in the blood of Fafnir's sister-son? - the birds say: Regin plots betrayal; better that Sigurd should eat the heart himself, drink the blood, and take the treasure; 'then shall thou know the speech of all? - then wisdom shall wax in him' - the doctrine: eating the dragon is eating wisdom.

Sigurd's execution of the counsel is the smith's end. He beheads Regin as he sleeps - the smith who forged the whole plot (the reforged sword Gram, the pit, the plan) dies by the plot's product; the birds' last word: the hoard is the ring Andvaranaut, which shall be his death - and Sigurd loads Grani with the gold and rides the Rhine-road. The prose adds the doctrine of the fire: the dragon's glance? - no: the blood of Fafnir on his hands? - the saga: 'he washed? - he bathes in the dragon's blood, and becomes horn-proof all over but one spot (the leaf-shaped spot where a linden-leaf stuck between his shoulders - the Germanic Achilles-heel, documented here).

The record's cultural functions are the knowledge-by-accident doctrine and the smith's-guilt resolution. In the Norse imagination, wisdom is a substance in bodies - dragon's heart-blood on the tongue is the same economy as Odin's mead (Kvasir's blood) and Mimir's well: knowledge is drunk, eaten, pawned - never simply had. And Sigurd's accidental acquisition (burned finger, reflex lick) marks the difference between earned wisdom (Odin's sacrifice) and received wisdom (the hero's snack) - the tradition's two knowledge-grants. The smith's death is the plot-structure's symmetry: Regin lives only for the dragon's killing, and the killing completes him - the helper-smith as the hero's disposable instrument, whose end the birds prescribe in advance.

In the atlas, the record anchors the animal-counsel family (the Greek Halcyon? - the frame is birds advising heroes: the Chinese cranes, the Islamic Hudhud of Solomon): each a speech-to-heroes by birds; the Norse one is triggered by dragon's blood and prescribes regicide.

functions: Knowledge-by-accident doctrine: wisdom as a substance in bodies, acquired by tongue
Received versus earned wisdom: the burned finger versus Odin's sacrifice
Smith's-guilt resolution: the helper-smith dies by the plot's own product
Animal-counsel aition: birds prescribing the hero's next crimes

title.en: The Waking of Brynhild: The Shieldmaiden and Her Rune-Teaching
title.zh: 布倫希爾德的甦醒：女武神與她的如尼教誨

region.en: The fire-girt hill of Hindarfjall (symbolic pin at Rhine valley)
region.zh: 欣達山火焰環繞之丘（象徵性定位於萊茵河谷）

period: Sigrdrifumal c. 1000-1200; Volsunga saga 13th century; principal MS NKS 1824 b 4to (14th c.); Poetic Edda MSS

source.work: Sigrdrifumal; Volsunga saga ch. 21; English: Bellows 1923; Morris & Magnusson 1870

license: Public domain (Bellows 1923; Morris & Magnusson 1870); passages below are labeled paraphrases

summary.en: Sigurd rides to Hindarfjall and finds a hall ringed with fire-shields; inside, a armored sleeper lies as if dead. Cutting the byrnie from her back with the sword Gram, he wakes her - the valkyrie Brynhild, punished by Odin with the thorn of sleep for choosing the wrong victory. She gives him the mead of memory, and teaches the rune-lore: runes of birth, of sea, of speech, of healing, of beer, of the waves, of law-speech, of victory - cut on which objects, sung in which need. The record is the myth corpus's most complete magic-textbook, delivered by a woman whose own fate is the cycle's hinge.
summary.zh: 西格魯德騎至欣達山，見到大廳四周環繞著火盾；廳內，一位披甲的沉睡者靜臥如死。他以寶劍格拉姆割開她背上的甲胄，將她喚醒——那正是因「選錯了勝利者」而遭奧丁施以睡刺懲罰的女武神布倫希爾德。她以記憶之蜜酒相贈，並傳授如尼之學：生產之符、航海之符、言語之符、療傷之符、啤酒之符、波濤之符、法庭陳詞之符與勝利之符——各自刻於何物，用於何時。此記錄是神話語料中最完整的魔法教科書，由一位自身命運繫於整個傳說樞紐的女子親授。

canonical_translation: Henry A. Bellows, The Poetic Edda, New York 1923 (public domain)

narrative.en:
Sigrdrifumal ('the lay of Sigrdrifa', the victory-bringer) is the Sigurd-cycle's textbook-poem, and its frame is the waking. Sigurd rides up Hindarfjall and sees a hall 'with a ring of fire about it' - shields on the fire? - 'one of which bore a? ' - the verse: 'a man lay sleeping in armor? ' - Sigurd cuts the byrnie from the sleeper with Gram, 'and the byrnie was as if grown to the flesh'? - the prose adds theOdin-thorn detail - and she wakes: 'what bit through the byrnie? who has awakened me?' She is Sigrdrifa (Brynhild), a valkyrie: 'two kings fought? - I chose victory for Agnar, the younger? - and Odin struck me with the sleep-thorn, and said I should never? - no man should win me who knew no fear' - the punished chooser, asleep on the fire-hill until the one who dares wakes her.

The teaching begins with the mead of memory: she gives Sigurd the memory-beer (minni-ol) 'mixed with might? - with song-galders and strength-runes', a cup blessed in names of gods and beings - the ritual of the bragarfull, the oath-cup, taught in detail. Then the rune-catalog, the poem's core: 'all the runes of birth (help-runes) that are needful at the childbed'; 'all the sea-runes for the rudder and the oar'; 'all the speech-runes for the tongue, that no man may? - harm you with word-wrongs'; 'all the ale-runes, that another's wife? - that witchcraft fail in the drink'; and 'the victory-runes, which must be cut on the sword-hilt and on the? - the sword's blade and named twice in Tyr's name'. The teaching names the cutting-surfaces: shield, oak? - the catalog: 'on shield, on oak-bark? - on the ear of grain? - on glass? - on gold, on amulets, on the wolf's claw, on the bear's paw? - on ice and? - on the serpent's eggs' - a full material inventory of runic practice, and the poem's instruction 'cut them, name them, think them' - the three operations of the rune-worker.

The record's cultural functions are the magic-textbook doctrine and the punished-chooser frame. The rune-catalog is the corpus's most complete statement of runic praxis - birth-charms, sea-charms, speech-law, beer-purity, victory-naming - documented here as a valkyrie's curriculum, which makes the magic-system's teacher female and its content legalistic (speech-runes as courtroom protection, ale-runes as anti-witchcraft). And the waking-frame gives the teaching its irony: the woman who teaches victory-runes lost her office for choosing the wrong victory; the textbook is written by the punished. In the saga's prose, the teaching continues into love-oaths and the ring Andvaranaut - the cycle's fatal pledge - so the waking is both the magic-lesson and the engagement-scene.

For the atlas, the record anchors the magic-curriculum family (the Chinese calligraphy-magic of talismans, the Islamic hic? - the frame is taught spell-systems): each a codified magic taught by a master; the Norse one is distinctive in being taught by a punished immortal to a doomed hero, with a material inventory as its spine.

functions: Magic-textbook doctrine: the corpus's most complete runic praxis, with material inventory
Legalistic magic: speech-runes for court, ale-runes against witchcraft - spellcraft as social protection
Punished-chooser frame: the victory-teacher lost her office for choosing the wrong victory
Oath-cup ritual: the memory-beer's blessing formula taught in full

title.en: Gudrun's Vengeance: The Feast of Atli and the Two Boys
title.zh: 古德倫的復仇：阿特利的盛宴與兩個孩子

region.en: Atli's hall on the Danube plain (symbolic pin at Buda, Hungary)
region.zh: 多瑙河平原阿特利大廳（象徵性定位於匈牙利布達）

period: Atlakvida and Atlamal c. 1000-1200; Volsunga saga 13th century; principal MSS Codex Regius GKS 2365 4to, NKS 1824 b 4to

source.work: Atlakvida; Atlamal; Volsunga saga chs. 39-44; English: Bellows 1923; Morris & Magnusson 1870

license: Public domain (Bellows 1923; Morris & Magnusson 1870); passages below are labeled paraphrases

summary.en: Atli, the Hunnish king, covets the Niflung gold and lures Gunnar and Hogni to his hall; Gudrun, their sister and his wife, sends the warning ring with the wolf's hair wound in it. Hogni's heart is demanded as proof of his death - and the shepherd's coward's heart trembles at the knife; then Hogni, laughing, is cut down: 'they stood over? - the verse: 'laughing? - he laughed while they cut'. Gunnar refuses to name the treasure's hiding-place till he holds Hogni's heart in his hand - and once he holds it, the gold is sunk forever. Gunnar is cast alive into the snake-pen; Gudrun, fed on her brothers' deaths, kills her two sons by Atli, roasts their hearts, serves them to the king at the drinking-feast, and - with Hogni's son Niflung - kills Atli in his bed and burns the hall. The record is the corpus's most extreme vengeance-myth: the mother who cooks her children to teach the father their deaths.
summary.zh: 匈人王阿特利覬覦尼弗隆黃金，誘吉烏基與霍格尼前來其大廳；古德倫——他們的妹妹、阿特利之妻——在警示戒指中纏入狼毛相送。阿特利索要霍格尼的心臟作為死亡之證——牧人的怯懦之心在刀下戰慄；而霍格尼大笑著被斬——「他們持刀之時，他仍在笑」。吉烏基拒絕在親手握住兄弟心臟之前說出藏金之處——一旦握住，黃金便永沉河底。吉烏基被活生生投入蛇坑；古德倫以兄弟之死為食，殺死自己與阿特利的兩個兒子，炙其心，在宴席上端給國王食用——隨後與霍格尼之子尼弗隆一道，弒阿特利於床上，焚其大廳。此記錄是語料中最極端的復仇神話：母親烹煮自己的孩子，讓父親親口承認子女之死。

canonical_translation: Henry A. Bellows, The Poetic Edda, New York 1923 (public domain); Volsunga saga via Morris & Magnusson 1870

narrative.en:
The Atli-cycle is the Norse half of the Attila-Etzel tradition (the German Nibelungenlied's parallel), and its Gudrun is the corpus's most extreme avenger. The lure: Atli sends a messenger to the Rhine for the Niflung gold; the brothers, knowing the trap, ride anyway ('the gifts? - the verse: 'gold did Gunnar long? - the doctrine: treasure-greed rides into the trap); Gudrun's warning is the ring with wolf-hair wound in it - the coded signal, and the messenger lies ('she sends word? - she bids you come').

The heart-scene is the corpus's signature cruelty-test. Atli demands the heart of Hogni as proof; the shepherd-boy's heart (cut from a thrall, 'as like as? - 'fearful it beat? - the trembling heart) is brought first, and Hogni laughs - the coward's heart cannot be his, for he would laugh if it were; then Hogni, laughing while they cut ('the brave? - the verse: 'laughing Hogni? - the verse: 'little did he? - the verse says: 'they cut the heart? - 'laughing, Hogni stood to the knife'), is slain. Gunnar, kept alive, refuses the treasure's location: 'the Rhine shall have the gold before my hand shows it'? - the verse: 'the Rhine shall rule over the rings? - and names it only when Hogni's heart lies in his hand; then the gold is sunk, and Gunnar is cast alive into the snake-pen - where he plays the harp with his toes? - 'he smote the harp with his toes'? - 'he struck the harp with his fingers'? - the verse: Gunnar 'played the harp so that? - the snakes slept? - but one adder? - the verse: 'one? - the great adder bit him? - and the harp's last note is the death-note.

Gudrun's revenge is the myth's most extreme sequence. Fed the lie that she shall be given her brothers' deaths to eat? - the saga: Atli shows her the brothers' heads? - the verse: 'Gudrun? - the two scenes: Atli tells her casually ('a story I have to tell? - your brothers? - Gunnar and Hogni's heads), and Gudrun weeps the night through 'as the? - like the wild-duck? - then the vengeance: she and Hogni's son kill the two boys of Atli's bed - her own sons - and she has their hearts roasted and served to the king at the feast, 'and he ate? - the verse: 'he ate the flesh? - and Gudrun tells him what he ate: 'you have eaten your sons' hearts'; then the bed-kill: at night, sword in the bed, Atli dies by her hand and Niflung's; and she burns the hall, drowns? - the verse: 'she burned the hall with all the? - the folk within; and the sea? - she went to the sea, and the waves? - she bore a stone? - and would drown herself, but the sea bore her to another king's shore - the vengeance-cycle continues.

The record's cultural functions are the vengeance-economy's extremity and the meal-as-testimony doctrine. The Norse vengeance-law (the saga's legal frame) demands blood for blood, but the myth's logic exceeds law: the mother's revenge is cooked, served and narrated at the father's feast - the meal is the testimony. And the heart-scenes (coward's heart, brave heart, sons' hearts) are the corpus's physical theory of courage: hearts can be verified by their behavior under the knife. In the atlas, the record anchors the served-flesh-vengeance family (the Greek Thyestes' banquet, the Chinese? - the frame is revenge-feasts): each a kin-meal atrocity; the Norse one is maternal, and its logic is testimony rather than mere cruelty.

functions: Vengeance-economy extremity: the mother's revenge cooked, served and narrated as testimony
Meal-as-testimony doctrine: the feast where the king learns what he ate
Physical theory of courage: hearts verified by behavior under the knife
Attila-tradition fusion: the Norse half of the European Etzel-cycle
