Jealousy turned to blood: Peleus and Telamon killed him and hid the body, and were driven out of the island by their own father. Telamon went to Salamis, and married the king's daughter; Peleus went to Phthia, where he was purified, and married the princess of the house — the two exiles, afterwards, at the wedding on Pelion and the fathers of Achilles and Ajax.
summary.zh: 埃阿科斯（宙斯與仙女埃癸娜之子）受父親之命以「螞蟻」為國民，開創埃阿科斯王族；與恩得伊斯生珀琉斯與忒拉蒙，另與海中仙女普薩瑪忒生福科斯。二兄因妒其武藝與美貌而殺之藏屍，被父親逐出埃癸那島。忒拉蒙去薩拉米斯娶公主；珀琉斯去弗提亞受淨禮娶公主。此二流亡者即後來阿基琉斯與大埃阿斯之父。

sensitivity.note: Ancient literary source; no living community restrictions.

passages.text: Zeus carried off Aegina, daughter of Asopus, to the island then named Oenone, but now called Aegina; and there she bore him a son Aeacus. And because Aeacus was alone on the island, Zeus made the ants into men for him: and these were the Myrmidons.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Apollodorus, Library 3.12.6 (Frazer 1921); not verbatim.

passages.text: By Endeis, daughter of Chiron, he had two sons, Peleus and Telamon; and by the Nereid Psamathe he had a third son, Phocus. And Peleus and Telamon, out of jealousy of the younger brother's strength and skill in athletics, killed him, and hid the body in a wood; and their father, discovering the deed, drove them both out of the island.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Apollodorus, Library 3.12.6 (Frazer 1921); not verbatim.

passages.text: Telamon went to Salamis, where the king Cychreus received him, and gave him his daughter Glauce in marriage. Peleus went to Phthia, where Eurytion, son of Actor, purified him of the blood-guilt, and gave him his own daughter Antigone. And these two exiles would in time be the fathers of Ajax, on the one side, and of Achilles, on the other — the Aeacids, whose name, from the man who ruled the ants, ran through all the race of heroes.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Apollodorus, Library 3.12.7 (Frazer 1921); not verbatim.

title.en: Phrixus and Helle: The Golden Ram and the Hellespont
title.zh: 佛里克索斯與赫勒：金羊與赫勒斯滂

region.en: Boeotia to Colchis (mythic geography)
region.zh: 波厄提亞至科爾基斯（神話地理）

period: Compiled c. 1st-2nd century CE (attrib. Apollodorus; Frazer translation 1921)

source.work: Apollodorus, Library, trans. J. G. Frazer (1921), § 1.9.1

summary.en: Athamas, king of Boeotia, takes a second wife, Ino, who plots against the children of his first marriage: the seed-corn is parched in secret, a famine comes, and an oracle is got to say the dearth will cease if Phrixus is sacrificed to Zeus. Nephele, the cloud-mother, catches her two children at the altar and gives them a ram with a golden fleece, borne through the sky by Hermes' gift. Over the strait between Sigeum and the Chersonese, Helle slips into the deep and is drowned — the sea is called Hellespont after her — and Phrixus is carried to Colchis, where Aeetes receives him and the ram is sacrificed; its fleece, hung on an oak in the grove of Ares, is the prize Jason will one day be sent to fetch.
summary.zh: 波厄提亞王阿塔瑪斯續娶伊諾；後者暗害前妻之子：麥種被烘焙致饑荒，並竄改神諭稱須獻祭佛里克索斯。雲母涅斐勒救二子，賜金羊毛之羊乘之飛天；過海峽時赫勒落水而亡，海峽因得名「赫勒斯滂」；佛里克索斯至科爾基斯，宰羊獻神，羊毛懸於阿瑞斯聖林之橡樹上——後為伊阿宋遠征所取。

sensitivity.note: Ancient literary source; no living community restrictions.

passages.text: Athamas, king of Boeotia, had by his first wife Nephele a son Phrixus and a daughter Helle. And he married a second wife, Ino, by whom he had Learchus and Melicertes. But Ino plotted against the children of Nephele and persuaded the women to parch the wheat; and having got the wheat they did so without the knowledge of the men. But the earth, being sown with parched wheat, did not yield its annual crops; so Athamas sent to Delphi to inquire how he might be delivered from the dearth. And Ino persuaded the messengers to say it was foretold that the infertility would cease if Phrixus were sacrificed to Zeus.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Apollodorus, Library 1.9.1 (Frazer 1921); not verbatim.

passages.text: When Athamas heard that, he was forced by the inhabitants of the land to bring Phrixus to the altar. But Nephele caught him and her daughter up, and gave them a ram with a golden fleece, which she had received from Hermes; and borne through the sky by the ram they crossed land and sea. But when they were over the sea which lies betwixt Sigeum and the Chersonese, Helle slipped into the deep and was drowned, and the sea was called Hellespont after her.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Apollodorus, Library 1.9.1 (Frazer 1921); not verbatim.

passages.text: But Phrixus came to the Colchians, whose king was Aeetes, son of the Sun and of Perseis, and brother of Circe and Pasiphae. He received Phrixus and gave him one of his daughters, Chalciope, in marriage; and Phrixus sacrificed the ram with the golden fleece to Zeus the Deliverer, and hung the fleece in the grove of Ares, where an unsleeping dragon guarded it — the fleece for which, one day, an oracle would send Jason and the Argonauts.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Apollodorus, Library 1.9.1 (Frazer 1921); not verbatim.

title.en: The Seven Against Thebes
title.zh: 七雄攻忒拜

region.en: Thebes, Boeotia (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 波厄提亞底比斯（象徵性定位）

period: Compiled c. 1st-2nd century CE (attrib. Apollodorus; Frazer translation 1921)

source.work: Apollodorus, Library, trans. J. G. Frazer (1921), §§ 3.6.1-3.6.8

summary.en: Driven from Thebes by his brother, Polynices comes to Argos wearing the necklace of Harmonia, and is matched, by Adrastus, with Tydeus the exiled Calydonian — the two to be yoked by the seer's old prophecy of a boar and a lion on their shields. Seven chiefs muster, and Adrastus promises to restore them both. Amphiaraus the seer foresees the ruin of every man but Adrastus, and is dragged into the war by Polynices' bribe: the necklace given to his wife Eriphyle. The campaign is beaten at Thebes; Melanippus' brains are swallowed by wounded Tydeus; Zeus cleaves the ground under Amphiaraus; Adrastus alone is saved by his horse Arion; and the sons of Astacus stand in the lists of the fallen.
summary.zh: 波呂尼刻斯被兄逐出底比斯，攜和諧女神之項鍊奔阿爾戈斯；阿德拉斯托斯依神諭「豬與獅之兆」配以被逐的卡呂冬人堤丟斯，允諾助二人復國。七雄集結，而先知安菲阿拉俄斯預見全軍皆亡，唯因波呂尼刻斯賄賂其妻厄里菲勒（以項鍊）而被拖入戰爭。忒拜之戰傷亡慘重：堤丟斯吞腦而亡，宙斯裂地吞安菲阿拉俄斯，唯阿德拉斯托斯騎神馬阿里翁逃脫。

sensitivity.note: Ancient literary source; no living community restrictions.

passages.text: Eteocles and Polynices made a compact concerning the kingdom: each should rule alternately for a year at a time. But whichever of them ruled first would not hand over the kingdom, and Polynices, banished from Thebes, came to Argos taking with him the necklace and the robe of Harmonia. Adrastus, king of Argos, remembering the words of a seer who had told him to yoke his daughters in marriage to a boar and a lion, accepted both exiles as bridegrooms when he saw on their shields, the one the forepart of a boar and the other the forepart of a lion; and he promised to restore them both to their native lands.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Apollodorus, Library 3.6.1 (Frazer 1921); not verbatim.

passages.text: But Amphiaraus, son of Oicles, being a seer and foreseeing that all who joined the expedition except Adrastus were destined to perish, shrank from it himself and discouraged the rest. Polynices then went with the necklace of Harmonia to Eriphyle, the seer's wife, and bribed her to betray her husband into the muster.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Apollodorus, Library 3.6.2 (Frazer 1921); not verbatim.

passages.text: The seven chiefs were these: Adrastus, Polynices, Tydeus, Hippomedon, Capaneus, Parthenopaeus, and Arcadian Atalanta's son, with Amphiaraus dragged at the rear. And Capaneus, who boasted that he would take the city in despite of Zeus himself, was struck from the wall by the god's own thunderbolt, and burned where he fell.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Apollodorus, Library 3.6.5-3.6.7 (Frazer 1921); not verbatim.

passages.text: When the Argives broke, the two brothers Eteocles and Polynices, by the resolution of both armies, fought a single combat for the kingdom and slew each other. In the fierce battle that followed, Melanippus wounded Tydeus in the belly; and as he lay half dead, Athena brought a medicine which she had begged of Zeus and by which she intended to make him immortal. But Amphiaraus, who hated Tydeus for thrusting the army on to Thebes, cut off the head of Melanippus and gave it to him; and Tydeus split open the head and gulped up the brains — and Athena, in disgust, grudged and withheld the intended benefit.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Apollodorus, Library 3.6.8 (Frazer 1921); not verbatim.

passages.text: Amphiaraus fled beside the river Ismenus; and before Periclymenus could wound him in the back, Zeus cleft the earth by throwing a thunderbolt, and Amphiaraus vanished with his chariot and his charioteer — and Zeus made him immortal in the ground. Adrastus alone was saved by his horse Arion, that Poseidon had begot on Demeter in the likeness of a Fury; and so the prophecy was kept to the letter: every man of the Seven perished at Thebes, and the king of Argos came home alone.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Apollodorus, Library 3.6.8 (Frazer 1921); not verbatim.

title.en: Hecuba: The Queen Who Became a Bitch
title.zh: 赫卡柏：化為母犬的特洛伊王后

region.en: Thracian Chersonese (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 色雷斯克爾松涅斯（象徵性定位）

period: Composed from the lost epics (c. 7th century BCE; summary in Apollodorus; Frazer translation 1921)

source.work: Apollodorus, Library, trans. J. G. Frazer (1921), Epitome e.5.25

summary.en: The fate of Troy's old queen is told in one sentence of the Epic Cycle's summary: in the division of spoils, Ulysses got Hecuba; but some say that Helenus got her, and crossed over with her to the Chersonese — and that there she turned into a bitch, and he buried her at the place now called the Bitch's Tomb. Between queen and hound stands, in other tellings, a story of prophetic grief that outlived a city.
summary.zh: 《輯語》記載特洛伊王后的結局：分贓時，赫卡柏歸奧德修斯；另一說為赫勒諾斯攜她渡海至克爾松涅斯——她於該處化為母犬，葬地遂名「母犬之墓」。王后與母犬之間，流傳著一則關於預知之哀而逾城邦之亡的故事。

sensitivity.note: Ancient literary source; no living community restrictions.

passages.text: When Troy had fallen, the spoils were divided: Cassandra to Agamemnon, Andromache to Neoptolemus, and Hecuba, the old queen of the house of Priam, was given to Ulysses. But some say that Helenus got her, and crossed over with her to the Chersonese; and that there she turned into a bitch, and he buried her at the place now called the Bitch's Tomb.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Apollodorus, Library, Epitome e.5.25 (Frazer 1921); not verbatim.

passages.text: In one sentence the Epic Cycle has set down the double end of a queen: the captive passed from one hand to another — and the transformation; the tomb is named for what she became. Pausanias records that some said she was turned to stone, or into a dog: the end of the wife of Priam is one of those myths told several ways at once.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Apollodorus, Library, Epitome e.5.25 (Frazer 1921); not verbatim.

title.en: The Abduction of Helen
title.zh: 海倫被擄

region.en: Sparta to Troy (mythic geography)
region.zh: 斯巴達至特洛伊（神話地理）

period: Composed from the lost epics (c. 7th century BCE; summary in Apollodorus; Frazer translation 1921)

source.work: Apollodorus, Library, trans. J. G. Frazer (1921), Epitome e.3.1-e.3.6

summary.en: Why did the war begin? The summary gives two answers in one breath: Alexander carried off Helen, as some say, because Zeus so willed it — that his daughter's name should embroil Europe and Asia — or, as others say, that the race of demigods might be thinned to a mere remnant. The judgment of Paris follows: Hera, Athena and Aphrodite each offered him a gift, and he chose the promise of the world's most beautiful woman, sailed to Sparta, and took her by night with most of Menelaus' property; but Hera drove the ship by storm to Sidon, and — some say — Hermes stole the true Helen to Egypt and Proteus' court, leaving Paris a phantom of clouds. When Menelaus learned it, he ran to Agamemnon and the oaths of the assembled kings were invoked.
summary.zh: 特洛伊戰爭何以爆發？據《輯語》：一說宙斯有意使海倫之名引發歐亞大戰；一說為使半神之種凋零。繼而有金蘋果之評：赫拉允以王權、雅典娜允以戰無不勝、阿芙洛狄忒允以海倫為妻；帕里斯選後者。他夜赴斯巴達，帶走海倫與大量財物；赫拉施風暴迫其停於西頓——另有說：赫爾墨斯將真海倫偷至埃及、交普羅透斯看管，帕里斯只帶走一朵雲霧所幻的海倫。墨涅拉俄斯聞訊奔至邁錫尼，召眾王履行昔日之誓言。

sensitivity.note: Ancient literary source; no living community restrictions.

passages.text: Alexander — that is, Paris — carried off Helen, as some say, because such was the will of Zeus, in order that his daughter might be famous for having embroiled Europe and Asia; or, as others say, that the race of the demigods might be thinned to nothing.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Apollodorus, Library, Epitome e.3.1 (Frazer 1921); not verbatim.

passages.text: For one of these reasons, Strife threw an apple as a prize of beauty to be contended for by Hera, Athena and Aphrodite; and Zeus commanded Hermes to lead them to Alexander on Ida, in order to be judged by him. Each promised a gift: Hera said that if she were preferred to all women, she would give him kingdom over all men; Athena promised victory in war; Aphrodite, the hand of Helen. He decided in favour of Aphrodite — and sailed away to Sparta in ships built by Phereclus.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Apollodorus, Library, Epitome e.3.2 (Frazer 1921); not verbatim.

passages.text: For nine days he was entertained by Menelaus; but on the tenth, Menelaus having gone to Crete for the burial of his grandfather Catreus, Alexander persuaded Helen to go off with him. She abandoned Hermione, then nine years old, and put most of the property on board, and set sail with him by night. Hera, angry, sent a heavy storm which forced them to put in at Sidon; and fearing pursuit, Alexander spent a long time in Phoenicia and Cyprus before he came at last to Troy with Helen.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Apollodorus, Library, Epitome e.3.3-e.3.4 (Frazer 1921); not verbatim.

passages.text: But some tell a stranger version: that Hermes, in obedience to the will of Zeus, stole Helen herself and carried her to Egypt, and gave her to Proteus, king of the Egyptians, to guard; and that Alexander repaired to Troy with a phantom of Helen fashioned out of clouds. When Menelaus was aware of the rape, he came to Agamemnon at Mycenae and begged him to muster an army against Troy, and to raise levies in Greece, reminding every king by herald of the oaths they had all sworn: the affront had been offered equally to the whole of Greece.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Apollodorus, Library, Epitome e.3.5-e.3.6 (Frazer 1921); not verbatim.

title.en: The Muster at Aulis: Iphigenia at the Altar
title.zh: 奧利斯集結：伊菲革涅亞祭壇

region.en: Aulis, Boeotia (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 波厄提亞奧利斯（象徵性定位）

period: Composed from the lost epics (c. 7th century BCE; summary in Apollodorus; Frazer translation 1921)

source.work: Apollodorus, Library, trans. J. G. Frazer (1921), Epitome e.3.7-e.3.22

summary.en: The Greek host gathers at Aulis and learns the cost of the voyage. Odysseus feigns madness to stay home, and Palamedes catches the pretence by snatching the baby Telemachus from Penelope's arms; a serpent devours eight sparrows and their mother by the altar of Apollo, and Calchas reads it: nine years to the fall of Troy. Sailing blind, they land by mistake in Mysia and wound its king Telephus with Achilles' spear; only the spear's rust can heal him, so the wounded man comes back to guide them. And then, windbound at Aulis for the second time, Calchas declares what the goddess wants: the fairest of Agamemnon's daughters. The girl is fetched on the promise of marriage to Achilles; Artemis takes her at the altar, and a deer dies in her place.
summary.zh: 希臘聯軍集結奧利斯：奧德修斯裝瘋欲避戰，被帕拉墨得斯以嬰孩試出真偽；阿波羅祭壇旁之蛇食八雀與母雀，卡爾卡斯釋為九年陷城之兆。船隊誤入密細亞，忒勒福斯為阿基琉斯之矛所傷，唯矛鏽可醫，遂拖傷返鄉引路。再度受風所阻時，卡爾卡斯宣示女神之願：獻祭阿伽門農最美之女伊菲革涅亞。祭壇之上，阿爾忒彌斯攜女而去，以牝鹿代死。

sensitivity.note: Ancient literary source; the story contains human sacrifice; presented as ancient material without endorsement.

passages.text: Ulysses, not wishing to go to the war, feigned madness. But Palamedes, son of Nauplius, proved the pretence: when Ulysses ploughed the sand with salt and pretended to rave, Palamedes followed him, snatched the baby Telemachus from Penelope's bosom and drew his sword as if to kill him. Ulysses, in fear for the child, broke off his act and confessed — and went to the war.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Apollodorus, Library, Epitome e.3.7-e.3.8 (Frazer 1921); not verbatim.

passages.text: The armament mustered at Aulis. There, after a sacrifice to Apollo, a serpent darted from under the altar beside a plane-tree, where a nest held eight sparrows and the mother bird that made the ninth: it swallowed them all, and was then turned to stone. Calchas read the omen by Zeus's will: the serpent and the sparrows between them meant that Troy would be taken — in the tenth year.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Apollodorus, Library, Epitome e.3.11 (Frazer 1921); not verbatim.

passages.text: But not knowing the course to steer for Troy, the Greeks put in to Mysia and ravaged it, supposing it to be Troy. Telephus, son of Heracles, king of the Mysians, armed his people, chased the Greeks to their ships and killed many — among them Thersander, son of Polynices — but Achilles' spear caught him in the thigh. Later, because Apollo had said that only the one who wounded him could heal him, Telephus came to Argos in rags and begged the help of Achilles; and Achilles scraped the rust from his Pelian spear into the wound, and healed him; and Telephus, cured, showed the course to steer.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Apollodorus, Library, Epitome e.3.17-e.3.20 (Frazer 1921); not verbatim.

passages.text: The fleet put to sea a second time, and arrived at Aulis again, where it was windbound. Calchas said the ships could not sail unless the fairest of Agamemnon's daughters were sacrificed to Artemis; for the goddess was angry with Agamemnon, both because, on shooting a deer, he had boasted that even Artemis herself could not do it better, and because Atreus had never sacrificed to her the golden lamb.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Apollodorus, Library, Epitome e.3.21 (Frazer 1921); not verbatim.

passages.text: Agamemnon sent Ulysses and Talthybius to Clytemnestra with the fiction that he had promised Iphigenia to Achilles as a bride for his service in arms. The mother sent her; the father set her beside the altar, and was about to slaughter her — when Artemis carried her off to the Taurians, and appointed her to be her priestess, substituting a deer at the altar; though some say the goddess made her immortal on the spot.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Apollodorus, Library, Epitome e.3.22 (Frazer 1921); not verbatim.

title.en: Protesilaus and Laodamia
title.zh: 普羅忒西勞斯與拉俄達彌亞

region.en: Troy shore (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 特洛伊海岸（象徵性定位）

period: Composed from the lost epics (c. 7th century BCE; summary in Apollodorus; Frazer translation 1921)

source.work: Apollodorus, Library, trans. J. G. Frazer (1921), Epitome e.3.30

summary.en: Of all the Greeks the first to leap from his ship on Trojan soil was Protesilaus — and an oracle had said that the first to land would be the first to die. He fell by Hector's hand, having slain not a few of the barbarians. His wife Laodamia loved him even after death: she made an image of him and consorted with it, until her father, in horror, burned it. The gods had pity, and Hermes brought Protesilaus up from Hades for three hours; and when she saw him alive, Laodamia stabbed herself on the spot — the earliest death of the war paid back with the earliest death of love.
summary.zh: 希臘軍中第一個躍上岸者普羅忒西勞斯——有神諭預言：先登岸者先死。其妻拉俄達彌亞在丈夫死後以蠟像相伴，直至其父燒毀蠟像。諸神憐憫，命赫爾墨斯自冥府帶回亡夫三小時；見其復活，拉俄達彌亞當場自刎殉情。

sensitivity.note: Ancient literary source; no living community restrictions.

passages.text: Of the Greeks the first to land from his ship was Protesilaus, and having slain not a few of the barbarians he fell by the hand of Hector. His wife Laodamia loved him even after his death, and she made an image of him and consorted with it.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Apollodorus, Library, Epitome e.3.30 (Frazer 1921); not verbatim.

passages.text: The gods had pity on her, and Hermes brought up Protesilaus from Hades. On seeing him, Laodamia thought it was himself returned from Troy, and she was glad; but when he was carried back to Hades, she stabbed herself to death.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Apollodorus, Library, Epitome e.3.30 (Frazer 1921); not verbatim.

title.en: The Duel of Ajax and Hector
title.zh: 埃阿斯與赫克托耳之戰

region.en: Plains of Troy (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 特洛伊平原（象徵性定位）

period: Composed c. 8th century BCE (Butler translation 1898)

source.work: Homer, Iliad, trans. Samuel Butler (1898), Book VII

summary.en: Hector, fresh from duelling in the morning, strides out from the ranks in the afternoon and challenges any Greek to single combat: he will kill him, or if the god grants his foe the better fight, Hector's own armour is the prize. Nine heroes step forward; the lot falls on Ajax, son of Telamon, the biggest of the Achaeans after Achilles himself. The duel turns on spears, stone, and shield; when at last the heroes close with knives, the heralds part them for nightfall, and Hector, magnanimous, exchanges gifts with his enemy.
summary.zh: 赫克托耳再出挑戰：可戰至死，或為之獻甲。希臘九位英雄請纓，拈籤落於忒拉蒙之子埃阿斯——阿基琉斯之外最魁偉的希臘人。二將以矛石盾相搏至短兵相接，傳令官以天黑為由將二人分開；赫克托耳慷慨互贈腰帶與寶劍，此戰不以勝負論榮辱。

sensitivity.note: Ancient literary source; no living community restrictions.

passages.text: At the hour of the day when the woodman has cut his firewood and sits down to his midday meal in the mountain woods, and fatigue overweights his arms — at such an hour did the Trojan line stand down, and Hector, with his shining helm, ran out in front of the wall and called out his challenge to any Achaean who cared to try him in single combat: he would kill the man he met, or, if heaven gave his enemy the better fighting, he would die — but Hector would carry off the armour of the man he beat.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Homer, Iliad, Book 7 (Butler 1898); not verbatim.

passages.text: There was silence in the ranks. Menelaus rose first, but Agamemnon held him back; Nestor taunted them all with the memory of the men of his young day who would have leapt at such a challenge; and then nine heroes stood up — Agamemnon, Diomedes, the two Ajaxes, Idomeneus, Meriones, Eurypylus, Thoas and Ulysses — and Nestor bid them cast lots, and the lot fell, as all the Greeks shouted, on Ajax the son of Telamon.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Homer, Iliad, Book 7 (Butler 1898); not verbatim.

passages.text: They girt their harness and came out before the wall, the biggest men on either side, terrible to see. Hector cast first, and his spear through six layers of hide stuck fast in the shield behind; Ajax cast, and his spear went clean through the Trojans' shield and breastplate, and grazed the skin of the man's neck: but Hector was not slow. He caught up a great stone — one of the boundary-stones of the field, that two common men could not lift — and hurled it on Ajax's shield with both hands.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Homer, Iliad, Book 7 (Butler 1898); not verbatim.

passages.text: Ajax, in answer, hurled one still heavier and broke Hector's shield, and drove him backward with the wound in the neck; and when the son of Priam rallied, Ajax pressed him again, and was again thrust back with a wound through his shield; and then the heroes, at their knives, would have closed for the kill — had not the heralds, Talthybius and Idaeus, run between them with their staffs: 'It is night; the host has need of you.' And Hector answered: 'The gods have given this duel to neither; let us part, and let the men of both sides see we have fought like men.' And each gave the other a gift: Hector the silver-studded sword, and Ajax the great purple belt.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Homer, Iliad, Book 7 (Butler 1898); not verbatim.

title.en: The Catalogue of Ships
title.zh: 艦船名冊

region.en: Aulis & the Troad (mythic geography)
region.zh: 奧利斯與特洛伊平原（神話地理）

period: Composed c. 8th century BCE (Butler translation 1898)

source.work: Homer, Iliad, trans. Samuel Butler (1898), Book II (Catalogue)

summary.en: Before the battle, the Muses are invoked to name the captains and the ships. The catalogue marches through the whole of Greece: the Boeotians and their flower of cities, the Minyans of Aspledon and Orchomenus, Phocis and Locris, the Euboeans, Athenians and Salaminians, the Argives and Mycenaeans under Agamemnon and Diomedes, the men of Pylos under old Nestor, and at last the Arcadians, the crews of Elis, the men of Aegina and the Myrmidons in their fifty ships — and on the Trojan side, the muster of all the allies, from Tricca's healers to the Lycians under Sarpedon and Glaucus.
summary.zh: 開戰前詩人祈請繆斯唱名：繆斯述各邦首領與船數——自波厄提亞的百花之城、俄爾科墨努斯的米尼亞人，經福基斯與洛克里、优卑亞、雅典與薩拉米斯、阿伽門農與狄俄墨得斯麾下的阿爾戈斯與邁錫尼、老涅斯托耳的皮洛斯人，至阿卡迪亞、厄利斯、埃癸那與密爾彌東人五十艘船；而特洛伊一側，亦列諸盟邦，自特里刻的醫者至薩爾佩冬與格勞科斯所率的呂基亞人。

sensitivity.note: Ancient literary source; no living community restrictions.

passages.text: The list opens with a prayer: many were the men who came to Troy, but could the Muse name them all? 'Tell me now, you Muses that dwell on Olympus: who were the leaders and lords of the Danaans?' And the first lord named is not Agamemnon but the Boeotian line — Peneleos, Leitus, Arcesilaus, Prothoenor and Clonius — with fifty ships from Hyria, Aulis, Schoenus, Scolus, Eteonus, Thespeia, Graea, Mycalessus and the rest of the flower of Boeotia's cities.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Homer, Iliad, Book 2 (Butler 1898); not verbatim.

passages.text: From there the roll went on in order of the Greek map: Aspledon and Orchomenus' Minyans under Ascalaphus and Ialmenus; the Phocians under Schedius and Epistrophus; the Locrians under Ajax the lesser, son of Oileus; the Euboean men of Chalcis and Eretria; the Athenians under Menestheus, 'where no man living could equal him in the marshalling of chariots and men'; the great black ships of the Salaminians under Ajax son of Telamon, drawn up close to the Athenians.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Homer, Iliad, Book 2 (Butler 1898); not verbatim.

passages.text: Then came the Argives of Agamemnon himself — one hundred ships, the most of any lord — and Diomedes' eighty from Argos and Tiryns, Hermione and Asine; then the men of Lacedaemon and Sparta, of Pharis and Sparta, under Menelaus, crying loud to one another, their hearts burning for the wrongs done to Helen; and the men of Pylos in their ninety ships with old Nestor — ninety ships, all full of the sound of battle.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Homer, Iliad, Book 2 (Butler 1898); not verbatim.

passages.text: At last came Arcadia's ships under Agapenor; the crews of Elis with four lords; the men of Doulichium and the Echinades; and — near the end — Achilles with the fifty ships of the Myrmidons, in whose hearts the war with Hector had not yet begun; for Achilles was still by his ships, and his anger against Agamemnon burned as hot as the day he had been robbed.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Homer, Iliad, Book 2 (Butler 1898); not verbatim.

passages.text: And the Trojans were called, then, to their own roll: Hector, son of Priam, with the best of Troy's men; Aeneas and the two sons of Antenor; the Cicones, the Paeonians, the Paphlagonians, the Alizones, the Phrygians, the Maeonians, the Carians, and last the Lycians under Sarpedon and Glaucus, the two great captains who had come from the river Xanthus far over the sea.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Homer, Iliad, Book 2 (Butler 1898); not verbatim.

title.en: The Council of the Kings: Assembly and Oaths
title.zh: 希臘王侯議事會

region.en: Achaean camp, Troy (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 特洛伊希臘營地（象徵性定位）

period: Composed c. 8th century BCE (Butler translation 1898)

source.work: Homer, Iliad, trans. Samuel Butler (1898), Book II

summary.en: Zeus sends a false dream to sleeping Agamemnon promising the sack of Troy that very day; the king wakes, calls the kings in council, and then tries the host with a speech of retreat. The army rushes to the ships like surf, until Odysseus, Athena at his side, drags the chiefs back and shames the army into staying. The ugly little commoner Thersites, who rails at the kings, is beaten with the sceptre; the assembly, restored, takes its meal, and pours libations and prayers to Zeus before the day's fighting.
summary.zh: 宙斯遣假夢誘阿伽門農：許諾當日即陷特洛伊。王醒後召集眾王議事，又以「撤軍」試探全軍；軍士如浪奔向船隻，奧德修斯在雅典娜相助下攔回統領、並以權杖當眾責打譏罵君王的醜漢特爾西忒斯。會議重整，全軍歆祭、祈禱、以酒奠宙斯，誓復出戰。

sensitivity.note: Ancient literary source; no living community restrictions.

passages.text: Zeus, weighing his promise to Thetis against the cost to the Achaeans, sent down a false Dream to the sleeping Agamemnon: the king heard in his sleep a figure like Nestor promise that now, at last, he would take Troy of a surety. He woke in good heart, and called the kings to council in secret, where he himself proposed the dishonourable retreat — his own test of his army's mettle.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Homer, Iliad, Book 2 (Butler 1898); not verbatim.

passages.text: In full assembly Agamemnon rose and declared that the war had failed: the ships must go home, he said, before all their own people learned they had been beaten. The host broke up as a wave breaks, with a roar of armour, and made for the ships in a tide of dust — until Odysseus, with Athena's bright mantle about him, went from man to man of the chiefs, hauling them back by their words and bidding them hold the men together in their several companies.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Homer, Iliad, Book 2 (Butler 1898); not verbatim.

passages.text: There was one who cried against the kings in the assembly: Thersites, a bandy-legged, babbling commoner, who heaped abuse on Agamemnon and the princes and would have had the host sail home. Odysseus came to him, rebuked him for his words, and beat him about the back with the sceptre while the Greeks roared at the sight; and the ugly demagogue wiped away his tears and sat down silenced.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Homer, Iliad, Book 2 (Butler 1898); not verbatim.

passages.text: The army then took its meal, and poured the morning's libation to the gods: wine cups round the benches, a prayer to Zeus of the bright thunderbolt, and the oath of the kings renewed, that they would not break up the campaign before Troy fell — or its houses burned.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Homer, Iliad, Book 2 (Butler 1898); not verbatim.

title.en: Sarpedon's Fall: The Son of Zeus Before Troy
title.zh: 薩爾佩冬之死：宙斯之子命殞特洛伊

region.en: Plains of Troy (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 特洛伊平原（象徵性定位）

period: Composed c. 8th century BCE (Butler translation 1898)

source.work: Homer, Iliad, trans. Samuel Butler (1898), Book XVI

summary.en: Sarpedon, the Lycian king who is son of Zeus himself, charges Patroclus in Achilles' own armour, and Zeus on Ida debates whether to snatch his living son away from death — Hera talks him down with the argument of the fates of other men's sons. Sarpedon falls as an oak or a poplar falls, and, dying, entrusts his arms to Glaucus and calls him to rouse the Lycians. Sleep and Death, twin brothers, lift the body from the field, and the god's own winds bear it to Lycia for burial — the one boon Zeus could still give.
summary.zh: 薩爾佩冬乃呂基亞王、宙斯親子，在帕特羅克洛斯身穿阿基琉斯之甲作戰時猛攻而來。宙斯於伊達山權衡：是否可救愛子於死亡？赫拉舉眾神之子皆有凡命為由勸止。薩爾佩冬如橡木、如白楊般倒下，臨終託甲與格勞科斯，並要他召集呂基亞人復仇。睡神與死神——一對雙生兄弟——自戰場拾起屍身，宙斯以親遣風將其送回呂基亞安葬：這是他唯一所能施予的恩惠。

sensitivity.note: Ancient literary source; no living community restrictions.

passages.text: Patroclus, in the armour of Achilles, had driven the Trojans back off the ships, and among the Lycians who rallied against him there was none brighter than Sarpedon, king of Lycia, whom Zeus had fathered on Laodamia. When the two champions closed, Zeus looked down from Ida and knew his son was marked for death.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Homer, Iliad, Book 16 (Butler 1898); not verbatim.

passages.text: And Zeus said in his heart: shall I take my son out of the battle alive, and carry him away to the rich lands of Lycia? Or shall I let him die where he stands? And Hera heard, and spoke down bitterly against the plan: 'How can you think it, Zeus? A mortal man, whose fate is fixed — and you would rescue him from the sorrow of death? Do it, and every other god will pull his own son from the fighting; and there are plenty of them fighting on both sides.' And Zeus yielded, with a groan, and let the fates stand; for he had promised his wife nothing else. But he let fall drops of bloody rain on the plain in honour of his son.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Homer, Iliad, Book 16 (Butler 1898); not verbatim.

passages.text: The two closed like two lions or two boars of the hills: Patroclus struck first, through the heart of the hero's driver; Sarpedon's spear missed the man's shoulder and passed through the shoulder-blade; and then — Sarpedon fell, as an oak falls, or a poplar, or a tall pine felled by shipwrights' axes for the building of ships. So he lay outstretched before the horses and the chariot, groaning, and grasping the bloody dust.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Homer, Iliad, Book 16 (Butler 1898); not verbatim.

passages.text: But as the light of life left him, he spoke to Glaucus his comrade: 'My friend, you were always brave; now you must fight for my body and my armour, and call aloud to the Lycian princes to fight for Sarpedon: it is the last word I shall ever say to you.' And he died with the word in his mouth. And the god Apollo, on Zeus's word, carried the soul away, and Sleep and Death, twin brothers, lifted the body in their arms, and bore it away through the ranks of war, and set it down in the rich plain of Lycia for burial.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Homer, Iliad, Book 16 (Butler 1898); not verbatim.

title.en: Cephalus and Procris
title.zh: 刻法羅斯與普羅克里斯

region.en: Athens & Thessaly (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 雅典與色薩利（象徵性定位）

period: Composed c. 8 CE (Latin; Riley translation 1851)

source.archive: Project Gutenberg eBook 21765 (H. T. Riley, trans.)
source.work: Ovid, Metamorphoses, Book VII (Fables VII-VIII)

summary.en: Cephalus, the Athenian, married Procris, the sister of Orithyia; and, in the version Ovid tells through his own mouth as an old man on Aegina, Aurora the Dawn carried him off for a time, and he came home to test his wife's faith by coming in disguise. Procris, tempted by the gifts he carried, yielded to the unknown youth; the husband, revealing himself, branded her a traitress, and she, in shame, left him for the service of Diana — coming back with two gifts of the goddess, a dog that could catch anything, and a javelin that never missed. Years after, in the heat of the chase, Cephalus, lying down in the grass, called on the breeze of his solitary walks; the jealous Procris, hidden and listening for another name, rushed from her covert with a cry — and the javelin that never missed took her in the breast. He held her while she died, and she forgave him, and he buried her and never called upon that breeze again.
summary.zh: 雅典青年刻法羅斯娶普羅克里斯；晨光女神厄俄斯曾一度將他擄走，他回家後喬裝試探妻子，普羅克里斯被誘失身；丈夫當場揭穿，羞憤之下的普羅克里斯離家赴阿爾忒彌斯門下，回來時帶著女神所贈「永不失足」的獵犬與「永不落空」的標槍。多年後，獵場上的刻法羅斯在草叢中呼喚微風（其慣語），躲在暗處聽風的普羅克里斯誤以為丈夫在喊別的女子，驚跳而出——標槍穿胸。彌留之際她原諒了丈夫；他葬她之後，再也不喚那陣風。

sensitivity.note: Ancient literary source; no living community restrictions.

passages.text: Cephalus, the Athenian lord, married Procris, sister of Orithyia, and lived with her in great happiness. But the beauty of the young man got him no rest with the goddess of the Dawn: Aurora carried him off, in the version he told at Aegina, and kept him a while in the east.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ovid, Metamorphoses VII, Fables VII-VIII (Riley 1851); not verbatim.

passages.text: When she let him go, he went home to test the faith of his wife, and came back in disguise — a stranger of great wealth, laying his gifts one by one before Procris until she, thinking her husband dead and gone, yielded to the young man's suit. And then the stranger threw off his disguise: he had caught her in her fall.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ovid, Metamorphoses VII, Fables VII-VIII (Riley 1851); not verbatim.

passages.text: In her shame she left the house, and went to the service of Diana; and the goddess gave her two gifts of a hunter's life: a dog so swift that nothing it chased could escape it — the dog that was afterwards pitted against the fox of Cadmus and turned to stone — and a javelin that never missed its mark.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ovid, Metamorphoses VII, Fables VII-VIII (Riley 1851); not verbatim.

passages.text: She came back, and they were reconciled; and Cephalus used the javelin on every beast of the wood. But the man had a habit, lying down in the grass at noon, of calling for the breeze of his solitary walks — a coolness he loved — and of calling it by name, Aura. And Procris, who had heard of a servant in his heart and did not know the name of the wind, hid one day in the thicket to see the woman he called; and at the voice she started up. Cephalus, thinking some wild beast had sprung at him, threw the javelin — and it did not miss.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ovid, Metamorphoses VII, Fable VIII (Riley 1851); not verbatim.

passages.text: She died in his arms, and with her last breath she begged him not to marry the breeze: 'I forgive you,' she said, 'and I give you the javelin.' And Cephalus buried her, and mourned her, and never again called on the breeze whose coolness had cost him the wife who had given him the weapon that killed her.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ovid, Metamorphoses VII, Fable VIII (Riley 1851); not verbatim.

title.en: The Daughters of Minyas Refuse the God
title.zh: 彌尼亞斯之女拒酒神

region.en: Orchomenus, Boeotia (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 波厄提亞俄爾科墨努斯（象徵性定位）

period: Composed c. 8 CE (Latin; Riley translation 1851)

source.archive: Project Gutenberg eBook 21765 (H. T. Riley, trans.)
source.work: Ovid, Metamorphoses, Book IV (Fable VI)

summary.en: The priest of Bacchus calls the women of Orchomenus to the festival, and three of them — the daughters of Minyas — stay at their looms. As they weave, they tell stories to pass the work; their webs grow green in mid-day, vines spring from the warp, grapes come out of the thread; torches light themselves; and beasts of the festival howl in the dark. The sisters hide in the smoky house, and out of the dark comes the change: a membrane over their small limbs, light wings instead of feathers, a voice grown thin and squeaking. They are bats — house-lovers, haters of the light, and from the late evening they take their name.
summary.zh: 俄爾科墨努斯祭司召婦女赴酒神慶典，彌尼亞斯之三女執意織布。織機上忽然生藤，經緯化作葡萄、綠藤；火把自燃，獸影在黑暗中嚎叫。三女躲入煙屋，肢體生出薄翼、聲音細如蟋蟀——化為蝙蝠：夜行、畏光，其名即源自「晚暮」。

sensitivity.note: Ancient literary source; no living community restrictions.

passages.text: There was now an end of their stories; and still do the daughters of Minyas go on with their work, and despise the God, and desecrate his festival. When, on a sudden, tambourines unseen resound with their jarring noise; the pipe, too, with the crooked horn, and the tinkling brass re-echo; myrrh and saffron shed their fragrant odors; and, a thing past all belief, their webs begin to grow green, and the cloth hanging in the loom to put forth foliage like ivy. Part changes into vines, and what were threads before are now turned into vine shoots; vine branches spring from the warp, and the purple lends its splendour to the tinted grapes.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ovid, Metamorphoses IV, Fable VI (Riley 1851); not verbatim.

passages.text: And now the day was past, and the time came on which you could neither call darkness nor light, but yet the very commencement of the dubious night along with the light. The house seemed suddenly to shake, and unctuous torches to burn, and the building to shine with glowing fires, and the fictitious phantoms of savage wild beasts to howl. Presently the sisters are hiding themselves throughout the smoking house, and in different places are avoiding the fires and the light.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ovid, Metamorphoses IV, Fable VI (Riley 1851); not verbatim.

passages.text: While they are seeking a hiding-place, a membrane is stretched over their small limbs, and covers their arms with light wings; nor does the darkness suffer them to know by what means they have lost their former shape. No feathers bear them up; yet they support themselves on pellucid wings; and, endeavouring to speak, they utter a voice very diminutive even in proportion to their bodies, and express their low complaints with a squeaking sound. They frequent houses, not woods; and, abhorring the light, they fly abroad by night. And from the late evening do they derive their name.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ovid, Metamorphoses IV, Fable VI (Riley 1851); not verbatim.

title.en: Medea's Cauldron: Aeson's Second Youth
title.zh: 美狄亞之釜：埃宋重返青春

region.en: Iolcus, Thessaly (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 色薩利伊奧爾科斯（象徵性定位）

period: Composed c. 8 CE (Latin; Riley translation 1851)

source.archive: Project Gutenberg eBook 21765 (H. T. Riley, trans.)
source.work: Ovid, Metamorphoses, Book VII (Fable II)

summary.en: Medea, come back to Thessaly with the fleece, begs a favour of the god of her arts: to renew her father-in-law Æson, old and nearly spent. She calls to the herbs of the world — the grasses of Ossa, of Olympus, of Pindus, of Pelion — and makes a fire under a cauldron of bronze, fills it with water and the roots she has gathered, and stirs with a dry branch of a successful olive-tree. Into the pot she throws the blood of one sacrificed old ram, the entrails of a wolf that had preyed on men, the hoof of a lion, the marrow of a stag, the shell of a tortoise, and the liver of a long-lived crow. Æson sleeps in the brew; the witch recites the charm; and he wakes twenty years younger — the daughters of Pelias, seeing the trick, set upon their own father with the same drugs, and kill him for nothing.
summary.zh: 美狄亞攜羊毛返色薩利，求其術神助她使衰老的公公埃宋重返青春：她自奧薩山、奧林波斯、皮同、珀利翁取來各種仙草，以銅釜燉水，加公羊血、食人狼之腸、獅蹄、鹿髓、龜殼、長壽烏鴉之肝，以橄欖枝攪拌；老人浴於湯中睡去，醒來年輕二十歲。佩利亞斯之女見狀，以為同法可使父返老還童，竟親手剁父煮之——卻只換得一場空。

sensitivity.note: Ancient literary source; violence presented as historical material without endorsement.

passages.text: Medea, come home from Colchis with the fleece and the ship, stood before her father-in-law's aged face and begged the gods of her art for a thing harder than any she had yet performed: the renewal of Æson's youth. To do it, she flew first to the herbs of the world, gathering on Ossa, on Olympus, on Pindus, and on Pelion the grasses her chariot drew out by the roots, testing some with the blade, some with her nails, and some with the sinews of the earth.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ovid, Metamorphoses VII, Fable II (Riley 1851); not verbatim.

passages.text: Then she built an altar of turf, two in the north, two in the south, one of the east, and one of the west, and called the god of her arts; and under the clear sky she dug a trench, and put into it the blood of one sacrificed old ram, and covered it over with warm ashes and the entrails of a wolf that had preyed on men, and the hoof of a lion, and the shell of a tortoise, and the marrow of a stag, and the liver of a long-lived crow.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ovid, Metamorphoses VII, Fable II (Riley 1851); not verbatim.

passages.text: She filled a cauldron of bronze with water, threw in the herbs she had gathered, and stirred it with a dry branch of a successful olive-tree, all the while reciting words that the poet does not repeat aloud. Then she placed the aged Æson in the brew and let him sleep; and he woke, not only rid of old age, but a young man of twenty — twenty years fewer than the day before, and as straight as a poplar.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ovid, Metamorphoses VII, Fable II (Riley 1851); not verbatim.

passages.text: And the daughters of Pelias, seeing the miracle, promised their father — by the same witch, under the same promises — that he would be made young again. So they set upon the old man with the knife, and cut him up, and boiled him: and the pot's contents boiled the man, and nothing came out of it but the ordinary steam. Medea's kin, for whom she had done all the things she had done, were undone; and Jason's own house, for all its triumph, turned, in one night, into the house of a father cooked by his daughters.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ovid, Metamorphoses VII, Fable II (Riley 1851); not verbatim.

title.en: Coresus and Callirhoe: The Oracle of Dodona
title.zh: 科勒索斯與卡利羅厄：多多納神諭

region.en: Calydon & Dodona (symbolic pins)
region.zh: 卡呂冬與多多納（象徵性定位）

period: Written c. 2nd century CE (Shilleto/Bohn translation; G. B. 68680)

source.archive: Project Gutenberg eBook 68680 (A. R. Shilleto, trans.)
source.work: Pausanias, Description of Greece VII.21

summary.en: Coresus, priest of Dionysus at Calydon, loved the maiden Callirhoe and she did not love him; and when all his gifts failed, he went as a suppliant to the statue of the god. Dionysus heard his priest's prayer, and the whole city became insane, as with drink, and died beside themselves. In terror, the Calydonians sent to the oracle of Dodona — the oak and the doves of Epirus — and were told that the wrath of Dionysus would not end till Coresus either sacrificed Callirhoe or some man who should volunteer to die in her place. At the altar Coresus turned the knife on himself instead of the girl; and Callirhoe, seeing him lying dead, repented, and cut her own throat at the well that has ever since been called Callirhoe.
summary.zh: 卡呂冬酒神祭司科勒索斯愛上少女卡利羅厄而遭拒；他向神像哀告，酒神遂使全城瘋狂如醉而亡。市民懼而遣使至多多納問卜——以橡樹與鴿子為靈之神諭——得知：除非科勒索斯獻祭卡利羅厄或自願代死，否則災疫不止。祭壇之上，科勒索斯反將利刃向己；卡利羅厄見其慘死，悔恨交加，自刎於井邊——該井從此以她為名。

sensitivity.note: Ancient literary source; no living community restrictions.

passages.text: In this part of the city there is also a temple to Dionysus under the title of Calydonian: because the statue of the god was brought from Calydon. And when Calydon was still inhabited, among other Calydonians who were priests to the god was one Coresus, who of all men suffered most grievously from love. He was enamoured of the maiden Callirhoe, but in proportion to the greatness of his love was the dislike of the maiden to him. And as by all his wooing and promises and gifts the maiden's mind was not in the least changed, he went as a suppliant to the statue of Dionysus.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Pausanias, Description of Greece 7.21 (Shilleto); not verbatim.

passages.text: And the god heard the prayer of his priest, and the Calydonians forthwith became insane, as with drink, and died beside themselves. They went therefore in their consternation to consult the oracle at Dodona: for those who dwell on this mainland, as the Aetolians and their neighbours the Acarnanians and Epirotes, believe in the oracular responses they get from doves and the oak there.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Pausanias, Description of Greece 7.21 (Shilleto); not verbatim.

passages.text: And they were oracularly informed at Dodona that it was the wrath of Dionysus that had caused this trouble, which would not end till Coresus either sacrificed to Dionysus Callirhoe, or somebody who should volunteer to die instead of her. And as the maiden found no means of escape, she fled to those who had brought her up, but obtaining no aid from them, she had nothing now left but to die.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Pausanias, Description of Greece 7.21 (Shilleto); not verbatim.

passages.text: But when all the preliminary sacrificial rites that had been ordered at Dodona had taken place, and she was led to the altar as victim, then Coresus took his place as sacrificial priest, and, yielding to love and not to anger, slew himself instead of her. And when she saw Coresus lying dead, the poor girl repented, and, moved by pity and shame at his fate, cut her own throat at the well in Calydon not far from the harbour, which has ever since been called Callirhoe after her.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Pausanias, Description of Greece 7.21 (Shilleto); not verbatim.

title.en: The Styx: The Oath-Water of the Gods
title.zh: 斯提克斯：諸神之誓水

region.en: The Underworld rivers (mythic geography)
region.zh: 冥府之河（神話地理）

period: Composed c. 700 BCE (Evelyn-White translation 1914)

source.work: Hesiod, Theogony, trans. Hugh G. Evelyn-White (1914), lines ca. 775-806

summary.en: Styx, eldest daughter of Ocean, is honoured above all the other gods' rivers: it is by her water that the immortals swear, and the oath once sworn has an inflexible punishment — the perjurer lies breathless for a year without ambrosia and nectar, in a swoon like death, and then, for nine years more, is banished from the councils and feasts of the gods. In the tenth year he may come back to the assemblies of Olympus; and Iris, the messenger, is sent to the rock of Styx with a golden jug whenever a god is suspected of lying.
summary.zh: 斯提克斯為俄刻阿諾斯長女，其水被諸神尊為立誓之媒：誓言一經違背，罰則不可更易——偽誓者躺臥一年不飲仙食、如昏死狀；再逐出神之議事與宴會九年；至第十年方能重返奧林波斯聚會。凡神涉偽誓，宙斯即遣伊里斯攜金瓶取斯提克斯之水。

sensitivity.note: Ancient literary source; no living community restrictions.

passages.text: And there dwells the goddess loathed by the deathless gods, terrible Styx, eldest daughter of back-flowing Ocean. She lives apart from the gods in her glorious house, vaulted over with great rocks and propped on silver pillars that reach to heaven.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Theogony, lines ca. 775-780 (Evelyn-White 1914); not verbatim.

passages.text: Iris, the swift-footed messenger of the gods, seldom comes to her with a message over the sea's wide back; and when strife and quarrel arise among the deathless gods, or when any of them lies, then Zeus sends Iris to bring a golden jug from the far rock: the great oath of the gods, the cold water that pours from the rock beneath the broad path of the earth.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Theogony, lines ca. 780-785 (Evelyn-White 1914); not verbatim.

passages.text: And the water runs under the earth, along the branch of Ocean — one part is given to Styx, and nine parts flow over the earth and the sea in silver eddies; and the part that falls from the rock is a great misery to the gods. So the tenth part is the oath-water, and the ninth are the waters of the world.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Theogony, lines ca. 785-795 (Evelyn-White 1914); not verbatim.

passages.text: And whoever of the deathless gods, that have their homes on Olympus, swears a false oath and pours out the water, lies breathless for a year — no ambrosia passes his lips, no nectar; he lies speechless on a bed, wrapt in a deep swoon, and the punishment is a coma that lasts a whole year. And when the year is ended, a worse punishment follows: for nine years he is cut off from the everlasting gods, from their councils and their feasts. In the tenth year he may come again to the assemblies of the deathless gods, who dwell in the house of Olympus; and such is the oath of the great gods, sworn upon the water of Styx.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Theogony, lines ca. 795-806 (Evelyn-White 1914); not verbatim.

title.en: Ask and Embla: The Variant Traditions of the First Humans
title.zh: 阿斯克與恩布拉：最初人類的異文傳統

region.en: The sea-shore of Midgard (symbolic pin at Pingvellir, Iceland)
region.zh: 米德加爾特海岸（象徵性定位於冰島辛格韋德利）

period: Voluspa c. 900-1000 CE; Gylfaginning c. 1220-1230; Lokasenna and skaldic parallels

source.work: Voluspa st. 17-18; Snorri, Gylfaginning ch. 9; Lokasenna st. 25-26; critical ed. Dronke (1997)

license: Public domain (Bellows 1923; Brodeur 1916); passages below are labeled paraphrases

summary.en: The first-humans motif collected across its witnesses: Voluspa's shore-walk (three gods, two trees, three gifts: breath, mind, colour), Snorri's systematization (Odin, Vili, Ve; life, wit, and speech-senses), Lokasenna's stray notices (the gods' shore-walk as a stock tale quoted in the flyting), and the name-lore (askr, ash; embla, elm or vine, on the disputed reading). The record is the motif's variant-file: what changes between tellings is the giver-list and the gift-list; what holds is the material (trees), the shore-setting and the threefold gift.
summary.zh: 最初人類母題的異文集：女先知的海灘巡行（三神、二木、三賜：氣息、心智、血色）、斯諾里的體系化（奧丁、維利、偉：生命、心智與言語感官）、《洛基的吵罵》中的零散引述（飛行中引用的「諸神海灘造人」套語），以及名物學（askr 梣木；embla 榆木或藤，讀法有爭議）。此記錄是該母題的異文檔案：各文本之間變動的是賜予者名單與恩賜清單，不變的是材質（樹木）、海岸場景與三分之賜。

canonical_translation: Henry A. Bellows, The Poetic Edda, New York 1923 (public domain); Gylfaginning via Brodeur 1916

narrative.en:
This collection-node holds the first-humans motif's witnesses side by side. Voluspa's version (the record norse-ask-embla holds the full doctrine): three gods walk the shore, find two trees 'without fate', and give the three gifts - Odin's breath (ond), Hoenir's mind (odr), Lodurr's warmth and colour (la and litr godr). Snorri's Gylfaginning renames the givers as Odin, Vili and Ve and re-divides the gifts (life and spirit; wit and feeling; countenance, speech, hearing, sight, and clothing) - the doctrine stable, the inventory fluid. Lokasenna's stray verse is the motif's oldest quotation-outside-the-poem: Loki taunting Njord with the shore-walk formula ('the? - 'gods? - 'who? - 'made? - man? - from? - the? - trees? - 'the? - flyting's stock-phrase) evidences that the shore-walk was a known tale before the Codex Regius.

The name-lore is the record's second register: askr is transparently 'ash', the tree-family the sagas use for kin-lines ('the? - 'family-tree? - idiom's? - mythic? - root); embla is disputed - 'elm' (the older dictionaries' reading) or 'vine' (the comparative-linguists' case, from the Indo-European *sbhloi? - the vine-word family), which would make the first couple a tree-and-vine pair, the wood-culture's own founding-materials. And the gift-grammar's comparative frame completes the file: the Greek clay-and-fire doctrine (Prometheus molding earth, Athena lending soul) and the Genesis dust-and-breath doctrine are the motif's nearest kin - the Norse version distinctive in the tripartite gift (breath, mind, colour) rather than a single ensouling.

The record's cultural functions are the variant-doctrine method (collecting the witnesses to show which elements are load-bearing: material, shore, threefold gift) and the name-ethnogenesis doctrine ('men? - 'are? - 'of? - Ask? - 'and? - Embla? - - the species named for its founders, as tribes are named for ancestors). In the atlas, the record anchors the variant-collection family: each a motif's witness-file; the Norse one is distinctive in the fluid giver-lists.

For the database, this node complements the doctrine-record (norse-ask-embla): there the motif told; here its witnesses laid side by side.

The record's gift-grammar completes the file: the three gifts' semantics debated (breath, mind and colour; or life, wit and speech) - the tripartite self's doctrine documented across the variant-lists, the human person as three loans. And the shore-setting's liminality completes it: the creation performed on the beach (the boundary between the sea-chaos and the land-order) - the first humans made on the world's threshold, the motif's geography as theology. The record's reception-note completes the file: the motif's medieval European echoes (the tree-birth tales of the conversion-era legends, the Ash-and-Elm pairing recalled in later origin-poems) - the variant-file's afterlife documented beyond the Edda-tradition, the first humans' wood-birth persisting in the North's imagination.

functions: Variant-collection node: the first-humans motif's witnesses compared
Load-bearing elements: tree-material, shore-setting, tripartite gift
Name-lore register: askr (ash) and the disputed embla (elm or vine)
Comparative frame: the Greek clay-and-fire and Genesis dust-and-breath kin

The first-humans motif collected across its witnesses: Voluspa's shore-walk (three gods, two trees, three gifts: breath, mind, colour), Snorri's systematization (Odin, Vili, Ve; life, wit, and speech-senses), Lokasenna's stray notices (the gods' shore-walk as a stock tale quoted in the flyting), and the name-lore (askr, ash; embla, elm or vine, on the disputed reading).

title.en: Aurgelmir's Line: The Primordial Giant Genealogies
title.zh: 奧爾蓋爾米爾之族：太古巨人的世系

region.en: Jotunheimr's deeps (symbolic pin at Jotunheimen, Norway)
region.zh: 約頓海姆深處（象徵性定位於挪威尤通黑門山）

period: Vafthrudnismal st. 28-35 c. 900-1000 CE; Snorri's genealogies c. 1220-1230; skaldic giant-genealogy verses

source.work: Vafthrudnismal st. 28-35; Snorri, Gylfaginning chs. 5-7; Skaldskaparmal genealogy-notices; critical ed. Dronke (1997)

license: Public domain (Bellows 1923; Brodeur 1916); passages below are labeled paraphrases

summary.en: The giant-lineages beyond Ymir collected: Aurgelmir (Ymir's name in the wisdom-contest), his odd physiogony (giants sweated from his left armpit; his feet engendered a son together), his descendants (Bergelmir, Thrudgelmir), the named giant-lines (Bolthorn, Bestla, Odin's giant-mother; Gymir and Aurboda, Gerd's parents; Hymir, Hlodi? - and the jotun-name book: Hrungnir, Thjazi, Geirrod, Hymir, Vafthrudnir), and the doctrine the genealogies serve: the giants are the gods' own kin, every god married or descended from a giant. The record is the corpus's giant-genealogy file.
summary.zh: 尤彌爾之外的巨人世系全集：奧爾蓋爾米爾（尤彌爾在智慧競賽中的異名）及其怪異的生理譜系（巨人自其左腋汗液而生，雙腳交合生出一子）、其後代（貝格爾米爾、斯魯德蓋爾米爾）、具名的巨人族系（博爾索恩與貝斯特拉——奧丁的巨人母系；基米爾與奧爾波達——葛德之父母；希米爾等——以及巨人名冊：赫朗格尼爾、夏茲、蓋爾羅德、希米爾、瓦夫特魯德尼爾），以及世系所服務的教義：巨人即諸神自身的親族——每一位神明皆娶巨人為妻或為巨人所生。此記錄是語料的巨人世系檔案。

canonical_translation: Henry A. Bellows, The Poetic Edda, New York 1923 (public domain); Gylfaginning via Brodeur 1916

narrative.en:
The giant-genealogy file holds the corpus's kinship-map of Jotunheim. Aurgelmir's name is the doctrine's hinge: in Vafthrudnismal the exam-giant answers Odin's oldest question with the name Aurgelmir ('the? - 'mud? - 'el? - 'boiler? - 'the? - wet-el? - one? - - the primordial giant under his exam-name, whom the sibyl calls Ymir) - the two names one being, the genealogies' own evidence that the giants' memory ran older than the poems. The physiogony is the record's strangest clause: Aurgelmir's left armpit sweated a son and a daughter? - a man and a maid - and his two feet engendered together a six-headed son (Thrudgelmir) - the giants reproducing without mate, the body itself the lineage's engine; and Thrudgelmir's son is Bergelmir, the flood-remnant (norse-bergelmir-flood holds the ark-doctrine), from whom 'the? - rime-giants? - 'are? - 'come.

The god-giant intermarriage is the genealogy's other half: Odin's mother Bestla is Bolthorn's daughter (the chief-god half giant); Thor's mother is Jord, a giantess (and his foster-mother? - the? - - the strength-god wholly giant-reared); Njord marries Skadi (Thjazi's daughter); Freyr wins Gerd (Gymir's daughter); Bragi marries Idunn? - the? - 'goddess? - list? - and even Loki is a giant's son (Farbauti's) married to a goddess-sworn wife - the record norse-loki-genealogy holds the brood. The name-book completes the file: the named giants of the corpus (Hrungnir, Thjazi, Geirrod, Hymir, Vafthrudnir, Utgard-Loki, Baugi, Suttungr, Gymir, Hrym) - each with a family-place, each encounter a kin-encounter.

The record's cultural functions are the kinship-enmity doctrine (the god-giant war as an ethnic myth inside one family: cousins at war, the corpus's own theory of enmity as kinship) and the genealogy-as-cartography doctrine (the jotun-names mapping the encounters: each hall named, each family placed). And the comparative frame completes it: the Greek Titan-genealogies and the Indo-European *Yemo? - the twin-sacrifice traditions - each a giant-lineage behind a divine order. In the atlas, the record anchors the giant-genealogy family: each a tradition's elder-race file; the Norse one is distinctive in the odd physiogony and the intermarried houses.

For the database, this node complements the creation-record (norse-creation-ymir) and the flood-record (norse-bergelmir-flood): here the lineage runs whole.

The record's name-lore completes the file: the giant-names' meanings (Aurgelmir 'mud-boiler', Farbauti 'dangerous-striker', Bolthorn 'evil-thorn', Hymir 'the? - dark? - one) - the genealogy as a name-dictionary, the elder race's identity carried in its titles. And the intermarriage-chart completes it: the gods' giant-kin tabulated (mothers, wives, fosterers) - the war of gods and giants as a family-feud documented genealogically.

title.en: Ginnungagap in Comparative Context: The Void Before the Worlds
title.zh: 金倫加鴻溝的比較視野：諸界之前的大虛空

region.en: The void between worlds (symbolic pin at Pingvellir, Iceland)
region.zh: 諸界之間的虛空（象徵性定位於冰島辛格韋德利）

period: Gylfaginning c. 1220-1230 (older material); comparative Indo-European and Near-Eastern parallels

source.work: Snorri, Gylfaginning chs. 3-4; comparative: Genesis 1.1-2; Enuma Elis; Rigveda 10.129 (Nasadiya); Apollodorus' Chaos; critical ed. Faulkes (1987)

license: Public domain (Brodeur 1916); passages below are labeled paraphrases

summary.en: The Norse void collected against its parallels: Ginnungagap ('the? - 'yawning? - 'gap? - 'the? - gap that had no bottom on any side) read beside the Hebrew tohu-bohu (the formless waste before light), the Babylonian Apsu-Tiamat (the mingled sweet and salt waters), the Rigveda's Nasadiya hymn ('neither? - being? - 'nor? - non-being? - 'then? - 'there? - was? - neither? - death? - 'nor? - the? - immortal), the Greek Chaos of Hesiod and Apollodorus, and the Chinese Hundun (the uncarved block). The record is the void-motif's comparative file: what the Norse version adds is the elemental polarity (ice and fire meeting in the gap) and the gap's survivor - it persists as the myth-world's border-sea.
summary.zh: 將北歐虛空與其平行文本並置對讀：金倫加鴻溝（「無論哪一側都沒有底的大張之口」）對照希伯來的「空虛混沌」（光前的無形荒野）、巴比倫的阿普蘇與提亞瑪特（甜水與鹹水的混合）、《梨俱吠陀》的「無有頌」（「既非存在亦非存在，無死亦無不死」）、赫西俄德與阿波羅多魯斯的卡俄斯，以及中國的「混沌」（未鑿之混沌）。此記錄是虛空母題的比較檔案：北歐版本的獨特之處在於元素兩極（冰與火於鴻溝中相遇），且鴻溝本身留存為神話世界的邊海。

language: Old Norse / Old Icelandic; comparative material in Hebrew, Akkadian, Sanskrit, Greek, Chinese
canonical_translation: Brodeur 1916 (public domain); comparative passages paraphrased from standard translations

narrative.en:
This comparative node holds the void-motif's witnesses. The Norse doctrine (norse-ginnungagap-void holds the full cosmogony): Ginnungagap is not nothing but a space - 'the? - 'gap? - 'that? - 'had? - no? - floor? - 'and? - no? - sky? - - and its two rims are the cosmos's elements (Niflheim's freezing rivers to the north, Muspell's fire to the south); creation happens in the gap where the elements meet, and the gap itself survives creation as the world's out-border (the record norse-world-serpent-midgard's enclosing sea reads as the gap's residue).

The parallels: Genesis's formless waste ('the? - 'earth? - 'was? - without? - form? - 'and? - void? - and? - darkness? - on? - the? - face? - of? - the? - deep? - - the deep as space, the spirit moving on the waters); the Enuma Elis's mingled waters (Apsu the sweet abyss, Tiamat the salt sea, their mingling begetting the gods - the polarity-doctrine in water-form); the Rigveda's Nasadiya hymn ('then? - 'there? - was? - neither? - being? - nor? - non-being? - 'no? - air? - 'no? - sky? - 'what? - stirred? - and? - where? - 'the? - one? - who? - looks? - down? - on? - it? - does? - not? - know? - - the void as an acknowledged question); Hesiod's Chaos ('first? - of? - all? - was? - the? - yawning? - chasm? - - the Greek void's own gaping-word, cognate-adjacent to the Norse gap); and the Chinese Hundun (the uncarved wholeness whose drilling kills it - the void as a living faceless thing).

The record's cultural functions are the comparative-motif doctrine (the void as a near-universal creation-motif with local inflections: space, water, question, chasm, block) and the polarity-doctrine (the Norse version's signature: the void is not neutral but polarized - the elements' meeting is the world's conception, creation as chemical event rather than command). And the gap's survival completes the motif-file: unlike most parallels' voids (which are replaced by the created order), Ginnungagap persists as the margin - the myth-world's border-sea where the serpent lies. In the atlas, the record anchors the void-motif family: each a tradition's pre-creation space; the Norse one is distinctive in polarity and persistence.

For the database, this node complements the creation-records (the void-doctrine; the giant-genealogies): here the motif's wider kin laid out.

The record's comparative-method completes the file: the void-motif's witnesses read as a typology (space, water, question, chasm, block) rather than as borrowings - each tradition's pre-creation space analyzed by its own inflection, the comparative file's method documented as database-practice. And the gap's cartographic persistence completes it: the border-sea where the serpent lies, the gap in the map's margin - the void surviving as geography.

Survival doctrine: the gap persisting as the world's border-sea
Creation-as-event: chemical conception rather than command

title.en: Svartalfaheimr and the Dwarf-Lore: The Two Dark Peoples
title.zh: 斯瓦特阿爾夫海姆與矮人學：兩支幽暗之族

region.en: The halls under rock and earth (symbolic pin at Falun, Sweden)
region.zh: 岩土之下的廳堂（象徵性定位於瑞典法倫）

period: Gylfaginning c. 1220-1230; Grimnismal st. 4? - Hervarar saga's dwarf-dialogues; sagas' dwarf-encounters

source.work: Snorri, Gylfaginning chs. 14, 17; Hervarar saga (the dwarfs' forge-dialogues); Volsunga saga (Andvari); critical ed. Faulkes (1987)

license: Public domain (Brodeur 1916; Kershaw 1921); passages below are labeled paraphrases

summary.en: The dark-peoples file collected: Snorri's two orders (the dark-elves below the earth, blacker than pitch; the dwarfs in Svartalfaheimr, the smith-race born of Ymir's maggots), the confusion-of-terms (svartalfar and dvergar overlapping in the sources), the dwarf-portraits (Andvari the pike-fisher, Dvalin and Durin the forced smiths, the dwarf-dialogues of Hervarar saga where Tyrfing is forged under duress), and the crafts-doctrine (the dwarfs make the gods' signature objects: Mjollnir, Draupnir, Skidbladnir, Gleipnir, the ship's? - the ring's? - the treasure-economy of the under-earth). The record is the subterranean peoples' file.
summary.zh: 幽暗之族的檔案：斯諾里筆下的兩個階序（居於地下的暗精靈，比柏油更黑；居於斯瓦特阿爾夫海姆的矮人——自尤彌爾蛆蟲所生的鍛造之族）、名稱的混淆（文獻中 svartalfar 與 dvergar 相互重疊）、矮人肖像（梭形垂釣的安德瓦利、被迫鍛劍的德瓦林與都林、《赫爾沃薩迦》中脅迫之下的鍛造對話），以及工藝教義（矮人鍛造諸神的標誌之物：妙爾尼爾、德羅普尼爾、斯基德布拉德尼爾、格雷普尼爾……地下世界的寶物經濟）。此記錄是地下民族之檔案。

canonical_translation: Brodeur 1916 (public domain); Hervarar saga via Kershaw 1921 (public domain)

narrative.en:
The dark-peoples file holds the under-earth's two orders and their confusion. The two-people doctrine (norse-alfheim-elves holds the light-elves' side): Snorri's dark-elves dwell below the earth, 'blacker? - 'than? - 'pitch? - 'and? - 'unlike? - the? - light-elves? - 'in? - deeds? - and? - looks; the dwarfs dwell in Svartalfaheimr ('the? - 'world? - 'of? - the? - 'black? - elves? - - Snorri's own name collapses the distinction: the dwarf-world is the dark-elf-world, and the sources use svartalfar and dvergar interchangeably) - the taxonomy's blur is the record's first datum: the two orders are one economy seen from above and below.

The dwarf-portraits: Andvari (the dwarf fishing in pike-shape, robbed of his hoard and laying the ring-curse - the record norse-andvari-ring-curse), Dvalin and Durin (the forced smiths of Tyrfing - the record norse-tyrfing-curse), the Dvergatal's catalog (norse-dvergatal-dwarfs holds the name-book), and the Hervarar-dialogues (the dwarfs speaking from the stone at dusk, forging under duress - the corpus's smith-dialogues where the underworld bargains by force). The crafts-doctrine: the dwarfs make the gods' signature objects - Mjollnir, Draupnir, Skidbladnir, Gungnir, Gleipnir, Brisingamen, the ship's? - the treasures-file (the record norse-mjolnir-forging holds the forge-competition) - so the under-earth is the gods' supply-chain: the dwarfs make, the gods circulate (Clunies Ross's exchange-economy).

The record's cultural functions are the under-earth-economy doctrine (smithcraft as the subterranean order's office, the treasures' provenance as a dwarf-claim) and the taxonomy-blur doctrine (the sources' own confusion documented as a datum: dark-elves and dwarfs as one seen from above). And the folk-afterlife completes it: the sagas' and ballads' dwarf-encounters (the mountain-king's daughter, the troll-women? - the? - later? - - the under-earth folk's persistence in post-conversion folklore). In the atlas, the record anchors the under-earth-people family: each a tradition's subterranean smith-folk; the Norse one is distinctive in the maggot-birth and the duress-dialogues.

For the database, this node complements the elf-record, the dwarf-catalog and the forge-records: here the dark-side runs whole.

The record's folk-afterlife completes the file: the under-earth folk's persistence in post-conversion folklore (the mountain-king's halls, the troll-women's brides, the fairy-mounds of the ballads) - the dwarf-economy's survival in the converted landscape's below. And the craft-lineage completes it: the smith-hero tradition (Völundr, the dwarfs' apprentices) as the under-earth's export - the subterranean order's heroes documented above ground. The record's taxonomic-note completes the file: the scholars' debate on svartalfar versus dvergar (one race under two names, or two races confused by Snorri's systematizing) - the dark-peoples' taxonomy as the corpus's own open question, documented here with both readings and the sources' usage-patterns.

title.en: The First Feasts of the Gods: Hospitality as Institution
title.zh: 諸神的最初宴席：作為制度的好客

region.en: Aegir's hall and the halls of Asgard (symbolic pin at Laeso, Denmark)
region.zh: 埃吉爾之廳與阿斯加德諸廳（象徵性定位於丹麥萊瑟島）

period: Skaldskaparmal c. 1220-1230 (older material); Hymiskvida; Lokasenna; Grimnismal's feasts

source.work: Snorri, Skaldskaparmal (the Aegir-feasts; the first feast of the gods); Hymiskvida; Lokasenna; critical ed. Faulkes (1987)

license: Public domain (Brodeur 1916; Bellows 1923); passages below are labeled paraphrases

summary.en: The feast-institution's origin-file collected: the gods' first communal feast (the mythic memory of the golden age's tables), the Aegir-feasts (the sea-giant's hall with the shining gold and self-pouring cups - the first hospitality the gods accept from a convert-giant), the kettle-quest that equips the feast (Hymir's mile-deep cauldron, stolen from the borderlands), and the feast-law (the cup-circles, the memory-toasts, the seat-rights and gift-cycles documented in the Hákon-chapter and the flyting's rules). The record is the divine-hospitality file: how the gods learned to eat together.
summary.zh: 宴席制度的起源檔案：諸神的第一次共食（黃金時代桌席的神話記憶）、埃吉爾宴（海巨人之廳金光閃爍、酒杯自斟——諸神首次接受一位皈依巨人的款待）、為宴席取來的巨釜（希米爾深達一里的鍋，自邊境奪得），以及宴席之法（傳杯之禮、追念之酒、座次之權與贈禮之環——見於哈康篇章與吵罵的規則）。此記錄是神聖好客的檔案：諸神如何學會同桌而食。

canonical_translation: Brodeur 1916 (public domain); Bellows 1923 (public domain)

narrative.en:
The divine-hospitality file holds the feast-institution's origins. The first communal feast: the golden age's tables (Voluspa's gleeful board-games and lack of gold - the record norse-golden-age-gods) are the feast's memory-image; but the institution's equipment is a theft: the gods cannot brew ale for all of them at once until Thor and Tyr fetch Hymir's mile-deep kettle from the borderlands (the record norse-hymir-kettle) - the feast's first hardware is war-booty, the communal feast founded on a raid.

The Aegir-feasts: the sea-giant converted to hospitality - his hall 'of? - 'shining? - 'gold? - 'the? - ale? - self-poured? - in? - the? - cups? - 'the? - - the gods accepting a giant's table (the record norse-lokasenna-flyting holds the feast's flyting); and the feast-law's grammar documented in the sources: the cup-circles by god (Odin for victory, Njord and Freyja for plenty), the memory-toasts (the bragafull), the seat-rights (Loki's blood-oath seat-claim), and the gift-cycles (the feast as the exchange-economy's ritual engine).

The record's cultural functions are the feast-as-institution doctrine (the communal feast as the gods' society's core ritual - what the kettle's absence prevents, the feast's presence produces: alliance, counsel, flyting and gift) and the hospitality-economics doctrine (the feast hosted by converts and enemies: Aegir the giant, the bonders' halls of the Hakon-chapter - the borderlands' hospitality absorbed into Asgard's ritual). And the Edda's own feast-frame completes it: Skaldskaparmal's teaching is staged at Aegir's feast - the textbook itself a banquet-scene, Bragi lecturing the convert-giant over the ale. In the atlas, the record anchors the divine-feast family: each a tradition's gods' banquet as social charter; the Norse one is distinctive in the stolen kettle.

For the database, this node complements the kettle-record, the Aegir-flyting record and the Yule-feast record: here the institution's file runs whole.

The record's banquet-grammar completes the file: the feast's outputs documented (alliance, counsel, flyting, gift, recruitment - the entry-oaths sworn over the cups) - the communal meal as the gods' society's parliament and recruiting-office. And the corpus's own feast-frames complete it: Skaldskaparmal, Lokasenna and the Eiriksmal each staged at a feast - the myth-textbook, the audit and the death-welcome all banquet-scenes, the institution's centrality documented by its frame-ubiquity. The record's Aegir-biography completes the file: the host-giant's own career (the sea-god of the drowned, the gold-hall's shining wealth) - the convert-host's profile documented beside his feast, the hospitality's donor as a bordered being of the deep. And the corpus’s own banquet-census completes it: the feasts named across the sources (the golden-age tables, Hymir’s ale, Aegir’s gold-hall, the Yule-feast at Hladir, Eirik’s welcome in Valhalla) - the institution’s scene-list documented, the gods’ social life measured in meals.

title.en: The Meeting of Fire and Ice: The Elemental Creation-Motif Collected
title.zh: 火與冰的相遇：元素創世母題集

region.en: The elemental rims of the world (symbolic pin at Pingvellir, Iceland)
region.zh: 世界的元素邊界（象徵性定位於冰島辛格韋德利）

period: Gylfaginning c. 1220-1230; Grimnismal; Voluspa; skaldic elemental kennings

source.work: Snorri, Gylfaginning chs. 4-5, 51; Grimnismal; Voluspa; critical ed. Faulkes (1987)

license: Public domain (Brodeur 1916; Bellows 1923); passages below are labeled paraphrases

summary.en: The fire-ice motif collected across the corpus: the creation's polarity (Niflheim's venom-rivers freezing; Muspell's fire-world fenced with flame; the thaw that quickens Ymir), the fire-world's persisting office (Surtr with the flaming sword at the world's rim; the Muspell-riders crossing Bifrost at the end), the ice-side's offices (Hrym's? - the frost-giants' realm; the poison-rivers of the underworld; the Fimbulwinter as the end's ice), and the poem-and-proverb echoes (the skalds' elemental kennings; the lore that the world ends in fire after living in cold). The record is the elemental-file: the two elements as the cosmos's bookends.
summary.zh: 火冰母題的語料全集：創世的兩極（尼福爾海姆的毒河凍結、穆斯貝爾海姆以火牆護衛、解凍催生尤彌爾）、火之國的恆久職能（蘇爾特持烈焰之劍守衛世界邊緣；末日之時穆斯貝爾之子騎越彩虹橋）、冰之國的職能（霜巨人之地、冥府毒河、末日之冰芬布爾之冬），以及詩與諺的迴響（吟遊詩人的元素隱喻；「世界生於嚴寒而終於烈火」的古訓）。此記錄是元素檔案：兩種元素即宇宙的書擋。

canonical_translation: Brodeur 1916 (public domain); Bellows 1923 (public domain)

narrative.en:
The elemental-file holds the fire-ice motif's witnesses. The creation-polarity: Niflheim's eleven venom-rivers freezing into rime at the gap's north rim, Muspell's fire-world fenced with flame at the south, and the thaw quickening Ymir in between (the record norse-ginnungagap-void holds the meeting) - the elements are not abstractions but countries, each with named geography and population (the frost-giants' realm; Muspell's sons, Surtr their captain).

The persisting offices: the fire-side holds the end's office (Surtr with the flaming sword 'at? - 'the? - 'world's? - rim? - 'since? - 'the? - 'beginning? - the record norse-ragnarok-battles holds the final burning; the riders of Muspell crossing Bifrost - the record norse-bifrost-gjallarhorn's scheduled demolition); the ice-side holds the underworld's office (the venom-rivers of Hel's realm - the record norse-hel-realm; the corpse-spring Hvergelmir; the Fimbulwinter as the doom's own ice - the record norse-fimbulwinter-wolves). The motif's proverb-form: the lore summarized as 'the? - 'world? - 'lives? - 'between? - fire? - 'and? - ice? - 'and? - 'ends? - in? - fire? - 'after? - 'ice? - - the elemental bookends doctrine.

The record's cultural functions are the elemental-geography doctrine (the elements as populated countries with named captains - the north's own climate-theology: winter as an inhabitable realm) and the bookend-doctrine (the cosmos bracketed by its two elements: born of their meeting, ended by the fire's return, renewed between them). And the skaldic kennings complete the file: the elemental diction (fire as 'Muspell's? - flame? - 'and? - 'the? - ice? - as? - 'the? - 'venom-rivers? - 'cold) evidencing the motif's poetic currency.
