title.en: Markandeya's Vision of the Dissolution
title.zh: 摩根德耶見劫滅之異象

region.en: Naimisha Forest, hermitage (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 尼彌沙林中仙居（象徵性定位）

period: Mahabharata, Vana Parva (Markandeya-Samasya), composition layers c. 400 BCE-400 CE (Ganguli translation, 1883-96)

source.work: The Mahabharata of Krishna-Dwaipayana Vyasa, trans. K. M. Ganguli (1883-96), Vana Parva, Markandeya's deluge vision (the child on the banyan leaf)

summary.en: In the forest, the aged seer Markandeya - the only being to survive every dissolution - answers Yudhishthira's questions about the end of the world: drought burns the earth, fires consume it, the oceans drink the world dry, and then the Lord sleeps alone on the waters. In the vision's heart, Markandeya sees himself drawn inside the sleeping child's body and finds the whole universe there, intact, with himself living within it.
summary.zh: 林中，經歷一切劫滅而獨存的年邁仙人摩根德耶回答堅戰關於世界終結的提問：大旱焚地、大火毀世、海洋飲盡世界，其後主獨臥於水上。異象核心處，摩根德耶被吸入沉睡孩童之身，竟於其中見完整宇宙，而他自己亦在其中生活。

sensitivity.note: Living tradition (epic recitation, temple discourse). Classified 'myth'.

passages.text: Yudhishthira, grieving and unsettled after years of forest exile, asks the old seer Markandeya to tell him what happens when the age ends. Markandeya, ancient beyond all others, answers that he alone has seen it: he has lived through a thousand dissolutions, and each time only he and the Lord remain. When the age runs out, a twelve-year drought sears the earth; creatures weaken and die; then the seven suns blaze, and fire consumes the three worlds.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Mahabharata, Vana Parva, Markandeya-Samasya sections (Ganguli 1883-96); not verbatim.

passages.text: The world burns like a cauldron's rim in the fire; the mountains tumble; the ocean, swollen, drinks the earth and then is itself swallowed, drawn up into a sky gone dark; darkness covers everything, and in that undivided night the wind alone moves. Then the Lord, Narayana, lies down upon the waters, alone, the sole being in the universes' sleep - the cosmos that was is wound up in him like a bed.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Mahabharata, Vana Parva, Markandeya-Samasya sections (Ganguli 1883-96); not verbatim.

passages.text: In the midst of that expanse Markandeya sees a banyan tree, and on a single leaf a small child, dark and lovely, asleep, sucking its toe. Drawn by an inexplicable tenderness, the sage approaches; the child smiles, opens its mouth, breathes him in - and Markandeya finds himself inside a world: oceans, mountains, cities, kingdoms, his own hermitage, people who know him, a life going on. He wanders this interior universe for years, seeking its edge, until at last the child breathes him out again.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Mahabharata, Vana Parva, Markandeya-Samasya sections (Ganguli 1883-96); not verbatim.

passages.text: Waking outside, the sage understands: the child is the Lord of all; the world is held inside him as a dream in a sleeper, creation his breathing out and dissolution his breathing in. The child smiles, identifies himself as the beginning, middle and end of all, and departs into the waters. Markandeya returns to the Pandavas with the certainty that only Vishnu stands when all else falls, and that the world's catastrophes are the motions of his sleep.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Mahabharata, Vana Parva, Markandeya-Samasya sections (Ganguli 1883-96); not verbatim.

canonical_translation: Kisari Mohan Ganguli, The Mahabharata of Krishna-Dwaipayana Vyasa, 1883-96 (public domain); modern: J. A. B. van Buitenen, The Mahabharata, vol. 3 (Vana Parva, incomplete), University of Chicago Press, 1975

narrative.en:
The Markandeya-Samasya section of the Vana Parva is the Mahabharata's principal eschatology: during the Pandavas' forest exile, the brothers come to the hermitage of the impossibly old seer Markandeya, and Yudhishthira - still reeling from his losses - asks the questions a bereaved king asks a survivor of everything: how does the world end, what remains, who rules after?

Markandeya's credentials frame the answer: he alone has lived through prior dissolutions, the sole being besides the Lord to remain when each kalpa closes. His account of the end is a sequence of un-creations. First, a twelve-year drought scorches the earth, and living things weaken as in a great famine. Then the seven suns rise and blaze; fire seizes the three worlds, and the world burns 'like the rim of a cauldron' - mountains topple, the sky itself smokes. The ocean, swollen with the melting world, first drinks the earth, then is swallowed in turn, drawn up as vapor into a sky gone dark. Nothing differentiates; darkness is undivided; only the wind still moves in the void. And in that night, the Lord - Narayana-Vishnu - lies down alone on the waters: the cosmos that was is wound up in him 'like a bed being rolled away', and he sleeps, the single being in the universes' rest.

The vision at the center is the epic's most famous image of interiority. In the featureless waters Markandeya sees a banyan tree; on one of its leaves, a small child - dark, lovely, asleep, sucking its toe. The old sage approaches with inexplicable tenderness, and the child smiles and opens its mouth. Markandeya is breathed in - and finds himself inside a complete world: seas and mountains, cities and rivers, his own hermitage, people who greet him by name, a whole life going on. He wanders this interior universe for what feels like years, searching for its edge, unable to find it; the inhabitants know nothing of being inside anyone. At last the child exhales, and the sage stands again on the leaf's rim, outside, looking at the sleeper.

The child wakes, smiles, and identifies himself: he is the beginning, the middle, and the end; the worlds are held in him as dreams are held by a sleeper; creation is his breathing out, dissolution his breathing in. (The episode thus fuses the epic's flood-with-Vishnu imagery with an almost Buddhist dream-ontology.) The child then departs into the waters, and Markandeya returns to the Pandavas with his doctrine: only Vishnu stands when everything falls; the catastrophes of worlds are the motions of his sleep; and the wise, knowing this, hold to dharma in the meantime - for the age will end, but the Self who witnesses it will not.

Function: this is the mythological engine of Hindu cyclical time - the same imagery the Vishnu Purana systematizes into kalpas, manvantaras and pralayas - and the epic's consolation for exile and loss: the world's destruction is real but contained; the container sleeps gently. The child-on-the-leaf image becomes the icon of Bhagavata devotion centuries later (Vishnu as the infant on the banyan leaf), and Markandeya becomes the tradition's recurring witness - the one who remembers, because he survives.
narrative.zh: 大森林篇之摩根德耶章為摩訶婆羅多主要末世論：般度五子在林居期間造訪年邁逾古的仙人摩根德耶之居所，堅戰仍為其失所動搖，向這位經歷一切而倖存者提出亡國之君的問題：世界如何終結？終結之後何者存留？摩根德耶的資歷框定答案：唯有他經歷過先前的劫滅，每一劫閉合之時，除主之外唯他獨存。他對終結的描述是一連串『逆創世』：先是十二年大旱灼燒大地，眾生如逢大饑而衰；繼而七日並出，烈火抓住三界，世界『如鍋沿』般燃燒——群山傾倒，天穹自亦冒煙。海因融化的世界而漲，先飲大地，繼而被吞，化為水汽升入昏暗之天。萬象無別，黑暗不分，唯風仍行於虛空。彼夜，主——那羅延-毘濕奴——獨臥於水上：曾為宇宙之物在彼之中『如床被捲起』般收攏，彼獨眠，為諸宇宙之息中唯一存者。中央的異象是史詩最著名的內在性意象：在無別之水上，摩根德耶見一株榕樹；一片葉上有一小童——膚色深美，熟睡，吮著腳趾。老仙人懷著無以名狀的慈愛走近；孩童微笑張口。摩根德耶被吸入——竟發現自己身在一個完整的世界：海洋群山、城池河流、他自己的仙居、以名相稱的人們，一整個生活正在進行。他漫遊這內在宇宙數年之久，尋覓其邊界而不可得；居民無人知道自己身處他人之內。最後孩童呼氣，仙人復立於葉緣之外，注視沉睡者。孩童醒來微笑，自陳：彼是始、中、終；諸世界如夢被睡者所持；創世是其呼氣，劫滅是其吸氣。（此幕遂將史詩的毘濕奴洪水意象與近乎佛教的夢之存在論熔於一爐。）孩童沒入水中，摩根德耶攜其教義歸告般度諸子：萬物傾覆之時唯毘濕奴獨立；世界之災乃其睡眠之動；智者知此，於其間持守正法——劫數將至，而見證之自我不滅。功能：此為印度循環時間觀之神話引擎（毘濕奴往世書將同一意象系統化為劫、摩奴期與滅劫），亦是史詩對流放與喪失的慰藉——世界之毀滅真實而受容；容納者溫柔地睡著。『葉上孩童』之像於數世紀後成為奉愛的圖像（毘濕奴為榕葉上的嬰兒），摩根德耶亦成為傳統中反覆現身的見證者——因他倖存，故他記得。

functions: Principal epic eschatology - the sequence of dissolution (pralaya) in narrative form
Icon of cosmic interiority: the universe as the sleeping child's dream
Consolation doctrine for exile and loss (worlds end; the witness does not)
Source matrix for Puranic kalpa/pralaya systematics and Bhagavata devotional imagery

title.en: The Four Ages and the Three Dissolutions (Vishnu Purana)
title.zh: 四期與三滅劫（毘濕奴往世書）

region.en: Gangadvar, Haridwar (symbolic pin at the Ganges' descent to the plain)
region.zh: 恆河出山口赫里德瓦爾（象徵性定位）

period: Vishnu Purana, c. 300-800 CE (Wilson translation, 1840)

source.work: The Vishnu Purana: A System of Hindu Mythology and Tradition, trans. H. H. Wilson (1840), Book I, chs. 3-6

summary.en: The Purana turns cosmic vision into arithmetic: the four ages (Krita, Treta, Dvapara, Kali) tick down like a clock losing its feet; each kalpa of a thousand ages is Brahma's day, each night a dissolution; and when Brahma's own life ends, the elements themselves dissolve into the Lord. Three kinds of pralaya are distinguished - and only the third is final, and only for a single soul.
summary.zh: 往世書將宇宙異象化為算術：四期（圓滿、三分、二分、爭鬥）如失足之鐘般倒數；千期為梵天一日，一夜即一滅劫；梵天自身壽盡時，諸元素亦溶解於主。滅劫分三種——唯第三種是終極，且僅對單一靈魂而言。

sensitivity.note: Living tradition (recited in temple discourse and scholarly study). Classified 'myth' (Puranic cosmological narrative).

passages.text: The ages are four: the Krita (perfect), the Treta, the Dvapara and the Kali. In the first, dharma stands on all four of its feet and men live long, equal and joyful; in each following age, dharma loses one foot, men's stature and years diminish, and virtue decays by quarters. The ages have dawns and twilights as well as middles, and the whole four, measured in divine years, amount to twelve thousand.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Vishnu Purana, Book 1, ch. 3 (Wilson 1840); not verbatim.

passages.text: A thousand of such four-age cycles is a day of Brahma, and his night is of equal length. At day's end, when the night of Brahma falls, creation is dissolved: the three worlds, consumed, are withdrawn into the waters, and the Lord abides upon the serpent's coil, holding the seed of the world as fire holds its heat and the seed its sprout - dormant, but not destroyed.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Vishnu Purana, Book 1, ch. 3 (Wilson 1840); not verbatim.

passages.text: Three dissolutions are taught. The occasional (naimittika) is the night of Brahma: creatures and worlds are withdrawn, and arise again at dawn. The elemental (prakritika) comes when Brahma's own life runs out: earth dissolves into water, water into fire, fire into air, air into ether, until only the Lord and primitive matter remain. The absolute (atyantika) is individual: the liberation of a soul, which ends for it all future dissolution. After Brahma's death the next Brahma wakes, and the wheel turns again.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Vishnu Purana, Book 1, chs. 3, 6 (Wilson 1840); not verbatim.

canonical_translation: Horace Hayman Wilson, The Vishnu Purana: A System of Hindu Mythology and Tradition, London, 1840 (public domain); modern survey: Ludo Rocher, The Puranas, Wiesbaden, 1986

narrative.en:
The Vishnu Purana's opening books convert the epic's apocalyptic visions (Markandeya's, Krishna's at Kurukshetra) into a complete cosmological timetable - the architecture of Hindu time that everything from temple festivals to astrological almanacs assumes.

The ages: time is a four-beat cycle. In the Krita (or Satya) age, dharma stands on all four feet; human beings live for centuries, equal in fortune and virtue, and no one needs to labor for truth - it is simply present. In the Treta, one foot is lost; in the Dvapara, two; in the Kali, dharma stands on one foot alone, and the age's signature is mixture - kingship by wealth, holiness by costume, truth bought and sold, bodies shorter and lives briefer. The ages run on a declining staircase, each shorter than the last, with dawns and twilights (sandhyas) at their edges; the four together, counted in divine years, make twelve thousand divine years - and a divine year is three hundred and sixty mortal ones. We live, says the Purana, deep in the Kali.

The calendar of worlds: a thousand of these four-age cycles is one day of Brahma, a kalpa; Brahma's night is equal. At each nightfall comes the first dissolution - the occasional or naimittika: the three worlds are consumed and withdrawn into the waters, and Brahma-Vishnu sleeps on the coils of the world-serpent Shesha, holding the world-seed 'as fire holds its heat, as the seed holds the sprout' - dormant, not dead. At dawn the creation resumes exactly where the timetable left off; the accumulated past is not erased but archived in the sleeper.

The second dissolution - elemental or prakritika - is vaster: when Brahma's own life completes its hundred years (each of his years a thousand kalpas), not only creatures but the elements themselves are rolled up: earth dissolves into water, water into fire, fire into air, air into ether, ether into its unmanifest source, until nothing remains but the Lord and primal matter (prakriti) in their embrace. Then - there is no dramatic 'then'; the Purana is content with the wheel - a new Brahma wakes and the kalpas begin again. The third dissolution is not cosmic at all: the atyantika ('absolute') dissolution is the individual soul's liberation - the one exit from the wheel, available to any being at any time, which ends for that soul all future endings.

Function: this arithmetic did three things to the tradition. It made every temple festival a punctual event on a cosmic clock (the almanacs locate us in the 28th four-age cycle of the 7th manvantara of Brahma's 51st year); it turned moral decline into a cosmology - the Kali age's corruption is built into the structure of time, so history has a direction without a final end; and it gave the renouncer a third option no apocalypse offers: to exit time entirely rather than wait for its renewal. Compared with Ragnarok or Revelation, the Hindu pralaya is neither final nor tragic - it is a breath held between syllables of an endless recitation.
narrative.zh: 毘濕奴往世書開篇將史詩的末世異象（摩根德耶、克里希那於俱盧之野）轉化為完整的宇宙時間表——從寺廟節慶到占星曆書所預設的印度時間架構。諸期：時間為四拍循環。圓滿期（Krita/Satya），正法四足而立；人壽數百年，福報德行均等，真理不假外求。三分期失一足；二分期失二足；至爭鬥期（Kali），正法僅餘一足，其時代的印記是混雜——以財富立王權、以服飾立聖潔、真理可買賣，身短壽促。諸期沿下行階梯遞短，邊緣有晨昏（sandhyas）；四期合計以神年計一萬二千神年——一神年為三百六十人年。往世書言：吾人現處爭鬥期之深處。世界曆法：一千個四期循環為梵天之一日（一劫 kalpa）；梵天之夜等長。每次夜臨便是第一種滅劫——間滅（naimittika）：三界被消耗並收攝入水，梵天-毘濕奴眠於世界蛇謝沙之盤曲上，持世界之種『如火持其熱、如種持其芽』——蟄伏而非死亡。黎明時創世依時表續行，累積的過去不被抹去，而被封存於睡眠者之中。第二種滅劫——元滅（prakritika）——更為浩大：當梵天自身壽命圓滿其百年（彼之一年等於一千劫），不只眾生，連元素本身亦被捲起：地溶於水、水溶於火、火溶於風、風溶於空，空溶於其不顯之源，直至唯餘主與原初質料（prakriti）相擁。然後——並無戲劇性的『然後』，往世書安於車輪——新梵天醒來，諸劫再始。第三種滅劫全然非宇宙性：終滅（atyantika）乃個體靈魂之解脫——唯一離開車輪的出口，任何時刻任何眾生皆可得，從此終結其一切未來的終結。功能：此算術為傳統做了三件事——使每場廟會成為宇宙時鐘上的準點事件；將道德衰退化為宇宙論——爭鬥期的腐化內建於時間結構，歷史因有方向而無終點；並給予出離者一個任何末日論皆不提供的第三選項：徹底離開時間，而非等待其更新。與諸神黃昏或啟示錄相比，印度滅劫既非終極亦非悲劇——它是無盡誦念的音節之間的一次屏息。

narrative.en:
The shrine's operation-log holds the martyr-king's cult beyond the core-record (norse-olaf-haraldsson-stiklestad). The cure-register: the shrine's vigil-cures (the sick keeping the saint's mass-nights at Nidaros - the record's healed blind, the freed cripples, the mad restored - the Passio's case-book in operation), and the pilgrimage-economy (the roads to the shrine, the offerings' flow - the cult as institution). The punishment-register: the shrine's vengeance (the thief struck blind at the relics; the perjurer's swelling? - 'the? - 'saint's? - 'judgment? - 'on? - 'the? - 'oath-breaker? - - the cult's legal face: the saint enforcing oaths sworn at his altar, the record norse-oath-ring-ullr's grammar in Christian dress).

The rescue-register: the king-at-sea (the drowning clients calling the saint's name - the shrine's patronage extended to the roads and waters), and the battle-standard (the saint's banner carried in the kings' wars - the cult as the state's flag). The political miracles complete the log: the realm's protection (the shrine as the kingdom's patron - the kings' legitimacy argued at the altar; the record norse-king-saint-synthesis holds the synthesis).

The record's cultural functions are the shrine-operation doctrine (the cult documented as a working institution: cures, punishments, rescues, standards - the hagiography as administration) and the oath-enforcement doctrine (the saint as the converted oath-law's guarantor - the pagan oath-ring's successor). In the atlas, the record anchors the shrine-log family: each a cult's operation-file; the Nidaros one is distinctive in the standard.

For the database, this node complements the core-record: here the shrine's daily business.

The log's documentary method completes the file: each cure dated, witnessed and deposed (the shrine's witnesses named, the healers' depositions recorded - the Passio's evidentiary apparatus applied to the shrine's daily business), so the miracle-log is an institution's registry rather than a legend-collection: the cures entered as evidence, the shrine's power audited in writing. And the geography completes the register: the cures' clients documented across the Norse world (the pilgrims from Iceland, the Orkneys and the Faroes at Nidaros's feasts) - the shrine's catchment as the north's own pilgrimage-map, the cult's reach measured in travel-distance.

The log's liturgical frame completes the file: the cures documented at the shrine's feasts (the mass-days and the vigil-nights as the miracles' stage - the cult's calendar driving the registry), so the operation-log's rhythm is the church-year's own: the saint's power celebrated on schedule, the cures clustering where the crowds came. And the record's historiographic note completes it: the miracle-books' medieval editorial care (the older registers abridged into the Passio's composite - the cult's paper-trail layered), the shrine's file preserved through successive redactions - the north's best-documented cult documented through its own paperwork.

narrative.en:
The royal-cult file holds the conversion's royal register. The sanctified kings: the model (St Óláfr's cult - the record norse-olaf-haraldsson-stiklestad; the martyr-king as the north's sanctity-template), the attempts (Óláfr Tryggvason's proposed cult at the mission-memorials; Knut the Saint of Denmark's 12th-century canonization - the Danish martyr-king, the second of the model), and the cults' politics (each sanctity a dynasty's charter: the relics legitimating the line).

The demonized kings complete the register: the sagas' villain-file (the oath-breaking, kin-slaying rulers of the narratives - the anti-saints whose deaths the sources relish: the blind? - the? - maimed? - kings? - 'the? - - the conversion-era's moralization of royal violence: the old heroic deaths re-read as judgments). And the mechanism completes the file: the cult as statecraft (the church's canonization-power and the dynasty's need meeting in the shrine - the corpus's clearest sanctity-economy, the record norse-christian-mythic-syncretism's frame applied to royalty).

The record's cultural functions are the royal-cult doctrine (the king's body as the realm's collateral, now paid in sanctity - the record norse-ynglinga-odin-migration's god-king doctrine's Christian successor) and the moralization-doctrine (the villain-register as the cult's mirror: sanctity defined by its negatives). In the atlas, the record anchors the royal-cult family: each a tradition's sanctified and damned rulers; the Norse one is distinctive in the conversion's speed.

For the database, this node synthesizes the king-records: here the cult-mechanism file.

The register's mechanism-completes the synthesis: the church's canonization-power and the dynasty's need meeting in the shrine (the cult granted for loyalty, the miracles certified by the bishops - the sanctity-economy's exchange documented: legitimacy for obedience), so the royal-cult file documents the north's own saint-making machine. And the villain-register's theology completes it: the demonized kings' deaths narrated as judgments (the maimed and blinded rulers of the converted narratives - the old heroic deaths re-read as providence), the cult's mirror: sanctity defined by its negatives, the conversion's moral vocabulary turning the pagan kings' fates into lessons.

The register's comparative frame completes the file: the royal-cults across the converted world (the Anglo-Saxon saint-kings, the Hungarian and Bohemian martyr-kings - the north's cults joining a European type), so the synthesis documents a genre, not an accident: the martyr-king as the age's standard charter, the Norse cases dated within the type's spread. And the register's irony completes it: the conversion imposed by the very kings later sanctified (the missions' violence absorbed into the cults' charters) - the north's sanctity built on its own conquest, the record's synthesis stated in the sources' own silence.

The legend's Oslo-charter completes the file: the city's cult-institutions documented (the cathedral's shrine, the feast-day's statute, the seal's imagery - the patron-saint's rights written into the town's charters), so the local-saint file documents a city's self-image: Oslo's founding-legend carried on its seal, the martyr's mercy as the town's identity. And the second-sun clause: 'the? - 'daughters? - 'of? - 'the? - sun? - 'riding? - 'their? - mother's? - path? - (the renewal's astronomy: the old sun swallowed, the daughter riding after - the record norse-svalinn-shield's shield-regime restored).

The file's liturgical-echo completes the register: the return-doctrine's resonance in the converted north (the resurrection-tide of the new faith's calendar read against the renewal-stanzas - the mission-preachers' use of the parallel), so the return-file documents a live argument in the conversion-generation: the missionaries' claims met by the natives' own renewal-lore - the record norse-christian-mythic-syncretism's layer dated to the mission-field itself. The eclipse-hypothesis: the sun-swallowing read as eclipse-lore (the wolves Skoll and Hati as the eclipse-creatures of folk-astronomy - the record norse-fimbulwinter-wolves' wolves decoded), and the comet-theories: the sky-fall read as a comet's passage (the stars falling from the heavens - the Völuspá's imagery argued as a remembered visitation).

The 536-CE debate: the Fimbulwinter read as climate-memory ('the? - 'years? - 'without? - summer? - - the late-antique dust-veil's northern famines: the tree-ring evidence of the 540s' failed summers read behind the mythic three winters - the corpus's most-cited naturalization: the doom dated to a real sky). The forest-fire and northern-lights readings complete the file: the Surt-fire argued as the fire-lore of the burned forests (the boreal fires' memory), and the flames on the sky read as the aurora - the mythic fire decoded as the north's own lights.

The record's cultural functions are the naturalization-method doctrine (the myth read as encoded observation: the scholars' decode-register) and the caution-doctrine (the readings' limits: the myth's dramatis personae outdate any single event - the corpus's warning against single-cause naturalization). And the medieval readings complete it: the conversion-era's own astronomical glosses (the learned Icelanders' eclipse-tables and the fate-terminology of the chroniclers) - the doom decoded already in the Middle Ages, the naturalization's first layer documented.

The file's source-horizon completes the register: the naturalization-projects' assumptions documented (the pagan myth treated as observation-log against the myth treated as poetry - the two schools' premises stated), so the record's method-note frames the whole file: the doom decoded only if one first decides what kind of speech it is. narrative.en:
The tree's folk-file holds Yggdrasil's local lives. The sacred groves: the temple-grove's divinity (Adam's clause - the record norse-uppsala-temple: every tree held sacred by the deaths hanging in it), and the groves' law (the tree-sanctuaries of the law-codes: the groves' inviolability - the corpus's grove-clauses).

The guardianship-trees: the farm's own tree (the vörðtrjá - 'the? - 'guard-tree? - 'whose? - 'health? - 'is? - 'the? - family's? - - the household's world-tree documented in the farm-customs: the tree fed, the tree's fall an omen, the family's fate read in the bark - the cosmology domesticated). The healing-tree lore completes the register: the ash's medicine (the bark's remedies, the tree's medical reputation in the farm-lore - the world-tree's species as the pharmacy). And the idiom-register: the family-tree speech ('the? - 'kin? - 'as? - 'branches? - - the micro-cosmology in everyday idiom: the households describing themselves in the tree's grammar).

The record's cultural functions are the tree-domestication doctrine (the world-tree's doctrine scaled to the farm: each household keeping its own Ash) and the idiom-doctrine (the cosmology's everyday speech: the myth's grammar surviving in language). In the atlas, the record anchors the local-tree family: each a tradition's world-tree folk-lives; the Norse one is distinctive in the guardianship-tree.

For the database, this node complements the Yggdrasil-record: here the tree's folk-lives.

The file's legal register completes the tree's folk-lives: the tree-sanctuaries' clauses (the groves' inviolability in the law-codes, the penalties for bark-cutting and branch-breaking - the tree's legal personhood documented), so the world-tree's doctrine scales down to statute: each grove a courthouse of its own, the sacred arbor protected by the same law that protected the thing-steads. And the churchyard-transplant completes the register: the holy trees of the converted parishes (the church-yards' ancient ashes standing beside the new altars) - the world-tree's folk-lives documented surviving conversion, the Ash outliving its own mythology.

The file's comparative-frame completes the register: the guardianship-trees across the north (the Scandinavian and German village-trees: the maypoles' predecessors, the dance-trees of the churchyards) - the Ash's folk-lives documented as a European register, the world-tree's doctrine shading into the maypole's festival. And the Yggdrasil-name's etymology completes it: 'Odin's horse' read as the gallows-tree's title (the tree of the god's own hanging - the record norse-havamal-runes) - the world-tree's name itself a gallows-joke, the cosmology's tree named for its owner's ordeal.

title.en: Macha Curses the Men of Ulster
title.zh: 瑪哈詛咒阿爾斯特男子

region.en: Emain Macha (Navan Fort), Co. Armagh, Northern Ireland
region.zh: 北愛爾蘭阿馬郡埃馬因·瑪哈堡（納萬堡）

period: Noinden Ulad tradition, medieval Irish MSS; Eleanor Hull retelling 1910

source.work: Eleanor Hull, Cuchulain, the Hound of Ulster (1910), Chapter IX, eBook #52963

summary.en: The war-goddess Macha comes to Ulster as a mortal woman to help a man of the province; the Ulstermen mock her in the assembly, and her curse falls on them — at every hour of their greatest need the pains of a mother in childbirth will seize the warriors of Ulster, so that a land of heroes lies helpless, and only the boy Cuchulainn is free.
summary.zh: 戰神瑪哈化身凡女救助阿爾斯特貴族，而該省男子於集會中嘲笑於她；其詛咒隨之降臨——每逢大敵當前，阿爾斯特戰士將如臨盆之母般陣痛無力，英雄之地任敵宰割，唯少年庫丘林免於此詛。

sensitivity.note: The childbirth-curse (ces noinden Ulad) is the Táin's master-motif; in the fuller Noínden Ulad tradition Macha wins a horse-race against the king's teams while in labour, gives birth to twins, and curses — a motif tied to Irish horse-cult lore.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase of Hull 1910: No common sickness lay upon the Province, but it came of the wrath and vengeance of the gods; for in days gone by the goddess Macha, one of the three fierce goddesses of war and battles, had visited Ulster as a mortal maid, to bring aid and comfort to one of the nobles of Ulster who was in sore distress. The king and people reviled her and brought shame and scoffing upon her, because they saw that she was not as one of themselves; they made game of her in the public assembly, crowding round her, scoffing at her courage and splendid form and at her swiftness of running beyond any of the men — for they knew not that she was one of the great gods. Not verbatim.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Hull 1910, ch. IX; not verbatim.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase: Then Macha cursed the men of Ulster and told them that in a time of danger and sore need, when all the chiefs and warriors of Ireland should gather round its borders, plundering and destroying, she would cast upon their warriors weakness and feebleness of body and of mind, so that they could not go forth in defence of the Province, and the land should be a prey to their enemies. Only upon Cuchulainn she laid not her curse, for he was young; and it fell not upon women and little children, but upon full-grown warriors only, because it was the men of Ulster who had insulted her. In dread of her they called the king's palace Emain Macha, the Brooch-pin of Macha, to this day. Not verbatim.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Hull 1910, ch. IX; not verbatim.

canonical_translation: Eleanor Hull, Cuchulain, the Hound of Ulster, London 1910 (public domain); underlying: Noinden Ulad (Ces Ulad), ed. and trans. Whitley Stokes and Kuno Meyer, Revue Celtique XI (1890), public domain

narrative.en:
The Táin Bó Cúailnge is only possible because of a woman the men of Ulster insulted; this tale, the Noínden Ulad or 'the Debility of the Ulstermen', is the fore-tale that switches off a whole heroic race.

Macha — one of the three war-goddesses, with Badb and the Morrígan — came to Ulster in the old days as a mortal maid, to bring aid and comfort to one of the nobles of the province who was in sore distress. Her origin is the otherworld: in the fuller versions she is the wife of Crunnchu, blessed by the sun, and visibly pregnant with twins when the Ulstermen test her. What is certain in every version is the insult: the king and people of Ulster reviled her, because they saw that she was not as one of themselves, and because they liked not that a woman greater than themselves should take up her abode amongst them. They made game of her in the public assembly, crowding round her, scoffing at her courage and her splendid form and at her swiftness of running, which was beyond any of the men. They knew not that she was one of the great gods.

In the classic tradition she is forced to race the king's horses while the pangs of labour are on her — and she wins, throws her twins at the winning-post, and pronounces the curse: at every hour of danger, when all the warriors of Ireland gather round the borders of Ulster plundering and destroying, the men of Ulster shall be seized with the pangs of a woman in her childbed, five days and four nights, or nine nines of hours, and in that weakness the land shall be a prey to its enemies. The men laughed — then the pains took them.

Only three exemptions the goddess allowed: the women, the little children, and Cuchulainn, young enough to stand outside the age-set that had insulted her. In Hull's telling the curse is activated at the hour of Medb's invasion: the warriors of Ulster lie prostrate while Connacht marches, and the province's whole fate passes to a seventeen-year-old with a sling and a spear. The Ulstermen, in dread of her, named the king's palace for her — Emain Macha, the Brooch-pin of Macha — and the great fort of Navan in Armagh bears that name in the landscape to this day.

The tale is the Irish mirror of a universal logic: the men who abused the divine feminine are unmanned at the exact moment they need their manhood. And it is an etiology of labor — the story that teaches that the pain a woman bears in childbed is the same pain a god can lay on an army, and that armies, like mothers, can be made helpless by it.
narrative.zh: 《奪牛記》得以成立，皆因阿爾斯特男子羞辱了一位女神；本篇（Noínden Ulad，「阿爾斯特人之衰弱」）即令整個英雄種族癱瘓之前篇。瑪哈——與巴德布、摩里岡並列的三位戰神之一——昔日化身凡女救助陷入困境的阿爾斯特貴族。完整傳說中她是克倫楚之妻、受太陽祝福，受試時身懷雙胎。各版本共通者為羞辱：王與民譏辱於她，不願勝過己者為女。眾人在集會中群聚嘲弄其勇武、絕色與超越男子的奔跑。古典傳說中，她被迫於陣痛之際與王之馬隊賽跑——她勝了，於終點產下雙胎並宣讀詛咒：大敵當前時，阿爾斯特男子必染產褥之痛五日四夜，全省任敵宰割。女神僅豁免婦女、孩童與庫丘林。據赫爾之述，此詛於梅芙入侵之際生效：戰士盡臥於地，全省之命運落於一名十七歲少年。阿爾斯特人畏之，以她之名命名王宮——埃馬因·瑪哈（瑪哈之胸針）——阿馬郡納萬大堡至今仍帶此名。此故事乃普世邏輯之鏡：虐待神聖女性者，於最需陽剛之時被去勢；亦為產痛之釋義——婦女產褥之痛，神亦可加於軍隊。

title.en: How Cuchulainn Wooed Emer
title.zh: 庫丘林求婚艾默

region.en: Forgall's fort at Lusk (the Gardens of Lugh), Co. Dublin, Ireland
region.zh: 愛爾蘭都柏林郡盧斯克福加爾堡（魯格之花園）

period: Tochmarc Emire tradition, 11th c. MSS; Eleanor Hull retelling 1910

source.work: Eleanor Hull, Cuchulain, the Hound of Ulster (1910), Chapter VIII, eBook #52963

summary.en: Cuchulainn rides south in festal chariot to the Gardens of the Sun-god Lugh and courts Emer in the riddling tongue of the poets — she demands that he first prove himself in deeds — and when the year is out he scythes through her father's guards, carries her off across the Boyne, and makes the White Field the Turf of Blood.
summary.zh: 庫丘林乘節慾戰車南行至太陽神魯格之花園，以詩人隱語向艾默求愛——艾默命其先以武功證己——一年期滿，他衝過其父衛隊，越博因河帶走艾默，白野自此改稱血原。

sensitivity.note: The riddling courtship dialogue (the six gifts of womanhood; the 'shy women' riddle) is one of the most studied scenes of the Ulster cycle; Emer's challenge is the Irish equivalent of a bride-test.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase of Hull 1910: It was on a day of the days of summer that Emer, daughter of Forgall the Wily, sat on a bench before her father's door, at his fort that is called Lusk to-day, but which in olden days men spoke of as the Gardens of the Sun-god Lugh, so sunny and so fair and fertile was that plain. Of all maids in Erin, Emer was the best, for hers were the six gifts of womanhood: the gift of loveliness, the gift of song, the gift of sweet and pleasant speech, the gift of handiwork, the gifts of wisdom and of modesty. Her father had sworn that none beneath a king or ruling prince should marry her, and any man who dared to woo her should never leave the fort alive. Not verbatim.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Hull 1910, ch. VIII; not verbatim.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase: Emer heard the chariot coming like thunder from the north; her sister Fiall described the two steeds like day and night, and the chariot-chief — 'gravely he looks, as though his mind revolved some serious thought, and yet a radiance as of the summer's day enfolds him round.' Emer spoke with him in the mystic ancient tongue of the bards; he claimed his strength — 'I can defend myself alone against twenty; I fear not to fight with forty; under my protection a hundred are secure; hosts fly before my name' — and named his fosterage by Conor and by the god Lugh. Emer teased him about her elder sister, then bade him go away and prove himself for a year by deeds of prowess before she would go with him as his one and only wife — and warned him that her father would try to have him killed. Not verbatim.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Hull 1910, ch. VIII; not verbatim.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase: For a whole year Cuchulainn was away, and Forgall guarded the fort so well that he could not come near Emer; at the year's end he wrote a message to her on a piece of stick, and came in his war-chariot with scythes upon its wheels with a band of hardy men who entered the outer rampart and carried off Emer, striking down men on every side; Forgall followed them to the earthen outworks and fell over the rath and was taken up lifeless. They were pursued to the Boyne; Cuchulainn set Emer in a house of safety, turned and destroyed his pursuers, and the White Field was called the Turf of Blood from that day. Then he and Emer reached their home at Dun Delgan in safety, nor were they henceforth parted until death. Not verbatim.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Hull 1910, ch. VIII; not verbatim.

canonical_translation: Eleanor Hull, Cuchulain, the Hound of Ulster, London 1910 (public domain); underlying: Tochmarc Emire, ed. and trans. Whitley Stokes and Holger Pedersen, 1899 (public domain)

narrative.en:
The wooing of Emer is the Ulster cycle's courtship masterpiece — a bride-test conducted entirely in riddles, in which the poet's language is the weapon and the dowry is proof of valor.

It was on a day of the days of summer that Emer, daughter of Forgall the Wily, sat on a bench before her father's door at his fort called Lusk to-day, but which in olden days men spoke of as the Gardens of the Sun-god Lugh — so sunny and so fair and fertile was that plain, with waving meadow-grass and buttercups and may-blossom girdling the fields. Her father was a man more learned than any druid and more cunning than any man of verse, and he had sworn that no one beneath a king or ruling prince should marry her, and that any man who dared to woo her should never leave the fort alive. Of all the maids of Ireland Emer was the best, for hers were the six gifts of womanhood: loveliness, song, sweet speech, handiwork, wisdom and modesty.

Cuchulainn came south in festal chariot with Laeg before him, and the girls on the rampart watched the thunder of the two horses — one grey like day, one black like night — and the young chariot-chief, 'gravely he looks, as though his mind revolved some serious thought, and yet a radiance as of the summer's day enfolds him round.' Emer knew at once the man of whom all Ulster spoke in whispers: the boy who fought grown warriors, killed the great hound, and was foredoomed to an early death — 'this were a man to win a woman's love.'

The courtship is conducted in the mystic tongue of the poets so that the listeners understand nothing. Emer lists her own excellences — 'I was brought up in noble behaviour as every queen is reared' — and he lists his: fostered by Conor among champions and poets, kin to Lugh the Long-handed, strength to fight alone against twenty and forty, protection to a hundred. She teases him about her elder sister Fiall — 'a younger sister in Ireland may not marry before an elder' — and he answers with the oath of a man in love: not Fiall but thee. Then the bride-test: 'go away and prove yourself for a year by deeds of prowess, and then, if you come again, I will go with you as your one and only wife' — and warning: her father will try to have you killed.

The year passed in the deeds the Táin later remembers — and in the fuller sources it passes in Scáthach's school in Alba, where Cuchulainn learns the gae bolga and wins the friendship of Ferdiad, and where the woman-warrior Aife bears him a son. When the year was out Forgall had locked the fort so well that no speech could pass; Cuchulainn wrote his message to Emer on a stick of wood, and came in the war-chariot with scythes on its wheels and a band of hard men, striking down the guards on every side and carrying her off over the ramparts. Forgall followed to the earthen outworks and fell over the rath and was taken up lifeless. They were pursued to the Boyne; Cuchulainn turned at the house of safety and destroyed the pursuers along the banks, and the White Field was called the Turf of Blood from that day. Then he and Emer reached Dun Delgan in safety, nor were they henceforth parted until death — a marriage that will be tested by fairy women, by queens, and by the whole luck of the cycle.
narrative.zh: 艾默求婚記乃阿爾斯特故事圈之求愛傑作——全程以謎語行聘禮之試，詩人之語言即兵器，嫁妝即武功之證。夏日之一日，狡詐者福加爾之女艾默坐在其父堡門前之長凳——該堡今日稱盧斯克，古時人稱太陽神魯格之花園——草原微波、毛茛金黃、山楂花環野。其父比任何德魯伊更博學、比任何詩人更狡黠，曾立誓：非王侯不得娶其女；凡敢求愛者必不得生離此堡。全愛爾蘭少女中以艾默為最，蓋其具婦女六藝：美、歌、慧言、手工、智、謙。庫丘林乘節慾戰車南來，萊格御於前，牆上少女聞雙馬之雷——一灰如晝、一黑如夜。求婚全以詩人隱語行之，旁人不解。艾默列其美德，他列其技：科恩王所養、魯格長手之親、可獨抗二十、不懼四十。她以其姊菲亞爾戲之——『愛爾蘭幼女不得先於長女嫁』——他以戀人之誓答之：非菲亞爾，是爾。繼而聘禮之試：『去以武功證己一年，再來時，我將為你唯一之妻』——並警告其父將殺你。此年為斯卡哈學校之年：庫丘林習得gae bolga、結識弗迪亞、女戰士艾菲為其生子。年期一滿，庫丘林以木棍書信傳予艾默，乘刃輪戰車率剛勇一隊而至，遍擊衛兵、越牆奪艾默。福加爾追至外土工事、跌落塹壕而死。眾追至博因河；庫丘林回身毀滅追兵，白野自此改稱血原。二人安然抵敦·德爾岡之家，至死不分離。

source.work: A. H. Leahy, Heroic Romances of Ireland, Volume I (1905), 'The Carving of Mac Dathó's Pig', eBook #5678

summary.en: Mac Dathó of Leinster promises his marvelous hound Ailbe to both Ulster and Connacht, so that both armies arrive on the same day; over a seven-year pig fed on the milk of fifty cows, the champions compete for the champion's portion — Ket puts the whole of Ulster to shame until Conall arrives — and the feast ends in a battle in which the house is ruined and the hound chooses his side.
summary.zh: 萊因斯特的麥克·達霍將神犬艾爾貝同時許給阿爾斯特與康諾特，致兩軍同日抵達；宴上以五十牛乳所養巨豬爭『勇士之份』——康特羞辱阿爾斯特全軍，直至科納爾到場——宴終於大戰，客棧被毀，神犬自擇其主。

sensitivity.note: The champion's portion contest is one of the defining institutions of the Ulster cycle; the tale is preserved complete only in the Book of Leinster.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase of Leahy 1905: Mac Datho of Leinster had a hound named Ailbe that guarded the whole of Leinster, and messengers came from both Ailill and Medb of Connacht and from Conor of Ulster asking for it, each offering treasures and cattle and a third of their realm. His wife's counsel ended his fasting misery: 'Of that hound to them both be thou giver, and who dies for it little we care.' He promised it to both provinces and arranged that both armies should arrive on the same day; the house had seven doors and fifty couches between each two doors, and it was no meeting of friends that was then seen in that house. Not verbatim.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Leahy 1905; not verbatim.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase: They slaughtered Mac Dathó's boar, nurtured seven years upon the milk of fifty cows; Bricriu called from above that the only test of division was the champion's portion: 'surely each man of you hath struck the other a buffet on the nose ere now!' Ket son of Maga rose above all the men of Ireland, hung his weapons higher than any, took a knife and stood at the boar: 'Find ye now one man among the men of Ireland who can equal my renown.' He put down Laegaire (pierced through in a border-raid), Angus son of Lama Gabaid (he had cut his father's hand off), Eogan (he had torn out one of his eyes), Munremur (the midmost of three heads he had taken was his firstborn son's), Mend the Sword-heeled (he had made his father's nickname by cutting off his heel), Celtchar (his spear had diseased him in leg and groin), and Cuscrid the Stammerer (whose first trial of arms had cost the third part of his folk and the sinews of his neck) — and the whole province of Ulster sat down before him. Not verbatim.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Leahy 1905; not verbatim.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase: Conall the Victorious entered the hall, and his claim was only this: 'I have seldom slept without the head of a slain man of Connaught as my pillow; and I have not let pass a day or a night in which a man of Connaught hath not fallen by my hand.' 'Thou art a better warrior than I,' said Ket; 'were but Anluan here!' 'Aye, but Anluan is here!' cried Conall, and plucked Anluan's head from his belt and threw it at Ket, so that its blood was dashed over his lips. Ket came away from the boar, and Conall took the tail, a load for nine men, and sucked it all into his mouth; to the men of Connaught he gave only the two fore-legs, and both hosts sprang up — the heap of bodies inside the house rose as high as its side-walls, blood flowed under the doors, Fergus tore up an oak-tree by the roots, and the battle went on outside, where Mac Dathó loosed the hound to see to which side its sense would turn; and the hound joined the men of Ulster, and rushed on the defeated Connachtmen. Not verbatim.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Leahy 1905; not verbatim.

narrative.en:
The pig-tale is the Ulster cycle's comic epic of the champion's portion — a duel of curriculum vitae conducted across a table, ending in architecture ruined by reputation.

Mac Dathó of Leinster kept a hound named Ailbe that guarded the whole of Leinster; messengers came to him from both Ailill and Medb of Connacht and from Conor of Ulster, each offering treasures, cattle, and a third of their realm for the dog. Mac Datho ate nothing and slept not, and his wife's verses solved the impasse: give the hound to them both, 'and who dies for it little we care.' So both armies were promised the same dog on the same day — and the house that received them had seven doors and fifty couches between each pair, for it was no meeting of friends: for three hundred years before the birth of Christ there had been war between Ulster and Connacht.

The feast-piece was Mac Dathó's boar, fed seven years on the milk of fifty cows, an animal so vast and so poisoned with enmity that many of the men of Ireland would die for it. Bricriu, from above, announced the law of the feast: there can be but one test of division, the champion's portion — 'surely each man of you hath struck the other a buffet on the nose ere now!' Then Ket son of Maga of Connacht rose above every man of Ireland, hung his weapons at a greater height than any, and took the knife: 'Find ye now one man among the men of Ireland who can equal my renown.' And he worked the hall like an advocate, undressing Ulster's heroes one by one: Laegaire the Triumphant who fled a border-raid pierced through with a spear; Angus son of Lama Gabaid, whose father's hand Ket had cut off with his own spear; Eogan of Fernmay, whose eye Ket had torn out; Munremur, whose firstborn's head Ket had taken; Mend, whose father's nickname (the Sword-heeled) was Ket's own work; Celtchar, diseased in leg and groin by Ket's spear; Cuscrid the Stammerer, whose first trial of arms had cost the third of his folk and the sinews of his neck. The whole province sat down.

Into that silence walked Conall the Victorious, straight from a raid, and his claim was one sentence: 'I have seldom slept without the head of a slain man of Connaught as my pillow, and I have not let pass a day or a night in which a man of Connaught hath not fallen by my hand.' Ket conceded the point — 'thou art a better warrior than I; were but Anluan here!' — 'Aye, but Anluan is here!' cried Conall, and plucked Anluan's head from his belt and threw it at Ket's chest so that the blood dashed over his lips. Conall took the boar's tail — a load for nine men — and sucked it into his mouth, and to Connacht he gave only the two fore-legs; and the hall exploded. The heap of bodies inside the house rose as high as its side-walls; blood flowed under the doors strong enough to drive a mill; Fergus tore up a great oak-tree by the roots; and the battle burst through the seven doors into the court. Outside, Mac Dathó loosed Ailbe to see which side the dog's sense would turn — and the hound joined the men of Ulster and rushed on the defeated Connachtmen, seizing the chariot-poles of Ailill and Medb at the ford that still bears the hound's name. The trick that ended in neither host gaining a dog, and in a hall's worth of champions dead of a division, is the Irish lawbook of status: worth is measured, in this world, in heads.
narrative.zh: 豬之分割記乃阿爾斯特故事圈中『勇士之份』的滑稽史詩——一場跨桌而行的履歷決鬥，終以名譽毀掉建築。萊因斯特的麥克·達霍畜神犬艾爾貝守護全萊因斯特；康諾特之艾利爾與梅芙、阿爾斯特之科恩各自遣使求犬，各許珍寶牛群與其地三分之一。麥克·達霍之妻以詩解困：『犬予兩家，死與否，吾等何懼。』兩軍遂約同日取犬——大屋有七門、每兩門之間五十張臥榻，蓋此聚非友朋之會。宴上主菜為五十牛乳養育七年之巨豬，巨而含毒，致愛爾蘭多人將為其死。布里克魯自高處宣布宴法：分割惟一之試，即勇士之份。康特·馬加之子於全場之上站起、執刀立於豬旁：『愛爾蘭可有聲名堪與我比者？』他如訟師逐一剝去阿爾斯特英雄之譽——萊加雷（邊境之戰中帶矛傷而逃）、安古斯（其父之手為康特之矛所斷）、伊奧甘（一目為康特所挖）、蒙雷穆爾（其長子之頭為康特所得）、劍踵者門德（其父之綽號乃康特斷其踵所贈）、克爾特查爾（腿股為康特之矛所傷致疾）、結巴者庫斯克里德（首試兵器即失三分之一族人、頸筋被斷）。全省之人皆坐。沉默中，科納爾·維克托里奧蘇斯直入大廳，其聲名僅一句：『自持矛以來，我幾無一夜不以康諾特人之頭為枕，無一日一夜無康諾特人死於我手。』康特讓之——『若安魯安在此！』——『安魯安在此！』科納爾自腰帶拔安魯安之頭擲於康特胸前，血濺其唇。科納爾取九人方可抬之豬尾全數吸入口中；予康諾特者僅前足兩條。大廳即時炸裂：屍堆高及牆垣、血自門下流洩、弗格斯連根拔起橡樹、戰鬥衝出七門。院外麥克·達霍放出艾爾貝——犬遂投阿爾斯特人，撲向敗逃之康諾特軍。詭計終局：兩軍皆未得犬，而一廳之英雄死於一場分割——此世之價值，以頭顱計量。

title.en: The Sick-Bed of Cuchulainn and Fand the Tear of Beauty
title.zh: 庫丘林病榻與美之淚芬德

region.en: Tete Brecc (the Sick-Bed), Emain Macha, Co. Armagh, Northern Ireland
region.zh: 北愛爾蘭阿馬郡埃馬因·瑪哈堡特特·布雷克（病榻之所）

period: Recorded in Leabhar na hUidre, c. 1100 (transcribed by Maelmuiri mac Ceileachair); Leahy translation 1905

source.work: A. H. Leahy, Heroic Romances of Ireland, Volume I (1905), 'The Sick-Bed of Cuchulain', eBook #5678

summary.en: Two birds linked by a chain of red gold lull the men of Ulster asleep at Samhain and put Cuchulainn into a year's sick-bed; from the Plain of Delight, Liban brings Fand — Manannan's released wife, whose beauty is compared only to a tear — to offer her love for a day's battle; Emer comes whetting knives, and Manannan shakes his cloak between the lovers, while the Druids give both husband and wife a drink of forgetfulness.
summary.zh: 薩溫之夜，紅金鏈相連之雙鳥使阿爾斯特男子入睡，並使庫丘林臥病一年；自宜人平原，莉班攜芬德——瑪南南已釋之妻，其美僅可比淚——以一日之戰事易其情愛；艾默攜磨利之刀而來；瑪南南於二情侶之間搖其斗篷，德魯伊則予夫妻二人遺忘之飲。

sensitivity.note: Fand ('tear') is Manannan's ex-wife in this tale; her resignation scene is one of the great love-debates of medieval literature. Retold from public-domain print.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase of Leahy 1905: At the Samhain festival on the Plain of Murthemne, two birds flying over the lake, linked together by a chain of red gold, sang a gentle song and a sleep fell upon all the men; Cuchulainn rose to pursue them, missed with stone and spear until the spear pierced the shield of the wing of one, and the birds went beneath the lake. He leaned his back against a pillar and a sleep fell on him; two women came to him in turn, one in a green mantle and one in a purple folded in five folds, laughing and striking him with a horsewhip until he was all but dead. For a year he lay speechless on the sick-bed at Tete Brecc, until Angus son of Aed Abra sang to the Ulstermen of the healing that Liban and Fand would bring. Not verbatim.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Leahy 1905; not verbatim.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase: Liban, from her spouse Labraid the Swift, Sword-Wielder, offered Cuchulainn Fand, daughter of Aed Abra, whose husband Manannan the Son of the Sea had released her, in exchange for one day's service in battle against Senach the Unearthly, Eochaid Juil and Yeogan the Stream. Fand is the name of the tear that runs from the eye — nothing in the world but a tear to which her beauty could be likened. Cuchulainn rose, fought the day's battle alone against three thousands in the otherworld's plain, and slept with the lady for a month; they made tryst at the Strand of the Yew-Tree's Head. Emer came there with fifty women and knives whetted to slay the lady, and found Cuchulainn and Laeg at chess. Not verbatim.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Leahy 1905; not verbatim.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase: Emer rebuked Cuchulainn before the women of Ulster, and he answered that Fand was fair and skilled and wealthy; Emer replied that the lady was in no way better than herself — 'fair seems all that's red; seems white what's new alone; and bright what's set o'erhead; and sour are things well known! Men worship what they lack; and what they have seems weak.' Fand resigned him: 'Emer! noble lady! Take thy man to thee; though my arms resign him, longing lives in me.' Manannan perceived her unequal war, came riding the maned waves of the sea, and asked whether she would go or stay; she chose Manannan — 'he hath no consort equal to himself, but Cuchulainn hath already.' Cuchulainn leaped three times into the air and made three leaps south to Tara Luachra, where he lay without meat or drink; the Druids bound him and gave him a drink of forgetfulness, and Emer one for her jealousy, and Manannan shook his cloak between Cuchulainn and Fand so that they might never meet again throughout eternity. Not verbatim.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Leahy 1905; not verbatim.

canonical_translation: A. H. Leahy, Heroic Romances of Ireland, Vol. I, London 1905 (public domain); underlying: Serglige Con Culainn (older edition: Windisch, Irische Texte I, 1870, public domain)

narrative.en:
The Sick-Bed of Cuchulainn is the Ulster cycle's answer to the Táin: after the epic of war, an epic of love, in which the hero of the ford is undone by a woman's tear.

Every year at Samhain the men of Ulster held festival on the Plain of Murthemne, where each man declared his combats, carrying in a pouch the tips of the tongues of the foes he had killed — and swords laid over thighs turned on any man who lied. Two birds came over the lake linked by a chain of red gold, singing a gentle song that put the whole assembly to sleep. Cuchulainn rose to hunt them, missed with stone and sling and spear until the spear went through the shield of the wing of one; the birds sang again and went beneath the lake, and a sleep fell on him. Two women appeared in turn — one in a green mantle, one in purple folded five-fold — and each struck him laughing with a horse-whip until he was all but dead. They left; a year he lay without speech on the sick-bed at Tete Brecc, refusing Emer's Dun Delga.

At the year's end the man Angus son of Aed Abra sang the diagnosis from the doorway: the women of the Sídhe had put their power on him, and healing lay in the Plain of Delight. At the pillar stone Liban appeared — wife of Labraid the Swift, Sword-Wielder — with an offer: Fand, daughter of Aed Abra, Manannan the Son of the Sea's released wife, for one day's battle against Senach the Unearthly, Eochaid Juil and Yeogan the Stream. Fand is the tear that runs from the eye; nothing in the world but a tear could her beauty be likened to. Laeg was carried across on the woman's shoulder to see the island of thrice-fifty couches and thrice-fifty welcome-song women.

Cuchulainn rose from the sick-bed like a man waking from death, crossed to the otherworld in Liban's bronze skiff, and fought the day's battle alone against three thousands — slaying Eochaid Juil bathing at the spring, thirty-three of his men, and Senach the Unearthly in a great fight — then cooled his heat in three vats of water, the first boiling over. He slept with Fand a month; they set a tryst at the Strand of the Yew-Tree's Head. Emer heard of it and came there with fifty women and knives whetted for the fairy's death, and found Cuchulainn and Laeg at chess. Fand saw the gold clasps and the green-edged knives first. Cuchulainn defended them both with a boast — but Emer answered with the most famous speech in the cycle, the truth of desire: 'Fair seems all that's red; seems white what's new alone; and bright what's set o'erhead; and sour are things well known! Men worship what they lack; and what they have seems weak.'

Fand released him with the grace of a queen: 'Emer, noble lady, take thy man to thee; though my arms resign him, longing lives in me.' Manannan, riding the maned waves of the sea where no vessel was needed, perceived his wife's unequal war, and asked her which she would do; she chose him, for Cuchulainn had a wife already and she none. As she went, Manannan shook his cloak between the mortal and the immortal so that they might never meet again throughout eternity. The Druids of Ulster hunted down the maddened hero in the mountains of Tara Luachra, bound him with fairy songs, and gave him — and gave Emer, for her jealousy was no better than his sickness — a drink of forgetfulness. So ends the cycle's one romance: with pharmaceutical forgetting standing in for mercy, and a god's cloak for a wall that time cannot build.
narrative.zh: 《庫丘林病榻》乃阿爾斯特故事圈對《奪牛記》之回應：戰爭史詩之後是愛之史詩——渡口英雄竟被一女子之淚擊倒。每年薩溫之夜，阿爾斯特男子在穆爾西姆尼平原集會驗功、袋中攜所殺之敵之舌尖——劍橫於腿上，誰若說謊，劍即反噬。紅金鏈相連之雙鳥飛過湖上、歌聲使全場入睡。庫丘林追之不中、矛貫其一鳥翼上之盾；雙鳥潛入湖底，睡意臨於英雄之身。兩女子輪流以馬鞭擊之至其垂死。此後一年，他臥於特特·布雷克病榻、不言不語。歲末，安古斯自門口唱出診斷：西德之女施加其力於他，愈病之方在宜人平原。石柱旁莉班現身獻議：芬德——瑪南南已釋之妻——以一日之戰相易。芬德者，眼中所流之淚也；其美惟淚可喻。庫丘林如死而復甦者起身、乘銅舟渡往彼岸，獨戰三千、殺敵而歸，於三缸水中冷卻其熱。與芬德同眠一月，相約紫杉首灘。艾默攜五十女子與磨利之刀而來，庫丘林與萊格正弈棋。艾默答以全圈最著名之言、慾望之真諦：『赤者看似美；新者看似白；高懸者看似亮；習見者轉為酸！人皆崇拜其所未有；所有者似弱。』芬德以女王之風讓之：『艾默，貴女，取回爾之男子；我雖放開雙臂，思念長存於我。』騎乘鬃浪之瑪南南問其去留；她擇瑪南南——因庫丘林有妻、而她無夫。瑪南南於凡人與不朽者之間搖其斗篷，使二人永世不得再會。德魯伊於塔拉·盧阿克拉斯山縛住瘋癲之英雄，予他——亦予艾默——遺忘之飲。全圈唯一戀曲如此終結：以遺忘代替慈悲，以神之斗篷代替時間不能築起之牆。

functions: Otherworld love-quest: the sick-bed as portal and the battle-service as bride-price, inverted

Doctrine of forgetting: the druids' drink of oblivion and Manannan's cloak as endings of unequal love
Etiology of the Samhain assembly and of the tongue-tips custom at festival

title.en: Deirdre and the Sons of Usnach
title.zh: 德爾德麗與烏斯納之子

region.en: Emain Macha (Navan Fort), Co. Armagh, Northern Ireland
region.zh: 北愛爾蘭阿馬郡埃馬因·瑪哈堡（納萬堡）

period: Longes mac nUisnenn, Book of Leinster and Glenn Masain versions, 11th-15th c.; Leahy translation 1905

source.work: A. H. Leahy, Heroic Romances of Ireland, Volume I (1905), 'The Exile of the Sons of Usnach', eBook #5678

summary.en: A baby cries in its mother's womb at a feast and Cathbad the druid names her Deirdre, the cause of ruin; the king rears her in seclusion to wed her, but she sees a raven drinking blood on snow and will love only the man with those three colors — Naisi, whom she seizes by the ears until he flees with her to Alba — until treachery brings the three brothers home and the whole Red Branch burns.
summary.zh: 宴上嬰兒於母腹中啼叫，德魯伊卡斯巴德命名其為德爾德麗——毀滅之因；王幽禁撫養欲娶之，她卻見烏鴉於雪上飲血，言必愛具此三色者——烏斯納之子奈西——她扯其耳直至兄弟攜她流亡阿爾巴；背信引三兄弟歸國，紅枝全軍化為灰燼。

sensitivity.note: Deirdre ('of the Sorrows') is the Helen of the Ulster cycle; the exiles' burning of Emain is historical for the cycle's chronology. Retold from public-domain print.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase of Leahy 1905: In the house of Feidlimid the storyteller the men of Ulster sat at their ale, and before them stood his wife, great with child; as she passed through the house the child cried out in her womb, a shriek heard through the whole house and the court without. Cathbad the druid laid his hand on her and prophesied: a fair maid with blue-centred eyes and cheeks like the foxglove, teeth faultless and lips like coral, for whose love many chiefs shall strive — 'Deirdre shall be her name, and evil woe shall be upon her... Usna's sons, the three chiefs sublime, to banishment forced shall be.' The young men cried 'Let that maiden be slain!'; but Conor said she should be reared to be his wife. Not verbatim.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Leahy 1905; not verbatim.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase: Deirdre was reared in a house of Conor's far from the court, seen by no man but her foster-father, foster-mother and Levorcham the witch. One winter day the calf's blood lay on the snow and a raven came down to drink it: 'That man only will I love who hath the three colours that I see here, his hair as black as the raven, his cheeks red like the blood, and his body as white as the snow.' Levorcham named Naisi the son of Usnach. Deirdre escaped to Emain's rampart where Naisi stood alone; he refused for fear of Cathbad's prophecy, she seized him by the two ears — 'Two ears of shame and of mockery shalt thou have if thou take me not with thee' — and Naisi, his brothers and thrice-fifty warriors went with her into exile in Alba. Not verbatim.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Leahy 1905; not verbatim.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase: At last Conor offered protection and Fergus, Dubhtach and Cormac as sureties; Fergus was delayed by an ale-feast contrived by Conor, and the three brothers, pledged to eat no food in Erin until they had eaten of Conor's, went on to the meadows of Emain. Eogan of Fernmay — whose peace Conor had just made — drove his spear through Naisi's back; Fiacha son of Fergus shielded Naisi with his body and died over him; there was murder through the meadow, Dubhtach slew Conor's son and daughter, and Fergus burned Emain before dawn. Deirdre lived a year in Conor's house smiling never, singing that sweeter than Conor's mead was the foam of the waterfall, more magic than horns and pipes the voice of Usna's sons; then — in the later Glenn Masain version Hull follows — she leapt from the chariot on the field and broke her head on the stones, and from her grave and Naisi's on either side of the loch two pines grew and entwined across the water until King Conor died. Not verbatim.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Leahy 1905 and Hull 1910; not verbatim.

canonical_translation: A. H. Leahy, Heroic Romances of Ireland, Vol. I, London 1905 (public domain); underlying: Longes mac nUisnenn (Book of Leinster version, ed. Whitley Stokes, 1902, public domain); Eleanor Hull retelling 1910

narrative.en:
Deirdre is the Ulster cycle's Helen and Cassandra at once — desired for a beauty druids read in her mother's womb, and fated to be the ruin of a kingdom that never once asks her consent.

In the house of Feidlimid son of Dall, Conor's storyteller, the men of Ulster sat at their ale; before them stood Feidlimid's wife, great with child. As she crossed the floor, the child cried out in her womb — a shriek that filled house and court — and Cathbad the druid laid his hand on her and read the future aloud: a fair maid with blue-centred eyes, cheeks like the foxglove, teeth faultless, lips like coral, for whose love many chiefs shall strive; her name shall be Deirdre, and evil woe shall be upon her: Usna's three sons forced to banishment; Fergus to exile; a son of Conor dead; a grim deed in wrath against the king of Ulster — and her own tiny grave. The young men cried 'Let that maiden be slain!' But Conor answered that she should be brought to him in the morning, reared to his will, and be his wife — the fated girl converted into the king's property.

She was reared in a house far from the court, seen of no man but her foster-father and foster-mother and Levorcham the witch, whom none could refuse. One winter day her foster-father skinned a calf on the snow to make her a roast; the blood lay red on the white, and a black raven came down to drink it. 'That man only will I love,' said Deirdre, 'who hath the three colours that I see here — his hair as black as the raven, his cheeks red like the blood, and his body as white as the snow.' Levorcham answered that such a man was near: Naisi, son of Usnach. Deirdre went out to the rampart of Emain where Naisi stood alone; he refused her for fear of Cathbad's prophecy — and she sprang on him and seized him by the two ears: 'Two ears of shame and of mockery shalt thou have if thou take me not with thee.' 'Release me, O my wife!' So they fled — three-times-fifty warriors with their women, dogs and servants — harried through Ireland, driven to the wildernesses of Alba, where they served the king in war and built themselves houses in the meadows for fear any man should see Deirdre.

The king of Alba's steward, seeing her beauty, asked her for his master; Deirdre told Naisi everything nightly. Snares and wars were set for the brothers, and they came safe out of all, until at last Conor offered protection under the surety of Fergus, Dubhtach and Cormac — sureties sacred in Irish law. Conor then contrived an ale-feast that held Fergus back, for the sons of Usnach were pledged to eat no food in Erin until they had eaten of Conor's hand. So the three walked into the meadows of Emain behind Fiacha son of Fergus, and Eogan of Fernmay — whose peace Conor had only just made — threw the spear that broke Naisi's back; Fiacha covered Naisi with his own body and died over him; murder ran through the meadow. Dubhtach slew Conor's son and daughter; three hundred of Ulster fell; and before dawn Fergus burned Emain — the Red Branch's whole glory — and went into exile with three thousand men, harrying Ulster for sixteen years.

Deirdre lived a year in Conor's house, smiling never, singing the laments whose every stanza measures Conor's court against Naisi's wilderness: sweeter than the mead of the hall, the foam of the waterfall; sweeter than horns and pipes, the voice of Usna's sons. In the Glenn Masain tradition Hull preserves, she struck her head on the stones from Conor's chariot on the field; and from her grave on one side of a loch and Naisi's on the other, two pines grew and entwined their branches across the water — and Conor would have cut them down, but the men of Ulster protected them until King Conor died. Love, in this telling, keeps growing across the king's borders after it has been killed.
narrative.zh: 德爾德麗兼具阿爾斯特故事圈之海倫與卡桑德拉：因其美貌而被覬覦——德魯伊於母腹中即讀出其美——並註定毀滅從不徵求她同意之王國。科恩之講古者費德利米德家中，阿爾斯特男子飲酒作樂；其懷孕之妻立於前，腹中嬰兒啼叫、聲滿屋院——德魯伊卡斯巴德按手讀出未來：藍心之目、狐花之頰、無瑕之齒、珊瑚之唇、群雄必爭之美女；名為德爾德麗，禍患隨之：烏斯納三子被迫流亡、弗格斯流放、科恩一子死亡、以及她自己的小小墳墓。眾青年喊『殺此女！』科恩答：按吾意撫養、為吾之妻。她被幽禁於遠離王廷之屋，除養父母與女巫萊沃坎外無男子可見。一日冬日，血紅於雪上、黑鴉落而飲之；德爾德麗曰：『我必愛具此三色之人——髮如鴉之黑、頰如血之紅、身如雪之白。』萊沃坎答：此人即烏斯納之子奈西。奈西因懼預言而拒——她抓住他雙耳：『若不帶我走，爾將有羞辱與嘲笑之雙耳。』三兄弟遂偕三九五十名戰士流亡阿爾巴荒野。阿爾巴王之總管代主求之；德爾德麗夜夜盡告奈西。直至科恩以弗格斯、達布塔赫與科爾馬克為保人賜予庇護——愛爾蘭法中神聖之保人。科恩設酒宴絆住弗格斯，因烏斯納之子曾誓：未食科恩之食不食愛爾蘭之食。甫與科恩講和之伊奧甘擲矛斷奈西之背；菲亞赫以己身護之而死；謀殺遍野、達布塔赫殺科恩之子與女、黎明前弗格斯焚埃馬因——紅枝之全部榮光——並率三千人流亡、蹂躪阿爾斯特十六年。德爾德麗居科恩家中一年、從不微笑，其哀詩每節皆以奈西之荒野衡量科恩之宮廷：比大廳蜜酒更甜者，瀑布之泡沫；比號角風笛更迷人者，烏斯納諸子之聲。格倫·馬辛傳統中，她自科恩戰車躍下、頭觸石而碎；其墓與奈西墓隔湖相對，兩株松樹自墓中生出、枝椏隔水相纏——科恩欲斬之，而阿爾斯特男子護之直至王死。愛，在被殺之後仍跨過國王之疆界繼續生長。

functions: Tragedy of foresight ignored: prophecy enacted exactly because no one changes course
Charter of surety law: Fergus's broken pledge as the legal hinge of Ulster's civil war
Etiology of the entwined pines and of Deirdre's grave across the loch
Ideology of the hero's cry: Naisi's warrior-call doubling the milk of every beast that hears

title.en: Yayati's Bargain with Old Age
title.zh: 耶耶提與衰老的交易

region.en: Pratishthana on the Ganges, Yayati's capital (symbolic pin near Prayagraj)
region.zh: 恆河畔耶耶提都城缽哩沙陀那（象徵性定位近般遮羅闍）

period: Mahabharata, Adi Parva (Sharmishtha Upaparva), composition layers c. 400 BCE-400 CE (Ganguli translation, 1883-96)

source.work: The Mahabharata of Krishna-Dwaipayana Vyasa, trans. K. M. Ganguli (1883-96), Adi Parva, the story of Yayati

summary.en: Cursed by his father-in-law to age before his time, the emperor Yayati begs each of his sons to trade him their youth. Four sons of Devayani refuse; his youngest, born of the servant Sharmishtha, agrees - and Yayati spends a thousand years of borrowed youth chasing pleasure, only to discover that desire is never satisfied by feeding it. He returns the youth, renounces the throne, and goes into the forest.
summary.zh: 耶耶提遭岳父之詛提前衰老，乞求諸子與之交易青春。德瓦亞尼所生四子皆拒；侍女沙爾蜜什陀所生之幼子應允——耶耶提以借來的千年青春追逐歡樂，終悟欲望愈餵愈飽不得。他歸還青春、放棄王位、入林而去。

sensitivity.note: Living tradition (epic recitation; katha retellings). Classified 'myth'.

passages.text: Devayani, daughter of the sage Shukra, married King Yayati in anger at the princess Sharmishtha; Sharmishtha followed her as a servant and bore Yayati secret sons. When Shukra learned of the union, his curse fell: Yayati would pass into old age, untimely, deprived of his pleasures in the prime of life.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Mahabharata, Adi Parva, Yayati episode (Ganguli 1883-96); not verbatim.

passages.text: Old age came upon the emperor like a guest he could not turn away. He went to his sons, each in turn: take my old age upon you, he said, and give me your youth, that I may enjoy the world a while longer and then hand it back. Four sons of Devayani refused - who would take a spent man's years for their own spring? Only Puru, the youngest, son of the servant, said: take it, father; I will bear your age and stand by your word.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Mahabharata, Adi Parva, Yayati episode (Ganguli 1883-96); not verbatim.

passages.text: With Puru's youth upon him Yayati resumed the pleasures of the senses - the gardens, the women, the hunts, the feasts - a thousand years of it, and every appetite only grew the more it was fed. At last he understood: desire is like fire; it is never satisfied by fuel. 'There is no end to desire,' he said; 'he who feeds it starves by feeding.' He gave Puru back his youth, declared Puru heir - disinheriting the elder line - and went to the forest with nothing, eating leaves, desiring nothing.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Mahabharata, Adi Parva, Yayati episode (Ganguli 1883-96); not verbatim.

canonical_translation: Kisari Mohan Ganguli, The Mahabharata of Krishna-Dwaipayana Vyasa, 1883-96 (public domain); modern: J. A. B. van Buitenen, The Mahabharata, vol. 1, University of Chicago Press, 1973

narrative.en:
The story of Yayati, told in the Adi Parva as part of the genealogy of kings, is the Mahabharata's sharpest fable about desire - and the charter myth of the Puru dynasty, the line from which the epic's own Bharata kings descend.

The tangle begins in a household war. Devayani, daughter of the preceptor Shukra, is humiliated by the Asura princess Sharmishtha and thrown into a well; Yayati rescues her; she marries him on condition that Sharmishtha be given to her as a servant. But Sharmishtha, in the palace as a maid, is soon secretly Yayati's mistress too, and bears him sons. When Shukra learns of it, his curse is precise and domestic: Yayati shall pass into untimely old age, cheated of his pleasures at their height.

The curse is also the experiment. Old age arrives, and Yayati - not yet done with the world - goes to his sons with the strangest request in the epic: give me your youth and carry my old age; I will enjoy the world a while and return what I borrow. The four sons of Devayani refuse, with the eldest speaking for them: what wise man would trade his springtime for another's winter? Only Puru, the youngest, son of the servant Sharmishtha - the unprivileged son - consents: 'take it, father; I will bear your age and stand by your word.'

So armed, Yayati re-enters the world's pleasures for a thousand years - the text lingers on the inventory: gardens, women, hunting, wine, festivity. And the experiment's result is the story's entire point: a thousand years of feeding desire leaves it hungrier, not quieter. Yayati's conclusion is spoken like a scientist closing his notebook: desire is a fire that no fuel satisfies; 'he who feeds it starves by feeding'; there is no end of wanting, only an end of the wanting man. He returns Puru's youth, makes Puru his heir - disinheriting the elder sons and founding the line of Puru that leads, in the epic's genealogy, to Bharata and to the Pandavas themselves - and walks into the forest owning nothing, 'desiring nothing, eating leaves and fruit'. The curse thus becomes a cure: the father-in-law's punishment delivers the hero to renunciation by the longest possible route.

Function: the story is recited as a teaching fable on craving (the epic's own frame commentary calls it the story of how even a thousand years of indulgence teaches only one sentence) and as a legitimation myth - the youngest servant-born son becomes the dynasty's founder because he alone paid his father's debt. In later retellings (Purana versions; Marathi and modern novel treatments, e.g. Vishnu Sakharam Khandekar's Yayati), the emphasis shifts between the erotic fable and the dynastic politics - the servant queen's line displacing the high-born one, a troubling undercurrent the epic leaves unresolved.
narrative.zh: 耶耶提的故事見於阿底篇王統之中，是摩訶婆羅多關於欲望最鋒利的寓言——也是補魯王朝的創建神話，史詩自身的婆羅多王族即出此系。家庭之戰開其端：仙人尸 訶之女德瓦亞尼受阿修羅公主沙爾蜜什陀之辱而墮井；耶耶提救之；她以沙爾蜜什陀為婢為條件嫁之。然沙爾蜜什陀居宮為婢，旋為耶耶提之秘密情人，生子數人。尸訶得知，其詛精確而家常：耶耶提將提前衰老，於歡樂正盛時被剝奪。詛咒亦即實驗。衰老降臨，耶耶提——未厭於世——向諸子提出史詩中最奇異的請求：予我青春而代我衰老；我將稍享世界而歸還所借。德瓦亞尼四子皆拒，長子代言：孰以己之春換他人之冬？唯侍女之子、最幼者補魯應允：『取之，父；我代父老，守父之言。』耶耶提遂攜補魯之青春重入感官之樂千年——經文細列清單：園林、婦女、田獵、酒宴——而實驗之果即故事全部之義：餵養欲望千年，欲望愈餵愈飢。耶耶提之結論如科學家合上筆記：欲望如火，燃料不能滿之；『餵它者因餵而餓』；欲無盡處，唯有欲者之盡。他歸還補魯之青春，立補魯為嗣——廢長支而建補魯之系，於史詩王統中直達婆羅多與般度諸子——且空手入林，『無所欲，食葉與果』。詛咒遂成療法：岳父之懲罰以最長之路將英雄送至出離。功能：此篇被誦為貪求之教寓言（史詩自註：縱千年之縱慾，所學僅一句），亦為正統神話——侍女所生之幼子因其獨償父債而成王朝之祖。後世重述（往世書；馬拉提語與現代小說，如坎德卡之《耶耶提》）於情欲寓言與王朝政治之間擺動——婢后之支取代嫡支，史詩留下未解的暗流。

functions: Teaching fable on desire: a thousand years of indulgence proves appetite unquenchable
Legitimation myth of the Puru-Bharata dynasty (the servant's son as founder)
Charter of renunciation as the end of the pleasure-path
Genealogical bridge from the gods' era to the epic's own royal line

variants.name: Katha retellings (Puranas and vernacular)
variants.summary: The story circulates as a stand-alone parable in Purana digests and oral katha, often with the moral stated explicitly: the man fed by all the world's pleasures died desiring.

title.en: Savitri Follows Death and Wins Back Her Husband
title.zh: 薩維特里隨死神而奪回夫君

region.en: Forest hermitage of Salva (symbolic pin at Chitrakoot)
region.zh: 薩羅訶王流放之林居（象徵性定位於質多羅俱吒）

period: Mahabharata, Vana Parva (Pativrata Upaparva), composition layers c. 400 BCE-400 CE (Ganguli translation, 1883-96)

source.work: The Mahabharata of Krishna-Dwaipayana Vyasa, trans. K. M. Ganguli (1883-96), Vana Parva, the story of Savitri and Satyavan

summary.en: Princess Savitri chooses as husband the exiled, doomed Satyavan, despite the seer Narada's prophecy that he will die within a year. On the fated day she follows her husband into the forest and trails Yama himself as he takes Satyavan's soul; her unanswerable courtesy and argument win three boons - and the third is worded so that the fourth, unasked, is his life.
summary.zh: 薩維特里公主不顧那羅陀仙人「夫將於一年內死」之預言，選流放而命定之薩蒂凡為夫。劫日當天，她隨夫入林，並尾隨親自取走薩蒂凡魂魄的閻摩；她以無可辯駁的禮數與言辭赢得三項恩諾——而第三項措辭巧妙，使未出口的第四項成為丈夫之命。

sensitivity.note: Living tradition: the story is ritually recited at Vat-Savitri Vrata (married women's fast). Classified 'myth'.

passages.text: King Ashvapati, childless, worshiped Savitri the sun-goddess with offerings; the goddess granted him a daughter, Savitri, radiant as the sun. When she was of marriageable age, her father sent her to choose - and she returned from the forests having fixed her heart on Satyavan, blind Dyumatsena's son, living in exile at a hermitage.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Mahabharata, Vana Parva, Savitri episode (Ganguli 1883-96); not verbatim.

passages.text: Narada the seer was present, and he pronounced the doom: Satyavan is virtuous beyond all men, but he has one defect - he shall die within a year. The king begged his daughter to choose another; Savitri answered that she had chosen once, for once only, whether he lives one year or more - she has made her choice. The marriage was performed, and she went to the forest, serving her husband's blind parents in homespun.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Mahabharata, Vana Parva, Savitri episode (Ganguli 1883-96); not verbatim.

passages.text: She counted the days. Four days before the term, she began a vigil, standing without food; on the fated day she obtained leave and went with Satyavan to the forest to cut firewood. He felled a tree, grew faint, and lay with his head in her lap; then came a dark-crowned figure with a rope - Yama, Death himself - who drew Satyavan's soul, small as a thumb, and turned south, binding it for the city of the dead.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Mahabharata, Vana Parva, Savitri episode (Ganguli 1883-96); not verbatim.

passages.text: Savitri followed. Yama told her to go back; she kept walking, speaking of duty and of the merit of following. Moved by her discourse, he offered boons: eyes and kingdom for her blind father-in-law; a hundred sons for her father; a hundred sons for herself. He had granted too much: a hundred sons require a living husband. Yama, bound by his own word and outmatched in argument, cut the rope, gave back the soul, and said: your husband shall live. Satyavan woke as from sleep, and the family's fortunes reversed from that day.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Mahabharata, Vana Parva, Savitri episode (Ganguli 1883-96); not verbatim.

canonical_translation: Kisari Mohan Ganguli, The Mahabharata of Krishna-Dwaipayana Vyasa, 1883-96 (public domain); modern: S. K. Belvalkar studies; also Julia Leslie's work on the Savitri vrata

narrative.en:
The Savitri episode (Vana Parva, told by Markandeya to Yudhishthira as the story of the perfect wife, pativrata) is the Mahabharata's great love-against-death narrative, and one of the most ritually alive stories in Hinduism: it is recited every year at the Vat-Savitri vrata, the fast married women keep for their husbands' longevity.

The choice: Ashvapati, king of Madra, is childless; he worships the sun-goddess Savitri with disciplined offerings, and she grants him a daughter as radiant as her namesake. When the girl is grown, the king - following custom - sends her on a pilgrimage of self-choice (svayamvara) in a chariot with aged counselors. She travels sanctuaries and hermitages and returns with her heart fixed: on Satyavan, son of the blind exiled king Dyumatsena, living in forest poverty. He is beautiful, dutiful - and doomed.

The oracle: Narada, the celestial seer, happens to be present and delivers the prophecy that gives the story its clock: Satyavan is virtuous beyond all men, but he has one defect - he shall die within a year. The father begs; the daughter's answer is the pivot of the story and the ethic it teaches: 'I have chosen once, whether he lives long or briefly; having chosen, I choose no more.' Death in a year is a defect of fate, not of the man. The marriage is performed with the doom standing, and Savitri goes to the hermitage in homespun, serving her blind parents-in-law.

The vigil: Savitri counts the days inward. Four before the term she begins a standing fast; her father-in-law tries to dissuade her; she answers with theology - the vow is kept, and what will be is known to the wise. On the fated day she obtains leave to go with her husband into the forest. He cuts firewood, faints, and lies with his head in her lap. Then she sees him: a dark-crowned figure carrying a rope, standing as if he owns the wood. It is Yama, and he draws Satyavan's soul - small as a thumb-length - binds it, and turns south toward his city.

The duel: Savitri follows. Yama three times commands her back; three times she stays, and her speeches - on dharma, on the company of the righteous, on the merit of following a husband - are so accomplished that Death himself concedes the conversation. He offers boons to get her to leave: for her father-in-law, eyes and his kingdom restored; for her father, a hundred sons; for herself, a hundred sons. The third boon is the trap she has been building: a hundred sons require a living husband. Yama, bound by his own granted word, laughs and releases the rope. 'Your husband shall live.' Satyavan wakes as from sleep; the exiled family's fortunes reverse; and the seers' prophecy is beaten not by force but by a wife's constancy, timed and worded.

Function: the story is the charter of the pativrata ideal - the devoted wife whose virtue has real cosmological purchase - and the ritual text of Vat-Savitri vrata, in which women fast, tie threads around a banyan, and retell Savitri's argument for their husbands' lives. Sri Aurobindo built his epic Savitri on it; comparative readers place it beside Orpheus (the descent for a wife, failed) and Psyche's tasks - here the descent is refused, and the argument wins where song could not.
narrative.zh: 薩維特里之章（大森林篇，由摩根德耶向堅戰講述，作為貞婦 pativrata 之典範故事）是摩訶婆羅多最偉大的抗死之愛敘事，也是印度教中儀式生命力最強的故事之一：每年 Vat-Savitri 齋戒——已婚婦女為夫壽而持之齋——都誦讀此篇。選擇：摩德羅王苑鏡婆底無子；他以嚴謹的供養禮拜太陽女神薩維特里，女神賜一女，光輝如其名。女長，王依俗遣其自擇夫婿（svayamvara）。她歷聖地與仙居，心有所定：薩蒂凡，盲眼流放王達優摩陀申之子，居林中貧困。彼俊美、孝謹——而命定將死。神諭：天界仙人那羅陀適在座，宣示預言，故事之鐘由此撥動：薩蒂凡德行冠世，然有一缺陷——他將於一年內死去。父懇求；女之回答是故事的樞紐與其教義：『我已擇定，無論其壽長壽促；既擇，不再擇。』一年之死乃命運之缺陷，非其人之缺陷。婚禮在預言成立之下舉行，薩維特里著粗衣至仙居，侍奉盲眼翁姑。守夜：薩維特里向內數日。期前四日始立齋；翁欲勸阻；她以神學作答——誓願已持，智者知其所將至。劫日，她求得許可與夫同入林中。伐木、昏厥，枕於她膝。隨即她見到他：頭戴暗冠、手持繩索之人，立於林間如主。是閻摩。他抽出薩蒂凡之魂——如拇指般小——繫之，轉向南往亡者之城。決鬥：薩維特里隨行。閻摩三令其返；三留，其言辭——論正法、論與義者同行、論隨夫之功——令死神自認辯不過。他為使其離去而賜恩諾：翁之眼與王國復得；父得百子；己得百子。第三項恩諾正是她步步築成的陷阱：百子需活著的丈夫。閻摩受己諾所縛，一笑斷繩：『汝夫將活。』薩蒂凡如從睡中醒來；流放之家時運逆轉；仙人之預言非為武力所破，而為一位妻子的堅貞——以恰當的時機與措辭——所破。功能：此篇為貞婦理想之憲章——貞婦之德具有真實的宇宙效力——亦為 Vat-Savitri 齋戒的儀式文本：婦女齋戒、於榕樹繫線、重述薩維特里的辯論以為夫爭命。室利阿羅頻多以此構築其史詩《薩維特里》；比較讀者置之於俄耳甫斯（為妻下行而失敗）之旁——此處下行被拒絕，歌所不能者，言辭得之。

functions: Charter of the pativrata ideal - wifely constancy with cosmological efficacy
Ritual text of Vat-Savitri vrata (annual fast for husbands' longevity)
Model of argumentative devotion: boons won by speech, not force
Narrative refutation of fatalism - prophecy beaten by timing and wording
