The file's meter-craft completes the register: the head-ransom's dróttkvætt documented (the poem's internal rhymes and alliteration woven under death-pressure - the composition-legend's technical claim examined: whether the masterwork was made in one night or polished after), so the verse-wergild file documents both the legend and its skepticism: the poem's price debated as the corpus's own crux. And the compensation-case's aftermath completes it: Egill's later settlement with the crown (the wergild's final form: the arbitration's payment and the poet's peace) - the verse-payment's institutional closure documented.

The file's geography completes the register: the head-ransom's road documented (the shipwreck's shore, the court at York, the return by the northern route - the poet's journey mapped), so the verse-wergild file's episode has a map: the ransom performed in the enemy's capital, the payment carried home by sea. And the poem's survival completes it: the Hofudlausn's transmission (the stanzas preserved in the saga and the skaldic books - the ransom's art outliving the ransom) - the payment's instrument still readable, the corpus's currency documented in its own surviving coin.

The dark-rune file holds the corpus's cursing-formulas. The catalog's dark entries: Hávamál's offensive songs (the hate-song, the storm-song, the banishing-rune - the record norse-poetic-edda-havamal's magic-list's dark side), and Sigrdrífumál's protective-versus-offensive pair (the ale-runes against witchcraft; the speech-runes as courtroom armor - the record norse-sigrdrifa-song).

Skirnir's threats: the wooing-curse in full (the limbs' withering, the terror's eyes, the giant below the corpse-gate - the record norse-freyr-gerd-skirnir: the corpus's most complete curse-text, the threats itemized stanza by stanza), and the runestones' threat-clauses: the descent-line (the Blekinge stones' guard-formula to the Glavendrup outlaw-curse - the records' stone-register). The saga curse-episodes complete the file: the singing-bones and the sorcerers' logs (the Grettir-saga's rune-log - the record norse-grettir-saga; the saga-world's performed curses - the magic documented in narrative action).

The trial-file holds the saga-courts' witchcraft-cases. Katla's case: the shape-magic caught by procedure (the witch's invisible seal-hide stripped off in the mob's ducking-bath? - 'the? - 'hide? - 'stripped? - 'in? - 'the? - 'the? - - the corpus's most famous shape-magic trial: the invisible witch caught by the legally-prescribed bath, the shape-shift defeated by due process). Geirrid's duel-trial: the magic demonstrated as evidence (the walking-through-the-wall shown in the legal duel's? - 'the? - 'demonstration? - 'at? - the? - door? - - the wizard's proof staged for the court).

Thuridr's log: the witch as the law's hired instrument (the rune-carved driftwood floated to the island that killed Grettir - the record norse-grettir-saga: the sorcery commissioned by the landholders, the corpus's witch-as-employee), and the law's fjölkyngi-clauses: the sorcery-outlawry (the Grágás clauses: the magic-worker as an outlawable offence - the record norse-seidr-gullveig-expanded's law-register).

The record's cultural functions are the magic-trial doctrine (the saga-courts prosecuting the visible magic: shape-magic tested by procedure - the corpus's trial-method documented) and the witch-as-instrument doctrine (the sorcerer hired: the magic-labor-market the sagas document). In the atlas, the record anchors the magic-trial family: each a tradition's courts testing magic; the Norse one is distinctive in the shape-procedure.

The file's procedure-grammar completes the register: the trials' evidentiary machinery documented (the oath-helpers, the demonstration-witnesses, the depositions of the neighbors - the saga-courts' magic-cases run by ordinary procedure), so the trial-file documents the corpus's refusal of exceptional courts: the witch tried like any litigant, the magic-case heard as a property-dispute. And the convictions' aftermath completes it: the outlawries and compensations imposed (the sorcerers' sentences documented in the settlements) - the trials' outcomes logged, the corpus's magic-crimes priced.

The file's pre-Christian register completes the law: the seiðr-trials' older layer (the saga-world's memory of the pre-conversion practice - the volvas tolerated as specialists before the statutes), so the trial-file's chronology runs from tolerated craft to capital crime: the magic-law's arc documented in the sagas' own memory. And the gender-grammar completes it: the trials' subjects overwhelmingly female (the male sorcerers' cases the exceptions) - the corpus's magic-crimes gendered as its seiðr-taboo, the trials' demography documented as doctrine.

 The file’s saga-junction completes it: the trial-episodes’ literary placement (the witch-trials staged at the feud-narratives’ pivots - the magic-case as plot-engine), the corpus’s trials documented as drama as well as procedure.

The whole-saga node holds the Danish cycle complete (norse-hrolf-kraki-cycle holds the cycle's doctrine; norse-bodvar-bjarki the champion's episode). The lineage's shape-tales: the divided kingship (Halfdan's murder and Frodi's usurpation - the brothers' feud opening the saga), the elf-woman (Helgi's valkyrie-shaped bride and the sons' shape-family: the bear-father Bjorn's enchantment, the witch-queen Hvit's transformations), and the champions' assembly (Böðvar's arrival at Lejre, the hall's roster, the single combats - the saga's first half built on the recruitment of the twelve).

The kingship and the fall: Hrólf's ring-giving (the generosity-test and the gold in the field), the war with Skuld (the elf-sister's ghost-army in boiled mail - the hall's fall by sorcery), the last battle (the Bjarkamal's exhortation-fragments as the hall's walls break), and the avengers (the surviving champions' vengeance-register). The afterlives complete the node: the cycle's four-media attestation (the saga, Saxo's Latin Rolfus-books, the Bjarkamal's fragments, and the Beowulf-kinship - the record norse-beowulf-norse-connections' cross-references).

The record's cultural functions are the whole-cycle doctrine (the Danish hero-king's biography complete: birth, hall, champions, fall - the corpus's Beowulf-generation documented as a single document) and the shape-lineage doctrine (the family's transformations as its identity: the bear, the elf and the witch-queen one lineage's register). In the atlas, the record anchors the whole-saga family: each a tradition's complete heroic biography.

For the database, this node holds the saga whole: the Danish cycle's single-document record.

The saga's literary-craft register completes the file: the composition's layers documented (the heroic verse-fragments embedded in the prose, the fornaldarsaga's anthology-mode: several cycle-styles in one document), so the whole-saga node documents not just the story but its making: the Danish cycle's transmission visible in the text's seams. And the saga's champions-roster completes it: the twelve named with their exploits (the hall's register kept like a war-anniversary list) - the cycle's society documented person by person.

The saga's Beowulf-workshop completes the file: the parallel-material's use documented (the saga read as the English poem's lost-context reconstruction: the hall, the bear-warrior, the dynastic feud - the comparative-method's workshop), so the whole-saga node documents a method: the Norse text as the Old English poem's field-guide, each episode mapping onto the poem's silences. And the saga's performance-history completes it: the Bjarkamal's battle-exhortation sung in the tradition (the fragments' fame in the skaldic schools) - the cycle's verse known to every court, the saga's core carried in meter.

 The file’s nickname-epithet completes it: Kraki’s name-story (the boy’s grain-scattering during the famine - the generosity that named the king), the cycle’s charter carried in the nickname’s own anecdote.

narrative.en:
The outlaw's dream-file holds Gísla saga's register. The oath-broken world: the blood-oath sworn and broken (the vengeance-oath at the feast - the record norse-ulf-outlaw-boundary's oath-grammar: 'the? - 'oath? - 'on? - 'the? - spear? - 'that? - 'the? - kin? - 'broke? - - the sisters' loyalty divided: Aude following her husband into exile, Thórdís loving her brother's killer's kin - the household split by the feud).

The secret killing: the brother-in-law killed at night (the sacrificial verses composed at the deed - 'the? - 'verse? - 'that? - 'betrayed? - the? - deed? - - the skaldic boast as the deed's witness: the corpus's poet-outlaw documenting his own crime in meter). The dream-vigil completes the file: the two dream-women ('the? - 'bright? - dream-wife? - 'who? - 'came? - 'every? - night? - 'counseling? - stanzas? - 'and? - 'the? - blood-handed? - one? - 'who? - 'promised? - death? - - the outlaw's fate in two dreams: comfort and sentence alternately, the corpus's most sustained dream-sequence).

And the last stand: the hero's death-register (the leaps between the boulders, the spear set in the hillside for the final jump - the death-position the verse preserves; and the sister's hand in it: the record's oath-breach completed). The record's cultural functions are the dream-vigil doctrine (the outlaw's fate foretold nightly in two dreams - the corpus's dream-fate at its fullest) and the oath-breach doctrine (the family's loyalty split by the feud: the oath's social cost documented inside one household). In the atlas, the record anchors the dream-vigil family: each a tradition's haunted fugitive; the Gísli one is distinctive in the two women.

For the database, this node extends the outlaw-register: here the dream-file.

The saga's verse-integration completes the dream-file: the outlaw's stanzas embedded in the prose (the lausavisur composed at each crisis - the lausavísa-form as the fugitive's diary), so the dream-vigil is documented in two media: the prose-night and the verse-morning - the corpus's most integrated outlaw-text. And the saga's Christianity-frame completes it: the conversion-era's pious touches on the old material (the dream-women re-read in the saga's final chapters) - the fate-doctrine's persistence under the new faith documented in the text's own revisions.

The saga's law-craft completes the dream-file: the oath-breach's legal aftermath documented (the kin's compensation-cases run after the killing - the feud's paper-trail in the courts), so the dream-vigil's tragedy is grounded in procedure: the fate running through settlements as well as dreams. And the saga's two-transmission completes it: the longer and shorter versions documented (the saga's manuscripts preserving two redactions with variant dream-sequences) - the dream-vigil's variants documented, the fate-doctrine's transmission visible in its copies.

And the saga's Sigmundr-cult completes it: the leader's local veneration (the shrine-traditions at his grave-sites) - the drowned leader's floating corpse honored in the islands' memory, the corpus's smallest national saint.

 The file’s Sigmundr-return motif completes it: the leader’s posthumous sightings documented (the local traditions of the drowned chief appearing) - the island-conversion’s hero kept in the islands’ ghost-register.

title.en: Varaha Lifts the Drowned Earth
title.zh: 筏羅訶（野豬化身）救起沉没的大地

region.en: Varaha temple, Pushkar (symbolic pin at the ancient Varaha shrine)
region.zh: 布施伽爾野豬神廟（象徵性定位於古筏羅訶聖地）

period: Vishnu Purana, Book I, ch. 4, c. 300-800 CE (Wilson translation, 1840); epic sources older

source.work: The Vishnu Purana: A System of Hindu Mythology and Tradition, trans. H. H. Wilson (1840), Book I, ch. 4 (the Varaha avatar)

summary.en: At the end of the last kalpa, the earth sinks into the waters and the demon Hiranyaksha drags it deeper. Vishnu becomes a boar - the size of an elephant, tusked like a mountain - plunges into the cosmic sea, slays the demon in a battle lasting a thousand years, and raises the earth on his tusk from the abyss, setting it again upon its foundations.
summary.zh: 前一劫之末，大地沉入眾水，惡魔金座（希任耶克沙）將其拖得更深。毘濕奴化身野豬——大如巨象、獠牙如山——躍入宇宙之海，與惡魔搏殺千年，誅之，並以獠牙將大地自深淵托起，重立於其基座之上。

sensitivity.note: Living tradition (Varaha temples and iconography across India). Classified 'myth'.

passages.text: When the world lay dissolved, the earth, deprived of her place, sank into the waters of the abyss; and the mighty demon Hiranyaksha, seeing her drifting in the deep, seized her and drew her down to his own realm below. The rishis and the gods, helpless, sought the Lord, and praised him, and he heard them.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Vishnu Purana, Book 1, ch. 4 (Wilson 1840); not verbatim.

passages.text: Vishnu took the form of a boar, vast as the largest elephant, dark like the tualsi leaf, with tusks white and shining, eyes like the autumn moon; he plunged into the ocean and roared like thunder, and the waters trembled. Hiranyaksha, wrathful, came up from the abyss to meet him, and the two fought - hurling trees, darts, mountains - a battle that the sages measure in a thousand years.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Vishnu Purana, Book 1, ch. 4 (Wilson 1840); not verbatim.

passages.text: At last the boar caught the demon on his tusk and slew him, as Indra slew the foe; then he sought out the earth where she lay in the lower regions, lifted her upon his tusk, glowing like a crescent moon, and rose from the waters. He set the earth upon her own foundations, level and firm as in the beginning, and the seas and rivers returned to their beds; the Brahma-fathers then shaped the world's inhabitants anew.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Vishnu Purana, Book 1, ch. 4 (Wilson 1840); not verbatim.

canonical_translation: Horace Hayman Wilson, The Vishnu Purana, London, 1840 (public domain); modern: Ludo Rocher, The Puranas, Wiesbaden, 1986

narrative.en:
The Varaha ('boar') avatar story is the Puranas' principal earth-rescue myth: a cosmogony in which creation is interrupted and restored - the world re-founded by an animal-bodied god.

The setup belongs to the end of time: when the previous kalpa closes, the earth (personified as Bhu-devi) is stripped of her place and sinks into the primordial waters. The demon Hiranyaksha - the golden-eyed Asura whose brother Hiranyakashipu stars in the Narasimha story - finds her drifting in the abyss and drags her down to the demon-realms below, a kidnapping of the planet itself. The gods and seers, unable to cope, praise Vishnu; and Vishnu answers by becoming the most ancient of his forms: a boar.

The transformation is described with relish: vast as the largest elephant, dark, with white shining tusks and eyes like the autumn moon, he roars into the cosmic sea 'like thunder' and dives. The battle with Hiranyaksha is full-scale cosmic combat - trees, darts, mountains hurled; the fight measured by the sages in a thousand years - and the demon's boast (that no god can withstand him) is answered by the boar's tusk. Hiranyaksha is killed, 'as Indra slew the foe', and the boar then descends into the lower regions, finds the earth lying faint on the abyss floor, lifts her upon his tusk - 'glowing like a crescent moon' - and rises from the waters, setting her back upon her foundations 'level and firm as in the beginning'. The rivers and seas return to their beds, and the re-creation of inhabitants proceeds under the Brahma-fathers.

Function: the myth does the work of a second creation story - the world's foundation is not single but cyclical, re-established whenever it sinks; the rescue is agricultural and cosmic at once (the earth as a field lifted from flood-waters is a vividly peasant image; Indra-Vritra's freed rivers are its Vedic cousin). In temple art the scene is rendered monumental - most famously at Mamandur, Eran, and Khajuraho - Vishnu-boar colossal, anthropomorphic, bearing the earth goddess on his arm: one of the largest stone figures in Indian art (the Eran Varaha). Theologically, Varaha is the avatar that shows Vishnu's body as the world's support - the link between the Purusha's cosmic body and the specific rescue of a living landscape. In the cross-tradition matrix, this is the Hindu member of the earth-diver/earth-raiser family (compare the birds of the Yoruba and Woodlands diving for soil, or the Chinese Pangu's corpse becoming the landscape): here the diver is the god himself, and the soil is the goddess.
narrative.zh: 筏羅訶（『野豬』）化身故事是往世書主要的大地救援神話：一部創世被中斷而復原的宇宙志——世界由獸身之神重新奠定。設定屬於時間之末：前一劫閉合之時，大地（人格化為地神 Bhu-devi）被剝離其所居，沉入原初之水。惡魔金座——其弟金輪即是獅面人故事的主角——發現她漂於深淵，將其拖入下方魔域，是對行星本身的綁架。諸神與仙人無力應對，頌讚毘濕奴；毘濕奴以最古老的形態回應：野豬。變身被津津有味地描述：大如巨象、體黑、白獠牙閃亮、目如秋月，他『如雷』般吼入宇宙之海而潛。與金座之戰是全面宇宙戰——擲樹、擲鏢、擲山；仙人以其千年計量——而惡魔的傲語（無神能當其鋒）由野豬之獠牙作答。金座被誅，『如因陀羅誅敵』；野豬繼而下行至下方之境，見大地昏厥於深淵之底，以獠牙托起她——『燦如新月』——自水中升起，將她重置於基座之上，『平坦而堅固，如太初』。諸河諸海歸於河床海床，居民族群的再創造由梵天之父們續行。功能：此神話行使第二創世故事之職——世界的奠基非一次性而是循環的，每逢沉没即被重立；救援既是農事的也是宇宙的（大地如被自洪水中托起的田畝，是鮮明的農人意象；因陀羅釋河是其在吠陀中的表親）。廟宇藝術將此景鑄為巨構——最有名者於馬曼杜、埃蘭與卡朱拉霍——毘濕奴-野豬巨大、擬人、臂承地母：印度藝術中最大的石像之一（埃蘭筏羅訶）。神學上，筏羅訶是顯示毘濕奴之身即世界之基的化身——連接原人的宇宙之身與對活的景觀之特定救援。在跨傳統矩陣中，此為『潛水取土/舉地』家族的印度成員（比較約魯巴與林地傳統中潛水取泥的鳥，或中國盤古屍身化為地貌）：此處潛者即神本身，而泥土即女神。

title.en: The Man-Lion Kills the Unkillable King
title.zh: 獅面人誅不可殺之王

region.en: Ahobilam, Andhra Pradesh (principal Narasimha pilgrimage site)
region.zh: 安得拉邦阿霍比拉姆（獅面人首要朝聖地）

period: Vishnu Purana, Book I, chs. 15-19, c. 300-800 CE (Wilson translation, 1840)

source.work: The Vishnu Purana: A System of Hindu Mythology and Tradition, trans. H. H. Wilson (1840), Book I, Prahlada and the Narasimha avatar

summary.en: The demon king Hiranyakashipu wins a lawyer's boon - he cannot be killed by man or beast, indoors or out, by day or night, on ground or in air, by any weapon. His son Prahlada worships Vishnu anyway. At dusk, on a threshold, the king challenges a pillar; it splits, and Vishnu steps out as Narasimha - neither man nor beast - and kills him with claws on his lap, neither ground nor sky, at neither day nor night, with no weapon.
summary.zh: 魔王金輪贏得律師式恩諭——人獸皆不能殺之、屋內外皆不能、晝夜皆不能、地上空中皆不能、任何兵器皆不能。其子布羅赫拉達偏偏崇拜毘濕奴。黃昏，於門檻上，王挑釁廊柱；柱裂，毘濕奴化身獅面人那羅辛哈步出——非人非獸——以爪於膝上殺之，非地非天，非晝非夜，不用兵器。

sensitivity.note: Living tradition with major temples (Ahobilam, Simhachalam) and Narasimha Jayanti observances. Classified 'myth'.

passages.text: Hiranyakashipu, brother of the slain Hiranyaksha, performed savage austerities until Brahma, shaken, granted his boon: let me not be slain by any being created by thee - man or beast, god or demon; let me not die inside a dwelling nor outside it, neither by day nor by night, neither on the ground nor in the air; no weapon shall reach me. Armed with impossibility, he conquered the three worlds and demanded worship.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Vishnu Purana, Book 1, chs. 15-16 (Wilson 1840); not verbatim.

passages.text: His son Prahlada, from the womb, knew the Lord; taught by sages, taught by Narada, the boy answered every tutor and every torture with the name of Vishnu. His father tried poison, fire, elephants, serpents; the boy was unharmed. Asked where this Vishnu was whom he worshiped, Prahlada said: He is in the pillar, as He is in me; the king, in fury, struck the pillar with his fist.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Vishnu Purana, Book 1, chs. 16-18 (Wilson 1840); not verbatim.

passages.text: The pillar split with a sound like the world cracking, and out stepped a being never before seen: to the waist a man, below a lion, eyes like flame, a mane like midnight. Narasimha - neither man nor beast - seized the demon king at the threshold (neither inside nor out), at dusk (neither day nor night), laid him on his lap (neither ground nor sky), and opened him with his claws (no weapon), at the hour of neither day nor night. The boon survived; the king did not.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Vishnu Purana, Book 1, chs. 18-19 (Wilson 1840); not verbatim.

canonical_translation: Horace Hayman Wilson, The Vishnu Purana, London, 1840 (public domain); modern: Ludo Rocher, The Puranas, Wiesbaden, 1986

narrative.en:
The Prahlada-Narasimha cycle is the Puranas' masterpiece of the boon-and-loophole plot - the tradition's most legally literate myth, in which omnipotence is demonstrated not by raw force but by reading a contract against its grantor.

The boon: Hiranyakashipu, brother of Hiranyaksha (the earth-stealing demon killed by the boar), performs ferocious austerities on the Mandara ridge until Brahma, scorching, grants his carefully drafted immunity: he shall not be slain by any being created by Brahma; not by man or beast, god or demon; not indoors or outdoors; not by day or night; not on ground or in air; not by any weapon; not by anything living or unliving that the creator made. With invulnerability drafted into every clause, he reconquers the three worlds and replaces worship of the gods with worship of himself.

The son: Prahlada - 'delight' - is the wrong kind of child for a demon-king. Instructed in the womb by Narada (the Purana's devotional theology: the name heard before birth takes root), he returns from every schooling with one curriculum: Vishnu is everywhere, in the pillar as in me. The father's countermeasures escalate through the Purana's catalogue of horrors - poison, fire, elephants, serpent-darts - and every attempt fails because the boy's protection is the very god his father excludes. The debates between father and son are the myth's real battleground: theology argued across a throne room.

The pillar: asked by his raging father whether his Vishnu is present in this pillar, Prahlada says yes - and the king strikes the column. It splits 'with a sound like the world cracking', and out steps a being the boon's author never created: Narasimha, to the waist a man, below a lion - outside every drafted category (neither man nor beast; not created by Brahma in any named kind). The kill is staged in the remaining loopholes: at the threshold (neither inside nor outside), at dusk (neither day nor night), on the god's own lap (neither ground nor sky), torn open by claws (no weapon). Each condition of the boon is honored; the king is dead; the contract is fulfilled and destroyed at once.

Aftermath: the gods fear the new form will not calm; Prahlada is asked to pacify him, and the boy's praise (the Prahlada-charita) does so - Narasimha crowns the child king of the demons. The imagery becomes one of the great iconographies of India: Narasimha bursting from the pillar carved on temple walls everywhere, the god's fury and the child's serenity paired.

Function: the story is the charter of bhakti's absolute claim (a child's faith defeats a demon's law) and of Vishnu's preserving justice - the lord answers prayers by arriving precisely where the rules say no one can. It is also the tradition's own satire of magical thinking: the boon that banishes every named possibility is beaten by a possibility the banisher forgot to name. In the boon-curse motif cluster, Narasimha is the perfect case: the boon is honored to the letter and inverted in spirit; the law is kept, and the lawbreaker's world ends.
narrative.zh: 布羅赫拉達-獅面人循環是往世書『恩諭-漏洞』情節的傑作——傳統中最具法律素養的神話：全能不以蠻力示人，而以按合同反治授予者示人。恩諭：金輪——被野豬所誅的竊地魔金座之弟——在曼陀羅山脊行兇暴苦行，直至梵天不堪炙烤而授予其精心起草的不死性：不被梵天所造之任何存在所殺；非人非獸、非神非魔；不在屋內屋外；非晝非夜；不在地上空中；不被任何兵器所及；不被造物主所造之任何有生或無生之物所殺。每一條款皆被豁免之後，他重新征服三界，並以對自身的崇拜取代對諸神的崇拜。其子：布羅赫拉達——意為『喜悅』——是魔王最不想要的兒子。經那羅陀於胎中教授（往世書奉愛神學：出生前聞名，其名生根），他自每一次求學歸來只帶一門課程：毘濕奴無所不在，在柱中亦在我中。父親的對策在往世書的恐怖目錄中升級——毒、火、巨象、蛇鏢——每一計皆敗，因孩童的護佑正是父親所排除的那位神。父子之辯是神話真正的戰場：神學在王座廳中交鋒。廊柱：被狂怒的父親問其毘濕奴是否在此柱中，布羅赫拉達答是——王以拳擊柱。柱『如世界碎裂之聲』裂開，走出一個恩諭作者未曾創造的存在：那羅辛哈，腰以上為人、以下為獅——在每一既定範疇之外（非人非獸；非梵天以任何命名之種所造）。誅殺在剩餘的漏洞中上演：在門檻（非內非外）、在黃昏（非晝非夜）、於神之膝上（非地非天）、以爪撕裂（無兵器）。恩諭的每一條件皆被遵守；王死；合同同時被履行與摧毀。後續：諸神懼新形態不能平息；布羅赫拉達被請去安撫，孩童的讚美（布羅赫拉達頌）奏效——獅面人立孩童為魔王之王。圖像成為印度最偉大的圖像學之一：獅面人自柱中迸出，雕於處處廟牆，神之怒與孩童之靜並列。功能：此故事是奉愛絕對主張的憲章（孩童之信勝魔王之法），也是毘濕奴護持之義——主應祈禱，恰在規則說無人能至之處降臨。它亦是傳統自身的魔法思維諷刺：排除一切已命名可能性的恩諭，被遺忘者未命名的一種可能性擊敗。在恩諭-詛咒母題群中，獅面人是完美案例：恩諭被逐字遵守而在精神上被反轉；法律被遵守，而違法者的世界終結。

title.en: The Dwarf's Three Steps: Vamana and King Bali
title.zh: 侏儒的三步：筏摩那與婆利王

region.en: Thrikkakara, Kerala (Vamana temple of the Onam festival)
region.zh: 喀拉拉邦特里卡卡拉（歐南節之筏摩那神廟）

period: Vishnu Purana, Book I-II (Bali's sacrifice), c. 300-800 CE (Wilson translation, 1840)

source.work: The Vishnu Purana: A System of Hindu Mythology and Tradition, trans. H. H. Wilson (1840), Book I, chs. 18-19 and Book II (Bali and the Dwarf avatar)

summary.en: The Asura king Bali, grandson of Prahlada, has conquered the three worlds by sacrifice and virtue, and the gods are homeless. Vishnu is born as a dwarf Brahmin and comes to Bali's great sacrifice asking for three paces of ground. Laughing at the tiny gift, Bali grants it - and the dwarf grows through sky and earth, taking heaven in one stride, earth in the second, and for the third steps on Bali's head, sending him to rule the netherworld. Each year, Bali is allowed home: the Onam festival.
summary.zh: 阿修羅王婆利——布羅赫拉達之孫——以祭祀與德行征服三界，諸神遂無家可歸。毘濕奴化身侏儒婆羅門，來到婆利的大祭上求三步之地。婆利笑許這份微小禮物——侏儒遂長貫天與地，一步取天，二步取地，第三步踏於婆利之首，遣其下治冥界。每年婆利獲准回家：此即歐南節。

sensitivity.note: Living tradition: Onam is Kerala's principal festival (celebrated across communities, with its own political readings of Bali). Classified 'myth'.

passages.text: Bali, grandson of the devotee Prahlada, ruled the three worlds by the power of sacrifice; he was just, generous, and invincible. The gods, stripped of their domains, went to Vishnu; and Vishnu, to restore them without breaking the law of the gift, was born as a dwarf Brahmin, Vamana, and came, staff in hand, to the vast sacrifice Bali was performing on the banks of the Narmada.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Vishnu Purana, Book 1, chs. 18-19 (Wilson 1840); not verbatim.

passages.text: The dwarf asked for a gift: three paces of ground. Bali's preceptor, Shukra, saw the trap and warned him; Bali answered that a Brahmin asking was a gift that could not be measured by size - and made the grant, water poured from his own hand. The dwarf then grew: his head rose through the worlds, the gods assembled in his body; one stride covered heaven, the second the earth and underworlds.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Vishnu Purana, Book 1, chs. 18-19 (Wilson 1840); not verbatim.

passages.text: For the third step there was nowhere left. Bali bowed his head; Vamana placed his foot upon it and pushed the king down to Patala, the netherworld, of which he was made the lord - honored, not humiliated. Because Bali's virtue was real, Vishnu granted him the annual return: each year, on the day kept as Onam, Bali comes up to see his people, and his kingdom for a day is the world again.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Vishnu Purana, Books 1-2 (Wilson 1840); not verbatim.

canonical_translation: Horace Hayman Wilson, The Vishnu Purana, London, 1840 (public domain); modern: Ludo Rocher, The Puranas, Wiesbaden, 1986

narrative.en:
The Vamana-Bali story is the Puranas' most elegant trickster myth - a conquest undone by a gift measured in steps - and it carries the one major Hindu festival whose hero is a demon.

The setup inverts the usual order: Bali, grandson of the great devotee Prahlada, is not a villain but an exemplary king - just, learned, generous, and undefeated because his power is sacrificial merit itself. Under his rule the three worlds are governed well; the problem is bookkeeping: if the Asuras hold everything, the gods have nothing to preside over. The gods complain to Vishnu, who refuses simple conquest - Bali's merit is real and the law of the gift protects it. Vishnu's solution is to be born as a dwarf Brahmin, Vamana ('the dwarf'), and to win back the worlds through the ritual economy: by asking.

The asking is staged at Bali's own great sacrifice on the Narmada's banks. A tiny Brahmin with an umbrella and a water-pot arrives; Bali receives him with full honor and asks his wish. The request - three paces of ground - is comically small, and Bali laughs as he grants it. But Shukra, the Asuras' preceptor, recognizes the shape of the trap (in the fuller tellings, Shukra shrinks himself into the spout of the water-vessel to block the gift, and Vamana blinds him with a blade of grass to clear the spout - the trickster answering the trickster). Bali, knowing the warning and granting anyway, chooses the law of the gift over prudence: a Brahmin's request cannot be refused, and a gift's worth is not its size. The water is poured; the grant is sealed.

Then the growth: Vamana's dwarf body expands through every world - gods assembled in his limbs - and he measures. One stride takes heaven; the second takes earth and the underworlds. For the third, there is nothing left but the giver. Bali bows and offers his own head; Vamana's foot sets upon it, and the king descends to Patala - not as a punished rebel but as the honored lord of the netherworld, a king of sorts still. The worlds return to the gods without a battle and without a broken promise.

The coda is what keeps the story alive: because Bali's virtue was real, Vishnu grants him a yearly return - each year Bali comes up to visit his kingdom and his people. In Kerala this day is Onam: the harvest festival at which households lay flower carpets and a feast (onasadya) to welcome the banished king's homecoming - a demon-king, exiled by the god, celebrated as the best of rulers. The festival's politics are part of the myth's afterlife: in Kerala, Mahabali's golden age is recalled as an era of equality (the proverb: all were equal when Maveli ruled), and modern movements have read Onam as the memory of a just order displaced. The record keeps both readings.

Function: the story teaches the ritual law of the gift (a promise made is a world transferred), the dwarf-as-god theology (smallness that contains all worlds), and the ambivalence of righteous conquest. Comparative readers place it beside the trickster-wager cluster and the three-strides motif known also in Indo-European poetry (the 'three paces' of Vishnu in the Rigveda are already cosmic - the myth is an epic expansion of a Vedic image).
narrative.zh: 筏摩那-婆利故事是往世書最優雅的詭計神話——一場以步為量度的贈禮所瓦解的征服——並且承載著印度教唯一一個以惡魔為主角的重大節日。設定反轉常規：婆利，大信徒布羅赫拉達之孫，並非惡棍而是模範之王——公正、博學、慷慨，因其力量即祭祀功德本身而不可戰勝。其治下三界井然；問題在於記帳：若阿修羅擁有一切，諸神便無所司掌。諸神向毘濕奴陳情，毘濕奴拒絕簡單的征服——婆利的功德真實，贈禮之法護佑之。毘濕奴之解為化身侏儒婆羅門筏摩那（『侏儒』），透過儀式經濟以『求』奪回世界。求取在婆利於納爾默達河畔舉行的大祭上上演。持傘與水罐的小婆羅門到來；婆利以全禮接待，問其所欲。所求——三步之地——小得可笑，婆利笑而允之。但阿修羅國師尸訶認出陷阱的形狀（較全的講述中，尸訶將自己縮入水器壺嘴以阻贈禮，筏摩那以草葉蔽其目以清壺嘴——詭計者對付詭計者）。婆利明知警告而仍允，以贈禮之法取勝於謹慎：婆羅門之求不可拒，禮之價不在其量。水已傾注；許諾封印。隨後是生長：筏摩那的侏儒之身擴張貫穿諸世界——諸神聚於其肢——而後丈量。一步取天；二步取地與冥界。第三步，唯餘施與者。婆利低首獻其頭；筏摩那之足踏其上，王下至缽陀羅（Patala）冥界——非為受罰之叛逆，而為受尊的冥界之主，仍是一種之王。世界未經一戰、未破一諾而歸於諸神。尾聲使故事長存：因婆利之德真實，毘濕奴准其年年歸返——每年婆利上來探望其王國與人民。在喀拉拉，此日即歐南節（Onam）：家家鋪花毯、設盛宴（onasadya）迎接被逐之王的歸來——一位被神放逐的魔王，被尊為最優的統治者。節日的政治是神話後續的一部分：在喀拉拉，摩訶婆利的黃金時代被追憶為平等之世（諺語：瑪韋利在位時人人平等），現代運動亦將歐南讀作被取代的公正秩序之記憶。本錄並存兩種讀法。功能：故事教授贈禮的儀式法（諾成則世界易主）、侏儒即神的神學（含納一切世界之小），以及義戰的曖昧。比較讀者置之於詭計者-賭注母題群與印歐詩歌已知的『三步』意象（梨俱吠陀中毘濕奴的三步已是宇宙性的——此神話是吠陀意象的史詩擴展）。

functions: Ritual law of the gift: a granted promise transfers worlds
Dwarf-theology: smallness containing all worlds (Vedic three strides expanded)
Festival charter of Onam - the annual return of the exiled demon-king
Ambivalence of righteous conquest: merit honored even as it is displaced

title.en: Krishna Born in Prison: The Midnight Child of Mathura
title.zh: 牢中誕生的克里希那：馬圖拉的午夜之子

region.en: Mathura, Krishna Janmabhoomi (birthplace temple)
region.zh: 馬圖拉（克里希那誕生地神廟）

period: Vishnu Purana, Book V, chs. 1-4, c. 300-800 CE (Wilson translation, 1840)

source.work: The Vishnu Purana: A System of Hindu Mythology and Tradition, trans. H. H. Wilson (1840), Book V, the birth of Krishna

summary.en: The tyrant Kamsa hears a prophecy - the eighth child of his cousin Devaki will kill him - and imprisons the couple, killing each infant at birth. The eighth child is born at midnight: Vishnu himself, who shows the parents his four-armed form, instructs the father to carry him across the Yamuna to Gokula, and vanishes into the herd-boys' world while a newborn girl is surrendered to Kamsa in his place.
summary.zh: 暴君甘薩聞預言——其表妹德瓦吉之第八子將殺之——遂囚禁夫婦，於每個嬰兒誕生時親手誅之。第八子於午夜誕生：即毘濕奴本人，向父母顯示四臂之形，囑父攜其渡亞穆納河至戈庫拉，隨即隱入牧童世界；甘薩則得一名代死的新生女嬰。

sensitivity.note: Living tradition of the highest intensity (Janmashtami, Mathura-Vraja pilgrimage). Classified 'myth' (Puranic narrative rather than scripture's legal sections).

passages.text: A voice from the sky told Kamsa at the wedding of Devaki: the eighth child of this union will slay thee. Kamsa drew his sword at once; Vasudeva pleaded, offering all his children; Kamsa spared the couple but imprisoned them, and destroyed each child as it was born.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Vishnu Purana, Book 5, chs. 1-2 (Wilson 1840); not verbatim.

passages.text: At midnight on the eighth day of the dark fortnight, in the month of Bhadra, the eighth child was born - and the prison filled with light. The parents saw the newborn as Vishnu himself, four-armed, with the conch, discus, mace and lotus; the babe spoke: take me to Nanda's house in Gokula and put the girl-child just born there in my place. Vasudeva carried him through the barred doors, the guards slept, the Yamuna parted, and the exchange was made.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Vishnu Purana, Book 5, chs. 3-4 (Wilson 1840); not verbatim.

passages.text: Kamsa came for the child, seizing the girl to dash her against stone; she slipped from his hands into the sky as the goddess, prophesying: thy destroyer lives, thy death is certain. Kamsa thereupon ordered the massacre of all infants in his realm; but the child grew up in Gokula among herdsmen as Krishna, son of Nanda and Yashoda - known in the village only as a darling, dark, and fond of butter.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Vishnu Purana, Book 5, chs. 4-6 (Wilson 1840); not verbatim.

canonical_translation: Horace Hayman Wilson, The Vishnu Purana, London, 1840 (public domain); modern sourcebook: Edwin F. Bryant, Krishna: A Sourcebook, Oxford, 2007

narrative.en:
The birth of Krishna in the Vishnu Purana is the tradition's fullest miracle-birth narrative - the infant god born under a death sentence, smuggled across a river, and raised in disguise as a cowherd's child.

The prophecy: at the wedding of his cousin Devaki to Vasudeva, a voice from the sky stops Kamsa's chariot: the eighth child of this marriage will kill you. Kamsa's response is immediate tyrant-logic: he seizes the couple, and - persuaded by Vasudeva to spare them - confines them in a guarded chamber and destroys each child at birth, one by one. The Purana is unsparing: six children die at their father-uncle's hands.

The eighth child: on the eighth day of the dark fortnight (the night kept today as Janmashtami), in the rain-month Bhadra, Devaki bears the eighth child at midnight - and the dungeon fills with light. The newborn is Vishnu himself: the parents see him four-armed, bearing the conch, the discus, the mace, the lotus - and the babe speaks, instructing them in the escape he has arranged. The theology is exact: this is not a god's avatara arriving later, but the lord born knowingly, giving orders as an infant.

The escape: Vasudeva carries the child out through the locked doors - the guards sunk in sleep by divine power, the chains unfastened, the Yamuna river (in flood, in the later tellings) parting or subsiding as he crosses to the herdsman's village of Gokula. There he exchanges the infant for the girl-child just born to Yashoda, Nanda's wife, and returns to his cell with the substitute. When Kamsa comes to kill the eighth child, the girl slips from his grip, rises into the air as the goddess, and prophesies his death - the tyrant is left with a massacre decree and no victim.

The disguise: the child grows in Gokula and Vraja as Krishna - 'the dark one' - darling of the cowherds, stealing butter, laughing, suckled by Yashoda who has no idea whose son she is raising. The Purana lets the disguise run for years before the prophecy closes: Kamsa's massacre (the slaughter of infants in his realm - a detail the Christian birth narrative mirrors, as scholars from Weber onward have noted), the demon attempts (Putana the poison-nurse among them in later books), and at last the wrestling-arena confrontation where the grown Krishna kills the tyrant who ordered his death at birth.

Function: this is the master narrative of Janmashtami, kept by fast and midnight vigil across India - the devotees imitate the vigil of the prison night. Theologically it fuses the avatara doctrine with the bhakti child-god: the same lord who is the cosmic sleeper on the waters is a baby that must be smuggled and hidden - omnipotence choosing helplessness, the adult god's disguise as a vulnerable child being the religion's central emotional engine. The birth scene's comparisons are direct: across the biblical mass-slaughter birth (Ramayana's and Christian telling both), the child smuggled past a tyrant is one of the world's oldest rescue plots; the Purana's version is distinctive in making the child the author of his own escape.
narrative.zh: 毘濕奴往世書中克里希那的誕生是該傳統最完整的奇蹟誕生敘事——嬰神在死刑之下誕生、被偷渡過河、偽裝為牧童之子養大。預言：表妹德瓦吉與婆藪提婆成婚之時，天外之聲止住甘薩的車：此婚之第八子將殺你。甘薩的反應是即刻的暴君邏輯：他抓住夫婦，經婆藪提婆求情饒其性命，將其囚於守衛之室，並在每個孩子誕生時逐一誅之。往世書毫不留情：六個孩子死於這位伯父之手。第八子：於黑半月初八之夜（今日守為建摩斯陀密節之夜）、雨月巴陀羅月，德瓦吉於午夜誕下第八子——牢獄充滿光芒。新生兒即毘濕奴本人：父母見其四臂，持法螺、輪、杵、蓮——而嬰兒開口，指示他已安排好的逃亡。神學精確：非神的化身後至，而是主自知而生，以嬰兒之身下達命令。逃亡：婆藪提婆抱子穿過緊鎖之門——守衛因神力沉睡，鎖鏈自解，泛濫的亞穆納河（後世講述中）在他渡往牧村戈庫拉時分開或退落。在那裡他以嬰兒換取耶雪陀（南陀之妻）剛生的女嬰，攜替身回獄。甘薩前來誅殺第八子時，女嬰自其掌中滑出，升空化為女神，預言其死——暴君落得一道屠殺令而無受害者。偽裝：孩子以克里希那——『黑者』——之名在戈庫拉與牧區長大，牛倌的寵兒，偷酪、嬉笑，由耶雪陀哺乳，而她並不知自己養的是誰的兒子。往世書讓偽裝持續多年，直至預言閉合：甘薩的屠殺（境內嬰兒盡誅——學者自韋伯以降皆注意到此細節與基督教誕生敘事的呼應）、妖魔的試探（後卷中的毒乳女普塔那等），最終在摔角場上，長成的克里希那誅殺那位在其誕生時即下令殺他的暴君。功能：此為建摩斯陀密節（Janmashtami）的主敘事，全印以齋戒與午夜守夜守持——信徒模仿牢獄之夜的守候。神學上它熔化身 doctrine 與奉愛的兒童神：臥於水上宇宙之眠的同一主，也是必須被偷渡與藏匿的嬰孩——全能選擇無助，成年神偽裝為易受傷的孩童，是此宗教情感的核心引擎。誕生場景的比較是直接的：跨越聖經的屠嬰誕生（羅摩衍那與基督教講述皆有），被偷渡越過暴君的孩子是世界上最古老的救援情節之一；往世書版本的獨特處在於讓孩子成為自己逃亡的作者。

functions: Master narrative of Janmashtami (midnight fast and vigil across India)
Avatara doctrine fused with the bhakti child-god: omnipotence choosing helplessness
Rescue plot of the doomed child smuggled past a tyrant
Pilgrimage charter of Mathura-Vraja (Janmabhoomi and Gokula sites)

title.en: Jimutavahana Gives His Body to the Garudas
title.zh: 吉穆多伐訶那以身餵金翅鳥

region.en: Malaya mountain, Vidyadhara realm (symbolic pin in the Vindhya uplands)
region.zh: 摩羅耶山，飛天國境（象徵性定位於溫迪亞高地）

period: Kathasaritsagara of Somadeva, c. 1070 CE, Kathapitha-lambaka, tarangas 22-24 (Tawney translation, 1880)

source.work: The Katha Sarit Sagara; or, Ocean of the Streams of Story, trans. C. H. Tawney (1880), vol. 1, the story of Jimutavahana

summary.en: Jimutavahana, prince of the Vidyadharas, renounces his throne for the life of a wandering ascetic and comes to a mountain where Garudas yearly carry off a Naga to eat. Finding a weeping serpent-child bound for the feast, he takes his place in the stone trough, offers his own body, and endures the voracious bird's first bite - whereupon the Garuda stops, transformed: the age of eating Nagas ends, and the prince, restored, is married to the princess he rescued on the way.
summary.zh: 飛天國王子吉穆多伐訶那放棄王位，過雲遊苦行生活，來到一座金翅鳥每年攫食一蛇的山。見一為盛宴被縛而泣的蛇童，他代之臥於石槽，獻出自己的身體，忍受貪饞之鳥的第一啄——金翅鳥遂止，轉化：食蛇之世終結；王子復原，娶途中相救的公主。

sensitivity.note: Secular-legendary katha literature read within living Sanskrit-katha traditions; the story also exists as the Buddhist-inflected Nagananda play tradition. Classified 'myth'.

passages.text: Jimutavahana, eldest of the Vidyadhara princes, felt no joy in a throne: he gave the kingdom to his brother and set out to wander, having freed the prisoners of his father's realm and taken nothing. On his way he restored to life the son of a merchant slain by a snake, and won the love of Malayavati; then, still seeking nothing, he came with his retinue to the slopes of Malaya mountain, where he heard weeping.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Kathasaritsagara, tarangas 22-24 (Tawney 1880); not verbatim.

passages.text: The weeper was a young Naga, bound and laid in a stone trough: once in every while, he said, the Garudas carry off one of our race and eat him, and this day the lot is mine. Jimutavahana, holding compassion dearer than his own body, bound the child, carried him home to his family, and laid himself in the trough in his place, oiling his own body to make it a proper meal.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Kathasaritsagara, tarangas 22-24 (Tawney 1880); not verbatim.

passages.text: The Garuda came, great as the clouds at the world's end, and fixed his beak in the prince's shoulder; the flesh gave way, and Jimutavahana, bleeding, did not move or cry out - only prayed that his sacrifice be accepted. The bird, tasting him, stopped: this flesh is not a serpent's, he said, and learned from the dying prince who he was. The Garuda wept, restored the body with heavenly charms, and vowed before fire that no Naga should ever be seized again; the age of eating serpents ended that day.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Kathasaritsagara, tarangas 22-24 (Tawney 1880); not verbatim.

passages.text: The Nagas, led by the rescued child's father, arrived to honor the sacrifice and found their intended victim alive; the prince was healed, married Malayavati, and returned to rule - a king whose throne had been refused and whose body had been spent, and who thereby ended a whole species' predator-prey war with one act of lying still.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Kathasaritsagara, tarangas 22-24 (Tawney 1880); not verbatim.

canonical_translation: C. H. Tawney, The Katha Sarit Sagara; or, Ocean of the Streams of Story, Calcutta, 1880-84 (public domain); annotated: N. M. Penzer, The Ocean of Story, 10 vols., 1924-28

narrative.en:
Somadeva's Kathasaritsagara ('Ocean of the Streams of Story', c. 1070) is Sanskrit literature's great story-collection - a Kashmiri recasting of the Brihatkatha cycle - and among its most celebrated episodes is the self-sacrifice of Jimutavahana, a story so beloved that the playwright Harsha made it the plot of the Nagananda, and Buddhist storytellers adopted it as a Jataka-style exemplar.

The prince who refuses: Jimutavahana ('whose chariot is the clouds'), eldest son of a Vidyadhara king, is the anti-hero of inheritance: he frees all prisoners in his father's realm, hands the throne to his brother, and walks out to be a wandering ascetic 'taking nothing'. On the road the story layers its ethics: he restores to life a merchant's son dead of snakebite (compassion already outranking death), and wins - almost involuntarily - the love of the princess Malayavati, whose father offers her; the prince, pledged to renunciation, is gently maneuvered by the narrative into accepting a marriage he did not seek.

The mountain: arriving at Malaya with his retinue, he hears weeping and follows it. A young Naga - serpent-being of the underworld race - is bound in a stone trough: by covenant of long standing, the Garudas (the great golden raptor-birds, enemies of the Nagas) periodically seize one of the serpent race and eat him; this day the lot has fallen to this child. Jimutavahana's decision is made without drama: he binds the child, carries him home to his parents, and lies down in the trough himself, anointing his own body with oil 'to make it a proper meal' - the story's black-comic realism in one gesture.

The feeding: the Garuda descends, 'great as the clouds at the world's end', and drives its beak into the prince's shoulder. Flesh tears; the prince does not cry out, does not move - he prays only that his gift be accepted. The bird, mid-bite, stops: this flesh is not a serpent's. From the dying man it learns who he is, and the predator's transformation is the story's climax: the Garuda weeps, restores the torn body with celestial charms (the resurrection beat), and vows before fire that no Naga shall ever again be seized. The Nagas arrive with garlands to mourn their savior and find him alive; the covenant of predation ends in a single act of stillness.

Function: the tale is the katha literature's ethics of ahimsa dramatized - the prince's self-gift does what no battle could, ending a war between species by feeding it. It is the Hindu-courts' answer to the Buddhist Jataka of the Bodhisattva feeding himself to a tigress (the mother-tigress story): shared grammar of compassionate self-donation, resurrection, and conversion of the predator. In Penzer's annotated Ocean of Story the episode's afterlives are traced: Harsha's Nagananda play (7th c.) built a full drama on it, stage traditions in Kerala (Nagananda-based performance) and modern retellings keep it current. Within the motif clusters, the story pairs with resurrection and parable-teaching: the body given is restored, and the restored body becomes a teaching that reforms an entire race of eaters.
narrative.zh: 索摩提婆的《故事海》（kathasaritsagara，約 1070 年）是梵語文學偉大的故事集——對《大故事》循環的克什米爾重鑄——其中最受讚頌的情節之一即吉穆多伐訶那的捨身，故事如此受愛戴，以致戲劇家曷沙王以其情節作《龍喜記》（Nagananda），佛教說書人亦採之為 Jataka 式典範。拒絕王位的王子：吉穆多伐訶那（『雲為其車』），飛天國王之長子，是繼承權的反英雄：他釋放父國的所有囚犯，將王位讓與其弟，徒步出走為雲遊苦行者『一無所取』。途中故事層疊其倫理：他復活一位死於蛇咬的商人之子（慈悲已勝過死亡），並幾乎不自願地贏得公主摩羅耶伐蒂之愛；誓願出離的王子被敘事溫和地推入一場他未曾求取的婚姻。山：攜隨從至摩羅耶山，聞泣聲而循之。一位年幼的龍族（Naga）——地下蛇族——被縛於石槽：依古老盟約，金翅鳥（Garuda，蛇族之大敵）定期攫取蛇族一人食之；此日籤落此童。吉穆多伐訶那的決定毫無戲劇性：他縛起孩童，送回其父母家中，自己臥入石槽，以油塗身『使其為一頓像樣的餐食』——故事黑色喜劇式的寫實盡在一舉。餵食：金翅鳥降臨，『大如世界之末的雲』，喙入王子之肩。血肉撕裂；王子不出聲、不動——只祈他的贈禮被接受。鳥於啄食中停頓：此肉非蛇肉。自垂死者處得知其為誰，捕食者的轉化即故事的高潮：金翅鳥泣，以天界咒法復其撕裂之軀（復活節拍），並於火前立誓：蛇族永不再被攫。龍族攜花環而來哀悼其救主，卻見其生還；捕食的盟約在一次次靜止的行動中終結。功能：此篇是 katha 文學中不害（ahimsa）倫理的戲劇化——王子的捨身做了任何戰爭都做不到的事，以餵食結束兩族的戰爭。它是梵廷宮廷文學對佛教本生經中菩薩捨身餵虎母故事的回應：共享的語法是慈悲捨身、復活、捕食者的皈依。彭澤爾註釋版《故事之洋》追溯了此篇的後續：曷沙的《龍喜記》（七世紀）據此構築全劇，喀拉拉的舞台傳統（基於《龍喜記》的演出）與現代重述使其至今流傳。在母題群中，此篇與復活及譬喻說法相配：被給出的身體被復原，而復原的身體成為改革整個食者之族的教導。

functions: Ethics of ahimsa dramatized: self-gift ends a war between species
Resurrection motif in katha literature - the torn body restored and the predator converted
Hindu-court counterpart of the Buddhist self-donation Jatakas
Charter of Harsha's Nagananda play and Kerala performance tradition

variants.summary: In most Purana tellings the Garuda-Naga enmity ends by contract (elbow-shells of amrita, the wager of the stakes); the katha version ends it by sacrifice instead - law versus love.

title.en: Pwyll and Arawn: a Year in Annwn
title.zh: 普維爾與阿朗：冥界一年

region.en: Glyn Cuch, Dyved (near Narberth), Pembrokeshire, Wales
region.zh: 威爾斯彭布羅克郡納伯斯附近格林·庫赫谷

period: Recorded in the Red Book of Hergest, c. 1382-1410; Lady Charlotte Guest translation 1849

source.work: The Mabinogion, trans. Lady Charlotte Guest (1849), 'Pwyll Prince of Dyved', eBook #5160

summary.en: Pwyll, prince of Dyved, sets his dogs on a stag already killed by a pack of white hounds with red ears — the hounds of Annwn; the insulted king Arawn trades shapes with him for a year and a night, and Pwyll, ruling the otherworld in his friend's form and refusing the second blow that once undid Arawn, wins for himself the title Pwyll Pen Annwn, chief of Annwn.
summary.zh: 迪維德親王普維爾縱犬逐已被冥界白身紅耳犬群所殺之牡鹿——此為冥界之犬；受辱之王阿朗與之換形一年一夜；普維爾以阿朗之形治理冥界，拒行昔日使阿朗落敗之第二擊，贏得『冥界之首』之名。

sensitivity.note: Annwn's hounds (white, red-eared) are the standard celtic otherworld color-code; the shape-trade is the founding scene of the Mabinogi's first branch.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase of Guest 1849: As Pwyll followed his dogs he lost his companions, and heard the cry of other hounds coming in the opposite direction; in a glade they had brought down a stag, and of all the hounds he had seen in the world he had never seen any like unto these, for their hair was of a brilliant shining white and their ears were red. He drove away those that had brought down the stag and set his own dogs upon it — and a horseman on a large light-grey steed drew near and spoke: 'Chieftain, I know who thou art, and I greet thee not... Greater discourtesy saw I never in man, than to drive away the dogs that were killing the stag and to set upon it thine own.' Not verbatim.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Guest 1849; not verbatim.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase: The horseman was Arawn, a king of Annwn, and his offer was the shape-trade: 'I will send thee to Annwvyn in my stead, and I will give thee the fairest lady thou didst ever behold to be thy companion, and I will put my form and semblance upon thee... And this shall be for the space of a year from to-morrow, and then we will meet in this place.' One year from that night Arawn was fixed to meet his enemy Havgan, king of Annwvyn, at the ford: 'be thou there in my likeness, and with one stroke that thou givest him, he shall no longer live. And if he ask thee to give him another, give it not, how much soever he may entreat thee, for when I did so, he fought with me next day as well as ever before.' Not verbatim.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Guest 1849; not verbatim.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase: The year was spent in hunting, minstrelsy and feasting with Arawn's queen — the fairest woman Pwyll had ever beheld — with whom he never lay, but turned his face away night after night, and they talked till morning. At the ford the two kings met alone: at the first thrust the man in Arawn's semblance clove Havgan's shield and helmet and bore him to the ground with a deadly blow. 'What right hast thou to cause my death?... But, for the love of Heaven, since thou hast begun to slay me, complete thy work.' 'Slay thee who may, I will not do so' — and Havgan died of the single stroke, and by noon the next day both kingdoms of Annwn were in Pwyll's power. At Glyn Cuch each took back his own form, and because of the year Pwyll had ruled Annwvyn the prince of Dyved lost his name and was called Pwyll Pen Annwvyn, chief of Annwn, from that time forward. Not verbatim.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Guest 1849; not verbatim.

canonical_translation: Lady Charlotte Guest, The Mabinogion, 1849 (public domain); underlying: Pedeir Keinc y Mabinogi, Red Book of Hergest (Jesus College Oxford MS 111, c. 1382-1410); modern ed. Patrick Ford, 1977 (copyright)

narrative.en:
The first branch of the Mabinogi opens with the smallest possible discourtesy — a hunting etiquette breach — and pays it off with a year in the otherworld: the tale that makes a mortal prince ruler of the land of the dead.

Pwyll, lord of the seven cantrevs of Dyved, was at Narberth his chief palace and minded to hunt in Glyn Cuch. He let loose the dogs, and following them lost his companions — and heard the cry of other hounds coming in the opposite direction, a cry different from his own. In a level glade they brought down a stag, and Pwyll looked not at the stag but at the dogs: of all the hounds he had ever seen he had never seen any like them, for their hair was of a brilliant shining white and their ears were red. And he came toward them, drove off those that had killed the stag, and set his own dogs upon it.

A horseman came up on a large light-grey steed, horn round his neck, clad in grey hunting-wool, and greeted him in the negative: 'Chieftain, I know who thou art, and I greet thee not.' The discourtesy was total and technical: to drive off another man's hounds and set one's own on their kill. 'Though I may not be revenged upon thee, yet I declare to Heaven that I will do thee more dishonour than the value of an hundred stags.' When Pwyll asked how he might redeem the friendship, the stranger named himself: Arawn, a king of Annwn — the otherworld kingdom — and named his enemy: Havgan, another king of Annwn, ever warring against him. And Arawn proposed the shape-trade, the mabinogi's first and greatest bargain: 'I will send thee to Annwvyn in my stead... I will put my form and semblance upon thee, so that not a page of the chamber, nor an officer, nor any other man that has always followed me shall know that it is not I.' For a year and a night. Pwyll asked only what would become of his own kingdom; Arawn answered that no one in Dyved would know he was not Pwyll.

So the year passed — hunting, minstrelsy, feasting — and with one exception that the tale watches closely: Arawn's queen, the fairest woman Pwyll had ever beheld, lay beside him every night, and every night he turned his back and face away, and they talked till morning. Friendship kept, honor kept — the tale is measuring Pwyll for kingship.

At the year's end came the ford. A knight arose: 'It is between two kings that this meeting is... do all of you stand aside and leave the fight to be between them.' At the first thrust the man in Arawn's semblance clove Havgan's shield and helmet and bore him an arm's and a spear's length over the crupper of his horse. 'What right hast thou to cause my death? I was not injuring thee in anything... But, for the love of Heaven, since thou hast begun to slay me, complete thy work.' And Pwyll refused — 'slay thee who may, I will not do so' — knowing that the second blow had been Arawn's undoing: the stroke that Havgan had asked of him was the stroke that had renewed Havgan each time he gave it. Havgan died of the one stroke; the nobles submitted; and by noon the next day both kingdoms of Annwn were in Pwyll's power.

At Glyn Cuch they met and each took back his own form. Arawn found his household unknowing of any absence; Pwyll found his people praising a wisdom, kindness and justice they had never seen in him before. He told them the truth, and they said: render thanks to Heaven that thou hast such a fellowship. And by reason of that year — and of uniting the two kingdoms in one day by his valor — Pwyll lost the name of Pwyll Prince of Dyved, and was called Pwyll Pen Annwvyn, chief of Annwn, from that time forward. The otherworld had tested him with a bed he would not sleep in and a stroke he would not give, and given him a title no other mortal holds.
narrative.zh: 馬比諾吉第一支以最小的失禮開篇——一樁狩獵禮儀之失——而以彼岸之一年償付：此篇使一凡俗親王成為冥土之主。迪維德七郡之主普維爾居納伯斯主宮、欲獵於格林·庫赫谷。縱犬逐獸、失其同伴——而聞另一犬群之吠聲自相反方向而來。平坦林間空地上，彼等擊倒一牡鹿；普維爾不視鹿而視犬：生平所見獵犬無一與之相似——毛為光耀之白、耳為紅色。他趨前驅開殺鹿之犬、縱己犬於其上。一騎士乘淺灰巨駿而來，頸掛號角、衣灰色獵服，以否定的方式問候：『首領，我識得你，而不向你問好。』失禮乃技術性的全然：驅他人之犬、縱己犬於其獵物。『我雖不能向你復仇，然我向天宣示：我將予你百鹿之價以上之羞辱。』普維爾問如何贖回誼；異客自名：阿朗，冥界（Annwn）之王——並名其敵：哈夫岡，另一冥界之王，與他長年交戰。阿朗遂提議換形——馬比諾吉之第一且最偉大之交易：『我將遣你代我入冥界……我將加我之形貌於你，使我宮中侍童、官員、乃至常隨之人無一人知其非我。』為期一年一夜。普維爾惟問其本國如何；阿朗答：迪維德無人知其非普維爾。於是為期一年——狩獵、樂事、宴飲——而有一例外為故事密切注視：阿朗之后、普維爾平生所見最美之婦人，每夜與之同榻，而他每夜背身轉面、與之言談至天明。友誼得守、名節得守——此篇正在為王位稱量普維爾。歲末至渡口。一騎士起立：『此乃二王之會……爾等皆退、留二人獨鬥。』首次交擊，代阿朗之形者劈裂哈夫岡之盾與盔、將其擊落馬後一臂一矛之距。『你有何權致我死命？我未傷你分毫……既已傷我，求天之下，將我殺死、成全此事。』而普維爾拒之——『能殺你者我亦不殺』——因知昔日哈夫岡所求於阿朗之第二擊，正是每次使哈夫岡復原之擊。哈夫岡死於單擊；群臣臣服；翌日正午，冥界二國盡入普維爾之手。格林·庫赫重逢，各復己形。阿朗歸而見家人對其離去一無所覺；普維爾歸而其民稱頌前所未有之智慧、仁慈與公義。他講出真相，眾人曰：感謝上天賜你此誼。因那一年——及其一日之內以勇武聯合二國之功——普維爾失『迪維德親王』之名，自彼時起被稱為普維爾·佩恩·安努文，冥界之首。彼岸以一張他不受之床與一擊他不肯出之劍試驗了他，而授予凡人所未曾有之頭銜。

title.zh: 白馬女子與袋中獾

region.en: Gorsedd Arberth, Narberth, Pembrokeshire, Wales
region.zh: 威爾斯彭布羅克郡納伯斯阿伯斯·阿貝斯王丘

summary.en: On the mound of Gorsedd Arberth a lady on a slow white horse passes pursuers who can never close the distance; Pwyll calls out her own words and she stops — Rhiannon, fleeing a marriage she does not want — but a rash boon given at the feast hands her to Gwawl, until she engineers the bag: however much is put in it never fills, until the man of wealth treads it down, and the game of Badger-in-the-Bag is played for the first time.
summary.zh: 阿伯斯王丘上，一白馬女子緩行而來、任何追者永不能縮短距離；普維爾以其自己的話呼之，她停步——這是萊安儂，逃離不願之婚約——但宴上輕許之諾把她讓給瓜爾；她設袋之計：袋中無論放入多少永不滿，直至富有之人踏之，『袋中獾』遊戲首次上演。

sensitivity.note: Rhiannon's white horse and slow pace mark her as a sovereignty/horse-goddess figure; the mound of Gorsedd Arberth carries its own rule — whoever sits on it gets wounds or a wonder.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase of Guest 1849: Pwyll went to the top of a mound above his palace called Gorsedd Arberth, though a courtier warned that 'whosoever sits upon it cannot go thence, without either receiving wounds or blows, or else seeing a wonder.' While he sat they saw a lady on a pure white horse of large size, with a garment of shining gold, coming along the highway; and the horse moved at a slow and even pace. A rider on foot followed her, and the greater his speed the further she was from him; a horse and the swiftest in the realm followed her, and still the more he urged his horse the further was she from him, yet she held the same pace as at first. Not verbatim.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Guest 1849; not verbatim.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase: On the third day Pwyll himself rode after her and called, 'O maiden, for the sake of him whom thou best lovest, stay for me.' 'I will stay gladly, and it were better for thy horse hadst thou asked it long since.' She was Rhiannon, daughter of Heveydd Hen: 'they sought to give me to a husband against my will. But no husband would I have, and that because of my love for thee... And hither have I come to hear thy answer.' She bade him meet her in a year at the palace of Heveydd, where a feast would be prepared. At the feast a tall auburn-haired youth entered and asked as his boon the lady Pwyll loved best — Gwawl son of Clud, the very man Rhiannon was fleeing — and Pwyll's rash answer bound him. Not verbatim.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Guest 1849; not verbatim.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase: Rhiannon set the stratagem of the bag: 'See that thou keep it well... I will cause that if all the meat and liquor that are in these seven Cantrevs were put into it, it would be no fuller than before... Say thou then that it never will, until a man of noble birth and of great wealth arise and press the food in the bag with both his feet, saying, Enough has been put therein.' A year later Pwyll came in ragged garments with the bag, asked only a bagful of food, and the more was put in the emptier it stayed; Gwawl rose and trod the food down — 'and Pwyll turned up the sides of the bag, so that Gwawl was over his head in it.

passages.text: And he shut it up quickly and slipped a knot upon the thongs, and blew his horn.' His hundred knights came down and every one struck a blow upon the bag, asking 'What is here?' 'A Badger' — 'The game of Badger in the Bag' — and thus was the game of Badger in the Bag first played. Gwawl was spared for sureties and gifts to suitors and minstrels, and never sought revenge. Not verbatim.

narrative.en:
The second movement of Pwyll's mabinogi is a courtship conducted on a mound with its own law, and resolved by the earliest game in Welsh literature.

Pwyll was at Narberth, his chief palace, where a feast had been prepared, and after the first meal he arose to walk — to the top of a mound above the palace called Gorsedd Arberth. A courtier warned him of the mound's peculiarity: 'whosoever sits upon it cannot go thence, without either receiving wounds or blows, or else seeing a wonder.' 'I fear not to receive wounds and blows in the midst of such a host as this, but as to the wonder, gladly would I see it.' So he sat upon the mound — and the wonder came riding toward him: a lady on a pure white horse of large size, in a garment of shining gold, at a slow and even pace. One of his men followed her on foot, and the greater his speed the further she was from him; the next day the swiftest horse in the realms followed her and could not close the gap; she held always the same pace. On the third day Pwyll rode after her himself — and when the horse failed, he did what no pursuer had done: he used words. 'O maiden, for the sake of him whom thou best lovest, stay for me.' 'I will stay gladly,' said she, 'and it were better for thy horse hadst thou asked it long since.' The riddle of the slow pursuit is the tale's theology: the sovereignty-goddess cannot be overtaken by force or wealth, only addressed.

She threw back her head-dress and fixed her eyes on him; and the beauty of all the maidens he had ever seen was as nothing compared to her. 'My chief quest was to seek thee,' said Rhiannon, daughter of Heveydd Hen: they sought to give her to a husband against her will, but no husband would she have because of her love for Pwyll. She set the tryst: this day twelvemonth, at the palace of Heveydd, with the feast prepared.

At the feast, in the middle of the carousal, a tall auburn-haired youth of royal bearing entered and claimed his boon — the lady whom Pwyll loved best, 'with the feast and the banquet that are in this place' — and Pwyll, whose wits the Mabinogi constantly tests, had already answered 'What boon soever thou mayest ask of me, as far as I am able, thou shalt have.' The suitor was Gwawl son of Clud — the very man Rhiannon had fled. 'Never did man make worse use of his wits than thou hast done,' said Rhiannon; and she laid the counter-plot herself. 'In thy hand will I give thee a small bag... I will cause that if all the meat and liquor that are in these seven Cantrevs were put into it, it would be no fuller than before... Say thou then that it never will, until a man of noble birth and of great wealth arise and press the food in the bag with both his feet, saying, Enough has been put therein.'

A year to the night, Pwyll came to the feast in coarse ragged garments and clumsy old shoes, asking nothing but a bagful of food for his need. Attendants filled the bag, and for all they put into it it was no fuller than at first; the seven cantrevs' meat and liquor went in and the bag stayed empty; and Gwawl, at Rhiannon's prompt, rose and trod the food down with both feet. 'And Pwyll turned up the sides of the bag, so that Gwawl was over his head in it. And he shut it up quickly and slipped a knot upon the thongs, and blew his horn' — the hundred knights came down from the orchard and took the host. Every knight that entered struck a blow on the bag and asked 'What is here?' 'A Badger,' said they; and so they played, each striking it with foot or staff, and thus was the game of Badger in the Bag first played. The bagged man asked not to die in a bag; Heveydd and Rhiannon counseled mercy — let him satisfy the suitors and minstrels in Pwyll's place, with sureties never to seek revenge. Pwyll wedded Rhiannon, and Gwawl's household in the otherworld kept the account: the mabinogi's later enchantment of Dyved will be billed to the Badger in the Bag.
narrative.zh: 普維爾馬比諾吉之第二樂章，是一場於帶法之丘上進行、並以威爾斯文學中最早之遊戲化解之求婚。普維爾居納伯斯主宮，初餐之後起身而行——登上宮上名為阿伯斯·阿貝斯之丘。廷臣警告此丘之特性：『凡坐其上者，非受傷受擊不得離去，或必見奇觀。』『於此等眾人中我不怕受傷受擊，至於奇觀，我樂於一見。』他坐於丘上——奇觀騎馬而來：一女子乘純白巨馬、披光耀金衣、緩步均速而來。其一人徒步追之，愈追愈遠；翌日全境最快之馬追之，距離如故；她始終保持同一速度。第三日普維爾親自乘馬追之——當馬力竭，他做了所有追者未做之事：用語言。『姑娘，為你最愛者之故，為我停留。』『我樂於停留——你若早說，你的馬也不至於此。』緩行追逐之謎即此篇之神學：主權女神不能被武力或財富追上，只能以言語召喚。她掀開面紗、定睛看他；他所見過的一切美女之美與她相比皆為烏有。『我此行主要為尋你，』希維德·亨之女萊安儂曰：族中欲違其願將她許嫁，而她因愛普維爾不從。她定約：一年後之今日，於希維德宮中相會，宴席已備。宴中行樂之際，一高挑紅髮王儀之青年入廳索取其諾——普維爾最愛之女子『與此地之宴與酒』——而普維爾早已答過『你所能求者，凡我能給者必予』。求婚者乃瓜爾·克魯德之子——即萊安儂所逃之人。『從無男子比你的機智用得更糟，』萊安儂曰；並親自定下反計。『我將一小袋交於你手……七郡之肉與酒縱然盡入其中，亦不比先前更滿……你當答曰：永不會滿，除非一位有田產財富之貴人起身以雙足踏實袋中之食，並說：已放足了。』一年後之是夜，普維爾著襤褸舊履而來，所求不過一袋之食。侍從填袋，愈填愈空；七郡之肉酒盡入而袋如故；瓜爾應萊安儂之催促起身、以雙足踏實其食。『普維爾翻起袋緣，使瓜爾沒頂其中。他迅速束緊袋帶、打了結、吹響號角』——百騎自果園直下、擒其從眾。每位入場騎士各擊袋一記問『此為何物？』『是一隻獾』——『袋中獾之戲』——袋中獾之戲遂首次上演。袋中人求勿死於袋中；希維德與萊安儂主寬——令其在普維爾之位上款待求婚者與吟遊詩人，並具保永不復仇。普維爾娶萊安儂；而彼岸瓜爾之族記下此帳：馬比諾吉後文迪維德之魔咒，帳單正開向袋中獾。

title.en: Rhiannon's Penance and the Child in the Satin Mantle
title.zh: 萊安儂之贖罪與緞衣中之嬰孩

region.en: Narberth, Pembrokeshire, Wales
region.zh: 威爾斯彭布羅克郡納伯斯

summary.en: Six watchwomen sleep through the night the heir of Dyved is born, then frame Rhiannon for devouring her own son — blood of puppies on her face and hands; she chooses penance over contention and sits seven years by the horseblock offering to carry guests into the palace, while on Gwent the stolen boy arrives in the same May-night claw that has taken every colt, and Teirnyon finds an infant in satin where the foal should have been.
summary.zh: 迪維德繼承人誕生之夜，六名守望婦女酣睡，事後誣萊安儂食其親子——以幼犬之血塗其面手；她選擇贖罪而非爭辯，於馬石旁坐七年、願背訪客入宮；同時在格溫特，被竊之嬰於五月之夜爪中抵達——特尼昂於本應得駒之處發現緞衣嬰孩。

sensitivity.note: The May-eve claw and the vanished foals are the Welsh mabinogi's version of the changeling/sacred-birth complex; Rhiannon's penance is the famous 'I will carry them on my back' image.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase of Guest 1849: Before the end of a year a son was born to Pwyll and Rhiannon at Narberth, and on the night that he was born six women were brought to watch the mother and the boy; before midnight every one of them fell asleep, and towards break of day they awoke and looked where they had put the boy, and behold he was not there. One counselled: 'There is here a stag-hound bitch, and she has a litter of whelps. Let us kill some of the cubs, and rub the blood on the face and hands of Rhiannon, and lay the bones before her, and assert that she herself hath devoured her son, and she alone will not be able to gainsay us six.' Not verbatim.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Guest 1849; not verbatim.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase: Rhiannon asked only for the truth, promising to defend them if they feared; the women held to their lie, and the story went throughout the land, and the nobles besought Pwyll to put away his wife. He answered that they had no cause save her having no children: 'But children has she now had, therefore will I not put her away; if she has done wrong, let her do penance for it.' The penance was that she should remain at Narberth to the end of seven years, sit every day near the horseblock without the gate, tell the story to all who came, and offer to carry guests and strangers on her back into the palace — but it rarely happened that any would permit. Not verbatim.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Guest 1849; not verbatim.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase: Teirnyon Twryv Vliant of Gwent Is Coed had a mare that foaled on the night of every first of May and whose colts always vanished; he armed and watched, and the mare foaled a large colt — then a claw came through the window and seized it by the mane, and Teirnyon struck off the arm at the elbow; tumult and wailing followed, and rushing out he came back to find at his door an infant boy in swaddling-clothes wrapped in a mantle of satin, very strong for his age. His wife called him Gwri Wallt Euryn for his gold hair; he grew faster than any child, and was given the colt saved the night he was found. Hearing of Rhiannon's punishment, Teirnyon saw in the boy a great likeness to Pwyll, went to Narberth, and refused the offered back: 'Think not that I will be one to be carried upon thy back.' At the feast he restored the boy — 'and whosoever told that lie concerning thee, has done wrong' — and Pendaran Dyved named him Pryderi, from the word his mother spoke when she received the joyful tidings. Not verbatim.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Guest 1849; not verbatim.

canonical_translation: Lady Charlotte Guest, The Mabinogion, 1849 (public domain); underlying: Pedeir Keinc y Mabinogi, Red Book of Hergest

narrative.en:
The birth of Pryderi is the Mabinogi's darkest domestic scene and its tenderest restoration: a queen libeled for cannibalism, a penance of patience, and a stolen child returned by the very claw that steals colts.

For two years Pwyll and Rhiannon ruled prosperously, and in the third the nobles grew sorrowful at having no heir. Pwyll asked a year; before it was out a son was born at Narberth, and on the night of his birth six women were brought to watch the mother and the boy. Before midnight every one of them slept, and toward break of day they awoke and the boy was not there. And they took counsel: 'There is here a stag-hound bitch, and she has a litter of whelps. Let us kill some of the cubs, and rub the blood on the face and hands of Rhiannon, and lay the bones before her, and assert that she herself hath devoured her son, and she alone will not be able to gainsay us six.' Rhiannon, waking, asked only where her son was; they told her she had struggled with them violently — 'hast thou not thyself devoured thy son?' She promised to defend them if they spoke from fear; they held to the lie. The story went through the land, the nobles besought Pwyll to put her away, and Pwyll answered with the law: they had no cause but childlessness, 'but children has she now had, therefore will I not put her away; if she has done wrong, let her do penance for it.'

Rhiannon chose penance over contention, and the penance was seven years at Narberth: every day she sat near the horse-block outside the gate, told her own story to strangers, and offered to carry them into the palace on her back — 'but it rarely happened that any would permit.' The great queen who rode a slow white horse past all pursuers now sits at a mounting-block waiting to carry men: the sovereignty of the land turned upside down by six liars.

Meanwhile in Gwent Is Coed, Teirnyon Twryv Vliant kept a mare than which none in the kingdom was more beautiful — and on the night of every first of May she foaled, and no one ever knew what became of the colt. One May night Teirnyon armed himself and watched. The mare foaled a large and beautiful colt; then he heard a great tumult, and a claw came through the window and seized the colt by the mane; Teirnyon drew his sword and struck off the arm at the elbow, so that the arm and the colt were in the house with him. Tumult and wailing followed; he rushed out after the noise — and remembered he had left the door open — and returned to find at his door an infant boy in swaddling-clothes, wrapped in a mantle of satin, and very strong for his age. His wife, who had never had a child, took the boy and feigned pregnancy; they baptized him Gwri Wallt Euryn, for the hair on his head was as yellow as gold, and he grew faster than any child in the world — at a year old he walked stoutly, before his fourth year he was bribing grooms to let him water the horses. And the colt, saved the night he was found, was broken in and given to the boy: each the twin of the other's deliverance.

When Teirnyon heard the tale of Rhiannon's penance, he looked steadfastly on the boy and saw the greatest likeness between father and son he had ever beheld — for he had of old been Pwyll's follower. Grieved at keeping another man's son while so excellent a lady was punished, he rode to Narberth with two knights, and Rhiannon rose beside the horse-block: 'go not further thus, I will bear every one of you into the palace, and this is my penance for slaying my own son and devouring him.' 'Oh, fair lady,' said Teirnyon, 'think not that I will be one to be carried upon thy back.' 'Neither will I,' said the boy. At the feast Teirnyon set the boy before Rhiannon: 'And behold here is thy son, lady. And whosoever told that lie concerning thee, has done wrong.' Pendaran Dyved gave the name: Pryderi — 'care, anxiety' — from the word his mother spoke when she received the joyful tidings; and thus ended the penance of Rhiannon and the secret nursling of Gwent.
narrative.zh: 普里德里誕生乃馬比諾吉最黑暗之家庭場景與最溫柔之復和：一位被誣食人的王后、一場以耐心行之贖罪、以及一個由偷駒之爪親手送回的被竊嬰孩。普維爾與萊安儂興治兩年；第三年貴族憂無嗣。普維爾求一年；未及滿年一子誕於納伯斯，誕生之夜六名婦女受命守護母子。午夜前人人入睡；天將明醒來，嬰孩不見。她們合謀：『此處有獵犬母犬及其幼犬。殺數隻幼犬、以血塗萊安儂之面與手、置骨於其前、堅稱她親自食其子——她一人無法反駁我們六人。』萊安儂醒來只問兒子何在；她們答其曾暴力掙扎——『你豈非自己食了兒子？』她許諾若因懼而說則必護她們；她們堅持謊言。消息傳遍全境，貴族請普維爾休妻，普維爾以法答之：除無子外別無理由休妻——『而今她有子，故我不休她；若她有過，令其贖罪。』萊安儂擇贖罪而非爭辯：納伯斯七年，每日坐於門外馬石旁、向來客講述自己的故事、並願背訪客入宮——『然極少有人允許。』曾騎白馬勝過一切追逐者的偉大女王，如今坐於上馬石旁等待背負男子：六名說謊者把土地的主權翻了過來。同時在格溫特伊斯科德，特尼昂·圖里夫·弗利安特畜一匹王國最美的母馬——每年五月朔夜產駒、而駒總是消失。一夜特尼昂披甲守候。母馬產下一匹大而美的駒；隨即他聞巨響，一爪自窗入、抓住駒鬣；特尼昂拔劍自肘部斬落其臂——斷臂與駒皆在屋內。喧嚷與哀哭隨之；他循聲衝出——記起門未關——回來時門邊有一襁褓嬰孩、裹緞衣、體力遠超其齡。從未育子的妻子收下男嬰、佯稱懷孕；為其洗禮命名格維·瓦爾特·尤林，因其髮黃如金；其成長快過世上任何孩童——一歲穩步、四歲前已賄馬伕牽馬飲水。而被救之夜所產之駒經馴後賜予此孩：各為彼此解救之雙生。特尼昂聞萊安儂贖罪之事，凝視男孩、見生平所未見之父子相似——因他昔日曾是普維爾隨從。為另一人之子而令賢后受罰，他不忍，遂偕二騎至納伯斯；萊安儂起身於馬石旁：『莫再前行，我願背爾等入宮，此乃我食親子之贖罪。』『美后，』特尼昂曰，『我斷不會讓你背負。』『我也不會，』男孩曰。宴上特尼昂置男孩於萊安儂前：『看，這是你的兒子，夫人。凡造此謊者，行不義。』彭達蘭·迪維德命名：普里德里——『憂念』——出自其母得喜訊時所說之詞；萊安儂之贖罪與格溫特之密養至此終結。

title.en: Branwen, the Cauldron of Rebirth and the Warring of Two Islands
title.zh: 布蘭溫、再生之釜與二島之戰

region.en: Aberffraw, Anglesey, Wales (wedding seat of the alliance)
region.zh: 威爾斯安格爾西島阿伯弗勞（聯姻之地）

summary.en: Matholwch king of Ireland weds Branwen to league Ireland with the Island of the Mighty; Evnissyen mutilates the wedding horses, the insult is paid with horses and the cauldron of rebirth, and still the foster-brothers dishonor Branwen — cook and daily blow on the ear — until she teaches a starling to carry her letter across the sea, and Brân walks the ocean with his fleet as a wood on the water.
summary.zh: 愛爾蘭王馬索爾奇娶布蘭溫以聯盟二島；埃文尼森殘害婚馬，以馬匹與再生之釜賠罪，而其乳兄弟仍辱布蘭溫——命其烹飪、每日批頰一記——直至她訓練椋鳥攜書渡海，白蘭徒步渡洋、其艦隊如海上之林。

sensitivity.note: The cauldron of rebirth (reviving the dead but mute) is the Mabinogi's central resurrection technology; the starling-letter is the cycle's most famous message-device.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase of Guest 1849: Matholwch king of Ireland sailed thirteen ships to Harlech to ask Branwen the daughter of Llyr, one of the three chief ladies of the island, that the Island of the Mighty might be leagued with Ireland. She was wedded to him at Aberffraw. But Evnissyen, the half-brother who would cause strife between his brothers when they were most at peace, 'rushed under the horses and cut off their lips at the teeth, and their ears close to their heads, and their tails close to their backs, and wherever he could clutch their eyelids, he cut them to the very bone, and he disfigured the horses and rendered them useless.' Matholwch left in anger, and atonements were made: a sound horse for every horse injured, a staff of silver as large and tall as himself, a plate of gold of the breadth of his face — and Branwen's counsel added the cauldron: 'the property of which is, that if one of thy men be slain to-day, and be cast therein, to-morrow he will be as well as ever he was at the best, except that he will not regain his speech.' Not verbatim.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Guest 1849; not verbatim.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase: In Ireland the foster-brothers of Matholwch rose in tumult over the insult, and the vengeance they took was 'to drive away Branwen from the same chamber with him, and to make her cook for the Court; and they caused the butcher after he had cut up the meat to come to her and give her every day a blow on the ear.' Ships and ferries were forbidden to Cambria for three years, that the thing be not known there. Branwen reared a starling in the cover of the kneading-trough, taught it to speak and to know her brother, wrote a letter of her woes and bound it to the root of the bird's wing; it found Brân at Caer Seiont in Arvon and alighted on his shoulder. He summoned sevenscore and four countries and sailed for Ireland — and his host appeared to the swineherds as a wood upon the sea, a mountain moving beside it, with a ridge between two lakes: the fleet's masts, Brân wading to the shore, and his two eyes wroth. Not verbatim.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Guest 1849; not verbatim.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase: The Irish broke the bridge over the Llinon and Brân said: 'he who will be chief, let him be a bridge. I will be so' — and lay down across the river, hurdles upon him, the host passing over. Peace was made in a great house built to contain him; but the Irish had hung leathern bags on each side of the hundred pillars with an armed man in each, and Evnissyen went the rounds feeling the bags — 'Meal, good soul' — and crushed every hidden head but one. At the peace feast he seized the boy Gwern by the feet and thrust him into the blazing fire; Branwen strove to leap in after her son, and Brân grasped her between shield and shoulder.

passages.text: The Irish kindled fire under the cauldron of renovation and cast their dead into it, and next day they came forth fighting-men as good as before, except that they could not speak. Evnissyen, seeing the men of the Island of the Mighty nowhere resuscitated, cast himself among the Irish dead, and was flung into the cauldron — and he stretched himself out in it and rent it into four pieces, and burst his own heart also. Only seven men of the Island of the Mighty escaped, and Brân himself was wounded in the foot with a poisoned dart. Not verbatim.
