region.en: Rasa, the far stream (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 羅娑，遠方之流（象徵性定位）

period: Rigveda, Books 1, 3, 10 (Griffith translation, 1896)

source.work: The Hymns of the Rigveda, trans. R. T. H. Griffith (1896), hymns naming Matarishvan (1.93, 3.29, 10.181)

summary.en: In the age before worship, the sacrificial fire lay hidden far away, kept among the waters by Ahi, the greedy watcher. The seer Matarishvan went, found the hidden flame where the great snake guarded it, and bore it to Bhrigu and Angiras, who first set it among men - the Vedic fire-theft that made worship possible.
summary.zh: 祭祀之火太古時遠藏他方，由貪守者阿希護於水中。仙人摩達利濕梵尋得藏於巨蛇守衛之處的隱焰，攜歸交予弗利伊與盎耆羅，二人首置火於人間——吠陀之盜火，使祭祀成為可能。

sensitivity.note: Ancient hymn; classified 'myth'. Fire-theft motif tag is a Euro-American index category - noted.

passages.text: In the earlier ages the god's flame lay hidden, withheld: it shone far off in the water, and the snake Ahi, the greedy one, kept guard over it where no worshipper could reach. Then the seer Matarishvan went where the fire lay hidden, passed the watcher, laid hold of the flame, and bore it back to the race of Bhrigu and Angiras, the first priests.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Rigveda hymns to Matarishvan (Griffith 1896); not verbatim.

passages.text: Bhrigu and Angiras set the fire among men and made from it the first offerings; by that flame the gods came to eat the sacrifice, and men came to speak with heaven. Every hearth lit since is a descendant of that stolen, carried light.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Rigveda hymns to Matarishvan (Griffith 1896); not verbatim.

canonical_translation: Ralph T. H. Griffith, 1896 (public domain)

title.en: The Miraculous Birth of Indra
title.zh: 因陀羅的奇蹟誕生

region.en: Punjab plains (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 旁遮普平原（象徵性定位）

period: Rigveda, Books 2, 8 (Griffith translation, 1896)

source.work: The Hymns of the Rigveda, trans. R. T. H. Griffith (1896), hymns on Indra's birth (2.12, 8.45, 10.73)

summary.en: Indra is born sidewise from his mother's flank so as not to be born normally - for he is already drunk with strength. He drinks the Soma his mothers offer, fills both worlds with his body, and before his first day is out has seized the thunderbolt and declared heaven and earth to be his.
summary.zh: 因陀羅自母體側腹斜出而生，非循常道——因其力已醉滿。他飲母親們獻上的蘇摩，軀體撐滿兩界，未滿一日已握雷霆杵，宣稱天地皆屬於他。

sensitivity.note: Ancient hymn; classified 'myth'.

passages.text: No ordinary womb could hold Indra; he turned himself as he was born and came out by his mother's side, and the mothers of the god stood about him offering the pressed Soma before he could even stand. He drank the Soma and grew - a body that filled two worlds; he overshadowed the sky and trod the earth, and the gods fled before their own newborn king until they set him at the head of all.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Rigveda hymns on Indra's birth (Griffith 1896); not verbatim.

passages.text: On the day of his birth he took the thunderbolt, made the sister-rivers flow, and slew the serpent - so the hymn compresses his whole career into his birthday: the king who does everything at once, before his first morning is over.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Rigveda hymns on Indra's birth (Griffith 1896); not verbatim.

canonical_translation: Ralph T. H. Griffith, 1896 (public domain)

title.en: The Maruts, the Howling Storm-Boys
title.zh: 摩魯多：呼嘯的風暴兄弟

region.en: Punjab plains (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 旁遮普平原（象徵性定位）

period: Rigveda, Books 1, 5, 8 (Griffith translation, 1896)

source.work: The Hymns of the Rigveda, trans. R. T. H. Griffith (1896), hymns to the Maruts (e.g. 1.85, 5.54, 8.20)

summary.en: The Maruts are the storm-brigade of young gods - spearmen with lightning in their fists, deer-clad, who tear up trees, split mountains, and can barely be distinguished from their own thunder. They follow Indra to his fights and howl like newborn lions; Rudra their father disowns their manners but not their worship.
summary.zh: 摩魯多為風暴青年兵團——持雷於拳、披鹿皮而鬧，拔樹裂山，其咆哮幾乎與雷聲難分。他們隨因陀羅赴戰，吼如新生的獅群；其父樓陀羅斥其行徑而未拒其崇拜。

sensitivity.note: Ancient hymn; classified 'myth'.

passages.text: They come as a cohort, not as a king: spears of light in their hands, golden breastplates, deerskins on their backs, and voices that break the frame of the sky. Where they go the trees are torn up by the roots and the mountains are carved like soft wood.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Rigveda hymns to the Maruts (Griffith 1896); not verbatim.

passages.text: They are the youths of Rudra the howler, and they take after their father; yet even Rudra is said to have disowned the manner of their birth - the hymn-writers joke that a god so disciplined has sons so unruly. With Indra they are invincible: the storm-king and his storm-brigade clear the sky of serpents and open the rains. Their favor is asked like the favor of weather itself, for they are the monsoon's own retinue.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Rigveda hymns to the Maruts (Griffith 1896); not verbatim.

canonical_translation: Ralph T. H. Griffith, 1896 (public domain)

title.en: Varuna's Thousand Ropes
title.zh: 伐樓那的千索

region.en: Punjab plains (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 旁遮普平原（象徵性定位）

period: Rigveda, Books 1, 7 (Griffith translation, 1896)

source.work: The Hymns of the Rigveda, trans. R. T. H. Griffith (1896), hymns to Varuna (e.g. 1.25, 7.86, 7.88)

summary.en: Varuna, king of the order of things, watches with spies the thousand witnesses he has set in heaven, and binds liars with a thousand ropes. The sinner Varuna's own poet sings his debt - 'not wilfully, but wine and dice and anger undid me' - and begs the god who fetters the guilty to loose the fetter.
summary.zh: 伐樓那，萬物秩序之王，以天中所置的千名見證者與密探監視，以千索縛謊者。詩人自詠其罪——『非有心，乃酒與骰與怒毀我』——乞那位縛罪者的神親手解索。

sensitivity.note: Ancient hymn; classified 'myth'.

passages.text: Varuna has numbered the breaths and winkings of men, set a thousand watchers over the lie, and placed his spies in heaven; his cords are said to be a hundred in his seat, a thousand as they go down the roads - whoever they seize shall not slip free.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Rigveda hymns to Varuna (Griffith 1896); not verbatim.

passages.text: The confession-hymns give Varuna a sinner's own voice: I told the lie, not wilfully - wine and dice and anger undid me; my elders erred, and I erred after them. O god, let not the stone break me, as a man breaks a dish.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Rigveda hymns to Varuna (Griffith 1896); not verbatim.

passages.text: The answer sought is not battle but release: loosen the bond that holds me, and my sin shall not again be found; and the poet dreams of going to Varuna's house to see the wise king whose order keeps the rivers running and the stars from straying.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Rigveda hymns to Varuna (Griffith 1896); not verbatim.

canonical_translation: Ralph T. H. Griffith, 1896 (public domain)

title.en: Ushas, the Awakener of Mankind
title.zh: 烏莎斯，人類的喚醒者

region.en: Punjab plains (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 旁遮普平原（象徵性定位）

period: Rigveda, Books 1, 7, 10 (Griffith translation, 1896)

source.work: The Hymns of the Rigveda, trans. R. T. H. Griffith (1896), hymns to Ushas (e.g. 1.113, 7.77, 10.73)

summary.en: Every dawn the goddess Ushas drives the same red-heifer chariot over the same road, and every dawn she is praised as if brand new - the hymns admit the joke: she is the 'old one' worshipped young, sister of Night, rival of the Sun, awakened by the priests' songs before the birds.
summary.zh: 每逢黎明，女神烏莎斯駕同一輛紅牛之車行同一條路，而每個黎明都被讚為嶄新——頌詩自承這一玩笑：她是『古老者』以青春受拜，夜之姊妹，日之勁敵，先於群鳥被祭司的歌聲喚醒。

sensitivity.note: Ancient hymn; classified 'myth'.

passages.text: Dawn comes to wake the world: she drives her bright heifer-car over the dark road, shakes open the closed eye of the sky, and the sleepers wake and the birds rise from their nests to sing before her. The hymns dare a human honesty: she is the old goddess come back with a new face - the same one we praised at every yesterday, and she goes before the Sun like a bride before a lord, or dances out of the east like a dancer out of the house.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Rigveda hymns to Ushas (Griffith 1896); not verbatim.

passages.text: Her power is mortal time itself: she extends the life of men, sets the many days upon their way, and casts down darkness as a matron casts out a drunkard; one dawn, the singers say, is worth all the nights of hoarded gold.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Rigveda hymns to Ushas (Griffith 1896); not verbatim.

canonical_translation: Ralph T. H. Griffith, 1896 (public domain)

title.en: Sarasvati, the Great River and the Word
title.zh: 薩拉斯瓦蒂：大河與言語

region.en: Sarasvati river course (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 薩拉斯瓦蒂河道（象徵性定位）

period: Rigveda, Books 2, 6, 10 (Griffith translation, 1896)

source.work: The Hymns of the Rigveda, trans. R. T. H. Griffith (1896), hymns to Sarasvati (e.g. 2.41, 6.61, 10.75 river hymn)

summary.en: Sarasvati is addressed as a real river - roaring from the mountains' ice, breaking ridges 'like a verdant elephant-horn', mightier than all other waters - and at the same time as the goddess of the Word that flows from the speaker's mouth. The river that later dried is the goddess that never did.
summary.zh: 薩拉斯瓦蒂被稱呼為真實的河流——自群山冰隙咆哮而下，『如青翠象牙』裂開山脊，壯於眾水——同時亦是自說者之口流出的言語女神。後來枯竭的河，成了永不枯竭的女神。

sensitivity.note: Ancient hymn; classified 'myth'.

passages.text: Sarasvati, mightiest of rivers, flows roaring from the mountains with the flood of her ice, breaking the ridges of the hills like a pierced elephant's tusk, a very army of waters going down to the sea. She is asked to enrich the sacrifice: come with thy floods, dear one, that our singers may be like rain-fed corn; she grants wealth, offspring and fame, and she is the mother of the Word itself. The same name runs through the tradition: the goddess of speech who later carries the veena, and the river whose dry bed stretches across the northwest plains - the geography the hymns loved and the language remembers.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Rigveda hymns to Sarasvati (Griffith 1896); not verbatim.

canonical_translation: Ralph T. H. Griffith, 1896 (public domain)

title.en: Rudra, the Howler of the Mountains
title.zh: 樓陀羅：山間的呼嘯者

region.en: Punjab plains (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 旁遮普平原（象徵性定位）

period: Rigveda, Books 1, 2, 7 (Griffith translation, 1896)

source.work: The Hymns of the Rigveda, trans. R. T. H. Griffith (1896), hymns to Rudra (e.g. 1.43, 1.114, 2.33)

summary.en: Rudra is the dangerous god: strong bow, hundred-faced darts, dogs with frightening mouths, dwelling in the mountains. The hymns are half praise, half bargaining - 'spare us, smite not us or our cattle; pass by us with thy felicity' - the first shape of the god who becomes Shiva.
summary.zh: 樓陀羅是危險之神：強弓、百面之鏢、嘴可畏的犬、居於群山。頌詩半為讚美，半為討價——『饒恕我們，勿擊我與我畜；攜吉慶繞過我們』——這就是後來成為濕婆之神的最初形態。

sensitivity.note: Ancient hymn; classified 'myth'.

passages.text: Rudra of the mountains, the strong one with the fair-limbed bow, has arrows that are sickness and darts that are fevers; his messengers are dogs with terrifying mouths, and his company walks the wild passes with him. The hymn prays like a neighbor soothing a temper: oh, divinity, be kind; spare us, injure not our strong steed nor our ram nor our offspring; put far from us thy bolt of heaven and thy stone of earth. But the danger is also medicine: he is the healer whose hand both strikes and cures, lord of herbs in the hill-forests, and the fierce god praised most sweetly becomes in the later tradition Shiva, the gracious one.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Rigveda hymns to Rudra (Griffith 1896); not verbatim.

canonical_translation: Ralph T. H. Griffith, 1896 (public domain)

title.en: Soma, the God That Is a Drink
title.zh: 蘇摩：即是飲料的神

region.en: Mujuvant mountains (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 木周萬特山（象徵性定位）

period: Rigveda, Book 9 (Soma Mandala) and others (Griffith translation, 1896)

source.work: The Hymns of the Rigveda, trans. R. T. H. Griffith (1896), Book 9, hymns to Soma Pavamana

summary.en: The Soma hymns praise the plant as it is pressed: the god filtered through sheep's wool, roaring as he runs, cleaning himself like a horse washed in a river. He is the drink that makes gods immortal and poets invincible - Indra's ammunition - and the whole ninth book is a single day's brewing turned into liturgy.
summary.zh: 蘇摩頌讚那正在榨汁的植物：神經羊毛衣而濾清，奔流時如雷而吼，如河浴之馬自淨。他是使諸神不死、使詩人無敵的飲料——因陀羅的彈藥——第九冊整卷即把一日的榨釀化作禮儀。

sensitivity.note: Ancient hymn; classified 'myth'.

passages.text: The Soma is brought down from the mountains in carts; it is pressed between stones, filtered through the sheep's wool, and as it streams it is called Pavamana, the flowing clear one - the god washing himself as he runs.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Rigveda Book 9 hymns (Griffith 1896); not verbatim.

passages.text: He mounts the sky as he flows: he begets light, sets the dawns in motion, drives the Sun upon his way, and puts strength into Indra's arms for the next serpent-slaying. The theology is intoxication made cosmic: whoever drinks of the pressed god becomes a seer; Indra himself grew so great on Soma that he filled two worlds - the hymns are the liturgy of a sacrament that means what it does.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Rigveda Book 9 hymns (Griffith 1896); not verbatim.

canonical_translation: Ralph T. H. Griffith, 1896 (public domain)

title.en: Mitra and Varuna: The Twin Upholders
title.zh: 密多羅與伐樓那：雙位撐持者

region.en: Punjab plains (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 旁遮普平原（象徵性定位）

period: Rigveda, Books 3, 5, 7 (Griffith translation, 1896)

source.work: The Hymns of the Rigveda, trans. R. T. H. Griffith (1896), dual hymns to Mitra-Varuna (e.g. 3.59, 5.62, 7.64)

summary.en: The twin sovereigns of the Vedic heaven: Mitra the friendship, Varuna the bond - together they prop the sky, direct the rivers, and sit as judges over oath and truth. Their shared hymns describe two kings of one law, one of them sovereign of the waters' deep and the other of the compact between men.
summary.zh: 吠陀天界的雙位君主：密多羅為友誼，伐樓那為盟約——同撐天穹、導引河流，並為誓言與真理之判官。其合頌描繪同一法律下的二王：一位為深水之主，一位為人際契約之王。

sensitivity.note: Ancient hymn; classified 'myth'.

passages.text: Mitra, when he speaks, stirs men to labor and to friendship; Varuna, when he decrees, holds the bound by their bonds. Together the two uphold the sky and the earth, and the hymns address them as one kingship with two names.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Rigveda dual hymns (Griffith 1896); not verbatim.

passages.text: They made the streams run to the sea, set the Sun upon his high road, and look down upon the dealings of men: the oath-breaker and the promise-keeper alike arrive at their seat, and the pair are invoked over every covenant. In the later spread of the god-language Mitra travels west - the Persian contract-god, the Roman Mithras - but in the Vedic home the two are the law's own face: order as friendship, order as fetter.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Rigveda dual hymns (Griffith 1896); not verbatim.

canonical_translation: Ralph T. H. Griffith, 1896 (public domain)

title.en: The Two Dogs of the Dead
title.zh: 亡者的雙犬

region.en: Yama's pasture road (symbolic pin at Gaya)
region.zh: 閻摩牧野之路（象徵性定位於伽耶）

period: Rigveda, Book 10 (Griffith translation, 1896)

source.work: The Hymns of the Rigveda, trans. R. T. H. Griffith (1896), Book 10, hymns 14, 135-136 (the dogs of Yama)

summary.en: On the path to Yama's pasture two four-eyed, broad-nosed dogs guard the road of the departed, dark of hue, with Sarama the divine bitch for their mother. The funeral hymns ask them to be lenient - to let the father through to the company of the old ones - while the dead man is sent ahead with gifts for the gate-keepers.
summary.zh: 通往閻摩牧野之路上，兩隻四眼闊鼻的犬守衛亡者之路，色暗，母親為神犬薩羅摩。葬歌求它們寬待——放父親入古者之群——死者則被先行差遣，攜禮物賄賂守門者。

sensitivity.note: Ancient funeral hymn; classified 'myth'.

passages.text: Run forward along the ancient paths, the hymn tells the dead man, where our forefathers have gone: there the two kings Yama and Varuna keep their seat, and the two dogs, the four-eyed ones, watch the path. The dogs are described by their mouths: broad-nosed, dark of body, drawn from the divine Sarama - one takes the black, one the parti-colored; they sit at Yama's city and lick at the lot of the dead.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Rigveda 10.14 (Griffith 1896); not verbatim.

passages.text: The offering is practical theology: give these two dogs of thine, O father, thy rice and thy cake - they watch the road of the fathers - and then enter, with the old ones and their flocks, to the pasture of delight.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Rigveda 10.14 (Griffith 1896); not verbatim.

canonical_translation: Ralph T. H. Griffith, 1896 (public domain)

title.en: The Coming of Finn: the Boy in the Wood and the Burning of Teamhair
title.zh: 芬恩之來臨：林中之童與塔拉大火

region.en: Slieve Bladhma (Slieve Bloom), Offaly/Laois, Ireland
region.zh: 愛爾蘭奧法利/萊斯郡斯利夫·布拉德瑪山（布盧姆山）

period: Fenian cycle (Fianaigecht), medieval Irish MSS; Gregory retelling 1904

source.work: Lady Augusta Gregory, Gods and Fighting Men (1904), Book One: Finn, Chapter I, eBook #14465

summary.en: Born after his father Cumhal is killed by the sons of Morna, the boy Demne is nursed in secret in the woods of Slieve Bladhma, trained by two women druids in running, leaping and swimming, given the name Finn — the Fair — at a swimming match, finds the crane-skin treasure-bag of Manannan, eats the salmon of knowledge at the Boinn, and keeps Teamhair safe for a night from Aillen of the Sídhe by holding a spear against his forehead until sleep cannot come — winning the headship of the Fianna from Goll's own hand.
summary.zh: 其父庫哈爾死於莫爾納諸子之手後出生的男孩德姆內，被秘密撫養於斯利夫·布拉德瑪山中；兩位女德魯伊訓練其跑、跳、泳；因游泳比賽得『芬恩』（俊美）之名；尋得瑪南南之鶴皮寶袋；於博因河食智慧之鮭；以矛抵額不眠、守塔拉整夜不被西德之艾倫焚毀——自戈爾之手贏得費恩納之首。

sensitivity.note: The salmon of knowledge episode overlaps the existing base record salmon-knowledge; this record cuts the whole coming-of-age arc, with the Aillen fire-fight as its climax. Finn's thumb of knowledge is the Fenian cycle's signature.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase of Gregory 1904: At the time Finn was born his father Cumhal of the sons of Baiscne, Head of the Fianna of Ireland, had been killed in battle by the sons of Morna that were fighting with him for the leadership; and his mother, beautiful long-haired Muirne, daughter of Tadg, son of Nuada of the Tuatha Dé Danann, did not dare to keep him with her; and two women, Bodhmall the woman Druid and Liath Luachra, came and brought him away to the woods of Slieve Bladhma and nursed him secretly. They gave him good training: one would run round a tree with a thorn switch, Finn after her with another switch; they left him in a field with hares and bid him not let the hares quit the field; to teach him swimming they threw him into the water and let him make his way out. Not verbatim.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Gregory 1904, Book One ch. 1; not verbatim.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase: Swimming against the lads of Magh Life, 'Fair he is and well shaped,' they said, and it was from that time he got the name of Finn, that is, Fair. He won seven games of chess from the king his mother had married, who guessed his blood and warned him away; he avenged a woman whose son had been killed, killing the champion who had given Cumhal his first wound, and took back the treasure-bag of crane-skin that had been Manannan's — Manannan's shirt and knife, Goibniu's belt and smith's hook, the shears of the King of Alban, the helmet of the King of Lochlann, the bones of Asal's pig — full at high tide and empty at ebb. Then for seven years he watched the salmon of the Boinn for the poet Finegas, and when it came and Finn roasted it, the blister on the skin burned his thumb and he put his thumb in his mouth: 'It is not Deimne but Finn your name is, and it is to you and not to myself the salmon was given in the prophecy.' Not verbatim.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Gregory 1904, Book One ch. 1; not verbatim.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase: At Samhain Finn went up to the gathering of the High King at Teamhair and declared himself: 'I am Finn, son of Cumhal.' For nine years Aillen son of Midhna of Sidhe Finnachaidh had come every Samhain playing music of the Sídhe that put all who heard it to sleep, then breathing a flame out of his mouth and burning Teamhair. Finn pledged to keep it safe till morning: when the sorrowful music came he stripped the covering from the head of a deadly spear and held it to his forehead, so that sleep could not come on him; Aillen let his flame out, and Finn held up his fringed crimson cloak against it till the flame fell through the air into the ground; then Finn followed Aillen back to the Sídhe and cast the spear through his heart as he entered, and struck off his head. 'Well, Goll, is it your choice to quit Ireland or to put your hand in Finn's hand?' — and Goll, son of Morna, was the first to strike his hand in Finn's hand, the way there would be less shame on the rest. Not verbatim.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Gregory 1904, Book One ch. 1; not verbatim.

canonical_translation: Lady Augusta Gregory, Gods and Fighting Men, London 1904 (public domain); underlying: Fianaigecht materials (MacNeill, 1908, public domain portions); Acallam na Senórach framework

narrative.en:
Every hero-cycle needs a foundling, and the Fenian cycle's foundling grows up in a wood with two druid-women for schoolmistresses — and becomes the most just, most generous king of a company of wild men.

At the time Finn was born his father Cumhal of the sons of Baiscne, Head of the Fianna of Ireland, had been killed in battle by the sons of Morna that were fighting with him for the leadership; and his mother, beautiful long-haired Muirne, daughter of Tadg — son of Nuada of the Tuatha Dé Danann and of Ethlinn, mother of Lugh of the Long Hand — did not dare to keep him with her. Two women, Bodhmall the woman Druid and Liath Luachra, came and brought him away to care for, to the woods of Slieve Bladhma, and nursed him secretly because of his father's enemies. His mother came once in six years, through every lonely place, to find the little hunting cabin and kiss him and sing him a sleepy song, and go away again.

His education was a chase. One woman would run round a tree with a thorn switch, Finn after her with another switch, each trying to hit the other; they would leave him in a field with hares and bid him not let the hares quit the field, but keep before them whichever way they went; to teach him swimming they threw him into the water and let him make his way out. He killed his first wild duck by a cast that cut the wings from her. A herd of mountain deer went past the cabin once, and Finn caught two stags and brought them home: 'I will get one for you.'

The name came at a swimming match in Magh Life: beating the lads of the plain at their own sport, 'Fair he is and well shaped,' they said — and it was from that time he got the name of Finn, the Fair, put on him like a crown for swimming. Jealousy drove him on: seven games of chess won from the king who had married Muirne — and that king knew his blood at once, 'you are the son that Muirne my wife bore to Cumhal. And do not stop here any longer, that you may not be killed under my protection.'

Then the spoils of ancestry. He avenged a woman whose only son had been killed, fighting and killing the great champion that had given Cumhal his first wound in his last battle — and took back from him the treasure-bag of crane-skin, whose pedigree runs through the whole mythological cycle: once the skin of Aoife, sweetheart of Ilbrec son of Manannan, changed to a crane through jealousy; kept in Manannan's house, holding Manannan's shirt and knife, Goibniu's belt and smith's hook, the shears of the King of Alban, the helmet of the King of Lochlann, and the bones of Asal's pig that the sons of Tuireann brought to Ireland — full at high tide and empty at ebb. It went from Manannan to Lugh son of Ethlinn, and after that to Cumhal, husband of Ethlinn's daughter: the Fenian cycle handing back to the Mythological cycle its own luggage.

Then poetry, and the salmon. Finn went to learn from Finegas the poet living at the Boinn, for the poets thought it was always on the brink of water poetry was revealed; and he gave no name of his own but took the name of Demne. Seven years Finegas had watched the salmon of the Boinn, for it was in the prophecy that he would eat it and have all knowledge after. At last it came; he bade Finn roast it and not taste it; and when Finn brought it back, 'Did you eat any of it at all, boy?' 'I did not; but I burned my thumb putting down a blister that rose on the skin, and after doing that I put my thumb in my mouth.' 'It is not Deimne, but Finn your name is, and it is to you and not to myself the salmon was given in the prophecy' — and Finegas gave him the whole of the salmon, and from that time Finn had the knowledge that came from the nuts of the nine hazels of wisdom that grow beside the well that is below the sea. A second draught followed by accident: hunting by the well of the moon of Beag son of Buan, whose three daughter-guardians would not part with a vessel of it for less than red gold, one of them threw the vessel's water at him to stop him, and a share went into his mouth — all the knowledge that well could give.

And then the master-feat of the cycle's beginning. At Samhain Finn went up to the High King's gathering at Teamhair and named himself before the horn of meetings: 'I am Finn, son of Cumhal... I am come now to get your friendship, and to give you my service.' For nine years, every Samhain, Aillen son of Midhna had come out of Sidhe Finnachaidh playing music of the Sídhe that put all who heard it to sleep — 'even women in their pains and men that were wounded would fall asleep' — and then breathed a flame out of his mouth and burned Teamhair. Finn pledged to keep it till morning, taking pledges of the king; and a fighting man, Fiacha son of Conga, who had loved Cumhal, sold him for a third of his winnings a deadly spear with a charm in its head: 'when you will hear the music of the Sídhe, let you strip the covering off the head of the spear and put it to your forehead, and the power of the spear will not let sleep come upon you.' The music came, the covering came off, the forehead took the spearhead's power; Aillen breathed his flame, and Finn held up his fringed crimson cloak against it until the flame fell down through the air and went into the ground. Then Finn followed Aillen back to the Sídhe and made the cast through his heart at the door, struck off his head and fixed it on a crooked pole at Teamhair till sunrise, while Aillen's mother keened: 'Nine times he burned Teamhair.'

The reward was the thing itself: 'Well, Goll, son of Morna, is it your choice to quit Ireland or to put your hand in Finn's hand?' 'By my word, I will give Finn my hand' — and when the charms of good luck had done their work, the chief men of the Fianna struck their hands in Finn's, Goll first, the way there would be less shame on the rest for doing it. The headship of the Fianna was Finn's until the end, at Almhuin of Leinster, in the white dun of Nuada of the Tuatha Dé Danann; and of him the sayings ran: a king and a seer and a poet; a Druid and a knowledgeable man; if his enemy and his own son had come before him to be judged, a fair judgment he would have given between them.
narrative.zh: 每個英雄故事圈都需要一個棄兒，而費恩納故事圈的棄兒在林中由兩位女德魯伊撫育成人——成為一隊野性男子的最公正、最慷慨之王。芬恩出生之時，其父——愛爾蘭費恩納之首、拜斯克尼之子庫哈爾——已在爭奪首領之位的戰鬥中被莫爾納諸子殺死；其母、美麗長髮的穆爾妮——塔德格之女、塔拉哈·迪·丹安之努阿達與魯格之母艾斯琳的後裔——不敢將他留在身邊。兩位婦女——女德魯伊波德馬爾與利亞·盧阿赫拉——將他帶往斯利夫·布拉德瑪山中秘密撫育。其母每六年穿過所有僻地來一次，尋到小獵屋、抱起他親吻、為他唱一支催眠短歌，而後離去。其教育即追逐：一名女子持棘枝繞樹奔跑、芬恩持另一枝追之互擊；他們把他與野兔留在田野、命他不許兔群離開田野、無論兔往何方都要趕在其前；教游泳之法是將他拋入水中、任其自行出水。他以一擊削去其翼殺死第一隻野鴨。一次一群山鹿經過小屋，芬恩追而捕得兩隻牡鹿帶回家：『我為你們弄一隻來。』其名得於馬格·利夫之游泳賽：他勝過平原上所有少年，眾人曰『他真俊美、身形真好』——自此他得名芬恩（俊美），如游泳之冠加於其身。嫉妒驅其前行：他從母親改嫁之王手中連勝七局棋——王即刻識出血統：『你便是穆爾妮為庫哈爾所生之子。別再停留於此，以免在我的庇護之下被殺。』繼而是祖先之戰利品。他為獨子被殺的婦人復仇，殺死曾在其父最後一戰中給予庫哈爾第一傷的巨漢——並取回鶴皮寶袋：其譜系貫穿整個神話故事圈——原為瑪南南之子伊爾布雷克之戀人艾奧菲因妒被化為鶴之皮；存於瑪南南家中，內藏瑪南南之衫與刀、戈伊布尼烏之帶與鍛鉤、阿爾巴王之剪、洛赫蘭王之盔、以及圖雷恩諾子攜來之阿薩爾豬骨——滿潮時滿、退潮時空。其袋由瑪南南傳至艾斯琳之子魯格、再至艾斯琳之女之夫庫哈爾：費恩納故事圈將神話故事圈自己的行李送還。繼而是詩與鮭。芬恩往博因河畔從詩人菲內加斯學詩——因詩人相信詩總在水邊顯現——隱名德姆內。菲內加斯守候博因智慧之鮭七年，因預言其食之而後得全知。鮭終至；他命芬恩烤之而不許嚐；芬恩捧鮭而回——『你究竟嚐過沒有，孩子？』『沒有；但皮上起了水泡、我按下去燙了拇指、隨後把拇指放進了嘴裡。』『你不叫德姆內，你的名字是芬恩，預言中的鮭是給你的、不是給我的』——菲內加斯將整條鮭給了他；自此芬恩擁有海底智慧泉旁九株榛樹堅果之知識。第二瓢知識又因意外而至：他在布安之子貝格的月亮井旁狩獵、三名持井之女不許他以少於赤金之價取水、其中一名擲水阻他、一口水入其口——該井所能給的知識盡歸於他。繼而是故事圈開篇之絕技。薩溫之夜芬恩上塔拉至至高王集會、於會議之角前自報家門：『我是芬恩、庫哈爾之子……我來求你的誼、獻我的忠。』九年來每逢薩溫，菲德納之子艾倫自北方菲納凱西德出來、奏西德之樂使聞者入睡——『連產中之婦與帶傷之男也會睡去』——繼而自口中吐火焚燒塔拉。芬恩立誓守至天明；曾敬庫哈爾的戰士菲亞赫以戰利品三分之一之價售他一支頭部藏咒的致命之矛：『聞西德之樂時，剝去矛頭之覆、以之抵額，矛之力便不容睡眠臨身。』樂聲至、覆布起、額頭承矛力；艾倫吐焰、芬恩舉紅穗斗篷相拒直至火焰穿空落地入土。隨後芬恩追艾倫至西德門前、乘其入門一矛穿心、斬首攜回塔拉、懸於彎杆至日昇，而艾倫之母哀哭：『他曾九次焚燒塔拉。』其賞即事物本身：『戈爾、莫爾納之子，你擇離開愛爾蘭、還是把手放進芬恩手中？』『我願把手交給芬恩』——吉兆咒行畢，費恩納首領們將手擊入芬恩手中、戈爾最先出手、好讓其餘之人少些羞恥。費恩納之首自始至終歸芬恩，於萊因斯特之阿爾文、塔拉哈·迪·丹安之努阿達所建白色雪堡之中；關於他的諺語如此流傳：王者、先知、詩人；德魯伊與博學之士；縱使仇敵與親子同至其前受審，他亦能公判。

summary.en: Grania, daughter of the High King, is betrothed to grey-haired Finn, Head of the Fianna, and regrets it at the wedding feast: a druid names each hero to her, the cap slips from Diarmuid's love-spot, an enchanted cup puts every man asleep, and she puts Diarmuid under geasa to carry her out — over the walls on the shafts of his spears, leaving unbroken bread behind him as proof he keeps his faith to Finn.
summary.zh: 至高王之女格蘭妮被許給灰髮的費恩納之首芬恩，婚宴之上心生悔意：德魯伊為她逐一唱名英雄、迪爾木德的愛痣帽落、施咒之杯使滿座入睡；她以geasa束縛迪爾木德攜她出走——踏矛桿越牆而過、身後留下未掰開之麵包以證他對芬恩守其忠信。

sensitivity.note: The elopement tale is Ireland's Helen-and-Paris story; the love-spot (ball seirce) granted to Diarmuid by the woman of the Sídhe makes consent literal and irresistible. Retold from public-domain print.

Oisin and Diorraing went to Teamhair to woo her; the king sent them to her own answer: 'If he is a fitting son-in-law for you, why would he not be a fitting husband for me?' But when Grania saw grey-haired Finn at the wedding, 'It is a great wonder it was not for Oisin Finn asked me, for he would be more fitting for me than a man that is older than my father.' narrative.en:
The Pursuit of Diarmuid and Gráinne is Ireland's great romance of the elopement — a bride who chooses for herself at her own wedding, and a hero who obeys the law of geasa into the tragedy it foretells.

Finn sat out alone on the green lawn of Almhuin of Leinster, without a wife or companion since Maighneis daughter of Black Garraidh had died from him, 'for quiet sleep is not used to come to a man that is without a fitting wife.' Oisin his son and Diorraing the Druid came to him, and Diorraing named the bride: Grania, daughter of the High King of Ireland, 'the woman of the best make and shape and the best speech of the women of the whole world.' Finn warned of the strife between himself and the High King; the two went to Teamhair to take the refusal for him. The king put them off to Grania's own answer — 'there is not a son of a king or of a great prince, there is not a champion in Ireland my daughter has not given a refusal to, and it is on me they all lay the blame' — and Grania answered with the wilful neatness of her whole character: 'If he is a fitting son-in-law for you, why would he not be a fitting husband for me?'

The wedding was set for a fortnight hence, and Finn gathered the seven battalions of the Fianna to Teamhair. But when Grania saw grey-haired Finn, she said it aloud: 'It is a great wonder it was not for Oisin Finn asked me, for he would be more fitting for me than a man that is older than my father.' Finn, who had the name of being quick with answers himself, set her riddles — what is whiter than snow (the truth), what is hotter than fire (the face of a hospitable man when he sees a stranger coming and the house empty), what is best for a champion (his doings to be high and his pride to be low), what is sharper than a sword ('the wit of a woman between two men'), what is quicker than the wind ('a woman's mind') — 'And indeed she was telling no lie when she said that.'

At the wedding feast, in the king's house of the Middle Court, the heroes were named to her one by one by a druid of Finn's people — Goll the ready fighter, Osgar son of Oisin, thin-legged Caoilte — and of the dark-haired man with cheeks like the rowan-berry, 'that is Diarmuid, grandson of Duibhne... the best lover of women in the whole world.' 'That is a good company,' said Grania. Diarmuid kept his cap always over the love-spot the woman of the Sídhe had left on his forehead — for no woman could see that spot but she would give him her love — and while he drove apart the fighting dogs, the cap fell; Grania saw it, and the blood rose in her heart. She sent for the great golden cup that held drink for nine times nine men, filled it with wine that had enchantment in it, and gave it first to Finn and then through the hall: all that drank fell into a heavy sleep, none waking but Oisin, Osgar, Caoilte, Diarmuid and Diorraing.

'Will you take my love, Diarmuid, son of Duibhne, and will you bring me away out of this house to-night?' 'I will not. I will not meddle with the woman that is promised to Finn.' 'If that is so, I put you under Druid bonds, to bring me out of this house to-night before the awaking of Finn and of the King of Ireland from their sleep.' It is under bad bonds you are putting me, Grania — and he polled his friends like a judge: Oisin ('you are not guilty if the bonds were laid on you'), Osgar ('it is a pitiful man that would break his bonds'), Caoilte ('it would be better to me than all the riches of the world Grania to have given me that love'), Diorraing ('follow Grania, although you will get your death by it'). All said follow. He stood up and stretched out his hand for his weapons, and every tear he shed was of the size of a mountain berry; then he went out to the wall of the dun, put the shafts of his two spears under him — for 'every fighting man has leave to pass over the walls of any dun and of any strong place at all by the shafts of his spears' — rose with a light leap and came down on the grass outside, where Grania met him.

He tried once more to be honorable — turn back, and Finn will never get news of what you are after doing — and she refused: 'I will never part with you till death parts us.' He carried her to horses, and from there on foot, and wherever they went 'Diarmuid left unbroken bread after him, as a sign to Finn he had kept his faith with him.' At Doire-da-Bhoth, the Wood of the Two Huts, he cut down the wood around them and built a fence with seven doors of woven twigs, and set out a bed of soft rushes and birch tops for Grania in the very middle of the wood. The trackers found the trail the next morning; Finn's jealousy rose like weather; Bran the hound and Caoilte's shouting servant were sent as warnings by Oisin and Osgar; and Finn surrounded the wood. 'O Diarmuid, which of us is the truth with, myself or Oisin?' 'You never failed from your good judgment, Finn, and indeed I myself and Grania are here' — and Angus Og came on the cold wind and lifted the eloping pair over the hosts on his own cloak, and the pursuit of a lifetime began.
narrative.zh: 《迪爾木德與格蘭妮之追尋》乃愛爾蘭私奔愛情之大篇——在自己的婚禮上為自己做選擇的新娘，與服從geasa之法走入其預言之悲劇的英雄。芬恩獨坐萊因斯特阿爾文草場，自黑加雷之女梅西斯死後無妻無伴，『蓋無賢妻者夜間少得安眠』。其子奧辛與德魯伊迪奧林至其處；迪奧林報出新娘之名：愛爾蘭至高王之女格蘭妮——『全世婦女中身形最好、言談最佳之女』。芬恩自陳與至高王素有嫌隙；二人赴塔拉代其受拒。王把問題交還格蘭妮本人——『王族貴胄、全國勇士，我女無一不拒，責任全在我』——格蘭妮以其全篇性格之果斷俏答：『若他配作你之佳婿，為何不配作我之夫？』婚期定於兩週後，芬恩集費恩納七營至塔拉。而格蘭妮一見灰髮之芬恩便出聲：『奇哉，芬恩所求何不是我為奧辛所求，他比我父更年長之人更配於我。』芬恩自誇機敏、以謎語相試——什麼比雪更白（真理）、什麼比火更熱（屋空客至時好客者之面）、什麼於武士最佳（功高而傲低）、什麼比劍更利（『兩男之間一女之機智』）、什麼比風更快（『一女之心』）——『她說此話確無虛言』。婚宴於中廷王屋舉行，芬恩族中一德魯伊為她逐一唱名眾英雄——善戰者戈爾、奧辛之子奧斯加、瘦腿的卡爾特——而對那位黑髮、頰如花楸果之男子曰：『此即迪布內之孫迪爾木德……舉世最得女子歡心者。』『好一群人物，』格蘭妮曰。迪爾木德常年以帽覆西德女子留在其額上之愛痣——因無女子見痣而不以身相許——他驅散相鬥之犬時帽落；格蘭妮見之、心血上湧。她遣人取九九八十一人量之大金杯、盛以咒酒、先奉芬恩、再傳全廳：飲者皆入沉睡、不醒者惟奧辛、奧斯加、卡爾特、迪爾木德與迪奧林五人。『迪爾木德、迪布內之子，你願受我之愛、今夜攜我出此屋否？』『不願。我不染指許給芬恩之女。』『既如此，我以德魯伊之束縛加於你：今夜、在芬恩與愛爾蘭王醒來之前，攜我出此屋。』『格蘭妮，你加於我的是惡縛』——他如法官逐一問計於同伴：奧辛（『縛非你自取，則你無罪；追隨格蘭妮』）、奧斯加（『毀縛者可鄙』）、卡爾特（『格蘭妮若以那愛予我，勝過世上一切財富』）、迪奧林（『追隨格蘭妮，縱因此得死，亦令我痛』）。皆曰追隨。他起身伸手取兵器、每滴淚大如山莓；出至堡牆、以雙矛之桿撐身——『凡戰士皆有權踏矛桿越任何堡壘之牆』——輕躍而下、落於牆外草上、格蘭妮在彼相迎。他再試一次求其正——回去吧，芬恩永不知道你所行之事——她拒絕：『至死我與你不分離。』他攜她至馬、繼而步行；所到之處『迪爾木德身後皆留未掰開之麵包，作為對芬恩守其忠信之證』。於兩茅屋之林（Doire-da-Bhoth）他伐林四周、築七門編枝之籬、為格蘭妮於林之正中鋪設柔薦與樺梢之床。翌晨追蹤者循跡而至；芬恩之妒如天氣驟起；奧辛與奧斯加遣忠犬布蘭與卡爾特之呼聲僕人預警；芬恩圍林。『迪爾木德，你我之間誰說真話——我還是奧辛？』『芬恩，你的判斷從無差錯——我和格蘭妮確實在此』——安古斯·歐格乘冷風而來、以自己的斗篷將私奔二人送過大軍之頂，一生的追捕自此開始。

functions: Charter of the geasa bond: the elopement compelled by debt-language as the cycle's central legal event
The love-spot doctrine: beauty as compulsion — consent engineered by the otherworld
The unbroken bread: loyalty display within betrayal — faith kept in the very act of its breach
Riddle-courtship of Finn and Grania: wisdom dialogue as character diagnosis before tragedy

title.en: The Boar of Beinn Gulbain: the Death of Diarmuid
title.zh: 本·古爾班之野豬：迪爾木德之死

region.en: Beinn Gulbain (Benbulben), Co. Sligo, Ireland
region.zh: 愛爾蘭斯萊戈郡本·古爾班山（本布爾本山）

period: Tóraigheacht Dhiarmada agus Ghráinne, medieval MSS (16th c. recension); Gregory retelling 1904

source.work: Lady Augusta Gregory, Gods and Fighting Men (1904), Book Seven: Diarmuid and Grania, Chapter VIII, eBook #14465

summary.en: At the peace-feast's end a hound's voice wakes Diarmuid in the night; against Angus's bonds and Grania's advice he takes the small weapons and meets the earless green boar of Beinn Gulbain — the very death Finn names for him; gored to the bowels he kills the boar with a sword-hilt, and calls on Finn for the drink from his two palms that would heal any sickness; Finn lets the water slip through his hands twice at the thought of Grania, and brings it the third time as Diarmuid dies.
summary.zh: 和宴之末，夜間犬吠聲喚醒迪爾木德；他不顧安古斯之禁與格蘭妮之勸、攜小兵器迎向本·古爾班之無耳綠豬——芬恩親口言明之死因；他被剖至腸出、以劍柄擊斃野豬，求芬恩以其雙掌之水療疾；芬恩因想起格蘭妮兩度令水自指間流去，第三度送到時迪爾木德已死。

sensitivity.note: The boar of Benbulben is the cycle's doom-beast (Angus's bond against hunting pigs); the healing drink from Finn's palms inverts the salmon of knowledge — the gift of life withheld. Benbulben is also W. B. Yeats's burial hill.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase of Gregory 1904: On the last night of the year of the peace-feast, Diarmuid was in his sleep at Rath Grania, and in the night he heard the voice of hounds; Grania caught him and bade him lie down — 'it is the Tuatha Dé Danann are doing that on you' — but the voice awakened him the third time, with the day come. 'Bring the Mor-alltach, the Great Fierce One, the sword of Manannan, with you, and the Gae Dearg,' said Grania. 'I will not; but I will take the Beag-alltach, the Little Fierce One, and the Gae Buidhe in the one hand, and the hound Mac an Chuill, the Son of the Hazel, in the other hand.' On the top of Beinn Gulbain he found Finn alone before him. 'It is the earless Green Boar of Beinn Gulbain is in it, and it is by him you will come to your death, and Angus knew that well when he put bonds on you not to go hunting pigs.' 'I never knew of those bonds; but however it is, I will not quit this through fear of him.' Not verbatim.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Gregory 1904, Book Seven ch. 8; not verbatim.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase: The Gae Buidhe gave the boar not a scratch; the Beag-alltach broke in two halves on his back; the boar charged, cut the sod from under Diarmuid's feet, and Diarmuid caught him on rising with a leg on each side and his face to his hinder parts, and rode him headlong down the hill and over the red stream of Ess Ruadh in three high leaps — until on the top of the mountain the boar freed himself, rushed at Diarmuid and ripped him open so his bowels came out about his feet. And Diarmuid made a cast at him with the hilt of his broken sword and dashed out his brains — and Rath na h-Amhrann, the Rath of the Sword Hilt, is the name of that place to this day. Not verbatim.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase: Finn came with the Fianna as the pains of death were coming on Diarmuid. 'It is well pleased I am to see you that way, Diarmuid... For all that, you have power to heal me, Finn, if you had a mind to do it. For the time you were given the great gift of knowledge at the Boinn, you got this gift with it, that any one you would give a drink to out of the palms of your hands would be young and well again from any sickness after it.' 'You are not deserving of that drink from me.' Then Finn went to the well and took the full of his two hands of the water; but when he was no more than half-way back, the thought of Grania came on him, and he let the water slip through his hands.

passages.text: A second time he let it slip. 'I swear by my sword and by my spear,' said Osgar, 'that if you do not bring the water without any more delay, Finn, there will not leave this hill but yourself or myself.' Finn went the third time and brought the water, but as he reached him the life went out of Diarmuid's body; and the Fianna gave three great heavy shouts, keening for Diarmuid. Not verbatim.

canonical_translation: Lady Augusta Gregory, Gods and Fighting Men, London 1904 (public domain); underlying: Tóraigheacht Dhiarmada agus Ghráinne, 16th c. recension

narrative.en:
The death of Diarmuid is the Fenian cycle's tragedy of small omissions: the small sword taken instead of the great, the third waking not heeded, the water spilled twice — and a hero dead of arithmetic.

Peace had been made. Grania had told Diarmuid it was a shame the two best men in Ireland — the High King and Finn — had never come to their house, and made a feast for them that lasted a year. And on the last night of the year, Diarmuid was in his sleep at Rath Grania, and in the night he heard the voice of hounds. He started up; Grania caught him with her two arms and bade him lie down — 'it is the Tuatha Dé Danann are doing that on you, on account of Angus of Brugh na Boinn.' The voice came again and he started up a second time; she caught him again. The third time, the day come with its full light, he said: 'I will go after the voice of the hound now, since the day is here.' 'If that is so,' said Grania, 'bring the Mor-alltach, the Great Fierce One, the sword of Manannan, with you, and the Gae Dearg.' 'I will not; but I will take the Beag-alltach, the Little Fierce One, and the Gae Buidhe in the one hand, and the hound Mac an Chuill, the Son of the Hazel, in the other hand.' The small weapons for a small errand: the whole tragedy in an inventory.

On the top of Beinn Gulbain he found Finn before him, without any one at all in his company. 'It is not a hunt I was making,' said Finn, 'but I and some of the Fianna went out after midnight, and one of our hounds came on the track of a wild boar... it is many a time the Fianna hunted him and he went away from them every time till now, and he has killed thirty of them this morning.' 'I will not leave the hill through fear of him,' said Diarmuid. 'It would be best for you, Diarmuid, for it is the earless Green Boar of Beinn Gulbain is in it, and it is by him you will come to your death, and Angus knew that well when he put bonds on you not to go hunting pigs.' 'I never knew of those bonds; but however it is, I will not quit this through fear of him. And let you leave Bran with me now, along with Mac an Chuill.' 'I will not,' said Finn, 'for it is often he met this boar before and could do nothing against him.' And Finn went away and left Diarmuid alone on the top of the hill. 'You made this hunt for my death, Finn; and if it is here I am to find my death, I have no use in going aside from it now.'

The fight is a lesson in wrong tools. The Gae Buidhe struck the boar full in the face and did not give him a scratch; the Beag-alltach made a full stroke at his back and broke in two halves. The boar charged and cut the sod from under Diarmuid's feet — and Diarmuid caught hold of him on rising, a leg on each side, his face to his hinder parts, and rode him headlong down the hill; the boar gave three high leaps over the red stream of Ess Ruadh backwards and forwards and could not rid himself of his rider; up the height of the mountain again, and at last he freed himself, rushed at the fallen man, and ripped him open, so that his bowels came out about his feet. And Diarmuid made a cast at him with the hilt of the broken sword yet in his hand, and dashed out his brains, so that he fell dead there and then — and Rath na h-Amhrann, the Rath of the Sword Hilt, is the name of that place to this day. Boar and man killed each other; the mountain kept the account.

Then the payment scene the whole cycle is remembered by. Finn came with the Fianna as the pains of death were coming on Diarmuid: 'It is well pleased I am to see you that way, Diarmuid, and it is a pity all the women of Ireland not to be looking at you now, for your great beauty is turned to ugliness.' 'For all that, you have power to heal me, Finn, if you had a mind to do it. For the time you were given the great gift of knowledge at the Boinn, you got this gift with it, that any one you would give a drink to out of the palms of your hands would be young and well again from any sickness after it.' 'You are not deserving of that drink from me.' Diarmuid recited the ledger of his service — the three red rushes round the burning house, fifty killed in every rush without a wound; the loosing of Finn from the House of the Quicken Tree with his own blood and the blood of the Three Kings of the Island of Floods — 'and if I had asked a drink of you that night, you would not have refused it.' Osgar, nearer in blood to Finn than to Diarmuid, said he would not let the drink be refused, and swore by his sword that if it were not brought without delay there would not leave this hill but one of them. Finn went to the well, took the full of his two hands of the water — and no more than half-way back, the thought of Grania came on him, and he let the water slip through his hands. A second time. 'I give my word,' said Diarmuid, 'it was of your own will you let it from you.' The third time, pressed by Osgar's oath, Finn brought the water to Diarmuid — but as he reached him, the life went out of his body; and the whole company gave three great heavy shouts, keening for Diarmuid. Angus came on the cold wind for his foster-son, gave three terrible cries, and bore the body to the Brugh in the lasting rocks: 'and if I cannot bring him back to life, I will put life into him the way he can be talking with me every day.'
narrative.zh: 迪爾木德之死乃費恩納故事圈關於微小遺漏之悲劇：取小劍而非大劍、第三次醒來未被理會、水兩度潑灑——一位英雄死於算術。和解已成。格蘭妮曾對迪爾木德言：愛爾蘭最好的兩人——至高王與芬恩——從未光臨其家是羞恥，遂為他們設宴一年。歲末最後一夜，迪爾木德在格蘭妮堡中睡臥、夜間聽見犬吠之聲。他驚起；格蘭妮雙臂抱住他、命他躺下——『這是塔拉哈·迪·丹安因安古斯之故對你所作』。聲音再至、他第二次驚起；她又抓住他。第三次，天已大亮，他說：『既然天亮了，我現在就去追犬吠之聲。』『既如此，』格蘭妮曰，『帶上瑪南南之劍、偉大兇猛者摩爾-奧爾塔赫，與紅矛蓋·迪爾格。』『我不帶；我只一手持小劍貝格-奧爾塔赫與黃矛蓋·布維、另一手帶獵犬榛子之子麥克·安·庫伊爾。』小事帶小兵器：全篇悲劇濃縮於一張清單。本·古爾班山頂他先見到芬恩、身邊一無一人。『我不是在狩獵，』芬恩曰，『我與數名費恩納午夜後外出、一犬遇上野豬蹤跡……費恩納多次獵牠、牠每次都逃脫，今晨已殺死三十人。』『我不會因怕牠離開此山，』迪爾木德曰。『迪爾木德，那對你最好——因為那是本·古爾班的無耳綠豬，你將因牠而死；安古斯對你下過不得獵豬之縛時深知此事。』『我從不知道那些縛；無論如何，我不會因懼牠離開。讓布蘭與麥克·安·庫伊爾留在我身邊。』『不會，』芬恩曰，『牠多次遇此豬而無能為力。』芬恩離去、獨留迪爾木德於山頂。『芬恩，你此獵是為我死而設；若我命終於此，我現在也無須避開。』搏鬥是一堂錯誤兵器之課。黃矛正中豬面而不傷分毫；小劍全力擊其背、斷為兩截。野豬衝撞、剷走迪爾木德足下之草皮——迪爾木德起身抱住牠、一腿跨一側、面朝其後軀、騎豬衝下山岡；野豬在埃斯·魯阿紅流上向前向後三度高躍、仍不能擺脫其騎者；再上山頂、終於掙脫、撲向倒地之人、剖開其身、腸流於足邊。迪爾木德以手中尚存之斷劍劍柄擲擊、擊碎其腦——野豬當場死亡——該地至今名為劍柄之堡（Rath na h-Amhrann）。人豬互斃；山岳記下此帳。繼而是全故事圈所銘記之償付場景。死痛臨身之際芬恩率費恩納而至：『見你如此我甚為快意，迪爾木德——可惜全愛爾蘭的女子此刻不能一睹你的容顏，你的大美已變為醜陋。』『儘管如此，芬恩，你若有意，便有能力醫我。你當年在博因河得大知識之賜時，隨之得了此能力：凡你以雙掌奉飲之人，飲後皆能從任何疾病中回復年輕康健。』『你不配從我這裡得此飲。』迪爾木德歷數其功之帳——燃屋三紅衝、每衝殺五十而自身無傷；以己血與洪流島三王之血自快活樹之屋釋放芬恩——『那夜我若向你求飲，你不會拒絕。』奧斯加——血緣上更近芬恩——言必不許拒絕，並以其劍起誓：若不即刻送水，此山將只餘你們二人之一。芬恩赴井、雙手掬滿泉水——行至半途、格蘭妮之念襲來、水自指間流去。第二次又如此。『我以言語起誓，』迪爾木德曰，『是你自己願意放開的。』第三次、在奧斯加之誓下，芬恩把水送到迪爾木德面前——但剛一伸手，生氣已離其身；全隊發出三聲沉重之呼、為迪爾木德哀哭。安古斯乘冷風而來為其養子、發三聲可怖之呼、將遺體帶往永石之堡（Brugh na Boinne）：『若我不能使他復生，我便賦予他生命，使他每日能與我交談。』

functions: Doom by inventory: the wrong weapons chosen as fate's mechanism — the small errand kills the great man
The healing drink withheld: Finn's palms as inverted sacrament of the salmon of knowledge
Guilt measured in water: two spilled handfuds as the cycle's precise unit of culpability
Etiology of Rath na h-Amhrann (the Rath of the Sword Hilt) on Beinn Gulbain

title.en: Oisin in Tir na nOg: the Three Hundred Years and the Touch of Earth
title.zh: 奧辛於青春之鄉：三百年與觸土之詛

region.en: Tir na nOg (the Country of the Young), western ocean otherworld (symbolic pin off Kerry)
region.zh: 青春之鄉（提爾納諾格），西方海洋彼岸世界（象徵定位：克里的近海）

period: Fenian cycle (Acallam na Senórach and later), medieval MSS; Gregory retelling 1904

source.work: Lady Augusta Gregory, Gods and Fighting Men (1904), Book Ten: The End of the Fianna, Chapters II-III, and Book Eleven, Chapter I, eBook #14465

summary.en: Niamh of the Golden Head rides out of the western sea on a white horse shod with gold and calls Oisin away from the last hunting of the Fianna to Tir na nOg — no death, no wasting, a hundred gifts — with one law: never set foot to ground. Three hundred years later he returns to Ireland for love of Finn's memory, helps a falling rider from his saddle by a stoop to the stone trough, and touches earth: the whole weight of the years falls on him at once, and the blind old man tells his story to Patrick.
summary.zh: 金髮尼芙乘金蹄白馬自西方海上而來，喚奧辛離開費恩納最後一次狩獵、前往青春之鄉——無死、無衰、百般贈禮——惟一法度：足不可觸地。三百年後他因思念芬恩返回愛爾蘭，為扶助落鞍之騎手俯身於石槽、觸地——歲月之全部重量瞬間壓身；失明的老人向帕特里克講述自己的故事。

sensitivity.note: Tir na nOg is the Irish otherworld of youth (Mag Mell/Tír Tairngire type); the saddle-and-earth taboo is the cycle's version of the touched-shore law seen in Bran's voyage.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase of Gregory 1904: One misty morning what were left of the Fianna were gathered together to Finn, hunting near the borders of Loch Lein, and they saw coming towards them from the west a beautiful young woman riding on a very fast slender white horse, with a queen's crown on her head and a dark cloak of silk down to the ground having stars of red gold on it — and the horse shod with shining gold. 'Niamh of the Golden Head is my name, and I have a name beyond all the women of the world, for I am the daughter of the King of the Country of the Young... I have given my love and my affection to your own son, Oisin of the strong hands.' Not verbatim.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Gregory 1904, Book Ten ch. 2; not verbatim.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase: She sang Oisin her country's charter: 'It is the country is most delightful of all that are under sun; the trees are stooping down with fruit and with leaves and with blossom. Honey and wine are plentiful there... no wasting will come on you with the wasting away of time; you will never see death or lessening... You will get the royal crown of the King of the Young... a hundred glad young girls shining like the sun... you will get everything I have said to you, and delights beyond them, that I have no leave to tell; and I myself will be with you as a wife.' 'I put on you the bonds of a true hero, you to come away with me now to the Country of the Young.' And Oisin kissed Finn his father and bade him farewell and went up on the horse with Niamh; at the strand the horse shook himself and neighed three times and made for the sea, and the Fianna gave three great sorrowful shouts. Not verbatim.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Gregory 1904, Book Ten ch. 2; not verbatim.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase: Hundreds of years — some say thousands — Oisin was in the Country of the Young, and it seemed short to him. He asked leave to go back to Ireland, and Niamh gave it three times warned: 'if you once get off the horse while you are away, or if you once put your foot to ground, you will never come back here again... you will be an old man, blind and withered.' He came back and found Finn gone and Almhuin's dun gone to weeds and nettles; and riding near a place where men were raising a stone, he saw a rider let his saddle-cushion slip, and he stooped to help him — 'and in the minute all the years came on me, and I was lying on the ground, and the horse took fright and went away and left me there, an old man, weak and spent, without sight, without shape, without comeliness, without strength or understanding, without respect.' And it was to Patrick Oisin was brought, and to him he told the whole story. Not verbatim.

narrative.en:
The last great story of the Fenian cycle is a three-hundred-year goodbye — the hero who accepts an offer of immortality, and loses it to an act of kindness.

One misty morning what were left of the Fianna were gathered together to Finn, hunting near the borders of Loch Lein, where the bushes were in blossom and the birds singing, and they were waking up the deer that were as joyful as the leaves of a tree in summer-time. And it was not long till they saw coming towards them from the west a beautiful young woman riding on a very fast slender white horse: a queen's crown on her head, a dark cloak of silk down to the ground with stars of red gold on it, her eyes blue and as clear as the dew on the grass, a gold ring hanging down from every golden lock of her hair, her cheeks redder than the rose, her skin whiter than the swan upon the wave, her lips as sweet as honey mixed through red wine — and the horse shod with shining gold, a silver crown on the back of his head.

'Niamh of the Golden Head is my name,' she said, 'and I have a name beyond all the women of the world, for I am the daughter of the King of the Country of the Young.' Finn asked her husband and her trouble; 'My husband is not gone from me, for I never went yet to any man. But O King of the Fianna, I have given my love and my affection to your own son, Oisin of the strong hands' — by reason of his great name, and the report of his bravery and comeliness. And when Oisin heard what she was saying, there was not a limb of his body that was not in love with beautiful Niamh.

She sang him the country's charter, the fullest otherworld advertisement in Irish: trees stooping down with fruit and leaves and blossom; honey and wine plentiful; 'no wasting will come on you with the wasting away of time; you will never see death or lessening'; feasts, music, silver and gold; a hundred swords, a hundred cloaks of the dearest silk, a hundred horses quickest in battle, a hundred willing hounds; the royal crown of the King of the Young; and 'delights beyond them, that I have no leave to tell; you will get beauty, strength and power, and I myself will be with you as a wife.' 'I put on you the bonds of a true hero,' she said, 'you to come away with me now to the Country of the Young.' Oisin kissed Finn his father, bade farewell to the Fianna, and went up on the horse; at the strand the horse shook himself and neighed three times, and made for the sea; and Finn said: 'It is my grief to see you going from me; and I am without a hope ever to see you coming back to me again.'

Hundreds of years — some say thousands — Oisin was in the Country of the Young, and it seemed short to him. He married Niamh, had two sons and a daughter, did not feel the time passing; and at last the desire came on him to see Finn and his comrades again. Niamh gave leave, and warned him three times with the same law: 'if you once get off the horse while you are away, or if you once put your foot to ground, you will never come back here again... you will be an old man, blind and withered, without liveliness, without mirth, without running, without leaping. And it is not now as it used to be, and you will not see Finn and his people, for there is not now in the whole of Ireland but a Father of Orders and armies of saints.'

He came back to green Ireland and looked about him, but there were no tidings to be got of Finn. A great troop of riders came toward him from the west and wondered at his size; and when he asked for Finn, they answered with the wound in one sentence: 'We often heard of Finn that lived long ago, and there is never was his equal for strength or bravery or a great name; and there is many a book written down by the sweet poets of the Gael about his doings and the doings of the Fianna.' Finn was a book now. At Almhuin of Leinster the great dun was weeds and nettles. Then the fatal kindness: riding near a place where men were raising a great stone, he saw a rider let his saddle-cushion slip, and, stooping to help him — 'I had such a wish and such a feeling for it that I forgot what I was told, and I got off the horse' — in the minute all the years came on him, and he was lying on the ground, and the horse took fright and went away and left him there, an old man, weak and spent, without sight, without shape, without comeliness, without strength or understanding, without respect.

It was to Patrick Oisin was brought; and in Patrick's house he told the whole story, and argued with the saint about Finn's soul — 'there is not a hell or a heaven there but I will put it down... if Osgar, my own son, is there, there is not in hell or in the Heaven of God a troop so great that he could not destroy it' — the last of the Fianna, keeping the old quarrel alive between the heroic age and the new one, one blind voice remembering everything.
narrative.zh: 費恩納故事圈最後的偉大故事是一場三百年的告別——接受不朽之邀的英雄，因一次善舉而失去它。一個多霧的清晨，費恩納的倖存者聚於芬恩身邊、在萊因湖畔狩獵——灌木開花、鳥兒歌唱、他們喚醒如夏日樹葉般歡欣的鹿群。不久他們見一絕美少女自西方乘一匹極快之細足白馬而來：頭戴王后之冠、身披及地黑絲斗篷綴赤金之星、雙眼湛藍清如草上之露、每縷金髮垂一金環、雙頰紅過玫瑰、膚白勝水上天鵝、唇甜如滲入紅酒之蜜——馬則釘著閃亮金蹄、腦後戴銀冠。『我的名字是金髮尼芙，我的名望超越世間所有女子，因我是青春之國王的女兒。』芬恩問其夫與其煩憂；『我沒有丈夫，因我從未嫁人。但費恩納之王啊，我已將我的愛戀與深情給了你的兒子、強手奧辛』——因他的大名與其勇武俊美之名。奧辛一聞此言，渾身無一處不愛美麗的尼芙。她為他唱出其國之憲章——愛爾蘭文學中最完整的彼岸廣告：果實、葉與花垂掛之樹；蜜與酒豐足；『隨時間流逝的衰竭不會臨於你；你永不見死亡或減損』；宴飲、音樂、金銀；百劍、百件極珍絲氅、百匹戰中最快之馬、百隻馴犬；青春之王的王冠；以及『更多樂趣，我無權言說；你將得美貌、力量與權柄，而我自己將為妻與你同在』。『我以真英雄之縛加於你：今夜隨我去青春之鄉。』奧辛親吻其父芬恩、辭別費恩納、上馬同行；至海灘馬嘶三聲、直奔大海；芬恩曰：『見你離我而去是我的悲痛；再見你歸來我已無望。』數百年——有人言數千年——奧辛居於青春之鄉，而於他恍如短暫。他娶尼芙、育二子一女、不覺時光流逝；最後思念芬恩與同伴之心湧起、求歸愛爾蘭。尼芙許之、三次以同一法度警示：『途中你若一次下馬、或一次足觸土地，便永不復返……你將成為盲而枯萎之老人，無生氣、無歡笑、無奔跑、無跳躍。而今日之愛爾蘭已非昔日，你將見不到芬恩與其族人，因全愛爾蘭今惟有一位修會之父與聖徒之軍。』他回到綠色的愛爾蘭、環顧四周、得不到芬恩的任何消息。一大隊騎者自西而來、驚其高大；他問起芬恩，他們一句話說出傷口：『我們常聽聞久遠之前的芬恩，其力量、勇武與大名無人能及；蓋爾甜美詩人所寫關於他與費恩納事蹟的書多得很。』芬恩如今是一本書。萊因斯特阿爾文的偉大白堡已蕪為雜草與蕁麻。繼而是致命的善舉：騎近眾人立石之處，他見一名騎者鞍墊滑落，俯身相助——『我對它有一種願望與情感，忘記了被告誡之事，下了馬』——一瞬之間，所有歲月一齊壓來，他倒在地上；馬受驚而逃、留下他於彼處——一位老者、衰弱力竭、無視力、無身形、無俊美、無力氣、無理解、無尊嚴。奧辛被送往帕特里克處；在聖人家中他講述整個故事、並就芬恩之靈與聖人爭辯——『無論地獄或天堂，無一支軍隊是我不敢摧毀的……若我子奧斯加在彼，地獄與上帝天堂之中無一支軍隊大到他能摧毀不了』——費恩納最後一人，在英雄時代與新時代之間讓舊日的爭吵繼續存活，一個失明的聲音記住了一切。

functions: Immortality's exchange-rate: three hundred years purchased by one foot touching the ground
The touched-shore law: the otherworld's irreversible exchange, replayed from Bran's voyage
Charter of the transition of ages: the Fianna dead, Finn become literature, Patrick's Ireland begun
Kindness as fate: the hero lost not through pride but through helping a fallen rider

title.en: The Bridal of Surya, the Sun's Daughter
title.zh: 蘇利耶（日女）的婚禮

region.en: Punjab plains (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 旁遮普平原（象徵性定位）

period: Rigveda, Book 10, Hymn 85, c. 1200-1000 BCE (Griffith translation, 1896)

source.work: The Hymns of the Rigveda, trans. R. T. H. Griffith (1896), Book 10, Hymn 85 (Surya's bridal)

summary.en: The most beautiful hymn of the Rigveda is a wedding: Surya, the Sun's daughter, is wooed over the sky-road by Soma, Gandharva, and Agni in turn, and weds Soma with all the gods as guests. The hymn is the charter of Vedic marriage itself - every Hindu wedding still recites its vows about the bride's sun-kissed, wide-prospering husband.
summary.zh: 梨俱吠陀最美的頌詩是一場婚禮：日女蘇利耶經天路先後受蘇摩、乾達婆與阿耆尼求聘，終嫁蘇摩，諸神皆為賓客。此頌即吠陀婚姻本身的憲章——至今印度婚禮仍誦其關於夫婿如日般廣受福澤的誓詞。

sensitivity.note: Living tradition: hymn recited at Hindu weddings; classified 'myth'.

passages.text: Truth was the beam of her bridal house, the rite its roof; the verses were the joining-car, and the songs its pillars - so the hymn builds Surya's house out of the sacrifice itself before her grooms arrive. Her suitors came over the high road of the sky: first Soma the moon won her, then Gandharva claimed her, then Agni held her - and to Soma, the gods gave the sun-maiden perfected: the wedding-gifts went round, the guests assembled.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Rigveda 10.85 (Griffith 1896); not verbatim.

passages.text: The vows are domestic and cosmic at once: pure, I give thee the husband of a wide and sun-shining dominion; may he prosper in thy keeping; and the crowd of the gods' people, the Anumatis, came to watch the daughter of the Sun carried in procession. The marriage of Surya became the marriage of every bride: the bridegroom's friends, the chariot, the veil, the swinging of the bride's foot over the threshold - the hymn invents in ritual what it names in myth.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Rigveda 10.85 (Griffith 1896); not verbatim.

canonical_translation: Ralph T. H. Griffith, 1896 (public domain)

title.en: The Ashvins Renew Old Chyavana
title.zh: 雙馬童使老仙人契耶凡納返老還童

region.en: Punjab plains (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 旁遮普平原（象徵性定位）

period: Rigveda, Book 1, Hymns 116-117, c. 1500-1200 BCE (Griffith translation, 1896)

source.work: The Hymns of the Rigveda, trans. R. T. H. Griffith (1896), Book 1, Hymns 116-117 (the Ashvins' deeds)

summary.en: The Ashvins, divine twin horsemen and physicians of the gods, renewed the aged sage Chyavana: they stripped the skin of his decrepitude from him as it were a garment, gave him a new body, and - in the Brahmana's telling - were rewarded with Soma, the only drink Indra denied them. Doctors of dawn and dusk, they save the drowning and mend the broken.
summary.zh: 雙馬童，諸神的騎手神醫，使年邁的仙人契耶凡納返老還童：他們如剝衣般剝下其老朽之皮，賜以新身——梵書言其因此獲得蘇摩，那是因陀羅唯一拒予雙神之飲。晨昏二位的醫者，既救溺水者，也修補折損者。

sensitivity.note: Ancient hymn; classified 'myth'.

passages.text: The two young heroes, the Nasatyas, ride the earliest car over sea and sky, thundering with their horses at daybreak and at dusk - healers who come at the hour between night and day, when no other god will answer.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Rigveda 1.116-117 (Griffith 1896); not verbatim.

passages.text: For Chyavana, grown old among his sons like a spent king, they stripped the withered skin from his body and wrapped him in new: the old man came out of his decrepitude with the beauty of youth restored. In the Brahmana's longer telling the twins' fee for the renewal was a draught of Soma, which Indra forbade to them; Chyavana, insulted, barred the door against Indra - and the god of a thousand eyes could not enter until the physicians of the gods had shared the cup.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Rigveda 1.116-117 (Griffith 1896); not verbatim. / Paraphrase of the Ashvins-Chyavana story (Brahmana tradition; Griffith 1896 hymns); not verbatim.

canonical_translation: Ralph T. H. Griffith, 1896 (public domain)

title.en: Sarama Tracks the Stolen Cattle
title.zh: 薩羅摩追蹤被竊的牛群

region.en: Vala's rock cave (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 伐羅岩洞（象徵性定位）

period: Rigveda, Book 10, Hymn 108, c. 1200-1000 BCE (Griffith translation, 1896)

source.work: The Hymns of the Rigveda, trans. R. T. H. Griffith (1896), Book 10, Hymn 108 (Sarama and the Panis)

summary.en: The Panis - the grasping merchant-demons - stole the cows of light into a rock cave. The divine hound Sarama, Indra's messenger, tracks them across the nine-and-ninety rivers and stands at the cave mouth; the Panis try to bribe her; she refuses, and her word for Indra is the war-cry that opens the rock.
summary.zh: 潘尼——貪婪的商魔——把光之牛群偷進岩洞。神犬薩羅摩，因陀羅的信使，跨九十九河追蹤，立於洞口；潘尼試圖賄賂她；她拒絕，其向因陀羅的回話即裂岩開洞的戰呼。

sensitivity.note: Ancient hymn; classified 'myth'.

passages.text: The Panis drove the kine of light into the hollow of the rock and hid them: their city of the stolen goods lies beyond the nine-and-ninety rivers, past which only the nose of the divine hound could follow. Sarama, sent as Indra's spy, found them and stood at the cave's mouth; the Panis offered her partnership - a share of the stolen herds if she would sell her lord's plan. She answered as a messenger must: I come to see your fortress, and my word is Indra's.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Rigveda 10.108 (Griffith 1896); not verbatim.

passages.text: Her report is the hymn's engine: let the Panis know their cattle will be carried back by force; and when Indra and the Angiras seers split the rock, the cows of the dawns lowed out of the cave to their old pastures - light ransacked back from the hoarders.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Rigveda 10.108 (Griffith 1896); not verbatim.

canonical_translation: Ralph T. H. Griffith, 1896 (public domain)

title.en: The Cave of Vala: Dawn Rescued from the Rock
title.zh: 伐羅之洞：自岩中救回的黎明

region.en: Vala's rock (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 伐羅之岩（象徵性定位）

period: Rigveda, Books 2, 10 (Griffith translation, 1896)

source.work: The Hymns of the Rigveda, trans. R. T. H. Griffith (1896), Book 10, Hymn 72 and hymns to Vala (e.g. 2.12, 1.62)

summary.en: Vala, a demon split from his own father's sacrifice, swallowed the dawns and the cows of light and sat on them inside stone. The Angiras seers - the poets themselves as priests of dawn - climbed the rock, sang the stone open, and Vala burst; the Ushases, the goddesses of dawn, lowed out like cows to the pastures of the sky.
summary.zh: 伐羅，自其父祭中裂出的惡魔，吞下黎明與光之牛，端坐於石內。盎耆羅仙人——詩人自己作為黎明的祭司——攀上岩石，以歌裂石，伐羅爆裂；烏莎斯諸女，黎明女神們，如母牛般哞叫著走向天上的牧野。

sensitivity.note: Ancient hymn; classified 'myth'.

passages.text: From the sacrifice of the gods Vala was split off, the first-born of seizure: he swallowed the cows and the dawns, and sat over them in the heart of stone - a hoard of light locked under rock. The Angiras, the chanters of old, set their song against the stone: they climbed it as men climb a ladder, and with their hymns carved like axes they cracked the mountain; the rocks opened like a split melon. Out of the cave came the Ushases lowing like kine at milking-time, finding their pastures of the sky again; the metaphor is the theology - dawn is cattle, and the poet's voice is the herdsman's tool.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Rigveda hymns to Vala (Griffith 1896); not verbatim.

canonical_translation: Ralph T. H. Griffith, 1896 (public domain)

title.en: Svarbhanu Pierces the Sun with Darkness
title.zh: 斯伐爾巴努以黑暗貫穿太陽

region.en: Punjab plains (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 旁遮普平原（象徵性定位）

period: Rigveda, Book 5, Hymn 40, c. 1500-1200 BCE (Griffith translation, 1896)

source.work: The Hymns of the Rigveda, trans. R. T. H. Griffith (1896), Book 5, Hymn 40 (the darkening of the Sun)

summary.en: The Asura Svarbhanu, the sun-swallower, pierced the Sun with darkness so that the sky itself could not see; the world went blind at midday. Indra struck down the demon, but the Sun's sight was broken - and the blind god was led, like a patient, to the Ashvins, the twin physicians, who restored his eye: the Vedas' own eclipse myth and its cure.
summary.zh: 阿修羅斯伐爾巴努，吞日者，以黑暗貫穿太陽，使天穹亦不能視；正午的世界陷入盲暗。因陀羅擊落惡魔，但日神之目已損——盲眼之神如病者被引至雙馬童，二位神醫復其目：吠陀自有的蝕神話與其療法。

sensitivity.note: Ancient hymn; classified 'myth'.

passages.text: O Surya, when the Asura's son Svarbhanu pierced thee through with darkness, all creatures looked like men bewildered who know not where they stand. Indra alone pierced the monster with his bolt; Atri, the sage, set the Sun upon the sky's road again - but the god's eye was hurt, and the night of midday did not lift.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Rigveda 5.40 (Griffith 1896); not verbatim.

passages.text: Then Atri took the blind Sun and led him to the two Ashvins as one leads a suffering king: they restored his sight with their remedies, and the hymn closes on the freed light - the eclipse explained, exorcised, and healed.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Rigveda 5.40 (Griffith 1896); not verbatim.

canonical_translation: Ralph T. H. Griffith, 1896 (public domain)

title.en: The Gambler's Lament
title.zh: 賭徒的哀歌

region.en: Punjab plains (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 旁遮普平原（象徵性定位）

period: Rigveda, Book 10, Hymn 34, c. 1200-1000 BCE (Griffith translation, 1896)

source.work: The Hymns of the Rigveda, trans. R. T. H. Griffith (1896), Book 10, Hymn 34 (the dice)

summary.en: The Rigveda's most personal poem is a confession of gambling ruin: the dice, 'born on a cold night with the magic herb', are praised as gods and blamed as demons; the speaker's wife hates him, his mother-in-law hunts him, and he ends homeless in the dark 'not knowing what I may get by the dice'. The oldest literature on addiction.
summary.zh: 梨俱吠陀最私人的一首詩是賭徒破產的自白：骰子『生於寒夜、與魔草相伴』，被譽為神又被斥為魔；說話者被妻所憎、被岳母所逐，最後『不知擲骰能得何物』地流落黑暗。關於成癮的最古老文獻。

sensitivity.note: Ancient hymn; classified 'myth'.

passages.text: The dice sprang high and rattled on the board; born on a cold night with the magic herb, they give delight and take a man's house: the gambler goes to the assembly hot from the hand, and never asks what fortune may do to him.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Rigveda 10.34 (Griffith 1896); not verbatim.

passages.text: The confession: my wife despised me for the dice, my mother-in-law even worse; no one lends to a gambler, and like an old horse worn out under the saddle I dwell in another man's house in the dark. The vow at the end is the first written self-reform: I will not play with them again; leave the men to their winnings, let me be - and the hymn ends with the dice's own fair warning: they have no pity even for the man who knows better.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Rigveda 10.34 (Griffith 1896); not verbatim.

canonical_translation: Ralph T. H. Griffith, 1896 (public domain)

title.en: Shunahshepa: The Boy Bound to the Post
title.zh: 設首施加：縛於祭柱的男孩

region.en: Varuna's realm (symbolic pin at Pushkar)
region.zh: 伐樓那之境（象徵性定位於布施伽爾）

period: Rigveda, Book 5, Hymns 2-3 (his own hymns); Aitareya Brahmana tradition (Griffith translation, 1896)

source.work: The Hymns of the Rigveda, trans. R. T. H. Griffith (1896), Book 5, Hymns 2-3 (hymns attributed to Shunahshepa), with the Brahmana narrative

summary.en: King Harishchandra, childless, vowed to Varuna that his first son would be sacrificed. The boy Rohita escaped into the wilds for years; at last he bought a poor man's son, Shunahshepa, to be tied to the post in his place. Bound before the fire, the boy sang to Varuna - and the god released him: he was adopted by the seer Vishvamitra and became a singer of hymns. The myth behind 'substitutionary sacrifice'.
summary.zh: 王哈利什陀羅無子，向伐樓那起誓以其首子獻祭。男孩羅希塔遁入荒野多年；終以貧者之子的兒子設首施加代替自己縛上祭柱。男孩縛於火前，向伐樓那唱頌——神遂釋之：他被維什瓦米陀收養，成為頌歌歌手。『替代祭』背後的神話。

sensitivity.note: Ancient hymn + Brahmana narrative; classified 'myth'.

passages.text: Harishchandra had vowed his son to Varuna for a son's sake; Rohita, grown, refused the stake and fled to the wilderness; the king was swollen with dropsy as long as the debt stood unpaid. In his wandering years the prince met Ajigarta the starving and bought his son Shunahshepa for a hundred kine - the father took the price and agreed to bind the boy; the boy agreed to go.
passages.note: Paraphrase of the Shunahshepa story (Brahmana tradition); not verbatim.

passages.text: Bound at the sacrificial post, the knife ready, Shunahshepa prayed to the gods with the hymns that still bear his name; Varuna, hearing, released the victim and healed the king - and Vishvamitra adopted the boy as a son among his hundred, calling him 'the singer saved at the post'.
passages.note: Paraphrase of the Shunahshepa story with Rigveda 5.2-3 (Griffith 1896); not verbatim.

canonical_translation: Ralph T. H. Griffith, 1896 (public domain)

title.en: Lopamudra and Agastya: The Wife's Reckoning
title.zh: 羅帕穆德拉與阿竭多：妻子之秤

region.en: Agastya's hermitage, southern hills (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 阿竭多仙居，南方山地（象徵性定位）

period: Rigveda, Book 1, Hymn 179, c. 1500-1200 BCE (Griffith translation, 1896)

source.work: The Hymns of the Rigveda, trans. R. T. H. Griffith (1896), Book 1, Hymn 179 (dialogue of Agastya and Lopamudra)

summary.en: Agastya, the pot-born dwarf sage, married the princess Lopamudra - chosen because her beauty was equal to heaven's. She told him plainly that austerity could not replace a household: 'the man who knows the gods, teach me; I desire offspring as a bride desires her lord'. He practiced austerity until his efforts bore two sons - and the Rigveda preserves her part of the argument, one of the oldest poems in the world spoken by a woman.
summary.zh: 罐中所生的矮小仙人阿竭多娶了公主羅帕穆德拉——因其美貌堪比天界。她直告他：苦行不能替代家室：『知神者，教我；我求子嗣，如新娘求其主。』他力行苦行直至生出二子——梨俱吠陀保存了她那一半的辯論，世上最古老的由女性口出的詩篇之一。

sensitivity.note: Ancient hymn; classified 'myth'.

passages.text: Agastya chose his bride with a strange standard: beauty that matched heaven; Lopamudra, framed by the gods and given to the king of Kashi, chose the ascetic's hut instead of the palace she left. The wife's verses press the point with wit: the aged sage grows old in austerity while the bride is a bride; not austerity, but giving, is the way of the ancestors - the fathers praised the seer and called his manliness incomplete.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Rigveda 1.179 (Griffith 1896); not verbatim.

passages.text: He answered with effort: the hymn counts his labors like an athlete's log - hundreds and thousands of recitations, hunger, thirst, heat - until by his exertion two sons were born, the first to milk and the second a singer; the couple's joint credit is recorded in the same breath.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Rigveda 1.179 (Griffith 1896); not verbatim.

canonical_translation: Ralph T. H. Griffith, 1896 (public domain)

title.en: The Hymn of the Frogs
title.zh: 青蛙頌

region.en: Punjab plains (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 旁遮普平原（象徵性定位）

period: Rigveda, Book 7, Hymn 103, c. 1500-1200 BCE (Griffith translation, 1896)

source.work: The Hymns of the Rigveda, trans. R. T. H. Griffith (1896), Book 7, Hymn 103 (the frogs)

summary.en: The Rigveda's comic masterpiece: the frogs of the dried pond wake when the rains come, 'one lows like a cow, one bleats like a goat, one is speckled' - and the hymn blesses them as Brahmins keeping vigil at the sacrifice of the year. Creation-by-monsoon, told with the priests' own jokes.
summary.zh: 梨俱吠陀的滑稽傑作：乾涸池塘的青蛙在雨至時醒來——『一者如母牛而哞，一者如山羊而咩，一者斑駁』——頌詩祝福牠們如守年度之祭的婆羅門。季風所造的世界，以祭司自己的笑話講述。

sensitivity.note: Ancient hymn; classified 'myth'.

passages.text: At rest for a year like Brahmins keeping a vow of silence, the frogs cry out when Parjanya, the rain-god, has watered the land: the voice rises from the drying pond like the singing of boys at school. They are catalogued with tenderness and fun: one lows like a cow, one bleats like a goat, one is speckled, one is green - and they come from out the waters to the pool, talking as their kind talk, laughing over the water's edge.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Rigveda 7.103 (Griffith 1896); not verbatim.

passages.text: The blessing is real: twelve months of drought they keep, and men cannot tell the season they mark; then the rain-year comes - and the hymn gives the frogs their reward, wealth of cows in a new monsoon, wealth of the singing word.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Rigveda 7.103 (Griffith 1896); not verbatim.

canonical_translation: Ralph T. H. Griffith, 1896 (public domain)

title.en: The Widow at the Husband's Pyre
title.zh: 丈夫火葬堆旁的寡婦

region.en: Punjab plains (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 旁遮普平原（象徵性定位）

period: Rigveda, Book 10, Hymn 18, c. 1200-1000 BCE (Griffith translation, 1896)

source.work: The Hymns of the Rigveda, trans. R. T. H. Griffith (1896), Book 10, Hymn 18 (funeral hymn; verses on the widow)

summary.en: The funeral hymn contains the tradition's earliest word on widowhood: the mourners address the woman at her husband's pyre - 'rise up, woman, to the world of the living; you lie by one whose life is spent' - and take the bow from the dead man's hand, breaking it for the living heir. The verse is the charter later cited against suttee; and the debate about its last lines has not ended.
summary.zh: 葬歌含傳統關於寡婦最早之言：哀悼者向火堆旁的女子說——『起來，女子，去活人的世界；你枕著的是一位生命已盡者』——並自死者手中取弓，為在世的繼承人折斷之。此節即後世反對寡婦殉葬者所引之憲章；而其末節的爭論至今未止。

sensitivity.note: Ancient funeral hymn, politically and morally contested in modern readings (suttee debate); classified 'myth'. The interpretive dispute is recorded here.

passages.text: The hymn sends the dead man forward to the fathers with his body, his eye to the Sun, his breath to the Wind - and turns to the living: let not our mothers weep; let the household be spared. To the widow the verse speaks with a hand on her shoulder: rise, come to the world of the living, woman; thou liest by this one whose life is gone - the husband taking thy hand was thy first duty; widowhood is the second.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Rigveda 10.18 (Griffith 1896); not verbatim.

passages.text: From the dead man's hand the bow is taken - a strong token for us, the mourners say - and broken, that he may not harm our fathers and may not harm us; the verse's margins hold the long later argument about what the woman was then commanded to do.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Rigveda 10.18 (Griffith 1896); not verbatim.

canonical_translation: Ralph T. H. Griffith, 1896 (public domain)

title.en: The Two Birds on the One Tree
title.zh: 一樹雙鳥

region.en: Atharvan school (symbolic pin at Kashi)
region.zh: 阿闥婆學派（象徵性定位於迦屍）

period: Mundaka Upanishad 3.1, late Vedic, c. 6th-2nd c. BCE (Müller translation, 1884)

source.archive: Internet Archive (Sacred Books of the East, vol. 15)
source.work: The Upanishads, Part II, trans. F. Max Müller (SBE 15, 1884), Mundaka Upanishad, Mundaka III, Khanda 1

summary.en: Two birds, fast friends, perch on the same tree: one eats the tree's sweet and bitter fruit, the other looks on without eating. When the eater, sunk in grief at his impotence, sees that other, his grief melts - and he knows it is he. The tree is the world, the birds are the self and the Self.
summary.zh: 雙鳥為友，同棲一樹：一隻啄食樹上的甘果與苦果，另一隻不食而觀。食果者陷於自力無能之悲，一旦望見那一位，悲即消融——他知那也是他自己。樹即世界，雙鳥即自我與大我。

sensitivity.note: Canonical scripture; classified 'religious'.

passages.text: Two birds, fast bound in friendship, sit on the same tree; one of them eats the sweet fig, the other, not eating, looks on. On the same tree the person sits, sunk and grieving, bewildered; but when he sees the other, the Lord, contented, and knows his glory, then his grief passes away from him. The knowing bird crosses: he becomes free, immortal, and light is shed on the tree's whole meaning - the image behind the later Sufi and Christian birds-on-a-branch alike, carried from the same Vedic source.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Mundaka Upanishad 3.1.1 (Müller 1884); not verbatim. / Paraphrase of Mundaka Upanishad 3.1.2 (Müller 1884); not verbatim. / Paraphrase of Mundaka Upanishad 3.1.3 (Müller 1884); not verbatim.

canonical_translation: F. Max Müller, SBE 15, 1884 (public domain)

title.en: Satyakama Jabala: The Boy Who Told the Truth
title.zh: 薩底耶迦摩：說真話的男孩

region.en: Kuru country (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 俱盧之地（象徵性定位）

period: Chandogya Upanishad 4.4-9, c. 8th-6th c. BCE (Müller translation, 1879)

source.archive: Internet Archive (Sacred Books of the East, vol. 1)
source.work: The Upanishads, Part I, trans. F. Max Müller (SBE 1, 1879), Chandogya Upanishad, Prapathaka IV

summary.en: The boy Satyakama wants to study, but has no father's name to claim. His mother Jabala tells him to say exactly what she told him - and the teacher Haridrumata accepts him because he did not swerve from truth. Sent to tend four hundred cows, he is taught the knowledge of Brahman one element at a time by a bull, fire, a swan and a diver-bird.
summary.zh: 男孩薩底耶迦摩欲求學，卻無父名可報。母親闍波羅囑其如實轉述；師哈里陀魯摩多因其不離真語而收之。遣其牧牛四百，牛、火、天鵝與潛水鳥逐一為其教授梵之知識，一次一種元素。

sensitivity.note: Canonical scripture; classified 'religious'.

passages.text: Satyakama, asking to be taught, named himself by his mother alone; asked what family he was of, he said: I have asked my mother, and she said she served many men in her youth, so she does not know - I am Satyakama Jabala, and I will tell you what she told me.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Chandogya Upanishad 4.4 (Müller 1879); not verbatim.

passages.text: The teacher answered: none but a Brahmin would speak so; fetch the fuel, my boy, I shall not let you swerve from truth - and he gave him four hundred cows to keep until they were a thousand, and told him not to come back until then.
