sensitivity.note: Continuation of the kern cycle; the cloud-thread hunt is a famous shapeshifting-contest episode (compare the pigkeepers' pursuit in cow-raid tradition). Death-and-restoration of the boy tagged 'resurrection' as a staged trick, not a religious miracle.

passages.text: After that he went to where Tadg O'Cealaigh was, having his old striped clothes and his old shoes as before, and when they asked him what art he had he said: "I am good at tricks. And if you will give me five marks I will show you a trick." With that the stranger put three rushes on the palm of his hand: "I will blow away the middle rush now, and the other two will stop as they are." So it was done. He showed too how he could wag the ear on one side of his head and the other would stay still.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Gregory 1904, Book IV, ch. IX; not verbatim.

passages.text: Then he took from his bag a thread of silk and gave a cast of it up into the air, that it was made fast to a cloud. He took a hare out of the same bag and it ran up the thread; then a little dog after the hare, yelping on its track; then a serving-boy after the hound; and out of another bag a beautiful, well-dressed young woman, bidden to follow them and not let the hare be torn by the dog. It was a delight to Tadg to look at them and listen to the hunt going on in the air.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Gregory 1904, Book IV, ch. IX; not verbatim.

passages.text: But the man of tricks said: "I am afraid there is some bad work going on up there. I am thinking the hound might be eating the hare, and the serving-boy courting the girl." He drew in the thread and found it so, and took his sword and struck the head off the boy; then, taking up the head, made a cast of it at the body, and it joined, but the face was turned backwards — and when Tadg said it would be better for him to be dead than living like that, he took hold of the boy and twisted his head straight, and he was as well as before.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Gregory 1904, Book IV, ch. IX; not verbatim.

title.en: Ciabhan and Cliodna's Wave
title.zh: 基亞班與克莉奧德娜之浪

region.en: Tonn Cliodhna (Glandore strand), Co. Cork, Ireland
region.zh: 愛爾蘭科克郡格蘭多爾海濱

period: Medieval Irish tradition; Lady Augusta Gregory retelling (1904)

source.work: Lady Augusta Gregory, Gods and Fighting Men (1904), Book IV, ch. XII, eBook #14465

summary.en: Ciabhan of the Curling Hair, the most beautiful young man of the world, is sent away from the Fianna for jealousy's sake and puts to sea; a rider on a dark grey horse rides under nine waves and rises with the tenth, and carries him to the Land of Promise. There Cliodna of the Fair Hair, who never loved before, gives him her love and sails away with him; but at Teite's Strand treachery plays her asleep with music, a great wave sweeps her off the strand, and the wave that took her bears her name for ever.
summary.zh: 鬈髮之基亞班為世間最美少年，因眾人妒忌而遭芬恩遣離，遂獨舟出海；一騎黑灰馬者潛行九浪、第十浪浮出，引他抵應許之地。彼處從未愛過人的仙姬克莉奧德娜對他一見傾心，隨他乘舟離去；然於泰特海濱，叛者以樂聲使她入睡，巨浪將她捲走。那浪因她得名，永存於世。

sensitivity.note: Tonn Cliodhna at Glandore is one of Ireland's three great waves; the drowning of the fairy bride at the strand is a wave-etiology. Coordinates are the traditional wave site.

passages.text: Ciabhan of the Curling Hair, the king of Ulster's son, was the most beautiful of the young men of the world at that time, but the Fianna grew tired of him because there was not a woman of their women but gave him her love, and Finn had to send him away at the last. He came to the Strand of the Cairn, saw a curragh with a narrow stern of copper, and put out to sea; great white shouting waves rose about him, every one the size of a mountain. Then he saw a rider coming towards him on a dark grey horse having a golden bridle, that would be under the sea for the length of nine waves and would rise with the tenth wave, and no wet on him at all. "What reward would you give to whoever would bring you out of this great danger?" "That you would give your service to whoever would give you his help," said Ciabhan, and he put his hand into the rider's hand, and was drawn on to the horse till they reached the shore of Tir Tairngaire, the Land of Promise.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Gregory 1904, Book IV, ch. XII; not verbatim.

passages.text: There was a feast made ready in Manannan's city, and when a clown had done his trick with nine willow rods, he put the rods in Ciabhan's hand, and Ciabhan stood up and did the feat before them all. Gebann, a chief Druid, had a daughter, Cliodna of the Fair Hair, that had never given her love to any man; but when she saw Ciabhan she gave him her love, and agreed to go away with him on the morrow. They went down to the landing-place and got into a curragh, and went on till they came to Teite's Strand in the south of Ireland.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Gregory 1904, Book IV, ch. XII; not verbatim.

passages.text: Ciabhan came on shore and went looking for deer under the thick branches of the wood, and he left the young girl in the boat on the strand. But the people of Manannan's house came after them having forty ships, and Iuchnu, that was in the curragh with Cliodna, did treachery, and played music to her till she lay down in the boat and fell asleep; and then a great wave came up on the strand and swept her away. And the wave got its name from Cliodna of the Fair Hair, that will be long remembered.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Gregory 1904, Book IV, ch. XII; not verbatim.

title.en: Tadg's Voyage to the Lake Island
title.zh: 塔格之湖島遠航

region.en: Inislocha, western ocean (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 西洋湖島（象徵定位）

period: Medieval Irish voyage-tale tradition; Lady Augusta Gregory retelling (1904)

source.work: Lady Augusta Gregory, Gods and Fighting Men (1904), Book IV, ch. XIV, eBook #14465

summary.en: Tadg son of Cian sails a forty-oxhide curragh to recover his wife and brothers, carried off by the king of Fresen, and is driven through wonder-islands — rams nine-horned as big as horses, birds whose eggs sprout feathers on the eaters — to Inislocha, the Lake Island. There he meets Cesair, first woman of Ireland, now living for ever; Connla of the Red Hair with his fairy bride; and Cliodna of the Fair Hair, who gives him a cup of wine-from-water and a prophecy of his death by a wild deer's wound in the green valley by the Boyne.
summary.zh: 吉安之子塔格乘四十牛皮大舟出海，尋找被弗雷森王擄走的妻子與兄弟；航經奇異群島——角如駿馬之九角公羊、食蛋生羽之奇鳥——終至湖島伊尼斯拉哈。彼處他遇見永生於此的愛爾蘭首位女子塞塞爾、與仙姬相伴的紅髮康拉、以及仙姬克莉奧德娜；她賜他化水為酒之杯，並預言他將死於博因綠谷野鹿之傷。

sensitivity.note: A full immram grafted onto the historical Tadg genealogy (Cian, father of Brian Boru's line); the island sequence is a Census of wonder-islands in the voyage genre. Cross-tradition parallel: voyage over the sea to islands of undying women.

passages.text: Tadg, son of Cian, was going his next heir's round into the west of Munster when Cathmann, king of the country of Fresen, slipped ashore with nine ships and took away Tadg's wife Liban and his two brothers, and put hardship on them — Eoghan to work a common ferry, Airnelach to cut firing, all their food barley seed and muddy water. Tadg escaped by his courage and the use of his sword, and made orders for a curragh that would be fit for a long voyage, with forty ox-hides of hard red leather soaked in bark, and masts and oars and pitch and everything that was wanting, and they put in every sort of meat and drink and clothes that would last a year.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Gregory 1904, Book IV, ch. XIV; not verbatim.

passages.text: They set out over the stormy heavy flood; on they rowed through twenty days and twenty nights till they got sight of a high land, and found it filled with sheep as big as horses, and one great ram of them all had nine horns, and he charged on Tadg's chief men, and Tadg killed him with a lucky cast of his spear that there was no escape from. On two islands after that were flocks of wonderful birds, and when some of the men began eating their eggs, feathers began to grow out on them on the moment, and dropped off again as quick as they came when they went bathing.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Gregory 1904, Book IV, ch. XIV; not verbatim.

passages.text: They came at last to a beautiful inver with green hills about it, and through apple gardens and a plain with a dew of honey over it, with a strong dun on every one of three steep hills. On the nearest hill a white-bodied woman welcomed Tadg: the dun of white marble was the home of the royal line of the kings of Ireland, and this island was Inislocha, the Lake Island. In the middle dun of gold he found Cesair, the first that ever reached Ireland, living for ever since she and the men that were with her came out of that dark unquiet land, and she told him every king and chief man of power in Ireland — Parthalon and Nemed, Firbolgs and Tuatha de Danaan — was in the dun beyond.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Gregory 1904, Book IV, ch. XIV; not verbatim.

passages.text: On the third hill were two comely lovers, a boy and a girl with gold chains about their necks; the boy had a sweet-smelling apple in his hand of which he would eat a third part, and it would never be less, and neither age nor sorrow could touch them that tasted it. "I am son to Conn of the Hundred Battles," he said; "it is Connla I am, and it is this girl of many shapes that brought me here." And Cliodna of the Fair Hair gave Tadg a green cup that turned water to wine, and warned him to keep it from escaping his hand, for at whatever time it escaped him his death would not be far away — a wandering wild deer would wound him in the green valley at the side of the Boinn, and after that strangers would put an end to him.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Gregory 1904, Book IV, ch. XIV; not verbatim.

title.en: Laeghaire Crimthann's Raid into Magh Mell
title.zh: 萊格爾·克里姆坦遠征幸福平原

region.en: Loch na nEan (Lake of Birds), Co. Galway, Ireland (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 愛爾蘭戈爾韋郡鳥湖（象徵定位）

period: Medieval Irish tradition; Lady Augusta Gregory retelling (1904)

source.work: Lady Augusta Gregory, Gods and Fighting Men (1904), Book IV, ch. XV, eBook #14465

summary.en: Fiachna of the Sidhe rises from the Lake of Birds to ask mortal help: his wife has been carried off by Goll, king of a people of Magh Mell, the Happy Plain. Laeghaire son of Crimthan Cass goes down into the lake with fifty fighting men, kills Goll in battle, restores the woman to Fiachna, and is rewarded with Fiachna's daughter Deorgreine, a Tear of the Sun, and fifty women for his fifty men — and for a year and a day the Sidhe keep them in the Happy Plain.
summary.zh: 仙族菲亞克納自鳥湖現身，請求凡人相助：其妻被幸福平原之王戈爾擄去。克里姆坦之子萊格爾率五十戰士入湖，陣斬戈爾，將女子歸還菲亞克納，並得菲亞克納之女「太陽之淚」德奧格萊恩為妻，其五十戰士各得一名仙女，眾人在幸福平原留居一年又一日。

sensitivity.note: A mortal raid into the underwater otherworld (descent-underworld by way of a lake); the sithchean (year and a day) elapsed among the Sidhe marks the otherworld-time motif. Lake pin symbolic; Magh Mell has no earthly coordinates.

passages.text: Laeghaire, son of the King of Connacht, Crimthan Cass, was out one day with his father near Loch na-n Ean, the Lake of Birds, and they saw a man coming to them through the mist, with long golden-yellow hair streaming after him, a gold-hilted sword at his belt, two five-barbed darts in his hand, and a five-folded crimson cloak about his shoulders. "I am come to look for the help of fighting men," said the stranger; "my name is Fiachna, son of Betach, of the men of the Sidhe; my wife was taken from my pillow and brought away by Eochaid, son of Sal; I killed him, and now she is gone to a brother's son of his, Goll, son of Dalbh, king of a people of Magh Mell. Seven battles I gave him, but they all went against me, and on this very day there is another to be fought, and I am come to ask help."
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Gregory 1904, Book IV, ch. XV; not verbatim.

passages.text: Fiachna went down into the lake, for it was out of it he had come, and Laegaire went down into it after him, fifty fighting men along with him. They saw a strong place before them and a company of armed men, and Goll, son of Dalbh, at the head of them. The two fifties attacked one another, and Goll fell, but Laeghaire and his fifty made a great slaughter of their enemies, so that not one of them made his escape. Laeghaire and his men went on to the dun of Magh Mell, and he called out to the men about it: "Your king has got his death, your chief men have fallen, let the woman come out, and I will give you your own lives." They agreed to that, and brought the woman out, and she made a complaint that got the name of "The Lament of the Daughter of Eochaid the Dumb." And that night Fiachna's daughter, Deorgreine, a Tear of the Sun, was given to Laeghaire as his wife, and fifty other women were given to his fifty fighting men, and they stopped with them there to the end of a year.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Gregory 1904, Book IV, ch. XV; not verbatim.

title.en: Ekalavya's Thumb
title.zh: 以卡拉維亞的拇指

region.en: Nishadha forest (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 尼沙陀森林（象徵性定位）

period: Mahabharata, Adi Parva, composition layers c. 400 BCE-400 CE (Ganguli translation, 1883-96)

source.work: The Mahabharata of Krishna-Dwaipayana Vyasa, trans. K. M. Ganguli (1883-96), Adi Parva, Ekalavya episode

summary.en: Rejected by Drona because of his forest birth, the Nishada prince Ekalavya built the master's statue in the woods and taught himself archery before it - becoming better than Arjuna. When Drona came demanding his fee, the boy cut off his own thumb and laid it before him: the epic's most-cited, most-contested parable of caste, loyalty and the price of a guru's word.
summary.zh: 因出身林野而被德羅納拒收的尼沙陀王子以卡拉維亞，在林中立師之像，對像自習射術——技藝勝過阿周那。當德羅納索其學資時，少年自斷拇指奉上：史詩中最常被引用、爭論最烈的關於種姓、忠誠與師言之價的寓言。

sensitivity.note: Living tradition and politically contested (caste readings); classified 'myth'.

passages.text: Drona refused the forest-born boy as a pupil - the teaching was reserved for princes - and Ekalavya went home, made a clay image of the master in the forest, and practiced before it until his hand was as true as the image's face.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Mahabharata, Adi Parva (Ganguli 1883-96); not verbatim.

passages.text: When dogs ran barking through the grove, seven arrows filled their mouths before they could cry; the princes traced the shot to a dark youth with a bow, and Arjuna went to his teacher, wounded in his pride: you promised me the best archer.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Mahabharata, Adi Parva (Ganguli 1883-96); not verbatim.

passages.text: Drona came and demanded his fee: thy right thumb. Ekalavya, glad to pay a master he had never been allowed to serve, cut it off at a stroke and held it out; his archery was gone in that instant, and the epic left the cost standing on the page for every age to argue.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Mahabharata, Adi Parva (Ganguli 1883-96); not verbatim.

canonical_translation: K. M. Ganguli, 1883-96 (public domain)

title.en: Karna's Basket: The Son of the Sun
title.zh: 迦爾納的竹籃：太陽之子

region.en: Ganges bank, Anga kingdom (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 恆河畔，鴦伽王國（象徵性定位）

period: Mahabharata, Adi Parva, composition layers c. 400 BCE-400 CE (Ganguli translation, 1883-96)

source.work: The Mahabharata of Krishna-Dwaipayana Vyasa, trans. K. M. Ganguli (1883-96), Adi Parva, the birth of Karna

summary.en: The maiden Kunti, testing a boon, called the Sun and bore a child already armored: born with golden ear-rings and a breastplate grown into his skin. Afraid, she set the basket on the river; it floated to the charioteer Adhiratha, who raised the boy as his son - and Karna lived his whole life paying for a birth his mother hid.
summary.zh: 少女恭蒂試驗恩賜，召日神而生下一個已然披甲的孩子：生而戴金環，胸鎧與皮肉同長。她因懼而將竹籃置於河上；竹籃漂至御者阿底羅陀之處，他將男孩養作己子——迦爾納的整個人生都在償付母親隱瞞的那次出生。

sensitivity.note: Living tradition; classified 'myth'.

passages.text: The boon was meant for practice; the Sun came as a bridegroom in full glory, and Kunti, unmarried, bore a child already wearing armor and ear-rings of gold - a birth like a dawn. The basket was set on the river at dawn; it floated down past reeds and towns to the charioteer's household, where Radha the childless took the armored boy for her own and named him Karna, the ear-ringed. The armor was his glory and his doom: a prince's courtesy could not outface a charioteer's son - and the sun-son's whole career was a bid to be honored as the person the armor proved he was.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Mahabharata, Adi Parva (Ganguli 1883-96); not verbatim.

canonical_translation: K. M. Ganguli, 1883-96 (public domain)

title.en: Draupadi's Swayamvara and the Fish's Eye
title.zh: 黑公主的自擇婚禮與魚眼

region.en: Panchala, capital of Drupada (symbolic pin at Bareilly)
region.zh: 般遮羅，德魯帕陀都城（象徵性定位於貝拿勒斯以北）

period: Mahabharata, Adi Parva, composition layers c. 400 BCE-400 CE (Ganguli translation, 1883-96)

source.work: The Mahabharata of Krishna-Dwaipayana Vyasa, trans. K. M. Ganguli (1883-96), Adi Parva, Chaitraratha and Draupadi sections

summary.en: Drupada raised a daughter from fire and a target no one could hit: a fish spinning above oil, to be pierced through the eye with a bow seen only in reflection. Kings failed; a brahmin youth stepped up, strung the bow, and shot the eye - Draupadi's garland fell on a poor student who was five husbands and two gods deep in disguise.
summary.zh: 德魯帕陀自火中生一女，並設下無人能中的的靶：懸於油面旋轉的魚，須以僅能於倒影中看見的弓，貫穿其眼。諸王皆敗；一名婆羅門青年上前張弓，射中魚眼——黑公主的花環落在一個貧寒學生身上，而此人實為五夫二神重重偽裝。

sensitivity.note: Living tradition; classified 'myth'.

passages.text: The target was a fish eye revolving above a smooth oil-pan, its bow heavy and its line of sight visible only in the oil's mirror - a test engineered so that no mortal aim could take it honestly. Karna of the golden armor lifted the bow to applause - and was refused by the princess herself, a brahmin-born's match for a suta's son; the slight he never forgave was minted here.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Mahabharata, Adi Parva (Ganguli 1883-96); not verbatim.

passages.text: The brahmin youth - Arjuna in beggar's garb - strung the great bow without a glance, took the eye in the oil's reflection, and the hall of kings watched a pauper take the fire-born bride; the brothers' laughter gave the game away.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Mahabharata, Adi Parva (Ganguli 1883-96); not verbatim.

canonical_translation: K. M. Ganguli, 1883-96 (public domain)

title.en: The Kirata and the Hunter: Arjuna Fights Shiva
title.zh: 基拉多與獵人：阿周那戰濕婆

region.en: Himalayan slopes above the Ganges (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 恆河上游喜馬拉雅坡地（象徵性定位）

period: Mahabharata, Vana Parva (Kiratarjuniya episode), composition layers c. 400 BCE-400 CE (Ganguli translation, 1883-96)

source.work: The Mahabharata of Krishna-Dwaipayana Vyasa, trans. K. M. Ganguli (1883-96), Vana Parva, Kirata-Arjuna section

summary.en: To win the weapons that would win the war, Arjuna performed fierce austerities in the Himalayas. When a boar charged him, he and a rough hunter - a Kirata of the hills - shot it at the same instant, and argued over the kill. The argument became a duel, the duel became a wrestling match that Arjuna could not win - and the hunter, laughing, revealed himself: Shiva, holding out the Pasupata, the weapon of destruction.
summary.zh: 為贏得足以贏得戰爭的武器，阿周那在喜馬拉雅行猛利苦行。當一頭野豬衝來，他與一名粗野的山中獵人——基拉多——同時放箭，為獵物之屬而爭。爭論化為決鬥，決鬥化為摔角，而阿周那不能取勝——獵人大笑現身：濕婆，遞出滅盡之器帕沙帕塔。

sensitivity.note: Living tradition; classified 'myth'.

passages.text: Arjuna's tapas burned so hot that the forest gods came to Shiva in complaint; the god chose the guise least suspected - a Kirata, a hill-hunter with a bow of bamboo and a dog for company. The boar died with two arrows in it; two hunters claimed the shot. Words went to blows, blows to wrestling - and the archer who felled armies could not move the mountaineer's shoulder.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Mahabharata, Vana Parva (Ganguli 1883-96); not verbatim.

passages.text: Exhausted, Arjuna made a clay linga and offered a garland - and the garland was already on the Kirata's neck. The god of gods gave him the Pasupata with the counsel: use it only against a foe no other weapon can end - and the war's arsenal was complete.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Mahabharata, Vana Parva (Ganguli 1883-96); not verbatim.

canonical_translation: K. M. Ganguli, 1883-96 (public domain)

title.en: Arjuna in Heaven: Indra's Court and the City of Nivatakavacha
title.zh: 阿周那天堂：因陀羅廷與尼婆達迦瓦遮之城

region.en: Svarga, Indra's heaven (symbolic pin at Meru)
region.zh: 須彌山頂因陀羅天界（象徵性定位）

period: Mahabharata, Vana Parva, composition layers c. 400 BCE-400 CE (Ganguli translation, 1883-96)

source.work: The Mahabharata of Krishna-Dwaipayana Vyasa, trans. K. M. Ganguli (1883-96), Vana Parva, Arjuna's ascent to heaven

summary.en: Indra's charioteer Matali came down and carried Arjuna bodily to heaven, where the god armed him for the war - and sent him first to kill the Nivatakavachas, demons armored in fog that no weapon could touch. Five years of heaven: the Gandharvas taught him music, the apsaras danced, and he returned to earth with every weapon in the gods' inventory.
summary.zh: 因陀羅的御者摩達利下凡，攜阿周那肉身登天；神為戰爭武裝他——並先遣他誅滅披霧之鎧、凡兵莫能觸及的尼婆達迦瓦遮群魔。五年的天堂：乾達婆授其樂，飛天為其舞，他攜諸神武庫之全部歸返大地。

sensitivity.note: Living tradition; classified 'myth'.

passages.text: Matali's chariot took the sky-road past clouds and stars; in Indra's court Arjuna was welcomed like a returning son - and sent, before any gift, to the city of the Nivatakavachas where the old demons had hidden behind armor of cloud.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Mahabharata, Vana Parva (Ganguli 1883-96); not verbatim.

passages.text: The battle was a siege of fog: with the gods' own weapons he cracked the cloud-armor and burned the city, and the heaven's oldest menace was cleared by a mortal's hand. The five years in Svarga armed the war: the conch Devadatta, the Gandiva bow, horses of the sun's stock, and a curriculum of music and dance - heaven's syllabus for a coming battlefield.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Mahabharata, Vana Parva (Ganguli 1883-96); not verbatim.

canonical_translation: K. M. Ganguli, 1883-96 (public domain)

title.en: Urvashi's Curse and Arjuna's Eunuch Year
title.zh: 鄔爾伐希的詛咒與阿周那的中性之歲

region.en: Svarga, Indra's heaven (symbolic pin at Meru)
region.zh: 因陀羅天界（象徵性定位於須彌）

period: Mahabharata, Vana Parva, composition layers c. 400 BCE-400 CE (Ganguli translation, 1883-96)

source.work: The Mahabharata of Krishna-Dwaipayana Vyasa, trans. K. M. Ganguli (1883-96), Vana Parva, Urvashi and Arjuna

summary.en: In heaven the apsara Urvashi offered herself to Arjuna; he refused with a bow to her years and his father's memory, and her curse fell: he shall live as a eunuch, desired by none. Indra softened the curse to one year of Arjuna's choosing - the year, it turned out, the war would need: as Brihannala the dance-teacher in Virata's court, his eunuch year kept the disguised heroes alive.
summary.zh: 在天界，飛天鄔爾伐希以身相許阿周那；他以其高齡與父親之誼婉拒，詛咒遂落：彼將以閹者之身度日，無人欲之。因陀羅將詛咒軟化為阿周那可自選的一年——而戰爭恰好需要那一年：作為毗羅陀王廷的舞師般厘哈那羅，其閹者之年使偽裝的英雄們得以存活。

sensitivity.note: Living tradition; gender readings contested; classified 'myth'.

passages.text: Urvashi came at midnight to the hero's chamber with love written in her walk; Arjuna folded his hands and refused - thou art the wife of my father's prime, and my mother in heaven's eyes. The apsara's curse answered the compliment's sting: thou shalt wander among women as a eunuch, fit for their music and unfit for their eyes - and Indra, arriving, cut the term to a single year at the cursed one's own choosing. Arjuna chose the thirteenth year of exile - and the curse became the disguise: in Virata's court as Brihannala, the eunuch dancing-master taught the princess and hid the archer of the age; the war's hinge was a curse, kept.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Mahabharata, Vana Parva (Ganguli 1883-96); not verbatim. / Paraphrase of Mahabharata, Vana Parva and Virata Parva (Ganguli 1883-96); not verbatim.

canonical_translation: K. M. Ganguli, 1883-96 (public domain)

title.en: The House of Lacquer
title.zh: 漆屋之計

region.en: Varanavata (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 婆羅那婆多（象徵性定位）

period: Mahabharata, Adi Parva, composition layers c. 400 BCE-400 CE (Ganguli translation, 1883-96)

source.work: The Mahabharata of Krishna-Dwaipayana Vyasa, trans. K. M. Ganguli (1883-96), Adi Parva, the house of lac

summary.en: Dhritarashtra sent his nephews to the festival-town of Varanavata - to a palace built of lac, pitch and straw by Duryodhana's order, ready to burn with them inside. Vidura's warning came in a riddle; the brothers tunneled out under cover of a harmless banquet, set fire themselves, and escaped through the earth while the city mourned their ashes - five bones and a mother, all false.
summary.zh: 持國遣其外甥赴慶典之城婆羅那婆多——入一幢由難敵下令以樹脂、瀝青與茅草所建的宮殿，屋內火起則五人與其母皆焚。維杜羅以謎語警示；兄弟們於無害宴會之掩護下掘地道遁走，自行縱火，於城中哀悼其灰燼之時自地底逃出——五副骨骸與一位母親，盡皆為偽。

sensitivity.note: Living tradition; classified 'myth'.

passages.text: The palace at Varanavata was handsome and hollow: walls of lacquer, floors of pitch, a bonfire waiting for a festival night - the uncle's love-letter to his nephews, written in kindling. Vidura's warning arrived in a language the watchers could not read: a house that catches fire from its own walls, said the uncle's riddle - the mouse escapes by digging; the brothers began the tunnel that night.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Mahabharata, Adi Parva (Ganguli 1883-96); not verbatim.

passages.text: On the night of the trap they burned the house themselves and slipped out the tunnel as the lac roared; a Nishada woman and her sons, drugged and drugged into the beds, were burned in their places - and the five Pandavas walked out of the ashes into the epic's next three hundred years.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Mahabharata, Adi Parva (Ganguli 1883-96); not verbatim.

canonical_translation: K. M. Ganguli, 1883-96 (public domain)

title.en: Bhima and Bakasura, the Village Eater
title.zh: 怖軍與婆迦蘇羅：食村的怪物

region.en: Ekachakra village (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 一輪村（象徵性定位）

period: Mahabharata, Adi Parva, composition layers c. 400 BCE-400 CE (Ganguli translation, 1883-96)

source.work: The Mahabharata of Krishna-Dwaipayana Vyasa, trans. K. M. Ganguli (1883-96), Adi Parva, Bakasura episode

summary.en: The rakshasa Bakasura held the village of Ekachakra to a tax of food and flesh, one household's meal and one child a day, carried by a boy on a cart. In disguise as brahmins, the Pandavas drew the turn of the woman of the house - Kunti sent Bhima, who ate the monster's delivery-cart dinner first, then the monster.
summary.zh: 羅剎婆迦蘇羅向一輪村徵收食物與血肉的稅——每日一家之餐與一童，由男孩推車送至。偽裝為婆羅門的般度五子恰好輪到屋主之女送稅——恭蒂遣怖軍前往，他先吃光怪物之車上餐點，再吃掉怪物本身。

sensitivity.note: Living tradition; classified 'myth'.

passages.text: The tax was simple and terrible: every day a cart of rice, two buffaloes, and a child - carried by the family whose lot had fallen, down the forest road to the cave of Bakasura. In the brahmin's rented hut the lot fell to Kunti's household; she sent her second son, the one who ate like ten, with the cart - telling him to enjoy the meal on the way.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Mahabharata, Adi Parva (Ganguli 1883-96); not verbatim.

passages.text: Bhima sat at the cave-mouth and ate the delivery; the monster, insulted, charged - and the wrestle ended when the boy's own arms were used as his last meal. The village's tax died with the eater; the beggars' household was richer by a secret.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Mahabharata, Adi Parva (Ganguli 1883-96); not verbatim.

canonical_translation: K. M. Ganguli, 1883-96 (public domain)

title.en: Draupadi and Kichaka in Virata's Court
title.zh: 黑公主與毗羅陀王廷的計迦迦

region.en: Virata's city, Matsya (symbolic pin at Jaipur)
region.zh: 毗羅陀王城，摩蹉國（象徵性定位於齋浦爾）

period: Mahabharata, Virata Parva, composition layers c. 400 BCE-400 CE (Ganguli translation, 1883-96)

source.work: The Mahabharata of Krishna-Dwaipayana Vyasa, trans. K. M. Ganguli (1883-96), Virata Parva, Kichaka episode

summary.en: In the thirteenth year of hiding, Draupadi served as a common maid in Queen Sudeshna's palace - and the general Kichaka wanted her. She refused; he shamed her publicly; she went to Bhima at night, and the general was found at dawn folded into a ball of flesh at the dancing-hall. Her five husbands, all disguised, could do nothing until the corpse spoke: the war's date was set by a maid's ruined honor.
summary.zh: 藏匿的第十三年，黑公主於王后蘇德什那宮中為侍婢——而大將計迦迦欲得之。她拒絕；他公開羞辱她；她夜見怖軍，黎明時大將被發現蜷成一團血肉於舞殿。她的五位丈夫皆在偽裝之中，在屍體說話之前皆無能為力：一名侍婦被毀的名譽定下了戰爭的日期。

sensitivity.note: Living tradition; classified 'myth'.

passages.text: Kichaka, the queen's brother and the army's pride, saw the new maid at the palace and pressed her with gifts and threats; Draupadi, a maid with five hidden husbands, refused - and he shamed her before the whole court. At night she found Bhima at the kitchens, his disguise as the royal cook; they laid the trap at the dancing-hall, and the general who came at midnight was folded like a wet cloth and left where he fell.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Mahabharata, Virata Parva (Ganguli 1883-96); not verbatim.

passages.text: The corpse told the story its finder could not: Kichaka's kinsmen tried to burn the maid on his pyre, Bhima rescued her in the night, and the king of Trigarta raised an army to avenge his ally - the heroes' year of silence ended with a war sized to fit.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Mahabharata, Virata Parva (Ganguli 1883-96); not verbatim.

canonical_translation: K. M. Ganguli, 1883-96 (public domain)

title.en: Nahusha, the Serpent King of Heaven
title.zh: 那護沙：天界的蛇王

region.en: Himalaya, Yudhishthira's forest road (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 喜馬拉雅，堅戰的林路（象徵性定位）

period: Mahabharata, Vana Parva, composition layers c. 400 BCE-400 CE (Ganguli translation, 1883-96)

source.work: The Mahabharata of Krishna-Dwaipayana Vyasa, trans. K. M. Ganguli (1883-96), Vana Parva, Nahusha episode

summary.en: When Indra fled heaven after killing Vritra, the gods crowned the mortal Nahusha in his place - and power made him drunk: he rode in a palanquin carried by the seers themselves, touching Agastya's head with his foot. The sage's curse turned him into an enormous python, lying across the forest road until a Yudhishthira came to answer his riddles and free him.
summary.zh: 因陀羅誅弗栗多後逃離天界，諸神立凡人那護沙代之——權力使之醉：他乘由仙人親自抬行的轎輦，以足觸阿竭多之首。仙人的詛咒化他為巨蟒，橫臥林路，直到一位堅戰前來解答其謎而釋放他。

sensitivity.note: Living tradition; classified 'myth'.

passages.text: Nahusha, a pious king of the lunar line, was lifted to Indra's vacant throne; the court bowed, the apsaras attended - and the seat taught him what thrones teach: that other men are furniture. His palanquin was carried by the seers of old; hurrying, he struck Agastya on the crown - and the sage's curse fell like a stone: be the snake you have behaved as, and lie across the world's roads until the right king frees you.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Mahabharata, Vana Parva (Ganguli 1883-96); not verbatim.

passages.text: A python the size of a hill lay on the Pandavas' forest road and seized Bhima; Yudhishthira answered its questions - What is liberation? What is the highest dharma? - and the serpent, satisfied, rose from the dust as Nahusha again, mounted to heaven, and returned Indra's throne unspoiled.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Mahabharata, Vana Parva (Ganguli 1883-96); not verbatim.

canonical_translation: K. M. Ganguli, 1883-96 (public domain)

title.en: Bhima Meets His Brother Hanuman
title.zh: 怖軍遇其兄哈奴曼

region.en: Gandhamadana mountain (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 甘陀摩達那山（象徵性定位）

period: Mahabharata, Vana Parva, composition layers c. 400 BCE-400 CE (Ganguli translation, 1883-96)

source.work: The Mahabharata of Krishna-Dwaipayana Vyasa, trans. K. M. Ganguli (1883-96), Vana Parva, Bhima and Hanuman

summary.en: Sent by Draupadi to fetch the scent-lotus of the north, Bhima came to an old monkey lying across the road, who asked the strong man to lift his tail out of the path. The tail would not lift. Enraged, Bhima grew huge - and the old monkey laughed, and grew huger: Hanuman, his half-brother by the same Wind-father, giving his kinsman a lesson in how large the family is.
summary.zh: 受黑公主之遣北上尋取香蓮的怖軍，遇一老猴橫臥路上，請壯士將其尾移出小徑。其尾不可舉。怖軍怒而身漲巨——老猴大笑，身漲更巨：哈奴曼，同以風神為父的異母兄，給其弟上了一課：家族之量。

sensitivity.note: Living tradition; classified 'myth'.

passages.text: The monkey lying in the mountain road asked only one courtesy: move my tail aside; I am old. Bhima, proud of his strength, pulled - and the tail did not move. He tried with shame and then with anger; the monkey, smiling, asked what his strength was for. Bhima grew vast - and the old shape grew vaster, filling the valley: it was Hanuman, son of the same Wind. The brothers embraced: Hanuman blessed the quest, promised to ride on Bhima's banner in the coming war, and sent him on to the lotus lake - the Ramayana's hero lending the Mahabharata his tail for a lesson.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Mahabharata, Vana Parva (Ganguli 1883-96); not verbatim.

canonical_translation: K. M. Ganguli, 1883-96 (public domain)

title.en: The Yaksha's Questions
title.zh: 夜叉之問

region.en: Dvaita lake, forest exile (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 陀夷多湖，林居（象徵性定位）

period: Mahabharata, Vana Parva, composition layers c. 400 BCE-400 CE (Ganguli translation, 1883-96)

source.work: The Mahabharata of Krishna-Dwaipayana Vyasa, trans. K. M. Ganguli (1883-96), Vana Parva, Yaksha Prashna

summary.en: A crane at a forest lake killed four brothers who drank without answering its riddle. Yudhishthira came last, gave the answers - 'the greatest wonder is that men die every day, and the living walk on as if immortal' - and was offered one brother's life. He chose Nakula, his stepmother's son: justice over blood, and the crane was Dharma, his father, giving him back all five.
summary.zh: 林中湖畔的怪鳥誅殺了四個未答其謎即飲水的兄弟。堅戰最後到來，給出答案——『最大的奇蹟是人們日日赴死，而生者仍如不死般行走』——並被允許救活一位兄弟。他選擇繼母之子無種：公道勝過血緣；而怪鳥即是正法，其父，歸還五子。

sensitivity.note: Living tradition; classified 'myth'.

passages.text: One by one the four Pandavas drank at the unseen lake and were struck down by its voice: this water is guarded; answer before you drink. Only their brother was left to come looking. Yudhishthira answered every question - what is the greatest marvel? Men die daily, and the living walk as if immortal; what is the best wealth? Knowledge; what is the greatest gain? Health; what is dharma? The conduct of the good.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Mahabharata, Vana Parva (Ganguli 1883-96); not verbatim.

passages.text: The reward offered was one brother; he chose Nakula, Madri's son, so that both his mothers would have a survivor - and the crane stood up as Dharma, the god of justice, his own father, restored all four: the ethics exam passed by the only student it was set for.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Mahabharata, Vana Parva (Ganguli 1883-96); not verbatim.

canonical_translation: K. M. Ganguli, 1883-96 (public domain)

title.en: The Dice Game in the Hall of Kauravas
title.zh: 俱盧族廷上的骰局

region.en: Hastinapura, gambling hall (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 象城，賭廳（象徵性定位）

period: Mahabharata, Sabha Parva, composition layers c. 400 BCE-400 CE (Ganguli translation, 1883-96)

source.work: The Mahabharata of Krishna-Dwaipayana Vyasa, trans. K. M. Ganguli (1883-96), Sabha Parva, the game of dice

summary.en: Summoned by a friendly invitation that was a trap, Yudhishthira sat down to dice against Shakuni, who played with his brother's charred bones - dice that obeyed him. Kingdom, brothers, self, Draupadi: all staked and lost in an afternoon. Her question in the assembly - 'whom have you lost first, yourself or me?' - broke the hall's law open; what followed made the war.
summary.zh: 以友善之名實為陷阱的邀請召堅戰入局，對手沙恭尼執其兄之焦骨所製之骰——骰子聽其號令。王國、兄弟、自身、黑公主：一個下午盡數押上並輸掉。她在集會上的質問——『你先輸的是你自己還是我？』——撕裂了廷堂之法；隨後之事釀成大戰。

sensitivity.note: Living tradition; classified 'myth'.

passages.text: Shakuni's dice were made from the bones of his own ruined family and obeyed him like servants; against them Yudhishthira, incapable of refusing a challenge, staked the kingdom as he had been taught dharma - by losing it. Brother by brother, self by self, he staked and lost - and when nothing was left, Dushasana was sent to drag Draupadi, dressed for menstruation, into the hall of men as the last stake won.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Mahabharata, Sabha Parva (Ganguli 1883-96); not verbatim.

passages.text: Her question to the assembly - was I lost before or after you lost yourself? - hung over the elders who kept their eyes down; the attempt to disrobe her was answered by the sari that would not end, and Bhima's vow that day put the war on its calendar.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Mahabharata, Sabha Parva (Ganguli 1883-96); not verbatim.

canonical_translation: K. M. Ganguli, 1883-96 (public domain)

title.en: Krishna's Last Embassy to Hastinapura
title.zh: 克里希那最後一次赴象城

region.en: Hastinapura (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 象城（象徵性定位）

period: Mahabharata, Udyoga Parva, composition layers c. 400 BCE-400 CE (Ganguli translation, 1883-96)

source.work: The Mahabharata of Krishna-Dwaipayana Vyasa, trans. K. M. Ganguli (1883-96), Udyoga Parva, Krishna's peace mission

summary.en: Before the war, Krishna went unarmed to Duryodhana's court to ask for five villages - anything, he said, rather than the blood of two houses. Duryodhana offered not a pin's point of land. Krishna's answer was the cosmic form shown to the court, the sanction of the war, and the choice given to each side - and the age chose.
summary.zh: 戰前，克里希那空手赴難敵之廷，求取五村——他說，兩族之血，任何代價都勝過。難敵連一根針尖之地也不予。克里希那的回答是向王廷顯示宇宙之形、戰爭之許可，以及給予雙方的選擇——而這個時代做出了選擇。

sensitivity.note: Living tradition; classified 'myth'.

passages.text: Krishna's offer was a masterpiece of smallness: five villages for five princes - a grain of the contested earth - so that no one could say war was chosen over land. Duryodhana refused even the pin's point, and ordered the envoy seized; Krishna rose from his seat, unfolded his cosmic form before the court, and the age saw what it was electing.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Mahabharata, Udyoga Parva (Ganguli 1883-96); not verbatim.

passages.text: The embassy's record stands in the epic as the last moral exit: the war was not forced by land-grab but by a court that would not grant a village's worth of peace - the doctrine that choices, not fates, made Kurukshetra.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Mahabharata, Udyoga Parva (Ganguli 1883-96); not verbatim.

canonical_translation: K. M. Ganguli, 1883-96 (public domain)

title.en: Karna and the Disguised Teacher
title.zh: 迦爾納與偽裝的教師

region.en: Himalayan hermitage (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 喜馬拉雅仙居（象徵性定位）

period: Mahabharata, Adi/Vana Parva traditions, composition layers c. 400 BCE-400 CE (Ganguli translation, 1883-96)

source.work: The Mahabharata of Krishna-Dwaipayana Vyasa, trans. K. M. Ganguli (1883-96), the curses of Karna

summary.en: Rejected by every teacher because of his charioteer birth, Karna learned from the sage Parashurama by pretending to be a brahmin. A nap in the teacher's lap ended the disguise: a bee's sting drew blood, the master woke to see a kshatriya's endurance, and the curse fell - the weapon you learned shall fail you when you need it. A cow's curse and a beggar's curse stacked the same verdict: the finest archer of the age was scheduled to die by accident of timing.
summary.zh: 因御者之子之出身被所有教師拒絕，迦爾納偽裝婆羅門從仙人婆羅沙羅學藝。在教師膝上午睡斷送了偽裝：一隻蜂螫出血，師醒見其剎帝利之忍耐，詛咒遂降——你所學的武器將在你最需要時背棄你。母牛之詛咒與乞者之詛咒疊出同一判決：當世最優的射手，被預定死於時機的偶然。

sensitivity.note: Living tradition; caste readings contested; classified 'myth'.

passages.text: Parashurama taught only brahmins; Karna wore the sacred thread of a brahmin's son and learned the Brahmastra and the bow of heaven - the century's best student under a false name. The bee found his shoulder in the teacher's lap; he bore the sting in silence rather than wake his sleeping master, and the blood woke him instead: a kshatriya's silence is not a brahmin's patience - the weapon shall fail thee at the hour of thy death.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Mahabharata (Ganguli 1883-96); not verbatim.

passages.text: The second curse came from a brahmin whose cow Karna had accidentally killed in practice - thy wheel shall sink in the earth at the last. Both curses kept their word at Kurukshetra: the weapon forgotten in the mouth, the wheel swallowed by the field - a life's talent bankrupted by a life's small sins.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Mahabharata (Ganguli 1883-96); not verbatim.

canonical_translation: K. M. Ganguli, 1883-96 (public domain)

title.en: The Death of Drona: A Lie Told for a War
title.zh: 德羅納之死：為戰爭而說的謊

region.en: Kurukshetra (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 俱盧之野（象徵性定位）

period: Mahabharata, Drona Parva, composition layers c. 400 BCE-400 CE (Ganguli translation, 1883-96)

source.work: The Mahabharata of Krishna-Dwaipayana Vyasa, trans. K. M. Ganguli (1883-96), Drona Parva, the fall of Drona

summary.en: Drona's chakravyuha was eating the Pandava army until Krishna proposed the one weapon that could stop him: a lie. An elephant named Ashwatthama was killed - and 'Ashwatthama is dead' was cried across the field, true of the elephant, false of the son. Drona asked Yudhishthira, the man who never lied; his broken answer - 'it is true, but not the man' - was lost in Krishna's conch, and the teacher dropped his bow.
summary.zh: 德羅納的輪陣正吞食般度軍隊，直到克里希那提出唯一能阻止他的武器：謊言。一頭名為馬音的大象被殺——『馬音已死』的呼喊傳遍戰場，於象為真，於子為假。德羅納問那個從不說謊的堅戰；他破碎的回答——『是，但不是那個人』——被克里希那的法螺聲吞沒，教師垂下了弓。

sensitivity.note: Living tradition; the ethics of the lie are debated in the tradition itself; classified 'myth'.

passages.text: The plan was honest about being dishonest: kill the elephant named Ashwatthama, then say the name - the teacher will ask only the man he trusts, and the man he trusts has never lied. Yudhishthira's answer tried to be both true and loyal: Ashwatthama is dead - the elephant, not the son - but the conch and the drums buried the second half of the sentence in the first half's sound.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Mahabharata, Drona Parva (Ganguli 1883-96); not verbatim.

passages.text: Drona, hearing his boy was gone, sat down on the field and closed his eyes in yoga; Dhrishtadyumna's sword did the rest - and the epic has argued ever since about the one sin that bought the war's turning point.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Mahabharata, Drona Parva (Ganguli 1883-96); not verbatim.

canonical_translation: K. M. Ganguli, 1883-96 (public domain)

title.en: Bhishma on the Bed of Arrows
title.zh: 箭床上的毗濕摩

region.en: Kurukshetra (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 俱盧之野（象徵性定位）

period: Mahabharata, Bhishma Parva, composition layers c. 400 BCE-400 CE (Ganguli translation, 1883-96)

source.work: The Mahabharata of Krishna-Dwaipayana Vyasa, trans. K. M. Ganguli (1883-96), Bhishma Parva

summary.en: The grandfather of both armies was held up for ten days by his own vow - he could not be killed while he chose not to fall, and would not fight women or women-born. Shikhandin was brought against him; Arjuna's arrows passed behind that shield and stitched Bhishma to the earth. He lay on the arrows-bed for fifty-eight nights, teaching the dharma of kings while the war raged over him.
summary.zh: 兩軍共同的祖父被自己的誓言懸於十天之久——他不能在自己不願倒下時被殺，且不與女子或由女子所生者為戰。希甘丁被引至其前；阿周那之箭越過那道盾，把毗濕摩縫在地上。他在箭床上躺了五十八夜，一邊於戰火之中講授王法。

sensitivity.note: Living tradition; classified 'myth'.

passages.text: Bhishma could not fall while he willed to stand: the boon of his father's blessing and the vow of his youth held him up while both armies battered; the age's finest archer was being killed by permission. The loophole was Shikhandin - the reborn Amba, whom he had wronged and could not fight; behind that shield Arjuna emptied his quiver, and the old man went down onto a bed of his own arrows.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Mahabharata, Bhishma Parva (Ganguli 1883-96); not verbatim.

passages.text: He chose the hour of his death: fifty-eight nights on the arrows, waiting for the sun's northern road, teaching Yudhishthira the duties of kings from a bed of pain - the epic's sage-parliament on the field it had helped to ruin.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Mahabharata, Bhishma Parva (Ganguli 1883-96); not verbatim.

canonical_translation: K. M. Ganguli, 1883-96 (public domain)

title.en: Abhimanyu in the Chakravyuha
title.zh: 阿毗曼紐入輪陣

region.en: Kurukshetra (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 俱盧之野（象徵性定位）

period: Mahabharata, Drona Parva, composition layers c. 400 BCE-400 CE (Ganguli translation, 1883-96)

source.work: The Mahabharata of Krishna-Dwaipayana Vyasa, trans. K. M. Ganguli (1883-96), Drona Parva, Abhimanyu episode

summary.en: Sixteen years old, Abhimanyu had heard in his mother's womb how to enter the Chakravyuha - but the exit lesson was interrupted. On the thirteenth day he broke into the wheel-formation alone, fought through its rings, and was killed in the closed center by six warriors breaking every rule of single combat. The boy's death broke the war's remaining decencies.
summary.zh: 十六歲的阿毗曼紐曾在母胎中聽聞入輪陣之法——但出口之課被打斷。第十三日，他獨自衝入車輪陣，連破其環，於封閉中心遭六名戰士違反單挑規則而圍殺。少年之死擊碎了戰爭僅存的體面。

sensitivity.note: Living tradition; classified 'myth'.

passages.text: The lesson was interrupted at the exit: Arjuna's wife fell asleep as he explained the labyrinth of rings, and the boy in her womb learned the way in but not the way out - the epic's cruelest incomplete education. On the thirteenth day, with the formation spinning and his uncles pinned, Abhimanyu broke through the mouth of the wheel alone and cut his way ring by ring toward its center.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Mahabharata, Drona Parva (Ganguli 1883-96); not verbatim.

passages.text: Six warriors closed on one boy - wheel-hubs, swords, bows from every side; he died fighting with a wheel-broken bow, and the code of the field broke with him: the war had run out of rules it was willing to keep.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Mahabharata, Drona Parva (Ganguli 1883-96); not verbatim.

canonical_translation: K. M. Ganguli, 1883-96 (public domain)

title.en: Gandhari's Curse
title.zh: 甘陀利的詛咒

region.en: Kurukshetra (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 俱盧之野（象徵性定位）

period: Mahabharata, Shalya/Sauptika Parvas, composition layers c. 400 BCE-400 CE (Ganguli translation, 1883-96)

source.work: The Mahabharata of Krishna-Dwaipayana Vyasa, trans. K. M. Ganguli (1883-96), the curse of Gandhari

summary.en: The blindfolded queen who had chosen her husband's darkness as her own walked through the field of her hundred dead sons and found Yudhishthira standing alive. Her grief opened - and her curse fell on Krishna: as thou hast watched my sons destroy each other, so shall thy house destroy itself, and the women of thy line shall weep as I do now. Thirty-six years later it came true.
summary.zh: 以布覆目、選擇與丈夫共享黑暗的王后，走過百子盡亡的戰場，發現堅戰仍活著。她的悲痛開口——詛咒降於克里希那：如你眼看我的兒子們互相毀滅，你的家也將自相殘殺，你家族的女子將如我今日般哭泣。三十六年後，此言應驗。

sensitivity.note: Living tradition; classified 'myth'.

passages.text: Gandhari had worn the bandage since her wedding, sharing her blind husband's world; her hundred sons died in eighteen days - she came to the field led by hand, over the bodies of her house. Her foot found Yudhishthira alive where all her sons were not; the queen who had cursed no one cursed the god who had permitted it - the same grief, turned toward its author.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Mahabharata (Ganguli 1883-96); not verbatim.

passages.text: Krishna took the curse as his due: in the thirty-sixth year the Yadavas fell on each other on the beach at Prabhasa, and the women of Dvaraka wept on the shore - the epic's oldest rule, that every grief writes its own future.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Mahabharata, Mausala Parva (Ganguli 1883-96); not verbatim.

canonical_translation: K. M. Ganguli, 1883-96 (public domain)

title.en: Karna's Wheel in the Mud
title.zh: 迦爾納陷於泥中的車輪

region.en: Kurukshetra (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 俱盧之野（象徵性定位）

period: Mahabharata, Karna Parva, composition layers c. 400 BCE-400 CE (Ganguli translation, 1883-96)

source.work: The Mahabharata of Krishna-Dwaipayana Vyasa, trans. K. M. Ganguli (1883-96), Karna Parva

summary.en: On the seventeenth day, at the last duel of the age's two archers, the earth took Karna's chariot wheel - the curses of his teachers arriving on schedule. He asked Arjuna for the decency of the code: wait till I lift the wheel. Krishna reminded Arjuna of Draupadi and of every Karna courtesy refused - and the arrow flew while the wheel was being lifted.
summary.zh: 第十七日，當世兩位神射手的最後決鬥中，大地吞下迦爾納的戰車之輪——其師之詛咒如期而至。他請阿周那遵守戰場規矩：待我舉輪。克里希那向阿周那重提黑公主與迦爾納每一次被拒的禮數——而箭在車輪被抬起之時飛出。

sensitivity.note: Living tradition; classified 'myth'.

passages.text: The wheel sank at the duel's hinge: two curses and a mother's missing gift stacked on one axle, and the sun-son stood half-buried asking for the code's mercy. Krishna's arithmetic was merciless: remember the dice-hall, remember the insults; the code was for men who kept it - and Arjuna's arrow was already loosed.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Mahabharata, Karna Parva (Ganguli 1883-96); not verbatim.

passages.text: The epic refuses to close the case: Karna died cursing the god's fairness, and the age's finest generosity - his lifelong giving - was spent on a battlefield that took it for weakness; the war's moral ledger stays open on this page.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Mahabharata, Karna Parva (Ganguli 1883-96); not verbatim.

canonical_translation: K. M. Ganguli, 1883-96 (public domain)

title.en: Ashwatthama's Night Massacre and the Jeweled Forehead
title.zh: 馬音的夜襲與寶石之額

region.en: Kurukshetra camp (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 俱盧之野營地（象徵性定位）

period: Mahabharata, Sauptika Parva, composition layers c. 400 BCE-400 CE (Ganguli translation, 1883-96)

source.work: The Mahabharata of Krishna-Dwaipayana Vyasa, trans. K. M. Ganguli (1883-96), Sauptika Parva

summary.en: His father murdered by a lie, Ashwatthama entered the sleeping Pandava camp at night and killed everyone he could find, including the princes in their beds, and set the Khandava forest-fire of vengeance alight. Caught, he threw the Brahmashirsha at the womb of the last heir; Krishna cursed him to roam immortal - wound-ridden, begging from village to village, the gem on his brow the only evidence of what he was.
summary.zh: 其父死於謊言，馬音夜入沉睡的般度營，見人即殺，連床上王子亦不例外，並燃起復仇的乾達婆之火。被擒後，他將婆羅摩首箭射向最後繼承人的子宮；克里希那詛咒他永世漂泊——帶傷而行，沿村乞食，額上寶石成為他身份的唯一證據。

sensitivity.note: Living tradition; classified 'myth'.

passages.text: The night raid avenged a father with a cemetery: the general's son swept the sleeping camp, killing princes in their beds and Draupadi's brothers in their tents - the war's last cruelty, done without a battle. His Brahmashirsha, aimed at Uttara's unborn son, was caught and turned by Krishna - the child was burned dark (hence Krishna, the dark one) and reborn as Parikshit, the survivor whose grandson would hear this very epic. The gem torn from his forehead was the price: immortal, festering, begging door to door for three ages - a walking sermon on what the war's last night cost the side that won it.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Mahabharata, Sauptika Parva (Ganguli 1883-96); not verbatim.

canonical_translation: K. M. Ganguli, 1883-96 (public domain)

title.en: King Sibi Weighs His Flesh Against a Dove
title.zh: 尸毗王以己肉秤鴿

region.en: Sibi's capital (symbolic pin, northwest)
region.zh: 尸毗都城（象徵性定位，西北）

period: Mahabharata, Vana Parva, composition layers c. 400 BCE-400 CE (Ganguli translation, 1883-96)

source.work: The Mahabharata of Krishna-Dwaipayana Vyasa, trans. K. M. Ganguli (1883-96), Vana Parva, the story of Sibi

summary.en: A dove fleeing a hawk fell into King Sibi's lap and begged protection; the hawk, cheated of its lawful prey, demanded its dinner. The king cut flesh from his own body to weigh against the dove - more and more, until he climbed onto the scale himself. The hawk was Indra and the dove Agni, testing the most generous king on earth.
summary.zh: 一鴿逃避獵鷹，落入尸毗王懷中求庇；鷹因失去合法獵物而索其晚餐。王自體割肉以秤鴿——愈割愈多，直至親自登上秤盤。鷹即因陀羅，鴿即阿耆尼，試探世上最慷慨的王。

sensitivity.note: Living tradition (also a Buddhist Jataka); classified 'myth'.

passages.text: The dove dropped into the king's lap like a falling leaf, and its voice was a voice: protect me, king; the hawk's claim is hunger, but my claim is shelter. Sibi's scale was exact: he cut his own thigh to equal the dove's weight - and the dove grew heavier with every cut, as if fed by the king's giving.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Mahabharata, Vana Parva (Ganguli 1883-96); not verbatim.

passages.text: At last he sat himself into the pan - and the gods dropped their disguises: the test of the most generous king on earth had weighed his whole self, and found it enough; his wounds healed as the flowers fell.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Mahabharata, Vana Parva (Ganguli 1883-96); not verbatim.

canonical_translation: K. M. Ganguli, 1883-96 (public domain)

title.en: Agastya Humbles the Vindhya Mountain
title.zh: 阿竭多折伏溫迪亞山

region.en: Vindhya range (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 溫迪亞山脈（象徵性定位）

period: Mahabharata, Vana Parva; Purana tellings (Ganguli translation, 1883-96; Wilson 1840)

source.work: The Mahabharata of Krishna-Dwaipayana Vyasa, trans. K. M. Ganguli (1883-96), Vana Parva, Agastya sections

summary.en: The Vindhya, jealous of Meru's height, grew until it blocked the sun's road: the south lived in shadow. Agastya, the dwarf seer journeying south, was asked by the mountain to pass over it; the sage asked in turn that it bow till he returned from the south - and he never returned. The mountain still waits, and the sun still passes.
summary.zh: 溫迪亞山妒於須彌之高，不斷生長直至遮斷日路：南方活在陰影之中。南行的矮小仙人阿竭多受山之請求從其上越過；仙人反請山俯首直到他自南方歸來——而他再未北返。山至今仍在等待，太陽至今仍在通行。

sensitivity.note: Living tradition; classified 'myth'.

passages.text: The mountain grew to rival Meru, higher and higher, until the sun's road bent around it and the lands of the south lay in permanent shade. Agastya came walking south and honored the obstacle: great one, bow till I cross; I shall return by this road - and the mountain, proud of its courtesy to a seer, folded down to the earth. The sage settled in the south and never took the northward road; the Vindhya keeps its bow, and the geography of two halves of India - sunlit south, waiting mountain - is one seer's promise, kept.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Mahabharata/Purana Agastya material (Ganguli 1883-96); not verbatim.

canonical_translation: K. M. Ganguli, 1883-96 (public domain)

title.en: Agastya Drinks the Ocean
title.zh: 阿竭多飲盡滄海

region.en: Indian Ocean (symbolic pin at Rameswaram)
region.zh: 印度洋（象徵性定位於羅摩梭瓦蘭）

period: Mahabharata, Vana Parva, composition layers c. 400 BCE-400 CE (Ganguli translation, 1883-96)

source.work: The Mahabharata of Krishna-Dwaipayana Vyasa, trans. K. M. Ganguli (1883-96), Vana Parva, the drinking of the ocean

summary.en: The Asuras Kalakeya had hidden in the ocean and raided the worlds from it; the gods came to Agastya, the seer whose appetite was his ancestor's gift. He knelt at the shore and drank the sea dry in three draughts - and the demons, standing on dry sand, were destroyed. The ocean's basin, one story says, is still the shape of that meal.
summary.zh: 迦羅迦耶群魔藏於海中，自海上襲擊世界；諸神來找阿竭多——那位以食欲為家傳的仙人。他跪於岸邊，三口飲乾滄海——群魔立足於乾沙之上，遂被誅滅。據一說，大洋的盆形至今仍是那頓飯的形狀。

sensitivity.note: Living tradition; classified 'myth'.

passages.text: The demons' fortress was the sea itself: no army could reach the Kalakeyas in the deep, and every raid ended with their retreat into the water. Agastya came to the shore, bowed to the ocean as to a host, and drank it - the whole weight of the sea taken into a body the size of a dwarf, three draughts and the bed lay dry. The exposed demons were cut down in the open; the gods crowned the seer, and the aition stood: why the ocean laps in a basin of that size - the appetite of the south's first sage.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Mahabharata, Vana Parva (Ganguli 1883-96); not verbatim.

canonical_translation: K. M. Ganguli, 1883-96 (public domain)

title.en: The Ramopakhyana: Rama's Story Told in the Mahabharata
title.zh: 羅摩傳：摩訶婆羅多中所講的羅摩故事

region.en: Markandeya's hermitage (symbolic pin at Naimisha)
region.zh: 摩根德耶仙居（象徵性定位於尼彌沙）

period: Mahabharata, Vana Parva (Ramopakhyana), composition layers c. 400 BCE-400 CE (Ganguli translation, 1883-96)

source.work: The Mahabharata of Krishna-Dwaipayana Vyasa, trans. K. M. Ganguli (1883-96), Vana Parva, Ramopakhyana

summary.en: Inside the Mahabharata, the sage Markandeya tells Draupadi the story of Rama: a wronged queen in exile finds hope in the epic of another exile - Rama, who won Sita back through forest, alliance and war. The Ramopakhyana is the tradition's own evidence that the two epics read each other: a Mahabharata woman comforted by a Ramayana plot.
summary.zh: 在《摩訶婆羅多》內部，仙人摩根德耶向黑公主講述羅摩的故事：一位受屈的王后在流亡中於另一流亡者的史詩裡找到希望——羅摩，經森林、結盟與戰爭而贏回悉多。《羅摩傳》是傳統自身展示兩部史詩互讀的證據：一位《摩訶婆羅多》的女子被《羅摩衍那》的情節安慰。

sensitivity.note: Living tradition; classified 'myth'.

passages.text: Draupadi, in the forest, asked Markandeya whether any woman had ever suffered what she suffered; the sage answered with a whole epic in brief - Rama's. The summary compresses the Ramayana to its skeleton: the exile, the abduction, the monkey-ally, the bridge, the war, the trial - a story shaped to console a queen that her own epic had abandoned in a forest. The embedded telling is textual gold: two epics quoting each other in the same mouth, a century or more before either reached its final form - the tradition's own first comparative literature.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Mahabharata, Vana Parva, Ramopakhyana (Ganguli 1883-96); not verbatim.

canonical_translation: K. M. Ganguli, 1883-96 (public domain)

title.en: Shuka's Ascension: The Sage Who Left Through the Sky
title.zh: 叔迦的升天：自天而出走的仙人

region.en: Shuka's hermitage (symbolic pin at Kurukshetra)
region.zh: 叔迦仙居（象徵性定位於俱盧之野）

period: Mahabharata, Shanti Parva, composition layers c. 400 BCE-400 CE (Ganguli translation, 1883-96)

source.work: The Mahabharata of Krishna-Dwaipayana Vyasa, trans. K. M. Ganguli (1883-96), Shanti Parva, Shuka's ascent

summary.en: Vyasa's son Shuka asked the one question his father's wisdom could not dodge: what lies beyond everything? The father sent him through a curriculum - kings, sages, women, heaven's own court - and each teacher returned the same answer in a new voice. Shuka's body rose from the earth into the sky and dissolved there: the epic's own account of a soul leaving through the crown of the head.
summary.zh: 毗耶娑之子叔迦問出一個父親的智慧無法迴避的問題：萬物之外是什麼？父親遣他完成一門課程——君王、仙人、女子、天廷——每位教師以新的聲音給出同一答案。叔迦之身自大地升入天空並於彼消融：史詩自身關於靈魂自頭頂出走的敘述。

sensitivity.note: Living tradition; classified 'myth'.

passages.text: Shuka's question was final: father, what is beyond the beyond? Vyasa, out-argued at last by his own son, sent him to ask everyone - the answer, he said, must be earned in every voice. The syllabus ran from Janaka's court to heaven's gate: kings and renouncers, women of wisdom and the gods themselves - and every teacher, asked about the beyond, answered with the Self. His ascension is described like weather: the body rose from the hermitage, the earth lost its hold, and the sage went out through the crown like a flame joining flame - the epic's witness to its own meaning's exit.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Mahabharata, Shanti Parva (Ganguli 1883-96); not verbatim.

canonical_translation: K. M. Ganguli, 1883-96 (public domain)

title.en: Vidura's Last Teaching and Death by Yoga
title.zh: 維杜羅的最後教導與瑜伽之死

region.en: Kurukshetra region (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 俱盧之野一帶（象徵性定位）

period: Mahabharata, Shanti/Anushasana Parvas, composition layers c. 400 BCE-400 CE (Ganguli translation, 1883-96)

source.work: The Mahabharata of Krishna-Dwaipayana Vyasa, trans. K. M. Ganguli (1883-96), Vidura's death

summary.en: Vidura, the palace's honest conscience, came out of retirement to teach Yudhishthira the final lessons of the dead - and died as he taught: fixed in yoga under a tree, his breath leaving upward, witnessed by the king he had warned all his life. The uncle who could not save the kingdom at least died in the posture of a man who had nothing left to lose.
summary.zh: 王廷中誠實的良知維杜羅走出退休，向堅戰傳授亡者的最後課程——並於授課中死去：瑜伽定於樹下，氣息向上而出，由他一生警告過的王親眼見證。這位無法拯救王國的伯父，至少以一無所失者的姿勢死去。

sensitivity.note: Living tradition; classified 'myth'.

passages.text: Vidura's last visit was a syllabus of warnings repeated too late: on dharma in defeat, on grief, on the self's path - the counsel of the only Kaurava who never wanted the war. Under a banyan in the ashram he sat in yoga with the king before him; the breath was drawn up through the spine, the body cooled in place - death as the final lesson, performed rather than described. Yudhishthira saw the truth of the death without horror: the uncle who had warned against every dice and every war died owning nothing and owing nothing - the epic's cleanest exit.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Mahabharata (Ganguli 1883-96); not verbatim.

canonical_translation: K. M. Ganguli, 1883-96 (public domain)

title.en: Parikshit's Seven Days
title.zh: 帕里格希的七天

region.en: Takshashila direction (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 怛叉始羅方向（象徵性定位）

period: Mahabharata, Adi Parva (Sambhava/Aranya sections), composition layers c. 400 BCE-400 CE (Ganguli translation, 1883-96)

source.work: The Mahabharata of Krishna-Dwaipayana Vyasa, trans. K. M. Ganguli (1883-96), Adi Parva, Parikshit and Takshaka

summary.en: The orphaned heir of the Pandavas, cursed by a seer's boy for a fruitless disrespect, was given seven days to live by the serpent-king Takshaka. He sealed himself in a tower of guards - and Takshaka came disguised as a worm in a fruit, took his true form in the king's sight, and closed the account. His son's revenge-sacrifice opens the epic itself.
summary.zh: 般度族孤兒繼承人因一場無意的輕慢觸怒仙人之子，被蛇王多剎迦給予七天之壽。他自封於守衛環繞的高塔——多剎迦化為果中之蟲潛入，於王眼前現出真身，閉合賬目。其子的復仇之祭開啟了史詩本身。

sensitivity.note: Living tradition (naga worship); classified 'myth'.

passages.text: The seer's son, ignored in the king's court, cursed through his brother's mouth: on the seventh day from this, Takshaka shall bite thee. The tower was sealed against every crawling thing - and the serpent-king bribed the envoys, arrived inside a fruit as a shining worm, and stood before the king in his own body with the days counted. The bite was the epic's first death: the crown passed to Janamejaya, whose snake-sacrifice - and the brahmin boy who stopped it - is where the Mahabharata begins to be recited.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Mahabharata, Adi Parva (Ganguli 1883-96); not verbatim.

canonical_translation: K. M. Ganguli, 1883-96 (public domain)

title.en: Uttanka and the Serpent's Earrings
title.zh: 鄔丹迦與蛇之耳環

region.en: King Paushya's court, netherworld (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 波希王廷，冥界（象徵性定位）

period: Mahabharata, Adi Parva (Astika Upaparva), composition layers c. 400 BCE-400 CE (Ganguli translation, 1883-96)

source.work: The Mahabharata of Krishna-Dwaipayana Vyasa, trans. K. M. Ganguli (1883-96), Adi Parva, Uttanka episode

summary.en: The seer's pupil Uttanka was asked, as a fee, for the divine earrings of a queen - which Takshaka's snakes had hidden in the netherworld. He rode with a blind man and an old woman who proved to be Indra and the Earth, dived into the serpent realm, charmed the snakes with a talking fire, and returned the earrings in time for the queen's vow - the epic's shortest quest, with Indra heckling from the roadside.
summary.zh: 仙人弟子鄔丹迦被索求王后之神聖耳環為學資——而多剎迦的蛇族已將其藏入冥界。他與盲者及老婦同乘（二人實為因陀羅與大地），潛入蛇域，以會言之火魅蛇，及時送回耳環——史詩中最短的探索之旅，因陀羅於路旁不斷戲弄。

sensitivity.note: Living tradition; classified 'myth'.

passages.text: The fee was absurd on purpose: the queen's divine ear-rings, kept in the netherworld by Takshaka's snakes - a teacher's test that doubles as a treasure-hunt. On the road Indra rode with him disguised - an old man on an ass, heckling the pupil with tests of hunger and trust - and the Earth herself lent the route; the underworld gate opened to a boy who knew its word.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Mahabharata, Adi Parva, Uttanka section (Ganguli 1883-96); not verbatim.

passages.text: In the serpent city the earrings were recovered with the help of a fire that spoke; Uttanka returned in time for the queen's vow, and Indra granted him the boon that named the epic's ending - rain whenever the world asked.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Mahabharata, Adi Parva, Uttanka section (Ganguli 1883-96); not verbatim.

canonical_translation: K. M. Ganguli, 1883-96 (public domain)

title.en: Sanatsujata: Death Is Not By Old Age
title.zh: 薩那特蘇鳩多：死不由於衰老

region.en: Dhritarashtra's hall (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 持國王廷（象徵性定位）

period: Mahabharata, Udyoga Parva (Sanatsujatiya), composition layers c. 400 BCE-400 CE (Ganguli translation, 1883-96)

source.work: The Mahabharata of Krishna-Dwaipayana Vyasa, trans. K. M. Ganguli (1883-96), Udyoga Parva, Sanatsujata episode

summary.en: Dhritarashtra, terrified before the war, asked the sage Sanatsujata: is there a way past death? The answer is the epic's purest philosophy in dialogue: 'men say that by renunciation, not by rites, the wise escape death' - truth and study are the road; the fear of death is the first lie. The conversation is the Gita's dry-run in a blind king's hall.
summary.zh: 戰前惶恐的持國問仙人薩那特蘇鳩多：可有越過死亡之路？答案是史詩中最純粹的對話哲學：『人言智者以出離、而非以儀軌，脫離死亡』——真理與學習即是道路；懼死是第一個謊言。這場對話是《薄伽梵歌》在盲王之廷的預演。

sensitivity.note: Living tradition; classified 'myth'.

passages.text: The king's question was the age's fear in one line: teach me a way beyond death; the sage's answer refused the premise - death is not escaped by rites but by knowledge. The dialogue strips fear to its error: the fool says 'this is I'; the knower says nothing - truth, study, self-restraint; the shadow of death falls only on the one who names himself twice. The Sanatsujatiya stands beside the Gita as the war's first philosophy: the same hall, the same fear, the same cure - study, taught a hundred chapters before Arjuna's chariot.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Mahabharata, Udyoga Parva (Ganguli 1883-96); not verbatim.

canonical_translation: K. M. Ganguli, 1883-96 (public domain)

title.en: Arjuna Lays Down His Bow: The Gita's First Scene
title.zh: 阿周那放下弓：《薄伽梵歌》首景

region.en: Kurukshetra, between the two armies (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 俱盧之野，兩軍之間（象徵性定位）

period: Mahabharata, Bhishma Parva (Bhagavad Gita 1), composition layers c. 400 BCE-400 CE (Arnold translation 1885 / Ganguli 1883-96)

source.work: The Song Celestial, trans. Sir Edwin Arnold (1885), Bhagavad-Gita ch. 1

summary.en: Krishna drove the chariot to a halt between the two armies and let Arjuna see what he was about to do: grandfathers, teachers, cousins, sons-in-law on both sides. The archer of the age dropped the Gandiva from his hand and sat down in the chariot saying he would not fight - the crisis out of which the eighteen chapters of the Gita grow.
summary.zh: 克里希那御車至兩軍之間停住，令阿周那看清他將要做的事：兩邊都是祖父、教師、表親、女婿。當世第一射手垂下手中之弓，坐於車中，說他不願作戰——《薄伽梵歌》十八章由此危機而生。

sensitivity.note: Living tradition (Gita recited as scripture); classified 'myth' (narrative frame rather than scripture's teaching sections).

passages.text: Krishna set the chariot before both armies and said: behold, Arjuna, what must be fought - and the hero looked at uncles and teachers and cousins arrayed to kill and be killed. The bow slipped from his hand: his mouth dried, his body trembled, his hair stood up - I will not fight, he said; what victory buys a heap of kin?
passages.note: Paraphrase of Bhagavad Gita 1 (Arnold 1885); not verbatim.

passages.text: The despondency was the opening question of the age's philosophy: is this my dharma or my crime? - and the friend on the chariot-box began to answer as the Lord, in the conversation the whole tradition has been reading since.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Bhagavad Gita 1-2 (Arnold 1885); not verbatim.

canonical_translation: Sir Edwin Arnold, The Song Celestial, 1885 (public domain)

title.en: The Trials of Entry into the Fianna
title.zh: 加入菲亞納的試煉

region.en: Almhuin (Hill of Allen), Co. Kildare, Ireland
region.zh: 愛爾蘭基爾代爾郡艾倫山

period: Fenian cycle, medieval Irish tradition; Lady Augusta Gregory retelling (1904)

source.work: Lady Augusta Gregory, Gods and Fighting Men (1904), Book I, ch. II, eBook #14465

summary.en: Finn's Household chapter preserves the Fianna's warrior code: no cattle by oppression, no refusal of any asker, no retreat before nine fighters — and the fearsome trials of entry: a man half-buried in a hole warding nine spears thrown at once, a hair-plaited run through the woods, a leap and a stoop at speed, and a thorn drawn out with the nail while running. Among the household the sweetest was Cnu Deireoil the Little Nut, come out of the Sidhe.
summary.zh: 菲亞納戰士法典載於本章：不強奪牛隻、不拒任何求助者、九敵之前不後退；入會試煉嚴酷——半身入土擋九矛齊射、辮髮疾奔林間不被追及、疾奔中跨越與俯身、以指甲拔除腳上荊棘。家臣中最甜美者為出自仙族的「小堅果」克努·迪爾奧爾。

sensitivity.note: This is a charter of the fianna warrior institution (ethics + initiation ordeals), a ritual-origin item under the project taxonomy rather than a narrative episode. Pin at Almhuin, Finn's seat.

passages.text: The number of the Fianna of Ireland at that time was seven score and ten chief men, every one of them having three times nine fighting men under him. And every man of them was bound to three things: to take no cattle by oppression, not to refuse any man as to cattle or riches, and no one of them to fall back before nine fighting men. There was no man taken into the Fianna until his tribe and his kindred would give securities for him; and there was no man taken till he knew the twelve books of poetry. And before any man was taken, he would be put into a deep hole in the ground up to his middle, having his shield and a hazel rod in his hand, and nine men would go the length of ten furrows from him and would cast their spears at him at the one time — and if he got a wound from one of them, he was not thought fit to join the Fianna.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Gregory 1904, Book I, ch. II; not verbatim.

passages.text: And after that again, his hair would be fastened up, and he put to run through the woods of Ireland, and the Fianna following after him, only the length of a branch between themselves and himself when they started; and if they came up with him and wounded him, or if his spears trembled in his hand, or if a branch of a tree undid the plaiting of his hair, or if he cracked a dry stick under his foot running, he was not let join them. And they would not take him among them till he had made a leap over a stick the height of himself, and stooped under one the height of his knee, and taken a thorn out from his foot with his nail, running his fastest.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Gregory 1904, Book I, ch. II; not verbatim.

passages.text: But if he had done all these things, he was of Finn's people. And of all his musicians the one Finn thought most of was Cnu Deireoil, the Little Nut, that came to him from the Sidhe: a small man about four feet in height, light yellow hair hanging to his waist, playing music on his harp that had no fault in it, come out of the place of the Sidhe in Slieve-nam-ban where ale is drunk and made; and there was never any music heard on earth but his was better.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Gregory 1904, Book I, ch. II; not verbatim.

title.en: The Birth of Bran and Sceolan
title.zh: 布蘭與斯克奧蘭之誕生

region.en: Fergus Fionnliath's harbour, Gallimh (Galway), Ireland
region.zh: 愛爾蘭戈爾韋費爾古斯港

period: Fenian cycle, medieval Irish tradition; Lady Augusta Gregory retelling (1904)

source.work: Lady Augusta Gregory, Gods and Fighting Men (1904), Book I, ch. III, eBook #14465

summary.en: Jealous of Iollan Eachtach's marriage to her mortal rival, the fairy Uchtdealb of the Fair Breast changes Tuiren into a hound and entrusts her, pregnant, to Fergus Fionnliath — the most dog-hating man in the world — who learns to love hounds through her. Iollan pledges lifelong fidelity to the fairy to win Tuiren's restoration, and the two whelps born in hound-shape are raised by Finn: Bran and Sceolan, who have human wits and will never be without fault.
summary.zh: 因妒忌伊奧蘭娶凡女蒂倫，仙女烏克特戴爾布將蒂倫化為母犬，託付給世上最恨狗的費爾古斯·芬利亞——他卻因她而愛上狗。伊奧蘭向仙女起誓終身不負，換回蒂倫人形；犬身所誕二犬被芬恩撫養——布蘭與斯克奧蘭，具人類心智而無一瑕疵。

sensitivity.note: Etiology of Finn's two great hounds (their names recur in birth-tales of Oisin); transformation-by-druid-rod tag from the fairy's hazel wand. Fergus Fionnliath's dog-hatred cured is a comic annex to the charm.

passages.text: Before Iollan Eachtach made his marriage with Tuiren, Finn's mother's sister, he had a sweetheart of the Sidhe, Uchtdealb of the Fair Breast; and great jealousy came on her when she knew he had taken a wife. She took the appearance of Finn's woman-messenger, came to the house where Tuiren was, and said: "Finn sends health and long life to you, queen, and he bids you to make a great feast; and come with me now till I speak a few words with you, for there is hurry on me." Tuiren went out with her, and when they were away from the house the woman of the Sidhe took out her dark Druid rod from under her cloak and gave her a blow of it that changed her into a hound, the most beautiful that was ever seen. Then she went on, bringing the hound with her, to the house of Fergus Fionnliath, king of the harbour of Gallimh, and it is the way Fergus was, he was the most unfriendly man to dogs in the whole world.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Gregory 1904, Book I, ch. III; not verbatim.

passages.text: Uchtdealb said to him: "Finn wishes you life and health, Fergus, and he says to you to take good care of his hound till he comes himself; and mind her well, for she is with young." Fergus said: "I wonder at that message, for Finn knows well there is not in the world a man has less liking for dogs than myself. But for all that I will not refuse Finn the first time he sent a hound to me." And when he brought the hound out to try her, she was the best he ever knew, and she never saw the wild creature she would not run down; and Fergus took a great liking for hounds from that out.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Gregory 1904, Book I, ch. III; not verbatim.

passages.text: When her time came she gave birth to two whelps. Iollan, called on for the pledge he had given the Fianna, went to the hill where Uchtdealb was, and promised to keep her as his sweetheart to the end of his life if she would free him from the danger; and she went to the house of Fergus Fionnliath and brought Tuiren away and put her own shape on her again, and gave her up to Finn. And as to the two whelps, they stopped always with Finn, and the names he gave them were Bran and Sceolan.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Gregory 1904, Book I, ch. III; not verbatim.

title.en: Sadbh the Fawn and the Finding of Oisin
title.zh: 雌鹿莎芙與歐辛的發現

region.en: Beinn Gulbain, Co. Kerry, Ireland
region.zh: 愛爾蘭克里郡古爾班山

period: Fenian cycle, medieval Irish tradition; Lady Augusta Gregory retelling (1904)

source.work: Lady Augusta Gregory, Gods and Fighting Men (1904), Book I, ch. IV, eBook #14465

summary.en: A beautiful fawn stops before Finn's hounds and lies on the grass to be licked by Bran and Sceolan; at Almhuin she becomes Sadbh, a woman changed into a deer for refusing the love of the Dark Druid. Finn loves and weds her, but a false likeness lures her from the dun and a hazel rod turns her back to a fawn. Seven years later, hounds penned in a ring on Beinn Gulbain reveal a naked wild boy — the son Sadbh bore — whom Bran and Sceolan play about like their own: Oisin, the maker of poems.
summary.zh: 一頭美麗母鹿在芬恩獵犬前止步，臥於草上任布蘭與斯克奧蘭舔撫；至艾倫山她化回莎芙——因拒絕黑德魯伊之愛而被變為雌鹿。芬恩娶她為妻，然幻影誘她出堡，榛杖將她復化為鹿。七年後，古爾班山上獵犬圍困一赤裸野童——莎芙所生之子。布蘭與斯克奧蘭如親族般親近他：此人即詩人歐辛。

sensitivity.note: The Sadbh-Oisin birth tale is the Fenian cycle's charter of wild-child adoption and of Finn's paternal line; the deception motif (false likeness) is a standard fairy abduction pattern. Pin at Beinn Gulbain, where the boy was found.

passages.text: It happened one time Finn and his men were coming back from the hunting, a beautiful fawn started up before them, and they followed after it, men and dogs, till at last they were all tired and fell back, all but Finn himself and Bran and Sceolan. And suddenly as they were going through a valley, the fawn stopped and lay down on the smooth grass, and Bran and Sceolan came up with it, and they did not harm it at all, but went playing about it, licking its neck and its face.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Gregory 1904, Book I, ch. IV; not verbatim.

passages.text: At Almhuin, when Finn was alone late that evening, a beautiful young woman having a rich dress came before him, and she told him it was she herself was the fawn: "It is for refusing the love of Fear Doirche, the Dark Druid of the Men of Dea, I was put in this shape, and through the length of three years I have lived the life of a wild deer in a far part of Ireland, and I am hunted like a wild deer. But a serving-man of the Dark Druid took pity on me and said that if I was once within the dun of the Fianna of Ireland, the Druid would have no more power over me. And I was safe with Bran and Sceolan, for they have human wits, and they knew my nature to be like their own."
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Gregory 1904, Book I, ch. IV; not verbatim.

passages.text: Finn gave her his love and took her as his wife, and so great was his love for her he gave up his hunting and all the things he used to take pleasure in. But the men of Lochlann came against Ireland, and while Finn was away fighting, a likeness of himself and of Bran and of Sceolan appeared before the dun, and Sadbh came out of the house and would not listen to them, but went running out towards the shadow with its arms stretched out to her. No sooner did she touch it than she gave a great cry, and the shadow lifted up a hazel rod, and on the moment it was a fawn was standing on the grass; the two hounds the shadow had with him took her by the throat and dragged her back to him, and then woman and fawn and Druid were not to be seen.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Gregory 1904, Book I, ch. IV; not verbatim.

passages.text: Seven years later Finn and his chief men were hunting on the sides of Beinn Gulbain, and the hounds went into some narrow place; and in a ring of the five hounds of Finn was a young boy, naked, with long hair and high looks, that Bran and Sceolan whined and licked about. Little by little he told them all he could remember of a deer he loved, his mother, that a dark-looking man spoke to softly and then in anger, and the last time struck her with a hazel rod and forced her to follow him. And the name the Fianna gave him was Oisin, and it is he was their maker of poems, and their good fighter afterwards.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Gregory 1904, Book I, ch. IV; not verbatim.

title.en: Caoilte's Rabble and the Ransom of Finn
title.zh: 卡爾特之「烏合群」與芬恩的贖身

region.en: Teamhair (Hill of Tara), Co. Meath, Ireland
region.zh: 愛爾蘭米斯郡塔拉王丘

period: Fenian cycle, medieval Irish tradition; Lady Augusta Gregory retelling (1904)

source.work: Lady Augusta Gregory, Gods and Fighting Men (1904), Book I, ch. V, eBook #14465

summary.en: The High King holds Finn prisoner at Tara for the Fianna's rebellion, and Caoilte avenges him with fire and slaughter until he can slip into the palace disguised as a servant. The king's impossible ransom — a mated couple of every wild creature in Ireland — Caoilte actually fulfils, herding birds and beasts and the very pigs of the son of Lir through the whole island; but at the last all the creatures scatter from Tara, and the people name the horde "Caoilte's Rabble."
summary.zh: 因菲亞納起事，至高王囚芬恩於塔拉；卡爾特縱火屠戮復仇，後喬裝僕役潛入宮中。國王索不可能之贖金——愛爾蘭所有野獸各一對——卡爾特竟真的橫越全島聚齊百獸，連利爾之子的豬也帶來；然而芬恩一獲自由，獸群四散，人稱此群為「卡爾特的烏合群」。
