sensitivity.note: The census-of-creatures episode is the Fenian analogue of Noah's ark and of Herakles' herculean labours — the impossible task ransom. Duplicate tag 'sacred-kingship' appears only once in the motif list per schema rules; kept once. Pin at Tara.

passages.text: Another time Caoilte brought Finn out of Teamhair, where he was kept by force by the High King, because of some rebellion the Fianna had stirred up. When Caoilte heard Finn had been brought away to Teamhair, he went out to avenge him: the first he killed was Cuireach, a king of Leinster that had a great name, and after that he made a great rout through Ireland, bringing sorrow into every house for the sake of Finn, killing a man in every place, and setting fire to the fields.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Gregory 1904, Book I, ch. V; not verbatim.

passages.text: And when he came to Teamhair he took the clothes off the door-keeper, and left his own worn sword in the king's sheath and took the king's sword that had great power in it, and went into the palace in the disguise of a servant. When evening came he held the candle at the king's feast, and the king said: "You will wonder at what I tell you, Finn, that the two eyes of Caoilte are in my candlestick." "Do not say that," said Finn, "and do not put reproach on my people; for it is a high mind Caoilte has, and he only does high deeds, and he would not stand serving with a candle for all the gold of the whole world."
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Gregory 1904, Book I, ch. V; not verbatim.

passages.text: Caoilte gave out a high sorrowful lament as he served the king with drink, and when the king knew him, he spoke out: "Tell me what way I can get freedom for my master." "There is no way but by doing one thing you can never do. If you can bring me together a couple of all the wild creatures of Ireland, I will give up your master to you then." Caoilte made no delay, but went through the whole of Ireland: two ravens from Fiodh da Bheann, two wild ducks from Loch na Seillein, two foxes from Slieve Cuilinn, two swans from blue Dobhran, two eagles from the Carraig of the stones, two deer from Sith Buidhe, two peacocks from Magh Mell, two cats from the Cave of Cruachan, and two pigs of the pigs of the son of Lir — and a horse and a mare of the beautiful horses of Manannan.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Gregory 1904, Book I, ch. V; not verbatim.

passages.text: When he brought them to Teamhair the king gave him a house with nine doors to put them up in for the night, and they raised a loud screech together through fifty openings, trying to make their escape. And when he brought out his troop, the name the people gave them was "Caoilte's Rabble." But all the profit the King of Ireland got from them was to see them together for that one time; for no sooner did Finn get his freedom than the whole of them scattered here and there, and no two of them went by the same road out of Teamhair.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Gregory 1904, Book I, ch. V; not verbatim.

title.en: Finn's Advice to a Young Champion
title.zh: 芬恩對年輕戰士的訓誡

region.en: Corraig Conluain, Slieve Bladhma, Co. Tipperary, Ireland
region.zh: 愛爾蘭蒂珀雷里郡布洛馬山科雷格·康盧因

period: Fenian cycle, medieval Irish tradition (speculum principis material); Lady Augusta Gregory retelling (1904)

source.work: Lady Augusta Gregory, Gods and Fighting Men (1904), Book I, ch. V, eBook #14465

summary.en: Lugaidh's Son, sluggish and quarrelsome among the Fianna, is nearly cast out; Finn gives him the famous advice of a champion — be quiet in a great man's house and surly in the narrow pass; give two-thirds of your gentleness to women, children, and poets; never promise what you cannot carry out, nor forsake a man under your protection. The advice stays with him, and he wins a great name among the poets of Ireland and Alban — and the love of Aoife, wife of the King of Alban, who sails to Ireland for him.
summary.zh: 盧蓋德之子在菲亞納中疏懶好鬥，幾被逐出；芬恩授以戰士經典訓誡——豪門之宅當謙、狹路之險當橫；把三分之二的溫柔留給婦孺與詩人；不作力不能及之諾，不棄受你庇護之人。此訓誡永伴其身，令他名揚愛爾蘭與阿爾巴詩壇——並贏得遠航來愛爾蘭的阿爾巴王后艾菲之愛。

sensitivity.note: The advice to Lugaidh's Son is a Teagusc na n-ingeh (conduct-instruction) embedded in narrative — Fenian wisdom literature rather than a plot episode; tagged parable-teaching deliberately.

passages.text: Lugaidh's Son, that was of Finn's blood, was put into Finn's arms as a child, and reared by Duban's daughter, that had reared eight hundred fighting men of the Fianna. He stopped through the length of a year with the Fianna, but he was someway sluggish through all that time, so that under his leading not more than nine of the Fianna got to kill so much as a boar or a deer; and along with that, he used to beat both his servants and his hounds. At last the three battalions of the Fianna made their complaint to Finn: "Make your choice now, will you have us with you, or will you have Lugaidh's Son by himself."
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Gregory 1904, Book I, ch. V; not verbatim.

passages.text: Then Finn gave him his advice, and it is what he said: "If you have a mind to be a good champion, be quiet in a great man's house; be surly in the narrow pass. Do not beat your hound without a cause; do not bring a charge against your wife without having knowledge of her guilt; do not hurt a fool in fighting, for he is without his wits. Let two-thirds of your gentleness be showed to women and to little children that are creeping on the floor, and to men of learning that make the poems, and do not be rough with the common people. Do not threaten or speak big words, for it is a shameful thing to speak stiffly unless you can carry it out afterwards. Do not forsake your lord so long as you live; do not give up any man that puts himself under your protection for all the treasures of the world.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Gregory 1904, Book I, ch. V; not verbatim.

passages.text: Do not refuse to share your meat; hold fast to your arms till the hard fight is well ended; and with that follow after gentleness." That advice stayed always with Lugaidh's Son, and he changed his ways, and after a while he got a great name among the poets of Ireland and of Alban. And Aoife, daughter of the King of Lochlann, wife of Mal, King of Alban, heard the great praise the poets were giving him and set her love on him, and came over the manes of the sea to Ireland with her nine foster-sisters to look for him; and when her husband Mal came to avenge her with three battalions, it was Mal fell by Lugaidh's Son at the last, and Aoife stood on a hill near by as long as the battle lasted.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Gregory 1904, Book I, ch. V; not verbatim.

title.en: The King of the Great World Invades Ireland
title.zh: 大世界之王入侵愛爾蘭

region.en: Fionntulach (the White Hill), Co. Kerry, Ireland
region.zh: 愛爾蘭克里郡白丘

period: Fenian cycle, medieval Irish tradition; Lady Augusta Gregory retelling (1904)

source.work: Lady Augusta Gregory, Gods and Fighting Men (1904), Book II, ch. I, eBook #14465

summary.en: The greatest battle the Fianna ever fought begins: Daire Donn, High King of the Great World, gathers the kings of Greece, France, Lochlann, the Dog-Heads and Cat-Heads, and Ogarmach the best woman-warrior of the world, to put Ireland under tribute. The exiled traitor Glas son of Bremen pilots them to Ireland, and only a shore of white sand at Corca Duibhne will do for the fairs and gatherings of so vast an army.
summary.zh: 菲亞納最宏偉之戰拉開序幕：大世界至高王達爾·東召集希臘、法蘭西、洛赫蘭諸王，犬首族、貓首族，以及世上最強女戰士奧加馬克，欲使愛爾蘭納貢。被逐出的叛徒格拉斯引艦隊入愛爾蘭，唯有科爾卡·迪夫尼的白沙灘足以容納此大軍的集市與集會。

sensitivity.note: The White Strand (Finntraigh) war-cycle is a world-invasion apocalypse of the Fenian cycle; the Dog-Headed and Cat-Headed peoples are marvel-races standard in voyage literature. Pin symbolic at the Kerry coast.

passages.text: Of all the great battles the Fianna fought to keep the foreigners out of Ireland, the greatest was the one that was fought at Finntraigh the White Strand, in Munster. One time the enemies of Ireland gathered together under Daire Donn, High King of the Great World, thinking to take Ireland and to put it under tribute. The King of Greece was of them, and the King of France, and the King of the Eastern World, and Lughman of the Broad Arms, King of the Saxons, and Tor the son of Breogan, King of the Great Plain, and Comur of the Crooked Sword, King of the Men of the Dog-Heads, and Caitchenn, King of the Men of the Cat-Heads, and Caisel of the Feathers, King of Lochlann, and three kings from the rising of the sun in the east, and Ogarmach, daughter of the King of Greece, the best woman-warrior that ever came into the world, and a great many other kings and great lords.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Gregory 1904, Book II, ch. I; not verbatim.

passages.text: The King of the World asked then: "Who is there can give me knowledge of the harbours of Ireland?" "I will do that for you, and I will bring you to a good harbour," said Glas, son of Bremen, that had been put out of Ireland by Finn for doing some treachery. Then the armies set out in their ships, and they were not gone far when the wind rose and the waves, and they could hear nothing but the wild playing of the sea-women, and the screams of frightened birds, and the breaking of ropes and of sails.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Gregory 1904, Book II, ch. I; not verbatim.

passages.text: But after a while, when the wind found no weakness in the heroes, it rose from them and went up into its own high place, and the sea grew quiet and the harbours friendly. They stopped for a while at an island that was called the Green Rock; but the King of the World said: "It is not a harbour like this you promised me, Glas, but a shore of white sand where my armies could have their fairs and their gatherings the time they would not be fighting." "I know a harbour of that sort in the west of Ireland," said Glas, "the Harbour of the White Strand in Corca Duibhne." So they went into their ships again, and went on over the sea towards Ireland.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Gregory 1904, Book II, ch. I; not verbatim.

title.en: Cael's Poem Wins Credhe
title.zh: 克爾的求婚詩贏得克蕾德

region.en: Loch Cuire, Paps of Dana, Co. Kerry, Ireland
region.zh: 愛爾蘭克里郡達娜山嶽庫雷湖

period: Fenian cycle, medieval Irish tradition; Lady Augusta Gregory retelling (1904)

source.work: Lady Augusta Gregory, Gods and Fighting Men (1904), Book II, ch. II, eBook #14465

summary.en: Gathering the Fianna against the invaders, Finn's host feeds on the nuts of the hazels of Cenntire and the salmon of Luimnech. Cael, who saw in a dream a woman of the Sidhe, wins Credhe daughter of the King of Ciarraighe Luachra by a poem no man can match — an inventory of her bowls, horns, crystal vats, apple-tree over the vat of bronze, and her house thatched with the crimson wings of birds — and she joins the march to the White Strand with a herd of cattle for the war.
summary.zh: 菲亞納出征集結，取食辛提里榛樹之果與利默里克之鮭。克爾曾夢見仙姬，今以無人能及之詩贏得西拉格·盧赫拉王之女克蕾德——詩中細數她的酒碗、牛角杯、水晶缸、銅缸上的蘋果樹，以及以緋紅鳥翼為瓦的宮室。她攜牛群隨軍出征白沙灘。

sensitivity.note: The courtship-poem (love-service verse) is the Fenian wedding-custom motif; Credhe is a Sidhe-bride from the Paps of Dana — the mountain named for the goddess Danu. The dream-woman motif links to the bruiden genre.

passages.text: When it was shown to Finn that the enemies of Ireland were coming, he called together the seven battalions of the Fianna, and the place where they gathered was on the hill that was called Fionntulach, the White Hill, in Munster. They had every sort of thing for food there, beautiful blackberries, haws of the hawthorn, nuts of the hazels of Cenntire, watercress at the beginning of summer; and birds out of the oak-woods, speckled eggs from the cliffs, and salmon out of Luimnech, and eels of the Sionnan. As they were going to set out southwards they saw one of their young men, Gael, grandson of Nemhnain, coming towards them.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Gregory 1904, Book II, ch. II; not verbatim.

passages.text: "It was about a high marriage and a woman of the Sidhe that was showed to me in a dream I was speaking with my nurse at Brugh na Boinne; Credhe it was I saw, daughter of the King of Ciarraighe Luachra." "Do you know this, Cael, that she is the greatest deceiver of all the women of Ireland? She will let no one come unless he is able to make a poem setting out the report of her bowls and her horns and her cups, her grand vessels and all her palaces." "I have all that ready," said Cael.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Gregory 1904, Book II, ch. II; not verbatim.

passages.text: They came to the door of the hill of the Sidhe at Loch Cuire and knocked at it with the shafts of their long gold-socketted spears, and Credhe herself came out, having three times fifty women with her. Cael rose up and sang his poem: "A journey I have to make, and it is no easy journey, to the house of Credhe against the breast of the mountain, at the Paps of Dana... There is a vat there of royal bronze, the juice of pleasant malt is running from it; over the vat is an apple-tree with its heavy fruit; when Credhe's horn is filled from the vat, four apples fall into it together...
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Gregory 1904, Book II, ch. II; not verbatim.

passages.text: She that owns all these things both at low water and at flood, Credhe from the Hill of the Three Peaks, she is beyond all the women of Ireland by the length of a spear-cast." Then Credhe took him for her husband, and the wedding-feast was made, and the whole of the Fianna stopped there through seven days at drinking and pleasure. And through the whole length of the battle that followed, that lasted a year and a day, she had new milk for them, and it was to her house the wounded were brought for healing.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Gregory 1904, Book II, ch. II; not verbatim.

title.en: Conn Crither and the Sisters of the Country of the Young
title.zh: 康恩·克里瑟與青春之國三姐妹

region.en: Finntraigh (White Strand), Corca Duibhne, Co. Kerry, Ireland
region.zh: 愛爾蘭克里郡科爾卡·迪夫尼白沙灘

period: Fenian cycle, medieval Irish tradition; Lady Augusta Gregory retelling (1904)

source.work: Lady Augusta Gregory, Gods and Fighting Men (1904), Book II, ch. III, eBook #14465

summary.en: The watchman Conn Crither sleeps through the landing of the invaders and wakes to flames and cries. Swearing to sell his life dearly, he is met on the way by three sisters from Tir nan Og who have all given him their love: they raise Druid armies from stalks of grass and watercress, blind the enemy with a mist, and keep a well of healing at the foot of the Eagle's Mountain. Alone he routs a province's worth of the foe and takes the head of the King of the Great Plain, boasting he will not leave it until the Fianna come.
summary.zh: 哨兵康恩·克里瑟在敵軍登陸時睡著，醒來見火光哭聲四起。他誓要戰死沙場，途中遇見三位來自青春之國的仙姝——她們皆已屬意於他：她們以草莖與水芹編成德魯伊幻軍，以霧障敵眼，並在鷹山麓保有療傷之泉。他獨自擊潰一省之敵，斬大平原王之首，誇言非至菲亞納來援不棄其首。

sensitivity.note: The healing well (Slieve Iolair) is the Fenian analogue of the Greek Kallichoron-style wound-restoring springs — tagged 'resurrection' for its wound-to-wholeness function, not a religious claim. The three sisters are the triple fairy-mistress pattern.

passages.text: The man that was keeping watch at the White Strand was Conn Crither, son of Bran, from Teamhair Luachra, and after he had been a long time watching, he fell asleep one night west from the Round Hill of the Fianna, called Cruachan Adrann; and while he was in his sleep the ships came, and what roused him was the noise of the breaking of shields and the clashing of swords, and the cries of women and children and of dogs and horses that were under flames. Conn Crither started up and said: "It is great trouble has come on the people through my sleep; and I will not stay living after this for Finn and the Fianna of Ireland to see me, but I will rush into the middle of the strangers, and they will fall by me till I fall by them."
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Gregory 1904, Book II, ch. III; not verbatim.

passages.text: On the way he saw three women dressed in battle clothes, and fast as he ran he could not overtake them. "Hold your hand," the nearest said, "for we are not come to harm you but to help you. We are three sisters, and we are come from Tir nan Og, the Country of the Young, and we have all three given you our love. We will make Druid armies about you from stalks of grass and from the tops of the watercress, and they will cry out to the strangers and will strike their arms from their hands, and take from them their strength and their eyesight.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Gregory 1904, Book II, ch. III; not verbatim.

passages.text: And we will put a Druid mist about you that will hide you from the armies of the strangers. And we have a well of healing at the foot of Slieve Iolair, the Eagle's Mountain, and its waters will cure every wound made in battle; and after bathing in that well you will be as whole and as sound as the day you were born." Conn Crither hurried on to the strand, took their spoils from the armies of the King of the Great Plain with the Druid army about him, fought the King himself, struck off his head, and lifted it up: "I will not let myself be parted from this body till some of the Fianna, few or many, will come to me."
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Gregory 1904, Book II, ch. III; not verbatim.

title.en: Glas son of Bremen Returns to Ireland
title.zh: 布雷門之子格拉斯歸國

region.en: Finntraigh (White Strand), Corca Duibhne, Co. Kerry, Ireland
region.zh: 愛爾蘭克里郡科爾卡·迪夫尼白沙灘

period: Fenian cycle, medieval Irish tradition; Lady Augusta Gregory retelling (1904)

source.work: Lady Augusta Gregory, Gods and Fighting Men (1904), Book II, ch. IV, eBook #14465

summary.en: Sent by the King of the World to identify the lone warrior boasting on the strand, Glas son of Bremen finds his own kinsman Conn Crither and turns his coat: no treasure of the world would keep him fighting against his blood once Finn's protection is promised. He asks the King to send his men one at a time, slaughters Madan of the Bent Neck in single combat, and his daily reports become the road by which the invaders are bled.
summary.zh: 大世界之王遣格拉斯去查明海灘上獨自誇耀的戰士是誰，格拉斯發現竟是自己族人康恩·克里瑟，隨即倒戈：只要芬恩許以庇護，世上任何財寶都不能令他與血親為敵。他請求國王逐一遣人上陣，單挑擊殺「彎頸」馬丹，其每日戰報遂成敵軍失血之路。

sensitivity.note: Traitor-redeemed is a Fenian stock figure; the single-combat tolling of the invaders runs through the whole cycle (compare Cuchulain's guard at the ford of the Tain). Prophesy aside: 'it was not in the prophecy that Glas would find his death there' shows the fate-motif of the Irish hero-tale.

passages.text: The King of the World heard the boast of the man on the strand and said: "Rise up now, Glas, son of Dremen, and see which of the Fianna of Ireland it is that is saying it." Glas left the ship and went to where Conn Crither was, and asked who was he. "I am Conn Crither, son of Bran, from Teamhair Luachra." "If that is so," said Glas, "you are of the one blood with myself, for I am Glas, son of Bremen from Teamhair Luachra." "It is not right for you to come fighting against me from those foreigners," said Conn. "It is a pity indeed; and but for Finn and the Fianna driving me from them, I would not fight against you or one of themselves for all the treasures of the whole world." "Do not say that, for I swear by my hand of valour, if you had killed Finn's own son and the sons of his people along with him, you need not be in dread of him if only you came under his word and his protection."
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Gregory 1904, Book II, ch. IV; not verbatim.

passages.text: "I think indeed the day is come for me to fight beside you," said Glas, and he went back to the King of the World and asked him not to let his armies land till the Fianna came, but to let one man only come to fight with each of them until that time. So two of the strangers were sent against them that day, and they got their death by Glas and by Conn Crither; then two men against each of them, and three times nine fell by them before night. And Conn Crither, covered with wounds, was bathed in the well of healing by the three sisters and made whole.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Gregory 1904, Book II, ch. IV; not verbatim.

passages.text: And Glas went down to the harbour: "O King of the World, there is a friend of mine in the ships, Madan of the Bent Neck, son of the King of the Marshes; and it is what he said in the great world in the east, that he himself would be enough to take Ireland for you. I ask you to let him come alone against me to-night, till we see which of us will fight best for Ireland." So Madan came to the land, and the two made a very hard fight; but as it was not in the prophecy that Glas would find his death there, it was the son of the King of the Marshes that got his death by him.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Gregory 1904, Book II, ch. IV; not verbatim.

title.en: The Men of Dea Come to the White Strand
title.zh: 神族馳援白沙灘

region.en: Dun Sesnain, Ui Conall Gabra, Co. Kerry, Ireland
region.zh: 愛爾蘭克里郡塞斯南堡

period: Fenian cycle, medieval Irish tradition; Lady Augusta Gregory retelling (1904)

source.work: Lady Augusta Gregory, Gods and Fighting Men (1904), Book II, ch. V, eBook #14465

summary.en: When Taistellach carries the alarm, Bran son of Febal goes to the Tuatha de Danaan feasting at Dun Sesnain. Dolb shames Bodb Dearg with the reminder that every king's son and Fianna leader has a wife or mother of the Sidhe, and the god-host musters in silk shirts and green shields — Midhir, Lir, Ilbrec son of Manannan, Abarthach, the Silver Hand, the Man of Sweet Speech. Abarthach slays the King of the Cat-Heads and, leaping down between Lir and the Dog-Head king, cuts off his legs at the knees and takes his head.
summary.zh: 泰斯特拉赫報警後，費巴爾之子布蘭前往在塞斯南堡設宴的神族。多爾布提醒波德·迪爾格：每位王子與菲亞納首領皆有一位仙族之妻母——神族遂著絲衫持綠盾集結：米德、利爾、瑪那南之子伊爾布雷克、阿巴爾塔赫、銀手、甜語者。阿巴爾塔赫斬貓首族王，又躍入利爾與犬首族王之間，斷其雙膝，取其首級。

sensitivity.note: The mythic-religious feature here is the alliance of the Tuatha de Danaan with their mortal kin — the aftermath of the Milesian settlement in reverse; the marvel-kings (Dog-Heads, Cat-Heads) belong to the Fenian marvel-race repertoire. Pin symbolic at Dun Sesnain.

passages.text: Taistellach that was one of Finn's messengers came to the White Strand asking news, and Conn bade him go back to where Finn was and tell him the way things were; and he sent him on to-night to the house of Bran, son of Febal his father, at Teamhair Luachra, to bid him gather all the Tuatha de Danaan to help them. Bran went out to gather the Tuatha de Danaan, and he went to Dun Sesnain in Ui Conall Gabra, where they were holding a feast at that time, and there he found Ilbrec the Many Coloured, son of Manannan, and Nemanach the Pearly, son of Angus Og, and Sigmall, grandson of Midhir.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Gregory 1904, Book II, ch. V; not verbatim.

passages.text: "There is a greater thing than this for you to do, Men of Dea," said Bran, and he told them the whole story. Dolb, son of Sesnan, went to Sidhe Bean Finn above Magh Femen to Bodb Dearg: "Young man," said Bodb Dearg, "we are no way bound to help the men of Ireland out of that strait." "Do not say that, for there is not a king's son or a prince or a leader of the Fianna of Ireland without having a wife or a mother or a foster-mother or a sweetheart of the Tuatha de Danaan; and it is good help they have given you every time you were in want of it."
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Gregory 1904, Book II, ch. V; not verbatim.

passages.text: "I give my word," said Bodb Dearg, "it is right to give a good answer to so good a messenger." He sent word to the Tuatha de Danaan in every place, and they gathered to him, and their leaders besides Bodb Dearg were Midhir of Bri Leith, and Lir of Sidhe Finnachaidh, and Ilbrec, son of Manannan, and Argat Lamh, the Silver Hand, from the Sionnan, and the Man of Sweet Speech from the Boinn. "O Men of Dea," said Abarthach, "let a high mind and high courage rise within you now in the face of the battle, for the doings of every one among you will be told till the end of the world." The King of the Dog-Heads and the King of the Cat-Heads went against them with five red-armed battalions like great red waves.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Gregory 1904, Book II, ch. V; not verbatim.

passages.text: Lir attacked the King of the Dog-Heads and was getting the worst of it, and Ilbrec and Sigmall and the five sons of Finnaistucan were all driven off; but Abarthach made an end of the King of the Cat-Heads, rose on his spear, made a leap, and came down between Lir and his enemy. He took his sword in his left hand, made a thrust with his spear through the king's armour, and as the king raised up his shield he cut off both his legs at the knees, and the king let fall his shield, and Abarthach struck off his head.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Gregory 1904, Book II, ch. V; not verbatim.

title.en: The King of Ulster's Son Slays Dolar Durba
title.zh: 阿爾斯特王子誅殺多拉·杜爾巴

region.en: Finntraigh (White Strand), Corca Duibhne, Co. Kerry, Ireland
region.zh: 愛爾蘭克里郡科爾卡·迪夫尼白沙灘

period: Fenian cycle, medieval Irish tradition; Lady Augusta Gregory retelling (1904)

source.work: Lady Augusta Gregory, Gods and Fighting Men (1904), Book III, ch. VIII, eBook #14465

summary.en: A twelve-year-old prince of Ulster, shut up by a father who thinks his bones too soft, escapes with twelve foster-brothers to join Finn at the White Strand. Conan mocks him; the invaders laugh when Finn's side sends a lad against their champion Dolar Durba — and in the mock they die, for the boy wounds Dolar again and again, grapples him when shields break, and the tide drowns them both locked together, Dolar beneath him.
summary.zh: 十二歲的阿爾斯特王子被父親以「骨骼尚軟」為由禁閉，卻攜十二名奶兄弟逃往白沙灘投奔芬恩。科南嘲弄他；當芬恩一方派出一少年迎戰敵方最強戰士多拉·杜爾巴時，敵軍大笑——然而大笑者皆亡：少年連創多拉，盾劍俱碎後相搏扭打，潮水將二人相鎖溺斃，多拉居其下。

sensitivity.note: The boy-hero episode is a Fenian stock type (compare Cuchulain's first exploits); the mutual drowning in a death-grip is the fixed 'sole to sole' death-motif of this cycle. Pin symbolic at the White Strand battle site.

passages.text: News of the great battle reached to the court of the King of Ulster, and the king's son, that was only twelve years of age and the comeliest of all the young men of Ireland, said to his father: "Let me go to help Finn, son of Cumhal, and his men." "You are not old enough, or strong enough, boy; your bones are too soft." When the boy went on asking, his father shut him up in some close place, and put twelve young men, his foster-brothers, in charge of him. "It is through courage and daring my father won a great name for himself in his young youth, and why does he keep me from winning a name for myself?" The boy talked on till he got round them all, and when the king was asleep they went into the house where the arms were kept, and every lad brought away a shield and a sword and a helmet and two spears and two greyhound whelps, and they went through Connacht of many tribes and into Ciarraighe, and so on to the White Strand.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Gregory 1904, Book III, ch. VIII; not verbatim.

passages.text: When they came there Dolar Durba was on the strand, boasting before the men of Ireland. "You are not a grown man," said Conan; "and neither yourself or your comrades are fit to face any fighting man at all." "I never saw the Fianna of Ireland till this day, but I know well that you are Conan Maol, that never says a good word of any man; and you will see now if I am in dread of that man on the strand, or of any man in the world, for I will go out against him by myself." But it was then Conan told him Dolar Durba was just after killing his twelve comrades.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Gregory 1904, Book III, ch. VIII; not verbatim.

passages.text: Great anger came on him, and he rushed down to the strand; and all the armies of the strangers gave a great shout of laughter, for they thought all Finn's men had been made an end of. When the boy heard that his courage grew the greater, and he fell on Dolar Durba and gave him many wounds before he knew he was attacked at all. They fought till their shields and their swords were broken in pieces, and then they grappled together and wrestled till the tide went over them and drowned them both; and when the ebb-tide came on the morrow, the two bodies were found cold and quiet, each one held fast by the other, but Dolar Durba was beneath the king's son, so they knew it was the young lad had got the victory.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Gregory 1904, Book III, ch. VIII; not verbatim.

title.en: The Fall of the King of Lochlann and His Sons
title.zh: 洛赫蘭王與三子之傾覆

region.en: Finntraigh (White Strand), Corca Duibhne, Co. Kerry, Ireland
region.zh: 愛爾蘭克里郡科爾卡·迪夫尼白沙灘

period: Fenian cycle, medieval Irish tradition; Lady Augusta Gregory retelling (1904)

source.work: Lady Augusta Gregory, Gods and Fighting Men (1904), Book III, ch. X, eBook #14465

summary.en: The royal house of Lochlann falls one after another on the strand: Forne falls to Oisin heartened by Fergus's praise, Tocha to Lugaidh's Son, Mongach of the Sea to Fidach of the Bretons in a mutual death of flail and sword. Last comes Caisel of the Feathers with the shield of the Fomor's smith that blazes even under the sea and burns men like oak-splinters — until Druimderg casts the Red-Socketed spear into his laughing mouth and the flame of the shield dies.
summary.zh: 洛赫蘭王室在白沙灘相繼傾覆：弗恩經費爾古斯讚美後的歐辛誅殺；托哈死於盧蓋德之子；海上之蒙古赫與布列塔尼之菲達赫同歸於盡。最後是持弗莫爾鐵匠神盾的羽翎王凱塞爾——盾焰入水不熄，焚人如燒橡柴——直到德魯姆德格擲出紅臼矛，正中其張口大笑之處，盾焰方熄。

sensitivity.note: The fire-shield of the Fomor's smith is a magical-weapon set-piece of the Fenian marvel repertoire; the mocking laugh that leaves only the mouth unarmoured is a fixed death-motif (compare Balor's eye, Siegfried's back). Pin symbolic at the strand.

passages.text: "I swear by the oath of my people," said the King of Lochlann, "if any man of the armies goes out against the Fianna before myself and my three sons, we will not go at all, for we would not get the satisfaction we are used to, unless our swords get their fill of blood." "I will go out against them alone," said Forne, the youngest son, with a red-edged sword in each of his hands, and he made the strand narrow with the bodies of the young men of the Fianna.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Gregory 1904, Book III, ch. X; not verbatim.

passages.text: Then Oisin gave out a great shout against him: "Stop here with me, king's son, until I fight with you for the Fianna." It seemed for a while that the battle was going against Oisin, and Fergus of the True Lips said to him: "There is great shame on the Fianna, Oisin, seeing you so low in this fight; and there is many a horseman from the daughters of the kings and princes of Ireland looking at you now." Great courage rose in Oisin then, and he drove his spear through the body of Forne. And Tocha, the second son, went on shore to avenge his brother, till Lugaidh's Son turned against him, and made a stroke that cut through the foreigner's sword, and then another that cut his heart in two halves.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Gregory 1904, Book III, ch. X; not verbatim.

passages.text: The third son, Mongach of the Sea, went on shore with a strong iron flail in his hand having seven balls of pure iron on it, and fifty iron chains, and fifty apples on every chain, and fifty deadly thorns on every apple. Fidach, son of the King of the Bretons, went out against him, and leaped aside from the flail and cut off his two hands at the joint, and made a blow at his middle that cut him into two halves; but as Mongach fell, an apple of the flail went into Fidach's comely mouth and through his brain, and it was foot to foot those two fell, and lip to lip.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Gregory 1904, Book III, ch. X; not verbatim.

passages.text: And the next that came was the King of Lochlann himself, Caisel of the Feathers, and the shield that was made for him by the smith of the Fomor had red flames coming from it; and if it was put under the sea itself, not one of its flames would stop blazing; and the flames he sent from his shield went through the bodies of men till they blazed up like a splinter of oak that had hung a year in the smoke of a chimney. Then Druimderg, grandson of the Head of the Fianna of Ulster, took the deadly spear, the Croderg, the Red-Socketed, that came down from one to another of the sons of Rudraighe, and looked at the King of Lochlann, and he could see no part of him without armour but his mouth that was opened wide, laughing at the Fianna; and he made a cast with the Croderg that hit him in the open mouth, and he fell, and his shield fell along with its master, and its flame went out.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Gregory 1904, Book III, ch. X; not verbatim.

title.en: Labran's Eagle Flight for the Fated Weapons
title.zh: 拉布蘭化身蒼鷹尋取宿命兵器

region.en: Dun of the King of the Country of the Fair Men (symbolic pin, western sea)
region.zh: 俊美者之國王的堡壘（象徵定位，西海）

period: Fenian cycle, medieval Irish tradition; Lady Augusta Gregory retelling (1904)

source.work: Lady Augusta Gregory, Gods and Fighting Men (1904), Book III, ch. XI, eBook #14465

summary.en: Tadg's wife recalls a birth-night prophecy: the smith of the Fomor made a shield and a sword for Daire Donn, King of the World, and no other arms will ever redden on him — and they lie with the King of the Country of the Fair Men, locked room by room behind seven locks. Labran flies there as a great eagle, borrows the weapons under a false love-errand, and nearly dies of the speed of his return; the wind-swift Aedh son of Aebinn carries them the last leg, and flashes of fire rise from the coverings as Finn takes them.
summary.zh: 塔格之妻憶及誕生夜之預言：弗莫爾鐵匠曾為大世界之王達爾·東鑄盾與劍，除此之外天下任何兵器均無法見血——如今七重鎖层层相扣，藏於俊美者之國王處。拉布蘭化身巨鷹飛往彼處，以假借之辭借得兵器，歸程急馳幾近衰竭；疾如風的艾德接力最後一程。芬恩揭開兵器之覆時，火光與致命之泡自其中升騰。

sensitivity.note: Fated weapons only able to kill a specific foe is a fixed Indo-European dragon-slayer motif (compare Sigurd, Mordred); the eagle-transformation flight is a shape-shifter errand of the Ulster-Tuatha interface. Symbolic pin; the Country of the Fair Men has no earthly coordinates.

passages.text: Fergus of the True Lips went through the length of Ireland till he came to the house of Tadg, son of Nuada, that was grandfather to Finn, and there was great grief on Muirne, Finn's mother, and on Labran of the Long Hand her brother. Tadg asked his wife who did she think would escape with their lives from the great fighting at the White Strand. "If all the living men of the world were on one side, Daire Donn, the King of the World, would put them all down, for there are no weapons in the world that will ever be reddened on him. And on the night he was born, the smith of the Fomor made a shield and a sword, and it is in the prophecy that he will fall by no other arms but those. And it is to the King of the Country of the Fair Men he gave them to keep, and it is with him they are now."
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Gregory 1904, Book III, ch. XI; not verbatim.

passages.text: They sent Labran looking for the weapons in the shape of a great eagle, and he went on from sea to sea till at noon on the morrow he came to the dun of the King of the Country of the Fair Men. There were seven rooms in the king's house that opened into one another, and on the first door was one lock, and on the second two locks, and so on to the door of the last room that had seven locks; and it was in that the sword and the shield that were made by the smith of the Fomor were kept.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Gregory 1904, Book III, ch. XI; not verbatim.

passages.text: Labran asked the loan of them under the story of a wife of a champion of the Fianna that had given him her love, and they were brought out and given to him, with stalks of luck put with them. He went back across the seas again, and reached his father's dun between the crowing of the cock and the full light of day, and the weakness of death came on him; and it was Aedh, son of Aebinn, that was as quick as the wind over a plain, carried them the last leg to the White Strand. Finn took the coverings off them, and there rose from them flashes of fire and deadly bubbles, and not one of the Fianna could stay looking at them, but it put great courage into them to know they were with Finn.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Gregory 1904, Book III, ch. XI; not verbatim.

title.en: Finn Slays the King of the World
title.zh: 芬恩誅殺大世界之王

region.en: Finntraigh (White Strand), Corca Duibhne, Co. Kerry, Ireland
region.zh: 愛爾蘭克里郡科爾卡·迪夫尼白沙灘

period: Fenian cycle, medieval Irish tradition; Lady Augusta Gregory retelling (1904)

source.work: Lady Augusta Gregory, Gods and Fighting Men (1904), Book III, ch. XII, eBook #14465

summary.en: On the last day the sea and hills and stones cry out the doom of the armies. Arcallach's axe turns on the King of the World's crown and sheds no blood; but when Finn meets him with the fated shield and sword, dread shakes the king and Finn cuts off his foot and then his head. The crown passes to Conmail, then to the woman-warrior Ogarmach — "it is in the prophecy the world will be owned by a woman" — until Finn cuts through the crown and her head; and the last two living men, Cael and Finnachta of the Teeth, drown one another hand to hand in the clear sea.
summary.zh: 末日之戰，海、山、石皆預鳴大軍之劫。阿卡拉克之斧劈王冠而不見血；然當芬恩持宿命之盾劍而來，恐懼令國王戰慄失色，芬恩斬其足而後斬其首。王冠先傳康麥爾，再傳女戰士奧加馬克——「預言曰：世界終將為女子所轄」——芬恩劈冠而斬其首。最後僅存的兩人，克爾與牙齒之芬納克特，在澄澈之海中手手相扼同溺而亡。

sensitivity.note: The doom-omens answered by the creatures of the high air are the Fenian Ragnarok-echo (sea chattering, stones crying, wind sobbing) — tagged 'world-renewal' as the cosmic reset after which the Fianna take charge of all Ireland. The crown-transfer sequence is a sacred-kingship motif.

passages.text: The King of the World came to the strand, and all that were left of the Fianna went out against them, and they were like thick woods meeting one another. Then the creatures of the high air answered to the battle, foretelling the destruction that would be done that day; and the sea chattered of the losses, and the waves gave heavy shouts keening them, and the water-beasts roared to one another, and the rough hills creaked with the danger of the battle, and the woods trembled mourning the heroes, and the grey stones cried out at their deeds, and the wind sobbed telling them, and the earth shook, foretelling the slaughter; and the cries of the grey armies put a blue cloak over the sun, and the clouds were dark.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Gregory 1904, Book III, ch. XII; not verbatim.

passages.text: Then the King of the World came towards Finn, and there was no one near him but Arcallach of the Black Axe, the first that ever brought a wide axe into Ireland. He made a terrible great blow of his axe at the king that went through his royal crown to the hair of his head, but did not take a drop of blood out of him, for the edge of the axe turned, and there went balls of fire over the plain from that blow; and the King of the World struck back at Arcallach and made two halves of him.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Gregory 1904, Book III, ch. XII; not verbatim.

passages.text: Then Finn and the King of the World turned on one another, and when the king saw the sword and the shield in Finn's hand, he knew those were the weapons that were to bring him to his death, and great dread came on him, and his comeliness left him, and his fingers were shaking. They fought like two days of judgment for the possession of the world, and Finn gave great strokes that broke his shield and his sword, and cut off his left foot, and at the last he struck off his head.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Gregory 1904, Book III, ch. XII; not verbatim.

passages.text: Finnachta of the Teeth took up the royal crown and set it on the head of Conmail; and when Goll Garbh made an end of him, he brought it to where Ogarmach was, the daughter of the King of Greece: "Put on that crown, Ogarmach, as it is in the prophecy the world will be owned by a woman; and it will never be owned by any woman higher than yourself." She went to look for Finn, and though the woman-warrior fought for a long time, a blow from Finn reached to her at last and cut through the royal crown, and with a second blow he struck her head off. And when the two armies were fallen side by side there were none left fit to stand but Cael, son of Crimthan, and Finnachta of the Teeth; and Cael, mortally hurt, had Fergus carry him to the sea to swim after the foreigner, and when Finnachta stretched out his hand to him, Cael took hold of it at the wrist and gave a strong pull that brought him over the side, and their hands shut across one another's bodies, and they went down to the sand and the gravel of the clear sea.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Gregory 1904, Book III, ch. XII; not verbatim.

title.en: Credhe's Lament and her Death for Cael
title.zh: 克蕾德之哀歌與其殉情

region.en: South of the White Strand, Corca Duibhne, Co. Kerry, Ireland
region.zh: 愛爾蘭克里郡白沙灘之南

period: Fenian cycle, medieval Irish tradition; Lady Augusta Gregory retelling (1904)

source.work: Lady Augusta Gregory, Gods and Fighting Men (1904), Book III, ch. XIII, eBook #14465

summary.en: Credhe searches the field of the dead for Cael. A crane above the marshes cannot shield both her nestlings from the fox; a stag nineteen days without grass or water laments the hind Finn killed — "it is no shame for me to die for grief after Cael." The waves put Cael's body back on the strand; she keens him in the famous harbour-lament, lays herself down beside him, dies of grief, and Caoilte raises the one stone over them. With the battle over, the great name of the armies of the World passes to the Fianna of Ireland for ever.
summary.zh: 克蕾德在屍橫遍野的戰場尋找克爾。澤上母鶴護不住兩隻雛鳥逃離狐狸；十九日不飲不食的牡鹿哀悼被芬恩射殺的母鹿——「我為克爾悲傷而死並不可恥」。海浪將克爾屍身推回沙灘，她為之唱起著名的港灣哀歌，隨即倒臥其側而死；卡爾特為二人立一石。大戰既畢，大世界大軍之名永歸愛爾蘭菲亞納。

sensitivity.note: The keening-lament (caoine) after battle is a real ritual genre embedded in narrative; the wife dying of grief beside her husband is a fixed death-motif ('dying of grief'). Post-war transfer of spoils and name marks the Fianna's world-guarantor role. Tag 'resurrection' here marks the ritual lament as renewal-of-the-dead practice, not belief claim.

passages.text: There came the women and the musicians and the physicians of the Fianna of Ireland to search out the kings and the princes of the Fianna and to bury them; and every one that might be healed was brought to a place of healing. Credhe, wife of Cael, went looking through the bodies for her comely comrade, crying as she went, and she saw a crane of the meadows and her two nestlings, and the cunning beast the fox watching the nestlings; and when the crane covered one of the birds to save it, he would make a rush at the other bird, the way she had to stretch herself out over the birds, and she would sooner have got her own death by the fox than her nestlings to be killed by him.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Gregory 1904, Book III, ch. XIII; not verbatim.

passages.text: "It is no wonder I to have such love for my comely sweetheart," said Credhe, "and the bird in that distress about her nestlings." Then she heard a stag in Druim Ruighlenn above the harbour, that was making great lamentations for his hind, for they had been nine years together and Finn had killed the hind, and the stag was nineteen days without tasting grass or water. "It is no shame for me to die for grief after Cael, since the stag is shortening his life sorrowing after the hind."
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Gregory 1904, Book III, ch. XIII; not verbatim.

passages.text: She met Fergus of the True Lips, and he had news: Cael and the last man left of the foreigners, Finnachta Fiaclach, were after drowning one another in the sea. And at that time the waves had put Cael back on the strand, and the women and the men of the Fianna raised him up and brought him to the south of the White Strand, and Credhe came to where he was and keened him: "The harbour roars, O the harbour roars, over the rushing race of the Headland of the Two Storms, the drowning of the hero of the Lake of the Two Dogs, that is what the waves are keening on the strand...
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Gregory 1904, Book III, ch. XIII; not verbatim.

passages.text: Since the son of Crimthann is drowned I will love no one after him for ever; many a king fell by his hand; his shield never cried out in the battle." After she had made that complaint, Credhe laid herself down beside Cael and died for grief after him, and they were put in the one grave, and it was Caoilte raised the stone over them. And the great name that was on the armies of the World went from them to the Fianna of Ireland; and they took the ships and the gold and the silver and all the spoils of the armies of the World, and from that time the Fianna had charge of the whole of Ireland until the time of their last battle, the sorrowful battle of Gabhra.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Gregory 1904, Book III, ch. XIII; not verbatim.

title.en: Manthara's Whisper and Kaikeyi's Boons
title.zh: 曼陀羅的耳語與凱凱伊的恩諾

region.en: Ayodhya, women's court (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 阿逾陀，內廷（象徵性定位）

period: Ramayana of Valmiki, oldest strata c. 2nd c. BCE-2nd c. CE (Griffith translation, 1870-74)

source.work: The Ramayan of Valmiki, trans. R. T. H. Griffith (1870-74), Ayodhya Kanda, Manthara episode

summary.en: On the eve of Rama's consecration, the hunchbacked maid Manthara talked Queen Kaikeyi out of her joy in ten minutes: her son Bharata would be a servant to Rama's crown. The two boons the king owed her from a battlefield - Bharata's throne, and Rama's fourteen years in the forest - were cashed that night, and the ideal reign was destroyed by a hairstyle's worth of vanity.
summary.zh: 羅摩加冕前夕，駝背侍女曼陀羅在十分鐘內說動了正為之歡喜的凱凱伊王后：其子婆羅多將為羅摩王冠之僕。國王於戰場上所欠的二項恩諾——婆羅多即位、羅摩流放十四年——當夜兌現，而理想之治毀於髮式般的虛榮。

sensitivity.note: Living tradition; classified 'myth'.

passages.text: Kaikeyi was dressed for joy - jewels for the consecration she thought her own son's day - when Manthara, the crooked-backed nurse, asked what she was celebrating; told, she threw down her ornament in a heap. The nurse's arithmetic: a mother's joy is her son's crown; a king's promise is a debtor's silence. Kaikeyi, told that Bharata would serve where he might reign, let the poison finish its work.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ramayana, Ayodhya Kanda (Griffith 1870-74); not verbatim.

passages.text: The boons were spoken in the anger-chamber, with the queen lying on the floor like a rejected petitioner: Bharata to the throne, Rama to the forest in bark garments - and the epic's engine was started by a maid with a grudge and a queen with a memory.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ramayana, Ayodhya Kanda (Griffith 1870-74); not verbatim.

canonical_translation: R. T. H. Griffith, 1870-74 (public domain)

title.en: Bharata and the Sandals of Rama
title.zh: 婆羅多與羅摩之履

region.en: Nandigrama, outside Ayodhya (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 難提伽羅摩，阿逾陀城外（象徵性定位）

period: Ramayana of Valmiki, oldest strata c. 2nd c. BCE-2nd c. CE (Griffith translation, 1870-74)

source.work: The Ramayan of Valmiki, trans. R. T. H. Griffith (1870-74), Ayodhya Kanda, Bharata's regency

summary.en: Bharata returned from his uncle's court to find a grieving city and a mother's crime done in his name. He chased Rama into the forest to give the throne back; Rama refused - a father's word was a father's word. So Bharata set Rama's sandals on the throne and governed from a hut outside Ayodhya for fourteen years, a regent who treated a pair of shoes as his king.
summary.zh: 婆羅多自舅家歸來，見城內舉哀，母親之罪假其名而行。他追入森林欲還其王位；羅摩不允——父親之言即是王命。於是婆羅多將羅摩之履置於王座，在阿逾陀城外的草廬中攝政十四年，以一雙鞋為其王。

sensitivity.note: Living tradition; classified 'myth'.

passages.text: Bharata's grief was double: the crown he was given was stolen goods, and the mother who stole it for him had emptied a city's joy - he refused the consecration and rode after his brother. In the forest Rama stood by the dead king's word: the exile was the promise, and a promise made to a queen in love is still a promise; the throne would keep for fourteen years. The compromise became the legend: Rama's sandals set upon the throne-cushion, and Bharata ruling not from the palace but from Nandigrama's hut, hair unbound, bark-garbed - a king dressed as an ascetic serving a pair of shoes.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ramayana, Ayodhya Kanda (Griffith 1870-74); not verbatim.

canonical_translation: R. T. H. Griffith, 1870-74 (public domain)

title.en: Sita Found in the Furrow
title.zh: 犁溝中的悉多

region.en: Mithila, Janaka's field (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 彌提羅，遮那迦之田（象徵性定位）

period: Ramayana of Valmiki, oldest strata c. 2nd c. BCE-2nd c. CE (Griffith translation, 1870-74)

source.work: The Ramayan of Valmiki, trans. R. T. H. Griffith (1870-74), Bala Kanda, Sita's birth

summary.en: King Janaka, ploughing the sacrificial ground, found a girl in the turned earth - a child as bright as a rising dawn, and he raised her as his daughter, naming her Sita, 'furrow'. The earth is her mother in the epic's own words, and the marriage-contest that Shiva's bow decides will break the bow instead.
summary.zh: 遮那迦王於祭祀之地上犁田，於翻起的土中得一女——明亮如初升朝霞的孩子——他養為己女，名之悉多，『犁溝』。史詩自言大地即其母；而決定其婚姻的濕婆神弓，最終被折斷。

sensitivity.note: Living tradition; classified 'myth'.

passages.text: Janaka was the plough-king of Mithila, and as he turned the first furrow of the sacred ground a child lay in the clods, bright as the dawn that was still in the sky. He lifted her from the earth and called her Sita - furrow - daughter of the ground he tilled; and the princess of the plough grew up in the palace with her origin kept in her name. The earth-mother of the epic is not a metaphor: at the poem's end the ground will open to receive her back - the furrow keeps its child from first page to last.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ramayana, Bala Kanda (Griffith 1870-74); not verbatim. / Paraphrase of Ramayana, Bala Kanda and Uttara Kanda (Griffith 1870-74); not verbatim.

canonical_translation: R. T. H. Griffith, 1870-74 (public domain)

title.en: The Death of Tataka the Yakshi
title.zh: 夜叉女多吒迦之死

region.en: Tataka's forest, Taraka's realm (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 多吒迦之林（象徵性定位）

period: Ramayana of Valmiki, oldest strata c. 2nd c. BCE-2nd c. CE (Griffith translation, 1870-74)

source.work: The Ramayan of Valmiki, trans. R. T. H. Griffith (1870-74), Bala Kanda, Tataka episode

summary.en: The forest that ate seers was ruled by Tataka, a yakshi cursed into a giant rakshasi's body. Vishvamitra led the teenage princes against her, with a logic he had to argue twice: a rakshasi may not be killed by a god's bolt - the deed belongs to a man. Rama's first arrows blinded her, his second flight cut her down, and the seers' fires burned unrobbed from that evening.
summary.zh: 吞食仙人的森林由多吒迦所轄——一位被詛咒為巨大羅剎女的夜叉。維什瓦米陀引少年王子前往，並須兩次論證其邏輯：羅剎女不可由神杵誅殺——此事屬於人。羅摩的第一輪箭使其盲目，第二輪將其斬落；自此仙人祭火不再被劫。

sensitivity.note: Living tradition; classified 'myth'.

passages.text: Tataka's story was a curse with a history: a yakshi of beauty, turned by a seer's word into a hill-sized demoness whose appetite emptied the hermitages of the district. Vishvamitra's law was stated like a rule of the hunt: no god's weapon may end her; this is a man's work - and Rama, a boy with his first great bow, was told the theology of manhood before his first battle.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ramayana, Bala Kanda (Griffith 1870-74); not verbatim.

passages.text: She came storming like a thundercloud; his first volley took her eyes, and in her blindness the second rained down and ended the forest's terror - the seers lit their fires that night without robbers at the edge of the light.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ramayana, Bala Kanda (Griffith 1870-74); not verbatim.

canonical_translation: R. T. H. Griffith, 1870-74 (public domain)

title.en: Surpanakha's Proposal and Mutilation
title.zh: 首哩薄那迦的求婚與毀容

region.en: Panchavati on the Godavari (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 哥達瓦里河畔般折婆提（象徵性定位）

period: Ramayana of Valmiki, oldest strata c. 2nd c. BCE-2nd c. CE (Griffith translation, 1870-74)

source.work: The Ramayan of Valmiki, trans. R. T. H. Griffith (1870-74), Aranya Kanda, Surpanakha episode

summary.en: The rakshasa princess Surpanakha found the exiles in the forest and proposed herself - to Rama, then to Lakshmana, with honest appetite. The brothers' answer was the epic's cruelest prank: she came back mutilated, nose and ears cut by Lakshmana's blade, and her wounded vanity summoned her brother Ravana to avenge the honor no court would give her.
summary.zh: 羅剎女公主首哩薄那迦在林中遇見流亡者，先向羅摩、再向羅什曼那求婚，態度坦率。兄弟的回答是史詩中最殘忍的惡作劇：她毀容而歸——鼻與耳被羅什曼那之刃割去——她受創的虛榮召來兄長羅波那，為任何廷堂都不肯給她的名譽復仇。

sensitivity.note: Living tradition; gendered violence readings contested; classified 'myth'.

passages.text: Surpanakha, sister of the lord of Lanka, saw the two exiled princes in the forest and offered herself first to Rama, then to Lakshmana - a proposal made with a demoness's frankness and refused with a mortal's caution. The prank that answered her was Lakshmana's blade: she flew at Sita and was cut - nose, ears - and the princes' hunting game sent the mutilated princess home to her brother. Her blood was the fuse of the war: the golden deer, the abduction, Lanka's ruin - the epic's course was set by a proposal nobody bothered to answer decently.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ramayana, Aranya Kanda (Griffith 1870-74); not verbatim.

canonical_translation: R. T. H. Griffith, 1870-74 (public domain)

title.en: The Golden Deer and Maricha's Last Trick
title.zh: 金鹿與摩哩遮的最後詭計

region.en: Panchavati forest (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 般折婆提森林（象徵性定位）

period: Ramayana of Valmiki, oldest strata c. 2nd c. BCE-2nd c. CE (Griffith translation, 1870-74)

source.work: The Ramayan of Valmiki, trans. R. T. H. Griffith (1870-74), Aranya Kanda, golden deer episode

summary.en: A deer of gold and jewels stepped into the hermitage clearing - Sita's delight, Rama's warning, and the demon Maricha in disguise. He led Rama leagues into the forest, and dying, imitated Rama's own voice crying for help; Lakshmana left the line only when Sita's anger drove him - and the clearing was empty for Ravana.
summary.zh: 一頭金鑲寶石之鹿踏進仙居空地——悉多所喜、羅摩所疑、實為摩哩遮的偽裝。牠引羅馬深入林中數里，臨死模仿羅摩自己的聲音呼救；羅什曼那只在悉多動怒後才離開界線——空地遂為羅波那讓出。

sensitivity.note: Living tradition; classified 'myth'.

passages.text: The deer was too beautiful to be real and too real to resist: silver hooves, sapphire eyes, a hide of beaten gold - and Rama went after it with the doubt still in his voice. Maricha led him a whole day's chase and, struck at last, threw his dying voice: Help, Sita, help, Lakshmana - Rama's own accent crying for rescue from the forest's far side. Lakshmana, bound by his brother's order and insulted by his sister-in-law's doubt, drew the line he would break - and the three minutes he was gone were the three minutes that emptied the world of the Ramayana.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ramayana, Aranya Kanda (Griffith 1870-74); not verbatim.

canonical_translation: R. T. H. Griffith, 1870-74 (public domain)

title.en: Jatayu's Last Fight
title.zh: 闍吒優私的最後一戰

region.en: Sky above the Deccan (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 德干上空（象徵性定位）

period: Ramayana of Valmiki, oldest strata c. 2nd c. BCE-2nd c. CE (Griffith translation, 1870-74)

source.work: The Ramayan of Valmiki, trans. R. T. H. Griffith (1870-74), Aranya Kanda, Jatayu episode

summary.en: The old vulture Jatayu, friend of Rama's father, saw Ravana's flying chariot cross the sky with Sita inside and attacked it - a bird of years against the ten-headed king of Lanka. He fought until his wings were cut; dying on the rock, he gave Rama the one fact that mattered: she lives; Lanka has her. His pyre was the first Rama lit for an ally.
summary.zh: 老鷹闍吒優私，羅摩之父的故友，見羅波那的飛車載著悉多越過天空，便攻擊之——以垂暮之鳥對抗楞伽的十首之王。戰至翼斷；死於岩上時，他給了羅摩唯一要緊的事實：她活著；楞伽藏她。羅摩為其盟友點燃的第一座火堆屬於他。

sensitivity.note: Living tradition; classified 'myth'.

passages.text: Jatayu met the abductor in the sky - an old vulture against a flying palace - and held the chariot in the clouds with beak and wing while Sita wept beneath the fight. Ravana cut the wings that held him; the bird fell like a stone among the rocks, and the king of Lanka flew on with his prize - the first casualty of the war, unwitnessed by either army.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ramayana, Aranya Kanda (Griffith 1870-74); not verbatim.

passages.text: Rama and Lakshmana found the wreck of the bird and heard the report that turned grief into a campaign: she lives, in the southern sea, in Ravana's island - and the pyre of a vulture was the war's first rite.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ramayana, Aranya Kanda (Griffith 1870-74); not verbatim.

canonical_translation: R. T. H. Griffith, 1870-74 (public domain)

title.en: Kabandha, the Headless Embrace
title.zh: 迦般陀：無首之抱

region.en: Dandaka forest (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 丹陀迦森林（象徵性定位）

period: Ramayana of Valmiki, oldest strata c. 2nd c. BCE-2nd c. CE (Griffith translation, 1870-74)

source.work: The Ramayan of Valmiki, trans. R. T. H. Griffith (1870-74), Aranya Kanda, Kabandha episode

summary.en: In the Dandaka the brothers met a monster with no head and a mouth in its belly, arms a league long: Kabandha, a gandharva cursed into the shape, who caught travelers as a bird catches fish. Disarmed by grief at first, they cut off his arms at last, burned him - and the freed spirit rose from the pyre to give them their road-map: Sugriva of Kishkindha, Hanuman, the south.
summary.zh: 在丹陀迦，兄弟們遇見一隻無首而口在腹中、雙臂長達一里路的怪物：迦般陀，被詛咒成此形的乾達婆，如鳥捕魚般捕捉旅人。初因悲痛而失手，終於斬其雙臂，焚其身——被解咒的靈魂自火堆中升起，交給他們整張路線圖：猴王須羯哩婆、哈奴曼、南方。

sensitivity.note: Living tradition; classified 'myth'.

passages.text: Kabandha's arms were the forest's trap: no head to reason with, a mouth in the belly, and a reach that closed like a net on anything that walked the dark path. When his arms were cut off at last and the body burned, the monster stood up out of the fire as a radiant gandharva - the curse ended by the very death he had forced on travelers. His gift was the plot: go to Kishkindha, to Sugriva the exile monkey-king; the monkey who leaps the ocean waits there - and the search for Sita found its map in a pyre's smoke.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ramayana, Aranya Kanda (Griffith 1870-74); not verbatim.

canonical_translation: R. T. H. Griffith, 1870-74 (public domain)

title.en: Shabari's Berries
title.zh: 莎婆利的野果

region.en: Pampa lake, Rishyamuka hill (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 般婆湖，黎沙牟迦山（象徵性定位）

period: Ramayana of Valmiki, oldest strata c. 2nd c. BCE-2nd c. CE (Griffith translation, 1870-74)

source.work: The Ramayan of Valmiki, trans. R. T. H. Griffith (1870-74), Aranya Kanda, Shabari episode

summary.en: The old ascetic woman Shabari had kept her master's ashram swept for years, waiting for two guests she had been promised. When Rama came, she fed him berries she had tasted first - the fruit a poor old woman could offer - and he accepted every one. Bhakti's first charter in the Ramayana: the devotional meal offered before the worthy offering.
summary.zh: 年邁的苦行女莎婆利多年來一直灑掃其師之道場，等待她被告知將會來到的兩位客人。羅摩來到時，她奉上自己先嚐過的野果——一位貧苦老婦所能獻出的果實——而他一一受之。奉愛在《羅摩衍那》中的第一份憲章：先於合儀之祭的奉愛之餐。

sensitivity.note: Living tradition; classified 'myth'.

passages.text: Shabari's ashram had been swept and waiting: her master, dying, had told her that Rama would come, and she kept the fire, the water-pots and the path for years of forest silence. She offered him the berries of the forest, each one tasted first for sweetness - the purest thing she had, given the only way she knew how to give. Rama ate what kings would have refused, and the poem's theology turned in his mouth: devotion outcounts ceremony - the first charter of bhakti hidden in a hunger-strike of an old woman's hospitality.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ramayana, Aranya Kanda (Griffith 1870-74); not verbatim.

canonical_translation: R. T. H. Griffith, 1870-74 (public domain)

title.en: The Death of Vali, Shot from Cover
title.zh: 婆黎之死：自掩蔽處射出的一箭

region.en: Kishkindha (symbolic pin at Hampi)
region.zh: 猴國吉什金陀（象徵性定位於漢皮）

period: Ramayana of Valmiki, oldest strata c. 2nd c. BCE-2nd c. CE (Griffith translation, 1870-74)

source.work: The Ramayan of Valmiki, trans. R. T. H. Griffith (1870-74), Kishkindha Kanda, Vali episode

summary.en: Vali, the monkey-king whose strength doubled from any foe he faced, had exiled his brother Sugriva and taken his wife. Rama agreed to help - and shot the king from behind a tree as he fought Sugriva. Dying, Vali asked the question the epic has answered ever since: where was the dharma in a hidden arrow? Rama's answer - the king who took his brother's wife - has satisfied fewer readers than the question.
summary.zh: 猴王婆黎的力量因面對之敵而倍增，曾放逐其弟須羯哩婆並奪其妻。羅摩應允相助——在婆黎與須羯哩婆相鬥時自樹後一箭射之。垂死的婆黎問出史詩至今仍要回答的問題：自掩蔽處放箭，正法何在？羅摩的答案——奪弟之妻之王——說服的讀者遠少於問題本身。

sensitivity.note: Living tradition; the shot's ethics are debated inside the tradition; classified 'myth'.

passages.text: Vali's strength was arithmetic: whatever he fought, he fought twice as strong - no army could beat him front-on, and his brother Sugriva lived only because exile was cheaper than war. The duel with Sugriva had turned once already; as the brothers closed again, an arrow came from the trees where Rama stood hidden, and the invincible king fell.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ramayana, Kishkindha Kanda (Griffith 1870-74); not verbatim.

passages.text: His dying argument named the problem: I wronged my brother, judge me in the open - why did the lord of dharma shoot from cover? Rama's answer (the wife taken, the code of allies) closed the case in the poem and reopened it in every retelling since.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ramayana, Kishkindha Kanda (Griffith 1870-74); not verbatim.

canonical_translation: R. T. H. Griffith, 1870-74 (public domain)

title.en: Hanuman Sets Lanka on Fire
title.zh: 哈奴曼火燒楞伽

region.en: Lanka (symbolic pin, Sri Lanka)
region.zh: 楞伽（象徵性定位，斯里蘭卡）

period: Ramayana of Valmiki, oldest strata c. 2nd c. BCE-2nd c. CE (Griffith translation, 1870-74)

source.work: The Ramayan of Valmiki, trans. R. T. H. Griffith (1870-74), Sundara Kanda, burning of Lanka

summary.en: Caught and humiliated by Ravana's guards, Hanuman answered with his tail: soaked in oil, set alight, he leapt free and used it as a torch, burning palace after palace through Lanka's rooftops - sparing only the grove where Sita sat. The message delivered on the way out: next time it will not be a monkey with a burning tail.
summary.zh: 被羅波那衛隊擒獲羞辱後，哈奴曼以尾作答：浸油、點燃，他躍脫羅網，以其為火炬，沿楞伽屋頂逐宮焚燬——唯獨繞過悉多所在的林苑。臨別的訊息：下次來的不是一隻尾巴著火的猴子。

sensitivity.note: Living tradition; classified 'myth'.

passages.text: The guards' insult was the plot's gift: they wrapped his tail in cloth and oil to burn him, and the monkey let them finish the torch before he moved. Shrunk, then sprung, he ran the city's ridgelines with a flame at his back: council halls, treasury, Ravana's own palace - the roofs went up one by one, and the sea-breeze carried the news. One grove he did not burn - the Ashoka grove where Sita waited; he doused his tail in the sea, took one last look at the enemy's capital, and leapt home over the ocean.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ramayana, Sundara Kanda (Griffith 1870-74); not verbatim.

canonical_translation: R. T. H. Griffith, 1870-74 (public domain)

title.en: Vibhishana's Defection
title.zh: 維毗沙那的投奔

region.en: Lanka court and Rama's camp (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 楞伽王廷與羅摩營地（象徵性定位）

period: Ramayana of Valmiki, oldest strata c. 2nd c. BCE-2nd c. CE (Griffith translation, 1870-74)

source.work: The Ramayan of Valmiki, trans. R. T. H. Griffith (1870-74), Yuddha Kanda, Vibhishana episode

summary.en: In Ravana's war council, the king's own brother Vibhishana said the unforgivable thing: give Sita back. Driven from the court with insults, he crossed the lines to Rama's camp - where the monkeys wanted to kill a rakshasa and Rama gave him shelter with one sentence: I take whoever comes to me, even once. The war's map changed hands that evening.
summary.zh: 在羅波那的戰爭廷議上，王的親弟維毗沙那說出不可饒恕之言：把悉多還回去。他被以侮辱逐出廷堂，越線投奔羅摩營地——猴族欲誅此羅剎，羅摩一句話收留他：凡來我此者，縱一次，我亦納之。戰爭的地圖於那個傍晚易手。

sensitivity.note: Living tradition; classified 'myth'.

passages.text: The council's honest voice belonged to the king's brother: return the wife of another, or die with her stolen - and Ravana's answer drove the only counselor who loved him out of Lanka. At Rama's camp the rakshasa's arrival split the monkeys - a spy, said some - until Rama's rule was stated once: whoever comes to me for shelter, once, is mine to keep. Vibhishana's knowledge of the city's gates, the ocean's ford, Kumbhakarna's bed - the war was won with the enemy's brother as cartographer, and the epic's hardest question (is treason ever dharma?) answered with a shelter, not an argument.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ramayana, Yuddha Kanda (Griffith 1870-74); not verbatim.

canonical_translation: R. T. H. Griffith, 1870-74 (public domain)

title.en: Waking Kumbhakarna
title.zh: 喚醒俱姆伽爾那

region.en: Lanka (symbolic pin, Sri Lanka)
region.zh: 楞伽（象徵性定位，斯里蘭卡）

period: Ramayana of Valmiki, oldest strata c. 2nd c. BCE-2nd c. CE (Griffith translation, 1870-74)

source.work: The Ramayan of Valmiki, trans. R. T. H. Griffith (1870-74), Yuddha Kanda, Kumbhakarna episode

summary.en: Ravana's giant brother slept six months at a stretch - the boon he had begged for eternity, mispronounced into eternal sleep. To wake him for the war, the rakshasas drove a thousand elephants over his body and hammered him with drums. He rose, ate his breakfast army, and asked the news; told that it was his brother's pride he was dying for, he went anyway - loyalty larger than judgment.
summary.zh: 羅波那的巨人弟弟一睡半年——本為求得永生而許之願，被誤唸成永眠。為喚其赴戰，羅剎們驅千象踩過其身，以鼓錘擊之。他起身，吞下早餐般的軍陣，問道新聞；得知自己是為兄長的驕傲而死，他仍然前往——忠誠大於判斷。

sensitivity.note: Living tradition; classified 'myth'.

passages.text: The boon at Brahma's gate had been mispronounced: nirdeva-vamsha (lordship without gods) heard as nidra-vamsha (a race of sleep) - and the giant who asked for the world's end got an appointment book with half the year dark. To raise him for the war the rakshasas stampeded elephants across his chest and rang the city's drums against his ears; he rose yawning, asked what was for breakfast, and ate the first regiment sent to greet him.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ramayana, Yuddha Kanda (Griffith 1870-74); not verbatim.

passages.text: Told the truth about the war - his brother's lust, not Lanka's honor - he chose his brother anyway: the epic's strangest loyalist, a giant who knew the cause was wrong and carried it to the field on his shoulders.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ramayana, Yuddha Kanda (Griffith 1870-74); not verbatim.

canonical_translation: R. T. H. Griffith, 1870-74 (public domain)

title.en: Indrajit's Serpent-Arrows and the Serpent-Noose
title.zh: 因陀羅耆的蛇箭與蛇索

region.en: Lanka battlefield (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 楞伽戰場（象徵性定位）

period: Ramayana of Valmiki, oldest strata c. 2nd c. BCE-2nd c. CE (Griffith translation, 1870-74)

source.work: The Ramayan of Valmiki, trans. R. T. H. Griffith (1870-74), Yuddha Kanda, Indrajit's serpent weapons

summary.en: Ravana's son Indrajit, invisible in war-chariot and sorcery, twice came near to ending the war in an afternoon: once with the Naga-pasha, the serpent-noose that bound Rama and Lakshmana both, and once with the arrow that left Lakshmana dying. Both times the counter-spell was a bird's: Garuda's wings, at whose approach the serpents fled, and the Sanjivana herb borne by Hanuman.
summary.zh: 羅波那之子因陀羅耆，隱形於戰車與咒術之中，兩度幾乎在一個下午結束戰爭：一次以蛇索縛住羅摩與羅什曼那二人，一次以一箭令羅什曼那垂死。兩次的破解皆為飛禽：金翅鳥之翼——蛇族見之而逃——以及哈奴曼所攜的還魂藥草。

sensitivity.note: Living tradition; classified 'myth'.

passages.text: Indrajit fought from the sky like a sound: invisible, his serpent-arrows became living nooses around the two brothers' bodies - and the sons of the Wind stood still, bound by snakes. The release came from above the food-chain: Garuda descended, and every serpent on the field let go - the bird that eats snakes had a claim on them older than any war. His second stroke - the Shakti that left Lakshmana dying - was answered by Hanuman's mountain: the whole peak of herbs flown north, the wound closed by the lift itself - the war's ambulance was a mountain.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ramayana, Yuddha Kanda (Griffith 1870-74); not verbatim. / Paraphrase of Ramayana, Yuddha Kanda and Sundara Kanda (Griffith 1870-74); not verbatim.

canonical_translation: R. T. H. Griffith, 1870-74 (public domain)

title.en: The Mountain of Life-Giving Herbs
title.zh: 還魂藥草之山

region.en: Dronagiri / Sanjivani mountain (symbolic pin in the Himalaya)
region.zh: 德羅那吉里／還魂山（象徵性定位於喜馬拉雅）

period: Ramayana of Valmiki, oldest strata c. 2nd c. BCE-2nd c. CE (Griffith translation, 1870-74)

source.work: The Ramayan of Valmiki, trans. R. T. H. Griffith (1870-74), Yuddha Kanda/Sundara Kanda, the Sanjivana mountain

summary.en: Lakshmana lay dying, and the physician-gods named the herb: Sanjivani, on a Himalayan peak that nobody could identify in time. Hanuman flew, failed to find the one plant among thousands, and solved it his way - he lifted the entire mountain and set it down on the battlefield. The mountain, the tradition says, has herbs still, and Himalayan villages argue about which peak it was.
summary.zh: 羅什曼那垂死，醫神指出藥草之名：還魂草，在喜馬拉雅一峰，無人能及時辨認。哈奴曼飛去，於千百藥草間無從分辨，遂以其法解之——舉起整座山，置於戰場之上。據傳統所說，那座山至今仍有藥草，喜馬拉雅村落至今仍爭論是哪一峰。

sensitivity.note: Living tradition (place-cults claim the peak); classified 'myth'.

passages.text: The diagnosis was divine: only the Sanjivani herb can bring him back, and it grows on a mountain of ten thousand look-alikes - the war had hours, not days. Hanuman flew north, searched the moonlit slope, and found the impossible shortlist: every plant in sight could be the one, and every minute cost blood.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ramayana (Griffith 1870-74); not verbatim.

passages.text: His solution was scale itself: he uprooted the mountain, flew it south under one arm, and set it on the field - the herb wherever it was, delivered; and the peak he returned (whichever it truly was) has been argued over ever since.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ramayana (Griffith 1870-74); not verbatim.

canonical_translation: R. T. H. Griffith, 1870-74 (public domain)

title.en: Ravana's Last Stand and the Brahmastra
title.zh: 羅波那的最後一戰與婆羅摩箭

region.en: Lanka battlefield (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 楞伽戰場（象徵性定位）

period: Ramayana of Valmiki, oldest strata c. 2nd c. BCE-2nd c. CE (Griffith translation, 1870-74)

source.work: The Ramayan of Valmiki, trans. R. T. H. Griffith (1870-74), Yuddha Kanda, Ravana's death

summary.en: Ravana's last day had the shape of a first-rate king's: quivers emptied, crowns broken, heads regrown as they were struck off. The deaths that would not stay dead ended with a single arrow - the Brahmastra, aimed at the navel where the nectar of his immortality was stored. Ravana fell still defending his city, and Rama ordered the funeral rites of a hero for the enemy who had ruined him.
summary.zh: 羅波那的最後一日有第一流君王的形狀：箭囊傾空，王冠碎裂，被斬之首一次次重新長出。不會死去的死亡終於由一枝箭終結——婆羅摩箭，瞄準其不死甘露所藏之臍。羅波那仍在守衛其城時倒下，而羅摩為這位毀了他的敵人舉行英雄之葬。

sensitivity.note: Living tradition; Ravana's dignity is read differently across South Asia; classified 'myth'.

passages.text: The duel was regicide as repair-work: heads cut off grew back, crowns shattered and were replaced - a king being killed in installments because his death refused to complete. Vibhishana, from the enemy's side, named the secret: the nectar in the navel - and Rama's Brahmastra went where no blow had reached, and the ten heads came off to stay. The fallen king got a hero's pyre at his slayer's order: the scholar-king of Lanka, veena-player and city-builder, buried as an adversary should be - with the honors he had earned and the judgment he had refused.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ramayana, Yuddha Kanda (Griffith 1870-74); not verbatim.

canonical_translation: R. T. H. Griffith, 1870-74 (public domain)

title.en: Lava and Kusha Sing the Epic in Their Father's Court
title.zh: 羅婆與俱舍於父廷誦唱史詩

region.en: Valmiki's ashram and Ayodhya (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 蟻垤仙居與阿逾陀（象徵性定位）

period: Ramayana of Valmiki, Uttara Kanda (critical edition appendix), c. 2nd c. BCE-2nd c. CE (Griffith translation, 1870-74)

source.work: The Ramayan of Valmiki, trans. R. T. H. Griffith (1870-74), Uttara Kanda, Lava and Kusha

summary.en: In Valmiki's forest school, two boys learned to sing a story they did not know was theirs: the exile, the abduction, the war - and the queen abandoned though proved pure. Brought to Ayodhya to sing before the court, they named their mother Sita and their father Rama, and the poem's audience discovered its own ending: the king had exiled a pregnant wife who was innocent by fire and by earth.
summary.zh: 在蟻垤的林中學堂，兩個男孩學唱一則不知屬於自己的故事：流放、被擄、戰爭——以及雖經證明清白仍被放棄的王后。他們被召至阿逾陀，於王廷獻唱，唱出其母悉多、其父羅摩之名，而詩的聽眾發現了自己的結局：這位王曾放逐一位以火與地雙證其清白的懷孕之妻。

sensitivity.note: Living tradition and contested narrative; classified 'myth'.

passages.text: The twins of the forest learned the poem as schoolwork: meter, melody, the whole career of a king who looked suspiciously like the founder of their song. Sung before the assembled court, the ballad came to its present - the queen proved by fire, and exiled pregnant all the same - and the hall went silent: the boys were singing the king's sin back to him.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ramayana, Uttara Kanda (Griffith 1870-74); not verbatim.

passages.text: The family reunion is the poem's last test: Sita summoned to the assembly, calling the earth to witness once more - and the furrow opened and took its daughter; the epic ends by returning its heroine to the soil that made her.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ramayana, Uttara Kanda (Griffith 1870-74); not verbatim.

canonical_translation: R. T. H. Griffith, 1870-74 (public domain)

title.en: The Pushpaka Chariot Flies Rama Home
title.zh: 布施帕迦飛車載羅摩歸國

region.en: Lanka to Ayodhya (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 自楞伽至阿逾陀（象徵性定位）

period: Ramayana of Valmiki, oldest strata c. 2nd c. BCE-2nd c. CE (Griffith translation, 1870-74)

source.work: The Ramayan of Valmiki, trans. R. T. H. Griffith (1870-74), Yuddha Kanda, the Pushpaka chariot

summary.en: The flying palace-chariot of Kubera, taken by Ravana, fell to the victors: Rama ordered it to the Ashoka grove for Sita, and it carried her, the monkey army, and the story home - over the bridge, the forests, the hermitages of the exile, each stop telling its own part of the war. Ayodhya lit the city for a midnight arrival: the first Diwali, the tradition says.
summary.zh: 財神俱毘羅的飛行宮車曾為羅波那所奪，如今歸於勝者：羅摩令其飛往無憂林苑接悉多，載著她、猴軍與故事歸國——越過橋樑、森林、流亡的仙居，每一處停靠自述其在戰爭中的一節。阿逾陀燃城以待午夜歸人：傳統言，此即第一個排燈節。

sensitivity.note: Living tradition (Diwali charter); classified 'myth'.

passages.text: The chariot flew at its rider's thought: Sita seated in state, the monkey commanders in their fur, the sky-road taken south to north over a war's whole geography. Each stop was a rite of return: the bridge of stones, Rishyashringa's hermitage, Bharata's hut outside the capital - the exile's road traveled backward at flying speed. Ayodhya heard the drums and lit every lamp in the city for the midnight entry: fourteen years of darkness ending in a street of fire - the charter of the festival of lights.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ramayana, Yuddha Kanda (Griffith 1870-74); not verbatim.

canonical_translation: R. T. H. Griffith, 1870-74 (public domain)

title.en: Kapila's Fire and the Sons of Sagara
title.zh: 迦毘羅之火與薩伽羅之子

region.en: Ocean depths (symbolic pin at Sagar Island)
region.zh: 海洋深處（象徵性定位於薩伽羅島）

period: Vishnu Purana, Book IV (dynasty of Sagara), c. 300-800 CE (Wilson translation, 1840)

source.work: The Vishnu Purana, trans. H. H. Wilson (1840), Book IV, the sons of Sagara and Kapila's fire

summary.en: King Sagara's sixty thousand sons dug the ocean in search of a stolen horse and burned everything in their way. The sage Kapila, interrupted in meditation by the horde, opened his eyes and burned all sixty thousand to ash - souls imprisoned in unburnt bones that no water could wash. Many generations later, Bhagiratha's descent of the Ganga (over Shiva's hair) freed them: the ocean is called Sagara for the diggers.
summary.zh: 王薩伽羅的六萬子為尋被竊之馬掘穿大洋，沿途焚燬一切。仙人迦毘羅於禪定中被打擾，睜眼之間，六萬人皆化為灰——其靈魂囚於水洗不去的未化之骨。數代之後，跋吉羅陀引恆河下降（經濕婆之髮）而釋之：大洋至今以掘者之名為名（薩伽羅）。

sensitivity.note: Living tradition (Sagar Island rites); classified 'myth'.

passages.text: The sacrificial horse was stolen to the underworld sea; Sagara's sixty thousand sons dug after it, turning the earth into the great basin of the ocean in their search. The sage Kapila sat in the depths where their spades arrived; the army's clamor broke his meditation, and one opened eye was a furnace - sixty thousand sons of a king burned to a single ash-heap. The ashes were the debt: no rite could free the souls until the Ganga herself came down to touch them - and the sea the diggers made still carries their king's name.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Vishnu Purana, Book IV (Wilson 1840); not verbatim.

canonical_translation: H. H. Wilson, 1840 (public domain)

title.en: Rama and Shambuka: The Ascetic Death
title.zh: 羅摩與首薄迦：苦行者的死亡

region.en: Ayodhya outskirts (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 阿逾陀城郊（象徵性定位）

period: Ramayana of Valmiki, Uttara Kanda (critical edition appendix), c. 2nd c. BCE-2nd c. CE (Griffith translation, 1870-74)

source.work: The Ramayan of Valmiki, trans. R. T. H. Griffith (1870-74), Uttara Kanda, Shambuka episode

summary.en: A child of Ayodhya died young; the seers traced the cause to a disorder in the order of castes: a Shudra named Shambuka was practicing austerities reserved for the twice-born, upside-down on a tree-branch. Rama went, confirmed the tale, and struck off the ascetic's head - and the child revived. The episode is the epic's hardest scene: dharma as hierarchy enforced by the ideal king, and the modern argument about it has never closed.
summary.zh: 阿逾陀之一孩童夭折；仙人們究其因於種姓秩序之亂：一名首陀羅名首薄迦者，倒懸於樹枝之上，修習唯再生者可修之苦行。羅摩前往，證實其事，斬下苦行者之頭——孩童於是復活。此幕是史詩最沉重的一幕：正法被理想之王以等級執行；而圍繞它的現代論爭從未閉合。

sensitivity.note: Living tradition and politically contested (caste politics); classified 'myth'. The contested modern readings are recorded here.

passages.text: The diagnosis of the kingdom's grief came from the seers: an ascetic of the wrong caste was heating the world with penance, and a child of the city paid the price. Rama found Shambuka hanging head-down on the branch, emaciated and luminous, and asked him his name and his vow; the answer confirmed the seers' account. The sword fell - and the dead child sat up in Ayodhya as the ascetic's life went out: the episode has made the Uttara Kanda the most argued section of the epic, and modern retellings often refuse it outright.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ramayana, Uttara Kanda (Griffith 1870-74); not verbatim.

canonical_translation: R. T. H. Griffith, 1870-74 (public domain)

title.en: Arthur of Britain Steals Finn's Hounds
title.zh: 不列顛之亞瑟竊取芬恩獵犬

region.en: Inver Mara Gamiach, coast of Britain
region.zh: 不列顛海岸卡拉馬基河口

period: Fenian cycle, medieval Irish tradition; Lady Augusta Gregory retelling (1904)

source.work: Lady Augusta Gregory, Gods and Fighting Men (1904), Book IV, ch. I, eBook #14465

summary.en: Arthur son of the King of Britain takes service with Finn, then runs off across the sea with the three hounds Bran, Sceolan and Adhnuall. Finn reads the theft in his pale-gold basin of water and sends nine champions after them; Goll spares Arthur's life, and the captive prince bonds with Finn and follows him till he dies.
