She bade him go to his comrades, and Diarmuid took leave of her and went back to the Fianna, and there was a great welcome before him; but for all that they were someway envious, Diarmuid to have got that grand house and her love from the woman they themselves had turned away.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Gregory 1904, Book VI, ch. III; not verbatim.

passages.text: Finn came towards her and asked one of the pups of Diarmuid's greyhound bitch, and she gave it; and Oisin came, and Caoilte, and each got a pup the same way. But every time Diarmuid came home and found a pup gone, he said it was because she remembered the way she was when she came to him; and the third time the house was gone and the woman was gone on the moment, and it was on the bare ground he awoke on the morrow. There was great sorrow on him then, and he said he would search in every place till he would find her again.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Gregory 1904, Book VI, ch. III; not verbatim.

title.en: The Cup of the Plain of Wonder and the Healing That Ended Love
title.zh: 奇觀平原之杯與終結愛情的治癒

region.en: Land-under-Wave, western ocean (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 浪下之國，西海（象徵定位）

period: Fenian cycle, medieval Irish tradition; Lady Augusta Gregory retelling (1904)

source.work: Lady Augusta Gregory, Gods and Fighting Men (1904), Book VI, ch. III, eBook #14465

summary.en: Searching for the vanished woman, Diarmuid rides a ship below the sea to Land-under-Wave, where the King's daughter is sick for love of him — she lost a drop of heart's blood at every thought of him on her seven-year enchanted journey. Her cure demands three draughts from the cup of the King of the Plain of Wonder, which no man ever got; Diarmuid destroys two armies, learns he was prophesied seven years before his birth, and takes the cup — but the red man, the messenger from beyond the world, warns that the healing will take his love with it, and so it does.
summary.zh: 尋找消失的女子，迪爾穆德乘船入海底之國「浪下之國」。國王之女正因思念他而病——七年魔困之旅中，每念他一次便失一滴心血。痊癒需奇觀平原之王之杯中的三口酒，而此杯無人可得；迪爾穆德殲滅兩軍，方知其毀滅早於出生七年已被預言。然而「界外信使」紅人警示：治癒之時，愛亦將隨之而去——果然如此。

sensitivity.note: The cup-of-healing quest under the sea is the Fenian grail-quest analogue; the love-destroying cure inverts the usual magical-healing plot and is a rare narrative device (love lost through the very act of saving the beloved). The messenger-from-beyond-the-world is a deus ex machina of the vision genre.

passages.text: Diarmuid followed the path she took down to the strand, and then he saw a ship, and leaned on the handle of his spear and made a light leap on to it; and the boat went out over the sea, and then down below it, and Diarmuid found himself on a plain. He met with three drops of blood on the way and put them in a napkin — the greyhound had lost them. He saw a woman gathering rushes: "The daughter of King Under-Wave is come home, and she was for seven years under enchantment, and there is sickness on her now, and all the physicians are gathered together and none of them can do her any good, and a bed of rushes is what she finds the wholesomest." The woman put the rushes about him and carried him to her on her back, and they took one another's hands, and were very joyful at that meeting. "Three parts of my sickness is gone from me now; but I am not well yet, and I never will be, for every time I thought of you, Diarmuid, on my journey, I lost a drop of the blood of my heart." "It is three draughts from the cup of the King of Magh an Ionganaidh, the Plain of Wonder, and no man ever got it or ever will get it."
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Gregory 1904, Book VI, ch. III; not verbatim.

passages.text: Diarmuid came to the little river before the Plain of Wonder, and there was a low-sized reddish man standing in the middle of it: "Come here and put your foot in the palm of my hand and I will bring you through." At the king's dun Diarmuid called out that the cup should be sent out to him, or champions to fight with him; twice eight hundred fighting men were sent, and in three hours there was not one of them left to stand against him; twice nine hundred better fighters again, and within four hours there was not one of them left. Then the King of the Plain of Wonder came out: "Where did the man come from that has brought destruction on the whole of my kingdom? For seven years before you were born it was put in the prophecy that you would come to destroy them.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Gregory 1904, Book VI, ch. III; not verbatim.

passages.text: And it is easy for me to give you the cup, whether or not there is healing in it." And the red man brought him back over the river: "I am the messenger from beyond the world, and I came to your help because your own heart is hot to come to the help of another. When you come where the woman is, put the water of the well in the cup, and one of the drops of blood in it, and she will drink it, and the same with the second drop and the third, and her sickness will be gone from her from that time. But there is another thing will be gone along with it, and that is the love you have for her." "That will not go from me," said Diarmuid. "It will go from you."
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Gregory 1904, Book VI, ch. III; not verbatim.

passages.text: So Diarmuid did as he bade him, and he brought the water and the cup and the drops of blood to the woman, and she drank them, and at the third draught she was healed. And no sooner was she healed than the love he had for her was gone, and he turned away from her. "O Diarmuid, your love is gone from me." "O, it is gone indeed," said he. Then there was music made in the whole place, and the lamenting was stopped, because of the healing of the king's daughter. And as to Diarmuid, he would take no reward and he would not stop there, but he asked for a ship to bring him home to Ireland, to Finn and the Fianna, and when he came where they were, there was a joyful welcome before him.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Gregory 1904, Book VI, ch. III; not verbatim.

title.en: The Gilla Decair and the Horse That Broke the Fianna
title.zh: 劣僕與拖垮菲亞納的怪馬

region.en: Aine Cliach, Co. Limerick, Ireland
region.zh: 愛爾蘭利默里克郡艾妮·克利亞

period: Fenian cycle, medieval Irish tradition; Lady Augusta Gregory retelling (1904)

source.work: Lady Augusta Gregory, Gods and Fighting Men (1904), Book VI, ch. IV, eBook #14465

summary.en: A huge gloomy Fomorian calls himself the Gilla Decair, the Hard Servant, comes to Finn for wages, and turns his starveling horse loose among the Fianna's horses to tear and kill. Conan, forced into horse-boy's service, mounts it with twelve men behind him and it will not stir; the Fomor taunts them and walks away slow — then tucks up his cloak and is gone like a swallow, leaving thirteen of the Fianna clinging to the horse that streams after him, the opening of the pursuit that ends in Tir fo Thuinn.
summary.zh: 一名陰鬱巨人自稱「劣僕」，前來芬恩處求佣，卻將其瘦骨嶙峋的怪馬放至菲亞納馬群中撕咬殘殺。科南被迫充當馬伕，攜十二人騎上怪馬，馬卻紋絲不動。弗莫爾譏嘲後慢步離開——隨即撩起斗篷，疾如飛燕而去，菲亞納十三人被怪馬拖拽緊追其後——一場終至「浪下之國」的大追逐就此開啟。

sensitivity.note: The Gilla Decair cycle (Acallam-material) is the source of the Land-under-Wave pursuit; Manannan is elsewhere identified with this trickster-figure in the corpus (Gregory's own remark). The wages-servant ruse is a fixed folktale opening (Aarne-Thompson 'work-avoidance servant'). Pin at Aine Cliach where the hunt stood.

passages.text: The Fianna went hunting one time in the two proud provinces of Munster, through the borders of Magh Breogain, over the level banks of the blue Siuir and over the green plain of Feman. Finn asked which of the men that were with him would go and keep watch on the side of the hill where they were, and Finnbane, son of Bresel, went; and he saw coming from the east a very big man, ugly and gloomy and deformed, a dark-coloured shield on his back, a wide sword on his crooked left thigh, his limbs as black as a quenched coal, leading a sulky bony horse by a rough iron halter, and striking blows on it with an iron cudgel to try and knock some going out of him.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Gregory 1904, Book VI, ch. IV; not verbatim.

passages.text: He saluted Finn, making signs of humility: "I am a man of the Fomor, travelling in search of wages to the kings of the earth, and I heard that Finn never refused wages to any man. There is nothing in the world is worse to me than a boy to be with me, for it is a hundred men's share of food that serves me for one day. The name I have is the Gilla Decair, the Hard Servant." And he turned his horse loose among the horses of the Fianna, and it began to tear and to kick and to bite at them, killing and maiming.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Gregory 1904, Book VI, ch. IV; not verbatim.

passages.text: "I will never bring him out of that; for I have no serving-boy to do it for me, and it is not work for me to be leading my horse by the hand." Conan rose up then and took the halter and put it on the horse: "You would never have done a horse-boy's service, Conan, to any one of the Fianna," said Finn; "if you will do what I advise, you will get up on the horse now and search out with him all the hills and hollows of Ireland, till his heart is broken in his body." Conan made a leap on to the horse and thirteen men of the Fianna went up behind him, but with all that the horse would not stir, and the big man went from them slow and weak, dragging himself along till he had put a little hill between himself and the Fianna; and as soon as he was on the other side of it, he tucked up his cloak to his waist, and away with him as if with the quickness of a swallow or a deer.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Gregory 1904, Book VI, ch. IV; not verbatim.

title.en: Kama Burned by the Third Eye
title.zh: 伽摩為第三眼所焚

region.en: Kailasa (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 吉羅娑（象徵性定位）

period: Puranic cycle, retold in Donald A. Mackenzie, Indian Myth and Legend (1913), ch. VIII (public domain)

source.work: Indian Myth and Legend, by Donald A. Mackenzie (1913), ch. VIII

summary.en: The gods needed Shiva married to Parvati to get a general against the demons - and the ascetic god would not look at her. They sent Kama, god of love, with his flower bow; one arrow found Shiva in meditation, and the god's third eye opened and burned the archer to ash. Desire died for the mission; Rati the wife's mourning earned his restoration as 'the bodiless one', Ananga - love that lives without a body.
summary.zh: 諸神需要濕婆娶波羅婆蒂以得對抗群魔的統帥——而苦行的神不肯看她。他們派出愛神伽摩執花弓；一箭射中禪定中的濕婆，神之第三眼開而將射手焚為灰燼。欲望為使命而死；其妻臘底的哀哭換來他以『無身者』（Ananga）復原——無形而活的愛。

sensitivity.note: Living tradition (Holi's Kamadeva burning); source is a public-domain scholarly retelling; recorded as such. Classified 'myth'.

passages.text: The plot was the gods' generalship: a demon-army needed a son of Shiva, and the only obstacle was Shiva's vow of not-looking - so they sent the one arrow that could make him look. The flower-bow found its mark; the meditation broke for a heartbeat - and the third eye, the god's alarm system, incinerated the intruder where he stood. Rati's grief argued the case in heaven: love without a body is still love - and the god was restored as Ananga, the bodiless; desire survives its own executions, which is the myth's whole point.
passages.note: Retold from Mackenzie, Indian Myth and Legend (1913), ch. VIII; not verbatim.

canonical_translation: Retold in English by Donald A. Mackenzie, 1913 (public domain)

title.en: Sita Under the Ashoka Tree
title.zh: 無憂樹下的悉多

region.en: Ashoka grove, Lanka (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 楞伽無憂林苑（象徵性定位）

period: Ramayana of Valmiki, oldest strata c. 2nd c. BCE-2nd c. CE (Griffith translation, 1870-74)

source.work: The Ramayan of Valmiki, trans. R. T. H. Griffith (1870-74), Sundara Kanda, the Ashoka grove

summary.en: In the grove of the Ashoka trees, Sita sat captive under guard - and Ravana came to court her with an empire: be my queen, he said, and the city is yours. She set a blade of grass between them and answered him in a dead level voice: my husband is coming, and your city will not survive the invitation. Her endurance in that grove is the epic's image of constancy.
summary.zh: 在無憂樹之苑中，悉多於看守下靜坐——羅波那前來以帝國求婚：作我的王后，他說，此城即屬於你。她於二人之間放下一根草葉，以平直如死的聲音回答：我的丈夫正在前來，而你的城市經不起這個邀請。她在苑中的堅忍是史詩恆常之德的意象。

sensitivity.note: Living tradition; classified 'myth'.

passages.text: The grove was a gilded prison: fruit and fountains, demoness guards in shifts, and a woman with one sentence on repeat - Rama is coming. Ravana's proposal came in state: jewels, thrones, a co-kingdom - and her answer was the grass-blade held between them, the smallest wall ever drawn, and her voice refusing without raising. The threat she named was the epic's own forecast: your city will not outlive my husband's arrival - and the monkey in the tree above heard it as a battle-plan confirmed.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ramayana, Sundara Kanda (Griffith 1870-74); not verbatim.

canonical_translation: R. T. H. Griffith, 1870-74 (public domain)

title.en: The Niyoga: Vyasa Fathers the Age's Two Armies
title.zh: 尼由伽：毗耶娑為時代兩軍之父

region.en: Hastinapura inner palace (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 象城內宮（象徵性定位）

period: Mahabharata, Adi Parva, composition layers c. 400 BCE-400 CE (Ganguli translation, 1883-96)

source.work: The Mahabharata of Krishna-Dwaipayana Vyasa, trans. K. M. Ganguli (1883-96), Adi Parva, the births of Dhritarashtra and Pandu

summary.en: With both princes dead and the dynasty heirless, the widows were given to Vyasa under the law of niyoga. Ambika closed her eyes and bore the blind Dhritarashtra; Ambalika turned pale and bore the pale Pandu; the maid, unafraid, bore the wise Vidura. Three looks, three natures, two armies - the epic's genealogy is a psychology experiment conducted in one afternoon.
summary.zh: 二王俱亡而王朝無嗣之際，依尼由伽之法，寡婦被交予毗耶娑。安比迦閉目而生盲眼持國；安波利迦面色轉白而生蒼白般度；侍女無懼而生睿智維杜羅。三種神色、三種天性、兩支大軍——史詩的譜系是一場於一個下午完成的心理實驗。

sensitivity.note: Living tradition; classified 'myth'.

passages.text: The succession was carried by visitation: the old seer came when called, and each widow's single meeting wrote the next generation's body and temperament. The closed eyes made the blind king; the pale face made the pale one; the maid's unflinching gaze made the wisest man of the age - looks as fate, recorded in the family's ledger. The two armies of Kurukshetra are, by this genealogy, one seer's afternoon: the epic's own way of saying that the war's sides were always one family's nerves.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Mahabharata, Adi Parva (Ganguli 1883-96); not verbatim.

canonical_translation: K. M. Ganguli, 1883-96 (public domain)

title.en: Gandhari's Hundred Sons in the Jar
title.zh: 甘陀利罐中的百子

region.en: Hastinapura (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 象城（象徵性定位）

period: Mahabharata, Adi Parva, composition layers c. 400 BCE-400 CE (Ganguli translation, 1883-96)

source.work: The Mahabharata of Krishna-Dwaipayana Vyasa, trans. K. M. Ganguli (1883-96), Adi Parva, the birth of the Kauravas

summary.en: Gandhari, pregnant for two years with a hundred-son blessing gone wrong, struck her iron-hard womb in rage - and delivered a single ball of flesh. Vyasa divided it into a hundred and one jars of ghee; from the first jar came Duryodhana, howling like a jackal at birth; the last, on schedule, was the girl Duhsala. The Kaurava legion was born from one fruit split into vessels.
summary.zh: 甘陀利懷著一項出錯的百子之福達兩年，怒擊其鐵般堅硬的子宮——產下一枚血肉之球。毗耶娑將其分入一百零一罐酥油；自第一罐生出的難敵出生時如豺狼般嚎叫；最後一罐依時而生者為女兒杜莎拉。俱盧軍團誕生於一枚被分割入器的果實。

sensitivity.note: Living tradition; classified 'myth'.

passages.text: The pregnancy that outlasted the year was a curse in slow motion: one ball of flesh where a hundred sons had been promised - the queen's blow made it worse, and Vyasa was sent for. The ball was divided with the care of a butcher-scholar: a hundred and one jars, ghee-cooled, each a cradle - the war's personnel grown in pantry vessels. The first-born's omen - howling like a jackal on the night of his birth - was reported to the king, and the king heard it as weather; the epic records the omen as the age's opening invoice.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Mahabharata, Adi Parva (Ganguli 1883-96); not verbatim.

canonical_translation: K. M. Ganguli, 1883-96 (public domain)

title.en: Jayadratha's Head at Sunset
title.zh: 日落時分的闍耶陀羅陀之首

region.en: Kurukshetra (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 俱盧之野（象徵性定位）

period: Mahabharata, Drona Parva, composition layers c. 400 BCE-400 CE (Ganguli translation, 1883-96)

source.work: The Mahabharata of Krishna-Dwaipayana Vyasa, trans. K. M. Ganguli (1883-96), Drona Parva, Jayadratha-vadha

summary.en: Jayadratha had held the gate against the Pandava rescuers while Abhimanyu died - Arjuna's vow: your head will leave your shoulders before tomorrow's sunset or I will burn myself. On the fourteenth day the sun went down and the vow had failed - until Krishna obscured the light: the fool raised his head in triumph at false sunset, the arrows flew, and the head was carried by the arrow to fall in his father's lap - a curse fulfilled twice.
summary.zh: 闍耶陀羅陀曾在阿毗曼紐死時守住營門抵抗般度救援軍——阿周那立誓：明日日落之前你的頭顱必離其肩，否則我自焚。第十四日，太陽落下而誓言已敗——直到克里希那遮蔽天光：那愚者在假日落時仰首慶賀，箭矢飛出，頭顱被箭攜至其父之膝落下——一個詛咒應驗兩次。

sensitivity.note: Living tradition; classified 'myth'.

passages.text: The vow was the war's most specific: one head, one sunset, one self-immolation - the kind of contract the field took as ordinary. The sunset arrived without the head; the archer drew for the pyre - and the light broke: a cloud made by a god gave the day a second evening. The false dusk brought the head up, the true arrows brought it down, and the father's curse (that it fall in his lap) closed like a latch - the epic's most surgical revenge, on schedule.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Mahabharata, Drona Parva (Ganguli 1883-96); not verbatim.

canonical_translation: K. M. Ganguli, 1883-96 (public domain)

title.en: The Epic's Frame: Vyasa, Vaishampayana and the Snake Sacrifice
title.zh: 史詩框架：毗耶娑、婆藪仙般耶那與蛇祭

region.en: Takshashila, sacrificial hall (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 怛叉始羅，祭祀之堂（象徵性定位）

period: Mahabharata, Adi Parva (Parvasangraha), composition layers c. 400 BCE-400 CE (Ganguli translation, 1883-96)

source.work: The Mahabharata of Krishna-Dwaipayana Vyasa, trans. K. M. Ganguli (1883-96), Adi Parva, the recitation frame

summary.en: The epic tells us how it was made: Vyasa composed it; his pupil Vaishampayana recited it first at Janamejaya's snake-sacrifice, to the grandson of the story's own heroes; sages collected it in the Naimisha forest from Ugrashravas the wandering bard. The Mahabharata builds its own reception history into its first book - a text about its own telling.
summary.zh: 史詩自述其成書：毗耶娑構作之；其弟子婆藪仙般耶那首於闍那彌覺耶的蛇祭上誦之，聽眾正是故事主角的曾孫；仙人們於尼彌沙林自雲遊詠者鄔伽什羅婆娑集之。《摩訶婆羅多》將自身的接受史寫入首卷——一部講述自身如何被講述的文本。

sensitivity.note: Living tradition (epic recitation); classified 'myth'.

passages.text: The chain of telling is the epic's first content: Vyasa composed; the pupil recited at the sacrifice; the bard carried it to the forest assembly - authorship as relay. The audience is inside the story: the king listening at the snake-sacrifice is the great-grandson of the heroes whose deaths the poem is already mourning. The frame makes the text its own archive: every recitation the reader imagines is one more link in the chain the first book lists - reception history as a genre.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Mahabharata, Adi Parva (Ganguli 1883-96); not verbatim.

canonical_translation: K. M. Ganguli, 1883-96 (public domain)

title.en: Shiva Drinks the World's Poison
title.zh: 濕婆飲下世界之毒

region.en: Cosmic ocean, churning site (symbolic pin at Kailasa)
region.zh: 宇宙之海，攪海之地（象徵性定位於吉羅娑）

period: Puranic cycle (Vishnu Purana, Book I, ch. 9; Bhagavata 8.7 tradition), c. 300-800 CE (Wilson translation, 1840)

source.work: The Vishnu Purana, trans. H. H. Wilson (1840), Book I, the churning and the poison (with Bhagavata tradition)

summary.en: In the Purana's churning, the first thing the ocean gave up was poison - halahala, black as midnight, hot enough to burn the three worlds. The gods fled to Shiva, who drank the world's poison down and held it in his throat; his neck turned blue, and the goddess pressed her hand there to stop it spreading. The blue-throated god is the cosmos' poison-sink: Nilakantha.
summary.zh: 往世書的攪海中，海洋吐出的第一物即是毒——黑如午夜、熱可焚三界的哈拉哈拉。諸神逃至濕婆，他將世界之毒一飲而盡，將其鎖於喉中；其頸轉為青色，女神以手按其喉以阻其擴散。青頸之神是宇宙的毒之受納者：尼羅迦陀。

sensitivity.note: Living tradition (Shivaratri, Nilakantha imagery); classified 'myth'. Purana locus for the poison episode varies by recension - noted.

passages.text: The first yield of the churning was not treasure but waste: a poison that darkened the sky and began to eat the worlds - the ocean's wages paid before its gifts. Shiva drank it as a drain takes a flood: the god held the whole dose in his throat, and the throat's blue is the receipt - Nilakantha, the blue-necked one, marked forever by service. The goddess's hand at his throat is the myth's tenderness: the poison is contained by a grip - the world's survival maintained by a wife's palm on her husband's neck.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Vishnu Purana, Book I (Wilson 1840); not verbatim.

canonical_translation: H. H. Wilson, 1840 (public domain)

title.en: Building the Fire-Altar: Agni's Body of Bricks
title.zh: 築火壇：磚砌的阿耆尼之身

region.en: Kuru-Panchala ritual ground (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 俱盧-般遮羅祭地（象徵性定位）

period: Shatapatha Brahmana 6-10, c. 8th-6th c. BCE (Eggeling translation, 1882-85)

source.archive: Internet Archive (Sacred Books of the East)
source.work: The Satapatha-Brahmana, trans. Julius Eggeling (SBE 41, 1885), the agnichayana chapters

summary.en: The Brahmana's grandest construction myth: the fire-altar is built as a person, in five layers of a thousand bricks, each brick named, each layer a world - earth, air, heaven and two between. The builder is rebuilding Agni's body (the god whose head was lost); when the five layers stand, the sacrificer climbs them to heaven's gate. Architecture as resurrection manual.
summary.zh: 梵書最宏大的營造神話：火壇以五層千磚築成一人之形，每一磚皆有名，每一層即一個世界——地、空、天與其間二者。築者是在重建阿耆尼之身（失去頭顱的神）；五層既成，祭者登之，直達天門。建築即復活手冊。

sensitivity.note: Brahmana ritual myth; classified 'myth'.

passages.text: The altar is a man made of masonry: five layers, a thousand bricks, each brick with a name and a verse - the sacrificed god rebuilt by contractors of ritual. The layers are the worlds in order: earth the base, air the middle, heaven the crown, with the transitional courses between - a skyline drawn as theology. The climax is structural: on the finished altar the sacrificer is lifted - the building's purpose is a doorway, and masonry is the road the dead man's body takes upward.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Shatapatha Brahmana, agnichayana chapters (Eggeling 1885); not verbatim.

canonical_translation: Julius Eggeling, SBE 41, 1885 (public domain)

title.en: The Pact of Rama and Sugriva
title.zh: 羅摩與須羯哩婆之盟

region.en: Rishyamuka hill (symbolic pin at Hampi)
region.zh: 黎沙牟迦山（象徵性定位於漢皮）

period: Ramayana of Valmiki, oldest strata c. 2nd c. BCE-2nd c. CE (Griffith translation, 1870-74)

source.work: The Ramayan of Valmiki, trans. R. T. H. Griffith (1870-74), Kishkindha Kanda, the alliance

summary.en: Two exiles made each other's wars their own: Rama would kill Vali for the throne; Sugriva would turn the monkey nations out for the search. The fire-pact was sworn at the hill - and the four directions were then dispatched as search parties, each named, each a catalogue of the world's monkey-tribes. The alliance is the epic's diplomatic charter: personal debt transmuted into a coalition.
summary.zh: 兩位流亡者將彼此的戰爭化為己任：羅摩為猴王之位誅婆黎；須羯哩婆則為搜索傾盡猴國之力。火前立盟於山巔——四方隨即被派作搜索隊，各有其名，各為一份世界猴族之清單。此盟是史詩的外交憲章：私人恩義化為聯軍。

sensitivity.note: Living tradition; classified 'myth'.

passages.text: The pact was struck like a treaty between states: one arrow for a throne, one army for a search - both parties investing their own blood in the other's cause. The fire was witness, and the dispatch orders that followed read like a census: north, east, west and south, each monkey-nation named and pointed at the horizon. The south-party found the quarry because its commander was the one monkey who could leap the sea - the alliance's return on investment measured in one flight to Lanka.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ramayana, Kishkindha Kanda (Griffith 1870-74); not verbatim.

canonical_translation: R. T. H. Griffith, 1870-74 (public domain)

title.en: Diarmuid Climbs the Rock and Dives the Enchanter's Well
title.zh: 迪爾穆德攀岩與躍入巫師之井

region.en: Grey cliff over the western sea, Corca Duibhne (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 科爾卡·迪夫尼西海外灰色絕壁（象徵定位）

period: Fenian cycle, medieval Irish tradition; Lady Augusta Gregory retelling (1904)

source.work: Lady Augusta Gregory, Gods and Fighting Men (1904), Book VI, ch. IV, eBook #14465

summary.en: Finn under bonds follows the Gilla Decair over sea, and thirteen of the Fianna hang from the mistletoe-cliff of a great grey rock. Fergus shames Diarmuid — reared by Manannan the Powerful and Angus Og — and he rises on Manannan's staves of power to the overhanging rock. There the Enchanter of the thicket fights him day after day at the enchanted well until both fall in; below lies a flowery plain, a royal city, and a house of healing where Diarmuid is made sound again.
summary.zh: 芬恩受誓追隨劣僕出海；菲亞納十三人懸於灰色巨岩之上。費爾古斯以「受教於大能瑪那南與安古斯·奧格」羞激迪爾穆德，他遂持瑪那南之力杖躍上懸岩。岩後密林中，巫師在魔井邊與他日復一日搏鬥，直至二人同墜井底；井底之下是繁花平原與王城，迪爾穆德在療傷之屋重獲健全。

sensitivity.note: The tree-horn-well sequence is the classic entry to the otherworld (the enchanted drink compels the duel — cf. the fixed well-and-keeper motif of immram literature). Manannan's staves of power are Diarmuid's inherited divine gifts. Symbolic pin.

passages.text: Finn and the Fianna rose up then, and they followed the Gilla Decair over every bald hill, and through every valley and every river, on to pleasant Slieve Luachra, into the borders of Corca Duibhne; and the big man, that was up on the horse then along with Conan and the rest, faced towards the deep sea, and Liagan Luath of Luachar took hold of the horse's tail with his two hands, and away with him over the sea, and Liagan along with him, holding on to his tail. "The Tuatha de Danaan left as a gift to the children of the Gael, that whoever might have to leave Ireland for a while had but to go to Beinn Edair, and however many would go along with him, they would find a ship that would hold them all." And Feradach, the Very Brave, son of the King of the Eastern World, struck three blows on his sling-stick with his carpenter's axe, and the whole of the bay and of the harbour was filled with ships and with fast boats.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Gregory 1904, Book VI, ch. IV; not verbatim.

passages.text: They went on over the restless hills of the great sea for three days and three nights, and saw a great rough grey cliff with a high round rock on its edge, having sides more slippery than an eel's back, and they found the track of the Hard Servant as far as to the foot of the rock. "It is no brave thing you are doing, Diarmuid, grandson of Duibhne, to hold back like this, for it was with Manannan the Powerful, son of Lir, you were reared and got your learning, in the Land of Promise and in the coasts of the harbours, and with Angus Og, the Dagda's son." Diarmuid's face reddened when he heard those words, and he took hold of Manannan's staves of power that were with him, and he rose on the staves and gave a leap, and got a standing-place for his two feet on the overhanging rock.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Gregory 1904, Book VI, ch. IV; not verbatim.

passages.text: He was not gone far when he saw a great tree with many twigs and branches, and a rock beside it, and a smooth-pointed drinking-horn on it, and a beautiful fresh well at its foot; and there was a great drouth on Diarmuid after the sea-journey, and he had a mind to drink a hornful of the water. But when he stooped to it he heard a great noise coming towards him, and he knew then there was enchantment in the water. "I will drink my fill of it for all that." And a Man of Enchantments came towards him armed: "It is no right thing to be walking through my thickets and to be drinking up my share of water." They fought till the end of the day, and the Enchanter made a leap into the bottom of the well; and in the evening, when the Enchanter was making his leap into the well again, Diarmuid threw his arms about his neck, thinking to stop him, but it is what happened, he fell in himself.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Gregory 1904, Book VI, ch. IV; not verbatim.

passages.text: Diarmuid went following after the Enchanter, and found before him a beautiful wide flowery plain, and a comely royal city in the plain; and when they saw him following after the Enchanter, they shut the gates, and the whole army turned on Diarmuid. But that put no fear on him, and he went through them and over them like a hawk would go through little birds, killing all before him; and Diarmuid, all full of hurts and wounds after the hard fight, lay down on the plain. A very strong daring champion came then and kicked at him: "It is not to do you any hurt or harm I am come, but to say to you it is a bad sleeping-place for you to have, and it on your ill-wisher's lawn." Diarmuid followed him a long, long way, till they came to a high-topped city, and there was a good welcome before him for his own sake and the sake of his people, and he was put in a house of healing, and good herbs were put to his hurts till he was smooth and sound again. Three days and three nights Diarmuid stopped in that city, and the best feast he ever found was given to him all through; and the champion told him it was Land-Under-Wave, and that the man that had fought with him was its king.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Gregory 1904, Book VI, ch. IV; not verbatim.

title.en: Finn Routs the High King of Greece
title.zh: 芬恩擊潰希臘至高王

region.en: Land of Sorcha, western ocean (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 索爾卡之國，西海（象徵定位）

period: Fenian cycle, medieval Irish tradition; Lady Augusta Gregory retelling (1904)

source.work: Lady Augusta Gregory, Gods and Fighting Men (1904), Book VI, ch. IV, eBook #14465

summary.en: Following Diarmuid's trail of meat-leavings, Finn is hosted by the King of Sorcha — himself once Finn's hired man — when the High King of Greece comes to put the whole world under him. Finn takes the protection of the country on himself, and with Osgar and Oisin and Goll makes such slaughter of the Greeks' champions that the King of Greece carries home what is left of his people, swearing to banish the Sons of the Gael to the ends of the earth.
summary.zh: 循迪爾穆德留下的肉屑而行，芬恩受「曾受雇於芬恩」的索爾卡王款待；此時希臘至高王正欲將全世界納入其轄下。芬恩立誓護國，與奧斯加、歐辛、戈爾將希臘勇士屠戮殆盡，希臘王攜殘部歸國，發誓要將蓋爾之子放逐至地極。

sensitivity.note: Finn's sea-expedition to protect a king who had served him years before turns employer-retainer law (wages never refused) into transmarine heroism; the Greek high-king parallels Daire Donn of the White Strand. Symbolic pin.

passages.text: Now, as to Finn and his people, when they thought Diarmuid was too long away from them, they made ladders of the cords of the ship and put them against the rock, looking for him, and after a while they found the leavings of the meat he had eaten, for Diarmuid never ate meat without leaving some after him. Finn looked then on every side, and he saw a rider coming towards him over the plain on a dark-coloured beautiful horse, having a bridle of red gold; and they went on till they came to a wide, large dwelling-place full of arms, and a great troop of armed men on the green before the fort. At the end of that time Finn asked what country was he in, and the man that brought him there told him it was the land of Sorcha, and that he himself was its king — "And I was with yourself one time, Finn, son of Cumhal, taking your wages through the length of a year in Ireland."
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Gregory 1904, Book VI, ch. IV; not verbatim.

passages.text: Then Finn and the King of Sorcha called a great gathering of the people, and while it was going on they saw a woman-messenger coming through the crowd: "The whole of the bay and the harbour is full of ships and of boats, and there are armies all through the country robbing all before them." "I know well, it is the High King of Greece is in it, for he has a mind to put the entire world under him, and to get hold of this country like every other." The King of Sorcha looked at Finn, and Finn understood it was help from him he was asking, and it is what he said: "I take the protection of this country on myself so long as I am in it." He and his people rose up, and the King of Sorcha along with them, and when they came up with the strange army they made great slaughter of its champions, and those they did not kill made no better stand than a flock of frightened birds, And at the last the King of Greece brought all his people back home.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Gregory 1904, Book VI, ch. IV; not verbatim.

passages.text: And then Finn and the King of Sorcha called another great gathering, and while it was going on, they saw coming towards them a great troop of champions, bearing flags of many-coloured silk, and grey swords at their sides and high spears reared up over their heads, and in the front of them was Diarmuid, grandson of Duibhne. And it would take too long to tell how Finn made the Hard Servant bring home his fifteen men that he had brought away; and when he had brought them back to Ireland, the whole of the Fianna were watching to see him ride away again, himself and his long-legged horse. But while they were watching him, he vanished from them, and all they could see was a mist, and it stretching out towards the sea. And that is the story of the Hard Servant, and of Diarmuid's adventures on the island Under-Wave.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Gregory 1904, Book VI, ch. IV; not verbatim.

title.en: Miodac's Riddles and the House of the Quicken Trees
title.zh: 米奧達克之謎與花楸樹之屋

region.en: Island of the Floods (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 洪流群島（象徵定位）

period: Fenian cycle, medieval Irish tradition; Lady Augusta Gregory retelling (1904)

source.work: Lady Augusta Gregory, Gods and Fighting Men (1904), Book VI, ch. V, eBook #14465

summary.en: Miodac, son of the King of Lochlann, passes himself off as a poet and tests Finn with verses: an army riding to victory with no horses but plants and branches — bees, says Finn; a woman swifter than any horse — the River Boinn, whose going never stops. Having found Finn out as a reader, he bids the Fianna into his House of the Quicken Trees: colour-fading walls, one door shut, a stenching fire, an enchantment that holds them to the floor — until Diarmuid makes an end of Miodac and the Three Kings of the Island of the Floods and takes the spell off the floor with their blood.
summary.zh: 洛赫蘭王之子米奧達克假扮詩人，以謎語試探芬恩：一支騎向勝利的軍隊卻無馬騎，只有草木枝葉——芬恩答曰蜂群；一位賽過駿馬的女子——芬恩答曰永不停止奔流的博因河。試出芬恩善解後，他將菲亞納誘入花楸樹之屋：彩壁褪色、七門僅存一閉門、香火轉惡臭、咒術使人黏地——直到迪爾穆德誅米奧達克與洪流群島三王，以其血破除地板咒術。

sensitivity.note: The riddle-contest (focusing Finn's wisdom) is the standard prelude to the enchanted-hostel trap; 'Quicken' = rowan, whose blood-breaking of enchantment echoes the rowan's protective uses in Gaelic belief. Symbolic pin.

passages.text: It was by treachery Miodac brought them in, giving himself out to be a poet, and making poems for Finn to make out the meaning of. A verse he made about a great army that he saw riding over the plains to victory, and robbing all before it, and the riders of it having no horses but plants and branches. "I understand that, it was an army of bees you saw, that was gathering riches from the flowers as it went." And another verse Miodac made was about a woman in Ireland that was swifter than the swiftest horse. "I know that; that woman is the River Boinn; and if she goes slow itself, she is swifter in the end than the swiftest horse, for her going never stops." And other verses he made about Angus' house at Brugh na Boinn, but Finn made them all out.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Gregory 1904, Book VI, ch. V; not verbatim.

passages.text: And after that he said he had a feast ready for them, and he bade them go into his House of the Quicken Trees till he would bring it; and it was a beautiful house, having walls of every colour, and foreign coverings of every colour on the floor, and a fire that gave out a very pleasant smoke.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Gregory 1904, Book VI, ch. V; not verbatim.

passages.text: But after a while Finn said: "It is a wonder such a beautiful house to be here." "There is a greater wonder than that; that fire that was so pleasant when we came in is giving out now the worst stench in the world." "There is a greater wonder than that; the walls that were of all colours are now but rough boards joined together." "There is a greater wonder than that; where there were seven high doors to the house there is now but one little door, and it shut." "Indeed, there is a more wonderful thing than that, for we sat down on beautiful coverings, and now there is nothing between us and the bare ground, and it as cold as the snow of one night." And he tried to rise up, but he could not stir, or any of the rest of them, for there was enchantment that kept them where they were; and it was the treachery of Miodac, and the spells of the Three Kings of the Island of the Floods, that had brought them into that danger.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Gregory 1904, Book VI, ch. V; not verbatim.

passages.text: And at the last it was Diarmuid that made an end of Miodac that was so treacherous, and of the Three Kings of the Island of the Floods, and took the enchantment off the floor of the House of the Rowan Trees with their blood.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Gregory 1904, Book VI, ch. V; not verbatim.

title.en: Grania Answers Finn at the Wedding of Tara
title.zh: 格拉尼亞在塔拉婚宴上妙答芬恩

region.en: Teamhair (Hill of Tara), Co. Meath, Ireland
region.zh: 愛爾蘭米斯郡塔拉王丘

period: Fenian cycle, medieval Irish tradition; Lady Augusta Gregory retelling (1904)

source.work: Lady Augusta Gregory, Gods and Fighting Men (1904), Book VII, ch. I, eBook #14465

summary.en: Betrothed to grey-haired Finn at Tara, Grania is put to the riddles of a man quick with questions and better with answers: whiter than snow — the truth; hotter than fire — a hospitable man's face when a stranger comes and the house is empty; sharper than a sword — the wit of a woman between two men; quicker than the wind — a woman's mind. She has no liking for Finn, and when the cap falls from Diarmuid's love-spot at the dogs' feast, her blood rises against the bridegroom forever.
summary.zh: 塔拉婚約既成，善問的芬恩以謎語相試，而格拉尼亞的回答更勝一籌：比雪更白——真理；比火更熱——客至而家空時好客之人的面容；比劍更利——兩男之間的女子之智；比風更疾——女子之心。她本無意於芬恩；群犬宴上迪爾穆德的帽子滑落、露出愛斑之際，她的心便永遠背離了新郎。

sensitivity.note: Grania's riddle-duel is a wisdom-contest embedded in the betrothal scene and quoted through the whole pursuit; the falling cap revealing the love-spot is the love-charm mechanism of the Diarmuid cycle. Tara pin, as the wedding was held at the seat of the High King.

passages.text: Finn gathered together the seven battalions of the Fianna to Teamhair, and when Grania saw grey-haired Finn she said: "It is a great wonder it was not for Oisin Finn asked me, for he would be more fitting for me than a man that is older than my father." But they talked together for a while, and Finn was putting questions to Grania, for she had the name of being very quick with answers. "What is whiter than snow?" "The truth." "What is the best colour?" "The colour of childhood." "What is hotter than fire?" "The face of a hospitable man when he sees a stranger coming in, and the house empty." "What has a taste more bitter than poison?" "The reproach of an enemy." "What is best for a champion?" "His doings to be high, and his pride to be low." "What is the best of jewels?" "A knife." "What is sharper than a sword?" "The wit of a woman between two men." "What is quicker than the wind?" "A woman's mind," said Grania. And indeed she was telling no lie when she said that.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Gregory 1904, Book VII, ch. I; not verbatim.

passages.text: At the wedding-feast in the king's feasting-house, a Druid of Finn's people named the champions for her at her asking — Goll the ready fighter, Osgar son of Oisin, thin-legged Caoilte, proud Lugaidh's Son — and then: "Who is that sweet-worded man with the dark hair, and cheeks like the rowan berry, on the left side of Oisin, son of Finn?" "That is Diarmuid, grandson of Duibhne, that is the best lover of women in the whole world." And after the feast had gone on a while, their own feast was made for the dogs outside; and Diarmuid was used to keep his cap always over the love-spot the woman had left on his forehead, and it chanced, while he was driving the dogs apart, the cap fell from him, and Grania was looking at him as it fell, and great love for him came on her there and then.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Gregory 1904, Book VII, ch. I; not verbatim.

passages.text: She filled the great golden cup with wine that had enchantment in it, and all that drank of it fell into a heavy sleep — Finn and the king and the whole company, but only Oisin and Osgar and Caoilte and Diarmuid and Diorraing; and when they were all in their sleep, Grania rose up softly, and turned her face to Diarmuid: "Will you take my love, Diarmuid, son of Duibhne, and will you bring me away out of this house to-night?"
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Gregory 1904, Book VII, ch. I; not verbatim.

title.en: Diarmuid's Trick Feats Kill the Green Champions
title.zh: 迪爾穆德的技戲誅殺綠衣勇士

region.en: Marsh of Finnliath, Co. Mayo, Ireland (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 愛爾蘭梅奧郡芬利阿沼澤（象徵定位）

period: Fenian cycle, medieval Irish tradition; Lady Augusta Gregory retelling (1904)

source.work: Lady Augusta Gregory, Gods and Fighting Men (1904), Book VII, ch. III, eBook #14465

summary.en: Sent by Finn to hunt the fugitive, the Green Champions of Muir-na-locht — two thousand men with three hounds fire cannot burn nor water drown — meet a fighting man who claims to have seen Diarmuid yesterday. Diarmuid rolls a tun of wine down the hill with men crushed beneath it, lights on the point of Manannan's upturned spear like a bird, and walks thrice along the edge of Angus's sword; each feat is copied to death, fifty in the wine alone.
summary.zh: 芬恩遣「穆爾納赫特綠衣勇士」——兩千戰士與三隻火不能焚、水不能溺的魔犬——追捕逃亡者；他們遇上一名自稱昨日見過迪爾穆德的戰士。迪爾穆德滾酒桶下山、壓斃模仿者，如飛鳥般立於瑪那南倒插長矛之尖，並在安古斯之劍刃上三度行走——每一次技戲皆被依樣模仿而死，僅酒桶一項已斃五十人。

sensitivity.note: The lethal-feat mimicry (hostiles die copying the hero's tricks) is a fixed chase-tale device of the Diarmuid pursuit; the weapons named — Crann Buidhe of Manannan, Mor-alltach of Angus, Gae Buidhe/Gae Dearg — are Diarmuid's charter arms from his god-fosterers. Symbolic pin.

passages.text: Diarmuid went up on a hill that was near, and saw a great fleet of ships coming from the west, and when they were come to land, nine times nine of the chief men came on shore. "Three kings we are of the Green Champions of Muir-na-locht, and Finn, son of Cumhal, sent looking for us by cause of a thief of the woods, and an enemy of his own that has gone hiding from him. We are twenty hundred good fighting men, and every one of us is a match for a hundred, and we have three deadly hounds with us; fire will not burn them, and water will not drown them, and arms will not redden on them." "I saw him yesterday," said Diarmuid, "and I myself am but a fighting man. And by my word, you will know Diarmuid's hand when you will meet it."
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Gregory 1904, Book VII, ch. III; not verbatim.

passages.text: "Is there wine in your ships? If you have a mind to bring out a tun of wine, I will do a trick for you." Diarmuid took the tun between his two hands and drank a drink out of it, and brought it to the top of the hill, and went up himself on the tun, and let it go down the steep of the hill till it was at the bottom; and he did that trick three times before the strangers. But they said he was a man had never seen a good trick when he called that a trick; and with that a man of them went up on the tun, but Diarmuid gave a stroke of his foot at it and the young man fell from it before it began to move, and it rolled over him and crushed him, that he died. Another man went on it, and another after him again, till fifty of them were killed trying to do Diarmuid's trick.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Gregory 1904, Book VII, ch. III; not verbatim.

passages.text: And the next day he put off his arms, all but the shirt next his skin, and struck the Crann Buidhe, the spear of Manannan, into the earth with the point upwards, and rose with a leap and lit on the point of the spear as light as a bird, and came down off it again without a wound on him — and a young man of the Green Champions came down heavily on the point, and it went through his heart. And the third day he put the sword of Angus Og, the Mor-alltach, between two forked poles on its edge, and walked on the sword three times from the hilt to the point, and came down and asked was there a man of them could do that feat; and a man rose up to walk on the sword, but came down heavily on it the way he was cut in two halves.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Gregory 1904, Book VII, ch. III; not verbatim.

title.en: Three Kings Die in Diarmuid's Bonds
title.zh: 三王死於迪爾穆德之縛

region.en: Slieve Luachra, Co. Kerry, Ireland
region.zh: 愛爾蘭克里郡盧赫拉山

period: Fenian cycle, medieval Irish tradition; Lady Augusta Gregory retelling (1904)

source.work: Lady Augusta Gregory, Gods and Fighting Men (1904), Book VII, ch. III, eBook #14465

summary.en: After the Green Champions fall, Diarmuid binds their three kings and leaves them alive, knowing only four men — Oisin, Osgar, Lugaidh's Son and Conan — can loosen bonds he tied. Muadhan's belt-whelp leaps into the first hound's throat; the Red Spear brings out the second's bowels; the third Diarmuid dashes its brains on the flagstone of Dubhan, then casts down the troop with the Gae Dearg. Finn's woman-messenger of the Black Mountain reports it all, and the three kings die under the hardness of the bonds.
summary.zh: 綠衣勇士潰滅後，迪爾穆德生擒並縛其三王——他知道僅有奧辛、奧斯加、盧蓋德之子、科南四人能解他所縛之縛。穆阿丹腰帶中的幼犬躍入第一隻魔犬咽喉；紅矛穿出第二隻內臟；第三隻被他在杜班石上撞破頭顱，繼而紅矛連誅三將。芬恩的「黑山信使」回報一切，三王竟死於堅不可解的束縛之中。

sensitivity.note: The unloosenable bonds (only four named looser-men) are a legalistic chain-of-bonds device characteristic of the cycle's geis logic; Muadhan's belt-whelp parallels Bran's whelp-rearing. The messenger-woman (fast as a weasel) repeats the cycle's shape-shifting courier pattern.

passages.text: Diarmuid drew his sword the Mor-alltach out of its sheath, and he made a fierce blow at the head nearest him that put it in two halves. Then he made an attack on the whole host of the Green Champions, and began to destroy them, cutting through the beautiful shining armour of the men of Muir-na-locht till there was hardly a man that could go back to give news of the fight, but only the three kings and a few of their people. He put his battle clothes on him, that no weapon could go through, and took the sword of Angus, that left no leavings after it, at his left side, and his two thick-handled spears, the Gae Buidhe and the Gae Dearg, the Yellow and the Red, that gave wounds there was no healing for; and he bound the three kings fast and firm: "There is no man of the heroes of Ireland can loosen those bonds but four only, Oisin, son of Finn, and Osgar, son of Oisin, and Lugaidh's Son of the Strong Hand, and Conan, son of Morna; and I know well none of those four will do it."
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Gregory 1904, Book VII, ch. III; not verbatim.

passages.text: They brought their three hounds out of the ship and laid them on Diarmuid's track, and when he saw them coming like that he was filled with great hatred of them. Then Muadhan turned back, and took a whelp out of his belt, and put it on the flat of his hand; and when the whelp saw the hound rushing towards him, and its jaws open, he rose up and made a leap from Muadhan's hand into the throat of the hound, and came out of its side, bringing the heart with it, and left the hound dead after him. Another hound was loosened after them, and Diarmuid said: "I often heard there is nothing can stand against weapons of Druid wounding," and he made a cast at the hound, and the spear went through its body and brought out its bowels.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Gregory 1904, Book VII, ch. III; not verbatim.

passages.text: The third hound overtook them at Lic Dhubhain, the flag-stone of Dubhan, on Slieve Luachra; Diarmuid took him by the two hind legs, and struck a blow of his carcase against the side of the rock till he had let out his brains through the openings of his head and of his ears. Then he made a good cast at the young man of the green cloak that was at the head of the troop, and killed him, and the second man, and the third man in the same way. And when Finn heard of the Kings of the Green Champions that were bound by Diarmuid, neither Oisin nor Osgar nor Conan nor Lugaidh's Son would loosen them; and they were not long talking about it till the three kings died under the hardness of the bonds that were on them. Then Finn made three wide-sodded graves for them, and a flag-stone was put over them, and another stone raised over that again, and their names were written in branching Ogham.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Gregory 1904, Book VII, ch. III; not verbatim.

title.en: The Rowan of Dubhros and the Hurling-Match of the Gods
title.zh: 杜布羅斯的花楸與神族擲球賽

region.en: Wood of Dubhros, Ui Fiachrach, Co. Mayo, Ireland
region.zh: 愛爾蘭梅奧郡杜布羅斯林地

period: Fenian cycle, medieval Irish tradition; Lady Augusta Gregory retelling (1904)

source.work: Lady Augusta Gregory, Gods and Fighting Men (1904), Book VII, ch. IV, eBook #14465

summary.en: Two daughters of Manannan quarrel over whose man is the better hurler, and the match between the Men of Dea and the Fianna runs three days and nights without a goal. Passing homeward through Ui Fiachrach, the gods drop a rowan berry of the Land of the Ever-Living Living Ones, and a tree springs up whose berries banish sickness, make the hundred-year-old young again, and turn any girl into a flower of beauty — a tree the Tuatha de Danaan must guard with the Surly One of Lochlann, a giant with one eye and a prophecy that he will not die till three strokes of his own iron club fall on himself.
summary.zh: 瑪那南的兩位女兒為誰的情人更善擲球而爭執，神族與菲亞納之賽遂歷時三日三夜不分勝負。神族歸途經過伊·菲赫拉赫時失落一顆「永生者之國」的花楸果，樹從果中生——食其果者百病不侵，百歲老人可返少年，少女可成絕色。神族不得不以獨眼巨人格瓦恩看守此樹——預言曰：唯有親受自己鐵棒三擊者方能殺他。

sensitivity.note: The rejuvenating rowan is the Fenian apple-of-immortality (Berries of the Land of Promise) — compare Goibniu's ale and Idunn's apples cross-traditionally; the hurling-match of gods and men is a distinctive Irish divine-game motif. Coordinates at the traditional Dubhros (Doo Lough) country.

passages.text: There rose a dispute one time between two women of the Tuatha de Danaan, Aine and Aoife, daughters of Manannan, son of Lir, for Aoife had given her love to Lugaidh's Son, and Aine had given her love to a man of her own race, and each of them said her own man was a better hurler than the other. It came from that dispute that there was a great hurling match settled between the Men of Dea and the Fianna of Ireland, on a beautiful plain near Loch Lein. The highest men and the most daring of the Tuatha de Danaan were there — the three Garbhs of Slieve Mis, and the three Mases of Slieve Luachra, and the three yellow-haired Murchadhs, and Bodb Dearg, son of the Dagda, and Manannan, son of Lir; and they themselves and the Fianna were playing the match through the length of three days and three nights, and neither of them winning a goal.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Gregory 1904, Book VII, ch. IV; not verbatim.

passages.text: Now the provision the Men of Dea had brought with them from the Land of Promise was crimson nuts, and apples, and sweet-smelling rowan berries. And as they were passing through the district of Ui Fiachrach by the Muaidh, a berry of the rowan berries fell from them, and a tree grew up from it. And there was virtue in its berries, and no sickness or disease would ever come on any person that would eat them, and those that would eat them would feel the liveliness of wine and the satisfaction of mead in them, and any old person of a hundred years that would eat them would go back to be young again, and any young girl that would eat them would grow to be a flower of beauty.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Gregory 1904, Book VII, ch. IV; not verbatim.

passages.text: And it is what they agreed, to send a young man of them in search of a man of Lochlann that would guard the tree by day and sleep in it by night; and his name was the Searbhan Lochlannach, the Surly One of Lochlann. Very black and ugly he was, having crooked teeth, and one eye only in the middle of his forehead. And he had a thick collar of iron around his body, and it was in the prophecy that he would never die till there would be three strokes of the iron club he had, struck upon himself.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Gregory 1904, Book VII, ch. IV; not verbatim.

title.en: The Surly One of Lochlann Dies by His Own Club
title.zh: 洛赫蘭悍翁死於己棒

region.en: Wood of Dubhros, Ui Fiachrach, Co. Mayo, Ireland
region.zh: 愛爾蘭梅奧郡杜布羅斯林地

period: Fenian cycle, medieval Irish tradition; Lady Augusta Gregory retelling (1904)

source.work: Lady Augusta Gregory, Gods and Fighting Men (1904), Book VII, ch. IV, eBook #14465

summary.en: Finn sets two sons of Morna, children of his father's killers, the price of peace: Diarmuid's head or a fistful of the quicken berries of Dubhros. Oisin warns them of both; they choose to fight for Diarmuid's berries instead, and are bound by him. Grania will not live without the berries, so Diarmuid wakes the Surly One, takes his three blows on the shield, then seizes the iron club and strikes three great blows on the giant — putting his brains out through his head, fulfilling the prophecy.
summary.zh: 芬恩向弒父仇人莫爾納之子索和，開價：迪爾穆德之頭，或一把杜布羅斯花楸果。歐辛警告二者皆不可得；他們選擇為迪爾穆德求果，反遭其縛。格拉尼亞誓言無果不活，迪爾穆德遂喚醒悍翁，先受其三擊於盾上，繼而奪其鐵棒，反擊三棒——巨漿迸腦而出，預言應驗。

sensitivity.note: Self-inflicted fatal blows fulfilling a prophecy is the classic paradoxical-death motif (cf. Balor's eye under Lug, Rhiannon's birds); the 'fine of peace' demanded of orphans of old enemies is a legal-fiction of Irish feud-settlement. Same pin as the rowan record.

passages.text: Finn and his people were not long at Almhuin till they saw fifty armed men coming towards them: "We are enemies of your own, and our fathers were at the killing of your father, and they themselves died for that deed. And it is to ask peace we are come now to you." "I must put a fine on you first in satisfaction for my father's death. I am asking but the head of a champion, or the full of a fist of the berries of the quicken-tree at Dubhros." "I will give you a good advice, children of Morna, to go back to the place you were reared, and not to ask peace of Finn through the length of your lives. For do you know whose head he is asking you to bring him? The head of Diarmuid, grandson of Duibhne; and if you were twenty hundred men in their full strength, Diarmuid would not let you take that head."
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Gregory 1904, Book VII, ch. IV; not verbatim.

passages.text: "Although the children of Morna do not go looking for those berries, I will not lie in a bed for ever till I get a share of them," said Grania, "and I will not live if I do not get them." Then Diarmuid went to the Surly One, and gave him a stroke of his foot, and said: "It is Grania, daughter of the High King, has a desire to taste those berries, and it is to ask a handful of them I am come." "If she is to die for it, she will never taste a berry of those berries." "Willing or unwilling, I will take those berries from you." When the Surly One heard that, he rose up on his feet and lifted his club and struck three great blows on Diarmuid, that gave him some little hurt in spite of his shield.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Gregory 1904, Book VII, ch. IV; not verbatim.

passages.text: But when Diarmuid saw him not minding himself, he threw down his weapons, and made a great leap and took hold of the club with his two hands. And when he had a hold of the club he struck three great blows on him that put his brains out through his head. And when they saw the Surly One was killed, Diarmuid plucked the berries for Grania and for the children of Morna, and they ate their fill of them, and the two young men went back to where Finn was with the load Diarmuid plucked for them.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Gregory 1904, Book VII, ch. IV; not verbatim.

title.en: The Fomor's Stake at Chess and the Broken Bread
title.zh: 弗莫爾的棋局賭注與碎麵包

region.en: Cave by the western sea, Ireland (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 愛爾蘭西海岩洞（象徵定位）

period: Fenian cycle, medieval Irish tradition; Lady Augusta Gregory retelling (1904)

source.work: Lady Augusta Gregory, Gods and Fighting Men (1904), Book VII, ch. V, eBook #14465

summary.en: Storm-bound in a sea cave, Diarmuid and Grania host Ciach the Fierce One of the Fomor; at chess Diarmuid wins, and the Fomor stakes Grania for his winnings. Grania, jealous of the touch, stabs Diarmuid's thigh — and he makes an end of the Fomor and will not speak to her. From the Quarrel come the famous farewell-laments of Diarmuid and Grania, and the sign to Finn of broken faith: henceforth broken bread, not whole, is left behind.
summary.zh: 風暴困於海洞，迪爾穆德與格拉尼亞款待弗莫爾悍者基亞赫；棋局迪爾穆德得勝，弗莫爾竟以格拉尼亞作為賭注索取。格拉尼亞妒火中燒，刺傷迪爾穆德大腿——他誅殺弗莫爾後拒與她言語。由此衍生迪爾穆德與格拉尼亞著名的離別哀歌，以及向芬恩示忠的標記——此後留下的不再是整塊麵包，而是碎屑。

sensitivity.note: Chess as a binding game with persons as stake is the fixed otherworld-gamble motif (cf. Midir and Etain, Finn and the chessboard oracles); Diarmuid's leaving bread as a fidelity-sign to Finn is the tracking device of the pursuit narrative. Symbolic pin.

passages.text: One night while they were there a great storm came on, so that they went into the far part of the cave. But bad as the night was, a man of the Fomor, Ciach, the Fierce One, his name was, came over the western ocean in a currach, with two oars, and he drew it into the cave for shelter. And Diarmuid bade him welcome, and they sat down to play chess together. And he got the best of the game, and what he asked as his winnings was Grania to be his wife, and he put his arms about her as if to bring her away. And Grania said: "I am this long time going with the third best man of the Fianna, and he never came as near as that to me." And Diarmuid took his sword to kill Ciach, and there was anger on Grania when she saw that, and she had a knife in her hand and she struck it into Diarmuid's thigh. And Diarmuid made an end of the Fomor, and he said no word to Grania, but ran out and away through the storm.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Gregory 1904, Book VII, ch. V; not verbatim.

passages.text: At the break of day she overtook him, and after a while they heard the cry of a heron: "Tell me that, Grandson of Duibhne, to whom I gave my love." "O Grania, daughter of the High King, woman who never took a step aright, it is because she was frozen to the rocks she gave that cry. O Grania of the beautiful hair, though you are more beautiful than the green tree under blossom, your love passes away as quickly as the cold cloud at break of day... I lost my people by you, and my lord, and my large bright ships on every sea; I lost my treasure and my gold; it is hunger you gave me through your love." And Grania said: "O Diarmuid of the face like snow, the sound of your voice was dearer to me than all the riches of the leader of the Fianna. The love-spot on your forehead is better to me than honey in streams...
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Gregory 1904, Book VII, ch. V; not verbatim.

passages.text: O Diarmuid of the beautiful hands, take me now the same as before; it was with me the fault was entirely; give me your promise not to leave me." But Diarmuid said: "How can I take you again, you are a woman too fond of words; one day you give up the Head of the Fianna, and the next day myself, and no lie in it." They came then to a place where there was a cave, and water running by it, and they stopped to rest; and Grania said: "Have you a mind to eat bread and meat now, Diarmuid? Give me a knife, so, till I cut it." "Look for the knife in the sheath where you put it yourself." She saw then that the knife was in his thigh where she had struck it, for he would not draw it out himself; so she drew it out then, and that was the greatest shame that ever came upon her.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Gregory 1904, Book VII, ch. V; not verbatim.

passages.text: They stopped then in the cave. And the next day when they went on again, Diarmuid did not leave unbroken bread like he had left every other day as a sign to Finn that he had kept his faith with him, but it was broken bread he left after him. And they went on wandering after that, all through Ireland, hiding from Finn in every place, sleeping under the cromlechs, or with no shelter at all, and wherever they went Finn would follow them, for he knew by his divination where they went; but one time he made out they were on a mountain, for he saw them with heather under them, and it was beside the sea they were, asleep on heather that Diarmuid had brought down from the hills for their bed; and so he went searching the hills and did not find them.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Gregory 1904, Book VII, ch. V-VI; not verbatim.

title.en: Grania's Sleep-Songs over the Wandering Bed
title.zh: 格拉尼亞的搖籃曲與流浪之床

region.en: Beinn Edair (Howth), Co. Dublin, Ireland
region.zh: 愛爾蘭都柏林郡埃達山（霍斯）

period: Fenian cycle, medieval Irish tradition; Lady Augusta Gregory retelling (1904)

source.work: Lady Augusta Gregory, Gods and Fighting Men (1904), Book VII, ch. VI, eBook #14465

summary.en: Watched over by the sleep of Diarmuid, Grania sings her songs of the sleep in the South and the North and the West and the East — then rouses him: the stag is not asleep, the hornless doe cries after her fawn, the bog lark is not sleeping between the streams. In a cave of Beinn Edair an old woman dips her cloak in the sea and lies of frost and rivers to hold them for Finn; Grania tastes salt on the cloak and Diarmuid arms — and Angus Og's boat carries them away in the nick of night.
summary.zh: 守著迪爾穆德的酣眠，格拉尼亞唱起南、北、西、東四方名人酣睡之歌——隨即喚醒他：雄鹿未眠，無角母鹿啼喚花斑幼鹿，雲雀仍在溪澗間守望。埃達山洞中，老嫗以海水蘸濕斗篷、謊稱嚴寒冰封以拖住二人等芬恩到來；格拉尼亞舌試斗篷嚐出鹹味，迪爾穆德披掛而起——安古斯·奧格之舟恰於深夜接應他們脫險。

sensitivity.note: Grania's sleep-song and rousing-song are quoted whole through the cycle and are among the most anthologised Fenian lyrics; the wet-cloak betrayal test (tasting salt) is a countersign motif. Pin at Beinn Edair cave tradition.

passages.text: And Grania would be watching over Diarmuid while he slept, and she would make a sleepy song for him: "Sleep a little, a little little, for there is nothing at all to fear, Diarmuid, grandson of Duibhne; sleep here soundly, soundly, Diarmuid, to whom I have given my love. It is I will keep watch for you, grandchild of shapely Duibhne; sleep a little, a blessing on you, beside the well of the strong field; my lamb from above the lake, from the banks of the strong streams. Let your sleep be like the sleep in the South, of Dedidach of the high poets, the time he took away old Morann's daughter, for all Conall could do against him. Let your sleep be like the sleep in the North, of fair comely Fionnchadh of Ess Ruadh, the time he took Slaine with bravery as we think, in spite of Failbhe of the Hard Head. Let your sleep be like the sleep in the West, of Aine, daughter of Gailian, the time she went on a journey in the night with Dubhthach from Doirinis, by the light of torches. Let your sleep be like the sleep in the East, of Deaghadh the proud, the brave fighter, the time he took Coincheann, daughter of Binn, in spite of fierce Decheall of Duibhreann."
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Gregory 1904, Book VII, ch. VI; not verbatim.

passages.text: And then to rouse him she would make another song: "Caoinche will be loosed on your track; it is not slow the running of Caoilte will be; do not let death reach to you, do not give yourself to sleep for ever. The stag to the east is not asleep, he does not cease from bellowing; the hornless doe is not asleep, crying after her speckled fawn; she is going over the bushes, she does not sleep in her home. The cuckoo is not asleep, the thrush is not asleep, the tops of the trees are a noisy place; the duck is not asleep, she is made ready for good swimming; the bog lark is not asleep to-night on the high stormy bogs; the sound of her clear voice is sweet; she is not sleeping between the streams."
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Gregory 1904, Book VII, ch. VI; not verbatim.

passages.text: One time they were in a cave of Beinn Edair, and there was an old woman befriending them and helping them to keep a watch; and one day she chanced to go up to the top of Beinn Edair, and saw an armed man coming towards her, and did not know him to be Finn: "It is looking for a woman I am come, and for a woman's love. And will you do all I will ask you?" "I will do that," she said, for she thought it was her own love he was asking; and she told him where Diarmuid was hiding. She dipped her cloak in the sea-water before she went into the cave, and made a complaint against the cold: "Cold, cold, cold to-night is the wide plain of Lurg; the snow is higher than the mountains, the deer cannot get at their share of food...
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Gregory 1904, Book VII, ch. VI; not verbatim.

passages.text: Ice is heaped up in every ford; it is for that I am saying and ever saying 'Cold.'" And when she was gone, Grania took hold of the cloak she had left there and put her tongue to it, and found the taste of salt water on it: "My grief, Diarmuid, the old woman has betrayed us. And rise up now, and put your fighting suit upon you." And no sooner were they outside than they saw Finn and the Fianna of Ireland coming towards them; then Diarmuid saw a little boat at hand in the shelter of the harbour, and they knew it was Angus was in it, that had come again to help them to escape from Finn, and they went back with him for a while to Brugh na Boinne.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Gregory 1904, Book VII, ch. VI; not verbatim.

title.en: Finn's Nurse and the Spearing through the Drowned Leaf
title.zh: 芬恩的奶母與洞穿枯葉之矛

region.en: Land of Promise, western ocean (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 應許之地，西海（象徵定位）

period: Fenian cycle, medieval Irish tradition; Lady Augusta Gregory retelling (1904)

source.work: Lady Augusta Gregory, Gods and Fighting Men (1904), Book VII, ch. VII, eBook #14465

summary.en: Beaten in Alban, Finn sails to the Land of Promise for his nurse, for it is not possible to put Diarmuid down by any strength of an army unless enchantment would put him down. Under a Druid mist she rises on a blast of Druid wind over the hunting Diarmuid with a drowned leaf, pierced like a mill-quern, and aims deadly spears through the hole — until Diarmuid, lying on his back, casts the Red Spear through the hole itself and the hag falls dead on the spot.
summary.zh: 阿爾巴受挫，芬恩遠航應許之地求助於奶母——「非魔力不能制服迪爾穆德」。她以德魯伊霧隱身，乘魔風升至打獵的迪爾穆德頭頂，持一片葉孔如磨盤的枯葉，穿孔擲出致命之矛——迪爾穆德仰臥舉紅矛，一擲洞穿葉孔，巫嫗當場斃命。

sensitivity.note: The nurse-enchantress of the Land of Promise is Finn's female counter-gift from the Sidhe (paralleling Manannan's fostering of Diarmuid); the millstone-holed leaf is one of the cycle's signature marvel-weapons. Symbolic pin.

passages.text: And after that, Finn went out again on the sea, and his people with him, and there is no word of them till they came to the Land of Promise where Finn's nurse was. And when she saw Finn coming she was very joyful before him. And Finn told her the whole story from beginning to end, and the cause of his quarrel with Diarmuid; and he said it was to ask an advice from her he was come, and that it was not possible to put him down by any strength of an army, unless enchantment would put him down. "I will go with you, and I will do enchantment on him."
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Gregory 1904, Book VII, ch. VII; not verbatim.

passages.text: And when they came to Brugh na Boinne, the nurse put a Druid mist around Finn and the Fianna, the way no one could know they were there. Now the day before that, Osgar had parted from Diarmuid, and Diarmuid was out hunting by himself. That was shown to the hag, and she took a drowned leaf having a hole in it, like the quern of a mill, and she rose with that by her enchantments on a blast of Druid wind over Diarmuid, and began to aim at him through the hole with deadly spears, till she had done him great harm, for all his arms and his clothing, and he could not make away he was so hard pressed.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Gregory 1904, Book VII, ch. VII; not verbatim.

passages.text: And every danger he was ever in was little beside that danger. And it is what he thought, that unless he could strike the old woman through the hole that was in the leaf, she would give him his death there and then. And he lay down on his back, and the Gae Dearg, the Red Spear, in his hand, and he made a great cast of the spear, that it went through the hole, and the hag fell dead on the spot. And he struck off her head and brought it back with him to Angus Og.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Gregory 1904, Book VII, ch. VII; not verbatim.

title.en: Peace with Finn and the Settling of Rath Grania
title.zh: 與芬恩議和與格拉尼亞堡的安定

region.en: Rath Grania, Ceis Corainn, Co. Kerry, Ireland (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 愛爾蘭克里郡格拉尼亞堡（象徵定位）

period: Fenian cycle, medieval Irish tradition; Lady Augusta Gregory retelling (1904)

source.work: Lady Augusta Gregory, Gods and Fighting Men (1904), Book VII, ch. VII, eBook #14465

summary.en: With Finn's nurse dead, Angus Og goes mediator: to Finn, to the High King, and home to Diarmuid, who will make peace only on conditions — his father's district of Ui Duibhne free of Finn's hunting and the King's tribute, Dumhais in Leinster, and Ceis Corainn as a marriage portion with the King's daughter. The terms are granted, sixteen years of hiding are forgiven, and at Rath Grania Grania bears him four sons and a daughter, richer in gold and cattle than any man living.
summary.zh: 巫嫗既死，安古斯·奧格充當調停人：先見芬恩，再見至高王，最後回到迪爾穆德處。後者僅在特定條件下方肯議和——父親封地伊·迪夫涅免於芬恩狩獵與王室貢賦、倫斯特之杜馬伊斯、以及隨王室之女作嫁妝的凱斯·科雷恩。條件獲准，十六年藏匿既往不咎；格拉尼亞在堡中為他誕下四子一女，金銀牛羊之富冠絕當世。

sensitivity.note: The peace-conditions are a land-grant legal episode (éiric and marriage-portion vocabulary); the sixteen-year term of hiding is the cycle's fixed chronology before the Boar of Beinn Gulbain. Pin symbolic at traditional Rath Grania.

passages.text: And the next morning early, Angus rose up, and he went where Finn was, and he asked would he make peace with Diarmuid, and Finn said he would. And then he went to the King of Ireland to ask peace for Diarmuid, and he said he would agree to it. And then he went back to where Diarmuid and Grania were, and asked him would he make peace with the High King and with Finn. "I am willing, if they will give the conditions I will ask. The district my father had, that is, the district of Ui Duibhne, without right of hunting to Finn, and without rent or tribute to the King of Ireland; and with that the district of Dumhais in Leinster, for they are the best in Ireland, and the district of Ceis Corainn from the King of Ireland as a marriage portion with his daughter; and those are the conditions on which I will make peace with them."
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Gregory 1904, Book VII, ch. VII; not verbatim.

passages.text: Then Angus went with that news to where the King of Ireland was with Finn, and they gave him all those conditions, and they forgave him all he had done through the whole of the time he had been in his hiding, that was sixteen years. And the place Diarmuid and Grania settled in was Rath Grania, in the district of Ceis Corainn, far away from Finn and from Teamhair; and Grania bore him children there, four sons and one daughter. And they lived there in peace, and the people used to be saying there was not a man living at the same time was richer as to gold and to silver, as to cattle and to sheep, than Diarmuid.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Gregory 1904, Book VII, ch. VII; not verbatim.

title.en: Tailc son of Treon and the Woman of the World's Three Walks
title.zh: 特雷昂之子塔爾克與三繞世界之女

region.en: Hill of the Fianna's gathering, Ireland (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 愛爾蘭菲亞納集結之丘（象徵定位）

period: Fenian cycle, medieval Irish tradition; Lady Augusta Gregory retelling (1904)

source.work: Lady Augusta Gregory, Gods and Fighting Men (1904), Book VIII, ch. I, eBook #14465

summary.en: Dark clouds of blood hang over the Fianna's feats, and Finn's dream shows Aodh Beag headless and Goll fighting a very strong man. A beautiful woman with a crimson cloak comes asking protection from her husband Tailc son of Treon — skin of coal, the head and tail of a cat — and Finn gives it against the seven battalions. Thousands fall in their thousands; Osgar fights Tailc five days and nights without food or sleep and strikes his head off — and the woman, seeing all the slaughter done on account of her, falls dead of shame.
summary.zh: 菲亞納演武之際，血雲密佈，芬恩夢見無首的艾德·貝格與強人搏鬥的戈爾。一紅衣美婦前來求庇護，躲避其夫特雷昂之子塔爾克——他膚如煤炭、首尾若貓。芬恩以七營之力相保；千人千人的部隊潰滅；奧斯加與塔爾克晝夜五日無食無眠地血戰，終斬其首——而那女子見因己身而致的大屠殺，羞慚倒地而亡。

sensitivity.note: The blood-cloud omen and dream-oracle open the Book of the Fianna's wearing-away; the cat-headed marvel-man repeats the marvel-race repertoire (compare the Cat-Heads king slain by Abarthach). The heroine dying of shame at the rescue echoes Credhe's death for Cael — inversion of the grief-death. Symbolic pin.

passages.text: One time the Fianna were all gathered together doing feats and casting stones, and the Druid of Teamhair that was with them said: "I am in dread, Finn of the Fianna, that there is some trouble near at hand; look now at those dark clouds of blood that are threatening us side by side overhead, and there is fear on me that there is some destruction coming on the Fianna." Finn lay down to sleep, and it was not long till he saw through his sleep Aodh Beag his son, and he without his head; and after that he saw Goll fighting with a very strong man. And then he heard a great shout, and saw Conan running, and the hounds after him; and when he came, Osgar asked him where was Aodh Beag. "Nothing troubles me but myself," said Conan; and Osgar found Aodh Beag with no fear or trouble on him at all, stopping there till he would hear the noise of the shields.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Gregory 1904, Book VIII, ch. I; not verbatim.

passages.text: They saw a great army coming as if in search of them, and a beautiful woman, having a crimson cloak, came to them over the plain, and her voice was as sweet as music: "I am the daughter of Garraidh, son of Dolar Dian, the Fierce; and my curse upon the King of Greece that bound me to the man that is following after me, and that I am going from, Tailc, son of Treon. For he has no good appearance, and his skin is of the colour of coal, and he has the head and the tail of a cat.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Gregory 1904, Book VIII, ch. I; not verbatim.

passages.text: And I have walked the world three times, and I did not leave a king or a great man without asking help from him, and I never got it yet." "I will give you protection, or the seven battalions of the Fianna will fall for your sake." A thousand of the Fianna went out to meet him and his men, and they all fell, and not one of them came back again; and another thousand of the best men of the Fianna, having blue and green shields, went out under Caoilte, son of Ronan, and they were worsted by Tailc and his people. Then Osgar asked leave of Finn to go out and fight the big man, and he himself and Tailc, son of Treon, were fighting through the length of five days and five nights without food or drink or sleep; and at the end of that time, Osgar made an end of Tailc, and struck his head off. And as to the young woman, when she saw all the slaughter that had been done on account of her, shame reddened her face, and she fell dead there and then.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Gregory 1904, Book VIII, ch. I; not verbatim.

title.en: Meargach of the Green Spears
title.zh: 綠矛之梅爾加赫

region.en: Hill of the Fianna's gathering, Ireland (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 愛爾蘭菲亞納集結之丘（象徵定位）

period: Fenian cycle, medieval Irish tradition; Lady Augusta Gregory retelling (1904)

source.work: Lady Augusta Gregory, Gods and Fighting Men (1904), Book VIII, ch. II, eBook #14465

summary.en: On the heels of Tailc's fall comes Meargach of the Green Spears, whose body no arms were ever reddened on, to avenge the queen-woman's death; Osgar fights him three days and at the last strikes off his head. Goll puts down Ciardan the Swift, and Conan — to Faolan's shame — takes Liagan the Nimble's head before the fight is begun: "If I could make an end of the whole army by one blow, I would do it, and I would not be ashamed."
summary.zh: 塔爾克既亡，梅爾加赫——「身經百戰而未嘗見血」的綠矛戰士——為王后之死而來復仇；奧斯加與其苦戰三日，終斬其首。戈爾誅「迅捷之基爾丹」；科南——令法奧蘭蒙羞——在交手之前便閃電般取下「敏捷之利亞根」首級：「若能一擊滅其全軍，我必為之而不以為恥。」

sensitivity.note: The honour-duel code (fair fight vs Conan's pragmatism) is debated in-text — a rare moment of the cycle commenting on its own ethics. Continuation record of the Tailc sequence; same symbolic pin.

passages.text: While the Fianna were gathered yet on the hill where Tailc, son of Treon, had been put down, they saw a very great champion coming towards them, having an army behind him; and he asked in a very rough voice where was Finn, the Head of the Fianna. "Meargach of the Green Spears is my name, and arms were never reddened yet on my body, and no one ever boasted of driving me backwards. Was it you, Finn, put down Tailc, son of Treon?" "It was not by me he fell, but by Osgar of the strong hand. And if it is satisfaction for her death or the death of Tailc you want, you can get it from a man of the Fianna, or you can go quietly from this place."
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Gregory 1904, Book VIII, ch. II; not verbatim.

passages.text: It was Osgar stood up against him, and they fought a very hard fight through the length of three days, and at one time the Fianna thought it was Osgar was worsted, and they gave a great sorrowful shout. But in the end Osgar put down Meargach and struck his head off, and the army of Meargach keened him very sorrowfully. And after that, the two sons of Meargach, Ciardan the Swift and Liagan the Nimble, came up and asked who would come against them, hand to hand, that they might get satisfaction for their father.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Gregory 1904, Book VIII, ch. II; not verbatim.

passages.text: And it was Goll stood up against Ciardan, and it was not long till he put him down; and Conan came out against Liagan, and Liagan mocked at him: "It is foolishness your coming is, bald man!" But Conan made a quick blow and struck his head off before the fight was begun at all. And Faolan said that was a shameful thing to do, not to stand his ground and make a fair fight. But Conan said: "If I could make an end of the whole army by one blow, I would do it, and I would not be ashamed, and the whole of the Fianna could not shelter them from me."
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Gregory 1904, Book VIII, ch. II; not verbatim.
