At the advice of a Druid he then built him a boat, or coracle, of skins lapped threefold one over the other; and the wizard also told him that seventeen men only must accompany him, and on what day he must begin the boat and on what day he must put out to sea. So when his company was ready he put out and hoisted the sail, but had gone only a little way when his three foster-brothers came down to the beach and entreated him to take them. "Get you home, for none but the number I have may go with me." But the three youths would not be separated from Maeldun, and they flung themselves into the sea. He turned back, lest they should be drowned, and brought them into his boat; and all were punished for this transgression, and Maeldun condemned to wandering until expiation had been made.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Rolleston 1911, ch. VII; not verbatim.

title.en: The Island of the Slaves and the Wind of Punishment
title.zh: 奴隸島與懲罰之風

region.en: Two bare islands of the western ocean (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 西海兩座荒島（象徵定位）

period: Voyage of Maeldun (Imram Maelduin), retold in T. W. Rolleston, Myths and Legends of the Celtic Race (1911)

source.work: T. W. Rolleston, Myths and Legends of the Celtic Race (1911), ch. VII, eBook #34630

summary.en: Rowing all day and half the night, the voyagers come to two small bare islands with two forts, and hear armed men quarrelling: 'Twas I slew Ailill of the Edge-of-Battle and burned the church of Doocloone over him, and no kinsman has avenged his death on me.' Maeldun is about to land for vengeance, but a great wind arises suddenly and blows them off into the boundless ocean — 'Ye have caused this to be, casting yourselves on board in spite of the words of the Druid' — and vengeance itself is postponed by the penalty of the broken rule.
summary.zh: 晝夜划行後，他們抵達兩座荒島，聽見武裝者的爭吵：「正是我殺了戰刃埃利爾、焚其教堂，至今無族人復仇。」梅爾敦欲登岸復仇，狂風驟起，將小舟吹入無垠大洋——「是你們違德魯伊之言擅自登舟，招此懲罰。」復仇因破誓之罰而延宕。

sensitivity.note: The wind that blows the avenger away from his vengeance is the immram's fixed moral device — the quest is penance, not reprisal; the two fort islands parallel the twin-fort openings of voyage literature (cf. the Coire Brecain twin isles). Symbolic pin.

passages.text: Maeldun and his crew had rowed all day and half the night when they came to two small bare islands with two forts in them, and a noise was heard from them of armed men quarrelling. "Stand off from me, for I am a better man than thou. 'Twas I slew Ailill of the Edge-of-Battle and burned the church of Doocloone over him, and no kinsman has avenged his death on me. And thou hast never done the like of that."
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Rolleston 1911, ch. VII; not verbatim.

passages.text: Then Maeldun was about to land, and German and Diuran the Rhymer cried that God had guided them to the spot where they would be. But a great wind arose suddenly and blew them off into the boundless ocean, and Maeldun said to his foster-brothers: "Ye have caused this to be, casting yourselves on board in spite of the words of the Druid." And they had no answer, save only to be silent for a little space.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Rolleston 1911, ch. VII; not verbatim.

title.en: The Little Cat and the Necklace of Ashes
title.zh: 小貓與化灰的項鍊

region.en: Tower island of the white houses (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 白屋高塔之島（象徵定位）

period: Voyage of Maeldun (Imram Maelduin), retold in T. W. Rolleston, Myths and Legends of the Celtic Race (1911)

source.work: T. W. Rolleston, Myths and Legends of the Celtic Race (1911), ch. VII, eBook #34630

summary.en: Hungry and thirsting, they reach a tall white tower of chalk reaching up to the clouds, and enter the great house where no man is — only a little cat playing on four stone pillars, leaping from one to the other; on the walls hang three rows of brooches, neck-torques as big as cask-hoops, and great swords with gold and silver hilts, and a roasted ox with abundance of liquor lies ready. They eat and sleep; and next morning the youngest foster-brother takes a necklace from the wall — and the cat leaps through him like a fiery arrow, and he falls a heap of ashes.
summary.zh: 飢渴交加之際，他們登上一座直插雲霄的白堊高塔之島；大屋中無人，唯有一隻小貓在四根石柱間跳躍嬉戲；牆上掛著三排金銀胸針、桶箍般大的金銀項圈與金柄寶劍，烤牛與美酒已備。他們飽食安睡；翌晨最年輕的乳兄弟竟從牆上取走項鍊——小貓如烈焰之箭穿身而過，他倒地化為一堆灰燼。

sensitivity.note: The cat that leaps 'like a fiery arrow' is the fixed guardian-sprite of the immram's wonder-houses (the Island of the Little Cat is the voyage's most famous theft-punishment); hospitality taken freely but a jewel stolen = death — a clean moral of otherworld property. Symbolic pin.

passages.text: This was, as it were, a tall white tower of chalk reaching up to the clouds, and on the rampart about it were great houses white as snow. They entered the largest of them, and found no man in it, but a small cat playing on four stone pillars which were in the midst of the house, leaping from one to the other. It looked a little on the Irish warriors, but did not cease from its play. On the walls of the houses there were three rows of objects hanging up, one row of brooches of gold and silver, and one of neck-torques of gold and silver, each as big as the hoop of a cask, and one of great swords with gold and silver hilts. Quilts and shining garments lay in the room, and there, also, were a roasted ox and a flitch of bacon and abundance of liquor.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Rolleston 1911, ch. VII; not verbatim.

passages.text: "Hath this been left for us?" said Maeldun to the cat. It looked at him a moment, and then continued its play. So there they ate and drank and slept, and stored up what remained of the food. Next day, as they made to leave the house, the youngest of Maeldun's foster-brothers took a necklace from the wall, and was bearing it out when the cat suddenly "leaped through him like a fiery arrow," and he fell, a heap of ashes, on the floor. Thereupon Maeldun, who had forbidden the theft of the jewel, soothed the cat and replaced the necklace, and they strewed the ashes of the dead youth on the sea-shore, and put to sea again.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Rolleston 1911, ch. VII; not verbatim.

title.en: The Mill That Grinds Men's Grudges
title.zh: 研磨人間怨恨的巨磨

region.en: Island of the Mill, western ocean (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 西海巨磨之島（象徵定位）

period: Voyage of Maeldun (Imram Maelduin), retold in T. W. Rolleston, Myths and Legends of the Celtic Race (1911)

source.work: T. W. Rolleston, Myths and Legends of the Celtic Race (1911), ch. VII, eBook #34630

summary.en: They find a great and grim-looking mill, and a giant miller grinding corn in it: 'Half the corn of your country is ground here. Here comes to be ground all that men begrudge to each other.' Heavy and many are the loads going to it, and all that is ground in it is carried away westwards — so they cross themselves and sail away. It is the voyage's clearest allegory, the sea-mill of envy standing where in later Irish sea-lore the whirlpool Corryvreckan turns.
summary.zh: 他們見到一座猙獰巨磨，巨人磨坊主正在磨穀：「爾國之穀，半數在此研磨；凡人間互相嫉恨之物，皆運至此研磨。」沉重的穀物源源運來，磨成之物皆向西流去——眾人畫十字而速去。此乃航程中最直白的寓意之島：嫉妒之海磨，正是後世愛爾蘭海傳說中迴漩的科里弗雷坎漩渦。

sensitivity.note: The grudge-mill is the immram's moral allegory (traditionally located at the whirlpool of Corryvreckan); the westward drift of what is ground away is the Irish eschatological geography (all rivers run west to the otherworld). Tagged 'world-renewal' for the sea-as-purgation reading, interpretive.

passages.text: Here they found a great and grim-looking mill, and a giant miller grinding corn in it. "Half the corn of your country," he said, "is ground here. Here comes to be ground all that men begrudge to each other." Heavy and many were the loads they saw going to it, and all that was ground in it was carried away westwards. So they crossed themselves and sailed away.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Rolleston 1911, ch. VII; not verbatim.

title.en: The Silvern Column and the Mesh of the Net
title.zh: 白銀巨柱與網眼之航

region.en: Sea of the silvern column (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 白銀巨柱之海（象徵定位）

period: Voyage of Maeldun (Imram Maelduin), retold in T. W. Rolleston, Myths and Legends of the Celtic Race (1911)

source.work: T. W. Rolleston, Myths and Legends of the Celtic Race (1911), ch. VII, eBook #34630

summary.en: One of the most striking episodes of the voyage: a great silvern column, four-square, rising from the boundless ocean, its summit lost in the sky, and from that summit a huge silver net flung far away into the sea. Through a mesh of the net they sail — and Diuran hacks away a piece of it: 'Destroy it not, for what we see is the work of mighty men.' 'For the praise of God's name I do this, that our tale may be believed; if I reach Ireland again, this silver shall be offered on the high altar of Armagh.' Two ounces and a half it weighed, measured afterwards in Armagh.
summary.zh: 航程最壯麗的一幕：四方白銀巨柱自無垠大洋拔海而起，柱頂沒入天際，一張巨大銀網自柱頂遠拋入海。眾人自網眼間駛過——狄烏蘭竟砍下一片：「勿毀之！此乃偉人所造。」「我以此榮耀神名，使我等傳說可信；若得歸國，此銀必供於阿馬大祭壇。」該銀片後在阿馬秤得二盎斯半。

sensitivity.note: The silvern column with its net is the immram's most abstract revelation-image (a cosmic fishing of the world); the relic taken for proof — weighed in Armagh — is the voyage's Christian-world verification device, unique among the islands. Symbolic pin.

passages.text: It was a great silvern column, four-square, rising from the sea. Each of its four sides was as wide as two oar-strokes of the boat. Not a sod of earth was at its foot, but it rose from the boundless ocean and its summit was lost in the sky. From that summit a huge silver net was flung far away into the sea, and through a mesh of that net they sailed.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Rolleston 1911, ch. VII; not verbatim.

passages.text: As they did so Diuran hacked away a piece of the net. "Destroy it not," said Maeldun, "for what we see is the work of mighty men." Diuran said: "For the praise of God's name I do this, that our tale may be believed, and if I reach Ireland again this piece of silver shall be offered by me on the high altar of Armagh." Two ounces and a half it weighed when it was measured afterwards in Armagh. And then they heard a voice from the summit of yonder pillar, mighty, clear, and distinct; but they knew not the tongue it spake, or the words it uttered.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Rolleston 1911, ch. VII; not verbatim.

title.en: The Island of the Women and the Clue of Twine
title.zh: 女人島與絲線之引

region.en: Dun of the seventeen maidens (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 十七少女的堡壘（象徵定位）

period: Voyage of Maeldun (Imram Maelduin), retold in T. W. Rolleston, Myths and Legends of the Celtic Race (1911)

source.work: T. W. Rolleston, Myths and Legends of the Celtic Race (1911), ch. VII, eBook #34630

summary.en: Within a mighty dun, seventeen maidens prepare a great bath; a rider richly clad comes up on a racehorse and is seen to be a woman — the queen. Maeldun is wedded to her, each of his men to a maiden, and she promises that old age will never fall on them if they stay. But the men weary — three months were three years — and put to sea while she is away judging the folk; she comes riding with a clew of twine and flings it, and it clings to Maeldun's hand so that he cannot free himself. So next time another man catches it, and Diuran smites off his hand, and it falls with the clew into the sea; and all the land was one cry of wailing as they escaped.
summary.zh: 宏偉堡壘內，十七位少女正備浴；一名衣飾華美的騎手乘賽馬而至——竟是女王。梅爾敦娶她為妻，部眾各配一女；她許諾：留此則永駐青春。然三月如三年，眾人思歸，趁女王出巡登舟而逃；她持絲線馳至擲出，線竟黏在梅爾敦掌上不能脫。下次由另一人接線，狄烏蘭揮劍斷其手，線與手俱落海中——全島哭聲震野，他們終於逃出女人島。

sensitivity.note: The queen's clew that clings is the binding-token motif (compare the ball of thread at the Land of Women in the Bran voyage — the two tales share the device); three months that are three years is the otherworld-time rule. Note the self-mutilation for escape is documented in the source. Symbolic pin.

passages.text: They landed to look on it, and sat on a hillock near by. Within the dun they saw seventeen maidens busy at preparing a great bath. In a little while a rider, richly clad, came up swiftly on a racehorse, and lighted down and went inside... And Maeldun was wedded to the queen, and each of the maidens to one of his men. "Stay here, and old age will never fall on you, but ye shall remain as ye are now for ever and ever... So they remained there for three months of winter; but at the end of that time it seemed they had been there three years, and the men wearied of it, and longed to set forth for their own country.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Rolleston 1911, ch. VII; not verbatim.

passages.text: But before they had gone far the queen came riding up with a clew of twine in her hand, and she flung it after them. Maeldun caught it in his hand, and it clung to his hand so that he could not free himself, and the queen, holding the other end, drew them back to land. Twice again the same thing happened, and the next time another man caught the clew, but it clung to his hand as before; so Diuran smote off his hand, and it fell with the clew into the sea. "When she saw that she at once began to wail and shriek, so that all the land was one cry, wailing and shrieking." And thus they escaped from the Island of the Women.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Rolleston 1911, ch. VII; not verbatim.

title.en: Rochad's Woman-Fight at Finnabair's Name
title.zh: 以芬娜芭爾之名挑起的「女子之戰」

region.en: North of the Tain route, Co. Monaghan, Ireland (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 愛爾蘭莫納亨郡奪牛記行軍路（象徵定位）

period: Tain Bo Cuailnge (LU recension), trans. L. Winifred Faraday (1904)

source.work: L. Winifred Faraday, The Cattle-Raid of Cualnge (1904), eBook #21557

summary.en: Cuchulainn sends his charioteer to Rochad Mac Fatheman of Ulster to come to his help; but Findabair loves Rochad, fairest of the Ulstermen, and she meets him by proxy in a horseman's shape: 'I have come from Findabair to meet you, that you come to speak with her.' The seven kings of the host, promised Findabair by Medb, lie in wait and Rochad slays a hundred of them at a time; the promise of the girl, made seven times over as a bribe, has raised a private war inside Meave's camp — the woman-fight by which the Tain's own bride-price logic devours it.
summary.zh: 庫丘林遣車伕召阿爾斯特的羅夏德前來相助；然芬娜芭爾鍾情於這位阿爾斯特最美的戰士，竟化身騎手傳話：「我奉芬娜芭爾之命來請你一見。」大軍中七位國王皆被梅芙許諾芬娜芭爾為酬，設伏相截；羅夏德一次斬殺百人。同一女子七次許諾的聘禮謊言，在梅芙營中釀成內戰——「女子之戰」反噬了《奪牛記》自己的贖金邏輯。

sensitivity.note: The woman-fight (ban-chath) is the LU's satiric name for the melee the promise of Findabair raises; Findabair as bride-bait recurs through the whole Tain (findabair promised to Nacrantal, to Fer Diad, to Loch), making her the cycle's currency. Pin symbolic on the route.

passages.text: Cuchulainn sent his charioteer to Rochad Mac Fatheman of Ulster, that he should come to his help. Now it happened that Findabair loved Rochad, for he was the fairest of the warriors among the Ulstermen at that time. The man goes to Rochad and told him to come. Rochad comes from the north with a hundred men. 'Rochad Mac Fatheman,' said he, 'and it is to help Cuchulainn he comes.' 'I have come from Findabair to meet you, that you come to speak with her,' said the horseman.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Faraday 1904, LU recension; not verbatim.

passages.text: It was promised to him that Findabair should be given to him, and he returned from them then. So that that is Rochad's Woman-fight. And the seven kings who had been promised Findabair by Medb lay in wait for Rochad, and Rochad slew a hundred of their men at a time; and the promise made seven times over as a bribe raised a private war inside the camp of Meave, so that the bride-price logic of the raid devoured the raid itself.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Faraday 1904, LU recension; not verbatim.

title.en: Cuchulainn and Findabair Make the Terms
title.zh: 庫丘林與芬娜芭爾議定條款

region.en: Tara of the Cattle-raid camp, Ireland (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 愛爾蘭奪牛記營地（象徵定位）

period: Tain Bo Cuailnge (LU recension), trans. L. Winifred Faraday (1904)

source.work: L. Winifred Faraday, The Cattle-Raid of Cualnge (1904), eBook #21557

summary.en: 'Let an offer go to him, that Findabair will be given to him,' says Ailill — and Cuchulainn, meeting the king's daughter by the ford, agrees to hold the host back for food and a champion a day, until the Ulstermen are cured. The maiden herself is made the guarantee of the truce that her own value has strained; the terms are broken within the day, and the host learns that the boy will not be bought with the girl he does not want.
summary.zh: 埃利爾提議：「向他許諾芬娜芭爾。」庫丘林與公主在渡口相會，允諾只要每日供食並遣一名勇士對決，便不襲擾大軍，直至阿爾斯特人痊愈。這位少女成了由她自己價值所繃緊的停戰擔保；條款當日即被撕毀，大軍也明白了：他們的少年戰士不會為他並不需要的姑娘所收買。

sensitivity.note: The meeting of Cuchulainn and Findabair (LU) sets the formal terms — daily champion and food — that structure the middle Tain; the breach-of-truce motif is the cycle's engine (compare the Fergus securities). Pin symbolic.

passages.text: 'Let an offer go to him,' said Ailill, 'that Findabair will be given to him, and a chariot, and the equipment of a chariot, and a maiden of the Connaughtmen with her.' And the maiden goes to Cuchulainn by the ford, and they make the terms between them: that he should not harass the host if he were supplied daily with food, and with a champion to meet him in single combat.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Faraday 1904, LU recension; not verbatim.

passages.text: The terms were made with him then, that he should have his food and his champion daily until the Ulstermen were cured of their sickness, and Findabair herself was the pledge of it; but the terms were broken within the day, for Meave sent men against him beyond the champion of the day; and the host learned that the boy would not be bought with the girl he did not want, and that a champion a day must pay for every breach.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Faraday 1904, LU recension; not verbatim.

title.en: The Two Bulls Fight at Tarbga
title.zh: 雙牛相搏於塔爾加

region.en: Tarbga in Mag Ai, Co. Roscommon, Ireland
region.zh: 愛爾蘭羅斯康芒郡阿伊平原塔爾加

period: Tain Bo Cuailnge (YBL recension ending), trans. L. Winifred Faraday (1904)

source.work: L. Winifred Faraday, The Cattle-Raid of Cualnge (1904), eBook #21557

summary.en: Routed, Meave blames Fergus — 'faults meet here to-day' — and his answer is the herding-law jibe: it is customary to every herd which a mare precedes. The Bull is driven home that morning and meets the White-horned at Tarbga in Mag Ai, where every man who escaped the battle watches only the two Bulls fighting. The Dun of Cualnge lighted on the horn of the other for a day and a night till Fergus plied the rod; the horn sprang to the Mountain of the Horn; and the conquering bull carries the loin and shoulder-blade and liver of the other on his horns from loch to loch, roaring through all the province, till he dies between Ulster and Iveagh at Druim Tairb. Ailill and Medb make peace, and for seven years after there is no wounding of men between them.
summary.zh: 潰敗後，梅芙怪罪費爾古斯——「今日你我各有過失」——他以牧群之律回敬：「母馬領群的牧群，向來如此。」當晨褐牛被驅回，於阿伊平原塔爾加與白角牛相遇，戰場脫生者皆屏息觀牛。庫爾涅褐牛之足踩住對方牛角一日一夜，費爾古斯以棍催其收足，角應聲彈上「牛角山」。勝牛角挑敵牛腰肉、肩胛與肝，逐湖而飲，吼聲震徹全省，最終死於阿爾斯特與伊威之間的德魯姆·塔爾布。埃利爾與梅芙議和，此後七年，兩族刀兵不入。

sensitivity.note: The bull-fight finale is the Tain's dindsenchas engine (Sliab n-Adarca, Ath Luain, Etan Tairb, Druim Tairb are all named from the bull's journey) — the epic's place-name charter; the seven-year peace after is the corpus's post-epic reset. Pin is the traditional Tarbga site.

passages.text: When the battle was broken, then said Medb to Fergus: 'Faults and meet here to-day, O Fergus.' 'It is customary to every herd which a mare precedes; after a woman who has ill consulted their interest.' They take away the Bull then in that morning of the battle, so that he met the White-horned at Tarbga in Mag Ai; every one who escaped in the fight was intent on nothing but beholding the two Bulls fighting. Bricriu Poison-tongue came with the rest then to see the combat of the Bulls; the two Bulls went in fighting over Bricriu, so that he died therefrom. That is the Death of Bricriu.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Faraday 1904, YBL ending; not verbatim.

passages.text: The foot of the Dun of Cualnge lighted on the horn of the other; for a day and a night he did not draw his foot towards him, till Fergus incited him and plied a rod along his body: 'Twere no good luck that this combative old calf which has been brought here should leave the honour of clan and race. Therewith he drew his foot to him so that his leg was broken, and the horn sprang from the other, and was in the mountain by him; it was Sliab n-Adarca, the Mountain of the Horn, afterwards.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Faraday 1904, YBL ending; not verbatim.

passages.text: He carried them then a journey of a day and a night, till he lighted in the loch which is by Cruachan, and he came to Cruachan out of it with the loin and the shoulder-blade and the liver of the other on his horns. He drank a draught in Findlethe; he drank another draught in Ath Luain; he gave forth his roar on Iraird Chuillend, and it was heard through all the province; there the liver of the other fell from his horns, hence is Tromma; and he went till he died between Ulster and Iveagh at Druim Tairb. Ailill and Medb made peace with the Ulstermen and with Cuchulainn; for seven years after there was no wounding of men between them. Findabair stayed with Cuchulainn, and the Connaughtmen went to their country, and the Ulstermen to Emain Macha with their great triumph. Finit, amen.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Faraday 1904, YBL ending; not verbatim.

title.en: The Renewed Eagle and Diuran's Drink
title.zh: 重生的巨鷹與狄烏蘭之飲

region.en: Island of the Eagle, western ocean (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 西海巨鷹之島（象徵定位）

period: Voyage of Maeldun (Imram Maelduin), retold in T. W. Rolleston, Myths and Legends of the Celtic Race (1911)

source.work: T. W. Rolleston, Myths and Legends of the Celtic Race (1911), ch. VII, eBook #34630

summary.en: On the island of the eagle they find the fifteenth man of the monks of St Brennan of Birr, last survivor of an ocean pilgrimage, with the holy Brennan's tablet. A cloud from the south-west proves an enormous bird, very old, plumage dull and decayed, eating berries from a branch as big as an oak; two eagles come at noon and pick the insects from its jaws and eyes and ears till vespers, and when it is cleansed it plunges in the lake and is renewed — 'thy youth is renewed like the eagle's' — and soars thrice round the island. Diuran bathes and drinks of the lake, and never again knew illness: not a tooth fell from his jaw nor a hair from his head.
summary.zh: 巨鷹島上住著聖布倫南修士團第十五人——海上朝聖的唯一倖存者。西南方一朵「雲」竟是羽色黯朽的蒼老巨鷹，正食橡木大枝上的葡萄狀紅果；正午兩鷹飛來，為其啄去目耳口間蟲豸直至晚禱；洗淨後巨鷹躍入湖中重生——「你的青春如鷹般更新」——繞島三匝而去。狄烏蘭入湖沐浴飲水，此後終身無病：齒不落，髮不脫。

sensitivity.note: The eagle renewed from age to youth is the immram's baptism-of-nature set-piece, glossed with Psalm 103 by the redactor; the healing lake parallels the well of healing of the Fenian cycle (cross-ref the Conn Crither record). Symbolic pin.

passages.text: One day they saw what seemed to be a cloud coming up from the south-west. As it drew near, however, they saw the waving of pinions, and perceived that it was an enormous bird. It came into the island, and, alighting very wearily on a hill near the lake, it began eating the red berries, like grapes, which grew on a huge tree-branch as big as a full-grown oak, that it had brought with it. And they saw that it was very old, and its plumage dull and decayed. At the hour of noon two eagles came up from the south-west and alit in front of the great bird, and after resting awhile they set to work picking off the insects that infested its jaws and eyes and ears. This they continued till vespers, when all three ate of the berries again.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Rolleston 1911, ch. VII; not verbatim.

passages.text: At last, on the following day, when the great bird had been completely cleansed, it plunged into the lake, and again the two eagles picked and cleansed it. Till the third day the great bird remained preening and shaking its pinions, and its feathers became glossy and abundant, and then, soaring upwards, it flew thrice round the island, and away to the quarter whence it had come, and its flight was now swift and strong; whence it was manifest to them that this had been its renewal from old age to youth, according as the prophet said, Thy youth is renewed like the eagle's. Then Diuran said: "Let us bathe in that lake and renew ourselves where the bird hath been renewed." But Diuran plunged in and drank of the water. From that time so long as he lived his eyes were strong and keen, and not a tooth fell from his jaw nor a hair from his head, and he never knew illness or infirmity.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Rolleston 1911, ch. VII; not verbatim.

title.en: The Island of the Flaming Rampart
title.zh: 烈焰護牆之島

region.en: Island of the flaming rampart, western ocean (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 西海烈焰護牆之島（象徵定位）

period: Voyage of Maeldun (Imram Maelduin), retold in T. W. Rolleston, Myths and Legends of the Celtic Race (1911)

source.work: T. W. Rolleston, Myths and Legends of the Celtic Race (1911), ch. VII, eBook #34630

summary.en: They come in sight of an island not large, encircled by a rampart of flame that circles round and round it continually; in one part of the rampart there is an opening, and when the opening comes opposite to them they see through it the whole island — men and women, beautiful, many, and wearing adorned garments, with vessels of gold in their hands, and the festal music comes to the ears of the wanderers. For a long time they linger there, watching this marvel, 'and they deemed it delightful to behold.'
summary.zh: 一座不大的島嶼出現眼前，四週烈焰之牆不斷迴旋；牆上有一開口，當開口轉至他們面前，他們便望見全島——眾多俊美的男男女女，衣飾華美，手捧金器，節慶樂聲傳到漂泊者耳中。他們久久滯留凝望此異象，「視之為賞心悅目之奇觀」。

sensitivity.note: The flaming rampart (fire-wall with a turning gate) is the immram's vision of the earthly paradise guarded by fire — the voyage's summit image, kin to the burning wall of the later St Brendan tradition; no landing is permitted. Symbolic pin.

passages.text: They now came in sight of an island which was not large, and it had about it a rampart of flame that circled round and round it continually. In one part of the rampart there was an opening, and when this opening came opposite to them they saw through it the whole island, and saw those who dwelt therein, even men and women, beautiful, many, and wearing adorned garments, with vessels of gold in their hands. And the festal music which they made came to the ears of the wanderers. For a long time they lingered there, watching this marvel, "and they deemed it delightful to behold."
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Rolleston 1911, ch. VII; not verbatim.

title.en: The Glass Bridge and the Lady Who Knew No Sin
title.zh: 玻璃橋與不知罪之女

region.en: Fortress of the glass bridge (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 玻璃橋堡壘（象徵定位）

period: Voyage of Maeldun (Imram Maelduin), retold in T. W. Rolleston, Myths and Legends of the Celtic Race (1911)

source.work: T. W. Rolleston, Myths and Legends of the Celtic Race (1911), ch. VII, eBook #34630

summary.en: One of the most elaborately wrought incidents of the voyage: an island with a fortress with a brazen door and a bridge of glass leading to it, which throws the crew backward when they seek to cross; a woman lifts a glass slab from the bridge and lowers her pail into the water beneath, and the melody of the smitten portcullis plunges them in slumber till the morrow, thrice over. On the fourth day she comes out over the bridge in a white mantle with a circlet of gold, and welcomes each man of the crew by his own name; her one pail gives every man what he most desires. Asked in marriage for Maeldun, she answers, 'I know not, nor have ever known, what sin is' — and by morning the island is gone.
summary.zh: 航程中最精緻的一幕：島上有銅門堡壘與一座玻璃橋，眾人欲過橋而橋將其拋回；女子自橋上揭起玻璃板，垂桶取水；敲擊銅閘之聲使他們昏睡至翌晨，如是者三。第四日，她身披白斗篷、金環飾髮，踏橋而出，一一喚出全體船員之名；她的一桶之水，人人得其所願。為梅爾敦提親時她答道：「我不知，也從不知何為罪。」翌晨，島嶼無蹤。

sensitivity.note: The glass bridge that rejects the uninvited is the immram's test-of-worthiness (kin to the glass mountain of later Celtic and Grail lore); the lady who 'knows not what sin is' is the voyage's vision of prelapsarian innocence — the doctrinal Christian overlay on the fairy-mistress motif. Symbolic pin.

passages.text: The island they now reached had on it a fortress with a brazen door, and a bridge of glass leading to it. When they sought to cross the bridge it threw them backward. A woman came out of the fortress with a pail in her hand, and lifting from the bridge a slab of glass she let down her pail into the water beneath, and returned to the fortress. They struck on the brazen portcullis before them to gain admittance, but the melody given forth by the smitten metal plunged them in slumber till the morrow morn; thrice over this happened, the woman each time making an ironical speech about Maeldun.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Rolleston 1911, ch. VII; not verbatim.

passages.text: On the fourth day, however, she came out to them over the bridge, wearing a white mantle with a circlet of gold on her hair, two silver sandals on her rosy feet, and a filmy silken smock next her skin. "My welcome to thee, O Maeldun," she said, and she welcomed each man of the crew by his own name... She gave them abundance of food and drink, all out of her one pail, each man finding in it what he most desired. They do woo the maiden for him, and she replies: "I know not, nor have ever known, what sin is." Twice over this is repeated. "To-morrow, you shall have your answer." When the morning breaks, however, they find themselves once more at sea, with no sign of the island or fortress or lady.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Rolleston 1911, ch. VII; not verbatim.

title.en: Tuan's History of the Five Invasions
title.zh: 圖安講述的五次入侵史

region.en: Ireland, from Partholon to the Milesians (symbolic pin, Tara)
region.zh: 愛爾蘭：自帕特隆至米利安（象徵定位塔拉）

period: Irish Fairy Tales, James Stephens (1920), Tuan mac Cairill cycle

source.work: James Stephens, Irish Fairy Tales (1920), The Story of Tuan Mac Cairill, eBook #28924

summary.en: Tuan mac Cairill, who watched Ireland's history from every shape he lived through, tells Finnian the tale of the invasions: Partholon and his people who perished of plague; Nemed who fought the Fomor and died of plague; the Firbolgs who came from Spain after the sack of towers and ruled till the Tuatha de Danaan beat them; the gods themselves who held the land until the Milesians came — and Tuan, last of all his kin, saw every age of it, remembering all his births, and told it to the new faith that came with Finnian.
summary.zh: 曾以各種形態親歷愛爾蘭歷史的圖安，向菲尼安講述入侵史：帕特隆一族盡歿於瘟疫；內梅德與弗莫爾交戰而終亡於疫；西班牙出逃的弗博爾格建國，直至神族將其擊敗；諸神居有此地，直到米利安人來臨。圖安——親族中僅存者——目睹每一紀元，銘記每次轉生，將歷史傳予隨菲尼安而來的新信仰。

sensitivity.note: Stephens' retelling of the Lebor Gabala frame through Tuan (a variant of the rebirth record): the five-invasion sequence is the standard Irish origin-list; Tuan as witness merges the rebirth-reincarnation motif with historiographic transmission. Variant record of the same tradition family as the Lebor Gabala chapters. Pin symbolic at Tara.

passages.text: And Tuan told Finnian of the coming of Partholon to Ireland, and of the plague that swept his people from the land, so that not one man of them was left; and of the coming of Nemed, and of his battles with the Fomor, and how his people also died of plague; and of the Firbolgs, who came from Spain after the sack of their towers, and divided Ireland into five provinces, and gave kings to it.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Stephens 1920, The Story of Tuan Mac Cairill; not verbatim.

passages.text: And he told him of the Tuatha de Danaan, who came out of the north of the world with their four cities and their treasures, and beat the Firbolgs in the first battle, and held Ireland under them till the Sons of Mil came from Spain; and how the gods went into the hills, and the Gael had the land, and Tuan, last of all his kin, watched every age of it, remembering all his births, and told it to the new faith that came with Finnian of the Bells.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Stephens 1920, The Story of Tuan Mac Cairill; not verbatim.

title.en: Fionn's First Exploits: the Fianna of the Boyhood
title.zh: 芬恩的初試鋒芒：少年菲亞納

region.en: Tara and the woods of Leinster, Ireland
region.zh: 愛爾蘭塔拉與倫斯特林地

period: Irish Fairy Tales, James Stephens (1920), Fenian cycle

source.work: James Stephens, Irish Fairy Tales (1920), eBook #28924

summary.en: Reared in secret in the wilds with his women guardians, Fionn learns his father's enemies wait for his name; he wins the salmon of knowledge, is claimed by the Fianna, and at Tara faces the burning Aillen — but it is Stephens' telling that sets the boy's bonds of hospitality: the boy who is fed must give thanks, the boy who is refused must wander, and the rule of the Fianna that no man shall refuse the asking of any is the law Fionn learns before he wears his father's place.
summary.zh: 芬恩自幼隨女眷隱居荒野，深知父親仇敵候其名而動；他贏得知識之鮭，被菲亞納接納，並在塔拉直面縱火的艾倫。而在斯蒂芬斯的敘事中，少年受的待客之誡尤為醒目：受食者當謝，被拒者當流浪——「任何求助者不可被拒」的菲亞納法典，是芬恩在繼承父位之前先學會的道理。

sensitivity.note: Stephens' version of the Coming of Finn overlaps Gregory's (existing celtic-fionn-boyhood-coming); this record keeps Stephens' hospitality-law frame distinct — the geis of never refusing the asking is the Fianna's charter in this recension. Pin at Tara.

passages.text: Fionn was reared in secret in the wilds, with his women guardians about him, for the enemies of his father waited on his name; and he learned the woods and the water, and the way a boy must hold his tongue and his courage. When the salmon of knowledge was given to him by the poet who had waited seven years for it, he took the wisdom of the nuts of the nine hazels of wisdom that grow beside the well that is below the sea.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Stephens 1920, Irish Fairy Tales; not verbatim.

passages.text: And he learned the law of the Fianna before ever he came to their number: that no man shall refuse the asking of any, that no man shall take cattle by oppression, that no man shall fall back before nine fighting men; and the boy who is fed must give thanks, and the boy who is refused must wander, and these are the rules by which Fionn held the headship of the Fianna of Ireland when his time came.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Stephens 1920, Irish Fairy Tales; not verbatim.

title.en: Agamemnon's Day of Slaughter
title.zh: 阿伽門農的殺戮之日

region.en: Plains of Troy (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 特洛伊平原（象徵性定位）

period: Composed c. 8th century BCE (Butler translation 1898)

source.work: Homer, Iliad, trans. Samuel Butler (1898), Book XI

summary.en: Zeus, by Iris, tells Hector to hold back while Agamemnon rages. The king charges first, kills Iphidamas — a bridegroom of twelve days — and Coon, and is wounded in the arm by the spear of Coon, Antenor's eldest son. As long as the blood is warm he goes on killing with spear, sword and stone; when the blood dries and the pain comes on him like the pangs of childbirth, he is driven to his chariot, and Hector, freed of his fear, takes the command.
summary.zh: 宙斯遣伊里斯告赫克托耳：阿伽門農逞威時暫避其鋒。王首當其衝，斬伊菲達瑪斯（僅成婚十二日的新郎）與科翁，又被科翁刺傷臂膊。血流溫熱時，他以矛、劍、巨石連連殺敵；血止痛起如產婦陣痛，方被迫登車；赫克托耳如釋重負，遂掌戰局。

sensitivity.note: Ancient literary source; no living community restrictions.

passages.text: Zeus sent Iris down to Hector: so long as Agamemnon headed his men and made havoc of the Trojan ranks, Hector was to keep aloof and bid the others bear the brunt; but when the king were wounded by spear or arrow and took to his chariot, then would Zeus vouchsafe him strength to slay till he reached the ships and night fell.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Homer, Iliad, Book 11 (Butler 1898); not verbatim.

passages.text: Iphidamas, son of Antenor, a bridegroom of twelve days, came first against the king: his spear struck the silver-studded girdle below the cuirass and was turned aside as if it had been lead; and Agamemnon caught it from his hand, drew him in with the fury of a lion, and killed him with a sword-cut on the neck. So there the poor fellow lay, 'sleeping a sleep as it were of bronze,' far from his wedded wife, of whom he had had no joy though he had given a hundred cattle and promised a thousand more.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Homer, Iliad, Book 11 (Butler 1898); not verbatim.

passages.text: Coon, Antenor's eldest son, crept up unseen and drove his spear through the king's forearm. Agamemnon was convulsed with pain, but did not leave off fighting: he sprang upon Coon as he dragged the dead body of his brother, and struck him with his bronze-shod spear, killing him over Iphidamas — and then cut off his head. Thus did the sons of Antenor meet their fate at the hands of the son of Atreus, and go down together into the house of Hades.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Homer, Iliad, Book 11 (Butler 1898); not verbatim.

passages.text: As long as the blood welled warm from the wound the king went on attacking the ranks of the enemy with spear and sword and great handfuls of stone; but when the blood dried and the pain came, sharp as the pangs which the Eilithuiae send upon a woman in labour, he sprang into his chariot with a cry to the two Ajaxes to save the host — and rode from the field.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Homer, Iliad, Book 11 (Butler 1898); not verbatim.

title.en: Briseis Weeps for Patroclus
title.zh: 布里塞伊斯哭帕特羅克洛斯

region.en: Achaean camp, Troy (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 特洛伊希臘營地（象徵性定位）

period: Composed c. 8th century BCE (Butler translation 1898)

source.work: Homer, Iliad, trans. Samuel Butler (1898), Book XIX

summary.en: Briseis, the war-prize returned to Achilles' tent, sees the mangled body of Patroclus laid out for the rites, and throws herself upon it. She laments: her own husband and three brothers were killed the same day in the sack of her city, and yet it was Patroclus who had comforted her then, promising that Achilles would marry her in Phthia. The women weep around her — in appearance for Patroclus, in truth for their own sorrows. And Achilles, refusing food, sits by the dead man through the night.
summary.zh: 布里塞伊斯——重返阿基琉斯帳中的戰利品——見帕特羅克洛斯殘軀陳列待殮，撲身其上痛哭。她哀悼：她的丈夫與三個兄弟皆在同日喪生，而當時安慰她的正是帕特羅克洛斯，他許諾阿基琉斯將在弗提亞娶她為妻。婦女們繞其哭泣——貌為亡者，實為己悲。阿基琉斯拒食，徹夜守屍。

sensitivity.note: Ancient literary source; no living community restrictions.

passages.text: Briseis, fair as Venus, when she saw the mangled body of Patroclus, flung herself upon it and cried aloud, tearing her breast, her neck, and her lovely face with both her hands. Beautiful as a goddess she wept and said: 'Patroclus, dearest friend, when I went hence I left you living; I return, O prince, to find you dead; thus do fresh sorrows multiply upon me one after the other. I saw him to whom my father and mother married me cut down before our city, and my three own dear brothers perished with him on the self-same day.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Homer, Iliad, Book 19 (Butler 1898); not verbatim.

passages.text: 'But you, Patroclus, even when Achilles slew my husband and sacked the city of noble Mynes, told me that I was not to weep, for you said you would make Achilles marry me, and take me back with him to Phthia, and we should have a wedding feast among the Myrmidons. You were always kind to me, and I shall never cease to grieve for you.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Homer, Iliad, Book 19 (Butler 1898); not verbatim.

passages.text: She wept as she spoke, and the women joined in her lament-making, as though their tears were for Patroclus, but in truth each was weeping for her own sorrows. Achilles, refusing meat and drink, lay by the dead man all night, and Zeus, looking down in pity, bade Athena drop nectar and ambrosia into his breast so that he might feel no hunger for what he had to do.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Homer, Iliad, Book 19 (Butler 1898); not verbatim.

title.en: The Fight for the Body of Patroclus
title.zh: 爭奪帕特羅克洛斯遺體

region.en: Plains of Troy (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 特洛伊平原（象徵性定位）

period: Composed c. 8th century BCE (Butler translation 1898)

source.work: Homer, Iliad, trans. Samuel Butler (1898), Book XVII

summary.en: Hector has the armour and wants the body; Ajax and Menelaus want it too, and the two hosts surge around it. Hippothous, son of the Pelasgian Lethus, drags it off by the foot — and Ajax strikes him through the helmet, so that the brain oozes through the crest-socket and the body falls. Phorcys, bestriding Hippothous, is next, and is stabbed in the belly so that his entrails pour out. Aeneas and Hector rally the Trojans; Ajax calls for a fighting retreat around the corpse, and the dead man is carried back to the ships under a rain of spears.
summary.zh: 赫克托耳已奪甲而欲奪屍；埃阿斯與墨涅拉俄斯亦力爭。色雷斯人希波托俄斯拖屍欲走，被埃阿斯一矛貫盔、腦漿溢出而亡；跨騎其上的福爾科斯腹中矛而死。埃涅阿斯與赫克托耳重整特洛伊軍勢；兩位埃阿斯呼籲圍屍且戰且退，終在如雨之矛下將遺體護回船陣。

sensitivity.note: Ancient literary source; no living community restrictions.

passages.text: At first the Trojans drove the Achaeans back, and they withdrew from the dead man daunted; the Trojans did not succeed in killing anyone, but they drew the body away. The Achaeans did not lose it long, for Ajax, foremost of the Danaans after Achilles, rallied them like a wild boar at bay on the mountains, and made towards the front through the phalanxes of the Trojans.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Homer, Iliad, Book 17 (Butler 1898); not verbatim.

passages.text: At this moment Hippothous, brave son of the Pelasgian Lethus, in his zeal for Hector and the Trojans, was dragging the body off by the foot through the press of the fight, having bound a strap round the sinews near the ankle. A mischief soon befell him from which none could save him: Ajax, son of Telamon, sprang forward and smote him on his bronze-cheeked helmet. The plumed headpiece broke about the point of the weapon, struck at once by the spear and the strong hand, so that the bloody brain came oozing out through the crest-socket; his strength failed him, and he let Patroclus' foot drop from his hand, as he fell full length dead upon the body.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Homer, Iliad, Book 17 (Butler 1898); not verbatim.

passages.text: Hector took aim at Ajax with a spear; the spear passed on and struck Schedius, son of noble Iphitus, captain of the Phocaeans, under the middle of the collarbone, and his armour rang as he fell. Ajax struck Phorcys, son of Phaenops, in the middle of the belly as he was bestriding Hippothous, and broke the plate of his cuirass; the spear tore out his entrails and he clutched the ground in his palm as he fell.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Homer, Iliad, Book 17 (Butler 1898); not verbatim.

passages.text: The Argives drew off the bodies of Phorcys and Hippothous and stripped them of their armour; and the two Ajaxes, calling the best of the Achaeans about the corpse of Patroclus, faced the Trojan line and fought round the dead man, giving ground slowly and carrying him with them, until, with the body safe between them, they had it once more among the ships.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Homer, Iliad, Book 17 (Butler 1898); not verbatim.

title.en: The Gods Restrained
title.zh: 眾神受制

region.en: Mount Olympus (mythic geography)
region.zh: 奧林波斯山（神話地理）

period: Composed c. 8th century BCE (Butler translation 1898)

source.work: Homer, Iliad, trans. Samuel Butler (1898), Book VIII

summary.en: Zeus forbids the gods to help either host, on pain of lightning and Tartarus, and announces his scale: he will not stay his hand until Hector reaches the Achaean ships. The gods sit silent; Athena alone, eager to go down, is checked with a threat; and Zeus hangs his golden scales from the sky, weighing the fates of the two armies, till the Trojans' side sinks toward the plain.
summary.zh: 宙斯嚴禁諸神援助兩軍，違者以雷霆與塔耳塔羅斯為罰，並預告其定局：赫克托耳將直逼希臘船陣。諸神默然；唯雅典娜欲下而止於威嚇之下。宙斯自天懸金秤，權衡兩軍之命，特洛伊一側下沉向平原。

sensitivity.note: Ancient literary source; no living community restrictions.

passages.text: When Morning in her robe of saffron began to suffuse light over the earth, Zeus called the gods in council on the topmost crest of Olympus: 'Hear me, gods and goddesses, that I may speak as I am minded. Let none of you, neither goddess nor god, try to cross me, but obey me every one, that I may bring this matter to an end.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Homer, Iliad, Book 8 (Butler 1898); not verbatim.

passages.text: The penalty, he said, would be swift: any god found working apart, on either side, would be hurled into the darkness of Tartarus by his own hand; and, so far from aiding the Greeks, he would go on letting Hector rage till the ships burned and the Greeks had paid for the wrong done to his anger.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Homer, Iliad, Book 8 (Butler 1898); not verbatim.

passages.text: So the gods sat silent in their places. Only Athena rose, because her heart was hot for the Achaeans, and stood before her father; and Zeus, smiling darkly, bade her sit down and not think of opening battle on her own account: the hand that wielded the thunderbolt was stronger than all Olympus. And she went back to her seat in silence, while the rest of the gods stayed where they were.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Homer, Iliad, Book 8 (Butler 1898); not verbatim.

passages.text: Then Zeus took his stand on Ida's highest crest and hung his golden scales from the sky: on one pan the fates of the Trojans, on the other the fates of the Achaeans, and he lifted the balance by the middle. The Achaeans' side sank down toward the plain; the Trojans' rose toward the heaven; and in that balance the day was given, until night should fall, to Hector and the men of Troy.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Homer, Iliad, Book 8 (Butler 1898); not verbatim.

title.en: Nestor's Tent and the Wounded Kings
title.zh: 涅斯托耳的帳篷與受傷的諸王

region.en: Achaean camp, Troy (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 特洛伊希臘營地（象徵性定位）

period: Composed c. 8th century BCE (Butler translation 1898)

source.work: Homer, Iliad, trans. Samuel Butler (1898), Book XI

summary.en: Machaon, wounded by an arrow, is carried out of the fight in Nestor's chariot. In the old man's tent the fair Hecamede mixes the famous cup — Pramnian wine, goat's-milk cheese grated with bronze, white barley-meal — in the two-handled cup with golden doves feeding on every rim, which none but Nestor could lift when full. As they drink, Nestor, wise as ever, tells how his own sons once fought; and Patroclus, sent by Achilles to learn who had been wounded, is moved by the old man's words to go back and beg Achilles for his armour.
summary.zh: 被箭射傷的瑪卡翁由涅斯托耳之車載出戰場。老將帳中，美貌的赫卡墨得調製名酒：普刺姆尼亞酒、青銅擦磨的山羊乳酪、白大麥粉——盛於四耳雙足、每耳有兩隻金鴿啄食之杯，此杯滿時唯涅斯托耳能舉。飲酒間，老人細述往事；帕特羅克洛斯奉阿基琉斯之命來探傷者，聞言動容，遂返營為友求甲。

sensitivity.note: Ancient literary source; no living community restrictions.

passages.text: Machaon the physician, wounded by an arrow, was taken out of the fight in Nestor's chariot; and the old man, setting his horses loose to graze, brought him to his tent by the sea, where Eurymedon took the horses from the chariot and they stood in the breeze to dry the sweat from their shirts.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Homer, Iliad, Book 11 (Butler 1898); not verbatim.

passages.text: Fair Hecamede, whom Nestor had had awarded to him from Tenedos when Achilles took it — a daughter of wise Arsinous, given to Nestor because he excelled all of them in counsel — mixed them a mess: a vessel of bronze, an onion for relish, honey and cakes of barley-meal; and in the cup of rare workmanship, studded with bosses of gold, with four handles on each of which two golden doves were feeding, she grated goat's-milk cheese with a bronze grater, threw in a handful of white barley-meal, and poured Pramnian wine. None but Nestor could lift that cup when it was full.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Homer, Iliad, Book 11 (Butler 1898); not verbatim.

passages.text: As they drank, Nestor turned the talk to the fortunes of the war and to the wounded kings, and blamed the army's faltering; and when Patroclus came, standing at the door in Achilles' armour of state, to learn who had been hurt, the old man took him by the words: he told him of the days when the Pylians had fought the Epeans, and begged him to carry to Achilles' ear the plight of the wounded host — for Achilles, he said, might yet save them all.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Homer, Iliad, Book 11 (Butler 1898); not verbatim.

passages.text: And Patroclus went back along the ships, remembering the old man's words, and carrying with him a comrade wounded in the shoulder — Eurypylus — for the old man's speech had lit in him the first spark of the pity that was to cost him his life.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Homer, Iliad, Book 11 (Butler 1898); not verbatim.

title.en: The Truce Broken
title.zh: 休戰破裂

region.en: Plains of Troy (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 特洛伊平原（象徵性定位）

period: Composed c. 8th century BCE (Butler translation 1898)

source.work: Homer, Iliad, trans. Samuel Butler (1898), Book IV

summary.en: The truce is sworn, but the gods are not done: Hera and Athena press Zeus to let the Trojans be made the first oath-breakers, and Athena, in the shape of Laodocus, goes down the Trojan ranks to the archer Pandarus with the promise of glory for shooting Menelaus. The arrow flies through belt and cuirass and grazes the flesh, and the wound bleeds like ivory streaked with purple. Agamemnon, his brother's blood on the wound, walks the host in person — praising the willing and shaming the laggards — and war is made again.
summary.zh: 和約既立而神明未息怒：赫拉與雅典娜促宙斯使特洛伊先毁誓；雅典娜化身拉俄多科斯，下至弓手潘達羅斯，許諾榮耀誘其射墨涅拉俄斯。箭穿腰帶與甲冑、擦破皮肉，如象牙染紫。阿伽門農見兄長傷口流血，親巡全軍——褒勇者、譴懦夫——戰火重燃。

sensitivity.note: Ancient literary source; no living community restrictions.

passages.text: The oaths had been sworn, the lambs sacrificed; but Zeus's daughter Athena, eager to see the Trojans made the first to break them, put on the shape of Laodocus, son of Antenor, and walked the ranks till she found Pandarus, son of Lycaon, the bowman of the Aesopus valley.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Homer, Iliad, Book 4 (Butler 1898); not verbatim.

passages.text: 'Brave son of Lycaon,' she said, 'if you dare send an arrow at Menelaus you will win honour and thanks from all the Trojans, and especially from Alexander, who would be the first to requite you handsomely if he could see Menelaus mount his funeral pyre. Take your aim now, and pray to Lycian Apollo, the famous archer, vowing a hecatomb of firstling lambs when you get home.' His fool's heart was persuaded.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Homer, Iliad, Book 4 (Butler 1898); not verbatim.

passages.text: He took out his bow of wild-ibex horn, sixteen palms long, gold-tipped by a worker in horn; he laid the arrow on the string and prayed to Lycian Apollo as he drew, and let fly. But the blessed gods did not forget Menelaus: Athena caught the shaft and turned it — through belt, cuirass and under-belt — till it grazed his skin, and the blood began to run, dark and purple, down his fair thighs like the streak on a piece of Meonian ivory.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Homer, Iliad, Book 4 (Butler 1898); not verbatim.

passages.text: Agamemnon saw the blood and shuddered; but Menelaus, looking at the arrow's barbs, said the wound was light. The king wept and cried aloud to the host that the Trojans had broken the truce; and with the guilt laid openly on the enemy he went through the ranks on foot, cheering the men he found eager and shaming, in terrible words, those he found shirking — that no Achaean might say the king had not set the war in order again.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Homer, Iliad, Book 4 (Butler 1898); not verbatim.

title.en: The Wall That Was Not Blessed
title.zh: 未經神許的城牆

region.en: Achaean wall, Troy (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 特洛伊希臘營牆（象徵性定位）

period: Composed c. 8th century BCE (Butler translation 1898)

source.work: Homer, Iliad, trans. Samuel Butler (1898), Book XII

summary.en: The Achaeans' trench and wall had been built without hecatombs to the gods, and so, the poet tells us, it did not last: after the war, Poseidon and Apollo turned the rivers of Ida on it and washed it into the sea. In its day, however, it stood. Asius, son of Hyrtacus, in his foolhardiness brought his horses to the wall and died there; Sarpedon led the Lycians over the trench on foot, and the Lycians scaled the wall with stones; and Ajax and Teucer held the parapet, shooting and shoving, until the tide of the assault broke and the Lycian captains turned back.
summary.zh: 希臘人的壕溝與城牆未經祭神便建成，故詩人言其不久存：戰後波塞冬與阿波羅引伊達諸河之水將其沖入海中。然而牆在時，阿西俄斯愚勇驅馬直衝而亡；薩爾佩冬徒步率呂基亞人越壕，攀牆投石；埃阿斯與透克羅斯於牆頭堅守，直到呂基亞攻勢潰退。

sensitivity.note: Ancient literary source; no living community restrictions.

passages.text: The Argives and Trojans fought desperately, and the trench and the high wall above it did not keep the Trojans in check longer; for they had built it to protect their ships, and dug the trench all round it, but they had not offered hecatombs to the gods. It had been built without the consent of the immortals, and therefore it did not last.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Homer, Iliad, Book 12 (Butler 1898); not verbatim.

passages.text: The poet stops the tale to tell its end: so long as Hector lived and Achilles nursed his anger, and so long as the city of Priam remained untaken, the great wall stood firm; but when the bravest of either side were gone, and the city was sacked in the tenth year, then Poseidon and Apollo turned on it the streams of all the rivers from Mount Ida — Rhesus, Heptaporus, Caresus, Rhodius, Grenicus, Aesopus and goodly Scamander with Simois — and for nine days Apollo drove the waters against it while Zeus rained, till the wall was washed into the sea and Neptune with his trident threw its beams and stones into the Hellespont, spreading a great beach of sand over the place where it had been.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Homer, Iliad, Book 12 (Butler 1898); not verbatim.

passages.text: While the wall yet stood, the Trojans and their allies followed the counsel of Polydamas, dismounting and coming over the trench on foot in five companies; but Asius, son of Hyrtacus, in his foolhardiness took his horses and his esquire with him toward the ships, nor did he fail to come by his end in consequence: death of ill-omened name overshadowed him ere he could return to wind-beaten Ilius exulting in his chariot.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Homer, Iliad, Book 12 (Butler 1898); not verbatim.

passages.text: Sarpedon led the Lycians over on foot, with Glaucus and Asteropaeus, and charged straight at the Danaans, holding his shield before him in the manner of a lion. And over the trench and up the wall the Lycians swarmed with stones, while on the parapet stood Ajax and Teucer, Ajax shoving down with great stones what came near, Teucer bending his bow and shooting; and when a Lycian came over the battlement, Ajax took him by the breastplate and cast him out; so the wall held for that day, and the Lycian captains, beaten back, turned again to their ships.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Homer, Iliad, Book 12 (Butler 1898); not verbatim.

title.en: The Bow of Iphitus
title.zh: 伊菲特斯之弓

region.en: Ithaca & Messene (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 伊薩卡與美塞尼（象徵性定位）

period: Composed c. 8th century BCE (Butler translation 1898)

source.work: Homer, Odyssey, trans. Samuel Butler (1898), Book XX

summary.en: Athena puts it into Penelope's mind to bring out the great bow; and the poet tells how Odysseus came by it. The bow had been left him by Iphitus, son of Eurytus, whom he met in Messene on a mission to recover sheep stolen from Ithaca; Iphitus had been hunting twelve lost brood mares when he fell in with Heracles — and Heracles, to his shame, killed his guest, fearing neither heaven nor the table he had set before Iphitus, and kept the mares. Iphitus had given Ulysses the bow that mighty Eurytus had carried, and Ulysses had given him a sword and a spear in return — a friendship that, for Heracles' crime, never got to be a visit.
summary.zh: 雅典娜令珀涅羅珀取出大弓；詩人敘其來歷：奧德修斯赴美塞尼追討失羊，途中遇伊菲特斯（歐律托斯之子）——後者為尋十二匹失馬而遇赫拉克勒斯，卻被其殺害，蓋神懼天譴、亦不敬所設之宴。伊菲特斯生前以父之強弓贈奧德修斯，奧德修斯回贈劍矛；友誼未及深交便為赫拉克勒斯之罪所斷。

sensitivity.note: Ancient literary source; no living community restrictions.

passages.text: Minerva now put it in Penelope's mind to make the suitors try their skill with the bow and with the iron axes, in contest among themselves, as a means of bringing about their destruction. She went upstairs and got the store-room key, which was made of bronze and had a handle of ivory, and went with her maidens into the store-room at the end of the house, where her husband's treasures were kept — and where was also his bow, and the quiver full of deadly arrows that had been given him by a friend whom he had met in Lacedaemon: Iphitus, son of Eurytus.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Homer, Odyssey, Book 20 (Butler 1898); not verbatim.

passages.text: The two fell in with one another in Messene, at the house of Ortilochus, where Ulysses was staying in order to recover a debt owing from the whole people — for the Messenians had carried off three hundred sheep from Ithaca, and had sailed away with them and with their shepherds. In quest of these Ulysses took a long journey while still quite young, for his father and the other chieftains had sent him on a mission to recover them.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Homer, Odyssey, Book 20 (Butler 1898); not verbatim.

passages.text: Iphitus had gone there also, to try to get back twelve brood mares that he had lost, with the mule foals that were running with them. These mares were the death of him in the end: for when he went to the house of Jove's son, mighty Heracles, who performed such prodigies of valour, Heracles, to his shame, killed him — though he was his guest, for he feared not heaven's vengeance, nor yet respected his own table which he had set before Iphitus, but killed him in spite of everything, and kept the mares himself.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Homer, Odyssey, Book 20 (Butler 1898); not verbatim.

passages.text: It was when claiming these that Iphitus met Ulysses, and gave him the bow which mighty Eurytus had been used to carry, and which, on his death, had been left to his son. Ulysses gave him in return a sword and a spear; and this was the beginning of a fast friendship, though they never visited at one another's houses, for Jove's son Heracles killed Iphitus before they could do so. And when Ulysses sailed for Troy the bow was left behind, a keepsake from a valued friend.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Homer, Odyssey, Book 20 (Butler 1898); not verbatim.

title.en: The Beggar in the Hall
title.zh: 大廳中的乞丐

region.en: Odysseus's hall, Ithaca (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 伊薩卡奧德修斯王宮（象徵性定位）

period: Composed c. 8th century BCE (Butler translation 1898)

source.work: Homer, Odyssey, trans. Samuel Butler (1898), Books XVII-XVIII

summary.en: Odysseus, in the disguise of a beggar, comes into his own hall with the swineherd, and the humiliation begins: Antinous throws a footstool at him and the household laughs; Melanthius the goatherd rails; and Irus, the town's other beggar — a hulking glutton called Arnaeus, named Irus for running errands — is set on by the suitors to fight him for the doorway. Athena thickens the limbs of the old man; Irus, once sobered by the sight, is beaten almost to death, and dragged out by the heels to be food for dogs and swine.
summary.zh: 偽裝乞丐的奧德修斯隨牧豬人步入自家大廳，羞辱隨之而來：安提諾俄斯擲凳、僕人訕笑、牧羊人墨蘭提俄斯斥罵；城中另一乞丐伊魯斯——本名阿耳奈俄斯、因跑腿而得名的貪食大漢——被求婚者慫恿，為爭門口而與「老乞」較量。雅典娜使老人的肢體粗壯；伊魯斯見狀膽怯仍戰，被幾近打死，拖足拖出，欲作狗豬之食。

sensitivity.note: Ancient literary source; no living community restrictions.

passages.text: There came a certain common tramp who used to go begging all over the city of Ithaca, and was notorious as an incorrigible glutton and drunkard — a great hulking fellow to look at, though he had no strength nor stay in him; his real name, the one his mother gave him, was Arnaeus, but the young men of the place called him Irus, because he used to run errands for anyone who would send him.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Homer, Odyssey, Book 18 (Butler 1898); not verbatim.

passages.text: As soon as he came he began to insult Ulysses, and to try to drive him out of his own house: 'Be off, old man, from the doorway, or you shall be dragged out neck and heels. Do you not see that they are all giving me the wink, and wanting me to turn you out by force?' Ulysses frowned and said there was room enough in the doorway for the pair of them; but Irus would not hear it, and Antinous, pleased at the quarrel, offered the victorious beggar sausages and a seat at the suitors' feast if he would clear the hall of the other.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Homer, Odyssey, Book 18 (Butler 1898); not verbatim.

passages.text: Athena stood by the true beggar and thickened his limbs, and when Irus saw the great size of the man's thighs he came near fainting; but the suitors had given their word, and the fight was fought in the hall for the prize of the puddings. Ulysses, mindful of his own plan, did not quite kill him: he broke him about the jaw, and he fell in the doorway with a thud, and the household laughed.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Homer, Odyssey, Book 18 (Butler 1898); not verbatim.

passages.text: And Eurymachus, in his mockery, hurled a footstool at the old man; the stool hit the cupbearer on his right hand and knocked him down, and his wine-jug rang to the ground. The suitors, in an uproar, wished the stranger gone — 'we cannot permit such disturbance about a beggar' — and Ulysses, nursing his anger, went out and sat among the swineherd and the cattle, saying to himself what he would do to the whole of them before the day was out.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Homer, Odyssey, Books 17-18 (Butler 1898); not verbatim.

title.en: Hecate's Threefold Honours
title.zh: 赫卡忒的三重榮光

region.en: Earth, sea & starry heaven (mythic geography)
region.zh: 大地、海洋與星空（神話地理）

period: Composed c. 700 BCE (Evelyn-White translation 1914)

source.work: Hesiod, Theogony, trans. Hugh G. Evelyn-White (1914), lines ca. 411-452

summary.en: Asteria, daughter of Coeus and Phoebe, bore Hecate, whom Zeus honoured above all: a portion of earth, of the barren sea, and of starry heaven; and whoever calls on her in prayer is heard, for she stands by kings in assembly, by horsemen in battle, by athletes in contest, by fishermen at their nets, and with Hermes increases the herds in the pens. She is nurse of all children who see the light of Eos; and her honours, given in the beginning, are never taken away.
summary.zh: 科俄斯與福柏之女阿斯特瑞亞生赫卡忒，宙斯予其榮光超越諸神：大地一份、荒海一份、星空一份。凡祈禱者皆蒙垂聽：她伴君王於議會、騎士於疆場、健兒於賽場、漁夫於網前；又與赫爾墨斯共掌畜群之興衰；並為初見晨光之孩童的乳母。其榮光自始不受剝奪。

sensitivity.note: Ancient literary source; no living community restrictions.

passages.text: Phoebe came to the bed of Coeus, and the goddess, pregnant with the god's love, bore dark-robed Leto, ever gentle, kind to men and to the deathless gods — kindest of those on Olympus. Phoebe also bore honourable Asteria, whom Perses led to his great house to become his wife.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Theogony, lines ca. 404-410 (Evelyn-White 1914); not verbatim.

passages.text: And Asteria bore Hecate, whom Zeus, Cronos' son, honoured above all others. He gave her splendid gifts: a portion of the earth and the barren sea, a share of the honour from the starry skies, and the highest honours from the immortal gods.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Theogony, lines ca. 411-416 (Evelyn-White 1914); not verbatim.

passages.text: Now, whenever humans on the earth pray for favours by offering beautiful sacrifices, they call on Hecate: much honour follows the ones whose prayers the goddess kindly accepts, and fortune follows those so blessed — such is her power. For all those born to Gaia and Ouranos were granted honours, and Hecate had her share too. Nor did the son of Cronos seek to deprive her of any honour she received from the Titans, and she retains all she was given in the beginning.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Theogony, lines ca. 416-422 (Evelyn-White 1914); not verbatim.

passages.text: When men arm themselves for deadly combat, she stands beside her chosen side, eager to grant victory and extend glory; she stands beside revered kings in the courts of justice; she stands beside horsemen, and beside those competing in the games. To those who work the gusty grey sea and pray to Hecate and the roaring Earth-shaker, she grants a great haul of fish, and just as easily takes it away. And along with Hermes she excels at increasing livestock in the pens, and can strengthen a herd or a flock or weaken it, whatever her spirit desires. And though she is her mother's only child, she is granted great honours among the immortals; and Cronos' son made her nurse to all children who see with their eyes the light of all-seeing Eos.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Theogony, lines ca. 422-452 (Evelyn-White 1914); not verbatim.

title.en: Nereus and the Fifty Daughters of Doris
title.zh: 涅柔斯與多里斯的五十女兒

region.en: The barren sea (mythic geography)
region.zh: 荒涼之海（神話地理）

period: Composed c. 700 BCE (Evelyn-White translation 1914)

source.work: Hesiod, Theogony, trans. Hugh G. Evelyn-White (1914), lines ca. 233-264

summary.en: Pontus fathered the truthful Nereus — the Old Man of the Sea, gentle and kind, who never forgets what is due and makes fair and honest plans — and Nereus, wedding Doris, daughter of Ocean, had fifty daughters in the barren sea. Of them all, the poet names only a handful before going through the rest: Protho, Eucrante, Sao, Amphitrite, Eudora, Thetis, Galene, Glauce, Cymothoe, Speo, Thalia, Pasithea, Erato, Eunice, Melite, Eulimene, Agave, Doto, Proto, Pherusa, Dynamene, Nessea, Actaea, Protomedea, Doris, Panope, Galatea, Hippothoe, Hipponoe, Cymodoce, Cymatolege, Cymo, Eione, Halimede, Glauconome, Pontoporea, Leagore, Euagore, Laomeda, Polynoe, Autonoe, Lusianassa, Euarne, Psamathe, Menippe, Neso, Eupompe, Themisto, Pronoe, Nemertes.
summary.zh: 旁托斯生下「海上老人」涅柔斯——溫厚誠實、不忘道義、謀劃公正；涅柔斯娶大洋之女多里斯，於荒海中生下五十位女兒：普羅托、歐克拉忒、薩奧、安菲特里忒、歐多拉、忒提斯、伽勒涅、格勞刻、庫墨托厄、斯佩俄、塔利亞、帕西忒亞、厄拉托、歐尼刻、墨利忒、厄利墨涅、阿伽瑪、多托、普洛托、費魯莎、狄娜墨涅、涅賽亞、阿克泰亞、普洛托墨狄亞、多里斯、帕諾珀、伽拉忒亞、希波托厄、希波諾厄、庫墨多刻、庫墨托勒革、庫摩、厄俄涅、哈利墨得、格勞科諾墨、蓬托波瑞亞、勒阿戈瑞、歐阿戈瑞、拉俄墨達、波呂諾厄、奧托諾厄、路西安那薩、歐阿耳涅、普薩瑪忒、墨尼珀、涅索、歐篷珀、忒彌斯托、普羅諾厄、涅墨耳忒斯。

sensitivity.note: Ancient literary source; no living community restrictions.

passages.text: Pontus fathered truthful and sincere Nereus, his eldest child: they call him the Old Man, for he is gentle and kind, never forgets what is due, and makes fair and honest plans. Then he mixed again with Gaia and begat great Thaumas, arrogant Phorcys, fair-cheeked Ceto, and Eurybia, whose heart is of steel. And many children, all greatly desired, were born in the barren sea to Nereus and fair-haired Doris, daughter of ever-circling Ocean.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Theogony, lines ca. 233-236 (Evelyn-White 1914); not verbatim. / Paraphrase of Theogony, lines ca. 237-242 (Evelyn-White 1914); not verbatim.

passages.text: These came from the illustrious Nereus: fifty daughters, all able to do great work — from Protho and Eucrante to Psamathe and Menippe, Neso and Eupompe, Themisto, Pronoe and Nemertes — sea-maidens whose company fills the waters of the Greek world, and of whom Thetis and Amphitrite would one day wed heroes and gods.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Theogony, lines ca. 240-264 (Evelyn-White 1914); not verbatim.

title.en: The River-Gods and the Oceanids
title.zh: 河神與大洋神女

region.en: World-encircling Oceanus (mythic geography)
region.zh: 環世大洋（神話地理）

period: Composed c. 700 BCE (Evelyn-White translation 1914)

source.work: Hesiod, Theogony, trans. Hugh G. Evelyn-White (1914), lines ca. 337-370

summary.en: Tethys bore to Oceanus the river-gods of the world — Nilus, Alpheus, Eridanus, Strymon, Meander, Ister, Phasis, Rhesus, the silver-eddying Achelous, Nessus, Rhodius, Haliacmon, Heptaporus, Grenicus, Aesepus, divine Simois, Peneius, Hermus, Caicus, the great Sangarius, Ladon, Parthenius, Euenus, Aldescus, and divine Scamander — and with them the daughters who with lord Apollo and the Rivers raise up young boys to be men. And there are three thousand more rivers, says the poet, too many for a mortal to name, but each known to the people who live beside it.
summary.zh: 忒堤斯為俄刻阿諾斯生下世間諸河神：尼羅河、阿爾甫斯、厄里達諾斯、斯特呂蒙、邁安德、伊斯特爾、法西斯、瑞索斯、銀旋的阿克洛俄斯、涅索斯、羅狄俄斯、哈利阿科門、赫普塔波魯斯、格瑞尼科斯、埃塞波斯、神聖的西摩伊斯、珀紐斯、赫爾穆斯、開科斯、大桑伽里烏斯、拉冬、帕爾忒尼俄斯、厄維諾斯、阿爾得索斯與神聖的斯卡曼德羅斯；此外還有三千條河，凡人無法一一唱名，卻皆為鄉人熟知。

sensitivity.note: Ancient literary source; no living community restrictions.

passages.text: Tethys bore to Oceanus the twisting rivers: Nilus, Alpheus, the deep-swirling Eridanus, Strymon, Meander, beautiful Ister, Phasis, Rhesus, the silver-eddying Achelous, Nessus, Rhodius, Haliacmon, Heptaporus, Grenicus, Aesepus, divine Simoeis, Peneius, Hermus, fair-flowing Caicus, the great Sangarius, Ladon, Parthenius, Euenus, Aldescus, and the divine Scamander.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Theogony, lines ca. 337-355 (Evelyn-White 1914); not verbatim.

passages.text: And she bore divine daughters who raised young boys into men, along with lord Apollo and the River-gods — for so Zeus charged them: Peitho, Admete, Ianthe, Electra, Doris, Prymno, divine-formed Ourania, Hippo, Clymene, Rhodea, Callirrhoe, Zeuxo, Clytie, Idyia, Pasithoe, Plexaura, Galaxaura, welcoming Dione, Melobosis, Thoe, shapely Polydora, fair-formed Cerceis, doe-eyed Pluto, Perseis, Ianeira, Acaste, Xanthe, charming Petraea, Menestho, Europa, Metis, Eurynome, saffron-veiled Telesto, Chryseis, Asia, fair Calypso, Eudora, Tyche, Amphiro, Ocyrhoe and Styx, who is without doubt the greatest of them all.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Theogony, lines ca. 355-362 (Evelyn-White 1914); not verbatim.

passages.text: These were the oldest of the maidens born to Oceanus and Tethys; but there are many others: three thousand thin-ankled daughters of Oceanus spread across the earth and the watery depths, all equal, shining children of goddesses. And many other loud-flowing rivers, sons of Oceanus, were born to queen Tethys; their names are difficult for a mortal to recite, but each is known to those who dwell beside them.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Theogony, lines ca. 362-370 (Evelyn-White 1914); not verbatim.

title.en: The Farmer's and the Sailor's Year
title.zh: 農人與水手的年曆

region.en: Ascra, Boeotia (Hesiod's village; symbolic pin)
region.zh: 波厄提亞阿斯克拉村（赫西俄德故鄉，象徵性定位）

period: Composed c. 700 BCE (Evelyn-White translation 1914)

source.work: Hesiod, Works and Days, trans. Hugh G. Evelyn-White (1914), lines ca. 383-694

summary.en: Hesiod sets out the working year by the stars: the Pleiades, Hyades, Orion, Sirius and Arcturus mark ploughing, harvest, threshing and sailing. Plough when the Pleiades rise and fall; harvest when Orion and Sirius are in the sky; cut wood when the leaves have fallen; thresh when Orion rises; sail fifty days after the solstice, when the sea is smooth, and bring the ship up on the sixth after the grape-picking is done. The story is the mythic origin of the Greek agricultural calendar: the stars are the gods' own clock, and the labourer who misses a season goes begging to his neighbours.
summary.zh: 赫西俄德以星辰劃分勞作之年：昴星團、畢宿、獵戶座、天狼星與大角星各標耕作、收穫、揚場與航行之時。昴星升落則犁地；獵戶與天狼當空則收割；葉落則伐木；獵戶升起則揚場；夏至後五十日宜航行；摘葡萄後第六日當收船。此即希臘農事曆之神話起源：星辰乃神明之鐘，誤時之勞作者唯向鄰人乞食。

sensitivity.note: Ancient literary source; no living community restrictions.

passages.text: Hesiod tells Perses to observe the signs from Zeus. The Pleiades, the Hyades, the strength of Orion, and the Bear, which men also call the Wagon, wheel about in the same place, and watch Orion: they alone bathe in the stream of Ocean. It is by the Bear that sailors steer, for she is bright and beautiful to see.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Works and Days, lines ca. 383-397 (Evelyn-White 1914); not verbatim.

passages.text: Harvest the crops when Pleiades, Atlas' daughters, begin to rise, and plough when they are about to set: for forty nights and days they are hidden, and again, as the year moves round, they first appear when the iron is being sharpened. This is the law of the plains and the sea-coast, and of the fertile glens far from the troubled deep: sow naked, plough naked, and reap naked, if you will harvest Demeter's work in due season.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Works and Days, lines ca. 415-426 (Evelyn-White 1914); not verbatim.

passages.text: When Orion and Sirius come into mid-sky, and Arcturus rises in rosy-fingered Dawn, then, Perses, cut your grapes, and bring them home; expose them to the sun ten days and ten, then five in the shade, and on the sixth draw the cups of the joyous wine-gift of Dionysus. And when Orion and Sirius come mid-sky, and Arcturus sees the rosy-fingered Dawn, then Perses, cut your grapes — that was the sign for the whole of the Greek vintage.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Works and Days, lines ca. 609-617, 656-668 (Evelyn-White 1914); not verbatim.

passages.text: For sailing, fifty days after the solstice is the season, when toilsome summer is come to its end: then there is no wind to break a ship, and no man to drown; unless Poseidon the Earth-shaker or Zeus wills it, for they are the keepers of the ends of the sea. But the wind is trustworthy then, and the sea, and the sea is tranquil: put the freight on board, and make for home quickly, and do not wait for the new wine and the autumn rain and the winter's harm, for the sea is then dangerous.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Works and Days, lines ca. 663-678 (Evelyn-White 1914); not verbatim.

title.en: Alcmaeon: The Last Curse of the Necklace
title.zh: 阿爾克邁翁：項鍊的最後詛咒

region.en: Psophis & the river Achelous (mythic geography)
region.zh: 普索菲斯與阿克洛俄斯河（神話地理）

period: Compiled c. 1st-2nd century CE (attrib. Apollodorus; Frazer translation 1921)

source.work: Apollodorus, Library, trans. J. G. Frazer (1921), §§ 3.7.5-3.7.7

summary.en: After the capture of Thebes, when Alcmaeon learned that his mother Eriphyle had been bribed to his undoing also, he was more incensed than ever; and, in accordance with an oracle of Apollo, he killed his own mother. The Fury of the matricide drove him mad: he wandered to Oicles in Arcadia, to Phegeus at Psophis, where he married the king's daughter Alphesiboea and gave her Harmonia's necklace as bride-gift; but his madness followed him everywhere, and the Delphic oracle told him the Fury would leave him nowhere but on land made new since his mother's blood. He found such a land in the silt of the Achelous, married the river's daughter Callirrhoe, and had by her two sons. Zeus, courted by Callirrhoe, made the boys full-grown in a day, and they killed Phegeus and his sons, dedicated the necklace and the robe at Delphi as Achelous had enjoined, and colonized Acarnania — from Acarnan, the elder.
summary.zh: 底比斯陷落後，阿爾克邁翁得知其母厄里菲勒亦受賄賣己，怒火更盛；依阿波羅神諭弒母。弒母之復仇女神使其瘋狂：他流亡至阿卡迪亞的俄伊克勒斯、普索菲斯的費革俄斯（娶其女阿爾斐西波亞，以和諧女神之項鍊為聘禮），然狂疾隨行；德爾菲諭曰：唯「母血未染之地」可避。他在阿克洛俄斯河淤積的新陸定居，娶河之女卡利羅厄，生二子。宙斯應卡利羅厄之請，使二子一夜成人；他們誅費革俄斯父子，依阿克洛俄斯之命將項鍊與嫁衣獻於德爾菲，開拓阿卡納尼亞。

sensitivity.note: Ancient literary source; no living community restrictions.

passages.text: After the capture of Thebes, when Alcmaeon learned that his mother Eriphyle had been bribed to his undoing also, he was more incensed than ever; and, in accordance with an oracle given to him by Apollo, he killed his mother. Some say that he killed her in conjunction with his brother Amphilochus, others that he did it alone.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Apollodorus, Library 3.7.5 (Frazer 1921); not verbatim.

passages.text: But Alcmaeon was visited by the Fury of his mother's murder; and going mad, he first repaired to Oicles in Arcadia, and thence to Phegeus at Psophis. And having been purified there, he married Alphesiboea, the daughter of Phegeus, and gave her the famous necklace and robe of Harmonia as bride-gifts.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Apollodorus, Library 3.7.5 (Frazer 1921); not verbatim.

passages.text: But as while he dwelt in Arcadia his madness became no better, he consulted the oracle at Delphi, and the Pythian priestess informed him that the Avenger of his mother Eriphyle would follow him to every place except to a spot which was most recent, and made by the action of the sea since he had stained himself with his mother's blood. And he found such a place: the Achelous had silted it up, and there he dwelt, and married Callirrhoe, the daughter of Achelous, according to the tradition of the Acarnanians, and had by her two sons, Acarnan and Amphoterus.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Apollodorus, Library 3.7.5-3.7.6 (Frazer 1921); not verbatim.

passages.text: Being apprized of Alcmaeon's untimely end, and courted by Zeus, Callirrhoe requested that the sons she had by Alcmaeon might be full grown in order to avenge their father's murder. And being suddenly full-grown, the sons went forth to right their father's wrong: they killed Phegeus and his sons, pursued the men who carried the necklace, and dedicated the necklace and robe at Delphi according to the injunction of Achelous; then they journeyed to Epirus, collected settlers, and colonized Acarnania, which took its name from the elder of the two.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Apollodorus, Library 3.7.6-3.7.7 (Frazer 1921); not verbatim.

title.en: The Golden Lamb: Atreus and Thyestes
title.zh: 金羔羊：阿特柔斯與堤厄斯忒斯

region.en: Mycenae (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 邁錫尼（象徵性定位）

period: Composed from the lost epics (c. 7th century BCE; summary in Apollodorus; Frazer translation 1921)

source.work: Apollodorus, Library, trans. J. G. Frazer (1921), Epitome e.2.10-e.2.14

summary.en: Atreus once vowed to sacrifice to Artemis the finest of his flocks; but when a golden lamb appeared, they say, he neglected the vow, choked the lamb and kept it in a box; and his wife Aerope gave it secretly to Thyestes, by whom she had been debauched. The Mycenaeans, having received an oracle that they should choose a king of the line of Pelops, sent for Atreus and Thyestes; and Zeus sent Hermes to Atreus with the stipulation that he should be king if the sun went backward. Thyestes agreed to the test, and the sun set in the east: so Atreus got the kingdom and banished his brother. Later, learning of the adultery, Atreus lured Thyestes back under a pretence of friendship, slaughtered his three sons — Aglaus, Callileon and Orchomenus — on the altar of Zeus as suppliants, boiled them limb from limb and served them up to their father; and when Thyestes had eaten heartily, Atreus showed him the extremities, and cast him out of the country. Thyestes then asked the oracle how to pay Atreus out, and was told to beget a son by his own daughter; and the son, Aegisthus, when grown, killed Atreus and restored the kingdom to Thyestes — the last link in the curse that ends with Agamemnon.
summary.zh: 阿特柔斯曾誓祭阿爾忒彌斯己群中最美之羊；金羔羊出現時卻毀誓，勒死羔羊藏於箱中；其妻厄洛珀暗將其交予情人堤厄斯忒斯。邁錫尼人得神諭「立珀羅普斯之裔為王」，召二兄弟；宙斯遣赫爾墨斯告阿特柔斯：若日反行則為王。堤厄斯忒斯同意，日竟自東而落；阿特柔斯得王位，放逐其弟。後阿特柔斯察其通姦，假意和解誘其歸，在其三子（阿格勞斯、卡利勒翁、俄爾科墨諾斯）於宙斯祭壇避難時殺之，肢解煮熟端上餐桌；待父食畢示其手足，再放逐之。堤厄斯忒斯問神諭如何復仇，神諭令其與親女交合生子；其子埃癸斯托斯成年後殺阿特柔斯、復其父位——此詛咒終至阿伽門農。

sensitivity.note: Ancient literary source; violence presented as historical material without endorsement.

passages.text: Now the wife of Atreus was Aerope, daughter of Catreus, and she loved Thyestes. And Atreus once vowed to sacrifice to Artemis the finest of his flocks; but when a golden lamb appeared, they say that he neglected to perform his vow, and having choked the lamb, he deposited it in a box and kept it there; and Aerope gave it to Thyestes, by whom she had been debauched.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Apollodorus, Library, Epitome e.2.10-e.2.11 (Frazer 1921); not verbatim.

passages.text: For the Mycenaeans had received an oracle which bade them choose a Pelopid for their king; so they sent for Atreus and Thyestes.
