title.en: Marsyas the Satyr Flayed Alive
title.zh: 薩提爾馬爾叙阿斯被活剝

region.en: Phrygia (mythic geography)
region.zh: 弗里吉亞（神話地理）

period: Composed c. 8 CE (Latin; Riley translation 1851)

source.archive: Project Gutenberg eBook 21765 (H. T. Riley, trans.)
source.work: Ovid, Metamorphoses, Book VI (Fable IV)

summary.en: The Satyr Marsyas, having challenged Apollo to a trial of skill on the flute, is overcome by the God on the Tritonian reed, and flayed alive for his presumption. 'Why dost thou tear me from myself?' he cries; 'alas! the flute is not of so much value!' As he shrieks aloud, his skin is stripped off from the surface of his limbs, nor is he aught but one entire wound: blood flows on every side, the nerves exposed appear, the quivering veins throb without any skin. The country-folk, the Fauns, his brothers the Satyrs, and Olympus, even then renowned, lamented him; and the fruitful earth, moistened, drank up the falling tears, and sent them forth a stream, the clearest river in Phrygia, which bears the name of Marsyas.
summary.zh: 薩提爾馬爾叙阿斯向阿波羅挑戰吹笛之技，敗於特里托尼亞蘆笛之神，因傲慢而被活剝。他哀嚎：「為何剝我離我自身？唉！笛聲不值得如此！」皮膚自四肢剝離，全身如一傷口：血四流、神經外露、無皮之脈搏動。鄉人、森林之神法翁、其兄弟薩提爾與名琴手奧林波斯皆為之哀悼；濕潤的大地飲下落淚，化為弗里吉亞最清澈之河，名馬爾叙阿斯河。

sensitivity.note: Ancient literary source; violence presented as historical material without endorsement.

passages.text: When thus one, who, it is uncertain, had related the destruction of these men of the Lycian race, another remembers that of the Satyr, whom, overcome in playing on the Tritonian reed, the son of Latona visited with punishment. 'Why,' said he, 'art thou tearing me from myself? Alas! I now repent; alas!' cried he, 'the flute is not of so much value!' As he shrieked aloud, his skin was stripped off from the surface of his limbs, nor was he aught but one entire wound. Blood is flowing on every side; the nerves, exposed, appear, and the quivering veins throb without any skin.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ovid, Metamorphoses VI, Fable IV (Riley 1851); not verbatim.

passages.text: You might have numbered his palpitating bowels, and the transparent lungs within his breast. The inhabitants of the country, the Fauns, Deities of the woods, and his brothers the Satyrs, and Olympus, even then renowned, and the Nymphs lamented him; and whoever besides on those mountains was feeding the wool-bearing flocks, and the horned herds.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ovid, Metamorphoses VI, Fable IV (Riley 1851); not verbatim.

passages.text: The fruitful earth was moistened, and, being moistened, received the falling tears, and drank them up in her lowest veins, which, when she had turned into a stream, she sent forth into the vacant air. And then, as the clearest river in Phrygia, running towards the rapid sea within steep banks, it bears the name of Marsyas.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ovid, Metamorphoses VI, Fable IV (Riley 1851); not verbatim.

title.en: Medea in Corinth
title.zh: 美狄亞在科林斯

region.en: Corinth (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 科林斯（象徵性定位）

period: Composed c. 8 CE (Latin; Riley translation 1851)

source.archive: Project Gutenberg eBook 21765 (H. T. Riley, trans.)
source.work: Ovid, Metamorphoses, Book VII (Fable III)

summary.en: Medea, after having killed Pelias, goes through several countries to Corinth, where, finding that Jason, in her absence, has married the daughter of king Creon, she sets fire to the palace, whereby the princess and her father are consumed. She then murders the two children which she had by Jason, before his face, and takes to flight; and unless she had mounted into the air with winged dragons, she would not have been exempt from punishment. Ovid follows her flight across the map of Greece, past Pelion and Othrys, past the fate of Cerambus who escaped Deucalion's flood on wings given by the nymphs, past the Hyrian lake that a mother's tears made, the Telchines whose eyes corrupted what they looked on, the king of Calaurea changed to a bird with his wife, Cyllene where Menephron lay with his mother, and Cephisus lamenting a grandson changed to a sea-calf — a catalogue of metamorphoses strung on the witch's route.
summary.zh: 美狄亞殺佩利亞斯後輾轉至科林斯；聞伊阿宋已另娶克瑞翁王之女，遂焚王宮，公主與其父一同葬身火海；復在其父面前親手殺害二子，乘飛龍車遁去，否則難逃懲罰。奧維德沿其飛行路線歷數希臘奇景：珀利翁、俄特律斯、乘仙女之翼躲過丟卡利翁洪水之凱朗布斯、希里亞母淚所成之湖、目光致毒的忒爾喀涅斯、卡勞瑞亞王夫婦化鳥、庫勒涅山上門涅夫戎之事、以及克菲索斯為化海豹之孫而泣——以女巫之路串起一串變形故事。

sensitivity.note: Ancient literary source; violence presented as historical material without endorsement.

passages.text: Medea, after having killed Pelias, goes through several countries to Corinth, where, finding that Jason, in her absence, has married the daughter of king Creon, she sets fire to the palace, whereby the princess and her father are consumed. She then murders the two children which she had by Jason, before his face, and takes to flight. And unless she had mounted into the air with winged dragons, she would not have been exempt from punishment.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ovid, Metamorphoses VII, Fable III (Riley 1851); not verbatim.

passages.text: She flies aloft, over both shady Pelion, the lofty habitation of the son of Phillyra, and over Othrys, and the places noted for the fate of the ancient Cerambus: he, by the aid of nymphs, being lifted on wings into the air when the ponderous earth was covered by the sea pouring over it, not being overwhelmed, escaped the flood of Deucalion. On the left side she leaves the Aeolian Pitane and the image of the long Dragon made out of stone, and the wood of Ida, in which Bacchus hid a stolen bullock beneath the appearance of a fictitious stag; the spot, too, where the father of Corythus lies buried beneath a little sand, and the fields which Maera alarmed by her unusual barking.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ovid, Metamorphoses VII, Fable III (Riley 1851); not verbatim.

passages.text: Phoebean Rhodes also, and the Ialysian Telchines, whose eyes, corrupting all things by the very looking upon them, Jupiter, utterly hating, thrust beneath the waves of his brother. She passed, too, over the Cartheian walls of ancient Cea, where her father Alcidamas was destined to wonder that a gentle dove could arise from the body of his daughter. After that, she beholds the lakes of Hyrie and Cycneian Tempe, which the swan that had suddenly become such frequented. For there Phyllius, at the request of the boy, had given him birds, and a fierce lion tamed; being ordered, too, to subdue a bull, he had subdued him; and, being angry at his despising his love so often, he denied him when begging the bull as his last reward. The other, indignant, said, 'Thou shalt wish that thou hadst given it;' and then leaped from a high rock. All imagined he had fallen; but, transformed into a swan, he hovered in the air on snow-white wings. But his mother, Hyrie, not knowing that he was saved, dissolved in tears, and formed a lake called after her own name.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ovid, Metamorphoses VII, Fable III (Riley 1851); not verbatim.

passages.text: After that, she sees the fields of Calaurea, sacred to Latona, conscious of the transformation of their king, together with his wife, into birds. Cyllene is on the right hand, on which Menephron was one day to lie with his mother, after the manner of savage beasts. Far hence she beholds Cephisus, lamenting the fate of his grandson, changed by Apollo into a bloated sea-calf; and the house of Eumelus, lamenting his son in the air. At length, borne on the wings of her dragons, she reached the Pirenian Ephyre. Here, those of ancient times promulgated that in the early ages mortal bodies were produced from mushrooms springing from rain.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ovid, Metamorphoses VII, Fable III (Riley 1851); not verbatim.

title.en: Phineus at the Wedding of Perseus
title.zh: 珀爾修斯婚宴上的菲紐斯

region.en: Ethiopia (mythic geography)
region.zh: 埃塞俄比亞（神話地理）

period: Composed c. 8 CE (Latin; Riley translation 1851)

source.archive: Project Gutenberg eBook 21765 (H. T. Riley, trans.)
source.work: Ovid, Metamorphoses, Book V (Fable I)

summary.en: As Perseus tells the story of Medusa among the guests of Cepheus, the hall fills with a raging multitude: Phineus, to whom Andromeda had been promised before Perseus rescued her, rushes in with an ashen spear, claiming his wife. Cepheus pleads for his son-in-law, and Phineus, pausing, throws his spear into the cushion. The combat turns on altars, goblets, and spears; Aconteus, a soldier of Perseus, is the first to look at the Gorgon and grow stiff with stone, and Astyages, striking the statue with his long sword, shares its nature. Two hundred more follow. Phineus, repenting, begs for his life, and Perseus turns the head on him where he stands — the suppliant face still turned aside, the hands hanging down, the posture of a coward, in stone forever.
summary.zh: 珀爾修斯於刻甫斯宮中講述美杜莎之事時，廳中突起大亂：先前與安德洛墨達有婚約的菲紐斯持槍闖入，稱「要奪回我的妻子」。刻甫斯為女婿求情；菲紐斯猶豫擲矛。戰鬥由祭壇、酒器、長矛展開；珀爾修斯部屬阿孔忒斯最先一瞥戈耳貢首級而石化，阿斯堤阿格斯以長劍擊石像亦隨之變石，另有兩百人同遭此命。菲紐斯悔而求生；珀爾修斯仍以蛇髮首級對準他——其祈求之容、垂手之姿，永化為石。

sensitivity.note: Ancient literary source; no living community restrictions.

passages.text: And while the hero, the son of Danaë, is relating these things in the midst of the company of the subjects of Cepheus, the royal courts are filled with a raging multitude; nor is the clamour such as celebrates a marriage-feast, but one which portends dreadful warfare. Foremost among them, Phineus, the rash projector of the onslaught, shaking an ashen spear with a brazen point, cries, 'Behold! now, behold! I am come, the avenger of my wife, ravished from me; neither shall thy wings nor Jupiter turned into fictitious gold deliver thee from me.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ovid, Metamorphoses V, Fable I (Riley 1851); not verbatim.

passages.text: Cepheus pleads for the son-in-law: it was not Perseus that took Andromeda from him, but the incensed majesty of the Nereids and horned Ammon and the monster of the sea; she was snatched from thee at the moment she was to have perished. Thou didst not come to save her, wilt thou now be grieving that she was saved? Phineus paused, and then, vainly, threw his spear: it stuck in the cushion; and Perseus, leaping off his couch, would have pierced his breast had not Phineus gone behind an altar — an altar, how unworthily, protecting a miscreant.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ovid, Metamorphoses V, Fable I (Riley 1851); not verbatim.

passages.text: The battle raged; and then, as one man, Aconteus by name, a soldier of Perseus, on beholding the Gorgon, grew hard with stone rising upon him. Astyages, thinking him still alive, struck him with his long sword; the sword resounded with a shrill ringing. While Astyages was in amazement, he took on himself the same nature, and the look of one in surprise remained on his marble features. Two hundred bodies, on beholding the Gorgon, grew stiff.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ovid, Metamorphoses V, Fable I (Riley 1851); not verbatim.

passages.text: Now at length Phineus repents of this unjust warfare. But what can he do? He sees statues varying in form, and he recognizes his friends, and demands help of them each, called by name; and not yet persuaded, he touches the bodies next him; they are marble. He turns away his eyes; and thus suppliant, stretching forth his hands that confessed his fault, he says: 'Perseus, thou hast conquered; remove the direful monster, and take away that stone-making face of thy Medusa, whatever she may be. I am not sorry to yield. Grant me nothing, most valiant man, beyond this life; the rest be thine.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ovid, Metamorphoses V, Fable I (Riley 1851); not verbatim.

passages.text: Upon his saying such things, and not daring to look upon him whom he is entreating with his voice, Perseus says: 'What am I able to give thee, most cowardly Phineus, and, a great boon to a craven, that will I give; lay aside thy fears; thou shalt be hurt by no weapon. Moreover, I will give thee a monument to last for ever, and in the house of my father-in-law thou shalt always be seen, that my wife may comfort herself with the form of her betrothed.' Thus he said, and he turned the daughter of Phorcys to that side towards which Phineus had turned himself with trembling face. Then, even as he endeavoured to turn away his eyes, his neck grew stiff, and the moisture of his eyes hardened in stone. But yet his timid features, and his suppliant countenance, and his hands hanging down, and his guilty attitude, still remained.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ovid, Metamorphoses V, Fable I (Riley 1851); not verbatim.

title.en: The Pierides and the Muses of Helicon
title.zh: 皮厄里得斯姊妹與赫利孔繆斯

region.en: Mount Helicon (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 赫利孔山（象徵性定位）

period: Composed c. 8 CE (Latin; Riley translation 1851)

source.archive: Project Gutenberg eBook 21765 (H. T. Riley, trans.)
source.work: Ovid, Metamorphoses, Book V (Fable II)

summary.en: Minerva, having seen the spring of Hippocrene opened by Pegasus' hoof, visits the Muses on Helicon and hears how their host Pyreneus tried to violate them as they sheltered from a storm, and, shut out, threw himself from the tower's height. Wings sounded in the air: nine magpies, lamenting their fate, were perched on the boughs. Urania explains: they are the daughters of Pierus of Pella, who challenged the Muses to a singing contest, offered to withdraw from the springs if beaten, and sang first a blasphemous song of the Giants and of the gods fleeing Typhoeus into Egypt and changing shapes — Jupiter a ram, Apollo a crow, Bacchus a goat, Diana a cat, Juno a cow, Venus a fish, Mercury an ibis. Then Calliope sang; the nymphs gave the victory to the Muses; and the daughters of Pierus, raging, began to abuse their judges, until they saw quills growing out of their nails and feathers on their arms, and the face of each shooting out into a hard beak.
summary.zh: 密涅瓦（雅典娜）見飛馬踏出之希波克瑞涅泉後，拜訪赫利孔繆斯；繆斯述其庇護人皮瑞涅斯欲施暴未遂、投塔自盡之事。此時空中傳來撲翅聲：九隻模仿人語的喜鵲棲於枝頭。烏拉尼亞告之：此乃皮厄羅斯之九女，曾向繆斯挑戰歌賽，敗則願棄泉而去，勝則繆斯須退至雪白之派俄尼亞。其先唱瀆神之歌：巨人戰敗、諸神奔埃及變形避難——宙斯化為羊、阿波羅為烏鴉、巴克庫斯為羊、狄安娜為貓、朱諾為牛、維納斯為魚、墨丘利為朱鷺。卡利俄佩繼唱；仙女判繆斯勝；皮厄里得斯姊妹怒而辱罵裁判，指甲生出羽、雙臂生出翼，面化鳥喙。

sensitivity.note: Ancient literary source; no living community restrictions.

passages.text: Hitherto Tritonia had presented herself as a companion to her brother; and, enwrapped in an encircling cloud, she makes for Thebes and Helicon, frequented by the virgin Muses. Having reached which mountain she stops, and thus addresses the learned sisters: 'The fame of the new fountain has reached my ears, which the hard hoof of the winged steed sprung from the blood of Medusa has opened. That is the cause of my coming. I wished to see this wondrous prodigy; I saw him spring from the blood of his mother.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ovid, Metamorphoses V, Fable II (Riley 1851); not verbatim.

passages.text: Urania replies: 'Whatever, Goddess, is the cause of thy visiting these abodes, thou art most acceptable to our feelings. However, the report is true, and Pegasus is the originator of this spring.' And then she conducts Pallas to the sacred streams. She, long admiring the waters produced by the stroke of his foot, looks around upon the groves of the ancient wood, the caves and the grass studded with flowers innumerable; and she pronounces the Mnemonian maids happy both in their pursuits and in their retreat.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ovid, Metamorphoses V, Fable II (Riley 1851); not verbatim.

passages.text: Wings resounded through the air, and a voice of some saluting them came from the lofty boughs. The daughter of Jupiter looked up, and asked whence tongues that speak so distinctly made that noise, and thought that a human being had spoken. They were birds; and magpies that imitate everything, lamenting their fate, they stood perched on the boughs, nine in number. As the Goddess wondered, thus did the Goddess Urania commence: 'Lately, too, did these, being overcome in a dispute, increase the number of the birds. Pierus, rich in the lands of Pella, begot them; the Paeonian Evippe was their mother.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ovid, Metamorphoses V, Fable II (Riley 1851); not verbatim.

passages.text: Nine times did she invoke the powerful Lucina, being nine times in labour. This set of foolish sisters were proud of their number, and came hither through so many cities of Haemonia and of Achaia, and engaged in a contest in words such as these: 'Cease imposing upon the vulgar with your empty melody. If you have any confidence in your skill, ye Thespian Goddesses, contend with us; we will not be outdone in voice or skill; and we are as many in number. Either, if vanquished, withdraw from the spring formed by the steed of Medusa and the Hyantean Aganippe, or we will retire from the Emathian plains, as far as the snowy Paeonians. Let the Nymphs decide the contest.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ovid, Metamorphoses V, Fable II (Riley 1851); not verbatim.

passages.text: The nymphs that are chosen swear by the rivers, and sit on seats made out of the natural rock. Then, without casting lots, she who had been the first to propose the contest sings the wars of the gods above, and gives the Giants honour not their due, and detracts from the actions of the great Divinities; and sings how that Typhoeus, sent forth from the lowest realms of the earth, had struck terror into the inhabitants of Heaven, until the land of Egypt received them in their weariness and the Nile, divided into its seven mouths. 'Jupiter,' she says, 'becomes the leader of the flock, whence, even at the present day, the Libyan Ammon is figured with horns. Apollo, the Delian God, lies concealed as a crow; the son of Semele as a he-goat; the sister of Phoebus as a cat; Juno, the daughter of Saturn, as a snow-white cow; Venus as a fish; Mercury, the Cyllenian God, beneath the wings of an Ibis.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ovid, Metamorphoses V, Fable II (Riley 1851); not verbatim.

passages.text: Thus far she had exerted her noisy mouth to the sound of the lyre; then the Muses were called upon, and Calliope rose, and, having her long hair gathered up with ivy, tuned with her thumb the sounding chords. The greatest of them finished her learned song; but the nymphs, with unanimous voice, pronounced that the goddesses who inhabit Helicon had proved the conquerors. Then the others, thus vanquished, began to scatter their abuse: since, they said, it is a trifling matter for you to have merited punishment by this contest, you add abuse too to your fault; and whither our resentment calls, we shall follow. The Emathian sisters smiled, and despised the threatening language; and, endeavouring to speak, and to menace with their insolent hands amid great clamour, they beheld quills growing out of their nails, and their arms covered with feathers; and they each saw the face of the other shooting out into a hard beak, and new birds being added to the woods.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ovid, Metamorphoses V, Fable II (Riley 1851); not verbatim.

title.en: Medea's Cup and the Sword-Token
title.zh: 美狄亞的毒杯與劍柄之記

region.en: Athens (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 雅典（象徵性定位）

period: Composed c. 8 CE (Latin; Riley translation 1851)

source.archive: Project Gutenberg eBook 21765 (H. T. Riley, trans.)
source.work: Ovid, Metamorphoses, Book VII (Fable IV)

summary.en: Theseus, after his exploits in the Isthmus, arrives at Athens, where Medea, now wedded to Aegeus, prepares a cup of wolfsbane for him — the aconite that sprang, they say, from the teeth of the Echidnean dog, from the white foam scattered by Cerberus as Heracles dragged him up from the dark cave in adamantine chains. The father presents the cup to his son as though to an enemy; Theseus, unsuspecting, has taken it in his right hand when his father perceives on the ivory hilt of his sword the tokens of his race, and strikes the draught from his mouth. Medea escapes death, having raised clouds by her enchantments.
summary.zh: 忒修斯在地峽建功後至雅典；此時美狄亞已嫁埃勾斯，為王子備下毒杯——其毒草「狼毒烏頭」相傳自刻耳柏洛斯齒間所生（赫拉克勒斯以金剛鏈拖犬上冥府時，其白沫落於沃土而成）。父親以「待敵之禮」將杯交給兒子；忒修斯毫無戒心地舉杯，埃勾斯卻在其劍柄上認出家族印記，當場打落毒酒。美狄亞以魔法召雲遁去。

sensitivity.note: Ancient literary source; no living community restrictions.

passages.text: Aegeus, to be blamed for this deed alone, shelters Medea; and hospitality is not enough, he also joins her to himself by the ties of marriage. And now was Theseus, his son, arrived, unknown to his father, who, by his valour, had established peace in the Isthmus between the two seas. For his destruction Medea mingles the wolfsbane, which she once brought with her from the shores of Scythia.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ovid, Metamorphoses VII, Fable IV (Riley 1851); not verbatim.

passages.text: This, they say, sprang from the teeth of the Echidnean dog. There is a gloomy cave with a dark entrance, wherein there is a descending path, along which the Tirynthian hero dragged away Cerberus, resisting, and turning his eyes sideways from the day and the shining rays of the Sun, in chains formed of adamant; he, filled with furious rage, filled the air with triple barkings at the same moment, and sprinkled the verdant fields with white foam. This, they suppose, grew solid, and, receiving the nourishment of a fruitful and productive soil, acquired the power of being noxious.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ovid, Metamorphoses VII, Fable IV (Riley 1851); not verbatim.

passages.text: This, by the contrivance of his wife, the father Aegeus himself presented to his son as though to an enemy. Theseus had received the presented cup with unsuspecting right hand, when his father perceived upon the ivory hilt of his sword the tokens of his race, and struck the guilty draught from his mouth. She escaped death, having raised clouds by her enchantments.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ovid, Metamorphoses VII, Fable IV (Riley 1851); not verbatim.

title.en: Demeter and the Cabiri
title.zh: 得墨忒耳與卡比里秘儀

region.en: The Cabirion near Thebes (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 底比斯卡比里圣所（象徵性定位）

period: Written c. 2nd century CE (Shilleto/Bohn translation; G. B. 68680)

source.archive: Project Gutenberg eBook 68680 (A. R. Shilleto, trans.)
source.work: Pausanias, Description of Greece IX.25

summary.en: By the Cabiri's sanctuary Pausanias refuses to say who the Cabiri were or what their rites are: 'I must be pardoned by the curious for passing over in silence.' But of the origin of the rites he publishes what the Thebans tell: there was a town here once, whose inhabitants were called Cabiri, and Demeter, getting acquainted with Prometheus, one of the Cabiri, and his son Aetnaeus, put something into their hands. What the deposit was and the circumstances of it, it is not lawful for him to disclose; but the mysteries of Demeter were a gift to the Cabiri. When the Epigoni captured Thebes, the Cabiri were driven out by the Argives, and the mysteries were not celebrated for a time; they were re-established afterwards by Pelarge, daughter of Potneus, and her husband Isthmiades — and because Pelarge celebrated them beyond the ancient boundaries, Telondes and the Cabiri who had left Cabiraea returned. And in consequence of an oracle from Dodona a victim big with young was ordered for Pelarge's sacrifice.
summary.zh: 鮑桑尼亞斯於卡比里圣所旁拒言其神與儀：「好奇者請恕我守口。」但可述底比斯人所傳之起源：此地昔有一城，居民稱卡比里人；得墨忒耳認識其中的普羅米修斯及其子埃特奈烏斯，將「某物」交其保管——所交為何、其事如何，「非我所能洩露」；得墨忒耳之秘儀乃卡比里人所得之賜。後起英雄（七雄之子）取底比斯時，卡比里人被阿爾戈斯人逐出，秘儀一度中斷；後由波忒紐斯之女珀拉爾革及其夫伊斯彌阿得斯重立——因珀拉爾革越古界舉行儀式，忒隆德斯與離開卡比里亞的卡比里人遂返。據多多納神諭，珀拉爾革之祭須以有孕之牲為犧。

sensitivity.note: Ancient literary source; no living community restrictions.

passages.text: By this grove is the temple of the Cabiri. Who they were and what are their rites or those of Demeter, I must be pardoned by the curious for passing over in silence. But nothing prevents my publishing to everybody the origin of these rites according to the Theban traditions. They say there was formerly a town here, the inhabitants of which were called Cabiri, and that Demeter, getting acquainted with Prometheus (one of the Cabiri) and Prometheus' son Aetnaeus, put something into their hands.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Pausanias, Description of Greece 9.25 (Shilleto); not verbatim.

passages.text: What this deposit was, and the circumstances relating to it, it is not lawful for me to disclose. But the mysteries of Demeter were a gift to the Cabiri. But when the Epigoni led an army against Thebes and captured it, the Cabiri were driven out by the Argives, and for some time the mysteries were not celebrated.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Pausanias, Description of Greece 9.25 (Shilleto); not verbatim.

passages.text: Afterwards however they are said to have been re-established by Pelarge, the daughter of Potneus, and her husband Isthmiades, who taught them to the person whose name was Alexiarus. And because Pelarge celebrated the mysteries beyond the ancient boundaries, Telondes and all of the Cabiri who had left Cabiraea returned. Pelarge, in consequence of an oracle from Dodona, was treated with various honours, and a victim big with young was ordered for her sacrifice.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Pausanias, Description of Greece 9.25 (Shilleto); not verbatim.

title.en: Phalanthus and the Rain from a Clear Sky
title.zh: 法蘭托斯與「晴空之雨」

region.en: Tarentum, Italy (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 義大利塔蘭托（象徵性定位）

period: Written c. 2nd century CE (Shilleto/Bohn translation; G. B. 68680)

source.archive: Project Gutenberg eBook 68680 (A. R. Shilleto, trans.)
source.work: Pausanias, Description of Greece X.10

summary.en: The Lacedaemonians colonized Tarentum under the Spartan Phalanthus, who, when he started on this colony, was told by an oracle from Delphi that he was to acquire land and found a city where he saw rain from a clear sky. At first he paid no great heed to the oracle, and sailed to Italy without consulting any interpreters; but when, after victories over the barbarians, he was unable to capture any of their cities or get possession of any of their land, he recollected the oracle, and thought the god had prophesied impossibilities — for it could not rain, he thought, from a clear and bright sky. And his wife, who had accompanied him from home, endeavoured to comfort him in various ways as he was in a despondent condition, and laid his head on her knees and began to pick out the lice; and in her goodwill it so fell out that she wept when she thought how her husband's affairs made no good progress. And she shed tears freely on Phalanthus' head; and then he understood the oracle: for his wife's name was Aethra — clear sky — and so, on the following night, he took from the barbarians Tarentum, the greatest and most prosperous of their maritime cities. They say the hero Taras was the son of Poseidon and a local nymph, and both the city and the river got their name from him.
summary.zh: 斯巴達人法蘭托斯奉命殖民意大利塔蘭托。德爾菲神諭言：「當見『晴空之雨』之處，即可得地建城。」初不以為意，征義大利屢敗，方悟神諭近乎不可能——晴空安得有雨？其妻見其沮喪，置其頭於膝上為之捉蝨，念其困頓而落淚；淚珠灑於夫頂。法蘭托斯頓悟：其妻名埃特拉，意即「晴空」——晴空落雨者，其妻之淚也。翌夜遂取塔蘭托。相傳英雄塔拉斯乃波塞冬與當地仙女之子，城與河皆以其為名。

title.en: Prometheus' Clay and the Grave of Tityus
title.zh: 普羅米修斯造人之泥與提提俄斯之墓

region.en: Panopeus, Phocis (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 福基斯帕諾珀俄斯（象徵性定位）

period: Written c. 2nd century CE (Shilleto/Bohn translation; G. B. 68680)

source.archive: Project Gutenberg eBook 68680 (A. R. Shilleto, trans.)
source.work: Pausanias, Description of Greece X.4

summary.en: Panopeus is a poor little town in Phocis, but Pausanias finds in its street a small building with a statue in Pentelican marble which some say is Asclepius and others Prometheus; and near the ravine lie stones, each large enough to fill a cart, in colour like the clay of sandy torrents, which smell, they say, very like the human body: the remains, the people claim, of the clay out of which the human race was fashioned by Prometheus. Near the ravine is the sepulchre of Tityus, whose mound Pausanias measures — a third of a stade around — and a Magnesian tells him he himself saw at Gades a sea-monster struck by lightning that covered five roods; so maybe Tityus, too, was as large as tradition says.
summary.zh: 福基斯小鎮帕諾珀俄斯雖貧瘠，卻有一間小磚樓、內立彭忒利科斯大理石像——或謂阿斯克勒庇俄斯、或謂普羅米修斯。後者之證據：峽谷旁有大石數塊，可載滿一車，色如山洪沖積之黏土，聞之「有如人體之氣味」——相傳即普羅米修斯造人之泥的遺存。峽谷旁另提提俄斯之墓，週長約三分之一斯塔德；一名瑪格尼西亚人向鮑桑尼亞斯自述曾在加德斯見被雷擊之海怪佔地五魯德，故提提俄斯之巨軀亦或可信。

sensitivity.note: Ancient literary source; no living community restrictions.

passages.text: But they have boundaries, and send members to the Phocian Council. They say that their town got its name from the father of Epeus, and that they were not Phocians originally, but Phlegyans who fled into Phocis from Orchomenia. There is in the street of Panopeus a building of unbaked brick of no great size, and in it a statue in Pentelican marble, which some say is Asclepius and others Prometheus. The last adduce the following to confirm their opinion: some stones lie near the ravine, each large enough to fill a cart, in colour like the clay found in ravines and sandy torrents, and they smell very like the human body. They say that these are remains of the clay out of which the human race was fashioned by Prometheus.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Pausanias, Description of Greece 10.4 (Shilleto); not verbatim.

passages.text: Near the ravine is also the sepulchre of Tityus, the circumference of the mound being about the third of a stade. Of Tityus it is said in the Odyssey: 'On the ground lying, and he lay nine roods.' But some say that this line does not state the size of Tityus, but that the place where he lay is called Nine Roods.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Pausanias, Description of Greece 10.4 (Shilleto); not verbatim.

passages.text: But Cleon, one of the Magnesians that live on the banks of the Hermus, said that people are by nature incredulous of wonderful things who have not in the course of their lives met with strange occurrences; and that he himself believed that Tityus and others were as large as tradition represented: for when he was at Gades, and he and all his companions sailed from the island according to the bidding of Heracles, on his return he saw a sea-monster who had been washed ashore, who had been struck by lightning and was blazing, and he covered five roods. So at least he said.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Pausanias, Description of Greece 10.4 (Shilleto); not verbatim.

title.en: Castor, Polydeuces, and the Cattle of Idas
title.zh: 卡斯托與波呂丟刻斯：伊達斯之牛

region.en: Lacedaemon (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 拉科尼亞（象徵性定位）

period: Composed c. 7th-6th century BCE (Cypria; Nagy translation)

source.archive: Center for Hellenic Studies (Gregory Nagy, trans.)
source.work: Epic Cycle, Cypria, Proclus summary (trans. Gregory Nagy)

license: Public domain (Proclus summary in Nagy translation)

summary.en: In the meantime, Kastor and Polydeukes are caught stealing the cattle of Idas and Lynkeus. Kastor is killed by Idas, but Idas and Lynkeus are killed by Polydeukes. And Zeus gives them both immortality on alternate days. Iris goes and tells Menelaos what has been happening at home. He returns and plans an expedition against Ilion with his brother.
summary.zh: 其間，卡斯托與波呂丟刻斯偷伊達斯與林叩斯之牛被發現。卡斯托為伊達斯所殺，伊達斯與林叩斯又為波呂丟刻斯所誅。宙斯遂賜二兄弟「隔日輪流」之永生。伊里斯將家中之事報與墨涅拉俄斯；他回國後與兄共謀遠征伊利翁。

sensitivity.note: Ancient literary source; no living community restrictions.

And Zeus gives them both immortality on alternate days. Iris goes and tells Menelaos what has been happening at home. He returns and plans an expedition against Ilion with his brother.

title.en: Zeus and Themis Plan the Trojan War
title.zh: 宙斯與忒彌斯謀劃特洛伊戰爭

region.en: Mount Olympus (mythic geography)
region.zh: 奧林波斯山（神話地理）

period: Composed c. 7th-6th century BCE (Cypria; Nagy translation)

source.archive: Center for Hellenic Studies (Gregory Nagy, trans.)
source.work: Epic Cycle, Cypria, Proclus summary (trans. Gregory Nagy)

license: Public domain (Proclus summary in Nagy translation)

summary.en: Zeus, together with Themis, plans the Trojan War. For Eris, while attending a feast of the gods at the wedding of Peleus, instigates a feud among Athena, Hera, and Aphrodite about beauty. They, by order of Zeus, are led by Hermes to Mount Ida for judgment by Alexandros. Alexandros judges for Aphrodite, encouraged by a promise of Helen in marriage. On the advice of Aphrodite, he has ships built; Helenos prophesies to him about what is going to happen; Aphrodite tells Aineias to sail with him; then Kassandra foretells the events of the future. When he gets to Lacedaemonia, Alexandros is entertained as a xenos by the sons of Tyndaros, and afterwards by Menelaos at Sparta; Alexandros gives Helen gifts during the feast. Menelaos sails off to Crete, telling Helen to provide proper hospitality for their xenoi while he is away; Aphrodite brings Helen and Alexandros together; and after their intercourse they load up a great many valuables and sail away by night.
summary.zh: 宙斯與忒彌斯共謀特洛伊戰爭。厄里斯（不和女神）赴珀琉斯婚宴，挑起雅典娜、赫拉、阿芙洛狄忒三女神之美貌之爭。宙斯命赫爾墨斯引三女神上伊達山，交由亞歷山德羅斯（帕里斯）評判；帕里斯因海倫之諾而判阿芙洛狄忒。他依阿芙洛狄忒之議造船；赫勒諾斯為他預言未來；阿芙洛狄忒命埃涅阿斯同行；卡珊德拉預言一切。帕里斯至斯巴達，受廷達瑞俄斯諸子與墨涅拉俄斯款待，宴中贈海倫禮物；墨涅拉俄斯赴克里特、囑海倫善待賓客；阿芙洛狄忒使二人結合，二人攜重寶夜遁。

sensitivity.note: Ancient literary source; no living community restrictions.

For Eris, while attending a feast of the gods at the wedding of Peleus, instigates a feud among Athena, Hera, and Aphrodite about beauty. They, by order of Zeus, are led by Hermes to Mount Ida for judgment by Alexandros. Alexandros judges for Aphrodite, encouraged by a promise of Helen in marriage.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Cypria, Proclus summary 1 (Nagy translation); not verbatim.

passages.text: On the advice of Aphrodite, he has ships built; Helenos prophesies to him about what is going to happen; Aphrodite tells Aineias to sail with him; then Kassandra foretells the events of the future. When he gets to Lacedaemonia, Alexandros is entertained as a xenos by the sons of Tyndaros, and afterwards by Menelaos at Sparta.

Aphrodite brings Helen and Alexandros together; and after their intercourse they load up a great many valuables and sail away by night. Hera sends a storm down upon them; landing at Sidon, Alexandros captures the city. They sail to Ilion; Alexandros marries Helen.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Cypria, Proclus summary 1 (Nagy translation); not verbatim.

title.en: Yu the Great Tames the Waters
title.zh: 大禹治水

region.en: Yellow River basin (Kaifeng)
region.zh: 黃河流域（開封）

period: Shujing traditions, compiled c. 4th c. BCE

source.work: Shujing (Book of Documents), Yugong; Shanhaijing

summary.en: For thirteen years Yu labors on channels and dredgings, passing his home three times without entering, and finally divides the Nine Provinces, guiding the flood to the sea.
summary.zh: 大禹疏川導滯十三年，三過家門而不入，終分九州，導洪水入於海。

passages.text: Yu dredged the rivers and opened the mountains; for thirteen years he passed the gate of his home three times and did not enter, until the waters were led down to the sea. Yu marked the Nine Provinces, measured the mountains and rivers, and set the grains to grow; the flood was mastered not by damming it in contention but by the way of the channels.

title.en: Vasilisa and Baba Yaga
title.zh: 瓦西麗莎與巴巴雅加

region.en: Vladimir, Russia
region.zh: 弗拉基米爾（俄羅斯）

period: 19th c. Russian collections (Afanasyev)

source.work: Vasilisa the Beautiful, in Alexander Afanasyev's collections

summary.en: Sent by her cruel stepmother to the witch Baba Yaga for fire, Vasilisa survives the impossible tasks with the help of a magic doll; she leaves with a skull full of burning coals — and the fire consumes the stepmother's house.
summary.zh: 繼母命瓦西麗莎往巫婆巴巴雅加處取火；她憑木偶之助通過種種試煉，攜一枚盛滿燃煤的骷髏歸家——骷髏之火焚盡繼母一家。

passages.text: The doll's eyes glowed like fire, and it whispered: 'Fear nothing, ask no questions till the time is ripe'; so Vasilisa served Baba Yaga's night, her day, and her pressing tasks of poppy-seed and dust. Baba Yaga gave her a skull with blazing eyes set on a stick; at home the eyes burned on the stepmother and her daughters and consumed them to coals, and Vasilisa was rid of them, and fire remained in her house.

title.en: The Siblings Who Became Sun and Moon
title.zh: 化為日月的兄妹

region.en: Andong, Korea
region.zh: 安東（韓國）

period: Korean oral folktale; 20th c. collections

source.archive: UNESCO APCIEU folktale anthology (rendering of the Korean folktale)
source.work: The Sun and the Moon (Haewa Dari Doen Onui), Korean folktale; earliest recorded telling narrated by O Su-hwa, South Gyeongsang, 1911

license: Oral tradition (public domain); anthology rendering (c) UNESCO APCIEU — passages paraphrased

summary.en: A tiger, having eaten their mother, hunts the brother and sister; praying, they draw down a rope from heaven and climb it — one becomes the sun, the other the moon, and the tiger, unable to climb, falls among the millet stalks.
summary.zh: 虎食其母而追兄妹二人；二人禱天，天上垂下繩索。兄化為日，妹化為月，登繩而升；虎攀繩不得，墜入高粱田中。

passages.text: The children prayed: 'Send down a rope, if we are innocent'; and a rope of silver came down from the sky; but where the tiger prayed, a rotten rope came down, and he fell into the millet. The brother became the moon, too cold and bright, and the sister became the sun — or the brother the sun, and she the moon — and that is why the moon's face bears the stains of the millet the tiger threw.
passages.note: Paraphrase of the Korean folktale "The Sun and the Moon" (O Su-hwa narration 1911, via UNESCO APCIEU anthology); not verbatim.

title.en: Lumawig on Earth: The Bean Miracle, the Wedding Feast, and the Man in the Rock
title.zh: 盧馬維格在人間：豆莢奇蹟、婚宴與石化於岩中者

region.en: Bontoc, Mountain Province, Luzon, Philippines (symbolic pin for the Igorot tale cycle)
region.zh: 菲律賓呂宋山省博托克（伊哥洛特故事圈之象徵定位）

period: Igorot oral tradition; recorded 1916 (Cole)

source.work: Mabel Cook Cole, Philippine Folk Tales (1916), Igorot: 'Lumawig on Earth', eBook #12814

summary.en: Lumawig the Great Spirit comes down to marry the girl Fukan, filling her bean baskets from a single pod, enlarging her chickens and pigs, and outdoing her mocking brother-in-law at the wedding feast. When the brother-in-law quarrels over water, Lumawig strikes a rock to create it and thrusts him into the rock, where his body becomes a spring; before returning to the sky Lumawig sets his wife afloat in a coffin that reaches Tinglayen, where a widower finds and marries her.
summary.zh: 大神盧馬維格下凡娶富坎，一豆莢滿其籃，令雞豬速大，於婚宴上戲弄譏諷之舅兄。舅兄因水起爭執，盧馬維格以矛擊石出水，將其推入岩中，其身軀化為泉源。臨歸天前，盧馬維格置妻於棺浮水，棺漂至丁格拉延，為鰥夫所拾並娶之。

sensitivity.note: Philippine oral tradition recorded from Igorot narrators; presented as an archival record, not as permission to speak for Igorot communities. The tale ends by etiologically explaining springs in rocks and a local place (Tinglayen), so a sacred-place motif tag is used.

passages.text: One day Lumawig, the Great Spirit who dwells in the sky, looked down and saw two sisters gathering beans, and he came down to visit them. When the younger sister Fukan told him how slow their work was, he asked for a single pod of beans, shelled it into the basket, and the basket was at once full. He filled another basket the same way, and when Fukan fetched three more, he filled them all. Her father, hearing the story of the young man who could fill a basket from one pod, said, "Go bring the young man here, for I think he must be a god." Lumawig helped carry the beans home, and when the father gave him water in a cocoanut shell he said, "If I stay here with you, I shall become very strong."
passages.note: Paraphrase of Mabel Cook Cole, Philippine Folk Tales (1916), 'Lumawig on Earth'; not verbatim.

passages.text: The next morning Lumawig fed the family's one hen and chicks rice meal, and as they ate they grew until they were cocks and hens; he fed the pigs sweet potato leaves, and they too grew to full size. The delighted father offered his elder daughter in marriage, but Lumawig chose the younger, Fukan. When the brother-in-law sneered that there was no rice, beef, pork, or chicken for a wedding feast, Lumawig answered, "I shall provide our wedding feast." He hurled two great pine trees to Lanao for the fire, set ten kettles boiling, and filled five of them full by passing one small basket of rice over them. He called deer and pigs from the forest for the people to catch, and though the brother-in-law chased the finest pig until he was exhausted, he could not seize it until Lumawig lifted it for him; then the pig cut loose and escaped twice more, until Lumawig himself carried it back.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Mabel Cook Cole, Philippine Folk Tales (1916), 'Lumawig on Earth'; not verbatim.

passages.text: After the feast they consulted the omen for the northern tribes, and when the hot, thirsty people asked Lumawig to create water, the brother-in-law taunted him for caring nothing for their thirst. They quarreled, and Lumawig told the people to rest; while they rested he struck the rock with his spear and water flowed out. The brother-in-law leaped to drink first, but Lumawig held him back and made him drink last; then he gave him a push that sent him into the rock, and water came from his body. "You must stay there," said Lumawig, "because you have troubled me a great deal," and they left him in the rock. Some time later Lumawig returned to the sky, first placing his wife in a wooden coffin with a dog at her feet and a cock at her head, bidding the coffin float without stopping until it reached Tinglayen. A widower sharpening his ax on the bank fished it out; Fukan cried out not to drive a wedge, and as the widower had no wife, he married her.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Mabel Cook Cole, Philippine Folk Tales (1916), 'Lumawig on Earth'; not verbatim.

title.en: How the First Head Was Taken
title.zh: 第一顆人頭如何被取下

region.en: Bontoc, Mountain Province, Luzon, Philippines (symbolic pin for the Igorot tale cycle)
region.zh: 菲律賓呂宋山省博托克（伊哥洛特故事圈之象徵定位）

period: Igorot oral tradition; recorded 1916 (Cole)

source.work: Mabel Cook Cole, Philippine Folk Tales (1916), Igorot: 'How the First Head was Taken', eBook #12814

summary.en: Kabigat the Moon, a woman, is molding a copper pot when a son of Chal-chal the Sun stops to watch her work. Annoyed by his staring, she strikes him with her paddle and cuts off his head, but the Sun hurries from afar, sets the head back on, and the boy lives again; the Sun then decrees that because of this act, people will forever cut off one another's heads on the earth.
summary.zh: 月神卡比加特為女性，正以拍打之法塑造銅釜；太陽查爾查爾之子駐足觀看。月神厭其凝視，以槳擊之，斬落其首；太陽遙知此事，趕至現場，將頭顱安回，男孩復生。太陽遂下斷言：因此事之故，世人從此將互相取下人頭。

sensitivity.note: Philippine oral tradition recorded from Igorot narrators; presented as an archival record. The story etiologically explains headhunting as a consequence laid on humankind by the Sun's decree; the Thompson-style taboo-transgression tag is an interpretive mapping (an act of violence whose consequence endures as a law of the world), noted here because the European motif index has no exact equivalent.

passages.text: One day the Moon, who was a woman named Kabigat, sat in the yard making a large copper pot. The copper was still soft and pliable like clay, and she squatted on the ground with the heavy pot against her knees while she patted and shaped it, pressing a stone against the inside and pounding the outside with a wooden paddle dripping with water until she had worked down the bulges and formed a smooth surface. A son of Chal-chal the Sun came by and stopped to watch her mold the form, standing still for some time, for he was greatly interested in seeing the jar grow larger, more beautiful, and smoother with each stroke. Suddenly the Moon looked up and saw him watching her, and instantly she struck him with her paddle and cut off his head.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Mabel Cook Cole, Philippine Folk Tales (1916), 'How the First Head was Taken'; not verbatim.

passages.text: The Sun was far away, but he knew as soon as the Moon had cut off his son's head. Hurrying to the spot, he put the boy's head back on, and he was alive again. Then the Sun said to the Moon, "You cut off my son's head, and because you did this ever after on the earth people will cut off each other's heads." In this way the tale explains the beginning of head-taking among the Igorot: the first severed head was that of the Sun's own son, taken not in war but in a moment of anger at a potter's wheel, and the custom follows from that first blow as its consequence.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Mabel Cook Cole, Philippine Folk Tales (1916), 'How the First Head was Taken'; not verbatim.

title.en: The Serpent Eagle
title.zh: 蛇鷹

region.en: Bontoc, Mountain Province, Luzon, Philippines (symbolic pin for the Igorot tale cycle)
region.zh: 菲律賓呂宋山省博托克（伊哥洛特故事圈之象徵定位）

period: Igorot oral tradition; recorded 1916 (Cole)

source.work: Mabel Cook Cole, Philippine Folk Tales (1916), Igorot: 'The Serpent Eagle', eBook #12814

summary.en: Two boys sent daily for firewood are starved and scolded by their mother no matter what wood they bring. Driven to despair, the elder climbs a tree and calls down "Here is some wood" as his own arm bones, leg bones, and finally all his bones drop to the ground; the younger carries the bundle of bones home, and the elder, transformed into a serpent eagle, flies overhead and cries that he no longer needs her food.
summary.zh: 兩兄弟每日為母拾柴，無論所拾為何皆受責罵且不得飽食。長兄絕望之餘攀上大樹，喊「這是柴火」，其臂骨、腿骨乃至全身骨骼紛紛落地。弟弟背起骨柴回家，長兄化為蛇鷹，盤旋於母親頭頂，啼叫自己不再需要她的食物。

sensitivity.note: Philippine oral tradition recorded from Igorot narrators; presented as an archival record, not as permission to speak for Igorot communities. Transformation tag marks the elder brother's becoming of a serpent eagle; the tale also etiologically explains the bird's cry.

passages.text: Two boys were sent by their mother every day to the forest to get wood for her fires. Each morning she gave them a little poor food for the trip, saying the wood they brought the day before was too poor to earn more. If they brought nice pine wood she scolded them; if they brought large dry reeds she said these were no good because they left too much ashes in the house. Try as they would, they failed to satisfy her, and their bodies grew very thin from working all day and from want of enough to eat. One morning she gave them a bit of dog meat, and the boys were very sad as they set out for the mountains.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Mabel Cook Cole, Philippine Folk Tales (1916), 'The Serpent Eagle'; not verbatim.

passages.text: In the forest one brother told the other to wait while he climbed a tree to cut branches. From above he called "Here is some wood," and the bones of his arm dropped to the ground. "Here is some more wood," and the bones of the other arm fell; then the bones of his legs, and so on, until all the bones of his body lay on the ground. "Take these home," he said, "and tell the woman that here is her wood; she only wanted my bones." The younger boy, alone and weeping, gathered up the bundle. As he finished, a serpent eagle called down from the treetops, "I will go with you, Brother," and the bird flew over the boy's head all the way home.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Mabel Cook Cole, Philippine Folk Tales (1916), 'The Serpent Eagle'; not verbatim.

passages.text: When the mother looked at the wood she was very much frightened and ran out of the house. The serpent eagle circled round and round above her head, crying "Quiukok! quiukok! quiukok! I do not need your food any more." The tale thus explains both the origin of the serpent eagle and the meaning of its call, told as a warning against mothers who starve the children who serve them.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Mabel Cook Cole, Philippine Folk Tales (1916), 'The Serpent Eagle'; not verbatim.

title.en: The Tattooed Men
title.zh: 紋身人

region.en: Bontoc, Mountain Province, Luzon, Philippines (symbolic pin for the Igorot tale cycle)
region.zh: 菲律賓呂宋山省博托克（伊哥洛特故事圈之象徵定位）

period: Igorot oral tradition; recorded 1916 (Cole)

source.work: Mabel Cook Cole, Philippine Folk Tales (1916), Igorot: 'The Tattooed Men', eBook #12814

summary.en: Two young friends, unhappy that neither has been tattooed, agree to mark each other. One works carefully over his friend's breast, back, arms, legs, and face, rubbing in soot so that he is beautifully tattooed; the other, taking revenge or jest too far, scrapes a great pile of pot soot and rubs it over his friend head to foot. They fight, and the beautifully tattooed one becomes a great lizard that hides in the tall grass while the sooty one becomes a crow that flies away over the village.
summary.zh: 兩位年輕摯友因未曾紋身而鬱鬱，相約互為對方紋身。一人細心為友在胸背、四肢、臉上刺紋並擦入鍋底煙灰，友人因而俊美；另一人卻刮起一大堆煙灰，將其從頭到腳塗滿全身。二人相鬥，俊美者忽化巨蜥遁入深草，滿身煙黑者化為烏鴉飛越村莊而去。

sensitivity.note: Philippine oral tradition recorded from Igorot narrators; presented as an archival record. Etiological tale of lizard and crow plumage and of tattooing customs.

passages.text: Two young men, very good friends, were unhappy because neither of them had been tattooed, and they felt they were not as beautiful as their friends. One day they agreed to tattoo each other. One marked the breast and back of the other, his arms and legs, and even his face; then he took soot from the bottom of a cooking-pot and rubbed it into all the marks, and the man was tattooed beautifully. The one who had done the work said, "Now, my friend, you are very beautiful, and you must tattoo me."
passages.note: Paraphrase of Mabel Cook Cole, Philippine Folk Tales (1916), 'The Tattooed Men'; not verbatim.

passages.text: But the newly tattooed man scraped a great pile of black soot off the cooking-pots, and before the other knew what was happening, he had rubbed it all over him from the top of his head to the bottom of his feet, leaving him black and greasy. Covered with soot, the man grew very angry and cried, "Why do you treat me so when I tattooed you so carefully?" They began to fight, but suddenly the beautifully tattooed one became a great lizard which ran away and hid in the tall grass, while the sooty one became a crow and flew away over the village.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Mabel Cook Cole, Philippine Folk Tales (1916), 'The Tattooed Men'; not verbatim.

title.en: Tilin, the Rice Bird
title.zh: 蒂林稻雀

region.en: Bontoc, Mountain Province, Luzon, Philippines (symbolic pin for the Igorot tale cycle)
region.zh: 菲律賓呂宋山省博托克（伊哥洛特故事圈之象徵定位）

period: Igorot oral tradition; recorded 1916 (Cole)

source.work: Mabel Cook Cole, Philippine Folk Tales (1916), Igorot: 'Tilin, the Rice Bird', eBook #12814

summary.en: A little girl begs raw rice while her mother pounds the evening meal, and is scolded for talking too much. Left alone while the mother fetches water, she lifts the winnower covering the basket of rice; the cover slips, she falls, and she is covered up inside. When the mother hears a bird crying from the basket and removes the cover, a little brown rice bird hops out, flying away and calling goodbye to the mother who would not give it any rice to eat.
summary.zh: 小女孩在母親舂晚餐米糧時討要生米，反被斥責多話。母親取水離家後，她掀開米籃上的簸箕蓋；蓋子一滑，她跌入籃中為米所覆。母親回來聽見籃中傳出鳥啼，掀蓋一看，一隻小棕雀跳出，一面飛去一面回頭喊道：再見，媽媽；你不肯給我米吃。

sensitivity.note: Philippine oral tradition recorded from Igorot narrators; presented as an archival record. Etiological tale of the rice bird (tilin) and its cry.

passages.text: One day a mother was pounding out rice to cook for supper when her little girl ran up crying, "Oh, Mother, give me some of the raw rice to eat." The mother said no, that it was not good for her until it was cooked, and told her to wait for supper. But the girl persisted until the mother, out of patience, cried, "Be still. It is not good for you to talk so much!" When the rice was pounded, the woman winnowed it, emptied it into her basket, covered it with the winnower, and set off to the spring for water.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Mabel Cook Cole, Philippine Folk Tales (1916), 'Tilin, the Rice Bird'; not verbatim.

passages.text: The little girl loved to go to the spring with her mother and play in the cool water, but this time she stayed behind, and as soon as the woman was out of sight she ran to the basket of rice and reached down to take a handful of grain. The cover slipped so that she fell, and was covered up in the basket. When the mother returned, she heard a bird crying "King, king, nik! nik! nik!" and, listening carefully, found the sound came from the basket. She removed the cover, and to her surprise a little brown rice bird hopped out. As it flew away it kept calling back, "Goodbye, Mother; goodbye, Mother. You would not give me any rice to eat."
passages.note: Paraphrase of Mabel Cook Cole, Philippine Folk Tales (1916), 'Tilin, the Rice Bird'; not verbatim.

title.en: How the Moon and the Stars Came to Be
title.zh: 月亮與星辰的由來

region.en: Bukidnon highlands, northern Mindanao, Philippines (symbolic pin for the Bukidnon tale cycle)
region.zh: 菲律賓民答那峨北部布基農高地（布基農故事圈之象徵定位）

period: Bukidnon oral tradition; recorded 1916 (Cole)

source.work: Mabel Cook Cole, Philippine Folk Tales (1916), Wild Tribes of Mindanao, Bukidnon: 'How the Moon and the Stars Came to Be', eBook #12814

summary.en: In the times when the sky was close to the ground and looked like coral rock, a spinster went out to pound rice, hanging her beads and comb on the sky. Each swing of her pestle struck the sky, and when she raised it too hard the sky rose up so far that she lost her ornaments forever: the comb became the moon and the beads became the scattered stars.
summary.zh: 天低近地、狀如珊瑚岩之時，一位女子外出舂米，將項珠與木梳掛於天上。杵每起落皆擊天空；一次她將杵舉得過重，天空驟然高升，飾物永不可得——木梳化為月亮，珠串化為散落之星。

sensitivity.note: Philippine oral tradition recorded from Bukidnon narrators; presented as an archival record, not as permission to speak for Bukidnon communities. Etiological tale: the rising sky and the transformation of ornaments into celestial bodies.

passages.text: One day, in the times when the sky was close to the ground and looked like coral rock, a spinster went out to pound rice. Before she began her work she took off the beads from around her neck and the comb from her hair, and hung them on the sky. Then she began working, and each time she raised her pestle into the air it struck the sky. For some time she pounded the rice in this way, and then she raised the pestle so high that it struck the sky very hard.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Mabel Cook Cole, Philippine Folk Tales (1916), 'How the Moon and the Stars Came to Be'; not verbatim.

passages.text: Immediately the sky began to rise, and it went up so far that she lost her ornaments. Never did they come down again, for the comb became the moon, and the beads became the stars that are scattered about the heavens. Thus the pounding of rice explains both why the sky is far above the world and why the moon and stars hang in it.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Mabel Cook Cole, Philippine Folk Tales (1916), 'How the Moon and the Stars Came to Be'; not verbatim.

title.en: The Great Crab and the Flood (Bukidnon)
title.zh: 巨蟹與洪水（布基農）

region.en: Bukidnon highlands, northern Mindanao, Philippines (symbolic pin for the Bukidnon tale cycle)
region.zh: 菲律賓民答那峨北部布基農高地（布基農故事圈之象徵定位）

period: Bukidnon oral tradition; recorded 1916 (Cole)

source.work: Mabel Cook Cole, Philippine Folk Tales (1916), Wild Tribes of Mindanao, Bukidnon: 'The Flood Story', eBook #12814

summary.en: A very big crab crawls into the sea and crowds the water out over all the earth, covering the land. A month earlier a wise man had warned the people to build a large raft; they bound three layers of trees together and fastened the raft with a long rattan cord to a pole in the earth. White water poured from the hills, the sea covered even the highest mountains, and all drowned except those on the raft, which the cord held near their old home when the waters sank — the only people left in the world.
summary.zh: 一隻巨蟹爬入海中，將海水擠出，漫覆大地。早在一個月前，智者已囑人建大木筏；他們以三層巨樹緊緊綁成筏，用長藤索繫於地上木柱。白水自山間傾瀉，海水淹沒至高峰；除筏上人畜外盡數溺亡。水退之後，因藤索未斷，木筏仍近故土——他們便是世上僅存的人類。

sensitivity.note: Philippine oral tradition recorded from Bukidnon narrators; presented as an archival record. Flood cluster: caused here by a giant crustacean displacing the sea — tagged world-serpent as an interpretive mapping (a vast creature whose movement unleashes the deluge), not a literal serpent.

passages.text: A long time ago there was a very big crab, and it crawled into the sea. As it went in, it crowded the water out so that the sea ran all over the earth and covered all the land. About one moon before this happened, a wise man had told the people that they must build a large raft. They did as he commanded and cut many large trees until they had enough to make three layers; these they bound tightly together, and when the raft was done they fastened it with a long rattan cord to a big pole in the earth.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Mabel Cook Cole, Philippine Folk Tales (1916), Bukidnon 'The Flood Story'; not verbatim.

passages.text: Soon the floods came. White water poured out of the hills, and the sea rose and covered even the highest mountains. The people and animals on the raft were safe, but all the others drowned. When the waters went down and the raft was again on the ground, it was near their old home, for the rattan cord had held. But these were the only people left on the whole earth, and from them the world began again.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Mabel Cook Cole, Philippine Folk Tales (1916), Bukidnon 'The Flood Story'; not verbatim.

title.en: Magbangal and the Self-Working Bolos
title.zh: 馬格邦加與自鳴刀斧

region.en: Bukidnon highlands, northern Mindanao, Philippines (symbolic pin for the Bukidnon tale cycle)
region.zh: 菲律賓民答那峨北部布基農高地（布基農故事圈之象徵定位）

period: Bukidnon oral tradition; recorded 1916 (Cole)

source.work: Mabel Cook Cole, Philippine Folk Tales (1916), Wild Tribes of Mindanao, Bukidnon: 'Magbangal', eBook #12814

summary.en: The powerful hunter Magbangal goes alone to clear land for planting, and his ten bolos and hatchets sharpen themselves on the stone and cut the forest with no hands to guide them. His wife, spying on him, breaks the magic: Magbangal wakes, seizes a bolo, and cuts off one of his own arms. He ascends to become the constellation Magbangal — appearing when it is time to plant rice — while his wife goes into the water and becomes a fish.
summary.zh: 獵人馬格邦加獨自前往墾地，其十柄波洛刀與斧頭自行就石磨利、無人操縱而砍伐林木。妻子窺探之舉破了法術：馬格邦加驚醒，抓起一刀自斷一臂。他升天化為馬格邦加星宿——稻作播種之季由此星昭示——妻子則入水化魚。

sensitivity.note: Philippine oral tradition recorded from Bukidnon narrators; presented as an archival record. The constellation is an agricultural sign-calendar; oracle-divination tag is used for the celestial sign that regulates the planting season.

passages.text: Magbangal was a good hunter who often went to a certain hill and killed wild pigs for food. One night, as the planting season neared, he told his wife he would go to the hill alone the next day to clear the land, and she was not to come. She begged to accompany him, but he refused, and in the morning she cooked rice and fish for him to eat on his return. He gathered up his ten hatchets and bolos, a sharpening stone, and a bamboo tube for water, and set out for the hill, where he cut small trees to make a bench and sat down upon it.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Mabel Cook Cole, Philippine Folk Tales (1916), 'Magbangal'; not verbatim.

passages.text: Then Magbangal spoke to his weapons: "You bolos must sharpen yourselves on the stone," and the bolos went to the stone and were sharpened. "You hatchets must be sharpened," and they also sharpened themselves. "Now you bolos cut all the small brush under the trees, and you hatchets must cut the large trees." The weapons went to work, and from his bench Magbangal watched the land being cleared while he slept. His wife, weaving a skirt at home, heard the trees continually falling and thought her husband must have found many helpers; walking toward the field, she stopped behind a tree and saw him asleep, while bolos and hatchets cut the trees with no hands to guide them.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Mabel Cook Cole, Philippine Folk Tales (1916), 'Magbangal'; not verbatim.

passages.text: She marveled that Magbangal had never told her of his power. Suddenly he jumped up, seized a bolo, and cut off one of his own arms; waking, he sat up and said, "Someone must be looking at me, for one of my arms is cut off." Knowing his wife was the cause, he went home with her, saying, "Now I am going away. It is better for me to go to the sky where I can give the sign to the people when it is time to plant; and you must go to the water and become a fish." Soon after he went to the sky and became the constellation Magbangal, and ever since, when the people see these stars appear, they know it is time to plant their rice.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Mabel Cook Cole, Philippine Folk Tales (1916), 'Magbangal'; not verbatim.

title.en: How Children Became Monkeys
title.zh: 孩童化猿猴

region.en: Bukidnon highlands, northern Mindanao, Philippines (symbolic pin for the Bukidnon tale cycle)
region.zh: 菲律賓民答那峨北部布基農高地（布基農故事圈之象徵定位）

period: Bukidnon oral tradition; recorded 1916 (Cole)

source.work: Mabel Cook Cole, Philippine Folk Tales (1916), Wild Tribes of Mindanao, Bukidnon: 'How Children Became Monkeys', eBook #12814

summary.en: A mother takes her two children along to color cloth in a carabao mud hole. As she stirs the dye pot, scalding water splashes her hand and she jumps and cries out; the children's laughter changes them into monkeys, and the shell spoons they hold become their tails. Their nails are still black from the days when, as children, they helped their mother dye cloth.
summary.zh: 母親攜二孩至水牛打滾的泥塘染布。攪動染鍋時滾水濺起燙手，她跳起驚叫；孩童大笑之際化作猿猴，手中貝殼湯匙化為其尾。猿猴的指甲至今仍黑——因為他們做孩子時曾幫母親染布。

sensitivity.note: Philippine oral tradition recorded from Bukidnon narrators; presented as an archival record. Etiological tale of monkey tails and black nails.

passages.text: One day a mother took her two children with her when she went to color cloth. Not far from her home was a mud hole where the carabao liked to wallow, and to this hole she carried her cloth, some dye pots, and two shell spoons. After she had put the cloth into the mud to let it take up the dark color, she built a fire and set over it a pot containing water and the leaves used for dyeing, and sat down to wait for the water to boil while the children played near by.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Mabel Cook Cole, Philippine Folk Tales (1916), 'How Children Became Monkeys'; not verbatim.

passages.text: By and by, when she went to stir the leaves with a shell spoon, some of the water splashed up and burned her hand, so that she jumped and cried out. This amused the children, and their laughter changed them into monkeys, and the spoons became their tails. The nails of the monkeys are still black, because while they were children they had helped their mother dye the cloth.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Mabel Cook Cole, Philippine Folk Tales (1916), 'How Children Became Monkeys'; not verbatim.

title.en: Bulanawan and Aguio: The Twin Brothers' Battle
title.zh: 布拉納萬與阿圭歐：雙生兄弟之戰

region.en: Bukidnon highlands, northern Mindanao, Philippines (symbolic pin for the Bukidnon tale cycle)
region.zh: 菲律賓民答那峨北部布基農高地（布基農故事圈之象徵定位）

period: Bukidnon oral tradition; recorded 1916 (Cole)

source.work: Mabel Cook Cole, Philippine Folk Tales (1916), Wild Tribes of Mindanao, Bukidnon: 'Bulanawan and Aguio', eBook #12814

summary.en: Twins Bulanawan and Aguio are separated in infancy when a whirlwind carries Bulanawan away to a far land, where he grows into a great warrior. Years later Aguio arrives in that land and, not knowing his brother, tries to steal his brother's wife; the duel shakes the earth. Rival second brothers sense the tremor and join the battle, and the quaking grows until Langgona's father, the twins' grandfather, arrives and makes peace — revealing that the combatants were brothers and grandsons.
summary.zh: 雙生子布拉納萬與阿圭歐幼時被旋風拆散，布拉納萬被吹至遠方，長成大勇士。多年後阿圭歐遠遊至此，不知彼此為兄弟，欲奪其嫂；二人決鬥撼動大地。各自的結拜兄弟感得地動，趕來助戰，震動加劇，大地幾乎崩裂。最後朗戈納之父——雙生子祖父——前來止戈，眾人方知交戰者竟是兄弟與孫輩。

sensitivity.note: Philippine oral tradition recorded from Bukidnon narrators; presented as an archival record. Twins/duality cluster: twin brothers whose battle shakes the cosmos, resolved by an elder peacemaker.

passages.text: Langgona and his wife had twin boys named Bulanawan and Aguio. When they were about two years old the mother took Bulanawan with her to the field to pick cotton, and while she was gathering more a great wind suddenly arose which wound the cotton around the baby and carried him away. Far away to a distant land the wind took Bulanawan, and in that place he grew up; when he was a man he became a great warrior. Aguio, too, grew into a great warrior, and one day he journeyed to this distant land, not knowing that his brother was there.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Mabel Cook Cole, Philippine Folk Tales (1916), 'Bulanawan and Aguio'; not verbatim.

passages.text: That same day Bulanawan and his wife sat resting on a large flat rock by the seashore, and Bulanawan fell asleep. Aguio, walking along the shore in his war-dress, thought the woman very beautiful and determined to steal her. He asked for some of her husband's betel-nut to chew; when she refused, he went forward to fight her husband, not knowing they were brothers. When his wife awakened him, Bulanawan sprang up, seized her, and put her in the cuff of his sleeve before coming forth to fight. They fought until their weapons were broken and the earth trembled.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Mabel Cook Cole, Philippine Folk Tales (1916), 'Bulanawan and Aguio'; not verbatim.

passages.text: Far away, the rival brothers of the two combatants felt the earth tremble, and each, fearing his brother was in trouble, hastened to the scene — one from the mountains, one by boat across the sea. They arrived at the same time and joined the battle. The trembling increased so much that Langgona, father of the twins, sought out the spot and tried to make peace, but he only made matters worse, and they all began fighting him, until the earth was in danger of falling to pieces.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Mabel Cook Cole, Philippine Folk Tales (1916), 'Bulanawan and Aguio'; not verbatim.

passages.text: Then the father of Langgona came and settled the trouble, and when all were at peace again they discovered that Aguio and Bulanawan were brothers and the grandsons of the peacemaker. Thus the tale binds the great quake-makers of the Bukidnon past into one family, and the shaking earth becomes the sign of kindred turned against kindred without knowing it.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Mabel Cook Cole, Philippine Folk Tales (1916), 'Bulanawan and Aguio'; not verbatim.

title.en: Origin: Toglai and Toglibon and the First Tribes
title.zh: 起源：托格萊與托格利邦及諸族之始

region.en: Cibolan, Mt. Apo, Davao, Mindanao, Philippines
region.zh: 菲律賓民答那峨達沃阿波火山錫博蘭

period: Bagobo oral tradition; recorded 1916 (Cole)

source.work: Mabel Cook Cole, Philippine Folk Tales (1916), Wild Tribes of Mindanao, Bagobo: 'Origin', eBook #12814

summary.en: The first couple Toglai and Toglibon live at Cibolan on Mt. Apo. After their eldest children depart across the waters — returning only as the Spaniards and Americans — a three-year drought dries every river, and the surviving children leave in pairs, each pair carrying some household thing from which a tribe takes its name: stones for the Magindanau, women's baskets for the Bilaan. Only a boy and girl too weak to travel remain; finding a single stalk of sugar-cane, they drink its water and survive, and their children are called Bagobo.
summary.zh: 初民夫婦托格萊與托格利邦居於阿波火山之錫博蘭。長子女渡水遠去，後裔即所謂西班牙人與美國人。其後三年大旱，河川盡涸；倖存子女兩兩離散，各攜一物——攜石者成馬京達瑙族，攜婦籃者成比拉蘭族，諸族之名皆源於所攜之物或所居之地。唯餘一對因飢渴過甚而無力遠行者，尋得一莖甘蔗飲汁度日；其子孫遂名巴戈博。

sensitivity.note: Philippine oral tradition recorded from Bagobo narrators; presented as an archival record, not as permission to speak for Bagobo communities. Ethnogenesis legend naming Bagobo, Bilaan, and Magindanau; the late-colonial framing (Spaniards and Americans) is retained as recorded, noting the tale's living tradition of adaptation.

passages.text: In the beginning there lived one man and one woman, Toglai and Toglibon. Their first children were a boy and a girl, and when they were old enough they went far away across the waters seeking a good place to live. Nothing more was heard of them until their children, the Spaniards and Americans, came back. After the first boy and girl left, other children were born to the couple, but they all remained at Cibolan on Mt. Apo with their parents, until Toglai and Toglibon died and became spirits.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Mabel Cook Cole, Philippine Folk Tales (1916), Bagobo 'Origin'; not verbatim.

passages.text: Soon after, a great drought came which lasted three years. All the waters dried up, so that there were no rivers and no plants could live. "Surely," said the people, "Manama is punishing us, and we must go elsewhere to find food and a place to dwell in." So they started out. Two went toward the sunset carrying stones from Cibolan River, and after a long journey they reached broad fields of cogon grass and abundance of water; their children still live there and are called Magindanau, because of the stones the couple carried when they left Cibolan.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Mabel Cook Cole, Philippine Folk Tales (1916), Bagobo 'Origin'; not verbatim.

passages.text: Two children went to the south carrying women's baskets (baraan), and settled where they found a good spot; their descendants are called Baraan or Bilaan, because of the women's baskets. So two by two the children of the first couple left the land of their birth, and in each place a new people developed — thus all the tribes in the world received their names from things the people carried out of Cibolan, or from the places where they settled.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Mabel Cook Cole, Philippine Folk Tales (1916), Bagobo 'Origin'; not verbatim.

passages.text: All the children left Mt. Apo save a boy and a girl whom hunger and thirst had made too weak to travel. One day, when they were about to die, the boy crawled out to the field to see if there was one living thing, and to his surprise he found a stalk of sugar-cane growing lustily. He eagerly cut it, and enough water came out to refresh him and his sister until the rains came. Because of this, their children are called Bagobo.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Mabel Cook Cole, Philippine Folk Tales (1916), Bagobo 'Origin'; not verbatim.

title.en: Lumabet and the White Deer: The Ascent to the Sky
title.zh: 盧馬貝特與白鹿：升天

region.en: Cibolan, Mt. Apo, Davao, Mindanao, Philippines
region.zh: 菲律賓民答那峨達沃阿波火山錫博蘭

period: Bagobo oral tradition; recorded 1916 (Cole)

source.work: Mabel Cook Cole, Philippine Folk Tales (1916), Wild Tribes of Mindanao, Bagobo: 'Lumabet', eBook #12814

summary.en: Lumabet, who could talk at one day old and worked wonders, chases a white deer around the world nine times, feeding himself by planting the skins of one banana and one camote each night. He has the people kill and revive his father eight times to prove his god-given power, then leads all who believe him through the moving, jaw-like sky to the world above — the sky keeping the last man as its agreed prize. His son follows on an arrow and a golden gun carried by white bees, while one homesick follower is lowered on a chain of karan leaves and becomes an owl.
summary.zh: 盧馬貝特生而一日能言，行諸奇事。他追白鹿環繞世界九匝，夜夜植蕉皮與薯皮為食。為證其神授之力，他八度命眾人殺其父並以頭帶復活之。其後他引信眾穿過開闔如口之天界，天得最後一人為酬；其子乘箭與金槍，由白蜂引路升天。而一名思鄉者被以卡蘭草鏈垂降，落地化為貓頭鷹。

sensitivity.note: Philippine oral tradition recorded from Bagobo narrators; presented as an archival record, not as permission to speak for Bagobo communities. Ascension cluster: a people-led migration to the sky at the horizon; resurrection tag covers the thrice-killed and revived father, an interpretive mapping.

passages.text: Soon after people were created on the earth there was born a child named Lumabet, who lived to be a very, very old man. He could talk when he was but one day old, and all his life he did wonderful things, until the people came to believe that he had been sent by Manama, the Great Spirit. As a young man he had a fine dog, and one day the dog scented a white deer. Lumabet and his companions pursued the swift deer but could not catch it; on and on they went until they had gone around the world, and one by one his companions dropped out.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Mabel Cook Cole, Philippine Folk Tales (1916), 'Lumabet'; not verbatim.

passages.text: All the time Lumabet had but one banana and one camote for food, but each night he planted the skins of these, and in the morning he found a banana tree with ripe fruit and a sweet potato large enough to eat. So he kept on until he had been around the world nine times, an old man with gray hair. At last he caught the deer, and he called all the people to a great feast. While they made merry, Lumabet told them to take a knife and kill his father. They were greatly surprised, but did as he commanded; when the old man was dead, Lumabet waved his headband over him and he came to life again. Eight times they killed the old man at Lumabet's command, and the eighth time he was small like a little boy, for each time they had cut off some of his flesh. They were certain Lumabet was a god.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Mabel Cook Cole, Philippine Folk Tales (1916), 'Lumabet'; not verbatim.

passages.text: One morning some spirits came to talk with Lumabet, and after they had gone he called the people into his house. Though the house was small and the people many, all went in and it did not seem crowded. Then he told them he was going on a long journey: all who believed in his power could go with him, while those who remained behind would be changed into animals and buso. He started out with many following, and those who refused were immediately changed into animals and buso. He led the people across the ocean to the place where the earth and sky meet, and there the sky moved up and down like a man opening and closing his jaws. "Sky, you must go up," commanded Lumabet, but the sky would not obey until Lumabet promised it the last man who tried to pass. The sky opened, the people entered, and near the last it shut down so suddenly that it caught not only the last man but also the long knife of the man before him.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Mabel Cook Cole, Philippine Folk Tales (1916), 'Lumabet'; not verbatim.

passages.text: On that same day Lumabet's son, out hunting, did not know his father had gone to the sky. Tired of the chase, he leaned an arrow against a baliti tree and sat on it; slowly it began to go down and carried him to his father's place, but he could find no people there — only a gun made of gold. White bees in the house said, "You must not weep, for we can take you to the sky where your father is," and they flew him up on the gun, reaching the sky in three days. Most of the followers were content in the sky, but one was unhappy, always looking down at the land below. The spirits made fun of him and wished to take out his intestines so he would be like them and never die, but he begged to go home. Finally Manama told them to allow it; they made a chain of the leaves of the karan grass, tied it to his legs, and let him down slowly head first — and when he reached the ground he was no longer a man but an owl.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Mabel Cook Cole, Philippine Folk Tales (1916), 'Lumabet'; not verbatim.

title.en: In the Beginning: The Four Beings on the Hat-Sized Island
title.zh: 太初：斗笠之島上的四神

region.en: Lake Sebu region, South Cotabato, Mindanao, Philippines (Bilaan homeland)
region.zh: 菲律賓民答那峨南哥達巴托省賽布湖（比拉蘭人故地）

period: Bilaan oral tradition; recorded 1916 (Cole)

source.work: Mabel Cook Cole, Philippine Folk Tales (1916), Wild Tribes of Mindanao, Bilaan: 'In the Beginning', eBook #12814

summary.en: Four beings live on an island no larger than a hat with a single bird; the bird flies across the waters and returns with earth, rattan, and fruit. Melu, the greatest, shapes and beats the soil like a woman molding pots, making the earth, and plants the fruit seeds. The beings first try to make people out of wax, which melts; then out of dirt — but Melu's companion sets the noses upside down. While his back is turned, Melu seizes each nose and turns it right, hurrying so that his finger-press at the root of the nose remains on every human face.
summary.zh: 四神居於僅如斗笠大小之島，島上唯彼等與一鳥。鳥飛越水域銜回泥土、藤與果實。至大者梅盧如婦人製陶般捶塑泥土而成大地，並植果核，藤蔓果樹滋長。四神先以蠟造人，置火即融；改以泥土塑形——同伴卻把鼻子捏反。趁其轉身，梅盧逐個扳正鼻樑，倉促之間以指壓鼻根，人臉上那道指痕至今猶在。

sensitivity.note: Philippine oral tradition recorded from Bilaan narrators; presented as an archival record. Clay-humans cluster (wax fails, earth succeeds, noses reversed).

passages.text: In the beginning there were four beings, and they lived on an island no larger than a hat. On this island there were no trees or grass or any other living thing besides these four people and one bird. One day they sent the bird out across the waters to see what it could find, and when it returned it brought some earth, a piece of rattan, and some fruit. Melu, the greatest of the four, took the soil and shaped it and beat it with a paddle in the same manner in which a woman shapes pots of clay, and when he finished he had made the earth. Then he planted the seeds from the fruit, and they grew until there was much rattan and many trees bearing fruit.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Mabel Cook Cole, Philippine Folk Tales (1916), Bilaan 'In the Beginning'; not verbatim.

passages.text: The four beings watched the growth for a long time and were well pleased, but finally Melu said, "Of what use is this earth and all the rattan and fruit if there are no people?" The others replied, "Let us make some people out of wax." So they took wax and worked long, fashioning it into forms; but when they brought the figures to the fire the wax melted, and they saw that men could not be made in that way.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Mabel Cook Cole, Philippine Folk Tales (1916), Bilaan 'In the Beginning'; not verbatim.

passages.text: Next they decided to try dirt, and Melu and one of his companions began working. All went well until they were ready to make the noses: the companion, working on that part, put them on upside down. Melu told him the people would drown if he left them that way, but he refused to change them. When his back was turned, however, Melu seized the noses one by one and turned them as they now are — but he was in such a hurry that he pressed his finger at the root, and it left a mark in the soft clay which you can still see on the faces of people.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Mabel Cook Cole, Philippine Folk Tales (1916), Bilaan 'In the Beginning'; not verbatim.

title.en: The Children of the Limokon
title.zh: 利莫康鳥之子

region.en: Mayo River, Davao Oriental, Mindanao, Philippines (Mandaya homeland)
region.zh: 菲律賓民答那峨東達沃省馬耀河（曼達雅人故地）

period: Mandaya oral tradition; recorded 1916 (Cole)

source.work: Mabel Cook Cole, Philippine Folk Tales (1916), Wild Tribes of Mindanao, Mandaya: 'The Children of the Limokon', eBook #12814

summary.en: In the very early days, the limokon doves were powerful and could talk like men. One limokon laid two eggs, one at the mouth of the Mayo River and one farther up its course; the first hatched a man, the second a woman. The man lived alone on the riverbank until a hair swept against his legs as he crossed the river; following the current upstream, he found the woman, and they married — their many children are the Mandaya still living along the Mayo River.
summary.zh: 太初之世，利莫康鳥神力無邊，形雖似鳥而言如人。一利莫康產二卵，一於馬耀河口，一於上游；前者孵化為男，後者為女。男子獨居河岸甚久，一日渡河時有髮絲強力沖撞其腿；溯流而上，終尋得女子，二人成婚——其眾多子孫即今居馬耀河畔之曼達雅人。

sensitivity.note: Philippine oral tradition recorded from Mandaya narrators; presented as an archival record. Ethnogenesis legend: humanity born of bird eggs on the river, with the first couple united by a hair in the current.
