secondary_sources.citation: Birrell 1993, Baltimore: Johns Hopkins University Press — annotated translation and dating of the Nüwa cycles.

secondary_sources.work: Derk Bodde, 'Myths of Ancient China'
secondary_sources.citation: Bodde 1961, in Mythologies of the Ancient World (ed. S. N. Kramer), New York: Doubleday — survey and stratigraphy of the Nüwa material.

source_urls.description: Wikisource (zh) — Fengsu Tongyi, public-domain Classical Chinese text

title.en: Nüwa and Fuxi: The Marriage of the Last Two
title.zh: 女媧伏羲兄妹為婚

region.en: Kunlun, the mountain of the divined marriage (symbolic pin: Kunlun range)
region.zh: 崑崙山（象徵性定位）

period: Duyi Zhi by Li Rong (Tang, c. 800 CE); cult images attested Han onward

source.archive: Internet Archive (reference; Duyi Zhi text in Tang collecting works)
source.work: Duyi Zhi (Records of the Singularity of Things), Li Rong, the Kunlun sibling-marriage episode

license: Public domain (Classical Chinese text; passages are compiler's renderings)

summary.en: When the flood of the world's ruin left only Nüwa and her brother Fuxi alive on Kunlun, they agreed to marry and beget mankind — but first asked heaven for a sign: two heaps of smoke that rose and twined together. Ashamed, she asked him to chase her; he caught her at a mulberry tree — the tree of unions — and from their marriage came the first people.
summary.zh: 宇初人民絕，唯女媧與其兄伏羲居崑崙而議為夫婦；羞恥相逐，兄追妹，妹以竹枝或扇自障，至桑下而合——煙柱相繞之占為天許，子孫遂眾。

sensitivity.note: Passages are the compiler's condensed paraphrases of the Duyi Zhi episode. The sibling-marriage motif appears across Han-tomb iconography (Nüwa and Fuxi with entwined serpent bodies) — recorded here as a mythic charter of the first marriage, not as endorsement of any practice.

passages.text: In the age when the people of the world had been swept away, Nüwa and her elder brother Fuxi alone survived, dwelling on Kunlun, the western mountain of the gods. With none left to marry, they spoke of becoming husband and wife to beget mankind — yet both were ashamed, for they were brother and sister.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Duyi Zhi, the Kunlun sibling-marriage episode (compiler's rendering); not verbatim.

passages.text: So they built two fires, and the smoke rose from each in a great column; the columns reached heaven and twined themselves about one another. 'Heaven consents,' they said. Still she fled him, and he chased her; nowhere could he catch her but under the great mulberry, whose shade hid them both — and from that marriage the people of the world were born again.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Duyi Zhi, smoke-divination and mulberry passages; not verbatim.

title.en: Gonggong Strikes Mount Buzhou, and the Sky Leans
title.zh: 共工觸不周山

region.en: Mount Buzhou, the imperfect northwest pillar (symbolic pin: northwest China)
region.zh: 西北不周山（象徵性定位）

period: Huainanzi, Tianwen Xun, c. 139 BCE

source.work: Huainanzi (Masters of Huainan), Tianwen Xun (Patterns of Heaven): Gonggong and Mount Buzhou

license: Public domain (Classical Chinese text; passages are compiler's renderings)

summary.en: Gonggong the water-power warred with Zhuanxu for the godhead; in rage and shame at defeat he struck his head on Mount Buzhou, the pillar of the northwest — and the pillar broke. Heaven's cables tore, so the sky tilts toward the northwest and the sun, moon and stars slide that way; the earth sinks in the southeast, so the rivers of China flow east.
summary.zh: 昔者共工與顓頊爭為帝，怒而觸不周之山，天柱折，地維絕——天傾西北，日月星辰移焉；地不滿東南，水潦塵埃歸焉。

sensitivity.note: Passages are the compiler's condensed paraphrases of the Huainanzi original. This is the aition of geography — sky's tilt and rivers' easterly flow — in one act of divine fury; a precursor to Nüwa's sky-mending (existing record 'nuwa-mending').

passages.text: Long ago Gonggong, the god of waters, contended with Zhuanxu for the lordship of the gods, and was beaten. In rage and shame he hurled himself against Mount Buzhou, the pillar that held up the sky in the northwest, and struck it with his head.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Huainanzi, Tianwen Xun, Gonggong passage (compiler's rendering); not verbatim.

passages.text: The pillar of heaven snapped and the cords of earth tore loose. So the sky leans to the northwest, and that is why the sun, the moon and the stars all slide in that direction; and the earth lies lower in the southeast — which is why the waters and the silt of China flow eastward to the sea.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Huainanzi, Tianwen Xun, aftermath passage; not verbatim.

title.en: Suiren-Shi, the Man Who Drilled Fire from Wood
title.zh: 燧人氏鑽木取火

region.en: The country of Suiming, where fire was found in the sun-tree (symbolic pin: northern China)
region.zh: 燧明國（象徵性定位）

period: Han Feizi, Wu Du chapter (c. 3rd c. BCE); expanded telling in Shiyi Ji (Wang Jia, 4th c. CE)

source.work: Han Feizi, Wu Du (Five Vermin): Suiren-Shi drills wood for fire; expanded in Shiyi Ji, juan 1: the fire-bird and the sun-tree of Suiming

license: Public domain (Classical Chinese text; passages are compiler's renderings)

summary.en: Before Suiren, people ate raw plants and shellfish and sickened their bellies; Suiren-Shi drilled dry wood and made fire, to cook what the world gave — and the people welcomed him as king. The later telling adds the pilgrim who reaches Suiming's country, sees a great fire-tree, and watches the birds peck it: sparks leap out, and he learns the drill.
summary.zh: 上古之世，民食果蓏蚌蛤，腥臊惡臭而傷害腹胃，民多疾病；有聖人作，鑽燧取火以化腥臊，而民說之，使王天下，號之曰燧人氏。拾遺記：燧明國有大樹，鳥啄其枝，燦然火出，聖人因取其枝以鑽火。

sensitivity.note: Passages are the compiler's condensed paraphrases of the Han Feizi and Shiyi Ji originals. Fire origin here is invention, not theft — a key contrast with the Greek Prometheus for the fire-theft cluster.

passages.text: In the uppermost age the people ate grasses, fruits, shellfish and raw flesh, and the rankness and stink of it wounded their stomachs, so that many were sick. Then a sage arose who drilled dry wood with a fire-stick and took out flame, and showed men to cook what they gathered — and the people were glad, and set him over the world; he was called Suiren-Shi, the Fire-Drill Master.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Han Feizi, Wu Du chapter (compiler's rendering); not verbatim.

passages.text: In the later telling, a wanderer travels to the country of Suiming, where the sun never sets and there grows a vast fire-tree; the birds of that land peck at its branches, and sparks flash out. The man takes a branch, drills it, and fire comes — and so, watching the birds, the human race learns the drill from the tree and the pecking beak.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Shiyi Ji, juan 1, Suiming fire-tree episode; not verbatim.

title.en: Cangjie Invents Writing, and Heaven Rains Grain
title.zh: 倉頡作書而天雨粟

region.en: The court of the Yellow Emperor (symbolic pin: Central Plains)
region.zh: 黃帝之廷（象徵性定位：中原）

period: Huainanzi, Benjing Xun (c. 139 BCE); Shuowen Jiezi preface (Xu Shen, c. 100 CE)

source.work: Huainanzi, Benjing Xun: Cangjie makes writing and heaven rains millet, ghosts weep at night; Shuowen Jiezi, Xu Shen's preface: the rope-knots before writing

license: Public domain (Classical Chinese text; passages are compiler's renderings)

summary.en: Cangjie, the recorder with four eyes who saw the tracks of birds and beasts, invented writing — and the cosmos shuddered: heaven rained down millet, and in the night the ghosts wept aloud, for with writing, cunning and record-keeping entered the world and its innocence ended.
summary.zh: 倉頡作書，天雨粟，鬼夜哭；倉頡四目，觀鳥獸之跡而畫卦象形——文字既作，詐偽萌生，神明之世終。

sensitivity.note: Passages are the compiler's condensed paraphrases of the Huainanzi and Shuowen preface. The boon-curse tag marks the dual reading: writing as civilizing gift and as the beginning of deceit.

passages.text: Before Cangjie, men governed by tying knots in cords and carved the memory of things in wood. Cangjie, the recorder of the Yellow Emperor, was born with four eyes and a gaze like a shining pair of stars; watching the tracks of birds and the prints of beasts on the earth, he saw that each creature's step could be told apart — and he drew the first signs, matching marks to things.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Shuowen Jiezi preface and traditional lore (compiler's rendering); not verbatim.

passages.text: The day Cangjie completed his characters, heaven rained down millet in wonder, and the ghosts wept through the night — for with writing, the cunning arts were born: contracts, quibbles, and the record of debts. Grain fell to feed the hungry who would now write; spirits wept because the age of trust was ending.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Huainanzi, Benjing Xun, Cangjie passage; not verbatim.

title.en: Gun Steals the Self-Spreading Soil and Dies for the Flood
title.zh: 鯀竊息壤

region.en: Yushan (Feather Mountain), where Gun was executed (traditional identification: near Lianyungang, Jiangsu)
region.zh: 羽山（今江蘇連雲港一帶）

period: Shanhaijing, Hai Nei Jing, compiled c. 4th-2nd c. BCE; variants in Chu Ci Tianwen (3rd c. BCE)

source.work: Shanhaijing (Classic of Mountains and Seas), Hai Nei Jing: Gun steals the xirang, is slain by Zhurong at Yushan, and gives birth to Yu; variants in Chu Ci, Tianwen

license: Public domain (Classical Chinese text; passages are compiler's renderings)

summary.en: When the floods raged without end, Gun stole from the Heavenly Emperor the xirang, the self-growing soil that rises wherever it is heaped, and tried to dam the waters without awaiting the decree — and the Emperor sent the fire-god Zhurong to kill him in the outskirts of Yushan. For three years Gun's body did not rot; when it was cut open, Yu was born from it, and Gun became a yellow dragon and sank into the Yu abyss.
summary.zh: 洪水滔天，鯀竊帝之息壤以堙洪水，不待帝命；帝令祝融殺鯀於羽郊。鯀復生禹，帝乃命禹卒布土以定九州——鯀三年不腐，剖之以吳刀，化為黃龍（一作黃熊）入羽淵。

sensitivity.note: Passages are the compiler's condensed paraphrases of the Shanhaijing original; the Chu Ci Tianwen parallel (Gun transformed) is paraphrased from the Classical Chinese. Cross-tradition flood-cluster record; the Tianwen's 'yellow bear' against the Guo Pu commentary's 'yellow dragon' variant is noted.

passages.text: The floods rose and raged, and there was nothing that could check them. Gun, the father of Yu, went up to heaven and stole the Emperor's xirang — the soil of unending growth, which swells higher wherever it is heaped — and without waiting for the Emperor's command he built dikes with it against the waters.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Shanhaijing, Hai Nei Jing, Gun passage (compiler's rendering); not verbatim.

passages.text: The Emperor was angered that the soil had been taken without his decree, and he sent the fire-god Zhurong to execute Gun in the outskirts of Feather Mountain. Gun's body lay there three years without rotting; when it was cut open with the knife of Wu, Yu sprang out of it — the son born from the father's death.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Shanhaijing, Hai Nei Jing, execution and birth of Yu; not verbatim.

passages.text: Gun himself did not vanish: he transformed into a yellow dragon — some tellers say a yellow bear — and sank into the abyss of Yu. And the Emperor, needing the work done, commanded Yu to take up the xirang lawfully and spread the soil to fix the Nine Provinces; the flood-tamer finished what the flood-thief had begun.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Shanhaijing, Hai Nei Jing, with the transformation and the Emperor's mandate to Yu; not verbatim.

canonical_translation: Compiler's English rendering from the public-domain original; consulted (copyright, summary only): Anne Birrell, Chinese Mythology: An Introduction, Johns Hopkins 1993

narrative.en:
The Chinese flood myth is not a single deluge-tale but a three-generation drama: flood, failed dammer, and successful channeler. The Shanhaijing's Hai Nei Jing chapter gives the sharpest version of its first act.

BEGINNING: THE WATER THAT HAD NO MEASURE. In the age before the Nine Provinces were settled, the waters rose and raged, flooding the world. Gun, a god of the divine lineage, could not bear it. He went up to heaven, and there he stole the xirang — the self-spreading soil, a magic earth that grows of itself wherever it is thrown, the ideal dam-filler. It is heaven's own property: the tool by which the sky-father would fix the world's waters when he chose.

MIDDLE: THE DAM WITHOUT A DECREE. Gun threw up dikes of xirang against the flood — but without the Emperor's command. In the Chinese mythic logic, the fatal flaw is procedural as much as hydraulic: he used heaven's means without heaven's mandate. The Emperor sent the fire-god Zhurong, lord of fire against the lord of water, to kill Gun in the outskirts of Feather Mountain. Gun's crime and his motive are both honored in later Chinese readings: he was an executor executed, the one who broke rank to try to save the drowning world.

END: THE BODY THAT GAVE BIRTH. For three years Gun's corpse would not decay. The officials sent to investigate cut it open with the knife of Wu — and Yu leapt out, born from his father's body. Gun himself transformed into a yellow dragon (in the Chu Ci Tianwen's question-form, a yellow bear) and sank into the deep pool of Yuyuan. The Emperor then gave Yu the mandate, and Yu — lawfully this time — spread the soil, dredged the channels, and fixed the Nine Provinces. The damming that failed as rebellion succeeded as obedience.

CULTURAL FUNCTION. This is China's flood-cluster narrative, and its shape differs from the Near Eastern pattern: there is no world-destruction by a vengeful god, but a cosmic infrastructure project in which the rebel dammer is executed and his son finishes the job with heaven's blessing. Gun became, in later ritual memory, a wronged benefactor — he is given a place among the honored dead in the Han dynasty state sacrifices, and the poet who questions heaven (Qu Yuan's Tianwen) asks pointedly why the one who tried to dam the flood was killed for it. The myth also founds Yu's legitimacy: the savior-child emerges from the executed rebel's undecayed body, proof that Gun's purpose was right even when his method was not.
narrative.zh: 洪水滔天，鯀竊息壤以堙洪水，不待帝命，帝令祝融殺鯀於羽郊；三年不腐，剖之以吳刀，禹出生於父腹；鯀化黃龍（天問作黃熊）入羽淵，帝乃命禹卒布土以定九州。中國洪水神話為三代之劇：洪水、盜壤築堤而被誅之父、受命成功之子；無神罰滅世之型，而為天道秩序下之水利工程——越命而救世者死，承命者成。鯀後世入祀典，屈原《天問》直問其冤。功能：解釋九州地理、王朝合法性自禹始、及『旨正而行違』之悲劇倫理。

functions: Aition of the Nine Provinces' geography as the flood-tamer's legacy
Charter of Yu's legitimacy: the savior born from the executed rebel
Tragic ethics of good intent against procedural order (theft of means without mandate)
Ritual memory of Gun as wronged benefactor in Han state sacrifice

variants.name: Chu Ci, Tianwen (3rd c. BCE) — the yellow bear
variants.summary: The Tianwen asks how Gun, changed into a yellow bear, could live on in the Yu abyss — the transformation into a bear rather than a dragon, and the poet's pointed sympathy for the executed dammer.

variants.name: Shiji, Xia Benji (c. 94 BCE)
variants.summary: The historiographic version strips the theft: Gun fails for nine years, is executed at Yushan as a public failure, and the empire's council names his son Yu to continue — history absorbing the myth.

variants.name: Guo Pu's commentary — the yellow dragon
variants.text_tradition: Guo Pu (Jin, 3rd-4th c. CE) commentary on the Shanhaijing
variants.summary: Guo Pu reads Gun's transformation as a yellow dragon entering the Yuyuan pool, and links the tale to the revived 'xirang' rite of Yu's earth-spreading.

primary_sources.citation: Compiled c. 4th-2nd c. BCE; Guo Pu recension; Gun passage (Gun steals xirang / execution at Yushan / birth of Yu). Classical Chinese via Wikisource.
Qu Yuan, 3rd c. BCE; Gun questions ('turns into a yellow bear, how can it live?').

secondary_sources.work: Anne Birrell, Chinese Mythology: An Introduction
secondary_sources.citation: Birrell 1993, Baltimore: Johns Hopkins University Press — annotated translation of the Gun-Yu cycle.

secondary_sources.work: Sarah Allan, The Shape of the Turtle: Myth, Art, and Cosmos in Classical China
secondary_sources.citation: Allan 1991, Albany: SUNY Press — structure of the flood and cosmogonic myths.

title.en: Houji, the Abandoned Child Who Invented Farming
title.zh: 后稷誕生與稼穡

region.en: Tai's footprints in the great marsh, Zhou homeland (symbolic pin: Wei River valley, Shaanxi)
region.zh: 周原邰地（象徵性定位：渭水流域）

period: Shi Jing (Book of Songs), Da Ya: Sheng Min, c. 8th-6th c. BCE compilation; Shiji, Zhou Ben Ji, c. 94 BCE

source.work: Shi Jing, Da Ya: Sheng Min (Birth of the People), the Houji birth poem; Shiji, Zhou Ben Ji: Jiang Yuan and the giant footprint

license: Public domain (Classical Chinese text; passages are compiler's renderings)

summary.en: Jiang Yuan steps into the footprint of God in the great marsh and becomes pregnant; her child, born clear as an egg and thrice abandoned (in a lane, in the woods, on the ice — saved each time), is named Qi, 'the Abandoned.' The boy plants beans and grain, teaches the six crops, founds the sacrifice to heaven — and the Zhou kings call him their ancestor, Houji, Lord Millet.
summary.zh: 姜嫄履帝武敏歆而生后稷；誕彌厥月，先生如達；三棄而三活——棄之隘巷、平林、寒冰，鳥覆翼之；名之曰棄。幼即如藝蓽菽，教民稼穡，樹藝五穀——周人祖之，是為后稷。

sensitivity.note: Passages are the compiler's condensed paraphrases of the Sheng Min hymn and Shiji narrative. The virgin-conception motif (footprint, no father named in the Shijing version) is a ritual-purity genealogy device, noted for the cross-tradition birth cluster.

passages.text: She who first bore the people of Zhou was Jiang Yuan. She went to sacrifice and pray that she might be spared childlessness, then trod in the great toe-print of God in the high ground of the marsh — and her heart stirred, and she conceived. When her months were full she bore a son clear and smooth as an egg of the lamb, and the household was alarmed, for a son of such birth must be ill-omened.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Shi Jing, Da Ya: Sheng Min, opening stanzas (compiler's rendering); not verbatim.

passages.text: They laid him in a narrow lane, but oxen and horses stepped around him; they set him in the woods, but woodcutters were there; they threw him onto the ice of the cold marsh, and birds came and sheltered him with their wings. When the birds flew off he cried out, loud and long — so at last his mother took him back and named him Qi, the Abandoned One.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Shi Jing, Sheng Min, the three abandonments; not verbatim.

passages.text: When Qi was a boy he grew up knowing how to plant beans, beans that flourished; then grain and hemp, gourds and melons. He taught the people the six kinds of crop and the rite of sacrifice to the Lord on High, and the Zhou dynasty counted him as its founder — the Lord of Millet, Houji.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Shi Jing, Sheng Min, agricultural stanzas; Shiji, Zhou Ben Ji parallel; not verbatim.

title.en: Jian Di Swallows the Black Bird's Egg: The Birth of the Shang
title.zh: 簡狄吞玄鳥卵

region.en: The bank of the Xuan Marsh, where Jian Di bathed (symbolic pin: northern Henan–southern Hebei)
region.zh: 玄丘之濱（象徵性定位：豫北冀南）

period: Shi Jing, Shang Song: Xuan Niao (c. 8th-6th c. BCE compilation); Shiji, Yin Ben Ji, c. 94 BCE

source.work: Shi Jing, Shang Song: Xuan Niao (The Dark Bird), the Shang origin hymn; Shiji, Yin Ben Ji: Jian Di and the egg

license: Public domain (Classical Chinese text; passages are compiler's renderings)

summary.en: Heaven commanded the dark bird to descend and bear the Shang: Jian Di, consort of Di Ku, bathing with her sisters, saw a dark bird drop its egg, took it and swallowed it — and bore Xie, ancestor of the Shang kings, whose descendant Tang received the mandate and ruled the four quarters.
summary.zh: 天命玄鳥，降而生商；簡狄為帝嚳次妃，行浴見玄鳥墮其卵，取吞之，孕而生契——商之王族由此而出，湯受命伐夏。

sensitivity.note: Passages are the compiler's condensed paraphrases of the Xuan Niao hymn and Shiji narrative. Bird-conception genealogies (black bird of Shang, Jumong's egg in Korea) form a northeast-Asian pattern — noted for comparative linking.

passages.text: Heaven sent down the dark bird to bear the house of Shang. Jian Di, the second consort of Di Ku, went with her two companions to bathe, and a dark bird flew over them and let fall its egg; Jian Di picked it up and swallowed it, and in that moment she conceived.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Shi Jing, Shang Song: Xuan Niao, with Shiji, Yin Ben Ji narrative (compiler's rendering); not verbatim.

passages.text: The child was Xie, the ancestor of the Shang. His descendants grew great, and in the time of Tang the house of Shang received the mandate and overthrew the Xia — for the song says the dark bird's gift was not one son but a dynasty, founded in a swallowed egg on the riverbank.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Shi Jing, Xuan Niao, dynastic stanzas; not verbatim.

title.en: Shennong Tastes the Hundred Herbs
title.zh: 神農嘗百草

region.en: The Hundred Herbs fields of the south (symbolic pin: Hubei–Hunan highlands, Shennongjia)
region.zh: 南方百草之野（象徵性定位：神農架一帶）

period: Huainanzi, Xiuxu Xun (c. 139 BCE); broader Shennong cycle in Han sources

source.work: Huainanzi, Xiuxu Xun: Shennong tastes the hundred herbs and meets seventy poisons in a day

license: Public domain (Classical Chinese text; passages are compiler's renderings)

summary.en: When the people of antiquity ate grasses, drank from streams and climbed trees for fruit, they fell sick and had no one to heal them; Shennong, the Divine Farmer, tasted the hundred herbs, met seventy poisons in a single day, and taught the people which plants were food, which medicine, and which death.
summary.zh: 古者民茹草飲水，採樹木之實，時多疾病毒傷之害；於是神農乃始教民播種五穀，嘗百草之滋味，一日而遇七十毒——辨可食者、可藥者。

sensitivity.note: Passages are the compiler's condensed paraphrases of the Huainanzi original. Tagging caveat: 'quest-immortality' marks Shennong's poison-testing as a search for life-giving herbs; the tradition's pharmaceutical canon (Bencao) claims him as founder.

passages.text: In the earliest age the people ate grass and drank from standing water, plucked the fruits of trees and the shellfish of rivers, and suffered always: the sick had no medicine, the poisoned no remedy, the bitten no cure. Then Shennong arose. He tasted the hundred herbs with his own mouth, met seventy poisons in one day, and went on tasting; he distinguished what could be eaten, what could heal, and what killed, and he taught the people to sow the five grains and to use the herbs as medicine. The hills and streams keep the marks of his testing — so the pharmacists of China say.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Huainanzi, Xiuxu Xun, opening (compiler's rendering); not verbatim. / Paraphrase of Huainanzi, Xiuxu Xun, with later Shennong lore; not verbatim.

title.en: The Opening of the Mouth: Rebirthing the Dead King
title.zh: 開口儀：亡王重生之術

region.en: Sakkarah (Saqqara), Egypt (pyramid chapels where the liturgy was cut)
region.zh: 埃及薩卡拉（金字塔祭堂，儀文刻壁處）

period: Pyramid Texts of the 5th-6th Dynasties, c. 2350-2175 BCE (Budge translation 1910)

source.work: The Literature of the Ancient Egyptians, trans. E. A. W. Budge (London, 1910), ch. II, 'The Book of Opening the Mouth'

summary.en: In the oldest recorded funerary rite, a priest wearing the bull's skin lies as if dead and then emerges — the king's rebirth as a spirit-body — while another priest cuts the bandages from the dead king's lips with the Pesh-Kef knife and chants the purification of Horus, so the king may walk and speak in the Other World.
summary.zh: 最古之葬儀：披牛皮的祭司臥而復起——亡王化為靈體重生；另一祭司以佩舍夫刀割去亡王唇上繃帶，誦荷魯斯淨化之辭，使王得以在冥界行走言語。

sensitivity.note: Ancient funerary liturgy; no living community restrictions. Budge's 1910 wording is dated in style but is the cited public-domain source, used without religious truth claims.

passages.text: First of all incense was burnt, and the priest said, 'Thou art pure,' four times. Water was then sprinkled over the statue and the priest said, 'Thou art pure. Thou art pure. Thy purifications are the purifications of Horus, and the purifications of Horus are thy purifications.' This formula was repeated three times, once with the name of Set, once with the name of Thoth, and once with the name of Sep. The priest then said, 'Thou hast received thy head, and thy bones have been brought unto thee before Keb.'
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Budge, Literature of the Ancient Egyptians (1910), ch. II, section I.

passages.text: The next ceremony, the ninth, represented the re-birth of the king, who was personified by a priest. The priest, wrapped in the skin of a bull, lay on a small bed and feigned death. When the chief priest had said, 'O my father,' four times, the priest representing the king came forth from the bull's skin, and sat up; this act symbolized the resurrection of the king in the form of a spirit-body (sahu). The chief priest then asserted that the king was alive, and that he should never be removed, and that he was similar in every way to Horus.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Budge (1910), ch. II.

passages.text: And the Osiris shall walk and shall talk, and his body shall be with the Great Company of the Gods who dwell in the Great House of the Aged One (i.e. the Sun-god) who dwelleth in Anu. And he shall take possession of the Urrt Crown therein before Horus, the Lord of mankind. Hail, Osiris! Horus hath opened thy mouth and thine eyes with the instruments Sebur and An, wherewith the mouths of the gods of the South were opened. All the gods bring words of power. They recite them for thee. They make thee to live by them. Thou becomest the possessor of twofold strength. Thou art protected, and thou shalt not die.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Budge (1910), ch. II.

title.en: The Liturgy of Funerary Offerings: Feeding the Ka of Unas
title.zh: 祭品禮文：餵養烏納斯之卡

region.en: Pyramid of Unas, Sakkarah, Egypt
region.zh: 埃及薩卡拉烏納斯金字塔

period: Pyramid Texts, reign of Unas (c. 2350-2300 BCE) (Budge translation 1910)

source.work: The Literature of the Ancient Egyptians, trans. E. A. W. Budge (1910), ch. II, 'The Liturgy of Funerary Offerings'

summary.en: About one hundred and fifty offerings — cold water, wine, onions, oils, bread — are presented one by one to the dead king's ka, and as each object is given the priest calls it the Eye of Horus, whose life-giving power transmutes the substance into food for the spirit in the Other World.
summary.zh: 約一百五十項祭品——冷水、酒、洋蔥、油脂、麵包——逐一呈於亡王之卡；祭司每奉一物皆稱其為荷魯斯之眼，其生命之力使實物轉化為冥界之靈糧。

sensitivity.note: Ancient funerary liturgy; no living community restrictions.

passages.text: This libation is for thee, Osiris, this libation is for thee, Unas. (Here offer cold water of the North.) It cometh forth before thy son, cometh forth before Horus. I have come, I have brought unto thee the Eye of Horus, that thy heart may be refreshed thereby. I have brought it and have set it under thy sandals, and I present unto thee that which flowed forth from thee. There shall be no stoppage to thy heart whilst it is with thee, and the offerings that appear at the command shall appear at thy word of command. (Recite four times.)
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Budge (1910), ch. II, section II, offering 32.

passages.text: Thou hast taken possession of the two Eyes of Horus, the White and the Black, and when they are in thy face they illumine it. (Here offer two jugs of wine, one white, one black.) — Day hath made an offering unto thee in the sky. The South and the North have given offerings unto thee. Night hath made an offering unto thee. An offering is brought unto thee, look upon it; an offering, hear it. There is an offering before thee, there is an offering behind thee, there is an offering with thee. (Here offer a cake for the journey.)
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Budge (1910), offerings 37-38.

passages.text: Osiris Unas, the white teeth of Horus are presented unto thee so that they may fill thy mouth. (Here offer five bunches of onions.) — O Ra, the worship that is paid to thee, the worship of every kind, shall be paid [also] to Unas. Everything that is offered to thy body shall be offered to the Double of Unas also, and everything that is offered to his body shall be thine. (Here offer the table of holy offerings.)
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Budge (1910), offerings 41 and 47.

passages.text: O ye oils, ye oils, which are on the forehead of Horus, set ye yourselves on the forehead of Unas, and make him to smell sweet through you. (Here offer oil of cedar of the finest quality.) — Make ye him to be a spirit-soul (khu) through possession of you, and grant ye him to have the mastery over his body, let his eyes be opened, and let all the spirit-souls see him, and let them hear his name. Behold, Osiris Unas, the Eye of Horus hath been brought unto thee, for it hath been seized for thee that it may be before thee. (Here offer the finest Thehenu oil.)
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Budge (1910), offerings 61-62.

title.en: Unas the Cannibal: The King Who Eats the Gods
title.zh: 食神之王烏納斯

region.en: Pyramid of Unas, Sakkarah, Egypt
region.zh: 埃及薩卡拉烏納斯金字塔

period: Pyramid Texts of Unas (c. 2350-2300 BCE; Budge translation 1910)

source.work: The Literature of the Ancient Egyptians, trans. E. A. W. Budge (1910), ch. II, the Cannibal Hymn of Unas

summary.en: The most fearsome passage of the Pyramid Texts: the dead king rises as a hunter in the sky, lassoes the gods, and butchers them in cauldrons so that he may swallow their magical powers and spirits of life, eating the Red Crown and the White Crown whole — a theology in which the dead king becomes greater than the gods by consuming them.
summary.zh: 《金字塔文》最可怖之篇：亡王化為天界獵手，套索縛神，於夜釜中割喉烹煮，吞其神力與靈魄，併吞紅冠白冠——亡王以噬神而凌駕諸神之上。

sensitivity.note: Ancient royal funerary text. Tagging note: 'dismembered-giant' is applied in reverse — here the king dismembers the gods for power, the inversion of the world-creation motif; recorded as an interpretive choice.

passages.text: The skies lower, the Star-gods tremble, the Archers quake, the bones of the Akeru gods tremble, and those who are with them are struck dumb when they see Unas rising up as a soul, in the form of the god who liveth upon his fathers, and who turneth his mothers into his food. Unas is the lord of wisdom, and his mother knoweth not his name. The adoration of Unas is in heaven, he hath become mighty in the horizon like Temu, the father that gave him birth, and after Temu had given him birth Unas became stronger than his father. The Doubles of Unas are behind him, the soles of his feet are beneath his feet, his gods are over him, his serpents are [seated] upon his brow, the serpent-guides of Unas are in front of him, and the spirit of the flame looketh upon [his] soul. Unas is a bull in heaven. He directeth his steps where he willeth.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Budge (1910), ch. II, section IV — the Cannibal Hymn (Unas text).

passages.text: He liveth upon the form which each god taketh upon himself, and he eateth the flesh of those who come to fill their bellies with the magical charms in the Lake of Fire. Unas is equipped with power against the spirit-souls thereof, and he riseth in the form of the mighty one, the lord of those who dwell in power. Unas hath taken his seat with his back turned towards Keb (the Earth-god). Unas hath weighed his words with the hidden god who hath no name, on the day of hacking in pieces the firstborn. Unas is the lord of offerings, the untier of the knot, and he himself maketh abundant the offerings of meat and drink. Unas devoureth men, and liveth upon the gods, he is the lord of envoys whom he sendeth forth on his missions.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Budge (1910), Cannibal Hymn.

passages.text: 'He who cutteth off hairy scalps,' who dwelleth in the fields, tieth the gods with ropes. Tcheser-tep shepherdeth them for Unas and driveth them unto him; and the Cord-master hath bound them for slaughter. Khensu, the slayer of the wicked, cutteth their throats, and draweth out their intestines, for it is he whom Unas sendeth to slaughter [them], and Shesmu cutteth them in pieces, and boileth their members in his blazing caldrons of the night. Unas eateth their magical powers, and he swalloweth their spirit-souls. The great ones among them serve for his meal at daybreak, the lesser serve for his meal at eventide, and the least among them serve for his meal in the night. The old gods and the old goddesses become fuel for his furnace.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Budge (1910), Cannibal Hymn.

passages.text: Unas is the Great Power, the Power of Powers, and Unas is the Chief of the gods in visible forms. Whatsoever he findeth upon his path he eateth forthwith, and the magical might of Unas is before that of all the spirit-bodies who dwell in the horizon. Unas is the firstborn of the firstborn gods. Unas is surrounded by thousands, and oblations are made unto him by hundreds; he is made manifest as the Great Power by Saah (Orion), the father of the gods. Unas repeateth his rising in heaven, and he is crowned lord of the horizon. He hath reckoned up the bandlets and the arm-rings [of his captives], he hath taken possession of the hearts of the gods. Unas hath eaten the Red Crown, and he hath swallowed the White Crown; the food of Unas is the intestines, and his meat is hearts and their words of power. Unas hath eaten the whole of the knowledge of every god, and the period of his life is eternity, and the duration of his existence is everlastingness.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Budge (1910), Cannibal Hymn.

title.en: The King Ascends: A Ladder to Heaven and the Field of Offerings
title.zh: 亡王登天：天梯與祭田

region.en: Pyramid of Pepi I, Sakkarah, Egypt
region.zh: 埃及薩卡拉佩皮一世金字塔

period: Pyramid Texts, 6th Dynasty, c. 2300-2200 BCE (Budge translation 1910)

source.work: The Literature of the Ancient Egyptians, trans. E. A. W. Budge (1910), ch. II, 'The King in Heaven' and the later text of Pepi

summary.en: The dead king is made a living star: Sothis draws him to heaven, Nut unfolds her arms, Ra sets a ladder between heaven and earth, and as a falcon and a goose he flies among his brethren the gods; a later text gives him a crystal throne between two great gods, where he judges and nothing can be denied him.
summary.zh: 亡王化作活星：天狼星引其升天，努特展臂相迎，拉置天梯於天地之間，王如鷹如雁翱翔於諸神之間；晚期文本更賜其雙大神間之水晶寶座，執掌裁決，無可駁斥。

sensitivity.note: Ancient royal funerary text; no living community restrictions.

passages.text: The sky hath withdrawn the life of the star Septet (Sothis, the Dog-star); behold Unas a living being, the son of Septet. The Eighteen Gods have purified him in Meskha (the Great Bear), [he is] an imperishable star. The house of Unas perisheth not in the sky, the throne of Unas perisheth not on the earth. Men make supplication [there], the gods fly [thither]. Septet hath made Unas fly to heaven to be with his brethren the gods. Nut, the Great Lady, hath unfolded her arms to Unas.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Budge (1910), ch. II, section IV.

passages.text: Unas cometh forth into heaven by thee, Ra. The face of Unas is like the [faces of the] Hawks. The wings of Unas are like [those of] geese. The nails of Unas are like the claws of the god Tuf. There is no [evil] word concerning Unas on earth among men. There is no hostile speech about him with the gods. Unas hath destroyed his word, he hath ascended to heaven. Upuatu hath made Unas fly up to heaven among his brethren the gods. Unas hath drawn together his arms like the Smen goose, he striketh his wings like a falcon, flying, flying. O men, Unas flieth up into heaven.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Budge (1910), section IV.

passages.text: Osiris hath commanded that Unas shall rise as a second Horus, and these Four Spirit-souls in Anu have written an edict to the two great gods in the Sky. Ra set up the Ladder in front of Osiris, Horus set up the Ladder in front of his father Osiris when he went to his spirit, one on this side [and] one on the other side; Unas is between them. Behold, he is the god of the pure seats coming forth from the bath. Unas standeth up, lo Horus; Unas sitteth down, lo Set. Ra graspeth his hand, spirit to heaven, body to earth.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Budge (1910), section IV.

passages.text: Pepi appeareth in heaven among the imperishable stars. His sister the star Sothis (the Dog-star), his guide the Morning Star (Venus) lead him by the hand to the Field of Offerings. He taketh his seat on the crystal throne, which hath faces of fierce lions and feet in the form of the hoofs of the Bull Sma-ur. He standeth up in his place between the Two Great Gods, and his sceptre and staff are in his hands. The Two Great Gods look on in their places, and they find Pepi acting as judge of the gods. The word of every spirit-soul is in him, and they make offerings to him among the Two Companies of the Gods.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Budge (1910), section IV, from the later Pyramid Text of Pepi.

title.en: The Sky-goddess Hymn: Nut Takes the King as Her Imperishable Star
title.zh: 天神頌：努特迎王為不滅之星

region.en: Pyramid of Pepi II, Sakkarah, Egypt
region.zh: 埃及薩卡拉佩皮二世金字塔

period: Pyramid Texts, reign of Pepi II (c. 2278-2184 BCE) (Budge translation 1910)

source.work: The Literature of the Ancient Egyptians, trans. E. A. W. Budge (1910), ch. II, the Hymn to Nut (ll. 61-64)

summary.en: A hymn from the Pyramid Texts in which the sky-goddess Nut stretches herself over the dead king, snatching him from the hand of Set; she who leapt unborn in the womb of Tefnut is asked to make the king like herself — an imperishable star that shall not die, with the whole earth under her hands.
summary.zh: 《金字塔文》頌詩：天神努特展身於亡王之上，自塞特之手奪回其子；未生而已在泰芙努特胎中躍動之努特，受請使王同化為己——不滅之星，永不死亡，大地盡在其雙手之下。

sensitivity.note: Ancient royal funerary hymn; no living community restrictions.

passages.text: [O] Nut, thou hast extended thyself over thy son the Osiris Pepi, Thou hast snatched him out of the hand of Set; join him to thyself, Nut. Thou comest, snatch thy son; behold, thou comest, form this great one [like] unto thyself. [O] Nut, cast thyself upon thy son the Osiris Pepi. Form thou him, O Great Fashioner; this great one is among thy children. Keb [was to] Nut. Thou didst become a spirit.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Budge (1910), ch. II, section III, the Hymn to Nut.

passages.text: Thou wast a mighty goddess in the womb of thy mother Tefnut when thou wast not born. Form thou Pepi with life and well-being; he shall not die. Strong was thy heart, Thou didst leap in the womb of thy mother in thy name of 'Nut.' [O] perfect daughter, mighty one in thy mother, who art crowned like a king of the North, Make this Pepi a spirit-soul in thee, let him not die.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Budge (1910), Hymn to Nut.

passages.text: [O] Great Lady, who didst come into being in the sky, who art mighty. Who dost make happy, and dost fill every place (or being), with thy beauty, The whole earth is under thee, thou hast taken possession of it. Thou hast encompassed the earth, everything is in thy two hands, Grant thou that this Pepi may be in thee like an imperishable star. Thou hast associated with Keb in thy name of 'Pet' (i.e. Sky). Thou hast united the earth in every place.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Budge (1910), Hymn to Nut.

passages.text: [O] mistress over the earth, thou art above thy father Shu, thou hast the mastery over him. He hath loved thee so much that he setteth himself under thee in everything. Thou hast taken possession of every god for thyself with his boat. Thou hast made them shine like lamps, Assuredly they shall not cease from thee like the stars. Let not this Pepi depart from thee in thy name of 'Hert' (ll. 61-64).
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Budge (1910), Hymn to Nut, closing lines.

title.en: The Monkey and the Turtle
title.zh: 猴子與海龜

region.en: Ilocos coast, northwestern Luzon, Philippines (symbolic pin for the Ilocano tale cycle)
region.zh: 菲律賓呂宋西北伊洛克斯海岸（伊洛卡諾故事圈之象徵定位）

period: Ilocano oral tradition; recorded 1916 (Cole)

source.work: Mabel Cook Cole, Philippine Folk Tales (1916), Christianized Tribes, Ilocano: 'The Monkey and the Turtle', eBook #12814

summary.en: The sad, hungry monkey joins the turtle in stealing banana plants, but plants his in a tree where it dies, while the turtle's rooted plant fruits. The monkey eats all the ripe fruit and is killed by the turtle's bamboo traps; the turtle cuts up the corpse, sells the meat to other monkeys, and when captured, tricks his captors into imitating his stone-weighted dive — the monkeys drown, and monkeys do not eat meat to this day.
summary.zh: 飢餓的猴子與海龜合夥偷香蕉苗；猴把苗種在樹上而枯死，龜的則結果纍纍。猴獨吞熟蕉，被龜以竹尖陷阱殺死；龜將猴屍切成肉塊賣給群猴，被擒時又誘群猴腰繫石頭潛水捕龍蝦——群猴溺斃，猴子至今不食肉。

sensitivity.note: Philippine oral tradition recorded from Ilocano narrators; presented as an archival record. Classic trickster/counter-trickster animal cycle tale.

passages.text: A monkey, looking very sad and dejected, was walking along the bank of the river one day when he met a turtle. He was hungry, for the farmer's squash had all been taken by other monkeys, and the turtle told him not to be discouraged: take a bolo and follow him, and they would steal some banana plants. They dug up some nice plants, but the monkey climbed a tree and planted his in it, while the turtle, who could not climb, dug a hole in the ground and set his there. Weeks later the monkey's plant was dead, for its roots had had no soil in the tree, but the turtle's was tall and bearing fruit.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Mabel Cook Cole, Philippine Folk Tales (1916), 'The Monkey and the Turtle'; not verbatim.

passages.text: The monkey sprang up the tree, leaving the poor turtle on the ground, and when the turtle begged for some to eat, the monkey threw him only a green one and ate all the ripe ones himself. When he had eaten all the good bananas the monkey stretched his arms around the tree and went to sleep. The turtle gathered sharp bamboo, stuck it all around under the tree, and cried, "Crocodile is coming! Crocodile is coming!" The monkey, startled, fell upon the sharp bamboo and was killed.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Mabel Cook Cole, Philippine Folk Tales (1916), 'The Monkey and the Turtle'; not verbatim.

passages.text: The turtle cut the dead monkey into pieces, put salt on it, and dried it in the sun; the next day he sold the meat to other monkeys in the mountains for squash, calling back as he left: "Lazy fellows, you are now eating your own body." The monkeys ran and caught him. "Let us take a hatchet," said one, "and cut him into very small pieces" — but the turtle laughed, showing the black scars on his shell: "That is just what I like." "Let us throw him into the water," said another, and at this the turtle cried and begged for his life, so they threw him in. He soon came up with a lobster, and when the astonished monkeys begged to know how to catch lobsters, he said he had tied a stone to a string around his waist to sink. They all tied strings and stones and plunged into the water, never to come up again. And to this day monkeys do not like to eat meat, because they remember the ancient story.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Mabel Cook Cole, Philippine Folk Tales (1916), 'The Monkey and the Turtle'; not verbatim.

title.en: The Poor Fisherman and His Wife
title.zh: 貧窮漁夫與其妻

region.en: Ilocos coast, northwestern Luzon, Philippines (symbolic pin for the Ilocano tale cycle)
region.zh: 菲律賓呂宋西北伊洛克斯海岸（伊洛卡諾故事圈之象徵定位）

period: Ilocano oral tradition; recorded 1916 (Cole)

source.work: Mabel Cook Cole, Philippine Folk Tales (1916), Christianized Tribes, Ilocano: 'The Poor Fisherman and His Wife', eBook #12814

summary.en: A poor fisherman catches a great white fish he believes is the town priest; his wife thinks it is the governor. Terrified of discovery, they flee their village on a holiday, hear bells at Pilar and think the people are pursuing them, then rush home — where, mounting their sons' horse in panic and forgetting to untie its rope, the fruit that falls from the shaken caramay tree convinces them they are being shot, and they die of fright.
summary.zh: 貧漁夫網得大白魚，自以為網到鎮上神父，其妻則說是省長。二人懼罪逃亡，逢節日炮響鐘鳴，愈發驚恐；至皮拉爾聞鐘聲，以為追兵又至，折返回家。慌亂中夫婦騎上兒子繫於卡瑪伊樹的馬，忘了解繩；馬拉扯繩索震落滿樹果子，二人以為中彈，驚懼而亡。

sensitivity.note: Philippine oral tradition recorded from Ilocano narrators; presented as an archival record. Comic fear-tale; taboo tag is interpretive (a forbidden catch treated as pollution and punished by panic).

passages.text: Many years ago a poor fisherman and his wife lived with their three sons in a village by the sea. One day the old man set his snare in the water, and at night found he had caught a great white fish such as he had never seen; it occurred to him that it was the priest of the town. He ran to his wife crying, "My wife, I have caught the priest!" But when she saw the fish she cried, "Oh, it is not the priest but the governor." The old man insisted it was the priest, and they went home trembling with fear.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Mabel Cook Cole, Philippine Folk Tales (1916), 'The Poor Fisherman and His Wife'; not verbatim.

passages.text: That night neither slept for wondering what they should do. The next day was a great holiday: at four o'clock cannons were fired and bells rang loudly, and the old couple, hearing the noise and not knowing the reason, thought their crime had been discovered and the people were searching for them to punish them, so they fled to the woods. Reaching the woods near Pilar, they heard the sexton ringing the bells for mass and thought the people there had been notified of their escape, so they turned and started home again.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Mabel Cook Cole, Philippine Folk Tales (1916), 'The Poor Fisherman and His Wife'; not verbatim.

passages.text: As they reached their house, the three sons tied their one horse to the trunk of the caramay tree, and at noon the bells rang again. Not thinking what time of day it was, the old man and woman ran out in terror, and seeing the horse, jumped on its back to ride to the next town before anyone could catch them — forgetting to untie the rope around the trunk. As they whipped the horse and it pulled at the rope, fruit fell from the tree upon the old man and woman. Believing they were shot, they were so frightened that they died.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Mabel Cook Cole, Philippine Folk Tales (1916), 'The Poor Fisherman and His Wife'; not verbatim.

title.en: The Presidente Who Had Horns
title.zh: 長角的鎮長

region.en: Ilocos coast, northwestern Luzon, Philippines (symbolic pin for the Ilocano tale cycle)
region.zh: 菲律賓呂宋西北伊洛克斯海岸（伊洛卡諾故事圈之象徵定位）

period: Ilocano oral tradition; recorded 1916 (Cole)

source.work: Mabel Cook Cole, Philippine Folk Tales (1916), Christianized Tribes, Ilocano: 'The Presidente who had Horns', eBook #12814

summary.en: An unjust presidente wishes he had horns to frighten his people, and horns grow on his head. His barber, forbidden on pain of hanging to tell, digs a hole under the bamboo and whispers the secret into the ground — and the bamboo itself begins to say that the presidente has horns. The councilmen hear it, force their way in, and kill him, saying he was no better than an animal.
summary.zh: 暴虐的鎮長一怒之下想長角嚇人，角果真生出。理髮師奉命不得外洩（否則處死），回思難抑，掘穴於竹林之下，低聲道出秘密——竹子卻替他宣揚：鎮長長角了！議員聞之破門而入，見角而殺之，言其與獸無異。

sensitivity.note: Philippine oral tradition recorded from Ilocano narrators; presented as an archival record. The whispered-secret motif (cf. Midas' barber) with the earth/bamboo broadcasting truth.

passages.text: Once there was a presidente who was very unjust to his people, and one day he became so angry that he wished he had horns so that he might frighten them. No sooner had he made this rash wish than horns began to grow on his head. He sent for a barber, and as the man worked the presidente asked what he saw on his head; the barber, though he could see the horns plainly, was afraid to say so. Soon the presidente felt the horns himself, and when he inquired again the barber told him he had two horns. "If you tell anyone what you have seen, you shall be hanged," said the presidente as the barber started away.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Mabel Cook Cole, Philippine Folk Tales (1916), 'The Presidente who had Horns'; not verbatim.

passages.text: At home the barber did not intend to tell anyone, but as he thought of his secret the desire to tell became so strong that he knew he could not keep it. Finally he went to the field, dug a hole under some bamboo, crawled in, and whispered that the presidente had horns; then he filled up the hole and went home. By and by people passing the bamboo stopped in amazement, for a voice came from the trees saying that the presidente had horns. The news spread through the town and to the councilmen, who also heard the voice.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Mabel Cook Cole, Philippine Folk Tales (1916), 'The Presidente who had Horns'; not verbatim.

passages.text: By this time the horns had grown a foot in length, and the presidente was so ashamed that he bade his wife say he could not talk. The councilmen insisted on seeing him, saying that if it were true he had horns he had no right to govern the people. She refused to let them in, so they broke down the door, saw the horns on the presidente's head, and killed him, saying he was no better than an animal.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Mabel Cook Cole, Philippine Folk Tales (1916), 'The Presidente who had Horns'; not verbatim.

title.en: The Story of a Monkey: The Thorn That Cost a Tail
title.zh: 猴子的故事：一根刺換走一條尾

region.en: Ilocos coast, northwestern Luzon, Philippines (symbolic pin for the Ilocano tale cycle)
region.zh: 菲律賓呂宋西北伊洛克斯海岸（伊洛卡諾故事圈之象徵定位）

period: Ilocano oral tradition; recorded 1916 (Cole)

source.work: Mabel Cook Cole, Philippine Folk Tales (1916), Christianized Tribes, Ilocano: 'The Story of a Monkey', eBook #12814

summary.en: A monkey with a thorn in his tail pays the barber with his tail-tip for the razor that cuts it off, then exacts the old woodcutter's firewood for his broken razor, the cake-maker's cakes for his burned wood, and dies just as he prospers — bitten by a dog which eats all the cakes.
summary.zh: 猴尾入刺，以尾梢換得理髮師的剃刀；又以斷刀換得老嫗的柴，以燒盡的柴換得婦人的糕餅。得逞之際卻被狗咬死，狗食盡其糕餅。

sensitivity.note: Philippine oral tradition recorded from Ilocano narrators; presented as an archival record. Cumulative chain-bargain trickster tale ending in the trickster's own death.

passages.text: One day when a monkey was climbing a tree in the forest he ran a thorn into his tail, and try as he would he could not get it out. He went to a barber in the town and offered to pay well to have it pulled; the barber tried with his razor, but in doing so cut off the end of the tail. The monkey cried, "Barber, Barber, give me back my tail, or give me your razor!" and as the barber could not put the tail back, he gave him the razor.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Mabel Cook Cole, Philippine Folk Tales (1916), 'The Story of a Monkey'; not verbatim.

passages.text: On the way home the monkey met an old woman cutting wood, and lent her the razor to cut more easily; before long it broke, and the monkey demanded a new one or all the firewood. She could not get a new razor, so she gave him the firewood. Going back to town to sell it, he saw a woman making cakes beside the road, and gave her his wood to bake more cakes; when the last stick was burned he cried that she must give him all her cakes, and she did. The monkey took the cakes and started for the town, but on the way he met a dog which bit him so that he died, and the dog ate all the cakes.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Mabel Cook Cole, Philippine Folk Tales (1916), 'The Story of a Monkey'; not verbatim.

title.en: The White Squash
title.zh: 白南瓜

region.en: Ilocos coast, northwestern Luzon, Philippines (symbolic pin for the Ilocano tale cycle)
region.zh: 菲律賓呂宋西北伊洛克斯海岸（伊洛卡諾故事圈之象徵定位）

period: Ilocano oral tradition; recorded 1916 (Cole)

source.work: Mabel Cook Cole, Philippine Folk Tales (1916), Christianized Tribes, Ilocano: 'The White Squash', eBook #12814

summary.en: A childless old couple whose garden always bore finds the vines suddenly barren; after long waiting one white squash grows. Opening it, they hear a voice begging them to be careful — inside is a talking baby boy. His bath water turns to gold, but on the third morning the child grows sad, flies away, and all the gold disappears, leaving the couple poor and alone again.
summary.zh: 無子的老夫婦花園常年結果，某年藤蔓忽然不結；久待之後僅得一白南瓜。剖瓜時瓜內傳聲請求小心——裡面竟是會說話的男嬰。嬰兒沐浴之水滴落皆化黃金；第三日晨，孩兒憂傷地飛去，黃金同時消失，老夫婦復歸於貧獨。

sensitivity.note: Philippine oral tradition recorded from Ilocano narrators; presented as an archival record. Miraculous birth from a plant; the vanishing-guest ending.

passages.text: In a queer little bamboo house in front of a big garden lived a man and his wife all alone. They had always been kind and good to everyone, but they were not happy, because the child for which they longed had never come, though they had prayed for a son or daughter every day for many years. In their garden grew fine white squash, and the vines bore the year around so they had never been in need of food — until one day they discovered that no new squash had formed to take the place of those they had picked.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Mabel Cook Cole, Philippine Folk Tales (1916), 'The White Squash'; not verbatim.

passages.text: Each day they examined the vines; the big yellow flowers bloomed and faded, but no squash grew on the stems. Finally one morning the woman cried out with delight, for she had discovered a little green squash. They decided to let it ripen for seed, and eagerly watched it grow into a beautiful white vegetable; but by the time it was large enough for food they were so hungry that they decided to eat it.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Mabel Cook Cole, Philippine Folk Tales (1916), 'The White Squash'; not verbatim.

passages.text: They brought a large knife and picked it, but scarcely had they started to open it when a voice cried out from within, "Please be careful that you do not hurt me." Thinking a spirit had spoken, they stopped; but when the voice again begged them to open the squash, they carefully opened it, and there inside was a nice baby boy who could already stand alone and talk. The couple were overjoyed. When the woman bathed him, the drops of water falling from his body were immediately changed to gold, until gold pieces covered the mat; a second bath brought more gold, enough to build a large house. But the third morning, when she brought the water, the boy grew very sad and flew away, and at the same time all the gold disappeared, and the man and his wife were left poor and alone.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Mabel Cook Cole, Philippine Folk Tales (1916), 'The White Squash'; not verbatim.

title.en: The Story of Benito: The Servant Who Outdid the King
title.zh: 貝尼托的故事：僕從勝於王

region.en: Laguna lake region, Luzon, Philippines (symbolic pin for the Tagalog tale cycle)
region.zh: 菲律賓呂宋拉古納湖區（他加祿故事圈之象徵定位）

period: Tagalog oral tradition; recorded 1916 (Cole)

source.work: Mabel Cook Cole, Philippine Folk Tales (1916), Christianized Tribes, Tagalog: 'The Story of Benito', eBook #12814

summary.en: Poor Benito enters a king's service and is sent to free a princess kept by giants across the sea. A bound sparrow-hawk, the King of the Fishes, and a magic sword from a strange woman help him. The princess then sets the king three impossible tasks — a lost ring, a lost earring, water from heaven and the lower world — which Benito fulfills with the fish-king, the mouse-king, and the dying sparrow-hawk; when the king bathes in the lower-world water and becomes a monster, the princess marries Benito, who becomes king.
summary.zh: 貧童貝尼托入宮為僕，受命渡海營救被巨人看守的公主。獲雀鷹、魚王相助，並得神劍誅巨人。公主卻向國王連出三難題：海底之戒指、林中耳環、天上與下界之水——皆由貝尼托借魚王、鼠王、雀鷹之力完成。國王以下界之水沐浴，化為怪物；公主遂嫁忠僕貝尼托，夫婦共治王國。

sensitivity.note: Philippine oral tradition recorded from Tagalog narrators; presented as an archival record. Tale-type: the prince's tasks fulfilled by the faithful servant.

passages.text: Benito was an only son who lived with his father and mother in a little village; they were very poor, and as the boy grew older he dreamed of being a help to them. Hearing of a young king who lived in a beautiful palace some distance away, he persuaded his parents to let him go and ask for work, and at last secured a place as a servant. One day the king sent for him: "I want you to bring to me a beautiful princess who lives in a land across the sea. Go at once, and if you fail you shall be punished severely." Benito's heart sank, but he answered, "I will, my lord."
passages.note: Paraphrase of Mabel Cook Cole, Philippine Folk Tales (1916), 'The Story of Benito'; not verbatim.

passages.text: In a thick forest he freed a large bird bound tightly with strings, which promised to help him whenever he called, its name being Sparrow-hawk. At the sea the King of the Fishes carried him on his back to the farther shore, and a strange woman gave him a magic sword that would kill instantly whatever it touched. At the castle many unarmed giants ran out to seize him, but he touched those in front with the sword and they fell dead, the others fleeing in panic. Benito freed the princess, who gladly returned with him to the palace.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Mabel Cook Cole, Philippine Folk Tales (1916), 'The Story of Benito'; not verbatim.

passages.text: When the king asked the princess to be his wife, she demanded first the ring she had lost crossing the sea. Benito's friend the King of the Fishes summoned all his subjects, found one fish too full to swim hiding under a stone, and had it cut open — inside was the lost ring. The princess next demanded the earring she lost in the forest: the King of Mice summoned his subjects and found one little mouse too full to walk in a hole among the bamboo; cut open, it yielded the earring. The princess's last request was some water from heaven and some from the lower world, and the king sent Benito on the hardest errand of all.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Mabel Cook Cole, Philippine Folk Tales (1916), 'The Story of Benito'; not verbatim.

passages.text: Benito called Sparrowhawk, who consented to fetch the water; two light cups of bamboo were fastened to the bird's legs, and it returned at nightfall with water from heaven on its right foot and from the lower world on its left. The journey had been too much for the bird and it was dying, and Benito sorrowfully buried it before hastening to the palace. The princess had herself cut in two and the water of heaven poured over her, growing into the most beautiful woman the king had ever seen. Eager to be handsome, the king begged the water of the lower world for himself: cut and bathed, he became a creature most ugly and horrible, which soon vanished out of sight. The princess then chose Benito, so faithful to his master and so kind to her, for her husband; they were married amid great festivities and became king and queen of that broad and fertile land, and Benito never forgot his parents, giving them one of the finest portions of his kingdom.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Mabel Cook Cole, Philippine Folk Tales (1916), 'The Story of Benito'; not verbatim.

title.en: The Adventures of Juan: The Goat, the Net, the Pot, and the Beating Stick
title.zh: 胡安歷險記：羊、網、飯鍋與神棍

region.en: Laguna lake region, Luzon, Philippines (symbolic pin for the Tagalog tale cycle)
region.zh: 菲律賓呂宋拉古納湖區（他加祿故事圈之象徵定位）

period: Tagalog oral tradition; recorded 1916 (Cole)

source.work: Mabel Cook Cole, Philippine Folk Tales (1916), Christianized Tribes, Tagalog: 'The Adventures of Juan', eBook #12814

summary.en: Lazy Juan spares a magic tree in exchange for a goat that shakes silver from its whiskers, a fish-filled net, and a self-replenishing pot — each of which his tuba-drinking friend steals and replaces with a common one, earning Juan beatings from his family. The fourth gift, a stick that beats anything at the words "Boombye, Boomba," defeats the thief and recovers all the treasures; Juan beats his scolding family until they make him head of the house, kills robbers, and marries a princess.
summary.zh: 懶惰的胡安饒過一棵魔樹，換得鬚間落銀之羊、自滿魚網與永不空乏的飯鍋——但每次都在朋友灌醉後被換成凡品，回家還挨打。第四次他得一根說「Boombye, Boomba」便自動打人的神棍，制服竊賊，取回全部寶物；又教訓譏其一生之家人，令其尊他為家主；後以神棍退賊、娶得公主。

sensitivity.note: Philippine oral tradition recorded from Tagalog narrators; presented as an archival record. The Juan cycle — the trickster hero whose luck and literal-mindedness carry the day.

passages.text: Juan was always getting into trouble: a lazy boy without good sense, whose family scolded and beat him whenever he did anything wrong. His mother gave him a bolo and sent him to the forest to cut firewood. Juan walked leisurely along, contemplating means of escape, until he came to a tree that seemed easy to cut — but it was a magic tree, and it said to him, "If you do not cut me I will give you a goat that shakes silver from its whiskers." Pleased both by curiosity and by not having to chop wood, Juan agreed at once, the bark separated, and a goat stepped out.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Mabel Cook Cole, Philippine Folk Tales (1916), 'The Adventures of Juan'; not verbatim.

passages.text: On the way home he met a friend more cunning than himself, who, knowing Juan's fondness for tuba, persuaded him to drink and substituted a common goat for the magic one while he was drunk. At home, when Juan commanded the animal to shake its whiskers, no money fell out, and his family, believing it another of Juan's tricks, beat and scolded him. He went back and threatened to cut the tree down for lying, but it offered a net which, cast on dry ground or even in the treetops, would return full of fish; the same friend again got him drunk and replaced the net with a common one, and again Juan was ridiculed at home. A third time the tree offered a magic pot, always full of rice, with spoons that provided whatever he wished to eat with it — and a third time the friend's tuba and substitution made Juan the subject of harder beatings.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Mabel Cook Cole, Philippine Folk Tales (1916), 'The Adventures of Juan'; not verbatim.

passages.text: Thoroughly angered, Juan sought the tree a fourth time and was on the point of cutting it down when it offered a stick which, at the words "Boombye, Boomba," would beat and kill anything he wished. When the friend asked what he had, Juan said, "Oh, it is only a stick, but if I say 'Boombye, Boomba' it will beat you to death." At the sound of the magic words the stick leaped from his hands and beat the friend until he cried that he would give back everything he had stolen. Juan then compelled the man to lead the goat and carry the net, jar, and spoons to his home; the goat shook its whiskers until his mother and brothers had all the silver they could carry, and they ate from the magic jar until filled.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Mabel Cook Cole, Philippine Folk Tales (1916), 'The Adventures of Juan'; not verbatim.

passages.text: Then Juan said to his family, "You have beaten me and scolded me all my life, and now you are glad to accept my good things. I am going to show you something else: 'Boombye, Boomba'." The stick leaped out and beat them all until they begged for mercy and promised that Juan should ever after be head of the house. From that time Juan was rich and powerful, never going anywhere without his stick; one night when thieves came to his house he would have been robbed and killed had not the magic words caused the death of all the robbers. Some time after this he married a beautiful princess, and because of the kindness of the magic tree they always lived happily.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Mabel Cook Cole, Philippine Folk Tales (1916), 'The Adventures of Juan'; not verbatim.

title.en: Juan Gathers Guavas
title.zh: 胡安摘番石榴

region.en: Laguna lake region, Luzon, Philippines (symbolic pin for the Tagalog tale cycle)
region.zh: 菲律賓呂宋拉古納湖區（他加祿故事圈之象徵定位）

period: Tagalog oral tradition; recorded 1916 (Cole)

source.work: Mabel Cook Cole, Philippine Folk Tales (1916), Christianized Tribes, Tagalog: 'Juan Gathers Guavas', eBook #12814

summary.en: Sent for ripe guavas to feed his father's guests, Juan eats all he can hold, then plays a joke instead of a feast: he bags a wasp's nest, locks the guests in, and watches. When his father opens the basket the wasps swarm the locked room, and the guests fight to escape through the windows — Juan opens the door and cries, "What fine, rich guavas you must have had! They have made you all so fat!"
summary.zh: 父親命胡安摘熟番石榴招待客人；胡安吃飽後卻以玩笑代盛宴——將黃蜂窩裝籃送入，反鎖房門。父親開籃，黃蜂滿室亂飛，賓客奪窗而逃。胡安開門見眾人臉腫，喊道：「你們吃的番石榴多麼肥美！把大家都吃胖了！」

sensitivity.note: Philippine oral tradition recorded from Tagalog narrators; presented as an archival record. Short Juan-cycle trickster anecdote.

passages.text: One day Juan's father sent him to get some ripe guavas, for a number of the neighbors had come in and he wanted to give them something to eat. Juan went to the guava bushes and ate all the fruit he could hold, and then he decided to play a joke on his father's guests instead of giving them a feast of guavas. A wasp's nest hung near by, and with some difficulty he succeeded in taking it down and putting it into the tight basket he had brought for the fruit.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Mabel Cook Cole, Philippine Folk Tales (1916), 'Juan Gathers Guavas'; not verbatim.

passages.text: He hastened home and gave the basket to his father, and as he left the room where the guests were seated he closed the door and fastened it. As soon as Juan's father opened the basket the wasps flew over the room, and when the people found the door locked they fought to get out of the windows. After a while Juan opened the door, and when he saw the swollen faces of the people he cried, "What fine, rich guavas you must have had! They have made you all so fat!"
passages.note: Paraphrase of Mabel Cook Cole, Philippine Folk Tales (1916), 'Juan Gathers Guavas'; not verbatim.

title.en: The Sun and the Moon (Visayan)
title.zh: 太陽與月亮（米沙鄢）

region.en: Cebu-Bohol seas, central Philippines (symbolic pin for the Visayan tale cycle)
region.zh: 菲律賓中部宿霧薄荷海域（米沙鄢故事圈之象徵定位）

period: Visayan oral tradition; recorded 1916 (Cole)

source.work: Mabel Cook Cole, Philippine Folk Tales (1916), Christianized Tribes, Visayan: 'The Sun and the Moon', eBook #12814

summary.en: The Sun and Moon were married with many star children, but the Sun's burning embrace destroyed the children he tried to hug, and the Moon forbade him to touch them. While she was washing at the spring he disobeyed and several children perished; in fury she raised a banana tree to strike him, and he threw sand in her face — the dark marks still on the Moon's face — and has chased her ever since, sometimes almost catching her.
summary.zh: 日月成婚，育有眾星辰子女；太陽欲擁抱子女，卻灼熱傷之，月亮遂禁其靠近。月亮去泉邊浣衣時，太陽違禁害死數子；月怒舉蕉樹擊之，太陽揚沙迷其面——月面暗痕至今可見——並自此永世追逐月亮，時近時遠。

sensitivity.note: Philippine oral tradition recorded from Visayan narrators; presented as an archival record. Celestial-family myth explaining moon markings and the sun's pursuit.

passages.text: Once upon a time the Sun and the Moon were married, and they had many children who were the stars. The Sun was very fond of his children, but whenever he tried to embrace any of them, he was so hot that he burned them up. This made the Moon so angry that finally she forbade him to touch them again, and he was greatly grieved.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Mabel Cook Cole, Philippine Folk Tales (1916), Visayan 'The Sun and the Moon'; not verbatim.

passages.text: One day the Moon went down to the spring to do some washing, and when she left she told the Sun that he must not touch any of their children in her absence. When she returned, however, she found that he had disobeyed her, and several of the children had perished. She was very angry, and picked up a banana tree to strike him, whereupon he threw sand in her face, and to this day you can see the dark marks on the face of the Moon. Then the Sun started to chase her, and they have been going ever since: sometimes he gets so near that he almost catches her, but she escapes, and by and by she is far ahead again.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Mabel Cook Cole, Philippine Folk Tales (1916), Visayan 'The Sun and the Moon'; not verbatim.

title.en: The First Monkey
title.zh: 第一隻猴子

region.en: Cebu-Bohol seas, central Philippines (symbolic pin for the Visayan tale cycle)
region.zh: 菲律賓中部宿霧薄荷海域（米沙鄢故事圈之象徵定位）

period: Visayan oral tradition; recorded 1916 (Cole)

source.work: Mabel Cook Cole, Philippine Folk Tales (1916), Christianized Tribes, Visayan: 'The First Monkey', eBook #12814

summary.en: A lazy grandson who gambles daily throws coconut shells at his industrious grandmother, who whips him with her cotton spindle — and he is transformed into an ugly animal, the cotton becoming his body hair and the stick his tail. He runs down to the town and whips his fellow gamblers with his tail, turning them into animals like himself; the people drive them all out, and they have lived in the trees as monkeys ever since.
summary.zh: 懶惰好賭的孫子因晚飯未備而擲椰殼擊打勤勞的祖母；祖母以紡錘抽打，少年頓化醜獸——棉花成其毛，紡錘成其尾。他奔下山，以尾抽打賭友，使之盡化同類。鎮民將他們逐出，從此棲於樹上，是為猴子。

sensitivity.note: Philippine oral tradition recorded from Visayan narrators; presented as an archival record. Etiological transformation tale.

passages.text: Many years ago at the foot of a forest-covered hill was a small town, and just above it on the hillside was a little house in which lived an old woman and her grandson. The old woman, very industrious, earned their living by removing the seeds from cotton, keeping near at hand a basket of cotton and a long stick she used for a spindle. The boy was lazy and would do nothing to help his grandmother, but went down to the town every day to gamble.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Mabel Cook Cole, Philippine Folk Tales (1916), 'The First Monkey'; not verbatim.

passages.text: One day, when he had been losing money, the boy went home and was cross because his supper was not ready. "I am hurrying to get the seeds out of this cotton," said the grandmother, "and as soon as I sell it, I will buy us some food." At this the boy fell into a rage and picked up some cocoanut shells and threw them at his grandmother. She became angry and began to whip him with her spindle, when suddenly he was changed into an ugly animal, the cotton becoming hair which covered his body, while the stick itself became his tail.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Mabel Cook Cole, Philippine Folk Tales (1916), 'The First Monkey'; not verbatim.

passages.text: As soon as the boy found he had become an ugly creature he ran down into the town and began whipping his companions, the gamblers, with his tail, and immediately they were turned into animals like himself. The people would no longer have them in the town, but drove them out; they went to the forest where they lived in the trees, and ever since they have been known as monkeys.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Mabel Cook Cole, Philippine Folk Tales (1916), 'The First Monkey'; not verbatim.

title.en: The Virtue of the Cocoanut: The Hunter and the Tuba
title.zh: 椰子之德：獵人與椰酒

region.en: Cebu-Bohol seas, central Philippines (symbolic pin for the Visayan tale cycle)
region.zh: 菲律賓中部宿霧薄荷海域（米沙鄢故事圈之象徵定位）

period: Visayan oral tradition; recorded 1916 (Cole)

source.work: Mabel Cook Cole, Philippine Folk Tales (1916), Christianized Tribes, Visayan: 'The Virtue of the Cocoanut', eBook #12814

summary.en: A hunter finds the first cocoanut tree and digs it up to take home; when the leaves wilt, he revives it in turn with the blood of the noisy bird, the mocking monkey, and the wild pig his dog has helped him kill. Planted at home it grows into a tall tree — the first from which tuba was drawn. The hunter teaches that the tree is like the three animals: the drinker of a few cups grows noisy as the bird, more makes him silly as the monkey, and the drunk sleeps like the pig in the mud-hole.
summary.zh: 獵人發現第一株椰樹，掘起帶回；葉屢枯，他依次以鳥、猴、豬之血澆灌使之復甦。植於家中成巨樹——第一株取椰酒之樹。獵人以此訓誡：飲椰酒三、四杯者聒噪如鳥，多飲者愚癲如猴，爛醉者則如泥塘酣睡之豬。

sensitivity.note: Philippine oral tradition recorded from Visayan narrators; presented as an archival record. Etiology of tuba and a temperance parable.

passages.text: One day a man took his blow-gun and his dog and went to the forest to hunt. Making his way through the thick woods, he chanced upon a young cocoanut tree growing in the ground, the first tree of this kind he had ever seen, and it seemed so peculiar that he stopped to look at it. Farther on he shot a noisy bird with his blow-gun, took aim at a large monkey that mocked him from a treetop, and that too fell dead at his feet; then, hearing his dog barking furiously, he hastened to it and found it biting a wild pig, which he killed after a hard struggle.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Mabel Cook Cole, Philippine Folk Tales (1916), 'The Virtue of the Cocoanut'; not verbatim.

passages.text: Satisfied with his success, the hunter took the three animals on his back and returned to the little plant. "I have decided to take you home with me, little plant," he said, "for I like you and you may be of some use to me." He dug it up carefully, but before he had gone far the leaves began to wilt, and having no water, he in despair cut the throat of the bird and sprinkled the blood on the cocoanut; the plant revived. When the leaves wilted again he revived it with the blood of the monkey, and a third time with the blood of the pig.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Mabel Cook Cole, Philippine Folk Tales (1916), 'The Virtue of the Cocoanut'; not verbatim.

passages.text: This was his last animal, so he made all the haste possible to reach home before his plant died. The cocoanut wilted again before he reached his house, but when he planted it in the ground it quickly revived and grew into a tall tree. This hunter was the first man to take the liquor called tuba from the cocoanut tree, and he told his friends: "The cocoanut tree is like the three animals whose blood gave it life when it would have died. The man who drinks three or four cups of tuba becomes like the noisy bird that I shot with my blow-gun. One who drinks more than three or four cups becomes like the big monkey that acts silly; and one who becomes drunk is like the pig that sleeps even in a mud-hole."
passages.note: Paraphrase of Mabel Cook Cole, Philippine Folk Tales (1916), 'The Virtue of the Cocoanut'; not verbatim.

title.en: Mansumandig, the Man Who Leans Back and Thinks
title.zh: 曼蘇曼迪：靠牆沉思者

region.en: Cebu-Bohol seas, central Philippines (symbolic pin for the Visayan tale cycle)
region.zh: 菲律賓中部宿霧薄荷海域（米沙鄢故事圈之象徵定位）

period: Visayan oral tradition; recorded 1916 (Cole)

source.work: Mabel Cook Cole, Philippine Folk Tales (1916), Christianized Tribes, Visayan: 'Mansumandig', eBook #12814

summary.en: To help his poor household, Mansumandig carries rice to the mines daily — but sells it for exactly the twenty-five centavos he paid, all year. Balancing accounts, he has made nothing; ashamed, he leans his head against the wall and thinks, which is why he is called Mansumandig. His wife then takes the same capital, weaves hemp into cloth, and makes three hundred pesos in a year; pitying him, she gives him the money to buy ten carabao, and they live comfortably ever after.
summary.zh: 曼蘇曼迪為養家而做米糧生意，卻整年以原價二十五分錢賣出。年底結帳分文未賺，羞愧地靠牆沉思——「曼蘇曼迪」（靠牆想者）之名由此而來。妻子以同樣本錢織麻布，一年掙得三百比索；她憐夫而以錢購十頭水牛耕田，從此生活安適。

sensitivity.note: Philippine oral tradition recorded from Visayan narrators; presented as an archival record. Humorous teaching tale on wit and industry; also etiological for the saying about leaning back and thinking.

passages.text: One day a man said to his wife: "My wife, we are getting very poor and I must go into business to earn some money." With his twenty-five centavos he bought a half-cavan of rice and carried it on his shoulder to the mines, where the people eagerly bought it — for the regular price of twenty-five centavos. His wife rejoiced that they would become very rich, and the man went on with his business for a year, each day buying a half-cavan of rice and selling it for the price he had paid for it.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Mabel Cook Cole, Philippine Folk Tales (1916), 'Mansumandig'; not verbatim.

passages.text: Then one day his wife said they would balance accounts, and she spread a mat on the floor. When she asked for the money he had made during the year, he handed her the twenty-five centavos. "Is that all you have received this year?" she cried angrily. He had paid twenty-five centavos and received twenty-five centavos. "Oh, my husband, how can you make any gain if you sell it for just what you paid for it?" The man leaned his head against the wall and thought; ever since then he has been called "Mansumandig," a man who leans back and thinks.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Mabel Cook Cole, Philippine Folk Tales (1916), 'Mansumandig'; not verbatim.

passages.text: Then the wife took the twenty-five centavos, bought hemp at the field where the people were gathering it, and wove it into cloth night and day — eight varas, sold for twelve and a half centavos a vara, the money reinvested in more hemp. At the end of a year she poured out her blanket of money, held aside her capital of twenty-five centavos, and counted three hundred pesos. Mansumandig, greatly ashamed that he had not made a cent, leaned his head against the wall and thought. After a while the woman pitied him, gave him the money, and told him to buy carabao; he bought ten and plowed his fields, and by raising good crops they lived comfortably all the rest of their lives.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Mabel Cook Cole, Philippine Folk Tales (1916), 'Mansumandig'; not verbatim.

title.en: Why Dogs Wag Their Tails
title.zh: 狗為何搖尾

region.en: Cebu-Bohol seas, central Philippines (symbolic pin for the Visayan tale cycle)
region.zh: 菲律賓中部宿霧薄荷海域（米沙鄢故事圈之象徵定位）

period: Visayan oral tradition; recorded 1916 (Cole)

source.work: Mabel Cook Cole, Philippine Folk Tales (1916), Christianized Tribes, Visayan: 'Why Dogs Wag their Tails', eBook #12814

summary.en: A rich man sends his dog and cat to carry a magic ring to his daughter at a convent. The dog bullies the cat into giving up the ring at the river crossing, drops it in the swift water, and flees in fear before reaching home. The cat returns alone to face the master, who commands all dogs in the world to join the search and have their tails cut off if found guilty — which is why every dog that meets another shows his teeth and wags his tail to prove his innocence, and why cats fear water.
summary.zh: 富人遣犬貓護送魔戒至修道院的女兒處。渡河時犬強奪魔戒，卻失手落入急流，未及回家便畏罪而逃。貓獨自回去面對主人；主人下令天下之犬搜捕此犬，見者截其尾——是以犬犬相遇必亮齒搖尾以自清白；貓亦自始懼水。

sensitivity.note: Philippine oral tradition recorded from Visayan narrators; presented as an archival record. Etiological animal tale.

passages.text: A rich man in a certain town once owned a dog and a cat, both very useful to him: the dog was old and toothless but a good guide, the cat strong and cunning. His daughter attended school at a convent some distance away, and very often he sent the two animals with presents. One day he called the faithful animals and bade them carry a magic ring to his daughter, the cat to carry it and the dog to guide her and keep her from harm.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Mabel Cook Cole, Philippine Folk Tales (1916), 'Why Dogs Wag their Tails'; not verbatim.

passages.text: All went well until they came to a river with neither bridge nor boat. As they were about to plunge into the water the dog said, "Let me take the magic ring." The cat refused — the master had given it to her to carry — but the dog argued that she could not swim well and threatened to kill her, and she reluctantly gave it up. The river was wide and the water swift, and just before they reached the opposite bank the dog dropped the ring.
