They searched carefully but could not find it anywhere; and just before reaching the house to report the loss, the dog was so overcome with fear that he turned and ran away and was never seen again.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Mabel Cook Cole, Philippine Folk Tales (1916), 'Why Dogs Wag their Tails'; not verbatim.

passages.text: The cat went on alone, and when the master saw her coming he called out to know what had become of her companion. The frightened cat explained how the ring had been lost and how the dog had run away. The master was very angry, and commanded that all his people should search for the dog, and that it should be punished by having its tail cut off. He also ordered that all the dogs in the world should join in the search — and ever since, when one dog meets another he says, "Are you the old dog that lost the magic ring? If so, your tail must be cut off." Then immediately each shows his teeth and wags his tail to prove that he is not the guilty one. Since then, too, cats have been afraid of water and will not swim across a river if they can avoid it.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Mabel Cook Cole, Philippine Folk Tales (1916), 'Why Dogs Wag their Tails'; not verbatim.

title.en: The Hawk and the Hen
title.zh: 鷹與母雞

region.en: Cebu-Bohol seas, central Philippines (symbolic pin for the Visayan tale cycle)
region.zh: 菲律賓中部宿霧薄荷海域（米沙鄢故事圈之象徵定位）

period: Visayan oral tradition; recorded 1916 (Cole)

source.work: Mabel Cook Cole, Philippine Folk Tales (1916), Christianized Tribes, Visayan: 'The Hawk and the Hen', eBook #12814

summary.en: A hawk wins a hen's promise to marry him once she has grown wings like his, giving her a ring as an engagement present. The cock claims her as his own and makes her throw the ring away. When the hawk returns with her dress of feathers, the frightened hen lies that a snake made her lose it; knowing she deceives him, the hawk decrees that she must always scratch the ground to look for the ring, and every chicken he finds he will snatch away — which hens do to this day.
summary.zh: 鷹向母雞求婚，雞允諾待其翅膀長成如鷹時成婚；鷹以戒指為聘。公雞卻聲稱雞本屬於他，逼其棄戒。鷹攜美羽而至，見戒已失；母雞謊稱蛇嚇致失。鷹洞穿其謊，判罰：母雞必須終生抓地覓戒，且其雛雞凡被鷹見者必遭奪取——母雞抓地之習至今猶然。

sensitivity.note: Philippine oral tradition recorded from Visayan narrators; presented as an archival record. Etiological animal tale of broken promise and punishment.

passages.text: A hawk flying about in the sky one day decided that he would like to marry a hen whom he often saw on earth. He flew down and searched until he found her, and then asked her to become his wife. She at once gave her consent on the condition that he would wait until she could grow wings like his, so that she might also fly high. The hawk agreed to this and flew away, after giving her a ring as an engagement present and telling her to take good care of it.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Mabel Cook Cole, Philippine Folk Tales (1916), 'The Hawk and the Hen'; not verbatim.

passages.text: The hen was very proud of the ring and placed it around her neck. The next day, however, she met the cock, who looked at her in astonishment and said, "Where did you get that ring? Do you not know that you promised to be my wife? You must not wear the ring of anyone else. Throw it away." And the hen threw away the beautiful ring.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Mabel Cook Cole, Philippine Folk Tales (1916), 'The Hawk and the Hen'; not verbatim.

passages.text: Not long after, the hawk came down bringing beautiful feathers to dress the hen. Frightened, she hid behind the door, but came out when he called — and the hawk at once saw that the ring was gone. The hen, ashamed to tell the truth, answered that a large snake had frightened her so in the garden that she ran to the house and then missed the ring. The hawk looked sharply at her, knowing she was deceiving him, and said: "When you have found the ring I will come down again and make you my wife. But as a punishment for breaking your promise, you must always scratch the ground to look for the ring. And every chicken of yours that I find, I shall snatch away." Then he flew away, and ever since all the hens throughout the world have been scratching to find the hawk's ring.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Mabel Cook Cole, Philippine Folk Tales (1916), 'The Hawk and the Hen'; not verbatim.

title.en: The Spider and the Fly
title.zh: 蜘蛛與蒼蠅

region.en: Cebu-Bohol seas, central Philippines (symbolic pin for the Visayan tale cycle)
region.zh: 菲律賓中部宿霧薄荷海域（米沙鄢故事圈之象徵定位）

period: Visayan oral tradition; recorded 1916 (Cole)

source.work: Mabel Cook Cole, Philippine Folk Tales (1916), Christianized Tribes, Visayan: 'The Spider and the Fly', eBook #12814

summary.en: Mr. Spider courts Miss Fly many times and is refused; when she closes her doors and windows against him and throws boiling water at his call, he vows everlasting enmity for himself and his descendants — which is why the spider still hates the fly to this day.
summary.zh: 蜘蛛先生屢次向蒼蠅小姐求婚均遭拒；一日她閉門閉窗，以滾水潑之。蜘蛛怒誓：己身及其子孫永世仇視蒼蠅、不得安寧——蜘蛛與蒼蠅之仇恨至今猶存。

sensitivity.note: Philippine oral tradition recorded from Visayan narrators; presented as an archival record. Short etiological tale; taboo tag interpretive (a hostile act answered with an enduring curse).

passages.text: Mr. Spider wanted to marry Miss Fly. Many times he told her of his love and begged her to become his wife, but she always refused, for she did not like him. One day when she saw Mr. Spider coming again, Miss Fly closed all the doors and windows of her house and made ready a pot of boiling water. When Mr. Spider called, begging her to allow him to enter, she answered by throwing boiling water at him.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Mabel Cook Cole, Philippine Folk Tales (1916), 'The Spider and the Fly'; not verbatim.

passages.text: This made Mr. Spider very angry, and he cried: "I will never forgive you for this, but I and my descendants will always despise you. We will never give you any peace." Mr. Spider kept his word, and even today one can see the hatred of the spider for the fly.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Mabel Cook Cole, Philippine Folk Tales (1916), 'The Spider and the Fly'; not verbatim.

title.en: The Battle of the Crabs
title.zh: 螃蟹之戰

region.en: Cebu-Bohol seas, central Philippines (symbolic pin for the Visayan tale cycle)
region.zh: 菲律賓中部宿霧薄荷海域（米沙鄢故事圈之象徵定位）

period: Visayan oral tradition; recorded 1916 (Cole)

source.work: Mabel Cook Cole, Philippine Folk Tales (1916), Christianized Tribes, Visayan: 'The Battle of the Crabs', eBook #12814

summary.en: The land crabs hold a council and decide to make war on the waves that sing so loudly they cannot sleep. A shrimp mocks their weak legs, is pinched into promising help, then laughs at and flees the first wave — while the crabs, all looking toward the shore, are covered with water and drowned.
summary.zh: 陸蟹集會，決議向終夜喧唱、令其不得安眠的海浪宣戰。蝦譏其腿弱，被鉗迫允諾助戰，旋即見浪而逃；眾蟹皆望岸而立，為浪所覆，盡數溺斃。

sensitivity.note: Philippine oral tradition recorded from Visayan narrators; presented as an archival record. Short comic etiological tale.

passages.text: One day the land crabs had a meeting, and one of them said, "What shall we do with the waves? They sing so loudly all the time that we cannot possibly sleep." "Well," answered one of the oldest of the crabs, "I think we should make war on them." The others agreed, and it was decided that the next day all the male crabs should get ready to fight the waves.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Mabel Cook Cole, Philippine Folk Tales (1916), 'The Battle of the Crabs'; not verbatim.

passages.text: As they started for the sea they met a shrimp, who asked where they were going. "We are going to fight the waves," answered the crabs, "for they make so much noise at night that we cannot sleep." "I do not think you will succeed," said the shrimp, "for the waves are very strong and your legs are so weak that even your bodies bend almost to the ground when you walk" — and he laughed loudly. This made the crabs very angry, and they pinched the shrimp until he promised to help them win the battle.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Mabel Cook Cole, Philippine Folk Tales (1916), 'The Battle of the Crabs'; not verbatim.

passages.text: Then they all went to the shore. But the crabs noticed that the eyes of the shrimp were set unlike their own, so they thought his must be wrong and laughed at him: "Friend shrimp, your face is turned the wrong way. What weapon have you to fight with the waves?" "My weapon is a spear on my head," replied the shrimp — and just then he saw a big wave coming and ran away. The crabs did not see it, however, for they were all looking toward the shore, and they were covered with water and drowned.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Mabel Cook Cole, Philippine Folk Tales (1916), 'The Battle of the Crabs'; not verbatim.

title.en: Yi Shoots Down Nine Suns and Slays the Monsters of the Burned Earth
title.zh: 堯使羿上射十日誅鑿齒

region.en: The scorched Nine Provinces under ten suns (symbolic pin: Central Plains)
region.zh: 十日並出之九州（象徵性定位：中原）

period: Huainanzi, Benjing Xun, c. 139 BCE (older Yi cycle in Shanhaijing, Hai Nei Jing)

source.work: Huainanzi, Benjing Xun: ten suns rise together, the monsters are slain by Yi under Yao's command

license: Public domain (Classical Chinese text; passages are compiler's renderings)

summary.en: In Yao's reign all ten suns rose together: crops burned, grasses scorched, the people without food. Monsters multiplied — Yayu the man-eater, Zaochi who chiseled teeth, Jiuying of the water-fire, the great wind-bird, the wild boar Fengxi, and the long snake Xiushe. Yao sent Yi of Qiong, who shot down nine suns with the red bow and killed the monsters, and the people rejoiced — Yao was set over the world as Son of Heaven.
summary.zh: 逮至堯之時，十日並出，焦禾稼，殺草木，民無所食；猰貐、鑿齒、九嬰、大風、封豨、修蛇皆為民害。堯使羿誅鑿齒於疇華之野，殺九嬰於凶水之上，繳大風於青丘之澤，斬修蛇於洞庭，禽封豨於桑林——萬民皆喜，堯乃為天子。

sensitivity.note: Passages are the compiler's condensed paraphrases of the Huainanzi original. Cross-tradition sun-capture cluster (Maui snares the sun); the Chinese version is archery — shooting, not snaring.

passages.text: In the time of Yao, the ten suns came out together. The grain burned in the fields and the grasses and trees were scorched; the people had nothing to eat. And out of the burning world came monsters of every kind: Yayu the man-eater of the west, Zaochi the chisel-toothed giant who slew men with his teeth, and the nine-headed Jiuying of the water and the fire.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Huainanzi, Benjing Xun, opening (compiler's rendering); not verbatim.

passages.text: Yao sent for Yi of Qiong, the master archer. Yi shot down the nine lesser suns with the red bow, and each burst into a golden crow and fell; he slew Zaochi in the Wild of Chouhua, killed Jiuying above the Water of Doom, snared the great wind-bird of Qingqiu with a corded arrow, cut off the long snake at Dongting, and took the wild boar Fengxi in the Mulberry Grove.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Huainanzi, Benjing Xun, Yi's campaign; not verbatim.

passages.text: One sun alone was left, and the sky grew gentle again. The ten thousand people rejoiced and set Yao over them as Son of Heaven, honored as one who had been made emperor in the dark of affliction — the world renewed under a single merciful sun.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Huainanzi, Benjing Xun, closing; not verbatim.

canonical_translation: Compiler's English rendering from the public-domain original; consulted (copyright, summary only): Anne Birrell, Chinese Mythology: An Introduction, Johns Hopkins 1993

narrative.en:
China's entry in the sun-capture cluster is the most violent of the world's sun myths: not a snare, not a trick — an execution by archery.

BEGINNING: THE WORLD UNDER TEN SUNS. In the age of Yao the sky's discipline broke. The ten suns, who should have taken the road one at a time from the Fusang tree of the east, rose all together. Ten suns poured down their heat: the grain in the fields burned, the grasses and trees withered, the people were left with nothing to eat. Out of the ruined world came monsters as if the heat itself had bred them — Yayu the man-eater, Zaochi the chisel-toothed slayer, the nine-headed Jiuying breathing water and fire, the great wind-bird that snapped trees and rooftops, the boar Fengxi that gorged in the fields, and the long snake Xiushe that swallowed an elephant in one gulp at Dongting. Humanity was caught between scorching sky and crawling earth.

MIDDLE: THE ARCHER AND HIS BOW. Yao sent for Yi of Qiong, the finest archer of the age — a culture-hero whose bow was of red lacquer, whose arrows were white plumed. Yi climbed the high ground, took aim at the blazing sky, and shot. Nine of the ten suns burst and fell; tradition says each falling sun revealed a great golden crow within, the sun-bird of the Shanhaijing's Fusang cosmology, dropping out of the sky like burning feathers. One sun was left, and it is that one that rises today — spared by mercy, as the tellers always add.

END: THE MONSTERS AND THE RENEWAL. With the sky reduced to order, Yi turned his bow on the earth. He killed Zaochi in the wild of Chouhua, the nine-headed Jiuying above the water of doom, snared the wind-bird at Qingqiu with a line-and-arrow, cut the long snake at Dongting, and caught the boar Fengxi at the Mulberry Grove, where its meat was cooked and offered. The ten thousand people rejoiced, and Yao — who had commanded the deed — was set over the world as Son of Heaven. The burned world was renewed under one sun.

FUNCTION AND AFTERMATH. The story explains why there is only one sun, and why there are droughts (the spared sun's heat is kept in check by ritual — in the Zhuolu cycle, the drought-maid Ba is exorcised). It also founds Yao's sacral kingship: the righter of the sky becomes the model of the sage-ruler. But Yi's own fate is tragic — denied immortality, betrayed by his wife Chang'e (who stole his elixir and flew to the moon), and finally murdered by his student Feng Meng with a peachwood club. The archer's sun-quest, the elixir, and the moon-flight form one continuous cycle of rise, failure, and transformation.
narrative.zh: 十日並出、羿射九日之神話見《淮南子·本經訓》：十日並出，焦禾稼、殺草木，猰貐、鑿齒、九嬰、大風、封豨、修蛇並起為害；堯使羿射九日、誅六害，萬民皆喜，堯乃為天子。此為中國太陽神話之『射日』型——與毛利毛伊縛日平行而以弓箭執行。羿之命運悲劇：不得長生，其妻嫦娥竊藥奔月，羿終為弟子逢蒙以桃杖殺之。射日、靈藥、奔月構成一連續之興衰循環。

functions: Aition of the single sun: why one sun remains and what a second sun costs
Founding of sage-kingship: Yao's mandate confirmed by the ordering of the sky
Agricultural renewal myth: the burned earth restored after monster-clearing
Setup of the elixir and moon-flight cycle (Yi-Chang'e tragedy)

variants.name: Shanhaijing, Hai Nei Jing — the emperor-god Yi
variants.text_tradition: Shanhaijing, Hai Nei Jing (Di Jun's grant of the bow)
variants.summary: An older layer makes Yi the Emperor Di Jun's own red bow granted to a lower heaven, and the suns are shot as birds — the myth as divine prerogative rather than sage-king's commission.

variants.name: Chu Ci, Tianwen — the arrow and the golden crow
variants.summary: The Tianwen asks how Yi shot the suns and why the crows' feathers fell — preserving an archaic version where each sun is a bird that drops its plumage when pierced.

variants.name: Miao/Hmong parallel — the sky too hot
variants.summary: In Miao tellings several suns or moons rise and are shot down by archer-brothers, with surviving sibling suns hiding — an ethnographic parallel suggesting wide distribution of the motif.

primary_sources.citation: c. 139 BCE, Liu An and his court, Huainan; ten-suns passage. Classical Chinese via Wikisource.
Older Yi layer: Di Jun grants the bow; Guo Pu recension.

secondary_sources.work: Anne Birrell, Chinese Mythology: An Introduction
secondary_sources.citation: Birrell 1993, Baltimore: Johns Hopkins University Press — Yi cycle and the archer's tragic arc.

secondary_sources.work: Derk Bodde, 'Myths of Ancient China'
secondary_sources.citation: Bodde 1961, in Mythologies of the Ancient World (ed. S. N. Kramer) — the ten-suns motif and drought rituals.

source_urls.description: Wikisource (zh) — Huainanzi, public-domain Classical Chinese text

title.en: Chang'e Steals the Elixir and Flies to the Moon
title.zh: 姮娥竊藥奔月

region.en: The moon palace (symbolic pin: the moon)
region.zh: 月宮（象徵性定位：月亮）

period: Huainanzi, Lanming Xun (c. 139 BCE); elixir narrative via Zhang Heng's Lingxian (2nd c. CE), quoted in later encyclopedias

source.work: Huainanzi, Lanming Xun: Heng'e steals the elixir of Yi and flies to the moon; Zhang Heng, Lingxian: the flight and the moon-toad (quoted in Taiping Yulan)

license: Public domain (Classical Chinese text; passages are compiler's renderings)

summary.en: Yi, who shot down nine suns, begged the Queen Mother of the West for the drug of immortality; his wife Chang'e (the old reading: Heng'e) stole it, ate it alone, and her body grew light and rose — she flew to the moon, where a cold moon-palace received her, and she became the moon's white toad, keeper of the elixir of the night sky.
summary.zh: 羿請不死之藥於西王母，姮娥竊以奔月，悵然有喪，無以續之；靈憲：嫦娥竊藥奔月，是為蟾蜍——月中蟾宮由是而立。

sensitivity.note: Passages are the compiler's condensed paraphrases of the Huainanzi line and the Lingxian narrative. Name: Han taboo forced Heng'e to be written Chang'e; both forms noted. Cross-tradition quest-immortality cluster.

passages.text: Yi, the archer who had shot down nine suns and saved the world, sought from the Queen Mother of the West the drug of deathlessness. She granted it — one dose, for one man, good for one life beyond all deaths. He brought it home and hid it, meaning to share its power with his wife Chang'e, or to take it himself at the proper season.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Huainanzi, Lanming Xun line with the Zhang Heng Lingxian narrative (compiler's rendering); not verbatim.

passages.text: Chang'e found the elixir and swallowed it entire. Her body grew light as if it had cast off its shadow; she rose from the ground and flew, higher and higher, past the clouds and the winds, until she reached the moon — and could not come back. There in the cold of the moon she looked down at the world she had left, and was stricken with the sorrow of what she had done and what she had become.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Lingxian flight narrative; not verbatim.

passages.text: The oldest tellers say she was changed into a toad, the pale toad of the moon, pounding the elixir beneath the cassia tree with the hare. Later ages, pitying her, made the toad only a shadow on the disc, and gave her instead a palace, attendants, and the long loneliness of the Queen of the Moon — the woman who chose to live forever alone rather than die with the man she betrayed.
passages.note: Paraphrase of moon-toad and moon-palace traditions; not verbatim.

canonical_translation: Compiler's English rendering from the public-domain original; consulted (copyright, summary only): Anne Birrell, Chinese Mythology: An Introduction, Johns Hopkins 1993

narrative.en:
The moon-elixir myth is China's quest-immortality tragedy: one drug, two claimants, and a transformation that is both reward and punishment.

BEGINNING: THE DOSE OF DEATHLESSNESS. Yi, the archer of the ten suns, had done the great labor of his age; but culture-heroes are mortal, and Yi knew he would die. He climbed to the far west, to the Jaguar-toothed Queen Mother of the West — the tiger-fanged goddess of calamities who, in the Han, had become keeper of the elixir of life. She granted him the drug: one dose, to be taken in due order. Some tellings say Yi was to share it; some say he hoarded it. Either way, the drug was hidden in his house.

MIDDLE: THE THEFT AND THE FLIGHT. His wife — written Heng'e in the oldest sources, renamed Chang'e when the Emperor Liu Heng's taboo made her name unspeakable — found the elixir. Why she stole it is retold many ways: fear of losing Yi to heaven without her, ambition, anger, or (in the tenderest reading) the wish not to be left mortal when her husband rose. She swallowed it all. The drug of deathlessness lightened her body until it broke the earth's hold; she flew through cloud and wind, up and up, to the moon.

END: THE COLD PALACE AND THE TOAD. The moon received her. The oldest explicit comment, in Zhang Heng's Lingxian, is harsh: in the moon she became a toad — the pale toad of the moon, who pounds the elixir beneath the cassia with the jade hare. Han mirrors carved the toad in the moon's disc. Later ages could not bear the image; they smoothed the toad into a shadow and gave Chang'e a palace of cold jade, attendants, the cassia tree, the hare — and the Mid-Autumn festival, when every household sets out mooncakes and looks up at the woman who traded husband, earth and death for a lonely forever.

FUNCTION. The myth is a cautionary etiology of the moon's nature: cold, bright, untouchable — what happens when the drug of life is taken without measure. It joins the quest-immortality cluster (Gilgamesh's herb lost to the snake; the Hanged God's runes) at the point where the quest is answered but the answer cannot be lived with. And it gives the Chinese moon its population: Chang'e, Yutu the hare, Wu Gang chopping the cassia — all punishments or refusals set into the disc to be watched every year.
narrative.zh: 姮娥奔月之悲劇：一劑不死之藥、二位覬覦者、一場得償所願而無法承受之變形。羿射九日而請藥於西王母；姮娥竊而盡服，身輕離地，飛昇入月；張衡《靈憲》謂其化為蟾蜍——漢鏡鑄月中蟾形；後世不忍其說，遂為月宮、玉兔、桂樹。中秋拜月之俗由此。與吉爾伽美什之草被蛇竊、日耳曼神之祭掛相似：不死之途皆有代價，得之者不得與人世同在。

functions: Etiology of the moon's imagery: toad, hare, cassia, the woman in the disc
Cautionary myth of immortality pursued by theft rather than merit
Ritual anchor of the Mid-Autumn festival (moon-worship, mooncakes, reunion)
Tragic closure of the Yi cycle: the savior-hero loses wife, elixir, and life

variants.name: Huainanzi, Lanming Xun — the bare theft
variants.summary: The earliest surviving telling is one sentence: Heng'e steals the drug Yi asked from the Queen Mother and flees to the moon, grieving, with no way back — the moral ambiguity already present.

variants.name: Zhang Heng, Lingxian — the toad
variants.text_tradition: 2nd c. CE astronomical rhapsody, quoted in later encyclopedias
variants.summary: Adds the transformation into the moon-toad and the flavor of punishment: the elixir-taker becomes the disc's crawling shadow, pounding the drug for the sky.

variants.name: Han-era Chang'e verses — the grief of Yi
variants.text_tradition: Attributed Han-chu song and later poetic tradition
variants.summary: Poetic expansions give Yi's side: left on earth with nothing to continue him, he grieves each full moon; the classical poets (Li Bai, Li Shangyin) keep her sorrow, not her guilt, at the center.

primary_sources.citation: c. 139 BCE; 'Yi begs the elixir from the Queen Mother of the West; Heng'e steals it and flees to the moon.' Classical Chinese via Wikisource.
2nd c. CE; the flight and the moon-toad, preserved in Taiping Yulan quotations.

secondary_sources.work: Anne Birrell, Chinese Mythology: An Introduction
secondary_sources.citation: Birrell 1993, Baltimore: Johns Hopkins University Press — the Yi-Chang'e cycle and the toad variant.

secondary_sources.work: David Leeming, 'A Dictionary of Creation Myths' and lunar myth surveys
secondary_sources.citation: Leeming, various — comparative context of moon-elixir myths.

source_urls.description: Wikisource (zh) — Huainanzi, public-domain Classical Chinese text

title.en: Kun the Fish Becomes Peng the Bird of Ninety Thousand Li
title.zh: 鯤化鵬徙於南冥

region.en: The Northern Dark (northern ocean) to the Southern Dark (symbolic pin: mythic ocean)
region.zh: 北冥至南冥（象徵性定位）

period: Zhuangzi, Xiaoyao You, c. 4th c. BCE; parallel in Liezi, Tang Wen

source.work: Zhuangzi, Xiaoyao You (Free and Easy Wandering): Kun and Peng; Liezi, Tang Wen, parallel passage

license: Public domain (Classical Chinese text; passages are compiler's renderings)

summary.en: In the Northern Dark lives a fish called Kun, so vast no one knows how many thousand li it is; it changes into a bird called Peng, whose back is like Mount Tai and whose wings hang like clouds from the sky. When the sea moves, the Peng strikes water three thousand li, rises on a whirlwind ninety thousand li, and sets off for the Southern Dark on the six months' wind — while the cicada and the dove laugh at it.
summary.zh: 北冥有魚，其名為鯤，化而為鳥，其名為鵬；背若泰山，翼若垂天之雲；水擊三千里，摶扶搖而上者九萬里，徙於南冥——蜩與學鳩笑之。

sensitivity.note: Passages are the compiler's condensed paraphrases of the Zhuangzi original. Tagging caveat: 'world-serpent' marks the giant-sea-being type (Kun); the Zhuangzi's point is philosophical — scale is relative — rather than combat.

passages.text: In the Northern Ocean there is a fish called Kun; no one knows how many thousand li its body runs. It changes of itself into a bird called Peng, whose back is like the great Mount Tai and whose wings hang from the sky like clouds across the heavens.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Zhuangzi, Xiaoyao You, Kun-Peng passage (compiler's rendering); not verbatim.

passages.text: When the sea heaves, the Peng strikes the water for three thousand li, then rises on the whirlwind ninety thousand li high, clears the blue, and sets its face toward the Southern Ocean on the wind of six months. The cicada and the little dove laugh at it: 'We hop from tree to tree — what does that creature think it needs all that height for?' The great and the small, says Zhuangzi, know their own limits, and that is the whole difference between them.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Zhuangzi, Xiaoyao You, with the cicada-and-dove commentary; not verbatim.

title.en: The Death of Hundun, Chaos Given Seven Holes
title.zh: 莊子鑿混沌七竅

region.en: The South Sea and North Sea, meeting at the center (symbolic pin: central plain)
region.zh: 南海北海之中央（象徵性定位）

period: Zhuangzi, Yinglei Diwang chapter, c. 4th c. BCE

source.work: Zhuangzi, Yinglei Diwang (The Normal Course for Rulers and Kings): Shu and Hu drill seven holes in Hundun

license: Public domain (Classical Chinese text; passages are compiler's renderings)

summary.en: The kings of the South Sea (Shu) and North Sea (Hu) met regularly in the land of Hundun, the central chaos, who treated them well; to repay him they decided to give him the senses everyone else had, and each day they bored one hole — seven days, seven holes — and on the seventh day Hundun died. Unity, given features, ceases to be itself.
summary.zh: 南海之帝為儵，北海之帝為忽，中央之帝為混沌；儵忽遇於混沌之地，報其德而欲鑿七竅——日鑿一竅，七日而混沌死。

sensitivity.note: Passages are the compiler's condensed paraphrases of the Zhuangzi original. Links to the Shanhaijing's faceless god Dijiang (chinese-shanhaijing-dijiang); the parable is anti-civilizing in Zhuangzi's hands.

passages.text: The emperor of the South Sea was Shu, and the emperor of the North Sea was Hu, and the emperor of the middle was Hundun — the undivided one, who had no face. Shu and Hu often met in Hundun's land, and Hundun treated them very well.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Zhuangzi, Yinglei Diwang, Hundun parable (compiler's rendering); not verbatim.

passages.text: They wished to repay his kindness, and reasoned that all men have seven openings — eyes, ears, nostrils, mouth — by which they see, hear, eat and breathe; Hundun alone had none. Each day they bored one hole in him. On the seventh day, the seventh hole was finished, and Hundun died. The undivided whole, given the features of the divided world, ceases to exist.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Zhuangzi, Yinglei Diwang, seven-holes passage; not verbatim.

title.en: The Giant of Longbo Hooks Away the Turtles of Penglai
title.zh: 龍伯釣六鰲

region.en: The five sacred isles far off in the Gulf of Bohai (symbolic pin: Bohai Sea)
region.zh: 渤海之東五神山（象徵性定位：渤海）

period: Liezi, Tang Wen chapter, c. 4th-3rd c. BCE

source.work: Liezi, Tang Wen (Questions of Tang): the five isles, the sixteen giant turtles, and the fisher-giant of Longbo

license: Public domain (Classical Chinese text; passages are compiler's renderings)

summary.en: Five magic isles floated without anchor in the eastern sea, and fifteen great turtles bore them on their backs in shifts; the giant of Longbo country strode the deep sea, hooked six turtles with a single cast, carried them home on his back to divine by the shells — and Daiyu and Yuanjiao, left drifting, drifted north and sank, so the gods had to relocate Penglai's survivors and forbid further wandering by giants.
summary.zh: 渤海之東有五山，常隨波上下，帝命禺疆使巨鰲十五舉首而戴之；龍伯之國大人一釣而連六鰲，負之馳歸，灼其骨以卜——岱輿、員嶠流於北極，沉於大海，仙聖播遷；帝怒，侵減龍伯之國使阨。

sensitivity.note: Passages are the compiler's condensed paraphrases of the Liezi original. The giant's casual fishing trip as cosmic catastrophe — trickster-scale humor.

passages.text: East of the Gulf of Bohai, far beyond the horizon, five sacred isles — Daiyu, Yuanjiao, Fanghu, Yingzhou, Penglai — floated on the waves without anchor, for they had no fixed ground beneath them; the immortals who lived there dreaded their drifting. So the High Emperor ordered the sea-god Yuqiang to command fifteen great turtles, who took the isles on their heads in shifts of sixty thousand years.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Liezi, Tang Wen, five-isles passage (compiler's rendering); not verbatim.

passages.text: But in the country of Longbo there lived giants taller than mountains. One of them, on a whim, strode into the deep sea, cast a line, and hooked six of the turtles at once; he slung them on his back and ran home to his own country, where he burned their shells to divine the future. Daiyu and Yuanjiao, losing their bearers, drifted to the far north and sank beneath the waves.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Liezi, Tang Wen, Longbo fishing episode; not verbatim.

passages.text: The immortals of the sunken isles were scattered, migrating in exile. The High Emperor was furious: he diminished the Longbo country to a few thousand li, and shrank its giants to a few feet — and so the surviving isles of Penglai and its sisters stand in the eastern sea to this day, and no giant wanders the deep again.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Liezi, Tang Wen, punishment and aftermath; not verbatim.

title.en: The Fool of the North Moves Two Mountains
title.zh: 愚公移山

region.en: Between Taihang and Wangwu, north of the Yellow River bend (symbolic pin: Shanxi–Henan border)
region.zh: 太行王屋二山（象徵性定位：晉豫交界）

period: Liezi, Tang Wen chapter, c. 4th-3rd c. BCE

source.work: Liezi, Tang Wen (Questions of Tang): Yugong, ninety years old, moves Taihang and Wangwu

license: Public domain (Classical Chinese text; passages are compiler's renderings)

summary.en: Ninety-year-old Yugong summoned his household to dig away the two mountains that blocked his road to the south, bucket by bucket, generation by generation — 'my sons will have sons; the mountains grow no taller.' The Wise Old Man of the River Bend laughed at him; Yugong answered, and the gods of the mountains, afraid, asked the Emperor of Heaven, who ordered the two sons of Kuae's giant to carry the mountains away on their backs — one to the east, one to the south.
summary.zh: 太行、王屋二山方七百里，懲山北之塞出入之迂；愚公年九十，率子孫荷擔者三夫，叩石墾壤，箕畚運於渤海之尾——子子孫孫無窮匱也，而山不加增。操蛇之神懼，帝感其誠，命夸娥氏二子負二山。

sensitivity.note: Passages are the compiler's condensed paraphrases of the Liezi original. The parable became a 20th-century Chinese political byword (Mao's 'Three Fairy Tales' speech) — noted as modern reception, not part of the mythic record.

passages.text: The two mountains Taihang and Wangwu blocked Yugong's household from the southern roads, a round trip of months. At ninety years, Yugong called his family together and proposed to dig away the mountains: they would carry the earth and stone, basket by basket, to the far shore of the Bohai Sea.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Liezi, Tang Wen, Yugong opening (compiler's rendering); not verbatim.

passages.text: The Wise Old Man of the River Bend came to laugh at him — an old man with months to live, against mountains seven hundred li around. Yugong answered: though I die, my son lives on; my sons will have sons, and sons will have sons, without end — but the mountain can add nothing to itself. Why should it not be leveled? The mountain-god, holding a snake, trembled at the resolve.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Liezi, Tang Wen, the dispute with the Wise Old Man; not verbatim.

passages.text: The gods of the two mountains, afraid, reported Yugong's resolve to the Emperor of Heaven, whose heart was moved by such constancy. He ordered the two sons of Kuae's giant to shoulder the mountains, one on each man's back, and set the one east of Shuofang and the other south of Yongzhou — and from that day, no hill stood between Yugong's house and the roads of the south.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Liezi, Tang Wen, divine intervention; not verbatim.

title.en: Yanshi Presents King Mu with a Mechanical Man
title.zh: 偃師獻假人

region.en: King Mu's western tour, beyond the Kunlun passes (symbolic pin: Hexi corridor)
region.zh: 穆王西巡昆侖之丘（象徵性定位）

period: Liezi, Mu Wang Pian chapter, c. 4th-3rd c. BCE

source.work: Liezi, Mu Wang Pian (Treatise on King Mu): the craftsman Yanshi and his walking, singing automaton

license: Public domain (Classical Chinese text; passages are compiler's renderings)

summary.en: Returning from his westward tour, King Mu was met by the craftsman Yanshi, who presented a man that walked, looked, sang and danced like a living being. At the height of the dance it winked at the king's ladies; Mu was furious — until Yanshi took the figure apart before him: skin, flesh, sinews, joints, heart, liver, intestines — all leather, wood, glue and paint, reassembled by night, and the machine sang again.
summary.zh: 偃師造能唱能舞之假人；其倡也，瞬其目而招王之左右侍妾——王大怒；偃師立剖散之：皆傅會革、木、膠、漆，內則肝膽心肺、腸胃外則筋骨支節——試廢其心則口不能言，廢其肝則目不能視。

sensitivity.note: Passages are the compiler's condensed paraphrases of the Liezi original. One of the world's oldest automaton tales; tagged 'quest-immortality' loosely for the King Mu elixir-tour frame, noted as interpretive.

passages.text: Returning from his journey to the west, King Mu of Zhou was met on the road by a craftsman called Yanshi, who asked for an audience and brought with him a man. 'This is my work,' said Yanshi — and the man could walk, could look about, could nod and bow, and when Yanshi sang it sang, and when he danced it danced, in a thousand varieties of movement.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Liezi, Mu Wang Pian, Yanshi episode (compiler's rendering); not verbatim.

passages.text: The king watched with his favorite ladies beside him — and at the height of the dance the automaton winked its eye at them. Mu raged and called it sorcery; Yanshi, terrified, took the figure apart on the spot before the king: inside there was nothing but leather, wood, glue and paint — organs of leather and timber, joints and sinews of cord — all artificial.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Liezi, Mu Wang Pian, the wink and the disassembly; not verbatim.

passages.text: Yanshi put it together again, and it moved and sang as before. Then, to test it, the king removed its heart — and its mouth could not speak; the liver — and its eyes could not see; the kidneys — and its feet could not walk. Mu exclaimed that human craft could equal the Creator's: he had the automaton loaded on the rear carriage and carried back to his capital.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Liezi, Mu Wang Pian, organ-removal test; not verbatim.

title.en: The Great Hymn to Amen-Ra, Bull of Karnak
title.zh: 阿蒙-拉大頌

region.en: Thebes, Egypt (temple of Amen-Ra at Karnak)
region.zh: 埃及底比斯（卡納克阿蒙-拉神廟）

period: New Kingdom hymn, c. 1600-900 BCE (Cairo papyrus; Budge translation 1910)

source.work: The Literature of the Ancient Egyptians, trans. E. A. W. Budge (1910), ch. XII, the Hymn to Amen-Ra

summary.en: The state hymn of the New Kingdom temple: Amen-Ra is hailed as the Bull of Karnak, the hidden creator who suspends the sky and hammers out the earth, maker of men and gods, one in form yet of many names, whose hidden name 'Amen' conceals him even from his own children the gods.
summary.zh: 新王國神廟國頌：阿蒙-拉被尊為卡納克之牛、懸天錘地之隱名造物主，造人亦造神，形一而名多——其隱名『阿蒙』連諸神子女亦不得窺知。

sensitivity.note: Ancient temple hymn quoted for comparative scholarship; no living community restrictions. Budge's 1910 wording is the cited public-domain source, presented without religious truth claims.

passages.text: Homage to thee, Amen-Ra, Lord of the throne of Egypt. Master of the Apts (Karnak). Kamutef at the head of his fields. The long-strider, Master of the Land of the South. Lord of the Matchau (Nubians), Governor of Punt, King of heaven, first-born son of earth, Lord of things that are, stablisher of things (i.e. the universe), stablisher of all things. One in his actions, as with the gods, Beneficent Bull of the Company of the Gods (or of the Nine Gods), Chief of all the gods, Lord of Truth, father of the gods, maker of men, creator of all animals, Lord of things that are, creator of the staff of life, Maker of the herbage that sustaineth the life of cattle.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Budge (1910), ch. XII, Hymn to Amen-Ra, sections II-III.

passages.text: The gods fall down awestruck at his feet, when they recognise His Majesty their Lord. Lord of terror, great one of victory, Great one of Souls, mighty one of crowns. He maketh offerings abundant, [and] createth food. Praise be unto thee, creator of the gods. Suspender of the sky, who hammered out the earth. — Homage to thee, Ra, Lord of Truth. Hidden is the shrine of the Lord of the gods. Khepera in his boat giveth the order, and the gods come into being. [He is] Tem, maker of the Rekhit beings, however many be their forms he maketh them to live, distinguishing one kind from another.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Budge (1910), sections VI and X.

passages.text: He heareth the cry of him that is oppressed. He is gracious of heart to him that appealeth to him. He delivereth the timid man from the man of violence. He regardeth the poor man and considereth [his] misery. He is the lord Sa (i.e. Taste); abundance is his utterance. The Nile cometh at his will. He is the lord of graciousness, who is greatly beloved. He cometh and sustaineth mankind. He setteth in motion everything that is made. He worketh in the Celestial Water, making to be the pleasantness of the light.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Budge (1910), sections XI-XII.

passages.text: He is Ra who is worshipped in the Apts. He is the one of many crowns in the House of the Benben Stone. He is the god Ani, the lord of the ninth-day festival. He maketh himself to be seen in the horizon, Chief of the beings of the Other World. His name is hidden from the gods who are his children, in his name of 'Amen.' — [He is] the Form One, the creator of everything that is. The One only, the creator of things that shall be. Men and women proceeded from his two eyes. His utterance became the gods. He maketh to live the fish in the river, and the geese and the feathered fowl of the sky. He giveth air to the creature that is in the egg.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Budge (1910), sections XIII and XV.

title.en: The Hymn to Amen: All the Gods Are Three
title.zh: 阿蒙頌：眾神合三為一

region.en: Thebes, Egypt (Leyden papyrus, Theban theology)
region.zh: 埃及底比斯（萊頓紙草，底比斯神學）

period: New Kingdom hymn, c. 1550-1200 BCE (Leyden papyrus; Budge translation 1910)

source.work: The Literature of the Ancient Egyptians, trans. E. A. W. Budge (1910), ch. XII, the Leyden papyrus extract on the power and glory of Amen

summary.en: A Theban hymn of divine omnipotence: Amen heals without medicine, rescues the doomed, stills the crocodile when his name is spoken, and stands behind the triune face of godhead — his face is Ra, his body Ptah — while the Nile rises from the hollow beneath his sandals and the luck and destiny of every man are in his hand.
summary.zh: 底比斯頌歌詠神之全能：阿蒙不假藥物而醫眼，救溺水者於冥府，其名一呼鱷魚失力；眾神合三為一——拉為其面，卜塔為其身；尼羅自其履下之穴湧出，萬民命運皆在其手。

sensitivity.note: Ancient temple hymn; no living community restrictions.

passages.text: He driveth away evils and scattereth diseases. He is the physician who healeth the eye without [the use of] medicaments. He openeth the eyes, he driveth away inflammation. He delivereth whom he pleaseth, even from the Tuat (the Other World). He saveth a man from what is ordained for him at the dictates of his heart. To him belong both eyes and ears, [he is] on every path of him whom he loveth. He heareth the petitions of him that appealeth to him. He cometh from afar to him that calleth [before] a moment hath passed.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Budge (1910), ch. XII, the Leyden papyrus extract.

passages.text: He maketh high (i.e. long) the life [of a man], he cutteth it short. To him whom he loveth he giveth more than hath been fated for him. [When] Amen casteth a spell on the water, and his name is on the waters, if this name of his be uttered the crocodile hath no power. The winds are driven back, the hurricane is repulsed. At the remembrance of him the wrath of the angry man dieth down. He speaketh the gentle word at the moment of strife. He is a pleasant breeze to him that appealeth to him. He delivereth the helpless one. He is more helpful than millions to the man who hath set him in his heart. One warrior [who fighteth] under his name is better than hundreds of thousands.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Budge (1910), Leyden papyrus extract.

passages.text: All the gods are three, Amen, Ra and Ptah, and there are none like unto them. He whose name is hidden is Amen. Ra belongeth to him as his face, and his body is Ptah. Their cities are established upon the earth for ever, [namely,] Thebes, Anu (Heliopolis), and Hetkaptah (Memphis). When a message is sent from heaven it is heard in Anu, and is repeated in Memphis to the Beautiful Face (i.e. Ptah). It is done into writing, in the letters of Thoth (i.e. hieroglyphs), and despatched to the City of Amen (i.e. Thebes), with their things.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Budge (1910), Leyden papyrus extract.

passages.text: His heart is Understanding, his lips are Taste, his Ka is all the things that are in his mouth. He entereth, the two caverns are beneath his feet. The Nile appeareth from the hollow beneath his sandals. His soul is Shu, his heart is Tefnut. He is Heru-Khuti in the upper heaven. His right eye is day. His left eye is night. He is the leader of faces on every path. His body is Nu. The dweller in it is the Nile, producing everything that is, nourishing all that is. He breatheth breath into all nostrils. The Luck and the Destiny of every man are with him. His wife is the earth, he uniteth with her, his seed is the tree of life, his emanations are the grain.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Budge (1910), Leyden papyrus extract.

title.en: Hymn to the Sun-god: The Judge of Words and Deeds
title.zh: 日神頌：言行之審判者

region.en: Cairo limestone ostracon provenance, New Kingdom Egypt
region.zh: 新王國埃及（開羅石灰岩陶片出土語境）

period: New Kingdom hymn written on limestone slices, c. 1300-1100 BCE (Budge translation 1910)

source.work: The Literature of the Ancient Egyptians, trans. E. A. W. Budge (1910), ch. XII, 'Hymns to the Sun-god'

summary.en: On a schoolboy's limestone slice a New Kingdom hymn praises the child of fire who sails the sky: he destroys the serpent-fiend Neka with the help of the Children of Horus, becomes Tem at evening to comfort the dead, and sits as Judge of words and deeds — to whom the hymnist prays that a wrongful usurper of his office be judged rightly.
summary.zh: 書童陶片上新王國頌詩讚火之子——日行天穹之童神：賀魯斯諸子合力誅蛇魔內卡；暮為阿圖姆而撫亡者；居於言行之審判座——頌者祈其審理奪其官職之不義者。

sensitivity.note: Ancient hymn; no living community restrictions.

passages.text: Well dost thou watch, O Horus, who sailest over the sky, thou child who proceedest from the divine father, thou child of fire, who shinest like crystal, who destroyest the darkness and the night. Thou child who growest rapidly, with gracious form, who restest in thine eye. Thou wakest up men who are asleep on their beds, and the reptiles in their nests. Thy boat saileth on the fiery Lake Neserser, and thou traversest the upper sky by means of the winds thereof.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Budge (1910), ch. XII, Hymns to the Sun-god.

passages.text: The two daughters of the Nile-god crush for thee the fiend Neka, Nubti (i.e. Set) pierceth him with his arrows. Keb seizeth (?) him by the joint of his back, Serqet grippeth him at his throat. The flame of this serpent that is over the door of thy house burneth him up. The Great Company of the Gods are wroth with him, and they rejoice because he is cut to pieces. The Children of Horus grasp their knives, and inflict very many gashes in him. Hail! Thine enemy hath fallen, and Truth standeth firm before thee.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Budge (1910), Hymns to the Sun-god.

passages.text: When thou again transformest thyself into Tem, thou givest thy hand to the Lords of Akert (i.e. the dead), those who lie in death give thanks for thy beauties when thy light falleth upon them. They declare unto thee what is their hearts' wish, which is that they may see thee again. When thou hast passed them by, the darkness covereth them, each one in his coffin. Thou art the lord of those who cry out (?) to thee, the god who is beneficent for ever.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Budge (1910), Hymns to the Sun-god.

passages.text: Thou art the Judge of words and deeds, the Chief of chief judges, who stablisheth truth, and doest away sin. May he who attacketh me be judged rightly, behold, he is stronger than I am; he hath seized upon my office, and hath carried it off with falsehood. May it be restored to me.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Budge (1910), Hymns to the Sun-god, closing petition.

title.en: The Hymn to Shu: He Who Stretches Out the Heavens
title.zh: 舒神頌：撐天者

region.en: British Museum Magical Papyrus (Harris No. 501), Egypt
region.zh: 埃及（大英博物館魔法紙草哈里斯501號）

period: Late New Kingdom / Third Intermediate hymn, c. 1100-900 BCE (Budge translation 1910)

source.work: The Literature of the Ancient Egyptians, trans. E. A. W. Budge (1910), ch. XII, the Hymn to Shu

summary.en: A hymn to the air-god Shu, flesh and bone of Ra and his firstborn son: he drives his spear into the serpent-fiend Nekau daily, Tefnut rides his head hurling fire at enemies, and he stretches out the heavens with his own hands — the self-created son who had no mother, twice great above the gods.
summary.zh: 頌大氣之神舒——拉之血肉長子：日日持矛刺蛇魔內考；泰芙努特踞其首，擲火焚敵；彼以雙手撐天——無母而自生之子，凌駕諸神兩倍之尊。

sensitivity.note: Ancient hymn from a magical papyrus; no living community restrictions.

passages.text: Homage to thee, O flesh and bone of Ra, thou first-born son who didst proceed from his members, who wast chosen to be the chief of those who were brought forth, thou mighty one, thou divine form, who art endowed with strength as the lord of transformations. Thou overthrowest the Seba fiends each day. The divine boat hath the wind [behind it], thy heart is glad. Those who are in the Antti Boat utter loud cries of joy when they see Shu, the son of Ra, triumphant, [and] driving his spear into the serpent fiend Nekau.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Budge (1910), ch. XII, Hymn to Shu.

passages.text: Ra setteth out to sail over the heavens at dawn daily. The goddess Tefnut is seated on thy head, she hurleth her flames of fire against thy enemies, and maketh them to be destroyed utterly. Thou art equipped by Ra, thou art mighty through his words of power, thou art the heir of thy father upon his throne, and thy Doubles rest in the Doubles of Ra, even as the taste of what hath been in the mouth remaineth therein.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Budge (1910), Hymn to Shu.

passages.text: Homage to thee, O son of Ra, who wast begotten by Temu himself. Thou didst create thyself, and thou hadst no mother. Thou art Truth, the lord of Truth, thou art the Power, the ruling power of the gods. Thou dost conduct the Eye of thy father Ra. They give gifts unto thee into thine own hands. Thou makest to be at peace the Great Goddess, when storms are passing over her. Thou dost stretch out the heavens on high, and dost establish them with thine own hands.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Budge (1910), Hymn to Shu.

passages.text: Every god boweth in homage before thee, the King of the South, the King of the North, Shu, the son of Ra, life, strength and health be to thee! Thou, O great god Pautti, art furnished with the brilliance of the Eye [of Ra] in Heliopolis, to overthrow the Seba fiends on behalf of thy father. Thou makest the divine Boat to sail onwards in peace. The mariners who are therein exult, and all the gods shout for joy when they hear thy divine name. Greater, yea greater (i.e. twice great) art thou than the gods in thy name of Shu, son of Ra.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Budge (1910), Hymn to Shu, closing.

title.en: The Great Hymn to the Aten: One God Over All Lands
title.zh: 阿頓大頌：萬國唯一之神

region.en: Akhet-Aten (Amarna), Egypt (tomb of Ay, where the hymn is inscribed)
region.zh: 埃及阿赫頓-阿頓（阿馬爾納，阿伊墓刻壁處）

period: Composed under Akhenaten, c. 1350-1334 BCE (tomb of Ay at Amarna; Budge translation 1923)

source.archive: Wikisource (from Budge, Tutankhamen: Amenism, Atenism and Egyptian Monotheism, 1923)
source.work: A Hymn of praise of Her-aakhuti (the Great Hymn to Aten), composed by Akhenaten, trans. E. A. Wallis Budge (1923)

summary.en: The most radical text of pharaonic religion: the sun's disk alone creates and sustains everything — people of every tongue and skin, beasts, fish, the chick in the egg — setting a Nile for foreign lands and a Nile in the underworld for Egypt; only Akhenaten, his son, knows him, and all other gods have been effaced from the world.
summary.zh: 法老宗教中最激進之文本：太陽之盤獨自創造並養活萬有——異語異膚之眾民、走獸游魚、卵中之雛——為外邦置天之尼羅，為埃及置冥府之尼羅；唯其子阿肯那頓識之，餘神盡廢於世。

sensitivity.note: Ancient royal hymn; no living community restrictions. Category 'religious' chosen deliberately: this is canonical liturgy of the Aten cult composed by the king himself, unlike the narrative myths of the tradition.

passages.text: Thy rising [is] beautiful in the horizon of heaven, O Aten, ordainer of life. Thou dost shoot up in the horizon of the East, thou fillest every land with thy beneficence. Thou art beautiful and great and sparkling, and exalted above every land. Thy arrows (i.e., rays) envelop (i.e., penetrate) everywhere all the lands which thou hast made. Thou art as Ra. Thou bringest [them] according to their number, thou subduest them for thy beloved son. Thou thyself art afar off, but thy beams are upon the earth; thou art in their faces, they [admire] thy goings.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Budge, Tutankhamen (1923), the Great Hymn to Aten (tomb of Ay), sections 2-3.

passages.text: Thou settest in the horizon of the west, the earth is in darkness, in the form of death. Men lie down in a booth wrapped up in cloths, one eye cannot see its fellow. If all their possessions, which are under their heads, be carried away they perceive it not. Every lion emergeth from his lair, all the creeping things bite, darkness [is] a warm retreat. The land is in silence. He who made them hath set in his horizon. The earth becometh light, thou shootest up in the horizon, shining in the Aten in the day, thou scatterest the darkness. Thou sendest out thine arrows (i.e., rays), the Two Lands make festival, [men] wake up, stand upon their feet, it is thou who raisest them up.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Budge (1923), sections 3-4.

passages.text: O how many are the things which thou hast made! They are hidden from the face, O thou One God, like whom there is no other. Thou didst create the earth by thy heart (or will), thou alone existing, men and women, cattle, beasts of every kind that are upon the earth, and that move upon feet (or legs), all the creatures that are in the sky and that fly with their wings, [and] the deserts of Syria and Kesh (Nubia), and the Land of Egypt. Thou settest every person in his place. Thou providest their daily food, every man having the portion allotted to him, [thou] dost compute the duration of his life. Their tongues are different in speech, their characteristics (or forms), and likewise their skins [in colour], giving distinguishing marks to the dwellers in foreign lands.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Budge (1923), sections 7-9.

passages.text: Thou settest a Nile in heaven, which cometh down to them. It maketh a flood on the mountains like the Great Green Sea, it maketh to be watered their fields in their villages. How beneficent are thy plans, O Lord of Eternity! A Nile in heaven art thou for the dwellers in the foreign lands (or deserts), and for all the beasts of the desert that go upon feet (or legs). Hapi (the Nile) cometh from the Tuat for the land of Egypt. Thy beams nourish every field; thou risest up [and] they live, they germinate for thee. Thou hast made millions of creations (or, evolutions) from thy one self (viz.) towns and cities, villages, fields, roads and river. Every eye (i.e., all men) beholdeth thee confronting it. Thou art the Aten of the day at its zenith.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Budge (1923), sections 9-11.

language: Egyptian (New Kingdom, late Middle Egyptian, wall inscription)
canonical_translation: E. A. Wallis Budge, Tutankhamen: Amenism, Atenism and Egyptian Monotheism (London, 1923), 'A Hymn to Aten' (tomb of Ay)

narrative.en:
The Great Hymn to the Aten is the centerpiece of the most ambitious religious revolution Egypt ever attempted. About year 5 of his reign, the king Amenhotep IV renamed himself Akhenaten ('Effective for the Aten'), abandoned Thebes and the temples of Amun, and built a new capital, Akhet-Aten ('Horizon of the Aten', modern Amarna), where the sun's disk alone was worshipped. The Great Hymn, composed in the king's own voice or court circle, was carved in the tombs of his nobles at Amarna — most completely in the tomb of Ay, later Tutankhamun's successor — so that its words would be forever available to the dead.

THE HYMN'S ARGUMENT. Unlike every other Egyptian hymn, which piles up epithets of one god among many, the Great Hymn describes a single creator whose power is light itself. Aten rises in the east and 'fillest every land with thy beneficence'; his rays are hands that 'subduest them for thy beloved son.' At sunset the world falls into darkness 'in the form of death': lions emerge, serpents bite, and a man's own possessions could be stolen over his head without his perceiving it. At dawn the Two Lands make festival, and every creature — cattle, birds, fish in the river, boats on the Nile — moves by the light's command.

CREATION BY LIGHT ALONE. The hymn then universalizes the creator. The Aten 'didst create the earth by thy heart, thou alone existing': men and women, cattle, birds, the creatures of Syria, Nubia, and Egypt alike. He sets every person in his place, apportions his food, and computes his lifespan. He gives each people its own tongue, form, and skin color — a striking acceptance of difference as divine ordinance rather than disorder. For the foreign lands he 'settest a Nile in heaven', a rain-flood watering their fields from the sky; for Egypt the true Nile rises 'from the Tuat', the underworld, by the god's plan. Even the unborn are his: the chick speaks in the shell, and the Aten gives it breath to crack the egg from within.

THE SOLITARY KING. The hymn's most exclusive claim comes near its close: 'Thou art in my heart. There is no other who knoweth thee except thy son Nefer-kheperu-Ra Ua-en-Ra' — Akhenaten alone understands the Aten's plans and power. The world that was 'millions of creations' from the one self is governed through one man. The hymn closes with the royal family named — the king 'great in the duration of his life' and Nefertiti 'living and young for ever and ever' — binding creation, light, and dynasty into one circuit.

HISTORY AND FAILURE. Within a generation of Akhenaten's death the temples of Amun were restored, Amarna was demolished, and the Aten hymns were chiseled out — surviving only because tomb walls hid them from the erasers. Egyptologists read the hymn both as the culmination of the old solar theology of Ra (the same creator-god by heart and tongue that the creation legends describe) and as the ancestor of a monotheistic form that would not recur in Egypt. It functions in this corpus as the tradition's most radical creation-and-theophany text, the pole at which Egyptian hymnody becomes exclusive religion.

functions: State liturgy of the Aten cult, carved in nobles' tombs for the eternal benefit of the dead
Exposition of solar monotheism: one creator known through light alone, without myth or temple image
Universalist theology of difference: every people given its own tongue, form, and skin by divine ordinance
Royal ideology: the sole god is known only through the sole king, Akhenaten and his household

variants.name: Shorter Hymn to the Aten (same Amarna corpus)
variants.text_tradition: Amarna tombs (Meryre II, Huya, Ay, Mahu), c. 1350-1334 BCE
variants.summary: A shorter, less radical hymn to the Aten survives in several Amarna tombs, hailing the rising sun in language close to traditional solar hymns; the Great Hymn's universalism and exclusive claims mark it as the genre's culmination.

variants.name: Traditional solar hymns (Ra-Khepera dawn hymn)
variants.text_tradition: Book of the Dead ch. 15, Papyrus of Ani, New Kingdom
variants.summary: The pre-revolution dawn liturgy hails Khepera rising amid a plural pantheon — Thoth, Maat, the celestial ferry — with the deceased petitioning for a seat in the solar barque; the Aten hymn strips out every god but the disk and its king.

variants.name: Restoration aftermath: Amun restored, Aten erased
variants.text_tradition: Restoration Stela of Tutankhamun (c. 1332 BCE, Cairo JE 31882)
variants.summary: Tutankhamun's Restoration Stela records temples of the gods fallen into ruin 'as if they had never been' during the Aten interlude and their refoundation under Amun — the state's official undoing of the hymn's world.

primary_sources.work: The Great Hymn to the Aten (A Hymn of Praise of Her-aakhuti)
primary_sources.citation: Tomb of Ay (Amarna tomb 25), south wall, reign of Akhenaten c. 1350-1334 BCE. Trans. E. A. W. Budge, Tutankhamen: Amenism, Atenism and Egyptian Monotheism (London, 1923), pp. 122-135. (Attribution to Akhenaten himself follows the tomb inscriptions; some scholars assign the text to Ay's circle.)

secondary_sources.work: Miriam Lichtheim, Ancient Egyptian Literature, vol. II
secondary_sources.citation: Lichtheim 1976, Berkeley: University of California Press — canonical modern translation and commentary on the Aten hymns (cited for scholarly context; copyrighted, not quoted).

secondary_sources.work: Jan Assmann, Moses the Egyptian
secondary_sources.citation: Assmann 1997, Cambridge, MA: Harvard University Press — the Aten revolution read as Egypt's counter-religion and its reception in European memory.

The Amarna Project — Akhet-Aten and the rock tombs where the hymn is inscribed

title.en: Suan's Good Luck: The Guesser Who Married the Princess
title.zh: 蘇安的好運氣：說中一切的賭徒

region.en: Laguna province, Luzon, Philippines (narrator's home province)
region.zh: 菲律賓呂宋內湖省（敘述者故鄉）

period: Tagalog oral tale; collected by D. S. Fansler, published 1921

source.work: Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 1a 'Suan's Good Luck', eBook #8299

summary.en: Lazy Suan, ridiculed for leaving school, pretends to be a diviner and 'guesses' what his mother cooks after spying on her. Hiding his father's plough and then 'finding' it, he wins a reputation as a prophet, beats rival datus' riddles by scoffing 'Nonsense!', survives the search for the princess's lost ring when his own cry of despair makes the guilty coachman confess, and marries the princess — every fortune falling to him by accident.
summary.zh: 輟學的懶漢蘇安佯稱通靈，先偷窺母親煮飯而『猜中』晚餐，再藏起父親的犁又『尋回』，博得神算之名。他以一句『胡說』贏過對賭的達圖；公主戒指失竊時，他一句絕望的哀嘆竟令真正的竊賊自首。他因此娶得公主——一切好運皆因巧合而降。

sensitivity.note: Tagalog droll recorded by Fansler from a Laguna narrator; archival record. The Juan/Suan cycle of the lucky anti-hero; Fansler notes its kinship with Grimm's 'Dr. Knowall' and Oriental king-wager tales.

passages.text: Suan left school because the other pupils mocked his pronunciation, and went home telling his mother to buy him a pencil and pad of paper, saying he was now the wisest boy in the town. That night he hid his father's plough in a creek near the house; when the plough could not be found next morning, Suan wrote figures of various shapes on the paper and chanted a rhyme that 'meant' the plough had been stolen by a neighbor and hidden in a creek. The father found it there, and in great wonder declared his son truly the wisest boy in town. Later, when Suan's uncle lost his carabao, the same performance traced it to the mountains, and the story of the good guesser spread.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 1 'Suan's Good Luck'; not verbatim.

passages.text: When a royal proclamation promised the princess's hand to whoever could name the thief of her lost ring — death to the one who failed — Suan's mother volunteered him. In the king's carriage Suan despaired aloud, 'Death is at hand!' — and the coachman, who was the real thief, believed himself discovered and knelt begging mercy. Suan shrewdly directed him to hide the ring inside one of the king's geese. The next day, with candle and Latin words, Suan 'divined' that the ring had been swallowed by a goose; the geese were killed and the ring found, and he married the princess.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 1 'Suan's Good Luck'; not verbatim.

passages.text: A rich datu then came to test the king's famous son-in-law with a golden ball whose contents no one could know, staking his wealth; Suan answered scornfully, 'Nonsense!' — and a bystander shouted that the ball contained nine cents, so Suan won fourteen cascos full of gold, and nobody doubted his merit again.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 1 'Suan's Good Luck'; not verbatim.

title.en: Suan Eket and the Ring in the Goose
title.zh: 蘇安·埃凱特與鵝腹之戒

region.en: Rizal province, Luzon, Philippines (narrator's home province)
region.zh: 菲律賓呂宋黎薩省（敘述者故鄉）

period: Tagalog oral tale; collected by D. S. Fansler, published 1921

source.work: Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 1b 'Suan Eket', eBook #8299

summary.en: Nicknamed 'Eket' for his inability to say the letter x, Suan quits school declaring himself the wisest boy in town. He 'divines' the plough he has hidden, then his uncle's carabao, and when the princess's ring is lost his despairing cry terrifies the thieving coachman into confessing; Suan orders the ring fed to a goose and divines it there. He wins a melon-seed contest by eavesdropping on the rival king's sailors in a floating tub, and is crowned heir when he smashes the dung-filled bottle crying 'I consider that you are all waste to me.'
summary.zh: 蘇安因發不清x音被喚作『埃凱特』，輟學自稱全鎮最聰明。他以紙上畫符『神算』尋回自藏的犁、舅舅的水牛；公主戒指失竊，他一聲絕望哀嘆嚇得竊賊馬夫自首，他遂令馬夫以鵝吞戒，次日『算』出戒在鵝腹。後又乘木盆漂海偷聽敵王艙中對話而贏瓜籽之賭；最後擲碎糞瓶喊『你們全是我眼中的廢物』——言中瓶中穢物，被加冕為儲君。

sensitivity.note: Tagalog droll recorded by Fansler from a Rizal narrator; archival record. Second variant of the lucky-guesser cycle (Tale 1).

passages.text: While studying in a private school Suan could not pronounce the letter x well — he called it 'eket' — so his schoolmates nicknamed him Suan Eket, and he left school, telling his mother to buy him a pencil and pad, for he was now the wisest boy in the town. One night he stole his father's plough and hid it in a creek; the next morning he wrote figures of various shapes on his paper, chanted 'Ararokes, ararokes, Na na nakawes, Ay na s'imburnales' — meaning the plough had been stolen by a neighbor and hidden in a creek — and when his father found it there he declared his son truly wise. The same trick with his uncle Pedro's carabao sent the whole town marveling at the good guesser.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 1 'Suan Eket'; not verbatim.

passages.text: Then the king's proclamation was read: the princess's ring was lost, and whoever could tell who stole it should have the king's daughter for his wife, while he who tried and failed would lose his head. Suan's mother boasted of her son, and the royal carriage came. In great sorrow Suan said aloud, 'Death is at hand! You will lose your life now' — and the coachman, who had himself stolen the ring, thought he was discovered. He knelt and begged pity; Suan bade him catch one of the king's geese that night and make it swallow the ring. Before the king Suan demanded a candle, went round a round table uttering Latin words, and concluded that the ring, not stolen, had been swallowed by a goose; the geese were killed, the ring found, and the wedding celebrated.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 1 'Suan Eket'; not verbatim.

passages.text: A rich foreign king, Mayabong, then challenged the King of Campao to a wager on melon seeds. Unable to guess, Suan rowed out to sea in a tub intending to drown himself where no one would find his body — but he drifted to Mayabong's casco and overheard the sailors counting the seeds of the green and yellow melons. He answered 'Five' and 'Six' and won the casco of gold. When Mayabong returned with a tightly covered bottle and a second wager, Suan, refusing at first, was compelled by his father-in-law; in rage he hurled the bottle down crying, 'I consider that you are all waste to me' — and the broken bottle proved to contain waste. In great joy the king crowned Suan to succeed him, and he lived happily with his wife the princess.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 1 'Suan Eket'; not verbatim.

title.en: The Charcoal-Maker Who Became King
title.zh: 炭夫為王

region.en: Manila, Luzon, Philippines (narrator's home city)
region.zh: 菲律賓呂宋馬尼拉（敘述者居地）

period: Tagalog oral tale; collected by D. S. Fansler, published 1921

source.work: Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 2 'The Charcoal-Maker who became King', eBook #8299

summary.en: A charcoal-maker's son wins the princess and crown by filling ten cars a day with silver from a magic purse; the princess drugs him and steals the purse. Fleeing, he eats fruit that sprouts horns on his forehead, then fruit that removes them, and returns unrecognized as a palace cook's helper. When the king's household grows horns from the contaminated food, the disguised 'doctor' cures the royal family — with whippings for the king and queen, a dance for the princess, and the condition of his stolen purse returned — marries her, and rules so wisely that the kingdom prospers.
summary.zh: 炭夫之子以神囊連續十日運銀十車，贏得公主與王位；公主灌醉他竊走錢囊。亡命途中，他誤食生角之果，又食脫角之果，遂扮作御廚幫工返宮。王室因毒食長角，他假扮醫師施治——鞭笞國王王后、與公主共舞——換回神囊，娶公主為妻；他雖出身寒微、不學無文，卻禮賢下士，國家因之大治。

sensitivity.note: Tagalog folktale recorded by Fansler from a Manila narrator; archival record. Fansler places it in Aarne's 'Three Magic Articles and the Wonderful Fruit' cycle.

passages.text: A king proclaimed that whoever could bring him ten car-loads of money for ten successive days should have his beautiful daughter and his crown, on pain of death for failure. The only son of a poor charcoal-maker heard the announcement and told his mother he would marry the princess and be king. Cutting a huge tree in the forest, he heard a voice say, 'Cut this tree no more. Dip your hand into the hole of the trunk, and you will find a purse which will give you all the money you wish.' He found the purse empty at first, but when he angrily threw it down, silver money rolled merrily out of it, and the stream of dollars seemed inexhaustible when he shook it at home.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 2 'The Charcoal-Maker who became King'; not verbatim.

passages.text: The youth filled the ten cars before the astonished guards, and for five days the money flowed. The princess, told by her guard that the purse was magical, entertained him regally and tricked him into sleep, stealing the purse and leaving him alone in the chamber. Doomed to die without fulfilling his contract, he fled the kingdom, ate little on his journey, and at last, starving, ate the fruit of a strange tree — and two horns appeared on his forehead. Another tree's fruit made the horns fall off. Collecting both fruits, unrecognizable after two years' travel, he took service unpaid in the royal kitchen, where he proved such an excellent cook that he did all the palace cooking.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 2 'The Charcoal-Maker who became King'; not verbatim.

passages.text: One day he ground the horn-producing fruit into the king's food and kept the other kind mixed with water in a jar. The king, queen, and princess, used to golden crowns set with diamonds, were seen at table with sharp ugly horns. The terrified cook was sent for a doctor, and the helper intercepted him, pretending the horns could be removed by himself — testing the food on the cook first, and curing him with the water. Dressed as a doctor of surgery, he promised the king not to unfold the matter to the people, and demanded, in return for one-half the kingdom and the princess's hand, the severest treatment: the king and queen to be whipped until they bled, the princess to dance with the doctor until exhausted.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 2 'The Charcoal-Maker who became King'; not verbatim.

passages.text: While the cruel scourging went nearly to killing the royal couple, the doctor fetched the jar of fruit-water and gave them drink; the horns fell off the king and queen, and from the exhausted princess after her dance. A few days afterwards the king and queen died, and the doctor succeeded to the throne with the princess as his wife — telling her that he was the poor charcoal-maker whose magic purse she had stolen. Though uneducated and unrefined, the new king welcomed all wise men to his palace as counsellors, and his kingdom prospered as it had never done under its previous rulers.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 2 'The Charcoal-Maker who became King'; not verbatim.

title.en: The Story of Carancal: The Span-Tall Strongman
title.zh: 卡蘭卡爾傳：一拃高的力士

region.en: Batangas, Luzon, Philippines (narrator's home province)
region.zh: 菲律賓呂宋八打雁省（敘述者故鄉）

period: Tagalog oral tale; collected by D. S. Fansler, published 1921

source.work: Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 3 'The Story of Carancal', eBook #8299

summary.en: Born a span long after his parents' prayers and prophecies, Carancal grows no taller than four feet but eats more than any man and out-wrestles all boys. Driven by poverty, his father twice tries to kill him — dropping a tree on him, sending him to dive at the net — and twice Carancal returns bearing the tree on his shoulders or a slain alligator. Exiled with a five-yard bolo, he defeats three strongmen in wrestling, burns the man-eating giant in the forest house, hurls the great stone out of sight, and marries off his companions to three princesses, remaining a bachelor and benefactor of three kings.
summary.zh: 夫婦祈禱得子，生下僅一拃長的卡蘭卡爾；他長不過四尺，食量驚人，摔跤無敵。貧困的父親兩度設計殺子——倒樹壓頂、誘其潛水——兩次他都肩扛大樹或手提鱷魚歸來。被逐出家門時，他攜五碼長刀上路，連勝三位力士，火燒林中食人巨魔，一舉甩飛巨石；他把三位同伴許配三國公主，自己終身不娶，為三王之恩人。

sensitivity.note: Tagalog folktale recorded by Fansler from a Batangas narrator; archival record. Eight Filipino variants of this cycle (Pusong, Cabagboc, Sandapal, Sandangcal, etc.); Fansler connects it to the European 'Strong Hans' and 'John the Bear' cycles and to Beowulf's underwater fight.

passages.text: A couple long married but childless begged God every Sunday for a son, and the town witches foretold that he would be born no longer than a span. After a year the boy was born exactly so, yet stronger than anyone would expect, eating a cavan of rice and twenty-five pounds of meat and fish a day by the time he stood four feet tall. Carancal led the town boys in wrestling. When his family's property was all sold to buy him food, his father resolved to kill him in the forest: he set the falling tree on his son and hurried home — but Carancal came back carrying the big tree on his shoulders, asking why he had been left alone. The second attempt, sending him to dive down and see that the net was sound, ended with the sea turning red and foaming — and Carancal walking in with a big alligator under his arm.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 3 'The Story of Carancal'; not verbatim.

passages.text: The discouraged mother finally told him to go earn his own living, and with a bolo five yards long Carancal set out. He challenged the first wanderer, Bugtongpalasan, to wrestle for the right to carry the bolo, and won; he defeated Tunkodbola, who could twist up a tree and hurl it out of sight, the earth trembling and trees uprooting as they wrestled; and Macabuhalbundok, who pushed hills over with a laugh, went down too. All four companions reached a large deserted house in the wood and devoured the food on its table. Three of them went hunting while one cooked — and each cook in turn was seized by a giant who came up the stairs crying 'Ho, bajo tao cainco: I smell a man whom I will eat', tying him to a post with a hair from his head.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 3 'The Story of Carancal'; not verbatim.

passages.text: When Carancal's turn came he had his companions shave his head. The giant, seeing the white head, laughed and demanded his own head be made white too; Carancal said heads must be shaved to be white, and it was a very difficult thing to shave a head. The impatient giant insisted, so Carancal tied him tightly to a post with ropes, smeared his body with wax, and set it on fire, destroying him; the four lived in the house as if it were their own. Then came the king's letter: a huge stone covered much ground in a kingdom across the sea, and its removal won the hand of the prettiest princess. After three weeks' swimming — discovering that the island they rested on was really a very big fish, which fortunately carried them near the kingdom — Carancal swung the great stone out of sight with one pull, and married one of his companions, Bugtongpalasan, to the princess instead of himself.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 3 'The Story of Carancal'; not verbatim.

passages.text: King Walangtacut next begged them to drag a monstrous decaying fish from his shore, and again only Carancal succeeded, marrying Tunkodbola to that princess in his place. A third king's letter told of a stone so big 'I thought it was the sky that fell'; Carancal moved it again, and Macabuhalbundok was married off. The three princes considered Carancal their father though he was younger than any of them, and as their fathers-in-law died one by one, all three became kings. Carancal at last visited his cruel parents with plenty of money, and lived once more with them, with three kings under him.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 3 'The Story of Carancal'; not verbatim.

title.en: Suac and His Adventures: The Boy Who Killed Pugut
title.zh: 蘇瓦克歷險：誅殺普古特的少年

region.en: Arayat, Pampanga, Luzon, Philippines (narrator's home town)
region.zh: 菲律賓呂宋邦板牙省阿拉亞特（敘述者故鄉）

period: Pampangan oral tale; collected by D. S. Fansler, published 1921

source.work: Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 4a 'Suac and his Adventures', eBook #8299

summary.en: Three young hunters on Mt. Telapayong lose each meal to Pugut, the huge black man in the tree who eats what is cooked beneath him. When Suac's turn comes to cook, he pushes the bearded ogre into the fire, lures him over a grass-covered pit, and finally shoves him into a crocodile's mouth. Taking Pugut's club, Suac kills the nightly man-eating giant of the town and then rids the islands of all wild monsters, becoming ruler over his people.
summary.zh: 三名少年獵人在特拉帕永山烹食，屢被樹上黑巨人普古特搶食。輪到蘇瓦克掌炊時，他先將普古特推入火中燒鬈其鬚，再誘其踏入草掩之陷阱，最後將其推入鱷口誅之。蘇瓦克持普古特之棒擊斃夜裡食人的巨人，繼而清除諸島所有野獸妖魔，成為族人之王。

sensitivity.note: Pampangan folktale recorded by Fansler from an Arayat narrator; archival record. The 'interrupted-cooking' ogre episode of the John the Bear cycle.

passages.text: In a certain town in Pampanga lived a boy named Suac, who went hunting with Sunga and Sacu on Mount Telapayong to try his fortune. Having caught a large hog, they left Sacu to cook under a large tree while the others hunted — and a horrible creature, a very large black man with a long beard named Pugut, called down from the treetop, 'Ha, ha! What a nice meal you are preparing! Hurry up! I am hungry.' Sacu resisted, but Pugut knocked him down and ate all the food; the same happened when Sunga cooked.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 4 'Suac and his Adventures'; not verbatim.

passages.text: When Suac was left to cook and roast the hog, Pugut threatened to eat him up along with the food. Suac placed the food near the fire, stood by it, and when Pugut tried to seize it, pushed him into the fire; Pugut's beard was burnt and became kinky. The boy ran to a deep pit, covered it with grass, and stood on the opposite side crying, 'I pray you, do not step on my grass!' Pugut stepped on the grass and fell into the pit, but Suac had not gone far when the ogre was following him again — until Suac, seeing a crocodile, waited resolutely, gave him a blow, and pushed him into the mouth of the crocodile. Thus Pugut was destroyed.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 4 'Suac and his Adventures'; not verbatim.

passages.text: Suac took his victim's club, and when he heard that a giant came every night into the neighborhood to devour people, he went to encounter him; one deadly blow of Pugut's club tumbled the giant down dead. Later Suac rid the islands of all the wild monsters, and became the ruler over his people.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 4 'Suac and his Adventures'; not verbatim.

title.en: The Three Friends, the Monkey, the Dog, and the Carabao: Against the Buñgisñgis
title.zh: 三友鬥班吉斯尼

region.en: Batangas, Luzon, Philippines (narrator's home province)
region.zh: 菲律賓呂宋八打雁省（敘述者故鄉）

period: Tagalog oral tale; collected by D. S. Fansler, published 1921

source.work: Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 4b 'The Three Friends — the Monkey, the Dog, and the Carabao', eBook #8299

summary.en: Three animal friends hunting in the country lose their meals one by one to the Buñgisñgis, who throws the carabao knee-deep into the earth and bullies the dog; the monkey alone sets a pitfall before cooking and buries the ogre. His foolish companions dig the ogre up and are killed and lamed; the monkey survives, cheats the Buñgisñgis into stirring a beehive and wearing a boa as a belt, and leads him to his death on a crocodile.
summary.zh: 猴、狗、水牛三友鄉間行獵，輪流掌炊；班吉斯尼巨人連連搶食，把水牛扔得膝陷入土，欺凌狗兒。唯有猴子先掘陷阱，禮讓巨人入座，一拉椅腿將其活埋。愚蠢的夥伴們挖開墳墓，反遭巨人殺死弄殘；猴子誘其去搖蜂窩『報時』、以蟒蛇作腰帶，終將其引至鱷口喪命。

sensitivity.note: Tagalog folktale recorded by Fansler from a Batangas narrator; archival record. The Buñgisñgis is the Tagalog one-eyed ogre; this is the animal-companion form of the interrupted-cooking episode.

passages.text: Once there lived three friends — a monkey, a dog, and a carabao — who, tired of city life, went to the country to hunt with rice, meat, and kitchen utensils.
