title.en: The Story of Zaragoza: The Thief the King Could Not Catch
title.zh: 薩拉戈薩傳：國王抓不到的賊

region.en: Manila, Luzon, Philippines (narrator's home city)
region.zh: 菲律賓呂宋馬尼拉（敘述者居地）

period: Tagalog oral tale; collected by D. S. Fansler, published 1921

source.work: Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 8a 'The Story of Zaragoza', eBook #8299

summary.en: Godfather to his friend Luis's infant son, the stranger Zaragoza joins him in tunneling into the king's treasury to punish the tax-burdening monarch. Luis is killed by a hidden arrow-trap, and Zaragoza, severing the head to hide the identity, outwits every royal snare: the widow's cry explained as his own, the soldiers drugged into sleep as a priest, the decoy gold sheep rendered untraceable by marking every door with a cross. Pardoned, he tricks the richest merchant with a 'Si'-saying fool dressed as a bishop, and abducts the hermit Tubal in an iron cage disguised as a gate of heaven — winning a knighthood.
summary.zh: 陌生人薩拉戈薩為教子之父，與友人路易斯同謀掘通王庫以懲暴君。路易斯誤中箭阱身亡；薩拉戈薩割其首以免身份敗露，此後一一破解王室圈套：寡婦的哀哭被他解釋為責子、扮神父以藥酒催眠衛兵、在滿城門戶畫上同樣的十字使金羊誘餌失效。國王赦免並重用他；他以說『Si』的傻瓜假扮主教騙取富商貨物，又以鐵籠假作天門『接引』隱士入宮——終獲冊封為騎士。

sensitivity.note: Tagalog folktale recorded by Fansler from a Manila narrator; archival record. A Rhampsinitus + Master Thief combination; Fansler compares Groome's gypsy 'The Two Thieves' and Herodotus ii, 121.

passages.text: Poor Luis, whose three children had died unbaptized, hastened to church with his newborn son and, in haste, asked a passing stranger to stand godfather; the child was named Luis after his father, and the godfather, Zaragoza, soon won the confidence of the household as a close friend. Hearing from Luis how the king oppressed the people with heavy taxes, Zaragoza resolved to avenge the wrongs of the people by stealing the treasure hidden in a cellar of the palace. Night after night the two carried away as many bags as they could manage, Zaragoza giving his share freely to the poor while the selfish Luis admonished him not to be too liberal.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 8 'The Story of Zaragoza'; not verbatim.

passages.text: When the king noticed his treasure dwindling, soldiers found the secret passage; the friends, resolved on one last trip, found it undisturbed — but as Luis lowered himself into the hole, the whiz of an arrow was heard and a faint cry: 'I am dying! Take care of my son!' Unable to pull the body free, Zaragoza shrewdly cut off the dead man's head and hurried home with it, lest Luis be recognized. When the king decreed that the headless body be carried through the streets, soldiers arresting anyone who showed sympathy for the dead man, Maria's cry of 'O my husband!' at the window betrayed her — until Zaragoza smilingly told the guard the remark was meant for himself, having unintentionally hurt their young son. The soldiers believed him and went on.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 8 'The Story of Zaragoza'; not verbatim.

passages.text: Disguised as a priest with a bottle of wine mixed with a strong narcotic, Zaragoza that night passed himself off as a pious traveler among the soldiers, who drank freely and fell asleep; he stole the corpse and buried it with the head. The king's next stratagem — a sheep covered with precious metal let loose in the streets, a spy marking the door of anyone who caught it — failed when Zaragoza drove it into his yard and then marked every door in the street with a cross. Giving up all hope of catching the thief, the king issued a proclamation of pardon, and Zaragoza confessed and was believed.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 8 'The Story of Zaragoza'; not verbatim.

passages.text: The king, promising a title of nobility if Zaragoza could trick Don Juan, the richest merchant, out of his most valuable goods, watched Zaragoza dress a fool in the guise of a bishop, asking him 'Does your grace wish to have this?' to every question, the fool's answer being always 'Si.' The carriage was loaded and Zaragoza drove off 'to fetch the money.' Next, ordered to bring an old hermit to the palace, Zaragoza placed an iron cage near the mouth of Tubal's cave and, in the guise of an angel on a high cliff, shouted that the gates of heaven were open: 'Go enter that cage, and you will see the way to heaven.' The meek hermit obeyed — and was carried before the king. Thoroughly satisfied, the king knighted Zaragoza and placed him among the chief advisers of the kingdom, where he lived with Maria and his godson under his protection as the most upright and generous man of the realm.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 8 'The Story of Zaragoza'; not verbatim.

title.en: Juan the Peerless Robber
title.zh: 無雙大盜胡安

region.en: Batangas, Luzon, Philippines (narrator's home province; tale set in Africa)
region.zh: 菲律賓呂宋八打雁省（敘述者故鄉；故事背景在非洲）

period: Tagalog oral tale; collected by D. S. Fansler, published 1921

source.work: Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 8b 'Juan the Peerless Robber', eBook #8299

summary.en: The famous brigand Juan flees to Africa, where he beats the Ethiopian robber Pedro at pickpocketing by unbuckling his belt. Hearing the King of Tunis reward the captor of the greatest robber alive, Juan robs the palace of one small bag, then lures his friend Pedro to jump into a tub of boiling water — collecting the reward for Pedro's own head. Disguised as an angel with two strong wings, he 'carries to heaven' a devout abbot, money-bag and all, to his cave; but the abbot's counsel reforms him, and they live together till death.
summary.zh: 大盜胡安亡命非洲，以解帶之術勝過衣索比亞同行佩德羅。突尼斯國王懸賞捉拿『國中第一大盜』；胡安先從王宮偷走一小袋財寶，再引佩德羅跳入他預置的滾水大盆——以故友的人頭領賞。之後他假扮天使、縛雙翼，從教堂穹頂將虔誠修道院長連人帶財寶『接引上天』至其洞穴；院長規勸他棄惡從善，二人同居至死。

sensitivity.note: Tagalog folktale recorded by Fansler from a Batangas narrator; archival record. Master-Thief cycle; Fansler compares the Persian Bahar-i-Danush. The tale's European/charlemagne framing is retained as recorded.

passages.text: Not many centuries after Charlemagne died, there lived a famous brigand named Juan, known from childhood as 'the deceitful Juan,' 'the unrivalled pilferer,' 'the treacherous Juan.' Forced at twenty to flee his native land, he visited Africa, where he met the famous Ethiopian robber Pedro; disputing which was the more skilful pickpocket, they stood face to face. 'Hey!' exclaimed Juan as Pedro began, 'don't take my handkerchief out of my pocket!' Then Juan unbuckled Pedro's belt and slipped it into his own pocket: 'Whose belt is this?' Pedro generously admitted defeat.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 8 'Juan the Peerless Robber'; not verbatim.

passages.text: Traveling in northern Africa, they heard the heralds of the King of Tunis proclaim that a big bag of money would be given to the captor of the greatest robber in the country. That night Juan climbed to the palace roof, made a hole as large as a peso, lowered himself by rope into a room filled with bags of gold and silver, pearls, carbuncles, diamonds, and other precious stones, and took the smallest bag he could find. When Pedro resolved to visit the palace the following night, Juan lowered a large tub through the same hole by day and filled it with boiling water at nightfall; the eager Pedro jumped straight into the room without the rope and perished in the fatal tub. Juan notified the king of the capture and death of the greatest of African robbers: 'Take your bag of money,' said the king.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 8 'Juan the Peerless Robber'; not verbatim.

passages.text: Juan then heard that a wealthy and devout abbot had been praying two days and nights for the angel of the Lord to come and take him to heaven. Providing himself with two strong wings, Juan made a hole through the dome of the church and called down, 'I have been sent by the Lord to take you to heaven. Come with me, and bring all your wealth.' The abbot put all his money into a bag, got into it at Juan's bidding, and after an hour's 'flight' — 'We are within one thousand miles of the abode of the blessed' — twenty minutes later they were in Juan's cave. Astounded, the abbot heard Juan's story and advised him to abandon his evil ways; Juan listened to the counsels of his new friend, became a good man, and he and the abbot lived together until their death.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 8 'Juan the Peerless Robber'; not verbatim.

title.en: The Seven Crazy Fellows
title.zh: 七個瘋子

region.en: Mangaldan, Pangasinan, Luzon, Philippines (narrator's home town)
region.zh: 菲律賓呂宋邦阿西楠省曼加爾丹（敘述者故鄉）

period: Pangasinan oral tale; collected by D. S. Fansler, published 1921

source.work: Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 9 'The Seven Crazy Fellows', eBook #8299

summary.en: Seven happy fools go fishing; Juan counts six, forgetting himself, and all dive for the drowned companion until an old man counts them properly and takes them into his service. Each fails his task: Felipe hangs his hat and rice on a deer's antlers believing them a running tree, Eulalio drowns nodding at his reflection, Pedro burns a chicken feather-and-all, and Mateo and Francisco kill the old mistress while swatting a fly from her nose — she dies smiling. They roll her body from a flat coffin, bury a live fagot-gathering old woman instead when the priest demands a corpse, and flee in terror at the sight of the 'ghost' they dropped by the roadside.
summary.zh: 七個快活的瘋子捕魚歸來清點人數，胡安漏數自己，以為少了一人，眾人紛紛潛水尋『溺亡』的夥伴，直至老者代為點數並收留他們。此後諸事皆錯：菲elipe把帽與飯掛上鹿角當『會跑的樹』、尤拉利歐向倒影點頭直至溺斃、佩德羅連毛帶炭煮雞、馬特奧與弗朗西斯科打蠅竟打死老婦——她含笑而逝。他們滾落棺中屍體，錯把拾柴老婦活埋，最後見到路旁遺屍驚呼鬼魂，散逃呂宋全島。

sensitivity.note: Pangasinan noodle-tale recorded by Fansler from a Mangaldan narrator; archival record. Bicol variant 'Juan and his Six Friends'; Fansler compares the Jataka fly-killing stories and Grimm's 'Seven Swabians.'

passages.text: In the northern part of Luzon lived seven crazy fellows — Juan, Felipe, Mateo, Pedro, Francisco, Eulalio, and Jacinto — happy all the day long. One morning Felipe asked his friends to go fishing, and about two o'clock Mateo said they were hungry and should go home. 'Before we go, let us count ourselves, to see that we are all here!' said Juan — but because he forgot to count himself, he found only six and said one of them had been drowned. All dived into the river for their lost companion; Francisco counted on their emergence and left himself out too, so in they dived again. An old man passing by asked what they were diving for, then counted them properly, and took them into his house as servants.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 9 'The Seven Crazy Fellows'; not verbatim.

passages.text: On the hunting trip Felipe, who had never seen a deer, thought the antlers of a standing deer were the branches of a small tree without leaves, and hung his hat and bag of rice on them — but the tree immediately ran away. At home the others fared no better: Eulalio nodded at his own reflection in the well until, tired, he jumped into the water and was drowned; Jacinto destroyed the garden fence instead of gathering sticks; Pedro cooked a chicken without removing the feathers and let it burn black as coal; and Mateo and Francisco, keeping flies off the old mistress's face, struck at one on her nose with big sticks and killed her — she died with seemingly a smile on her face, and the two fools agreed she was very much pleased by their work.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 9 'The Seven Crazy Fellows'; not verbatim.

passages.text: They made a flat coffin with nothing to prevent the corpse from falling off, and on the way to the church ran so hard that the body rolled off; running, they agreed, made their burden lighter. When the priest found the corpse missing and sent them back, they met an old woman picking up sticks by the roadside and, binding her, carried her to the church — where the priest, who was also crazy, performed the burial-ceremony over her, answering her cries that she was alive with the remark that since he had her burial-fee he did not care whether she was alive or not. Returning home, they saw the corpse that had fallen from the coffin, and Francisco cried that it was the ghost of the old woman; terribly frightened, they ran away in different directions and became scattered all over Luzon.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 9 'The Seven Crazy Fellows'; not verbatim.

title.en: The Jinghe Dragon Loses a Rain-Bet and His Head
title.zh: 涇河龍王犯天條

region.en: Chang'an and the Jing River (pin: Shaanxi)
region.zh: 長安涇河（陝西）

period: Journey to the West, 16th c. (attrib. Wu Cheng'en, ch. 10)

source.work: Journey to the West, ch. 10: the fortune-teller's fish-price, the rain-bet, and Wei Zheng's dream-execution

license: Public domain (Ming novel; passages are compiler's renderings)

summary.en: A fisherman prospered by the word of a diviner, and the Jinghe dragon, furious that his shrimp-ministers were sold by the pound, went up as a white-robed scholar to humble the fortune-teller Yuan Shoucheng — who set him a rain-wager. The dragon held heaven's rain-docket, and altered the decree by an inch of rain and an hour of time: a small cheat, a capital crime. The executioner was the minister Wei Zheng — and the Emperor, keeping him awake beside him at chess, could not stop the blade that fell in Wei Zheng's dream.
summary.zh: 涇河龍王與袁守誠賭雨，擅改玉帝旨意，剋扣雨點時辰，犯下死罪；監斬者乃人曹官魏徵；太宗以棋絆之，魏徵夢中斬龍——龍頭落於剮龍臺。

sensitivity.note: Passages are the compiler's condensed paraphrases of the novel.

passages.text: A diviner at Chang'an market told a fisherman where to cast, and the fisherman's baskets came up silver; the shrimps and carp of the Jinghe river were his daily catch, and the river's dragon resolved to drive the star-reader from the city. He came up as a white-robed scholar and challenged the fortune-teller to name tomorrow's rain to the inch and the hour.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Journey to the West, ch. 10 (compiler's rendering); not verbatim.

passages.text: The next day heaven's rain-docket arrived and matched the prediction to the point — except that the dragon, to win the bet, cut the fall short by one inch of rain and one hour of time. That was treason against the decree of heaven: by the law of the rain, a river-god who alters the Heavenly Ordinance must die, and the blade belonged to Wei Zheng, a mortal minister who executed in his sleep.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Journey to the West, ch. 10, the altered decree; not verbatim.

passages.text: The dragon begged the Emperor to keep Wei Zheng beside him all day, and the Emperor did — at the chess board. But at midday the minister nodded, and in his dream he mounted a cloud, drew his sword, and cut the dragon's head from its body; the head fell on the execution terrace of the sky, and the dragon's ghost came nightly to demand of the Emperor the life he had promised to save.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Journey to the West, ch. 10, dream-execution; not verbatim.

title.en: Emperor Taizong's Journey Through the Underworld
title.zh: 唐太宗入冥

region.en: The underworld courts and the Naihe bridge (symbolic pin: Fengdu, Sichuan)
region.zh: 幽冥地府（象徵性定位：豐都）

period: Journey to the West, 16th c. (attrib. Wu Cheng'en, chs. 10-11); older Tang tale 'Taizong Ruming' preserved in Dunhuang manuscripts

source.work: Journey to the West, chs. 10-11: the death of the Emperor, the tour of the Ten Courts, and the return with twenty years

license: Public domain (Ming novel; passages are compiler's renderings)

summary.en: The dragon-king's ghost dragged the dying Emperor to the underworld courts, where the Ten Kings called him to answer for the fratricide of his brothers; a bribed judge altered the ledger to add twenty years, the six kings of the six paths displayed their realms, the Ghost Gate and the iron city held the murdered brothers of his own past, and the Emperor, released at the Naihe bridge with a promise of a grand water-mass for the dead, came back to life to hold the Grand Mass and send a monk west for true scriptures.
summary.zh: 魏徵修書托崔玨；崔判官私改生死簿，添太宗二十年陽壽；六道輪迴、枉死城中兄建成弟元吉索命；奈何橋、業鏡輪迴——還陽後做水陸大會，選玄奘取經——取經之緣由此結成。

sensitivity.note: Passages are the compiler's condensed paraphrases of the novel. Cross-tradition descent-to-underworld cluster; also a satirical mirror of bureaucratic corruption (a judge amending the ledger for a donor) — noted as the novel's deliberate irony.

passages.text: The dragon-king's ghost, dragged to death by a dream-blade, came to the Emperor's bedside nightly until the Emperor sickened and died. Wei Zheng, who had beheaded him, wrote a letter of recommendation to his friend Cui Jue, a judge among the Ten Courts of the underworld, and slipped it into the Emperor's sleeve for the journey down.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Journey to the West, ch. 10-11 (compiler's rendering); not verbatim.

passages.text: In the Hall of Darkness the Ten Kings asked Wei Zheng's letter; the judge Cui Jue, reading it, quietly took the ledger of life and death and altered the Emperor's allotted years from thirty-three to fifty-three — twenty years added by a single stroke of a bureaucrat's brush. But the six paths were shown to the Emperor all the same: the mountain of knives, the ice of the guilty, the iron city where his two murdered brothers — Li Jiancheng and Li Yuanji — seized his robe and screamed for restitution.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Journey to the West, ch. 11, the ledger and the iron city; not verbatim.

passages.text: Released at the Naihe bridge with a promise of a Grand Mass of Water-and-Land to feed the hungry ghosts of the six paths, the Emperor climbed back into his body as it lay in the coffin, and the mourners fled the vault as the dead man coughed. He lived his twenty added years, founded the mass for the dead — and, told that only the true scriptures of the west could finish the salvation of the drowned and murdered souls, sent Xuanzang out through the western gate.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Journey to the West, ch. 11-12, return and commission; not verbatim.

canonical_translation: Compiler's English rendering from the public-domain original; consulted (copyright, summary only): Anthony C. Yu, Journey to the West, 1977-1986; W. J. F. Jenner, Journey to the West, 1982

narrative.en:
The underworld journey of Emperor Taizong is the deepest structural episode of Journey to the West — the descent to the dead that sets the whole pilgrimage in motion. It reworks a Tang-dynasty tale, 'Taizong enters the underworld' (Taizong Ruming), preserved in Dunhuang manuscripts, which the novel expands into a full bureaucratic tour of the Chinese hell.

BEGINNING: A DEBT OF BLOOD. The dragon-king of the Jing River, beheaded in a dream by the minister Wei Zheng, haunts the Emperor nightly until the Emperor dies. His soul goes down with a letter of recommendation sewn into his sleeve — the dead travel with connections in the novel's world. At the Hall of Darkness the Ten Kings sit in judgment; the judge Cui Jue, who owes Wei Zheng a favor, takes the ledger of life and death and quietly amends the Emperor's entry: thirty-three years become fifty-three. Twenty years of life added by one clerk's stroke.

MIDDLE: THE TOUR OF THE SIX PATHS. But justice has its own bureaucracy. The Emperor is shown the six paths of rebirth and the machinery of punishment — the mountain of knives, the boiling pots, the ice cells, the bridge of the three crossings — and, in the iron city, the ghosts of his own murdered brothers, Li Jiancheng and Li Yuanji, the princes he destroyed in the coup of 626, who seize his sleeves and demand justice before all the dead. History's fratricide becomes the underworld's open wound. The Emperor promises a Grand Mass of Water-and-Land, the great Chinese rite of feeding the dead, to quiet the hungry ghosts.

END: THE RETURN AND THE COMMISSION. The judge escorts him to the Naihe bridge; the Emperor refuses the cup of Meng Po's broth of forgetting, and climbs back into the body laid out in the coffin, coughing in the presence of the mourning court. He lives his added twenty years, holds the mass — and learns from Guanyin, manifested at the mass, that only the scriptures of the west can complete the salvation of the dead souls. So he selects the monk Xuanzang, gives him his own surname Tang and the title 'pilgrim of the scriptures,' and sends him out the western gate with a bowl, a horse, and the mandate of two worlds.

FUNCTION. The episode is three things at once: a descent-myth with the full inventory of the Chinese underworld (Ten Courts, ledgers, the six paths, hungry ghosts); a political satire (even the Emperor's fate can be bought with the right connection — the novel's wry mirror of Tang legal bureaucracy); and the narrative engine of the whole book, converting a personal debt of the Emperor into the salvation-quest of a monk. In cross-tradition terms it stands with Odysseus's Nekyia and Er's myth: a king returns from the dead with a program for the living.
narrative.zh: 唐太宗入冥為全書樞紐：魏徵修書、崔判私改生死簿添壽、枉死城兄弟索命、奈何橋還陽、設水陸大會、選玄奘西行。敦煌《唐太宗入冥記》古本與小說對讀：冥府科層、簿籍、六道俱全，而判官改簿之諷刺直指官僚制度。功能：下冥之型（十殿、六道、餓鬼）、政治諷喻、取經之動機——國王之債轉為沙門之願。

functions: Full inventory descent-myth: Ten Courts, ledgers of fate, six paths, hungry ghosts
Satire of bureaucracy: twenty years bought by a letter of recommendation
Conversion of imperial debt into monastic quest (the engine of the pilgrimage)
Charter of the Water-and-Land mass for the dead (ritual anchor)

variants.name: Dunhuang 'Taizong Ruming' tale (Tang)
variants.text_tradition: Dunhuang manuscript fragments (S.2630 etc.), ed. Wang Zhongmin
variants.summary: The Tang prototype: the Emperor's soul dragged to court, interrogated by a dead official, and sent back to found the mass for the dead — without the dragon-king frame or the added years.

variants.name: Novel chs. 10-11 — the amended ledger
variants.text_tradition: Journey to the West, 1592 Shidetang edition
variants.summary: The novel adds the dragon-king backstory, Wei Zheng's dream-execution, the judge's twenty-year amendment, and the murdered brothers in the iron city.

primary_sources.citation: Attributed Wu Cheng'en, 1592 Shidetang edition; Classical vernacular Chinese via Wikisource.
Tang tale, Dunhuang MSS; cited in scholarship on the novel's sources.

secondary_sources.work: Andrew H. Plaks, The Four Masterworks of the Ming Novel
secondary_sources.citation: Plaks 1987, Princeton: Princeton University Press — structural allegory of the novel's descent.

secondary_sources.work: Anthony C. Yu, introduction and translation of Journey to the West
secondary_sources.citation: Yu 1977-1986, Chicago: University of Chicago Press — historical notes on the underworld chapters.

source_urls.description: Wikisource (zh) — Journey to the West, public-domain Ming text

title.en: The Golden-Horn and Silver-Horn Kings of Flat-Top Mountain
title.zh: 平頂山金角銀角

region.en: Flat-Top Mountain Lotus-Flower Cave (pin: mythic westward route)
region.zh: 平頂山蓮花洞

period: Journey to the West, 16th c. (attrib. Wu Cheng'en, chs. 32-35)

source.work: Journey to the West, chs. 32-35: the five treasures — the gourd, the vase, the sword, the fan, the rope — and the name-calling contest

license: Public domain (Ming novel; passages are compiler's renderings)

summary.en: Two demon kings of Flat-Top Mountain held five magic treasures — chief among them a red-gold gourd that, if you answered to your own name, swallowed you and melted you to pus in an instant. The demon boys tricked the pilgrims into naming themselves; Wukong stole the gourd, called the kings' own names in answer, drank them both, and turned out the treasure: the two demons were the tending boys of Laozi's own furnace, sent down to try the pilgrims — and were carried back to the Tushita palace by the old man himself.
summary.zh: 平頂山蓮花洞金角銀角大王持五寶：紫金紅葫蘆、羊脂玉淨瓶、幌金繩、七星劍、芭蕉扇；叫名即吸——悟空騙得葫蘆，反叫二魔之名吸入瓶中；太上老君收回二童（爐中看爐之童子下界）。

sensitivity.note: Passages are the compiler's condensed paraphrases of the novel.

passages.text: Two demon kings guarded Lotus-Flower Cave with five treasures of heaven-forging: a purple-gold gourd, a white-jade vase, a golden rope, a seven-star sword and a plantain fan. The gourd was the terror of the country: called by its true name, a man answered — and once the answer left his lips, he was sucked inside and dissolved to soup in an instant.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Journey to the West, chs. 32-33 (compiler's rendering); not verbatim.

passages.text: The demons' boys, sent with the gourd to capture the monk, were out-witted by the monkey, who stole the gourd and filled it with a replica of himself. The demon kings called his name; the monkey answered with a false name and was not swallowed; then Wukong, holding the stolen gourd, called the true names of the two kings — and they answered, and the gourd took them both.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Journey to the West, ch. 35, the name-contest; not verbatim.

passages.text: Opening the gourd, he poured out two streams of water — the demons dissolved. And Laozi descended to reclaim his treasure: the two kings had been the tending-boys of his furnace, sent down to earth to make trial of the pilgrims' hearts. The five treasures went back to the Tushita palace, and the road west lay open again.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Journey to the West, ch. 35, Laozi's retrieval; not verbatim.

title.en: The False King of Wuji and the Well's Drowned Ghost
title.zh: 烏雞國假國王

region.en: Wuji Kingdom on the western road (pin: mythic westward route)
region.zh: 烏雞國

period: Journey to the West, 16th c. (attrib. Wu Cheng'en, chs. 36-39)

source.work: Journey to the West, chs. 36-39: the ghost of the true king, the well of the Crystal Palace, and the lion-demon exposed

license: Public domain (Ming novel; passages are compiler's renderings)

summary.en: The true king of Wuji drowned three years ago in a well, murdered by a demon who took his shape, his throne and his queen; his ghost begged the Tang monk for justice, and the monkey fished the body from the well — preserved whole by a well-dragon's pearl. With the fake elixir of a pill the soul was called back into the corpse, the false king was exposed before the court — and he was a lion of Manjusri's own stable, sent down to pay a kingly insult to the Bodhisattva.
summary.zh: 烏雞國王三年前被獅猁怪推入井中，妖魔變作國王霸其國；真王鬼魂託夢三藏；悟空井中撈屍，太上老君還魂丹救活；假王現形，乃文殊菩薩坐下獅子——為償國王捆縛菩薩三日之報。

sensitivity.note: Passages are the compiler's condensed paraphrases of the novel.

passages.text: The ghost of a drowned king came to the pilgrims' night-fire and told his tale: three years past, a demon in a Taoist robe brought rain in a drought, was made brother of the king — and pushed the king into a well at the Back Garden, took his shape and his crown, and has sat on the throne ever since.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Journey to the West, chs. 36-37 (compiler's rendering); not verbatim.

passages.text: Wukong went down the well with a sea-fork and found at its bottom a Crystal Palace of the well-dragon, and the king's body laid out whole and fresh, kept incorrupt by a pearl of the dragon's keeping. He bore it up in the night to the prince, told the truth to the boy — and the prince, on his mother's word, believed.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Journey to the West, ch. 38, the well-body; not verbatim.

passages.text: The false king was lured into the open court; the true body, with a pill of revivification from Laozi's own crucible, sat up and named its murderer. The demon unmasked was a lion of the stable of Manjusri — sent down because the king of Wuji had once bound the Bodhisattva and soaked him three days in the river: the lion's three years of theft were the payment of a king's insult.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Journey to the West, ch. 39, the trial and Manjusri's lion; not verbatim.

title.en: Red Boy of Fire-Cloud Cave, Adopted by Guanyin
title.zh: 紅孩兒善財童子

region.en: Fire-Cloud Cave, Hao-thorn ridge west of Flaming Mountains (pin: mythic westward route)
region.zh: 號山枯松澗火雲洞

period: Journey to the West, 16th c. (attrib. Wu Cheng'en, chs. 40-42)

source.work: Journey to the West, chs. 40-42: the boy-demon's samadhi fire, the five carts, and the conversion into Sudhana

license: Public domain (Ming novel; passages are compiler's renderings)

summary.en: The demon Red Boy, son of the Bull Demon King, had cultivated the true fire of samadhi for three hundred years: from five magic carts he poured a fire even the rain-gods could not quench, and from his breath he blew a smoke that struck the Monkey King's heart and nearly killed him. Wukong fetched Guanyin, who lured the boy onto a lotus seat of spears, subdued him with rings of gold — and took him to Potalaka as her page: the demon became the boy Sudhana, attendant of the Bodhisattva.
summary.zh: 紅孩兒乃牛魔王之子，三百年修得三昧真火，五輛車子三昧真火焚天；悟空請觀音，蓮花寶座化刀，金箍套頸——收為善財童子，隨侍紫竹林。

sensitivity.note: Passages are the compiler's condensed paraphrases of the novel.

passages.text: The demon Red Boy was a child in looks only: three hundred years of cultivation had won him the true fire of samadhi, drawn from the mouth and nostrils, hotter than any flame of wood. He stationed five magic carts of fire about his cave and breathed the fire of them at whatever came near — and the Monkey King, struck by the smoke of it, plunged into a stream and nearly burst his heart.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Journey to the West, chs. 40-41 (compiler's rendering); not verbatim.

passages.text: The dragons rained and could not quench it; the monkey fetched Guanyin. The Bodhisattva sent a message, lured the boy to a lotus seat of blades that turned to thorns and rings of gold, and bound him hand and foot — the demon, disarmed, transformed into a boy of great beauty, barefoot and garlanded.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Journey to the West, ch. 41-42, Guanyin's subduing; not verbatim.

passages.text: Guanyin led him back to Potalaka to stand beside her as a page — the boy Sudhana, the Child of Wealth, attendant of the Bodhisattva of Mercy. The fire demon of the western road became one of the gentlest presences in the Buddhist heavens: a conversion the Tang monk's party watched with awe, and the demon's father, the Bull Demon King, never forgave.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Journey to the West, ch. 42, adoption as Sudhana; not verbatim.

title.en: The Inspiration King of the Cross-Heaven River
title.zh: 通天河靈感大王

region.en: Tongtian River, Chen family village (pin: mythic westward route)
region.zh: 通天河陳家莊

period: Journey to the West, 16th c. (attrib. Wu Cheng'en, chs. 47-49)

source.work: Journey to the West, chs. 47-49: the yearly sacrifice of a child, the ice-bridge of the frozen river, and the goldfish of Guanyin's pond

license: Public domain (Ming novel; passages are compiler's renderings)

summary.en: By the Cross-Heaven River a demon called himself the Inspiration King and took each year a boy and a girl from the Chen household as his sacrifice. Wukong and Bajie took the children's places, fought the demon, and drove him under the ice; the monk was carried off through the frozen river's hole, and only Guanyin, wading barefoot with fish-baskets, could draw her goldfish — escaped from her own pond, nine years unattended — from the riverbed.
summary.zh: 靈感大王每年食童男童女；八戒悟空代之，冰凍通天河；三藏被水底攝去；觀音以魚籃收金魚精——原是蓮池中金魚，觀音未梳妝而至。

sensitivity.note: Passages are the compiler's condensed paraphrases of the novel.

passages.text: The Chen family by the river offered a boy and a girl each year to the Inspiration King, whose flood-temple stood on the bank, and the two children of this year wept in the offering hall until the pilgrims took their places — Bajie in the girl's dress and Wukong in the boy's, sitting in the sacrifice to await the god.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Journey to the West, ch. 47 (compiler's rendering); not verbatim.

passages.text: The demon came as a winter gale; the brothers fought him off, and he fled down into the deep. In the night the river froze bridge-hard, the monk crossed on the ice — and the demon, striking through the frozen surface, carried him down to his Water-Turtle Palace. The frozen river thawed, the monk was gone, and only the white dragon horse wept that his master was under the water.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Journey to the West, chs. 48-49, the ice and the abduction; not verbatim.

passages.text: Guanyin came barefoot and unadorned, wove a fish-basket of wands, and drew from the river a great goldfish — her own pond's pet, escaped nine years before to become the scourge of the river villages. She hung the basket on her shoulder and went back to the South Sea; and an old white turtle of the riverbed ferried the pilgrims across the water to the western shore.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Journey to the West, ch. 49, the goldfish and the turtle; not verbatim.

title.en: The Three Demon Immortals of Cart-Slow Kingdom
title.zh: 車遲國三妖鬥法

region.en: Cart-Slow (Chechi) Kingdom (pin: mythic westward route)
region.zh: 車遲國

period: Journey to the West, 16th c. (attrib. Wu Cheng'en, chs. 44-46)

source.work: Journey to the West, chs. 44-46: rain-calling by decree, the meditation-box gamble, and the three lethal contests

license: Public domain (Ming novel; passages are compiler's renderings)

summary.en: In Cart-Slow Kingdom three demon-immortals — tiger, deer and goat in their true shapes — had enslaved two thousand Buddhist monks to haul carts up a mountain ridge. The pilgrims freed the monks, and the demons demanded a trial by magic: rain-summoning (won by Wukong's manipulation of the rain-bureaucracy), meditation on high platforms (won by Bajie's hair-transformed louse), then head-removal, gut-plucking, and oil-boiling — lethal contests in which each demon lost his life to the monkey's mimicry.
summary.zh: 車遲國虎力、鹿力、羊力三大仙役使和尚拉車；悟空解放僧人，三妖鬥法求雨、雲梯坐禪、隔板猜物；賭砍頭、剖腹、下油鍋——虎力斷頭不歸、鹿力剖腹現羊、羊力油炸現羚羊——三妖皆死。

sensitivity.note: Passages are the compiler's condensed paraphrases of the novel. The demons are fake Daoists — the novel's satire on corruption of both Buddhist and Daoist establishments; noted.

passages.text: In Cart-Slow Kingdom the three national immortals — Tiger-Power, Deer-Power and Antelope-Power — had turned two thousand Buddhist monks into haulers of carts up a ridge of rock for the building of the three demons' temples. The pilgrims freed them in the night, and the demons demanded justice before the king: a trial by magic between the monks and the masters of the road.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Journey to the West, chs. 44 (compiler's rendering); not verbatim.

passages.text: First, rain: the demons danced their papers and calls, and the monkey went up to the rain-bureaucracy and ordered the weather bureau around — wind, cloud, thunder and rain falling only at the monk's nod, and bright sun at his frown. Then the guessing-contest through a cabinet: the monkey, changing into a moth and a cricket, spoiled every guess and put right every one of his own side's.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Journey to the West, ch. 45, the contests; not verbatim.

passages.text: Then came the lethal games. Head-cutting: the Tiger immortal's head did not return, and a hawk took it away — the demon died. Gut-plucking: the Deer immortal's bowels were pecked by a hawk in the shape of the monkey's own trick, and he collapsed in his true form, a deer. The Antelope immortal boiled in oil; the monkey blew the oil cold, then heated it himself, and the demon, cooked in his turn, rose as a scorched antelope. Three contests, three deaths, and the Buddhist monks of Cart-Slow went free.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Journey to the West, ch. 46, the lethal contests; not verbatim.

title.en: The Women's Kingdom of Xiliang and the Scorpion of Pipa Cave
title.zh: 女兒國與琵琶洞蠍子精

region.en: Women's Kingdom of Xiliang, west of the Childless River (pin: mythic westward route)
region.zh: 西梁女國、解陽山琵琶洞

period: Journey to the West, 16th c. (attrib. Wu Cheng'en, chs. 53-55)

source.work: Journey to the West, chs. 53-55: the pregnancy river, the queen's proposal, and the scorpion-demon's bridal cave

license: Public domain (Ming novel; passages are compiler's renderings)

summary.en: Drinking from the Childless River, the Tang monk and Bajie grew heavy with child, and had to drink the abortive waters of the Spring of Delivered Motherhood — guarded by a jealous immortal of the true stream. In the Women's Kingdom, a realm of queens and no men, the young queen proposed marriage to the monk for his kingdom's sake — and while the pilgrims staged the wedding-escort, the Scorpion Demon of Pipa Cave snatched the monk to her cave; her poisoned stinger had wounded even the Buddha, and only the Star Officer Mao, the celestial rooster, could crow her out of her hole.
summary.zh: 子母河水使三藏八戒胎動，落胎泉水解之；女兒國女王願以一國相托婚配三藏；假親脫網之計，琵琶洞蠍子精攝三藏——蠍尾毒曾螫如來；昴日星官現本相（雞）鳴而蠍死。

sensitivity.note: Passages are the compiler's condensed paraphrases of the novel.

passages.text: At the Childless River the monk and the pig drank greedily of the current, and by evening both were heavy with child. The midwives of the village sent them west to the Spring of the Delivered Mother, where a single draught dissolved the pregnancy — but the spring was guarded by a vengeful immortal whose own spring Wukong had to conquer first.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Journey to the West, ch. 53 (compiler's rendering); not verbatim.

passages.text: In the Women's Kingdom — a country of queens, never men — the young queen heard of the monk and proposed to marry him, offering him the whole state. The pilgrims, needing to pass, staged a betrothal as a ruse: the queen and her court loaded the monk into the royal carriage, and at the moment of parting Wukong sprung the trap and freed his master — only for a whirlwind to snatch the monk away to the Scorpion Demon's cave.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Journey to the West, ch. 54, the false betrothal; not verbatim.

passages.text: The Scorpion Demon had once stung even the Buddha's finger and lived. Her poisoned tail-sting drove back the monkey and the pig with swollen heads; the monk was held for her bridal. Wukong fetched the Star Officer Mao, the celestial rooster of the eastern palace: the god crowed twice, revealing his true form of a great golden bird, and the scorpion, stretched out of her hole, lay dead on the ground.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Journey to the West, ch. 55, the scorpion's death; not verbatim.

title.en: The True and False Monkey Kings
title.zh: 真假美猴王

region.en: From Flower-Fruit Mountain to the Thunderclap Monastery (pin: mythic westward route)
region.zh: 花果山至雷音寺

period: Journey to the West, 16th c. (attrib. Wu Cheng'en, chs. 57-58)

source.work: Journey to the West, chs. 57-58: the indistinguishable double, the halls of heaven and the Sea of Suffering, and the Buddha's naming of the Six-Eared Macaque

license: Public domain (Ming novel; passages are compiler's renderings)

summary.en: Banished once more for killing a bandit, Wukong's place was taken by a double — identical in face, staff, skill and name-lore — who felled the Tang monk and took the luggage to found his own scripture-school. Heaven's mirror could not tell them apart; Guanyin could not; the underworld's ledger named one 'Sun Wukong,' but the macaque had never been in it. Only the Buddha could read the creature: a Six-Eared Macaque, a being that hears the past and the future through six ears — and as the two grappled beneath his palm, the true one revealed the false, and the Great Sage killed his own image with one blow.
summary.zh: 悟空再遭逐，六耳獼猴假扮美猴王打傷三藏，欲自去取經；照妖鏡、緊箍、諦聽皆不能辨；如來道破：乃六耳獼猴，善聆音、能察理、知前後——悟空一棒打死，師徒復和。

sensitivity.note: Passages are the compiler's condensed paraphrases of the novel. Readers have long read the double as the monkey's own shadow-self — a modern interpretive frame, noted but not asserted.

passages.text: Banished for a second killing, the Great Sage had barely gone before a double appeared to the monk in his shape, with his staff, his face and his manners — offered water, was refused in fear of poison, and struck the Tang monk down and took the luggage. Two identical Sun Wukongs now argued before the courts of heaven, each with his own story of the other.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Journey to the West, ch. 57 (compiler's rendering); not verbatim.

passages.text: The Jade Emperor's demon-revealing mirror showed two identical monkeys. Guanyin, tightening the fillet on both at once, could not tell them. The underworld's beast-listening god Diting heard everything and told no one; the register of souls named one Sun Wukong — but the other had never entered the book at all.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Journey to the West, ch. 58, the failed identifications; not verbatim.

passages.text: Before the Buddha the truth was spoken: the false monkey was a Six-Eared Macaque, a creature that hears a thousand li and knows past and future — one of four monkey-kinds beyond the reach of the ten categories of beings. As the two monkeys grappled under the Buddha's golden bowl, the true Wukong saw his chance and killed his double with a single blow — and the Buddha gently reproved him not for killing, but for the anger that had let the double in.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Journey to the West, ch. 58, the naming and the killing; not verbatim.

title.en: The Flaming Mountains and the Iron-Fan Princess
title.zh: 火焰山芭蕉扇

region.en: Flaming Mountains, 800 li of fire (pin: Turfan basin echo)
region.zh: 火焰山（八百里火焰）

period: Journey to the West, 16th c. (attrib. Wu Cheng'en, chs. 59-61)

source.work: Journey to the West, chs. 59-61: the borrowed fan, the swallowed fan, the Bull Demon King's true form

license: Public domain (Ming novel; passages are compiler's renderings)

summary.en: Eight hundred li of fire — kindled, said the locals, when Wukong kicked over Laozi's furnace five hundred years before — blocked the road; only the Iron-Fan Princess's plantain fan could quench it. She was the wife of the Bull Demon King and mother of the demon Red Boy, and she hated the monkey. He was blown fifty thousand li by her fan, swallowed a wind-stilling pill, sneaked into her belly as a bug and forced the loan; the false fan fanned the fire higher — and the war with the Bull Demon King ended when heaven's armies closed in and the Bull, in his great white bull form, yielded: the fan was surrendered, forty-nine waves quenched the mountains, and the monk passed west.
summary.zh: 火焰山乃悟空當年蹬倒丹爐之火；鐵扇公主持芭蕉扇，一扇五萬四千里；悟空定風丹、變蟲入腹索扇；假扇扇火更旺；牛魔王大戰，天兵圍攻，老牛現白牛本相，獻扇滅火四十九扇，山火永熄。

sensitivity.note: Passages are the compiler's condensed paraphrases of the novel.

passages.text: The road west crossed eight hundred li of burning mountain — flames that had burned since, the locals said, the day the Great Sage kicked over Laozi's crucibles five hundred years before. Only the plantain fan of the Iron-Fan Princess, one wave for dying, two for a wind, three for rain, could quench the fire; and the princess hated the monkey, whose capture had sent her son Red Boy to a bodhisattva's service.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Journey to the West, ch. 59 (compiler's rendering); not verbatim.

passages.text: Her first fan blew Wukong fifty-four thousand li, to the gates of the Little Sumeru hill; the Buddha of that hill gave him a wind-stilling pill. Returning as a gnat, he hid in the foam of her tea, entered her belly, and kicked and turned inside it until she gave up the true fan — which, waved in haste, only fanned the flames higher, for it was a false one made of apricot leaves.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Journey to the West, ch. 59, the thefts and the false fan; not verbatim.

passages.text: Then the Bull Demon King himself took the field — a war of transformations, of feasts and disguises, until the heavenly hosts closed in and the Bull, struck down in his great white bull form, surrendered: the true fan, forty-nine waves, and the mountains quenched forever. The road west lay clear, the rain fell green over the hills, and the pilgrims went on — with the monkey owing a debt to the Bull's family that the final chapters of the novel will still be collecting.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Journey to the West, ch. 61, the Bull's surrender; not verbatim.

title.en: The Taking of Joppa: Tahutia's Two Hundred Sacks
title.zh: 攻克雅法：塔胡提亞的兩百麻袋

region.en: Joppa (Jaffa), Canaan (rebel city on the Phoenician coast)
region.zh: 迦南雅法（腓尼基海岸之叛城）

period: Tale set in the reign of Thutmose III (c. 1479-1425 BCE); Petrie translation 1895

source.work: Egyptian Tales, Second Series, ed. W. M. Flinders Petrie (London, 1895), 'The Taking of Joppa'

summary.en: The general Tahutia pretends to defect to the rebel of Joppa, carries the king's magic cane in a bundle of reeds, strikes the rebel senseless with it, and hides two hundred Egyptian soldiers in grain-sacks; the city hauls its own doom through the gates and the power of Pharaoh seizes it — the oldest version of the trick that becomes the Wooden Horse and Ali Baba.
summary.zh: 大將塔胡提亞詐降雅法叛首，以蘆葦捆藏王之魔杖，一擊使叛首昏厥；再以穀袋暗藏二百埃及士兵——城門自啟，引祸入城，法老之權遂掌此邑——此計乃特洛伊木馬與阿里巴巴之最古原型。

sensitivity.note: Ancient literary tale on an historical basis; no living community restrictions.

passages.text: And thereupon the Foe in Joppa said to Tahutia, 'My heart is set on examining the great cane of Men-kheper-ra, which is named . . . tautnefer. By the ka of the King Men-kheper-ra it will be in thy hands to-day; now do thou well and bring thou it to me.' And Tahutia did thus, and he brought the cane of King Men-kheper-ra. And he laid hold on the Foe in Joppa by his garment, and he arose and stood up, and said, 'Look on me, O Foe in Joppa; here is the great cane of King Men-kheper-ra, the terrible lion, the son of Sekhet, to whom Amen his father gives power and strength.' And he raised his hand and struck the forehead of the Foe in Joppa, and he fell helpless before him.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Petrie, Egyptian Tales Second Series (1895), The Taking of Joppa.

passages.text: He put him in the sack of skins and he bound with gyves the hands of the Foe in Joppa, and put on his feet the fetters with four rings. And he made them bring the two hundred sacks which he had cleaned, and made to enter into them two hundred soldiers, and filled the hollows with cords and fetters of wood, he sealed them with a seal, and added to them their rope-nets and the poles to bear them. And he put every strong footman to bear them, in all six hundred men, and said to them, 'When you come into the town you shall open your burdens, you shall seize on all the inhabitants of the town, and you shall quickly put fetters upon them.'
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Petrie (1895), The Taking of Joppa.

passages.text: Then one went out and said unto the charioteer of the Foe in Joppa, 'Thy master is fallen; go, say to thy mistress, A pleasant message! For Sutekh has given Tahutia to us, with his wife and his children; behold the beginning of their tribute,' that she may comprehend the two hundred sacks, which are full of men and cords and fetters. So he went before them to please the heart of his mistress, saying, 'We have laid hands on Tahutia.' Then the gates of the city were opened before the footmen: they entered the city, they opened their burdens, they laid hands on them of the city, both small and great, they put on them the cords and fetters quickly; the power of Pharaoh seized upon that city.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Petrie (1895), The Taking of Joppa, closing.

passages.text: After he had rested Tahutia sent a message to Egypt to the King Men-kheper-ra his lord, saying, 'Be pleased, for Amen thy good father has given to thee the Foe in Joppa, together with all his people, likewise also his city. Send, therefore, people to take them as captives that thou mayest fill the house of thy father Amen Ra, king of the gods, with men-servants and maid-servants, and that they may be overthrown beneath thy feet for ever and ever.'
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Petrie (1895), the dispatch to Egypt.

title.en: The Doomed Prince: Crocodile, Serpent, and Dog
title.zh: 受詛王子：鱷、蛇與犬

region.en: Naharaina (Upper Syria), frontier state of New Kingdom Egypt
region.zh: 納哈林那（上敘利亞），新王國之邊邦

period: Tale of the close of the 18th Dynasty (c. 1350-1300 BCE), Harris papyrus 500; Petrie translation 1895

source.work: Egyptian Tales, Second Series, ed. W. M. Flinders Petrie (1895), 'The Doomed Prince'

summary.en: The Hathors decree that a long-awaited prince will die by crocodile, serpent, or dog; his father walls him in a desert house, but the prince demands his fate: 'Let God do what is in His heart.' He wins the princess of Naharaina by climbing to her seventy-windowed tower, she saves him from the serpent with a bowl of milk, and the tale breaks off with the crocodile — 'I am thy doom, following after thee' — still waiting.
summary.zh: 哈托爾諸女神判一位盼來之子將死於鱷、蛇或犬；父王築屋於荒漠困之，王子卻道：『願神行其心中所欲。』他攀上納哈林那公主七十扇窗的高塔而娶之；公主以一碗牛乳救他於蛇吻——故事至鱷魚一句『我是你的命，一路跟隨你』戛然而止。

sensitivity.note: Ancient literary tale; no living community restrictions. The papyrus breaks off mid-story; the ending is unknown.

passages.text: There once was a king to whom no son was born; and his heart was grieved, and he prayed for himself unto the gods around him for a child. They decreed that one should be born to him. And his wife, after her time was fulfilled, brought forth a son. Then came the Hathors to decree for him a destiny; they said, 'His death is to be by the crocodile, or by the serpent, or by the dog.' Then the people who stood by heard this, and they went to tell it to his majesty. Then his majesty's heart sickened very greatly. And his majesty caused a house to be built upon the desert; it was furnished with people and with all good things of the royal house, that the child should not go abroad.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Petrie, Egyptian Tales Second Series (1895), The Doomed Prince.

passages.text: Then when the days increased after this, and when the child became grown in all his limbs, he sent a message to his father saying, 'Come, wherefore am I kept here? Inasmuch as I am fated to three evil fates, let me follow my desire. Let God do what is in His heart.' They agreed to all he said, and gave him all sorts of arms, and also his dog to follow him, and they took him to the east country, and said to him, 'Behold, go thou whither thou wilt.' His dog was with him, and he went northward, following his heart in the desert, while he lived on all the best of the game of the desert. He went to the chief of Naha-raina.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Petrie (1895), The Doomed Prince.

passages.text: Behold, there had not been born to the chief of Naharaina, except one daughter. Behold, there had been built for her a house; its seventy windows were seventy cubits from the ground. And the chief caused to be brought all the sons of the chiefs of the land of Khalu, and said to them, 'He who reaches the window of my daughter, she shall be to him for a wife.' — He climbed, and he reached the window of the daughter of the chief of Naharaina. She kissed him, she embraced him in all his limbs.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Petrie (1895), the tower and its conquest (condensed).

passages.text: And when the evening came he lay down on his bed, sleep seized upon his limbs; and his wife filled a bowl of milk, and placed it by his side. Then came out a serpent from his hole, to bite the youth; behold his wife was sitting by him, she lay not down. Thereupon the servants gave milk to the serpent, and he drank, and was drunk, and lay upside down. Then his wife made it to perish with the blows of her dagger. And they woke her husband, who was astonished; and she said unto him, 'Behold thy God has given one of thy dooms into thy hand; He will also give thee the others.' And he sacrificed to God, adoring Him, and praising His spirits from day to day. — He came to the river, and entered the river behind his dog. Then came out the crocodile, and took him to the place where the mighty man was. And the crocodile said to the youth, 'I am thy doom, following after thee.' [Here the papyrus breaks off.]
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Petrie (1895), the serpent episode and the tale's broken ending.

title.en: Anpu and Bata: The Brother Whose Soul Sat in a Blossom
title.zh: 安普與巴塔：魂寄花上之弟

region.en: Valley of the Acacia (symbolic pin, Eastern Delta pine land) and the royal house of the Two Lands
region.zh: 金合歡谷（象徵定位，東三角洲松地）與兩地之王室

period: Papyrus d'Orbiney (BM EA 10183), property of Sety II as crown prince, 19th Dynasty c. 1250-1200 BCE (Petrie-Griffith translation 1895)

source.work: Egyptian Tales, Second Series, ed. W. M. Flinders Petrie (1895), 'Anpu and Bata'

summary.en: The greatest of Egyptian folk-myths: the falsely accused younger brother Bata cuts off his own flesh, plants his soul in the topmost blossom of an acacia, is betrayed woman after woman and transformed bull after tree after child, until he becomes king of Egypt for thirty years — while his elder brother Anpu, who once hunted him with a knife, ends as his heir.
summary.zh: 埃及民間神話之最：遭誣陷的弟弟巴塔自斷己肉，將魂魄置於金合歡最高之花；他歷經一女又一女的背叛、由牛化樹化子——最終為埃及之王三十年；而當年持刀追殺他的兄長安普，竟繼承其位。

sensitivity.note: Ancient literary myth-tale; no living community restrictions. The Joseph parallel (false accusation motif) is noted by Petrie and Griffith and flagged for the Compare view.

passages.text: Once there were two brethren, of one mother and one father; Anpu was the name of the elder, and Bata was the name of the younger. Now, as for Anpu he had a house, and he had a wife. But his little brother was to him as it were a son; he it was who made for him his clothes; he it was who followed behind his oxen to the fields; he it was who did the ploughing; he it was who harvested the corn; he it was who did for him all the matters that were in the field. Behold, his younger brother grew to be an excellent worker, there was not his equal in the whole land; behold, the spirit of a god was in him.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Petrie, Egyptian Tales Second Series (1895), Anpu and Bata.

passages.text: And she conversed with him, saying, 'There is great strength in thee, for I see thy might every day.' And her heart knew him with the knowledge of youth. And she arose and came to him, and conversed with him, saying, 'Come, stay with me, and it shall be well for thee, and I will make for thee beautiful garments.' Then the youth became like a panther of the south with fury at the evil speech which she had made to him; and she feared greatly. And he spake unto her, saying, 'Behold thou art to me as a mother, thy husband is to me as a father, for he who is elder than I has brought me up. What is this wickedness that thou hast said to me? Say it not to me again.'
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Petrie (1895), the wife's temptation.

passages.text: And Ra stood and heard all his cry; and Ra made a wide water between him and his elder brother, and it was full of crocodiles; and the one brother was on one bank, and the other on the other bank... And the younger brother called unto him, saying, 'I shall go to the valley of the acacia. And this is what shall come to pass, that I shall draw out my soul, and I shall put it upon the top of the flowers of the acacia, and when the acacia is cut down, and it falls to the ground, and thou comest to seek for it, if thou searchest for it seven years do not let thy heart be wearied. For thou wilt find it, and thou must put it in a cup of cold water, and expect that I shall live again.' And the youth went to the valley of the acacia; and his elder brother went unto his house... he slew his wife, he cast her to the dogs, and he sat in mourning for his younger brother.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Petrie (1895), the separation and the soul in the blossom.

passages.text: The Nine Gods talked one with another, and they said unto him, 'Ho! Bata, bull of the Nine Gods, art thou remaining alone?' And Ra Harakhti said to Khnumu, 'Behold, frame thou a woman for Bata, that he may not remain alive alone.' And Khnumu made for him a mate to dwell with him. She was more beautiful in her limbs than any woman who is in the whole land. The essence of every god was in her. The seven Hathors came to see her: they said with one mouth, 'She will die a sharp death.' — And they cut the flower upon which was the soul of Bata, and he fell dead suddenly... They grew as two great Persea trees, and each of them was excellent. — But a chip flew up, and it entered into the mouth of the princess; she swallowed it, and after many days she bore a son. And the king raised him to be the royal son of Kush. And when he had fulfilled many years as heir, his majesty flew up to heaven. He was thirty years king of Egypt, and he died, and his elder brother stood in his place on the day of burial.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Petrie (1895), elided between the divine wife, the deaths and transformations, and the ending.

canonical_translation: F. Ll. Griffith in W. M. F. Petrie, Egyptian Tales, Second Series (London, 1895)

narrative.en:
The Tale of Anpu and Bata is the longest and strangest of Egyptian narratives — a folk-myth that begins as a rustic idyll and ends with a dynasty. It survives on a single papyrus that once belonged to Sety II as crown prince; Petrie and Griffith, its English translators, detected an older, beautiful opening tale that some Ramesside compiler stretched out with marvels, and its closing curse on meddlers ('He who speaks against this roll, may Tahuti smite him') suggests the compiler knew he had been meddling.

BEGINNING: THE HOUSEHOLD AND THE FALSE ACCUSATION. Anpu has a house and a wife; Bata, the younger brother, lives with him 'as it were a son' — he makes Anpu's clothes, herds his cattle, ploughs and harvests, bakes the bread before dawn, and sleeps in the stable with the oxen. 'Behold, the spirit of a god was in him': even the cattle speak to him, and he leads them to the pasture they desire. At ploughing-time Anpu sends Bata to the farm for seed; Anpu's wife, dressing her hair, sees his strength and 'her heart knew him with the knowledge of youth.' She offers herself; Bata answers like a startled panther — 'Behold thou art to me as a mother... Say it not to me again' — and goes back to the field. Fearing exposure, the wife smears herself with fat, lies beaten and wordless, and tells Anpu that the boy attacked her; Anpu sharpens his knife and waits behind the stable door. But the foremost cow warns Bata: 'Behold thy elder brother standing before thee with his knife.' Bata flees; Anpu pursues; and Ra-Harakhti, hearing Bata's cry — 'My good Lord! Thou art he who divides the evil from the good' — sets a wide water full of crocodiles between the brothers. Bata takes the first severing into his own hands: he cuts off his flesh and casts it to the fish, then plants his soul in the topmost blossom of an acacia in the valley of the acacia, telling Anpu to search seven years for it and steep it in cold water to restore him. Anpu goes home and gives his lying wife to the dogs.

MIDDLE: THE DIVINE WIFE AND THE THREE DEATHS. In the valley the Nine Gods pass by and pity Bata alone; Ra-Harakhti orders Khnumu to 'frame a woman for Bata' — the potter-god's masterpiece, more beautiful than any woman on earth, 'the essence of every god in her.' The Seven Hathors pronounce her doom with one mouth: 'She will die a sharp death.' Bata warns her: he cannot be killed while his soul is on the acacia flower, but 'if another find it, I must fight with him.' The sea covets her; she flees; a lock of her hair drifts to Egypt and its perfume convicts the royal fullers. Pharaoh's sages read the hair — 'a daughter of Ra-Harakhti... a tribute to thee from another land' — and soldiers fetch her to the king, who raises her to high estate. To keep her secret, she orders the acacia cut down; the blossom falls and Bata dies. But Anpu, warned by the troubled cup of beer, comes searching; in the fourth year he finds a seed, steeps it in cold water, and Bata shudders back to life. Bata's transformations now cascade: he becomes a great bull marked with every good sign and carries Anpu to Pharaoh's court; the queen recognizes him, has the bull slaughtered at a feast, and two drops of his blood grow by night into two great Persea trees before the palace gates; she has the felled trees made into planks while she watches, and a flying chip enters her mouth — she swallows it, and bears a son.

END: THE KING OF THIRTY YEARS. The child is brought to Pharaoh as 'a son born to thee'; the king, delighted, makes him Royal Son of Kush and heir. When Pharaoh dies the heir assembles the nobles and 'judged with her' — the tale's single sentence of justice — then makes Anpu, who comes to court, hereditary prince over all the land. Bata reigns thirty years; at his death his elder brother, once his murderer and then his restorer, stands in his place on the day of burial.

FUNCTION. The tale is a theological folk-drama of wrong and restoration: the innocent sufferer repeatedly dies and repeatedly returns — from body cut to fish, bull, tree, and finally child — a folk brother of Osiris' own death-and-resurrection, staged in farmhouse and palace. Petrie's remarks note the striking parallel with the Joseph story in Genesis (the wife's accusation), and Egyptologists have long compared Bata's vegetative rebirths with the Osiris-Persea tree cult. It also gives the earliest literary portrait of a woman whose beauty is literally the essence of every god, and whose 'sharp death' prophecy the Hathors pronounce — the same fate-decreeing Hathors of the Doomed Prince.

functions: Folk theology of death and rebirth: the soul kept in a blossom and re-quickened in cold water, a rustic mirror of the Osiris resurrection
Etiology of royal succession: a tale of a pretender's line told in the household of Sety II, legitimizing the heir's rule
The false-accusation motif: earliest full version of the story-type best known from Joseph and Potiphar's wife
Female liminality: the divine-made wife as the instrument of the hero's deaths and of his final rebirth as a king

variants.name: The Contendings of Horus and Seth (same transformation logic in the divine realm)
variants.text_tradition: Papyrus Chester Beatty I, New Kingdom
variants.summary: Horus' own litigation against Seth uses the same weapons of disguise, contest, and transformation; the folk tale and the divine myth are two registers of the same restoration plot.

variants.name: The Joseph story (Genesis 39, false-accusation type)
variants.text_tradition: Hebrew Bible, composed c. 1st millennium BCE
variants.summary: The master's wife who tries and falsely accuses the beautiful servant, and the servant's rise in a foreign court, parallels Bata's opening and its aftermath (noted by Petrie and Griffith).

variants.name: Persea-tree rebirth cult
variants.text_tradition: Persea (Mimusops) trees in Egyptian temple cult, New Kingdom
variants.summary: Bata's rebirth through blood drops becoming Persea trees reflects the actual cult of Persea trees at Memphis and Heliopolis, in which the tree was an avatar of rebirth and kingship records were written on its leaves.

primary_sources.citation: Papyrus d'Orbiney (BM EA 10183), recto, 19th Dynasty, c. 1250-1200 BCE. Ed. E. Naville (facsimile, 1870); trans. F. Ll. Griffith in W. M. F. title.en: Setna and the Magic Book of Thoth
title.zh: 塞特納與托特魔法書

region.en: Memphis, Egypt (cemetery and tomb of Naneferkaptah) and Koptos in the Thebaid
region.zh: 埃及孟菲斯（奈奈弗爾卡普塔墓園）與底比斯之科普托斯

period: Demotic tale written in the Ptolemaic period, colophon dated year 35 (Petrie-Hess rendering 1895)

source.work: Egyptian Tales, Second Series, ed. W. M. Flinders Petrie (1895), 'Setna and the Magic Book'

summary.en: Setna Khaemwaset, the king's scholar son, breaks into a tomb to steal the Book of Thoth, which grants power over heaven and earth and the speech of birds and fish; the dead prince wins it back at the game of 52 points, sinking him into the earth three games deep, then destroys him with a dream of the courtesan Tabubua — until Setna restores the book, forked stick in hand and fire-pan on head, and reunites the dead family in one tomb.
summary.zh: 王子書吏塞特納破墓欲奪托特之書——其書能御天地、通鳥獸魚語；亡王子以五十二點棋局三度勝之，令其陷入土中至耳，再以名妓塔布布阿之夢毀之——直至塞特納持叉杖、頂火盤還書於墓，並聚合亡者一家於一塋。

sensitivity.note: Ancient literary ghost tale; no living community restrictions. Petrie's edition restores the lost opening and summarizes the Tabubua episode (marked in passages).

passages.text: The mighty King User-maat-ra (Ra-meses the Great) had a son named Setna Kha-em-uast who was a great scribe, and very learned in all the ancient writings. And he heard that the magic book of Thoth, by which a man may enchant heaven and earth, and know the language of all birds and beasts, was buried in the cemetery of Memphis. And he went to search for it with his brother An-he-hor-eru; and when they found the tomb of the king's son, Na-nefer-ka-ptah, son of the king of Upper and Lower Egypt, Mer-neb-ptah, Setna opened it and went in. Now in the tomb was Na-nefer-ka-ptah, and with him was the ka of his wife Ahura; for though she was buried at Koptos, her ka dwelt at Memphis with her husband, whom she loved.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Petrie, Egyptian Tales Second Series (1895), Setna and the Magic Book.

passages.text: This book is in the middle of the river at Koptos, in an iron box; in the iron box is a bronze box; in the bronze box is a sycamore box; in the sycamore box is an ivory and ebony box; in the ivory and ebony box is a silver box; in the silver box is a golden box, and in that is the book. It is twisted all round with snakes and scorpions and all the other crawling things around the box in which the book is; and there is a deathless snake by the box. — And Na-nefer-ka-ptah then went to the place where he found the box. He uncovered a box of iron, and opened it... and then he found a box of gold; he opened that, and found the book in it. He took the book from the golden box, and read a page of spells from it. He enchanted the heaven and the earth, the abyss, the mountains, and the sea; he knew what the birds of the sky, the fish of the deep, and the beasts of the hills all said.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Petrie (1895), Ahura's narration of the theft.

passages.text: And as we went on Thoth discovered all that Na-nefer-ka-ptah had done with the book; and Thoth hastened to tell Ra, and said, 'Now know that my book and my revelation are with Na-nefer-ka-ptah, son of the King Mer-neb-ptah. He has forced himself into my place, and robbed it, and seized my box with the writings, and killed my guards who protected it.' And Ra replied to him, 'He is before you, take him and all his kin.' — And after this hour, the little boy Mer-ab, going out from the awning of the royal boat, fell into the river... Then Na-nefer-ka-ptah then went out of the awning of the royal boat and fell into the river. He cried on Ra; and all those who were on the bank made an outcry, saying, 'Great woe! Sad woe! Is he lost, that good scribe and able man that has no equal?'
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Petrie (1895), the deaths of the family.

passages.text: And Na-nefer-ka-ptah rose from his seat and said, 'Are you Setna, to whom my wife has told of all these blows of fate, which you have not suffered? If, indeed, you can play games with me, let us play a game, then, of 52 points.' And Setna said, 'I am ready,' and the board and its pieces were put before him. And Na-nefer-ka-ptah won a game from Setna; and he put the spell upon him, and defended himself with the game board that was before him, and sunk him into the ground above his feet. He did the same at the second game... He did the same at the third game, and made him sink into the ground up to his ears. — [Petrie's edition here summarizes the Tabubua episode: the courtesan-daughter of a priest of Bast beguiles Setna into surrendering all he has and slaying his children, then vanishes; he awakens stripped of everything in an unknown place, and finds his children alive.] — So Setna went out from before the king, with a forked stick in his hand, and a fire-pan on his head... And Na-nefer-ka-ptah laughed, and he said, 'This is the business that I told you before.'
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Petrie (1895), with the Tabubua episode marked as the edition's summary; not verbatim for that section.

canonical_translation: J. J. Hess, Der Demotische Roman von Stne Ha-m-us (Leipzig, 1888), as rendered in W. M. F. Petrie, Egyptian Tales, Second Series (1895)

narrative.en:
Setna and the Magic Book is the first and greatest of the Setna cycle — a Ptolemaic-era demotic ghost story set three centuries earlier, starring Setna Khaemwaset, a real son of Ramesses II whose reputation as scholar prince made him Egypt's stock hero of learning and its comic foil. The tale exists in a single papyrus, its opening lost; Petrie's edition restores the frame from clues in the text.

BEGINNING: THE TOMB ROBBER. Setna, son of Ramesses the Great, hears that the magic book of Thoth — by which a man may enchant heaven, earth, abyss, mountains and sea, know the language of birds and beasts and the speech of fish, and see the sun shining with all its gods — lies in the Memphis tomb of Naneferkaptah, son of Mernebptah. He breaks in and finds the dead prince with the ka of his wife Ahura, who though buried at Koptos dwells at Memphis 'with her husband, whom she loved.' When he demands the book, Ahura begs him to hear first 'what we have suffered for it': the royal couple who were brother and sister by the queen's decree, the mocking priest who sold Naneferkaptah the book's secret, the nested coffins — iron, bronze, sycamore, ebony-and-ivory, silver, gold — in the middle of the river at Koptos, the deathless serpent killed and cut in two with sand between the halves, and the theft that enchanted the world. But Thoth told Ra, and Ra decreed: 'take him and all his kin.' One by one the boy Mer-ab and then Ahura fell from the boat's awning into the river and drowned, read back to speech by spell only to tell of Thoth's decree; and Naneferkaptah, unable to face the king, bound the book to himself with striped byssus and stepped into the river. The royal boat came on to Memphis; the king hid the book and buried his son 'in his resting-place.'

MIDDLE: THE GAME OF 52 POINTS AND THE DREAM. Setna, unmoved by grief he has not suffered, demands the book by force. Naneferkaptah rises: 'Are you Setna...? If, indeed, you can play games with me, let us play a game, then, of 52 points.' The dead prince wins the first game and sinks Setna into the ground above his feet; the second, to his waist; the third, to his ears. Setna, at his brother's word, is saved by the talisman of Ptah, seizes the book, and walks out with a Light before him and Darkness behind him; Ahura weeps the contrast — 'Glory to the King of Darkness! Hail to the King of Light! all power is gone from the tomb' — but Naneferkaptah promises: 'I will make him bring back this book, with a forked stick in his hand, and a fire-pan on his head.' The king's warning goes unheeded; Setna reads the book to everybody. Then comes the revenge: in the temple court he sees the courtesan Tabubua, daughter of a priest of Bast, irresistible; she strips him of rank after rank, wealth after wealth, then of his children — he consents to everything at her command — until she gives 'a fearful cry' and vanishes, and he wakes alone, stripped, in an unknown place while crowds gather to mock him. His children appear alive: the whole degradation was spun for him from the tomb.

END: RESTITUTION AND REUNION. Setna returns the book in the foretold state — 'a forked stick in his hand, and a fire-pan on his head' — and Naneferkaptah laughs: 'This is the business that I told you before.' As the tomb fills with sunlight ('The sun was in the whole tomb'), the dead prince asks one last service of the scribe: Ahura and Mer-ab lie buried at Koptos; let Setna find their resting-place and bring their bodies to the tomb at Memphis, by the skill of a good scribe. Diggers search three days and nights through all the catacombs of Koptos without finding them; Naneferkaptah himself comes up as a very old man and reveals the spot beneath the south corner of the town of Pehemato, promising its safety. Setna brings the two bodies up the Nile as honored persons, lays them with Naneferkaptah, and smooths the earth over them; the dead family is reunited, the scholar has paid for his learning, and the colophon — written in the 35th year — closes the oldest ghost-and-roller-dice story in literature.

FUNCTION. The tale is a theology of restricted knowledge: the Book of Thoth is exactly the sort of knowledge that must not be taken — its theft kills a royal family and its restitution is the only cure. It mocks the over-confident scholar (Setna is Shimon-Setna's type across three centuries of tales), and its dream-technique — a punishment that seems real until it is withdrawn — made it a template for the visions-and-illusions plot from late antiquity onward. Its tomb-board game at 52 points is among the earliest known uses of a board game as a contest with Death, a cousin of the games the dead play for their souls in other traditions.

functions: Warning tale of restricted knowledge: the Book of Thoth may be read by no living man without the price of a royal family's blood
Cult of the scholar prince: Setna Khaemwaset historicized as both Egypt's great antiquarian and its chastened tomb robber
Ghost-justice ritual: restitution performed with forked stick and fire-pan, and the reunification of a scattered dead family in one tomb
Dream-punishment narrative: the Tabubua episode as an enacted illusion that restores the wrong-doer to terror and humility

variants.name: The Sealed Letter (Setna cycle, second tale)
variants.text_tradition: Demotic Setna II (Cairo papyrus), Ptolemaic period
variants.summary: A later Setna tale in which the ghost-son Se-Osiris travels to Amentet and reads the sealed letter of another age — the descent-to-the-underworld register of the same hero; planned as a pending record.

variants.name: The Shipwrecked Sailor's isle and the speech of creatures
variants.summary: The Book of Thoth's promise of the languages of birds and fish echoes the older tale in which the serpent-prince speaks and the sailor's correct speech saves him — knowledge and speech as salvific power across Egyptian literature.

variants.name: Naneferkaptah as historical reading
variants.text_tradition: Egyptological literature on the setem-priest Naneferkaptah
variants.summary: Egyptologists read the tale as demotic fiction attached to an earlier historical figure; the Koptos episode uses a real temple of Isis and real geography (Petrie's remarks, 1895).

title.en: Juan Manalaksan: The Wood-Cutter and the Glass of Giants
title.zh: 胡安·馬納拉克桑：樵夫與巨人玻璃

region.en: Arayat, Pampanga, Luzon, Philippines (narrator's home town)
region.zh: 菲律賓呂宋邦板牙省阿拉亞特（敘述者故鄉）

period: Pampangan oral tale; collected by D. S. Fansler, published 1921

source.work: Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 10a 'Juan Manalaksan', eBook #8299

summary.en: The wood-cutter Juan saves the choking datu's son Pedro, and on an old woman's advice asks not for gold but for the glass Pedro keeps in his right armpit: a stick pushed through its hole summons giants who grant any wish. The charm cures a sick datu and wins Juan his daughter, but Pedro's soldiers steal wife and glass. Advised by an old mankukulam, Juan captures the king of the cats; thrown into a rat-cell, he looses the cat, and the rats buy their lives by bringing back every glass in the village — including his own, with which he orders the giants to kill Pedro and his father and bring his wife home.
summary.zh: 樵夫胡安救了噎住的達圖之子佩德羅；依老嫗之囑，他不索金銀，只要佩德羅右腋下的玻璃——穿孔小棍一捅，巨人現身有求必應。他以此符治癒達圖、娶得其女；佩德羅遣兵掠走其妻與玻璃。老巫婆指點他擒獲貓王；被囚鼠牢時他放出貓，鼠輩為保命搬來村中所有玻璃——胡安重得神符，命巨人誅佩德羅父子，迎回妻子。

sensitivity.note: Pampangan folktale recorded by Fansler from an Arayat narrator; archival record. Magic Ring/Aladdin cycle variant; the charm is a piece of glass rather than a ring, which Fansler reads as a sign of primitiveness.

passages.text: In a certain village lived a brave datu whose only son Pedro amused himself hunting deer and wild boars; nearby lived the poor wood-cutter Juan Manalaksan. Hunting on the mountain, Pedro choked on a piece of meat at their noon meal, and his father cried out loudly not knowing what to do for his dying son. Juan, cutting wood near by, ran quickly and pulled the piece of meat out of Pedro's throat, saving his life; grateful, Pedro promised a reward. On the way to the palace Juan met an old woman who warned him not to accept money or wealth, but to ask for the glass Pedro kept in his right armpit — as large as a peso, with a small hole in the centre: push a small stick through the hole, and giants who could give anything would surround him.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 10 'Juan Manalaksan'; not verbatim.

passages.text: Juan asked for nothing but the glass, hurried home to his starving mother, punched a small stick through the hole, and found himself surrounded by giants who fetched food at his command — though his mother ate so much that she became sick and died. In a neighboring village a datu fell ill, and proclaimed that the man who could cure him should have his daughter for a wife; the giants gave Juan medicine, the datu swallowed it and at once became well, and the next morning Juan was married and took his wife to live in his small hut in the woods.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 10 'Juan Manalaksan'; not verbatim.

passages.text: One day while Juan was away cutting trees, Pedro ordered soldiers to steal the wood-cutter's wife and magic glass. Going to his father-in-law for help, Juan met an old mankukulam, who told him to catch the king of the cats at a certain tree and always keep it with him. Soon after, Pedro's father commanded his soldiers to cut off the ears of all the men in the village, placing any who refused in a room full of rats; Juan refused, was seized and shut up — but he had his cat with him all the time, and as soon as the door closed he turned it loose. The rats, seeing they would all be killed, begged to serve him: 'Bring me all the glasses in this village,' said Juan, and one rat soon returned carrying the magical glass. Pushing the stick through its hole, Juan ordered the giants to kill Pedro and his father, and bring him his wife again. Thus Juan got his wife back, and they lived happily together till they died.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 10 'Juan Manalaksan'; not verbatim.

title.en: Juan the Poor, Who Became Juan the King
title.zh: 窮胡安稱王

region.en: Batangas, Luzon, Philippines (narrator's home province)
region.zh: 菲律賓呂宋八打雁省（敘述者故鄉）

period: Tagalog oral tale; collected by D. S. Fansler, published 1921

source.work: Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 10b 'Juan the Poor, who became Juan the King', eBook #8299

summary.en: Lazy Juan spares the monster in the tree he cuts, taking from its tongue a white oval stone that grants every wish; the stone builds a castle in the bay in one night and wins him the princess Maria.
