A defeated general hires a witch, who in the guise of Maria's old nurse steals the stone from under the sleeping princess's pillow. A huge bird strips Juan to his wood-cutter's clothes; crossing three mountains he is three times knocked down by the same cat, which he finally bags — and in the general's rat-cell the cat spares the rat-king on condition it fetch back the stolen stone. The stone destroys the castle, kills the general, frees Maria and the king, and Juan rules wisely after his father-in-law's death.
summary.zh: 懶漢胡安饒過樹中之怪，從其舌上取白色橢圓寶石，有求必應；一夜間在海灣建成城堡，娶得公主瑪利亞。敗將僱巫婆假扮乳母偷走枕下寶石；巨鳥剝去胡安華服。他三度遭同一隻貓撲倒，第三度將其裝袋；在敵國鼠牢中，貓以鼠王性命要脅取回寶石。寶石毀城堡、誅敵將、救出妻與岳王；岳王死後胡安登基，治國有道。

sensitivity.note: Tagalog folktale recorded by Fansler from a Clemente narrator; archival record. Magic Ring cycle variant with a wishing-stone.

passages.text: In a small hut at the edge of a forest lived a father and son so poor that the son was named Juan the Poor. Ordered to fetch firewood, the lazy boy marked every good tree, began cutting one with a hole in its trunk — and a monster came out of the hole as soon as the tree fell. Juan raised his axe: 'Good sir, forbear, And my life spare, If you wish a happy life And, besides, a pretty wife,' chanted the monster, and told him to take from the middle of its tongue a white oval stone from which he could ask for and get whatever he wanted. Juan tested the charm by summoning men who cut down trees and carried the wood to his house, then hurried home and lay down again behind the fireplace.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 10 'Juan the Poor'; not verbatim.

passages.text: Remembering the pretty wife, Juan went to the king's palace to ask for his daughter's hand; the king, scorning the rustic suitor, demanded a castle built in the middle of the bay within three days, on pain of losing his head. Two days Juan did nothing; at midnight of the third he bade his stone build a fort in the middle of the bay, and the next morning, dressed like a prince, presented it as the king bathed to the sound of cannon-shots. He married the princess Maria. When war broke out he led his father-in-law's army and conquered the mighty enemy with the stone's help — and the defeated general, never beaten before, offered half his property to anyone who could get Juan's power for him.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 10 'Juan the Poor'; not verbatim.

passages.text: A witch who knew Juan's secret flew to the general, then to Juan's house one hot afternoon, smiling at Maria: 'Do you not recognize me, pretty Maria? I am the one who nursed you when you were a baby.' The princess believed her, treated her kindly, and lay down to a siesta; fanning her to sleep, the witch took from under the pillow the magical stone Juan had forgotten to take hunting, and rewarded herself with half the general's riches. As Juan enjoyed his hunt, a huge bird swooped down and seized his horse and clothes, his inner garments changing back into his old wood-cutter's clothes — an ill omen that sent him hastening home on foot to find house and palace deserted.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 10 'Juan the Poor'; not verbatim.

passages.text: Concluding that the general had his stone, Juan crossed three mountains toward the general's country — and each time a cat came running after him and knocked him down. He dashed out its life against a rock twice, but the same cat tumbled him a third time; filled with curiosity, he caught it and put it in his bag. At the castle he begged a mouthful of rice; recognized, he was thrown into the cell of rats. Remembering his cat, he let it loose, and it killed all the rats except their king. 'Now you shall die if you do not promise to get for Juan his magical stone, which your master has stolen,' said the cat — and the rat-king ran quickly to the general's room and took the stone from the table. Juan then said to his stone, 'Pretty stone, destroy this house with the general and his subjects, and release my father-in-law and wife from their prison.' The earth trembled, the castle was destroyed, the general and his subjects dead, and his wife and father-in-law free. After the death of the king, Juan ascended to the throne and ruled wisely, living long happily with his lovely wife.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 10 'Juan the Poor'; not verbatim.

title.en: Lucas the Strong: The Golden Carriage and the Four Companions
title.zh: 力士盧卡斯：金車與四同伴

region.en: Laguna lake region, Luzon, Philippines (Tagalog narrator's home)
region.zh: 菲律賓呂宋拉古納湖區（他加祿敘述者故鄉）

period: Tagalog oral tale; collected by D. S. Fansler, published 1921

source.work: Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 11a 'Lucas the Strong', eBook #8299

summary.en: Lazy Lucas bites off the end of a boa-constrictor's tail — the reptile's seat of strength — and becomes the strongest man in his barrio. When the king promises the princess to whoever gives him a golden carriage, his hardworking brothers fail and spurn a begging leper, but Lucas shares his meat with her and receives carriage, clothes, and shoes from her promise. On the road he wrestles four prodigies into his service: Runner, Sharpshooter, Farsight, and Blower. Set against the king's giant messenger for a bottle of the water of youth, Runner is drugged with a gold ring in his bottle, but Farsight spies, Blower blows the giant to the eighth mountain, and Sharpshooter shoots the bottle's head to wake Runner — Lucas marries the princess.
summary.zh: 懶漢盧卡斯咬下蟒蛇尾尖——蛇之力源——成為村中最強者。國王懸賞金車以聘公主；兩位勤勞兄長掘金失敗且拒施捨癩婦，盧卡斯分肉與之，遂得金車、衣履。途中他以摔跤收服四人：飛毛腿、神射手、千里眼、大風。國王令巨人與之競取『不老泉』；巨人以金戒使飛毛腿昏睡，千里眼偵察，大風將巨人吹回第八座山，神射手射穿瓶頭喚醒飛毛腿——盧卡斯終娶公主。

sensitivity.note: Tagalog folktale recorded by Fansler from a Macasaet narrator; archival record. Skilful-Companions cycle; the boa's tail-tip as seat of strength is a local belief.

passages.text: A man had three sons — Juan, Pedro, and Lucas — his wife dying young; Juan and Pedro were hard workers, but Lucas was lazy, rambling about the forests and river-banks looking for guavas and birds' nests. One day in the woods Lucas saw a boa-constrictor and knew that this reptile carried the centre of its strength in the horny appendage at the end of its tail; wishing to become strong, for the men of strength in his barrio were the most influential, he approached the snake like a cat, bit off the end of its tail with his sharp teeth, and ran away with all his might. The boa followed but could not overtake him, for it had lost its strength, and Lucas soon became the strongest man in his barrio, defeating the man who used to be the Hercules of the place.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 11 'Lucas the Strong'; not verbatim.

passages.text: The king proclaimed that whoever gave him a carriage made of gold should have the princess for his wife. Juan dug for gold on a mountain and refused his lunch to an old leper with her child — 'Go away! You are very dirty' — and after three weeks gave up; Pedro fared no better and was also unkind to the old leper. When the woman begged of Lucas, he gave her half his meat, and she promised him not only the golden carriage but a pair of shoes, a coat, and trousers. Nine days she did not come, and Lucas repented his kindness — until she appeared, told him what he had been thinking, and vanished; the next day he saw the golden carriage drawn by a pair of fine fat horses, with the clothes inside, and she showed him how to wear them.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 11 'Lucas the Strong'; not verbatim.

passages.text: Driving toward the palace, Lucas met and wrestled into his service four prodigies: Runner, son of the good runner; Sharpshooter, son of the famous shooter; Farsight, son of the great Sharp-Eyes; and Blower, son of the great blower. At the palace the king set a final challenge: fetch a bottle of the water that gives youth and health from the foot of the seventh mountain, faster than his messenger — a giant — or lose his head. Runner ran with all his might and caught up with the giant, but the giant secretly put a gold ring in Runner's bottle to make him sleep. Farsight saw Runner sleeping and the giant very near the city; Blower blew the giant back to the eighth mountain; Sharpshooter shot the head of the bottle so that Runner woke up, ran and got the precious water, and arrived in the city in twelve hours. Lucas presented the water to the king, and the monarch was obliged to accept the young man as his son-in-law — though the third day after the nuptials the giant reached the palace claiming a heavy wind had blown him back to the eighth mountain.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 11 'Lucas the Strong'; not verbatim.

title.en: Juan and His Six Companions: The Golden Egg of King Jaime
title.zh: 胡安與六同伴：海梅王的金蛋

region.en: Balayan, Batangas, Luzon, Philippines (origin of the narrator's tale)
region.zh: 菲律賓呂宋八打雁省巴蘭彥（故事原鄉）

period: Tagalog oral tale; collected by D. S. Fansler, published 1921

source.work: Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 11b 'Juan and His Six Companions', eBook #8299

summary.en: King Jaime promises his daughter to whoever wins the golden egg from the moss-grown oak on the Mountain of the Golden Egg; fleets of suitors perish. Pedro and Fernando both spurn a begging old man and are killed when their axe-blows on the oak rebound; the pious Juan bathes, dresses, and feeds the old man, who rewards him — the egg, then a golden ship — and six prodigies join him on the voyage: Corrin Corron the runner, Mirin Miron the far-seer, Puntin Punton the sure-shot, Carguin Cargon the mountain-carrier, Soplin Soplon the blower, Oirin Oiron the hear-all. When the thrice-perfidious king still refuses, Carguin Cargon overturns the kingdom, Oirin Oiron overhears the surrender, and Soplin Soplon scatters the pursuing army like chaff; Juan marries Maria and is crowned the same day.
summary.zh: 海梅王允諾：取回苔橡樹上金蛋者可娶公主。艦隊盡沒；佩德羅與費爾南多皆拒施老丐，揮斧時木片反彈斃命。虔誠的胡安為老人沐浴、更衣、進食，得金蛋與金船；六位奇人登船同行——飛毛腿、千里眼、神射手、負山人、吹風者、順風耳。背信三次的國王仍不允婚，負山人傾覆其國，順風耳竊聽降語，吹風者將追兵吹散如草屑；胡安與瑪利亞成婚，當日加冕。

sensitivity.note: Tagalog folktale recorded by Fansler from a Hilario narrator (hearing it from an old woman of Balayan); archival record. Skilful-Companions cycle in grand style.

passages.text: Not very long after the death of our Saviour on Calvary, a powerful king named Jaime ruled a far-away land, devoted to establishing a strong government of moderation and justice; his daughter Maria was a pearl of the kingdom, and neither Venus nor Helen of Troy could compare with her in beauty. After consulting with his advisers, the monarch proclaimed: 'He who shall succeed in getting the golden egg from the moss-grown oak in yonder mountain shall be my son-in-law and heir.' For five days and five nights crowds of lovers, adventurers, and ruffians set sail for the Mountain of the Golden Egg, but none ever reached the place — some shipwrecked, some driven to strange lands, the rest forced back by horrible sights of broken planks and mangled bodies. Three orphan brothers then rose from obscurity: Pedro, Fernando, and Juan, agreeing that Pedro should try first.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 11 'Juan and His Six Companions'; not verbatim.

passages.text: On the mountain an old gray-headed man in tattered clothes came limping toward Pedro asking for help, but the selfish Pedro pushed him away with disrespect; when his axe struck the oak, a large piece of wood broke off and hit him in the right temple, killing him instantly. Fernando suffered the same fate as his haughty brother. Juan alone remained: after invoking God's help he set sail, met the same old man, and bathed, dressed, and fed him. 'You shall be amply requited,' said the old man, disappearing; with one stroke of his axe Juan broke the oak in two, and in a circular hole lined with down he found the golden egg. But the shrewd king did not want a rustic son-in-law: 'You shall not marry my daughter unless you bring me a golden ship.' The old man appeared again on the mountain and directed Juan to a splendidly equipped ship that moved smoothly over stumps and stones.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 11 'Juan and His Six Companions'; not verbatim.

passages.text: As the golden ship traveled along, Juan gathered six prodigies: Corrin Corron, son of the great runner, who was taking his daily exercise by running around the mountain in less than a minute; Mirin Miron, son of the great Farsight, watching a game seven miles away; Puntin Punton, son of the great Sureshot, about to kill a bat-fly annoying a sheep three miles off; Carguin Cargon, son of the great Strong-Back, carrying a mountain on his shoulders to build a dam — when he cast it down, the whole kingdom was shaken so violently that the inhabitants thought all the volcanoes had burst into eruption; Soplin Soplon, son of the great Blast-Blower, exercising his lungs by blowing down long lines of trees like grain before a hurricane; and Oirin Oiron, son of the great Hear-All, lying with his ear to the ground listening to lovers' ditties twelve miles away.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 11 'Juan and His Six Companions'; not verbatim.

passages.text: At the palace gate Juan asked for the princess's hand, but the king said, 'Never!' When the ship was beyond the frontier, Juan ordered Carguin Cargon to overturn the king's realm; many houses were destroyed and hundreds crushed. Oirin Oiron heard the king seven miles off promise his daughter if Juan restored the kingdom; the kingdom was rebuilt, but the king again refused, and again the realm was overturned. At last Oirin Oiron heard the tramp of horses and the clash of spears: King Jaime's vast host in hot pursuit, nine miles away. 'Let the army approach,' said Soplin Soplon, and when it was within eight hundred yards he blew forcible blasts that scattered the soldiers and horses in all directions like chaff before a wind; only a handful survived, crippled for life. Again the king sued for peace, and this time kept his word: Juan and Maria were married amidst the most imposing ceremonies, and that very day King Jaime abdicated in favor of his more powerful son-in-law. On the site of the destroyed houses were built larger and more handsome ones — the lumber felled by Soplin Soplon's blasts and carried by Carguin Cargon — and the royal couple and the six gifted men led a glorious life, conquering new lands and ruling their kingdom well.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 11 'Juan and His Six Companions'; not verbatim.

title.en: The Miraculous Cow
title.zh: 神異之牛

region.en: Manila, Luzon, Philippines (narrator's home city)
region.zh: 菲律賓呂宋馬尼拉（敘述者居地）

period: Tagalog oral droll; collected by D. S. Fansler, published 1921

source.work: Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 15 'The Miraculous Cow', eBook #8299

summary.en: Two boys steal a farmer's cow tied behind his carreton, and the cunning Ambrosio ties himself in the animal's place. When the farmer looks back and shouts, Ambrosio explains that his angry mother once transformed him into a cow, and now, restored, he begs his freedom; the kind-hearted wife of the farmer releases 'by the great mercy of God' the rascal, who rejoins his friend to laugh over the two simple folks.
summary.zh: 二少年偷牽農夫拴在車後的母牛；狡黠的安布羅西奧以自己代替牲口拴在原處。農夫回頭見是個男孩大驚；安布羅西奧哭訴『昔日母親盛怒將我變為牛，今日還形』，農婦心生憐憫，以『上帝大恩』放他自由——頑童與同伴相視大笑。

sensitivity.note: Tagalog droll recorded by Fansler from a Manila narrator; archival record. Fansler traces the tale to the Arabian Nights 'Simpleton and the Sharper' and Spanish variants; transformation-by-parental-curse is widespread in serious Philippine etiological myths.

passages.text: There was once a farmer driving home from his farm in his carreton, his cow tied to the back of the cart as he was accustomed to do every evening. Two boys, Felipe and Ambrosio, saw him, and Felipe whispered, 'Do you see the cow tied to the back of that carreton? Well, if you will untie it, I will take it to our house.' Ambrosio approached slowly, untied the cow, handed the rope to Felipe, and tied himself in the place of the animal.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 15 'The Miraculous Cow'; not verbatim.

passages.text: When the farmer happened to look back he was frightened to find a boy instead of his cow tied to the carreton, and shouted furiously, 'Rascal, give me my cow!' 'Oh, don't be angry with me!' said Ambrosio. 'Once, when I was a small boy, my mother became very angry with me. She cursed me, and suddenly I was transformed into a cow; and now I am changed back into my own shape. It is not my fault that you bought me: I could not tell you not to do so, for I could not speak at the time. Now, generous farmer, please give me my freedom! for I am very anxious to see my old home again.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 15 'The Miraculous Cow'; not verbatim.

passages.text: The farmer did not know what to do, for he was very sorry to lose his cow; but at home his kind-hearted wife said, 'Husband, what can we do? We ought to set him free. It is by the great mercy of God that he has been restored to his former self.' So the wily boy got off, rejoined his friend, and they had a good laugh over the two simple folks.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 15 'The Miraculous Cow'; not verbatim.

title.en: The Clever Husband and Wife: Two Funerals for One Couple
title.zh: 機智夫妻：一對夫妻兩場喪事

region.en: Pagsanjan, La Laguna, Luzon, Philippines (narrator's home town)
region.zh: 菲律賓呂宋內湖省帕桑漢（敘述者故鄉）

period: Tagalog oral droll; collected by D. S. Fansler, published 1921

source.work: Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 16 'The Clever Husband and Wife', eBook #8299

summary.en: Married off with a dowry by his kindly master the doctor, Pedro and his wife Marta squander everything. Pedro reports his own wife dead (onion-juice in his eyes) and receives burial money; Marta reports Pedro dead to the doctor's sister and receives masses money. When doctor and sister compare notes and send servants, the couple take turns lying 'dead' in bed; examined in person, they are found both feigning death — and the delighted benefactor takes them home, laughing at the joke.
summary.zh: 醫師成全僕人婚事並予二百金；夫妻揮霍殆盡後，佩德羅以洋蔥汁拭淚謊報『亡妻』領喪葬費；瑪爾塔又向醫師之妹謊報『亡夫』領彌撒錢。兄妹比對消息互遣僕探，夫妻輪流僵臥裝死；兄妹親至，發現二人在裝死——卻為玩笑與舊僕無恙而大喜，帶他們回家同住。

sensitivity.note: Tagalog droll recorded by Fansler from a Cordero narrator; archival record. Fansler derives it from the Abu-l-Hasan story of the 1001 Nights (The Sleeper Awakened).

passages.text: Pedro had been living as a servant in a doctor's house for more than nine years and wanted very much to have a wife, but had no business of any kind to support one. His master, noticing his dejection, married him to the woman he loved, let the couple live in a cottage near the hacienda, and gave them two hundred pieces of gold. In time the money was spent, and a second gift of twenty pieces vanished as quickly.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 16 'The Clever Husband and Wife'; not verbatim.

passages.text: Early one day Pedro went to the doctor's house weeping — he had rubbed onion-juice on his eyes — saying that his wife had died and he had nothing for her burial. The doctor pitied him: 'Take this money and see that she gets a decent burial.' A month later Marta went to the doctor's married sister with the same story of her husband's death, and was given money for masses for his soul. That evening the doctor visiting his sick nephew was told that Marta's husband had died — 'No,' answered the doctor, 'it was Marta who died' — and they argued until they decided to send a servant to see which one was dead.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 16 'The Clever Husband and Wife'; not verbatim.

passages.text: When Pedro saw the servant coming he told his wife to lie flat and stiff in the bed as if she were dead; the servant reported that it was Marta. The sister would not believe him, so another servant was sent — this time Marta made Pedro lie down stiff and flat, and he was reported dead. Neither knew what to believe, so the next morning the doctor and his sister together visited the cottage and found the couple both lying as if dead. After examining them, however, the doctor realized that they were merely feigning death; he was so pleased by the joke, and so glad to find his old servants alive, that he took them home with him and made them stay at his house.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 16 'The Clever Husband and Wife'; not verbatim.

title.en: The Seven Spider Demons of Coiled-Silk Cave
title.zh: 盤絲洞蜘蛛精

region.en: Coiled-Silk Cave and Yellow-Flower Abbey (pin: mythic westward route)
region.zh: 盤絲洞、黃花觀

period: Journey to the West, 16th c. (attrib. Wu Cheng'en, chs. 72-73)

source.work: Journey to the West, chs. 72-73: the spider-sisters of the bath-pool, the silk-entrapment, and the centipede-poison of the Many-Eyeds

license: Public domain (Ming novel; passages are compiler's renderings)

summary.en: Seven spider-sisters bathed in the Scouring Pool and hung silk like ten-thousand-li nets over the mountain; the monkey, watching the monk go to alms, saw the webs take him and could not cut through the silk with any weapon. The centipede demon of Yellow-Flower Abbey — the Many-Eyeds, whose thousand eyes shot golden light — poisoned the pilgrims' tea, and only the embroidered-gold needle of the Bodhisattva Bilanpo could break the demon's glare and set the bathers free.
summary.zh: 盤絲洞七蜘蛛精濯垢泉洗澡，絲繩網山；黃花觀百眼魔君（蜈蚣精）毒茶害四眾；毗藍婆菩薩以繡花針破金光，收蜈蚣精歸紫雲山——遂解之。

sensitivity.note: Passages are the compiler's condensed paraphrases of the novel.

passages.text: The Tang monk went to beg his own meal and walked into the bath-pool of seven spider-sisters, who took him prisoner and spun their silk over the mountain like a net of ten thousand li. Wukong's staff, cudgels and even the sea-pillar could not cut the silk ropes; the pig was rolled into the pool; the brothers freed themselves by trickery, and burned out the demons' web-nests with a furnace-rat fire.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Journey to the West, ch. 72 (compiler's rendering); not verbatim.

passages.text: The sisters fled to Yellow-Flower Abbey and its master, the Many-Eyeds — a centipede in human shape, whose thousand eyes, when opened, shot golden rays of light that no sword or staff could touch. He brewed the pilgrims' tea with his own poison, and three of the four lay stiff as wood on the abbey floor.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Journey to the West, ch. 73, the poison; not verbatim.

passages.text: Wukong sought help from Bilanpo, the Bodhisattva of the Purple Cloud Mountain, whose son was the Rooster Star Officer himself. She came with a needle of embroidered gold, flew it into the demon's light-rays, and the golden glare burst like a shattered mirror: the centipede, blinded, shrank to his true form and was carried off into the Bodhisattva's keeping — and the pilgrims' poison was cured with her dew.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Journey to the West, ch. 73, the needle and the cure; not verbatim.

title.en: Lion-Camel Ridge: The Three Great Demons of the Eight Hundred Li
title.zh: 獅駝嶺三魔

region.en: Lion-Camel Ridge and Lion-Camel Kingdom, eight hundred li of bones (pin: mythic westward route)
region.zh: 獅駝嶺、獅駝國

period: Journey to the West, 16th c. (attrib. Wu Cheng'en, chs. 74-77)

source.work: Journey to the West, chs. 74-77: the green lion, the white elephant, the golden-winged roc, and the swallower of armies

license: Public domain (Ming novel; passages are compiler's renderings)

summary.en: Eight hundred li of ridge, forty-eight thousand demon soldiers, and a kingdom where every living person had been eaten — the three great demons of Lion-Camel Ridge were the gravest foes of the whole journey: a green lion who swallowed the monkey whole, a white elephant who crushed him with his trunk, and a golden-winged roc who could cover ninety thousand li in one flap and snatch even the monkey out of the sky. The roc alone was senior to the Buddha himself — the Buddha's uncle by hatchling — and only the Buddha's own palm, descending over the sky, could bring him to yield.
summary.zh: 獅駝嶺青獅、白象、大鵬三魔，四萬八千小妖，獅駝國人食盡；青獅吞悟空入腹，白象卷之，大鵬一翅九萬里——如來親至，言大鵬乃其母舅（孔雀大明王所生），如來親至，文殊普賢收坐騎，大鵬困於佛掌而歸依。

sensitivity.note: Passages are the compiler's condensed paraphrases of the novel.

passages.text: The demon-baron of Lion-Camel Ridge told Wukong, by way of warning, the census of the mountain: forty-eight thousand named soldiers, eight hundred li of ridge, and a Lion-Camel Kingdom beyond where every living soul had been eaten five hundred years before — so that the city the pilgrims saw from afar was a city of nothing but bones. Three brothers ruled the mountain: a green lion, a white elephant and a golden-winged roc.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Journey to the West, ch. 74 (compiler's rendering); not verbatim.

passages.text: The green lion opened his jaws a thousand fathoms wide and swallowed the Monkey King whole — inside his belly the monkey set up a gymnastics of terror, kicked the demon's liver and made the lion beg for mercy from within. The white elephant wound his trunk around the monkey's waist; the roc, in one stroke of his wings, covered the sky and snatched the Tang monk out of the air — and for a while the pilgrimage stood at the brink of ruin, three demons holding its heart.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Journey to the West, chs. 75-76; not verbatim.

passages.text: At last the Buddha himself came, with Manjusri and Samantabhadra to collect their own steeds — for the lion and the elephant were the two Bodhisattvas' mounts escaped to earth. The roc could not be caught: he was senior to the Buddha in hatchling, born of the same egg-tree as the peacock. The Buddha spread his palm over the whole sky, and the roc, unable to fly beyond it, yielded — and was seated at the Buddha's head, above all the hosts of the western heaven.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Journey to the West, ch. 77, the Buddha's palm; not verbatim.

title.en: The Bhikkhu Kingdom and the Deer-Skinned Immortal
title.zh: 比丘國白鹿精

region.en: Bhikkhu (Monk) Kingdom (pin: mythic westward route)
region.zh: 比丘國

period: Journey to the West, 16th c. (attrib. Wu Cheng'en, chs. 78-79)

source.work: Journey to the West, chs. 78-79: the elixir of boy-hearts, the white deer and the fox-queen, Longevity Star's retrieval

license: Public domain (Ming novel; passages are compiler's renderings)

summary.en: The king of Bhikkhu had sickened, and his Taoist physician prescribed the elixir of a thousand and eleven boy-hearts: every household's child was named and caged. The physician was a white deer escaped from the Longevity Star's mountain, and the queen his daughter a white fox. Wukong exposed the cage-city, saved the boys, unmasked the deer, and the Star of Longevity himself came down to collar his pet and prescribe the king a different diet.
summary.zh: 比丘國王欲取一千一百一十一個小兒心肝做藥引；國丈乃南極壽星之白鹿，美后為白面狐狸；悟空救眾小兒，破白鹿本相，壽星收回坐騎。

sensitivity.note: Passages are the compiler's condensed paraphrases of the novel.

passages.text: In Bhikkhu Kingdom the king, sick of long years, had been given a prescription by his immortal physician: the elixir of a thousand and eleven boy-hearts, to be drawn from children gathered into cages at the palace gate. Every household wept; the monkey, with his fiery eyes, saw through the city's grief to the palace's secret.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Journey to the West, ch. 78 (compiler's rendering); not verbatim.

passages.text: The physician demanded also the Tang monk's heart as the finishing ingredient. Wukong transformed himself into his master, opened his own chest, and offered a rack of hearts — loyalty, mercy, cunning, every heart but the black one the demon demanded. The demon drew back; the monkey unmasked him in the court: a white deer of the Longevity Star's own mountain, the beautiful queen beside him a white fox.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Journey to the West, ch. 79, the heart-contest; not verbatim.

passages.text: The Star of Longevity came down the sky on a crane to collar his escaped deer, called it a pet turned scourge, and prescribed the king instead the plain diet of rice gruel and vegetables. The boys of Bhikkhu went home to their families, the kingdom renounced the deer's regimen, and the pilgrims passed on toward the holy city.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Journey to the West, ch. 79, the Star's retrieval; not verbatim.

title.en: The Bottomless Cave and the Golden-Nosed White Rat
title.zh: 無底洞金鼻白毛老鼠精

region.en: Bottomless Cave, Black Rooster ridge westward (pin: mythic westward route)
region.zh: 陷空山無底洞

period: Journey to the West, 16th c. (attrib. Wu Cheng'en, chs. 80-83)

source.work: Journey to the West, chs. 80-83: the demoness's bridal snare, the shrine of Li Jing, and the sky-lord's arrest

license: Public domain (Ming novel; passages are compiler's renderings)

summary.en: A demoness with a golden nose and white fur, once a rat of the Vulture Peak who ate the Buddha's candle-oil, had taken the Tang monk for her bridal cave and set up a shrine to the Pagoda-Bearing Heavenly King Li Jing as her adoptive father. Wukong fought through her endless cave with three mouths and no floor, found the shrine, flew to heaven with the tablets, and Li Jing and Nezha came down themselves to arrest their own 'daughter' and take her back to the court of the Jade Emperor.
summary.zh: 金鼻白毛老鼠精，曾在靈山偷食如來香花寶燭，認托塔李天王為父；無底洞攝三藏成親；悟空上天告狀，李天王父子拿妖歸案。

sensitivity.note: Passages are the compiler's condensed paraphrases of the novel.

passages.text: The demoness of the Bottomless Cave, a rat-spirit of the Vulture Peak who had once eaten the lamp-oil of the Buddha's hall, spun a bridal snare: a woman bound to a tree begging rescue, an offered meal, and a whirlwind to carry the monk down the cave's endless dark to be her husband.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Journey to the West, ch. 80-81 (compiler's rendering); not verbatim.

passages.text: The cave had no floor — three mouths, a thousand turns, wine flowing in channels, and a spring to drown pursuers. Wukong went down as a fly and a cricket, found at last a shrine with tablets to the Pagoda-Bearing Heavenly King and Prince Nezha, and carried the tablets up to the Jade Emperor: the demoness had sworn kinship with heaven's own constable.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Journey to the West, ch. 81-83, the shrine of Li Jing; not verbatim.

passages.text: Li Jing, furious to be named father by a rat, came down with Nezha and his pagoda, seized his 'daughter' with the tower's own chains, and hauled her back to heaven for sentencing. The monk was freed from the bridal cave, and the Bottomless Cave had at last a bottom: the rod of the third prince, driven through its dark.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Journey to the West, ch. 83, the arrest; not verbatim.

title.en: Thorn-Ridge: The Tree-Spirits' Night of Poetry
title.zh: 荊棘嶺木仙夜談

region.en: Thorn-Ridge, eight hundred li of thorns (pin: mythic westward route)
region.zh: 荊棘嶺

period: Journey to the West, 16th c. (attrib. Wu Cheng'en, ch. 64)

source.work: Journey to the West, ch. 64: the tree-spirits' literary party in the Stone House, and the abduction of the Tang monk for a poetry contest

license: Public domain (Ming novel; passages are compiler's renderings)

summary.en: Eight hundred li of thorn-thickets blocked the road, and in their heart stood a stone house where the tree-spirits of the ridge — an old cypress, an old juniper, a bamboo, a plum and a maple — kept a literary salon. They abducted the Tang monk in a wind of petals for a night of linked verses, and the plum-spirit, appearing as a beautiful woman, pressed him with love-poems; the monk, flustered but constant, recited only of the Way — until the monkey arrived and cut down the poets: the cypress, the juniper, the maple and the plum roots of the ridge.
summary.zh: 荊棘嶺木仙庵：十八公（柏）、拂雲叟（竹）、赤身鬼（楓）、杏仙（杏）等樹精攝三藏吟詩談禪；杏仙欲薦枕席；悟空尋至，八戒築倒眾樹根。

sensitivity.note: Passages are the compiler's condensed paraphrases of the novel. A rare quiet episode: the novel's meditation on poetry, temptation and rootedness.

passages.text: Thorn-Ridge lay eight hundred li deep in thorns, and the pilgrims hacked their way through on a stone track left by an old road. In the heart of the thorns the Tang monk was stolen away in a wind of flower-petals, and set down before a stone house lit with lanterns, where four venerable tree-spirits awaited him: an ancient cypress, an ancient juniper, a red maple and a fair plum-spirit in woman's form.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Journey to the West, ch. 64 (compiler's rendering); not verbatim.

passages.text: They asked for linked verses, and the monk, finding their learning deep, chanted of the Chan mind and the moon; the plum-spirit, gathering her breath, sang of love under the blossom and hinted at the bridal couch — the one temptation of the road that came dressed as poetry. The monk refused her with a face like iron, and the party of trees, amused, did not insist.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Journey to the West, ch. 64, the plum-spirit's poems; not verbatim.

passages.text: Then the Monkey King and the pig came crashing through the thorns, and the spirits scattered into their true forms. Bajie, maddened by the wasted night, swung his rake and uprooted the cypress, the juniper, the maple and the plum — and blood and sap ran from the roots, and the thorn-thickets of the ridge opened a road that has stayed open ever since.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Journey to the West, ch. 64, the felling; not verbatim.

title.en: The Jade-Hua Princes and the Nine-Headed Lion
title.zh: 玉華州收徒與九靈元聖

region.en: Jade-Hua Princely Court (pin: mythic westward route)
region.zh: 玉華州

period: Journey to the West, 16th c. (attrib. Wu Cheng'en, chs. 88-90)

source.work: Journey to the West, chs. 88-90: three princes apprenticed, the stolen weapons, and the nine-headed lion of the Taiyi Jiuku sect

license: Public domain (Ming novel; passages are compiler's renderings)

summary.en: The three princes of Jade-Hua begged to learn the staff, the rake and the staff-of-sand; Wukong taught them, and had copies of the three weapons forged — which the furnace-light drew up a lion-demon from the Bamboo-Mountain, who stole the weapons at night. The demon lord was a nine-headed lion, grandsire of all lion-spirits and uncle-slave of the Taiyi Rescuer; when he seized the monk, only the heavenly master Taiyi Jiuku Tianzun, summoned by Wukong's own shout, could whistle the beast home and collar it.
summary.zh: 玉華州三王子拜師學藝，仿造三般兵器；豹頭山黃獅精盜寶；其祖九靈元聖（九頭獅）攝三藏八戒；太乙救苦天尊收坐騎——獅祖歸位。

sensitivity.note: Passages are the compiler's condensed paraphrases of the novel.

passages.text: The three princes of Jade-Hua State saw the three weapons of the pilgrims and begged to be taught. Wukong taught the eldest the staff, Bajie the second the rake, and the sand-monk the third his priest's staff; and for practice the smiths of the court forged replicas of all three — the fire of whose forging shone up into the mountains like a beacon.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Journey to the West, ch. 88-89 (compiler's rendering); not verbatim.

passages.text: A yellow lion of the Leopard-Head Mountain saw the light and stole the three replicas by night for his own armory. The pilgrims crushed his cave and took the weapons back — but his grandfather, the Nine-Spirit Sovereign, a nine-headed lion of the Taiyi sect's stables, came with the whole lineage of lion-demons to seize the monk and the pig in vengeance.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Journey to the West, ch. 89-90, the theft and the vengeance; not verbatim.

passages.text: The nine-headed lion was the mount of the Heavenly Master Taiyi Jiuku Tianzun, the Rescuer of the Afflicted. Wukong flew to the Master's eastern paradise, shouted his complaint at the gate, and the Master descended, whistled the beast's name — and the nine heads bowed to the collar. The lion-lineage of the mountain went home to heaven, the princes were made masters of their weapons, and Jade-Hua built the pilgrims a temple to remember them by.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Journey to the West, ch. 90, the Master's whistle; not verbatim.

title.en: The Jade Rabbit of India and the Thrown Embroidered Ball
title.zh: 天竺國玉兔拋繡球

region.en: India (Tianzhu), Capital of the western heaven-road (pin: mythic India)
region.zh: 天竺國

period: Journey to the West, 16th c. (attrib. Wu Cheng'en, chs. 93-95)

source.work: Journey to the West, chs. 93-95: the false princess, the embroidered-ball betrothal, and Chang'e's hare brought home

license: Public domain (Ming novel; passages are compiler's renderings)

summary.en: On the last road to the Thunderclap Monastery, the king of India chose a son-in-law by thrown embroidered ball — and the ball landed on the Tang monk. The bride was not the princess but the Jade Rabbit of the moon-palace, escaped to earth to avenge a slight of Chang'e, holding the monk for her wedding night. Wukong fought her through the night sky to the edge of the moon-mountain, and Chang'e and the Star of the Taiyin came down to lead the runaway hare home by the ear.
summary.zh: 天竺國公主拋繡球招親擊中三藏；假公主乃月宮玉兔，為報一掌之仇私逃下界；悟空戰之，太陰星君與嫦娥收玉兔歸月——真公主乃出生時被妖調換。

sensitivity.note: Passages are the compiler's condensed paraphrases of the novel.

passages.text: The king of India cast an embroidered ball from his tower to choose his daughter's husband, and the ball, steered by more than wind, fell upon the Tang monk's cowl. The whole court prepared the wedding of the year — while the monkey's fiery eyes saw at once that the bride was no princess but a demoness of the moon.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Journey to the West, ch. 93-94 (compiler's rendering); not verbatim.

passages.text: The false princess was the Jade Rabbit, pounding-maid of Chang'e's palace, who had fled the moon eighteen years before to pay back a slight of the goddess's hand. She had exchanged the true princess for herself at birth and now demanded the monk for her wedding night; her pestle of jade was a weapon no staff could match.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Journey to the West, ch. 95, the rabbit's story; not verbatim.

passages.text: The monkey chased her into the sky, and at the moon-mountain the Star of the Great Yin and Chang'e herself came down in glory to claim the runaway hare and lead her home by the ear. The true princess was restored to the king of India, the wedding was given to the rightful heir, and the pilgrims, four days later, saw the first towers of the Thunderclap Monastery over the western ridge.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Journey to the West, ch. 95, the rabbit's retrieval; not verbatim.

title.en: The Attainment: Five Saints and the Scriptures Carried East
title.zh: 功成行滿

region.en: Thunderclap Monastery, Vulture Peak (pin: mythic India)
region.zh: 靈山雷音寺

period: Journey to the West, 16th c. (attrib. Wu Cheng'en, chs. 98-100)

source.work: Journey to the West, chs. 98-100: the river-crossing to the other shore, the true scriptures, and the investiture of the five

license: Public domain (Ming novel; passages are compiler's renderings)

summary.en: At the last river an empty bottomless boat ferried the pilgrims across, and from its floor the corpse of the Tang monk's own mortal body floated away downstream — he saw his own flesh dead and was glad. In the Thunderclap Monastery the Buddha's hosts delivered the true scriptures, and the five were invested: the Tang monk a Buddha of the sandalwood merit, the monkey a Buddha victorious in strife, Bajie the altar-cleanser (for his gluttony remained), the sand-monk a golden-bodied arhat, and the white horse back to dragonhood in the lake of the gate — the journey over, the books carried east, and the empire of Tang transcribed them forever.
summary.zh: 凌雲渡無底船渡三藏，脫去凡胎；雷音寺取得真經三十五部；功德圓滿：三藏為旃檀功德佛，悟空為鬥戰勝佛，八戒為淨壇使者，沙僧為金身羅漢，白馬化龍盤於擎天華表柱。

sensitivity.note: Passages are the compiler's condensed paraphrases of the novel.

passages.text: Beyond the last ridge a river lay without bridge or ford, and an old boat came — a boat without a bottom. The monk stepped in trembling, and as it crossed, a corpse floated past his face: his own body, dead. His disciples cried out in joy, for he had seen his own flesh fall away — the crossing was done, and the man who crossed was no longer the man who had embarked.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Journey to the West, ch. 98 (compiler's rendering); not verbatim.

passages.text: In the Thunderclap Monastery the Buddha's hosts gave out the true scriptures — thirty-five canons, five thousand and forty-eight scrolls, the number of the completion of one great kalpa. The monks of the library, asked for a gratuity, gave scrolls blank as river-reeds; the Buddha smiled and said that the scriptures of the empty hand were meant for those of the empty mind — then granted, at the East's request, the true word-filled scrolls as well.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Journey to the West, ch. 98, the scriptures; not verbatim.

passages.text: The five were invested by name before all the hosts: the Tang monk, Buddha of Sandalwood Merit; the monkey, Buddha Victorious in Strife; the pig, Cleanser of the Altars — for he still loved offerings and was given the altars of the world to eat them clean; the sand-monk, Arhat of the Golden Body; and the white horse, restored to dragonhood, coiled upon the pillar of the gate. They rode the clouds home to Chang'an, and the Emperor received the books as a nation's treasure.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Journey to the West, chs. 99-100, the investiture and return; not verbatim.

title.en: The King's Poem in the Palace of Nüwa
title.zh: 紂王題詩女媧宮

region.en: Nüwa's palace at the Zhaoge court (pin: Shang capital, Henan)
region.zh: 朝歌女媧宮（河南）

period: Investiture of the Gods (Fengshen Yanyi), 16th c. novel, ch. 1

source.work: Fengshen Yanyi, ch. 1: King Zhou's lewd poem and the goddess's summoning of the three demons of Xuanyuan tomb

license: Public domain (Ming novel; passages are compiler's renderings)

summary.en: King Zhou, at the seventh-year pilgrimage, entered the newly renovated temple of Nüwa and, seeing the goddess's painted beauty, wrote a lewd poem on the golden wall promising to make her his own. The goddess, returning from the Fire-Cloud Palace, read the verse and flew into fury: she summoned the three demons of the Xuanyuan tomb — the thousand-year fox, the nine-headed pheasant and the jade pipa — and sent them down to bewitch the king and ruin the Shang, setting the whole Investiture of the Gods in motion.
summary.zh: 紂王進香女媧宮，見聖像之美，題淫詩於粉壁：『但得妖嬈能舉動，取回長樂侍君王。』女媧大怒，喚軒轅墳三妖——千年狐狸、九頭雉雞精、玉石琵琶精——隱其妖形，託身宮院，惑亂君心，敗成湯天下。

sensitivity.note: Passages are the compiler's condensed paraphrases of the novel. The goddess's wrath frames the dynastic change as divine decree — the novel's theology of the Mandate.

passages.text: In the seventh year of his reign King Zhou went with his court to offer incense at the temple of Nüwa, the goddess who had mended the sky, newly painted for his visit. Behind the curtain stood the image of the goddess, and the king, gazing at her painted beauty, felt his heart burn.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Fengshen Yanyi, ch. 1 (compiler's rendering); not verbatim.

passages.text: He took up a brush and wrote on the golden wall a poem in praise of her loveliness, ending: 'If only the enchanting one could move and live, I would bring her back to Chang-le to serve her king.' The courtiers trembled; the king laughed and returned to his palace.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Fengshen Yanyi, ch. 1, the poem; not verbatim.

passages.text: The goddess came back from the Fire-Cloud Palace, read the verse on her own wall, and her face went black with rage: a mortal king had spoken to the mender of heaven as to a woman of the market. She summoned the three demons of the Xuanyuan tomb and charged them: assume beautiful forms, enter the palace, bewitch the king — and the fall of the Shang, six hundred years in the building, was decreed in one afternoon of lewd verse.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Fengshen Yanyi, ch. 1, the summoning; not verbatim.

title.en: The Fox Takes the Body of Su Daji
title.zh: 妲己被狐妖附體

region.en: Enzhou, Su Hu's fief (pin: Hebei–Henan border)
region.zh: 冀州蘇護府

period: Investiture of the Gods (Fengshen Yanyi), 16th c. novel, ch. 4

source.work: Fengshen Yanyi, ch. 4: Su Hu's daughter offered to the court, the fox's possession on the road, and the false Daji

license: Public domain (Ming novel; passages are compiler's renderings)

summary.en: Ordered to surrender his daughter Su Daji to the king's harem, the border-lord Su Hu marched her to the capital; at the Enzhou post-house a thousand-year fox-spirit, sent by Nüwa, killed the girl and took her body, arriving at court as the loveliest of the king's three thousand — and the true Daji was never seen again. The fox-queen of the novel's middle chapters, with her basin of burning bronze and her garden of frozen souls, is that possessed body.
summary.zh: 蘇護獻女妲己入宮；恩州驛狐狸精吸盡妲己魂魄，借體成形——入宮為妃，蠱惑紂王：酒池肉林、炮烙之刑、剖腹驗胎、敲骨視髓，皆出假妲己之手。

sensitivity.note: Passages are the compiler's condensed paraphrases of the novel. The fox-spirit figure echoes the nine-tailed fox of Qingqiu — an inversion from auspicious omen (chinese-shanhaijing-jiuweihu) to dynastic poison; noted.

passages.text: The border-lord Su Hu was ordered to send his daughter Daji to King Zhou's palace, and marched her with an escort to the capital. At the post-house of Enzhou a black wind shook the inn: it was the thousand-year fox, sent by the goddess to take a human body for her work at court.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Fengshen Yanyi, ch. 4 (compiler's rendering); not verbatim.

passages.text: The fox drew out the girl's soul with a breath and poured its own spirit into her body; the serving-maids saw nothing amiss, and the escort moved on. At court the false Daji was received in splendor — and King Zhou, one look at her, forgot the altars, the ancestral temple and the remonstrances of his ministers forever.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Fengshen Yanyi, ch. 4, the possession; not verbatim.

passages.text: What followed the novel tells as the inventory of a kingdom's ruin: pools of wine and forests of roasted meat, the bronze pillar heated for the loyal, the dissected bodies of pregnant women for the king's amusement, the bones of the old broken to see the marrow. Every atrocity came from the fox in the stolen body — and every atrocity added a name to the register of the gods the ending would confer.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Fengshen Yanyi, chs. 4-26, the reign of the false Daji; not verbatim.

title.en: Jiang Ziya Descends the Mountain to Wait Forty Years
title.zh: 姜子牙下山

region.en: Kunlun's Jade Void Palace and the market of Song family village (pin: Henan–Shaanxi)
region.zh: 崑崙玉虛宮至宋家莊

period: Investiture of the Gods (Fengshen Yanyi), 16th c. novel, chs. 15-16

source.work: Fengshen Yanyi, chs. 15-16: Yuanshi Tianzun sends Jiang Ziya down the mountain; the burning of the pipa-spirit; the failed fortune-telling and the failed marriage

license: Public domain (Ming novel; passages are compiler's renderings)

summary.en: Yuanshi Tianzun told the seventy-two-year-old Jiang Ziya that his destiny was not the immortal path but the throne of a minister: he was sent down Kunlun to aid the Zhou and to confer the titles of the gods. On earth he divined for a living, burned out a pipa-spirit in the palace of the king, and married the shrew Ma Shi, who left him when his fortunes fell — the general who would marshal heaven's armies spent his sixties as a market fortune-teller and a failed husband.
summary.zh: 元始天尊命姜子牙下山輔周滅紂、封神；子牙宋家莊算卦，火燒玉石琵琶精顯道術；娶馬氏，賣笊籬、賣麵皆折本——後往渭水垂釣，以待文王。

sensitivity.note: Passages are the compiler's condensed paraphrases of the novel.

passages.text: Jiang Ziya had studied on Kunlun forty years, and at seventy-two the Patriarch Yuanshi told him plainly: he was not born for the elixir — his fate was a chancellor's seal on earth. 'Go down the mountain,' said the master, 'aid the house of Zhou against the Shang, and confer the investitures of the gods; you will be born again into honor when your work is done.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Fengshen Yanyi, ch. 15 (compiler's rendering); not verbatim.

passages.text: Down the mountain he lodged with an old friend in the Song family village, married the sharp-tongued Ma Shi, and failed at every trade she set him: baskets, flour, cattle, a wine-shop. He found work at last as a fortune-teller at court, where he sniffed out a jade pipa-spirit sitting among the king's ladies and burned its true form out of the consort's body with the fire of his own arts — winning the enmity of the fox-queen and a posting to the frontier as reward.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Fengshen Yanyi, ch. 16, the pipa-spirit; not verbatim.

passages.text: Ma Shi left him for a poorer man when his post was lost, and the future Grand Marshal of the Investiture sat by the Wei River with a straight hook, waiting forty years' worth of years for a king — the novel's long joke that becomes the founding of a dynasty.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Fengshen Yanyi, chs. 16-23, the marriage and the fishing; not verbatim.

title.en: The Straight Hook of the Wei River and the Carriage of King Wen
title.zh: 渭水文王拉縴

region.en: Panxi, the bend of the Wei River (pin: Baoji, Shaanxi)
region.zh: 渭水磻溪（陝西寶雞）

period: Investiture of the Gods (Fengshen Yanyi), chs. 23-24; historical layer in Shiji, Qi Taigong Shijia, c. 94 BCE

source.work: Fengshen Yanyi, chs. 23-24: King Wen divines the fisher, the straight hook with no bait, and the carriage pulled by the king himself

license: Public domain (Ming novel; passages are compiler's renderings)

summary.en: King Wen, divining that a great minister waited by the river, went hunting and found Jiang Ziya fishing with a straight hook three feet above the water — 'not for the fish that live in the river, but for the king that will come.' The king bore him home in his own carriage, pulling the shafts eight hundred paces himself; Jiang Ziya answered that the Zhou would hold the realm eight hundred years — one year for every pace.
summary.zh: 文王占得飛熊，獵於渭陽，遇子牙直鉤釣渭——『寧在直中取，不向曲中求』；文王親拉車八百步，子牙許周八百年天下——西伯载歸，拜為太師。

sensitivity.note: Passages are the compiler's condensed paraphrases of the novel and the Shiji chapter. The carriage-pull prophecy is the novel's addition to Sima Qian's historical meeting.

passages.text: King Wen of Zhou, divining before a hunt, read in the crack a promise of the great teacher his line had lacked; he rode to the bend of the Wei and found an old man fishing — with a straight hook, and no bait, held three feet above the water.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Fengshen Yanyi, ch. 23 (compiler's rendering); not verbatim.

passages.text: 'The hook is not bent for the fish that swim,' said the fisher, 'but for the king that comes to the water. I would rather take in the straight way than beg in the crooked one.' King Wen bowed to the bank, invited him into the carriage, and — as the old man's price — pulled the shafts himself eight hundred paces, sweating at the task the Son of Heaven of the west performed for his minister.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Fengshen Yanyi, ch. 24, the carriage-pull; not verbatim.

passages.text: Jiang Ziya counted the paces and prophesied: the house of Zhou should hold the realm eight hundred years, one for every step the king had drawn. The king bore him home and made him Grand Tutor; the eighty years of the old man's waiting were over in an afternoon — and the dynasty's chronology was set by the length of a courtyard.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Fengshen Yanyi, ch. 24, the prophecy; not verbatim.

title.en: Nezha Born as a Ball of Flesh at Chen-Tang Pass
title.zh: 哪吒陳塘關出世

region.en: Chen-Tang Pass on the Shang frontier (pin: Sichuan Yibin tradition / Henan?; symbolic pin at Yibin)
region.zh: 陳塘關（象徵性定位）

period: Investiture of the Gods (Fengshen Yanyi), chs. 12-14; Nezha's cult attested Tang onward

source.work: Fengshen Yanyi, ch. 12: Lady Yin's three-year pregnancy, the ball of flesh, and Taiyi Zhenren's naming of the child

license: Public domain (Ming novel; passages are compiler's renderings)

summary.en: Lady Yin was three years and six months with child and had borne no child but a ball of flesh that rolled on the floor; her husband struck it with a sword, and a boy leapt out, wearing a red sash, with a golden bracelet on his right wrist. Taiyi Zhenren of the Qianyuan Mountain named him Nezha, took him as a disciple, and gave him the universe-sash and the universe-ring as weapons — a child of heaven sent down to be the vanguard of the coming war of the gods.
summary.zh: 殷夫人懷胎三年六月，產下一肉球，滴溜溜圓轉；李靖劍劈肉球，跳出一男孩，右手套一金鐲，腹纏紅綾；乾元山金光洞太乙真人收徒，取名哪吒，贈乾坤圈、混天綾。

sensitivity.note: Passages are the compiler's condensed paraphrases of the novel.

passages.text: Lady Yin, wife of the garrison commander of Chen-Tang Pass, had carried her child three years and six months without bearing it; the household whispered omens, and at last she was delivered — not of a child, but of a ball of flesh that rolled shining on the floor.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Fengshen Yanyi, ch. 12 (compiler's rendering); not verbatim.

passages.text: Li Jing struck it with his sword — and the ball split, and a boy leapt out of it, white and full-faced, with a red silk sash wrapped about him and a golden bracelet on his right wrist. The father, half in terror, was preparing to kill what might be a demon, when an immortal of the Qianyuan Mountain came to the gate and claimed the child.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Fengshen Yanyi, ch. 12, the splitting of the ball; not verbatim.

passages.text: Taiyi Zhenren named him Nezha, took him as a disciple, and gave him two weapons: the Universe-Ring of gold and the Universe-Sash of red silk. The child grew at a stride, a son of heaven posted to earth's frontier — and before he was seven, the river outside the pass would know his name.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Fengshen Yanyi, ch. 12-13, naming and gifts; not verbatim.

title.en: Nezha Flays the Dragon Prince
title.zh: 哪吒鬧海抽龍筋

region.en: The Nine-Bend River outside Chen-Tang Pass (symbolic pin: river of the pass)
region.zh: 陳塘關九灣河

period: Investiture of the Gods (Fengshen Yanyi), chs. 13-14

source.work: Fengshen Yanyi, chs. 13-14: the washing of the sash, the death of Ao Bing, and Nezha's return of his own body to his parents

license: Public domain (Ming novel; passages are compiler's renderings)

summary.en: Washing his universe-sash in the river, the child shook the Crystal Palace of the sea; the dragon-king's patrol came up to chide him and Nezha killed him with a ring-stroke. The third prince Ao Bing came in war-paint; Nezha beat the dragon from the clouds, flayed him, and pulled out his sinews to weave his father a belt. The four dragon-kings came to the pass to drown the town and seize the parents — and Nezha cut his own flesh back to his mother and his bones to his father, so that the debt of the body was paid and the dragons went home.
summary.zh: 哪吒混天綾攪海，震動水晶宮；打死巡海夜叉李艮，又殺三太子敖丙，抽其龍筋；四海龍王水淹陳塘關索命；哪吒削骨還父、削肉還母——魂魄飄蕩，求母建行宮。

sensitivity.note: Passages are the compiler's condensed paraphrases of the novel.

passages.text: The seven-year-old Nezha washed his red sash in the Nine-Bend River, and the silk of heaven churned the water until the Crystal Palace of the Eastern Sea rocked on its pillars. The dragon-king sent up a patrol to seize the bather, and the child killed him with one turn of his golden ring.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Fengshen Yanyi, ch. 13 (compiler's rendering); not verbatim.

passages.text: The third prince Ao Bing descended in war-paint; Nezha met him in the air, broke the dragon's halberd, felled him to the sand, and — flaying the dragon as his father flayed oxen — pulled out the sinews of the prince's tail to twist into a belt for Li Jing. Three dragons of the sea came up the river in fury to drown the pass and seize the parents in payment.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Fengshen Yanyi, chs. 13-14, the flaying and the siege; not verbatim.

passages.text: To save them, the child stepped forward and settled the debt of the body: he cut his flesh from his bones and returned it to his mother, and his bones to his father, saying that he had borrowed a body from them and was now giving it back — with not one strand of sinew owed. The dragons went home; the child's soul fled on the wind to his master's mountain, and his mother raised a temple to a son who had no body left to be buried.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Fengshen Yanyi, ch. 14, the return of the body; not verbatim.

title.en: Lotus Roots and Lotus Flowers: The Rebirth of Nezha
title.zh: 哪吒蓮花化身

region.en: Qianyuan Mountain, Golden Light Cave (pin: mythic mountain)
region.zh: 乾元山金光洞

period: Investiture of the Gods (Fengshen Yanyi), ch. 14

source.work: Fengshen Yanyi, ch. 14: Taiyi Zhenren gathers lotus roots and flowers and rebuilds Nezha's body

license: Public domain (Ming novel; passages are compiler's renderings)

summary.en: The bodiless soul of Nezha came to Qianyuan Mountain, and Taiyi Zhenren went to the lotus pond, took two lotus roots and three leaves, laid them out in the pattern of a body — bones of the root, flesh of the flower, sinews of the leaf — and with a breath of immortal qi and a word of incantation called a boy into being: Nezha reborn, taller and fiercer than before, whose body could no longer be touched by the river-floods of the dragons or the arrows of men, for it was made of lotus and light, not of the flesh his parents had lent him.
summary.zh: 太乙真人取荷葉荷梗藕節，按三才佈局，拆開父子之情，還他世界本性——蓮花化身；點化再生，賜火尖槍、風火輪——哪吒重生，不懼水火，身非血肉所成。

sensitivity.note: Passages are the compiler's condensed paraphrases of the novel. Cross-tradition resurrection cluster; the lotus-body is a Buddhist-inflected image (lotus birth) welded to a Daoist master's craft.

passages.text: The soul of Nezha, homeless on the wind, came weeping to the Golden Light Cave of Qianyuan Mountain; his master Taiyi looked at the ghost of a child and said there was a way — not a way of flesh, for flesh had been returned, but a way of flower.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Fengshen Yanyi, ch. 14 (compiler's rendering); not verbatim.

passages.text: Taiyi went down to the lotus pond and gathered what it offered: two stalks of lotus root, three leaves, and a blossom yet unclosed. He laid the roots for bones and the petals for flesh, folded the leaves for sinews and skin, and breathed on the heap the true breath of immortals — and drew with his finger the pattern of a boy of eight years.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Fengshen Yanyi, ch. 14, the lotus construction; not verbatim.

passages.text: He called the name, and the lotus figure sat up: Nezha, alive again, taller and brighter than the child the dragons had killed, his body no longer the flesh his parents had given and he had returned, but flower and root and light — a body that rivers could not drown, blades could not gash, and fires could not burn. His master armed him with the fire-tipped spear and the wind-fire wheels, and sent him down the mountain into the war of the gods.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Fengshen Yanyi, ch. 14, rebirth and rearming; not verbatim.

canonical_translation: Compiler's English rendering from the public-domain original; consulted (copyright, summary only): modern translations of Fengshen Yanyi

narrative.en:
The lotus rebirth of Nezha is the Chinese tradition's resurrection cluster: a hero who dies in childhood, gives his body back as payment of a debt, and is rebuilt from plants by a master-craftsman immortal.

BEGINNING: A CHILD WHO KILLS AND IS KILLED FOR IT. Nezha, the miraculous third son of Li Jing, born from a ball of flesh after three years in the womb, kills the river-gods who come to chide his play: the Dragon King's third prince is flayed, his sinews drawn out for a belt. The dragon-kings retaliate by threatening to flood Chen-Tang Pass and seize the parents. To pay the debt of blood without his family paying it, Nezha performs the novel's most piercing act: he cuts his flesh from his bones and returns it to his mother, cuts his bones and returns them to his father — 'the body was borrowed from you; I return it, with nothing owing' — and his soul flees, bodiless, to his master's mountain.

MIDDLE: THE MOTHER'S TEMPLE AND THE FATHER'S AXE. The ghost-boy asks his mother to build him a temple where he may receive incense and grow a body of worship; she does, on King Wu's road, and the boy gains a measure of power from three years of offerings. His father, hearing of it, comes in fury and smashes the temple with his axe — a father striking the shrine of the son whose body he accepted back. The soul, now truly homeless and fatherless, returns to Qianyuan Mountain.

END: THE LOTUS BODY. Taiyi Zhenren goes to the lotus pond and builds a body from what the pond gives: lotus roots for bones, petals for flesh, leaves for sinews, sealed with a breath of immortal qi and a drawn pattern. The lotus figure sits up — Nezha again, eight years old and stronger than before, his body no longer flesh at all: rivers cannot drown it, blades cannot gash it, and the father's axe, in later tellings, cannot touch it. He receives the fire-tipped spear and the wind-fire wheels and descends into the war of the gods as its fiercest child.

FUNCTION AND CROSS-TRADITION NOTES. The lotus rebirth gathers three motifs: resurrection (the dead child restored), transformation (flesh to plant), and the miraculous second birth. The lotus frame is Buddhist — the flower of rebirth from the waters — while the craftsman-creator is pure Daoist alchemy; the novel welds the two into the most famous child-hero of Chinese myth. In cross-tradition terms the body-as-debt motif (bones returned to the father) is a distinctive Chinese ethics of embodiment: resurrection here is not a god's favor but a craft-work performed on materials honestly surrendered.
narrative.zh: 哪吒蓮花化身為中國復活型神話之代表作：削骨還父、削肉還母——身體為借貸之物，還清則魂魄自由；太乙真人以荷為骨、蓮為肉、葉為筋，仙氣點化而成——花身不懼水火刀兵。廟宇被父砸毀一段寫父子之倫的決裂；重生後哪吒持火尖槍、踏風火輪下山大鬧封神之戰。跨傳統比較：佛教蓮花再生意象 + 道教煉形之術；復活非神恩而是誠實歸還材料後的工藝再造。

functions: Resurrection by craft: the master as rebuilder rather than rescuer
Ethics of the body as debt: bones and flesh returned honestly before rebirth
Aition of Nezha's invulnerability in cult and opera (lotus-body, not flesh)
Buddhist lotus imagery welded to Daoist form-making alchemy

variants.name: Fengshen Yanyi ch. 14 — the temple destroyed
variants.summary: The novel adds Li Jing's smashing of Nezha's memorial temple, which turns rebirth into filial war — Nezha returns from the lotus determined to punish his father.

variants.name: Precious Scroll of Nezha (folk paojuan) — the sister's bones
variants.summary: Folk versions make the lotus body depend on a sister's sacrifice or on bones borrowed from a temple statue — the craft of rebirth done with borrowed materials.

primary_sources.citation: 16th c. novel, attributed Xu Zhonglin / Lu Xixing; lotus-rebirth chapter. Vernacular Chinese via Wikisource.

secondary_sources.work: Meir Shahar, 'The Lingyanji and the temples of Nezha' and related studies of Chinese child-gods
secondary_sources.citation: Shahar, various — history of the Nezha cult and its texts.

secondary_sources.work: Anne Birrell, Chinese Mythology: An Introduction
secondary_sources.citation: Birrell 1993, Baltimore: Johns Hopkins University Press — Nezha in the mythic corpus.

source_urls.description: Wikisource (zh) — Fengshen Yanyi, public-domain Ming text

title.en: Bigan Gives Up His Heart
title.zh: 比干剖心

region.en: Zhaoge, Shang capital (pin: Henan)
region.zh: 朝歌（河南）

period: Investiture of the Gods (Fengshen Yanyi), ch. 26; older lore in Lüshi Chunqiu and Shiji

source.work: Fengshen Yanyi, ch. 26: the fox feast in the tower, the seven-apertured heart, and the amulet of the heartbeatless

license: Public domain (Ming novel; passages are compiler's renderings)

summary.en: The king's uncle Bigan, his heart famed for its seven apertures, was demanded by the fox-queen for medicine; Jiang Ziya left him a written amulet: 'Say nothing at all.' The heart was cut out; Bigan rode out of the city without a word, silent as his amulet — until a woman selling heartless greens called out that a heartless man cannot live, and he fell from his horse and died. The foxes at the feast were flayed; their skins stuffed the mattresses of the loyal.
summary.zh: 比干有心七竅；妲己設計取心為藥引；子牙留符曰『不可言語』；比干剖心而不語，行出城——見賣無心菜婦人言『菜無心可活，人無心即死』，墜馬而亡——封神榜上封為文曲星。

sensitivity.note: Passages are the compiler's condensed paraphrases of the novel.

passages.text: Bigan, uncle of the king, discovered the fox-queen's kinsmen at a midnight feast in the terrace of the stars, and had every fox pelt flayed for stuffings — the fox-queen, widowed of her tribe, resolved on his heart in payment.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Fengshen Yanyi, ch. 26 (compiler's rendering); not verbatim.

passages.text: She sickened, and her physician prescribed the heart of a man of seven apertures — and there was one man in the kingdom with such a heart. The king summoned his uncle; Jiang Ziya, foreseeing it, had left him a written charm: 'Say nothing at all, whatever you hear, and you will be safe.' Bigan cut out his own heart without a word, cast it down before the throne, and rode out of the gate in silence, his blood falling behind his horse.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Fengshen Yanyi, ch. 26, the amulet; not verbatim.

passages.text: Through the streets he rode, silent, and no blood touched him — until a woman by the road called her greens: 'Heartless heartless greens!' and he asked her, despite the charm, whether a heartless man could live. 'The greens live without a heart,' she said, 'but a man without a heart dies.' The word spoken, the charm was broken: Bigan fell from his horse and died. He was numbered among the stars of the Investiture, the star of the loyal heart that was taken.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Fengshen Yanyi, ch. 26, the greens-seller; not verbatim.

title.en: Lei Zhenzi, the Thunder Child Hatched from an Egg
title.zh: 雷震子食杏生翅

region.en: Yan-shan thunder-field and the Cloud-Brocade cave (symbolic pin: Shaanxi–Shanxi)
region.zh: 燕山雷鳴、終南山雲中子洞府

period: Investiture of the Gods (Fengshen Yanyi), chs. 3, 21-22

source.work: Fengshen Yanyi, chs. 3 and 21-22: the egg found after thunder, the seven years, and the two magic apricots that grew wings

license: Public domain (Ming novel; passages are compiler's renderings)

summary.en: After a thunderclap on Yan-shan, the returning court of King Wen found an egg-like child in the rain, and the immortal of the Cloud-Brocade cave named him Lei Zhenzi — Thunder-Startled — and took him as a disciple. Seven years later, sent to rescue his father from the siege of Tong Pass, the boy was fed two magic apricots: his face turned blue, his hair red, his teeth fangs, and wings of wind and thunder sprang from his sides — and he flew his father over the pass on his back.
summary.zh: 文王得雷雨中異兒，雲中子收為徒，名雷震子；七歲下山救父，食仙杏二枚——面如藍靛，髮似硃砂，肋下生風雷二翅；背負文王飛出五關。

sensitivity.note: Passages are the compiler's condensed paraphrases of the novel.

passages.text: King Wen, returning from his journey, heard thunder split the sky at Yan-shan, and in the rain found a child as smooth as an egg; the immortal of the Cloud-Brocade cave claimed him as a son of thunder and named him Lei Zhenzi — Thunder-Startled — and carried him up the mountain to be raised.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Fengshen Yanyi, ch. 3 (compiler's rendering); not verbatim.

passages.text: Seven years on, word came that King Wen was besieged at Tong Pass on his road home. The immortal gave the boy two apricots of the magic grove: he ate them, and his face turned the blue of indigo, his hair the red of cinnabar, his mouth grew elephant-fangs — and two wings of wind and two of thunder sprouted from his ribs, wide as the span of a cart.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Fengshen Yanyi, chs. 21-22, the apricots; not verbatim.

passages.text: On his new wings he flew to the pass, bore his father on his back over the walls and the pursuing soldiers, and set him down beyond the mountains — the thunder-child repaying in one flight the seven years of a father's finding.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Fengshen Yanyi, ch. 22, the rescue-flight; not verbatim.

title.en: Huang Feihu Crosses the Five Passes
title.zh: 黃飛虎反出五關

region.en: Zhaoge to Xiqi, through the five passes (pin: Henan to Shaanxi corridor)
region.zh: 朝歌至西岐五關

period: Investiture of the Gods (Fengshen Yanyi), chs. 30-34

source.work: Fengshen Yanyi, chs. 30-34: the death of Lady Jia, the rebellion of the king's own general, and the crossing of the five passes

license: Public domain (Ming novel; passages are compiler's renderings)

summary.en: Huang Feihu, the Shang king's own brother-in-law and keeper of the realm's armies, saw his wife driven from the terrace of the stars by the fox-queen's spite and fall to her death; his sister, the western concubine, was thrown from the tower after her. He gathered his father's troops, his sons and his fathers-in-arms, and fought his way out through the five passes of the Shang frontier — the highest-ranked defection of the whole epic, which turned the war from skirmish to revolution and carried to the Zhou court the man who knew every gate of the Shang.
summary.zh: 黃飛虎乃商之鎮國武成王；妲己害其妻賈氏墜樓，其妹（西宮黃妃）亦被紂王摔死；飛虎反出朝歌，率黃明、周紀等過五關——臨潼關、潼關、穿雲關、界牌關、汜水關——投西岐，拜開國武成王。

sensitivity.note: Passages are the compiler's condensed paraphrases of the novel.

passages.text: The fox-queen, nursing her grudge, lured Lady Jia, wife of the marshal Huang Feihu, up to the terrace of the stars on New Year's Day and set her before the drunken king; the lady, to keep her honor, threw herself from the tower. The marshal's own sister, the king's concubine, cast herself down after her in rage — and was dashed to death by the king's own hand.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Fengshen Yanyi, ch. 30 (compiler's rendering); not verbatim.

passages.text: Huang Feihu, keeper of the Shang armies, drank his grief all night, then took up his iron whip and raised the flag of rebellion: his four sworn brothers, his sons, a thousand veterans. He fought through the five passes of the frontier — five gates, five garrisons, five battles — each commander a friend or a demon in the pay of the fox.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Fengshen Yanyi, chs. 31-34, the rebellion; not verbatim.

passages.text: At Xiqi the defector was received as an equal, made Grand Marshal of the west, and invested after his death as the God of the Eastern Peak — the mountain of the dead. The man who crossed the five passes with his family's ashes behind him became the warden of the underworld's gate.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Fengshen Yanyi, chs. 34 and 99, reception and investiture; not verbatim.

title.en: The Formation of the Ten Thousand Immortals
title.zh: 萬仙陣

region.en: The field before Tong Pass (pin: Henan–Shaanxi border)
region.zh: 汜水關前（萬仙陣）

period: Investiture of the Gods (Fengshen Yanyi), chs. 84-87

source.work: Fengshen Yanyi, chs. 84-87: the last formation, the battle of the two sects, and the fates of the intercepted immortals

license: Public domain (Ming novel; passages are compiler's renderings)

summary.en: The Master of the Intercepts marshalled his whole sect — ten thousand immortals, beasts and bugbears of every shape — in the last great formation before the passes; the Patriarchs of the West broke it with the banners of the two illuminations, and the field filled with the trampled, the captured and the slain. The intercepted were led to the Register; the beasts of the mountain-lines were ground to their true shapes; and the Master of the Intercepts, ruined, retreated with his survivors to the western sea — the war of gods ended, the list of the invested ready for the Grand Marshal's brush.
summary.zh: 通天教主擺萬仙陣，聚截教群仙；老子、元始破陣，接引、準提助之；群仙或死或擒，封神榜上有名者盡歸其位——萬仙陣破，截教敗，封神之局定。

sensitivity.note: Passages are the compiler's condensed paraphrases of the novel.

passages.text: The Master of the Intercepts called up every disciple of his sect — immortals, beast-spirits, bugbears of the islands — and marshalled them in the last formation, ten thousand strong, its gates hung with the banners of his teaching. The Patriarchs of the West came down in force — Laozi with his cart, Yuanshi with his seal, and the two Buddhas of the western gate with their own banners — and the formation was broken from within: the sea of immortal disciples flooded, and the field filled with the captured, the slain and the beasts ground back to their true shapes.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Fengshen Yanyi, ch. 84 (compiler's rendering); not verbatim. / Paraphrase of Fengshen Yanyi, ch. 85, the breaking of the formation; not verbatim.

passages.text: The Master of the Intercepts left the field with the remnant of his sect for the western sea; the war of the gods was over, and the Register of the Investiture lay open for the Grand Marshal's brush — three hundred and sixty-five thrones of wind, rain, mountain, and plague to be filled with the names of the fallen.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Fengshen Yanyi, chs. 86-87 and 99, aftermath; not verbatim.

title.en: The Investiture: Jiang Ziya Confers Three Hundred and Sixty-Five Gods
title.zh: 姜子牙封三百六十五位正神

region.en: The altars of Qishan (pin: Shaanxi)
region.zh: 岐山封神臺

period: Investiture of the Gods (Fengshen Yanyi), ch. 99

source.work: Fengshen Yanyi, ch. 99: the reading of the Register and the conferring of the divine titles

license: Public domain (Ming novel; passages are compiler's renderings)

summary.en: On the altar at Qishan, Jiang Ziya opened the Register of the Investiture and read out the names: every soul that died in the war of the gods — loyalists, rebels, demons and beasts — was called by name and given a post: the God of the Eastern Peak, the Five Gods of the Thunder, the Twenty-Eight Mansions of the sky, the God of Plague, the God of Wealth, the Goddess of the Bedchamber — three hundred and sixty-five thrones, one for every day of the year, the dead of the war made into the civil service of heaven.
summary.zh: 子牙登封神臺，展開封神榜，逐一宣讀：柏鑑引魂、三百六十五位正神就位——東嶽大帝、雷部、火部、瘟部、二十八宿、財神趙公明、坑三姑娘娘娘……戰死之魂盡列神班，一年之日各有一神司之。

sensitivity.note: Passages are the compiler's condensed paraphrases of the novel. The investiture is the novel's theology: the dead re-ordered into the bureaucracy of heaven — China's pantheon in a payroll register.

passages.text: On the altar at Qishan, hung with the flags of the eight trigrams, the Grand Marshal of the Investiture unrolled the Register and called the first name: Bai Jian, the usher of souls, led up from the shadow a troop of the war's dead, and each, at his name, bowed and went to his throne.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Fengshen Yanyi, ch. 99 (compiler's rendering); not verbatim.

passages.text: The thrones were read out in departments: the Eastern Peak to keep the registers of birth and death; the Thunder-gods and the Rain-gods; the Gods of Plague; the Twenty-Eight Mansions of the zodiac; the Gods of Wealth, of the Kitchen, of the Bedchamber, of the Doors — three hundred and sixty-five thrones, a post for every day of the year, filled by the soldiers, generals, demons and immortals the war had spent.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Fengshen Yanyi, ch. 99, the departments; not verbatim.

passages.text: When the last name was read, the heavens accepted their new civil service: the dead of the war became the gods of the living, and the temple-bells of China rang for powers that had once been mortal. The Grand Marshal himself, who held the Register, took no throne for his own — his reward was to remain a chancellor in the world of men.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Fengshen Yanyi, ch. 99, conclusion; not verbatim.

title.en: The Turtle and the Monkey: The Trial among the Monkeys
title.zh: 海龜與猴子：猴群審判

region.en: Mexico, Pampanga, Luzon, Philippines (narrator's home town)
region.zh: 菲律賓呂宋邦板牙省墨西哥鎮（敘述者故鄉）

period: Pampangan oral fable; collected by D. S. Fansler, published 1921

source.work: Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 55a 'The Turtle and the Monkey', eBook #8299

summary.en: A monkey and a turtle divide a floating banana-stalk — the monkey takes the leafy top that dies, the turtle the roots that fruit. The monkey eats all the ripe bananas; the turtle rings the tree with pointed sticks and the monkey, frightened by a cry of 'The hunters are coming!', leaps to his death. The turtle sells the meat to other monkeys, is betrayed by leftover fur, tried, and sentenced to be burned and cut — punishments he claims to relish — until the fools 'drown' him, and he surfaces laughing.
summary.zh: 猴與龜分食浮來的蕉莖——猴得頂梢而枯，龜得根莖而實。猴獨吞熟蕉；龜環樹插尖竹，喊『獵人來了』嚇得猴跳下喪命。龜剝皮賣肉給群猴，因殘留猴毛被識破，受審判刑——火燒刀砍皆不懼，佯懼溺水——群猴投之於湖，龜浮出水面大笑。

sensitivity.note: Pampangan fable recorded by Fansler from a Garcia narrator; archival record. The monkey-and-turtle cycle is Philippines-wide; Fansler traces it to the Kacchapa-jataka (No. 273) and related Jatakas, arguing a pre-Spanish, ultimately Indian origin with the Bagobo version as a connecting link.

passages.text: It was mid-day, and a monkey and a turtle were having a good time on the shady river-bank, discussing the past, present, and future, when they saw a banana-stalk floating by. 'Can you swim?' replied the turtle when the monkey proposed getting it; the turtle agreed to fetch it on condition that they divide it, and demanded the upper part where the leaves are — but the monkey took the leaves himself and gave the turtle only the roots. Unable to fight the monkey, the humble turtle planted his share in the woods, and it was not strange that the monkey's part died while the turtle's brought forth clusters of ripe bananas in time.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 55 'The Turtle and the Monkey'; not verbatim.

passages.text: When the monkey learned that the bananas were ripe, he visited his friend, who offered half the bananas if the monkey would climb the stalk and get the fruit. In less than a minute the monkey was at the top, eating all he could and throwing down only banana-peelings. 'I know what I'll do!' said the turtle to himself, gathering pointed sticks and setting them all around the base of the tree; then he cried out, 'The hunters are coming! The hunters are coming!' The monkey, very much frightened, jumped down in the hope of escaping, was pierced by the sharp sticks, and died in a few hours — thus the turtle got his revenge on the selfish monkey.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 55 'The Turtle and the Monkey'; not verbatim.

passages.text: The turtle skinned the monkey, dried his meat, and sold it to the other monkeys in the neighborhood — but, careless, he left parts of the fur sticking to the meat, and the monkeys which had bought the meat judged the turtle guilty of the murder of one of their brethren, taking him before their chief. Sentenced to be burned, he said, 'Fire does not do me any harm...
