My father has burned me many times'; sentenced to be cut to pieces, he showed the scars — 'My father used to cut me over and over again.' At last the brightest fellow in the group said, 'We will drown him in the lake,' and as soon as the turtle heard this he felt happy, for he knew that he would not die in the water; he pretended to be very much afraid and implored them not to throw him in. The monkeys took him to the lake and threw him in; the turtle dived, then stuck his head above the surface, laughing very loud at them — his life saved because he had used his brains in devising a means of escape.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 55 'The Turtle and the Monkey'; not verbatim.

title.en: The Monkey and the Turtle: The Exchange by the Banana-Tree
title.zh: 猴與龜：蕉樹下調包

region.en: Batangas, Luzon, Philippines (narrator's home province)
region.zh: 菲律賓呂宋八打雁省（敘述者故鄉）

period: Tagalog oral fable; collected by D. S. Fansler, published 1921

source.work: Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 55c 'The Monkey and the Turtle' (Katigbak version), eBook #8299

summary.en: The selfish monkey carries away his patient turtle friend's whole food-supply on a journey, mocks him, and leaves him to be caught by a hunter — who kindly ties the turtle by a banana-tree and feeds him hourly. Envying the turtle's easy life, the monkey begs to swap places at night; the turtle yields, goes off happy, and the hunter, taking the tied 'thief' for a banana-stealer, shoots the monkey dead at dawn.
summary.zh: 自私的猴子旅途上吃光龜友的乾糧、一路嘲笑，終令龜被獵人捕走——獵人卻待之甚厚，縛於蕉樹旁按時餵食。猴子夜裡羨慕不已，央求調換；龜欣然讓位而去。清晨獵人見『被縛者』似在偷蕉，一槍擊斃猴子。

sensitivity.note: Tagalog fable recorded by Fansler from a Katigbak narrator; archival record. Version (c) of the monkey-and-turtle cycle with the hunter-exchange episode.

passages.text: Once upon a time there was a turtle who was very kind and patient, with many friends, among them a monkey who was very selfish and always wanted the best part of everything. Journeying to the next village, the monkey took little food, not liking to carry a heavy load, while the turtle took a big supply and advised the monkey to take more — but the monkey only laughed. After five days the monkey's food was gone and the greedy turtle had to feed him, then carry all the food; the monkey ran ahead, ate everything, and mocked his hungry friend. When they met a hunter, the monkey climbed a tree, but the man caught the turtle and took it home.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 55 'The Monkey and the Turtle' (Tagalog version); not verbatim.

passages.text: The monkey laughed at his friend's misfortune — but the hunter was kind to the turtle: he tied it near a banana-tree and gave it food every hour. Passing the house a few hours later, the monkey saw how the turtle was fed and envied his situation; when night came and the hunter was asleep, he went up to the turtle and said, 'Let me be in your place.' 'No, I like this place,' answered the turtle; but the monkey kept urging and begging, so that finally the turtle yielded, set the monkey free, and went off happy — while the monkey tied himself to the tree, so pleased that he could hardly sleep for thinking of the food the hunter would give him in the morning.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 55 'The Monkey and the Turtle' (Tagalog version); not verbatim.

passages.text: Early the next morning the hunter woke and looked out of his window, caught sight of the monkey, and thought that the animal was stealing his bananas; so he took his gun and shot him dead. Thus the turtle became free, and the monkey was killed. Moral: Do not be selfish.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 55 'The Monkey and the Turtle' (Tagalog version); not verbatim.

title.en: The Monkey and the Crocodile: The Liver Left on the Tree
title.zh: 猴子與鱷魚：留在樹上的肝

region.en: Manila, Luzon, Philippines (narrator's home city)
region.zh: 菲律賓呂宋馬尼拉（敘述者居地）

period: Tagalog oral fable; collected by D. S. Fansler, published 1921

source.work: Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 56a 'The Monkey and the Crocodile' (Tagalog version), eBook #8299

summary.en: A monkey courts a crocodile's help to cross the river, riding on his back; midstream the crocodile laughs that he will eat the monkey's liver and kidneys. The monkey calmly explains that he left them hanging on the macopa-tree in their haste, and the gullible crocodile turns back — whereupon the monkey leaps ashore, scampers up the tree, and the crocodile confesses, 'I am a fool.'
summary.zh: 猴子請鱷魚載他渡河；行至中流，鱷魚大笑要吃猴肝猴腎。猴子鎮定回答：匆忙出門，肝腎忘了取下，正掛在河邊的蒲桃樹上——鱷魚信以為真折返；猴一躍上岸、攀上樹梢。鱷魾自嘆：『我真傻。』

sensitivity.note: Tagalog fable recorded by Fansler from an Abasola narrator; archival record. Fansler derives the cycle from the Vanarinda-jataka (No. 57) and Sumsumara-jataka (No. 208), via the Pancatantra and Kalilah wa-Dimnah.

passages.text: One day, while a clever monkey was searching for his food along the river-bank, he saw a tall macopa-tree laden with ripe fruits, standing just by the shore of a river where a young crocodile lived. After eating all the fruit he wanted, the monkey conceived the desire of getting to the other side of the wide river, and finding no means, asked the just-woken crocodile in a friendly way to do him a favor. The crocodile was greatly surprised by this amicable salutation, but answered humbly that he would be glad to help, and told the monkey to sit on his back.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 56 'The Monkey and the Crocodile'; not verbatim.

passages.text: When they reached the middle of the stream, the crocodile began to laugh aloud: 'Now, you foolish monkey! I'll eat your liver and kidneys, for I'm very hungry.' The monkey became nervous but concealed his anxiety: 'To be sure! I thought myself that you might be hungry, so I prepared my liver and kidneys for your dinner; but unfortunately, in our haste to depart, I left them hanging on the macopa-tree. Let us return, and I'll get you the food.' The foolish crocodile, convinced that the monkey was telling the truth, turned back toward the shore — and when they were near, the monkey nimbly jumped onto the dry land and scampered up the tree. When the crocodile saw how he had been deceived, he said, 'I am a fool.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 56 'The Monkey and the Crocodile'; not verbatim.

title.en: The Monkey and the Crocodile (Zambal): The King's Red Breads
title.zh: 猴與鱷（三描）：國王的紅麵包

region.en: Zambales coast, western Luzon, Philippines (narrator's tale-source)
region.zh: 菲律賓呂宋西岸三描禮士（故事原鄉）

period: Zambal oral fable; collected by D. S. Fansler, published 1921

source.work: Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 56b 'The Monkey and the Crocodile' (Zambal version), eBook #8299

summary.en: Promised a lifetime supply of monkeys by a drowning-scare monkey, the crocodile ferries him across, only to be mocked from a tree. Playing dead later, the crocodile seizes the monkey — who claims to be the king's cook guarding the bright-red 'breads' of the pepper-bushes and promises them freely; the crocodile gulps the chilies, coughs and sneezes his way back to the river while the monkey laughs from above.
summary.zh: 猴子假意許諾帶鱷魾去『一生吃不完的猴群之地』，渡河後攀樹嘲笑。鱷魾裝死復又突襲擒猴；猴子自稱國王御廚，指點椒叢紅果為『御賜紅麵包』，任其取食。鱷魾大嚼辣椒，咳嗆抓舌，狼狽竄回河中——猴在樹上大笑。

sensitivity.note: Zambal fable recorded by Fansler from an Uichanco narrator (hearing it from a Zambales native); archival record. Contaminated form blending the crocodile cycle with the king's-fruit episode of the monkey-and-turtle group.

passages.text: One stormy day a monkey stood by the shore of a river, wondering how to get to the other side; the water was deep, and all he saw was a large crocodile with its mouth wide open, ready to seize him. Very much frightened, he said, 'O Mr. Crocodile! pray, do not kill me! Spare my life, and I will lead you to a place where you can get as many monkeys as will feed you all your life.' The crocodile agreed and carried him across on his back — but just before they reached the bank the monkey jumped to land, ran as fast as he could, and climbed up a tree where his mate was, while the crocodile could only return to the water saying, 'The time will come when you shall pay.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 56 'The Monkey and the Crocodile' (Zambal version); not verbatim.

passages.text: Not long afterwards the monkey found the crocodile lying motionless, as if dead, about low Chile pepper-bushes loaded with numerous bright-red fruits like ornaments on a Christmas tree. Playing with the crocodile's tail, the monkey was suddenly seized so tightly that he could not escape. 'Think first, think first!' said the monkey. 'I am now the cook of his Majesty the king. Those bright-red breads have been intrusted to my care.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 56 'The Monkey and the Crocodile' (Zambal version); not verbatim.

passages.text: The moment you kill me, the king will arrive with thousands of well-armed troops, and will punish you.' Frightened, the crocodile promised to set him free if he might eat as many pieces of bread as would relieve his hunger — 'Eat all you can; they are free to you,' responded the monkey kindly — and without another word the crocodile rushed at the heavily-laden bushes. The monkey slipped away secretly and climbed up a tree to enjoy the discomfiture of his voracious friend, who began to cough, sneeze, and scratch his tongue; when he rushed to the river to cool his mouth, the monkey only laughed at him. Moral: Use your own judgment; do not rely on the counsel of others, for it is the father of destruction and ruin.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 56 'The Monkey and the Crocodile' (Zambal version); not verbatim.

title.en: The Monkeys and the Dragon-Flies
title.zh: 群猴與蜻蜓之戰

region.en: Catanduanes, Philippines (where the story is very common)
region.zh: 菲律賓卡坦端內斯島（故事甚為流行）

period: Bicol oral fable; collected by D. S. Fansler, published 1921

source.work: Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 57 'The Monkeys and the Dragon-Flies', eBook #8299

summary.en: A weary dragon-fly resting on a monkeys' branch is mocked and stoned. Her brother the king declares war; the monkeys come armed with heavy clubs, the dragon-flies unarmed — and when the monkey-king shouts 'Strike the flying creatures with your clubs!', King Dragon commands his soldiers to alight on the foreheads of their enemies. Each blow falls on a companion's head; the quick dragon-flies are untouched and the foolish strong monkeys annihilate themselves.
summary.zh: 疲憊的蜻蜓在猴樹枝上歇腳，遭猴嘲弄、擲枝相擊。其兄蜻蜓王宣戰；群猴持重棍而來，蜻蜓則兩手空空。猴王一令『用棍擊打飛蟲』，蜻蜓王即命部下停在敵人額上——每一棍都落在同伴頭上。敏捷的蜻蜓毫髮無傷，強壯而愚笨的猴群自相殘滅。

sensitivity.note: Bicol fable recorded by Fansler from a Sorreta narrator; archival record. War of the winged and four-footed creatures; Fansler compares Grimm's 'Willow-Wren and the Bear' and the Latukika-jataka.

passages.text: One day, when the sun was at the zenith and the air was very hot, a poor dragon-fly, fatigued with her long journey, alighted to rest on a branch of a tree in which a great many monkeys lived. A monkey approached her: 'Aha! What are you doing here, wretched creature?' She begged to rest while the sun was so hot, but the monkey, mocking, cried 'We don't allow any weak creature such as you are to stay under our shelter. Go away!' — and, taking a dry twig, threw it at the poor creature. The dragon-fly, very quick, flew away before he could hit her, hurried to her brother the king, and told him what had happened; the king became very angry and resolved to make war on the monkeys, sending three soldiers with a challenge to the king of the monkeys.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 57 'The Monkeys and the Dragon-Flies'; not verbatim.

passages.text: The monkey-king laughed at the challenge: 'Let your king and his soldiers come to the battle-field, and they will see how well my troops fight.' When the reply came, King Dragon immediately ordered his soldiers to go to the battle-field — but without anything to fight with. The monkeys came, each armed with a heavy stick, and the monkey-king shouted, 'Strike the flying creatures with your clubs!' When King Dragon heard this order, he commanded his soldiers to alight on the foreheads of their enemies. Then the monkeys began to strike at the dragon-flies which were on the foreheads of their companions; the dragon-flies were very quick and were not hurt at all, but the monkeys were all killed. Thus the light, quick-witted dragon-flies won the victory over the strong but foolish monkeys.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 57 'The Monkeys and the Dragon-Flies'; not verbatim.

title.en: Li Ji, the Girl Who Volunteered to Slay the Serpent
title.zh: 李寄斬蛇

region.en: Dongyue, the Peak of the East (Fujian, snake country)
region.zh: 東越閩中庸嶺

period: Soushen Ji (In Search of the Supernatural) by Gan Bao, c. 350 CE, juan 19

source.work: Soushen Ji, juan 19: the great serpent of Yong ridges, the yearly maiden, and Li Ji

license: Public domain (Classical Chinese text; passages are compiler's renderings)

summary.en: An eight-zhang serpent in the eastern hills demanded a maiden of twelve or thirteen every August, and the officials, offering slaves and land, sent nine girls to their deaths. Li Ji, the sixth daughter of a poor clerk, volunteered against her parents' weeping: she took a sword and a snake-sniffing hound, loaded rice-balls with honeyed sesame, and in the mouth of the cave baited, killed and beheaded the serpent — and found in its lair the skulls of the nine before her, saying as she came out that the timid ones had deserved their deaths.
summary.zh: 東越閩中庸嶺大蛇長八丈，歲八月輒送十二三歲女充祭，已食九女；將樂縣李誕家六女李寄自請應募——囓犬、斫密劍、蜜麨數石；蛇出食犬，寄以劍砍之——得九女髑髏，歎曰『汝曹怯弱，為蛇所食』，遂緩步而歸。

sensitivity.note: Passages are the compiler's condensed paraphrases of the Soushen Ji original.

passages.text: In the eastern land of Dongyue a serpent lay coiled in the hills, eighty feet long, that had once shown itself to the town and eaten the girls sent to charm it: every August the officers bought or seized a girl of twelve or thirteen, shut her in a chamber by the serpent's cave-mouth, and let the beast take her. Nine girls had gone to the chamber; the town went on sending.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Soushen Ji, juan 19, Li Ji episode (compiler's rendering); not verbatim.

passages.text: Li Ji, sixth daughter of a poor clerk, offered herself against her parents' tears, took the reward of slaves and grain for her family, and prepared her own equipment: a sharp sword, a hound that loved to kill snakes, and several bushels of rice-balls kneaded with honeyed sesame. She set the sweet rice at the cave-mouth and waited with the hound behind her.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Soushen Ji, juan 19, the preparations; not verbatim.

passages.text: The serpent came out, boiling with the sweetness, and plunged its head into the rice; the hound fastened on its throat, and Li Ji hacked at the wound until the beast died. In the lair she found the skulls of the nine maidens before her, and said to them, coming out unhurried: 'You were too soft to save yourselves.' She went home a heroine, and was married to the king of Yue.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Soushen Ji, juan 19, the killing and the skulls; not verbatim.

title.en: The Swords of Gan Jiang and Mo Ye, and the Head in the Cauldron
title.zh: 干將莫邪三王墓

region.en: The Chu court and the southern mountains (pin: Hubei)
region.zh: 楚國

period: Soushen Ji by Gan Bao, c. 350 CE, juan 11 (older tellings in Lüshi Chunqiu and Wuyue Chunqiu)

source.work: Soushen Ji, juan 11: the sword-smith's three years, the male sword in the pillar, and the boy's head boiled in the cauldron

license: Public domain (Classical Chinese text; passages are compiler's renderings)

summary.en: The sword-smith Gan Jiang forged a pair of swords for the king of Chu; three years in the furnace, the king killed him in anger — but the smith had hidden the male sword in a pillar and told his unborn son. The boy Mei-jian-chi grew, learned the riddle, dug out the sword, and met a stranger who offered to avenge him if he would give up his head and sword; the head, boiled in a cauldron, leapt a thousand times and would not scald, and the stranger cut off his own head to join it — three heads in one cauldron, buried together as the Tomb of the Three Kings.
summary.zh: 干將為楚王作劍三年乃成，王怒殺之；留雄劍於柱中，囑子出而取之。子赤比（眉間尺）得劍，遇客願為報仇，索頭與劍；頭鑊中三日照不爛，客自刎以頭助之——三首俱爛，合葬一處，是為三王墓。

sensitivity.note: Passages are the compiler's condensed paraphrases of the Soushen Ji original.

passages.text: Gan Jiang and his wife Mo Ye forged swords for the king of Chu; the metal was of such temper that the furnace took three years. When the king came in anger to demand them, the smith showed him only the female sword, and died by his blade — but he had hidden the male sword inside a pillar of the gate-tower, and told his pregnant wife: 'If the child is a boy, tell him to come out of the south gate, look at the pillar of the north hill, and find the sword in the wood.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Soushen Ji, juan 11, Gan Jiang episode (compiler's rendering); not verbatim.

passages.text: The boy grew up asking about his father, learned the riddle, split the pillar and took the sword. The king dreamed of a boy with a brow like an inch-wide measure, and set a price on his head; the boy fled to the hills, singing his grief — until a stranger asked his story, and offered to do the vengeance if the boy would give him his head and the sword.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Soushen Ji, juan 11, Mei Jianchi episode; not verbatim.

passages.text: The boy cut off his own head and stood holding it and the sword, waiting for the promise; the stranger took both and went to the king, presenting the head in a cauldron of boiling water. Three days it boiled and would not scald; the head glared from the water. 'This head will not melt,' said the stranger, 'look closer' — and when the king bent over the cauldron, the stranger cut off the king's head, then his own, and all three heads boiled together. The courtiers buried the three in one mound, and the Tomb of the Three Kings stood in Yichun to be seen.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Soushen Ji, juan 11, the cauldron and the tomb; not verbatim.

title.en: Han Ping and His Wife: The Mandarin Ducks of Kangle
title.zh: 韓憑夫婦鴛鴦

region.en: Kangwang Terrace, Song state (Henan)
region.zh: 宋康王之青陵臺

period: Soushen Ji by Gan Bao, c. 350 CE, juan 11

source.work: Soushen Ji, juan 11: the wife taken by the king, the double suicide, and the trees that grew together

license: Public domain (Classical Chinese text; passages are compiler's renderings)

summary.en: King Kang of Song coveted the wife of his gate-clerk Han Ping, seized her, and sent Han Ping to hard labor; the wife sent him a coded letter of garters, the king laughed, and both took their lives — she jumped from the terrace, he hanged himself. The king buried them apart, saying they could not join in death if they had loved in life; in ten days two trees grew from the graves, curved toward each other, entwined their roots and branches — and mandarin ducks nested in the canopy, crying day and night.
summary.zh: 宋康王舍人韓憑妻何氏美，王奪之，罰憑築城；妻陰遺書，『其雨淫淫，河大水深，日出當心』——夫婦相繼自殺；王使冢分埋之，兩墳各生梓木，屈體相就，根交於下、枝錯於上；鴛鴦恆棲樹上，晨夕不去——宋人哀之，號其木曰相思樹。

sensitivity.note: Passages are the compiler's condensed paraphrases of the Soushen Ji original. Aition of the 'lovers' tree' (xiangsi shu) and of mandarin-duck symbolism for wedded fidelity.

passages.text: The wife of Han Ping, a clerk in the court of Song, was so beautiful that King Kang took her for himself and sent Han Ping to a chain-gang by the Great Wall. The wife sent her husband a letter in three riddling lines — rain that falls and falls, a river too deep to measure, the sun rising on a set heart — and both king and court read it and laughed, for only the husband knew it said: the king has me, the way is far, and I will die.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Soushen Ji, juan 11, Han Ping episode (compiler's rendering); not verbatim.

passages.text: Han Ping hanged himself in the laborers' camp. His wife, walking the king's terrace, had her robes lined with paper: she leapt from the height, her dress burst open in the air like a butterfly's wings, and the king, striking at the falling paper, could not save her. In her girdle was a plea: to be buried with her husband in one grave.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Soushen Ji, juan 11, the two deaths; not verbatim.

passages.text: The king buried the lovers apart, in plots within sight of each other, saying the dead could not undo his taking. In ten days a catalpa tree grew from each grave, bending toward the other until the roots met beneath the earth and the branches crossed in the air; and mandarin ducks came and nested in the canopy, crying to each other night and morning. The people of Song named the trees the Trees of Longing, and the terrace the Terrace of the Loving Couple.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Soushen Ji, juan 11, the entwined trees; not verbatim.

title.en: Dong Yong Sells Himself to Bury His Father, and a Weaver Girl Comes Down
title.zh: 董永賣身葬父織女相助

region.en: Qiancheng, northern Shandong (Han commandery)
region.zh: 千乘（山東）

period: Soushen Ji by Gan Bao, c. 350 CE, juan 1 (Han iconography of Wuliang shrine, 2nd c. CE)

source.work: Soushen Ji, juan 1: Dong Yong's sale of himself, the ten-day cloth, and the weaving-girl who descended for ten days

license: Public domain (Classical Chinese text; passages are compiler's renderings)

summary.en: Dong Yong, too poor to bury his dead father, sold himself into servitude for the funeral money and walked to the master's house to work it off. On the road a girl met him and asked to be his wife; in the master's house she wove in ten days a hundred bolts of cloth that should have taken a year — then told him, rising into the air: 'I am one of the Weaving Maidens of heaven; the Emperor of Heaven, moved by your filial piety, sent me to pay your debt.' And she was gone.
summary.zh: 董永喪父貧，賣身以葬；道遇一女求為妻，織縑百匹十日而畢——女凌空而去，曰『我天上織女，天帝感君孝，命我助君償債』——漢畫像石已見此圖。

sensitivity.note: Passages are the compiler's condensed paraphrases of the Soushen Ji original. The Cowherd-Weaver cycle's ethical core (filial piety rewarded) is anachronistic with the later love-tragedy version; both strands recorded.

passages.text: Dong Yong of Qiancheng was so poor at his father's death that he could not afford a coffin; he sold himself to a rich household for ten thousand cash, to be worked off as a servant, and walked to the master's house with the funeral done.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Soushen Ji, juan 1, Dong Yong episode (compiler's rendering); not verbatim.

passages.text: On the road a girl met him, saying she wished to be his wife; the master was told and agreed to set her to weaving, and the girl sat at the loom for ten days and wove a hundred bolts of fine cloth — the full price of the bond — and the debt was paid.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Soushen Ji, juan 1, the weaving; not verbatim.

passages.text: The girl left the loom, rose into the air before him, and said: 'I am one of the Weaving Maidens of heaven. The Emperor of Heaven was moved by your filial piety, and sent me down for ten days to clear your debt.' And she was gone — the first telling of the heaven-sent weaver whose ten days of cloth redeemed a bondsman.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Soushen Ji, juan 1, the ascent; not verbatim.

title.en: The Girl Who Was Wrapt in the Horse's Hide: The Origin of Silkworms
title.zh: 馬皮蠶女

region.en: The silk country of the west (Sichuan–Shaanxi borders)
region.zh: 西蜀蠶鄉

period: Soushen Ji by Gan Bao, c. 350 CE, juan 14

source.work: Soushen Ji, juan 14: the girl of the old tale, the promised horse, and the wrapping of the silkworm

license: Public domain (Classical Chinese text; passages are compiler's renderings)

summary.en: A girl missed her father on a far journey and teased the family horse: bring him back and you shall have me. The horse broke its tether, carried the father home, and — remembered the promise — would not eat; the father killed and flayed it, drying the hide in the yard. The hide rolled itself up, swept the girl from the courtyard, and flew away with her to the mulberry trees, where both were found as a white silkworm wrapt in horse-hide — the origin of silkworms, and of the silkworm-princess worshipped in the sericulture lands.
summary.zh: 舊說太古之時，女念父不歸，戲語馬曰『汝得迎父，吾嫁汝』；馬絕韁迎父歸，不肯食；父殺之曝皮；皮忽卷女飛去，棲於桑樹之間——化為蠶，食桑葉，吐絲成繭——蠶神馬頭娘之由來。

sensitivity.note: Passages are the compiler's condensed paraphrases of the Soushen Ji original. Aition of sericulture and of the 'horse-head lady' (matou niang) silkworm goddess.

passages.text: In the oldest times, so the tale runs, a girl alone at home missed her father gone on a long journey, and teased the house's horse: 'If you bring him back, I will marry you.' The horse broke its tether that day, ran the roads until it found the father, and carried him home on its back — and thereafter would eat nothing, stamping and rearing whenever it saw the girl.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Soushen Ji, juan 14, silkworm-girl episode (compiler's rendering); not verbatim.

passages.text: The father asked the reason, learned the promise, and said a match between man and horse could not be; he shot the horse dead in the yard and had the hide spread out to dry. One day the girl walked over the hide — and the hide rolled itself up and swallowed her, and flew off with her into the sky.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Soushen Ji, juan 14, the hide; not verbatim.

passages.text: The father searched for days, and found daughter and hide at last in the mulberry trees above the house — for there the pair had changed into a creature like a silkworm, eating mulberry leaves and spinning silk from itself. The sericulture lands built shrines to the girl as the Silkworm Princess, and the mulberry trees of the silk country are said to grow thickest where she was wrapt.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Soushen Ji, juan 14, the silkworm and the cult; not verbatim.

title.en: Song Dingbo Catches a Ghost and Sells It
title.zh: 宋定伯捉鬼

region.en: Wanling, on the night road (Henan)
region.zh: 南陽宛陵夜路

period: Soushen Ji by Gan Bao, c. 350 CE, juan 16 (also in Lieyichuan)

source.work: Soushen Ji, juan 16: the night walk, the questions of the ghost, and the ghost spat into a market sale

license: Public domain (Classical Chinese text; passages are compiler's renderings)

summary.en: Walking to market by night, Song Dingbo met a ghost and, told what it was, answered that he was a ghost too. They carried each other by turns; the ghost, heavy as a man made of nothing, taught him its one weakness — human saliva. At the market crossing the ghost turned a goat; Song spat on it, held it, and sold it in the morning for fifteen hundred cash — the merchant's saying ever after: 'Song Dingbo sold a ghost for fifteen hundred.'
summary.zh: 宋定伯夜行逢鬼，問曰『汝復誰』——『我亦鬼』；鬼言唯不喜人唾；共遞相擔，至宛市，鬼化為羊，定伯唾之，賣得錢千五百——『定伯賣鬼，得錢千五百』。

sensitivity.note: Passages are the compiler's condensed paraphrases of the Soushen Ji original.

passages.text: Song Dingbo, a man of Nanyang, walked to market by night and met a figure on the road. 'Who goes?' said the figure. 'I am a ghost too,' said Song, coolly; and the two walked on together, the ghost asking what weighed so heavily on Song's shoulders — 'newly dead,' said Song, 'nothing is light for me yet.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Soushen Ji, juan 16, Song Dingbo episode (compiler's rendering); not verbatim.

passages.text: They carried each other by turns across the streams; the ghost, borne by Song, was light as a leaf. Song asked what ghosts feared; the ghost answered: 'Only the saliva of living men.' At the ford of the river the ghost bade Song cross silently; Song plunged through with a splash and said he was newly dead and knew no better.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Soushen Ji, juan 16, the ferrying; not verbatim.

passages.text: As the sky lightened at the market-gate, the ghost turned into a goat and tried to run; Song spat on it and held it fast, and sold it in the morning market for fifteen hundred cash. The merchants of Nanyang told the tale ever after as a price-list: 'Song Dingbo sold a ghost for fifteen hundred.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Soushen Ji, juan 16, the sale; not verbatim.

title.en: Liu Yi Delivers a Letter to the Dragon Palace of Dongting
title.zh: 柳毅傳書

region.en: Dongting Lake and the Jing River (Hunan–Shaanxi)
region.zh: 洞庭龍宮、涇川

period: Taiping Guangji, juan 419, from Li Chaowei's chuanqi 'Liuyi Zhuan' (Tang, c. 794 CE)

source.work: Taiping Guangji, juan 419: Liu Yi's letter-bearing, the sheep-herding lady on the Jing River, and the fire of the Qiantang dragon

license: Public domain (Classical Chinese text; passages are compiler's renderings)

summary.en: A failed examinee, Liu Yi, met a girl herding sheep on the Jing River who wept that she was the daughter of the Dragon King of Dongting, married off and abused by her husband's house; she gave him a letter, and told him to strike a tree by Dongting. In the Crystal Palace the wrathful younger brother, the Qiantang dragon, burst from the water as a red dragon a thousand feet long, ate the offending husband, and brought the lady home; Liu Yi refused a marriage of gratitude, and only years later — after a wife who died, a fisher of Wuzhou who was the lady in disguise — wed her as she truly was, a dragon-daughter immortal, and rose with her into the clouds.
summary.zh: 柳毅下第，涇陽遇牧羊龍女託書；至洞庭擊橘社树，龍宮震動；錢塘君怒誅涇川次子，救侄女歸；毅拒婚，後娶盧氏（即龍女所化），同登仙籍——傳書之報。

sensitivity.note: Passages are the compiler's condensed paraphrases of the Taiping Guangji text.

passages.text: Liu Yi, failing the examination, passed the Jing River and saw a girl herding a flock that were not sheep but water-thunder in sheep's shape; she wept that she was the daughter of the Dragon King of Dongting, married into the Jing River's house and beaten by its lord, and begged him to carry a letter — strike the tree of the orange-terrace by Dongting, and a messenger will come.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Taiping Guangji, juan 419, Liuyi Zhuan (compiler's rendering); not verbatim.

passages.text: At Dongting he struck the tree thrice, and the lake opened into a corridor of water-walls, and servants of the Dragon King led him to the Crystal Palace. When the letter was read, a wail rose through the palace — and from the sky burst the Qiantang dragon, the wrathful younger brother, a red thunder a thousand feet tall, who seized the offending husband of the Jing River and ate him, then carried his niece home in triumph.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Taiping Guangji, juan 419, the Qiantang dragon; not verbatim.

passages.text: The palace feasted him and offered the lady in marriage out of gratitude; Liu Yi, proud, refused and went home. Years later, his wife dead, he married a fisher-woman of Wuzhou who grew rich and mysterious — and at last she told him she was the dragon-daughter, who had not forgotten the man who carried her letter; they rose together into the clouds and were seen no more among the people of Dongting.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Taiping Guangji, juan 419, the marriage and the ascent; not verbatim.

title.en: The Dream of Nanke: A Career in an Ant Kingdom
title.zh: 南柯一夢

region.en: The locust tree of Guangling (Yangzhou)
region.zh: 廣陵郡槐樹

period: Taiping Guangji, juan 475, from Li Gongzuo's chuanqi 'Nanke Taishou Zhuan' (Tang, c. 813 CE)

source.work: Taiping Guangji, juan 475: Chunyu Fen's dream of the Great Locust Kingdom, his twenty years as governor, and the digging of the tree

license: Public domain (Classical Chinese text; passages are compiler's renderings)

summary.en: Chunyu Fen, drunk under a great locust tree, was carried off in a gilded carriage to a kingdom in the tree's hollow: he married the king's daughter, governed Nanke for twenty years, raised children, knew honor and disgrace — and woke at dusk under the same tree. Digging beneath it, his friends found an ant-city of perfect order in the hollow of the trunk, and a second colony to the west: Nanke, the kingdom of his career, one afternoon's dream in the life of a mound of ants.
summary.zh: 淳于棼夢入大槐安國，尚公主，守南柯郡二十年；夢醒，與客掘樹——樹下一蟻國，枝下一南柯郡——人生如蟻國一夢。

sensitivity.note: Passages are the compiler's condensed paraphrases of the Taiping Guangji text.

passages.text: Chunyu Fen sat drinking under the great locust tree of his garden and fell asleep; two purple-clad envoys carried him in a gilded carriage through a hole in the trunk into a kingdom whose gates bore the name Great Locust Ancestral Peace.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Taiping Guangji, juan 475, Nanke Taishou Zhuan (compiler's rendering); not verbatim.

passages.text: The king married him to his golden-braided daughter, posted him as governor of Nanke, and he reigned twenty years of the dream: good harvests, honors, sons and daughters, then disgrace and exile by the king's displeasure. The dream kingdom packed him back through the same hole in the trunk as dawn was near, and he woke in the dusk of his own garden with the wine-cups still unwashed.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Taiping Guangji, juan 475, the reign and the waking; not verbatim.

passages.text: His friends dug under the locust tree and found in the hollow a city of ants in perfect order — palaces, gates, guards — and beneath the western branch a second smaller colony: the Nanke of the dream. A storm that night scattered both cities to the winds; Chunyu Fen took vows and did not drink again under that tree.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Taiping Guangji, juan 475, the ant-city; not verbatim.

title.en: The Yellow Millet Dream on the Handan Road
title.zh: 黃粱一夢

region.en: Handan post-road, Hebei
region.zh: 邯鄲道旅舍

period: Taiping Guangji, juan 82, from Shen Jiji's chuanqi 'Zhenzhong Ji' (Tang, c. 750 CE)

source.work: Taiping Guangji, juan 82: the pillow of Lü Weng, the millet still cooking, and the whole life of Lu Sheng

license: Public domain (Classical Chinese text; passages are compiler's renderings)

summary.en: A young man at the Handan post-house, lamenting his poverty to a Taoist with a magic pillow, fell asleep as the millet was set to cook: he lived in the dream a whole career — the brilliant marriage, the examination, the governorships, the wars, the chancellorship, the slanders, the exile, the old age — and died in the dream among his grandchildren. He woke, and the millet was not yet done; the Taoist smiled, and the young man bowed and went home having seen what a life is.
summary.zh: 呂翁於邯鄲道遇盧生，授青瓷枕——夢中娶崔氏、登第、陝州鑿河、大破吐蕃、拜相、遭讒、流放、復起、壽終——炊黃粱未熟。盧生悟，作禮而去。

sensitivity.note: Passages are the compiler's condensed paraphrases of the Taiping Guangji text.

passages.text: At the post-house of Handan a young man named Lu lamented to a Taoist traveler that he was born to nothing: talent without opportunity, poverty without end. The Taoist drew from his bag a pillow of green porcelain and said: 'Sleep on this; you will find in it all that you desire.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Taiping Guangji, juan 82, Zhenzhong Ji (compiler's rendering); not verbatim.

passages.text: Lu slept, and in the dream lived seventy years: he married the daughter of a great house, passed the examinations, governed provinces, drained the Yellow River's flood for the land's good, broke a Tibetan invasion, became grand chancellor — was slandered, exiled, recalled, honored — raised sons, married daughters, and died old and full of days in his bed among his grandchildren.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Taiping Guangji, juan 82, the life in the dream; not verbatim.

passages.text: He woke on the post-house bench: the Taoist sat beside him, and the innkeeper's millet on the stove was not yet done cooking. Lu sat up a long time and then bowed: 'Glory and poverty, favor and loss, death and life — I have seen them all. Sir, you have quieted the passions of my heart.' He bowed again and went home, and the Yellow Millet Dream passed into the language of China as the name of every ambition seen whole.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Taiping Guangji, juan 82, the waking; not verbatim.

title.en: The Three-Lives Stone: Yuan Ze and Li Yuan
title.zh: 三生石

region.en: Tiantai Mountain and the Tianzhu Temple at Hangzhou
region.zh: 天臺山、杭州天竺寺

period: Ganze Yao (Tang, c. 800 CE), 'Yuan Guan'; reprinted in the Taiping Guangji collections

source.work: Ganze Yao: Yuan Ze and Li Yuan's pact, the rebirth at the well of Tianzhu, and the Twelve-year meeting at the Three-Lives Stone

license: Public domain (Classical Chinese text; passages are compiler's renderings)

summary.en: Li Yuan, a retired general, and the monk Yuan Ze traveled toward Mount Emei; at a stream the monk saw a pregnant woman washing and went pale: his rebirth waited there. He asked Li Yuan to sing a song at the birth three days later, and to find him in twelve years at the Tianzhu temple of Hangzhou. Yuan Ze died, the child was born and spoke; twelve years on, Li Yuan came to Hangzhou, and a herd-boy by the Three-Lives Stone sang the promised song: 'the old soul on the third-life stone' — and was gone over the hills.
summary.zh: 李源與圓觀（一作圓澤）同遊；至江峽見妊婦汲水，觀曰『我託生之所』——約三日後浴兒相見、十二年後天竺寺相尋；圓觀坐化，兒生而能言；十二年李源至杭州天竺寺，牧童扣牛角歌曰『三生石上舊精魂』——遂杳然而去。

sensitivity.note: Passages are the compiler's condensed paraphrases of the Ganze Yao text.

passages.text: Li Yuan, a general grown old in retreat, and his friend the monk Yuan Ze set out together for the mountains of the west; at a stream near the gorges Yuan Ze stopped, went pale at sight of a woman washing at the water, and said to Li Yuan: 'My rebirth waits in that house. I have put off going until now, but no one goes past it twice.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ganze Yao, Yuan Guan episode (compiler's rendering); not verbatim.

passages.text: He asked a last favor: come to the house in three days, and if the newborn smiles at you, that smile is mine; then find me in twelve years at the Tianzhu temple of Hangzhou, by the Three-Lives Stone. He bathed, sat upright, and died — and the child was born that night, and smiled at Li Yuan when he came.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ganze Yao, Yuan Guan episode, the pact; not verbatim.

passages.text: Twelve years later Li Yuan came to Hangzhou, and by the Three-Lives Stone of the Tianzhu temple a herd-boy sat on an ox, singing the very song Yuan Ze had promised: 'The old soul on the third-life stone; I do not regret the moon-song or the wind; my shame is only to meet you again, yet be a stranger going and coming.' He bowed across the distance, and was gone into the mists of the hill — friendship surviving death, by appointment.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ganze Yao, Yuan Guan episode, the meeting; not verbatim.

title.en: The White Snake and the Leifeng Pagoda
title.zh: 白娘子永鎮雷峰塔

region.en: West Lake and Leifeng Pagoda, Hangzhou
region.zh: 杭州西湖雷峰塔

period: Jingshi Tongyan by Feng Menglong, 1624 CE, juan 28

source.work: Jingshi Tongyan, juan 28: the white snake of West Lake, the umbrella at the broken bridge, the red-swallowing? truth, and the pagoda

license: Public domain (Ming collection; passages are compiler's renderings)

summary.en: At the Broken Bridge of West Lake a white snake in woman's form sheltered a young pharmacy clerk Xu Xian with his umbrella, married him, and made his fortune with her silver — silver that had been stolen, so that he was twice exiled for her sake. A Taoist tried to exorcise her, a monk Fahai of Jinshan pursued her: the white snake flooded the temple with the water of the whole lake, was captured, and sealed under the Leifeng Pagoda to wait a thousand years — the great love-story of the snake and the man, told by Feng Menglong as a warning, loved by the people as a tragedy.
summary.zh: 西湖斷橋白蛇借傘許仙，成親開藥鋪；銀兩皆來路不明，許仙兩度充軍；道士除妖不成，金山寺法海鬥法水漫金山；白娘子被缽收，鎮於雷峰塔下——『雷峰塔倒，白蛇出世』。

sensitivity.note: Passages are the compiler's condensed paraphrases of the Feng Menglong text.

passages.text: At the Broken Bridge of West Lake, in the rain, a woman in white and her green-robed maid sheltered a young clerk of the medicine shops and lent him an umbrella; he called for it next day, drank tea, and before the month was out the white-clad lady was his wife, her dowry of fifty taels of silver furnishing the house.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Jingshi Tongyan, juan 28 (compiler's rendering); not verbatim.

passages.text: The silver was traced: it had been stolen from an official's house, and Xu Xian was arrested twice for goods that appeared from nowhere. The truth was worse than theft: his wife was a white snake of a thousand years' cultivation, her maid a green snake, and a wandering Taoist who tried to hang a charm on the marriage was driven off with a strip of her serpent's tail.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Jingshi Tongyan, juan 28, the truth; not verbatim.

passages.text: At last the monk Fahai of Jinshan temple took the case. When the white snake flooded his temple with the whole of West Lake to rescue her husband, he brought forth the alms-bowl of the Buddha: she was caught in it, sealed with the Leifeng Pagoda built over her on the lake shore, and told she would wait under it a thousand years — until the pagoda falls, said the storytellers, and the white snake comes out again.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Jingshi Tongyan, juan 28, the pagoda; not verbatim.

title.en: Xiao Shi and Nong Yu: The Flute That Called the Phoenixes
title.zh: 蕭史弄玉鳳凰臺

region.en: Phoenix Terrace, the palace of Duke Mu of Qin (Shaanxi)
region.zh: 秦穆公鳳凰臺

period: Liexian Zhuan (Biographies of Immortals), attributed Liu Xiang, Han dynasty

source.work: Liexian Zhuan: Xiao Shi the flute-player, the duke's daughter Nong Yu, and the phoenixes of the terrace

license: Public domain (Classical Chinese text; passages are compiler's renderings)

summary.en: Duke Mu of Qin had a daughter, Nong Yu, who loved the pan-pipes; a young man called Xiao Shi played the xiao flute so that peacocks and phoenixes gathered on his roof. He married the princess and taught her; they lived half a life above the terrace they were given, and one morning, playing, they called down the phoenix and the dragon — she rode the phoenix, he rode the dragon, and both rose together into the sky, leaving the Qin court a tower and a lesson: music, sincerely practiced, is the road of the immortals.
summary.zh: 蕭史善簫，能致孔雀白鶴；穆公以女弄玉妻之；居鳳樓數年，一朝隨鳳凰昇天——秦作鳳女祠，簫聲之仙由此立。

sensitivity.note: Passages are the compiler's condensed paraphrases of the Liexian Zhuan text.

passages.text: Xiao Shi of the Qin lands played the xiao so that its notes drew the cries of peacocks and the songs of white cranes; the Duke Mu heard of it, married him to his daughter Nong Yu, who was herself a master of the pan-pipes, and gave the pair a tower of their own.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Liexian Zhuan, Xiao Shi biography (compiler's rendering); not verbatim.

passages.text: For several years the two played together on the tower morning and night, until their music called down the phoenixes themselves: great birds settled on the tower's roof, and the duke built a terrace of phoenix and named the city's gate for them.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Liexian Zhuan, Xiao Shi biography, the phoenixes; not verbatim.

passages.text: One morning the flute called a pair down for the last time: Nong Yu mounted the phoenix, Xiao Shi the dragon that came with it, and husband and wife rose together into the sky, never to be seen in Qin again — leaving the duke a terrace, a shrine, and the teaching that the flute of the immortals is played by two.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Liexian Zhuan, Xiao Shi biography, the ascent; not verbatim.

title.en: The Monkey, the Turtle, and the Crocodile
title.zh: 猴、龜與鱷

region.en: Batangas town, Luzon, Philippines (where the story is common)
region.zh: 菲律賓呂宋八打雁鎮（故事流行之地）

period: Tagalog oral fable; collected by D. S. Fansler, published 1921

source.work: Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 58 'The Monkey, the Turtle, and the Crocodile', eBook #8299

summary.en: The deceiving monkey offers two exhausted travelers — a turtle and a crocodile — lodging and food, leading them to a field of ripe pumpkins, then goes home to sleep. The plantation owner arrives, summons laborers with long poles and bolos, and the two beasts flee clinging together — the turtle refusing to release the crocodile's tail, 'or else there will be no one to push you' — until the men overtake and kill them both.
summary.zh: 慣於欺騙的猴子假意款待兩位疲憊旅人——龜與鱷——領他們到熟南瓜田飽餐一頓後自回家睡覺。園主回來，召來持長棍與波洛刀的工人；二獸倉皇奔逃，龜仍死抓鱷尾——『不放，不然誰來推你』——終被追上，雙雙喪命。

sensitivity.note: Tagalog fable recorded by Fansler from a Hilario narrator; archival record. A compensation story in which the monkey gets even with his two traditional opponents.

passages.text: There was once a monkey who used to deceive everybody whom he met, and as is the case with most deceivers, he had many enemies who tried to kill him. One day, walking in the streets of his native town, he met in a by-lane a turtle and a crocodile so tired they could hardly breathe. 'I'll try to deceive these slow creatures of the earth,' said the monkey to himself, and approached them with kind words. The two travelers, so much affected, told him all about themselves with the greatest candor: they were strangers from their native town, not knowing where to get food or spend the cold night. 'I'll conduct you to a place where you can spend the night and get all you want to eat,' said the monkey.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 58 'The Monkey, the Turtle, and the Crocodile'; not verbatim.

passages.text: He brought them to a field full of ripe pumpkins — 'Eat all the pumpkins you want, and then rest here. Meanwhile I'll go home and take my sleep, too' — and while the two hungry travelers enjoyed a hearty meal, the owner of the plantation happened to pass by. Seeing the crocodile, he called to his laborers to bring long poles and their bolos. The turtle clung to the tail of the crocodile, and away they went. 'Don't cling to my tail! I cannot run fast if you cling to my tail. Let go! for the men will soon overtake us,' said the crocodile. 'I have to cling to your tail, or else there will be no one to push you,' said the turtle. But their attempt to escape was unsuccessful: the men overtook them and killed them both. Such was the unhappy end of the turtle and the crocodile. Moral: Never trust a new friend or an old enemy.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 58 'The Monkey, the Turtle, and the Crocodile'; not verbatim.

title.en: The Iguana and the Turtle
title.zh: 鬣蜥與海龜

region.en: Binalonan, Pangasinan, Luzon, Philippines (where the story is fairly common)
region.zh: 菲律賓呂宋邦阿西楠省比納隆安（故事流行之地）

period: Pangasinan oral fable; collected by D. S. Fansler, published 1921

source.work: Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 59 'The Iguana and the Turtle', eBook #8299

summary.en: Caught poaching in a pond-owner's pond, the turtle persuades the wife-hungry iguana to swap places by pretending he is tied there for refusing to marry the old man's daughter. The iguana cries 'I want to marry your daughter' until beaten at; later the turtle tricks him into putting his mouth between two wind-rubbed bamboos to hear 'the pipe of my grandfather up there' — his mouth badly pinched, he falls, and the turtle disappears.
summary.zh: 海龜在塘主池中偷魚被捕，拴於屋下；他謊稱『老翁逼婚、我不肯』，誘得想娶妻的鬣蜥換位受縛。鬣蜥連喊『我要娶你的女兒』直至挨打掙脫；再遇海龜時，又被騙去聽風中相磨的雙竹——『那是我祖父的笛聲』——竹片夾嘴，跌落於地，海龜早已不見蹤影。

sensitivity.note: Pangasinan fable recorded by Fansler from a Guico narrator; archival record. Fansler compares the related Tinguian tale (Fay-Cooper Cole, No. 78) and a Borneo mouse-deer story.

passages.text: Once upon a time there lived two good friends, an iguana and a turtle, who always went fishing together. One day the turtle invited the iguana to catch fish in a certain pond that he knew of; after about two hours the old man who owned the pond came along, the iguana escaped, but the turtle was caught. The old man took the turtle home, tied a string around its neck, and fastened it under the house. Early in the morning the iguana wandered everywhere looking for his friend and finally found him under the old man's house, tied to a post.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 59 'The Iguana and the Turtle'; not verbatim.

passages.text: 'What are you doing here, my friend?' said the iguana. 'That old man wants me to marry his daughter, but I do not want to marry her,' said the turtle. The iguana, who very much wanted a wife, was delighted at this chance, and asked to be allowed to take the turtle's place; the turtle consented, the iguana released the turtle and was tied up in his place, and the turtle made off as fast as he could. When the old man woke up he heard some one saying over and over again, 'I want to marry your daughter'; angry, he went down and found the iguana saying it, and picked up a big stick to beat its head — but the iguana cut the string and ran away.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 59 'The Iguana and the Turtle'; not verbatim.

passages.text: On his way he came across the turtle again, listening to the sound produced by the rubbing of two bamboos when the wind blew. 'What! are you here again?' said the iguana. 'Be quiet! I am listening to the pipe of my grandfather up there. Don't you hear it?' said the turtle. The iguana wanted to see the turtle's grandfather, so he climbed up the tree and put his mouth between the two bamboos that were rubbing together; his mouth was badly pinched, and he fell down to the ground. The turtle meanwhile had disappeared. Moral: This teaches that the one who believes foolishly will be injured.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 59 'The Iguana and the Turtle'; not verbatim.

title.en: The Trial among the Animals: Sinukuan's Court on Mt. Arayat
title.zh: 動物受審：阿拉亞特山蘇努庫安法庭

region.en: Mount Arayat, Pampanga, Luzon, Philippines
region.zh: 菲律賓呂宋邦板牙省阿拉亞特山

period: Pampangan oral legend; collected by D. S. Fansler, published 1921

source.work: Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 60a 'The Trial among the Animals', eBook #8299

summary.en: Sinukuan, driven from his town by envy of his strength, dwells in a cave of Mount Arayat, wins the friendship of the animals by taking whatever form they do, and is made their judge. A noisy frog blames the turtle carrying his house, the turtle blames the firefly playing with fire, the firefly blames the mosquito's dagger — each freed with a good reason — until the mosquito, without excuse, is sentenced to three days' imprisonment and loses his voice: since then the male mosquito has had none and fears to carry his dagger.
summary.zh: 蘇努庫安因力大遭人妒恨，退居阿拉亞特山洞穴，能化身任何前來的動物，被眾獸奉為法官。夜噪的蛙推諿於『背屋的龜』，龜推諿於『玩火的螢』，螢推諿於『帶匕首的蚊』——個個理由得直、當庭開釋；唯有蚊子無辭可辯，被判三日監禁，從此失聲——公蚊啞然，且不敢再帶匕首。

sensitivity.note: Pampangan tale recorded by Fansler from a Pineda narrator; archival record. Sinukuan is the great Pampangan mountain-spirit of Mt. Arayat; sacred-place tag marks the cave court. The 'clock' story chain has four further Philippine variants (The Pugu's Case, Why Mosquitoes Hum, A Tyrant, The Bacuit's Case).

passages.text: In ancient times Sinukuan, the judge of the animals, lived in one of the caves of Mount Arayat. He had formerly lived in a neighboring town; but, since he was so brave and strong, the people began to envy him, then to hate him, and at last made so many plots against his life that he gave up all his property and friends in the town, and went to live in Mount Arayat, where he devoted all his time to gaining the friendship of the animals there. It was not hard for Sinukuan to win the love of the animals, for he had the power of changing himself into whatever form he pleased, and always took the form of those animals who came to him; before long all the animals realized the power, wisdom, and justice of their good companion, and made him their judge.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 60 'The Trial among the Animals'; not verbatim.

passages.text: One day a bird came to Sinukuan's court and asked him to punish the frog for being so noisy during the night. The frog answered respectfully, 'Sir, I was only crying for help, because the turtle was carrying his house on his back, and I feared that I might be buried under it' — and was freed. The turtle, in turn, replied that he carried his house because the firefly was playing with fire and he was afraid it might set fire to his home: 'Is it not right to protect one's house from fire?' — and was freed. The firefly said he had no other means to protect himself from the sharp-pointed dagger of the mosquito — and was liberated too. Finally the mosquito was tried; and, since he did not have any good reason to give for carrying his dagger, Sinukuan sentenced him to three days' imprisonment. The mosquito was obliged to submit; and it was during this confinement that he lost his voice. Ever since, the male mosquito has had no voice, and he has been afraid to carry his dagger, for fear of greater punishment.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 60 'The Trial among the Animals'; not verbatim.

title.en: Why Mosquitoes Hum and Try to Get into the Holes of Our Ears
title.zh: 蚊為何嗡嗡繞耳

region.en: Bohol, central Philippines (tale's home province)
region.zh: 菲律賓薄荷島（故事原鄉）

period: Visayan oral etiological tale; collected by D. S. Fansler, published 1921

source.work: Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 60c 'Why Mosquitoes hum and try to get into the Holes of our Ears', eBook #8299

summary.en: Crab-king Mangla of old Bohol orders the bataktak to guard his house in silence; their laughter at a snoring king during heavy rain leads to a trial-chain: the bataktak laughed seeing Hu-man carrying his house, Hu-man for fear of Aninipot's fire, Aninipot because Lamoc the mosquito kept biting him. When Lamoc is summoned he pre-arranges his companions to follow, bites the king's face, and is killed by the sheriff Cagang, whose pursuers cannot enter his deep burrow — they remain humming around the doors; the mosquitoes mistake the holes of our ears for the house of Cagang, and that is why they hum about our ears.
summary.zh: 古時薄荷島蟹王曼格拉令小蟹守夜禁聲；大雨之夜眾蟹見『人背屋』而笑，被審——人因怕螢火蟲背屋、螢火蟲因蚊叮而持火。蚊王拉莫克早令同伴跟隨，到場便咬王面，被郡守卡岡誅殺；其同伴追至卡岡深居的地下巢穴，無法攻入，遂終日繞門嗡嗡——今人耳孔被誤作卡岡之家，蚊聲因此繞耳不絕。

sensitivity.note: Visayan etiological tale recorded by Fansler from a Torralba narrator (Bohol); archival record. Explains mosquito humming as the siege of the crab-sheriff's burrow.

passages.text: In those very early times, in the province of Bohol, there lived a creature called Mangla; he was king of the crabs. One night, tired and sleepy, Mangla ordered his old sheriff Cagang, leader of the small land-crabs, to call his followers, the Bataktak, before him, and told them: 'You must all watch my house while I am sleeping; but do not make any noise that will waken me.' While he was snoring, it began to rain so hard that the guards could not help laughing. The king awoke very angry, but being still tired and sleepy, waited till morning, and then asked the Bataktak why they had laughed when he had told them not to make any noise.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 60 'Why Mosquitoes Hum'; not verbatim.

passages.text: The Bataktak answered softly, 'We could not help laughing, because last night we saw our old friend Hu-man carrying his house on his shoulder' — and the king pardoned them, then summoned Hu-man, who replied humbly that he was carrying his house because Aninipot was bringing fire and he was afraid his only dwelling would be burned. Aninipot, summoned next, answered in a trembling voice that he was carrying fire because Lamoc was always trying to bite him, and to protect himself he would carry fire all the time. The king realized there was a great deal of trouble brewing in his kingdom, and sent for Lamoc — who, before leaving his own house, had told all his companions to follow him, for he expected trouble.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 60 'Why Mosquitoes Hum'; not verbatim.

passages.text: Before Lamoc reached the palace the king was already shouting with rage, so Lamoc approached the king and bit his face. Mangla cried out, 'It is true, what I heard from Bataktak, Hu-man, and Aninipot!' and ordered his sheriff to kill Lamoc; Cagang killed him, but Lamoc's companions, bent on avenging the murder, rushed at him and followed him to his home — very deep under the ground, where they could not get in, so they remained and hummed around the door. Even to-day at the doors of the houses of Cagang and his followers there are many friends of Lamoc humming and trying to go inside. It is said that the Lamoc mistake the holes of our ears for the house of Cagang, and that that is the reason mosquitoes hum about our ears now.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 60 'Why Mosquitoes Hum'; not verbatim.

title.en: A Tyrant: The King Who Died Swatting a Mosquito
title.zh: 暴君之死：拍蚊而亡

region.en: Jaen, Nueva Ecija, Luzon, Philippines (narrator's home town)
region.zh: 菲律賓呂宋新怡詩夏省哈恩（敘述者故鄉）

period: Tagalog oral tale; collected by D. S. Fansler, published 1921

source.work: Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 60d 'A Tyrant', eBook #8299

summary.en: A tyrant's law of silence is extended to the animals; a croaking frog is tried, and excuses himself for laughing at the snail carrying his house; the snail fears the firefly's fire; the firefly fears the mosquito's bite. Tired of the trial, the king forbids the mosquito ever to bite again and seizes his mallet; the mosquito alights on the king's forehead, the blow kills the insect — and ends the tyranny with it.
summary.zh: 暴君禁聲之律竟施於動物。蛙因『笑蝸牛背屋』受審；蝸牛怕螢火燒屋；螢火怕蚊叮。國王厭倦長審，下令蚊蟲永不許叮人，並舉槌欲擊；蚊飛落國王額頭，一槌下去蚊死——暴政亦隨之而終。

sensitivity.note: Tagalog tale recorded by Fansler from an Esquivel narrator; archival record. Fourth link of the 'clock' story chain; moral: It is foolish to carry matters to extremes.

passages.text: Once there lived a tyrannical king. One of his laws prohibited the people from talking loudly; even when this law had been put in force he was still not satisfied, so he ordered the law to be enforced among the animals. One of his officers once heard a frog croak, caught it, and carried it before the king. 'Don't you know that there is a law prohibiting men and animals from making a noise?' began the trial. 'Yes, your Majesty, but I could not help laughing to see the snail carrying his house with him wherever he goes,' said the frog — and the king was satisfied and dismissed him.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 60 'A Tyrant'; not verbatim.

passages.text: The snail said he was always afraid the firefly was going to burn his house; the firefly said the mosquitoes would bite him if he did not carry his fire; and the mosquito, asked why he was always trying to bite some one, said, 'Why, sir, I cannot live without biting somebody.' The king was tired of the long trial, so with the mosquito he determined to end it: 'From now on you must not bite anybody. You have no right to do so.' When the mosquito tried to protest the sentence, the king seized his mallet and determined to crush him with it; but the mosquito alighted on the forehead of the king. The king became very angry at this insult and hit the mosquito hard — he killed the mosquito, but he also put an end to his own tyranny. Moral: It is foolish to carry matters to extremes.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 60 'A Tyrant'; not verbatim.

title.en: The Greedy Crow
title.zh: 貪心的烏鴉

region.en: Taal, Batangas, Luzon, Philippines (narrator's home town)
region.zh: 菲律賓呂宋八打雁省塔阿爾（敘述者故鄉）

period: Tagalog oral fable; collected by D. S. Fansler, published 1921

source.work: Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 61 'The Greedy Crow', eBook #8299

summary.en: A crow eating his meat sees a kasaykasay fly past with a dead rat; enraged at being ignored, he abandons his own meal to chase the faster little bird, fails, and returns to find a hawk has carried off the meat — and the hawk, passing again, taunts him: 'I am very sorry for you.'
summary.zh: 烏鴉正食腐肉，見小雀卡賽卡賽叼死鼠掠過；小雀不理會他的呼喝，烏鴉怒而棄食追趕，卻追不上。折返樹頭，肉已被路過的老鷹叼走；鷹再度經過時嘲笑道：『現在告訴你是我拿的——我真為你難過。』

sensitivity.note: Tagalog fable recorded by Fansler from a Gaa narrator; archival record. Fansler considers it native, distantly related to the Culladhanuggaha-jataka (No. 374) and 'The Dog and his Shadow.'

passages.text: One day a crow found a piece of meat on the ground, picked it up, and flew to the top of a tree to eat it. A kasaykasay, a small bird, passed by carrying a dead rat and flying very fast. The crow called to her, 'Kasaykasay, where did you get that dead rat that you have?' But the small bird did not answer: she flew on her way. When the crow saw that she paid no attention to him, he was very angry, and called out, 'Kasaykasay, Kasaykasay, stop and give me a piece of that rat, or I will follow you and take the whole thing for myself!' Still the small bird paid no attention to him. At last, full of greed and rage, the crow determined to have the rat by any means, and left the meat he was eating to fly after the small creature — but although she was only a little bird, the Kasaykasay could fly faster than the crow, and he could not catch her.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 61 'The Greedy Crow'; not verbatim.

passages.text: While the crow was chasing the Kasaykasay, a hawk happened to pass by the tree where the crow had left his meat, saw it, and at once seized it in his claws and flew away. Though the crow pursued the Kasaykasay a long time, he could not overtake her, and gave up at last; but when he came to the spot and found the meat gone, he was almost ready to die of disappointment and hunger. By and by the hawk which had taken the meat passed the tree again and called to the crow, 'Mr. Crow, do you know that I am the one who took your meat? If not, I will tell you now, and I am very sorry for you.' The crow did not answer, for he was so tired and weak that he could hardly breathe. Moral: Do not be greedy. Be contented with what you have, and do not wish for what you do not own.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 61 'The Greedy Crow'; not verbatim.

title.en: The Humming-Bird and the Carabao
title.zh: 蜂鳥與水牛

region.en: Cavite province, Luzon, Philippines (narrator's home province)
region.zh: 菲律賓呂宋甲米地省（敘述者故鄉）

period: Tagalog oral fable; collected by D. S. Fansler, published 1921

source.work: Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 62 'The Humming-Bird and the Carabao', eBook #8299

summary.en: A tiny humming-bird bets the carabao he can drink more river water. The carabao drinks against the rising tide until he nearly bursts — 'you have added more water to the river instead' — while the little bird merely dips his bill and waits for the ebb, 'drinking' as the river empties. The beaten carabao is left stupefied by all the water he swallowed.
summary.zh: 蜂鳥誇口喝水勝過水牛。漲潮之際，水牛拚命吞飲，肚子將裂——『你沒喝，倒往河裡添水了』——蜂鳥僅將喙點入水中，靜候退潮，『喝乾』了整條河。水牛被大量河水脹得頭昏眼花，認輸認得莫名其妙。

sensitivity.note: Tagalog fable recorded by Fansler from a Lopez narrator (Cavite); archival record. Fansler compares the nearly identical North Borneo tale 'The Kandowei and the Kerbau.'

passages.text: One hot April morning a carabao was resting under the shade of a quinine-tree which grew near the mouth of a large river, when a humming-bird alighted on one of the small branches above him. After the friendly greeting, little Hum said he was so thirsty that he had come down to drink, and the carabao answered jestingly, 'I wonder how much you can drink! You are so small, that a drop ought to be more than enough to satisfy you.' 'Yes, Friend Carabao? I bet you that I can drink more than you can! You drink first, and we shall see.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 62 'The Humming-Bird and the Carabao'; not verbatim.

passages.text: So old carabao, ignorant of the trick that was being played on him, walked to the bank of the river and began to drink. He drank and drank and drank; but it so happened that the tide was rising, and, no matter how much he swallowed, the water in the river kept getting higher and higher. At last he could drink no more, and the humming-bird began to tease him: 'Why, Friend Carabao, you have not drunk anything. It seems to me that you have added more water to the river instead.' 'You fool!' answered the carabao angrily, 'can't you see that my stomach is almost bursting?'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 62 'The Humming-Bird and the Carabao'; not verbatim.

passages.text: But the humming-bird only pretended to drink. He knew that the tide would soon be going out, so he just put his bill in the water, and waited until the tide did begin to ebb. The water of the river began to fall also. The carabao noticed the change, but he could not comprehend it; he was surprised, and agreed that he had been beaten. Little Hum flew away, leaving poor old Carabao stupefied and hardly able to move, because of the great quantity of water he had drunk.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 62 'The Humming-Bird and the Carabao'; not verbatim.

title.en: The Camanchile and the Passion
title.zh: 卡曼奇勒樹與西番蓮

region.en: Ilagan, Isabela, Luzon, Philippines (narrator's home town)
region.zh: 菲律賓呂宋伊莎貝拉省伊拉甘（敘述者故鄉）

period: Ilocano oral fable; collected by D. S. Fansler, published 1921

source.work: Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 63 'The Camanchile and the Passion', eBook #8299

summary.en: A flowerless camanchile-tree laments that travelers pass him by, and the low-growing Passion vine climbs him to display her blossoms on his crown. Months later the tree realizes he is being smothered and begs her to leave; Passion will not go, and Camanchile dies. Moral: Be yourself.
summary.zh: 無花的卡曼奇勒樹嘆息旅人不屑一顧；低矮的西番蓮藤攀上樹冠，以花朵為其添彩。數月後樹木窒息難耐，哀求藤蔓離開；西番蓮不肯，卡曼奇勒遂枯死。寓意：做你自己。

sensitivity.note: Ilocano fable recorded by Fansler from a Maramag narrator; archival record. Fansler compares the Palasa-jataka (No. 370) on a tree destroyed by a parasitic banyan-shoot.

passages.text: Once upon a time there grew in a forest a large camanchile-tree with spreading branches. Near it grew many other trees with beautiful fragrant flowers that attracted travellers; the camanchile had no fragrant flowers, but its crown was beautifully shaped, for the leaves received as much light as the leaves of the other trees. Yet the beauty of the crown proved of no attraction, and travellers passed the tree by.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 63 'The Camanchile and the Passion'; not verbatim.

passages.text: One day Camanchile exclaimed aloud, 'Oh, what a dreary life I lead! I would that I had flowers like the others, so that travellers would visit me often!' A vine by the name of Passion, which grew near by and received only a small amount of light, heard the exclamation and thought this its opportunity to improve its condition: 'Oh, that's easy! Just let me climb on you, and I'll display on your crown my beautiful flowers. Then many persons will come to see you.' Camanchile consented, and after a few days Passion reached the top of the tree and soon covered the crown.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 63 'The Camanchile and the Passion'; not verbatim.

passages.text: A few months later Camanchile realized that he was being smothered: he could not get light, so he asked Passion to leave him. 'O Passion! what pain I am in! I can't get light. Your beauty is of no value. I am being smothered: so leave me, I beg of you!' Passion would not leave Camanchile, however, and so Camanchile died. Moral: Be yourself.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 63 'The Camanchile and the Passion'; not verbatim.

title.en: Auac and Lamiran: The Hawk Who Sang Away His Fish
title.zh: 奧瓦克與拉米蘭：唱掉魚的鷹

region.en: Arayat, Pampanga, Luzon, Philippines (where the story is well known)
region.zh: 菲律賓呂宋邦板牙省阿拉亞特（故事著名之地）

period: Pampangan oral fable; collected by D. S. Fansler, published 1921

source.work: Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 64 'Auac and Lamiran', eBook #8299

summary.en: The hawk Auac, dining on a stolen salted fish, is flattered by the squirrel Lamiran — his shiny feathers, his kingly gait — until he is asked to sing. Opening his beak with 'Uac-uac-uac-uac!', he drops the fish, and Lamiran gets it. A heron on a carabao's back delivers the moral: do not always believe what others tell you, and remember that ill-gotten gains never prosper.
summary.zh: 鷹奧瓦克享用偷來的鹹魚時，被松鼠拉米蘭連番奉承——羽毛油亮、步態如王——直至被請求一展歌喉。牠張口『哇—哇—哇』，魚落於地，為松鼠所得。近旁水牛背上的蒼鷺贈言：勿盡信他人之言，且記『不義之財終不昌』。

sensitivity.note: Pampangan fable recorded by Fansler from a Villegas narrator; archival record. Philippine form of the Fox-and-Crow type; Fansler compares the Jambu-khadaka-jataka (No. 294) and Anta-jataka (No. 295).

passages.text: Once Auac, a hawk, stole a salted fish which was hanging in the sun to dry, and flew with it to a branch of a camanchile-tree, where he sat down and began to eat. As he was eating, Lamiran, a squirrel who had his house in a hole at the foot of the tree, looked up and said, 'What beautiful shiny black feathers you have, Auac!' When he heard this praise the hawk looked very dignified, nevertheless he was much pleased, and fluttered his wings. 'You are especially beautiful, Auac, when you walk; for you are very graceful,' continued the squirrel, and Auac, not understanding the trick, hopped along the branch with the air of a king.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 64 'Auac and Lamiran'; not verbatim.

passages.text: 'I heard some one say yesterday that your voice is so soft and sweet, that every one who listens to your song is charmed. Please let me hear some of your notes, you handsome Auac!' said the cunning Lamiran. Auac, feeling more proud and dignified than ever, opened his mouth and sang, 'Uac-uac-uac-uac!' As he uttered his notes, the fish in his beak fell to the ground, and Lamiran got it. A heron which was standing on the back of a water-buffalo near by saw the affair, and said, 'Auac, let me give you a piece of advice. Do not always believe what others tell you, but think for yourself; and remember that ill-gotten gains never prosper.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 64 'Auac and Lamiran'; not verbatim.

title.en: Why the Ant Is Not So Venomous as the Snake
title.zh: 螞蟻之毒為何不及蛇

region.en: Lipa, Batangas, Luzon, Philippines (tale recorded only here)
region.zh: 菲律賓呂宋八打雁省利帕（此故事僅見於此地）

period: Tagalog oral etiological tale; collected by D. S. Fansler, published 1921

source.work: Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 65 'Why the Ant is not so Venomous as the Snake', eBook #8299

summary.en: God first created the earth, then threw a rock from it onto the surface, breathing life into the fragments. The snake asks for the power to kill the rebellious, receives poison for its teeth; the ant, overjoyed at receiving the same privilege, runs off at such speed that it pays no attention when God calls — so God, enraged, takes away some of the ant's power, and the ant's bite is not so poisonous as the snake's. In a second Lipa telling, it is Bathala who slighted by a lazy ant transfers its intended gift to the snake and condemns ants to be pinched to death by those they bite.
summary.zh: 上帝造地後，又擲石碎塊、吹入生氣。蛇求誅惡之力，得齒中劇毒；螞蟻獲賜同權後狂喜奔走，上帝呼喚竟不應——上帝震怒，收回其部分之力。故今日蟻毒不及蛇毒。另一利帕傳說中，懶蟻怠慢巴哈拉，蛇得其原賜之能，蟻族則註定被其所咬者捏死。

sensitivity.note: Tagalog etiological tale recorded by Fansler from an Africa narrator (Lipa, Batangas); archival record. Fansler notes a second local variant invoking Bathala; the tale is unrecorded outside Lipa.

passages.text: God first created the earth. Then he took a rock from the earth and threw it on the terrestrial surface; when the rock was broken into many small pieces, he breathed into them the breath of life, and they became living creatures. Among these creatures were the snake and the ant. One day the snake went to God to ask for power to kill all those that were rebellious and troublesome, and God answered, 'Hereafter you are endowed with the power to store in your teeth this poison. When you bite the vile and contemptible, inject into the wound some of this poison, and they will be killed; but first of all, observe their actions, and be conscientious and thoughtful.' The snake returned to the earth in great joy.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 65 'Why the Ant is not so Venomous as the Snake'; not verbatim.

passages.text: When the ant heard that the snake was endowed with such power, it at once went to God to ask that the same privilege be granted it. 'Give me the same power, and I will be of great aid to the snake in destroying sinners,' it said; and God, thinking that the snake might need an assistant, gave the ant the same privilege that he had given the snake. The ant was so greatly overjoyed that it ran as fast as it could to the earth; when God saw it running he called to the ant, but it paid no attention to him. Then God, being very much enraged, took away some of the ant's power, lest the ant might use it unreasonably. And so to-day the ant's bite is not so poisonous as the snake's.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 65 'Why the Ant is not so Venomous as the Snake'; not verbatim.

title.en: Why Locusts Are Harmful
title.zh: 蝗害之始

region.en: Lipa, Batangas, Luzon, Philippines (with Bicol and Zambales variants)
region.zh: 菲律賓呂宋八打雁省利帕（另有比科爾、三描禮士變體）

period: Tagalog oral etiological tale; collected by D. S. Fansler, published 1921

source.work: Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 66 'Why Locusts are Harmful', eBook #8299

summary.en: In the dawn of humanity angels headed by Satanas revolt against God; in battle Satanas throws a handful of sand into God's face, and God laughs — 'I turn the sand back to thee. The particles shall become the scourge of all ages to thee and to thy followers' — and the sand becomes a mighty swarm of locusts. Bicol and Zambales variants explain the pest instead from a greedy datu's exploding granaries and a goddess-beggar denied shelter by an ungrateful rich farmer.
summary.zh: 人類之晨，撒塔納斯率天使叛上帝；戰中撒沙入上帝之面。上帝大笑：『沙還於你——這些微粒將成為你與你的追隨者萬世之禍！』言畢沙粒化作鋪天蝗群。比科爾變體謂貪婪達圖糧倉爆裂、稻米化蟲；三描禮士變體謂富農拒施捨喬裝乞婦的財富女神，其稻穀化為蝗災。

sensitivity.note: Tagalog etiological tale recorded by Fansler from an Africa narrator; archival record. The notes' Bicol ('Origin of Locusts' from a hoarding datu) and Zambales (Kayamanan the goddess of riches disguised as a beggar) variants are paraphrased in the final passage as named variants.

passages.text: During the dawn of humanity, some angels headed by Satanas revolted against God; they wanted to establish a kingdom for themselves. In a battle against the army of God, in which God himself was present, Satanas threw a handful of sand into God's face; but the heavenly monarch just laughed, and said, 'I turn the sand back to thee. The particles shall become the scourge of all ages to thee and to thy followers, O Satanas!' No sooner had God uttered these words than the particles of sand became a mighty swarm of locusts that flew in all directions — such was the beginning of the pest.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 66 'Why Locusts are Harmful'; not verbatim.

passages.text: A Bicol variant explains the pest from greed: a valley datu hoarded his people's rice until, in a famine year, seven starving petitioners came begging and the datu, lunging at them from his ladder, fell and was left for dead; the next morning his bursting granaries exploded, and all the rice flew away in the form of insects — the doron — vanishing from his sight. In a Zambales variant an ambitious farmer, enriched by the goddess Kayamanan beyond six full barns, neglected his thank-feasts and drove away a beggar at whose plea he threatened to loose his dog; the beggar, who was the goddess in disguise, asked God for the power of changing anything to any form she wished, and doomed his rice to turn to a swarm of locusts which would destroy the crops of farmers everywhere — and the punishment was carried out, leaving the farmer destitute.
passages.note: Paraphrase of the variants printed in Fansler's notes to Tale 66 (Bicol by Maximina Navarro; Zambales by Felix de la Llana); not verbatim.

title.en: How Lansones Became Edible
title.zh: 蘭撒果如何變得可食

region.en: Laguna de Bay region, Luzon, Philippines (Paete and La Laguna versions)
region.zh: 菲律賓呂宋內湖灣區（派提與內湖省版本）

period: Tagalog oral etiological tale; collected by D. S. Fansler, published 1921

source.work: Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 67 'How Lansones became Edible', eBook #8299

summary.en: Lansones fruit was once so poisonous its juice could bring leprosy. A starving religious pilgrim in the forest is fed the deadly fruit by an angel from heaven, and his hunger is removed — ever since, lansones have been good to eat, and all the fruits still bear the marks of the angel's fingers. In the Paete saint-legend, it is the Virgin Mary walking with her child who pinches the pulp with her white fingers, and the finger-prints of the Virgin may be seen in any lanzon opened today.
summary.zh: 昔日蘭撒果劇毒，汁液可致癩病。朝聖老者在林中飢疲交加，天使奉天而來，親手摘果餵之，飢餓頓消——自此蘭撒果甘美可食，果肉上至今留有天使指痕。派提鎮聖像傳說則謂聖母攜聖子親指甲果，開果可見聖母指印。

sensitivity.note: Tagalog etiological tale recorded by Fansler from an Africa narrator; archival record. Fansler notes the name-play lanson/lason ('poison') and the Paete Virgin-Mary legend (Benitez). Christianity-inflected etiology of a Malaysian fruit tree.

passages.text: Once upon a time the fruit of the lansone-tree was very poisonous; its very juice could make a man sick with leprosy. One day a very religious old man was passing through a forest to attend the fiesta of the neighboring town. When he reached the middle of the thick wood he became very hungry and tired, and felt that he could go no farther; no matter where he looked he could see nothing but the poisonous lansone-trees. So he lay down on the soft grass. Hardly a moment had passed when a winged being from heaven approached him and said, 'My good Christian pilgrim, take some of these lansone-fruits, eat them, and you will be much relieved.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 67 'How Lansones became Edible'; not verbatim.

passages.text: At first the old man would not do it, but the angel picked some of the fruits and handed them to the pilgrim.
