This is the more probable as this misfortune is said to have happened to Osiris in the month of Hathor, precisely at that season of the year when, upon the cessation of the Etesian or north winds the Nile returns to its own bed, and leaves the country everywhere bare and naked. At this time the priests celebrate doleful rites, and they exhibit as a suitable representation of the grief of Isis a gilded ox covered with a fine black linen cloth.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Budge (1912), Plutarch sec. XXXIX.

passages.text: On the nineteenth of the month Pachons they march in procession to the sea, whither the priests and other officials carry the sacred chest, wherein is enclosed a small boat of gold; into this they first pour some water, and then all present cry out with a loud voice, 'Osiris is found.' This done, they throw some earth, scent, and spices into the water, and mix it well together, and work it up into the image of a crescent, which they afterwards dress in clothes. This shows that they regard the gods as the essence and power of water and earth.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Budge (1912), Plutarch sec. XXXIX.

title.en: The Column of Curses against Menes: The King Who Learned Poverty
title.zh: 詛咒美尼斯之柱：嘗貧之王

region.en: Thebes, Egypt (temple column inscribed with curses)
region.zh: 埃及底比斯（神廟刻咒之柱）

period: Story set in the reign of Tafnekht (24th Dynasty, c. 730 BCE), recorded in Plutarch, De Iside 8 (Budge translation 1912)

source.work: Legends of the Gods, trans. E. A. W. Budge (1912), Plutarch, The History of Isis and Osiris, sec. VIII

summary.en: King Technatis, eating mean soldier's food on the Arabian campaign and sleeping on the bare ground, conceived such love of poverty that with the priests' permission he raised in the temple of Thebes a column full of curses against Menes, the first king who had drawn the Egyptians from their frugal course of life.
summary.zh: 塔夫奈赫特王遠征時食兵卒之粗食、臥於赤地，遂生出對儉樸之深情，得祭司之許，於底比斯神廟立柱，刻滿詛咒——咒那第一位使埃及人離儉樸生活之王美尼斯。

sensitivity.note: Ancient anecdote-myth via Plutarch; no living community restrictions. Budge's footnote doubts Tafnekht's authority at Thebes.

passages.text: All agree, however, in saying that so great was the abhorrence which the ancient Egyptians expressed for whatever tended to promote luxury, expense, and voluptuousness, that in order to expose it as much as possible they erected a column in one of the temples of Thebes, full of curses against their king Meinis, who first drew them off from their former frugal and parsimonious course of life. The immediate cause for the erection of the pillar is thus given: Technatis, the father of Bocchoris, leading an army against the Arabians, and his baggage and provisions not coming up to him as soon as he expected, was therefore obliged to eat some of the very poor food which was obtainable, and having eaten, he lay down on the bare ground and slept very soundly. This gave him a great affection for a mean and frugal diet, and induced him to curse the memory of Meinis, and with the permission of the priests he made these curses public by cutting them upon a pillar.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Budge, Legends of the Gods (1912), Plutarch sec. VIII. / Verbatim excerpt of Budge (1912), Plutarch sec. VIII.

title.en: Ares Comes to His Mother: The Battle of Staves at Papremis
title.zh: 阿瑞斯探母：帕普雷米斯的棍戰

region.en: Papremis, Nile Delta, Egypt (festival of the war-god)
region.zh: 埃及三角洲帕普雷米斯（戰神祭日）

period: Recorded by Herodotus, Histories II.63 (5th century BCE; Macaulay translation 1890)

source.work: The History of Herodotus, trans. G. C. Macaulay (1890), Book II, secs. 62-63

summary.en: At the festival of the war-god (Ares) at Papremis, the image is drawn in its shrine toward the temple while a thousand men with clubs block the gate — for the god, once grown away from his mother, had to fight his way past her temple attendants to visit her; hence, say the priests, the ritual combat in his honor, in which heads are broken and (Egyptians insist) no one dies.
summary.zh: 帕普雷米斯戰神祭日，神像乘車欲入神廟，千名持棍者封門相拒——蓋因神自幼離母，長成後欲探母而不獲准入，遂引外人破門而入。祭司稱：此棍戰之禮即由此而立，且謂傷者眾而死者無。

sensitivity.note: Ancient ethnographic myth via Herodotus; no living community restrictions. 'ritual-origin' is the intended topic tag; see ledger note.

passages.text: At Papremis they do sacrifice and worship as elsewhere, and besides that, when the sun begins to go down, while some few of the priests are occupied with the image of the god, the greater number of them stand in the entrance of the temple with wooden clubs, and other persons to the number of more than a thousand men with purpose to perform a vow, these also having all of them staves of wood, stand in a body opposite to those: and the image, which is in a small shrine of wood covered over with gold, they take out on the day before to another sacred building.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Macaulay, Herodotus (1890), Book II.63.

passages.text: The few then who have been left about the image, draw a wain with four wheels, which bears the shrine and the image that is within the shrine, and the other priests standing in the gateway try to prevent it from entering, and the men who are under a vow come to the assistance of the god and strike them, while the others defend themselves. Then there comes to be a hard fight with staves, and they break one another's heads, and I am of opinion that many even die of the wounds they receive; the Egyptians however told me that no one died.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Macaulay, Herodotus (1890), Book II.63.

passages.text: This solemn assembly the people of the place say that they established for the following reason: — the mother of Ares, they say, used to dwell in this temple, and Ares, having been brought up away from her, when he grew up came thither desiring to visit his mother, and the attendants of his mother's temple, not having seen him before, did not permit him to pass in, but kept him away; and he brought men to help him from another city and handled roughly the attendants of the temple, and entered to visit his mother. Hence, they say, this exchange of blows has become the custom in honour of Ares upon his festival.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Macaulay (1890), Book II.63.

title.en: The Voyage to Bubastis: Egypt's Wildest Festival
title.zh: 赴布巴斯提斯之舟：埃及最狂歡的節日

region.en: Nile from the Delta towns to Bubastis (temple of Bastet, Greek Artemis)
region.zh: 尼羅河自三角洲諸城至布巴斯提斯（貝斯特/阿爾忒彌斯神廟）

period: Recorded by Herodotus, Histories II.59-60 (5th century BCE; Macaulay translation 1890)

source.work: The History of Herodotus, trans. G. C. Macaulay (1890), Book II, secs. 59-60

summary.en: The greatest of Egypt's pilgrim feasts: men and women sail to Bubastis together in one boat, women rattling sistra, men piping; at every riverside town the women jeer at the shore-women and dance, some pulling up their garments; at Bubastis more wine is drunk in the festival than in the rest of the year, and, the natives say, seven hundred myriads of people gather yearly.
summary.zh: 埃及最盛大的朝節：男女同舟赴布巴斯提斯，婦人搖鈴，男子吹笛；沿途每城，船上的女人向岸上的女人叫喊戲謔，且舞且起衣；至布巴斯提斯，一節所耗之酒多於全年其餘時日——當地人稱歲歲聚者達七十萬眾。

sensitivity.note: Ancient festival description via Herodotus; no living community restrictions.

passages.text: The Egyptians hold their solemn assemblies not once in the year but often, especially and with the greatest zeal and devotion at the city of Bubastis for Artemis, and next at Busiris for Isis; for in this last-named city there is a very great temple of Isis, and this city stands in the middle of the Delta of Egypt; now Isis is in the tongue of the Hellenes Demeter: thirdly, they have a solemn assembly at the city of Sais for Athene, fourthly at Heliopolis for the Sun (Helios), fifthly at the city of Buto in honour of Leto, and sixthly at the city of Papremis for Ares.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Macaulay, Herodotus (1890), Book II.59.

passages.text: Now, when they are coming to the city of Bubastis they do as follows: — they sail men and women together, and a great multitude of each sex in every boat; and some of the women have rattles and rattle with them, while some of the men play the flute during the whole time of the voyage, and the rest, both women and men, sing and clap their hands; and when as they sail they come opposite to any city on the way they bring the boat to land, and some of the women continue to do as I have said, others cry aloud and jeer at the women in that city, some dance, and some stand up and pull up their garments. This they do by every city along the river-bank; and when they come to Bubastis they hold festival celebrating great sacrifices, and more wine of grapes is consumed upon that festival than during the whole of the rest of the year. To this place (so say the natives) they come together year by year even to the number of seventy myriads of men and women, besides children.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Macaulay (1890), Book II.60.

title.en: The Black Doves of Thebes: The Origin of the Oracles
title.zh: 底比斯黑鴿：神諭之源

region.en: Thebes, Egypt (temple of Zeus/Amon; whence the oracle-priestesses were carried)
region.zh: 埃及底比斯（宙斯/阿蒙神廟；神諭女祭司自此被擄）

period: Recorded by Herodotus, Histories II.54-57 (5th century BCE; Macaulay translation 1890)

source.work: The History of Herodotus, trans. G. C. Macaulay (1890), Book II, secs. 54-57

summary.en: The priests of Theban Zeus/Amon claim two consecrated women were carried off by Phoenicians, one sold to Libya, one to Greece — founding the oracles of Ammon and of Dodona; the Dodona priestesses themselves say two black doves flew from Thebes, one to an oak at Dodona speaking with human voice, one bidding the Libyans make an oracle; Herodotus half-believes: the 'doves' were Egyptian women, whose foreign speech sounded like birds.
summary.zh: 底比斯阿蒙祭司稱：兩名侍神女子被腓尼基人擄走，一售利比亞、一售希臘——分別創立阿蒙與多多納神諭；多多納女祭司則言：兩隻黑鴿自底比斯飛出，一落橡樹作人言，一令利比亞人立神諭。希羅多德半信半疑：『鴿』實為埃及女子，其異語聽來如鳥啼。

sensitivity.note: Ancient origin myth via Herodotus; no living community restrictions.

passages.text: The priests of the Theban Zeus told me that two women in the service of the temple had been carried away from Thebes by Phenicians, and that they had heard that one of them had been sold to go into Libya and the other to the Hellenes; and these women, they said, were they who first founded the prophetic seats among the nations which have been named: and when I inquired whence they knew so perfectly of this tale which they told, they said in reply that a great search had been made by the priests after these women, and that they had not been able to find them, but they had heard afterwards this tale about them which they were telling.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Macaulay, Herodotus (1890), Book II.54.

passages.text: They say that two black doves flew from Thebes to Egypt, and came one of them to Libya and the other to their land. And this latter settled upon an oak-tree and spoke with human voice, saying that it was necessary that a prophetic seat of Zeus should be established in that place; and they supposed that that was of the gods which was announced to them, and made one accordingly: and the dove which went away to the Libyans, they say, bade the Libyans to make an Oracle of Ammon; and this also is of Zeus.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Macaulay (1890), Book II.55.

passages.text: Moreover, I think that the women were called doves by the people of Dodona for the reason that they were Barbarians and because it seemed to them that they uttered voice like birds; but after a time (they say) the dove spoke with human voice, that is when the woman began to speak so that they could understand; but so long as she spoke a Barbarian tongue she seemed to them to be uttering voice like a bird: for had it been really a dove, how could it speak with human voice? And in saying that the dove was black, they indicate that the woman was Egyptian.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Macaulay (1890), Book II.57.

title.en: Melampus Learns the Phallos Procession in Egypt
title.zh: 墨蘭普斯在埃及習得陽具遊行

region.en: Egyptian villages and Boeotia (transmission of the Dionysos rites)
region.zh: 埃及村莊與玻俄提亞（狄俄倪索斯祭祀之傳播）

period: Recorded by Herodotus, Histories II.48-49 (5th century BCE; Macaulay translation 1890)

source.work: The History of Herodotus, trans. G. C. Macaulay (1890), Book II, secs. 48-49

summary.en: Egyptian women carry cubit-high dancing figures of Dionysos with movable phallos through the villages behind a flute, singing his praises — the rites, says Herodotus, that Melampus son of Amytheon learned in Egypt and taught to the Greeks, who thereafter carried the phallos in procession for Dionysos.
summary.zh: 埃及婦女攜一肘高之狄俄倪索斯舞像巡行村落，像之陽具以線操動，笛聲前導，頌歌隨行——希羅多德謂：墨蘭普斯習此於埃及，而後傳授希臘人，故希臘有陽具遊行之祭。

sensitivity.note: Ancient ritual-origin account via Herodotus; no living community restrictions.

passages.text: Then for Dionysos on the eve of the festival each one kills a pig by cutting its throat before his own doors, and after that he gives the pig to the swineherd who sold it to him, to carry away again; and the rest of the feast of Dionysos is celebrated by the Egyptians in the same way as by the Hellenes in almost all things except choral dances, but instead of the phallos they have invented another contrivance, namely figures of about a cubit in height worked by strings, which women carry about the villages, with the privy member made to move and not much less in size than the rest of the body: and a flute goes before and they follow singing the praises of Dionysos.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Macaulay, Herodotus (1890), Book II.48.

passages.text: Now I think that Melampus the son of Amytheon was not without knowledge of these rites of sacrifice, but was acquainted with them: for Melampus is he who first set forth to the Hellenes the name of Dionysos and the manner of sacrifice and the procession of the phallos. Strictly speaking indeed, he when he made it known did not take in the whole, but those wise men who came after him made it known more at large. I say then that Melampus being a man of ability contrived for himself an art of divination, and having learnt from Egypt he taught the Hellenes many things, and among them those that concern Dionysos, making changes in some few points of them.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Macaulay (1890), Book II.49.

title.en: The Phoenix Carries Its Father to the Temple of the Sun
title.zh: 不死鳥負父赴日廟

region.en: Heliopolis, Egypt (temple of the Sun, where the phoenix appears)
region.zh: 埃及赫利奧波利斯（不死鳥顯現之日神廟）

period: Recorded by Herodotus, Histories II.73 (5th century BCE; Macaulay translation 1890)

source.work: The History of Herodotus, trans. G. C. Macaulay (1890), Book II, sec. 73

summary.en: The people of Heliopolis say the phoenix comes at intervals of five hundred years, when its father dies: partly gold-feathered and partly red, like an eagle in outline, it flies from Arabia bearing its father — plastered up in myrrh — to the temple of the Sun, and buries him there. Herodotus saw the bird only in painting, and says he cannot believe the story.
summary.zh: 赫利奧波利斯人言：不死鳥每五百年一至，值其父死時而來；羽半金半赤，形若鷹，自阿拉伯攜其父——以沒藥封裹——負至日神廟而葬之。希羅多德僅於畫中見之，自言未敢盡信。

sensitivity.note: Ancient wonder-tale via Herodotus; no living community restrictions. The Egyptian Bennu bird underlies the Greek phoenix.

passages.text: There is also another sacred bird called the phoenix which I did not myself see except in painting, for in truth he comes to them very rarely, at intervals, as the people of Heliopolis say, of five hundred years; and these say that he comes regularly when his father dies; and if he be like the painting, he is of this size and nature, that is to say, some of his feathers are of gold colour and others red, and in outline and size he is as nearly as possible like an eagle. This bird they say (but I cannot believe the story) contrives as follows: — setting forth from Arabia he conveys his father, they say, to the temple of the Sun plastered up in myrrh, and buries him in the temple of the Sun.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Macaulay, Herodotus (1890), Book II.73.

passages.text: And he conveys him thus: — he forms first an egg of myrrh as large as he is able to carry, and then he makes trial of carrying it, and when he has made trial sufficiently, then he hollows out the egg and places his father within it and plasters over with other myrrh that part of the egg where he hollowed it out to put his father in, and when his father is laid in it, it proves (they say) to be of the same weight as it was; and after he has plastered it up, he conveys the whole to Egypt to the temple of the Sun.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Macaulay (1890), Book II.73.

title.en: The Ibis and the Winged Serpents of Arabia
title.zh: 朱鷺與阿拉伯飛蛇

region.en: Mountain pass opposite Buto, edge of Egypt (where the ibis meets the flying serpents)
region.zh: 埃及邊境布托對面之山口（朱鷺迎擊飛蛇之地）

period: Recorded by Herodotus, Histories II.75-76 (5th century BCE; Macaulay translation 1890)

source.work: The History of Herodotus, trans. G. C. Macaulay (1890), Book II, secs. 75-76

summary.en: Each spring winged serpents fly from Arabia toward Egypt, and the ibises meet them at the narrow pass and kill them; heaps of their bones and spines cover the ground — the aition, Herodotus reports, of the ibis' great honour in Egypt, who saw the heaps himself and learned the tale from both Arabians and Egyptians.
summary.zh: 每歲春分，飛蛇自阿拉伯撲向埃及，朱鷺守狹口而擊殺之——蛇骨蛇棘遍堆於地，為埃及尊崇朱鷺之由。希羅多德自稱親見其堆，且此事得自阿拉伯人與埃及人兩方之口。

sensitivity.note: Ancient aition via Herodotus; no living community restrictions.

passages.text: There is a region moreover in Arabia, situated nearly over against the city of Buto, to which place I came to inquire about the winged serpents: and when I came thither I saw bones of serpents and spines in quantity so great that it is impossible to make report of the number, and there were heaps of spines, some heaps large and others less large and others smaller still than these, and these heaps were many in number. This region in which the spines are scattered upon the ground is of the nature of an entrance from a narrow mountain pass to a great plain, which plain adjoins the plain of Egypt; and the story goes that at the beginning of spring winged serpents from Arabia fly towards Egypt, and the birds called ibises meet them at the entrance to this country and do not suffer the serpents to go by but kill them. On account of this deed it is (say the Arabians) that the ibis has come to be greatly honoured by the Egyptians, and the Egyptians also agree that it is for this reason that they honour these birds.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Macaulay, Herodotus (1890), Book II.75. / Verbatim excerpt of Macaulay (1890), Book II.75.

title.en: Sesostris the Conqueror: Pillars, Scythians, and the Fire of Daphnai
title.zh: 征服者塞索斯特里斯：石柱、斯基泰與達夫奈之火

region.en: From the Erythraian Sea to the Phasis (Sesostris' march; symbolic pin at Daphnai, Pelusium)
region.zh: 自紅海至法西斯河（塞索斯特里斯之遠征；象徵定位於達夫奈/佩魯西翁）

period: Priests' account of an Old or New Kingdom conqueror, recorded by Herodotus, Histories II.102-110 (5th century BCE; Macaulay translation 1890)

source.work: The History of Herodotus, trans. G. C. Macaulay (1890), Book II, secs. 102-110

summary.en: Sesostris sails the Erythraian Sea, marches over the continent setting up pillars — brave nations get his name, cowards get the emblem of a woman — until he crosses to Europe and subdues the Scythians; returning through Daphnai, his brother invites him to a feast and piles the house with brushwood; his wife counsels laying two of his six sons upon the pyre as a bridge, and the king escapes over their bodies while the brothers burn.
summary.zh: 塞索斯特里斯先航紅海，後率大軍征陸，凡遇勇敢死戰之國則立柱刻名，懦弱者則刻女陰以辱之；及至歐洲，降斯基泰而返。歸途達夫奈，其弟邀宴，積薪焚宅；其妻獻策：以二子伏火為橋，王履之而過，二子焚死，餘者得生。

sensitivity.note: Ancient heroic legend via Herodotus; no living community restrictions. Egyptologists identify Sesostris with Senusret I/III or Ramesses II.

passages.text: Passing these by I shall make mention of the king who came after these, whose name was Sesostris. He (the priests said) first of all set out with ships of war from the Arabian gulf and subdued those who dwelt by the shores of the Erythraian Sea, until as he sailed he came to a sea which could no further be navigated by reason of shoals: then secondly, after he had returned to Egypt, according to the report of the priests he took a great army and marched over the continent, subduing every nation which stood in his way: and those of them whom he found valiant and fighting desperately for their freedom, in their lands he set up pillars ...; but as to those of whose cities he obtained possession without fighting or with ease, on their pillars he inscribed words after the same tenor as he did for the nations which had shown themselves courageous, and in addition he drew upon them the hidden parts of a woman, desiring to signify by this that the people were cowards and effeminate.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Macaulay, Herodotus (1890), Book II.102, condensed with ellipsis; not verbatim throughout.

passages.text: Thus doing he traversed the continent, until at last he passed over to Europe from Asia and subdued the Scythians and also the Thracians. These, I am of opinion, were the furthest people to which the Egyptian army came, for in their country the pillars are found to have been set up, but in the land beyond this they are no longer found.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Macaulay (1890), Book II.103.

passages.text: As this Egyptian Sesostris was returning and bringing back many men of the nations whose lands he had subdued, when he came (said the priests) to Daphnai in the district of Pelusion on his journey home, his brother to whom Sesostris had entrusted the charge of Egypt invited him and with him his sons to a feast; and then he piled the house round with brushwood and set it on fire: and Sesostris when he discovered this forthwith took counsel with his wife, for he was bringing with him (they said) his wife also; and she counselled him to lay out upon the pyre two of his sons, which were six in number, and so to make a bridge over the burning mass, and that they passing over their bodies should thus escape. This, they said, Sesostris did, and two of his sons were burnt to death in this manner, but the rest got away safe with their father.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Macaulay (1890), Book II.107.

title.en: Pheros Casts His Spear into the River: Ten Years Blind
title.zh: 斐羅斯擲矛入河：十年失明

region.en: The Nile in flood and the temple of the Sun, Heliopolis (Pheros' obelisks)
region.zh: 泛濫之尼羅與赫利奧波利斯日神廟（斐羅斯方尖碑）

period: Priests' account recorded by Herodotus, Histories II.111 (5th century BCE; Macaulay translation 1890)

source.work: The History of Herodotus, trans. G. C. Macaulay (1890), Book II, sec. 111

summary.en: In his eighteenth-cubit flood year, King Pheros in presumptuous folly hurls a spear into the eddies of the Nile and goes blind for ten years; the oracle of Buto promises sight if he washes his eyes with the tears of a woman faithful to her own husband — tested wife by wife until one cures him — and the king burns the faithless women alive in the city of Erythrabolos and weds the faithful one.
summary.zh: 尼羅漲至十八肘之歲，王斐羅斯愚妄投矛於漩流，遂盲十年；布托神諭許之：以忠於其夫之婦人之淚洗目可復明——逐一試之，至一婦而愈——王遂於埃里特拉波羅斯城焚諸不貞之婦，娶其貞者。

sensitivity.note: Ancient king-legend via Herodotus; no living community restrictions.

passages.text: Now after Sesostris had brought his life to an end, his son Pheros, they told me, received in succession the kingdom, and he made no warlike expedition, and moreover it chanced to him to become blind by reason of the following accident: — when the river had come down in flood rising to a height of eighteen cubits, higher than ever before that time, and had gone over the fields, a wind fell upon it and the river became agitated by waves: and this king (they say) moved by presumptuous folly took a spear and cast it into the midst of the eddies of the stream; and immediately upon this he had a disease of the eyes and was by it made blind.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Macaulay, Herodotus (1890), Book II.111.

passages.text: For ten years then he was blind, and in the eleventh year there came to him an oracle from the city of Buto saying that the time of his punishment had expired, and that he should see again if he washed his eyes with the water of a woman who had accompanied with her own husband only and had not knowledge of other men: and first he made trial of his own wife, and then, as he continued blind, he went on to try all the women in turn; and when he had at last regained his sight he gathered together all the women of whom he had made trial, excepting her by whose means he had regained his sight, to one city which now is named Erythrabolos, and having gathered them to this he consumed them all by fire, as well as the city itself; but as for her by whose means he had regained his sight, he had her himself to wife.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Macaulay (1890), Book II.111.

passages.text: Then after he had escaped the malady of his eyes he dedicated offerings at each one of the temples which were of renown, and especially (to mention only that which is most worthy of mention) he dedicated at the temple of the Sun works which are worth seeing, namely two obelisks of stone, each of a single block, measuring in length a hundred cubits each one and in breadth eight cubits.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Macaulay (1890), Book II.111.

title.en: Helen in Egypt: The Judgment of King Proteus at Memphis
title.zh: 海倫在埃及：孟菲斯王普羅透斯之審

region.en: Memphis, Egypt (the enclosure of Proteus and the temple of the foreign Aphrodite)
region.zh: 埃及孟菲斯（普羅透斯聖域與異邦阿佛洛狄忒神廟）

period: Priests' account recorded by Herodotus, Histories II.112-116 (5th century BCE; Macaulay translation 1890)

source.work: The History of Herodotus, trans. G. C. Macaulay (1890), Book II, secs. 112-116

summary.en: The Egyptian counter-story to the Trojan War: winds drove Alexander (Paris) and Helen to Egypt, where his slaves fled to the asylum of the temple of Heracles and accused him; King Proteus of Memphis summoned the seducer, condemned him — 'thou didst go in to the wife of thine own host' — kept Helen and the treasure for Menelaos, and sent Paris empty away; Herodotus swears Homer knew this version and turned from it.
summary.zh: 特洛伊戰爭之埃及異聞：風將帕里斯與海倫吹至埃及，其僕逃入赫拉克勒斯神廟聖域而發其罪；孟菲斯王普羅透斯召而審之——『汝通主母』——奪海倫與財留還墨涅拉俄斯，逐帕里斯空手而歸；希羅多德斷言荷馬知此說而捨之。

sensitivity.note: Ancient myth via Herodotus; no living community restrictions. Cross-tradition link: the Egyptian Helen episode behind Stesichorus' palinode and Euripides' Helen.

passages.text: After him, they said, there succeeded to the throne a man of Memphis, whose name in the tongue of the Hellenes was Proteus; for whom there is now a sacred enclosure at Memphis, very fair and well ordered, lying on that side of the temple of Hephaistos which faces the North Wind. Round about this enclosure dwell Phenicians of Tyre, and this whole region is called the Camp of the Tyrians. Within the enclosure of Proteus there is a temple called the temple of the 'foreign Aphrodite,' which temple I conjecture to be one of Helen the daughter of Tyndareus, not only because I have heard the tale how Helen dwelt with Proteus, but also especially because it is called by the name of the 'foreign Aphrodite.'
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Macaulay, Herodotus (1890), Book II.112.

passages.text: And the priests told me, when I inquired, that the things concerning Helen happened thus: — Alexander having carried off Helen was sailing away from Sparta to his own land, and when he had come to the Egean Sea contrary winds drove him from his course to the Sea of Egypt; and after that, since the blasts did not cease to blow, he came to Egypt itself, and in Egypt to that which is now named the Canobic mouth of the Nile and to Taricheiai. Now there was upon the shore, as still there is now, a temple of Heracles, in which if any man's slave take refuge and have the sacred marks set upon him, giving himself over to the god, it is not lawful to lay hands upon him.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Macaulay (1890), Book II.113.

passages.text: At length Proteus declared to them this sentence, saying, 'Were it not that I count it a matter of great moment not to slay any of those strangers who being driven from their course by winds have come to my land hitherto, I should have taken vengeance on thee on behalf of the man of Hellas, seeing that thou, most base of men, having received from him hospitality, didst work against him a most impious deed. For thou didst go in to the wife of thine own host; and even this was not enough for thee, but thou didst stir her up with desire and hast gone away with her like a thief.'
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Macaulay (1890), Book II.115.

title.en: Rhampsinitos and the Master Thief
title.zh: 拉美西尼圖斯與神偷

region.en: Memphis, Egypt (the stone treasury of the king)
region.zh: 埃及孟菲斯（王者石室寶庫）

period: Priests' tale recorded by Herodotus, Histories II.121 (5th century BCE; Macaulay translation 1890)

source.work: The History of Herodotus, trans. G. C. Macaulay (1890), Book II, sec. 121

summary.en: The treasury's own builder leaves his sons a removable stone; the thief caught in a trap sends his brother to cut off his head, the mother forces the survivor to reclaim the corpse, the guards are made drunk on wine-skins and shaved in mockery, and finally — at the king's own daughter's stews — the thief, clutching a dead man's arm in the dark, confesses his two crimes and escapes, winning pardon, a great reward, and the king's daughter.
summary.zh: 寶庫建造者臨終授子以可移之石；兄落阱，弟受命斷其首；母迫生者索還屍身——以酒囊灌醉守衛、剃其右頰以嘲之；末至王女之室，暗中持死人臂以代己，自陳兩樁罪——王服其智，赦而賞之，並以其女妻焉。

sensitivity.note: Ancient folk-tale via Herodotus; no living community restrictions. One of the oldest recorded trickster-cycle tales in world literature.

passages.text: This king, they said, got great wealth of silver, which none of the kings born after him could surpass or even come near to; and wishing to store his wealth in safety he caused to be built a chamber of stone, one of the walls whereof was towards the outside of his palace: and the builder of this, having a design against it, contrived as follows, that is, he disposed one of the stones in such a manner that it could be taken out easily from the wall either by two men or even by one. So when the chamber was finished, the king stored his money in it, and after some time the builder, being near the end of his life, called to him his sons (for he had two) and to them he related how he had contrived in building the treasury of the king, and all in forethought for them, that they might have ample means of living.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Macaulay, Herodotus (1890), Book II.121(a).

passages.text: When the thieves had come as at former times and one of them had entered, then so soon as he came near to one of the vessels he was straightway caught in the trap: and when he perceived in what evil case he was, straightway calling his brother he showed him what the matter was, and bade him enter as quickly as possible and cut off his head, for fear lest being seen and known he might bring about the destruction of his brother also. And to the other it seemed that he spoke well, and he was persuaded and did so; and fitting the stone into its place he departed home bearing with him the head of his brother.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Macaulay (1890), Book II.121(b-c).

passages.text: He contrived for his purpose a device as follows: — Providing himself with asses he filled some skins with wine and laid them upon the asses, and after that he drove them along: and when he came opposite to those who were guarding the corpse hung up, he drew towards him two or three of the necks of the skins and loosened the cords with which they were tied... and in the end he made them a present of one of the skins in addition to what they had. Upon that they lay down there without more ado, being minded to drink... Then as it was now far on in the night, he first took down the body of his brother, and then in mockery shaved the right cheeks of all the guards; and after that he put the dead body upon the asses and drove them away home.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Macaulay (1890), Book II.121(d).

passages.text: He caused his own daughter to sit in the stews, and enjoined her to receive all equally, and before having commerce with any one to compel him to tell her what was the most cunning and what the most unholy deed which had been done by him in all his life-time... the thief, hearing for what purpose this was done and having a desire to get the better of the king in resource, did thus: — from the body of one lately dead he cut off the arm at the shoulder and went with it under his mantle: and having gone in to the daughter of the king, and being asked that which the others also were asked, he related that he had done the most unholy deed when he cut off the head of his brother... and she when she heard it tried to take hold of him, but the thief held out to her in the darkness the arm of the corpse... but the thief left it in her hands and departed, escaping through the door. Rhampsinitos greatly marvelled at him, and gave him this daughter of his to wife, counting him to be the most knowing of all men.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Macaulay (1890), Book II.121(e-f).

title.en: Rhampsinitos Plays Dice with Demeter in Hades
title.zh: 拉美西尼圖斯冥府與得墨忒爾擲骰

region.en: The temple of Demeter, twenty furlongs from the city (symbolic pin, Egyptian underworld journey)
region.zh: 距城二十弗隆之地母神廟（象徵定位，埃及冥府之旅）

period: Priests' tale recorded by Herodotus, Histories II.122 (5th century BCE; Macaulay translation 1890)

source.work: The History of Herodotus, trans. G. C. Macaulay (1890), Book II, sec. 122

summary.en: After the thief's pardon, King Rhampsinitos went down alive to the place the Greeks call Hades, played dice with Demeter, sometimes winning and sometimes losing, and returned bearing a gift of a handkerchief of gold; ever after, at the feast of his descent, the priests weave a robe in a single day, blindfold one of their number, and two wolves lead the blind priest twenty furlongs to the temple of Demeter and back again.
summary.zh: 神偷既赦，王拉美西尼圖斯生入希臘人所稱冥府，與得墨忒爾擲骰，互有勝負，懷其金帕而返；自是其降冥之日成節：祭司一日織成一袍，蒙其一目，兩狼引之二十弗隆至地母廟，復引之而歸。

sensitivity.note: Ancient underworld-visit tale via Herodotus; no living community restrictions. Cluster: descent to the underworld.

passages.text: After these things they said this king went down alive to that place which by the Hellenes is called Hades, and there played at dice with Demeter, and in some throws he overcame her and in others he was overcome by her; and he came back again having as a gift from her a handkerchief of gold: and they told me that because of the going down of Rhampsinitos the Egyptians after he came back celebrated a feast, which I know of my own knowledge also that they still observe even to my time; but whether it is for this cause that they keep the feast or for some other, I am not able to say.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Macaulay, Herodotus (1890), Book II.122.

passages.text: However, the priests weave a robe completely on the very day of the feast, and forthwith they bind up the eyes of one of them with a fillet, and having led him with the robe to the way by which one goes to the temple of Demeter, they depart back again themselves. This priest, they say, with his eyes bound up is led by two wolves to the temple of Demeter, which is distant from the city twenty furlongs, and then afterwards the wolves lead him back again from the temple to the same spot.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Macaulay (1890), Book II.122.

title.en: The Soul's Round of Three Thousand Years
title.zh: 靈魂三千年之輪迴

region.en: Egypt, land of the first doctrine of the immortal soul (symbolic pin, Thebes)
region.zh: 埃及，不死靈魂之說首傳之地（象徵定位，底比斯）

period: Priests' doctrine recorded by Herodotus, Histories II.123 (5th century BCE; Macaulay translation 1890)

source.work: The History of Herodotus, trans. G. C. Macaulay (1890), Book II, sec. 123

summary.en: Herodotus records the Egyptian doctrine that the soul of man is immortal: at death it enters another creature coming to birth, and after passing through all creatures of land, sea, and air, enters a human body again — a round of three thousand years; certain Greeks, he notes pointedly, adopted the doctrine 'as if it were their own invention.'
summary.zh: 希羅多德錄埃及之教：人之靈魂不死——身死而魂入新生之物，遍歷陸海空萬類之後，復入人身，其輪迴之期為三千年；並譏某希臘人襲取此說而自詡為其發明。

sensitivity.note: Ancient doctrinal report via Herodotus; no living community restrictions. The doctrine is the Pythagorean-Orphic transmigration in its Egyptian source-form.

passages.text: The Egyptians say that Demeter and Dionysos are rulers of the world below; and the Egyptians are also the first who reported the doctrine that the soul of man is immortal, and that when the body dies, the soul enters into another creature which chances then to be coming to the birth, and when it has gone the round of all the creatures of land and sea and of the air, it enters again into a human body as it comes to the birth; and that it makes this round in a period of three thousand years. This doctrine certain Hellenes adopted, some earlier and some later, as if it were of their own invention, and of these men I know the names but I abstain from recording them.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Macaulay, Herodotus (1890), Book II.123. / Verbatim excerpt of Macaulay (1890), Book II.123.

title.en: Cheops the Tyrant: Ten Years on the Causeway
title.zh: 暴君胡夫：築道十年

region.en: Giza, Egypt (the great pyramid and its causeway)
region.zh: 埃及吉薩（大金字塔與其石道）

period: Priests' account recorded by Herodotus, Histories II.124-125 (5th century BCE; Macaulay translation 1890)

source.work: The History of Herodotus, trans. G. C. Macaulay (1890), Book II, secs. 124-125

summary.en: The priests' curse-memory of the pyramid age: Cheops shut the temples, stopped the sacrifices, and drove every Egyptian to labour for him — a hundred thousand men at a time, three months each, ten years for the causeway alone and twenty for the pyramid — and the Egyptians, hating him, refuse even to name the kings, calling the pyramids after the shepherd Philitis.
summary.zh: 祭司所詛之金字塔時代：胡夫閉神廟、禁祭品、驅全民為其勞作——每批十萬人，三月一換，僅石道即築十年，塔又二十年——埃及人恨之入骨，拒呼王名，而以牧人菲利提斯之名稱金字塔。

sensitivity.note: Ancient king-legend via Herodotus; no living community restrictions. Herodotus' hostile account is a literary tradition, not an archaeological record.

passages.text: Down to the time when Rhampsinitos was king, they told me there was in Egypt nothing but orderly rule, and Egypt prospered greatly; but after him Cheops became king over them and brought them to every kind of evil: for he shut up all the temples, and having first kept them from sacrificing there, he then bade all the Egyptians work for him. So some were appointed to draw stones from the stone-quarries in the Arabian mountains to the Nile, and others he ordered to receive the stones after they had been carried over the river in boats, and to draw them to those which are called the Libyan mountains; and they worked by a hundred thousand men at a time, for each three months continually.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Macaulay, Herodotus (1890), Book II.124.

passages.text: Of this oppression there passed ten years while the causeway was made by which they drew the stones, which causeway they built, and it is a work not much less, as it appears to me, than the pyramid; for the length of it is five furlongs and the breadth ten fathoms and the height, where it is highest, eight fathoms, and it is made of stone smoothed and with figures carved upon it. For the making of the pyramid itself there passed a period of twenty years; and the pyramid is square, each side measuring eight hundred feet, and the height of it is the same.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Macaulay (1890), Book II.124.

passages.text: Here then they reckon one hundred and six years, during which they say that there was nothing but evil for the Egyptians, and the temples were kept closed and not opened during all that time. These kings the Egyptians by reason of their hatred of them are not very willing to name; nay, they even call the pyramids after the name of Philitis the shepherd, who at that time pastured flocks in those regions.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Macaulay (1890), Book II.128.

title.en: The King's Daughter and Her Pyramid of Stones
title.zh: 王女與其一石一塔

region.en: Giza, Egypt (the middle of the three queens' pyramids, one side 150 feet)
region.zh: 埃及吉薩（三后金字塔之中者，每邊一百五十英尺）

period: Priests' account recorded by Herodotus, Histories II.126 (5th century BCE; Macaulay translation 1890)

source.work: The History of Herodotus, trans. G. C. Macaulay (1890), Book II, sec. 126

summary.en: Driven to want of money, Cheops sent his own daughter to the stews; she not only raised the appointed sum but asked each visitor for one stone toward her building — and of these stones, the Egyptians told Herodotus, the middle of the three small pyramids was built, one hundred and fifty feet on every side.
summary.zh: 胡夫財匱，遣親女入妓院斂金；女不但足額，更向每位客人索一石以備營造——埃及人告希羅多德：此三小金字塔中間之一，即以此諸石砌成，每邊一百五十英尺。

sensitivity.note: Ancient folk aition via Herodotus; no living community restrictions.

passages.text: Cheops moreover came, they said, to such a pitch of wickedness, that being in want of money he caused his own daughter to sit in the stews, and ordered her to obtain from those who came a certain amount of money (how much it was they did not tell me); but she not only obtained the sum appointed by her father, but also she formed a design for herself privately to leave behind her a memorial, and she requested each man who came in to her to give her one stone upon her building: and of these stones, they told me, the pyramid was built which stands in front of the great pyramid in the middle of the three, each side being one hundred and fifty feet in length.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Macaulay, Herodotus (1890), Book II.126.

title.en: Mycerinus and the Golden Cow: The Sun Once a Year
title.zh: 門卡烏拉與金牛：歲見日光一次

region.en: Sais, Western Delta, Egypt (the royal palace chamber of the gilded cow)
region.zh: 埃及西三角洲薩伊斯（王宮鍍金牛之室）

period: Priests' account recorded by Herodotus, Histories II.129-132 (5th century BCE; Macaulay translation 1890)

source.work: The History of Herodotus, trans. G. C. Macaulay (1890), Book II, secs. 129-132

summary.en: The just king Mycerinus loses his only daughter and buries her in a hollow cow of wood covered with gold; the rival tale makes him her lover and the girl strangled herself — her mother cutting off the hands of the maids who betrayed her, hence the handless colossi; the cow still stood at Sais in Herodotus' day, carried into the sunlight once a year, for the daughter dying asked to see the sun once in the year.
summary.zh: 賢王門卡烏拉喪獨女，製中空鍍金牛以葬之；異聞謂王亂其女，女自縊，母斷洩密侍女之手——故其裸體巨像皆無手。此牛至希羅多德時仍陳於薩伊斯，歲一出室見日一次——蓋女臨終求其父：歲見日光一次。

sensitivity.note: Ancient king-legend via Herodotus; no living community restrictions.

passages.text: But while Mykerinos was acting mercifully to his subjects and practising this conduct which has been said, calamities befell him, of which the first was this, namely that his daughter died, the only child whom he had in his house: and being above measure grieved by that which had befallen him, and desiring to bury his daughter in a manner more remarkable than others, he made a cow of wood, which he covered over with gold, and then within it he buried this daughter who, as I said, had died.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Macaulay, Herodotus (1890), Book II.129.

passages.text: Some however tell about this cow and the colossal statues the following tale, namely that Mykerinos was enamoured of his own daughter and afterwards ravished her; and upon this they say that the girl strangled herself for grief, and he buried her in this cow; and her mother cut off the hands of the maids who had betrayed the daughter to her father; wherefore now the images of them have suffered that which the maids suffered in their life. In thus saying they speak idly, as it seems to me, especially in what they say about the hands of the statues; for as to this, even we ourselves saw that their hands had dropped off from lapse of time.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Macaulay (1890), Book II.131.

passages.text: The cow is covered up with a crimson robe, except only the head and the neck, which are seen, overlaid with gold very thickly; and between the horns there is the disc of the sun figured in gold. The cow is not standing up but kneeling, and in size it is equal to a large living cow. Every year it is carried forth from the chamber... for they say that she asked of her father Mykerinos, when she was dying, that she might look upon the sun once in the year.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Macaulay (1890), Book II.132.

title.en: Mycerinus Defies the Oracle: Nights Made into Days
title.zh: 門卡烏拉抗神諭：以夜為晝

region.en: Buto, Nile Delta, Egypt (the oracle that doomed a just king)
region.zh: 埃及三角洲布托（判賢王短命之神諭）

period: Priests' account recorded by Herodotus, Histories II.133 (5th century BCE; Macaulay translation 1890)

source.work: The History of Herodotus, trans. G. C. Macaulay (1890), Book II, sec. 133

summary.en: An oracle from Buto gives the pious Mycerinus six years only — while his impious father and uncle had reigned long; he sends a reproach to the god and receives back the terrible answer: it is precisely his justice that hastens the end, for Egypt is doomed to suffer one hundred and fifty years. So the king lights lamps every night and lives a life of pleasure night and day, turning night into day to prove the oracle false.
summary.zh: 布托神諭判虔敬之王門卡烏拉僅餘六年——而其不敬之父叔皆長壽；王遣使責神，復得駭人回語：正因爾之公義，故速爾之終——埃及當受一百五十年之災。王遂夜夜燃燈，晝夜行樂，以夜作晝，欲證神諭之妄。

sensitivity.note: Ancient king-legend via Herodotus; no living community restrictions.

passages.text: An oracle came to him from the city of Buto, saying that he was destined to live but six years more, in the seventh year to end his life: and he being indignant at it sent to the Oracle a reproach against the god, making complaint in reply that whereas his father and uncle, who had shut up the temples and had not only not remembered the gods, but also had been destroyers of men, had lived for a long time, he himself, who practised piety, was destined to end his life so soon: and from the Oracle there came a second message, which said that it was for this very cause that he was bringing his life to a swift close; for he had not done that which it was appointed for him to do, since it was destined that Egypt should suffer evils for a hundred and fifty years, and the two kings who had risen before him had perceived this, but he had not.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Macaulay, Herodotus (1890), Book II.133.

passages.text: Mykerinos having heard this, and considering that this sentence had been passed upon him beyond recall, procured many lamps, and whenever night came on he lighted these and began to drink and take his pleasure, ceasing neither by day nor by night; and he went about to the fen-country and to the woods and wherever he heard there were the most suitable places for enjoyment. This he devised (having a mind to prove that the Oracle spoke falsely) in order that he might have twelve years of life instead of six, the nights being turned into days.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Macaulay (1890), Book II.133.

title.en: Sabacos' Dream: The Ethiopian Who Refused to Cut the Priests
title.zh: 薩巴科斯之夢：不肯割裂祭司的埃塞俄比亞王

region.en: Egypt under Ethiopian rule, capital at Memphis (Sabacos' fifty years)
region.zh: 埃塞俄比亞統治下的埃及（薩巴科斯五十年）

period: Priests' account recorded by Herodotus, Histories II.137-140 (5th century BCE; Macaulay translation 1890)

source.work: The History of Herodotus, trans. G. C. Macaulay (1890), Book II, secs. 137-140

summary.en: Sabacos the Ethiopian rules Egypt for fifty years, never putting a wrongdoer to death but setting each to raise an embankment around his own city; then a dream stands by him counselling the impious deed of cutting all Egypt's priests in two, and he reads it as the gods' snare: his prophesied fifty years are expired — he departs of his own free will.
summary.zh: 埃塞俄比亞王薩巴科斯治埃及五十年，從不誅犯者，而令各就其城築堤贖罪；後夢中一人立於身側，勸其割裂全埃及之祭司——王悟為神之誘餌，且其神諭之五十年已滿，遂自願離國而去。

sensitivity.note: Ancient king-legend via Herodotus; no living community restrictions.

passages.text: In his reign the Ethiopians and Sabacos the king of the Ethiopians marched upon Egypt with a great host of men; so this blind man departed, flying to the fen-country, and the Ethiopian was king over Egypt for fifty years, during which he performed deeds as follows: — whenever any man of the Egyptians committed any transgression, he would never put him to death, but he gave sentence upon each man according to the greatness of the wrong-doing, appointing them work at throwing up an embankment before that city from whence each man came of those who committed wrong. Thus the cities were made higher still than before.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Macaulay, Herodotus (1890), Book II.137.

passages.text: The final deliverance from the Ethiopian came about (they said) as follows: — he fled away because he had seen in his sleep a vision, in which it seemed to him that a man came and stood by him and counselled him to gather together all the priests of Egypt and cut them asunder in the midst. Having seen this dream, he said that it seemed to him that the gods were foreshowing him this to furnish an occasion against him, in order that he might do an impious deed with respect to religion, and so receive some evil either from the gods or from men: he would not however do so, but in truth (he said) the time had expired, during which it had been prophesied to him that he should rule Egypt before he departed thence. For when he was in Ethiopia the Oracles which the Ethiopians consult had told him that it was fated for him to rule Egypt fifty years: since then this time was now expiring, and the vision of the dream also disturbed him, Sabacos departed out of Egypt of his own free will.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Macaulay (1890), Book II.139.

title.en: Sethos and the Field-Mice: The Night Egypt's Enemies Were Disarmed
title.zh: 塞托斯與田鼠：一夜之間敵軍盡失其器

region.en: Pelusium, Egypt (Sennacherib's invasion; the temple of Hephaistos/Ptah)
region.zh: 埃及佩魯西翁（辛那赫里布之侵；赫菲斯托斯/卜塔神廟）

period: Priests' account of Sennacherib's campaign (c. 701 BCE), recorded by Herodotus, Histories II.141 (5th century BCE; Macaulay translation 1890)

source.work: The History of Herodotus, trans. G. C. Macaulay (1890), Book II, sec. 141

summary.en: When Sennacherib marched on Egypt the warrior caste refused to serve the priest-king Sethos, who had stripped them of their twelve yokes of land; the king wept in the sanctuary until the god stood by him in a dream and promised helpers — and by night field-mice swarmed the Assyrian camp, eating quivers, bows and shield-handles; his statue in the temple holds a mouse: 'Let him who looks upon me learn to fear the gods.'
summary.zh: 辛那赫里布侵埃之際，被奪十二份田之戰士階層拒為祭司王塞托斯出戰；王泣於神廟聖所，夢中神立其旁許以援手——夜間田鼠蜂擁亞述營中，齧毀箭囊、弓與盾柄，敵軍赤手而潰。廟中其像手托一鼠，銘曰：『見我者當敬畏諸神。』

sensitivity.note: Ancient miracle tradition via Herodotus; no living community restrictions. A cousin of the Assyrian plague-of-the-camp tradition (Herodotus here transposes 2 Kings 19).

passages.text: After this, Sanacharib king of the Arabians and of the Assyrians marched a great host against Egypt. Then the warriors of the Egyptians refused to come to the rescue, and the priest, being driven into a strait, entered into the sanctuary of the temple and bewailed to the image of the god the danger which was impending over him; and as he was thus lamenting, sleep came upon him, and it seemed to him in his vision that the god came and stood by him and encouraged him, saying that he should suffer no evil if he went forth to meet the army of the Arabians; for he himself would send him helpers. Trusting in these things seen in sleep, he took with him, they said, those of the Egyptians who were willing to follow him, and encamped in Pelusion, for by this way the invasion came: and not one of the warrior class followed him, but shop-keepers and artisans and men of the market.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Macaulay, Herodotus (1890), Book II.141.

passages.text: Then after they came, there swarmed by night upon their enemies mice of the fields, and ate up their quivers and their bows, and moreover the handles of their shields, so that on the next day they fled, and being without defence of arms great numbers fell. And at the present time this king stands in the temple of Hephaistos in stone, holding upon his hand a mouse, and by letters inscribed he says these words: 'Let him who looks upon me learn to fear the gods.'
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Macaulay (1890), Book II.141.

title.en: The Sun Rose Where It Sets: Egypt's Twice-Changed Sky
title.zh: 日出改處：埃及天空四度之變

region.en: Thebes, Egypt (the priests' reckoning of eleven thousand years)
region.zh: 埃及底比斯（祭司所記一萬一千年之推算）

period: Priests' cosmological account recorded by Herodotus, Histories II.142 (5th century BCE; Macaulay translation 1890)

source.work: The History of Herodotus, trans. G. C. Macaulay (1890), Book II, sec. 142

summary.en: The priests of Thebes, counting 341 generations of kings and chief-priests, declare that within those eleven thousand years no god ever appeared in human form — but the sun moved four times from his accustomed place of rising: twice rising where he now sets, and twice setting where he now rises; meanwhile nothing in Egypt changed — not the fruits of the earth, nor the river, nor diseases, nor deaths.
summary.zh: 底比斯祭司推算三百四十一代王與大祭司，共一萬一千年，其間從無神以人形顯現——惟太陽四度改其常規出沒之地：今沒處曾兩度為其出處，今出處曾兩度為其沒處；而其間埃及百物不變——土地所產、河之水、疾病、死亡，皆如故。

sensitivity.note: Ancient cosmological report via Herodotus; no living community restrictions. Read by some as a memory of precessional or calendrical shifts.

passages.text: So far in the story the Egyptians and the priests were they who made the report, declaring that from the first king down to this priest of Hephaistos who reigned last, there had been three hundred and forty-one generations of men, and that in them there had been the same number of chief-priests and of kings: but three hundred generations of men are equal to ten thousand years, for a hundred years is three generations of men; and in the one-and-forty generations which remain, those I mean which were added to the three hundred, there are one thousand three hundred and forty years. Thus in the period of eleven thousand three hundred and forty years they said that there had arisen no god in human form.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Macaulay, Herodotus (1890), Book II.142.

passages.text: In this time they said that the sun had moved four times from his accustomed place of rising, and where he now sets he had thence twice had his rising, and in the place from whence he now rises he had twice had his setting; and in the meantime nothing in Egypt had been changed from its usual state, neither that which comes from the earth nor that which comes to them from the river nor that which concerns diseases or deaths.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Macaulay (1890), Book II.142.

title.en: The Floating Island of Chemmis: Where Leto Gave Birth
title.zh: 克米斯浮島：勒托誕子之處

region.en: Chemmis, near Buto, Nile Delta, Egypt (the floating island in the deep water)
region.zh: 埃及三角洲布托附近克米斯（深水中的浮島）

period: Recorded by Herodotus, Histories II.156 (5th century BCE; Macaulay translation 1890)

source.work: The History of Herodotus, trans. G. C. Macaulay (1890), Book II, sec. 156

summary.en: In the deep water near Buto floats the island of Chemmis, drifting wherever the river carries it; there, the Egyptians say, Leto received and secretly nursed Apollo and Artemis when in fear of Typhon — at her request Poseidon anchored it with four diamond-footed anchors hidden under the water, and the island still moves, and no one may set foot on it.
summary.zh: 布托附近深水中有浮島克米斯，隨河漂移；埃及人言：勒托懼提豐，攜阿波羅與阿爾忒彌斯至此隱匿哺育——應其請，波塞冬以四枚鑽石足之錨沉於水下繫島，故島雖浮而不得行，且無人得踏上其土。

sensitivity.note: Ancient place-myth via Herodotus; no living community restrictions. The Egyptian name Chemmis (Akh-biten) matches the 'hidden nest of Horus' of the Isis cycle.

passages.text: This house then of all the things that were to be seen by me in that temple is the most marvellous, and among those which come next is the island called Chemmis. This is situated in a deep and broad lake near by in Thebes, and the Egyptians say that it is a floating island. I will set down how it is according to the account given to me, and in what manner it moves: the Egyptians say that in this island, which was not previously fixed or made fast to the mainland, Leto, one of the eight gods first existing, dwelling in Buto where this oracle of hers is, received Apollo and Artemis from Isis, and hid them for safety from Typhon, and supported and concealed them there.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Macaulay, Herodotus (1890), Book II.156 (the house-of-single-stone introduction trimmed).

title.en: The Courtesan Rhodopis and Her Pyramid: A Slander Corrected
title.zh: 名妓羅多庇斯與其金字塔：闢謠

region.en: Naucratis, Egypt (the courtesans' city; Delphi for the iron spits)
region.zh: 埃及諾克拉提斯（名妓之城；鐵籤則獻於德爾菲）

period: Recorded by Herodotus, Histories II.134-135 (5th century BCE; Macaulay translation 1890)

source.work: The History of Herodotus, trans. G. C. Macaulay (1890), Book II, secs. 134-135

summary.en: Greeks said the third pyramid was built by the courtesan Rhodopis; Herodotus, who knew better, corrects the tale: Rhodopis of Thrace — fellow-slave of Aesop the fable-maker, ransomed by Charaxos, brother of Sappho — was famous in Amasis' reign, centuries too late; her tithe went not to a pyramid but to iron spits of ox-piercing size, dedicated at Delphi, where they still lay in his day.
summary.zh: 希臘人謂第三金字塔為名妓羅多庇斯所建；希羅多德闢之：色雷斯女奴羅多庇斯——寓言家伊索的同門奴、薩福之弟卡拉克索斯贖其身——盛名在阿馬西斯之世，晚於建塔之王數百年；其什一之財非建塔，乃鑄巨鐵籤獻於德爾菲，希氏時猶陳於廟後。

sensitivity.note: Ancient biographical legend via Herodotus; no living community restrictions.

passages.text: This pyramid some of the Hellenes say was built by the courtesan Rhodopis, not therein speaking rightly: and besides this it is evident to me that they who speak thus do not even know who Rhodopis was, for otherwise they would not have attributed to her the building of a pyramid like this, on which have been spent (so to speak) innumerable thousands of talents: moreover they do not know that Rhodopis flourished in the reign of Amasis, and not in this king's reign; for Rhodopis lived very many years later than the kings who left behind the pyramids. By descent she was of Thrace, and she was a slave of Iadmon the son of Hephaistopolis a Samian, and a fellow-slave of Esop the maker of fables.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Macaulay, Herodotus (1890), Book II.134.

passages.text: As for Rhodopis, she came to Egypt brought by Xanthes the Samian, and having come thither to exercise her calling she was redeemed from slavery for a great sum by a man of Mytilene, Charaxos son of Scamandronymos and brother of Sappho the lyric poet. Thus was Rhodopis set free, and she remained in Egypt and by her beauty won so much liking that she made great gain of money for one like Rhodopis, though not enough to suffice for the cost of such a pyramid as this.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Macaulay (1890), Book II.135.

passages.text: Rhodopis wished to leave behind her a memorial of herself in Hellas, namely to cause a thing to be made such as happens not to have been thought of or dedicated in a temple by any besides, and to dedicate this at Delphi as a memorial of herself. Accordingly with the tithe of her wealth she caused to be made spits of iron of size large enough to pierce a whole ox, and many in number, going as far therein as her tithe allowed her, and she sent them to Delphi: these are even at the present time lying there, heaped all together behind the altar which the Chians dedicated.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Macaulay (1890), Book II.135.

title.en: The Book of Breathings: Salvation in a Few Pages
title.zh: 呼吸之書：數頁之內的救恩

region.en: Egypt, Graeco-Roman period funerary workshops (symbolic pin, Thebes)
region.zh: 希臘-羅馬時期埃及喪葬作坊（象徵定位，底比斯）

period: Ptolemaic-Roman period condensation of the Book of the Dead (c. 200 BCE-100 CE; Budge translation 1910)

source.work: The Literature of the Ancient Egyptians, trans. E. A. W. Budge (1910), ch. V, the Shai en Sensen (Book of Breathings), British Museum papyrus

summary.en: When only the wealthy could afford the whole Book of the Dead, scribes condensed the essential chapters: the Book of Breathings declares the deceased washed in the Field of Offerings, purified by Uatchet and Nekhebet, vindicated by the Goddess of Truth before Osiris — 'thy soul breathe[s] for ever and ever, and thy form is renewed with life upon earth.'
summary.zh: 亡靈書全卷非富人莫辨，書吏遂刪要成篇：呼吸之書宣告亡者洗於祭品之田，為瓦傑特與奈赫貝特所淨，於奧西里斯前受真理女神之辯護——『爾之靈永世呼吸，爾之形於人間更新而得生』。

sensitivity.note: Ancient funerary scripture; no living community restrictions.

passages.text: Hail, Osiris Kersher, son of Tashenatit! Thou art pure, thy heart is pure. Thy fore parts are pure, thy hind parts are cleansed; thy interior is cleansed with incense and natron, and no member of thine hath any defect in it whatsoever. Kersher is washed in the waters of the Field of Offerings, that lieth to the north of the Field of the Grasshoppers. The goddesses Uatchet and Nekhebet purify thee at the eighth hour of the night and at the eighth hour of the day. Come then, enter the Hall of Truth, for thou art free from all offence and from every defect, and 'Stone of Truth' is thy name.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Budge, Literature of the Ancient Egyptians (1910), ch. V, the Book of Breathings.

passages.text: Thou enterest the Tuat (Other World) as one exceedingly pure. Thou art purified by the Goddesses of Truth in the Great Hall. Holy water hath been poured over thee in the Hall of Keb (i.e. the earth), and thy body hath been made pure in the Hall of Shu (heaven). Thou lookest upon Ra when he setteth in the form of Tem at eventide. Amen is nigh unto thee and giveth thee air, and Ptah likewise, who fashioned thy members for thee; thou enterest the horizon with Ra. Thy soul is received in the Neshem Boat of Osiris, thy soul is made divine in the House of Keb, and thou art made to be triumphant for ever and ever.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Budge (1910), Book of Breathings.

passages.text: Hail, Osiris Kersher! Thy name flourisheth, thy earthly body is stablished, thy spirit body germinateth, and thou art not repulsed either in heaven or on earth. Thy face shineth before Ra, thy soul liveth before Amen, and thy earthly body is renewed before Osiris. Thou breathest the breath of life for ever and ever. — Thoth, the most mighty god, the Lord of Khemenu (Hermopolis), cometh to thee, and he writeth the 'Book of Breathings' with his own fingers. Then doth thy soul breathe for ever and ever, and thy form is renewed with life upon earth.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Budge (1910), Book of Breathings.

title.en: The Book of Traversing Eternity: A Soul That Visits the Festivals
title.zh: 遍歷永恆之書：能赴節會之魂

region.en: Egypt, Graeco-Roman period (symbolic pin, Abydos, the great festival circuit)
region.zh: 希臘-羅馬時期埃及（象徵定位，阿拜多斯，大祭之旅）

period: Ptolemaic-Roman period funerary book, fullest copy on a Vienna papyrus (Budge translation 1910)

source.work: The Literature of the Ancient Egyptians, trans. E. A. W. Budge (1910), ch. V, the Book of Traversing Eternity

summary.en: The shortest road to the whole of Egypt for the dead: the Book of Traversing Eternity promises the soul freedom to travel from one end of the land to the other, visit all the holy places, attend every festival, commune with the gods and — tenderest of clauses — with the living kinsfolk it left behind, floating in the air, following the gods, traveling with the stars, at will by night and by day.
summary.zh: 亡者遊遍埃及之最簡之路：遍歷永恆之書許諾靈魂可自由行遍全國、遍訪聖地、赴每一祭節、與神靈相通——最溫柔者：與其在世之親族相見——浮於空氣，追隨諸神，同行星宿，晝夜任意往來。

sensitivity.note: Ancient funerary scripture; no living community restrictions.

passages.text: This work describes how the soul of the deceased, when armed with the power which the Book of Traversing Eternity will give it, shall be able to travel from one end of Egypt to the other, and to visit all the holy places, and to assist at the festivals, and to enjoy communion not only with the gods and spirits who assemble there, but also with its kinsfolk and acquaintances whom it left behind alive on the earth. The object of the book was to secure for the deceased the resurrection of his body; it opens with the following words: 'Thy soul liveth in heaven in the presence of Ra. Thy Ka hath acquired the divine nature of the gods. Thy body remaineth in the deep house (i.e. tomb) in the presence of Osiris. Thy spirit-body becometh glorious among the living. Thy descendants flourish upon the earth.'
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Budge, Literature of the Ancient Egyptians (1910), ch. V (opening description and text).

passages.text: Thou comest forth by day, thou art joined to the Sun-god Aten. The text goes on to state that the deceased breathes, speaks, eats, drinks, sees, hears, and walks, and that all the organs of his body are in their proper places, and that each is performing its proper functions. He floats in the air, hovers in the shadow, rises in the sky, follows the gods, travels with the stars, dekans, and planets, and moves about by night and by day on earth and in heaven at will.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Budge (1910), Book of Traversing Eternity.

title.en: The Festival Songs of Isis: The Hair Like Lapis
title.zh: 伊西斯節歌：髮如青金石

region.en: Abydos, Upper Egypt (sung at the great Osiris festival, 22nd-26th of Khoiak)
region.zh: 埃及上埃及阿拜多斯（荷阿克月22-26日大祭中咏唱）

period: Graeco-Roman copies of Osiris-festival liturgy (c. 200 BCE-100 CE; Budge translation 1910)

source.work: The Literature of the Ancient Egyptians, trans. E. A. W. Budge (1910), ch. V, the Festival Songs of Isis and Nephthys

summary.en: Sung by two virgins with wool fillets and tambourines at the five-day festival of Osiris: 'Come, come, run to me, O strong heart! ... My heart burneth as with fire at thy escape from the Fiend' — and the bridal hymn to the risen god: 'Thy hair is like turquoise as thou comest forth from the Fields of Turquoise... thy skin and body are like southern alabaster, and thy bones are of silver.'
summary.zh: 兩名頭束羊毛帶、手持鈴鼓之處女於奧西里斯五日大祭中詠唱：『來，來，奔向我，剛毅之心！……爾脫於魔爪，我心如焚』——另有婚頌迎復活之神：『爾髮如松石，爾自松石之田而來……爾膚若南方雪花石膏，爾骨為白銀。』

sensitivity.note: Ancient ritual song; no living community restrictions.

passages.text: The second work, the 'Festival Songs of Isis and Nephthys,' was sung during the great festival of Osiris, which took place in the fourth month of the Season of Akhet and lasted five days (from the twenty-second to the twenty-sixth day). It was sung by two virgins who wore fillets of sheep's wool on their heads, and held tambourines in their hands; one was called Isis and the other Nephthys. According to the rubrical directions given in the British Museum papyrus, the sections were sung by both women together.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Budge, Literature of the Ancient Egyptians (1910), ch. V rubric.

passages.text: 'Come, come, run to me, O strong heart! Let me see thy divine face, for I do not see thee, and make thou clear the path that we may see thee as we see Ra in heaven, when the heavens unite with the earth, and cause darkness to fall upon the earth each day. My heart burneth as with fire at thy escape from the Fiend, even as my heart burneth with fire when thou turnest thy side to me; O that thou wouldst never remove it from me! O thou who unitest the Two Domains (i.e. Egypt, North and South), and who turnest back those who are on the roads, I seek to see thee because of my love for thee.'
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Budge (1910), Festival Songs.

passages.text: 'Thou fliest like a living being, O Everlasting King; thou hast destroyed the fiend Anrekh. Thou art the King of the South and of the North, and thou goest forth from Tatchesert. May there never be a moment in thy life when I do not fill thy heart, O my divine brother, my lord who goest forth from Aqert. My arms are raised to protect thee, O thou whom I love. I love thee, O Husband, Brother, lord of love; come thou in peace into thy house. Thy hair is like turquoise as thou comest forth from the Fields of Turquoise, thy hair is like unto the finest lapis-lazuli, and thou thyself art more blue than thy hair. Thy skin and body are like southern alabaster, and thy bones are of silver.'
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Budge (1910), Festival Songs.

title.en: Making Splendid the Spirit of Osiris: The Nile Rises at His Word
title.zh: 使奧西里斯之靈光榮：尼羅應其口而漲

region.en: Abydos, Upper Egypt (sung November-December at the Osiris mysteries)
region.zh: 埃及上埃及阿拜多斯（十一至十二月奧西里斯秘祭中詠唱）

period: Graeco-Roman copies of the Osiris liturgy, Paris papyrus (Budge translation 1910)

source.work: The Literature of the Ancient Egyptians, trans. E. A. W. Budge (1910), ch. V, the Book of Making Splendid the Spirit of Osiris

summary.en: The third great Osiris liturgy: Isis speaks as both sister and mother of the faith — 'I, a woman, made a man child for thee... He pleaded thy case... Set fell under his knife' — and the risen god is hailed as the source of the flood itself: 'The Nile appeareth at the command of thy mouth... When thou comest that which is dead springeth into life, and the plants in the marshes put forth blossoms.'
summary.zh: 奧西里斯第三大禮文：伊西斯以姊兼母之口言說——『我，一介女子，為你生下男兒……他為你申冤……塞特倒於其刀下』——復活之神被尊為洪源：『尼羅應爾口而漲……爾至之時，死者復生，沼中草木開花。』

sensitivity.note: Ancient ritual liturgy; no living community restrictions.

passages.text: Come to thy house, come to thy house, O An. Come to thy house, O Beautiful Bull, lord of men and women, the beloved one, the lord of women. O Beautiful Face, Chief of Akert, Prince, Khenti Amentiu, are not all hearts drunk through the love of thee, O Un-Nefer, whose word is truth? The hands of men and gods are lifted up and seek thee, even as the hands of a babe are stretched out to his mother. Come thou to them, for their hearts are sad, and make them to rejoice.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Budge, Literature of the Ancient Egyptians (1910), ch. V, the Book of Making Splendid the Spirit of Osiris.

passages.text: Hail, Osiris Khenti Amentiu! I am thy sister Isis. No god and no goddess have done for thee what I have done. I, a woman, made a man child for thee, because of my desire to make thy name to live upon the earth. Thy divine essence was in my body, I brought him forth on the ground. He pleaded thy case, he healed thy suffering, he decreed the destruction of him that caused it. Set fell under his knife, and the Smamiu fiends of Set followed him. The throne of the Earth-god is thine, O thou who art his beloved son. There is health in thy members, thy wounds are healed, thy sufferings are relieved, thou shalt never groan again in pain.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Budge (1910), Making Splendid the Spirit of Osiris.

passages.text: The Nile appeareth at the command of thy mouth; thou makest men to live on the effluxes that proceed from thy members, and thou makest every field to flourish. When thou comest that which is dead springeth into life, and the plants in the marshes put forth blossoms. Thou art the Lord of millions of years, the sustainer of wild creatures, and the lord of cattle; every created thing hath its existence from thee. What is in the earth is thine. What is in the heavens is thine. What is in the waters is thine. Thou art the Lord of Truth, the hater of sinners, whom thou overthrowest in their sins.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Budge (1910), Making Splendid the Spirit of Osiris.

title.en: Wenamun in Byblos: The Ambassador of Amun and the Cedars of Lebanon
title.zh: 文阿蒙在比布魯斯：阿蒙使臣與黎巴嫩雪松

region.en: Byblos, Phoenician coast (harbour of Zakar-Baal, prince of Byblos)
region.zh: 腓尼基海岸比布魯斯（比布魯斯王札克爾-巴爾之港）

period: Papyrus written in the 11th century BCE (year 5 of the Whm-Mswet era; Budge translation 1910)

source.work: The Literature of the Ancient Egyptians, trans. E. A. W. Budge (1910), ch. X, the Journey of the Priest Unu-Amen (Wenamun) into Syria

summary.en: The elder priest of Amun sails to buy cedar for the god's great boat, is robbed, stranded for twenty-nine days in Byblos harbour while the prince orders him out daily, haggle-humiliated — 'I am not thy servant, nor the servant of him that sent thee' — and wins his timbers only by invoking the sleeping statue of Amun travelling with him; shipwrecked at last on Cyprus, he pleads his mission to the queen.
summary.zh: 阿蒙大祭司奉命購雪松以造大神舟，途中遭竊，滯留比布魯斯港二十九日，王子日日逐客，又遭折辱——『我非爾之僕，亦非遣爾者之僕』——直至其以同行睡臥之阿蒙神像相脅，方得巨木；終又遭遇海難漂至塞浦路斯，向女王哀陳使命。

sensitivity.note: Late New Kingdom narrative (historical romance); no living community restrictions. Treated in this corpus as a mythic travel tale of the god's ambassador.

passages.text: On the eighteenth day of the third month of the season of the Inundation, of the fifth year, Unu-Amen, the senior priest of the Hait chamber of the house of Amen, the Lord of the thrones of the Two Lands, set out on his journey to bring back wood for the great and holy Boat of Amen-Ra, the King of the Gods, which is called 'User-hat,' and floateth on the canal of Amen. — And a man who belonged to the crew of my boat ran away, having stolen vessels of gold that weighed five teben, and four vessels of silver that weighed twenty teben, and silver in a leather bag that weighed eleven teben.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Budge, Literature of the Ancient Egyptians (1910), ch. X.

passages.text: And I passed nineteen days in the port of Byblos, and the governor passed his days in sending messages to me each day, saying, 'Get thee gone out of my harbour.' Now on one occasion when he was making an offering to his gods, the god took possession of a certain young chief of his chiefs, and he caused him to fall into a fit of frenzy, and the young man said, 'Bring up the god. Bring the messenger who hath possession of him. Make him to set out on his way. Make him to depart immediately.'
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Budge (1910), ch. X.

passages.text: He answered and said unto me, 'On what matter of business hast thou come hither?' And I said unto him, 'The matter concerning which I have come is wood for the great and holy Boat of Amen-Ra, the King of the Gods. What thy father did [for the god], and what thy father's father did for him, do thou also.' And he said unto me, 'They certainly did do work for it. Give me a gift for my work for the boat, and then I also will work for it... As for me, I am assuredly not thy servant, and indeed I am not the servant of him that made thee to set out on thy way. If I were to cry out now, and to shout to the cedars of Lebanon, the heavens would open, and the trees would be lying spread out on the sea-shore.'
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Budge (1910), ch. X.

passages.text: And I said unto him, 'What a shameful thing [to say]! It is not a beggarly journey whereon I have been despatched by those among whom I live. And besides, assuredly there is not a single boat that floateth that doth not belong to Amen. To him belong the sea and the cedars of Lebanon, concerning which thou sayest, They are my property... Amen-Ra, the King of the Gods, spake and told Her-Heru, my lord, to send me forth; and therefore he caused me to set out on my journey together with this great god. Now behold, thou hast caused this great god to pass nine and twenty days here in a boat that is lying at anchor in thy harbour.'
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Budge (1910), ch. X.

title.en: The Dawn Liturgy: A Seat in the Boat of Ra
title.zh: 黎明禮文：拉舟中之一席

region.en: Thebes, Egypt (Papyrus of Ani, funerary liturgy)
region.zh: 埃及底比斯（阿尼紙草喪禮經文）

period: Book of the Dead ch. 15, Theban recension c. 1550-1292 BCE (Budge translation 1910)

source.work: The Literature of the Ancient Egyptians, trans. E. A. W. Budge (1910), ch. IV, the funerary hymn to Ra from the Papyrus of Ani

summary.en: The scribe Ani's daily liturgy for the risen sun: Khepera is hailed as creator, the serpent-fiend is cast into the fire headlong, and the deceased petitions his place in the cosmic day — to see the Abtu and Ant fishes of the barque, to hold the bows of the Evening Boat and the stern of the Morning Boat, and to be received into the presence of Osiris 'in the Land where Truth is spoken.'
summary.zh: 書吏阿尼之日昇禮文：頌凱佩拉為造物主，蛇魔被頭朝下投於火中，亡者為自己祈求宇宙白晝之位——得見日舟之阿布圖與安特雙魚、執暮舟之首與晨舟之尾，並蒙接引至奧西里斯前『在其言真實之國』。

sensitivity.note: Ancient funerary liturgy; no living community restrictions.

passages.text: Homage to thee, O thou who art in the form of Khepera, Khepera the creator of the gods. Thou risest, thou shinest, thou illuminest thy mother [the sky]. Thou art crowned King of the Gods. Mother Nut welcometh thee with bowings. The Land of Sunset (Manu) receiveth thee with satisfaction, and the goddess Maat embraceth thee at morn and at eve. Hail, ye gods of the Temple of the Soul (i.e. heaven), who weigh heaven and earth in a balance, who provide celestial food! And hail, Tatunen, One, Creator of man, Maker of the gods of the south and of the north, of the west and of the east!
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Budge, Literature of the Ancient Egyptians (1910), ch. IV, funerary hymn to Ra (Papyrus of Ani).

passages.text: Those who dwell in the heights and those who dwell in the depths worship thee. Thoth and the goddess Maat have laid down thy course for thee daily for ever. Thine Enemy the Serpent hath been cast into the fire, the fiend hath fallen down into it headlong. His arms have been bound in chains, and Ra hath hacked off his legs; the Mesu Betshet shall never more rise up. The Temple of the Aged God [in Anu] keepeth festival, and the sound of those who rejoice is in the Great House. The gods shout for joy when they see Ra rising, and when his beams are filling the world with light.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Budge (1910), funerary hymn to Ra.

passages.text: O be thou at peace with me, and let me behold thy beauties! Let me appear on the earth. Let me smite [the Eater of] the Ass. Let me crush the Serpent Seba. Let me destroy Aapep when he is most strong. Let me see the Abtu Fish in its season and the Ant Fish in its lake. Let me see Horus steering thy boat, with Thoth and Maat standing one on each side of him. Let me have hold of the bows of [thy] Evening Boat and the stern of thy Morning Boat. Grant thou unto the Ka of me, the Osiris the scribe Ani, to behold the disk of the Sun, and to see the Moon-god regularly and daily. Let there be prepared for me a seat in the Boat of Ra on the day when the god goeth forth. Let me be received into the presence of Osiris, in the Land where Truth is spoken.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Budge (1910), funerary hymn to Ra.

title.en: The Litany of Osiris: Homage to the Nine Forms
title.zh: 奧西里斯連禱：九形之敬拜

region.en: Thebes, Egypt (Papyrus of Ani, introduction to ch. 15)
region.zh: 埃及底比斯（阿尼紙草第十五章引文）

period: Book of the Dead ch. 15, Theban recension c. 1550-1292 BCE (Budge translation 1910)
