source.work: The Literature of the Ancient Egyptians, trans. E. A. W. Budge (1910), ch. IV, the Litany from the Papyrus of Ani

summary.en: Ani's introduction to the Osiris litany: the god of Amentet makes the earth shine 'like refined copper', the dead rise up to breathe the air when his disk rises — and the litany hails him form by form, Heliopolis to Busiris to Abydos to Herakleopolis, each homage answered by the same refrain: 'Grant thou unto me a path whereon I may pass in peace, for I am just and true.'
summary.zh: 阿尼之連禱引文：冥國之神使大地亮如精煉之銅，日盤升起時亡者起而呼吸——連禱逐一頌其形相，自赫利奧波利斯至布西里斯、阿拜多斯、赫拉克利奧波利斯，每頌一呼必應：『賜我一途，使我能安然通行，因我公義真實。』

sensitivity.note: Ancient funerary liturgy; no living community restrictions.

passages.text: Praise be unto thee, O Osiris, lord of eternity, Un-Nefer, Heru-Khuti, whose forms are manifold, whose attributes are majesty, [thou who art] Ptah-Seker-Tem in Heliopolis, lord of the Sheta shrine, creator of Het-ka-Ptah (Memphis) and of the gods who dwell therein, thou Guide of the Other World, whom the gods praise when thou settest in the sky. Isis embraceth thee contentedly, and she driveth away the fiends from the mouth of thy paths. Thou turnest thy face towards Amentet, and thou makest the earth to shine like refined copper. The dead rise up to look upon thee, they breathe the air, and they behold thy face when [thy] disk riseth on the horizon. Their hearts are at peace, inasmuch as they behold thee, O thou who art Eternity and Everlastingness.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Budge, Literature of the Ancient Egyptians (1910), ch. IV, Litany introduction.

passages.text: 1. Homage to thee, O [Lord of] the Dekans in Heliopolis and of the heavenly beings in Kheraha, thou god Unti, who art the most glorious of the gods hidden in Heliopolis. Grant thou unto me a path whereon I may pass in peace, for I am just and true; I have not spoken lies wittingly, nor have I done aught with deceit. — 5. Homage to thee, O Lord of the Acacia. The Seker Boat is on its sledge; thou turnest back the Fiend, the worker of evil; thou makest the Eye of the Sun-god to rest upon its throne. — 9. Homage to thee, O Creator of the gods, King of the South, King of the North, Osiris, Conqueror, Governor of the world in thy gracious seasons! Thou art the Lord of the heaven of Egypt (Atebui).
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Budge (1910), Litany sections 1, 5, and 9 (response repeated after each petition).

title.en: The Scribe of Truth: Hunefer's Hymn of Clean Hands
title.zh: 真理之書吏：胡內弗之潔手頌

region.en: Thebes, Egypt (Papyrus of Hunefer)
region.zh: 埃及底比斯（胡內弗紙草）

period: Book of the Dead, 19th Dynasty (c. 1300-1200 BCE; Budge translation 1910)

source.work: The Literature of the Ancient Egyptians, trans. E. A. W. Budge (1910), ch. IV, the Hymn to Osiris from the Papyrus of Hunefer

summary.en: A royal scribe stands before Osiris 'holding in my hands truth, and my heart hath in it no cunning': the gods bow in fear at the terror of Ra upon the god — and the petitioner claims the identity of the perfect judge's scribe: 'I am Thoth, the perfect scribe, whose hands are pure... what I abominate is sin.'
summary.zh: 王家書吏立於奧西里斯之前：『我手執真理，我心無詭詐』——因神身負拉之威，諸神望而畏懼——祈者更自認為完美審判者之書吏：『我即托特，潔手之完美書吏……我所憎者惟罪。』

sensitivity.note: Ancient funerary hymn; no living community restrictions.

passages.text: The gods come unto thee, bowing low before thee, and they hold thee in fear. They withdraw and depart when they see thee endued with the terror of Ra, and the victory of Thy Majesty is over their hearts. Life is with thee, and offerings of meat and drink follow thee, and that which is thy due is offered before thy face. I have come unto thee holding in my hands truth, and my heart hath in it no cunning (or deceit). I offer unto thee that which is thy due, and I know that whereon thou livest. I have not committed any kind of sin in the land; I have defrauded no man of what is his. I am Thoth, the perfect scribe, whose hands are pure. I am the lord of purity, the destroyer of evil, the scribe of truth; what I abominate is sin.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Budge, Literature of the Ancient Egyptians (1910), ch. IV, Hymn to Osiris from the Papyrus of Hunefer. / Verbatim excerpt of Budge (1910), Hymn to Osiris (Papyrus of Hunefer).

title.en: Prayer Before the Four Ape-gods: Sin Washed Away
title.zh: 四猿神前之禱：洗除己罪

region.en: Thebes, Egypt (Book of the Dead ch. 126, the boat of Ra at dawn)
region.zh: 埃及底比斯（亡靈書第一二六章，拉舟黎明處）

period: Book of the Dead ch. 126, Theban recension (Budge translation 1910)

source.work: The Literature of the Ancient Egyptians, trans. E. A. W. Budge (1910), ch. IV, Chapter CXXVI of the Book of the Dead

summary.en: The rare Book of the Dead prayer for forgiveness: the four Ape-gods in the bows of Ra's boat — who live upon truth and to whom wickedness is abomination — are asked to do away with the petitioner's evil deeds, and they answer with absolution: 'Come, for we have done away with thy wickedness... Enter, therefore, into Rastau, and cakes, and ale, and sweetmeats shall be given unto thee.'
summary.zh: 亡靈書中罕有的赦罪之禱：拉舟首的四猿神——以真理為食、視邪惡為可憎者——被祈求除去祈者之罪孽，且應答赦免：『來吧，我等已除去爾之罪惡……故爾可入臘斯陶，餅與酒與甜食必賜予爾。』

sensitivity.note: Ancient funerary prayer; no living community restrictions.

passages.text: Hail, ye four Ape-gods who sit in the bows of the Boat of Ra, who convey truth to Nebertchet, who sit in judgment on my weakness and on my strength, who make the gods to rest contented by means of the flame of your mouths, who offer holy offerings to the gods, and sepulchral meals to the spirit-souls, who live upon truth, who feed upon truth of heart, who are without deceit and fraud, and to whom wickedness is an abomination, do ye away with my evil deeds, and put ye away my sin, which deserved stripes upon earth, and destroy ye every evil thing whatsoever that clingeth to me, and let there be no bar whatsoever on my part towards you.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Budge, Literature of the Ancient Egyptians (1910), ch. IV, Book of the Dead ch. 126.

passages.text: The four Ape-gods reply: 'Come, for we have done away with thy wickedness, and we have put away thy sin, which deserved stripes, which thou didst commit upon earth, and we have destroyed all the evil that clung to thee. Enter, therefore, into Rastau, and pass in through the secret gates of Amentet, and cakes, and ale, and sweetmeats shall be given unto thee, and thou shalt go in and come out at thy desire, even as do those whose spirit-souls are praised [by the god], and [thy name] shall be proclaimed each day in the horizon.'
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Budge (1910), ch. 126, the gods' reply.

title.en: My Heart, My Mother: The Heart-Scarab Spell
title.zh: 吾心吾母：心聖甲蟲之咒

region.en: Hall of Judgement, Egyptian Other World (symbolic pin, Thebes)
region.zh: 埃及冥界審判之廳（象徵定位，底比斯）

period: Book of the Dead ch. 30B; tradition as old as the 12th Dynasty (Budge translation 1910)

source.work: The Literature of the Ancient Egyptians, trans. E. A. W. Budge (1910), ch. IV, Chapter XXXB of the Book of the Dead

summary.en: Possibly the oldest prayer in the world, said over a green-stone heart-scarab hung on the dead: 'My heart, my mother. My heart whereby I came into being. Mayest thou not be separated from me in the presence of the Keeper of the Balance... Let not that which is false be uttered against me before the Great God, the Lord of Amentet' — so that the heart shall not betray its owner at the weighing.
summary.zh: 或為世上最古之禱文，誦於繫於亡者頸間的綠石心形聖甲蟲之上：『吾心，吾母。吾賴以生成之心。於司秤者面前勿與我分離……勿使虛妄之言在偉大神主、冥國之主前指斥於我』——使心在稱量之時不出賣其主。

sensitivity.note: Ancient funerary spell; no living community restrictions.

passages.text: My heart, my mother. My heart, my mother. My heart whereby I came into being. Let none stand up to oppose me at my judgment. May there be no opposition to me in the presence of the Tchatchau. Mayest thou not be separated from me in the presence of the Keeper of the Balance. Thou art my Ka (i.e. Double, or vital power), that dwelleth in my body; the god Khnemu who knitteth together and strengthened my limbs. Mayest thou come forth into the place of happiness whither we go. May the Shenit officers who decide the destinies of the lives of men not cause my name to stink [before Osiris]. Let it (i.e. the weighing) be satisfactory unto us, and let there be joy of heart to us at the weighing of words (i.e. the Great Judgment). Let not that which is false be uttered against me before the Great God, the Lord of Amentet (i.e. Osiris). Verily thou shalt be great when thou risest up [having been declared] a speaker of the truth.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Budge, Literature of the Ancient Egyptians (1910), ch. IV, Book of the Dead ch. 30B.

passages.text: In many papyri this prayer is followed by a Rubric, which orders that it is to be said over a green stone scarab set in a band of tchamu metal (i.e. silver-gold), which is to be hung by a ring from the neck of the deceased. Some Rubrics order it to be placed in the breast of a mummy, where it is to take the place of the heart, and say that it will 'open the mouth' of the deceased. A tradition which is as old as the twelfth dynasty says that the Chapter was discovered in the town of Khemenu (Hermopolis Magna) by Herutataf, the son of Khufu, in the reign of Menkaura, a king of the fourth dynasty. It was cut in hieroglyphs, inlaid with lapis-lazuli on a block of alabaster, which was set under the feet of Thoth.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Budge (1910), the rubric and tradition of ch. 30B.

title.en: I Shall Not Rot: The Spells Against Decay and the Second Death
title.zh: 我不朽壞：抗腐與抗二死之咒

region.en: Egyptian Other World (symbolic pin, Thebes)
region.zh: 埃及冥界（象徵定位，底比斯）

period: Book of the Dead chs. 154 and 175, Theban recension (Budge translation 1910)

source.work: The Literature of the Ancient Egyptians, trans. E. A. W. Budge (1910), ch. IV, Chapters CLIV and CLXXV of the Book of the Dead

summary.en: From first to last the Book of the Dead fights corruption: 'I shall not decay, I shall not rot, I shall not putrefy, I shall not turn into worms' — and when the scribe Ani arrives and finds the Other World 'black as the blackest night', he asks how long he shall live, and Osiris answers: 'It is decreed that thou shalt live for millions of millions of years, a life of millions of years.'
summary.zh: 亡靈書自始至終與腐朽抗爭：『我不腐壞，我不朽爛，我不化膿，我不生蛆』——及書吏阿尼至，見冥界『黑如至黑之夜』，問能活多久，奧西里斯答：『命定爾將活百萬之百萬年，一個百萬年之生命。』

sensitivity.note: Ancient funerary spells; no living community restrictions.

passages.text: Homage to thee, O my divine father Osiris, thou livest with thy members. Thou didst not decay. Thou didst not turn into worms. Thou didst not waste away. Thou didst not suffer corruption. Thou didst not putrefy. I am the god Khepera, and my members shall have an everlasting existence. I shall not decay. I shall not rot. I shall not putrefy. I shall not turn into worms. I shall not see corruption before the eye of the god Shu. I shall have my being, I shall have my being. I shall live, I shall live. I shall flourish, I shall flourish. I shall wake up in peace. My inward parts shall not perish. I shall not suffer injury. Mine eye shall not decay. The form of my visage shall not disappear. Mine ear shall not become deaf. My head shall not be separated from my neck. My tongue shall not be carried away. My hair shall not be cut off. Mine eyebrows shall not be shaved off. No baleful injury shall come upon me. My body shall be established, and it shall neither crumble away nor be destroyed on this earth.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Budge, Literature of the Ancient Egyptians (1910), ch. IV, Book of the Dead ch. 154.

passages.text: The passage that refers to everlasting life occurs in Chapter 175, wherein the scribe Ani is made to converse with Thoth and Temu in the Tuat, or Other World. Ani, who is supposed to have recently arrived there, says: 'What manner of country is this to which I have come? There is no water in it. There is no air. It is depth unfathomable, it is black as the blackest night, and men wander helplessly therein. In it a man may not live in quietness of heart; nor may the affections be gratified therein.' After a short address to Osiris, the deceased asks the god, 'How long shall I live?' And the god says, 'It is decreed that thou shalt live for millions of millions of years, a life of millions of years.'
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Budge (1910), Book of the Dead ch. 175.

title.en: The Blood of Isis: The Tet Amulet Spell
title.zh: 伊西斯之血：泰特護符之咒

region.en: Egyptian funerary workshops (symbolic pin, Thebes)
region.zh: 埃及喪葬作坊（象徵定位，底比斯）

period: Book of the Dead ch. 156, Theban recension (Budge translation 1910)

source.work: The Literature of the Ancient Egyptians, trans. E. A. W. Budge (1910), ch. IV, Chapter CLVI of the Book of the Dead (the tet amulet)

summary.en: The spell for the tet amulet — the knot-shaped pillar that represented a portion of Isis' body — recited over carnelian steeped in ankham-flower water and set in a sycamore frame at the funeral: 'The blood of Isis, the power of Isis, the words of power of Isis shall be strong to protect this mighty one... and one hand of his shall be towards heaven and the other towards earth, regularly and continually.'
summary.zh: 泰特護符之咒——該結形柱乃伊西斯身體之一部分所成——於葬日誦於浸過安卡姆花水、鑲於梧桐木框之紅玉髓上：『伊西斯之血、之力、之言辭之力，將強而護此偉大者……其一手指天，一手指地，恆常不變。』

sensitivity.note: Ancient amuletic spell; no living community restrictions.

passages.text: The blood of Isis, the power of Isis, the words of power of Isis shall be strong to protect this mighty one (i.e. the mummy), and to guard him from him that would do unto him anything which he abominateth (or, is taboo to him).
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Budge, Literature of the Ancient Egyptians (1910), ch. IV, Book of the Dead ch. 156.

passages.text: [This spell] shall be said over a tet made of carnelian, which hath been steeped in water of ankham flowers, and set in a frame of sycamore wood, and placed on the neck of the deceased on the day of the funeral. If these things be done for him the powers of Isis shall protect his body, and Horus, the son of Isis, shall rejoice in him when he seeth him. And there shall be no places hidden from him as he journeyeth. And one hand of his shall be towards heaven and the other towards earth, regularly and continually.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Budge (1910), the rubric of ch. 156.

title.en: I Am Ra, the Self-Protected: Spells Against the Crocodiles
title.zh: 我乃拉，自護者：驅鱷之咒

region.en: The Nile of the Other World (symbolic pin, the river journey of the dead)
region.zh: 冥界之尼羅（象徵定位，亡者之河旅）

period: Book of the Dead chs. 31-32, Theban recension (Budge translation 1910)

source.work: The Literature of the Ancient Egyptians, trans. E. A. W. Budge (1910), ch. IV, Chapters XXXI-XXXII of the Book of the Dead

summary.en: The dead face crocodiles from all four quarters of the river and answer them with identity-spells — 'Get thee back, thou Crocodile of the West... I am set... I am Osiris... I am Sept... I am Tem' — until the climax of pure solar self-protection: 'Created things are in the hollow of my hand, and the things that are not yet made are inside me... I am Ra, the self-protected, no evil thing whatsoever shall overthrow me.'
summary.zh: 亡者四面遇鱷，以同體之咒應之——『退去吧，西方之鱷……我已定。我是奧西里斯……我是塞普特……我是阿圖姆』——末句乃純粹太陽式自護宣言：『已成之物在我掌心，未成之物在我懷中……我即拉，自護者，任何邪惡皆不能勝我。』

sensitivity.note: Ancient funerary spells; no living community restrictions.

passages.text: Away with thee! Retreat! Get back, O thou accursed Crocodile Sui. Thou shalt not come nigh me, for I have life through the words of power that are in me. If I utter thy name to the Great God he will make thee to come before the two divine messengers Betti and Herkemmaat. Heaven ruleth its seasons, and the spell hath power over what it mastereth, and my mouth ruleth the spell that is inside it. My teeth which bite are like flint knives, and my teeth which grind are like unto those of the Wolf-god. O thou who sittest spellbound with thine eyes fixed through my spell, thou shalt not carry off my spell, thou Crocodile that livest on spells.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Budge, Literature of the Ancient Egyptians (1910), ch. IV, Book of the Dead ch. 31.

passages.text: Get thee back, thou Crocodile of the West, that livest on the never-resting stars. That which is thy taboo is in me. I have eaten the brow (or, skull) of Osiris. I am set. — Get thee back, thou Crocodile of the East. The serpent Nau is inside me. I will set it on thee, thy flame shall not approach me... Get thee back, thou Crocodile of the South... I will fetter thee. My charm is among the reeds. I will not yield unto thee. — Get thee back, thou Crocodile of the North... I am Tem. — Created things are in the hollow of my hand, and the things that are not yet made are inside me. I am clothed in and supplied with thy spells, O Ra, which are above me and beneath me. I am Ra, the self-protected, no evil thing whatsoever shall overthrow me.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Budge (1910), Book of the Dead ch. 32.

title.en: The Kingdom of Osiris: Fields of Reeds and the Island of Truth
title.zh: 奧西里斯之國：蘆葦之田與真理之島

region.en: The Fields of Reeds (Sekhet Aaru), Egyptian Other World (symbolic pin, Abydos region)
region.zh: 埃及冥界蘆葦之田（象徵定位，阿拜多斯一帶）

period: Descriptions from the Book of Gates and Book of the Dead ch. 110, New Kingdom (Budge, The Book of the Dead, 1901/1920)

source.work: The Book of the Dead, by E. A. Wallis Budge (1901), ch. VIII, 'The Kingdom of Osiris'

summary.en: Egypt's heaven is a working farm: fields crossed by canals with 'no fish and no worms', on one island of which Osiris dwells with his saints — the Island of Truth, where the ferryman carries none who was not declared 'true of word' at the Great Reckoning; the beautified, seven cubits tall, reap wheat three cubits high, ears that are 'the members of Osiris', and eat the body of their god daily as the Bread of Everlastingness.
summary.zh: 埃及的天堂是一座農場：田野為運河所交錯，『無魚亦無蛇』；其中一小島為奧西里斯與其聖徒所居——『真理之島』，非經托特與諸神於大清算中宣告『言真實』者，奧西里斯之渡者不載；蒙福者高七肘，刈三肘高之麥——麥穗即『奧西里斯之肢體』——日日以神之身為糧，是謂『永恆之餅』。

sensitivity.note: Ancient funerary cosmography; no living community restrictions. Coordinates symbolic over the Abydos region where theologians placed the kingdom.

passages.text: According to the Book of Gates and the other 'Guides' to the Egyptian Under World, the Kingdom of Osiris formed the Sixth Division of the Tuat; in very early times it was situated in the Western Delta, but after the XIIth dynasty theologians placed it near Abydos in Upper Egypt, and before the close of the Dynastic Period the Tuat of Osiris had absorbed the Under World of every nome of Egypt. When the soul in its beautified or spirit body arrived there, the ministers of Osiris took it to the homestead or place of abode which had been allotted to it by the command of Osiris, and there it began its new existence.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Budge, The Book of the Dead (1901), ch. VIII.

passages.text: The large vignette to the CXth Chapter shows us exactly what manner of place the abode of the blessed was. The country was flat and the fields were intersected by canals of running water in which there were 'no fish and no worms' (i.e., water snakes). In one part of it were several small islands, and on one of them Osiris was supposed to dwell with his saints. It was called the 'Island of Truth,' and the ferry-man of Osiris would not convey to it any soul that had not been declared 'true of word' by Thoth, Osiris and the Great Gods at the 'Great Reckoning.' The portion of the Kingdom of Osiris depicted in the large Books of the Dead represents in many respects a typical Egyptian farm, and we see the deceased engaged in ploughing and reaping and driving the oxen that are treading out the corn.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Budge (1901), ch. VIII.

passages.text: One corner of this region was specially set apart for the dwelling place of the aakhu, i.e., beautified souls, or spirit-souls, who were said to be seven cubits in height, and to reap wheat or barley which grew to a height of three cubits. Near this spot were moored two boats that were always ready for the use of the denizens of that region; they appear to have been 'spirit boats,' i.e., boats which moved of themselves and carried the beautified wheresoever they wanted to go without any trouble or fatigue on their part.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Budge (1901), ch. VIII.

passages.text: In the texts that accompany these scenes the ears of wheat are said to be the 'members of Osiris,' and the wheat plant is called the maat plant. Osiris was the Wheat-god and also the personification of Maat (i.e., Truth), and the beautified lived upon the body of their god and ate him daily, and the substance of him was the 'Bread of Everlastingness.' Osiris says to them, 'Ye are truth of truth; rest in peace.' And of them he says, 'They were doers of truth whilst they were upon earth, they did battle for their god, and they shall be called to the enjoyment of the Land of the House of Life with Truth... Ye shall live there even as they live, and ye shall have dominion over the cool waters of your land.'
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Budge (1901), ch. VIII.

title.en: The Divine Youth, Self-Created: The Opening Hymn of the Dead
title.zh: 自生之聖子：亡者開篇頌

region.en: Egypt, opening hymn of the great Book of the Dead papyri (symbolic pin, Heliopolis)
region.zh: 埃及，亡靈書大紙草之開篇頌（象徵定位，赫利奧波利斯）

period: Hymn to Ra, standard opening of Book of the Dead papyri from the 4th Dynasty onward (Budge, The Book of the Dead, 1901)

source.work: The Book of the Dead, by E. A. Wallis Budge (1901), ch. IX, the Hymn to Ra that opens the great papyri

summary.en: Every great Book of the Dead papyrus opens with this hymn to Ra, sung by the deceased: 'Thou art the God One, who camest into being in the beginning of time. Thou didst create the earth, and man, thou didst make the sky and the celestial river Hep... Thou art the lord of heaven and earth' — and at its heart the confession of the Unknowable: 'Thou art unknowable, and no tongue can describe thy similitude; thou existest alone.'
summary.zh: 所有亡靈書大紙草皆以此拉之頌開篇，由亡者自誦：『爾乃太初自生之唯一神。爾造大地、造人，爾造蒼穹與天河水赫普……爾為天地之主』——其核心乃不可知者之告白：『爾不可知，無舌能言爾之像；爾獨存。』

sensitivity.note: Ancient hymn; no living community restrictions.

passages.text: Homage to thee, O Ra, at thy beauteous rising. Thou risest, thou risest; thou shinest, thou shinest at the dawn. Thou art King of the Gods, and the Maati goddesses embrace thee. The Company of the Gods praise thee at sunrise and at sunset. Thou sailest over the heights of heaven and thy heart is glad. Thy Morning Boat meeteth thy Evening Boat with fair winds. Thy father is the Sky-god and thy mother is the Sky-goddess, and thou art Horus of the Eastern and Western skies. O thou Only One, O thou Perfect One, O thou who art eternal, who art never weak, whom no mighty one can abase; none hath dominion over the things which appertain to thee.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Budge, The Book of the Dead (1901), ch. IX.

passages.text: Homage to thee in thy characters of Horus, Tem, and Khepera, thou Great Hawk, who makest man to rejoice by thy beautiful face. When thou risest men and women live. Thou renewest thy youth, and dost set thyself in the place where thou wast yesterday. O Divine Youth, who art self-created, I cannot comprehend thee. Thou art the lord of heaven and earth, and didst create beings celestial and beings terrestrial. Thou art the God One, who camest into being in the beginning of time. Thou didst create the earth, and man, thou didst make the sky and the celestial river Hep; thou didst make the waters and didst give life unto all that therein is. Thou hast knit together the mountains, thou hast made mankind and the beasts of the field to come into being, and hast made the heavens and the earth. The fiend Nak is overthrown, his arms are cut off.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Budge (1901), ch. IX.

passages.text: O thou Divine Youth, thou heir of everlastingness, self-begotten and self-born, One, Might, of myriad forms and aspects, Prince of An (i.e., On), Lord of Eternity, Everlasting Ruler, the Company of the Gods rejoice in thee. As thou risest thou growest greater: thy rays are upon all faces. Thou art unknowable, and no tongue can describe thy similitude; thou existest alone.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Budge (1901), ch. IX.

title.en: The Hymn to Hapy: The God Who Cannot Be Figured in Stone
title.zh: 哈皮頌：不可雕像之神

region.en: The Nile from the First Cataract to the sea (the god of the flood)
region.zh: 自第一瀑布至海口之尼羅（洪水之神）

period: Hymn of the Middle Kingdom or earlier (Budge translation 1899, from Maspero's Hymnes au Nil)

source.work: Egyptian Ideas of the Future Life, by E. A. W. Budge (1899), ch. I, the Hymn to Hapi

summary.en: The great hymn to the Nile-god opens with paradox: Hapy comes in peace 'to make Egypt to live', waters the fields Ra created, gives every tooth its food — and yet cannot be figured in stone, cannot be found in inscribed shrines, has no habitation that can contain him; his living place is unknown and his form cannot be conceived in the heart.
summary.zh: 尼羅神大頌以悖論開篇：哈皮『安然而來使埃及得生』，澆灌拉所造之田，賜每顆牙齒以食——然彼不可雕像，不可見於刻銘神龕，無一居所可容其身；其居所不可知，其形不可心構。

sensitivity.note: Ancient hymn quoted in Budge 1899; no living community restrictions. The paradox passage is discussed by Budge with the observation that actual pictures of Hapy survive — the invisibility belongs to his divine aspect.

passages.text: Homage to thee, O Hapi! Thou comest forth in this land, and dost come in peace to make Egypt to live, O thou hidden one, thou guide of the darkness whensoever it is thy pleasure to be its guide. Thou waterest the fields which Ra hath created, thou makest all animals to live, thou makest the land to drink without ceasing; thou descendest the path of heaven, thou art the friend of meat and drink, thou art the giver of the grain, and thou makest every place of work to flourish, O Ptah! If thou wert to be overcome in heaven the gods would fall down headlong, and mankind would perish. Thou makest the whole earth to be opened (or ploughed up) by the cattle, and prince and peasant lie down to rest. His disposition (or form) is that of Khnemu; when he shineth upon the earth there is rejoicing, for all people are glad, the mighty man receiveth his meat, and every tooth hath food to consume.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Budge, Egyptian Ideas of the Future Life (1899), ch. I, the Hymn to Hapi.

passages.text: He cannot be figured in stone; he is not to be seen in the sculptured images upon which men place the united crowns of the South and the North furnished with uraei; neither works nor offerings can be made to him; and he cannot be made to come forth from his secret place. The place where he liveth is unknown; he is not to be found in inscribed shrines; there existeth no habitation which can contain him; and thou canst not conceive his form in thy heart.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Budge (1899), ch. I, the Hymn to Hapi.

title.en: God Is One and Alone: The Epithets of the Hidden One
title.zh: 神乃唯一：隱者之尊號

region.en: Egypt, all periods (a composite of epithets from texts of every age)
region.zh: 埃及，歷代諸時期（集各時代文本之尊號）

period: Epithets collected by H. Brugsch from texts of all periods (Religion und Mythologie, 1885-88); Budge translation 1899

source.work: Egyptian Ideas of the Future Life, by E. A. W. Budge (1899), ch. I, the classified epithets of God

summary.en: Budge's classification of the epithets applied to the supreme Being across Egyptian texts: God is One and alone, a hidden spirit, from the beginning, eternal, hidden from gods and men, truth that liveth by truth, father and mother that begat himself, the primeval Potter who turned men and gods out of his hands — stretching out the heavens and founding the earth, so that what his heart conceived came to pass straightway.
summary.zh: 伯奇自歷代文本輯錄之至尊尊號：神乃唯一而獨存、隱秘之靈、太初已存、永恆無窮、為神與人所不能見之隱者、以真理為食之真理、自生之父與母、於陶匠之桌上摶人摶神之太初陶匠——展天立地，心之所念，言出即成。

sensitivity.note: Ancient liturgical epithets quoted in Budge 1899; no living community restrictions. The 'potter' epithet supplies the clearest native witness of the clay-humans motif.

passages.text: God is One and alone, and none other existeth with Him; God is the One, the One Who hath made all things. God is a spirit, a hidden spirit, the spirit of spirits, the great spirit of the Egyptians, the divine spirit. God is from the beginning, and He hath been from the beginning; He hath existed from of old and was when nothing else had being. He existed when nothing else existed, and what existeth He created after He had come into being. He is the father of beginnings. God is the eternal One, He is eternal and infinite; and endureth for ever and aye; He hath endured for countless ages, and He shall endure to all eternity.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Budge (1899), ch. I, the classified epithets of God.

passages.text: God is the hidden Being, and no man hath known His form. No man hath been able to seek out His likeness; He is hidden from gods and men, and He is a mystery unto His creatures. No man knoweth how to know Him, His name remaineth hidden; His name is a mystery unto His children. His names are innumerable, they are manifold and none knoweth their number. God is truth, and He liveth by truth, and he feedeth thereon. He is the King of truth, He resteth upon truth, He fashioneth truth, and He executeth truth throughout all the world.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Budge (1899), ch. I.

passages.text: God is father and mother, the father of fathers, and the mother of mothers. He begetteth, but was never begotten; He produceth, but was never produced; He begat Himself and produced Himself. He createth, but was never created; He is the maker of His own form, and the fashioner of His own body. God hath made the universe, and He hath created all that therein is... God is the father of the gods, and the father of the father of all deities; He made His voice to sound, and the deities came into being, and the gods sprang into existence after He had spoken with His mouth. He formed mankind and fashioned the gods. He is the great Master, the primeval Potter Who turned men and gods out of His hands, and He formed men and gods upon a potter's table.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Budge (1899), ch. I.

passages.text: The heavens rest upon His head, and the earth supporteth His feet; heaven hideth His spirit, the earth hideth His form, and the underworld shutteth up the mystery of Him within it. His body is like the air, heaven resteth upon His head, and the new inundation [of the Nile] containeth His form. God is merciful unto those who reverence Him, and He heareth him that calleth upon Him. He protecteth the weak against the strong, and He heareth the cry of him that is bound in fetters; He judgeth between the mighty and the weak, God knoweth him that knoweth Him, He rewardeth him that serveth Him, and He protecteth him that followeth Him.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Budge (1899), ch. I.

title.en: I Evolved the Evolving of Evolutions: The Longer Creation of Nesi-Amsu
title.zh: 我演化演化之演化：內西-阿姆蘇長本創世記

region.en: Thebes, Egypt (British Museum Papyrus 10,188, the Book of Overthrowing Apep)
region.zh: 埃及底比斯（大英博物館紙草10188號，滅阿波菲斯之書）

period: British Museum Papyrus 10,188, copied c. 300 BCE, older doctrine (Budge translation 1899)

source.work: Egyptian Ideas of the Future Life, by E. A. W. Budge (1899), ch. I, the second version of the creation in the Papyrus of Nesi-Amsu

summary.en: The longer, stranger version of the creation legend: 'I evolved the evolving of evolutions... I uttered my own name, as a word of power, from my own mouth, and I straightway evolved myself. I was alone' — the speaker names himself Osiris, the germ of primeval matter, emits Shu and Tefnut ('from being One I became Three'), and men and women come from the tears of the Eye of Khepera.
summary.zh: 創世傳說之更長奇本：『我演化演化之演化……我以己名為力言，自口而出，我頃刻自化。我獨存』——言者自名為奧西里斯、原初物質之胚，吐出舒與泰芙努特（『由一而為三』），而人類則自凱佩拉之眼所落之淚而生。

sensitivity.note: Ancient creation text quoted in Budge 1899; no living community restrictions. Cross-refers to the short-version record of the same papyrus cut from Budge 1912.

passages.text: I evolved the evolving of evolutions. I evolved myself under the form of the evolutions of the god Khepera, which were evolved at the beginning of all time. I evolved with the evolutions of the god Khepera; I evolved by the evolution of evolutions — that is to say, I developed myself from the primeval matter which I made, I developed myself out of the primeval matter. My name is Ausares (Osiris), the germ of primeval matter. I have wrought my will wholly in this earth, I have spread abroad and filled it, I have strengthened it [with] my hand.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Budge, Egyptian Ideas of the Future Life (1899), ch. I, Papyrus of Nesi-Amsu.

passages.text: I was alone, for nothing had been brought forth; I had not then emitted from myself either Shu or Tefnut. I uttered my own name, as a word of power, from my own mouth, and I straightway evolved myself. Nothing existed on this earth then, and I made all things. There was none other who worked with me at that time. I performed all evolutions there by means of that divine Soul which I fashioned there, and which had remained inoperative in the watery abyss. I found no place there whereon to stand. But I was strong in my heart, and I made a foundation for myself, and I made everything which was made. I was alone.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Budge (1899), ch. I, Papyrus of Nesi-Amsu.

passages.text: I made a foundation for my heart (or will), and I created multitudes of things which evolved themselves like unto the evolutions of the god Khepera, and their offspring came into being from the evolutions of their births. I emitted from myself the gods Shu and Tefnut, and from being One I became Three; they sprang from me, and came into existence in this earth. Shu and Tefnut brought forth Seb and Nut, and Nut brought forth Osiris, Horus-khent-an-maa, Sut, Isis, and Nephthya at one birth.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Budge (1899), ch. I, Papyrus of Nesi-Amsu.

title.en: The King and Neter: God in the Pyramid Texts and the Precepts
title.zh: 王與奈特爾：金字塔文與箴言中的神

region.en: Sakkarah and Memphis, Egypt (the earliest uses of the word Neter)
region.zh: 埃及薩卡拉與孟菲斯（『奈特爾』一詞最早之用法）

period: Pyramid Texts c. 2350-2175 BCE and the Precepts of Ptah-hetep (Budge translation 1899)

source.work: Egyptian Ideas of the Future Life, by E. A. W. Budge (1899), ch. I, the word Neter in the Pyramid Texts and the Precepts

summary.en: The earliest religious usage of the supreme word: in the text of Unas the king exists 'at the side of God'; of Teta it is said 'he weigheth words, and behold God hearkeneth unto that which he saith'; of Pepi, 'This Pepi is God, the son of God'; while the Precepts of Ptah-hetep teach the oldest ethics of the word — 'What is loved of God is obedience; God hateth disobedience.'
summary.zh: 至尊之詞最早的宗教用法：烏納斯文中王『立於神之側』；論泰塔云『其權衡言辭，而神聽其所言』；論佩皮云『此佩皮乃神，神之子』；而卜塔-赫特普箴言授此詞最古之倫理——『神所愛者為順從；神所憎者為悖逆』。

sensitivity.note: Ancient royal and wisdom texts quoted in Budge 1899; no living community restrictions.

passages.text: In the text of Unas, a king who reigned about B.C. 3300, we find the passage: 'That which is sent by thy ka cometh to thee, that which is sent by thy father cometh to thee, that which is sent by Ra cometh to thee, and it arriveth in the train of thy Ra. Thou art pure, thy bones are the gods and the goddesses of heaven, thou existest at the side of God, thou art unfastened, thou comest forth towards thy soul, for every evil word (or thing) which hath been written in the name of Unas hath been done away.'
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Budge (1899), ch. I, quoting the Pyramid Text of Unas.

passages.text: And, again, in the text of Teta, in the passage which refers to the place in the eastern part of heaven 'where the gods give birth unto themselves, where that to which they give birth is born, and where they renew their youth,' it is said of this king, 'Teta standeth up in the form of the star...he weigheth words (or trieth deeds), and behold God hearkeneth unto that which he saith.' And of Pepi I., who reigned about B.C. 3000, it is said, 'This Pepi is God, the son of God.'
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Budge (1899), ch. I, quoting the Pyramid Texts of Teta and Pepi I.

passages.text: The idea of God held by Ptah-hetep is illustrated by the following passages: 'Thou shalt make neither man nor woman to be afraid, for God is opposed thereto; and if any man shall say that he will live thereby, He will make him to want bread.' — 'If thou abasest thyself in the service of a perfect man, thy conduct shall be fair before God.' — 'What is loved of God is obedience; God hateth disobedience.' — 'Verily a good son is of the gifts of God.'
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Budge (1899), ch. I, quoting the Precepts of Ptah-hetep.

title.en: Ptah Creates by Heart and Tongue: The Memphite Theology
title.zh: 卜塔以心與舌創世：孟菲斯神學

region.en: Memphis, Egypt (temple of Ptah, city of the artificer god)
region.zh: 埃及孟菲斯（工藝之神卜塔神廟）

period: Memphite doctrine (Shabaka Stone copy, 25th Dynasty); retold in D. A. Mackenzie, Egyptian Myth and Legend (1913)

source.archive: Global Grey Ebooks (public domain facsimile of Mackenzie, Egyptian Myth and Legend)
source.work: Donald A. Mackenzie, Egyptian Myth and Legend (London, 1913), ch. VI, 'The City of the Elf God'

summary.en: Memphis' own account of creation: Ptah, chief of the eight dwarfish Khnumu, first appeared as an egg laid by the chaos goose and fashioned the sun egg and the moon egg on his potter's wheel; in the higher doctrine the Memphite priests eulogize him as 'the mind and tongue of the gods', the creator whose ideas take material shape the moment he gives them expression.
summary.zh: 孟菲斯之創世記：卜塔，八位矮小庫努姆之首，初為混沌鵝所生之卵，於陶輪上造太陽之卵與月亮之卵；其高階教義則謂他為『眾神之心與舌』——其意念一經表達，即化為實物。

sensitivity.note: Ancient Memphite theology retold in a public-domain synthesis (Mackenzie 1913); all passages are his retelling, marked as such. The Shabaka Stone's own text is fragmentary; Mackenzie's rendering preserves the heart-and-tongue doctrine.

passages.text: At the beginning, according to Memphite belief, Ptah shaped the world and the heavens, assisted by his eight workmen, the dwarfish Khnumu. He was also the creator of mankind, and in Egyptian tombs are found numerous earthenware models of these 'elves', who were believed to have had power to reconstruct the decaying bodies of the dead. As their dwellings were underground, they may have also been 'artisans of vegetation', like the spirits associated with Tvashtar, the 'master workman' of the Rig-Veda hymns and the 'black dwarfs' of Teutonic mythology.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Mackenzie, Egyptian Myth and Legend (1913), ch. VI.

passages.text: Like Ra, Ptah was also believed to have first appeared as an egg, which, according to one of the many folk beliefs of Egypt, was laid by the chaos goose which came to be identified with Seb, the earth god, and afterwards with the combined deities Amon-Ra. Ptah, as the primeval 'artificer god', was credited with making 'the sun egg' and also 'the moon egg', and a bas-relief at Philae shows him actively engaged at the work, using his potter's wheel.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Mackenzie (1913), ch. VI.

passages.text: A higher and later conception of Ptah represents him as a sublime creator god who has power to call into existence each thing he names. He is the embodiment of mind from which all things emerge, and his ideas take material shape when he gives them expression. In a philosophic poem a Memphite priest eulogizes the great deity as 'the mind and tongue of the gods', and even as the creator of other gods as well as of 'all people, cattle, and reptiles', the sun, and the habitable world.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Mackenzie (1913), ch. VI.

title.en: The War of the Gods at Heracleopolis: The Great Cat and the Fiery Door
title.zh: 赫拉克利奧波利斯之諸神之戰：巨貓與火門

region.en: Heracleopolis Magna (Khenen-su), Middle Egypt (the lakes of natron and of truth)
region.zh: 埃及中埃及赫拉克利奧波利斯（ natron 湖與真理湖）

period: Heracleopolitan theology of the 9th-10th Dynasties; retold in D. A. Mackenzie, Egyptian Myth and Legend (1913)

source.archive: Global Grey Ebooks (public domain facsimile of Mackenzie, Egyptian Myth and Legend)
source.work: Donald A. Mackenzie, Egyptian Myth and Legend (1913), ch. XIV, 'Father Gods and Mother Goddesses'

summary.en: The local creation myth of Heracleopolis: Ra rises from the deep as the sun egg or the lotus flower — 'He who said: I am but One... He who is Yesterday (Osiris) and the Morrow (Ra)'; in its two sacred lakes Ra cleanses himself; at the height of the war of the gods Set flings filth in Horus' face and Horus mutilates Set, until Ra, as the Great Cat of the Persea tree, strangles the Apep serpent; and at the door of the fiery region crouches the greyhound-headed devourer of the condemned.
summary.zh: 赫拉克利奧波利斯本地創世記：拉以日卵或蓮花自深處升起——『彼自言：吾乃唯一……彼乃昨日（奧西里斯）與明日（拉）』；於其二聖湖中淨身；諸神之戰方酣，塞特擲穢於荷魯斯之面，荷魯斯殘塞特之體；末則拉化身為柏塞亞樹間之巨貓，勒斃阿波菲斯之蛇；火獄之門蹲踞著灰犬首之噬魂者。

sensitivity.note: Ancient theology retold in Mackenzie 1913; passages verbatim from the retelling. The Great Cat of Heliopolis slashing the Apep serpent is the scene depicted in BD ch. 17 vignettes.

passages.text: Heracleopolis Magna, which the Egyptians called Khenen-su is of special mythological interest. It came to be recognized as the scene of the great creation myth of the sun worshippers. There Ra, at the beginning, rose from the primeval deep in the form of the sun egg, or the lotus flower — He that openeth and he that closeth the door; He who said: 'I am but One'. Ra, who was produced by himself; Whose various names make up the group of gods; He who is Yesterday (Osiris) and the Morrow (Ra).
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Mackenzie, Egyptian Myth and Legend (1913), ch. XIV.

passages.text: Khenen-su district was the scene of the 'war of the gods', who contended against one another at Ra's command — a myth which suggests the everlasting struggle between the forces of nature, which began at Creation's dawn, and is ever controlled by the sun. Somewhere in the nome were situated the two mythical lakes, 'the lake of natron' and 'the lake of truth', in which Ra cleansed himself, and there, too, at the height of their great struggle — symbolized as the struggle between good and evil — Set flung filth in the face of Horus, and Horus mutilated Set. The ultimate victory was due to Ra, who, in the form of the Great Cat that haunted the Persea tree at Heliopolis, fought with the Apep serpent and overcame it.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Mackenzie (1913), ch. XIV.

passages.text: In the vicinity of Khenen-su was the fiery region. At its entrance crouched the demon who had human skin and the head of a greyhound. He was concealed by the door, and pounced unexpectedly upon 'the damned'; he tore out their hearts, which he devoured, and he swallowed their spirits. So the faithful sun worshippers were wont to pray: 'O Ra-tum give me deliverance from the demon who devoureth those who are condemned — he who waits at the door of the fiery place and is not seen. Save me from him who clutcheth souls, and eateth all filth and rottenness by day and by night. Those who dread him are helpless.'
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Mackenzie (1913), ch. XIV.

passages.text: At Khenen-su lived the Phoenix — the 'Great Bennu'. It resembled an eagle, and had feathers of red and golden colour. Some authorities identify this mythical bird with the planet Venus, which, as the morning star, was 'the guide of the sun god'.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Mackenzie (1913), ch. XIV.

title.en: Her-shef the Self-created: Head in Heaven, Feet on Earth
title.zh: 自生之神赫爾-舍夫：首在蒼天，足在大地

region.en: Heracleopolis Magna (temple of Her-shef, its chief god)
region.zh: 埃及赫拉克利奧波利斯（其主神赫爾-舍夫神廟）

period: Heracleopolitan state cult, 9th-10th Dynasties onward; retold in D. A. Mackenzie, Egyptian Myth and Legend (1913)

source.archive: Global Grey Ebooks (public domain facsimile of Mackenzie, Egyptian Myth and Legend)
source.work: Donald A. Mackenzie, Egyptian Myth and Legend (1913), ch. XIV, 'Father Gods and Mother Goddesses'

summary.en: The chief god of Heracleopolis is a self-created Great Father: his head in the heavens and his feet upon the earth, his right eye the sun and his left the moon, his soul the light he sheds over the world — and he breathes from his nostrils the north wind that gives life to every living being, for 'wind' and 'breath' and 'spirit' were one word to the Egyptians.
summary.zh: 赫拉克利奧波利斯主神乃自生之偉大父神：首在蒼天、足在大地；右眼為日、左眼為月；其魂即其照世之光——且自鼻息中呼出賦生於萬物之北風，蓋『風』『息』『靈』於埃及人本為一詞。

sensitivity.note: Ancient cult retold in Mackenzie 1913; passages verbatim from the retelling.

passages.text: The chief god was Her-shef, who bears a stronger resemblance to Ptah Tanen than to Horus. He was a self-created Great Father, whose head was in the heavens while his feet rested upon the earth. His right eye was the sun and his left the moon, while his soul was the light that he shed over the world. He breathed from his nostrils the north wind, which gave life to every living being.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Mackenzie, Egyptian Myth and Legend (1913), ch. XIV.

passages.text: 'Wind' and 'breath' and 'spirit' were believed by many primitive peoples to be identical. Her-shef was therefore the source of universal life. As a 'wind god' he resembles the southern deity Khnumu, who was also called Knef (the Kneph of the Greeks). The Egyptian knef means 'wind', 'breath', and 'spirit' — 'the air of life'.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Mackenzie (1913), ch. XIV.

title.en: The Arch of Nut: From Eastern Toes to Western Fingertips
title.zh: 努特之拱：自東足至西指尖

region.en: The sky over Egypt (the body-arch of the sky-goddess)
region.zh: 埃及上空（天神身軀之拱）

period: The Heliopolitan creation cosmology, retold in D. A. Mackenzie, Egyptian Myth and Legend (1913)

source.archive: Global Grey Ebooks (public domain facsimile of Mackenzie, Egyptian Myth and Legend)
source.work: Donald A. Mackenzie, Egyptian Myth and Legend (1913), ch. I, 'Creation Legend of Sun Worshippers'

summary.en: The picture every Egyptian knew: Ra commands earth and heaven to rise from the waste of water, and Shu the uplifter raises Nut on high — she forms the vault arched over Seb, who lies prostrate beneath her, from where at the eastern horizon she is poised upon her toes to where at the western horizon, bending with outstretched arms, she rests upon her finger tips; in the darkness the stars sparkle upon her unwearied limbs.
summary.zh: 每個埃及人都熟悉的圖景：拉命大地與蒼天自洪荒之水升起，『舉天者』舒將努特高舉——她成拱頂，覆於俯臥之塞布其上，自東方地平以足尖點立，至西方地平則屈身舒臂，以指尖著地；黑暗中，星宿閃耀於她不知疲倦的肢體之上。

sensitivity.note: Ancient cosmology retold in Mackenzie 1913; passages verbatim from the retelling.

passages.text: Then came into being Seb, the earth god, and Nut, the goddess of the firmament, who became the parents of Osiris and his consort Isis and also of Set and his consort Nepthys. Ra spake at the beginning of Creation, and bade the earth and the heavens to rise out of the waste of water. In the brightness of his majesty they appeared, and Shu, the uplifter, raised Nut upon high. She formed the vault, which is arched over Seb, the god of earth, who lies prostrate beneath her from where, at the eastern horizon, she is poised upon her toes to where, at the western horizon, bending down with outstretched arms, she rests upon her finger tips. In the darkness are beheld the stars which sparkle upon her body and over her great unwearied limbs.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Mackenzie, Egyptian Myth and Legend (1913), ch. I.

passages.text: When Ra, according to his desire, uttered the deep thoughts of his mind, that which he named had being. When he gazed into space, that which he desired to see appeared before him. He created all things that move in the waters and upon the dry land. Now, mankind were born from his eye, and Ra, the Creator, who was ruler of the gods, became the first king upon earth. He went about among men; he took form like unto theirs, and to him the centuries were as years.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Mackenzie (1913), ch. I.

title.en: Sebek the Crocodile: The Radiant Green Disk of the Fayum
title.zh: 鱷神塞貝克：法尤姆的翠綠日盤

region.en: Crocodilopolis, the Fayum, Egypt (the sacred lake of the tamed crocodile)
region.zh: 埃及法尤姆鱷城（馴鱷聖湖）

period: Cult of the 12th-13th Dynasties onward (observed by Herodotus and Strabo); retold in D. A. Mackenzie, Egyptian Myth and Legend (1913)

source.archive: Global Grey Ebooks (public domain facsimile of Mackenzie, Egyptian Myth and Legend)
source.work: Donald A. Mackenzie, Egyptian Myth and Legend (1913), ch. XVIII, 'Myths and Lays of the Middle Kingdom'

summary.en: The crocodile god of the Middle Kingdom rose to prominence with the Fayum kings: Sebek is 'the radiant green disk — the creator', who rose from Nu 'in many shapes and in many colours'; at Ombos he is the earth giant 'husband of his mother'; and in the sacred lake of Crocodilopolis lived his living image — a tame crocodile with crystal-set golden earrings and bracelets on its fore paws, fed by its priests with cakes, flesh and honey wine.
summary.zh: 中王國鱷神隨法尤姆諸王而興：塞貝克乃『放射之翠綠日盤——創造者』，自努『以多形多色』升起；在翁博斯為『母之夫』的大地巨人；而在鱷城聖湖中則有其活像——馴鱷戴金耳環嵌水晶、前爪有鐲，祭司以餅、肉與蜜酒飼之。

sensitivity.note: Ancient cult retold in Mackenzie 1913; passages verbatim from the retelling.

passages.text: Along with the new royal faces new religious beliefs also came into prominence. The rise of Sebek, the crocodile god, may have been due to the tendency shown by certain of the Pharaohs to reside in the Fayum. The town of Crocodilopolis was the chief centre of the hitherto obscure Sebek cult. — Sebek-Tum-Ra ultimately became the crocodile of the sun, as Mentu became 'bull of the sun', and he symbolized the power and heat of the orb of day. In this form he was the 'radiant green disk' — 'the creator', who rose from Nu 'in many shapes and in many colours'.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Mackenzie, Egyptian Myth and Legend (1913), ch. XVIII.

passages.text: At Ombos, Sebek was a form of Seb, the earth giant, the son of Nut, and 'husband of his mother'. He was called the 'father of the gods' and 'chief of the Nine Bow Barbarians'. — But his worshippers believed that he would lead souls by 'short cuts' and byways to the Egyptian paradise. In the Pyramid Texts he has the attributes of the elfin Khnumu... for he renews the eyes of the dead, touches their tongues so that they can speak, and restores the power of motion to their heads.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Mackenzie (1913), ch. XVIII.

passages.text: Strabo, who visited Egypt in the Roman period, relates that he saw a sacred crocodile in an artificial lake at Crocodilopolis in the Fayum. It was quite tame and was decorated with gold ear-rings, set with crystal, and wore bracelets on its fore paws. The priests opened its jaws and fed it with cakes, flesh, and honey wine. When the animal leapt into the water and came up at the other side, the priests followed it and gave it a fresh offering.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Mackenzie (1913), ch. XVIII, citing Strabo.

title.en: Neith the Veiled: The Unknown One Whose Veil Was Never Raised
title.zh: 蒙面之奈特：面紗未曾掀起之未知者

region.en: Sais, Western Delta, Egypt (temple of Neith, the Libyan Great Mother)
region.zh: 埃及西三角洲薩伊斯（利比亞大母神奈特神廟）

period: Cult of Neith from predynastic Libya through the 26th Dynasty (recorded in Mackenzie 1913 and Plutarch)

source.archive: Global Grey Ebooks (public domain facsimile of Mackenzie, Egyptian Myth and Legend)
source.work: Donald A. Mackenzie, Egyptian Myth and Legend (1913), ch. XVIII, 'Myths and Lays of the Middle Kingdom'

summary.en: In the Pyramid Texts Sebek is the son of Neith, the Libyan Earth Mother, who personified the female principle and was self-sustaining as she had been self-produced: 'the unknown one' and 'the hidden one', whose veil had never been uplifted — like other virgin goddesses she had a fatherless son, 'the husband of his mother'.
summary.zh: 金字塔文中塞貝克乃奈特之子——利比亞大地母神，體現女性本原，自足如自生：『未知者』『隱者』，其面紗未曾掀起——如他處女神，育無父之子，即『母之夫』。

sensitivity.note: Ancient cult retold in Mackenzie 1913; passages verbatim from the retelling. Cross-refers to the Sais veil inscription cut from Plutarch.

passages.text: In the texts of Unas, Sebek is referred to as the son of Neith, the Libyan 'Earth Mother', who personified the female principle, and was believed to be self-sustaining, as she had been self-produced. She was 'the unknown one' and 'the hidden one', whose veil had never been uplifted. Like other virgin goddesses, she had a fatherless son, the 'husband of his mother', who may have been identified with Sebek as a result of early tribal fusion.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Mackenzie, Egyptian Myth and Legend (1913), ch. XVIII.

passages.text: To this purpose, likewise, is that inscription which they have engraved upon the base of the statue of Athene at Sais, whom they identify with Isis: 'I am everything that has been, that is, and that shall be: and my veil no man hath raised.'
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Budge, Legends of the Gods (1912), Plutarch, De Iside sec. IX, quoted here as the Sais-temple parallel to the Neith tradition.

title.en: The Lay of the Harper: Drink, for No One Returns
title.zh: 琴師之歌：飲吧，無人復返

region.en: Egyptian banquet halls (the skeleton carried round at feasts; symbolic pin, Thebes)
region.zh: 埃及宴廳（宴中巡示之骷髏；象徵定位，底比斯）

period: Song of the Old Kingdom type, sung at banquets into the Middle Kingdom (metrical rendering in Mackenzie 1913)

source.archive: Global Grey Ebooks (public domain facsimile of Mackenzie, Egyptian Myth and Legend)
source.work: Donald A. Mackenzie, Egyptian Myth and Legend (1913), ch. XVIII, 'The Lay of the Harper'

summary.en: Egypt's great carpe-diem song, chanted at banquets while a model coffin was carried round: 'No soul comes back to tell us how he fares... Where are the tombs of Imhotep and Hordadaf? Long fallen, their places unknown... Revel in pleasure while your life endures and deck your head with myrrh... for no man takes his riches to the grave; yea, none returns again when he goes hence.'
summary.zh: 埃及最著名之及時行樂之歌，宴中偕小棺巡示而詠：『無魂歸來告我以彼界之事……英霍特普與霍爾代代夫之墓安在？傾頹無跡……趁生而行樂，以沒藥飾首……無人能攜富貴入墓；離去者無一復返。』

sensitivity.note: Ancient banquet song in Mackenzie's metrical rendering; passages verbatim from the rendering. The skeleton custom matches the Maneros record cut from Plutarch.

passages.text: One of the most popular Egyptian poems is called 'The Lay of the Harper'. It was chanted at the banquets given by wealthy men. 'Ere the company rises,' wrote Herodotus, 'a small coffin which contains a perfect model of the human body is carried round, and is shown to each guest in rotation. He who bears it exclaims: Look at this figure. After death you will be like it. Drink, therefore, and be merry.' The 'lay' in its earliest form was of great antiquity. Probably a real mummy was originally hauled through the banquet hall.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Mackenzie, Egyptian Myth and Legend (1913), ch. XVIII introduction.

passages.text: 'Tis well with this good prince; his day is done, His happy fate fulfilled. So one goes forth While others, as in days of old, remain. The old kings slumber in their pyramids, Likewise the noble and the learned, but some Who builded tombs have now no place of rest, Although their deeds were great. Lo! I have heard The words Imhotep and Hordadaf spake — Their maxims men repeat. Where are their tombs? Long fallen, e'en their places are unknown, And they are now as though they ne'er had been.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Mackenzie (1913), the Lay of the Harper, first stanza.

passages.text: No soul comes back to tell us how he fares — To soothe and comfort us ere we depart Whither he went betimes. But let our minds Forget of this and dwell on better things. Revel in pleasure while your life endures And deck your head with myrrh. Be richly clad In white and perfumed linen; like the gods Anointed be; and never weary grow In eager quest of what your heart desires — Do as it prompts you, until that sad day Of lamentation comes, when hearts at rest Hear not the cry of mourners at the tomb, Which have no meaning to the silent dead. Then celebrate this festal time, nor pause — For no man takes his riches to the grave; Yea, none returns again when he goes hence.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Mackenzie (1913), the Lay of the Harper, closing stanza.

title.en: The Two Judgments: Ra at Sunrise, Osiris at Midnight
title.zh: 兩重審判：晨之拉，夜半之奧西里斯

region.en: Near Abydos, Egypt (where the Judgment of Osiris was held at midnight)
region.zh: 埃及阿拜多斯近郊（奧西里斯午夜審判之處）

period: Doctrinal synthesis from the Book of the Dead and Book of Gates (Budge, The Book of the Dead, 1901)

source.work: The Book of the Dead, by E. A. Wallis Budge (1901), chs. VI-VII, 'Osiris as Judge of the Dead' and 'The Judgment of Osiris'

summary.en: Egypt's hell was annihilation, not torment: the Judgment of Ra at sunrise threw the wicked into pits of fire, consuming body, soul, shadow and heart; the Judgment of Osiris sat at midnight near Abydos, where Shesmu the headsman cut off the heads of the damned and burned their members — 'the infliction of punishment never ceased' only because the wicked were condemned anew each day.
summary.zh: 埃及之地獄是滅絕而非受苦：晨間拉之審判將惡者投入火坑，身、魂、影、心俱焚；夜半於阿拜多斯近郊行奧西里斯之審判，其劊子手舒斯姆斬罪者之首，肢解其身而焚之——刑罰之所以『無有止息』，唯因每日重新定罪而已。

sensitivity.note: Ancient funerary cosmology; no living community restrictions.

passages.text: This region of the dead, or Dead-land, is called 'Tat,' or 'Tuat,' but where the Egyptians thought it was situated is not quite clear... Wherever it was it was not underground, and it was not originally in the sky or even on its confines; but it was located on the borders of the visible world, in the Outer Darkness. The Tuat was not a place of happiness, judging from the description of it in the Book of the Dead. When Ani the scribe arrived there he said, 'What is this to which I have come? There is neither water nor air here, its depth is unfathomable, it is as dark as the darkest night, and men wander about here helplessly.' In the Tuat there was neither tree nor plant, for it was the 'land where nothing grew'; and in primitive times it was a region of destruction and death, a place where the dead rotted and decayed, a place of abomination, and horror and terror, and annihilation.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Budge, The Book of the Dead (1901), ch. VI.

passages.text: When the belief gained ground among them that Osiris, the God of the Dead, had himself risen from the dead, and had been acquitted by the gods of heaven after a searching trial, and had the power to 'make men and women to be born again,' and 'to renew life' because of his truth and righteousness, they came to regard him as the Judge as well as the God of the Dead. As time went on, and moral and religious ideas developed among the Egyptians, it became certain to them that only those who had satisfied Osiris as to their truth-speaking and honest dealing upon earth could hope for admission into his kingdom.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Budge (1901), ch. VI.

passages.text: But, as according to the cult of Ra, the wicked, the rebels, and the blasphemers of the Sun-god suffered swift and final punishment, so also all those who had sinned against the stern moral Law of Osiris, and who had failed to satisfy its demands, paid the penalty without delay. The Judgment of Ra was held at sunrise, and the wicked were thrown into deep pits filled with fire, and their bodies, souls, shadows and hearts were consumed forthwith. The Judgment of Osiris took place near Abydos, probably at midnight, and a decree of swift annihilation was passed by him on the damned. Their heads were cut off by the headsman of Osiris, who was called Shesmu, and their bodies dismembered and destroyed in pits of fire. There was no eternal punishment for men, for the wicked were annihilated quickly and completely; but inasmuch as Osiris sat in judgment and doomed the wicked to destruction daily, the infliction of punishment never ceased.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Budge (1901), ch. VI.

title.en: The Beetle and the Ball of Seed: Why the Scarab Is the Emblem of Creation
title.zh: 甲蟲與土球：聖甲蟲何以成創世徽記

region.en: Egypt (the scarab engraved on every soldier's seal)
region.zh: 埃及（刻於士兵印璽上的聖甲蟲）

period: Recorded by Plutarch, De Iside 10 (Budge translation 1912)

source.work: Legends of the Gods, trans. E. A. W. Budge (1912), Plutarch, The History of Isis and Osiris, sec. X

summary.en: Plutarch's famous aition for the scarab seal: there is no female of the species — all beetles are male — and they propagate their kind by casting their seed into round balls of dirt, which serve both as the hatching-place of the young and their first food; hence the self-created beetle became the hieroglyph of the self-created god Khepera.
summary.zh: 普魯塔克論聖甲蟲印璽之故：此蟲無雌——皆為雄——其繁衍之法乃將精種投於圓土球中，土球既為孵化之所，亦為幼蟲初糧；故此自生之蟲遂成自生之神凱佩拉之象形符號。

sensitivity.note: Ancient aition via Plutarch; no living community restrictions. Plutarch's biology is wrong but his report of the symbolism is the classic ancient testimony.

passages.text: Of a like nature is the Beetle which we see engraven upon the seals of the soldiers, for there is no such thing as a female beetle of this species; for they are all males, and they propagate their kind by casting their seed into round balls of dirt, which afford not only a proper place wherein the young may be hatched, but also nourishment for them as soon as they are born.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Budge, Legends of the Gods (1912), Plutarch sec. X.

passages.text: And I myself am of the opinion that, when the Pythagoreans appropriated the names of several of the gods to particular numbers, as that of Apollo to the unit, of Artemis to the duad, of Athene to the seven, and of Poseidon to the first cube, in this they allude to something which the founder of their sect saw in the Egyptian temples, or to some ceremonies performed in them, or to some symbols there exhibited.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Budge (1912), Plutarch sec. X.

title.en: The Handless Judges of Thebes: Statues That Teach Justice
title.zh: 底比斯無手法官：教誨公義之像

region.en: Thebes, Egypt (statues of the judges in the temple)
region.zh: 埃及底比斯（神廟中法官之像）

period: Recorded by Plutarch, De Iside 10 (Budge translation 1912)

source.work: Legends of the Gods, trans. E. A. W. Budge (1912), Plutarch, The History of Isis and Osiris, sec. X

summary.en: The statues of the judges at Thebes are without hands, and their chief is carved with his eyes turned downward — 'which signifies that justice ought not to be obtainable by bribes, nor guided by favour or affection' — a sermon in stone on how the divine court itself is conducted.
summary.zh: 底比斯法官像皆無手，主審者之目向下——『其意謂公義不可賄得，不可因私情而偏』——以石為講章，教示神庭審判之道。

sensitivity.note: Ancient temple-symbolism anecdote via Plutarch; no living community restrictions.

passages.text: Much in the same way are those statues of the Judges at Thebes without hands, and their chief, or president, is represented with his eyes turned downwards, which signifies that justice ought not to be obtainable by bribes, nor guided by favour or affection.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Budge, Legends of the Gods (1912), Plutarch sec. X.

passages.text: Their great king and lord Osiris is represented by the hieroglyphics for an eye and a sceptre, the name itself signifying 'many-eyed', as we are told by some who would derive it from the words os, 'many', and iri, an 'eye', which have this meaning in the Egyptian language. Similarly, because the heavens are eternal and are never consumed or wax old, they represent them by a heart with a censer placed under it.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Budge (1912), Plutarch sec. X.

title.en: The Ass of Typhon: Asses Cast Down, Trumpets Forbidden
title.zh: 提豐之驢：投驢於崖、禁吹號角

region.en: Koptos, Busiris and Lycopolis, Egypt (the towns of the ass taboo)
region.zh: 埃及科普托斯、布西里斯與呂科波利斯（驢之禁俗諸城）

period: Recorded by Plutarch, De Iside 30-31 (Budge translation 1912)

source.work: Legends of the Gods, trans. E. A. W. Budge (1912), Plutarch, The History of Isis and Osiris, secs. XXX-XXXI

summary.en: The taboo-codes of Set's animal: red being Typhon's colour, the men of Koptos cast asses down precipices, the towns of Busiris and Lycopolis never use trumpets because their sound resembles the ass's braying, the festival cakes of Paoni and Paopi are stamped with a fettered ass — and Typhon himself, says the tradition, escaped from Horus by a flight of seven days on an ass.
summary.zh: 塞特聖獸之禁忌：紅為提豐之色，科普托斯人驅驢投崖；布西里斯與呂科波利斯人永不吹號——以其聲似驢鳴；帕奧尼與帕奧皮祭日之餅上印有縛驢之像——相傳提豐曾騎驢七日而遁於荷魯斯之手。

sensitivity.note: Ancient taboo traditions via Plutarch; no living community restrictions.

passages.text: Typhon is held by the Egyptians in the greatest contempt, and they do all they can to vilify him. The colour red being associated with him, they treat with contumely all those who have a ruddy complexion; the ass being usually of a reddish colour, the men of Koptos are in the habit of sacrificing asses by casting them down precipices. The inhabitants of Busiris and Lycopolis never use trumpets, because their sounds resemble the braying of an ass. The cakes which are offered at the festivals during Paoni and Paopi are stamped with the figure of a fettered ass.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Budge, Legends of the Gods (1912), Plutarch sec. XXX (Budge's summary of Plutarch's text).

passages.text: The ass is identified with Typhon not only because of his colour, but also because of his stupidity and the sensuality of his disposition. The Persian king Ochus was nicknamed the 'Ass', which made him to say, 'This ass shall dine upon your ox,' and accordingly he slew Apis. Typhon is said to have escaped from Horus by a flight of seven days on an ass.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Budge (1912), Plutarch sec. XXXI (Budge's summary of Plutarch's text).

passages.text: In a hymn the deceased prays, 'May I smite the Ass, may I crush the serpent-fiend Sebau,' but the XLth Chapter of the Book of the Dead is entitled, 'Chapter of driving back the Eater of the Ass.' The vignette shows us the deceased in the act of spearing a monster serpent which has fastened its jaws in the back of an ass. In Chapter CXXV. there is a dialogue between the Cat and the Ass.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Budge (1912), footnote to Plutarch sec. XXX, citing the Book of the Dead.

title.en: Red Bulls Only: The Seal on Every Sacrificial Beast
title.zh: 惟紅牛可祭：祭牲身上的印記

region.en: The sacrificial courts of Egyptian temples (symbolic pin, Memphis)
region.zh: 埃及神廟祭牲之圈（象徵定位，孟菲斯）

period: Recorded by Plutarch, De Iside 31 (Budge translation 1912)

source.work: Legends of the Gods, trans. E. A. W. Budge (1912), Plutarch, The History of Isis and Osiris, sec. XXXI

summary.en: The ritual logic of the Egyptian altar: only red-coloured bulls may be sacrificed — a single black or white hair disqualifies the victim — because the sacrificed creatures are believed to hold the souls of the wicked, confined in beasts for punishment; hence the custom of cursing the animal, cutting off its head and throwing it into the Nile, and the priests' seal: a man on his knees, hands bound behind him, a sword pointed at his throat.
summary.zh: 埃及祭壇之禮制：惟純赤之牛可祭——祭牲身上一毫黑白之毛即為不合格——蓋彼等信祭牲體內囚有惡人之魂，受罰於獸身；故有咒詛祭牲、斬其首而投於尼羅之俗，且祭牲必佩祭司印記：一人跪地，反縛雙手，利劍加頸。

sensitivity.note: Ancient ritual doctrine via Plutarch; no living community restrictions.

passages.text: The Egyptians only sacrifice red-coloured bulls, and a single black or white hair in the animal's head disqualifies it for sacrifice. They sacrifice creatures wherein the souls of the wicked have been confined, and through this view arose the custom of cursing the animal to be sacrificed, and cutting off its head and throwing it into the Nile. No bullock is sacrificed which has not on it the seal of the priests who were called 'Sealers.' The impression from this seal represents a man upon his knees, with his hands tied behind him, and a sword pointed at his throat.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Budge, Legends of the Gods (1912), Plutarch sec. XXXI (Budge's summary of Plutarch's text).

title.en: Osiris the Earth: The Nile from the Sweat of His Hands
title.zh: 大地奧西里斯：尼羅出於其掌汗

region.en: Egypt, the black land itself (the god who bears the earth on his shoulders)
region.zh: 埃及黑土之邦（肩負大地之神）

period: New Kingdom hymn written on limestone ostracon (Budge translation 1910)

source.work: The Literature of the Ancient Egyptians, trans. E. A. W. Budge (1910), ch. XII, the Hymn to Osiris on the Cairo limestone slices

summary.en: The earth-hymn of Osiris: the divine mummy lies on the sand, the earth rests upon his shoulders, its corners upon him 'as far as the four pillars of heaven'; if he stirs, the earth quakes; the Nile appears from the sweat of his two hands, and men live by the breath of his throat — 'Thou art the father and mother of men and women, they live by thy breath, they eat the flesh of thy members. Pautti, the Primeval God, is thy name.'
summary.zh: 奧西里斯大地之頌：神聖木乃伊臥於沙上，大地載於其肩，四極倚其身『直抵天之四柱』；彼若微動，大地震顫；尼羅自其掌汗湧出，人賴其喉息而活——『爾乃人類之父與母，彼等賴爾息而活，食爾肢體之肉。太初之神『保提』乃爾之名。』

sensitivity.note: Ancient hymn; no living community restrictions. The hymn identifies Osiris with the earth itself and its fertility.

passages.text: [Praise be] unto thee, O thou who extendest thine arms, who liest asleep on thy side, who liest on the sand, the Lord of the earth, the divine mummy. Thou art the Child of the Earth Serpent, of great age. Thy head ... and goeth round over thy feet. Ra-Khepera shineth upon thy body, when thou liest on thy bed in the form of Seker, so that he may drive away the darkness that shroudeth thee, and may infuse light in thy two eyes. He passeth a long period of time shining upon thee, and sheddeth tears over thee.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Budge, Literature of the Ancient Egyptians (1910), ch. XII, Hymn to Osiris.

passages.text: The earth resteth upon thy shoulders, and its corners rest upon thee as far as the four pillars of heaven. If thou movest thyself, the earth quaketh, for thou art greater than.... [The Nile] appeareth out of the sweat of thy two hands. Thou breathest forth the air that is in thy throat into the nostrils of men; divine is that thing whereon they live. Through thy nostrils (?) subsist the flowers, the herbage, the reeds, the flags (?), the barley, the wheat, and the plants whereon men live.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Budge (1910), Hymn to Osiris.

passages.text: If canals are dug ... and houses and temples are built, and great statues are dragged along, and lands are ploughed up, and tombs and funerary monuments are made, they [all] rest upon thee. It is thou who makest them. They are upon thy back. There is no vacant space on thy back, they all lie on thy back, and yet [thou sayest] not, 'I am [over] weighted therewith.' Thou art the father and mother of men and women, they live by thy breath, they eat the flesh of thy members. 'Pautti' (i.e. Primeval God) is thy name.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Budge (1910), Hymn to Osiris.

title.en: Jiufeng, the Nine-Headed Bird of the Northern Polar Mountain
title.zh: 九鳳九首人面

region.en: Beiji Tiangui, the northern polar mountain (symbolic pin: far north)
region.zh: 北極天櫃（象徵性定位）

period: Shanhaijing, Da Huang Bei Jing, compiled c. 4th-2nd c. BCE

source.work: Shanhaijing, Da Huang Bei Jing: the nine-headed god Jiufeng of the northern polar mountain (Guo Pu recension)

license: Public domain (Classical Chinese text; passages are compiler's renderings)

summary.en: On the northern polar mountain, where the sea pours in from the north, dwells a god with nine heads on a bird's body and human faces — Jiufeng, the great nine-headed bird whom the Chu poets would later honor and storytellers fear: ancestor of the fire-birds and the ghost-phoenix of the south.
summary.zh: 大荒北經北極天櫃：海水北注焉；有神九首，人面鳥身，名曰九鳳——楚地火鳥與鬼鳳之祖。

sensitivity.note: Passages are the compiler's condensed paraphrases of the Shanhaijing original. The nine-headed bird later becomes the 'nine-headed ghost-bird' (guiche/ye xiao) of Chinese folklore — a feared omen; the descent is noted.

passages.text: In the midst of the Great Waste there is a mountain called the Northern Polar Heaven-Cabinet, into which the sea pours itself from the north. On that mountain dwells a god with nine heads, human-faced, borne on a bird's body, and his name is Jiufeng, Nine-Phoenixes.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Shanhaijing, Da Huang Bei Jing, Jiufeng entry (compiler's rendering); not verbatim.

passages.text: The nine heads face nine ways at once, so the god sees the whole waste in every wind; commentators of the Chu lands took him for a form of the great fire-bird, and folklorists of later ages for the nine-headed night-owl that calls over village roofs — the same bird, feared when it is heard.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Shanhaijing entry with Guo Pu's traditional commentary; not verbatim.

title.en: Tianwu, the Water God with Eight Heads and Eight Tails
title.zh: 天吳八首八尾

region.en: Chaoyang Valley, the valley of the morning sun (symbolic pin: eastern waters)
region.zh: 朝陽之谷（象徵性定位）

period: Shanhaijing, Hai Wai Dong Jing, compiled c. 4th-2nd c. BCE

source.work: Shanhaijing, Hai Wai Dong Jing: the god Tianwu of Chaoyang Valley (Guo Pu recension)

license: Public domain (Classical Chinese text; passages are compiler's renderings)

summary.en: In Chaoyang Valley dwells the god Tianwu, Lord of the Waters: eight human faces on a body of eight tiger-colored parts, eight legs, eight tails, yellow-green all over — a god of the waters whose crest of backs was carved on Han-era water-gates and whose name means Heaven-Growl.
summary.zh: 朝陽之谷，神曰天吳，是為水伯；其為獸也，八首人面、八足八尾，皆青黃——水伯天吳。

sensitivity.note: Passages are the compiler's condensed paraphrases of the Shanhaijing original.

passages.text: The valley of the morning sun is in the wild of the east, and its god is Tianwu, the Lord of the Waters: eight human faces in a ring, eight feet, eight tails, his whole body banded green-yellow like a tiger's hide.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Shanhaijing, Hai Wai Dong Jing, Tianwu entry (compiler's rendering); not verbatim.

passages.text: He is the Water-Count of the book's gazetteer — the power of rivers and tides in animal form; later votive art puts a many-headed water god with beast faces on the gates of dams and wells, where the tiger-bands and eight tails still show the shape of Tianwu.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Shanhaijing entry with traditional commentary; not verbatim.

title.en: Luwu, Guardian of Kunlun and the Emperor's Parks
title.zh: 陸吾司崑崙

region.en: Kunlun, the mountain of the gods (symbolic pin: Kunlun range)
region.zh: 崑崙之丘（象徵性定位）

period: Shanhaijing, Xi Ci Er Jing, compiled c. 4th-2nd c. BCE

source.work: Shanhaijing, Xi Ci Er Jing: Kunlun and the guardian god Luwu (Guo Pu recension)

license: Public domain (Classical Chinese text; passages are compiler's renderings)

summary.en: On Kunlun, the emperor's own mountain below the sky, dwells the god Luwu: body of a tiger, nine tails, a human face, claws like tiger's talons — the steward who administers the nine provinces of heaven and the seasons of the imperial game-parks. His salt-ponds flash red and his water-margins flash gold.
summary.zh: 崑崙之丘，是實惟帝之下都，神陸吾司之：虎身九尾，人面虎爪；司天之九部及帝之囿時——崑崙之守。

sensitivity.note: Passages are the compiler's condensed paraphrases of the Shanhaijing original.

passages.text: Kunlun is the emperor's lower capital below the sky, and the god set over it is Luwu: a tiger's body with nine tails, a human face, and talons like a tiger's — he administers the nine districts of heaven and the seasons of the emperor's own hunting-parks.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Shanhaijing, Xi Ci Er Jing, Kunlun entry (compiler's rendering); not verbatim.

passages.text: On the mountain are salt-ponds that flash red and waters that flash gold at the margins; beasts of every kind live around them, and Luwu, with his nine tails and tiger-claws, is the steward of it all — the game-warden of heaven's own estate.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Shanhaijing, Xi Ci Er Jing; not verbatim.

title.en: Yingzhao, the Horse-Faced Warden of the Four Seas
title.zh: 英招徇於四海

region.en: Huaijiang Mountain, west of Kunlun (symbolic pin: Kunlun west)
region.zh: 槐江之山（象徵性定位）

period: Shanhaijing, Xi Ci San Jing, compiled c. 4th-2nd c. BCE

source.work: Shanhaijing, Xi Ci San Jing: Huaijiang Mountain and the god Yingzhao (Guo Pu recension)

license: Public domain (Classical Chinese text; passages are compiler's renderings)

summary.en: Huaijiang Mountain, in sight of the Hanging Gardens, is held by the god Yingzhao: a horse's body with a human face, tiger-striped and winged, whose cry sounds like a rolling winnow, and who patrols the four seas crying aloud — the warden whose shout carries around the world's rim.
summary.zh: 槐江之山，實惟帝之平圃；神英招司之，其狀馬身而人面，虎文而鳥翼，徇於四海，其音如榴——巡守四極之神。

sensitivity.note: Passages are the compiler's condensed paraphrases of the Shanhaijing original.

passages.text: Huaijiang Mountain, looking up at the emperor's Hanging Gardens, is governed by the god Yingzhao — a horse's body with a human face, tiger-striped, with a bird's wings, and a voice that rolls like a winnowing-hail. His office is the circuit of the four seas: he patrols the coasts of the world crying aloud, and the book adds that the Yellow River's spring rises from this mountain — the warden's rounds begin where the great water begins.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Shanhaijing, Xi Ci San Jing, Yingzhao entry (compiler's rendering); not verbatim. / Paraphrase of Shanhaijing, Xi Ci San Jing; not verbatim.

title.en: Erfu Kills Yayu, and the Murdered God Becomes a Man-Eater
title.zh: 貳負殺窫窳

region.en: Shushu Mountain, where the murderer was bound (symbolic pin: far west)
region.zh: 疏屬山（象徵性定位）

period: Shanhaijing, Hai Wai Xi Jing, compiled c. 4th-2nd c. BCE

source.work: Shanhaijing, Hai Wai Xi Jing: Erfu and the murder of Yayu; Guo Pu's note on the revived monster

license: Public domain (Classical Chinese text; passages are compiler's renderings)

summary.en: Yayu, a god with a snake's body and a human face, was murdered by Erfu and his minister Wei; the Emperor bound the murderers to Shushu Mountain with their right feet shackled. But Yayu's corpse revived wrongly — he rose again as a monster with a dragon's head, eating men, one of the very monsters Yi the archer would later shoot down in the ten-sun age.
summary.zh: 貳負之臣曰危，與貳負殺窫窳，帝乃梏之疏屬之山，桎其右足；窫窳者蛇身人面——後復甦為龍首食人之獸，為羿所誅。

sensitivity.note: Passages are the compiler's condensed paraphrases of the Shanhaijing original. Links to the Yi ten-suns record (chinese-huainanzi-yi-ten-suns): the revived god is one of Yi's prey.

passages.text: Erfu, a god of the west, and his minister Wei murdered Yayu, a god with a snake's body and a human face — a killing among gods that could not go unpunished, for the murdered one was of the divine kindred.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Shanhaijing, Hai Wai Xi Jing, Erfu entry (compiler's rendering); not verbatim.

passages.text: The Emperor had the murderers seized and bound to Shushu Mountain, their right feet shackled in stone and their arms pierced and locked behind their backs to the mountain's rock. There the two stood until their term should run.
