passages.text: He returned to find her dead of the waiting. At the tomb-mound her spirit came out of the earth in jeweled robes, sang him a farewell in five lines, and brought him down into the grave for three days of feast; then she gave him the pearls and sent him up into the light.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Soushen Ji, juan 16, the tomb-wedding; not verbatim.

passages.text: The king called it grave-robbery and would have him arrested; the daughter rose out of the tomb before the whole court in her grave-ornaments, stood in the air before her father, named the pearls hers and gave, and sank back into the mound — and the king, undone, had her tomb raised higher. The story keeps both its grief and its proof.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Soushen Ji, juan 16, the court and the ending; not verbatim.

title.en: Lu Chong's Grave-Wedding in the House of Cui
title.zh: 盧充幽婚

region.en: The hunting-field west of Cui's tomb (Hebei)
region.zh: 崔少府墓

period: Soushen Ji by Gan Bao, c. 350 CE, juan 16

source.work: Soushen Ji, juan 16: Lu Chong's hunt, the Cui household in the tomb, the wedding, and the three-year son

license: Public domain (Classical Chinese text; passages are compiler's renderings)

summary.en: Hunting west of the city, Lu Chong shot a roe that ran into a mansion whose gate read Cui Shaofu's Tomb: within, the master of the house — dead these years — greeted him, produced his daughter, and explained the marriage was arranged before her birth. They were wed; four days on, the living groom was sent home with his bride's gold bowl. Three years later, on the river, the bowl was filled by their son, sent up from the tomb in a boat — and the boy, raised four years more among ghosts, came out to live in the world.
summary.zh: 盧充逐麞入崔少府府（墓）；府君曰『尊府君與僕有婚姻之約』——與其女成婚四日，贈金碗而歸；三年後河上見送三歲兒者——幽婚生子，幽明兩全。

sensitivity.note: Passages are the compiler's condensed paraphrases of the Soushen Ji original.

passages.text: Lu Chong, hunting west of the city, shot at a roe and followed it into a mansion whose gate-plate read the Tomb of Cui Shaofu; within, a lord greeted him by name and asked whether he knew the marriage contract his own father had signed before the girl's birth.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Soushen Ji, juan 16, Lu Chong entry (compiler's rendering); not verbatim.

passages.text: The daughter came out and was married to him in the tomb-house; four days on, her father sent the living groom home with his bride's gold bowl, saying the child of the marriage would be found when three years had run.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Soushen Ji, juan 16, the wedding; not verbatim.

passages.text: On the river three years later a boat came up carrying the bowl, filled and warm, and the boy of three years old beside it; the ghost-household raised him four years more and then sent him out to live among the living — Lu Chong's line continued from a tomb that kept its own accounts.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Soushen Ji, juan 16, the son; not verbatim.

title.en: The Lovers of Hejian: Opened in Death, Married in Life
title.zh: 河間郡男女

region.en: Hejian commandery, the tomb and the bridal bed (Hebei)
region.zh: 河間郡

period: Soushen Ji by Gan Bao, c. 350 CE, juan 15

source.work: Soushen Ji, juan 15: the buried-alive girl, the tunnel of love, and the resurrection by the official's order

license: Public domain (Classical Chinese text; passages are compiler's renderings)

summary.en: A girl of Hejian was buried while still breathing, and her lover dug a tunnel to the coffin and kept vigil there until she woke — and they lived as man and wife in the grave-mound. The discovery scandalized the county; the case went up to the court, and the judge's verdict is the tale's point: the love of an earlier betrothal is the finest of bonds — let them be wed. And the two came up out of the earth, put on wedding clothes, and the county that had called it a crime gave the feast.
summary.zh: 河間郡男女私悅而女生埋；男開冢穴而居之，女既更蘇；官司上聞，議曰『私情之篤，許其婚』——遂以禮娶之。

sensitivity.note: Passages are the compiler's condensed paraphrases of the Soushen Ji original.

passages.text: A girl of Hejian, betrothed in love and buried before her breath had left her, lay in the mound alive — and her lover, learning it, dug a tunnel to the coffin and took up a watchman's life beside her grave.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Soushen Ji, juan 15, Hejian entry (compiler's rendering); not verbatim.

passages.text: She woke in the tunnel's air, and the two lived as man and wife in the mound — a scandal that reached the court, where the officials argued the letter of the law against the facts of the lovers' constancy.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Soushen Ji, juan 15, the tunnel-life; not verbatim.

passages.text: The verdict went to the lovers: the bond of a betrothal was the finest of bonds, and the pair were given leave to wed. They came up out of the earth, put on the clothes of a wedding, and the county that had prosecuted them gave the feast — the law bowing, once, to the tunnel.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Soushen Ji, juan 15, the verdict; not verbatim.

title.en: Jiang Ji's Dead Son Asks for a Better Post
title.zh: 蔣濟亡兒託夢

region.en: The court of the Lord of Mount Tai (pin: Shandong)
region.zh: 泰山府君之署

period: Soushen Ji by Gan Bao, c. 350 CE, juan 16

source.work: Soushen Ji, juan 16: the dream of Jiang Ji's son, the underworld's job market, and the prefect's letter

license: Public domain (Classical Chinese text; passages are compiler's renderings)

summary.en: Jiang Ji, a minister of Wei, dreamed his dead son came weeping: in the underworld he served as a common soldier under a bureau-chief of the dead, and his father's name could buy him the post he wanted, if a letter came. The father wrote to a dead acquaintance of the family who now served as secretary to the Prefect of Mount Tai; the son was transferred; and the dream-detail that indicts the bureaucracy is the tale's whole point: the dead of the Chinese underworld are promoted and retired like clerks, and connections cross the river of death freely.
summary.zh: 蔣濟亡兒託夢求遷：其子隸泰山府君之伍伯；濟作書與故吏（已亡者）託之；旬日夢兒來謝——幽冥亦有選曹。

sensitivity.note: Passages are the compiler's condensed paraphrases of the Soushen Ji original. The underworld-as-bureaucracy satire.

passages.text: Jiang Ji, a minister of Wei, dreamed that his dead son stood weeping before him: in the courts below he served as a common soldier under a bureau-chief, and wanted a post in the ranks of the Prefect of Mount Tai — a post his father's name could obtain with one letter.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Soushen Ji, juan 16, Jiang Ji entry (compiler's rendering); not verbatim.

passages.text: The father wrote to an old family acquaintance — dead these years and now secretary to the underworld's own prefect — and posted the letter by the only road that carries such things: he laid it on the grave and spoke the address aloud.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Soushen Ji, juan 16, the letter; not verbatim.

passages.text: Days later the son came again in the dream, this time in new robes, bowing with the thanks of a promoted clerk. The tale's point needs no ghost at all: the underworld of the Chinese imagination runs on the same paper as the court above it — recommendations, favor, and the price of a father's signature.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Soushen Ji, juan 16, the thanks; not verbatim.

title.en: Guo Pu Divines His Own Death and the Rain of Two Prefectures
title.zh: 郭璞占己

region.en: Jiankang, the eastern capital (Nanjing)
region.zh: 建康

period: Soushen Ji by Gan Bao, c. 350 CE, juan 9 (Guo Pu, d. 324 CE)

source.work: Soushen Ji, juan 9: Guo Pu's divinations — the dry rain-prayer, the drowned rider, and his own appointment with the executioner

license: Public domain (Classical Chinese text; passages are compiler's renderings)

summary.en: Guo Pu, the greatest diviner of his age, was asked by the general Wang Dun — plotting revolt — to read his own fate; Pu answered with the cold number: inauspicious, and you will not succeed. Wang Dun had him killed; Pu asked only to choose the place of his execution, walked to a ground where the trees of his divination grew, and died exactly where he had ranked the spot. Earlier, asked for rain by a drought-bound prefecture, he had called for a green-scaled river-lord fetched up from the water, and an afternoon of rain that drenched two counties to their field-stones.
summary.zh: 郭璞為王敦占筮曰『無成』；敦怒殺之；璞自擇行刑之地——璞自言命盡於今日，至南岡松柏之下行刑——其術通神，死生皆自占。

sensitivity.note: Passages are the compiler's condensed paraphrases of the Soushen Ji original.

passages.text: Guo Pu, master of the stalk and the compass, was brought before the general Wang Dun, who wanted one number: will my rising succeed? Pu cast and answered with the coldest word in the diviner's repertoire: inauspicious — you will not succeed.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Soushen Ji, juan 9, Guo Pu entry (compiler's rendering); not verbatim.

passages.text: Wang Dun ordered him killed. Pu asked one courtesy — to choose the ground — and walked to a spot among the trees where, as he had already told the household that morning, his span would end; there he knelt, and the blade fell exactly where he had ranked it.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Soushen Ji, juan 9, the chosen ground; not verbatim.

passages.text: The same book keeps his rain-call for the drought-bound prefecture: a boat and a green-scaled river-lord fetched up from the water, and an afternoon of rain that drenched two counties to their field-stones — the diviner who read the sky so exactly that his own death had a street address.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Soushen Ji, juan 9, the rain; not verbatim.

title.en: Wang Daoping and the Wife Who Came Back Twice
title.zh: 王道平還魂

region.en: The border camps and the tomb of the pledged girl (pin: northern frontier)
region.zh: 沙場與父? 墓

period: Soushen Ji by Gan Bao, c. 350 CE, juan 15

source.work: Soushen Ji, juan 15: Wang Daoping's war-exile, the girl's death and burial, and the ghost who named her rescuer

license: Public domain (Classical Chinese text; passages are compiler's renderings)

summary.en: Wang Daoping and the girl Tang Wenyu was pledged from youth; he was conscripted and gone ten years; her parents, sure he was dead, married her to another. She grieved, sickened, died, and was buried. Her ghost came to Daoping in his camp, told him where the mound stood, and bade him open it; he did, and she sat up alive — and the lawsuit that followed gave her back to the first, the court reading the tomb-opening as proof of a betrothal the living had forgotten.
summary.zh: 王道平與唐文喻自幼誓為夫婦；平從軍十年，父母聘女他氏，女憂憤而卒；魂託夢於平，使發冢——開棺而蘇——復歸故夫。

sensitivity.note: Passages are the compiler's condensed paraphrases of the Soushen Ji original.

passages.text: Wang Daoping and the girl he had loved from childhood were pledged in youth; the draft took him for ten years, her parents married her to another in his absence, and she grieved herself into the grave within three years of the wedding.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Soushen Ji, juan 15, Wang Daoping entry (compiler's rendering); not verbatim.

passages.text: Her ghost found him at the front, told him where the mound stood, and gave him the single instruction: open it. He came home on leave, dug, and the girl sat up in the coffin — three years buried, alive, and asking first about the man the court had given her.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Soushen Ji, juan 15, the opening; not verbatim.

passages.text: The lawsuit went to the officials, who read the resurrection as the sky's own testimony: a bride who could not stay dead for her betrothed was a bride betrothed in truth. She was returned to Daoping, and the second household was paid off with the county's apology.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Soushen Ji, juan 15, the verdict; not verbatim.

title.en: Ding Lingwei Becomes a Crane and Returns to a Changed City
title.zh: 丁令威化鶴

region.en: Liaodong, the crane's home city (Liaoning)
region.zh: 遼東城

period: Soushen Hou Ji (In Search of the Supernatural, Continued), attributed Tao Qian, c. 5th c. CE, juan 1

source.work: Soushen Hou Ji, juan 1: Ding Lingwei of Liaodong, the thousand years on Lingxu Mountain, and the crane's song on the city pillar

license: Public domain (Classical Chinese text; passages are compiler's renderings)

summary.en: Ding Lingwei of Liaodong went to the Spirit-Emptiness Mountain to study the Way and became a crane; after a thousand years he flew home, lighted on the city pillar, and sang his song to the gathered people: 'There was a bird, a bird named Ding Lingwei — a thousand years gone from home, and now returned: the walls are as they were, and the people are not; why not study the immortals, and leave the mounds of dust?' — and rose into the sky, leaving the city a proverb it has never quite finished pronouncing.
summary.zh: 丁令威，本遼東人，學道於靈虛山，後化鶴歸遼，集城門華表柱；時有少年舉弓欲射之——鶴乃飛，徘徊空中而言曰：『有鳥有鳥丁令威，去家千年今始歸。城郭如故人民非，何不學仙冢壘壘。』遂高上沖天。

sensitivity.note: Passages are the compiler's condensed paraphrases of the Soushen Hou Ji original.

passages.text: Ding Lingwei of Liaodong went up into the Spirit-Emptiness Mountain to study the Way, and learned it so thoroughly that a thousand years on he came home as a white crane, and lighted on the pillar of the city gate where he used to loiter as a boy.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Soushen Hou Ji, juan 1, Ding Lingwei entry (compiler's rendering); not verbatim.

passages.text: A young archer raised his bow at the crane; the crane rose in the air, circled, and sang its four lines to the crowd: a bird named Ding Lingwei, a thousand years from home; the walls as they were, the people not; why not study the immortals, for the mounds of the dead are stacking up. Then it flew into the sky and was not seen again — the city's mourning for its own century, delivered by a bird.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Soushen Hou Ji, juan 1, the song; not verbatim.

title.en: A-Xiang and the Thunder-Cart
title.zh: 阿香推雷車

region.en: The post-house of the new-yang road (pin: Henan–Shaanxi)
region.zh: 新陽道中

period: Soushen Hou Ji (In Search of the Supernatural, Continued), attributed Tao Qian, c. 5th c. CE, juan 5

source.work: Soushen Hou Ji, juan 5: the girl pushing the thunder-cart at the inn, and the hail that came on her word

license: Public domain (Classical Chinese text; passages are compiler's renderings)

summary.en: At an inn on the New-yang road a tired guest was shown to sleep by a girl who, in the night, went out to the yard, took the handles of a small cart, and pushed it into the sky — at which the thunder rolled. He told the innkeeper at breakfast; the old man turned pale: that was A-Xiang, the thunder-maid, hired to drive the storm-cart, and she has left this inn tonight for good. Wherever she pushes, hail and thunder fall — the aition of the thunder's labor: pushed, not thrown.
summary.zh: 雨夜有女子推雷車而雷聲大作；主人曰『此阿香推雷車也』——雷車之由來：雷乃人推，非神怒。

sensitivity.note: Passages are the compiler's condensed paraphrases of the Soushen Hou Ji original.

passages.text: At a road-inn on the New-yang road a traveler was shown to his straw by a hired girl of the house; at midnight he heard her go down to the yard, seize the handles of a small cart, and strain it upward — and the thunder answered from the sky.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Soushen Hou Ji, juan 5, A-Xiang entry (compiler's rendering); not verbatim.

passages.text: At breakfast he told the innkeeper what he had seen and heard; the old man went white and looked at the empty bed: that was A-Xiang, the thunder-maid, engaged to drive the storm-cart, and her term here ends tonight. Wherever she pushes, hail and thunder fall on the fields — and the tale fixes the thunder's origin as labor: pushed, not thrown.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Soushen Hou Ji, juan 5; not verbatim.

title.en: The Three Brothers: The Spy-Glass, the Ship, and the Thief
title.zh: 三兄弟：千里鏡、造船與神偷

region.en: Ilocos region, northwestern Luzon, Philippines (narrator's home region)
region.zh: 菲律賓呂宋西北伊洛克斯地區（敘述者故鄉）

period: Ilocano oral tale; collected by D. S. Fansler, published 1921

source.work: Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 12a 'The Three Brothers', eBook #8299

summary.en: A poor widow sends her three sons out for nine years of training. An-no learns glass-making and brings home a spy-glass in which all hidden things are visible; Berto becomes an expert boat-builder; the youngest falls in with robbers and becomes their most skillful member. With the glass the brothers locate the kidnapped Princess Amelia in a guarded island tower, Berto builds the ship, and Tito steals her out; when all three claim her, the king refuses the marriage and divides half his wealth equally among them.
summary.zh: 貧寡母遣三子外出九年學藝。長兄學製玻璃，攜回一窺千里、能見隱秘之物的千里鏡；次兄成造船巧匠；幼弟卻落入強盜之夥，練就全幫最精妙的偷技。三人憑千里鏡尋得被劫的阿梅莉亞公主，次兄造船，幼弟隻身入守衛森嚴的塔樓竊出公主。三位求娶者相持不下，國王索性不嫁，將半數家產均分三人。

sensitivity.note: Ilocano folktale recorded by Fansler from a Garcia narrator; archival record. Rival-Brothers type; Fansler compares Grimm No. 129 and Straparola VII, 5.

passages.text: There was once an old woman who had three sons; the father died when Tito, the youngest, was only five years old, and the good widow worked hard to bring them up. When her strength began to fail she called her sons before her: 'As you see my strength is failing me, I want each of you to go into the world to seek his fortune. After nine years, come back home and show me what you have learned to do.' At the crossroads where the wide road branched in three directions they agreed that An-no should take the north branch, Berto the south, and Tito the east, and that at the end of the nine years they should all meet there before presenting themselves to their mother.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 12 'The Three Brothers'; not verbatim.

passages.text: At the end of the nine years the three brothers met again at the place designated. An-no had been in the company of glass-makers and had learned the art of glass-making, bringing home a spy-glass in which everything hidden from the eyes of men could be seen; Berto had been employed in a shipyard and become an expert boat-builder; the youngest, unfortunately, had fallen into the company of notorious robbers, and while with this band had become the best and most skilful robber in the gang. Their mother was very glad to have all her sons with her once more.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 12 'The Three Brothers'; not verbatim.

passages.text: Shortly after the family was re-united, the king issued a proclamation stating that his daughter, the beautiful princess Amelia, had been kidnapped by a brave stranger, and that whoever could give any information about her and restore her to the palace should be allowed to marry her. An-no looked through his glass and saw her confined in a tower on an island; Berto built a ship, and when it was finished the three brothers sailed to the island — but the tower was so closely guarded by armed soldiers that it seemed impossible to get into it. 'Well, that is easy,' said Tito. 'You stay here and wait for my return. I will bring the princess with me.' Through his skill the famous young robber succeeded in rescuing her and bringing her to the ship, and the four sailed directly for the king's palace.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 12 'The Three Brothers'; not verbatim.

passages.text: With great joy the king received them, and a great feast was held in the palace in honor of the rescue of his daughter. After the feast the king asked the three brothers to which of them he should give his daughter's hand; each claimed the reward, and a quarrel arose among them. The king, seeing that all had played important parts in the rescue of the princess, decided not to bestow his daughter on any of them — instead, he gave half his wealth to be divided equally among An-no, Berto, and Tito.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 12 'The Three Brothers'; not verbatim.

title.en: Three Brothers of Fortune: The Book, the Mat, and the Magic Stones
title.zh: 三兄弟的運氣：神書、飛毯與魔石

region.en: Rosales, Pangasinan, Luzon, Philippines (narrator's tale-source)
region.zh: 菲律賓呂宋邦阿西楠省羅薩利斯（故事原鄉）

period: Pangasinan oral tale; collected by D. S. Fansler, published 1921

source.work: Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 12b 'Three Brothers of Fortune', eBook #8299

summary.en: Three idle brothers skip school and wander abroad, buying a life-restoring book from an old woman, a flying mat from another, and finding two stones that unite things of the same kind. Ambo revives a drowned girl, Iloy flies the party to the seashore, and Suan mends their storm-wrecked boat with his stones. When all three claim the girl, the king's savage judgment divides her body three ways — and it is Suan, re-uniting the useless portions with his stones, who brings her back to life and marries her.
summary.zh: 三位遊手好閒的兄弟棄學出走：一人購得還魂書，一人購得飛行蓆，一人拾得能合併同類之物的雙石。安波救活溺水女子，伊洛伊以飛毯載眾至海濱，蘇安以魔石修補風暴中的破船。三人爭奪女子時，國王竟判將屍身三分——蘇安以石合其三份，女子復活，嫁蘇安而樂。

sensitivity.note: Pangasinan folktale recorded by Fansler from an Estayo narrator (story heard from a native of Rosales); archival record. The dismemberment judgment is garbled (Fansler notes it as 'inhuman') — retained as recorded; cf. Vetâlapancavinçati No. 2.

passages.text: In former times there lived in a certain village a wealthy man who had three sons — Suan, Iloy, and Ambo. As this man was a lover of education, he sent all his boys to another town to school; but the three brothers did not study: they spent their time in idleness and extravagance. When vacation came they were ashamed to go back to their home town, so instead they wandered from town to town seeking their fortunes. In the course of their travels they met an old woman broken with age, who sold Ambo a book: 'If you want to restore a dead person to life, just open this book before him, and in an instant he will be revived.' Another old woman sold Iloy a mat: 'If you want to travel through the air, just step on it, and in an instant you will be where you desire to go.' Suan alone had no charm — until he saw two stones which would meet and unite to form one round black stone, and then separate again; believing they possessed magical power to unite things of the same or similar kind, he picked them up.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 12 'Three Brothers of Fortune'; not verbatim.

passages.text: Not long afterward they came upon a crowd of persons weeping over the dead body of a beautiful young lady. Ambo told the parents that he would restore her to life if they would pay him a reasonable sum; they gladly agreed, he opened his book, and the dead lady was brought back to life. As soon as he had received his reward, Iloy placed his mat on the ground, told his two brothers to hold the young woman, and stepped on the mat: in an instant all four were transported to the seashore. From there they took ship to another country; but when they were in the middle of the sea a severe storm came and their boat was wrecked — all on board would have been drowned had not Suan repaired the broken planks with his two magical stones.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 12 'Three Brothers of Fortune'; not verbatim.

passages.text: When they landed, a quarrel arose among the three brothers as to which one was entitled to the young woman. 'I am the one who should have her, for it was I who restored her to life,' said Ambo. 'But if it had not been for me, we should not have the lady with us,' said Iloy. 'And if it had not been for me, we should all be dead now, and nobody could have her,' said Suan. As they could not come to any agreement, they took the question before the king, who decided to divide the young woman into three parts to be distributed among the three brothers; his judgment was carried out. Iloy and Ambo were discontented because their portions were useless, so they threw them away; but Suan picked up the shares of his two brothers and united them with his own. The young woman was brought to life again, and lived happily with Suan — so, after all, Suan was the most fortunate.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 12 'Three Brothers of Fortune'; not verbatim.

title.en: Pablo and the Princess: The Carpet, the Book, and the Ivory Tube
title.zh: 帕布洛與公主：魔毯、奇書與象牙管

region.en: La Laguna, Luzon, Philippines (narrator's home province)
region.zh: 菲律賓呂宋內湖省（敘述者故鄉）

period: Tagalog oral tale; collected by D. S. Fansler, published 1921

source.work: Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 12c 'Pablo and the Princess', eBook #8299

summary.en: Three friends take three roads and are each rewarded for their kindness: Pedro a transport carpet, Juan a book that knows everything happening in the world, Pablo an ivory tube that cures the dying. Juan's book reveals a dying princess, Pedro's carpet carries them to her, and Pablo's tube revives her — but when the king sets a shooting-match at the banana-flower that represents her heart, only Pablo refuses to shoot at it, for he loves her too dearly; and so he wins her.
summary.zh: 三位好友分道而行，各因善行得寶：佩德羅得可瞬間抵達任意之地的魔毯、胡安得知曉天下事的奇書、帕布洛得能起死回生的象牙管。書中傳來公主病危的消息，魔毯將三人送至王宮，象牙管救活公主。國王以香蕉花代表公主之心，令三人射箭定婚——只有帕布洛拒射：『我愛她太深。』於是公主屬於帕布洛。

sensitivity.note: Tagalog folktale recorded by Fansler from a Zafra narrator (La Laguna); archival record. Rival-suitors type with the arrow contest (cf. the 1001 Nights Prince Ahmed).

passages.text: Once upon a time there lived three friends, Pedro, Juan, and Pablo, who met one morning at the junction of three roads and agreed to each take one road and set out to find his fortune, promising to meet again in the same place, the first who came to wait for the others. Pedro took the road to the right: after three months' travelling he met an old man who asked him for food, and gave him his bread; in return the old man gave him a carpet — whoever sits on it may be transported instantly to any place he desires. Juan took the road to the left, and after three months and a half likewise shared his dinner-bread with a hungry old man, receiving a book by which he could read everything that was happening in the world at all times. Pablo took the middle road, and after travelling four months gave his bread to another old man, receiving an ivory tube that cures all sick persons of every disease — even a dying patient is restored instantly to perfect health if you blow through one end of the tube into his nose.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 12 'Pablo and the Princess'; not verbatim.

passages.text: At the crossroads they congratulated one another and exchanged fortunes. While Pedro was looking in Juan's book he read that a certain princess in a distant kingdom was very sick, and that the king her father had promised her hand and his heirship to whoever could cure her. They seated themselves on the carpet and were transported in a flash to the king's palace; led into the room of the sick princess, Pablo took his tube and blew through one end of it into her nose. She immediately opened her eyes, sat up, and began to talk.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 12 'Pablo and the Princess'; not verbatim.

passages.text: Before the king each claimed the princess: 'It is true, Pablo, that you are the one who cured my daughter; but could you have contrived to cure her if you had not known from Juan's book that she was sick, and if Pedro's carpet had not brought you here without delay? Your book, Juan, revealed that my daughter was sick; but the knowledge of her illness would have been of no service had it not been for Pedro's carpet and Pablo's tube. And it is just the same way with your carpet, Pedro.' Unable to choose among them, the king proposed a contest: 'Go and procure, each one of you, a bow and an arrow. I will hang up the inflorescence of a banana-plant. This will represent the heart of my daughter. The one who shoots it in the middle shall be the husband of my daughter, and the heir of my kingdom.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 12 'Pablo and the Princess'; not verbatim.

passages.text: Pedro shot first, and his arrow passed directly through the middle of the banana-flower; Juan shot second, and his arrow passed through the same hole Pedro's arrow had made. Now came Pablo's turn — but when Pablo's turn came, he refused to shoot, saying that if the banana-flower represented the heart of the princess, he could not shoot it, for he loved her too dearly. When the king heard this answer he said, 'Since Pablo really loves my daughter, while Pedro and Juan do not, for they shot at the flower that represents her heart, Pablo shall marry the princess.' And so Pablo married the king's daughter, and in time became king of that country.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 12 'Pablo and the Princess'; not verbatim.

title.en: Legend of Prince Oswaldo: The Old Man Who Was the Capitalist
title.zh: 奧斯瓦爾多王子傳：自稱『出資人』的老人

region.en: Calamba, La Laguna, Luzon, Philippines (narrator's home town)
region.zh: 菲律賓呂宋內湖省卡蘭巴（敘述者故鄉）

period: Tagalog oral legend; collected by D. S. Fansler, published 1921

source.work: Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 12d 'Legend of Prince Oswaldo', eBook #8299

summary.en: A groaning old man at the crossroads gives three youths a hundred pesos each and directs them to buy the first things they find sold: a rain-coat that carries its wearer anywhere, a book that tells all the world's happenings, a violet bottle that restores the dead. The book announces the death of the princess of Berengena; the coat carries all three there; Juan risks his head to revive her and wins her — until all three sue. An old man then claims none of them, as he was the capitalist: 'the interest is mine' — and marries her, becoming the young Prince Oswaldo the moment the sun rises, freed from enchantment by his marriage.
summary.zh: 十字路口呻吟的老人各賜百金，囑三青年買下路旁所售第一物：可任意飛行的雨衣、知曉天下事的奇書、能起死回生的紫色瓶。書中傳來貝倫赫納公主的死訊；雨衣攜三人瞬至靈堂；胡安以性命為注，將公主救活並求娶。三人相爭之際，一老人挺身而出：『你們誰也不能娶——是我指給你們寶物之路、給你們本錢，我是出資人，利息歸我。』他娶了公主；日出之光中，老人化作解除魔咒的年輕王子奧斯瓦爾多，登基為王。

sensitivity.note: Tagalog legend recorded by Fansler from an Uichanco narrator (Calamba); archival record. Rival-brothers type with an enchanted-prince resolution.

passages.text: Once upon a time, on a moonlight night, three young men were walking monotonously along a solitary country road, and when they came to a place where the road branched into three they stopped there like nails attracted by a powerful magnet. At this crossroads a helpless old man lay groaning as if in mortal pain; the three companions ran to him, helped him up, and fed him a part of the rice they had with them. He thanked them, gave each of the companions a hundred pesos, and said, 'Each one of you shall take one of these branch-roads. At the end of it is a house where they are selling something. With these hundred pesos that I am giving each of you, you shall buy the first thing that you see there.' Pedro, on the left branch, bought a rain-coat: 'It will take you wherever you wish to go.' Diego, on the middle road, bought a book: 'It will tell you what is going on in all parts of the world.' Juan, on the third road, bought a bottle of violet-colored liquid: 'It brings the dead back to life.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 12 'Legend of Prince Oswaldo'; not verbatim.

passages.text: When Diego opened his book he read what appeared on the page: 'The beautiful princess of Berengena is dead. Her parents, relatives, and friends grieve at her loss.' 'Good!' answered Juan. 'Then there is an occasion for us to test this bottle. It restores the dead back to life.' 'Then we shall have occasion to use my rain-coat,' said Pedro, and wrapping it about all three of them wished them in Berengena; within a few minutes they reached that country, where the princess was already in the church, her parents weeping over her and everybody wearing deep mourning. When the three strangers boldly entered the church the guard arrested them, for they had on red clothes; and when Juan protested that the princess was only sleeping, the king called him a fool — until Juan, staking his head, secured a formal agreement: success would win the princess and the heirship, failure the scaffold.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 12 'Legend of Prince Oswaldo'; not verbatim.

passages.text: Blinded by his love for the beautiful princess, Juan tremblingly uncorked his bottle of violet liquid and held it under the nose of the princess — an hour, hours, while the people grew impatient and the scaffold waited. 'Nameless stranger! upon your honor, tell us the truth! Can you do it, or not? Speak. I command it!' Just as Juan was about to reply, he saw the right hand of the princess move; soon she moved her other hand and opened her eyes, exclaiming, 'Oh, where am I?... No, there is my father, there is my mother, there is my brother.' The king was fully satisfied; he ordered Juan's clothes exchanged for prince's garments so that the celebration of the marriage might take place at once, and the people shouted, 'Long live Juan! Long live the princess!'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 12 'Legend of Prince Oswaldo'; not verbatim.

passages.text: When Diego and Pedro heard the shout they could not help feeling cheated, and made their way through the crowd: 'If it had not been for my book, we could not have known that the princess was dead... And Juan's good luck is due to my rain-coat.' The king was overwhelmed — each of the three had a good reason, but all three could not marry the princess, and even the counsellors could not decide. While they were puzzling over it, an old man sprang forth from the crowd and declared that he would settle the difficulty: 'None of you shall marry the princess. You, Juan, shall not marry her, because you intended to obtain your fortunes regardless of your companions; and you, Pedro and Diego, shall not have her, because you did not accept your misfortune quietly and thank God for it. None of you shall have her. I will marry her myself. I am the one who showed these three companions where to get their bottle, rain-coat, and book. I am the one who gave each of them a hundred pesos. I am the capitalist: the interest is mine.' The old man was right; the crowd clapped their hands, and the princess, bitterly weeping, gave her hand to the old man, who seemed to be her grandfather. But just then the sun began to rise, and the whole church was flooded with light: when the people recovered, they found their princess walking with her husband, not an old man, but a gallant young prince — none other than Prince Oswaldo, who had just been set free from the bonds of enchantment by his marriage. He was seated on the throne, the crown and sceptre were transferred to him, and he was hailed as King Oswaldo of Berengena.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 12 'Legend of Prince Oswaldo'; not verbatim.

title.en: The Rich and the Poor: The Ring in the Fat Fish
title.zh: 富者與貧者：肥魚腹中的戒指

region.en: Pasig and Laguna de Bay, Luzon, Philippines (story localized there)
region.zh: 菲律賓呂宋帕西格與內湖灣（故事發生地）

period: Tagalog oral tale; collected by D. S. Fansler, published 1921

source.work: Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 13a 'The Rich and the Poor', eBook #8299

summary.en: Two friends wager which can make a poor wood-cutter rich. Mayaman's six gifts of money are stolen each time by dishonest neighbors, and his magic wish-ring is lost when its commanded wind sinks the banca — into the lake. Mahirap's five centavos buy the very fish whose belly holds the lost ring; talking aloud to it, the wood-cutter startles the thieves into returning every stolen bag, and he becomes the richest man in town.
summary.zh: 二友打賭誰能讓貧苦樵夫致富。富人梅雅曼六次贈金六次遭竊；他賜的許願戒指因一句『起風』弄沉小船而失落湖中。窮人馬希拉普僅以五仙買下一尾肥魚——魚腹中正是那枚戒指！樵夫捧戒高歌，竊金鄰人以為被識破，捧著全部贓物前來求恕。樵夫自此富甲全鎮。

sensitivity.note: Tagalog folktale recorded by Fansler from a Gomez narrator (Rizal); archival record. Localized on Laguna de Bay; Fansler connects it with the Arabian Nights 'Khevajah Hasan al-Habbal.'

passages.text: Once upon a time there lived in the town of Pasig two honest men who were intimate friends, called Mayaman and Mahirap because one was much richer than the other. One pleasant afternoon they took a long walk into the neighboring woods, and saw in the distance a poor wood-cutter busy cutting and collecting fagots for sale, who maintained his family by selling wood from the forest. 'Now, which one of us can make that wood-cutter rich?' said Mayaman. 'Well, even though I am much poorer than you,' said Mahirap, 'I can make him rich with just the few cents I have in my pocket.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 13 'The Rich and the Poor'; not verbatim.

passages.text: Mayaman tried first: evening after evening he gave the wood-cutter four bags of money, and six times the dishonest neighbors who found out that the wood-cutter had much money in the house secretly stole the bags. Finally, on his sixth application, Mayaman presented him with a beautiful ring instead: 'This ring will preserve you from harm, and will give you everything you ask for. With it you can become the richest man in town; but be careful not to lose it!' Sailing home, the wood-cutter asked it for food — twelve different kinds of food appeared in his banca — and then, the wind having calmed, he said to the ring, 'O beautiful ring! blow my banca very hard, so that I may reach home quickly.' The wind rose suddenly, the sail and mast were blown away, the banca sank, and the unfortunate man, swimming for his life, reached the shore to find he had lost his valuable ring.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 13 'The Rich and the Poor'; not verbatim.

passages.text: Mayaman had nothing more to give, so it was Mahirap's turn: he gave the poor wood-cutter five centavos, all he had in his pocket, and told him to go to the market and buy a fish with it for his supper. At the fish-stalls the wood-cutter saw a very fine fat fish and, unable to bargain it down, gave all his money for it. When he went home and opened the fish to clean it, what did he find inside but the precious ring he had lost in the lake! He was so rejoiced at getting back his treasure that he walked up and down the streets talking out loud to his ring — 'Ha, ha, ha, ha!
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 13 'The Rich and the Poor'; not verbatim.

passages.text: I have found you now; you are here, and nowhere else.' When his neighbors who had stolen his bags of money heard these words, they thought the wood-cutter had found out they were the thieves and was addressing these words to them; they ran up to him with all the bags of money, saying, 'O wood-cutter! pardon us for our misdoings! Here are all the bags of money that we stole from you.' With his money and the ring, the wood-cutter soon became the richest man in his town — and so Mahirap, with five centavos only, succeeded in making the wood-cutter rich.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 13 'The Rich and the Poor'; not verbatim.

title.en: Lucas the Rope-Maker: The Lead That Was Worth Twenty Thousand Pesos
title.zh: 搓繩人盧卡斯：價值兩萬的鉛

region.en: Pagsanjan, La Laguna, Luzon, Philippines (story well known there, set in 'Bagdad')
region.zh: 菲律賓呂宋內湖省帕桑漢（故事聞名之地，背景設於『巴格達』）

period: Tagalog oral tale; collected by D. S. Fansler, published 1921

source.work: Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 13b 'Lucas the Rope-Maker', eBook #8299

summary.en: Kindhearted Luis twice gives his friend the rope-maker Lucas money, and twice it vanishes — an eagle snatching the hat with the second sum; even the third gift, a thousand pesos, is lost when his starving wife fills the money-jar with darak for the rice-seller. Given a piece of lead instead, Lucas lends it to a neighbor; the fish her husband catches holds a bright stone, which Lucas sells for twenty thousand pesos, becoming the kindliest rich man in town.
summary.zh: 仁厚的路易斯兩度贈金給搓繩人盧卡斯，兩度失散——鷹叼走藏錢的帽子；妻子又把藏千金的空甕裝滿豆麩償還米商。第三次，路易斯只給他一塊鉛：盧卡斯把鉛借給鄰婦作漁線墜，其夫釣回的大魚腹中藏一寶石——盧卡斯以兩萬比索售出，從此成為鎮上最仁厚的富翁。

sensitivity.note: Tagalog folktale recorded by Fansler from a Cordero narrator (Pagsanjan), who says the story is well known and old; archival record. Fansler derives it from the Arabian Nights 'History of Khevajah Hasan al-Habbal.'

passages.text: Luis and Isco were intimate friends in a country called Bagdad; Luis believed that gentleness and kindness were the second heaven, while Isco believed that wealth was the source of happiness. That afternoon they went to a town called Cohija, where they saw a rope-maker, Lucas by name, whose condition showed his great suffering from poverty; he had six little children to support but no money with which to feed them, nor could he get anything from his rope-making. Approaching Lucas, Luis gave him a roll of paper money, saying, 'Now, Lucas, take this money and spend it judiciously.' Lucas was overjoyed, hardly knowing what to do.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 13 'Lucas the Rope-Maker'; not verbatim.

passages.text: With his hundred pesos Lucas bought two pounds of meat and a roll of cañamo; but as he walked home an eagle, attracted by the smell of the meat, flew about his head and snatched off the hat in the corner of which he had put the leftover money — and when he searched, the money was gone. His wife Zelima scolded him roundly, and after the family had eaten the meat they were as poor as before, even pale because of hunger. Later, Luis and Isco found Lucas weeping under a mango-tree and, perceiving he told the truth, Luis gave him a thousand pesos; Lucas hid the bulk of the money in an empty jar in the corner of the room and went out to buy food — and while he was gone his starving wife, having nothing with which to repay the rice-seller who gave her rice, filled the jar with darak and gave it away. When Lucas came home and found the money gone he was in despair, and tried to kill himself, but his children prevented him.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 13 'Lucas the Rope-Maker'; not verbatim.

passages.text: Two months later Luis and Isco again visited their friend, and Luis, who had found a big piece of lead in the street, gave it to Lucas, saying, 'Now, take care of that! Maybe your wealth will come from it.' Lucas accepted it unwillingly, thinking he was mocked, and threw the lead in the corner; but during the night a neighbor knocked at their door, asking for a piece of lead for her husband's fishing-line, and Zelima found the lead and gave it to her, receiving the promise of the first fish her husband should catch. The next morning the neighbor was there with a big fish, and while Zelima was cleaning it she found a bright stone inside it; ignorant of its value, she gave it to her youngest son to play with, and the children quarrelled over it. Don Juan, the rich man in front of whose house they lived, heard the noise of the quarrelling children, and his wife saw the stone and wanted it very much.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 13 'Lucas the Rope-Maker'; not verbatim.

passages.text: Don Juan offered the rope-maker a thousand pesos for the stone, but Lucas refused, for now he suspected it was worth more than that; at last he sold it for twenty thousand pesos. Lucas was now a rich man: he bought clothes for his wife and children, renewed his falling house, and bought a machine for making rope, then another; but although he was the richest man in town he was very kind — his house was open to every comer, he supported crippled persons, and gave alms to the poor. When Luis and Isco visited Lucas the last time they were surprised and delighted to see him so rich, and Lucas gave a banquet in honor of these two men, telling them every detail of all that had happened to him. Luis was now convinced that Lucas was honest, and had told the truth on former occasions; and Lucas lived in his big house happily and in peace with his wife and children.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 13 'Lucas the Rope-Maker'; not verbatim.

title.en: The King and the Dervish: Deer, Nightingale, and Dog
title.zh: 國王與苦行僧：鹿、夜鶯與犬

region.en: Batangas, Luzon, Philippines (narrator's home province)
region.zh: 菲律賓呂宋八打雁省（敘述者故鄉）

period: Tagalog oral tale; collected by D. S. Fansler, published 1921

source.work: Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 14a 'The King and the Dervish', eBook #8299

summary.en: A dervish who can leave his body and enter dead creatures teaches the king the charm; mid-hunt the dervish seizes the king's vacated body and orders the marked deer killed. The king flees through a nightingale's body into the palace cage, pecking the false king whenever he is touched; when the dervish leaves to revive the 'dead' bird, the king darts from the dog's body into his own and kills the ungrateful bird — and the queen dies of grief at learning she was deceived.
summary.zh: 能離體附身的苦行僧授國王咒術；狩獵之中，僧人趁虛入主王體，下令獵殺帶記號的鹿。真國王藉夜鶯之屍逃入王宮鳥籠，每被假王觸碰便啄之；待苦行僧離體去『救活』夜鶯，國王自犬身返回本體，手刃忘恩之鳥——而王后知曉被欺，悲傷而死。

sensitivity.note: Tagalog folktale recorded by Fansler from a Hilario narrator (Batangas); archival record. Fansler derives it from the 1001 Days story of Prince Fadlallah; the transformation requires a dead body to enter.

passages.text: Once there lived a young and brave king with his gentle and loving wife; he ruled his people well, and she always cheered her husband when he was sad. One day a dervish came to the palace and told the king that he possessed magical power, and straightway they became friends. This dervish had the power to leave his body and enter that of a dead animal or person. The king was fond of hunting, and once he took his new friend with him to shoot deer; after a few hours of hard chasing they succeeded in killing a buck, and to show his power the dervish left his body and entered that of the dead deer, then resumed his former shape.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 14 'The King and the Dervish'; not verbatim.

passages.text: The king was very anxious to be able to do the same thing; the dervish gave him minute instructions and taught him the necessary charms — and then the king left his body and took possession of that of the deer, while in an instant the dervish entered the king's body and went home as the monarch, giving orders that a deer with certain marks should be hunted out and killed. The true king was very unhappy, especially when he saw his own men chasing him to take his life.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 14 'The King and the Dervish'; not verbatim.

passages.text: In his wanderings through the forest he saw a dead nightingale, and left the deer's body and entered the bird's. Now he was safe, so he flew to his palace and sang so sweetly that the queen ordered her attendants to catch him; he gladly allowed himself to be caught and to be cared for by the queen. Whenever the dervish took the bird in his hands, the bird pecked him; but the beautiful singer always showed signs of satisfaction when the queen smoothed his plumage. Not long after the bird's capture, a dog died in the palace, and the king underwent another change, leaving the bird's body and entering that of the dog.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 14 'The King and the Dervish'; not verbatim.

passages.text: On waking up in the morning the queen found that her pet was dead, and began to weep; unable to see her so sad, the dervish comforted her and told her he would give the bird life again. Consequently he left the king's body and entered the bird's — and seeing his chance, the real king left the dog's body and resumed his original form, going at once to the cage and killing the ungrateful bird, the dervish. The tender queen protested against the king's act of cruelty; but when she heard that she had been deceived by the dervish, she died of grief.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 14 'The King and the Dervish'; not verbatim.

title.en: The Mysterious Book: The Transformation Chase
title.zh: 神秘之書：變形追逐

region.en: Calamba, La Laguna, Luzon, Philippines (narrator's home town)
region.zh: 菲律賓呂宋內湖省卡蘭巴（敘述者故鄉）

period: Tagalog oral tale; collected by D. S. Fansler, published 1921

source.work: Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 14b 'The Mysterious Book', eBook #8299

summary.en: Idle Juan opens his master Don Luzano's seventh, gem-bound box and is carried into the air by the triangular gold book inside — pursued by his raging master. Whoever has touched the book can change into any form: steed against mule, bird against hawk, fish against fish hiding in a crack of the well — until the princesses of the well catch the seven-scaled fish. When Don Luzano, promising to cure the sick princess, demands her fish as payment, the fish becomes a gold ring, the ring a shower of mungo seeds, the crow that devours them is torn apart by the cat Juan has become — and Juan stands an embroidered prince beside his beloved.
summary.zh: 懶漢胡安開啟主人東·盧薩諾的第七重寶匣，被匣中金鑲鑽的三角奇書捲上天空——主人在後暴怒追趕。凡觸書者可任意變形：小馬對騾、小鳥對鷹、小魚對大魚躲入井壁裂縫——直到井邊三位公主釣起七彩鱗的小魚。東·盧薩諾假意醫病、索討公主之魚為酬；魚化金戒、戒化滿地豆粒、吞食豆粒的烏鴉被化貓的胡安撕裂——胡安以錦袍王子之姿站在所愛身旁。

sensitivity.note: Tagalog folktale recorded by Fansler from an Uichanco narrator (Calamba); archival record. Transformation-combat cycle; Fansler compares Grimm's 'The Thief and his Master' and Dasent's 'Farmer Weathersky,' tracing the family to India.

passages.text: Once upon a time there lived a poor father and a poor son — the father old, named Pedro; the son, Juan, afraid of work though they were very poor. One day, with not a single grain of rice in the house, Juan went to a neighboring town to seek a master, and found one in the person of Don Luzano, a fine gentleman of fortune. Don Luzano treated Juan like a son, and in time intrusted him with the most precious valuables in the house. One morning, going out hunting, he left Juan alone as usual; while Juan was sweeping and cleaning his master's room, he caught sight of a highly polished box lying behind the post in the corner.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 14 'The Mysterious Book'; not verbatim.

passages.text: Curious, Juan opened the box: there appeared another box; he opened this box and another box still was disclosed — one box after another until Juan came to the seventh, which contained a small triangular-shaped book bound in gold and decorated with diamonds and other precious gems. Disregarding the consequences, Juan picked up the book and opened it — and at once he was carried up into the air. When he looked back, whom did he see but Don Luzano pursuing him with eyes full of rage and an enormous deadly-looking bolo in his hand. The book had the wonderful power of changing anybody who had laid his hands on it into whatever form that person wished to assume: Juan became a little steed galloping down the street — Don Luzano a big fast mule with bubbling and foaming mouth; Juan a pretty little bird — Don Luzano a big hawk about to swoop down on him; then Juan suddenly leaped into a well he was flying over and became a little fish, Don Luzano assuming the form of a big fish — until the little fish entered a small crack in the wall of the well where the big fish could not pursue him farther, and Don Luzano had to give up and go home in great disappointment.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 14 'The Mysterious Book'; not verbatim.

passages.text: The well belonged to three beautiful princesses, and one morning while they were looking into the water they saw the little fish with its seven-colored scales moving gracefully through the water. The eldest lowered her bait, but the fish would not see it; the second sister tried her skill, but the fish released its hold just as it was being drawn out; the youngest sister's turn came, and the fish allowed itself to be caught and held in the tender hands of this beautiful girl, who placed it in a golden basin of water and cared for it very tenderly. Several months later the king issued a proclamation saying that the youngest princess was sick and promising half his kingdom to anyone who could cure her.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 14 'The Mysterious Book'; not verbatim.

passages.text: 'Ay, what foolishness!' exclaimed Don Luzano when he heard the news. 'The sickness! Pshaw! That's no sickness, never in the wide world!' — and the following morning he told the king he had already cured many similar cases, asking as token only the fish the princess kept in her room. On the third day, before beginning any part of the treatment, he requested that the fish be given him; but as he was about to dip his hand into the basin, the princess boldly stopped him, saying he would soil with his hands the golden basin of the monarch — she would pour the fish into his hands. Before the fish could reach them it jumped out; in its stead was a beautiful gold ring adorning the finger of the princess. Don Luzano tried to snatch the ring, but as the princess jerked her hand back the ring fell to the floor, and in its place were countless little mungo seeds scattered about the room. Don Luzano instantly took the form of a greedy crow, devouring the seeds with extraordinary speed — but Juan, contained in one of the seeds that had rolled beneath the feet of the princess, suddenly became a cat, and rushing out attacked the bird: as soon as you could wink your eyes, the crow was dead, miserably torn to pieces, and in place of the cat stood Juan in an embroidered suit, looking like a gay young prince. 'This is my beloved,' confessed the princess to her father; and the king forgave his daughter and gladly welcomed his new son-in-law — rid of his formidable antagonist, with a beautiful princess for a wife, and an excellent chance of inheriting the throne.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 14 'The Mysterious Book'; not verbatim.

title.en: Ren Shi, the Fox-Woman Who Wanted an Ordinary Marriage
title.zh: 任氏傳

region.en: Chang'an, the west market and the hunting parks (Tang capital)
region.zh: 長安西市

period: Taiping Guangji, juan 452, from Shen Jiji's chuanqi 'Renshi Zhuan' (Tang, c. 780 CE)

source.work: Taiping Guangji, juan 452: Ren Shi the fox-woman, Zheng Liu's marriage, and the hounds of the hunting field

license: Public domain (Classical Chinese text; passages are compiler's renderings)

summary.en: Zheng Liu met the loveliest woman of Chang'an by the west market — a fox, his companion's hound told them, and she fled with the fox's speed of nine turns. But she came back, and married Zheng: she fed his poor household from stores no one could trace, turned down a great man's lust with the fox's wit, and died at last on the road south — not by hound but by chance — where she had once said, laughing, that foxes have no luck but what they make.
summary.zh: 任氏為狐，遇鄭六於長安西市；犬逐之，任氏遁而復返，與鄭六同居；富家供給、拒豪家之暴；後隨鄭南行，卒於道——『異類之有情者』。

sensitivity.note: Passages are the compiler's condensed paraphrases of the Taiping Guangji text.

passages.text: Zheng Liu met her by the west market, the loveliest woman in Chang'an; his friend's hound broke loose and ran at her, and she fled with a fox's nine turns of speed — a fox, then. But she came back to Zheng by her own road, and asked of him no fortune: only a house, a table, and the name of wife.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Taiping Guangji, juan 452, Renshi Zhuan (compiler's rendering); not verbatim.

passages.text: She furnished his poverty from stores no ledger could trace, fed his friends, and when a great man of the city took her by force, she broke his grip with words alone — shamed him, reasoned him, and walked free while he stood red-faced in his own hall.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Taiping Guangji, juan 452; not verbatim.

passages.text: She died on the south road, not by hound but by chance, as the foxes' luck ran; and the storyteller's point outlasts the plot: of all the strange women in the tales, the fox was the most faithful — the supernatural judged not by its shape but by its keeping of an ordinary promise.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Taiping Guangji, juan 452, the ending; not verbatim.

title.en: Nie Yinniang, the Nun's Assassin and the Magistrate's Daughter
title.zh: 聶隱娘

region.en: The Wei-bo camp and the stone caves of the mountains (Tang frontier)
region.zh: 魏博節度使府

period: Taiping Guangji, juan 194, from the 'Nie Yinniang' chuanqi (Tang, c. 820 CE)

source.work: Taiping Guangji, juan 194: the stolen daughter, the five years of knife-training, and the two assassins who married

license: Public domain (Classical Chinese text; passages are compiler's renderings)

summary.en: A nun took the five-year-old daughter of the Wei-bo garrison commander from her garden and returned her five years later as a knife that killed in the dark without a sound; the commander set her on his rivals. She married a mirror-polisher, defected to a worthier lord with one warning gift, and ended the tale as a chemical hermit — swallowed a drug, grew like a clam-shell, and told her husband to to wait: twenty years, then a crane called at the grave. The first great assassin of Chinese fiction, and its first story of a woman choosing her own lord.
summary.zh: 尼竊魏博大將之女隱娘，五年歸，能於暗中刺人；許嫁磨鏡少年；棄魏帥而事劉昌裔；終以藥化形，不知所之——唐傳奇第一刺客。

sensitivity.note: Passages are the compiler's condensed paraphrases of the Taiping Guangji text.

passages.text: The nun came to the garrison commander's garden, lifted his five-year-old girl out of play, and was gone; five years later she returned the child grown silent and sure — a knife trained in the dark caves to take lives without a sound, as practice on men the nun called the wicked.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Taiping Guangji, juan 194, Nie Yinniang entry (compiler's rendering); not verbatim.

passages.text: The father set her on his enemies, and she served — until she met the one lord worth serving, warned him by a mirror-gift left at his gate, and went over to his camp against her father's own paymaster; her husband, a mere mirror-polisher, was kept on as her assistant: the tale's quiet joke about marriages arranged by nuns.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Taiping Guangji, juan 194, the defection; not verbatim.

passages.text: She ended as the tale's strangest image: a drug that made her body close like a clam, a husband told to wait twenty years by a grave, and a crane that called at last from the cloud-line where she had gone. The knife became a hermit; the daughter of a warlord walked out of her father's war entirely.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Taiping Guangji, juan 194, the clam-shell ending; not verbatim.

title.en: The Kunlun Slave and the Locked Tower of the Cui Mansion
title.zh: 崑崙奴磨勒

region.en: Chang'an, the Cui mansion and the locked red tower (Tang capital)
region.zh: 長安崔府紅綃樓

period: Taiping Guangji, juan 194, from the 'Kunlun Nu' chuanqi (Tang, c. 830 CE)

source.work: Taiping Guangji, juan 194: the slave Mole, the walls of the great house, and the fifty dogs of the garden

license: Public domain (Classical Chinese text; passages are compiler's renderings)

summary.en: The young scholar Cui fell for a singing-girl kept in a locked tower of the great marshal's compound; his house-servant Mole, a man of Kunlun with iron wrists, carried him over the walls at night, dropped the guard dogs with thrown stones, brought the girl down with the scholar, and did it twice more before the marshal's men came with halberds. Mole fought them off, walked out of the compound, and vanished: the first great emancipator-hero of Chinese fiction, a slave who freed three people and himself with the same pair of wrists.
summary.zh: 崑崙奴磨勒負崔生逾牆入紅綃女宅，遣猛犬，竊紅綃與崔生俱出；軍士圍捕，磨勒脫身而去——異域之力士。

sensitivity.note: Passages are the compiler's condensed paraphrases of the Taiping Guangji text. The Kunlun figure reflects Tang-era African/Indian Ocean servitude — the tale's exoticizing frame is noted critically.

passages.text: Cui the young scholar loved a singing-girl kept in a locked tower of the great marshal's household; his servant Mole, a man of Kunlun with wrists of iron, said only: show me the wall — and carried the scholar over it at midnight, past the dogs of the garden, into the tower's chamber.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Taiping Guangji, juan 194, Kunlun Nu entry (compiler's rendering); not verbatim.

passages.text: The girl asked to be carried out of her gilded prison with him; Mole took her down the wall on his back and walked her home through the sleeping city, and did the same errand twice more before the marshal's men finally traced the escapes and came with halberds to the servants' quarters.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Taiping Guangji, juan 194; not verbatim.

passages.text: Mole scattered the halberdiers with his two hands, stepped over the compound wall unhurried, and was never seen in the city again — a slave who freed a scholar, a girl, and himself with the same skill, and paid for it with nothing but his own disappearance.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Taiping Guangji, juan 194, the ending; not verbatim.

title.en: Hongxian, the Red Thread Across a Governor's Pillow
title.zh: 紅線盜盒

region.en: The camps of Luzhou and Weibo (Tang frontier, Hebei–Shanxi)
region.zh: 潞州至魏博

period: Taiping Guangji, juan 195, from the 'Hongxian' chuanqi (Tang, c. 830 CE)

source.work: Taiping Guangji, juan 195: the maidservant who flew three hundred li, took a gold box, and stopped a war with it

license: Public domain (Classical Chinese text; passages are compiler's renderings)

summary.en: The governor of Luzhou's household held a maidservant, Hongxian, who could fly three hundred li in a night with a red thread tied to her brow. When the warlord of Weibo massed an army to destroy the governor, she rode the night wind into his bedroom, stood at his sleeping head with her knife — and took, instead of his life, the gold box at his pillow, flying home by dawn. The box laid on the warlord's own breakfast-table stopped the war; the maidservant was, she said, a man of an earlier age reborn to pay a debt of one city's blood.
summary.zh: 紅線夜入魏博節度使田承嗣寢帳，取其枕前金盒而歸；承嗣懼而罷兵——紅線自言前生為男子，以誤傷人命，謫為女子償之。

sensitivity.note: Passages are the compiler's condensed paraphrases of the Taiping Guangji text.

passages.text: When the warlord of Weibo massed his armies to destroy the governor of Luzhou, the governor's own maidservant Hongxian asked for one night and a red thread tied at her brow; she flew the three hundred li to the warlord's camp in the dark.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Taiping Guangji, juan 195, Hongxian entry (compiler's rendering); not verbatim.

passages.text: In his bedroom she stood over the sleeping man with her knife at his head, and considered — the war to be paid in one life, or taught in one theft. She took the gold box from his pillow, left the knife, and flew home before dawn with the proof of how far a servant can reach.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Taiping Guangji, juan 195, the theft; not verbatim.

passages.text: The box was laid on the warlord's own breakfast-table by his own envoy, with a courteous letter; the warlord, understanding in one look that his bedroom had been visited by the household he meant to destroy, recalled his armies. The maidservant said farewell to her master and vanished — a man of an earlier age, she said, reborn as a woman to pay an old debt, and paid.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Taiping Guangji, juan 195, the ending; not verbatim.

title.en: Laozi Born Old, and the Ox Through the Western Pass
title.zh: 老子出關

region.en: The Hangu Pass, west of Luoyang (Shaanxi–Henan)
region.zh: 函谷關

period: Shenxian Zhuan (Biographies of Divine Immortals) by Ge Hong, c. 300 CE, Laozi biography

source.work: Shenxian Zhuan, 'Laozi': the ancient mother's plum-? — the ancient origin, the keeper Yin Xi's request, and the five thousand characters

license: Public domain (Classical Chinese text; passages are compiler's renderings)

summary.en: The immortal biographies make Laozi the oldest of beings, born as an old man with white hair, and a keeper of archives in the declining Zhou. When the age decayed he rode a black ox toward the western passes; the gate-keeper Yin Xi saw the purple vapor riding the east wind and held the gate until the sage wrote down, in five thousand characters, the Way and its Power — then rode on west, leaving behind the smallest book and the largest theology.
summary.zh: 老子生而皓首，故稱老子；周室衰，乘青牛西出關；關令尹喜見紫氣東來，留之——為著五千言《道德經》，遂西去莫知所終。

sensitivity.note: Passages are the compiler's condensed paraphrases of the Shenxian Zhuan biography; the historical Laozi of the Shiji is a different genre — both are kept apart in the corpus.

passages.text: The immortal record says Laozi was older than heaven and earth, and was born with white hair — hence his name, the Old Child — and served the declining house of Zhou as keeper of the archives, watching the world's receipts pile up without its wisdom growing.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Shenxian Zhuan, Laozi biography (compiler's rendering); not verbatim.

passages.text: When the dynasty could no longer be helped, he mounted a black ox and rode west toward the passes. The gate-keeper Yin Xi, a student of the skies, saw a purple vapor riding the east wind and knew a sage was coming: he held the gate and asked for the teaching as toll.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Shenxian Zhuan, Yin Xi episode; not verbatim.

passages.text: Laozi stayed the night and wrote, in five thousand characters, the book of the Way and its Power; then he rode on through the pass and west beyond all records — the smallest book and the largest theology left at a customs gate, and the sage gone where no account of him follows.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Shenxian Zhuan, the departure; not verbatim.

title.en: The Yellow Emperor Casts the Tripod and Rides the Dragon From Dinghu
title.zh: 黃帝鼎湖騎龍

region.en: Mount Jing and the tripod-pool of Dinghu (Shaanxi)
region.zh: 荊山鼎湖

period: Shenxian Zhuan by Ge Hong, c. 300 CE, Huangdi biography; parallel in Shiji, Fengshan Shu

source.work: Shenxian Zhuan, 'Huangdi': the first tripod cast at Mount Jing, the dragon that came down, and the ministers clinging to the whiskers

license: Public domain (Classical Chinese text; passages are compiler's renderings)

summary.en: Having united the world, the Yellow Emperor mined the copper of Mount Jing and cast a tripod at the pool called Dinghu; when it was done a dragon came down with its whiskers hanging, and the emperor, his household and seventy ministers climbed aboard and rose. Those who could not climb seized the dragon's whiskers, which tore out and fell with the bows the crowd had clutched — and the village keeps the names to this day: Whisker Row, Bow-Grasping Hamlet, and the pool named Tripod-Lake.
summary.zh: 黃帝採首山銅，鑄鼎於荊山下；鼎既成，有龍垂胡髯下迎黃帝；黃帝上騎，群臣後宮從上者七十餘人；小臣不得上，持龍髯，髯拔墮，弓亦墮地；百姓抱弓而號，其弓曰烏號，其地曰鼎湖。

sensitivity.note: Passages are the compiler's condensed paraphrases of the Shenxian Zhuan biography and the Shiji parallel.

passages.text: The Yellow Emperor, having set the world in order, mined the copper of the first mountain and cast a great tripod at the pool of Dinghu — the cauldron of the state's completion, cast in the one metal worth the sky's attention.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Shenxian Zhuan, Huangdi biography (compiler's rendering); not verbatim.

passages.text: The tripod finished, a dragon came down with its whiskers trailing, and the emperor with his family and seventy of his ministers climbed upon it and rose from the pool into the clouds; the crowd below seized the whiskers and the bows of the departing — and the whiskers tore out and fell, and with them the bows. The villages of that mountain keep the names the fall earned: Whisker Row where the beard landed, Bow-Grasping Hamlet where the crowd held on, and the pool named Tripod-Lake — the founding emperor's exit from history filed as geography.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Shenxian Zhuan, the ascension; not verbatim. / Paraphrase of Shenxian Zhuan with the Shiji parallel; not verbatim.

title.en: The Queen Mother of the West Feasts Emperor Wu, and the Peach Thieves Come
title.zh: 漢武帝內傳西王母降

region.en: The palace of Emperor Wu at Chang'an (Han court)
region.zh: 漢宮

period: Han Wudi Neizhuan (Inner Biography of Emperor Wu), c. 4th-5th c. CE; parallel in Han Wudi Zhuan

source.archive: Internet Archive (reference; the text via digitized collections)
source.work: Han Wudi Neizhuan: Xiwangmu's descent on the azure bird, the seven peaches of three-thousand-year ripening, and Dongfang Shuo caught at the window

license: Public domain (Classical Chinese text; passages are compiler's renderings)

summary.en: On the seventh month's seventh day the Queen Mother of the West came down to Emperor Wu's palace on a chariot of purple clouds drawn by azure birds; she brought with her attendants and, wrapped in leaves, seven peaches of the garden where one ripening takes three thousand years. She gave two to the Emperor; the third vanished from the tray — and the Queen Mother laughed, for she knew who had taken it: Dongfang Shuo, her own thieving courtier, caught at the window with the peach in his mouth.
summary.zh: 漢武帝好仙道，西王母以七月七日降於宮中，命侍女索桃；桃盤盛七枚，大如鴨卵；王母以四枚與帝，自食其三，帝收其核欲種之——東方朔窺桃竊之，王母笑指之：『此桃三千年一生實。』

sensitivity.note: Passages are the compiler's condensed paraphrases of the Neizhuan text.

passages.text: The Emperor Wu of Han, hungry for the Way of the immortals, purified a palace tower, and on the night of the seventh month the Queen Mother of the West descended on a cloud-chariot of purple vapor, drawn by the azure birds that serve her and attended by a train of her singing-women.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Han Wudi Neizhuan (compiler's rendering); not verbatim.

passages.text: She called for peaches, and a plate was brought from heaven's orchard: seven peaches of a size like a duck's egg, from the tree that ripens once in three thousand years. She gave two to the emperor, who ate and wanted the kernels to plant — and she laughed at the wish, for the tree of that garden does not grow in soil such as his.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Han Wudi Neizhuan, the peaches; not verbatim.

passages.text: A third peach vanished from the plate while she spoke; the Queen Mother looked at the window and said, still laughing, the thief's name: Dongfang Shuo, her courtier, was already swallowing it behind the lattice — the peach-thief of heaven's garden employed, for the joke of it, in the emperor's own council hall.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Han Wudi Neizhuan, Dongfang Shuo episode; not verbatim.

title.en: Du Zichun, the Man Who Could Not Stay Silent in Hell
title.zh: 杜子春

region.en: The tower of the ascetics on Mount Song (Henan)
region.zh: 嵩山煉丹院

period: Taiping Guangji, juan 16, from the 'Du Zichun' tale (Tang, c. 750 CE)

source.work: Taiping Guangji, juan 16: the squanderer made rich twice, the vow of silence, and the hell of every passion

license: Public domain (Classical Chinese text; passages are compiler's renderings)

summary.en: Du Zichun, a squanderer made rich twice by a strange old man, was given one trial for the third gift: keep silent in a tower for a day, whatever comes. All day hell came to him — lightning, demons, boiling cauldrons, the general's blade at his neck, his wife's head dropped in the fire, rebirth as a girl mute and scorned, marriage, a son — and his child, dashed against a stone, laughed in his face. At that his tongue unlocked with one cry of grief — and the tower's fire went out: the elixir needed a heart with no passions left, and his had one.
summary.zh: 杜子春兩受老人贈金；第三試：嵩山煉丹爐前終日緘口；歷雷電、刀山、油鼎、畜生道，為啞女生子；兒撲石而笑，子春失聲而呼——爐火遂熄，丹不成。

sensitivity.note: Passages are the compiler's condensed paraphrases of the Taiping Guangji text.

passages.text: Du Zichun had squandered one fortune and been given a second by a strange old man in the market; squandered that too, and been given a third with a condition: a day's vigil of total silence in the old man's mountain tower, whatever came for him there.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Taiping Guangji, juan 16, Du Zichun entry (compiler's rendering); not verbatim.

passages.text: The day brought hell in order: a storm that split the tower, generals and demons who beat and boiled and burned him, his wife's head dropped screaming into the fire — and he held. Then he was reborn in the vision as a mute girl, sold, married, given a son; and the son, at her silent mother's knee, laughed and stumbled toward the well.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Taiping Guangji, juan 16, the trials; not verbatim.

passages.text: The child was dashed on the stones and laughed up at her, and Du Zichun's silence broke with one cry of love. The old man's voice came through the smoke: the elixir was ready but the heart was not — for the Way of the immortals wants no passions, and his had one, and it had cost them the furnace. He went home rich for the last time, having failed magnificently.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Taiping Guangji, juan 16, the failure; not verbatim.

title.en: The Old Man Under the Moon and the Red Thread Ledger
title.zh: 月下老人

region.en: The temple garden near Song city (Henan)
region.zh: 宋城龍興寺

period: Taiping Guangji, juan 159, from the 'Dinghun Dian' tale (Tang, c. 810 CE)

source.work: Taiping Guangji, juan 159: the moonlit ledger of marriages and the red thread that cannot be broken

license: Public domain (Classical Chinese text; passages are compiler's renderings)

summary.en: Wei Gu, walking in the moonlight at a temple near Song, found an old man reading a ledger against a bag of red threads; the ledger, the man said, was the book of all marriages, and one thread tied ankle to ankle joined two people wherever they ran. Wei Gu laughed at the entry that assigned him a greengrocer's baby daughter — and the old man, to settle it, took him by night to the vegetable market, where a woman with a scarred child of the vegetable stall sat selling greens. Wei Gu sent a servant to stab the child; she survived the knife with a scar over the brow. Years on, the magistrate gave him a daughter of beauty and brow-scarred: the greengrocer's baby, led by the red thread he had tried to cut.
summary.zh: 韋固遇月下老人於宋城，赤繩繫足以定婚姻；固怒遣僕刺菜市女孩，十四年後娶妻眉間有刀痕——月老祠由此立。

sensitivity.note: Passages are the compiler's condensed paraphrases of the Taiping Guangji text. The child-stabbing episode is recorded as the tale's darker layer.

passages.text: Wei Gu walked in the moonlight outside a temple near Song and found an old man on the steps reading a ledger, with a bag of red threads at his feet; the ledger, the man said, was the book of all marriages, and a single red thread, tied ankle to ankle, joined every pair it named — however far they ran to escape it.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Taiping Guangji, juan 159, Dinghun Dian entry (compiler's rendering); not verbatim.

passages.text: He showed Wei Gu his own entry: a daughter of the vegetable market, a baby in a cradle by the greens. Wei Gu, insulted, sent a servant that night to stab the child; the knife left a scar over the brow and the child lived.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Taiping Guangji, juan 159, the stabbing; not verbatim.

passages.text: Fourteen years on, the magistrate gave Wei Gu his daughter in marriage — a beauty, and brow-scarred; she told him at her mirror how she had been a grocer's baby stabbed in the cradle and adopted by an uncle. Wei Gu told her about the old man with the threads; both believed, and the temple of the Old Man Under the Moon has stood in the tale's honor ever since.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Taiping Guangji, juan 159, the marriage; not verbatim.

title.en: Pei Hang and the Blue-Bridge of the Jade Mortar
title.zh: 裴航藍橋

region.en: The Blue-Bridge post-station on the Shang mountain road (Shaanxi)
region.zh: 藍橋驛

period: Taiping Guangji, juan 50, from Pei Xing's 'Pei Hang' tale (Tang, c. 860 CE)

source.work: Taiping Guangji, juan 50: the jade pestle and the hundred days of pounding herbs at the Blue Bridge

license: Public domain (Classical Chinese text; passages are compiler's renderings)

summary.en: Pei Hang, riding home in splendor, stopped at the Blue-Bridge station for water and heard the girl behind the curtain sing his own verse back at him — Yunying, the hostess's daughter, a girl of heaven's stock. An old woman demanded his jewels for the marriage; a master of the mountains told him the true price: a jade pestle, and a hundred days of pounding the herb of the immortals in the inn's own courtyard. He bought the pestle, pounded for a hundred days in the drizzle, and married Yunying — and the two were seen later riding a jade-lion into the clouds, inviters of the household of the immortals.
summary.zh: 裴航藍橋驛遇雲英；老嫗索玉杵臼為聘，航傾財購之，搗藥百日而娶雲英——夫婦俱仙去。

sensitivity.note: Passages are the compiler's condensed paraphrases of the Taiping Guangji text.

passages.text: Pei Hang, richly dressed and riding home from a failed examination, stopped at the Blue-Bridge station for water; behind the partition a girl's voice sang three lines that matched his own heart's verse — Yunying, the innkeeper's daughter, who was not of the innkeeper's stock.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Taiping Guangji, juan 50, Pei Hang entry (compiler's rendering); not verbatim.

passages.text: The old hostess named a bride-price no man could pay: a jade pestle and mortar of the immortals, and a hundred days of pounding the herb that opens the Way. Pei Hang sold his estates, hunted the jade through the markets of the capital, found it, and came back to the Blue Bridge to work.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Taiping Guangji, juan 50; not verbatim.

passages.text: A hundred days he pounded in the courtyard, hands in the drizzle, herbs to powder, powder to medicine; on the last night the doors of the inn opened on a hill of light, and the household came up the mountain as immortal guests. Years after, travelers saw two riders on a jade lion in the clouds and knew the pairing at the Blue Bridge had ended in heaven's register.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Taiping Guangji, juan 50, the ascent; not verbatim.

title.en: The Passion Play of Osiris at Abydos
title.zh: 阿拜多斯奧西里斯受難劇

region.en: Abydos, Upper Egypt (temple, processional way, and the plain of Peqer)
region.zh: 埃及上埃及阿拜多斯（神廟、巡行道與佩克爾平原）

period: Annual play attested by the stele of I-kher-nefert, 12th Dynasty (c. 1900 BCE), reproducing Old Kingdom rites (Budge, Osiris and the Egyptian Resurrection vol. II, 1911)

source.work: E. A. W. Budge, Osiris and the Egyptian Resurrection, vol. II (London, 1911), ch. XIV, 'The Shrines, Miracle Play, and Mysteries of Osiris' (stele of I-kher-nefert, Berlin 1024)
