Finally the time came when the unmarried humpbacks had to depend on the other one for food; naturally this arrangement was very displeasing to the wife, and in time her hate grew so intense that she planned to kill all her brothers-in-law.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 33 'The Seven Humpbacks'; not verbatim.

passages.text: One day, when her husband was away on business, she murdered the six brothers. Next she hired a man to come and bury a corpse, telling him of only one corpse because she wanted to deceive the man. When he had buried one of the bodies he came back to get paid for his work; the woman, before he had time to speak, began to reproach him for not burying the man in the right place: 'See here! You did not do your work well. Go and bury the body again. Remember that I will not pay you until you have buried the man so that he stays under the earth.' The man took the second corpse and buried it; but when he returned, there it was again. And so on: he repeated the operation until he thought that he had buried the same corpse six times.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 33 'The Seven Humpbacks'; not verbatim.

passages.text: But after the sixth, the last humpback, had been buried, the married humpback came home from his work. When the grave-digger saw this other humpback, he immediately seized and killed him, thinking he was the same man he had buried so many times before. When the wicked woman knew that her very husband had been killed, she died of a broken heart.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 33 'The Seven Humpbacks'; not verbatim.

title.en: Respect Old Age: The Half-Blanket and the Wooden Plate
title.zh: 敬老：半條毯與木盤

region.en: Malabon, Rizal, and Mangaldan, Pangasinan, Luzon, Philippines (two tellings)
region.zh: 菲律賓呂宋黎薩省馬拉翁與邦阿西楠省曼加爾丹（兩則講述）

period: Tagalog and Pangasinan oral exempla; collected by D. S. Fansler, published 1921

source.work: Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 34a 'Respect Old Age' and 34b 'The Golden Rule', eBook #8299

summary.en: Two Filipino tellings of the old-age exemplum: forced on a rainy morning to send his eighty-year-old father to a farm hut, the boy cuts the carrying-blanket in two — 'When you grow old, I will leave you in a hut, and give you this half' — and the father recalls the order; and in Pangasinan, the son who must eat from a wooden plate because his trembling hands break the china begins carving boards 'for you and my mother when you are old,' and the father weeps and seats the old man at the table again.
summary.zh: 兩則菲律賓孝道故事：雨晨被迫送八十歲老父去農舍的父親，見兒子把毯子剪成兩半——『您老了，我就用這半條送您去小屋』——連忙召回祖父；另一則裡，因老人手抖摔盤而被罰用木盤吃飯的孩子，竟在屋下雕起木板：『給您和媽媽老了用』——父親流淚，從此老人重上飯桌。

sensitivity.note: Two related exempla recorded by Fansler from an Ignacio narrator (Malabon, Rizal) and a Serafica narrator (Mangaldan, Pangasinan); archival record. A Pampango variant ('The Old Man, his Son, and his Grandson' with the rope 'to have it ready when your turn comes') was printed by H. E. Fansler. Known in many countries.

passages.text: Once there lived a poor man who had to support his family: a hot-headed wife who predominated over the will of her husband, a small boy of ten, and an old man of eighty, the boy's grandfather. The old man could no longer work because of his feebleness, and was the cause of many quarrels between the husband and wife, though he was loved by their son. One rainy morning the husband was forced by his wife to send his father away; he called his son and ordered him to carry a basket full of food and also a blanket, telling the boy they were to leave the old man in a hut on their farm some distance away. The boy wept and protested against this harsh treatment of his grandfather, but in vain; he then cut the blanket into two parts, and when he was asked to explain his action, he said to his father, 'When you grow old, I will leave you in a hut, and give you this half of the blanket.' The man was astonished, hurriedly recalled his order concerning his father, and thereafter took good care of him.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 34 'Respect Old Age'; not verbatim.

passages.text: A long time ago there lived in a town a couple who had a son, and the father of the husband lived with his son and daughter-in-law happily for many years; but when he grew very old he became very feeble, and every time he ate at the table he always broke a plate, because his hands trembled so. The old man's awkwardness soon made his son angry, and one day he made a wooden plate for his father to eat out of; the poor old man had to eat all his food from this wooden plate.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 34 'The Golden Rule'; not verbatim.

passages.text: When the grandson noticed what his father had done, he took some tools and went down under the house, and there took a piece of board and began to carve it. When his father saw him and said, 'What are you doing, son?' the boy replied, 'Father, I am making wooden plates for you and my mother when you are old.' As the son uttered these words, tears gushed from the father's eyes; from that time on, the old man was always allowed to eat at the table with the rest of the family, nor was he made to eat from a wooden plate. Moral: Do unto others as you want them to do unto you.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 34 'The Golden Rule'; not verbatim.

title.en: The Trial of Osiris Before the Great Gods: Thoth the Advocate
title.zh: 諸神前之奧西里斯審判：辯護者托特

region.en: Celestial Anu (Heliopolis), Egypt (the Hall of Judgment of the Great Gods)
region.zh: 埃及天界赫利奧波利斯（諸神審判之廳）

period: Ancient tradition retold from Pyramid Text hints (Budge, The Book of the Dead, 1901, ch. V)

source.work: The Book of the Dead, by E. A. Wallis Budge (1901), ch. V, 'Thoth and Osiris'

summary.en: Set's case against his murdered brother is tried before the Greater and Lesser Companies assembled in celestial Anu: Isis and Nephthys bring Osiris in, Horus 'the avenger of his father' comes to watch, Thoth appears as scribe — and as advocate, proving Set's charges unfounded and Set himself a liar; the gods order Osiris a Great God with rule of the Under World, throw Set down, make Osiris mount upon his back, bind him 'with cords like a beast for sacrifice,' and hack him in pieces before Thoth.
summary.zh: 塞特訟其被害之兄，案審於天界赫利奧波利斯之大小二神團前：伊西斯與奈芙蒂斯引奧西里斯至，荷魯斯『復父仇者』臨庭監審，托特以書記之職而兼辯護——證塞特之訟皆虛、其人乃謊者；諸神遂判奧西里斯為大神、王冥界；塞特被擊倒於地，奧西里斯登其背以示勝，復縛之『如祭祀之獸』，於托特之前碎其身。

sensitivity.note: Ancient theological narrative via Budge 1901; no living community restrictions.

passages.text: The Egyptians were not satisfied with the mere possession of the texts of Thoth, when their souls were being weighed in the Great Scales in the Judgment Hall of Osiris, but they also wished Thoth to act as their Advocate on this dread occasion and to prove their innocence as he had proved that of Osiris before the great gods in prehistoric times.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Budge, The Book of the Dead (1901), ch. V.

passages.text: The Greater and the Lesser Companies of the Gods assembled in the celestial Anu, or Heliopolis, and ordered Osiris to stand up and defend himself against the charges brought against him by Set. Isis and Nephthys brought him before the gods, and Horus, 'the avenger of his father,' came to watch the case on behalf of his father, Osiris. Thoth appeared in the Hall of Judgment in his official capacity as 'scribe,' i.e., secretary to the gods, and the hearing of the evidence began. Set seems to have pleaded his own cause, and to have repeated the charges which he had made against Osiris.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Budge (1901), ch. V.

passages.text: The defence of Osiris was undertaken by Thoth, who proved to the gods that the charges brought against Osiris by Set were unfounded, that the statements of Set were lies, and that therefore Set was a liar. The gods accepted Thoth's proof of the innocence of Osiris and the guilt of Set, and ordered that Osiris was to be considered a Great God and to have rule over the Kingdom of the Under World, and that Set was to be punished. Thoth convinced them that Osiris was 'MAA KHERU,' 'true of word,' i.e., that he had spoken the truth when he gave his evidence, and in texts of all periods Thoth is frequently described as S-MAA KHERU ASAR, i.e., he who proved Osiris to be 'true of word.'
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Budge (1901), ch. V.

passages.text: As for Set the Liar, he was seized by the ministers of the Great Gods, who threw him down on his hands and face and made Osiris mount upon his back as a mark of his victory and superiority. After this Set was bound with cords like a beast for sacrifice, and in the presence of Thoth was hacked in pieces.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Budge (1901), ch. V.

title.en: The Crocodile and the Trochilus: The Bird That Enters the Mouth
title.zh: 鱷與鶺鴒：入其口之鳥

region.en: The Nile and the lake of Moiris, Egypt (where the tamed crocodiles wear golden earrings)
region.zh: 埃及尼羅與莫伊里斯湖（馴鱷戴金耳環之處）

period: Recorded by Herodotus, Histories II.68-70 (5th century BCE; Macaulay translation 1890)

source.work: The History of Herodotus, trans. G. C. Macaulay (1890), Book II, secs. 68-70

summary.en: The sacred-crocodile rite: around Thebes and the lake of Moiris each people keeps one crocodile trained to tameness, hung with ornaments of molten stone and gold in its ears and anklets on its front feet, fed on appointed food and sacrificial victims — while at Elephantine they eat them, 'not holding them to be sacred'; and the trochilus, the one bird at peace with the crocodile, enters its open mouth to swallow the leeches.
summary.zh: 聖鱷之禮：底比斯與莫伊里斯湖畔各奉一馴鱷，耳懸熔石與金飾、前足戴環，以定制之食與祭牲飼之——而象島之民竟食之，『不以為聖』；獨有鶺鴈與鱷相安，入其啟口而吞其螞蟥。

sensitivity.note: Ancient ethnography via Herodotus; no living community restrictions.

passages.text: Now for some of the Egyptians the crocodiles are sacred animals, and for others not so, but they treat them on the contrary as enemies: those however who dwell about Thebes and about the lake of Moiris hold them to be most sacred, and each of these two peoples keeps one crocodile selected from the whole number, which has been trained to tameness, and they put hanging ornaments of molten stone and of gold into the ears of these and anklets round the front feet, and they give them food appointed and victims of sacrifices and treat them as well as possible while they live, and after they are dead they bury them in sacred tombs, embalming them: but those who dwell about the city of Elephantine even eat them, not holding them to be sacred.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Macaulay, Herodotus (1890), Book II.69.

passages.text: Whereas all other birds and beasts fly from him, the trochilus is a creature which is at peace with him, seeing that from her he receives benefit; for the crocodile having come out of the water to the land and then having opened his mouth (this he is wont to do generally towards the West Wind), the trochilus upon that enters into his mouth and swallows down the leeches, and he being benefited is pleased and does no harm to the trochilus.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Macaulay (1890), Book II.68.

title.en: Cats to Bubastis, Hawks to Buto: The Burial Map of Sacred Animals
title.zh: 貓葬布巴斯提斯、鷹葬布托：聖獸葬地圖

region.en: Egypt, the sacred animal cemeteries (Bubastis, Buto, Hermopolis)
region.zh: 埃及聖獸墓群（布巴斯提斯、布托、赫爾莫波利斯）

period: Recorded by Herodotus, Histories II.65-67 (5th century BCE; Macaulay translation 1890)

source.work: The History of Herodotus, trans. G. C. Macaulay (1890), Book II, secs. 65-67

summary.en: A geography of grief: whoever kills one of the sacred animals willingly dies, and the killer of an ibis or hawk dies whatever his intent; when fire breaks out the cats leap into the flames 'divinely possessed' and great mourning comes upon Egypt; the dead cats are carried to Bubastis and embalmed, dogs buried in city tombs, shrew-mice and hawks to Buto, ibises to Hermopolis.
summary.zh: 哀悼之地理：擅殺聖獸者死，殺朱鷺或鷹者不問有心無心皆死；火起之時，貓『如神所憑』躍入火中，全埃及為之舉哀——貓死運至布巴斯提斯製為木乃伊；犬葬城中聖墓；鶹鶹與鷹運至布托；朱鷺運至赫爾莫波利斯。

sensitivity.note: Ancient ethnography via Herodotus; no living community restrictions.

passages.text: If any one kill any of these animals, the penalty, if he do it with his own will, is death, and if against his will, such penalty as the priests may appoint: but whosoever shall kill an ibis or a hawk, whether it be with his will or against his will, must die.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Macaulay, Herodotus (1890), Book II.65.

passages.text: Moreover when a fire occurs, the cats seem to be divinely possessed; for while the Egyptians stand at intervals and look after the cats, not taking any care to extinguish the fire, the cats slipping through or leaping over the men, jump into the fire; and when this happens, great mourning comes upon the Egyptians. And in whatever houses a cat has died by a natural death, all those who dwell in this house shave their eyebrows only, but those in whose houses a dog has died shave their whole body and also their head.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Macaulay (1890), Book II.66.

passages.text: The cats when they are dead are carried away to sacred buildings in the city of Bubastis, where after being embalmed they are buried; but the dogs they bury each people in their own city in sacred tombs; and the ichneumons are buried just in the same way as the dogs. The shrew-mice however and the hawks they carry away to the city of Buto, and the ibises to Hermopolis; the bears (which are not commonly seen) and the wolves, not much larger in size than foxes, they bury on the spot where they are found lying.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Macaulay (1890), Book II.67.

title.en: Three Ways of Embalming: Cedar Oil, Natron, and Seventy Days
title.zh: 三種防腐之法：雪松油、泡鹼與七十日

region.en: The embalmers' workshops of Egypt (symbolic pin, Memphis)
region.zh: 埃及防腐師作坊（象徵定位，孟菲斯）

period: Recorded by Herodotus, Histories II.86-88 (5th century BCE; Macaulay translation 1890)

source.work: The History of Herodotus, trans. G. C. Macaulay (1890), Book II, secs. 86-88

summary.en: The undertakers' price-list in three grades: for the costliest, the brain drawn out through the nostrils with a crooked iron tool, the belly cleansed with palm-wine and pounded spices, filled with pure myrrh and cassia, sewn and kept in natron for seventy days — 'and when the seventy days are past... they have a wooden figure made in the shape of a man' to enclose the corpse; the middle grade is filled with cedar oil through the breech, and the third is the least expensive of all.
summary.zh: 殯儀之三等價目：上等以鐵鉤自鼻孔抽腦，以棕櫚酒洗腹、填純沒藥與桂皮而縫之，納於泡鹼七十日——『七十日既滿……乃製一木製人形』以納屍；中等以雪松油自後竅注入；下等最廉。

sensitivity.note: Ancient mortuary practice via Herodotus; no living community restrictions.

passages.text: In this occupation certain persons employ themselves regularly and inherit this as a craft. These, whenever a corpse is conveyed to them, show to those who brought it wooden models of corpses made like reality by painting... Then they after they have agreed for a certain price depart out of the way, and the others being left behind in the buildings embalm according to the best of these ways thus: — First with a crooked iron tool they draw out the brain through the nostrils, extracting it partly thus and partly by pouring in drugs; and after this with a sharp stone of Ethiopia they make a cut along the side and take out the whole contents of the belly, and when they have cleared out the cavity and cleansed it with palm-wine they cleanse it again with spices pounded up: then they fill the belly with pure myrrh pounded up and with cassia and other spices except frankincense, and sew it together again.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Macaulay, Herodotus (1890), Book II.86.

passages.text: Having so done they keep it for embalming covered up in natron for seventy days, but for a longer time than this it is not permitted to embalm it; and when the seventy days are past, they wash the corpse and roll its whole body up in fine linen cut into bands, smearing these beneath with gum, which the Egyptians use generally instead of glue. Then the kinsfolk receive it from them and have a wooden figure made in the shape of a man, and when they have had this made they enclose the corpse, and having shut it up within, they store it then in a sepulchral chamber, setting it to stand upright against the wall.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Macaulay (1890), Book II.86.

passages.text: But for those who desire the middle way and wish to avoid great cost they prepare the corpse as follows: — having filled their syringes with the oil which is got from cedar-wood, with this they forthwith fill the belly of the corpse, and this they do without having either cut it open or taken out the bowels, but they inject the oil by the breech, and having stopped the drench from returning back they keep it then the appointed number of days for embalming.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Macaulay (1890), Book II.87.

title.en: The Blind King's Island of Ashes: Elbo, Hidden Seven Hundred Years
title.zh: 盲王之灰島：隱匿七百年之埃爾博

region.en: The marshes of the Delta, Egypt (the secret island Elbo, ten furlongs each way)
region.zh: 埃及三角洲沼澤（秘密之島埃爾博，每邊十弗隆）

period: Recorded by Herodotus, Histories II.140 (5th century BCE; Macaulay translation 1890)

source.work: The History of Herodotus, trans. G. C. Macaulay (1890), Book II, sec. 140

summary.en: The blind king Anysis, driven into the marshes by the Ethiopian Sabacos, rules from a secret island he built by heaping up ashes: every visitor who brought him food was commanded to bring ashes as a gift; the island, named Elbo, ten furlongs each way, remained hidden from every king of Egypt for more than seven hundred years, until Amyrtaios.
summary.zh: 盲王阿尼西斯為埃塞俄比亞王所逐，遁於沼澤，積灰壘土而成密島：凡攜食來見者皆奉灰為禮；此島名埃爾博，每邊十弗隆——七百餘年間，歷代埃及諸王皆未能尋獲，直至阿米爾塔伊奧斯。

sensitivity.note: Ancient king-legend via Herodotus; no living community restrictions.

passages.text: Then when the Ethiopian had gone away out of Egypt, the blind man came back from the fen-country and began to rule again, having lived there during fifty years upon an island which he had made by heaping up ashes and earth: for whenever any of the Egyptians visited him bringing food, according as it had been appointed to them severally to do without the knowledge of the Ethiopian, he bade them bring also some ashes for their gift.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Macaulay, Herodotus (1890), Book II.140.

passages.text: This island none was able to find before Amyrtaios; that is, for more than seven hundred years the kings who arose before Amyrtaios were not able to find it. Now the name of this island is Elbo, and its size is ten furlongs each way.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Macaulay (1890), Book II.140.

title.en: Piromis Son of Piromis: The Priests Refuse a Divine Descent
title.zh: 善人之子善人：祭司拒認神裔

region.en: Thebes, Egypt (the sanctuary where 345 statues of chief-priests stood)
region.zh: 埃及底比斯（陳列三百四十五尊大祭司像之聖所）

period: Recorded by Herodotus, Histories II.143 (5th century BCE; Macaulay translation 1890)

source.work: The History of Herodotus, trans. G. C. Macaulay (1890), Book II, sec. 143

summary.en: When Hecataeus the historian traced his descent to a god in the sixteenth generation, the priests of Theban Zeus led him into the great sanctuary, counted the 345 wooden statues of chief-priests, and refused the claim: each statue, they said, had been a piromis — 'an honourable and good man' — son of a piromis, 'and neither with a god nor a hero did they connect their descent.'
summary.zh: 史家赫卡泰奧斯自溯為第十六代之神裔，底比斯宙斯之祭司乃引之入大聖所，指陳三百四十五尊大祭司木像，而拒其說：謂每一像皆『善人』（piromis）之子為善人，『其世系不繫於神亦不繫於英雄』。

sensitivity.note: Ancient anecdote via Herodotus; no living community restrictions.

passages.text: And formerly when Hecataios the historian was in Thebes, and had traced his descent and connected his family with a god in the sixteenth generation before, the priests of Zeus did for him much the same as they did for me (though I had not traced my descent). They led me into the sanctuary of the temple, which is of great size, and they counted up the number, showing colossal wooden statues in number the same as they said; for each chief-priest there sets up in his lifetime an image of himself.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Macaulay, Herodotus (1890), Book II.143.

passages.text: And when Hecataios had traced his descent and connected his family with a god in the sixteenth generation, they traced a descent in opposition to this, besides their numbering, not accepting it from him that a man had been born from a god; and they traced their counter-descent thus, saying that each one of the statues had been piromis son of piromis, until they had declared this of the whole three hundred and forty-five statues, each one being surnamed piromis; and neither with a god nor a hero did they connect their descent. Now piromis means in the tongue of Hellas 'honourable and good man.'
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Macaulay (1890), Book II.143.

title.en: Cochinango: The Ass, the Buyo, and the Dancing Guitar
title.zh: 科奇南戈：驢、檳榔與舞曲吉他

region.en: Laoag, Ilocos Norte, Luzon, Philippines (narrator's grandmother's home town)
region.zh: 菲律賓呂宋北伊洛克斯省佬沃（敘述者祖母故鄉）

period: Ilocano oral tale; collected by D. S. Fansler, published 1921

source.work: Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 35 'Cochinango', eBook #8299

summary.en: A palmer foretells that the 'fool' Cochinango will dine with the king, kiss the princess, marry her, and be king. Kindness on the road wins him a question-answering buyo, a food-furnishing cane, an inexhaustible purse, and — for his ass — a guitar that makes anyone dance. Winning the princess's riddle-contest earns only prison; but the cane feeds his fellow-prisoners, the purse buys his dinner with the king, and a night of inescapable guitar music wins the marriage — after which his dancing enemies save the kingdom from raiding Moros.
summary.zh: 朝聖者預言：被喚作『傻瓜』的科奇南戈終將與王共餐、親吻公主、娶她為妻、繼而為王。一路行善，他先後得能答萬問的檳榔、予食的拐杖、取之不竭的錢袋，並以毛驢換得令人起舞的吉他。贏了猜謎卻被囚；拐杖餵飽獄友，錢袋換來御宴，一曲通宵達旦的吉他迫使國王允婚——此後他以舞曲退摩洛海寇，繼位為王。

sensitivity.note: Ilocano folktale recorded by Fansler from a Velasco narrator (grandmother from Laoag); archival record. The magic buyo is likely native Ilocano belief or Tinguian-influenced (Fansler); the closing reference to raiding Moros 'appears to be a remnant of very old native tradition.'

passages.text: Once upon a time there lived in a small village on the border of a powerful kingdom a poor farmer who had a son. This son was called a fool by many; but a palmer predicted that Cochinango would some day dine with the king, kiss the princess, marry her, and finally would himself be king. Cochinango wondered how he could ever marry the princess and himself be king, for he was very poor — until one day he heard that the king had summoned all those who would like to attempt to answer the questions of the princess, the person who could answer them all without fail to marry her; so he mounted his ass and rode toward the king's palace.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 35 'Cochinango'; not verbatim.

passages.text: On his way Cochinango had to pass through a wide forest, where he met a weary traveller and asked him for buyo, having forgotten to bring any; the traveller gave him a magic buyo that would answer any question he put to it, in exchange for food. At a stream he offered to carry across an old man too weak to swim, and in return received his cane, which would furnish food at any time — and this old man was the same one who had given him the magic buyo: it was God himself, who had come down on earth to test Cochinango and to reward him for his kindness. Then, out of pity, he gave a centavo to a wretched old woman and received an empty purse from which he could ask any sum of money he wanted; and God, again in the form of a jolly young fellow with a small guitar, asked him to exchange his ass for the guitar, since he could make anybody dance by plucking its strings. Cochinango had to proceed on foot, and it took him two days to reach the gates of the palace.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 35 'Cochinango'; not verbatim.

passages.text: Luckily he arrived on the very day of the guessing-contest, and in spite of his mean dress he was admitted. The princess was much astonished at Cochinango's appearance and disgusted by his boldness — but she was even more chagrined when he rightly answered her first question; she denied that his answer was correct, and asked him two more questions, the most difficult she could think of, but Cochinango, with the help of his magic buyo, answered both. She shrunk from the idea of being married to a poor, foolish, lowly-born man, and asked her father the king to imprison the insolent peasant, which was instantly done.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 35 'Cochinango'; not verbatim.

passages.text: In the prison Cochinango found many nobles who, like himself, were victims of the guessing-match; night came, and they were given no food, for the princess wanted to starve them to death. Cochinango told them not to worry: he struck a table with his cane, and instantly choice food appeared. When this was reported to the princess she went to the prison and begged Cochinango to give her the cane; but he would not give it up unless she allowed him to kiss her. At last she consented and went away with the cane, thinking this was the only way she could starve her prisoners — but the next day Cochinango asked a large sum of money from his magic purse, distributed it among his companions and the guards, and they had no difficulty in getting food. Again the princess went to the prison and asked for the purse; he would give it up only on condition that he be allowed to dine with the king — and accordingly he was taken to the king's table, where he ate with the king and the princess, though he was put in prison again as soon as the dinner was over.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 35 'Cochinango'; not verbatim.

passages.text: At last Cochinango began to be tired of prison life, so he took up his wonderful guitar and began to play it: no sooner had he touched the strings than his fellow-prisoners and the guards began to dance; he played louder and louder, and the inmates of the palace heard it and they too began to dance; he kept on playing throughout the night, and the king, princess, and all got no rest whatsoever — by morning most of them were tired to death. At last the king ordered the guards to open the prison doors and let the prisoners go free; but Cochinango would not stop playing until the king consented to give him the princess in marriage, and the princess also at last had to agree to accept Cochinango as her husband. The next day they were married with great pomp and ceremony. Thus the poor, foolish boy was married to a princess; more than once he saved the kingdom from the raiding Moros by playing his guitar, for all his enemies were obliged to dance when they heard the music, and thus they were easily captured or killed. When the king died, Cochinango became his successor, and he and the princess ruled happily for many years.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 35 'Cochinango'; not verbatim.

title.en: Pedro and the Witch: The Red and White Handkerchiefs
title.zh: 佩德羅與巫婆：紅白兩巾

region.en: San Narciso, Zambales, Luzon, Philippines (narrator's home town)
region.zh: 菲律賓呂宋三描禮士省聖納爾西索（敘述者故鄉）

period: Zambal oral tale; collected by D. S. Fansler, published 1921

source.work: Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 36 'Pedro and the Witch', eBook #8299

summary.en: Left alone at nightfall, Pedro opens the door to Boroka, the bird-winged, horse-footed witch with a woman's head who devours children's livers; obedient, he becomes her housekeeper and befriends a visiting horse. When children grow scarce and the witch plans to serve Pedro at a feast of witches, the horse gives him two handkerchiefs and carries him off — the red one becomes a fire that burns off the witches' wings, the white one a wide sea they cannot pass.
summary.zh: 夜幕中應門的佩德羅落入巫婆博羅卡之手——鳥翼馬足、人頭食童肝的怪物。他乖順地當起管家，並與常來探望的馬結為好友。孩童漸稀、巫婆擬以他為宴饗之時，馬兒贈他兩方手帕、載他狂奔：紅巾化烈火燒盡巫婆之翼，白巾化大海阻斷追兵。

sensitivity.note: Zambal tale recorded by Fansler from a Dumlao narrator (San Narciso, Zambales); archival record. Fansler regards it as the detritus of a literary tradition from Europe (the Pampangan corrido 'Pugut Negro' / Don Octavio cycle and the widely-known 'Juan Tiñoso'), noting Boroka is a native demon-name.

passages.text: Pedro was the son of a poor man; he lived with his father and mother by the seashore. Early one morning his parents went to look for food, leaving him alone in the house; he stayed there all day waiting for them to return. Evening came, but his father and mother did not appear — some misfortune had overtaken them. Pedro felt very hungry, but he could find no food in the house. In the middle of the night he heard someone tapping at the door; thinking that it was his mother, he arose and went to meet her — but when he opened the door, he saw that it was not his mother who had rapped, but Boroka, whom children are very much afraid of. Now, Boroka was a witch: she had wings like a bird, four feet like a horse, but a head like that of a woman. She devoured boys and girls, and was especially fond of their liver. As soon as Pedro opened the door, she seized him and carried him off to her home in the mountains.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 36 'Pedro and the Witch'; not verbatim.

passages.text: Pedro was not afraid of the witch; he was obedient to her, and soon she made him her housekeeper. Whenever she went out at night to look for food, he was sure to have flesh and liver for breakfast the next day. Whenever the witch was away, Pedro used to amuse himself riding on the back of a horse that would often come to see him; it taught him how to ride well, and the two became great friends.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 36 'Pedro and the Witch'; not verbatim.

passages.text: One day when children began to get scarce, and Boroka was unable to find any to eat, she made up her mind to kill Pedro: she left the house and went to invite the other witches, so that they might have a great feast. While she was gone, the horse came and told Pedro of his danger, and advised him what to do; it gave him two handkerchiefs, one red and the other white. Then Pedro jumped on the horse's back, and the horse ran away as fast as it could. Not long afterward he noticed that the witches were pursuing them; when they came nearer, Pedro dropped the red handkerchief, which was immediately changed into a large fire — the wings of the witches were all burnt off. However, the witches tried to pursue the horse on foot, for they could run very fast; when they were almost upon him again, Pedro dropped the white handkerchief, which became a wide sea through which the witches could not pass. Pedro was now safe, and he thanked the horse for its great help.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 36 'Pedro and the Witch'; not verbatim.

title.en: The Woman and Her Coles Plant
title.zh: 婦人與通天甘藍

region.en: Batangas city, Luzon, Philippines (tale common there)
region.zh: 菲律賓呂宋八打雁城（故事流行之地）

period: Tagalog oral exemplum; collected by D. S. Fansler, published 1921

source.work: Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 37 'The Woman and her Coles Plant', eBook #8299

summary.en: A beggar-woman's coles seed grows to the sky; climbing it she begs St. Peter for a wand that grants any wish, feasts on summoned tables — and grows so proud she no longer knows her friends. Demanding that the church bells toll for her, she is struck senseless by the swinging bell; recovering, she climbs again for another gift, but the plant breaks halfway to heaven and she is killed by her fall — punished for her vanity.
summary.zh: 乞婦種下甘藍，藤蔓直上雲霄。她攀至天界，向聖彼得求得『要什麼有什麼』的神杖，從此錦衣玉食、目中無友。她竟令教堂鐘為她而鳴——鐘錘當頭將她擊昏；醒後再度攀藤求賜，藤蔓半途折斷，她墜地而亡——虛榮之罰。

sensitivity.note: Tagalog exemplum recorded by Fansler from a Hilario narrator (Batangas); archival record. Jack-and-the-Beanstalk machinery joined to the Fisherman-and-his-Wife moral; Fansler derives it from a French or Italian Märchen, probably through the clergy.

passages.text: Once there lived a very poor woman. She lived practically by begging, but sometimes she got money with which to buy rice by selling small vegetables in the market; she had a little garden, and one day planted some seeds. Out of one of these seeds there grew up a plant which we call coles: this plant grew very fast, and in a few months it reached the sky.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 37 'The Woman and her Coles Plant'; not verbatim.

passages.text: Out of curiosity, one day the woman began to climb the plant; when she was assured that it was strong she kept on climbing, and did not stop until she reached the sky. There she called to St. Peter, and asked him to give her a magic wand from which she could ask anything she wished; St. Peter gave her what she asked for, but told her not to disturb him again. Then she descended, and went down so quickly that she almost hurt herself. When she reached her little hut, she at once asked the wand for food: immediately there appeared a table on which was the best food in the world; when she had finished eating, she commanded the table to disappear, and it disappeared instantly. Now she became very proud on account of her wonderful possession — she did not recognize her friends any more.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 37 'The Woman and her Coles Plant'; not verbatim.

passages.text: One day an archbishop arrived in the town in which she was living, and all the bells were rung in his honor; she then became very angry, and wondered why the bells were not rung for her whenever she passed in front of the church. So she went to the tower where the bells were, and commanded them to toll for her. They began to ring — but she was struck on the head and was knocked senseless. When she recovered, she hastened home and began to climb the plant to ask St. Peter for another gift; but, before she had covered one-half the distance to the sky, the plant broke, and she was killed by her fall. Thus she was punished for her vanity.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 37 'The Woman and her Coles Plant'; not verbatim.

title.en: A Negrito Slave: The Three Questions
title.zh: 小黑奴與三問

region.en: Valladolid, Negros Occidental, Philippines (narrator's home town)
region.zh: 菲律賓西內格羅省瓦利亞多利德（敘述者故鄉）

period: Visayan oral tale; collected by D. S. Fansler, published 1921

source.work: Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 38 'A Negrito Slave', eBook #8299

summary.en: A Negrito with a wish-granting ring whitens his skin, masks himself as his young master, and answers the princess-king's three questions in his place: God owns the kingdom; the king is worth thirty pieces of silver, like the Saviour; and he can drink all the fresh water in the world once the king separates it from the salt. The youngest prince marries the princess; the Negrito receives the maid of honor.
summary.zh: 有許願戒指的小黑奴以法美白膚、戴上酷似少主的面具代其應答三問：王國屬於上帝；國王值三十塊銀元——救主被賣的價錢；只要國王先把海水與淡水分開，他便能喝盡天下淡水。少年王子娶得公主，小黑奴則得女儐相為妻。

sensitivity.note: Visayan folktale recorded by Fansler from a de la Rama narrator (Valladolid, Negros Occidental); archival record. Fansler traces the three-questions cycle to Europe (Grimm No. 152, 'The King and the Bishop' family), the Negrito taking the miller's role; the record retains the period's colonial framing and naming, noted here.

passages.text: Once upon a time there were three princes who owned a Negrito slave; although he was called a slave he was not really one, for the princes, especially the youngest, whom he loved most, treated him kindly. One striking characteristic of this Negrito was that his grinning was like that of a monkey, and he often grinned without cause; he would often follow his young master when he went out for a walk, and he had a suit similar to the prince's, so that, when they were out on the street, they looked very much alike — the only difference was that he was black, and the prince was white. Yet he owned a ring, a charm which had been given him by a woman for saving her from the hands of a robber; this ring gave him power to call for anything he wanted, and this was the reason, doubtless, why he was treated with kindness by his masters.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 38 'A Negrito Slave'; not verbatim.

passages.text: In a neighboring land there was a king who had a beautiful daughter who wanted to marry; so desirous was she of having a companion that she could not sleep day or night, meditating on how she could have a husband that would suit both herself and her father. At last, won over by her many entreaties, the king proclaimed to all the world that his daughter would marry anyone who had a handsome appearance and who could answer his three difficult questions; those who came to the court and were unable to answer the questions of the king were to lose their lives. The three princes were all handsome; the two elder brothers tried to answer the king's questions, but lost their lives. The youngest remained, and although he wanted to try, he was sure he would fail too. The Negrito determined to help him: by means of his ring he was able to make his skin white, and he also got a mask that was exactly like the face of his young master; then he dressed himself to resemble the prince, and went to the court of the king. 'Will you have your head cut off, too?' said the king. 'Yes, if I cannot answer your questions; but let us see!'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 38 'A Negrito Slave'; not verbatim.

passages.text: 'Who owns this kingdom?' 'God owns this kingdom.' The king was surprised at his bold reply; however, he could not say that it was not God's, for that would be untrue: therefore he could not compel the prince to answer that it was his. 'How much am I worth?' 'You are not worth more than thirty pieces of silver.' The king was furious, and said that, if the prince could not give a good reason for his insulting words, he would be put to death instantly. 'Yes, yes! Our Saviour was sold for that much: therefore you, who are inferior to the Saviour, cannot be worth more than he was sold for.' The people at the court were astounded, and murmured to one another, 'The prince is wise. He is wise, indeed!' 'Well, answer this third question, and you shall be married to my daughter: Can you drink all the fresh water in the world?' 'Yes... But here, in many parts of the world the water of the ocean mixes with the fresh water: so, before I drink, you must separate the fresh water from the salt.' As the king was unable to do this, he acknowledged himself vanquished.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 38 'A Negrito Slave'; not verbatim.

passages.text: 'All right. To-morrow come here for the wedding.' The Negrito hastened home and told his young master all that had happened; the prince gave him five thousand pesetas, and promised him that he would urge the princess to give her consent to the marriage of the Negrito with her maid of honor. The next morning the prince and the princess were married, and the following day the Negrito received the maid of honor for his wife.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 38 'A Negrito Slave'; not verbatim.

title.en: Alberto and the Monsters: Seven Heads, Ten Heads, Twelve Heads
title.zh: 阿爾貝托降魔記：七首、十首、十二首

region.en: Casiguran (Tayabas coast) and Sinucuan (Mt. Arayat) — Philippine frame for an imported tale, Luzon (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 菲律賓呂宋卡西古蘭與蘇努庫安（外來故事之在地框架，象徵定位）

period: Tagalog oral tale; collected by D. S. Fansler, published 1921

source.work: Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 39 'Alberto and the Monsters', eBook #8299

summary.en: A whirlwind carries off King Luis's three daughters; Prince Alberto of Sinucuan wins the magic boot, rusty key, and invisibility hat from quarrelers, drinks the monsters' pails of water until his iron chairs and beds break under him, and cuts off the seven-, ten-, and twelve-headed monsters head by head through the invisible door. Restoring all three princesses before the third day, he picks his bride by the handkerchief he slipped to the youngest.
summary.zh: 旋風捲走國王路易的三位女兒；蘇努庫安王子阿爾貝托以巧計贏得魔靴、鏽鑰與隱身帽，飲下魔怪的水桶直至鐵椅鐵床應聲而碎，隔著隱身之門將七首、十首、十二首巨魔逐一斬首。三日之限前送回三位公主，並以悄悄塞給幼女的手帕擇定新娘。

sensitivity.note: Tagalog folktale recorded by Fansler from a Cordero narrator (Pagsanjan); archival record. Fansler connects it to the Servian storm-stolen princesses (Wuk No. 5), the Bear's-Son underworld monsters, and Strong Hans (Grimm No. 166); Sinucuan is the legendary King of Pampanga of Mt. Arayat, who figures in the corpus record pampangan-crow-black-sinukuan.

passages.text: Once there was a king in Casiguran named Luis, who had three beautiful daughters, the youngest the fairest of all. One day the three princesses went to the orchard to amuse themselves; it happened that on that day the wind blew very hard, and they were swept away. The king felt very sad over the loss of his daughters, and issued proclamations in all parts of his kingdom, saying that anyone who could find his daughters within three days would be allowed to choose one of the three for his wife. At that time there was also in the neighboring kingdom of Sinucuan a king who had a brave son named Alberto; when Alberto heard of the matter, he went to the king and said that he would look for his lost daughters, and King Luis accepted his offer.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 39 'Alberto and the Monsters'; not verbatim.

passages.text: Prince Alberto walked and walked until he came to a large forest where he found two boys fighting over a boot which, if worn by anyone, would carry him to whatever place he wanted to go, provided he kicked the ground. 'Go over by that large tree, and the one who can run here first shall have the boot,' said the prince — and while the boys were walking toward the tree, he put on the boot and kicked the ground, and was at once carried far away. In the same manner he won from two young men a rusty key which, knocked against a stone, would open the stone however hard it might be, and from two old men a hat which made its wearer's body invisible. The boot brought him before a huge rock with a small hole in it; Alberto put the key in the hole, and the rock suddenly opened, revealing a street leading to a palace, where a beautiful princess met him.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 39 'Alberto and the Monsters'; not verbatim.

passages.text: Before Alberto could say a word, the princess told him to go away, for a seven-headed monster was living with her; 'If that is the case, show me his sword, and I will kill him.' The sword was too heavy for him to move — until the princess gave him a pail of water to drink, the water the monster always drank before touching his sword; he drank it and sat down on an iron chair, and the chair broke. 'The princess now told him that he was strong.' Soon steps were heard on the stairs: Prince Alberto put on his hat and stood by the door, sword in hand. When the monster came up, he thrust one of his heads through a window near the door and said, 'I smell something human!' — and the prince cut off that head. 'Somebody must be here!' cried the monster, but the princess answered that there was no one there with her; the prince then cut off the monster's heads one after another until only the main one was left, and when at last the monster entered the door, the prince cut off his last head and he fell dead. Inexpressible was the joy of the princess, who told him she was one of the daughters of King Luis and that her two sisters were kept prisoners in the same way.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 39 'Alberto and the Monsters'; not verbatim.

passages.text: He went outside and kicked the ground, and was brought before another huge rock; after two pails of water and a broken iron bed, he killed the ten-headed monster in the same way, and then the twelve-headed monster of the eldest princess — who, seeing him without his hat, thought he could easily kill him now that he could see him, and 'had scarcely spoken these words when Alberto cut off his remaining head.' Alberto took the princess in his arms, kicked the ground, and all three princesses were carried from palace to palace and brought back to their father's kingdom, for the third day was nearly gone. When they arrived at the palace, King Luis was overjoyed to see his daughters again, and told the prince to decide which one he wanted for a wife. While the three princesses were talking about their life with the monsters, Alberto managed, without being noticed, to give his handkerchief to the youngest. 'Have you decided whom you are going to take for a wife?' said the king the next day. 'The one who has a handkerchief just like mine shall be my wife' — and so the youngest was married to him; for three days banquets of thanksgiving were held, the marriage festivities lasted two days, and the other two princesses were also married to kings' sons.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 39 'Alberto and the Monsters'; not verbatim.

title.en: Juan and Maria: The Beggar's Children Who Became King and Queen
title.zh: 胡安與瑪利亞：乞丐子女封王封后

region.en: Arayat, Pampanga, Luzon, Philippines (often told by Pampangan grandmothers)
region.zh: 菲律賓呂宋邦板牙省阿拉亞特（祖母們常講的故事）

period: Pampangan oral tale; collected by D. S. Fansler, published 1921

source.work: Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 40 'Juan and Maria', eBook #8299

summary.en: Chased from a beggar's hut, Juan and Maria find shelter with a kind old woman; a talking black deer leaves Juan golden armor in its hide, and the hen's egg Maria carries hatches a cock that crows victory at the cockpit. In golden armor Juan wins the tournament for the princess's hand and the throne; a lost prince marries Maria — and both children seek out the parents who drove them off, whose father weeps for his former cruelty.
summary.zh: 被乞丐父母逐出的兄妹胡安與瑪利亞，得善良老嫗收留。黑鹿託夢留金甲於皮中；瑪利亞拾的雞蛋孵出必勝鬥雞。金甲加身的胡安贏得比武、迎娶公主、加冕為王；林中迷途的王子娶瑪利亞為后。兄妹衣錦還鄉探望狠心的父母——父親見子女為王為后，痛哭昔日之殘忍。

sensitivity.note: Pampangan folktale recorded by Fansler from a Pascual narrator (Arayat); archival record. Fansler compares the Tagalog corrido 'Juan and Maria' and the Tagalog 'Pitong' (Hop o' my Thumb), judging the common source European but the folk-tale nativized.

passages.text: Once there lived in a barrio an old beggar couple who had a son named Juan and a daughter Maria; the proceeds from their begging were hardly enough to support the family. One day, after the old man had returned home from town, he ordered his wife to cook the rice that had been given him; when he saw that the rice was not enough for him and his wife and children, he angrily said to her, 'From now on, don't let me see our children in this house. Chase them as far as you can, and let them find their own food.' The old mother wept when she heard the words of her cruel husband; she did not want to be separated from her children, but she feared that she would be whipped if she kept them, so she obeyed the cruel order. At first the poor children did not want to go away; but, when they saw that their bad father was going to kick them, they ran off crying.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 40 'Juan and Maria'; not verbatim.

passages.text: Soon the children came to a wild forest. 'Maria, what will become of us here?' said Juan. 'I am very hungry,' said the little girl. By good luck Juan found a guava-tree with one small fruit on it, climbed up for the guava, and gave it to his hungry sister; and as they were walking along, Maria found a hen's egg on the grass, which she picked up and carried along with her in her dirty ragged skirt. At last they saw a very small hut roofed with dry talahib; an old woman in the hut welcomed them and promised that she would treat them as her little son and daughter. From that time on Juan and Maria lived with the kind old woman: Juan grew to be a strong fine man, spending almost all his time hunting in the mountains and woods, and Maria became a beautiful young woman.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 40 'Juan and Maria'; not verbatim.

passages.text: One morning Juan caught a black deer; while he was taking the animal home, the deer said to him, 'Juan, as soon as you reach your home, kill me, eat my flesh, and put my hide in your trunk. After three days open your trunk, and you will see something astonishing.' When Juan reached home he did as the deer had told him to do, and on the third day he found in the trunk golden armor — he was greatly delighted by the precious gift. Maria's egg had hatched into a chick which soon grew into a fine fighting cock; one morning the cock crowed, 'Tok-to-ko-kok! Take me to the cockpit. I'll surely win!' — and the next Sunday the rooster was victorious and won much money for Juan.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 40 'Juan and Maria'; not verbatim.

passages.text: One day Juan heard that a tournament would be held in front of the king's palace, the winner of the contest to become the husband of the princess and inherit the throne; Juan quickly put on his golden armor and hastened to the palace to try his skill, defeating all his opponents. The next day his bridal ceremony was celebrated, and the crown was placed on his head; that very day he ascended the throne to rule over the kingdom. Although Juan was now king, he was not proud; he and the queen visited Maria to get her to live in the palace, but the old woman would not allow her to go with her brother, as she had no other companion in the hut. One day a prince was lost in the forest, and happened to come across the hut in which Maria was living; he fell in love with her and wanted to marry her, and as the old woman offered no objections, the following day Maria became a queen, just as her brother had become king. Although the parents of Juan and Maria had been very cruel, yet the king and queen did not forget them: the brother and sister visited their father and mother, whom they found in the most wretched condition, and when the father saw that his children had become king and queen, he wept greatly for his former cruelty to them.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 40 'Juan and Maria'; not verbatim.

title.en: Pitong: The Seven Brothers and the Giant
title.zh: 皮通：七兄弟與巨人

region.en: Pagsanjan, La Laguna, Luzon, Philippines (narrator's home town)
region.zh: 菲律賓呂宋內湖省帕桑漢（敘述者故鄉）

period: Tagalog oral tale; collected by D. S. Fansler, published 1921

source.work: Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), notes to Tale 40, 'Pitong', eBook #8299

summary.en: Seven sons of a poor woodman are twice led to the forest to be abandoned; the wisest, Pitong, marks the way with white stones and then with bread-crumbs the ants devour. Lost, they knock at a banquet-lighted house whose giant husband eats human beings; warned by the wife, Pitong swaps his brothers' rough clothes for the giant's sons' rich garments, so the father's axe at midnight beheads his own children. Escaping with the giant's magic boot, cap, and cane stolen as he sleeps, the boys are carried home, and the powerless giant dies in the woods.
summary.zh: 貧苦樵夫的七個兒子兩度被帶入林中遺棄；最機智的皮通先以白石、後以麵包屑（被螞蟻吃光）記路。迷途中他們投宿巨人妖宅；忠心的女主人示警，皮通讓兄弟們與巨人七子換衣——深夜巨斧落下的，是巨人自己的七個兒子。少年們盜走巨人的魔靴、魔帽、魔杖逃回家中；失去法力的巨人餓斃林中。

sensitivity.note: Tagalog folktale recorded by Fansler from a Cordero narrator (Pagsanjan); archival record. Tagalog form of Hop o' my Thumb, which Fansler says must have been received directly from Europe, retaining the received form with few modifications; no other Oriental form recorded.

passages.text: Melanio and Petrona had seven sons; the father was a woodman, and they were so poor that sometimes the whole family went without dinner. One day Melanio said to his wife, 'Petrona, our children are growing, and I don't see how we shall be able to support them all... Don't you think we should get along better without them?' — 'Yes, if we could only get rid of them some way!' — 'Well, to-morrow I will take them to the forest to gather fuel. While they are busy, I will leave them on the pretext of looking for better kinds of wood, and will hurry home. They will not be able to get home, for they won't know the way.' The wife agreed to this cruel plan; but the youngest son overheard the conversation, and told his brothers about it. At last Pitong (seventh), for that was the name of the youngest, and he was the wisest of all, made this suggestion: 'Before we go to the forest to-morrow, I will pick up white stones. I will carry them with me, and as we go along I will drop them one by one... Then, if he leaves us, we can easily follow the track of stones back home.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of the Tagalog folktale printed in Fansler's notes to Tale 40, 'Pitong'; not verbatim.

passages.text: The next day the children marched straight into the forest with their father as if they were going on a picnic, and Pitong dropped his stones one by one; their father commanded them to get together what sticks they could find, then left them, promising to meet them in a certain place — but really he hurried home and told his wife, 'We are now rid of a heavy burden.' The boys followed the track of stones and reached home safely, and the parents were astounded. The next morning Melanio took his sons out again; this time all the boys took white stones with them, but the part of the forest to which they went was so far that all the stones were used up before they got there — Pitong did not eat his bread, but broke it into pieces and dropped them on the ground as they went along, and the pieces were eaten by the ants. When they could not find the track they cried out, 'Father, father! Where are you?' until they sat down on the ground and began to weep.
passages.note: Paraphrase of the Tagalog folktale printed in Fansler's notes to Tale 40, 'Pitong'; not verbatim.

passages.text: It began to grow dark. Pitong advised his brothers to pluck up courage and said to them, 'Follow me.' In about a half-hour they came to a tall tree, and Pitong climbed it: 'Brothers, I see a lighted house from here.' When they came near, they saw that it was well lighted and richly adorned, as if there were a banquet going on — only it was very quiet. Pitong, followed by his brothers, knocked at the door; a woman kindly admitted them, and the boys begged for some food, telling her how they had been deserted by their selfish father. 'I have a giant husband who is a great eater of human beings. If he finds you here, you will surely be devoured; but I can give you something to eat. I will hide you before he comes, and you must remain perfectly still.' The boys had hardly finished dinner when a loud sound was heard from without: 'Here comes my husband! Boys, follow me into that room! You all get into this big trunk and stay here.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of the Tagalog folktale printed in Fansler's notes to Tale 40, 'Pitong'; not verbatim.

passages.text: The door was suddenly flung open: as soon as the giant entered, he said in a fierce voice, 'I smell something human: somebody must be here' — and although the wife did not want to show him the boys, she finally did so, for she feared she would be punished. 'Welcome, my young friends!' said the giant. 'Give these boys some food, and prepare them a comfortable bed. To-morrow early in the morning they will all be killed.' These words increased the terror of the six older brothers, who could not swallow a morsel more of food; but Pitong kept trying to think of a plan by which he could save them all. Now, the room in which they were to sleep was also the room of the giant's seven sons, who were about the same height as the woodman's sons, but had on rich garments. At midnight Pitong awoke his brothers, and they quietly and carefully exchanged clothes with the giant's sons, then pretended to sleep. At four o'clock in the morning the giant came in; he paused before the two beds, but at last turned to the one his sons were in, and when he felt their rough clothes he thought them the strangers, and with his axe he cut off the heads of all seven — his own children. Now Pitong and his six brothers stealthily hurried away into the forest; when the giant found that he had killed his own children he was enraged, and at once took his magic cane, put on his magic boots and cap, and pursued them. The boys hid in a big hole they had dug, and when the keen-scented giant at last leaned against a tree and fell asleep, Pitong called out to his brothers, and they quickly stole the magic boot, cap, and cane of the giant, and were soon carried home. Their parents were very much surprised to see them back, but welcomed their children when they knew of the magic objects; by means of these the family became rich. As for the giant, when he awoke he was deprived of all his power: he was so weak that he could not even get up from the ground, so he died there in the woods.
passages.note: Paraphrase of the Tagalog folktale printed in Fansler's notes to Tale 40, 'Pitong'; not verbatim.

title.en: The Enchanted Prince: The Monkey in the Tallest Tree
title.zh: 被施咒的王子：最高樹上的猿猴

region.en: Virac, Catanduanes, Philippines (narrator's home island)
region.zh: 菲律賓卡坦端內斯島維拉克（敘述者故鄉）

period: Bicol oral tale; collected by D. S. Fansler, published 1921

source.work: Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 41 'The Enchanted Prince', eBook #8299

summary.en: Forced by his father to marry a woman not the witch he loved, Prince Ucay is cursed: his city becomes a forest of beautiful trees, he a monkey in the tallest tree for five centuries, until a girl loves him more than anything else. Two captured ladies die of fear; a girl disappointed in love, whom a noble look in the monkey's eyes keeps alive, lives on strange fruits until her love outgrows everything — and on the tenth evening she wakes beside a gallant prince, crowned next morning queen of the restored subjects.
summary.zh: 被迫另娶的烏卡伊王子遭女巫詛咒：城池化為秀美之林，他化為最高樹上的猿猴，五百年間唯有真心愛他的少女方能解咒。先前兩位被擄女子皆驚懼而死；唯有一位失戀的姑娘，在猴眼中看出高貴的神情而倖存，以奇果為生，愛意日深——第十夜醒來，身旁已是英俊王子；翌日她加冕為后，全城子民復得人身。

sensitivity.note: Bicol tale recorded by Fansler from a Sorreta narrator (Virac); archival record. Fansler judges it old native tradition, vaguely suggesting the Beauty-and-Beast and Sleeping-Beauty cycles, and notes the number 500 and the monkey-prince suggest Buddhistic lore.

passages.text: Many years ago there lived a very rich king in a beautiful city near a wild forest, the home of many wicked witches. The king had a gallant son named Ucay, who fell in love with a beautiful young witch, the daughter of the most bitter enemy of his father. When Ucay became old enough to marry, his father requested him to select the most beautiful lady in the city for his wife; but the prince would neither select one, nor would he tell his father about his love for the witch. So the rich king ordered his soldiers to bring to the palace all the beautiful women that could be found in the kingdom; none of the girls suited the prince, so the king took the matter of selection into his own hands, and, after choosing a very handsome girl, forced his son to marry her.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 41 'The Enchanted Prince'; not verbatim.

passages.text: Out of fear, Ucay consented to do as his father bade him — but the beautiful young witch to whom he had already pledged his love became angry with him for his timidity, and so she resolved to change the city into a forest of beautiful trees. Her fickle lover she transformed into a monkey, who should live in the tallest tree, and who should not be able to recover his human shape till five centuries had passed, when a charming girl would live with him and love him more than anything else; moreover, she changed the king's subjects into other animals as she pleased. No sooner had the marriage of the prince been proclaimed, then, than the desire of the witch was accomplished, to the great surprise of the neighboring cities.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 41 'The Enchanted Prince'; not verbatim.

passages.text: Four centuries had already passed; the wonderful disappearance of the city was already forgotten, and people from other places began to build houses in the enchanted city. The monkey-prince was always watching for an opportunity to catch a beautiful girl who should break the spell that kept him in his miserable condition; soon a church was built near the foot of the tree in which he lived. He had already succeeded in capturing two ladies, but they had died of fear. After incalculable suffering and extraordinary patience, the time for his recovery came at last.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 41 'The Enchanted Prince'; not verbatim.

passages.text: One Sunday morning before the mass was over, a very beautiful girl, the daughter of a poor man, came out of the church and sat at the foot of the tree; she had been disappointed in her love with a rich man's son, who had forsaken her in order to marry the daughter of a rich man, so she wished to die. When the monkey-prince saw her sitting there alone, he noiselessly went down, carefully took her by the right hand, and carried her to the top of the tree. She would have died of fright, as was the fate of the two former women, had she not seen in the monkey's eyes a noble look that filled her with wonder and sympathy. As days went by, she lived on delicious fruits which were entirely strange to her; and her love for the poor creature grew greater and greater, until at last she loved him more than anything else. On the evening of the tenth day she was surprised to find herself beside a gallant prince in a richly-decorated room; at first she thought she was dreaming, but when the prince woke up, kissed her, and then told her the history of his life, she knew that it was real — 'Ah, me! God is wise!' The next morning she was crowned queen of her husband's happy subjects, whom she had restored from the enchantment of the wicked witch; every one in the kingdom loved his new queen as long as he lived.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 41 'The Enchanted Prince'; not verbatim.

title.en: The Prince's Dream: The Mirror of the King of the Demons
title.zh: 王子之夢：魔王之鏡

region.en: Tigaon, Camarines, Bicol region, Luzon, Philippines (narrator's home town)
region.zh: 菲律賓呂宋比科爾地區蒂高安（敘述者故鄉）

period: Bicol oral tale; collected by D. S. Fansler, published 1921

source.work: Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 42 'The Prince's Dream', eBook #8299

summary.en: A dream-ghost sends the prince to the city of Black, then home to his own cellar, where he finds diamond columns and a final chamber that 'none can unlock but the wealthiest Negro in the city of Black.' The Negro leads him through the sphinx-ferry and fire-gated walls to the king of the demons, who demands in exchange a woman 'whose heart is untainted by any worldly passion' — tested by an oval mirror that clouds at a false heart. The one pure girl is a poor farmer's daughter, whom the prince falls in love with on the road; the demon, unveiling the veiled figures in the final chamber, gives her to the prince — but keeps the diamond column.
summary.zh: 夢中幽靈引王子至『黑城』又折返自家地窖，尋得鑽石柱與最後密室——『唯黑城首富能開』。黑人引他渡獅身人面之舟、過雷火之門，謁見魔王；魔王索求一位『心無塵欲』的女子為酬——以一面照心的橢圓魔鏡驗之。純真的女子竟是貧農之女；王子途中愛上她。魔王揭開帷中人——竟將姑娘賜予王子，卻收回了鑽石柱。

sensitivity.note: Bicol tale recorded by Fansler from a Frondoso narrator (Tigaon, Camarines); archival record. Fansler notes (per Boas) that the story is from the Arabian Nights 'The Tale of Zayn Al-Asnam.'

passages.text: Once there lived a young prince who, after his father's death, succeeded to the throne as the sole heir of a vast, rich kingdom. He indulged himself in all worldly pleasures, gave dances, and all sorts of merry-making surrounded his court; meanwhile the royal treasury was being drained, and his subjects were becoming disloyal to him. Disappointed by his conduct, his counsellors plotted to dismiss him from the realm; the prince's mother, the widowed queen, learned of their plot and said to him, 'My son, I wish you would turn from your foolish trifling, and govern your people as you ought to do; for your advisers are planning to dethrone you.' The prince, who was not bad at heart, followed his mother's sensible advice, and his ministers gave up their plan.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 42 'The Prince's Dream'; not verbatim.

passages.text: One noon, when the prince was taking his siesta, he had a dream: a ghost appeared to him and spoke in this manner, 'Your father left a hidden treasure of gold and diamonds, which he forgot to mention in his will. Should you care to have that treasure, go to the city of Black. There you will find a Negro, the richest in that city, who will tell you all about the treasure.' 'Undeceive yourself,' said his mother. 'Never believe in dreams.' In spite of her words he set out disguised as a poor traveller; the gates were closed for the night, and while he slept outside the walls the very same ghost appeared to him: 'Go back to your palace, prince, and there in the cellar you will find the treasure I spoke of.' Early one morning, without the knowledge of his mother, he took a pointed iron bar and went down into the cellar, digging until his bar struck something hard which produced a metallic sound; he uncovered an iron platform locked with a padlock, and beneath it a low ladder made of diamond bars, leading down into a small apartment all shining bright as if it were day.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 42 'The Prince's Dream'; not verbatim.

passages.text: He found two columns of diamond bars, each a foot in thickness and a metre in height, whose brightness shot through all the corners like sunbeams; the subterranean chamber led to another with a big safe, from which gold coins flowed like water in torrents from a cliff. 'Are these gold coins and diamonds real, or am I simply dreaming?' — he filled his cap with the coins and went up into the sunlight to assure himself they were of pure gold. In a third chamber were two more columns of diamonds; in a fourth, behind a wide curtain of silk on which were embroidered in big golden letters the words: 'Inside this chamber is another column of diamonds twice as large and twice as high as those in the other two; none can unlock this apartment but the wealthiest Negro in the city of Black.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 42 'The Prince's Dream'; not verbatim.

passages.text: Disguised again as a poor traveller, the prince found the Negro, who received him kindly — and, hearing the prince's story, knelt down before him: 'My prince, I was the most beloved servant of your father. I acknowledge you as my master... There is but one man who can unlock it, who knows very well your dead father, and who was his friend... This man is the king of the demons. And to him we will go together.' They feasted, then journeyed to the palace of the king of the demons, crossing a river in a banca paddled by a sphinx and passing through two circular walls — at the knock of the first gate it became dark all around them, lightnings flashed, and it thundered; at the second gate two lions ran out with eyes glowing like balls of fire, ready to devour them — until, recognizing the Negro, these two kings of beasts wagged their tails as a sign of welcome. 'I gave that diamond column to your father as a gift which he might bequeath to his son; and if you are his son, you shall have it. But, before giving it to you, I should like to have you do me a favor in return for that rich gift. If you will bring me a very beautiful woman to be my companion, one whose heart is untainted by any worldly passion, I will unlock for you your wished-for treasure, the diamond room.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 42 'The Prince's Dream'; not verbatim.

passages.text: The king of the demons gave the prince a small oval mirror: 'If you see a beautiful woman, hold this mirror before her face. If the surface of the mirror becomes clouded, leave her; but if the surface of the mirror remains as clear as before, bring her to me, for she is the one I want for my comfort.' In three days they searched through three cities and three villages, but every girl that looked on the magic mirror clouded its surface — until, resting in a small village on their discouraged return, they found a most beautiful girl, the daughter of a poor farmer, whose looking on the mirror left its surface as clear as before. On the way the prince, fascinated by her beauty, fell in love with the girl, and did not want to give her up to the king of the demons; but the Negro would not consent, and the prince gave up his plan on condition that the girl's face be veiled. When they arrived at the palace, the king of the demons gladly met them: 'Now you have fulfilled my wish. You may go back to your palace, and there you will find the diamond apartment unlocked for you.' The sorrowing prince went home with heavy heart, no longer thinking of the treasure but of the beautiful maiden he had given up. Yet, to divert his mind, he went to the subterranean apartment, where he found the last chamber unlocked; inside were two veiled figures, the one in the form of a king with his sceptre and crown, the other a maiden. He unveiled the one with the crown and was astounded to find the very same king of the demons. 'Prince, unveil that figure,' said the king of the demons — and the young king did so, and to his great joy saw the beautiful maiden he had lost his heart to. 'Young king, since on your way to my palace you fell in love with this maiden, I deem it fit that you should have her for your companion; but do not expect the diamond column any more.' Then the king of the demons disappeared; the prince at once embraced the maiden and conducted her up to his palace, and that same day their marriage was celebrated with pomp and luxury.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 42 'The Prince's Dream'; not verbatim.

title.en: The Wicked Woman's Reward: The Corpse the Birds Would Not Give Up
title.zh: 惡婦的下場：群鳥護屍

region.en: Camarines, Bicol region, Luzon, Philippines (told by a father to his son)
region.zh: 菲律賓呂宋比科爾地區甘馬粦（父親講給兒子聽的故事）

period: Bicol oral tale; collected by D. S. Fansler, published 1921

source.work: Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 43 'The Wicked Woman's Reward', eBook #8299

summary.en: A jealous concubine smothers her own daughter, steals her rival's boy and puts a newborn cat in its place; the king drowns the accused mother without investigation and marries the thief. But the drowned woman's corpse floats fragrant down the river, covered by the birds with flowers — and when the king comes to see the miracle, the corpse rises and tells him of the theft before sinking away. He hurls the treacherous wife from the palace window, buries the innocent woman among the noble dead, and her son grows to rule the kingdom well.
summary.zh: 妒忌的侍妾悶死親女、竊走情敵之子，以新生的小貓掉包。國王未經查問便將被誣者沉河，並娶竊賊為妻。然而被溺女屍順流而飄，芳香撲鼻，群鳥啣花覆體——國王親臨觀奇，屍身忽起，泣訴冤情而後沉去。暴怒的國王將惡婦拋出窗外、懸屔示眾，以王禮厚葬無辜者；其子長成，治國有道。

sensitivity.note: Bicol tale recorded by Fansler from a Frondoso narrator (Camarines); archival record. Animal-substitution motif; Fansler knows no other versions of the story as a whole.

passages.text: Once there lived a certain king. He had concubines, five in number; two of them he loved more than the others, for they were to bear him children, and he said that the one who should give birth to a male baby he would marry. Soon one of them bore a child, but it was a girl, and shortly afterward the other bore a handsome boy. The one which had given birth to the baby girl was restless: she wished that she might have the boy, and in order to satisfy her wish thought of an ingenious plan whereby she might get possession of him.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 43 'The Wicked Woman's Reward'; not verbatim.

passages.text: One midnight, when all were sound asleep, she killed her own baby and secretly buried it; then she quietly crept to her rival's bed and stole her boy, putting in his place a newborn cat. Early in the morning the king went to the room of his concubine who had borne the boy, and was surprised to find a cat by her side instead of a human child; he was so enraged that he immediately ordered her to be drowned in the river, and his order was at once executed. Then he went into the room of the wicked woman: the moment he saw the boy baby he was filled with great joy, and he smothered the child with kisses; as he had promised, he married the woman, sent away all his other concubines, and harbored a deep love for his deceitful wife.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 43 'The Wicked Woman's Reward'; not verbatim.

passages.text: Soon afterwards there was a great confusion throughout the kingdom: everybody wondered why it was that the river smelled so fragrant, and the people were very anxious to find out the cause of the sweet odor. It was not many days before the townspeople along the river-bank found the corpse of the drowned woman floating in the water — and this was the source of the sweetness that was causing their restlessness; it was full of many different kinds of flowers which had been gathered by the birds. When the people attempted to remove the corpse from the water, the birds pecked them, and would not let the body be taken away. At last the news of the miracle was brought to the ears of the king, who himself went to the river to see the wonderful corpse; as soon as he saw the figure of the drowned woman, he was tortured with remorse — then, to his great surprise and fear, the corpse suddenly stood up out of the water, and said to him in sorrowful tones, 'O king! As you see, my body has been floating on the water. The birds would have buried me, but I wanted you to know that you ordered me to be killed without any investigation of my fault. Your wife stole my boy, and, as you saw, she put a cat by my side.' The ghost vanished, and the king saw the body float away again down the river.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 43 'The Wicked Woman's Reward'; not verbatim.

passages.text: The king at once ordered the body of his favorite to be taken out of the water and brought to the palace, and he himself was driven back to the town, violent with rage and remorse; there he seized his treacherous wife and hurled her out of the window of the palace, and he even ordered her body to be hanged. Having gotten rid of this evil woman, the king ordered the body of the innocent woman to be buried among the noble dead: the corpse was placed in a magnificent tomb, and was borne in a procession with pompous funeral ceremonies; he himself dressed entirely in black as a sign of his genuine grief for her. Yet, in spite of his sorrow for his true wife, he took comfort in her son, who grew to be a handsome boy; as time went on the prince developed into a brave youth, able to perform the duties of his father the king — so, as his father became old, no longer able to bear the responsibilities of regal power, the prince succeeded to the throne and ruled the kingdom well, proving himself to be the son of the good woman by his wise and just rule over his subjects.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 43 'The Wicked Woman's Reward'; not verbatim.

title.en: The Magic Ring: Carlos and the Goddess of the Sea
title.zh: 魔戒：卡洛斯與海之女神

region.en: Jaro, Iloilo, central Philippines (story very popular among the Visayans)
region.zh: 菲律賓怡朗省哈羅（故事甚為流行）

period: Visayan oral tale ('Ang Singsing nga Tantanang'); collected by D. S. Fansler, published 1921

source.work: Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 44 'The Magic Ring (Ang Singsing nga Tantanan)', eBook #8299

summary.en: Ashamed to beg, Carlos stands beneath the princess's window and is spat upon; his retort — that the Goddess of the Sea, star on forehead and moon on throat, would not dare — costs him his head unless she appears within a week. An eagle and the king of the fishes carry him to her golden house; she gives him her diamond ring — touch it thrice for her help, six times and she appears. When the whole court waits for the goddess, Carlos touches the ring six times and is saved; he marries Florentina, builds a chapel of gold, and his mother dies of happiness — though he never learns the meaning of his name.
summary.zh: 恥於行乞的卡洛斯立於公主窗下，竟被唾面；他反唇譏她不及『額有星、喉有月的海之女神』，遂以性命為注：一週內請不來女神便處絞。鷹王與魚王引他至女神金宮；女神贈鑽戒——叩三下得助，叩六下現身。滿朝引頸等待之時，卡洛斯六叩金戒，女神降臨，全場震懾。他娶得佛洛倫蒂娜，以黃金造禮拜堂，老母含笑而逝——唯其名字之義，至死未明。

sensitivity.note: Visayan folktale recorded by Fansler from a Gonzaga narrator (Jaro, Iloilo); archival record. Fansler knows no variants; the helpful animals lack the usual motivation.

passages.text: In the town of X, not far from the kingdom of Don Fernando, there lived an old religious woman named Carmen, who had a son named Carlos; she had been a widow since Carlos was nine months old, and was poor, poor even to raggedness. 'I have named you Carlos because I love you. For me, no name is prettier than yours. Every letter in it means something' — but when Carlos asked her to tell him the meaning of his name she said, 'I'll tell it to you later. First go to the king's palace, and there beg something for us to eat. O my son! If you only knew the miseries I have had to endure to bring you up, you would not refuse this request of your poor mother.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 44 'The Magic Ring'; not verbatim.

passages.text: Carlos pitied his mother very much, so he ran towards the king's palace to beg some food; but when he reached the gate he hesitated to enter, for he was ashamed to beg, and went and stood silently under the orange-tree which was not far from the princess's window. As Carlos was looking at the declining sun with tears in his eyes, the princess raised her window and unintentionally spit on his head.
