The August Grandchild left his heavenly rock-seat, clove his way with an awful path-cleaving through the eight-fold clouds of heaven, and descended on the Peak of Takachiho of So in Hiuga. He took his stand on a level part of the floating sand-bank, traversed the desert land of Sojishi from the Hill of Hitawo in search of a country, and came to Cape Kasasa in Ata-no-nagaya, where a man of that land, Koto-katsu-kuni-katsu Nagasa, told him there was a country and begged him to roam through it at his pleasure.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Nihongi, Book II §9 (trans. Aston 1896); not verbatim.

passages.text: Amaterasu gave the August Grandchild the three treasures, the curved jewel of Yasaka gem, the eight-hand mirror, and the sword Kusanagi, joining to him as attendants Ame no Koyane, first ancestor of the Nakatomi; Futo-dama, first ancestor of the Imibe; Ame no Uzume, first ancestor of the Sarume; Ishi-kori-dome, first ancestor of the mirror-makers; and Tamaya, first ancestor of the jewel-makers — gods of five Be. She commanded him: this Reed-plain-1500-autumns fair-rice-ear Land is the region which her descendants should be lords of; let him proceed thither and govern it, and may his dynasty, like heaven and earth, endure for ever. She also gave over to him the rice-ears of the sacred garden of which she partook in the Plain of High Heaven.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Nihongi, Book II §11–12 (trans. Aston 1896); not verbatim.

passages.text: Amaterasu took the precious mirror in her hand, gave it to Ame no Oshi-ho-mimi and uttered a prayer: my child, when thou lookest upon this mirror, let it be as if thou wert looking on me; let it be with thee on thy couch and in thy hall, a holy mirror. The Koyane and Futo-dama were commanded to guard it well. At the descent itself, one sent in advance returned and reported that at the eight-cross-roads of heaven dwelt a god the length of whose nose was seven hands and of whose back more than seven fathoms, with light shining from his mouth and posteriors, and eyeballs like an eight-hand mirror with a ruddy glow like the winter-cherry. None of the eighty-myriad deities dared confront him.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Nihongi, Book II §12–13 (trans. Aston 1896); not verbatim.

passages.text: So Uzume was specially commanded to question him, being superior in the power of her looks. She bared her breasts, pushed the band of her garment down below her navel, and confronted him with a mocking laugh. The god of the crossways asked what this behaviour meant; she replied by asking who he was to remain in the road by which the child of Amaterasu was to make his progress. He answered: hearing that the child of Amaterasu was about to descend, he had come respectfully to meet and attend upon him — his name was Saruta-hiko. Asked whether he would go before or she, he chose to go before and be the harbinger, directing the Grandchild to the Peak of Kushifuru of Takachiho and himself to the upper waters of the River Isuzu at Sanada in Ise. Uzume attended him, and for having discovered him received the designation Sarume no Kimi, from which the male and female Lords of Sarume were both styled Kimi.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Nihongi, Book II §13 (trans. Aston 1896); not verbatim.

title.en: Nihongi: Konohana-sakuya's Ordeal by Fire
title.zh: 日本書紀·木花咲耶姬火中產子

region.en: Cape Kasasa, Ata, in Hiuga (modern Kagoshima, Kyushu)
region.zh: 日向國阿多之笠沙岬(今鹿兒島)

period: Nihongi compiled 720 CE (trans. Aston 1896)

source.work: Nihongi: Chronicles of Japan from the Earliest Times to A.D. 697, Vol. I, trans. W. G. Aston (1896)

summary.en: At Cape Kasasa the August Grandchild Ninigi meets the fair maiden Konohana-sakuya, daughter of the mountain god Oho-yama-tsu-mi, and weds her after rejecting her elder sister Iha-naga — who curses the race of man to brief lives like the flowers of the trees. When Konohana conceives in one night, Ninigi doubts the child is his; she builds a doorless parturition hut, swears an ordeal by fire, sets it alight, and from the flames are born her three or four sons unharmed — including Hiko-hoho-demi, ancestor of the emperors.
summary.zh: 瓊瓊杵尊至笠沙岬,遇大山祇神之女木花咲耶姬,娶之;嫌其姊石長姬醜而退之,石長姬羞憤咒曰:若取吾則子孫壽如磐石,今唯娶妹,帝祚當如木花之易謝——此人命所以短也。木花咲耶姬一夜有孕,瓊瓊杵尊疑非己子;姬立無戶之產室,誓曰:若所懷非天孫之胤,願焚死;遂入室自焚,火中先後生火須勢理命、火明命、彥火火出見尊,母子皆無恙。

sensitivity.note: Ancient Japanese court myth (Nihongi, Book II); passages are condensed paraphrases of public-domain translations, presented for comparative mythology.

passages.text: After his descent the August Grandchild erected a palace-hall at Cape Kasasa, and walking afterwards by the sea-shore saw a beautiful woman, Kami-ataka-ashi-tsu-hime, also called Ko-no-hana-saku-ya-hime, daughter of the mountain god Oho-yama-tsu-mi. He asked her in marriage; her father sent his two daughters with a hundred tables of food and drink. The Grandchild thought the elder sister Iha-naga ugly and would not take her, but took the noted younger sister, who conceived in one night. Iha-naga was greatly ashamed and cursed him: had he taken her, the children born to him would have been long-lived, enduring like the massy rocks; but since he had married her sister only, the children born to him would be decadent like the flowers of the trees — and in one version she spat and wept that the race of visible mankind should change swiftly like the flowers of the trees and decay and pass away. This is the reason why the life of man is so short.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Nihongi, Book II §14–15 (trans. Aston 1896); not verbatim.

passages.text: Konohana-sakuya announced her pregnancy; the August Grandchild declared that though he was a heavenly deity, how could he cause any one to become with child in one night, and that the child in her bosom was assuredly not his. Wroth and ashamed, she made a doorless muro, a parturition-hut, and made a vow: if the child she had conceived were the offspring of another deity, might it assuredly be destroyed; but if it were truly the offspring of the Heavenly Grandchild, might it surely live unharmed. Then she entered the muro and set it on fire.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Nihongi, Book II §15 (trans. Aston 1896); not verbatim.

passages.text: When the flames first broke out, a child was born who was named Ho-no-susori; when the flame reached its height, a child was born named Ho-no-akari; and the next child born was Hiko-hoho-demi — three children in all, the fire failing to harm them and the mother unharmed. A variant writing has four sons who announce themselves from the fire, one at the first brightness, one at its height, one when the flames were becoming extinguished, and one as she recoiled from the heat; the mother came forth from the embers unscathed, and the Grandchild confessed that his mockery had been deliberate, to let every one know that a heavenly deity can cause pregnancy in one night. From the bamboo knife with which she cut their navel-strings there eventually sprang up a bamboo grove, and the place was called Takaya.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Nihongi, Book II §15–16 (trans. Aston 1896); not verbatim.

passages.text: Konohana-sakuya, by divination, fixed upon a rice-field which she named Sanada, and from the rice grown there brewed heavenly sweet sake with which she entertained the Grandchild — the mythic counterpart of the annual Nihi-name festival of first-fruits. A long time after, the August Grandchild died and was buried in the Misasagi of Hiuga-no-ye in Tsukushi, closing the story of the divine ancestor's earthly career.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Nihongi, Book II §16 (trans. Aston 1896); not verbatim.

title.en: Nihongi: Hohodemi and the Lost Fish-Hook at the Sea-God's Palace
title.zh: 日本書紀·彥火火出見失鉤與海神宮

region.en: Sea-palace of the Sea-God Toyotama-hiko (symbolic pin on the Hiuga coast, Kyushu)
region.zh: 海神豐玉毘古之宮(象徵定位:日向海岸)

period: Nihongi compiled 720 CE (trans. Aston 1896)

source.work: Nihongi: Chronicles of Japan from the Earliest Times to A.D. 697, Vol. I, trans. W. G. Aston (1896)

summary.en: Hiko-hoho-demi, who has a mountain-gift, trades talents with his sea-gifted elder brother Ho-no-susori and loses his brother's fish-hook. Grieving on the shore, he is sunk in a basket-boat to the Sea-God's crenellated palace, where he marries the Sea-God's daughter Toyotama-hime and lives three years; the lost hook is recovered from the mouth of the red tai, and the Sea-God sends him home with the tide-flowing and tide-ebbing jewels. With them he drowns and humbles his brother, whose descendants become the Hayato mimes of the imperial court.
summary.zh: 火須勢理命有海幸,彥火火出見尊有山幸;二兄易其利器,俱不得利。弟失兄之釣鉤,造新鉤數千不獲允;海濱悲泣,遇鹽椎老翁,編竹籃沉之海底,至海神之宮。綿津見神款待之,以女豐玉毘賣妻焉;三年後欲歸,海神於赤女(鯛)口中得鉤,授以潮滿珠、潮涸珠,教以咒鉤之辭。弟歸,以潮滿珠溺其兄,兄乃稱臣為俳優,子孫世為隼人,侍於皇宮。

sensitivity.note: Ancient Japanese court myth (Nihongi, Book II); passages are condensed paraphrases of public-domain translations, presented for comparative mythology.

passages.text: The elder brother Ho-no-susori had by nature a sea-gift, and the younger brother Hiko-hoho-demi a mountain-gift. They exchanged gifts for trial, but neither gained aught by it. The elder repented and demanded his fish-hook back; the younger had already lost it, made another, then forged thousands from his cross-sword and heaped them in a winnowing tray — all refused. His grief was profound; he went and made moan by the shore of the sea, where he met Shiho-tsutsu no Oji. The old man made a basket without interstices, placed him in it, and sank it in the sea. Hohodemi found himself at a pleasant strand and arrived suddenly at the palace of the Sea-God, provided with battlements and turrets and stately towers, with a well before the gate over which grew a many-branched cassia-tree.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Nihongi, Book II §29 (trans. Aston 1896); not verbatim.

passages.text: A beautiful woman came out from within, took a jewel-vessel, and was about to draw water when, raising her eyes, she saw him and was alarmed, returning to tell her father and mother of the rare stranger at the foot of the tree. The Sea-God prepared an eight-fold cushion and led him in, and heard all the circumstances from first to last. He assembled the fishes, both great and small, and required an answer of them; all knew not, only the Red-woman (the red tai) had had a sore mouth for some time past. She was summoned peremptorily, her mouth examined, and the lost hook was found. Then Hohodemi took the Sea-God's daughter Toyotama-hime to wife and dwelt in the sea-palace; for three years he enjoyed peace and pleasure, but still longed for his own country and sighed deeply from time to time.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Nihongi, Book II §30–31 (trans. Aston 1896); not verbatim.

passages.text: The Sea-God returned the hook with instructions: when giving it to the elder brother, first call to it secretly 'a poor hook', or in one version recite 'the origin of poverty, the beginning of starvation, the root of wretchedness', and in another spit thrice; and if the brother should cross the sea, the Sea-God would stir up the blasts and billows to overwhelm him. He gave also the jewel of the flowing tide and the jewel of the ebbing tide: dip the first and the tide shall drown the brother; dip the second and the tide shall ebb and save him — by harassing him thus the elder brother would of his own accord render submission. One writing adds advice about fields: if the elder brother makes high fields, the younger should make puddle fields, and conversely, so that the Sea-God might in all sincerity lend his aid.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Nihongi, Book II §31 (trans. Aston 1896); not verbatim.

passages.text: Back in his own palace, Hohodemi followed the god's instructions. The elder brother, in the utmost straits, of his own accord admitted his offence: henceforward he would be his subject to perform mimic dances — spare my life. In the fuller variant he is drowned thrice: the tide-flowing jewel submerges field, plain and mountain, and at the last he climbs a lofty tree and cries that his descendants for eighty generations shall serve as mimes in ordinary — one version has dog-men. In another, the younger brother stands on the sea-shore and whistles; a sudden tempest overwhelms the fishing fleet, and the elder brother, with nothing but his waistcloth, smears his face and palms with red earth, and, kicking up his feet, practises the manner of his drowning struggles: foot-divination when the tide reaches his feet, raised feet at his knees, circling at his thighs, hands on his breast, thrown-up hands at his neck. From that time until now this custom has never ceased, and the Hayato who guard the imperial palace serve instead of barking dogs.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Nihongi, Book II §32–34 (trans. Aston 1896); not verbatim.

title.en: Nihongi Variant: Toyotama-hime's Childbirth by the Sea
title.zh: 日本書紀異傳·豐玉毘賣臨海產子

region.en: Parturition-house on the shore of Hiuga (modern Miyazaki coast)
region.zh: 日向國海濱產室

period: Nihongi compiled 720 CE (trans. Aston 1896)

source.work: Nihongi: Chronicles of Japan from the Earliest Times to A.D. 697, Vol. I, trans. W. G. Aston (1896)

summary.en: The sea-born bride Toyotama-hime promises to come ashore in raging winds and waves, and begs Hohodemi to build her a parturition-house and not look upon her in travail. Unable to restrain himself, he peers in and sees her changed into a great sea-monster of eight fathoms; in shame she abandons the newborn, bars the sea-path, and departs — forfeiting the friendship between sea and land. The child, born before the cormorant-feather thatch was finished, is named Hiko-nagisa-take-u-gaya-fuki-ahezu, and is reared by his aunt Tama-yori-hime, whom he later marries: their sons include Kamu-yamato-ihare-biko, the future Emperor Jimmu.
summary.zh: 豐玉毘賣自誓:當以怒風怒浪之日來產,請造產室相待,臨蓐勿窺。彥火火出見尊不能忍,竊自窺之,則見其化為八尋大鰐,方蟠委而產。妃大慚,曰:本欲使海陸相通,永不睽隔;今既見辱,何以親睦?乃以葦纏兒置之渚,塞海途而返。兒因產室以鸕羽葺之未竟而生,名曰彥波瀲武鸕鶿草葺不合尊。後玉依毘賣育之,尊娶姨為妃,生四子,季子神日本磐余彥,即神武天皇之祖。

sensitivity.note: Ancient Japanese court myth (Nihongi, Book II); passages are condensed paraphrases of public-domain translations, presented for comparative mythology.

passages.text: When Hohodemi was about to return home, Toyotama-hime addressed him: thy handmaiden is already pregnant, and the time of her delivery is not far off; on a day when the winds and waves are raging, I will surely come forth to the sea-shore, and I pray thee make for me a parturition-house and await me there. She fulfilled her promise, bringing with her her younger sister Tama-yori-hime, and bravely confronting the winds and waves came to the sea-shore. When the time of her delivery was at hand she besought him: when thy handmaiden is in travail, do not look upon her. The Heavenly Grandchild could not restrain himself, but went secretly and peeped in.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Nihongi, Book II §33–34 (trans. Aston 1896); not verbatim.

passages.text: Toyotama-hime was just in childbirth, and had changed into a dragon — in another telling, into an enormous sea-monster of eight fathoms, wriggling about on her belly. Greatly ashamed, she said: hadst thou not disgraced me, I would have made the sea and land communicate with each other, and for ever prevented them from being sundered; but now that thou hast disgraced me, wherewithal shall friendly feelings be knit together? So she wrapped the infant in rushes and abandoned it on the sea-shore; then she barred the sea-path and passed away. Accordingly the child was called Hiko-nagisa-take-u-gaya-fuki-ahezu — because in one version the parturition-house by the sea-shore was thatched with cormorants' feathers and the child was born before the tiles had met.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Nihongi, Book II §34 (trans. Aston 1896); not verbatim.

passages.text: Variant writings supply the name more fully. In one, Hohodemi built the parturition-house of cormorants' feathers for thatch, and Toyotama-hime arrived riding on a great tortoise with her younger sister Tama-yori-hime, throwing a splendour over the sea; her months were already fulfilled, so she entered before the thatching was completed. Asked by what name the child ought to be called, she answered Hiko-nagisa-take-u-gaya-fuki-ahezu and departed straight across the sea. Another account has her withhold the child at first out of resentment, then send it back with Tama-yori-hime, having taken the coverlet of the true couch and rushes to wrap him in — and for this reason, it is said, there is no communication between land and sea. She later sent the verse of poetry of the island of wild-ducks, regretting the parting; the provisioning of wet-nurses, boiled-rice-chewers and washerwomen for the infant is given as the origin of the practice of engaging wet-nurses.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Nihongi, Book II §34–36 (trans. Aston 1896); not verbatim.

passages.text: Hiko-nagisa-take-u-gaya-fuki-ahezu took his aunt Tama-yori-hime as his consort, and had by her four male children: Hiko-itsu-se, Ina-ihi, Mi-ke-iri-no, and Kamu-yamato-ihare-biko — the youngest variously styled Sano in childhood, and, after he had cleared and subdued the realm, honoured with the title by which he is known as the first emperor. Long after, Hiko-nagisa died in the palace of the western country and was buried in the Misasagi on the top of Mount Ahira in Hiuga; his father Hohodemi before him had been buried on the summit of Mount Takaya.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Nihongi, Book II §38–39 (trans. Aston 1896); not verbatim.

title.en: Hwanung Descends to Mount Taebak
title.zh: 桓雄降於太白山

region.en: Myohyang-san, North Pyongan (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 妙香山，平安北道（象徵性定位）

period: Gojoseon annal tradition, recorded in Hulbert's History of Korea (1905); episode dated 2332 BC

source.work: Homer B. Hulbert, The History of Korea, Vol. 1 (1905), ch. 1, eBook #52127

summary.en: In the primeval ages the divine being Hwanin (Che-so, the Creator) permits his son Hwanung, weary of heaven, to descend and found a mundane kingdom. With three thousand spirit companions he alights on Mount Taebak, gathers his followers under an ancient pak-tal tree, proclaims himself King of the Universe, and governs through three viceregents: the Wind General, the Rain Governor, and the Cloud Teacher.
summary.zh: 太初之世，神人桓因（帝釋）允許其子桓雄厭倦天界、下凡建國。桓雄率三千從神降於太白山，聚眾神於古檀樹下，自稱天王，以風伯、雨師、雲師三輔臣治理天下。

sensitivity.note: Ancient chronicle tradition retold by a 1905 Western historian; no living-community restriction.

passages.text: In the primeval ages, so the story runs, there was a divine being named Whan-in, or Che-so, the Creator. His son, Whan-ung, being affected by a celestial weariness, obtained permission to descend to the earth and found a mundane kingdom.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Hulbert, History of Korea, Vol. 1, ch. 1 (1905); not verbatim.

passages.text: Armed with this warrant, Whan-ung with three thousand spirit companions descended upon Ta-bak Mountain, the mountain now known as Myo-hyang San in Pyongan Province. It was in the twenty-fifth year of the Emperor Yao of China, a date the annals set at 2332 BC.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Hulbert, History of Korea, Vol. 1, ch. 1 (1905); not verbatim.

passages.text: He gathered his spirit friends beneath the shade of an ancient sandalwood tree, and there proclaimed himself King of the Universe. He governed through his three vice-regents, the Wind General, the Rain Governor, and the Cloud Teacher; but as he had not yet taken human shape, he found it difficult to assume control of a purely human kingdom, and so searched for a means of incarnation.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Hulbert, History of Korea, Vol. 1, ch. 1 (1905); not verbatim.

title.en: Ungnyeo and the Breath of the Wind
title.zh: 熊女與風息成胎

region.en: Sandalwood hill, Myohyang-san (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 檀木山（象徵性定位）

period: Gojoseon annal tradition, recorded in Hulbert's History of Korea (1905); episode dated c. 2332 BC

source.work: Homer B. Hulbert, The History of Korea, Vol. 1 (1905), ch. 1, eBook #52127

summary.en: Having endured the cave ordeal and become a perfect woman, the bear Ungnyeo's first wish is motherhood, and she cries out for a son. Hwanung, the Spirit King, passing on the wind beholds her sitting beside the stream; he circles round her, breathes upon her, and her cry is answered. She cradles the babe in moss beneath the sandalwood tree.
summary.zh: 熊女忍過洞中苦行化為完美女子後，初願是為人母，呼求賜子。桓雄乘風而過，見其坐於溪畔，繞行其身，噓氣吹拂，其願得償。她將嬰兒安置於檀樹下的苔蘚中。

sensitivity.note: Ancient chronicle tradition; the conception-by-wind episode parallels Greek cloud-shaped unions (cf. Danae) and is tagged interpretively.

passages.text: At early dawn a tiger and a bear met upon the mountainside and held a colloquy: would that they might become men. Whan-ung overheard them, and a voice from the void bade each eat twenty garlics and a piece of artemisia and retire from the sun's light for thrice seven days. The tiger, fierce by nature, broke the restraint and came out early; the bear waited in faith and stepped forth a perfect woman.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Hulbert, History of Korea, Vol. 1, ch. 1 (1905); not verbatim.

passages.text: The first wish of the bear-woman's heart was maternity, and she cried, 'Give me a son.' Whan-ung, the Spirit King, passing on the wind, beheld her sitting beside the stream. He circled round her, breathed upon her, and her cry was answered. She cradled her babe in moss beneath that same sandalwood tree, and it was there that in after years the wild people of the country found the child sitting, and made him their king.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Hulbert, History of Korea, Vol. 1, ch. 1 (1905); not verbatim.

title.en: Dangun Teaches the Nine Wild Tribes
title.zh: 檀君教化九夷

region.en: Pyongyang, ancient Asadal (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 平壤古都（象徵性定位）

period: Gojoseon annal tradition, recorded in Hulbert's History of Korea (1905); episode dated c. 2333 BC

source.work: Homer B. Hulbert, The History of Korea, Vol. 1 (1905), ch. 1, eBook #52127

summary.en: The child found under the sandalwood tree, Dangun Wanggeom, Lord of the Pak-tal Tree, is made king over the nine wild tribes (Ku-i) who love drink, dancing and song. He teaches them the relation of king and subject, the rite of marriage, cooking, house-building, the binding of the hair, the cutting of trees and the tilling of fields, and makes Pyongyang his capital.
summary.zh: 檀樹下所生的檀君王儉（檀木之主）為九夷之首領。九夷嗜酒善歌舞，以草織為衣，穴居野處。檀君教以君臣之義、婚姻之禮、烹飪築室之術、束髮之俗、伐木墾田之法，並定都平壤。

sensitivity.note: Ancient chronicle tradition; no living-community restriction.

passages.text: The babe was the Tan-gun, the Lord of the Pak-tal Tree, also less widely known as Wang-gum. At that time the country was peopled by the nine wild tribes commonly called the Ku-i: the Kyun, Pang, Whang, Fak, Chuk, Hyun, P'ung, Yang and U.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Hulbert, History of Korea, Vol. 1, ch. 1 (1905); not verbatim.

passages.text: These aborigines were fond of drinking, dancing and singing. They dressed in woven grass and ate nuts, roots and berries; in summer they lived beneath the trees, in winter in a rudely covered hole in the ground. When the Tan-gun became their king he taught them the relation of king and subject, the rite of marriage, the art of cooking and the science of house-building. He taught them to bind up the hair with a cloth about the head, to cut down trees and to till fields. He made P'yung-yang the capital of his kingdom, and there tradition says he reigned until the coming of Ki-ja in 1122 BC.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Hulbert, History of Korea, Vol. 1, ch. 1 (1905); not verbatim.

title.en: Dangun Raises the Altar on Mari-san
title.zh: 檀君祭摩離山壇

region.en: Mari-san, Ganghwa Island (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 摩離山，江華島（象徵性定位）

period: Gojoseon annal tradition, recorded in Hulbert's History of Korea (1905); episode dated 2265 BC

source.work: Homer B. Hulbert, The History of Korea, Vol. 1 (1905), ch. 1, eBook #52127

summary.en: In 2265 BC Dangun offers the first sacrifice at Hyul-gu on the island of Kang-wha, building a stone altar on Mari-san that remains to this day. The people call it Tan-gun's Altar, or the Ch'am-sung Altar; nearby stands the Sam-nang fortress said to have been built by Dangun's three sons, and at Mun-wha a shrine honors the Korean trinity of Whan-in, Whan-ung and Tan-gun.
summary.zh: 公元前2265年，檀君首祭於江華島血谷，並在摩離山上築石壇，至今猶存。民稱之為檀君壇，又名朝天壇；鄰近峻德城相傳為檀君三子所築，牡室又有桓因、桓雄、檀君三聖祠。

sensitivity.note: Ancient chronicle tradition; the altar remains a site of modern veneration; presented as historical record.

passages.text: We learn that in 2265 BC the Tan-gun first offered sacrifice at Hyul-gu on the island of Kang-wha. For this purpose he built an altar on Mari San which remains to this day. On the top of Mari San is a stone platform or altar known as the Tan-gun's Altar, popularly believed to have been used by the Tan-gun four thousand years ago; it is called also the Ch'am-sung Altar. On Chun-dung San there is a fortress called Sam-nang, believed to have been built by the Tan-gun's three sons. At Mun-wha there is a shrine to the Korean trinity, Whan-in, Whan-ung and Tan-gun; and though the Tan-gun later resumed his spirit form, his grave is still shown at Kang-dong, four hundred and ten feet in circumference.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Hulbert, History of Korea, Vol. 1, ch. 1 (1905); not verbatim.

title.en: Dangun Retires to Kuwol-san and Becomes Spirit
title.zh: 檀君退隱不注山化神

region.en: Kuwol-san, Munwha, Hwanghae (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 不注山，黃海道月嶽（象徵性定位）

period: Gojoseon annal tradition, recorded in Hulbert's History of Korea (1905); episode dated 1122 BC

source.work: Homer B. Hulbert, The History of Korea, Vol. 1 (1905), ch. 1, eBook #52127

summary.en: Upon the arrival of the sage Ki-ja at Pyongyang, Dangun withdraws to Ku-wul San, the old Korean A-sa-dal, in present Mun-wha. There he resumes his spirit form and disappears forever from the earth, ending the Dangun line and clearing the way for the Ki-ja dynasty.
summary.zh: 箕子東來之際，檀君退隱於不注山（古稱阿斯達，在今黃海道牡室），復其神形，永離人間，檀君之世遂終，箕子朝鮮開端。

sensitivity.note: Ancient chronicle tradition; no living-community restriction.

passages.text: It is said that upon the arrival of Ki-ja, the Tan-gun retired to Ku-wul San, known in pure Korean as A-sa-dal, in the present town of Mun-wha in Whang-ha Province. There he resumed his spirit form and disappeared forever from the earth. His wife, tradition adds, was a woman of Pi-so-ap, whose location is unknown.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Hulbert, History of Korea, Vol. 1, ch. 1 (1905); not verbatim.

passages.text: The Tan-gun's kingdom is generally believed to have extended from Mun-gyung in the south to the Heuk-yong River in the north, and from the Japan Sea in the east to Yo-ha in the west; and the word Tan-gun, some think, refers to a line of native chieftains who antedated the coming of Ki-ja.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Hulbert, History of Korea, Vol. 1, ch. 1 (1905); not verbatim.

title.en: Dangun Sends Puru to the Court of the Great Yu
title.zh: 檀君遣夫婁聘大禹

region.en: To-san, China; Amur valley (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 塗山會盟，阿穆爾河谷（象徵性定位）

period: Gojoseon annal tradition, recorded in Hulbert's History of Korea (1905); episode dated 2187 BC

source.work: Homer B. Hulbert, The History of Korea, Vol. 1 (1905), ch. 1, eBook #52127

summary.en: When the great Ha-u-si (Yu the Great), who drained the waters covering the interior of China, summoned all vassal kings to his court at To-san, Dangun sent his son Puru as envoy. Another work affirms that when Ki-ja later came to Korea, Puru fled northward and founded the kingdom of North Pu-yu, which later moved and became Eastern Pu-yu.
summary.zh: 大禹疏九河、會諸侯於塗山時，檀君遣其子夫婁為使入貢。另一說謂箕子東來後，夫婁北走而建立北夫餘，後遷都為東夫餘。

sensitivity.note: Ancient chronicle tradition with conflicting dates; Hulbert himself flags the discrepancies.

passages.text: When the great Ha-u-si, who drained off the waters which covered the interior of China, called to his court at To-san all the vassal kings, the Tan-gun sent his son, Pu-ru, as an envoy. This was supposed to be in the year 2187 BC.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Hulbert, History of Korea, Vol. 1, ch. 1 (1905); not verbatim.

passages.text: Another work affirms that when Ki-ja came to Korea, Pu-ru fled northward and founded the kingdom of North Pu-yu, which at a later date moved to Ka-yup-wun and became Eastern Pu-yu. These stories show such enormous discrepancies in dates that they are alike incredible, and yet it may be that the latter story has some basis in fact; at any rate it gives us our only clue to the founding of the kingdom of Pu-yu.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Hulbert, History of Korea, Vol. 1, ch. 1 (1905); not verbatim.

title.en: P'ang-o, Warden of Roads and Waters
title.zh: 逄蒙治道水

region.en: U-su-ju, Chun-ch'un (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 牛首州，春川（象徵性定位）

period: Gojoseon annal tradition, recorded in Hulbert's History of Korea (1905); episode dated late Dangun dynasty

source.work: Homer B. Hulbert, The History of Korea, Vol. 1 (1905), ch. 1, eBook #52127

summary.en: Late in the Dangun dynasty a minister named P'ang-o holds special charge of road-making and drainage. One authority says the Emperor of China ordered P'ang-o to cut a road between the eastern tribe Ye-mak and Cho-sun; a stone tablet to P'ang-o stands at Ox-hair Town, the old U-su-ju near Chun-ch'un, whose Ox-head Plain still confirms the ancient name.
summary.zh: 檀君朝末年有大臣逄蒙，專司修路治水。一說中國天子命逄蒙開濊貊與朝鮮間之通道。春川古稱牛首州，今尚有牛頭坪，並立逄蒙石碑以紀其事。

sensitivity.note: Ancient chronicle tradition; no living-community restriction.

passages.text: Late in the Tan-gun dynasty there was a minister named P'ang-o who is said to have had as his special charge the making of roads and the care of drainage. One authority says that the Emperor of China ordered P'ang-o to cut a road between Ye-mak, an eastern tribe, and Cho-sun. From this we see that, according to some authorities, the word Cho-sun antedates the coming of Ki-ja. The town of Chun-ch'un, fifty miles east of Seoul, was known in this period as U-su-ju, Ox-hair Town, and a plot of ground there is still called the U-du-bol, Ox-head Plain, where a stone tablet to P'ang-o is erected.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Hulbert, History of Korea, Vol. 1, ch. 1 (1905); not verbatim.

title.en: Tal-geui the Nine-Tailed Fox
title.zh: 妲己九尾狐現形

region.en: Mountain cave, western peaks (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 西嶺山洞（象徵性定位）

period: Shang-dynasty legend carried in Korean annal tradition, recorded in Hulbert's History of Korea (1905); episode dated c. 1050 BC

source.work: Homer B. Hulbert, The History of Korea, Vol. 1 (1905), ch. 2, eBook #52127

summary.en: The emperor's concubine Tal-geui is so beautiful that whoever she smiles upon is enslaved. The statesman Pi-gan, suspecting a fox that has drunk from a twenty-year-old skull, has detectives track her to a mountain cave where foxes fawn upon her, and slays her kin. Robed in their white breast-fur, he unmasks her at court: when he dies by her demand, he curses her to resume her true form — a white fox with nine tails — and she leaps from the window and escapes.
summary.zh: 紂王寵姬妲己美艷無雙，笑則媚人。比干疑其為飲枯顱之水而得人形之狐，遣偵探跡其獨登之山洞，見群狐獻媚，遂盡誅之，剝其胸前白毛為裘。妲己知親族已死，以媚惑帝求剖比干之心以驗七竅；比干臨刑斥其現形，頃刻毛髮怒長，化為九尾白狐，破窗而遁。

sensitivity.note: The kumiho (nine-tailed fox) motif is one of Korea's defining folklore figures; tagged with the fox-woman transformation sense of 'transformation'.

passages.text: The concubine Tal-geui was wonderfully beautiful, but surpassingly so when she smiled. At such times the person upon whom she smiled was fascinated as by a serpent and forced to comply with whatever request she made. Pondering this, Pi-gan decided that she must be a fox in human shape, for it is well known that if an animal tastes of water that has lain twenty years in a human skull it acquires the power to assume human shape at will.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Hulbert, History of Korea, Vol. 1, ch. 2 (1905); not verbatim.

passages.text: Inquiries showed that monthly she ascended a certain mountain alone, leaving her attendants at the foot. Armed detectives followed her unseen and saw her enter a cave near the summit; she emerged accompanied by a pack of foxes who leaped and fawned upon her. When she left, the spies entered, put the foxes to the sword, and cut from each body the piece of white fur always found on the breast of the fox.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Hulbert, History of Korea, Vol. 1, ch. 2 (1905); not verbatim.

passages.text: When Tal-geui next met the emperor, dressed in a sumptuous white fur robe, she shuddered but did not guess the truth, until a month later, entering the cave, she beheld the festering remains of her kindred. Adorning herself in all her finery she exerted her fascination to the utmost, and when the net was well woven about the royal dupe she said: 'I hear there are seven orifices in the heart of every good man. I fain would put it to the test. I would see the heart of Pi-gan.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Hulbert, History of Korea, Vol. 1, ch. 2 (1905); not verbatim.

passages.text: As the executioner's knife was plunged into the victim's breast, Pi-gan cried: 'You are no woman; you are a fox in disguise, and I charge you to resume your natural shape.' Instantly hair sprang forth upon her face, her nails grew long, and bursting from her garments she stood revealed, a white fox with nine tails. With one parting snarl at the assembled court she leaped from the window and made good her escape.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Hulbert, History of Korea, Vol. 1, ch. 2 (1905); not verbatim.

title.en: Ki-ja and the Great-Law from the Tortoise
title.zh: 箕子洪範龜書

region.en: Nak River, China (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 洛水（象徵性定位）

period: Shang-Zhou legend carried in Korean annal tradition, recorded in Hulbert's History of Korea (1905); episode dated c. 1122 BC

source.work: Homer B. Hulbert, The History of Korea, Vol. 1 (1905), ch. 2, eBook #52127

summary.en: Before emigrating east, the imprisoned sage Ki-ja presents Emperor Mu-wang with the Hong-bum, the Great-Law, found long before inscribed on the back of a fabled tortoise that rose from the waters of the Nak River in the days of Ha-u-si — a text no one had been able to decipher until Ki-ja took it in hand. Then with five thousand followers he passes eastward into the peninsula.
summary.zh: 箕子囚於獄，武王釋之而求道。箕子乃以《洪範》獻王——相傳此大法初見於大禹時洛水神龜背上之文，千載無人能解，至箕子始通其義。遂率五千眾東渡朝鮮。

sensitivity.note: Legend of the Chinese classic Hongfan as transmitted in Korean historiography; no living-community restriction.

passages.text: Ki-ja, sole survivor of the great trio of statesmen, had saved his life only by feigning madness, and was now in prison; but Mu-wang came to his door and besought him to become Prime Minister. Loyalty to the fallen dynasty compelled him to refuse.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Hulbert, History of Korea, Vol. 1, ch. 2 (1905); not verbatim.

passages.text: He secured the Emperor's consent to his plan of emigrating to Cho-sun, but before setting out he presented the Emperor with that great work, the Hong-bum or Great-Law, which had been found inscribed upon the back of the fabled tortoise that came up out of the waters of the Nak River in the days of Ha-u-si over a thousand years before, and which no one had been able to decipher till Ki-ja took it in hand. Then with his five thousand followers he passed eastward into the peninsula of Korea, to found a kingdom that would last almost a thousand years.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Hulbert, History of Korea, Vol. 1, ch. 2 (1905); not verbatim.

title.en: Ki-ja Plants a Kingdom of Five Thousand
title.zh: 箕子五千東遷建國

region.en: Pyongyang (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 平壤（象徵性定位）

period: Ki-ja Choson legend, recorded in Hulbert's History of Korea (1905); episode dated 1122 BC

source.work: Homer B. Hulbert, The History of Korea, Vol. 1 (1905), ch. 2, eBook #52127

summary.en: Ki-ja settles at Pyongyang, the old Dangun capital, bringing the principles of history and poetry, the sciences of manners, music, medicine and incantation, and teachers of a hundred useful trades. His short penal code matches crime to punishment; a clay broad-brim hat keeps quarrelsome males at arm's length; the well-field system yields a ninth of the harvest; and willows planted along the Ta-dong give the city a name of peace.
summary.zh: 箕子都平壤，率五千移民，攜詩書之教、禮樂醫巫之學、百工之技。立法簡嚴：殺人者償、爭訟者罰穀、盜者沒為奴而可贖。又製陶冠以杜鬥毆，行井田九一之貢，沿大同江植柳萬株，民呼其水為朝鮮之黃河。

sensitivity.note: Ki-ja (Jizi) founding is a historiographic legend, contested by modern scholarship; recorded here as myth-history.

passages.text: In whatever way he came, Ki-ja finally settled at the town of P'yung-yang which had already been the capital of the Tan-gun dynasty. He found the country semi-barbarous, and the reforms he instituted give abundant evidence of his genius. His penal code was short: murder was punished with death inflicted in the same manner as the crime; brawling was punished by a fine paid in grain; theft was punished by enslaving the offender, who could regain freedom by a heavy fine. To prevent quarrelling, it is said, he compelled all males to wear a broad-brimmed hat of clay pasted on a framework; if the hat was doffed or broken the offender was severely punished, which kept the men at arm's length.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Hulbert, History of Korea, Vol. 1, ch. 2 (1905); not verbatim.

passages.text: He picked men from the various districts, trained them in the duties of government, reduced the language of the people to writing, and taught the arts and sciences he had brought. All arable land was divided into squares of nine parts; whoever cultivated the eight surrounding squares must also till the central one for the government, which received a ninth of the produce. Prosperity was seen on every side, and the people called the Ta-dong River the Yellow River of Korea.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Hulbert, History of Korea, Vol. 1, ch. 2 (1905); not verbatim.

title.en: Ki-ja Weeps in the Barley Field
title.zh: 箕子麥秀歌

region.en: Ruins of the Shang capital, China (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 殷墟（象徵性定位）

period: Zhou-era elegy tradition, recorded in Hulbert's History of Korea (1905); episode dated c. 1120 BC

source.work: Homer B. Hulbert, The History of Korea, Vol. 1 (1905), ch. 2, eBook #52127

summary.en: Though made King of Cho-sun without vassalage, Ki-ja is permitted to send envoys to worship at the tombs of the fallen Shang. He visits the site of the ancient capital himself, finds it sown with barley, and weeps, composing an elegy on the spot before going on to swear allegiance to the new emperor — an act the Cho-so history calls his weakness, for he had sworn never to do so.
summary.zh: 武王封箕子於朝鮮而不臣。箕子嘗遣使祭殷墓，又親往殷墟，見宮室毀壞、生禾黍，悲而作《麥秀歌》，後乃朝周。史稱此為其弱點，蓋曾誓不仕周也。

sensitivity.note: Classic Chinese elegy tradition (Maixiu ge) embedded in Korean annals; no living-community restriction.

passages.text: From the very first Korea was an independent kingdom, for though Emperor Mu-wang made Ki-ja King of Cho-sun he neither demanded nor received his allegiance as vassal, and even allowed Ki-ja to send envoys to worship at the tombs of the fallen dynasty.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Hulbert, History of Korea, Vol. 1, ch. 2 (1905); not verbatim.

passages.text: It is said that Ki-ja himself visited the site of the ancient Shang capital, but when he found it sown with barley he wept and composed an elegy on the occasion, after which he went and swore allegiance to the new Emperor.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Hulbert, History of Korea, Vol. 1, ch. 2 (1905); not verbatim.

passages.text: The work entitled Cho-so says that he mounted a white cart drawn by a white horse and went to the new capital and swore allegiance; and it adds that in this he showed his weakness, for he had sworn never to do so.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Hulbert, History of Korea, Vol. 1, ch. 2 (1905); not verbatim.

title.en: The Luminous Egg of Hyokkose
title.zh: 赫居世日光卵

region.en: Kyongju, Silla capital (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 新羅都城慶州（象徵性定位）

period: Silla founding legend from Korean annals, recorded in Hulbert's History of Korea (1905); episode dated 57 BC

source.work: Homer B. Hulbert, The History of Korea, Vol. 1 (1905), ch. 6, eBook #52127

summary.en: The chiefs of six Chin-han states meet and merge their fiefs into a kingdom with its capital Su-ya-bul, near modern Kyongju. On the mountainside revellers behold a ball of light on which a white horse stands grazing; as they approach, the horse rises into the air and vanishes, leaving a great luminous egg. It opens of itself and discloses a handsome boy, amid vivid light and thunder, who is set on the throne as Hyokkose.
summary.zh: 辰韓六部酋長會盟，併為一國，都於徐耶伐（今慶州）。會中有眾見山上白光如月，中有白馬伏跪；眾近之，馬凌空而沒，餘一大卵。俄而卵自開，出一俊秀男嬰，光芒燦然，雷聲震地。眾立為王，是為朴赫居世。

sensitivity.note: Silla dynastic founding legend; no living-community restriction.

passages.text: In the year 57 BC the chiefs of the six great Chin-han states held a great council and agreed to merge their separate fiefs into a kingdom. They named the capital of the new kingdom Su-ya-bul, whence the present word Seoul is probably derived, and it was situated where Kyong-ju now stands.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Hulbert, History of Korea, Vol. 1, ch. 6 (1905); not verbatim.

passages.text: They placed upon the throne a boy of thirteen years named Hyuk-ku-se with the royal title Ku-se-gan. The story of his advent is typically Korean: a company of revellers beheld upon a mountainside a ball of light on which a horse was seated. As they approached, the horse rose straight into the air and disappeared, leaving a great luminous egg. This soon opened of itself and disclosed a handsome boy, the wonder accompanied by vivid light and the noise of thunder.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Hulbert, History of Korea, Vol. 1, ch. 6 (1905); not verbatim.

title.en: Alyong, the Bird-Bill Bride of the Spring
title.zh: 閼英鳥喙井邊女

region.en: Nan-yong Spring, Kyongju (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 南泉井，慶州（象徵性定位）

period: Silla founding legend from Korean annals, recorded in Hulbert's History of Korea (1905); episode dated 53 BC

source.work: Homer B. Hulbert, The History of Korea, Vol. 1 (1905), ch. 6 & 7, eBook #52127

summary.en: Beside the Yun-yung Spring a hen raises her wing and from her side comes forth a female child with a mouth like a bird's bill; washed in the spring, the bill falls off and she becomes like other children, so the well is named Pal-ch'un, the Falling of the Bill. In the fifth year of his reign the boy-king Hyokkose espouses her, and Koreans see in them the perfect marriage; when he dies she follows him within seven days, so completely were they one.
summary.zh: 閼英井（雲慶井）畔有雞開翼，自肋下出一女嬰，喙如鳥嘴；浴於井水而喙落，乃如常兒，井因名泊蓮（喙落）。赫居世王五年迎娶之，國人視為夫婦之範。王薨七日，后亦隨逝，若不能獨存者。

sensitivity.note: Silla dynastic legend; 'resurrection' tagged loosely for the joint-death motif, interpretively.

passages.text: Not long after the wonder of the luminous egg another was seen. Beside the Yun-yung Spring a hen raised her wing, and from her side came forth a female child with a mouth like a bird's bill; but when they washed her in the spring the bill fell off and left her like other children. For this reason the well was named the Pal-ch'un, which refers to the falling of the bill.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Hulbert, History of Korea, Vol. 1, ch. 6 (1905); not verbatim.

passages.text: Another tradition says that she was formed from the rib of a dragon which inhabited the spring. In the fifth year of his reign the youthful king espoused this girl, and they typify to all Koreans the perfect marriage. In 4 AD Hyuk-ku-se, the wise king of Sil-la, died, and seven days later his queen followed him. It is said that they were so completely one that neither could live without the other. Nam-ha his son built a shrine to his father and reigned in his stead.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Hulbert, History of Korea, Vol. 1, ch. 6 (1905); not verbatim. / Paraphrase of Hulbert, History of Korea, Vol. 1, ch. 7 (1905); not verbatim.

title.en: The Golden Frog under the Boulder
title.zh: 金蛙出石

region.en: Forest stream, North Buyeo (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 北夫餘林溪（象徵性定位）

period: Buyeo origin legend from Korean annals, recorded in Hulbert's History of Korea (1905); episode dated c. 50 BC

source.work: Homer B. Hulbert, The History of Korea, Vol. 1 (1905), ch. 6, eBook #52127

summary.en: King Ha-bu-ru of North Pu-yu grieves that Providence has given him no son. Riding in the forest he prays to the Great Spirit at a rushing stream; his horse stands with bowed head before a great boulder, tears rolling down its face. He turns the boulder over and finds beneath it a child of the color of gold in the form of a toad, and names him Keum-wa, Golden Toad. Soon after, the kingdom removes to East Pu-yu, near Paektu Mountain.
summary.zh: 北夫餘王解夫婁無子，乘馬獵於林，至急流之畔祈天求嗣。馬低首立於巨石之前，淚落如雨。王翻其石，得金色蛙形之兒，乃名金蛙。未幾國遷於東夫餘，近白頭山之地。

sensitivity.note: Buyeo dynastic legend; no living-community restriction.

passages.text: It must have been about fifty years before the beginning of our era that King Ha-bu-ru sat upon the throne of North Pu-yu. His great sorrow was that Providence had not given him a son. Riding one day in the forest he reached the bank of a swift rushing stream, and there dismounting he besought the Great Spirit to grant him a son. Turning to remount, he found the horse standing with bowed head before a great boulder while tears were rolling down its face. He turned the boulder over and found beneath it a child of the color of gold, with a form resembling a toad. Thus was his prayer answered. He took the curious child home and gave it the name Keum-wa, Golden Toad. Soon after this the kingdom removed to East Pu-yu, near the White Head Mountain, known as Pak-tu San.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Hulbert, History of Korea, Vol. 1, ch. 6 (1905); not verbatim.

title.en: Jumong Outwits the Royal Stables
title.zh: 朱蒙瘦馬奇計

region.en: East Buyeo royal stables (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 東夫餘王廄（象徵性定位）

period: Goguryeo founding cycle from Korean annals, recorded in Hulbert's History of Korea (1905); episode dated c. 40 BC

source.work: Homer B. Hulbert, The History of Korea, Vol. 1 (1905), ch. 6, eBook #52127

summary.en: The egg-born archer boy Chu-mong is no favorite at court, and his rivals seek his death; the king makes him keeper of the royal stables. Like Jacob of Holy Writ he turns wits to the situation: by fattening the poorer horses and starving the good ones he reserves the fleetest steeds for himself, so that in every hunt he leads the rout and secures the lion's share of the game — and earns the mortal hatred of his seven brothers.
summary.zh: 卵生神箭童子朱蒙不見喜於宮中，仇家欲害之；王乃命其掌王廄。彼如雅各弄智，故意肥劣馬而瘦良馬，暗留駿足自乘，故每獵必先馳而多獲。七兄弟由此恨之入骨，共謀殺之。

sensitivity.note: Goguryeo dynastic legend; no living-community restriction.

passages.text: The egg at last burst and disclosed a fine boy. This precocious youth at seven years of age was so expert with the bow that he won the name of Chu-mong, the Skillful Archer. He was not a favorite with the people, and they tried to compass his death; but the king protected him and made him keeper of the royal stables. Like Jacob of Holy Writ he brought his wits to bear upon the situation: by fattening the poorer horses and making the good ones lean, he succeeded in reserving for his own use the fleetest steeds.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Hulbert, History of Korea, Vol. 1, ch. 6 (1905); not verbatim.

passages.text: Thus in the hunt he always led the rout and secured the lion's share of the game. For this his seven brothers hated him and determined upon his death; by night his mother sought his bedside and whispered the word of warning.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Hulbert, History of Korea, Vol. 1, ch. 6 (1905); not verbatim.

title.en: Yuri and the Broken Sword-Blade
title.zh: 類利剖柱得刀

region.en: Buyeo marketplace (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 夫餘市井（象徵性定位）

period: Goguryeo founding cycle from Korean annals, recorded in Hulbert's History of Korea (1905); episode dated c. 19 BC

source.work: Homer B. Hulbert, The History of Korea, Vol. 1 (1905), ch. 6, eBook #52127

summary.en: When Chu-mong fled south he left behind a wife and son, Yuri. Playing with pebbles in the street, Yuri breaks a woman's water jar; her taunt — you are a child without a father — drives the boy to seek a knife for self-destruction before his mother reveals the truth: his father is a great king in the south, who hid a token under a tree. Wearied by searching, Yuri sits in despair until he hears a picking sound from a house post; digging beneath it he unearths half a broken blade, carries it south, and when the halves match, his father proclaims him heir.
summary.zh: 朱蒙南奔，留妻與子類利。類利戲於市以礫石，誤碎汲者水甕；婦人怒斥：『無父之子！』類利慚欲自裁，母乃告以實情：父為南方大王，去時留信物於樹下。類利遍尋不獲，倦極坐於屋後，忽聞柱中有剝啄之聲，曰：『此樹也！』掘柱下得斷劍之半。負劍南下，父子各持其半，合之而吻合，遂立為儲君。

sensitivity.note: Token-recognition episode parallels wide-spread broken-token heirship tales; tagged interpretively.

passages.text: When Chu-mong fled southward from Pu-yu he left behind him a wife and son, the latter named Yu-ri. Tradition says that one day while playing with pebbles in the street he accidentally broke a woman's water jar. In anger she exclaimed, 'You are a child without a father.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Hulbert, History of Korea, Vol. 1, ch. 6 (1905); not verbatim.

passages.text: The boy went sadly home and asked his mother if it was true. She answered yes, to see what the boy would do. He went out and found a knife and was on the point of plunging it into his body when she threw herself upon him, saying: 'Your father is living and is a great king in the south. Before he left he hid a token under a tree, which you are to find and take to him.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Hulbert, History of Korea, Vol. 1, ch. 6 (1905); not verbatim.

passages.text: The boy searched everywhere but could not find the tree. At last, wearied out, he sat down behind the house in despair, when suddenly he heard a sound as of picking, coming from one of the posts of the house, and said, 'This is the tree, and I shall now find the token.' Digging beneath the post he unearthed the broken blade of a sword.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Hulbert, History of Korea, Vol. 1, ch. 6 (1905); not verbatim.

passages.text: With this he started south, and when he reached his father's palace he showed the token. His father produced the other half of the broken blade, and as the two matched he received the boy and proclaimed him heir to the throne.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Hulbert, History of Korea, Vol. 1, ch. 6 (1905); not verbatim.

title.en: Onjo and Biryu Found Baekje
title.zh: 溫祚百濟開國

region.en: Han River valley, Chik-san (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 漢江流域，稷山（象徵性定位）

period: Baekje founding legend from Korean annals, recorded in Hulbert's History of Korea (1905); episode dated 18 BC

source.work: Homer B. Hulbert, The History of Korea, Vol. 1 (1905), ch. 6, eBook #52127

summary.en: When Yuri appears as heir, Chu-mong's younger sons Biryu and Onjo flee southward. Ascending Sam-gak San behind Seoul they survey the land: Biryu chooses the western coast at Mi-ch'u-hol, Onjo goes directly south to Chik-san, where the king of Ma-han grants him land. Biryu finds his settlement sterile and unhealthy and rejoins his brother, then dies of chagrin at his failure; Onjo sets up the little kingdom of South Pu-yu, which history knows as Paek-je.
summary.zh: 類利立為儲，朱蒙別子沸流、溫祚懼而南奔。登首爾背後之三角山，望野而議：沸流取海濱彌鄒忽之地，溫祚南徑至稷山。馬韓王賜溫祚膏腴之地，遂建小國，號南夫餘。沸流所居地瘠氣惡，乃復歸其弟，旋因愧恨而卒。國名百濟，或謂始名十濟，後以眾增而改。

sensitivity.note: Baekje dynastic founding legend; no living-community restriction.

passages.text: Yu-ri had two half-brothers, Pi-ryu and On-jo, sons of a wife Chu-mong had taken more recently. When Yu-ri appeared on the scene these two brothers, knowing how proverbially unsafe the head of a king's relative is, feared for their lives and fled southward.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Hulbert, History of Korea, Vol. 1, ch. 6 (1905); not verbatim.

passages.text: Ascending Sam-gak San, the mountain immediately behind the present Seoul, they surveyed the country southward. Pi-ryu the elder chose the country along the sea, settling at Mi-ch'u-hol, now In-ch'un; On-jo struck southward into what is now Ch'ung-ch'ung Province and settled at Eui-rye-sung, now the district of Chik-san. There he was given a generous tract of land by the king of Ma-han, and set up a little kingdom which he named South Pu-yu.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Hulbert, History of Korea, Vol. 1, ch. 6 (1905); not verbatim.

passages.text: The origin of the name Paek-je is not definitely known. Some say it was because a hundred men constituted the whole of On-jo's party; others say it was at first called Sip-je, and changed to Paek-je when the numbers were swelled by Pi-ryu's party. The latter had found the land sterile and the climate unhealthy at Mi-ch'u-hol, and so was constrained to join his brother again. Not long after he rejoined him he died of chagrin at his own failure.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Hulbert, History of Korea, Vol. 1, ch. 6 (1905); not verbatim.

title.en: The Autumn Gathering in the Susin Cave
title.zh: 神穴秋祭

region.en: Susin cave, east-coast mountains (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 神穴，嶺東山間（象徵性定位）

period: Ethnographic tradition on Goguryeo rites, recorded in Hulbert's History of Korea (1905); describing customs of the early centuries AD

source.work: Homer B. Hulbert, The History of Korea, Vol. 1 (1905), ch. 6, eBook #52127

summary.en: The worship of spirits is universal among the people of Ko-gu-ryu. Every autumn a great religious festival gathers the tribes in the eastern part of the peninsula at a famous cave called Su-sin, where singing and drinking fill the night — and at the same time the captives are set free.
summary.zh: 高句麗之俗，舉國事神。歲秋大祭，嶺東部族會於神穴，歌飲連宵，並縱囚徒以祓不祥。

sensitivity.note: Ethnographic record of Goguryeo religious customs; no living-community restriction.

passages.text: The worship of spirits was universal among the people of Ko-gu-ryu. In the autumn there was a great religious festival. In the eastern part of the peninsula there was a famous cave called Su-sin where a great religious gathering occurred each autumn. Their religious rites included singing and drinking, and at the same time captives were set free.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Hulbert, History of Korea, Vol. 1, ch. 6 (1905); not verbatim.

title.en: The Bullock Slain for Omens before Battle
title.zh: 戰前屠牛占兆

region.en: Goguryeo war camp (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 高句麗軍營（象徵性定位）

period: Ethnographic tradition on Goguryeo rites, recorded in Hulbert's History of Korea (1905); describing customs of the early centuries AD

source.work: Homer B. Hulbert, The History of Korea, Vol. 1 (1905), ch. 6, eBook #52127

summary.en: On the eve of battle the men of Ko-gu-ryu slaughter a bullock and examine its body for omens, reading the fate of the coming fight in the carcass before they march.
summary.zh: 高句麗人臨戰，必屠牛祭神，驗其臟腑以觀吉凶，然後進兵。

sensitivity.note: Ethnographic record of Goguryeo divination customs; no living-community restriction.

passages.text: The worship of spirits was universal among the people of Ko-gu-ryu, and their religious rites included singing, drinking, and the freeing of captives at the autumn festival. They worshipped likewise on the eve of battle, slaughtering a bullock and examining the body for omens, reading the fate of the coming contest in the carcass before they marched.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Hulbert, History of Korea, Vol. 1, ch. 6 (1905); not verbatim.

title.en: The Escaped Pig that Found a Capital
title.zh: 逐豬得都

region.en: Kung-na district, near Ch'o-san (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 骨乃，楚山附近（象徵性定位）

period: Goguryeo annal tradition, recorded in Hulbert's History of Korea (1905); episode dated AD 2

source.work: Homer B. Hulbert, The History of Korea, Vol. 1 (1905), ch. 7, eBook #52127

summary.en: The king of Ko-gu-ryu is about to sacrifice a pig to his gods when the animal escapes and is chased by the courtier Sul-chi into the district of Kung-na. Catching it near Wi-na Cliff, Sul-chi returns and describes the place as rough, rich in deer, fish and turtles, and therefore suited for a capital. The king moves his court there, and the city remains the capital for two hundred and six years.
summary.zh: 高句麗王將祭神，豕忽逸去，臣燧追至骨乃界、威那崖畔而獲之。歸述其地山川險阻、麋鹿魚鱉甚眾，宜為國都。王遂遷都於彼，凡二百零六年。

sensitivity.note: Goguryeo annal anecdote; no living-community restriction.

passages.text: We read that in 2 AD the king of Ko-gu-ryu was about to sacrifice a pig to his gods, when the pig escaped and, taking to its heels, was chased by the courtier Sul-chi into the district of Kung-na. He caught the animal near Wi-na Cliff, north of the Ch'o-san of today.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Hulbert, History of Korea, Vol. 1, ch. 7 (1905); not verbatim.

passages.text: When he returned he described the place to the king as being rough and consequently suitable for the site of a capital; deer, fish and turtles also abounded there. He gave such a glowing account that the king moved his capital to that place, where it remained for two hundred and six years.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Hulbert, History of Korea, Vol. 1, ch. 7 (1905); not verbatim.

title.en: Seok Talhae, the Egg that Drifted across the Japan Sea
title.zh: 昔脫解浮卵渡海

region.en: A-jin Harbor, Silla coast (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 阿珍浦，新羅海濱（象徵性定位）

period: Silla annal legend, recorded in Hulbert's History of Korea (1905); episode dated early first century AD

source.work: Homer B. Hulbert, The History of Korea, Vol. 1 (1905), ch. 7, eBook #52127

summary.en: In the kingdom of Ta-p'a-ra in northeastern Japan a woman pregnant for seven years brings forth an egg. The neighbors think it an omen and would destroy it, but the mother wraps it in silk and cotton, sets it in a strong chest and commits it to the Japan Sea. The chest drifts to A-jin Harbor on the Silla coast, where an old fisherwoman draws it ashore and finds a beautiful child. Magpies follow the boy in flocks wherever he goes, giving him the name Suk, from the word for magpie, with Tal for 'to put off' from the egg and Ha for the fishwife who opened the chest. The child becomes a giant in body and mind, enters the service of the statesman Pyo-gong, marries the king's daughter and becomes vicegerent of Silla.
summary.zh: 東方旦伐羅國有孕七歲之婦，產一卵。鄰人以為不祥將毀之，母乃以繒裹卵納諸櫝，投於海中。櫝浮至新羅阿珍浦，老嫗取而剖之，得一兒。兒行處，喜鵲隨而翔集，故名鵲（昔）；脫者，出卵也；解者，嫗剖櫝也。兒長成魁偉多智，事大臣瓢公，尚王女，遂為新羅執政。

sensitivity.note: Silla dynastic legend; no living-community restriction.

passages.text: Somewhere in north-eastern Japan there was a kingdom known as Ta-p'a-ra, and there a woman, pregnant for seven years, brought forth an egg. The neighbors thought it a bad omen and were minded to destroy it, but the mother, aware of their intentions, wrapped the egg in silk and cotton and, placing it in a strong chest, committed it to the waters of the Japan Sea.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Hulbert, History of Korea, Vol. 1, ch. 7 (1905); not verbatim.

passages.text: In time it drifted to A-jin Harbor on the coast of Sil-la, where an old fisherwoman drew it ashore and found upon opening it a beautiful child. She adopted him and reared him in her humble home. It was noticed that wherever the child went the magpies followed him in flocks, so they gave him the name of Suk, the first part of the Chinese word for magpie; Tal means 'to put off', for his having broken forth from the egg, and Ha means 'to open', for the fishwife opened the chest.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Hulbert, History of Korea, Vol. 1, ch. 7 (1905); not verbatim.

passages.text: The boy developed into a giant both physically and mentally. His foster-mother gave him what education she could afford and then sent him to enter the service of the great statesman Pyo-gong, who recognized his merit and introduced him at court. His rise was so rapid that he married the king's daughter and became vicegerent of the realm, the king resigning into his hands the greater part of the business of state.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Hulbert, History of Korea, Vol. 1, ch. 7 (1905); not verbatim.

title.en: Kyon-mo-ju Weds the Being from the Sky
title.zh: 伽倻山神感天婚

region.en: Ka-ya Mountain (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 伽倻山（象徵性定位）

period: Gaya founding legend, recorded in Hulbert's History of Korea (1905); episode dated legendary antiquity

source.work: Homer B. Hulbert, The History of Korea, Vol. 1 (1905), ch. 7, eBook #52127

summary.en: Of the five Gaya states subject to Ka-rak, the founder of one is known: he was descended from Kyon-mo-ju, the female divinity of Ka-ya Mountain, who wedded the celestial being Yi-ja-ga. Their offspring, Yi-i-a-si, founded one of the Gaya states — a union of mountain goddess and sky being at the root of a polity.
summary.zh: 加羅所屬五伽倻，其一之祖可考：乃伽倻山女神己慕主與天人夷刀伽所生。其子悅己斯遂建一伽倻之國，山神天人之合，遂啟一方之業。

sensitivity.note: Gaya dynastic legend; no living-community restriction.

passages.text: Ka-rak had five dependencies, the districts known under the common name of Ka-ya. Of these Ka-ya states we know the founder of only one. He was descended from Kyon-mo-ju, the female divinity of Ka-ya Mountain, who wedded a celestial being, Yi-ja-ga. Their offspring, Yi-i-a-si, founded one of the Ka-ya states.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Hulbert, History of Korea, Vol. 1, ch. 7 (1905); not verbatim.

title.en: The Serpent of Su-ro's Grave
title.zh: 首露墓蛇誅盜

region.en: Su-ro's tomb, Kim-hae (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 首露王陵，金海（象徵性定位）

period: Gaya legend recorded in Korean annals, cited in Hulbert's History of Korea (1905); episode dated 935 and later

source.work: Homer B. Hulbert, The History of Korea, Vol. 1 (1905), ch. 7, eBook #52127

summary.en: When Silla falls in 935, worthless wretches defile the grave of Keum Su-ro, founder of Ka-rak — and are mysteriously killed, one by a falling beam, one by an invisible archer, and nine others by a serpent eighteen feet long. Three centuries later Japanese invaders who open the same tomb find vast store of gold and jade, a skull of prodigious size, and beside the body two women whose features are preserved but dissolve when exposed to the air.
summary.zh: 新羅亡時（935年），有匪徒盜掘駕洛國始祖首露王陵，旋遭橫死：一為梁壓，一為無形弓矢所射，餘九人皆為十八尺大蛇所噬。三百年後日軍再掘其墓，得金玉甚富，王顱異常巨大，屍側二女面貌如生，見風而化。

sensitivity.note: Tomb-guardian-serpent legend; 'resurrection' tagged loosely for the incorrupt-dead motif; interpretively.

passages.text: It is also affirmed that when Sil-la fell in 935, some worthless wretches who defiled the grave of Keum Su-ro were mysteriously killed, one by the falling of a beam, one by an invisible archer, and nine others by a serpent eighteen feet long.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Hulbert, History of Korea, Vol. 1, ch. 7 (1905); not verbatim.

passages.text: The records say that when the Japanese, at the time of the great invasion three centuries ago, dug open this king's grave, they found great store of gold and jade. The skull of the monarch was of prodigious size, and beside his body lay two women whose features were well preserved but which dissolved and melted away when exposed to the air.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Hulbert, History of Korea, Vol. 1, ch. 7 (1905); not verbatim.

title.en: The Council in Darkness: Earth Spoken into Being
title.zh: 黑暗中的議會：大地由言語而成

region.en: Q'umarkaj (Utatlan), K'iche' highlands, Guatemala (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 危地馬拉高地庫馬爾卡赫（烏塔特蘭）（象徵性定位）

period: K'iche' text written c. 1554-78; Ximenez transcription c. 1701-03

source.work: Popol Wuj (K'iche' text c. 1554-78; transcription by Francisco Ximenez c. 1701-03), French ed. Brasseur de Bourbourg, 1861

license: Public domain (Brasseur 1861 French edition); modern translations only paraphrased

summary.en: Before the world there is only sea, sky, and the gods gathered in darkness. The Framer, the Shaper, Sovereign Plumed Serpent, and Heart of Sky confer, and by merely speaking and thinking — agreeing on the ripening of the dawn — they raise the earth out of the water: mountains rise, valleys open, and the forests bring forth life.
summary.zh: 世界之前只有海洋、天空與在黑暗中聚合的諸神。塑造者、羽蛇主宰與天之心相商，僅憑言語與思想——就黎明的成熟達成一致——便將大地自水中升起：山巒隆起，谷地張開，森林萌發生命。

sensitivity.note: Living K'iche' tradition; the Popol Wuj is treated by some Maya communities as sacred counsel. Only published translations are paraphrased; no restricted or unpublished ceremonial text is reproduced.

passages.text: There is not yet one person, one animal, bird, fish, crab, tree, rock, hollow, canyon, meadow, or forest. Alone, the sky exists. The face of the earth has not appeared. There is only the sea's calm expanse and the expanse of heaven. Nothing has been brought together, nothing has been raised. The beach, the sea and the sky are the only things there are; nothing has gathered, only stillness, only silence, only night, only the lonely expanse.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Popol Wuj, Part 1 opening (Brasseur 1861; Tedlock 1996); not verbatim.

passages.text: Then the Framer and the Shaper, the Sovereign and Quetzal Serpent, the Bearer and Begetter, and Heart of Sky — Hurricane, Newborn Thunderbolt, Sudden Thunderbolt — come together and speak the ripening of the dawn in the darkness, in the night. They confer, ponder, and reflect, and what they agree upon is spoken: the earth rises like a cloud from the middle of the sea. Mountains appear from the water at once, and the valleys and ravines push apart; the cypresses and pines shoot forth on the ridges, and the meadows, vines, and bushes bloom.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Popol Wuj, Part 1 (Brasseur 1861; Tedlock 1996); not verbatim.

passages.text: The Sovereign Plumed Serpent and Heart of Sky ask what has happened, and it is told: the earth has been raised, as it should be. The gods call it 'earth' in the gathering of light and shadow, of night and dawn. And the Framer and Shaper say: it was merely their word alone that brought it forth — no stone had been laid, no tree planted; by their thought alone the earth stood fast. This is the first sign of the place of the horizon where the dawn will come.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Popol Wuj, Part 1 (Brasseur 1861; Christenson 2003); not verbatim.

canonical_translation: Brasseur de Bourbourg, Popol Vuh (French, 1861); Dennis Tedlock, Popol Vuh, rev. ed. 1996

narrative.en:
The Popol Wuj opens with a cosmogony of pure speech. Before anything exists there is only stillness: the calm sea and the empty sky, night alone, and the gods assembled within it — the Framer and the Shaper, the Bearer and the Begetter, Hunahpu Pos, Hunahpu Utiu, the Sovereign and Quetzal Serpent (the great plumed serpent couple), the Heart of Lake, the Heart of Sea, and above all Heart of Sky, whose three aspects are Hurricane, Newborn Thunderbolt, and Sudden Thunderbolt, the trinity of storm gods who speak as one voice.

The gods talk together, think, and meditate upon the appearance of light, upon the dawn, upon what will need to exist for the people to be nourished. There is nothing yet: no person, no beast, no bird, no fish, no tree, no stone, no canyon, no meadow. Then comes the essential gesture of Maya creation: they agree on it in their minds, and they speak it. Merely by word and thought the earth is born. It rises like a cloud or like a mist from the sea; mountains come forth out of the water immediately and stand apart; the cypresses, pines, and gullies of the ridges shoot forth; the meadows and the vines and the bushes grow green. The Framer and the Shaper call it 'earth' in the presence of the sky, in the gathering of night and dawn.

Then Heart of Sky and Sovereign Plumed Serpent converse about the newly made earth. 'It has been raised,' they say; 'the earth is there, as it truly is.' They add the horizon: they make the small cords of light and shadow and the measures of night and dawn, and they mark the place of the horizon where the dawn will appear. Creation here is not a battle between cosmic opponents (as in Babylon or Norse myth) but a council: power flows from consensus, from a speech act ratified by every divine will present. This reflects the Maya political world, where authority required the agreement of councils and where words — oaths, day-names, prayers — carried causal weight.

The episode grounds everything that follows: the creations of animals, of mud and wood and maize people, are successive attempts to finish what this council began. Its ritual function is to authorize speech itself: what is said in agreement among the governing lines will stand, as the earth stood when the gods said 'earth'.

functions: Explains the origin of the earth as a speech act of divine council, authorizing councils and speech in K'iche' political life
Establishes Heart of Sky (Hurricane trio) as the storm triad that later floods the failed creations
Sets the horizon and the count of night and dawn, founding calendrical time

variants.name: Cakchiquel opening of the Annals
variants.summary: The Cakchiquel account likewise begins in darkness and the word: 'there was nothing yet, only the sea and the sky', and the creation proceeds from speech among the gods at Tulan before the crossing of the waters.

variants.name: Yucatec Chilam Balam creation
variants.text_tradition: Book of Chilam Balam of Chumayel (Roys trans. 1933)

title.en: The Daykeepers Divine the Creation
title.zh: 日守者占問造世

region.en: Q'umarkaj (Utatlan), K'iche' highlands, Guatemala (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 危地馬拉高地庫馬爾卡赫（烏塔特蘭）（象徵性定位）

period: K'iche' text written c. 1554-78; Ximenez transcription c. 1701-03

source.work: Popol Wuj, Part 1, French ed. Brasseur de Bourbourg, 1861

license: Public domain (Brasseur 1861 French edition); modern translations only paraphrased

summary.en: After the earth is raised, the grandmother Xmucane and the grandfather Xpiyacoc — the divine matchmakers and daykeepers — cast the corn kernels and the days to learn whether the world should be made. Their divination is itself a thing of the primordial night: asking the days before asking the gods.
summary.zh: 大地升起後，祖母徐穆坎與祖父希皮亞科克——神聖的媒合者與日守者——擲玉米粒與日名，以知世界是否應造。此占問本身即是太初黑夜中的事物：先問日子，再問神明。

sensitivity.note: Living K'iche' divinatory tradition; paraphrase of published translation only.

passages.text: Then Xmucane and Xpiyacoc, named as matchmakers, are called: grandmother of day, grandmother of light. The two of them speak in council about what should be done, and they divine: they sort the days and the corn kernels, casting them to see whether the making of the earth and the sky is a thing to be done or not done. This was the first divination, made while the world was still young, when the days themselves were newborn.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Popol Wuj, Part 1 (Brasseur 1861; Tedlock 1996); not verbatim.

passages.text: The two daykeepers throw the kernels in fours, on the right and the left, reading the day signs that answer. It is the day itself that speaks to them in the throw, and they listen: the sign falls in the direction that shows the earth should be formed, and the forming of it is good. So the answer comes not as thunder but as a pattern of grains and day names — the same count that every later daykeeper of the K'iche' would consult before naming a child or planting a field.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Popol Wuj, Part 1 (Brasseur 1861; Tedlock 1996); not verbatim.

title.en: The Animals Are Made and Condemned
title.zh: 獸類受造而受譴

region.en: Q'umarkaj (Utatlan), K'iche' highlands, Guatemala (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 危地馬拉高地庫馬爾卡赫（烏塔特蘭）（象徵性定位）

period: K'iche' text written c. 1554-78; Ximenez transcription c. 1701-03

source.work: Popol Wuj, Part 1, French ed. Brasseur de Bourbourg, 1861

license: Public domain (Brasseur 1861 French edition); modern translations only paraphrased

summary.en: Heart of Sky and the Plumed Serpent fashion the deer, birds, jaguars, and serpents and assign each its home and its food. But the animals can only squawk and howl — they cannot speak the names of their makers — so their flesh is sentenced to be caught and killed. Their speechlessness founds the human privilege of language and the eating of meat.
summary.zh: 天之心與羽蛇塑造鹿、鳥、美洲豹與蛇，並為其各定居所與食物。然而獸類只能鳴叫嘶吼——無法呼其造物者之名——故其肉身被判為可捕可食。獸之無言，奠基了人的語言特權與食肉之權。

sensitivity.note: Paraphrase of published translation; no living-community restriction.

passages.text: Heart of Sky speaks to the Sovereign Plumed Serpent: the dawn has come, but the earth is empty of persons, of creatures that would tend it. So they make the animals of the mountains: the deer and the birds alone first, and they say to the deer, 'you shall walk in fours' — thus their legs — and to the birds, 'you shall live in the branches of the trees and in the vines.' Then the greater animals: jaguars, coyotes, peccaries, and serpents, each given its own den and its own way of feeding.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Popol Wuj, Part 1 (Brasseur 1861; Tedlock 1996); not verbatim.

passages.text: But when the gods ask the animals to speak, to name their makers and pray to them, the animals can only squawk, chatter, and howl. They manage no words, each merely its own call. So the gods speak their sentence: 'You will be changed, because you could not make yourselves understood. Your flesh will be ground and eaten.' Thus it was settled that deer and birds would be caught and killed, and that their meat would feed those who could speak.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Popol Wuj, Part 1 (Brasseur 1861; Tedlock 1996); not verbatim.

passages.text: The animals look for the rising of the sun, and they do not find it; they do not know where it will come from. This is why they are silent in the count of days: they have names for places but no words of praise. Having failed in speech, they are failed in turn, and they go to their mountains and their canyons, the homes assigned to them at the beginning.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Popol Wuj, Part 1 (Brasseur 1861; Christenson 2003); not verbatim.

title.en: The Mud People That Would Not Hold
title.zh: 不成形的泥人

region.en: Q'umarkaj (Utatlan), K'iche' highlands, Guatemala (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 危地馬拉高地庫馬爾卡赫（烏塔特蘭）（象徵性定位）

period: K'iche' text written c. 1554-78; Ximenez transcription c. 1701-03

source.work: Popol Wuj, Part 1, French ed. Brasseur de Bourbourg, 1861

license: Public domain (Brasseur 1861 French edition); modern translations only paraphrased

summary.en: The gods' first human figures are shaped of wet earth, but they crumble and dissolve: they cannot turn their heads, walk, or hold a shape. They are undone by water and left unfinished, the first failed attempt at humankind before wood and then maize.
summary.zh: 諸神最初以濕土塑人形，但泥人崩解消融：不能轉頭、行走，也無法保持形狀。他們被水所毀，成為造人未竟的第一次失敗——其後才有木人與玉米人。

sensitivity.note: Paraphrase of published translation; no living-community restriction.

passages.text: The gods speak again: 'Let us make one who will nourish and sustain us.' Then they try a figure of earth, mud, wet clay. It is molded and given a face, but it cannot move of itself; it cannot turn its head; it slides apart and collapses as if in water. Its strength dissolves, its face slumps; it cannot walk, and it cannot multiply.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Popol Wuj, Part 1 (Brasseur 1861; Tedlock 1996); not verbatim.

passages.text: The Framer and the Shaper look at the mud people and speak among themselves: this is not what should be. The thing is lopsided and soft, without strength either to stand or to speak. So they take it apart and wash the earth away, and the first attempt is undone — the mud people are spoken of no more, except as the memory of a failure in the materials of the world.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Popol Wuj, Part 1 (Brasseur 1861; Christenson 2003); not verbatim.

title.en: The Hearthstones Bite: Tools Revolt Against the Wood People
title.zh: 灶石反噬：器物起而攻木人

region.en: Q'umarkaj (Utatlan), K'iche' highlands, Guatemala (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 危地馬拉高地庫馬爾卡赫（烏塔特蘭）（象徵性定位）

period: K'iche' text written c. 1554-78; Ximenez transcription c. 1701-03

source.work: Popol Wuj, Part 1, French ed. Brasseur de Bourbourg, 1861

license: Public domain (Brasseur 1861 French edition); modern translations only paraphrased

summary.en: When Heart of Sky destroys the wooden people with resinous rain, their own household implements rise against them: the grinding stones, cooking pots, dogs, and hearthstones that had been abused now gnash and bite, speaking the vengeance of tools. The survivors climb into the trees and become monkeys.
summary.zh: 天之心以松脂之雨毀滅木人時，其家中器物紛紛起而攻之：被虐待的石磨、陶鍋、狗與灶石出聲反擊，道出器物的復仇。倖存者攀樹而逃，化為猴子。

sensitivity.note: Paraphrase of published translation; no living-community restriction.

passages.text: Then Heart of Sky blows a wind of resin through the sky, and a black rain falls day and night. The wooden people run everywhere, seeking shelter, but the shelters do not want them. The grinding stones say: 'You have beaten us and ground us without mercy; now it is our turn.' The cooking pots and cups answer: 'You have burned us over the fire and scraped us; now you will feel our teeth.' The dogs and the turkeys cry out and bite the faces of their masters.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Popol Wuj, Part 1 (Brasseur 1861; Tedlock 1996); not verbatim.

passages.text: The hearthstones themselves — the three stones of the fireplace — rise up and throw themselves out of the fire at the wooden people, and the tortilla griddles spin at their heads. All of them flee to their houses, but the houses collapse, to the trees, but the trees shake them off, to the caves, but the caves shut before them. Only a few get away up high, and these become the monkeys in the trees, which is why the monkeys look like the shape of a person — a parody of humanity left over from the third creation.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Popol Wuj, Part 1 (Brasseur 1861; Tedlock 1996); not verbatim.

title.en: Seven Macaw, the False Sun
title.zh: 七鸚鵡，偽日

region.en: Q'umarkaj (Utatlan), K'iche' highlands, Guatemala (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 危地馬拉高地庫馬爾卡赫（烏塔特蘭）（象徵性定位）

period: K'iche' text written c. 1554-78; Ximenez transcription c. 1701-03

source.work: Popol Wuj, Part 1, French ed. Brasseur de Bourbourg, 1861

license: Public domain (Brasseur 1861 French edition); modern translations only paraphrased

summary.en: Between the failed creations and the true dawn, Vucub Caquix, Seven Macaw, boasts in a nance tree: 'I am the sun, I am the moon, I am the light of the world.' His glittering metal teeth and eyes dazzle the survivors of the flood, and the world is lit only by his vanity until two boys come with a blowgun.
summary.zh: 在失敗的創造與真正的黎明之間，武庫布·卡魁希（七鸚鵡）於南美櫻桃樹上自誇：「我是太陽、月亮、世界之光。」其金屬牙齒與眼珠光耀炫目，炫惑洪水倖存者；直至兩個男孩持吹箭而來，世界只由其虛榮照明。

sensitivity.note: Paraphrase of published translation; no living-community restriction.

passages.text: This was when there was still no sun: Vucub Caquix would climb his nance tree and cry out: 'I am great! My place is higher than the human. I am their sun and their moon, and my light shines on the whole world. I am the guide for those who walk. My beak of metal shines; my teeth glitter with jewels. I am the eyes of the earth.' And the glitter of his mouth was so great that it cast a light over the earth, and everyone looked up at him in the dark before the true dawn.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Popol Wuj, Part 1 (Brasseur 1861; Tedlock 1996); not verbatim.

passages.text: But he was not the sun, only a bird swollen with pride, his mouth and eyes of chipped metal that the gods destined for the grave. Heart of Sky speaks of him with anger: this one is not right; he would be a sun and a moon by vanity alone. And the two boys, Hunahpu and Xbalanque, are told to bring him down, for the true dawn must not be preceded by a counterfeit.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Popol Wuj, Part 1 (Brasseur 1861; Tedlock 1996); not verbatim.

title.en: The Twins Shoot Seven Macaw and Take His Teeth
title.zh: 雙子射七鸚鵡而取其牙
