title.en: Aroni, the One-Legged Master of Forest Herbs
title.zh: 阿羅尼——獨腿林中藥師

region.en: Yoruba forest fastness (symbolic pin: deep forest near Ile-Ife)
region.zh: 約魯巴深林（象徵定位：伊費近郊密林深處）

period: Yoruba oral tradition; recorded 1894 (Ellis)

source.work: A. B. Ellis, The Yoruba-speaking Peoples of the Slave Coast of West Africa (London, 1894), ch. III

summary.en: Aroni, the forest-god, has one leg, a dog's head and a dog's tail, and knows all medicine. Those who meet him and run are devoured; those who stand their ground are led two or three months into the depths of the forest and taught the secrets of the plants — then dismissed with a single hair from his tail as proof of initiation. A whirlwind swirling the dead leaves is his manifestation.
summary.zh: 森林之神阿羅尼一目一腿，狗首犬尾，通曉百藥。林中遇他而逃跑者，必被吞噬；昂然而立、面無懼色者，則被引至林中秘所兩三個月，學盡草木藥性，臨別得他尾上一毛以為憑證。林間捲起枯葉的旋風，正是他現身之兆。

sensitivity.note: Living Yoruba tradition; herbalist-initiation figure recorded 1894. Presented as archival record.

passages.text: Aroni is the Forest-god, and, like Osanhin, the god of medicine, has a knowledge of medicine, though the cure of disease is not his special function. The name means One having a withered limb, and Aroni is always represented as of human shape but with only one leg, the head of a dog, and a dog's tail.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ellis, The Yoruba-speaking Peoples, ch. III (1894); not verbatim.

passages.text: Aroni seizes and devours those who meet him in the forest and attempt to run away when they see him; but if a man faces him boldly and shows no sign of fear, he leads him to his dwelling in the fastnesses of the forest, and keeps him there for two or three months, during which time he teaches him the secrets of the plants and their medicinal properties. When the pupil has no more to learn Aroni dismisses him, giving him a hair from his tail to prove to the incredulous that he has really been initiated. An eddy of wind, rushing through the forest and swirling up the dead leaves, is considered a manifestation of Aroni.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ellis, The Yoruba-speaking Peoples, ch. III (1894); not verbatim.

title.en: Aja, the Foot-High Teacher of Herbs
title.zh: 阿賈——一尺高的采藥之師

region.en: Yoruba forest (symbolic pin: vine thicket near Ile-Ife)
region.zh: 約魯巴森林（象徵定位：伊費近郊藤叢）

period: Yoruba oral tradition; recorded 1894 (Ellis)

source.work: A. B. Ellis, The Yoruba-speaking Peoples of the Slave Coast of West Africa (London, 1894), ch. III

summary.en: Aja, a deity like Aroni but smaller than a child of two feet, carries off those who meet her into the depths of the forest and teaches them the medicinal properties of plants — but she never harms anyone. The aja vine that shares her name is used by women to cure inflamed breasts.
summary.zh: 阿賈是一位類似阿羅尼的神祇，身高不過一二尺。遇見她的人會被帶入森林深處，學習草木的藥性——但她從不傷人。與她同名的阿賈藤，至今仍為婦女醫治乳腺腫痛之藥。

sensitivity.note: Living Yoruba tradition; gentle forest-teacher deity recorded 1894.

passages.text: Aja, whose name appears to mean a wild vine, is a deity somewhat similar to Aroni. Like Aroni, she carries off persons who meet her into the depths of the forest, and teaches them the medicinal properties of plants; but she never harms anyone. Aja is of human shape, but very diminutive, she being only from one to two feet high. The aja vine is used by women to cure inflamed breasts.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ellis, The Yoruba-speaking Peoples, ch. III (1894); not verbatim.

title.en: Oye, the Giant of the Harmattan
title.zh: 奧耶——哈馬丹風的巨人

region.en: North of Ilorin, Nigeria (the cavern whence the dry wind blows)
region.zh: 奈及利亞伊洛林以北（乾風所出的巨洞）

period: Yoruba oral tradition; recorded 1894 (Ellis)

source.work: A. B. Ellis, The Yoruba-speaking Peoples of the Slave Coast of West Africa (London, 1894), ch. III

summary.en: Oye, the god of the Harmattan wind, is a giant who, according to some, lives in a cavern to the north of Ilorin, while others say he resides on the mountain named Igbeti, where Elegba is supposed to have his palace.
summary.zh: 哈馬丹風之神奧耶是位巨人。一說他住在伊洛林以北的巨洞中，另一說他棲於伊格貝蒂山——那裡也是艾萊格巴傳說中的宮殿所在。

sensitivity.note: Living Yoruba tradition; wind-deity fragment recorded 1894.

passages.text: Oye, the god of the Harmattan wind, is a giant who, according to some, lives in a cavern to the north of Ilorin, while others say that he resides on the mountain named Igbeti, where Elegba is supposed to have his palace.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ellis, The Yoruba-speaking Peoples, ch. III (1894); not verbatim.

title.en: Ibeji: Keeping the Lost Twin Among the Living
title.zh: 伊貝吉——讓逝去的雙生留在人間

region.en: Erapo, Nigeria (symbolic pin: twin shrine on the Lagos-Badagry lagoon)
region.zh: 奈及利亞埃拉波（象徵定位：拉哥斯至巴達格利間潟湖的雙生神廟）

period: Yoruba oral tradition; recorded 1894 (Ellis)

source.work: A. B. Ellis, The Yoruba-speaking Peoples of the Slave Coast of West Africa (London, 1894), ch. III

summary.en: Ibeji, the tutelary deity of twins, has for sacred animal a small black mangrove monkey that twins and their parents may not eat. When one of twins dies, the mother carries a small wooden figure of the dead child beside the surviving one — to keep the living child from pining and to give the departed spirit a dwelling that will not disturb its twin. At Erapo stands a celebrated temple of Ibeji, whither twins and their parents make pilgrimage from far around.
summary.zh: 伊貝吉是雙生子之守護神，聖獸為紅樹林中的小黑猴，雙生子及其父母不得食其肉。孿生之一夭折時，母親便雕一具小木偶隨存活的孩子隨身攜帶——既免活著的孩子思念成疾，也給亡靈一個居所，免擾同胞。埃拉波的伊貝吉大廟遠近聞名，雙生子與其父母千里朝聖。

sensitivity.note: Living Yoruba tradition; Ibeji twin-cult (ere-ibeji figures) is a world-renowned living practice. The Yoruba Ibeji is the key African parallel in the twins motif cluster (cf. maya-popol-vuh-creation-twins, Romulus and Remus). Cross-refs: maya-popol-vuh-creation-twins.

passages.text: Ibeji, Twins, is the tutelary deity of twins. A small black monkey, generally found amongst mangrove trees, is sacred to Ibeji; offerings of fruit are made to it, and its flesh may not be eaten by twins or the parents of twins. This monkey is called Edon dudu, or Edun, and one of twin children is generally named after it.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ellis, The Yoruba-speaking Peoples, ch. III (1894); not verbatim.

passages.text: When one of twins dies, the mother carries, with the surviving child, a small wooden figure seven or eight inches long, roughly fashioned in human shape and of the sex of the dead child, to keep it from pining for its lost comrade and also to give the spirit of the deceased child something to enter without disturbing the living child. Such figures are nude, as an infant would be, with beads round the waist. At Erapo, a village on the lagoon between Lagos and Badagry, there is a celebrated temple to Ibeji, to which all twins, and the parents of twins, from a long distance round make pilgrimages.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ellis, The Yoruba-speaking Peoples, ch. III (1894); not verbatim.

title.en: Oshumare, the Rainbow-Serpent of the Underneath
title.zh: 奧舒馬雷——地底彩虹巨蛇

region.en: Yoruba country (symbolic pin: rainbow arching above the earth's rim, near Ile-Ife)
region.zh: 約魯巴地方（象徵定位：伊費附近天際虹弧）

period: Yoruba oral tradition; recorded 1894 (Ellis)

source.work: A. B. Ellis, The Yoruba-speaking Peoples of the Slave Coast of West Africa (London, 1894), ch. III

summary.en: Oshumare is the Rainbow-god, the Great Snake of the Underneath, who comes up at times above the edge of the earth to drink water from the sky; the python called ere is his sacred messenger. By some accounts he serves Shango, carrying water from the earth up to the thunderer's palace in the clouds.
summary.zh: 彩虹之神奧舒馬雷是「地底的大蛇」，不時升至大地邊緣之上，仰首飲天。大蟒「埃雷」為其聖使。又一說他是尚戈的僕役，專司把地上之水運上雲中雷宮。

sensitivity.note: Living Yoruba tradition; rainbow-serpent parallel (cf. Australian Rainbow Serpent) noted by comparativists; tagged to the world-serpent motif cluster as an interpretive act. Cross-refs: norse-world-serpent-midgard.

passages.text: Oshumare is the Rainbow-god, the Great Snake of the Underneath, who comes up at times above the edge of the earth to drink water from the sky. A variety of the python, called by the Yorubas ere, is the messenger of the rainbow-god, and is sacred to him. According to some natives, Oshumare, the Rainbow, is the servant of Shango, his office being to take up water from the earth to the palace in the clouds.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ellis, The Yoruba-speaking Peoples, ch. III (1894); not verbatim.

title.en: Oke and the Self-Sealing Cavern of Abeokuta
title.zh: 奧凱與阿貝奧庫塔的自閉石洞

region.en: Abeokuta, Nigeria (the rocky cavern of the mountain god)
region.zh: 奈及利亞阿貝奧庫塔（山神岩洞）

period: Yoruba oral tradition; recorded 1894 (Ellis)

source.work: A. B. Ellis, The Yoruba-speaking Peoples of the Slave Coast of West Africa (London, 1894), ch. III

summary.en: Oke, the god of mountains, rolls down boulders and sweeps landslips on the forgetful; a falling rock is always his handiwork and a sign that something is required. At Abeokuta a rocky cavern is his shrine, and the other tribes believe that when the Egbas are defeated in war they can retire into it, which then hermetically seals itself until the danger is past.
summary.zh: 山神奧凱若遭怠慢，便滾石砸屋、土崩掩舍；落石從來都是他的手筆，也是「該有所奉獻」的警示。阿貝奧庫塔有一處岩洞即其聖所；別族相傳，埃格巴人戰敗時可退入洞中，洞門自合，封閉至險情過去。

sensitivity.note: Living Yoruba tradition; Abeokuta (founded 1830 as a war refuge) literally means under-the-rock; the cavern legend explains the city's own name.

passages.text: Oke, mountain, or hill, is the god of Mountains, and is worshipped by those who live in mountainous or rocky country. If neglected, he is apt to roll down huge masses of rock upon the habitations of those who have been forgetful of his wants, or to sweep them away by a landslip. When any great mishap of this nature occurs, a human victim is offered up to turn away his anger. The falling of boulders or detached pieces of rock is always considered the handiwork of Oke and a sign that something is required. The emblem of Oke is a stone or fragment of rock.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ellis, The Yoruba-speaking Peoples, ch. III (1894); not verbatim.

passages.text: At Abeokuta there is a rocky cavern in which Oke is worshipped. It is popularly believed by the other tribes that the Egbas, when defeated in war, can retire into this cavern, which then hermetically seals itself till the danger is past.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ellis, The Yoruba-speaking Peoples, ch. III (1894); not verbatim.

title.en: The Sun Drives Out His Sons; Yemaja Makes Them Fish
title.zh: 日逐諸子，耶莫雅化之為魚

region.en: Yoruba sky-country (symbolic pin: where sky meets sea, off the Lagos coast)
region.zh: 約魯巴天空之境（象徵定位：拉哥斯海外天海相接處）

period: Yoruba oral tradition; recorded 1894 (Ellis)

source.work: A. B. Ellis, The Yoruba-speaking Peoples of the Slave Coast of West Africa (London, 1894), ch. III

summary.en: The stars are the daughters of the sun and moon. The boy-suns, growing up, tried to follow their father across the sky to the place where sea and sky meet — where, say the Yorubas, the white men go and fill their ships — but the Sun, jealous of his power, turned on them and tried to kill them. Some fled to Olosa, some to Olokun, and the rest to their grandmother Yemaja, who turned them into fish; so all the sons were driven out of the sky, while the daughters remain with their mother by night.
summary.zh: 星辰是日月的女兒。長大的小太陽們想跟隨父親橫越天穹，往天海相接之處——約魯巴人說，白人就是在那裡把船裝滿的——但太陽怕大權旁落，回頭便要殺他們。有的逃到奧洛薩處，有的投奔奧洛貢，其餘的躲進祖母耶莫雅懷裡，被她化作游魚。諸子盡逐於天外，女兒們則夜夜伴著母親。

sensitivity.note: Living Yoruba tradition; celestial-family myth recorded 1894. Tagged sun-capture as nearest cluster motif (jealous sun expelling rival suns).

passages.text: According to the myth, the sun, moon, and stars came from the body of Yemaja. Orun, the Sun, and Oshu, the Moon, are gods. The stars are the daughters of the sun and moon. The boys, or young suns, on growing up tried to follow their father in his course across the sky to where the sea and the sky meet, and which, say the Yorubas, is the place where the white men go and find all the things with which they fill their ships; but he, jealous of his power, turned upon them and tried to kill them.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ellis, The Yoruba-speaking Peoples, ch. III (1894); not verbatim.

passages.text: Some of them sought refuge with Olosa, some with Olokun, and the remainder with their grandmother, Yemaja, who turned them into fish. Thus all the sons were driven out of the sky, but the daughters remained with their mother and still accompany her by night. To see the new moon is lucky, and an eclipse of the moon is supposed to indicate that the sun is beating her, steps being taken to drive him away.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ellis, The Yoruba-speaking Peoples, ch. III (1894); not verbatim.

title.en: Egungun, the Masked One from Deadland
title.zh: 埃貢貢——自冥土歸來的假面

region.en: Yoruba town streets (symbolic pin: festival streets of a Yoruba town near Ile-Ife)
region.zh: 約魯巴城鎮街衢（象徵定位：伊費近郊慶典街道）

period: Yoruba oral tradition; recorded 1894 (Ellis)

source.work: A. B. Ellis, The Yoruba-speaking Peoples of the Slave Coast of West Africa (London, 1894), ch. VI

summary.en: Egungun — the word means bone, skeleton — is supposed to be a man risen from the dead, robed in grass and masked in wood, who returns to the land of the living to see what goes on and to carry away the troublesome. To touch him is death; days after a funeral he calls the deceased by name through the night streets, and then brings the family news from Deadland — usually that the dead arrived safely and is well — receiving in return a hidden feast and messages for the departed.
summary.zh: 埃貢貢，本義為「骨」，相傳是死而復返之人：身披草衣、面覆木雕，自冥土回來察看生者世界，專收擾鄰不安之人。觸之即死。葬禮數日後，他率蒙面隨從夜巡街市，高呼亡者之名；再數日，他到喪家報信——亡者已安抵冥土、一切安好。家人備下酒食退出房間（見其進食者死），再託他捎信給逝者。

sensitivity.note: Living Yoruba tradition; Egungun masquerade remains a central ancestral institution (also carried into the diaspora and Freetown). Ellis 1894 describes the rite; presented as archival record, not as an insider account.

passages.text: Egungun really means bone, hence skeleton, and Egungun himself is supposed to be a man risen from the dead, acted by a man disguised in a long robe, usually made of grass, and a mask of wood representing a hideous human face, or sometimes the head of an animal. He appears in the streets by day or night, leaping, dancing, or walking grotesquely, and uttering loud cries. He is supposed to have returned from the land of the dead in order to ascertain what is going on in the land of the living, and his function is to carry away those persons who are troublesome to their neighbours — a kind of supernatural inquisitor into the general domestic conduct of people, particularly of women.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ellis, The Yoruba-speaking Peoples, ch. VI (1894); not verbatim.

passages.text: Although it is very well known that Egungun is only a disguised man, it is popularly believed that to touch him, even by accident, causes death; to raise the hand against him is punished with death, and women are forbidden, on pain of death, to laugh at him or say he is not one who has risen from the dead. In June there is an annual feast for Egungun lasting seven days, during which lamentations are made for those who have died within the last few years — a kind of All-Souls festival.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ellis, The Yoruba-speaking Peoples, ch. VI (1894); not verbatim.

passages.text: Egungun also appears in connection with funeral ceremonies. A few days after the funeral an Egungun, accompanied by masked and disguised men, parades the streets of the town at night, and, as in the Roman conclamatio, calls upon the deceased loudly by name, a half-frightened crowd following and listening for any response. A few days later he proceeds to the house in which the death took place and brings to the relatives news of the deceased, usually that he has arrived in Deadland safely and is quite well. In return the family set food, rum, and palm-wine in a room of the house and, inviting Egungun to partake, themselves retire — for to see Egungun eating is death. When he and his followers have consumed everything, loud groans are heard from the room, a sign that he is about to depart; the family re-enter and entrust him with messages for the deceased.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ellis, The Yoruba-speaking Peoples, ch. VI (1894); not verbatim.

title.en: Oro and the Bull-Roarer That Women Must Not See
title.zh: 奧羅與婦人不得目睹的呼嘯板

region.en: Ondo, Nigeria (symbolic pin: Oro's forest edge outside the town)
region.zh: 奈及利亞翁多城（象徵定位：奧羅巡行的城外林緣）

period: Yoruba oral tradition; recorded 1894 (Ellis)

source.work: A. B. Ellis, The Yoruba-speaking Peoples of the Slave Coast of West Africa (London, 1894), ch. VI

summary.en: Oro — fierceness, tempest — is personified executive power, haunting the forest near towns, his approach known by a strange whirring roar made by whirling a thin strip of wood: the bull-roarer, known also to the mysteries of Ancient Greece and Australia. No woman may see the instrument and live; criminals given to Oro are never seen again, their clothes found entangled in a lofty tree.
summary.zh: 「奧羅」意為烈性、風暴，是執行權力的化身，盤踞城鎮近郊的樹林；他的到來以奇異的呼嘯聲為號——那是旋轉薄木片所發的聲響，與古希臘秘儀及澳洲部落所用的「牛吼板」同源。婦女見此物者死。被判交予奧羅的罪犯從此消失，只在參天樹梢尋得纏繞的衣物——人已被他於半空吞噬。

sensitivity.note: Living Yoruba tradition; Oro society rites are restricted and still practiced; Ellis's 1894 description of secret instruments is presented as an outsider ethnographic record. Restricted rites themselves are not described here beyond what Ellis published.

passages.text: The word Oro means fierceness, tempest, or provocation, and Oro himself appears to be personified executive power. He is supposed to haunt the forest in the neighbourhood of towns, and he makes his approach known by a strange, whirring, roaring noise. As soon as this is heard, all women must shut themselves up in their houses and refrain from looking out on pain of death. The voice of Oro is produced by whirling round and round a thin strip of wood fastened to a stick by a long string — the instrument known to English boys as the bull-roarer, which has been shown to have been used in the mysteries of Ancient Greece, Australia, New Mexico, New Zealand, and South Africa. No women may see the bull-roarer and live.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ellis, The Yoruba-speaking Peoples, ch. VI (1894); not verbatim.

passages.text: In Yoruba country Oro is manipulated by the Ogboni Society. Criminals condemned to death are sometimes given to Oro, in which case they are ordinarily never seen again, but their clothes are shown entangled in the branches of a lofty tree, where Oro is said to have left them when flying through the air; in such a case Oro is said to have devoured the bodies. Unlike Egungun, Oro only appears on his feast-days, when the voice of Oro is heard from morning to night, all women closely confined to their houses, while Oro himself, in a long robe hung with shells and a wooden mask painted white, with the lips smeared with blood, parades the town with a numerous following. In Ondo there is an annual festival to Oro lasting three lunar months; and a large boulder of granite called Olumo, on the summit of a hill in Abeokuta, is sacred to Oro, and no one may ascend it.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ellis, The Yoruba-speaking Peoples, ch. VI (1894); not verbatim.

title.en: Abiku: The Hungry Spirits Who Kill Children
title.zh: 阿比庫——奪走孩童的飢靈

region.en: Yoruba bush (symbolic pin: uninhabited tracts where the Abiku dwell, near Ile-Ife)
region.zh: 約魯巴荒野（象徵定位：伊費近郊無人居處，阿比庫所棲）

period: Yoruba oral tradition; recorded 1894 (Ellis)

source.work: A. B. Ellis, The Yoruba-speaking Peoples of the Slave Coast of West Africa (London, 1894), ch. VI

summary.en: The empty bush swarms with hungry Abiku spirits who enter the bodies of new-born babes and live on their food, sharing it with the comrades outside until the child pines and dies. Mothers fight back with iron: rings and bells on the ankles, chains on the neck, peppers cut into the flesh to burn the indwelling spirit — and a dead child, buried without ceremony in the bush, may be beaten and mutilated so the Abiku feels every blow and fears to return.
summary.zh: 空曠的野地擠滿飢餓的阿比庫之靈，他們鑽入新生嬰兒體內，奪其食糧，還要與體外的同夥分食，孩子日漸枯瘦而死。母親以鐵相抗：足踝繫鐵環銅鈴、頸掛鐵鏈，甚至以尖椒割入兒身灼燒體內之靈。若孩子夭亡，屍身無葬儀、棄於野，甚或被擊打毀損——阿比庫身受其痛，心生畏懼，不敢再入這位母親日後的孩子。

sensitivity.note: Living Yoruba tradition; the Abiku belief inspired the modern Yoruba novels of Wole Soyinka (The Interpreters imagery) and J. P. Clark's poem Abiku. Descriptions of painful folk remedies reported as 1894 ethnography; handled without endorsement.

passages.text: Abiku means predestined to death, and is used to mean the spirits of children who die before reaching puberty, and also a class of evil spirits who cause children to die. The general idea is that the uninhabited tracts of country abound with evil spirits who suffer from hunger, thirst, and cold, since nobody offers sacrifice to them, and who are constantly endeavouring to improve their condition by entering the bodies of new-born babes. Only one Abiku can enter and dwell in the body of the same child; as there is great competition for such a position, an Abiku is only suffered to enter peaceably on condition of his promising his companions a share of the comforts he is about to obtain.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ellis, The Yoruba-speaking Peoples, ch. VI (1894); not verbatim.

passages.text: When an Abiku has entered a child he takes for his own use, and for the use of his companions, the greater part of the food that the child eats, who in consequence begins to pine away. It is the incessant demands made by the hungry Abikus outside which destroy the child; when a child is peevish and fretful it is believed that the outside Abikus are hurting him to make the indwelling Abiku give them more to eat. A mother who sees her child wasting away concludes that she has given birth to an Abiku.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ellis, The Yoruba-speaking Peoples, ch. VI (1894); not verbatim.

passages.text: To get rid of the indwelling Abiku and his companions, the anxious mother offers a sacrifice of food and, while the Abikus are supposed to be devouring its spiritual part, attaches iron rings and small bells to the ankles of the child and hangs iron chains round his neck — the jingling keeping the Abikus at a distance, hence the number of children seen with their feet weighed down with iron. If the child grows worse, the mother endeavours to drive out the Abiku by making small incisions in the child's body and putting green peppers or spices in them, believing she thereby causes pain to the Abiku and makes him depart; the poor child screams, but the mother hardens her heart in the belief that the Abiku is suffering equally. Should the child die, it is buried without ceremony in the bush; sometimes the corpse is beaten, pounded, and mutilated while threats and curses are invoked upon the Abiku, who is believed to feel every blow and to be terrified by the threats, so that he fears to enter the body of any other infant the mother may bear.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ellis, The Yoruba-speaking Peoples, ch. VI (1894); not verbatim.

title.en: Tree-Spirits: The Ashorin Lure and the Glowing Apa
title.zh: 樹靈：阿紹林之餌與夜光的阿帕樹

region.en: Yoruba forest (symbolic pin: timber groves near Ile-Ife)
region.zh: 約魯巴森林（象徵定位：伊費近郊伐木林地）

period: Yoruba oral tradition; recorded 1894 (Ellis)

source.work: A. B. Ellis, The Yoruba-speaking Peoples of the Slave Coast of West Africa (London, 1894), ch. VI

summary.en: Several trees are inhabited by spirits, hamadryads rather than gods. The woodman who would fell an Ashorin sets out palm-oil as a lure and cuts while the spirit licks it up. The Apa, African mahogany, is an evil spirit's tree, glowing phosphorescent by night, propitiated with a fowl before its drum-wood may be cut, and by night the haunt of wizards in owl-form. The Iroko silk-cotton tree needs only that the feller rub palm-oil on his own forehead, invoking the spirit of his own head.
summary.zh: 多種大樹內棲樹靈——似古希臘的樹仙女而非大神。伐阿紹林樹者須先在地上抹棕櫚油為餌，趁樹靈舔油時下斧。非洲桃花心木「阿帕」則棲惡靈，夜發磷光，伐其鼓木前須以雞祭之；而巫者夜聚，亦化為貓頭鷹聚於此樹之下。伐伊羅科木棉者，只須以油抹額，喚起自家「頭靈」即可無恙。

sensitivity.note: Living Yoruba tradition; tree-spirit beliefs and woodcutter rites recorded 1894.

passages.text: Several varieties of trees are believed to be inhabited by indwelling spirits, which are not exactly gods, but answer more to the hamadryads of Ancient Greece, or to the elves of mediaeval Europe. The Ashorin tree is one which is inhabited by a spirit who, it is believed, would, if its attention were not diverted, drive away anyone who attempted to fell the tree. The woodman therefore places a little palm-oil on the ground as a lure, and when the spirit leaves the tree to lick up the delicacy, proceeds to cut down its late abode.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ellis, The Yoruba-speaking Peoples, ch. VI (1894); not verbatim.

passages.text: The Apa, frequently called the African mahogany, is inhabited by an evil spirit, and is commonly seen encircled with palm-leaves, with an earthen pot at its foot to receive the offerings of woodcutters. It is believed to emit a phosphorescent light by night. Before it can be cut down the spirit must be propitiated by an offering, usually a fowl and some palm-oil; the Apa is the emblem of vengeance. The Iroko (silk-cotton tree) is also inhabited by a spirit, but not a powerful or malicious one, and when a man desires to fell such a tree it is sufficient protection for him to invoke the indwelling spirit of his own head by rubbing a little palm-oil on his forehead.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ellis, The Yoruba-speaking Peoples, ch. VI (1894); not verbatim.

passages.text: Wizards and witches are by the Yorubas believed to hold nocturnal meetings at the foot of trees tenanted by spirits, more especially the Apa, whose indwelling spirit is believed to assist them in their malpractices. Here, too, the owl again appears; instead of being the messenger of the tree spirit, it is the witch himself or herself who metamorphoses into an owl and proceeds on the mission of death.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ellis, The Yoruba-speaking Peoples, ch. VI (1894); not verbatim.

title.en: Bola's Baby of Otta: The Spirit Who Grew at Market-Time
title.zh: 奧塔的博拉之子——赴市而長的精靈

region.en: Otta, Nigeria (village on the River Ilo, near the Ogun)
region.zh: 奈及利亞奧塔村（伊洛河畔，近奧貢河）

period: Yoruba oral tradition; recorded 1894 (Ellis)

source.work: A. B. Ellis, The Yoruba-speaking Peoples of the Slave Coast of West Africa (London, 1894), ch. VI

summary.en: At Otta, a woman named Bola leaves her baby fastened in the house and finds on every market-day that the food has vanished — though the door was never opened. A neighbour demands repayment of cowries the child borrowed, insisting she saw him grown to the size of a ten-year-old. The father hides and watches the baby stand, swell into a big boy, and begin to eat — springing back to infancy at the sight of him. Parents beat the child to drive out the possessing spirit, and the spirit fled.
summary.zh: 奧塔村的博拉每次鎖門赴市，歸來總發現家中食物被吃光，門閂卻分毫未動。鄰婦上門討債——「你的孩子以你的名義借了我的貝幣」，並說來借錢的孩子約莫十歲模樣，比眼前的嬰兒大得多。夫親藏身屋內窺探：只見嬰孩站起，長成大男孩，正要取食——被父親當場撞破，瞬間縮回嬰兒啼哭。父母鞭打驅靈，精靈終於遁去。

sensitivity.note: Living Yoruba tradition; Ellis notes this is the Yoruba counterpart of the European changeling — a strong cross-tradition parallel for the Compare view. Cross-refs: none recorded in corpus for changeling; closest thematic relative is the Abiku cycle.

passages.text: There lived at Otta, a village on the River Ilo, a woman named Bola, who had a male child. When the child was small the mother carried him on her back to market, but when he was about nine months old she used to lay him on a mat in her house, fasten the door, and go to market by herself. After this it always happened that when she returned from market she found that all the food she had left in the house had disappeared — though the door-fastening was always untouched. One day a neighbour came to demand repayment of the string of cowries that Bola had sent her little boy to borrow; Bola protested that the child was too young to walk or talk, but the neighbour, looking closely at the sleeping child, solemnly declared that it was really he who had come to her — though when he came he was much bigger, with the appearance of a child of about ten years of age.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ellis, The Yoruba-speaking Peoples, ch. VI (1894); not verbatim.

passages.text: When Bola heard this she was much distressed, fearing her child was possessed by an evil spirit; she paid the cowries and begged the neighbour to say nothing, then told her husband the whole story. The father hid himself in the house one day while mother and child were out; scarcely had Bola gone and fastened the door than the father saw the baby stand up and begin to grow till he became a big boy, going to the calabashes where the food was kept and beginning to eat. Immediately the child saw his father he became a little baby again and lay on the floor crying. He was possessed by a spirit. His mother came back, and they beat him to drive the spirit out, so that the spirit fled.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ellis, The Yoruba-speaking Peoples, ch. VI (1894); not verbatim.

title.en: The Man-Hyena of the Night Forest
title.zh: 夜林中人形鬣狗

region.en: Yoruba night-forest (symbolic pin: dark paths beyond the town, near Ile-Ife)
region.zh: 約魯巴夜林（象徵定位：伊費城外夜路）

period: Yoruba oral tradition; recorded 1894 (Ellis)

source.work: A. B. Ellis, The Yoruba-speaking Peoples of the Slave Coast of West Africa (London, 1894), ch. VI

summary.en: The hyena is often supposed to be a man who assumes that disguise at night to prey upon sheep and cattle — and, if the opportunity offers, upon human beings. Such man-hyenas can, by certain howls and cries, compel people to come out to them in the dark forest to be devoured; the weird laugh of the hyena and its nocturnal habits account for the belief.
summary.zh: 約魯巴人常謂鬣狗實為夜間易形之人，白日為人，夜著獸形，捕食羊牛——有機可乘時，也吃人。這種人形鬣狗能以特殊嚎叫與呼喚，逼人深夜走進黑暗的樹林任其吞噬。鬣狗那怪異的「笑聲」與夜行習性，正是此一信念的根源。

sensitivity.note: Living Yoruba tradition; were-hyena belief, the African analogue of the werewolf, recorded 1894 (cf. Abyssinia).

passages.text: We also find a superstition which recalls that of the were-wolf, for the hyena is often supposed to be a man who assumes that disguise at night, to prey upon sheep and cattle, and, if the opportunity offers, upon human beings.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ellis, The Yoruba-speaking Peoples, ch. VI (1894); not verbatim.

passages.text: Such man-hyenas are believed to be able, by means of certain howls and cries, to compel people to go out to them in the dark forest to be devoured. A similar belief is found in Abyssinia. The weird laugh of the hyena, and its nocturnal habits, no doubt account for this superstition, just as similar causes have led to the owl being universally regarded as a bird of ill omen.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ellis, The Yoruba-speaking Peoples, ch. VI (1894); not verbatim.

title.en: Iyewa Becomes a Lagoon to Save Her Children
title.zh: 伊耶瓦化潟湖救幼子

region.en: Odo Iyewa lagoon, Nigeria (the water named for the mother)
region.zh: 奈及利亞伊耶瓦潟湖（以母親之名為名的水域）

period: Yoruba oral tradition; recorded 1894 (Ellis)

source.work: A. B. Ellis, The Yoruba-speaking Peoples of the Slave Coast of West Africa (London, 1894), ch. VI

summary.en: A poor woman, Iyewa, gathered firewood daily with her two children; one day, deep in the forest, they lost the path, and, tormented with thirst, the children cried for water until they lay near death. Prostrating herself, Iyewa called upon the gods, who changed her into a lagoon at which the children drank and recovered. When they grew up they built their house beside the water and named it Odo Iyewa — the Lagoon of Iyewa.
summary.zh: 貧婦伊耶瓦日日攜二子入林拾柴換糧。某日迷途林中，孩子渴極哀號，氣息奄奄。她伏地呼神求救；眾神應允，將她化作一泓潟湖。孩子俯身痛飲，得救生還。二人成年後在水畔築屋，命名「伊耶瓦之湖」，永誌其母。

sensitivity.note: Living Yoruba tradition; metamorphosis-and-place-name legend recorded 1894. The Iyewa lagoon lies near the Badagry creek country.

passages.text: The Iyewa lagoon is also said to have been a woman. A poor woman, named Iyewa, had two children whom she had a hard struggle to support; but she used every day to go with them into the forest to gather firewood, which she carried to the town and sold for food. One day, finding wood scarce, she and the children wandered further into the forest than usual, and when it was time to return they could not find their way out. They walked hither and thither looking for the path, but in vain, and at last, tired out and tormented with thirst, they lay down to rest under a large tree.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ellis, The Yoruba-speaking Peoples, ch. VI (1894); not verbatim.

passages.text: This rested their limbs, but their thirst increased, and the two children filled the forest with their lamentations, crying to their mother for water. The poor woman, half distracted, sprang to her feet and again searched in every direction for the path and for water, but fruitlessly; and when at last she returned to her children she found them almost at the last gasp. Then, prostrating herself upon the earth, she called upon the gods to come to her assistance and save her children. The gods listened to her prayer, and Iyewa was at once changed into a lagoon, at which the children drank and so recovered; while next day they were found by neighbours and taken back to the town. When the children grew up they built a house by the side of the lagoon, which, in memory of their mother, they called Odo Iyewa — the Lagoon of Iyewa.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ellis, The Yoruba-speaking Peoples, ch. VI (1894); not verbatim.

title.en: The Goblin and the Two Palm-Oil Sellers
title.zh: 妖靈與兩個賣油女

region.en: Yoruba market-roads to Deadland (symbolic pin: road from the market at Ile-Ife)
region.zh: 約魯巴通往冥土的市路（象徵定位：伊費市集外的大路）

period: Yoruba oral tradition; recorded 1894 (Ellis)

source.work: A. B. Ellis, The Yoruba-speaking Peoples of the Slave Coast of West Africa (London, 1894), ch. XIV

summary.en: A short-changed girl follows a goblin past head-pounders, a river of filth, a bloody river, gloomy forest, and a craggy mountain, into the land of the dead, where she does everything backwards — oil for the dregs, fruit for the peel — and is rewarded with three ados that break into slaves, herds, and a houseful of cowries. The jealous head-wife sends her own daughter, who cheats the goblin and does everything forwards — and the last ado she breaks calls up lions, leopards, hyenas and snakes that tear her apart at her own door.
summary.zh: 賣油女被妖靈短找一枚貝幣，鍥而不捨追進冥土：經過頭杵搗薯之國、穢水之河、血河、幽林與危崖。在那裡她事事反著做——油自留、渣奉主、果自吃、皮奉主——得三枚小葫蘆為賞：途中碎一枚，奴馬隨行；門前碎一枚，牛羊雞群湧至；入屋碎一枚，貝幣盈室。妒忌的大婦遣親女效仿，卻欺妖賴帳、事事順做，最後一枚葫蘆一碎，獅豹鬣蛇蜂擁而出，將她咬死在自家門檻。

sensitivity.note: Living Yoruba tradition; classic two-sisters wonder tale with a katabasis (journey to the land of the dead). Cross-tradition parallels abound; descent to the underworld cluster. Cross-refs: greek-odyssey-nekuia (motif family only).

passages.text: A woman's little girl made palm-oil and stayed in the market selling it until it was quite dark, when a goblin came to buy and paid her with cowries — one short. She cried that her mother would beat her, and followed the goblin, who warned her to turn back, for no one can enter the country where he lives. "Wherever you go I will follow, until you pay me my cowry," she said. So she followed past the country where people stand on their heads in their mortars and pound yams with their heads, past a river of filth, a bloody river, a gloomy forest, and a craggy mountain — he singing "You must turn back," she singing "Save I get my cowry, I'll not leave your track" — until they arrived at the land of dead people.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ellis, The Yoruba-speaking Peoples, ch. XIV (1894); not verbatim.

passages.text: There the goblin gave her palm-nuts to make oil and bade her eat the oil and give him the ha-ha, the stringy remains; but when it was made she gave him the oil and ate the ha-ha herself, and he said, "Very well." He gave her a banana and told her to eat it and bring him the skin; she peeled it and gave him the fruit and ate the skin herself. Then he told her to pick three small calabashes, not those which cried "Pick me, pick me, pick me," but those which said nothing, and to break one half-way home, one at the house-door, and one inside. At the first break slaves and horses appeared and followed her; at the second, sheep, goats, and fowls, more than two hundred; and at the third the house was filled to overflowing with cowries.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ellis, The Yoruba-speaking Peoples, ch. XIV (1894); not verbatim.

passages.text: The mother carried a royal present of cloths, beads, sheep and fowls to the head wife, who refused them and sent her own daughter to do the same. This girl short-changed the goblin herself, hiding a cowry and demanding payment, and followed him to the land of the dead — where she did everything exactly as told: ate the oil and gave him the ha-ha, ate the banana and gave him the skin, and picked the three calabashes that cried "Pick me." Half-way home she broke the first, and numbers of lions, leopards, hyenas and snakes appeared, harassing and biting her all the way to the door; at the second break more ferocious beasts came upon her, and there, upon the threshold — the deaf person within hearing nothing — the wild beasts killed the little girl.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ellis, The Yoruba-speaking Peoples, ch. XIV (1894); not verbatim.

title.en: The Aranran Bird and the Two Mothers
title.zh: 阿蘭蘭神鳥與兩位母親

region.en: Yoruba forest (symbolic pin: tall tree in the woodcutting wood, near Ile-Ife)
region.zh: 約魯巴森林（象徵定位：伊費近郊伐木高樹）

period: Yoruba oral tradition; recorded 1894 (Ellis)

source.work: A. B. Ellis, The Yoruba-speaking Peoples of the Slave Coast of West Africa (London, 1894), ch. XIV

summary.en: A poor young woman's baby is snatched into a tall tree by the aranran bird; three times she sings her plea, refusing coral beads and treasure until the bird brings down the child itself — and she goes home rich. The head-wife, greedy for the same fortune, sets another wife's child under the tree: the bird eats it, and answers her songs with a bag of filth, a broken calabash of water, and the child's bones — for which murder the king has her put to death.
summary.zh: 貧婦伐薪時，幼子被神鳥阿蘭蘭攫上高樹。她三度唱歌求還，先拋下珊瑚珠串、再拋下財寶，她皆不取，直至神鳥親銜孩子落地——她從此富貴。大婦豔羨，竟將別房妻室的孩子置於樹下。神鳥食之，回以一袋穢物、一破甕冷水、一捧孩骨。事發，國王判大婦死刑。

sensitivity.note: Living Yoruba tradition; the discomfiture of the iyale (head-wife) is a favourite Yoruba tale-theme, noted by Ellis. Contains the killing of a child within the tale; reported as recorded.

passages.text: There was a poor young woman who had a child, so poor that she could not even buy a cloth to wear, her child held on her back with a plantain-leaf. Going into the forest to cut firewood, she put the child to sleep in the shade of a tall tree; and in this tree there was an aranran, a bird of prey, which while she worked seized the child and carried it up into the tree-top. When she could not find her baby she ran to and fro crying, till she looked up and saw him in the claws of the bird, and began to sing: "Aranran, wild bird of the bush, give me back my child; here is a rope of tie-tie; quickly let my child down."
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ellis, The Yoruba-speaking Peoples, ch. XIV (1894); not verbatim.

passages.text: At her song the bird threw down a bag of coral beads; the child was not in it, so she sang again, and the aranran threw down all kinds of valuable property; still no child. She sang a third time, and the bird took the child and flew down with it and placed it gently on the ground. She carried him home on her back, picked up all the things the bird had thrown down, and from being poor became rich. Returning, she offered the iyale (head wife) twenty strings of coral beads; but the iyale, when she learned how they were come by, refused them and declared she would send her own child and get as much.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ellis, The Yoruba-speaking Peoples, ch. XIV (1894); not verbatim.

passages.text: The iyale took a child belonging to one of the other wives and carried it into the bush, setting it under the tree of the aranran, and went away to cut wood. While she was away the bird carried off the child and killed and ate it. When she returned she sang the young woman's song; but the bird voided copiously into a bag and threw it down, then made water in a large calabash which broke upon her head, and at the third song threw down the bones of the child. She cried that it was not her child and went home — but the true mother demanded her baby, and after three months carried the case before the king. "If this woman belonged to you, what would you do with her?" asked the king; and all the people replied, "We would put her to death." And so the iyale was killed.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ellis, The Yoruba-speaking Peoples, ch. XIV (1894); not verbatim.

title.en: Why the Ajao Remained Unburied
title.zh: 阿賈奧狐蝠無人送葬之由

region.en: Yoruba village (symbolic pin: burial ground near Ile-Ife)
region.zh: 約魯巴村落（象徵定位：伊費近郊墓地）

period: Yoruba oral tradition; recorded 1894 (Ellis)

source.work: A. B. Ellis, The Yoruba-speaking Peoples of the Slave Coast of West Africa (London, 1894), ch. XIV

summary.en: The ajao, a great flying-fox, dies alone. The birds refuse the funeral — he has no feathers; the rats refuse it — he has no tail. Having no relations, the ajao remained unburied.
summary.zh: 大狐蝠阿賈奧病歿屋中。鄰人先請鳥族送葬——鳥說他無羽，非我族類；再請鼠族——鼠說他無尾，亦非親眷。兩邊不認，阿賈奧遂暴屍無葬。

sensitivity.note: Living Yoruba tradition; animal etiology, the in-between creature refused by both kin-groups — cf. the Ogumefu bat tale and the Kipling-era motif of the outcast bat.

passages.text: The ajao lay in his house very sick, and there was no one to tend him. The ajao died. The neighbours said, "The ajao is dead; we must call his relatives to come and perform the funeral ceremonies and bury him." And they went and called the birds, saying, "Your relation is dead." The birds came, and when they saw that the deceased was an ajao they said, "This is not one of our family. All our family wear feathers, and you see the ajao has none. He does not belong to us." And they went away.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ellis, The Yoruba-speaking Peoples, ch. XIV (1894); not verbatim.

passages.text: The neighbours consulted together: "The birds are right. The ajao has no feathers, and is not of the family of birds. He must be of the family of rats." And they went and called the rats, saying, "Your relation is dead." The rats came, but when they saw that the deceased was an ajao they also denied him: "This is not one of our family. Everyone who is of our family has a tail, and you see the ajao has none." And they went away. Thus the ajao, having no relations, remained unburied.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ellis, The Yoruba-speaking Peoples, ch. XIV (1894); not verbatim.

title.en: The Kini-Kini Bird and the King's Slap
title.zh: 基尼基尼鳥與國王一巴掌

region.en: Yoruba royal town (symbolic pin: cleared ground before the palace, near Oyo)
region.zh: 約魯巴王城（象徵定位：奧約宮前空地）

period: Yoruba oral tradition; recorded 1894 (Ellis)

source.work: A. B. Ellis, The Yoruba-speaking Peoples of the Slave Coast of West Africa (London, 1894), ch. XIV

summary.en: The king calls all the birds to clear his ground — but forgets the kini-kini, who each noon sings the grass and bush back up over their work. Trapped at last with birdlime, the bird buys pardon by voiding cowries at every slap of the king's hand; when it escapes through a boy's curiosity, the furious king cuts off his son's ear. The boy drums the bird out of hiding, catches it, and a dead leaf laid where the ear was softens and grows into an ear.
summary.zh: 國王召群鳥墾地，獨忘基尼基尼。正午鳥雀歇工，牠飛上臭椿高唱，草莽隨聲復生，一連三日。群鳥以黏鳥膠擒之，鳥以貝幣贖命——國王一拍手，牠便噴出滿屋貝幣。後王子偷揭籃蓋縱鳥，王怒削其子一耳。孩子以小鼓誘鳥出林就擒；王取枯葉補耳，枯葉竟軟化生肉，長成一隻新耳。

sensitivity.note: Living Yoruba tradition; bird-trickster tale with a healing miracle ending. Note: the king mutilates his own son within the tale; reported as recorded.

passages.text: One day the king called all the birds to come and clear a piece of ground, but he forgot to call the kini-kini, the small black-and-white doctor-bird. All the birds came and cleared a large piece of ground; but in the middle stood an odan tree, and at mid-day, when the sun was hot and the birds had left their work, the kini-kini came and perched on it and sang his song, and the grass and bush sprang up over the cleared ground. This happened again the next day and the day after; and when the birds saw what had happened the third time, they asked the king for authority to seize the trickster, and put a great quantity of birdlime on the odan tree. At mid-day the kini-kini came, sang his song, found himself held by the birdlime, and was seized and brought before the king.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ellis, The Yoruba-speaking Peoples, ch. XIV (1894); not verbatim.

passages.text: "What have I done to you?" asked the king. "When you called all my companions to clear the ground you left me out, therefore I have revenged myself," said the bird. The king raised his hand to slap it. "Pardon, pardon — if I find any cowries I will give them to you." The king gave him a slap, and the kini-kini voided out cowries till the room was filled; a second slap brought still more. The king summoned all his people for the fifth day to see the marvel, but his little son uncovered the basket to slap the bird himself and it flew away. In his anger the king beat the boy and cut off one of his ears, and pushed him out to find the bird.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ellis, The Yoruba-speaking Peoples, ch. XIV (1894); not verbatim.

passages.text: The boy made a little drum and sat down where the birds were accustomed to come; he beat on his drum, and all the birds flocked round and danced in turn. The kini-kini refused, but at last, begged by all, he twisted and turned, dancing closer and closer, until the boy thrust out his hand and seized him by the leg. "Here he is. Won't you do something now to restore my ear?" Then the king got up, took a dead leaf and put it in the place of the ear; and the dead leaf softened and changed into an ear.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ellis, The Yoruba-speaking Peoples, ch. XIV (1894); not verbatim.

title.en: Sigo in the Tortoise's Drum
title.zh: 西戈困於龜鼓

region.en: Yoruba hunting country (symbolic pin: rain-gully on the hunting road, near Ile-Ife)
region.zh: 約魯巴獵場（象徵定位：伊費近郊獵路雨溝）

period: Yoruba oral tradition; recorded 1894 (Ellis)

source.work: A. B. Ellis, The Yoruba-speaking Peoples of the Slave Coast of West Africa (London, 1894), ch. XIV

summary.en: A cloudburst washes the young hunter Sigo into a gully, and Tortoise — the bald-headed elf — pulls him out on terms of slavery, then shuts him inside a big drum whose song tells the whole story at court. The mistresses who own Sigo free him at a dance while the elf gorges and sleeps; and when Tortoise beats the rescued drum, out croaks only a crow.
summary.zh: 驟雨把少年獵人西戈沖入深溝。禿頭精靈龜君救他出水，代價是為奴——並把他藏進一面大鼓。龜鼓在宮廷上一敲便唱出全部來歷，舉座驚駭。西戈的主母們趁龜君宴飲醉眠，開鼓放人、原樣封好。龜君醒後再擊鼓，鼓中只剩一隻烏鴉呱呱作響。

sensitivity.note: Living Yoruba tradition; Tortoise (Ijapa/Awon) trickster cycle; the talking-drum-singer conceit is native to Yoruba drum culture. Ellis's tale; greed defeats the trickster.

passages.text: Olu had a son named Sigo, and Sigo determined to be a hunter. His father gave him a horse, his mother a sheep, and he rode away into the bush with bow and arrows. At last he arrived at the haunt of animals; then the sky became overcast, the rain poured in torrents, and Sigo was washed by the water into a deep gully, whence he could not get out, but remained weeping and lamenting. The rain ceased, and Tortoise, always on the look-out for opportunities, came to the gully. "What will you give me if I pull you out?" he asked. "I will be your slave," replied Sigo; and the bald-headed elf climbed down and took him out.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ellis, The Yoruba-speaking Peoples, ch. XIV (1894); not verbatim.

passages.text: "I am going to make a large drum, and shall put you inside it," said Tortoise. "When we come to any house and I begin playing on the drum, take care that you sing well." At his own town Tortoise boasted of the fine sound of his drum before the king, who summoned the whole town to a dance. The drum sounded, singing: "Sigo is the son of Olu — ah, let me be rescued! His mother gave him a sheep, his father gave him a horse, and told him to go and hunt; he went to the elephant's haunt, to the buffalo's lair; the flood of the rain washed him into the cleft; and so he became the Tortoise's slave — ah, let me be rescued!" The people clapped their hands to their mouths in wonder.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ellis, The Yoruba-speaking Peoples, ch. XIV (1894); not verbatim.

passages.text: Before long the mistresses of the house to which Sigo belonged asked Tortoise to come and beat his drum at a dance. They made gruel of Indian corn and bought rum; Tortoise ate and drank, and, becoming drunk, fell asleep. When he was asleep they took his drum, took off the drum-head, took Sigo out, and put the head back as it was before. When Tortoise awoke and began beating on it, a crow croaked in the drum; he beat harder and quicker, and the crow croaked louder, and he cried: "Why, when you were eating, did you not give something to eat to the drum? Why, when you were drinking, did not you give some of the rum to the drum?" He went home, took off the drum-head, and found a crow in the drum.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ellis, The Yoruba-speaking Peoples, ch. XIV (1894); not verbatim.

title.en: Tortoise Makes the Dumb Princess Speak
title.zh: 龜君讓啞公主開口

region.en: Yoruba royal town (symbolic pin: princess's bush cottage near Oyo)
region.zh: 約魯巴王城（象徵定位：奧約城外公主林舍）

period: Yoruba oral tradition; recorded 1894 (Ellis)

source.work: A. B. Ellis, The Yoruba-speaking Peoples of the Slave Coast of West Africa (London, 1894), ch. XIV

summary.en: For half his palace, Tortoise undertakes to make the king's dumb daughter speak. He lays a bottle of honey in the bush, hides, and slaps the princess crying "Thief!" — and rope and slander-song wring her first words from her. The king, hearing his daughter answer the trickster's taunts in song, divides his house, and that is how Tortoise succeeds in everything.
summary.zh: 龜君立誓讓啞語的公主開口，酬勞是半座宮殿。他在林中放一瓶蜜，藏身其後，待公主伸手便衝出拍她肩：「賊！偷我蜜吃！」又以繩縛之，編歌誣其為竊。公主羞憤難抑，開口以歌相答。國王聞女兒之歌聲驚喜交集，分宮半座予龜君——龜君事事得逞，此其一例。

sensitivity.note: Living Yoruba tradition; Tortoise trickster cycle. The trick is deceptive slander within the tale; reported as recorded.

passages.text: The king had a daughter who was dumb. The girl's name was Bola. He did all he could to make her speak, but all was of no avail, so he did not keep her in the town; he sent her to live in the country. Tortoise, of the thousand cunning tricks, came to the king and said: "What will you give me if I make your child speak?" "I will divide my house into two halves, and I will give you one half," said the king. The bald-headed elf bought a bottle of honey, went to the bush where the girl was living, put the honey on the ground and hid himself.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ellis, The Yoruba-speaking Peoples, ch. XIV (1894); not verbatim.

passages.text: The girl came, saw the honey, and put out her hand to it. Tortoise came out of his hiding-place, came behind her, and gave her a slap, crying: "Thief! So it is you who steal my honey and eat it." "I?" said the girl. "I have stolen your honey to eat?" Then Tortoise tied her with a rope and sang: "Bola stole honey to eat; Bola is a cunning cheat; Bola is a shameless thief." And the young girl sang back: "Into the wood of the elephant I went with the elephant; into the wood of the buffalo I went with the buffalo; and Tortoise has come to accuse me of stealing honey to eat." Tortoise led her back to the town, he singing and she answering, until before the king the father cried out with astonishment: "My daughter, who has never been heard to speak, speaks to-day!" The king divided his palace in half and gave one half to Tortoise, the bald-headed elf. That is how Tortoise succeeds in everything.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ellis, The Yoruba-speaking Peoples, ch. XIV (1894); not verbatim.

title.en: Tortoise Rides the Elephant to Town
title.zh: 龜騎象入城

region.en: Yoruba forest-to-town road (symbolic pin: road from the bush into Oyo)
region.zh: 約魯巴林間入城道（象徵定位：自林入奧約之路）

period: Yoruba oral tradition; recorded 1894 (Ellis)

source.work: A. B. Ellis, The Yoruba-speaking Peoples of the Slave Coast of West Africa (London, 1894), ch. XIV

summary.en: Tortoise wagers the animals he will ride the elephant into town. He flatters the beast that all the world mocks him as too big for town, climbs aboard on the plea of tired legs, and engineers a gallop — "my father's slave!" The enraged elephant hurls him where Tortoise begs to be thrown, into the swamp, where the elf dives and surfaces elsewhere, crowing his triumph; and since then the elephant has not come to town any more.
summary.zh: 龜君與眾獸打賭：他能騎象入城。他先煽動大象「眾獸笑你笨重不敢入城」，再以腿軟為由討騎，又教象「我抓背你就跑，我敲背你快跑」——一路疾馳入城，口口聲聲「我父親的奴僕！」大象羞怒欲摔死他，龜君反求「扔我去沼澤吧」。象信以為真，把牠扔進爛泥，龜卻潛水他處浮出，再次高呼得勝。自此大象再也不肯進城。

sensitivity.note: Living Yoruba tradition; Tortoise trickster cycle. The elephant's humiliation etiology; the title slavery-language is the tale's own rhetoric of boasting.

passages.text: The bald-headed elf one day told the other animals that he would ride the elephant, but they said: "No, you can't ride the elephant." "Well, I will make a wager that I will ride the elephant into town." So Tortoise went into the forest and met the elephant. "My father, all the animals say you are too stout and big to come to town." The elephant was vexed: "The animals are fools. If I do not come to town it is because I prefer the forest. Besides, I do not know the way." "Then come with me; I will show you the way, and you can put all the animals to shame." When they were near the town, "My father, I am tired. Will you kindly allow me to get on your back?" The elephant knelt down, and Tortoise climbed up.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ellis, The Yoruba-speaking Peoples, ch. XIV (1894); not verbatim.

passages.text: "When I scratch your back you must run, and when I knock my head against your back you must run faster; then you will make a fine display in the town." Near the town Tortoise scratched the elephant's back and he began to run; he knocked his back with his head and the elephant ran faster. The animals, frightened, went into their houses but looked out of their windows; and Tortoise called out: "Did I not say I would ride my father's slave to town?" "What do you mean by your father's slave?" said the elephant, growing angry. "I am only praising you," said Tortoise. "I will throw you down on the hard stones here and break you to pieces!" "Yes, that is right — throw me down here; then I shall not die. If you really want to kill me, carry me to a swamp: there the mud and water will drown me at once."
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ellis, The Yoruba-speaking Peoples, ch. XIV (1894); not verbatim.

passages.text: The elephant believed the bald-headed elf, ran to the swamp, and threw Tortoise into the mud; then he stretched out his foot to kick him, but the elf dived in the mire and came up in another place. The other animals were looking on, and Tortoise called out again: "Did I not say I would ride my father's slave to town?" When the elephant found he could not catch him, he ran at full speed back to the forest and told the other elephants what that broken-back had done to him. They said, "You were a fool to carry that broken-back to town." Since then the elephant has not come to town any more.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ellis, The Yoruba-speaking Peoples, ch. XIV (1894); not verbatim.

title.en: Adun and the Borrowed-Limbs Suitor
title.zh: 阿敦與借肢求婚者

region.en: Yoruba country (symbolic pin: market-day road near Ile-Ife)
region.zh: 約魯巴地方（象徵定位：伊費附近趕集之路）

period: Yoruba oral tradition; recorded 1894 (Ellis)

source.work: A. B. Ellis, The Yoruba-speaking Peoples of the Slave Coast of West Africa (London, 1894), ch. XIV

summary.en: The beautiful Adun, who has refused rich and chief and king alike, accepts on market-day a stranger assembled of borrowed legs, arms and body. On the road home each lender reclaims his part until only the head remains, and Adun, nearly dead with fear, is taken to the head's house. Tortoise, set to sound the horn if she tries to escape, is bribed with ekuru cakes stuffed into his horn — he eats, eats, eats, and Adun runs away.
summary.zh: 美婦阿敦拒盡富豪酋王，卻在趕集日心許一位借得雙腿、雙臂、身軀拼成的「完人」。歸途中債主逐一討回，最後只剩一顆頭顱獨行，阿敦嚇得魂飛魄散，被帶回首顱之家。頭顱命龜君守望報信；阿敦按祭師之計，把浸油的豆餅塞滿號角——龜君吹號即食，食而不已，阿敦趁機奔逃。

sensitivity.note: Living Yoruba tradition; variant of the disembodied-suitor tale. Strong parallel with Ogumefu's Head tale and with European Horned-Women/demon-lover plots. Cross-refs: yoruba-the-head-body-borrowing.

passages.text: Adun was very beautiful, and all the men wanted her; they were always entreating her, but she always refused. One market-day a person borrowed legs from one, arms from another, and a body from a third, joined all together, and went to the market. He wanted Adun, and he would have her. His appearance pleased her, and they talked together; although he belonged to a distant country, she consented to go with him, and her mothers said, "Very well, go with him."
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ellis, The Yoruba-speaking Peoples, ch. XIV (1894); not verbatim.

passages.text: They went. On the road, the master of the legs took away the legs, the master of the arms took away the arms, and the master of the body took away the body. Nothing was left but the head. And the head went on, on, while Adun, nearly dead with fear, could not run away. They arrived at the house of the head. Next morning, before he went to work in his plantation, the head said to Tortoise: "If Adun tries to run away, sound the horn to warn me." Scarcely had he gone out of sight when Adun took her bundle and began to run away; Tortoise sounded the horn, and the head ran up and made big round eyes. Every day Adun tried to run away, but without success, until she went to ask the babalawo what she should do. "Buy plenty of ekuru cakes, soak them in palm-oil, and stuff them into Tortoise's horn," said the diviner. She did as she was told, took up her bundle, and started off; Tortoise took the horn to blow it, the ekurus came into his mouth, he ate and ate and ate — and Adun ran away.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ellis, The Yoruba-speaking Peoples, ch. XIV (1894); not verbatim.

title.en: Tortoise, the Lizard, and the Yam-Rock
title.zh: 龜、蜥與藥薯岩

region.en: Yoruba farm country (symbolic pin: yam plantation rock near Ile-Ife)
region.zh: 約魯巴農鄉（象徵定位：伊費近郊薯田巨岩）

period: Yoruba oral tradition; recorded 1894 (Ellis)

source.work: A. B. Ellis, The Yoruba-speaking Peoples of the Slave Coast of West Africa (London, 1894), ch. XIV

summary.en: In famine, the lizard learns a farmer's secret — "Rock, open... Rock, shut" — and feeds daily. Tortoise wheedles his way in, loads himself with yams, and forgets the closing words; caught by the owner and tied to the lizard as informer, he finds the lizard playing dead. The farmer smashes Tortoise, and the cockroach and the ant come and mend him — the rough patches of the tortoise's shell are where they mended him.
summary.zh: 饑年，蜥蜴偷學到農夫的口訣——「岩石，開！……岩石，合！」——日日取薯。龜君哄其同行，貪多延宕，忘了合巖咒語；被農夫捉住，又被縛去對質裝死的蜥蜴。農夫一怒把龜砸個粉碎。蟑螂與螞蟻前來替他拼補——龜甲上那些粗糙的補丁，正是牠倆修補之處。

sensitivity.note: Living Yoruba tradition; Tortoise trickster cycle with a shell etiology, the greed-moral Ellis notes in his commentary.

passages.text: There was a famine, and a great scarcity of food all through the country. One day the lizard, searching in a plantation, found a large rock full of yams, and saw the owner cry "Rock, open," go in, take yams, come out, and say "Rock, shut" — whereupon the rock closed up. Every morning at cock-crow the lizard did the same. One day Tortoise met the lizard carrying yams, and wheedled out the secret: "No, I will not say a word to anyone. Please take me." They agreed to go together at cock-crow.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ellis, The Yoruba-speaking Peoples, ch. XIV (1894); not verbatim.

passages.text: At the rock the lizard opened it, took yams, and warned Tortoise it was time to go; but the bald-headed elf stayed behind, putting yams on his back, his head, his arms and his legs. The lizard went home, lit a fire, and lay on his back with his feet in the air as if dead. When Tortoise was ready to go he could not remember the right words; he said many words, but not the right ones, and the rock remained shut. By-and-by came the plantation-owner, opened the rock, found Tortoise inside, and beat him badly.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ellis, The Yoruba-speaking Peoples, ch. XIV (1894); not verbatim.

passages.text: "Who brought you here?" "It was the lizard who brought me." So the man tied a string to Tortoise and took him to the lizard's house, where the lizard lay on his back with his feet in the air. "I?" said the lizard. "You can see for yourself it is impossible. I am not in a state to go out. I have been sick here for three months, lying on my back." Then the man took Tortoise and smashed him. And Tortoise, groaning and moaning, said in a pitiful voice: "Cockroach, come and mend me. Ant, come and mend me." And the cockroach and the ant mended him — and the places where they mended him are those parts of Tortoise which are rough.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ellis, The Yoruba-speaking Peoples, ch. XIV (1894); not verbatim.

title.en: Yorimasa Slays the Night Monster
title.zh: 頼政誅夜怪

region.en: The Imperial palace, Kyoto
region.zh: 京都御所

period: Recorded 1912 (Davis, Myths & Legends of Japan)

source.work: F. Hadland Davis, Myths & Legends of Japan (1912)

summary.en: A shape-shifting night-haunt on the palace roof is driving the Emperor to death; the archer Yorimasa waits through thunder and lightning, brings the beast down with a single steel-headed arrow, and is rewarded with the sword King of Lions and the hand of Lady Ayame.
summary.zh: 夜怪每夜伏於紫宸殿頂，致天皇病篤；武士賴政於雷雨中張弓一箭射落此猿首虎身蛇尾之怪，獲賜獅子王之劍並娶女官菖蒲。

sensitivity.note: Medieval Japanese warrior legend recorded 1912 in Davis; passages are condensed paraphrases of a public-domain retelling, presented for comparative mythology.

passages.text: An Emperor lay seriously ill, kept from sleep every night by a horrible unaccountable noise on the roof of the Purple Hall of the North Star. At sunset a dark cloud crept from the eastern horizon and settled on the palace roof, and the courtiers who waited in the imperial bedchamber heard scratching sounds as if the cloud had changed into a beast with gigantic claws. Night after night the visitant returned and the Emperor grew worse, until it was clear that unless the monster was destroyed his Majesty would die.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Myths & Legends of Japan, ch. II 'Yorimasa' (Davis 1912); not verbatim.

passages.text: The court named Yorimasa as the one knight valiant enough for the task. He made his preparations - best bow, steel-headed arrows, armour under a hunting-dress and a ceremonial cap - and lay in concealment at sunset while thunder crashed and wind shrieked like a pack of wild demons. At midnight a black cloud rushed through the sky and stopped at the north-east corner of the roof; lightning flashed, and Yorimasa saw the gleaming eyes of a large animal. Noting the position, he bent his bow round as the full moon and shot. There was a roar of anger and a heavy thud as the monster rolled from the roof to the ground.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Myths & Legends of Japan, ch. II 'Yorimasa' (Davis 1912); not verbatim.

passages.text: Yorimasa and his retainer ran forward and despatched the creature, which was as large as a horse, with an ape's head, the body and claws of a tiger, a serpent's tail, bird's wings, and the scales of a dragon. From the moment it died the Emperor's health improved. His Majesty ordered the skin kept for ever in the Imperial treasure-house, presented Yorimasa with the sword Shishi-wo, the King of Lions, promoted him at court, and finally gave him the Lady Ayame, most beautiful of the ladies-in-waiting.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Myths & Legends of Japan, ch. II 'Yorimasa' (Davis 1912); not verbatim.

title.en: Yoshitsune and Benkei on Gojo Bridge
title.zh: 義經與弁慶五條橋之會

region.en: Gojo Bridge, Kyoto
region.zh: 京都五條大橋

period: Recorded 1912 (Davis, Myths & Legends of Japan)

source.work: F. Hadland Davis, Myths & Legends of Japan (1912)

summary.en: Trained by the King of the Tengu, the exiled boy Yoshitsune defeats the giant priest Benkei - who has collected 999 swords waylaying knights on Gojo Bridge - and wins him as a retainer for life.
summary.zh: 牛若丸（義經）受天狗之王傳授武藝，於五條大橋擊敗奪得九百九十九柄刀的強梁僧兵弁慶，弁慶遂終身追隨。

sensitivity.note: Medieval Japanese heroic legend recorded 1912 in Davis; passages are condensed paraphrases of a public-domain retelling, presented for comparative mythology.

passages.text: Yoshitomo had been killed fighting the all-powerful Taira, whose cruel leader Kiyomori sought to destroy his children. Their mother Tokiwa fled into hiding and at last consented to become the hated Kiyomori's wife - the only way to save her sons' lives - keeping Yoshitsune with her and whispering daily: remember your father Minamoto Yoshitomo; grow strong and avenge his death. At seven the boy was sent to a monastery to be made a monk, but in a lonely valley he flourished a little wooden sword against the rocks, singing fragments of war-songs and longing to right the wrongs the Taira had heaped on his family.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Myths & Legends of Japan, ch. II 'Yoshitsune and the Taira' (Davis 1912); not verbatim.

passages.text: One night a thunderstorm broke over the valley and a mighty giant with a long red nose, glaring eyes, bird-like claws and feathered wings stood before the boy - the King of the Tengu, ruler of the elves of the mountains. Admiring the boy's perseverance, he offered to teach him all there was to know of swordsmanship, and soon Yoshitsune could vanquish twenty small tengu at once. At fifteen he heard of Benkei, a wild giant of a bonze who waylaid knights on the Gojo Bridge of Kyoto and had already won nine hundred and ninety-nine swords. Yoshitsune went to meet him, playing his flute to show his unconcern.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Myths & Legends of Japan, ch. II 'Yoshitsune and the Tengu' (Davis 1912); not verbatim.

passages.text: Benkei disdained to fight what looked like a dreamy flute-playing boy, and this contempt so angered Yoshitsune that he kicked the halberd from the giant's hands. Leaping from side to side with tengu-trained agility, he mocked Benkei's swinging strokes until the giant grew weary, tripped him, and mounted triumphantly on his back. Amazed at defeat by so slight a victor - the son of Lord Yoshitomo - Benkei begged to become his retainer, and from that hour the two names were linked: together they drove the Taira to their last ruin at Dan-no-ura.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Myths & Legends of Japan, ch. II 'Yoshitsune and Benkei Fight' (Davis 1912); not verbatim.

title.en: The Ghost Armies of Dan-no-ura
title.zh: 壇之浦亡靈

region.en: Dan-no-ura strait, Shimonoseki
region.zh: 下關壇之浦

period: Recorded 1912 (Davis, Myths & Legends of Japan)

source.work: F. Hadland Davis, Myths & Legends of Japan (1912)

summary.en: Sailing past Dan-no-ura, Yoshitsune and Benkei meet a ghostly company of the drowned Taira clan; Benkei stills the phantoms with a rosary and prayers, and the crabs with warrior markings on their backs are said to be the ghosts of the defeated.
summary.zh: 義經與弁慶舟過壇之浦，遭平家亡靈阻擋；弁慶持數珠誦經鎮靜亡魂。漁人至今見幽軍出沒，謂背有甲紋之蟹乃平家武士之靈。

sensitivity.note: Medieval Japanese ghost legend recorded 1912 in Davis; passages are condensed paraphrases of a public-domain retelling, presented for comparative mythology.

passages.text: Yoshitsune and his henchman Benkei had arranged to cross in a ship from the province of Settsu to Saikoku. When they reached Dan-no-ura a great storm arose: mysterious noises came from the towering waves, a far-away echo of the din of battle, the rushing of ships, the whirling of arrows, the footfall of a thousand men. From the lashing crests there arose a ghostly company of the Taira clan, their armour torn and blood-stained, thrusting out vaporous arms to stop the boat.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Myths & Legends of Japan, ch. II 'Yoshitsune and Benkei Fight' (Davis 1912); not verbatim.

passages.text: Yoshitsune cried out for revenge even upon the ghosts of the Taira dead; but Benkei, always shrewd and circumspect, bade his master lay aside the sword, took out a rosary, and recited Buddhist prayers. Peace came to the great company of ghosts; the wailing ceased and the sea grew calm. Fishermen still see ghostly armies come out of the sea, wailing and shaking their long arms, and say the crabs with markings on their backs are the wraiths of the Taira warriors who drowned there.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Myths & Legends of Japan, ch. II (Davis 1912); not verbatim.

title.en: Raiko Slays the Goblin of Oyeyama
title.zh: 賴光退大江山鬼

region.en: Mount Oye (Oeyama), near Kyoto
region.zh: 大江山

period: Recorded 1912 (Davis, Myths & Legends of Japan)

source.work: F. Hadland Davis, Myths & Legends of Japan (1912)

summary.en: The Goblin King Shutendoji kidnaps and devours the young of Kyoto from his iron palace on Mount Oye; Raiko and five knight-companions go disguised as mountain priests, trick the goblins into drinking heaven-sent poison sake, and behead the monster in his sleep.
summary.zh: 大江山之鬼王酒吞童子擄食京都少年男女。賴光與四天王偽裝山伏潛入鐵宮，以神賜之毒酒灌醉群鬼，斬鬼王首級，救出被擄女子。

sensitivity.note: Medieval Japanese demon-slaying legend recorded 1912 in Davis; passages are condensed paraphrases of a public-domain retelling, presented for comparative mythology.

passages.text: In the reign of the Emperor Ichijo a demon dwelt on Mount Oye who could assume many forms. Slipping into Kyoto as a human being, he left home after home destitute of well-loved sons and daughters, whom he carried back to his mountain stronghold to mock and finally devour. Even the sacred Court was not exempt: the Goblin King Shutendoji snatched away the beautiful daughter of Kimitaka, and the Emperor summoned his council to plan the creature's destruction. All agreed that the doughty knight Raiko should be sent, with chosen companions, on this perilous adventure.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Myths & Legends of Japan, ch. II 'The Goblin of Oyeyama' (Davis 1912); not verbatim.

passages.text: Raiko chose five companions and bade them go disguised as mountain priests, armour hidden in unsuspicious knapsacks. Two knights prayed at the temple of Hachiman, God of War, two at the shrine of Kwannon the Goddess of Mercy, and two at the temple of Gongen. On Mount Oye's formidable path of rocks, forests, and bottomless chasms, three old men suddenly appeared - the deities themselves, now vindicating the prayers - and gave Raiko a jar of magical sake called Shimben-Kidoku-Shu, a cordial for men but poison for goblins, before vanishing into the clouds in miraculous light.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Myths & Legends of Japan, ch. II 'The Goblin of Oyeyama' (Davis 1912); not verbatim.

passages.text: A weeping princess washing a blood-stained garment in a stream led the band to a great palace of black iron and satisfied the sentinels with the mountain-priest story. In the mighty hall sat the Goblin King, gigantic, red-skinned, with a mass of white hair, feasting on food served by captive Kyoto women. When the feast was in full swing Raiko politely offered the magic sake; the Goblin King drank one cup, then a second, and all his goblins drank until they slept. The three deities appeared once more to say the demon's limbs were bound. Raiko's sword crashed down on the monster's neck; the severed head shot into the air, pouring smoke and fire from its nostrils, and a second blow laid it dead. The knights carried out the grim head, followed by a company of happy maidens released at last.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Myths & Legends of Japan, ch. II 'Raiko Slays the Goblin' (Davis 1912); not verbatim.

title.en: Raiko and the Mountain Spider
title.zh: 賴光誅山蜘蛛

region.en: Rendai plain and Kagura-ga-Oka, near Kyoto
region.zh: 京都近郊

period: Recorded 1912 (Davis, Myths & Legends of Japan)

source.work: F. Hadland Davis, Myths & Legends of Japan (1912)

summary.en: In Kenko Hoshi's darker version, Raiko and Tsuna follow a flying skull to a ruined mansion crowded with goblins; a beautiful woman turns out to be the Mountain Spider, whose carcass bursts open to yield 1,990 human skulls.
summary.zh: 另一傳本：賴光與碓井隨飛空骷髏至廢屋，遇百鬼夜行與妖女；妖女實為山蜘蛛，斬其腹竟湧出一千九百九十顆骷髏。

sensitivity.note: Medieval yokai legend (Kenko Hoshi variant) recorded 1912 in Davis; passages are condensed paraphrases of a public-domain retelling, presented for comparative mythology.

passages.text: In another version, written by Kenko Hoshi, Raiko left Kyoto with Tsuna, the most worthy of his retainers, and as they crossed the plain of Rendai a skull rose in the air and flew before them like a wind-driven thing until it vanished at Kagura-ga-Oka. There they found a ruined mansion where an old woman of strange aspect, dressed in white with white hair, opened her eyes with a small stick and let her breasts fall upon her knees. 'I am two hundred and ninety years old,' she said; 'I serve nine masters, and the house in which you stand is haunted by demons.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Myths & Legends of Japan, ch. II 'Another Version' (Davis 1912); not verbatim.

passages.text: From the kitchen Raiko saw a storm brewing, heard ghostly footsteps, and watched a great company of goblins crowd into the room. Then came a nun-like being with a face two feet long and arms white as snow and thin as threads, which laughed and vanished like mist; and when a cock crowed, a lovely woman appeared instead, more graceful than willow branches waving in the breeze. Her radiant beauty blinded him for a moment, and he found himself enveloped in countless cobwebs; he struck with his sword, and she disappeared, leaving the blade buried in the floor planks, its point broken, and covered with white blood.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Myths & Legends of Japan, ch. II 'Another Version' (Davis 1912); not verbatim.

passages.text: Search uncovered a den where a monster lay with many legs and an enormous downy head, its mighty eyes shining like sun and moon as it groaned that it was sick and in pain. The broken sword-point projected from its body; Raiko and Tsuna dragged it out and cut off its head, and from the wound in its stomach gushed nineteen hundred and ninety skulls, with spiders as large as children. Within the entrails were the ghostly remains of human corpses: the monster was the Mountain Spider.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Myths & Legends of Japan, ch. II 'Another Version' (Davis 1912); not verbatim.

title.en: Momotaro, or the Son of a Peach
title.zh: 桃太郎

region.en: A mountain village and the Demon Island of the North-Eastern Sea (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 桃太郎之島（象徵定位）

period: Recorded 1912 (Davis, Myths & Legends of Japan)

source.work: F. Hadland Davis, Myths & Legends of Japan (1912)

summary.en: An old couple find a boy born from a peach; at fifteen Momotaro sails to the devils' island with a dog, a monkey, and a pheasant bought with rice-cakes, slays the Demon King, frees the captives, and brings home treasure for his foster-parents.
summary.zh: 老夫婦拾桃得子，桃太郎十五歲攜飯糰上路，以飯糰收犬、猿、雉為從，渡海討鬼島，斬鬼王、救俘虜、奪寶歸鄉。

sensitivity.note: Classic Japanese folktale recorded 1912 in Davis; passages are condensed paraphrases of a public-domain retelling, presented for comparative mythology.

passages.text: While an old woman stood by a stream washing clothes, an enormous peach came floating down the water. Poor and hungry, she remembered the little verse about distant water being bitter and near water sweet, and sang it until the fruit stopped at her feet. That evening her husband was about to cut the peach open when it burst open of its own accord and the prettiest child imaginable tumbled out with a merry laugh. 'The Gods have heard how much you desired a child,' he said, 'and have sent me to be a solace and comfort in your old age.' They called him Momotaro, Son of a Peach.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Myths & Legends of Japan, ch. II 'The Adventures of Momotaro' (Davis 1912); not verbatim.

passages.text: At fifteen the lad towered above his fellows and longed for knightly heroism. He asked leave to sail to an island in the North-Eastern Sea where devils had captured a great company of innocent people and ate many of them, meaning to kill the devils, free the captives, and bring back the plunder for his foster-parents. His father consented, sure that no devil could harm a child sent from heaven. With rice-cakes from the old woman, Momotaro won over a growling dog, then a monkey, then a pheasant - each eating half a cake and joining the expedition.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Myths & Legends of Japan, ch. II 'The Triumph of Momotaro' (Davis 1912); not verbatim.

passages.text: The pheasant flew ahead to the devils' castle and demanded surrender and broken horns, but the devils only laughed and hurled iron bars. On shore Momotaro found two daimyos' daughters weeping over blood-soaked washing, and they showed him a way into the castle. Inside, the little band fought tenaciously; many devils fell from the parapets and were dashed to pieces, and all were destroyed except the Demon King, who begged for his life and was refused. Momotaro gave the captive King into the monkey's keeping, freed the prisoners, and gathered much treasure; the dog and pheasant carried the spoils home, and his foster-parents ended their days in peace and plenty.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Myths & Legends of Japan, ch. II 'The Triumph of Momotaro' (Davis 1912); not verbatim.

title.en: Tawara Toda, My Lord Bag of Rice
title.zh: 俵藤太退百足

region.en: Seta bridge, Lake Biwa
region.zh: 近江瀬田橋・琵琶湖

period: Recorded 1912 (Davis, Myths & Legends of Japan)

source.work: F. Hadland Davis, Myths & Legends of Japan (1912)

summary.en: The hero Hidesato climbs over a sleeping dragon on a bridge and so wins the Dragon King of Lake Biwa's trust; with saliva-smeared arrows he slays the monstrous centipede of Mount Mikami and receives inexhaustible rice, silk, and a fireless cooking-pot.
summary.zh: 俵藤太跨過橋上臥龍不懼，龍王請其誅食其子孫之百足怪；以唾塗箭簇射腦誅之，獲寶米、寶綢、寶鍋，遂號俵藤太。

sensitivity.note: Medieval Japanese hero legend recorded 1912 in Davis; passages are condensed paraphrases of a public-domain retelling, presented for comparative mythology.

passages.text: The great Hidesato came one day to the bridge over beautiful Lake Biwa and found the way blocked by a great serpent-dragon fast asleep. Without a moment's hesitation he climbed over the monster and walked on - and behind him the dragon became a man with red hair and a dragon-shaped crown, bowing with much ceremony. He was the Dragon King of Lake Biwa, who had taken a hideous shape to test for a fearless mortal; all men had fled at the sight of him, but a monstrous centipede came down from Mount Mikami, destroyed his children and grandchildren, and soon he himself would be devoured.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Myths & Legends of Japan, ch. II 'My Lord Bag of Rice' (Davis 1912); not verbatim.
