passages.text: They guard nine rivers; they guard nine mountains. The red flint stone is the stone of the red Mucencab. The red ceiba tree of abundance is his arbor which is set in the east. Reddish are their yellow turkeys; red toasted corn is their corn.
passages.note: Condensed from Roys translation (1933), ch. I; not verbatim throughout.

passages.text: The white flint stone is their stone in the north, with the white ceiba tree of abundance for arbor. The black flint stone is their stone in the west, with black speckled corn, black beans, and black wild pigeons for turkeys. The yellow flint stone is the stone of the south, with the yellow ceiba tree of abundance and yellow-green corn.
passages.note: Condensed from Roys translation (1933), ch. I; not verbatim throughout.

passages.text: The red wild bees are in the east, with the red Plumeria for their flower and a large red blossom for their cup; the white bees in the north, the black bees in the west, the yellow bees in the south. Then they swarmed at Cozumel in great numbers among the magueys, the calabash trees, the ceiba trees and the chulul trees of the land, and Kin Pauahtun was their priest.
passages.note: Condensed from Roys translation (1933), ch. I; not verbatim throughout.

title.en: The Sky Falls: Bolon-ti-ku Seizes Oxlahun-ti-ku
title.zh: 天空傾覆：博倫捉拿奧克斯拉洪

region.en: Chumayel, Yucatan, Mexico
region.zh: 墨西哥猶加敦丘馬耶爾

period: Chumayel MS. written late 18th c.; Roys translation 1933

source.work: The Book of Chilam Balam of Chumayel, trans. Ralph L. Roys, 1933, ch. X

license: Public domain (Roys 1933, not renewed at US Copyright Office)

summary.en: In Katun 11 Ahau the Ah Mucenca come forth to blindfold the faces of the Oxlahun-ti-ku, the thirteen sky gods; Bolon-ti-ku, the nine, seizes Oxlahun-ti-ku, wounds his head and despoils him of his insignia. Fire, rope, rocks and trees descend; the sky falls upon the earth; the four Bacabs are set up — and after the destruction, the four trees of abundance and the pillar of the sky raise a new world, which dawns with the count thirteen-plus-seven.
summary.zh: 十一阿赫卡特倫之際，穆肯卡布前來蒙蔽十三位天神奧克斯拉洪-提-庫的面容；博倫-提-庫擒之，傷其首，奪其徽記。火、繩、石、樹降下；天空塌落於大地；四巴卡布被立起——毀滅之後，四棵豐盈之樹與天柱立起新世界，以十三加七之數破曉。

sensitivity.note: Published colonial-era Yucatec text; quote/paraphrase of Roys public-domain translation only.

passages.text: It was Katun 11 Ahau when the Ah Mucenca came forth to blindfold the faces of the Oxlahun-ti-ku; but they did not know his name, except for his older sister and his sons. This was after the creation of the world had been completed, but they did not know it was about to occur. Then Oxlahun-ti-ku was seized by Bolon-ti-ku.
passages.note: Quoted from Roys translation (1933), ch. X; lightly condensed; not verbatim throughout.

passages.text: Then it was that fire descended, then the rope descended, then rocks and trees descended. Then came the beating of things with wood and stone. Then Oxlahun-ti-ku was seized, his head was wounded, his face was buffeted, he was spit upon, and he was thrown on his back as well. After that he was despoiled of his insignia and his smut.
passages.note: Quoted from Roys translation (1933), ch. X; lightly condensed; not verbatim throughout.

passages.text: There would be a sudden rush of water when the theft of the insignia occurred. Then the sky would fall, it would fall down upon the earth, when the four gods, the four Bacabs, were set up, who brought about the destruction of the world. Then, after the destruction of the world was completed, they placed a tree to set up in its order the yellow cock oriole. Then the white tree of abundance was set up. A pillar of the sky was set up, a sign of the destruction of the world.
passages.note: Quoted from Roys translation (1933), ch. X; lightly condensed; not verbatim throughout.

passages.text: He came from the seventh stratum of the earth when he came to fecundate Itzam-kab-ain, when he came with the vitality of the angle between earth and heaven. They moved among the four lights, among the four layers of stars. The world was not lighted; there was neither day nor night nor moon. Then they perceived that the world was being created. During the creation thirteen infinite series added to seven was the count of the creation of the world. Then a new world dawned for them.
passages.note: Quoted from Roys translation (1933), ch. X; lightly condensed; not verbatim throughout.

canonical_translation: Ralph L. Roys, The Book of Chilam Balam of Chumayel, Carnegie Institution of Washington, 1933

narrative.en:
The creation chapter of the Chumayel tells a cosmic coup. The ordered sky of the Oxlahun-ti-ku, the thirteen gods of the upper layers, is overthrown by Bolon-ti-ku, the nine gods of the lower layers, working through the Ah Mucenca — the earth-bearers who blindfold the faces of the thirteen so they cannot see what is coming. Once the thirteen are seized, the world above collapses: fire descends, the rope descends, rocks and trees descend, the sky itself falls upon the earth. Oxlahun-ti-ku is wounded, spat upon, thrown on his back, and despoiled of his insignia; with his regalia goes the order of the old world.

Then the water rushes in — the sky's fall brings the flood — and the four Bacabs, the gods who hold up the corners of the sky, are set up 'who brought about the destruction of the world'. After destruction, rebuilding begins in ritual order: the trees of abundance are planted in the four quarters and at the center (white north, black west, yellow south, green center), each with its bird perched as a sign; a pillar of the sky is raised as the record of the destruction; and the Piltec messengers are stationed at the four directions to conduct people to their lord. Ah Uuc Cheknal comes up from the seventh stratum of the earth to fecundate Itzam-kab-ain, the earth-crocodile, 'with the vitality of the angle between earth and heaven'.

What emerges is neither chaos-mystery nor flood alone but a calendar cosmology: the new world dawns with the count 'thirteen infinite series added to seven', the arithmetical signature of the Maya Long Count itself (13 and 7 being the root numbers of the tzolkin). The world is destroyed and re-created as a counting operation, and the red, white, black and yellow foundations and rulers are 'set up' like day signs. Greed descends from the heart of the sky; the first sun is snatched from the earth; famine follows; and the chapter ends by warning that the law of the katun will run its course and 'God will bring about a great deluge again which will be the end of the world' — the Maya end-of-katun doctrine fused, in this colonial text, with the Christian Second Coming over the valley of Jehoshaphat.

The ritual function of this chapter is renewal: it is the mythic charter of the New Year and katun-ending ceremonies in which the Bacabs, the world trees, and the four-colored foundations are ritually re-erected so that time may begin again. It is also a theological commentary on colonial conquest: the fall of the thirteen sky gods mirrors the fall of the old order before the 'perishable men, the perishable rulers' of the new katun.

functions: Charter of katun-ending and New Year renewal rites (Bacabs, world trees, four-colored foundations)
Explains the cosmological basis of the 13-7 arithmetic of the Maya calendar
Frames conquest-era suffering as one more cosmic overturning in a series

variants.name: Popol Wuj flood of the wooden people
variants.summary: The highland account likewise destroys a failed creation by black rain and re-creates the world; here the flood follows the theft of divine insignia and the fall of the sky.

sensitivity_guidance: The Chumayel is a colonial synthesis of pre-conquest myth and Christian commentary. Present it as a colonial-era document, not as timeless 'Maya belief'; note the Christian overlay rather than erasing it.

title.en: The Ritual of the Angels: Seven Graces in the Night
title.zh: 天使之儀：夜中七恩典

region.en: Chumayel, Yucatan, Mexico
region.zh: 墨西哥猶加敦丘馬耶爾

period: Chumayel MS. written late 18th c.; Roys translation 1933

source.work: The Book of Chilam Balam of Chumayel, trans. Ralph L. Roys, 1933, ch. XI

license: Public domain (Roys 1933, not renewed at US Copyright Office)

summary.en: When there was neither heaven nor earth, seven angels are born one by one in seven katuns of infinite night, each naming himself through his own effort: Alpilcon, Alba Congel, Atea Ohe, Decipto, Conlamil. Then God the Father awakens alone in the three-cornered precious stone of grace, declares 'I am the beginning and I shall be the end', and the heavens are set up with the four colored Pauahtuns.
summary.zh: 天地未分之時，七位天使在七個卡特倫的無盡黑夜中逐一誕生，各自獨力自名：阿爾皮爾康、阿爾巴·康格爾、阿特亞·奧赫、德西普托、康拉米爾。隨後天父獨自於三角恩典寶石中甦醒，宣告「我是始者，亦將是終者」，並以四色鮑豪頓立起諸天。

sensitivity.note: Published colonial-era text; quote/paraphrase of Roys public-domain translation only.

passages.text: Dominus vobiscum ended the words of their song when there was neither heaven nor earth. When the world was submerged, when there was neither heaven nor earth, the three-cornered precious stone of grace was born, after the divinity of the ruler was created, when there was no heaven. Then there were born seven tuns, seven katuns, hanging in the heart of the wind, the seven chosen ones.
passages.note: Quoted from Roys translation (1933), ch. XI; lightly condensed; not verbatim throughout.

passages.text: Thereupon he became man in the second infinite precious stone of grace. Then there arrived in the second katun Alpilcon, as the angel was named when he was born. In the third infinite precious stone of grace the angel was named Alba Congel; in the fourth, Atea Ohe, who said: 'Oh god, the ruler! I am after all nothing in myself.' In the fifth the angel was Decipto, who declared: 'Who might I be? I am a god, a ruler, after all.' And the seventh grace was born, and Conlamil was the name of his angel.
passages.note: Condensed from Roys translation (1933), ch. XI; not verbatim throughout.

passages.text: Then God the Father awoke to consciousness alone in person; in the three-cornered precious stone of grace he awoke to consciousness. There was one seal in the darkness, one seal on high. 'I am the beginning and I shall be the end.' These are his words in their mighty entirety. And these are the angels of the winds which were set up while he created the star, when the world was not yet lighted: the Red Pauahtun, the White Pauahtun, the Black Pauahtun, the Yellow Pauahtun.
passages.note: Condensed from Roys translation (1933), ch. XI; not verbatim throughout.

title.en: The Song of the Itza: Heresy Was Favored at Chichen Itza
title.zh: 伊察之歌：奇琴伊察縱容異端

region.en: Chichen Itza, Yucatan, Mexico
region.zh: 墨西哥猶加敦奇琴伊察

period: Chumayel MS. written late 18th c.; Roys translation 1933

source.work: The Book of Chilam Balam of Chumayel, trans. Ralph L. Roys, 1933, ch. XII

license: Public domain (Roys 1933, not renewed at US Copyright Office)

summary.en: A ritual lament sung by the Itza: Adam was created on the plain of Damascus, the black stone of terror was born, and then — 'a tender boy was laid at Chichen, when the evil man, the master of the army, came to seize the land.' Imix was the day the ruler was seized; 'Buried, buried!' was the cry; and the song remembers being 'tame animals to Mizcit Ahau' until his roguery ended.
summary.zh: 伊察人的儀式輓歌：亞當在大馬士革平原受造，恐怖的黑石誕生，隨後——「一個稚嫩的男孩被安置在奇琴，當那惡人、軍隊之主前來奪取土地之時。」伊米希之日王被擒；「埋了，埋了！」是眾人的哭喊；歌中又憶及自己曾是米茲西特·阿豪的「馴養之獸」，直至其暴虐終結。

sensitivity.note: Published colonial-era text; quote/paraphrase of Roys public-domain translation only.

passages.text: Damascus was the name of the plain where our first father, Adam, was created by God. Drops of moisture formed on the stones and bushes for the first time, created when there was no sky. However, at the same time there was born in the stone, the black stone of terror, the one named Verbum-tuorum, Ix-coal-tun, Ix-coal-cab, taken by the mistress of the world.
passages.note: Condensed from Roys translation (1933), ch. XII; not verbatim throughout.

passages.text: Ho! What is so precious as we are? It is the precious jewel worn on the breast. What is the distinction of righteous men? It is my mantle, my loin-cloth. So spoke the god. Then do you mourn for anyone? No one. A tender boy was laid at Chichen, when the evil man, the master of the army, came to seize the land. Woe! At Chichen Itza heresy was favored!
passages.note: Condensed from Roys translation (1933), ch. XII; not verbatim throughout.

passages.text: Imix was the day when the ruler was seized at Chikin-chen. Where thou art, there is the god. Buried, buried! This was their cry. On that first day of Yaxkin, that mighty day, 2 Akbal, they came. Woe! Force was brought to bear for the second time. For the third time was established the religious festival of our enemies. We were like tame animals to Mizcit Ahau; but an end comes to his roguery. I die, he said, because of the town festival; I shall come, he said, because of the destruction of the town.
passages.note: Condensed from Roys translation (1933), ch. XII; not verbatim throughout.

title.en: The Creation of the Uinal: Twenty Days That Made the World
title.zh: 烏納爾之創造：二十日造世

region.en: Chumayel, Yucatan, Mexico
region.zh: 墨西哥猶加敦丘馬耶爾

period: Chumayel MS. written late 18th c.; Roys translation 1933

source.work: The Book of Chilam Balam of Chumayel, trans. Ralph L. Roys, 1933, ch. XIII

license: Public domain (Roys 1933, not renewed at US Copyright Office)

summary.en: The first priest Napuc Tun records how the twenty-day month was created before the world: God marches east with his grandmothers and measures his own footstep, and then day by day creates — the first stairway from heaven on 2 Eb, the first candle on 6 Cib, death itself invented on 3 Cimi, the waters of the flood on 6 Muluc, and on 13 Akbal he waters the ground and shapes it into man.
summary.zh: 第一位祭司納普克·圖恩記載：世界未成之前，二十日之月已先受造——上帝偕祖母們向東而行，量其足跡；然後逐日創造：二厄布之日造自天而降的第一道階梯，六希布之日造第一支蠟燭，三西米之日發明死亡，六穆盧克之日諸谷沒於洪水，十三阿克巴爾之日澆水於地、塑之以成人。

sensitivity.note: Published colonial-era text; quote/paraphrase of Roys public-domain translation only.

passages.text: Thus it was recorded by the first sage, Melchisedek, the first prophet, Napuc Tun, the priest, the first priest. This is a song of how the uinal came to be created before the creation of the world. Then he began to march by his own effort alone, and his maternal grandmother, his maternal aunt, his paternal grandmother and his sister-in-law marched with him. There in the east he measured the footstep of our Lord, God the Father — this was the reason it was called counting off the whole earth.
passages.note: Condensed from Roys translation (1933), ch. XIII; not verbatim throughout.

passages.text: On 2 Eb he made the first stairway, descending from the midst of the heavens, in the midst of the water. On 3 Ben he made all things, as many as there are. On 4 Ix sky and earth were tilted. On 6 Cib the first candle was made; it became light when there was neither sun nor moon. On 7 Caban honey was first created. On 9 Cauac hell was first considered. On 10 Ahau wicked men went to hell. On 11 Imix rocks and trees were formed. On 12 Ik the breath of life was created — there was no death in it.
passages.note: Condensed from Roys translation (1933), ch. XIII; not verbatim throughout.

passages.text: On 13 Akbal he took water and watered the ground. Then he shaped it and it became man. On 1 Kan he first created anger because of the evil he had created. On 3 Cimi he invented death; it happened that our Lord God invented the first death. On 5 Lamat he established the seven great waters of the sea. On 6 Muluc all valleys were submerged, when the world was not yet created. Then the uinal was created, the earth was created; sky, earth, trees and rocks were set in order; all things were created by our Lord God, the Father.
passages.note: Condensed from Roys translation (1933), ch. XIII; not verbatim throughout.

title.en: The Itza Name the Towns and Wells
title.zh: 伊察為城鎮與水井命名

region.en: Yucatan, Mexico
region.zh: 墨西哥猶加敦

period: Chumayel MS. written late 18th c.; Roys translation 1933

source.work: The Book of Chilam Balam of Chumayel, trans. Ralph L. Roys, 1933, ch. II

license: Public domain (Roys 1933, not renewed at US Copyright Office)

summary.en: Marching from town to town, the Itza give every place a name that records what happened there: at Ake they were born; at Chikin-conot their faces turned west; at Tah-cab they stirred the honey; at Panabha they dug for water; at Mani their language was forgotten by them; at Caucel they all shivered with cold. The land is named by the story of the walking of the people.
summary.zh: 伊察人逐城而行，所經之處皆以其事命名：在阿克誕生；在奇金-科諾特面向西方；在塔-卡伯攪拌蜂蜜；在帕納巴挖井得水；在馬尼遺忘己語；在考塞爾人人發冷。大地之名，即是族人行走的故事。

sensitivity.note: Published colonial-era text; quote/paraphrase of Roys public-domain translation only.

passages.text: Then they arrived at Ppoole, where the remainder of the Itza were increased in number; they took the women of Ppole as their mothers. Then they arrived at Ake; there they were born at Ake. Then they came to Tixchel, where their words and discourse were prolonged. Then they arrived at Chikin-conot, where their faces were turned to the west.
passages.note: Condensed from Roys translation (1933), ch. II; not verbatim throughout.

passages.text: Then they arrived at Tzuc-oop, where they remained apart under the Anona tree. Then they arrived at Tah-cab, where the Itzas stirred the honey. Then they arrived at Panabha, where they dug for water. Then they arrived at Yobain, where the crocodile bewitched them through their maternal grandfather, their ruler at the seashore. Then they arrived at Caucel, where they all shivered with cold. Then they went to Mani, where their language was forgotten by them.
passages.note: Condensed from Roys translation (1933), ch. II; not verbatim throughout.

passages.text: These are the names of whatever towns there were and the names of the wells, in order that it may be known where they passed in their march, to see whether this district was good, whether it was suitable for settlement here. But these were the people who named the district, who named the wells, who named the villages, who named the land, because no one had arrived here in this neck of the land when we arrived here.
passages.note: Condensed from Roys translation (1933), ch. II; not verbatim throughout.

title.en: Hunac Ceel Puts Out His Head from the Sacred Well
title.zh: 胡納克·塞爾自聖井探首

region.en: Sacred Cenote of Chichen Itza, Yucatan, Mexico
region.zh: 墨西哥猶加敦奇琴伊察聖井

period: Chumayel MS. written late 18th c. (events legendary, Katun 13 Ahau); Roys translation 1933

source.work: The Book of Chilam Balam of Chumayel, trans. Ralph L. Roys, 1933, ch. II

license: Public domain (Roys 1933, not renewed at US Copyright Office)

summary.en: The Itza begin casting victims into the well of Chichen so their rulers may hear a prophecy — but no prophecy comes. Then Cauich, Hunac Ceel, puts out his head at the south lip of the well and comes forth to declare the prophecy himself. The court proclaims him ruler; he is seated in the house on high, the eagle is said to be his mother, and he removes the stones of Itzam into the water.
summary.zh: 伊察人開始將犧牲者投入奇琴之井，欲使統治者聽得神諭——然而神諭未至。此時考伊奇，即胡納克·塞爾，於井南緣探出其首，現身親自宣告神諭。朝臣遂擁之為王；他被安置於高屋之中，人言鷹為其母；他更將伊察姆之石投入水中。

sensitivity.note: Published colonial-era text; quote/paraphrase of Roys public-domain translation only.

passages.text: Then they began to be served; then those who were to be thrown arrived; then they began to throw them into the well that their prophecy might be heard by their rulers. Their prophecy did not come. It was Cauich, Hunac Ceel, Cauich was the name of the man there, who put out his head at the opening of the well on the south side.
passages.note: Quoted from Roys translation (1933), ch. II; lightly condensed; not verbatim throughout.

passages.text: Then he went to take it. Then he came forth to declare the prophecy. Then began the taking of the prophecy. Then began his prophecy. Then they began to declare him ruler. Then he was set in the seat of the rulers by them. Then they began to declare him head-chief. He was not the ruler formerly; that was only the office of Ah Mex Cuc. Now the representative of Ah Mex Cuc was declared ruler. The eagle, they say, was his mother.
passages.note: Quoted from Roys translation (1933), ch. II; lightly condensed; not verbatim throughout.

passages.text: Then he was set in the house on high in 13 Ahau, the sixth reign. Then he began to be treated as a lord; then obedience to the name of Ah Mex Cuc began; then he was served there at the mouth of the well. Chichen Itzam was its name because the Itza went there. Then he removed the stones of the land, the stones of the sowed land, the place of Itzam, and they went into the water. Then began the introduction of misery there at Chichen Itza.
passages.note: Condensed from Roys translation (1933), ch. II; not verbatim throughout.

title.en: The Face of the Sun Is Eaten
title.zh: 日面被食

region.en: Chichen Itza, Yucatan, Mexico
region.zh: 墨西哥猶加敦奇琴伊察

period: Chumayel MS. written late 18th c. (events of Katun 8 Ahau); Roys translation 1933

source.work: The Book of Chilam Balam of Chumayel, trans. Ralph L. Roys, 1933, ch. II

license: Public domain (Roys 1933, not renewed at US Copyright Office)

summary.en: In Katun 8 Ahau drought comes: the hoofs of animals burn, the seashore burns, a sea of misery. The face of the sun is eaten and darkened and extinguished, and terror fills the sky. Then comes Ix-Tziu-nene to introduce sin, a numerous army is seen, a gallows is built, and the archery of Ox-halal Chan begins — the blood of the rulers taken by the archers.
summary.zh: 八阿赫卡特倫之時，大旱降臨：獸蹄灼熱，海岸焚燒，苦難如海。日面被食、被蔽、被熄，恐怖彌天。隨後伊希-茲尤-內內前來引入罪孽，大軍現身，刑架築起，奧克薩拉爾·張之箭術始行——統治者之血為弓手所取。

sensitivity.note: Published colonial-era text; quote/paraphrase of Roys public-domain translation only.

passages.text: Katun 8 Ahau came. 8 Ahau was the name of the katun when their government occurred. Then there was a change of the katun, then there was a change of rulers. Then they introduced the drought. That which came was a drought, according to their words, when the hoofs of the animals burned, when the seashore burned, a sea of misery.
passages.note: Condensed from Roys translation (1933), ch. II; not verbatim throughout.

passages.text: Then the face of the sun was eaten; then the face of the sun was darkened; then its face was extinguished. They were terrified on high, when it burned at the word of their priest to them, when the word of our ruler was fulfilled. Then began the idea of painting the exterior of the sun. When they heard of that, they saw the moon.
passages.note: Condensed from Roys translation (1933), ch. II; not verbatim throughout.

passages.text: Then came the rulers of the land. It was Ix-Tziu-nene who introduced sin to us, the slaves of the land, when he came. Whereupon a numerous army was seen, and they began to be killed. Then a thing of terror was constructed, a gallows for their death. Now began the archery of Ox-halal Chan. Then the rulers of the land were called. Their blood flowed, and it was taken by the archers.
passages.note: Condensed from Roys translation (1933), ch. II; not verbatim throughout.

title.en: Prophecy for Katun 11 Ahau: The Beginning of Misery
title.zh: 十一阿赫卡特倫預言：苦難之始

region.en: Ichcaanziho (Merida), Yucatan, Mexico
region.zh: 墨西哥猶加敦伊察安西霍（梅里達）

period: Chumayel MS. written late 18th c.; Roys translation 1933

source.work: The Book of Chilam Balam of Chumayel, trans. Ralph L. Roys, 1933, ch. III

license: Public domain (Roys 1933, not renewed at US Copyright Office)

summary.en: Katun 11 Ahau is set upon the mat and the throne; Yaxal Chac is its face; the heavenly fan and bouquet descend. It is the beginning of the count because it is the katun when the foreigners arrived from the east, and with them: the beginning of tribute, of church dues, of purse-snatching, of blow-gun strife, of trampling on people, of robbery with violence, of forced debts — the beginning of our misery.
summary.zh: 十一阿赫卡特倫安設於席與座之上；亞克薩爾·查克為其面容；天扇與天花束自天而降。此乃計數之始，因其為異邦人自東方而來之卡特倫；隨之而來的是：貢賦之始、教稅之始、扒竊之始、吹箭之爭之始、踐踏人民之始、暴力劫掠之始、強制債務之始——我們苦難之始。

sensitivity.note: Published colonial-era text; quote/paraphrase of Roys public-domain translation only.

passages.text: Katun 11 Ahau is set upon the mat, set upon the throne, when their ruler is set up. Yaxal Chac is its face to their ruler. The heavenly fan, the heavenly wreath and the heavenly bouquet shall descend. The drum and rattle of the lord of 11 Ahau shall resound, when flint knives are set into his mantle.
passages.note: Quoted from Roys translation (1933), ch. III; lightly condensed; not verbatim throughout.

passages.text: 11 Ahau is the beginning of the count, because this was the katun when the foreigners arrived. They came from the east when they arrived. Then Christianity also began. The katun is established at Ichcaanziho. With the true God, the true Dios, came the beginning of our misery.
passages.note: Condensed from Roys translation (1933), ch. III; not verbatim throughout.

passages.text: It was the beginning of tribute, the beginning of church dues, the beginning of strife with purse-snatching, the beginning of strife with blow-guns, the beginning of strife by trampling on people, the beginning of robbery with violence, the beginning of forced debts, the beginning of debts enforced by false testimony, the beginning of individual strife, a beginning of vexation, a beginning of robbery with violence.
passages.note: Quoted from Roys translation (1933), ch. III; lightly condensed; not verbatim throughout.

title.en: Five Days of Eclipse: The Torch of Katun 13 Ahau
title.zh: 五日蝕：十三阿赫卡特倫之火炬

region.en: Yucatan, Mexico
region.zh: 墨西哥猶加敦

period: Chumayel MS. written late 18th c.; Roys translation 1933

source.work: The Book of Chilam Balam of Chumayel, trans. Ralph L. Roys, 1933, ch. XI

license: Public domain (Roys 1933, not renewed at US Copyright Office)

summary.en: The sky is set in its place by the first pope, the burden of Katun 13 Ahau — but the face of the sun shall be turned from its course and turned face down in the reign of the perishable rulers. For five days the sun is eclipsed, and then the torch of Katun 13 Ahau is seen: God's sign that death shall come to the rulers of the land and the first rulers driven from their towns.
summary.zh: 首任教皇——十三阿赫卡特倫之重負——將天空安置於其位；然而在朽壞統治者的朝代，日面將偏離其軌、翻身朝下。太陽蝕沒五日，其後十三阿赫卡特倫的火炬顯現：此乃上帝之兆，宣告死亡必臨此地統治者，最初的王將被逐出其城。

sensitivity.note: Published colonial-era text; quote/paraphrase of Roys public-domain translation only.

passages.text: Then the sky was put in its place, Corporales ti ojales, by the first pope, the face of the katun, the burden of the Katun 13 Ahau. The face of the sun shall be turned from its course, it shall be turned face down during the reign of the perishable men, the perishable rulers.
passages.note: Quoted from Roys translation (1933), ch. XI; lightly condensed; not verbatim throughout.

passages.text: Five days the sun is eclipsed, and then shall be seen the torch of Katun 13 Ahau, a sign given by God that death shall come to the rulers of this land. Thus it shall come about that the first rulers are driven from their towns. Then Christianity shall have come here to the land. The descendants of the former rulers are dishonored and brought to misery; we are christianized, while they treat us like animals.
passages.note: Condensed from Roys translation (1933), ch. XI; not verbatim throughout.

title.en: The Great Deluge Again: The Descent over Jehoshaphat
title.zh: 大洪水再臨：於約沙法谷降臨

region.en: Yucatan, Mexico
region.zh: 墨西哥猶加敦

period: Chumayel MS. written late 18th c.; Roys translation 1933

source.work: The Book of Chilam Balam of Chumayel, trans. Ralph L. Roys, 1933, ch. X

license: Public domain (Roys 1933, not renewed at US Copyright Office)

summary.en: When the law of the katun shall have run its course, God will bring about a great deluge again which will be the end of the world. When this is over, the Lord Jesus Christ shall descend on a great cloud over the valley of Jehoshaphat beside Jerusalem, to level off the world for the good and the bad, the conquerors and the captives.
summary.zh: 卡特倫之法運行既畢，上帝必再降大洪水，以為世界之終。洪荒既過，主耶穌基督將乘大雲降於耶路撒冷旁約沙法谷之上，為善人與惡人、征服者與被俘者，夷平世界。

sensitivity.note: Published colonial-era text; quote/paraphrase of Roys public-domain translation only.

passages.text: But when the law of the katun shall have run its course, then God will bring about a great deluge again which will be the end of the world. When this is over, then our Lord Jesus Christ shall descend over the valley of Jehoshaphat beside the town of Jerusalem where he redeemed us with his holy blood.
passages.note: Quoted from Roys translation (1933), ch. X; lightly condensed; not verbatim throughout.

passages.text: He shall descend on a great cloud to bear true testimony that he was once obliged to suffer, stretched out on a cross of wood. Then shall descend in his great power and glory the true God who created heaven and earth and everything on earth. He shall descend to level off the world for the good and the bad, the conquerors and the captives.
passages.note: Quoted from Roys translation (1933), ch. X; lightly condensed; not verbatim throughout.

title.en: The Language of Zuyua: The Interrogation of the Chiefs
title.zh: 祖尤瓦之語：審問諸酋

region.en: Zuyua (mythic place of power), Yucatan, Mexico
region.zh: 祖尤瓦（神權之地），墨西哥猶加敦

period: Chumayel MS. written late 18th c.; Roys translation 1933

source.work: The Book of Chilam Balam of Chumayel, trans. Ralph L. Roys, 1933, ch. IX

license: Public domain (Roys 1933, not renewed at US Copyright Office)

summary.en: The first head-chief interrogates the chieftains in the Language of Zuyua — a riddle-speech that only the lineage learned may answer. 'Bring me the firefly of the night' means a smoking tube of tobacco; 'the beckoning tongue of the jaguar' is fire; 'your daughter, pale of face' is a calabash of atole; 'the winged jaguar' is a horse with bells and a red-thread crest. Those who know are cheerful; the ignorant shall be sad and lose their seats.
summary.zh: 第一酋首以祖尤瓦之語審問諸酋——此謎語之言，唯受教於族系者能答。「夜之螢火蟲」意指煙管中的菸草；「 jaguar 的招引之舌」是火；「面容蒼白的妳的女兒」是一碗阿托莱玉米糊；「有翼的 jaguar」是繫鈴戴紅線冠的馬。知者喜悅，不知者憂愁而失其位。

sensitivity.note: Published colonial-era text; quote/paraphrase of Roys public-domain translation only.

passages.text: 'Son, bring me the firefly of the night. Its odor shall pass to the north and to the west. Bring with it the beckoning tongue of the jaguar.' 'It is well, father.' What he asks for is a smoking tube filled with tobacco. The beckoning tongue of the jaguar for which he asks is fire.
passages.note: Quoted from Roys translation (1933), ch. IX; lightly condensed; not verbatim throughout.

passages.text: 'Son, bring me your daughter that I may see her. Pale is her face and very beautiful. White are her head-covering and her sash.' What he asks for is a white calabash cup filled with atole. 'Son, bring me a woman with a very white and well rounded calf.' He wants a jicama: tucking back the skirt is peeling the skin. 'Bring me a very beautiful woman with a very white countenance; I will cast down her skirt and her loose dress before me.' This is a turkey-hen for him to eat; casting down her skirt means plucking its feathers.
passages.note: Condensed from Roys translation (1933), ch. IX; not verbatim throughout.

passages.text: Then our lord, the first head-chief, calls the chiefs: 'If you are head-chiefs here in the land, go and get the winged jaguar, and come and give it to me to eat. Put his bead collar on him properly, put on his crest properly.' Those who are ignorant shall be sad at heart and say nothing. This jaguar for which he asks is the chief's horse which he wishes to eat: the bead collar is its little bells; the crest is a red thread; it is to be completely saddled and bridled. The language of Zuyua.
passages.note: Condensed from Roys translation (1933), ch. IX; not verbatim throughout.

title.en: The Mounds the Great Men Built
title.zh: 偉人們所築之丘

region.en: Yucatan, Mexico
region.zh: 墨西哥猶加敦

period: Chumayel MS. written late 18th c.; Roys translation 1933

source.work: The Book of Chilam Balam of Chumayel, trans. Ralph L. Roys, 1933, ch. IV

license: Public domain (Roys 1933, not renewed at US Copyright Office)

summary.en: The history of how the mounds came to be constructed by the heathen: for three score and fifteen katuns they were constructed by the great men, thirteen katuns and six years in all — fifteen four-hundreds of scores of mounds and fifty more, all over the land, from the sea to the base of the land, with names for them and for the wells.
summary.zh: 記異教徒如何築丘：丘由偉人們築造，歷三又十五卡特倫，共十三卡特倫又六年——丘之總數十五個四百之計又五十，遍布全地，自海至地之基，丘與井皆有名字。

sensitivity.note: Published colonial-era text; quote/paraphrase of Roys public-domain translation only.

passages.text: The history which I have written of how the mounds came to be constructed by the heathen. During three score and fifteen katuns they were constructed. The great men made them. On this day I have written how the great mounds came to be built by the lineages and all the things which the rulers did; they were the ones who built the mounds.
passages.note: Condensed from Roys translation (1933), ch. IV; not verbatim throughout.

passages.text: It took thirteen katuns and six years for them to construct them. Fifteen four-hundreds were the scores of their mounds, and fifty more made the total count of the mounds they constructed all over the land. From the sea to the base of the land they created names for them as well as for the wells.
passages.note: Condensed from Roys translation (1933), ch. IV; not verbatim throughout.

title.en: The Foreigners Who Sucked Pond-Apples
title.zh: 吸食番荔枝的異邦人

region.en: Port of Ecab, Yucatan, Mexico
region.zh: 墨西哥猶加敦埃卡布港

period: Chumayel MS. written late 18th c.; Roys translation 1933

source.work: The Book of Chilam Balam of Chumayel, trans. Ralph L. Roys, 1933, ch. V

license: Public domain (Roys 1933, not renewed at US Copyright Office)

summary.en: In Katun 11 Ahau the foreigners seized the port of Ecab, coming from the east. They were the first to eat the pond-apple for breakfast, and so they were named: the foreigners who ate pond-apples, the foreigners who sucked pond-apples. Nacom Balam, the householder they seized at Ecab, was the first to be taken by the first captain, Don Juan de Montejo.
summary.zh: 十一阿赫卡特倫之際，異邦人自東方而來，奪取埃卡布港。他們是最早以番荔枝為早餐的人，因此得名：食番荔枝的異邦人、吸食番荔枝的異邦人。他們在埃卡布擒獲的屋主納科姆·巴拉姆，是首位被初代隊長胡安·德·蒙特霍擒獲的人。

sensitivity.note: Published colonial-era text; quote/paraphrase of Roys public-domain translation only.

passages.text: A record of the katuns and years when the Province of Yucatan was first seized by the foreigners, the white men. It was, they say, in Katun 11 Ahau that they seized the port of Ecab. They came from the east when they arrived. They say they were the first to eat the pond-apple for breakfast; this was the reason they called them the foreigners who ate pond-apples, foreigners who sucked pond-apples.
passages.note: Condensed from Roys translation (1933), ch. V; not verbatim throughout.

passages.text: This is the name of the householder whom they seized at Ecab: Nacom Balam was his name. He was the first to be seized at Ecab by the first Spanish captain, Don Juan de Montejo, the first conqueror. It was still the same katun when they arrived at Ichcaanziho. After the Itza were dispersed, it was fifteen score years when the foreigners arrived.
passages.note: Condensed from Roys translation (1933), ch. V; not verbatim throughout.

title.en: The Katun of the Plumeria Flower: Submit or Be Uprooted
title.zh: 雞蛋花卡特倫：順服或被連根拔起

region.en: Yucatan, Mexico
region.zh: 墨西哥猶加敦

period: Chumayel MS. written late 18th c.; Roys translation 1933

source.work: The Book of Chilam Balam of Chumayel, trans. Ralph L. Roys, 1933, ch. XV

license: Public domain (Roys 1933, not renewed at US Copyright Office)

summary.en: In the katun of the Plumeria flower comes the forceful one: head like a jaguar, long of tooth, body withered, heart pierced with sorrow — his speech false and mad. Chilam Balam counsels submission to the unhappy destiny of the katun: refuse, and you shall be moved from where your feet are rooted, gnaw the trunks of trees, and die as the deer die, going forth from your settlement.
summary.zh: 雞蛋花卡特倫之際，強橫者將至：首如 jaguar，齒長身枯，心如刀割——其言偽而狂。奇拉姆·巴拉姆勸眾順服卡特倫之厄運：若不順服，必被從立足之處連根拔起，啃食樹幹草莖，如鹿之死，倉皇離去。

sensitivity.note: Published colonial-era text; quote/paraphrase of Roys public-domain translation only.

passages.text: Then there shall be present the forceful one, there would be Nine Mountains, Yuma-une-tziuit, the quetzal, the green bird. No one understands the penance among the rulers in the twelfth tun when he declared his name. Like a jaguar is his head, long is his tooth, withered is his body, like a dog is his body. His heart is pierced with sorrow. Sweet is his food, sweet is his drink.
passages.note: Quoted from Roys translation (1933), ch. XV; lightly condensed; not verbatim throughout.

passages.text: Give yourselves up, my younger brothers, my older brothers, submit to the unhappy destiny of the katun which is to come. If you do not submit, you shall be moved from where your feet are rooted. If you do not submit, you shall gnaw the trunks of trees and herbs. If you do not submit, it shall be as when the deer die, so that they go forth from your settlement.
passages.note: Quoted from Roys translation (1933), ch. XV; lightly condensed; not verbatim throughout.

passages.text: Then even when the ruler himself goes forth, he shall return within your settlement bearing nothing. There shall come such a pestilence that the vultures enter the houses, a time of great death among the wild animals. There shall be three kinds of bread: the bread-nut shall be their bread in the katun of the Plumeria flower.
passages.note: Condensed from Roys translation (1933), ch. XV; not verbatim throughout.

title.en: The Birth of Shango in Nupeland
title.zh: 尚戈誕生於努佩之地

region.en: Oyo-Ile and Nupeland (symbolic pin: Old Oyo, Shango's royal seat)
region.zh: 舊奧約與努佩地帶（象徵定位：尚戈的王都舊奧約）

period: Yoruba oral tradition; recorded 1910-12 (Frobenius)

source.work: Leo Frobenius, The Voice of Africa, vol. I (London, 1913), ch. XI

summary.en: The Ibadan tellers make Oranjan (Oranyan) Shango's father: a great warrior who conquered and lost Ife, went to Okuland and married Yemodia, a woman of Takpa (Nupe) blood, taking no second wife; Shango was born in Nupeland and ruled at Old Ojo. The coast version says simply that Shango was the mightiest of the sons the All-Mother Yemaya bore at Ife — first royal ruler of the country, whose posterity still give Yoruba its kings.
summary.zh: 伊巴丹的講述者以奧蘭揚為尚戈之父：這位大戰士曾攻克伊費復又失守，遠行奧庫之地娶塔卡（努佩）血統的耶莫迪亞為妻，終生不二色。尚戈生於努佩之地，都於舊奧約。海濱版本則直言：尚戈乃是太母耶莫雅在伊費所生諸子中最強者——本國第一位君王，其子孫至今擁立約魯巴的國王。

sensitivity.note: Living Yoruba tradition; the royal genealogy tying the Alaafin line to Shango, recorded 1910-12 by Frobenius. Two competing origin versions (Ife theogony vs Nupeland genealogy) are preserved side by side as the source states.

passages.text: What was told in Ibadan was this: Oranjan was Shango's sire. His mother was Yemodia; Laro was Oranjan's father, and Yemodia's Aussi. Oranjan was a great warrior in Yoruba. He once conquered Ilife (Ife), but was driven forth again. He went to Okuland; there lived Yemodia, who was of Takpa (or Nupe) blood. There Oranjan married Yemodia. She was his only wife, and he took no second, as negroes do. Then Shango was born in Nupeland. Oranjan became king in Oduma-ushe. But Shango ruled in Old-Ojo.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Frobenius, The Voice of Africa, vol. I, ch. XI (1913); not verbatim.

passages.text: The myths on the Coast relate that Shango was the mightiest man born of the All-Mother, Yemaya, in Ife — as powerful, as warlike and as mighty a God as was ever created in the minds of a nation striving for self-expression in great ideas. This country's first royal ruler sprang, as its people believe, from his loins; his posterity still have the right to give the country its kings.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Frobenius, The Voice of Africa, vol. I, ch. XI (1913); not verbatim.

title.en: Shango Forces His Two Captains to Fight
title.zh: 尚戈逼使二將相殘

region.en: Old Oyo, Nigeria (the court where the king demanded endless war)
region.zh: 奈及利亞舊奧約（國王索戰不休的宮廷）

period: Yoruba oral tradition; recorded 1910-12 (Frobenius)

source.work: Leo Frobenius, The Voice of Africa, vol. I (London, 1913), ch. XI

summary.en: Passionately devoted to war, King Shango sent his two high officers, Mokwa and Timi, out day after day to raze towns in his name — and spat fire at them for not doing more. When the two complained together, he constrained them to fight each other; Mokwa at length slew his friend Timi, then declared he would kill the king too. Shango bade him call the people; the assembly decreed that Shango must depart the land within five days, and he went of his own free will.
summary.zh: 尚戈王酷嗜征伐，日日遣兩員重臣莫克瓦與蒂米出兵毀城，稍有不力便口噴烈焰。二人同來陳情，王竟逼他們自相殘殺；莫克瓦終手刃摯友蒂米，繼而宣言亦要誅王。尚戈命他召集群眾公斷；民意裁定：五日之內，王必須離境。尚戈遂自願出走。

sensitivity.note: Living Yoruba tradition; the expulsion of the war-king that precedes his deification (Frobenius 1913). Mokwa and Timi survive as the names of real Yoruba chieftaincies (Mokwa, Timi of Ede).

passages.text: When Shango was King of Ojo he had two Ironse (high officers or courtiers). One was Mokwa (or Mogba), the other Timi Agbala-Olofa-no. Shango was passionately devoted to war, so he often sent Timi and Mokwa out, who waged war and destroyed towns in his name. He was so warlike that at last the people of Ojo assembled, saying: "Our king wastes all the country round; we desire a ruler who will give us, not slaves, but meat." They sent an embassy to Shango: "Thou hast been king; thou wert too strict; thou wert too cruel; wicked thou art. Therefore, thou shalt cease to be king."
passages.note: Paraphrase of Frobenius, The Voice of Africa, vol. I, ch. XI (1913); not verbatim.

passages.text: Mokwa related: "Shango sent forth Timi and Mokwa every day to wage war. He said at morn, 'Go, do thus and thus!' At night we came, saying, 'It has been done!' Shango answered: 'Nay, I am not content. To-morrow ye must forth, and do yet more.' Each day we went; Shango spat fire and bade us go. One day we two came unto him, saying: 'Thou dost naught but vomit flames from forth thy mouth. Enough!' Then said Shango: 'Ye are come one with the other to complain of me. But, now, I will constrain ye that ye fight one with another.' So we fought, for we were compelled. I, Mokwa, slew Timi at length. Timi, Mokwa's friend, lay dead. Then Mokwa spake to Shango: 'Thou forcedst me to slay this man. He was not mine enemy. Therefore I will slay thee also.' Shango spake: 'How? Thou wouldst slay me? Call the people together in the city; hearken unto them. And mark thou what cometh to pass.'"
passages.note: Paraphrase of Frobenius, The Voice of Africa, vol. I, ch. XI (1913); not verbatim.

passages.text: Mokwa called the people and spoke unto them thus: "Each day Royal Shango sent Mokwa and Timi forth to raze the cities and to slay. They waxed faint. They complained. Shango constrained them to contend. They contended. Mokwa slew Timi. Mokwa said to Shango the king: 'Now will I kill thee also.' Shango said: 'Call the people.' I, Mokwa, did so. Ye are here; say ye what shall be done!" The people cried: "Shango must depart the land within five days." Thus they spake to Shango. He took a rope and went away into the forest. This is how it came to pass. It is true that none could slay Shango. He departed of his own free-will.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Frobenius, The Voice of Africa, vol. I, ch. XI (1913); not verbatim.

title.en: "What Mokwa Can, I Can": Shango Burns and Rises
title.zh: 「莫克瓦能者吾亦能」——尚戈焚而復生

region.en: Old Oyo, Nigeria (the pyre in the middle of the road)
region.zh: 奈及利亞舊奧約（大道中央的柴堆）

period: Yoruba oral tradition; recorded 1910-12 (Frobenius)

source.work: Leo Frobenius, The Voice of Africa, vol. I (London, 1913), ch. XI

summary.en: In one account of Shango's passing, the king orders a wood-pile twenty-four feet high piled in the middle of the road, drenched with palm kernels and oil, and sets the torch — then throws his captain Mokwa upon it. Mokwa is consumed, and comes to life again. Astonished, Shango declares, "What Mokwa can, I can. But I will not be a man, I will become an Orisha!" and hangs himself in the bush wearing his skin apron and sixteen cowries; he becomes an Orisha and ascends into heaven, the cowries sacred to him ever after, and Mokwa becomes his first priest.
summary.zh: 一說尚戈命人在大道中央堆起二十四尺高的柴堆，澆以棕櫚油與果仁，親自點火——隨即把部將莫克瓦擲上火堆。莫克瓦焚盡，竟又復活。尚戈大驚，宣言：「莫克瓦能者，吾亦能。然吾不願再為人，吾將成神！」遂披皮裙、佩十六貝幣，入林自縊；自此他成為奧里莎，直上青天。貝幣從此為其聖物，莫克瓦則成其首位祭司。

sensitivity.note: Living Yoruba tradition; the death-and-apotheosis of Shango (Frobenius 1913). Strong cross-tradition fit for the death-and-resurrection cluster. Cross-refs: egyptian-osiris-cycle, norse-ragnarok (renewal), christian-passion-resurrection.

passages.text: Once, when Mokwa was at war, Shango sent word to the people of Ojo to make a wood-pile not less than twenty-four feet high in the middle of the road. Palm kernels and palm oil were to be poured upon it. Everything was prepared and Shango applied the torch. When the blaze was at its height, Shango threw Mokwa on top of it. But when Mokwa had been consumed he came to life again. Shango was greatly astonished. He said: "What Mokwa can, I can. But I will not be a man, I will become an Orisha!"
passages.note: Paraphrase of Frobenius, The Voice of Africa, vol. I, ch. XI (1913); not verbatim.

passages.text: Thereupon he took his apron, which was made of skin, and sixteen cowrie shells. He went into the bush and hanged himself upon an Anjo tree. So Shango became an Orisha and ascended into heaven; the cowries were sacred to him, for one throws them for him (oracle), and thus Mokwa became his first priest.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Frobenius, The Voice of Africa, vol. I, ch. XI (1913); not verbatim.

title.en: Shango's Triple Commandment
title.zh: 尚戈三誡

region.en: Old Oyo and Kushi, Nigeria (the Anjo tree on the road to Kushi)
region.zh: 舊奧約與庫希（往庫希路旁的自縊之樹）

period: Yoruba oral tradition; recorded 1910-12 (Frobenius)

source.work: Leo Frobenius, The Voice of Africa, vol. I (London, 1913), ch. XI

summary.en: Shango, born in Takpaland, set his people a threefold law: first truth — lying he loathed; second, none should poison another; third, none should steal or break the bounds of mine and thine. Whoso offends against this triple commandment, Shango — now an Orisha — will slay: he appears in the Ara, the thunderstorm, and kills with the stone Ara-dung, the meteorite. As a living king he was an Oni-Sheggo, a sorcerer; his two deputies were the good Ossenj and the wicked Edju, and setting out to meet Edju at Kushi he hanged himself on an Anjo tree by the way, then went up into the sky by a chain.
summary.zh: 生於塔卡之地的尚戈為民立三誡：一曰真——謊言為其所憎；二曰無相鴆；三曰勿竊、勿逾你我之界。凡犯此三誡者，已成神的尚戈必誅之：他顯形於「阿剌」雷暴之中，以「阿剌敦」隕石殺人。生前他是行蠱的「奧尼謝戈」；麾下二將，善者奧森傑，惡者埃茹。他往庫希去會埃茹，途中在一棵安喬樹上自縊，而後循鐵鏈升天。

sensitivity.note: Living Yoruba tradition; the ethical commandments attached to Shango's cult (Frobenius 1913) — an unusual theomorphic law-code. Recorded 1910-12.

passages.text: Shango the King was born in Takpaland. The first thing he demanded was the truth; lying he loathed. Nor, secondly, was it his will that people should poison each other. Thirdly, he set his face against the Yorubans stealing from each other and going into each other's houses in the cities and disregarding the laws of meum and tuum. If any offend against this triple commandment, Shango, who is to-day an Orisha, will slay him. Shango will appear in the Ara, the Thunderstorm, and he kills with the stone Ara-dung, or our meteorite.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Frobenius, The Voice of Africa, vol. I, ch. XI (1913); not verbatim.

passages.text: While Shango lived he was an Oni-Sheggo and ascended to heaven by a chain. He killed himself on high, and this was the way of it: in war he had two Enondje (deputies or envoys), one of whom was very good, the other very evil. The bad one was Edju, the good one Ossenj. One day Ossenj said to the King, then dwelling in Ojo, that Edju had told him Shango could not return. Now, Edju was then in Kushi in Yorubaland. So Shango set out to meet him, but hanged himself on his way on an Anjo tree. This is why the people still appeal to him always as Obaku-su! Then he went up into the sky by a chain.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Frobenius, The Voice of Africa, vol. I, ch. XI (1913); not verbatim.

title.en: Shango on the Storm-Ram, and the Stones in the Fields
title.zh: 雷羊背上的尚戈與田中石斧

region.en: Ibadan, Nigeria (symbolic pin: the fields where thunderbolts are found)
region.zh: 奈及利亞伊巴丹（象徵定位：拾得雷石的田間）

period: Yoruba oral tradition; recorded 1910-12 (Frobenius)

source.work: Leo Frobenius, The Voice of Africa, vol. I (London, 1913), ch. XI

summary.en: Shango rides the storm: "When Shango rides across the heavens in a storm, he stands upon the backs of goats, and his favourite food is ram." Stone axes dug from the fields are his missiles — a peasant who finds one sets it on the god's altar and prays for rains and plenty; and his effigies show two dynasties, the elder Taba Shango masked as a ram over his fire-medicine, the later Mesi Shango always on horseback.
summary.zh: 尚戈乘風而行：「雷暴橫天之時，尚戈足踏群羊之背；公綿羊是他至愛的祭饌。」田中掘得的石斧即其飛石——農夫拾得便供上神壇，禱求風調雨順、五穀豐登。其神像分兩朝：古老的塔巴尚戈以公羊假面覆其火藥秘藏；後起的梅西尚戈則永遠跨騎戰馬。

sensitivity.note: Living Yoruba tradition; the thunderbolt-stone (celt) cult is well attested across the Sudan (Frobenius 1913). The sun-ram parallel (Ammon) is Frobenius's comparison; tagged sun-capture only as interpretive cluster link.

passages.text: On the last day of my stay in Ibadan I was looking in the yard at my horse, which was fresh and lustily pawing the ground. An old Yoruban looked at it admiringly and compared the freshness of my steed to the vigour of Shango's rams. The old fellow, on further questioning, said: "When Shango rides across the heavens in a storm, he stands upon the backs of goats and his favourite food is ram." Shango's effigy in Ojo is a ram's mask which conceals his holy, light-giving magic.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Frobenius, The Voice of Africa, vol. I, ch. XI (1913); not verbatim.

passages.text: The symbols of divinity are almost always present on all royal gates as well as on the portals leading to temples: little stone axes, the missiles of the God; the wedges decorated with stone hatchet heads, the Ose-Shango; the long-handled Shango-rattles; and the great leathern wallets, or Laba-Shango. There is a plethora of emblems set up in the temples and on country roadsides, which always express the twofold prayer to the God to send the blessed and fertilizing rain without the loss of human life by strokes of lightning. But when the peasant finds an ancient stone axe in his fields, he carefully picks it up and puts it among his produce or upon the altar of the God as the symbol and instrument of his might, praying him to bless his crops and send him rains.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Frobenius, The Voice of Africa, vol. I, ch. XI (1913); not verbatim.

passages.text: One of the royal house said that most certainly the Alafins derived their descent from Shango the Thunder God, but that there had been two different Shangos: the elder was the Takpa or Taba, and the other the Mesi, Shango. The name of the former shows that he came from Nupeland, but the latter from Borgu, where Mesi, in all the old histories and tales, is the name of the King. Legend maintains that the Mesi Shango dynasty was conquered and driven out by reason of the Taba Shango's renewed accession to power. Mesi Shango are said to be always represented on horseback; Shango Taba, however, was always shown in the guise of a ram. There are two such ram-masks in Ojo, forming the lid of a casket which had held the fire medicine of this God.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Frobenius, The Voice of Africa, vol. I, ch. XI (1913); not verbatim.

title.en: The Fire-Dance of Shango: Ear, Tongue and Eye Restored
title.zh: 尚戈踏火之舞——耳舌眼復生

region.en: Ibadan, Nigeria (the fire-pot carried in the great festival)
region.zh: 奈及利亞伊巴丹（大祭中頂在頭上的火壇）

period: Yoruba oral tradition; recorded 1910-12 (Frobenius)

source.work: Leo Frobenius, The Voice of Africa, vol. I (London, 1913), ch. XI

summary.en: At Shango's great festival the fire-dancer carries a ritual pot of the Jena, Shango's fire, on his head. Charged with magic, he works miracles: stoops and picks up a handful of earth that turns to salt or cowries; cuts off an ear which the sacred flame replaces; removes his tongue and it grows again; plucks out an eye, burns it, swallows it — and sees with the recreated optic as distinctly as ever. But the performer must first have made the power of Ossenj his own, for no miracles without Ossenj. At the solstice every hearth is extinguished and each family carries home a brand from Shango's fire: the birth of the new year.
summary.zh: 尚戈大祭之日，踏火者頭頂盛著「耶納」聖火的祭壇。他借符力顯奇：俯身拾土，土化為鹽或貝幣；割下一耳，聖火為之再生；扯下舌頭，復又長回；剜出一眼，燒之吞下——新生的眼卻看得分明如昔。但行奇蹟者必先得「奧森傑」之力——無奧森傑則無奇蹟。冬至之祭，萬火俱熄，家家自尚戈聖火取一根火種而歸：新年由此誕生。

sensitivity.note: Living Yoruba tradition; Shango fire-dance (Frobenius 1913) — fire-walking with the Ose-Shango remains part of Shango devotional performance. Recorded 1910-12; described as the source states it.

passages.text: One of the most interesting of the cult's offerings is the fire-dance. The dancer has a ritual pot (Adjeri) or basket (Agba) on his head, in which burns the Jena, or Shango fire. He at first takes an apparently reckless turn or two, which completely loads him up with magic forces, enabling him to perform miracles with ease. He can stoop and pick up a handful of earth which turns into salt or cowrie-shells. He can cut off one of his ears, which the sacred flame on his head will replace. He can remove his tongue from his neck, and the sacred flame will make it grow again there. He pulls out an eye, burns it and swallows it; but the fire-dancer's optic will be recreated and he will see with it again as distinctly as ever. This kind of dance is carried out at the great seven-day festival and the Batta drummer drums to it.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Frobenius, The Voice of Africa, vol. I, ch. XI (1913); not verbatim.

passages.text: Through it all we must not forget that these people believe that the great god Shango himself could not do these marvellous things without help: the fire-dancer has first to make the power of Ossenj his own. The fire-pot is brought back to the Shango priest at the close of this magical day; and when it is relighted in the following year the Shaman will well knead the head and the body of the dancer, so as to shield him from the hurt of the fire. No miracles without Ossenj! Should this festival be held at the time of the solstice, fires are everywhere extinguished and every one takes a brand from the burning fire of Shango to his home. Then this is the birth of the New Year for the ministers of Shango.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Frobenius, The Voice of Africa, vol. I, ch. XI (1913); not verbatim.

title.en: Elogun-Shango: The God Seizes a Dancer
title.zh: 埃洛貢尚戈——神附舞者之身

region.en: Ibadan, Nigeria (the temple court and the road to the Bale's house)
region.zh: 奈及利亞伊巴丹（廟庭與通往巴萊宅邸的街路）

period: Yoruba oral tradition; recorded 1910-12 (Frobenius)

source.work: Leo Frobenius, The Voice of Africa, vol. I (London, 1913), ch. XI

summary.en: Shango descends quite unexpectedly on some dancer's head: the inspired one rushes to the temple chamber, seizes the carved Ose-Shango club or the holy rattle, and capers before the crowd — and everyone agrees one possessed by Shango dances differently from ordinary folk. The Batta drummer joins; the whole procession follows the dancer home, and the Bale takes off his own cap and lays it on the ground before the deity in human shape — the utmost homage a man whose forehead never bends to earth can be expected to pay. One man told Frobenius he woke to find all doing him obeisance, not remembering what had happened.
summary.zh: 尚戈突降於某舞者之頂：被附身者狂奔入廟，抓起雕工精美的奧謝尚戈杖或聖鈴，在眾人前手舞足蹈——人皆言，被尚戈附身者舞姿迥異常人。鼓師擊巴塔鼓相隨，全城尾隨舞者歸宅；巴萊（村長）竟摘下自家冠帽置於神附之身前的地上——額不觸地之人所能致的最高敬禮。一名經歷者自述：醒來方知眾人皆向自己跪拜，事前渾然不覺。

sensitivity.note: Living Yoruba tradition; orisha-possession (Elogun-Shango) remains central to Shango devotion in Yorubaland and the diaspora. Frobenius records a first-person account; presented as archival testimony.

passages.text: The stories told by those who have assisted at these festivals and exaltations of feeling sound very much the same. Shango descends quite unexpectedly upon some man or woman dancer's head. The inspirationist rushes madly to the Banga, seizes an Ose-Shango, a beautifully carved club, or a Shere-Shango, that is, the holy rattle. This individual begins to caper before the others. The afflatus is patent. All agree in this: a being possessed by Shango or any other Orisha dances quite differently from ordinary folk. The beater of the sacred Batta drum joins the dancer, and they leave the temple court with all the rest at their heels. He dances to his own house, followed by them all, and then everyone well knows that this person is a friend, a darling of Shango's.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Frobenius, The Voice of Africa, vol. I, ch. XI (1913); not verbatim.

passages.text: Arrived at his home, the God-favoured one will provide sacrificial rams, cowries, kola and drink for the commune, so that they all may know and experience the gratitude he feels. In Ibadan there is one road always taken by these temporary inspired ones: it leads to the house of the Bale in office. The dance goes on in the courtyard, and the master of the house will certainly honour this dancer by the grace of God: he takes off his Bale cap, the Akitajo, and lays it on the ground before the deity in human shape — the utmost homage which so great a man, whose forehead never bends to earth unless the headsman's glaive parts head from trunk, can be expected to pay.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Frobenius, The Voice of Africa, vol. I, ch. XI (1913); not verbatim.

passages.text: A highly-esteemed person told how, some years ago, Shango had made him his mouthpiece to the people. He had danced with the rest and danced very swiftly; someone asked whether there was likely to be an Elogun-Shango (a God-inspired one) that day, and somebody said you never could tell — not even the augur, nor even the person himself, for it might happen to anyone. Then he had felt very strange; he was compelled to rush to the temple chamber and snatch up an Ose-Shango. What came next he was unable to say; but he felt very jolly and drank a lot that evening and went to sleep drunk. Everyone did him obeisance next day, and that was the first time he heard what had happened.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Frobenius, The Voice of Africa, vol. I, ch. XI (1913); not verbatim.

title.en: Oya Sweeps the Road Before the Thunderer
title.zh: 奧雅為雷神清道

region.en: River Niger country (symbolic pin: the storm-wind preceding the storm over the Niger)
region.zh: 奈及利亞尼日河鄉（象徵定位：雷暴前掃過尼日河的疾風）

period: Yoruba oral tradition; recorded 1910-12 (Frobenius)

source.work: Leo Frobenius, The Voice of Africa, vol. I (London, 1913), ch. XI

summary.en: In the Ibadan version Shango's only wife was Oja, the lake — a mighty huntress of leopard, antelope and elephant with her younger brother at her side; after Shango's marriage and self-sought death she transformed herself into the River Niger. An Ilesha man added that she had first been married to Ogun, who was so evil she ran away to Shango; she still performs her wifely duty and sweeps the road before him clean in the wind that heralds the storm, ranks as mother of Shango's children and thus of the Alafins, and abides in the sky with him. Her priests and priestesses always sacrifice sheep, never goats; goats are forbidden to be killed or eaten.
summary.zh: 伊巴丹版本中，尚戈唯一的妻子是湖澤女神奧雅——豹鹿象皆其所獵的巾幗獵手，幼弟常隨左右。尚戈自縊之後，她化身為尼日河。伊萊沙的講述者又說：她原嫁暴戾的奧貢，不堪其惡而逃奔尚戈；至今雷暴之前的疾風，正是她為夫君清道；她是尚戈諸子、亦即歷代阿勞芬王的母親，與夫同住天界。其祭司只獻羊，永不殺羊、永不食羊。

sensitivity.note: Living Yoruba tradition; Oya (Oja) as the Niger and storm-wind, recorded 1910-12. Goat taboo in Oya cult reported by Frobenius.

passages.text: In the Ibadan version, Shango's only wife was Oja, the lake. Now, Oja was a mighty huntress and followed the chase with exceeding skill; she hunted all the wild things in the bush, leopards, antelopes and elephants, and had a younger brother, her constant companion on the trail. After Shango's marriage and suicide, Oja transformed herself into the River Niger.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Frobenius, The Voice of Africa, vol. I, ch. XI (1913); not verbatim.

passages.text: An Ilesha man supplied this supplement: Oja was Shango's spouse; she still performs her wifely duty and sweeps the road before him clean. She had before been married to Ogun, who was so evil that she ran away to Shango, married and lived with him. Oja ranks as the mother of Shango's children and thus of the Alafins, the blood-royal of Ojo. In her present form she abides in the sky with Shango. When the festival of Oja is at hand, i.e., in December or January, many people go to the river and make her offerings. Oja's priests and priestesses always sacrifice sheep, but never goats to this deity: goats are forbidden to be killed or eaten.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Frobenius, The Voice of Africa, vol. I, ch. XI (1913); not verbatim.

title.en: Nini, the Son of Shango, Is No More
title.zh: 尚戈之子尼尼已逝

region.en: Old Oyo, Nigeria (the Batta drum sounding the death proclamation)
region.zh: 奈及利亞舊奧約（巴塔鼓宣告死訊之地）

period: Yoruba oral tradition; recorded 1910-12 (Frobenius)

source.work: Leo Frobenius, The Voice of Africa, vol. I (London, 1913), ch. XI

summary.en: Shango had a son, Nini, killed in one of his many wars. The drum, Batta, was beaten and proclamation made: "Nini, the son of Shango, is no more!" And since that time Nini's death is a topic forbidden at the dying hour of a Shango descendant — a prohibition tied, it is said, to some magical spell whose quintessence could not be grasped even by Frobenius.
summary.zh: 尚戈有一子名尼尼，歿於連年征戰之一。巴塔大鼓擂響，宣告於眾：「尚戈之子尼尼已逝！」自那時起，凡尚戈子孫臨終之際，「尼尼之死」便成禁忌之語——相傳此事繫於某種咒法，其真義連記錄者也未能參透。

sensitivity.note: Living Yoruba tradition; a death-taboo etiology inside the Shango cycle (Frobenius 1913).

passages.text: There is a wonderful story of Nini's death. For Shango, namely, had a son, called Nini, killed in one of his many wars. The drum, Batta, was beaten and proclamation made: "Nini, the son of Shango, is no more!" And since that time, Nini's death is a topic forbidden at the dying hour of a Shango descendant. I never could grasp this legend's quintessence, which is said to relate to some magical spell.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Frobenius, The Voice of Africa, vol. I, ch. XI (1913); not verbatim.

title.en: Children of the Gods: Clans, Taboos and the Speech of the Old Man
title.zh: 神之子嗣——氏族、禁忌與老者之言

region.en: Northern Yoruba (symbolic pin: clan compounds of Ibadan)
region.zh: 約魯巴北部（象徵定位：伊巴丹的氏族院落）

period: Yoruba oral tradition; recorded 1910-12 (Frobenius)

source.work: Leo Frobenius, The Voice of Africa, vol. I (London, 1913), ch. X

summary.en: The whole Yoruban nation is totemistically organized in clans, each descended from a God through the male line; the divine founder's food-taboo (Ewuo) descends to his youngest offspring, and exogamy forbids marriage between children of the same Godship. When Frobenius asked whether one might leave one's clan for another Orisha, he was laughed at — even a convert to Islam or Christianity cannot escape the bonds of the clan: "You have a father and a mother... you can honour or dishonour them, but you will never be able to disown them and choose others. So also it is with the Orishas."
summary.zh: 整個約魯巴族按圖騰氏族組織，每族經父系溯源於一位神祇；開族之神的食物禁忌（埃武奧）傳給最幼的後嗣，同神子孫不得通婚。當弗羅貝紐斯問能否改投別神的氏族，人們為之失笑——即使改宗回教或基督教，也脫不了氏族之羈絆：「你總有父母。可以敬他們，也可以辱他們，但永遠不能撇開他們另認他人。奧里莎亦復如是。」

sensitivity.note: Living Yoruba tradition; the clan-descendant (omo-orisha) structure recorded 1910-12. The old man's speech is paraphrased from Frobenius's account.

passages.text: The whole Yoruban nation is totemistically organized in several clans, at the head of each of which there is a God from whom all its members derive descent. Some animals are unpleasing in this God's sight, for which reason his descendants must eschew them, and this is the foundation of totemistic food-taboo, or Ewuo. This food-taboo is handed down in the paternal line from the divine founder of the clan to his youngest offspring. The law imposes exogamy, prohibiting intermarriage between descendants of the same Godship; and although branches of the same family may have diverged so far that no member of them can call to mind any relation to the paternity of the other line, two young people observing the same food-taboo must give each other a wide berth, by reason of their assumed consanguinity.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Frobenius, The Voice of Africa, vol. I, ch. X (1913); not verbatim.

passages.text: No person can ever leave his or her clan in order to adopt the paternal and original ancestorship of another Orisha. Whenever anyone was questioned as to this possibility, the questioner was laughed at for his pains, because of the implied absurdity of such an inquiry; for even though one should become a Mahommedan or a Christian, he cannot any way escape from the bonds of the clan. An old black gentleman to whom the query was put answered it very simply: "You have a father and a mother. You should honour these, your parents. You can, however, also disgrace your father and mother. But you will never be able to disown them and choose others. Everyone comes from two parents and he cannot alter the fact. The only question is, whether he honours or dishonours them. So also it is with the Orishas."
passages.note: Paraphrase of Frobenius, The Voice of Africa, vol. I, ch. X (1913); not verbatim.

title.en: Breaking Kola for the Orisha: How the House-Priest Is Chosen
title.zh: 為神剖柯拉果——家祭司之選

region.en: Yoruba compound (symbolic pin: the family altar within a compound near Ile-Ife)
region.zh: 約魯巴院落（象徵定位：伊費近郊家宅祭壇）

period: Yoruba oral tradition; recorded 1910-12 (Frobenius)

source.work: Leo Frobenius, The Voice of Africa, vol. I (London, 1913), ch. X

summary.en: When the family priest, the Abosha, dies, the whole family meets at the altar with a vessel of water and two kola-nuts; kneeling with foreheads in the dust, they ask the Orisha to choose a new Abosha. Each candidate's name is put as the nuts are thrown — four sections flat, four convex means divine consent; any other split means rejection and another name is tried. At the year's great festival the same oracle asks the family God whether anyone of the household will die this year; if the answer is unfavourable, the wrath of the God — usually the transgression of a food-taboo — must be bought off with ever more ample sacrifice until the nuts fall even.
summary.zh: 家祭司「阿博夏」去世後，闔族攜清水一壺與柯拉果兩枚到祭壇前，跪地額觸塵土，請神自選新祭司。逐一唱名擲果：四瓣平面朝上、四瓣凸面朝上即為神許；否則換名再擲。年終大祭時，同法問神：家宅中今年是否有人將死？若卦象不吉——多半是有人犯了食物禁忌——便須祭品重重、一再加碼，直至柯拉果八瓣均分，神怒方平。

sensitivity.note: Living Yoruba tradition; household divination recorded 1910-12. The kola-oracle (Acqua-bi-fosa, breaking kola for the Orisha) is described in detail by Frobenius.

passages.text: At the decease of an Abosha the whole family meets to elect a new one. The family approaches the altar with a vessel full of water and two kola-nuts. The water and the nuts having been offered up, they pray the Orisha, on bended knees and with their foreheads in the dust, to choose for them a new Abosha of the house and compound to conduct henceforth the sacrifices and the festivals. The two kola-nuts are divided into their eight natural sections, which are thrown while the name of an honoured member of the family is mentioned in the question: "Wilt thou have M.N. for thy Abosha?" The person so named becomes the Abosha by the Orisha's choice, if four of the sections fall on the flat, and four on the convex side; but if they fall unequally divided, it signifies the named one's rejection, and the oracle game is repeated with different names until the positions of the sections are equal, which indicates the divine consent to the appointment.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Frobenius, The Voice of Africa, vol. I, ch. X (1913); not verbatim.

passages.text: At the great festival the Chief of the Compound begs the Abosha to perform the sacrificial rites. The entire family — all the adherents of the Orisha here worshipped — meet in front of the altar. The Abosha offers up the water and the kola-nuts, extends them on his palm towards the altar, saying, "Behold!" and asks: "Will anybody of this household die this year?" He throws them down and interprets the augury by the relative positions of the segments, favourably or the reverse. If the latter, a hostile influence must be placated: the probable explanation, as they think, is that the anger of the God has been caused by some member of the family's transgression of a food-taboo, or Ewuo, at some time or other. He must therefore be appeased, and the most ample, most numerous and most valuable sacrifices must be offered; these made, the Abosha repeats the business with the nuts until they lie four and four in similar positions, an assurance that for this year at least the ancestral deity will not demand the death of any member of the family.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Frobenius, The Voice of Africa, vol. I, ch. X (1913); not verbatim.

title.en: The Egun Dancer: Speaking in the Dead's Piping Treble
title.zh: 埃貢舞者——以亡者之聲開言

region.en: Yoruba town (symbolic pin: funeral courtyard near Ile-Ife)
region.zh: 約魯巴城鎮（象徵定位：伊費近郊喪儀庭院）

period: Yoruba oral tradition; recorded 1910-12 (Frobenius)

source.work: Leo Frobenius, The Voice of Africa, vol. I (London, 1913), ch. X

summary.en: At a person's death and funeral, the shroud is removed from the body once more before being for ever hidden; a wooden mask has been prepared and is assumed by one of the mourners, who, wrapping the shroud around him, dances among the relatives, speaks to them in the piping treble of the dead so represented, consoles, exhorts and talks with them concerning work. This Egun dancer is regarded as a direct personification of the departed; the mask is set up when offerings are made to the shade, and is often held in estimation as an Orisha — though, being the impersonation of the dead, it can in reality be nothing more than a small fraction of the deity.
summary.zh: 人死出殯之際，裹屍布在永藏之前要再展開一次；木雕面具早已備好，由一名送葬者戴上，裹以屍布，在親屬之間起舞，以亡者的尖細假聲與眾人對話——安慰、勉勵、交代家中事務。這位埃貢舞者被視為亡者的直接化身；向亡靈獻祭時面具亦被設座受祭，常被尊為奧里莎——雖然它只是亡者的一角化身。

sensitivity.note: Living Yoruba tradition; Egun/Egungun ancestral masquerade recorded 1910-12 (Frobenius's account complements Ellis 1894). Cross-ref: yoruba-egungun-messenger-deadland.

passages.text: Another is Egun or Egungun. Egun is at first a mask. At a person's death and his funeral, the shroud is removed from the body once more before being for ever hidden. A wooden mask has been prepared and assumed by one of the mourners, who, wrapping the shroud around him, dances among the relatives, speaks to them in the piping treble of the dead so represented, consoles, exhorts and talks with them concerning work and so on. This Egun dancer is regarded as a direct personification of the departed.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Frobenius, The Voice of Africa, vol. I, ch. X (1913); not verbatim.

passages.text: This mask is set up when offerings are made to the shade, and it is assumed that it receives them itself. This Egun is also often held in estimation as an Orisha, without having any justifiable claim to this high title, since, being the impersonation of the dead, it can in reality be nothing more than a small fraction of the deity.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Frobenius, The Voice of Africa, vol. I, ch. X (1913); not verbatim.

title.en: Esse, the Fish with Breasts and a Human Face
title.zh: 埃塞——有乳房與人面的魚

region.en: The great river, Northern Yoruba (symbolic pin: manatee waters of the Niger at Lokoja)
region.zh: 約魯巴北部大河（象徵定位：洛科賈附近的尼日河儒艮水域）

period: Yoruba oral tradition; recorded 1910-12 (Frobenius)

source.work: Leo Frobenius, The Voice of Africa, vol. I (London, 1913), ch. X

summary.en: In the great river lives a large fish which has breasts and a human face: the Esse. Hunters of it fasten an Ogu, a magic, at the head of their javelins; after three days' hunting and prodding the Esse puts in an appearance, its flesh is distributed at discretion, but the shaman gets the bones. It is caught on the seashore when it comes to land to graze — Frobenius identified it as the manatee. It was once worshipped as an Orisha; one day, owing to some misunderstanding, there was a quarrel with it, since when the Yorubans kill it wherever they can — though a clan in the land of Lubu still pays it honour, its myths having trickled in from the Mande and Fulbe.
summary.zh: 大河之中棲著一尾巨魚，有乳房、具人面，名為「埃塞」。獵者以符咒繫於標槍之首，追獵三日，埃塞方才現身；其肉任人分食，骨架歸巫師。據說牠有時上岸吃草，因此也被人於海濱捕獲——弗羅貝紐斯斷定此即儒艮。牠曾被人奉為奧里莎；後因誤會與人結怨，自此約魯巴人見之即殺——但盧布之地仍有一氏族向牠致敬，其神話由曼德與富爾貝部落傳入。

sensitivity.note: Living Yoruba tradition; the deified-then-demoted manatee (Esse), recorded 1910-12 — an example of orisha manufacture and abandonment noted by Frobenius.

passages.text: In the great river there lives a large fish which has breasts and a human face. Its name is Esse. The hunters of it fasten an Ogu, or magic, at the head of their Ofas (a javelin). After three days' hunting and prodding, the Esse puts in an appearance. Its flesh is distributed at discretion, but the Shaman gets the bones. Sometimes this Esse is caught on the seashore when it comes to land to graze.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Frobenius, The Voice of Africa, vol. I, ch. X (1913); not verbatim.

passages.text: It was once worshipped as an Orisha. But one day, owing to some misunderstanding, there was a quarrel with it, since when the Yorubans see in it only a fish like any other and kill it wherever they can. Yet everybody knows that the Esse once upon a time was a human being living in Lubu on the borders of Enjille. There in the land of Lubu there is a clan which still pays honour to Esse. But the Orisha of that ilk is at present unknown in Yoruba proper. It was tracked and found to be nothing but the Manatee, the Ma of the Mande tribe and the Adju of the Houssas; the myths about it, current among the Mande and Fulbe tribes, trickled into North Yoruba, and in this way a new Orisha appeared on this people's horizon.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Frobenius, The Voice of Africa, vol. I, ch. X (1913); not verbatim.

title.en: Ossenj: The Wizard-Power Behind Every God
title.zh: 奧森傑——諸神身後的巫力

region.en: Yoruba country (symbolic pin: the shaman's house of iron staves near Ile-Ife)
region.zh: 約魯巴地方（象徵定位：伊費近郊巫師宅中的鐵柱）

period: Yoruba oral tradition; recorded 1910-12 (Frobenius)

source.work: Leo Frobenius, The Voice of Africa, vol. I (London, 1913), ch. X

summary.en: Behind the whole Orisha system stands Ossenj — the power of wizardry — worked by the Ada-ushe, the shaman-physicians. Only a child of Ossenj may become a shaman; the art is inherited from a dying father, perfected by years of travel to famous masters, and stamped by the god's medicine. Every orisha priest is subordinate to the shaman, for from Ossenj alone comes the magic that animates gods and men: the Shango priest must fetch his fire-protection from a shaman before dancing with fire, and even the great god Shango, they say, could only win the height of his power through the witchcraft of a shaman.
summary.zh: 整個奧里莎體系的背後，矗立著「奧森傑」——巫術之力，由「阿達烏謝」（巫醫）執掌。唯奧森傑之子可為巫；其術承自垂死的父親，再歷經多年遊歷名師而後大成，並以神賜之「藥」為印。凡奧里莎祭司皆隸屬於巫——因為能賦神與人以靈力的，唯有奧森傑：尚戈祭司欲在祭典踏火，必先向巫師求取護身之力；傳說連大神尚戈本人的威權，也是從一位巫師的巫術中得來的。

sensitivity.note: Living Yoruba tradition; the shaman (Ada-ushe, Onisegun) institution recorded 1910-12. Ossenj = Osun (the medicine power), distinct from the river goddess Oshun in Frobenius's usage.

passages.text: The Yorubans, in common with almost all other African nations, believe in malignant, unrealizable, supernatural powers at the beck and call of but a very few persons specially endowed by heredity to control them. Only one class of man can afford such defence and is able to do battle against these nocturnal beings, namely, the Shamans, whom the Yorubans call Ada-ushe. This Ada-ushe's ordinary calling is that of a medicine-man, or physician, who is a master of much pharmaceutical knowledge. But it is possible to possess this not so much by descent from Ossenj, but rather by being inspired because of this descent; and the art has to be regularly learnt and carefully studied.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Frobenius, The Voice of Africa, vol. I, ch. X (1913); not verbatim.

passages.text: When an aged Ada-ushe feels the pressure of years all too heavy upon him and is plagued by premonitions of death, he begins to indoctrinate his son, so that he may, in time, be his equal in knowledge and skill. After his own father's induction he has to take up his staff and go travelling for many a year, visiting famous exponents of his father's professional caste, paying for his lore and instruction, and wends his way onwards. Only an Om-Ossenj (child of the Ossenj) may become an Ada-ushe, and this Godhead gives him the medicine which stamps him as a Shaman of the first water. Every Orisha priest is also subordinate to the Ada-ushe, for from Ossenj alone is derived the source of the power of magic, which animates both Gods and men: before the ministrant to Shango dances with the fire at this deity's holy feast, he fetches the power to protect himself from an Ada-ushe. And even the God Shango, in the beginning of things, could only win the height of his power and might through the witchcraft of an Ada-ushe — thus, from Ossenj.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Frobenius, The Voice of Africa, vol. I, ch. X (1913); not verbatim.

title.en: Edju Brings the Sixteen Palm-Nuts Down to Men
title.zh: 埃茹攜十六聖果下凡

region.en: Kukuruku border country (symbolic pin: the palm-plantation where the monkeys dropped the nuts)
region.zh: 庫庫魯庫邊地（象徵定位：群猴擲果的棕櫚園）

period: Yoruba oral tradition; recorded 1910-12 (Frobenius)

source.work: Leo Frobenius, The Voice of Africa, vol. I (London, 1913), ch. XII

summary.en: The Gods went hungry: men no longer offered them burnt sacrifice, and even pestilence and lightning-bolts could not bring them back to the altars. Yemaya counselled Edju that men do not fear death — give them something so good they will yearn to go on living. Orungan told him of a great thing made of sixteen palm-nuts; the monkeys gave him the nuts and counselled him to go round the world and ask their meaning everywhere, sixteen sayings in each of sixteen places. Edju went, returned to the sky, and told the Gods; knowledge passed to men, who could then read each day's fate and escape what was coming by offering sacrifice — and this was the way Edju brought the Ifa palm-nuts down to men.
summary.zh: 眾神斷糧：人間久無燔祭，瘟疫與雷擊也嚇不回信眾。耶莫雅教埃茹：人不怕死——須賜他們求之若渴之物，他們才想活下去。奧倫岡指點他：有一件由十六枚棕櫚仁織成的「大事」；群猴獻果，並教他環遊世界、十六處各聽十六訓，方能解其玄機。埃茹依言行遍天下，歸天轉授眾神；知識下及人間，人們從此能日日占知禍福、以祭品消災——這便是埃茹把伊法聖果帶到人間的經過。

sensitivity.note: Living Yoruba tradition; the Edju version of the Ifa-origin myth (Frobenius 1910-12), the trickster-teacher variant complementing the Elegba bargain variant. Cross-ref: yoruba-ifa-elegba-bargain.
