Waking at the moor of Tajihi, the emperor learned of the fire and sang of the flames still bright at Naniha; at the Ohosaka mountain a woman warned him that armed men barred the way, so he went round by Tagima and dwelt in the temple of the Deity of Isonokami.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Kojiki, Wikisource pages 373-375 (trans. Chamberlain 1882); not verbatim.

passages.text: His brother Midzu-ha-wake came for an audience, and was told: 'I am in doubt whether perhaps you may not be of like mind with King Sumi-no-ye-no-naka-tsu. Return down and slay him, and come up again; then I will surely meet and speak with thee.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Kojiki, Wikisource pages 375-376 (trans. Chamberlain 1882); not verbatim.

passages.text: Midzu-ha-wake bribed the man-at-arms Sobakari with the promise of the Prime Ministership; Sobakari watched his king enter the privy and thrust him to death with a spear. At a halt and sudden feast at the mountain entrance the King bestowed the promised rank, then - while the great cup hid the traitor's drinking face - drew a sabre laid under the matting and cut off his head, judging that one who had slain his lord could not be suffered to live; the place was called Chika-tsu-Asuka. Going up to Isonokami he reported the deed done, and was received.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Kojiki, Wikisource pages 376-377 (trans. Chamberlain 1882); not verbatim.

title.en: Ingyou's Cure and the Hot-Water Trial of Surnames
title.zh: 允恭天皇療疾與湯沸定姓

region.en: Amakashi cape, Asuka (Nara), Japan
region.zh: 甘樫丘（飛鳥）

period: Kojiki compiled 712 CE (trans. Chamberlain 1882)

source.work: Kojiki, trans. Basil Hall Chamberlain (1882)

summary.en: Wo-asa-dzu-ma-waku-go (Ingyou), long sick, at first declines the throne; the ruler of Shiragi dutifully sends eighty-one tribute vessels whose chief envoy, deeply versed in medicine, cures him. To end the confusion of false surnames and gentile names, he sets jars of boiling water at the Wondrous Cape of Eighty Evils in Words at Amakashi and settles the surnames of the eighty heads of companies by ordeal.
summary.zh: 雄朝津間稚子宿禰天皇（允恭）久病辭位，新羅獻貢船八十一艘，其大使妙於醫術，醫愈天皇之疾。又患天下氏姓錯亂，於甘樫丘之誓湯丘設沸湯之鼎，令八十氏族長就湯以定氏姓。

sensitivity.note: Ancient Japanese court myth (Kojiki); passages are condensed paraphrases of public-domain translations, presented for comparative mythology.

passages.text: The Heavenly Sovereign Wo-asa-dzu-ma-waku-go-no-sukune dwelt in the Palace of Toho-tsu-Asuka and ruled the Empire. When first about to rule the succession of Heaven's Sun, he declined, saying: 'I have a long sickness; I cannot rule the sun's succession' - but from the Empress downwards all the magnates strongly urged him, and he forthwith ruled.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Kojiki, Wikisource pages 379-380 (trans. Chamberlain 1882); not verbatim.

passages.text: At this time the ruler of Shiragi dutifully sent eighty-one vessels with august tribute across the sea. The chief envoy who accompanied the tribute, Komu-ha-chimu-kamu-ki-mu, was a man deeply versed in the medical art, and with his skill he cured the Heavenly Sovereign's august sickness - the long illness that had made him refuse the throne was healed.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Kojiki, Wikisource page 380 (trans. Chamberlain 1882); not verbatim.

passages.text: Lamenting the transgressions in the surnames and gentile names of the people - many claiming names that were not theirs - the emperor placed jars for trial by hot water at the Wondrous Cape of Eighty Evils in Words at Amakashi, and deigned to establish by ordeal the surnames and gentile names of the eighty heads of companies.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Kojiki, Wikisource pages 380-381 (trans. Chamberlain 1882); not verbatim.

title.en: Karu and the Great Lady of Karu: Banishment and Double Death
title.zh: 輕皇子與輕大娘皇女：流放與殉死

region.en: Iyo hot springs (Dogo Onsen), Japan
region.zh: 伊予溫泉（道後）

period: Kojiki compiled 712 CE (trans. Chamberlain 1882)

source.work: Kojiki, trans. Basil Hall Chamberlain (1882)

summary.en: Chosen to succeed but discovered to have debauched his younger sister, the Great Lady of Karu, the Heir Apparent Karu of Ki-nashi loses all support to Prince Anaho, flees, is besieged and surrendered by the Noble Oho-mahe Wo-mahe, and is banished to the hot waters of Iyo. The Queen So-tohoshi follows him out of love, and when she at last reaches him they sing and kill themselves together.
summary.zh: 草香幡梭皇子之妹輕大娘皇女（衣通姬）之美動天下。輕皇子與其妹私通，事聞，眾叛而歸安康王。輕皇子遁於忍馬屋小前老女之家被圍，由大前小前宿禰獻出，流放伊予溫泉。衣通姬追之不得，二人相會而歌，遂同時自殺。

sensitivity.note: Ancient Japanese court myth (Kojiki); passages are condensed paraphrases of public-domain translations, presented for comparative mythology.

passages.text: After the decease of the Heavenly Sovereign it was settled that King Karu of Ki-nashi should rule the Sun's succession. But in the interval before his accession he debauched his younger sister the Great Lady of Karu, singing proud rustic songs of sleeping well whatever people might plot against him.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Kojiki, Wikisource pages 382-383 (trans. Chamberlain 1882); not verbatim.

passages.text: Therefore all the officials and likewise the people of the Empire turned from the Heir Apparent Karu to the August Child Anaho. Karu, alarmed, fled into the house of the Noble Oho-mahe Wo-mahe and made implements of war; Anaho likewise, raised an army, and beleaguered the house, singing through the heavy ice-rain at the gate.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Kojiki, Wikisource pages 383-384 (trans. Chamberlain 1882); not verbatim.

passages.text: The Noble Oho-mahe Wo-mahe came dancing and singing, 'Come not with arms against the King thine elder brother - people will surely laugh. I will secure him and present him to thee.' Anaho disbanded his troops; the noble secured Prince Karu, presented him, and the captive prince was banished to the hot waters of Iyo, singing on the road of the mats he might not defile and of his sister whom he loved like a true jewel and a mirror.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Kojiki, Wikisource pages 384-386 (trans. Chamberlain 1882); not verbatim.

passages.text: Queen So-tohoshi presented a song to the banished prince, and being unable to restrain her love went after him. When she reached the place where he pensively waited he sang: if they said his sister, whom he loved like a true jewel, were there, he would go home and long for his country - and having thus sung, they forthwith killed themselves together.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Kojiki, Wikisource pages 387-389 (trans. Chamberlain 1882); not verbatim.

title.en: The Child King Mayowa Avenges His Father
title.zh: 安康天皇與稚子熊娃之復仇

region.en: Yamato court (Nara), Japan
region.zh: 大和宮廷（奈良）

period: Kojiki compiled 712 CE (trans. Chamberlain 1882)

source.work: Kojiki, trans. Basil Hall Chamberlain (1882)

summary.en: The Grandee of Ne steals the jewel headdress sent as a gift by King Oho-kusaka and slanders him, so the Heavenly Sovereign Anaho slays Oho-kusaka and takes his wife as empress. Warning his drowsing empress that he fears her son Mayowa will one day avenge his father, the emperor is overheard by the seven-year-old boy himself, who watches until Anaho sleeps and cuts off his head with the great sword, then flees to the Grandee Tsubura.
summary.zh: 根臣竊取大草香皇子所獻印齒珠而讒之，穴穗天皇遂殺大草香皇子，奪其妻為后。后携前夫之子稚子熊娃居宮中。天皇語后：「吾懼其子長大知我弒其父而復仇。」時七歲稚子熊娃在廊下聞之，俟帝晝寢，取大刀斬帝首，逃入平群臣之家。

sensitivity.note: Ancient Japanese court myth (Kojiki); passages are condensed paraphrases of public-domain translations, presented for comparative mythology.

passages.text: The Heavenly Sovereign sent the Grandee of Ne to King Oho-kusaka on behalf of his younger brother Prince Oho-hatsuse, to command the presentation of the King's younger sister Queen Waka-kusaka in marriage. Oho-kusaka dutifully promised her and sent back, as a ceremonial gift for the emperor, a push-wood jewel headdress.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Kojiki, Wikisource page 390 (trans. Chamberlain 1882); not verbatim.

passages.text: The Grandee of Ne stole the jewel headdress and slandered the King, reporting that Oho-kusaka had refused the Imperial Commands and grasped his sword in anger. The Heavenly Sovereign, in great anger, slew King Oho-kusaka, took that King's chief wife Nagata-no-oho-iratsume, and made her Empress.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Kojiki, Wikisource page 390 (trans. Chamberlain 1882); not verbatim.

passages.text: Sleeping at midday, the emperor asked his Empress what was on her mind, and she answered nothing - for her former husband's child, King Ma-yowa, seven years old, was playing just outside the apartment. Not knowing the boy could hear, the emperor said: 'I have constantly something upon my mind - the fear that thy child King Ma-yowa, when he comes to man's estate and learns that I slew the King his father, will requite me with a foul heart.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Kojiki, Wikisource page 391 (trans. Chamberlain 1882); not verbatim.

passages.text: The child caught the words, watched for the Heavenly Sovereign to be augustly asleep, took the great sword that lay at his side, struck off his head, and fled into the house of the Grandee Tsubura. Thus the wronged orphan avenged his father's blood before he was old enough to fear.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Kojiki, Wikisource page 391 (trans. Chamberlain 1882); not verbatim.

title.en: Ohohatsuse Seizes the Throne
title.zh: 雄略天皇染血即位

region.en: Yamato to Afumi (Nara/Biwa), Japan (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 大和至近江（象徵座標）

period: Kojiki compiled 712 CE (trans. Chamberlain 1882)

source.work: Kojiki, trans. Basil Hall Chamberlain (1882)

summary.en: Told of Anaho's murder, the lad Oho-hatsuse strangles his unconcerned elder brother Kuro-biko and buries his brother Shiro-biko alive up to the loins; he then besieges the Grandee Tsubura, whose loyal speech ends with the prince's death and Tsubura's own suicide. On a Afumi moor he ambushes King Oshiha under his clothes, shoots him, cuts up the body into a horse's manger, and the orphaned princes Ohoke and Woke flee into Harima as grooms.
summary.zh: 雄略（大泊瀨）聞天皇遇弑，責兄黑彥王冷漠而扼殺之，又活埋白彥王於畝旁。圍平群臣之家，平群臣力戰不支，殺皇子與己身以殉。又獵近江蒲原野，甲胄伏於衣內，突射殺其兄意祁王，碎屍納馬槽而埋之。意祁王之子億計王、弘計王亡命播磨，為馬夫牧童。

sensitivity.note: Ancient Japanese court myth (Kojiki); passages are condensed paraphrases of public-domain translations, presented for comparative mythology.

passages.text: Prince Oho-hatsuse, then a lad, was grieved and furious at the murder of the Heavenly Sovereign, and went to his elder brother King Kuro-biko: 'They have slain the Heavenly Sovereign. What shall be done?' Kuro-biko was not startled but unconcerned - so Oho-hatsuse clutched him by the collar, dragged him out, drew his sword, and slew him.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Kojiki, Wikisource pages 392-393 (trans. Chamberlain 1882); not verbatim.

passages.text: His other elder brother King Shiro-biko showed the same unconcern; Oho-hatsuse clutched him too, and on reaching Woharida dug a pit and buried him standing, so that when he was buried to the loins both his eyes burst out and he died.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Kojiki, Wikisource pages 392-393 (trans. Chamberlain 1882); not verbatim.

passages.text: Raising an army, he beleaguered the house of the Grandee Tsubura, who sheltered both Mayowa and the maiden Princess Kara. Arrows fell like reeds; Tsubura came forth unarmed and offered the princess and five granaries, declaring that grandees hide in kings' palaces, but kings do not hide in grandees' houses, and a loyal slave must die rather than desert a prince who trusted him. When their strength and arrows were spent, the prince begged death: Tsubura thrust the prince through with his sword and then cut off his own head.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Kojiki, Wikisource pages 393-394 (trans. Chamberlain 1882); not verbatim.

passages.text: Told of boars and deer in abundance at Kuta on the moor of Kaya in Afumi, Oho-hatsuse went hunting with King Ichi-no-be-no-oshiha. Warned that Oshiha was a violent-spoken prince, he put armour under his clothes, girded bow and arrows, rode level with the other king in a sudden interval, shot Oshiha down, cut his body to pieces, put them into a horse's manger, and buried them level with the earth. Oshiha's children, Kings Ohoke and Woke, fled across Yamashiro and the River Kusuba into Harima, where an old tattooed boar-herd once seized their provisions - and they hid in a native's house, working as grooms and cow-herds.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Kojiki, Wikisource pages 394-395 (trans. Chamberlain 1882); not verbatim.

title.en: The Raised-Roof House and the White Dog
title.zh: 志紀懸屋與白狗

region.en: Kafuchi (Osaka), Japan
region.zh: 河内（大阪）

period: Kojiki compiled 712 CE (trans. Chamberlain 1882)

source.work: Kojiki, trans. Basil Hall Chamberlain (1882)

summary.en: Progressing through Kafuchi, Emperor Oho-hatsuse sees a subject's house built with a raised roof-frame like his own and has it set on fire; the trembling lord offers a white dog clothed in cloth with a bell round its neck, and the burning is stopped. The emperor then sends the strange dog as a wooing-gift to Queen Waka-kusaka-be, who answers that she will come up to serve him, and he sings to her of intertwined bamboos not yet entwined.
summary.zh: 雄略天皇幸河內，見志紀縣主屋頂作懸屋，怒曰：賤奴僭擬御殿！命焚其屋。縣主戰懼獻白狗，披布繫鈴；天皇乃止焚，又以白狗為聘，遣人致若草香部郎女。郎女答曰：背日臨幸可畏，吾將上京奉仕。天皇登歌於山而詠之。

sensitivity.note: Ancient Japanese court myth (Kojiki); passages are condensed paraphrases of public-domain translations, presented for comparative mythology.

passages.text: In the beginning, when the Empress dwelt at Kusaka, the Heavenly Sovereign made a progress into Kafuchi by way of the Tadagoye road. Climbing a mountain-top and gazing over the country, he saw a house built with a raised roof-frame, and asked whose it was: 'It is the house of the great Departmental Lord of Shiki.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Kojiki, Wikisource pages 397-398 (trans. Chamberlain 1882); not verbatim.

passages.text: 'What! a slave builds his own house in imitation of the august abode of the Heavenly Sovereign!' - and he forthwith sent men to burn the house down. The Great Departmental Lord, trembling and bowing his head, pleaded that being a slave he had built overmuch in ignorance, and presented as an offering of entreaty a white dog clothed in cloth with a bell hung round its neck, led by a string by his kinsman Koshihaki. The emperor ordered the burning to desist.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Kojiki, Wikisource pages 397-398 (trans. Chamberlain 1882); not verbatim.

passages.text: Making a progress to the residence of Queen Waka-kusaka-be, he sent the dog as a present with the message that this strange thing got on the road was a thing to woo with. She answered that it was very alarming he should come with his back to the sun, so she would come up straight to the capital and respectfully serve him - and the emperor, standing on the mountain ascent, sang to his beloved of bamboos not yet intertwined.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Kojiki, Wikisource pages 398-399 (trans. Chamberlain 1882); not verbatim.

title.en: Akawi-ko: Eighty Years' Vigil at the Miwa River
title.zh: 引田部赤猪子八十年待命

region.en: Miwa river (Sakurai, Nara), Japan
region.zh: 三輪川（奈良櫻井）

period: Kojiki compiled 712 CE (trans. Chamberlain 1882)

source.work: Kojiki, trans. Basil Hall Chamberlain (1882)

summary.en: By the river Miwa the emperor meets the beautiful Akawi-ko of the Hiketa Tribe washing clothes and forbids her to marry: 'I will send for thee.' Eighty years she reverently awaits the summons; grown lean and withered, she comes up with a hundred tables of merchandise to show her faithfulness. The emperor, startled and pitiful, cannot wed her aged form but confers on her songs of the sacred dwelling, and sends her back plentifully endowed.
summary.zh: 雄略天皇幸三輪川，見美少女引田部赤猪子浣衣，命勿嫁，曰：吾將召汝。赤猪子待命八十年，形容枯槁，乃陳百几之調物以表忠貞。天皇愕然而憐之，欲娶而嫌其老，遂賜御歌而厚贈遣歸。

sensitivity.note: Ancient Japanese court myth (Kojiki); passages are condensed paraphrases of public-domain translations, presented for comparative mythology.

passages.text: Once when the Heavenly Sovereign went out for amusement and reached the River Miwa, there was a girl of very beautiful aspect washing clothes by the river-side. Asked whose child she was, she answered: 'My name is Akawi-ko of the Hiketa Tribe.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Kojiki, Wikisource pages 399-400 (trans. Chamberlain 1882); not verbatim.

passages.text: The emperor caused her to be told: 'Do not thou marry a husband. I will send for thee,' and returned to the palace. Eighty years passed while she reverently awaited the Heavenly Sovereign's commands; then, thinking her face and form lean and withered and hope gone, yet unable to bear hiding her faithfulness, she caused merchandise on a hundred tables to be carried and came forth to present it as tribute.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Kojiki, Wikisource pages 400-401 (trans. Chamberlain 1882); not verbatim.

passages.text: The emperor, who had quite forgotten the command of long ago, asked what old woman she was. She declared how in such a month of such a year she had received his command and waited eighty years, her prime passed away in vain. 'This is very pitiful,' he said; in his heart he wished to marry her, but shrank from her extreme age, and instead conferred on her an august song.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Kojiki, Wikisource pages 400-401 (trans. Chamberlain 1882); not verbatim.

passages.text: At the great august song the tears that Akawi-ko wept quite drenched the red-dyed sleeve she wore, and in reply she sang songs of her own unchangeable faith - that for every reason it had been impossible for her ever to give her affections to another, and that she had come up to the capital to demonstrate to him who had forgotten her the constancy of her heart. Then the old woman was sent back plentifully endowed.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Kojiki, Wikisource pages 401-402 (trans. Chamberlain 1882); not verbatim.

title.en: The Dancer of Yeshinu
title.zh: 吉野舞女

region.en: Yeshinu (Yoshino, Nara), Japan
region.zh: 吉野（奈良）

period: Kojiki compiled 712 CE (trans. Chamberlain 1882)

source.work: Kojiki, trans. Basil Hall Chamberlain (1882)

summary.en: Progressing to Yeshinu the emperor weds a beautiful girl of the river bank. On a later visit he raises a great august throne on the very spot of their meeting, seats himself, plays his lute, and makes the maiden dance; for her good dancing he composes an august song in her praise.
summary.zh: 雄略天皇幸吉野，娶川畔美少女。再幸其地，即舊逢處設御座，自彈琴而令女舞；嘉其舞之善，作歌贊之。

sensitivity.note: Ancient Japanese court myth (Kojiki); passages are condensed paraphrases of public-domain translations, presented for comparative mythology.

passages.text: When the Heavenly Sovereign made a progress to the palace of Yeshinu, there was on the bank of the Yeshinu river a girl of beautiful appearance. Having wedded this girl he returned to the Palace, but the meeting-place by the river stayed in his memory through the seasons that followed.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Kojiki, Wikisource page 402 (trans. Chamberlain 1882); not verbatim.

passages.text: Afterwards, when he again made a progress to Yeshinu, he halted where he had first met the girl, raised a great august throne in that place, seated himself upon it, played on his august lute, and made the maiden dance.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Kojiki, Wikisource page 402 (trans. Chamberlain 1882); not verbatim.

passages.text: For the maiden's good dancing he composed an august song in her praise, wedding the memory of their first meeting to the music of the lute in the river valley. Thus the emperor of the age made of one riverside encounter a royal romance, a dance, and a song that kept her name alive.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Kojiki, Wikisource pages 402-403 (trans. Chamberlain 1882); not verbatim.

title.en: The Dragonfly that Named Akitsushima
title.zh: 蜻蛉啖虻與秋津島

region.en: Moor of Akidzu, Yamato (Nara), Japan (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 秋津野（象徵座標）

period: Kojiki compiled 712 CE (trans. Chamberlain 1882)

source.work: Kojiki, trans. Basil Hall Chamberlain (1882)

summary.en: Hunting from his throne on the moor of Akidzu, the emperor is bitten on the arm by a horse-fly; a dragonfly at once comes, eats up the horse-fly, and flies away. He composes a song of thanks, and from that time the moor is called Akidzu-nu - whence Akitsushima, Dragonfly Island, the poetic name of Japan itself.
summary.zh: 雄略天皇於秋津野御座而獵，牛虻齧其臂，忽有蜻蛉飛來啖虻而去。天皇作歌謝之，其野遂名秋津洲，日本之雅稱由此而來。

sensitivity.note: Ancient Japanese court myth (Kojiki); passages are condensed paraphrases of public-domain translations, presented for comparative mythology.

passages.text: When the Heavenly Sovereign made a progress to the Moor of Akidzu and augustly hunted, he sat on an august throne. A horse-fly bit his august arm, and forthwith a dragonfly came and ate up the horse-fly, and flew away.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Kojiki, Wikisource page 403 (trans. Chamberlain 1882); not verbatim.

passages.text: Thereupon he composed an august song in thanks for the dragonfly's service, for the insect had avenged the august arm of the sovereign with a sudden flash of wings. From that time that moor was called by the name of Akidzu-nu, the Dragonfly Moor, and the hunters remembered the song as long as they walked the field.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Kojiki, Wikisource pages 403-404 (trans. Chamberlain 1882); not verbatim.

passages.text: From the moor's name comes Akitsushima, the Island of the Dragon-fly - the poetic name of Japan itself. The commentators even reversed the common assumption: it was not the island that was called after Japan, but Japan that was called after the dragon-fly, so that the country's loveliest old name was born from one small winged avenger on a hunting morning.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Kojiki, Wikisource page 404 (trans. Chamberlain 1882); not verbatim.

title.en: The Boar of Kadzuraki and the Deity Lord of One Word
title.zh: 葛城山豬與一言主神

region.en: Mount Kadzuraki (Nara/Osaka border), Japan (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 葛城山（象徵座標）

period: Kojiki compiled 712 CE (trans. Chamberlain 1882)

source.work: Kojiki, trans. Basil Hall Chamberlain (1882)

summary.en: On Mount Kadzuraki a wounded boar roars back at the emperor, who climbs an alder and sings. On a later progress a retinue exactly like his own - garments, red cords, order of march - ascends the opposite acclivity; arrows are fixed on both sides until the other declares himself the Great Deity of Kadzuraki, Lord of One Word, who dispels evil and good with a word. The emperor strips his hundred officials of their garments as offerings, and the deity escorts him down the mountain.
summary.zh: 雄略天皇射葛城山豬，豬怒吼反撲，帝懼而登榿木而歌。又幸葛城山，見對山上人馬服飾與御仗儀仗無異；兩軍張弓相峙，對方自報：吾乃一言主神，善言則善、惡言則惡之神。天皇戰慄致敬，脫百官衣裳并自佩弓劍進獻，神擊掌受之，且送帝至葛城山麓。

sensitivity.note: Ancient Japanese court myth (Kojiki); passages are condensed paraphrases of public-domain translations, presented for comparative mythology.

passages.text: Once the Heavenly Sovereign made a progress up to the summit of Mount Kadzuraki, and a large wild boar ran out. He shot it with a whizzing barb, but the boar, furious, came towards him roaring; alarmed at the roaring, he climbed up to the top of an alder and sang there of his peril and the mercy of his great lord.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Kojiki, Wikisource pages 404-405 (trans. Chamberlain 1882); not verbatim.

passages.text: Again, on a progress up Mount Kadzuraki, all the officials were clothed in green-stained garments with red cords. On the opposite mountain acclivity people ascended quite similar to the order of the Heavenly Monarch's retinue - the habiliments and the very people indistinguishable. 'There being no other king in Yamato excepting myself,' the emperor demanded, 'what person goeth thus?'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Kojiki, Wikisource pages 405-406 (trans. Chamberlain 1882); not verbatim.

passages.text: Very angry, he fixed his arrow, and the officials all fixed theirs - and those people also fixed their arrows. 'Let each tell his name, and then let fly his arrow.' The reply: 'I was the first to be asked, I will be the first to tell my name. I am the deity who dispels with a word the evil and with a word the good - the Great Deity of Kadzuraki, Lord of One Word.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Kojiki, Wikisource pages 405-406 (trans. Chamberlain 1882); not verbatim.

passages.text: The Heavenly Sovereign trembled and reverenced the Great Deity; beginning with his great august sword and bow and arrows, he took off the garments of the hundred officials and worshipfully presented them, and the Deity, clapping his hands, accepted the offering. Descending the mountain, the Great Deity respectfully escorted the emperor to the entrance of the Hatsuse mountain - so it was that the Lord of One Word was revealed.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Kojiki, Wikisource page 406 (trans. Chamberlain 1882); not verbatim.

title.en: The Leaf in the Liquor Cup and the Maid of Mihe
title.zh: 盃中落葉與三女汀采女

region.en: Hatsuse (Sakurai, Nara), Japan
region.zh: 初瀨（奈良櫻井）

period: Kojiki compiled 712 CE (trans. Chamberlain 1882)

source.work: Kojiki, trans. Basil Hall Chamberlain (1882)

summary.en: Going to wed Princess Wodo of Kasuga, the emperor sees a girl hide behind a mound and sings of digging her out with five hundred metal spades - whence the Mound of the Metal Spade. At a feast under a hundred-branching tsuki-tree, a leaf falls into the liquor-cup of the maid from Mihe, and he is about to cut off her head; her inspired song of the sacred palace and the falling leaves wins pardon, and she is praised and plentifully endowed.
summary.zh: 雄略天皇幸春日欲婚幡梭郎女，途中少女匿於塚畔，帝歌以五百鐵鍬掘山取之，其塚遂名鐵鍬塚。又於初瀨百枝木下大宴，三女汀采女奉杯，落葉浮於盃中；帝拔劍欲斬，采女歌詠日御門與建木之靈義而得赦，大加褒賞。

sensitivity.note: Ancient Japanese court myth (Kojiki); passages are condensed paraphrases of public-domain translations, presented for comparative mythology.

passages.text: Again when the Heavenly Sovereign made a progress to Kasuga to wed Princess Wodo, daughter of the Grandee Satsuki of Wani, a maiden met him by the way, and, seeing the Imperial progress, ran and hid on the side of a mound. The emperor composed an august song, jesting that he desired five hundred metal spades like hers wherewith to break down the hill-side and dig her out - and so that mound was called the Mound of the Metal Spade.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Kojiki, Wikisource pages 406-407 (trans. Chamberlain 1882); not verbatim.

passages.text: When he made a copious feast under a hundred-branching tsuki-tree at Hatsuse, a female attendant from Mihe in the land of Ise lifted up the great august cup and presented it to him. From the tree there fell a leaf and floated in the great august cup; not knowing it, the maid did not desist from presenting the liquor, but the emperor, perceiving the leaf, knocked her down, put his sword to her neck, and was about to cut off her head.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Kojiki, Wikisource pages 407-408 (trans. Chamberlain 1882); not verbatim.

passages.text: 'Slay me not! There is something that I must say to thee,' the maid cried, and sang: the palace of Hishiro at Makimuku shines with the morning and evening sun, and on the hundred-fold flourishing tsuki-tree the leaves fall from branch to branch into the fresh jewelled goblet, curdle-curdle - a very awful thing, August Child of the High-Shining Sun, and the tradition of the thing, too, this!
passages.note: Paraphrase of Kojiki, Wikisource pages 407-408 (trans. Chamberlain 1882); not verbatim.

passages.text: Her song of heavenly words recalled how drops of brine that fell curdling became the first island of the archipelago - so that a leaf falling into liquor must be a good omen rather than a crime. The emperor sang in reply, and at that copious feast the female attendant from Mihe was praised and plentifully endowed.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Kojiki, Wikisource pages 409-411 (trans. Chamberlain 1882); not verbatim.

title.en: The Fire-Tenders' Dance in Harima
title.zh: 播磨灶童之舞

region.en: Harima (Himeji, Hyogo), Japan
region.zh: 播磨（兵庫姬路）

period: Kojiki compiled 712 CE (trans. Chamberlain 1882)

source.work: Kojiki, trans. Basil Hall Chamberlain (1882)

summary.en: After Seinei's death the realm seeks a king and finds Princess Ihi-toyo. Wodate, newly appointed governor of Harima, comes to the new-cave rejoicing of Shizhimu, where two young fire-tending children dance with princely courtesy, each yielding precedence to the other. The younger's chant of the red-painted sword and banners hidden among the bamboos reveals them as beggarly descendants of emperors - the hidden princes Ohoke and Woke, whose father Ichinobe was slain.
summary.zh: 清寧天皇崩而無嗣，求飯豐王女為主。山背守小楯宿禰幸播磨志染神社新屋大宴，二灶童相讓起舞；弟詠赤旗之劍藏於竹叢之歌，自曝為乞食流亡之皇孫，即億計、弘計二王。

sensitivity.note: Ancient Japanese court myth (Kojiki); passages are condensed paraphrases of public-domain translations, presented for comparative mythology.

passages.text: The Heavenly Sovereign Shiraka-no-oho-yamato-ne-ko had no Empress and no august children; after his decease there was no King to rule the Empire, and enquiry was made for one to rule the sun's succession. Wodate, Chief of the Mountain Clan, was appointed governor of the land of Harima, and arrived just at the time of a rejoicing for the new cave of an inhabitant called Shizhimu.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Kojiki, Wikisource pages 413-414 (trans. Chamberlain 1882); not verbatim.

passages.text: When the feasting and drinking were at their height, all danced in turns; two young children employed to light the fire sat beside the furnace, and were made to dance. 'Do thou the elder brother dance first.' 'Do thou the younger brother dance first.' Laughing at their mutual yielding, the assembly waited till the elder at last danced; then, when the younger was about to dance, he chanted.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Kojiki, Wikisource pages 414-415 (trans. Chamberlain 1882); not verbatim.

passages.text: The chant spoke of a sword painted and decorated with red streamers, of red banners hidden behind the thick leaves of the bamboo-grove - as the Imperial origin of the two young princes was hidden beneath the vile office they filled in Shizhimu's household - and ended with the words 'beggarly descendants,' by which the singer revealed his own and his brother's princely birth.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Kojiki, Wikisource pages 415-416 (trans. Chamberlain 1882); not verbatim.

title.en: The Song-Hedge Quarrel with the Grandee Shibi
title.zh: 志比臣歌垣之爭

region.en: Uda and Yamato (Nara), Japan
region.zh: 宇陀與大和（奈良）

period: Kojiki compiled 712 CE (trans. Chamberlain 1882)

source.work: Kojiki, trans. Basil Hall Chamberlain (1882)

summary.en: As the two princes are about to assume rule, the Grandee Shibi seizes in a song-hedge the maiden Ofuwo whom Prince Woke is about to wed, and taunts him with tunny-metaphors in alternating songs. The princes resolve that no better time to act can come than when the Grandee's gate stands empty of men, raise an army, besiege and slay Shibi, and then cede the empire to one another until the younger Woke rules first.
summary.zh: 二王將即位，平群臣志比於歌垣中奪弘計王將娶之乙媛，以鰹魚之喻相譏相和。王等伺志比宅門無人，舉兵圍而殺之。既而兄弟互讓帝位，弟弘計王以兄讓而先即位。

sensitivity.note: Ancient Japanese court myth (Kojiki); passages are condensed paraphrases of public-domain translations, presented for comparative mythology.

passages.text: When the government of the Empire was about to be assumed, the Grandee Shibi, ancestor of the Grandees of Heguri, mixed in the Songs and took the hand of the beautiful person whom Prince Woke was about to wed - the maiden Ofuwo, daughter of one of the Headmen of Uda. Woke likewise mixed in the Song-Hedge, and they taunted one another in alternating songs.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Kojiki, Wikisource pages 416-418 (trans. Chamberlain 1882); not verbatim.

passages.text: Song answered song in growing anger: the prince likened himself to a fisherman who would fain spear the great tunny, the Grandee jeered at the dilapidated palace and the sorry fortunes of the princes, and the war of words mounted to threats of cutting and burning one another's houses down.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Kojiki, Wikisource pages 417-419 (trans. Chamberlain 1882); not verbatim.

passages.text: The princes took counsel together: 'Unless it be now, it were hard to plot against him, for there is nobody at the gate' - and forthwith they raised an army, beleaguered the house of the Grandee Shibi, and slew him, ending the song-hedge rivalry with spears instead of verses.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Kojiki, Wikisource pages 418-419 (trans. Chamberlain 1882); not verbatim.

passages.text: Then each of the two Princes ceded the Empire to the other. Ohoke urged: 'Had not Thine Augustness revealed our names when we dwelt in the house of Shizhimu in Harima, we should never have arrived at being the lords of the Empire. Though I be the elder brother, do Thine Augustness rule first.' Unable to refuse, His Augustness Woke ruled the Empire first.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Kojiki, Wikisource pages 419-420 (trans. Chamberlain 1882); not verbatim.

title.en: Emperor Woke Finds His Father's Bones
title.zh: 顯宗天皇尋父骨與老嫗置目

region.en: Kaya moor, Afumi (Lake Biwa), Japan
region.zh: 近江蒲原野（象徵座標）

period: Kojiki compiled 712 CE (trans. Chamberlain 1882)

source.work: Kojiki, trans. Basil Hall Chamberlain (1882)

summary.en: Emperor Woke, searching for the august bones of his murdered father King Ichinobe, receives a poor old woman from Afumi who alone knows the grave - and can tell the skeleton by its teeth. The bones are dug up, interred in a new mausoleum, and the old woman, named Oki-me, is housed beside the palace and summoned daily by a bell; when she begs to go home the emperor sees her off with songs.
summary.zh: 顯宗天皇弘計求其父市之邊王之骨。近江有一老嫗自言知埋骨處，且能以齒辨之。發土得骨，葬於蒲原野東山陵，使賀富臣子孫守之。天皇召嫗入宮，賜名置目，宮畔築屋，擊鈴而召之；後老嫗乞歸鄉，天皇賜歌送之。

sensitivity.note: Ancient Japanese court myth (Kojiki); passages are condensed paraphrases of public-domain translations, presented for comparative mythology.

passages.text: His Augustness Woke-no-ihasu-wake dwelt at the palace of Chika-tsu-Asuka and ruled the Empire. At the time when the Heavenly Sovereign was searching for the august bones of the King his father, King Ichinobe, there came out from the land of Afumi to the palace a poor old woman, who said: 'The place where the prince's august bones are buried is specially well known to me, and moreover his skeleton can be known by his august teeth.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Kojiki, Wikisource pages 419-420 (trans. Chamberlain 1882); not verbatim.

passages.text: People were set to dig the ground and search; the bones were forthwith obtained, an august mausoleum was made on the mountain east of the Moor of Kaya, and they were interred there, with the children of Kara-fukuro set to guard it. Afterwards the august bones were brought up to the Capital.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Kojiki, Wikisource pages 419-420 (trans. Chamberlain 1882); not verbatim.

passages.text: The emperor sent for the old woman, praised her for having kept the place in mind without forgetting, and conferred on her the name of the Old Woman Oki-me. He built her a house close to the palace, always sent for her every day, hung a bell by the door of the great hall, and always rang it when he wished to call her, singing a song of her long journey from valley and moor.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Kojiki, Wikisource pages 420-421 (trans. Chamberlain 1882); not verbatim.

passages.text: The old woman said she was very aged and would fain depart to her native land; the Heavenly Sovereign let her depart according to her request, saw her off, and sang a farewell song of the hundred stages by which she had come.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Kojiki, Wikisource page 421 (trans. Chamberlain 1882); not verbatim.

title.en: Woke's Vengeance on the Herdman and the Mausoleum
title.zh: 顯宗天皇之復仇

region.en: Asuka river and Mozu mound (Nara/Osaka), Japan
region.zh: 飛鳥川與百舌鳥古墳

period: Kojiki compiled 712 CE (trans. Chamberlain 1882)

source.work: Kojiki, trans. Basil Hall Chamberlain (1882)

summary.en: The boar-herd who seized the princes' provisions in their days of flight is hunted out, beheaded in the bed of the river Asuka, and all his kindred have their knee-tendons cut, so his descendants limp to this day when they come up to Yamato. Wishing revenge on the spirit of Yuryaku, Woke would demolish his mausoleum; his brother Ohoke undertakes the deed, only slightly excavating its side, arguing that an emperor's tomb must be spared while the insult suffices as a token to future ages.
summary.zh: 顯宗天皇尋得昔日奪食之野豬飼夫，斬於飛鳥川之原，並刳其族人之膝筋，故其子孫至今上大和而自跛。又欲掘雄略天皇之陵以報父仇；兄億計王自任其事，僅微掘陵側而還，奏曰：叔父雖為父仇，然曾君臨天下，盡毀其陵恐遭後世非議，微掘以為後世之鑒足矣。

sensitivity.note: Ancient Japanese court myth (Kojiki); passages are condensed paraphrases of public-domain translations, presented for comparative mythology.

passages.text: The Heavenly Sovereign searched for the old boar-herd who had seized his august provisions at the time when he first met with adversity and was fleeing; having sought him out, he sent for him up to the Capital, beheaded him in the bed of the River Asuka, and cut the knee-tendons of all his kindred. Wherefore down to the present time his descendants, on the day when they come up to Yamato, always limp of their own accord; the man's abode had been well seen and divined, so the place was named Shimesu.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Kojiki, Wikisource pages 421-422 (trans. Chamberlain 1882); not verbatim.

passages.text: Deeply hating the Heavenly Sovereign Oho-hatsuse, who had slain the King his father, the emperor wished to be revenged on his spirit by destroying his august mausoleum. His elder brother Ohoke addressed him: 'To demolish this august mausoleum thou shouldst not send other people. None but myself shall go.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Kojiki, Wikisource pages 422-423 (trans. Chamberlain 1882); not verbatim.

passages.text: Ohoke proceeded down, slightly excavated the side of the mausoleum, and reported the deed done. Challenged on his quick return, he explained: revenge on their father's foe is just, but Oho-hatsuse was still their uncle and a Heavenly Sovereign who ruled the Empire - to demolish wholly the mausoleum of a ruler would be reviled by after-generations, so a slight excavation will suffice as a token to future ages. 'This also is very just,' said the emperor, and let it be.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Kojiki, Wikisource pages 422-423 (trans. Chamberlain 1882); not verbatim.

title.en: No Heir: Keitai Sent For and the Revolt of Ihawi
title.zh: 繼體天皇入繼與磐余之叛

region.en: Ihare (Nara) and Tsukushi, Japan
region.zh: 磐余（奈良）與筑紫

period: Kojiki compiled 712 CE (trans. Chamberlain 1882)

source.work: Kojiki, trans. Basil Hall Chamberlain (1882)

summary.en: Emperor Buretsu dies childless, leaving no prince to inherit; Ohoda, fifth descendant of Emperor Homuda, is sent for from Afumi, married to Princess Tashiraka, and presented with the Empire, ruling from the palace of Tamaho. In his reign Ihawi, Lord of Tsukushi, defies the imperial decrees, and the Great Chieftain Mononobe-no-arakawi and the Chieftain Ohotomo-no-kanamura are both sent to slay him.
summary.zh: 武烈天皇崩而無嗣，乃迎近江之彥太（繼體天皇，譽田天皇五世孫），婚於手白香皇女，奉以帝位，居磐余玉穰宮。其世筑紫國造磐井不遵朝命，大逆無道，乃遣物部麁鹿火大連與大伴金村連俱誅之。

sensitivity.note: Ancient Japanese court myth (Kojiki); passages are condensed paraphrases of public-domain translations, presented for comparative mythology.

passages.text: His Grandeur Wo-hatsuse-no-waka-sazaki dwelt in the palace of Namiki at Hatsuse and ruled the Empire for eight years, having no august children; the Wo-hatsuse Tribe was established as his august proxy. On his death there was no prince anywhere to inherit the Empire, and the imperial line itself seemed about to fail.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Kojiki, Wikisource page 424 (trans. Chamberlain 1882); not verbatim.

passages.text: So His Augustness Ohoda, the fifth descendant of the Heavenly Monarch Homuda, was sent for down from the land of Afumi, married to Her Augustness Tashiraka, and presented with the Empire. Dwelling in the Palace of Tamaho at Ihare, he ruled as the Heavenly Sovereign Keitai.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Kojiki, Wikisource pages 424-425 (trans. Chamberlain 1882); not verbatim.

passages.text: In this august reign Ihawi, Lord of Tsukushi, was disobedient to the Imperial Decrees and was exceedingly disrespectful. So the Great Chieftain Mononobe-no-arakawi and the Chieftain Ohotomo-no-kanamura were both sent to slay Ihawi - the lord of the great clans going together against the rebel of the western road.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Kojiki, Wikisource page 425 (trans. Chamberlain 1882); not verbatim.

title.en: The Oracle of Oho-tata-neko and the Sacred Sake of Miwa
title.zh: 大田田根子神託與三輪神酒之歌

region.en: Plain of Kami-asachi and Miwa, Yamato
region.zh: 大和神淺茅原與三輪

period: Nihongi compiled 720 CE (trans. Aston 1896)

source.work: Nihongi (Chronicles of Japan), Vol. I, trans. W. G. Aston (1896)

summary.en: A great pestilence half-destroys the realm under Emperor Sujin. Divining with the eighty myriad deities, he learns through the possessed princess Yamato-toto-hi-momoso-hime that the land-god Oho-mono-nushi must be worshipped; the god's dream-instruction names his own child Oho-tata-neko as priest. The man is found at Suye and installed, the plague ceases and the grain returns, and the brewer Ikuhi presents the sacred sake with a famous punning song.
summary.zh: 崇神天皇六年國中大疫，人民死過半。天皇憂懼，齋服於神淺茅原，會八十萬神而卜。倭跡跡日百襲姬命為大物主神所憑曰「帝何為憂國？若敬祀我，則當自平」。問其神名，答曰「吾是倭國域內之神，名曰大物主神」。拜而不效，再夢神諭：以吾子大田田根子主祭。遣使求之於茅淳縣水下縣戶之村，尋獲，立為大物主神之祭主，設八十万神之祠，疫乃止，五穀登成，百姓安泰。命意岐多為造酒神之釀酒者，進神酒而歌「此御酒非吾所醸，乃大物主神所醸之御酒」。

sensitivity.note: Ancient Japanese court myth (Nihongi): Emperor Sujin's founding of the state cult, sacred to Shinto tradition; passages are condensed paraphrases of the public-domain Aston translation, presented for comparative mythology.

passages.text: In the fifth year there was much pestilence throughout the country, and more than one half the people died; the next year the people took to vagabondage and there was rebellion. The Emperor, rising early and full of awe until the evening, requested punishment of the Gods of Heaven and Earth. He dreaded the power of the two deities worshipped within his Great Hall and entrusted Amaterasu to be worshipped at Kasanuhi in Yamato. In the seventh year he resolved to commit the matter to the Sacred Tortoise and ascertain the cause of the calamity: he proceeded to the plain of Kami-asachi, assembled the eighty myriads of Deities, and inquired of them by divination. At this time the Gods inspired Yamato-toto-hi-momoso-hime no Mikoto, who said: 'Why is the Emperor grieved at the disordered state of the country? If he duly did us reverent worship, it would assuredly become pacified of itself.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Nihongi, Book V, §§5–7 (trans. Aston 1896); not verbatim.

passages.text: Asked what God it was that instructed him, the answer came: 'I am the God who dwells within the borders of the land of Yamato, and my name is Oho-mono-nushi no Kami.' He worshipped as he was told, but without effect; then, having bathed and practised abstinence, he prayed to be further instructed in a dream. That night a man of noble appearance stood opposite him in the door of the hall, announcing himself as Oho-mono-nushi, and said: 'Let the Emperor grieve no more for the disorder of the country. This is my will. If thou wilt cause me to be worshipped by my child, Oho-tata-neko, then will there be peace at once; moreover the lands beyond the sea will of their own accord render submission.' Four people - the Emperor's aunt, Oho-mina-kuchi-no-Sukune and two others - had the same dream on the same night, and reported it.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Nihongi, Book V, §§7–8 (trans. Aston 1896); not verbatim.

passages.text: By proclamation to the Empire the Emperor sought Oho-tata-neko, who was found in the village of Suye in the district of Chinu. Asked whose child he was, he answered: 'My father's name is Oho-mono-nushi no Oho-kami; my mother's name is Ikudama-yori-bime.' The Emperor said, 'Now we shall be prosperous.' The articles for worship were made by the hands of the eighty Mononobe, Oho-tata-neko was appointed master of the worship of Oho-mono-nushi, and Nagaochi master of the worship of Yamato no Oho-kuni-dama. The eighty myriads of Deities were separately worshipped, shrines assigned to Heaven and Earth, and land and houses allotted for the service of the Gods. Thereupon the pestilence ceased, the country had peace, the five kinds of grain were produced, and the peasantry enjoyed abundance.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Nihongi, Book V, §§8–9 (trans. Aston 1896); not verbatim.

passages.text: In the eighth year the brewer Ikuhi was appointed to the Great Deity, and when Oho-tata-neko worshipped the Great Deity, Ikuhi in person presented sacred sake to the Emperor with a song: 'This sacred sake is not my sacred sake: 'tis sacred sake brewed by Oho-mono-nushi of Yamato - how long ago! how long ago!' (a pun on the brewer's own name). Having sung, they feasted in the shrine of the God, and afterwards the high officials and the Emperor answered with songs about the morning-door of the Hall of Miwa, of sweet sake fame; so the door of the shrine was thrown open and the Emperor proceeded on his way.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Nihongi, Book V, §10 (trans. Aston 1896); not verbatim.

title.en: The Four Generals of the Roads and the Maiden's Warning Song
title.zh: 崇神遣四道將軍與少女警世之歌

region.en: Wani acclivity, Yamashiro
region.zh: 山城和邇坂

period: Nihongi compiled 720 CE (trans. Aston 1896)

source.work: Nihongi (Chronicles of Japan), Vol. I, trans. W. G. Aston (1896)

summary.en: Sujin sends four generals with seals and ribbons to the four quarters - Oho-hiko to the north, Takenu-kaha-wake to the Eastern Sea, Kibi-tsu-hiko to the western road, Tamba-no-chi-nushi to Tamba. At the Wani acclivity Oho-hiko hears a roadside maiden sing a song warning that some are stealthily preparing to cut the thread of the Emperor's life; she vanishes, and the shrewd Yamato-toto-hi-momoso-hime reads the omen as Take-hani-yasu's coming treason and orders the generals recalled.
summary.zh: 崇神天皇十年，詔選群臣遣於四道，賜印綬為將軍：大彥命主北道，武渟川別主東海道，吉備津彥主西道，丹波道主命主丹波，誡曰「有不順者即擊之」。大彥命至和邇坂之上，見路旁少女歌曰「呀彌動高日!豈知竊防竊欲絕王命之緒，逍遙如少女者!」復詠而忽滅。跡跡日百襲姬命占之，知武埴安彥將謀反，其妻吾田媛已取香山土以咒國土，乃悉召四道將軍還。

sensitivity.note: Ancient Japanese court myth (Nihongi); passages are condensed paraphrases of the public-domain Aston translation, presented for comparative mythology.

passages.text: The Emperor proclaimed to his ministers that for the guidance of the people the chief thing is education: the distant savages did not yet receive the calendar, being unaccustomed to the civilizing influences of rule, so ministers would be sent to the four quarters to make the Imperial Will known. He sent Oho-hiko no Mikoto to the northern region, Takenu-kaha-wake to the Eastern Sea, Kibi-tsu-hiko to the western road, and Tamba-no-chi-nushi no Mikoto to Tamba, addressing them: 'If there be any who do not receive our instructions, prepare war and smite them.' He granted them all alike seals and ribbons and appointed them generals; later, in winter, the four generals set out on their journeys simultaneously.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Nihongi, Book V, §§12–13 (trans. Aston 1896); not verbatim.

passages.text: Oho-hiko no Mikoto arrived at the top of the Wani acclivity - another version has the Hira-zaka acclivity in Yamashiro. There was by the road-side a young woman who sang: 'Ah! Prince Mimaki-iri! Unaware that some are stealthily preparing to cut the thread of thine own life, thou amusest thyself like a lady!' Wondering at this, Oho-hiko inquired what words these were; she answered that she was only singing, sang the song over again, and suddenly disappeared. Oho-hiko returned and reported the circumstances to the Emperor.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Nihongi, Book V, §14 (trans. Aston 1896); not verbatim.

passages.text: Yamato-toto-hi-momoso-hime no Mikoto, the Emperor's aunt, a shrewd and intelligent person who could foresee the future, understood what was portended by the song, and told the Emperor that it was a sign that Take-hani-yasu-hiko was about to plot treason. 'I have heard,' she said, 'that Ata-bime, Take-hani-yasu-hiko's wife, came secretly and took earth from Mount Kako in Yamato, which she wrapped in her neckerchief and prayed over, saying: This earth represents the Land of Yamato - and turned it upside down. By this I know that there will be troubles. If thou dost not speedily take measures, it will assuredly be too late.' Hereupon the Emperor recalled all the generals and consulted with them.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Nihongi, Book V, §14 (trans. Aston 1896); not verbatim.

title.en: Yamato-toto-hime and the Snake Husband of Mount Mimoro
title.zh: 倭跡跡姬婚大物主蛇神，簪刺而崩

region.en: Mount Mimoro (Miwa), Yamato
region.zh: 大和三輪山

period: Nihongi compiled 720 CE (trans. Aston 1896)

source.work: Nihongi (Chronicles of Japan), Vol. I, trans. W. G. Aston (1896)

summary.en: Yamato-toto-hi-momoso-hime becomes the wife of Oho-mono-nushi, who visits her only by night. Begging to behold his majesty, she is told he will enter her toilet-case at dawn - where she finds a beautiful little snake the length of a garment-cord. She cries out in fright; the shamed god puts her to shame in turn, treads the Great Void and ascends Mount Mimoro. She stabs herself in remorse with a chopstick, and her tomb is built by men in the daytime and by gods at night.
summary.zh: 倭跡跡日百襲姬命為大物主神之妻。神惟夜至，不見晝形。姬曰「願得仰覩尊之威容」，神許以朝入其櫛笥。姬旦視笥中，見小蛇，其色如錦續子，長大如衣緒，大驚而叫。神慚，忽化人形，語其妻曰「汝不慎忍，令我羞恥；我還令汝知恥」，遂踏大虛，登三輪山而止。姬仰而悔之，則於座上以箸撞陰而死，葬大市。時人號其墓曰箸墓。墓晝人作、夜神作，運大坂山石築之。

sensitivity.note: Ancient Japanese court myth (Nihongi): the serpent-husband episode of the Miwa cult, a standard snake-suit motif in comparative mythology; passages are condensed paraphrases of the public-domain Aston translation, presented for comparative mythology.

passages.text: After this Yamato-toto-hi-momoso-hime no Mikoto became the wife of Oho-mono-nushi no Kami. This God, however, was never seen in the daytime, but came at night. Yamato-toto-hime said to her husband: 'As my Lord is never seen in the daytime, I am unable to view his august countenance distinctly. I beseech him to delay a while, that in the morning I may look upon the majesty of his beauty.' The Great God answered: 'What thou sayest is clearly right. To-morrow morning I will enter thy toilet-case and stay there. I pray thee be not alarmed at my form.' She wondered secretly at this, and waiting until daybreak, looked into her toilet-case. There was there a beautiful little snake, of the length and thickness of the cord of a garment.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Nihongi, Book V, §17 (trans. Aston 1896); not verbatim.

passages.text: Thereupon she was frightened and uttered an exclamation. The Great God was ashamed, and changing suddenly into human form, spoke to his wife: 'Thou didst not contain thyself, but hast caused me shame. I will in my turn put thee to shame.' So treading the Great Void, he ascended to Mount Mimoro. Yamato-toto-hime looked up and had remorse. She flopped down on a seat and with a chopstick stabbed herself in the pudenda so that she died. She was buried at Oho-chi, and the men of that time called her tomb the Hashi no haka, the Chopstick Tomb.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Nihongi, Book V, §17 (trans. Aston 1896); not verbatim.

passages.text: This tomb was made by men in the daytime and by Gods at night. It was built of stones carried from Mount Oho-saka, the people standing close to each other and passing the stones from hand to hand from the mountain to the tomb. The men of that time made a song about this: 'If one passed from hand to hand the rocks built up on Oho-saka, how hard 'twould be to send them!'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Nihongi, Book V, §17 (trans. Aston 1896); not verbatim.

title.en: The White Stone Becomes a Maiden: Arashito's Lost Divine Bride
title.zh: 白石化麗姬：阿羅斯等失神女

region.en: Kara (southern Korea) and Naniha (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 加耶與浪速（象徵錨點）

period: Nihongi compiled 720 CE (trans. Aston 1896)

source.work: Nihongi (Chronicles of Japan), Vol. I, trans. W. G. Aston (1896)

summary.en: A variant account of Arashito: when villagers slaughter his lost ox, an old man advises him to demand not treasures but the god of the village - a white stone. Carried home, the stone becomes a beautiful maiden; while he is away she vanishes eastwards, and drifting far over the sea he arrives in Japan following her. The maiden becomes the Deity of the Himegoso shrines at Naniha and in the Land of Toyo.
summary.zh: 一說：都怒我阿羅斯等在本國以牛載田器而行，牛忽亡。跡入一村，村人宰牛欲食之，一老人教之曰「求償勿求珍寶，但求其村所祭之神」。其神乃白石化之。持歸寢室，忽化為美好少女。阿羅斯等欲婚之，暫離其間，女忽遁而東去。逐之，漂流泛海，遂至日本。女至浪速為比古佐之神，又至豐國許岐山，亦為比古佐之神，兩所祀之。

sensitivity.note: Ancient Japanese court myth (Nihongi); passages are condensed paraphrases of the public-domain Aston translation, presented for comparative mythology.

passages.text: In the beginning, when Tsunoga-arashito was still in his own land, he went into the country with an ox loaded with implements of husbandry. The ox suddenly disappeared, and seeking for it by its tracks, he found that the foot-prints ceased in a certain village. An old man there told him that the village chiefs had slain and eaten the ox to use the implements, and instructed him: 'If thou art asked what thing thou desirest as the price of the ox, do not ask for treasures, but say that thou wishest to have the God worshipped by the village.' The God whom they worshipped was a white stone. So they gave the white stone to the owner of the ox, and he brought it away with him and placed it in his bed-chamber.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Nihongi, Book VI, §6 (trans. Aston 1896); not verbatim.

passages.text: This divine stone became changed into a beautiful maiden, upon which Arashito was greatly rejoiced and wished to be united to her. But while he was away in another place the maiden suddenly disappeared. Arashito was greatly alarmed, and inquired of his wife where the maiden had gone; she replied that she had gone towards the East. So he went in search of her, and at length, drifting far over the sea, he thus arrived in Japan. The maiden whom he sought came to Naniha, where she became the Deity of the Himegoso shrine; then proceeding to the district of Kusaki in the Land of Toyo, she afterwards became the Deity of the Himegoso shrine there. She is worshipped in both these places.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Nihongi, Book VI, §6 (trans. Aston 1896); not verbatim.

title.en: Ama-no-hi-hoko Brings the Divine Treasures of Silla
title.zh: 天日槍獻新羅寶物

region.en: Harima and Tajima (Sea of Japan coast)
region.zh: 播磨與但馬

period: Nihongi compiled 720 CE (trans. Aston 1896)

source.work: Nihongi (Chronicles of Japan), Vol. I, trans. W. G. Aston (1896)

summary.en: Ama-no-hi-hoko, son of the King of Silla, gives his realm to his younger brother and sails to Japan with seven (or eight) treasures - gems, sun-mirror, Idzushi sword and spear, and a Kuma-himorogi. Allowed to seek his own dwelling, he tours by way of Lake Biwa and Wakasa and settles in Tajima; the potters of Kagami become his servants, and through his wife Matawo he becomes great-grandfather of Tajima-mori.
summary.zh: 垂仁天皇三年，新羅王子天日槍來。獻寶物七種（一說八種）：葉細珠、足高珠、鹿石赤石珠、出石短劍、出石槍、日鏡、熊神籬（及伊莎莎刀）。帝命擇播磨宍鹿或淡路出島而居，天日槍請自遊行諸國擇所愿之地，歷近江、若狹而定居但馬。近江鏡谷土師皆其奴。娶出石真緋女，四世而至田道間守。

sensitivity.note: Ancient Japanese court myth (Nihongi) on the Korean (Silla) transmission of cult objects to Japan; passages are condensed paraphrases of the public-domain Aston translation, presented for comparative mythology.

passages.text: The Silla prince, Ama-no-hi-hoko, arrived, bringing seven objects in all: one Ha-buto gem, one Ashi-daka gem, one red-stone Ukaka gem, one Idzushi short sword, one Idzushi spear, one sun-mirror, and one Kuma-himorogi. These were stored in the Land of Tajima and made divine things for ever.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Nihongi, Book VI, §7 (trans. Aston 1896); not verbatim.

passages.text: One version says that in the beginning Ama-no-hi-hoko, riding in a ship, anchored at the land of Harima and dwelt in the village of Shisaha. Inquired who he was, he answered that he was the son of the King of Silla: hearing that in the Land of Japan there was a sage monarch, he had given his country to his younger brother Chiko and come to offer his allegiance with his treasures. The Emperor gave orders that he should dwell in Shisaha in Harima or Idesa in the island of Ahaji at his pleasure. Ama-no-hi-hoko asked that he might himself visit the various provinces to seek the place agreeable to his mind; ascending the river Uji he went north to the village of Ana in Ohomi, proceeded through Wakasa, and going westward arrived at the province of Tajima, where he fixed his dwelling. Therefore the potters of Kagami-no-hasama in Ohomi are the servants of Ama-no-hi-hoko. Ama-no-hi-hoko took to wife Matawo, daughter of Futomimi, a man of Idzushi in Tajima, who bore to him Tajima Morosuke - father of Tajima-no-Hinaraki, father of Kiyohiko, father of Tajima-mori.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Nihongi, Book VI, §7 (trans. Aston 1896); not verbatim.

title.en: Sahohiko's Treason and the Rice-Castle of Fire
title.zh: 沙本毘古之叛與稻城之火

region.en: Makimuku, Yamato
region.zh: 大和纏向

period: Nihongi compiled 720 CE (trans. Aston 1896)

source.work: Nihongi (Chronicles of Japan), Vol. I, trans. W. G. Aston (1896)

summary.en: The Empress's brother Sahohiko asks whom she loves best and entreats her to murder Suinin with a hidden dagger. As she bends over her sleeping husband her tears fall on his face; his dream of a brocade snake coiled round his neck and rain from Saho wrings the whole plot from her. Sahohiko resists a month in a castle of piled rice-stalks; the Empress enters with her child to plead for his life, leaves as it burns, and dies with her brother, recommending five ladies of Tamba to the Emperor.
summary.zh: 垂仁后沙本姬之兄沙本毘古欲弒帝，誘妹曰「汝愛兄與夫孰深」，予小刀使藏於衣，伺帝寢而刺其頸。姬泣於帝膝枕之側，帝覺而占夢曰「錦蛇繞頸，大雨自沙本潦面」，姬懼而盡吐其情。帝曰「非汝罪」，起兵遣筒田連田狹命誅沙本毘古。毘古積稻作稻城而拒，一月不拔。后抱皇子入稻城，帝圍之益急，趣送后與皇子出。后曰「臣妾罪當死，但願以妾所主之五后宮宅奉帝」，言訖，於烈火中與兄俱死。其后丹波有五女，皆賢，後召入後宮。

sensitivity.note: Ancient Japanese court myth (Nihongi); passages are condensed paraphrases of the public-domain Aston translation, presented for comparative mythology.

passages.text: The Empress's elder brother by the mother's side, Prince Sahohiko, plotted treason and tried to endanger the State. Watching an occasion when the Empress was at leisure, he asked her whom she loved best - her elder brother or her husband - and she innocently answered, her elder brother. Then he enticed her: 'If one serves a man by beauty, when the beauty fades his affection will cease... I wish to ascend to the immense felicity and rule over the Empire along with thee. So making high our pillows, we shall complete a long hundred years. I beg thee, therefore, to slay the Emperor for me.' He took a dagger and gave it to the Empress: 'Gird on this dagger among thy garments, and when the Emperor goes to sleep, do thou stab him in the neck and thus kill him.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Nihongi, Book VI, §§8–9 (trans. Aston 1896); not verbatim.

passages.text: The Emperor took his noonday sleep with the Empress's knees as his pillow. She thought vainly that this would be the time to accomplish her brother's plot, and her tears fell on the Emperor's face. He woke and said: 'To-day We have had a dream. A small brocade-coloured snake coiled itself round Our neck and a great rain arose from Saho, which coming hither wet Our face. What does this portend?' Knowing she could not conceal the plot, she bowed herself to the earth and told him all: the small brocade-coloured snake is nothing else than the dagger given her; the great rain is her own tears. The Emperor said, 'This is not thy crime', raised a force from the neighbouring districts, and commanded Yatsunada to slay Sahohiko.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Nihongi, Book VI, §§9–10 (trans. Aston 1896); not verbatim.

passages.text: Sahohiko withstood him with an army, hastily piling up rice-stalks to make a castle so solid it could not be breached - a rice-castle. A month passed and it did not surrender. The Empress, grieving, said that though she was Empress she could not preside over the Empire after bringing ruin on her brother; she took the Imperial Prince Homutsu-wake in her arms and entered the rice-castle. The Emperor increased his army, surrounded the castle on all sides, and proclaimed to those within to send out the Empress and Prince quickly, but they would not. So the general Yatsunada set fire to the castle. The Empress, taking the child in her bosom, crossed over the castle and came out, beseeching the Emperor: her flight into the castle had been in hope of absolving her brother for her sake; that failing, there was nothing for her but to strangle herself - only she prayed that her palace be granted to fair mates for him, and that five virtuous ladies, daughters of Prince Michi-no-Ushi of Tamba, be placed in the side courts. To this the Emperor agreed; then the fire blazed up, the castle was destroyed, and Sahohiko and his younger sister died together inside it. Yatsunada was commended and granted the new name Yamato-hi-muke-take-hi-muke-hiko.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Nihongi, Book VI, §10 (trans. Aston 1896); not verbatim.

passages.text: In the fifteenth year the five women of Tamba were sent for and placed in the side-court: Hibasu-hime, Nuba-tani-iri-hime, Matonu-hime, Azami-ni-iri-hime, and Takano-hime. Hibasu-hime was appointed Empress and her three younger sisters made concubines; Takano-hime, on account of the ugliness of her form, was sent back to her own country. In her shame at being sent back, when she came to Kadono she purposely tumbled from the carriage and was killed; therefore that place received the name of Ochi-kuni, Fall-country.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Nihongi, Book VI, §15 (trans. Aston 1896); not verbatim.

title.en: Nomi no Sukune and Kuyehaya: The First Wrestling-Match
title.zh: 野見宿禰與當麻蹶速相撲

region.en: Daini district (Taima), Yamato
region.zh: 大和當麻

period: Nihongi compiled 720 CE (trans. Aston 1896)

source.work: Nihongi (Chronicles of Japan), Vol. I, trans. W. G. Aston (1896)

summary.en: The courtiers report a champion of the Empire, Kuyehaya of Taima, who can break horns and straighten hooks and challenges all comers. A minister recalls the valiant Nomi no Sukune of Idzumo; the two men stand opposite and kick at each other until Sukune breaks Kuyehaya's ribs and loins and kills him. Taima's land is seized and given to Sukune, and the field of the broken loins keeps its name - the origin of sumo.
summary.zh: 垂仁七年，人奏當麻蹶速力絕人，能折角勾曲，揚言四海之內莫己若者，欲得力者比試生死。帝問群臣，有奏「出雲國有野見宿禰，宜召而試之」。即遣使者召之。二人相對踢蹴，宿禰踢蹶速脅而折其肋，又踢而折其腰，遂殺之。取其地悉賜宿禰，故其地有腰折田之名。是為相撲之始。

sensitivity.note: Ancient Japanese court myth (Nihongi): the legendary origin of sumo wrestling; passages are condensed paraphrases of the public-domain Aston translation, presented for comparative mythology.

passages.text: The courtiers represented to the Emperor: 'In the village of Taima there is a valiant man called Kuyehaya of Taima. He is of great bodily strength, so that he can break horns and straighten out hooks. He is always saying to the people: You may search the four quarters, but where is there one to compare with me in strength? O that I could meet with a man of might, with whom to have a trial of strength, regardless of life or death.' Hearing this, the Emperor proclaimed to his ministers that Kuyehaya was the champion of the Empire and asked if there might be any to compare with him. One of the ministers came forward and said that in the Land of Idzumo there was a valiant man named Nomi no Sukune, whom it would be desirable to send for and match with Kuyehaya.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Nihongi, Book VI, §12 (trans. Aston 1896); not verbatim.

passages.text: That same day the Emperor sent Nagaochi to summon Nomi no Sukune, who came from Idzumo, and straightway he and Taima no Kuyehaya were made to wrestle together. The two men stood opposite to one another; each raised his foot and kicked at the other, when Nomi no Sukune broke with a kick the ribs of Kuyehaya and also kicked and broke his loins, and thus killed him. Therefore the land of Taima no Kuyehaya was seized and was all given to Nomi no Sukune. This was the cause why there is in that village a place called Koshi-ore-da, the field of the broken loins. Nomi no Sukune remained and served the Emperor.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Nihongi, Book VI, §12 (trans. Aston 1896); not verbatim.

title.en: The Living Burial of Yamato-hiko's Tomb
title.zh: 倭彥命陵活殉之慟

region.en: Tsukizaka in Musa, Yamato
region.zh: 大和身狹桃花鳥坂

period: Nihongi compiled 720 CE (trans. Aston 1896)

source.work: Nihongi (Chronicles of Japan), Vol. I, trans. W. G. Aston (1896)

summary.en: When Yamato-hiko, the Emperor's brother, dies, his personal attendants are buried alive upright in the precinct of the tomb. For several days they do not die but weep and wail day and night until they rot, and dogs and crows eat them. Hearing the sound of their weeping, Suinin is grieved and decrees an end to the practice of following the dead - the story later generations attach to the age of Kōrei.
summary.zh: 垂仁二十八年，倭彥命崩，葬身狹桃花鳥坂。乃集其從僕數十人，悉生埋於陵域。數日不死，夜哭晝泣，遂腐而畢，犬烏聚而食之。帝聞哭聲，心甚哀慟，詔左右曰「生者殉死，甚可痛傷。古雖如此，何用追從？自今以後，議而止之」。

sensitivity.note: Ancient Japanese court myth (Nihongi) concerning junshi, the burial of attendants with their lord; passages are condensed paraphrases of the public-domain Aston translation, presented for comparative mythology.

passages.text: Yamato-hiko no Mikoto, the Emperor's younger brother by the mother's side, died, and was buried at Tsukizaka in Musa. Thereupon his personal attendants were assembled and were all buried alive upright in the precinct of the misasagi. For several days they died not, but wept and wailed day and night. At last they died and rotted. Dogs and crows gathered and ate them.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Nihongi, Book VI, §19 (trans. Aston 1896); not verbatim.

passages.text: The Emperor, hearing the sound of their weeping and wailing, was grieved in heart, and commanded his high officers: 'It is a very painful thing to force those whom one has loved in life to follow him in death. Though it be an ancient custom, why follow it, if it is bad? From this time forward, take counsel so as to put a stop to the following of the dead.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Nihongi, Book VI, §19 (trans. Aston 1896); not verbatim.

title.en: Nomi no Sukune Substitutes Clay Figures for Living Men
title.zh: 野見宿禰造土偶代生人

region.en: Tomb of Hibasu-hime, Yamato
region.zh: 大和日葉酢媛命陵

period: Nihongi compiled 720 CE (trans. Aston 1896)

source.work: Nihongi (Chronicles of Japan), Vol. I, trans. W. G. Aston (1896)

summary.en: When Empress Hibasu-hime dies, the abolished yet still-expected practice of following in death poses a problem. Nomi no Sukune proposes an expedient: he summons a hundred clay-workers' men from Idzumo and has them shape figures of men, horses and other objects. These haniwa are first set up at her tomb, and a decree orders clay figures, not harmed men, at all tumuli henceforth - and the Hashi no Muraji superintend imperial burials ever after.
summary.zh: 垂仁三十二年，日葉酢媛命崩。帝曰「從死之風不良已悟，今葬何宜？」野見宿禰進曰「於君之陵生埋人，非良，何傳後世？請進一事」。乃遣使自出雲召土師部工人百，自執作土牛馬等物以獻，曰「自今以後，以土物代生人，置於陵域，以為後世法」。帝大喜，命此土物曰埴輪。下詔「陵必置土物，無傷人」。宿禰獲賞，掌土師部，故土師連執掌帝葬至今。

sensitivity.note: Ancient Japanese court myth (Nihongi): the legendary origin of the haniwa clay figures; passages are condensed paraphrases of the public-domain Aston translation, presented for comparative mythology.

passages.text: The Empress Hibasu-hime no Mikoto died. Some time before the burial, the Emperor commanded his Ministers: 'We have already recognized that the practice of following the dead is not good. What should now be done in performing this burial?' Thereupon Nomi no Sukune came forward and said: 'It is not good to bury living men upright at the tumulus of a prince. How can such a practice be handed down to posterity? I beg leave to propose an expedient which I will submit to Your Majesty.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Nihongi, Book VI, §20 (trans. Aston 1896); not verbatim.

passages.text: He sent messengers to summon up from the Land of Idzumo a hundred men of the clay-workers' Be, and himself directed them to take clay and form therewith shapes of men, horses and various objects, which he presented to the Emperor: 'Henceforward let it be the law for future ages to substitute things of clay for living men, and to set them up at tumuli.' The Emperor was greatly rejoiced and commanded Nomi no Sukune: 'Thy expedient hath greatly pleased Our heart.' The things of clay were first set up at the tomb of Hibasu-hime, and a decree was issued: 'Henceforth these clay figures must be set up at tumuli: let not men be harmed.' Sukune was bountifully rewarded, received a kneading-place and the charge of the clay-workers' Be, and was thenceforth called Hashi no Omi; this was how it came to pass that the Hashi no Muraji superintend the burials of the Emperors.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Nihongi, Book VI, §20 (trans. Aston 1896); not verbatim.

title.en: Yamato-hime Carries Amaterasu to Ise of the Divine Wind
title.zh: 倭姬命奉天照大神祀伊勢

region.en: Ise (Isuzu river, Province of Ise)
region.zh: 伊勢國五十鈴川畔

period: Nihongi compiled 720 CE (trans. Aston 1896)

source.work: Nihongi (Chronicles of Japan), Vol. I, trans. W. G. Aston (1896)

summary.en: Amaterasu is taken from Toyo-suki-iri-hime and entrusted to the princess Yamato-hime, who wanders through Sasahata, Ohomi and Mino seeking a shrine, until the Great Goddess names the secluded and pleasant land of Ise of the divine wind as her dwelling. There an abstinence palace is built on the Isuzu. In a variant, the Emperor makes Yamato-hime his august staff offered to the Goddess. The Great God of Yamato also possesses a minister to rebuke Sujin's incomplete worship, and Nunaki-waka-hime is divined as priestess.
summary.zh: 垂仁二十五年三月，以天照大神自豐鍬入姬命傳於倭姬命。倭姬命求鎮坐之地，歷宇陀、近江、美濃而後至伊勢。大神託曰「神風伊勢者，常世之浪打寄之國，此地美哉，願居此」。乃奉齋於五十鈴川畔，建齋宮，是為伊勢齋宮之始。一說帝以倭姬為御杖，奉於天照大神。又大倭大國魂神託物部大磯城，諫帝祭祀不周，帝乃廣加奉祭。

sensitivity.note: Ancient Japanese court myth (Nihongi) on the founding of the Grand Shrine of Ise, sacred to living Shinto tradition; passages are condensed paraphrases of the public-domain Aston translation, presented for comparative mythology.

passages.text: Ama-terasu no Oho-kami was taken from Toyo-suki-iri-hime no Mikoto and entrusted to Yamato-hime no Mikoto. Yamato-hime sought for a place where she might enshrine the Great Goddess: she proceeded to Sasahata in Uda, then turning back entered the land of Ohomi, went round eastwards to Mino, and arrived in the province of Ise. Now Amaterasu instructed her: 'The province of Ise, of the divine wind, is the land whither repair the waves from the eternal world, the successive waves. It is a secluded and pleasant land. In this land I wish to dwell.' In compliance with this instruction a shrine was erected to her in the province of Ise, and an Abstinence Palace was built at Kaha-kami in Isuzu - the palace of Iso.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Nihongi, Book VI, §17 (trans. Aston 1896); not verbatim.

passages.text: One story is that the Emperor made Yamato-hime no Mikoto his august staff, that is his assistant or deputy, and offered her to Amaterasu: she enshrined the Goddess at Idzu-kashi-no-Moto in Shiki and offered sacrifice, and thereafter, in compliance with the Goddess's instructions, removed in winter to the Palace of Watarahi in the province of Ise.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Nihongi, Book VI, §17 (trans. Aston 1896); not verbatim.

passages.text: At this time the Great God of Yamato inspired Ohominakuchi no Sukune and admonished the Emperor by his mouth: 'At the time of the Great Beginning it was covenanted that Amaterasu should govern all the Plain of Heaven, and that her august Imperial descendants should hold absolute rule over the eighty spiritual beings of the Central Reed-plain Land. My personal tenure of the governance of the great land is already at an end. Although the late Emperor Mimaki maintained the worship of the Gods in Heaven and Earth, he failed to search out the root of the matter, wanting in thoroughness: therefore that Emperor was short-lived. Do thou show regret for his shortcomings and be watchful as to the ceremonies of worship; so thine august life will be long and the Empire will have peace.' By divination Nunaki-waka-hime was appointed to conduct the worship of the Great God of Yamato; her body being already emaciated and unfit to sacrifice, Nagaochi offered the sacrifices in her stead.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Nihongi, Book VI, §17 (trans. Aston 1896); not verbatim.

title.en: The Ugly Boy Who Could Not Be Moved
title.zh: 撼不動之妖童

region.en: Nobleman's house, Seoul (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 漢京貴族宅（象徵性定位）

period: Collected by Im Bang; English ed. Gale, Korean Folk Tales (1913)

source.work: James S. Gale (trans.), Korean Folk Tales (1913), tale 'The Awful Little Goblin', eBook #51002

summary.en: At a great feast in a nobleman's house an uncombed, ugly boy of fifteen appears in the women's quarters and will not go. Servants, then ten men with ropes, then giants with clubs try to move or crush him — he is like a rock fast in the earth, and the club-blows sound like reverberating thunder without turning a hair of him. The crowd, fearing this is not a man but a god, bow and supplicate until he gives a sarcastic smile, goes out of the gate and disappears. From that day the people of the house are taken ill; those who scolded him, tied him and pounded him all die within a few days. It was commonly held that the boy was the Too-uk Spirit.
summary.zh: 漢京貴族宴客，有垢面醜童忽然立於婦人房前，喝之不去。以繩縛、以巨木擊，皆如撼山擊卵，童子紋絲不動。眾懼，以為神，羅拜乞哀。童冷笑而出，旋杳。自是闔家及諸客相繼病歿。俗謂此即土尤之神云。

sensitivity.note: Goblin-visitor tale; no living-community restriction.

passages.text: There was an occasion for a celebration in the home of a nobleman of Seoul. In front of the women's quarters there suddenly appeared an uncombed, ugly-looking boy about fifteen years of age. One of the women guests sent a servant to reprimand him and put him out, but the boy stood stock-still with no word of reply.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Gale, Korean Folk Tales, 'The Awful Little Goblin' (1913); not verbatim.

passages.text: Several took hold of him to pull him, but he was like a fixed rock fast in the earth, absolutely immovable. They sent ten strong men with ropes to bind him, but like a giant mountain he remained fast; five or six giant fellows with clubs laid on with all their might, the sound of their pounding like reverberating thunder, yet not a hair did he turn, not a wink did he give. The crowd began to fear, saying, 'This is not a man, but a god,' so they entered the courtyard, one and all, and began to bow before him, joining their hands and supplicating earnestly.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Gale, Korean Folk Tales, 'The Awful Little Goblin' (1913); not verbatim.

passages.text: At last the boy gave a sarcastic smile, turned round, went out of the gate and disappeared. The company, frightened out of their wits, called off the feast. From that day on, the people of that house were taken ill, including host and guests; those who scolded him, those who tied him with ropes, those who pounded him, all died in a few days. It was commonly held that the boy was the Too-uk Spirit.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Gale, Korean Folk Tales, 'The Awful Little Goblin' (1913); not verbatim.

title.en: God's Way: The Lightning Strikes the Mother-Beater
title.zh: 天雷殛逆子

region.en: Buckwheat field outside a country town (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 郊野蕎麥田（象徵性定位）

period: Tale by Yi Ryuk; English ed. Gale, Korean Folk Tales (1913)

source.work: James S. Gale (trans.), Korean Folk Tales (1913), tale 'God's Way', eBook #51002

summary.en: A man of fierce and ungovernable disposition beats his mother, who screams: 'Oh, God, why do you not strike dead this wicked man who beats his mother?' Thrusting his sickle through his belt he goes to reap buckwheat under a fine clear sky — until a dark fleck of cloud appears in mid-heaven and all the sky becomes black. Furious thunder follows; the villagers see in the field a man with lifted sickle trying to ward off the flashes, and when the storm clears they find the mother-beater struck dead and riven to pieces. God takes note of evil doers on this earth, and deals with them as they deserve.
summary.zh: 有悍夫常毆其母，母呼天曰：『天何不殛此逆子！』其人攜鐮往田刈蕎。晴空萬里，忽黑雲一點，頃刻天晦，雷雨大作。村人遙見田中一人舉鐮遮雷。雨霧往視，則逆子已遭雷殛，碎裂於地。天道報應，可不畏哉。

sensitivity.note: Moral exemplum of filial piety; no living-community restriction.

passages.text: In a certain town there lived a man of fierce and ungovernable disposition, who in moments of anger used to beat his mother. One day, thus beaten, the parent screamed out, 'Oh, God, why do you not strike dead this wicked man who beats his mother?'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Gale, Korean Folk Tales, 'God's Way' (1913); not verbatim.

passages.text: The son thrust his sickle through his belt and went slowly off to the fields where he was engaged by a neighbour in reaping buckwheat. The day was fine and the sky beautifully clear, when suddenly a dark fleck of cloud appeared in mid-heaven, and a little later all the sky became black. Furious thunder followed, and rain came on.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Gale, Korean Folk Tales, 'God's Way' (1913); not verbatim.

passages.text: The village people looked out toward the field, where the flashes of lightning were specially noticeable; they seemed to see there a man with lifted sickle trying to ward them off. When the storm had cleared away, they went to see, and lo, they found the man who had beaten his mother struck dead and riven to pieces.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Gale, Korean Folk Tales, 'God's Way' (1913); not verbatim.

title.en: The Old Man in the Dream Beseeches for the Turtle
title.zh: 夢中老人乞龜

region.en: Lotus Lake near Seoul (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 漢京蓮池（象徵性定位）

period: Tale by Yi Ryuk; English ed. Gale, Korean Folk Tales (1913)

source.work: James S. Gale (trans.), Korean Folk Tales (1913), tale 'The Old Man in the Dream', eBook #51002

summary.en: Kwon Jai, high in rank and given to sport, dreams that an old man bows low in tears: 'Sir, Minister Hong wishes to kill off me and all my posterity. Please save me — if you desist, Hong will give it up and I shall live and all mine.' A rap at the door wakes him: it is Hong, come to invite him to fish for turtles at Lotus Lake. Then Kwon knows the turtle appeared in the dream in the form of an old man, and declines, saying he is ill — and he learned later that Hong also did not go.
summary.zh: 權居士夢一老人泣拜曰：『洪公欲盡誅吾族，公救之。』覺而洪公適來邀，往蓮池釣龜。權悟夢中之老人即龜也，辭以疾。後聞洪公亦未往。

sensitivity.note: Animal-dream omen tale; no living-community restriction.

passages.text: Kwon Jai was a man high in rank and well advanced in years, much given to sport and various kinds of pleasure. One night he had a dream, when an old man came to him, bowed low, and in tears said, 'Sir, Minister Hong wishes to kill off me and all my posterity. Please save me, won't you?'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Gale, Korean Folk Tales, 'The Old Man in the Dream' (1913); not verbatim.

passages.text: 'Hong will assuredly ask Your Excellency to help him. Desist from it, please, for if you do, Hong will give it up and I shall live and all mine,' said the old man. A little later there came a rap at the door, when Kwon awakened and asked, 'Who is there?'
