It was Hong, who that day had planned an excursion to Lotus Lake to fish for turtles, and now had come specially to invite Kwon to go with him. Then Kwon knew that the turtle had appeared to him in a dream in the form of an old man, so he declined, saying he was ill. It was learned later that Hong also did not go.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Gale, Korean Folk Tales, 'The Old Man in the Dream' (1913); not verbatim.

title.en: Softy, the Priest Who Took the Floggings
title.zh: 軟和尚代刑

region.en: Pagoda Temple, Seoul (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 漢京塔寺（象徵性定位）

period: Tale by Yi Ryuk; English ed. Gale, Korean Folk Tales (1913)

source.work: James S. Gale (trans.), Korean Folk Tales (1913), tale 'The Perfect Priest', eBook #51002

summary.en: A priest called Namnu has perfected his ways in Buddhist doctrine: he undresses and gives his clothing to the cold, and everybody calls him Softy. Whenever he sees anyone sentenced to a flogging in the temple or official yamen, he invariably begs to take the culprit's place. At a great function at Pagoda Temple he tells Prince Hong of Yon-san, 'You are indeed a very great man,' takes a box on the ear, and laughs: 'Please, Hong, don't do that, it hurts! it hurts!' Before the Temple he looks at Prince Yi and says, 'I know your face, but I have forgotten your name. Oh, I remember now, you are Yi Sok-hyong' — to the scandal of the monastery priests, who hurry to apologize: 'Softy was born so, God made him so.'
summary.zh: 有僧曰南婁，戒行圓滿，遇寒者輒解衣衣之，人呼曰軟和尚。凡見受笞者必以身代。於塔寺大會中謂燕山君之子曰『公真偉人也』，被批頰，笑曰『勿爾，痛哉』。又於寺前直呼親王名諱，僧眾大驚謝罪，曰『此天生如此，惟乞恕之』。

sensitivity.note: Holy-fool (holy fool/palmun) figure in Buddhist context; no living-community restriction.

passages.text: There was once a priest called Namnu who had perfected his ways in the Buddhistic doctrine. Whenever he had clothing of his own he would willingly undress and give it to those who were cold. His spirit was gentle, with no creases or corners in it. Everybody, high and low, rich and poor, called him by the nickname of Softy.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Gale, Korean Folk Tales, 'The Perfect Priest' (1913); not verbatim.

passages.text: Whenever he saw any one sentenced to a flogging in the temple or official yamen, Namnu invariably begged that he might take the culprit's place. Once, when there was a great function in progress at Pagoda Temple and many high officials were assembled, Softy, too, was seen kneeling at the side. He suddenly remarked to Prince Hong of Yon-san, 'You are indeed a very great man.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Gale, Korean Folk Tales, 'The Perfect Priest' (1913); not verbatim.

passages.text: Hong replied, 'What do you mean by great man, you impudent brat? Take that,' and gave him a box with his fist on the ear. Softy laughed, and said, 'Please, Hong, don't do that, it hurts! it hurts!' Later, stopping before the Temple with Prince Yi and other high officials, Softy looked at Yi and said, 'I know your face, but I have forgotten your name. Afterwards he said, Oh, I remember now, you are Yi Sok-hyong.' The priests of the monastery who heard this familiarity were scandalized, and hurried to make no end of apology to the Prince: 'Softy was born so, God made him so. Please, Your Excellency, forgive him.' The Prince forgave him and so he was not disturbed.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Gale, Korean Folk Tales, 'The Perfect Priest' (1913); not verbatim.

title.en: The Propitious Magpie and the Imitation Nest
title.zh: 鵲巢報喜

region.en: Outside the South Gate, Seoul (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 漢城南門外（象徵性定位）

period: Tale by Yi Ryuk (1439-1498), with personal testimony; English ed. Gale, Korean Folk Tales (1913)

source.work: James S. Gale (trans.), Korean Folk Tales (1913), tale 'The Propitious Magpie', eBook #51002

summary.en: People say that when the magpie builds its nest directly south of a home, the master of the house will be promoted. King T'ai-jong's poor friend, failing in all his projects, sends a servant to build an imitation magpie's nest in a propitious place before the royal procession; caught and questioned, the servant explains the belief, and the King takes pity and orders the appointment at once. Yi Ryuk testifies from his own life: as a boy he moved a fallen nest to a propitious tree south of his home, and that very winter his father was promoted three degrees; when a slave pulled down the nest at his Chong-pa summer-house the magpies built again the next year, and in that year Ye-jong came to the throne and Yi was promoted again; a third nest by his office brought a third promotion. 'There is a spiritual power in the magpie surely.'
summary.zh: 俗云鵲巢於宅南者，主人必遷官。太宗有貧友，遣僕於蹕路造偽鵲巢以邀福；事發，僕直陳其故，王憐而即予除目。柳夢寅自記：少時移鵲巢於宅南楮樹，其冬父連升三級；後館前鵲巢被婢拆作薪，次年復營，是年睿宗即位而柳復遷官。鵲之有靈，信矣。

sensitivity.note: Bird-omen belief; no living-community restriction.

passages.text: People say that when the magpie builds its nest directly south of a home, the master of the house will be promoted in office. King T'ai-jong had a friend once who was very poor and had failed in all his projects; he decided to wait till the King went out on procession and then send a servant to build an imitation magpie's nest in some propitious place before him.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Gale, Korean Folk Tales, 'The Propitious Magpie' (1913); not verbatim.

passages.text: The King saw it and asked the man what he was doing. He said in reply that when a magpie builds its nest straight south of a home the master of the house instantly gets promotion; his master had waited so long and nothing had come, that he was building an imitation nest to bring it about. The King took pity on him and ordered his appointment at once.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Gale, Korean Folk Tales, 'The Propitious Magpie' (1913); not verbatim.

passages.text: When I was young myself a magpie built its nest before our home, but with other boys I cut off the branch so that the whole nest fell to the ground; feeling sorry and afraid, on a propitious site to the south I had the nest hung up on a tree, where the young all lived and flourished and flew away. In that very winter my father was promoted three degrees in rank. Afterwards, before my summer-house at Chong-pa, magpies built a nest in a date tree; a woman slave pulled it down for fuel, but they came again the next year and built once more, and that year Ye-jong came to the throne and I was promoted again. In the spring of 1471 magpies built their nest in a tree just south of my office: 'There is a spiritual power in the magpie surely, as men have said from olden times and as I myself have proven.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Gale, Korean Folk Tales, 'The Propitious Magpie' (1913); not verbatim.

title.en: The Old Buddha Rides Past the Magistrates
title.zh: 老佛過橋

region.en: Kai-ryong county riverbank (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 鶏龍縣江干（象徵性定位）

period: Tale by Yi Ryuk; English ed. Gale, Korean Folk Tales (1913)

source.work: James S. Gale (trans.), Korean Folk Tales (1913), tale 'The Old Buddha', eBook #51002

summary.en: Prime Minister Choi Yun-tok, mourning his mother, rides south with a single horse and one servant through the county of Kai-ryong, where district magistrates are drinking under a tent by the riverbank. Offended that the mourner does not dismount, they arrest his servant and demand his master's name. 'Choi, the Old Buddha.' 'But what's his real name?' 'The old Buddha.' Beaten over the head, the servant says slowly: he is called Choi the Buddha, but his real name is Yun-tok, on his way to his country home in Chang-won. The magistrates recognize the Prime Minister, strike their tent, clear away the eatables, and run to make their deepest salaam and ask pardon for their sin.
summary.zh: 崔有敦相公居喪南行，道經鶏龍縣。縣令宴於江亭，怒其不下馬，逮其僕問主人名。僕曰『老佛崔公』；再問，曰『老佛』。笞之，僕徐言曰『佛者字也，諱有敦，今往昌原私第』。令等大懼，撤席奔拜請罪。老佛者，相公之別號也。

sensitivity.note: Officialdom anecdote; no living-community restriction.

passages.text: Prime Minister Choi Yun-tok was in mourning once for his mother. With a single horse and one servant he made a journey to the south where the road led through the county of Kai-ryong. At that very time two or three of the district magistrates had pitched a tent on the bank of the river and were having refreshments.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Gale, Korean Folk Tales, 'The Old Buddha' (1913); not verbatim.

passages.text: They said to one another, 'Who is that mourner that goes riding by without dismounting? It must be some country farmer who has never learned proper manners. We shall certainly have to teach him a lesson.' They sent an attendant to arrest and bring his servant, and asked who his master was. 'Choi, the Old Buddha.' 'But what's his real name?' 'The old Buddha.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Gale, Korean Folk Tales, 'The Old Buddha' (1913); not verbatim.

passages.text: Then they grew very angry and beat him over the head. Then the servant said slowly, 'He is called Choi the Buddha, but his real name is Yun-tok, and he is now on his way to his country home in Chang-won.' At once they recognized that it was no other than the Prime Minister, and great fear overcame them. They struck their tent, cleared away the eatables, and ran to make their deepest salaam and to ask pardon for their sin.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Gale, Korean Folk Tales, 'The Old Buddha' (1913); not verbatim.

title.en: The Kill-Devil Pills of Prince Cheung
title.zh: 殺鬼丸

region.en: Minister's mansion, Seoul (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 漢京相府（象徵性定位）

period: Tale by Yi Ryuk; English ed. Gale, Korean Folk Tales (1913)

source.work: James S. Gale (trans.), Korean Folk Tales (1913), tale 'A Wonderful Medicine', eBook #51002

summary.en: Prince Cheung, First Minister for thirty years and now nearly ninety, has his home attacked by goblins and devils: in broad daylight they snatch the hat from a young official's head and crumple it, and keep throwing stones till the whole court is in confusion. The Prince escapes to another house, prepares a special medicine called sal-kwi-whan, kill-devil-pills, which he offers in prayer — and from that time the goblins depart. After five or six years no sign of them has reappeared, and Prince Cheung is well and strong and free from sickness.
summary.zh: 張相公府中為鬼所擾，白晝擲石，奪客之帽而揉之，闔宅大亂。相公避居別第，製藥曰殺鬼丸，持咒服之。自是群鬼遁去，五六載不復至，相公亦康強無恙。

sensitivity.note: Exorcism-medicine anecdote; no living-community restriction.

passages.text: Prince Cheung had been First Minister of the land for thirty years, a man just and upright, now nearly ninety years of age. His home was suddenly attacked by goblins and devils: when a young official came to call on him, these mysterious beings in broad daylight snatched the hat from his head and crumpled it up.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Gale, Korean Folk Tales, 'A Wonderful Medicine' (1913); not verbatim.

passages.text: They threw stones, too, and kept on throwing them so that all the court was reduced to confusion. Prince Cheung made his escape and went to live in another house, where he prepared a special medicine called sal-kwi-whan, kill-devil-pills, which he offered in prayer. From that time the goblins departed, and now after five or six years no sign of them has reappeared; Prince Cheung, too, is well and strong and free from sickness.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Gale, Korean Folk Tales, 'A Wonderful Medicine' (1913); not verbatim.

title.en: Mo, the Slave Wife Who Died Rather than Part
title.zh: 無娘殉情

region.en: Camel Mountain ridge, Seoul (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 駱山嶺（象徵性定位）

period: Tale by Yi Ryuk, told by kin of the scholar An Yun; English ed. Gale, Korean Folk Tales (1913)

source.work: James S. Gale (trans.), Korean Folk Tales (1913), tale 'Faithful Mo', eBook #51002

summary.en: An Yun, a noted scholar, loves Mo, the beautiful daughter of Prince Ha's slave, and takes her for his wife. The furious Prince has her arrested to marry her to one of his bondsmen; she escapes over the wall back to An, and together they swear to die rather than be parted. Arrested again, she is found hanging by the neck dead. Months later, returning from the Confucian Temple over Camel Mountain ridge in the autumn moonlight, An is musing love verses to her memory when a soft footfall comes from among the pines — there is Mo. Knowing her long dead, he runs to catch her hand: 'How did you come here?' — and she disappears. He cries out, falls ill, cannot swallow, and dies of a broken heart. 'Faithful unto death was she. Even of the faithful among the ancients was there ever a better than Mo?'
summary.zh: 安允與婢女無娘私結為夫婦，主人家怒而執之。無娘踰牆歸安，誓死不離。再被捕，縊死。後安自廟還，月夜過駱山嶺，忽聞松間履聲，則無娘也。安知其鬼，然情不能自已，趨執其手，瞬息而滅。安慟而病，粒食不下，遂卒。或曰：『至死靡他，雖士族之婦有不及者。』

sensitivity.note: Love-tragedy ghost tale; depicts Joseon slave status; no living-community restriction.

passages.text: Prince Ha had a slave who was a landed proprietor and lived in Yang-ju county; he had a daughter, fairest of the fair, whom he called Mo. An Yun was a noted scholar, a man of distinction in letters. He saw Mo, fell in love with her and took her for his wife. Prince Ha heard of this and was furiously angry: 'How is it that you, a slave, dare to marry with a man of the aristocracy?'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Gale, Korean Folk Tales, 'Faithful Mo' (1913); not verbatim.

passages.text: He had her arrested and brought home, intending to marry her to one of his bondsmen. Mo learned of this with tears and sorrow, made her escape over the wall and went back to An; together they took an oath to die rather than to be parted. Later Prince Ha sent his underlings to arrest her again and carry her off; after this all trace of her was lost till Mo was discovered one day in a room hanging by the neck dead.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Gale, Korean Folk Tales, 'Faithful Mo' (1913); not verbatim.

passages.text: Months of sorrow passed over An till once, under cover of the night, he was returning from the Confucian Temple to his house over the ridge of Camel Mountain. It was early autumn and the wooded tops were shimmering in the moonlight. Musing longingly of Mo, and repeating love verses to her memory, he suddenly heard a soft footfall as though coming from among the pines — there was Mo. An knew that she was long dead, but because he was so buried in thought of her, doubting nothing, he ran to her and caught her by the hand, saying, 'How did you come here?' — but she disappeared. An gave a great cry and broke into tears. He fell ill; a little later he died of a broken heart.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Gale, Korean Folk Tales, 'Faithful Mo' (1913); not verbatim.

title.en: The Minister in Plain Clothes and the Proud Scholar
title.zh: 微行相公折傲士

region.en: Roadside pavilion, southern journey (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 南行道旁亭（象徵性定位）

period: Tale by Yi Ryuk; English ed. Gale, Korean Folk Tales (1913)

source.work: James S. Gale (trans.), Korean Folk Tales (1913), tale 'The Renowned Maing', eBook #51002

summary.en: Minister of State Maing Sa-song, dressed in plain clothes, is overtaken by rain and shelters in a side pavilion where the young scholar Whang Eui-hon, hands behind his back, reads the verse-boards. 'Well, grand-dad, do you know the flavour of verses like these?' The Minister pretends ignorance and asks the meaning; Whang lectures him on the great men of the past and living pictures in poetry. Then pack-horses, servants, tent poles and canvas packs come in a long procession, and Whang, to his amazement, learns the old man is Maing Sa-song, and drops unconsciously onto his knees in a deep and long obeisance. The Minister laughs: 'There is no difference in the value of mere men; they are high or low according to the thoughts that prompt them, but unfortunately all are born with a proud heart. You are not a common scholar; why, therefore, should you be so proud to begin with and so humble now?' — and comforts him and sends him away.
summary.zh: 蕭瑟松微服南行，避雨於亭。有書生黃義憲方負手讀壁上題詠，傲然問曰『老丈解此詩味否』。松佯為不知，請其講解。俄而行李駝馬續至，黃始知即蕭相公，不覺長跪。松笑曰：『人之貴賤在乎其心，而不在於貌。子始倨而後恭，何也？』乃慰而遣之。

sensitivity.note: Moral anecdote; no living-community restriction.

passages.text: Minister of State Maing Sa-song once upon a time, dressed in plain clothes, started south on a long journey. On the way he was overtaken by rain, and turned into a side pavilion for rest and shelter. There was a young scholar already in the pavilion by the name of Whang Eui-hon, who with his two hands behind his back was reading the pavilion inscription board.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Gale, Korean Folk Tales, 'The Renowned Maing' (1913); not verbatim.

passages.text: At last he turned to the old man and said, 'Well, grand-dad, do you know the flavour of verses like these?' The famous Minister, pretending ignorance, arose and said, 'An old countryman like myself, could you expect him to know? Please tell me the meaning.' Whang said, 'These verses were written by the great men of the past. What they saw and experienced they wrote down to inspire the souls of those who were to come after them. They are like pictures of sea and land, for there are living pictures in poetry, you know.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Gale, Korean Folk Tales, 'The Renowned Maing' (1913); not verbatim.

passages.text: A little later came pack-horses loaded with all sorts of things, servants and retainers, tent poles, canvas packs and other equipment, a long procession. Whang, surprised, made inquiry, and to his amazement learned that the old man was none other than Maing Sa-song; unconsciously he dropped onto his knees in a deep and long obeisance. The Minister laughed and said, 'That will do; there is no difference in the value of mere men, they are high or low according to the thoughts that prompt them, but unfortunately all are born with a proud heart. You are not a common scholar; why, therefore, should you be so proud to begin with and so humble now?' The Minister took him by the hand, led him to his mat, made him sit down, comforted him and sent him away.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Gale, Korean Folk Tales, 'The Renowned Maing' (1913); not verbatim.

title.en: Who Decides, God or the King?
title.zh: 富貴在天

region.en: Heung-yang Palace, Seoul (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 漢城慶熙宮（象徵性定位）

period: Tale by Yi Ryuk; story of King Tae-jong (r. 1400-1418); English ed. Gale, Korean Folk Tales (1913)

source.work: James S. Gale (trans.), Korean Folk Tales (1913), tale 'Who Decides, God or the King?', eBook #51002

summary.en: Resting in Heung-yang Palace, King Tae-jong overhears two eunuchs arguing whether riches and honour are in the king's hand or ordered of God. To test it, he writes a secret despatch — 'Raise the bearer of this letter one degree in rank' — and commands A to deliver it. At the palace gate a furious pain takes A in the stomach, and he begs B to go in his place. The next day the record of promotions shows B advanced, and not one word about A. King Tae-jong makes inquiry, and when he knows the circumstances he gives a sudden start of wonder and remains long in deep thought.
summary.zh: 太宗休於宮中，聞二閹辯富貴由王抑由天。乃手書密札曰『持此札者進一階』，命甲賫送。甲至宮門腹痛如割，倩乙代往。明日甲名不與，而乙登籍。太宗驚愕，沉思良久。

sensitivity.note: Fate-vs-royal-power tale; no living-community restriction.

passages.text: King Tai-jong was having a rest in Heung-yang Palace, while outside two eunuchs were talking together over the law that governs the affairs of men, as to whether it is man or God. One said, 'Riches and honour are all in the king's hand.' The other said, 'Nothing of the kind; every atom of wealth and every degree of promotion are all ordered of God. Even the king himself has no part in it and no power.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Gale, Korean Folk Tales, 'Who Decides, God or the King?' (1913); not verbatim.

passages.text: The King, overhearing what was said, wrote a secret despatch, saying, 'Raise the Bearer of this letter one degree in rank.' He sealed it and commanded the first eunuch to take it. He made his bow and departed, but just when he was about to leave the palace enclosure a furious pain took him in the stomach, so that he begged his fellow to take his place and go into the city.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Gale, Korean Folk Tales, 'Who Decides, God or the King?' (1913); not verbatim.

passages.text: The next day, when the record of promotions was placed before the King, he read how the second had been advanced, but not one word was there about the first. King Tai-jong made inquiry, and when he knew the circumstances he gave a sudden start of wonder and remained long in deep thought.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Gale, Korean Folk Tales, 'Who Decides, God or the King?' (1913); not verbatim.

title.en: Im Sung-jong's Three Years on the Door-sill
title.zh: 任世宗三絕苦練

region.en: Outside the South Gate, Seoul (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 漢城南門外（象徵性定位）

period: Tale by Yi Ryuk; story of the reign of King Se-jong; English ed. Gale, Korean Folk Tales (1913)

source.work: James S. Gale (trans.), Korean Folk Tales (1913), tale 'Three Things Mastered', eBook #51002

summary.en: Im Sung-jong, a relative of the king and the first performer of his time on the harp, is seen every morning for three years kneeling on the sill of his front door beating his hands up and down on his knees — people think him mad, but thus he learns the motions required for the harp. Night and day he blows and practises with his fingers for three years to learn the motions for the flute; and being light of body and poor at riding and archery, he sighs that he must yet know how to make the bull's-eye, takes his bow into the hills every morning and shoots all day long for three years till he becomes a renowned archer.
summary.zh: 任世宗為王之懿親，善琴。日日跪於門限上以手擊膝，如是者三年，人皆以為狂，而琴法遂成。又畫夜吹簫習指，三年而簫法成。體弱不善騎射，乃日日擕弓矢入山射之，三年而為名射。精誠所至，金石為開。

sensitivity.note: Self-cultivation exemplum; no living-community restriction.

passages.text: There was a relative of the king, named Im Sung-jong, who was a gifted man in thought and purpose. He was the first performer of his time on the harp. King Se-jong said of him, 'Im's harp knows but one master, and follows no other man.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Gale, Korean Folk Tales, 'Three Things Mastered' (1913); not verbatim.

passages.text: His home was outside the South Gate, and every morning he was seen kneeling on the sill of his front door beating his hands upwards and downwards on his knees, and this practice he carried on for three years. People could not imagine what he meant by it, but thought him mad. Thus he learned the motions required for the harp. Also he blew with his mouth and practised with his fingers day and night without stopping, and kept this up for three years and so learned the motions for the flute.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Gale, Korean Folk Tales, 'Three Things Mastered' (1913); not verbatim.

passages.text: He was a lightly built man in body, and poor at riding and at archery. He often sighed over this defect, and said, 'Though I am weak and stupid and not able to shoot a long distance, I shall yet know how to hit the target and make the bull's-eye. This also must be acquired by practice.' So every morning he took his bow and arrows and went off into the hills, and there he shot all day long, keeping it up for three years, till he became a renowned archer.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Gale, Korean Folk Tales, 'Three Things Mastered' (1913); not verbatim.

title.en: The Dead General Who Came Back to Shoot a Thief
title.zh: 故將軍鬼射賊

region.en: General Kim's former home (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 金故宅（象徵性定位）

period: Tale by Yi Ryuk; story of Kim Tok-saing, honored at the court of Tae-jong; English ed. Gale, Korean Folk Tales (1913)

source.work: James S. Gale (trans.), Korean Folk Tales (1913), tale 'Strangely Stricken Dead', eBook #51002

summary.en: Kim Tok-saing, a soldier of fortune several times generalissimo, has been dead ten years and more when one night his intimate friend is twice awakened with a fright. He has just seen General Kim riding a white horse with bow and arrows at his belt: 'A thief has just entered my home, and I have come to shoot him dead' — and returning, drew an arrow with blood marks on it: 'I have just shot him, he is dead.' In the morning the friend goes to Kim's former home and learns that that very night Kim's young widow had decided to remarry, and as soon as the chosen fiancé entered her home a terrible pain shot him through; before morning he died in great agony.
summary.zh: 金德星歿已十年。一夕其故友連驚醒，言夢見將軍乘白馬佩弓矢來曰『有賊入吾家，吾射殺之矣』，且出矢示之，矢上血痕宛然。晨往其故宅問之，則是夜其寡婦方議改適，所聘者甫入門，暴痛而絕於床。鬼射之說，駭人聽聞。

sensitivity.note: Ancestor-ghost vigilante tale; no living-community restriction.

passages.text: There was once a man called Kim Tok-saing, a soldier of fortune who had been specially honoured at the Court of Tai-jong, and had several times been generalissimo of the army. Kim had been dead now for some ten years and more, when one night this friend of his was awakened with a start and gave a great outcry.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Gale, Korean Folk Tales, 'Strangely Stricken Dead' (1913); not verbatim.

passages.text: 'I have just seen General Kim riding on a white horse, with bow and arrows at his belt. He called to me and said, A thief has just entered my home, and I have come to shoot him dead. He went and again returned, and as he drew an arrow from his quiver, I saw that there were blood marks on it. He said, I have just shot him, he is dead.' The husband and wife in fear and wonder talked over it together.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Gale, Korean Folk Tales, 'Strangely Stricken Dead' (1913); not verbatim.

passages.text: When morning came the friend went to General Kim's former home to make inquiry. He learned that that very night Kim's young widow had decided to remarry, but as soon as the chosen fiancé had entered her home, a terrible pain shot him through, and before morning came he died in great agony.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Gale, Korean Folk Tales, 'Strangely Stricken Dead' (1913); not verbatim.

title.en: The Archers under the Hoi Tree
title.zh: 海樹下之射者

region.en: Inside the Great East Gate, Seoul (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 漢城東大門內（象徵性定位）

period: Tale by Yi Ryuk; English ed. Gale, Korean Folk Tales (1913)

source.work: James S. Gale (trans.), Korean Folk Tales (1913), tale 'The Mysterious Hoi Tree', eBook #51002

summary.en: Before Prince Pa-song's house inside the great East Gate stands a large Hoi tree. One night the Prince's son-in-law, passing the archers' pavilion, sees a great company of bowmen shooting at the target, practising riding, throwing spears and hurling bowls till the road is blocked. 'Look at that impudent rascal! He attempts to ride by without dismounting.' They catch and beat him till a tall fellow comes out of the ranks: 'He is my master; why do you treat him so?' — undoes his bonds and leads him home. At the gate the son-in-law looks back and sees the man walk under the Hoi tree and disappear: all the crowd of archers were spirits, and the tall one had come forth from their particular Hoi tree.
summary.zh: 怕松公宅在東大門內，門前有海樹一本。其婿夜過射亭，見無數射手習射馳馬擲矛，喧然塞路。眾怒其不下馬，執而笞之。忽有一偉者出曰『此吾主也，何得如此』，為解其縛而送之歸。至門回顧，其人已行入海樹下而滅。蓋群射者皆鬼，偉者即樹中之神也。

sensitivity.note: Tree-spirit lore; no living-community restriction.

passages.text: Prince Pa-song's house was situated just inside of the great East Gate, and before it was a large Hoi tree. On a certain night the Prince's son-in-law was passing by the roadway that led in front of the archers' pavilion. There he saw a great company of bowmen, more than he could number, all shooting together at the target; a moment later he saw them practising riding, some throwing spears, some hurling bowls, some shooting from horseback, so that the road in front of the pavilion was blocked against all comers.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Gale, Korean Folk Tales, 'The Mysterious Hoi Tree' (1913); not verbatim.

passages.text: Some shouted as he came by, 'Look at that impudent rascal! He attempts to ride by without dismounting.' They caught him and beat him, paying no attention to his cries for mercy, till one tall fellow came out of their serried ranks and said in an angry voice, 'He is my master; why do you treat him so?' He undid his bonds, took him by the arm and led him home.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Gale, Korean Folk Tales, 'The Mysterious Hoi Tree' (1913); not verbatim.

passages.text: When the son-in-law reached the gate he looked back and saw the man walk under the Hoi tree and disappear. He then learned, too, that all the crowd of archers were spirits and not men, and that the tall one who had befriended him was a spirit too, and that he had come forth from their particular Hoi tree.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Gale, Korean Folk Tales, 'The Mysterious Hoi Tree' (1913); not verbatim.

title.en: Ta-hong, Who Hid Herself until the Honours Came
title.zh: 桃花潛身待郎君

region.en: Chang-eui ward, Seoul; Keumsan county (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 漢京彰義坊（象徵性定位）

period: Story of Minister Sim Heui-su (1535-1622), told before his death; collected by Im Bang; English ed. Gale, Korean Folk Tales (1913)

source.work: James S. Gale (trans.), Korean Folk Tales (1913), tale 'Ta-hong', eBook #51002

summary.en: At sixteen, the beautiful boy Sim Heui-su sees the kisaeng Ta-hong, Flower-bud, at a banquet and cannot forget her. Days later she alights before him in the street, reveals she asked his name that night, and plights her troth: he must first win first place at the examination and his three days of public rejoicing, and until then she will hide herself in safety. He studies day and night for her sake, marries at his parents' word without joy, and five years after their farewell wins his honours — and on the third evening, called in to an old Minister's house by the Sillai whistle, finds her. For a year she has been a voluntary slave in that house, 'called my concubine in name lest my nephews should steal her away,' confident to the end. She becomes his only wife, forbids their too-frequent happiness as interfereing with duty, and in Keumsan county announces her own death four or five days beforehand: 'Our life is ordered, God decides it all; bury me by my master, that we may meet again.' After her death she still comes to warn him of things to come, never with a mistake, until the dream in which she says 'Master, the time of your departure has come' — and Sim dies the day following, as was foretold.
summary.zh: 沈羲壽十六歲遇名妓桃花（花苞），一見傾心。數日後桃花馬上相認，與之盟曰：『君登科之日乃我歸期，我自匿身以全其節。』沈乃發憤苦讀五年而魁天下。第三日夜誤入某老相公家，桃花果在。原來伊自願為婢於其家，託名側室以避匪人。後為沈正室，賢而克勤。任金山縣令時，桃花預言己死期，至日果卒。遺言葬於夫塋之側。死後猶託夢預告家事，末乃告夫死期，翌日果卒。

sensitivity.note: Love-and-fidelity tale with prophecy; no living-community restriction.

passages.text: Minister Sim Heui-su was, when young, handsome as polished marble and white as the snow. At about sixteen years of age he went with a half-dozen comrades to see a banquet with dancing-girls, where among them was a young woman whose face was very beautiful, not like an earthly person, but like some angelic being: her name was Ta-hong, Flower-bud.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Gale, Korean Folk Tales, 'Ta-hong' (1913); not verbatim.

passages.text: Ten days later, carrying his books along the main street, he suddenly met a pretty girl beautifully dressed, riding a handsome horse, who alighted just in front of him and taking his hand said, 'Are you not Sim Heui-su?' It was Ta-hong. 'I saw you at the gathering, and to me your face was like a god's. From that day on I longed to meet you. Our meeting thus is surely of God's appointment.' They plighted their troth in her aunt's house. 'You have your parents to think of. As I reflect upon your ability and chances for promotion, I see you already a Minister of State. Let us separate just now, and I'll keep myself for you till the time when you win the first place at the Examination and have your three days of public rejoicing. I have a plan by which to hide myself away in safety.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Gale, Korean Folk Tales, 'Ta-hong' (1913); not verbatim.

passages.text: From that time forth, with all his might, he went at his lessons, day and night, not for the sake of the Examination, but for the sake of once more meeting her. It was five years after his farewell to Ta-hong that he won his honours, but on the first day and the second he did not meet her, and the third day was passing with no word. Evening was falling, when his father sent him to call on an old friend in Chang-eui ward; as he was returning, just as he was passing a high gateway, he heard the Sillai call and was obliged to dismount and enter the house of an old Minister, who entertained him and then lifted his glass and inquired, 'Would you like to meet a very beautiful person?' When she came, it was his lost Ta-hong: 'Is this not within the three days of your public celebration, and according to the agreement by which we parted?'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Gale, Korean Folk Tales, 'Ta-hong' (1913); not verbatim.

passages.text: The old man told her history: 'On a certain day this young girl came to us saying, May I have the place of slave with you? I am not running away from any master. She called herself my concubine so as to be safe, lest my nephews or some younger members of the clan should steal her away. We watched the Examination reports, and this time on looking over the list I found your name. She is first of all a faithful woman: I have not known her like before.' His parents gave consent that he should have her, and she was made a member of his family, really his only wife. A little later, as magistrate of Keumsan county, he heard her say one day, 'I am going to die, for my span of life is finished.' In four or five days she fell ill, and a day or two later died, saying, 'Our life is ordered, God decides it all. As I die I ask only that my body be buried where it may rest by the side of my master when he passes away, so that when we meet in the regions beyond I shall be with you once again.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Gale, Korean Folk Tales, 'Ta-hong' (1913); not verbatim.

passages.text: After her death, whenever anything serious was to happen in his home, she always came to tell him beforehand, and never was there a mistake in her announcements. For several years it has continued thus, till a few days ago she appeared in a dream saying, 'Master, the time of your departure has come, and we are to meet again. I am now making ready for your glad reception.' Last night she came once more and said, 'To-morrow is your day.' In the morning, when he awoke, marks of tears were still upon his cheeks: 'This is not because I fear to die, but because I have seen my Ta-hong.' So Sim died, as was foretold, on the day following.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Gale, Korean Folk Tales, 'Ta-hong' (1913); not verbatim.

title.en: The Oriole That Sings for Kim
title.zh: 黃鳥呼金

region.en: Royal palace, Seoul (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 漢城王宮（象徵性定位）

period: Folk legends of birds collected by H.N. Allen, Korean Tales (1889)

source.work: Horace N. Allen, Korean Tales (1889), ch. 3 'The Rabbit and other Legends', eBook #55539

summary.en: One of the numerous ladies at court once had a love affair with a palace official, a Mr. Kim. It was discovered and the poor thing lost her life; but her spirit could not be killed, and unappeased it entered the oriole, in which form she returned to the palace singing 'Kim-pul-lah-go', 'tell Kim to come', and, receiving no response, mournfully entreating 'Kim-poh-go-sip-so', 'I want to see Kim'. Even to this day the women and children feel sad when they hear these plaintive notes, and their hearts go out in pity for the poor lone lover ever searching in vain for her Kim.
summary.zh: 相傳宮中嬪御與內官金某私通，事泄被誅。其魂不滅，附於黃鳥，飛回宮中，啼曰『金不喇高』（喚金），無應，復哀鳴『金潑高息潑』（思見金）。至今婦孺聞此鳥聲，無不感傷。

sensitivity.note: Bird-origin legend; no living-community restriction.

passages.text: Once upon a time, one of the numerous ladies at court had a love affair with one of the palace officials, a Mr. Kim. It was discovered, and the poor thing lost her life. Her spirit could not be killed, however, and, unappeased, it entered this bird, in which form she returned to the palace.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Allen, Korean Tales, ch. 3 (1889); not verbatim.

passages.text: She sang, 'Kim-pul-lah-go' — 'tell Kim to come' — and then, receiving no response, would mournfully entreat, 'Kim-poh-go-sip-so' — 'I want to see Kim.' So, even to this day, the women and children feel sad when they hear these plaintive notes, and unconsciously their hearts go out in pity for the poor lone lover who is ever searching in vain for her Kim.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Allen, Korean Tales, ch. 3 (1889); not verbatim.

title.en: The Magpie's News and the Goose of Constancy
title.zh: 鵲報吉凶鵝定情

region.en: Village houses, Korea (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 鄉村宅院（象徵性定位）

period: Folk legends of birds collected by H.N. Allen, Korean Tales (1889)

source.work: Horace N. Allen, Korean Tales (1889), ch. 3, eBook #55539

summary.en: The magpie is in great favor in Korea: should he come to the house with his song in the morning, good news may be expected during the day — father returning from a long journey, a brother succeeding in his examination; in the afternoon, a guest may be expected with an appetite equal to a family of children; after dark, thieves may be dreaded. He is also champion of the swallows, dashing at the head of the house-snake that has eaten their young. The wild goose participates in every wedding ceremony, for these observing people once noticed that a goose whose mate was killed returned year after year to mourn her loss, and such constancy they seek to commend to their wives, pledging each other: 'Black is the hair that now crowns our heads, yet when it has become as white as the fibres of the onion root, we shall still be found faithful to each other.'
summary.zh: 朝鮮人最喜鵲。晨鵲鳴於門，是日必有喜事：或遠人歸，或子弟登科；午則有客至；暮則防盜。鵲又為燕之友，啄食蛇頭以護雛。雁則婚礼必用之，以雁失偶後歲歲哀鳴，取其貞也。夫婦交拜時互誓云：『今結髮皆黑，他年皓首，此心如雁不改。』

sensitivity.note: Bird-omen and wedding-custom etiology; no living-community restriction.

passages.text: The magpie, that impudent, noisy nuisance, is in great favor, so much so that his great ugly nest is safe from human disturbance. When one of the great lazy house-snakes comes out to sun himself after a meal of young swallows, the bereaved parents fly off for the saucy magpie, who comes promptly and dashes at the snake's head amid the encouraging jabbering of the swallows.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Allen, Korean Tales, ch. 3 (1889); not verbatim.

passages.text: Should the magpie come to the house with his song in the morning, good news may be expected during the day: father will return from a long journey; brother will succeed in his examination and obtain rank. Should the magpie come in the afternoon, a guest may be expected with an appetite equal to that of a family of children; while, if the magpie comes after dark, thieves may be dreaded.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Allen, Korean Tales, ch. 3 (1889); not verbatim.

passages.text: The wild goose is one of the most highly prized birds in Korea. It always participates in the wedding ceremonies; for no man would think himself properly married had he not been presented by his bride with a wild goose. The reason is that these observing people once noticed that a goose whose mate was killed returned to the place year after year to mourn her loss; and such constancy they seek, by this pretty custom, to commend to their wives. They further pledge each other at this time: 'Black is the hair that now crowns our heads, yet when it has become as white as the fibres of the onion root, we shall still be found faithful to each other.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Allen, Korean Tales, ch. 3 (1889); not verbatim.

title.en: The White Heron Who Pecked the Temple Bell
title.zh: 白鶴擊鐘

region.en: Mountain temple (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 山寺（象徵性定位）

period: Folk legends of birds collected by H.N. Allen, Korean Tales (1889)

source.work: Horace N. Allen, Korean Tales (1889), ch. 3, eBook #55539

summary.en: The white heron is the especial friend of man. Many are the tales told of the assistance it has rendered: in one case the generous-hearted creature is said to have pecked off its bill in its frantic attempts to ring a temple bell for the salvation of a man. In another, a hunter who shot an arrow through the head of a snake about to devour some newly hatched herons was in turn saved by the mother bird, who pecked to death a snake that had gotten into the man's stomach while he was drinking at a spring — the pecking so expertly done as not to injure the man.
summary.zh: 白鶴為人之友。相傳曾自啄其喙，以撞寺鐘而活一人。又一獵者射蛇以救雛鶴，後鶴母啄出其腹中之蛇，毫髮無傷，以報其恩。

sensitivity.note: Bird-gratitude legend; no living-community restriction.

passages.text: The white heron seems to be the especial friend of man. Many are the tales told of the assistance it has rendered individuals: in one case the generous-hearted creature is said to have pecked off its bill in its frantic attempts to ring a temple bell for the salvation of a man.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Allen, Korean Tales, ch. 3 (1889); not verbatim.

passages.text: One of the early stories relates how a hunter, having shot an arrow through the head of a snake that was about to devour some newly hatched herons, was in turn saved by the mother bird, who pecked to death a snake that had gotten into the man's stomach while he was drinking at a spring — the pecking, further, was so expertly done as not to injure the man.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Allen, Korean Tales, ch. 3 (1889); not verbatim.

title.en: The Rabbit Who Kept Both His Eyes
title.zh: 龜騙兔目

region.en: Undersea palace of the fish-king (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 龍宮（象徵性定位）

period: Animal folktale collected by H.N. Allen, Korean Tales (1889)

source.work: Horace N. Allen, Korean Tales (1889), ch. 3 'The Rabbit and other Legends', eBook #55539

summary.en: The king of fishes gets a hook through his nose and grows very ill; in solemn council the turtle declares that a poultice made from the fresh eye of a rabbit would cure him, and undertakes to bring one up from the beach. Feigning that the view from the hills is nothing to the sights of the undersea world, the turtle lures the curious rabbit onto his back and carries him down to the palace, where the doctors explain the plot of securing his eyes before he should die. The rabbit saves himself with a happy thought: he always carries two pairs of eyes, real ones and a pair of mountain crystal for dusty weather — and fearing the water would injure the real ones, he buried them in the sand before mounting. Let him ride back and dig them up. Marvelling at the rabbit's courtesy, the fishes are ashamed; once released on the sand, the rabbit shakes the water from his coat, winks at his clumsy betrayer, tells him to dig for the eyes himself, and tears away up the mountainside, ever after giving the turtle a wide berth.
summary.zh: 魚王誤吞魚鉤，群醫束手。老龜獻策：以兔眼為膏藥可治，遂上山誘兔曰『海底之勝過於山巔』。兔好奇，伏龜背而入海。至龍宮，醫者密議於兔死之前取其目。兔聞之大恐，詭言『吾有二目，真目畏水，已埋於沙，今所用者水晶目也。願歸取一目以奉大王』。魚眾愧其詐而放之。兔登岸大笑，令龜自掘，遂遁入山，終身避龜。

sensitivity.note: Animal trickster tale; parallels the Tortoise-and-Hare and Brer Rabbit types and the Dragon Palace visit (cf. Urashima).

passages.text: The king of fishes, while snapping greedily at a worm, got a hook through his nose. He succeeded in breaking the line, but he could in no way remove the cruel hook, and his finny majesty grew very ill; all the officials of his kingdom were summoned and met in solemn council. At last the turtle announced his firm belief that a poultice made from the fresh eye of a rabbit would remove the disorder of their sovereign at once.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Allen, Korean Tales, ch. 3 (1889); not verbatim.

passages.text: The turtle concealed his excitement under an air of indifference, boasting of the magnificent sights under the water, and offered to carry the rabbit down on his back. The rabbit was charmed and bewildered by the magnificence of everything he saw, and especially by the gorgeous palace, through which he was escorted to the sick chamber of the king. While sitting in an elegant chair he chanced to hear a discussion concerning the best way of securing his eyes before he should die; questioning an attendant, the whole plot was explained to him. The poor fellow scratched his head and wondered if he would ever get out of the place alive.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Allen, Korean Tales, ch. 3 (1889); not verbatim.

passages.text: At last a happy thought struck him. He explained that he always carried about two pairs of eyes, his real ones and a pair made of mountain crystals to be used in dusty weather; fearing that the water would injure his real eyes, he had buried them in the sand before getting upon the turtle's back, and was now using his crystal ones. He was most willing to let them have one of his real eyes to cure his majesty's disorder, if they would but carry him back to the spot where he had buried them.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Allen, Korean Tales, ch. 3 (1889); not verbatim.

passages.text: Marvelling much at the rabbit's courtesy, the fishes slunk away into the corners for very shame at their own rude conduct in forcibly kidnapping him. The turtle was rather roughly commanded to carry the guest to the place designated. Once released to dig for the eyes in the sand, the rabbit shook the water from his coat, and winking at his clumsy betrayer told him to dig for the eyes himself, that he had only one pair, and those he intended to keep. With that he tore away up the mountain side, and has ever after been careful to give the turtle a wide berth.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Allen, Korean Tales, ch. 3 (1889); not verbatim.

title.en: The Enchanted Wine-Jug
title.zh: 寶瓶酒泉

region.en: Riverbank wine-shop (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 江畔酒壚（象徵性定位）

period: Folk tale collected by H.N. Allen, Korean Tales (1889); origin-legend of the enmity of cats and dogs

source.work: Horace N. Allen, Korean Tales (1889), ch. 4 'The Enchanted Wine Jug', eBook #55539

summary.en: An old childless wine-seller by the ferry once gave his last drink to a weary divine stranger, who gave him a bit of amber: drop it in your jug and you will never want for drink. His wine never gave out; his deputy children, an old dog and an old cat, guarded the secret. One day the wine fails — the gem has been poured into a customer's jug — and the dog and cat organize a great search, cross the frozen river, recruit the rat guild to gnaw the soapstone tobacco-box, and retrieve the gem. On the way back, riding on the swimming dog's back, the cat laughs at the schoolchildren's jeering and drops the gem into the river; the dog dives, the cat clings, both are nearly drowned, and from that day cat spits at dog and dog barks at cat. In the end the dog spears a fish through the ice for his master, and the lost gem is found in the fish's belly — whereupon the old man, learning the amber duplicates whatever he wishes, becomes immensely wealthy.
summary.zh: 江畔老翁憐一疲客，傾壺與之。客贈琥珀一粒，投入瓶則酒不竭。老翁畜一犬一貓，相依為命。一日酒盡，蓋寶石誤入客瓶矣。犬貓結伴尋之，渡冰河，賂鼠齧石匣，卒得其寶。歸渡時，貓笑學童之譁，失口落寶於江；犬潛水取之，貓爪其背，幾皆溺。自此貓犬成讎。後犬於冰下啣魚歸獻主人，剖魚腹而寶石出焉。老翁乃知其能倍增萬物，遂成巨富。

sensitivity.note: Etiological animal tale; no living-community restriction.

passages.text: The old man had befriended a divine being in the form of a weary human traveller, to whom he gave the last drink his jug contained; and when the contents had gurgled down the stranger's throat in a long unbroken draught, the stranger gave him a trifling little thing that looked like a bit of amber, saying: 'Drop this into your jug, old man, and so long as it remains there, you will never want for a drink.' The dog and cat knew the secret, and had ever a watchful eye upon the jug.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Allen, Korean Tales, ch. 4 (1889); not verbatim.

passages.text: One day the news flashed around the neighborhood that the old man's supply of wine was exhausted; not a drop remained in his jug. He concluded that he must have poured the bit of amber into a customer's jug; and the dog and cat, listening attentively, puzzled their brains as to what was to be done. Their plan was adopted that very night: the cat called on the cats indoors and kept his smellers open, the dog chatted with the dogs outside, and they searched every house in the neighborhood, night after night, then extended the search across the frozen river.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Allen, Korean Tales, ch. 4 (1889); not verbatim.

passages.text: The cat at last traced the odor to a soapstone tobacco box on a high clothes-press, too fastened to open; the dog's wisdom enlisted the chief of the rat guild, who gnawed a hole through the stone, and a mouse pushed the gem out. The cat bore the treasure in his teeth mounted on the swimming dog's back; but nearing the bank a party of school-children burst into uproarious laughter at the absurd sight, the cat's merriment shook the dog into great gulps of water, and in his hearty laugh the cat dropped the precious gem into the river. The dog dove at once; the cat, sticking his claws into the dog's skin in his agony of suffocation, caused such pain that the dog missed his object and came to the surface. The cat got ashore, greatly angered, and climbed a tree, and has ever since been careful to avoid the dog — this accounts for the scarcity of cats and the popularity of dogs.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Allen, Korean Tales, ch. 4 (1889); not verbatim.

passages.text: The dog dove many times in vain, and spent most of the following days on the river's bank. One day he espied a man spearing fish through a hole in the ice, grabbed a fish as it was laid down, and rushed off with it to his master, who was almost reduced to begging. When the old man slit the fish open, to his infinite joy his long-lost gem fell out of the fish's belly. Sitting down to think, the whole truth dawned upon him: he had been content to use his talisman simply to run a wine-shop, while he might have had money and everything else in abundance by simply giving the charm a chance to work — and so he eventually became immensely wealthy, for he could always duplicate anything with his piece of amber.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Allen, Korean Tales, ch. 4 (1889); not verbatim.

title.en: Ching Yuh and Kyain Oo, the Star-Lovers
title.zh: 牽牛織女鵲橋

region.en: Heavenly river (Milky Way) (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 天河（象徵性定位）

period: Heavenly-lore prelude to the tale collected by H.N. Allen, Korean Tales (1889)

source.work: Horace N. Allen, Korean Tales (1889), ch. 5 'Ching Yuh and Kyain Oo', eBook #55539

summary.en: Ching Yuh and Kyain Oo were stars attendant upon the Sun. They fell madly in love, and, obtaining the royal permission, were married; but as the honey-moon bade fair to continue during the rest of their lives, rendering them unfit for the discharge of their duties, their master banished them — one to the farthest edge of the eastern heavens, the other to the opposite bank of the great river that divides the heavenly plains. They may meet but one short night in the year, when the bridge is completed by the crows, who carry the materials for its construction upon their heads — any one may know it, who cares to notice how bald and worn are the heads of the crows during the seventh moon. This sad meeting occurs on the night of the seventh day of the seventh moon; their grief at parting manifests itself in weeping tears so copious that the whole earth beneath is deluged with rains.
summary.zh: 秦玉與堅牛本日邊侍星也，相愛成婚，形影不離，廢其職守。天帝怒，一謫東極，一謫天河西岸。惟歲七夕烏鵲填橋，得一宵之聚。既別，悲泣成雨，人間因有霖雨之候。烏鵲頭頂為之禿，故七月烏頂皆禿。

sensitivity.note: Korean version of the East Asian Weaver-and-Cowherd (Chilseok) myth; shared Sinosphere heritage, tagged as heavenly lore.

passages.text: Ching Yuh and Kyain Oo were stars attendant upon the Sun. They fell madly in love with each other, and, obtaining the royal permission, they were married. It was to them a most happy union; but as the honey-moon bade fair to continue during the rest of their lives, rendering them unfit for the discharge of their duties, their master decided to punish them: he banished them, one to the farthest edge of the eastern heavens, the other to the extreme opposite side of the great river that divides the heavenly plains.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Allen, Korean Tales, ch. 5 (1889); not verbatim.

passages.text: They were sent so far away that it required full six months to make the journey. They could only hope to journey back and forth for the scant comfort of spending one short night in each other's company, and could cross the broad river only at the season when the great bridge is completed by the crows, who carry the materials for its construction upon their heads — as any one may know who cares to notice how bald and worn are the heads of the crows during the seventh moon.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Allen, Korean Tales, ch. 5 (1889); not verbatim.

passages.text: Naturally this fond couple are always heart-broken and discouraged at being so soon compelled to part after such a brief but long-deferred meeting, and 'tis not strange that their grief should manifest itself in weeping tears so copious that the whole earth beneath is deluged with rains. This sad meeting occurs on the night of the seventh day of the seventh moon; if prevented by some untoward circumstance, the usual rainy season is withheld, and the parched earth unites in lamentation with the fond lovers.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Allen, Korean Tales, ch. 5 (1889); not verbatim.

title.en: The Fan Betrothal by the Roadside
title.zh: 路旁贈扇定情

region.en: Shady roadside, two districts (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 道旁樹蔭（象徵性定位）

period: Story collected by H.N. Allen, Korean Tales (1889)

source.work: Horace N. Allen, Korean Tales (1889), ch. 5, eBook #55539

summary.en: Two childless households pray to heaven. You Tah Jung's wife dreams of a beautiful boy riding down from the North Star on a white feather fan — the attendant of the North Star, banished to earth, sent to her with the fan that will one day save both their lives; with the spring-tide a beautiful boy is born, Pang Noo. Cho Sung Noo's wife, moon-gazing for the meeting of the star-lovers, dreams of a little girl borne on five soft clouds, an attendant of the Queen of Heaven banished for mischief — she had driven the crows away and ruined the seventh-moon bridge out of a spirit of mischief; a daughter is born, Uhn Hah, the divine maiden. At ten, resting by the road, Uhn Hah meets Pang Noo on his way to school; for two oranges he writes on the fan: 'No girl was ever possessed of such incomparable graces as the beautiful Uhn Hah. I now betroth myself to her, and vow never to marry other so long as I live.' The fan closes; the characters are concealed; she puts it away unread.
summary.zh: 柳、趙二家皆乏嗣，各禱於天。柳妻夢北極星侍童乘白羽扇降，曰『謫降人間，此扇將活爾母子之命』，果生神童逢午。趙妻月下夢雲輦仙女，自言乃天帝侍女，以戲毀鵲橋致旱而被謫，遂生神女嫣夏。十歲時，逢午上塾過其地，以二橘易題扇曰：『天下之麗莫若嫣夏，吾誓終身不娶他人。』扇闔而字隱，女珍藏之。

sensitivity.note: Star-birth romance; no living-community restriction.

passages.text: One night the wife of You Tah Jung fell asleep while praying, and dreamed a remarkable dream: a most beautiful boy came down to her riding upon a wonderful fan made of white feathers. 'I am the attendant of the great North Star, and because of a mistake I made I am banished to earth for a term of years, telling me to come to you and bring this fan, which will eventually be the means of saving your life and my own.' With the succeeding spring-tide a beautiful boy came to them; they called the boy Pang Noo.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Allen, Korean Tales, ch. 5 (1889); not verbatim.

passages.text: The wife of Cho Sung Noo, sitting in the moonlight gazing into the heavens hoping to witness the meeting of Ching Yuh and Kyain Oo, dreamed that the four winds were bearing to her a beautiful litter supported upon five rich, soft clouds, in which reclined a little girl far lovelier than any being she had ever dreamed of. 'I was an attendant upon the Queen of Heaven, but I have been very bad, though I meant no wrong, and I am banished to earth for a season.' When the annual union of Ching Yuh and Kyain Oo takes place, she hears them mourning because they can only see each other once a year; in a spirit of mischief she drove the crows away and ruined their bridge before they could reach each other — not counting on the drought that would occur, and the consequent suffering entailed on mortals. A daughter was really born to them, known popularly as the divine maiden.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Allen, Korean Tales, ch. 5 (1889); not verbatim.

passages.text: One day, resting by the road-side on her nurse's back, Uhn Hah was confronted by Pang Noo on his way to school. Seeing some oranges in her lap, he stepped up and spoke politely to the nurse: 'I am You Pang Noo, a lad on my way to school, and I am very thirsty; won't you ask your little girl to let me have one of her oranges?' In her confusion she gave him two oranges. 'If you will allow me I will write your name on this fan and present it to you.' He wrote: 'No girl was ever possessed of such incomparable graces as the beautiful Uhn Hah. I now betroth myself to her, and vow never to marry other so long as I live.' The fan being closed, no one read the characters, and Uhn Hah carefully put it away without examining it sufficiently close to discover the written sentiment.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Allen, Korean Tales, ch. 5 (1889); not verbatim.

title.en: Uhn Hah Refuses the General and Wins the Rock Test
title.zh: 擲石試力請纓

region.en: Royal court, Seoul (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 漢城王廷（象徵性定位）

period: Story collected by H.N. Allen, Korean Tales (1889)

source.work: Horace N. Allen, Korean Tales (1889), ch. 5, eBook #55539

summary.en: Pang Noo wins the great examination and is made a Ussa, the King's disguised inspector; Uhn Hah, discovering at last the vow written on her fan, vows to be his or never marry. When a cruel general asks for her hand for his son, she refuses — 'I am already the wife of Pang Noo in my heart; kill me, if you will, but spare me this' — and the family must flee to another province, her parents dying on the road. In male disguise she is seized by Pang Noo's father the Governor for her fan, and released; an old man of the night feeds her a pill of superhuman strength; a blind man prophesies that her husband is fighting the rebels, nearly dead, but 'he will not die, for she will rescue him.' Petitioning the King for a command, she proves herself before the court: she throws a weather-worn stone over the enclosing wall as easily as two men could lift it from the ground, and whirls the General's sword into one continuous ring of burning steel, till the wicked General cowers in abject terror — and the King gives her the choicest battalion.
summary.zh: 逢午科舉奪魁，授暗察使。嫣夏始見扇上盟文，誓死不他適。大將軍為子求婚，女泣拒曰『妾心已屬逢午，寧死不從』，舉家避禍，父母道死。兄妹裝（易男裝）北行，為柳父所疑，繫獄得釋。夜遇老人賜大力丸；瞽者卜曰『夫在軍中將歿，然卿至則活』。女上書請纓，王命試其力：嫣夏擲庭前巨石踰牆，如提兩人之力；復舞劍如環，寒光繞身。王大悅，授精兵一營，命往平叛。

sensitivity.note: Heroine-warrior romance; no living-community restriction.

passages.text: Uhn Hah at last discovered the characters on the fan, and great was her surprise and delight at the message. She concluded it was a heaven-arranged union, and vowed she would be his or never marry at all. When one of His Majesty's greatest generals, who had a reputation for bravery and cruelty as well, asked to betroth his son to Cho's daughter, the girl was struck dumb: 'He has pledged himself to me, and I know he is even now coming to me. Would you ask one woman to marry two men? I am already the wife of Pang Noo in my heart. Kill me, if you will, but spare me this, I beg and entreat.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Allen, Korean Tales, ch. 5 (1889); not verbatim.

passages.text: The parents loved her too well to withstand her pleadings; they dispatched a letter declining the offer, and the General, in a towering rage, sent soldiers to arrest Mr. Cho. The honest local magistrate listened to Cho's story, believed the strange case, and bade them collect what they could and go to another province to live; in a distant hamlet the worn and discouraged parents were taken sick and passed on to join their ancestors. Uhn Hah and her old nurse donned male attire and journeyed on, till the Governor's procession passed by and the Governor, espying the peculiar feather fan, had the supposed men seized and questioned at the yamen. 'It is a family relic,' replied Uhn Hah; she would die rather than part with it, and was locked up — then dismissed with the steward's pity and a parting gift.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Allen, Korean Tales, ch. 5 (1889); not verbatim.

passages.text: Darkness overtook them at a little hut occupied by an old man reading a book, who called her by her true name, Cho Nang Jah, and said, 'I have been waiting for you and expecting you. You are soon to do great things. Never mind your hunger, but devour this pill; it will give you superhuman strength and courage.' When they awoke it was bright morning, the birds singing above them, their only shelter — the hut and the old man had disappeared entirely; she devoutly bowed in grateful acknowledgment of the gracious manifestation. At a wayside inn a blind man prophesied for the people: 'This is a woman in disguise; she is seeking for her husband, who is fighting the rebels, and searching for her. He is now nearly dead; but he will not die, for she will rescue him.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Allen, Korean Tales, ch. 5 (1889); not verbatim.

passages.text: Learning that Pang Noo had been carried captive by the rebels, Uhn Hah petitioned the King to be given a body of soldiers to punish the rebels and liberate her husband. The King bade her come before him; her beauty and dignity of carriage won attention, but the General suggested she first give some evidence of her strength and prowess. She breathed a prayer to her departed parents, remembered the promise of the pill, and seizing a large weather-worn stone that stood in an ornamental rock basin in the court, threw it over the enclosing wall as easily as two men would have lifted it from the ground. Then, taking the General's sword, she manipulated it, increasing gradually, till the movement became so rapid that the sword seemed like one continuous ring of burning steel, menacingly near the wicked General, who cowered in abject terror. His Majesty was completely captivated, and himself gave the orders for her expedition, raising her to relative rank and giving her the choicest battalion of troops.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Allen, Korean Tales, ch. 5 (1889); not verbatim.

title.en: Hungbu, the Swallow-King's Gourds of Plenty
title.zh: 興夫瓢中福

region.en: Chulla province, southern Korea (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 全羅道（象徵性定位）

period: Folk tale collected by H.N. Allen, Korean Tales (1889)

source.work: Horace N. Allen, Korean Tales (1889), ch. 6 'Hyung Bo and Nahl Bo', eBook #55539

summary.en: In Chullado lived two brothers: rich Nahl Bo, who kept the whole inheritance and reduced his brother to abject misery, and poor Hyung Bo with his starving family in a hut of broom straw. When a roof-snake devours the swallow nestlings, Hyung binds up the broken legs of the one survivor with fish-skin splints; the bird flies south to the king of birds, and in spring returns bearing a seed engraved in gold: bury me in soft earth and give me plenty of water. The gourd-vine climbs the hut and bears four enormous gourds: out of the first step two beautiful boys with wine and a jade table — one bottle restores life to the dead, one sight to the blind, tobacco that gives speech to the dumb, wine that wards off age and death; the second gourd pours out household furniture, silk and satins; the third produces carpenters who build a fine house with courts, stables and granaries before the family can rise from the ground; the fourth yields a maiden of matchless beauty, sent by the bird king to be his concubine — and Hyung's wife, who sees only a rival, is sternly reprimanded and sent to reign in the women's quarters.
summary.zh: 全羅道有兄弟二人：兄諾夫富而吝，弟興夫貧而仁。燕為蛇所噬，興夫以魚皮裹其折足而療之。燕南歸告鳥王，春返啣金書之種，種之則瓜蔓滿屋，結四巨瓜。剖之：一瓜出二仙童，奉生死人藥酒、明目酒、啞者能言之煙與長生之酒；二瓜出金帛器物；三瓜出工匠，俄頃成大廈，牛馬僕從畢至；四瓜出絕色女子，云奉鳥王之命來為媵。興夫之妻妒而叱之，被夫所責，退居內舍。

sensitivity.note: Korean Cinderella-boys analog (Hungbu-Nolbu); no living-community restriction.

passages.text: In the province of Chullado, in Southern Korea, lived two brothers. One was very rich, the other very poor. For in dividing the inheritance, the elder brother, instead of taking the father's place and providing for the younger children, kept the whole property to himself, reducing Hyung Bo to a condition of abject misery; he had built himself a hut of broom straw so poor that when it rained they were deluged inside.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Allen, Korean Tales, ch. 6 (1889); not verbatim.

passages.text: When the little birds were taking their first lesson in flying, Hyung was lying on his back on the ground and saw a huge roof-snake crawl along and devour several little birds before he could arise and help them. One bird struggled from the reptile and fell, catching both legs in the meshes of a reed-blind, and hung helplessly within the snake's reach. Hyung hastily snatched it down, and with the help of his wife bound up the broken limbs, using dried fish-skin for splints, laying the little patient in a warm place, till the bird soon began to hop around the room and finally flew away to join his fellows.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Allen, Korean Tales, ch. 6 (1889); not verbatim.

passages.text: The bird paid homage to the king of birds in the bird-land beyond the frosts and related his rescue by a very poor but very kind man. His bird majesty gave the little cripple a seed engraved with fine characters in gold, denoting that the seed belonged to the gourd family. In the spring the bird dropped the seed, with a message: 'Bury me in soft earth, and give me plenty of water.' The stem shot up and climbed all over the house, blossoming into four small gourds that grew to an enormous size.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Allen, Korean Tales, ch. 6 (1889); not verbatim.

passages.text: Hyung got a saw and sawed open the first huge gourd: out of it stepped two beautiful boys, with fine bottles of wine and a table of jade set with dainty cups — the bird king's presents to the benefactor of one of his subjects. One wine would restore life to the dead; another would restore sight to the blind; one gold bottle contained tobacco which, being smoked, would give speech to the dumb, while the other gold bottle contained wine which would prevent the approach of age and ward off death. The next gourd poured out all manner of household furniture, clothing and rolls of fine silk and satin; the third produced a body of carpenters, who put up a fine house with courts and servants' quarters, stables and granaries before the family could arise from the ground; and out of the fourth stepped a maiden as beautiful as were the gifts that had preceded her, sent by the bird king to be this man's concubine. The wife grew dark in the face and ordered her away, upbraiding her husband for his greed in opening the fourth gourd; he commanded her to go at once to the women's quarters, where she should reign supreme.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Allen, Korean Tales, ch. 6 (1889); not verbatim.

title.en: Nahlbu's Twelve Gourds of Ruin
title.zh: 諾夫瓜中禍

region.en: Nahl Bo's compound, Chulla (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 全羅道諾夫宅（象徵性定位）

period: Folk tale collected by H.N. Allen, Korean Tales (1889)

source.work: Horace N. Allen, Korean Tales (1889), ch. 6, eBook #55539

summary.en: Nahl Bo hears of his brother's transformation and demands the secret, then goes home to strike at all the birds he can see, breaking one bird's legs and binding them in splints to counterfeit his brother's kindness. The bird tells the king of the man's cruelty, and in spring a seed comes — and Nahlbu's vines bear twelve gourds that groan the great beams of his house. Opened one by one at a thousand cash a gourd, they disgorge: rope-dancers who demand 5,000 cash, Buddhist priests begging for their temple, paid mourners following a corpse, dancing girls who sing of the wind god and the twelve months, an acrobatic pair, a jester, yamen runners and an official announcing that Nahl Bo is now a serf owing heavy tribute, soothsayers with drums to exorcise disease-demons, blind fortune-tellers, a juggler who throws him headlong and stands him on his head, a giant who carries him off till ransomed — and at last a gourd that splits rotten with an awful stench, followed by a gale that destroys the buildings, which take fire from the kang, and the last of his property is swept forever from him. The seed that brought prosperity to the honest brother turned prosperity into ruin to the cruel, covetous Nahl Bo.
summary.zh: 諾夫聞弟驟富，忌且妬，乃效之傷燕足以邀福。燕訴於鳥王，春啣種至。蔓生十二巨瓜。剖之：一雜技班討錢、一僧眾化緣、一喪班哭屍、一歌伎獻曲、一戲班、一傀儡師，皆索金五千；一官差至，宣判諾夫為某公之奴，歲納重賦；一巫女擊鼓驅疫、一瞽者占卜、一力士倒拋諾夫、一巨人負之去，贖金乃放。最後一瓜臭不可近，烈風大作，屋焚產蕩。諾夫遂依弟之施捨度日。

sensitivity.note: Punitive-twin motif; no living-community restriction.

passages.text: When Nahl Bo heard of the wonderful change taking place at his brother's establishment, he began to upbraid his brother with dishonest methods; Hyung Bo frankly told him how he had saved the bird from the snake and bound up its broken limbs. The covetous man insisted on having the fair maiden too, and in a rage departed, fully determined to use the secret of his brother's success for all it was worth. Going home he struck at all the birds he could see, and after killing many succeeded in catching one, and, breaking its legs, took fish-skin and bound them up in splints.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Allen, Korean Tales, ch. 6 (1889); not verbatim.

passages.text: The bird told the bird king of the man's cruelty in killing so many birds and then breaking its own legs; the king gave the little cripple a seed to present to the wicked man on its return in the spring. The vines were most luxurious, and instead of one gourd, or even four, the new vines bore twelve gourds, which grew till the great beams of his house fairly groaned under their weight. The carpenter insisted upon the enormous sum of 1,000 cash for opening each gourd.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Allen, Korean Tales, ch. 6 (1889); not verbatim.

passages.text: Out of the first came a party of rope-dancers who refused to leave until he had paid them 5,000 cash; number two yielded a body of Buddhist priests begging for their temple; the third a procession of paid mourners followed by a corpse. From the fourth came a band of dancing girls, one from each province, singing of the wind god, of the money christening placed on the roof tree of every house, of the twelve months that make the year — then demanding their pay. A jester came forth demanding expense money; yamen runners followed by an official read a paper announcing that Nahl Bo was the serf of a certain lord and must pay heavy tribute; a bevy of soothsayers came forth with drums to exorcise disease-demons; blind men offered to tell fortunes; a juggler threw him headlong over his own back, nearly breaking his neck, and stood him on his head; and a giant seized him and carried him off upon his shoulders till ransomed.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Allen, Korean Tales, ch. 6 (1889); not verbatim.

passages.text: The carpenter opened the last remaining gourd, and had only sawed a very little when it split open as though it were rotten, while a most awful stench arose, driving every one from the premises. This was followed by a gale of wind so severe as to destroy the buildings, which, in falling, took fire from the kang, and while the once prosperous man looked on in helpless misery, the last of his remaining property was swept forever from him. The seed that had brought prosperity to his honest, deserving brother had turned prosperity into ruin to the cruel, covetous Nahl Bo, who now had to subsist upon the charity of his kind brother, whom he had formerly treated so cruelly.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Allen, Korean Tales, ch. 6 (1889); not verbatim.

title.en: Chun Yang on the Swing at Kwanghallu
title.zh: 春香蕩鞦韆

region.en: Kwang-han Pavilion, Namwon (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 廣寒樓，南原（象徵性定位）

period: Pansori tale set c. 1600s; collected by H.N. Allen, Korean Tales (1889)

source.work: Horace N. Allen, Korean Tales (1889), ch. 7 'Chun Yang', eBook #55539

summary.en: In Namwon lived the Prefect's son Ye Toh Ryung, a dutiful scholar of sixteen, who rides out in the first spring weather to Kwang-han Pavilion, the rarest of all views, where the spirits themselves, it is said, frequent the place for its beauty. Leaning on one arm he sees a vision shoot into the air: a beautiful girl swinging in her dooryard — a dazzle of bright silks, shoeless white-stockinged feet shooting up among the peach blossoms till her hairpin falls and breaks with a sharp click. She is Chun Yang Ye, Fragrant Spring, daughter of Uhl Mah the dancing girl. The servant is sent running; brought before the young man, she matches him in age — twice eight and four fours — born at midnight of the eighth of the fourth moon, the lantern festival, one hour later than his own. 'Surely the gods had some motive in sending us into the world at the same time,' he says, and pleads that heaven must have intended them man and wife.
summary.zh: 南原使君之子李夢龍，春日遊廣寒樓。方倚欄看山，忽見鄰院少女蕩鞦韆直上雲際，羅衣生風，繡履掠桃，釵墮而折。急問之，乃歌伎月梅之女成春香也。召至，同年同月同日生，惟相差一時辰。夢龍曰：『此天作之合也。』遂求婚。

sensitivity.note: Pansori classic Chunhyang; no living-community restriction.

passages.text: In the city of Nam Won, in Chull Lah Do, lived the Prefect Ye Tung Uhi, the happy father of a son of some sixteen years of age, a bright, quick-minded, dutiful boy. As the mild spring weather approached and the buds began to open to the singing of the joyful birds, Ye Toh Ryung felt that he must get out and enjoy nature, and asked his pang san concerning the neighboring views. 'But of all rare views, Kang Hal Loo is the rarest,' said the servant. 'Officers from the eight provinces come to enjoy the scenery, and the temple is covered with verses they have left in praise of the place.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Allen, Korean Tales, ch. 7 (1889); not verbatim.

passages.text: 'That is true; so true, in fact, that it is well known that the spirits do frequent this place for its beauty.' As he said this, Toh Ryung had raised himself, gazing out to one side, when, as though it were one of the spirits just mentioned, the vision of a beautiful girl shot up into the air and soon fell back out of sight in the shrubbery of an adjoining court-yard. The vision arose again, and he then had time to see that it was but a beautiful girl swinging in her dooryard — the jewels sparkling on the gay robes, the dainty white hands and full round arms, and, as she flew higher in her wild sport, two little shoeless feet encased in white stockings shot up among the peach blossoms, causing them to fall in showers all about her. In the midst of the sport her hairpin loosened and fell, allowing her raven locks to float about her shoulders; the costly ornament fell on a rock and broke, for Toh Ryung could hear the sharp click where he sat.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Allen, Korean Tales, ch. 7 (1889); not verbatim.

passages.text: 'She is Uhl Mahs' daughter, a gee sang of this city; her name is Chun Yang Ye — fragrant spring.' The servant ran and called her. 'What is your name?' asked he. 'My name is Chun Yang Ye,' she said, with a voice that resembled silver jingling in a pouch. 'How old are you?' 'My age is just twice eight years.' 'Ah ha! how fortunate; you are twice eight, and I am four fours. We are of the same age. Your name, Fragrant Spring, is the same as your face — very beautiful.' 'My birthday occurs at midnight on the eighth day of the fourth moon.' 'That is the date of the lantern festival, and it is also my own birthday, only I was born at eleven instead of twelve. Surely the gods had some motive in sending us into the world at the same time, and thus bringing us together at our sixteenth spring-tide. Heaven must have intended us to be man and wife.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Allen, Korean Tales, ch. 7 (1889); not verbatim.

title.en: The Written Contract for a Hundred Years
title.zh: 春香執券

region.en: Kwang-han Pavilion, Namwon (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 廣寒樓，南原（象徵性定位）

period: Pansori tale set c. 1600s; collected by H.N. Allen, Korean Tales (1889)

source.work: Horace N. Allen, Korean Tales (1889), ch. 7, eBook #55539

summary.en: Toh Ryung begs Chun Yang to marry him, but she is no silly foolish thing: 'The son of a nobleman may not marry a gee sang without the consent of his parents... should we be privately married, and your father be ordered to duty at some other place, you would not dare take me with you. Then you would marry the daughter of some nobleman, and I would be forgotten.' He swears a yangban has but one mouth and cannot speak two ways; she answers that words fly out of the mouth and are soon lost — ink and paper are more lasting. Instantly he writes: 'Desiring to enjoy the spring scenery, I came to Kang Hal Loo. There I saw for the first time my heaven-sent bride. Meeting for the first time, I pledge myself for one hundred years; to be her faithful husband. Should I change, show this paper to the magistrate.' That night, scaling the back wall after his father sleeps, he comes to her house with its banner praying that a century be short to span her life and happiness; over the wine she sings that the flowers can bloom but a few days at best, and they pledge that when death should overtake them she will enter a flower, while he becomes a butterfly, coming and resting on her bosom and feasting off her fragrant sweetness.
summary.zh: 夢龍欲娶，春香曰：『貴公子不得私娶伎女；且異日尊翁遷任，君必不能攜我，則娶高門而棄我矣。』夢龍誓之，春香曰：『言出無憑，立券為信。』夢龍即書券曰：『遊廣寒樓，始遇天配之妻，百年偕老；若負此心，持券告官。』夜逾牆而至其家，酒酣對酌，相誓曰：『他日我為蝶，汝為花，蝶常棲花懷而餐其香。』

sensitivity.note: Pansori classic; no living-community restriction.

passages.text: 'You know,' she said, 'the son of a nobleman may not marry a gee sang without the consent of his parents. I know I am a gee sang by name, the fates have so ordained, but, nevertheless, I am an honorable woman, always have been, and expect to remain so.' 'Certainly, we cannot celebrate the six customs ceremony, but we can be privately married just the same.' 'No, it cannot be. Your father would not consent, and should we be privately married, and your father be ordered to duty at some other place, you would not dare take me with you. Then you would marry the daughter of some nobleman, and I would be forgotten. It must not, cannot be.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Allen, Korean Tales, ch. 7 (1889); not verbatim.

passages.text: 'I will never forsake you, or marry another. I swear it. And a yang ban has but one mouth, he cannot speak two ways. Even should we leave this place I will take you with me, or return soon to you.' 'But suppose you change your mind or forget your promises; words fly out of the mouth and are soon lost, ink and paper are more lasting; give me your promises in writing,' she says. Instantly the young man took up paper and brush, and wrote: 'A memorandum. Desiring to enjoy the spring scenery, I came to Kang Hal Loo. There I saw for the first time my heaven-sent bride. Meeting for the first time, I pledge myself for one hundred years; to be her faithful husband. Should I change, show this paper to the magistrate.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Allen, Korean Tales, ch. 7 (1889); not verbatim.

passages.text: When the lights were extinguished and his father had gone to sleep, he took his trusty servant, and, scaling the back wall, they hurried to the house of Chun Yang Ye. On the door leading to her little parlor hung a banner inscribed with verses to her ancestors and descendants, praying that a century be short to span her life and happiness.
