title.en: Itzamna, the Priest Who Named Everything
title.zh: 伊察姆納：為萬物命名的大祭司

region.en: Izamal, Yucatan, Mexico
region.zh: 墨西哥猶加敦伊扎馬爾

period: Recorded c. 1566 (Landa) and 1633 (Lizana); Tozzer edition 1941

source.work: Diego de Landa, Relacion de las cosas de Yucatan, trans. Alfred M. Tozzer (1941); Fray Bernardo de Lizana, Devocionario (1633)

license: Landa's sixteenth-century text public domain; Tozzer translation copyrighted and only paraphrased

summary.en: Itzamna — called Zamna, 'the lizard house', god of the heavens and of day and night — was the priest of the gods: he invented letters, the calendar, and the count of days, gave each thing its name, and healed the sick without payment. At Izamal his temple was the greatest of the land, and the pilgrims of the old religion came there as to Rome and Jerusalem.
summary.zh: 伊察姆納——又稱扎姆納，意為「蜥之家」，天空之神、晝夜之主——是諸神的大祭司：他發明文字、曆法與日數，為萬物命名，並不取分文地醫治病人。伊扎馬爾的神廟為全地之最，舊教朝聖者視之如羅馬與耶路撒冷。

sensitivity.note: Sixteenth-century colonial record; paraphrase of published translations only.

passages.text: The Yucatec held Itzamna to be a god of the heavens, the maker and lord of day and of night, and the priest of their gods in the time of the ancients: it was he who gave each thing its name, and who taught them the letters, the count of the years, months and days, and the feasts and ceremonies that go with the count.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Landa, Relacion, sections on the gods (Tozzer trans. 1941); not verbatim.

passages.text: He was so devoted to his people that he healed them, they say, of every sickness, and never asked a fee: medicine and writing and the calendar came to them as gifts. Because of this they built him the temple at Izamal, and made roads to it from all the ends of the land, so that all the province came to worship there as the Christians to Rome.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Lizana, Devocionario (1633), on Zamna and Izamal (Tozzer ed. 1941); not verbatim.

language: Sixteenth-century Spanish record of Yucatec tradition
canonical_translation: Tozzer, Landa's Relacion (1941); Lizana trans. via Tozzer notes

narrative.en:
Diego de Landa, writing about 1566, records that the Yucatec worshipped as a principal god Itzamna, whom they called also Zamna, the 'house of the lizard', a god of the heavens who had been the priest of the gods in the time of the ancients. It was Itzamna who gave names to the rivers, the places, and the things of the world; who invented the letters and the books; and who worked out the calendar — the count of the years, months, days, and feasts — teaching it to the priests who came after him. His cult center was Izamal, where the great pyramids of the town were said to be his, and Lizana, writing in 1633 from local memory, adds the detail that Zamna healed the sick of every illness and never asked a fee, and that four great roads were made from the ends of the land to his temple, as causeways to Rome and Jerusalem are made for pilgrims.

The Itzamna record is the Maya culture-hero cycle of Yucatán: a founder who is at once god, priest, physician, and civilizer. His healing without payment marks him as a god of free grace, unlike the priced covenants of Tohil in the highlands; his invention of writing and of the calendar marks him as the patron of the Ah Kin, the day-priests, whose title means literally 'he of the sun'; and his naming of everything echoes the Popol Wuj's creation by word — in Yucatán, the power of naming is remembered as the gift of a god who walked among the people.

At Izamal the memory of Itzamna is fused with that of Kinich Kakmó, 'the sun-faced', an idol which had its temple on the highest mound of the city, where from the top the sea itself could be seen. Landa's contemporaries reported the founders of Izamal as figures named Kinich Kabul, Kinich Kakmo, Cit Ah Cutz, and Cit Ah Coyi — 'father of the turkey lineage' and 'father of the coyote lineage' — founder-gods whose names became the patronymics of living families. Ritual function: Izamal remained the pilgrimage center of Yucatán under colonial rule; the Franciscans deliberately built their monastery on Itzamna's platform (1549), converting the god's own geography into Christian space while the roads of the god continued to carry pilgrims.

For the comparative study of culture heroes, Itzamna belongs beside Osiris, Thoth, and Quetzalcoatl: the god who gives writing, calendar, and medicine as a single civilizing gift. His Yucatec specificity lies in the way the gift is staged - naming. To give a thing its name, in the Maya world, is to bring it into the count of days; and Itzamna is remembered as the first counter, the priest whose naming made the calendar possible. The survival of his name into the Lacandon pantheon (Ioana, the caretaker of the underworld, as Tozzer found it in 1907) shows how long the office of the naming priest remained a living institution.

functions: Culture-hero charter of writing, calendar, and healing in Yucatán
Explains the sacred geography of Izamal as pilgrimage center with roads from all quarters
Authorizes the Ah Kin priesthood as heirs of the god's own office

title.en: Kukulcan, the Feathered Serpent, Comes from the West
title.zh: 羽蛇庫庫爾坎自西方而來

region.en: Chichen Itza, Yucatan, Mexico
region.zh: 墨西哥猶加敦奇琴伊察

period: Recorded c. 1566 (Landa, Herrera); Tozzer edition 1941

source.work: Diego de Landa, Relacion de las cosas de Yucatan, trans. Alfred M. Tozzer (1941); Antonio de Herrera, Historia General (1601-15)

license: Sixteenth-century texts public domain; Tozzer translation only paraphrased

summary.en: At Chichen Itza there reigned a great lord called Kukulcan — a man of good ability, without wife or children, public-spirited, and therefore considered a god. Whether he came before, after, or with the Itzas none agreed; but he ruled in peace, and after his return to Mexico he was worshipped there as Quetzalcoatl.
summary.zh: 奇琴伊察曾有一位偉大的君主庫庫爾坎——才幹出眾，無妻無子，熱心公益，因此被視為神。其到來早於、晚於抑或伴隨伊察人，眾說不一；但他治世以和平；回墨西哥之後，即被尊為羽蛇神克薩爾科亞特爾。

sensitivity.note: Sixteenth-century colonial record; paraphrase of published translations only.

passages.text: Among them there is a belief that a great lord called Kukulcan reigned, and all agree that he entered from the direction of the west; the difference of opinion which exists concerning this is only whether he entered before or after the Itzas or with them. He was a man of good ability; he had no wife nor children; he was very public-spirited and for this reason considered a god.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Herrera, Historia General (1601-15), Appendix A (Tozzer 1941); not verbatim.

passages.text: They say that he was favorably disposed, and that after his return he was regarded in Mexico as one of their gods and called Quetzalcouatl; and they also considered him a god in Yucatan, because of his great virtues and his gentleness. It is said he taught them, and that a beautiful building was dedicated to his name at Chichen Itza, with the serpent of the balustrade, by which his arrival was remembered.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Landa, Relacion, on Kukulcan (Tozzer 1941); not verbatim.

title.en: Kukulcan Builds the Walled City of Mayapan
title.zh: 庫庫爾坎築牆城馬雅潘

region.en: Mayapan, Yucatan, Mexico
region.zh: 墨西哥猶加敦馬雅潘

period: Recorded c. 1566 (Landa, Herrera); Tozzer edition 1941

source.work: Diego de Landa, Relacion de las cosas de Yucatan, trans. Alfred M. Tozzer (1941); Antonio de Herrera, Historia General (1601-15)

license: Sixteenth-century texts public domain; Tozzer translation only paraphrased

summary.en: To quiet the country, Kukulcan agrees that a new city should be founded where all affairs could go. Eight leagues inland from Merida they built a circle of dry stone wall with only two doors, raised the temples, named the largest for Kukulcan, and divided the land among the lords — the beginning of the government of Mayapan.
summary.zh: 為平定邦國，庫庫爾坎議定另建一城，使諸務皆歸於此。眾人在梅里達城址以內八里格處，築乾砌石牆圓城，僅開兩門；建諸神廟，最大者以庫庫爾坎為名，並將土地分予諸侯——馬雅潘政權由此而始。

sensitivity.note: Sixteenth-century colonial record; paraphrase of published translations only.

passages.text: In order to tranquillize the country he agreed to found another city where all affairs should go. They chose a site for this eight leagues further inland from where the city of Merida now is and fifteen from the sea, and there they made a circle of about an eighth of a league consisting of a wall in stone laid dry, leaving only two doors.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Herrera, Historia General (1601-15), Appendix A (Tozzer 1941); not verbatim.

passages.text: They made their temples and called the largest Kukulcan, and they also built the houses of the lords near the enclosure. Kukulcan divided the land among the latter, and the city was called Mayapan; and in this way peace returned and the government endured in that place for many generations, until the tyrant Cocom brought ruin on it.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Landa, Relacion (Tozzer 1941); not verbatim.

title.en: The Three Brothers of Chichen Itza
title.zh: 奇琴伊察的三兄弟

region.en: Chichen Itza, Yucatan, Mexico
region.zh: 墨西哥猶加敦奇琴伊察

period: Recorded c. 1566 (Landa, Herrera); Tozzer edition 1941

source.work: Diego de Landa, Relacion de las cosas de Yucatan, trans. Alfred M. Tozzer (1941)

license: Sixteenth-century texts public domain; Tozzer translation only paraphrased

summary.en: Chichen Itza was ruled, they say, by three lordly brothers who came from the west and lived very chastely with their wives; they built the great temples. But when one of them died, the other two began to act unjustly and indecently; the people hated them, put them to death, and abandoned the place and its buildings.
summary.zh: 據言奇琴伊察由三位自西方而來的君王兄弟共治，其妻皆守貞潔；他們建造了宏偉的神廟。然而其中一人死後，其餘二人開始行事不義不端；民眾惡之，遂誅二人，棄城而去，連其偉大建築也一併拋下。

sensitivity.note: Sixteenth-century colonial record; paraphrase of published translations only.

passages.text: It is said that Chichen Itza was ruled by three lords who were brothers, who came into that country from the west; they were very devout, and they built very beautiful temples, and their wives lived very chastely. One of them died or went away, upon which the other two acted unjustly and indecently, and for this they were put to death.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Landa, Relacion (Tozzer 1941); not verbatim.

passages.text: In time, they say, one of them died, and his absence left so great a flaw that the other two began to be dishonest and partial, and to such a degree that the people hated them; so they killed them and abandoned the place and left the buildings, especially the most honorable, which is ten leagues from the sea. Those who settled Chichen Itza are called the Itzas.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Herrera, Historia General, Appendix A (Tozzer 1941); not verbatim.

title.en: Governor Cocom Covets Riches: The Mexicans Enter Mayapan
title.zh: 科科姆總督貪財：墨西哥人入馬雅潘

region.en: Mayapan, Yucatan, Mexico
region.zh: 墨西哥猶加敦馬雅潘

period: Recorded c. 1566 (Landa); events of the 13th-15th c.; Tozzer edition 1941

source.work: Diego de Landa, Relacion de las cosas de Yucatan, trans. Alfred M. Tozzer (1941)

license: Sixteenth-century texts public domain; Tozzer translation only paraphrased

summary.en: Governor Cocom begins to covet riches and arranges with the Mexican garrisons kept at Tabasco and Xicalango to hand over his city. The Mexican troops enter Mayapan, the governor oppresses the poor and makes slaves — the first to do so, the record insists — and the Yucatecans, learning the use of the bow, the lance and the axe, cease to fear them.
summary.zh: 科科姆總督起貪財之心，與墨西哥人在塔巴斯科與希卡蘭戈的衛戍部隊相約，欲將其城交出。墨西哥軍入馬雅潘，總督欺凌貧民、役使奴隸——史載此為奴役之始——而猶加敦人習得弓、矛、斧之用，自此不再畏懼他們。

sensitivity.note: Sixteenth-century colonial record; paraphrase of published translations only.

passages.text: The Governor Cocom began to covet riches, and for this reason he arranged with the troops of the garrison which the kings of Mexico kept at Tabasco and Xicalango to hand over the city to them. And thus he brought the Mexican people into Mayapan, and oppressed the poor and made many slaves; and the lords would have put him to death but for the fear which they had of the Mexicans.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Landa, Relacion (Tozzer 1941); not verbatim.

passages.text: The lord of the Tutul Xius never consented to this. And the Yucatecans, finding themselves in this situation, learned from the Mexicans the use of arms, and they soon became masters of the bow and arrow, the lance and the axe, their shields and jackets made strong with cotton, so that finally they neither admired the Mexicans nor feared them, but took little account of them.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Landa, Relacion (Tozzer 1941); not verbatim.

title.en: The Fall of Mayapan: Tyranny and the Absent Son
title.zh: 馬雅潘之傾覆：暴政與倖存的獨子

region.en: Mayapan, Yucatan, Mexico
region.zh: 墨西哥猶加敦馬雅潘

period: Recorded c. 1566 (Landa); fall c. 1441-60; Tozzer edition 1941

source.work: Diego de Landa, Relacion de las cosas de Yucatan, trans. Alfred M. Tozzer (1941)

license: Sixteenth-century texts public domain; Tozzer translation only paraphrased

summary.en: A haughty successor of Cocom's house makes a second league with Tabasco, introduces more Mexicans, and plays the tyrant, enslaving the poor. The nobles join the just Tutul Xiu, conspire against Cocom, kill him and all his sons but one who is absent, sack his house, and take back his lands — and after five hundred years of dwelling there, the parties abandon Mayapan, each returning to his own country.
summary.zh: 科科姆家族的繼任者傲慢仿其先人，再與塔巴斯科結盟，引入更多墨西哥人，行暴政而奴役貧民。諸侯遂擁公正的圖圖爾·希烏，密謀誅科科姆——殺其與其諸子，唯獨缺席的一子倖免；劫其家，奪其可可田與果園以償所奪。城居五百餘年之後，各方棄城而去，各歸其國。

sensitivity.note: Sixteenth-century colonial record; paraphrase of published translations only.

passages.text: Among the successors of the house of Cocom was a very haughty man, an imitator of Cocom, and he made another league with the men of Tabasco, and he introduced more Mexicans into the city, and he began to play the tyrant and to make slaves of the poorer people. On this account the nobles joined with the party of Tutul Xiu, who was a just statesman like his ancestors, and they conspired to put Cocom to death.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Landa, Relacion (Tozzer 1941); not verbatim.

passages.text: This they did, killing at the same time all his sons, except one who was absent. They sacked his house and took away the lands which he had in cacao and in other fruits, saying that they paid themselves for what he had taken from them. The quarrels between the Cocoms, who said they had been unjustly expelled, and the Xius lasted so long that after they had lived in that city for more than five hundred years, they abandoned it and left it in solitude, each party returning to his own country.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Landa, Relacion (Tozzer 1941); not verbatim.

title.en: The Well of Chichen: Living Men, Precious Stones, and the Voice from Below
title.zh: 奇琴之井：活人、寶石與井下之聲

region.en: Sacred Cenote of Chichen Itza, Yucatan, Mexico
region.zh: 墨西哥猶加敦奇琴伊察聖井

period: Recorded c. 1566 (Landa); Tozzer edition 1941

source.work: Diego de Landa, Relacion de las cosas de Yucatan, trans. Alfred M. Tozzer (1941)

license: Sixteenth-century texts public domain; Tozzer translation only paraphrased

summary.en: From a paved causeway running from the court of the great building, a well opens in the living rock, green with the groves around it. Into it, in times of drought, they threw living men as sacrifice, believing they did not die though they never saw them again; with them precious stones and things they prized, gold cup and bowl, so great was their devotion. If the country had had gold, they say, all of it would be in that well.
summary.zh: 自大神殿前庭有一石鋪大道，通往岩層中天然開口的深井，井水因四圍林木而呈綠色。大旱之時，人們將活人投入井中獻祭，堅信其人未死、只是不再被人看見；同投者有寶石與珍愛之物、金杯與金碗，奉獻之誠如此。人言：若此地有金，皆在井中。

sensitivity.note: Sixteenth-century colonial record; paraphrase of published translations only.

passages.text: From the court in front of these stages a wide and handsome causeway runs as far as a well which is about two stones' throw off. Into this well they have had, and then had, the custom of throwing men alive as a sacrifice to the gods in times of drought, and they believed that they did not die though they never saw them again.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Landa, Relacion (Tozzer 1941); not verbatim.

passages.text: They also threw into it a great many other things, like precious stones and things which they prized. And so, if this country had possessed gold, it would be this well that would have the greater part of it, so great was the devotion which the Indians showed for it. The well is more than seven stadia deep down to the water, and more than one hundred feet broad, marvellously formed by a circular and perpendicular opening in the living rock, and the water appears green, which they say is caused by the groves with which it is surrounded.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Landa, Relacion (Tozzer 1941); not verbatim.

language: Sixteenth-century Spanish record of Yucatec practice
canonical_translation: Tozzer, Landa's Relacion (1941)

narrative.en:
Landa's description of the Sacred Cenote is the classic colonial account of Maya pilgrimage sacrifice. A wide paved causeway (the sacbe still traceable today) runs from the great pyramid's court northward to a natural well — the cenote — cut by a circular perpendicular opening in the living rock, more than a hundred feet across, its water green from the groves around it. Into this well, Landa records, the Yucatec 'have had, and then had', the custom of throwing living men as sacrifice to the gods in time of drought, believing that they did not die though they were never seen again; with the victims went precious stones, cups of gold, bowls, and everything they prized — so much so, Landa observes, that if the country had possessed gold, the greater part of it would have been at the bottom of that well.

The rite was divinatory as much as propitiatory. The Relacion of Valladolid (recorded in Tozzer's notes from the 1580s) describes the full procedure: the lords of all the provinces fasted sixty days without raising their eyes to their wives or to those who brought them food; at break of dawn they threw into the well Indian women who had been told to ask the gods for a good year; at exactly midday the one who was to come out shouted for a rope, and when she was drawn up half-dead, great fires were made around her and she was censed with copal. Revived, she reported that many of her race were below, men as well as women, who received her, and that when she raised her head they struck her neck so that she would keep it bowed. She answered their questions — good year or bad — and if the demon was angry with a lord, his woman did not ask to be taken out at noon, and never came out.

The 1562 idolatry testimonies taken under Landa's own inquisition add a village-level echo: messengers carried a boy to Chichen, threw him into the cenote, waited a day to hear 'the reply of what their gods had told him' about pestilence or food or sterility, and, when he did not come out, returned to report. And a post-conquest episode — the Xiu pilgrimage for rain, with its Cocamb ambush — shows the well still commanding the politics of the peninsula long after the conquest had begun.

Archaeologically, Edward H. Thompson's dredging (1904-10) recovered the gold and copper bells, jade beads, carved plaques, wooden objects, human bones, and copal balls that verify the accounts. The well's cultural function is threefold: it is an oracle (the victim returns with the year's answer), a covenant of rain (drought victims, boys and girls, sent to speak with the rain gods), and a treasury of the community's wealth surrendered to the water. In Maya cosmology the cenote is an entrance to the watery underworld — Xibalba's channels — and the sacrifice at noon (midday, the hour of the divinatory return) marks the axis between the living town and the dead water.

functions: Rain covenant in drought: living victims sent to petition the water gods
Oracle: the survivor returns at noon with the year's answer
Community treasury: gold, jade, and prized goods surrendered to the water

variants.name: Relacion of Valladolid (1580s)
variants.summary: Gives the fasting, the dawn casting, the noon rope, the subaquanean people, and the angry-lord rule.

variants.name: Chumayel: Hunac Ceel's prophecy from the well
variants.text_tradition: Book of Chilam Balam of Chumayel (Roys 1933)
variants.summary: When the prophecy fails to come, Hunac Ceel puts out his head from the well's south lip and declares the prophecy himself, rising to rulership.

primary_sources.work: Diego de Landa, Relacion de las cosas de Yucatan
primary_sources.citation: c. 1566; Tozzer trans. 1941, pp. 179-84

primary_sources.work: Relacion of the city of Valladolid
primary_sources.citation: Relaciones de Yucatan, 2: 24-6; in Tozzer 1941

title.en: The Xius Walk to the Well and Are Burned on the Road
title.zh: 希烏人朝聖於井，途中遭焚

region.en: Road from Mani to Chichen Itza, Yucatan, Mexico
region.zh: 墨西哥猶加敦自馬尼往奇琴伊察之路

period: Recorded c. 1566 (Landa); events of the 1550s-60s; Tozzer edition 1941

source.work: Diego de Landa, Relacion de las cosas de Yucatan, trans. Alfred M. Tozzer (1941)

license: Sixteenth-century texts public domain; Tozzer translation only paraphrased

summary.en: Rain fails in the whole land and there is famine; the lords of Mani, of the Xiu lineage, agree on a solemn sacrifice and take male and female slaves to throw into the well of Chichen Itza. To reach it they must pass through Cocom country; the Cocoms, wanting vengeance, let them pass — then burn the pilgrims alive and shoot down those who flee.
summary.zh: 全地無雨，饑饉大作；馬尼的希烏族君長議定行莊嚴之祭，攜男女奴隸投入奇琴伊察之井。前往之路必經科科姆之地；懷恨已久的科科姆人表面允其通行——旋即將朝聖者活活燒死，以箭射殺逃脫者。

sensitivity.note: Sixteenth-century colonial record; paraphrase of published translations only.

passages.text: Rain being lacking in the whole land, little bread was gathered, and they came to such great extremity that they ate barks of trees. As a result of this famine the lords of Mani, who are those of the Xiu lineage, agreed to make a solemn sacrifice to the idols, and taking certain male and female slaves in order to throw them into the well of Chichen Itza.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Landa, Relacion (Tozzer 1941); not verbatim.

passages.text: It was necessary to pass through the pueblo of those of the Cocom lineage, their ancient and capital enemies; and not believing that they would renew the old passions at such a time, they sent to them to give an account of their journey and ask to be allowed to pass. The Cocoms, who were desirous of avenging ancient injuries, cautiously replied all right, they might go. Having reached a pueblo two leagues from Cocom, they lodged in a large house, where the Cocoms set fire to them and burned them, and shot with arrows those who escaped.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Landa, Relacion (Tozzer 1941); not verbatim.

title.en: The Five Unlucky Days: The Bacabs at the Four Entrances of the Town
title.zh: 五個凶日：鎮口四方的巴卡布

region.en: Yucatan, Mexico
region.zh: 墨西哥猶加敦

period: Recorded c. 1566 (Landa); Tozzer edition 1941

source.work: Diego de Landa, Relacion de las cosas de Yucatan, trans. Alfred M. Tozzer (1941)

license: Sixteenth-century texts public domain; Tozzer translation only paraphrased

summary.en: For the New Year the Maya used the five unlucky days before the first of Pop. In the Kan year, whose omen is Hobnil of the south, they made a hollow figure of clay called Kan u Uayeyab, set it on a heap of stones at the southern entrance of the town, and raised the statue of Bolon Dzacab in the chief's house; the priest and lords assemble, chase out the evil spirit, pierce ears and tongues, anoint the idols, and so begin the year.
summary.zh: 歲首之祭用一月波普之前的五個凶日。坎年之兆為南方之霍布尼爾；眾人塑名為坎·烏·瓦耶亞布的黏土空心神像，置於鎮南入口的石堆之上，並在酋長家中立起博倫·察卡布之神像；祭司與諸侯齊聚，驅逐惡靈，穿耳穿舌，塗聖諸像，然後歲曆更新。

sensitivity.note: Sixteenth-century colonial record; paraphrase of published translations only.

passages.text: For celebrating the festival of the New Year, this people, with great rejoicing and with much dignity according to their unhappy ideas, made use of the five unlucky days which were regarded by them as such before the first day of the new year. In these days they held many services for the Bacabs and for the gods called Kan u Uayeyab, Chac u Uayeyab, Sac u Uayeyab and Ek u Uayeyab.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Landa, Relacion (Tozzer 1941); not verbatim.

passages.text: It was the custom in all the towns in Yucatan that there should be two heaps of stone facing each other at the entrance of the town on all four sides — east, west, north and south. In the Kan year the omen was Hobnil, and they ruled in the region of the south; they made an image or hollow figure of the god of clay, which they called Kan u Uayeyab, and carried it to the heaps of dry stone raised at the southern side.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Landa, Relacion (Tozzer 1941); not verbatim.

passages.text: They chose a chief of the town in whose house the festival was celebrated, and made the statue of a god called Bolon Dzacab, which they placed in the house of the principal, adorned, in a public place where everyone could go to it. Then the lords, the priest and the men of the town assembled, and they began by chasing away from themselves the evil spirit, in order to perform the ceremony the better — sometimes by prayers and benedictions, at other times by offerings and sacrifices.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Landa, Relacion (Tozzer 1941); not verbatim.

language: Sixteenth-century Spanish record of Yucatec ritual
canonical_translation: Tozzer, Landa's Relacion (1941)

narrative.en:
Landa's longest ritual description is the set of four New Year ceremonies attached to the four year-bearers of the Yucatec calendar: Kan, Muluc, Ix, and Cauac, each with its color (red east, white north, black west, yellow south), its Bacab, its Pauah Tun, its Xib Chac, and its Uayeyab idol. The ceremonies were held in the five 'unlucky' nameless days (the Uayeb) before the first of Pop, when the old year is dying and the new one must be carried across the threshold.

In each of the four rites the pattern is the same in shape and different in color and direction: two heaps of dry stone face each other at the entrance of the town on the side belonging to the year's color; a hollow figure of baked clay, named for the year (Kan u Uayeyab, and so on), is carried to the stone heaps and seated on the crossbars of green poles; a statue of the year's god (for instance Bolon Dzacab) is set up in the house of the chief chosen to give the feast; the evil spirit is chased away first — by prayers, benedictions, offerings — because no ceremony can proceed while he lingers; and then come the sacrifices. Hearts of quail are burned; the Chacs, the four assistants of the rite, draw blood by piercing tongues and ears with blades, and anoint the idols; the dancers carry the god on a litter to the sound of drum and conch and flute, singing, and drink a wine of fermented bark until they are overcome.

Each year also brings its specific calamities to avert, and Landa lists them: in the Kan year, the south's dominion, the evils are those of the yellow (kan) color; in the Muluc year the omen is Can tzic nal and the direction east; in the Ix year, Sac cimi and the north; in the Cauac year, Hosan ek and the west. The tunkul (split drum), the conch, and the flute give the sound of the transition; the fire, the new idols, and the swept courts give its material form.

As a corpus record this is the Maya counterpart of the New Year renewal clusters in other traditions: the world is renewed by re-coloring it, by re-stationing its gods at the four gates, and by feeding them blood before the calendar turns. The connection to the Dresden Codex pages 25-28 and Tro-Cortesianus 34-37 — which picture the same Uayeb rites — makes this one of the few places where a colonial text, a codex, and living practice (the Cha-chaac rain rites recorded among the modern Maya) describe the same liturgy.

functions: Renewal of time: the year is inaugurated by re-stationing the direction gods at the four gates
Expiation: the evil spirit must be driven off before any ceremony
Blood covenant: tongue and ear piercing with ac-grass blades feeds the year-gods
Links the colonial liturgy to Dresden 25-28 and to modern Cha-chaac rain rites

title.en: The Feast of the Hunters: Deer Skulls and Ac Grass
title.zh: 獵人之祭：鹿首與茅草

region.en: Yucatan, Mexico
region.zh: 墨西哥猶加敦

period: Recorded c. 1566 (Landa), month Zip; Tozzer edition 1941

source.work: Diego de Landa, Relacion de las cosas de Yucatan, trans. Alfred M. Tozzer (1941)

license: Sixteenth-century texts public domain; Tozzer translation only paraphrased

summary.en: In the month Zip the hunters' festival is held. The priests drive out the evil spirit, set up the sacrifice apparatus with new fire and blue bitumen, and invoke the gods of the chase. Some dance holding anointed deer skulls and arrows; others pierce their ears and tongues and pass seven wide blades of ac grass through the holes, then pour out the wine until they are overcome.
summary.zh: 希普月行獵人之祭。祭司驅逐惡靈，備祭器、新火與藍色樹脂，召請狩獵諸神。有人執塗聖的鹿首與箭起舞；有人穿耳穿舌，以七片寬茅草葉貫穿孔竅；禮成之後，傾酒痛飲，直至醉倒。

sensitivity.note: Sixteenth-century colonial record; paraphrase of published translations only.

passages.text: The priests came and drove away the evil spirit as usual. After he had been driven out they placed in the middle the apparatus for the sacrifice, incense and new fire, and the blue bitumen. And the hunters devoutly invoked the gods of the chase, Acanum, Suhui Dzip, Tabai and others, and distributed the incense which they threw into the brazier.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Landa, Relacion (Tozzer 1941); not verbatim.

passages.text: While it was burning, each took an arrow and the skull of a deer, which the Chacs anointed with the blue bitumen. And some danced holding these thus anointed in their hands, while others pierced their ears and others their tongues, and passed through the holes seven rather wide blades of a kind of grass called ac. This done, the priest first, and then the officers of the festival, offered the gifts; and so dancing, the wine was poured out, and they got drunk until they were overcome.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Landa, Relacion (Tozzer 1941); not verbatim.

title.en: The Fishermen Cut Their Ears and Set Up the Pole
title.zh: 漁人割耳立柱

region.en: Coast of Yucatan, Mexico
region.zh: 墨西哥猶加敦海岸

period: Recorded c. 1566 (Landa), month Zec; Tozzer edition 1941

source.work: Diego de Landa, Relacion de las cosas de Yucatan, trans. Alfred M. Tozzer (1941)

license: Sixteenth-century texts public domain; Tozzer translation only paraphrased

summary.en: The day after the hunters, the fishermen celebrate their feast: they anoint their fishing implements, cut their ears round the edges instead of piercing them, dance the Chohom, bless a tall thick pole and set it upright — and then the lords go to the shore with a great company to catch fish with rejoicing.
summary.zh: 獵祭次日，漁人行其祭：他們塗聖漁具，不以穿孔而沿耳緣割切，跳卓霍姆之舞，祝聖一根粗高的木柱而立之——然後君長們率大隊人馬前往海濱，歡騰捕魚。

sensitivity.note: Sixteenth-century colonial record; paraphrase of published translations only.

passages.text: At once on the following day the fishermen celebrated the festival in the same way as the others, except that the things which they anointed were their fishing implements, and they did not pierce their ears, but they cut them round the edges, and they danced a dance called Chohom.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Landa, Relacion (Tozzer 1941); not verbatim.

passages.text: When all this was done, they blessed a tall and thick pole, and set it upright. When this festival was ended in the towns, the lords were accustomed to go to celebrate it with a large number of people on the shore, where they caught a large number of fish with rejoicings, carrying a large supply of trammel nets, hooks and other instruments for fishing.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Landa, Relacion (Tozzer 1941); not verbatim.

title.en: The Sun-Faced Idol of Izamal
title.zh: 伊扎馬爾的日面神像

region.en: Izamal, Yucatan, Mexico
region.zh: 墨西哥猶加敦伊扎馬爾

period: Recorded c. 1566 (Landa) and 1633 (Lizana); Tozzer edition 1941

source.work: Diego de Landa, Relacion de las cosas de Yucatan, trans. Alfred M. Tozzer (1941); Lizana, Devocionario (1633)

license: Sixteenth-century texts public domain; Tozzer translation only paraphrased

summary.en: On the highest mound of Izamal stood the temple of Kinich Kakmó, 'the sun with a face'. The first inhabitants of the city were remembered as founder-gods — Kinich Kabul, Kinich Kakmo, Cit Ah Cutz ('father of the turkey lineage'), Cit Ah Coyi ('father of the coyote lineage') — whose names became the patronymics of living families. From the temple's top one saw the whole land and the sea.
summary.zh: 伊扎馬爾最高的丘上，立有基尼奇·卡克莫——「有面之日」——的神廟。城中初民被記為創族之神：基尼奇·卡布爾、基尼奇·卡克莫、西特·阿·庫茨（火雞氏之父）、西特·阿·科伊（郊狼氏之父），其名成為後世家族的姓氏。自廟頂可望全境與大海。

sensitivity.note: Sixteenth-century colonial record; paraphrase of published translations only.

passages.text: There was also another mound at Izamal which is today the highest one, and it is called Kinich Kakmo, the reason being that there was a temple on top of it and in it an idol which had this name, which in our language means 'the sun with a face'. From the top of the chapel one sees wonderfully well, as far as the sight can reach, and the sea is visible.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Lizana, Devocionario (1633), and Landa (Tozzer 1941); not verbatim.

passages.text: The first inhabitants of the city were Kinich Kabul, Kinich Kakmo, Cit Ah Cutz and Cit Ah Coyi, from whom descended the Xols, the Mos and the Coyes. These first inhabitants should be considered founder gods: their names became the surnames of the lineages that still bear them, so that the god of the sun-faced temple is also the ancestor in the count of families.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of the Relacion of Izamal and Lizana (Tozzer 1941); not verbatim.

title.en: The Flood Page: The Goddess of the Cloud-Burst
title.zh: 洪水頁：雲爆女神

region.en: Dresden Codex (Yucatec tradition), symbolic pin at Uxmal, Yucatan
region.zh: 德累斯頓抄本（猶加敦傳統），以墨西哥猶加敦烏斯馬爾為象徵定位

period: Codex drawn c. 1200-1250 (pre-conquest copy of older tradition); Forstemann facsimile 1880

source.work: Dresden Codex, p. 74, Forstemann facsimile (1880); commentary in Schellhas, Representation of Deities of the Maya Manuscripts, trans. Parker & Rau, 1904

license: Public domain (Forstemann facsimile 1880; Schellhas 1904 BAE translation)

summary.en: Dresden page 74: the aged water-goddess — crowned with the knotted serpent and wearing the cross-bones of the death-god — pours water from an overturned jar, while below stretches the great world-serpent and the blackened sun. Schellhas reads her as the personification of water in its quality of destroyer: the goddess of floods and cloud-bursts, the end of a world.
summary.zh: 德累斯頓抄本第74頁：頭戴蛇結、身佩死神交叉骨的老水神，自傾覆之罐倒出大水；其下橫陳巨大世界之蛇，太陽黝黑。謝爾哈斯讀之為「以毀滅者形象現身的水」——洪水與雲爆之女神，即一個世界的終結。

sensitivity.note: Published codex facsimile and public-domain commentary; paraphrase of scholarly description only.

passages.text: The aged goddess appears repeatedly with claws of feet of the jaguar; she wears on her head a knotted serpent and with her hands pours water from a vessel. Evidently we have here a personification of water in its quality of destroyer, a goddess of floods and cloud-bursts, which, as we know, play an important part in Central America.
passages.note: Condensed from Schellhas, Representation of Deities of the Maya Manuscripts (1904), on goddess I; not verbatim.

passages.text: In accordance with this character, on Dresden page 74, where something resembling a flood is represented, she wears the cross-bones of the death-god. In the Madrid manuscript the same goddess distinguished by symbols of flood and water appears; in both she is invariably marked by the serpent on her head, the symbol of the water flowing along and forming waves — and with her come the signs of the evil days.
passages.note: Condensed from Schellhas (1904), on goddess I and Dresden 74; not verbatim.

canonical_translation: Forstemann facsimile (1880); Schellhas commentary, trans. Parker & Rau (1904)

narrative.en:
Page 74 of the Dresden Codex is the Maya 'flood page' — a picture with no Long Count dates, unlike almost everything else in the book, set apart as a mythic scene of the ending of a world. In the upper register the aged water-goddess (Schellhas's Goddess I, generally identified with Ix Chel) turns an overturned jar and pours a stream of water out upon the world; she wears on her head the knotted serpent — the symbol of flowing, wave-forming water — and on her body the cross-bones of the death-god, marking the pouring as destruction rather than irrigation. The stream that falls from her jar is black, and the sun on the page is blackened: the sky's light is going out. Below stretches the great serpent frame of the sky, the double-headed world-serpent on which the heavens rest, and along its body the rain-gods (the Chacs with their lightning axes) and the uprooted trees and birds of the doomed world.

The page belongs to the cluster of world-destruction by water that runs through Maya narrative from the Popol Wuj's black-rain flood that ends the wooden people, through the Chilam Balam's 'sudden rush of water when the sky fell', to the colonial-era prophecies of a final deluge. In the codex it is likely the mythic template behind the katun-ending and New Year rites: the world is periodically drowned and re-founded, and the poured jar of the goddess is the picture of the boundary between a finished count and a new one.

Its comparative weight in the Motif Atlas is high: the Maya flood belongs with the Sumerian Utanapishtim flood, Deucalion, Noah, Manu, and Bergelmir — but with a distinctive calendrical theology. The Maya flood is not punishment for a single sin; it is the end of a count, a period that has run its course. Ritual function: at the year-turning, the pouring of water (from jars, from the rain gods, from the cenote) re-enacts both the destruction and the renewal; the flood page is the template of that double act.

In the corpus of world floods the Dresden page stands out for its pictorial economy: no names, no dates, no words of dialogue - only the act. The goddess pours; the sun goes black; the serpent frame holds; the trees come down. This economy has made the page a touchstone for every discussion of Maya eschatology, from Forstemann onward, and its imagery is close enough to the descriptions of the Chilam Balam and the Popol Wuj floods that the three traditions are usually read together as one theology of periodic world-ending. For the Motif Atlas the page is the Maya anchor of the flood cluster, cross-referenced to the Mesopotamian, Hebrew, Hindu, and Norse deluge records, and to the Maya wooden-people flood whose black rain it mirrors.

functions: Picture-template of world destruction by water at the end of a count
Goddess I (Ix Chel) as destroyer: water with the death-god's cross-bones
Anchors the flood cluster in the Maya codical tradition

variants.name: Popol Wuj: the black-rain flood
variants.summary: The highland flood that destroys the wooden people — a resinous black rain day and night, with the implements in revolt.

variants.name: Chumayel: sky falls and water rushes in
variants.text_tradition: Book of Chilam Balam of Chumayel (Roys 1933)
variants.summary: The seizure of Oxlahun-ti-ku's insignia brings the sky down and a sudden rush of water.

secondary_sources.citation: Schellhas, 1904, Washington: Bureau of American Ethnology (Annual Report 16)

title.en: The Venus Table: The Morning Star's Spears
title.zh: 金星表：晨星之矛

region.en: Dresden Codex (Yucatec tradition), symbolic pin at Uxmal, Yucatan
region.zh: 德累斯頓抄本（猶加敦傳統），以墨西哥猶加敦烏斯馬爾為象徵定位

period: Codex drawn c. 1200-1250; Forstemann facsimile 1880

source.work: Dresden Codex, pp. 46-50, Forstemann facsimile (1880); commentary in Schellhas (1904)

summary.en: The Venus table counts 584-day years: five pages in which the planet's heliacal rising is drawn as a god hurling a spear — the star's rays weaponized against victims below. Schellhas computes the grand period 1,366,560 days, thirteen Venus cycles of 584, and finds the same number again at Chichen Itza — the calendar war of the Morning Star.
summary.zh: 金星表以584日為一年：五頁之中，行星的晨曦初升被繪為投擲長矛的神明——星光化作武器，射向下方的犧牲者。謝爾哈斯計得總數1,366,560日，即13個金星年，並發現同數出現於奇琴伊察——晨星之曆戰。

sensitivity.note: Published codex facsimile and public-domain commentary; paraphrase only.

passages.text: The Venus table of the Dresden Codex, pages 46-50, counts the planet in Venus years of 584 days: its heliacal rising as the Morning Star, its greatest brilliancy, its disappearance and return. In each of the five pages the rising star is pictured as a god of war hurling a spear downward — the star's light drawn as a weapon, and its victims below.
passages.note: Condensed from Schellhas (1904) commentary and Forstemann's analysis of the Venus table; not verbatim.

passages.text: The grand period of the table is 1,366,560 days, that is, precisely 416 solar years of 365 days each, or 260 Venus years of 584 days each — the product of the Tonalamatl multiplied by the Venus years. Seler finds this same period on a relief of Chichen Itza: the astronomy of the codex and the architecture of the city carry the same count.
passages.note: Condensed from Schellhas (1904), on the Venus table numbers; not verbatim.

title.en: Sun and Moon Combat on the Eclipse Page
title.zh: 日月相搏：蝕之頁

region.en: Dresden Codex (Yucatec tradition), symbolic pin at Uxmal, Yucatan
region.zh: 德累斯頓抄本（猶加敦傳統），以墨西哥猶加敦烏斯馬爾為象徵定位

period: Codex drawn c. 1200-1250; Forstemann facsimile 1880

source.work: Dresden Codex, pp. 59-60, Forstemann facsimile (1880); commentary in Schellhas (1904)

summary.en: On Dresden page 60 sun and moon stand on a platform in combat — the moon the assailant, the sun making only a proud defensive gesture — and the animal beneath them embodies the eclipses to which they at times succumb. Venus triumphs over weak Mercury; Jupiter over bound Saturn, whose slowness of motion is his chains.
summary.zh: 德累斯頓第60頁：日與月立於臺上相搏——月亮為進攻者，太陽僅作傲然自衛之勢——其下之獸即日月時或屈服的蝕之化身。金星勝過軟弱的墨丘利；木星勝過戴鐐的土星，其緩行即其囚禁。

sensitivity.note: Published codex facsimile and public-domain commentary; paraphrase only.

passages.text: The sun and moon stand on the platform in the upper picture; their combat is equivalent to the eclipses to which they at times succumb. The moon is the assailant and the sun makes only a proud defensive gesture. The animal under the two persons is the embodiment of the eclipses, which the Aztecs interpreted as the act of being devoured by the jaguar.
passages.note: Condensed from Schellhas (1904), on Dresden page 60; not verbatim.

passages.text: At the left, bottom, the powerful Venus triumphs over the weak Mercury; the two planets are real chronometers, by reason of the regular alternation of their appearance as morning and evening stars, and each is accompanied by a serpent, the usual symbol of time. On the right, Jupiter as the stronger has vanquished Saturn, whose bound arms symbolize his slowness of motion and his confinement to the same region of the sky.
passages.note: Condensed from Schellhas (1904), on Dresden page 60; not verbatim.

title.en: The Sacrificial Scene of Dresden 3
title.zh: 德累斯頓第3頁的獻祭圖

region.en: Dresden Codex (Yucatec tradition), symbolic pin at Uxmal, Yucatan
region.zh: 德累斯頓抄本（猶加敦傳統），以墨西哥猶加敦烏斯馬爾為象徵定位

period: Codex drawn c. 1200-1250; Forstemann facsimile 1880

source.work: Dresden Codex, p. 3, Forstemann facsimile (1880); commentary in Schellhas (1904)

summary.en: On the upper half of page 3 a woman lies bound hand and foot on the sacrificial stone, the incision above the stomach already made, her eyes closed. Behind her rises the tree of life with a bird in its branches holding an end of the ribbon issuing from the victim's eyes; four gods surround the scene — the storm-god K above, the maize-god E with a dish of fruit, the serpent-god H, and the rain deity at the destroyed upper left.
summary.zh: 第3頁上半：一名女子手足被縛，臥於祭石之上，胃上方切口已開，雙目緊閉。其後立生命之樹，枝上有鳥，銜著自犧牲者眼中抽出之物的一端；四神環繞——上方為風暴之神K，左下為持果盤的玉米神E，右下為蛇神H，左上之雨神像已殘。

sensitivity.note: Published codex facsimile and public-domain commentary; paraphrase only.

passages.text: We come now to the sacrificial scene proper, which practically fills the upper half of the page. The victim, a woman, lies bound hand and foot on the sacrificial stone, just as in Cortesianus 41-42; the incision above the stomach is already made and the eyes are closed. Behind her rises the tree of life with a bird (vulture?) sitting in its branches, which holds in its bill one end of an object resembling a ribbon issuing from the eyes of the victim.
passages.note: Condensed from Schellhas (1904), commentary on Dresden page 3; not verbatim.

passages.text: This picture is surrounded by four gods. At the right above is K, the storm-god; the figure at the left above is almost entirely destroyed — a rain deity, so that these two gods signify the productive season. The two gods below may refer to the blessing upon the harvest and chase resulting from the season and the sacrifice: at the left below, the maize deity E holding a dish of fruit; at the right below sits the serpent deity H, and in front of him an animal with the noose still around its neck.
passages.note: Condensed from Schellhas (1904), commentary on Dresden page 3; not verbatim.

title.en: God A: The Death-God with Skeleton Face and Owl
title.zh: 神A：骷髏面與貓頭鷹的死神

region.en: Dresden Codex (Yucatec tradition), symbolic pin at Uxmal, Yucatan
region.zh: 德累斯頓抄本（猶加敦傳統），以墨西哥猶加敦烏斯馬爾為象徵定位

period: Codex drawn c. 1200-1250; Schellhas 1904

source.work: Schellhas, Representation of Deities of the Maya Manuscripts, trans. Parker & Rau, 1904

summary.en: The death-god is a figure with exposed bony spine, truncated nose, and grinning teeth — a walking skull. He wears the stiff feather collar, the globular bells on hands and feet, and carries the owl as his animal; his hieroglyph is the head of a corpse with closed eyes beside a skull, and his sign is the day Cimi, death.
summary.zh: 死神之形：裸露的骨脊椎、殘鼻與咧齒——行走的骷髏。佩硬羽領，手足綴鈴鐺，以貓頭鷹為其獸象；其神符為閉目屍首與骷髏之頭，其日名即西米（死亡）。

sensitivity.note: Published public-domain commentary; paraphrase only.

passages.text: God A is represented as a figure with an exposed bony spine, truncated nose and grinning teeth. It is plainly to be seen that the head of this god represents a skull and that the spine is that of a skeleton. The pictures of the death-god are so characteristic in the Maya manuscripts that the deity is always easily recognized.
passages.note: Condensed from Schellhas (1904), on God A; not verbatim.

passages.text: A distinguishing ornament of the death-god consists of globular bells or rattles which he wears on his hands and feet, on his collar and as a head ornament. Among the symbols of the death-god a cross of two bones should be mentioned, which is also found in the Mexican manuscripts; it occurs as a death-sign and as the sign for the day Cimi, death.
passages.note: Condensed from Schellhas (1904), on God A; not verbatim.

title.en: God B: The God with the Large Nose and Lolling Tongue
title.zh: 神B：巨鼻垂舌之神

region.en: Dresden Codex (Yucatec tradition), symbolic pin at Uxmal, Yucatan
region.zh: 德累斯頓抄本（猶加敦傳統），以墨西哥猶加敦烏斯馬爾為象徵定位

period: Codex drawn c. 1200-1250; Schellhas 1904

source.work: Schellhas, Representation of Deities of the Maya Manuscripts, trans. Parker & Rau, 1904

summary.en: The most frequently represented deity of the manuscripts has a long proboscis-like pendent nose and a tongue or fangs hanging out of the mouth, with the knotted-bow head ornament. God B is evidently one of the most important of the Maya pantheon — a universal deity to whom the most varied elements, natural phenomena and activities are subject: the rain-god Chac.
summary.zh: 抄本中最常出現的神祇：長鼻如象、舌齒垂於口外，頭飾如結環。神B顯然是馬雅萬神殿最重要者之一——無所不統的神，自然現象與諸般活動皆受其轄：即雨神查克。

sensitivity.note: Published public-domain commentary; paraphrase only.

passages.text: The deity represented most frequently in all the manuscripts is a figure with a long, proboscis-like, pendent nose and a tongue (or teeth, fangs) hanging out in front and at the sides of the mouth, also with a characteristic head ornament resembling a knotted bow and with a peculiar rim to the eye. God B is evidently one of the most important of the Maya pantheon.
passages.note: Condensed from Schellhas (1904), on God B; not verbatim.

passages.text: He must be a universal deity, to whom the most varied elements, natural phenomena and activities are subject. He is represented with different attributes and symbols of power, with torches, with the serpent, and in the year-bearer pages of the Dresden Codex as the god who opens the sky in the four directions with the lightning axe — the Chac of the colonial texts.
passages.note: Condensed from Schellhas (1904), on God B, and Thompson's identification with Chac; not verbatim.

title.en: God D: The Moon- and Night-God
title.zh: 神D：月與夜之神

region.en: Dresden Codex (Yucatec tradition), symbolic pin at Uxmal, Yucatan
region.zh: 德累斯頓抄本（猶加敦傳統），以墨西哥猶加敦烏斯馬爾為象徵定位

period: Codex drawn c. 1200-1250; Schellhas 1904

source.work: Schellhas, Representation of Deities of the Maya Manuscripts, trans. Parker & Rau, 1904

summary.en: An old man with aged face and sunken toothless mouth, distinguished by the Akbal (darkness, night) sign in his head ornament and surrounded by dots as an indication of the starry sky. His second name-sign consists of two sacrificial knives and the sign of the day Ahau — king. The moon glyph is his head in cursive form, doubled as the number 20.
summary.zh: 一位面容衰老、口無牙的老者，頭飾中含阿克巴爾（黑暗、夜）之符，四圍星點以示星空。其第二神符由兩把祭刀與阿豪（王）日符組成。月之符即其頭的簡筆，兼作數字20。

sensitivity.note: Published public-domain commentary; paraphrase only.

passages.text: This is a deity who is pictured in the form of an old man with an aged face and sunken, toothless mouth. He is frequently characterized by a long, pendent head ornament, in which is the sign Akbal, darkness, night, which also appears in his hieroglyph before the forehead of the deity, surrounded by dots as an indication of the starry sky.
passages.note: Condensed from Schellhas (1904), on God D; not verbatim.

passages.text: The second sign consists of two sacrificial knives and the sign of the day Ahau, which is equivalent to 'king'. The head of this deity appears in reduced, cursive form as the sign of the moon; this character also has the significance of 20 as a number sign in the calendar — the association of moon, night, and the completed count.
passages.note: Condensed from Schellhas (1904), on God D; not verbatim.

title.en: God E: The Maize-God
title.zh: 神E：玉米之神

region.en: Dresden Codex (Yucatec tradition), symbolic pin at Uxmal, Yucatan
region.zh: 德累斯頓抄本（猶加敦傳統），以墨西哥猶加敦烏斯馬爾為象徵定位

period: Codex drawn c. 1200-1250; Schellhas 1904

source.work: Schellhas, Representation of Deities of the Maya Manuscripts, trans. Parker & Rau, 1904

summary.en: The maize-god bears on his head the Kan-sign and above it the ear of maize with leaves. His head was evolved out of the conventional drawing of the ear of maize: what was originally a head ornament finally passed into the form of the head itself, so that the god appears now as an ear of maize surrounded by leaves — the person of the corn itself.
summary.zh: 玉米神頭戴坎符，其上為帶葉的玉米穗。其頭部由玉米穗的程式化描繪演化而來：原本的頭飾終於化為頭形本身，使神的面容即成被葉所繞的玉米穗——玉米本身即神身。

sensitivity.note: Published public-domain commentary; paraphrase only.

passages.text: This god bears on his head the Kan-sign and above it the ear of maize with leaves. The hieroglyph is definitely determined. The god is identical with the figures recurring with especial frequency in the Madrid manuscript, the heads of which are prolonged upward and curved backward in a peculiar manner.
passages.note: Condensed from Schellhas (1904), on God E; not verbatim.

passages.text: This head was evolved out of the conventional drawing of the ear of maize: what was originally a head ornament finally passed into the form of the head itself, so that the latter appears now as an ear of maize surrounded by leaves. Compare the pictures of the maize plant in the Codex Troano with the head ornament of the god — the person of the corn become the corn itself.
passages.note: Condensed from Schellhas (1904), on God E; not verbatim.

title.en: God F: The God of War and Human Sacrifice
title.zh: 神F：戰爭與人祭之神

region.en: Dresden Codex (Yucatec tradition), symbolic pin at Uxmal, Yucatan
region.zh: 德累斯頓抄本（猶加敦傳統），以墨西哥猶加敦烏斯馬爾為象徵定位

period: Codex drawn c. 1200-1250; Schellhas 1904

source.work: Schellhas, Representation of Deities of the Maya Manuscripts, trans. Parker & Rau, 1904

summary.en: A deity closely related to the death-god, resembling the Aztec Xipe, and without hesitation the god of human sacrifice — perhaps, more generally, of death by violence. His hieroglyph contains the number 11, and his distinguishing mark is a single black line running down the face near the eye.
summary.zh: 一位與死神關係密切的神祇，形似阿茲特克的希佩，無疑是人祭之神——或更廣泛地，死於暴力之神。其神符含數字11；其面部近眼處一道黑線為其標記。

sensitivity.note: Published public-domain commentary; paraphrase only.

passages.text: This is a deity closely related to the death-god A, resembling the Aztec Xipe, and may, I think, without hesitation be regarded simply as the god of human sacrifice, perhaps even more generally as the god of death by violence. His hieroglyph contains the number 11.
passages.note: Condensed from Schellhas (1904), on God F; not verbatim.

passages.text: The characteristic mark of god F is a single black line usually running perpendicularly down the face in the vicinity of the eye. These pictures of the maize-god E can always be unfailingly recognized by the peculiar shape of the head and should be distinguished from those representing F.
passages.note: Condensed from Schellhas (1904), on God F; not verbatim.

title.en: God G: The Sun-God
title.zh: 神G：太陽之神

region.en: Dresden Codex (Yucatec tradition), symbolic pin at Uxmal, Yucatan
region.zh: 德累斯頓抄本（猶加敦傳統），以墨西哥猶加敦烏斯馬爾為象徵定位

period: Codex drawn c. 1200-1250; Schellhas 1904

source.work: Schellhas, Representation of Deities of the Maya Manuscripts, trans. Parker & Rau, 1904

summary.en: God G's hieroglyph contains as its chief factor the sun-sign Kin, one of the signs with the Ben-ik prefix, doubtless denoting a month dedicated to the sun. It is surprising that a deity who from his nature must be considered very important is represented with such comparative infrequency.
summary.zh: 神G的神符以太陽符「金」為主，屬帶貝-伊克前綴的符號之一，無疑表示獻給太陽的月份。令人訝異的是：這樣一位本性上必極重要的神，在抄本中出現得如此稀少。

sensitivity.note: Published public-domain commentary; paraphrase only.

passages.text: God G's hieroglyph contains as its chief factor the sun-sign Kin. It is one of the signs which has the Ben-ik prefix and doubtless denotes a month dedicated to the sun. There is no difference of opinion regarding the significance of this deity.
passages.note: Condensed from Schellhas (1904), on God G; not verbatim.

passages.text: It is surprising that a deity who from his nature must be considered as very important is represented with such comparative infrequency. He occurs only a few times in the Dresden manuscript, and in the Codex Tro-Cortesianus — the sun in the codices is more often present as the day Kin than as a personal god.
passages.note: Condensed from Schellhas (1904), on God G; not verbatim.

title.en: God H: The Chicchan-God with the Serpent's Scale
title.zh: 神H：帶蛇鱗的奇坎神

region.en: Dresden Codex (Yucatec tradition), symbolic pin at Uxmal, Yucatan
region.zh: 德累斯頓抄本（猶加敦傳統），以墨西哥猶加敦烏斯馬爾為象徵定位

period: Codex drawn c. 1200-1250; Schellhas 1904

source.work: Schellhas, Representation of Deities of the Maya Manuscripts, trans. Parker & Rau, 1904

summary.en: A god of frequent occurrence characterized by a skin-spot or a scale of a serpent on his temple, of the same shape as the hieroglyph of the day Chicchan (serpent). His representations differ so much that there are almost no other positive, unvarying characteristic marks to be specified.
summary.zh: 一位常見的神，其太陽穴有蛇之鱗或皮斑，形如奇坎（蛇）日的神符。其形貌變化極大，幾乎無其他恆定的特徵可指認。

sensitivity.note: Published public-domain commentary; paraphrase only.

passages.text: The figure of a deity of frequent occurrence in the Dresden manuscript is a god who is characterized by a skin-spot or a scale of a serpent on his temple of the same shape as the hieroglyph of the day Chicchan (serpent). The representations of the god himself differ very much, so that there are almost no other positive, unvarying characteristic marks to be specified.
passages.note: Condensed from Schellhas (1904), on God H; not verbatim.

passages.text: The hieroglyph belonging to this deity likewise displays the Chicchan-sign as its distinguishing mark; several variants occur. The serpent of his temple-mark connects him with the great serpent of the sky band and the serpent deity who receives the catch in the sacrificial scenes.
passages.note: Condensed from Schellhas (1904), on God H; not verbatim.

title.en: Goddess I: The Water-Goddess with the Knotted Serpent
title.zh: 女神I：戴蛇結的水神

region.en: Dresden Codex (Yucatec tradition), symbolic pin at Uxmal, Yucatan
region.zh: 德累斯頓抄本（猶加敦傳統），以墨西哥猶加敦烏斯馬爾為象徵定位

period: Codex drawn c. 1200-1250; Schellhas 1904

source.work: Schellhas, Representation of Deities of the Maya Manuscripts, trans. Parker & Rau, 1904

summary.en: The water-goddess is distinguished by tiger claws on her feet and by the knotted serpent on her head, the symbol of the water flowing along and forming waves. With her appear the oblong signs which Forstemann interprets as the sign of evil days — she is both the giver of the rain and the goddess of floods and cloud-bursts.
summary.zh: 水神女神：足有虎爪，頭戴蛇結——即流淌成波之水的符號。與其相伴者有弗斯特曼讀為「凶日」符的長形符號——她既是賜雨者，亦是洪水與雲爆之神。

sensitivity.note: Published public-domain commentary; paraphrase only.

passages.text: The goddess distinguished in the Madrid manuscript by symbols of flood and water is doubtless the same as goddess I of the Dresden manuscript; her unmistakable character of water-goddess in both manuscripts is in favor of this. In both manuscripts she is invariably distinguished by the serpent on her head, which, as we know, is a symbol of the water flowing along and forming waves.
passages.note: Condensed from Schellhas (1904), on Goddess I; not verbatim.

passages.text: The well-known oblong signs, which Forstemann interprets as the sign for evil days, frequently occur with her. This would be appropriate for the goddess of floods — in the Dresden manuscript a few similar figures of women are found who, like goddess I, wear a knotted serpent on the head.
passages.note: Condensed from Schellhas (1904), on Goddess I; not verbatim.

title.en: Gods L and M: The Old Black God and the Black God with Red Lips
title.zh: 神L與神M：老黑神與紅唇黑神

region.en: Dresden and Madrid Codices, symbolic pin at Uxmal, Yucatan
region.zh: 德累斯頓與馬德里抄本，以墨西哥猶加敦烏斯馬爾為象徵定位

period: Codices drawn c. 1200-1250; Schellhas 1904

source.work: Schellhas, Representation of Deities of the Maya Manuscripts, trans. Parker & Rau, 1904

summary.en: God L is the old black god with the sunken toothless mouth and the black face, appearing entirely black in Dresden 7a; he does not occur in the Madrid or Paris manuscripts. God M, the black god with the red lips, is represented with special frequency in the Madrid manuscript, which treats of this deity with great fullness of detail — the merchant's god, Ek Chuah.
summary.zh: 神L為老黑神，口無牙、面黑，在德累斯頓7a全黑示人；不見於馬德里與巴黎抄本。神M為紅唇黑神，在馬德里抄本中出現尤多、描繪極詳——即商人之神埃克·丘瓦。

sensitivity.note: Published public-domain commentary; paraphrase only.

passages.text: God L's features are those of an old man with sunken, toothless mouth. His hieroglyph is characterized by the black face. God L, who is also black, must not be confounded with M whose description follows. He is represented in Dresden 14b and 14c and 46b; he appears entirely black in Dr. 7a. This deity does not occur in the Madrid and Paris manuscripts.
passages.note: Condensed from Schellhas (1904), on Gods L and M; not verbatim.

passages.text: God M is found in the Dresden manuscript only three times; on the other hand, god M appears with special frequency in the Madrid manuscript, which treats of this deity with great fullness of detail. While he is represented in the Dresden manuscript with his body striped, in the Madrid he is the black god with the red lips — the god of cacao traders and merchants, Ek Chuah of the later tradition.
passages.note: Condensed from Schellhas (1904), on Gods L and M; not verbatim.

title.en: God N: The God of the End of the Year
title.zh: 神N：歲末之神

region.en: Dresden Codex (Yucatec tradition), symbolic pin at Uxmal, Yucatan
region.zh: 德累斯頓抄本（猶加敦傳統），以墨西哥猶加敦烏斯馬爾為象徵定位

period: Codex drawn c. 1200-1250; Schellhas 1904

source.work: Schellhas, Representation of Deities of the Maya Manuscripts, trans. Parker & Rau, 1904

summary.en: A deity with the features of an old man wearing a head ornament which contains the sign for the year of 360 days. His hieroglyph consists of the numeral 5 with the sign of the month Zac. Forstemann has recognized in god N the god of the five Uayeyab days, the unlucky intercalary days added at the end of the year — the god of the end of the year.
summary.zh: 一位老者相貌的神，頭飾中含360日之年的符號。其神符由數字5與月份扎克之符組成。弗斯特曼認出神N即五個瓦耶亞布日——歲末所加的凶日——之神，即歲末之神。

sensitivity.note: Published public-domain commentary; paraphrase only.

passages.text: We have here a deity with the features of an old man and wearing a peculiar head ornament, which contains the sign for the year of 360 days. The god's hieroglyph consists of the numeral 5 with the sign of the month Zac. Forstemann has recognized in god N the god of the five Uayeyab days, which were added as intercalary days at the end of the original year of 360 days, and were considered unlucky days.
passages.note: Condensed from Schellhas (1904), on God N; not verbatim.

passages.text: N is, therefore, the god of the end of the year. He can be recognized in the Dresden manuscript in the passages of the year-bearer pages, where the old god presides over the five dangerous days before the new year is counted — the counterpart in picture of the rites that Landa records.
passages.note: Condensed from Schellhas (1904), on God N; not verbatim.

title.en: God P: The Frog-God Who Sows
title.zh: 神P：播種的蛙神

region.en: Madrid Codex, symbolic pin at Uxmal, Yucatan
region.zh: 馬德里抄本，以墨西哥猶加敦烏斯馬爾為象徵定位

period: Codex drawn c. 1200-1250; Schellhas 1904

source.work: Schellhas, Representation of Deities of the Maya Manuscripts, trans. Parker & Rau, 1904

summary.en: We call him the frog-god because in Codex Troano 31 he is pictured with the club-shaped fingers of a frog. The blue background, his attribute twice in the same passage, points to a connection with water; and that the god has to do with agriculture may be deduced from the fact that he is pictured sowing seed and making furrows with the planting-stick.
summary.zh: 所以稱蛙神，因在《特羅阿諾抄本》31頁，其手指呈蛙的棒狀。同頁兩次出現的藍色背景指向其與水的關係；而其播種、以播杖開溝的圖像，則表明此神與農耕有關。

sensitivity.note: Published public-domain commentary; paraphrase only.

passages.text: We call him the frog-god because in the Codex Troano 31, he is pictured in the first and second lines with the club-shaped fingers of a frog, which occur only on this figure. The blue background, which is his attribute twice in the same passage, likewise points to a connection with water.
passages.note: Condensed from Schellhas (1904), on God P; not verbatim.

passages.text: That the god also has something to do with agriculture may be deduced from the fact that he is pictured sowing seed and making furrows with the planting-stick. His head ornament is very characteristic and contains the sign for the year of 360 days; he therefore bears some unknown relation also to the end of the year.
passages.note: Condensed from Schellhas (1904), on God P; not verbatim.

title.en: The Moan Bird, the Dog, and the Vulture: Mythological Animals
title.zh: 莫安鳥、犬與兀鷲：神話之獸

region.en: Dresden and Madrid Codices, symbolic pin at Uxmal, Yucatan
region.zh: 德累斯頓與馬德里抄本，以墨西哥猶加敦烏斯馬爾為象徵定位

period: Codices drawn c. 1200-1250; Schellhas 1904

source.work: Schellhas, Representation of Deities of the Maya Manuscripts, trans. Parker & Rau, 1904

summary.en: Besides the gods, the codices keep a bestiary of mythic animals: the Moan bird that rests on a hand held beneath it in the sacrifice scenes; the serpent as the usual symbol of time accompanying the planets; the dog that carried the dead across the water; the vulture in the tree of life; the jaguar as devourer; the tortoise that carried the reassembled head.
summary.zh: 除諸神外，抄本中還有一部神話獸譜：獻祭圖中歇於手持之上的莫安鳥；作為時間符號伴隨行星的蛇；載亡者渡水的犬；生命之樹上的兀鷲；吞噬者的美洲豹；以及承載復合之首的龜。

sensitivity.note: Published public-domain commentary; paraphrase only.

passages.text: In addition to those discussed in this paper, there are a few animals in the manuscripts which probably also have a partial mythologic significance: the deer, while idealization with human bodies, with torches, hieroglyphic character on the head should be considered as an unmistakable sign of mythologic meaning. A mythologic significance also seems to belong to the bee which plays so prominent a part in the Madrid manuscript.
passages.note: Condensed from Schellhas (1904), on mythological animals; not verbatim.

passages.text: The serpent appears in the manuscripts in connection with figures of gods as the usual symbol of time, accompanying the planets; the scorpion seems also to have an important mythologic significance, appearing with figures of gods. The Moan bird rests on a hand held beneath it in the sacrifice scenes; the vulture sits in the tree of life; the dog carries the dead across the water of the underworld; the tortoise carries the reassembled head of the ballplayer.
passages.note: Condensed from Schellhas (1904), on mythological animals; not verbatim.

title.en: The Ceremonies for Kukulcan in Dresden 65-69
title.zh: 德累斯頓65-69頁：庫庫爾坎之祭

region.en: Dresden Codex (Yucatec tradition), symbolic pin at Uxmal, Yucatan
region.zh: 德累斯頓抄本（猶加敦傳統），以墨西哥猶加敦烏斯馬爾為象徵定位

period: Codex drawn c. 1200-1250; Brinton 1882

source.work: Brinton, Aids to the Study of the Maya Codices (1882), on Dresden pp. 65-69; Forstemann facsimile 1880

summary.en: Through the lower division of pages 65 to 69 of the Dresden Codex runs a remarkably regular series of figures and written characters apparently devoted entirely to representations of incidents in the life of the culture-hero Kukulcan — the god with the snake-like tongue — or to the ceremonies to be performed in his honor.
summary.zh: 德累斯頓抄本65至69頁下半部貫穿著一組異常規整的人物與文字系列，顯然專為描繪文化英雄庫庫爾坎——蛇舌之神——生平中的事蹟，或為在其名下舉行的祭典而設。

sensitivity.note: Published public-domain commentary; paraphrase only.

passages.text: A remarkably regular series of figures and written characters runs through the lower division of pages 65 to 69 of the Dresden Codex, apparently devoted entirely to representations of incidents in the life of the culture-hero Kukulcan, the deity mentioned on a subsequent page as the 'unknown god with the snake-like tongue', or to ceremonies to be performed in honor of this deity.
passages.note: Condensed from Brinton, Aids to the Study of the Maya Codices (1882); not verbatim.

passages.text: Over each figure are three lines of written characters, in groups — one group of six compound characters over each figure of the series; there are thirteen glyphs of the left and thirteen of these groups of characters in the series. The third character of each group is the symbol of the deity and corresponds in the text with the figure of the god in the pictures.
passages.note: Condensed from Brinton (1882), on Dresden 65-69; not verbatim.

title.en: The Beekeeping Pages of the Madrid Codex
title.zh: 馬德里抄本的養蜂頁

region.en: Madrid Codex (Maya east coast tradition), symbolic pin at Cozumel
region.zh: 馬德里抄本（馬雅東岸傳統），以科蘇梅爾為象徵定位

period: Codex drawn c. 1300-1500; Schellhas 1904

source.work: Madrid (Tro-Cortesianus) Codex, pp. 103-112, in Schellhas (1904) and Villacorta & Villacorta, Codices Mayas (1933)

summary.en: Ten pages of the Madrid Codex are given to the bees: the bee-god appears among hives, honey is offered, gods tend the stingless hives of Yucatan, and rites for the swarms are prescribed — the codex keeps a liturgy of beekeeping, the one surviving Maya book of agricultural ceremony.
summary.zh: 馬德里抄本十頁皆記蜂事：蜂神現於蜂巢之間，蜂蜜獻祭，諸神照管猶加敦的無刺蜂群，並為蜂群規定祭儀——抄本中竟存有一部養蜂禮書，即碩果僅存的馬雅農事經典。

sensitivity.note: Published public-domain commentary; paraphrase only.

passages.text: In Codex Tro-Cortesianus, pp. 103-112, there is a long portion which has to do with the bees. The god of the bees is pictured among the hives; there is a rite, probably an offering of corn in some form in honor of the bee god, and the figures handle the stingless hives of Yucatan as objects of ceremony.
passages.note: Condensed from Schellhas (1904) and Tozzer (1907), on the beekeeping pages; not verbatim.

passages.text: A mythologic significance also seems to belong to the bee which plays so prominent a part in the Madrid manuscript; the gods of the wild bees of the four quarters appear in the Dresden Codex with their flowers for cups — the red bees of the east, the white of the north, the black of the west, the yellow of the south.
passages.note: Condensed from Schellhas (1904) and the Chumayel ritual of the four world-quarters; not verbatim.

title.en: The Flood over Madrid 35
title.zh: 馬德里第35頁的洪水

region.en: Madrid Codex, symbolic pin at Cozumel
region.zh: 馬德里抄本，以科蘇梅爾為象徵定位

period: Codex drawn c. 1300-1500; Schellhas 1904

source.work: Madrid (Tro-Cortesianus) Codex, p. 35, in Schellhas (1904)

summary.en: In the Madrid manuscript the goddess distinguished by symbols of flood and water appears; she is doubtless the same as goddess I of the Dresden Codex — the water-goddess invariably marked by the serpent on her head, the symbol of the water flowing along and forming waves, bringing the evil days with her.
summary.zh: 馬德里抄本中以洪水與水之符號為標記的女神出現；她無疑即德累斯頓抄本的女神I——頭戴蛇結的水神，蛇即流淌成波之水的符號，伴隨凶日而來。

sensitivity.note: Published public-domain commentary; paraphrase only.

passages.text: The goddess distinguished in the Madrid manuscript by symbols of flood and water is doubtless the same as goddess I of the Dresden manuscript described above; her unmistakable character of water-goddess in both manuscripts is in favor of this. In both manuscripts she is invariably distinguished by the serpent on her head, which is a symbol of the water flowing along and forming waves.
passages.note: Condensed from Schellhas (1904), on Goddess I in the Madrid Codex; not verbatim.

passages.text: The figure corresponding to her in the Madrid manuscript, in Troano 27 and 34c, displays some variations, in particular the tiger claws on the feet and the red-brown color of the body are lacking; but the agreement cannot be questioned when we recall that the Maya manuscripts doubtless originated in different ages and different areas of civilization.
passages.note: Condensed from Schellhas (1904); not verbatim.

title.en: The Paris Codex: The Cycle of the Thirteen Katuns
title.zh: 巴黎抄本：十三卡特倫之週期

region.en: Paris Codex (Yucatec), symbolic pin at Chichen Itza
region.zh: 巴黎抄本（猶加敦），以奇琴伊察為象徵定位

period: Codex drawn c. 1250-1400; Schellhas 1904

source.work: Paris Codex (Perez Codex), katun cycle, in Schellhas (1904) and Villacorta & Villacorta, Codices Mayas (1933)

summary.en: The Paris Codex preserves the cycle of the thirteen katuns — the prophetic wheel by which each twenty-year period has its lord, its omen, and its end: the Maya zodiac and the katun prophecies that would later be written out in the Books of Chilam Balam.
summary.zh: 巴黎抄本保存了十三卡特倫之週期——預言的輪盤，每個二十年各有其主、其兆與其終：即馬雅黃道帶，也就是後來寫入《奇拉姆·巴拉姆之書》的卡特倫預言。

sensitivity.note: Published public-domain commentary; paraphrase only.

passages.text: The Paris manuscript preserves the cycle of the thirteen katuns, the count in which each katun of twenty years is ruled by its own lord and carries its own prophecy. The wheel of the katuns is the Maya zodiac: figures of the katun lords with their dates and their omens, the frame into which the Books of Chilam Balam pour their histories.
passages.note: Condensed from Schellhas (1904) and standard descriptions of the Paris Codex katun cycle; not verbatim.

passages.text: With the katun cycle the Paris Codex gives the divisions of the sky and the creatures set in them; Spinden suggested that the Maya zodiac is shown in its pages — the serpent, the birds, and the monsters that carry the years.
passages.note: Condensed from Schellhas (1904) and Spinden's suggestion on the Maya zodiac; not verbatim.

title.en: Braima Hew the Idols in Pieces
title.zh: 布萊瑪碎神像記

region.en: The East ('Mecca' of Yoruba tradition; symbolic pin: the road of the 90 days' flight westward)
region.zh: 傳說中的東方（約魯巴傳統的「麥加」；象徵定位：九十日西行的流亡之路）

period: Yoruba tradition recorded 1921 (Johnson); the migration legend itself older

source.work: Rev. Samuel Johnson, The History of the Yorubas (London, 1921), Part I ch. I

summary.en: Asara, priest and image-maker of the idolatrous Crown Prince Oduduwa, had a son Braima, brought up a Mohammedan, who hated his father's trade and cried "Who would purchase falsehood?" When the men were away hunting for three days, Braima hewed the idols in pieces and left the axe hanging on the neck of the chief idol. "Ask that huge idol who did it," he said; "Can he speak?" "Then why do you worship things which cannot speak?" He was condemned to be burnt alive — a thousand loads of wood were heaped for the stake — and the signal for civil war was given: Lamurudu the king was slain, and Oduduwa's party driven from the town.
summary.zh: 奉偶像教之王儲奧杜杜瓦的祭司兼造像師阿薩拉，有一子名布萊瑪，自幼信奉回教，憎惡父業，賣像時高呼「誰要買謊言？」趁獵人出城三日，他將眾神像剁碎，斧頭掛在大神像頸上。「問那尊大神像是誰幹的！」「牠會說話嗎？」「既然不能說話，你們為何拜牠？」他被判活焚——千擔柴堆於刑柱之下——內戰自此爆發：國王拉穆魯杜被殺，奧杜杜瓦一黨被逐出城。

sensitivity.note: Recorded 1921 by the Yoruba pastor-historian Samuel Johnson. Johnson himself notes the tale is a garbled scriptural story (Gideon, Judges 6:28-33) — the Yoruba migration legend braided with Biblical memory. Religious-conflict content reported as the recorded tradition states it.

passages.text: The Crown Prince Oduduwa relapsed into idolatry during his father's reign, and as he was possessed of great influence, he drew many after him. His purpose was to transform the state religion into paganism, and hence he converted the great mosque of the city into an idol temple, and this Asara, his priest, who was himself an image maker, studded with idols. Asara had a son called Braima, who was brought up a Mohammedan. During his minority he was a seller of his father's idols, an occupation which he thoroughly abhorred, but which he was obliged to engage in; but in offering for sale his father's handiwork he usually invited buyers by calling out: "Who would purchase falsehood?"
passages.note: Paraphrase of Johnson, The History of the Yorubas, Part I ch. I (1921); not verbatim.

passages.text: When Braima was old enough he seized the opportunity of one of the king's hunting absences to destroy the gods whose presence had caused the sacred mosque to become desecrated. The axe with which the idols were hewed in pieces was left hanging on the neck of the chief idol, a huge thing in human shape. Enquiry being made, it was soon discovered who the iconoclast was, and when accosted, he gave replies not unlike those which Joash gave to the Abiezrites who accused his son Gideon of a similar act. Said Braima, "Ask that huge idol who did it." The men replied, "Can he speak?" "Then," said Braima, "Why do you worship things which cannot speak?" He was immediately ordered to be burnt alive for this act of gross impiety. A thousand loads of wood were collected for a stake, and several pots of oil were brought for the purpose of firing the pile. This was signal for a civil war: Lamurudu the King was slain, and all his children, with those who sympathized with them, were expelled from the town.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Johnson, The History of the Yorubas, Part I ch. I (1921); not verbatim.

title.en: The Ninety Days' Flight: Oduduwa Comes to Ile-Ife
title.zh: 九十日流亡——奧杜杜瓦抵達伊費

region.en: Ile-Ife, Nigeria (end of the eastward flight)
region.zh: 奈及利亞伊費城（東來流亡的終點）

period: Yoruba tradition recorded 1921 (Johnson)

source.work: Rev. Samuel Johnson, The History of the Yorubas (London, 1921), Part I ch. I

summary.en: The Yorubas say they sprang from Lamurudu, one of the kings of "Mecca"; driven out after the civil war, the princes went their ways — westward to Gogobiri and Kukawa, eastward Oduduwa, who travelled ninety days and finally settled at Ile-Ife, where he met Agbonniregun (Setilu), the founder of the Ifa worship. Oduduwa's party escaped with two idols; Sahibu's army sent against them was defeated, and among the booty was a copy of the Koran, preserved in a temple and worshipped to this day as Idi, Something Tied Up. Johnson notes that "Mecca" is really the East — the Yoruba came from the East, and their "Mecca" is their word for it.
summary.zh: 約魯巴人自述乃「麥加」王拉穆魯杜之裔；內戰之後諸王子四散——西往戈戈比里與庫卡瓦，東行者奧杜杜瓦則走了九十日，終於定居伊萊-伊費，並在此遇見伊法崇拜的創始者阿貢尼雷貢（塞蒂盧）。奧杜杜瓦一行攜兩尊神像逃出；前來征討的薩希布大軍戰敗，戰利品中有一部《可蘭經》，供奉於廟中，至今以「伊迪」（綁起之物）之名受拜。約翰遜指出：此「麥加」實指東方——約魯巴人自東而來，「麥加」即他們口中的東方。

sensitivity.note: Recorded 1921; the migration charter of the Yoruba royal tradition. Johnson's critical argument (Mecca = the East; Ife marbles Egyptian in form) is reported alongside the tradition. Cross-refs: yoruba-ife-navel-world, yoruba-oduduwa-sand-hen.

passages.text: The Yorubas are said to have sprung from Lamurudu one of the kings of Mecca, whose offspring were: Oduduwa, the ancestor of the Yorubas, and the Kings of Gogobiri and of the Kukawa, two tribes in the Hausa country. The Crown Prince Oduduwa's party, expelled after the civil war, went their ways: the Princes who became Kings of Gogobiri and of the Kukawa went westwards, and Oduduwa eastwards. He travelled 90 days from Mecca, and after wandering about finally settled down at Ile Ife, where he met with Agbonniregun (or Setilu) the founder of the Ifa worship.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Johnson, The History of the Yorubas, Part I ch. I (1921); not verbatim.

passages.text: Oduduwa and his children had escaped with two idols to Ile Ife. Sahibu, being sent with an army to destroy or reduce them to submission, was defeated, and amongst the booty secured by the victors was a copy of the Koran. This was afterwards preserved in a temple and was not only venerated by succeeding generations as a sacred relic, but is even worshipped to this day under the name of Idi, signifying Something Tied Up. That the Yorubas came originally from the East there cannot be the slightest doubt, as their habits, manners and customs all go to prove: with them the East is Mecca and Mecca is the East.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Johnson, The History of the Yorubas, Part I ch. I (1921); not verbatim.

title.en: The Child Who Kept the Crown
title.zh: 抱走王冠的孩子

region.en: Ile-Ife, Nigeria (the king's knees where the crown was claimed)
region.zh: 奈及利亞伊費城（王膝上得冠之地）

period: Yoruba tradition recorded 1921 (Johnson)

source.work: Rev. Samuel Johnson, The History of the Yorubas (London, 1921), Part I ch. I

summary.en: Oduduwa's eldest daughter chose to marry her father's priest, and from them came Olowu, ancestor of the Owus.
