Playing on his grandfather's knees, the child pulled at the crown on the old king's head; the indulgent parent set it on the child's head, and like some spoiled children he refused to give it up — so it was left with him. When he fell asleep in his mother's arms she returned it, but the king told her to keep it for her son, he seemed so anxious to have it. Hence the right of the Olowu to wear a crown like his uncles — and the same right was afterwards accorded to the Alaketu, progenitor of the Ketu people.
summary.zh: 奧杜杜瓦的長女下嫁其父的祭司，所生之子即奧武人之祖「奧洛烏」。此兒在祖父膝上玩耍，伸手去抓老人頭上的王冠；溺愛的祖父便把王冠扣在孩子頭上——這孩子嬌縱不還，祖父只得另戴一頂。孩子戴著王冠在母親懷中睡去；母親欲奉還，國王卻道：既如此珍愛，便留給你的兒子吧。奧洛烏遂得與諸叔王同等戴冠之權——其後阿凱圖（凱圖人之祖）亦援此例。

sensitivity.note: Recorded 1921; crown-right etiology of the Owu royal line, told of a princess who married a commoner priest.

passages.text: The Yoruba princesses had (and still have) the liberty of choosing husbands according to their fancy from any rank in life; the King's eldest daughter chose to marry her father's priest, for whom she had the Olowu. This young prince was one day playing on his grandfather's knees, and he pulled at the crown on his head; the indulgent parent thereupon placed it on the child's head, but like some spoiled children, he refused to give it up when required, and so it was left with him, the grandfather putting on another.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Johnson, The History of the Yorubas, Part I ch. I (1921); not verbatim.

passages.text: The child had the crown on his head until he fell asleep in his mother's arms, when she took it off and returned it to her father; but the latter told her to keep it for her son, as he seemed so anxious to have it. Hence the right of the Olowu to wear the crown like his uncles. The same right was subsequently accorded to the Alaketu, i.e., the progenitor of the Ketu people.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Johnson, The History of the Yorubas, Part I ch. I (1921); not verbatim.

title.en: Oranyan Inherits the Land
title.zh: 奧蘭揚承地為業

region.en: Ile-Ife, Nigeria (the partition of Oduduwa's estate)
region.zh: 奈及利亞伊費城（家產分封之地）

period: Yoruba tradition recorded 1921 (Johnson)

source.work: Rev. Samuel Johnson, The History of the Yorubas (London, 1921), Part I ch. I

summary.en: On Oduduwa's death the inheritance was divided: the King of Benin got the money, the Orangun of Ila the wives, the King of Sabe the cattle, the Olupopo the beads, the Olowu the garments, the Alaketu the crowns — and nothing was left Oranyan but the land. Some say he was away on a warlike expedition when the partition was made. But Oranyan turned his portion to good account: he held his brothers as tenants on the land which was his, and for rents received money, women, cattle, beads, garments and crowns — hence the common saying "Alafin l'oni ile," the Alafin is the lord of the land. Another account gives him only a rag of earth, twenty-one pieces of iron and a cock on a world covered with water, the cock scattering the earth until dry land appeared, his brothers paying annual tribute to live on it.
summary.zh: 奧杜杜瓦身後分產：貝寧王得錢財，伊拉之奧蘭貢得妻妾，薩貝王得牛群，奧盧波波得珠子，奧洛烏得衣裳，阿凱圖得王冠——留給奧蘭揚的唯有土地。或謂分產時他正領兵在外。但他把家業經營得蒸蒸日上：諸兄皆為他土地上的佃戶，歲納金錢、婦女、牛群、珠貝、衣冠為租——故有諺語「阿勞芬乃土地之主」。另一說：他只得一方裹於布中的泥土、二十一塊鐵器與一隻雄雞，當時大地盡為洪水所覆；雞爪撒土，乾地處處浮現，諸兄欲居陸上者歲納貢賦。

sensitivity.note: Recorded 1921; the dynastic inheritance charter (Johnson's version of the Oranyan tale, complementing Ogumefu's folk version yoruba-oranyan-iron-cock-soil). Johnson calls the flood version a travesty of creation or flood stories.

passages.text: On the death of the King, their grandfather, his property was unequally divided among his children as follows: the King of Benin inherited his money (consisting of cowry shells), the Orangun of Ila his wives, the King of Sabe his cattle, the Olupopo the beads, the Olowu the garments, and the Alaketu the crowns, and nothing was left for Oranyan but the land. Some assert that he was absent on a warlike expedition when the partition was made, and so he was shut out of all movable properties. Oranyan was, however, satisfied with his portion, which he proceeded forthwith to turn to good account with the utmost skill: he held his brothers as tenants living on the land which was his; for rents he received money, women, cattle, beads, garments, and crowns, which were his brothers' portions, as all these were more or less dependent on the soil.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Johnson, The History of the Yorubas, Part I ch. I (1921); not verbatim.

passages.text: According to another account, Oranyan had only a bit of rag left him, containing earth, 21 pieces of iron, and a cock. The whole surface of the earth was then covered with water. Oranyan laid his portion on the surface of the water, and placed on it the cock, which scattered the earth with his feet; the wide expanse of water became filled up, and the dry land appeared everywhere. His brothers, preferring to live on dry land rather than on the surface of the water, were permitted to do so on their paying an annual tribute for sharing with their younger brother his own portion. It will be noticed that both traditions attribute the land to Oranyan; hence the common saying "Alafin l'oni ile" (the Alafin is the lord of the land): the pieces of iron representing underground treasures, and the cock such as subsist on the land.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Johnson, The History of the Yorubas, Part I ch. I (1921); not verbatim.

title.en: Follow the Boa: How Oyo Was Founded
title.zh: 跟著巨蟒走——奧約建城記

region.en: Oyo-Ile (Katunga), Nigeria (the hill Ajaka where the boa vanished)
region.zh: 奈及利亞舊奧約城（卡通加；巨蟒消失的阿賈卡山下）

period: Yoruba tradition recorded 1921 (Johnson)

source.work: Rev. Samuel Johnson, The History of the Yorubas (London, 1921), Part I ch. I

summary.en: Marching to avenge his great-grandfather against "Mecca," Oranyan found the old route impassable — an army of black ants had blocked the path — and took the Tapa road instead. At Igangan his brothers quarrelled over a pot of beer and dispersed. Reaching the Niger he could not force a crossing, and to return to Ife was too humiliating; so he consulted the King of Ibariba, who made a charm, fixed it on a boa constrictor, and advised him to follow the track of the boa and build his town wherever it remained seven days and then disappeared. At the foot of a hill called Ajaka the reptile did so, and there Oranyan built Oyo Ajaka — the ancient city of Oyo, Katunga.
summary.zh: 奧蘭揚率師東征「麥加」以報曾祖之仇，舊路卻被成群的螞蟻堵死，只好改走塔帕（努佩）之路。行至伊甘貢，諸弟為一壺啤酒爭吵四散。他兵抵尼日河，無法強渡，返回伊費又覺羞辱；遂問計於伊巴里巴王。王製符咒繫於巨蟒之身，教他跟隨蟒蹤——蟒若在一處停留七日而後消失，便在彼建城。蟒行至阿賈卡山下果然如此；奧蘭揚遂建「奧約阿賈卡」城——即古奧約，卡通加。

sensitivity.note: Recorded 1921; founding legend of the Oyo capital by oracle-guided serpent. Cross-ref: yoruba-staff-of-oranyan (Ogumefu's version of his return).

passages.text: It is said that the route by which they came from "Mecca" and which occupied 90 days was by this time rendered impassable owing to an army of black ants blocking up the path, and hence Oranyan was obliged to take another route which led through the Nupe or Tapa country. All his brothers but the eldest joined him, but at Igangan they quarrelled over a pot of beer and dispersed, refusing to follow his lead. The eldest brother, calculating the distance through the Tapa country, lost courage and went eastward. Oranyan pushed on until he found himself on the banks of the River Niger.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Johnson, The History of the Yorubas, Part I ch. I (1921); not verbatim.

passages.text: The Tapas are said to have opposed his crossing the river, and as he could not force his way through, he was obliged to remain for a while near the banks, and afterwards resolved to retrace his steps. To return, however, to Ile Ife was too humiliating to be thought of, and hence he consulted the King of Ibariba near whose territory he was then encamping as to where he should make his residence. Tradition has it that the King of Ibariba made a charm and fixed it on a boa constrictor and advised Oranyan to follow the track of the boa, and wherever it remained for 7 days and then disappeared, there he was to build a town. Oranyan and his army followed his directions and went after the boa up to the foot of a hill called Ajaka, where the reptile remained 7 days and then disappeared. According to instructions Oranyan halted there, and built a town called Oyo Ajaka — the ancient city of Oyo, marked in ancient maps as Eyeo or Katunga.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Johnson, The History of the Yorubas, Part I ch. I (1921); not verbatim.

title.en: The Son of the Sacrificial Victim: How the Oni Got His Name
title.zh: 祭品之子——奧尼之名的由來

region.en: Ile-Ife, Nigeria (the custodianship of the national treasures)
region.zh: 奈及利亞伊費城（王室珍寶守護之地）

period: Yoruba tradition recorded 1921 (Johnson)

source.work: Rev. Samuel Johnson, The History of the Yorubas (London, 1921), Part I ch. I

summary.en: Oranyan left Adimu, one of his father's trusty servants, in charge of the royal treasures and the charms, with strict injunction to observe the customary worship of the national gods Idi and Orisa Osi during his absence. Adimu was originally the son of a woman condemned to death who, being found at execution to be in the way of becoming a mother, was temporarily reprieved; the child was dedicated to the perpetual service of the gods, especially Obatala, to whom his mother was to have been sacrificed. When the kings and princes around were told of the appointment, all asked "And who is this Adimu?" The answer: "Omo Oluwo ni" — the son of a sacrificial victim — contracted to Ooni. When the seat of government moved permanently to Oyo, Adimu became supreme at Ile-Ife, and his successors to this day are the Ooni, high priests of the whole Yoruba nation.
summary.zh: 奧蘭揚東征之前，將王室珍寶與符咒託付乃父的忠僕阿迪穆，囑其謹守國神「伊迪」與「奧里莎奧西」的常祭。阿迪穆本是死囚之子：其母臨刑時已懷身孕，獲暫緩死刑，嬰孩生下便被永獻神前——尤其獻給其母本應祭予的奧巴塔拉。當諸王聞知此任命，皆問「阿迪穆是何人？」答曰：「奧莫奧盧沃尼」——祭品之子。此語縮為「奧尼」。王都既永久遷奧約，阿迪穆便為伊費之主，其後裔至今即全約魯巴的大祭司——奧尼。

sensitivity.note: Recorded 1921; the Ooni title etymology, anchored in a reprieve-from-sacrifice birth. Historical human-sacrifice context reported as the recorded tradition states it.

passages.text: He left Adimu one of his father's trusty servants in charge of the royal treasures and the charms, with a strict injunction to observe the customary worship of the national gods Idi and Orisa Osi. But this Adimu, who became of so much consequence from his performing royal functions, was originally the son of a woman condemned to death, but being found at the time of execution to be in the way of becoming a mother she was temporarily reprieved, until the child was born. This child at its birth was dedicated to the perpetual service of the gods, especially the god Obatala, to which his mother was to have been sacrificed. He was said to be honest, faithful and devoted to the King as to his own father, and therefore he was loved and trusted.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Johnson, The History of the Yorubas, Part I ch. I (1921); not verbatim.

passages.text: When Adimu was announced to the Kings and Princes all around as the person appointed by the King to take charge of the treasures, and to worship the national deities during his absence, it was generally asked "And who is this Adimu?" The answer comes: "Omo Oluwo ni" — the son of a sacrificial victim: this is contracted to Ooni (Oluwo being the term for a sacrificial victim). So in subsequent years, when the seat of government was removed permanently to Oyo but not the national deities, Adimu became supreme at Ile Ife, and his successors to this day have been termed the Ooni — the high priests to the king and people of the whole Yoruba nation, the duties of the office being not local or tribal, but national.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Johnson, The History of the Yorubas, Part I ch. I (1921); not verbatim.

title.en: Oranyan's Sword: No King May Order an Execution Without It
title.zh: 奧蘭揚之劍——無劍不得行刑

region.en: Ile-Ife, Nigeria (the grave from which the sword is fetched)
region.zh: 奈及利亞伊費城（取劍之王陵）

period: Yoruba tradition recorded 1921 (Johnson)

source.work: Rev. Samuel Johnson, The History of the Yorubas (London, 1921), Part I ch. I

summary.en: As the Yorubas worship the dead and believe prayers at an ancestor's grave potent for blessing, all succeeding kings on their accession, before coronation, send to perform acts of worship at the grave of Oduduwa and receive the benediction of the priest. The sword of justice known as Ida Oranyan (Oranyan's sword) must be brought from Ile-Ife, where Oranyan is buried, and ceremoniously placed in the new king's hands; without this, the king has no authority whatever to order an execution. Oranyan himself, though he died (as is probable) at Oko, is shown buried at Ife — for the Yoruba custom is to pare the nails and shave the head of anyone dying far from his burial-place and bury those relics there with full obsequies; his grave bears the obelisk called Opa Oraniyan, with characters said to suggest a Phoenician origin.
summary.zh: 約魯巴人拜祭亡者，深信在祖陵前祈禱可致福佑；故歷代君王即位加冕之前，必遣人赴伊費奧杜杜瓦陵前致祭，並受祭司祝禱。稱為「伊達奧蘭揚」（奧蘭揚之劍）的正義之劍必自伊費——奧蘭揚安葬之地——迎來，莊嚴地置於新王之手；未經此儀，國王無權下令處決任何人。相傳奧蘭揚雖或卒於奧科，伊費卻有其陵——按風俗，客死遠方者剪指甲、剃髮攜歸安葬，葬儀與全屍無異。陵上立有碑柱「奧帕奧蘭揚」，其上刻文，或謂有腓尼基之源。

sensitivity.note: Recorded 1921; the coronation charter binding every crowned Yoruba king to Ife. Cross-ref: yoruba-staff-of-oranyan.

passages.text: As the Yorubas worship the dead, and have the belief that prayers offered at the grave of deceased ancestors are potent to procure temporal blessings, all succeeding Yoruba kings on their accession and before coronation are expected to send to perform acts of worship at the grave of Oduduwa and to receive the benediction of the priest. The sword of justice known as Ida Oranyan (Oranyan's sword) is to be brought from Ile Ife and ceremoniously placed in their hands; without this being done, the King has no authority whatever to order an execution.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Johnson, The History of the Yorubas, Part I ch. I (1921); not verbatim.

passages.text: Oranyan may have actually died at Oko, but his grave with an obelisk over it is certainly shown at Ile Ife to this day. It is a custom among the Yorubas, observed to this day, to pare the nails and shave the head of anyone who dies at a considerable distance from the place where they would have him buried; these relics are taken to the place of interment and there decently buried, the funeral obsequies being scrupulously observed as if the corpse itself were buried there. The most notable of the Ife marbles is what is known as the Opa Oraniyan (Oraniyan's staff), an obelisk standing on the site of Oraniyan's supposed grave, having characters cut in it which suggest a Phoenician origin.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Johnson, The History of the Yorubas, Part I ch. I (1921); not verbatim.

title.en: Obanita: The Sacrifice on the Highway Who Lived
title.zh: 奧巴尼塔——路口祭壇上的生還者

region.en: Ijebu country, Nigeria (the Aha forest where the survivor ascended to heaven)
region.zh: 奈及利亞伊傑布之地（生還者升天的阿哈森林）

period: Yoruba tradition recorded 1921 (Johnson)

source.work: Rev. Samuel Johnson, The History of the Yorubas (London, 1921), Part I ch. II

summary.en: The Ijebus themselves claim descent from Oba-nita — "servants of Obanita." Tradition says he was a victim of sacrifice by the Olowu, offered where two roads cross: a sacrifice on the highway, Ebo-ni-ita. The victim was mangled and left for dead, but revived at night, crawled into the forest, recovered and survived — living on fruits and the chase, then a little farming. As the oldest man in those parts he was regarded as the father of newcomers, and the tribe that grew around him took his name: Ebonita, a sacrifice on the highway, converted to Obanita, a king on the highway. There never really was anyone of that name; a forest near the village of Aha is still shown where he is annually worshipped, whence he is supposed to have ascended into heaven. The annual victim of Obanita was never killed, but made demented by unknown arts and left to wander the Aha Forest until he perished — as the ancestor himself was not killed outright.
summary.zh: 伊傑布人自稱乃「奧巴尼塔的僕人」之後。相傳此人是奧洛烏王在兩路交叉口所獻的祭品——所謂「路口之祭」。他被剁傷棄置等死，卻在夜間甦醒，爬入森林，活了下來，以野果狩獵為生，後又墾荒。因其為當地最年長者，陸續前來的移民皆奉之為父；其後裔遂稱他為祖先——「路口之祭」（埃博尼塔）遂轉訛為「路口之王」（奧巴尼塔）。其實並無此人。阿哈村附近至今猶存一片森林，歲歲向他致祭，相傳他即由此升天。獻給奧巴尼塔的年度祭品從不處死，卻被不知名的法術弄得神智失常，在阿哈林中遊蕩至死——正如其先祖未曾被殺死。

sensitivity.note: Recorded 1921; tribe-origin legend of the Ijebu from a surviving sacrificial victim. Johnson notes both Ijebu accounts derive the tribe from human-sacrifice victims ('the food of the deep' and Obanita). Presented as the recorded tradition states it.

passages.text: The Ijebus themselves claim to have descended from Oba-nita, as they say of themselves, "Ogetiele, eru Obanita" — Ogetiele, servants of Obanita. But who was this Oba-nita? Tradition says he was a victim of sacrifice by the Olowu, or King of Owu. It was said that the Olowu offered in sacrifice a human being where two roads cross; this was termed Ebo-ni-ita, a sacrifice on the highway, the victim being mangled and left for dead. He, however, revived at night, and crawled away into the forest, where he subsequently recovered and survived.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Johnson, The History of the Yorubas, Part I ch. II (1921); not verbatim.

passages.text: He lived on fruits, on the chase, and then did a bit of farming. With an access of population, being the oldest man met in those parts, he was regarded as the father, and subsequent generations call him their ancestor, and so the Ijebu tribe was formed, and the term Ebonita (a sacrifice on the highway) was converted to Obanita (a king on the highway). There was really nobody of that name. A forest is still shown near the village of Aha where he is annually worshipped, from whence he was supposed to have ascended into heaven.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Johnson, The History of the Yorubas, Part I ch. II (1921); not verbatim.

passages.text: It is rather curious that both accounts should have made them descended from victims of human sacrifice. The victim also usually offered to Obanita annually was always a human being, but this was never killed; he was, however, always acted upon in some way or other unknown (by magic arts) that he always became demented, and left to wander about sheepishly in the Aha Forest until he perished there. This is no doubt due to the fact that the ancestor Ebonita himself, when a victim, was not killed outright.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Johnson, The History of the Yorubas, Part I ch. II (1921); not verbatim.

title.en: Ijesa: The Food of the Gods, and the Sons of Sticks
title.zh: 伊傑薩——眾神之食與木棍之子

region.en: Ibokun and Ilesa, Nigeria (the cattle-pen of victims and the okra king's garden)
region.zh: 奈及利亞伊博昆與伊萊薩（祭品欄與秋葵王的花園）

period: Yoruba tradition recorded 1921 (Johnson)

source.work: Rev. Samuel Johnson, The History of the Yorubas (London, 1921), Part I ch. II

summary.en: Two accounts tell of the Ijesas. In the earliest times, before Shango's reign, human sacrifices were common; to have victims ready to hand a number of slaves were purchased and located in the district of Ibokun, tended as cattle under the care of Owaju, from whom selections were made for sacrificial purposes — hence the term Ijesa, from Ije Orisa, the food of the gods. Another legend says that when the royal family were appointing kings from Ile-Ife, a brave young scion appointed first Owa over the Ijesas complained his subjects were too few; the sire ordered a large bundle of sticks and converted them into human beings for him — hence the Ijesas are nicknamed Omo Igi, offspring of sticks. Johnson calls this a pure myth of wily neighbours. Yet one fact held into modern times: the Ifes preferred an Ijesa victim to any other, sacrifices being considered more acceptable as the food of the gods. When the later Ijesas migrated and took the country, they spared the kindly old principal chief called Oba Ila, the Okra King, from his okra plantation, and made him second in rank — a title, Obala, continued to this day.
summary.zh: 關於伊傑薩人有兩說。最古之世（尚戈王之前），人祭盛行；為求祭品隨手可得，人們購買奴隸圈養於伊博昆之地，由奧瓦茹看管如牛群，不時挑選獻祭——「伊傑薩」即「眾神之食」之意。又一傳說：王室自伊費分封諸王時，受封伊傑薩的青年勇士抱怨子民太少；先王命取一大捆木棍，化為人形賜他添丁——故伊傑薩人被鄰族謔稱「奧莫伊吉」，木棍之子。約翰遜斥此為刁滑鄰邦編造的神話。然而直到近代，伊費人獻祭時總優先挑選伊傑薩人，因其為「眾神之食」。後來伊傑薩人東山再起奪回鄉土時，獨獨放過了慈祥的老酋——因種秋葵而得名的「秋葵王」奧巴拉——尊為次席，其號「奧巴拉」沿用至今。

sensitivity.note: Recorded 1921. Contains historical human-sacrifice practice ('food of the gods') reported as the recorded tradition states it, in Johnson's own frankly critical register; the Omo-Igi sticks myth parallels Ogumefu's Sons of Sticks (yoruba-sons-of-sticks).

passages.text: The first account relates to the earliest period when the Yorubas had just entered into and subdued the country, and the Alafins then resided at Ile Ife, i.e., prior to the reign of Shango. Human sacrifices were common in those days, and in order to have victims ready to hand, a number of slaves were purchased and located in the district of Ibokun; there they were tended as cattle, under the care of Owaju, and from them selections were made from time to time for sacrificial purposes; hence the term Ijesa from Ije Orisa (the food of the gods).
passages.note: Paraphrase of Johnson, The History of the Yorubas, Part I ch. II (1921); not verbatim.

passages.text: There is also a legend that when the nations began to disperse from Ile Ife and members of the Royal Family were appointed kings and rulers in divers places, a young and brave scion of the house was appointed the first Owa or king over the Ijesas, but he returned to the Alafin and complained that his territory was too small and his subjects few; the sire thereupon ordered a large bundle of sticks to be brought to him, and these sticks he converted into human beings for the Owa, in order to increase the number of his subjects. Hence to this day the Ijesas are often termed by their neighbours Omo Igi (offspring of sticks!). This, of course, is a pure myth invented by their more wily neighbours to account for the notorious characteristics of the Ijesas generally, who are as proverbially deficient in wit as they are remarkably distinguished for brute strength.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Johnson, The History of the Yorubas, Part I ch. II (1921); not verbatim.

passages.text: The other account relates chiefly to the present day Ijesas of Ilesa (the home of the gods). They hailed from the Ekitis, or from the neighbourhood of Ibokun, migrating first to Ipole near Ondo and thence back to Ilesa. Finding game plentiful, the climate agreeable, and the inhabitants simple, peaceful, and unwarlike, while at home they endured much oppression from their Owa, they there and then settled, and reduced the aboriginal inhabitants into subjection. They spared the principal chief, a kindly old gentleman who had an extensive garden plantation, called Oba Ila, the Okra King, from his Okra plantation, and placed him next in rank to the chief of the marauders; that nickname is continued to the present time as the title Obala, conferred on the most distinguished chief after the Owa of Ilesa.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Johnson, The History of the Yorubas, Part I ch. II (1921); not verbatim.

title.en: Ajaka and the Salt Water from the Sea
title.zh: 阿賈卡與取自大海的鹽水

region.en: Ile-Ife and Ilesa, Nigeria (the blind king's palace and the sea-road)
region.zh: 伊費與伊萊薩（失明老王的宮廷與尋海之路）

period: Yoruba tradition recorded 1921 (Johnson)

source.work: Rev. Samuel Johnson, The History of the Yorubas (London, 1921), Part I ch. II

summary.en: When the Olofin of Ife became blind from old age, a man came forward with a sure remedy containing salt water — but none of his children would go to fetch it except his youngest grandson, the warlike prince Ajaka, "one who fights everywhere." Away many years and given up for lost, the king divided his property: to the Oloyo, most beloved, the land — "settle nowhere till you come to a slippery place"; hence Oyo, the slippery, and hence Oyos are such slippery customers. Then the young adventurer turned up with water from the sea; the king used it as prescribed and regained his sight — hence the Ijesas, who became his subjects, are called Omo Obokun, children of the brine procurer. Having nothing left, he gave Ajaka his own sword with leave to attack any of his brothers and possess himself of their wealth; the Owa cut the fringes off his grandfather's crown in wantonness, and the old man swore never to wear a fringed crown again — and took away Aregbajo's crown, never returning it: kings of Igbajo wear none to this day.
summary.zh: 伊費的老王奧洛芬因年老而失明，有人獻上含鹽水的良方——可兒子們無一人肯去取水，唯幼孫阿賈卡（綽號「處處開戰者」）慨然請行。去經多年、音信全無，老王分了家產：把土地給最寵愛的奧約奧——「遇到濕滑之地方可定居」——故名奧約（濕滑之意），奧約人也因此出了名的滑頭。不料少年探險者竟攜海水而歸！老王照方服用，重見光明——其後裔伊傑薩人遂稱「奧莫奧博貢」，取鹽水者之子。家產已盡，他便把佩劍賜給阿賈卡，許他攻打任何兄弟、奪其財貨。而阿賈卡探視祖父時，竟揮劍削去王冠的流蘇；老王大怒立誓：有生之年再戴無蘇之冠；他還奪走阿雷加喬的王冠不還——伊巴喬之王至今無冠。

sensitivity.note: Recorded 1921; the Obokun (brine-procurer) etiology of the Ijesa royal house and the Oyo-slippery name etiology in one narrative complex.

passages.text: The Olofin (Alafin) king of Ife had several children, grandchildren and great-grandchildren. When the Olofin became blind from old age he was much depressed in mind; efforts were put forth to effect his cure, all of which proved fruitless, when a certain man came forward and prescribed for him a sure remedy which among other ingredients contained salt water. He put the case before his children, but none made any effort to procure some for him save his youngest grandson, a very brave and warlike prince who bore the title of Esinkin among the King's household warriors, and was surnamed Ajaka, i.e., one who fights everywhere, on account of his proclivities, being fond of adventures. He volunteered to go and fetch some wherever procurable.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Johnson, The History of the Yorubas, Part I ch. II (1921); not verbatim.

passages.text: Having been away for many years and not heard of, the aged sire and everyone else despaired of his ever coming back; so the King divided his property among the remaining grown-up children. Although the Alado (king of Benin) was the eldest, yet the Oloyo was the most beloved, and to him he gave the land, and told him to scour it all over, and settle nowhere till he came to a slippery place, and there make his abode; hence the term Oyo (slippery), and hence Oyos are such slippery customers! After they had all gone and settled in their respective localities, all unexpectedly, the young adventurer turned up with water from the sea! The monarch made use of it as per prescription and regained his sight! Hence the Ijesas who subsequently became his subjects are sometimes termed Omo Obokun, children of the brine procurer.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Johnson, The History of the Yorubas, Part I ch. II (1921); not verbatim.

passages.text: Having distributed all his property he had nothing left for Ajaka; he therefore gave him a sword lying by his side with leave to attack any of his brothers, especially the Alara or Alado, and possess himself of their wealth, but should he fail, to retire back to him; hence the appellation Owa Ajaka Onida raharaha (Owa the ubiquitous fighter, a man with a devastating sword). The Owa Ajaka settled a little way from his grandfather, and on one occasion he paid him a visit, and found him sitting alone with his crown on his head — and out of sheer wantonness he cut off some of the fringes with his sword. The old man was enraged by this act, and swore that he would never wear a crown with fringes on. The Aregbajo was one of those who had a crown given to him, but the Owa Ajaka, paying him a visit, saw it, took it away, and never returned it: hence the kings of Igbajo never wear a crown to this day.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Johnson, The History of the Yorubas, Part I ch. II (1921); not verbatim.

title.en: The Spared Twins of Ode Ondo
title.zh: 奧德奧恩多——被赦的雙生子

region.en: Ode Ondo, Nigeria (the settlement named The Settlers)
region.zh: 奈及利亞奧恩多城（名為「定居者」的城邑）

period: Yoruba tradition recorded 1921 (Johnson)

source.work: Rev. Samuel Johnson, The History of the Yorubas (London, 1921), Part I ch. II

summary.en: The custom of killing twins prevailed all over the country in early times; it has died out so long ago that no one can say precisely when or by whom a stop was put to it. But it happened once upon a time, when the practice still prevailed, that one of the wives of the Alafin (King Ajaka) gave birth to twins, and the King was loth to destroy them; he gave orders that they should be removed, with the mother, to a remote part of the kingdom and there remain, and be regarded as dead. So she left with a large number of friends and retinue to the site of the present Ode Ondo, then sparsely peopled by a tribe named Idoko, and there settled — hence the term Ondo, the Settlers. The people of the district, knowing who the strangers were, yielded ready obedience, and the strangers became rulers of the district. Probably it was from this time that infanticide received its death-blow in Yoruba proper.
summary.zh: 太古之世，殺嬰之俗遍行全國，廢除已久，無人能確言起於何時何人。相傳尚在行此俗的年代，阿勞芬王（阿賈卡王）的一位妃子誕下雙生子，王不忍加誅，遂下令將母子連同大批親隨遷往王國邊陲，視同已死。一行人來到今日奧德奧恩多城之地——其時此地稀疏地住著名叫伊多科的部落——定居下來，故名「奧恩多」：定居者。當地人得知來歷，俯首聽命，客居者遂為其主。殺嬰之俗在約魯巴本部的死刑，大概自此而始。

sensitivity.note: Recorded 1921; twin-sparing legend founding the Ondo kingdom — the key Yoruba record for the twins motif cluster alongside Ibeji devotion. Cross-refs: yoruba-ibeji-ere-figures, yoruba-twin-brothers-ajaka, maya-popol-vuh-creation-twins.

passages.text: The custom of killing twins prevailed all over the country in early times; it has died out all over the greater part of it so long ago that no one can say precisely when or by whom a stop was put to it. But it happened once upon a time when the practice still prevailed that one of the wives of the Alafin (King Ajaka) gave birth to twins, and the King was loth to destroy them; he thereupon gave orders that they should be removed — with the mother — to a remote part of the kingdom and there to remain and be regarded as dead.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Johnson, The History of the Yorubas, Part I ch. II (1921); not verbatim.

passages.text: So she left with a large number of friends and retinue to the site of the present Ode Ondo, then sparsely peopled by a tribe named Idoko, and there settled, hence the term Ondo, signifying the Settlers. The people of the district, knowing who the strangers were, yielded them ready obedience, and the strangers became rulers of the district. Probably it was from this time that infanticide received its death blow — in Yoruba Proper at least.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Johnson, The History of the Yorubas, Part I ch. II (1921); not verbatim.

title.en: The Osile Who Walked on Blood: Oko, the Pelting Stone
title.zh: 踏血而行的奧西勒——「投石」之城

region.en: Oko (Egba Oke-Ona), Nigeria (the Ogboni house doorway)
region.zh: 奈及利亞奧科城（奧格博尼會堂門檻）

period: Yoruba tradition recorded 1921 (Johnson)

source.work: Rev. Samuel Johnson, The History of the Yorubas (London, 1921), Part I ch. II

summary.en: The Osile is said to be an unfortunate title because, more than any of the other divisions, the Oke-Ona people were prone to slaughter human victims: every time the Osile entered the Ogboni house he must walk on the blood of a male victim, and when he came out, on that of a female. Also, Osiles never die a natural death; when their excesses became unbearable they were usually stoned to death — hence the appellation of their chief town, Oko, a pelting stone. For that reason the Egbas were reluctant to resuscitate the title at Abeokuta until 1897, when the Governor of Lagos ordered the Egbas to reorganise their government and fill up vacant titles.
summary.zh: 「奧西勒」據說是個不祥的尊號：奧克-奧納人最嗜人祭——奧西勒每次進奧格博尼會堂，須踏過男祭品之血；出門時，又須踏過女祭品之血。而且奧西勒從無善終者：惡行積重難返之時，民眾便以石擊殺之——其都城因此得名「奧科」，即投石之邑。因此埃格巴人遲遲不肯在阿貝奧庫塔復設此號，直至1897年拉哥斯總督下令重整政制、補齊虛銜方才恢復。

sensitivity.note: Recorded 1921; kingship-blood taboo etiology reported as the recorded tradition states it. Human-sacrifice content handled without graphic detail.

passages.text: The Osile is said to be an unfortunate title because, more than any of the other divisions, the Oke Ona people were more prone to slaughter human victims; every time the Osile entered the Ogboni house, he must walk on the blood of a male victim, and when he comes out on that of a female! Also that Osiles never die a natural death; when their excesses became unbearable they were usually stoned to death; hence the appellation of their chief town, Oko — i.e., a pelting stone.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Johnson, The History of the Yorubas, Part I ch. II (1921); not verbatim.

passages.text: For that reason the Egbas were reluctant to resuscitate the title at Abeokuta until Governor McCallum of Lagos in 1897, on the occasion of the Queen's Diamond Jubilee, ordered the Egbas and others to reorganise their government, and fill up vacant titles.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Johnson, The History of the Yorubas, Part I ch. II (1921); not verbatim.

title.en: Nohochakyum and the Four Brothers of Yaxchilan
title.zh: 諾霍查庫姆與亞希蘭的四兄弟

region.en: Yaxchilan (home of the gods), Usumacinta River, Chiapas
region.zh: 恰帕斯烏蘇馬辛塔河亞希蘭（諸神之家）

period: Recorded 1901-03 (Tozzer fieldwork among the Lacandones), published 1907

source.work: Alfred M. Tozzer, A Comparative Study of the Mayas and the Lacandones (1907), Part II: Religion of the Lacandones

summary.en: Nohochakyum, head of the Lacandón pantheon, lives in the ruins of Yaxchilan; the sun itself is his servant, and constellations and thunder carry out his commands. He is one of four brothers — one for each direction — and at the end of the world he will wear around his waist the body of Hapikern, the snake who draws men to him by his breath and slays them.
summary.zh: 拉坎敦萬神殿之首諾霍查庫姆居於亞希蘭遺址；太陽亦是其僕從，星座與雷聲皆聽其號令。他有四位兄弟——四方各一——而在世界末日，他將以哈皮克爾恩之身為腰帶：那條以吐息引人近身而殺之的巨蛇。

sensitivity.note: Published public-domain ethnography (1907); paraphrase/quote only. Living Lacandón Maya religion — describe respectfully.

passages.text: Nohochakyum is at the head of Lacandone pantheon. It is to him that the greatest reverence is paid. Two flowers, the red Plumeria and the white Plumeria, are considered the father and mother respectively of Nohochakyum; these two flowers are used in some of the rites, one of each kind being placed on the mouth of the brasero containing the idol.
passages.note: Condensed from Tozzer (1907), Part II; not verbatim.

passages.text: Nohochakyum of the Lacandones lives at the ruins of Yaxchilan. The spirits of the east, Yalanquin, are regarded as the servants of this main god. The sun itself occupies an inferior place in the pantheon: it is regarded as a servant ready to carry out the commands of his master, Nohochakyum. Many of the constellations and the spirit of the thunder are regarded as other servants of 'the great lord.'
passages.note: Condensed from Tozzer (1907), Part II; not verbatim.

passages.text: It is supposed that at the end of the world Nohochakyum will wear around his waist as a belt the body of Hapikern, a very bad spirit in the form of a snake, who draws people to him by his breath and slays them. Nohochakyum is one of four brothers: Yantho the oldest, with the spirit of the north; Usukun, who has the earthquake as his servant; and Uyin, the youngest, whose power is always for the good.
passages.note: Condensed from Tozzer (1907), Part II; not verbatim.

title.en: The Many-Headed Snake of Kukulkan
title.zh: 庫庫爾坎的多頭巨蛇

region.en: Lake Petha region, Chiapas
region.zh: 恰帕斯佩塔湖地區

period: Recorded 1901-03 (Tozzer fieldwork), published 1907

source.work: Alfred M. Tozzer, A Comparative Study of the Mayas and the Lacandones (1907), Part II

summary.en: The name of the old Yucatec culture hero Kukulcan survives among the Lacandones as a mythical snake with many heads, living only near the home of Nohochakyum. This snake is killed and eaten only at the time of great national peril — during an eclipse of the moon, and especially that of the sun.
summary.zh: 昔日猶加敦文化英雄庫庫爾坎之名，在拉坎敦人中存留為一多頭的神話巨蛇，僅居於諾霍查庫姆之家附近。此蛇唯有在民族大難之時——月蝕，尤以日蝕——方可殺而食之。

sensitivity.note: Published public-domain ethnography (1907); paraphrase/quote only.

passages.text: The name of the other culture hero of the early natives of Yucatan, Kukulcan, is still retained among the Lacandones as the name of a mythical snake with many heads, living only in the vicinity of the home of Nohochakyum. This snake is killed and eaten only at the time of great national peril, as during an eclipse of the moon and especially that of the sun.
passages.note: Condensed from Tozzer (1907), Part II; not verbatim.

title.en: Kisin Below: The Earthquake Who Hates the Rain
title.zh: 井下基辛：憎雨的地震之神

region.en: Metnal (underworld), Chiapas
region.zh: 恰帕斯梅特納爾（冥界）

period: Recorded 1901-03 (Tozzer fieldwork), published 1907

source.work: Alfred M. Tozzer, A Comparative Study of the Mayas and the Lacandones (1907), Part III

summary.en: Below the earth is the abode of Kisin, the earthquake and god of the underworld, a god of evil. The Yumchacob send down the rain which refreshes the earth; this makes the ground cold and uncomfortable for Kisin, so he makes a wind in the sky to drive away the rain clouds. In metnal live the spirits of those who killed themselves by throwing themselves into a cenote.
summary.zh: 地下為基辛之居——地震與冥界之神，邪惡之神。諸雨神降下甘霖，大地得潤；然雨令地下陰冷難耐，基辛遂於天中起風，驅散雨雲。自沉於聖井者之靈，即居於此冥界。

sensitivity.note: Published public-domain ethnography (1907); paraphrase/quote only.

passages.text: Below the earth is the abode of Kisin, the earthquake and god of the underworld (metnal). He is a god of evil. The Yumchacob send down the rain which refreshes the earth. This makes the ground cold and uncomfortable for Kisin, so that he makes a wind in the sky to drive away the rain clouds.
passages.note: Condensed from Tozzer (1907), Part III; not verbatim.

passages.text: It is in this underworld that the spirits of those live who have committed suicide by throwing themselves into a cenote, or by some other means. The spirits of all people who die go here for a short time, after which they pass through the several heavens, finally arriving at the seventh, where they live in happiness forever.
passages.note: Condensed from Tozzer (1907), Part III; not verbatim.

title.en: Usukun: The Brother Kept Apart
title.zh: 烏蘇昆：被隔開的兄弟

region.en: Lake Petha region, Chiapas
region.zh: 恰帕斯佩塔湖地區

period: Recorded 1901-03 (Tozzer fieldwork), published 1907

source.work: Alfred M. Tozzer, A Comparative Study of the Mayas and the Lacandones (1907), Part II

summary.en: The second brother of Nohochakyum is Usukun — 'his older brother'. He lives in a cave, has the earthquake Kisin as his servant, and is not of good intention. His idol is always placed apart from the rest, as if its presence would be harmful near the braseros of the other gods; yet it is not neglected but placated with offerings of food and drink.
summary.zh: 諾霍查庫姆的次兄名烏蘇昆——意即「其兄」。他居於洞穴，以地震神基辛為僕，居心不良。其神像常與他神分開，彷彿近他神之香爐則有害；然其像亦非被忽略，仍以飲食祭品安撫之。

sensitivity.note: Published public-domain ethnography (1907); paraphrase/quote only.

passages.text: The second brother, according to age, is called Usukun, which in Maya means his older brother. He is thus named in respect to Nohochakyum. This god lives in a cave. He has the earthquake, Kisin, as his servant, and is not of good intention.
passages.note: Condensed from Tozzer (1907), Part II; not verbatim.

passages.text: His idol is usually found, however, in every collection of the sacred ollas, but it is always placed apart from the rest, as if its presence would be harmful when in the vicinity of the braseros of the other gods. The idol of Usukun is not neglected, however, but it is placated with offerings of food and drink as are those of the other gods.
passages.note: Condensed from Tozzer (1907), Part II; not verbatim.

title.en: Akna, the Mother: Goddess of Childbirth
title.zh: 阿克納之母：生育女神

region.en: Yaxchilan, Usumacinta River, Chiapas
region.zh: 恰帕斯烏蘇馬辛塔河亞希蘭

period: Recorded 1901-03 (Tozzer fieldwork), published 1907

source.work: Alfred M. Tozzer, A Comparative Study of the Mayas and the Lacandones (1907), Part II

summary.en: Next in importance to the four brothers is the goddess Akna, the Mother — mother of certain of the lesser gods and goddess of childbirth. Prayers and offerings are made to her especially on the birth of a child; when serving in this capacity she is called Ixsel — the same deity the early authorities record as goddess of medicine and of childbirth.
summary.zh: 地位僅次於四兄弟者為女神阿克納——「母」，為某些小神之母，亦是生育女神。凡產子之時，祈禱與祭品尤敬於她；當此之時其名為伊希塞爾——即早期文獻所記掌醫藥與生育的女神。

sensitivity.note: Published public-domain ethnography (1907); paraphrase/quote only.

passages.text: Next in importance to the four brothers is the goddess Akna (the mother). She is considered the mother of certain of the lesser gods as Nohochakyum is the father of many of the gods. Akna is the goddess of childbirth. Prayers and offerings are made especially to her on the birth of a child. When serving in this capacity she is called Ixsel. This is the same deity mentioned by the early authorities as goddess of medicine and of childbirth.
passages.note: Condensed from Tozzer (1907), Part II; not verbatim.

title.en: When the Sun Is Ill: Eclipse Rites of the Lacandones
title.zh: 太陽患病之時：拉坎敦的蝕祭

region.en: Lake Petha region, Chiapas
region.zh: 恰帕斯佩塔湖地區

period: Recorded 1901-03 (Tozzer fieldwork), published 1907

source.work: Alfred M. Tozzer, A Comparative Study of the Mayas and the Lacandones (1907), Part II

summary.en: When there is an eclipse of the sun it is said that Nohochakyum is ill; rites are held and offerings made to the gods, every one abstains from secular work, and each family remains in its own home for the period of the eclipse. An eclipse of the moon is a less serious event: it is a sign that the daughter of Nohochakyum is ill.
summary.zh: 日蝕之時，人言諾霍查庫姆患病；遂舉行祭儀、向神獻供，人人停止俗務，蝕期各家閉戶自守。月蝕則較輕：那只是諾霍查庫姆之女患病的兆頭。

sensitivity.note: Published public-domain ethnography (1907); paraphrase/quote only.

passages.text: When there is an eclipse of the sun, it is said that Nohochakyum is ill. Rites are held and offerings are made to the gods. Every one abstains from secular work of all kinds, and each family remains in their own home during the period of an eclipse. All kinds of animals may be freely eaten.
passages.note: Condensed from Tozzer (1907), Part II; not verbatim.

passages.text: An eclipse of the moon is a less serious event. It is regarded as a sign that the daughter of Nohochakyum is ill. A rite is celebrated as in the case of an eclipse of the sun — the sun belongs to the great lord, and the moon to his child.
passages.note: Condensed from Tozzer (1907), Part II; not verbatim.

title.en: Asking the Stone: Divination for the Idol's Journey
title.zh: 問石：為神像之旅占卜

region.en: Lake Petha region, Chiapas
region.zh: 恰帕斯佩塔湖地區

period: Recorded 1901-03 (Tozzer fieldwork), published 1907

source.work: Alfred M. Tozzer, A Comparative Study of the Mayas and the Lacandones (1907), Part II

summary.en: A god may only be brought home as an idol after he has shown himself willing: the father or oldest son of the settlement performs two acts of divination, one with a strip from the leaf of a palm, chanting as a necessary part of the rite, to learn whether the god consents to come and exert his beneficent influence over the encampment.
summary.zh: 唯有神明自願，方能以神像迎入家中：由聚落的父親或長子行兩種占卜之一——以棕櫚葉條為器，誦禱為祭禮必需——以知神是否允諾降臨，施福於此營地。

sensitivity.note: Published public-domain ethnography (1907); paraphrase/quote only. Living ritual — describe respectfully.

passages.text: There are two methods of divination by which it may be ascertained whether or not a god is willing to have his idol placed in the sacred hut, thus showing his consent to come and exert a beneficent influence over the encampment in question. These acts of divination may only be performed by the father or oldest son of the settlement, and it is only they and their direct line who understand the rite. Chanting is a necessary part to this ceremony of divination.
passages.note: Condensed from Tozzer (1907), Part II; not verbatim.

passages.text: One of these rites is performed with a strip from the leaf of a palm, and a part of the detached leaf is burned; the god answers in the fall and pattern of the strip. Only those gods are represented in an encampment to whose shrine a pilgrimage has been made and a stone either carved or otherwise brought back — journeys which cannot be made at will, but only after the god has shown himself willing.
passages.note: Condensed from Tozzer (1907), Part II; not verbatim.

title.en: The Four Epochs: Dwarfs in Darkness and the Cut Rope
title.zh: 四紀元：黑暗中的侏儒與斷繩

region.en: Valladolid, Yucatan, Mexico
region.zh: 墨西哥猶加敦巴利亞多利德

period: Recorded 1901-03 (Tozzer fieldwork among the Mayas of Yucatan), published 1907

source.work: Alfred M. Tozzer, A Comparative Study of the Mayas and the Lacandones (1907), Part III: Religion of the Mayas of Yucatan

summary.en: This world is in its fourth period. In the first epoch lived the Saiyam-koob, the Adjusters: dwarfs who built the ruins in darkness before there was any sun, and turned to stone when the sun appeared. From Tuloom and Coba to Chichen Itza and Uxmal there ran a road suspended in the sky — a living rope with blood flowing in the middle, by which food was sent to the ancient rulers — until it was cut, and the rope vanished forever. Three more floods separate the epochs.
summary.zh: 今世已歷四紀。第一紀元住著賽亞姆-庫布，即「調整者」：一群侏儒，在日出之前的黑暗中建造了遺址，日出即化為石。自圖盧姆與科巴至奇琴伊察與烏斯馬爾，懸於天空有一條路——一根有血於中流的活繩，古人由此向遺址中的君王輸送食物——繩斷之後，永不再現。其後三場洪水分隔諸紀。

sensitivity.note: Published public-domain ethnography (1907); paraphrase/quote only.

passages.text: According to the information obtained from the Mayas in the vicinity of Valladolid, this world is now in the fourth period of its existence. In the first epoch there lived the Saiyamwinkoob, the Adjusters. These composed the primitive race of Yucatan. They were dwarfs and were the ones who built the ruins. This work was all done in darkness before there was any sun. As soon as the sun appeared, these people turned to stone. Their images are found to-day in many of the ruins.
passages.note: Condensed from Tozzer (1907), Part III; not verbatim.

passages.text: It was at this period that there was a road suspended in the sky, stretching from Tuloom and Coba to Chichen Itza and Uxmal. This pathway was called the white road. It was in the nature of a large rope supposed to be living, and in the middle flowed blood. It was by this rope that the food was sent to the ancient rulers who lived in the structures now in ruins. For some reason this rope was cut, the blood flowed out, and the rope vanished forever.
passages.note: Condensed from Tozzer (1907), Part III; not verbatim.

passages.text: This first epoch was separated from the second by a flood, water over the earth. In the second period of the history of the earth there lived the Offenders. Again a flood destroyed the greater part of the world, after which the Mayas of the present time came into power. Still again there was a flood which gave way to the fourth period. In this last epoch there is a mixture of all the previous peoples inhabiting Yucatan.
passages.note: Condensed from Tozzer (1907), Part III; not verbatim.

canonical_translation: Tozzer, A Comparative Study of the Mayas and the Lacandones (1907)

narrative.en:
Tozzer's third part records the cosmology of the Maya of Valladolid as told in field interviews around 1900 — a complete world-ages cycle surviving under the surface of Catholic language. The world is now in its fourth period. In the first epoch lived the Saiyam-winkoob, the Adjusters, the primitive race of Yucatán: dwarfs who built the great ruins in darkness, before there was any sun, and who turned to stone when the sun first appeared — their images are the stone figures still standing in the ruins. In that epoch a road was suspended in the sky, stretching from Tuloom and Coba to Chichén Itzá and Uxmal: the sacbe, the white road, described as a living rope with blood flowing in its middle, by which food was sent up to the ancient rulers. For some reason the rope was cut; the blood flowed out and the rope vanished forever — the mythic image of a covenant between heaven and earth broken.

The first epoch was separated from the second by a flood called 'water over the earth'. In the second period lived the Oolob, the Offenders; again a flood destroyed the greater part of the world, after which the Mayas of the present time came into power; and still again a flood gave way to the fourth period, in which all previous peoples are mixed. The Catholic priests, Tozzer notes, took advantage of this belief to teach that in the last flood all spirits of the race were killed except three who escaped in a canoe — Dios Yumbil, Dios Mehenbil, and Dios Espirito Santo, the Trinity in Maya terms. Above the earth are seven heavens, each with a hole in the center one directly above the other; a giant ceiba growing in the exact center of the earth rears its branches through the successive holes to the seventh, where 'El Gran Dios' lives; by this tree, or by a ladder of vines through the same holes, the spirits of the dead ascend from world to world until they reach the topmost heaven and remain.

The record belongs to the cross-tradition cluster of world ages ending in flood (Hindu yugas, Norse Ragnarök cycles, Aztec suns) and of humans molded and remade — the dwarfs who became stone are the Maya counterpart of petrification myths worldwide. Its ritual function is calendrical and moral: epochs end, each flood is a judgment on the epoch's offenders, and the present age is understood as mixed and therefore fragile; the ascending ceiba explains the funerary rites by which food is set on the grave to provision the spirit's climb.

functions: Explains ruins as the stone bodies of the sun-blind dwarf builders
Frames the present as the fourth, mixed epoch, with three floods behind and judgment ahead
Charter of the seven-heaven ascent and of grave offerings provisioning the soul's climb

variants.name: Aztec Five Suns
variants.text_tradition: Codex Vaticanus A / Historia de los Mexicanos por sus pinturas
variants.summary: Successive creations each ended by flood or destruction, the present sun being the fifth — the Mesoamerican analog of the four epochs.

variants.name: Popol Wuj creation sequence
variants.summary: Successive failed creations of mud, wood, and maize parallel the epochal 'peoples' who fail in each age.

primary_sources.work: Tozzer field interviews among the Maya of Valladolid
primary_sources.citation: Tozzer, 1907, Part III, pp. 154-155

secondary_sources.work: Alfred M. Tozzer, A Comparative Study of the Mayas and the Lacandones
secondary_sources.citation: Tozzer, 1907, New York: Macmillan

secondary_sources.work: David Freidel, Linda Schele, Joy Parker, Maya Cosmos
secondary_sources.citation: Freidel, Schele & Parker, 1993, New York: William Morrow

sensitivity_guidance: This is living Yucatec cosmology collected as folklore; treat as living doctrine and avoid reducing it to 'mere legend'.

title.en: The Giant Ceiba Through the Seven Heavens
title.zh: 貫穿七重天的巨大木棉

region.en: Valladolid, Yucatan, Mexico
region.zh: 墨西哥猶加敦巴利亞多利德

period: Recorded 1901-03 (Tozzer fieldwork), published 1907

source.work: Alfred M. Tozzer, A Comparative Study of the Mayas and the Lacandones (1907), Part III

summary.en: There are seven heavens above the earth, each with a hole in the center, one directly above the other. A giant ceiba growing in the exact center of the earth rears its branches through the successive holes until it reaches the seventh, where El Gran Dios lives; by this tree the dead spirits ascend from one world to the other until they reach the topmost one. A cenote lies directly beneath the sacred tree, and a hawk lives in the topmost branch — the spirit of the tree.
summary.zh: 地上有七重天，各天中央有一孔，層層直上。一株巨木棉生於大地正中，枝幹依次穿過諸孔，直抵第七重天——西班牙人的大上帝居於彼處；亡靈即沿此樹自一界攀至另一界，直至最高一層而止。聖樹正下方有一聖井，最高枝上棲一鷹，即樹之靈。

sensitivity.note: Published public-domain ethnography (1907); paraphrase/quote only.

passages.text: According to the natives of Yucatan, there are seven heavens above the earth, each of which has a hole in the center, one directly above the other. According to one idea, a giant ceiba growing in the exact center of the earth rears its branches through the successive holes in the heavens until it reaches the seventh, where 'El Gran Dios' of the Spaniards lives. It is by means of this tree that the dead spirits ascend from one world to the other until they reach the topmost one, where they finally remain.
passages.note: Condensed from Tozzer (1907), Part III; not verbatim.

passages.text: Another explanation is that there is a ladder made of vines running from the earth up through the holes in the heavens to the seventh, and it is by this vine that the souls ascend. One ceiba was supposed to have grown in Valladolid: it was cut down, but it grew again and had four branches, one for each of the cardinal points. A cenote was directly beneath the tree, and a hawk lived in the topmost branch, the spirit of the tree; the bird's cry was the name given to the town.
passages.note: Condensed from Tozzer (1907), Part III; not verbatim.

title.en: The Yum Balamob: Guardians at the Four Crosses
title.zh: 尤姆·巴拉姆：四十字口的守護者

region.en: Valladolid, Yucatan, Mexico
region.zh: 墨西哥猶加敦巴利亞多利德

period: Recorded 1901-03 (Tozzer fieldwork), published 1907

source.work: Alfred M. Tozzer, A Comparative Study of the Mayas and the Lacandones (1907), Part III

summary.en: In the first heaven above the earth live the Yum Balamob, for the special protection of Christians. Invisible by day, they are awake at night, seated at the crosses set up at the entrances of the pueblos — four of them, one for each cardinal point, mounting guard over the town. The worked obsidian flakes scattered over Yucatan are their tools: they cut through the wind with them and signal to their companions at the other entrances.
summary.zh: 第一重天上住著尤姆·巴拉姆，專司庇護基督徒。晝間隱形，夜間醒著，坐於鎮口所立十字架旁——共四位，各鎮一方，輪值守衛全鎮。猶加敦散落的黑曜石片即其工具：他們以之切風為聲，向各口同僚傳訊。

sensitivity.note: Published public-domain ethnography (1907); paraphrase/quote only.

passages.text: In the first heaven above the earth lived the Yumbalamob. They are for the special protection of 'cristianos'. They are invisible during the day, but at night they are awake and remain seated at the crosses set up at the entrance of the pueblos. There are four of the Yumbalamob, one for each of the cardinal points. They mount guard over the town and protect the people from the animals of the forest and other dangers.
passages.note: Condensed from Tozzer (1907), Part III; not verbatim.

passages.text: The pieces of worked obsidian often found throughout Yucatan are supposed to have been used by the Balamob to cut through the wind, and by the sounds thus produced to make signs to their companions stationed at the other entrances to the town. These obsidian flakes are also used to hurl at animals who are about to attack men.
passages.note: Condensed from Tozzer (1907), Part III; not verbatim.

title.en: The Rain Gods Ride: Whips, Arrows, and Thrown Cigars
title.zh: 雨神騎行：鞭、箭與拋棄的雪茄

region.en: Valladolid, Yucatan, Mexico
region.zh: 墨西哥猶加敦巴利亞多利德

period: Recorded 1901-03 (Tozzer fieldwork), published 1907

source.work: Alfred M. Tozzer, A Comparative Study of the Mayas and the Lacandones (1907), Part III

summary.en: The rain gods rush everywhere in the storm; the thunder is the drum that announces their coming, and the lightning is the whip with which they lash their horses. They carry bows and arrows and often fell trees in their journeys — the arrowheads found in the forest. And the comets are explained as the cigars being thrown away by the rain gods.
summary.zh: 風雨之時，雨神們馳騁四野；雷是其來臨的鼓聲，閃電是抽打坐騎的鞭子。他們持弓帶箭，途中每每伐倒大樹——林中所見的箭鏃即其遺留。而彗星，便是雨神拋棄的雪茄。

sensitivity.note: Published public-domain ethnography (1907); paraphrase/quote only.

passages.text: The gods of rain, Yumchacob, are said to be rushing everywhere in a storm, and they use the thunder to announce their coming. The lightning is the whip with which they lash their horses. The rain gods carry bows and arrows and often fell trees in their journeys; sometimes the points of their arrows are found in the midst of the forest. This is the explanation given when a meteorite is found.
passages.note: Condensed from Tozzer (1907), Part III; not verbatim.

passages.text: The Yumchacob are great smokers. Comets are explained as the cigars which are being thrown away by the rain gods. As among the Lacandones, both the sun and his consort, the moon, are regarded as servants of the main god: the deities themselves never do any real work, and as the sun and moon are continually in motion, they cannot be regarded as anything more than servants.
passages.note: Condensed from Tozzer (1907), Part III; not verbatim.

title.en: Biting the Sun: The Noise of the Eclipse
title.zh: 咬日：蝕時之喧

region.en: Yucatan, Mexico
region.zh: 墨西哥猶加敦

period: Recorded 1901-03 (Tozzer fieldwork); Cogolludo 1688; published 1907

source.work: Alfred M. Tozzer, A Comparative Study of the Mayas and the Lacandones (1907), Part III; Diego Lopez de Cogolludo, Historia de Yucathan (1688)

summary.en: When the sun or moon is in eclipse, it is believed that an evil being is biting them. A great noise is made to frighten the animal away, and the children are struck so that they will cry. Cogolludo recorded the same tradition in 1688: at eclipses the Indians make their dogs howl, pinch them, and beat the boards, benches and doors, saying that the moon is dying or is being stung by a kind of ant called Xulab.
summary.zh: 日蝕或月蝕之時，人們相信有邪物正咬噬日月。於是制造巨響以驅其獸，並拍打孩童令其啼哭。科戈柳多1688年即記此俗：蝕時印第安人使犬哀嚎、擰其身、擊板凳門扉，言月亮垂死，或正被一種名為蘇拉布的蟻叮咬。

sensitivity.note: Published public-domain ethnography; paraphrase/quote only.

passages.text: When the sun or moon is in eclipse, it is believed that an evil being is biting them. A great noise is made to frighten the animal away. The children are struck so that they will cry. No trace of this idea can be found among the Lacandones; the belief that a great noise must be made is found among the Mexicans, and its origin may possibly be traced to them.
passages.note: Condensed from Tozzer (1907), Part III; not verbatim.

passages.text: Cogolludo (1688) records the same tradition: 'In the eclipses of Sun and Moon they use, by tradition of their ancestors, to make their dogs howl or cry out, pinching their body or ears, and give blows on the boards, benches and doors. They say the Moon is dying, or is being stung by a kind of ant that they call Xulab.'
passages.note: Condensed from Cogolludo, Historia de Yucathan (1688), Bk. IV, ch. 4, as quoted in Tozzer (1907); not verbatim.

title.en: The Clay Figure in the Doorway: Trial by Witchcraft
title.zh: 門檻下的黏土人：巫審

region.en: Yucatan, Mexico
region.zh: 墨西哥猶加敦

period: Recorded 1901-03 (Tozzer fieldwork), published 1907

source.work: Alfred M. Tozzer, A Comparative Study of the Mayas and the Lacandones (1907), Part III

summary.en: If a man is suspected of murder and the murdered man's family want him tried, one of the pulahob — the witch-spirits — is invoked: a small human figure of clay is made, a thorn placed in its head or heart, and it is secretly buried in the doorway of the suspect's hut. As he passes over it he becomes ill; if he is guilty he dies, otherwise he recovers.
summary.zh: 若有人涉嫌謀殺，而死者家屬欲究其罪，便召喚普拉霍布巫靈之一：塑一小黏土人，置荊刺於其頭或心，秘密埋於嫌疑者的門檻之下。他跨過之時即病；若有罪則死，無罪則癒。

sensitivity.note: Published public-domain ethnography (1907); paraphrase/quote only.

passages.text: The Pulahoob are a class of spirits corresponding to our idea of witches. They are employed to work evil toward wrongdoers. Their power can be exerted only over evil. If a person is supposed to be a murderer, and the family of the murdered man want him killed if he be the guilty one, one of the hechiceros (pulahoob) is invoked, and a small human figure in clay is made. In this effigy a thorn is placed either in the head or heart. This is then secretly buried in the doorway of the supposed murderer's hut.
passages.note: Condensed from Tozzer (1907), Part III; not verbatim.

passages.text: As he passes over it, he immediately becomes ill. If the man in question is guilty, he dies; otherwise he recovers. If one desires to send fever to punish a wrongdoer, chili is rubbed on the clay figure to be buried; and the guilty one who eats the poisoned food vomits forth tarantulas, snakes, earth, ashes, and pieces of crystal, and finally dies in great agony — while the innocent suffer no harm.
passages.note: Condensed from Tozzer (1907), Part III; not verbatim.

title.en: The Stabai in the Forks of Trees
title.zh: 樹杈間的斯塔拜

region.en: Yucatan, Mexico
region.zh: 墨西哥猶加敦

period: Recorded 1901-03 (Tozzer fieldwork), published 1907

source.work: Alfred M. Tozzer, A Comparative Study of the Mayas and the Lacandones (1907), Part III

summary.en: Stabai is a name used by Lacandones and Mayas alike. Among the Mayas it is the name given to a class of demons of snake form living in caves; they lie in wait, ready to spring out in human form and capture men, carrying them into the underworld or throwing them into a cenote. They are sometimes female in form, sitting in the forks of trees combing their hair.
summary.zh: 斯塔拜之名，拉坎敦人與馬雅人皆用。於馬雅人，乃指居於洞穴的蛇形惡靈一類；它們潛伏待機，化人形躍出擒人，或攜入冥界，或投之聖井。其形有時為女子，坐於樹杈之間梳理長髮。

sensitivity.note: Published public-domain ethnography (1907); paraphrase/quote only.

passages.text: Stabai is a term used both by the Lacandones and the Mayas, both now and at the time of the Conquest. It is given by Brasseur de Bourbourg as a god of the chase. Among the Lacandones it is a goddess residing in the rocks of the forest. Among the Mayas it is the name given to a class of demons of snake form living in caves.
passages.note: Condensed from Tozzer (1907), Part III; not verbatim.

passages.text: They lie in wait, ready to spring out in human form and capture men. These they carry into the underworld, or throw them into a cenote. They are sometimes female in form, and sit in the forks of trees combing their hair. The Yoyolche are in the same class as the stabai: each of their steps is half a league in length; they walk in the night and shake the houses as they pass.
passages.note: Condensed from Tozzer (1907), Part III; not verbatim.

title.en: Moremi's Vow at the Stream Esinmirin
title.zh: 莫雷米在埃辛米林溪畔的誓願

region.en: Ile-Ife, Nigeria (the stream Esinmirin where Moremi vowed)
region.zh: 奈及利亞伊費城（許願之溪埃辛米林）

period: Yoruba tradition recorded 1921 (Johnson)

source.work: Rev. Samuel Johnson, The History of the Yorubas (London, 1921), Part II ch. I, 'The Legend of Moremi and her Son'

summary.en: Moremi, wife of one of the ancient heroes of Ile-Ife — probably Oranmiyan — was a woman of great beauty and virtue with an only son, Ela or Olurogbo. The Ifes attributed their repeated sufferings under Igbo raids to the displeasure of their gods, for the attackers seemed not to be human beings but gods or demi-gods. Moremi resolved to find out what the Igbos really were: she repaired to the stream Esinmirin and vowed to its deity that if her plans proved successful she would offer the most costly sacrifice she could afford. "But," she said, "if I perish, I perish." She let herself be captured, was given among the booty to the King of the Igbos, learnt all their secrets — the raiders were mere men covered head to foot in Ekan grass and bamboo fibres — and extracted the secret of attacking them: "If your people know how to make a torch, and have the courage to rush amongst them with lighted torches, they cannot stand that."
summary.zh: 莫雷米乃伊費古英雄（或即奧蘭米揚）之妻，貌美德厚，獨子名埃拉（或奧盧羅格博）。伊費人飽受伊格博人劫掠，以為來犯者非人乃神，遂求諸神而無應。莫雷米決意查明真相：她到埃辛米林溪畔向溪神許願，若計成必獻上最貴重的祭品。「但若我死，便死吧。」她故意被擄，作為戰利品之一被獻給伊格博王，贏得信任，探得全部機密——所謂神兵不過是裹著埃坎草與竹纖維的凡人；又從丈夫口中套得破敵之法：「只要你們會造火把，敢舉著火把衝進他們陣中，他們必潰。」

sensitivity.note: Recorded 1921; the fullest written version of the Moremi legend, which Johnson compares to Jephthah's vow and to the Virgin-and-Child story 'perverted'. Moremi remains a honoured heroine of Ife (Edi festival). Cross-ref: yoruba-moremi-igbo-raid (Ogumefu's folk version).

passages.text: Moremi was the wife of one of the ancient heroes of Ile Ife, probably Oranmiyan. She was a woman of great beauty and virtue, and had an only son named Ela or Olurogbo. It happened that the city of Ife was at one time in a state of frequent commotion and unrest, owing to the repeated raids of a tribe of people called the Igbos. The Ifes attributed this affliction and distress to the displeasure of their gods, because those that attacked them from the Igbo territory appeared not to be human beings, but gods or demi-gods, and consequently the Ifes felt they could not withstand them; so these raiders used to make away with easy plunder, including their valuables, with their women and children. For this they propitiated and called upon their gods for help, but received no response.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Johnson, The History of the Yorubas, Part II ch. I (1921); not verbatim.

passages.text: Now this Moremi, fired with zeal and patriotism, was determined to do what she could to free her country from this calamity. She was resolved to find out what these Igbos really were, and how to fight them. To this end she repaired to a stream called Esinmirin, and there made a vow to the deity thereof that if she was enabled to carry out her plans and they proved successful, she would offer to the god the most costly sacrifice she could afford. Her plan was to expose herself to the raiders and get caught, and be taken to their country where she could best learn their secrets. "But," she said, "if I perish, I perish."
passages.note: Paraphrase of Johnson, The History of the Yorubas, Part II ch. I (1921); not verbatim.

passages.text: At the time of the next raid she was caught by the Igbos and taken to their country; being a woman of great beauty, she was given up, amongst others and sundry booty, to their king. Her beauty and virtue soon won her a place in the country and the confidence of the people; she became familiar with all their customs and learnt all their secrets: then she also learnt that those who were such objects of terror to her people were mere men, who covered themselves from head to foot with Ekan grass and bamboo fibres, making them appear extra human, and are nicknamed Eluyare. She extracted from her husband also the secret of attacking them successfully: "If your people know how to make a torch, and have the courage to rush amongst them with lighted torches, they cannot stand that."
passages.note: Paraphrase of Johnson, The History of the Yorubas, Part II ch. I (1921); not verbatim.

title.en: Olurogbo, Half Dead on the Altar, Climbs to Heaven
title.zh: 祭壇上半死的奧盧羅格博攀天而去

region.en: Ile-Ife, Nigeria (the altar where the vow was paid)
region.zh: 奈及利亞伊費城（還願的祭壇）

period: Yoruba tradition recorded 1921 (Johnson)

source.work: Rev. Samuel Johnson, The History of the Yorubas (London, 1921), Part II ch. I, 'The Legend of Moremi and her Son'

summary.en: Having freed her country for ever from the raids of the men once their terror, Moremi repaired to the stream with her offerings of lambs, rams and goats; but the god would not accept any of them. She offered a bullock, and the god refused that also. She prayed the priests to divine what would be acceptable, and the god demanded of her her only son. She gave up her only son in sacrifice to the gods in fulfilment of her vows; the Ife nation bewailed her loss and promised to be to her sons and daughters for the loss she had sustained for the salvation of her country. But Olurogbo, when supposed to be killed, was but half dead; he afterwards revived and rose again, and made a rope with which he climbed up into heaven — and all Ifes to this day have a full hope that he will come again to this world and reap the full reward of his good deeds.
summary.zh: 莫雷米以火攻秘計永絕大患之後，攜羊羔、公羊、山羊赴溪還願；神皆不納。獻上公牛，仍遭拒絕。她請祭司占問何物可納，神竟索其獨子。她依誓將獨子獻為祭品；伊費舉國哀慟，許諾永為其兒女，以補她為救國所失。然而祭壇上的奧盧羅格博僅是半死；他甦醒起身，編繩攀天而去——至今伊費人仍深信他終將重返人間，收穫善行的全數報償。

sensitivity.note: Recorded 1921; the vow's price and the promised return — a Yoruba death-and-return figure (Johnson notes the confused echo of Jephthah). Strong member of the resurrection cluster. Cross-refs: yoruba-moremi-esinmirin-vow, christian-passion-resurrection.

passages.text: Moremi feeling she was now conversant with everything amongst the Igbos, having disarmed any suspicion they may have entertained of her as a captive, suddenly escaped one day to her native land, and by making use of the secrets she had learnt, freed her country for ever from the raids of the men once their terror. It remained now for her to fulfil her vows.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Johnson, The History of the Yorubas, Part II ch. I (1921); not verbatim.

passages.text: She repaired to the stream with her offerings of lambs, rams, and goats for sacrifice, but the god would not accept any of these. She then offered a bullock, which the god also refused to accept; then she prayed the priests to divine for her what would be acceptable; this was done, and the god demanded of her her only son! She then gave up her only son in sacrifice to the gods in the fulfilment of her vows. The Ife nation bewailed her loss and promised to be to her sons and daughters, for the loss she had sustained for the salvation of her country.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Johnson, The History of the Yorubas, Part II ch. I (1921); not verbatim.

passages.text: Olurogbo however, when supposed to be killed, was but half dead; he afterwards revived and rose again, and made a rope with which he climbed up into heaven; and all Ifes to this day have a full hope that he will come again to this world, and reap the full reward of his good deeds.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Johnson, The History of the Yorubas, Part II ch. I (1921); not verbatim.

title.en: Sango Learns His Dead Mother's Name: Torosi
title.zh: 尚戈得知亡母之名——托羅西

region.en: Tapa (Nupe) country (symbolic pin: Elempe's grave where the name was spoken)
region.zh: 塔帕（努佩）之地（象徵定位：埃倫佩王陵——報名之處）

period: Yoruba tradition recorded 1921 (Johnson)

source.work: Rev. Samuel Johnson, The History of the Yorubas (London, 1921), Part II ch. I

summary.en: Sango, possessed with a desire to worship at the grave of his dead mother, could not so much as remember her name — she died when he was but a babe, a daughter of Elempe, the Nupe king who gave her to Oranyan in marriage. He commissioned a Tetu and a Hausa slave to go to the Tapa country and obtain from Elempe a horse and a cow for the sacrifice, charging them to listen carefully to the first name uttered in the invocation, which would be his mother's. The messengers were heartily welcomed and highly entertained; the Hausa forgot himself and his duty, but at the sacrifice the priest said at the grave: "Torosi, iya gbodo, listen to us, thy son Sango is come to worship thee." The Tetu noted the name Torosi; the drunken Hausa paid no heed. On their return the faithful Tetu was highly rewarded and the Hausa slave severely punished — 122 razor cuts slashed all over his body as a lasting warning.
summary.zh: 尚戈欲往亡母陵前致祭，卻連母親的名字也不記得——她在他還是嬰孩時便已去世；她是努佩王埃倫佩嫁給奧蘭揚的女兒。尚戈派一名特圖人與一名豪薩奴隸前往塔帕之地，向埃倫佩求一馬一牛為祭，並囑二人：祭祀時神職呼喊的第一個名字，必是他母親之名。二使受到盛情款待；豪薩人樂而忘形。祭司在墓前祝曰：「托羅西，伊亞格博多，聽著，你的兒子尚戈前來祭拜你了。」特圖人默記「托羅西」；醉醺醺的豪薩人卻渾然不覺。歸國之後，忠謹的特圖人重賞，豪薩奴隸重罰——全身剃刀紋一百二十二道，永為鑒戒。

sensitivity.note: Recorded 1921; the Torosi-name and razor-cut etiology in Johnson's royal history — the fuller court version of Ogumefu's tribal-marks tale (yoruba-sango-tribal-marks).

passages.text: Sango was now possessed with a desire of performing an act of filial piety. He wished to worship at the grave of his dead mother, but he did not so much as remember her name, for she died when he was but a babe. She was the daughter of Elempe, a Nupe king, who formed an alliance with Oranyan by giving him his daughter to wife, of which marriage Sango was the issue. Sango therefore commissioned a Tetu and a Hausa slave to proceed to the Tapa country, to his maternal grandfather Elempe, for the purpose of giving them a horse and a cow for the sacrifice. The King's charge to these messengers was, that they should listen carefully to the first name uttered in the invocation which evidently will be his mother's name.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Johnson, The History of the Yorubas, Part II ch. I (1921); not verbatim.

passages.text: The messengers were heartily welcomed and highly entertained by Elempe, their King's grandfather, so much so that the Hausa forgot himself and the duty he was charged with. At the time of the sacrifice, the priest said at the grave: "Torosi, iya gbodo, listen to us, thy son Sango is come to worship thee." The Tetu noted the name Torosi, but the Hausa, being far from sober, paid no heed to what was said; therefore, on their return home, the Tetu who had faithfully carried out his orders was highly rewarded, and the Hausa slave severely punished. The punishment meted out to him was 122 razor cuts slashed all over his body as a lasting warning for all time.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Johnson, The History of the Yorubas, Part II ch. I (1921); not verbatim.

title.en: The Scars That Took the Fancy of the King's Wives
title.zh: 王妃豔羨的疤紋與中計的奧約科羅

region.en: Oyokoro (Oyo), Nigeria (the city whose chiefs were marked as a trap)
region.zh: 奈及利亞奧約科羅（酋長們受紋中計之城）

period: Yoruba tradition recorded 1921 (Johnson)

source.work: Rev. Samuel Johnson, The History of the Yorubas (London, 1921), Part II ch. I

summary.en: The scars left by the 122 razor cuts strangely took the fancy of the King's wives, who thought they added comeliness and beauty, and advised that such marks should in future be made not upon a slave but on actual members of the royal family as distinctive of royalty. Sango took the advice and placed himself first in the hands of the markers, Babajegbe Osan and Babajegbe Oru; but he could stand only two cuts on each arm — these are the Ey o, two broad ribbon-marks from shoulder to wrist still worn by the royal family, whose members are termed Akeyo. When Sango determined to take Oyokoro, he sent the marked Hausa slave to show how beautiful the marks looked, and advised the prince of Oyokoro to submit himself and his principal chiefs to be thus marked for rank and beauty. On the third day, when they were very sore, Sango appeared with his forces: no resistance could be offered, and the city fell — shamefully and brutally he put to death the prince and his chiefs, the dupes of his stratagem. Thus the seat of government was permanently removed to Oyo.
summary.zh: 那一百二十二道剃刀疤竟令王妃們傾心，以為平添俊美；她們進言：此後刀紋不當施於奴隸，而應行於王室成員之身，以為王族之標記。尚戈率先受紋——由紋師巴巴傑格貝-奧桑與巴巴傑格貝-奧魯執刀——但他只能忍受每臂兩道：這便是「埃約」——肩至腕的兩道寬帶紋，至今仍是王族記號，族人稱「阿凱約」。尚戈欲取奧約科羅，便派帶紋的豪薩奴隸前往示美，勸該城王子與諸酋長為榮銜美觀而受紋。第三日，他們創痛難當之際，尚戈大軍壓境；城中無力抵抗，城池陷落——他殘忍處死中了圈套的王子與酋長們。王都自此永久遷於奧約。

sensitivity.note: Recorded 1921; the Akeyo royal marks etiology joined to a stratagem of war, in Johnson's royal history. Executions reported without graphic detail.

passages.text: The scars left by these wounds strangely took the fancy of the King's wives who thought that they added comeliness and beauty to the man, and therefore they advised that in future such marks should not be performed upon a slave, but on actual members of the royal family as distinctive of royalty. Sango took this advice, and placed himself first in the hands of the Olowolas (the markers) named Babajegbe Osan and Babajegbe Oru; but he could stand only two cuts on each arm, and forbade them to proceed any further. This is what is termed Ey o. The marks are to this day retained in the royal family, as a distinctive badge of royalty, and hence members of the royal family are termed Akeyo. They are two broad ribbon marks on the arms from the shoulder to the wrist.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Johnson, The History of the Yorubas, Part II ch. I (1921); not verbatim.

passages.text: When the King had determined upon taking Oyokoro, it occurred to him to employ this as a device by which he could effect his purpose easily without loss of lives. He thereupon sent the Hausa slave to Oloyo-koro, for him to see how beautiful this slave looks with these marks, and that it has been resolved to use the same as a mark of royalty; he therefore advised the Oloyo-koro to submit himself to be thus marked, with his principal chiefs for rank and beauty, stating that he himself had done so. To this they consented, and Babajegbe Osan and Babajegbe Oru were sent over there, and admirably did they perform their tasks. But on the third day, when the Oloyo-koro and his chiefs were very sore, Sango appeared with his forces against them; no resistance could be offered, and the city fell easily into his hands: shamefully and brutally he put to death the prince and his chiefs, the dupes of his stratagem. Thus the seat of government was permanently removed from Oko to Oyo the ancient Eyeo or Katunga.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Johnson, The History of the Yorubas, Part II ch. I (1921); not verbatim.

title.en: The Charm Tested on His Own Palace: Sango's Long Road to Koso
title.zh: 咒藥先試己宮——尚戈走向庫索的不歸路

region.en: Oyo and Koso, Nigeria (the hill Oke-Ajaka above the burning palace)
region.zh: 奧約與庫索（焚宮所在的奧凱-阿賈卡山）

period: Yoruba tradition recorded 1921 (Johnson)

source.work: Rev. Samuel Johnson, The History of the Yorubas (London, 1921), Part II ch. I

summary.en: Sango reigned seven years, marked by restlessness; he was said to have the knowledge of a preparation by which he could attract lightning. The palace at Oyo stood at the foot of the hill Oke-Ajaka; one day the King ascended it with his courtiers and slaves, among them his two favourites Biri and Omiran, minded to try the preparation — thinking it might have been damp and useless, he first made the experiment on his own house. A storm was raised, the lightning struck the palace before they came down the hill, and the buildings were on fire; many of Sango's wives and children perished. From a broken heart he resolved to abdicate and retire to the court of his maternal grandfather Elempe; all Oyo was astir to dissuade him, but he could not bear opposition and slew with his own sword some of the loyal subjects who remonstrated; he was said to have caused 160 persons to be slain in a fit of anger. Setting out with a few followers, his favourites Biri and Omiran one after another regretted the step and forsook him; left alone, ashamed to return, he climbed a shea-butter tree and hanged himself.
summary.zh: 尚戈在位七年，征伐不休；相傳他通曉一種引雷之法。奧約王宮築於奧凱-阿賈卡山麓；一日王與近臣、奴僕（含寵臣比里與奧米蘭）登山，欲試其藥——只因疑心藥已受潮失效，竟先在自己宮殿上試驗。頃刻風暴大作，眾人尚未下山，雷已殛宮，烈焰沖天；尚戈的多位妻室與子孫葬身火中。他心碎欲狂，決意退位投奔外祖埃倫佩。全城苦諫，他卻容不得半點異議，親手斬殺進言的忠臣；一怒之下被殺者達一百六十人。他僅攜少數隨從啟程；寵臣比里、奧米蘭先後悔悟棄他而去。孤身無助、歸又無顏，他攀上一株乳油木，自縊於枝頭。

sensitivity.note: Recorded 1921; Johnson's full court version of the charm-fire and flight (complementing Ogumefu yoruba-sango-lightning-storm and Frobenius's variants). Suicide reported as the recorded tradition states it.

passages.text: Sango reigned for seven years, the whole of which period was marked by his restlessness. He fought many battles and was fond of making charms. He was said to have the knowledge of some preparation by which he could attract lightning. The palace at Oyo was built at the foot of a hill called Oke Ajaka (Ajaka's hill). One day the King ascended this hill accompanied by his courtiers and some of his slaves, among whom were two favourites, Biri and Omiran; some of his cousins went with him, but none of his children. He was minded to try the preparation he had in hand; thinking it might have been damp and useless, he first made the experiment on his own house.
