But it took effect: a storm was immediately raised and the lightning had struck the palace before they came down the hill, and the buildings were on fire. Many of Sango's wives and his children perished in this catastrophe.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Johnson, The History of the Yorubas, Part II ch. I (1921); not verbatim.

passages.text: Sango, who was the author of his own misfortunes, became alarmed and dismayed at what had happened, and from a broken heart he was resolved to abdicate the throne and retire to the court of his maternal grandfather, Elempe, king of the Nupes. All Oyo was now astir, not only to sympathize with the King, but also to dissuade him from carrying out his resolution; but he could not bear any opposition, and so mad was he that he even used his sword against some of his loyal subjects who ventured to remonstrate with him, and who promised to replace for him his dead wives by others. He was said to have caused 160 persons to be slain in a fit of anger, of those who were showing much concern and over-anxiety on his behalf, and who would prevent him by force from carrying out his resolve.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Johnson, The History of the Yorubas, Part II ch. I (1921); not verbatim.

passages.text: Thus determined he set out on his fateful journey with a few followers. Biri his head slave and favourite was the first to regret the step taken, and to urge on his master to yield to the entreaties of those citizens of Oyo who with all loyalty promised to replace his losses and rebuild the palace; but finding the King inexorable, he forsook him and returned to the city with all his followers; Omiran likewise followed his example, and the King was thus left alone. He now repented his rashness, especially when he found himself deserted by his favourite Biri. He could not proceed alone, and for shame he could not return home, and so he was resolved to put an end to his own life; and climbing on a shea butter tree, he hanged himself.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Johnson, The History of the Yorubas, Part II ch. I (1921); not verbatim.

title.en: They Died With Their King: Biri at Koso, Oya at Ira
title.zh: 以身殉王——比里歿於庫索，奧雅歿於伊拉

region.en: Koso, Ira, Papo, Sele and Jakuta, near Oyo, Nigeria (the suicide-sites of the King's party)
region.zh: 庫索、伊拉、帕波、塞萊與賈庫塔（近奧約，王黨殉節之地）

period: Yoruba tradition recorded 1921 (Johnson)

source.work: Rev. Samuel Johnson, The History of the Yorubas (London, 1921), Part II ch. I

summary.en: On hearing of the King's death his personal friends followed his example and died with him: Biri committed suicide at Koso (where the King died), Omiran did the same, his cousin Omo Sinda at Papo, Babayanmi at Sele, Obei at Jakuta, and Oya his favourite wife at Ira. Sango was afterwards deified and is still worshipped by all of the Yoruba race as the god of thunder and lightning; in every Yoruba and Popo town, whenever a flash of lightning is followed by a peal of thunder, the populace shouts "Ka biye si" — welcome to your majesty, long live the King. Deified heroes and heroines are never spoken of as dead, but as having disappeared: "Oya disappeared in the town of Ira; Sango disappeared at Koso."
summary.zh: 噩耗傳來，王的近臣相繼以身相殉：比里歿於庫索（王崩之地），奧米蘭同之，堂親奧莫辛達歿於帕波，巴巴揚米歿於塞萊，奧貝歿於賈庫塔，愛妃奧雅歿於伊拉。尚戈後被尊為神，至今全約魯巴人奉為雷電之神；凡約魯巴與波波城鎮，電光之後雷聲一響，民眾便高呼「卡比耶西」——恭迎王駕，國王萬歲！成神者從不言「死」，只道「隱去」：諺云「奧雅隱於伊拉城，尚戈隱於庫索山」。

sensitivity.note: Recorded 1921; the martyr-list and disappearance formula. Suicides within the recorded tradition; reported without graphic detail.

passages.text: His friends hearing of this tragedy went immediately and performed for him the last act of kindness, by burying his remains under the same tree. On hearing of the King's death, his personal friends followed his example, and died with him: Biri committed suicide at Koso (where the King died), Omiran did the same, his cousin Omo Sinda committed suicide at Papo, Babayanmi at Sele, Obei at Jakuta, and Oya his favourite wife at Ira.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Johnson, The History of the Yorubas, Part II ch. I (1921); not verbatim.

passages.text: Thus ended the life of this remarkable personage, who once ruled over all the Yorubas and Popos. He was afterwards deified, and is still worshipped by all of the Yoruba race as the god of thunder and lightning. In every Yoruba and Popo town to this day, whenever there is a flash of lightning followed by a peal of thunder, it is usual to hear from the populace shouts of "Ka biye si" (welcome to your majesty, long live the King). Deified heroes and heroines are never spoken of as dead, but as having disappeared. Thus the saying: "Oya wole ni ile Ira, Sango wole ni Koso" — Oya disappeared in the town of Ira, Sango disappeared at Koso.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Johnson, The History of the Yorubas, Part II ch. I (1921); not verbatim.

title.en: Ajaka and the Nine Medicine-Men Who Could Not Be Kept
title.zh: 阿賈卡與留不住的九位術士

region.en: Oyo, Nigeria (the royal court where the magicians vanished)
region.zh: 奈及利亞奧約城（術士遁走的宮廷）

period: Yoruba tradition recorded 1921 (Johnson)

source.work: Rev. Samuel Johnson, The History of the Yorubas (London, 1921), Part II ch. I

summary.en: King Ajaka kept in his service medicine-men who made charms for him — Atagbin, Omo-onikoko, Abitibiti Onisegun, Paku, Teteoniru, Yonk, Oko-adan Egbeji, Alari baba isegun, and Elenre. After his wars, some humbly prayed to be allowed to return home; the King refused, fearing lest other kings might come into possession of the charms they had made. As they were determined to go, they showed by demonstrative proofs that the request was but courtesy: Paku fell down before him and disappeared; Teteoniru, Abitibiti Onisegun and Alari did the same; Egbeji threw up a ball of thread which hung suspended in space, climbed it and vanished. Elenre alone remained standing. "Kill me if you can," he replied; the sword broke in two, the spear bent and the spearman's arm withered, the great stone fell on him as light as a ball of cotton-wool.
summary.zh: 阿賈卡王豢養九位術士為他造符：阿塔格賓、奧莫-奧尼科科、阿比提比提、帕庫、泰特奧尼魯、約恩克、奧科-阿丹埃格貝吉、阿拉里與埃倫雷。戰事既畢，諸術士謙辭還鄉；王恐符咒落入他國之手而不許。他們遂以實證表明去意難留：帕庫當場倒地隱沒；泰特奧尼魯、阿比提比提、阿拉里相繼消失；埃格貝吉拋出一團懸空的線球，攀線升空而去。唯埃倫雷屹立不動。「殺我？你若能！」寶劍應聲兩斷，長矛彎折、矛手手臂枯萎，巨石壓身輕如棉絮。

sensitivity.note: Recorded 1921; Johnson's royal version of the magicians' contest (cf. Ogumefu yoruba-three-magicians-elenre), with Johnson's own note that the fable is Elijah 'in a perverted form'.

passages.text: He had in his service certain medicine men who made charms for him, viz., Atagbin, Omo-onikoko, Abitibiti Onisegun, Paku, Teteoniru, Yonk, Oko-adan Egbeji, Alari baba isegun, and Elenre. After his wars, some of these medicine men went up to him and humbly prayed to be allowed to return home; but the King refused to grant them leave, fearing lest their services might be required by some other kings, and in that way others might be in possession of the charms they made for him. As they were determined to go home they showed the King by demonstrative proofs that they made the request simply out of courtesy but that the King could not detain them: Paku fell down before him, and disappeared. Teteoniru, Abitibiti Onisegun, and Alari baba Isegun performed the same feat and vanished. Egbeji threw up a ball of thread which hung suspended in space, and he climbed up it and disappeared. Elenre alone remained standing before him.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Johnson, The History of the Yorubas, Part II ch. I (1921); not verbatim.

passages.text: Then said the King to him: "Elenre, you had better follow the examples of your colleagues and vanish, or I shall wreak my vengeance upon you for their disobedience." "Kill me if you can," replied Elenre. The King thereupon ordered him to be decapitated; but the sword was broken in two on the attempt. He then ordered him to be speared, but the spear became bent and the spearman's arm withered! He ordered a large stone to be rolled over him to crush him to death, but it fell on him as light as a ball of cotton-wool.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Johnson, The History of the Yorubas, Part II ch. I (1921); not verbatim.

title.en: The Head in the King's Hand Becomes a River
title.zh: 王掌中的頭顱化作長河

region.en: Oyo, Nigeria (Odo Elenre, Elenre's river, and Ijaechin's stagnant pool)
region.zh: 奈及利亞奧約城（埃倫雷之河與伊亞埃欽的死水潭）

period: Yoruba tradition recorded 1921 (Johnson)

source.work: Rev. Samuel Johnson, The History of the Yorubas (London, 1921), Part II ch. I

summary.en: The King and executioners were at their wits' end until one bethought himself to "plough with his heifer": Elenre's wife Ijaechin, prevailed upon, told them that no iron or steel could affect him — "Pull off a single blade of grass from the thatch of the house, and with that you can decapitate him." This was done; but instead of falling to the ground the head fell into the King's hand, and he involuntarily grasped it. He tried all he could to drop it, to no avail: any food brought to the King the head devoured, and drank all the water likewise, and the King, famishing, was really dying of hunger. Medicine-men of every tribe were sent for; as soon as anyone entered, the head would call him by name, tell out the composition of his charms, and ask "Do you think that can affect me?" — until came Agawo, who prostrated at a distance and entreated: "Who am I to oppose you? I came only in obedience to the King's commands, as I dare not refuse to come." "I will respect you because you are wise and respect yourself; I yield to your entreaties." Then, falling suddenly from the King's hands, Elenre's head became a flowing river known at Oyo to this day as Odo Elenre. His wife Ijaechin, who disclosed the secret, was also converted into a stream — but Elenre's head said to it "Thou shalt not flow," and she became a stagnant pool. From this incident King Ajaka made it a rule that no king should be present in person at an execution.
summary.zh: 君臣束手無策之際，有人想起「借他家中母牛犁田」：埃倫雷之妻伊亞埃欽受迫吐露——鋼鐵傷他不得，「從屋頂茅草抽一根草葉，便能斷他首級」。依計行之，頭顱落地卻不墜地，竟落進王掌之中，王身不由己緊握不放。任何飲食送到王前，那頭顱便吃盡喝光；王餓得形容枯槁，幾乎喪命。全國術士奉召前來驅邪——誰一進門，頭顱便喚其名、報出其符方，問「你以為這能奈何我？」直至阿加奧前來，遠遠俯伏哀求：「我何德何能敢與您為敵？我不過奉王命而來，不敢不來。」頭顱答：「你自重，我亦敬你；我依你所請。」言畢頭顱驟然離手落地，化作奔流長河——即今日奧約的「埃倫雷之河」。洩密的伊亞埃欽也化為溪流，頭顱卻道「你不許流動」，遂成死水一潭。自此阿賈卡王定規：君王永不親臨刑場。

sensitivity.note: Recorded 1921; the river-and-pool etiology completing the Elenre cycle (Johnson notes the Jordan parallel in his Elijah comparison). Cross-ref: yoruba-three-magicians-elenre.

passages.text: The King and the executioners were now at their wits' end, and then it occurred to one of them to plough with his heifer. His wife Ijaechin being prevailed upon, told them that no iron or steel can affect him: "Pull off a single blade of grass from the thatch of the house, and with that you can decapitate him." This was done, and the head was struck off, but instead of falling to the ground, it fell into the King's hand, and he involuntarily grasped it. The King tried all his best to drop it off, but to no avail. Any food brought to the King the head devoured, and drank all the water likewise. The King soon became famished, he was losing flesh, and was really dying from hunger.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Johnson, The History of the Yorubas, Part II ch. I (1921); not verbatim.

passages.text: All the medicine men of every tribe in the kingdom were sent for, to disenchant this alarming phenomenon: as soon as anyone entered, the head would call him by name, tell out the composition of his charms, and then ask "Do you think that can affect me?" Thus many were baffled, until at last came one Agawo; this man at once prostrated at a distance and entreated the head to forbear with him, saying: "Who am I to oppose you? In what am I better than my predecessors whom you have already foiled?
passages.note: Paraphrase of Johnson, The History of the Yorubas, Part II ch. I (1921); not verbatim.

passages.text: I came only in obedience to the King's commands as I dare not refuse to come." The head replied: "I will respect you because you are wise and respect yourself; I yield to your entreaties." Then, falling suddenly from the King's hands, Elenre's head became a flowing river known at Oyo to this day as Odo Elenre (Elenre's river). His wife Ijaechin who disclosed the secret of his strength was also converted into a stream, but Elenre's head said to it "Thou shalt not flow," therefore Ijaechin became a stagnant pool at Oyo unto this day. From this incident King Ajaka made it a rule that from henceforth no King should be present in person at an execution.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Johnson, The History of the Yorubas, Part II ch. I (1921); not verbatim.

title.en: Ajaka's Birds of War Across the Niger
title.zh: 阿賈卡的飛鳥大軍渡尼日河

region.en: The Niger crossing, Tapa country (symbolic pin: the Niger where the birds flew)
region.zh: 塔帕之地的尼日渡口（象徵定位：飛鳥掠過的尼日河）

period: Yoruba tradition recorded 1921 (Johnson)

source.work: Rev. Samuel Johnson, The History of the Yorubas (London, 1921), Part II ch. I

summary.en: King Ajaka, dethroned for being too peaceful, proved after his re-instatement a totally different man, more warlike even than his brother Sango. He led an expedition into the Tapa country, and tradition has it that he employed large and well-trained birds armed with arrows, and after crossing the Niger they showered down these deadly weapons upon the maternal relations of his brother Sango. What is certain is that the expedition was successful — but by what means it is not really known; for with the Yorubas, as with all superstitious peoples, brave deeds and extraordinary acts of daring are always attributed to the supernatural.
summary.zh: 因太過溫和而一度被廢的阿賈卡王，復位後判若兩人，比其兄尚戈更好征戰。他領兵遠征塔帕之地；相傳他動用受過大規模訓練的飛鳥，鳥爪縛箭，渡過尼日河後，便向其兄尚戈的母系親族漫天傾瀉這些奪命之矢。可以確定的是征伐大獲全勝——至於用何手段，實難考證；因為約魯巴人一如所有崇信神異的民族，凡勇武奇功，皆歸於超自然之力。

sensitivity.note: Recorded 1921; a marvel-tale of archer-birds reported by Johnson with his own sceptical note.

passages.text: King Ajaka who was dethroned for being too peaceful was now recalled to the throne. He proved after his re-instatement a totally different man to what he had been before, and showed himself more warlike than even his brother Sango. He led an expedition into the Tapa country. Tradition has it that he employed large and well-trained birds, armed with arrows, and after crossing the Niger they showered down these deadly weapons upon the maternal relations of his brother Sango. What is certain is that the expedition was successful, but by what means it is not really known. But thus it was with the Yorubas, as with all superstitious people, that brave deeds and extraordinary acts of daring are always attributed to the supernatural.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Johnson, The History of the Yorubas, Part II ch. I (1921); not verbatim.

title.en: The Thousand Skulls Worshipped as Orishala
title.zh: 千顆骷髏——奧里夏拉崇拜之源

region.en: Oyo, Nigeria (the reliquary of skulls kept in the royal city)
region.zh: 奈及利亞奧約城（王城中的骷髏聖龕）

period: Yoruba tradition recorded 1921 (Johnson)

source.work: Rev. Samuel Johnson, The History of the Yorubas (London, 1921), Part II ch. I

summary.en: Ajaka spent the latter part of his years waging intestine wars with 1060 of his chiefs and princes, among them the principal vassal kings, the Onikoyi, the Olugbon and the Aresa. He put to death all the vassal kings, 1060 in number, taken in war; the relics of their skulls were put together and are worshipped under the name of Orishala to this day — this, says Johnson, is the probable origin of that worship. He goes on to read the reign of the mythological heroes as garbled forms of scriptural stories: Elijah's slaughter of the priests of Baal perverted into Ajaka slaying his vassal kings, Egbeji climbing a cord into heaven as Elijah's ascent, Elenre's head becoming a river as Jordan was crossed.
summary.zh: 阿賈卡晚年與一千零六十名酋長王子連年內戰——其中不乏奧尼科伊、奧盧貢、阿雷薩等大藩之王。他把戰敗被俘的一千零六十位藩王盡數處死；其頭骨遺骸收集一處，至今以「奧里夏拉」之名受人崇拜——約翰遜認為，這很可能就是該崇拜的源頭。他又指出，這些神話時代君王的傳說皆是聖經故事的訛變：以利亞屠殺巴力眾祭司，被改寫成阿賈卡誅殺千位藩王；埃格貝吉攀繩上天，猶如以利亞升天；埃倫雷頭顱化河，彷彿約旦河的渡越。

sensitivity.note: Recorded 1921; cult-origin legend with mass execution of vassal kings reported as the recorded tradition states it, non-graphically. Johnson's Biblical-parallelistic reading is his own and is reported as such.

passages.text: He spent the latter part of his years in waging intestine wars with his subjects. He was said to have been engaged in civil wars with 1060 of his chiefs and princes, among whom were the principal vassal or provincial kings, the Onikoyi, the Olugbon, and the Aresa. He put to death all the vassal kings, 1060 in number, taken in war; the relics of their skulls were put together and are worshipped under the name of Orishala to this day. This is the probable origin of that worship.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Johnson, The History of the Yorubas, Part II ch. I (1921); not verbatim.

passages.text: The reign of the mythological heroes abound in garbled forms of scriptural stories, showing, as was remarked in the earlier part of this history, that the ancestors of the Yorubas were acquainted with Christianity in the land of their origin. The fable here related is evidently the story of Elijah in a perverted form: his putting to death so many priests of Baal has been perverted into Ajaka slaying all his vassal kings and their skulls converted to an object of worship; Egbeji climbing up a cord and disappearing as the saying goes, Egbeji ta kun o lo si Orun — Egbeji suspended a cord and by it went up to heaven; and the river Jordan crossed by Elijah suggested Elenre's head becoming a river.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Johnson, The History of the Yorubas, Part II ch. I (1921); not verbatim.

title.en: Gbonka Sits in the Fire and Walks Out of It
title.zh: 貢邦卡坐火而無恙

region.en: Oyo, Nigeria (the single combat and the pyre in the royal court)
region.zh: 奈及利亞奧約城（宮廷決鬥與柴堆）

period: Yoruba tradition recorded 1921 (Johnson)

source.work: Rev. Samuel Johnson, The History of the Yorubas (London, 1921), Part II ch. II

summary.en: Timi, the kinglet of Ede who had stopped paying his tribute of five cowries per trader, routed the King's troops. Eliri-onigbajo the Gbonka — the only man who dared oppose the King's own encroachments — was appointed to bring him in, the King secretly hoping his champion might fall. In the single combat Gbonka carried a viol of a drug with strong narcotic properties when inhaled, and Timi, rendered unconscious, was dispossessed and taken bound to Oyo. The King, pretending to doubt the fairness of the fight, ordered it repeated before him; Gbonka was again victorious, and Timi was instantaneously killed by the victor before the King and without his orders. To strike terror into the King, Gbonka ordered a pile made and pots of palm oil, nut oil and shea butter poured on it, went coolly and sat on the top, and ordered it set on fire — and when the pile was ablaze, the Gbonka disappeared. Tidings soon reached the court that he was seen dancing about the town; he entered the palace and challenged His Majesty to display feats similar to his own — and the King, having no alternative, took poison and died.
summary.zh: 伊德的小王蒂米停繳每商五貝幣的稅金，還擊潰了王師。宮中舉薦貢邦卡（埃利里-奧尼加喬）——唯一敢於抗衡王權擴張之人——前去拿人；王暗自指望他的勇士命喪其手。單打獨鬥中，貢邦卡攜一只嗅之即昏迷的藥瓶，蒂米不省人事，被繳械縛送奧約。王假意懷疑勝負是否公平，命二人當廷再戰；貢邦卡再勝，竟未奉王命當場擊斃蒂米。為震懾君王，貢邦卡命人堆起柴垛，澆以棕櫚油、堅果油與乳油，自己泰然坐上柴頂，命人點火——烈焰騰起，貢邦卡蹤影全無。不久王廷傳來消息：他正隨鼓手在城中起舞！他闖進王宮，喝令君王也顯一手同樣的神通——國王別無他法，服毒自盡。

sensitivity.note: Recorded 1921; the fire-ordeal of Gbonka mirrors Shango's fire-pile motif (cf. yoruba-shango-fire-pile-resurrection) in a court-legend register. Executions reported without graphic detail.

passages.text: Eliri-onigbajo the Gbonka was proposed to the King as the only man equal to the task of arresting Timi. But the Gbonka was already a powerful subject at Oyo, being the only man who dared to oppose the King's encroachments upon the liberties of the people; therefore he was at first loth to accede to this proposal, lest a success might add an additional lustre to the Gbonka's glory; but on second consideration he consented, secretly hoping he might fall by the hand of his brave antagonist. So the Gbonka was appointed.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Johnson, The History of the Yorubas, Part II ch. II (1921); not verbatim.

passages.text: The fight was limited to a single combat between the two chieftains. Timi armed himself with his bow and arrows, but the Gbonka carried a shield with which to defend himself against the powerful darts of his assailant. His own weapon of offence was a viol containing a drug with strong narcotic properties when inhaled, and by means of this Timi was soon rendered unconscious, and in this state he was dispossessed of his weapons and taken bound to Oyo. The King, pretending to be dissatisfied with the issue of the contest, doubting its fairness, ordered the same to be repeated in his presence. To his mortification the Gbonka was again victorious amid shouts of applause from the people. Timi was not only subdued but was also instantaneously killed by the victor before the King and without his orders.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Johnson, The History of the Yorubas, Part II ch. II (1921); not verbatim.

passages.text: The Gbonka, to show further what he could do, and to strike terror into the King, ordered a pile to be made, and pots of palm oil, nut oil, and shea butter to be poured on it; he then went coolly and sat on the top of it, and ordered it to be set on fire. All present were anxious for the consequence; but when the pile was ablaze, the Gbonka disappeared. Courtiers now began to congratulate the King on the fall of his enemy by his own hands; but he was apprehensive of some other issues. Tidings soon reached the court that the Gbonka, followed by drummers, was seen dancing about the town. The Gbonka, knowing the public feeling towards the King and his unpopularity, entered the palace and challenged His Majesty to display feats similar to his own, and said if he could not, he would be rejected. There being no alternative, the King took poison and died.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Johnson, The History of the Yorubas, Part II ch. II (1921); not verbatim.

title.en: Oluaso: The King of 320 Years and Three Sets of Twins
title.zh: 奧盧阿索——在位三百二十年與三對雙生

region.en: Oyo, Nigeria (the fifty-four palaces of the royal twins)
region.zh: 奈及利亞奧約城（五十四座王宮）

period: Yoruba tradition recorded 1921 (Johnson)

source.work: Rev. Samuel Johnson, The History of the Yorubas (London, 1921), Part II ch. II

summary.en: The unfortunate King was succeeded by a handsome and amiable prince called Oluaso, remarkable for his longevity and peaceful reign — his agnomen Osarewa S'akin, handsome but strong. He was a wise and affable sovereign fabled to have reigned 320 years and had 1460 children! Three times did nine of his wives bear him male twins in one day: the first set he named Omoja, the second Ona-aka, and the third Ona-isokun. Of these three sets of twins the last were the most popular, and kings were chosen from amongst them and their descendants; these names have become hereditary titles unto this day. The King built fifty-four palaces for them.
summary.zh: 不幸的國王之後，繼位的是俊美和藹的王子奧盧阿索，以長壽與太平之治著稱——綽號「奧薩雷瓦薩金」，俊美而剛強。相傳這位賢君在位三百二十年，得子女一千四百六十人！一日之間，九位王妃竟三度為他誕下男嬰雙生：第一對名奧莫賈，第二對奧納阿卡，第三對奧納伊索昆。三對之中，末對最得人望，歷代君王皆出自這一系及其後裔；這些名字至今仍為世襲尊號。國王為他們建了五十四座宮殿。

sensitivity.note: Recorded 1921; the hyperbolic reign-lengths and triple twin-births of Oluaso, anchoring the Ona-isokun royal line. Cross-refs: yoruba-ondo-twins-exile, yoruba-ibeji-ere-figures.

passages.text: The unfortunate King was succeeded by a handsome and amiable prince called Oluaso, who was remarkable for his longevity and peaceful reign. His agnomen was Osarewa S'akin, i.e., handsome but strong. He was a wise and affable sovereign fabled to have reigned for 320 years, and had 1460 children! Three times did nine of his wives bear him male twins in one day. The first set he named Omoja, the second Ona-aka, and the third Ona-isokun. Of these three sets of twins the last (Ona-isokun) were the most popular, and kings were chosen from amongst them and their descendants. These names have become hereditary titles unto this day. The King built 54 palaces for these.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Johnson, The History of the Yorubas, Part II ch. II (1921); not verbatim.

title.en: The Son Prayed For at the Grave: Iyayun and Kori
title.zh: 陵前求來的兒子——伊亞貴與科里

region.en: Oyo, Nigeria (Aganju's grave where the dynasty's survival was prayed for)
region.zh: 奈及利亞奧約城（在阿甘朱陵前求嗣之地）

period: Yoruba tradition recorded 1921 (Johnson)

source.work: Rev. Samuel Johnson, The History of the Yorubas (London, 1921), Part II ch. II

summary.en: Aganju, Ajaka's son who tamed wild animals and venomous reptiles and kept a tame leopard, waged war at the end of his reign on a namesake, the Onisambo, for refusing him the hand of his daughter Iyayun: four chiefs were captured, their towns destroyed, and the bride forcibly secured. His only son Lubego was discovered in illicit intercourse with the beloved Iyayun; the stern father pronounced the extreme penalty, and it was rigidly carried out — but the King was overcome with grief and died soon after, before the birth of a successor. The late king having no surviving son, the Basorun Erankogbina managed the kingdom, and the only hope of a direct successor was the child of Iyayun still unborn: sacrifices were offered frequently on the grave of Aganju, praying him to grant Iyayun a son, if his name was not to be forgotten and the dynasty end with him. When in due course Iyayun gave birth to a son, the joy of the populace was unbounded; he was named Kori. During Kori's minority Iyayun was declared Regent: she wore the crown, put on the royal robes, and was invested with the Ejigba, the Opa ileke and other royal insignia, and ruled the kingdom as a man until her son was of age.
summary.zh: 阿賈卡之子阿甘朱能馴服猛獸毒蛇，還養著一頭溫馴的花豹。他晚年為強娶同名藩王奧尼桑博之女伊亞貴而興兵：四位酋長被擒、城池被毀、新娘被強奪。其獨子盧貝戈竟與愛妃伊亞貴私通；嚴父判以極刑，依法執行——但國王悲慟欲絕，未及見嗣子出生便撒手人寰。先王無嗣，巴西倫埃蘭科格比納代攝國政；王統唯一的希望是伊亞貴腹中的孩子：人們頻頻到阿甘朱陵前獻祭，禱求他賜伊亞貴一子，否則他的名號將被遺忘、王朝亦將終絕。伊亞貴果真誕下男嬰，萬民歡騰；孩子取名科里。科里年幼，伊亞貴被立為攝政：她戴上王冠、穿上王服、受「埃吉巴」權杖與「奧帕伊萊克」等御物，儼然以男子之姿治國，直至兒子成年。

sensitivity.note: Recorded 1921; a queen-regent legend with posthumous-heir grave-prayers. The execution of Lubego is reported without graphic detail.

passages.text: Aganju, Ajaka's son, had a remarkable faculty of taming wild animals and venomous reptiles, several of which may be seen crawling about him; he had also in his house a tame leopard. Towards the end of his reign he waged war with a namesake of his, Aganju the Onisambo, for refusing him the hand of his daughter Iyayun. In this war four chiefs, viz. the Onisambo and his allies the Onitede, the Onimeri and the Alagbona, were captured, their towns destroyed, and the bride forcibly secured. The close of his reign was clouded by great domestic troubles: his only son Lubego was discovered having illicit intercourse with his beloved Iyayun, on whose account so many princes and people have lost their lives. The stern father was enraged beyond words, the sentence pronounced on him was the extreme penalty of the law, and it was rigidly carried out. But the King was overcome with grief; he died not long after this, even before the birth of a successor to the throne.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Johnson, The History of the Yorubas, Part II ch. II (1921); not verbatim.

passages.text: The late King having no surviving son, Erankogbina the Basorun was left to manage the affairs of the kingdom. The only hope of a direct successor to the throne was the child of Iyayun still in utero; hence sacrifices were offered frequently on the grave of Aganju, praying him to grant Iyayun a son, if his name is not to be forgotten and the dynasty end with him. When in due course therefore Iyayun gave birth to a son, the joy of the populace was unbounded; he was named Kori. During Kori's minority, Iyayun was declared Regent; she wore the crown, and put on the royal robes, and was invested with the Ejigba, the Opa ileke and other royal insignia, and ruled the kingdom as a man until her son was of age.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Johnson, The History of the Yorubas, Part II ch. II (1921); not verbatim.

title.en: "My Father Will Find the Koran for Me"
title.zh: 「我父自會為我尋回《可蘭經》」

region.en: Oyo, Nigeria (the Basorun's house struck the next morning)
region.zh: 奈及利亞奧約城（次日遭雷擊的巴西倫宅邸）

period: Yoruba tradition recorded 1921 (Johnson)

source.work: Rev. Samuel Johnson, The History of the Yorubas (London, 1921), Part III ch. I

summary.en: One Alaja-eta, a Hausa trader at Oyo, was plundered of his goods under the pretext that he was bringing bad charms into the city; among the confiscated goods was his Koran, which he prized more than all else. He appealed to King Aole, who from a sense of justice ordered everything restored — all but the Koran. The Hausa appealed again; the King insisted that search be made and the lost Koran restored. The Basorun, in whose possession it probably was, refused, and told the King it could not be found. His Majesty felt this keenly as an insult to his dignity: "Very well then, if you cannot find it, my father (meaning the deified Sango) will find the Koran for me." As the god Sango is reputed to take vengeance on thieves and liars by burning their houses, so the next day, when lightning struck the Basorun's house, great was his rage against the King for being instrumental in convicting him of theft and lying — the ceremony of appeasing the god entailing heavy expenses on him who, had it been another man's house, might have gone shares in the fines. Thus he became the King's enemy.
summary.zh: 奧約城中的豪薩商人阿拉賈-埃塔被誣「攜邪符入城」，貨物盡遭搶奪；被抄之物中有一部他視若性命的《可蘭經》。他向阿奧萊王申冤；王秉公下令全數發還——唯經書未還。豪薩人再訴，王堅持搜查歸還。經書多半在巴西倫（首相）之手，他卻拒不交出，回稟「查無此物」。國王深以為辱：「好——你既尋不著，我父（即指已故成神的尚戈）自會為我尋回！」尚戈素以火焚宅第懲治竊賊謊者；次日雷電果然擊中巴西倫的房屋。他怒不可遏——王藉神明之力坐實了他竊盜與說謊之罪，而安神謝罪的巨費本可由他分潤罰金。自此他成了國王的死敵。

sensitivity.note: Recorded 1921; the lightning-justice episode that opens the Oyo revolution, in Johnson's historical narrative.

passages.text: One Alaja-eta, a Hausa trader at Oyo, was plundered of his goods, under the pretext that he was bringing bad charms into the city. Among his confiscated goods was his Koran, which he prized more than all his other stolen property. He appealed to the King, and he, from a sense of justice, ordered that all his goods be restored to him. All but the Koran were accordingly restored. The Hausa again appealed to the King for this his most valued treasure; the King insisted that search should be made and the lost Koran be restored. The Basorun, in whose possession it probably was, or who at any rate knew where it could be found, refused to restore it, and told the King it could not be found!
passages.note: Paraphrase of Johnson, The History of the Yorubas, Part III ch. I (1921); not verbatim.

passages.text: His Majesty felt this keenly as an insult to his dignity; he was heard to say: "Is it come to this that my commands cannot be obeyed in my own capital? Must it be said that I failed to redress the grievance of a stranger in my town? That he appealed to me in vain?" Turning to the Basorun and pointing upwards, he said: "Very well then, if you cannot find it, my father (meaning the deified Sango) will find the Koran for me." As the god Sango is reputed to take vengeance on thieves and liars by burning their houses, so the next day, when lightning struck the Basorun's house, great was his rage against the King for being instrumental in convicting him of theft and lying! The ceremony of appeasing the god by the devotees entailed heavy expenses on the Basorun, who, had it been another man's house, might have gone shares with the Alafin in the fines imposed upon the sufferers. In this way he became the King's enemy.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Johnson, The History of the Yorubas, Part III ch. I (1921); not verbatim.

title.en: Apata Odaju, the Rock of the Heartless
title.zh: 阿帕塔奧達茹——無情者之岩

region.en: Apomu, Nigeria (the frontier market and the rock where the sold friend was rescued)
region.zh: 奈及利亞阿波穆（邊貿市集與救人時的無情之岩）

period: Yoruba tradition recorded 1921 (Johnson)

source.work: Rev. Samuel Johnson, The History of the Yorubas (London, 1921), Part III ch. I

summary.en: Apomu was the market town where Oyos, Ifes, Owus and Ijebus met for trade, in Ife territory on the border of the Olowu's dominion; raiding and man-stealing were rife, and Oyos coming from afar were in the greatest danger. Aole, then a private man, used to trade there with a friend who was also his attendant — and on one occasion he bartered away his own friend for merchandise! The Ijebus were actually taking him away when word reached the Bale of Apomu that an Oyo man was being sold; by the Bale's prompt action the man was rescued at a spot named Apata Odaju, the rock of the heartless. Investigation showed who the slave-dealer was; but as Aole was an Akeyo, a prince, who could not be more severely dealt with, he was ordered by the Bale to be severely flogged — and when Aole came to the throne he named the Bale of Apomu as his enemy, and Apomu was doomed. The faithful Bale took refuge with the Ooni of Ife, his over-lord, but the offence being against the Suzerain, even the Ooni could not save him: to save his town and people from destruction he committed suicide, and his head was cut off and sent to Oyo to appease the offended monarch.
summary.zh: 阿波穆是奧約人、伊費人、奧武人與伊傑布人互市的邊貿重鎮，地處伊費境內、奧洛烏轄區邊緣；掠人販奴之風盛行，遠道而來的奧約人首當其衝。布衣時代的阿奧萊常與一位兼任侍從的好友在此貿易——他竟把摯友折價換了貨物！伊傑布人正要將人帶走時，有人報知阿波穆的巴萊：有奧約人正被販賣。巴萊當機立斷，在一處名叫「阿帕塔奧達茹」——無情者之岩——的地方將人救下。查明販奴者正是阿奧萊；但他是王族「阿凱約」，不能重懲，巴萊便下令重責鞭刑。阿奧萊登基後，點名巴萊為敵，阿波穆遂遭滅頂之災。忠直的巴萊投奔宗主奧尼求庇，但此仇直犯宗主，奧尼亦無能為力；為免全城生靈塗炭，他自盡殉城，頭顱被送往奧約以平息盛怒的君王。

sensitivity.note: Recorded 1921; the slave-selling anecdote and the loyal Bale's suicide that sparked the destruction of Apomu. Suicide reported as the recorded tradition states it.

passages.text: Apomu was the market town where Oyos, Ifes, Owus, and Ijebus met for trade. It was situated in Ife territory, and in the border of the Olowu's dominion. Raiding and man-stealing were rife at those times. Oyos particularly were in greater danger, as they came from afar. Aole, who was then a private man, used to trade in these parts with a friend who was also his attendant; and on one occasion, he bartered away his friend for merchandise! So faithless and heartless were the princes in those days. The Ijebus were actually taking him away when it was reported to the Bale of Apomu that an Oyo man was being sold away; fortunately for the man, by the prompt action of the Bale, he was rescued at a certain spot named Apata Odaju (the rock of the heartless), perhaps so named from this circumstance, and brought before the Bale.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Johnson, The History of the Yorubas, Part III ch. I (1921); not verbatim.

passages.text: Investigation soon showed who the slave-dealer was; but as Aole was an Akeyo (Prince) and could not more severely be dealt with, in order that justice may not miscarry, he was ordered by the Bale to be severely flogged. This was the reason why Aole now named the Bale of Apomu as his enemy, and hence Apomu was doomed. When the Bale of Apomu heard that war was declared against his town on his account, he took refuge in the court of the Ooni of Ife his over-lord, whose orders he had obeyed. But as the offence was against the Suzerain, even the Ooni could not save him; so this faithful chief, in order to save his town and his people from destruction, committed suicide, and his head was cut off and sent to Oyo to appease the offended monarch.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Johnson, The History of the Yorubas, Part III ch. I (1921); not verbatim.

title.en: Aole's Three Arrows: The Curse That Broke the Empire
title.zh: 阿奧萊的三支箭——裂帝國之咒

region.en: Oyo, Nigeria (the palace quadrangle where the arrows were loosed)
region.zh: 奈及利亞奧約城（放箭發咒的王宮庭院）

period: Yoruba tradition recorded 1921 (Johnson)

source.work: Rev. Samuel Johnson, The History of the Yorubas (London, 1921), Part III ch. I

summary.en: Sent against Iwere — impregnable to the simple weapons of the day — under oaths binding the Kakanfo to conquer within three months or die, the army mutinied before its walls: "O Ya!" — now is the time — and the royal party was massacred. Forty-two days the insurgent army stood before Oyo; at last an empty covered calabash was sent to the King — for his head. There being no alternative, His Majesty set his house in order; but before he committed suicide he stepped out into the palace quadrangle with face stern and resolute, carrying in his hands an earthenware dish and three arrows. He shot one to the North, one to the South, and one to the West, uttering those ever-memorable imprecations: "My curse be on ye for your disloyalty and disobedience, so let your children disobey you. If you send them on an errand, let them never return to bring you word again. To all the points I shot my arrows will ye be carried as slaves. My curse will carry you to the sea and beyond the seas; slaves will rule over you, and you their masters will become slaves." Then he raised and dashed the earthenware dish on the ground, smashing it into pieces: "Igba la isu a ki isu awo, beheni ki oru mi o se to! to!" — a broken calabash can be mended, but not a broken dish; so let my words be — irrevocable! He then took poison and died, after which the camp was broken up and each of the chiefs repaired to his own place; from this time the spirit of rebellion spread throughout the kingdom, and tribute was no longer paid to the King.
summary.zh: 卡坎佛（大元帥）受誓約束：三月不克，唯有自裁。諸侯便設計把大軍誘到天險奧維雷城下，軍中一聲「奧雅！」——時機已到——王黨盡遭屠戮。叛軍圍奧約四十二日；末了，一只有蓋空葫蘆被送入宮中——向王索頭。君王自知無路可走，先安排好家事；臨終之前，他面色沉毅地走進王宮庭院，手捧一件陶盤與三支箭。他向北、向南、向西各射一箭，朗聲立下永載史冊的咒誓：「爾等不忠不順，我咒爾等！爾之子孫亦必忤逆爾等。爾差遣他們辦事，叫他們一去不回、音信全無。我箭射向何方，爾等便被賣作奴隸流落何方。我的詛咒要把你們帶到海濱、越過重洋；奴隸將統治你們，而你們這些主人也要淪為奴隸。」隨後他把陶盤高舉擲地，摔得粉碎：「葫蘆碎了尚可修補，陶盤碎了便無可挽回——我言已出，絕不更改！」言畢服毒而崩。叛營隨之散去，諸侯各歸封地；自此叛離之風蔓延全國，貢賦再也不入王庭。

sensitivity.note: Recorded 1921; the famous dying curse of Aole (Arogangan), the prophetic charter of the Yoruba nineteenth-century wars and slave-raiding in Johnson's history. Suicide reported as the recorded tradition states it. Cross-tradition cluster: prophetic curse (cf. celtic-fedelm-prophecy-red).

passages.text: The King's counsellors advised that the Kakanfo and the army should be sent against Iwere, a place fortified by nature and by art, and impregnable to the simple weapons of those days; and as the Kakanfo, by the oaths of his office, must either conquer within three months or die, and Iwere is impregnable, he will have no other alternative but, as in honour bound, to make away with himself. It was arranged that he should not be forewarned but decoyed to that place until he found himself at the foot of the hill on which Iwere was built.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Johnson, The History of the Yorubas, Part III ch. I (1921); not verbatim.

passages.text: But private intelligence had reached the Kakanfo at Ilorin of all the plots and intrigues going on in the capital. The army at length stood before Iwere, and the royal party, pointing to it, said: "This is the town to be taken by the order of the Alafin." The time was now come for the mutiny to break out: the watchword was given "O Ya!" (now is the time) and so the whole army turned their swords upon the royal party and massacred them. Chief Opele of Gbogun in particular was famous as a swordsman, and took to himself a name "A ri agada pa aburo Oba" — one who has a blade for slaying the King's brother.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Johnson, The History of the Yorubas, Part III ch. I (1921); not verbatim.

passages.text: The siege was immediately raised, and the whole army stood before the city for forty and two days. At last an empty covered calabash was sent to the King — for his head. A plain indication that he was rejected. There being no alternative, His Majesty set his house in order; but before he committed suicide, he stepped out into the palace quadrangle with face stern and resolute, carrying in his hands an earthenware dish and three arrows. He shot one to the North, one to the South, and one to the West, uttering those ever-memorable imprecations: "My curse be on ye for your disloyalty and disobedience, so let your children disobey you. If you send them on an errand, let them never return to bring you word again. To all the points I shot my arrows will ye be carried as slaves. My curse will carry you to the sea and beyond the seas; slaves will rule over you, and you their masters will become slaves."
passages.note: Paraphrase of Johnson, The History of the Yorubas, Part III ch. I (1921); not verbatim.

passages.text: With this he raised and dashed the earthenware dish on the ground, smashing it into pieces, saying: "Igba la isu a ki isu awo, beheni ki oru mi o se to! to!" — a broken calabash can be mended, but not a broken dish; so let my words be — irrevocable! He then took poison and died, after which the camp was broken up, and each of the chiefs repaired to his own place. From this time the spirit of rebellion and independence began to spread throughout the kingdom: tribute was no longer paid to the King, and this was the commencement of the break-up of the unity of the Yoruba kingdom and the beginning of the tribal independence.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Johnson, The History of the Yorubas, Part III ch. I (1921); not verbatim.

title.en: The Dwarf of Uxmal and the House of the Diviner
title.zh: 烏斯馬爾的侏儒與占卜者之屋

region.en: Uxmal, Yucatan, Mexico
region.zh: 墨西哥猶加敦烏斯馬爾

period: Collected from local tradition c. 1840 (Stephens 1841-43); retold by Charnay 1887

source.work: Desire Charnay, The Ancient Cities of the New World (1887), reproducing the legend collected by John Lloyd Stephens (Incidents of Travel in Yucatan, 1843)

summary.en: A childless old woman hatches a dwarf from an egg; he grows wise but not tall. In trials of strength before the king he matches every feat — the stone, the bundles of cogoiol wood beaten on the head — because his mother's tortilla protects him. Ordered to build a palace taller than any other overnight, he wakes in the finished palace that still stands at Uxmal; the second blow of his little hand breaks the king's skull, and the people proclaim the dwarf their sovereign.
summary.zh: 無子的老嫗自一枚蛋孵出侏儒；他聰慧過人卻不再長高。國王面前，他力試屢勝——舉石、以硬木束互擊頭顱——因其母的玉米餅護其頭。國王限其一夜建成高於一切的宮殿，翌晨侏儒已睡於竣工的宮殿之中——即烏斯馬爾今存的占卜者之屋；而他小手的第二擊便碎了國王的頭顱，眾人遂擁侏儒為王。

sensitivity.note: Yucatec folk legend recorded by travelers; paraphrase of public-domain texts only.

passages.text: An old woman lived alone in her hut, rarely leaving her chimney-corner. She was much distressed at having no children; in her grief, one day she took an egg, wrapped it up carefully in a cotton cloth, and put it in a corner of her hut. She looked at it every day with great anxiety; one morning, however, she found the shell broken, and a lovely tiny creature was stretching out its arms to her.
passages.note: Quoted from Charnay (1887) reproducing Stephens (1843); lightly condensed; not verbatim throughout.

passages.text: The old woman was in raptures; she took it to her heart, gave it a nurse, and was so careful of it that at the end of a year the baby walked and talked as well as a grown-up man, but he stopped growing. She exclaimed that the baby should be a great chief, and one day told him to go to the king's palace and engage him in a trial of strength. The dwarf begged hard not to be sent on such an enterprise, but the old woman insisted, and he was obliged to obey.
passages.note: Condensed from Charnay (1887) reproducing Stephens (1843); not verbatim throughout.

passages.text: The king smiled and asked him to lift a stone of three arobes; the child returned crying to his mother, who sent him back, saying: 'If the king can lift the stone, you can lift it too.' The king did take it up, but so did the dwarf. His strength was tried in many other ways, but all the king did was as easily done by the dwarf. Wroth at being outdone by so puny a creature, the prince told the dwarf that unless he built a palace loftier than any in the city, he should die.
passages.note: Condensed from Charnay (1887) reproducing Stephens (1843); not verbatim throughout.

passages.text: The affrighted dwarf returned to the old woman, who bade him not despair, and the next morning they both awoke in the palace which is still standing. The king, amazed, sent for the dwarf to collect two bundles of cogoiol, with one of which he would strike the dwarf on the head and consent to be struck in return. The old woman placed a tortilla on his head. The king broke his whole bundle on the dwarf's head without hurting him in the least; the dwarf struck, and at the second blow the king's skull was broken to pieces. The spectators immediately proclaimed the victorious dwarf their sovereign.
passages.note: Condensed from Charnay (1887) reproducing Stephens (1843); not verbatim throughout.

canonical_translation: Stephens, Incidents of Travel in Yucatan (1843), via Charnay (1887)

narrative.en:
The dwarf legend is the signature folk narrative of Uxmal, told to John Lloyd Stephens at the ruins in 1841-43 and retold by Desiré Charnay from his pages. A childless old woman, alone in her hut, grieves that she has no children; one day she takes an egg, wraps it in a cotton cloth, and sets it in a corner of her hut. It does not change until one morning the shell is broken and a tiny, lovely creature stretches out its arms to her. She gives it a nurse and tends it so carefully that within a year the baby walks and talks like a grown man — but then he stops growing. In her joy the old woman declares the child will be a great chief, and sends him to the king's palace to engage the sovereign in a trial of strength.

The trials follow the folk-tale pattern of the outwitted king. The king bids the dwarf lift a stone of three arobes; the child runs home crying, but his mother sends him back with the words 'If the king can lift it, you can lift it too' — and the dwarf lifts what the king lifts, and matches every feat. Furious at being outdone by a puny creature, the king sets a deadly condition: build a palace loftier than any in the city overnight, or die. The old woman forbids despair, and the next morning the dwarf awakes in the completed palace — the House of the Dwarf, the Casa del Adivino or Pyramid of the Magician, the tallest and steepest structure at Uxmal, whose enormous rounded pyramid still dominates the site.

The final ordeal closes the tale as a succession myth: the king must break a bundle of cogoiol wood over the dwarf's head and take a blow in return, with the ordeal held before all the grandees of the state. The old woman places a tortilla on the dwarf's head; the king shatters his whole bundle to no effect; when his own word binds him to the return blow, the dwarf strikes once and then a second time, and the king's skull breaks to pieces. The spectators proclaim the victorious dwarf their sovereign, and the old woman vanishes — only to reappear, in the tale's coda, as the water-selling woman by the subterranean river at Mani, whose serpent devours the innocent babies.

As a corpus record the episode is the Maya counterpart of the 'unfinished palace in a night' cycle (parallels exist in Irish and South American tale types) fused with a kingship-transfer myth: the dwarf's victory founds a new dynasty of the diviner's house. The Casa del Adivino's own architecture — built over and enclosing an older inner temple — was read by travelers as the material signature of the legend's claim that the dwarf's palace rose in a single night over an older world.

functions: Founding legend of the House of the Dwarf / Pyramid of the Magician at Uxmal
Succession myth: the smallest challenger replaces the proud king
Etiology of the Casa del Adivino's enclosed older inner temple

title.en: The Old Woman of Mani and the Water-Selling Serpent
title.zh: 馬尼老嫗與賣水的巨蛇

region.en: Mani, Yucatan, Mexico
region.zh: 墨西哥猶加敦馬尼

period: Collected c. 1840 (Stephens 1843); retold by Charnay 1887

source.work: Desire Charnay, The Ancient Cities of the New World (1887), reproducing the Uxmal legend cycle of Stephens (1843)

summary.en: After the dwarf's victory the old woman disappeared; but at Mani, fifty miles away, a deep well leads to a subterraneous passage reaching as far as Merida, where an old woman sits on the bank of a river shaded by a great tree, with a serpent by her side. She sells water in small quantities and accepts no money — she must have human beings, innocent babies, which are devoured by the serpent. She is the dwarf's mother.
summary.zh: 侏儒得勝之後，老嫗消失；但在五十里外的馬尼，一口深井通向遠及梅里達的地下甬道，一老嫗坐於河畔大樹之蔭，旁有巨蛇。她零星賣水，不收金錢——她要的是人，是無辜的嬰兒，皆為巨蛇所吞。她正是侏儒之母。

sensitivity.note: Yucatec folk legend recorded by travelers; paraphrase of public-domain texts only.

passages.text: After this the old woman disappeared; but in the village of Mani, fifty miles distant, is a deep well leading to a subterraneous passage which extends as far as Merida. In this passage is an old woman sitting on the bank of a river shaded by a great tree, having a serpent by her side.
passages.note: Quoted from Charnay (1887) reproducing Stephens (1843); lightly condensed; not verbatim throughout.

passages.text: She sells water in small quantities, accepting no money, for she must have human beings, innocent babies, which are devoured by the serpent. This old woman is the dwarf's mother — the giver of the palace gone down into the water, the price of whose gifts is still paid in children.
passages.note: Condensed from Charnay (1887) reproducing Stephens (1843); not verbatim throughout.

title.en: The House of the Old Woman
title.zh: 老嫗之屋

region.en: Uxmal, Yucatan, Mexico
region.zh: 墨西哥猶加敦烏斯馬爾

period: Building named in local tradition; described by Stephens 1843

source.work: John Lloyd Stephens, Incidents of Travel in Yucatan, vol. I (1843), on the ruins of Uxmal

summary.en: Among the buildings of Uxmal, near the Governor's Palace and the House of the Turtles, stands the Casa de la Vieja — the House of the Old Woman — named in local tradition for the aged mother of the dwarf, the sorceress of the hatched egg, whose hut is remembered in the stone of the city she helped to raise.
summary.zh: 烏斯馬爾諸建築之間，在總督宮與龜屋之旁，立有名為卡薩·德拉·維赫的「老嫗之屋」——以侏儒之母、孵蛋的老巫嫗為名；傳說中其草屋所居，被記於其助建之城的石構之中。

sensitivity.note: Yucatec folk legend recorded by travelers; paraphrase of public-domain text only.

passages.text: In the foreground is the inner facade of the front range of the Monjas; to the left, in the distance, appears the Casa de la Vieja, or of the Old Woman; and rising grandly above the front of the Monjas are the House of the Turtles, that of the Governor, and the Casa de Palomos, or the House of the Pigeons.
passages.note: Condensed from Stephens, Incidents of Travel in Yucatan, vol. I (1843); not verbatim throughout.

passages.text: The name preserves the old woman of the dwarf legend: the childless sorceress who hatched the egg, protected her son with a tortilla, and vanished when he became sovereign — remembered at Uxmal in a stone house, as her own hut was of thatch in the tale.
passages.note: Condensed from Stephens (1843) and the dwarf legend cycle; not verbatim throughout.

title.en: Fresh Copal in the House of the Dwarf, 1656
title.zh: 1656年，侏儒之屋中仍燃新柯巴脂

region.en: Uxmal, Yucatan, Mexico
region.zh: 墨西哥猶加敦烏斯馬爾

period: Recorded by Cogolludo 1656; reproduced in Charnay 1887

source.work: Diego Lopez de Cogolludo, Historia de Yucathan (1688), as reproduced in Charnay, The Ancient Cities of the New World (1887)

summary.en: Padre Cogolludo, who visited the temple at Uxmal in 1656, complains of the steep staircase that made his head swim, and finds in one of its apartments offerings of cocoa and copal burned very recently — fifteen years after the Conquest the natives were still sacrificing to their gods and practising their superstitions in their own temples.
summary.zh: 1656年訪烏斯馬爾神廟的科戈柳多神父，抱怨其陡階令人眩暈，並在其一室中發現不久前焚燒的可可與柯巴脂祭品——征服後十五年，土人仍在自家神廟中向其神獻祭、行其舊俗。

sensitivity.note: Colonial missionary record; paraphrase of public-domain text only.

passages.text: Padre Cogolludo, who visited this temple in 1656, is the first to complain of the steep staircase, which caused his head to swim. He found in one of these apartments offerings of cocoa and copal which had been burnt very recently; consequently, fifteen years after the Conquest the natives were still sacrificing to their gods, and practising their superstitions in their own temples.
passages.note: Condensed from Charnay (1887) quoting Cogolludo; not verbatim throughout.

title.en: The Indians Cling to Their Ruins: The Title Papers of Uxmal
title.zh: 土人戀其遺址：烏斯馬爾地契文書

region.en: Uxmal, Yucatan, Mexico
region.zh: 墨西哥猶加敦烏斯馬爾

period: Title documents 1683-88; reproduced by Stephens 1843

source.work: John Lloyd Stephens, Incidents of Travel in Yucatan, vol. I (1843), title papers of Uxmal

summary.en: The title papers of Uxmal record that, one hundred and forty years after the founding of Merida, the buildings were still regarded with reverence by the Indians, forming the nucleus of a scattered population resorting to them for religious rites at a distance from the eyes of the Spaniards; Cogolludo had seen in the House of the Dwarf 'the marks of copal recently burned', the evidence of some idolatry recently committed.
summary.zh: 烏斯馬爾地契文書記載：梅里達建城一百四十年後，土人仍崇敬其建築，散落的人群以之為核，避西班牙人耳目而行其祭儀；科戈柳多曾在侏儒之屋見「新焚柯巴脂之痕」，證明新近仍有偶像崇拜。

sensitivity.note: Colonial-era documents; paraphrase of public-domain text only.

passages.text: The reader will perceive that we have here two distinct, independent witnesses testifying that, one hundred and forty years after the foundation of Merida, the buildings of Uxmal were regarded with reverence by the Indians; that they formed the nucleus of a dispersed and scattered population, and were resorted to for the observance of religious rites at a distance from the eyes of the Spaniards.
passages.note: Condensed from Stephens, Incidents of Travel in Yucatan, vol. I (1843); not verbatim throughout.

passages.text: Cogolludo saw in the House of the Dwarf the 'marks of copal recently burned', 'the evidence of some idolatry recently committed'; and the private title papers show that it was the policy of the government to break up the Indian customs and drive the natives away from their consecrated buildings, which they were openly and notoriously worshipping in these ancient buildings.
passages.note: Condensed from Stephens (1843), on the title papers of Uxmal; not verbatim throughout.

title.en: Cerro de los Sacrificios: The Mound of Sacrifice at Uxmal
title.zh: 烏斯馬爾的祭儀之丘

region.en: Uxmal, Yucatan, Mexico
region.zh: 墨西哥猶加敦烏斯馬爾

period: Named in local tradition; described by Charnay 1887

source.work: Desire Charnay, The Ancient Cities of the New World (1887), on Uxmal

summary.en: To the rear of the Dwarf's House rises a great pyramid crowned by a vast platform without monuments, known as the Cerro de los Sacrificios, the Mound of Sacrifice — planned like the Mexican temples, with small wooden chapels containing idols upon its summit.
summary.zh: 侏儒之屋之後，聳起一座巨大的金字塔，頂部為一空闊平台，無有任何建築，人稱塞羅·德·洛斯·薩克里菲西奧斯——祭儀之丘；其規制如墨西哥神廟，頂上原立有小木龕以奉神像。

sensitivity.note: Paraphrase of public-domain travel description only.

passages.text: To the rear, a great pyramid crowned by a vast platform, without monuments, known as 'Cerro de los Sacrificios', Mound of Sacrifice. It is on the plan of the Mexican temples, which consisted, like this monument, of a pyramid with small wood chapels containing idols.
passages.note: Condensed from Charnay (1887), on Uxmal; not verbatim throughout.

title.en: The Mysterious Well of Xcoch
title.zh: 希科赫的神秘之井

region.en: Xcoch, near Nohcacab, Yucatan, Mexico
region.zh: 墨西哥猶加敦諾卡卡布附近的希科赫

period: Described by Stephens 1843

source.work: John Lloyd Stephens, Incidents of Travel in Yucatan, vol. I (1843), ruins of Xcoch

summary.en: At the ruins of Xcoch, under the high mound visible from the House of the Dwarf, Stephens explores a mysterious well: a circular cavity with a great grove, a mouth opening into passages explored by torchlight, used by the village for its water — the subterranean world beneath a Maya mound.
summary.zh: 在希科赫遺址——侏儒之屋可望見的高丘之下——斯蒂芬斯探一神秘之井：圓形井穴與秀美林地，井口通入甬道，秉炬而探；村人至今汲水於此——馬雅土丘之下別有幽冥世界。

sensitivity.note: Paraphrase of public-domain travel description only.

passages.text: The ruins of Xcoch: a mysterious well, with a fine grove and a circular cavity, the mouth of the well opening into passages which we explored with torches; the well was in use by the village, which drew its water from the passages under the mound — the underground world beneath a Maya ruin.
passages.note: Condensed from Stephens, Incidents of Travel in Yucatan, vol. I (1843), ch. XV; not verbatim throughout.

title.en: El Laberinto: The Mound with Secret Chambers
title.zh: 拉貝林托：藏有密室的土丘

region.en: Hacienda of San Felipe, Yucatan, Mexico
region.zh: 墨西哥猶加敦聖費利佩莊園

period: Described by Stephens 1843

source.work: John Lloyd Stephens, Incidents of Travel in Yucatan, vol. I (1843), the Labyrinth

summary.en: The Indians told of a subterraneous structure called El Laberinto, the Labyrinth, 'which had no end'. Entering by a half-buried door under a mound, Stephens finds long passages, branching in every direction, choked at last by fallen earth — and realizes the labyrinth runs inside the body of a great mound, giving rise to the idea that all the great mounds of the country contain secret and unknown chambers.
summary.zh: 土人言及一地下結構，名拉貝林托——迷宮，「無有盡頭」。斯蒂芬斯自丘下半掩之門而入，見甬道綿長、四向分歧，終為塌土所阻——於是恍然：迷宮竟貫穿巨大土丘之腹，由此推想，全地諸大丘之中或皆藏有未知的密室。

sensitivity.note: Paraphrase of public-domain travel description only.

passages.text: I was sure of going on to the end and discovering something, when all at once I found the passage choked up and effectually stopped; the ceiling had fallen in, crushed by a great mass of superincumbent earth, and farther progress was utterly impossible. I told the Indians to put an end to their lying stories about the Laberinto and its having no end.
passages.note: Condensed from Stephens, Incidents of Travel in Yucatan, vol. I (1843); not verbatim throughout.

passages.text: On examining outside, I found that what I had taken for an irregular natural formation was a pyramidal mound of the same general character with all the rest; the door of El Laberinto opened into this mound, and the labyrinth, instead of being subterraneous, was in the body of the mound — a discovery which gave rise to the exciting idea that all the great mounds scattered over the country contained secret, unknown, and hidden chambers.
passages.note: Condensed from Stephens (1843); not verbatim throughout.

title.en: Kubiya, the Leper King in His Farm Hut
title.zh: 庫比亞——蟄居田舍的麻瘋王

region.en: Abeokuta district, Nigeria (the farm hut of the deposed king)
region.zh: 奈及利亞阿貝奧庫塔近郊（廢王蟄居的田舍）

period: Yoruba tradition recorded 1910 (Dennett)

source.work: R. E. Dennett, Nigerian Studies (London, 1910), ch. XVI

summary.en: Two rival traditions explain Orisha Oko, the harvest god. In Keribo's account his name was Kubiya: he was a king and a tyrant, poisoned by one of his subjects and stricken with leprosy. His people built him a hut in the farm (oko), and as he was reluctant to leave home, kingly reverence was promised him in this retreat — a promise fulfilled, so that after his death men repair thither to worship him; the white and red marks used by his devotees indicate the chalk and camwood he is in the habit of using to conceal the leprous spots in their initial stage. In another account his name was again Kubiya, but he was a trapper of guinea fowls who became an extraordinary physician and diviner, called Orisa-Oko, the village god, because he lived in a village.
summary.zh: 關於農耕神奧里莎奧科有兩種說法。柯里博記載：他本名庫比亞，是位暴君，被臣下毒害而染麻瘋。族人為他在田中（奧科）搭起茅舍；他不願遠離家園，人們便許諾在此奉他為王——諾言果然兌現，他死後世人至今前往其舍祭拜。信眾額上、身上的白紅斑記，正是他用白堊與紅木粉遮掩初期麻瘋斑點的遺痕。另一說他名叫庫比亞，原是捕珠雞的獵手，後成醫術通神的名醫與占者；因住在村中而被稱為「奧里莎奧科」——村落之神。

sensitivity.note: Recorded 1910; rival euhemeristic traditions for the harvest god collected by Dennett. Leprosy described as the recorded tradition states it, respectfully. Cross-ref: yoruba-orisa-oko-demon-polo, yoruba-orisa-oko-witch-cave.

passages.text: His name was Kubiya. He was a king and a tyrant. He was poisoned by one of his subjects and was leprous. His people thereafter built him a hut in the farm (oko), and as he was reluctant to leave home, kingly reverence was promised him in this retreat. This promise was fulfilled, so that after his death men repair thither to worship him. The white and red marks used by its devotees indicate the chalk and camwood he is in the habit of using to conceal the leprous spots in their initial stage.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dennett, Nigerian Studies, ch. XVI (1910); not verbatim.

passages.text: Orisha Oko's name was Kubiya. His first occupation was to catch wild guinea fowls and sell them. He afterwards became a physician, and was such an extraordinary man that his powers were considered supernatural. He resided in a village where all men came to him, for he was a very skilful medical man and diviner. He was called Orisa-Oko (village god) because he lived in a village.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dennett, Nigerian Studies, ch. XVI (1910); not verbatim.

title.en: Oke Visits Men in Dreams to Fix the Rain-Feast
title.zh: 奧凱託夢定雨祭之期

region.en: Ibadan, Nigeria (the hill-goddess who commands the drought festival)
region.zh: 奈及利亞伊巴丹（吩咐旱祭日期的山神）

period: Yoruba tradition recorded 1910 (Dennett)

source.work: R. E. Dennett, Nigerian Studies (London, 1910), ch. XVI

summary.en: The Orisha Oke may well be called the titular goddess of Ibadan: when the chiefs were asked what emblem should figure on the medals of their agricultural show, they unanimously selected Oke, photographed as a fine-looking woman, her breasts exposed and her arms raised towards heaven as if to welcome her children — a picture of fruitfulness. She is the hill Orisha connected with fire; her festival used to be held when the land was at its driest and rain was most required to quench its thirst. She would appear to a man in a dream and tell him to go to the Bale and ask him to fix a day for the feast; if the Bale took no notice, she would visit another man in a dream; if the Bale hesitated she threatened to send fire down from heaven to burn his house. Her demands varied — sometimes a man as a sacrifice, sometimes 200 pigeons, sometimes a bullock or a sheep — and on the festival day no trade was done, and anyone coming into the town was robbed of all he brought.
summary.zh: 山神奧凱堪稱伊巴丹的守護女神：酋長們為農業賽會的獎章選徽記時，不約而同選中奧凱——一位豐滿美婦的形象，袒露雙乳、雙臂高舉向天，如迎自己的兒女——一幅豐饒之圖。她是與火相連的山嶽之神；她的祭典總在大地最乾渴、最盼雨時舉行。她會在夢中向某人顯現，命他去請巴萊（村長）定下祭日；巴萊若置之不理，她便託夢另一人再去催請；巴萊若仍遲疑，她便威脅降天火焚其宅。她的索求時而是一名活人為祭，時而是二百隻鴿子，時而是一頭牛或一隻羊。祭日當天全城罷市，誤入城中者財物盡失。

sensitivity.note: Recorded 1910. Dennett also describes a licensed festival attached to this rite; that material is summarized in the corpus only in its ritual-and-rain aspects, without explicit description. Human sacrifice demands reported as the recorded tradition states it.

passages.text: The Orisha Oke may well be called the titular goddess of Ibadan. When the chiefs of that place were asked what animal or sign they would like as an emblem to figure on the medals to be given away at their agricultural show, they unanimously selected Oke. They had the photograph of a fine looking woman taken, her breasts exposed, and her arms raised towards heaven, as if to welcome her children — a picture of fruitfulness. She is the hill Orisha, connected with fire. Her festival used to be held when the land was at its driest and rain was most required to quench its thirst.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dennett, Nigerian Studies, ch. XVI (1910); not verbatim.

passages.text: She would appear to a man in a dream and tell him to go to the Bale and ask him to fix a day for the feast. Perhaps the Bale would take no notice, and then she would visit another man in a dream and ask him to go. If the Bale hesitated, she threatened to send fire down from heaven to burn his house and cause him a great loss. She sometimes demanded a man as a sacrifice, sometimes 200 pigeons, sometimes a bullock or a sheep. Notice would be sent round to all the villages and the day stated; everyone had to be in the town the day before the date fixed, and anyone coming into the town on the day of the festival would be robbed of all he might be bringing with him. No trade was done.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dennett, Nigerian Studies, ch. XVI (1910); not verbatim.

title.en: The Sixteen Odus as the Order of Propagation
title.zh: 十六奧杜——孕育之序

region.en: Yoruba country (symbolic pin: the diviner's tray at Ile-Ife)
region.zh: 約魯巴地方（象徵定位：伊費的占卜托板）

period: Yoruba oral tradition; recorded 1910 (Dennett)

source.work: R. E. Dennett, Nigerian Studies (London, 1910), ch. XV

summary.en: Dennett took the order of the Ifa odus from an Ifa priest, Oliyitan, verified three months later, and read them as the order of propagation: Iroshun and Owourin, filtration and drizzle — water; Obara, that which bears the oil seed — earth; Okoron, the dry bed of a river, and Oguda, that which pounds and creates marriage; Osa, that which dries and evaporates — loss; Ika, he who reaps, and Oturupon, he who gathers — first harvest, the conception of man; Otura and Irete, ease, happiness and hope, when there is no anxiety about food — pregnancy; Oshe, that which shall be — emission; Ofu, to appear in the wrong month without being expected — pain, suffering, travail. The categories of creation, reproduction, death and salvation he found at the back of the Yoruba babalawo's mind as well as the Congolese.
summary.zh: 德內特向伊法祭司奧利伊坦請得十六奧杜之序，三月後再問，次序絲毫不差。他將其讀作孕育之序：伊羅舜與奧烏林——滲濾與細雨，屬水；奧巴拉——負油之種，屬土；奧科隆（乾涸河床）與奧古達（舂捣而造）——論婚嫁；奧薩——曬乾蒸發，屬損耗；伊卡（收割者）與奧圖魯彭（聚合者）——初獲，即人的受孕；奧圖拉與伊雷特——安然、喜樂與盼望，無糧食之憂，即懷孕之期；奧謝——將至之事，即臨盆；奧富——不期而至於不當之月，即陣痛與分娩之苦。他認為創造、孕育、死亡與救贖的次序，同樣潛藏於約魯巴巴巴拉奧與剛果巫祝的心底。

sensitivity.note: Recorded 1910; Dennett's structural reading of the Ifa odu sequence (his interpretation, reported as such). Complements the Johnson and Frobenius accounts of Ifa's corpus. Cross-ref: yoruba-opele-servant-oracle.

passages.text: I obtained the order of the Odus from Oliyitan, an Ifa priest, and to make sure that the order was correct so far as he was concerned, I asked him to give me the order again about three months afterwards. As it was exactly the same I have adopted this as correct.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dennett, Nigerian Studies, ch. XV (1910); not verbatim.

passages.text: Taking the order as given to me by the babalawo, and remembering the order of the seasons, there can be no doubt that they tell us of the order of propagation: Iroshun, filtration, and Owourin, that which drizzles — water; Obara, that which bears the oil seed — earth; Okoron, the dry bed of a river, and Oguda, that which pounds and creates — marriage; Osa, that which dries and evaporates — loss; Ika, he who reaps, harvest, and Oturupon, he who gathers — the first harvest, man's conception; Otura and Irete, translated to me as ease, happiness, hope, when there is no anxiety about food, a time of fruitfulness — the time when the woman shows signs of pregnancy and she is happy and hopeful; Oshe, that which shall be — emission; Ofu, to appear in the wrong month without being expected — pain, suffering, travail.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dennett, Nigerian Studies, ch. XV (1910); not verbatim.

title.en: The Broken Calabash of Ife
title.zh: 伊費碎葫蘆記

region.en: Ile-Ife, Nigeria (the King's courtyard where the broken world-calabash was mended)
region.zh: 奈及利亞伊費城（修補破碎天地葫蘆的王宮前庭）

period: Yoruba oral tradition; recorded 1910 (Dennett, from Mr. George)

source.work: R. E. Dennett, Nigerian Studies (London, 1910), ch. XV, quoting the story of the breaking of Igba at Ife

summary.en: All the world met in the King's courtyard to discuss the breaking of the world-renowned Igba, the calabash of Ife — Heaven and Earth in one shell. They called Awlawta to put it together again, but he could not; Beni-ado of Ife and Owo of Otu; Ogun also was sent for, which means war was declared over the breakage — but none of them could put the calabash together again. People farmed and waited for the rain, but none came; then hunger came, and man and beast mourned for their dead. Obalufon from Iyinde, Laberinjo from Ido, Jigure from Otun Moba, Esegba an Egba, Asadu from Ijesa, Akoda from Ife, Aseda Araba the law-giving cotton tree their father, Olumo from Imori, Ogun of Alara, Ogbon of Ijero, and Odudugbundu of Eshemaiva, the father devil who lived in Ketu — all these could do nothing. Then Ototo Enia, the truthful one, blew his trumpet — the elephant ran to the bush, the wild ox to its field, the rat to its hole, beans to the brook, the dog to the land of meditation, the sheep to the country of stupidity, all beasts to beastland — and Ajalaiye, Ajalorun, and Ajirilogbon were called. The people confessed their filth and prayed that the broken calabash might be patched; Ajirilogbon told them to find the leaf of a tree called Ewe-Alashuwalu, capable of remodelling a man's evil character; they could not find it, so he took it out of the bag of Egede, the bag of deep mystery, and mended the broken Igba of Ife — and rain fell, and healed all the people, and stopped the calamity from causing further harm.
summary.zh: 聞名天下的伊費葫蘆「伊格巴」——合天地於一殼——忽然破碎，萬民齊聚王宮前庭商議。請阿烏拉塔來修，修不好；伊費的貝尼-阿多、奧圖的奧沃也請來了；連奧貢都請動了——意味著為此碎裂而宣戰——依然無人能將葫蘆復原。人們照常耕作、盼雨，雨卻不來；接著饑荒降臨，人獸同哀亡者。伊延德的奧巴魯豐、伊多的拉貝林喬、奧圖莫巴的吉古雷、埃格巴人埃塞格巴、伊傑薩的阿薩杜、伊費的阿科達、「賜法木棉」阿塞達-阿拉巴（眾人之父）、伊莫里的奧盧莫、阿拉拉的奧貢、伊傑羅的奧貢、以及居於凱圖的眾魔之父奧杜格本杜——全都無能為力。此時「誠實者」奧托托-埃尼亞吹響號角：大象奔入林、野牛歸田、老鼠入洞、豆落溪、犬往冥想之鄉、羊往愚魯之國，眾獸各歸獸國——接著「與地上事務角力者」阿賈拉伊耶、「與天界事務角力者」阿賈洛倫、「司視與智慧者」阿吉里洛貢被一一請到。民眾懺悔罪污，求補破葫蘆；阿吉里洛貢命他們尋一種能重塑人的惡習的樹葉「埃韋-阿拉舒瓦盧」；眾人尋不得，他便從「埃格德」——深奧之秘的袋子——中取出此葉，補好了伊費的碎葫蘆。雨隨即落下，醫愈萬民，災殃自此不再蔓延。

sensitivity.note: Recorded 1910 by Dennett from Mr. George's account; the fall-and-restoration of the Ife calabash (Heaven-and-Earth shell), with the famine that follows its breaking. Dennett notes the Humpty Dumpty parallel. Cross-refs: yoruba-odudua-blind-calabash, yoruba-olokun-flood-chained.

passages.text: They called Awlawta to come and put it together again, but he could not. Beni ado from Ife, and Owo from Otu were called. Ogun also is sent for; which means that war was declared over this breakage. But none of them could put the calabash together again. People farmed and waited for the rain, but none came. Then hunger came, and man and beast mourned for their dead.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dennett, Nigerian Studies, ch. XV (1910); not verbatim.

passages.text: The Obalufon from Iyinde, Laberinjo from Ido, Jigure from Otun Moba, Esegba an Egba, Asadu from Ijesa, Akoda from Ife, Aseda Araba (the law-giving cotton tree), their father, Olumo from Imori, Ogun of Alara, Ogbon of Ijero, Odudugbundu of Eshemaiva, the father devil who lived in Ketu — but all these could do nothing. They call Akonilogbon and Afonahanni and ask their assistance; they advised them to call in Ototo Enia, the truthful one. From the beginning at the creation of the world this duty of trumpeter to the man from heaven was specially laid on him. Then he blew his trumpet, and the elephant went quickly to the Eselu bush, the wild ox to Elugu apako, the bird Kekeke flies to the ale plant, the rat runs to its hole, the beans to the brook, the dog to the land of meditation, the sheep to the country of stupidity — all beasts go to beastland, beings go to the land of beings.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dennett, Nigerian Studies, ch. XV (1910); not verbatim.

passages.text: Ajalaiye, he who strives with earthly affairs; Ajalorun, he who strives with heavenly affairs; Ajirilogbon, he who strives with matters concerning sight and wisdom, were called. The people confess their filth and pray that he should patch the broken calabash, and Ajirilogbon tells them to go and find the leaf of a tree called Ewe-Alashuwalu (which is said to be capable of remodelling a man's evil character). They cannot find it. He then takes it out of the bag of Egede (the bag of deep mystery), and mends the broken Igba of Ife, and rain falls, and so heals all the people, and stops the calamity from causing further harm.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dennett, Nigerian Studies, ch. XV (1910); not verbatim.

title.en: Idowu Recites the Names of Shango
title.zh: 伊多沃念誦尚戈諸名

region.en: Oyo and Akure, Nigeria (the festival procession of the Odushushango)
region.zh: 奧約與阿庫雷（尚戈男信眾的祭典行列）

period: Yoruba oral tradition; recorded 1910 (Dennett)

source.work: R. E. Dennett, Nigerian Studies (London, 1910), ch. XVI

summary.en: Jakuta is the name of Shango's day: Shango is the Alafin of Oyo's great Orisha and is sometimes called Oba Kuso, the king of Kuso, a hill near Oyo sacred to him. An Odushushango named Idowu recited his names: Alada Ogun, the one who splits the mortar that Ogun is said to wear on his head; Ako aja abinrinja lese, the he-dog that walks as one about to fight; Aja jumoni koto kpanije, the one who frightens one before he kills and eats him; Olilu tun ilu re she, one who puts his town in order; Ebi ti ka waw ponyin shoro, the one who with his hands behind his back does him an injury; Akuwarapa abija kaka, the one who has fits and is extraordinarily strong. His wife Oya runs on ahead when Shango goes out to fight, the strong tornado wind; Oshun is the gathering darkness and Oba the wild clouds that meet — these two stay at home to keep house. His sacred tree is the Ayan, from which his staff is made; his food taboos (ewaws) are the Sese beans, the Eligidi pumpkin, the Esuro antelope, the Ekun rabbit, and the Eku-ago, the white-bellied rat which the Alafin of Oyo is seen at times to raise to his lips as if to kiss.
summary.zh: 「賈庫塔」是尚戈的聖日之名；尚戈是奧約阿勞芬的大神，又稱「奧巴庫索」——庫索王，即奧約附近獻給他的聖山。尚戈男信眾（奧杜舒尚戈）伊多沃誦其諸名：奧拉達奧貢（劈開奧貢頭上木杵者）；如欲鬥之犬而行的公犬；先嚇後殺的噬人者；整飭其城者；反手傷人者；癲狂而神力無匹者。其妻奧雅是尚戈出征時一馬當先的龍捲狂風；奧舜是聚攏的黑暗，奧巴是相撞的烏雲——此二人留守家中。其聖樹為阿揚木（神杖即取材於此）；其食忌為塞塞豆、南瓜、羚羊、野兔，以及白腹鼠——奧約阿勞芬時而把它舉到唇邊，彷彿親吻。

sensitivity.note: Recorded 1910; the praise-name roll and food taboos of Shango's cult, complementing Ellis's chant (yoruba-shango-fiery-stones) and Frobenius's ram cycle (yoruba-shango-ram-thunderbolt).

passages.text: Jakuta is the name of Shango's day. Shango is the Alafin of Oyo's great Orisha and is sometimes called Oba Kuso, the king of Kuso, a hill near Oyo which is sacred to him. His male followers are called Odushushango and the female Esin nla (the great horse). An Odushushango named Idowu gave the following information: another name is Alada Ogun, the one who splits the mortar that Ogun is said to wear on his head; Ako aja abinrinja lese, the he-dog that walks as one about to fight; Aja jumoni koto kpanije, the one who frightens one before he kills and eats him; Olilu tun ilu re she, one who puts his town in order; Ebi ti ka waw ponyin shoro, the one who with his hands behind his back does him an injury; Akuwarapa abija kaka, the one who has fits and is extraordinarily strong.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dennett, Nigerian Studies, ch. XVI (1910); not verbatim.

passages.text: His wife Oya is she who runs on ahead when Shango goes out to fight, the strong tornado wind. Oshun is the gathering darkness and Oba the wild clouds that meet. These two stay at home to keep house. They sacrifice the cow, the sheep and the cock to Shango. His sacred tree is the Ayan from which his staff is made. His ewaws (food taboos) are the Sese (beans), the Eligidi (pumpkin), the Esuro (antelope), the Ekun (rabbit), and the Eku ago or white-bellied rat which the Alafin of Oyo is seen at times to raise to his lips as if to kiss.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dennett, Nigerian Studies, ch. XVI (1910); not verbatim.

title.en: Naming the Child's Guardian Orisha: Footprints of Fate
title.zh: 為嬰孩問出守護神——命運的足印

region.en: Yoruba country (symbolic pin: the naming-day threshold near Ile-Ife)
region.zh: 約魯巴地方（象徵定位：伊費近郊命名日的門前）

period: Yoruba oral tradition; recorded 1910 (Dennett)

source.work: R. E. Dennett, Nigerian Studies (London, 1910), ch. XVI

summary.en: From marriage to birth there are no Orisha ceremonies; but when the child is born the parents ask the priest to what Orisha they owe this good fortune, and when he tells them they sacrifice to it. Three days after the birth they call in the priest and ask him to name the child's Ese entele — its footprints: the babalawo consults Ifa, and as the priest mentions an Orisha, shakes his head until that which is to become the guardian spirit of the child is mentioned. The child, as soon as it is able, fetches water for this Orisha and sacrifices to it on all great occasions during its life; if Obatala is the Orisha, the child must wear white and must not drink palm wine nor eat dog. The grandparents as well as the parents each thank their separate Orishas on the safe delivery; if a girl, a name is given on the seventh day, if a boy, on the ninth.
summary.zh: 自婚至產並無奧里莎之儀；孩子降生後，父母便請祭司指點：此番好運該歸功於哪位神？指明之後便向祂獻祭。產後三日請祭司為孩子問出「埃塞恩特勒」——命運的足印：巴巴拉奧求問伊法，祭司逐一念神名，直到搖出將成為孩子守護神的那一位為止。孩子稍長，便為這位奧里莎取水、逢大典獻祭；若守護神是奧巴塔拉，孩子終身必穿白衣、不得飲棕櫚酒、不得食犬。平安產後，祖輩與父母各自感謝自己的守護神；女嬰第七日命名，男嬰第九日。

sensitivity.note: Recorded 1910; the life-cycle rite of guardian-orisha attribution, reported from the marriage-birth chapter of Dennett's informants (Odedaino).

passages.text: From the time of marriage to the time of birth there are no Orisha ceremonies, but when the child is born they ask the priest to what Orisha they owe this good fortune, and when he tells them they sacrifice to it. Three days after the birth they call in the priest and ask him to name the child's Ese entele, or footprints. The babalawo consults Ifa, who, as the priest mentions an Orisha, shakes his head until that which is to become the guardian spirit of the child is mentioned. The child, as soon as it is able, fetches water for this Orisha and sacrifices to it on all great occasions during its life. If Obatala is the Orisha then the child must wear white and must not drink palm wine nor eat dog.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dennett, Nigerian Studies, ch. XVI (1910); not verbatim.

passages.text: The grandparents as well as the parents on the safe delivery of their child each thank their separate Orishas. The priest gives the mother medicine for the preservation of the child. If it be a girl, a name is given to it on the seventh day; if a boy, on the ninth.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dennett, Nigerian Studies, ch. XVI (1910); not verbatim.

title.en: The Koran on the Peg: How the Worship of Odudua Began
title.zh: 釘上的《可蘭經》——奧杜杜瓦崇拜之源

region.en: Ile-Ife, Nigeria (the wall where the bag hung)
region.zh: 奈及利亞伊費城（掛袋的牆壁）

period: Yoruba oral tradition; recorded 1910 (Dennett, from F. S.)

source.work: R. E. Dennett, Nigerian Studies (London, 1910), ch. VI

summary.en: Many years after the death of Odudua, a Hausa Mussulman came to Ife. He used to call the inhabitants together and read to them passages from the copy of the Koran which he brought with him, saying in imperfect Yoruba: "Let us worship Allah; He created the Mountain, He created the lowland, He created everything, He created us." He did this from time to time without gaining a single proselyte, and died a few months after his arrival. After his death his Koran was found hanging on a peg on the wall in a bag; some of the men who saw it said: "The late Hausaman told us this was the personage who created existence — this is Odudua; let us therefore worship him" — misunderstanding the Mussulman. So they removed the bag containing the Koran from the peg, put it on the ground, covered it with a pot and began to worship it: so commenced the worship of Odudua.
