passages.text: The concubine Tal-geui was wonderfully beautiful, but surpassingly so when she smiled: at such times the person upon whom she smiled was fascinated as by a serpent and forced to comply with whatever request she made. Pondering this, Pi-gan decided that she must be a fox in human shape, for it is well known that if an animal tastes of water that has lain twenty years in a human skull it acquires the power to assume human shape at will.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Hulbert, History of Korea, Vol. 1, ch. 2 (1905); not verbatim.

passages.text: Armed detectives followed her unperceived and saw her enter a cave near the summit of the mountain; she presently emerged accompanied by a pack of foxes who leaped about her and fawned upon her in evident delight. When she left, the spies entered, put the foxes to the sword, and cut from each dead body the piece of white fur which is always found on the breast of the fox.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Hulbert, History of Korea, Vol. 1, ch. 2 (1905); not verbatim.

passages.text: Adorning herself in all her finery, she entered the imperial presence and exerted her power of fascination to the utmost. I hear that there are seven orifices in the heart of every good man; I would that I might see the heart of Pi-gan. As the executioner's knife was plunged into the victim's breast, Pi-gan cried: You are no woman; you are a fox in disguise, and I charge you to resume your natural shape. Instantly her face began to change; hair sprang forth upon it, her nails grew long, and, bursting forth from her garments, she stood revealed — a white fox with nine tails. With one parting snarl at the assembled court, she leaped from the window and made good her escape.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Hulbert, History of Korea, Vol. 1, ch. 2 (1905); not verbatim.

title.en: The Revolt of Prince Oshikuma and the Cut Bow-Strings
title.zh: 忍熊王之叛與斷弦之計

region.en: Uji river and the Seta crossing, Afumi (Lake Biwa)
region.zh: 近江宇治與瀨田渡

period: Nihongi compiled 720 CE (trans. Aston 1896)

source.work: Nihongi (Chronicles of Japan), Vol. I, trans. W. G. Aston (1896)

summary.en: Princes Kakosaka and Oshikuma, Chuai's elder sons, plot against the newborn heir while Jingu is in Korea: they raise a misasagi at Akashi with stones rafted from Awaji. At a hunt-prayer a wild boar leaps on Kakosaka and kills him. Oshikuma waits at Sumiyoshi; Takechi no Sukune deceives him into cutting every bow-string and flinging every sword into the river, then reveals spare strings hidden in the top-knots and real swords, routs him at Afusaka, and pursues him to the Seta crossing, where the Prince and Isachi no Sukune drown together like grebes.
summary.zh: 香坂王與忍熊王聞帝崩、后西征又生皇子，謀叛。借營山陵之名至播磨作明石陵，連舟運淡路之石，執兵以待后。獵祈於兔寸野，忽有赤豕突起噬香坂王而卒。忍熊王退屯住吉。后遣武內宿禰等率數萬擊之。宿禰密令全軍藏副弦於髻，佩木劍，詐謂各斷弦棄兵以示和，王信而全軍斷弦投河。宿禰軍復弦佩真劍渡河擊之，破於逢坂，追至栗隅柴，血流入栗隅村，故至今栗隅之果不薦於御膳。王與狹穗彥弟彥宿禰同沉瀨田渡而死。

sensitivity.note: Ancient Japanese court myth (Nihongi); passages are condensed paraphrases of the public-domain Aston translation, presented for comparative mythology.

passages.text: Now Prince Kakosaka and Prince Oshikuma, hearing of the Emperor's decease, as well as of the Empress's expedition to the West, and of the recent birth of an Imperial Prince, plotted secretly, saying: 'The Empress has now a child, and all the ministers obey her. They will certainly consult together and establish an infant sovereign. But shall we, the elders, obey our younger brother?' So, pretending that it was in order to build a misasagi for the Emperor, they went to Harima and raised a misasagi at Akashi, joining boats together in a string across to the island of Ahaji and transporting the stones of that island to build it. Now they made every man take a weapon, and so awaited the Empress. Hereupon Kurami-wake, ancestor of the Kimi of Inugami, and Isachi no Sukune, ancestor of the Kishi, joined themselves unto Prince Kakosaka, who made them his generals.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Nihongi, Book IX, sec. 18 (trans. Aston 1896); not verbatim.

passages.text: The two Princes went forth together to the moor of Toga and made a hunt-prayer, saying: 'If our project is to be successful, then surely let us take some good game.' The two Princes sat each in his shelter, when a wild-boar sprang out suddenly, and climbing on to the shelter, bit Prince Kakosaka and killed him. The soldiers every one shuddered with fear. Then Prince Oshikuma addressed Kurami-wake: 'This is a very ominous thing. We ought not to await the enemy here.' So he withdrew his troops and encamped at Sumiyoshi. At this time the Empress heard that Prince Oshikuma had raised an army and was awaiting her. She commanded Takechi no Sukune to take in his bosom the Imperial Prince and go out across by way of the south-sea provinces to anchor in the harbour of Kii, while the Empress's ship made straight for Naniha. At this time the Empress's ship swerved towards the midst of the sea and was unable to proceed; she returned to the harbour of Muko and made divination, and the Gods instructed her where each should be enshrined, so that she was enabled to cross the sea in peace.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Nihongi, Book IX, secs. 18-19 (trans. Aston 1896); not verbatim.

passages.text: The Empress commanded Takechi no Sukune and Take-furu-kuma to lead an army of several tens of thousands of men to attack Prince Oshikuma. They went out by way of Yamashiro as far as Uji and encamped north of the river. Kuma-no-Kori, who formed the vanguard of Oshikuma's army, encouraged his men with a loud song of the pine-clad plain beyond the river. Then Takechi no Sukune made an order that every man should bind his hair mallet-wise, conceal spare bow-strings in his top-knot, and gird on wooden swords; then he deluded Prince Oshikuma, saying: 'I am not greedy to possess the Empire. Only, while cherishing the infant Prince, we will obey my Lord the Prince. I pray thee let us both cut our bow-strings, fling away our weapons, and be in harmony together.' So he openly gave orders to his army to cut their bow-strings and fling their swords into the river. Prince Oshikuma believed these deluding words and ordered all his troops to do likewise. Upon this Takechi no Sukune commanded the three divisions of his army to produce their spare bow-strings, string their bows again, and, girt with their real swords, advance across the river.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Nihongi, Book IX, secs. 20-21 (trans. Aston 1896); not verbatim.

passages.text: Prince Oshikuma, seeing that he had been deceived, said to Kurami-wake and Isachi no Sukune: 'We have been deceived, and have now no spare weapons. How shall we be able to fight?' He withdrew his forces and gradually retreated; Takechi sent forth his choice troops, came up with him at Afusaka and put him to the rout. The army took to flight and ran as far as Kurusu in Sasanami, where many were slain; the blood overflowed into Kurusu, and in horror of this, until this day, the fruit of Kurusu is not offered to the Imperial Palace. Prince Oshikuma, not knowing whither to betake himself in his flight, called to him Isachi no Sukune and made a song: 'Come, my child Isachi Sukune! Rather than receive a severe wound from the mallet of Uchi no Aso, like unto the grebe let us make a plunge!' So they sank together in the crossing-place of Seta and died. Takechi no Sukune made a song over the birds that dived at the ferry of Seta: 'Since with my eyes I cannot see them, can they be still alive?' Several days after they came out on the river-bank at Uji, and Takechi made a song: 'Passing Tanakami, have been caught at Uji.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Nihongi, Book IX, sec. 21 (trans. Aston 1896); not verbatim.

title.en: The Eternal Night: Two Priests Buried in One Grave
title.zh: 晝如夜之咎與神靈託地

region.en: Muko harbour and Shinu palace, Kahachi
region.zh: 河內武庫與忍宮

period: Nihongi compiled 720 CE (trans. Aston 1896)

source.work: Nihongi (Chronicles of Japan), Vol. I, trans. W. G. Aston (1896)

summary.en: Sailing for Naniha to meet the rebels, the Empress's ship swerves into mid-sea and will not move; divination at Muko brings instructions from four deities - Amaterasu's rough spirit, Waka-hiru-me, Koto-shiro-nushi and the three water-gods - each naming the land where he wishes to be worshipped, and only then can she cross in peace. Later, at the palace of Shinu, the day is dark as night for many days; an old man explains it is the calamity of the two priests of Shinu and Amano, friends buried in one grave; the tombs are opened and re-interred separately, and daylight returns.
summary.zh: 后舟向浪速而漂於海心不得進，還武庫而卜。天照大神荒魂、稚日霙姬、事代主神與水底三神各託辭求祀地，后依而祀之乃得安渡。至忍宮，晝如夜者多日。野老曰此乃忍神與天神二神主同穴而葬之咎。發墓視之果然，乃改葬各異其棺，日光乃出。

sensitivity.note: Ancient Japanese court myth (Nihongi); passages are condensed paraphrases of the public-domain Aston translation, presented for comparative mythology.

passages.text: At this time the Empress's ship swerved towards the midst of the sea, and was unable to proceed. She returned again to the harbour of Muko, where she made divination as to this. Hereupon Ama-terasu no Oho-kami admonished her, saying: 'My rough spirit may not approach the Imperial residence. Let him dwell in the land of Hirota in Mikokoro.' So Hayama-hime, daughter of Yamashiro-neko, was appointed to worship him. Moreover, Waka-hiru-me no Mikoto admonished the Empress, saying: 'I wish to dwell in the land of Nagawo in Ikuta.' So Una-gami no Isachi was appointed to worship her. Again, Koto-shiro-nushi no Mikoto admonished her, saying: 'Worship me in the land of Nakata in Mikokoro.' So Naga-hime, younger sister of Hayama-hime, was appointed to worship him. Again the three Gods, Uha-tsutsu no wo, Naka-tsutsu no wo, and Soko-tsutsu no wo, admonished her, saying: 'Let our gentle spirits dwell at Nagawo in Nunakura in Ohotsu, so that they may look upon the ships passing back and forward.' Hereupon these Gods were enshrined in accordance with their instructions, and the Empress was enabled to cross the sea in peace.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Nihongi, Book IX, sec. 19 (trans. Aston 1896); not verbatim.

passages.text: The Empress proceeded southwards to the land of Kii, and met the Prince Imperial at Hitaka. She removed to the Palace of Shinu. It so happened that at this time the day was dark like night. Many days passed in this manner, and the men of that time said: 'This is the Eternal Night.' The Empress inquired of Toyomimi, the ancestor of the Atahe of Ki, saying: 'Wherefore is this omen?' Then there was an old man who said: 'I have heard by tradition that this kind of omen is called Atsunahi no tsumi.' She inquired what it meant. He answered: 'The priests of the two shrines have been buried together.' Therefore she made strict investigation in the village.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Nihongi, Book IX, secs. 19-20 (trans. Aston 1896); not verbatim.

passages.text: There was a man who said: 'The priest of Shinu and the priest of Amano were good friends. The priest of Shinu fell ill and died. The priest of Amano wept and wailed, saying: We have been friends together since our birth. Why in our death should there not be the same grave for both? So he lay down beside the corpse and died of himself, so that they were buried together. This is perhaps the reason.' So they opened the tomb, and on examination found that it was true. Therefore they again changed their coffins and interred them separately, upon which the sunlight shone forth, and there was a difference between day and night.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Nihongi, Book IX, secs. 19-20 (trans. Aston 1896); not verbatim.

title.en: A-chik-ki and Wang-in: The Coming of Chinese Learning
title.zh: 阿直岐與王仁：漢學東漸

region.en: Court at Naniha and Karu, Yamato
region.zh: 難波與大和輕坂

period: Nihongi compiled 720 CE (trans. Aston 1896)

source.work: Nihongi (Chronicles of Japan), Vol. I, trans. W. G. Aston (1896)

summary.en: The King of Pekche sends A-chik-ki with two quiet horses as tribute; they are stabled at the acclivity of Karu, named Mumaya-saka, Stable-hill. A-chik-ki is able to read the classics and becomes teacher to the Heir Apparent. Asked whether any learned man is his superior, he names Wang-in of Pekche; envoys are sent to summon him, and Wang-in arrives to teach the prince the classical books - the beginning of Chinese learning in Japan.
summary.zh: 百濟王貢良馬二匹，牧於輕坂，因名廄坂。阿直岐能讀經典，為菟道稚郎子之師。帝問更有勝汝之博士乎，對曰有王仁。乃遣上毛野君等往百濟徵之。王仁至，皇子受諸書，無不通曉，是為漢學之始。

sensitivity.note: Ancient Japanese court myth (Nihongi); Aston dates this transmission of writing 120 years later; passages are condensed paraphrases of the public-domain Aston translation, presented for comparative mythology.

passages.text: The King of Pekche sent A-chik-ki with two quiet horses as tribute. So they were fed in stables on the acclivity of Karu, and A-chik-ki was appointed to have charge of their foddering. Therefore the place where the horses were kept was named Mumaya-saka, Stable-hill. Moreover, A-chik-ki was able to read the classics, and so the Heir Apparent made him his teacher. Hereupon the Emperor inquired of A-chik-ki, saying: 'Are there other learned men superior to thee?' He answered and said: 'There is Wang-in, who is superior.' Then Areda wake, ancestor of the Kimi of Kodzuke, and Kamu-nagi wake were sent to Pekche to summon Wang-in.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Nihongi, Book X, sec. 15 (trans. Aston 1896); not verbatim.

passages.text: Wang-in arrived, and straightway the Heir Apparent took him as teacher and learnt various books from him. There was none which he did not thoroughly understand. Therefore the man called Wang-in was the first ancestor of the Fumi no Obito, the chiefs of writing. In the same year King Ahwa of Pekche died, and the Emperor sent for Prince Tyen-chi and addressed him: 'Do thou return to thy country and succeed to the royal Dignity.' Accordingly he further granted to him the territory of Eastern Han and so dismissed him. Meanwhile, Kidzu no Sukune of Heguri and Tada no Sukune of Ikuba had been sent to Kara with choice troops to assail Silla and open a way for Sotsuhiko, whose return had been long delayed: the King of Silla was afraid, confessed his guilt, and they brought away with them the people of Kungwol and Sotsuhiko.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Nihongi, Book X, secs. 15-16 (trans. Aston 1896); not verbatim.

passages.text: In the twentieth year, autumn, ninth month, Achi no Omi, ancestor of the Atahe of the Aya of Yamato, and his son Tsuga no Omi immigrated to Japan, bringing with them a company of their people of seventeen districts. Earlier, in the fourteenth year, the King of Pekche had sent as tribute a seamstress named Maketsu, first ancestress of the seamstresses of Kume; and the Lord of Yutsuki came from Pekche to offer his allegiance, saying that, coming with one hundred and twenty districts of the people of his own land, the men of Silla had prevented them and forced them to remain in the land of Kara. Katsuraki no Sotsuhiko was sent to bring the men of Yutsuki from Kara, but three years passed and he did not come.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Nihongi, Book X, secs. 14 and 20 (trans. Aston 1896); not verbatim.

title.en: The Descent of Ninigi: Amaterasu's Grandson Comes Down to Takachiho
title.zh: 瓊瓊杵尊天降高千穗

region.en: The peak of Kuzhifuru, Takachiho in Tsukushi (symbolic pin at the Takachiho plateau, Miyazaki)
region.zh: 筑紫日向高千穗峰狹梶山頂（宮崎高千穗高原象徵性定位）

period: Kojiki compiled 712 CE (trans. Chamberlain 1882)

source.work: Kojiki, trans. Basil Hall Chamberlain (1882)

summary.en: With the Central Land subdued, the heir proposes that his child Prince-Rice-ear-Ruddy-Plenty (Ninigi) descend instead; at the eight-forking road of Heaven a deity of blinding radiance is confronted by the Heavenly-Alarming-Female Uzume, who learns he is the Deity Prince of Saruta come to serve as vanguard. The Heavenly Deities attach the mirror and curved jewels that once lured Amaterasu from the Rock-Dwelling, the Herb-Quelling-Great-Sword, and five chief companies, charge Ninigi to regard the mirror as their very spirit, and he descends, pushing asunder the eight-fold clouds, onto the peak of Takachiho.
summary.zh: 天之石屋既平葦原中國，皇孫命其子天邇岐志國邇岐志天津日高日子番能邇邇藝命降臨。於天上八衢遇輝光普照之神，命天鈿女命問之，乃猿田毗古神自薦為嚮導。遂以八尺瓊勾玉與八咫鏡、草薙大刀，並思兼神、手力男神、天石屋戶神等五部眾授之，敕曰：以此鏡視為我靈，當如視我而奉之。邇邇藝命遂離天之石座，排八重天雲，分道而下，降於筑紫日向高千穗之狹梶山頂。

sensitivity.note: Ancient Japanese court myth (Kojiki): Ninigi's descent and the mirror-charge are the charter myth of the imperial regalia and Ise shrine; present comparatively and critically. Passages are condensed paraphrases of public-domain translations.

passages.text: Then the Heaven-Shining-Great-August-Deity and the High-Integrating-Deity charged the Heir Apparent, His Augustness Truly-Conqueror-I-Conquer-Conquering-Swift-Heavenly-Great-Great-Ears: The Brave-Awful-Possessing-Male-Deity says he has now finished pacifying the Central Land of Reed-Plains; do you, in accordance with our gracious charge, descend to it, dwell in it, and rule over it. The Heir Apparent replied: While I have been getting ready to descend, there has been born to me a child whose name is His Augustness Heaven-Plenty-Earth-Plenty-Heaven's-Sun-Height-Prince-Rice-ear-Ruddy-Plenty. This child should be sent down. So the Heavenly Deities laid their command on Prince-Rice-ear-Ruddy-Plenty: This Luxuriant Reed-Plain Land of Fresh Rice-ears is the land over which you shall rule; and he answered that he would descend from Heaven according to their commands.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Kojiki, pp. 192-193 (trans. Chamberlain 1882); not verbatim.

passages.text: When the prince was about to descend, at the eight-forking road of Heaven there stood a deity whose refulgence reached up to the Plain of High Heaven and down to the Central Land of Reed-Plains, so that his light made the way doubtful. The Heavenly Deities charged the Heavenly-Alarming-Female-Deity: Though you are but a delicate female, you are a deity who conquers in facing other deities; go and ask: This being the road by which our august child is about to descend from Heaven, who is it that stands there? To this gracious question he replied: I am an Earthly Deity named the Deity Prince of Saruta. Having heard of the intended descent of the august child of the Heavenly Deities, I have come humbly to meet him and respectfully offer myself as his vanguard.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Kojiki, pp. 193-194 (trans. Chamberlain 1882); not verbatim.

passages.text: So they joined to him five chiefs of companies — the Heavenly-Beckoning-Ancestor-Lord, Grand-Jewel, the Heavenly-Alarming-Female, I-shi-ko-ri-do-me, and Jewel-Ancestor — and to the prince they joined the eight-feet curved jewels and the mirror that had allured the Heaven-Shining-Great-August-Deity from the Rock-Dwelling, and the Herb-Quelling-Great-Sword, together with the Deity Thought-Includer, the Hand-Strength-Male-Deity, and the Deity Heavenly-Rock-Door-Opener of Eternal Night, charging him: Regard this mirror exactly as if it were our august spirit, and reverence it as if reverencing us; and let the Deity Thought-Includer take in hand our affairs and carry on the government.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Kojiki, pp. 194-197 (trans. Chamberlain 1882); not verbatim.

passages.text: Then the prince, leaving the Heavenly Rock-Seat, pushing asunder the eight-fold heavenly spreading clouds, and dividing a road with a mighty road-dividing, set off floating shut up in the Floating Bridge of Heaven, and descended onto the peak of Kuzhifuru, which is Takachiho in Tsukushi. His attendant deities, taking the heavenly rock-quivers on their backs, the mallet-headed swords at their sides, the heavenly vegetable-wax-tree bows in their hands, and clasping the heavenly true deer-arrows under their arms, stood in his august van in respectful attendance. He looked about him and said: This place is opposite to the land of Kara; one comes straight across to the august Cape of Kasasa; it is a land whereon the morning sun shines straight and the evening sun's sunlight illumines — an exceedingly good place. Having thus spoken, he made stout the temple-pillars on the nethermost rock-bottom, made high the cross-beams to the Plain of High Heaven, and dwelt there. He then charged the Heavenly-Alarming-Female to escort the Deity Prince of Saruta back, to bear that deity's august name, and to serve him; wherefore the Duchesses of Saru bear the name of the Prince of Saruta to this day.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Kojiki, pp. 197-199 (trans. Chamberlain 1882); not verbatim.

title.en: Kaguya-hime: The Shining Princess Returns to the Moon
title.zh: 輝夜姬：月宮公主歸月

region.en: A bamboo grove outside the Heian capital; the moon capital above (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 京城郊外竹林；天上月之都（象徵定位）

period: Taketori Monogatari composed c. late 9th–early 10th century CE (oldest surviving tale in Japanese; trans. Dickins 1888)

source.archive: Internet Archive / Project Gutenberg (Dickins 1888 translation; Davis 1912 retelling)
source.work: Taketori Monogatari (The Tale of the Bamboo-Cutter), trans. Frederick Victor Dickins, 1888; retold in F. Hadland Davis, Myths & Legends of Japan (1912)

summary.en: A childless bamboo-cutter finds a four-inch girl shining inside a bamboo stalk; in three months she grows into the peerless Lady Kaguya, whose impossible quests defeat five noble suitors and even the emperor's love. As the full moon approaches she remembers she was sent from the moon capital; the Moonfolk descend, dress her in the robe that erases mortality, and ascend — leaving the elixir of life that the emperor burns on Japan's highest peak, giving Fuji its name, 'Never-Dying'.
summary.zh: 老翁於竹中拾得四寸輝夜姬；三月而成絕色，以難題卻五大臣，帝亦不得其身。望月之期將至，公主憶起月都之命；月人乘雲而降，為其著羽衣，塵心頓忘，乘雲昇天。所遺不死之藥，帝命焚於駿河最高之山，故富士山名曰「不死」。

sensitivity.note: Court tale (monogatari) of the Heian period drawing on moon-veneration imagery; passages are condensed paraphrases of public-domain translations (Dickins 1888; Davis 1912), presented for comparative mythology. The 'elixir gives Fuji its name' aetiology is read as folk etymology, not as an imperial claim.

passages.text: An old bamboo-cutter named Taketori no Okina went into the groves and cut reeds as he had always done, until one stalk glowed like sunlight and split open to reveal a girl four inches tall. He carried her home, and he and his wife reared her in a basket. Every time he cut cane thereafter, gold appeared among the stems, and in three months the child grew to a woman of peerless beauty, who was named Kaguya-hime, the Shining Princess. The old man's house filled with suitors, and their ranks swelled until five noblemen of the highest courts remained, vowing to win her.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Taketori Monogatari, opening (trans. Dickins 1888; cf. Davis 1912); not verbatim.

passages.text: Kaguya-hime demanded what could not be gotten: the stone begging-bowl of the Buddha of India; jeweled branches from the island of Hōrai; a robe of fire-rat fur that no flame can burn; a jewel from the dragon's neck that changes colour through five hues; and a cowry born from the swallow. Each suitor returned with a counterfeit, and she unmasked them one by one — the bowl proved common, the branch's jewels were paste, the fire-rat robe burned in the fire-test, the dragon jewel was bought from a conjurer's merchant, and the swallow's cowry was a bird's droppings. Word of her beauty reached the emperor himself, but the princess refused the palace; still he wrote to her, and she answered him in verses until his heart grew ever more tender.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Taketori Monogatari, the five impossible quests episode (trans. Dickins 1888; cf. Davis 1912); not verbatim.

passages.text: As the autumn moon grew fuller, Kaguya-hime wept when she saw it, and at last confessed to the old couple: she was not of this world, but of the moon capital, whence she had been sent for a fault, and the day of her return was at hand. The emperor, told of this, sent two thousand soldiers to guard the house against the moon-people, yet when the moon rose, a shining cloud descended, and no bow-arm could draw against it. The messenger from the moon hung a robe of wings beside her; whoever wore it ceased to feel love or grief. She wrote her last verses to the emperor, prayed him never to send again for her, donned the robe so that her mortal thoughts fell away with her tears, and ascended with the cloud, leaving behind a vial of the elixir of immortality and a letter.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Taketori Monogatari, the moon-descension and ascent (trans. Dickins 1888; cf. Davis 1912); not verbatim.

passages.text: The emperor, seeing the elixir without the one being who could make life sweet, ordered it burned on the mountain nearest heaven, where the smoke rose highest; the mount of Suruga ever after bore the name Fuji, meaning 'Never-Dying', and smoke was said to rise from its summit to this day. The letters of the princess he kept, and his own men who had gazed upon the moon wept at the summit of that smoke.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Taketori Monogatari, the Fuji aetiology (trans. Dickins 1888; cf. Davis 1912); not verbatim.

narrative.en:
The Taketori Monogatari, commonly called the Tale of the Bamboo-Cutter, is the oldest surviving monogatari in Japanese literature, composed around the end of the ninth or the beginning of the tenth century CE. Though a courtly romance rather than a shrine myth, its matter is entirely mythic: a divine child from the moon who enters the human world by miraculous birth, blesses it with gold, defeats its most powerful men with impossible quests, and finally re-ascends, refusing the immortality of heaven to anyone who cannot share it with her. It is Japan's great otherworld-voyage tale told in reverse — the visitor is the otherworld, and the mortals are the ones who long to follow.

The tale opens on a poor bamboo-cutter, Taketori no Okina, who cuts cane for a living and has neither son nor daughter. One night a stalk shines at the base like sunlight, and inside he finds a girl four inches tall, of exquisite form. He carries her home to his wife, and the couple raise the child in a basket with tenderness. From that day every stalk he cuts bears gold, and the cutter grows rich in a few months. The child, meanwhile, grows from four inches to full stature in three months, more radiant than any woman in Japan, and is named Kaguya-hime. Word of her spreads; suitors fill the house night after night until only the most determined remain — five noblemen of the highest rank — and the old man, anxious for his foster-daughter, urges her to take a husband.

Kaguya-hime sets each suitor an impossible quest: the stone begging-bowl of the Buddha in India; jeweled branches from the immortal island of Hōrai; the fur robe of the fire-rat that no flame can burn; the jewel from the dragon-king's neck that shifts through five colours; and the cowry-shell that lies in the nest of the swallow. Each man returns with a treasure, and each treasure proves counterfeit: the bowl is common crockery, the jewels on the branch are paste that runs, the fur robe burns in the hearth, the dragon-jewel comes from a conjurer's merchant, and the cowry from the swallow is bird's dung. The suitors slink away in disgrace, and the tale lingers over their humiliation — the closest the monogatari comes to social satire, ridiculing wealth, rank and bravado before a girl who cannot be bought.

Last of all the emperor himself hears of the princess and visits; her radiance dazzles him, he begs her to come to the palace, and she refuses. Still he writes to her, and she answers in verse, and for three years they exchange poems while he does not press his claim further — an almost unprecedented gesture of restraint in a Heian tale of imperial desire.

But the princess has been looking at the moon with tears. As autumn's full moon draws near she confesses to the old couple that she is not of this world: she was sent down from the moon capital as punishment, and the time of her recall has come. The emperor, hearing of it, orders two thousand soldiers to encircle the house, yet when the moon rises a cloud of light descends, and against the moon-people no arrow will fly. The celestial messenger hangs a robe of wings beside her, and whoever wears it forgets all mortal grief. She writes her farewell to the emperor, praying him never to send for her again, for in heaven he cannot be followed; she sets down a letter and a vial of the elixir of immortality; she robes herself and her tears and her love fall away like a garment, and she ascends with the cloud into the moon.

The emperor, unable either to follow her or to make his court immortal without her, orders the elixir burned on the summit of the mountain in Suruga nearest to heaven. The smoke rises highest there, and the mountain takes the name Fuji, 'Never-Dying'; its summit is said to smoke to this day. The princess's letters he keeps with his own until his death. The tale thus closes its double aetiology — of Fuji's name and of the unbridgeable distance between men and gods — and the old cutter and his wife are left with the house their gold built and a daughter's empty room.
narrative._comment: narrative in prose; functions array separately

functions: Aetiology of Mount Fuji's name (fushi, 'never-dying') and of the elixir of immortality motif in Japanese narrative; the mountain is the smoke-channel between heaven and earth.
Charter for moon-veneration imagery in Japanese court poetry and the autumn full-moon festival (Jūgoya); the moon is a homeland, not a lamp.
Satire of Heian aristocratic courtship: the five suitors and their counterfeits ridicule status, wealth and bravado, making the tale a mirror of court society.
Refusal of imperial authority: even the emperor cannot bind the divine visitor, dramatising the gulf between human rule and heavenly beings.

title.en: Urashima Taro and the Dragon Palace
title.zh: 浦島太郎與龍宮

region.en: Midzunoe fishing village, Tango province; Dragon Palace beneath the sea (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 丹後國水之江漁村；海底龍宮（象徵定位）

period: Oldest versions in Nihongi (720 CE) and Man'yōshū poems (c. 759 CE); popular folktale recorded 1912 (Davis)

source.work: F. Hadland Davis, Myths & Legends of Japan (1912), ch. XXVII 'Legends of the Sea'; earliest variants in Nihongi, trans. W. G. Aston (1896)

summary.en: The fisher-lad Urashima of Midzunoe spares a tortoise, is carried to the Dragon Palace as reward, and marries the princess Otohime in a land where all four seasons linger at once. Three days there are three hundred years on earth; opening his wife's forbidden jewel-box releases his old age, and he dies on the shore of a world he can no longer recognise.
summary.zh: 丹後水之江漁童浦島救龜，受邀入龍宮，娶乙姬為妻，居四時同在之樂土。龍宮三日，人間三百年；違禁開啟玉手箱，頓成皓首之翁，倒斃於再不識的故鄉海岸。

sensitivity.note: Ancient Japanese folktale with official-annals variants (Nihongi Book X); passages are condensed paraphrases of public-domain translations (Davis 1912; Aston 1896), presented for comparative mythology.

passages.text: Urashima, a fisher-lad of the little village of Midzunoe in Tango province, caught a tortoise in his nets; because tortoises live many thousands of years, he spared the creature and let it return to the sea. As he dozed at his oars a sweet voice called his name: the tortoise, able to speak, thanked him for his kindness and offered to carry him to the ryūgū, the Palace of the Dragon King. Riding the tortoise's back he glided through the sea at tremendous speed, and his clothes never once grew wet.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Davis, Myths & Legends of Japan, ch. XXVII (1912); not verbatim.

passages.text: At the Sea King's palace the red bream, flounder, sole and cuttlefish came out to welcome him, and the Dragon King led him to an inner chamber where the princess Otohime sat in garments of red and gold, the colours of a wave under sunlight. She explained that the tortoise had been herself, testing his kindness of heart, and as reward for his virtue she offered to be his bride in a land of eternal youth. Fishes in ceremonial robes bore coral trays of delicacies, music was played, and the wedding cup of sake was drunk on the white sand.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Davis, Myths & Legends of Japan, ch. XXVII (1912); not verbatim.

passages.text: The marvel of that country was that all four seasons lingered together: eastward plum and cherry bloomed with butterflies above the blossom; southward the trees stood in full summer and the cricket sang; westward the maples burned like fire; northward lay snow and a pond of ice. After three days Urashima remembered his old parents and asked leave to go home. Otohime wept and begged him to stay one day more, but he promised to return, and she gave him a keepsake, the Tamate-bako, the Box of the Jewel Hand, forbidding him ever to open it.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Davis, Myths & Legends of Japan, ch. XXVII (1912); not verbatim.

passages.text: Mounting the tortoise he reached his own country, but his father's cottage had vanished and only the little stream remained. A passer-by told him that a fisher-lad named Urashima had gone to sea three hundred years ago and was drowned, and all his kin lay long in their graves; then he remembered that in the divine land one day was a hundred years. Hearing the murmur of the sea, he thought Otohime called him, and that if he opened the box it might reveal the way back. He untied the red silk thread and lifted the lid: a little white cloud rushed out and rolled away over the sea, and the sacred promise broken, the handsome youth became old and wrinkled, staggered toward the waves, and fell dead upon the shore.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Davis, Myths & Legends of Japan, ch. XXVII (1912); not verbatim.

narrative.en:
Urashima Taro is Japan's classic otherworld-voyage tale, and one of its oldest: traces of the story appear in the official annals (Nihongi, Book X, where a fisher named Urashima-no-ko visits the Eternal Land of Tokoyo and returns aged) and in two famous Man'yōshū laments that take the story for granted, so that the ballad must be centuries older than its oldest written forms. In the popular version the fisher-lad of Midzunoe in Tango province spares a tortoise; the tortoise is the sea-princess Otohime in disguise, come to test his kindness, and she repays him with a voyage to the Dragon Palace of the sea-god, her father.

The Dragon Palace (ryūgū) is an otherworld of perfect abundance and suspended time: fish in ceremonial robes serve the wedding feast, and the seasons stand together in one landscape — spring in the east, summer in the south, autumn in the west, winter in the north — a ritual image of the world renewed and unchanging, akin to the Evergreen Land of Tokoyo in the annals. Urashima marries Otohime and dwells in this bliss for what he believes are days.

The return home supplies the tale's tragic engine. Three days in the palace are three hundred years on earth; the village, the parents, the whole world he knew have passed away. Otohime's parting gift, the Tamate-bako (jewel-box), is a taboo-object: it holds either his vanished years or the road back to the sea — the tellings differ — and it must never be opened. Lonely among strangers and hearing the sea call like a wife's voice, Urashima opens it. A white cloud escapes, and his mortality, banked for three centuries, settles on him at once; in the Davis retelling he falls dead on the shore; in the Man'yōshū he becomes a crane and departs, and his wife flies up from the sea as a tortoise; in the Nihongi he simply grows old and dies, a witness of Tokoyo's time-slip.

The tale functions as Japan's great meditation on time and death: bliss bought by kindness, forfeited by curiosity, and unrecoverable because the otherworld's clock cannot be reconciled with ours. It also aetiologises the summer sea-longsing: the shore of Midzunoe, the boy's tomb and casket were still shown at a Kanagawa temple in Chamberlain's day, and Mount Fuji's name 'never-dying' echoes the same immortality-longing in the Taketori tale. As a comparative text it sits with the Celtic otherworld voyages (Oisín in Tír na nÓg is nearly the same plot) and with the boxed-years motif found from Polynesia to China, making it one of the strongest cross-tradition matches in the Japanese corpus.

functions: Etiology of the time-slip: explains human mortality and the irreversibility of age through a contrast between divine and human time (one palace day = one hundred years).
Charter for kindness-to-animals motifs in Japanese folk ethics: the test of the tortoise rewards compassion with otherworld hospitality.
Ritual image of world-renewal: the four seasons abiding together in the Dragon Palace mirror Tokoyo, the Evergreen Land of the annals, as an image of unchanging abundance.
Festival and shore-lore anchor: Urashima's tomb, fishing-line and casket were shown at a Kanagawa temple, and the tale is recited in summer sea-songs and Noh (Urashima, Takasago's companion pieces).

title.en: The Serpent That Called the Reef to Rise
title.zh: 喚起礁石之蛇

region.en: Admiralty Islands, Papua New Guinea (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 阿德米羅提群島，巴布亞新幾內亞（象徵定位）

period: Oral tradition; recorded in R. B. Dixon, Oceanic Mythology, 1916

source.work: Roland B. Dixon, Oceanic Mythology, The Mythology of All Races Vol. IX (Boston: Marshall Jones, 1916), 'Melanesia' ch. I

summary.en: In the beginning nothing existed but a wide sea, and in it swam a great serpent. Wanting a resting place, the serpent called out, 'Let the reef rise!' — and the reef rose from the ocean and became dry land.
summary.zh: 太初唯有一片汪洋，巨蛇游於其中。蛇欲得一棲息之所，便呼曰『礁石升起吧！』——礁石遂自海中浮出，化為陸地。

sensitivity.note: Recorded by a museum anthropologist (Dixon 1916) from Admiralty Islands informants; colonial-era collection, heritage held by Manus communities.

passages.text: A part of the people of the Admiralty Islands believed that once there was nothing in the world but a wide-spread sea. In this primeval ocean swam a great serpent, and because the serpent had no place on which he might rest, he called out, 'Let the reef rise!' And the reef rose up out of the ocean and became dry land. In this way the first solid ground in the world came into being — the serpent's own words lifting the foundation of the islands out of the endless water.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dixon, Oceanic Mythology, 'Melanesia' ch. I (1916); not verbatim.

title.en: The Couple on the Driftwood
title.zh: 浮木上的一對

region.en: Admiralty Islands, Papua New Guinea (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 阿德米羅提群島，巴布亞新幾內亞（象徵定位）

period: Oral tradition; recorded in R. B. Dixon, Oceanic Mythology, 1916

source.work: Roland B. Dixon, Oceanic Mythology, The Mythology of All Races Vol. IX (Boston: Marshall Jones, 1916), 'Melanesia' ch. I

summary.en: A variant Admiralty Islands creation story: a man and a woman floated on the primeval sea on a piece of driftwood, watching to see whether the ocean would dry up. When the waters retired they planted trees and created the food plants on the barren new land.
summary.zh: 阿德米羅提群島另一創世異文：一男一女乘浮木漂流於太初之海，觀察海水是否退去。水退陸現，惟大地荒蕪無物，二人遂種樹、造百種食物。

sensitivity.note: Colonial-era collection (Dixon 1916); heritage held by Manus communities.

passages.text: Another Admiralty Islands version differs from the serpent's reef: a man and a woman, after having floated upon the primeval sea, climbed upon a piece of driftwood and wondered whether the ocean would ever dry up. At last the waters wholly retired, and land appeared, covered with hills — but barren and without life. Whereupon the two beings planted trees and created foods of various sorts, stocking the empty world with forest and garden from their driftwood vantage.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dixon, Oceanic Mythology, 'Melanesia' ch. I (1916); not verbatim.

title.en: To-Kabinana and To-Karvuvu Fish Up the Land
title.zh: 托卡比納那與托卡武武釣起陸地

region.en: Gazelle Peninsula, New Britain (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 新不列顛加澤爾半島（象徵定位）

period: Oral tradition; recorded in R. B. Dixon, Oceanic Mythology, 1916

source.work: Roland B. Dixon, Oceanic Mythology, The Mythology of All Races Vol. IX (Boston: Marshall Jones, 1916), 'Melanesia' ch. I

summary.en: On New Britain the familiar Polynesian-style myth of fishing land from the bottom of the sea is told of the culture-hero brothers To-Kabinana and To-Karvuvu, who haul up islands from the deep for their people.
summary.zh: 新不列顛島流傳與波利尼西亞相仿的『釣起陸地』神話：文化英雄兄弟托卡比納那與托卡武武自深海拉起島嶼，為其子民造地。

sensitivity.note: Colonial-era collection (Dixon 1916); Tolai heritage of the Gazelle Peninsula.

passages.text: Among the coastal tribes of the Gazelle Peninsula of New Britain we find the familiar story of the fishing of the land from the bottom of the sea, a task accomplished by the two culture-hero brothers, To-Kabinana and To-Karvuvu. The wise elder brother drew the land upward from the deep, and the islands of their coasts rose where he pulled; the fool of a younger brother lent his hand to the same work, his blunders marking the imperfections of the new earth. Some of their other deeds — the making of the first women, the carved shark, the roasted mother — fill the rest of the Gazelle cycle.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dixon, Oceanic Mythology, 'Melanesia' ch. I (1916); not verbatim.

title.en: Fishing Up the Land in the Southern New Hebrides
title.zh: 新赫布里底群島南部的釣地神話

region.en: Southern New Hebrides (Tanna–Erromango) (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 新赫布里底群島南部（塔納—埃羅芒加）（象徵定位）

period: Oral tradition; recorded in R. B. Dixon, Oceanic Mythology, 1916

source.work: Roland B. Dixon, Oceanic Mythology, The Mythology of All Races Vol. IX (Boston: Marshall Jones, 1916), 'Melanesia' ch. I

summary.en: The same conception of land fished up from the bottom of the sea, told in slightly greater detail, is found in the southern New Hebrides — the southernmost reach of the tale, far from its New Britain home.
summary.zh: 『自海底釣起陸地』之說亦見於新赫布里底群島南部，敘述稍詳——此乃該神話分布之最南端，遠離其新不列顛故地。

sensitivity.note: Colonial-era collection (Dixon 1916); heritage of southern Vanuatu communities.

passages.text: Dixon notes that the story of the fishing of the land from the bottom of the sea, told on New Britain by To-Kabinana and To-Karvuvu, is found also in the southern New Hebrides in slightly greater detail. There the first dry ground of the islands was likewise drawn up from the deep — a striking instance of one tale-idea travelling the full length of the Melanesian chain, from the Bismarck Archipelago to the islands that lie nearly opposite New Caledonia.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dixon, Oceanic Mythology, 'Melanesia' ch. I (1916); not verbatim.

title.en: Manual Carves a Wife from Wood
title.zh: 曼努爾刻木為妻

region.en: Admiralty Islands, Papua New Guinea (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 阿德米羅提群島，巴布亞新幾內亞（象徵定位）

period: Oral tradition; recorded in R. B. Dixon, Oceanic Mythology, 1916

source.work: Roland B. Dixon, Oceanic Mythology, The Mythology of All Races Vol. IX (Boston: Marshall Jones, 1916), 'Melanesia' ch. I

summary.en: Manual, alone in the Admiralty Islands, longed for a wife. He felled a tree, shaped the trunk into a woman's figure, and spoke: 'My wood there, become a woman!' — and the image came to life.
summary.zh: 阿德米羅提群島的曼努爾獨居渴偶。他入林伐木，將樹幹雕成女子之形，念咒曰：『我的木頭啊，成為女人吧！』木像遂活。

sensitivity.note: Colonial-era collection (Dixon 1916); Manus heritage. Motif 'clay-humans' used for its making-by-speech parallel.

passages.text: In the Admiralty Islands it is said that Manual was alone and longed for a wife. So he took his axe, went into the forest, and cut down a tree, and after he had fashioned the trunk into the figure of a woman, he spoke to it: 'My wood there, become a woman!' And the image came to life — the first marriage of mankind made not by finding a bride but by carving one, the carver's speech turning wood into flesh.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dixon, Oceanic Mythology, 'Melanesia' ch. I (1916); not verbatim.

title.en: Qat Carves the First Six Humans
title.zh: 卡特刻出最早之六人

region.en: Banks Islands, Vanuatu (symbolic pin: Gaua/Mota)
region.zh: 瓦努阿圖班克斯群島（象徵定位：高阿島／莫塔島）

period: Oral tradition; recorded in R. B. Dixon, Oceanic Mythology, 1916 (from Codrington's Mota texts)

source.work: Roland B. Dixon, Oceanic Mythology, The Mythology of All Races Vol. IX (Boston: Marshall Jones, 1916), 'Melanesia' ch. I

summary.en: Qat, the first maker of men, cut wood of the dracaena tree into six figures — three men and three women — hid them three days, then danced and drummed before them until they stirred and stood alive; he joined them into three married pairs.
summary.zh: 卡特首造人類：以龍血樹之木刻成六像，三男三女；藏之三日，取出立起，於其前跳舞擊鼓，木像漸動而得自立——『如是誘之入生』；遂配為三對夫妻。

sensitivity.note: Missionary-era Mota collection via Dixon 1916; cross-ref qat-creation (same episode in Codrington).

passages.text: In the Banks Islands, Qat was the first to make man, cutting wood out of the dracaena-tree and forming it into six figures, three men and three women. When he had finished them, he hid them away for three days, after which he brought them forth and set them up. Dancing in front of them and seeing that they began to move, he beat the drum before them, and they moved still more, and thus he beguiled them into life, so that they could stand of themselves. Then he divided them into three pairs as man and wife — the first marriages of the Banks Islands made by Qat's own hand.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dixon, Oceanic Mythology, 'Melanesia' ch. I (1916), after Codrington's Mota texts; not verbatim.

title.en: Marawa Buries His People: The Origin of Death
title.zh: 馬拉瓦埋活人：死亡之起源

region.en: Banks Islands, Vanuatu (symbolic pin: Gaua/Mota)
region.zh: 瓦努阿圖班克斯群島（象徵定位：高阿島／莫塔島）

period: Oral tradition; recorded in R. B. Dixon, Oceanic Mythology, 1916 (from Codrington's Mota texts)

source.work: Roland B. Dixon, Oceanic Mythology, The Mythology of All Races Vol. IX (Boston: Marshall Jones, 1916), 'Melanesia' ch. I

summary.en: Marawa, envious of Qat, copied his wooden figures and drummed them alive; then he buried his people seven days in a pit lined with coconut fronds — and dug them up lifeless and decomposed. So death came among men.
summary.zh: 馬拉瓦嫉妒卡特，仿其法刻木鼓而活之；卻將其所造之人埋入鋪椰葉之坑七日——掘出時已死而腐。人類之死，由此而始。

sensitivity.note: Missionary-era Mota collection via Dixon 1916; cross-ref qat-creation.

passages.text: Now Marawa, who was a malicious, envious fellow, saw what Qat had made and determined to do likewise. So he took wood of another sort, and when he had fashioned the images, he set them up and beat the drum before them, and gave them life as Qat had done. But when he saw them move, he dug a pit and covered the bottom with coco-nut fronds, burying his men and women in it for seven days; and when he dug them up again, he found them lifeless and decomposed. This was the origin of death among men — mortality entering the world through the envy of the copyist.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dixon, Oceanic Mythology, 'Melanesia' ch. I (1916), after Codrington's Mota texts; not verbatim.

title.en: The Clay Man and the Twig Woman
title.zh: 紅土男子與樹枝之女

region.en: Banks Islands, Vanuatu (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 瓦努阿圖班克斯群島（象徵定位）

period: Oral tradition; recorded in R. B. Dixon, Oceanic Mythology, 1916 (from Codrington's Mota texts)

source.work: Roland B. Dixon, Oceanic Mythology, The Mythology of All Races Vol. IX (Boston: Marshall Jones, 1916), 'Melanesia' ch. I

summary.en: In another Banks Islands version, Qat made the first man of red clay, and the first woman of supple rods and rings covered with the spathes of sago palms — exactly as the people themselves make the tall dance-hats of the sacred ceremonies.
summary.zh: 班克斯群島另一異文：卡特以紅土造首男，以柔枝與環、外覆西米棕櫚葉鞘造首女——正如島民製作聖舞高帽之法。

sensitivity.note: Missionary-era Mota collection via Dixon 1916.

passages.text: According to another version from the same Banks Islands area, while the first man was made of red clay by Qat, he created the first woman of rods and rings of supple twigs covered with the spathes of sago palms — just as they make the tall hats which are used in the sacred dances. Man and woman of the first day were thus made of the two most ritual materials of the islands: the earth itself, and the ceremonial craft of the dance.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dixon, Oceanic Mythology, 'Melanesia' ch. I (1916), after Codrington's Mota texts; not verbatim.

title.en: Takaro's Ten Mud Men and the First Woman
title.zh: 塔卡羅造十泥人與首位女子

region.en: New Hebrides (Ambae/Aoba) (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 新赫布里底群島（安巴埃島）（象徵定位）

period: Oral tradition; recorded in R. B. Dixon, Oceanic Mythology, 1916

source.work: Roland B. Dixon, Oceanic Mythology, The Mythology of All Races Vol. IX (Boston: Marshall Jones, 1916), 'Melanesia' ch. I

summary.en: Takaro made ten figures from mud and breathed life into them; unsatisfied with a world of men, he changed one into a woman with a thrown fruit, then sent each man to her for fire and water until the last she called husband.
summary.zh: 塔卡羅以泥塑十人像，吹氣使活；世間皆男，塔卡羅不滿，擲果一枚使其化為女子，令九男依次向她求火、求水，逐一被稱為兄長，唯末一人稱為夫。

sensitivity.note: Colonial-era collection (Dixon 1916); Ambae heritage.

passages.text: A tale of the creation of man from earth is told in the New Hebrides. Takaro made from mud ten figures of men. When they were finished, he breathed upon them — upon their eyes, their ears, their mouths, their hands, their feet — and thus the images became alive. But all the people he had made were men, and Takaro was not satisfied.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dixon, Oceanic Mythology, 'Melanesia' ch. I (1916); not verbatim.

passages.text: So he told them to light a fire and cook some food, then ordered them to stand still while he threw a fruit at one of them — and lo, one of the men was changed into a woman. Takaro sent the woman to dwell by herself in a house. One by one he sent the nine men to her, first to ask for fire, then for water; each she greeted as her elder brother, her younger brother, her kinsman — all but the last, and him she called her husband. So Takaro said to him, 'Take her as your wife, and you two shall live together.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dixon, Oceanic Mythology, 'Melanesia' ch. I (1916); not verbatim.

title.en: Drawn in Blood: The Birth of the Two Brothers
title.zh: 血繪地畫：二兄弟之生

region.en: Gazelle Peninsula, New Britain (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 新不列顛加澤爾半島（象徵定位）

period: Oral tradition; recorded in R. B. Dixon, Oceanic Mythology, 1916

source.work: Roland B. Dixon, Oceanic Mythology, The Mythology of All Races Vol. IX (Boston: Marshall Jones, 1916), 'Melanesia' ch. I

summary.en: A being drew two figures of men on the ground, cut himself with a knife, sprinkled the drawings with his blood, and covered them with leaves; they came to life as To-Kabinana and To-Karvuvu. The elder then threw two unripe coconuts to earth and two women burst from them.
summary.zh: 有神者於地上畫二男形，以刀自割，以其血灑畫，覆之以葉；畫遂活為托卡比納那與托卡武武。兄攀椰樹擲青椰二枚落地，爆裂而化為二女，娶之為妻。

sensitivity.note: Colonial-era collection (Dixon 1916); Tolai heritage.

passages.text: In the beginning, a being drew two figures of men upon the ground, and then, cutting himself with a knife, he sprinkled the two drawings with his blood and covered them over with leaves. The result was that they came to life as To-Kabinana and To-Karvuvu, the wise and the foolish brother of the Gazelle Peninsula.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dixon, Oceanic Mythology, 'Melanesia' ch. I (1916); not verbatim.

passages.text: To-Kabinana then climbed a coco-nut-tree which bore light yellow nuts, and picking two unripe ones, he threw them to the ground, where they burst and changed into two women, whom he took as his wives. His brother asked how he had come to be possessed of the two women, and To-Kabinana told him.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dixon, Oceanic Mythology, 'Melanesia' ch. I (1916); not verbatim.

title.en: To-Karvuvu's Ugly-Nosed Wives
title.zh: 托卡武武之塌鼻妻子

region.en: Gazelle Peninsula, New Britain (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 新不列顛加澤爾半島（象徵定位）

period: Oral tradition; recorded in R. B. Dixon, Oceanic Mythology, 1916

source.work: Roland B. Dixon, Oceanic Mythology, The Mythology of All Races Vol. IX (Boston: Marshall Jones, 1916), 'Melanesia' ch. I

summary.en: To-Karvuvu copied his brother's coconut trick, but his nuts fell on their under side and burst into two women with depressed, ugly noses. Jealous, he abandoned his own wives and took one of To-Kabinana's.
summary.zh: 托卡武武仿兄擲椰，然其椰以底觸地，爆出二女，鼻樑低塌貌醜。他嫉妒兄之美妻，遂棄己二妻，而奪托卡比納那之一妻。

sensitivity.note: Colonial-era collection (Dixon 1916); Tolai heritage.

passages.text: To-Karvuvu also climbed a tree and likewise threw down two nuts; but they fell so that their under side struck the ground, and from them came two women with depressed, ugly noses. So To-Karvuvu was jealous because his brother's wives were better looking than his, and he took one of To-Kabinana's spouses, abandoning the two ugly females who were his own — the foolish brother's first great blunder, and the tale's aition of why some families prosper and some do not.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dixon, Oceanic Mythology, 'Melanesia' ch. I (1916); not verbatim.

title.en: The Light and Dark Coconut Women
title.zh: 白椰女與黑椰女

region.en: Gazelle Peninsula, New Britain (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 新不列顛加澤爾半島（象徵定位）

period: Oral tradition; recorded in R. B. Dixon, Oceanic Mythology, 1916

source.work: Roland B. Dixon, Oceanic Mythology, The Mythology of All Races Vol. IX (Boston: Marshall Jones, 1916), 'Melanesia' ch. I

summary.en: To-Kabinana tied a light-coloured coconut to his canoe and it became a handsome woman; the foolish brother's dark nut became a black-skinned woman. From the two descends mankind, divided into two classes, and with the dark woman death entered the world: 'if all of us were only light of skin, we should not die.'
summary.zh: 托卡比納那以白椰繫舟尾，化為俊美女子；弟之黑椰則化黑膚女子。兩類人由此而生：白皮者不致於死，黑椰女一脈則必死——托卡武武之愚遂為人類招致死亡與分化。

sensitivity.note: Colonial-era collection (Dixon 1916). The tale encodes a local dual-marriage-class rule; recorded as ethnographic material, not endorsement.

passages.text: To-Kabinana said to To-Karvuvu, 'Do you get two light-coloured coco-nuts. One of them you must hide, then bring the other to me.' To-Karvuvu, however, did not obey, but got one light and one dark nut, and having hidden the latter, he brought the light-coloured one to his brother, who tied it to the stern of his canoe and paddled out to sea. Soon the coco-nut turned into a handsome woman, who sat on the stern of the canoe and steered while To-Kabinana paddled.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dixon, Oceanic Mythology, 'Melanesia' ch. I (1916); not verbatim.

passages.text: When To-Karvuvu brought the other coco-nut, his brother saw that it was dark-coloured and upbraided him: 'You are indeed a stupid fellow. You have brought misery upon our mortal race.' They tied the dark nut to the stern and paddled away, and it turned into a black-skinned woman. Then To-Kabinana said: 'Alas, you have only ruined our mortal race. If all of us were only light of skin, we should not die. Now, however, this dark-skinned woman will produce one group, and the light-skinned woman another, and the light-skinned men shall marry the dark-skinned women, and the dark-skinned men shall marry the light-skinned women.' And so To-Kabinana divided mankind into two classes.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dixon, Oceanic Mythology, 'Melanesia' ch. I (1916); not verbatim.

title.en: The Dove's Son
title.zh: 鳩之子

region.en: Admiralty Islands, Papua New Guinea (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 阿德米羅提群島，巴布亞新幾內亞（象徵定位）

period: Oral tradition; recorded in R. B. Dixon, Oceanic Mythology, 1916

source.work: Roland B. Dixon, Oceanic Mythology, The Mythology of All Races Vol. IX (Boston: Marshall Jones, 1916), 'Melanesia' ch. I

summary.en: One Admiralty Islands version of human origins: a dove bore two young, one of which was a bird and one a man, who became the ancestor of the human race by incestuous union with his mother.
summary.zh: 阿德米羅提群島人類起源之一說：一鳩產二雛，一為鳥，一為人；此人與其母鳩结合，遂為人類之祖。

sensitivity.note: Colonial-era collection (Dixon 1916); Manus heritage.

passages.text: In the Admiralty Islands, according to one version, a dove bore two young, one of which was a bird and one a man. The man became the ancestor of the human race by incestuous union with his mother — the first people of the islands descending from a bird's brood.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dixon, Oceanic Mythology, 'Melanesia' ch. I (1916); not verbatim.

title.en: The Tortoise's Ten Eggs
title.zh: 龜之十卵

region.en: Admiralty Islands, Papua New Guinea (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 阿德米羅提群島，巴布亞新幾內亞（象徵定位）

period: Oral tradition; recorded in R. B. Dixon, Oceanic Mythology, 1916

source.work: Roland B. Dixon, Oceanic Mythology, The Mythology of All Races Vol. IX (Boston: Marshall Jones, 1916), 'Melanesia' ch. I

summary.en: Another Admiralty Islands recension: a tortoise laid ten eggs, from which were hatched eight tortoises and two human beings, a man and a woman, who married and became the ancestors of both light-skinned and dark-skinned people.
summary.zh: 阿德米羅提群島另一異文：一龜產十卵，孵化得八龜與二人——一男一女；二人成婚，遂為白膚與黑膚人種之共祖。

sensitivity.note: Colonial-era collection (Dixon 1916); Manus heritage.

passages.text: Another recension has it that a tortoise laid ten eggs, from which were hatched eight tortoises and two human beings, one man and one woman. These two, marrying, became the ancestors of both light-skinned and dark-skinned people — the human stock of the Admiralties hatched from a single clutch beside their tortoise siblings.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dixon, Oceanic Mythology, 'Melanesia' ch. I (1916); not verbatim.

title.en: Ndengei Hatches the First Pair
title.zh: 恩登蓋孵出初民二性

region.en: Viti Levu, Fiji (Nakauvadra range, symbolic pin)
region.zh: 斐濟維提島（納夸瓦德拉山，象徵定位）

period: Oral tradition; recorded in R. B. Dixon, Oceanic Mythology, 1916

source.work: Roland B. Dixon, Oceanic Mythology, The Mythology of All Races Vol. IX (Boston: Marshall Jones, 1916), 'Melanesia' ch. I

summary.en: In Fiji, a bird laid two eggs which were hatched by Ndengei, the great serpent — a boy coming from one and a girl from the other. The serpent-god of the Nakauvadra cave thus brooded mankind into being.
summary.zh: 斐濟神話：一鳥產二卵，由巨蛇恩登蓋孵化——一卵出男，一卵出女。納夸瓦德拉山洞中之蛇神遂成孵育人類之祖。

sensitivity.note: Colonial-era collection (Dixon 1916); iTaukei heritage. Cross-ref thomson-fijians records.

passages.text: In Fiji it is said that a bird laid two eggs which were hatched by Ndengei, the great serpent — a boy coming from one and a girl from the other. Thus the first Fijians were brooded into life by the serpent who dwells in the earth, and Ndengei, the old stone-eating snake-god of the Nakauvadra, stands at the head of the race as its incubator rather than its maker.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dixon, Oceanic Mythology, 'Melanesia' ch. I (1916); not verbatim.

title.en: From the Egg a Worm, from the Worm a Man
title.zh: 卵生蛆、蛆化人

region.en: Eastern Torres Strait Islands (Mer) (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 托雷斯海峽東部群島（摩爾島）（象徵定位）

period: Oral tradition; recorded in R. B. Dixon, Oceanic Mythology, 1916

source.work: Roland B. Dixon, Oceanic Mythology, The Mythology of All Races Vol. IX (Boston: Marshall Jones, 1916), 'Melanesia' ch. I

summary.en: According to the Eastern Islanders of Torres Strait, a bird having laid an egg, a maggot or worm was developed from it, which then was transformed into human shape.
summary.zh: 托雷斯海峽東部島民之說：一鳥產卵，卵中生出蛆蟲，蛆蟲再變化為人形。

sensitivity.note: Colonial-era collection (Dixon 1916); Meriam heritage of Torres Strait.

passages.text: A variant of the egg-origin tale is found in Torres Straits where, according to the Eastern Islanders, a bird having laid an egg, a maggot or worm was developed from it, which then was transformed into human shape — life passing in three stages, from the bird's egg through the lowly worm to the first human form.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dixon, Oceanic Mythology, 'Melanesia' ch. I (1916); not verbatim.

title.en: Hi-asa's Blood, Two Eggs
title.zh: 希阿莎之血化雙卵

region.en: Admiralty Islands, Papua New Guinea (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 阿德米羅提群島，巴布亞新幾內亞（象徵定位）

period: Oral tradition; recorded in R. B. Dixon, Oceanic Mythology, 1916

source.work: Roland B. Dixon, Oceanic Mythology, The Mythology of All Races Vol. IX (Boston: Marshall Jones, 1916), 'Melanesia' ch. I

summary.en: The woman Hi-asa, living alone, cut her finger while shaving pandanus strips and caught the blood in a mussel-shell. After eleven days the blood held two eggs, which burst into a man and a woman — the parents of the human race.
summary.zh: 獨居女子希阿莎削露兜樹條時割傷手指，以蚌殼接血覆蓋之。十一日後血中化二卵，數日卵裂，出一男一女——人類之父母由此而生。

sensitivity.note: Colonial-era collection (Dixon 1916); Manus heritage.

passages.text: One version from the Admiralty Islands tells of an origin of mankind from a clot of blood. A woman named Hi-asa, who lived alone, one day cut her finger while shaving pandanus strips. Collecting the blood from the wound in a mussel-shell, she put a cover over it and set it away; but when, after eleven days, she looked in the shell, it contained two eggs. She covered them up, and after several days they burst, one producing a man and the other a woman, who became the parents of the human race.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dixon, Oceanic Mythology, 'Melanesia' ch. I (1916); not verbatim.

title.en: The Old Woman's Arms: Blood of the Pandanus
title.zh: 老嫗之臂：露兜樹血種

region.en: Gazelle Peninsula, New Britain (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 新不列顛加澤爾半島（象徵定位）

period: Oral tradition; recorded in R. B. Dixon, Oceanic Mythology, 1916

source.work: Roland B. Dixon, Oceanic Mythology, The Mythology of All Races Vol. IX (Boston: Marshall Jones, 1916), 'Melanesia' ch. I

summary.en: An old woman wading for shellfish scratched her aching arms with sharp pandanus strips and laid the blood-covered strips in a refuse heap. The pile swelled, and from the blood of her right arm grew To-Kabinana, from her left To-Karvuvu.
summary.zh: 一老嫗涉水拾貝，雙臂痠痛，以利露兜樹條先後割左右臂，將染血樹條棄於垃圾堆中。日後垃圾堆隆起，右臂之血生托卡比納那，左臂之血生托卡武武。

sensitivity.note: Colonial-era collection (Dixon 1916); Tolai heritage.

passages.text: While an old woman was wading in the sea searching for shellfish, her arms pained her, and so, taking two sharp strips of pandanus, she scratched and cut first one arm and then the other. The two strips of pandanus, thus covered with her blood, she laid away in a heap of refuse which she intended to burn; but after a time the pile began to swell, and when she was about to set fire to it, she saw that two boys had grown from her blood — from the blood of her right arm, To-Kabinana, and from that of her left arm, To-Karvuvu.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dixon, Oceanic Mythology, 'Melanesia' ch. I (1916); not verbatim.

title.en: The Sprouting Sugar-Cane
title.zh: 甘蔗生人

region.en: Solomon Islands (symbolic pin: Guadalcanal)
region.zh: 所羅門群島（象徵定位：瓜達爾卡納爾）

period: Oral tradition; recorded in R. B. Dixon, Oceanic Mythology, 1916

source.work: Roland B. Dixon, Oceanic Mythology, The Mythology of All Races Vol. IX (Boston: Marshall Jones, 1916), 'Melanesia' ch. I

summary.en: In the Solomon Islands, mankind came from plants: two knots began to sprout on a stalk of sugar-cane, and when the cane below each sprout burst, from one issued a man and from the other a woman — the parents of the race.
summary.zh: 所羅門群島之說：一節甘蔗生出兩個芽瘤，芽下之莖先後爆裂，一瘤出男、一瘤出女——人類之父母自此而生。

sensitivity.note: Colonial-era collection (Dixon 1916); Solomon Islands heritage.

passages.text: An origin of the human race from plants seems definitely stated only in the Solomon Islands, where it is said that two knots began to sprout on a stalk of sugar-cane, and when the cane below each sprout burst, from one issued a man and from the other a woman — these becoming the parents of mankind. Humanity thus sprouting from the cane that still sweetens Solomon feasts.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dixon, Oceanic Mythology, 'Melanesia' ch. I (1916); not verbatim.

title.en: The Woman in the Wild Cane
title.zh: 野蔗中之女子

region.en: Gazelle Peninsula, New Britain (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 新不列顛加澤爾半島（象徵定位）

period: Oral tradition; recorded in R. B. Dixon, Oceanic Mythology, 1916

source.work: Roland B. Dixon, Oceanic Mythology, The Mythology of All Races Vol. IX (Boston: Marshall Jones, 1916), 'Melanesia' ch. I

summary.en: Two men (some say To-Kabinana and To-Karvuvu) netted a piece of wild sugar-cane three times and planted it. The planted cane swelled, burst, and a woman stepped out to cook their food secretly, until they caught and kept her.
summary.zh: 兩個男人（或謂托卡比納那與托卡武武）夜漁三網得一根野蔗，棄之不去，遂種之。蔗株日漸膨脹，一日爆裂，走出一名女子為他們暗備飯食；二人潛伏捉住她，其一娶之為妻，人類自此傳衍。

sensitivity.note: Colonial-era collection (Dixon 1916); Tolai heritage.

passages.text: Two men (sometimes described as To-Kabinana and To-Karvuvu) were fishing at night, and while they were so engaged a piece of wild sugar-cane floated into the net, where it became entangled. Disengaging it, they threw it away, but again it was enmeshed and was once more discarded. When, however, it was caught for the third time, they determined to plant it, and did so. Taking root, the cane grew, and after a time it began to swell, until one day, while the two men were absent at work, the stalk burst and from it came out a woman who cooked food for the men and then returned to her hiding-place.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dixon, Oceanic Mythology, 'Melanesia' ch. I (1916); not verbatim.

passages.text: The men came back from their work and were much surprised to find their food ready; and since the same thing occurred the next day, on the following morning they hid themselves to see who it was that had prepared their food. After a time the stalk opened and the woman came out, whereupon they immediately seized her and held her fast. In some versions, the woman then became the wife of one of the men, and all mankind are supposed to be descended from the pair.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dixon, Oceanic Mythology, 'Melanesia' ch. I (1916); not verbatim.

title.en: Woman from the Tree, Man from the Ground
title.zh: 樹出女、地出男

region.en: Elema country, Gulf of Papua (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 巴布亞灣埃勒馬地區（象徵定位）

period: Oral tradition; recorded in R. B. Dixon, Oceanic Mythology, 1916

source.work: Roland B. Dixon, Oceanic Mythology, The Mythology of All Races Vol. IX (Boston: Marshall Jones, 1916), 'Melanesia' ch. I

summary.en: Among the Papuan Elema of British New Guinea, the first woman sprang from a tree and the first man from the ground.
summary.zh: 英屬新幾內亞埃勒馬巴布亞人之說：首位女子生於樹，首位男子生於地。

sensitivity.note: Colonial-era collection (Dixon 1916); Elema heritage.

passages.text: Among the Papuan tribes of Elema in British New Guinea, an origin is given of the first woman from a tree and of the first man from the ground — the two first ancestors drawn from the forest and from the soil on which the tribe still plants its sago and taro.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dixon, Oceanic Mythology, 'Melanesia' ch. I (1916); not verbatim.

title.en: The Cowrie-Shell Woman
title.zh: 寶螺化女

region.en: New Hebrides (symbolic pin: Espíritu Santo)
region.zh: 新赫布里底群島（象徵定位：聖靈島）

period: Oral tradition; recorded in R. B. Dixon, Oceanic Mythology, 1916

source.work: Roland B. Dixon, Oceanic Mythology, The Mythology of All Races Vol. IX (Boston: Marshall Jones, 1916), 'Melanesia' ch. I

summary.en: In the New Hebrides, the first female being is said to have sprung from a cowrie-shell which turned into a woman.
summary.zh: 新赫布里底群島之說：第一位女性由一枚寶螺所化，螺殼開而成人形女子。

sensitivity.note: Colonial-era collection (Dixon 1916); Vanuatu heritage.

passages.text: In the New Hebrides the first female being is said to have sprung from a cowrie-shell which turned into a woman — the cowrie, prized across Melanesia as wealth and ornament for the bride-price, becoming in the story the very shell of womanhood itself.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dixon, Oceanic Mythology, 'Melanesia' ch. I (1916); not verbatim.

title.en: The Sun and Moon Marry: Stones and Birds
title.zh: 日月成婚：石化為男、鳥化為女

region.en: Baining country, Gazelle Peninsula, New Britain (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 新不列顛加澤爾半島拜寧人之地（象徵定位）

period: Oral tradition; recorded in R. B. Dixon, Oceanic Mythology, 1916

source.work: Roland B. Dixon, Oceanic Mythology, The Mythology of All Races Vol. IX (Boston: Marshall Jones, 1916), 'Melanesia' ch. I

summary.en: The Baining say that at first only the sun and moon existed; they married, and from their union were born stones and birds — the stones turning into men, the birds into women, from whom the Baining are descended.
summary.zh: 拜寧人之說：太初唯有日月；日月成婚，生出石頭與鳥——石化為男人，鳥化為女人，拜寧人即由此傳下。

sensitivity.note: Colonial-era collection (Dixon 1916); Baining heritage.

passages.text: An origin of man from stone is told by the Baining of New Britain. At first the only beings in the world were the sun and the moon, but they married, and from their union were born stones and birds, the former subsequently turning into men, the latter into women, and from these the Baining are descended. The first ancestors were thus children of the two great lights, solid as the stones of the mountains and swift as the birds of the air.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dixon, Oceanic Mythology, 'Melanesia' ch. I (1916); not verbatim.

title.en: The Tiny Sea in the Tapa-Cloth Cover
title.zh: 樹皮布下的小小海

region.en: Baining country, Gazelle Peninsula, New Britain (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 新不列顛加澤爾半島拜寧人之地（象徵定位）

period: Oral tradition; recorded in R. B. Dixon, Oceanic Mythology, 1916

source.work: Roland B. Dixon, Oceanic Mythology, The Mythology of All Races Vol. IX (Boston: Marshall Jones, 1916), 'Melanesia' ch. I

summary.en: The sea began as a tiny water-hole under a tapa cloth, owned by an old woman for flavouring food. Her sons tore the cover open, and the water spread until it became the sea; the old woman planted twigs along the shore to stop the ocean from destroying all things.
summary.zh: 太初之海僅為老嫗藏於樹皮布下的一小水窪，供她取鹹水調味。二子偷窺後撕開覆布，水洞愈撕愈大，二人攜布角奔逃，水漫成海，幾滅萬物；老嫗急植樹枝於岸邊，方遏止海洋。

sensitivity.note: Colonial-era collection (Dixon 1916); Baining heritage.

passages.text: In the beginning the sea was very small — only a tiny water-hole, belonging to an old woman, from which she got the salt water for the flavouring of her food. She kept the hole concealed under a cover of tapa cloth, and though her two sons repeatedly asked her whence she obtained the salt water, she refused to answer.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dixon, Oceanic Mythology, 'Melanesia' ch. I (1916); not verbatim.

passages.text: So they determined to watch, and eventually surprised her in the act of lifting the cover and dipping up the salt water. When she had gone they went to the spot and tore the cover open; and the farther they tore, the larger became the water-hole. Terrified by this, they ran away, each carrying a corner of the cloth; and thus the water spread and spread until it became the sea, which rose so that only a few rocks, covered with earth, remained above it. When the old woman saw that the sea constantly grew larger, she feared that the entire world would be covered by it, so she hastily planted some twigs along the edge of the shore, thus preventing the ocean from destroying all things.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dixon, Oceanic Mythology, 'Melanesia' ch. I (1916); not verbatim.

title.en: The Two Mushrooms Thrown to the Sky
title.zh: 擲天之二菇：日與月

region.en: Admiralty Islands, Papua New Guinea (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 阿德米羅提群島，巴布亞新幾內亞（象徵定位）

period: Oral tradition; recorded in R. B. Dixon, Oceanic Mythology, 1916

source.work: Roland B. Dixon, Oceanic Mythology, The Mythology of All Races Vol. IX (Boston: Marshall Jones, 1916), 'Melanesia' ch. I

summary.en: When the sea had dried and the first two beings had planted trees and made food, they made two mushrooms: the man threw one into the sky to create the moon, the woman tossed the other upward and formed the sun.
summary.zh: 海水退去、初民種樹造食之後，首二人又造二菇：男將一菇擲入天空，化為月亮；女將另一菇拋上去，化為太陽。

sensitivity.note: Colonial-era collection (Dixon 1916); Manus heritage.

passages.text: In the Admiralty Islands it is said that when the sea had dried so that man appeared, the first two beings, after planting trees and creating food plants, made two mushrooms, one of which the man threw into the sky, creating the moon, while the woman tossed the other upward and formed the sun. Thus the two lights of the world were the work of the first couple's hands, flung up from their garden on the new land.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dixon, Oceanic Mythology, 'Melanesia' ch. I (1916); not verbatim.

title.en: The Moon Dug Up Too Soon
title.zh: 太早掘出的月亮

region.en: Port Moresby district, British New Guinea (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 英屬新幾內亞莫爾茲比港一帶（象徵定位）

period: Oral tradition; recorded in R. B. Dixon, Oceanic Mythology, 1916

source.work: Roland B. Dixon, Oceanic Mythology, The Mythology of All Races Vol. IX (Boston: Marshall Jones, 1916), 'Melanesia' ch. I

summary.en: A man digging a deep hole uncovered the moon as a small bright object. It grew in his hands, escaped, and rose into the sky — but because it was taken out prematurely, it sheds only feeble rays instead of the brighter light it would have given had it been left to be born naturally.
summary.zh: 有人掘深坑時掘出一小小發亮之物——月亮。月亮在他手中漸漸長大，掙脫而出，升上天空；惟因早產而出，其光微弱，未能如自然誕生時那般明亮。

sensitivity.note: Colonial-era collection (Dixon 1916); Motu/Koita heritage.

passages.text: A different account of the moon is given by the people of southern British New Guinea. A man was digging a deep hole one day when he uncovered the moon as a small bright object. After he had taken it out, it began to grow, and finally, escaping from his hands, rose high into the sky. Had the moon been left in the ground until it was born naturally, it would have given a brighter light; but since it was taken out prematurely, it sheds only feeble rays — the dim moonlight of every night since bearing the mark of that man's impatience.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dixon, Oceanic Mythology, 'Melanesia' ch. I (1916); not verbatim.

title.en: The Moon in the Jar
title.zh: 罐中之月

region.en: German New Guinea coast (symbolic pin: Huon Gulf)
region.zh: 德屬新幾內亞海岸（象徵定位：休恩灣）

period: Oral tradition; recorded in R. B. Dixon, Oceanic Mythology, 1916

source.work: Roland B. Dixon, Oceanic Mythology, The Mythology of All Races Vol. IX (Boston: Marshall Jones, 1916), 'Melanesia' ch. I

summary.en: The moon was kept hidden in a jar by an old woman until boys discovered and opened it; the moon flew out and rose into the sky, bearing the marks of their hands on its surface.
summary.zh: 太初月亮藏於一老嫗之罐中。幾個男孩偷開罐口，月亮飛出，掙脫他們的手，升上天空——月面上至今仍留著他們的指印。

sensitivity.note: Colonial-era collection (Dixon 1916); New Guinea coast heritage.

passages.text: A tale from German New Guinea recounts how the moon was originally kept hidden in a jar by an old woman. Some boys discovered this, and coming secretly, opened the jar, whereupon the moon flew out; and though they tried to hold it, it slipped from their grasp and rose into the sky, bearing the marks of their hands on its surface — the mottled face of the moon the print of the boys' fingers on the day it was freed.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dixon, Oceanic Mythology, 'Melanesia' ch. I (1916); not verbatim.

title.en: The Stolen Fire Cast into the Sky
title.zh: 被竊之火拋上天空

region.en: Woodlark Island, Massim (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 馬西姆伍德拉克島（象徵定位）

period: Oral tradition; recorded in R. B. Dixon, Oceanic Mythology, 1916

source.work: Roland B. Dixon, Oceanic Mythology, The Mythology of All Races Vol. IX (Boston: Marshall Jones, 1916), 'Melanesia' ch. I

summary.en: An old woman of Woodlark Island was sole owner of fire, while others ate raw food. Her son stole flame and gave it to mankind; in anger she divided what remained into two parts and threw them into the sky — the larger becoming the sun, the smaller the moon.
summary.zh: 伍德拉克島一老嫗獨霸火種，餘人皆食生冷。其子斥她殘忍，偷火分與眾人；老嫗怒，將所餘之火分作兩半擲上天空——大者成日，小者成月。

sensitivity.note: Colonial-era collection (Dixon 1916); Massim heritage.

passages.text: The people of Woodlark Island have a tale in which the origin of the sun and moon is connected with the origin of fire. In the beginning an old woman was the sole owner of fire, and she alone could eat cooked food, while other people must devour theirs raw. Her son said to her: 'You are cruel. You see that the taro takes the skin off our throats, yet you do not give us fire with which to cook it'; but since she proved obdurate, he stole some of the flame and gave it to the rest of mankind.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dixon, Oceanic Mythology, 'Melanesia' ch. I (1916); not verbatim.

passages.text: In anger at his action, the old woman seized what was left of her fire, divided it into two parts, and threw them into the sky, the larger portion thus becoming the sun, and the smaller the moon — the stolen fire of mankind leaving the two great lights behind in the heavens as the thief's mother's revenge.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dixon, Oceanic Mythology, 'Melanesia' ch. I (1916); not verbatim.

title.en: Dudugera, the Fish-Fathered Sun
title.zh: 杜杜格拉：魚父之子化為毒日

region.en: Massim district, eastern British New Guinea (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 英屬新幾內亞東部馬西姆地區（象徵定位）

period: Oral tradition; recorded in R. B. Dixon, Oceanic Mythology, 1916

source.work: Roland B. Dixon, Oceanic Mythology, The Mythology of All Races Vol. IX (Boston: Marshall Jones, 1916), 'Melanesia' ch. I

summary.en: A woman playing with a great fish in the surf bore from a swelling on her leg a son, Dudugera. Taunted for his parentage, he was carried east by his fish-father, climbed into the sky, and as the sun nearly destroyed all things with his heat — until his mother threw lime into his face as he rose.
summary.zh: 一婦人與巨魚在海浪中嬉遊，腿上腫處迸出男嬰杜杜格拉。他因出身遭同儕辱罵，被魚父攜往東方，攀上天空化為太陽，烈炎幾滅萬物——其母登高，以石灰罐撒向初升之日，日閉目而炎減。

sensitivity.note: Colonial-era collection (Dixon 1916); Massim heritage.

passages.text: A woman who was watching her garden close to the ocean, seeing a great fish sporting in the surf, walked out into the water and played with the fish, continuing to do this for several days. By and by the woman's leg, against which the fish had rubbed, began to swell and became painful until at last she got her father to make a cut in the swelling, when out popped an infant. The boy, who was named Dudugera, grew up among the other children of the village until one day, in playing a game, he threw his dart at the other children rather than at the mark, whereupon they became angry and abused him, taunting him with his parentage.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dixon, Oceanic Mythology, 'Melanesia' ch. I (1916); not verbatim.

passages.text: Fearing lest the others might really harm him, Dudugera's mother determined to send him to his father; so she took the boy to the beach, whereupon the great fish came, seized him in his mouth, and carried him far away to the east. Before he left, Dudugera warned his mother and relatives to take refuge under a great rock, for soon, he said, he would climb into a pandanus-tree and thence into the sky, and, as the sun, would destroy all things with his heat. So indeed it came to pass, for excepting his mother and her relatives, who heeded Dudugera's advice, nearly everything perished. To prevent their total annihilation his mother took a lime-calabash, and climbing upon a hill near which the sun rose, cast the lime into his face as he came up, which caused the sun to shut his eyes and thus to decrease the amount of heat.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dixon, Oceanic Mythology, 'Melanesia' ch. I (1916); not verbatim.

title.en: Qat Releases the First Night
title.zh: 卡特釋出首夜

region.en: Banks Islands, Vanuatu (symbolic pin: Gaua/Mota)
region.zh: 瓦努阿圖班克斯群島（象徵定位：高阿島／莫塔島）

period: Oral tradition; recorded in R. B. Dixon, Oceanic Mythology, 1916 (from Codrington's Mota texts)
