source.work: Roland B. Dixon, Oceanic Mythology, The Mythology of All Races Vol. IX (Boston: Marshall Jones, 1916), 'Melanesia' ch. I

summary.en: Daylight was perpetual until Qat sailed to buy night from Night himself at Vava in the Torres Islands, blackened eyebrows, sleep, and the dawn. He released it on his terrified brothers and cut it with red obsidian at cockcrow — so night became short, as it now is.
summary.zh: 白晝本永無盡頭。卡特聞托雷斯群島之瓦瓦有夜，遂買夜而歸，並學得睡意、黎明與晨鳥。他對驚恐的兄弟們釋出黑夜，教他們閉眼而眠；雞鳥報曉之際，以紅色黑曜石割開黑夜——於是夜短如今日。

sensitivity.note: Missionary-era Mota collection via Dixon 1916; cross-ref qat-creation (Codrington telling of buying the night).

passages.text: In the Banks Islands, after Qat had formed men, pigs, trees, and rocks, he still did not know how to make night, for daylight was continuous. His brothers said to him, 'This is not at all pleasant. Here is nothing but day. Can't you do something for us?' Now Qat heard that at Vava in the Torres Islands there was night, so he took a pig, and went to Vava, where he bought night from I-Qong, Night, who lived there. Other accounts say that Qat sailed to the edge of the sky to buy night from Night, who blackened his eyebrows, showed him sleep and taught him how to make the dawn.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dixon, Oceanic Mythology, 'Melanesia' ch. I (1916), after Codrington's Mota texts; not verbatim.

passages.text: Qat returned to his brothers, bringing a fowl and other birds to give notice of the dawn. He begged his brothers to prepare beds of coco-nut fronds. Then for the first time, they saw the sun sinking in the west, and they cried out to Qat that it was crawling away. 'It will soon be gone,' said he, 'and if you see a change on the face of the earth, that is night.' Then he let go the night. 'What is this coming out of the sea,' they cried, 'and covering the sky?' 'That is night,' said he, 'sit down on both sides of the house, and when you feel something in your eyes, lie down and be quiet.' Presently it was dark, and their eyes began to blink. 'Qat! Qat! what is this? Shall we die?' 'Shut your eyes,' said he, 'that is it, go to sleep.' When night had lasted long enough the cock began to crow and the birds to twitter; Qat took a piece of red obsidian and cut the night with it; the light over which the night had spread itself shone forth again, and Qat's brothers awoke.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dixon, Oceanic Mythology, 'Melanesia' ch. I (1916), after Codrington's Mota texts; not verbatim.

title.en: The Dog That Swam for Fire
title.zh: 渡海取火之犬

region.en: Motu villages, Port Moresby (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 莫爾茲比港莫圖村落（象徵定位）

period: Oral tradition; recorded in R. B. Dixon, Oceanic Mythology, 1916

source.work: Roland B. Dixon, Oceanic Mythology, The Mythology of All Races Vol. IX (Boston: Marshall Jones, 1916), 'Melanesia' ch. I

summary.en: The ancestors of the Motu ate raw food until smoke was seen rising from a far island. Snake, bandicoot, bird, and kangaroo all tried and failed to cross the sea; only the dog swam out, seized a blazing brand from the cooking women, and brought fire home to all the people.
summary.zh: 莫圖人先祖無火，日晒煮食。一日見遠島升起炊煙，蛇、袋狸、鳥、袋鼠相繼渡海取火，皆因浪大而返；唯犬游至島上，見婦女炊食，奪一支燃薪，游泳而歸，將火分與眾人。

sensitivity.note: Colonial-era collection (Dixon 1916); Motu heritage.

passages.text: According to a version told by the Motu, the ancestors of the present people had no fire, and ate their food raw or cooked it in the sun until one day they perceived smoke rising out at sea. A dog, a snake, a bandicoot, a bird, and a kangaroo all saw this smoke and asked, 'Who will go to get fire?' First the snake said that he would make the attempt, but the sea was too rough, and he was compelled to come back. Then the bandicoot went, but he, too, had to return. One after another, all tried but the dog, and all were unsuccessful.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dixon, Oceanic Mythology, 'Melanesia' ch. I (1916); not verbatim.

passages.text: Then the dog started and swam and swam until he reached the island whence the smoke rose. There he saw women cooking with fire, and seizing a blazing brand, he ran to the shore and swam safely back with it to the mainland, where he gave it to all the people — the first hearth of the Motu villages lit by a dog's swim through the open sea.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dixon, Oceanic Mythology, 'Melanesia' ch. I (1916); not verbatim.

title.en: Goga's Body-Fire and the Snake That Saved It
title.zh: 葛嘎之體火與護火之蛇

region.en: Massim district, eastern British New Guinea (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 英屬新幾內亞東部馬西姆地區（象徵定位）

period: Oral tradition; recorded in R. B. Dixon, Oceanic Mythology, 1916

source.work: Roland B. Dixon, Oceanic Mythology, The Mythology of All Races Vol. IX (Boston: Marshall Jones, 1916), 'Melanesia' ch. I

summary.en: The old woman Goga kept fire hidden in her own body and cooked for herself while ten youths ate sun-warmed food. The youngest spied her secret, stole the firebrand, and leapt a felled tree to escape; when her rain quenched all flame, fire survived only in a snake's burning tail — and the trees of the firebrands became totems.
summary.zh: 老嫗葛嘎藏火於己身，自煮自食，十名少年只得以日晒暖食。最幼者窺得其密，奪火把而逃，躍過倒木擺脫追趕；火把燙手落地，燒著枯草與露兜樹。老嫗降雨欲滅火，唯樹洞中蛇尾如炬未熄。雨停，眾少年拔蛇而取其燃尾，堆柴引火，各村聞訊來取火種——各氏族取薪之樹，遂成其圖騰。

sensitivity.note: Colonial-era collection (Dixon 1916); Massim heritage. Includes local totem aition.

passages.text: Among the Massim tribes of eastern British New Guinea, people had no fire in the beginning, but simply warmed and dried their food in the sun. There was, however, a certain old woman called Goga who thus prepared food for ten of the youths, but for herself she cooked food with fire, which she obtained from her own body. Before the boys came home each day, she cleared away all traces of the fire and every scrap of cooked food, lest they should know her secret; but one day a piece of boiled taro accidentally got among the lads' food, and when the youngest ate it, he found it much better than what was usually given him.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dixon, Oceanic Mythology, 'Melanesia' ch. I (1916); not verbatim.

passages.text: The youths resolved to discover the secret; the youngest hid and saw the old woman take the fire from her body and cook with it. They cut down a huge tree over which all tried to jump, but only the youngest succeeded, so they selected him to steal the fire. Creeping back to the house, he seized the firebrand when the old woman was not looking, and ran off with it; she chased him, but he jumped over the tree, which she was unable to do. As he ran, the brand burned his hand and he dropped it in the dry grass, which caught the blaze and set fire to a pandanus-tree near.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dixon, Oceanic Mythology, 'Melanesia' ch. I (1916); not verbatim.

passages.text: Now, in a hole in this tree, lived a snake, whose tail caught fire and burned like a torch. The old woman, finding that she could not overtake the thief, caused a great rain to fall, hoping thus to quench the fire, but the snake stayed in his hole, and his tail was not extinguished. When the rain had stopped, the boys found the hole, pulled out the snake, and broke off its tail, which was still alight. Then making a great pile of wood, they set fire to it, and people from all the villages came and got flame, which they took home with them. Different folk used different kinds of wood for their firebrands, and the trees from which they took their brands became their totems.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dixon, Oceanic Mythology, 'Melanesia' ch. I (1916); not verbatim.

title.en: Fire from the Serpent's Belly
title.zh: 蛇腹取火

region.en: Admiralty Islands, Papua New Guinea (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 阿德米羅提群島，巴布亞新幾內亞（象徵定位）

period: Oral tradition; recorded in R. B. Dixon, Oceanic Mythology, 1916

source.work: Roland B. Dixon, Oceanic Mythology, The Mythology of All Races Vol. IX (Boston: Marshall Jones, 1916), 'Melanesia' ch. I

summary.en: The daughter of Ulimgau married a serpent who spoke with a man's voice. Their children ate raw fish until the serpent father sent the boy into his own belly to fetch fire and teach his sister to cook — the beginning of cooked food among mankind.
summary.zh: 烏林皋之女嫁與一條口吐人言之蛇。所生兒女以日光烤魚，食之猶生。蛇父令子鑽入己腹取火，交與其妹；二人以火炊魚——人間炊食自此而始。

sensitivity.note: Colonial-era collection (Dixon 1916); Manus heritage.

passages.text: A version from the Admiralty Islands runs as follows. The daughter of Ulimgau went into the forest. The serpent saw her, and said, 'Come!' and the woman replied, 'Who would have you for a husband? You are a serpent. I will not marry you.' But he replied, 'My body is indeed that of a serpent, but my speech is that of a man. Come!' And the woman went and married him, and after a time she bore a boy and a girl, and her serpent husband put her away, saying, 'Go, I will take care of them and give them food.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dixon, Oceanic Mythology, 'Melanesia' ch. I (1916); not verbatim.

passages.text: And the serpent fed the children and they grew. One day they were hungry, and he told them to catch fish and cook them; but they replied, 'The sun has not yet risen,' and by and by they ate the fish still raw and bloody. Then the serpent said to them, 'You two are spirits, for you eat your food raw. Perhaps you will eat me. You, girl, stay; and you, boy, crawl into my belly.' The boy was afraid, but his father said 'Go,' and he crept into the serpent's belly, took the fire, and brought it out to his sister. And the boy and girl lit a fire and cooked the food, and when they had eaten, the serpent asked, 'Is my kind of food or your kind of food the better?' And they answered, 'Your food is good, ours is bad.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dixon, Oceanic Mythology, 'Melanesia' ch. I (1916); not verbatim.

title.en: Emakong and the Village Under the Water
title.zh: 埃馬孔與水下之村

region.en: Sulka country, northern New Britain (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 新不列顛北部蘇爾卡人之地（象徵定位）

period: Oral tradition; recorded in R. B. Dixon, Oceanic Mythology, 1916

source.work: Roland B. Dixon, Oceanic Mythology, The Mythology of All Races Vol. IX (Boston: Marshall Jones, 1916), 'Melanesia' ch. I

summary.en: Diving for a lost ornament, Emakong found a village at the bottom of the stream whose people turned into snakes to sleep and owned fire, night, crickets, and the dawn-birds. He returned bearing them all, and taught the Sulka their use — though the people first fled in terror from the crackling flame.
summary.zh: 蘇爾卡人埃馬孔潛水尋找失落飾物，竟至溪底一村，村中人夜化為蛇而眠，有火、有夜、有蟋蟀與報曉之鳥。同名者贈其夜、火、蟋蟀與晨鳥之包，他攜之升水而歸；眾人見火而逃，他追告其用途，人間始有火與夜。

sensitivity.note: Colonial-era collection (Dixon 1916); Sulka heritage.

passages.text: There was once a time when the Sulka were ignorant of fire; but one day a man named Emakong lost one of his ornaments, which fell into a stream. Taking off his loin-cloth, he jumped in and dove to recover the lost object, but was amazed, on reaching the bottom, to find himself in the yard of a house. Many people came up and asked him his name, and when he replied that he was called Emakong, one of them said, 'Oh, that is also my name,' whereupon he took the bewildered man to his house and gave him a new loin-cloth.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dixon, Oceanic Mythology, 'Melanesia' ch. I (1916); not verbatim.

passages.text: Great was Emakong's astonishment to see a fire in the house. At first he was afraid of it, but after he had been given cooked food and had found this much better than the raw viands which he had always eaten before, he lost his fear of the new thing. When it became night, the crickets began to sing, and his terror grew still greater when he heard resounding claps of thunder from every side and saw all the people turn into snakes in order to sleep. His namesake reassured him, saying that this was their custom, and that when day came again all would return to their human form. Then, with a loud report, he also changed into a snake, and Emakong alone retained the shape of man.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dixon, Oceanic Mythology, 'Melanesia' ch. I (1916); not verbatim.

passages.text: In the morning, when the birds sang to announce the coming day, he awoke, and with a crash all the serpents again turned into men. His namesake now did up a package for him, containing night, some fire, some crickets, and the birds that sing at dawn, and with this Emakong left, rising through the water. On reaching the shore, he threw the fire into dry grass, but when the people saw the blaze and heard the crackling of the flame, they were greatly alarmed and all fled. Emakong, however, ran after them and, telling them of his adventures, explained to them the use of the things that he had brought.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dixon, Oceanic Mythology, 'Melanesia' ch. I (1916); not verbatim.

title.en: The Gods Debate the Death of Man
title.zh: 二神議死：蛻皮抑或埋葬

region.en: Ambrym, New Hebrides (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 新赫布里底群島安布里姆島（象徵定位）

period: Oral tradition; recorded in R. B. Dixon, Oceanic Mythology, 1916

source.work: Roland B. Dixon, Oceanic Mythology, The Mythology of All Races Vol. IX (Boston: Marshall Jones, 1916), 'Melanesia' ch. I

summary.en: After man was made, the good deity proposed that old men be flayed like eels so that a new skin would grow and they would renew their youth like snakes. The malicious deity answered that they must be buried in the ground — and because the one who has the last word prevails, death came into the world.
summary.zh: 人造成之後，善神說：老人皮皺則如剝鱔般剝其皮，新皮自生，人可如蛇蛻皮而不死。惡神卻道：老則掘坑埋之。因『末語者勝』，死亡遂入人間。

sensitivity.note: Colonial-era collection (Dixon 1916); Ambrym heritage.

passages.text: According to the version current in Ambrym, the good and the malicious deities were discussing man after he had been made. The former said: 'Our men seem to get on well, but haven't you noticed that their skins have begun to wrinkle? They are yet young, but when they are old, they will be very ugly. So when that happens, we will flay them like an eel, and a new skin will grow, and thus men shall renew their youth like the snakes and so be immortal.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dixon, Oceanic Mythology, 'Melanesia' ch. I (1916); not verbatim.

passages.text: But the evil deity replied: 'No, it shall not be that way. When a man is old and ugly, we will dig a hole in the ground and put the body in it, and thus it shall always be among his descendants.' And because the one who has the last word prevails, death came into the world — a grave-rule set by the malice of the speaker who closed the debate.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dixon, Oceanic Mythology, 'Melanesia' ch. I (1916); not verbatim.

title.en: The Old Skin That Floated Away
title.zh: 漂走之舊皮

region.en: Banks Islands, Vanuatu (symbolic pin: Gaua/Mota)
region.zh: 瓦努阿圖班克斯群島（象徵定位：高阿島／莫塔島）

period: Oral tradition; recorded in R. B. Dixon, Oceanic Mythology, 1916 (from Codrington's Mota texts)

source.work: Roland B. Dixon, Oceanic Mythology, The Mythology of All Races Vol. IX (Boston: Marshall Jones, 1916), 'Melanesia' ch. I

summary.en: Men once cast their skins like snakes and crabs and so never died. An old woman who shed hers in a stream went unrecognized by her own child; to quiet its crying she put the old skin on again — and from that time men ceased to renew their youth and died when they grew old.
summary.zh: 太初之人如蛇蟹蛻皮，蛻而復少，永不死。一老嫗於溪中蛻皮，新顏返家，其子不識，啼哭不止；她為哄幼兒，重回溪邊取回舊皮穿上——自此人不再蛻皮，老而至死。

sensitivity.note: Missionary-era Mota collection via Dixon 1916.

passages.text: In the Banks Islands it is said that in the beginning men did not die, but cast their skins like snakes and crabs, and thus renewed their youth. One day an old woman went to a stream to change her skin and threw the old one into the water where, as it floated away, it caught upon a stick. When she went home, her child refused to recognize her in her new and youthful form, and to pacify the infant, who cried without ceasing, she returned and got her old skin, and put it on again. From that time men have ceased to cast their skins and have died when they grew old — mortality entangled by a mother's tenderness.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dixon, Oceanic Mythology, 'Melanesia' ch. I (1916), after Codrington's Mota texts; not verbatim.

title.en: Qat Summons Mate, and Tagaro the Foolish Watches the Wrong Path
title.zh: 卡特召馬特；愚塔加羅守錯路

region.en: Banks Islands, Vanuatu (symbolic pin: Gaua/Mota)
region.zh: 瓦努阿圖班克斯群島（象徵定位：高阿島／莫塔島）

period: Oral tradition; recorded in R. B. Dixon, Oceanic Mythology, 1916 (from Codrington's Mota texts)

source.work: Roland B. Dixon, Oceanic Mythology, The Mythology of All Races Vol. IX (Boston: Marshall Jones, 1916), 'Melanesia' ch. I

summary.en: Because property stuck forever in the same hands, Qat summoned a man called Mate — 'Death' — laid him on a board, and held a funeral feast. Tagaro the Foolish, sent to watch the parting of the ways at Panoi, sat before the wrong path, and Mate went down to the lower world; all men have followed him since.
summary.zh: 太初人不死，惟財產永歸一手，紛擾不堪。卡特遂召一名『馬特』（死）之人，置於板上覆蓋，殺豬分其財產，舉行喪宴。第五日吹螺驅魂，啟板視之，馬特已去，僅餘白骨。卡特派愚塔加羅守帕諾伊岔路口，防馬特下界；愚者卻坐在上界之路口，馬特遂下冥府——世人從此皆循其路。

sensitivity.note: Missionary-era Mota collection via Dixon 1916; cross-ref funeral-feast aition.

passages.text: In the Banks Islands it is said that in the beginning men lived forever, casting their skins, and that the permanence of property in the same hands led to much trouble. Qat, therefore, summoned a man called Mate ('Death') and laid him on a board and covered him over; after which he killed a pig and divided Mate's property among his descendants, all of whom came and ate of the funeral feast. On the fifth day, when the conch-shells were blown to drive away the ghost, Qat removed the covering, and Mate was gone; only his bones were left.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dixon, Oceanic Mythology, 'Melanesia' ch. I (1916), after Codrington's Mota texts; not verbatim.

passages.text: Meanwhile Qat had sent Tagaro the Foolish to watch the way to Panoi, where the paths to the underworld and the upper regions divide, to see that Mate did not go below; but the Fool sat before the way of the world above so that Mate descended to the lower realms; and ever since that time all men have followed Mate along the path he took.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dixon, Oceanic Mythology, 'Melanesia' ch. I (1916), after Codrington's Mota texts; not verbatim.

title.en: The Sun Calls All Things to Live Forever
title.zh: 日召萬物得不死，獨人不至

region.en: Baining country, Gazelle Peninsula, New Britain (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 新不列顛加澤爾半島拜寧人之地（象徵定位）

period: Oral tradition; recorded in R. B. Dixon, Oceanic Mythology, 1916

source.work: Roland B. Dixon, Oceanic Mythology, The Mythology of All Races Vol. IX (Boston: Marshall Jones, 1916), 'Melanesia' ch. I

summary.en: The sun called all things together and asked which wished to live forever. All came except man; so the stones and the snakes live forever, but man must die — for had he obeyed the sun's summons, he too might have changed his skin like the snake.
summary.zh: 一日召集萬物，問誰願永生。萬物皆至，唯人不至；故石與蛇長存，人則必死——若人應召，本可如蛇蛻皮而得永生。

sensitivity.note: Colonial-era collection (Dixon 1916); Baining heritage.

passages.text: Thus the Baining in New Britain say that one day the sun called all things together and asked which wished to live forever. All came except man; so the stones and the snakes live forever, but man must die. Had man obeyed the sun, he would have been able to change his skin from time to time like the snake, and so would have acquired immortality — the missing summons the one missed appointment that set the human lot.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dixon, Oceanic Mythology, 'Melanesia' ch. I (1916); not verbatim.

title.en: The Cheated Tree of Refuge
title.zh: 受欺之庇護樹

region.en: Admiralty Islands, Papua New Guinea (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 阿德米羅提群島，巴布亞新幾內亞（象徵定位）

period: Oral tradition; recorded in R. B. Dixon, Oceanic Mythology, 1916

source.work: Roland B. Dixon, Oceanic Mythology, The Mythology of All Races Vol. IX (Boston: Marshall Jones, 1916), 'Melanesia' ch. I

summary.en: Fleeing an evil spirit, a man hid in a tree that opened and closed for him; the tree asked two white pigs as payment. He brought only one true white pig and another blackened with chalk — and the tree revoked its shelter, dooming the race to mortality and the enmity of evil spirits.
summary.zh: 一人遭惡靈追殺，大樹開合庇之；樹索白豬二頭為酬。此人以白垩塗黑豬充數，樹責其忘恩：『若你誠實，遇險皆可入我身避之；如今不能，你必死。』人類之必死與惡靈之仇，皆由此不誠而起。

sensitivity.note: Colonial-era collection (Dixon 1916); Manus heritage.

passages.text: A man once went out fishing; but since an evil spirit wished to kill and eat him, he fled into the forest. There he caused a tree to open, and creeping inside, the tree closed again, so that when the evil being came, he did not see his victim and went away, whereupon the tree opened, and the man came out. The tree said to him, 'Bring to me two white pigs.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dixon, Oceanic Mythology, 'Melanesia' ch. I (1916); not verbatim.

passages.text: So the man went to his village and got two pigs, but he cheated the tree in that he brought only a single white one, the other being black whitened with chalk. For this the tree rebuked him and said: 'You are unthankful, though I was good to you. If you had done what I had asked, you might have taken refuge in me whenever danger threatened. Now you cannot, but must die.' So, as a result of this man's ingratitude, the human race is doomed to mortality and cannot escape the enmity of evil spirits.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dixon, Oceanic Mythology, 'Melanesia' ch. I (1916); not verbatim.

title.en: Raudalo Turns Back the Flood
title.zh: 蛇王勞達洛止洪水

region.en: Southern British New Guinea coast (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 英屬新幾內亞南部海岸（象徵定位）

period: Oral tradition; recorded in R. B. Dixon, Oceanic Mythology, 1916

source.work: Roland B. Dixon, Oceanic Mythology, The Mythology of All Races Vol. IX (Boston: Marshall Jones, 1916), 'Melanesia' ch. I

summary.en: A great flood overflowed the hills of British New Guinea; people and animals fled to the peak of Tauaga. Only the serpent-king Raudalo did not fear: he touched the angry waters with his forked tongue, and the sea turned and flowed back down the mountain to its bed.
summary.zh: 洪水暴發，海沒群山，人畜奔逃至最高峰陶阿加。唯蛇王勞達洛不懼，屢問僕蛇水勢，終以舌端觸水，海水頓止而退；蛇王更追洪下山，以舌驅之，直至海復其位，洪水乃平。

sensitivity.note: Colonial-era collection (Dixon 1916); coastal PNG heritage. Cross-tradition flood cluster.

passages.text: Once a great flood occurred, and the sea rose and overflowed the earth, the hills being covered, and people and animals hurrying to the top of Tauaga, the highest mountain. But the sea followed and all were afraid. Yet the king of the snakes, Raudalo, did not fear. At last he said to his servants, 'Where now are the waters?' And they answered, 'They are rising, lord.' Yet looked he not upon the flood.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dixon, Oceanic Mythology, 'Melanesia' ch. I (1916); not verbatim.

passages.text: And after a space he said again, 'Where now are the waters?' and his servants answered as they had done before. And again he inquired of them, 'Where now are the waters?' But this time all the snakes, Titiko, Dubo and Anaur, made answer, 'They are here, and in a moment they will touch thee, lord.' Then Raudalo turned him about and put forth his forked tongue, and touched with the tip of it the angry waters which were about to cover him. And on a sudden the sea rose no more, but began to flow down the side of the mountain. Still was Raudalo not content, and he pursued the flood down the hill, ever and anon putting forth his forked tongue that there might be no tarrying on the way. Thus went they down the mountain and over the plain country until the sea shore was reached, and the waters lay in their bed once more and the flood was stayed.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dixon, Oceanic Mythology, 'Melanesia' ch. I (1916); not verbatim.

title.en: Abaia the Lake Eel Drowns the Village
title.zh: 湖鰻阿拜亞淹村

region.en: British New Guinea lake country (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 英屬新幾內亞湖區（象徵定位）

period: Oral tradition; recorded in R. B. Dixon, Oceanic Mythology, 1916

source.work: Roland B. Dixon, Oceanic Mythology, The Mythology of All Races Vol. IX (Boston: Marshall Jones, 1916), 'Melanesia' ch. I

summary.en: A village plundered the fish of a lake whose depths held the magic eel Abaia. When a woman even laid hold of the great eel, he raised a night of rain; the lake rose and drowned them all save one old woman who had not eaten of the fish and saved herself in a tree.
summary.zh: 村民捕盡一湖之魚，湖底潛有神鰻阿拜亞。一婦人竟捉住大鰻，鰻怒而興連夜大雨，湖水暴漲，村人盡沒；唯未食魚之一老嫗攀樹得生。

sensitivity.note: Colonial-era collection (Dixon 1916); PNG heritage.

passages.text: One day a man discovered a lake in which were many fish; and at the bottom of the lake lived a magic eel, but the man knew it not. He caught many fish and returned the next day with the people of his village whom he had told of his discovery; and they also were very successful, while one woman even laid hold of the great eel, Abaia, who dwelt in the depths of the lake, though he escaped her.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dixon, Oceanic Mythology, 'Melanesia' ch. I (1916); not verbatim.

passages.text: Now Abaia was angry that his fish had been caught and that he himself had been seized, so he caused a great rain to fall that night, and the waters of the lake also rose, and all the people were drowned except an old woman who had not eaten of the fish and who saved herself in a tree. The old eel's deluge spared only her who had kept the taboo of the lake's abundance.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dixon, Oceanic Mythology, 'Melanesia' ch. I (1916); not verbatim.

title.en: To-Karvuvu Roasts His Mother: The Origin of Cannibalism
title.zh: 托卡武武烤母：食人之始

region.en: Gazelle Peninsula, New Britain (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 新不列顛加澤爾半島（象徵定位）

period: Oral tradition; recorded in R. B. Dixon, Oceanic Mythology, 1916

source.work: Roland B. Dixon, Oceanic Mythology, The Mythology of All Races Vol. IX (Boston: Marshall Jones, 1916), 'Melanesia' ch. II

summary.en: To-Kabinana told his fool of a brother to look after their mother. To-Karvuvu poured water over her, killed her with hot stones, and laid her in the oven — 'I thought you said to kill her!' His brother's rebuke becomes the aition of cannibalism among their descendants.
summary.zh: 托卡比納那命弟照顧母親。愚弟托卡武武以水淋母、以熱石殺母、置於爐中烤之——『我以為你叫我去殺她！』兄斥之：『你這蠢貨，必先我而死；你的子孫從此將煮食人肉。』食人之俗，由此愚行而生。

sensitivity.note: Colonial-era collection (Dixon 1916); Tolai heritage. The tale explains (and frames) cannibalism as a curse from a blunder.

passages.text: To-Kabinana and To-Karvuvu were one day walking in the fields when the former said to the latter, 'Go, and look after our mother.' So To-Karvuvu went, filled a bamboo vessel with water, poured it over his mother, heated stones in the fire, killed her, and laid her in the oven to roast, after which he returned to To-Kabinana, who asked him how their parent was and if he had taken good care of her.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dixon, Oceanic Mythology, 'Melanesia' ch. II (1916); not verbatim.

passages.text: To-Karvuvu replied, 'I have roasted her with the hot stones,' whereupon his brother demanded, 'Who told you to do that?' 'Oh,' he answered, 'I thought you said to kill her!' But To-Kabinana declared, 'Oh, you fool, you will die before me. You never cease doing foolish things. Our descendants now will cook and eat human flesh.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dixon, Oceanic Mythology, 'Melanesia' ch. II (1916); not verbatim.

title.en: The House Roofed on the Inside
title.zh: 內鋪屋頂之屋

region.en: Gazelle Peninsula, New Britain (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 新不列顛加澤爾半島（象徵定位）

period: Oral tradition; recorded in R. B. Dixon, Oceanic Mythology, 1916

source.work: Roland B. Dixon, Oceanic Mythology, The Mythology of All Races Vol. IX (Boston: Marshall Jones, 1916), 'Melanesia' ch. II

summary.en: The brothers each built a house, but To-Karvuvu roofed his on the inside; in the night's rain he sat weeding, wet and blind under the darkness, until the pitying To-Kabinana told him to abandon his house and live with him.
summary.zh: 兄弟各建一屋，托卡比納那於外鋪頂，愚弟卻把屋頂鋪在屋內。夜裡行雨，黑暗沉沉，雨水穿透內頂滴落其身，托卡武武哭訴；兄憐之，命其拆屋不必，同住自己屋中。

sensitivity.note: Colonial-era collection (Dixon 1916); Tolai heritage.

passages.text: To-Kabinana said to his brother, 'Come, let us each build a house,' and accordingly each constructed a dwelling, but To-Kabinana roofed his house outside, while his foolish brother covered his on the inside. Then To-Kabinana said, 'Let us make rain!' so they performed the proper ceremony, and in the night it rained.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dixon, Oceanic Mythology, 'Melanesia' ch. II (1916); not verbatim.

passages.text: The darkness pressed heavily on To-Karvuvu so that he sat up, and the rain came through the roof of his house and fell upon him, and he wept. In the morning he came to his brother, saying, 'The darkness pressed upon me, and the rain-water wet me, and I cried.' But when To-Kabinana asked, 'How did you build your house?' the other replied, 'I covered it with the roof covering inside. It is not like yours.' Then they both went to look at it, and To-Karvuvu said, 'I will pull it down and build like yours.' But his brother had pity on him and said, 'Do not do that. We will both of us live together in my house.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dixon, Oceanic Mythology, 'Melanesia' ch. II (1916); not verbatim.

title.en: The Carved Shark
title.zh: 雕刻之鯊

region.en: Gazelle Peninsula, New Britain (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 新不列顛加澤爾半島（象徵定位）

period: Oral tradition; recorded in R. B. Dixon, Oceanic Mythology, 1916

source.work: Roland B. Dixon, Oceanic Mythology, The Mythology of All Races Vol. IX (Boston: Marshall Jones, 1916), 'Melanesia' ch. II

summary.en: To-Kabinana carved a thum-fish that drove shoals ashore for the people to catch. The fool copied it wrongly, carving a shark, which ate the other fish — and would eat people too: the origin of the shark's appetite.
summary.zh: 托卡比納那刻木為松魚，投之於海使其成活，松魚驅馬利瓦蘭魚群上灘，眾人得以捕撈。愚弟欲仿之，兄明言當刻松魚，他卻刻成一鯊。鯊不驅魚上灘，反把眾魚吃光，哭訴於兄；兄嘆：『你這蠢貨，禍及子孫：此魚食盡他魚，亦將食人。』鯊魚之害，由此而生。

sensitivity.note: Colonial-era collection (Dixon 1916); Tolai heritage.

passages.text: One day To-Kabinana carved a thum-fish out of wood and let it float on the sea and made it alive so that it might always be a fish; and the thum-fish drove the malivaran-fish ashore in great numbers so that they could be caught. Now To-Karvuvu saw them, and asked his brother where were the fish that forced the malivaran-fish ashore, saying that he also wished to make some. Accordingly, To-Kabinana told him to make the figure of a thum-fish.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dixon, Oceanic Mythology, 'Melanesia' ch. II (1916); not verbatim.

passages.text: But instead the stupid fellow carved the effigy of a shark and put it in the water. The shark, however, did not drive the other fish ashore, but ate them all up, so that To-Karvuvu went crying to his brother and said, 'I wish I had not made my fish, for he eats all the others'; whereupon To-Kabinana asked, 'What kind of a fish did you make?' and he replied, 'A shark.' Then To-Kabinana said, 'You are indeed a stupid fellow. You have brought it about that our descendants shall suffer. That fish will eat all the others, and he will also eat people as well.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dixon, Oceanic Mythology, 'Melanesia' ch. II (1916); not verbatim.

title.en: Qat, the Crab-Hole Stone, and Ro Lei
title.zh: 卡特、蟹穴巨石與羅萊

region.en: Banks Islands, Vanuatu (symbolic pin: Gaua/Mota)
region.zh: 瓦努阿圖班克斯群島（象徵定位：高阿島／莫塔島）

period: Oral tradition; recorded in R. B. Dixon, Oceanic Mythology, 1916 (from Codrington's Mota texts)

source.work: Roland B. Dixon, Oceanic Mythology, The Mythology of All Races Vol. IX (Boston: Marshall Jones, 1916), 'Melanesia' ch. II

summary.en: Qat's eleven brothers, all named Tagaro, conspired to kill him for his wife Ro Lei and his canoe. They toppled a stone over him in a crab's hole; but calling on Marawa by name, Qat was carried round about to Ro Lei and sat beside her before his murderers reached the village.
summary.zh: 卡特十一位兄弟皆名塔加羅，合謀害他以奪其妻羅萊與獨木舟。他們引卡特入蟹穴挖蟹，翻石壓之，以為他已死，便奔往村中搶妻。卡特在石下呼名求救：『馬拉瓦！帶我繞到羅萊那裡去。』兄弟抵村時，卡特已坐在妻子身邊。諸兄弟屢屢設計害他，皆不能勝。

sensitivity.note: Missionary-era Mota collection via Dixon 1916; cross-ref qat-marawa-canoe (canoe episode, Codrington).

passages.text: After this, the brothers tried to destroy Qat in order that they might possess his wife and canoe. One day they took him to the hole of a land-crab under a stone, which they had already so prepared by digging under it that it was ready to topple over upon him. Qat crawled into the hole and began to dig for the crab; his brothers tipped over the stone upon him, and thinking him crushed to death, ran off to seize Ro Lei and the canoe.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dixon, Oceanic Mythology, 'Melanesia' ch. II (1916), after Codrington's Mota texts; not verbatim.

passages.text: But Qat called on Marawa by name, 'Marawa! take me round about to Ro Lei,' and by the time that his brothers reached the village, there was Qat to their astonishment sitting by the side of his wife. They tried to kill him in many other ways, but Qat was always the victor, and their plans were frustrated.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dixon, Oceanic Mythology, 'Melanesia' ch. II (1916), after Codrington's Mota texts; not verbatim.

title.en: Tagaro and Suqe-matua Toss Up the World
title.zh: 塔加羅與蘇蓋馬圖亞拋物定善惡

region.en: New Hebrides, Vanuatu (symbolic pin: Ambae)
region.zh: 瓦努阿圖新赫布里底群島（象徵定位：安巴埃）

period: Oral tradition; recorded in R. B. Dixon, Oceanic Mythology, 1916

source.work: Roland B. Dixon, Oceanic Mythology, The Mythology of All Races Vol. IX (Boston: Marshall Jones, 1916), 'Melanesia' ch. II

summary.en: Tagaro wanted everything good and would have no pain; Suqe-matua would have all things bad. When Tagaro made things, he or Suqe-matua tossed them into the air: what Tagaro caught is good for food, what he missed is worthless.
summary.zh: 塔加羅願萬物皆善，不容痛苦；蘇蓋馬圖亞偏要萬物皆惡。塔加羅造物之後，或由他、或由蘇蓋馬圖亞拋向空中——塔加羅接住的便為可食之物，他失手的便一文不值。

sensitivity.note: Colonial-era collection (Dixon 1916); Vanuatu heritage.

passages.text: In the New Hebrides, Tagaro wanted everything to be good, and would have no pain or suffering; Suqe-matua would have all things bad. When Tagaro made things, he or Suqe-matua tossed them up into the air; what Tagaro caught is good for food, what he missed is worthless. In a neighbouring island Tagaro is one of twelve brothers, and usually another of them is Suqe-matua, who continually thwarts him.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dixon, Oceanic Mythology, 'Melanesia' ch. II (1916); not verbatim.

title.en: Tagaro and Suqe-matua Share the Work of Creation
title.zh: 塔加羅與蘇蓋馬圖亞分創天地

region.en: Lepers Island (Aoba), New Hebrides (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 新赫布里底群島麻瘋島（安巴埃）（象徵定位）

period: Oral tradition; recorded in R. B. Dixon, Oceanic Mythology, 1916

source.work: Roland B. Dixon, Oceanic Mythology, The Mythology of All Races Vol. IX (Boston: Marshall Jones, 1916), 'Melanesia' ch. II

summary.en: On Lepers Island Tagaro and Suqe-matua shared creation, but everything Suqe-matua did was wrong: his trees bore bitter fruit; he wanted men to walk like pigs and sleep in sago-palm trunks, while Tagaro said they should walk upright and dwell in houses. Tagaro's word always prevailed.
summary.zh: 麻瘋島上，塔加羅與蘇蓋馬圖亞同司創造，然蘇蓋馬圖亞所為皆謬：其所植樹果實苦澀；他欲人行如豬、眠於西米棕櫚樹幹，塔加羅則命人直立而行、居於屋中。二人常相爭，終以塔加羅之言為勝。

sensitivity.note: Colonial-era collection (Dixon 1916); Aoba heritage.

passages.text: In Lepers Island Tagaro and Suqe-matua shared the work of creation, but whatever the latter did was wrong. Thus when they made the trees, the fruit of Tagaro's were good for food, but Suqe-matua's were bitter; when they created men, Tagaro said they should walk upright on two legs, but Suqe-matua said that they should go like pigs; Suqe-matua wanted to have men sleep in the trunks of sago palms, but Tagaro said they should work and dwell in houses. So they always disagreed, but the word of Tagaro prevailed. Tagaro was said to be the father of ten sons, the cleverest of whom was Tagaro-Mblti.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dixon, Oceanic Mythology, 'Melanesia' ch. II (1916); not verbatim.

title.en: Tagaro and the Hen-Dung Hair Oil
title.zh: 塔加羅與雞糞髮油之計

region.en: Lepers Island (Aoba), New Hebrides (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 新赫布里底群島麻瘋島（安巴埃）（象徵定位）

period: Oral tradition; recorded in R. B. Dixon, Oceanic Mythology, 1916

source.work: Roland B. Dixon, Oceanic Mythology, The Mythology of All Races Vol. IX (Boston: Marshall Jones, 1916), 'Melanesia' ch. II

summary.en: Meragbuto admired Tagaro's oiled hair and asked the secret. Tagaro told him to sit under the roosting hens and anoint himself with what they threw down — and Meragbuto proudly went to a festival reeking, learning too late that he had been tricked.
summary.zh: 梅拉布托見塔加羅髮油光可鑒，羨而問其方。塔加羅答：『待雞棲樹後，坐樹下，以雞從上拋下之物塗身。』梅拉布托依言以雞糞塗遍全身，翌日盛裝赴宴，人人掩鼻而逃，方知中計，倉皇下海洗身。

sensitivity.note: Colonial-era collection (Dixon 1916); Aoba heritage.

passages.text: In another portion of Lepers Island, Tagaro's opponent, here known as Meragbuto, becomes more of a simple fool, and many are the tricks that Tagaro plays upon him. One day Meragbuto saw Tagaro, who had just oiled his hair with coco-nut oil, and admiring the effect greatly, asked how this result had been produced. Tagaro asked him if he had any hens, and when Meragbuto answered that he had many, Tagaro said: 'Well, when they have roosted in the trees, do you go and sit under a tree, and anoint yourself with the ointment which they will throw down to you.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dixon, Oceanic Mythology, 'Melanesia' ch. II (1916); not verbatim.

passages.text: Meragbuto carried out the instructions exactly and rubbed not only his hair, but his whole body with the excrement of the fowls. On the following day he went proudly to a festival, but as soon as he approached every one ran away, crying out at the intolerable odour; only then did Meragbuto realize that he had been tricked, and washed himself in the sea.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dixon, Oceanic Mythology, 'Melanesia' ch. II (1916); not verbatim.

title.en: The Endless Coconut and the Broken Tabu
title.zh: 吃不盡之椰與犯禁之死

region.en: Lepers Island (Aoba), New Hebrides (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 新赫布里底群島麻瘋島（安巴埃）（象徵定位）

period: Oral tradition; recorded in R. B. Dixon, Oceanic Mythology, 1916

source.work: Roland B. Dixon, Oceanic Mythology, The Mythology of All Races Vol. IX (Boston: Marshall Jones, 1916), 'Melanesia' ch. II

summary.en: Tagaro placed a tabu on all coconuts; Meragbuto devoured them anyway. Tagaro then set a half-scraped nut before him — however much he scraped, more was always left — and made him eat until he burst and died. Had he not perished, there would have been no more coconuts at all.
summary.zh: 塔加羅下令所有椰子皆禁食；梅拉布托置若罔聞，幾乎吃光。塔加羅遂取一椰，刮去一半果肉而留殼置之，誘其食盡——他刮而復刮，椰肉始終有餘，食至腹破而死。若他未死，椰子早被他食盡。

sensitivity.note: Colonial-era collection (Dixon 1916); Aoba heritage.

passages.text: Another time Tagaro placed a tabu upon all coco-nuts so that no one should eat them; but Meragbuto paid no attention to this prohibition, eating and eating until he had devoured nearly all of them. Thereupon Tagaro took a small coco-nut, scraped out half the meat, and leaving the rest in the shell, sat down to await the coming of Meragbuto, who appeared by and by, and seeing the coco-nut, asked Tagaro if it was his. 'Yes,' said Tagaro, 'if you are hungry, eat it, but only on condition that you eat it all.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dixon, Oceanic Mythology, 'Melanesia' ch. II (1916); not verbatim.

passages.text: So Meragbuto sat down and scraped the remainder of the nut and ate it; but though he scraped and scraped, more was always left, and so he continued eating all day. At night Meragbuto said to Tagaro, 'My cousin, I can't eat any more, my stomach pains me.' But Tagaro answered, 'No. I put a tabu on the coco-nuts, and you disregarded it; now you must eat it all.' So Meragbuto continued to eat until finally he burst and died. If he had not perished, there would have been no more coco-nuts, for he would have devoured them all.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dixon, Oceanic Mythology, 'Melanesia' ch. II (1916); not verbatim.

title.en: The Burning-House Pit
title.zh: 火屋之坑

region.en: Lepers Island (Aoba), New Hebrides (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 新赫布里底群島麻瘋島（安巴埃）（象徵定位）

period: Oral tradition; recorded in R. B. Dixon, Oceanic Mythology, 1916

source.work: Roland B. Dixon, Oceanic Mythology, The Mythology of All Races Vol. IX (Boston: Marshall Jones, 1916), 'Melanesia' ch. II

summary.en: To destroy Meragbuto at last, Tagaro dug a pit beneath his own house, begged his rival to burn him alive, and survived the fire in the pit. Meragbuto, 'when it is night, do you come and set fire to my house,' was burned to death while Tagaro urged him to bear it bravely.
summary.zh: 塔加羅欲除梅拉布托，先在自家屋下掘深坑覆以枝葉，再請他來縱火燒屋：『如此你我妻兒皆焚而死，你便成唯一首領。』火起，塔加羅一家鑽入坑中得生；梅拉布托醒而探視，見其無恙，竟求同一死法。塔加羅如約縱火，聽他在火中哀號，只回一句：『你不會死，我當日也是如此；勇敢忍耐，很快便完。』愚者遂被燒盡。

sensitivity.note: Colonial-era collection (Dixon 1916); Aoba heritage.

passages.text: At last Tagaro determined to destroy Meragbuto, and accordingly he said, 'Let us each build a house.' This they did, but Tagaro secretly dug a deep pit in the floor of his house and covered it over with leaves and earth; after which he said to Meragbuto: 'Come, set fire to my house, so that I and my wife and children may be burned and die; thus you will become the sole chief.' So Meragbuto came and set fire to Tagaro's house, and then went to his own and lay down and slept. Tagaro and his family, however, quickly crawled into the pit which he had prepared, and so they escaped death.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dixon, Oceanic Mythology, 'Melanesia' ch. II (1916); not verbatim.

passages.text: When the house had burned, they came up out of their hiding-place and sat down among the ashes. After a time Meragbuto awoke, and saying, 'Perhaps my meat is cooked,' he went to where Tagaro's house had been, thinking to find his victims roasted. Utterly amazed to see Tagaro and his family safe and sound, he asked how this had happened, and Tagaro replied that the flames had not harmed him at all. 'Good!' said Meragbuto, 'when it is night, do you come and set fire to my house and burn me also.' So Tagaro set fire to Meragbuto's house, but when the flames began to burn him, Meragbuto cried out, 'My cousin! It hurts me. I am dying.' Tagaro, however, replied, 'No, you will not die; it was just that way in my case. Bear it bravely; it will soon be over.' And so it was, for Meragbuto was burned up and entirely destroyed.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dixon, Oceanic Mythology, 'Melanesia' ch. II (1916); not verbatim.

title.en: Tamus, Pupal, and the Coconut-Shell Oracle
title.zh: 塔穆斯、帕帕與椰殼神諭

region.en: Sulka country, northern New Britain (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 新不列顛北部蘇爾卡人之地（象徵定位）

period: Oral tradition; recorded in R. B. Dixon, Oceanic Mythology, 1916

source.work: Roland B. Dixon, Oceanic Mythology, The Mythology of All Races Vol. IX (Boston: Marshall Jones, 1916), 'Melanesia' ch. III

summary.en: Abandoned because she was pregnant while a cannibal couple ravaged the land, Tamus bore a son who turned a dracaena plant into a companion, Pupal. The two boys slew the cannibals and sent the ogress's breasts afloat in a coconut shell as an oracle that sank only when the fugitives spoke the truth.
summary.zh: 食人夫婦肆虐，村人棄孕婦塔穆斯而逃。她產下一子，其子以龍血樹造出同伴帕帕。二童築滑障、練武藝，誘食人者前來而誅之；塔穆斯將母食人妖之乳裝入椰殼放流，設下神諭：若流亡者撒謊則浮，說真話則沉。村民依諭而返，二童先拒其登岸，以棄母之罪責之，後宥之，眾人重聚故里。

sensitivity.note: Colonial-era collection (Dixon 1916); Sulka heritage.

passages.text: Once there was a cannibal and his wife who had killed and eaten a great many persons, so that, fearing lest they should all be destroyed, the people resolved to abandon their village and seek safety in flight. But Tamus, one of the women of the village, was with child, whence the others refused to take her with them; she swam after them, however, and clung to the stern of one of the canoes, but they beat her off, compelling her to return to the deserted village and to live there alone. In due time she bore a son, and warned him never to talk or laugh, lest the cannibals should hear.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dixon, Oceanic Mythology, 'Melanesia' ch. III (1916); not verbatim.

passages.text: One day his mother left him a dracaena-plant as a plaything, and when she was gone he said to himself, 'What shall I make out of this, my brother or my cousin?' Then he held the dracaena behind him, and presently it turned into a boy, with whom he played and talked — Pupal, hidden behind a partition in the house. When their mother discovered the companion, the two boys reassured her: 'Have no fear; we shall kill them, if they dare to come.' Making shields and spears, practising marksmanship, and raising a slippery barricade, they set up a swing near the house and called out, 'Where are you? We are here, come and eat us.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dixon, Oceanic Mythology, 'Melanesia' ch. III (1916); not verbatim.

passages.text: When the cannibals tried to climb the barricade, they slipped and fell, and the boys rushing out succeeded in killing them both after a hard fight. Tamus cut up the bodies and burned them, saving only the breasts of the ogress, which she put in a coco-nut-shell and set afloat on the sea: 'Go to the people who ran away from here, and if they ask, Have the cannibals killed Tamus? — remain floating; but if they say, Has Tamus borne a son and has he killed the cannibals? — then sink!' All occurred as Tamus had foreseen, and through the aid of the coco-nut-shell the people learned the truth. When the fugitives set out for their old home, Pupal and Tamus's son attacked them, saying, 'Ye abandoned my mother and cast her away. Now, ye shall not come back'; but after a while he relented and allowed the people to land, and all lived together again happily and safely in their old home.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dixon, Oceanic Mythology, 'Melanesia' ch. III (1916); not verbatim.

title.en: The Twins of the Dead Mother Avenge Taso
title.zh: 亡母雙子誅食人者塔索

region.en: New Hebrides, Vanuatu (symbolic pin: Espíritu Santo)
region.zh: 瓦努阿圖新赫布里底群島（象徵定位：聖靈島）

period: Oral tradition; recorded in R. B. Dixon, Oceanic Mythology, 1916

source.work: Roland B. Dixon, Oceanic Mythology, The Mythology of All Races Vol. IX (Boston: Marshall Jones, 1916), 'Melanesia' ch. III

summary.en: The cannibal Taso killed Qatu's pregnant sister and left her body in a thicket, where twin boys were born of the dead woman. Reared by their uncle on sago-frond bows, they ripened a tabued banana bunch bottom-up as their victory sign, then crushed Taso with the hot stones of his own oven.
summary.zh: 食人者塔索殺害孕姊，棄屍灌叢；雙生子竟由亡母腹中誕生，以雨水嫩芽活命。舅父卡圖收養之，以西米葉小弓練其射技。長成後，二人在蕉樹上設禁：若蕉串自頂向下熟，即塔索殺我；自底向上熟，即我殺塔索。二人潛入塔索屋中之男子會所，以爐中熱石砸殺塔索，誅其母，焚屋而歸，舅父聞竹爆聲急往，途中遇之，知母仇已報。

sensitivity.note: Colonial-era collection (Dixon 1916); Vanuatu heritage.

passages.text: There was once a cannibal named Taso, who came one day upon the sister of Qatu and killed her, but did not eat her because she was with child. So he abandoned her body in a thicket, and there, though their mother was dead, twin boys were born. They found rain-water collected in dead leaves, and shoots of plants that they could eat; and when they grew old enough to walk, they wandered in the forest until one day they found a sow belonging to their uncle Qatu, eating its provisions daily until he caught them — and, hearing who they were, welcomed them as his nephews.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dixon, Oceanic Mythology, 'Melanesia' ch. III (1916); not verbatim.

passages.text: Qatu made little bows of sago fronds for them, and when they could shoot lizards, he broke the bows, giving them larger ones with which they brought down greater game; and thus he trained them until they were grown up and could shoot anything. When they were young men, Qatu told them about Taso and how he had murdered their mother. The twins determined to kill the cannibal, so they set a tabu on a banana-tree belonging to them and said to their uncle: 'If our bunch of bananas begins to ripen at the top and ripens downwards, you will know that Taso has killed us; but if it begins to ripen at the bottom and ripens upwards, we shall have killed him.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dixon, Oceanic Mythology, 'Melanesia' ch. III (1916); not verbatim.

passages.text: When they came to his house, Taso had gone to the beach to sharpen his teeth, and only his mother was at home. The twins sat in the gamal, the men's house, roasting yams and heating stones in the blaze; and Taso's mother sang a song, telling him that there were two men in the gamal and that they should be food for him and for her. The cannibal quickly returned from the shore, moving his head from side to side and striking the trees so that they went crashing down. When he climbed over the door-rail of the gamal, the boys immediately threw at him all the hot rocks from the oven and knocked him down, and then with their clubs they beat him until he was dead, after which they killed his mother, and setting fire to the house over them, went away. Now Qatu, hearing the popping of the bamboos as the house burned, said, 'Alas, Taso has probably burned the boys!' Hastening to see what had happened, he met them on the way and heard from them that they had killed Taso and had revenged their mother whom he had slain.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dixon, Oceanic Mythology, 'Melanesia' ch. III (1916); not verbatim.

title.en: The Four Brothers and the Cannibal Who Killed His Own House
title.zh: 四兄弟與自滅滿門之食人妖

region.en: Melanesia (tale of general distribution; symbolic pin: Solomon Islands)
region.zh: 美拉尼西亞通用故事（象徵定位：所羅門群島）

period: Oral tradition; recorded in R. B. Dixon, Oceanic Mythology, 1916

source.work: Roland B. Dixon, Oceanic Mythology, The Mythology of All Races Vol. IX (Boston: Marshall Jones, 1916), 'Melanesia' ch. III

summary.en: Three brothers each answered a cannibal's challenge to 'call my brothers' by making buried fish reply, so the ogre let them take his breadfruit. The youngest, who had killed his fish outright, was trapped in the tree — but he talked the stupid monster into felling every tree he stood near, his own children, his wife, and last his own hand, before coming down and slaying him.
summary.zh: 長兄射魚埋沙，攀食人妖之麵包樹，妖令其呼弟為證，埋魚齊聲應之，妖懼而放行。二弟三弟效之皆得手。幼弟殺魚不埋，無魚應聲，被困樹上；他卻誘妖：『我將從那棵樹上下來』——妖連砍週遭樹木，又殺自己幼女、妻子，最後砍斷己手；男子下樹而誅之。

sensitivity.note: Colonial-era collection (Dixon 1916); tale of general Melanesian distribution.

passages.text: In a village lived four brothers, the eldest of whom one day took his bow and went out to shoot fish. Those which were only wounded he buried in the sand, and so went on until his arrow hit and stuck in the trunk of a bread-fruit-tree; whereupon, looking up and seeing ripe fruit, he climbed the tree and threw several of them down. An old cannibal heard the sound as they dropped and said, 'Who is that stealing my fruit?' The man in the tree replied, 'It is I with my brothers,' and the old ogre answered, 'Well, let us see if what you say is true. Just call to them.' Accordingly the man shouted, 'My brothers!' and all the fish that he had buried in the sand replied, so that it sounded as if many men were near; whereupon the cannibal was frightened and said, 'It is true, but hurry up, take what you will, only leave me the small ones.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dixon, Oceanic Mythology, 'Melanesia' ch. III (1916); not verbatim.

passages.text: The second brother followed his tracks and imitated his procedure and came back with fish and fruit; the third brother did the same. Then came the turn of the fourth, who failed to bury the wounded fish but killed them, and when the cannibal asked him to call his brothers, there was no reply. 'Aha,' said the cannibal, 'now I have got you. You must come down from the tree.' 'Oh, yes!' said the youngest brother, 'I shall come down on that tree there.' Quickly the ogre took his axe and cut down the tree, and in this way he felled every one that stood near. 'Now, I surely have you,' said he, but the youngest brother replied, 'No, I will come down on your youngest daughter there.' So the cannibal rushed at her and gave her a fatal blow; and thus the man in the tree induced the stupid monster to kill all his children and his wife and lastly to cut off his own hand, whereupon the man came down from the tree and slew the ogre.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dixon, Oceanic Mythology, 'Melanesia' ch. III (1916); not verbatim.

title.en: The Widower's Armbands and the Flooded Tree-Root
title.zh: 鰥夫臂環與樹根洪刑

region.en: Melanesia (tale of general distribution; symbolic pin: Solomon Islands)
region.zh: 美拉尼西亞通用故事（象徵定位：所羅門群島）

period: Oral tradition; recorded in R. B. Dixon, Oceanic Mythology, 1916

source.work: Roland B. Dixon, Oceanic Mythology, The Mythology of All Races Vol. IX (Boston: Marshall Jones, 1916), 'Melanesia' ch. III

summary.en: A cave-monster stole a household's stored food and walled wife and children alive in a cave. The widower mourned a year, then lured the cannibal to sleep on a tree-root in a dammed river-bed with the promise of plaited armlets; the birds broke the dam, and the flood drowned the monster while the man tore off his mourning bands.
summary.zh: 洞穴妖盜食藏糧，又將婦人與孩童封入洞中餓死。鰥夫居喪編臂環，妖羨而求之；他答：『須先睡，方能編得工整。』遂密令群鳥截流，引妖臥於乾河床之大樹根上，以藤索縛之；鳥決堤，洪水奔下。妖問『這涼物是什麼？』男子答曰：『你這惡洞妖，食物本是為我們備的，你吃光並害死我妻兒，如今還想要臂環？』遂撕下喪環擲地，洪水沒頂，妖溺斃。

sensitivity.note: Colonial-era collection (Dixon 1916); Dixon notes close Indonesian parallels.

passages.text: A man and his family had dried and prepared a great quantity of food, which they stored on a staging in their home; and one day, when the man had gone off to his field to work, a cannibal came to the house. Seeing all the provisions, he resolved to get them. So he said to the man's wife, 'Your cousin told me to tell you to give me a package of food.' The woman gave him one, and he hid it in the forest, after which he returned and repeated his request, thus carrying away all the food which the people had stored. Finally he seized the woman and her children, shut them up in a cave, and went away.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dixon, Oceanic Mythology, 'Melanesia' ch. III (1916); not verbatim.

passages.text: When the husband returned, he found his house empty; his wife and family starved to death in the cave he could not open, and he returned to his town and plaited the widower's wristlets and arm-bands for himself. One day the old cannibal came by, and seeing him sitting there, admired the plaited ornaments and asked the man to make him some like them. The widower agreed: 'You must first go to sleep, then I can make them properly.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dixon, Oceanic Mythology, 'Melanesia' ch. III (1916); not verbatim.

passages.text: So they went to seek a suitable place, and the man, after secretly telling the birds to dam up the river, led the cannibal to a great tree-root in the channel of the stream. Believing him, the cannibal lay down on the root and slept, whereupon the man took strong rattans and vines and tied the monster fast, after which he called out to the birds to break the dam and let the flood come down the river. When the cannibal, awakened by the water which rose higher and higher, cried out, 'What is this cold thing which touches me?' the man replied: 'You evil cave-monster, surely it was for you that we prepared all the food, and you came and ate it up. You also killed my wife and children, and now you want me to plait an arm-band for you.' Then he tore off his own arm-bands and signs of mourning and threw them away, while the water rose above the head of the cannibal and drowned him.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dixon, Oceanic Mythology, 'Melanesia' ch. III (1916); not verbatim.

title.en: Garawada in the Fig-Tree
title.zh: 困於無花果樹之加拉瓦達

region.en: Melanesia (tale of general distribution; symbolic pin: Solomon Islands)
region.zh: 美拉尼西亞通用故事（象徵定位：所羅門群島）

period: Oral tradition; recorded in R. B. Dixon, Oceanic Mythology, 1916

source.work: Roland B. Dixon, Oceanic Mythology, The Mythology of All Races Vol. IX (Boston: Marshall Jones, 1916), 'Melanesia' ch. III

summary.en: The witch mother-in-law imprisoned Garawada in a fig-tree by magic; her son was born and fell to the jungle floor, where he grew alone, fed his mother from below, and sang the identity song 'I have sucked the shoots of dabedabe; my mother is Garawada.' Rescued by his uncle's villagers, Garawada slipped free of the falling tree and turned into a crab.
summary.zh: 巫婆岳母施法夾困加拉瓦達於無花果樹杈間。她產子墜地，兒獨自長於叢林，採果奉母，並習唱認親歌：『我食過達貝達貝之嫩枝，吾母加拉瓦達也。』一日誤傷村童，其舅父出而認之，率眾伐樹救母；樹倒之際，加拉瓦達脫身奔至海灘，化為蟹，鑽入沙穴而去。兒隨舅返村，村童自此不再怕他。

sensitivity.note: Colonial-era collection (Dixon 1916); tale of general Melanesian distribution.

passages.text: A woman named Garawada one day went with her mother-in-law into the jungle to gather figs. Coming to a fig-tree, Garawada climbed up and began to eat the ripe fruit, while she threw down the green ones to her mother-in-law. The latter, angered at this, called to Garawada to come down, but when she reached the fork in the tree, the old woman, who was a witch, caused the forks to come together, thus imprisoning her daughter-in-law, after which she went away and left her.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dixon, Oceanic Mythology, 'Melanesia' ch. III (1916); not verbatim.

passages.text: For many days the woman remained in the tree, and finally bore a son; but after a while the child fell to the ground, and though his mother feared that he would die, he found wild fruits and water, and lived. One day he looked up into the tree and discovered his mother, and from that time he gave her fruits and berries in order that she might not starve. 'Mother, teach me my pari, that I may sing it when I find my people, and that thus they may know me' — and she taught him the spell: 'I have sucked the shoots of dabedabe; My mother is Garawada.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dixon, Oceanic Mythology, 'Melanesia' ch. III (1916); not verbatim.

passages.text: The child ran off to seek his way out of the jungle and came to the edge of the forest, where children threw darts at a rolled coco-nut; missing his aim, he struck one of the children in the arm, and all ran shrieking home. On the third visit the father of one of them ran out and caught him; the boy told his story and sang his song, and the man said, 'Truly thou art my nephew. Come, let us go and set thy mother free.' So they went with many of the villagers and cut down the tree; but as the tree fell, Garawada slipped away and ran swiftly to the beach, and there, turning into a crab, crawled into a hole in the sand. Her son wept because he knew that his mother had left him, but his uncle led him back to the village and took him into his own home, and the children no longer were afraid to have him for a playfellow.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dixon, Oceanic Mythology, 'Melanesia' ch. III (1916); not verbatim.

title.en: Tagaro and the Winged Maiden of the Sky-Land
title.zh: 塔加羅與天界羽女

region.en: Lepers Island (Aoba), New Hebrides (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 新赫布里底群島麻瘋島（安巴埃）（象徵定位）

period: Oral tradition; recorded in R. B. Dixon, Oceanic Mythology, 1916

source.work: Roland B. Dixon, Oceanic Mythology, The Mythology of All Races Vol. IX (Boston: Marshall Jones, 1916), 'Melanesia' ch. III

summary.en: Tagaro stole the wings of a bathing sky-maiden and married her; when her weeping over scolded yams wore the earth from her hidden wings, she flew back to heaven with her child. Tagaro built an arrow-chain to the sky and climbed a banian-root that crept down it — but halfway down his wife cut the root beneath her, and Tagaro fell to earth alone.
summary.zh: 塔加羅窺天女下凡沐浴，竊其翼藏於屋柱下，娶為妻。妻觸薯蔓而薯自熟，遭妯娌責罵，入屋倚柱而泣，淚滴蝕土露出雙翼，遂攜子飛回天上。塔加羅百箭連環射空成梯，天界榕根循箭而下，他攜飾物攀根而上尋妻；歸途夫妻相讓先下，行至半空，妻抽斧斷根，塔加羅與鳥墜地，妻與子重返天界。

sensitivity.note: Colonial-era collection (Dixon 1916); Aoba heritage. Swan-maiden type, well developed in the New Hebrides.

passages.text: A party of heavenly, winged maidens once flew down to earth to bathe, and Tagaro watched them. He saw them take off their wings, stole one pair, and hid them at the foot of the main pillar of his house. He then returned and found all fled but the wingless one, and he took her to his house and presented her to his mother as his wife. After a time Tagaro took her to weed his garden, when the yams were not yet ripe, and as she weeded and touched the yam vines, ripe tubers came into her hand. Tagaro's brothers thought she was digging yams before their time and scolded her; she went into the house and sat weeping at the foot of the pillar, and as she wept her tears fell, and wearing away the earth pattered down upon her wings. She heard the sound, took up her wings, and flew back to heaven.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dixon, Oceanic Mythology, 'Melanesia' ch. III (1916); not verbatim.

passages.text: Another version adds that the returning sky-maiden took her child with her; and Tagaro, finding the wings gone, knew that his wife and child had returned to the sky-land. He called a bird: 'Fly up and seek for them in their country, for you have wings and I have not.' The bird perched in the sky-country, scratched upon a fruit pictures of Tagaro, the child, and its mother, and dropped it at their feet. The sky-woman bade the bird tell Tagaro that he must ascend to the sky-land, for only if he should come up to her would she agree to descend to earth again.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dixon, Oceanic Mythology, 'Melanesia' ch. III (1916); not verbatim.

passages.text: Quickly making a powerful bow and a hundred arrows, Tagaro shot one of them at the sky; it stuck firmly, and he shot another into the butt of the first, and a third into the butt of the second, making an arrow-chain until the end of it reached the earth. Then from the sky a banian-root crept down the arrow-chain and took root in the earth; Tagaro breathed upon it, and it grew larger and stronger, whereupon he and the bird climbed the banian-root to the sky. His wife gathered up her mats and followed him down; but when they were half way down, she took out a hatchet which she had concealed and cut the banian-root just beneath her, so that Tagaro and the bird fell to earth, while she and her child climbed back again to the sky.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dixon, Oceanic Mythology, 'Melanesia' ch. III (1916); not verbatim.

title.en: The Isle of Women
title.zh: 女人之島

region.en: Gazelle Peninsula, New Britain (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 新不列顛加澤爾半島（象徵定位）

period: Oral tradition; recorded in R. B. Dixon, Oceanic Mythology, 1916

source.work: Roland B. Dixon, Oceanic Mythology, The Mythology of All Races Vol. IX (Boston: Marshall Jones, 1916), 'Melanesia' ch. III

summary.en: Chasing a snared pigeon, a man came to an isle of women whose only husbands were tortoises. One woman saw him reflected in the spring and secreted him; discovered at last, he became husband to them all — until, homesick, he paddled home and his own wife, furious at the wasted funeral beads, felled him with an axe.
summary.zh: 男子追捕網中之鴿，遠航至女人之島——島上女子皆以龜為夫。一女在泉中窺見樹上男影，藉故折返留其日盾，密藏男子於家。事洩後眾女出資共聘之為夫。及其子長成，男子思鄉，解舟而歸；家人以為他已溺亡。夜叩鼓歸家，其妻舉火視之，怒斥：『你害我們白費葬禮珠錢，卻無恥地與別的女人過活！』舉斧擊之，男子遂死。

sensitivity.note: Colonial-era collection (Dixon 1916); Tolai heritage.

passages.text: A man one day set some snares in a tree to catch pigeons. One of the birds was caught, but succeeded in tearing the snare loose and flew away over the sea. The man, thinking to secure it, followed it in his canoe, and after having paddled all day and all night, in the morning he saw an island and the bird perched upon a tree. Concealing his canoe, he started after the bird, but hearing people coming, he hurriedly climbed into a tree and hid himself.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dixon, Oceanic Mythology, 'Melanesia' ch. III (1916); not verbatim.

passages.text: The tree stood directly over a spring, and soon many women appeared, coming to get water. One of them, as she stooped to dip up water, saw the reflection of the man in the surface of the pool; whereupon she called out to her companions, 'I will fill your water-vessels for you.' She secretly left her sun-shield behind, went back to the spring, and asked the man to marry her; and thus she alone of all the women had a man for her husband, for all the rest had only tortoises. In due time she had a child; and when the other women discovered the secret, they paid the sisters to let them all marry the man, so that he had very many spouses.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dixon, Oceanic Mythology, 'Melanesia' ch. III (1916); not verbatim.

passages.text: After the man's first child had grown, he determined to leave the island; uncovering his canoe, he paddled away to his own home, where he saw the signs put up in the house of the dead, for all thought him drowned. It was evening when he reached his village, and as he rapped on the drum to let his wife know that he had returned, she called out, 'Who is there?' to which he answered, 'It is I.' She lit a torch and came out of the house and looked at him; but was angry, and saying, 'You are the one who caused us to spend all our bead-money in vain on your funeral ceremonies, while you have been living shamelessly with other wives,' she seized an axe and struck him so that he died.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dixon, Oceanic Mythology, 'Melanesia' ch. III (1916); not verbatim.

title.en: The Tapa-Beater That Became a Woman
title.zh: 化為女子之打布棒

region.en: German New Guinea coast (symbolic pin: Huon Gulf)
region.zh: 德屬新幾內亞海岸（象徵定位：休恩灣）

period: Oral tradition; recorded in R. B. Dixon, Oceanic Mythology, 1916

source.work: Roland B. Dixon, Oceanic Mythology, The Mythology of All Races Vol. IX (Boston: Marshall Jones, 1916), 'Melanesia' ch. III

summary.en: A tapa-beater transformed itself into a woman, lured her bedfellow out night-fishing, and abandoned her on an island of driftwood. A sea-eagle hatched from an egg in her hand fed her, brought fire, and at last carried her home; her father burned the deceptive beater.
summary.zh: 夜裡，一根打布棒自化為女子之形，喚同屋女子：『起來，我們捕魚去。』二人秉炬出海，至漂流木之小島；天明，同伴現出打布棒原形，棄她而去。女子拾得海雕之卵，孵化育之；雕鳥捕魚奉食，並銜火枝予她炊食，終以巨木試力，攜她飛回本島。父母大喜，厚養雕鳥；父聞打布棒之詐，燃起大火，將棒投入焚之。

sensitivity.note: Colonial-era collection (Dixon 1916); New Guinea coast heritage.

passages.text: One night, while two women were sleeping in a house, a tapa-beater transformed itself into a woman resembling one of the pair, and waking the other, said to her, 'Come, it is time for us to go fishing.' So the woman arose, and they took torches and went out to sea in a canoe. After a while she saw an island of drift-wood, and as the dawn came on, perceived that her companion had turned into a tapa-beater, whereupon she said: 'Oh, the tapa-beater has deceived me. While we were talking in the evening, it was standing in the corner and heard us, and in the night it came and deceived me.' Landing her on the island, the tapa-beater paddled away and abandoned her.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dixon, Oceanic Mythology, 'Melanesia' ch. III (1916); not verbatim.

passages.text: But she sought for food, and found a sea-eagle's egg which she held in her hand until it broke and hatched out a young bird, for which she cared until it grew large. Then the bird would fly off and get fish for her to eat, and also brought her a fire-brand, so that she could cook her food. When the bird said that he would carry her to the shore, she doubted whether he was strong enough; then the bird seized a great log of wood and showed her that he could lift that, so she trusted him and was borne safely back to her own island. Her father was angry at the tapa-beater's deception, and building a great fire, threw the tapa-beater into it and burned it up.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dixon, Oceanic Mythology, 'Melanesia' ch. III (1916); not verbatim.

title.en: The Ghost and His Own Corpse
title.zh: 鬼搬己屍

region.en: Kai country, Huon Gulf, German New Guinea (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 德屬新幾內亞休恩灣凱人之地（象徵定位）

period: Oral tradition; recorded in R. B. Dixon, Oceanic Mythology, 1916

source.work: Roland B. Dixon, Oceanic Mythology, The Mythology of All Races Vol. IX (Boston: Marshall Jones, 1916), 'Melanesia' ch. III

summary.en: A youngest brother fell from a tree and died; his ghost lied its way down, secretly wrapped and hid the body, and played the 'I forgot something' trick on the other brothers. The village shut its doors; only an old woman's door stood open, and the ghost bargained her grandson against his own corpse until dawn forced him to yield — and he became a wild tero-plant, his body a piece of bark.
summary.zh: 凱人兄弟爬樹採製臂環之料，幼弟失足墜亡；其鬼謊稱踏斷枯枝，先下樹裹屍藏之，途中屢以『忘了東西』為名回去搬屍，兄弟疑而逃歸，全村閉戶。唯老嫗與孫未聞警，門仍敞開。鬼擲屍入屋，老嫗擲出，鬼接而復擲；相持間老嫗誤將孫兒擲出，鬼大喜：『此可為我食矣！』天將曉，嫗呼日出，鬼懼日光，終以孫換屍，不再能隱，化為野特羅草，其屍則成一片樹皮。

sensitivity.note: Colonial-era collection (Dixon 1916); Kai heritage.

passages.text: A number of brothers who were gathering material for making arm-bands had climbed into a great tree, when the youngest made a mis-step, and falling to the ground, was killed. The other brothers, who could not see what had happened because of the thick foliage, called out, 'What was that which fell?' The ghost of the dead brother, however, still stood in the tree and said, 'I stepped on a dead branch which broke,' and thus lying to his brothers, he descended from the tree before them, wrapped his body in leaves, and hid it. On the way back he repeated the trick of going back for 'something he had left' until his brothers, becoming suspicious, watched and found out how they had been deceived. Thereupon they all fled, and coming to the village, cried out, 'We have seen something mysterious. Shut your doors.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dixon, Oceanic Mythology, 'Melanesia' ch. III (1916); not verbatim.

passages.text: By and by the ghost came, carrying his body on his back. He tried to throw his corpse into the first house, but it struck against the closed door and fell down again; so he picked it up and cast it at the next with like result. Thus he tried them all until he came to the last house, in which the old woman lived; and here, because the door was open, the ghost succeeded and threw his body into the house. Quickly the old woman seized the bundle and tossed it out again, but the ghost caught it and hurled it back. Thus they continued to send the body to and fro; but at last the old woman seized her grandson by mistake and threw him out, at which the ghost cried, 'That is great! Now you have given me something to eat.' The old woman then said, 'Throw him back again,' but the ghost replied, thinking to cheat her, 'Do you first throw out my body. Then I will throw him back.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dixon, Oceanic Mythology, 'Melanesia' ch. III (1916); not verbatim.

passages.text: So they argued until dawn was near, when the old woman shouted, 'The dawn is coming. Does that mean something for you or for me?' Since the ghost replied, 'For me!' the woman delayed until the day had come. The light of the sun put the ghost in danger, so he threw the grandson back and received his own body in return; but being no longer able to conceal himself, he was changed into a wild tero-plant, while his body became a piece of bark.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dixon, Oceanic Mythology, 'Melanesia' ch. III (1916); not verbatim.

title.en: How the Rat Got His Tail and the Rail His Red Brow
title.zh: 鼠尾與紅額秧雞之由來

region.en: Banks Islands, Vanuatu (symbolic pin: Gaua/Mota)
region.zh: 瓦努阿圖班克斯群島（象徵定位：高阿島／莫塔島）

period: Oral tradition; recorded in R. B. Dixon, Oceanic Mythology, 1916 (from Codrington's Mota texts)

source.work: Roland B. Dixon, Oceanic Mythology, The Mythology of All Races Vol. IX (Boston: Marshall Jones, 1916), 'Melanesia' ch. III

summary.en: A rat and a rail quarrelled over a gariga-fruit tree. The rat ate all the ripe fruit and threw down only stones; one struck the rail on the forehead and stuck there — the rail's red brow. Coming down, the rat was jabbed with a dracaena leaf that stuck fast in his rump: his tail.
summary.zh: 鼠與秧雞爭爬一樹，鼠食盡熟果，只擲石下來。秧雞誘其擲一枚，石果正中其額黏住——秧雞之紅額由此而來。鼠下樹時，秧雞以龍血樹葉插其臀，葉黏不去——鼠尾便是那片龍血樹葉。

sensitivity.note: Missionary-era Mota collection via Dixon 1916.

passages.text: In the Banks Islands it is said that a rat and a rail, once finding a gariga-tree full of ripe fruit, disputed which should climb the tree. At last the rat went up, but instead of throwing ripe fruit down to the rail, he ate them himself and tossed down only stones. Finding that the rat refused to give him any fully ripe fruit, the bird said, 'Throw me down that one. It is only red ripe,' whereupon the rat took the fruit and tossed it at the rail, so that it hit him on his forehead and stuck fast.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dixon, Oceanic Mythology, 'Melanesia' ch. III (1916), after Codrington's Mota texts; not verbatim.

passages.text: The rail was angry, and as the rat came down from the tree, he thrust the unfolded leaf of a dracaena into the rat's rump, where it stuck fast. So the tail of the rat is the leaf of the dracaena that the rail put there, and the red lump on the head of the rail is the gariga-fruit which the rat threw at him.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dixon, Oceanic Mythology, 'Melanesia' ch. III (1916), after Codrington's Mota texts; not verbatim.

title.en: The Yam That Ate a Chicken
title.zh: 食雞之薯與好薯壞薯

region.en: Lepers Island (Aoba), New Hebrides (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 新赫布里底群島麻瘋島（安巴埃）（象徵定位）

period: Oral tradition; recorded in R. B. Dixon, Oceanic Mythology, 1916

source.work: Roland B. Dixon, Oceanic Mythology, The Mythology of All Races Vol. IX (Boston: Marshall Jones, 1916), 'Melanesia' ch. III

summary.en: A wild yam rose up and devoured one of a hen's ten chickens; the survivors took shelter under a kite, which seized the man-eating yam and dropped it, and a second kite split it in two. The two halves fell to the two kites — whence some yams are good and some are bad.
summary.zh: 麻瘋島上，一母雞率十雛遇野薯，薯起身吞食一雛。倖存者呼鳶庇護，藏於其翼下；野薯質問，鳶怒而抓薯高飛擲地，另一鳶再抓再擲，薯裂為二——兩鳶分而食之，故今之薯有好有壞。

sensitivity.note: Colonial-era collection (Dixon 1916); Aoba heritage.

passages.text: In Lepers Island in the New Hebrides the origin of good and bad yams is given as follows. One day a hen and her ten chickens came across a wild yam, which got up after a while and ate one of the chickens. The survivors called to a kite, which said to the hen, 'Put the chickens under me,' and when the yam came and asked the kite where the chickens were, the bird replied, 'I don't know.' Thereupon the yam scolded the kite, and the latter, seizing the yam, flew high into the air and dropped it to the ground.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dixon, Oceanic Mythology, 'Melanesia' ch. III (1916); not verbatim.

passages.text: Then another kite took it up and let it fall from a great height, so that the yam was broken into two parts; and thus the two kites divided the yam between them and ate it, whence some yams are good for food and some are bad — the garden patch carrying to this day the memory of the chicken-eating wild yam and the two birds that broke it.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dixon, Oceanic Mythology, 'Melanesia' ch. III (1916); not verbatim.

title.en: How the Turtle Got His Shell
title.zh: 龜殼之由來

region.en: British New Guinea coast (symbolic pin: Port Moresby)
region.zh: 英屬新幾內亞海岸（象徵定位：莫爾茲比港）

period: Oral tradition; recorded in R. B. Dixon, Oceanic Mythology, 1916

source.work: Roland B. Dixon, Oceanic Mythology, The Mythology of All Races Vol. IX (Boston: Marshall Jones, 1916), 'Melanesia' ch. III

summary.en: The turtle and the wallaby raided Binama the hornbill's garden. The wallaby leapt away; the turtle was caught for the morrow's feast, bribed Binama's children with games and finery, and plunged into the sea wearing a great wooden bowl — which the stones of the pursuing birds could not break. To this day all turtles carry the bowl of Binama's house on their backs.
summary.zh: 龜與袋鼠同入犀鳥比納馬之園偷食蕉蔗。袋鼠一躍而逃，龜被縛於架上以待翌日宴殺。龜哄比納馬之子女解縛同戲，戴上珠串、貝釧，背上負一大木碗，趁眾人歸而奔海。眾人追至岸邊擲石，擊碎雙釧與珠串，木碗卻堅不可破；龜遂遠遁。至今龜背所負，即是比納馬家中之木碗。

sensitivity.note: Colonial-era collection (Dixon 1916); PNG coastal heritage.

passages.text: The turtle and the wallaby, being hungry one day, went together to the hornbill's garden and began to eat his bananas and sugar-cane. While they were thus engaged, the birds were preparing a feast, and Binama, the hornbill, asked one of them to go to the shore for some salt water with which to flavour the food; the wagtail agreed to go, and on the way passed through Binama's garden, where he saw the wallaby and the turtle feasting. The wagtail returned to the village by another path and cried out, 'Friends, the turtle and the wallaby are eating in our master's garden.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dixon, Oceanic Mythology, 'Melanesia' ch. III (1916); not verbatim.

passages.text: Then all the people were angry, and getting their spears, they ran and surrounded the garden. The wallaby, seeing his danger, made a tremendous leap and escaped, but the turtle, having no means of flight, was caught and carried prisoner to Binama's house, where he was tied to a pole and laid upon a shelf until the morrow, when Binama and the others intended to kill the turtle at a feast. Only Binama's children were left in the house, and the turtle, speaking softly to them, said, 'Loosen my bonds, O children, that we may play together.' This the children did, and at the turtle's request got the best of their father's ornaments, which the turtle donned: a great bead necklace, shell armlets, and a huge wooden bowl on his back.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dixon, Oceanic Mythology, 'Melanesia' ch. III (1916); not verbatim.

passages.text: By and by the people could be heard returning; and as soon as the turtle became aware of this, he ran swiftly to the sea and dived out of sight. The birds hurled great stones at him and broke one of the armlets, then the other, and hit the necklace so that the string gave way and the beads were lost. Then for a last time calling to the turtle to show himself, they threw very large stones which fell upon the wooden bowl on his back, but they did not break it, and the turtle was not harmed. Then he fled far away over the sea, and to this day all turtles carry on their backs the bowl that once was in the house of Binama.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dixon, Oceanic Mythology, 'Melanesia' ch. III (1916); not verbatim.

title.en: The Dog, the Kangaroo, and the Broken Forepaws
title.zh: 犬、袋鼠與斷掌之計

region.en: Gazelle Peninsula, New Britain (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 新不列顛加澤爾半島（象徵定位）

period: Oral tradition; recorded in R. B. Dixon, Oceanic Mythology, 1916

source.work: Roland B. Dixon, Oceanic Mythology, The Mythology of All Races Vol. IX (Boston: Marshall Jones, 1916), 'Melanesia' ch. III

summary.en: The kangaroo tricked the dog into eating filth for a yellow lafua-fruit; the dog repaid him by boasting of his own broken forepaws until the kangaroo snapped his off — then killed the maimed trickster. Ever since, the kangaroo has had short forepaws.
summary.zh: 袋鼠食黃色拉富阿果，狗問其口何以黃；袋鼠指穢物謊稱即是，狗食之受騙。狗懷恨，先埋掌於沙，謊稱自斷前掌故而短美，誘袋鼠效之；袋鼠自斷雙掌，狗躍起曰：『我掌仍在！是你騙我食穢。』撲而殺之。袋鼠短掌之形，自此而傳。

sensitivity.note: Colonial-era collection (Dixon 1916); Tolai heritage. Dixon notes close parallels with Australian tales.

passages.text: One day when the kangaroo was going along, followed by the dog, he ate a yellow lafua-fruit and was asked by the dog, when the latter came up with him, 'Tell me, what have you eaten that your mouth is so yellow?'
