summary.zh: 在「印加之宴」,純印加血統的少年接受瓦拉卡(吊索)、楚斯帕(小袋)與瓦拉(褲)。據說瓦拉卡以龍舌蘭纖維與羊筋製成,先祖自帕卡里坦波走出時便佩戴此物。在瓦納考里獻五羔祭後,祭司向空中吹羊毛,禱曰:「瓦納考里,我們的父親,願造物主、太陽與雷永葆青春!」叔伯父母鞭打少年手足,曰:「像我當年那樣勇敢!」騎士們在阿納瓦爾基賽跑——相傳自洪水時代起,此瓦卡如獅般奔跑;在勞拉納山,神廟供兩隻石隼,係帕查庫特克·尤潘琪所立,瓦伊納·卡帕克又自馬拉斯人偶像處取隼飾之。受武者於此得褲、金耳飾與羽冠。此節由曼科·卡帕克為其子辛奇·羅卡而設;「瓦里」之歌乃造物主在曼科走出坦波洞穴時所授,唯此節可唱。

sensitivity.note: Full initiation sequence from Molina's compilation; the lineage rules exclude non-Inca youths, recorded as given.

passages.text: Each of the youths who were about to be armed had a sheep prepared for sacrifice. They all went, with their relations, to the hill called Huanacauri. That night they slept at the foot of the hill, at a place called Matahua, and at sunrise, all fasting, they ascended the hill until they came to the huaca Huanacauri. When they reached the top of the hill, the Tarpuntays took five lambs and sacrificed them before the huaca, then divided the wool among the youths who were about to be made knights. The youths and chiefs then blew the wool into the air while the sacrifices were being consumed, with these words: 'O Huanacauri! our father, may the Creator, the Sun, and the Thunder ever remain young, and never become old. May thy son the Ynca always retain his youth, and grant that he may prosper in all he undertakes. And to us, thy sons and descendants who now celebrate this festival, grant that we may ever be in the hands of the Creator, of the Sun, of the Thunder, and in thy hands.'
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Molina, Fables and Rites, Ccapac Raymi (Markham 1873); not verbatim.

passages.text: At the ninth hour of the day they put huaracas and bags called chuspas into the hands of the youths, and on presenting them with the huaracas they said: 'Now that our father Huanacauri has given the huaracas as a sign of valour, live henceforth as brave men.' They were made of aloe fibre and the sinews of sheep, and it was said that their ancestors, when they came forth from Paccari-tampu, wore them. Then they walked on until they came to a ravine called Quiras-manta, where they were met by the uncles and parents and chiefs, who whipped them on the arms and legs, saying, 'Be brave as I have been, and receive these gifts that you may imitate me.' Then they chaunted a song called Huari.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Molina, Fables and Rites, Ccapac Raymi (Markham 1873); not verbatim.

passages.text: The reason why they went to the huaca of Anahuarqui to perform a sacrifice was that, on this day, they had to run a race, to try which was the best runner. The tradition had been handed down from the time of the deluge that this huaca ran like a lion. The youthful knights stood in a row before the huaca of Anahuarqui, behind them a second row of arm bearers, and in their rear a third row whose duty it was to aid those who fell; in front of all was an Indian very gaily dressed who gave the word. They all began to run at full speed and with all their force; those who fell or fainted were assisted by the men in the rear, but some died of the falls. Those who reached the goal received drink from the maidens, and drank as they ran.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Molina, Fables and Rites, Ccapac Raymi (Markham 1873); not verbatim.

passages.text: The huaca of Raurana consisted of two falcons in stone, placed upon an altar on the summit of the hill. It was instituted by Pachacutec Ynca Yupanqui as the place where they should receive the breeches which they call huara. This huaca was at first the idol of the Indians of Maras, and Huascar Ynca caused the falcons to be brought here to beautify it. Manco Ccapac instituted this feast, and caused these ceremonies to be observed in the case of his son Sinchi Rocca. With reference to the taqui so often repeated in the ceremony, they say that, in the time of Manco Ccapac, when he came forth from the Cave of Tampu, it was given to him by the Creator with a command that it should be sung at this festival, and at no other.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Molina, Fables and Rites, Ccapac Raymi (Markham 1873); not verbatim.

canonical_translation: C. R. Markham, Narrative of the Rites and Laws of the Yncas (Hakluyt Society, 1873)

title.en: Chocanaco: Hanan against Hurin in the Thistle-Seed Battle
title.zh: 喬卡納科:哈南對烏林的薊籽之戰

region.en: Cuzco great square (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 庫斯科大廣場(象徵性標記)

period: Recorded by Cristóbal de Molina at Cuzco, c. 1575; publ. Markham 1873

source.work: Molina of Cuzco, 'An Account of the Fables and Rites of the Yncas', in Narratives of the Rites and Laws of the Yncas, trans. C. R. Markham, Hakluyt Society, 1873

summary.en: On the first day of Camay-quilla the newly armed knights of the lineages of Hanan Cuzco and Hurin Cuzco came into the great square with slings and hurled coco - the missiles found on certain thistles - against one another, at times coming to close quarters to prove the muscles of their arms, until the Inca, who was present, rose up and restored order. It was called chocanaco, a trial of strength to see who were the strongest and bravest.
summary.zh: 卡馬伊基利亞月初一,新受武的哈南庫斯科與烏林庫斯科兩世系騎士各執吊索入大廣場,互擲「科科」(一種薊上的籽實),時或近身角力以較臂力,直至在場的印加王起身喝止。此謂「喬卡納科」,較力之戲,以試誰最強最勇。

sensitivity.note: Martial game opening the December rites; the Hanan/Hurin duality is central to Cuzco social myth.

passages.text: On the first day of the month, those who had been armed as knights, as well those of the lineage of Hanan Cuzco as of Hurin Cuzco, came out into the square, with slings in their hands called huaraca, and the youths of Hanan Cuzco hurled against those of Hurin Cuzco; their missiles were called coco, which are found on certain thistles. At times they came to close quarters, to prove the muscles of their arms; until the Ynca, who was present, rose up and restored order. They called this chocanaco, and it was a trial of strength, to see who were the strongest and bravest.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Molina, Fables and Rites, month of December (Markham 1873); not verbatim.

canonical_translation: C. R. Markham, Narrative of the Rites and Laws of the Yncas (Hakluyt Society, 1873)

title.en: Charcoal and Toads: Souls with the Creator or with Supay
title.zh: 炭與蟾蜍:歸造物主之魂與墮蘇帕伊之魂

region.en: Heaven above and the place of punishment below (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 上天與受罰之所(象徵性標記)

period: Recorded by Cristóbal de Molina at Cuzco, c. 1575; publ. Markham 1873

source.work: Molina of Cuzco, 'An Account of the Fables and Rites of the Yncas', in Narratives of the Rites and Laws of the Yncas, trans. C. R. Markham, Hakluyt Society, 1873

summary.en: Food and drink were offered to the embalmed dead as if they were alive, saying: 'When you were alive you used to eat and drink of this; may your soul now receive it and feed on it, wheresoever you may be.' For they believed and held it for certain that souls did not die, but that those of good men went to rest with the Creator, who would see them from heaven; they charged their families to perform all they had left them to do. But there was a place of punishment for bad men, where they were tormented by demons called Supay: there they suffered much hunger and thirst, and their food was charcoal, snakes, toads, and other things of that kind; while those who went to heaven ate and drank the best that the Creator had, and also received the food and liquor their relations offered up.
summary.zh: 人們向死者木乃伊供上食物與酒,如同其生前:說「你生前曾如此飲食,願你的靈魂今在何處都能領受而食之」。因他們確信靈魂不死,善人之魂歸造物主安息,自天上眷顧子孫,臨終時囑咐家人完成遺命。惡人之魂則墮入受罰之所,為名喚「蘇帕伊」的惡魔所折磨:飢渴交迫,所食者為炭、蛇、蟾蜍之類;而升天者得享造物主所有之至美飲食,亦能領受親人所供之食。

sensitivity.note: Andean eschatology as recorded by a missionary observer; 'Supay' later became the name for the Christian devil - here it is the native term for punishing demons.

passages.text: For this feast they brought all the huacas into the square, as well as the bodies of the dead Yncas, to drink with them; placing those who had belonged to the Hanan Cuzco on the side where that lineage was stationed, and the same with those of Hurin Cuzco. Then they brought food and drink to the dead bodies, as if they were alive, saying: 'When you were alive you used to eat and drink of this; may your soul now receive it and feed on it, wheresoever you may be.'
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Molina, Fables and Rites, month of December (Markham 1873); not verbatim.

passages.text: For they believed and held it for certain that souls did not die, but that those of good men went to rest with the Creator. When they died they declared this belief, and charged their families and relations to perform all that they had left them to do, and that they would see them from heaven. They also believed that there was a place of punishment for bad men, where they were tormented by demons called Supay. They said that those who went there suffered much hunger and thirst, and that their food was charcoal, snakes, toads, and other things of that kind. Those who went to heaven, on the other hand, ate and drank the best that the Creator had, and they also received the food and liquor which their relations offered up.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Molina, Fables and Rites, month of December (Markham 1873); not verbatim.

canonical_translation: C. R. Markham, Narrative of the Rites and Laws of the Yncas (Hakluyt Society, 1873)

title.en: Moro-urco: The Four-Coloured Cable Wound Like a Serpent
title.zh: 莫羅-烏爾科:四色繩索如蛇盤繞

region.en: Moro-urco house near the temple of the Sun, Cuzco (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 庫斯科太陽神廟旁莫羅-烏爾科之屋(象徵性標記)

period: Recorded by Cristóbal de Molina at Cuzco, c. 1575; publ. Markham 1873

source.work: Molina of Cuzco, 'An Account of the Fables and Rites of the Yncas', in Narratives of the Rites and Laws of the Yncas, trans. C. R. Markham, Hakluyt Society, 1873

summary.en: At the full moon of December the people went to the house called Moro-urco near the houses of the Sun, to take out a very long cable woven in four colours, black, white, red and yellow, with a stout ball of red wool at the end. Every one took hold of it, men on one side and women on the other, performing the taqui called yaqauyra; coming to the square they made their reverences to the huacas and the Inca, and kept going round and round until they were the shape of a spiral shell. Then they dropped the cable on the ground and left it coiled up like a snake. A lamb was sacrificed for the cable and for rain and the winter time, saying to the winter: 'Why hast thou rained?'
summary.zh: 十二月望月之夜,人民齊往太陽神廟旁的「莫羅-烏爾科」之屋,取出一條極長的繩索——以黑、白、紅、黃四色織成,末端繫一紅色羊毛大球。男女分列兩側,共執此繩,且行且歌。入廣場拜過瓦卡與印加王後,眾人繞行不止,直至隊形成螺旋貝狀,然後將繩索擲於地上,任其盤繞如蛇。為繩索與雨水獻祭一羔,並向冬天發問:「你為何降雨?」

sensitivity.note: The coiled four-coloured cable (huascar) is tagged to the world-serpent cluster for its serpent-coil imagery; the tag is interpretive.

passages.text: The rest of the people had gone to a house called Moro-urco, near the houses of the Sun, to take out a very long cable which was kept there, woven in four colours, black, white, red, and yellow, at the end of which there was a stout ball of red wool. Every one took hold of it, the men on one side, and the women on the other, performing the taqui called yaqauyra. When they came to the square, after making reverences to the huacas and the Ynca, they kept going round and round until they were the shape of a spiral shell. Then they dropped the huascar on the ground, and left it coiled up like a snake. They called this cable Moro-urco.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Molina, Fables and Rites, month of December (Markham 1873); not verbatim.

passages.text: Presently, they brought a lamb to be sacrificed for the cable, and for rain, and the winter time, saying to the winter: 'Why hast thou rained?' From noon to sunset was passed in rejoicings, and in drinking with the huacas and dead bodies.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Molina, Fables and Rites, month of December (Markham 1873); not verbatim.

canonical_translation: C. R. Markham, Narrative of the Rites and Laws of the Yncas (Hakluyt Society, 1873)

title.en: Mojocati: The Year's Sacrifices Sent Down the River to Ollantay-tampu
title.zh: 莫霍卡蒂:歲祭順流送至歐雁台

region.en: Capi-mayu river, Cuzco to Ollantay-tampu (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 庫斯科卡皮河至歐雁台(象徵性標記)

period: Recorded by Cristóbal de Molina at Cuzco, c. 1575; publ. Markham 1873

source.work: Molina of Cuzco, 'An Account of the Fables and Rites of the Yncas', in Narratives of the Rites and Laws of the Yncas, trans. C. R. Markham, Hakluyt Society, 1873

summary.en: In December they collected all kinds of food, ajis, coca, cloths, shoes, llautus, plumes, sheep, flowers, gold and silver, and all the ashes of the year's sacrifices, and threw them into the dammed-up river Capi-mayu; the first dam was thrown down and the water rushed out with such fury that it carried the other dams away with it and all the sacrifices. Indians stationed with torches along the ten-league route by night accompanied the offerings to the bridge of Ollantay-tampu over the great river flowing to the North Sea, where two bags of coca were thrown from the bridge as the sacrifices flowed past. The reason given was that, as the Creator had granted them a good year, they should offer these things that they might not appear ungrateful. Those who had gone furthest carried salt lances and falcons; the laggards carried salt toads, and the people laughed at them.
summary.zh: 十二月,人們收齊各色食物、辣椒、古柯袋、衣裳、鞋履、勞圖頭帶、羽冠、羊、花、金銀,以及全年祭祀積存的灰燼,投入築壩蓄水的卡皮河。推倒第一道壩,洪水洶湧而出,連同諸壩與祭品一併沖走。沿途村落居民持火把排列於十萊格的夜路上,護送祭品直至歐雁台大橋——橋下大河奔向北海。祭物流過時,自橋上投入兩袋古柯。其理由是:造物主既賜他們豐年,便當以所得之物還祭,以免顯得不感恩。行得最遠者手持鹽製長矛與隼,落後者捧鹽製蟾蜍,惹得眾人哄笑。

sensitivity.note: The December river-sending rite; tagged with world-renewal as the year's accumulated sacra are washed to the sea.

passages.text: A small river flows through the centre of Cuzco called Capi-mayu and Huaca-puncu-mayu. In the ravines above the town they constructed dams to confine the water, although it was winter, in order that it might bear away the sacrifices with greater force. On this day they collected all kinds and sorts of food, all the different sorts of ajis, great quantities of bags of coca, all kinds of cloths of different colours and shoes, llautus and plumes, sheep, flowers, gold and silver, and every other sort of thing that they used, as well as all the ashes and cinders of all the sacrifices that had been preserved throughout the year.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Molina, Fables and Rites, month of December (Markham 1873); not verbatim.

passages.text: All these things were thrown into the river, the first dam was thrown down, and the water rushed out with such fury that it carried the other dams away with it, and all the sacrifices. Many people were assembled on both sides of the river, outside the city of Cuzco, at a place called Pumap-chupa. The Indians on both sides of the river were commanded by the Lord Ynca, who was present, to go with the sacrifices to Ollantay-tampu, ten leagues from Cuzco by the round. Indians of the villages by which they had to pass were stationed at intervals with torches, in order to give light during the night, and no part of the sacrifices was allowed to remain in the river. When they reached the bridge of Ollantay-tampu, over a great river flowing to the North Sea, they threw two bags of coca, called pilculuncu paucar uncu, from the bridge as the sacrifices flowed past.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Molina, Fables and Rites, month of December (Markham 1873); not verbatim.

passages.text: The reason for throwing these sacrifices into the river was that, as the Creator of all things had granted them a good year, it seemed well that, out of the things that he had given them, they should offer these sacrifices, that they might not appear ungrateful, beseeching him to receive them, wheresoever he might please to be. Those who had gone furthest carried in their hands lances and falcons made of salt; while those who lagged behind had toads made of salt, as a sign that they had gone slowly, which made the people laugh at them.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Molina, Fables and Rites, month of December (Markham 1873); not verbatim.

canonical_translation: C. R. Markham, Narrative of the Rites and Laws of the Yncas (Hakluyt Society, 1873)

title.en: Mama Huaco's First Maize: The Farm of Sausiru
title.zh: 瑪瑪·瓦科的初植玉米:薩烏西魯田

region.en: Farm of Sausiru beneath the fortress of Cuzco (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 庫斯科要塞下薩烏西魯田(象徵性標記)

period: Recorded by Cristóbal de Molina at Cuzco, c. 1575; publ. Markham 1873

source.work: Molina of Cuzco, 'An Account of the Fables and Rites of the Yncas', in Narratives of the Rites and Laws of the Yncas, trans. C. R. Markham, Hakluyt Society, 1873

summary.en: In the harvest month of Ayrihuay the newly armed knights went to the farm of Sausiru, beneath the citadel, to fetch the reaped maize; there, they say, Mama-huaco, the sister of Manco Ccapac, sowed the first maize. The farm was cultivated every year for the body of this Mama-huaco, making from the crop the chicha necessary for the service of the embalmed body, which was delivered to those who had charge of it. The maize of the harvests of the Creator, the Sun, the Moon, the Thunder, the Ynca, Huanacauri and all the dead lords was brought in small baskets, singing a chaunt called yaravi and dressed in gay clothes.
summary.zh: 收穫月艾里瓦伊,新受武的騎士前往要塞下的薩烏西魯田運取已收之玉米。相傳瑪瑪·瓦科——曼科·卡帕克之姊妹——在此播下第一粒玉米。此田歲歲耕種,專為瑪瑪·瓦科之遺體:以其收成釀奇恰酒,交由管理木乃伊之人以供祭祀。造物主、太陽、月亮、雷神、印加王、瓦納考里及歷代先王的收穫玉米,皆由人們盛於小籃,身著華服,唱著名為「雅拉維」的哀歌,一一運回。

sensitivity.note: Etiological farm of the first maize, tied to the ancestral mother-warrior Mama Huaco; gendered founder narrative preserved from a male-priest compilation.

passages.text: The month of April was called Ayrihuay. In it they reaped the crops and got in the harvests. Those who had received arms as knights went to the farm of Sausiru, to fetch the maize that had been reaped there, which is beneath the citadel. It is here they say that Mama-huaco, the sister of Manco Ccapac, sowed the first maize.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Molina, Fables and Rites, month of April (Markham 1873); not verbatim.

passages.text: They cultivated this farm every year for the body of this Mama-huaco, making from the crop the chicha that was necessary for the service of the body, and delivering this chicha to those who had charge of the body, which was embalmed. Then, in their order, they brought the maize of the harvests of the Creator, the Sun, the Moon, the Thunder, the Ynca, and Huanacauri, and of all the dead lords. They brought it in small baskets, singing a chaunt called yaravi, and dressed in gay clothes.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Molina, Fables and Rites, month of April (Markham 1873); not verbatim.

passages.text: All the rest of the people of Cuzco went to bring in this maize, except on the first day, when it was brought by the youths who had received knighthood. The priests, called Tarpuntays, offered up a lamb in sacrifice, beseeching the Creator ever to grant them good harvests. This lasted for four days, after which they went back to their farms; and so the year ended.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Molina, Fables and Rites, month of April (Markham 1873); not verbatim.

canonical_translation: C. R. Markham, Narrative of the Rites and Laws of the Yncas (Hakluyt Society, 1873)

title.en: Tawhaki Calls Down the Overwhelming of Mataaho
title.zh: 塔瓦基降下大洪水之怒

region.en: Lofty hillfort, Hauraki coast, Aotearoa (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 紐西蘭豪拉基海岸山巔要塞（象徵性定位）

period: Oral tradition; recorded 1855 (Grey, Polynesian Mythology)

source.work: George Grey, Polynesian Mythology and Ancient Traditional History of the New Zealand Race, ch. 3, The Legend of Tawhaki (London 1855)

summary.en: Two of Tawhaki's brothers-in-law attempt to murder him on the way home from a fishing trip and bury him insensible. His wife Hinepiripiri finds him alive, carries him home, and at his direction brings a whole unchopped tree as firewood, naming their first son Wahieroa - 'long log for the fire' - to recall the duty of revenge. Recovered, Tawhaki builds a fort on a lofty mountain and calls on the gods his ancestors, who let the floods of heaven descend; the earth is overwhelmed and all human beings of that race perish, an event named 'The Overwhelming of the Mataaho'.
summary.zh: 塔瓦基與四個連襟出海捕魚，其中二人心懷不軌，歸途中謀害他並將其草草埋葬。妻子希內皮里皮里尋獲尚有一息的他，背回家中，依其囑咐扛回整根不劈之樹作柴火，並為長子取名瓦希耶羅亞——『長柴之火』——以銘記復仇之責。塔瓦基傷癒後於高山築寨，呼喚祖神復仇；天洪傾瀉，大地沒頂，該族人類盡亡，史稱『馬塔阿霍大沒』。

sensitivity.note: Flood-cluster record: revenge-deluge variant where a hero summons the flood, not a survival tale.

passages.text: Tawhaki, son of Hema and Urutonga, having taken Hinepiripiri as a wife, went one day with his brothers-in-law to fish from a flat reef of rocks running far out into the sea. Two of them, tired of fishing, returned toward their village with him; when they drew near the village they attempted to murder him, and, thinking they had slain him, buried him. The others, questioned by their young sister, claimed the party had all gone home together long since; the wife suspected her husband had been killed and ran off to search for him.
passages.note: Paraphrase of George Grey, Polynesian Mythology, ch. 3 (1855); not verbatim.

passages.text: She found where he had been buried, and on examining him ascertained he had only been insensible, not quite dead; with great difficulty she got him on her back, carried him home, carefully washed his wounds and staunched the bleeding. When he had somewhat recovered he told her to fetch wood and light a fire, and to fell any tall tree growing near, bringing the whole of it: she put the entire tree upon the fire without chopping it into pieces. It was this circumstance that led her to give the name of Wahieroa - long-log-of-wood-for-the-fire - to their first son, that the duty of avenging his father's wrongs might often be recalled to his mind.
passages.note: Paraphrase of George Grey, Polynesian Mythology, ch. 3 (1855); not verbatim.

passages.text: As soon as Tawhaki had recovered from his wounds he left the place where his faithless brothers-in-law lived, took all his own warriors and their families, and built a fortified village on the top of a very lofty mountain where he could easily protect himself. Then he called aloud to the gods, his ancestors, for revenge, and they let the floods of heaven descend; the earth was overwhelmed by the waters and all human beings perished, and the name given to that event was 'The Overwhelming of the Mataaho', and the whole of that race perished.
passages.note: Paraphrase of George Grey, Polynesian Mythology, ch. 3 (1855); not verbatim.

title.en: Tawhaki and Karihi Destroy the Ponaturi
title.zh: 塔瓦基兄弟誅滅波納圖里族

region.en: Manawa-Tane, Ponaturi house (symbolic pin, coast)
region.zh: 波納圖里族大屋馬納瓦塔內（象徵性定位）

period: Oral tradition; recorded 1855 (Grey, Polynesian Mythology)

source.work: George Grey, Polynesian Mythology and Ancient Traditional History of the New Zealand Race, ch. 3, The Legend of Tawhaki (London 1855)

summary.en: Tawhaki and Karihi seek revenge on the Ponaturi, an underwater race who slew their father Hema and kept their captive mother as 'Tatau the Door', watching for dawn at the threshold of the house Manawa-Tane. Hiding in the thatch, the brothers stop every chink of the house; when Tatau at last answers 'Yes, it is dawn', the light streams in and the whole Ponaturi tribe withers before the sun's rays. Only the leaping kanae escapes by springing back to the sea; the brothers burn their father's bones and carry them home with their mother.
summary.zh: 塔瓦基與卡里希兄弟為父復仇：殺父奪屍的是海底種族波納圖里人，他們囚母於大屋馬納瓦塔門口，令其守候黎明，得名『塔陶之門』。兄弟藏身屋茅之內，封死屋中每道縫隙；老嫗終答『已破曉』，晨光灌入，全族在日光下枯萎而死，唯善跳之鰆魚躍水而逃。兄弟取下父骨焚之，攜母親與父親遺骨歸返故土。

sensitivity.note: Colonial-era collection; the sun-kill tagging links the episode to the solar-death cluster.

passages.text: It was a different race who had carried off and slain the father of Tawhaki; the name of that race was the Ponaturi, whose country was underneath the waters, but who had a large house on the dry land to which they resorted to sleep at night, named Manawa-Tane. They had carried off the father's body, and kept his wife alive as a captive. When Tawhaki and his younger brother Karihi drew near the house there was no one there but their mother sitting near the door, while the bones of their father were hung up inside under the high sloping roof; at the approach of night the whole tribe would return to the house.
passages.note: Paraphrase of George Grey, Polynesian Mythology, ch. 3 (1855); not verbatim.

passages.text: As the brothers came repeating incantations, the bones of their father rattled loudly together where they hung, for gladness, knowing the hour of revenge had come; their mother Urutonga heard Tawhaki's voice and wept for gladness. She warned them the people were very fierce and savage, and only kept her alive to watch for the rising of the dawn; they named her 'Tatau', the Door, calling out through the night, 'Ho, Tatau, is it dawn yet?' and she answering, 'No, no, it is deep night - sleep on.' The brothers climbed to the ridge-pole, made holes in the thick layers of reeds that formed the thatch, and crept into them; their mother charged them, when it drew near dawn, to stop up every chink in the house so that no single ray of light might shine in.
passages.note: Paraphrase of George Grey, Polynesian Mythology, ch. 3 (1855); not verbatim.

passages.text: When the sun sank beneath the ocean the whole tribe left the water in a body. A scout sniffed round the house and nearly found the strangers' scent, but the tribe came crowding in thousands and the scent was lost; the house filled up with sleeping Ponaturi. At midnight the brothers stole down and whispered with Tatau at the doorway; she counselled them to let the sun kill the people, its rays would destroy them. Time and again the old men called, 'Ho, Tatau, is it dawn yet?' and she answered, 'It is night, it is lasting night, sleep soundly.' At last dawn had broken and the sun shone brightly; she answered 'Yes' and cried to her children, 'Pull out the stoppings!' The bright rays of the sun came streaming into the house and the whole of the Ponaturi perished before the light - not by the hand of man, but withered before the sun's rays; only the leaping kanae escaped by successive springs back to the water. The brothers took down their father's bones, burnt them with fire, and returned to their own country with their mother and the bones of their father.
passages.note: Paraphrase of George Grey, Polynesian Mythology, ch. 3 (1855); not verbatim.

title.en: Tangotango, the Bride from the Skies
title.zh: 天女湯戈湯戈下嫁塔瓦基

region.en: Tawhaki's village, Hauraki (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 塔瓦基村居，豪拉基（象徵性定位）

period: Oral tradition; recorded 1855 (Grey, Polynesian Mythology)

source.work: George Grey, Polynesian Mythology and Ancient Traditional History of the New Zealand Race, ch. 3, The Legend of Tawhaki (London 1855)

summary.en: Fame of Tawhaki's courage and beauty reaches Tangotango, a maiden of the heavenly race, who descends nightly to lie by the sleeping hero and vanishes before dawn. Pregnant, she discloses herself and lives with him for love of his people; but when Tawhaki calls their newborn daughter smelly, the insulted mother rises into the sky from the ridge-pole carving. Her parting counsel - grasp the vine that has struck root into the earth, not the loose swaying one - becomes the key to his later ascent, and Arahuta is carried to heaven.
summary.zh: 塔瓦基之勇武俊美遠播天界，天女湯戈湯戈夜夜下凡偎依熟睡的英雄，晨光前離去。及至有孕，她吐露身份，為愛留居人間。然塔瓦基嫌初生女兒『氣味難聞』，天女含悲攜女自屋脊雕飾處凌空而去，留下一句訣別之言：握住那已深深扎入土中的藤蔓，莫握高空搖曳的鬆蔓——此話後來成為他登天的鑰匙。

sensitivity.note: Sacred-marriage cluster: hero marries a sky-born woman; motif tags interpretive.

passages.text: The fame of Tawhaki's courage in destroying the race of Ponaturi, and a report also of his manly beauty, chanced to reach the ears of a young maiden of the heavenly race who live above in the skies; so one night she descended from the heavens to visit Tawhaki and judge for herself whether these reports were true. She found him lying sound asleep, gazed on him for some time, stole to his side and laid herself down by him; when he was disturbed by her he thought it was only some female of this lower world, and slept again; before dawn the young girl stole away and ascended once more to the heavens.
passages.note: Paraphrase of George Grey, Polynesian Mythology, ch. 3 (1855); not verbatim.

passages.text: From that time Tangotango, the girl of the heavenly race, stole every night to the side of Tawhaki, and lo, in the morning she was gone - until she found she had conceived a child, afterwards named Arahuta. Then, full of love for Tawhaki, she disclosed herself fully to him and lived constantly in this world with him, deserting for his sake her friends above; and he discovered that she who had so loved him belonged to the race whose home is in the heavens.
passages.note: Paraphrase of George Grey, Polynesian Mythology, ch. 3 (1855); not verbatim.

passages.text: When the child came - a little girl - Tawhaki took it to a spring to wash it before baptism, then held it away from him as if it smelt badly, and said, 'Faugh, how badly the little thing smells.' Tangotango, hearing this said of her own dear baby, sobbed and cried bitterly, and at last rose up with her child and began to take flight towards the sky, pausing one minute with one foot resting on the carved figure at the end of the ridge-pole above the door. Tawhaki rushed forward and springing up tried to catch his wife, entreating, 'Mother of my child, oh return once more to me!' She called down that she would never return; but at his plea for a remembrance she gave him her parting counsel: take care to lay hold not of the loose root of the creeper which drops from aloft and sways to and fro in the air, but rather of that which, hanging down from on high, has again struck its fibres into the earth. Then she floated up into the air and vanished from his sight.
passages.note: Paraphrase of George Grey, Polynesian Mythology, ch. 3 (1855); not verbatim.

title.en: Tawhaki Climbs the Vine of Heaven
title.zh: 塔瓦基攀天藤而上

region.en: Matakerepo's guard post at the world's rim (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 盲眼祖妣守藤之天際之地（象徵性定位）

period: Oral tradition; recorded 1855 (Grey, Polynesian Mythology)

source.work: George Grey, Polynesian Mythology and Ancient Traditional History of the New Zealand Race, ch. 3, The Legend of Tawhaki (London 1855)

summary.en: Grieving for wife and daughter, Tawhaki travels with Karihi to the road's end where the tendrils hanging from heaven touch the earth, guarded by their blind ancestress Matakerepo. Tawhaki's taro-counting prank restores her sight with a touch, and she reveals the way. Karihi seizes a loose tendril and is swept to the horizon's edge and back before Tawhaki's shout frees him; Tawhaki alone climbs with a powerful incantation, keeping hold of the rooted vine, until he pulls himself up into the heavens.
summary.zh: 塔瓦基思念妻女成疾，偕弟卡里希行至天藤垂地之處，守藤者為雙目失明的祖妣馬塔凱雷波。塔瓦基以偷數芋頭的惡作劇戲弄她，繼以手觸復其明目；老嫗指路並囑咐：待明日晨光再攀，中途不可俯視下界，亦須握緊扎入土中的藤蔓。卡里希誤抓鬆藤，被風吹至天際又墜回，得兄呼喊方脫險；塔瓦基獨自攀天，一路誦唸強力咒語，終於拉身登上天界。

sensitivity.note: Ascension cluster: hero climbs to the heavens to reclaim his family.

passages.text: Tawhaki remained plunged in grief, for his heart was torn by regrets for his wife and his little girl. One moon had waned after her departure, when, unable longer to endure such sufferings, he called to Karihi to go and search for his little girl, and they departed with two slaves as companions. He warned the unclean, unconsecrated slaves not to look up at the enchanted fortress of Tongameha as the road passed it; one slave looked up, and his eye was immediately torn out by the magical arts of Tongameha and he perished.
passages.note: Paraphrase of George Grey, Polynesian Mythology, ch. 3 (1855); not verbatim.

passages.text: At last they reached the spot where the ends of the tendrils which hang down from heaven reach the earth, and found an old ancestress of theirs quite blind, named Matakerepo, appointed to take care of the tendrils and holding the ends of one of them in her hands. She was counting ten taro roots she was about to cook; Tawhaki quietly slipped away the tenth, then the ninth, until she guessed somebody was playing a trick upon her. She pulled her weapon from beneath her and swept it round; the brothers lay flat and her weapon passed over them. Karihi struck her a blow upon the face, and as she threw up her hands crying out, Tawhaki touched both her eyes, and lo, she was at once restored to sight, knew her grandchildren, and wept over them. Then she pointed to the tendrils: 'Up there lies your road; but do not begin the ascent so late in the day; wait until the morning.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of George Grey, Polynesian Mythology, ch. 3 (1855); not verbatim.

passages.text: Tawhaki presented his slave to the old lady as an acknowledgment for her kindness, and at first peep of dawn prepared food for strength. As he started, she called out to him: lay fast hold of the tendrils with your hands and climb on; when you get midway between heaven and earth, take care not to look down upon this lower world again, lest you become charmed and giddy and fall; and take care not by mistake to lay hold of a tendril which swings loose, but rather of one which, hanging down from above, has again firmly struck root into the earth.
passages.note: Paraphrase of George Grey, Polynesian Mythology, ch. 3 (1855); not verbatim.

passages.text: Karihi sprang and caught a loose one, and away he swung to the very edge of the horizon; a blast of wind blew him back to the other side of the skies, another swept him up, and down he was blown again - until Tawhaki shouted, 'Now, my brother, loose your hands!' and he stood upon the earth once more. Tawhaki, alarmed for his brother, sent him home to care for their families, and began the ascent alone, his old ancestress calling 'Hold fast, my child!' and repeating a powerful incantation as he climbed, until at length he reached the heavens and pulled himself up into them.
passages.note: Paraphrase of George Grey, Polynesian Mythology, ch. 3 (1855); not verbatim.

title.en: The Ugly Old Slave Is Tawhaki
title.zh: 醜老奴原是塔瓦基

region.en: Canoe-building forest in the heavens (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 天界造舟之林（象徵性定位）

period: Oral tradition; recorded 1855 (Grey, Polynesian Mythology)

source.work: George Grey, Polynesian Mythology and Ancient Traditional History of the New Zealand Race, ch. 3, The Legend of Tawhaki (London 1855)

summary.en: Entering the heavens, Tawhaki disguises himself as an ugly old man; the very brothers-in-law who had tried to murder him seize him as a slave to carry axes and firewood. Each evening he secretly adzes their canoes to perfection; when the suspicious brothers-in-law hide to watch, he sheds his disguise in incantations and stands resplendent. Tangotango questions the 'slave' and wins back her husband, who snatches up his little daughter; Tawhaki makes the whole place tapu, performs the noble rites for the child, and lightning flashes from his arm-pits - for he dwells in the skies still, and thunder is said to be his footsteps.
summary.zh: 塔瓦基登天後自毀俊容，化身醜陋老者；謀害過他的連襟們竟把他當作奴隸，令其背斧扛柴。每晚他暗自以斧精修其獨木舟，成品完美令眾驚疑；連襟埋伏窺視，只見他在咒語中褪去偽裝、恢復煥發儀容。湯戈湯戈上前質問，夫婦相認，塔瓦基抱起幼女，全場被其神威立為禁地。他為女兒行貴族洗禮之禮，腋下電光迸射——相傳塔瓦基至今仍居天界，雷聲即其腳步。

sensitivity.note: Grey's footnote notes the tapingu of the courtyard and the thunder/lightning worship of Tawhaki.

passages.text: At length Tawhaki reached the heavens, and pulled himself up into them, and then by enchantments disguised himself, changing his handsome and noble appearance into the likeness of a very ugly old man. He followed the road into a dense forest where his brothers-in-law, with a party of their people, were hewing canoes from the trunks of trees; they saw him and, little thinking who he was, called out that here was an old fellow who would make a nice slave, and made him carry the heavy axes home. At evening, coming near the village, he was taken up by two women gathering firewood and made to carry a load as well - so was this mighty chief treated as a slave, even by female slaves.
passages.note: Paraphrase of George Grey, Polynesian Mythology, ch. 3 (1855); not verbatim.

passages.text: Little did his wife Tangotango think that the slave they were insulting was her own husband Tawhaki. He carried his load of firewood straight up to her fire-place; all present cried that he would become tapued from sitting near Tangotango, but on he went. Next evening, after the others were out of sight, he turned back and rapidly adzed a canoe from bow to stern, and lo, one side was finished, then the other, beautifully finished; next day the brothers-in-law found a second canoe transformed. On the third evening they hid in the forest to watch; and Tawhaki, repeating the necessary incantations, put off his disguise and took again his own appearance, noble and handsome, and commenced his work at the canoe. The watchers whispered that this must be a demi-god, ran to the village, asked Tangotango to describe her husband, and found the man exactly like the description.
passages.note: Paraphrase of George Grey, Polynesian Mythology, ch. 3 (1855); not verbatim.

passages.text: When Tawhaki reappeared, disguised again as an ugly old man, Tangotango questioned him: 'Now tell me, who are you? Are you Tawhaki?' He murmured assent, still walking on until he reached her side, then snatched up his little daughter and pressed her to his heart. The persons present all rushed out of the court-yard, for the whole place was made tapu by Tawhaki, and murmurs of gratification arose on every side at the splendour of his appearance. He retired with his wife, saying he came that their little daughter might undergo the ceremonies usual for the children of nobles; at daybreak they broke an opening through the end of the house opposite the door, that the little girl's rank might be seen by her being carried out that way, repeated the prescribed prayers, and lightnings flashed from the arm-pits of Tawhaki as they plunged her into the water. It is said Tawhaki still dwells in the skies, worshipped as a god, and that thunder and lightning are caused by his footsteps when he moves.
passages.note: Paraphrase of George Grey, Polynesian Mythology, ch. 3 (1855); not verbatim.

title.en: Hinauri, the Stranded Log of Timber
title.zh: 海娜烏里：擱淺之木

region.en: Wairarawa beach, northern Aotearoa (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 紐西蘭北部懷拉拉瓦海灘（象徵性定位）

period: Oral tradition; recorded 1855 (Grey, Polynesian Mythology)

source.work: George Grey, Polynesian Mythology and Ancient Traditional History of the New Zealand Race, ch. 4, Rupe's Ascent into Heaven (London 1855)

summary.en: After her self-drowning over Irawaru, Hinauri drifts for months in the sea and is thrown up on the beach of Wairarawa, overgrown with seaweed and barnacles. Two brothers, Ihuatamai and Ihuwareware, gently scrape her clean and nurse her back; she takes a new name, Ihungarupaea, the Stranded-log-of-timber. When her husband Tinirau's other wives curse and try to kill her, one incantation fells them both dead, and Hinauri is left mistress of Motu-tapu.
summary.zh: 海娜烏里因丈夫化犬而投海，隨波漂流數月，終被衝上懷拉拉瓦海灘，身上纏滿海草藤壺。伊胡阿塔邁與伊胡瓦雷瓦雷兄弟憐惜相救，輕刮其身、悉心照料；她隱去舊名，自稱『擱淺之木』伊洪加魯派亞。後被酋長蒂尼勞娶為妻，遭其另二妻咒罵追打；她僅誦一咒，二婦撲地即斃，從此獨占島嶼家宅。

sensitivity.note: Resurrection-cluster edge case: recovery from apparent death rather than true return from the underworld.

passages.text: We left Hinauri floating out into the ocean; for many months she floated through the sea, and was at last thrown up by the surf on the beach at a place named Wairarawa. She was found there, lying as if dead upon the sandy shore, by two brothers named Ihuatamai and Ihuwareware; her body was in many parts overgrown with seaweed and barnacles from the length of time she had been in the water, but they could still see some traces of her beauty, and pitying the young girl they lifted her in their arms, carried her home, laid her carefully beside a fire, and scraped off very gently the seaweed and barnacles from her body, and thus by degrees restored her.
passages.note: Paraphrase of George Grey, Polynesian Mythology, ch. 4 (1855); not verbatim.

passages.text: When she had quite recovered, Ihuatamai and Ihuwareware looked upon her with pleasure and took her as a wife between them both; she did not disclose her name, but changed it and called herself Ihungarupaea, the Stranded-log-of-timber. After she had lived with the brothers a long time, Ihuwareware went to pay a visit to his superior chief Tinirau and related her adventures; Tinirau came to bring away the young stranger as a wife for himself, and she was given up to him - though by Ihuatamai she had already conceived a child.
passages.note: Paraphrase of George Grey, Polynesian Mythology, ch. 4 (1855); not verbatim.

passages.text: Tinirau took her home to his residence on the island called Motu-tapu, where he had two other wives, Harataunga and Horotata. When they saw the young stranger coming along in their husband's company they could not endure it; they abused Hinauri for her conduct, at last proceeded so far as to attempt to strike and kill her, and cursed her bitterly. The heart of Hinauri became gloomy with grief and mortification, so she began to utter incantations against them, and repeated one so powerful that hardly had she finished when the two women fell flat on the ground with the soles of their feet projecting upward, and lay quite dead, and her husband was left free for her alone.
passages.note: Paraphrase of George Grey, Polynesian Mythology, ch. 4 (1855); not verbatim.

title.en: Rupe's Ascent through the Ten Heavens
title.zh: 魯佩穿越十重天

region.en: Te Putahi-nui-o-Rehua, tenth heaven (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 第十重天雷胡瓦居所（象徵性定位）

period: Oral tradition; recorded 1855 (Grey, Polynesian Mythology)

source.work: George Grey, Polynesian Mythology and Ancient Traditional History of the New Zealand Race, ch. 4, Rupe's Ascent into Heaven (London 1855)

summary.en: Rupe, once called Maui-mua, grieves for his lost sister Hinauri and ascends heaven after heaven - each inhabited level refusing that the next can be reached - until he forces through ten skies to Rehua's home. Rehua shakes tui birds from his sacred locks for the feast, which Rupe reverently refuses to eat, and reveals that a murmur from Motu-tapu has reached him. As a pigeon, Rupe spears his way down to Tinirau's window, reveals himself, and carries his sister and her newborn back to heaven; on the way the dropped afterbirth becomes the shark's eggs, and a later rite explains the red stain of the sky as Kaitangata's blood.
summary.zh: 魯佩——原名毛伊穆阿——思念失散的姐姐海娜烏里，逐重攀登天界：每層天人都說再上一層不可達；他強行穿破，直至第十重天抵達雷胡瓦居所。雷胡瓦抖動神聖髮結，放出在其中棲息覓蟲的圖伊鳥充宴，魯佩敬畏不敢下箸。雷胡瓦透露下方島上消息，魯佩化鴿飛降，於窗台顯形，攜姐與新生兒同歸天上；途中遺落的胞衣被鯊吞食，即鯊腹多卵之由；而雷胡瓦之子卡伊唐加塔血染天際，即晚霞之紅。

sensitivity.note: Layered-heavens cosmology record; the tui-from-locks episode is a classic tapu food test.

passages.text: All this time Hinauri was lost to her friends and home, and her young brother Maui-mua, afterwards called Rupe, could do nothing but think of her; excessive love for his sister and sorrow at her departure so harassed him that he could no longer remain at rest, but must go and seek her. He visited every place he could think of without missing one, yet could nowhere find his sister; at last he thought he would ascend to the heavens to consult his great ancestor Rehua, who dwelt there at a place named Te Putahi-nui-o-Rehua.
passages.note: Paraphrase of George Grey, Polynesian Mythology, ch. 4 (1855); not verbatim.

passages.text: Rupe continued his ascent; at each inhabited place he asked whether the heavens above were inhabited and whether he could reach them, and each people answered, 'You cannot reach them; those heavens were fixed there by Tane.' But Rupe forced a way up through those heavens, and so he continued until he reached the tenth heaven and the abode of Rehua. Rehua welcomed the stranger with a lamentation; when they had ended, he called for a fire and cooking. Rupe wondered whence the food would come, and saw Rehua slowly loosen the thick bands about his locks and shake his long hair, from which came flying flocks of tui birds that had been nestling there feeding upon insects. The slaves caught and cooked them, but Rupe said, 'Nay, I cannot eat this food; I saw these birds loosened and take wing from thy locks; who would dare to eat birds that had fed upon insects in thy sacred head?'
passages.note: Paraphrase of George Grey, Polynesian Mythology, ch. 4 (1855); not verbatim.

passages.text: Rupe ventured to ask whether a confused murmur of voices from the world below had reached Rehua concerning a subject in which he was interested; Rehua answered that such a murmur had come from the island of Motu-tapu. Immediately Rupe changed himself into a pigeon and flew down to the dwelling of Tinirau; the people tried to spear and snare the bird, but his young sister Hinauri suspected something, looked well at it, knew her brother, and greeted him with the poem of Toetoetu. That very day her child was born; hardly had she finished her answering lament before Rupe caught her up with her new-born baby, and in a moment they were gone, carrying the afterbirth for burial. As they passed through the air it was dropped, fell into the sea, and was devoured by a shark - which caused the multitude of large eggs now found inside the shark.
passages.note: Paraphrase of George Grey, Polynesian Mythology, ch. 4 (1855); not verbatim.

passages.text: At Rehua's dwelling Rupe cleansed the filthy court-yard with two wooden shovels he named Tahitahia and Rakerakea, and added a building to the dwelling; but one beam being badly fixed, Rehua's son Kaitangata was one day killed hanging on to it - thrown down as it gave way and sprang back. His blood, running about over part of the heavens, stained them and formed what we now call a ruddiness in the sky; when therefore a red and ruddy tinge is seen in the heavens, men say, 'Ah! Kaitangata stained the heavens with his blood.' Kupe's first name was Maui-mua; it was after he was transformed into a bird that he took the name of Rupe.
passages.note: Paraphrase of George Grey, Polynesian Mythology, ch. 4 (1855); not verbatim.

title.en: Kae Rides Tutunui to Death
title.zh: 凱騎毙鯨魚圖圖努伊

region.en: Te Tibi-o-Manono, Kae's village (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 凱的村莊特提比奧馬諾諾（象徵性定位）

period: Oral tradition; recorded 1855 (Grey, Polynesian Mythology)

source.work: George Grey, Polynesian Mythology and Ancient Traditional History of the New Zealand Race, ch. 5, Kae's Theft of the Whale (London 1855)

summary.en: Tinirau brings the magician Kae to enchant his infant son Tuhuruhuru, slaughters a slice of his tame whale Tutunui for the feast, and lends the whale to carry Kae home. Kae, who has tasted how savoury the flesh is, ignores the signal to jump off when the whale touches bottom, presses it down until its blow-holes stop with sand and it dies; his tribe drags Tutunui ashore and roasts it in ovens lined with koromiko leaves - still greasy today, says the proverb. When the savoury scent drifts across the sea, Tinirau knows his pet is eaten, and sends forty women to take revenge.
summary.zh: 蒂尼勞請老法師凱為嬰兒祝福，宰殺愛鯨圖圖努伊一塊款待；歸程借鯨代舟。凱既嘗其鮮美，歸途中鯨觸底示警，他卻死抱不放，將鯨壓向海底，噴氣孔被沙堵死，鯨斃命。族眾將屍拖上岸，以科羅米科香葉墊灶烹之——至今葉上猶留油脂，諺語云『這是圖圖努伊的餘香』。美味之氣飄洋而過，蒂尼勞知寵鯨被食，遂遣四十女子渡海復仇。

sensitivity.note: Colonial-era collection; etiological tail for greasy koromiko leaves.

passages.text: Soon after Tuhuruhuru was born, Tinirau endeavoured to find a skilful magician who might perform the necessary enchantments and incantations to render the child a fortunate and successful warrior, and Kae was the name of the old magician brought to him for this purpose. Kae arrived at Tinirau's village and performed the proper enchantments over the infant. When all was rightly concluded, Tinirau gave a signal to a pet whale he had tamed, whose name was Tutunui; it left the ocean in which it was sporting and came to the shore, and its master laid hold of it and cut a slice of its flesh off to make a feast for the old magician, cooked it, and gave a portion of it to Kae, who found it very savoury and praised the dish very much.
passages.note: Paraphrase of George Grey, Polynesian Mythology, ch. 5 (1855); not verbatim.

passages.text: Shortly afterwards Kae said it was necessary for him to return to his own village, Te Tibi-o-Manono; Tinirau ordered a canoe to be got ready, but Kae made excuses and said he did not like to go back in the canoe - a mere trick, his real object being to get leave to ride back upon the whale, upon Tutunui, for he now knew how savoury the flesh of that fish was. Tinirau at last lent Tutunui, with very particular directions: when you get so near the shore that the fish touches the bottom, it will shake itself to let you know, and you must then, without any delay, jump off on the right side.
passages.note: Paraphrase of George Grey, Polynesian Mythology, ch. 5 (1855); not verbatim.

passages.text: When they came close to the shore at Kae's village and the whale felt the bottom, it shook itself as a sign for Kae to jump off and wade ashore; but it was of no use - the old magician stuck fast to the whale and pressed it down against the bottom as hard as he could. In vain the fish continued to shake itself; Kae held on and would not jump off, and in its struggles the blow-holes of Tutunui got stopped up with sand, and it died. Kae and his people dragged up the body intending to feast upon it; they cut it up and cooked it in ovens, covering the flesh with the fragrant leaves of the koromiko before heaping earth upon them, and the fat of Tutunui adhered to the leaves - which continue greasy to this day, so that if koromiko boughs are put on the fire and become greasy, the proverb says, 'There's some of the savouriness of Tutunui.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of George Grey, Polynesian Mythology, ch. 5 (1855); not verbatim.

title.en: Forty Women Carry Off the Sleeping Kae
title.zh: 四十女子智擒酣睡之凱

region.en: Kae's meeting-house (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 凱的聚會大屋（象徵性定位）

period: Oral tradition; recorded 1855 (Grey, Polynesian Mythology)

source.work: George Grey, Polynesian Mythology and Ancient Traditional History of the New Zealand Race, ch. 5, Kae's Theft of the Whale (London 1855)

summary.en: To identify the gap-toothed Kae among his tribe, Tinirau's forty women stage an evening of games, flutes and comic songs until the magician laughs aloud - and the flesh of Tutunui is seen still between his uneven teeth ('There's Kae laughing', says the proverb). Deceiving his mother-of-pearl eye-discs with dim firelight, they enchant the whole house into sleep and pass the rolled-up magician hand to hand down a living chain into their canoe. Waking at Tinirau's in a house exactly like his own, Kae is disoriented by the forged cries of 'Here comes Tinirau', recognizes the changed window, bows his head, and is slain.
summary.zh: 蒂尼勞之四十女子以歌舞遊戲誘老法師開口大笑——他齒參差不齊，齒縫間猶嵌圖圖努伊之肉，『凱笑了』從此成諺。眾女借熄火之機施展咒術，令全屋陷入沉睡，再列成長鏈，將裹於氈毯的凱手手相傳至獨木舟。凱醒來時身處一模一樣的屋中，又被『蒂尼勞來訪』的假呼聲所惑；待看清窗戶位置不對，方知大禍臨頭，垂首受戮。

sensitivity.note: The identification-by-teeth is a classic Maori trickster ruse; proverbial in Maori speech.

passages.text: Just before the canoe started, Tinirau's youngest sister asked him what marks they should know Kae by, and he answered, 'You cannot mistake him; his teeth are uneven and all overlap one another.' They paddled to the village of the old magician, and towards night a fire was lighted in Kae's great house, crowded with visitors on one side and his own people on the other; Kae sat at the foot of the main pillar. To find him out, Tinirau's people resolved to try by wit and fun to make everybody laugh, and when they opened their mouths to watch whose teeth lapped across one another.
passages.note: Paraphrase of George Grey, Polynesian Mythology, ch. 5 (1855); not verbatim.

passages.text: Raukatauri exhibited all her amusing tricks: she made them sing and play on flute and putorino, beat castanets, play at mora and at the stick-throwing game in time to song, played a jew's-harp, made puppets dance and whizgigs spin - yet the man they thought was Kae never once laughed. At last they all burst into a droll comic song, making curious faces and shaking their arms in time; the old magician could not help laughing out heartily, and those watching saw pieces of the flesh of Tutunui still sticking between his teeth. From this a proverb is preserved among the Maori to the present day - if anyone laughs at a story, a bystander says, 'Ah, there's Kae laughing.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of George Grey, Polynesian Mythology, ch. 5 (1855); not verbatim.

passages.text: The women made an excuse to let the fire burn dim so they might work their enchantments unseen; but Kae, suspecting, stuck a round piece of mother-of-pearl shell in the socket of each eye, so that the faint reflected rays might make the strangers think the whites of his eyes were open. The women went on and by their magical arts threw everyone in the house into an enchanted sleep. Then they ranged themselves in a long row from Kae's sleeping-place to the canoe, and two of them lifted the old magician gently up, rolled in his cloaks as he lay, and passed him from hand to hand until he reached the arms of the two women standing in the canoe - and thus Kae was carried off by Hine-i-te-iwaiwa and Raukatauri.
passages.note: Paraphrase of George Grey, Polynesian Mythology, ch. 5 (1855); not verbatim.

passages.text: They laid him fast asleep close to the central pillar of Tinirau's house, so that the place where he slept was exactly like his own sleeping-place - though Kae's own house was circular, with rafters springing from a central pillar, while Tinirau's was a long house with a ridge-pole. Tinirau ordered his tribe, when he passed in the morning, to call out loud 'Here comes Tinirau' as if he were arriving at Kae's own village; Kae started up drowsy and confused, declared 'This is my house', and could not say where his window was. The whole appearance of his house had changed; he guessed at once that the house belonged to Tinirau, and the old magician, seeing that his hour had come, bowed down his head in silence to the earth. They seized him, dragged him out, and slew him; and his tribe, the descendants of Poporokewa, later avenged his death by attacking Tinirau's fortress and slaying Tinirau's son.
passages.note: Paraphrase of George Grey, Polynesian Mythology, ch. 5 (1855); not verbatim.

title.en: Vladimir's Pantheon of 980: Perun with the Silver Head
title.zh: 弗拉基米爾九八〇年神殿：銀首金髯之佩倫

region.en: Kiev hill by the Dnieper (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 第聶伯河畔基輔山丘（象徵性定位）

period: Event of 980; recorded in the Russian Primary Chronicle (Cross translation 1930); retold by Machal 1918

source.work: Jan Machal, Slavic Mythology, Mythology of All Races III (1918), Part III ch. 1, after the Russian Primary Chronicle

summary.en: In 980 Prince Vladimir set idols on the hill before his palace at Kiev: Perun the Thunderer with a silver head and golden beard, Khors, Dazhbog, Stribog, Simargl, and Mokosh; his uncle Dobrynya raised a like image for Perun on the Volkhov at Novgorod, and the city sacrificed to it.
summary.zh: 九八〇年弗拉基米爾王公於基輔王宮前山丘立神像：銀首金髯之雷神佩倫、霍爾斯、達日博格、斯特里博格、西馬爾格爾與莫科什；其叔多布雷尼亞於諾夫哥羅德沃爾霍夫河畔為佩倫立像，舉城祭之。

sensitivity.note: Chronicle source.

passages.text: The chief god of the pagan Russians was Perun, whose wooden idol Prince Vladimir set on a hill before his palace at Kiev in 980; it had a silver head and a golden beard. Around it stood the statues of Khors, Dazhbog, Stribog, and other deities of the old pantheon. Vladimir's uncle Dobrynya erected a similar image of Perun at Novgorod on the river Volkhov, and the inhabitants sacrificed to it.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Machal, Slavic Mythology, Mythology of All Races III (1918), Part III ch. 1, after the Primary Chronicle; not verbatim.

passages.text: The name Perun comes from the root 'to strike': he is the maker of thunder and lightning, the Thunderer, the Zeus of the Slavs — the old Bulgarian Alexander-romance actually translates the Greek Zeus as Perun, and in the apocryphal Dialogue of the Three Saints, asked who created thunder, Vasiliy answers that there are two angels of thunder: the Greek Perun and the Jew Khors. Hills called Perun-dub and Peruna-Dubrava mark his worship from Slovenia to Bulgaria.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Machal, Slavic Mythology, Mythology of All Races III (1918), Part III ch. 1; not verbatim.

title.en: Swearing on Perun: Igor's Treaty with Byzantium, 945
title.zh: 佩倫前立誓：伊戈爾九四五年拜占庭盟約

region.en: Hill of Perun outside Kiev (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 基輔郊外佩倫之丘（象徵性定位）

period: Event of 945; recorded in the Russian Primary Chronicle (Cross translation 1930); retold by Machal 1918

source.work: Jan Machal, Slavic Mythology, Mythology of All Races III (1918), Part III ch. 1

summary.en: Before the Byzantine envoys, Prince Igor laid aside his armour on the hill of Perun and swore the treaty there, while the Christian Russians of his retinue took the same oath in the church of St. Elias: may the treaty-breakers never have aid from God or Perun, protection from their shields, or anything but their own swords.
summary.zh: 拜占庭使節之前，伊戈爾王公於佩倫丘上卸甲立誓；其扈從中之基督徒則在聖伊利亞堂作同誓：背約者不得蒙神與佩倫之佑、不得賴盾護身，唯受己劍之戮。

sensitivity.note: Chronicle source.

passages.text: In his name the Russians swore to keep their compacts with other nations. When Prince Igor was about to make a treaty with the Byzantines in 945, he summoned the envoys in the morning and went with them to a hill where Perun's statue stood. Laying aside their armour and shields, Igor and his pagan followers took a solemn oath before the god, while the Christian Russians did the same in the church of St. Iliya (Elias).
passages.note: Paraphrase of Machal, Slavic Mythology, Mythology of All Races III (1918), Part III ch. 1, after the Primary Chronicle; not verbatim.

passages.text: The formula directed against those who should violate the treaty ran: 'Let them never receive aid either from God or from Perun; let them never have protection from their shields; let them be destroyed by their own swords, arrows, and other weapons, and let them be slaves throughout all time to come.' So the same hill held both the thunder-god and, in the church below, his eventual successor, the prophet Elias who rides the storm.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Machal, Slavic Mythology, Mythology of All Races III (1918), Part III ch. 1; not verbatim.

title.en: Perun Down the Dnieper: The Idol of 988
title.zh: 佩倫順第聶伯而去：九八八年神像遭逐

region.en: Dnieper rapids below Kiev (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 基輔以下第聶伯急灘（象徵性定位）

period: Event of 988; recorded in the Russian Primary Chronicle (Cross translation 1930); retold by Machal 1918

source.work: Jan Machal, Slavic Mythology, Mythology of All Races III (1918), Part III ch. 1

summary.en: When Vladimir was baptized in 988 he ordered the idols broken or burned; Perun alone was tied to a horse's tail, dragged down to the stream, beaten by twelve men to disgrace the demon who had deceived men, and pushed through the rapids — landing forever on the sands called Perunya Ren, Perun's Sands.
summary.zh: 九八八年弗拉基米爾受洗，命毀諸神像；獨佩倫像被繫於馬尾、拖至河邊，十二人笞之，以辱惑眾之魔，並推其過灘——神像終擱淺於後世稱『佩倫灘』之沙洲。

sensitivity.note: Chronicle source.

passages.text: When Prince Vladimir received baptism in 988 he went to Kiev and ordered all idols to be broken, cut to pieces, or thrown into the fire. The statue of Perun, however, was tied to a horse's tail and dragged down to a brook, where twelve men beat it with rods — not because the wood could feel pain, but that the demon which had deceived men might be disgraced.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Machal, Slavic Mythology, Mythology of All Races III (1918), Part III ch. 1, after the Primary Chronicle; not verbatim.

passages.text: As the idol was carried to the Dnieper the pagans wept, for they had not yet been baptized. When it was thrown into the river Vladimir gave the command: 'If it stops, thrust it from the banks until it has passed the rapids; then let it alone.' The order was carried out, and no sooner had the idol passed through the rapids than it was cast upon the sands, which after that time were called Perunya Ren — Perun's Sands. Where the image once stood Vladimir built a church of St. Basil; yet Perun's worship did not finally disappear from the land until the end of the eleventh century.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Machal, Slavic Mythology, Mythology of All Races III (1918), Part III ch. 1; not verbatim.

title.en: 'Be Off with You!': Perun Floated Down the Volkhov, 989
title.zh: 『滾吧！』：九八九年佩倫像漂下沃爾霍夫河

region.en: Novgorod, river Volkhov (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 諾夫哥羅德沃爾霍夫河（象徵性定位）

period: Event of 989; recorded in Novgorod chronicle tradition; retold by Machal 1918

source.work: Jan Machal, Slavic Mythology, Mythology of All Races III (1918), Part III ch. 1

summary.en: Archbishop Akim of Korsun destroyed the pagan idols of Novgorod in 989 and ordered Perun cast into the Volkhov; dragged through the mire and beaten so the demon cried out with pain, the image floated downstream — until a man on the banks of the Pidba pushed it away with a pole: 'Now, little Perun, you have had enough to eat and drink; be off with you!'
summary.zh: 九八九年科爾松的阿基姆主教毀諾夫哥羅德諸神像，命將佩倫投入沃爾霍夫河；神像被拖過泥濘、笞至魔泣，順流而下——皮德巴河畔一男子以竿推之：『小佩倫，吃夠喝足了，滾吧！』

sensitivity.note: Chronicle-legend source.

passages.text: The pagan idols of Novgorod were destroyed by Archbishop Akim Korsunyanin in 989, and the command went forth that Perun should be cast into the Volkhov. Binding the image with ropes they dragged it through the mire to the river, beating it with rods and causing the demon, as the chronicle says, to cry out with pain.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Machal, Slavic Mythology, Mythology of All Races III (1918), Part III ch. 1, after the Novgorod tradition; not verbatim.

passages.text: In the morning a man dwelling on the banks of the Pidba, a small stream flowing into the Volkhov, saw the idol floating toward the shore; he thrust it away with a pole, saying: 'Now, Perunisce — little Perun — you have had enough to eat and to drink; be off with you!' The god of the Volkhov drifted on toward Lake Ladoga, and the place where he was thrown remained for centuries a place of dread.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Machal, Slavic Mythology, Mythology of All Races III (1918), Part III ch. 1; not verbatim.

title.en: The Thunder-Saint: Perun Becomes St. Iliya the Prophet
title.zh: 雷鳴聖徒：佩倫化身聖伊利亞

region.en: Rhodope mountains and Russia (symbolic pin in the Rhodopes)
region.zh: 羅多彼山與俄羅斯（象徵性定位於羅多彼山）

period: Custom recorded 19th c. (Machal 1918)

source.work: Jan Machal, Slavic Mythology, Mythology of All Races III (1918), Part III ch. 1

summary.en: After the conversion the worship of Perun passed to the prophet Elias, who rides the storm: on St. Iliya's Day no man may work the fields lest the Saint slay him with his thunderbolt, and bulls and calves are slaughtered and consecrated for his feast — the old sacrifices of the Thunderer under a new name.
summary.zh: 皈依之後，佩倫之祀歸於乘雷之先知伊利亞：聖伊利亞日，田間不得勞作，違者聖徒以雷殛之；宰牛羊祭於堂，即雷神舊祭之改裝。

sensitivity.note: Living rite; classic survival-of-paganism case.

passages.text: In the Christian period the worship of Perun was transferred to St. Iliya (Elias). The chronicle itself shows the seam: at Igor's treaty the pagan Russians swore by Perun and the Christians in the church of St. Iliya. On July 20, St. Iliya's Day, great reverence is still kept in Russia; in places they prepare a feast and slaughter bulls, calves, and lambs after consecrating them in church, and it is considered a great sin not to partake of such banquets.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Machal, Slavic Mythology, Mythology of All Races III (1918), Part III ch. 1; not verbatim.

passages.text: The Serbians call St. Iliya Gromovnik, 'the Thunderer', and pray to him as the dispenser of good harvests. Among the Southern Slavs no man does work in the fields on his day, no woman weaves or spins; he who dared to labour would make the Saint angry, and instead of help with the crops he would be slain with the thunderbolt. In the Rhodope Mountains the festival is kept on a lofty summit with a bull or a cow killed for the solemn banquet — all doubtless nothing less than a survival of the feasts long before celebrated in honour of Perun.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Machal, Slavic Mythology, Mythology of All Races III (1918), Part III ch. 1; not verbatim.

title.en: Dazhbog, Czar-Sun: Grandfather of the Russians
title.zh: 達日博格——太陽沙皇：羅斯人之祖

region.en: Kiev (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 基輔（象徵性定位）

period: Recorded in the Primary Chronicle and the Tale of Igor's Campaign, 12th c. (Machal 1918)

source.work: Jan Machal, Slavic Mythology, Mythology of All Races III (1918), Part III ch. 2

summary.en: Dazhbog, 'the Giving God', Czar-Sun and Son of Svarog, stood beside Perun on the Kiev hill; early Russian texts translate Helios by his name, and the Tale of Igor's Campaign calls the princes of Russia his grandchildren — while in Serbian fairy-tale he lingers as Dabog, the tsar on earth set against God in heaven.
summary.zh: 達日博格——『施予之神』、太陽沙皇、斯瓦羅格之子——立於基輔丘上佩倫之側；古羅斯文獻以之名譯希臘之赫利俄斯，《伊戈爾遠征記》稱羅斯王公為其孫；塞爾維亞童話中猶存為達博格——地上之沙皇，與天上之神相對。

sensitivity.note: Chronicle source.

passages.text: The statue of Dazhbog, whose name probably means 'the Giving God', stood on the hill in the courtyard of the castle at Kiev beside the idols of Perun, Khors, and Stribog. Old chronicles term him 'Czar Sun' and 'Son of Svarog'; early Russian texts frequently translate the name of the Greek Helios as Dazhbog, which may be taken as proof that he was worshipped as a solar deity.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Machal, Slavic Mythology, Mythology of All Races III (1918), Part III ch. 2; not verbatim.

passages.text: In the old Russian epic, the Tale of Igor's Campaign, Vladimir and the Russians call themselves the grandchildren of Dazhbog — the ancient Slavs often derived their origin from divine beings. Dazhbog was known among the Southern Slavs too, his memory preserved in the Serbian fairy-tale of Dabog: 'Dabog, the Czar, was on earth, and the Lord God was in heaven' — the old pagan sun-king refigured as an evil being, since early Christianity counted the old gods devilish.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Machal, Slavic Mythology, Mythology of All Races III (1918), Part III ch. 2; not verbatim.

title.en: Svarog the Smith: Who Forged the First Marriage Law
title.zh: 斯瓦羅格鐵匠：鑄造第一婚姻法

region.en: Kiev (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 基輔（象徵性定位）

period: Recorded in the Khronika of Malalas redaction, c. 1261; recorded by Machal 1918

source.work: Jan Machal, Slavic Mythology, Mythology of All Races III (1918), Part III ch. 3

summary.en: Svarog, the heavenly smith identified with Hephaestus, forged the sun in his sky-forge and set it in heaven; the chronicle's scholia make him the founder of legal marriage — one man, one wife — ordaining that adulterers be cast into a fiery furnace.
summary.zh: 斯瓦羅格，天之鐵匠，被比為赫菲斯托斯；於天上火爐鑄太陽而置於蒼穹；編年史註疏謂其創婚姻之法——一男一妻，犯者投烈火之爐。

sensitivity.note: Chronicle scholia; the solar smith parallels Tvasty/Ilmarinen.

passages.text: Svarozic was worshipped by the Russians as the god of fire, his name a patronymic meaning 'Son of Svarog'. Svarog himself is mentioned in an old Russian chronicle — the Russian redaction of John Malalas — which identifies him with the Greek Hephaistos. In the Lithuanian redaction the celestial smith Telyaveli 'forged for Perkunas the sun as it shines on earth, and set the sun in heaven'; the same forge-craft belongs to the Slavic sky-smith.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Machal, Slavic Mythology, Mythology of All Races III (1918), Part III ch. 3; not verbatim.

passages.text: The chronicle speaks of Svarog as the founder of legal marriage: under him it was made a law for every man to have only one wife, and for every woman to have only one husband; and whosoever trespassed against this command was to be cast into a fiery furnace. The tradition implies the centrality of fire — hearth and fire-side — for settled family life: the smith-god who forged the sun also forged the law that binds households.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Machal, Slavic Mythology, Mythology of All Races III (1918), Part III ch. 3; not verbatim.

title.en: Veles: God of Cattle and Plaited Beard of the Harvest
title.zh: 韋萊斯：牛群之神與收割的『編辮』

region.en: Russia (symbolic pin at Rostov)
region.zh: 俄羅斯（象徵性定位於羅斯托夫）

period: Recorded in the Primary Chronicle (10th-11th c.); recorded by Machal 1918

source.work: Jan Machal, Slavic Mythology, Mythology of All Races III (1918), Part III ch. 5

summary.en: Veles, god of flocks, shared the Russians' oaths with Perun and was cast into the river Pochayna at the baptism; to this day southern Russian reapers plait the last handful of ears and call it 'plaiting the beard of Veles', leaving a piece of bread among the ears.
summary.zh: 牛群之神韋萊斯與佩倫同受羅斯人之誓，受洗時其像被投入波恰伊納河；至今南俄收割者將最後一把麥穗打結，稱『為韋萊斯編鬚』，穗中猶置麵包一塊。

sensitivity.note: Chronicle and living custom.

passages.text: Veles, the god of flocks, was held in high honour by the Russians, who swore by him as well as by Perun when making a treaty. When Vladimir was baptized in 988 he caused the idols of Veles to be thrown into the river Pochayna; a stone statue of the same deity, worshipped by Slavic tribes in the neighbourhood of Finland, was destroyed by Abraham of Rostov, who preached Christianity on the banks of the Volga in the twelfth century. The Tale of Igor's Campaign calls the minstrel Boyan 'the grandson of Veles'.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Machal, Slavic Mythology, Mythology of All Races III (1918), Part III ch. 5; not verbatim.

passages.text: The memory of Veles still lives among the Russian people: in southern Russia it is customary at harvest-time to tie the last handful of ears into a knot, 'plaiting the beard of Veles' or 'leaving a handful of ears for Veles's beard'; in some districts a piece of bread is put among such ears, probably a reminiscence of the sacrifices offered to the god. After the conversion his worship was transferred to St. Blasius, shepherd and martyr of Caesarea, guardian of flocks — while in Bohemia his very name came to mean simply 'the devil'.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Machal, Slavic Mythology, Mythology of All Races III (1918), Part III ch. 5; not verbatim.

title.en: Stribog: Grandfather of the Winds
title.zh: 斯特里博格：眾風之祖父

region.en: Kiev hill (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 基輔山丘（象徵性定位）

period: Recorded in the Primary Chronicle and the Tale of Igor's Campaign; recorded by Machal 1918

source.work: Jan Machal, Slavic Mythology, Mythology of All Races III (1918), Part III ch. 5

summary.en: Stribog's idol stood on the Kiev hill beside Perun's; the Tale of Igor's Campaign calls the winds 'the grandsons of Stribog' — a god of cold and frost, from whose breath the winds themselves were thought to blow.
summary.zh: 斯特里博格之像立於基輔丘佩倫像之側；《伊戈爾遠征記》稱風為『斯特里博格之孫』——乃寒霜之神，風即自其呼息而生。

sensitivity.note: Chronicle source.

passages.text: Stribog, whose idol stood on the hill in Kiev beside that of Perun, was most probably the god of cold and frost. In the Tale of Igor's Campaign the winds are called 'the grandsons of Stribog' — a conception of the winds as the result of cold and frost, children and children's children of the frozen god.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Machal, Slavic Mythology, Mythology of All Races III (1918), Part III ch. 5; not verbatim.

passages.text: The chronicler Cosmas testifies that the Bohemians worshipped deities similar to Jupiter, Mars, Bellona, and Ceres, making idols of them; but their names are lost. Dlugosz records a crowd of Polish divinities, though his late and classicizing report is unreliable. Of the old Kiev pantheon, Stribog and Simargl stand as the barest names — the wind-god and the winged sentinel of the Persian imagination, both set one day on the same Dnieper hill as Perun.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Machal, Slavic Mythology, Mythology of All Races III (1918), Part III ch. 5; not verbatim.

title.en: The Sun in the Tower: Why the Iron Hammer Is Worshipped
title.zh: 塔中日頭：鐵錘受拜之故

region.en: Lithuania (symbolic pin at Vilnius)
region.zh: 立陶宛（象徵性定位於維爾紐斯）

period: Recorded by Aeneas Sylvius (Pius II, d. 1464) from missionary Jerome; recorded by Gray 1918

source.work: L. H. Gray, Baltic Mythology, Mythology of All Races III (1918), Part V, after Aeneas Sylvius

summary.en: A mighty king once imprisoned the sun for months in a strongly fortified tower; the signs of the zodiac broke the tower with a huge hammer and set the sun free — which is why, the missionaries reported, the old Lithuanians worshipped an iron hammer of rare size.
summary.zh: 古有強王將太陽囚於堅塔數月；黃道諸宮以巨錘破塔救日——傳教士所記立陶宛人敬奉特大鐵錘之由即在此。

sensitivity.note: Early missionary report through Papal circles; tagged interpretively.

passages.text: Aeneas Sylvius (afterward Pope Pius II) reports, on the information of the Camaldolite hermit Jerome who had long served as missionary in Lithuania, that a Lithuanian people worshipped the sun and venerated with curious cult an iron hammer of rare size. When the priests were asked what the veneration meant, they answered that once upon a time the sun was not seen for several months, because a most mighty king had imprisoned it in the dungeon of a tower right strongly fortified.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Gray, Baltic Mythology, Mythology of All Races III (1918), Part V, after Aeneas Sylvius; not verbatim.

passages.text: Then the signs of the zodiac bore aid to the sun, broke the tower with a huge hammer, and restored to men the liberated sun — so that the instrument by which mortals regained the light was held worthy of veneration. Mannhardt read the myth as the darkening of the sun in winter and its return in the storms of spring; the real destroyer of the tower was Perkunas, god of thunder and chief Baltic deity. Lithuanians call the prehistoric stone celt 'Perkunas's ball' or 'Perkunas's stone' — the parallel with Thor's hammer is immediate.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Gray, Baltic Mythology, Mythology of All Races III (1918), Part V; not verbatim.

title.en: Perkune Tete, Mother of Lightning: Who Bathes the Weary Sun
title.zh: 雷母佩爾庫內·泰特：為倦日沐浴

region.en: Lithuania (symbolic pin at Kaunas)
region.zh: 立陶宛（象徵性定位於考納斯）

period: Recorded from Lithuanian folk tradition; recorded by Gray 1918

source.work: L. H. Gray, Baltic Mythology, Mythology of All Races III (1918), Part V

summary.en: Perkune Tete, mother of lightning and thunder, receives at night the weary, dusty sun; she washes her and sends her forth on the morrow bathed and shining — the nightly return of the day.
summary.zh: 雷電之母佩爾庫內·泰特，夜間迎回塵勞之倦日；為之沐浴，翌晨送其容光煥發而升——晝夜更替即如此夜夜重演。

sensitivity.note: Folk fragment.

passages.text: The second of the two old myths recorded of the Lithuanians is still briefer than the first: Perkune Tete, 'Mother of Lightning and Thunder', receives at night the weary, dusty sun, whom she sends forth on the morrow bathed and shining.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Gray, Baltic Mythology, Mythology of All Races III (1918), Part V; not verbatim.

passages.text: In the dainas the same daily round is sung as an economy: Morning Star makes the Sun's fire and Evening Star prepares her couch; the golden cock on the edge of the Great Water rouses the sun's daughter to spin the silver thread of dawn. The Baltic sky is run like a great household, and the mother of lightning is the bath-keeper of the world's light.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Gray, Baltic Mythology, Mythology of All Races III (1918), Part V; not verbatim.

title.en: Why the Moon Wanes: The Moon Who Forsook the Sun
title.zh: 月之所以虧：棄日而奔晨星之月

region.en: Latvia (symbolic pin at Riga)
region.zh: 拉脫維亞（象徵性定位於里加）

period: Daina recorded 19th c. (Mannhardt); material pre-Christian; recorded by Gray 1918

source.work: L. H. Gray, Baltic Mythology, Mythology of All Races III (1918), Part V, after the dainas collected by Mannhardt

summary.en: In the primal spring the Moon wedded the Sun, but he forsook her and loved the Morning Star; Perkunas, filled with wrath, smote the Moon with his sword — 'Wherefore hast thou left thy Sun?' — and the god's grief-struck blow is the waning of the moon.
summary.zh: 原初之春，月娶日，旋棄之而愛晨星；佩爾庫納斯怒不可遏，拔劍擊月——『何故棄汝之日？』——那一擊之痛，即月之盈虧。

sensitivity.note: Celestial-marriage cluster parallel to Sumerian Nanna-Sarru? tagged as daina translation (Mannhardt's German rendering, PD).

passages.text: Home the Moon once led the Sun in the very primal spring; early did the Sun arise, but the Moon from her withdrew. Leaving her, he roamed afar, and the Morning Star he loved. Perkunas then was filled with wrath, and with his sword he smote the Moon: 'Wherefore hast thou left thy Sun? Wherefore roam'st thou alone by night? Wherefore lovest thou Morning Star?' Full of sorrow was his heart.
passages.note: Paraphrase of the daina as rendered by Gray, Baltic Mythology, Mythology of All Races III (1918), Part V; not verbatim.

passages.text: The daina holds the myth of the conjunction of sun and moon, their gradual divergence until the moon stands with the morning star, the wrath of Perkunas — who is not merely god of thunder but the great Baltic deity — and the explanation of the moon's changing form as he wanes. In the Baltic languages the sun is feminine and the moon masculine; the Lettish variant carries the tale further, for there the moon and sun have many children, the stars.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Gray, Baltic Mythology, Mythology of All Races III (1918), Part V; not verbatim.

title.en: The Broken Oak at the Wedding: The Sun's Daughter Washes Out the Blood
title.zh: 婚禮上斷裂的橡樹：日之女洗滌血漬

region.en: Latvia (symbolic pin at Riga)
region.zh: 拉脫維亞（象徵性定位於里加）

period: Daina recorded 19th c. (Mannhardt); recorded by Gray 1918

source.work: L. H. Gray, Baltic Mythology, Mythology of All Races III (1918), Part V

summary.en: When Morning Star wed the Sun's daughter, Perkunas rode through the doorway and shattered the green oak; its blood — the red rays of evening — spattered the bride's garments, and for three years she gathered the seared leaves, asking where to wash, where to dry, where to don her white — 'upon that day when nine suns shall be shining.'
summary.zh: 晨星娶日之女之日，佩爾庫納斯縱馬穿門、劈裂綠橡；橡之血——即暮空紅霞——濺遍新娘衣裙；三年間她拾枯葉，問何處可洗、何處可晾、何處可著素衣——『待九日同輝之時。』

sensitivity.note: Daina.

passages.text: When Morning Star was wedded, Perkunas rode through the doorway and the green oak he shattered; then forth the oak's blood spurted, besprinkling all the bride's garments and her crownlet. With streaming eyes the Sun's daughter for three years collected the leaves, all sear and withered.
passages.note: Paraphrase of the daina as rendered by Gray, Baltic Mythology, Mythology of All Races III (1918), Part V; not verbatim.

passages.text: 'Oh where, oh where, my mother, shall I now wash my garments, and where wash out the blood-stains? — My daughterling, so youthful, swift haste unto the fountain wherein nine brooks are flowing. And where dry them in the breezes? — In the garden where roses nine are blooming. And where don my garments bright gleaming in their whiteness? — Upon that day, my daughter, when nine suns shall be shining.' The fountain of nine brooks, the nine roses, the nine suns, the apple-tree of nine branches — all are the rays of the sun.
passages.note: Paraphrase of the daina as rendered by Gray, Baltic Mythology, Mythology of All Races III (1918), Part V; not verbatim.

title.en: The Devil Struck Down for Seven Years: Perkunas and the Unending Battle
title.zh: 魔墮七年：佩爾庫納斯與無盡之戰

region.en: Lithuania (symbolic pin at Vilnius)
region.zh: 立陶宛（象徵性定位於維爾紐斯）

period: Folk belief recorded 19th c.; recorded by Gray 1918
