title.en: Five Days of Darkness: Stones Knocking Against Each Other
title.zh: 五日長夜:石擊石的世界

region.en: Provinces of Huarochiri, Mama and Chaclla (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 瓦羅奇里、瑪瑪與查克利亞三省(象徵性標記)

period: Huarochiri manuscript collected by Francisco de Avila, 1608; publ. Markham 1873

source.work: Francisco de Avila, 'A Narrative of the Errors, False Gods and other Superstitions... of Huarochiri, Mama and Chaclla', in Narratives of the Rites and Laws of the Yncas, trans. C. R. Markham, Hakluyt Society, 1873

summary.en: They relate that, a long time ago, the sun disappeared and the world was dark for a space of five days; that the stones knocked one against the other; and that the mortars, which they call mutca, and the pestles called marop, rose against their masters, who were also attacked by their sheep, both those fastened in the houses and those in the fields. Avila, who records it, wonders whether this may have been the eclipse which occurred when the Redeemer died, and objects that, as these people had no watches, they could not have counted five days by the absence of the sun.
summary.zh: 相傳很久以前,太陽隱去,世界陷入五日黑暗;石頭相互碰撞;搗穀的石臼(穆特卡)與石杵(馬羅普)起而反抗主人;主人們又遭自家羊群攻擊——無論圈在屋內的,還是放牧在外的。記錄此故事的阿維拉猜測這或許是救主受難時的日蝕,又質疑:既無時計,他們何以知道太陽缺席了五日。

sensitivity.note: Cosmic-disturbance tale; the animated tools and attacking flocks parallel the day-of-darkness cluster in other traditions.

passages.text: They relate that, a long time ago, the sun disappeared and the world was dark for a space of five days; that the stones knocked one against the other; and that the mortars, which they call mutca, and the pestles called marop, rose against their masters, who were also attacked by their sheep, both those fastened in the houses and those in the fields.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Avila, Narrative of the Errors of Huarochiri, ch. 3 (Markham 1873); not verbatim.

passages.text: This may have been the eclipse which occurred when our Redeemer died; but I cannot clearly make this out, for when it was day in that hemisphere it was night here... The rest of the story consists of lies, for, as these people had no watches, how could they tell that the sun was absent for five days, seeing that we count days by the absence and presence of the sun?
passages.note: Avila's commentary condensed (Markham 1873); the gloss is the recorder's, the tale is the tradition.

language: Spanish record of a Quechua tradition
canonical_translation: C. R. Markham, Narrative of the Rites and Laws of the Yncas (Hakluyt Society, 1873)

title.en: The Speaking Llama and the Mountain of Villca-coto
title.zh: 開口的駝馬與維爾卡-科托山

region.en: Villca-coto, between San Damian and San Geronimo de Surco (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 聖達米安與聖哲羅姆-德-蘇爾科之間的維爾卡-科托山(象徵性標記)

period: Huarochiri manuscript collected by Francisco de Avila, 1608; publ. Markham 1873

source.work: Francisco de Avila, 'A Narrative of the Errors, False Gods and other Superstitions... of Huarochiri, Mama and Chaclla', in Narratives of the Rites and Laws of the Yncas, trans. C. R. Markham, Hakluyt Society, 1873

summary.en: An Indian was tethering his llama in a place where there was good pasture, and the animal resisted, showing sorrow and moaning after its manner, crying 'yu' yu''. The master, who happened to be eating a choclo (ear of maize), observing this, threw the core (coronta) at the llama, saying: 'Fool, why do you moan and refrain from eating? Have I not put you where there is good pasture?' The llama thus replied: 'Madman! what do you know? Learn that I am not sad without good cause; for within five days the sea will rise and cover the whole earth, destroying all there is upon it.' The man, wondering that his llama should speak, asked whether there was any way by which they could save themselves. The llama said that the man must follow it quickly to the summit of a high mountain called Villca-coto, between the parish of San Damian and San Geronimo de Surco, taking food for five days. He did as he was told, carrying his load on his back and leading the llama, and found on the summit many different kinds of birds and animals assembled. Just as they reached the top the sea began to rise: the water filled the valleys and covered the tops of the hills, except that of Villca-coto; the animals were crowded together, for the water rose so high that some could hardly find foothold. Among these was a fox, whose tail was washed by the waves - which is the reason that the tips of foxes' tails are black. At the end of five days the waters began to abate, and the sea returned to its former bounds; but the whole earth was without inhabitants except that solitary man, from whom descend all the people who now exist.
summary.zh: 一人正在好牧場拴駱馬,駝馬不肯安臥,悲鳴「喲!喲!」。主人正吃著玉米棒,見狀擲出玉米芯,罵道:「蠢畜,好草不吃,鳴什麼?」駝馬答道:「蠢人!你懂什麼?我悲鳴自有緣故:不出五日,海水將漲,淹沒大地,毀滅其上一切。」那人驚詫駝馬竟能人言,忙問可有生路。駝馬命他快隨己登一座極高的名為維爾卡-科托之山——在聖達米安與聖哲羅姆-德-蘇爾科教區之間——並帶足五日糧食。他依言背糧牽駝登頂,見山巔早已聚滿各色飛禽走獸。他們剛到頂,海水便開始上漲:填滿山谷,漫過群山峰頂,唯維爾卡-科托山不沒。獸群擠作一團,水高得連立足之處都快沒了。其中一隻狐狸,尾巴被浪打濕——所以狐尾尖至今是黑的。五日之後,水勢漸退,大海復歸故道;大地之上唯存此孤身一人,今日世上的人類皆其後裔。

sensitivity.note: The Huarochiri flood: an animal-warning deluge narrative of the messenger-fails type in reverse (the animal warns, the man heeds); a flagship cross-cluster record.

passages.text: An Indian was tethering his llama in a place where there was good pasture, and the animal resisted, showing sorrow and moaning after its manner, which it does by crying 'yu' yu''. The master, who happened to be eating a choclo, observing this, threw the core (which they call coronta) at the llama, saying: 'Fool, why do you moan and refrain from eating? Have I not put you where there is good pasture?' The llama thus replied: 'Madman! what do you know, and what can you suppose? Learn that I am not sad without good cause; for within five days the sea will rise and cover the whole earth, destroying all there is upon it.'
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Avila, Narrative of the Errors of Huarochiri, ch. 4 (Markham 1873); not verbatim.

passages.text: The man, wondering that his llama should speak, answered it by asking whether there was any way by which they could save themselves. The llama then said that the man must follow it quickly to the summit of a high mountain called Villca-coto, taking with him food for five days, and that he might thus be saved. The man did as he was told, carrying his load on his back and leading the llama, and he arrived on the summit of the mountain, where he found many different kinds of birds and animals assembled.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Avila, Narrative of the Errors of Huarochiri, ch. 4 (Markham 1873); not verbatim.

Among these was a fox, whose tail was washed by the waves, which they say is the reason that the tips of foxes' tails are black. At the end of five days the waters began to abate, and the sea returned to its former bounds; but the whole earth was without inhabitants except that solitary man, from whom, they say, descend all the people who now exist.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Avila, Narrative of the Errors of Huarochiri, ch. 4 (Markham 1873); not verbatim.

title.en: Five Eggs on Condorcoto: The Birth of Pariacaca and His Brothers
title.zh: 孔多爾科托的五枚蛋:帕里亞卡卡誕生

region.en: Condorcoto mountain, between Huarochiri and Chorrillo (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 瓦羅奇里與喬里略之間的孔多爾科托山(象徵性標記)

period: Huarochiri manuscript collected by Francisco de Avila, 1608; publ. Markham 1873

source.work: Francisco de Avila, 'A Narrative of the Errors, False Gods and other Superstitions... of Huarochiri, Mama and Chaclla', in Narratives of the Rites and Laws of the Yncas, trans. C. R. Markham, Hakluyt Society, 1873

summary.en: After the deluge, in every district the Indians chose the richest and most valiant man among them for their leader, and this period they call Purun-pacha - the time when there was no king. In those days there appeared five large eggs on a mountain between Huarochiri and Chorrillo towards the south, called Condorcoto - the origin of Pariacaca. At that time there lived a poor and ill-clad Indian named Huathiacuri, who was a son of Pariacaca, and who learnt many arts from his father; he was called Huathiacuri because his food was all huatyasca, parboiled, not properly cooked food, being poor he could afford nothing better.
summary.zh: 洪水之後,各地印第安人推舉其中最富最勇者為首領,此期稱為「普龍-帕查」——無王之世。其時,在瓦羅奇里與喬里略之間偏南的一座名為孔多爾科托的山上,出現了五枚巨卵——此即帕里亞卡卡之來歷。當時有一個衣衫襤褸的貧苦印第安人,名叫瓜提亞庫里,乃帕里亞卡卡之子,從其父學得諸多法術;因其所食皆為半生不熟的「瓜蒂亞斯卡」(貧者唯能如此),遂得此名。

sensitivity.note: Egg-born mountain god; tagged miraculous-birth against the cluster of divine births.

passages.text: It must now be understood that in the time after the deluge, in every district, the Indians chose the richest and most valiant man among them for their leader, and this period they call Purun-pacha, which means the time when there was no king. They say that in those days there appeared five large eggs on a mountain between Huarochiri and Chorrillo, towards the south, (and this is the origin of Pariacaca) called Condorcoto.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Avila, Narrative of the Errors of Huarochiri, ch. 5 (Markham 1873); not verbatim.

passages.text: At that time there lived a poor and ill-clad Indian named Huathiacuri, who, they say, was a son of Pariacaca, and who learnt many arts from his father. They say that he was called Huathiacuri because his food was all huatyasca, which means parboiled, not properly cooked, or, as we say here, roasted en barbacoa. Being poor, he could afford nothing better.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Avila, Narrative of the Errors of Huarochiri, ch. 5 (Markham 1873); not verbatim.

title.en: The Foxes' Conversation: The Cure of the Rich Man Who Called Himself Creator
title.zh: 狐語診病:自稱造物主的富人得醫

region.en: Anchicocha and Latallaco heights (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 安奇科查與拉塔利亞科高地(象徵性標記)

period: Huarochiri manuscript collected by Francisco de Avila, 1608; publ. Markham 1873

source.work: Francisco de Avila, 'A Narrative of the Errors, False Gods and other Superstitions... of Huarochiri, Mama and Chaclla', in Narratives of the Rites and Laws of the Yncas, trans. C. R. Markham, Hakluyt Society, 1873

summary.en: A very rich and great lord had his house on Anchicocha, its roof made of the yellow and red feathers of certain birds, the walls covered with curious materials; he had llamas of red, blue, yellow and other bright colours, so that to make mantles it was unnecessary to dye the wool. People came to him from all directions, and he made himself out to be very wise, even saying that he was the God and Creator. But he fell sick of a tedious and disgusting disease, and everybody wondered that a man who was a God and Creator should be so ill and unable to cure himself; they began to murmur against him. Huathiacuri, journeying towards the sea, slept on the height called Latallaco, where he saw a fox going towards the sea and another coming from the coast: one asked the other for news. 'All is well except that the rich man is very sick... the real cause is that, when his wife was toasting a little maize, one grain fell on her skirt. She gave it to a man who ate it, and afterwards she committed adultery with him. This is the reason that the rich man is sick, and a serpent is now hovering over his beautiful house to eat it, while a toad with two heads is waiting under his grinding-stone with the same object. But no one knows this.' Huathiacuri, having heard what the foxes said, went to the place where the rich man lay sick, and asked the beautiful young daughter - in payment for her favour - to let him cure her father. He commenced the cure by saying: 'Do you know that your wife has committed adultery, and that this is the reason of your sickness? Do you know that there are two great serpents above your house waiting to eat you? and that there is a toad with two heads underneath that grind-stone? Before everything else we must kill those animals, and then you will begin to recover. But when you are well you must worship and reverence my father, who will appear before many days; for it is quite clear that you are neither God nor Creator. If you were God you would not be ill, nor would you be in need of a cure.' Search was made and the two serpents found on the top of the house and killed; the wife confessed her adultery; the grindstone was raised and out hopped a toad with two heads, which went to a spring that now flows by Anchicocha, where they say it still lives, making those who go to it lose their way, and become mad, and die. The sick man became well, and gave Huathiacuri his young daughter to wife.
summary.zh: 安奇科查住著一位巨富之主:屋頂覆黃紅羽毛,牆壁飾奇珍;駝馬有紅、藍、黃諸色,織毯無須染色。四方之人皆來拜謁,他自詡明智,甚至自稱是神、是造物主。然而他得了纏綿惡疾,舉族驚異:神與造物主豈會臥病而無自救之能?人們開始抱怨他。瓜提亞庫里赴海途中宿於拉塔利亞科高地,見一狐向海而去,一狐自海岸來;來者問訊,去者答:「一切安好,唯那富人病重……真正緣故是:其妻烘玉米時,一粒玉米落在裙上,她拾起給一男子吃了,隨後與他私通。富人之病由此而起;如今有一條大蛇盤踞其美宅之上欲食之,磨石之下又伏著一隻雙頭蟾蜍,同樣等著吃他。只是無人知曉。」瓜提亞庫里聽罷,便至病榻,對病主的幼女說:若肯以身相許,他便醫好其父。醫治之始,他直言:「你可知道,你妻子與人私通,這正是你生病的原因?你可知道,屋頂之上有兩條巨蛇等著吃你,磨石之下伏著雙頭蟾蜍?先殺了這些動物,你的病才會好。病癒之後,你須敬奉我父親——他不久將顯現。你顯然既非神、亦非造物主;你若是神,豈會生病、需要醫治?」眾人驚訝。其妻怒斥誣謗,但富人求治心切,命人搜查:屋頂果然有兩蛇,殺之;其妻承認私通;掀起磨石,雙頭蟾蜍蹦出,逃至今安奇科查旁的一眼泉邊——相傳它至今仍住在那裡,使誤飲其水者迷路、發狂、死去。富人病癒,以幼女妻之。

sensitivity.note: The fox-lore diagnosis of adultery-sickness; the rich man who claimed creatorhood is unmasked - a theodicy episode of the Huarochiri cycle.

passages.text: A very rich and great lord had his house on Anchicocha, about a league and a half from the place where the five eggs appeared. His house was very richly and curiously adorned, for the roof was made of the yellow and red feathers of certain birds, and the walls were covered with similar and even more curious materials. This lord had a great number of llamas - some red, others blue and yellow and of other bright colours, so that, to make mantles, it was unnecessary to dye the wool. For these reasons people came to him from all directions to pay their respects; and he made himself to be very wise, even saying that he was the God and Creator. But at last a great misfortune befell him: he fell sick of a tedious and disgusting disease, and everybody wondered that a man who was so wise and rich, and was a God and Creator, should be so ill and be unable to cure himself. So they began to murmur against him.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Avila, Narrative of the Errors of Huarochiri, ch. 5 (Markham 1873); not verbatim.

passages.text: At this time they say that Huathiacuri journeyed towards the sea, and slept on that height called Latallaco. While he was there he saw a fox going towards the sea, and another coming from the coast towards Anchicocha. The one coming from the sea asked the other whether there was any news, and the other answered that all was well except that the rich man was very sick... But, added the fox, the real cause is that, when his wife was toasting a little maize, one grain fell on her skirt. She gave it to a man who ate it, and afterwards she committed adultery with him. This is the reason that the rich man is sick, and a serpent is now hovering over his beautiful house to eat it, while a toad with two heads is waiting under his grinding-stone with the same object. But no one knows this.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Avila, Narrative of the Errors of Huarochiri, ch. 5 (Markham 1873); not verbatim.

passages.text: Having heard what the foxes said, he went to the place where the rich man was lying sick, and asked a young and beautiful girl - daughter to the sick God - if any one was ill... He entered, and said that he could certainly effect a cure if the sick man would give his young daughter to him for a wife. The wise Huathiacuri commenced the cure by saying: 'Do you know that your wife has committed adultery, and that this is the reason of your sickness? Do you know that there are two great serpents above your house waiting to eat you? and that there is a toad with two heads underneath that grind-stone? Before everything else we must kill those animals, and then you will begin to recover your health. But, when you are well, you must worship and reverence my father, who will appear before many days, for it is quite clear that you are neither God nor Creator. If you were God you would not be ill, nor would you be in need of a cure.'
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Avila, Narrative of the Errors of Huarochiri, ch. 5 (Markham 1873); not verbatim.

passages.text: The sick man was so desirous to be cured that he ordered search to be made, and they found the two serpents on the top of the house and killed them. Then the sage reminded the wife that when she was toasting maize one grain had fallen on her skirt... So she confessed. The sage then caused the grindstone to be raised, and there hopped from underneath a toad with two heads, which went to a spring that now flows by Anchicocha, where they say that it still lives, making those who go to it lose their way, and become mad, and die. Having done all this, the sick man became well, and the wise Huathiacuri enjoyed the girl.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Avila, Narrative of the Errors of Huarochiri, ch. 5 (Markham 1873); not verbatim.

language: Spanish record of a Quechua tradition
canonical_translation: C. R. Markham, Narrative of the Rites and Laws of the Yncas (Hakluyt Society, 1873)

title.en: Faridun's Birth and the Peacock Cow
title.zh: 法里東誕生與孔雀母牛

region.en: Forests of Mazandaran (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 馬贊德蘭林間（象徵性定位）

period: Composed c. 1010 CE (Warner translation 1905)

source.work: Firdausi, Shahnama, trans. A. G. & E. Warner (1905), vol. I, Zahhak secs. 3-4

summary.en: Abtin, a descendant of Tahmuras who warred against Zahhak, is captured and put to death, and his wife Faranak flees with the newborn Faridun, the bearer of Jamshid's lost Grace. She entrusts the babe to a keeper of the wondrous peacock-coloured cow Birmaya, whose milk rears him for three years; when the search closes in, the mother carries him to a holy hermit on Mount Alburz, while Zahhak in rage slays Birmaya and burns Faridun's empty home.
summary.zh: 阿卜丁——塔胡穆拉斯後裔、討伐扎哈克者——被擒處死。其妻法拉娜克攜新生兒法里東（賈姆希德失落之天恩所託）逃亡，將嬰孩託付孔雀羽色神牛比爾瑪雅的牧人，以牛乳哺育三年。追兵漸近，母親攜子避往阿爾布茲山聖隱士處；扎哈克盛怒之下殺比爾瑪雅、焚其空宅。

sensitivity.note: Epic literary source; hidden-infant-hero motif. No living community restriction.

passages.text: Years passed away and calamity approached the dragon-king: the blessed Faridun was born and the fashion of the world was changed. Of cypress height he shone forth with the Grace of kings of kings which erst Jamshid possessed, was like the sun, as needful as the rain to earth, and fit as knowledge to the mind; revolving heaven loved him tenderly.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Firdausi, Shahnama, Zahhak sec. 3 (Warner 1905); not verbatim.

passages.text: Then lived the cow Birmaya, chief of kine, born with a coat all bright and peacock-hued, a marvel the archmages flocked to see. Meanwhile Zahhak searched everywhere till Faridun became a source of danger to his sire Abtin, who fled for life but met certain followers of Zahhak, who seized him and bore him before the Shah, and the Shah had him put to death.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Firdausi, Shahnama, Zahhak sec. 3 (Warner 1905); not verbatim.

passages.text: When Faridun's wise mother Faranak perceived her husband's fate she fled heart-broken to the field of the beautiful Birmaya, and bade the hind: protect this suckling for me, be a father to him, and give him milk of yon fair cow. The guardian fed the child for three years with Birmaya's milk; but as the cow was talked of everywhere the mother bore the babe in haste to a devotee on Mount Alburz, charging him to father it, for this her noble son would discrown Zahhak and tread his girdle in the dust. When the rumour reached Zahhak he went like a mad elephant, slew Birmaya, and burned the lofty palace of Faridun to the ground.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Firdausi, Shahnama, Zahhak secs. 3-4 (Warner 1905); not verbatim.

title.en: Faridun Learns His Blood and Girds for Revenge
title.zh: 法里東知身世而興復仇之志

region.en: Plains of Iran (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 伊朗平原（象徵性定位）

period: Composed c. 1010 CE (Warner translation 1905)

source.work: Firdausi, Shahnama, trans. A. G. & E. Warner (1905), vol. I, Zahhak sec. 4

summary.en: At sixteen Faridun seeks out his mother and demands the truth of his lineage. She tells him of Abtin of royal race, of the two serpents that suck Iran's life-breath, of the brains of his father taken to feed them, and of the peacock cow that nursed him. Faridun's heart aches for revenge, but Faranak counsels patience: thou canst not stand alone against the world, for Zahhak has throne, crown, and a hundred thousand strong.
summary.zh: 十六歲的法里東尋母問出身。母親道出：父阿卜丁乃王族、被殺取腦以飼扎哈克肩上雙蛇，那雙蛇吸食伊朗的生命之息；又述孔雀母牛哺乳之事。法里東胸中燃起復仇之火，母親卻勸其忍耐：扎哈克有王冠、寶座與十萬大軍，孤身不可與天下為敵。

sensitivity.note: Epic literary source; no living community restriction.

passages.text: Faridun, when twice eight years had passed, sought out his mother on the plain: disclose thy secret, say who is my father, what is my lineage, whom shall I declare myself in public. She said: I will tell all, my noble boy. Within Iran erewhile lived one Abtin, of royal race, sprung from Tahmuras; Abtin knew all the pedigree. Thy sire and my dear spouse was he; my days were dark when we were parted.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Firdausi, Shahnama, Zahhak sec. 4 (Warner 1905); not verbatim.

passages.text: Now on Zahhak the warlock's shoulders grew two serpents which sucked the life-breath of Iran, and thy sire's brains were taken from his head to feed them. I came on an open pasture and there beheld a cow like jocund spring, the cow of peacock hues supplying thee with milk that made thee thrive, until the tidings of cow and meadow reached the Shah; then I bare thee from the pasture in all haste, and he came and slew the noble tender nurse and turned our home to ditch.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Firdausi, Shahnama, Zahhak sec. 4 (Warner 1905); not verbatim.

passages.text: The prince, enraged thereat, mused on revenge: the lion groweth brave by venturing, and since the sorcerer hath done his part, mine is to take my scimitar and lay his palace in the dust. She said: this is not well; thou canst not stand alone against the world; view not the world with boyish eyes, give all words save thy mother's to the wind.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Firdausi, Shahnama, Zahhak sec. 4 (Warner 1905); not verbatim.

title.en: Kava the Smith Raises the Kawian Standard
title.zh: 鐵匠卡瓦高舉卡維戰旗

region.en: Zahhak's palace, Babylon (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 扎哈克王宮（象徵巴比倫）

period: Composed c. 1010 CE (Warner translation 1905)

source.work: Firdausi, Shahnama, trans. A. G. & E. Warner (1905), vol. I, Zahhak sec. 5

summary.en: Zahhak, tormented by dreams of Faridun, makes the notables sign a scroll attesting his goodness. In bursts Kava the smith, seventeen of his eighteen sons taken to feed the serpents, accusing the Shah to his face. He tears the scroll in fury, hoists his leathern apron on a spear as a rallying flag — the ruler here is Ahriman, God's foe — and leads the crowd to Faridun. Faridun brocades the apron with jewels and names it the Kawian flag, the royal standard of Shahs for ages after.
summary.zh: 扎哈克被法里東之夢所擾，迫群臣在其善行文書上署名。鐵匠卡瓦闖入——十八子被征去餵蛇，僅存其一——當面控訴王之暴虐。他怒撕文書，以鐵匠皮圍裙縛於矛尖為旗：「此地之主乃阿赫里曼，神之敵！」率眾投奔法里東。法里東以錦繡寶石飾之，定名卡維戰旗，後世歷代君王皆以此為國旗。

sensitivity.note: Epic literary source; the Kawian flag is an Iranian national symbol etiology. No living community restriction.

passages.text: Zahhak had Faridun upon his lips both day and night; he called the notables from every province and asked them to sign a scroll: our monarch soweth naught but seeds of good. Those upright men subscribed their names upon the Dragon's document against their wills, because they feared the Shah. Just then was heard outside the palace-gate the voice of one that clamoured for redress.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Firdausi, Shahnama, Zahhak sec. 5 (Warner 1905); not verbatim.

passages.text: O Shah, my name is Kawa and I sue for justice, cried the smith. I have had many an outrage at thy hands. I had once in this world eighteen sons: but one is left! My youth is gone, my children are no more, and all will be aghast if they shall show that this my son hath perished in his turn with all the rest to feed those snakes of thine. They set the young man free, but when Zahhak bade him subscribe the scroll Kawa shouted: confederates of the Div with impious hearts! I will not subscribe; and, rising in fury, rent the scroll and trampled it.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Firdausi, Shahnama, Zahhak sec. 5 (Warner 1905); not verbatim.

passages.text: In the market-place he took a leathern apron such as smiths wear to protect their legs while at the forge, stuck it upon a spear's point, and passed along exclaiming: whosoever would 'scape the fetters of Zahhak, let him resort with me to Faridun; the ruler here is Ahriman, God's foe. So that poor leather discriminated friends and enemies. Faridun marked the apron on the spear and hailed the omen, decked it with brocade of jewelled patterns on a golden ground, and named it the Kawian flag; thenceforth when any Shah acceded to the throne he hung the smith's worthless apron with still more jewels, and Kawa's standard grew to be a sun amid the gloom of night.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Firdausi, Shahnama, Zahhak sec. 5 (Warner 1905); not verbatim.

title.en: The Crag Above the Sleeping Prince and the Swim Across the Tigris
title.zh: 墜崖巨石與橫渡底格里斯河

region.en: Tigris at Baghdad (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 巴格達附近底格里斯河（象徵性定位）

period: Composed c. 1010 CE (Warner translation 1905)

source.work: Firdausi, Shahnama, trans. A. G. & E. Warner (1905), vol. I, Zahhak sec. 6

summary.en: Faridun's two elder brothers envy his rising fortune: at a night halt they scale a cliff above their sleeping brother and loose a mighty crag upon his brow, but God rouses the sleeper, who with his magic art arrests the stone in mid-career and keeps the matter secret. Advancing on Zahhak's capital, Faridun finds the river-guard forbidden to launch boats, so he plunges his rose-red charger into the Tigris and his host swims over like a phantom cohort of a dream.
summary.zh: 法里東兩位兄長嫉妒其鴻運：夜宿時攀上峭壁，對沉睡之弟鬆落巨石；神使其醒，法里東以法術止石於半空，並秘而不宣。進軍至扎哈克都城，渡口官奉命不予船隻，法里東遂騎赤駿直入底格里斯河，全軍如夢中幻影般泅水而過。

sensitivity.note: Epic literary source; no living community restriction.

passages.text: Faridun had two brothers, both of noble birth and older than himself, hight Kaimish and prosperous Purmaya. His brothers, seeing that God sped his cause, departed without delay to compass his destruction. There was above their heads a lofty cliff, and underneath the Shah slept peacefully. His two abandoned brothers scaled the height unseen, and, scrupling at no crime, set loose a mighty crag upon the brow to fall directly on their brother's head and kill him in his sleep.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Firdausi, Shahnama, Zahhak sec. 6 (Warner 1905); not verbatim.

passages.text: The crashing crag, for God so ordered, roused the slumberer, who by his magic art arrested it in mid-career: it stopped dead. Faridun went on his way but kept the matter secret. In front marched Kawa with the Kawian standard, soon to become the ensign of the realm, and Faridun advanced toward the Arwand, which the Arabs call the Dijla.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Firdausi, Shahnama, Zahhak sec. 6 (Warner 1905); not verbatim.

passages.text: The river-guard sent not his boats but made reply: the Shah gave privy orders to launch no boat without a passport under his own seal. The prince, enraged and fearless of the stream, plunged with his rose-red charger in the flood; with one accord his comrades turned toward the stream and plunged over saddle-back, their heads reeling while their swift steeds struggled with the tide, so that they seemed the phantom cohort of a dream. The warriors reached the dry land and set their faces toward Gang-i-Dizhukht, the tall palace of Zahhak.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Firdausi, Shahnama, Zahhak sec. 6 (Warner 1905); not verbatim.

title.en: Faridun Binds Zahhak on Mount Damawand
title.zh: 法里東縛扎哈克於達馬萬德山

region.en: Mount Damawand (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 達馬萬德山（象徵性定位）

period: Composed c. 1010 CE (Warner translation 1905)

source.work: Firdausi, Shahnama, trans. A. G. & E. Warner (1905), vol. I, Zahhak secs. 7-8

summary.en: Zahhak returns by byway to his usurped palace, descends a roof by lasso with a poniard drawn against the two queens, and Faridun rushes on him like the wind, beating in his helm with the ox-head mace. The blessed Suriish stays the blow — his time hath not yet come — and Faridun binds the Dragon with a lasso of lion's hide and chains him in a nail-studded chasm of Mount Damawand, where he hangs, his heart's blood trickling to the ground.
summary.zh: 扎哈克潛回王宮，以繩縋下屋頂，拔匕首欲刺二后；法里東疾風般撲上，牛首狼牙棒擊碎其盔。聖靈蘇魯什喝止：「其死期未至，當縛之。」法里東以獅皮繩縛龍，將其釘於達馬萬德山釘滿鐵釘的深谷岩隙間，令其懸吊，心血滴落於地。

sensitivity.note: Epic literary source. Zahhak is bound, not slain — his death is deferred to the eschaton (Keresaspa); cf. persian-zahhak-dream-faridun and Bundahishn eschatology records. No living community restriction.

passages.text: Zahhak, mailed, approached the palace in jealous fear, armed with a lasso sixty cubits long, scaled the lofty edifice, and saw beneath him dark-eyed Shahrinaz toying bewitchingly with Faridun. He drew a keen-edged poniard from its sheath, told not his purpose or his name, and clutched the steel-blue dagger in his hand, athirst for the blood of those two beauteous dames.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Firdausi, Shahnama, Zahhak sec. 7 (Warner 1905); not verbatim.

passages.text: His feet no sooner rested on the ground than Faridun rushed on him like the wind and beat his helm in with the ox-head mace. Strike not, cried blest Suriish, who hurried thither: his time hath not yet come, but bind him vanquished firm as a rock and bear him to some gorge where friends and kinsmen will not come to him. When Faridun heard that he gat a lasso made of lion's hide and bound Zahhak around the arms and waist with bonds that no huge elephant could snap.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Firdausi, Shahnama, Zahhak sec. 8 (Warner 1905); not verbatim.

passages.text: He bore Zahhak fettered to Mount Damawand, and having marked a chasm of viewless depth, and studded it with heavy nails whereon the brain might chafe, he secured Zahhak bound by the hands upon a crag, that so his anguish might endure. Thus was he left to hang, his heart's blood trickling to the ground. The binding of Zahhak, that loathly one devoid of justice, was the chief deed done: he next avenged the murder of Abtin and purged the surface of earth clean of madmen.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Firdausi, Shahnama, Zahhak sec. 8 (Warner 1905); not verbatim.

title.en: Faridun Founds the Feast of Mihrgan
title.zh: 法里東創立米赫爾甘節

region.en: Istakhr of Pars (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 帕爾斯伊斯塔赫爾（象徵性定位）

period: Composed c. 1010 CE (Warner translation 1905)

source.work: Firdausi, Shahnama, trans. A. G. & E. Warner (1905), vol. I, Faridun sec. 1

summary.en: Firm on the throne, Faridun orders crown and palace according to the usance of old times and on the first of Mihr sets on the royal diadem. He bids men kindle bonfires, burning ambergris and saffron, and thus founds the feast of Mihrgan, that time of rest and festival whose memorial is still the month of Mihr. In five centuries of sway he dedicates not a single day to evil.
summary.zh: 法里東穩坐王位後，依古禮整飭冠冕宮室，於米赫爾月初一加冕。他令百姓燃起篝火，焚乳香與藏紅花，遂創米赫爾甘節——休憩歡宴之期，米赫爾月之名永為其紀念。五百載統治，無一日行惡。

sensitivity.note: Epic literary source; festival etiology. No living community restriction.

passages.text: When Faridun attained his wish and reigned supreme on earth, he ordered crown and throne according to the usance of old times within the palace of the king of kings, and on the first of Mihr, a blessed day, set on his head the royal diadem. In those days, apprehensive of no evil, all men began to tread the path of God, abstaining from contention and observing a feast inaugurated royally.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Firdausi, Shahnama, Faridun sec. 1 (Warner 1905); not verbatim.

passages.text: Then sages sat rejoicing and each held a ruby goblet; the wine was bright, the new Shah's face was bright, and all the world itself was brightened as that month began. He bade men kindle bonfires and the people burned ambergris and saffron; thus he founded Mihrgan. That time of rest and festival began with him, and his memorial is still the month of Mihr. He banished then all grief and labour from the minds of men, and dedicated not a single day to evil in five centuries of sway.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Firdausi, Shahnama, Faridun sec. 1 (Warner 1905); not verbatim.

title.en: Sarv of Yaman Proves the Princes by Sorcery
title.zh: 也門王沙爾夫以法術試駙馬

region.en: Court of Sarv in Yaman (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 也門沙爾夫王庭（象徵性定位）

period: Composed c. 1010 CE (Warner translation 1905)

source.work: Firdausi, Shahnama, trans. A. G. & E. Warner (1905), vol. I, Faridun secs. 4-5

summary.en: Faridun sends to Sarv, king of Yaman, for three royal sisters to wed his three nameless sons. Sarv tries them twice: first he ranges his daughters by inverted age at a feast, which the princes answer as their father taught them; then he works a killing frost over their sleeping bower, and the three sons, by the Grace of God and their own skill, oppose the spell and keep the frost away. Beaten twice, Sarv gives up his three Eyes with crowns and trinkets and sends the brides to Faridun.
summary.zh: 法里東遣使向也門王沙爾夫求三姐妹為其三子擇偶。沙爾夫兩度試探：先於宴上按長幼顛倒排列三女，王子們依父所授答破其計；再以殺人寒霜襲其睡處，三子賴天恩與己術，破咒禦霜。兩度挫敗，沙爾夫獻出三女，攜冠飾送往法里東處。

sensitivity.note: Epic literary source; sorcery trial episode. No living community restriction.

passages.text: Faridun perceived his three sons fit to rule and called Jandal, a noble counsellor: go round the world and select three maidens of noble lineage worthy of my sons, three sisters in full blood with fairy faces. The shrewd and holy man at length reached Sarv, the monarch of Yaman, and explained the embassy: my three sons well deserve to reign, and I have news that thou hast three maiden daughters as yet unnamed.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Firdausi, Shahnama, Faridun secs. 2-4 (Warner 1905); not verbatim.

passages.text: Sarv brought his daughters out of their bowers and ranged them just as Faridun had foretold he would — the youngest walking first, the eldest last, the mid in age in the midst — and asked the eldest prince which of the three Stars was the youngest. They answered as they had been taught, and so sewed up the eyelids of his craft, while he and all his warriors were lost in wonder. The introduction ended in betrothal.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Firdausi, Shahnama, Faridun sec. 4 (Warner 1905); not verbatim.

passages.text: Then Sarv assembled boon-companions, and when wine had prevailed he bade set couches by a fountain of rose-water, where the three athelings slept in a bower of roses. Meanwhile the sorcerer-king prepared his spells: he brought a frost and mighty blast, and over hill and plain it froze so sharply that the crows grew numb. Faridun's three sons leapt from their couches at the grievous cold and, by the Grace of God and their own skill, by kingly magic and hardihood, opposed the spell and kept the frost away. Sarv beheld three princes like new moons and knew that spells had failed him; he opened his treasury and gave his three bright Eyes to the princes, with crowns and trinkets, sending the brides to Faridun.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Firdausi, Shahnama, Faridun sec. 5 (Warner 1905); not verbatim.

title.en: The Father Turns Dragon: Salm, Tur, and Iraj
title.zh: 父化為龍試三子：薩爾姆、圖爾與伊朗支

region.en: Roads of Iran (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 伊朗道路（象徵性定位）

period: Composed c. 1010 CE (Warner translation 1905)

source.work: Firdausi, Shahnama, trans. A. G. & E. Warner (1905), vol. I, Faridun sec. 6

summary.en: Hearing the princes returned with brides, Faridun changes himself to a raging dragon to prove their mettle. The eldest flees — be thou Salm, for thou soughtest safety; the second strings his bow — be thou Tur, a lion brave; the youngest speaks him fair and names himself — be thou Iraj, who chose the middle course 'twixt dust and flame. The Shah then reads their horoscopes: Jupiter for Salm, the Sun in the Lion's House for Tur, and for Iraj the Moon in Cancer — a destiny of strife and woe.
summary.zh: 聞三子攜新婦歸來，法里東化身為咆哮巨龍以試其膽。長子逃遁——得名薩爾姆（求安全者）；次子彎弓——得名圖爾（勇獅）；幼子言辭得體——得名伊朗支（擇塵與火之中道者）。王更觀星象：薩爾姆得木星，圖爾得太陽居獅宮，而伊朗支得巨蟹座之月——註定紛爭與悲慟。

sensitivity.note: Epic literary source. Names encode ethnonyms (Salm/Rum, Tur/Turan, Iraj/Iran). No living community restriction.

passages.text: When tidings reached Faridun that the princes had returned he went to meet them, longing, by trial of their characters, to end his boding fears; so changed him to a dragon, one no lion could escape, which hissed and bellowed with its jaws aflame. He rushed in fury toward his eldest son, that prince of many virtues, who exclaimed: no man of sense and wisdom thinketh good to fight with dragons; then he showed his back and fled.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Firdausi, Shahnama, Faridun sec. 6 (Warner 1905); not verbatim.

passages.text: The father turned toward the second son, who when he saw the dragon strung up his bow and drew it: when fight is toward, what matter if the foe be roaring lion or brave cavalier? But when the youngest son came up he cried: thou art a leopard; ware the lions' path! If e'er the name of Faridun hath reached thine ears contend not with us, for we three are sons of his, and I will discrown thee of thy loathly face unless thou turnest from thy waywardness.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Firdausi, Shahnama, Faridun sec. 6 (Warner 1905); not verbatim.

passages.text: The glorious Faridun thus proved their mettle and returned as their sire with pomp and kettledrums. That loathly dragon was your own father, he told them, who desired to prove your mettle. Now in my wisdom I have chosen fit names: thou soughtest safety, be thou Salm; thou from the first showedst fight, whose courage is more ardent than a flame, be thou Tur; and the youngest, who chose the middle course 'twixt dust and flame, the prudent man's, be he Iraj, and may his end be all supremacy. Then he spread the catalogue of stars before him: Salm's horoscope was Jupiter in Sagittarius, Tur's the Sun ascendant in the Lion's House, but for Iraj the Moon in Cancer revealed a destiny of strife and woe, and the Shah could not be but filled with grave anxiety.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Firdausi, Shahnama, Faridun sec. 6 (Warner 1905); not verbatim.

title.en: Tamure Outmagics the Sorcerer Kiki
title.zh: 塔穆雷鬥法勝基基

region.en: Waikato River (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 懷卡托河（象徵性定位）

period: Oral tradition; recorded 1855 (Grey, Polynesian Mythology)

source.work: George Grey, Polynesian Mythology and Ancient Traditional History of the New Zealand Race, ch. 18, The Two Sorcerers (London 1855)

summary.en: Kiki's shadow withers shrubs; sliding back his door as canoes pass, he kills the crews at a glance - 'the offspring of Kiki wither shrubs'. Tamure of Kawhia crosses the ranges to duel him, repeats the incantation Mata-tawhito before landing, enchants the threshold and door, and feeds his enchanted meal to his daughter, who slips most of it under her clothes. Leaving, Tamure instructs a downstream village to tell pursuers the canoe is far ahead; Kiki's men, misled, turn back, and Kiki dies by Tamure's spells.
summary.zh: 巫師基基的影子能令灌木枯萎；河上舟過，他拉開屋門便使舟中人僵斃——『基基的子嗣使灌木枯萎』。卡菲亞的塔穆雷越山赴會決鬥：登岸前誦『馬塔陶希托』護身咒，到村後詛咒門檻與門扉，又讓女兒吃下詛咒之食——她卻把大部分食物藏於衣下。臨別時他囑下游村人：若有人追問，便答『那舟早已遠去』。基基族人被誤導而折返，基基死於塔穆雷咒術之下。

sensitivity.note: Sorcery-duel legend; Grey notes descendants of both sorcerers were living in his day.

passages.text: Kiki was a celebrated sorcerer and skilled in magical arts; he lived upon the river Waikato. The inhabitants of that river still have this proverb, 'The offspring of Kiki wither shrubs.' This proverb had its origin in the circumstance of Kiki being such a magician that he could not go abroad in the sunshine; for if his shadow fell upon any place not protected from his magic, it at once became tapu, and all the plants there withered. If any parties coming up the river called at his village in their canoes as they paddled by, he still remained quietly at home, but just drew back the sliding door of his house so that it might stand open, and the strangers stiffened and died; or even as canoes came paddling down from the upper parts of the river, he drew back the sliding wooden shutter to the window of his house, and the crews on board were sure to die.
passages.note: Paraphrase of George Grey, Polynesian Mythology, ch. 18 (1855); not verbatim.

passages.text: At length the fame of this sorcerer spread exceedingly and resounded through every tribe, until Tamure, a chief who dwelt at Kawhia, thought he would go and contend in the arts of sorcery with Kiki. He selected two of his people as companions and took his young daughter with him; they crossed the mountain range from Kawhia and came down upon the river Waipa, and paddled down towards the village of Kiki, managing so well that before they were seen by anybody they had arrived at the landing-place. Tamure was not only skilled in magic but also a very cautious man; whilst still afloat he repeated an incantation of the kind called Mata-tawhito to preserve him safe from all arts of sorcery, and other incantations to ward off spells, collect good genii round him, keep off evil spirits and shield him from demons.
passages.note: Paraphrase of George Grey, Polynesian Mythology, ch. 18 (1855); not verbatim.

passages.text: The old sorcerer called out that they were welcome and invited them up; in the square some of Kiki's people kindled fire in an enchanted oven and began to cook food for the strangers. Tamure sat on the ground just outside the entrance to the house and repeated incantations over the threshold, so that Kiki might be enchanted as he stepped over it to come out. When the food was cooked and spread upon clean mats, the old sorcerer made his appearance and invited Tamure to eat with him - but the food was all enchanted, and his object in asking Tamure was that the enchanted food might kill him. Tamure said his young daughter was very hungry and would eat of the food; he kept repeating Mata-tawhito, Whakangungu and Parepare, protections against enchanted food, and as she ate she also continued to repeat them; even when she stretched out her hand to take a sweet potato she dropped the greater part of it at her feet and hid it under her clothes, then only ate a little bit. Kiki waited for Tamure to begin to eat that he might soon die; meanwhile Tamure repeated incantations which might render the door enchanted also, so that Kiki might be certain not to escape when he passed out of it.
passages.note: Paraphrase of George Grey, Polynesian Mythology, ch. 18 (1855); not verbatim.

passages.text: Tamure now ordered his people to launch his canoe, and they paddled away; a little time after they had left the village Kiki became unwell. As they passed a village where there were many people on the river's bank, Tamure stopped and said to them, 'If you should see any canoe pulling after us, and the people in the canoe ask you, Have you seen a canoe pass up the river? would you be good enough to say, Yes, a canoe has passed by here; and then if they ask you, How far has it got? would you be good enough to say, Oh, by this time it has got very far up the river.' Some time after Tamure's party had left, the old sorcerer became very ill indeed; his people knew this had been brought about by the magical arts of Tamure and sprang into a canoe to follow after him as hard as they could. When they reached the village on the river's bank they called out and asked how far the canoe had reached, and the villagers answered, 'Oh, that canoe must have got very far up the river by this time.' The pursuers, upon hearing this, returned again to their own village, and Kiki died from the incantations of Tamure. He overcame every other sorcerer until he met Tamure, but he was vanquished by him and had to bend the knee before him.
passages.note: Paraphrase of George Grey, Polynesian Mythology, ch. 18 (1855); not verbatim.

title.en: Hakawau Storms the Sacred Mount
title.zh: 哈卡瓦烏攻打聖山

region.en: Sacred Mount fortress near Waitara, Taranaki (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 塔拉納基懷塔拉附近聖山要塞（象徵性定位）

period: Oral tradition; recorded 1855 (Grey, Polynesian Mythology)

source.work: George Grey, Polynesian Mythology and Ancient Traditional History of the New Zealand Race, ch. 19, The Magical Wooden Head (London 1855)

summary.en: Puarata and Tautohito keep a carved wooden head on the Sacred Mount whose mighty cry kills every traveller who passes; armies sent to destroy the sorcerers all perish, the corpses strewing the track over Waimatuku. Hakawau dreams his genius stands head in heaven and feet on earth, then walks the fatal road in safety, warding off malignant spirits with ceaseless incantations. His genii feign retreat, lead the fortress spirits into pursuit, and storm the undefended place; the wooden head can only wail, and as Hakawau smites the threshold in leaving, every soul in the fortress dies.
summary.zh: 普阿拉塔與陶托希托供奉一尊木雕頭顱於聖山之上：其大吼一聲，過路人便皆斃命；征討的大軍無一生還，屍骸遍布懷馬圖庫道上。大巫哈卡瓦烏夢見自己的精靈頭頂天、腳立地，遂踏上死路卻平安無事。其精靈佯敗誘敵、後軍突襲空城；木雕頭顱只餘低泣。哈卡瓦烏臨行以手拍擊門檻——剛出要塞，全寨之人盡數倒斃。

sensitivity.note: Magic-duel legend; the head's killing cry is the central motif.

passages.text: This head bewitched all persons who approached the hill where the fortress in which it was kept was situated, so that, from fear of it, no human being dared to approach the place, which was thence named the Sacred Mount. Upon that mount dwelt Puarata and Tautohito with their carved head, and its fame went through all the country - to the river Taranaki, to Kaipara, to the tribes of Ngapuhi, to Akau, to Waikato, to Kawhia, to Mokau, to Hauraki, and to Tauranga. Everywhere reports were heard that so great were its magical powers none could escape alive from them; and although many warriors and armies went to the Sacred Mount to try to destroy the sorcerers to whom the head belonged, and to carry it off as a genius for their own district, they all perished in the attempt. No mortal could approach the fortress and live; even parties of people who were travelling along the forest track northwards towards Muriiwhenua all died by the magical powers of that head, whether they went in large armed bodies or simply as quiet travellers - their fate was alike.
passages.note: Paraphrase of George Grey, Polynesian Mythology, ch. 19 (1855); not verbatim.

passages.text: At last the report reached a very powerful sorcerer named Hakawau, who, confiding in his magical arts, said he was resolved to go and see this magic head and the sorcerers who owned it. He called upon all the genii who were subservient to him, in order that he might be thrown into an enchanted sleep and see what his fate in this undertaking would be; and in his slumber he saw that his genius would triumph in the encounter, for it was so lofty and mighty that in his dream its head reached the heavens whilst its feet remained upon earth. Having by his spells ascertained this, he started on his journey with one friend, passing Maraetai, Putataka, Rukuwai, Waitara, Te Weta, and at length reaching the most fatal place of all - Waimatuku. Here they smelt the stench of the carcases of the numbers who had been previously destroyed, so bad that it was quite suffocating; but Hakawau kept on unceasingly working at his enchantments which might ward off the attacks of evil genii and collect good genii about them, and thus they passed over Waimatuku, looking with horror at the many corpses strewed about the beach and in the dense fern and bushes which bordered the path.
passages.note: Paraphrase of George Grey, Polynesian Mythology, ch. 19 (1855); not verbatim.

passages.text: Nevertheless they died not on the dreadful road, but went straight along the path till they came to the place where it passes over some low hills, from whence they could see the fortress which stood upon the Sacred Mount. Hakawau, with his incantations, sent forth many genii to attack the spirits who kept watch over the fortress and magic head; some in advance, charged others to follow at some distance. As soon as the spirits who guarded the fortress saw them, they all issued out to attack; the good genii feigned a retreat, the evil ones following, and whilst they were thus engaged in the pursuit, some of the thousands of good genii stormed the fortress now left without defenders; and when the evil spirits turned to protect the fortress, the genii of Hakawau caught them one after the other, and thus all the spirits of the old sorcerer Puarata were utterly destroyed.
passages.note: Paraphrase of George Grey, Polynesian Mythology, ch. 19 (1855); not verbatim.

passages.text: When the watchmen of the fortress, to their great surprise, saw strangers coming, Puarata hurried to his magic head to call upon it: 'Strangers, come here! Two strangers come!' But it uttered only a low wailing sound; for since the good genii of Hakawau had destroyed the spirits who served Puarata, the old sorcerer addressed in vain his supplications to the magic head - it could no longer raise aloud its powerful voice as in former times. Could it have cried out with a loud voice, straightway Hakawau and his friend would both have perished; for thus it was, when armies and travellers had in other times passed the fortress, Puarata addressed supplications to his magic head, and when it cried out with a mighty voice, the strangers all perished as they heard it. Hakawau went quietly on over the gateway without paying the least attention to the angry words of those who called out to him, and went direct to all the most holy places of the fortress where no person who had not been made sacred might enter. When at length they departed, he smote his hands on the threshold of the house in which they had rested, and they had hardly got well outside the fortress before every soul in it was dead - not a single one of them was left alive.
passages.note: Paraphrase of George Grey, Polynesian Mythology, ch. 19 (1855); not verbatim.

title.en: Kahukura Learns Netting from the Fairies
title.zh: 卡胡庫拉向精靈學織網

region.en: Rangiaowhia beach, far north Aotearoa (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 紐西蘭最北蘭吉奧希亞海灘（象徵性定位）

period: Oral tradition; recorded 1855 (Grey, Polynesian Mythology)

source.work: George Grey, Polynesian Mythology and Ancient Traditional History of the New Zealand Race, ch. 20, Kahukura and the Fairies (London 1855)

summary.en: Travelling north, Kahukura finds mackerel cleaned on the sand by night footprints and no crushed reeds - fairies fish here. He returns after dark, mixes with the pale-skinned Patupaiarehe hauling their net, and keeps delaying dawn by untying the slip-knot a fairy kindly ties for him, so that his string of fish keeps falling. At full daylight the fairies see he is a man and scatter, abandoning their rush net and flax-stem canoes - and with the net the art of net-making passes to Kahukura, who teaches it to his children and so to the whole Maori race.
summary.zh: 卡胡庫拉北上途中發現沙灘上有人夜間清理鯖魚——足跡卻無蘆草壓痕，必是精靈所為。當夜他潛入精靈的拖網隊伍，因其膚色近乎精靈之白而未被識破；他屢次解開精靈好心替他繫好的結，讓魚串墜地，拖延到天光大亮。精靈們看清他是凡人，倉皇四散，棄網棄舟——舟竟是亞麻莖所化。編網之術從此傳於卡胡庫拉，再由他傳子孫，澤被整個毛利民族。

sensitivity.note: Etiological origin of Maori net-making (Patupaiarehe fairies); interpretive tagging.

passages.text: Once upon a time a man of the name of Kahukura wished to pay a visit to Rangiaowhia, a place lying far to the northward, near the country of the tribe called Te Rarawa. As he was on his road he passed a place where some people had been cleaning mackerel, and he saw the inside of the fish lying all about the sand on the sea-shore; surprised at this, he looked about at the marks, and saw that the people who had been fishing had made their footmarks in the night-time, not that morning, nor in the day. He said to himself, 'These are no mortals who have been fishing here - spirits must have done this; had they been men, some of the reeds and grass which they sat on in their canoe would have been lying about.' He felt quite sure from several circumstances that spirits or fairies had been there.
passages.note: Paraphrase of George Grey, Polynesian Mythology, ch. 20 (1855); not verbatim.

passages.text: That night he returned to the place where he had observed all these things, and just as he reached the spot, back had come the fairies too, to haul their net for mackerel; some of them were shouting out, 'The net here! the net here!' Then a canoe paddled off to fetch the other in which the net was laid, and as they dropped the net into the water they began to cry out, 'Drop the net in the sea at Rangiaowhia, and haul it at Mamaku.' These words were sung out by the fairies as an encouragement in their work and from the joy of their hearts at their sport in fishing. As the fairies were dragging the net to the shore, Kahukura managed to mix amongst them and hauled away at the rope; he happened to be a very fair man, so that his skin was almost as white as that of these fairies, and from that cause he was not observed by them.
passages.note: Paraphrase of George Grey, Polynesian Mythology, ch. 20 (1855); not verbatim.

passages.text: As the net came close in to the shore the fairies began to cheer and shout, 'Go out into the sea some of you, in front of the rocks, lest the nets should be entangled in Tawatawauia a Teweteweuia', for that was the name of a rugged rock standing out from the sandy shore. When the first fish reached the shore, thrown up in the ripples driven before the net, the fairies had not yet remarked Kahukura, for he was almost as fair as they were. It was just at the very first peep of dawn that the fish were all landed; every one took up what fish he liked and ran a twig through their gills, calling out, 'Make haste, run here, all of you, and finish the work before the sun rises.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of George Grey, Polynesian Mythology, ch. 20 (1855); not verbatim.

passages.text: Kahukura kept on stringing his fish with the rest of them. He had only a very short string, and, making a slip-knot at the end of it, when he had covered the string with fish, he lifted them up, but had hardly raised them from the ground when the slip-knot gave way from the weight of the fish, and off they fell. Then some of the fairies ran good-naturedly to help him to string his fish again, and one of them tied the knot at the end of the string for him; but the fairy had hardly gone after knotting it before Kahukura had unfastened it and again tied a slip-knot at the end. Then he began stringing his fish again, and when he had got a great many on, up he lifted them, and off they slipped as before. This trick he repeated several times, delaying the fairies in their work by getting them to knot his string for him. At last full daylight broke, so that there was light enough to distinguish a man's face, and the fairies saw that Kahukura was a man; then they dispersed in confusion, leaving their fish and their net, and abandoning their canoes, which were nothing but stems of the flax. Now was first discovered the stitch for netting a net, for they left theirs with Kahukura, and it became a pattern for him. He thus taught his children to make nets, and by them the Maori race were made acquainted with that art, which they have now known from very remote times.
passages.note: Paraphrase of George Grey, Polynesian Mythology, ch. 20 (1855); not verbatim.

title.en: Te Kanawa Offers the Fairies the Shadows of His Jewels
title.zh: 特卡納瓦以珠影贈精靈

region.en: Mount Pukemore, Waikato, Aotearoa (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 紐西蘭懷卡托普凱莫爾山（象徵性定位）

period: Oral tradition; recorded 1855 (Grey, Polynesian Mythology)

source.work: George Grey, Polynesian Mythology and Ancient Traditional History of the New Zealand Race, ch. 21, Te Kanawa's Adventure with the Fairies (London 1855)

summary.en: Kiwi-hunting overnight on Mount Pukemore, Te Kanawa's party hear a whole troop of fairies - men, women and children - approaching in the dark. They peep over the great tree-roots at the handsome chief whenever the fire burns low, singing merrily. Te Kanawa, nearly frightened to death, hangs his greenstone neck-ornament and ear-rings on a stick as an offering; the fairies take only the shadows of the jewels, handing them from one to another, and vanish - leaving the jewels themselves, 'the hearts of the fairies being quite contented at getting the shadows alone'.
summary.zh: 特卡納瓦一行夜宿普凱莫爾山頂獵奇維鳥，黑暗中忽然聽見大隊精靈——男女老幼——歡歌而來。火光一暗，精靈便從巨樹盤根後偷看這位俊美酋長。特卡納瓦嚇得半死，心生一計：將碧玉頸飾與耳環繫於木棒獻上。精靈們只取寶石的影子，一一傳遞把玩，隨即消失無蹤——寶石原物留了下來，『精靈的心，得影即足』。

sensitivity.note: Fairy-encounter tale; Grey notes the fairies' fair hair and skin, unlike the Maori.

passages.text: Te Kanawa, a chief of Waikato, was the man who fell in with a troop of fairies upon the top of Puke-more, a high hill in the Waikato district. This chief happened one day to go out to catch kiwis with his dogs, and when night came on he found himself right at the top of Puke-more. So his party made a fire to give them light, for it was very dark. They had chosen a tree to sleep under - a very large tree with immense roots sticking up high above the ground; they slept between these roots, and made the fire beyond them.
passages.note: Paraphrase of George Grey, Polynesian Mythology, ch. 21 (1855); not verbatim.

passages.text: As soon as it was dark they heard loud voices, like the voices of people coming that way; there were the voices of men, of women, and of children, as if a very large party of people were coming along. They looked for a long time but could see nothing; till at last Te Kanawa knew the noise must proceed from fairies. His people were all dreadfully frightened, and would have run away if they could; but where could they run to? for they were in the midst of a forest, on the top of a lonely mountain, and it was dark night. For a long time the voices grew louder and more distinct as the fairies drew nearer and nearer, until they came quite close to the fire; Te Kanawa and his party were half dead with fright.
passages.note: Paraphrase of George Grey, Polynesian Mythology, ch. 21 (1855); not verbatim.

passages.text: At last the fairies approached to look at Te Kanawa, who was a very handsome fellow. To do this, they kept peeping slily over the large roots of the tree under which the hunters were lying, and kept constantly looking at him whilst his companions were quite insensible from fear. Whenever the fire blazed up brightly, off went the fairies and hid themselves, peeping out from behind stumps and trees; and when it burnt low, back they came close to it, merrily singing as they moved: 'Here you come climbing over Mount Tirangi to visit the handsome chief of Ngapuhi, whom we have done with.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of George Grey, Polynesian Mythology, ch. 21 (1855); not verbatim.

passages.text: A sudden thought struck Te Kanawa, that he might induce them to go away if he gave them all the jewels he had about him; so he took off a beautiful little figure carved in green jasper which he wore as a neck ornament, and a precious carved jasper ear-drop from his ear. Te Kanawa was only trying to amuse and please them to save his life, but all the time he was nearly frightened to death. He took a stick, and fixing it into the ground, hung his neck ornament and ear-rings upon it. As soon as the fairies had ended their song, they took the shadows of the ear-rings and handed them about from one to the other until they had passed through the whole party, which then suddenly disappeared, and nothing more was seen of them. The fairies carried off with them the shadows of all the jewels of Te Kanawa, but they left behind them his jasper neck ornament and his ear-rings, so that he took them back again, the hearts of the fairies being quite contented at getting the shadows alone; they saw, also, that Te Kanawa was an honest, well-dispositioned fellow. However, the next morning, as soon as it was light, he got down the mountain as fast as he could without stopping to hunt longer for kiwis.
passages.note: Paraphrase of George Grey, Polynesian Mythology, ch. 21 (1855); not verbatim.

title.en: Takarangi Carries Water to the Besieged
title.zh: 塔卡蘭基賜水解圍城

region.en: Pa Whakarewa, Taranaki, Aotearoa (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 紐西蘭塔拉納基瓦卡雷瓦要塞（象徵性定位）

period: Oral tradition; recorded 1855 (Grey, Polynesian Mythology)

source.work: George Grey, Polynesian Mythology and Ancient Traditional History of the New Zealand Race, ch. 22, The Loves of Takarangi and Rau-mahora (London 1855)

summary.en: Investing the fortress of Rangirarunga, the Ngati-Awa army leaves its people dying of thirst. The aged chief cries for one drop of water, and calabashes are broken in his hands by the hard-hearted. Seeing his white heron plume, the old man challenges the young leader: can he still the wrathful surge? 'The wrathful surge shall be stilled; this arm of mine is one which no dog dares to bite.' Takarangi fills a calabash at Fount Oringi in dead silence and carries it up - for himself, he is thinking of Rau-mahora, the daughter. They gaze long at each other, she consents to be his bride, and the war ends for ever.
summary.zh: 納蒂阿瓦大軍圍困瓦卡雷瓦要塞，城中糧水俱絕。老酋長在牆頭哀求一滴水，心狠者當眾打碎水葫蘆。他望見敵酋頭上白鷺羽飾，便高聲發問：『你能否平息這憤怒的浪濤？』塔卡蘭基朗聲答道：『浪濤必平；吾臂非犬可噬。』他自奧林吉泉注滿葫蘆，萬軍肅然；葫蘆遞上牆頭——『這水給你，也給那年輕的姑娘。』兩人久久對視；姑娘應允下嫁，干戈就此永息。

sensitivity.note: Grey names the descendants dwelling in Wellington (Te Puni) as living witness of the genealogy.

passages.text: There was, several generations since, a chief of the Taranaki tribe named Rangirarunga. His pa was called Whakarewa; it was a large pa, renowned for the strength of its fortifications. This chief had a very beautiful daughter whose name was Rau-mahora; she was so celebrated for her beauty that the fame of it had reached all parts of these islands, and had come to the ears of Te Rangi-apitirua, a chief of the Ngati-Awa tribes, whose pa was Puke-ariki, on the hill where the Governor's house stood in New Plymouth. This chief had a son named Takarangi; he was the hero of his tribe, and it may be that his heart sometimes dwelt long on the thoughts of such great loveliness. In those days there arose a war between the tribes of Te Rangi-apitirua and of the father of Rau-mahora.
passages.note: Paraphrase of George Grey, Polynesian Mythology, ch. 22 (1855); not verbatim.

passages.text: The army of the Ngati-Awa tribes marched to Taranaki to attack the pa of Rangirarunga, and the army invested that fortress and sat before it night and day, yet they could not take it; they constantly made assaults, so that its inhabitants became worn out from want of provisions and water, and many of them were near dying. At last the old chief of the pa, Rangirarunga, overcome by thirst, stood on the top of the defences and cried out to the men of the enemy's army, 'I pray you to give me one drop of water.' Some of his enemies, pitying the aged man, said 'Yes', and one ran with a calabash to give him water; but the majority, being more hard-hearted, were angry at this, and broke the calabash in his hands, so that not a drop reached the poor old man; and this was done several times, whilst his enemies continued disputing amongst themselves.
passages.note: Paraphrase of George Grey, Polynesian Mythology, ch. 22 (1855); not verbatim.

passages.text: The old chief still stood on the top of the earthen wall, and he saw the leader of the hostile force with the symbols of his rank fastened on his head - a long white comb made from the bone of a whale, and a plume of the long downy feathers of the white heron, the emblems of his chieftainship. Then was heard by all the voice of the aged man as he shouted from the top of the wall, 'Who art thou?' And the other cried out, 'Lo, he who stands here before you is Takarangi.' And the aged chief called down to him, 'Young warrior, art thou able to still the wrathful surge which foams on the hidden rocks of the shoal of O-rongo-mai-ta-kupe?' meaning, hast thou, although a chief, power to calm the wrath of these fierce men? Then proudly replied the young chief, 'The wrathful surge shall be stilled; this arm of mine is one which no dog dares to bite' - meaning that no plebeian hand dared touch his arm, made sacred by his deeds and rank, or to dispute his will.
passages.note: Paraphrase of George Grey, Polynesian Mythology, ch. 22 (1855); not verbatim.

passages.text: But what Takarangi was really thinking in his heart was, 'That dying old man is the father of Rau-mahora, of that so lovely maid. Ah, how I should grieve if one so young and innocent should die tormented with the want of water.' Then he arose, and slowly went to bring water for that aged man and for his youthful daughter; he filled a calabash, dipping it up from the cool spring which gushes up from the earth and is named Fount Oringi. No word was spoken or movement made by the crowd of fierce and angry men, but all, resting upon their arms, looked on in wonder and in silence. Calm lay the sea that was before so troubled, all timid and respectful in the lowly hero's presence; and the water was taken by Takarangi and by him held up to the aged chief. Then was heard by all the voice of Takarangi as he cried aloud to him, 'There - said I not to you, No dog would dare to bite this hand of mine? Behold the water for you - for you and for that young girl.' Then they drank, both of them, and Takarangi gazed eagerly at the young girl, and she too looked eagerly at Takarangi; long time gazed they, each one at the other; and as the warriors of the army looked on, lo, he had climbed up and was sitting at the young maiden's side; and they said amongst themselves, 'O comrades, our lord Takarangi loves war, but one would think he likes Rau-mahora almost as well.' At last a sudden thought struck the heart of the aged chief, so he said to his daughter, 'O my child, would it be pleasing to you to have this young chief for a husband?' and the young girl said, 'I like him.' Then the old man consented that his daughter should be given as a bride to Takarangi, and he took her as his wife. Thence was that war brought to an end, and the army dispersed, each man to his own village, and they came back no more to make war against the tribes of Taranaki - for ever were ended their wars against them.
passages.note: Paraphrase of George Grey, Polynesian Mythology, ch. 22 (1855); not verbatim.

title.en: Puhihuia's Elopement from Maunga-whau
title.zh: 普希惠亞私奔芒加懷烏

region.en: Mount Eden fortress, Tamaki isthmus, Aotearoa
region.zh: 紐西蘭伊甸山要塞，塔馬基地峽

period: Oral tradition; recorded 1855 (Grey, Polynesian Mythology)

source.work: George Grey, Polynesian Mythology and Ancient Traditional History of the New Zealand Race, ch. 23, The Stratagem of Puhihuia's Elopement with Te Ponga (London 1855)

summary.en: After a war of stalemates, Waikato makes peace with the fortress town on Mount Eden. At the welcome dance Puhihuia, daughter of the chief, dances 'her full-orbed eyes clear and brilliant as the full moon', and Te Ponga's heart grows wild. His slave's stratagem: call loudly for water, let the chieftainess fetch it. 'You are the water that I thirsted for', says Te Ponga at the spring; they arrange to escape. At the farewell, Puhihuia slips behind scoria rocks and runs; canoes are pre-cut of lashings and plugs, and the pursuing war party can drag only top-sides off the beach, cursing in vain.
summary.zh: 懷卡托人與伊甸山要塞僵持不下，終於議和。歡迎之夜的舞會上，酋長之女普希惠亞『明眸皎如初升滿月』，令客人首領特蓬加心旌搖蕩。他的奴僕獻計：大聲喊渴，引酋長之女親自取水。泉邊相會，特蓬加道：『你就是我所渴的水。』二人約定私奔。辭別宴上，普希惠亞閃身躲入火山岩後疾奔；早被割斷繫繩拔掉木塞的獨木舟令追兵徒勞無功，只能呆立灘頭。

sensitivity.note: Colonial-era collection.

passages.text: There was formerly a large fortified town upon Mount Eden; its defences were massive and strong, and a great number of persons inhabited the town. In the days of olden time a war was commenced by the tribes of Awhitu and of Waikato against the people who inhabited the town at Mount Eden or Maunga-whau. They engaged in a fierce war: one side first persisted in their efforts for victory until they were successful in beating the other party; then the other side in their turn succeeded in resisting their enemies and gained a victory in their turn; thus the tribes of Waikato did not succeed in destroying their enemies as they desired. Seeing no way to accomplish this, they determined to make peace; so at last they arranged a peace, and it appeared to be a sure one.
passages.note: Paraphrase of George Grey, Polynesian Mythology, ch. 23 (1855); not verbatim.

passages.text: When this peace had been made, Te Ponga, a chief from Awhitu, and one of the fiercest enemies of the people of that town, went attended by a large company to Maunga-whau; the people ran to the gates of the fortress calling out, 'Welcome, oh welcome, strangers from afar!' The strangers walked direct to the large court-yard in front of the house of the chief of the town, and there they all seated themselves. The chiefs of each party stood up and made speeches; the women lighted fires to cook food for the strangers, and when the ovens were opened the food was ranged in a long pile before the visitors. The strangers, however, ate very slowly, knowing they had better take but little food, in order not to surfeit themselves, and so that their waists might be slim when they stood up in the ranks of the dancers; and as they sat they kept on thinking, 'When will night come and the dance begin?'
passages.note: Paraphrase of George Grey, Polynesian Mythology, ch. 23 (1855); not verbatim.

passages.text: As soon as it began to get dark the dancers began, and whilst they sprang nimbly about, Puhihuia, the young daughter of the chief of the village, stood watching a good opportunity to bound forward before the assembly; when the beating time by the assembly with their feet and hands and the deep voices of the men were all in exact unison, was the fitting moment for her to bound forward into the dance. Then, just as they were all beating time together, Puhihuia perceived the proper moment had come, and forth she sprang before the assembled dancers; first she bends her head with many gestures towards the people upon the one side, and then towards those upon the other, as she performed her part beautifully; her full-orbed eyes seemed clear and brilliant as the full moon rising in the horizon, and whilst the strangers looked at the young girl they all were quite overpowered with her beauty, and Te Ponga, their young chief, felt his heart grow wild with emotion when he saw so much loveliness before him. Then up sprang the strangers to dance in their turn; the young chief Te Ponga stood peeping over them, and at last forth he bounded, and he, too, performed beautifully! The people of the village were so surprised at his agility and grace that they could do nothing but admire him, and as for the young girl Puhihuia, her heart conceived a warm passion for Te Ponga.
passages.note: Paraphrase of George Grey, Polynesian Mythology, ch. 23 (1855); not verbatim.

passages.text: At length the dance concluded, and all dispersed; all reclined in slumber except Te Ponga, who lay tossing from side to side, unable to sleep from his great love for the maiden, and devising scheme after scheme. At last a project originated in the suggestions of his private slave, who said, 'Sir, I have found out a plan by which you may accomplish your wishes. To-morrow evening, just at nightfall, as you sit in the court-yard of the chief of the village, feign to be very thirsty, and call to me to bring you a draught of water; I will take care to be at a distance, but do you continue to shout loudly and angrily to me, Sirrah, I want water, fetch me some - call loudly, so that the father of the young girl may hear; then he will probably say to his daughter, My child, why do you let our guest call in that way for water without running to fetch some for him? Then, when the young girl runs down the hill to fetch water from the fountain for you, do you follow her to the spring; but when you rise to follow her, pretend to be in a great passion with me - Where is that deaf slave of mine? I'll go and find the fellow.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of George Grey, Polynesian Mythology, ch. 23 (1855); not verbatim.

passages.text: The next evening Te Ponga called out loudly for water, louder and louder, until the chief of the village said to his young daughter, 'My child, run and fetch some water for our guest; why do you allow him to go on calling for water in that way?' Then the maiden arose, and, taking a calabash, went off to fetch water; and no sooner did Te Ponga see her starting off than he too arose and went out of the house, feigning by his voice to be very angry with his slave, but as soon as he was out he went straight after the young girl, led by her voice, who tripped along the path singing blithely and merrily as she went. When the maiden arrived at the brink of the fountain and was about to dip her calabash into it, she heard some one behind her, and, turning suddenly round - ah! there stood Te Ponga himself. She stood quite astonished for some time, and at length asked, 'What can have brought you here?' He answered, 'I came here for a draught of water.' But the girl replied, 'Ha, indeed! Did not I come here to draw water for you? Why, then, did you come?' Then Te Ponga answered, 'You are the water that I thirsted for.' She thought within herself, 'He, then, has fallen in love with me'; they conversed together, and before they separated they arranged a time when they might escape together.
passages.note: Paraphrase of George Grey, Polynesian Mythology, ch. 23 (1855); not verbatim.

passages.text: When the appointed time had arrived, he desired some chosen men of his followers to go to the landing-place on Manuka harbour, where the canoes were all hauled on shore, there to prepare one canoe in which he and all his followers might escape, to launch it and keep it afloat with every paddle in its place, and further to go round every one of the other canoes, to cut the lashings which made the top sides fast to the hulls, and to pull out all the plugs, so that those following them might find they had no canoes in which to continue the pursuit. The next morning Te Ponga, having told his host that he must return to his own country, was presented with the chief's jade mere to establish the peace, and gave his own jade mere in turn. Just before the strangers started, Puhihuia and some of the young girls of the village stole a little way along the road to accompany the strangers; Puhihuia's father seeing his daughter was going so far called out, 'Children, children, come back here!' The other girls stopped, but Puhihuia's heart beat but to the one thought of escaping with her beloved Te Ponga. So she began to run. She drew near to some large scoria rocks and glided behind them, and, when hidden from the view of those in the village, she redoubled her speed - well done, well done, young girl! She runs so fast that her body bends low as she speeds forward. When Te Ponga saw Puhihuia running in this hurried manner, he called aloud to his men, 'What is the meaning of this? let us be off as fast as we can too.' Then began a swift flight, like a feather drifting before the gale. When the people of the village saw that their young chieftainess was gone, there was a wild rushing to and fro for weapons, and whilst they thus lost their time the elopement went unmolestedly on its way. When the pursuers came out ready for the pursuit and laid hold of another canoe to haul it down towards the water, the lashings of the top sides were cut - they dragged nothing but the top sides, there lay the bottom of the canoe unmoved. Pursuit was impossible; the party that had come to make peace escaped, and returned uninjured and joyful to their own country, carrying off with them the young chieftainess, who could only be seen standing on the shore stamping with rage and threatening them in vain.
passages.note: Paraphrase of George Grey, Polynesian Mythology, ch. 23 (1855); not verbatim.

title.en: The Frog Princess of the Wilna Marshes
title.zh: 維爾紐斯沼澤的蛙公主

region.en: Wilna (Vilnius), eastern Poland / Belarus (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 維爾紐斯，波蘭東部／白俄羅斯（象徵性定位）

period: Collected by A. J. Glinski, printed at Wilna 1862; trans. Biggs 1920

source.work: A. J. Glinski, Polish Fairy Tales, trans. Maude Ashurst Biggs (1920), 'The Frog Princess'

summary.en: The youngest prince's arrow falls into a lake where a frog sits on the reeds, and she is his bride; her carpets, loaves, and dances outdo the human brides until he burns her frog-skin in his haste — and he must win her back at three huts on crooked legs.
summary.zh: 幼王子之箭落於湖中蘆葦上的青蛙處，蛙即其新娘；她織毯、烤麵包、起舞皆勝凡人新娘——直到他性急焚其蛙皮；須至三座曲腿小屋方能尋回。

sensitivity.note: Classic frog-bride tale.

passages.text: The old king, grown heavy with the cares of government, sends his three sons to the tower to shoot their arrows: where each arrow falls, there each prince must seek his wife. The eldest's arrow falls on a senator's palace, the second's on a rich man's country-house — and the youngest's flies through the green wood and falls into a lake, where a frog sits on the reeds looking fixedly at him.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Glinski, Polish Fairy Tales (Biggs trans. 1920), 'The Frog Princess'; not verbatim.

passages.text: 'Take me for your wife, and I will give it to you,' says the frog; and the prince, instructed to say he has married an Eastern lady who must be seen by no one, carries her home in his pocket. To the king's tests she answers like no other bride: she weaves a carpet so fine that it shines like the sun, bakes bread that fills whole armies, and dances at the ball more beautifully than any princess living — for at night, in the prince's own chamber, she slips off her frog-skin and is the loveliest lady in the world.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Glinski (Biggs 1920); not verbatim.

passages.text: The prince, mad to keep her beautiful forever, burns the frog-skin in the stove — and she vanishes, for her mother's enemies are still alive and the skin was her safety. He follows a ball of thread to three queer huts, saying 'Little house, move on your crooked legs free; turn your back to the wood, and your front door to me.' At the third hut, when the duck-bride at last cannot escape him, he breaks the spindle she becomes across his knee — and holds instead the hands of his beautiful princess. She builds a crystal bridge hundreds of miles long to his father's gallery, and they drive home in a golden coach to be crowned.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Glinski (Biggs 1920); not verbatim.

title.en: Princess Miranda and Prince Hero
title.zh: 米蘭達公主與英雄王子

region.en: Green island in the wide ocean (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 廣大洋中的綠島（象徵性定位）

period: Collected by A. J. Glinski, 1862; trans. Biggs 1920

source.work: A. J. Glinski, Polish Fairy Tales, trans. Maude Ashurst Biggs (1920), 'Princess Miranda and Prince Hero'

summary.en: Kosciey, king of the underground realm, gazes at the world through his telescope and sees Miranda asleep; his poisonous breath sleeps whole armies, and a twelve-headed dragon guards the iron rampart around her hill — until the prince of her dreams, Hero, with the invisible mace, comes to wake the island.
summary.zh: 地下之王科謝伊以望遠鏡窺見沉睡的米蘭達；其毒息令千軍入睡，十二首巨龍守衛山丘四周鐵壁——直到她夢中之人，持隱形狼牙棒的英雄王子降臨，喚醒全島。

sensitivity.note: Folk tale.

passages.text: On a green island in the wide ocean lives Miranda, the most beautiful princess in the world, with twelve maidens grown up beside her; whoever would force her to marriage she turns to ice with a glance.
