passages.text: The chief sorcerer of Kauhi's family told him to take the large and delicate leaves of the ape-plant and spread them over the place where Kahala must walk and sit before the judges; a human being could not touch these leaves without tearing and bruising them, but a ghost walking upon them could make no impression. Untorn leaves would condemn Mahana to the ovens, and the spirit catchers would seize the escaped ghost. The leaves were secretly placed; Kahala drew near, attended by the two spirit-sisters who had saved her, and they knew at once the ghost test by which she was to be tried: the test would only prove more evidently that she was a living human being, but would prove that they themselves were ghosts. They whispered to her to break as many of the leaves on either side of her as she could without attracting undue attention, and Kahala bruised and broke as many of the leaves as she could quietly. She was recognized at once as the child of the divine rain and wind of Manoa Valley; the torn leaves afforded ample and indisputable testimony, and Kauhi in despair recognized the girl whom he had several times tried to slay. A second form of ghost-testing was proposed by Akaaka: any face reflected in a pool or calabash of water was a spirit face, which the watcher grasped and crushed, destroying the spirit. The chief sorcerer eagerly ordered a calabash of water brought; in his anxiety he forgot himself and leaned over the calabash. His own spirit face was the only one reflected on the surface; before he could leap back and restore his spirit to his body, Akaaka leaped forward, thrust his hands down into the water and seized and crushed this spirit face between his mighty hands. The chief sorcerer fell dead by the side of the calabash by means of which he had hoped to destroy the friends of the rainbow-maiden. Kauhi was punished for his crimes: he was baked alive in the imu prepared on his own land at Waikiki, and his lands and retainers were given to Kahala and Mahana.
passages.note: Paraphrase of W. D. Westervelt, Legends of Gods and Ghosts, ch. 11 (1915); not verbatim.

title.en: How Milu Became King of the Ghosts
title.zh: 米盧如何成為鬼王

region.en: Waipio Valley, Hawaii Island, and Po (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 夏威夷島懷皮奧谷與幽冥（象徵性定位）

period: Hawaiian oral tradition; retold 1915 (Westervelt)

source.work: W. D. Westervelt, Legends of Gods and Ghosts (Hawaiian Mythology), ch. 12 (New York 1915)

summary.en: The healing god Kamaka spits into the mouth of the red-skinned farmer Lono and makes him the father of Hawaiian medicine. Milu, chief of Waipio, is healed by Lono but warned to dwell quietly in a ti-leaf house and never look out. A giant bird tears out his liver when he peeps; Lono restores him with the wrapped blood. Warned again, Milu goes surf-riding, and two returning waves crush him under. Lono remains the ancestor of good healing priests, but Milu becomes ruler of the Under-world, where ghosts surf, gamble, box and feast as they did in life.
summary.zh: 治病之神卡馬卡向紅膚農夫龍諾口中吐唾，使其成為夏威夷醫術之祖。懷皮奧酋長米盧得龍諾救治，卻被告誡：幽居芋葉小屋、切莫窺探窗外。一日巨鳥撲落，撕取其肝；龍諾以布裹血敷創救之。再被告誡後，米盧仍忍不住出海弄潮——兩道回擊的巨浪將他捲入海底。龍諾成為良醫之祖，米盧則成幽冥之王：鬼魂在其治下衝浪、博弈、角力、宴飲，一如生前。

sensitivity.note: Under-world cosmology: Milu vs. New Zealand Miru noted by Westervelt.

passages.text: Lono was a chief living on the western side of the island Hawaii. He had a very red skin and strange-looking eyes; his choice of occupation was farming, and this man had never been sick. One time he was digging with the oo, a long sharp-pointed stick or spade, and cut his foot; a stranger, Kamaka, a god of healing, was sent for and bound pounded popolo fruit and leaves with salt upon the wound. As he journeyed on, Lono followed, saying he had left his lands in the care of friends and hastened after him to learn how to heal other people. The god said, 'Lono, open your mouth!' This Lono did, and the god spat in his mouth, so that the saliva could be taken into every part of Lono's body; thus a part of the god became a part of Lono, and he became very skilful in the use of all healing remedies.
passages.note: Paraphrase of W. D. Westervelt, Legends of Gods and Ghosts, ch. 12 (1915); not verbatim.

passages.text: The god said, 'It is not right for us to stay together; you must go to a separate place and give yourself up to healing people.' Lono turned aside to dwell in Waimanu and Waipio Valleys and began to practise healing, becoming very noted. Another god, Kalae, was trying to find some way to kill Milu, chief of Waipio, and was always making him sick; Milu heard of the skill of Lono, who came, slapped Milu all over the body and healed him from all the sickness inside the body caused by Kalae. But there was danger from outside, so he said: 'You must build a ti-leaf house and dwell there quietly for some time, letting your disease rest. If a company should come by the house making sport with a great noise, do not go out, because when you go they will come up and get you for your death. Do not open the ti leaves and look out; the day you do this you shall die.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of W. D. Westervelt, Legends of Gods and Ghosts, ch. 12 (1915); not verbatim.

passages.text: For some time Milu remained in the house; then Waipio was full of resounding noises and a great bird appeared in the sky, resplendent in all kinds of feathers, swaying from precipice to precipice, while the people shouted until the valley re-echoed. Milu became tired of that great noise and could not patiently obey his physician, so he pushed aside some of the ti leaves of his house and looked out upon the bird. That was the time when the bird swept down upon the house, thrusting a claw under Milu's arm and tearing out his liver. Lono saw this and ran after the bird, which flew to a deep pit in the lava and dashed inside, leaving blood spread on the stones; Lono came, saw the blood, took it and wrapped it in a piece of tapa cloth and returned to the place where the chief lay almost dead. He poured some medicine into the wound and pushed the tapa and blood inside, and Milu was soon healed. The place where the bird hid is called to this day Ke-ake-o-Milu, the liver of Milu.
passages.note: Paraphrase of W. D. Westervelt, Legends of Gods and Ghosts, ch. 12 (1915); not verbatim.

passages.text: Then Lono told him that another death threatened him and would soon appear; he must dwell in quietness. For some time Milu lived in peace; then one day the surf of Waipio became very high and the people entered into surf-riding with great joy and loud shouts. Milu was impatient of the restraint and forgot the words of Lono, and went out to bathe in the surf. He let the first and second waves go by and launched himself upon the third; he went out again, and as he came to the shore the first and second waves were hurled back from the shore in a great mass against the wave upon which he was riding; the two great masses of water struck and pounded Milu, whirling and crowding him down, while the surf-board was caught in the raging waters and thrown toward the shore. Milu was completely lost in the deep water. The people cried, 'Milu is dead! The chief is dead!' The god Kalae thought he had killed Milu, so he with the other poison-gods went on a journey to Mauna Loa, where Kapo and Pua, the poison-gods of Maui, joined them; they discovered a forest on Molokai and entered into the trees of that forest as kupua spirits, becoming the medicinal or poison qualities in the trees. Lono remained in Waipio Valley, becoming the ancestor and teacher of all the good healing priests of Hawaii, but Milu became the ruler of the Under-world, where he established ghostly sports like those his subjects had enjoyed before death - kilu with polished cocoanut shells, konane, gambling, boxing and wrestling, leaping from precipices into ghostly swimming-pools, feasting and fighting - living the ghost life as they had on earth. Sometimes the ruler was forgotten and the ancient Hawaiians called the Under-world by his name, Milu; the New Zealanders frequently gave their Under-world the name Miru.
passages.note: Paraphrase of W. D. Westervelt, Legends of Gods and Ghosts, ch. 12 (1915); not verbatim.

title.en: Ka-ilio-hae Visits the King of Ghosts
title.zh: 野狗魂朝見鬼王

region.en: Kekaa, Lahaina, Maui, and the ghost-land (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 毛伊島拉海納凱卡與幽冥（象徵性定位）

period: Hawaiian oral tradition; retold 1915 (Westervelt)

source.work: W. D. Westervelt, Legends of Gods and Ghosts (Hawaiian Mythology), ch. 13 (New York 1915)

summary.en: The wild dog Ka-ilio-hae sinks into death; his spirit creeps from the left eye, perches like a bird, and is borne toward Kekaa, doorway of Maui's ghosts. His ghost-sister, an aumakua-ho-ola, warns him never to taste the shadow-food, and coaches him through the three watchmen and the two blocking heads to the court of the ghost king Walia: answer 'Walia' and 'The Great Death', push the heads aside, and cry 'He comes to see the Divine One'. Before the third call seals the walls, she drives him home and shoves the shivering spirit back into the foot, up the body, to life.
summary.zh: 『野狗』卡伊利奧哈埃沉入彌留；魂魄自左眼竄出，如鳥棲枝，被引往毛伊鬼魂之門凱卡。其幽魂姐姐——能起死回生的奧馬庫阿——告誡他勿食幻影之食，並傳授過三關、避雙頭、朝見鬼王瓦利亞的口訣。第三聲召喚將封閉石牆之前，姐姐硬將他拖回海濱；亡魂畏懼軀體的氣味屢屢逃縮，被姐姐自腳踝推入、順體而上——胸口起伏，家人知道他又活過來了。

sensitivity.note: Detailed ghost-topography record.

passages.text: When any person lay in an unconscious state it was supposed by the ancient Hawaiians that death had taken possession of the body and opened the door for the spirit to depart. Ka-ilio-hae, the wild dog, had been sick for days and at last sank into unconsciousness. The spirit of life crept out of the body and finally departed from the left eye into a corner of the house, buzzing like an insect; it looked back over the body it had left, which appeared like a massive mountain with eyes like deep caves. The spirit became afraid, went outside and rested on the roof of the house; the people began to wail loudly, and the ghost fled from the noise to a cocoanut-tree and perched like a bird in the branches. Soon he felt the impulse of the spirit-land moving him away from his old home; he leaped from tree to tree and flew from place to place, wandering toward Kekaa, the place from which the ghosts leave the island of Maui for their home in the permanent spirit-land, the Under-world.
passages.note: Paraphrase of W. D. Westervelt, Legends of Gods and Ghosts, ch. 13 (1915); not verbatim.

passages.text: Near this doorway to the spirit-world he met the ghost of a sister who had died long before, to whom was given the power of sometimes turning a ghost back to its body again - an aumakua-ho-ola, a spirit making alive. She called to him and warned him that when her husband was at home he must not yield to any invitation from him to enter their house nor partake of any of the food her husband might urge him to eat: the home and the food would be only the shadows of real things, and would destroy his power of becoming alive again. She led him to the place of whirlwinds where many spirits were planning to enjoy all the sports of their former life - surf-riding, rolling the ulu-maika, boxing, wrestling, gambling games, and crowds around the hulas. There was a strange quality which fettered every new-born ghost: he could only go in the direction into which he was pushed by the hand of some stronger power; the newcomer started to join the games, but the sister slapped him on the breast and drove him away, for these were shadow games into which those who entered could never go back to the substantial things of life.
passages.note: Paraphrase of W. D. Westervelt, Legends of Gods and Ghosts, ch. 13 (1915); not verbatim.

passages.text: Then the sister led her brother to a great field, stone walled, in which were such fine grass houses as were built only for chiefs of the highest rank, and pointed to a narrow passage into which he must enter by himself. 'This is the home of Walia, the high chief of the ghosts living in this place. You must go to him. Listen to all he says to you. Say little. Return quickly. There will be three watchmen guarding this passage. The first will ask you, What is the fruit of your heart? You will answer, Walia. The second watchman will ask why you come; again answer, Walia. At the end of the entrance the third guardian stands holding a raised spear ready to strike; call to him, Ka-make-loa, the Great Death - that is the name of his spear - then reply, To see the chief. When you stand at the door of the great house you will see two heads bending together so that you cannot enter; point your hands straight before you between them and open your arms, pushing these guards off on each side, then the ala-nui, the great way, will be open for you. You will see kahilis moving over the chiefs; the king will awake and call, Why does this traveller come? You will reply quickly, He comes to see the Divine One. Listen and remember and you will be alive again.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of W. D. Westervelt, Legends of Gods and Ghosts, ch. 13 (1915); not verbatim.

passages.text: Ka-ilio-hae did as he was told with the three watchmen, and each one stepped back, saying 'Noa' - the tabu is lifted - and he pushed by. At the door he shoved the two heads to the side and entered the chief's house, falling on his hands and knees while the servants waved the kahilis. The chief awoke, looked at him and said: 'Aloha, stranger, come near. Who is the high chief of your land?' Then Ka-ilio-hae gave the name of his king and the genealogy from ancient times of the chiefs dead and in the spirit-world. The queen of ghosts arose, and the kneeling spirit saw one more beautiful than any woman in all the island, and fell on his face before her. The king told him to go back and enter his body and tell his people about troubles near at hand. While he was before the king twice he heard messengers call that the sports were all over; any one not heeding would be thrown into the darkest place of the home of the ghosts when the third call had been sounded. The sister knew that at the third call the stone walls around the king's houses would close and her brother would be held fast forever in the spirit-land; she uttered her incantations, passed the guard, softly called, seized him and pushed him outside. She knew well what must be done to restore the spirit to the body; when they came to the place where the body lay she found a hole in the corner of the house and pushed the spirit through. When he saw the body he was very much afraid and tried to escape, but the sister caught him and pushed him inside the foot up to the knee; he did not like the smell of the body and tried to rush back, but she pushed him inside again and held the foot fast and shook him and made him go to the head. The family heard a little sound in the mouth and saw breath moving the breast, then they knew that he was alive again; they warmed the body and gave a little food, and when strength returned he told his family all about his wonderful journey into the land of ghosts.
passages.note: Paraphrase of W. D. Westervelt, Legends of Gods and Ghosts, ch. 13 (1915); not verbatim.

title.en: Kalai-pahoa, the Poison-god of the Trees
title.zh: 毒神卡萊帕霍亞

region.en: Mauna Loa forest, Molokai (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 摩洛凱島冒納羅亞林（象徵性定位）

period: Hawaiian oral tradition; retold 1915 (Westervelt)

source.work: W. D. Westervelt, Legends of Gods and Ghosts (Hawaiian Mythology), ch. 14 (New York 1915)

summary.en: After Milu's death the death-gods left Waipio for Maui and entered the trees of a Mauna Loa forest, becoming the medicine and poison of the woods. The ruined gambler Kane-ia-kama, told in dream to 'bet your bones', wins everything and is shown which trees hold the gods; offerings set, he sends woodcutters whose sap-blood and flying chips kill them - until leaf cloaks of ieie protect the men. The chief cuts the gods from their trees; the strongest, named Kalai-pahoa, killed all who drank at a poisoned spring, passed from Kahekili to Kamehameha, and lies in the Bishop Museum today.
summary.zh: 米盧死後，諸死神自懷皮奧遷往毛伊，遁入冒納羅亞林中諸樹，化為草木之藥性與毒性。傾家賭徒卡內亞卡馬夜聞神諭『以骨為注』，連戰連勝，又被指認諸神所棲之樹。他遣人伐木取神：樹血飛濺，伐木者暴斃；以伊埃藤葉為衣方得安然。最強之神名『卡萊帕霍亞』——意為『被石斧所刻者』——其毒泉曾使飲者全滅；後由毛伊王卡赫基利傳至卡美哈梅哈，今藏於檀香山主教博物館。

sensitivity.note: Poison-rite (pule-ana-ana) summarized; no operational detail beyond the legend's own terms.

passages.text: The Bishop Museum of Honolulu has images of many of the gods of long ago: a helmeted head of wicker-work covered with red feathers bordered with yellow - the mighty war-god of Kamehameha - and a squat rough image crudely carved out of wood, Kamehameha's poison-god. The ancient Hawaiians were acquainted with poisons of various kinds; one Hawaiian writer said: 'The opihi-awa is a poison shell-fish, bitter and deadly; Kalai-pahoa is also a tree in which there is the power to kill.' Kamehameha's poison-god was called Kalai-pahoa because it was cut from that tree which grew in the upland forest on the island of Molokai.
passages.note: Paraphrase of W. D. Westervelt, Legends of Gods and Ghosts, ch. 14 (1915); not verbatim.

passages.text: When the priest wanted Kalai-pahoa he was taken down and anointed with cocoanut-oil and wrapped in a fresh kapa cloth, set up above the altar with a feast before him - awa to drink, and pig, fish, and poi to eat. The priest who had special care of this god would scrape off a little from the wood, put it in an awa cup, hold the cup before the god, chanting a prayer for the life of the king, the government and the people; one of the priests would drink the contents and quickly take food. Those watching would see a red flush creep over his cheeks while the eyes became glassy and the breath short like that of a dying man; then the priest would touch his lips to the stick Mai-ola and have his life restored - Mai-ola was a god who had another tree, and when Kalai-pahoa entered his tree on Molokai, Mai-ola entered another tree and became the enemy of the poison-god. The priests of the poison-god were powerful in the rite called pule-ana-ana, praying to death: it was believed they scraped the body of the image and put the pieces in the food of the one they wished to pray to death.
passages.note: Paraphrase of W. D. Westervelt, Legends of Gods and Ghosts, ch. 14 (1915); not verbatim.

passages.text: A legend told by the old people explained the coming of medicinal and poisonous properties into the trees. After the death of Milu the gods left Waipio Valley and crossed the channel to Maui; these gods had all kinds of power for evil - stopping the breath, chilling or burning the body, inflicting death. Pua and Kapo, goddesses having medicinal power, joined the party, and all the gods went up Mauna Loa into a large and magnificent forest which they loved and of which they became gods. Near this forest lived Kane-ia-kama, a high chief who was a very great gambler and had gambled away all his possessions; in sleep he heard a voice, 'O Kane-ia-kama, begin your play again', and when he protested he had nothing left, the voice said, 'Bet your bones, and see what will happen.' He bet his body and won until he had more wealth than any one on the island.
passages.note: Paraphrase of W. D. Westervelt, Legends of Gods and Ghosts, ch. 14 (1915); not verbatim.

passages.text: Then the voice showed him the trees into which the gods had entered, explained all their characteristics, and ordered him to take offerings of pigs, fish, cocoanuts, bananas, chickens and kapas and place them at the roots of these trees. For some reason he sent woodcutters to cut the gods out of them with their stone axes. They began to cut: the koko, the blood of the trees as the natives termed the flowing sap, and the chips flying out struck some of the woodcutters and they fell dead. Kane-ia-kama made cloaks of the long leaves of the ieie vine and tied them around his men so that their bodies could not be touched, then the work was easily accomplished. The chief kept these images of gods cut from the medicinal trees; the most powerful was that whose voice he had heard in the night, to which he gave the name Kalai-pahoa, The-one-cut-by-the-stone-axe. It was said that when Kane-kulana-ula changed into his tree form he leaped into it with a tremendous flash of lightning, thus the great mana went into that tree. A piece of this tree fell into a spring at Kaakee near the maika field on Molokai, and all the people who drank at that spring died; they filled it up, and the chiefs ruled that no one should keep branches or pieces of the tree - only the carved gods were to be preserved. Kahekili, king of Maui, had these images as household gods and told Kamehameha to wait and he should have the poison-god and the government over all the islands; after Kahekili's death Kamehameha did conquer all the islands and Kalai-pahoa came into his possession. The overthrow of idolatry came in 1819, when most of the wooden gods were burned or thrown into ponds and rivers, but a few were concealed by their caretakers, among them the two gods now in the Bishop Museum.
passages.note: Paraphrase of W. D. Westervelt, Legends of Gods and Ghosts, ch. 14 (1915); not verbatim.

title.en: Puna Escapes the Dragon-goddess Kiha-wahine
title.zh: 普納逃出龍女神之掌

region.en: Molokai to Kilauea, Hawaii (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 摩洛凱至基拉韋厄（象徵性定位）

period: Hawaiian oral tradition; retold 1915 (Westervelt)

source.work: W. D. Westervelt, Legends of Gods and Ghosts (Hawaiian Mythology), ch. 16 (New York 1915)

summary.en: Out surfing, chief Puna is lured to Molokai by Kiha-wahine, who keeps him in a cave-house as husband. Her brother Hinole recognizes him and coaches his escape: ask for the ice-water of Poliahu, and bore a hole in the jar. The dragon goes for the water, finds it leaking on the ground, and Puna has reached Pele's pit. Gathering all the dragons of the islands, she threatens to fill the crater; they spit drool that almost quenches the fire - but the flames rise, burn the dragons, and Kiha-wahine leaps into the shadow-lake Loko-aka. Her brother Hinole becomes the hinalea fish; Puna returns to Haumea, and is later hanged in a breadfruit tree by chief Kou - the tree opens and swallows his wife, whose akala skirt still grows as a vine.
summary.zh: 衝浪之時，酋長普納被龍女基哈瓦希內誘至摩洛凱，囚於洞屋為夫。其兄希諾勒認出他並授計逃脫：求取冒納凱阿雪山之冰水，並在水罐上鑽孔。龍女負罐遠行，發現罐水漏盡，普納已抵佩蕾火山口。她召來群島之龍圍攻火山口，口吐涎沫幾滅神火；火勢驟起，燒斃群龍，龍女跳入影湖羅科阿卡。其兄希諾勒化為海鏢鱸魚；普納返歸妻室，後被酋長庫縊於麵包樹——樹身裂開吞入其妻，其紅藤裙至今仍生為藤蔓。

sensitivity.note: Dragon (mo-o) cycle; Westervelt notes this is a reworking of 'The Wonderful Breadfruit Tree'.

passages.text: Haumea is said to have taken as her husband Puna, a chief of Oahu. He and his people were going around the island; the surf was not very good and they wanted to find a better place. At last they found a fine surf-place where a beautiful woman was floating on the sea. She called to Puna, 'This is not a good place for surf'; he asked where there was one, and she answered, 'I know where there is one, far outside.' She desired to get Puna; they swam way out in the sea until they were out of sight, and forgot everything else but each other. This woman was Kiha-wahine. The people on the beach wailed but did not take canoes to help them; they swam over to Molokai, left their surf-boards on the beach and went inland to the cave house of the woman. Puna stayed there as a kind of prisoner and obeyed her commands; she took care of him and prepared his food, and they lived as husband and wife for a long time, until at last his real body began to change.
passages.note: Paraphrase of W. D. Westervelt, Legends of Gods and Ghosts, ch. 16 (1915); not verbatim.

passages.text: Once he went out of the cave and heard voices loud and confused, but could not go, because the woman had laid her law on him that if he went away he would be killed. In the morning he went down to the sea and saw many sports; while he was watching, one of the men, Hinole, the brother of his wife, saw him and was pleased, inviting him to eat and talk. Hinole asked whence he came; Puna told him all the story, and Hinole told him his wife was a goddess: 'When you return and come near to the place, go very easily and softly, and you will see her in her real nature as a mo-o, or dragon; but she knows all that you are doing and what we are saying. Your first wife, Haumea, is the first born of all the other women. It is my thought to save your life, so that you can look into the eyes of your first wife.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of W. D. Westervelt, Legends of Gods and Ghosts, ch. 16 (1915); not verbatim.

passages.text: Puna went slowly and softly back and saw his wife as a dragon; she heard his breathing, quickly changed to a human body and cursed him for coming quietly and hiding, saying, 'Perhaps I will eat your eyes.' But they dwelt together and had peace. One day Puna was breathing hard, for he was thirsty and wanted the water of the gods - the water of Poliahu of Mauna Kea, the snow-covered mountain of Hawaii, cold and heavy with ice, which his good grandparents always brought for him in his youth. The woman said, 'Your desire for water is not a hard thing to satisfy; I will go and get the water.' Before he had spoken of his desire he had made a little hole in the water-jar, as Hinole had told him, that the woman might spend a long time and let him escape. She arose and went away; he also arose and followed, found a canoe and crossed to Maui, another boat going to Hawaii, and landed at Kau. He went up and stood on the edge of the pit of Pele; those living in the crater saw him and cried out, 'Here is a man, a husband for our sister.' He quickly went down into the crater and dwelt with them.
passages.note: Paraphrase of W. D. Westervelt, Legends of Gods and Ghosts, ch. 16 (1915); not verbatim.

passages.text: Kiha-wahine went to Poliahu, but could not fill the water-jar: when the jar was lifted it became light, and she saw the water lying on the ground and her husband far beyond at the pit of Pele. She became angry and called all the dragons of Molokai, Lanai, Maui, Kahoolawe and Hawaii; when she had gathered them she went up to Kilauea and stood on the edge of the crater, telling the people below to give her the husband. They refused, crying out, 'Where is your husband? This is the husband of our sister; he does not belong to you, O mischief-maker.' Then the dragon-goddess said, 'If you do not give up this man, I will send all my people and fill up this crater and capture all your fires.' The dragons threw their drooling saliva in the pit and almost destroyed the fire where Pele lived; then the fire moved and began to rise with great strength, burning off all the saliva, and Kiha-wahine and the rest of the dragons could not stand the heat; the fire caught them and killed a large part, while earthquakes opened the rocks and fire followed the fleeing dragons. Kiha-wahine ran and leaped down the precipice into a fish-pond called by the name of the shadow of the dragon, Loko-aka, the shadow lake; so she was imprisoned in the pond, husbandless, scarcely escaping with her life. When she went back to Molokai she meant to kill Hinole for aiding Puna to escape, but he leaped into the sea and became the Hinalea, a fish dearly loved by the fishermen of the islands; she caught him at last in a basket baited with pounded sea-eggs and crabs - this is the way the Hinalea is caught to this day - and compelled him ever after to retain the form of the fish.
passages.note: Paraphrase of W. D. Westervelt, Legends of Gods and Ghosts, ch. 16 (1915); not verbatim.

passages.text: After Puna had escaped according to the directions of Hinole he returned to Oahu and saw his wife Haumea. After Puna disappeared, Kou became the new chief of Oahu, and Puna went to live in the mountains above Kalihi-uka. One day he came to a banana plantation, ate, and lay down to rest; the watchmen of the new chief found him, took his loin-cloth, tied his hands behind his back, and brought him to Kou, who killed him and hung the body in the branches of a breadfruit-tree at Wai-kaha-lulu below the steep diving rocks of the Nuuanu stream. When Haumea returned from gathering moss and fish she heard of the death of her husband; as she hurried down all the people shouted, 'This is the wife of the dead man.' She found Puna hanging on the branches; then she made that breadfruit-tree open. Leaving her pa-u on the ground where she stood, she stepped inside the tree and bade it close about her and appear the same as before; the akala of which the pa-u had been made took root and grew into a large vine. The fat of the body of Puna fell down through the branches and the dogs ate below the tree; one of these dogs belonged to the chief Kou: it came back to the house, played with the chief, then leaped, caught him by the throat and killed him.
passages.note: Paraphrase of W. D. Westervelt, Legends of Gods and Ghosts, ch. 16 (1915); not verbatim.

title.en: Hiku Swings His Bride Up from Milu
title.zh: 希庫鞦韆吊回亡妻

region.en: Waipio pit of Milu, Hawaii Island (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 夏威夷島懷皮奧米盧之坑（象徵性定位）

period: Hawaiian oral tradition (Kalakaua family version); retold 1915 (Westervelt)

source.work: W. D. Westervelt, Legends of Gods and Ghosts (Hawaiian Mythology), ch. 18 (New York 1915)

summary.en: Ku's children Hiku and Kewalu wed by the tabu surf of Kona. Hiku pines for the upland forest and slips away through fog, vines and rain; Kewalu, entangled in the ieie she chased him through, winds the vines about her neck - the first suicide in Hawaiian story - and her spirit creeps down to Milu. Ku teaches Hiku the one daring remedy: rub himself with rancid kukui oil, descend by an ieie rope through the Waipio pit, and win the ghost unnoticed. Among the ghosts he wins a kilu game, answers Kewalu's mele with the secret response, swings her in his lap and shrinks her spirit smaller and smaller until Ku hauls them up; sealed in a cocoanut shell, her ghost is poured in at the feet and charmed upward until the eyes open.
summary.zh: 庫神之子女希庫與凱瓦魯在科納聖灘結為夫婦。希庫思慕山林，趁夜遁走；凱瓦魯追夫不成，被伊埃藤纏頸自縊——夏威夷神話中第一宗自殺——其魂徐徐墮入幽冥米盧。庫授奇策：以腐臭寇阿油塗身，循懷皮奧之坑沿伊埃藤而下。冥界中他贏得基盧賭局，以密語應和她之歌；鞦韆戲中攬其入懷，一邊搖盪一邊誦咒使她越縮越小，直至父親收繩上提。魂被封入椰殼，自足底灌入遺體，誦咒引魂上行——雙目終於重開。

sensitivity.note: Descent-resurrection cluster flagship; Westervelt links it to the Maori 'Deceiving of Kewa' chant.

passages.text: Ku, one of the most widely known gods of the Pacific Ocean, was thought by the Hawaiians to have dwelt as a mortal for some time on the western side of the island Hawaii. He chose a chiefess by the name of Hina as his wife, and to them were born two children. When he withdrew from his residence among men he left a son on the uplands of North Kona, and a daughter on the seashore of the same district. The son, Hiku-i-kana-hele, Hiku of the forest, lived with his mother; the daughter, Kewalu, dwelt under the care of guardian chiefs and priests by a temple, and was perfected in all arts pertaining to the very high chiefs. Hiku was proficient in all the feats of manly strength and skill upon which chiefs of the highest rank prided themselves; to him were given many of the supernatural powers of his father, though his mother guarded him from the knowledge that he had a sister.
passages.note: Paraphrase of W. D. Westervelt, Legends of Gods and Ghosts, ch. 18 (1915); not verbatim.

passages.text: Day after day the young chief heard the rejoicing of people by the sea; a trusty retainer reported that he had found certain tabu surf waters of the Kona beach where a very high chiefess alone played with her surf-board, her beauty and skill so great that the people clapped their hands like many thunder-storms. Hiku prepared the best surf-board that could be made, anointed his body with kukui oil until it glistened like polished leaves, and went boldly to the tabu surf waters of his sister. The gods of the sea favored Hiku: he carried the surf-board more royally than any chief the people had ever known, and rode to the shore on the crests of the highest waves performing wonderful feats by his magic power. Kewalu took the wreath of rare and fragrant flowers which she wore and threw it around his shoulders as a token to all the people that she had taken him to be her husband; thus Hiku married his sister, Kewalu, according to the custom of that time, because she was the only one of all the people equal to him in rank and beauty.
passages.note: Paraphrase of W. D. Westervelt, Legends of Gods and Ghosts, ch. 18 (1915); not verbatim.

passages.text: Hiku at last grew weary of the life by the sea and wanted the forest on the mountain and the cold air of the uplands. One night he rose up very quietly and passed out into the darkness; the leaves rustled in welcome and the night birds hastened him on, but Kewalu was awakened and hastened after him, her plaintive cry louder and clearer than the voices of the night birds: 'E Hiku, return! O my love, wait for Kewalu!' Hiku by his magic power sent thick fogs and mists around her, threw the long flexible vines of the ieie down into the path, so that she stumbled and fell again and again; the rain destroyed the kapa mantle she had thrown around her. The ancient chant says: Hiku is climbing up the hill; branches and vines are in the way; hopeless the quest, but Kewalu is calling, E Hiku, beloved! At last she could no longer hear the retreating footsteps; chilled and desolate she crept back to the village and into the grass house, intending to put an end to her life. The ieie vines held her arms and legs, but she partially disentangled herself and wound them around her head and neck; soon the tendrils grew tight and slowly but surely choked the beautiful chiefess to death - this was the first suicide in the records of Hawaiian mythology. As the body became lifeless the spirit crept upward to the lua-uhane, the little hole in the corner of the eye, the spirit-door, and slowly and sadly journeyed to Milu, the Under-world home of the ghosts.
passages.note: Paraphrase of W. D. Westervelt, Legends of Gods and Ghosts, ch. 18 (1915); not verbatim.

passages.text: His father, the god Ku, had been watching him and had seen the suicide of the beautiful Kewalu. He called Hiku and told him how heedless he had been in his treatment of Kewalu, and that only by the most daring effort could he hope to regain his loved bride: he could go to the Under-world, meet the ghosts and bring his sister back, but if the ghosts discovered and captured him they would punish him with the severest torments. Hiku was determined. He prepared a cocoanut-shell full of oil made from decayed kukui nuts, very vile and foul smelling, and a long stout rope of ieie vines. Ku knew where the door to the Under-world was, a hole near the seashore in the valley of Waipio. Hiku rubbed his body all over with the rancid kukui oil, gave the ieie vine into the keeping of his father, and slowly Ku let the vine down until at last Hiku stood in the strange land of Milu. He rubbed his body once more thoroughly with the oil and disfigured himself with dirt; as he passed from place to place searching for Kewalu the ghosts said, 'What a bad-smelling spirit!' and turned away from him as if he were one of the most unworthy ghosts dwelling in Milu.
passages.note: Paraphrase of W. D. Westervelt, Legends of Gods and Ghosts, ch. 18 (1915); not verbatim.

passages.text: In the realm of Milu he saw the people in the game of rolling cocoanut-shells to hit a post; Kulioe had lost all his property to the daughter of Milu, and saw Hiku: 'If you are a skilful man perhaps you should play with these two girls.' Kulioe bet his bones; Hiku swung the cup, and it glided and twisted around the floor and struck the post, counting five and winning the first bet; then he threw the cup numbered twenty, won all the property and gave it back to Kulioe. At last he found Kewalu by the side of the high chief Milu, who had seen the beautiful princess as she came into the Under-world and called her at once to the highest place in his court. While she was singing her mele the people were startled to hear a clear voice chanting the response which was known by no other person but Hiku. She wandered from place to place looking for Hiku; the only one very close was a foul-smelling, dirt-covered ghost, and Hiku in a low tone warned her to be very careful and not recognize him, but assured her that he had come in person to rescue her and take her back to her old home.
passages.note: Paraphrase of W. D. Westervelt, Legends of Gods and Ghosts, ch. 18 (1915); not verbatim.

passages.text: When Hiku came to the place where the vine was hanging he took hold to see if Ku was still carefully guarding the other end; having made himself sure of the aid of the god, he tied the end into a strong loop and seated himself in it, beginning to swing back and forth, sometimes rising high and sometimes resting with his feet on the ground. Kewalu came near and begged to be allowed to swing; he would only consent on the condition that she would sit in his lap. The ghosts thought this would be an excellent arrangement and shouted their approval. Then Hiku took the spirit of Kewalu in his strong arms and began to swing slowly, then more and more rapidly, higher and higher, while he gave the signal to Ku to pull them up; almost imperceptibly the swing receded from the spirit world. All this time he had been gently rubbing the spirit and softly uttering charm after charm, so that while they were swaying in the air she was growing smaller and smaller. Suddenly it dawned upon some of the beholders that the vine was being drawn up to the Upper-world: the cry arose, 'He is stealing the woman!' The Under-world was in a great uproar; some of the ghosts leaped as high as they could, others called for Hiku to return, others uttered charms to cause his downfall; but no one could leap high enough to touch Hiku, and the power of all the charms was defeated by the god Ku, who rapidly drew the vine upward. Hiku succeeded in charming the ghost of Kewalu into the cocoanut-shell and stopping the opening tight with his fingers, so that the spirit could not escape, and brought her back to the land of mortals. The spirits of the dead must find their way back little by little through the body from the feet to the eyes; Hiku knelt at the feet, cold and stiff in death, placed the small hole in the end of the shell against the tender spot in the bottom of one of the cold feet, removed his finger and uttered the incantations which would allure the ghost into the body. Little by little the soul of Kewalu came back, and the body grew warm from the feet upward, until at last the eyes opened and the soul looked out upon the blessed life restored to it by the skill and bravery of Hiku.
passages.note: Paraphrase of W. D. Westervelt, Legends of Gods and Ghosts, ch. 18 (1915); not verbatim.

title.en: The Silver Saucer and the Transparent Apple
title.zh: 銀碟與晶蘋果

region.en: Russian village (symbolic pin at Rostov)
region.zh: 俄羅斯村莊（象徵性定位於羅斯托夫）

period: Retold by Arthur Ransome, 1916

source.work: Arthur Ransome, Old Peter's Russian Tales (1916), 'The Tale of the Silver Saucer and the Transparent Apple'

summary.en: A kind stepdaughter finds a silver saucer and a transparent apple in a beggar's pack; rolled on the saucer, the apple shows any city she wishes — until it shows her the drowned daughter of the tsar, and only her kind answer to the drowning woman can end the tale.
summary.zh: 善良繼女自乞丐行囊中得銀碟與晶蘋果；蘋果置碟上滾動，可照見心中所願之城——直至映出溺水而亡的沙皇之女；唯她善意作答，方能終結亡靈之囑。

sensitivity.note: Folk tale.

passages.text: A poor widow's little daughter gives her bread to a beggar at the gate, and the beggar leaves in the pack a silver saucer and a transparent apple. Rolled on the saucer, the apple shows any city she asks for — and the stepmother's own daughter, greedy to see more, asks for the one city no one may look on: the city of the dead tsar's daughter, drowned in the river.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ransome, Old Peter's Russian Tales (1916), 'The Silver Saucer and the Transparent Apple'; not verbatim.

passages.text: In the crystal city of the dead the daughter of the tsar sits in a white chamber, and her voice comes through the apple: 'Who loves me more than all the world?' The kind girl answers, 'I do, poor drowned daughter of the tsar,' and takes up the saucer — but the voice is not done. She runs weeping to the river and tells the tsar; they drag the river, find the princess with a silver moon on her breast, and lay her in the palace in a glass coffin among flowers.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ransome (1916); not verbatim.

passages.text: Then the kind girl is sent for, and the drowned tsar's daughter rises in her coffin and gives her the silver saucer and the transparent apple as her own — for the kind girl had been the only one who ever answered her. The stepmother and her lazy daughter are shut out of the house for ever, and the tsar makes the kind girl his daughter; and some say the drowned princess took her dulcimer and swam back into the Volkhov to look for the little shepherd who had loved her.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ransome (1916); not verbatim.

title.en: Sadko and the Sea-King: The Gusli That Stopped the Sea
title.zh: 薩德科與海王：令海止息的古斯里琴

region.en: Novgorod and Lake Ilmen (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 諾夫哥羅德與伊爾門湖（象徵性定位）

period: Retold by Arthur Ransome, 1916

source.work: Arthur Ransome, Old Peter's Russian Tales (1916), 'Sadko'

summary.en: The poor gusli-player Sadko plays so beautifully on the shore of Lake Ilmen that the Sea-King rises to thank him; taught how to win gold at the merchants' feast, Sadko becomes the richest trader in Novgorod — until the sea demands him, and he plays the king to sleep among the daughters of the sea.
summary.zh: 貧苦琴師薩德科於伊爾門湖畔奏古斯里琴，樂聲之美令海王升水面致謝；習得商宴贏金之法，遂為諾夫哥羅德首富——直至大海索其人；他在海王眾女間奏樂催眠。

sensitivity.note: Novgorod bylina as retold for children.

passages.text: Poor Sadko sits twelve days on the shore of Lake Ilmen without a bite, and at last, because he has nothing else, he plays his gusli. The water of the lake stirs, and the Sea-King himself rises out of the waves to thank him: 'You have played so well that you have made the sea move when it did not wish to move — now the sea is calm again, and you shall be paid for your music.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ransome, Old Peter's Russian Tales (1916), 'Sadko'; not verbatim.

passages.text: He teaches Sadko how to win a wager from the merchants of Novgorod — 'buy every fish with golden fins in the market, whatever the price' — and Sadko becomes the richest man in the city, buys ships, and sails the seas trading. But the Sea-King has not forgotten him: at sea a storm rises that no sacrifice can calm, and the lot falls to Sadko to go down into the water to the Sea-King, playing his gusli all the while.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ransome (1916); not verbatim.

passages.text: Down in the crystal palace Sadko plays for the daughters of the sea; when the Sea-King rises to dance, the storms above wreck ships, until St. Nicholas sends word that Sadko should break his gusli — for a landman cannot live under the sea. He breaks the strings, wakes on the shore of the Volkhov, and builds the church of St. Nicholas that still stands by the market in Novgorod.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ransome (1916); not verbatim.

title.en: Frost: The Red Nose Who Cracks the Trees
title.zh: 嚴寒：裂樹的紅鼻老人

region.en: Russian winter forest (symbolic pin at Suzdal)
region.zh: 俄羅斯冬日森林（象徵性定位於蘇茲達爾）

period: Retold by Arthur Ransome, 1916

source.work: Arthur Ransome, Old Peter's Russian Tales (1916), 'Frost'

summary.en: Sent to freeze in the forest by a stepmother, the little stepdaughter is found by Frost — red-nosed, cracking the branches above her — who comes down lower and lower with his bitter words; her courteous answers make him cloak her in furs instead, while the stepmother's own daughter, rude to the cold, is frozen where she sits.
summary.zh: 繼母遣繼女凍死林中；紅鼻的嚴寒老人在樹上咔咔作響、步步逼近；她彬彬有禮的回答竟令他為她裹上皮裘——而繼母親女出言無禮，就地凍斃。

sensitivity.note: Morozko tale.

passages.text: The stepmother sends the old man into the winter forest to leave his daughter; the girl sits under a tree with her poor coat worn through, and Frost the red-nosed winter-god comes down crackling from branch to branch, freezing everything within reach. 'Are you cold, little maid?' 'No, thank you, kind Frost — I am warm.' Each time he comes lower and crackles louder, and each time she answers courteously, though her hands are benumbed.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ransome, Old Peter's Russian Tales (1916), 'Frost'; not verbatim.

passages.text: Frost has never been answered kindly in all his winters; he wraps her in a great fur cloak and gives her a chest of silver. At home the little dog under the table barks that she is coming home in a coach of gold; the stepmother sends her own daughter into the same forest in her best clothes to earn the same — and the rude girl answers Frost as rudely as her mother taught her, until the cold takes her voice, and she is frozen sitting, where the kind girl had been wrapped in warmth.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ransome (1916); not verbatim.

title.en: The Fool of the World and the Flying Ship
title.zh: 世間的傻子與飛船

region.en: Village and royal palace (symbolic pin at Vladimir)
region.zh: 村莊與王宮（象徵性定位於弗拉基米爾）

period: Retold by Arthur Ransome, 1916

source.work: Arthur Ransome, Old Peter's Russian Tales (1916), 'The Fool of the World and the Flying Ship'

summary.en: The tsar promises his daughter to whoever brings him a flying ship; the fool's kindness to an old man wins him the ship, and the strange servants he feeds on the road — Hearer, Sighter, Swift-Gone, Shooter, Drinker, Eater, Frost-Blower, Wood-Thrower — win the princess against the tsar's own tests.
summary.zh: 沙皇許諾以女兒嫁獻飛船者；傻子善待老人而得船；路上以飯食所收的奇僕——善聽、善視、疾行、神射、豪飲、大食、吐寒氣、擲巨木——一一破解沙皇的刁難。

sensitivity.note: Classic tale (Seven Simeons cycle).

passages.text: The tsar of a great country hears that a flying ship has been seen, and offers his daughter to whoever brings it to the palace. The fool of the world, sent out with crusts while his clever brothers ride with loaves, shares his crust and his flask with an ancient old man; the old man teaches him a charm, and at a word a flying ship stands in the field, and the fool sails it toward the city.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ransome, Old Peter's Russian Tales (1916), 'The Fool of the World and the Flying Ship'; not verbatim.

passages.text: On the way he takes aboard all the strange men who beg a seat: the man who hears everything, the man who sees a hundred versts, the man who can be across the world and back with whatever you name before the water cools, the marksman, the man who drinks the sea, the man who eats the baked earth, the man who blows frost from his mouth, and the man who can carry a forest on his back.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ransome (1916); not verbatim.

passages.text: The tsar sets the fool tasks to lose his head: to have dinner ready in a moment (the Eater swallows the kitchen and the Drinkers drain the wells), to bring running water from no well (the Hearer hears where it runs under the earth), to fetch the sword that hangs a hundred versts off (the Swift-Gone fetches it before the water cools), and to defeat the greatest archer in the empire (the Shooter beats the tsar's archer from the edge of the world). At last the fool wins the princess, and the tsar is ashamed to have tested the servants of the flying ship.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ransome (1916); not verbatim.

title.en: The Cat Who Became Head-Forester
title.zh: 當上林務總管的貓

region.en: Village and forest (symbolic pin at Murom)
region.zh: 村莊與森林（象徵性定位於穆羅姆）

period: Retold by Arthur Ransome, 1916

source.work: Arthur Ransome, Old Peter's Russian Tales (1916), 'The Cat Who Became Head-Forester'

summary.en: An old peasant sends his cat to the forest to earn a living; the cat's arched back and furious tail frighten the wolves into service, then the bear, and he ends as head-forester of all the woods with the fox as his housekeeper.
summary.zh: 老農遣貓入林自謀生計；貓弓背豎尾之怒嚇得群狼供食、棕熊上樹，終為全林總管，以狐狸為管家。

sensitivity.note: Animal tale.

passages.text: The old peasant, unable to feed his cat, carries him to the forest: 'Live by your wits.' The cat, hungry, meets the fox, who trades on his terror — and meets the wolf, at whom he arches his back, sets all his fur on end, and says, very distinctly, 'Who are you? and how dare you?' — and the wolf, who has never seen anything sit still and dare him, brings him a lamb to keep the peace.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ransome, Old Peter's Russian Tales (1916), 'The Cat Who Became Head-Forester'; not verbatim.

passages.text: Then comes the bear, wanting the lamb's meat; the cat sends him up the tallest tree 'to see the hunters coming', and the fox below cries that the hunters have arrived. The bear, believing the guns are for him, jumps from the top of the tree, lands badly, and is glad to escape with his life. Thereafter the wolf brings game, the bear brings an ox, the cat lives in the fox's hole as a lord, and the forest gives him the title of head-forester, with the fox for his housekeeper and fresh meat all the days of his life.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ransome (1916); not verbatim.

title.en: The Little Daughter of the Snow
title.zh: 雪中少女

region.en: Russian village in winter (symbolic pin at Novgorod)
region.zh: 冬日俄羅斯村莊（象徵性定位於諾夫哥羅德）

period: Retold by Arthur Ransome, 1916

source.work: Arthur Ransome, Old Peter's Russian Tales (1916), 'The Little Daughter of the Snow'

summary.en: An old couple make a little girl of snow, and by evening she is alive — Snegurochka, the Snow Maiden, who runs and leaps with the village children all winter; but when the sun comes, a fire is built, and the little Snow Daughter jumps over it and melts into mist, reappearing with Frost her father and Snow her mother.
summary.zh: 老夫婦以雪塑小女孩，入夜竟活——雪中少女斯涅古羅奇卡，整個冬天與村童奔跳；然春陽既至，篝火燃起，雪女躍火而過，化為輕霧，與父親嚴寒、母親白雪同去。

sensitivity.note: Snegurochka tale; living New Year icon in Russia.

passages.text: An old couple who have no children mold a little girl of snow in the courtyard, and by evening she is alive — warm, laughing, and real, 'though her hair is snow and her eyes blue as spring water'. All winter she runs and leaps with the children of the village, and no cold can touch her; but as spring comes she grows paler and thinner, and watches the others out of doors with longing.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ransome, Old Peter's Russian Tales (1916), 'The Little Daughter of the Snow'; not verbatim.

passages.text: At last the girls of the village build a great fire to leap over, and the little Snow Daughter, who cannot refuse, runs and jumps — and melts into a little white mist that is gone. The old couple weep; but that summer the little Prince of the village dreams of her, and one winter's night a white mist drifts again over the snow and the Snow Maiden stands there once more, come from Frost her father and Snow her mother, who carried her away over the seas.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ransome (1916); not verbatim.

title.en: Little Master Misery
title.zh: 小苦惱老爺

region.en: Russian village (symbolic pin at Tver)
region.zh: 俄羅斯村莊（象徵性定位於特維爾）

period: Retold by Arthur Ransome, 1916

source.work: Arthur Ransome, Old Peter's Russian Tales (1916), 'Little Master Misery'

summary.en: A poor peasant shares his last crust with Misery, the ugly little man who squats on men's shoulders and eats their luck; in gratitude Misery leaves him, but when the peasant tries to fob Misery off on rich households and ends up selling him in a barrel to a drunkard's town, the whole city learns what the luck-eater can do.
summary.zh: 貧農以最後一塊麵包施捨蹲在人肩上吞食運氣的小苦惱；苦惱感恩離去；農夫卻試圖把苦惱轉嫁富戶，最終將其裝桶賣給酒鬼之城——全城遂識得『運氣吞食者』之能。

sensitivity.note: Misery (Nedolya) tale.

passages.text: Misery, the ugly little man in a torn coat, comes to squat on the shoulder of a ruined peasant and eat his luck. The peasant, having nothing else, gives Misery his last crust and half of his last drop — and Misery, who has never been treated kindly in his life, gets off the man's shoulder, and luck pours into the house: the fish fill the nets, the hens lay, the prince rides by.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ransome, Old Peter's Russian Tales (1916), 'Little Master Misery'; not verbatim.

passages.text: But the peasant grows careless, thrusts Misery out into the cold, and tries to be rid of him forever — selling him shut up in a barrel to the keeper of a tavern in a drunken town. In the barrel Misery calls himself a treasure, and the whole town is soon at ruin: every man who drinks from the barrel carries Misery home on his shoulder, luck drains out of the houses, and the drunkards' town comes to beggardom.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ransome (1916); not verbatim.

passages.text: The peasant comes to see the mischief he has sold, opens the barrel and speaks kindly to Misery again; the little man climbs back to the shoulder of the man who shares with him — and luck returns with him, while the drunkards of the town sit in their ruined taverns, poorer than the peasant they bought their treasure from.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ransome (1916); not verbatim.

title.en: Alenoushka and Her Brother
title.zh: 阿廖努什卡與其弟

region.en: Russian village and forest (symbolic pin at Murom)
region.zh: 俄羅斯村莊與森林（象徵性定位於穆羅姆）

period: Retold by Arthur Ransome, 1916

source.work: Arthur Ransome, Old Peter's Russian Tales (1916), 'Alenoushka and Her Brother'

summary.en: Warned not to drink from the hoof-print pool, little Ivanushka drinks and becomes a kid; the witch rides into the house as Alenoushka's double, and only the lamb that bleats at the river's edge — and the white lamb that weeps so that all hear — can bring the true sister back from the bottom of the pond.
summary.zh: 小伊萬努什卡不聽勸，飲蹄印池之水而化為小羊；女巫化身冒充阿廖努什卡入主家門；唯河畔哀鳴之羔羊——白羊泣聲令眾人皆聞——方能使真姊自池底歸來。

sensitivity.note: Classic tale (ATU 450).

passages.text: Alenoushka and her little brother Ivanushka walk to the fields; a cow-herd witch with evil eyes gives Alenoushka a ring to carry home her cows, and the ring works a wicked bargain. On the road the children grow thirsty, and there is a pool with a hoof-print — 'who drinks of this shall be a calf,' warns Alenoushka — and Ivanushka, minding it not, drinks and becomes a little white lamb.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ransome, Old Peter's Russian Tales (1916), 'Alenoushka and Her Brother'; not verbatim.

passages.text: Home again, the witch rides into the courtyard in the shape of Alenoushka and takes her place in the house; the true sister is thrown into the pond at the bridge with a stone round her neck, and only the lamb knows. Every day the lamb runs to the river's edge and bleats, 'Sister Alenoushka, the water is heavy on me, the stones lie cold on me!' — and the witch hears it and bids her false orders have the lamb killed.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ransome (1916); not verbatim.

passages.text: But the little white lamb stands on the bank weeping so that all the village hears, and the truth comes out; the witch is seized, the stone taken from Alenoushka's neck, and she rises from the pond once more her own little self, to live with her brother Ivanushka, who is a boy again and never drinks from a hoof-print pool again.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ransome (1916); not verbatim.

title.en: The Fire-Bird, the Horse of Power, and Princess Vasilissa
title.zh: 火鳥、神駒與瓦西麗莎公主

region.en: Russian fairyland, blue sea garden (symbolic pin at Kiev)
region.zh: 俄羅斯童話之境，藍海花園（象徵性定位於基輔）

period: Retold by Arthur Ransome, 1916

source.work: Arthur Ransome, Old Peter's Russian Tales (1916), 'The Fire-Bird, the Horse of Power, and the Princess Vasilissa'

summary.en: The archer's mare bears him a foal that speaks — the Horse of Power — and with its advice he catches the Fire-Bird with golden feathers that burn like flame, is sent to fetch Princess Vasilissa from her silver boat on the blue sea, and wins all three by keeping faith with his horse.
summary.zh: 射手的老馬產下會說話的馬駒——神駒；依其計擒得羽如火焰的金色火鳥；又奉命往藍海銀舟中迎回瓦西麗莎公主——全憑對神駒守信而三願皆成。

sensitivity.note: Classic Fire-Bird tale.

passages.text: The archer's grey mare bears a foal that speaks, the Horse of Power: 'Sell me not, for we shall have great adventures together.' Sold and set free, the Horse of Power returns and helps the archer catch the Fire-Bird with a sack of grain scattered where it feeds — the bird with feathers of gold and eyes like living coals.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ransome, Old Peter's Russian Tales (1916), 'The Fire-Bird, the Horse of Power, and the Princess Vasilissa'; not verbatim.

passages.text: The tsar, wanting more, sends the archer to fetch Princess Vasilissa, who lives in a silver boat on the blue sea, rowing with golden oars among the fish. The Horse of Power leaps with him into the water; Vasilissa, half-fish and wholly beautiful, is carried off to be the tsar's bride — and the archer, who has done everything, is thrown into a pit to starve for having seen her.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ransome (1916); not verbatim.

passages.text: But the Horse of Power comes to the pit's mouth with the water of life and the water of death, and brings the archer out; and when the tsar sends his armies to seize the princess, the Horse of Power tramples them, and the archer rides into the palace with Vasilissa, who was never meant for the tsar. The archer marries the princess of the silver boat, and the Horse of Power says at last: 'You have kept faith with me, and I with you — now you need me no more.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ransome (1916); not verbatim.

title.en: Salt: The Ship to the Salt Island
title.zh: 鹽：駛向鹽島之船

region.en: Russian port and the salt seas (symbolic pin at Arkhangelsk)
region.zh: 俄羅斯港口與鹽海（象徵性定位於阿爾漢格爾斯克）

period: Retold by Arthur Ransome, 1916

source.work: Arthur Ransome, Old Peter's Russian Tales (1916), 'Salt'

summary.en: The merchant's youngest son sails for salt and is blown to an island where a devil sleeps on a casket of salt; the devil's own gold makes the voyage — and the son who was mocked for having no gift trades with a golden crown and forgives his brothers, for salt is worth more than gold.
summary.zh: 商人幼子出海尋鹽，被風吹至魔怪枕鹽箱而眠之島；借魔怪之金成此航；曾被譏『一無所有』的幼子以金冠易鹽，寬宥其兄——蓋鹽貴於金。

sensitivity.note: Salt tale (ATU 665).

passages.text: The old merchant sends his sons to sea: the eldest with precious stones, the second with silver and gold cloth — and the youngest, mocked for having nothing, with a shipload of simple iron wares and a hold of salt, the cheapest thing in the port. A storm drives the little ship to an island where no man lives, and the youngest son goes ashore to see what an empty island may hold.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ransome, Old Peter's Russian Tales (1916), 'Salt'; not verbatim.

passages.text: In a cave sleeps a devil on a casket of salt — mountains of white salt, more than all the ships of the world could carry — and beside him lie bags of gold. The young merchant fills his hold with salt and trades in the golden bags for the salt he needs; then, when the devil wakes, he sings the devil to sleep again with his own games, and sails home by the storm that brought him.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ransome (1916); not verbatim.

passages.text: Home, the brothers laugh that salt is worth nothing — until they understand what the youngest has: in the whole wide world salt is the one thing every kitchen must have, and the youngest son, who began with nothing, trades a golden crown's worth for every sack, and forgives the brothers who mocked him; for the merchant of the house says at last, 'Salt, my children, is worth more than gold.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ransome (1916); not verbatim.

title.en: Caribs as Children of Tigers and of Snakes
title.zh: 加勒比人為虎與蛇之後

region.en: Orinoco country (Achagua and Saliva tribes)
region.zh: 奧里諾科阿查瓜-薩利瓦之地

period: Orinoco tribal traditions recorded by Gili; summarized 1915 (Roth)

source.work: Walter E. Roth, An Inquiry into the Animism and Folk-lore of the Guiana Indians (33rd Annual Report, Bureau of American Ethnology, 1915), ch. IV 'Creation of Man', §§53-54

summary.en: The Achagua held that the Caribs were the legitimate descendants of tigers: chavi meant 'tiger', whence chavinavi, 'arising from a tiger', their name for a Carib — or, from 'tiger' and 'pike', the children of tigers with pikes. The Salivas told that the son of Puru slew a monstrous snake that was devouring the nations of the Orinoco; from the worms that bred in the rotting monster's entrails there arose, each one, a Carib Indian and his woman — and as the serpent was the bloody enemy of all nations, so her children were savage, inhuman, and cruel.
summary.zh: 阿查瓜人言加勒比人乃虎之後裔：『虎』曰查維，故稱之『虎生』；或云『虎與矛』之子女。薩利瓦人言普魯之子誅食人之巨蛇；蛇屍腸中生蟲，每蟲化為加勒比男女——蛇為萬國之仇，其子孫亦兇殘不仁。

sensitivity.note: Orinoco tribal traditions summarized in Roth 1915 from Gili's colonial-era record; archival record, read critically.

passages.text: Thus the Achagua maintain that the Caribs are legitimate descendants of tigers: chavi in their language signifies a tiger, whence they deduce chavinavi, 'arising from a tiger', which is their term for a Carib. Other branches of the Achagua explain the term more satisfactorily: chavi is a tiger and chavina the spear, lance and pike; and from these two words, 'tiger' and 'pike', they derive chavinavi as being the children of tigers with pikes.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Roth 1915, §53 (from Gili); not verbatim.

passages.text: The Salivas say that the son of Puru conquered and put to death a horrible snake that had been destroying and devouring the nations of the Orinoco. But as soon as the monster began to putrefy, certain large worms began to develop in her entrails; and from each worm there finally arose a Carib Indian and his woman. In the same way that the snake had been so bloody an enemy of all those nations, so her children were savage, inhuman, and cruel.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Roth 1915, §54 (from Gili); not verbatim.

title.en: The Warrau Tale of the Water-Snake and the Birth of the Carib Nation
title.zh: 瓦勞水蛇傳說與加勒比民族之生

region.en: Pomeroon River, Guyana (Warrau)
region.zh: 蓋亞那波默龍河瓦勞之地

period: Warrau oral tradition; recorded 1915 (Roth)

source.work: Walter E. Roth, An Inquiry into the Animism and Folk-lore of the Guiana Indians (33rd Annual Report, Bureau of American Ethnology, 1915), ch. IV 'Creation of Man', §55

summary.en: A Warrau man warned his sister never to bathe in a certain pond at her unwell times; forgetting, she was caught by the great water-camudi snake and grew pregnant. In bullet-tree season she came home loaded with seeds though she took no ax: watching, her brother saw the snake leave her body, climb the tree as a man, shake down the seeds, and return into her. The watchers hacked the serpent to pieces as it left her; she gathered the fragments under a heap of mold, and each piece grew into a Carib. Peace endured until the old mother of the Caribs, revenging her slain lover, ordered the Warrau child killed — and a blood feud began that ended with the Caribs overwhelming the Warraus.
summary.zh: 瓦勞男子誡妹毋於忌日浴於某池；妹忘之，為大水蛇所獲而孕。采子歸而無斧；兄窺之，見蛇出其身，化人登樹搖子，復入其身。眾遂斬蛇成段；妹集屍片於土下，每片化為加勒比人。後蛇母復仇，令殺瓦勞童子；血仇遂起，加勒比終滅瓦勞。

sensitivity.note: Warrau oral tradition recorded 1915 (Roth); archival record, read critically.

passages.text: A Warrau man warned his sister not to bathe in a certain neighboring pond at those regular periods when she happened to be unwell. For a long time she obeyed; but after a time, forgetting all about the warning, she went to bathe at the forbidden spot and time, and was caught by a large snake, the water-camudi Uamma. By and by she became pregnant. In bullet-tree season the Indians cut down the trees for the excellent eating seed, and it was noticed that this woman, although she took no ax away with her in the morning, invariably returned in the afternoon with a large quantity of the delicious seed.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Roth 1915, §55; not verbatim.

passages.text: Suspecting, the brother followed her next day and saw the Uamma snake come out of her body, coil around a huge bullet-tree, and climb into the topmost branches, where it changed into a man who shook the boughs so the seeds fell for the woman to gather. Then, reverting to its original form, the snake descended and again entered her body. The brother told his friends, who watched and rushed up as the snake reached the ground, cutting it into thousands of pieces. The woman grieved sorely but collected all the fragments under a heap of mold and leaves, and each piece by and by grew into a Carib.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Roth 1915, §55; not verbatim.

passages.text: Many years passed; the Caribs grew strong and numerous and became a nation, living in harmony with the Warraus: when one tribe caught some game they would send a child with a piece of it over to the other. This lasted a long time, until one day the original mother of the Caribs — a very old woman now — told them to kill the child which the Warraus had sent to them, in revenge for the way the Warraus had slain her snake lover years before. The Warraus in turn slaughtered the Carib child, and thus a blood feud arose between the two nations, the Caribs finally overwhelming the Warraus.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Roth 1915, §55; not verbatim.

title.en: The Carib Nation Grows from a Baby Serpent
title.zh: 自幼蛇而生之加勒比民族

region.en: Upper Pomeroon River, Guyana (Carib)
region.zh: 蓋亞那波默龍河上游加勒比之地

period: Carib oral tradition; recorded 1915 (Roth)

source.work: Walter E. Roth, An Inquiry into the Animism and Folk-lore of the Guiana Indians (33rd Annual Report, Bureau of American Ethnology, 1915), ch. IV 'Creation of Man', §56

summary.en: The water-camudi had an Indian woman for a sweetheart, a snake by day and 'a people like myself' by night; they met at the waterside so her parents knew nothing. A baby camudi was born, swam about the river bank, and took its father's place each time he left. The brothers watched, were told by the old father to kill both snakes, hacked the baby serpent far back in the bush into many pieces — and months later, coming on voices, found four houses full of Indians grown out of the fragments, who welcomed their two uncles with paiwarri. And thus the Carib nation arose from a water-camudi.
summary.zh: 水蛇為印第安女子之情郎，日為蛇夜為人。生幼蛇，常候河畔。兄長受命誅二蛇，將幼蛇剁於深林。數月後聞聲尋至，見四屋之人皆自蛇段而生，迎二舅共飲——加勒比民族遂自水蛇而生。

sensitivity.note: Carib oral tradition recorded 1915 (Roth); archival record, read critically.

passages.text: The water-camudi had an Indian woman for a sweetheart. During the day he took the form of a snake; at night he was 'a people' like myself. The couple used to meet at the water side, and hence the girl's parents knew nothing of their being so fond of each other. After she became pregnant a baby camudi was born; the little one used to appear when she reached the river bank, swim about, and after a time return to its nesting place.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Roth 1915, §56; not verbatim.

passages.text: As she stayed so long each time at the water side, the old father asked his two sons why their sister took so long to bathe. Watching her go down to the stream, they saw the small serpent leave and the huge camudi enter, and saw the father bring his infant something to eat and the baby take his place when he left. The old man told them to kill both the snakes. On the next occasion they killed the huge camudi, and seizing the baby serpent carried it far away back into the bush, where they chopped it up into many small pieces.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Roth 1915, §56; not verbatim.

passages.text: Some months afterward, when hunting in the neighborhood, the brothers heard a great noise and the sound of voices, and going to ascertain the cause found four houses in the very spot where they had cut up the baby camudi, all occupied by Indians who had grown out of the fragments of the snake. In the first hut the house-master welcomed his two uncles; in the other three the occupants wanted to kill them for having destroyed their sister's child. But the first house-master said: 'No, don't do that, because these two visitors are uncles to all of you.' And the old father came to see his numerous progeny, and they all drank paiwarri. And thus the Carib nation arose from a water-camudi.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Roth 1915, §56; not verbatim.

title.en: Makunaima Cuts the First Beings from the Great Tree
title.zh: 馬庫納伊瑪自巨樹削造眾生

region.en: Upper Mazaruni country (Akawai and Makusi)
region.zh: 馬扎魯尼上游阿卡瓦-馬庫希之地

period: Akawai/Makusi tradition recorded 19th c.; summarized 1915 (Roth)

source.work: Walter E. Roth, An Inquiry into the Animism and Folk-lore of the Guiana Indians (33rd Annual Report, Bureau of American Ethnology, 1915), ch. IV 'Creation of Man', §57

summary.en: The Akawai and Makusi idea of creation is that, coeval with Makunaima, there was a large tree: having mounted this tree, he cut pieces of wood with a stone ax and, throwing them into the river, the pieces became animated beings. The Arawaks held that from his seat on the silk-cotton tree the Mighty One scattered twigs and bark in the air, on the land, and in the water, and from these pieces arose birds, beasts, reptiles, fish — and also men and women; the sire of the Arawaks was Wadili.
summary.zh: 阿卡瓦-馬庫希人言：與馬庫納伊瑪同時有巨樹；彼登樹以石斧削木，擲諸河，木片即化為有靈之物。阿拉瓦克人言：大能者坐木棉樹上，散枝皮於天、於陸、於水，眾鳥獸蟲魚與男女由此而生；阿拉瓦克之父乃瓦迪利。

sensitivity.note: Akawai/Makusi traditions summarized in Roth 1915; archival record, read critically.

passages.text: The Akawai and Makusi idea of creation is that, co-eval with Makunaima, there was a large tree, and that, having mounted this tree, he cut pieces of wood with a stone ax which, having been thrown into the river, became animated beings.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Roth 1915, §57; not verbatim.

passages.text: The Arawaks hold that from his seat on the silk-cotton tree the Mighty One scattered twigs and bark in the air, on the land, and in the water, and that from these pieces arose the birds, beasts, reptiles, and fish, and also men and women. The sire of the Arawaks was Wadili.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Roth 1915, §57; not verbatim.

title.en: Tamanaku Mountain and the Palm-fruits That Became People
title.zh: 塔瑪納庫山與化人之棕果

region.en: Tamanaku mountain, upper Orinoco (Tamanac/Maipure)
region.zh: 奧里諾科上游塔瑪納庫山塔馬納克-邁普雷之地

period: Tamanac tradition recorded by Humboldt; summarized 1915 (Roth)

source.work: Walter E. Roth, An Inquiry into the Animism and Folk-lore of the Guiana Indians (33rd Annual Report, Bureau of American Ethnology, 1915), ch. IV 'Creation of Man', §57

summary.en: The Maipures and the Tamanacs say that in early days the whole earth was submerged in water, only two people — a man and a woman — saving themselves on the top of the high mountain Tamanaku. As they wandered round the mountain in deep distress over the loss of their friends, they heard a voice which told them to throw the fruits of the Mauritia palm behind them over their shoulders; and as they did so, the fruit which the man threw became men, and that which the woman threw became women.
summary.zh: 邁普雷與塔馬納克人言：上古洪水盡沒大地，惟男女二人登塔瑪納庫高山而免。二人環山悲泣，聞聲命以肩後擲瑪里提亞棕之果；男擲者化為男，女擲者化為女。

sensitivity.note: Tamanac/Maipure tradition recorded by Humboldt, summarized in Roth 1915; archival record, read critically.

passages.text: The Maipures and, according to Humboldt, similarly the Tamanacs, say that in early days the whole earth was submerged in water, only two people, a man and a woman, saving themselves on the top of the high mountain Tamanaku, the last dry height standing above the waste of waters.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Roth 1915, §57 (from Humboldt); not verbatim.

passages.text: As they wandered around the mountain in deep distress over the loss of their friends, they heard a voice which told them to throw the fruits of the Mauritia palm behind them over their shoulders. As they did so, the fruit which the man threw became men, and that which the woman threw became women.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Roth 1915, §57 (from Humboldt); not verbatim.

title.en: Children of Rocks, Soil, and Rivers
title.zh: 石土河之子孫

region.en: Barraguan promontory, Orinoco (Otomac/Mapoya/Saliva)
region.zh: 奧里諾科巴拉瓜恩岬奧托馬-馬波亞-薩利瓦之地

period: Orinoco tribal traditions recorded by Gili/Humboldt; summarized 1915 (Roth)

source.work: Walter E. Roth, An Inquiry into the Animism and Folk-lore of the Guiana Indians (33rd Annual Report, Bureau of American Ethnology, 1915), ch. IV 'Creation of Man', §58

summary.en: The Otomacs said a three-part pyramid of stones on the rock called Barraguan was their earliest ancestress, and a monstrous rock on a pinnacle two leagues off their first ancestor — indeed, every stone of the bare promontory was one of their predecessors, whose skulls they dug up yearly to set among the crevices to change into stone. The Mapoyas called such a stone Uruana, the source of their tribe. Some Salivas declared themselves children of the soil — the earth once breeding men and women as it now produces thorns and hidden rocks — and certain Achagua held their origin from rivers.
summary.zh: 奧托馬人言巴拉瓜恩石上三合之石乃其始祖，二里外巨巖乃其初祖——岬上諸石皆其先人；歲掘死者之顱置石隙中，冀化為石。馬波亞人名其源石曰烏魯阿納。薩利瓦人自稱土之子，謂古時大地生人如生荊棘；阿查瓜人則言源出江河。

sensitivity.note: Orinoco tribal traditions summarized in Roth 1915; archival record, read critically.

passages.text: The Otomacs used to say that a stone made up of three parts, arranged in the form of a pyramid upon the summit of a rock called Barraguan, was their earliest ancestress; and that another monstrous rock, serving as the summit of another pinnacle two leagues distant, was their first ancestor. Being consistent, they believed that all the rocks and stones of which the said Barraguan — a high promontory of large rocks bearing hardly a particle of earth — was formed, were each of them one of their predecessors. Although these Otomacs buried their dead, they dug up the skulls at the end of a year, and placed them among the crevices and holes between the rocks and stones of the promontory, where they expected them in their turn to change into stone.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Roth 1915, §58; not verbatim.

passages.text: The Mapoyas would call such a stone as that serving for the summit of the pinnacle Uruana, describing it as the source of their tribe. Some of the Salivas would declare that they were children of the soil, and that in former times the earth used to breed men and women in the same way that it now produces thorns and hidden rocks. Those of the Achaguas who believed in their origin from rivers distinguished themselves by the name Uni-verrenais — children of the river.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Roth 1915, §58; not verbatim.

title.en: Makunaima Sends the Waters; the Survivor Throws Stones
title.zh: 馬庫納伊瑪降洪水；倖存者擲石再殖大地

region.en: Roraima country (Makusi)
region.zh: 羅賴馬馬庫希之地

period: Makusi tradition recorded by Schomburgk; summarized 1915 (Roth)

source.work: Walter E. Roth, An Inquiry into the Animism and Folk-lore of the Guiana Indians (33rd Annual Report, Bureau of American Ethnology, 1915), ch. IV 'Creation of Man', §58

summary.en: According to the Makusi tradition, Makunaima sent great waters upon the world: only one man escaped. This one man who survived the flood threw stones behind him, and thus peopled the earth anew.
summary.zh: 馬庫希人言：馬庫納伊瑪降大水於世，惟一人得免。此人擲石於肩後，遂再殖大地。

sensitivity.note: Makusi tradition summarized in Roth 1915 from Schomburgk; archival record, read critically. Flood-cluster motif for cross-tradition comparison.

passages.text: According to the Makusi tradition, Makunaima sent great waters upon the world, flooding it from end to end: only one man escaped, the sole survivor in all the drowned country. This one man who survived the flood threw stones behind him as he went, and thus the earth was peopled anew from the stones of the flood-survivor.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Roth 1915, §58 (from Schomburgk); not verbatim.

title.en: The First Fruit Trees Grow from a Spirit's Ashes
title.zh: 自鬼灰而生之諸果樹

region.en: Arawak country, Guyana
region.zh: 蓋亞那阿拉瓦克之地

period: Arawak oral tradition; recorded 1915 (Roth)

source.work: Walter E. Roth, An Inquiry into the Animism and Folk-lore of the Guiana Indians (33rd Annual Report, Bureau of American Ethnology, 1915), ch. IV 'Creation of Man', §59

summary.en: Three sisters alone in the house were visited by a young man with a powis — in truth an Adda-kuyuha, a Tree Spirit. He broke the calabash they offered, returned at night, and broke the youngest sister's neck-bone while she lay in her hammock, eating all but her head, which he bore to his mother. The elder sisters watched and told the returning piai; they fired the hollow tree where the spirit family lived, heard the grandmother reviling her wicked grandson amid the flames, and from the ashes grew the first fruit trees of our forefathers — the plantain, the pineapple, and the cocoanut, with all the others. But the piai had to taste the fruit before others might touch it.
summary.zh: 三姊妹夜遇青年，實樹鬼也。鬼折其甕，夜返殺季妹，食之而留其首攜歸。姊窺其蹤，告歸來之醫師；焚其空心樹，鬼家老嫗火中咒其孫。灰中遂生先祖之諸果樹——香蕉、鳳梨、椰子及其他。然醫師先嘗之，眾人方得食。

sensitivity.note: Arawak oral tradition recorded 1915 (Roth); archival record, read critically.

passages.text: There were three sisters alone in the house, preparing drink; the men-folk were away at a party. Early in the afternoon a young man came along bringing a powis with him. He was not what he appeared to be, a friend, but an Adda-kuyuha, a Tree Spirit. The girls asked him inside and offered him pepper-pot and cassiri; he refused the former and broke the calabash containing the latter, which made the girl who handed it to him laugh. He told her on departing that he would pay her another visit later in the evening.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Roth 1915, §59; not verbatim.

passages.text: Night fell, and the young man appeared again as arranged. The elder sisters watched. He got into the hammock where the youngest sister was lying and began caressing her; as he continued troubling her she asked what he wanted, and with that he slipped his arm round her neck and broke her neck-bone, killing her. He then began eating her body and finished all except the head by early dawn. Belching, he said: 'Yes! I am indeed satisfied. My mother told me to bring her the head, so I must spare it for her.' Holding the head up by its beautiful long hair, he carried it away into the bush and disappeared with it in a hollow tree, of which the sisters took note.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Roth 1915, §59; not verbatim.

passages.text: When the men-folk returned, among them a piai, the sisters told exactly what had happened. The piai told them to collect plenty of firewood and bring it to the hollow tree; they piled it around and fired it. It burned right merrily, and in the din of the cracking timber, enveloped in smoke and flame, you could hear the whole Tukuyuha family screaming, and the old grandmother reviling her wicked grandson for having brought so much trouble on them. Soon the hollow tree and the whole family of spirits were reduced to ashes — and from the ashes grew the first fruit trees of our forefathers, the plantain, the pineapple, and the cocoanut, with all the others. But the piai had to taste the fruit before the others were allowed to touch it.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Roth 1915, §59; not verbatim.

title.en: Allepdntepo: the Wonderful Tree and the Greedy Tapir
title.zh: 阿萊潘鐵波神樹與貪貘

region.en: Carib country, Guyana
region.zh: 蓋亞那加勒比之地

period: Carib oral tradition; recorded 1915 (Roth)
