source.work: Walter E. Roth, An Inquiry into the Animism and Folk-lore of the Guiana Indians (33rd Annual Report, Bureau of American Ethnology, 1915), ch. IV 'Creation of Man', §60

summary.en: When the Caribs had no cassava, all starved except the tapir, who went out every morning and returned each evening sleek and fat, dropping banana-skins as he went. The bush-rat followed him to the immense tree Allepdntepo, on whose branches grew everything one could wish for — plantains, cassava, yams, plums, pines, and all the fruits Caribs love. Stone axes hacked for thirty days before the tree fell; the greedy tapir, punished with a sifter that never held water, got back too late and has had only plums ever since. The Indians planted what they took, and the Bunia bird explained how each was to be propagated and cooked.
summary.zh: 加勒比人饑饉，惟貘日日出行而歸必肥，遺蕉皮為跡。田鼠隨之至巨樹阿萊潘鐵波，凡可欲之果皆在其枝。石斧斫三十日而樹仆；貪貘以簍取水，水皆漏盡——罰也——歸時惟餘李子，至今食李而已。眾植所得，斑鳩教其栽煮之法。

sensitivity.note: Carib oral tradition recorded 1915 (Roth); archival record, read critically.

passages.text: Time was when the Caribs had no cassava to eat; they all starved. Animals and birds also had nothing to eat; they likewise starved. It was the Maipuri alone who, going out regularly every morning and returning home of an evening, always appeared sleek and fat. The others, noticing his droppings — banana-skins, cane strips, etc. — said one to another: 'Maipuri must have found a good place to get food. Let us watch him.' So next morning they sent the bush-rat to dog his footsteps, and the rat followed Maipuri a long, long way into the bush, where he saw him pause under the shade of an immense tree and gather the fruit that had fallen.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Roth 1915, §60; not verbatim.

passages.text: This tree was the Allepdntepo, very wonderful, in that everything you could wish for grew upon its branches — plantains, cassava, yams, plums, pines, and all the other fruits that Caribs love. As soon as Maipuri had had his fill the bush-rat climbed the tree, picked on the corn to satisfy his hunger, and brought back a grain to show the others. The Indians followed him to the tree and cleaned up everything that had fallen, then agreed to cut it down. They hacked with their stone axes for ten days — it would not fall; another ten days — still it would not fall; so big was Allepdntepo. At the expiration of another ten days of continuous cutting the tree at last fell.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Roth 1915, §60; not verbatim.

passages.text: Their work made them thirsty, so the Indians gave calabashes to all the animals except the Maipuri, to whom they gave a sifter; when they reached the waterside, the water poured out of his sifter as fast as it was poured in — part of his punishment for being so greedy in keeping the secret of the bountiful tree all to himself. The Indians took away all the cassava, cane, yams, plantains, potatoes, bananas, pumpkins, and watermelons; by the time Maipuri got back only the plums were left, and with these he has had to remain content even to the present day. What the Indians took they planted in their provision fields; but it was the Bunia bird who explained how each was to be propagated and cooked, and how some, like the bitter cassava juice, had to be boiled before drinking, while others could be eaten raw.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Roth 1915, §60; not verbatim.

title.en: The Fountain in the Stump: the Flood That Followed the Wonderful Tree
title.zh: 樹樁之泉：繼神樹而來之洪水

region.en: Carib-Akawai country, Guiana highlands
region.zh: 圭亞那高地加勒比-阿卡瓦之地

period: Carib/Akawai tradition recorded by Brett; summarized 1915 (Roth)

source.work: Walter E. Roth, An Inquiry into the Animism and Folk-lore of the Guiana Indians (33rd Annual Report, Bureau of American Ethnology, 1915), ch. IV 'Creation of Man', §61

summary.en: Brett adds to the tale of the wonderful tree a fountain of swelling waters in the stump or under its roots, its overflow checked only by a rugged rock — or, in the Akawai version, an inverted basket. Owing to the reputed wickedness of the people in the one case, and the mischief of a howling monkey in the other, the waters were let loose and a flood overwhelmed nearly everything. Some tried to escape by climbing a high kokerite palm whose top reached the heavens; a poor woman, unable to climb, led the way halfway up and was turned into stone by terror and exhaustion, and all who tried to pass over her became rocks likewise. A few survivors climbed a komoo palm and saved themselves.
summary.zh: 布雷特續神樹之傳：樹樁根下有湧泉，以巨石（阿卡瓦人言倒置之籃）塞之。人因惡行（一說吼猴之擾），泉決為洪，幾滅萬類。眾攀其顛及天之柯基里棕而逃；一孕婦先登，半途驚疲化石，後至者欲越亦皆化石。倖存者攀孔摩棕乃免。

sensitivity.note: Carib/Akawai tradition recorded by Brett, summarized in Roth 1915; archival record, read critically.

passages.text: Brett ascribes the wonderful tree to Tamosi among the Caribs, in the same way that he gives Makunaima credit for the similarly wonderful Akawai tree. To the story he adds the mention of a fountain or swelling waters in the stump, or under the roots, of this wonderful tree, the overflowing of which is temporarily checked by means of a rugged rock (Carib) or an inverted basket (Akawai).
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Roth 1915, §61 (from Brett); not verbatim.

passages.text: Owing to the reputed wickedness of the people in the one case, and the mischief of a howling monkey in the other, the waters are let loose, and a flood occurs, which overwhelms nearly everything, most of the people being destroyed. Some try to escape by climbing a high kokerite palm whose top reaches the heavens, but a poor woman not in a condition to climb led the way, and halfway up was turned into stone by terror and exhaustion: none could help her and none could pass over her, and all who tried to do so became rocks likewise. A few survivors then climbed a komoo palm and so saved themselves.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Roth 1915, §61 (from Brett); not verbatim.

title.en: 'You Will Change Your Skins': Amalivaca and the Origin of Death
title.zh: 『汝將換皮』：阿馬利瓦卡與死之由來

region.en: Tamanac country, Orinoco
region.zh: 奧里諾科塔馬納克之地

period: Tamanac tradition recorded by Humboldt; summarized 1915 (Roth)

source.work: Walter E. Roth, An Inquiry into the Animism and Folk-lore of the Guiana Indians (33rd Annual Report, Bureau of American Ethnology, 1915), ch. V 'The Body and Its Associated Spirits', §64

summary.en: After Amalivaca had lived a long while with the Tamanacas, he took his corial to return across the salt water whence he had come. Just as he was taking his departure he sang out to them, 'You will change your skins' — that is, 'You will always be young', like the snakes that cast theirs. But one doubting old dame called out 'Oh!', which annoyed Amalivaca so much that he said instead: 'You shall die!' So death came into the world through a single doubting voice.
summary.zh: 阿馬利瓦卡久居塔馬納克人間，將乘舟歸故海。臨別呼曰：『汝等將換皮』——意謂恆如蛇之蛻皮而長生。一老嫗疑而呼『哦！』。神怒，乃改口曰：『汝等當死！』死由是入世。

sensitivity.note: Tamanac tradition recorded by Humboldt, summarized in Roth 1915; archival record, read critically. Origin-of-death cluster parallel (messenger/failed-blessing type).

passages.text: Other phases of the idea of an immortal body are met with in the myths relative to changed skins: the Indian belief is that those creatures which undergo ecdysis live forever. After Amalivaca had lived a long while with the Tamanacas, he took his corial to reach the other side of the salt water whence he had come. Just as he was taking his departure he sang out to them, 'You will change your skins' — that is, 'You will always be young', like snakes and such creatures.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Roth 1915, §64 (from Humboldt); not verbatim.

passages.text: But one doubting old dame called out an impatient interjection, which annoyed Amalivaca so much that he now said instead: You shall die! And so, through one old woman’s single word of doubt, the Tamanacs exchanged the perpetual renewal of skins for the ending of life, and death entered their world.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Roth 1915, §64 (from Humboldt); not verbatim.

title.en: Korurumanni Takes Away the Arawaks' Everlasting Life
title.zh: 科魯魯瑪尼奪阿拉瓦克之永生

region.en: Arawak country, Guiana coast
region.zh: 蓋亞那濱海阿拉瓦克之地

period: Arawak tradition recorded by Schomburgk; summarized 1915 (Roth)

source.work: Walter E. Roth, An Inquiry into the Animism and Folk-lore of the Guiana Indians (33rd Annual Report, Bureau of American Ethnology, 1915), ch. V 'The Body and Its Associated Spirits', §64

summary.en: When Kururumanni [Kororomanna] came to earth to see what the Arawaks were doing, he found them so bad that he wished to destroy them; on that account he took away their everlasting life and bestowed it instead on those creatures who cast their skins — the snakes, the lizards, and the cockroaches. That is why those creatures never die of old age, and why men do.
summary.zh: 科魯魯瑪尼下凡觀阿拉瓦克所為，見其甚惡，欲滅之；遂奪其永生，而賜於蛻皮之物——蛇、蜥與蟑螂。故彼等不老不死，而人則必死。

sensitivity.note: Arawak tradition summarized in Roth 1915 from Schomburgk; archival record, read critically. Origin-of-death cluster parallel.

passages.text: When Kururumanni [Kororomanna] came to earth to see what the Arawaks were doing, he found them so bad that he wished to destroy them; on which account he took away their everlasting life and bestowed it on those creatures who cast their skins — snakes, lizards, and cockroaches.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Roth 1915, §64 (from Schomburgk); not verbatim.

title.en: The Monkey Wife and the Man with a Bad Temper
title.zh: 猴妻與暴夫

region.en: Pomeroon River, Guyana (Warrau)
region.zh: 蓋亞那波默龍河瓦勞之地

period: Warrau oral tradition; recorded 1915 (Roth)

source.work: Walter E. Roth, An Inquiry into the Animism and Folk-lore of the Guiana Indians (33rd Annual Report, Bureau of American Ethnology, 1915), ch. V 'The Body and Its Associated Spirits', §64A

summary.en: A couple caught a girl monkey and 'minded' her; when the household was away she took off her skin, hung it on a beam, dressed in their ornaments, and cooked and ate the cassava. A hidden young man seized her, promised never to ill-treat her, and threw the monkey skin into the fire. But tired of her he began lashing her and calling her 'Monkey'; she fled into the bush, resuming her four-legged gait and her tree-jumping, with her little boy imitating her. At a wide river her people made the shores draw together, tree touched tree, and mother and child leapt across. 'You must swim after us if you want us!' — and the man went home and destroyed everything that had belonged to the woman.
summary.zh: 一家畜幼猴；家中無人時，猴褪皮懸樑，飾以飾物，炊薯而食。青年捉之，誓不相虐，焚其猴皮。後夫厭之，鞭而呼『猴』；婦攜子遁入林，復四足之行，攀樹如猿。至大河，其族人令兩岸相合，母子越而返。『欲得吾等，泅水而來！』夫歸而盡毀其婦之物。

sensitivity.note: Warrau oral tradition recorded 1915 (Roth); archival record, read critically.

passages.text: A man and woman once caught a girl monkey and 'minded' her: she became quite tame, and when the old people went away for a while they would often leave the monkey in charge. One day, when they had gone on a visit, the monkey took off her skin, threw it over one of the house-beams, and replaced it with the apron-belt and other ornaments the household had left behind. She then cooked and ate the cassava, and finally put on her skin again. On the next occasion a young man remained behind, hidden, to watch; he rushed up and seized her as she baked the cassava, and a hard struggle took place.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Roth 1915, §64A; not verbatim.

passages.text: 'I am not fit to be your wife,' said the girl. 'But I want you badly,' was the rejoinder. When he assured her he would never ill-treat her, she consented, and as soon as she agreed he pulled the monkey skin down from the beam and threw it into the fire. They remained together a long time, and she bore him a little boy. But getting tired of her he began lashing her and kept calling her 'Monkey' and annoying her in every way he could.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Roth 1915, §64A; not verbatim.

passages.text: Suffering so much, she resolved to return to her people: telling her husband she was going to bathe in the pond, she went far away into the bush, limping on a stick, trying to get back into her original style of walking on four legs and jumping from tree to tree, her little boy beginning to imitate her movements. When the husband came on her, there she was with the baby jumping from the top of one tree to another; only the child, who felt sorry for his father, threw down the spiders and insects for him to eat. At a wide river she cried to her people 'Katanni-tan — come and fetch us!', and they made the wind blow so strongly that the opposite shore came close over, tree touching tree, and mother and child jumped across. 'You must swim after us if you want us!' cried the monkey; and the man went home and destroyed everything that had belonged to the woman — cut up her hammock, broke her calabash, and smashed her goblets. What a bad temper he must have had!
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Roth 1915, §64A; not verbatim.

title.en: The Sorcerer's Daughter and the Magic Skin
title.zh: 巫師之女與魔皮

region.en: Guiana coast (after Brett)
region.zh: 圭亞那濱海（據布雷特）

period: Guiana oral tradition; recorded 1880 (Brett), retold 1915 (Roth)

source.work: Walter E. Roth, An Inquiry into the Animism and Folk-lore of the Guiana Indians (33rd Annual Report, Bureau of American Ethnology, 1915), ch. V 'The Body and Its Associated Spirits', §64B (adapting Brett 1880)

summary.en: The daughter of a piai fell in love with a brave young hunter and begged her father to make her like one of the young man's dogs so that she might always be with him. He put a magic skin over her shoulders and she became a dog. Each time the youth went out hunting with his four dogs, one always ran home and would never join the fray; and when he got home in the afternoon there was the fire burning and the cassava ready. Tying up the three dogs, he returned without a sound, saw a lovely maiden making cassava with the charmed skin hanging at one side, rushed in, threw the skin on the already lighted fire — and claimed the girl from her father for his wife.
summary.zh: 巫師之女愛獵人，求父化之為犬以隨之。父以魔皮覆肩，遂成犬。獵人每出獵，一犬必先歸；歸家則火已燃、薯已備。縶三犬，悄然返家，見美婦炊薯，魔皮懸於側；疾入擲皮於火，向其父求以為妻。

sensitivity.note: Guiana tradition from Brett 1880, retold in Roth 1915; archival record, read critically.

passages.text: The daughter of a piai fell in love with a brave young hunter, who did not seemingly pay her any too much attention. She begged her father to make her like one of the young man's dogs so that she might always be with him. He put a magic skin over her shoulders and she became a dog. Thus it came about that each time the youth went out hunting with his four dogs, one always ran back home and would never join in the fray; more than this, whenever he got home in the afternoon, there was the fire burning, the cassava ready, and all neat and clean.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Roth 1915, §64B (from Brett); not verbatim.

passages.text: He thought this was due to some of his neighbors, and went to thank them, but they denied all knowledge. On the next occasion, as soon as he missed one of his dogs, he tied the three up to a tree and returned home without making the slightest sound. Taking an advantageous position, he saw a lovely maiden there making cassava and doing other things, while at one side there hung the charmed skin. He swiftly rushed in, seized the skin, and threw it on the already lighted fire. He then claimed the girl from her father for his wife.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Roth 1915, §64B (from Brett); not verbatim.

title.en: The River of Life and the Search for the Happy Land
title.zh: 生命之河與樂土之尋

region.en: Florida (Arawak Islander tradition)
region.zh: 佛羅里達（島民阿拉瓦克傳說）

period: Island Arawak tradition reported to Spaniards; summarized 1915 (Roth)

source.work: Walter E. Roth, An Inquiry into the Animism and Folk-lore of the Guiana Indians (33rd Annual Report, Bureau of American Ethnology, 1915), ch. V 'The Body and Its Associated Spirits', §65

summary.en: Some old Island Indians, presumably of the Arawak stock, assured Ponce de Leon that far to the north there existed a land abounding in gold and in all manner of delights, but above all possessing a river of such wonderful virtue that whoever bathed in it would be restored to youth. They added that in times past, before the arrival of the Spaniards, a large party of the natives of Cuba had departed northward in search of this happy land and this River of Life, and, never returning, were concluded to be flourishing in renovated youth, detained by the pleasure of that enchanting country.
summary.zh: 島民阿拉瓦克老人告西班牙人：北方有沃土，金銀百物具足，尤有一河，浴之者返老還童。昔西班牙人未至時，古巴土人結伴北尋此樂土與生命之河，一去不返；人皆以為彼等飲浴其間，樂而忘歸，永保青春。

sensitivity.note: Island Arawak tradition as reported to early Spanish colonizers, summarized in Roth 1915; archival record, read critically.

passages.text: Far to the north there existed a land abounding in gold and in all manner of delights; but above all, possessing a river of such wonderful virtue that whoever bathed in it would be restored to youth. In times past, before the arrival of the Spaniards, a large party of the natives of Cuba had departed northward in search of this happy land and this River of Life, and, having never returned, it was concluded that they were flourishing in renovated youth, detained by the pleasure of that enchanting country.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Roth 1915, §65; not verbatim.

title.en: Perkunas and the Perpetual Oak-Fire: The Drought Sacrifice
title.zh: 佩爾庫納斯與長明橡火：求雨祭

region.en: Lithuania (symbolic pin at Vilnius)
region.zh: 立陶宛（象徵性定位於維爾紐斯）

period: Rite recorded by early chroniclers; retold by Frazer 1922

source.work: J. G. Frazer, The Golden Bough, abridged ed. (1922), ch. XVII 'Fire-Festivals', section on Perkunas

summary.en: Oaks are Perkunas's trees; a fire of oak-wood burned day and night in his honour, rekindled by friction of the sacred wood if ever it died — and in drought the people sacrificed a black heifer, a black he-goat, and a black cock in the depths of the woods, carrying a bowl of beer thrice round the fire and praying the thunder-god for rain.
summary.zh: 橡樹乃佩爾庫納斯之樹；橡木之火晝夜長燃，熄則以聖木鑽摩復燃——旱時眾人聚於密林，以黑母牛、黑山羊、黑公雞祭雷神，捧啤酒繞火三匝、傾酒於焰，祈神降雨。

sensitivity.note: Frazer's comparative framing; the sacrifice is described ethnographically.

passages.text: The chief deity of the Lithuanians was Perkunas, god of thunder and lightning, whose likeness to Zeus and Jupiter has often been pointed out. Oaks were sacred to him, and when the Christian missionaries cut them down the people loudly complained that their sylvan deities were destroyed. Perpetual fires, kindled with the wood of certain oak-trees, were kept up in his honour; if such a fire went out, it was lighted again by friction of the sacred wood.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Frazer, The Golden Bough, abridged ed. (1922), ch. XVII; not verbatim.

passages.text: Men sacrificed to oak-trees for good crops, while women sacrificed to lime-trees — the oaks counted male and the limes female. And in time of drought, when they wanted rain, they sacrificed a black heifer, a black he-goat, and a black cock to the thunder-god in the depths of the woods. The people assembled in great numbers from the country round about, ate and drank, and called upon Perkunas; they carried a bowl of beer thrice round the fire, poured the liquor on the flames, and prayed the god to send showers.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Frazer (1922); not verbatim.

title.en: Waizganthos and the Standing Girl: The Flax-God's Omen
title.zh: 瓦伊茲甘托斯與立姿少女：亞麻神之兆

region.en: Old Prussia (symbolic pin at Gdansk)
region.zh: 古普魯士（象徵性定位於格但斯克）

period: Rite recorded 19th c.; retold by Frazer 1922

source.work: J. G. Frazer, The Golden Bough, abridged ed. (1922), ch. on temporary kings, Prussian flax ceremony

summary.en: The tallest girl of the household stands on one foot upon a seat, lap full of cakes and brandy in her right hand, and prays the flax-god Waizganthos that the flax may grow as high as she stands; if her foot goes down, the crop may fail.
summary.zh: 家中最高少女單足立於凳上，膝抱糕餅、右手持白蘭地，向亞麻神瓦伊茲甘托斯祈願：亞麻當如她所立之高而生長；足若落地，收成或歉。

sensitivity.note: Homeopathic magic rite (Frazer's term); flagged as Victorian interpretation.

passages.text: A ceremony observed by the old Prussians puts the crop and the girl's body into one measure: the tallest girl, standing on one foot upon a seat, with her lap full of cakes, a cup of brandy in her right hand and a piece of elm-bark or linden-bark in her left, prays to the god Waizganthos that the flax may grow as high as she is standing.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Frazer, The Golden Bough, abridged ed. (1922); not verbatim.

passages.text: Then, after draining the cup, she has it refilled and pours the brandy on the ground as an offering to Waizganthos, and throws down the cakes for his attendant sprites. If she remains steady on one foot throughout the ceremony, it is an omen that the flax crop will be good; but if she lets her foot down, it is feared that the crop may fail.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Frazer (1922); not verbatim.

title.en: Swinging for Flax: The Lettish Spring Custom
title.zh: 盪鞦韆以助亞麻：拉脫維亞春俗

region.en: Latvia (symbolic pin at Riga)
region.zh: 拉脫維亞（象徵性定位於里加）

period: Custom recorded 19th c.; retold by Frazer 1922

source.work: J. G. Frazer, The Golden Bough, abridged ed. (1922), ch. on temporary kings

summary.en: Between Easter and St. John's Day every Lettish peasant devotes his leisure hours to swinging diligently — for the higher he rises in the air, the higher his flax will grow that season.
summary.zh: 復活節至聖約翰日之間，拉脫維亞農人皆勤於盪鞦韆——空中愈高，是季亞麻愈高。

sensitivity.note: Living custom.

passages.text: In the spring and early summer, between Easter and St. John's Day (the summer solstice), every Lettish peasant is said to devote his leisure hours to swinging diligently; for the higher he rises in the air, the higher will his flax grow that season. The same logic underlies the Prussian girl who stands on one foot for the flax-god: the height of the body is the height of the crop.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Frazer, The Golden Bough, abridged ed. (1922); not verbatim.

passages.text: Frazer reads such customs as imitative magic — the swing, the standing girl, the king's raised seat are all charms to lift the crop into the sky. In the Baltic the flax-field itself was the scale on which the year was weighed, and every leap into the air was a prayer the whole village could see.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Frazer (1922); not verbatim.

title.en: Sabarios: The Lithuanian Feast of Mixed New Corn
title.zh: 薩巴里奧斯：立陶宛新穀合和之宴

region.en: Lithuania (symbolic pin at Kaunas)
region.zh: 立陶宛（象徵性定位於考納斯）

period: Rite recorded 19th c.; retold by Frazer 1922

source.work: J. G. Frazer, The Golden Bough, abridged ed. (1922), ch. on eating the god, Lithuanian Sabarios

summary.en: At the autumn sowing each Lithuanian farmer holds the Sabarios: nine handfuls of every crop, each divided three ways, mixed into one heap; from it little loaves for each of the household and the year's first beer — with a cock and hen of the same brood given 'O God, and thou, O earth, we give you this cock and hen as a free-will offering'.
summary.zh: 秋播之際，立陶宛農家行薩巴里奧斯祭：九種穀物各取九把、每把三份，合為一堆；以其烘焙家宅小麵包、釀歲首新酒——並以同窩公雞母雞獻曰：『神啊，大地啊，我們以雞為自由奉獻。』

sensitivity.note: Sacrificial offering described ethnographically.

passages.text: About the time of the autumn sowing, when all the corn has been got in and the threshing begun, each Lithuanian farmer holds a festival called Sabarios, 'the mixing or throwing together'. He takes nine good handfuls of each kind of crop — wheat, barley, oats, flax, beans, lentils, and the rest — divides each handful into three parts, and throws the twenty-seven portions of each grain on a heap, all mixed together; the grain must be that first threshed and winnowed and kept for the purpose.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Frazer, The Golden Bough, abridged ed. (1922); not verbatim.

passages.text: Of the mixed grain he bakes little loaves, one for each of the household, and brews the year's first beer. On the chosen evening, kneeling before the barrel, he pours a jugful on the bung, saying, 'O fruitful earth, make rye and barley and all kinds of corn to flourish'; a cock and hen of the same brood, hatched within the year, lie bound on the parlour floor, and the family gives thanks 'O God, and thou, O earth, we give you this cock and hen as a free-will offering' — the fowls killed with a wooden spoon, for the head might not be cut off.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Frazer (1922); not verbatim.

passages.text: The fowls boiled in a new pot, the loaves and flesh set on an upturned bushel with three unused mugs, the family kneels while the father prays and drinks the three mugs; all follow, the beer going round till each has emptied each mug nine times. Nothing may remain over; the bones are given to the dog, and what the dog leaves is buried under the dung in the cattle-stall. No bad word may be spoken that day — for the new corn of all the fields is in the house, and the year is born again.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Frazer (1922); not verbatim.

title.en: The Old Rye-Woman: Killing the Corn-Spirit in Lithuania
title.zh: 老黑麥婦：立陶宛的殺穀靈之俗

region.en: Lithuania, near Ragnit and Tilsit (symbolic pin at Sovetsk)
region.zh: 立陶宛拉格尼特與提爾西特附近（象徵性定位於蘇維埃茨克）

period: Custom recorded 19th c.; retold by Frazer 1922

source.work: J. G. Frazer, The Golden Bough, abridged ed. (1922), ch. on the corn-spirit as old woman

summary.en: In Lithuania the Old Woman — Boba, the Old Rye-woman — sits in the last handful of standing corn; the reaper who cuts it 'has cut off the Boba's head', and the man whose flail falls last 'has struck the Old Rye-woman dead' — each killer paying for the deed in brandy and drenched with water by the farmer's wife.
summary.zh: 立陶宛田中末把之穀內棲『老婦』（波巴，老黑麥婦）；割其穗者謂『斬波巴之首』，末落連枷者謂『擊斃老黑麥婦』——皆需以白蘭地贖罪，且被農婦以水澆頭。

sensitivity.note: Corn-spirit parallels the Old Woman of European harvest lore.

passages.text: Near Ragnit, in Lithuania, the last handful of corn is left standing by itself, with the words, 'The Old Woman (Boba) is sitting in there.' Then a young reaper whets his scythe and, with a strong sweep, cuts down the handful; it is now said of him that 'he has cut off the Boba's head', and he receives a gratuity from the farmer and a jugful of water over his head from the farmer's wife.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Frazer, The Golden Bough, abridged ed. (1922); not verbatim.

passages.text: Every Lithuanian reaper makes haste to finish his task, for the Old Rye-woman lives in the last stalks, and whoever cuts the last stalks kills her, and by killing her brings trouble on himself. At threshing the same: when only a single pile of corn remains, all the threshers step back a few paces as if at the word of command, then fall upon the last bundle with almost frantic fury — and the man whose flail is the last to fall after the shout of 'Halt!' has 'struck the Old Rye-woman dead', and must treat his fellows to brandy.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Frazer (1922); not verbatim.

passages.text: Sometimes the slain corn-spirit was represented by a puppet: a female figure made of corn-stalks, dressed in clothes, and placed on the threshing-floor under the heap to be threshed last — whoever gave the last stroke thereby 'struck the Old Woman dead'. In the Baltic field the goddess of the year dies in every harvest and is reborn in every sowing; the reapers only carry out what the dainas sing of Saule and her daughters.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Frazer (1922); not verbatim.

title.en: The Mock Birth on the Harvest-Field: Zytniamatka
title.zh: 收割場上的模擬分娩：穀之母

region.en: West Prussia (symbolic pin at Gdansk)
region.zh: 西普魯士（象徵性定位於格但斯克）

period: Custom recorded 19th c.; retold by Frazer 1922

source.work: J. G. Frazer, The Golden Bough, abridged ed. (1922), ch. on Demeter and the harvest-field custom

summary.en: In West Prussia a Corn-mother and a Corn-baby are acted out on the stubble at harvest: the pretended mother of the ripe grain and the pretended child of next year's crop — a charm to ensure a crop, and Frazer's glimpse of a savage Demeter behind the classical one.
summary.zh: 西普魯士於收穫之田行模擬分娩：扮『穀母』者代表今歲熟穀，扮『穀嬰』者代表來年之穀——此為保豐收之巫術，弗蕾澤稱其為野蠻的德墨忒爾之回聲。

sensitivity.note: Frazer's interpretation flagged; the rite itself documented.

passages.text: The West Prussian custom of the mock birth of a child on the harvest-field: the pretended mother represents the Corn-mother (Zytniamatka); the pretended child represents the Corn-baby, and the whole ceremony is a charm to ensure a crop next year. In the mother-sheaf of Europe generally a large figure made of the last sheaf carries a small corn-doll inside — the mother and the daughter still unborn.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Frazer, The Golden Bough, abridged ed. (1922); not verbatim.

passages.text: Frazer reads the custom beside the Greek legend that Iasion begat the child Plutus — 'abundance' — by Demeter on a thrice-ploughed field: the myth and the Prussian mimic birth alike point to an older practice of performing among the sprouting crops or the stubble one of those acts of procreation by which primitive man seeks to infuse vigorous life into the languid energies of nature. The Corn-mother of this year is Demeter; the Corn-child of next year, taken from her seed and sown in autumn, is Persephone, gone down into the lower world to rise again in spring.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Frazer (1922); not verbatim.

title.en: The Fortieth Day: Feasting the Dead in Prussia and Lithuania
title.zh: 第四十日：普魯士立陶宛的祭亡宴

region.en: Prussia and Lithuania (symbolic pin at Vilnius)
region.zh: 普魯士與立陶宛（象徵性定位於維爾紐斯）

period: Custom recorded 19th c.; retold by Frazer 1922

source.work: J. G. Frazer, The Golden Bough, abridged ed. (1922), ch. on feast of All Souls

summary.en: On the fortieth day after a funeral the old Prussians and Lithuanians feasted the dead — the day on which, the Slavs believed, the soul finally leaves the house it has haunted for six weeks: the whole village ate and drank with the departed at the graveside.
summary.zh: 舊普魯士人與立陶宛人於葬後第四十日設宴饗亡者——斯拉夫俗信中，魂靈於逝後四十日始離其徘徊之宅：全村聚於墓旁與逝者同餐共飲。

sensitivity.note: Ancestor rite.

passages.text: On the fortieth day after the funeral the old Prussians and Lithuanians held their feast of the dead — the day, in Slavic belief, when the soul leaves the places it haunted for six weeks and rises toward the sun or the stars, or wanders into the forests, waters, and mountains. Food and drink were set for the deceased at the graveside and at the family board, part of every dish set aside for the one who could no longer eat.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Frazer, The Golden Bough, abridged ed. (1922); not verbatim.

passages.text: The custom belongs to the same calendar of the dead as the autumn Dziady of White Russia and the Lithuanian October commemoration the old writers noted: the living eat with the dead at fixed seasons of the year, so that the ancestors, well fed and remembered, will guard the seed and the herd. In the Baltic household the boundary between the living and the dead was not a wall but a table laid twice over.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Frazer (1922); not verbatim.

title.en: Hanan and Hurin Cuzco: The Two Branches of the Inca Lineage
title.zh: 哈南與烏林庫斯科:印加王族的兩支

region.en: Valley of Cuzco (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 庫斯科谷地(象徵性標記)

period: Report by Polo de Ondegardo, written c. 1561-71; publ. Markham 1873

source.work: Polo de Ondegardo, 'Report by Polo de Ondegardo', in Narratives of the Rites and Laws of the Yncas, trans. C. R. Markham, Hakluyt Society, 1873

summary.en: The lineage of these Yncas was divided into two branches, the one called Hanan Cuzco and the other Hurin Cuzco. From this it may be concluded that they were natives of the valley of Cuzco, although some pretend that they came from other parts to settle there - but no credit should be given to them, for they also say that this happened before the flood. From the traditions of the present time it is not more than three hundred and fifty to four hundred years since the Yncas only possessed and ruled over the valley of Cuzco as far as Urcos and the valley of Yucay. They preserve the memory of these Lords by their quipus; but, judged by the time each is said to have lived, the historical period cannot be placed further back than four hundred years at the earliest.
summary.zh: 印加王族分為兩支:一稱「哈南庫斯科」(上庫斯科),一稱「烏林庫斯科」(下庫斯科)。由此可斷:他們本是庫斯科谷地的土著;雖有人稱其自他處遷來——但此說不足信,因那些人還說遷來之事發生在洪水之前。就現存傳說推算,印加人僅據庫斯科谷地——東至烏爾科斯、北至尤卡伊谷——不過三百五十年至四百年。諸王之名以結繩「基普」記憶;但按諸王在位年數推算,信史至多上溯四百年。

sensitivity.note: Polo's source-critical frame: the Hanan/Hurin duality as the oldest social fact of Cuzco; his skepticism about pre-flood origins is quoted.

passages.text: It must be understood, in the first place, that the lineage of these Yncas was divided into two branches, the one called Hanan Cuzco, and the other Hurin Cuzco. From this it may be concluded (and there is no memory of anything to the contrary) that they were natives of the valley of Cuzco, although some pretend that they came from other parts to settle there. But no credit should be given to them, for they also say that this happened before the flood.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Polo de Ondegardo, Report (Markham 1873); not verbatim.

passages.text: From what can be gathered and conjectured in considering the traditions of the present time, it is not more than three hundred and fifty to four hundred years since the Yncas only possessed and ruled over the valley of Cuzco as far as Urcos, a distance of six leagues, and to the valley of Yucay, which is not more than five leagues. They preserve the memory of these Lords by their quipus, but if we judge by the time that each is said to have lived, the historical period cannot be placed further back than four hundred years at the earliest.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Polo de Ondegardo, Report (Markham 1873); not verbatim.

canonical_translation: C. R. Markham, Narrative of the Rites and Laws of the Yncas (Hakluyt Society, 1873)

title.en: The Pururaucas: Seven from the Cave and Warriors Sent from Heaven
title.zh: 普魯勞卡斯:洞中七人與天降援兵

region.en: Paccari-tampu, five leagues from Cuzco (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 庫斯科附近帕卡里坦波(象徵性標記)

period: Report by Polo de Ondegardo, written c. 1561-71; publ. Markham 1873

source.work: Polo de Ondegardo, 'Report by Polo de Ondegardo', in Narratives of the Rites and Laws of the Yncas, trans. C. R. Markham, Hakluyt Society, 1873

summary.en: Having resolved to conquer and subjugate other nations, the Yncas sought some colour and pretext for prosecuting their objects. The first story they put forward was that, after the deluge, seven men and women had come out of a cave which they call Paccari-tampu, five leagues from Cuzco, where a window was carved in masonry in most ancient times; that these persons multiplied and spread over the world - hence every province had a like place of worship where people came forth after the universal destruction. His father having been defeated by the Chancas, Pachacuti formed an army from the fugitives, the garrison of Cuzco and the men of Canes and Canches; before he set out his mother had a dream that the reason of the Chanca victory was that more veneration was shown for the Sun than for Pachayachachic, the universal Creator. Henceforward a promise was made that more sacrifices and prayers should be offered to that statue; then the son was promised a victory over the Chancas, and that men should be sent from Heaven to reinforce him. With this title he went forth and conquered, and thence arose the idea of the Pururaucas - the stone allies - most important for the Yncas as a title in extending their conquests. All who were subjugated were taught that Cuzco was the abode and home of the gods; throughout that city there was not a fountain, nor a well, nor a wall, which they did not say contained some mystery - more than four hundred such places of worship are enumerated in the report on Cuzco.
summary.zh: 印加人決意征服他邦,便需尋一藉口。最初提出的說法是:洪水之後,七位男女自庫斯科附近(五萊格)一處名「帕卡里坦波」的洞穴走出——那裡的古牆上鑿有一窗;此七人繁衍子孫,遍布天下——故各省皆有同類聖地,相傳大毀滅後人們皆從那裡走出。帕查庫提之父為昌卡人所敗,退保庫斯科;帕查庫提以潰卒、城防軍與卡內斯、坎切斯人重組大軍。出征之前,其母得一夢:昌卡人獲勝,是因世人崇太陽過於崇「帕查亞查奇」——造化萬物之主。自此立誓,對造物主之像多獻祭多祈禱;隨後有人許諾:其子必勝昌卡,且天將遣神兵相助。他持此「天命」出征而克,遂生「普魯勞卡斯」之說——化石為兵者——成為印加擴張最重要的名義。凡被征服者皆受教:庫斯科是諸神的居所;全城之內,無一泉、一井、一牆不含神異——庫斯科聖所清單所載,不下四百處。

sensitivity.note: Polo's uniquely candid analysis of Inca conquest ideology as manufactured title; the Pururaucas (petrified allies) are the political theology of the Chanca war.

passages.text: Having resolved to conquer and subjugate other nations, the Yncas sought some colour and pretext for prosecuting their objects. The first story that these Yncas put forward, though it was not the title which they finally asserted, was an idea that, after the deluge, seven men and women had come out of a cave which they call Paccari-tampu, five leagues from Cuzco, where a window was carved in masonry in most ancient times; that these persons multiplied and spread over the world. Hence every province had a like place of worship where people came forth after the universal destruction.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Polo de Ondegardo, Report (Markham 1873); not verbatim.

passages.text: His father had been defeated by the Chancas, and retreated to Cuzco, leaving his troops in a Pucara or fortress. Then the son formed an army out of the fugitives, and out of the garrison of Cuzco, and out of the men of Canes and Canches, and turned back to attack the Chancas. Before he set out his mother had a dream that the reason of the victory of the Chancas was that more veneration was shown for the Sun than Pachayachachic, who was the universal Creator. Henceforward a promise was made that more sacrifices and prayers should be offered to that statue. Then the son was promised a victory over the Chancas, and that men should be sent from Heaven to reinforce him. With this title he went forth and conquered, and thence arose that idea of the Pururaucas, which was one which was most important for the Yncas as a title in extending their conquests.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Polo de Ondegardo, Report (Markham 1873); not verbatim.

passages.text: Sacrifices of many kinds were continually invented, and all who were subjugated were taught that Cuzco was the abode and home of the gods. Throughout that city there was not a fountain, nor a well, nor a wall, which they did not say contained some mystery, as appears in the report on the places of worship in that city, where more than four hundred such places are enumerated.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Polo de Ondegardo, Report (Markham 1873); not verbatim.

canonical_translation: C. R. Markham, Narrative of the Rites and Laws of the Yncas (Hakluyt Society, 1873)

title.en: The Lands of the Sun and of the Inca: Singing Work-Parties
title.zh: 太陽之田與印加之田:歌聲中的勞作

region.en: Village lands of Ttahuantin-suyu (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 大蘇尤各村田地(象徵性標記)

period: Report by Polo de Ondegardo, written c. 1561-71; publ. Markham 1873

source.work: Polo de Ondegardo, 'Report by Polo de Ondegardo', in Narratives of the Rites and Laws of the Yncas, trans. C. R. Markham, Hakluyt Society, 1873

summary.en: In every place where a settlement was formed, the land was divided as follows: one portion was set apart for the support of religion, being divided between the Sun and the Pachayachachic, and the thunder which they called Chuquilla, and the Pacha-mama and their ministers, and other huacas and places of worship. Every notable thing was made an object of worship - springs, fountains, streams, stones, valleys, and hill summits, which they called apachetas - each with its people whose duty it was to perform the sacrifices. The lands of the tribute of the Ynca and of religion were sown and reaped in the same order; when the people worked upon them they ate and drank at the cost of the Ynca and of the Sun. This work was not performed by gangs: all the inhabitants went forth except the aged and infirm, dressed in their best clothes, and singing songs appropriate for the occasion. Although the crops were devoted to the tribute, the land itself belonged to the people themselves; the aged, infirm, and widows did not join in the work.
summary.zh: 凡立村之處,土地如此分配:一份供養宗教——分歸太陽、帕查亞查奇、名喚「楚基利亞」的雷神、帕查-瑪瑪(地母)及其祭司,以及其他瓦卡與聖所。凡可注目之物皆成崇拜對象——泉、井、溪流、石、谷、峰頂(所謂「阿帕凱塔斯」)——各配專司祭祀之人。印加與宗教的貢田,播種收穫皆依同例;勞作之時,飲食皆由印加與太陽供給。此勞非按隊攤派:除老弱之外,全體居民盛裝而出,唱著應時的歌謠下田。雖收穫盡歲貢,土地本身仍屬人民;老弱與寡婦不與此役。

sensitivity.note: Polo's administrative description of the religious economy; the singing-work detail is a rare social texture.

passages.text: In every place where a settlement or village community was formed, the land was divided in the following manner: one portion was set apart for the support of religion, being divided between the Sun and the Pachayachachic, and the thunder, which they called Chuquilla, and the Pacha-mama and their ministers, and other huacas and places of worship. For each town was divided in the same way as Cuzco, and every notable thing was made an object of worship, such as springs, fountains, streams, stones, valleys, and hill summits, which they called apachetas. Each of these things had its people whose duty it was to perform the sacrifices.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Polo de Ondegardo, Report (Markham 1873); not verbatim.

passages.text: The lands set apart for the tribute of the Ynca and of religion were sown and reaped in the same order; but it must be understood that when the people worked upon them, they ate and drank at the cost of the Ynca and of the Sun. This work was not performed by gangs, nor were the men told off for it, but all the inhabitants went forth except the aged and infirm, dressed in their best clothes, and singing songs appropriate for the occasion. In these two kinds of tribute there were two things that seem worthy of note: one is that the aged, infirm, and widows did not join in it; the other is, that although the crops and other produce of these lands were devoted to the tribute, the land itself belonged to the people themselves.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Polo de Ondegardo, Report (Markham 1873); not verbatim.

canonical_translation: C. R. Markham, Narrative of the Rites and Laws of the Yncas (Hakluyt Society, 1873)

title.en: Ccapac-llama and Huachay-llama: The Flocks of the Rich and the Poor
title.zh: 卡帕克-利亞馬與瓜恰伊-利亞馬:富畜與貧畜

region.en: High pastures of the Collao (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 科利亞奧高原牧場(象徵性標記)

period: Report by Polo de Ondegardo, written c. 1561-71; publ. Markham 1873

source.work: Polo de Ondegardo, 'Report by Polo de Ondegardo', in Narratives of the Rites and Laws of the Yncas, trans. C. R. Markham, Hakluyt Society, 1873

summary.en: Those flocks belonging to religion and to the Ynca were called Ccapac-llama, and the others Huachay-llama, which means rich and poor beasts. A division was prohibited, and to this day they are all enjoyed in common. There was a rule that females should never be killed, and thus the flocks multiplied exceedingly, for neither were those of the Ynca or of religion killed except for sacrifices. If any beast was attacked with carache, the disease by which so many have been lost in our times, the rule was that they should not be fed or cured, but buried at once, deep in the ground, as the disease was infectious. The flock of the community was shorn at the proper season, and the wool was divided amongst the people, each getting the quantity he required for himself, his wife, and children; so that all were clothed.
summary.zh: 歸宗教與印加所有的畜群稱「卡帕克-利亞馬」,其餘稱「瓜恰伊-利亞馬」——意即「富畜」與「貧畜」。此種劃分不許取消,至今全民共用。律有一條:母畜永不得宰殺——故畜群繁殖極盛;印加與宗教的畜群,除祭祀外亦不輕宰。若有牲畜染上「卡拉切」疫病(近世因此損失甚眾),律令不得餵養醫治,須立即深埋土中,以防傳染。村中公畜按時剪毛,羊毛按人分配——本人、妻、子各得所需——故人人有衣。

sensitivity.note: Pastoral law with a ritual naming; the no-female-slaughter rule framed as taboo.

A division was prohibited, and to this day they are all enjoyed in common. There was a rule that females should never be killed, and thus the flocks multiplied exceedingly, for neither were those of the Ynca or of religion killed except for sacrifices.

title.en: No Sowing, No Share: The Ayllu's Common Harvest Rule
title.zh: 不耕者不得食:世系公田之分穀律

region.en: District of Cuzco (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 庫斯科地區(象徵性標記)

period: Report by Polo de Ondegardo, written c. 1561-71; publ. Markham 1873

source.work: Polo de Ondegardo, 'Report by Polo de Ondegardo', in Narratives of the Rites and Laws of the Yncas, trans. C. R. Markham, Hakluyt Society, 1873

summary.en: On the death of an owner of land, the heirs and descendants possessed it in common, without the power of dividing it; but the person who represented the Ayllu had the charge, and all the rest enjoyed the fruits in common, divided among them as follows: if a son of the first possessor had six sons, and another son had two, each one had equal shares, and there were as many shares as persons. At the time of sowing they all had to be present to divide the crop; and at the harvest if any one, even though a descendant, had not been at the sowing, he could neither take his share nor give it to another. Yet even if he was absent ten years, he did not lose his right, if he chose to be at the sowing; and even when there were so many descendants that there was scarcely a mazorca of maize for each, the rule was still observed; and it is still kept up in the district of Cuzco. Thus the lands belonged to the whole village, and he who did not work at the sowing had no share in the harvest.
summary.zh: 田主身故,其子孫共同擁有田地,不得分拆;由代表世系「阿伊柳」者掌其事,眾人共享其利,分配之法如下:長子若生六子、次子若生二子,則八人均分——人各一份,不以房支為限。播種之時,人人須到場分穀;收穫之際,凡未參與播種者——即便是嫡系子孫——既不得取其份,亦不得轉讓他人。然而縱使缺席十年,只要播種之日願來,其權不滅;乃至子孫繁衍到每人幾乎分不到一根玉米穗,此律依然奉行——今日庫斯科地區猶遵行之。故田屬全村:不播者,不得收。

sensitivity.note: Andean land-tenure custom described by the colonial judge; a social ethic ('no sowing, no share') rather than myth strictly - tagged ritual-origin as a customary-law story.

At the time of sowing they all had to be present to divide the crop; and at the harvest if any one, even though a descendant, had not been at the sowing, he could neither take his share nor give it to another.

title.en: Minuchihr Slays Tur in the Night Battle
title.zh: 米努奇赫爾夜戰誅圖爾

region.en: Plains of Turan (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 圖蘭平原（象徵性定位）

period: Composed c. 1010 CE (Warner translation 1905)

source.work: Firdausi, Shahnama, trans. A. G. & E. Warner (1905), vol. I, Faridun secs. 19-22

summary.en: Faridun sends young Minuchihr with Karan, Garshasp, and Sam against the two murderers of Iraj. When Tur plans a night-attack, Minuchihr arranges an ambush of thirty thousand chosen warriors; Tur's host of a hundred thousand meets banners flying, and the young prince springs from ambush, surrounds him, hurles a dart into his back, and cuts off his head, sending it in a casket to Faridun: I have slain him as he slew Iraj.
summary.zh: 法里東遣米努奇赫爾率卡蘭、加爾沙斯普與薩姆征討弑伊朗支之二人。圖爾謀夜襲，米努奇赫爾預伏三萬精兵；圖爾十萬之軍夜出，見旌旗嚴陣。年輕王子自伏兵中殺出，合圍圖爾，擲鏢中背，斬其首，裝匣送呈法里東：「我以他弑伊朗支之法誅之。」

sensitivity.note: Epic literary source; no living community restriction.

passages.text: The Shah was told that a host had crossed Jihun, and bade prince Minuchihr to pass the frontier. The Shah was told a host had crossed, and bade prince Minuchihr pass the frontier toward the desert: a youth predestined to be fortunate may ensnare a mountain-sheep while hunters are before and pards behind; but having patience, prudence, sense, and wits, he will take savage lions in his toils.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Firdausi, Shahnama, Faridun sec. 19 (Warner 1905); not verbatim.

passages.text: The armies fought till night, till Minuchihr obtained the victory. Noon passed; the brothers met for consultation and said: let us attempt a night-attack and fill the desert with blood. That night those miscreants drew their army out bent on a camisade; the Iranian scouts gat news thereof and sped to Minuchihr. That shrewd man heard and planned a counter-ruse: he left Karan the host and led himself an ambuscade with thirty thousand warriors, all men of name.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Firdausi, Shahnama, Faridun secs. 20-21 (Warner 1905); not verbatim.

passages.text: Tur came at night and brought one hundred thousand men prepared for fight, but found the foe arrayed with banners flying and saw that battle was his sole resource. Minuchihr sprang from his ambush and surrounded Tur, who wheeled and fled mid wailings of despair from his own troops. Stay, miscreant, cried the prince, hot for revenge, who lovest fight so well and cuttest off the heads of innocents! He hurled a dart against Tur's back, whose sword fell from his grasp; then Minuchihr like wind unseated him, cast him to earth, slew him, cut off his head, and left the body for the beasts of prey.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Firdausi, Shahnama, Faridun sec. 21 (Warner 1905); not verbatim.

passages.text: Then Minuchihr wrote to Shah Faridun: since Tur had placed within a golden casket his royal brother's head in foul contempt, and had no ruth or reverence for him, God delivered Tur to me, and I have slain him as he slew Iraj; and will lay waste his realm and dwelling-place. The messenger approached with confidence and laid the head of Tur before the Shah, who prayed to God, the righteous Judge, to pour on Minuchihr his blessings evermore.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Firdausi, Shahnama, Faridun sec. 22 (Warner 1905); not verbatim.

title.en: Salm Falls by the Hand of Minuchihr
title.zh: 薩爾姆伏誅

region.en: Castle of the Alans (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 阿蘭要塞（象徵性定位）

period: Composed c. 1010 CE (Warner translation 1905)

source.work: Firdausi, Shahnama, trans. A. G. & E. Warner (1905), vol. I, Faridun secs. 23-25

summary.en: Karan the avenger takes Tur's signet-ring and royal standard, gains entry to the sea-castle of the Alans as a pretended envoy, raises the standard at break of day, and Shirwi storms the gate: by noon castle and castellan had vanished, and twice six thousand of the foe were slain. Kakwi, grandson of Zahhak, then fights Minuchihr and is dragged from his steed and gashed. Salm flees to the sea, finds not a spar of vessel, and Minuchihr overtakes him and cleaves the king of Rum asunder from the neck, setting his head upon a spear.
summary.zh: 復仇者卡蘭取圖爾印信戰旗，偽作使者混入臨海阿蘭要塞，黎明高舉戰旗，希爾維奪門而入——正午時要塞與守將俱滅，敵軍一萬二千人被誅。扎哈克之孫卡克維來戰，被拖下馬砍創。薩爾姆逃至海邊，無船可渡；米努奇赫爾追及，自頸將羅姆王劈為兩半，其首懸於矛尖。

sensitivity.note: Epic literary source; no living community restriction.

passages.text: News of the fight and of that Moon's eclipse reached Salm, who purposed making a retreat upon a lofty castle in his rear — the hold of the Alans, whose head is in the clouds, built by cunning from the ocean's depths. Karan chose six thousand veterans of name and said: I will secure Salm's only gate for combat or for retreat; for this exploit I need Tur's royal standard and his signet-ring, then will I make a shift to seize the hold.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Firdausi, Shahnama, Faridun sec. 23 (Warner 1905); not verbatim.

passages.text: Disguised as envoy to the castellan, Karan showed Tur's signet-ring and gave a forged charge from Tur; the castellan recognised the signet and they oped the castle-gates: he saw the seeming, but he saw no more. At break of day Karan set up a standard like the moon full-orbed and made signals to Shirwi, who seized on the gate and threw in his troops. By noon the castle's form and castellan's had vanished; at sunset hold and plain were level, and twice six thousand of the foe were slain.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Firdausi, Shahnama, Faridun secs. 23, 25 (Warner 1905); not verbatim.

passages.text: Kakwi the grandson of Zahhak then came forth like a div, and Minuchihr advanced with Indian sword in hand; they fought till noon like pards, and as day declined the prince caught the girdle of Kakwi, dragged his elephantine form from his steed, flung him upon the burning sand, and gashed his chest with the scimitar. Kakwi being dead, Salm ceased to seek revenge and fled toward the sea, but saw not a spar of any vessel there.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Firdausi, Shahnama, Faridun secs. 24-25 (Warner 1905); not verbatim.

passages.text: The Iranian host pursued apace, and Minuchihr, hard upon the king of Rum, cried: thou who art guilty of the blackest crime, who murderedst thy brother for his crown, whither wilt thou flee? I bring thee now a crown and throne: the royal Tree hath come to bearing fruit. As thus he spake he urged his steed along, and in another moment overtook and clave the king asunder from the neck, then bade the head be set upon a spear.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Firdausi, Shahnama, Faridun sec. 25 (Warner 1905); not verbatim.

title.en: The Death of Faridun
title.zh: 法里東之死

region.en: Tammisha (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 塔米沙（象徵性定位）

period: Composed c. 1010 CE (Warner translation 1905)

source.work: Firdausi, Shahnama, trans. A. G. & E. Warner (1905), vol. I, Faridun sec. 27

summary.en: Reunited with the heads of all three of his sons, Faridun lives out his days in tears and austerities: my days are changed and darkened by these three, who were my heart's delight and grief withal. Minuchihr girds a blood-stained girdle, rears a charnel of ruddy gold and lapislazuli with a throne of ivory within, hangs a crown above it, bids the dead farewell as ritual requires, and shuts the charnel-door. One sennight the whole city mourns with its mourning sovereign.
summary.zh: 三子之首皆在身側，法里東以淚與苦行度其餘年：「我的歲月被這三子改變而黯淡，他們曾是我心中的歡喜與悲傷。」米努奇赫爾繫血染腰帶，以赤金與青金石築陵，內置象牙御座，其上懸冠，依禮向死者道別而閉陵門。全城為哀慟之君服喪七日。

sensitivity.note: Epic literary source; no living community restriction.

passages.text: This done, the great king's day and fortune changed, the leafage withered on the royal tree; he quitted crown and throne and with the heads of those three kings beside him lived in tears and in austerities: my days are changed and darkened by these three, who were my heart's delight and grief withal, thus slain before me miserably. Such ills befell them through their perversity and evil deeds; they disobeyed me and the world frowned on them. His heart was full, his face all tears till death.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Firdausi, Shahnama, Faridun sec. 27 (Warner 1905); not verbatim.

passages.text: Then Minuchihr put off the royal crown, he girt a blood-stained girdle round his loins, and reared a charnel as the Shahs were wont of ruddy gold and lapislazuli. They placed a throne of ivory within and hung a crown above it, visited the dead to say farewell, as was the use and ritual, then shut the charnel-door: in such ill case that dear one left the world. One sennight Minuchihr gave up to grief, and for a sennight city and bazar were mourning with their mourning sovereign.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Firdausi, Shahnama, Faridun sec. 27 (Warner 1905); not verbatim.

title.en: The Legendary Places of Ancient Kou
title.zh: 古都庫之地靈譜

region.en: Kou (ancient Honolulu), Oahu
region.zh: 瓦胡島庫（古檀香山）

period: Hawaiian oral tradition; retold 1915 (Westervelt)

source.work: W. D. Westervelt, Legends of Old Honolulu, ch. 2 (New York 1915)

summary.en: A gazetteer of myth around old Honolulu: the surf Ke-kai-o-Mamala named for the chiefess Mamala; Kewalo, where the Kauwa servants were drowned and where owls would later defeat king Kakuhihewa; Punchbowl, hill of human sacrifice under the 'raging tabu fire of Keaka'; Waolani, wilderness home of the gods, where the god Kahano lay with one hand on Kahiki and one on Oahu, and over his arms the Menehune fairies crossed to build fish-ponds and temples; the magic breadfruit tree, the burial place of Maikoha, father of the wauke kapa tree, and the Canoe of the Dragon stone in the Nuuanu stream.
summary.zh: 古檀香山（庫）神話地誌：以女衝浪手瑪瑪拉得名的『瑪瑪拉之海』浪；凱瓦洛——僕隸溺亡之地，後亦為群鴉勝國王之戰場；火山彈坑山——『凱卡之烈焰禁忌』下的人祭之丘；瓦奧拉尼——眾神荒野之家，神卡哈諾一臂擱塔希提、一臂擱瓦胡，梅內胡內小矮人便沿其臂跨海而來築塘造廟；尚有魔法麵包樹、卡帕之樹的埋葬地，以及努瓦努溪中『龍之舟』聖石。

sensitivity.note: Gazetteer record consolidating place-lore; sacrifice details summarized.

passages.text: Ho-no-lu-lu is a name made by the union of the two words Hono and lulu; the old Hawaiians said Hono means abundance and lulu means calm, or peace - abundance of peace. Kakuhihewa was a king of Oahu in the long, long ago, so noted that for centuries the island has been named after him 'The Oahu of Kakuhihewa'; what is now Honolulu was almost always mentioned as Kou, after the chief Kou, an ilamuku under King Kakuhihewa. Ke-kai-o-Mamala was the name of the surf which came in the outer entrance of the harbor of Kou, named after Mamala, a chiefess who loved to play konane, drink awa, and ride the surf. Kewalo was the place where the Kauwa, a very low class of servants, were drowned by holding their heads under water, a custom known as Ke-kai-heehee, the sliding of the servants under the waves of the sea; it was also the nesting-ground of the owl who was the cause of a battle between the owls and the king Kakuhihewa.
passages.note: Paraphrase of W. D. Westervelt, Legends of Old Honolulu, ch. 2 (1915); not verbatim.

passages.text: Puu-o-wai-na, or Punchbowl, was a hill of sacrifice according to the meaning of the native words. Kamakau says: 'Formerly there was an imu ahi, a fire oven, for burning men on this hill; chiefs and common people were burned as sacrifices in that noted place; people could be burned in this place for violating the tabus of the tabu divine chiefs.' Part of an ancient chant concerning Punchbowl reads: 'O the raging tabu fire of Keaka, O the high ascending fire of the sacrifice! Tabu fire, scattered ashes. Tabu fire, spreading heat.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of W. D. Westervelt, Legends of Old Honolulu, ch. 2 (1915); not verbatim.

passages.text: Nuuanu Valley's most interesting legendary place is the little valley called Waolani, the wilderness home of the gods, belonging to the eepa people, almost the same as the ill-shaped gnomes of European fairy tales. In this valley was the heiau Waolani built for Ka-hanai-a-ke-Akua, the chief brought up by the gods, long before the days of Kakuhihewa. It was said that the divine caretakers of this chief were Kahano and Newa, and that Kahano was the god who lay down on the ocean stretching out his hands until one rested on Kahiki and the other rested on Oahu; over his arms as a great bridge walked the Menehunes, or fairy people, to Oahu.
passages.note: Paraphrase of W. D. Westervelt, Legends of Old Honolulu, ch. 2 (1915); not verbatim.

passages.text: They came to be servants for the young chief; they built fish-ponds and temples, lived in Manoa Valley and on Punchbowl Hill, and their master Ku-leo-nui could call them any evening, his voice heard over all the island, each task finished before the rising sun drove them to their hidden resorts. Nearer the banks of the Nuuanu stream was the great bread-fruit tree into which a woman thrust her husband by magic power when he was about to be offered as sacrifice; at the foot of the valley Pu-iwa was where the father Maikoha told his daughters to bury his body, that from it might spring the wauke tree used for making kapa; and in the bed of the stream is the legendary stone called The Canoe of the Dragon.
passages.note: Paraphrase of W. D. Westervelt, Legends of Old Honolulu, ch. 2 (1915); not verbatim.

title.en: The Tree That Became the God of Pakaka Temple
title.zh: 化為帕卡卡廟神之樹

region.en: Pakaka temple, Kou, Oahu (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 瓦胡島庫帕卡卡神廟（象徵性定位）

period: Hawaiian oral tradition; retold 1915 (Westervelt)

source.work: W. D. Westervelt, Legends of Old Honolulu, ch. 3 (New York 1915)

summary.en: In Kahiki the ancestress Haumea demands a singing-flower tree as the price of saving mother and child in childbirth; the wavering princess pays at last, and Haumea plants the tree by the Wai-hee stream of Maui, where it takes root. A flood hurls it to the sea: one branch becomes the fish-gathering god Makalei, another the Maui god Ku-ke-olo-ewa, and the trunk, found rolling on the beach by a childless couple after omens, is carved as Ku-hoo-nee-nuu and enshrined at Pakaka, the most noted temple of Oahu, school of its priests for centuries.
summary.zh: 遠國卡希基，女祖豪梅亞以一株開歌聲之花的奇樹為價救活難產母女；公主三度反悔、三度復許，終於獻樹。豪梅亞攜樹渡海，種於毛伊懷希溪畔，樹遂生根。山洪暴發，樹被捲入海：一枝成為聚魚之神馬卡萊伊，一枝成毛伊庫克奧洛埃瓦，樹幹則被無嗣夫婦按夢兆於灘上拾得，雕為庫呼尼努神，供於瓦胡島最負盛名的帕卡卡神廟——百餘年來祭司學堂之所在。

sensitivity.note: God-image origin legend; healing bargain paraphrased.

passages.text: Olopana had sailed away from Waipio, Hawaii, for the islands of distant seas, and somewhere in the great number of islands grouped under the general name Kahiki found a home. Here his daughter Mu-lei-ula was experiencing great trouble being near to childbirth. For some reason Haumea, one of the divine Polynesian ancestors, had stopped for a time to visit the people of that land. When the friends were afraid that Mu-lei-ula would die, Haumea came to help, saying: 'In our land the mother lives; the mother and child both live.' She demanded as payment a beautiful tree with two strange but glorious flowers, 'the tree of changing leaves', with one kind of flower singing sharply and the other singing from time to time. Gladly the sick girl and her friends promised to give this beautiful tree to Haumea, and the chiefess rapidly grew stronger; but she repented the gift and cried, 'I will not give the tree' - and immediately began to lose strength. Twice she renounced and re-promised, and Olopana in agony cried to his daughter to give up her tree; then Haumea, with the most powerful incantations, gave her the final strength, and mother and child both lived and became well and strong.
passages.note: Paraphrase of W. D. Westervelt, Legends of Old Honolulu, ch. 3 (1915); not verbatim.

passages.text: Haumea took the tree and travelled over the far seas to Hawaii, finding no place to plant it; she crossed to Maui and came to the four rivers, where she prepared the awa of the gods but needed fresh water to mix with it. She laid her tree on the ground at Puu-kume by the Wai-hee stream and went down after water; when she returned the tree had rooted, and while she looked it began to stand up and send forth branches. She built a stone wall around it, and when it blossomed returned to her divine home in Nuumealani, the land of mists and shadows where the gods dwelt.
passages.note: Paraphrase of W. D. Westervelt, Legends of Old Honolulu, ch. 3 (1915); not verbatim.

passages.text: A man with his stone axe went out to cut a tree, perhaps to make a god, and after hours of labor cut down the new short beautiful tree. That night a fierce and mighty storm came down from the mountains; blood-red were the streams of water pouring down into the valleys. During twenty nights and twenty days the angry rain punished the land, built up hills and dug ravines, crushed the wall, scattered the stones, and bore the tree down a deep ravine; the branches were carried far out into the ocean. For six months the waves tossed this burden, and at last threw the largest branch on the reef near the beach of Kailua on Hawaii; where this branch lay stranded, fish of many kinds gathered leaping around it, and the chiefs took it inland and made the god Makalei, a god of Hawaii for generations. Another branch became the Maui god Ku-ke-olo-ewa.
passages.note: Paraphrase of W. D. Westervelt, Legends of Old Honolulu, ch. 3 (1915); not verbatim.

passages.text: The body of the tree rolled back and forth along the beach; a chief and his wife who had not yet found a god for their home were led by omens down to the beach, saw a dim haze playing over it in the moonlight, took the tree, cut out their god and called it Ku-hoo-nee-nuu. They built a temple for this god, named Waihau, and made it tabu to the priests and high chiefs; the mana of this god was very great, from Hawaii to Kauai. The king living on Oahu heard about the tree, sent servants to Maui, and the chief readily gave up his god; so the temple was built at Kou and the god placed in it - this was Pakaka, the most noted temple on Oahu, and its god, the log of the tree from a foreign land, became the god of the chiefs of Oahu.
passages.note: Paraphrase of W. D. Westervelt, Legends of Old Honolulu, ch. 3 (1915); not verbatim.

title.en: Papa and the Tabu Breadfruit Tree
title.zh: 帕帕與禁忌麵包樹

region.en: Nuuanu Valley and Kalihi, Oahu
region.zh: 瓦胡島努瓦努谷與卡利希

period: Hawaiian oral tradition; retold 1915 (Westervelt)

source.work: W. D. Westervelt, Legends of Old Honolulu, ch. 4 (New York 1915)

summary.en: Papa (Haumea) and Wakea, the first residents of Oahu, live in the uplands by Kilohana precipice. Ruler Lele-hoo-mao's servants seize Wakea as a sacrifice for Pakaka temple. Papa overtakes the captive at the tabu breadfruit tree at Nini, and the tree opens; she leaps inside with him, passes through its other side, and hurls away her vine skirt - the morning-glory - as they escape. The cutters' chips kill all who touch them until the priest Wohi recognizes Papa from Kahiki, orders sacrifice and coconut oil, and the tree is felled into a goddess, Ka-meha-i-kana, whose image later passed to Kamehameha as a war-winning god.
summary.zh: 波利尼西亞始祖帕帕與瓦基亞定居瓦胡高地。統領萊勒呼毛奧的僕役捕瓦基亞獻祭帕卡卡廟。帕帕在尼尼的禁忌麵包樹下追上押解隊伍；古樹忽啟，她攜夫躍入樹心，自彼端破壁而出，將藤裙化作牽牛花隨手拋去。伐木者斧屑濺身即斃，祭司沃希認出此乃卡希基來的帕帕女神，命眾獻黑豬黑卡瓦紅魚、以椰油塗身，方敢伐樹——樹被雕為女神卡梅哈伊卡納，其神像後為卡美哈梅哈的開國戰神。

sensitivity.note: Variant of the Puna/Kiha-wahine breadfruit legend; cross-referenced below.

passages.text: The wonderful bread-fruit tree was a great tree growing on the eastern bank of the rippling brook Puehuehu; it was a tabu tree, set apart for the high chief from Kou and the chiefs from Honolulu to rest under while on their way to bathe in the celebrated diving-pool Wai-kaha-lulu. That tree became a god. Papa and Wakea were the ancestors of the great scattered sea-going people living in all the islands now known as Polynesia; they came to the island of Oahu, and according to almost all the legends were the first residents. Papa was a kupua - a woman having many wonderful and miraculous powers - sometimes called Haumea, but at last she left her power and a new name, Ka-meha-i-kana, in the magic bread-fruit tree.
passages.note: Paraphrase of W. D. Westervelt, Legends of Old Honolulu, ch. 4 (1915); not verbatim.

passages.text: On the Honolulu side of the mountains were many chiefs, among them Lele-hoo-mao, the ruler, whose fields were often despoiled by Papa and her husband; it was his servants who, searching the country around these fields, had found and captured Wakea, forcing him toward the temple Pakaka to be offered in sacrifice, shouting, 'We have found the mischief-maker and have tied him.' Papa threw around her some of the vines she had fashioned into a skirt and ran over the hills to the edge of Nuuanu Valley; a man by the stream told her a man had been carried by who was to be baked in an oven that day. She took a stone and smashed it against the ground, breaking through into a pool of water, drank and hastened on to the bread-fruit tree at Nini, where she overtook her husband and the men who guarded him. Wailing that she must kiss him, she rushed to him and began pushing and pulling him, whirling him around and around. Suddenly the great bread-fruit tree opened and she leaped with him through the doorway into the heart of the tree; the opening closed in a moment. By her miraculous power she opened the tree on the other side, and they passed through and went rapidly up the mountain-side. As they ran, Papa threw off her vine pa-u; the vine became the beautiful morning-glory, delicate in blossom and powerful in medicinal qualities. The astonished men had lost their captive; as the ancient proverb says, 'Their fence was around the field of nothingness.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of W. D. Westervelt, Legends of Old Honolulu, ch. 4 (1915); not verbatim.

passages.text: The chiefs consulted together and decided to cut down the tree and take the captive out of his hiding-place. The leader of the tree-cutters struck the tree with his stone axe; a chip leaped from the tree, struck him, and he fell dead. Another caught the axe - again chips flew and the workman fell dead. Whenever a chip hit any one he died, and the sap of the tree flowed out and was spattered under the blows of the stone axes; whenever a drop touched a workman or a bystander he fell dead. The people were filled with fear and cried to their priest for help. Wohi, the priest, came to the tree, bowed before it and remained in silent thought a long time, then raised his head and said: 'It was not a woman who went into that tree. It was Papa from Kahiki. She is a goddess and has a multitude of bodies. If we treat her well we shall not be destroyed.' He commanded the people to offer sacrifices at the foot of the tree - a black pig, black awa and red fish - then to rub themselves bountifully with coconut oil and go fearlessly to their work; chips struck them and the sap was spattered over them, but they toiled on unhurt until the great tree fell. Out of this magic bread-fruit tree a great goddess was made. Papa gave to it one of her names, Ka-meha-i-kana, and endowed it with power so that it was noted from Kauai to Hawaii; it became one of the great gods of Oahu, but was taken to Maui, where Kamehameha secured it as his god to aid in establishing his rule over all the islands.
passages.note: Paraphrase of W. D. Westervelt, Legends of Old Honolulu, ch. 4 (1915); not verbatim.

passages.text: After a time Papa had a daughter, Kapo, who also had kupua power; Kapo had many names, such as Kapo-ula-kinau and Laka, and was a high tabu goddess of the ancient Hawaiian hulas, having the power of assuming many bodies at will, from the mo-o, or lizard, to a human being. Kapo was born from the eyes of Haumea, or Papa. Papa looked away from Kapo and there was born from her head a sharp pali, often mist-covered - this was Ka-moho-alii. Then Pele was born, the one who had mighty battles with Kamapuaa, the pig-man, who almost destroyed the volcano Kilauea; it was Ka-moho-alii who rubbed sticks and rekindled the volcanic fires for his sister Pele, thus driving Kamapuaa down the sides of Kilauea into the ocean. These three, according to the Honolulu legends, were the highest-born children of Papa and Wakea. Down the Kalihi stream below Papa's home were two stones to which the Hawaiians gave eepa power: if a traveller passes, he stops, gathers leaves, makes leis and places them on these stones, that there may be no trouble in all that day's wanderings - hence the proverb of Kalihi Valley, 'Here is the sharp-headed rain of Kalihi.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of W. D. Westervelt, Legends of Old Honolulu, ch. 4 (1915); not verbatim.

title.en: Kane and Kanaloa Strike Springs from the Rock
title.zh: 卡內與卡納洛亞擊石得泉

region.en: Kalihi and Manoa Valley, Oahu
region.zh: 瓦胡島卡利希與馬諾阿谷

period: Hawaiian oral tradition; retold 1915 (Westervelt)

source.work: W. D. Westervelt, Legends of Old Honolulu, ch. 5 (New York 1915)

summary.en: Four great gods come from Kahiki to Nuuanu Valley: Ku, Lono, Ka-ne and Kanaloa. Kane and Kanaloa are the water-finders, each pool a Ka-Wai-a-ke-Akua. Walking Kauai unheeded as men, they drink awa from coast to coast; at Kalihi Kane smashes his great staff into the lava bed and water leaps up - the water-door of Kalihi; in Manoa Valley he splits the precipice for the pool still called the Water Provided by a God, whose bearers cried their warning and made all fall prostrate before Kamehameha's royal drink.
summary.zh: 四大神自卡希基來到努瓦努谷：庫、龍諾、卡內與卡納洛亞。卡內與卡納洛亞是尋水之神，凡泉池皆稱『神賜之水』。二人如凡人般走遍考愛島無人禮拜，便一路啜卡瓦酒至瓦胡。卡利希處，卡內以巨杖猛擊熔岩，清泉迸湧——『卡利希水門』；馬諾阿谷中，他劈開崖壁成潭，至今猶名『神賜之水』。卡美哈梅哈王時代，取水使者沿途高呼，行人皆伏身於王之神飲之前。

sensitivity.note: Westervelt explicitly notes the motif is not Biblical-derived.

passages.text: Four great gods with a large retinue of lesser gods came from Kahiki to the Hawaiian Islands: Ku, Lono, Ka-ne and Kanaloa. Ka-ne and Kanaloa were the water-finders, opening springs and pools over all the islands, each pool known as Ka-Wai-a-ke-Akua, the water provided by a god. In one of the very old Hawaiian newspapers the question was asked, 'What are the waters of Ka-ne?' and the answers came: the heavy showers of life-giving rain, the mountain stream swelling into a torrent, the rainbow-colored rain loved by Ka-ne, the continually flowing brooks of the valleys - these were the waters of Ka-ne. Prayers were offered to the two gods in all the different stages of farming, with the prayer, 'Here is food, O Gods, Ka-ne and Kanaloa! Give life to us and our family, life for the parents feeble with age, life for all in the household, when digging and planting our land; this is our prayer. Amama.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of W. D. Westervelt, Legends of Old Honolulu, ch. 5 (1915); not verbatim.

passages.text: Ka-ne and Kanaloa were great travellers. Together they journeyed over Kauai, coming from far-away lands; they appeared more like men than gods, and the Kauai people did not worship them, so they opened up only a few springs and crossed over to Oahu. Throughout all the islands the awa root has been found, bitter and very astringent, but when crushed and mixed with water the juice became a liquor greatly loved - 'These two gods drank awa from Kauai to Hawaii', so the old legends say. At Kalihi a number of fine awa roots were growing; they pulled up the roots and prepared them for chewing. When the awa was ready Kanaloa looked for fresh water but could not find any, and said to Ka-ne, 'Our awa is good, but there is no water in this place. Where can we find water for this awa?' Ka-ne said, 'There is indeed water here.' He had a large and strong staff, in some of the legends called a spear; he began to strike the earth, deep went the point into the rock, smashing and splintering it and breaking open a hole out of which water leaped for them to mix with their prepared awa. This pool has been known since the days of old as Ka-puka-Wai-o-Kalihi, the water door of Kalihi.
passages.note: Paraphrase of W. D. Westervelt, Legends of Old Honolulu, ch. 5 (1915); not verbatim.

passages.text: They passed Nuuanu Valley and went into Manoa Valley, the home of the rainbow princess. There the gods found most excellent awa, and Kanaloa cried, 'O my brother, this is awa surpassing any other we have found; but where shall I go to find water?' Ka-ne replied, 'Here in this hillside is water.' So he took his staff and struck it fiercely against the precipice; rapidly the rocks were broken off, the precipice crept back from the mighty strokes of the god, and a large pool of clear, cool water appeared among the great stones which had fallen. There they mixed awa and water and drank again and again until the sleep of the drunkard came.
passages.note: Paraphrase of W. D. Westervelt, Legends of Old Honolulu, ch. 5 (1915); not verbatim.

passages.text: This pool is still at the head of Manoa Valley, called Ka-Wai-a-ke-Akua, the water provided by a god. In the days of Kamehameha I very often messengers came from this pool with calabashes full of water swinging from the ends of sticks laid over their shoulders; when they came near any individual or group of Hawaiians they had to call out loudly, giving warning so that all by whom they passed could fall prostrate before the gift of the gods to the great king. Kane and Kanaloa made many springs of fresh water in all the different islands, and went to Kohala, Hawaii, where they lived in a temple so long that the people thought they were gods and offered sacrifices and worship.
passages.note: Paraphrase of W. D. Westervelt, Legends of Old Honolulu, ch. 5 (1915); not verbatim.

title.en: The Quest for the Water of Life of Ka-ne
title.zh: 追尋卡內之生命之水

region.en: Sorcerer-king's palace in the far lands (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 遠國巫王之宮（象徵性定位）

period: Hawaiian oral tradition; retold 1915 (Westervelt)

source.work: W. D. Westervelt, Legends of Old Honolulu, ch. 6 (New York 1915)

summary.en: A dying king's three sons seek the water of life of Ka-ne, which restores the dead and makes the old young again. Two rough sons push aside the dwarf who bars the path and are strangled in living vines; the youngest speaks gently, receives a strong staff and three bundles of food, strikes the sorcerer's wall thrice, feeds the two dragons at its fountain, and fills his calabash at midnight. Betrayed by jealous brothers who swap the water for sea-salt, he is exiled, until three grateful kings tell his father the truth - and the maiden of Kane's palace walks straight to him along her line in the air.
summary.zh: 老王垂危，三子奉命尋取卡內的生命之水——它能起死回生、返老還童。兩位粗暴的兄長推開守路的侏儒，被活藤縛斃於林中；幼子溫言求助，獲神杖與三束祭食，三擊破巫王之牆，以食飼雙龍，午夜前灌滿葫蘆。歸途兄弟以鹹海水偷換聖水，父王反被毒害，幼子蒙冤流放；直至三國君王攜禮來謝、真相大白——而卡內宮中的公主沿著空中劃線直奔他而來，選他為夫。

sensitivity.note: Water-of-life cluster: ATU 551-type tale in Hawaiian dress.

passages.text: When the moon dies she goes to the living water of Ka-ne, to the water which can restore all to life, even the moon to the path in the sky - so runs the Maori legend. The Hawaiians of long ago shared the belief that somewhere along the deep sea beyond the horizon, or somewhere in the cloud-land above the heavens, there was a land known as the land of the water of life of the gods, in which was a lake of living water in which always rested the power of restoration to life - Ka wai ola a Ka-ne. Mention of this wai ola is found in New Zealand, the Tongas, Samoa, Tahiti and the Hawaiian Islands. Ka-ne was one of the four greatest gods of the Polynesians; in his hands was placed the care of the water of life; a sick person drinking it would recover health, and a dead person sprinkled with it would be restored to life.
passages.note: Paraphrase of W. D. Westervelt, Legends of Old Honolulu, ch. 6 (1915); not verbatim.

passages.text: In the misty past a king was very, very ill, and all his friends thought he was going to die. An old man, a stranger, passing by the three wailing sons said slowly: 'I have heard of something which would make your father well. He must drink of the water of life of Ka-ne. But this is very hard to find and difficult to get.' The eldest son ran to his father for permission, and as he went along a path through the forest, suddenly an ugly little man, a dwarf, appeared in his path and called out, 'Where are you going that you are in such a hurry?' The prince answered roughly, pushed the little man aside and ran on; the dwarf made the path twist and turn and grow narrow, until the prince fell, crawling and fighting against tangled masses of ferns and clinging tendrils of the vines of the land of fairies and gnomes; they twined around him and tied him tight with living coils, and he lay like one who was dead. The second son, thinking the selfish thought that he might win the kingdom, met the same little man, spoke roughly, pushed him out of the way, and was caught in the tangled woods and held fast like one who was dead.
passages.note: Paraphrase of W. D. Westervelt, Legends of Old Honolulu, ch. 6 (1915); not verbatim.

passages.text: Then the last, the youngest son, took his calabash and went away thinking he might be able to rescue his brothers as well as get the water of life for his father. He told the dwarf about the king's illness and the report of the water of life of Ka-ne, and asked if he could aid in any way. The little man said, 'Because you have spoken gently and have asked my help and have not been rough and rude as were your brothers, I will tell you where to go and will give you aid. The path will open before you at the bidding of this strong staff which I give you. You will come to the palace of a king who is a sorcerer; in his house is the fountain of that water of life.
