Take three bundles of food in one hand and your strong staff in the other; strike the door of that king's house three times and an opening will be made. Then you will see two dragons with open mouths ready to devour you; quickly throw food in their mouths and they will become quiet. Fill your calabash with the living water and hurry away. At midnight the doors will be shut, and you cannot escape.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of W. D. Westervelt, Legends of Old Honolulu, ch. 6 (1915); not verbatim.

passages.text: The prince came to the strange land and the sorcerer's house; three times he struck until he broke the wall and made a door for himself. He saw the dragons and threw the food into their mouths, making them his friends. He saw some young chiefs, who welcomed him and gave him a war-club and a bundle of food; in another room he met a beautiful maiden whom he loved at once with all his heart, who told him that after a time they would meet again and live as husband and wife, and showed him where he could get the water of life. He dipped his calabash in the spring and leaped through the door just at the stroke of midnight. He found his brothers in the tangled path and sprinkled a little of the water of life over them, so that strength returned; but they were jealous and angry at the success of their younger brother. They passed lands where the high chief was resisting rebels; the young prince gave them part of the bundle of food from the house of the god Ka-ne, and they ate and became very strong, and the war-club destroyed the rebels. At the seacoast of their own land the wicked brothers took his calabash of the water of life and poured the water into their water-jars, filling his calabash with salt, sickish sea-water. The king drank deeply of the salt water and was made more seriously sick, almost to death; then the older brothers gave him the real water of life and he immediately became strong as in the days of his youth. The king was very angry with the youngest son and sent him away with an officer, a friend who helped him find a safe hiding-place. By and by three great kings came from distant lands with presents for the prince who had given them peace and prosperity; the father acknowledged the wrong he had done. Meanwhile one of the most beautiful princesses of all the world had sent word everywhere that she would be seated in her house and any prince who could walk straight to her along a line drawn in the air by her sorcerers, without turning to either side, should be her husband. The brothers had both failed, but the young prince went with swift steps of love straight to a door which opened of its own accord; out leaped the maiden of the palace of the land of Ka-ne, and into his arms she rushed. The brothers ran away to distant lands and never returned; the prince and the princess became king and queen and lived in great peace and happiness.
passages.note: Paraphrase of W. D. Westervelt, Legends of Old Honolulu, ch. 6 (1915); not verbatim.

title.en: Mamala Rides the Sea of Kou
title.zh: 瑪瑪拉踏浪庫港

region.en: Kou harbor entrance, Honolulu, Oahu
region.zh: 瓦胡島檀香山庫港入口

period: Hawaiian oral tradition; retold 1915 (Westervelt)

source.work: W. D. Westervelt, Legends of Old Honolulu, ch. 7 (New York 1915)

summary.en: Mamala, a kupua chiefess - great lizard, shark and beautiful woman in one - dances on the roughest outer waves of the harbor entrance whose surf still bears her name. Leaving her shark-man husband Ouha for the chief Hono-kau-pu, she drives him away; humiliated when the shrimps in his offered basket leap back to the sea amid the women's taunts, Ouha casts off humanity and becomes the great shark-god of the coast between Waikiki and Koko Head, while the mele of Hono-kau-pu keeps her riding 'from the top of the tossing surf waves'.
summary.zh: 瑪瑪拉是庫普阿族女酋——巨蜥、鯊與絕色美人三位一體——於港口外最洶湧的浪頭上翩然起舞，港之浪濤至今仍冠其名。她離開鯊人丈夫烏哈改嫁霍諾考普；烏哈獻蝦求恕，蝦群躍水而逃，遭婦人嘲笑；他拋卻人身，化為威基基與科科角之間海岸的大鯊神。霍諾考普的古歌至今傳唱：『我自濤尖盼君歸——今夜，庫港的雙眼終得相會。』

sensitivity.note: Surf-lore etiology; chant paraphrased.

passages.text: Kou was a noted place for games and sports among the chiefs of long ago. Straight out toward the ocean was the narrow entrance to the harbor, through which rolled the finest surf waves of old Honolulu; the surf bore the name Ke-kai-o-Mamala, the sea of Mamala, and when it rose high it was called Ka-nuku-o-Mamala, the nose of Mamala. Mamala was a chiefess of kupua character: she was a mo-o, a gigantic lizard or crocodile, as well as a beautiful woman, and could assume whichever shape she most desired; one of the legends says that she was a shark and woman. She had for her first husband the shark-man Ouha, afterward a shark-god having his home in the ocean near Koko Head; Mamala and Ouha drank awa together and played konane on the large smooth stone at Kou.
passages.note: Paraphrase of W. D. Westervelt, Legends of Old Honolulu, ch. 7 (1915); not verbatim.

passages.text: Mamala was a wonderful surf-rider; very skilfully she danced on the roughest waves. The surf in which she most delighted rose far out in the rough sea, where the winds blew strong and whitecaps rolled in rough disorder into the bay of Kou; the people on the beach, watching her, filled the air with resounding applause, clapping their hands over her extraordinary athletic feats. The chief Hono-kau-pu chose to take Mamala as his wife, so she left Ouha and lived with her new husband.
passages.note: Paraphrase of W. D. Westervelt, Legends of Old Honolulu, ch. 7 (1915); not verbatim.

passages.text: Ouha was angry and tried at first to injure Hono and Mamala, but he was driven away; he fled to the lake Ka-ihi-Kapu toward Waikiki, where he appeared as a man with a basketful of shrimps and fresh fish, which he offered to the women of that place, saying, 'Here is life for the children.' He opened his basket, but the shrimps and the fish leaped out and escaped into the water. The women ridiculed the god-man; as the ancient legendary characters of all Polynesia could not endure anything that brought shame or disgrace upon them in the eyes of others, Ouha fled from the taunts of the women, casting off his human form and dissolving his connection with humanity - thus he became the great shark-god of the coast between Waikiki and Koko Head.
passages.note: Paraphrase of W. D. Westervelt, Legends of Old Honolulu, ch. 7 (1915); not verbatim.

passages.text: The surf-rider was remembered in the beautiful mele coming from ancient times and called the mele of Hono-kau-pu: 'The surf rises at Koolau, blowing the waves into mist, into little drops, spray falling along the hidden harbor. There is my dear husband Ouha, there is the shaking sea, the running sea of Kou, the crab-like moving sea of Kou. Prepare the awa to drink, the crab to eat; the small konane board is at Hono-kau-pu. My friend on the highest point of the surf: this is a good surf for us. My love has gone away. Smooth is the floor of Kou, fine is the breeze from the mountains. I wait for you to return; the games are prepared. Leap away to Tahiti by the path to Nuumealani, home of the gods - will that lover return? I belong to Hono-kau-pu, from the top of the tossing surf waves; the eyes of the day and the night are forgotten. Kou has the large konane board; this is the day, and to-night the eyes meet at Kou.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of W. D. Westervelt, Legends of Old Honolulu, ch. 7 (1915); not verbatim.

title.en: Ka-ehu Pushes the Man-eater Pehu into the Shallows
title.zh: 卡埃胡智懲食人鯊佩胡

region.en: Waikiki surf, Oahu
region.zh: 瓦胡島威基基浪區

period: Hawaiian oral tradition; retold 1915 (Westervelt)

source.work: W. D. Westervelt, Legends of Old Honolulu, ch. 8 (New York 1915)

summary.en: Ka-ehu, the little yellow shark of Pearl Harbor gifted with wisdom by the shark-god Ka-moho-alii, pines for his home in Puna and sets out for Hawaii. At Waikiki he meets Pehu, a man-eating shark from Maui, 'catching a crab' for breakfast among the surf-riders. Pretending to help, Ka-ehu stations Pehu by the reef, signals his sharks at the right wave, shoves the surfers aside, and tosses the leaping Pehu head-first into a deep coral hole; the surf-riders kill him and find hair and bones inside - proof of his meals - and burn the pieces in a great oven at Pele-ula.
summary.zh: 珍珠港的小黃鯊卡埃胡蒙鯊神卡莫霍阿利賜予智慧，思鄉而返夏威夷。途經威基基，遇毛伊來的食人鯊佩胡在衝浪者間『捉蟹當早餐』。卡埃胡假意相助，令其藏身礁影，並約定：浪頭來時群鯊齊發。時機一到，衝浪者被推至一側，躍起撲食的佩胡被眾鯊拋得團團轉，頭朝下栽進深珊瑚洞；衝浪者合力誅之，剖腹見髮見骨——皆其食人罪證——碎屍於佩雷烏拉大灶焚化。

sensitivity.note: Shark-justice legend.

passages.text: Among the legendary characters of the early Hawaiians was Ka-ehu, the little yellow shark of Pearl Harbor, who had been given magic power and great wisdom by his ancestor Ka-moho-alii, the shark-god, brother of the fire goddess Pele. Part of his life had been spent with his parents, who guarded the sea precipices of the Coast of Puna in the southern part of the island Hawaii. While at Pearl Harbor he became homesick for the beauty of Puna, and chanted: 'O my land of rustling lehua-trees! Rain is treading on your budding flowers; they meet the fish in the sea. This is the day when love meets love; my longings are stirring within me for the spirit friends of my land. They call me back to my home; I must return.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of W. D. Westervelt, Legends of Old Honolulu, ch. 8 (1915); not verbatim.

passages.text: Ka-ehu called his shark friends and started along the Oahu shores on his way to Hawaii. At Waikiki they met Pehu, a shark visitor from Maui, who lived in the sea belonging to Hono-ka-hau; Pehu was a man-eating shark, swimming back and forth at Kalehua-wike waiting for some surf-rider to go out far enough to be caught. Ka-ehu asked him what he was doing there; he replied, 'I am catching a crab for my breakfast.' Ka-ehu said, 'We will help you catch your crab', and told Pehu to go near the coral reef while he and his large retinue of sharks would go seaward: when a number of surf-riders were far out they would appear and drive them shoreward in a tumultuous rush, and then Pehu could easily catch the crab. This pleased the shark from Maui, so he went close to the reef and hid himself in its shadows.
passages.note: Paraphrase of W. D. Westervelt, Legends of Old Honolulu, ch. 8 (1915); not verbatim.

passages.text: Ka-ehu said to his friends: 'We must kill this man-eating shark who is destroying our people. This will be a part of our pay to them for honoring us at Puu-loa, Pearl Harbor; we will all go and push Pehu into the shallow water.' A number of surf-riders poised on the waves, and Pehu called for the other sharks to come, but Ka-ehu told him to wait for a better chance. Soon two men started on a wave from the distant dark blue sea where the high surf begins. Ka-ehu gave a signal for an attack: his friends were to rush in under the great wave and, as it passed over the waiting Pehu, crowd the men and their surf-boards to one side and push the leaping Pehu so that he would be upset; then, while he was floundering in the surf, they must hurl him over the reef.
passages.note: Paraphrase of W. D. Westervelt, Legends of Old Honolulu, ch. 8 (1915); not verbatim.

passages.text: As Pehu leaped to catch one of the coming surf-riders he was astonished to see the man shoved to one side, then as he rose almost straight up in the water he was caught by the other sharks and tossed over and over until he plunged head first into a deep hole in the coral; he thrashed his great tail about, but only forced himself farther in so that he could not escape. The surf-riders went out to the hole and killed him and cut his body in pieces; inside the body they found hair and bones, showing that this shark had been destroying some of their people. They took the pieces to Pele-ula, where they made a great oven and burned them. Ka-ehu passed on toward Hawaii as a knight-errant, meeting many adventures and punishing evil-minded residents of the great sea.
passages.note: Paraphrase of W. D. Westervelt, Legends of Old Honolulu, ch. 8 (1915); not verbatim.

title.en: Maikoha and the Birth of Kapa
title.zh: 邁科哈與樹皮布之誕生

region.en: Pu-iwa, Nuuanu Valley, Oahu
region.zh: 瓦胡島努瓦努谷普伊瓦

period: Hawaiian oral tradition (Kuokoa 1865); retold 1915 (Westervelt)

source.work: W. D. Westervelt, Legends of Old Honolulu, ch. 9 (New York 1915)

summary.en: In the days before kapa the oldest clothes were dried banana leaves and ti-leaf cloaks. The farmer Maikoha of Pu-iwa, dying, bids his daughters bury him by the stream: a tree will grow from the grave, its bark for kapa. The wauke springs up; the daughters pound its bark into the first beaten cloth, and every broken branch takes root and spreads island to island. Maikoha becomes the ancestor-god of kapa-makers, his daughters the gods of pounding and of patterned beaters, Ehu the dyer's god - and Hina, mother of Maui, beats her kapa in the sky, where thunder is her rolling stones and lightning the flash between cloud-sheets.
summary.zh: 樹皮布問世之前，先民以乾蕉葉、露兜葉蔽體。普伊瓦農夫邁科哈臨終囑女兒將其葬於溪畔：墳上將生一樹，樹皮可製卡帕。瓦烏凱樹應聲而出；女兒們搗樹皮成最初的『捶打之物』，斷枝隨處生根，由島及島。邁科哈成為樹皮布匠的祖先神，二女分司搶打與花紋，染師敬染神埃胡——而毛伊之母希娜在天上捶打雲布：雷是她滾落的鎮布石，電是雲層間躍動的日光。

sensitivity.note: Craft-origin myth; technical details of kapa-making summarized.

passages.text: The old people said that in the very long ago their ancestors did not have anything like the kapa cloth which has been known for many centuries; there was no kapa maoli - nothing in nature which provided clothing or covering. The clothing of the oldest time was sometimes made by tying dried banana leaves around the body; the long fragrant leaves of the ti plant were dried, soaked in water until soft, then fastened together by braiding, making a very warm cloak worn by bird-catchers to shed rain and keep out cold. For many generations the Hawaiians made most beautiful and costly feather garments, braiding a foundation mesh of fine vegetable fibres and covering it with the most brilliant red and golden feathers from the birds of the forest.
passages.note: Paraphrase of W. D. Westervelt, Legends of Old Honolulu, ch. 9 (1915); not verbatim.

passages.text: This was the valley supposed to have been the first habitation of the gods, from which all life spread over the island group; here the gnomes, or eepa people, had their home, and here the Menehunes built a temple for the child adopted by the gods. At Pu-iwa, by the side of the running water, a farmer by the name of Maikoha lived with his daughters. Years passed by and Maikoha became weak and ill; on his death-bed he called his daughters and commanded them to listen carefully and obey his words, saying: 'When I die, bury my body close to the waters of our pleasant stream. A tree will grow from that burial-place. This tree will be to you for kapa, from which you will make all things good for clothing as well as covering when you sleep or are ill. The bark of this tree is the part you will use.' When death came, the daughters buried their father by the running water, and after a time a tree grew from the grave - not tall and large, but throwing out a number of small, spreading branches. This was the wauke tree. The daughters believed it was a gift from the aumakua, the ghost-god into which the spirit of their father had been changed; reverently they touched the tree, broke off some branches, stripped off the bark, and pounded and pounded until the pieces were fastened together in a rude kind of cloth - thus they found kapa, the beaten thing, and learned how to make it into small and large pieces and to fashion such clothing as met their need.
passages.note: Paraphrase of W. D. Westervelt, Legends of Old Honolulu, ch. 9 (1915); not verbatim.

passages.text: Wherever they cut or broke the branches of this new tree the broken pieces took root, or, caught by the swift-flowing stream, were tossed on the bank or carried and scattered over the plain, until they grew even to the sea; branches were carried to the other islands, thus the wauke became a blessing to all the people - this tree under the name aute, which is the same as wauke, was a blessing to many Polynesians from Tahiti to New Zealand. Maikoha became the chief aumakua, or ancestor-god, of the Hawaiian kapa-makers, and has been worshipped for generations: when they planted the wauke branches prayers, incantations and sacrifices were offered to Maikoha. One of his daughters, Lau-hu-iki, became the aumakua of all those who pounded the prepared bark; the other, Laa-hana, was worshipped by those who used especially marked clubs while beating the bark into patterns, for she learned how to scratch the clubs with sharks' teeth so that marks would be left in the pounded sheets. Ehu was made the aumakua of kapa-dyers because he learned how to dip the cloth in dyes and give it color, discovering the red dye in the blood of the kukui tree.
passages.note: Paraphrase of W. D. Westervelt, Legends of Old Honolulu, ch. 9 (1915); not verbatim.

passages.text: In the early time a flat stone was used upon which to pound out the sheets of kapa, but blocks of wood and long heavy sticks - called kua-kuku - gave the best results, giving back a soft sound with the rhythmic beat of the mallets, accompanied by the makers' own chants and incantations to Maikoha or one of the other aumakuas. Hina, the mother of the demi-god Maui, was the great kapa-maker of the legends of the ancient Hawaiians: it is said that she still spreads her kapas in the sky - they are the beautiful clouds of all colors, sometimes piled up and sometimes lying in sheets. When fierce winds blow and lift and toss the cloud kapas and roll off the stones which Hina has placed on them to hold them down, or when she throws off the stones herself, the noise of the rolling stones is the thunder which men hear; and when Hina rolls the cloud sheets together, the folds glisten and flash in the light of the sun - thus what men call lightning is the sunlight leaping from sheet to sheet of Hina's kapas in cloudland.
passages.note: Paraphrase of W. D. Westervelt, Legends of Old Honolulu, ch. 9 (1915); not verbatim.

title.en: Kamakau's Creation of the First Man
title.zh: 卡馬考傳：造人之說

region.en: Mokapu islet, Oahu (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 瓦胡島莫卡普小島（象徵性定位）

period: Hawaiian tradition recorded by Kamakau c. 1860s; retold 1915 (Westervelt)

source.work: W. D. Westervelt, Legends of Old Honolulu, ch. 10 (New York 1915)

summary.en: Kamakau's native-history version: the earth is a calabash, its cover the sky, sun and moon of its flesh, stars of its seeds. On Mokapu Kane kneads red dirt into the form of a man; Kanaloa's mockery of dirt lacks life and is turned to stone. Ku and Lono push a spirit of the air into the image, and Kane calls it alive - 'Hiki au, E-ola!' - and the man Wela-ahi-lani-nui stands. Sleeping, he is opened and a woman taken from his body: his shadow, aka, changed into 'The-heaven-changed-shadow', Ke-aka-huli-lani, ancestress of Hawaiians and all the peoples of the great ocean.
summary.zh: 卡馬考所記：大地如葫蘆，葫蓋化天，日月出其肉，星辰出其籽。莫卡普島上，卡內以紅土捏成人形；卡納洛亞嘲弄仿製的泥像無生氣，被咒為石。庫與龍諾將空中之靈推入泥像，卡內呼曰『我來，活吧！活吧！』——巨人韋拉阿希拉尼努伊應聲而起。他熟睡之際，諸神剖其身取出一女子：那便是曾隨他左右的名為『影子』的東西，如今名為『天變之影』——夏威夷人與大洋諸島萬民之祖。

sensitivity.note: Westervelt notes part of this Kamakau account is thoroughly Biblical; kept as recorded tradition with that caveat. Humans-molded-from-clay cluster.

passages.text: Ku, Ka-ne, Lono and Kanaloa were the first gods made. The gods had come from far-off unknown lands; they brought with them the mysterious people who live in precipices and trees and rocks - the invisible spirits of the air. The earth was a calabash; the gods threw the calabash cover upward and it became the sky; part of the thick flesh became the sun, another part was the moon, and the stars came from the seeds.
passages.note: Paraphrase of W. D. Westervelt, Legends of Old Honolulu, ch. 10 (1915); not verbatim.

passages.text: The gods went over to a small island called Mokapu, and thought they would make man to be chief over all other things. Mololani was the crater hill which forms the little island; on the sunrise side of this hill, near the sea, was the place where red dirt lay mixed with dark blue and black soil. Here Ka-ne scratched the dirt together and made the form of a man. Kanaloa ridiculed the mass of dirt and made a better form, but it did not have life.
passages.note: Paraphrase of W. D. Westervelt, Legends of Old Honolulu, ch. 10 (1915); not verbatim.

passages.text: Ka-ne said, 'You have made a dirt image; let it become stone.' Then Ka-ne ordered Ku and Lono to carefully obey his directions; they were afraid he would kill them, so at once they caught one of the spirits of the air and pushed it into the image Ka-ne had made. When the spirit had been pushed into the body, Ka-ne stood by the image and called, 'Hiki au, E-ola! E-ola!' - I come, live! live! Ku and Lono responded 'Live! live!' Then Ka-ne called again, 'I come, awake! awake!' and the other two responded, and the image became a living man. Then Ka-ne cried, 'I come, arise! arise!' and the image stood up - a man with a living spirit. They named him Wela-ahi-lani-nui, the great heaven burning hot.
passages.note: Paraphrase of W. D. Westervelt, Legends of Old Honolulu, ch. 10 (1915); not verbatim.

passages.text: The gods took this man to their home and nourished him. When he became strong he went out to walk around the home of the gods; soon he noticed a shadow going around with his body - it walked when he walked, and rested when he rested. He wondered what this thing was, and called it aka, shadow. When he slept, Ku, Ka-ne and Lono tore open his body, and Ka-ne took out a woman, leaving Ku and Lono to heal the body; then they put the woman by the side of the man and they were alike. Wela-ahi-lani-nui woke and found a beautiful one lying by him, and thought: 'This is that thing which has been by my side, my aka. The gods have changed it into this beautiful one.' So he gave her the name Ke-aka-huli-lani, the heaven-changed-shadow. These were the ancestors of the Hawaiians and all the peoples of the islands of the great ocean. It must be remembered that there are many other Hawaiian legends which mention other first men and women as ancestors of the Hawaiian people.
passages.note: Paraphrase of W. D. Westervelt, Legends of Old Honolulu, ch. 10 (1915); not verbatim.

title.en: Ku-ilio-loa, the Great Dog of the Clouds
title.zh: 雲中巨犬庫伊利洛阿

region.en: Mountain cave, Oahu (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 瓦胡島山穴（象徵性定位）

period: Hawaiian oral tradition; retold 1915 (Westervelt)

source.work: W. D. Westervelt, Legends of Old Honolulu, ch. 12 (New York 1915)

summary.en: The dog-god Ku-ilio-loa follows three rainbows to the bathing-pool of the chief's daughter Na-pihe-nui as a little white dog; discovered, he demands her in marriage and, refused, devours the chief's people one by one - sometimes falling like lightning on a group and striking far away almost instantly. Hidden women withstand the siege in a cave; in a final terrific battle Ku is overpowered, cut in two, and the priest's power turns the halves into two great stones. He still stretches from peak to peak among the changing clouds of Oahu - the nature-myth of the dog-shaped cloud.
summary.zh: 犬神庫伊利洛阿循三道彩虹而至酋長之女沐浴池畔，化身小白犬；被識破後索婚不遂，遂逐個吞食族人，時如閃電擊群、瞬息遠襲。酋長將婦孺藏於洞穴死守；決戰中巨犬力竭，身被斬為兩半，祭司施法使其化作兩塊巨石。至今它仍橫亙瓦胡群峰之間，隱現於變幻雲影——犬形雲的自然神話。

sensitivity.note: Cannibalism summarized; nature-myth reading per Westervelt.

passages.text: Ku, the dog-man, decided to come down from the clouds and visit mankind, so he assumed the form of a little dog and went around almost unnoticed. Ku saw a group of three rainbows moving from place to place or resting for a long time above the home of a high chief: sometimes the rainbows went up to the forests of ohia and kukui-trees, sometimes they rested over the deep pools made by the waterfalls of the swiftly descending mountain streams, and most frequently the beautiful colors were arched over a small grove of trees around a bathing-pool. Here Na-pihe-nui, the daughter of the high chief, came daily with her company of maidens to bathe and sport in the water. One day one of the girls saw something moving on the shore; they hastened to the place where their clothes had been thrown down and found a little white dog lying on the kapa mantle of the princess. For a time they played with the little stranger, delighted with his unusual intelligence, and took him with them and cared for him.
passages.note: Paraphrase of W. D. Westervelt, Legends of Old Honolulu, ch. 12 (1915); not verbatim.

passages.text: The high chief Polihale was interested in the peculiar powers possessed by this strange dog; his suspicions were aroused and the dog was watched. Soon the chief learned that this was a man of marvellous ability who could appear as a dog or a man at his own pleasure, and ordered his retainers to kill the dog; it dashed into the woods and made its escape. It was the great dog Ku, who had seen the three rainbows and followed them to the bathing-pool and then, having seen the princess, had determined to carry her away as his wife. Then Ku changed himself into a man of fine appearance and came boldly to the high chief's home demanding the princess in marriage, but the chief, warned by the omens studied by his soothsayers, refused. Ku was in great anger and threatened to kill the chief's people, but the high chief drove him away.
passages.note: Paraphrase of W. D. Westervelt, Legends of Old Honolulu, ch. 12 (1915); not verbatim.

passages.text: A dream came to the high chief in which he saw the strange man coming as a great dog, stretching itself out of a cave on the mountain-side; he knew this dog with magical powers would be a very difficult enemy to overcome. The chief soon learned that Ku was catching his people one by one and devouring them, and decided to take final issue with his enemy. He hid all the women of his family in a cave, placing the princess in their care with provisions for a long siege, water found in the cave itself, and stones placed before the opening. Then the high chief and his followers waged war against Ku, the dog-man, but Ku was very strong and overthrew his pursuers; many times he killed some of the chief's people and carried their bodies away to feast upon them, and he was so swift that sometimes he fell like a flash of lightning upon a group of his foes and in an incredibly short time would make an attack in a far distant place.
passages.note: Paraphrase of W. D. Westervelt, Legends of Old Honolulu, ch. 12 (1915); not verbatim.

passages.text: The high chief offered sacrifices to his gods and secured charms from his priests; incantations and prayers were prepared against Ku. At last a terrific battle was fought and Ku was overpowered and beaten to the ground; still he fought fiercely, but the hard wooden spears pierced him and the heavy clubs broke his bones, until he lay a crushed and bleeding mass at the feet of his conquerors. They cut his body in two pieces, throwing one to one side and the other to a place some distance away; then the power of the priests was invoked and the two parts of the body of Ku-ilio-loa became two great stones which have been objects of veneration among the Hawaiians for many years. Ku stretches his form along the mountains and sometimes reveals himself as the great dog among the myriad shapes which the changing clouds are ever assuming - sometimes in the clouds of Oahu, and then again his form is in the skies of other islands.
passages.note: Paraphrase of W. D. Westervelt, Legends of Old Honolulu, ch. 12 (1915); not verbatim.

title.en: The Battle of the Owls of Kakuhihewa
title.zh: 卡庫希黑瓦王與群鴞之戰

region.en: Waikiki heiau, Oahu
region.zh: 瓦胡島威基基神廟

period: Hawaiian oral tradition; retold 1915 (Westervelt)

source.work: W. D. Westervelt, Legends of Old Honolulu, ch. 18 (New York 1915)

summary.en: Kapoi, moved by an owl's plea, gives back her seven stolen eggs, adopts her as his family god, builds her a temple at Manoa and lifts his own tabu - death under king Kakuhihewa's decree. In Waikiki's heiau the owl-king of Manoa calls the owls of every island by drum: in one day Hawaii, Lanai, Maui and Molokai's owls gather at Kalapueo, Oahu's at Kanoniakapueo, Kauai and Niihau's at Pueo-hulu-nui. At daybreak the sky is covered; owls tear eyes and faces, befoul the warriors, and Kapoi is freed - 'Your god has mana greater than my god; your god is a true god.'
summary.zh: 卡波伊為鴞之哀求所動，歸還其七枚卵，奉其為家神，於馬諾阿為之建廟，並自設又自解禁忌——依卡庫希黑瓦王之法，此乃死罪。囚於威基基神廟之際，馬諾阿的鴞王擊鼓召集各島之鴞：一日之內，夏威夷、拉奈、毛伊、摩洛凱之鴞集於卡拉普埃奧，考愛與尼豪之鴞集於普埃霍胡魯努伊。破曉時分，天空盡為鴞翼所蔽；它們啄眼撲面、污及眾武士，卡波伊得釋——王亦承認：『你的神法力高於我的神，你的神是真神。』

sensitivity.note: Owl-worship origin legend; also covers the Pueo trials establishing proof before punishment.

passages.text: Pueo, the owl-god, was also Pueo-alii, king of owls; he had kahunas who consulted him by signs, and the aumakuas, or ghost gods, sometimes in oracles. From his own residence on Owl's Hill he governed all Manoa Valley. It was said that one of the natives in the valley displeased him; he captured the man and at once ordered the death penalty, calling him a rebel. The man secured the attention of the owl-god for a moment and presented the plea that he ought to be permitted to say something for himself before he was punished; the execution was delayed, the man proved that he was innocent of the charge against him, and the owl-god established a law that a person must be proved guilty before he could be condemned and punished. This came to be a custom among the Hawaiians as the years passed by.
passages.note: Paraphrase of W. D. Westervelt, Legends of Old Honolulu, ch. 18 (1915); not verbatim.

passages.text: Down Pauoa Valley dashes a stream of beautiful clear water, passing the eastern edge of Punchbowl Hill. Here at Kahehuna lived a man by the name of Kapoi, whose grass house was decaying, its thatch falling to pieces. Kapoi went to the Kewalo marsh near the beach, where tall pili grass was growing, to get a bundle for thatching; he found a nest of owl's eggs, took up his bundle of grass and the nest and returned home. In the evening he prepared to cook the eggs, making a fire in his small imu with his fire-sticks; an owl flew down and sat on the wall by the gate. Kapoi had almost finished wrapping the eggs in ti leaves and was about to lay them on the hot stones when the owl called to him: 'O Kapoi! Give me my eggs.' 'How many eggs belong to you?' 'I have seven eggs.' 'I am cooking these eggs for I have no fish.' 'O Kapoi! You are heartless, and you have no sorrow for me if you do not give back my eggs.' Kapoi was touched, and said, 'Come and get your eggs.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of W. D. Westervelt, Legends of Old Honolulu, ch. 18 (1915); not verbatim.

passages.text: Because of this kindness the owl became Kapoi's god, and commanded him to build a heiau and make a raised place and an altar for sacrifice at Manoa. He laid a sacrifice and some bananas on the altar, established the day for the tabu to begin and the day when the tabu should be lifted. This was talked about by the people, and by and by the high chief heard that a man had built a temple for his god, had made it tabu and had lifted the tabu. Kakuhihewa was living at Waikiki, the king after whom the island Oahu was named Oahu-a-Kakuhihewa; he had made a law for the temple he was building at Waikiki, decreeing that if any chief or man should build a temple with a tabu on it and should lift that tabu before the tabu on the king's temple should be over, that chief or man should pay the penalty of death as a rebel. The king sent out his servants and captured Kapoi; they brought him to Waikiki and placed him in the king's heiau Kapalaha, where he was to be killed and offered in sacrifice to the offended god of the king's temple.
passages.note: Paraphrase of W. D. Westervelt, Legends of Old Honolulu, ch. 18 (1915); not verbatim.

passages.text: His owl-god was grateful for the return of the eggs and determined to reward him for his kindness and protect him as a worshipper. This owl-god was a family god belonging only to Kapoi and his immediate household; according to Hawaiian custom any individual could select anything he wished as the god for himself and family. Kapoi's owl-god secured the aid of the king of owls, who lived in Manoa Valley on Owl's Hill, and the king of owls sent out a call for the owls of all the islands to come and make war against the king of Oahu and his warriors. Kauai legends say that the sound of the drum of the owl-king was so penetrating that it could be heard across all the channels by the owls on the different islands; in one day the owls of Hawaii, Lanai, Maui and Molokai had gathered at Kalapueo, the owls of Koolau and Kahikiku of Oahu in Kanoniakapueo, and the owls of Kauai and Niihau in Pueo-hulu-nui near Moanalua. Kakuhihewa had set apart the day of Ka-ne as the day when Kapoi should be sacrificed; in the morning of that day the priests were to slay Kapoi and place him on the altar in the presence of the king and his warriors. At daybreak the owls rallied around that temple; as the sun rose its light was obscured - the owls were clouds covering the heavens. Warriors and chiefs and priests tried to drive the birds away; the owls flew down and tore the eyes and faces of the men of Kakuhihewa, scratched dirt over them and befouled them. Such an attack was irresistible: Kakuhihewa's men fled, and Kapoi was set free. Kakuhihewa said to Kapoi: 'Your god has mana, miraculous power, greater than my god. Your god is a true god.' Kapoi was saved, the owl was worshipped as a god, and the place of that battle was Kukaeunahio-ka-pueo, the confused noise of owls rising in masses.
passages.note: Paraphrase of W. D. Westervelt, Legends of Old Honolulu, ch. 18 (1915); not verbatim.

title.en: The Maihisikiri Takes the Woman for a Bush Spirit
title.zh: 邁希斯基里攜婦化為林鬼

region.en: Pomeroon River, Guyana (Warrau)
region.zh: 蓋亞那波默龍河瓦勞之地

period: Warrau oral tradition; recorded 1915 (Roth)

source.work: Walter E. Roth, An Inquiry into the Animism and Folk-lore of the Guiana Indians (33rd Annual Report, Bureau of American Ethnology, 1915), ch. VIII 'Spirits of the Bush', §§97-97A

summary.en: The Maihisikiri is a Yawahu wandering the bush that can assume the very face and body of a woman's husband; woe to the woman who yields to it, for she will die within days — unless she is shrewd enough to look at the left foot, which lacks its big toe. One woman was taken in three times; when at last she challenged it, the spirit confessed and led her away. Her husband found her lying in the distance laughing, all soft, without a single bone in her body — she had become a Bush Spirit herself, and told him, 'You will have to die before you can become one.'
summary.zh: 邁希斯基里乃林中鬼，能幻作婦人之夫；婦若信之，數日必死——惟察其左足無大趾者可辨。一婦三受其欺；末詰之，鬼自認而攜之去。夫尋至，見妻笑臥於野，遍體無骨——已化林鬼。婦曰：『夫須先死，方能為鬼。』

sensitivity.note: Warrau oral tradition recorded 1915 (Roth); archival record, read critically.

passages.text: The Maihisikiri is a particular Yawahu wandering about the bush and in and among the trees, of which the native women have to be especially careful. Such spirits can assume the identical material appearance of their real husbands or lovers, but woe betide those poor women who yield to their solicitations, for they will surely die in a few days. The shrewd woman can always tell whether she is dealing with the real man or not — she has only to look at the left foot: in the case of a spirit wooer this is always minus the big toe.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Roth 1915, §97; not verbatim.

passages.text: A man went out hunting, leaving his wife behind; a Maihisikiri appeared, and believing it to be her husband, the woman allowed it to act like one. On the third visit, knowing her husband had gone to a distant locality, she asked: 'How can you be my husband? He is gone far away.' Only then did it admit it was a Bush Spirit in her husband's likeness, and told her to come away. When the real husband returned the house was empty; he found her prostrate, laughing because the Maihisikiri was sporting with her. When he seized her arm it was all soft, with no bones in it — she had not a single bone left in her body. 'I do not really want to leave you, husband, but the Maihisikiri is too strong for me. I am now a Bush Spirit. And though you must not be sorry for me, I am indeed sorry for you, for you will have to die before you can become one.'
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Roth 1915, §97A; not verbatim.

title.en: The Man Who Always Hunted Scrub-Turkey
title.zh: 恆獵鷸鳥之人

region.en: Arawak country, Guyana
region.zh: 蓋亞那阿拉瓦克之地

period: Arawak oral tradition; recorded 1915 (Roth)

source.work: Walter E. Roth, An Inquiry into the Animism and Folk-lore of the Guiana Indians (33rd Annual Report, Bureau of American Ethnology, 1915), ch. VIII 'Spirits of the Bush', §98

summary.en: A man celebrated for his skill in hunting maam (scrub-turkey) brought home four or five a day until people warned him he would get into trouble with the bird's 'mother' — the Spirit. He did not care. One evening, following the calling of the birds deeper and deeper into the forest, he found a woman's leg roosting among the branches: the arch Spirit of the maams. He shot the foot through the center; the leg fell and became an extraordinarily big scrub-turkey, which he cooked and ate whole, giving away not the smallest particle. Thereafter he hunted more successfully than ever, and feared nothing.
summary.zh: 一獵人善獵鷸，日獲四五隻；人誡其勿犯鳥之『母』——即鳥鬼——而彼不聽。一夜循鳴聲入深林，見枝上有婦人之足，乃鷸之大鬼。射其足心，足落地化為特大之鷸；烹而盡食之，分毫不與人。自後獵愈多，無所懼矣。

sensitivity.note: Arawak oral tradition recorded 1915 (Roth); archival record, read critically.

passages.text: There was a man celebrated for his skill in hunting 'maam' (scrub-turkey); he would regularly bring home four or five of these birds, and people warned him that if he continued in this way he would get into trouble with the maam's 'mother' — the Spirit — for killing so many of her brood. But he did not care, and went on destroying the birds in the same wasteful manner.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Roth 1915, §98; not verbatim.

passages.text: One occasion he stayed out later than usual, tracking the calls deeper and deeper until he found himself deep in the forest. Locating the tree, he peered in among the branches to see where the bird was calling — but could see only a woman's leg. Recognizing this to be the arch Spirit of the maams, he took careful aim and shot an arrow right into the center of the foot. The leg fell down, and directly it touched ground changed into an extraordinarily big scrub-turkey, which he killed and carried home. His friends knew it at once to be the maam's 'mother', and advised him to cook and eat the whole of it himself, not giving away even the smallest particle. He did what was advised, and was ever after even more successful than before — and now that he had destroyed the maam-Spirit, he was not afraid of killing as many birds as he liked.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Roth 1915, §98; not verbatim.

title.en: The Shrewd Little Boy and the Hebu
title.zh: 小兒智破林鬼

region.en: Pomeroon River, Guyana (Warrau)
region.zh: 蓋亞那波默龍河瓦勞之地

period: Warrau oral tradition; recorded 1915 (Roth)

source.work: Walter E. Roth, An Inquiry into the Animism and Folk-lore of the Guiana Indians (33rd Annual Report, Bureau of American Ethnology, 1915), ch. VIII 'Spirits of the Bush', §99

summary.en: Kau-nassa, a Hebu disguised as their old grandmother, led two little girls away 'to your mother' and drowned them in a closed basket dropped into a creek. At a second house the shrewd boy was told not to play behind her back — and so of course slipped behind, seeing the old woman's lower back aglow with the fire she carried there. Knowing her for a Hebu, he carried his little sister home, calling out her name: Kau-nassa! So angered and dismayed was the Spirit at being discovered that she burst into wind and flame and flew away.
summary.zh: 鬼卡烏納薩偽裝老嫗，誘二女往『見母』，織籃閉之沉於溪而溺之。至第二家，誡小兒毋戲其背——兒故潛至其後，見其下背火光熒然，知為林鬼。攜妹歸，呼其名曰：卡烏納薩！鬼羞怒，化風焰而飛去。

sensitivity.note: Warrau oral tradition recorded 1915 (Roth); archival record, read critically.

passages.text: A woman having to go to make starch out of the ite tree left her little children, two girls, behind the house. While she was away Kau-nassa, a Bush Spirit, came along disguised as their old grandmother and said: 'Come along, my little girls. I will take you to your mother.' Instead she led them far into the bush to a creek, sat down and made a basket; when it was completed she told the youngsters to get inside, closed the top, and threw it into the water, where the children were soon drowned.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Roth 1915, §99; not verbatim.

passages.text: Kau-nassa then went to another house where a little boy and girl had been left in charge, similarly disguised as their grandmother. At the creek she said: 'You children must not play behind my back. Play in front of me where I can see you.' The very fact of being told not to go behind her made the boy all the more anxious to do what had been forbidden: he slipped away behind and saw the lower part of the old woman's back all aglow with the fire she carried there. He knew now that she was a Hebu, and getting back to his little sister, carried her home. But before going he called out, 'Kau-nassa! Kau-nassa!' So angered and dismayed was the Spirit at being discovered and hearing her name called that she burst into wind and flame and flew away.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Roth 1915, §99; not verbatim.

title.en: The Spirit's Brain and the Goat-Suckers
title.zh: 鬼腦與夜鷹

region.en: Arawak-Carib country, Guyana
region.zh: 蓋亞那阿拉瓦克-加勒比之地

period: Arawak/Carib oral tradition; recorded 1915 (Roth)

source.work: Walter E. Roth, An Inquiry into the Animism and Folk-lore of the Guiana Indians (33rd Annual Report, Bureau of American Ethnology, 1915), ch. VIII 'Spirits of the Bush', §103

summary.en: Waiting for rain to draw land-crabs, a hunter pressed a calabash over his head; a Konoko-kuyuha marveling at his 'fine smooth head' was persuaded to have his own cut round and peppered, while the man slipped away. Years later the spirit recognized him by the pepper bushes grown on his skull and swore revenge. 'The person who really did it has been dead a long time,' said the man, leading him to a stack of deer bones; they danced with the bones rattling, and when the spirit bent his head low over the baking-stone the man crushed it. From each scattered piece of brain there grew a wokorai-yu, the goat-sucker — that is why we Indians dread these birds and leave them severely alone: they come from the spirits of the bush and give warning of evil.
summary.zh: 獵人候雨捕蟹，以瓢覆首；林鬼見其『光首』，羨而求己首亦環割敷椒；獵人遁去。多年後鬼認之，欲殺之。獵人曰：『其人久死矣』，引至鹿骨堆；共舞骨歌，鬼俯首近烤石，被擊碎腦——腦片各生一夜鷹。故印第安人畏夜鷹而不敢害之：彼等自林鬼而出，報凶之兆也。

sensitivity.note: Arawak/Carib oral tradition recorded 1915 (Roth); archival record, read critically.

passages.text: A man went out hunting for land crab, waiting for the rain to fall, for only under this condition does the animal creep out of its hole. When the rain fell it wet his hair; the huntsman, using his calabash like a cap, pressed it firmly down upon his head. A Konoko-kuyuha put in an appearance, and seeing the man in this guise could not help exclaiming: 'What a fine smooth head you have! How did you manage to get it?' The man told him he had just taken a knife and cut his head all the way round, and offered to do the same for the spirit, who was delighted, allowed the skin round his head to be cut and peppers rubbed over the raw surface to make it heal the quicker — groaning in pain while the huntsman quietly slipped out of sight.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Roth 1915, §103; not verbatim.

passages.text: Many years later, the same man met the same Konoko-kuyuha and recognized him by the peppers on his head, which had grown into big bushes. 'You are the man who peeled off my head. I will kill you.' — 'No. The person who really did it has been dead a long time. Come with me and I will show you his bones.' He led him to a stack of deer bones; the spirit threw them one by one into his basket and said: 'Let us dance, and make his bones rattle.' Singing, 'It was you that peeled my head... How do you like to hear your own bones rattling for music?', they danced until the man directed the spirit onto a fine flat baking-stone and told him to bend his head lower, lower still — and suddenly crushed it thereon.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Roth 1915, §103; not verbatim.

passages.text: The Spirit's brains were thus scattered, and from each piece there 'grew' a wokorai-yu — the goat-sucker. This is why we Indians always dread these birds, and leave them severely alone; they come from the Spirits of the Bush, and give us warning of evil — a token that we may expect trouble of various sorts.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Roth 1915, §103; not verbatim.

title.en: The Mutilated Husband Is Made Whole
title.zh: 碎夫復活

region.en: Pomeroon River, Guyana (Warrau)
region.zh: 蓋亞那波默龍河瓦勞之地

period: Warrau oral tradition; recorded 1915 (Roth)

source.work: Walter E. Roth, An Inquiry into the Animism and Folk-lore of the Guiana Indians (33rd Annual Report, Bureau of American Ethnology, 1915), ch. VIII 'Spirits of the Bush', §106

summary.en: A wife traveled in male attire to an all-male work camp, and when found out, the two men who coveted her tried three times to kill her husband — twice frustrated, the third time tied in a corial to drift out to sea, from which a tiger gnawed him free. A house-master who was really a Spirit sent him with a spirit friend to seek her; the guilty couple chopped him up with an ax, but the spirit restored him — again and again, until the keeper burned the body and scattered the ashes, and the spirit gathered the ashes in a palm leaf and made them into a living person again. Only spirits can do such things: the revived husband then destroyed his faithless wife and her paramour, whom their friends could not piece alive.
summary.zh: 婦扮男裝隨夫至男子聚作之所；事露，二男欲得其婦，三謀殺其夫——末縛之於舟，漂流出海，虎嚙繩縱之。一實為鬼之屋主遣鬼友偕往尋妻；奸夫婦以斧碎之，鬼復活之——三次皆然，末焚其屍而散其灰，鬼聚灰於棕葉，復成人形。惟鬼能為此。復活之夫乃誅其妻與其姦夫。

sensitivity.note: Warrau oral tradition recorded 1915 (Roth); archival record, read critically.

passages.text: A man told his wife he was going to another village to work for the headman; she was so importunate to come that he yielded and insisted on her traveling in male attire — hair cut short, breasts hidden with cotton and hog-tooth neck-chains, a strip of bark covering her nakedness. The others at the settlement wondered why the new-comer would never bathe with them, and set watch; discovering it was a woman, they determined on killing the husband so as to secure possession of the wife.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Roth 1915, §106; not verbatim.

passages.text: They tried twice, but each time something went wrong with their plans. The third time they tied him in a corial and let it drift out to sea, but the sea cast it back on shore, where a tiger, scenting him, gnawed through the ropes and set him free — for pure selfishness, telling his captive he now intended punishing him. 'Don't do that; haven't I been punished enough in losing my wife?' pleaded the man, and the tiger let him go. The house-master who received him was really a Spirit; he told the man to shut his eyes, and when he opened them again another Spirit was present to guide him to his wife.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Roth 1915, §106; not verbatim.

passages.text: The guilty couple, recognizing the husband, chopped him up with an ax — but the Spirit friend restored him to life. They killed him a second time; the Spirit again made him whole. A third time the keeper burned the body and scattered the ashes; this made no difference, for the Spirit collected the ashes together in a palm leaf and made them into a living person again. The resurrected husband, acting under advice, then destroyed his faithless wife as well as her paramour: their friends tried to piece the bits together and 'make them alive', but could not. It is only Spirits who can do such things.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Roth 1915, §106; not verbatim.

title.en: How Pain, Misery, and Death Came into the World
title.zh: 苦難與死亡之由來

region.en: Pomeroon district, Guyana (Carib)
region.zh: 蓋亞那波默龍加勒比之地

period: Carib oral tradition; recorded 1915 (Roth)

source.work: Walter E. Roth, An Inquiry into the Animism and Folk-lore of the Guiana Indians (33rd Annual Report, Bureau of American Ethnology, 1915), ch. VIII 'Spirits of the Bush', §108

summary.en: In the olden times there was no contention, all were happy, and no one became sick or died: the Yurokons came and lived among the Caribs as friends. One came as a woman with a baby at the breast; the pepper-pot burned her mouth, and while she went to the water for a drink some worthless woman threw her baby into the boiling cassiri pot. Stirring the pot, she found her child's body rise to the surface. Then she upbraided the people: 'Your children shall all die, and this will make you weep as I am weeping. You shall suffer pain and trouble at their birth. And you men shall have great trouble when you go out to catch fish.' So fishing was made a toil of poisoning pools, and pain, misery, and death entered the world.
summary.zh: 上古無爭，人人安樂，無病無死：林鬼亦為友。一鬼幻為哺乳之婦；辣鍋灼口，取水間嬰兒被擲沸酒鍋中。攪酒而嬰屍浮。鬼怒咒曰：『汝等之子必死，令汝如我之泣；產子必受痛；捕魚必受勞。』於是毒魚為業，苦難與死亡遂入世。

sensitivity.note: Carib oral tradition recorded 1915 (Roth); archival record, read critically. Origin-of-death cluster parallel.

passages.text: In the olden times, there was no contention, all were happy, and no one became sick or died. It was then that the Yurokons used to come and live among us as our friends and associates; they were short people like ourselves. One Yurokon in particular used to come and drink paiwarri with my people regularly once a month. The last time he came, he appeared as a woman with a baby at the breast.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Roth 1915, §108; not verbatim.

passages.text: The Caribs gave her of the pepper-pot, into which she dipped the cassava; it was so hot that it burned the inside of her mouth and 'heart', and this made her ask for water. Leaving her baby up at the house, she went down to the waterside and quenched her thirst. On her return her little child was nowhere to be seen, because during her absence some worthless woman among the company had thrown it into the boiling cassiri pot. By and by Yurokon went to stir the cassiri with the usual paddle-spoon, and, while she stirred, the body of her baby rose to the surface.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Roth 1915, §108; not verbatim.

passages.text: She wept, and then, turning on the people, upbraided them: 'Why have you punished me in this way? I have never had a bad mind against any of you, but now I will make you pay me. In future your children shall all die, and this will make you weep as I am weeping. And when children are born to you, you shall suffer pain and trouble at their birth. Furthermore, I will give you great trouble when you go out to catch fish.' — for in those days the Caribs only had to bail the water out of the streams and pick up the fish left exposed at the bottom, putting the water back to breed fish once more. Yurokon altered all this, made fish-poisoning the toil it now is, killed the worthless Indian who had thrown her boy into the cassiri — and pain, misery, and death entered the world.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Roth 1915, §108; not verbatim.

narrative.en: The Caribs of the Pomeroon district tell that in the olden times there was no contention: all were happy, and no one became sick or died. In those days the Yurokons — the hairy little forest spirits, short people like the Caribs themselves — used to come and live among men as friends and associates. One Yurokon in particular came regularly once a month to drink paiwarri with the narrator's people. The last time he came he appeared as a woman with a baby at the breast. The Caribs gave her pepper-pot, into which she dipped her cassava; it burned her mouth and 'heart', and she asked for water, was told there was none, and went down to the water-side with her calabash, leaving the baby at the house. While she was gone some worthless woman among the company threw the child into the boiling cassiri pot. When she returned and stirred the drink with the paddle-spoon, the body of her baby rose to the surface. She wept, then turned on the people with the curse that re-ordered the world: 'Why have you punished me in this way? I have never had a bad mind against any of you, but now I will make you pay me. In future your children shall all die, and this will make you weep as I am weeping. And when children are born to you, you shall suffer pain and trouble at their birth. Furthermore, with regard to you men, I will give you great trouble when you go out to catch fish.' So fishing, which in those days meant simply bailing out a stream and picking the fish from the exposed bed before letting the water back to breed again, became the toil of poisoning pools with roots; and sickness, the pain of childbirth, and death entered the world — a Guianese parallel to the world-wide origin-of-death tales in which a spirit's child is killed and the loss is repaid in the only coin mortals have.

functions: Origin-of-death tale: explains mortality, the pain of childbirth, and the labour of fish-poisoning as a single compensation for the murdered spirit-child
Codes hospitality: guests — even disguised spirits — must not be wronged, for the wronged spirit's curse binds the whole community
Sanctions food-processing taboos around menstruation, pregnancy, and drinking-feasts within which such 'worthless women' offences were policed
Anchors the ritual authority of the piai, whose spirit-friends are the Yurokons now estranged from men

variants.name: Kururumanni version (Arawak, after Schomburgk)
variants.text_tradition: Arawak, recorded by Schomburgk and summarised by Roth
variants.summary: Kururumanni came to earth to see what the Arawaks were doing, found them so bad that he wished to destroy them, and took away their everlasting life, bestowing it on the creatures that cast their skins — snakes, lizards, and cockroaches.

variants.name: Tamanac version (after Humboldt)
variants.text_tradition: Tamanac, recorded by Humboldt, summarised in Roth 1915
variants.summary: Amalivaca, departing across the salt water, sang to the Tamanacs 'You will change your skins' — perpetual youth — until one doubting old woman cried out, and he revoked the blessing: 'You shall die!'

variants.name: Warrau version (after Roth)
variants.summary: A man who married a Water Spirit disobeyed her one command — that at her moon-sickness she must stay in the hut — and she died in the women's out-house; her father decreed that sickness, accident and death should henceforth come to the Warraus from the Water People.
