Such is the narrowness of her territory that her knees and chin touch, no other position being possible. Vari-ma-te-takere was very anxious for progeny. One day she plucked off a bit of her right side, and it became a human being - the first man Avatea, or Vatea, the father of gods and men, half man and half fish, the division being like the two halves of the human body; thus one eye of Vatea was human, the other a fish-eye; his right side was furnished with an arm, the left with a fin; he had one proper foot, and half a fish-tail. But there is another, and probably far more ancient, account of Vatea, which means moon in all the dialects of Eastern Polynesia: Vatea is a man possessed of two magnificent eyes, rarely visible at the same time - whilst one, called by mortals the sun, is seen in this upper world, the other eye, called by men the moon, shines in Avaiki.
passages.note: Paraphrase of W. W. Gill, Myths and Songs from the South Pacific, ch. 1 (1876); not verbatim.

passages.text: The land assigned by the Great Mother to Vatea was Te-papa-rairai, the thin land - the bright land of Vatea, implying the perfect contrast between the brightness of noon-day and the utter gloom of Po. On another occasion Vari-ma-te-takere tore off a second bit from that same right side, and it became Tinirau, Innumerable, who, like his brother, had a second and fishy form; the Great Mother gave him the land of Motu-Tapu, the Sacred Isle, where were his celebrated ponds full of all kinds of fish - Tinirau was lord of the finny inhabitants of the sea, from the shark downwards. Another day Vari took a bit off her left side, and it became Tango, Support, who went to live at Enua-Kura, the land of red parrot-feathers. A fourth child was Tumuteanaoa, Echo, whose home was Te-parai-tea, the hollow grey rocks; Echo is represented as a female.
passages.note: Paraphrase of W. W. Gill, Myths and Songs from the South Pacific, ch. 1 (1876); not verbatim.

passages.text: A fifth child was Raka, Trouble, who presides, like Aeolus, over the winds; Raka found a congenial home in Moana-Irakau, Deep-ocean, and received from Vari a great basket in which the winds were hidden, also the knowledge of many useful inventions; the children of Raka are the numerous winds and storms which distress mankind, and to each child is allotted a hole at the edge of the horizon through which he blows at pleasure. Vari, finding that her left side had been more injured than her right, resolved to make both sides alike by taking a third bit from the right side, and named this, her last child, Tu-metua, Stick-by-the-parent, who lives with the Great Mother in that narrow strip of territory constituting the very bottom of Avaiki, the mute land, where the only language known is that of signs - such as nods, elevated eye-brows, grimaces, and smiles.
passages.note: Paraphrase of W. W. Gill, Myths and Songs from the South Pacific, ch. 1 (1876); not verbatim.

title.en: Maui Wins the Fire-god's Secret in the Shades
title.zh: 毛伊冥界取火記

region.en: Avaiki, nether-world of Mangaia (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 曼加亞冥界阿瓦伊基（象徵性定位）

period: Hervey Islands oral tradition; recorded 1876 (Gill)

source.work: W. W. Gill, Myths and Songs from the South Pacific, ch. 4, The Exploits of Maui: The Fire-god's Secret (London 1876)

summary.en: Peeping into his mother Buataranga's basket, Maui finds cooked food - the secret of fire lies in Avaiki. Borrowing Tane's red pigeon Fearless, he speaks the chasm-opening charm his mother taught him and descends into the shades, where the fire-god Mauike hurls him higher than any coconut tree - and is caught like a ball. Tortured in mid-air, Mauike bargains for life: the fire-sticks oronga and especially the banyan, and the friction-song. Maui sets all nether-world aflame, rescues the pigeon's tail, and returns to the upper world with the two fire-sticks of Mauike.
summary.zh: 毛伊偷窺母親布瓦塔蘭嘎的食籃，發現熟食——火的秘密在冥界。他借得塔內的紅鴿『無畏』，誦母親所授的裂石咒，自岩隙降入幽冥。火神毛伊凱接連將他拋向高空——高過任何椰子樹——他卻如球般被接住；精疲力竭的火神討饒求活，吐露火之奧秘：奧龍伽木、尤以榕木為要，與鑽木咒歌。毛伊縱火燒盡冥界，修復鴿尾，攜火種兩枚重返陽世。

sensitivity.note: Fire-theft cluster: Mangaian Maui descends to the shades for fire.

passages.text: Originally fire was unknown to the inhabitants of this world, who of necessity ate raw food. In nether-world (Avaiki) lived four mighty ones: Mauike, god of fire; the Sun-god Ra; Ru, supporter of the heavens; and lastly, his wife Buataranga, guardian of the road to the invisible world. To Ru and Buataranga was born a famous son, Maui. At an early age Maui was appointed one of the guardians of this upper world where mortals live. The mother occasionally visited her son, but always ate her food apart, out of a basket brought with her from nether-land. One day, when she was asleep, Maui peeped into her basket and discovered cooked food; upon tasting it he was decidedly of opinion that it was a great improvement upon the raw diet to which he was accustomed. This food came from nether-world; it was evident that the secret of fire was there. To nether-world, the home of his parents, he would descend to gain this knowledge, so that ever after he might enjoy the luxury of cooked food.
passages.note: Paraphrase of W. W. Gill, Myths and Songs from the South Pacific, ch. 4 (1876); not verbatim.

passages.text: On the following day Buataranga was about to descend to Avaiki, when Maui followed her through the bush without her knowing it, peering through the tall reeds, and saw his mother standing opposite a black rock, which she addressed with the magic words: 'Buataranga, descend thou bodily through this chasm. The rainbow-like must be obeyed. As two dark clouds parting at dawn: Open, open up my road to nether-world, ye fierce ones.' At these words the rock divided, and Buataranga descended. Maui carefully treasured up these magic words; and without delay started off to see the god Tane, the owner of some wonderful pigeons. Nothing would content Maui but the possession of Akaotu, Fearless, a red pigeon specially prized by Tane; Tane, who was loth to part from his pet, extracted a promise from Maui that the pigeon should be restored uninjured. Maui set off carrying the red pigeon, pronounced the magic words, and to his great delight the rock opened; entering the pigeon, he descended. Some assert that Maui transformed himself into a small dragon-fly and perched upon the back of the pigeon. The two fierce guardian demons of the chasm made a grab at the pigeon intending to devour it, but only succeeded in getting possession of the tail, whilst the pigeon, minus its beautiful tail, pursued its flight to the shades.
passages.note: Paraphrase of W. W. Gill, Myths and Songs from the South Pacific, ch. 4 (1876); not verbatim.

passages.text: Arrived at nether-land, Maui sought the home of his mother, guided by the sound of her cloth-flail. The red pigeon alighted on an oven-house opposite the open shed where Buataranga was beating out cloth; she guessed the red pigeon to be a visitor from the upper world, as none of the pigeons in the shades were red. 'Are you not come from daylight?' The pigeon nodded assent. 'Are you not my son Maui?' Again the pigeon nodded. Maui resumed his proper human form and went to embrace his mother, avowing that he had come to learn the secret of fire. Buataranga said the secret rested with the fire-god Mauike, whose dwelling was called Are-aoa, house-of-banyan-sticks; she entreated Maui to be careful, for the fire-god is a terrible fellow of a very irritable temper. Maui walked up boldly to the house of the fire-god and demanded a fire-brand, extinguished it in the stream, returned, and extinguished a second and a third; the fourth time Mauike was beside himself with rage, and ordered him away under pain of being tossed into the air. But the visitor said he should enjoy nothing better than a trial of strength with the fire-god.
passages.note: Paraphrase of W. W. Gill, Myths and Songs from the South Pacific, ch. 4 (1876); not verbatim.

passages.text: Mauike boldly seized him with both hands and hurled him to the height of a cocoa-nut tree; Maui contrived in falling to make himself so light that he was in no degree hurt. Maddened that his adversary should yet breathe, Mauike next hurled him far higher than the highest cocoa-nut tree that ever grew; yet Maui was uninjured, whilst the fire-god lay panting for breath. It was now Maui's turn: seizing the fire-god he threw him up to a dizzy height and caught him again like a ball with his hands, without allowing Mauike to touch the ground. Assured that this was but preparation for a final toss which would seal his fate, the panting and thoroughly exhausted Mauike entreated Maui to stop and to spare his life. Maui said, 'Only on one condition will I spare you: tell me the secret of fire. Where is it hidden? How is it produced?' Mauike gladly promised to tell all he knew, and led him inside his wonderful dwelling, where bundles of fire-yielding sticks - the oronga and particularly the aoa, the banyan tree - were all dry and ready for use; two smaller sticks lay by themselves, and as the fire-god plied one on the other he sang his fire-song: 'Grant, oh grant me thy hidden fire, thou banyan tree! Perform an incantation; utter a prayer to the spirit of the banyan tree! Kindle a fire for Mauike of the dust of the banyan tree!' By the time this song was completed Maui to his great joy perceived a faint smoke arising out of the fine dust produced by the friction of one stick upon another, a slight flame arose, and the grand secret of fire was secured. But the victor resolved to be revenged by setting fire to his fallen adversary's abode; in a short time all nether-world was in flames, which consumed the fire-god and all he possessed - even the rocks cracked and split with the heat: hence the ancient saying, 'The rocks at Orovaru are burning.' Ere leaving the land of ghosts Maui carefully picked up the two fire-sticks, restored the tail of the pigeon to avoid the anger of Tane, and once more pronouncing the words he learnt from Buataranga, got safely back to this upper world.
passages.note: Paraphrase of W. W. Gill, Myths and Songs from the South Pacific, ch. 4 (1876); not verbatim.

title.en: Miru's Shades: The Bua Tree and the Fatal Net
title.zh: 米露冥府：巨樹與奪魂之網

region.en: Auraka chasm, Mangaia (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 曼加亞奧拉卡裂谷（象徵性定位）

period: Hervey Islands oral tradition; recorded 1876 (Gill)

source.work: W. W. Gill, Myths and Songs from the South Pacific, ch. 8, Hades; or, The Doctrine of Spirit-world (London 1876)

summary.en: Avaiki, the hollow under Mangaia, is reached at death by a leaping-place of souls facing the setting sun. A gigantic bua tree springs up from the shades to receive the spirit, with a branch for each clan; at the foot Akaanga spreads the net of innumerable meshes, and the drowned ghosts are dragged before the ruddy Miru, who feeds her visitors on red earth-worms and black beetles, stews them in her ever-burning oven. Warriors slain in battle escape her - only women, cowards and children are annihilated.
summary.zh: 阿瓦伊基——曼加亞之下的空洞——亡魂自面西的『魂躍之地』一躍而下。冥土升起一株巨大布瓦樹，枝幹各歸各族；樹底阿卡安加張開『千孔之網』，溺魂被拖至紅面米露前：以紅蚯蚓與黑甲蟲飼之，置於永不熄滅之灶蒸煮。唯戰場陣亡的武士得免——婦孺與懦夫皆被吞滅。

sensitivity.note: Death-eschatology record; the spirit's road closed by Tiki noted in passages.

passages.text: The proper name for Hades is Avaiki; in Tahitian, Hawaii; in New Zealand, Hawaiki. As the dead were usually thrown down the deepest chasms, it was not unnatural for their friends to imagine the earth to be hollow, and the entrance to this vast nether-world to be down one of these pits: the outer portion of Mangaia is a honeycomb, the rock being pierced in every direction with winding caves and frightful chasms. The inland opening to this subterranean territory was the grand repository of the dead, and is known by the significant name of Auraka - murder; doubtless this is the true origin of their idea of the whereabouts of spirit-world. The proper denizens of Avaiki are the major and lesser divinities with their dependants; these marry, multiply, and quarrel like mortals; they wear clothing, plant, cook, fish, build, and inhabit dwellings of exactly the same sort as exist on earth. The visible world itself is but a gross copy of what exists in spirit-land: if fire burns, it is because latent flame was hidden in the wood by Mauike in Hades.
passages.note: Paraphrase of W. W. Gill, Myths and Songs from the South Pacific, ch. 8 (1876); not verbatim.

passages.text: The high-road to Avaiki is for ever closed; this was not the fault of mankind, but the penalty of the excesses of the denizens of spirit-land. They became very troublesome to mankind - continually afflicting them with disease and death; they occasioned great dearth by stealing all kinds of food, and even ravished the women of this world. The brave and beautiful Tiki, the sister of Veetini, determined to put an end to these annoyances; for this purpose she rolled herself alive down into the gloomy opening, which immediately closed upon her. From that memorable day the spirits of mortals have been compelled to descend to Avaiki by a different route; happily, however, the natives of Avaiki no longer dare molest mankind, and the closed chasm is known by the name of Tiki's hole.
passages.note: Paraphrase of W. W. Gill, Myths and Songs from the South Pacific, ch. 8 (1876); not verbatim.

passages.text: The point of departure for spirit-land is called a reinga vaerua; there are three on Mangaia, all facing the setting sun. The standard and esoteric teaching of the priests was that the souls of the dying leave the body ere breath is quite extinct, and travel to the edge of the cliff at Araia near the marae of Rongo, facing the west. If a friendly spirit should meet the solitary wanderer at any point of the sad but inevitable journey and should say, 'Go back and live', the now joyful ghost at once returns to its old home and re-inhabits the once forsaken body - this is the native theory of fainting. But if no friendly spirit interfere, the departing soul pursues its mournful travels and eventually reaches the extreme edge of the cliff. Instantly a large wave approaches to the base, and at the same moment a gigantic bua tree, covered with fragrant blossom, springs up from Avaiki to receive on its far-reaching branches unhappy human spirits; even at this last moment a friendly voice may send the spirit-traveller back to life and health. Otherwise he is mysteriously impelled to climb the particular branch reserved for his own tribe and conveniently brought nearest to him: the worshippers of Motoro have a branch to themselves, the worshippers of Tane have another - the tree having just as many branches as there are principal gods in Mangaia.
passages.note: Paraphrase of W. W. Gill, Myths and Songs from the South Pacific, ch. 8 (1876); not verbatim.

passages.text: Immediately the human soul is safely lodged upon this gigantic tree, the bua goes down with its living burden to nether-world; while yet on the tree the wretched spirit looks down to the root, and to his horror sees a great net spread out beneath to catch it - hence the proverb in regard to the dying, 'Will be caught in the net of innumerable meshes', the net of Akaanga. This net, from the strong meshes of which there is no escape, is firmly held by Akaanga and his assistants; the doomed spirit at last falls into this fatal net, and is at once submerged in a lake of fresh water near the foot of the gigantic bua tree, named Vai-roto-ariki, the royal fresh-water lake; in these treacherous waters captive ghosts exhaust themselves by wriggling like fishes in the vain hope of escape. The great net is eventually pulled up, and the half-drowned spirits tremblingly enter the presence of the inexpressibly ugly Miru, generally called the ruddy, because her face reflects the glowing heat of her ever-burning oven. The hag feeds her unwilling visitors with red earth-worms, black beetles, crabs, and small blackbirds. The grand secret of Miru's power over her intended victims is the kava root, one vast root named by her Tevoo, her own peculiar property; her four lovely daughters are directed to prepare bowls of this strong kava for her unwilling visitors. Utterly stupefied with the draught, the unresisting victims are borne off to the oven and cooked; Miru, with her son and peerless daughters, subsist on these human spirits. Such is the inevitable fate of those who die a natural death - that is, of women, cowards, and children; they are annihilated. Not so warriors slain on the field of battle: the spirits of these lucky fellows for a while wander about amongst the rocks and trees in the neighbourhood of which their bodies were thrown.
passages.note: Paraphrase of W. W. Gill, Myths and Songs from the South Pacific, ch. 8 (1876); not verbatim.

title.en: Veetini, the First to Die, Returns on the Sun's Path
title.zh: 首位逝者維蒂尼循日路歸來

region.en: Rangikapua hill, Mangaia
region.zh: 曼加亞蘭吉卡普阿山丘

period: Hervey Islands oral tradition; recorded 1876 (Gill)

source.work: W. W. Gill, Myths and Songs from the South Pacific, ch. 9, Veetini; or, The Immortality of the Soul (London 1876)

summary.en: Veetini, first to die a natural death in Mangaia, is mourned with the dirge, funeral games and black pakoko garments invented for him. His spirit returns once along the sun's golden path, granted a detained sun by great Tangaroa to converse with his parents at a booth on Karanga-iti, teaches mortals the food-offerings for the dead, and at Vairorongo, Rongo's sacred stream, shouts 'Thrust down the sun, that I may descend to nether-land' - grasped at, he is only a shadow, and vanishes forever in the train of the setting sun.
summary.zh: 維蒂尼——曼加亞首位自然死亡者——其親人為之創制輓歌、喪舞與染黑的帕科科喪服。其魂循太陽的金色軌跡一度歸來：經坦加羅亞恩准，太陽為之停留，他在卡拉恩加伊提的涼棚下與父母敘談，教世人以食物祭亡者；至瓦伊羅龍戈——龍戈聖溪——他高呼『沉下太陽，我好下降冥府』。父母伸手挽留，抓住的只是影子；他隨落日金光，永逝而去。

sensitivity.note: Origin-legend of Mangaian funeral rites and food-offerings to the dead.

passages.text: The first who ever died a natural death in Mangaia was Veetini. He was the only and much beloved son of Tueva and his wife Manga. But Veetini, when in the prime of early manhood, sickened and died. The parents, in their grief, instituted those signs of mourning and funeral games which were ever afterwards observed amongst these islanders. The chief mourners were Tueva, Manga, and the lovely Tiki, the attached sister of Veetini. All these, with the more distant relatives, blackened their faces, cut off their hair, slashed their bodies with shark's teeth, and wore only pakoko, or native cloth, dyed red in the sap of the candle-nut tree and then dipped in the black mud of a taro-patch - the very offensive smell of this mourning garment is symbolical of the putrescent state of the dead. It was on account of Veetini that the eva, or dirge, in its four varieties, and the mourning dance, were invented and performed by the sorrowing relatives day by day. During the entire period of mourning no beating of bark for native cloth was permitted in the district where the death occurred, to avoid giving offence to the female demon Mueu, who introduced cloth-beating to this world, but who herself beats out cloth of a very different texture: her cloth-flail is the stroke of death - hence the proverb when a person dies, 'Ah! Mueu's flail is once more at work!'
passages.note: Paraphrase of W. W. Gill, Myths and Songs from the South Pacific, ch. 9 (1876); not verbatim.

passages.text: The last resting-place of Veetini is at Rangikapua, a green spot about half a mile from the sea, a hill about 100 feet above the level of the ocean, on which the rays of the setting sun fall. On the evening he was buried the dirges and dances that had been invented in his honour were performed, and the parents and the sister looked wistfully towards the north, hoping for his return to their midst - but in vain! The mourning band walked in sad procession along the western shore, chanting dirges; they sought the lost one on the southern and almost inaccessible shore of Mangaia, and at last arrived at the eastern coast, gazing over the vast expanse swept by the life-giving trade-winds. At night they occupied the Ruddy Cave, Ana-kura, its entrance washed by the surf. Ere dawn Tueva rose from his stony couch to watch the rising of the sun; as it rose in all its wonted glory he noticed a tiny dark speck beneath on the ocean, which grew larger and drew nearer, passing over the ocean in the bright trail of the sun - on arriving nearer still, this wonderful object, lightly skimming over the crest of the waves, proved to be no other than their own lost Veetini!
passages.note: Paraphrase of W. W. Gill, Myths and Songs from the South Pacific, ch. 9 (1876); not verbatim.

passages.text: The now rejoicing parents rushed forwards to kiss their son, who was indeed Veetini, yet not altogether like his former self. He said to the joyful throng that he had been permitted to revisit this upper world in consequence of the passionate lamentations of his parents, and to comfort their sorrowing hearts; he also came to show mortals how to make offerings of food to please the dead. For himself, he had come and must depart in the bright track of the sun, being now a denizen of spirit-land. However, to gratify his parents and friends, Veetini asked great Tangaroa to detain the sun for a short time in its course, in order that he might rest and converse awhile with his relatives; the prayer was granted, and the sun was detained while Veetini and his friends pleasantly rested in a sort of extempore house erected for him on the spot known as Karanga-iti.
passages.note: Paraphrase of W. W. Gill, Myths and Songs from the South Pacific, ch. 9 (1876); not verbatim.

passages.text: At length Veetini rose, and led the half-glad and half-sorrowful procession along the beach towards the west; at last they reached Vairorongo, Rongo's sacred stream, directly facing the setting sun. Here they rested a few minutes only, as day was fast fading away. As the sun disappeared beneath the horizon Veetini said he must go; the weeping parents begged him to stay with them. The son replied, 'I cannot; I do not belong to this world now', and then shouted impatiently: 'Thrust down the sun, that I may descend to nether-land!' The parents now endeavoured to detain him by force; but lo! they grasped at a shadow. They watched him gliding swiftly over the western ocean in the ruddy track of the sun, and, with its last rays, Veetini, now a tiny distant speck in the train of the king of day, for ever disappeared.
passages.note: Paraphrase of W. W. Gill, Myths and Songs from the South Pacific, ch. 9 (1876); not verbatim.

title.en: The Ghost Train That Follows the Setting Sun
title.zh: 隨落日西行的幽魂列車

region.en: Ana-kura red cave and reinga, Mangaia
region.zh: 曼加亞紅洞與魂躍之地

period: Hervey Islands oral tradition; recorded 1876 (Gill)

source.work: W. W. Gill, Myths and Songs from the South Pacific, ch. 8 (London 1876)

summary.en: Mangaian ghosts wander the shore in ghostly net-work and turbaned red twine, most delighted to follow the sun. They muster at the red cave Ana-kura or at Karanga-iti, dance and revisit old homes, and when their leader gives the word, flit along the coast to Vairorongo and, at sunset, enter Avaiki through the very aperture by which the Sun-god descends - 'Tis night now in spirit-land; for 'tis light in this upper world.' A laggard must wait a whole season, dancing the dance of the starved.
summary.zh: 曼加亞幽魂披幽網、纏紅繩，沿濱流浪，最喜追隨太陽。它們聚於紅洞阿納庫拉或小迎地卡拉恩加伊提，歌舞盤桓、重訪舊居；待首領一聲令下，便沿海岸飄至瓦伊羅龍戈，日落時分循日神下冥之口而入——『此刻冥府正夜；而陽世正晝。』落伍的孤魂則須苦候一季，跳『餓鬼之舞』消磨光陰。

sensitivity.note: Eschatological topography; solar-death pathway parallel.

passages.text: The spirits of the dead were often spoken of as wandering along the margin of the sea most disconsolately, not a little annoyed at the extreme sharpness of the rocks, and the entanglement of their feet in the bindweed and thick vines. They were arrayed in ghostly net-work, and a fantastic mourning of weeds picked upon the way, relieved, however, by the fragrant heliotrope which grows freely on the barren rocks; a red creeper, resembling dyed twine, wound round and round the head like a turban, completed their ghostly toilet. Rather inconsistently with this, a smooth, shelving piece of coral rock on the western coast is known as 'the place where ghosts blanch their new-made garments', as if during the weary months of their wanderings they were driven, like the living, to prepare new clothing from time to time. The great delight of these weeping, melancholy spirits was to follow the sun: at the summer solstice, January, he apparently rises out of the ocean opposite to Ana-kura, the red-cave; at the winter solstice, June, rising at Karanga-iti. These points became, therefore, grand rendezvous of disembodied spirits: those belonging to the northern half of the island assembling at the last-named rendezvous, those belonging to the southern half meeting at the former.
passages.note: Paraphrase of W. W. Gill, Myths and Songs from the South Pacific, ch. 8 (1876); not verbatim.

passages.text: Many months might elapse ere the projected departure of the ghosts took place. This weary interval was spent in dances and in revisiting their former homes, where the living dwell affectionately remembered by the dead; at night-fall they would wander amongst the trees and plantations nearest to these dwellings, sometimes venturing to peep inside. As a rule these ghosts were well-disposed to their own living relatives, but often became vindictive if a pet child was ill-treated by a step-mother or other relatives. Sometimes wearied with these wanderings, the ghosts huddled together in the Red-cave, or clambered up the open lawn-like place above it - now a favourite resting-place for fishermen - known as One-ma-kenu-kenu, the smooth spot. The precise period for final departure was fixed by the leader of the band; but if no distinguished person was amongst them, they must of course wait until such a leader was obtained; thus in the classic laments for Vera, he is represented as the chosen captain of the dead.
passages.note: Paraphrase of W. W. Gill, Myths and Songs from the South Pacific, ch. 8 (1876); not verbatim.

passages.text: The chief of this disconsolate throng resolves to depart; messages are sent to collect those stray ghosts who may yet be lingering near their ancient haunts. With many tears and last lingering looks they assemble at the Red-cave, intently watching the rising of the sun. At the first streak of dawn the entire band take their departure to meet the rising sun; this done, they follow in his train as nearly as may be - he in the heavens above, they at first on the ocean beneath, but afterwards over the rocks and stones, always avoiding the interior of the island - until late in the afternoon of the appointed day they are all assembled at Vairorongo, facing the setting sun.
passages.note: Paraphrase of W. W. Gill, Myths and Songs from the South Pacific, ch. 8 (1876); not verbatim.

passages.text: At last the congregated throng, whose eyes are fixed upon the setting sun, feel that the moment has come when they must for ever depart from the cherished scenes of earth, despite the tears and solicitations of relatives, who are frequently represented as chasing their loved ones over rocks and across fearful precipices round half the island. The sun now sinks in the ocean, leaving a golden track; the entire band of ghosts take a last farewell, and, following their earthly leader, flit over the ocean in the train of the Sun-god Ra, but not like him destined to reappear on the morrow; the ghostly train enter Avaiki through the very aperture by which the Sun-god descends in order to lighten up for a time those dark subterranean regions - as the priest Teka sang in 1794: 'Tis night now in spirit-land; for 'tis light in this upper world.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of W. W. Gill, Myths and Songs from the South Pacific, ch. 8 (1876); not verbatim.

title.en: Five Nuts for the Dead: Offerings Taught by Veetini
title.zh: 亡者五椰：維蒂尼所授祭食

region.en: Graveside of Auraka, Mangaia (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 曼加亞墳塋（象徵性定位）

period: Hervey Islands oral tradition; recorded 1876 (Gill)

source.work: W. W. Gill, Myths and Songs from the South Pacific, ch. 9, Veetini Meeting His Father (London 1876)

summary.en: 'I came to instruct you in making food-offerings to the dead,' said Veetini to his weeping father. From that teaching came the rite: five old coconuts opened and poured out in turn, wrapped in leaves and cloth and thrown towards the grave - or down the chasm of Auraka - each time the name of the departed called loudly, 'Here is thy food; eat it'; and at the fifth, 'Farewell! we come back no more to thee!'
summary.zh: 維蒂尼對泣父言：『我來教你祭奠亡者之法。』由此傳下祭禮：依次開啟五枚老椰，傾汁於地，以葉布裹之擲向墳塋——或拋入奧拉卡深谷——每次高呼亡者之名：『此乃你的食物，吃吧！』至第五枚並布丁擲下，則道：『別了！我們不再來看你！』

sensitivity.note: Funeral-rite origin; includes Gill's later anecdote of the last heathen mourner Arikikaka.

passages.text: Tueva, who seven times lamented for his boy, asked, 'Why didst thou return to this world?' 'I came', said Veetini, 'to instruct you in making food-offerings to the dead: offerings to those in spirit-world; gifts from their relatives who yet linger in this upper world.' Such was the belief and practice of heathenism. As soon as the corpse was committed to its last resting-place, the mourners selected five old cocoa-nuts, which were successively opened, and the water poured out upon the ground; these nuts were then wrapped up in leaves and native cloth, and thrown towards the grave; or, if the corpse were let down with cords into the deep chasm of Auraka, the nuts and other food would be successively thrown down upon it. Calling loudly each time the name of the departed, they said, 'Here is thy food; eat it.' When the fifth nut and the accompanying raroi, or pudding, were thrown down, the mourners said, 'Farewell! we come back no more to thee!'
passages.note: Paraphrase of W. W. Gill, Myths and Songs from the South Pacific, ch. 9 (1876); not verbatim.

passages.text: Seventeen years before Gill wrote, Arikikaka, the last heathen of Mangaia, lost his only son, a consistent church member; the old man was inconsolable. The corpse was buried with his mother's deceased relatives on the west of the island, and the friends dispersed to their respective homes. A day or two after, Arikikaka and his wife walked with difficulty across the island, arriving at dusk at the grave of their beloved son with a basket of cooked food and some unopened cocoa-nuts; with many tears and affectionate words they called upon their boy to eat the food and drink the nuts - carefully opened for the convenience of the ghost at the grave, the contents poured out upon the earth - which they had carried six miles. The aged couple slept under a tree close to the last resting-place of their son, and at dawn on the following morning departed. Gill adds that in May, 1865, Arikikaka and his wife were baptized - 'at eventime there was light.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of W. W. Gill, Myths and Songs from the South Pacific, ch. 9 (1876); not verbatim.

title.en: Tinirau, Innumerable, Lord of the Fish
title.zh: 魚王蒂尼勞：無數者

region.en: Motu-Tapu, the Sacred Isle, Avaiki (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 阿瓦伊基聖島莫圖塔普（象徵性定位）

period: Hervey Islands oral tradition; recorded 1876 (Gill)

source.work: W. W. Gill, Myths and Songs from the South Pacific, ch. 1 (London 1876)

summary.en: Torn from Vari's right side as her second son, Tinirau - Innumerable - is half man, half sprat, with fish-ponds at the Sacred Isle teeming with every fin from shark downwards. He is the father of the Tinirau cycle: the fish-ponds that draw Ina, the pet whale ridden by Kae, the ten daughters - a divine ancestor whose name the Maori south-sea traditions share.
summary.zh: 自瓦里右側撕下的第二子蒂尼勞——『無數者』——半人半鯡，聖島上池塘魚群自鯊以下無所不有。他是蒂尼勞傳說之祖：引伊娜前來的魚塘、被凱竊騎的寵鯨、眾多女兒——其名亦見於毛利與南方海域傳統。

sensitivity.note: Divine genealogy record connecting to the Kae/whale cycle.

passages.text: On another occasion Vari-ma-te-takere tore off a second bit from that same right side, and it became Tinirau, Innumerable, who, like his brother, had a second and fishy form; the sort of fish which composed his half fish body was of the sprat-kind. The Great Mother gave him the land of Motu-Tapu, the Sacred Isle, as his own domain; there were his celebrated ponds full of all kinds of fish, and Tinirau was lord of the finny inhabitants of the sea, from the shark downwards.
passages.note: Paraphrase of W. W. Gill, Myths and Songs from the South Pacific, ch. 1 (1876); not verbatim.

passages.text: At Ngatangiia, Rarotonga, there is an islet, covered with cocoa-nut trees, so named Motu Tapu - this is, of course, a modern identification; the Sacred Isle is supposed to be in the shades. Tinirau became in later myth the father of the great Tinirau cycle of the south seas - the lord of the fish-ponds to which the fairy voyager Ina was carried, the owner of the pet whale which Kae rode and destroyed, and the father of the many daughters sung in the day-songs of Mangaia.
passages.note: Paraphrase of W. W. Gill, Myths and Songs from the South Pacific, ch. 1 (1876); not verbatim.

title.en: Ancoallo: The Embalmed Brother Who Led the Chancas to War
title.zh: 安科阿約:率昌卡出征的兄弟乾屍

region.en: Andahuaylas, Chanca country (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 昌卡人的安達瓦伊利亞斯(象徵性標記)

period: Inca tradition as given to Sarmiento de Gamboa, 1572; trans. Markham 1907

source.work: Pedro Sarmiento de Gamboa, History of the Incas, ch. 26, trans. Sir Clements Markham, Hakluyt Society, 1907

summary.en: In the province of Andahuaylas, thirty leagues west of Cuzco, there were two Sinchis named Uscovilca and Ancovilca, who coming on an expedition from near Huamanca had settled in the valley and formed a state. They were brothers. Uscovilca, the elder and principal, instituted a tribe called Hanan-chancas or upper Chancas; Ancovilca formed another called Hurin-chancas or lower Chancas. These chiefs, after death, were embalmed, and because they were feared for their cruelties in life, were kept by their people. The Hanan-chancas carried the statue of Uscovilca with them in their raids and wars; although they had other Sinchis, they always attributed their success to the statue of Uscovilca, which they called Ancoallo.
summary.zh: 庫斯科以西三十萊格的安達瓦伊利亞斯省,有兩位辛奇——烏斯科維爾卡與安科維爾卡——自瓦曼卡一帶遷來,在谷中建邦。二人為兄弟:兄長烏斯科維爾卡立「哈南昌卡」(上昌卡)部,安科維爾卡立「烏林昌卡」(下昌卡)部。二酋死後,因其生前兇名赫赫,遺體被製成木乃伊,由族人奉養。哈南昌卡人出征劫掠,必抬烏斯科維爾卡的神像隨行;雖另有辛奇統兵,卻總把勝利歸功於那尊名為「安科阿約」的烏斯科維爾卡神像。

sensitivity.note: The Chanca war-god as ancestor mummy; the mirror image of the Inca guauqui system on the enemy side.

passages.text: In this province there were two Sinchis, named Uscovilca and Ancovilca who, coming on an expedition from near Huamanca with some companies, had settled in the valley of Andahuaylas, and had there formed a state. They were brothers. Uscovilca being the elder and principal one, instituted a tribe which he called Hanan-chancas or upper Chancas. Ancovilca formed another tribe called Hurin-chancas or lower Chancas.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Sarmiento, History of the Incas, ch. 26 (Markham 1907); not verbatim.

passages.text: These chiefs, after death, were embalmed, and because they were feared for their cruelties in life, were kept by their people. The Hanan-chancas carried the statue of Uscovilca with them, in their raids and wars. Although they had other Sinchis, they always attributed their success to the statue of Uscovilca, which they called Ancoallo.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Sarmiento, History of the Incas, ch. 26 (Markham 1907); not verbatim.

canonical_translation: Sir Clements Markham, History of the Incas (Hakluyt Society, 1907)

title.en: 'I Will Not Abandon the House of the Sun': Cusi Rebukes His Father
title.zh: 「我決不捨棄太陽之屋」:庫西斥父逃亡

region.en: Cuzco (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 庫斯科(象徵性標記)

period: Inca tradition as given to Sarmiento de Gamboa, 1572; trans. Markham 1907

source.work: Pedro Sarmiento de Gamboa, History of the Incas, ch. 26, trans. Sir Clements Markham, Hakluyt Society, 1907

summary.en: The news of the Chanca advance spread terror among the orejones of Cuzco, for they doubted the powers of Inca Viracocha, who was now very old and weak. Viracocha called a Council of his sons and captains Apu Mayta and Vicaquirau. These captains said to him: 'After careful consideration it appears to us that, as you are old and infirm, it will not be well that you should attempt so great a business, dangerous and with victory doubtful. The wisest counsel is that you should leave Cuzco, and proceed to the place of Chita, and thence to Caquia Xaquixahuana, which is a strong fort, whence you may treat for an agreement with the Chancas.' But when Cusi Inca Yupanqui found that his father was determined to leave Cuzco, they say that he thus addressed him: 'How father can it fit into your heart to accept such infamous advice as to leave Cuzco, city of the Sun and of Viracocha, whose name you have taken, whose promise you hold that you shall be a great lord, you and your descendants.' Though a boy, he said this with the animated daring of a man high in honour. The father answered that he was a boy and that he spoke like one, in talking without consideration, and that such words were of no value. Inca Yupanqui replied that he would remain where they would be remembered, that he would not leave Cuzco nor abandon the House of the Sun. So Viracocha left Cuzco and went to Chita; his son Inca Yupanqui remained at Cuzco, resolved to defend the city or die in its defence. Seven chiefs remained with him.
summary.zh: 昌卡進逼的消息令庫斯科的耳垂貴胄膽寒——老王維拉科查年老體衰,威望堪憂。維拉科查召集諸子與大將阿普·馬雅塔、維卡基勞議事。二將進言:「您年邁勞損,不宜親冒大險。上策是放棄庫斯科,退往奇塔,再據堅城卡基亞-夏基夏瓜納,與昌卡人議和。」庫西·印加·尤潘琪得知父親決意棄城,便直言進諫:「父親!您怎忍心聽從這等可恥的建議,捨棄庫斯科——太陽與維拉科查之城?您取了神的名,神許您與子孫成為大主!」雖是少年,他說話卻如大丈夫般無畏。父親斥他:「你還是個孩子,說話不知輕重,不值一提。」庫西答道:「我願留在讓人們記住的地方。我決不離開庫斯科,決不捨棄太陽之屋!」於是維拉科查攜庶子烏爾庫、索索退往奇塔;庫西留守庫斯科,誓與城共存亡。七位首領與他同守。

sensitivity.note: The defiance that made the king; Sarmiento undercuts it by attributing the scene to Apu Mayta's intrigues.

passages.text: These captains said to him: 'Inca Viracocha!... After careful consideration it appears to us that as you are old and infirm owing to what you have undergone in former wars, it will not be well that you should attempt so great a business, dangerous and with victory doubtful... The wisest counsel respecting the course you should adopt is that you should leave Cuzco, and proceed to the place of Chita, and thence to Caquia Xaquixahuana, which is a strong fort, whence you may treat for an agreement with the Chancas.'

passages.text: But when Cusi Inca Yupanqui found that his father was determined to leave Cuzco, they say that he thus addressed him: 'How father can it fit into your heart to accept such infamous advice as to leave Cuzco, city of the Sun and of Viracocha, whose name you have taken, whose promise you hold that you shall be a great lord, you and your descendants.' Though a boy, he said this with the animated daring of a man high in honour. The father answered that he was a boy and that he spoke like one... Inca Yupanqui replied that he would remain where they would be remembered, that he would not leave Cuzco nor abandon the House of the Sun.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Sarmiento, History of the Incas, ch. 26 (Markham 1907); not verbatim.

passages.text: So Viracocha left Cuzco and went to Chita, taking with him his two illegitimate sons Inca Urco and Inca Socso. His son Inca Yupanqui remained at Cuzco, resolved to defend the city or die in its defence. Seven chiefs remained with him: Inca Rocca his elder and legitimate brother, Apu Mayta, Vicaquirau, Quillis-cacha, Urco Huaranca, Chima Chaui Pata Yupanqui, Viracocha Inca Paucar, and Mircoy-mana the tutor of Inca Yupanqui.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Sarmiento, History of the Incas, ch. 26 (Markham 1907); not verbatim.

canonical_translation: Sir Clements Markham, History of the Incas (Hakluyt Society, 1907)

title.en: The Vision at Susurpuquio: A Mirror Showing the Provinces to Come
title.zh: 蘇蘇爾普基奧顯聖:映出未來疆土的明鏡

region.en: Susurpuquio spring on the road to Xaquixahuana (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 通往夏基夏瓜納路上的蘇蘇爾普基奧泉(象徵性標記)

period: Inca tradition as given to Sarmiento de Gamboa, 1572; trans. Markham 1907

source.work: Pedro Sarmiento de Gamboa, History of the Incas, ch. 27, trans. Sir Clements Markham, Hakluyt Society, 1907

summary.en: While this was proceeding with the messengers of the Chancas, the Chanca army was coming nearer to Cuzco. Inca Yupanqui made great praying to Viracocha and to the Sun to protect the city. One day he was at Susurpuquio in great affliction, thinking over the best plan for opposing his enemies, when there appeared a person in the air like the Sun, consoling him and animating him for the battle. This being held up to him a mirror in which the provinces he would subdue were shown, and told him that he would be greater than any of his ancestors: he was to have no doubt, but to return to the city, because he would conquer the Chancas who were marching on Cuzco. With these words the vision animated Inca Yupanqui. He took the mirror, which he carried with him ever afterwards, in peace or war, and returned to the city, where he began to encourage those he had left there.
summary.zh: 昌卡軍日益逼近。印加·尤潘琪向維拉科查與太陽苦苦祈禱,求佑城池。一日,他懷著沉重的憂思來到蘇蘇爾普基奧,盤算退敵之策。忽然,空中現出一人,形貌如太陽,撫慰他、為他壯膽。那神人舉起一面明鏡,鏡中映出他日後將要征服的各省,並說:他必超越歷代先王;叫他勿疑,速回城中——進犯庫斯科的昌卡人必為他所敗。異象之言使印加·尤潘琪勇氣倍增。他取過那面明鏡,從此不離左右——和平時帶著,征戰時也帶著——隨即回城,鼓舞留守軍民。

sensitivity.note: The mirror of conquest - the central legitimation vision of Pachacuti; Molina tells a crystal variant of the same spring episode.

title.en: Chanan-ccuri Coca: The Woman Who Turned the Chanca Assault
title.zh: 查南-庫里-科卡:獨退昌卡攻城的女子

region.en: Chocos-chacona suburb, Cuzco (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 庫斯科喬科斯-查科納坊(象徵性標記)

period: Inca tradition as given to Sarmiento de Gamboa, 1572; trans. Markham 1907

source.work: Pedro Sarmiento de Gamboa, History of the Incas, ch. 27, trans. Sir Clements Markham, Hakluyt Society, 1907

summary.en: Those who entered by a suburb called Chocos-chacona were valiantly repulsed by the inhabitants. They say that a woman named Chanan-ccuri-coca here fought like a man, and so valiantly opposed the Chancas that they were obliged to retire. This was the cause that all the Chancas who saw it were dismayed.
summary.zh: 自喬科斯-查科納坊突入的昌卡兵,被城中居民奮勇擊退。相傳一位名叫查南-庫里-科卡的女子在此如男子般奮戰,拼死抗擊昌卡人,終使他們被迫退卻。親眼目睹的昌卡人無不喪膽。

sensitivity.note: The named woman defender of Cuzco; a rare female combat hero in the dynastic tradition.

title.en: Men Sent by the Creator: The First Victory and the Name Pachacuti
title.zh: 造物主遣來的神兵:首捷與「帕查庫提」之名

region.en: Cuzco and the hills around (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 庫斯科及其四郊山嶺(象徵性標記)

period: Inca tradition as given to Sarmiento de Gamboa, 1572; trans. Markham 1907

source.work: Pedro Sarmiento de Gamboa, History of the Incas, ch. 27, trans. Sir Clements Markham, Hakluyt Society, 1907

summary.en: The Inca Yupanqui meanwhile was so quick and dexterous with his weapon that those who carried the statue of Uscovilca became alarmed, and their fear was increased when they saw great numbers of men coming down from the hills. They say that these were sent by Viracocha, the creator, as succour for the Inca. The Chancas began to give way, leaving the statue of Uscovilca, and they say even that of Ancovilca. Attacking on two sides, Inca Rocca, Apu Mayta, and Vicaquirau made great havock among the Chancas. The men of Cuzco continued the pursuit for more than two leagues. The Cuzcos rejoiced at this victory won with so little expectation or hope. They honoured Inca Yupanqui with many epithets, especially calling him PACHACUTI, which means 'over-turner of the earth', alluding to the land and farms which they looked upon as lost by the coming of the Chancas; for he had made them free and safe again. From that time he was called Pachacuti Inca Yupanqui.
summary.zh: 印加·尤潘琪揮器如飛,令扛抬烏斯科維爾卡神像的昌卡人心生恐懼;而當他們望見大群戰士從山上滾滾而下時,恐懼更甚。相傳那些人正是造物主維拉科查為援助印加而遣來的神兵。昌卡軍開始潰退,丟下烏斯科維爾卡的神像——據說連安科維爾卡的神像也丟了。印加·羅卡、阿普·馬雅塔與維卡基勞兩面夾擊,殺得昌卡人屍橫遍野;庫斯科人追擊兩萊格有餘。這場誰也沒想到能贏的大捷令全城歡騰。人們以種種美名尊稱印加·尤潘琪,尤其是「帕查庫提」——意即「翻轉大地者」,指那些因昌卡來犯而被視為必失的土地田園;因為他使它們重獲自由與安寧。自此他便被稱為帕查庫提·印加·尤潘琪。

sensitivity.note: The petrified-ally (pururaucas) miracle behind the name Pachacuti; the divine-reinforcement motif of the conquest ideology.

title.en: Treading on the Spoils: A Father's Refusal and a Son's Triumph
title.zh: 踐踏戰利品:父王的推拒與兒子的凱旋

region.en: Chita and Caquia Xaquixaguana (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 奇塔與卡基亞-夏基夏瓜納(象徵性標記)

period: Inca tradition as given to Sarmiento de Gamboa, 1572; trans. Markham 1907

source.work: Pedro Sarmiento de Gamboa, History of the Incas, ch. 27, trans. Sir Clements Markham, Hakluyt Society, 1907

summary.en: As soon as the victory was secure, Inca Yupanqui did not wish to enjoy the triumph. He wished to give his father the glory of such a great victory. So he collected the most precious spoils, and took them to his father who was in Chita, with a principal orejon named Quillis-cachi Urco Huaranca. By him he sent to ask his father to enjoy that triumph and tread on those spoils of the enemy, a custom they have as a sign of victory. When Quillis-cachi Urco Huaranca arrived before Viracocha Inca, he placed those spoils of the Chancas at his feet with great reverence, saying: 'Inca Viracocha! thy son Pachacuti Inca Yupanqui, to whom the Sun has given such a great victory... sends me to salute you, and says that, as a good and humble son he wishes you to triumph over your victory and to tread upon these spoils of your enemies.' Inca Viracocha did not wish to tread on them, but said that his son Inca Urco should do so, as he was to succeed to the Incaship. Hearing this the messenger rose and gave utterance to furious words, saying that he did not come for cowards to triumph by the deeds of Pachacuti. He added that if Viracocha did not wish to receive this recognition from so valiant a son, it would be better that Pachacuti should enjoy the glory for which he had worked. With this he returned to Cuzco, and told Pachacuti what had happened with his father.
summary.zh: 大捷甫定,印加·尤潘琪不願獨享凱旋,欲將榮光歸於父親。他收集最珍貴的戰利品,由重臣基利斯-卡奇·烏爾科·瓦蘭卡押送至奇塔父王行轅,請父王踐踏敵酋遺物、共享凱旋——這是他們表示勝利的禮制。使者到後,恭恭敬敬將昌卡戰利品置於維拉科查足前:「印加·維拉科查!您的兒子帕查庫提·印加·尤潘琪——太陽賜予他如此大捷——命我前來問安。他願以孝順謙卑之子之身,請父親享受凱旋,踐踏敵人的戰利品。」維拉科查卻不肯踐踏,說應由儲君印加·烏爾庫代行。使者聞言霍然起身,憤然說道:「我可不是來讓懦夫借帕查庫提的功勞沾光的!您若不肯受這樣勇武之子的尊崇,那便請帕查庫提自己享用他拚來的榮耀吧!」言畢返回庫斯科,將父親的態度告訴了帕查庫提。

sensitivity.note: The triumph ritual (treading the spoils) turned into a legitimacy contest between father and son.

title.en: Child of the Sun, Guardian of Cuzco: The Reply and the Hatchet
title.zh: 太陽之子、庫斯科守護者:答書與戰斧

region.en: Ichu-pampa, five leagues west of Cuzco (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 庫斯科以西五萊格的伊丘-潘帕(象徵性標記)

period: Inca tradition as given to Sarmiento de Gamboa, 1572; trans. Markham 1907

source.work: Pedro Sarmiento de Gamboa, History of the Incas, ch. 28, trans. Sir Clements Markham, Hakluyt Society, 1907

summary.en: As soon as the two forces came in sight of each other, Asto-huaraca, full of arrogance, sent to Inca Yupanqui to tell him that they were not like him coming from the poverty stricken Cuzco, and that unless he repented the past and became a tributary and vassal to the Chancas, Asto-huaraca would dye his lance in an Inca's blood. But Inca Yupanqui was not terrified by the embassy. He answered: 'Go back, brother, and say to Asto-huaraca, your Sinchi, that Inca Yupanqui is a child of the Sun and guardian of Cuzco, the city of Ticci Viracocha Pachayachachi, by whose order I am here guarding it. For this city is not mine but his; and if your Sinchi should wish to own obedience to Ticci Viracocha, or to me in His name, he will be honourably received. If your Sinchi should see things in another light, show him that I am here with our friends, and if he should conquer us he can call himself Lord and Inca. But let him understand that no more time can be wasted in demands and replies. God (Ticci Viracocha) will give the victory to whom he pleases.' The two armies approached each other in Ichu-pampa, encountered, and mixed together... At last Pachacuti made a way to where Asto-huaraca was fighting, attacked him and delivered a blow with his hatchet which cut off the Chanca's head. Tomay-huaraca was already killed. The Inca caused the heads of these two captains to be set on the points of lances, and raised on high to be seen by their followers. The Chancas, on seeing the heads, despaired of victory without leaders.
summary.zh: 兩軍望見彼此时,驕横的阿斯托-瓦拉卡遣使羞辱印加·尤潘琪:你們不過來自窮困的庫斯科;若不悔過稱臣,他的長矛必染印加之血。印加·尤潘琪絲毫不為所動,答曰:「回去告訴你們的辛奇阿斯托-瓦拉卡:印加·尤潘琪是太陽之子、庫斯科的守護者——庫斯科乃提基·維拉科查·帕查亞查奇之城,奉其命我守衛於此。此城非我所有,乃神之城。你們的辛奇若願向提基·維拉科查——或以神之名向我——俯首,必受禮遇。若他執迷不悟,那就叫他看著:我與我的朋友們在此;他若能勝我,自可稱主稱王。但叫他明白:索貢與回文,到此為止。勝利屬於誰,提基·維拉科查自會定奪。」兩軍在伊丘-潘帕相撞混戰。終於,帕查庫提殺開血路,直取阿斯托-瓦拉卡,一斧揮落其頭顱;托馬伊-瓦拉卡已先被擊斃。印加王命將二酋首級懸於長矛頂端,高高舉起示眾。昌卡人見酋首,自度無主必敗,潰散而逃。

sensitivity.note: The war-embassy exchange formulates Inca conquest theology in one sentence: the city belongs to Viracocha.

passages.text: Asto-huaraca, full of arrogance, sent to Inca Yupanqui to tell him that he could see the power of the Chancas and the position they now held. They were not like him coming from the poverty stricken Cuzco, and if he did not repent the past and become a tributary and vassal to the Chancas; Asto-huaraca would dye his lance in an Inca's blood. But Inca Yupanqui was not terrified by the embassy. He answered in this way to the messenger: 'Go back brother and say to Asto-huaraca, your Sinchi, that Inca Yupanqui is a child of the Sun and guardian of Cuzco, the city of Ticci Viracocha Pachayachachi, by whose order I am here guarding it. For this city is not mine but his; and if your Sinchi should wish to own obedience to Ticci Viracocha, or to me in His name, he will be honourably received... But let him understand that no more time can be wasted in demands and replies. God (Ticci Viracocha) will give the victory to whom he pleases.'
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Sarmiento, History of the Incas, ch. 28 (Markham 1907); not verbatim.

passages.text: At last Pachacuti made a way to where Asto-huaraca was fighting, attacked him and delivered a blow with his hatchet which cut off the Chanca's head. Tomay-huaraca was already killed. The Inca caused the heads of these two captains to be set on the points of lances, and raised on high to be seen by their followers. The Chancas, on seeing the heads, despaired of victory without leaders. They gave up the contest and sought safety in flight.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Sarmiento, History of the Incas, ch. 28 (Markham 1907); not verbatim.

canonical_translation: Sir Clements Markham, History of the Incas (Hakluyt Society, 1907)

title.en: The Fringe Found on the Image: How the Sun's Oracle Crowned Pachacuti
title.zh: 神像自戴王纓:太陽神諭為帕查庫提加冕

region.en: Inti-cancha, House of the Sun, Cuzco (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 庫斯科太陽之屋因蒂-坎恰(象徵性標記)

period: Inca tradition as given to Sarmiento de Gamboa, 1572; trans. Markham 1907

source.work: Pedro Sarmiento de Gamboa, History of the Incas, ch. 29, trans. Sir Clements Markham, Hakluyt Society, 1907

summary.en: When the Inca Yupanqui found himself so strong and that he had been joined by so many people, he determined not to wait for the nomination of his father, much less for his death. With this object he caused a grand sacrifice to be offered to the Sun in the Inti-cancha or House of the Sun, and then went to ask the image of the Sun who should be Inca. The oracle of the devil, or perhaps some Indian who was behind to give the answer, replied that Inca Yupanqui Pachacuti was chosen and should be Inca. On this answer being given, all who were present at the sacrifice prostrated themselves before Pachacuti, crying out 'Ccapac Inca Intip Churin' - Sovereign Lord Child of the Sun. Presently they prepared a very rich fringe of gold and emeralds wherewith to crown him. Next day they took Pachacuti Inca Yupanqui to the House of the Sun, and when they came to the image of the Sun, which was of gold and the size of a man, they found it with the fringe, as if offering it of its own will. First making his sacrifices, according to their custom, he came to the image, and the High Priest called out in his language 'Intip Apu' - Governor of things pertaining to the Sun. With much ceremony and great reverence the fringe was taken from the image and placed, with much pomp, on the forehead of Pachacuti Inca Yupanqui. Then all called his name and hailed him 'Intip Churin Inca Pachacuti' - Child of the Sun Lord, over-turner of the earth.
summary.zh: 印加·尤潘琪羽翼已豐,歸附者日眾,遂決意不再等候父親的冊立——更不必等他壽終。他在太陽之屋向太陽隆重獻祭,然後叩問太陽神像:誰當為印加王?神諭——薩爾米恩托說是「魔鬼的神諭,或許只是躲在像後傳話的某個印第安人」——答道:帕查庫提·印加·尤潘琪已被選中,當為印加王。此言一出,與祭眾人皆拜倒於帕查庫提之前,高呼「卡帕克·印加·因蒂普·丘林」——太陽之子、至尊之主。眾人隨即製備鑲祖母綠的華美金王纓。次日,眾人擁帕查庫提至太陽之屋;行至金鑄的、如真人大小太陽神像前,卻見王纓已掛在神像之上——彷彿神像自願奉出。他依俗獻祭完畢,走近神像;大祭司以土語高呼「因蒂普·阿普」——司太陽之事之主。於是,在極隆重的儀式中,王纓自神像取下,莊嚴地繫於帕查庫提·印加·尤潘琪的額前。眾人齊呼其號:「因蒂普·丘林·印加·帕查庫提」——太陽之主的兒子,翻轉大地者。

sensitivity.note: The self-offering oracle fringe; Sarmiento's aside ('or perhaps some Indian who was behind') is preserved as part of the record - a rare colonial demystification embedded in the myth.

On this answer being given, all who were present at the sacrifice, prostrated themselves before Pachacuti, crying out 'Ccapac Inca Intip Churin,' which means 'Sovereign Lord Child of the Sun.'

title.en: The Sun Watches Through the Pillars: Sucanca and Inti-huatana
title.zh: 陽光穿柱:蘇坎卡與拴日石

region.en: Hill east of Cuzco (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 庫斯科以東山丘(象徵性標記)

period: Inca tradition as given to Sarmiento de Gamboa, 1572; trans. Markham 1907

source.work: Pedro Sarmiento de Gamboa, History of the Incas, ch. 30, trans. Sir Clements Markham, Hakluyt Society, 1907

summary.en: In order that the precise time of sowing and harvesting might be known, and that nothing might be lost, the Inca caused four poles to be set up on a high mountain to the east of Cuzco, about two varas apart, on the heads of which there were holes, by which the sun entered, in the manner of a watch or astrolabe. Observing where the sun struck the ground through these holes, at the time of sowing and harvest, marks were made on the ground. Other poles were set up in the part corresponding to the west of Cuzco, for the time of harvesting the maize. Having fixed the positions exactly by these poles, they built columns of stone for perpetuity in their places, of the height of the poles and with holes in like places. All round it was ordered that the ground should be paved; and on the stones certain lines were drawn, conforming to the movements of the sun entering through the holes in the columns. Thus the whole became an instrument serving for an annual time-piece, by which the times of sowing and harvesting were regulated. Persons were appointed to observe these watches, and to notify to the people the times they indicated. Markham's note identifies the pillars as the Sucanca - the two pillars denoting the beginning of winter, whence the year was measured, were called Pucuy Sucanca; those notifying the beginning of spring were Chirao Sucanca - and the equinox column before the temple of the Sun as the Inti-huatana, the 'sun-seizer', where a line was drawn from east to west and they watched when the shadow of the pillar was on the line and there was no shadow at noon.
summary.zh: 為使播種收穫各得其時、寸陰不廢,印加王命人在庫斯科以東的高山上豎立四根木柱,間距約兩瓦拉,柱頭鑿孔,讓陽光穿孔而入——一如日晷或星盤。播種與收穫之時,觀察日光穿孔投於地面的位置,在地面做下記號。庫斯科以西相應之處也豎立木柱,以定收玉米之期。位置定準之後,便在原處砌起石柱,以垂永久——石柱與木柱同高,孔位相同;柱基四周鋪石,石面刻線,與陽光穿孔的移動軌跡相合。整座裝置遂成為一座年度報時儀,用以規定播種與收穫之期;又設專人值守觀測,向民眾宣告時令。據馬卡姆注,這些石柱稱「蘇坎卡」:標誌冬季開始(即歲首)的兩柱稱「普庫伊·蘇坎卡」,標誌春季開始的稱「奇勞·蘇坎卡」;而太陽神廟前空地中央立於大圓圈內的石柱,則是「因蒂-瓦塔納」——「拴日石」:自東至西畫一條線,日出至日落間柱影落在線上而正午無影之時,便是春分秋分。

sensitivity.note: Astronomical pillars as calendrical ritual technology; the 'sun-seized' etymology of Inti-huatana is Markham's.

passages.text: In order that the precise time of sowing and harvesting might be known, and that nothing might be lost, the Inca caused four poles to be set up on a high mountain to the east of Cuzco, about two varas apart, on the heads of which there were holes, by which the sun entered, in the manner of a watch or astrolabe. Observing where the sun struck the ground through these holes, at the time of sowing and harvest, marks were made on the ground... Having fixed the positions exactly by these poles, they built columns of stone for perpetuity in their places... Thus the whole became an instrument serving for an annual time-piece, by which the times of sowing and harvesting were regulated. Persons were appointed to observe these watches, and to notify to the people the times they indicated.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Sarmiento, History of the Incas, ch. 30 (Markham 1907); not verbatim.

passages.text: The pillars at Cuzco to determine the time of the solstices were called Sucanca. The two pillars denoting the beginning of winter, whence the year was measured, were called Pucuy Sucanca. Those notifying the beginning of spring were Chirao Sucanca... To ascertain the time of the equinoxes there was a stone column in the open space before the temple of the Sun in the centre of a large circle. This was the Inti-huatana. A line was drawn across from east to west and they watched when the shadow of the pillar was on the line from sunrise to sunset and there was no shadow at noon.
passages.note: Markham's note condensed (Hakluyt Society 1907); reported as editorial annotation to Sarmiento's text.

canonical_translation: Sir Clements Markham, History of the Incas (Hakluyt Society, 1907)

title.en: Golden Doors on the Window: Pachacuti Honours the Cave of Origins
title.zh: 金門封窗:帕查庫提朝拜始祖之洞

region.en: Tampu-tocco (Paccari-tampu) (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 坦波-托科(帕卡里坦波)(象徵性標記)

period: Inca tradition as given to Sarmiento de Gamboa, 1572; trans. Markham 1907

source.work: Pedro Sarmiento de Gamboa, History of the Incas, ch. 30, trans. Sir Clements Markham, Hakluyt Society, 1907

summary.en: As he was curious about the things of antiquity, and wished to perpetuate his name, the Inca went personally to the hill of Tampu-tocco or Paccari-tampu - names for the same thing - and entered the cave whence it is held for certain that Manco Ccapac and his brethren came when they marched to Cuzco for the first time. After he had made a thorough inspection, he venerated the locality and showed his feeling by festivals and sacrifices. He placed doors of gold on the window Ccapac-tocco, and ordered that from that time forward the locality should be venerated by all, making it a prayer place and huaca, whither to go to pray for oracles and to sacrifice.
summary.zh: 帕查庫提酷好古事,又欲名垂不朽,便親往坦波-托科(即帕卡里坦波,同名異稱)之山,鑽進那傳說中曼科·卡帕克與兄弟們首次出征庫斯科時所出的洞穴。他仔細察看之後,對聖地行禮致敬,以節慶與祭祀表達敬意;又命人在卡帕克-托科之窗安上黃金之門,下令從此全民崇敬此處,奉為祈禱之所與瓦卡——人們可到那裡求取神諭、舉行獻祭。

sensitivity.note: The dynasty's birthplace shrine refurbished by its greatest restorer; gold doors on the emergence window.

title.en: The Ludki: First People of Lusatia
title.zh: 魯德基：勞西茨的初民

region.en: Lusatia (Lausitz) (symbolic pin at Bautzen)
region.zh: 勞西茨（象徵性定位於包岑）

period: Belief recorded 19th c. (Machal 1918)

source.work: Jan Machal, Slavic Mythology, Mythology of All Races III (1918), Part I ch. 3

summary.en: The Ludki were the first inhabitants of Lusatia: small, big-headed, with protruding eyes and red caps, living in burrows like ovens, grinding corn between two stones — they taught mankind smithcraft and the building of houses, and their funeral urns were the urns and lachrymatories the graves give up.
summary.zh: 魯德基為勞西茨之初民：身材短小、頭大眼凸、戴紅帽，居於爐形土穴，以雙石磨穀——彼教人類鍛工與築屋之術；古墓出土之甕與淚壺，即其葬器。

sensitivity.note: Folk belief.

passages.text: In the belief of the Lusatian Serbs the Ludki — the Little People — were the first inhabitants of Lusatia, small in stature, with disproportionately large heads and protruding eyes, gaily dressed and wearing big hats or red caps. They could not endure the ringing of bells and left the country when it came; their abodes were burrows like bakers' ovens, furnished like ordinary houses.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Machal, Slavic Mythology, Mythology of All Races III (1918), Part I ch. 3; not verbatim.

passages.text: They grew corn, picking the kernels with an awl, ground it between two stones, and were familiar with every handicraft, especially the smith's trade — it was they who taught mankind the art of building houses. They were endowed with prophecy, loved music, waged fierce wars among their own households, and repaid the human family that gave them millet and courtesy. When a Ludek died his relatives burned the body, collected the tears of the mourners in little jars, and buried them filled — whence the urns and lachrymatories still found in the old graves.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Machal (1918); not verbatim.

title.en: The Polevik: Corn-Stalk Tall, Stubble Small
title.zh: 波列維克：麥稈之高，麥茬之矮

region.en: Russia (symbolic pin at Voronezh)
region.zh: 俄羅斯（象徵性定位於沃羅涅日）

period: Belief recorded 19th c. (Machal 1918)

source.work: Jan Machal, Slavic Mythology, Mythology of All Races III (1918), Part I ch. 8

summary.en: The Polevik, the field-spirit, stands about the height of a corn-stalk until harvest, when he shrivels to the size of stubble; he runs before the scythe and hides in the standing ears, and the man who naps at noon is ridden over or stricken with disease.
summary.zh: 田野精靈波列維克，收割前身高如麥稈，收割後縮至麥茬之小；他在鐮刀之前奔逃、藏於未割之穗間；正午小睡者或被其馬踏過，或罹疾。

sensitivity.note: Folk belief.

passages.text: Besides the Poludnica the Russians have a field-spirit named Polevik or Polevoy, about the height of a corn-stalk until harvest-time, when he shrivels to the size of stubble. He runs away before the swing of the scythe and hides among the stalks that are still standing; when the last ears are cut he gets into the hands of the reaper and is brought to the barn with the final sheaf.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Machal, Slavic Mythology, Mythology of All Races III (1918), Part I ch. 8; not verbatim.

passages.text: He appears at noon or before sunset, and at that time it is unsafe to take a nap in the field: the Polevik, roaming about on horseback, will ride over those who are sleeping there, or will send disease upon them. The field is his until the last sheaf is carried in.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Machal (1918); not verbatim.

title.en: Belun: The Old Man Who Walks the Harvest-Field
title.zh: 別倫：行走於收割田中的老者

region.en: White Russia (symbolic pin at Minsk)
region.zh: 白俄羅斯（象徵性定位於明斯克）

period: Belief recorded 19th c. (Machal 1918)

source.work: Jan Machal, Slavic Mythology, Mythology of All Races III (1918), Part I ch. 8

summary.en: The White Russians tell of Belun, an old man with a long white beard and gown, who helps the reapers and bestows rich presents on them; he shows himself only by day, and guides aright those who have lost their way.
summary.zh: 白俄羅斯人傳說別倫——白髮白袍之老者——助割麥人並厚贈之；他只在白晝顯形，為迷途者指引正路。

sensitivity.note: Folk belief; parallel to Vile's gift-giving wanderers.

passages.text: The White Russians tell stories about the Belun, an old man with a long white beard and gown, who helps the reapers and bestows rich presents upon them. He shows himself only during the day, and guides aright those who have lost their way — the kind old field-walker, the opposite number of the noon-spirit who asks riddles.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Machal, Slavic Mythology, Mythology of All Races III (1918), Part I ch. 8; not verbatim.

passages.text: Belun belongs to the family of wanderers who walk the roads of Slavic belief giving gifts: the old men who swap tables and packs in the Czech tales, the gods who travel unrecognized. In the harvest-field his favour is the simplest of bargains — help the reapers, and the help comes back.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Machal (1918); not verbatim.

title.en: The Jezinky: Cave Witches Who Put Out Travelers' Eyes
title.zh: 葉津卡：掏眼的洞穴女巫

region.en: Bohemia, cave country (symbolic pin at Prague)
region.zh: 波希米亞洞穴之地（象徵性定位於布拉格）

period: Belief recorded 19th c. (Machal 1918)

source.work: Jan Machal, Slavic Mythology, Mythology of All Races III (1918), Part I ch. 7

summary.en: The Jezinky of the old Czechs had the faces of women, the bodies of sows, and the legs of horses; living in caves, they lulled travellers to sleep and put out their eyes, feeding stolen children on dainties in their caverns.
summary.zh: 古捷克葉津卡女巫：婦人之面、母豬之軀、馬之腿；穴居洞中，先催眠旅人再掏其眼，並於洞中餵養被竊孩童以美食。

sensitivity.note: Folk belief; the Jezibaba (Baba Yaga of Bohemia) belongs to the same family.

passages.text: The ancient Czechs were familiar with Jezinky — lamias said to have the faces of women, the bodies of sows, and the legs of horses. Living in caves, they put out the eyes of human beings after lulling them to sleep, and they kidnap small children, whom they feed on dainty morsels in their caverns.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Machal, Slavic Mythology, Mythology of All Races III (1918), Part I ch. 7; not verbatim.

passages.text: The old Poles knew them too, and still tell stories of Jendzyna, who figures in popular fairy-tales as Jaga-baba, Jezibaba, Jendzibaba — the Bohemian cousin of the Russian Baba Yaga. In Moravia the Wild Beings are small and ungainly, living in the fields and changing into all sorts of animals; their own children are ugly, so they steal those of mankind and treat them very well.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Machal (1918); not verbatim.

title.en: The Children of the Sun and Moon
title.zh: 日月之子

region.en: Latvia (symbolic pin at Riga)
region.zh: 拉脫維亞（象徵性定位於里加）

period: Daina recorded 19th c. (Mannhardt); recorded by Gray 1918

source.work: L. H. Gray, Baltic Mythology, Mythology of All Races III (1918), Part V

summary.en: In the Lettish variant the sun and the moon have many children — the stars; and the betrothed of the Lettish Morning Star is the sun's own daughter, conceived of a union with Pehrkons himself — a thunderstorm at dawn.
summary.zh: 拉脫維亞版本中，日月育有多子——即群星；而晨星之未婚妻正是日之親女，乃日與佩爾康臨時結合所生——即黎明的雷雨。

sensitivity.note: Daina; celestial family structure parallels Vedic and Greek sky genealogies.

passages.text: A Lettish variant of the moon-and-sun myth carries the story a little further: the sun and the moon have many children, the stars; and the betrothed of the masculine Lettish Morning Star is none other than the sun's own daughter, the fruit of a temporary union with Pehrkons himself — a clear personification of a thunderstorm at dawn.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Gray, Baltic Mythology, Mythology of All Races III (1918), Part V; not verbatim.

passages.text: The moon, in shame and anger, avoids his spouse: he is visible only by night, while she appears by day in the sight of all mankind. The whole starry family is thus one kin-group — a sky-household of children, daughters, wooers, and a thunder-father — exactly as the farm below, which the songs never let the sky forget.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Gray (1918); not verbatim.

title.en: The Silver Stone: The Sun Strikes the Moon
title.zh: 銀石：太陽擊月

region.en: Latvia (symbolic pin at Riga)
region.zh: 拉脫維亞（象徵性定位於里加）

period: Daina recorded 19th c. (Mannhardt); recorded by Gray 1918

source.work: L. H. Gray, Baltic Mythology, Mythology of All Races III (1918), Part V

summary.en: She strikes the moon with a silver stone — her rising orb obliterates the moon — and this is the cause of three days' battle with God.
summary.zh: 她以銀石擊月——初升之日輪抹去月亮——此即與神三日之戰的緣由。

sensitivity.note: Daina.

passages.text: She strikes the moon with a silver stone — in other words, her rising orb obliterates the moon — and this is the cause of three days' battle with God. The three days' battle is the new moon's darkness: for three nights the sky is at war between the sun's blow and the god's repairing, until the silver stone has done its work and the light can be rebalanced. The daina keeps the quarrel in the family — wife, husband, and father-in-law — exactly as the farm keeps its own.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Gray, Baltic Mythology, Mythology of All Races III (1918), Part V; not verbatim. / Paraphrase of Gray (1918); not verbatim.

title.en: Two Lights in the Sea: The Sons of God Build a Bridal Chamber
title.zh: 海中雙火：神之子築婚房

region.en: Latvia (symbolic pin at Riga)
region.zh: 拉脫維亞（象徵性定位於里加）

period: Dainas recorded 19th c. (Mannhardt); recorded by Gray 1918

source.work: L. H. Gray, Baltic Mythology, Mythology of All Races III (1918), Part V

summary.en: Seeking to win the daughter of the sun, God's son makes for her an island in the midst of the sea — the first light at dawn or the first shadow at evening; or the two sons kindle two lights in the sea and in the centre of the ocean build a bridal chamber, which she enters trembling, urged to wake early, for God's sons are coming to roll apples.
summary.zh: 為求娶日之女，神之子為她於海中造島——即黎明初光或黃昏初影；或二子於海中燃起雙火，於大洋中央築起婚房；她顫抖著走入，被催促早醒，因神之子將來滾蘋果。

sensitivity.note: Daina.

passages.text: Seeking to win the daughter of the sun, God's son makes for her an island in the midst of the sea — either the first dark shadows of evening or the first bits of light at dawn; or the two sons kindle two lights in the sea, awaiting her, and in the centre of the ocean they build a bridal chamber, which she enters tremblingly.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Gray, Baltic Mythology, Mythology of All Races III (1918), Part V; not verbatim.

passages.text: She is urged to awake early, for God's sons are coming to roll apples — the apple-play of the Baltic wedding, where the fruit stands for the disk of the light. The wooing of dawn by the morning star is thus built in the sea itself: every daybreak raises the island, lights the fires, and rolls the apple again.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Gray (1918); not verbatim.

title.en: Usching: The Horse-God of the Southeast
title.zh: 烏希格：東南方的馬神

region.en: Ludzen and Rossitten, southeastern Lithuania (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 立陶宛東南部盧任與羅西滕（象徵性定位）

period: Recorded in a Jesuit mission report of 1606; recorded by Gray 1918

source.work: L. H. Gray, Baltic Mythology, Mythology of All Races III (1918), Part V, citing the Jesuit mission report of 1606

summary.en: A few dainas remain in honour of a deity Usching, whom a Jesuit mission report of 1606 declares to have been a horse-god worshipped in the vicinity of Ludzen and Rossitten, in the extreme south-east of Lithuania.
summary.zh: 尚存數首達伊納尊奉一神名烏希格；一六〇六年耶穌會傳教報告謂其為馬神，受祀於立陶宛東南部盧任與羅西滕一帶。

sensitivity.note: Fragmentary deity; interpretive reconstruction flagged.

passages.text: There are a few dainas in honour of a deity Usching, whom a Jesuit mission report of 1606 declares to have been a horse-god worshipped in the vicinity of Ludzen and Rossitten, in the extreme south-east of Lithuania. Gray adds that these are not of mythological value — the god's tales are lost, and only the name and the horse remain. Yet the horse was the great beast of the Baltic sky: God rides with smoke-grey horses, the sun keeps her hundred brown horses, and the hooves in the dainas always belong to someone. Usching is the horse-god by name; his stories, whatever they were, have gone the way of the Prussians. (Fragmentary; interpretive reconstruction flagged.)
passages.note: Paraphrase of Gray, Baltic Mythology, Mythology of All Races III (1918), Part V; not verbatim. / Paraphrase of Gray (1918) with caveat; not verbatim.

title.en: Zal at the Court of Mihrab of Kabul
title.zh: 扎勒訪喀布爾米赫拉布王庭

region.en: Kabul (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 喀布爾（象徵性定位）

period: Composed c. 1010 CE (Warner translation 1905)

source.work: Firdausi, Shahnama, trans. A. G. & E. Warner (1905), vol. I, Minuchihr sec. 7

summary.en: Zal rides a royal progress through Kabul, Dunbar, Mai and Ind, and is met with treasure by Mihrab, the wealthy king of Kabul who pays yearly tribute to Sam. Mihrab's praise of Zal — in heart a lion, in strength an elephant; when he is on the throne he scattereth gold, when he is in the fray he scattereth heads — lights a fire in the heart of Rudaba, Mihrab's daughter, whom Zal has never seen.
summary.zh: 扎勒巡行喀布爾、敦巴爾、邁與信德，受到向薩姆納貢的富裕王米赫拉布厚禮相迎。米赫拉布讚扎勒「心為獅、力如象；登座則撒金，臨陣則落首」——此語在未曾謀面的米赫拉布之女魯達貝心中點燃愛火。

sensitivity.note: Epic literary source; no living community restriction.

passages.text: One day Zal set forth on a royal progress with chiefs attached to him in rede and Faith, to view Kabul, Dunbar, Margh, Mai and Ind. At every stage he set him up a throne and called for wine and harp and minstrelsy, and reached Kabul with gladness in his heart.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Firdausi, Shahnama, Minuchihr sec. 7 (Warner 1905); not verbatim.

passages.text: There was a certain monarch hight Mihrab, a wealthy and successful potentate, descended from Zahhak, who ruled Kabul but, having not the power to fight with Sam, paid yearly tribute. Hearing that Sam's son had come, he left Kabul at dawn with treasure and steeds and dinars and musk and rubies and brocade of gold, and Zal went to meet and greet him courteously. They came together to the turquoise throne and a table fit for paladins was spread.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Firdausi, Shahnama, Minuchihr sec. 7 (Warner 1905); not verbatim.

passages.text: Mihrab observed the son of Sam, and said to Sindukht: of all the warrior-paladins of earth not one can tread his steps; he is in heart a lion and in strength an elephant. When he is on the throne he scattereth gold, when he is in the fray he scattereth heads. He hath this one defect: his hair is white. On hearing this Rudaba blushed, with cheeks red as pomegranate-blossoms, while her heart became fulfilled with fire for love of Zal, and passion usurped the place of wisdom.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Firdausi, Shahnama, Minuchihr secs. 7-8 (Warner 1905); not verbatim.

title.en: The Damsels at the River and the Rosary of Roses
title.zh: 河畔侍女與薔薇花園

region.en: Kabul riverside (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 喀布爾河畔（象徵性定位）

period: Composed c. 1010 CE (Warner translation 1905)

source.work: Firdausi, Shahnama, trans. A. G. & E. Warner (1905), vol. I, Minuchihr secs. 8-10

summary.en: Rudaba confides her love to her five Turkman waiting-maids — I am in love, and like a raging sea whose billows surge to heaven — and when they warn her of Zal's white hair and ignoble fostering she flares up: I want not Caesar or Faghfur of Chin; Zal, son of Sam, is tall enough for me. At Farwardin the maids go gathering roses by the river where Zal's tents stand, and the two camps talk of nothing but the other side.
summary.zh: 魯達貝向五名突厥侍女吐露愛情——「我墜入愛河，如浪濤沖天之怒海。」侍女們勸其勿慕白髮之孤兒，她怒斥：「我不求愷撒或中國王；扎勒之子薩姆已足矣。」法爾瓦爾丁月，侍女們至扎勒營旁河邊採薔薇，兩營談論的盡是對岸之人。

sensitivity.note: Epic literary source; no living community restriction.

passages.text: Rudaba had five Turkman waiting-maids, five faithful slaves, all girls of prudent minds. To them she said: I am in love, and like a raging sea whose billows surge to heaven; mine ardent heart is full of love for Zal, and in my sleep I cannot tear my thoughts from him. His love possesseth me, heart, mind, and wits; I muse upon his features day and night.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Firdausi, Shahnama, Minuchihr sec. 8 (Warner 1905); not verbatim.

passages.text: The slaves thought in amaze and rose at her like so many Ahrimans: wouldst thou clasp upon thy bosom one whose own father hath rejected him, one fostered on a mountain by a fowl? Rudaba heard, her heart flared up like fire before a blast of air, and she shrieked: I want not Caesar or Faghfur of Chin, or any of the princelings of Iran; Zal, son of Sam, is tall enough for me; I do not love his face and hair but him; 'tis for his merits that I seek his love.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Firdausi, Shahnama, Minuchihr sec. 8 (Warner 1905); not verbatim.

passages.text: So donning raiment of brocade of Rum, and twisting roses in their hair, they went toward the river-side: 'twas Farwardin, the first month of the year, and Zal's encampment was beside the stream. Zal, spying them from his high throne, inquired who were these flower-worshippers, and one said: the Beauty of Kabulistan hath sent forth from the palace of bright-souled Mihrab her waiting-maidens to the rosary. Zal's heart beat fast, and being love-distraught he walked beside the stream with a single slave.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Firdausi, Shahnama, Minuchihr sec. 9 (Warner 1905); not verbatim.

title.en: The Lasso of Tresses
title.zh: 以秀髮為繩

region.en: Palace of Mihrab, Kabul (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 米赫拉布王宮（象徵性定位）

period: Composed c. 1010 CE (Warner translation 1905)

source.work: Firdausi, Shahnama, trans. A. G. & E. Warner (1905), vol. I, Minuchihr sec. 11

summary.en: At dusk a damsel tells Zal all is prepared. Rudaba from the roof cries: thou art well come; and when Zal asks why she should be on the roof and he below, she doffs her scarlet wimple and looses her tresses over the battlements till they reach the ground: seize these black tresses which hang down beside me, all dedicate to thee. Zal will not wound her heart with his hand; he takes a lasso from his servant instead, and hand clasped in hand the two descend intoxicate with love.
summary.zh: 黃昏時侍女告知扎勒一切已備。魯達貝在屋頂喊道：「君至矣！」扎勒問為何她居高而他居低；她便褪下猩紅頭巾，將長髮垂下牆頭直至地面：「抓住這為你而留的黑髮吧！」扎勒不忍以手攀其心，改用僕人的繩索登牆；二人攜手，沉醉愛河而下。

sensitivity.note: Epic literary source; no living community restriction.

passages.text: At dusk they locked the gate and took the key, and then a damsel went to Zal and said: all is prepared, so come. Thereat the chief, all wooer-like, set out toward the palace. Meanwhile black-eyed and rosy-cheeked Rudaba went to the roof, and, when the son of Sam appeared, that high-born maid unlocked her coral lips and cried to him: thou art well come, O youth of noble birth.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Firdausi, Shahnama, Minuchihr sec. 11 (Warner 1905); not verbatim.

passages.text: Oh find some means to let me look on thee, said Zal, for why shouldst thou be on the roof and I below? The fairy-faced one heard the chieftain's words and doffed her scarlet wimple instantly; then from her lofty cypress-form she loosed a lasso, such as none could plait, of musk. She loosed her tresses o'er the battlements, and when they straightened out they reached the ground.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Firdausi, Shahnama, Minuchihr sec. 11 (Warner 1905); not verbatim.

passages.text: Now speed thee quickly, spake Rudaba from the wall above, and seize these black tresses which hang down beside me, all dedicate to thee. Zal gazed on her in marvel and said: this is not well; may no sun shine when I shall lay a wanton hand upon my Life. He took a lasso from his servant, coiled and lightly flung it; the noose caught and he mounted. She clasped his hand, and both intoxicate with love descended hand clasped in hand to her pavilion, a Paradise adorned.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Firdausi, Shahnama, Minuchihr sec. 11 (Warner 1905); not verbatim.

passages.text: The Shah will ne'er consent, and Sam will wring his hands and storm, said Zal, but still by God I swear that I will never break my troth to thee. Rudaba answered: I too swear by Him, the God of Faith and right, that none but Zal shall be my lord; the Maker is my witness. Their love waxed ever as the moments sped, for wisdom was afar and passion near; then from aloft Zal dropped his lasso and descending straight went from the palace of his lovely mate.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Firdausi, Shahnama, Minuchihr sec. 11 (Warner 1905); not verbatim.

title.en: Sindukht Finds the Go-Between and the Ring
title.zh: 辛杜赫特識破傳信婦人

region.en: Palace of Mihrab, Kabul (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 米赫拉布王宮（象徵性定位）

period: Composed c. 1010 CE (Warner translation 1905)

source.work: Firdausi, Shahnama, trans. A. G. & E. Warner (1905), vol. I, Minuchihr sec. 15

summary.en: A dame of honied speech bears the lovers' greetings to and fro, and Sindukht, Rudaba's mother, suspects the visitor who passes in and out.
