summary.en: Some addition has been made to that legend, grave and old, since our fathers surveyed steel-clad white men, strong and bold, who with blood-hounds, we are told, hunted men — and all for gold! 'Not from the Komaka tree sprang the whites,' our sages say: 'they, from wood cast on the sea, rose amidst wild ocean's spray, finding land on which to stay over the waters — far away.' 'If from wood our race has sprung, did it in these forests grow? Did it to green-heart belong, locust, or balata? Did its foliage ruddy glow with a mora's strength below? Ask no more, friend, you are wrong: those trees give us bark, gums, and timber strong — but the white man's stock, they say, good for nought, was cast away!' Smiles on every face appear; red men seated on the ground laugh to hear that satire old — a mild revenge which poor men found who escaped Spanish arcabuz and hound in the swamps around.
summary.zh: 自先祖見鋼甲白人以血犬獵人、專為掠金，古傳說遂增一篇。耆老言：『白人非自柯瑪卡樹出；乃擲海之木，起於怒濤之間，覓遠方之陸而居。』或問：『若吾族出自木，則此木生於此林乎？綠心木耶？洋槐耶？巴拉塔耶？』答曰：『毋多問，君誤矣。此諸樹日日賜我樹皮、樹膠、堅材；白人之材，無用而見棄者也！』紅人席地而笑——逃西班牙火銃與獵犬者之小復仇也。

sensitivity.note: Arawak oral tradition recorded by the missionary Brett 1880; a satire on the Spanish conquest embedded in the legend cycle, read critically.

passages.text: Some addition has been made to that legend, grave and old, since our fathers here surveyed steel-clad white men, strong and bold. They, with blood-hounds, we are told, hunted men — and all for gold! 'Not from the Komaka tree sprang the whites,' our sages say: 'they from wood cast on the sea rose amidst wild ocean's spray, finding land on which to stay over the waters — far away.'
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Brett 1880, 'Origin of the White Race'; not verbatim.

passages.text: 'If from wood our race has sprung, did it in these forests grow? Did it to green-heart belong, locust, or balata? Ask no more, friend, you are wrong. Those trees give us, day by day, bark, or gums, and timber strong: useful gifts they all convey. But the white man's stock, they say, good for nought, was cast away!' Smiles on every face appear; red men, seated on the ground, laugh that satire old to hear: a mild revenge, which poor men found who escaped, in swamps around, Spanish arcabuz and hound!
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Brett 1880, 'Origin of the White Race'; not verbatim.

title.en: The Fire: the First Destruction of the Arawak World
title.zh: 天火：阿拉瓦克世界之首滅

region.en: Arawak country, Guiana coast
region.zh: 圭亞那濱海阿拉瓦克之地

period: Arawak oral tradition; recorded 1880 (Brett)

source.work: W. H. Brett, Legends and Myths of the Aboriginal Indians of British Guiana (1880), Part I 'Legends of the Arawaks', 'The Fire and the Flood'

summary.en: The Arawaks, peculiar, understood that fire had swept the earth before the water-flood. Fire is mighty, all-subduing: once its fury came when the Maker, roused, was viewing deeds of blood and shame — evil raging, goodness failing — then on earth His wrath prevailing came the burning flame. Timely warning came from heaven: 'Fire shall sweep the land!' One who heard that warning sought a reef of sand and led his little band to dig a pit, hide wives and children under a strong timber roof, and to fell and burn all around until nothing on which flames could fasten remained. Clouds of smoke came rolling nigher, then fierce flames wrapped the woods in fire: the blazing torrent came onward, the burnt clearing stayed its current — there the flames expired. Thither, from that danger flying, birds and beasts repaired; and in their vault those men were lying, bearing smoke and heat while the fiery hail was pouring, finding safety there. Coming forth they saw the ruin through the lurid fume: blackened skeletons showed where men and beasts, when flying, met their awful doom.
summary.zh: 阿拉瓦克人獨知：洪水之前，先有天火。火威莫禦；造物主見人間血腥與醜惡，怒而生焰。天降警曰：『火將燎原！』一酋聞之，率眾至沙礁，鑿窖藏婦孺，以堅木覆之；又伐燒四周，使無可燃之物。煙雲漸近，烈焰裹林；火洪滾滾而至，遇焚清之地而止——焰乃熄。飛禽走獸亦奔集焉；窖中人忍煙受熱，得免於焚。出而視之：灰燼遍地，黑骸橫陳，皆奔逃者之終也。

sensitivity.note: Arawak oral tradition recorded by Brett 1880 in metrical form; paraphrased into prose. Fire-before-flood destruction, read critically.

passages.text: Fire is mighty — all-subduing! Once its fury came, when the Maker, roused, was viewing deeds of blood and shame — evil raging, goodness failing — then on earth, His wrath prevailing, came the burning flame. Timely warning came from heaven: 'Fire shall sweep the land!' One who heard that warning given sought a reef of sand; by that chieftain's wisdom guided, some a refuge there provided for their little band.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Brett 1880, 'The Fire and the Flood'; not verbatim.

passages.text: 'Here,' said he, 'a pit preparing, wives and children hide; timber strong, the sand-roof bearing, we must first provide. Felling next the trees, and burning all around make clear; shrubs and grass to ashes turning, leave we nothing here — nothing on which flames can fasten. Clear and burn! O brothers! hasten, ere the flames appear!'
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Brett 1880, 'The Fire and the Flood'; not verbatim.

passages.text: Clouds of smoke, the sun concealing, came still rolling nigher; then fierce flames, their might revealing, wrapped the woods in fire. Onward came the blazing torrent: that burnt clearing stayed its current — there the flames expired. Thither, from that danger flying, birds and beasts repaired; in their vault those men were lying, smoke and heat they bore, while the flames around were roaring, and the fiery hail was pouring — finding safety there. Coming forth they saw the ruin through the lurid fume: blackened skeletons there lying showed where men and beasts, when flying, met their awful doom!
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Brett 1880, 'The Fire and the Flood'; not verbatim.

title.en: Marerewana's Canoe and the Bush-Rope Mooring
title.zh: 馬雷瓦納之舟與藤索之繫

region.en: Arawak country, Guiana coast
region.zh: 圭亞那濱海阿拉瓦克之地

period: Arawak oral tradition; recorded 1880 (Brett)

source.work: W. H. Brett, Legends and Myths of the Aboriginal Indians of British Guiana (1880), Part I 'Legends of the Arawaks', 'The Fire and the Flood', part II

summary.en: Time flowed on; punishment became a stranger, and all had gone astray. When a new warning told them of a flood impending, none believed it true — till Marerewana, fearing for his wife and children, made a great canoe. Some of his neighbours said he was to blame; others, mocking at his labours, strove to give him shame: 'Make it large, Marerewana! Over forest and savannah float — the deluge through!' Still he worked, morning and evening, until the great waters came. An arched roof he thatched above it with strong warm palm leaves. 'When this flood shall come, we may drift, perhaps to-morrow, through the salt-sea foam!' he said with sorrow — and a voice answered: 'That great tree near thee: moor to that — thy craft shall bear thee safely near thy home!' Then, with lengthened bush-ropes mooring, he and his, the flood enduring, weathered surge and swell; and when the waters left them stranded, near their former home they landed — known, and loved, so well!
summary.zh: 時流而罰寢，眾皆放僻。洪水之警再至，無人信之——惟馬雷瓦納懼妻孥之亡，造巨舟。鄰人或咎之，或嘲之：『造大些，馬雷瓦納！漂過林野，浮出洪水！』彼朝夕勤作，不辭勞苦，直至大水至。舟上覆拱頂，以厚棕葉蔽之。彼憂曰：『洪水至時，吾儕恐漂入鹹海之沫。』有聲答曰：『近有大樹，繫舟其上——水退必近故里！』乃以長藤繫之；洪經而舟安，水退登岸，故里宛然在望。

sensitivity.note: Arawak oral tradition recorded by Brett 1880; variant of the flood record already in the corpus, read critically.

passages.text: Time flowed on. That fearful danger long had passed away; punishment became a stranger; all had gone astray. Violence and wrong abounded; men with evil good confounded, growing worse each day. Evil ways have evil ending: when a warning new told them of a flood impending, none believed it true — till Marerewana, hearing, for his wife and children fearing, made a great canoe.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Brett 1880, 'The Fire and the Flood' II; not verbatim.

passages.text: Some among his nearest neighbours said he was to blame; others, mocking at his labours, strove to give him shame. Still they found him at it working, morn and eve, no labour shirking, ere 'great waters' came. 'Make it large, Marerewana! Strong and fair to view: over forest and savannah float — the deluge through!' Thus they mocked their anxious neighbour, laughed at his canoe. An arched roof he thatched above it, palm leaves strong and warm; firm, that no fierce wind might move it, ready for the storm.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Brett 1880, 'The Fire and the Flood' II; not verbatim.

passages.text: Still he feared, and said with sorrow: 'When this flood shall come, we may drift, perhaps to-morrow, through the salt-sea foam!' Said a voice: 'That great tree near thee, moor to that — thy craft shall bear thee safely near thy home!' Then, with lengthened bush-ropes mooring (so our legends tell), he and his, the flood enduring, weathered surge and swell. When the waters left them stranded, near their former home they landed — known, and loved, so well!
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Brett 1880, 'The Fire and the Flood' II; not verbatim.

title.en: The Elder of Cuba and the Two Ways of the Soul
title.zh: 古巴老者與靈魂之兩路

region.en: Isle of Cuba (Arawak)
region.zh: 古巴島（阿拉瓦克）

period: Taino tradition as told to Columbus; retold 1880 (Brett)

source.work: W. H. Brett, Legends and Myths of the Aboriginal Indians of British Guiana (1880), Part I 'Legends of the Arawaks', 'Ideas of a Future State'

summary.en: Columbus told how, on fair Cuba's isle, where, spent with toil, he sought repose awhile, and gentle natives welcomed him to land, a venerable elder took his hand. Full fourscore years had bowed that old man's head, and to the Admiral thus solemnly he said: 'Great is thy power, O chief! But be not vain, and from all violence and wrong abstain. For, after death, there are before the soul two ways, each ending in a final goal: to light and life all the kind-hearted go; the cruel and unkind to dark and dismal woe!'
summary.zh: 哥倫布述古巴島事：其倦而登陸，土人善遇之；一老者執其手——年已八十——肅然言曰：『酋長！權大勿驕，戒暴戒虐。人死之後，靈前有二路，各有終點：仁善者向光明與生；殘忍者向幽暗與苦！』

sensitivity.note: Taino tradition as retold through Columbus and Brett 1880; archival record, read critically.

passages.text: Columbus told how, on fair Cuba's isle, where, spent with toil, he sought repose awhile, and gentle natives welcomed him to land, a venerable elder took his hand. Full fourscore years had bowed that old man's head, and to the Admiral thus solemnly he said: 'Great is thy power, O chief! But be not vain, and from all violence and wrong abstain. For, after death, there are before the soul two ways, each ending in a final goal: to light and life all the kind-hearted go; the cruel and unkind to dark and dismal woe!'
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Brett 1880, 'Ideas of a Future State'; not verbatim.

title.en: Arawanili and the Orehu, the Lady of the Sea
title.zh: 阿拉瓦尼利與海母奧雷胡

region.en: Kaieri island, Antilles (Arawak)
region.zh: 安的列斯群島凱里島（阿拉瓦克）

period: Arawak oral tradition; recorded 1880 (Brett)

source.work: W. H. Brett, Legends and Myths of the Aboriginal Indians of British Guiana (1880), Part I 'Legends of the Arawaks', 'Arawanili and the Orehu'

summary.en: A chieftain grave, both wise and brave — good Arawanili — stood mournful by the silver wave of the wide-spread ocean sea. His heart was sore: the plume he wore as chief of Kaieri drooped, while he listened on the shore to the sigh of that ocean sea. Throughout the isle man, wife, and child lay crushed by fever, driven wild by the demons' arrows — the dire shafts of the Yauhahu; and none without a charm could face them. Then in his view bright Orehu, the Water-Mother, rose glistening from the ocean sea: 'Go, plant with care this branch I bear, and rear the ida tree; when fruit is found, take that which first falls on the ground, and meet me by the sea!' He emptied the calabash's rind through holes; she brought its feathered handle, and, diving, brought the gems of ocean and stones of shining white; tobacco too, which none then knew, brought she; with charms which made all Yauhahu dread Arawanili. To her he owed the power he showed — none since like him could be. Still in stream or bay the Orehu men see; but 'high above', grown old, they say, rests Arawanili.
summary.zh: 智勇之酋阿拉瓦尼立於銀浪之濱而悲。凱里島中老幼為熱病所苦，為雅烏哈胡之毒箭所傷；無符者莫能當之。海母奧雷胡自波中出，曰：『植我所授之枝，育伊達樹；初落之果取而攜至海濱見我。』遂剖葫蘆為鈴，得羽柄；彼潛海而得白石；並授菸草——時人未知者也——與鎮雅烏哈胡之符。其能皆出於彼；至今無匹。今人猶於溪灣見奧雷胡；而阿拉瓦尼則老而高棲於天。

sensitivity.note: Arawak oral tradition recorded by the missionary Brett 1880 in verse; paraphrased into prose and read critically.

passages.text: A chieftain grave, both wise and brave — good Arawanili — stood mournful by the silver wave of the wide-spread ocean sea. His heart was sore; the plume he wore as chief of Kaieri drooped, while he listened on the shore to the sigh of that ocean sea. 'Tis for the dead, the chieftain said, for whom I nought could do, to help them ere their spirits fled from torturing Yauhahu: throughout this isle, man, wife, or child, by fever crushed I view; by demons' arrows driven wild — dire shafts of Yauhahu! But none, without a charm, I trow, can face the Yauhahu.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Brett 1880, 'Arawanili and the Orehu'; not verbatim.

passages.text: Then, in his view, bright Orehu — the Water-Mother she — rose, glistening as with drops of dew, or pearls, from the ocean sea. 'Tell me thy grief, O chief! And I, perchance, may bring relief from the depths of the ocean sea. Go, plant with care this branch I bear, and rear the ida tree; when fruit is found, full large and round, take that which first falls on the ground, and meet me by the sea!'
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Brett 1880, 'Arawanili and the Orehu'; not verbatim.

passages.text: Its rind with care he emptied there through holes; she brought its handle, feathered fair; and while he wrought, she dived and sought the gems of ocean sea, and stones of shining white she brought. Tobacco too, which none then knew (though common now), brought she: with charms which made all Yauhahu dread Arawanili. To her he owed the power he showed — none since like him could be. Still, to this day, in stream or bay, the Orehu men see; but 'high above', grown old, they say, rests Arawanili.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Brett 1880, 'Arawanili and the Orehu'; not verbatim.

title.en: Biter Bit: the Piai and the Sick White Man
title.zh: 反噬：巫醫與詐病之白人

region.en: Guiana backwoods (Arawak piai practice)
region.zh: 圭亞那內地（阿拉瓦克巫俗）

period: Arawak piai lore; recorded 1880 (Brett)

source.work: W. H. Brett, Legends and Myths of the Aboriginal Indians of British Guiana (1880), Part I 'Legends of the Arawaks', 'Appendix to the Legend (Biter Bit)'

summary.en: Allusion was made to the tricks in their trade which Indian sorcerers have commonly played — here is what really happened a few years ago. Two white men went through the backwoods wishing to learn the piai mystery; one feigned sickness, and his friend begged the famous piai-man near by to come and cure 'this sick white man'. The sorcerer sternly bade the females take themselves away, made up his sacred fire to burn the sacred weed, commenced incantations terrible to hear, inhaled tobacco smoke and blew it over and up the sick man's nose, rubbed the affected part till the patient shook with stifled laughter he could hold out no more — then, according to their ancient rules, applied his mouth to suck out what was causing the pain, gripping with his teeth full sore until, with a yell, the patient fell out on the earthen floor. The cool doctor by signs made his meaning plain: 'Get back into that hammock; I must operate again!' — and the white man, cash and fame secure, walked off triumphantly, having told him he had made a cure and given a handsome fee. And when a man is learning the mysteries of his vocation, he is shut up and half-starved, drinks tobacco decoction as strong as can be, till he sinks in a trance — and revives an M.D.!
summary.zh: 巫醫行技之詭，姑舉一實事。二白人入林欲學巫秘；一人詐病，友人請近地名巫醫來治。巫驅婦人，焚聖草，誦咒震耳，吸菸而吹病者鼻中，搓其痛處；病者忍癢不禁，笑聲大作——巫面不改色。依古法以口吸其痛處，齧之極痛；病者呼而仆地。巫以手示意：『回床！吾須再施術！』白人自知技窮，乃賞金而稱其治愈，揚長而去。至若學巫之人：閉戶半饑，飲至濃之菸汁，昏眩而醒——即成醫師矣！

sensitivity.note: Arawak piai practice described by the missionary Brett 1880; a colonial-era anecdote about shamanic curing technique, read critically — it records real ritual procedure (tobacco fumigation, sucking extraction) alongside colonial mockery.

passages.text: Two white men through our backwoods went, the Indian life to see, and much they wished of piai-men to learn the mystery. But 'twas in vain, till one declared that he was 'taken sick', and begged his friend to lend a hand to carry out the trick. They knew a famous piai-man lived at a place near by: 'Oh come and cure this sick white man!' He answered: 'I will try.' He first the females sternly bade to take themselves away; they all forthwith fled like the wind, too much afraid to stay. He then made up his sacred fire to burn the sacred weed; his incantations then commenced, most terrible to hear.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Brett 1880, 'Appendix to the Legend'; not verbatim.

passages.text: He next inhaled tobacco smoke, much as his mouth could hold, and blew it on the sick white man. He next on the affected part his hands began to rub; the patient grew convulsed at that — with strong but stifled laughter his body shook all over: he could hold out no more! He laughed outright, then feebly tried to make that laugh a groan: the doctor knew the difference of tone, saw that he was being tricked, yet went on with his work, not altering a muscle, but as grave as any Turk.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Brett 1880, 'Appendix to the Legend'; not verbatim.

passages.text: According to their ancient rules, his mouth he next applied to suck out what was causing pain in that white man's inside; he seized him boldly with his teeth — it was a grip full sore — and, with a yell, the patient fell out on the earthen floor! Most cool the doctor was: by signs he made his meaning plain: 'Get back into that hammock, I must operate again!' The other shook his head, showed his injured side, and said 'twas bitten through — but he replied: 'This savage doctor knows a thing or two; I'll tell him he has made a cure, and give a handsome fee.' So he, with cash and fame secure, walked off triumphantly. When a man's on probation, learning the mysteries of his vocation, he's shut up and half-starved; drinks tobacco decoction as strong as can be, till he sinks in a trance: and revives — an M.D.!
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Brett 1880, 'Appendix to the Legend'; not verbatim.

title.en: Arawidi the Sun and the Woodpecker Watchman
title.zh: 太陽阿拉威迪與啄木守望

region.en: Arawak country, Guiana coast
region.zh: 圭亞那濱海阿拉瓦克之地

period: Arawak oral tradition; recorded 1880 (Brett)

source.work: W. H. Brett, Legends and Myths of the Aboriginal Indians of British Guiana (1880), Part I 'Legends of the Arawaks', 'Arawidi (A Fragment)'

summary.en: 'Adaili is the glorious sun' — thus their first legend ran — 'but when of old on earth he came, then Arawidi was his name: his fashion, that of man.' Once, fishing on a favourite stream, he made a dam or weir, and said: 'This stream must not run dry, lest, in my visits from the sky, I find no fishes here.' The otters heard; they broke his dam and let the waters flow. Then he, compelled to seek for aid, made the woodpecker his watchman here below. One day, while passing through the sky, loud tapping caught his ear: swift darting to that spot below he found a fierce and mailed foe — the alligator — near. He seized him with a mighty hand, and smote to make the reptile yield with his war club upon his head and tail. 'Oh, Arawidi, slay me not!' the alligator cried: 'Cease to wound! Thy suppliant spare, and I will give a maiden fair to be thy beauteous bride.' He called his friends the water-sprites, the maiden to provide; and soon a girl of wondrous charms was placed in Arawidi's arms. The reptile's wounds were healed, but still their marks are seen, 'tis said, indented on his battered head and notched along his tail.
summary.zh: 『阿達利即榮耀之日』——其首傳如此——『古時降凡，名阿拉威迪，形貌如人。』彼於慣釣之溪築堰，曰：『此水毋涸，免我自天再臨時無魚。』水獺聞而毀堰；彼遂以啄木鳥為守望。一日自天過，聞叩聲甚急；俯臨其地，見鱷——披甲之勁敵也。執之以巨手，以戰杖擊其首尾。鱷呼曰：『阿拉威迪，毋殺我！饒我，當獻美女為爾妻。』遂召水靈獻女；美人入懷。鱷創雖愈，而其首之凹痕、尾之齒痕，至今猶見。

sensitivity.note: Arawak oral tradition recorded by Brett 1880 in verse; paraphrased into prose. Variant of the Roth Arawidi record.

passages.text: 'Adaili is the glorious sun' (thus their first legend ran), 'but when of old on earth he came, then Arawidi was his name: his fashion — that of man. Once, fishing on a fav'rite stream, he made a dam, or weir, and said: This stream must not run dry, lest, in my visits from the sky, I find no fishes here. The otters heard. They broke his dam, and let the waters flow. Then he, compelled to seek for aid, its guardian the woodpecker made — his watchman — here below.'
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Brett 1880, 'Arawidi'; not verbatim.

passages.text: 'One day, while passing through the sky, loud tapping caught his ear. Swift darting to that spot below, he found a fierce and mailed foe — the alligator — near. He seized him with a mighty hand, whose grip could never fail; then smote, to make the reptile yield, with that war club he well could wield, upon his head and tail. Oh, Arawidi, slay me not! the alligator cried: cease, cease to wound! Thy suppliant spare, and I will give a maiden fair to be thy beauteous bride.'
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Brett 1880, 'Arawidi'; not verbatim.

passages.text: 'He called his friends, the water-sprites, the maiden to provide; and soon a girl, of wondrous charms, was placed in Arawidi's arms. The reptile's wounds were healed; those blows no more his hide assail; but still their marks are seen, 'tis said, indented on his battered head and notched along his tail!'
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Brett 1880, 'Arawidi'; not verbatim.

title.en: Kapikoa, the Black Cockatoo, and the Girl Without Fire
title.zh: 黑鸚鵡卡皮科亞與無火之女

region.en: Wamira district, British New Guinea (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 英屬新幾內亞瓦米拉地區（象徵定位）

period: Oral tradition; recorded by Annie Ker, Papuan Fairy Tales, 1910

source.work: Annie Ker, Papuan Fairy Tales (London: Macmillan, 1910), 'Kapikoa, the Black Cockatoo'

summary.en: The great chief Kapikoa gave his servants only the husk of his betel nut; on a western journey his servants muddied the stream, sent him thirsty to its source, and sailed away with the canoe. Abandoned, he threw a scratched fig down to a girl filling her water bottles, won her for his wife — and taught her and all her land fire, for no fire was known there and food was eaten raw or sun-warmed; and so do all women cook to this day.
summary.zh: 大酋長黑鸚鵡卡皮科亞苛待僕從，食檳榔只給他們嚼殼。西行途中，僕從們把溪水攪渾，支他源頭飲水，卻乘舟棄他而去。他流落異鄉，從樹上擲下一枚刻了花紋的榕果給汲水的少女，少女識得非風落之物，喚他下樹，結為夫妻。妻子不知火為何物——她的家鄉無火，食物生食或晒暖而食。卡皮科亞取兩段木相搓，吹燃成火；她驚懼之餘學會炊食。自那日起，該地婦女皆如此炊煮，至今依然。

sensitivity.note: Colonial-era collection (Ker 1910); Wamira heritage.

passages.text: In the old days, Kapikoa, the black cockatoo, was a very great chief. His servants were many, but he treated them evilly, for when he ate betel nut he gave them only the husk, and kept the substance for himself. One day he said to his servants, 'Get ready my canoe, for I wish to travel to the west.' So they made all ready, and went on board, they and their master, and paddled a long way, and at last they landed. Now the servants had made a plot among themselves to rid them of their greedy master. They said, 'Let us go away, and leave him alone, where he will have no one to take his betel husk.' So they went to Kapikoa, and said, 'Lord, we would ask thee a boon. Wilt thou remain by the canoe whilst we go to drink water?' Then said he, 'Ye may go.' They therefore followed up the stream, and made its waters dark by stirring up the mud as they went. But when they got higher they drank fair water at the source.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ker, Papuan Fairy Tales, 'Kapikoa, the Black Cockatoo' (1910); not verbatim.

passages.text: Now when they had thus done they went back to Kapikoa and said, 'Let us now remain by the canoe, lord, whilst thou drinkest.' Kapikoa was athirst, therefore he did as his servants had said. But when he reached the stream he found the water was muddied. He walked on and on until he reached the source. Then he drank and returned to the shore. But no canoe there lay, for his servants had already launched it and put out to sea, leaving their master's bag on the beach. When they were a safe distance from the shore they laid down their paddles and let the canoe float. Then was Kapikoa wroth when he saw them, and he cried with a loud voice, 'Come hither that I may go on board.' But the servants made answer, 'Nay! Thou hast given us only the husk of thy betel nut, while thou hast eaten the substance thyself. Remain there alone, for we will not have pity on thee.' Then they took up their paddles, and steered for home.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ker, Papuan Fairy Tales, 'Kapikoa, the Black Cockatoo' (1910); not verbatim.

passages.text: There he saw a big fig tree on the bank, and he climbed into it. As he sat in the branches, a beautiful girl passed under it, and bent down at the river to fill her coconut water bottles. Kapikoa scratched a design on a fig and threw it down, hoping that the maiden would see him. She looked up when it splashed in the water, but could see nought, therefore she stooped once more. Kapikoa threw down yet another fig, and the girl, seeing the design upon it, knew that it had not fallen with the wind, but that someone had thrown it. Therefore she gazed long at the tree, and saw Kapikoa in the branches. Then she called to him, 'Come down, I pray thee.' Kapikoa did as she had said, and when he saw how fair she was he loved her, and they were married, and went away together.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ker, Papuan Fairy Tales, 'Kapikoa, the Black Cockatoo' (1910); not verbatim.

passages.text: Then said he, 'Now thou art my wife thou must cook my food.' The girl took some taro and peeled it and laid it in the sun to become warm. Her husband asked her, 'Is there here no fire?' Then said the girl, 'Nay, lord, I know not of what thou speakest.' For in her land fire was not known, and food was eaten raw, or was but warmed by the rays of the sun. Then said Kapikoa, 'Bring me hither two pieces of wood,' and she brought them and gave them to him. Then he rubbed them together and they smouldered, and he blew on them until they blazed. Now the girl was afraid when she saw the flames, for she knew not whence they were. But her husband said, 'Fear not. Now thou canst cook my food, since I have shown thee how.' So the girl made ready taro and cooked it and gave it to her husband, and they both ate of it. And when the meal was eaten, Kapikoa said to his wife, 'Behold, now thou knowest how to deal with fire.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ker, Papuan Fairy Tales, 'Kapikoa, the Black Cockatoo' (1910); not verbatim.

title.en: The Mouse and the Butterfly
title.zh: 鼠與蝶

region.en: Wamira district, British New Guinea (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 英屬新幾內亞瓦米拉地區（象徵定位）

period: Oral tradition; recorded by Annie Ker, Papuan Fairy Tales, 1910

source.work: Annie Ker, Papuan Fairy Tales (London: Macmillan, 1910), 'The Mouse and the Butterfly'

summary.en: In the days when the animals were bariawa and spake as men, the Mouse and the Butterfly made a canoe that came apart in the sea. Ashore they quarrelled over sugarcane and bananas; the Mouse bit through a heavy cane that fell and crushed him, and his friend wrapped him in a taro leaf for burial. A great Hawk swooped on the bundle and ate the dead Mouse in a mouthful — till the Butterfly's brother felled him with a sling-stone, avenging the dishonour done to the dead body.
summary.zh: 太古之世，獸類皆如人言語。鼠與蝶合造一舟出海，舟解於浪，二者泅水登岸。登島後爭食：鼠往啃蔗，蝶去尋蕉。蝶食香蕉時忽聞遠處慘呼『Kaidara kiki!』——是鼠被一株粗蔗倒下壓死了。蝶含悲取芋葉裹友屍，負往葬地。沿途鳥雀皆問『你裹的是什麼？』蝶皆答『你不會想知道的東西』；最後遇上大鷹，厲聲喝問，一撲奪包，登樹一口把死鼠吞了。蝶含憤奔告其兄；兄弟二人攜彈弓而至，一石擊斃惡鷹，為亡友雪恥，然後歸家。

sensitivity.note: Colonial-era collection (Ker 1910); Wamira heritage.

passages.text: In the times of which I tell thee, it so befell that the Mouse and the Butterfly made a canoe. They hollowed it out with their stone axes, and fastened a great outrigger to it. Then they launched it, and set out for the islands, that they might there seek for food. But alas! not far had they gone when the canoe came apart, and the two on board were struggling in the water. The fur on the back and sides of the Mouse was sorely bedraggled, and the Butterfly's wings were heavy with water. Yet were they not faint at heart, and after a time they reached the shore. There they bethought them where they might seek food, for what they had brought was now at the bottom of the sea. 'Let us eat sugarcane,' said the Mouse. 'Nay,' answered the Butterfly sharply. 'Bananas are best, and we must search for them.' 'That will I never do,' said the Mouse. 'I go now to the sugarcane patch, and will eat my fill there.' And thus did he.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ker, Papuan Fairy Tales, 'The Mouse and the Butterfly' (1910); not verbatim.

passages.text: The Butterfly, left alone, searched until he found bananas which were ripe, and ate. But while he ate, he heard a cry from afar, 'Kaidara kiki!' 'Surely that is the voice of my friend,' said he in his heart, and, tarrying not, he left his meal to seek for the Mouse, whose voice had called him. Now this is what had befallen the Mouse. He had found a large patch of sugarcane, and had begun to bite the tough stalks and to suck out the sweet juice. So was his heart gladdened, but at last he bit through a stalk of heavy cane, which fell on him and crushed him. It was his death-cry his friend had heard. The Butterfly found the Mouse lying dead on the ground, and could now only make him ready for burial. This he did by plucking a taro leaf, and wrapping his friend in it. Then he set forth for the burial ground, bearing the Mouse.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ker, Papuan Fairy Tales, 'The Mouse and the Butterfly' (1910); not verbatim.

passages.text: He soon reached the gardens where the birds grew their food. Some small Finches were turning over the ground, and looked up as the Butterfly drew near. 'What hast thou there?' said they. 'Nought for which ye would care,' said the Butterfly, and he passed on. But he had not gone far ere he reached the place where the Wagtails were digging. Then did they ask the same question, and the Butterfly gave the same answer, and went on. Then he passed through the Cockatoos' plantation, and after that the Hornbills', and was asked and answered in the same manner. In this time the Butterfly was weary, and hoped that he would meet no one else. But he was still some distance from the burying ground when he met a great Hawk. Then said the Hawk in a harsh voice, 'What hast thou wrapped up there?' 'Nought for which thou wouldst care, my lord,' said the Butterfly, and his voice was small with fear. 'Nay, but I will judge of that,' said the Hawk, and he swooped down upon the bundle which the Butterfly carried.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ker, Papuan Fairy Tales, 'The Mouse and the Butterfly' (1910); not verbatim.

passages.text: But the Butterfly did not tarry to see what would befall. He made haste to find his brother, who was older and stronger than he. And when he had found him he cried, 'Bring thy sling with thee, brother,' and together the two Butterflies sped to where the Hawk was still sitting on the bough of the tree. The Butterfly's brother waited not. He placed a stone in his sling, and whirling it round his head let fly at the Hawk. The great bird fell to the ground, and was dead. Then the two Butterflies, having avenged the dishonour done to the dead body of the Mouse, returned home.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ker, Papuan Fairy Tales, 'The Mouse and the Butterfly' (1910); not verbatim.

title.en: Tauribolena, the Man Who Could Not Be Killed
title.zh: 殺不死之人陶里波雷納

region.en: Iriwavo island, British New Guinea (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 英屬新幾內亞伊里瓦沃島（象徵定位）

period: Oral tradition; recorded by Annie Ker, Papuan Fairy Tales, 1910

source.work: Annie Ker, Papuan Fairy Tales (London: Macmillan, 1910), 'The Man Who Could Not Be Killed'

summary.en: The scythes leaped aside from, the fire would not hold him, and when the great clam closed on his hand at the bottom of the sea his brothers-in-law went home glad — but at high tide the clam opened and cast his swollen body on the beach, where the birds' beaks could not pierce him till the tia flew from the moon and let the sea-water out. He rose singing his wife-tracking song — and it was the red-hot stone under the roasted kumika, thrown into his open mouth by his own wives, that at last rid the land of the man who could not be killed.
summary.zh: 妻兄們的鐮刀砍他不著，火圈燒他不死，海底大蚌鉗住他的手——漲潮之時蚌開，把他漲脹的屍身拋上沙灘；百鳥啄不透他的皮肉，唯最小的鳥 tia 自月亮高處俯衝而下，啄破皮膚放出海水，他竟一躍而起，唱著尋妻之歌『Kaipokina kivi! Kautauvaona kivi!』（不育者之足跡！哺乳者之足跡！）繼續作威作福。最後他的兩個妻子設計：烤熱的 kumika 果一枚枚拋進他張開的嘴，末了把燒紅的炙石也拋了進去。他吞下滾石，口冒黑煙，怒而取回斧石袋擲入海中，泅往遠方的伊里瓦沃島——從此人們再沒見過他。

sensitivity.note: Colonial-era collection (Ker 1910); Wamira heritage.

passages.text: In the old days a great chief named Tauribolena lived in the mountains with his two wives, Rekubole, an old woman, and Kauavira, who was still young. It came to pass that one day he told them that they were to go with him to the sea shore, and he set out carrying his child, and the two women walking behind, carrying heavy bags of food, which were slung from their heads. Tauribolena nursed the child so badly that it cried, and he needs must give it to his wives that they might stop its wailing. The women hated their husband for that he was cruel to the child, therefore they lay hid with it in the grass, and hoped that Tauribolena would not find them. But in a little he missed them, and turned back, singing as he walked — 'Kaipokina kivi! Kautauvaona kivi!' ('Footsteps of the barren woman! Footsteps of the nursing woman!') Then he found them, and forced them to go with him to the shore.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ker, Papuan Fairy Tales, 'The Man Who Could Not Be Killed' (1910); not verbatim.

passages.text: 'Rest in peace, sisters,' answered one of the men. 'We go on the morrow to the fields to mow the long grass, and Tauribolena shall not escape our scythes.' On the morrow, the brothers asked Tauribolena if he would go with them. He was willing, and soon the brothers were slashing with their wooden scythes, nigh to where Tauribolena stood. Swish! swish! went the scythes, but each time Tauribolena leaped aside, else would his legs have been broken. The mowers soon wearied of their fruitless task, and returned to the house, Tauribolena with them. Then they made another plan, which they determined to carry out in the morning. When the sun rose, the men said to their brother-in-law, 'We go a hunting; wilt thou come with us?' Then Tauribolena said that if they would lend him spears, he was fain to go with them. The brothers therefore took down a handful of spears from the dadabi, the rack over the fire, and gave them to Tauribolena. Then one took a burning coal and laid it in a piece of coconut husk, and, whistling to the dogs, they all set forth.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ker, Papuan Fairy Tales, 'The Man Who Could Not Be Killed' (1910); not verbatim.

passages.text: The way to the hunting ground was long, but it was reached at last. Then the three went each his way, and made ready to watch the long grass, which would ere long be burning, and out of which they hoped many beasts would rush. But the brothers had parted only to meet in secret, and they had soon kindled the grass in such a manner that Tauribolena was surrounded by a ring of leaping flames. The men watched to see their brother-in-law overcome by the clouds of rolling smoke, but on a sudden he made a great effort, and with one mighty leap cleared the barrier of flames and stood by their side. So that plan failed as had the other. On the morrow the sea was calm, and the men asked Tauribolena to go fishing with them. They all went on board a canoe, and paddled hither and thither, looking for clams under the clear water. At last they spied a big one, but it lay in deep water. Tauribolena's brothers-in-law asked him if he would dive for it, and he said that he would do so.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ker, Papuan Fairy Tales, 'The Man Who Could Not Be Killed' (1910); not verbatim.

passages.text: Now it came to pass that by and by the tide turned, and at high tide the great clam opened its shell and set free the body of Tauribolena, which floated to the surface, and was thrown upon the beach by the waves. There it lay, being swollen with the sea water he had drunk. Many people, as they passed, stopped to look, and said, 'Now he is indeed dead.' Then all the birds of the air came down and tried to peck at his flesh. First came the pigeon, then the black cockatoo, next a hawk, a crow, a bird of paradise, and many others. But they pecked in vain. Tauribolena's flesh was too tough for their beaks to pierce. At last came the turn of the tia, which is the smallest of birds. The tia flew high up in the air until it reached the moon. Then it rushed swiftly down, and with its little beak pecked at the body of Tauribolena until the sea water had all escaped.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ker, Papuan Fairy Tales, 'The Man Who Could Not Be Killed' (1910); not verbatim.

title.en: The Brush Turkeys of Mulawa
title.zh: 穆拉瓦的叢塚雉

region.en: Mulawa, British New Guinea (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 英屬新幾內亞穆拉瓦（象徵定位）

period: Oral tradition; recorded by Annie Ker, Papuan Fairy Tales, 1910

source.work: Annie Ker, Papuan Fairy Tales (London: Macmillan, 1910), 'The Brush Turkeys'

summary.en: Two children, jealous because their mother's parting charge was all for the dog, killed it, cooked it, and fled the village singing 'Aloulo! we are offended, we are going away.' The girl climbed a mountain and the boy rounded the cape — and each was turned into a brush turkey. Their wings were weak, and could not fly well; therefore the brush turkey heaps leaves and earth on the ground and lays its eggs there, as you may see for yourself among the trees of Mulawa.
summary.zh: 父母下園前只叮嚀孩子照顧愛犬，兄妹妒而生恨：哥哥把狗擊石殺死，與妹妹同煮而食，席捲檳榔，唱著『Aloulo! 我們受了委屈，我們要走了』逃離村莊。妹妹登上高山，哥哥繞過海角——二者皆化為叢塚雉。化鳥之後翅膀仍弱，不善飛翔；故叢塚雉至今不孵蛋於腹，只把落葉堆土成塚、產卵其中。此事你自己到穆拉瓦的樹林間一看便知。

sensitivity.note: Colonial-era collection (Ker 1910); Wamira heritage.

passages.text: In a certain village dwelt a man and his wife, whose children were two, a boy and a girl. The father and mother went to the gardens, and the children stayed at home. Before she went away, the mother said to the girl, 'Cook some food, and chew it till it is soft. Then feed the dog with it,' and she said to the boy, 'Take the dog down to the river and give it a bath.' Now the children were angry with their mother, because, when she was leaving, she seemed to be careful only for the dog, not caring for them. And so they were jealous. Therefore the little girl stayed in the house, and her brother took the dog down to the river, and dashed its head against a stone and killed it. Then he brought it back to the house, and the children cooked it in a big earthenware pot. When it was now nearly time for the father and mother to come home, the children thought it best to flee from the village ere they were found out.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ker, Papuan Fairy Tales, 'The Brush Turkeys' (1910); not verbatim.

passages.text: The little boy climbed a palm, on which grew his father's betel nuts, and he picked a great many of them. Then he came down and filled a leaf basket with them. He also put the dog which they had cooked in another basket, which he slung on his shoulder, and he took the basket of betel nuts and hung it on his little sister's head, so that it lay on her back. Then they left the village, and as they went they sang, 'Aloulo! a dudula, A nenae.' ('Aloulo! we are offended, We are going away.') Now when the father and mother came back they called to the children, but there was no voice to answer them. And they searched for long, but found them not, nor the dog, which the woman loved. And she was much grieved for that the dog was gone, yet after a time, she cared not for it, but mourned only for the children who returned not.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ker, Papuan Fairy Tales, 'The Brush Turkeys' (1910); not verbatim.

passages.text: Now when the children left the village they journeyed until they came to a mountain, and the girl climbed it, but the boy went on till he had rounded the cape. Then was each turned into a brush turkey. Now when they were thus changed, though they became birds, yet were their wings weak, nor could they fly well. Therefore it is so that when a brush turkey makes its nest, it heaps up leaves and earth on the ground, and lays its eggs there. And this mayest thou see for thyself, amongst the trees of Mulawa.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ker, Papuan Fairy Tales, 'The Brush Turkeys' (1910); not verbatim.

title.en: The Enchanted Pillow
title.zh: 魔枕

region.en: Potuma village, British New Guinea (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 英屬新幾內亞男子會所之村（象徵定位）

period: Oral tradition; recorded by Annie Ker, Papuan Fairy Tales, 1910

source.work: Annie Ker, Papuan Fairy Tales (London: Macmillan, 1910), 'The Enchanted Pillow'

summary.en: A fierce villager beat a visitor's little son out of the men's house, and the father went out silent — and returned when all were fishing, leaving a carved head-rest in the empty potuma. 'This is now my pillow,' claimed the violent man, and slept; and in the morning he was dead. A second claimant died likewise; a watcher saw the pillow fly through the air and kill a child that climbed in — and the village burned it, groaning 'A-ge-ge-ge-ge-ge! A-ke-ke-ke-ke-ke!' while the ashes flew over the hills to the mountain village of the man who had thus taken vengeance for the ill done to his little son.
summary.zh: 一名兇橫的村民把投宿會所的外山人的幼子毒打出門；父親一言不發，抱子而去。數日後趁全村捕魚，他悄然潛回空蕩的會所，留下一只雕花木枕。兇徒見枕，照例喝道『這枕頭從今歸我，誰要便來搶』，枕頸而眠——清晨眾人發現他已斃命。次夜第二人照樣認枕而眠，亦死。村人設伏，親眼看見那枕頭騰空而起，把一個爬進會所玩耍的孩子砸死，又落回原位。眾人堆薪縱火，把枕擲入火心；枕如活物般扭動，哀鳴『A-ge-ge-ge! A-ke-ke-ke!』直至化為灰燼。灰燼隨風越過樹林山丘，飄向山頂——那正是報了辱子之仇的山人所在。至今上得山去，莫在他村中過夜，否則你的枕頭也會要你的命。

sensitivity.note: Colonial-era collection (Ker 1910); Wamira heritage.

passages.text: In the old days there was a certain village in which three died to avenge a wrong done to a child. It came to pass that on a day a man from the hills came into the village leading his little son. And when it was night, he went into the potuma, where the men slept, to pass the night, and he took with him the child. Now in the potuma was a man of the village who was fierce and violent in all his ways. When, therefore, he saw the hill man about to sleep in the potuma, he arose and beat the little child, saying, 'What doest thou here, O child? Knowest thou not that this is a house for men? Begone!' Now the child's father saw and heard, but he said nothing. And he rose up and took his little son in his arms, and went out of the potuma. Then the fierce man was glad, and he said, 'So will I deal with all strangers,' and he lay down to sleep.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ker, Papuan Fairy Tales, 'The Enchanted Pillow' (1910); not verbatim.

passages.text: It came to pass not many days after that all the people of the village were fishing at the river, and none saw the hill man return and creep into the empty potuma. Now when he entered he had somewhat in his hand, but when he came forth his hands were empty. And he made haste back to the hills. At even the men of the village came back, and, after they had eaten, they went into the potuma and made ready to sleep, for they were weary after fishing. And it befell that the violent man saw before him a head-rest carved of wood, and he desired that it should be his. (But he knew not that it was the hill man who had placed it there.) Therefore, as was his custom, he laid hold of it, saying, 'This is now my pillow. If any wish for it let him take it from me if he can.' Then he lay down and rested his neck on the wooden pillow, and was soon asleep, for none of the men were willing to wrestle with him as he had said.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ker, Papuan Fairy Tales, 'The Enchanted Pillow' (1910); not verbatim.

passages.text: Now in the morning the men woke and one by one came forth from the potuma into the village. But the violent man came not forth, and the others marvelled for what cause he tarried so long, such not being his custom. Therefore, after a time, one of them made bold to go once more into the potuma and to draw near to the violent man to waken him. But he was not able to do so, though he shook him and called to him many times. Then, looking upon him, he saw that he was dead, and he called the others, and they saw it and were afraid, for they knew not why he had died so quietly, and they said, 'Who hath bewitched him?' Then he was buried, and his name was no more spoken amongst them for that he was dead. But on the next night, another man, seeing the pillow lying without one to claim it as his, took it for his own, and lay down to sleep. And on the morrow, he also was dead when the other men arose.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ker, Papuan Fairy Tales, 'The Enchanted Pillow' (1910); not verbatim.

passages.text: Then they bethought them of the pillow which had caused the death of three people, and they made ready to take vengeance. They brought faggots of wood, and lit a great fire. Then one who was strong and brave went into the potuma and brought out the pillow and cast it into the heart of the fire. The pillow writhed as though it were alive, and it groaned, 'A-ge-ge-ge-ge-ge! A-ke-ke-ke-ke-ke!' until it was burned to ashes. And the ashes flew on the wind over the trees and over the hills to a mountain village, where sat the man from the hills who had thus taken vengeance for the ill done to his little son. Now, if thou climbest the hills and comest to the village where dwells the hill man, sleep not in his village, else may thy pillow slay thee as it slew the three who died in the old days.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ker, Papuan Fairy Tales, 'The Enchanted Pillow' (1910); not verbatim.

title.en: The Unlucky Man: Betrayed at Sea, Slain in the Hills
title.zh: 薄命人：海上見棄、山中遇刺

region.en: Iriwavo to the hill country, British New Guinea (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 英屬新幾內亞伊里瓦沃至山地（象徵定位）

period: Oral tradition; recorded by Annie Ker, Papuan Fairy Tales, 1910

source.work: Annie Ker, Papuan Fairy Tales (London: Macmillan, 1910), 'The Unlucky Man'

summary.en: A wicked sister-in-law's lying tales made an elder brother drop his boar tusk overboard and abandon the younger in the deep — 'There is thy canoe, brother' — flinging in a bunch of sprouting coconuts. The castaway drifted eating gelaruru, commanding the east wind 'biraigu' and courting the north, till the coconut roots had twined round his legs; ashore in a strange land a maiden who had met him in dream found and healed him — till a jealous witch stabbed him in his sleep and fled, leaving the child lying in its dead father's blood.
summary.zh: 長兄娶妻後遠赴伊里瓦沃購野豬牙，把妻子交託幼弟照看；嫂子心毒，因弟不肯事事依她，便向丈夫進讒。長兄信讒，借出海尋飛魚卵之機，佯裝失手把豬牙丟入海中，喝令弟弟潛水打撈，隨即劃舟遠遁；弟弟呼救，他答『你這樣的人，休想再上船』，拋下一串已發芽的椰子：『這就是你的舟了。』弟弟抱椰漂流多日，以飛魚卵為食，向東風喊『biraigu（止步）』，向北風求渡；椰根纏腿、椰葉纏髮，終被吹至異鄉海灘。夢中見過他的少女尋至，治其瘡、解其髮，招他為夫；卻有嫉妒的巫女趁他熟睡以利刃刺死他，遠逃無蹤——妻子歸來時，只見丈夫與幼兒臥於血泊。

sensitivity.note: Colonial-era collection (Ker 1910); Wamira heritage.

passages.text: There were once two brothers, and they lived in peace until a woman caused strife between them. The elder brother married a wife, and soon after set out for the island of Iriwavo to buy a boar's tusk to hang round his neck, for so would he show that he was a chief. Now when he went he left his younger brother to care for his wife. But she was a wicked woman, and because her brother-in-law would not give her everything she wanted, she made a plan that she might punish him. Therefore when her husband came home she took him apart and told him lying tales of his brother, and the man, being her husband, believed her. It came to pass that on the morrow the elder brother bade the younger go with him to look for gelaruru, which is the spawn of the flying fish. And they set out together in a canoe. When they were far out to sea the elder man dropped his boar tusk overboard, as though by accident, and he cried to his brother, 'Look, the boar tusk has fallen into the sea. Dive quickly for it, before it is gone.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ker, Papuan Fairy Tales, 'The Unlucky Man' (1910); not verbatim.

passages.text: Then the younger brother dived overboard to look for the tusk. But when he came up to breathe the canoe was already far away. Then he called, 'Come back, brother, and let me get on board.' But his brother answered, 'Thou shalt never come on board, for that thy deeds were evil while I was yet at Iriwavo.' 'Nay, brother,' cried the man in the water, 'is it then an evil deed to hinder thy wife from doing wrong?' Then was his brother yet more angry for that he had spoken thus of his wife. Therefore he flung in to the water a bunch of coconuts which were already sprouting, and said, 'There is thy canoe, brother, I will now return; stay thou here.' And he paddled swiftly homewards. Now when he reached the shore his wife said to him, 'Where is now thy brother?' He told her what he had done, and, moreover, what the other had said concerning her, and the woman was much afraid lest the truth should be known.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ker, Papuan Fairy Tales, 'The Unlucky Man' (1910); not verbatim.

passages.text: Now it came to pass that the younger brother, when he was left to die in the sea, rested his arms upon the coconuts which had floated to him, and thus he remained many days, eating the gelaruru which lay upon the face of the water. And when the east wind blew he cried, 'O Lauraibo, biraigu, biraigu,' so that it might no longer blow upon him. For when the east wind blew it drove him further from land. Then when the north wind came he cried, 'O Lauraibo, newaigu, newaigu,' for thus he prayed it to carry him to the shore. And the north wind blew, and after many days he reached a strange land, which he knew not. So long had he been in the water that the roots of the coconuts had twined round his legs, and their leaves were tangled in his hair. He was also feeble for want of food, and he laid himself down under a tree and slept. And as he slept he dreamed that a beautiful maiden was near him.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ker, Papuan Fairy Tales, 'The Unlucky Man' (1910); not verbatim.

passages.text: Then she took him to the hill village where she dwelt, and undid the coconut roots which were twined about him, and when he had bathed she laid healing leaves upon his skin, and anointed him with coconut oil, and removed the tangles from his hair. Then was he fair to look upon once more, and a girl, who was also a witch, beholding him, loved him, and she said to the beautiful maiden, 'It is I who should have married the stranger.' 'Nay, sister,' answered the beautiful girl, 'did I not find him upon the shore? It is for that cause that he is mine.' Then the witch went away, but hatred and jealousy still lived in her heart. But as for the man and his wife, they cared little for that, and for a time no ill came of it. When the sun rose far out to sea many moons after, a little son was born to them, and they loved him dearly.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ker, Papuan Fairy Tales, 'The Unlucky Man' (1910); not verbatim.

title.en: The Snake Child: How Taro Came to Bolanai
title.zh: 蛇子與芋之來歷

region.en: Bolanai, British New Guinea (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 英屬新幾內亞波拉奈（象徵定位）

period: Oral tradition; recorded by Annie Ker, Papuan Fairy Tales, 1910

source.work: Annie Ker, Papuan Fairy Tales (London: Macmillan, 1910), 'The Snake Child'

summary.en: A girl of Kulawa begged piece after piece of a smoked snake — tail, middle, and at last the head — and gave birth to a son in form like a snake. She fled him from island to island; at Bolanai she set sharp stakes and had the villagers cut him to pieces, boil and eat him — and an old woman, loath that the memory of so good a food should fade, planted a piece in her garden. It sprouted and grew high above the earth: the plant is TARO, chief of all food, and the people of Bolanai have it ever in their gardens in plenty and of great size.
summary.zh: 庫拉瓦村的獵人燻了一條蛇準備晚食；一女子討了一截又一截——尾、中段、直到最後把蛇頭也吃了。此後她產下一個蛇形的兒子，大駭，棄之渡海而逃。蛇子冒雨雷泅水追母；她再逃至波拉奈，令村人削尖木樁、守株待蛇，入村即剁。村人把蛇屍剁碎、煮而食之，讚不絕口。一老嫗惜此美味失傳，討得一塊種入園中；數日後竟發芽抽莖，長得高出土面——眾人折枝分種，根塊甘美異常。此物便是芋，百食之長；波拉奈人的園圃至今芋頭繁茂碩大。

sensitivity.note: Colonial-era collection (Ker 1910); Wamira heritage.

passages.text: In the old days, it befell that the men of Kulawa, who were out hunting, found a snake and killed it. When they returned home they smoked it, and would have eaten it at their evening meal. But a girl who was near said, 'Ye are about to eat of the snake. Will ye not give me a little that I may taste it?' Then they, willing to please her, gave her the tail, and she ate it. And so much did she love the taste of its flesh that she said again, 'I pray you, give me a little of the snake that I may eat.' So they gave her the middle, and she ate it all. Again she asked for more, and they gave it to her, and again, until the head was all that was left. Then she prayed that they would give her the head also, and they gave it to her, and she ate it and went away.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ker, Papuan Fairy Tales, 'The Snake Child' (1910); not verbatim.

passages.text: Now it came to pass that after a time the woman gave birth to a son, in form like to a snake, and she feared him greatly. Therefore she left him and crossed the sea to the great island, Iriwavo. Much rain fell, and the voice of the thunder was loud, nevertheless the snake swam after his mother that he might be with her. The people of Iriwavo seeing him draw near said, 'What is this which we see?' The woman looked also, and cried 'It is a snake.' Then she fled across the sea once more, and landed at Bolanai. Yet she knew that not here would she be safe from her son. Therefore she said to the men of Bolanai, 'Cut stakes many and sharp.' They did her bidding, and she said, 'Watch in this place and I will stay in the house. And presently a snake will come to this village. Spare him not, but cut it in pieces.' The men did as she said, and cut the snake into many pieces as soon as he entered the village.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ker, Papuan Fairy Tales, 'The Snake Child' (1910); not verbatim.

passages.text: Then they scraped the pieces and boiled them and gathered together that they might eat them. 'We have done well to obey the voice of the woman,' said they, 'for the eating is good indeed.' Then said an old woman to them, 'It were a pity for the memory of this good food to fade. Give me some to plant in my garden, that we may see if perchance it will live there.' So they gave the old woman some of the flesh, and she planted it in her garden. And it came to pass that after not many days it sprouted and grew high above the earth. Then came many people and broke off shoots from the strange plant which grew in the old woman's garden, and planted them in their own gardens, where the shoots grew and waxed strong. And many did eat of the roots, and found them good indeed, for the name of the plant is TARO, which is the chief of all food. Thus was it that taro came to us, and for this reason is it that the people of Bolanai have it ever in their gardens in plenty and of great size.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ker, Papuan Fairy Tales, 'The Snake Child' (1910); not verbatim.

title.en: The Ant and the Pheasant
title.zh: 螞蟻與野雞

region.en: Wamira district, British New Guinea (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 英屬新幾內亞瓦米拉地區（象徵定位）

period: Oral tradition; recorded by Annie Ker, Papuan Fairy Tales, 1910

source.work: Annie Ker, Papuan Fairy Tales (London: Macmillan, 1910), 'The Ant and the Pheasant'

summary.en: The Pheasant fled his watch and lied of mud on his wings; the Ant said nothing, but slew the next pig alone — and when the Pheasant lost the entrails to an eel, the Ant's mat held a dead hornbill he had killed with his own hands. All the birds gathered to avenge their cousin, and each in turn he slew from the tree-top where he gummed himself a leafy house — until the great raven plucked down the nest and swallowed him on the shore.
summary.zh: 螞蟻與野雞結伴捕豬。設網之時野雞臨陣退縮，飛上樹頂，任豬脫網而逃；回來卻把翅膀塗上爛泥謊稱搏鬥受挫。螞蟻不揭穿，互換位置後獨自網住殺死一豬。歸家後螞蟻命野雞去河邊洗豬內臟；野雞空手回來，謊稱被鰻搶走。屋中獨守的螞蟻早被門口咆哮的大犀鳥激怒，一躍而誅之，屍藏於蓆下。野雞見屍大驚，跑去召集百鳥復仇；螞蟻上樹結葉為巢，來一鳥殺一鳥，百鳥莫奈。最後一隻大鴉啄下掛巢的細枝，把螞蟻連巢叼至海邊一口吞下——犀鳥之仇方雪。

sensitivity.note: Colonial-era collection (Ker 1910); Wamira heritage.

passages.text: In the old days, so our fathers have told us, the Ant and the Pheasant were friends, and one day they made a plan to go hunting. So they took their pig-net and set out. When they had reached the proper place, they put up their net, and the Pheasant said he would watch while the Ant drove beasts towards it. It came to pass that after a time the Ant found a pig, and drove it into the net. Now when the Pheasant saw the wild pig rushing upon him he was much afraid, and flew up into a tree. Then was the pig glad, and he made his way out of the net with haste, for there was none to let him. Then came the Pheasant down from the tree, and laid mud upon his wings, and waited for his friend. In a little the Ant came and said, 'Where is the pig?' The Pheasant made answer, 'I caught the pig and held him, but he threw me down in the mud. Look now at my wings!' Now this Pheasant was very deceitful, for he had lied even to his friend.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ker, Papuan Fairy Tales, 'The Ant and the Pheasant' (1910); not verbatim.

passages.text: The Ant did not reproach him. He said, 'Come, let us try another place with our net, and thou shalt hunt the game whilst I watch.' They did so, and it came to pass that a pig ran into the net and was killed at once by the Ant. By and by the Pheasant came back and said, 'Where is our pig?' Then answered his friend the Ant, 'Thou wilt find it over yonder by the tree.' The Pheasant looked by the tree, and there in truth was a pig lying. Then the two friends bound it tightly to a pole, and carried it home upon their shoulders. When they came to the house they cut up the pig, and the Ant said to the Pheasant, 'Take the entrails of the pig to the river and wash them.' The Pheasant went to do what the Ant bade him, and the Ant stayed alone in the house.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ker, Papuan Fairy Tales, 'The Ant and the Pheasant' (1910); not verbatim.

passages.text: Now as he was thus alone, a great hornbill stood in the doorway and said, in a terrible voice, 'Ga-a-a-a-a!' Yet did the Ant not fear, but his heart grew hot within him for anger, and he leapt up and killed the hornbill, and hid him in a mat. Then the Pheasant returned, but bearing nought. 'Friend,' said the Ant, 'where are the entrails of the pig?' 'An eel snatched them from me,' answered the Pheasant. 'It matters not,' said the Ant gently. 'But, I pray thee, come hither, and bring my mat with thee, for I would fain sit upon it.' The Pheasant took up the mat, but straightway saw the dead hornbill, and he cried out, 'Friend, why hast thou killed my cousin? Didst thou not know that his kinsfolk are many, and that they will of a surety avenge his death?' But the Ant hardened his heart, and said, 'I fear not thee nor thy kinsfolk. Go now to them, I pray thee, and tell them what thou hast seen here.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ker, Papuan Fairy Tales, 'The Ant and the Pheasant' (1910); not verbatim.

passages.text: Then went the Pheasant, and told all the birds what the Ant had done. They gathered together in one place and took counsel what they should do. At last they determined to kill the Ant for that he had killed the hornbill. The Ant climbed into the top of a tree, and each bird which in turn tried to attack him he slew. Then he made for himself a house by gumming leaves together, and he sat therein, and his heart was glad for that he had conquered his enemies. But while he thus sat quietly inside the leaves, a great raven flew up, and with his sharp beak plucked off the little branch on which hung the Ant's nest. Then he carried the leaves to the shore, and swallowed the Ant, thus making an end of him. So did he perish, and so was the death of the hornbill avenged.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ker, Papuan Fairy Tales, 'The Ant and the Pheasant' (1910); not verbatim.

title.en: The Boar Slayer and the Raft of Bristles
title.zh: 誅野豬者與鬃筏傳信

region.en: Abandoned village and Iriwavo, British New Guinea (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 英屬新幾內亞棄村與伊里瓦沃（象徵定位）

period: Oral tradition; recorded by Annie Ker, Papuan Fairy Tales, 1910

source.work: Annie Ker, Papuan Fairy Tales (London: Macmillan, 1910), 'The Boar Slayer'

summary.en: Left behind when her people fled the man-eating boar, a woman dug a burrow and bore a son in the dark; he grew up and built platforms half a league long toward the den, hurling bundle after bundle of spears from each in turn. His mother's two great spears — Karaganigani and Karakatekate — ended it; and a raft of the boar's bristles, charged to land only where mourners stood, drew the fugitives home, where the lad became their chief.
summary.zh: 惡野豬日日噬人，村人棄地而逃，唯一名孕婦被遺落。她在地下掘穴藏身，夜間偷入荒園取食，產子撫養於黑暗之中。兒子長成，逼問母親，得知原委，誓言除害。他建造一路相距不遠的小平台，直達半里之遙，末座緊鄰豬穴；又縛好一束束長矛分置各台，另鑄兩桿大矛——卡拉加尼加尼與卡拉卡特卡特——交母親保管。他投矛挑釁，野豬追影而來；他逐台而跳、逐台擲矛，矛如落葉紛紛被抖落。最後母親遞上雙神矛：一矛入其脅，血涌不止，野豬仍進；第二矛全力貫入，巨獸倒地而亡。母子擊鼓而舞。他削下野豬鬃縛上小筏，吩咐鬃毛：『海浪與風會送你們到遠方；所到之處，若無服喪之人便莫靠岸；見有戴孝者方可登陸。』筏漂流至族人避居之地，只在服喪者手中停留。五位族人駕舟回探，見燻好的豬肉大駭；少年答『是我獨自誅之』。全村遂返故里，飽食豬肉，奉少年為酋長，由他賢明地統治。

sensitivity.note: Colonial-era collection (Ker 1910); Wamira heritage.

passages.text: In a certain land was a fierce boar, and the people of that land feared him greatly, for each day one or other of their number came not back to the village at even, and all knew that he had been seized and eaten by the boar, and each trembled lest on the morrow his turn should come to enter the evil den of the dread beast. Many plans they laid whereby to ensnare the boar, but they came to nought, and the old men, who were wise, counselled that all should flee to another land, where they might dwell in safety. And the people hearing this word knew that it was good, and gathered their goods upon canoes and set out secretly for a country whither the boar might not follow them. Now it came to pass that in their haste one woman was left behind. When she found that she was indeed alone, she wept for her companions, but, being not faint-hearted, she soon arose and dug a hole in the earth, where she might hide from the boar.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ker, Papuan Fairy Tales, 'The Boar Slayer' (1910); not verbatim.

passages.text: Sometimes the child would cry in anger or in pain, but ever his mother would silence him, saying, 'Hush, my son, or the boar will devour us.' And the child would forbear to cry, but wondered much what this boar might be whose wrath his mother feared. It fell upon a day that the lad said to his mother, 'Tell me, mother, why do we live in this hole in the earth, and why dost thou fear the light of the sun?' Then said his mother, 'It hath not always been so, my son. Thy grandparents and thine uncles and I lived many years in the light of the sun. But a cruel enemy arose and killed and ate many of our people, and I only was left. Therefore I hollowed out this place where we dwell, and it was here thou wast born.' The lad hearkened to his mother's words, and made answer, 'It is true, mother, that I could not protect thee while I was a child. But I am now a man, and I will deliver thee from thine enemy.' Whereupon he built a house, and began to make ready to fight with the boar.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ker, Papuan Fairy Tales, 'The Boar Slayer' (1910); not verbatim.

passages.text: His mother was sore afraid, and said, 'Son, the boar is very fierce. He will surely fall upon us and slay us.' 'We shall see,' said the lad. 'Cook me some food, that I may eat.' His mother did as he had bidden her, and set food before him and he ate, and set forth to fight with the boar. When he reached the platform nearest to the den he stood upon it and brake the fastening of the bundle of spears which lay there. Then he launched a dart into the den where the beast lurked. The monster rushed out on feeling the prick of the spear as it fell upon him, and the lad at the same moment cast the spears which were in his hand at the boar, who shook them off as though they had been but dead leaves. The lad turned to fly, and the boar followed, tracking him by the shadow which fell upon the ground beside the platform.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ker, Papuan Fairy Tales, 'The Boar Slayer' (1910); not verbatim.

passages.text: Joy filled the hearts of the woman and her son at the fall of their enemy, and they beat upon the drum and danced for gladness. Then the lad cut up the flesh of the boar, and smoked great portions of it. Moreover, he made a raft, and placed thereon bristles which he had plucked from the dead boar's back. And he said to the bristles, 'The waves and the wind will carry you to distant countries. Wheresoever ye see men who bear no marks of mourning ye must not land. But if mourners appear on that shore ye are to land. Go.' And he sent the raft forth, and fell to beating the drum once more. The little raft floated hither and thither as the wind blew upon it and as the waves drew it, and was carried nigh to a shore where children played. One among them spied the raft, and cried to his comrades that they should help him draw it to land; but as their hands were stretched out to lay hold of the raft, it floated backwards until it was out of their reach.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ker, Papuan Fairy Tales, 'The Boar Slayer' (1910); not verbatim.

title.en: The Man with the Open Throat
title.zh: 喉中有孔之叟

region.en: Wamira district, British New Guinea (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 英屬新幾內亞瓦米拉地區（象徵定位）

period: Oral tradition; recorded by Annie Ker, Papuan Fairy Tales, 1910

source.work: Annie Ker, Papuan Fairy Tales (London: Macmillan, 1910), 'The Man with the Open Throat'

summary.en: Two grandsons laughed at the old man whose food came out of a hole in his neck; he lured them to sea with lying promises of coconuts and cane, and marooned them on a desolate shore — 'I will return, but not until six days are past.' A witch who had dreamed of them nourished them, and on the sixth day commanded Sun to scorch and Rain to drown the returning grandfather, then stopped a stream with her pearl shell and loosed the water into his throat as he stooped to drink, choking him: hence the saying, 'Eat first and afterwards drink, else will thy liver be pierced by the water which shall be swallowed.'
summary.zh: 老叟喉上有孔，吃飯時食物從孔中漏出，兩個孫兒見狀忍不住發笑，他便懷恨在心。他謊稱舟上已備好椰子與甘蔗，誘二孫出海，把他們丟在無人荒灘：『六日後我回來接你們。』一個巫婆夢見兩個孩子在荒灘吸露兜果，尋至照拂。第六日她見老叟駕舟將至，便命烈日曝曬他、暴雨淋他，如此反覆；又用珠貝截斷溪流，待老人俯身就涓滴而飲之際猛然撤貝，激流灌喉，把他嗆死——兩個孩子得救。因他死狀如此，至今有一句諺語：『先吃後飲，否則水入喉穿肝。』

sensitivity.note: Colonial-era collection (Ker 1910); Wamira heritage.

passages.text: In the old days there lived in a certain village a man in whose neck was a hole, so that when he ate his food passed not down his throat, but came forth at the hole. Now it came to pass that his two grandsons saw him eating in this manner, and could not forbear to laugh. Therefore he resolved to punish them for mocking him. So with gentle voice he said to them, 'I am about to go a journey in my canoe, and if ye desire it ye shall also come.' Then said the elder, 'Truly we would fain go with thee. But let me first get a water bottle to put on board, for my little brother will perchance be thirsty while we are on the sea.' 'Nay, trouble not,' said their grandfather. 'It is already on board.' This he said to deceive them. 'Ah,' said the child, 'but I must get some young coconuts for us to drink.' 'I have already heaped young coconuts on the canoe,' lied the man. Then the child spake of fetching taro and sugarcane, but the man gave ever the same answer, and all being ready they went on board.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ker, Papuan Fairy Tales, 'The Man with the Open Throat' (1910); not verbatim.

passages.text: Now as they paddled the sun grew hot and the children weary. Therefore the elder said to his grandfather, 'We are athirst. Give us, I pray thee, a coconut that we may drink.' 'Why didst thou not bring thy coconut with thee?' said the man. 'There are here none for thee.' 'May we not have then a stick of sugarcane to suck?' said the child. 'Where is sugarcane for thee?' asked his grandfather. 'Thou shouldst have brought it with thee.' Once more spake the child. 'Grandfather, my little brother is very thirsty. Give us, I pray thee, the stopper of the water bottle that he may suck it and be refreshed.' 'Nay,' said the man fiercely. 'If ye want water ye should have brought it with you.' Then the children were silent, and paddled on once more. At last they came to a dreary place where no house was, and where food grew not. Then the man bade the children help him pull the canoe up on the beach, and they did so, and then ran to a pandanus tree which grew near and began sucking its fruit.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ker, Papuan Fairy Tales, 'The Man with the Open Throat' (1910); not verbatim.

passages.text: The children wept bitterly, for they were much afraid to be alone in this strange place where no people were. But being hungry, they climbed into the pandanus tree, and sucked many of the fruit which they found. Now it came to pass that while they were thus doing, an old woman who was a witch dreamed that she saw two children in a lonely place sucking pandanus fruit. Therefore she arose and journeyed until she came to the place of which she had dreamed. There indeed she found them, but they knowing her to be a witch, feared to come down. Then said she to them, 'What do ye in the pandanus?' They said, 'Our grandfather brought us to this desolate land and left us here, saying that he would return in six days.' The witch hearing their tale, pitied them and said, 'Come down now to me, and let us see what may be done.' 'Nay,' said they, 'for if we do thou mayest kill us.' 'I will not harm you,' said the witch.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ker, Papuan Fairy Tales, 'The Man with the Open Throat' (1910); not verbatim.

passages.text: Now it came to pass on the sixth day, that the witch saw he was drawing nigh, and she bade the Sun burn him with its rays. And the Sun shone forth, and the old man was burned and thirsty. Then said the witch to the Rain, 'Rain upon this man.' And the Rain rained until the man was like to be drowned. Then the witch bade that the Sun should scorch him once more, and again the Rain that it should rain upon him, and then once more the Sun, that it should burn the man. Now he was close to the land, and he was very thirsty. Therefore he hasted to a little stream hard by, and stooped to drink. But the witch with her pearl shell had stopped the water from flowing, and only a few drops trickled. Therefore the man stooped low to drink what little was there, and at that moment the witch took away her pearl shell, and the water rushed mightily forward and down the man's throat, and choked him. So were the children delivered from their enemy who had wrought them much ill.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ker, Papuan Fairy Tales, 'The Man with the Open Throat' (1910); not verbatim.

title.en: Borevui and Her Three Brothers
title.zh: 波雷維伊與三兄弟

region.en: Mountain country, British New Guinea (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 英屬新幾內亞山地（象徵定位）

period: Oral tradition; recorded by Annie Ker, Papuan Fairy Tales, 1910

source.work: Annie Ker, Papuan Fairy Tales (London: Macmillan, 1910), 'Borevui and Her Three Brothers'

summary.en: On their mother's grave grew the red-leaved bush Borevui — their little sister, though they knew it not. She stepped down each day to cook for them, till the youngest caught her; when the brothers claimed her for a wife she told them she was their sister. Then a mountain man carried her off and killed each brother in turn as he came seeking — but Borevui saved each liver in a bowl of water, and at the last blew on the water until the three stood before her alive; her husband ate pig-food that night and was slain by the brothers he had cooked.
summary.zh: 母親墳上長出一株紅葉灌木——波雷維伊，實是化生的妹妹，兄長們卻不知。她日日下墳化身少女，為哥哥們備好飯食再化回灌木。最幼的弟弟藏於蔗堆後捉住她，兄長們爭相要以她為妻；她答：『我是你們的妹妹，願日日照料你們、為你們煮飯。』後來一個山人把她搶走成婚；三位哥哥先後尋妹而至，皆被妹夫殺死烹食。波雷維伊不哭不怨，只討得每人的肝，浸在椰殼水碗中。末了丈夫命她入山墾園，她攜重袋先行，回家吹拂那碗靜水——三兄弟漸漸成形，活生生站在她面前。她以熱飯款待兄弟，卻給丈夫備下豬食；他入門見豬食大怒欲毆，三兄弟聞聲而起，把這食人者剁碎燒屋。兄妹遂返故里，永世安泰。

sensitivity.note: Colonial-era collection (Ker 1910); Wamira heritage.

passages.text: There was once a woman who had three sons but no daughters. After a time she died and was buried, and her sons mourned for her. And it came to pass that one day a little red-leaved plant sprung up on the woman's grave, and became a beautiful bush, called Borevui. The red leaves waved in the wind, and the lads saw that they were fair, but they knew not that it was their little sister who was there. One day they went hunting game, which was to be eaten at the death feast in honour of their mother. While they were all away Borevui stepped down from the grave and became a girl. Then she entered her brothers' house, and cooked some food for them. After she had done this, she ran back to the grave and became Borevui once more. Now the three lads were hungry when they came from their long day's hunting, and they found a big pot of food waiting for them. They turned to their old grandmother, who sat in the corner, and said, 'Grandmother, who cooked our food?' 'Who knows?' said the old woman.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ker, Papuan Fairy Tales, 'Borevui and Her Three Brothers' (1910); not verbatim.

passages.text: When it was morning, the two elder brothers hid the youngest in a stack of sugar-cane, which they leaned against the wall. Then they left him, and it came to pass that the little sister came once more into the house to cook for her brothers. The youngest brother watched while she took a piece of taro and peeled it with a sharp pearl shell. Then he came quickly from his hiding-place, and laid hold of the girl. He saw how fair she was, and said, 'Aio, be my wife!' But the girl made answer, 'I cannot be thy wife, for I am thy sister.' Then the two brothers came home and saw the beautiful girl, and they said, 'She is to be my wife,' 'She is to be my wife.' But the girl told them that she was their sister, and would take care of them all and cook their food day by day.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ker, Papuan Fairy Tales, 'Borevui and Her Three Brothers' (1910); not verbatim.

passages.text: On the morrow the brothers went out hunting, as was their custom, and Borevui went to the spring to fill her coconut water bottles. Now as she was leaning over the spring, a man who was hiding there leapt out, picked her up in his arms, and carried her off to his home far in the mountains. After a time, when the brothers had waited in vain for Borevui to return, the eldest said that he would go and look for her. After searching for long, he found her at last, and was greeted by his sister and her husband. 'Go to the gardens,' said the man to Borevui, 'and bring food home and cook it, that our brother may eat.' The girl did as he bade her, and returned with some food, but, alas! she found that her brother had been killed by her husband, and that his flesh was to be eaten. But she did not cry out or reproach her husband.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ker, Papuan Fairy Tales, 'Borevui and Her Three Brothers' (1910); not verbatim.

passages.text: The youngest brother, who was now at home alone with their grandmother, said, 'I must needs go to see why my brothers have not yet returned.' And he set out. But the same fate overtook him, and ere long his flesh was cooking over the fire. And Borevui could do nought but save the lad's liver, which she placed in the bowl of water where the others already lay. Then her husband bade her follow him to their mountain garden. There they toiled for long, and Borevui cut down a tree which was in the road, and helped her husband clear the ground for a great distance. At last he said, 'Go home now, when thou shalt have dug up some food, and cook it. I will follow thee.' Borevui obeyed and went home, carrying the heavy bag of food slung from her head. She cooked a great pot full, and then went to the bowl of water where lay the livers of her three brothers.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ker, Papuan Fairy Tales, 'Borevui and Her Three Brothers' (1910); not verbatim.

title.en: The Mud People and the House of Rei
title.zh: 泥屋與茅屋

region.en: Lake of Apogi, mountains, British New Guinea (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 英屬新幾內亞山區阿波吉湖（象徵定位）

period: Oral tradition; recorded by Annie Ker, Papuan Fairy Tales, 1910

source.work: Annie Ker, Papuan Fairy Tales (London: Macmillan, 1910), 'The Mud People'

summary.en: In the old days men dwelt in caves and holes, till two men agreed to build shelters on the face of the earth. One wove the long grass rei thickly over a frame of sticks; the other plastered mud over his. The mud-builder decried the rei — 'will not the sharp rei enter thine eye and blind thee?' — then besought the lake spirit Apogi for rain, which crumbled his own walls; and beaten upon the closed doorway he was answered with his own words, till the rain-builder's wife won shelter for the children. From that day mud is contemned and houses are built of rei.
summary.zh: 太古人穴居野處。有二人相約造屋：一個用長茅草『雷』密密編在木架上，滴水不漏；另一個只用泥漿糊在立木之上。泥屋主人先貶低茅屋：『茅草鋒利，怕不戳瞎你的眼？扎破你孩子的皮？』隨後他上阿波吉湖邊念咒求雨，大雨果然傾落——他的泥牆自己先塌了。一家人哭著奔向茅屋求收留，茅屋主人卻把他自己的話原樣擲回：『茅草鋒利，怕不戳瞎你的眼？』泥屋主人啞口無言；茅屋主人之妻心軟求情，才開門收留。雨過之後，泥屋主人羞愧難當，疾起仿建茅屋——自那日起泥屋為人所鄙，家家皆以茅草造屋，直到如今。

sensitivity.note: Colonial-era collection (Ker 1910); Wamira heritage.

passages.text: In the old days men lived not in houses, but dwelt in caves and holes in the ground, for none knew how they might fashion a shelter which would keep out rain and sun. Now it came to pass that two men talking idly together agreed to attempt to build some shelter on the face of the earth where their families might dwell safe from sun and rain, and nevertheless live in the light of day and not in the dark earth as heretofore. They therefore arose and each went his way, neither did either see the face of other until the work was accomplished. Then came one and said to his fellow, 'Come, let us go now and I will show thee the house I have fashioned.' And they went both together until they came to where the man had built his house, and behold, it was a fair sight indeed. For the man had taken of the long grass which is called rei, and had woven it thickly upon a frame of sticks, so that no ray of sun nor drop of rain might pierce the roof or walls of his house.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ker, Papuan Fairy Tales, 'The Mud People' (1910); not verbatim.

passages.text: But the other looking upon it saw that it was better than his own, and set about to decry it, that it might be worthless in the eyes of him who had built it. 'This then is thy shelter, brother,' quoth he. 'It were better for thee and thine to dwell therein than for me and mine. For I should fear greatly lest perchance the sharp rei should enter my eye, and so blind me. Moreover, it must needs be that it will prick thy skin and cause a rash to rise upon it. But come now,' he said, turning away, 'and I will show thee mine.' So they went together to see the other house.
