passages.text: As the shades of night close o'er them, to their hammocks all repair; little reck they that before them stand grim death and dark despair. From the grove come, mockingly, cries of 'Waters cover me!' They respond: 'O friend, we hear them!' laugh, and turn to slumber on — till the rush of waters near them terrifies the stoutest one. And these words, in solemn tone, issue from the outraged stone: 'Lo! the swelling floods before you; see their waters cover me! Soon they will be closing o'er you; I no more your help can be.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Brett 1880, 'The Rock and the Wood' (with its footnote); not verbatim.

passages.text: Yet had you but faithful been, death no man would e'er have seen!' Swell the mighty floods, prevailing — yet to three or four is given safety till the floods subside, for a komoo palm (by heaven made to grow) surmounts the tide: all whom that tree does not save sink, as rocks, beneath the wave. There is an episode, usually given here, of a cocorite palm whose top reached the heavens: a poor woman, not in a condition to climb, led the way, and halfway up was turned into stone by terror and exhaustion; none could help her, and all who tried to pass over her became rocks likewise.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Brett 1880, 'The Rock and the Wood' (with its footnote); not verbatim.

narrative.en: The Carib cycle of Tamosi Kabo-tano — 'the Ancient One of Heaven', the Supreme Being — reaches its crisis in the legend of the Rock and the Wood. Under the roots of the wonderful tree from which all cultivated plants first came, some saw a sacred grotto, and in it the Water-Mother bathing in her loved abode; that it was her form none other, the swelling waters soon showed, for a gushing flood burst out that would have swept all mankind away — had not a rugged rock, by what power none can know, closed the fountain. The people drew near to their saviour, and the rock gave forth oracles: 'Though I from the waters save you, there may come a day when yourselves, your sons and daughters, in a flood will pass away. Listen, then, mankind, to me, that your years like mine may be. In yon wood are spirits dwelling, who will tempt you day by day. If you dread the waters swelling, answer not, whate'er they say! You are safe while you obey, heeding well your rock-stone grey. And if age bring evils on you — wrinkled skin and whitening hair — you at will may cast them from you, youth renewing, bright and fair, as the serpent glideth clear from the slough he scorns to wear.' Thus the rock offered both the covenant of safety and the serpent's gift of skin-renewal, the Guianese form of earthly immortality. Time passed; men grew careless, and their hearts, long hesitating, obeyed the voices from the wood. From the grove came Yarrekaru, the monkey, sent by man's malignant foes; none prevented him while, alone, he undermined their guardian stone. From the grove came mockingly the cries of 'Waters cover me!' — the people answered 'O friend, we hear them!', laughed, and turned to slumber on, until the rush of waters near them terrified the stoutest. The outraged stone spoke in solemn tone: 'Lo! the swelling floods before you; I no more your help can be. Yet had you but faithful been, death no man would e'er have seen!' The floods prevailed, and death returned to the world with them. Only three or four survived on a komoo palm that heaven made to grow above the tide; all the rest sank like rocks beneath the wave — for in the usual episode of the cycle, those who strove to climb the cocorite palm, whose top reached the heavens, found the way blocked by a poor woman turned to stone by terror and exhaustion halfway up, and every climber who tried to pass over her became rock likewise. The tale is told by the Rev. W. H. Brett in metrical form from Carib informants of British Guiana, and its imagery — the guardian stone, the tempting wood, the tree whose crown reaches the sky, the serpent's skin — binds the Guianese flood cycle to the wider American pattern of the broken covenant and the second creation.

functions: Flood-and-covenant myth: the guardian rock's oracle establishes the pact of obedience whose breach restores death to the world
Explains standing rocks and stones as the petrified dead of the deluge, and names the komoo palm as the ark of the Carib remnant
Locates the serpent-skin renewal — sloughing as youth-renewal — in the same moral field as the covenant, joining origin-of-death to origin-of-taboo
Legitimises the siesta of fear: the voices from the wood are real, and the tale teaches silence in their season

title.en: Amalivaca Carves the Rocks and Tames the Rivers (Brett Version)
title.zh: 阿馬利瓦卡刻石馴河（布雷特版）

region.en: Orinoco headwaters and cataracts
region.zh: 奧里諾科上游與灘區

period: Tamanac-Carib tradition recorded by Humboldt; versified 1880 (Brett)

source.work: W. H. Brett, Legends and Myths of the Aboriginal Indians of British Guiana (1880), Part III 'Legends of the Caribs', 'Legend of Amalivaca'

summary.en: While the deluge was subsiding from some land of unknown name, over the mighty waters gliding, great Amalivaca came, sailing on where now are seen widespread plains and forests green. Doubtless sent our race to raise, helping men in many ways. In the sculptures so high on the rocks his work you see: waters at that height were flowing, so he carved them easily, carved them from his great canoe, taught mankind to carve them too — each device and time-worn figure had, of old, its well-known lore, voiceless all, they spake with vigour to the eye in days of yore; but our wisest all allow none can read their lessons now. When the mighty floods were failing and the land again was seen, wildly rugged all the ground then Amalivaca found; but his brother gave assistance, and by that good brother's aid, overcoming all resistance, smooth and gentle slopes he made. Men asked him for canoes and streams: 'But when we pass the tidal power, going up no help is found. Now exert thy wondrous skill — strive to remedy this ill.' Then he spent much toil and trouble on great Orinoco's flood, and strove to make its current double: one side up, the other down. Orinoco answered 'No!' Then he strove the tides of ocean to the upper stream to bring; but the river said: 'You seek a fatal thing: if the tide should higher go, all will be submerged below!' This Amalivaca learned; and from fruitless labour turned — and from that time nevermore comes he to this Western shore. Humboldt considers those rock-carvings to be traces of an ancient civilisation.
summary.zh: 洪水將退，阿馬利瓦卡自異邦乘巨舟而來，行於今之平原綠林之上。蓋為興我族、濟眾生而至。高崖之刻畫，即其手澤——其時水至彼處，故自舟中刻之甚易；且教人亦刻。古之圖形各有其義，今之智者亦莫能讀矣。水退地見，丘壑叢雜；其弟助之，平為緩坡。人求通舟之川；告以潮之難；彼欲使奧里諾科上下同流——河曰『否』！又欲引海潮上溯——河曰：『此取死之道：潮高則下皆沒矣！』阿馬利瓦卡乃知水非其造者莫能改，遂罷。臨去，眾揮淚送舟；自此不復西來。洪堡謂崖刻乃古文明之遺跡云。

Ocean waves he had crossed over, sailing in his large canoe; from that other side a rover, seeking lands and people new: doubtless sent our race to raise, helping men in many ways.

Waters at that height were flowing, so he carved them easily — carved them from his great canoe, taught mankind to carve them too. Each device and time-worn figure had, of old, its well-known lore: voiceless all, they spake with vigour to the eye in days of yore; but our wisest all allow none can read their lessons now. When the mighty floods were failing and the land again was seen, wildly rugged all the ground then Amalivaca found; but his brother gave assistance, and by that good brother's aid, overcoming all resistance, smooth and gentle slopes he made.

passages.text: 'But when a canoe is bearing, heavy burdens light become' — the men said: 'When we pass the tidal power, going up no help is found; heavy is the work each hour. Now exert thy wondrous skill — strive to remedy this ill.' Then he spent much toil and trouble on great Orinoco's flood, and strove to make its current double: one side up, the other down. Orinoco answered: 'No!' Then he strove the tides of ocean to the upper stream to bring; but the river, with emotion, said: 'You seek a fatal thing: if the tide should higher go, all will be submerged below!' This Amalivaca learned; and from fruitless labour turned — and from that time nevermore comes he to this Western shore. When the black-robed teachers found us, we inquired if they had seen him who left such marks around us — and we grieved when all said 'No!'

title.en: Manarowa and the Falls: the Carib Chief and the Amphibious Race
title.zh: 馬納羅瓦與瀑：加勒比酋長與兩棲之族

region.en: Essequibo Falls (Mandrowa fall), Guyana
region.zh: 蓋亞那埃斯塞基博瀑（曼德羅瓦瀑）

period: Carib historical legend of the 18th-19th c.; recorded 1880 (Brett)

source.work: W. H. Brett, Legends and Myths of the Aboriginal Indians of British Guiana (1880), Part III 'Legends of the Caribs', 'Legend of Manarowa'

summary.en: Sweet is his Essequibo home; yet still Manarowa will roam to gain more power and fame: from Orinoco to Corentyne fighting and plundering he has been — the Indians round him own his sway, and slaves, as tribute, to him pay: all, save the Taruma. They on that stream above are found; but he, to reach them, must go round, ascending the Rewa — for the great Essequibo Falls, never yet passed, like mighty walls, confront Manarowa. 'Those Tarumas we must invade, and take them by surprise: o'er those grim cataracts we will haul our light canoes, and on them fall, as coming from the skies!' He scaled one wat'ry wall where a small island in the fall gave precarious footing; then, no footing to be found, 'We now must clear a pathway through the forest here, and drag our vessels round.' Thus they, still toiling day by day, o'er falls and rapids worked their way — and the rocks are high, the Caribs nigh, no power is theirs to fight or fly: the Tarumas hid themselves and woodskins in caverns deep beneath the tide, and thus eluded the chase. 'Have we thus far come through such perils to make war on an amphibious race?' The tale had to a legend grown, of that amphibious race eluding him who ventured o'er a path no mortal man before, or after, dared to trace — for near one hundred years, until a white explorer, Mr. C. B. Brown in 1870, crossed o'er every dangerous fall, giving that highest, worst of all its name — Mandrowa. And when Great Britain put down the slave-trade his business was gone: small-pox and rum consumed his clan; he saw them dying man by man, grieved, and his spirit fled.
summary.zh: 馬納羅瓦之埃斯塞基博家園固美，然彼猶四出以求權名：自奧里諾科至科倫丁，戰而掠之；四周部落皆臣，貢以奴隸——惟塔魯馬不臣。欲達之，必遡雷瓦河而上——蓋埃斯塞基博大瀑未嘗有人過者，如牆當道。酋曰：『當突襲塔魯馬：曳輕舟過惡灘，自天而降！』攀一瀑而藉小嶼立足；再遇無立足者，遂曰：『當闢林徑，曳舟繞行。』日日力作，越灘而行——然兩棲之族匿其身與皮舟於潮下深穴，蹤跡遂失。酋歎曰：『歷此萬險，乃與兩棲之族戰乎？』此事百年成為傳說——至1870年白人探險家布朗越諸瀑，名最高最險者為曼德羅瓦瀑。英國禁奴販，其業遂盡；天花與朗姆滅其族——目睹族人相繼死，憂憤而亡。

sensitivity.note: Carib historical legend recorded by the missionary Brett 1880; a colonial-era chief narrative, read critically.

passages.text: Sweet is his Essequibo home; yet still Manarowa will roam to gain more power and fame. Though, from that river's sources south to Dutch plantations near its mouth, the tribes all fear his name: from Orinoque to Corentyne, fighting and plundering he has been — the bold Manarowa! The Indians round him own his sway, and slaves, as tribute, to him pay: all, save the Taruma. They on that stream above are found; but he, to reach them, must go round, ascending the Rewa — for the great Essequibo Falls, never yet passed, like mighty walls, confront Manarowa.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Brett 1880, 'Legend of Manarowa'; not verbatim.

passages.text: The chief has pondered long, and said: 'Those Tarumas we must invade, and take them by surprise. O'er those grim cataracts we will haul our light canoes, and on them fall, as coming from the skies!' Now he has scaled one watery wall, where a small island in the fall precarious footing gave. With toil they hoist and carry o'er their craft. With that great fall they scarce have done, ere they come to a greater one: no footing there is found. 'We now must clear a pathway through the forest here, and drag our vessels round.' Thus they, still toiling day by day, o'er falls and rapids work their way with labour most severe.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Brett 1880, 'Legend of Manarowa'; not verbatim.

passages.text: The rocks are high, the Caribs nigh, no power is theirs to fight or fly: the Tarumas themselves and woodskins now hide in caverns deep beneath the tide, and thus elude our chase! 'Have we thus far come through such perils to make war on an amphibious race?' To all on Essequibo known, the tale had to a legend grown, of that amphibious race eluding him who ventured o'er a path no mortal man before, or after, dared to trace — for near one hundred years, until a white explorer crosses, o'er every dangerous fall, giving that highest, worst of all its name — Mandrowa. And when Great Britain put down the slave-trade, his business was gone: small-pox and rum consumed his clan; he saw them dying, man by man; grieved, and his spirit fled!
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Brett 1880, 'Legend of Manarowa'; not verbatim.

title.en: Sixteen Years Behind the Golden Doors: Tupac Inca Presented to the Sun
title.zh: 金門後十六年:圖帕克·印加獻於太陽之前

region.en: House of the Sun, Cuzco (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 庫斯科太陽之屋(象徵性標記)

period: Inca tradition as given to Sarmiento de Gamboa, 1572; trans. Markham 1907

source.work: Pedro Sarmiento de Gamboa, History of the Incas, ch. 42, trans. Sir Clements Markham, Hakluyt Society, 1907

summary.en: He then said that he named his son Tupac Inca, and ordered him to come forth from the house. He had been there for 15 or 16 years to be brought up, without any one seeing him except very rarely and as a great favour. He was now shown to the people, and the Inca presently ordered a fringe of gold to be placed in the hand of the image of the Sun. After Tupac Inca had made his obeisance to his father, they went before the image of the Sun, made their sacrifices and offered capa cocha to that deity; then they offered the new Inca Tupac Yupanqui, beseeching the Sun to protect and foster him, and to make him so that all should hold and judge him to be a child of the Sun and father of his people. The priests took the fringe from the hands of the image, which they call mascapaycha, and placed it over the head of Tupac Inca Yupanqui until it rested on his forehead. He was declared Inca Ccapac and seated in front of the Sun on a seat of gold, garnished with emeralds. Seated there, they clothed him in the ccapac uncu, placed the suntur paucar in his hand, and the priests raised him on their shoulders. His brother Amaru Tupac Inca, the eldest legitimate son who had been named successor years before, came to see him: when Amaru saw him in such majesty of wealth and surroundings he fell on his face to the earth, adoring, offering sacrifices and obedience; on learning that it was his brother, Tupac Inca raised him and saluted him in the face.
summary.zh: 印加王宣布立子圖帕克·印加為儲,命他出屋。此子在屋中養育十五六年,除極少數特許之外,無人得見。此時他方被引見於民;印加王命人將金王纓置於太陽神像手中。圖帕克·印加向父王行禮後,眾人先向太陽神像獻祭,並行卡帕-科查人祭;再獻上新印加圖帕克·尤潘琪,祈求太陽護佑他,使萬民奉他為太陽之子、民眾之父。祭司從神像手中取下王纓——即「瑪斯卡帕恰」——戴於圖帕克·印加·尤潘琪頭上,直至額前。他被宣布為「卡帕克·印加」,坐於太陽像前鑲祖母綠的金座之上;眾人為他披上卡帕克上衣,把孫圖爾-保卡爾放入他手中,祭司們將他扛上肩頭。此前曾被立為儲的嫡長子阿瑪魯·圖帕克·印加前來相見;阿瑪魯見兄弟富貴威儀如此,當即伏地叩拜,獻祭稱臣;得知確是自己的兄弟,圖帕克·印加扶他起來,與他貼面相慶。

sensitivity.note: The secluded heir revealed; the mascapaycha taken from the image's own hands as in Pachacuti's coronation.

passages.text: He then said that he named his son Tupac Inca, and ordered him to come forth from the house. He had been there for 15 or 16 years to be brought up, without any one seeing him except very rarely and as a great favour. He was now shown to the people, and the Inca presently ordered a fringe of gold to be placed in the hand of the image of the Sun... Then they offered the new Inca Tupac Yupanqui, beseeching the Sun to protect and foster him, and to make him so that all should hold and judge him to be a child of the Sun and father of his people.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Sarmiento, History of the Incas, ch. 42 (Markham 1907); not verbatim.

passages.text: The priests took the fringe from the hands of the image, which they call mascapaycha, and placed it over the head of Tupac Inca Yupanqui until it rested on his forehead. He was declared Inca Ccapac and seated in front of the Sun on a seat of gold, called duho, garnished with emeralds and other precious stones. Seated there, they clothed him in the ccapac uncu, placed the suntur paucar in his hand, gave him the other insignia of Inca, and the priests raised him on their shoulders.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Sarmiento, History of the Incas, ch. 42 (Markham 1907); not verbatim.

passages.text: There came to the Inca Pachacuti his son Amaru Tupac Inca, who had been named by his father as his successor some years before... he desired to see him and offer sacrifice to him. When Amaru saw him in such majesty of wealth and surroundings, he fell on his face to the earth, adoring, offering sacrifices and obedience. On learning that it was his brother, Tupac Inca raised him and saluted him in the face.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Sarmiento, History of the Incas, ch. 43 (Markham 1907); not verbatim.

canonical_translation: Sir Clements Markham, History of the Incas (Hakluyt Society, 1907)

title.en: Eyebrows Blown in Offering: The Roads Cleared for Tupac Inca
title.zh: 吹毛為獻:為圖帕克·印加清道的眾生

region.en: Roads of Chinchaysuyu (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 欽查蘇尤大道(象徵性標記)

period: Inca tradition as given to Sarmiento de Gamboa, 1572; trans. Markham 1907

source.work: Pedro Sarmiento de Gamboa, History of the Incas, ch. 44, trans. Sir Clements Markham, Hakluyt Society, 1907

summary.en: Tupac went in such pomp and majesty that, where he passed, no one dared to look him in the face, in such veneration was he held. The people left the roads along which he had to pass and, ascending the hills on either side, worshipped and adored. They pulled out their eyebrows and eyelashes, and blowing on them, they made offering to the Inca. Others offered handfuls of a very precious herb called coca. When he arrived at the villages, he put on the dress and head-gear of that district, for all were different in their dress and head-gear: for Inca Yupanqui, so as to know each nation he had conquered, ordered that each one should have a special dress and head-gear, which they call pillu, llaytu and chuco, different one from the other, so as to be easily distinguished and recognized. Seating himself, Tupac Inca made a solemn sacrifice of animals and birds, burning them in a fire kindled in his presence; and in this way they worshipped the sun, which they believed to be God.
summary.zh: 圖帕克出行,儀仗威嚴:所過之處,無人敢直視其面。百姓離開王駕必經的道路,登上兩側山坡,頂禮膜拜;他們拔下自己的眉毛睫毛,向王吹獻為禮;另有人捧上名貴的古柯葉為獻。王至各村,便換上該地的服飾頭冠——各族衣冠各異;印加·尤潘琪為便於辨識所征各族,特命各族服飾頭飾各有專式,名為「皮尤」「勞圖」「丘科」,一望可辨。圖帕克·印加端坐,就地焚燒牲畜飛鳥,行莊嚴獻祭——他們如此崇拜太陽,奉之為神。

sensitivity.note: The eyebrow-blowing offering recorded as the standard act of reverence before the king.

passages.text: Tupac went in such pomp and majesty that, where he passed, no one dared to look him in the face, in such veneration was he held. The people left the roads along which he had to pass and, ascending the hills on either side, worshipped and adored. They pulled out their eyebrows and eyelashes, and blowing on them, they made offering to the Inca. Others offered handfuls of a very precious herb called coca.

For Inca Yupanqui, so as to know each nation he had conquered, ordered that each one should have a special dress and head-gear, which they call pillu, llaytu and chuco, different one from the other, so as to be easily distinguished and recognized.

canonical_translation: Sir Clements Markham, History of the Incas (Hakluyt Society, 1907)

title.en: Antarqui Flies Over the Sea: The Necromancer Who Reconnoitred the Islands
title.zh: 安塔爾基飛越重洋:偵島的巫師

region.en: Islands of Avachumbi and Ninachumbi, western sea (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 西海阿瓦瓊比與尼納瓊比群島(象徵性標記)

period: Inca tradition as given to Sarmiento de Gamboa, 1572; trans. Markham 1907

source.work: Pedro Sarmiento de Gamboa, History of the Incas, ch. 46, trans. Sir Clements Markham, Hakluyt Society, 1907

summary.en: There arrived at Tumbez some merchants who had come by sea from the west, navigating in balsas with sails. They gave information of the land whence they came, which consisted of some islands called Avachumbi and Ninachumbi, where there were many people and much gold. Tupac Inca was a man of lofty and ambitious ideas, and was not satisfied with the regions he had already conquered. So he determined to challenge a happy fortune, and see if it would favour him by sea. Yet he did not lightly believe the navigating merchants, for such men, being great talkers, ought not to be credited too readily. In order to obtain fuller information, he called a man who accompanied him in his conquests, named Antarqui, who, they all declare, was a great necromancer and could even fly through the air. Tupac Inca asked him whether what the merchant mariners said was true. Antarqui answered, after having thought the matter well out, that what they said was true, and that he would go there first. They say that he accomplished this by his arts, traversed the route, saw the islands, their people and riches, and, returning, gave certain information of all to Tupac Inca.
summary.zh: 通貝斯港來了幾名自西方乘帆筏渡海而來的商人。他們說起故鄉所在:海中有島,名「阿瓦瓊比」與「尼納瓊比」,人煙稠密,黃金遍地。圖帕克·印加志存高遠,不滿足於已得之地,決意試探海上的命運。然而他並不輕信這些誇誇其談的水商;為求確證,他召來隨征的安塔爾基——眾人都說此人法力高強,甚至能凌空飛行。圖帕克問他:商人所言可真?安塔爾基深思之後答道:所言屬實,而且他願先行探路。相傳他果然以法術飛越航線,親見群島、島民與富饒,然後回報,把一切確切告知圖帕克·印加。

sensitivity.note: The flying necromancer as pre-expedition scout; Markham's note identifies the islands (perhaps) with the Galapagos.

title.en: The Jawbone of a Horse: Tupac Inca's Voyage to Avachumbi
title.zh: 馬的頜骨:圖帕克·印加的遠航

region.en: Islands of Avachumbi and Ninachumbi (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 阿瓦瓊比與尼納瓊比群島(象徵性標記)

period: Inca tradition as given to Sarmiento de Gamboa, 1572; trans. Markham 1907

source.work: Pedro Sarmiento de Gamboa, History of the Incas, ch. 46, trans. Sir Clements Markham, Hakluyt Society, 1907

summary.en: The Inca, having this certainty, determined to go there. He caused an immense number of balsas to be constructed, in which he embarked more than 20,000 chosen men, taking with him as captains Huaman Achachi, Cunti Yupanqui, Quihual Tupac (all Hanan-cuzcos), Yancan Mayta, Quisu Mayta, Cachimapaca Macus Yupanqui, Llimpita Usca Mayta (Hurin-cuzcos); his brother Tilca Yupanqui being general of the whole fleet. Tupac Inca navigated and sailed on until he discovered the islands of Avachumbi and Ninachumbi, and returned, bringing back with him black people, gold, a chair of brass, and a skin and jaw bone of a horse. These trophies were preserved in the fortress of Cuzco until the Spaniards came. An Inca now living had charge of this skin and jaw bone of a horse. He gave this account, and the rest who were present corroborated it. His name is Urco Huaranca. The duration of this expedition was nine months, others say a year, and, as he was so long absent, every one believed he was dead. But to deceive them and make them think that news of Tupac Inca had come, Apu Yupanqui, his general of the land army, made rejoicings. This was afterwards commented upon to his disadvantage, and it was said that he rejoiced because he was pleased that Tupac Inca Yupanqui did not appear. It cost him his life.
summary.zh: 印加王既有確證,便決意遠征。他命人造筏無數,載精兵兩萬餘人;將領有瓜曼·阿查奇、昆蒂·尤潘琪、基瓦爾·圖帕克(皆哈南庫斯科),揚坎·馬雅塔、基蘇·馬雅塔、卡奇馬帕卡·馬庫斯·尤潘琪、伊利皮塔·烏斯卡·馬雅塔(皆烏林庫斯科);其弟蒂爾卡·尤潘琪統領全船隊;陸軍則由阿普·尤潘琪統率留守。圖帕克·印加揚帆遠航,直至發現阿瓦瓊比與尼納瓊比二島,然後返航——帶回黑人、黃金、一把銅椅,還有一張馬皮與一副馬的頜骨。這些戰利品一直珍藏在庫斯科的堡壘中,直至西班牙人到來。尚在人世的一位印加老人烏爾科·瓦蘭卡,曾親自保管那張馬皮與馬頜骨,如此作證,在場眾人皆附和其說。遠征歷時九月,或說一年;因王久出不歸,舉國都當他已死。陸軍統帥阿普·尤潘琪為安人心,詐稱圖帕克·印加有信,下令歡慶——此事後來成為他的罪狀:人們說他歡慶,是因為高興王不回來。這條謠言,竟要了他的性命。

sensitivity.note: The most extraordinary trans-Pacific claim in Andean tradition; the horse relics are the evidentiary core (Sarmiento swore witnesses) and remain a famous crux.

title.en: I Was Born as a Flower of the Field: Pachacuti's Dying Words
title.zh: 我生如野花:帕查庫提的臨終之歌

region.en: Cuzco (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 庫斯科(象徵性標記)

period: Inca tradition as given to Sarmiento de Gamboa, 1572; trans. Markham 1907

source.work: Pedro Sarmiento de Gamboa, History of the Incas, ch. 47, trans. Sir Clements Markham, Hakluyt Society, 1907

summary.en: Being in the highest prosperity and sovereignty of his life, he fell ill of a grave infirmity, and, feeling that he was at the point of death, he sent for all his sons who were then in the city. In their presence he first divided all his jewels and contents of his wardrobe. Next he made them plough furrows in token that they were vassals of their brother, and that they had to eat by the sweat of their hands. He also gave them arms in token that they were to fight for their brother. He next sent for the Incas orejones of Cuzco, his relations, and for Tupac Inca his son, to whom he spoke with a few words: 'Son! you now see how many great nations I leave to you, and you know what labour they have cost me. Mind that you are the man to keep and augment them. No one must raise his two eyes against you and live, even if he be your own brother. I leave you these our relations that they may be your councillors. Care for them and they shall serve you. When I am dead, take care of my body, and put it in my houses at Patallacta. Have my golden image in the House of the Sun, and make my subjects, in all the provinces, offer up solemn sacrifice, after which keep the feast of purucaya, that I may go to rest with my father the Sun.' Having finished his speech they say that he began to sing in a low and sad voice, with words of his own language: 'I was born as a flower of the field, as a flower I was cherished in my youth, I came to my full age, I grew old, now I am withered and die.' Having uttered these words, he laid his head upon a pillow and expired.
summary.zh: 正當盛年威福之極,帕查庫提忽染重疾,自知大限將至,便召在城諸子。當著他們的面,他先分完所有珍寶衣物;再命諸子扶犁開溝——以示他們是兄弟的藩屬,當以雙手汗水謀食;又授兵刃——以示他們當為兄弟而戰。隨後召庫斯科的印加耳垂貴胄與其子圖帕克·印加,簡言囑道:「兒啊!你看我留給你多少大邦,你知我為此耗費多少辛勞。你要守成,更要拓土。任何人不得仰視你而活——縱是你的親兄弟也不行。我把這些親族交給你作謀臣;善待他們,他們便侍奉你。我死之後,妥善安置我的遺體,放入帕塔利亞克的我的宮室;把我的金像供在太陽之屋;命各行省臣民舉行隆重獻祭,然後行普魯卡亞之祭——好讓我與我父太陽同歸安息。」言畢,相傳他以本族語言低聲悲唱:「我生如野地之花,幼時如花受呵護,及至成年又衰老,如今枯萎而凋零。」唱罷,他頭枕憑几,溘然長逝。

sensitivity.note: The flower death-song (Castilian rendering of a Quechua elegy) and the furrow-ploughing vassalage rite at the deathbed.

title.en: Condin Savana the Shapechanger: Hunting Smoke in the Forests of the Antis
title.zh: 變形者孔丁-薩瓦納:安蒂林海中獵煙

region.en: Forests of Antisuyu, east of Cuzco (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 庫斯科以東安蒂蘇尤林海(象徵性標記)

period: Inca tradition as given to Sarmiento de Gamboa, 1572; trans. Markham 1907

source.work: Pedro Sarmiento de Gamboa, History of the Incas, ch. 49, trans. Sir Clements Markham, Hakluyt Society, 1907

summary.en: The forests were very dense and full of evil places; so that they could not force their way through, nor did they know what direction to take in order to reach the settlements of the natives, which were well concealed in the thick vegetation. To find them the explorers climbed up the highest trees, and pointed out the places where they could see smoke rising. So they worked away at road making through the undergrowth until they lost that sign of inhabitants and found another. In this way the Inca made a road where it seemed impossible to make one. The Sinchi of the greater part of these provinces of the Antis was Condin Savana, of whom they say that he was a great wizard and enchanter, and they had the belief, and even now they affirm that he could turn himself into different shapes. Tupac Inca and his captains penetrated into this region of the Antis, which consists of the most terrible and fearful forests, with many rivers, where they endured immense toil, and the people who came from Peru suffered from the change of climate; the soldiers became sick, and many died. Tupac Inca himself, with a third of his men who came with him to conquer, were lost in the forests, and wandered for a long time, without knowing whether to go in one direction or another, until he fell in with Uturuncu Achachi who put him on the route.
summary.zh: 安蒂的森林密不透風,兇險四伏;大軍無法強行穿過,又不知土人村落藏於何處——全都隱沒在濃密的草木之中。探路人只好攀上最高的樹,瞭望何處炊煙升起,便朝那裡砍路開道;待到煙跡消失,再尋新煙,如此節節推進。印加王就這樣在看似無路之地開出了一條路。這些安蒂省份大部歸辛奇孔丁-薩瓦納統轄;相傳他是位大巫師、大幻術家,能隨意變換形體——至今人們猶如此深信。圖帕克·印加與諸將深入這片最可怖的林海,河川縱橫,勞苦不堪;來自乾寒秘魯的兵士水土不服,病者甚眾,死者相繼。圖帕克·印加本人連同三分之一的部眾迷失林中,長久徘徊,不知何往,直至遇上烏圖倫庫·阿查奇,方才認路歸隊。

sensitivity.note: Amazonian frontier campaign; the shapeshifting sinchi as guardian of the forest world.

passages.text: The forests were very dense and full of evil places; so that they could not force their way through, nor did they know what direction to take in order to reach the settlements of the natives, which were well concealed in the thick vegetation. To find them the explorers climbed up the highest trees, and pointed out the places where they could see smoke rising... In this way the Inca made a road where it seemed impossible to make one.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Sarmiento, History of the Incas, ch. 49 (Markham 1907); not verbatim.

passages.text: The Sinchi of the greater part of these provinces of the Antis was Condin Savana, of whom they say that he was a great wizard and enchanter, and they had the belief, and even now they affirm that he could turn himself into different shapes.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Sarmiento, History of the Incas, ch. 49 (Markham 1907); not verbatim.

passages.text: Tupac Inca himself, with a third of his men who came with him to conquer, were lost in the forests, and wandered for a long time, without knowing whether to go in one direction or another until he fell in with Uturuncu Achachi who put him on the route.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Sarmiento, History of the Incas, ch. 49 (Markham 1907); not verbatim.

canonical_translation: Sir Clements Markham, History of the Incas (Hakluyt Society, 1907)

title.en: The False Pachacuti: Coaquiri Steals a Dead Man's Name
title.zh: 偽帕查庫提:科阿基里盜用亡王之名

region.en: Collao (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 科利亞奧(象徵性標記)

period: Inca tradition as given to Sarmiento de Gamboa, 1572; trans. Markham 1907

source.work: Pedro Sarmiento de Gamboa, History of the Incas, ch. 49, trans. Sir Clements Markham, Hakluyt Society, 1907

summary.en: During the campaign an Indian of the Collas, named Coaquiri, fled from his company, reached the Collao, and spread the report that Tupac Inca was dead. He said that there was no longer an Inca, that they should all rise, and that he would be their leader. Presently he took the name of Pachacuti, the Collas rose, and chose him as their captain. This news reached Tupac Inca in Anti-suyu where he was in the career of conquest. He resolved to march against the Collas and punish them. He left the forests, leaving Uturuncu Achachi to complete the conquest, with orders to return into Peru when that service was completed, but not to enter Cuzco triumphing until the Inca should come. Having returned from the Antis, he increased his army and advanced to the Collao. The Collas had constructed four strong places at Llallaua, Asillo, Arapa, and Pucara. The Inca captured the chiefs and the leader of all, who was Chuca-chucay Pachacuti Coaquiri - afterwards these were the drummers of Inca Tupac.
summary.zh: 征戰期間,一名科利亞人科阿基里脫隊而逃,回到科利亞奧,散佈流言說圖帕克·印加已死。他說:印加已無,眾人當起事,他來做首領。不久他便自取「帕查庫提」之名;科利亞人群起,推他為帥。消息傳到正在安蒂蘇尤征戰的圖帕克·印加耳中,他決意回師討伐。他離開林海,留烏圖倫庫·阿查奇完成征服,命其事畢返回秘魯,但非待印加王親至,不得擅自凱旋入庫斯科。圖帕克·印加自安蒂回師,擴軍進逼科利亞奧。科利亞人築四座要塞於利亞勞阿、阿西略、阿拉帕、普卡拉。印加王擒獲諸酋,連同他們的總頭領「丘卡-丘卡伊·帕查庫提」科阿基里——這批人後來都成了圖帕克·印加的鼓手。

sensitivity.note: Name-theft as rebellion; the captured pretender turned royal drummer is a pointed humiliation.

passages.text: During the campaign an Indian of the Collas, named Coaquiri, fled from his company, reached the Collao, and spread the report that Tupac Inca was dead. He said that there was no longer an Inca, that they should all rise and that he would be their leader. Presently he took the name of Pachacuti, the Collas rose, and chose him as their captain.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Sarmiento, History of the Incas, ch. 49 (Markham 1907); not verbatim.

passages.text: The Inca captured the chiefs and the leader of all, who was Chuca-chucay Pachacuti Coaquiri, he who, as we have said, fled from Anti-suyu. Afterwards these were the drummers of Inca Tupac. Finally, owing to the great diligence of Inca Tupac, although the war occupied some years, the Incas conquered and subdued all.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Sarmiento, History of the Incas, ch. 50 (Markham 1907); not verbatim.

canonical_translation: Sir Clements Markham, History of the Incas (Hakluyt Society, 1907)

title.en: Ndengei, the Serpent in the Cave of Nakauvadra
title.zh: 納夸瓦德拉洞中蛇神恩登蓋

region.en: Kauvandra mountain above Rakiraki, Viti Levu, Fiji (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 斐濟維提島拉基拉基上方考萬德拉山（象徵定位）

period: Oral tradition; recorded by Basil Thomson, The Fijians, 1908, ch. on religion

source.work: Basil Thomson, The Fijians: A Study of the Decay of Custom (London: Heinemann, 1908), 'The Ndengei Myth'

summary.en: Ndengei is supreme among the Kalou-vu, the original gods; in serpent form he lies coiled in a cavern in the Kauvandra mountain above Rakiraki, and when he turns himself the earth quakes. Priests crawl to his cave-mouth with hundreds of hogs and turtle and come out holding yam, dripping with rain, or flinging fire-brands; in some versions he has only the head and neck of a serpent, the rest of his body being stone. He is the creator of mankind, with no emotion but hunger — and his son Rokomautu scraped the land up from the ocean bed and taught men how to produce fire.
summary.zh: 恩登蓋為原初神（Kalou-vu）之首，全維提島及外島皆奉其號令。蛇形之軀盤踞於拉基拉基上方考萬德拉山的岩洞之中；他一翻身，大地便震動。拉基拉基人以數百頭豬與海龜獻於洞口，祭司跪爬至洞前進洞請願：求芋豐收則捧芋而出，求雨則滴水而歸，求戰勝則有火把擲出、兵器交擊之聲應殺敵之數。有的版本說他只有蛇頭蛇頸，身軀皆石。他造人類，卻無喜無怒，唯飢而已。其子羅科馬烏圖自海底刮起陸地：衣裾拖過處成沙灘，衣裾撩起處成石岸；又教人取火之術。

sensitivity.note: Colonial administrator-anthropologist record (Thomson 1908); iTaukei heritage. Thomson argues Ndengei is Melanesian, not Polynesian.

passages.text: Ndengei is supreme among the Kalou-vu (original gods), and his authority was recognized by the whole of Vitilevu and its outlying islands, and by the western half of Vanua-levu. The oldest tradition in which his name occurs mentions him as one of the first immigrants with Lutu-na-somba-somba, but his fame far exceeded that of his companions, and so many myths gathered about his name, that when the first missionaries arrived he had come to be a counterpart of Zeus himself. In serpent form he lay coiled in a cavern in the Kauvandra mountain above Rakiraki, and when he turned himself the earth quaked. Enormous offerings of food were made to him by the Rakiraki people.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Thomson, The Fijians, 'The Ndengei Myth' (1908); not verbatim.

passages.text: Several hundred hogs and turtle were carried to the mouth of the cavern, which the priests approached, crawling on their knees and elbows. One of the priests then entered the cave to proffer the request. If it was for a good yam-crop he would reappear, holding a piece of yam which the god had given him; if for rain, he would be dripping with water; if for victory, a fire-brand would be flung out in token that the enemy would be consumed, or a clashing of clubs would be heard, one for each of the enemy that would be slaughtered.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Thomson, The Fijians, 'The Ndengei Myth' (1908); not verbatim.

passages.text: Beyond the limits of his own district he had scarcely a temple, and little actual worship was paid to him, though in the great drought of 1838 King Tanoa of Mbau sent propitiatory offerings to him. In some versions Ndengei has the head and neck only of a serpent, the rest of his body being of stone. He is the creator of mankind, but he has no emotions, sensations, or appetites except hunger. Another version describes him as sending forth his son, Rokomautu, to create the land. He scraped it up from the ocean-bed, and where his flowing garment trailed across it there were sandy beaches, and where the skirt was looped up the coast was rocky. He also taught men how to produce fire.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Thomson, The Fijians, 'The Ndengei Myth' (1908); not verbatim.

title.en: The Shooting of Turukawa, Ndengei's Awakener
title.zh: 射殺神鴿圖魯卡瓦

region.en: Kauvandra mountain, Viti Levu, Fiji (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 斐濟維提島考萬德拉山（象徵定位）

period: Oral tradition; recorded by Basil Thomson, The Fijians, 1908 (version of Ilai Motonithothoko)

source.work: Basil Thomson, The Fijians: A Study of the Decay of Custom (London: Heinemann, 1908), 'The Ndengei Myth — The Shooting of the Sacred Pigeon'

summary.en: The twin grand-nephews of Ndengei tamed a pigeon, Turukawa, whose cooing at sunrise roused the somnolent old god; a messenger carried it off on the father's assurance, and when the twins found their bird in Ndengei's village they shot it with the bow called Summer-lightning and fortified themselves with Rokola's carpenters. There was war in Kauvandra such as Fiji has never seen since — and a vine-bridge snare that swung Ndengei's warriors into the fortress to be clubbed at leisure.
summary.zh: 恩登蓋的兩個孫侄輩雙生子馴得一隻鴿子，取名圖魯卡瓦；晨昏潮汐，鴿鳴遠播——老人恩登蓋嗜睡，全靠這鴿子喚醒。使者趁兄弟外出，憑其父一句『不必他們同意』把鴿子取走。雙子聞鴿鳴於神村，大怒：『這就是你們對待人類子孫的方式嗎？』遂以名喚『夏之閃電』的弓射殺神鴿，並入羅科拉的木匠村，倚其戰柵自固。考萬德拉山由此爆發斐濟史上從未有過的大戰：恩登蓋與羅科穆托的聯軍圍攻韋西木戰柵，屢攻不克；羅科拉更設毒計——在裂谷上張藤橋，橋畔暗設鴨網式的繩套，敵兵一踏上便被高吊入堡，任憑處置。恩登蓋軍心大沮。

sensitivity.note: Record of a native-written version (Ilai Motonithothoko) via Thomson 1908; iTaukei heritage.

passages.text: When Ndengei had grown old the settlement on the Kauvandra mountain consisted of several villages, one of which belonged to Rokola and his carpenter clan, and the grandsons of the first arrivals were grown men. In the village of Nai-lango-nawanawa, on the slopes of the mountain, lived two twin grand-nephews of Ndengei, named Na-thiri-kau-moli and Na-kau-sambaria, who having brought down a pigeon with an arrow without injuring it, clipped its wings and tamed it. They gave the bird the name of Turukawa, and every morning and evening, and at flood-tide and ebb-tide, its cooing resounded far and wide over the mountain. Old Ndengei, hearing its voice, sent a messenger to ask the youths to give it to him, but they were absent from home, and the messenger, assured by their father that their consent was not necessary, took the bird to his master. Ndengei wanted the bird for a practical purpose. Elderly Fijians are somnolent, and the pigeon's cooing at sunrise was useful in arousing him from slumber.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Thomson, The Fijians, 'The Ndengei Myth' (1908), version of Ilai Motonithothoko; not verbatim.

passages.text: Next morning the twin brothers were startled at hearing their pigeon cooing in Ndengei's village, and when they heard that it had been taken away without their consent, they flew into a rage, crying, 'Sombo! is this to be the way with us children of men?' And they made ready their bow, which was called Livaliva-ni-singa (Summer-lightning), and set forth to shoot Turukawa. And when they drew near the banyan-tree in which he was perched, they doffed their turbans; therefore the place is called Ai-thavu-thavu-ni-sala (the Doffing-place) to this day. And they shot an arrow at Turukawa, who fell dead to the ground. And they drew out the arrow, and went to the carpenters' village, Narauyamba, because it was fortified, and their own village was not fortified. For four days Ndengei missed the cooing of his Awakener, and he sent Uto, his messenger, to see what had become of him.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Thomson, The Fijians, 'The Ndengei Myth' (1908), version of Ilai Motonithothoko; not verbatim.

passages.text: And Uto came to the banyan-tree, and found the body of Turukawa, and saw the arrow-wound, and said, 'There is none who would so forget Ndengei as to kill his Awakener but the twin brothers whose bird he was.' Then Ndengei sent to them to come to him, and they refused. And his anger blazed up within him, and he cried with a terrible voice, 'Go, tell them to depart to a land where I am not known!' But this also they refused to do, and Rokola ordered his carpenters to build a war-fence of vesi timber, very high, with neither joint nor chink in it.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Thomson, The Fijians, 'The Ndengei Myth' (1908), version of Ilai Motonithothoko; not verbatim.

passages.text: Then there was war in Kauvandra — such a war as has never since been seen in Fiji. Joined to Ndengei were Rokomouto and his clan, who had settled on Viwa, and together they laid siege to the fortress. Many heroes fell on either side, but never a warrior could storm the wall of vesi built by the carpenters. But now Rokola devised a dreadful engine of war. Before the gate of his fortress there was a ragged rift in the mountain-side. He sent out his warriors to cut stout vines in the forest, and suspended a bridge of twisted vines over the chasm. From the tops of two stout posts, planted within the fortress, he stretched ropes that appeared to be mere supports to the bridge, but were in reality a trap such as the men of Notho use when they would snare wild duck in their taro-beds. For when a man trod upon them he was caught fast in a noose, and the defenders hauled suddenly upon the ropes, and swung him high over the rampart into their midst, where they could club him at leisure.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Thomson, The Fijians, 'The Ndengei Myth' (1908), version of Ilai Motonithothoko; not verbatim.

title.en: The Deluge of the Vungayali-Tree and the Lifeboat
title.zh: 武恩加亞利樹之洪與救命舟

region.en: Kauvandra to the western ocean, Fiji (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 斐濟考萬德拉至西海（象徵定位）

period: Oral tradition; recorded by Basil Thomson, The Fijians, 1908 (version of Ilai Motonithothoko)

source.work: Basil Thomson, The Fijians: A Study of the Decay of Custom (London: Heinemann, 1908), 'The Ndengei Myth — The Great Deluge'

summary.en: When Ndengei could not take the fortress by force, a traitor's dream told him to cut the vungayali-tree by the rampart: water gushed from the wound, flooded the fortress knee-deep by nightfall, and became a river flowing south. The carpenters built canoes in haste and sailed to a new land — the ancestors of the carpenter clan at Rewa — while the twin brothers, for Rokola's sake, were given time to build the Nai-vaka-nawanawa, the Lifeboat, 'a vessel such as has never since been seen in Fiji,' and sailed into the western ocean, never heard of more.
summary.zh: 恩登蓋力攻不下，便尋得與木匠同族卻為己方效力的叛徒姆巴坎德羅蒂，命他獻計破敵。當夜神靈入夢，教他砍伐戰柵旁那株 vungayali 樹。斧落樹根，泉水噴涌而出——整日灌入堡中，入夜已深及膝，且仍在漲。木匠們商議，既神明相助，不如乞和；恩登蓋與眾酋議定：『這批工匠太有用，不可殺，改判流放！』泉水已成南流的大河，木匠們倉促造舟，順流而下，至新陸定居——這便是雷瓦木匠氏族的祖先。至於雙生子，罪無可赦，本應終身放逐；但看在羅科拉的情面，准其造舟自贖。羅科拉為他們造出一艘斐濟空前的巨舟，命名『納伊瓦卡納瓦納瓦』——救命舟；兄弟二人順流入西海而去，從此杳無音訊。

sensitivity.note: Record of a native-written version via Thomson 1908; iTaukei heritage. Flood cluster; cross-ref melanesian-dengei-flood-canoe-builders (Fison recension).

passages.text: There were traitors in Ndengei's camp, who were conspiring with the enemy, and carrying food to him by night. These men were seized, and being found guilty on their own confession, were exiled from Kauvandra for ever. Now, when Ndengei saw that he could not prevail against the fortress, he sought out one Mbakandroti, a man related to the carpenters, who had chosen to take part with Ndengei against his own kin, and bade him devise a plan for betraying the fortress. That night a spirit appeared to Mbakandroti in a dream, and told him to cut down a vungayali-tree that grew close to the rampart. And when he had related his dream, one Vueti was appointed to cut it down. He had scarce laid his stone axe to the root when water began to gush forth from the wound. All that day the water poured into the fortress, and by nightfall it was knee-deep, and rising still. So the carpenters took counsel, and resolved to ask pardon of Ndengei, since the gods were with him. So Ndengei took counsel with his chiefs, and they said, 'These craftsmen are too valuable; we cannot destroy them; let them be exiled!'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Thomson, The Fijians, 'The Ndengei Myth' (1908), version of Ilai Motonithothoko; not verbatim.

passages.text: The fountain had now become a mighty river flowing southward from the mountain, and the craftsmen built them canoes in haste, and embarked, and sailed down the stream till they came to a new land, and there they settled. These are the ancestors of the carpenter clan at Rewa. But there was no pardon for the twin brothers; to their exile there was to be no limit. Yet, for Rokola's sake, they were given time to build their canoe. And Rokola built them a vessel such as has never since been seen in Fiji, and named it Nai-vaka-nawanawa (the Lifeboat), and sailed away down the stream into the western ocean, and were never heard of more; only the prophecy remains that when they reappear on earth the power of Ndengei, which is the Old Serpent, would continue in the ascendant, for the twins were gods.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Thomson, The Fijians, 'The Ndengei Myth' (1908), version of Ilai Motonithothoko; not verbatim.

title.en: The Origin of the Tagai Constellation
title.zh: 塔蓋星座之由來

region.en: Murray Island (Mer), Torres Strait (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 托雷斯海峽摩爾島（象徵定位）

period: Oral tradition; recorded by A. C. Haddon, Head-Hunters Black, White and Brown, 1901

source.work: A. C. Haddon, Head-Hunters Black, White and Brown (London: Methuen, 1901), 'Marriage Customs and Star Myths — The Origin of the Tagai Constellation'

summary.en: Tagai the captain speared fish from the bow while Kareg poled the canoe through the reef; the hot sun made the crew thirsty, and they drank the ship's water-bamboo dry. Tagai made a rope fast round the necks of six men and cast them into the sea — 'All you fellow Usiam' — then killed the rest with two wooden skewers through their necks and called them Seg; only Kareg, who never stole his water, was spared, and Tagai and Kareg and canoe stop in one place, Usiam in another, and Seg in another — the sky's almanack of yam and turtle seasons.
summary.zh: 船長塔蓋立於船首叉魚，卡雷格在船尾撐篙過礁。烈日炙人，全體船員口渴難耐，偷飲了船長的竹筒飲水。塔蓋舉起空筒喝問『誰喝了水？』無人應答。他怒極，取繩套住六人的脖子拋入海中：『你們就是「烏西亞姆」！』又取兩支木針，把其餘水手一一殺死，以針穿頸拋海，名之『塞格』。唯卡雷格無過得生：『你留下，你不偷水，你一直撐船。』如今塔蓋、卡雷格與舟停於天上一處，烏西亞姆一處，塞格一處——這便是漁民與農夫的天曆：烏西�姆報新芋之期，塔蓋報海龜之汛，夜航則循塔蓋左手而行。

sensitivity.note: Field record (Haddon 1901, informant's own words); Meriam heritage of Torres Strait.

passages.text: A man named Tagai, with uplifted and outstretched hands bearing a spear, is supposed to stand upon a canoe, which is represented by the bowed row of stars that forms the scorpion's tail. Below the front end of the canoe is a single star, the anchor of the canoe, and near its other end is a red star that represents a man named Kareg. A cluster of stars is called Usiam, and another linear constellation is named Seg. Tagai is an important constellation, not only as an indication of the approach of certain seasons, but also for navigation purposes. 'Usiam he vick for new yams.' 'Seg he vick next kind of yam.' 'Tagai he vuk for turtle season. Two hand he come first; all turtle go to islands to leeward (to the west), and they eat turtle first. By-and-by face belong Tagai he come up; Dauarle get turtle, and then all the rest of Murray Island.' In sailing by night from Erub (Darnley Island) to Mer (Murray Island) they steer for the left hand of Tagai.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Haddon, Head-Hunters, 'Marriage Customs and Star Myths' (1901); not verbatim.

passages.text: One man, Tagai, he got a canoe. Tagai he stop in forehead (the bow or front end of the canoe) and look out and spear fish. Kareg he stop in stern. Plenty men crew. They go over reef; Kareg he pole canoe. Tagai he spear fish. Sun hot on reef, all men thirsty, and steal water in canoe belong captain. Tagai say, 'Why you no pole canoe good? I no spear fish.' By-and-by he say, 'Where water-bamboo?' He take bamboo and shake it; it empty. 'Who drink water?' Men no talk. Tagai get wild. He get one rope and make fast round neck of six men and chuck into sea. He put name to them, 'All you fellow Usiam.' Tagai take two wooden skewers and call other men in canoe, and kill plenty, and stick the skewers through their necks and chuck them in the sea, and call them 'Seg.' Kareg he live. Tagai tell Kareg, 'You stop; you no steal my water, you push canoe all time.' Man stop in sky all the time. Tagai, Kareg, and canoe stop in one place, Usiam stop in another place, and Seg stop in another place.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Haddon, Head-Hunters, 'The Origin of the Tagai Constellation' (1901), given in the informant's own words; not verbatim.

title.en: Metakorab the Dorgai and Bu
title.zh: 多蓋妖女梅塔科拉布與布

region.en: Boigu and Kerpai, Torres Strait (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 托雷斯海峽博伊古島與克爾派村（象徵定位）

period: Oral tradition; recorded by A. C. Haddon, Head-Hunters Black, White and Brown, 1901

source.work: A. C. Haddon, Head-Hunters Black, White and Brown (London: Methuen, 1901), 'Star Myths — A Dorgai Constellation'

summary.en: Digging mound-bird eggs on Boigu, Nadai pulled and pulled at what would not come — and dragged out of the ground a sleeping Dorgai, Metakorab, wearing great white cowries tied at her chin. Every village he ran to for help emptied itself at her terrible face; only at Kerpai did Bu stay in the bachelors' quarters, shoot her with pig-arrows, and kill her. Both are now in the sky — the Dorgai going first, continually followed by Bu: Altair the body, the stars each side her arms, and the cluster Bu, that belongs to the north-west monsoon and calls the dances.
summary.zh: 博伊古島的納代去掘塚雉的蛋，一連拔出幾枚拔不動的『蛋』——原來是多蓋妖女梅塔科拉布睡在土塚之下，頷下繫著幾枚大白寶螺。他嚇得魂飛，逃回村中呼眾殺妖；可是各村的武士一見妖面便棄械而逃，環島皆然。最後到克爾派村，眾人仍然跑了，唯有名喚布的男子留在單身漢屋裡，張弓搭上射豬用的利箭，一箭斃妖。如今二者皆在天上：多蓋在前，布緊隨其後——多蓋便是牛郎星（他們稱 gaum『身體』），兩側是她的雙臂，而布則是那一簇星。這組星座屬西北季風；『多蓋升起之時，正是跳舞之季。』

sensitivity.note: Field record (Haddon 1901, told in Mabuiag 1888); Torres Strait heritage.

passages.text: Once upon a time a man named Nadai, living on the Island of Boigu, went into the bush to collect the eggs of the mound-bird, a bird that lays its eggs in a great mound of earth which it scratches up with its strong feet. He found a large mound, and dug into it till he came to what he thought was an egg. He tried to pull it up, but it stuck fast; then he tried to get another, but neither would that come away. It so happened that a Dorgai named Metakorab was sleeping under the mound, and she was wearing several large white cowry shells, and it was these that Nadai was pulling at, mistaking them for eggs. Nadai at last caught hold of the shell, which was tied on to the Dorgai's chin, and giving a tremendous pull he dragged the Dorgai out of the ground. He was so terrified at her appearance, that he fled back to the village and called out to the inhabitants to arm themselves and kill the Dorgai, who was sure to follow after him.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Haddon, Head-Hunters, 'A Dorgai Constellation' (1901); not verbatim.

passages.text: By-and-by a fly came, and behind it came the Dorgai; but the men no sooner saw her terrible face than they threw down their weapons and ran away in a fright. Then Nadai went on to the next village, but the same thing happened again. So he went on all round the island, but it always happened as before. At last Nadai came to a village called Kerpai, on the north side of the island, and he begged the people to stand firm and attack the Dorgai. They armed themselves, but when the fly came, and after it the Dorgai, they all took to their heels, as the others had done before, with the exception of one man named Bu. He remained in the bachelors' quarters, and armed himself with a bow and with arrows that are used for shooting wild pigs. When the Dorgai arrived, Bu shot her and killed her. Both are now in the sky; the Dorgai going first, being continually followed by Bu.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Haddon, Head-Hunters, 'A Dorgai Constellation' (1901); not verbatim.

title.en: Kabi and the House of the Sun
title.zh: 卡比訪日宮

region.en: Dauan and Saibai, Torres Strait (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 托雷斯海峽道安島與賽拜島（象徵定位）

period: Oral tradition; recorded by A. C. Haddon, Head-Hunters Black, White and Brown, 1901 (from Robert Bruce at Daru)

source.work: A. C. Haddon, Head-Hunters Black, White and Brown (London: Methuen, 1901), 'Star Myths — Sun, Moon, and Night'

summary.en: At Kadau all men yammed that Sun, Moon, and Night were all the same one; Kabi alone said No, and when the assembly threatened to kill him he set out in his canoe to find where the Sun stopped. The Sun carried Kabi's canoe in one hand like a boy's toy, entertained him with bananas, yams, taro, and coconuts, hitched a rope to his head and towed him home through three big waves — and when Kabi shook the rope loose before all the people, they believed: 'Sun, Moon, and Darkness each got their own work to do.'
summary.zh: 道安島卡道的村人閒談皆言『日、月、夜原是同一個』。唯卡比說：『瞎說！你們看：日出之時月即落；月升之時日即沉——分明是三個。』眾人惱怒欲殺他；卡比便說『明天我去日月夜所居之地，親眼看給你們』。他駕舟遠航，過賽拜、越大洋，果真尋到日之所居。太陽單手提起他的小舟，如孩童提玩具一般放上屋頂，又以大珠貝佩胸出迎，待以蕉、芋、薯、椰之宴。臨別，太陽以繩繫其頭，拖舟而行；三大浪相繼，一波送他半程，一波至賽拜，一波直送道安。他登岸對眾人說：『我去過日月之家——他們是兩個，不是一個。你們看這繩——』解繩之時，繩竟向天而去。眾人這才信了：『日、月、黑夜，各司其職。』

sensitivity.note: Field record (Haddon 1901, from Robert Bruce at Daru); Torres Strait heritage.

passages.text: Plenty men sit down and yarn at Kadau (a village in the island of Dauan). All man he yarn about Sun, and Moon, and Night. All man speak, 'Sun, Moon, and Night he all the same one.' One man called Kabi he speak, 'No good you talk all the same; suppose you look. You see. Sun he come up, that time Moon he go down. Moon he come up, and Sun he go down.' Then all man too much wild; some man he speak, 'Very good, we kill Kabi; he talk no good.' Kabi he hear, he afraid. Kabi he then speak, 'You fellow, look, I go to-morrow; I go place belong Sun, and Moon, and Night.' At small daylight he go in his canoe, his woman stop behind. He go across to Saibai. All man in Saibai speak, 'Where you go, Kabi?' He speak, 'I go to look place where Sun he stop.' Him go — go — go. All islands he come up. He go big deep water. He catch him place where Sun he stop.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Haddon, Head-Hunters, 'Sun, Moon, and Night' (1901), from Robert Bruce; not verbatim.

passages.text: Kabi he look, Sun he come out house belong him. Kabi he think, 'Sun he no good, as Sun he no got good things on.' Kabi pulled his canoe on beach and sat down. Sun then come out of door of his house and looked at Kabi. Sun then go inside house belong him and put on all flash things — one big pearl-shell he put on breast and one big shell on body. Sun he walk along and come close to Kabi. Kabi he very much afraid; he think inside, 'Big man he come now. I think he kill me.' Sun he speak, 'Kabi, come on, you and me go house.' Sun he carry canoe belong Kabi in his one hand, all same as boy carry canoe belong play; then he put canoe on top of his house.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Haddon, Head-Hunters, 'Sun, Moon, and Night' (1901), from Robert Bruce; not verbatim.

passages.text: Then Sun he speak, 'Kabi, what name you come here for?' Kabi he speak, 'All man he growl for you; he all speak, Sun, and Moon, and Night he one. Me, one fellow, speak, No, Sun he one. Moon he one, and Night he one. Then all man he wild.' Sun he speak, 'All right, you come house.' Sun he speak, 'Me one, Moon another one.' Then Sun and Moon he bring Kabi kaikai (food). Sun he give kaikai belong Sun — bananas, yams, taro, sweet potatoes, coconuts. Moon he give him all the same.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Haddon, Head-Hunters, 'Sun, Moon, and Night' (1901), from Robert Bruce; not verbatim.

passages.text: Sun he take canoe belong Kabi, and put it in the water; then they put all kaikai in canoe. Kabi he get afraid when he think of the long journey he got to take. Sun he speak, 'Kabi, I make rope fast along your head, then you and me go together; I tow you. When you come to place belong you, you shake rope; by-and-by when you loose rope, you shake it, then that time I pull up.' Kabi he then start in his canoe. Three big waves come; one wave lift him half-way, the next lift him along to Saibai, the next wave lift his canoe to Dauan. Kabi then went ashore and told all the people, 'I been to place where Sun and Moon he stop. You hear me now when I speak. He no one fellow, he two fellow. Sun he pull me here.' Then Kabi got all people in one place. He speak, 'You see this rope fast on top of my head. You look when I take this rope off my head.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Haddon, Head-Hunters, 'Sun, Moon, and Night' (1901), from Robert Bruce; not verbatim.

title.en: Kwoiam of Mabuiag, the Berserker of the Straits
title.zh: 馬布瓦格狂戰士克沃伊亞姆

region.en: Mabuiag, Torres Strait (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 托雷斯海峽馬布瓦格島（象徵定位）

period: Oral tradition; recorded by A. C. Haddon, Head-Hunters Black, White and Brown, 1901

source.work: A. C. Haddon, Head-Hunters Black, White and Brown (London: Methuen, 1901), 'The Cult of Kwoiam'

summary.en: Cursed by his blind mother for a stolen strip of plaiting-leaf, Kwoiam killed her and went on the rampage 'to pay for mother,' returning with a canoe-load of heads; he slew whole villages and every expedition sent against him until his throwing-stick broke, and he backed slowly up his hill and crouched and gave up the ghost. 'No cut him head; he great man' — his foes heaped their weapons over him, and the cairn on Kwoiam's hill still carries three shell trumpets, while the spring his spear drove into the rock flows yet, its upper pool forbidden to the unworthy, whose penalty is premature grey-ness.
summary.zh: 克沃伊亞姆與盲母同住，舅父為其隨從。一日他以腳趾抽走母親編席的一片葉，受母咒罵；他怒而出門，取椰芽飾身，竟弒母，繼而『為母償血』，掀起殺伐：先屠數島，直上新幾內亞大陸，歸來載回一舟頭顱。巴杜人拒他魚食戲弄於他，他追至普魯島午寢之地盡殲之。兩批復仇大軍皆被誅盡；至第三批，他的擲矛杆折斷，手無寸鐵的他且戰且退，退上山頂，俯身而亡。敵方一名巴杜勇士喝止行刑者：『莫砍他的頭！他是偉人，讓他躺在這裡——他是這些島嶼的主人。』敵人反以弓箭矛棒為其堆塚。今日克沃伊亞姆崗上石塚猶存，塚置三枚古貝號。岩隙中他那矛鑿出的泉水至今長流：上池唯老者尊者可飲，僭飲者必早生華髮。

sensitivity.note: Field record (Haddon 1901); Kwoiam cult heritage of Mabuiag. Records head-hunting warfare as remembered history.

passages.text: Kwoiam lived with his mother, who was blind, and he had an uncle for his henchman. One day, when his mother was plaiting a mat, Kwoiam abstracted with his toes a strip of leaf his mother was about to use, and missing it she asked who had taken it. Kwoiam confessed, and his mother cursed him; this made him angry, and he went outside the hut and called to his uncle to get the sprouting leaf of a coconut palm that he might deck himself for the war-path. When he was so accoutred he killed his mother, and then went on the rampage to avenge her death, or as it was told to me, 'to pay for mother.' He went to several islands and to the mainland of New Guinea, sometimes slaying the population of a whole village, at other times merely requesting food or a new canoe. Eventually Kwoiam returned with a canoe-load of human heads, and he ordered his uncle to clean them for him.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Haddon, Head-Hunters, 'The Cult of Kwoiam' (1901); not verbatim.

passages.text: On one occasion certain Badu men fooled him, refusing to give him some fish for which he had civilly asked them. These men retired to the island of Pulu for a midday siesta; Kwoiam followed them there and killed them all except two, who made their escape, but one of them had his leg transfixed by a javelin hurled by Kwoiam. An expedition of Moa and Badu men was sent to retaliate; but Kwoiam killed all who were sent against him except four men. A second very large avenging expedition was sent, but when fighting against these Kwoiam's throwing-stick broke, and he was helpless. He slowly retreated backwards up his hill, and when the enemy pressed too closely upon him, he rushed forward, unarmed as he was, and frightened back his foes; this happened several times.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Haddon, Head-Hunters, 'The Cult of Kwoiam' (1901); not verbatim.

passages.text: As soon as Kwoiam reached the summit of the hill he crouched in a prone position and gave up the ghost. A Moa man rushed up to him and began to cut off his head with a bamboo knife, but he had only made a small incision when he was stopped by another Badu man, who said, 'No cut him head; he great man. Let him lie where he stop; he master over all these islands.' So instead of insulting the dead warrior they did him honour, and piled over his body their bows, arrows, javelins, and stone clubs, saying that now Kwoiam was dead all the fighting was over. The cairn erected over his grave remains to this day, and on it are placed three ancient shell trumpets.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Haddon, Head-Hunters, 'The Cult of Kwoiam' (1901); not verbatim.

passages.text: On the plain near the sea is a large oval boulder, the head of the luckless mother. As we ascended the hill called Kwoiamantra we passed between a long double row of stones that represented the heads taken by Kwoiam on the famous voyage when he paid the blood-price for the death of his mother. A short distance up the hill were some rocks, from out of a cleft in which a perennial stream flows. It arose in this wise. One day Kwoiam was thirsty, and he drove his spear into the rock, and water gushed forth and has never ceased to flow. The water fills a rock basin, and from this it trickles into a lower pool, and thence the stream flows down the hill. Ten years before I was informed that only old and important men might drink from the upper pool, whereas the lower was free to all; the penalty of unworthily drinking from the upper pool was premature greyness. I asked if I might drink there, and they were good enough to think that my claims were sufficiently strong. Apparently I was presumptuous, as the penalty has been inflicted!
passages.note: Paraphrase of Haddon, Head-Hunters, 'The Cult of Kwoiam' (1901); not verbatim.

title.en: The Fifth Course: Ulad is Taken by the Lasso
title.zh: 七關之五：擒獲烏拉德

region.en: Corn-lands of Mazandaran marches (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 馬贊德蘭邊境麥田（象徵性定位）

period: Composed c. 1010 CE (Warner translation 1905)

source.work: Firdausi, Shahnama, trans. A. G. & E. Warner (1905), vol. II, Kai Kaus sec. 10 (Fifth Course)

summary.en: Rustam passes a murk black as a negro's face — the sun is captive and the stars are lassoed — and emerges into a land like painted silk with crops, where Rakhsh strays into the corn and a watchman beats the sleeper and loses his ears for it. Ulad the marchlord rides against him: my name is Cloud, replies Rustam, if a cloud hath lion's claws; he shears two chieftains' heads at every stroke, then flings his sixty-coiled lasso and takes Ulad, who guides him to Kaus' prison, the White Div's cavern, and Pulad son of Ghundi.
summary.zh: 魯斯塔姆穿越黑如夜幕的昏暗地帶——「太陽被囚，星辰被縛」——來到如錦繡的沃野；拉赫什闖入麥田，守田人驅馬而被英雄扭下雙耳。地方領主烏拉德來戰；「吾名『雲』，若雲有獅爪者」。魯斯塔姆一擊落二人首級，擲出六十圈套索擒烏拉德，令其引路指向卡烏斯囚地與白魔巢穴。

sensitivity.note: Epic literary source; no living community restriction.

passages.text: He journeyed on and reached a place of gloom black as a negro's face, a murky night without a star or moon; thou wouldst have said: the sun is captive and the stars are lassoed! When he emerged to light he saw a land like painted silk with crops, where all was verdure and streams; the old world had renewed its youth. He unbridled Rakhsh and loosed him in the corn, then couched like a mighty lion in the grass.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Firdausi, Shahnama, Kai Kaus sec. 10 (Warner 1905); not verbatim.

passages.text: The watchman of the plain, on seeing Rakhsh among the crops, ran up with hue and cry; he smote the hero smartly with a stick upon the foot: O Ahriman! why didst thou loose thy steed among the corn to eat where others toiled? But Rustam, angered, seized the watchman's ears, wrung them and tore them off without a word. There was Ulad the marchlord, a brave and famous youth, hunting there with other nobles; they rode to find out who he was.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Firdausi, Shahnama, Kai Kaus sec. 10 (Warner 1905); not verbatim.

passages.text: What is thy name? Ulad cried. My name is Cloud, said Rustam, if a cloud hath lion's claws, with swords and maces only for its fruit, and beareth on its lap the heads of chieftains. With that he drew his baleful Crocodile, came like a lion midst a flock, and slew all that were in his reach; at every stroke he sheared two chieftains' heads. Then Rustam, with sixty coils of lasso on his arm, flung his mighty lasso, ensnared that chieftain's head, and then alighting made fast his hands.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Firdausi, Shahnama, Kai Kaus sec. 10 (Warner 1905); not verbatim.

passages.text: If thou speak the truth and art faithful, then from the monarch of Mazandaran will I take crown and throne and massive mace, and thou shalt be the ruler of the land. Ulad said: there are between us now and Kai Kaus a hundred leagues; whence to the White Div is another hundred; the road is through a gorge, a fearful spot o'er which no eagle flieth; there is a cavern midst two hundred others, and there twelve thousand warriors, all divs, keep watch by night; their captain is Pulad son of Ghundi. Of all the divs the White Div is the chief; at him the mountains shake like willow-leaves, and thou wilt find his person mountain-tall.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Firdausi, Shahnama, Kai Kaus sec. 10 (Warner 1905); not verbatim.

title.en: The Sixth Course: Arzhang's Head Hurled at His Troops
title.zh: 七關之六：阿爾章之魔伏誅

region.en: Mount Ispuruz camp (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 伊斯普魯茲山營地（象徵性定位）

period: Composed c. 1010 CE (Warner translation 1905)

source.work: Firdausi, Shahnama, trans. A. G. & E. Warner (1905), vol. II, Kai Kaus sec. 11 (Sixth Course)

summary.en: At midnight watch-fires spring up on every side, for the div Arzhang is ever noisy at the entrance of Mazandaran. Rustam binds Ulad to a tree and goes in royal helm and tiger-skin to shout his challenge; the div comes leaping from the camp at that tremendous shout, and Rustam, grasping his head and ears and neck, tears off his head and flings it at his troops; the divs' hearts burst in terror at the sight of Rustam's iron mace, and son and sire go off pell mell.
summary.zh: 夜半四野燃起警戒之火——入口處有魔阿爾章夜夜喧囂。魯斯塔姆縛烏拉德於樹，頂盔披虎皮大喊叫陣；魔自營中躍出，英雄抓住其頭、耳、頸，如獅撕裂其首並擲回敵陣；眾魔見其鐵錘膽裂魂飛，父子倉皇而逃。

sensitivity.note: Epic literary source; no living community restriction.

passages.text: At midnight shoutings went up from the plain; the folk lit watch-fires in Mazandaran and torches everywhere. Then matchless Rustam asked of Ulad: what is the cause that fires are springing up to right and left of us? It is the entrance to Mazandaran, Ulad replied; the more part of each night none dareth sleep; the div Arzhang is there and he is ever noisy. Rustam slept till dawn, then took Ulad, bound him in anguish against a tree, and departed confident and full of ruse.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Firdausi, Shahnama, Kai Kaus sec. 11 (Warner 1905); not verbatim.

passages.text: In royal helm and sweat-soaked tiger-skin he sought, intent on fight, the chief Arzhang, and shouted in the middle of the host; thou wouldst have said the hills and seas are rent! The div Arzhang came leaping from the camp at that tremendous shout, while Rustam spurring came on him like Azargashasp, grasped boldly his head and ears and neck, then lion-like tore off his head and flung it at his troops.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Firdausi, Shahnama, Kai Kaus sec. 11 (Warner 1905); not verbatim.

passages.text: The divs' hearts burst in terror at the sight of Rustam's iron mace, and son and sire, forgetting land and crops, went off pell mell, while Rustam drew his vengeful scimitar and cleared the neighbourhood. At set of sun he made all speed back to Mount Ispuruz, untied Ulad, and hurried on led by Ulad afoot. When he arrived Rakhsh gave a thundering neigh, which Kai Kaus, who heard it, understood and told the Iranians: our evil days are all but over now; I heard the neigh of Rakhsh; it made my heart and spirit young.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Firdausi, Shahnama, Kai Kaus sec. 11 (Warner 1905); not verbatim.

title.en: The Seventh Course: Rustam Wrings the White Div's Neck
title.zh: 七關之七：力搏白魔

region.en: Abysmal cave of the White Div (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 白魔深穴（象徵性定位）

period: Composed c. 1010 CE (Warner translation 1905)

source.work: Firdausi, Shahnama, trans. A. G. & E. Warner (1905), vol. II, Kai Kaus sec. 12 (Seventh Course)

summary.en: Rustam pauses till noon when the divs sleep, then charges the guards, parts heads from trunks, and finds a pit like Hell where a mountain blots all within, with sable face and hair like lion's mane. He will not slay the div asleep but rouses him with a leopard's roar; the White Div seizes a millstone and draves at him like smoke; they wrestle, tearing out each other's flesh, till all the ground is puddled with their blood — if I survive this day, thinks Rustam, I ne'er shall die. At last he reaches out, clutches the div neck-high, dashes the life-breath from him, stabs him to the heart and plucks out the liver.
summary.zh: 魯斯塔姆待至正午魔怪沉睡，直搗巢穴，斬首級如切草；地穴深淵中一個「黑面獅鬃」的山巒擋住一切。他不肯趁睡偷襲，如豹吼醒白魔；白魔抓起磨石擲來如煙；二搏至血流成窪——魯斯塔姆心想：今日不死，則永不死。終於攥住魔頸高高舉起，摔斷其命息，復以匕首刺心，剜出其肝。

sensitivity.note: Epic literary source. The White Div's blood cures the blindness of the captive Shahs — leechcraft motif. No living community restriction.

passages.text: He went girt up, all battle and revenge; he took Ulad and made Rakhsh go like wind. As soon as Rakhsh had reached the seven mountains, with all their troops of valiant divs, the chieftain drew near the abysmal cave, saw them on guard. Ulad made answer: when the sun is hot the divs will sleep and thou wilt overcome them. So Rustam paused till noon, then mounted Rakhsh, unsheathed his warlike Crocodile, and shouted his name like thunder, came like flying dust among the troops, and parted heads from trunks.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Firdausi, Shahnama, Kai Kaus sec. 12 (Warner 1905); not verbatim.

passages.text: Thence radiant as the sun he went to seek the White Div, found a pit like Hell, but saw not the sorcerer for the murk. He rubbed his eyelids, bathed his eyes, and searched the cave till in the gloom he saw a mountain that blotted all within, with sable face and hair like lion's mane, a world to see! Now Rustam hasted not to slay the div asleep, but roused him with a leopard's roar.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Firdausi, Shahnama, Kai Kaus sec. 12 (Warner 1905); not verbatim.

passages.text: He charged at Rustam like a gloomy mountain with iron helm and brassards, seized a millstone and drave at him like smoke. The hero quailed and thought: mine end is come! Yet like a lion enraged he struck full at the div and lopped from that enormous bulk a hand and foot, so mighty was he with his trenchant sword. They wrestled, tearing out each other's flesh, till all the ground was puddled with their blood, and Rustam thought: if I survive this day I ne'er shall die.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Firdausi, Shahnama, Kai Kaus sec. 12 (Warner 1905); not verbatim.

passages.text: While elephantine Rustam in God's strength strove mightily in anguish and revenge, till sore bestead he reached out, clutched the div, raised him neck-high, and dashed the life-breath from him on the ground; then with a dagger stabbed him to the heart and plucked the liver from his swarthy form: the carcase filled the cave, and all the world was like a sea of blood. He came back to Shah Kai Kaus with the liver, and the Shah said: now put the White Div's blood upon mine eyes and those of all my folk. They anointed his dim eyes, which grew as bright as Sol, and forthwith Rustam anointed all the others with the blood; their eyes grew bright, and all the world to them a rosary.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Firdausi, Shahnama, Kai Kaus sec. 12 (Warner 1905); not verbatim.

title.en: Rustam the Envoy Uproots a Tree and an Executioner
title.zh: 使節魯斯塔姆拔樹裂刑吏

region.en: Court of the King of Mazandaran (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 馬贊德蘭王庭（象徵性定位）

period: Composed c. 1010 CE (Warner translation 1905)

source.work: Firdausi, Shahnama, trans. A. G. & E. Warner (1905), vol. II, Kai Kaus secs. 13-14

summary.en: Sent as envoy with Kaus' letter of advice, Rustam uproots a wayside tree before the assembled chiefs and hurls it over their cavaliers; a strength-assayer squeezes his hand and loses his own strength, falling off his steed, and Kalahur the famous duelist has his nails fall off like leaves. The king of Mazandaran defies Iran, orders the envoy seized, and Rustam, roaring like a lion, catches the executioner by the wrists, flings him down, and, holding one foot fast with his own upon the other, rents the man asunder — none e'er saw a sight like that.
summary.zh: 魯斯塔姆奉命持書出使：路旁拔樹擲向列陣騎兵；「試力者」握其手反被捏得力盡墜馬；名劍客卡拉胡爾握其手而指甲如落葉紛紛。馬贊德蘭王傲然拒絕，喝令拿下使者；魯斯塔姆如獅怒吼，抓住刑吏雙腕摔倒在地，一腳踩定另一腳，竟將其撕裂——聞所未聞之狀！

sensitivity.note: Epic literary source; no living community restriction.

passages.text: A skilled scribe wrote upon white silk a letter both kind and harsh, inspiring hope and fear: if God is just why should His laws be broken? Quit thou thy throne and from Mazandaran come, like our other subjects, to our court, and, as thou canst not strive with Rustam, pay such tax and tribute as we may demand. The letter done, the Shah affixed his seal of musk and spicery and sent Farhad to convey to yonder div this letter of advice.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Firdausi, Shahnama, Kai Kaus sec. 13 (Warner 1905); not verbatim.

passages.text: The king read the letter and writhed, then gave his answer: my court is more exalted than thine own; mine are a thousand thousand troops and more; I will lead forth an army lion-like and rouse those heads of yours from their sweet slumbers. Thereat Kaus called Rustam, who said: myself will go to him as envoy; at my words the rivers shall run blood. The Shah replied: the signet and the crown gain light from thee, who art at once ambassador, bold Tiger, and haughty Lion of the battlefield.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Firdausi, Shahnama, Kai Kaus secs. 13-14 (Warner 1905); not verbatim.

passages.text: The letter sealed, aspiring Rustam flung his mace upon the saddle and approached Mazandaran. As he saw the welcoming chiefs he beheld beside the road a spreading tree, seized on two branches, and twisting round the tree with might and main uprooted it, himself unscathed the while, then poised it like a dart, while all the troops looked on astound; as they came up he hurled the tree, whose boughs hid many cavaliers. One of the chiefest of Mazandaran seized Rustam's hand and squeezed it to assay his fortitude in pain, but Rustam laughed while all the company looked on in wonder, and as he laughed he crushed the other's hand.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Firdausi, Shahnama, Kai Kaus sec. 14 (Warner 1905); not verbatim.

passages.text: There was a cavalier hight Kalahur whose fame rang through the land; the king sent him forth to shame the envoy, and Kalahur came lion-like to Rustam and took and squeezed the Elephantine's hand till it turned blue with pain, who bore it lightly and stoutly wrung the hand of Kalahur, whose nails fell off like leaves. The king was wroth and cried: arrest the envoy in my presence, disseat him and behead him. Instantly an executioner approached the throne to seize his wrists, but Rustam, roaring like a lion, caught the executioner's wrists and dragged him close, then flung him down and, holding one foot fast, set his own foot upon the other one and rent the man asunder! None e'er saw a sight like that.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Firdausi, Shahnama, Kai Kaus sec. 14 (Warner 1905); not verbatim.

title.en: The Sorcerer-King Turns to a Boulder
title.zh: 魔王化為巨岩

region.en: Field of Mazandaran (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 馬贊德蘭戰場（象徵性定位）

period: Composed c. 1010 CE (Warner translation 1905)

source.work: Firdausi, Shahnama, trans. A. G. & E. Warner (1905), vol. II, Kai Kaus sec. 15

summary.en: For a week the glory-seeking hosts encounter; on the eighth day Kaus weeps before the Judge and Guide, dons his helm, and joins his famous troops. Elephantine Rustam charges the quarter where the monarch of Mazandaran stands, invokes the name of God, strikes the king's girdle, and pierces him through the mail — and the sorcerer turns to a boulder by his magic arts before the Iranian host. All the strongest of the host essay in vain to move the mass, but Rustam raises it unaided, shoulders the rock, and warns: quit these black arts or else with this sharp steel and battle-ax will I break up the stone; the stone dissolves like mist, the king is seen with a boar's head and tushes, and Rustam hales him from the presence of Kaus to be hewn in pieces.
summary.zh: 兩軍鏖戰七日；第八日卡烏斯泣禱於造物主之前，重披戰甲親征。魯斯塔姆呼神之名直取馬贊德蘭王，擊其腰帶、貫其甲胄——魔王竟施法化作巨岩！全軍之力不能撼動分毫，魯斯塔姆卻獨力舉起扛回營前，喝令其解除妖術否則以斧劈石。岩石如霧消散，現出豬首獠牙的魔形，被拖出宮前碎屍萬段。

sensitivity.note: Epic literary source; no living community restriction.

passages.text: Thus for a week those glory-seeking hosts encountered; on the eighth day Shah Kaus took from his head the royal casque and stood before the Judge and Guide of this world, weeping: O Judge whose word is truth, who madest sea and land! Give me to quell these divs who fear not Thee, and grace for me the throne of king of kings. He donned his helm and joined his famous troops; there rose a shout and trumpet-blare, the host moved like a mountain.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Firdausi, Shahnama, Kai Kaus sec. 15 (Warner 1905); not verbatim.

passages.text: Then elephantine Rustam charged with a mighty power against the quarter where stood the monarch of Mazandaran, who with his divs and elephants of war awhile maintained his ground. Then Rustam gave his pointed lance to one to hold, invoked the name of God, raised high his mace, and raged; his voice filled all the air, the divs became dispirited, the elephants confounded. Then calling for a spear he charged the king; both roared like thunder. When the king beheld the spear of Rustam wrath and courage failed, while Rustam, seething with revenge, sent up a mighty lion's roar, struck the king's girdle, and pierced him through the mail.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Firdausi, Shahnama, Kai Kaus sec. 15 (Warner 1905); not verbatim.

passages.text: The sorcerer turned to a boulder by his magic arts before the Iranian host, while matchless Rustam stood in amaze. I will carry him to camp, perchance he will resume his shape, he said. Then all the strongest of the host essayed in vain to move the mass, howbeit Rustam raised it unaided to the troops' amaze, then shouldering the rock walked off therewith with all the people shouting at his back.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Firdausi, Shahnama, Kai Kaus sec. 15 (Warner 1905); not verbatim.

passages.text: He set a guard and said: quit these black arts and sorceries to take thy proper shape, or else with this sharp steel and battle-ax will I break up the stone. The sorcerer heard, the stone dissolved like mist, the king was seen in helmet and cuirass, but he had a loathly face, a lanky shape and boar's head, neck, and tushes. Kais recalled the past with pain and sighs, then bade a headsman hew the div in pieces, whom matchless Rustam taking by the beard haled from the presence of Kaus. They hewed the div to pieces as the great king bade, and gathered all the booty from the camp.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Firdausi, Shahnama, Kai Kaus sec. 15 (Warner 1905); not verbatim.

title.en: Tane Prop Raki up with Four Posts
title.zh: 塔內四柱撐天：朗基的告別

region.en: Sky and Papa, Aotearoa (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 紐西蘭天與地（象徵性定位）

period: Maori oral tradition; recorded 1887 (White, Nga-i-tahu recension)

source.work: John White, The Ancient History of the Maori, vol. 1, pp. 141-143 (Wellington 1887)
