title.en: 'The Boy Chief': How the Fringe Was Stolen Back for Huayna Capac
title.zh: 「少年君王」:為瓦伊納·卡帕克奪回王纓

region.en: Cuzco and Huanacauri (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 庫斯科與瓦納考里(象徵性標記)

period: Inca tradition as given to Sarmiento de Gamboa, 1572; trans. Markham 1907

source.work: Pedro Sarmiento de Gamboa, History of the Incas, ch. 55-56, trans. Sir Clements Markham, Hakluyt Society, 1907

summary.en: A woman who had been a concubine of the late Inca, named Ccuri Ocllo, a kinswoman of Ccapac Huari, spoke to her relations: 'Know that Tupac Inca is dead and that, when in health, he had named Ccapac Huari for his successor, but at the end, being on the point of death, he said that Titu Cusi Hualpa, son of Mama Ocllo, should succeed him. You ought not to consent to this. Rather call together all your relations and friends, and raise Ccapac Huari, your elder brother, son of Chuqui Ocllo, to be Inca.' The plot became known to the late Inca's brother, Huaman Achachi: he assembled friends, made them arm themselves, went to where Titu Cusi Hualpa was concealed, proceeded to where the friends of Ccapac Huari had assembled, and killed many of them. Ccapac Huari was banished to Chinchero, never allowed to enter Cuzco again; his mother Chuqui Ocllo, a rebel and witch who had killed her lord Tupac Inca, was put to death; the woman Ccuri Ocllo was also killed. The city being pacified, Huaman Achachi went to Quispicancha where Titu Cusi Hualpa was concealed, brought his nephew to the House of the Sun; after the sacrifices and accustomed ceremonies the image of the Sun delivered the fringe to Titu Cusi Hualpa. The new Inca was placed in a rich litter and borne to the huaca Huanacauri, where he offered a sacrifice; the orejones returned to Cuzco by the route taken by Manco Ccapac. Arrived at the first square, called Rimac-pampa, the accession was announced to the people: when they all assembled and saw how young he was, never having seen him before, they all raised their voices and called him Huayna Ccapac, which means 'the boy chief'; for this reason he was called Huayna Ccapac from that time. He also placed, with great solemnity, the caul in which he was born, in the great edifices he erected at Tumipampa where he had himself been born.
summary.zh: 先王生前的一位妾室——庫里·奧克略,卡帕克·瓦里一黨的親族——向親屬喊話:「知道嗎,圖帕克·印加已死!他生前曾立卡帕克·瓦里為儲;但臨終之際,卻改口要瑪瑪·奧克略之子圖帕克·庫西·瓦爾帕繼位。你們豈能依從!快召集親族好友,擁立你們的長兄——楚基·奧克略之子卡帕克·瓦里——為印加王!」此謀為先王之弟瓜曼·阿查奇得知:他召集心腹,披甲執械,先護住藏匿的圖帕克·庫西·瓦爾帕,再突襲卡帕克·瓦里一黨聚會之所,誅殺甚眾。卡帕克·瓦里被放逐欽切羅,至死不得再入庫斯科;其母楚基·奧克略——既係叛黨,又是毒殺其主圖帕克·印加的女巫——被處死;庫里·奧克略亦遭誅。京城既定,瓜曼·阿查奇赴基斯皮坎查迎回藏匿的侄兒,送入太陽之屋;獻祭行禮之後,太陽神像將王纓授予圖帕克·庫西·瓦爾帕。新王乘華轎赴瓦納考里瓦卡獻祭,耳垂貴胄沿曼科·卡帕克當年之路返回庫斯科。抵達第一座廣場——里馬克-潘帕——時,向民眾宣布新王登基:眾人聚攏,見王如此年幼,前所未見,齊聲高呼「瓦伊納·卡帕克」——意即「少年君王」。自此,「圖帕克·庫西·瓦爾帕」之名不再使用,皆稱瓦伊納·卡帕克。他曾在自己出生的通米潘帕大興土木,並以隆重的儀式,將自己出生時的胎衣供奉於彼。

sensitivity.note: Succession coup and counter-coup; the caul relic ties the king's body to his birthplace shrine.

passages.text: The plot of the party of Ccapac Huari became known to the late Inca's brother, Huaman Achachi. He assembled some friends, made them arm themselves, and they went to where Titu Cusi Hualpa was retired and concealed. They then proceeded to where the friends of Ccapac Huari had assembled, and killed many of them, including Ccapac Huari himself... His mother Chuqui Ocllo was taken and, being a rebel as well as a witch who had killed her lord Tupac Inca, she was put to death. Ccapac Huari was banished to Chinchero... never allowed to enter Cuzco again until his death.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Sarmiento, History of the Incas, ch. 55 (Markham 1907); not verbatim.

passages.text: After the sacrifices and accustomed ceremonies, the image of the Sun delivered the fringe to Titu Cusi Hualpa. The new Inca having been invested with all the insignia of Ccapac, and placed in a rich litter, they bore him to the huaca Huanacauri, where he offered a sacrifice. The orejones returned to Cuzco by the route taken by Manco Ccapac. Arrived at the first square, called Rimac-pampa, the accession was announced to the people... they all raised their voices and called him Huayna Ccapac which means 'the boy chief' or 'the boy sovereign.'
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Sarmiento, History of the Incas, ch. 56 (Markham 1907); not verbatim.

canonical_translation: Sir Clements Markham, History of the Incas (Hakluyt Society, 1907)

title.en: The Lake Coloured with Blood, and the Drum Made of Pinto's Skin
title.zh: 血染之湖與以平托之皮製成的鼓

region.en: Lake Yahuar-cocha, near Ibarra, Ecuador (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 厄瓜多伊瓦拉附近亞瓦爾-科查湖(象徵性標記)

period: Inca tradition as given to Sarmiento de Gamboa, 1572; trans. Markham 1907

source.work: Pedro Sarmiento de Gamboa, History of the Incas, ch. 60, trans. Sir Clements Markham, Hakluyt Society, 1907

summary.en: Auqui Toma attacked the fortress of the Cayambis, captured four lines of defence and the outer wall, which was composed of five; but at the entrance the Cayambis killed Auqui Toma, captain of the Cuzcos, who had fought most valorously. The attack and defence was so obstinate and long continued that an immense number of men fell, and the survivors had nowhere to fight except upon heaps of dead men. The desire of both sides to conquer or die was so strong that they gave up their lances and arrows and took to their fists. At last, when they saw that their captain was killed, the Incas began to retreat towards a river into which they went without any care for saving their lives; the river was in flood and a great number of men were drowned. Huayna Ccapac was not dismayed; he marched in person, sent Michi with a third of the army to pass on one side of the fortress without being seen, feigned a flight, drew the Cayambis out in pursuit, and while they were at a distance the detachment entered the fortress and set it on fire. The Cayambis fled towards a lake, thinking to hide among the reeds; the Inca gave instructions that the lake should be surrounded, and in the lake and the swamps on its borders the troops made such havock and slaughter, fighting most furiously in person, that the lake was coloured with the blood of the dead Cayambis: from that time forward the lake has been called Yahuar-cocha, the lake of blood. In the middle of this lake there was an islet with two willow trees, up which some Cayambis climbed, among them their two chiefs named Pinto and Canto, most valiant Indians. The troops of Huayna Ccapac pelted them with stones and captured Canto, but Pinto escaped with a thousand brave Canaris. When at last Pinto surrendered after his hide-out was surrounded and hunger forced him, he had such hatred against Huayna Ccapac that even after his capture, when the Inca had presented him with gifts and treated him kindly, he never could see his face; so he died out of his mind, and Huayna Ccapac ordered a drum to be made of his skin. The drum was sent to Cuzco, and so this war came to an end: it was at Cuzco in the taqui or dance in honour of the Sun.
summary.zh: 奧基·托馬攻打卡揚比要塞,連破四道防線與外牆(共五道);然而在要塞入口,卡揚比人殺死了驍勇無雙的庫斯科統帥奧基·托馬。此役攻防相持之久、之烈,死傷無數,倖存者竟只能踩著屍山而戰;雙方勝負之志如此決絕,索性棄了長矛弓箭,赤手相搏。最後,印加人見主帥已亡,向河邊潰退——不顧死活地跳入正在暴漲的河中,大批人馬溺斃。瓦伊納·卡帕克不以為餒,親自督師:遣米奇率三分之一兵力潛行繞至要塞一側,自己佯敗而走,誘卡揚比人出城追擊;敵軍既遠,奇兵直入要塞,四處縱火。卡揚比人見老巢火起,逃往湖畔,想藏身蘆葦叢中。瓦伊納·卡帕克下令四面圍湖,親自奮戰最烈;湖中湖畔殺戮之慘,湖水竟被卡揚比死者的血染紅——此湖從此名為「亞瓦爾-科查」,血湖。湖心有一小洲,洲上兩株柳樹;一些卡揚比人攀上樹去,其中有其二酋——平托與坎托,皆至勇之士。印加兵以石投之,擒坎托;平托卻帶一千卡尼亞里勇士脫逃,遁入林莽。後來印加王圍其藏身之地,斷糧迫使平托出降。平托勇烈蓋世,恨瓦伊納·卡帕克入骨:縱然王以厚禮相待、善待有加,他始終不肯與王見面;終至瘋癲而死。瓦伊納·卡帕克命人以他的皮蒙鼓,送至庫斯科——就在祭祀太陽的舞樂「塔基」中使用。這場戰爭就此了結。

sensitivity.note: The Yahuar-cocha etiology (a real lake name near Ibarra) and the skin-drum trophy of the Sun dance.

passages.text: This attack and defence was so obstinate and long continued that an immense number of men fell, and the survivors had nowhere to fight except upon heaps of dead men. The desire of both sides to conquer or die was so strong that they gave up their lances and arrows and took to their fists... The river was in flood and a great number of men were drowned.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Sarmiento, History of the Incas, ch. 60 (Markham 1907); not verbatim.

passages.text: In order that none might escape he gave instructions that the lake should be surrounded. In that lake, and the swamps on its borders, the troops of Huayna Ccapac, he fighting most furiously in person, made such havock and slaughter, that the lake was coloured with the blood of the dead Cayambis. From that time forward the lake has been called Yahuar-cocha, which means the 'lake of blood.'
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Sarmiento, History of the Incas, ch. 60 (Markham 1907); not verbatim.

passages.text: This Pinto was very brave and he had such hatred against Huayna Ccapac that even, after his capture, when the Inca had presented him with gifts and treated him kindly, he never could see his face. So he died out of his mind, and Huayna Ccapac ordered a drum to be made of his skin. The drum was sent to Cuzco, and so this war came to an end. It was at Cuzco in the taqui or dance in honour of the Sun.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Sarmiento, History of the Incas, ch. 60 (Markham 1907); not verbatim.

canonical_translation: Sir Clements Markham, History of the Incas (Hakluyt Society, 1907)

title.en: Kaus Weds Sudaba and Loses His Freedom
title.zh: 卡烏斯娶蘇達貝而失自由

region.en: Hamavaran (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 哈馬瓦蘭（象徵性定位）

period: Composed c. 1010 CE (Warner translation 1905)

source.work: Firdausi, Shahnama, trans. A. G. & E. Warner (1905), vol. II, Kai Kaus Part II secs. 1-4

summary.en: Flushed with his Mazandaran triumph, Kai Kaus marches on Hamavaran, demands the king's daughter Sudaba in marriage, and is made prisoner with all his host by the crafty king. The news reaches Zabul, and Afrasiyab, scenting Iran leaderless, invades the land. In the Zamyad Yasht this is the moment when Afrasiyab is recorded to have seized at last the kingly Glory which Zahhak himself sought in vain.
summary.zh: 馬贊德蘭大捷後，卡烏斯揮師哈馬瓦蘭，索娶國王之女蘇達貝，卻中奸計連同全軍被擒。消息傳到扎布勒；阿弗拉西亞卜趁伊朗無主而入侵。《扎姆亞德頌》記載：此時阿弗拉西亞卜終於奪得連扎哈克都求而不得的王權光榮。

sensitivity.note: Epic literary source. Cross-ref: Zamyad Yasht's account of Frangrasyan seizing the xvarənah (glory); cf. persian-rustam-course-lion context. No living community restriction.

passages.text: How Kai Kaus warred with the King of Hamavaran: the Shah, flushed with victory over Mazandaran, heard that the king of Hamavaran had a daughter named Sudaba, fairer than sun or moon. He demanded her to wife, and the wily king used the occasion to entrap him.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Firdausi, Shahnama, Kai Kaus Part II secs. 1-2 (Warner 1905); not verbatim.

passages.text: When the Shah was within his reach the king of Hamavaran made Kaus prisoner with his host, and the throne of Iran stood empty of its master. News came to Zabul, and Afrasiyab, hearing that Iran was Shahless and its army leaderless, invaded the land.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Firdausi, Shahnama, Kai Kaus Part II secs. 3-4 (Warner 1905); not verbatim.

title.en: Rustam Fights Three Kings and Frees Kaus
title.zh: 魯斯塔姆力戰三王救主

region.en: Plains of Hamavaran (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 哈馬瓦蘭平原（象徵性定位）

period: Composed c. 1010 CE (Warner translation 1905)

source.work: Firdausi, Shahnama, trans. A. G. & E. Warner (1905), vol. II, Kai Kaus Part II sec. 6

summary.en: Rustam arrays his forces against the armies of three monarchs and three realms, with eight score elephants of Barbaristan foaming like the Nile and a hundred more of Hamavaran: keep your eyelashes well apart to-day, he harangues; be the foe a hundred or a hundred thousand horse, their sum importeth not. Deigning not to slaughter common folk he charges the king of Sham and lassoes him, snatching him from the saddle like a ball struck by a polo-stick. The king of Barbar and forty chiefs are taken, the king of Hamavaran asks quarter, gives up Kaus and the treasures, and three hosts disband.
summary.zh: 魯斯塔姆列陣對抗三王聯軍：巴巴里斯坦八頭象口沫如尼羅河，哈馬瓦蘭又添百象。他訓誡部眾：「睜大雙眼盯緊矛尖；敵軍百人萬人，皆不足懼。」他不屑屠戮小卒，直取沙姆之王，套索擒之如擊馬球般擲落；巴巴里國王與四十酋長就擒；哈馬瓦蘭王乞降獻出卡烏斯，三軍解散。

sensitivity.note: Epic literary source; no living community restriction.

passages.text: Next day they set the battle in array and raised their standards. When the peerless Rustam had led his forces to the field and viewed the armies of three monarchs and three realms, he thus harangued his noble warriors: keep your eyelashes well apart to-day, and look to mane and forelock, steed and rein, with both eyes on your spearpoints. Be the foe a hundred or a hundred thousand horse, their sum importeth not, for, since the All-holy is our ally, I will bring down their heads to dust.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Firdausi, Shahnama, Kai Kaus Part II sec. 6 (Warner 1905); not verbatim.

passages.text: Barbaristan sent eight score elephants all foaming like the Nile, Hamavaran contributed a hundred more, huge beasts, and thirdly was arrayed the power of Misr. The atmosphere was darkened, earth was hidden, and thou hadst said: the world is all of iron. Then were the claws and hearts of lions rent, and lusty eagles flung their plumes away, for how could anything oppose such troops?
passages.note: Paraphrase of Firdausi, Shahnama, Kai Kaus Part II sec. 6 (Warner 1905); not verbatim.

passages.text: The peerless hero urged on Rakhsh and, deigning not to slaughter common folk, charged at the king of Sham and lassoed him, then snatched him from the saddle, like a ball struck by a polo-stick, and flung him down. They captured sixty of name and deluged plain and hill with blood; the monarch of Barbar and forty chiefs were taken prisoners, and when the monarch of Hamavaran beheld valiant Rustam creating Doomsday on the battlefield he felt this day is one of bale, and sent to Rustam to ask quarter, promising to give up Kai Kaus and restore the treasures, crowns, and jewels. They made a peace and then disbanded three hosts; the monarch of Hamavaran went home, sent and fetched Kaus, and righted him.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Firdausi, Shahnama, Kai Kaus Part II sec. 6 (Warner 1905); not verbatim.

title.en: Kaus Ascends the Sky on the Eagle Throne
title.zh: 卡烏斯乘鷹輦登天

region.en: Forest near Amul (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 阿穆爾附近森林（象徵性定位）

period: Composed c. 1010 CE (Warner translation 1905)

source.work: Firdausi, Shahnama, trans. A. G. & E. Warner (1905), vol. II, Kai Kaus Part II secs. 9-10

summary.en: Iblis sends a shrewd div as a flattering youth to wean Kaus from God: heaven is thy fit home and earth thy slave; now take the heaven also in thy toils. The Shah, though the sky is ladderless and though stars be many, God but One, feeds eaglets a year on lamb and kabab, builds an aloe-wood throne with lamb's legs hung from the spear-tips, and ties the ravenous birds to it; they strive for the flesh and bear throne, spears, and Shah cloudward — and long flew the eagles, but they stopped at last, sulking exhausted, and brought the Shah down to a forest near Amul, where he tarried in shame, imploring relief from Almighty God.
summary.zh: 伊布利斯遣巧魔化為諂媚青年：「天堂才是你的歸宿；如今把天空也納入掌握吧！」卡烏斯不知「天梯之不存在、星辰雖眾神唯一」，以羊腿懸於輦角、縛饑鷹於寶座，鷹爭食而起，載王與矛輦沖天——然而鷹終有盡時，筋疲力盡地將王摔落阿穆爾森林；羞愧的王在林中祈求真主寬宥。

sensitivity.note: Epic literary source. Hubris-flight motif paralleling Icarus/Bellerophon; Warner notes alternate versions of the motive. No living community restriction.

passages.text: One dawn Iblis, unknown to Kai Kaus, addressed the assembled divs: our daily task is one of cruel labour for the Shah; we need a div shrewd and presentable to tempt him, soil his Grace, wean him from God, and thus abate his tyranny. At length a wicked div arose and said: be mine this subtile task; I will pervert his mind from God as none but I can do.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Firdausi, Shahnama, Kai Kaus Part II sec. 9 (Warner 1905); not verbatim.

passages.text: Appearing as a youth of good address and mien, he waited till the famous Shah went hunting from Pahlav, approached with roses to present, then kissed the ground and said: thy glory and thy Grace are such that heaven is thy fit home and earth thy slave. How is it that the sun concealeth from thee the secret of its rising and its setting? What is the moon? Thou hast the earth and all thou didst desire; now take the heaven also in thy toils.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Firdausi, Shahnama, Kai Kaus Part II sec. 9 (Warner 1905); not verbatim.

passages.text: The Shah's heart strayed, he tarried not to think, convinced that turning heaven favoured him. He knew not that the sky is ladderless, nor that, though stars be many, God but One. He bade men scale the aeries while the eagles were sleeping, had those eaglets fed a year and more with fowl, kabab, and at some whiles with lamb; when they were strong as lions he made a throne of aloe from Kumar with seats of gold, bound a lengthy spear at every corner, suspended a lamb's leg from every spear-head, brought four strong eagles, tied them to the throne, and took his seat, a cup of wine before him.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Firdausi, Shahnama, Kai Kaus Part II sec. 9 (Warner 1905); not verbatim.

passages.text: The swift-winged eagles, ravenous for food, strove lustily to reach the flesh, and raising the throne above earth's surface bore it cloudward. Kaus essayed the sky to outsoar angels. Long flew the eagles, but they stopped at last, like other slaves of greed; they sulked exhausted, they drooped their sweating wings and brought the Shah, his spears, and throne down from the clouds to earth, alighting in a forest near Amul. The world preserved him by a miracle; in answer to his prayers a duck appeared, for something must be had to eat and drink; instead of sitting on his throne in might his business then was penitence and travail, and he tarried in the wood in shame and grief imploring from Almighty God relief.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Firdausi, Shahnama, Kai Kaus Part II sec. 9 (Warner 1905); not verbatim.

title.en: Aukele Wins the Water of Life in the Far-off Helani
title.zh: 奧克勒遠國取生命之水

region.en: Kua-i-Helani, far-away Helani (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 遙遠的海拉尼（象徵性定位）

period: Hawaiian oral tradition (Aukele-nui-a-Iku chant); retold 1917 (Westervelt)

source.work: W. D. Westervelt, Hawaiian Historical Legends, ch. 3 (New York 1917)

summary.en: The Self-reliant Dragon arms the youngest son Aukele with a bamboo stick holding Lono's image, a food-leaf, and her own skin - a cloak that shatters enemies into ashes. His warrior brothers wreck the mission by calling their boat a war canoe and are destroyed; Aukele alone survives to marry the chiefess, defeat the cannibal god Ku-waha-ilo - father of Pele - and, grieving for his drowned brothers, fly toward the sunrise for Kane's living water: past the moon ancestress whose food thins her to a new moon, into the pit of watchmen, past the dirty calabash, to the pure water of life which sprinkles his brothers back to standing.
summary.zh: 自信龍神以竹杖賜予幼子奧克勒：內藏龍諾神像、取之不竭的食葉與她自剝的神皮——披之則敵化飛灰。好戰的兄長們自毀使命、命喪海底；唯奧克勒倖存，娶得女酋，擊敗佩蕾之父——食人神庫瓦希伊洛。為救溺亡的兄長，他朝日出行空遠征：途經啃薄自己化為新月的月亮祖母，躍過守水者的深坑，辨別濁水與真水，終以生命之水灑海，喚起沉船中的兄弟。

sensitivity.note: Water-of-life cluster, Hawaiian Aukele-nui-a-Iku recension.

passages.text: The Self-reliant Dragon is frequently mentioned in the oldest Hawaiian legends; she dwelt in one of the mysterious islands mentioned in the Hawaiian chants as Kua-i-Helani, the Far-away Helani, lying in the ancient far western home of the Polynesians. Iku was the chief, and the youngest of his sons was Aukele-nui-a-Iku, Aukele the Great Son of Iku. Aukele was a favorite of the Self-reliant Dragon; she gave him a large bamboo stick, inside which she placed an image of the god Lono, and also a magic leaf which could provide plenty of food for any one who touched the leaf to his lips, and put in a part of her own skin. She said, 'This skin is a cloak for you. If you lift it up against any enemies, they will fall to pieces as dust and ashes.' The brothers, who were great warriors, determined to sail away, find a new land and conquer it by fighting; Aukele persuaded them to take him.
passages.note: Paraphrase of W. D. Westervelt, Hawaiian Historical Legends, ch. 3 (1917); not verbatim.

passages.text: After a long time on the sea all their food was gone and they were starving and lying in the bottom of the boat; Aukele fed them from the leaf which he touched to their lips. Some days passed and Aukele said, 'To-morrow we will come to a land where a woman is the ruler; let me tell why we journey.' The chiefess of that land looked out and saw a boat in the ocean, and sent some birds to see what the boat was doing and learn whether it was a war canoe or a travelling boat; Aukele wanted his brothers to say it was a travelling boat, but the birds asked and the brothers said, 'This is a war canoe.' The birds went away. Aukele took up the bamboo stick and threw it in the sea, and leaped in after it. The brothers threw the cloak of Aukele on the beach; the chiefess found the cloak and shook it toward the boat, then threw it away - the brothers broke into small dust and were destroyed, the boat and the brothers sinking to the bottom of the sea. Aukele swam to the beach, pulled up his stick, found his cloak, lay down under a tree and slept.
passages.note: Paraphrase of W. D. Westervelt, Hawaiian Historical Legends, ch. 3 (1917); not verbatim.

passages.text: A watchdog came out and smelled the man and barked; the chiefess called two women and told them to see who it was and, if they found any one, kill him. The women came and he greeted them, knowing their names; they were ashamed because he had found their names, and one said, 'What can we give him for naming us?' - 'We will let him be the husband of our ruler.' The chiefess turned the dog out again; at once there was more barking, and she told her bird brothers to go and look over the land. Lono told Aukele: 'When they come you say their names quickly and welcome them.' This knowledge gave him power over them, and they could not harm him. When he went up to the house he stood at the door; the dog ran out and tried to bite Aukele through the magic cloak, and the dog became ashes. The brothers came with food put in moss-covered calabashes; he never touched it - it was the death food; he went to where green calabash vines were growing, took a calabash, broke it and found good food inside. Then they lived as man and wife; the chiefess had been a cannibal but at this time stopped eating men. Soon a son was born.
passages.note: Paraphrase of W. D. Westervelt, Hawaiian Historical Legends, ch. 3 (1917); not verbatim.

passages.text: The chiefess told her brothers to go away into the heavens and find her father, Ku-waha-ilo, a cannibal god, also the father of Pele, the goddess of volcanic fire. The father saw Aukele flying and was angry. Lono told Aukele to put on his magic cloak; the cannibal father made fire, called Kuku-ena, the lightning, and Ikuwa, a stone crashing like thunder; the lightning and the crashing stone were struck by the cloak and rattled into ashes. After the battle the bird brothers told their father that the daughter was well and this was her husband. After this flight and this victory over the cannibal god, Aukele returned to his wife. After a time the ghosts of his brothers appeared to him and reminded him of their grave in the sea; Aukele ate nothing for days, and his wife told him if he had strength enough to find the living water of Kane he could still restore his brothers. She made a straight line toward the East, the sunrise, and told him to fly straight, not swerving to either side.
passages.note: Paraphrase of W. D. Westervelt, Hawaiian Historical Legends, ch. 3 (1917); not verbatim.

passages.text: He thought he was flying in a straight line, but one arm became tired because the stick was under it; he changed the stick, and this moved his direction. His god saw this and told him he was leaving the straight line and flying to some other place. There was fire far below; all the people had fled except one. 'Let us go straight till we come to that one; then you catch him and hold him fast; we shall have life.' This was the moon, who was an ancestress of his wife; the moon had been cooking food, and she arose to take up her food and get ready to go; but Aukele caught her, held her and ate her food - she thus became thin, a new moon, and the traveller gained strength to return to his home. Aukele tried again according to his wife's line: he flew straight a long time until he found a strange land with a deep pit lined with trees and wonderful plants, at the bottom the spring of the water of life. He leaped down upon the back of a watchman on the edge of the pit, who had been put there to kill any one coming after the water; 'Who are you? My grandchild, the brother of Pele, never got on my back. Who are you?' Aukele gave his name and ancestors, and told the watchman he had come for the water of life for his brothers.
passages.note: Paraphrase of W. D. Westervelt, Hawaiian Historical Legends, ch. 3 (1917); not verbatim.

passages.text: The watchman told him to fly to another watchman, who told him to go straight to the bottom of the pit: 'There a blind woman will be sitting. Look at the place where she is cooking bananas. She will take them one by one; you eat all her bananas. Then she will become angry and throw ashes; if she throws on the right side you must fly to the left; watch if she strikes with a stick, then run quickly, sit in her lap, and tell her who you are.' When he had done all these things and all attempts to kill him had failed, Aukele made the old blind woman lie down under a cocoanut tree, got two young cocoanuts and told her to turn her eyes toward the sky; he dropped the cocoanuts in her eyes; she wept sorely because of the pain, rubbed the water out of her eyes and said, 'I can see you.' She told him what he must do to get the water of life: bring the stem of a water plant and a bush with white flowers; she squeezed the water from the plants into a cup, took charcoal and mixed them until black, then painted Aukele's hands very black, like the hands of the brother of Pele - those watching the water of life would look at the hands reaching for water and make no mistake; they would tightly cover up the water if a white hand came down. 'Wait until the guardian god is asleep; then go to the door and one will give you some water. The first will be dirty water; throw it away. Put your hand down again; they will give you another calabash of water. This will be the living water of Kane; take it.' He went down and put his hand in for the water; the watchman handed out a calabash of dirty water, he threw it away and again thrust his black hand down the pit, and the watchman gave him a calabash of the pure water of life. He flew rapidly along the path to the outside world; in his haste he struck the leaves of the groves of trees, and the sound swept through the land of the water of life like rolling thunder. The brother of Pele and his servants awoke and followed, but Aukele fled through the heavens to the place where the ghosts of his brothers lay in the sunken ship. The chiefess told her husband to pour the water of life in his hand; she put her fingers in the water and sprinkled drops over the sea. Out in the ocean under the moving surface was a boat, its mast coming up through the waves; in a little while they saw men standing in the boat - these were the brothers of Aukele. After the welcome, he gave them lands and homes. In that strange far-off land of the ancestors - the mysterious Floating Island, the Hidden Island of Kane - it is said they still live under the rule of their younger brother.
passages.note: Paraphrase of W. D. Westervelt, Hawaiian Historical Legends, ch. 3 (1917); not verbatim.

title.en: Hawaii-loa, the First Viking of the Pacific
title.zh: 夏威夷洛亞：太平洋首位航海王

region.en: Land of Kane to Hawaiian islands (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 卡內之土至夏威夷群島（象徵性定位）

period: Hawaiian chant tradition (Kumu Honua); retold 1917 (Westervelt)

source.work: W. D. Westervelt, Hawaiian Historical Legends, ch. 4 (New York 1917)

summary.en: The Polynesian meles rival the Viking sagas: bold expeditions, stirring adventures, voyages to far-off lands, naming each new country. In the long chant of Kumu Honua, the first created, Hawaii-loa is the first sea-king of the Polynesians, reported as making long journeys and discovering the Hawaiian Islands - an ancestor of islands rather than of families, who lived in the land of the handsome golden god Kane, near the green precipiced paradise where the water of life gave forth healing even for the dead.
summary.zh: 波利尼西亞之歌可與北歐維京薩迦媲美：壯舉與遠航層見疊出，所到之地皆以己意命名。在『初造者』庫穆霍努阿的長篇頌歌中，夏威夷洛亞是波利尼西亞首位海上王者——遠航發現夏威夷群島，成為島嶼而非宗族之祖。他居於金神卡內的土地，鄰近生命之水湧流、連死者亦可癒合的翠崖樂園。

sensitivity.note: Ethnogenetic tradition; Westervelt's Viking comparison retained as framing.

passages.text: History is frequently legendary. Legends are the indistinct memories of nations, and are of real value when there is any opportunity for comparison. Early Norse history was told in song legends; the sagas of the Vikings are rivalled in some measure by the meles of the Hawaiians. The Hawaiians have both the chant - the mele, and the tradition - the olelo; from these come Hawaiian ancient history. The Vikings, sea kings, the men who sailed out from the vicks, the fjords of the Scandinavian coast, were brave mariners; they swept the European coast, infested Mediterranean waters, found the North Atlantic islands, and named the countries newly discovered after their own fancies. The Polynesian folklore abounds in stories of remarkable men, bold expeditions, stirring adventures and voyages to far-off lands; the Vikings of the Pacific gave to their foreign lands the names by which these lands were then known and by which they are known to-day.
passages.note: Paraphrase of W. D. Westervelt, Hawaiian Historical Legends, ch. 4 (1917); not verbatim.

passages.text: In the long Hawaiian chant of Kumu Honua, the first created, there is a part devoted to Hawaii-loa, the first sea-king of the Polynesians. He is reported as making long journeys and discovering the Hawaiian Islands; besides this chant there are many legends and references which make him an important ancestor among Hawaiians, an ancestor of islands rather than of families. He lived in the land of the handsome or golden god Kane; to the north lay the land Ulu-nui, the Great Ulu; his home was near the green precipiced paradise of Hawaiian legend, the place where the water of life gave forth healing even for the dead.
passages.note: Paraphrase of W. D. Westervelt, Hawaiian Historical Legends, ch. 4 (1917); not verbatim.

title.en: Paao Sails from Samoa to the Voice of Hawaii
title.zh: 帕阿奧自薩摩亞循聲赴夏威夷

region.en: Upolu, Samoa, to Puna, Hawaii (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 自薩摩亞烏波盧至夏威夷普納（象徵性定位）

period: Hawaiian tradition dated c. 1100 CE; retold 1917 (Westervelt)

source.work: W. D. Westervelt, Hawaiian Historical Legends, ch. 7 (New York 1917)

summary.en: On Upolu the priest Paao, accused by his elder brother Lonopele of fruit-theft, slays his own son and opens his stomach to prove innocence - then, in anger, kills Lonopele's son and flees north. Storms, a magic bird pouring waves, fish pushing the boats, and at last a wind with no salt in it: 'I hear no voice - Hawaii! Hawaii!! and the strong voice of the Maile blossoms... The fingers of the morning touch the mountains of Hawaii.' He lands in state, builds Wahaula temple, and his priestly line runs to Hewahewa, who burned the same temples seven hundred years later.
summary.zh: 烏波盧島祭司帕阿奧遭兄長誣子竊果，竟剖愛子之腹以自證清白——繼而憤殺兄子，舉族北逃。途中風暴驟起、魔鳥傾浪、群魚推舟，直至聞得那無鹹味的風：『夏威夷！夏威夷！邁蕾花香嘹亮，甘蔗低吟，麵包果呼喚——晨曦的手指已觸到夏威夷的群山。』他盛裝登陸，建瓦豪拉神廟；其祭司世系綿延至赫瓦赫瓦——七百年後親手焚毀同廟之人。

sensitivity.note: Child-sacrifice episode recorded as in the tradition; Paao is the traditional founder of the Hawaiian high-priest line.

passages.text: Hawaiians never reckoned history by dates, but by genealogies, as did the Hebrews; they measured time not by the years but by the lives of men, not by the days passed but by the deeds done. When Ka-meha-meha became king of the Rainbow Islands his royal chant took the supreme place: he traced his royal blood to Pili, from a foreign land, and through Pili back to Wa-kea, a Polynesian chief of perhaps the second century, and thence back through a series of hero-gods to Kumu-Honua, the first created. Not far from the year 1100 A.D., two priest brothers were living on Upolu, one of the Samoan Islands: Lonopele, the elder, lived in one of the luxurious valleys opening upon the seacoast; Paao, the younger, was a seaman as well as a priest, and lived near the beach, where he kept a small fleet of canoes.
passages.note: Paraphrase of W. D. Westervelt, Hawaiian Historical Legends, ch. 7 (1917); not verbatim.

passages.text: In some way bitter feeling arose between the two households. One day Lonopele came to the temple where his brother was making ready to sacrifice a sacred black hog, and cried, 'Where are you, O Paao, that you prepare a sacrifice for the favour of the gods, when you do not watch your oldest boy? Some of my choice fruits, brought from Tahiti, are beginning to ripen; and each night Kaino, your son, creeps under the low branches and gathers whatever is good.' 'It is false!' angrily replied the father. Theft was considered the greatest of crimes among the Polynesians. 'No! It is true. He is coming even now from his feast. If he touches my fruit again he shall die. It is tabu.' The boy came near, evidently having just been eating. 'Have you taken fruit from Lonopele in the night?' 'No. I have fruit at home, but better are the baked dog and fish; I would not eat his fruit.' Lonopele became angry and cried out: 'May the god, Kanaloa, curse you and break your body into fragments, for your falsehood.' 'Cut open my stomach, O my uncle, and I shall be proved innocent.' Paao determined to substitute his son for the sacrifice he was preparing, and thus prove his guilt or innocence; no trace of fruit was found in the body. Lonopele bowed his head in shame and hastened away. The Hawaiian traditions say that after this act he determined to leave Upolu, and agreed with a few trusted friends to prepare their large canoes and go with him, seeking the Burning-Java, or Hawaii, somewhere toward the north.
passages.note: Paraphrase of W. D. Westervelt, Hawaiian Historical Legends, ch. 7 (1917); not verbatim.

passages.text: The sides of the boats were to be built two or three feet higher, hewing boards with stone axes and sewing them to each other through holes drilled by bones, using cords of cocoanut fibre for thread - thus canoes were prepared capable of carrying thirty to sixty persons; dried bananas, pigs, fish and pounded taro were made ready. One day Paao saw his brother's son coming near the boats, and in a fit of anger rushed upon the boy and slew him. Lonopele soon discovered the murder and made war upon Paao. Paao and his friends launched their canoes as fast as possible, placing in them their families and such provisions as were at hand; his warriors, defeated by Lonopele, hastened to the canoes and shoved out into the deep waters. The battle was evidently fierce, for the legends say that some of the prophet friends who could not escape to their canoes leaped from the precipitous cliffs to fly to the boats, and were dashed to pieces on the rocks below. One of the priest-friends leaped into the water, calling for Paao to return and rescue him. 'Not so', answered Paao, 'we have left the shore; it would be an evil omen to turn back. We will wait for you where we are.' The legends say the priest flew like a bird to the canoes and was warmly received. Lonopele sent a storm to destroy the canoes; two great fish aided the fugitives - the Aku pushed the boats, and the Opelea hindered the storm waves by opposing his great body and breaking their force. Lonopele ordered his magic bird to take up great waves of water and pour them from the sky, overwhelming the fugitives; the canoe-men hurriedly arranged mats covering the boats, and the water was turned into the sea. Thus they escaped.
passages.note: Paraphrase of W. D. Westervelt, Hawaiian Historical Legends, ch. 7 (1917); not verbatim.

passages.text: The days passed; sometimes showers fell upon the mats arranged like funnels, filling the water calabashes afresh; sometimes they passed through a school of fish and caught all they could, drying them for future use; some died and descended to the bountiful islands in the world under the waters; some of the canoes were abandoned. One day Paao said: 'I was watching the stars last night and my thought is that some water-god has put his hands under our boats and moved us away from Hawaii.' That night Paao could not sleep; he studied the stars; he felt a breeze that seemed to him in some way different from the ordinary sea-breezes. 'Do you feel the new wind from the eastern star?' he said softly to his steersmen. 'Aye! we have to hold the steering paddles more firmly.' Paao awakened his prophet and whispered: 'Does the new wind have a voice for you?' The prophet sniffed the air, then stepped upon the high prow and breathed again. 'Aye, the wind has the voice of smoke, perhaps the smoke of the burning-mountain. Say nothing about the voice; we will change our course and sail toward the bright star.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of W. D. Westervelt, Hawaiian Historical Legends, ch. 7 (1917); not verbatim.

passages.text: In the very early morning of the third day, as Paao was restlessly looking eastward, his wife crept to his side: 'O my Paao, I am about to die. I have just dreamed of the green-walled paradise; I smelled the sweet Maile blossoms and the leaves of our marriage wreath; I saw the spirits of my sons stand by the cocoanut tree. The vision is from the gods; I must surely die.' 'Hush', said Paao quickly, 'I too have heard the voice of the Maile born on the winds but I was awake. You shall not die. Call the astrologer, and then listen to his words.' The astrologer came quickly; Paao handed his friend a calabash with a little precious water, bidding him bathe his parched mouth and nostrils. 'Now what do the winds say?' 'Hawaii! Hawaii!! and the strong voice of the Maile blossoms, and the gentle voice of the sugar-cane. I can hear the bread-fruit call Come and eat. The Lau-hala's voice comes over the sea. Awake, awake, oh canoe-men! The fingers of the morning touch the mountains of Hawaii; the morning is raising its hand to beckon us on. O friends of the canoes, awake! Hear the land voices. Hear the wind that has no salt in it. Awake and hear Hawaii.' In a moment shouts and songs of gladness were heard from all the canoes; new life, new strength pervaded the weakened wanderers, and the steersmen unconsciously changed the course of the boats toward the blue haze of land outlined by the dawn. Bundles of feather robes were unrolled; native cloth, brilliantly coloured, was taken from its wrappings; Paao robed himself in a high-priest's tabu mantle of black feathers, wearing a white helmet ornamented with black plumes. Thus, as the new morning dawned, they came to Hawaii; thus they landed as if their journey had known nothing of starvation and death. The language of the newcomers was almost identical in meaning and pronunciation with the native tongue; the priests with new gods were received with offerings, food and clothing in abundance were given, and land in Puna, near Hilo, was set apart for their dwelling-place. Paao, aided by the Hawaiians, at once built a temple at Wahaula, which after being twice restored was destroyed in 1820. From Paao the high priest's family, highest in priestly rank of all dwelling in the islands, was perpetuated until Ka-meha-meha's high priest, Hewa-hewa, a lineal descendant of Paao, in 1819 aided in destroying the temples of the gods - with his own hands Hewa-hewa set fire to shrines and idols, overthrowing the system of worship and sacred tabu which Paao had established nearly 700 years before.
passages.note: Paraphrase of W. D. Westervelt, Hawaiian Historical Legends, ch. 7 (1917); not verbatim.

title.en: Neva and Taife: the Good Spirit and the Bad Spirit of the North-West Amazons
title.zh: 涅瓦與泰費：西北亞馬遜善靈與惡靈

region.en: Issa-Japura region, Witoto-Boro country
region.zh: 伊薩-哈普拉河維托托-博羅之地

period: Witoto-Boro oral tradition; recorded 1915 (Whiffen)

source.work: Thomas Whiffen, The North-West Amazons (1915), ch. XVII 'The Indians' Magico-Religious System'

summary.en: So far as these Indians believe in anything they believe in the existence of supreme good and bad spirits. The Good Spirit — Neva in Boro, Usiyamoi in Witoto, the Tupano of the Tupi-Guarani — is a spirit of benevolent passivity, good for no other reason than that he is not evil; no prayer or invocation is offered to him. The Bad Spirit — Navena in Boro, Taife in Witoto, whose dread true name Apuehana is never pronounced above a whisper — is affirmative in character and always active: he must be placated at all costs as the supreme author of sickness and misfortune. The Bad Spirit may be materialised sufficiently to carry a child bodily away or steal a woman should she stray into the forest by herself; women who run away from their husbands are consequently said by them to have been taken by the devil.
summary.zh: 維托托-博羅人信至善至惡二靈。善靈博羅名涅瓦，維托托名烏西亞莫伊——靜而不動，以其非惡故為善；無祈無禱。惡靈博羅名納維納，維托托名泰費，真名阿普埃哈納惟耳語乃出——恆動而為病厄之首，必百計安之。惡靈可具形攫獨行之童婦；婦逃夫者，眾皆謂為魔所攝。

sensitivity.note: Witoto-Boro beliefs recorded by Whiffen 1915; read critically — the record names colonial-era rubber-regime informants' communities; no restricted ritual content included.

passages.text: So far as they believe in anything they believe in the existence of supreme good and bad spirits. In essence the idea of God is not that of a Supreme Being, but rather that of a Superior Being, possessed by an indulgent tolerance for all mankind; he is a spirit of benevolent passivity, good for no other reason than that he is not evil; there is no particularised sanctity in his name, only an unquestioning acquiescence in his benignity. The Good Spirit may be more potent, but he is certainly more remote than the Bad Spirit — too remote for ordinary people to be brought into any degree of contact with him whatsoever.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Whiffen 1915, ch. XVII; not verbatim.

passages.text: This Devil, or Bad Spirit, is affirmative in character, and is always active. He must not be invoked, but he is to be prevented by charms and magic from wreaking his vengeance on mankind, and must be placated at all costs as the supreme author of sickness and misfortunes. It is noteworthy that the Bad Spirit may be materialised sufficiently to be able to carry a child bodily away, or to steal a woman should she stray out into the forest by herself. For this reason usually no woman will go alone into the bush: women who run away from their husbands are consequently said by them to have been taken by the devil — a favourite theory, as the man may thereby avoid the censure of the tribe.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Whiffen 1915, ch. XVII; not verbatim.

passages.text: In the Boro language we have the word Neva as an equivalent for God, the good or sympathetic deity, and the word Navena for the Devil, the great evil spirit. But inasmuch as neva stands also for the sun, the dawn, and the morning, while navena is used for any spirit however humble, we may postulate that such are not the true names of these deities, but those that may be used without offence. In Witoto Usiyamoi has the meaning of God, Taife is the Devil; the Taife, the all-pervading evil genius, is named Apuehana, a word never pronounced above a whisper — here we may have reached a true secret name.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Whiffen 1915, ch. XVII; not verbatim.

title.en: The Visit of Neva to Earth: the Savannahs and the Whisper to the Tigers
title.zh: 涅瓦降世：草原之語與虎群之囑

region.en: Open savannahs, Issa-Japura region
region.zh: 伊薩-哈普拉河草原

period: Boro oral tradition; recorded 1915 (Whiffen)

source.work: Thomas Whiffen, The North-West Amazons (1915), ch. XVII 'The Indians' Magico-Religious System'

summary.en: Once Neva had forgotten the puny human factor, so he took the guise of a man and came to earth. The open spaces — the natural savannahs or geological outcrops — are where he spoke to the Indians, and it is a sign of his speaking and of his erstwhile presence that these are now open to the sun and the sky. But one Indian vexed Neva, the Good Spirit, and he was wrath with all men, so he went again to sit on the roof of the world. Before he departed he whispered into the ears of all the tigers that they were to kill the Indians and their children: that is why the tigers to-day are wicked and sometimes are the habitations of the most evil spirits. Before this time the tigers were good to men, and they hunted together like brothers; they lived together in the houses, ate and drank and licked tobacco in amity round the fire.
summary.zh: 涅瓦忽念塵世之人，遂化人形而降。曠野草原——即其訓人之所——今猶向日而敞，是其曾臨之徵。後一人觸其怒，大神忿而返天頂之座；臨行俯語眾虎：『當戮印第安人與其子孫。』故今虎性惡，且常為惡靈所棲。昔虎與人如兄弟，同獵同食，環火而舐菸，相善也。

sensitivity.note: Boro oral tradition recorded by Whiffen 1915; Whiffen himself doubted how far the tale was a genuine folk-tale or a perverted Biblical version — the record keeps that caution visible.

But one Indian vexed Neva, the Good Spirit, and he was wrath with all men, so he went again to sit on the roof of the world.

title.en: Neva and the Young Chief: the Tobacco Palaver's Verdict
title.zh: 涅瓦與少主：菸議之判

region.en: Boro maloka, Issa-Japura region
region.zh: 伊薩-哈普拉河博羅大屋

period: Boro oral tradition; recorded 1915 (Whiffen)

source.work: Thomas Whiffen, The North-West Amazons (1915), ch. XVII 'The Indians' Magico-Religious System'

summary.en: On the occasion of hearing this story of the visit of the Good Spirit to earth, Whiffen related, to the best of his ability, the Christian story. After the tribesmen had listened they held a tobacco palaver which lasted some six hours; then the chief appeared — the medicine-man was surly and remote — and this was the burden of his wisdom: his own people were greater than the people from the clouds, the white people, for the Good Spirit, Neva himself, came to the Indians, whereas only the Young Chief visited the clouds. And the Indians were better than the white people, for the white people killed the Young Chief, but the Indians listened to Neva, and only one among them vexed him.
summary.zh: 博羅人聞涅瓦降世之傳；白人乃述基督教之事。眾人聚而合菸（菸議），歷六小時；酋長出而言曰：『我族大於雲外之人：大神涅瓦親臨我族，而雲外之人僅得少主一顧。我族亦優於彼：彼弒少主，而我族聽涅瓦之言，觸其怒者惟一人耳。』

sensitivity.note: Boro oral tradition recorded by Whiffen 1915; a colonial-era comparative exchange, recorded and read critically.

passages.text: After they had listened to my story the tribesmen held a tobacco palaver, which lasted some six hours. Then the chief — the medicine-man was surly and remote — appeared, and this was the burden of his wisdom: his own people were greater than the people from the clouds — the white people — for the Good Spirit, Neva himself, came to the Indians, whereas only the Young Chief visited the clouds. And the Indians were better than the white people, for the white people killed the Young Chief, but the Indians listened to Neva, and only one among them vexed him.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Whiffen 1915, ch. XVII; not verbatim.

title.en: The Bad Spirit Imitates the Hunter's Call
title.zh: 惡靈效獵者之呼

region.en: Forest thickets, Issa-Japura region
region.zh: 伊薩-哈普拉河叢林

period: Witoto-Boro oral tradition; recorded 1915 (Whiffen)

source.work: Thomas Whiffen, The North-West Amazons (1915), ch. XVII 'The Indians' Magico-Religious System'

summary.en: The Bad Spirit wanders with his myrmidons in the forest every night. Sometimes he takes the form of a tiger or other fierce animal; sometimes he resembles a man who can disappear at will. He imitates the call of the hunter who has found game, or the call of an animal to be hunted; he entices his victim by these and similar contrivances to venture deeper and deeper into the bush, until the wretched wanderer is utterly lost — according to tribal belief he is then destroyed, or spirited bodily away. As confirmation of his real presence an Indian will sometimes whisper the evil name as he points out the track of an abnormal-sized tapir, which is curiously reminiscent to the European of the cloven hoof of his own Devil.
summary.zh: 惡靈夜夜率其黨徜徉林間；或化猛虎，或如隱形之人。效獵者得獸之呼、獸之鳴，誘其人愈行愈深，至迷失不知所返——傳說其時彼即被毀，或舉體被攝。土人指巨大異常之貘跡，必耳語惡名——白人觀之，儼然己魔之蹄印也。

sensitivity.note: Witoto-Boro oral tradition recorded by Whiffen 1915; read critically.

passages.text: The Bad Spirit wanders with his myrmidons in the forest every night. Sometimes he takes the form of a tiger, or other fierce animal; sometimes, as alternative to the tiger-lifting theory, he resembles a man who can disappear at will. He imitates the call of the hunter who has found game, or the call of an animal to be hunted. He entices his victim by these and similar contrivances to venture deeper and deeper into the bush, until the wretched wanderer is utterly lost — according to tribal belief he is then destroyed, or spirited bodily away.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Whiffen 1915, ch. XVII; not verbatim.

passages.text: As confirmation of his real presence an Indian will sometimes whisper the evil name as he points out the track of an abnormal-sized tapir, which is curiously reminiscent to the European of the cloven hoof of his own Devil; no corroborative evidence, however, is ever forthcoming from the victim himself.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Whiffen 1915, ch. XVII; not verbatim.

title.en: The Land of the After-Life: a World in Miniature
title.zh: 來世之土：縮微之世界

region.en: Upstream, toward the setting sun
region.zh: 溯河而上，日落之方

period: Witoto-Boro oral tradition; recorded 1915 (Whiffen)

source.work: Thomas Whiffen, The North-West Amazons (1915), ch. XVII 'The Indians' Magico-Religious System'

summary.en: Man's soul in Indian belief is immortal — that is to say it exists as long as it continues to appear in the dreams and the thoughts of the survivors: a thing forgotten has never existed, and the soul of a remembered being lives for ever. The ghost lingers near the body after death, then goes at length to the happy grounds of the Good Spirit — among some tribes above the skies, among others away up some river, in the far and mythical distance, approximately towards the setting sun. This land of the After-Life is a diminutive replica of the ordinary world, with evil things eliminated and joyful things emphasised: all is on a lower scale, stunted forests and pigmy game; hunting is fruitful always, women are beautiful and amenable, and the men are all the old familiar friends of earth. Individual possessions are buried with the dead, and the Kuretu confess this is done to prevent the return of the soul in search of them — burial sets free the soul-part of each object to take in the miniature world a position corresponding to that held here on earth. The Zaparo believe the good and brave souls pass into birds of beautiful plumage and feed on the most delicate fruits, while the bad and cowardly are condemned to a future existence in the guise of objectionable reptiles.
summary.zh: 土人謂魂不死：憶之則存，忘之則無。魂初依屍，後往善靈之樂土——或在天上，或在河源，日落之方。彼土乃人間之縮本，去惡揚善：林矮獸小，獵常豐，婦皆美，友皆故。殉葬其物者，使物之魂隨主人而去，各安其位於縮微之世。薩帕羅人言：善勇之魂化為麗羽之鳥，食美果；怯惡之魂化為可憎之蟲蛇。

sensitivity.note: Witoto-Boro-Zaparo beliefs recorded by Whiffen 1915; read critically.

passages.text: Man's soul in Indian belief is immortal, that is to say it exists as long as it is felt to exist, whilst it continues to appear in the dreams, in the thoughts of the survivors — for so long, in fact, as it is remembered. Surely this is immortality: a thing forgotten has never existed; and, per contra, the soul of a remembered being lives for ever. The disembodied spirit lingers near the body after death, and then indefinitely the soul wanders farther afield, and goes at length to the happy grounds of the Good Spirit — above the skies, or away up some river in the far and mythical distance, approximately towards the setting sun.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Whiffen 1915, ch. XVII; not verbatim.

passages.text: This land of the After-Life is a diminutive replica of the ordinary world, but with evil things eliminated and joyful things emphasised: all is on a lower scale, stunted forests and pigmy game. Life in this enigmatic sphere has everything most prized in this world: hunting is fruitful always, women are beautiful and amenable, and the men are all the old familiar friends of earth. Individual possessions are buried with the dead, and the Kuretu confess that this is done to prevent the return of the soul in search of them: burial sets it at liberty to take in the miniature world of the After-Life a position corresponding in every detail to that which has been held here on earth.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Whiffen 1915, ch. XVII; not verbatim.

passages.text: Of the Zaparo belief the good and brave souls will pass into birds of beautiful plumage and feed on the most delicate fruits, while the bad and cowardly are condemned to a future existence in the guise of objectionable reptiles.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Whiffen 1915, ch. XVII; not verbatim.

title.en: The Dreaming Soul and the Deadly Sneeze
title.zh: 夢魂與致命之嚏

region.en: Maloka fireside, Issa-Japura region
region.zh: 伊薩-哈普拉河大屋火畔

period: Witoto-Boro oral tradition; recorded 1915 (Whiffen)

source.work: Thomas Whiffen, The North-West Amazons (1915), ch. XVII 'The Indians' Magico-Religious System'

summary.en: Not only do the Indians hold that a man's soul leaves his body at death, but they believe it may do so during life for a limited period: in sleep the spirit is out of the body and wanders about, for in dreams the soul passes through the mouth and has adventures in the outer world — dreams are a portion of the man's real life, and a man will not hesitate to declare that he has done what he dreamed he was doing. This is involuntary disembodiment, differing only from actual death in that it is of temporary duration; but if the soul make a violent effort to escape that apparently entails fatal consequences, for the Indians declare when anybody sneezes it is the soul attempting to leave the body and so cause death. Voluntary disembodiment is believed possible in certain favoured cases: the medicine-man may free his spirit for magical purposes, either remaining disembodied and invisible, or lurking in the form of some animal, a tree, a stone — or even in the wind, the rain, or the river.
summary.zh: 土人言魂於生前亦可暫離其體：睡時魂出而遊，夢中魂經口而出，歷於外界——夢乃真歷也，故其人自認夢中所為。魂若猛然欲遁，則致命：土人謂人之嚏者，魂欲離體而致死之兆也。醫師能自纵其魂以行法：或隱而不見，或寄於獸、於樹、於石，乃至風雨川河之中。

sensitivity.note: Witoto-Boro beliefs recorded by Whiffen 1915; read critically.

passages.text: We have examples in sleep, they argue, when the spirit is out of the body and wanders about; for in dreams, they say, the soul passes through the mouth and has adventures in the outer world. Dreams are, in fact, a portion of the man's real life: his spirit has ventured forth and actually gone through the experience his fancy paints. They realise, therefore, that individuality is not in the body itself, but in the spirit that inhabits the body; so if a man dreams he will not hesitate to declare that he has done what he dreamed he was doing.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Whiffen 1915, ch. XVII; not verbatim.

passages.text: This is an example of involuntary disembodiment, differing only from actual death in that it is of temporary duration: the soul has gone quietly, and will return. But if the soul make a violent effort to escape that apparently entails fatal consequences, for the Indians declare when anybody sneezes it is the soul attempting to leave the body and so cause death. Voluntary disembodiment is believed to be possible in certain favoured cases: the medicine-man may free his spirit for magical purposes, either remaining disembodied and invisible, or lurking for a time in the form of some animal or object, a tree, a stone — or even in the wind, the rain, or the river.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Whiffen 1915, ch. XVII; not verbatim.

title.en: The Virgin and the Manioc: Origin of Cassava Cultivation
title.zh: 處女與木薯：薯田之起源

region.en: Manioc plantation upriver, Issa-Japura region
region.zh: 伊薩-哈普拉河上游薯田

period: Witoto-Boro oral tradition; recorded 1915 (Whiffen)

source.work: Thomas Whiffen, The North-West Amazons (1915), ch. XVIII 'Myths'

summary.en: The Good Spirit when he came to earth showed the Indians a manioc plant and taught them how to extract the evil spirit's influence — but he did not seem to have explained how the plant might be reproduced. The Indians searched for seeds and found none; they buried the young tuberous roots to no effect; the Good Spirit was vexed with them, which is why he did not divulge the secret. But long, long after, a virgin of the tribe, a daughter of the chief, was found to be with child. Questioned, she replied that long ago, when sick to death under the medicine-man's narcotic magic, she had wandered far into the bush and found a beautiful manioc plant: she was seduced by the tuberous root — some say the plant was metamorphosed into a beautiful young hunter — and in due course gave birth to a girl-child who could both talk and walk at birth. This child took the women of the tribe to a beautiful plantation of manioc far up a certain river, and there the precocious infant explained how to reproduce the plant with bits of the stalks. So to this day the chief food of all the peoples is cassava.
summary.zh: 善靈臨世，示人以木薯，教以去其毒；然未示其殖法。眾覓種而無，埋根而無效——蓋神怒而秘其術。久之，酋之處女有孕；自言昔病篤，受巫之麻醉，迷行林中，得一美薯；為塊根所誘（或言其化為美少年獵者），遂產一女——生而能言行。此女攜族中婦人至河上之美田，示以莖枝插殖之法。故至今諸族以木薯為主食。

sensitivity.note: Witoto-Boro oral tradition recorded by Whiffen 1915; read critically.

passages.text: The Good Spirit when he came to earth showed the Indians a manioc plant, and taught them how to extract the evil spirit's influence; but he did not seem to have explained how the plant might be reproduced. The Indians searched for seeds, but found none; they buried the young tuberous roots, but to no effect. The Good Spirit was vexed with them — that is why he did not divulge the secret.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Whiffen 1915, ch. XVIII; not verbatim.

passages.text: But long, long after, a virgin of the tribe, a daughter of the chief, was found to be with child. When questioned she replied that long, long ago, when sick to death, and under the medicine-man's narcotic magic, she wandered far, far into the bush. In the bush she found a beautiful manioc plant. She was seduced by the tuberous root — some Indians say the plant was metamorphosed into a beautiful young hunter — and in due course she gave birth to a girl-child, who could both talk and walk at birth.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Whiffen 1915, ch. XVIII; not verbatim.

passages.text: This child took the women of the tribe to a beautiful plantation of manioc, far, far up a certain river, and there the precocious infant explained how to reproduce the plant with bits of the stalks. So to this day the chief food of all the peoples is cassava. A different version is told among more northern tribes at Sao Gabriel: a bird discovered to the Indians the use of the mandiocca, then a great and solitary tree; all the tribes came to procure the roots, and when none were left carried off branches — hence the varieties of mandiocca now grown.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Whiffen 1915, ch. XVIII (with Spruce's variant); not verbatim.

title.en: Komuine the Monkey-Man: the Boro Tribe That Was No More
title.zh: 猴夫科穆伊內：烏蒂格內族之亡

region.en: Utiguene lands, Issa-Japura region
region.zh: 伊薩-哈普拉河烏蒂格內之地

period: Boro oral tradition; recorded 1915 (Whiffen)

source.work: Thomas Whiffen, The North-West Amazons (1915), ch. XVIII 'Myths: Boro tribal tale'

summary.en: Once a large tribe lived there, one of the most powerful and most numerous of all: a chief of the Utiguene had a daughter who was not only ugly but bird-rumped, and the medicine-man gave her the name of Komuine — monkey. Going into the bush to pick peppers and berries she did not return. A tiger must have carried her off, said the tribe; a tribal hunt was instituted, but in the bush they were attacked by a wicked tribe which killed them in great numbers. Long after, Komuine reappeared in the great house and sang her complaint-solo: 'The chief's daughter was lost in the forest, and no one came to find the spoor...' Dancing, her bird-rump was covered with nikwako, hair; the old women rubbed rubber latex on her to remove it — but as it was removed more came, and the hairier she grew. When she was covered with leaves she told her story: a komuine had come and taken her by force into the bush to be his woman; she gave birth to twins, and the second was buried, for even komuine have but one child — and the child was hairy like a komuine but had the face of a man. Because of the unsightliness and the pollution, and the blood-feud which had cost the tribe so many warriors, it was decided to destroy her; she fled into the forest, and all the komuine came and robbed the plantation — no manioc, no fruit. The lianas were like a net in the path, and the tribe got thinner and thinner, and now to-day there is no tribe of the Utiguene.
summary.zh: 昔有大族，兵強人眾；酋有女，貌陋而臀有羽；巫名之曰科穆伊內——猴也。入林採椒不返；眾謂虎攫之，大索而遇敵族，戰歿甚眾。久之，女歸大屋而歌其怨：『酋女迷林，無人尋跡……』舞而臀毛叢生；老嫗塗膠拔之，愈拔愈多。葉覆其身，乃自述：猴強暴之，攜入林為婦；產雙生，埋其一——猴惟一子也——其子毛如猴而面如人。族恥其穢，又痛血仇之損，議誅之；女遁於林，群猴至而掠其田——薯果俱盡。藤蔓如網塞徑，族日削，今烏蒂格內無存矣。

sensitivity.note: Boro oral tradition recorded by Whiffen 1915; Whiffen notes it may equally be a traditional account of an actual rape by a hostile tribe — the Amazonian version of Helen and Troy; the record keeps both readings and is read critically.

passages.text: Once a large tribe lived there, one of the most powerful of all the tribes, and also one of the most numerous. But long, long ago a chief of this tribe of the Utiguene had a daughter, who was not only ugly but bird-rumped; the Chekobe, the medicine-man, gave her the name of Komuine — monkey. When she was about five feet high Komuine went into the bush to pick peppers and berries, but did not return. The tribe said a tiger must have carried her off; so a tribal hunt was instituted, and the bush searched — but in the bush they were attacked by a wicked tribe, which fell upon them and killed them in great numbers. So they returned with great sadness to the maloka.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Whiffen 1915, ch. XVIII; not verbatim.

passages.text: Long, long after this Komuine reappeared in the great house of the tribe, and sang a solo, as is the custom among the people when making a complaint: 'The Chief's daughter was lost in the forest, and no one came to find the spoor; the branches were broken, the leaves were turned, and no one came to find the spoor; and where were my brothers, and the sons of the chief's brothers?' And while Komuine was dancing it was noticed, to the disgust of the tribe, that her bird-rump was covered with nikwako, hair; so the old women came and rubbed latex upon her to remove the unsightliness — but as it was removed more unsightliness came, and the hairier she grew. When she was covered with leaves she told her story: 'When I was in the forest picking peppers a komuine came to me, and taking me by force he deflowered me; he took me with him into the bush to become his woman, and I gave birth to twins, and the second one was buried, for even komuine have but one child. And the child was hairy like a komuine, but had the face of a man.'
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Whiffen 1915, ch. XVIII; not verbatim.

passages.text: The tribe then had a tobacco palaver, and because of the unsightliness, and the pollution, and the blood-feud with their enemies which had cost the tribe so many warriors, it was decided to destroy her. When she heard this she fled into the forest, and all the komuine came and robbed the plantation: there was no manioc, and no fruit. And when the men of the Utiguene went out to hunt, the lianas were like a net in the path, and so thick no one could pass. And the tribe got thinner and thinner, and now to-day there is no tribe of the Utiguene.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Whiffen 1915, ch. XVIII; not verbatim.

title.en: The Jaguar and the Anaconda: Magic Beasts and the Feast of Revenge
title.zh: 豹與蚺：靈獸與復仇之宴

region.en: Issa-Japura rivers
region.zh: 伊薩-哈普拉諸河

period: Witoto-Boro oral tradition; recorded 1915 (Whiffen)

source.work: Thomas Whiffen, The North-West Amazons (1915), ch. XVII 'The Indians' Magico-Religious System'

summary.en: Two of the forest denizens, the jaguar and the anaconda, occupy outstanding positions in connection with spirits and magic: independently of spiritual possession they are magical beasts. The anaconda is looked upon as an evil spirit, the embodiment of the water spirit, the Yacu-mama, the mother, the spirit of the streams, whose coils may bar the passage of the streams — the Indian goes in terror of it. Tigers are never killed wantonly: the tribesman is anxious not to provoke war with the tiger tribe, for Indians look upon animals as capable of a prolonged blood-feud with humans who may have wronged them. But when an Indian is killed, or a child lost — tigers are usually credited with the destruction of any child missing from its home — the medicine-man proceeds to discover that it was a tribal enemy working in disguise, probably the spirit of a hostile medicine-man; the tiger is then to be treated as a human enemy. A big tribal hunt is organised, and if the quarry be secured a feast of tiger-flesh follows, a feast of revenge, very similar in detail to the anthropophagous orgies. At no other time does the Indian eat jaguar meat; the tiger-skin becomes the property of the medicine-man, whose magic has thus triumphed over the magic of a rival.
summary.zh: 豹與大蚺者，獸中之靈也；非附魂而自具魔法。蚺為水母雅庫瑪瑪——川后之靈——其身可斷河流，人莫不畏之。豹非挑釁不殺：獸亦能血仇。然人有橫死、嬰有失蹤——皆歸咎於豹——醫師必察之，言乃敵族巫者之靈所化；於是豹即人敵，大舉族獵。獲而烹豹肉，設復仇之宴；此外不食豹肉。豹皮歸於醫師——其術勝敵巫之術也。

sensitivity.note: Witoto-Boro beliefs recorded by Whiffen 1915; read critically. The comparative note on cannibal-feast parallels is kept as description, not endorsement.

passages.text: Two of the forest denizens, the jaguar and the anaconda, occupy outstanding positions in this connection with spirits and magic to all the other beasts of the wild: the 'tiger' and the great water-snake, independently of such spiritual possession, are magical beasts. The anaconda is looked upon as an evil spirit: it is the embodiment of the water spirit, the Yacu-mama, whose coils may bar the passage of the streams, and the Indian goes in terror of it. The Yacu-mama, as the name signifies, is the mother, the spirit of the streams; it occupies the place in Amazonian folk-tales filled by the sea-serpent of Europe.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Whiffen 1915, ch. XVII; not verbatim.

passages.text: Tigers are not killed unless they be the aggressors — that is to say they are never killed wantonly: the reason for this is not cowardice, but fear of further aggression on the part of the tiger family, or from the family of the medicine-man who has assumed tiger form. Indians look upon animals as having the same instincts as themselves, and therefore capable of a prolonged blood-feud with humans who may have wronged them.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Whiffen 1915, ch. XVII; not verbatim.

passages.text: When an Indian is killed, or a child lost — and tigers are usually credited with the destruction of any child missing from its home — the medicine-man is called upon, and he proceeds to discover that it was a tribal enemy working in disguise, probably the spirit of a hostile medicine-man. The tiger is in these circumstances to be treated as a human enemy: a big tribal hunt is organised, and if the quarry be secured a feast of tiger-flesh follows, a feast of revenge. At no other time does the Indian eat jaguar meat; the tiger-skin becomes the property of the medicine-man, whose magic has thus triumphed over the magic of a rival.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Whiffen 1915, ch. XVII; not verbatim.

title.en: The Sun and His Wife the Moon, the Stars as Souls of Chiefs
title.zh: 日與其妻月，星為酋長之魂

region.en: Issa-Japura region
region.zh: 伊薩-哈普拉之地

period: Witoto-Boro oral tradition; recorded 1915 (Whiffen)

source.work: Thomas Whiffen, The North-West Amazons (1915), ch. XVII 'The Indians' Magico-Religious System'

summary.en: Finally, the tribes south of the Japura are concerned with the sun and the moon: these are venerated, the sun as a great and sympathetic spirit, but not an incarnation of the great Good Spirit; the moon as his wife, who is sent betimes by the sun into the heavens at night to prevent the evil spirits from depopulating the world. Of the stars these people seem to have the vaguest ideas, and only one Boro explained that they were the souls of the chiefs and of the great men of his tribe. The moon's inconstant appearances are accounted for by the suggestion that she is sent periodically by the sun her husband to drive away the evil spirits of the night that await the stray or heedless loiterers in the forest thickets — though this protective character is denied to the moon by other tribes, and some South American Indians will hide young infants lest the moon should injure them.
summary.zh: 哈普拉以南諸族尊日月：日為偉大仁慈之靈，非善靈之化身；月為其妻，夫遣之夜行於天，以阻惡靈之滅人。星則其識甚淺；一博羅人言星乃其族酋長與大人之魂也。月之隱現，蓋夫遣妻驅林間伺人之夜鬼——然他族不然，或有匿嬰以防月之害者。

sensitivity.note: Witoto-Boro beliefs recorded by Whiffen 1915; read critically.

Of the stars these people seem to have the vaguest ideas, and only one Boro explained to me that they were the souls of the chiefs and of the great men of his tribe.

title.en: The Camera That Stole Souls
title.zh: 竊魂之照箱

region.en: Boro-Witoto malokas
region.zh: 博羅-維托托大屋

period: Boro-Witoto beliefs; recorded 1915 (Whiffen)

source.work: Thomas Whiffen, The North-West Amazons (1915), ch. XVII 'The Indians' Magico-Religious System'

summary.en: Anything abnormal or unknown is regarded with suspicious dread; Whiffen's camera was naturally endowed by Indian imagination with magical properties, the most general idea among the Boro being that it was an infernal machine designed to steal the souls of those who were exposed to its baleful eye. The Indian was brought face to face with his naked soul, represented by the miniature of himself in the photographic plate: one glance, and one only, could he be induced to give; never again would he be privy to such magic. The Witoto women believed more material magic was afoot, and feared that, should they suffer exposure to the camera, they would bear resultant offspring to whom the camera — or the photographer — would stand in paternal relation.
summary.zh: 凡異常之物，皆疑而懼之。白人之照箱，博羅人以為地獄之器，凡受其凶目所照者，魂皆被竊。相版中縮小之影，即其赤裸之魂也；一見之後，永不復視。維托托婦人則懼其為形體之術：若受照，所產之子，當以照箱或照相者為父也。

sensitivity.note: Boro-Witoto beliefs recorded by Whiffen 1915; a colonial-era encounter, read critically.

The Indian was brought face to face with his naked soul, represented by the miniature of himself in the photographic plate: one glance, and one only, could he be induced to give — never again would he be privy to such magic.

title.en: The White Indians Who Sleep by Day
title.zh: 晝眠之白印第安人

region.en: Upper rivers of Guiana and Amazonia
region.zh: 圭亞那與亞馬遜上游諸河

period: South American folk tradition; recorded 1915 (Whiffen)

source.work: Thomas Whiffen, The North-West Amazons (1915), ch. XVIII 'Myths'

summary.en: A story prevalent throughout South America tells of a race of white Indians who sleep in the daytime, and only go abroad at night. This tale was laughed at when repeated at a recent meeting of the Royal Geographical Society, but it is certainly in existence among the tribes; and Crevaux states that the Ouayana will not go near one river, 'à cause des singuliers habitants qui habiteraient près des sources... des Indiens aux chevaux blonds qui dorment le jour et marchent toute la nuit' — because of the strange dwellers near the sources, Indians with blond horses who sleep the day and march all night. Where tribal differentiation of colour is so marked it is only natural that tales should be told of some mythical 'white' folk.
summary.zh: 南美遍傳白印第安人之說：晝眠而夜行。皇家地理學會曾哂之，然土族中確有其傳。克雷沃言：瓦亞納人不近某河，『以河源有異民居之：白膚金髮之印第安人，晝眠而夜行也。』部落膚色既異，則幻設白人之族，固其宜也。

sensitivity.note: South American folk tradition recorded by Whiffen 1915; read critically.

passages.text: A story that is prevalent throughout South America tells of a race of white Indians who sleep in the daytime, and only go abroad at night. This tale was laughed at when repeated at a recent meeting of the Royal Geographical Society, but it is certainly in existence among the tribes; and Crevaux states that the Ouayana will not go near one river — because of the strange dwellers near the sources: Indians with blond horses who sleep the day and march all night.

title.en: Cane Joints Full of Lice: The Tribute of the Disabled Poor
title.zh: 裝滿蝨子的竹節:貧弱者的貢賦

region.en: Villages of Ttahuantin-suyu (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 大蘇尤各村(象徵性標記)

period: Written by Garcilaso de la Vega (Inca), publ. Markham trans. 1871

source.work: Garcilasso de la Vega (El Inca), First Part of the Royal Commentaries of the Yncas, trans. C. R. Markham, London 1871

summary.en: Another sort of tribute was imposed upon those who could not work, and were called poor: at certain intervals they had to deliver a specified number of cane joints full of lice to the governor of their village. They say that the Yncas imposed this tribute in order that no one (except those exempted from tribute) should contribute nothing, however poor he might be; and therefore from those who were disabled from paying tribute in personal service was exacted a tribute of lice. It was also said that the chief reason of the Yncas for requiring this tribute was a loving care for these poor people, that they might be obliged to clean themselves, and not become a prey to the lice. For such thoughtful care as this the Yncas were called the Friends of the Poor. The Decurions were expected to see that this tribute was paid.
summary.zh: 另一種貢賦加於不能勞作、被稱為「貧者」的人:他們須定期向村中長官繳交一定數量、裝滿蝨子的竹節。相傳印加王立此貢,是為使任何人——除非免貢之人——縱然赤貧,也不致一無所獻;故對無力以勞役納貢者,便徵「蝨貢」。又有一說:印加王設此貢,本出於對貧民的體恤,使他們不得不清潔自身,免遭蝨害。因有此等細緻入微的關懷,印加王被稱為「貧者之友」。十戶之長(十夫長)負責督察此貢的繳納。

sensitivity.note: Garcilaso's most tender anecdote of Inca social policy; read with his own apologetic purpose in mind.

passages.text: Another sort of tribute was imposed upon those who could not work, and were called poor; and this was that, at certain intervals, they had to deliver a specified number of cane joints full of lice to the governor of their village. They say that the Yncas imposed this tribute in order that no one (except those exempted from tribute) should contribute nothing, however poor he might be; and therefore from those who were disabled from paying tribute in personal service was exacted a tribute of lice.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Garcilasso de la Vega, Royal Commentaries (Markham 1871); not verbatim.

passages.text: It was also said that the chief reason of the Yncas for requiring this tribute was a loving care for these poor people, that they might be obliged to clean themselves, and not become a prey to the lice. For such thoughtful care as this, which the Yncas showed in all things, they were called the Friends of the Poor. The Decurions were expected to see that this tribute was paid.
