title.en: The Stones and Bushes Turned to Men: Garcilaso's Skeptical Pururaucas
title.zh: 石與灌木化為人形:加爾西拉索筆下的普魯勞卡斯

region.en: Yahuar-pampa, near Cuzco (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 庫斯科附近亞瓦爾-潘帕(象徵性標記)

period: Written by Garcilaso de la Vega (Inca), publ. Markham trans. 1871

source.work: Garcilasso de la Vega (El Inca), First Part of the Royal Commentaries of the Yncas, trans. C. R. Markham, London 1871

summary.en: The Yncas, being a people who strove to magnify their deeds by fables and false pretensions, seeing these new friends (the reinforcements), resolved not to lose the occasion, but to turn it to advantage as was their custom. They cried out that the very stones and bushes of the plain were turning into men, and coming to fight in the service of the Prince, because the Sun and the god Uiracocha had so ordered it. The Chancas, being a credulous people, were much amazed by this fable; and afterwards it was believed by all the common people throughout that empire, as Father Friar Geronimo Roman says: 'So that the field remained in the power of the Ynca. To this day all the Indians declare, in speaking of this famous battle, that the stones in the plain turned into men to fight for them, and that all this was done by the Sun to fulfil the promise that he had given to the brave Pachacuti Ynca Yupanqui.' Garcilaso, quoting Acosta's account, adds that from the time of that victory Uiracocha was held to be the universal lord; that the prince announced to his soldiers that they had not conquered their enemies, but that the victory had been gained by certain bearded men sent by the Uiracocha who were visible to none but himself, and that they had afterwards been turned into stones: they collected a great quantity of stones near the mountains which he selected, took them to the war with much devotion, holding that victory was certain with their assistance, and called them Pururaucas. Yet Garcilaso corrects the record: the Indians never had more than two gods, which were Pachacamac, who was invisible and unknown, and the Sun, who was visible and notorious; they held that Uiracocha and the other Yncas were children of the Sun.
summary.zh: 印加人素有以神話浮誇誇大戰功之風;見到援兵到來,便照例抓住時機,大肆利用。他們高喊:平原上的石頭和灌木叢都變成了人,奉太陽與維拉科查之命,來為王子助戰!昌卡人性喜輕信,聞之大駭;此後全帝國的平民也都信以為真——赫羅尼莫·羅曼神父記道:「至今所有印第安人談起這場著名會戰,仍說平原上的石頭化為人形為他們作戰,這一切都是太陽為履行他對英勇的帕查庫提·印加·尤潘琪的許諾而行的。」加爾西拉索又引阿科斯塔:自那場大捷之後,維拉科查被尊為至高之主;王子向將士宣布,此勝非人力所取,而是維拉科查所遣的、唯有王子能見的鬚髯神兵所建,戰後神兵化為石頭——人們於是拾取他所點的山邊巨石,奉為瓦卡,虔誠地抬上戰場,相信有神石相助則必勝,稱之為「普魯勞卡斯」。但加爾西拉索糾正道:印加人自來只有兩位神——隱而無名的帕查卡馬克,與顯而有名的太陽;維拉科查與歷代印加王,皆只是太陽的兒子。

sensitivity.note: The mestizo historian explicitly frames the pururaucas as an Inca propaganda invention while preserving the belief record - a uniquely critical native-voiced version.

passages.text: The Yncas, being a people who strove to magnify their deeds by fables and false pretensions, seeing these new friends, resolved not to lose the occasion, but to turn it to advantage as was their custom. They cried out that the very stones and bushes of the plain were turning into men, and coming to fight in the service of the Prince, because the Sun and the god Uiracocha had so ordered it. The Chancas, being a credulous people, were much amazed by this fable; and afterwards it was believed by all the common people throughout that empire.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Garcilasso de la Vega, Royal Commentaries (Markham 1871); not verbatim.

passages.text: To this day all the Indians declare, in speaking of this famous battle, that the stones in the plain turned into men to fight for them, and that all this was done by the Sun to fulfil the promise that he had given to the brave Pachacuti Ynca Yupanqui. [Acosta quoted:] From the time of that victory Uiracocha was held to be the universal lord... As soon as he had gained the victory over the Chancas, he announced to his soldiers that they had not conquered their enemies, but that the victory had been gained by certain bearded men sent by the Uiracocha who were visible to none but himself, and that they had afterwards been turned into stones... They called them Pururaucas, and took them to the war with much devotion, holding that victory was certain with their assistance.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Garcilasso quoting Roman and Acosta (Markham 1871); not verbatim.

passages.text: That they placed a statue of Uiracocha higher than that of the sun is a new invention of the Indians, to flatter the Spaniards... This was not so, for they never had more than two gods, which were Pachacamac, who was invisible and unknown, and the Sun, who was visible and notorious. They held that Uiracocha and the other Yncas were children of the Sun.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Garcilasso de la Vega, Royal Commentaries (Markham 1871); not verbatim.

canonical_translation: C. R. Markham, First Part of the Royal Commentaries of the Yncas (1871)

title.en: The Field of Blood: Eight Hours at Yahuar-pampa
title.zh: 血野:亞瓦爾-潘帕八小時血戰

region.en: Yahuar-pampa, Chanca country (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 昌卡地亞瓦爾-潘帕(象徵性標記)

period: Written by Garcilaso de la Vega (Inca), publ. Markham trans. 1871

source.work: Garcilasso de la Vega (El Inca), First Part of the Royal Commentaries of the Yncas, trans. C. R. Markham, London 1871

summary.en: The battle, having been so hardly won and having lasted for eight hours, was very bloody. The Indians declare that, besides the blood that was shed on the ground, a dry bed of a stream that crossed the plain also flowed with blood; hence the plain was called from that time forward Yahuar-pampa, which means 'the field of blood.' More than 30,000 Indians died, 8000 on the side of the Ynca, and the rest belonging to the nations Chanca, Hanco-huallu, Uruinarca, Vilca, Untun-sulla, and others. The two rebel masters of the camp, and the general Hanco-hualla, were made prisoners.
summary.zh: 此役得之極難,酣戰八小時,血染沙場。印第安人相傳:除了灑在地面上的鮮血,那片平原上乾涸的河床也流滿了血;自此這片平原便名為「亞瓦爾-潘帕」——血野。死者逾三萬:印加一方八千,餘者屬昌卡、安科-瓦尤、烏魯伊納爾卡、維爾卡、溫通-蘇利亞諸族。叛軍的兩位統帥與主將安科-瓦利亞俱被生擒。

sensitivity.note: Yahuar-pampa is the standard Garcilaso name for the decisive Chanca battlefield (Yuncaypampa in other sources).

The Indians declare that, besides the blood that was shed on the ground, a dry bed of a stream that crossed the plain also flowed with blood; hence the plain was called from that time forward Yahuar-pampa, which means 'the field of blood.'

title.en: Drinking with the Sun: Evaporation as the God's Draught
title.zh: 與太陽對飲:蒸發即神飲

region.en: Temple of the Sun, Cuzco (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 庫斯科太陽神廟(象徵性標記)

period: Written by Garcilaso de la Vega (Inca), publ. Markham trans. 1871

source.work: Garcilasso de la Vega (El Inca), First Part of the Royal Commentaries of the Yncas, trans. C. R. Markham, London 1871

summary.en: For these Yncas, although they held the Sun to be god, treated him as if he had been a man like themselves. Among other things that they did to him in his supposed character of a man was to drink with him, and they poured the Sun's drink into a half tinajon of gold, which they placed in the court where they held their festivals, or in the temple. They declared that what appeared to be gone had been drank by the Sun, and they said truly, for the Sun's heat had evaporated the liquor. They also put out plates of meat that the Sun might eat. And when a great event happened, like this victory, they sent a special messenger to tell the Sun what had happened, and to offer up thanks to him. In accordance with this ancient custom, the prince Uiracocha Ynca sent a messenger to the Sun with the news of the victory, and with orders to the priests to get together those who had fled, that they might offer up thanksgivings and make new sacrifices. He sent another messenger to the virgins dedicated to the Sun, with the news of the victory which had been granted in return for their prayers and merits.
summary.zh: 印加人雖奉太陽為神,卻像對待族人一般與他相處。其中一樁,便是與太陽對飲:他們把太陽的酒漿倒入一只半人高的金缸,安放在舉行節宴的庭院或神廟之中;眾人眼中「消失不見」的酒,便算是太陽飲下的——他們這話倒也不假,因為那正是太陽的熱力把酒蒸發了。他們還擺上肉盤,請太陽進食。凡遇大事——如這場大捷——便遣專使向太陽報喜致謝。照這古禮,維拉科查·印加王子遣使赴太陽神廟報捷,並命祭司召集逃散之人回來謝恩獻祭;另遣一使往太陽的貞女處報喜——說這場勝利是報答她們的祈禱與功德。

sensitivity.note: The famous evaporation anecdote - the most-quoted passage of Garcilaso; his rationalist wink inside the ritual description.

title.en: The Blood-Omen Fulfilled: The Dethroned King Keeps His Yellow Fringe
title.zh: 血兆應驗:廢王仍戴黃纓

region.en: Rumi-colca palace, between Muyna and Quespicancha (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 穆伊納與基斯皮坎恰之間的魯米-科爾卡宮(象徵性標記)

period: Written by Garcilaso de la Vega (Inca), publ. Markham trans. 1871

source.work: Garcilasso de la Vega (El Inca), First Part of the Royal Commentaries of the Yncas, trans. C. R. Markham, London 1871

summary.en: The prince returned to the city, put aside the yellow fringe, and adopted the red one. But though he wore the red fringe himself, he never would consent that his father should leave it off, caring little for the outward insignia, so long as he possessed the reality of dominion and power. As soon as the palace was finished it was supplied with servants and all other necessaries, so that, except the government of the kingdom, the Ynca Yahuar-huaccac was deprived of no other thing. The poor king passed the rest of his life in this solitude, deprived of his kingdom by his own son. The Indians say that this dethronement was prognosticated by the evil omen of his having wept blood in his childhood. They also say, reasoning amongst themselves and recalling the memory of past events, that if this Ynca, when he began to fear the disposition of his son, had resorted to the remedy of giving him a little poison (according to the custom of tyrants, which was practised by the sorcerers in some of the provinces of that empire) he would not have been dethroned. Others, defending the conduct of the prince, say that if his father had fallen into the hands of the enemy still worse would have befallen him. Others, who were held to be religious, said that even if the use of poison had been possible, all his predecessors would rather have died than have used it.
summary.zh: 王子回到城中,摘下黃纓,改用紅纓。然而他自己雖戴紅纓,卻始終不許父親摘下黃纓——在他看來,只要實權在握,外在的徽記無足輕重。宮殿一成,僕從用度俱全;除了失去國政,廢王亞瓦爾-瓦卡克別無所失。可憐的老王在這片幽居中度過餘生——江山斷送在親生兒子手上。印第安人說,這場廢立早有預兆:他幼年泣血的凶兆,如今應驗了。人們私下議論:這位印加王若在察覺兒子野心之初,便用上那劑小小的毒藥——暴君之間的慣技,帝國某些省份的巫師確曾使用——便不會遭此下場。另一些人為王子辯護:若老王落入敵手,下場只會更慘;棄城而逃者,性命、江山、子孫基業都將不保。還有些信教虔誠的人說:縱使毒計可行,歷代先王寧死也不肯用毒。

sensitivity.note: The wept-blood omen fulfilled; the fringe colours as rank semiotics; the poison debate is Garcilaso's moral commentary in native voices.

passages.text: The Ynca Uiracocha entered Cuzco on foot... put aside the yellow fringe, and adopted the red one. But though he wore the red fringe himself, he never would consent that his father should leave it off, caring little for the outward insignia, so long as he possessed the reality of dominion and power... The poor king passed the rest of his life in this solitude, deprived of his kingdom by his own son.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Garcilasso de la Vega, Royal Commentaries (Markham 1871); not verbatim.

passages.text: The Indians say that this dethronement was prognosticated by the evil omen of his having wept blood in his childhood. They also say, reasoning amongst themselves, and recalling the memory of past events, that if this Ynca, when he began to fear the disposition of his son, had resorted to the remedy of giving him a little poison (according to the custom of tyrants, which was practised by the sorcerers in some of the provinces of that empire) he would not have been dethroned. Others, who were held to be religious, and highly extolled the nobility and generosity of their Yncas, said that even if the use of poison had been possible, all his predecessors would rather have died than have used it.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Garcilasso de la Vega, Royal Commentaries (Markham 1871); not verbatim.

title.en: Tahmina Comes to Rustam by Night
title.zh: 塔米娜夜訪魯斯塔姆

region.en: Palace of Samangan (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 薩曼甘王宮（象徵性定位）

period: Composed c. 1010 CE (Warner translation 1905)

source.work: Firdausi, Shahnama, trans. A. G. & E. Warner (1905), vol. II, Suhrab secs. 3-4

summary.en: Rustam's Rakhsh is lassoed by Turkmen horsemen while he sleeps, and he tramps afoot to Samangan, where the king feasts him. At midnight a slave with an ambergris taper leads in a moon-faced girl: Tahmina, sole daughter of the king of Samangan, who has heard the romances of the man who fears not div and lion and has sacrificed her prudence to her passion, hoping God may lay upon her breast a child of his. They are wed by the usual rites, and Rustam, leaving at dawn, gives her his famous armlet as a token for the child: if a daughter, plait it in her hair; if a son, bind it round his arm, for he will be like Sam in stature and bring down soaring eagles.
summary.zh: 魯斯塔姆熟睡時拉赫什被突厥騎手套走，他徒步前往薩曼甘，受國王盛宴款待。半夜，一名手持龍涎香燭的侍女引來月貌少女——國王獨女塔米娜。她傾慕傳說中「不懼魔獅」的英雄，情勝理智，只盼真主在她懷中賜下他的孩子。二人依禮成婚；黎明分別時，魯斯塔姆解下名貴臂鐲相贈：「若是女兒，編入髮辮；若是兒子，繫於其臂——他將如薩姆一般雄偉，能擊落翱翔之鷹。」

sensitivity.note: Epic literary source; the armlet is the recognition-token whose failure causes the tragedy. No living community restriction.

passages.text: Some Turkman horsemen chanced upon the plain and marked the tracks of Rakhsh. These they pursued beside the stream, surrounded him, and with their royal lassos essayed to take him. Rakhsh raged like a mighty lion: lashing out he laid two Turkmans low and with his teeth tore off another's head; at length the others threw from every side their lassos, caught him round the neck and took him. When Rustam woke and needed docile Rakhsh he looked about the mead but found him not, whereat in dudgeon and astound he hurried toward Samangan, thus armed with quiver, mace, helm, scimitar, and tiger-skin cuirass, and went in evil case and much discouragement.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Firdausi, Shahnama, Suhrab secs. 2-3 (Warner 1905); not verbatim.

passages.text: At noon of night, while Phosphor crossed the sky, there came mysterious whispers: Rustam's door was softly opened, and a slave who bare a taper savouring of ambergris walked stately toward the drunken sleeper's couch. Behind the slave there was a moon-faced girl sun-bright, all scent and hue, with arching eyebrows and locks that hung in tresses lasso-like, in stature like a lofty cypress-tree. The lion-hearted Rustam marvelled at her and asked: thy name? What seek'st thou midst the murk of night?
passages.note: Paraphrase of Firdausi, Shahnama, Suhrab sec. 4 (Warner 1905); not verbatim.

passages.text: She said: Tahmina; and thou well mayst say that mine affliction teareth me in twain. Sole daughter of the king of Samangan, there is no mate for me among the kings. Many and many a story have I heard of thee, just like romance: how div and lion, pard and crocodile thou fearest not; how eagles seeing thy naked sword dare not to swoop upon their quarry. God hath ordained thy sojourn in this city, and now if thou wilt have me I am thine, for I have sacrificed my prudence to my passion; haply God Almighty may lay upon my breast a child of thine.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Firdausi, Shahnama, Suhrab sec. 4 (Warner 1905); not verbatim.

passages.text: He bade an archimage go and demand the maiden from her sire. The king, that noble Cypress, was well pleased to be affined to Rustam and bestowed Tahmina on him with the usual rites. He wore an armlet, a famous one; that gave he to Tahmina, and said: keep this. If thou shalt bear a daughter then plait it in her hair; while if the stars vouchsafe to thee a son bind round his arm this token of his father. He will be like Sam son of Nariman in stature and bring down soaring eagles; the sun will scorch not him. Then homeward to Zabulistan he went, but no one heard him speak of this event.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Firdausi, Shahnama, Suhrab sec. 4 (Warner 1905); not verbatim.

title.en: The Birth and Boyhood of Sohrab
title.zh: 蘇赫拉布誕生

region.en: Samangan (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 薩曼甘（象徵性定位）

period: Composed c. 1010 CE (Warner translation 1905)

source.work: Firdausi, Shahnama, trans. A. G. & E. Warner (1905), vol. II, Suhrab sec. 5

summary.en: Nine months pass and a moon-like babe is born; thou wouldst have said 'tis elephantine Rustam or lion-Sam; and since the babe smiled and was bright of blee Tahmina gave to him the name Suhrab. He looked a year old in a month, his chest was like his sire's; at three he exercised in arms, at five he had a lion-heart, at ten none dared encounter him in fight. He bluntly asks his mother who his father is, and Tahmina, to keep the secret of her love, tells him that Rustam, son of Zal, is his father — and the boy's heart swells: I must go to Iran and set my father on the throne of Kai Kaus.
summary.zh: 九月期滿，誕下皎月般的嬰孩——「彷彿巨象般的魯斯塔姆，又如雄獅般的薩姆」；因嬰兒容光煥發，塔米娜為其取名蘇赫拉布（「光彩奪目」）。滿月如周歲，三歲習武，五歲膽壯，十歲無人敢與之角力。他直問母親生父是誰；塔米娜道出「扎勒之子魯斯塔姆」——少年壯志頓生：我要去伊朗，助父登上卡烏斯的王座！

sensitivity.note: Epic literary source; no living community restriction.

passages.text: Nine months passed and a moon-like babe was born; thou wouldst have said: 'tis elephantine Rustam, or else: 'tis lion-Sam, or Nariman; and since the babe smiled and was bright of blee Tahmina gave to him the name Suhrab. He looked a year old in a month, his chest was like his sire's; at three he exercised in arms, at five he had a lion-heart, at ten none dared encounter him in fight.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Firdausi, Shahnama, Suhrab sec. 5 (Warner 1905); not verbatim.

passages.text: He bluntly asked his mother once: now tell me, since none of my milk-fellows can compare with me, and my head reacheth to the sky, who is my sire? Tahmina, to keep the secret of her love, told him that Rustam, son of Zal, the hero of Zabul, was his father, and his heart swelled with the desire to go to Iran and set his father on the throne of Kai Kaus.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Firdausi, Shahnama, Suhrab sec. 5 (Warner 1905); not verbatim.

title.en: Tuli Complains and Tangaloa Fishes Up the Land
title.zh: 鷸鳥啼訴：坦加羅亞釣起大地

region.en: Skies over Samoa (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 薩摩亞上空（象徵性定位）

period: Samoan oral tradition; recorded 1897 (Stair)

source.work: John B. Stair, Old Samoa, ch. 9 (London 1897)

summary.en: Tangaloa of the Skies, principal god and creator, sent his son the plover Tuli down to the ocean's surface; finding no place to rest, Tuli returned to complain, and Tangaloa threw down a stone which became land - or fished one up from the bottom of the sea with his great fish-hook, raising it higher on a second cast when the waves still wetted Tuli's feet. The reclining rock gave place to the spreading, sitting and upright rocks, then earth and grass and conquering convolvulus - whose rottenness bred the two grubs out of which Ngai-tosi and Ngai-va'a-va'ai shaped the first two bodies of mankind, part by part named for Tuli.
summary.zh: 天主坦加羅亞遣其子——鷸鳥圖利——下探海面；無處棲身，鷸鳥啼訴於天，父乃擲下巨石化為陸地——或以神鉤自海底釣起山岩，浪濤仍濕其足，遂二次揚鉤升高陸地。臥岩讓位於蔓延岩、坐岩、立岩；其後泥土、青草、藤蔓相繼而出——腐藤之中化出兩條幼蟲，恩加伊托西與恩加伊瓦瓦艾將其塑為兩具人形，各部皆冠以圖利之名。

sensitivity.note: Samoan creation; fish-hook parallels the Maori Maui and Hawaiian creation.

passages.text: The Samoans had several superior divinities and a host of inferior ones, and they were also accustomed to deify the spirits of deceased chiefs. Of the primitive gods the chief place is assigned to Tangaloa, or, as he is sometimes called, Tangaloa-langi, Tangaloa of the Skies. He was always spoken of as the principal god, the creator of the world and progenitor of the other gods and mankind. In one tradition that gives an account of the formation of the earth mention is made of other divinities or helpers, Tangaloa-tosi, also styled Ngai-tosi (Ngai the marker), and Ngai-va'a-va'ai (Ngai the seer or beholder), also called Tangaloa-va'a-va'ai; these two helpers are introduced as being sent by Tangaloa to complete the formation of the bodies of the first two of mankind, and to impart life to them.
passages.note: Paraphrase of John B. Stair, Old Samoa, ch. 9 (1897); not verbatim.

passages.text: The son of Tangaloa was the Tuli, a species of plover. Tuli went down from the heavens to the surface of the ocean, but found no place on which to rest, and returned to complain to his father. On this his father threw down a stone from the heavens, which became land. Another account of the origin of the earth states that, in answer to Tuli's complaint of want of a resting-place, Tangaloa fished up a large stone from the bottom of the sea with a fish-hook; having raised the stone to the surface, he gave it to his son for his dwelling-place. On going thither to take possession of his new home Tuli found that every wave or swell of the ocean partially overflowed it, which compelled him to hop from one part to another of the stone to prevent his feet being wetted by each succeeding wave; annoyed at this, he returned to the skies to complain to his father, who, by a second application of the mighty fish-hook, raised the land to the desired height. This version is also given by the inhabitants of other groups in Polynesia.
passages.note: Paraphrase of John B. Stair, Old Samoa, ch. 9 (1897); not verbatim.

passages.text: This tradition also gives the history of the worm of the earth. Popo-taoto, the reclining rock, was succeeded by Popo-sosolo, the spreading rock; Papa-sosolo was succeeded by Papa-nofo, the sitting rock; Papa-nofo was succeeded by Papa-tu, the upright rock. The rock was succeeded by the earth or mould, which was then spread over with grass; after this the fue (convolvulus) grew and overcame the grass. Tuli returned to his father, Tangaloa, having obtained his land, but there was no man to reside on it. His father said to him, 'You have got your land. What grows on it?' Tuli answered, 'The fue.' His father told him to go and pull it up, which he did, and on its rotting produced two grubs, which moved a little as Tuli looked upon them; he again returned to the skies to tell his father of their birth.
passages.note: Paraphrase of John B. Stair, Old Samoa, ch. 9 (1897); not verbatim.

passages.text: Upon this Tuli was told to return to the earth and take with him Tangaloa-tosi, or Ngai-tosi, the marker, and Tangaloa-va'a-va'ai, the seer, who were told to operate upon the two grubs; on their arrival they began to form them into the shape of men, commencing at the head. When the head was completed Tuli said, 'Let my name be joined with that of the head', a portion of which was then named O le-tuli-ulu; they then proceeded to give sight by forming the eyes, when Tuli made the same request as before, upon which a portion of the eye was called O le-tuli-mata; the different members of the body were successively formed, each having the name of Tuli prefixed to the portion of the body as formed: as the elbow, O le-tuli-lima, and the knee, O le-tuli-vae.
passages.note: Paraphrase of John B. Stair, Old Samoa, ch. 9 (1897); not verbatim.

title.en: The First Man Dies by the Little Fish Lo
title.zh: 初人之死：小魚羅致禍

region.en: New-formed Samoa (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 新成之薩摩亞（象徵性定位）

period: Samoan oral tradition; recorded 1897 (Stair)

source.work: John B. Stair, Old Samoa, ch. 9 (London 1897)

summary.en: The two shaped bodies lived, but were both males. One day, fishing with a net called the faamutu, one of them was injured by a small fish called the lo, which caused his death. Tuli returned to the skies and bewailed the loss of one of the inhabitants of his land; Ngai-tosi was directed by Tangaloa to proceed to the earth and reanimate the dead body, changing the sex of the deceased male to that of a female - and the two became man and wife, the parents of the human race.
summary.zh: 所塑的兩具身體活了，卻皆為男子。一日以『法阿姆圖圖』漁網捕魚，其一被小魚『羅』所傷而死。圖利上天空哀悼其民之喪；坦加羅亞遣恩加伊托西下界復活屍身——並將死者由男易女。二人遂結為夫婦，成為人類之父母。

sensitivity.note: Origin of death and of the human pair in the Stair recension.

passages.text: On the formation of the two bodies being complete they lived, but were both males, and dwelt on the land on which they were formed. One day, whilst fishing with a net called the faamutu, one of them was injured by a small fish called the lo, which caused his death. Upon this Tuli returned to the skies, and bewailed the loss of one of the inhabitants of his land to his father, when Ngai-tosi was directed by Tangaloa to proceed to the earth and reanimate the dead body; previously to which, however, he changed the sex of the deceased male to that of a female. The two then became man and wife, and the parents of the human race.
passages.note: Paraphrase of John B. Stair, Old Samoa, ch. 9 (1897); not verbatim.

passages.text: In connexion with this history of Tangaloa it may be mentioned that occasional visits are stated to have been made to the abode of the august Tangaloa by parties from the earth, who returned with some useful benefaction from the deity - as, for instance, Losi, who is reputed to have been the benefactor of his countrymen by bringing taro.
passages.note: Paraphrase of John B. Stair, Old Samoa, ch. 9 (1897); not verbatim.

title.en: The Leaping Stone and the Two Roads of the Dead
title.zh: 躍魂之石與亡者兩途

region.en: Falealupo, west point of Savaii (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 薩瓦伊島西端法萊阿盧波（象徵性定位）

period: Samoan oral tradition; recorded 1897 (Stair)

source.work: John B. Stair, Old Samoa, ch. 9 (London 1897)

summary.en: The disembodied spirit retains the exact resemblance of its former self and immediately begins its solitary journey to the Fafa, westward of Savaii: from Manuka the ghost swims island to island to the west point of Savaii, where at the leaping-stone all spirits leap into the sea. There are two roads - O le Lua-loto-o-Alii, the deep hole of chiefs, to Pulotu the abode of the blest; and O le Lua-loto-o-tau-fanua, the deep hole of the common people, to Le nu'u-o-nonoa, the land of the bound, another name for the dreadful Sa-le-Fe'e. Natives have assured Stair that spirits passed them on the road and returned no answer.
summary.zh: 亡魂離體，貌如生前，即刻啟程獨行冥府法法——位於薩瓦伊之西：自毛卡出發的魂靈逐島泅渡，至薩瓦伊西端『躍魂之石』縱身入海。冥途有二：『酋長深穴』通往福地普洛圖；『平民深穴』通往『受縛者之鄉』——即可怖的薩勒費埃。斯泰爾親聞土人說：魂靈曾與他們同行於路，呼之而不應。

sensitivity.note: Samoan eschatology; two-roads parallel to Tongan Pulotu/Sa-le-Fe'e.

passages.text: O le Fafa, Sa-le-Fe'e, and Pulotu are places which occupy a prominent position in Samoan mythology, and seem in some manner to be connected the one with the other. O le Fafa (Hades) is alike the entrance to Sa-le-Fe'e, the Samoan Tartarus, or dread place of punishment, and also to Pulotu, the abode of the blest; the one entrance being called O le Lua-loto-o-Alii, or deep hole of chiefs, by which they passed to Pulotu; the other, O le Lua-loto-o-tau-fanua, or deep hole of the common people, by which they passed to Le nu'u-o-nonoa, or the land of the bound, which is simply another term for the much-dreaded Sa-le-Fe'e. The idea of the superiority of the chiefs over the common people was thus perpetuated, none but chiefs or higher ranks gaining entrance to the Samoan Elysium.
passages.note: Paraphrase of John B. Stair, Old Samoa, ch. 9 (1897); not verbatim.

passages.text: The disembodied spirit was supposed to retain the exact resemblance of its former self, and immediately on leaving the body it was believed to commence its solitary journey to the Fafa, which was located to the westward of Savaii, the most westerly of the group, and towards this point disembodied spirits from all the islands bent their way immediately after death. Thus in case of a spirit commencing its journey at Manuka, the most easterly of the group, it journeyed on to the western end of that island from whence it started, where it dived into the sea and swam to the nearest point of Tutuila, where, having journeyed along the shore to the extreme west point of that island, it again plunged into the sea and pursued its solitary way to the next island, and thus onward throughout the entire group until it reached the extreme west point of Savaii, where it finally dived into the ocean and pursued its solitary way to the mysterious Fafa.
passages.note: Paraphrase of John B. Stair, Old Samoa, ch. 9 (1897); not verbatim.

passages.text: At the west point of Upolu the land terminates in a narrow rocky point, which is still known as O le fatu-osofia, the leaping-stone, from which all spirits were said to leap into the sea en route to the Fafa. This was a much-dreaded point, where the lonely travellers were said to be certainly met with, and their company was anything but desired. Many times natives have assured me that disembodied spirits have passed them on the road when travelling; when asked how they knew them, they answered, 'Why, we knew them personally, and spoke to them, but received no answer', which was quite sufficient in their estimation to determine the spiritual nature of the parties met, since it is the invariable custom of the Samoans to return an answer when accosted on a journey - to do otherwise being looked upon as an insult.
passages.note: Paraphrase of John B. Stair, Old Samoa, ch. 9 (1897); not verbatim.

passages.text: The priesthood, Taula-aitu (anchors of the spirits), were divided into four classes: priests of the war-gods, keepers of the war-gods, family priests, and prophets or sorcerers. The Taula-aitu-o-aitu-tau were important personages, being consulted upon all warlike occasions; this class invoked the assistance of various war-gods, but most of all Nafanua, a female deity who was reverenced by the entire population, and who in conjunction with Savea-se'u-leo may be considered the national gods of war. It was one of this class, the representative of Le Tamafainga, that usurped the regal power of the islands and reigned with great tyranny over the whole of Samoa until the year 1829, when he was slain by the people of A'ana - he was worshipped as combining both regal and divine attributes.
passages.note: Paraphrase of John B. Stair, Old Samoa, ch. 9 (1897); not verbatim.

title.en: Pachacamac, Whom No One Had Seen: Adoration Without Image
title.zh: 無人見過的帕查卡馬克:無像之拜

region.en: Valley of Pachacamac, coast below Lima (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 帕查卡馬克谷地（象徵性定位）

period: Written by Garcilaso de la Vega (Inca), publ. Markham trans. 1871

source.work: Garcilasso de la Vega (El Inca), First Part of the Royal Commentaries of the Yncas, trans. C. R. Markham, London 1871

summary.en: The Yncas kings of Peru, with the light of nature which God had bestowed on them, had attained to a conception of the Maker of all things, whom they called Pachacamac, the word signifying the maker and sustainer of the universe. They said that Pachacamac was invisible, and that consequently they neither built temples nor offered sacrifices to him, as to the sun, but adored him inwardly with the greatest veneration, in accordance with the outward demonstrations they made with heads, eyes, arms, and body, when they used his name. Those who had adopted this belief before they were conquered by the Yncas were the ancestors of king Guismancu, who built a temple to Pachacamac and gave the same name to the valley where it stood. The Yuncas placed their idols in this temple, which were figures of fishes, and among them there was the image of a fox. The valley of Rimac, four leagues to the north, took its name from an idol there in the shape of a man, which spoke and gave answers to questions like the oracle of the Delphic Apollo: Rimac signifies 'He who speaks', and the city of Lima was founded in that valley.
summary.zh: 秘魯的印加諸王,憑上帝所賦的自然之光,已能體認造化萬物之主,稱之為「帕查卡馬克」——此名意即「宇宙的造就者與扶持者」。他們說帕查卡馬克隱而無形,故不像對太陽那樣為他建廟獻祭,只在內心以至高崇敬拜他;而每當提及他的名號,便以頭、眼、臂、身作出外在的敬意。此信仰廣布帝國;早在印加人到來之前便已信奉此道的,是庫伊斯曼庫王的先祖——他們為帕查卡馬克建了一座大神廟,並以其名命名所在的河谷。永卡人把偶像供在廟裡:是些魚形神像,其中還有一尊狐像。以北四萊格的利馬谷,則得名於一尊人形神像——它開口言事、有問必答,如德爾斐阿波羅的神諭;「里馬克」即「發言者」之意;今日利馬城便建於該谷。

sensitivity.note: Garcilaso's natural-theology reading of Pachacamac as an unimaged Creator - the classic passage on Andean henotheism.

passages.text: The Yncas kings of Peru, with the light of nature which God had bestowed on them, had attained to a conception of the Maker of all things, whom they called Pachacamac, the word signifying the maker and sustainer of the universe. They said that Pachacamac was invisible, and that consequently they neither built temples nor offered sacrifices to him, as to the sun, but adored him inwardly with the greatest veneration, in accordance with the outward demonstrations they made with heads, eyes, arms, and body, when they used his name.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Garcilasso de la Vega, Royal Commentaries (Markham 1871); not verbatim.

passages.text: Those who more particularly had adopted this belief before they were conquered by the Yncas were the ancestors of king Guismancu, who built a temple to Pachacamac, and gave the same name to the valley where it stood. The Yuncas placed their idols in this temple, which were figures of fishes, and among them there was the image of a fox.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Garcilasso de la Vega, Royal Commentaries (Markham 1871); not verbatim.

passages.text: The valley of Rimac is four leagues to the north of Pachacamac. The word Rimac is the present participle, and signifies 'He who speaks.' The valley was so called from an idol there, in the shape of a man, which spoke and gave answers to questions, like the oracle of the Delphic Apollo and many others mentioned in the histories of the ancient heathens. So they called it 'He who speaks' because it talked, and the valley was given the same name.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Garcilasso de la Vega, Royal Commentaries (Markham 1871); not verbatim.

canonical_translation: C. R. Markham, First Part of the Royal Commentaries of the Yncas (1871)

title.en: The Fox, the Ocean, and the Peace with Cuismancu
title.zh: 狐與海:與庫伊斯曼庫的和平之約

region.en: Valleys of Pachacamac and Rimac (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 帕查卡馬克與里馬克兩谷(象徵性標記)

period: Written by Garcilaso de la Vega (Inca), publ. Markham trans. 1871

source.work: Garcilasso de la Vega (El Inca), First Part of the Royal Commentaries of the Yncas, trans. C. R. Markham, London 1871

summary.en: The great lord Cuismancu replied that his people had no need of another lord; that the laws and customs he observed were those which had been received from his ancestors; that his people had no wish to put away their gods, for these gods were very powerful: among them was Pachacamac, whom they believed to be the creator and preserver of the universe, and therefore necessarily a greater god than the sun. They had built a temple to Pachacamac, where they offered up the best of everything they had, even sacrificing men, women and children; and such was the veneration in which they held him that they used not even to look upon his image, but the king and the priests entered the temple to worship, walking backwards, and went out so as to avoid raising their eyes. They also worshipped Rimac, a god that spoke and gave replies; their other objects of worship were the fox, which they respected for his cunning and sagacity, and the ocean, because it supplied them with fish. Cuismancu concluded by saying that these gods were sufficient for them: the sun less than any, as they needed no more heat than they already experienced. The Yncas resolved not to make war but to subdue the Yuncas by reasoning and kindness. A peace was concluded: the Yuncas agreed to worship the sun like the Yncas, and to build a separate temple; that no human sacrifices should be made, because to kill a man was contrary to the laws of nature, and the custom was to be entirely abolished; that the idols should be removed from the temple of Pachacamac, and that he should henceforth be worshipped in the heart, no statue being set up because no one had ever seen him; that a house of chosen virgins of the sun should be established, the two things the provinces most desired to possess being a temple of the sun and a convent of virgins, for by possessing these they resembled Cuzco; and the Yncas agreed to hold in high veneration the oracle Rimac.
summary.zh: 庫伊斯曼庫答道:他的子民不需要別的主;他的法度皆承自祖先;他們也無意拋棄自己的神——那些神威力無邊,其中有創造並扶持宇宙的帕查卡馬克,自然比太陽更偉大。他們為他建廟,獻上最好的所有,甚至人祭;崇敬之至,連神像也不敢仰視——王與祭司入廟禮拜,須倒退而行,出廟時亦不得抬眼。他們還拜里馬克——那尊會說話、有問必答的神;此外尊狐之狡智,敬海洋之賜魚。庫伊斯曼庫說:有這些神便夠了;太陽嘛,他們並不需要更多的熱。印加人聞言大喜,決定不以兵戎,而以理喻與善意收服永卡人。和平條款如下:永卡人奉拜太陽,另建太陽神廟;廢除人祭——殺人違逆自然之法;偶像盡出帕查卡馬克神廟——他既無形無像,自當「心拜」而不立像;並建太陽貞女之屋——各地最慕者,莫過太陽神廟與貞女院,有此二者便如庫斯科;印加人亦允崇奉里馬克神諭,令全境敬之。

sensitivity.note: A negotiated theology: Garcilaso presents the Inca conquest of the coast as a religious peace treaty; the fox-and-ocean cult detail is unique.

passages.text: He replied that his people had no need of another lord... that they had no wish to put away their gods, for these gods, he said, were very powerful. Among them was Pachacamac, whom they believed to be the creator and preserver of the universe, and therefore necessarily a greater god than the sun... such was the veneration in which they held him, that they used not even to look upon his image, but the King and the priests entered the temple to worship, walking backwards, and went out so as to avoid raising their eyes. They also worshipped Rimac, a god that spoke and gave replies to those who sought him. Their other objects of worship were the fox, which they respected for his cunning and sagacity, and the ocean, because it supplied them with fish... the sun less than any, as they needed no more heat than they already experienced.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Garcilasso de la Vega, Royal Commentaries (Markham 1871); not verbatim.

passages.text: The Yuncas agreed to worship the sun like the Yncas, and to build a separate temple... but that no human sacrifices should be made, because to kill a man was contrary to the laws of nature, and the custom was to be entirely abolished. It was agreed that the idols should be removed from the temple of Pachacamac... Pachacamac was henceforth to be worshipped in the heart, and no statue to him was to be set up; because, as no one had ever seen him, it was impossible to know his figure, or to make an image of him. It was also arranged, for the greater honour and glory of the valley of Pachacamac, that a house of chosen virgins of the sun should be established... The Yncas agreed to hold in high veneration the oracle Rimac.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Garcilasso de la Vega, Royal Commentaries (Markham 1871); not verbatim.

canonical_translation: C. R. Markham, First Part of the Royal Commentaries of the Yncas (1871)

title.en: The Voice from the Corners of the Temple: Pachacamac's New Oracle
title.zh: 神廟角落的聲音:帕查卡馬克神諭的革新

region.en: Temple of Pachacamac (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 帕查卡馬克神廟(象徵性標記)

period: Written by Garcilaso de la Vega (Inca), publ. Markham trans. 1871

source.work: Garcilasso de la Vega (El Inca), First Part of the Royal Commentaries of the Yncas, trans. C. R. Markham, London 1871

summary.en: It is worthy of note that the Devil, as soon as he saw that the Yncas had subjugated the valley of Pachacamac, and that the temple was cleared of the numerous idols that it formerly contained, sought to make himself the special lord of it, in the character of the unknown god whom the Indians venerated so highly, so as to obtain worship in various ways, and to sell his lies at a higher price in some places than in others. With this object he began to speak from the corners of the temple to the priests of the highest position and character, saying that he wished to reply to their questions and inquiries, not when all were assembled, but to the most respected alone, because it was beneath his dignity to speak to men of low degree. He added that he could only condescend to converse with kings and great lords, but that he would order the idol Rimac, who was his slave, to speak to the common people, and to answer all their inquiries. From that time it was the rule to consult the oracle on matters of state in the temple of Pachacamac, and for the people to resort to that of Rimac. The latter idol thus had his name of 'Speaker' confirmed, for as he was obliged to answer all, he had to talk a great deal.
summary.zh: 值得注意的是:魔鬼一見印加人征服帕查卡馬克谷、神廟中原有的諸多偶像盡被清除,便趁機自封為此廟特別之主——假冒印第安人至為崇敬的那位「無名之神」,以便受人崇拜、把謊言賣得更貴。為此,他開始從神廟的角落向地位最高、品行最尊的祭司們講話:說他不願當眾作答,只肯對受尊崇者開口——向卑微之人說話有失他的尊嚴;還說他只肯屈尊與君王和大領主交談,至於平民的問詢,則命他的奴僕——里馬克神像——代答。自此以後,國家大事便到帕查卡馬克廟中問神,平民之事則赴里馬克廟求問;「發言者」之名就此坐實——因為他須有問必答,只好喋喋不休。

sensitivity.note: The missionary demonology of oracle differentiation: state cult vs popular cult, narrated in Garcilaso's inherited frame.

From that time, it was the rule to consult the oracle on matters of state in the temple of Pachacamac, and for the people to resort to that of Rimac.
