canonical_translation: C. R. Markham, First Part of the Royal Commentaries of the Yncas (1871)

title.en: Sohrab Chooses His Charger and Marches on Iran
title.zh: 蘇赫拉布擇駿出征

region.en: Herds of Samangan (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 薩曼甘馬群（象徵性定位）

period: Composed c. 1010 CE (Warner translation 1905)

source.work: Firdausi, Shahnama, trans. A. G. & E. Warner (1905), vol. II, Suhrab secs. 5-7

summary.en: Sohrab demands a charger swift of foot with hoofs of steel flint-shattering; his might breaks down many a noble steed until a warrior brings a colt of the breed of Rakhsh, in strength a lion and as fleet as wind, whose leap is like the lightning. Mounted, Sohrab appears like Mount Bisitun, his spear pillar-like, and asks his grandsire's leave to seek Iran and see his glorious sire. Afrasiyab, delighted, sends Barman and Human with twelve thousand troops and a secret policy: the father must not recognise his son, that matchless Rustam may be slain — and should the boy perish by his father's hand, that hero's heart will never cease to burn.
summary.zh: 蘇赫拉布索求鋼蹄碎石、疾如飛鳥的戰馬；他的神力折服諸多駿馬，直到有人獻上「拉赫什血統」的雄駒——力如獅、疾如風、躍如閃電。少年上馬如比斯通山聳立，向祖父請命赴伊朗「拜見生父」。阿弗拉西亞卜大喜，遣巴爾曼與胡曼率一萬二千人並授密計：務使父子互不相認，讓無敵的魯斯塔姆隕落；若少年死於父親之手，那位英雄之心將永燃悔恨之火。

sensitivity.note: Epic literary source; Afrasiyab's intrigue is the tragic engine of the Sohrab story. No living community restriction.

passages.text: Thou shalt see my prowess, said Sohrab, but I must have a charger swift of foot with hoofs of steel flint-shattering, in strength like elephants, in flight like birds, in water like fish, and on the land like deer. His mother bade the herdsman bring his herds of horses for Sohrab to choose a charger; and when some large-limbed, lusty steed appeared Sohrab flung round its neck the leathern noose, then laid his hand upon the beast to prove it and made it grovel. Thus his might broke down full many a noble steed.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Firdausi, Shahnama, Suhrab sec. 6 (Warner 1905); not verbatim.

passages.text: At length a warrior approached the elephantine youth and said: I have a colt, one of the breed of Rakhsh, in strength a lion and as fleet as wind; beneath the stamping of his hoofs the Bull-fish quaketh; his leap is like the lightning; on the mountains he goeth like the raven, on the water like fish, upon the desert like shaft from bow. Sohrab laughed out for joy, both proved and approved it, saddled and mounted; he appeared like Mount Bisitun, his spear was pillar-like. Since I have gotten such a steed I must ride forth at once and turn the day of Kai Kaus to gloom.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Firdausi, Shahnama, Suhrab sec. 6 (Warner 1905); not verbatim.

passages.text: Afrasiyab had news: Suhrab hath launched his ship, a host hath gathered unto him; although his mouth still savoureth of milk his mind is set on shaft and scimitar. He chose two chiefs, Human and Barman, gave them twelve thousand valiant troops and said: be this your secret policy: the father must not recognise his son by any ties of instinct, love, or race; so, when the twain encounter, the matchless Rustam will be put to it; it may be that this lion-man will slay him. Then will we press Kaus and seize on Iran with Rustam gone; while should he perish by his father's hand, that hero's heart will never cease to burn.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Firdausi, Shahnama, Suhrab sec. 7 (Warner 1905); not verbatim.

title.en: Gurdafrid Unmasks before White Castle
title.zh: 古爾達弗里德城堡前現真容

region.en: White Castle of Iran (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 伊朗白堡（象徵性定位）

period: Composed c. 1010 CE (Warner translation 1905)

source.work: Firdausi, Shahnama, trans. A. G. & E. Warner (1905), vol. II, Suhrab secs. 8-11

summary.en: At White Castle veteran Hajir rides out against the boy and is thrown like a boulder to the earth; his daughter Gurdafrid, a woman ever famous in the fight, arms herself, conceals her tresses under her mail, and showers arrows on Sohrab, who abashed charges, rents her mail with a dart, and snatches off her helm — her hair escapes, her face shines like the sun: it is a girl! He lassoes her round the waist, but she bargains: chiefs should be wise, so let us keep it dark; our troops and stronghold are at thy command. Then from the ramparts she mocks him: when news shall reach the Shah, he will march forth with Rustam whom ye cannot stand against; woe is me that such a neck and shoulder should disappear within the maw of pards.
summary.zh: 白堡守將海吉爾出戰，竟被少年如巨石般摔落於地。其女古爾達弗里德——征戰聞名的巾幗英雄——披甲藏髮出戰，箭如飛蝗；蘇赫拉布慚愧而奮擊，一鏢撕裂其鎧甲，奪其盔——長髮飄散、面容如日：「原來是女子！」他以套索擒其腰；她卻與之講和：「智者不逞匹夫之勇，堡壘兵馬任憑差遣。」隨後在城頭譏笑他：等卡烏斯與魯斯塔姆大軍一到，你這等英偉的脖頸怕要葬身獅腹！

sensitivity.note: Epic literary source; Gurdafrid's taunt plants the fatal ambiguity of Sohrab's identity. No living community restriction.

passages.text: White Castle was a stronghold of Iran and veteran Hajir was castellan, a man of might and courage; for Gazhdaham was failing though still brave and venturesome. His daughter, who was proud, renowned, and malapert, bore arms and fought on horseback. As Sohrab approached, Hajir sped forth upon the field. Suhrab rushed from the host as 'twere a blast: what are thy name and lineage? She that bare will have to weep for thee.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Firdausi, Shahnama, Suhrab sec. 8 (Warner 1905); not verbatim.

passages.text: Hajir laughed out and charged; brave Sohrab, strong as an elephant, came on like fire upon his moving mountain of a steed. Hajir thrust at his waist; the spearpoint glanced. Sohrab struck with the butt his foe's waist lustily and threw him like a boulder to the earth, astound in heart and soul. Suhrab dismounted, sat on his foeman's breast; Hajir entreated quarter, was made fast in bonds, and sent to Human.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Firdausi, Shahnama, Suhrab sec. 8 (Warner 1905); not verbatim.

passages.text: A woman like some valiant cavalier was she and ever famous in the fight; her name was Gurdafrid, and none as yet had seen her match. Time pressed, she armed, concealed her tresses underneath her mail, secured her Ruman casque upon her head, and came down, like a lion, from the hold with girded waist upon a wind-foot steed. What lusty Crocodile is there among you to match himself with me in single combat? she cried in thunder-tones.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Firdausi, Shahnama, Suhrab sec. 9 (Warner 1905); not verbatim.

passages.text: He thrust a deadly dart with all his strength, struck Gurdafrid upon the belt and rent her coat of mail, but even as she reeled she drew her sword and clave the dart asunder; he pressed upon her, jostled her, and snatched her helm: her hair escaped, her face shone like the sun. It is a girl! he said amazed. He caught her round the waist, but she showed her face and said: chiefs should be wise, so let us keep it dark; our troops and stronghold are at thy command. Then, laughing, from the ramparts she mocked him: when news shall reach the Shah that a chief is leading an army from Turan, he will march forth with Rustam whom ye cannot stand against, and all thy host will perish; woe is me that such a neck and shoulder should disappear within the maw of pards.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Firdausi, Shahnama, Suhrab secs. 9-11 (Warner 1905); not verbatim.

title.en: Kana, Born a Rope, Grows into the Sky
title.zh: 繩形所生的巨人卡納

region.en: Piihonua, Hilo, Hawaii Island
region.zh: 夏威夷島希洛皮伊霍努阿

period: Hawaiian oral tradition; recorded 1916-1917 (Fornander Collection)

source.work: Fornander Collection of Hawaiian Folk-lore, vol. 4, Legend of Kana and Niheu (Honolulu 1916-1917)

license: Public domain (Bishop Museum Memoirs vol. IV, 1916-1917)

summary.en: Hakalanileo and Hina's first-born Kana is born as a piece of rope; grandmother Uli, famed sorceress, keeps it until it assumes human form and brings the child up at Piihonua in Hilo. His body grows so tall and terrible to behold that the house Halauoloolo must be lengthened from the mountain almost to the sea - the Jack-and-beanstalk growth of the Hawaiian hero who will one day reach the deep blue of the heavens.
summary.zh: 哈卡拉尼萊奧與希娜的長子卡納降生時竟是一段繩索，並無人形；祖母烏里——巫術界著名的女神——將其收藏，待其成人形後扶養於希洛皮伊霍努阿。其身軀猛長，可怖驚人，以致居屋哈勞洛洛不得不自山腳一延至海——這便是日後直上藍天的夏威夷英雄的傑克豆蔓式成長。

sensitivity.note: Kana is a figure of great antiquity in Hawaiian legendary lore; Uli the sorcerer-goddess.

passages.text: Hakalanileo was the father and Hina the mother of Kana, the first-born, and Niheu was the younger brother of Kana; Uli was the grandmother. Hamakualoa, Maui, was the land in which Kana was born, and Halauoloolo was the name of the house. At the birth of Kana he was in the form of a piece of rope; he had no human form. After the birth of Kana, Uli took and kept it until it assumed a human form, then she brought the child up. The place where Kana was brought up was in Piihonua, Hilo, Hawaii, a place lying to the east of Wailuku, where his house was built, called Halauoloolo.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Fornander Collection of Hawaiian Folk-lore, vol. 4, Legend of Kana and Niheu (1916-1917); not verbatim.

passages.text: In this legend it is said that the body of Kana grew to be very tall and large and was terrible to behold. While he was being brought up he grew so fast that the house had to be lengthened, so that it extended from the mountain until it was almost to the edge of the sea - such is the story as told of this house, Halauoloolo. Hina in this story has been called Hawaii's Helen of Troy; she has been a prolific inspiration of freaks and foibles in the folk-lore not only of these islands but throughout Polynesia, and Niheu was said to have special power, Sampson-like, through his long hair.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Fornander Collection of Hawaiian Folk-lore, vol. 4, Legend of Kana and Niheu (1916-1917); not verbatim.

title.en: Kana Snaps the Flippers of the Turtle Hill Haupu
title.zh: 卡納折斷龜山霍普之鰭

region.en: Haupu hill, Pelekunu, Molokai
region.zh: 摩洛凱島佩萊庫努霍普山

period: Hawaiian oral tradition; recorded 1916-1917 (Fornander Collection)

source.work: Fornander Collection of Hawaiian Folk-lore, vol. 4, Legend of Kana and Niheu (Honolulu 1916-1917)

license: Public domain (Bishop Museum Memoirs vol. IV, 1916-1917)

summary.en: The floating hill Haupu - in truth the great turtle Kahonunuimaeleka - carries off Hina to Molokai with chief Kapepeekauila. Uli's gods carry the double canoe Kaumaielieli down from Paliuli; Niheu fells the swordfish-man Keauleinakahi mid-channel and catches the hurled boulder in Kana's right hand. Fed at last by grandmother Uli, Kana towers over Haupu, makes eyes at it until it strains upward to meet him, then breaks the flippers right and left - the hill falls to pieces into the sea, leaving the Rocks of Kana at the mouth of Waikolu Valley.
summary.zh: 漂浮之山霍普——實為巨龜卡霍努努伊馬埃萊卡——攜走希娜至摩洛凱酋長卡佩佩考伊拉處。烏里之神眾自帕利烏里抬下雙舟考邁埃利埃利；尼赫烏中流斃劍魚勇士克勞萊納卡希，卡納右手接住山上擲來的巨石。祖母烏里以食慰之後，卡納拔身凌駕霍普之上，以目相逼——山將其鰭折斷，霍普頓失其力，崩落入海，遺下瓦伊科魯谷口的『卡納之岩』。

sensitivity.note: Molokai landmark legend; prophetic dream of priest Moi summarized in passages.

passages.text: Once upon a time this hill, Haupu, moved or floated to Mokuola in Hilo, Hawaii, carrying along the chief and the people and the things that grew on the hill. When Hina the mother of Kana and Niheu saw that the land was pleasant to the eye she climbed on up the hill with the idea of taking a look at the place; as soon as Hina was on the hill of Haupu it immediately moved back to Molokai, thus leaving Hakalanileo to mourn for her loss. When Hakalanileo saw that his wife was being carried away he tried to recover her but found it impossible to do so; after his failure he proceeded to Niheu and informed him that Hina had been taken away by the hill of Haupu. When Niheu heard this report from his father he said: 'I cannot get her; there is only one person who can do it, and that is Kana. You must go to him personally; don't be afraid of him and run away if he should turn and look at you.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Fornander Collection of Hawaiian Folk-lore, vol. 4, Legend of Kana and Niheu (1916-1917); not verbatim.

passages.text: When Kana heard this he said to Hakalanileo: 'Go and issue a call that the people come together throughout Hawaii, and instruct the men to go and hew out canoes, by which we will get to Molokai and get back your wife.' With this the canoe hewers all around Hawaii came together and a large double canoe of ten fathoms in length was hewed out and made ready; but when Kana stretched out his hands and placed them on the canoe, the canoe sunk out of sight - the hands of Kana alone were too much for the canoe, and it too sunk out of sight, thus leaving them without a canoe to get to Molokai in. Therefore Hakalanileo went to the presence of Niheu, who said: 'You go to Uli and ask for a canoe; she has the canoe that will take you to Molokai, and she will direct you what to do.' Uli made reply: 'Yes, there is a canoe; it is in Paliuli; but you must go and call all the people together to go and drag down the canoes.' Hakalanileo did so and collected eight times forty men, and they proceeded to the uplands of Paliuli, where Uli prayed for a double canoe for Kana; after the people had all returned, the double canoe Kaumaielieli was lifted by the gods and carried down and placed in the sea.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Fornander Collection of Hawaiian Folk-lore, vol. 4, Legend of Kana and Niheu (1916-1917); not verbatim.

passages.text: While Kana and Niheu were making their preparations to sail on the double canoe Kaumaielieli to do battle with Kapepeekauila, the chief on the top of Haupu hill, Moi dreamed a dream - Moi was the priest to the chief Kapepeekauila, a very great priest, learned in his profession and all-powerful, his predictions always coming true. In the night of Kane he dreamed: 'A long man, a short man; a stunted youth, a male god. The eyes touched the heaven; the earth was overshadowed. Say Kamauhili, Ku is routed. Such is my dream, the priest.' After telling the dream Moi gave an interpretation of its meaning, but the chief would not believe it; seeing this Moi prophesied: 'If you are not going to take heed to my warning, you will surely be dispossessed. I saw a long man, and it was by him that the borders of Haupu were broken and the hill fell to pieces into the sea; therefore depart now while death is yet at a distance.' Kapepeekauila refused to take heed of this warning, saying: 'You are the one I shall cause to die, you deceiving priest. My hill of Haupu shall never be conquered. However, let it stand; if my hill is not conquered in the coming fight, I will kill you.' Moi then replied: 'Yes, well and good. The paths of the priests are narrow and can never be reached by crawling.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Fornander Collection of Hawaiian Folk-lore, vol. 4, Legend of Kana and Niheu (1916-1917); not verbatim.

passages.text: When the chief Kapepeekauila heard the words of Moi he sent his swiftest messengers, Kolea and Ulili, to fly and look for Kana and Niheu; when the two came to the harbor of Punahoa in Hilo they flew away up high so as to be out of the reach of Kana, and from up there called out to him. When Kana heard the call he reached up with his hands while still lying down, but did not catch them, though the wind of his hands made them swing away in haste, and in doing this they fell down on the hill of Haupu in Molokai. When the chief heard the report of the two birds he sent them to tell Keauleinakahi, his warrior who had charge of the ocean - a warrior who could thrust through a canoe with his snout. On the day when Kana and Niheu completed their preparations they boarded the canoe taking their father Hakalanileo, and set sail; Kana was wrapped up in the form of a large package placed on the platform, the length of the package extending the full length of the double canoe. While they had reached a point between Hawaii and Maui they were met by Keauleinakahi, who made an attack on the double canoe with the intention of breaking it to pieces with his sharp snout; while it was preparing for the attack Niheu stood up with his war club, Wawaikalani by name, and as Keauleinakahi made the attack Niheu struck it with his club, killing it. The voyage was resumed until they arrived at Waikolu, Molokai, near where the Haupu hill was standing, and here the canoe was moored; a large rock was rolled down from the hill aimed at the canoe, and as Kana was lying on the platform he heard the cry 'Say, there comes a large rock! We will be killed!' - he reached out his right hand and held the rock, while with the left hand he reached for a small stone and lodged it fast between the palis, where it is to this day; thus Kana and the canoes of Kaumaielieli escaped the death of the rock.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Fornander Collection of Hawaiian Folk-lore, vol. 4, Legend of Kana and Niheu (1916-1917); not verbatim.

passages.text: The real name of the hill was Kahonunuimaeleka, a turtle, and had flippers on the sides; whenever these flippers closed the hill would extend up to the heaven. Around this hill was a fence called Paehumu composed of ti-leaf of Koaea and the ulei of Nuuhiwa, which grew so close together that they served as a windbreak, and no wind could touch the chief's house, called Halehuki. When Niheu came up to the fence he beat down the ti-leaf and ulei with his war club, causing the wind to enter Halehuki; Kapepeekauila asked what had caused the wind to enter, and Hina spoke up: 'It must be Niheu, our brave son; he is without fear; we shall be killed.' While she was speaking Niheu came in and taking hold of Hina started off with her - but before Niheu came into the house Hina had told Kolea and Ulili the place wherein the strength of Niheu laid, it being in the strands of his hair, called Wilikalinoamohalaikaekaeka, and told them to take hold of the strands and pull on them, which would cause Niheu to let go of her, for this would cause him to lose his strength. When Kolea and Ulili saw that Hina was being taken away they flew and held Niheu by the hair; Niheu let go of Hina, took up his war club and struck at the two birds, and while he was doing this Hina ran back to the house to her new husband. Kana said to Niheu, 'You stay here on our canoe while I go after our mother'; with this Kana stood up in the canoe and peeped over the hill of Haupu - at this the hill extended on up, and Kana also extended upward too, until he had to go up to the highest heaven, in the deep blue sky, and his body was in the form of a spider's web, for he was in great need of food and meat.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Fornander Collection of Hawaiian Folk-lore, vol. 4, Legend of Kana and Niheu (1916-1917); not verbatim.

passages.text: When Niheu saw that the legs of Kana were thin and in the form of a spider's web he felt that it was because he was starving, so he called out in a loud voice to Kana: 'Lie toward Kona, to Uli our grandmother, where you will be able to get food and meat.' Niheu had to repeat this call for three days before Kana heard him; when Kana heard the call of Niheu he bent himself over across Molokai, over the top of Haleakala, over the mountain whereby a groove was formed across Haleakala which can be seen to this day. When Kana reached Kona and the home of Uli his grandmother he laid down by the doorway until Uli awoke in the morning, and when she came out she saw Kana her grandson, woke him up and began feeding him; when Kana was satisfied the increase of his body began to come down until it reached his feet which were in the canoe, where Niheu was still waiting. When Niheu looked and saw that the legs were increasing he arose and cut off one, for he was angry with Kana for eating till satisfied; the numbness from this cut went up until it reached the head of Kana, and upon informing his grandmother of this fact Uli said: 'Your younger brother Niheu got angry with you because you partook of food without remembering him, so he has cut off one of your legs.' After this Uli said to Kana: 'You have conquered over your opponent. When you rise up you must extend upward until you tower above the Haupu hill, then make eyes at the hill and when it extends up to meet you, you reach down and break off the flippers on the right side; then break off the flippers on the left side; then it will have no more strength.' After these instructions had been imparted Kana arose and stood upright until he towered over Haupu, when he made eyes at the hill; at seeing this Haupu extended upward to meet Kana, and Kana then reached down and broke off the flippers - as soon as the flippers were broken the power of Haupu ceased. Kana then stepped down on the hill and it fell to pieces, and as the pieces fell into the sea they were left there in the form of small hills, which can be seen to this day at the mouth of the Waikolu Valley, overgrown with loulou palms. By the death of Haupu the chief Kapepeekauila was conquered and Hina was recovered, and she was brought back to live with her first husband Hakalanileo - this ended the war between Kana and the Haupu hill.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Fornander Collection of Hawaiian Folk-lore, vol. 4, Legend of Kana and Niheu (1916-1917); not verbatim.

title.en: Hanaaumoe, the Flattering Spirit of Spirit-Oahu
title.zh: 阿諛之靈哈瑙毛埃

region.en: Kou landing, Oahu (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 瓦胡島庫港（象徵性定位）

period: Hawaiian oral tradition; recorded 1916-1917 (Fornander Collection)

source.work: Fornander Collection of Hawaiian Folk-lore, vol. 4, Legend of Hanaaumoe (Honolulu 1916-1917)

license: Public domain (Bishop Museum Memoirs vol. IV, 1916-1917)

summary.en: Old Oahu was the island of spirits under king Halalii, and Hanaaumoe the flatterer guarded its coasts, luring canoes ashore to be eaten. The lame Kaneopa, suspicious, digs a hole beneath the door sill where the spirit king will sit, and alone survives the night of feasting - 'your flesh, your bones, your bowels, your blood, your eyes, will all be eaten up'. He tells his king; the priest orders ten thousand wooden images; the spirits bite them, cry 'How tough!', and the Kauai men burn the long house over them all, sparing only the escaping flatterer.
summary.zh: 舊日瓦胡乃群靈之島，王哈拉利伊治之；阿諛者哈瑙毛埃守其海岸，誘舟登陸以供群靈果腹。跛足的卡內奧帕起疑，在門檻下掘穴藏身——群靈入屋、王坐門檻，一聲啖食，眾人皆歿，唯彼得免。歸告其王；祭司命造木偶萬計以代人。群靈囓之，連呼『真硬！』——考愛人縱火焚長屋，群靈盡燼，唯阿諛者遁去。

sensitivity.note: Spirit-island Oahu tradition; gourd-count of gods cited in source (471, 40,000...).

passages.text: Hanaaumoe was a flattering spirit who lived in Oahu, as the island of Oahu in the olden days, during the reign of Halalii, was the home of the spirits. The duty of this spirit Hanaaumoe was to meet all the canoes that arrived from other lands and through his cunning and flattery urge the people to land; in this way several people were killed and eaten by the spirits. As this spirit had no equal in the art of flattery he was delegated by Halalii, the king of the spirits, to guard all the points along the coast of Oahu. While he was on duty one day he saw canoes approaching Oahu from the west; in the double canoe was Kahaookamoku the friend of the king of Kauai, several men, and Kaneopa, a lame fellow - these people were from Kauai and were on their way to Hawaii to make a visit.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Fornander Collection of Hawaiian Folk-lore, vol. 4, Legend of Hanaaumoe (1916-1917); not verbatim.

passages.text: Hanaaumoe upon seeing these people invited them to come ashore: 'Come ashore, land your canoe. Don't go to Hawaii, for that island is filled with spirits: Hawaii has spirits, for Kanikaa lives there; Maui has spirits, for Keoloewa lives there; Lanai has spirits, for Pahulu lives there; Molokai has spirits, for Kaunolu lives there. Here is the island that has no spirits; land the canoe. There is food ashore, there are houses, there are women for each; the paddlers shall have two apiece as wives, and your chief Kahaookamoku shall have five wives.' When the people heard the invitation extended by Hanaaumoe they came ashore at the landing at Kou, hauled the canoes on to the beach, entered the long shed where they slept awaiting the things promised them by Hanaaumoe.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Fornander Collection of Hawaiian Folk-lore, vol. 4, Legend of Hanaaumoe (1916-1917); not verbatim.

passages.text: Late that evening Hanaaumoe came to the door of the house where the strangers were sleeping and called out: 'Asleep are you? Piled on one another, scattered here and there, are you all asleep?' Everybody was fast asleep except Kaneopa, who was still sitting up; upon hearing the call Kaneopa answered: 'We are not asleep, we are still awake waiting for the food, and meat and our wives.' Hanaaumoe then resorted to falsehood: 'The things cannot arrive in a hurry, as the road from Nuuanu down is long, the climb from Kapukaki is long and the plain Kulaokahua is also afar off.' Hanaaumoe soon after this returned to Halalii and the rest of the spirits. At midnight Hanaaumoe again returned and called the second time; Kaneopa answered as before. Certain thoughts then entered Kaneopa that the island of Oahu was full of spirits and they would all be eaten by them, so he looked for a place within the house where he could conceal himself; after studying the matter for a while he at last decided to dig a hole under the door sill, for he reasoned that the king would, upon entering the house, naturally sit on the door sill. All this time the rest of the people were in a deep sleep; Kaneopa tried to keep himself awake but could only last until the crowing of the first cock, when he too became so overcome with sleep and moved under the door sill and sat in the hole.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Fornander Collection of Hawaiian Folk-lore, vol. 4, Legend of Hanaaumoe (1916-1917); not verbatim.

passages.text: Just as soon as he entered the hole Hanaaumoe arrived and again called as before, for the third time; there was no answer; he called again - again there was no answer. Hanaaumoe then said: 'You will surely be all killed. Why didn't you sleep at Kauai instead of coming and sleeping on the island of Halalii where the spirits live? You are as good as dead; there is no escape; your flesh, your bones, your bowels, your blood, your eyes will all be eaten up.' During all this talk by Hanaaumoe Kaneopa was listening; at the end Hanaaumoe returned to Halalii. Halalii then asked him: 'How is it, are they asleep?' 'Yes, they are asleep; let us be going', said Hanaaumoe to the rest of the spirits. When the spirits arrived at the long house where Kaneopa and his companions were sleeping they all entered, and Halalii sat on the door sill; the spirits were so numerous that they were without number - the number of the gods was 471, 40,000 gods, 400,000 gods, 4,000 gods. They made but one smack and the people disappeared, all eaten up by the spirits; the spirits then began digging up the floor of the house except that portion under the sill where Halalii was sitting. At the approach of day the spirits all returned to their home and Kaneopa came out of his hiding place, and limping to the canoe he pushed it into the sea and set sail for Kauai.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Fornander Collection of Hawaiian Folk-lore, vol. 4, Legend of Hanaaumoe (1916-1917); not verbatim.

passages.text: While Kaneopa was on his way to Kauai Hanaaumoe appeared on the coast and beckoned to him, inviting him to land, saying: 'Come ashore; let the canoe come ashore.' Kaneopa then answered angrily: 'You are a filthy old spirit; didn't you eat up our chief? I will not come ashore.' Upon Kaneopa's arrival at Kauai he informed the king and people how his companions had been eaten up by the spirits of Oahu, and how he was saved only through his wit. The king then asked the priest what must be done, and the priest Hanakapiai answered: 'Proceed and hew out a countless number of wooden images that will look as near as possible to human beings.' After the images were ready the king, the priest and a large number of followers set sail for Oahu, and in course of time hove to directly off Leahi, when they saw Hanaaumoe appear on the coast and call out as he did the other time; Kaneopa, who was in the company on this second visit, said to the people: 'That is Hanaaumoe the great flatterer; that is the spirit who deceived us and got us to land.' The people then all came ashore and approached the long house where Kahaookamoku and his companions had stayed and were eaten up by the spirits. Toward dusk that same evening the priest instructed the people: 'Let everybody retire to where the canoes are lying and leave the wooden images in the house; let everybody be supplied with lights with which to set the house on fire as soon as all the spirits have entered the house.' Late that evening the flatterer Hanaaumoe came to the house and called out his formula; no one answered from within; he called a second time, still no answer. Hanaaumoe then spoke to himself: 'Ha, ha! Why didn't you sleep on Kauai instead of coming here and sleeping on the spirit island of Halalii? Dead, you will not be saved.' At the end of his call Hanaaumoe returned to Halalii and reported that the people were all asleep; upon hearing this report Halalii issued a call that all the spirits be brought together, and they proceeded to the long house at the beach; upon coming up to the house the spirits all entered and Halalii sat on the door sill.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Fornander Collection of Hawaiian Folk-lore, vol. 4, Legend of Hanaaumoe (1916-1917); not verbatim.

passages.text: The spirits then took up the wooden images and began eating them: 'Oh, how tough!' was heard from one of the spirits; 'so is the one I am eating', said another. It was customary in days gone by for the king to receive the choicest portions of the meat, so these portions were given to Halalii by the spirits; upon taking a bite at one of these choice portions Halalii remarked, 'Very tough.' The rest of the spirits answered: 'All these people are very tough, not one of them is fat; they are all thin and tough; they are not at all like the first lot that came.' While the spirits were busy eating the wooden images the Kauai people surrounded the house and set it on fire, killing all the spirits with the exception of Hanaaumoe, who somehow managed to escape.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Fornander Collection of Hawaiian Folk-lore, vol. 4, Legend of Hanaaumoe (1916-1917); not verbatim.

title.en: Eleio the Runner Restores Kanikaniaula to Life
title.zh: 飛毛腿埃萊奧救活卡尼卡尼奧拉

region.en: Lele (Lahaina), Maui
region.zh: 毛伊島萊萊（拉海納）

period: Hawaiian oral tradition (reign of Kakaalaneo); recorded 1916-1917 (Fornander Collection)

source.work: Fornander Collection of Hawaiian Folk-lore, vol. 4, Legend of Eleio (Honolulu 1916-1917)

license: Public domain (Bishop Museum Memoirs vol. IV, 1916-1917)

summary.en: Eleio, swifter than the wind - three circuits of Maui a day - is king Kakaalaneo's awa-fish runner. On the Kaupo road he greets a woman sitting by the wayside, Kanikaniaula, who is in truth a dead chiefess of Hawaii lying in her husband's puoa tomb. Undertaking her revival, he restores her on the fourth day; she gives him her hidden feather cape for the king, is nearly baked in the umu with the rescued hero, and becomes queen of Maui - mother of the breadfruit-puller Kaululaau.
summary.zh: 埃萊奧快逾疾風——一日可繞毛伊三匝——為卡卡拉內奧王跑腿取鰆魚。赴考烏坡路上他與路旁女子招呼——卡尼卡尼奧拉，實為已亡的夏威夷貴婦，停屍於其夫的普瓦阿靈屋中。埃萊奧應允救活她，至第四日死者復生如初；她將珍藏的羽披風贈予其主卡卡拉內奧，幾乎與英雄同入大灶，終成毛伊王后——拔面包果的庫盧勞之母。

sensitivity.note: Resurrection cluster; feather-cape rarity detail retained.

passages.text: Eleio, otherwise known as Lahaina in Maui, is the country in which the events of this legend took place, and the time was during the reign of Kakaalaneo, who was king of the whole island of Maui. Eleio was a very fast runner, faster than the wind, and could make three complete circuits of the island of Maui in one day; because of his great speed he was made runner to King Kakaalaneo, and it was his duty as runner to bring awa fish from Hana for the king: when a meal was about ready Eleio would set out for Hana to bring fish and would always return before the king sat down to eat. Once while he was on his way back he met on the road Kaahualii, a spirit, who asked him for some fish; Eleio answered: 'Take the hairs on your behind for the fish and your urine for water.' When Kaahualii heard this he chased Eleio; upon coming by Kamaalaea Eleio's sister, who was residing at this place, saw that her brother was out of breath, so she took down her pau and exposed herself to the spirit - this action so shamed the spirit that it abandoned Eleio. Being chased by this spirit on three different occasions along this same road, Eleio upon his next return trip went around the west side of Hana by way of Kaupo; upon his arrival at Kaupo one day he found a woman by the name of Kanikaniaula sitting by the roadside, but he passed right along without noticing her; she called out after him, 'Say, are you going to pass right along without greetings?' When Eleio heard this call he turned back and greeted her, and she invited him to the house.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Fornander Collection of Hawaiian Folk-lore, vol. 4, Legend of Eleio (1916-1917); not verbatim.

passages.text: Kanikaniaula at the time when this conversation was taking place was dead: although she appeared in the form of a live person it was really in spirit. She was a very fine woman and came from a line of high chiefs of Hawaii; upon coming to live in Kaupo, Maui, she married a person of low rank who lived in the back country. Upon her death the husband built a tomb, a small house of poles in the form of a pyramid, in which he placed the dead body of his wife; when she came to Maui to live she brought along with her from Hawaii a feather cape which was the insignia of a very high chief, but which article she had hidden up to the time of her death, nor had she ever once alluded to her rank as a high chiefess. When Eleio arrived at the house he saw a man occupying it but the woman was not to be seen. 'Where is my companion?' 'Who is your companion?' 'My companion was a woman.' 'She is dead, my own wife; she is laid in that small house yonder.' 'How many days has she been lying there?' 'Two days already; this is the third day in which we are speaking.' 'Yes, I will undertake to bring your wife to life again', said Eleio; he then proceeded, and at the end of the fourth day Kanikaniaula was brought back to life and in all respects became as she was before her death.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Fornander Collection of Hawaiian Folk-lore, vol. 4, Legend of Eleio (1916-1917); not verbatim.

passages.text: Kanikaniaula then asked Eleio: 'What indeed shall I give you as a recompense? Shall it be myself?' Eleio answered: 'I will not take anything in payment from you, but I wish you to become the wife of my lord, Kakaalaneo.' Kanikaniaula consented to this, saying: 'Yes, he shall be my lord; but here is a present which I wish you to take to him - a feather cape.' At this the husband for the first time was made aware that Kanikaniaula was a chiefess. 'You may now return, and in the nights of Kane you may come for me; I am going to my place on Hawaii and shall return in a few days.' Eleio then returned wearing the feather cape tied around his neck - feather capes at this time were so rare that even Kakaalaneo the king of Maui did not have one in his possession. As Eleio had been absent a number of days Kakaalaneo became very angry and ordered his chief officers to start an umu and make it very hot, in which to bake Eleio upon his return; he had posted spies along the Aalaloloa cliffs to watch for the return of Eleio, and when seen to start a fire as a signal to the people at Lele of his approach, when the umu was to be started and made hot before the arrival of Eleio.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Fornander Collection of Hawaiian Folk-lore, vol. 4, Legend of Eleio (1916-1917); not verbatim.

passages.text: As Eleio came running at full speed with the feather cape over his shoulders, on arrival at Lele and seeing the umu burning and the king sitting near it, he jumped right into the hot umu. When the king saw something red and pretty on Eleio's shoulders he called out to the men, 'Seize Eleio! Seize Eleio!!'; at this the people got hold of Eleio and he was pulled out of the umu and was saved, but the feather cape was torn to pieces - a small piece, however, was saved in the hands of Eleio. Kakaalaneo then called Eleio to come to him, and when he got in the presence of the king asked him, 'Where did you get this beautiful thing?' Eleio replied: 'This was the cause of my delay. Kanikaniaula, a very handsome woman, was dead, and I brought her to life again; I have told her that you are to be her husband.' When Eleio arrived at Kaupo in the nights of Kane he found that Kanikaniaula had returned from Hawaii with some of the chiefs, their servants, and with feather capes; when they reached Lele and stood before the king Kakaalaneo took Kanikaniaula and they dwelt together, husband and wife. Not very long after this Kanikaniaula conceived a child.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Fornander Collection of Hawaiian Folk-lore, vol. 4, Legend of Eleio (1916-1917); not verbatim.

title.en: Kaululaau Outwits the Spirits of Lanai
title.zh: 庫盧勞智取拉奈群靈

region.en: Lanai island (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 拉奈島（象徵性定位）

period: Hawaiian oral tradition (reign of Kakaalaneo); recorded 1916-1917 (Fornander Collection)

source.work: Fornander Collection of Hawaiian Folk-lore, vol. 4, Relating to Kaululaau (Honolulu 1916-1917)

license: Public domain (Bishop Museum Memoirs vol. IV, 1916-1917)

summary.en: Prince Kaululaau, who pulls up the breadfruit trees of Lele for sport, is exiled by his father to spirit-haunted Lanai with a cooked store. Warned by his aumakua in dream, he hides each night in a cave and by day answers the spirits' question with a different lie - the thistle patch, the thorny vines, the great surf - until the spirits are worked to death, only Pahulu escaping to Kahoolawe. The king, seeing the fire still burning, sends for his mischievous son: 'He was sent to Lanai to be devoured by the spirits, but no! What does it mean? Well and good.'
summary.zh: 王子庫盧勞以拔光萊萊的面包果為戲，被父放逐到群靈盤踞的拉奈島。夜夢中祖靈示警，他夜宿岩穴、晝答群靈以謊——今宿刺茄叢、明宿棘藤、又宿大浪之中——直把群靈追索至死，唯帕胡魯遁往卡胡拉維。國王遙見島上火光不熄，問：『庫盧勞莫非未被靈所食？』遂遣雙舟迎回：『本欲以靈飼之，孰料竟不然——也罷。』

sensitivity.note: Companion to the Hanaaumoe cycle; Pahulu named as the Lanai spirit-king.

passages.text: On the day when it was discovered that the queen was with child, Kakaalaneo sent out his messengers to make a circuit of Maui and find out all the chiefesses who were also with child on that same day, the intention of the king being to procure servants and playmates for the coming heir. In due course of time the queen gave birth to a baby boy and he was called Kaululaau, known as the one who pulled up the breadfruit trees of Lele; all the children who were born on the same day on Maui were brought to the king and reared with the prince Kaululaau. As Kaululaau grew to manhood, so also grew his playmates, and as he grew older he became more and more mischievous: it was customary for the boys with him to climb the breadfruit trees and pick the fruit, and when the fruit got fewer and beyond their reach Kaululaau would then pull up the trees with his hands; this was done so often that the trees became scarce in the district of Lele. At last the father Kakaalaneo took pity on the people, knowing that they would some day go hungry, and ordered that all the boys be sent home to their parents; but instead of improving Kaululaau grew worse. After considering the matter for some time the father at last told the queen and attendants to take Kaululaau and abandon him on Lanai with the spirits; the chiefs and people agreed, the food and meat were cooked, kapa and other things were gotten ready, and the canoes set out with Kaululaau - upon their arrival at Lanai he was put ashore with all the things prepared for him and the canoes returned.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Fornander Collection of Hawaiian Folk-lore, vol. 4, Relating to Kaululaau (1916-1917); not verbatim.

passages.text: When Kaululaau landed on Lanai he entered a patch of reeds and slept there; while in his sleep his god came to him and said: 'Say, Kaululaau, get up and enter the cave with all your belongings.' When Kaululaau woke up he looked about him and saw a cave opening near by, so he got up and entered it in obedience to the instructions given him in his sleep. Lanai was an island of spirits: no people could live on this island, as the spirits killed and ate everybody who came there; Kaululaau was, however, an exception to this, for he was not eaten up - but this was because he was too cunning in telling falsehoods, just like Punia, who was considered the champion liar of his time. That night Kaululaau slept in the cave, and at daylight he left it and returned to the patch of reeds, where he was found by the spirits, who asked him: 'Say, Kaululaau, where did you sleep last night?' Kaululaau replied: 'In the small patch of thistles.' 'Is that so?
passages.note: Paraphrase of Fornander Collection of Hawaiian Folk-lore, vol. 4, Relating to Kaululaau (1916-1917); not verbatim.

passages.text: No wonder you were not found last night', remarked the spirits. On the approach of the next night he again entered the cave, when the spirits went about looking for him the whole night; at daylight Kaululaau went to the beach on the dry sand and sat there, where the spirits came and asked him: 'Where did you sleep last night?' 'In the patch of thorny vines growing there; that is the place where I slept.' The spirits again asked him: 'Where are you going to sleep to-night?' Kaululaau replied: 'In the large surf where it rolls as high as a house; that is where I will sleep.' On the approach of night Kaululaau would again retire to the cave, and at daylight go out on the sand where he would be met by the spirits, who would ask him: 'Where did you sleep last night?' 'In the small surf; you were all at the large surf', Kaululaau would reply.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Fornander Collection of Hawaiian Folk-lore, vol. 4, Relating to Kaululaau (1916-1917); not verbatim.

passages.text: Through these deceiving answers the spirits got so overworked that they mostly all died off, leaving but very few of them alive; Pahulu was one of the spirits that was saved, because he left Lanai and went over to Kahoolawe to live. Kaululaau after this kept a fire burning all the time he remained on Lanai; Kakaalaneo upon seeing the fire burning on Lanai so continuously asked the people: 'Say, Kaululaau could not have been killed by the spirits?' 'No', replied the people. Therefore Kakaalaneo sent some people in a canoe to go to Lanai and see if Kaululaau was indeed still alive or not; when the canoe arrived at Lanai the people saw that Kaululaau was indeed still alive and was still keeping the fire burning. The canoe then returned to Lele and the people told Kakaalaneo the king of what they had seen; when the king heard this he remarked: 'Yes, he was sent to Lanai to be devoured by the spirits, but no! What does it mean? Well and good.' He then ordered a double canoe to go and bring Kaululaau home - this is how Kaululaau was saved, and his history and life on Lanai has become famous even unto this day.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Fornander Collection of Hawaiian Folk-lore, vol. 4, Relating to Kaululaau (1916-1917); not verbatim.

title.en: Women Like Valiant Men: The Amazons of Chugara
title.zh: 如勇男般的女子:丘加拉的亞馬遜

region.en: Chugara, province of the Canas (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 卡納斯省丘加拉(象徵性標記)

period: Written by Cieza de León, publ. Markham trans. 1883 (Second Part)

source.work: Pedro de Cieza de León, The Second Part of the Chronicle of Peru, trans. and ed. Sir Clements Markham, Hakluyt Society, 1883

summary.en: They affirm of a certainty that, after that powerful captain arose in Hatuncollao, there appeared in the province of the Canas, which lies between the Canches and Collao, near the village called Chugara, some women who were like valiant men. Taking up arms they subdued those who were in the district where they lived, and, almost like what is told of the Amazons, they made homes for themselves, without husbands. These people, after this had gone on for some years, and they had performed some famous deeds, came to fight with Zapana, he who had become Lord of Hatuncollao; and to defend themselves against his power, which was great, they made fortresses and walls, which still exist. But after they had done all to the utmost of their power, they were taken and killed, and their name disappeared.
summary.zh: 據說確有其事:繼哈通科利亞奧那位強大的酋長崛起之後,在卡納斯省——坎切斯與科利亞奧之間——的丘加拉村附近,出現了一批勇武如男子的女子。她們執兵而戰,征服了所居之地的居民;幾乎如傳說中的亞馬遜,她們自立門戶,不嫁不婚。數年之間,她們建立功業,聲名遠播,竟至與哈通科利亞奧之主薩帕納交鋒;為抗其強權,她們築起堡壘與城牆——至今猶存。然而她們雖竭盡全力,終被擒殺,其名自此湮沒無聞。

sensitivity.note: The land-of-women topos grounded in named ruins; Cieza records it from witnesses who visited the site.

title.en: The Sun Shining Very Brightly Came Forth from the Island of Titicaca
title.zh: 太陽燦然出自的的喀喀島

region.en: Island of Titicaca, lake of the Collao (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 科利亞奧大湖的的喀喀島(象徵性標記)

period: Written by Cieza de León, publ. Markham trans. 1883 (Second Part)

source.work: Pedro de Cieza de León, The Second Part of the Chronicle of Peru, trans. and ed. Sir Clements Markham, Hakluyt Society, 1883

summary.en: Before the Incas reigned in these kingdoms, or had ever been heard of, the Indians relate another thing much more notable than all things else that they say. For they declare that they were a long time without seeing the sun, and that, suffering much evil from its absence, great prayers and vows were offered up to their gods, imploring for the light they needed. Things being in this state, the sun, shining very brightly, came forth from the island of Titicaca, in the great lake of the Collao, at which every one rejoiced.
summary.zh: 早在印加人稱王、甚至無人聽說過印加之前,印第安人還講著一件比一切傳說更著名的事。他們說:曾經很長時間看不見太陽,因太陽缺席而受盡苦難,便向他們的神極力祈禱、許願,哀求賜下所需的光明。就在此時,太陽燦然生輝,從科利亞奧大湖的的喀喀島上噴薄而出——眾人皆大歡喜。

sensitivity.note: Cieza's version of the sun-emergence: darkness-then-light, no creator sequence included - a minimal solar theogony.

passages.text: They declare that they were a long time without seeing the sun, and that, suffering much evil from its absence, great prayers and vows were offered up to their gods, imploring for the light they needed. Things being in this state, the sun, shining very brightly, came forth from the island of Titicaca, in the great lake of the Collao, at which every one rejoiced.

canonical_translation: Sir Clements Markham, The Second Part of the Chronicle of Peru (Hakluyt Society, 1883)

title.en: The White Man of Great Stature Who Made Water Flow from Stones
title.zh: 身量高大的白人:點石出水者

region.en: Roads of the mountains to the sea coast (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 山路至海濱(象徵性標記)

period: Written by Cieza de León, publ. Markham trans. 1883 (Second Part)

source.work: Pedro de Cieza de León, The Second Part of the Chronicle of Peru, trans. and ed. Sir Clements Markham, Hakluyt Society, 1883

summary.en: Presently afterwards, they say, there came from a southern direction a white man of great stature, who, by his aspect and presence, called forth great veneration and obedience. This man who thus appeared had great power, insomuch that he could change plains into mountains, and great hills into valleys, and make water flow out of stones. As soon as such power was beheld, the people called him the Maker of created things, the Prince of all things, Father of the Sun. For they say that he performed other wonders, giving life to men and animals, so that by his hand marvellous great benefits were conferred on the people. Such was the story that the Indians who told it to me say that they heard from their ancestors, who in like manner heard it in the old songs which they received from very ancient times. They say that this man went on towards the north, working these marvels along the way of the mountains; and that he never more returned so as to be seen. In many places he gave orders to men how they should live, and he spoke lovingly to them and with much gentleness, admonishing them that they should do good, and no evil or injury one to another, and that they should be loving and charitable to all. In most parts he is generally called Ticiviracocha, but in the province of the Collao they call him Tuapaca, and in other places Arnauan. In many parts they built temples in which they put blocks of stone in likeness of him, and offered up sacrifices before them. It is held that the great blocks at Tiahuanacu were from that time.
summary.zh: 此後不久——相傳——自南方來了一位身量高大的白人,儀表威嚴,令人望之生敬、順服。此人神力無邊:他能把平原變作高山,把崇嶺夷為深谷,能點石而出泉。人們見此神威,便稱他為「造物之主」「萬有之王」「太陽之父」。相傳他還行過別樣奇事:使男子與畜類復生,親手降下莫大恩惠於人民。向我講述此事的印第安人說,這故事是他們從祖先那裡聽來的,而祖先又是從極古的歌謠中傳承下來的。相傳此人繼續北上,沿著山路一路顯聖;此後再未現身。他在許多地方教人如何生活,言語溫存柔和,勸人行善,勿相互傷害,當彼此仁愛、施惠於人。各地對他稱呼不一:多稱「提基維拉科查」,科利亞省稱「圖阿帕卡」,另一些地方稱「阿爾瑙安」。許多地方為他建廟,廟中供上狀似其形的石塊,在其前獻祭。人們說,蒂亞瓦納科的巨石便是那個時代留下來的。

sensitivity.note: Cieza's white culture-hero heard in the old songs; the apostle speculation is his own editorial frame.

title.en: The Fire from Heaven at Cacha, and the Mantle That Entered the Waves
title.zh: 卡查天火與入海之氅

region.en: Village of Cacha (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 卡查村(象徵性標記)

period: Written by Cieza de León, publ. Markham trans. 1883 (Second Part)

source.work: Pedro de Cieza de León, The Second Part of the Chronicle of Peru, trans. and ed. Sir Clements Markham, Hakluyt Society, 1883

summary.en: They say that, a long time having passed, they again saw another man resembling the first, whose name they do not mention; but they received it from their forefathers as very certain that wherever this personage came and there were sick, he healed them, and where there were blind he gave them sight by only uttering words. Through acts so good and useful he was much beloved by all. In this fashion, working great things by his words, he arrived at the province of the Canas, in which, near to a village which has the name of Cacha, the people rose against him, threatening to stone him. They saw him upon his knees, with his hands raised to heaven, as if invoking the divine favour to liberate him from the danger that threatened him. Presently there appeared a great fire in the heaven, which they thought to be surrounding them. Full of fear and trembling, they came to him whom they had wanted to kill, and with loud clamour besought him to be pleased to forgive them. For they knew that this punishment threatened them because of the sin they had committed in wishing to stone the stranger. Presently they saw that when he ordered the fire to cease, it was extinguished, so that they were themselves witnesses of what had come to pass; and the stones were consumed and burnt up in such wise as that large blocks could be lifted in the hand, as if they were of cork. Leaving the place where these things happened, the man arrived on the sea coast, where, holding his mantle, he went in amongst the waves and was never more seen. And as he went, so they gave him the name of Viracocha, which means 'the foam of the sea.' Soon afterwards they made a temple in this village of Cacha, on the other side of a river which passes near, where they set up an idol of stone, very large, but in a somewhat narrow recess. Some gold was found in holes near it. Whether this or any other was intended for one of the glorious apostles who, in the days of his preaching, had passed this way, God Almighty knows.
summary.zh: 相傳良久之後,他們又見到一位與前者相像的人;其名不傳。但祖先們確鑿相告:此人每到之處,病者得愈,盲者一聞其言便得復明。他善行廣布,深得眾愛。他以言語創行大事,行至卡納斯省,在卡查村附近,當地人群起欲以石擊之。眾人見他屈膝跪地,雙手向天,似在祈求上蒼解其危難。霎時間,天現大火,彷彿要將他們團團圍住。眾人戰慄恐懼,紛紛來到方才欲殺之人面前,大聲哀求饒恕——他們明白:這懲罰是因他們欲以石擊客人之罪而降。隨後,那人一聲令下,天火頓熄;眾人親眼所見:石塊盡被燒枯,燒得如此輕盈,大石竟可單手舉起,輕如木栓。那人離開此地,行至海濱,展其氅衣,步入波濤,從此不再現身。他如此離去,人們便稱他為「維拉科查」——意即「海之泡沫」。不久,卡查村便在近旁河對岸建起一座神廟,供上一尊極大的石像,安置於略顯狹窄的壁龕之中;像旁洞穴曾掘得黃金。至於這尊石像或其他,是否為昔日傳道途中經此的某位榮耀使徒,唯有全能的上帝知曉。

title.en: Worse than Supais: The Name Viracocha Given and Taken Back
title.zh: 比魔鬼還壞:維拉科查之名的予與奪

region.en: Curicancha, Cuzco (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 庫斯科科里坎查(象徵性標記)

period: Written by Cieza de León, publ. Markham trans. 1883 (Second Part)

source.work: Pedro de Cieza de León, The Second Part of the Chronicle of Peru, trans. and ed. Sir Clements Markham, Hakluyt Society, 1883

summary.en: Treating of this name Viracocha, I wish to disabuse the reader of the popular belief that the natives called the Spaniards by the name of Viracocha, which means foam of the sea. So far as the word is concerned it is true, for vira is the word for grease, and cocha is the sea. And seeing that the Spaniards came by sea, that name has been attributed to them. But this is a wrong interpretation, according to the explanation which I received at Cuzco, and which the Orejones give. They say that before Atahuallpa was taken prisoner by the Spaniards in the province of Caxamarca, there had been great wars between him and his brother Huascar Inca... While these passions were at their height, Atahuallpa had been made prisoner and had agreed with Pizarro to give him a house of gold as his ransom. Martin Bueno, Zarate, and Moguer went to Cuzco to receive it, the greater part being in the Sun temple called Curicancha. As these Christians arrived at Cuzco at the time when the party of Huascar was suffering under the above calamity, the oppressed Yncas rejoiced when they heard of the imprisonment of Atahuallpa, and with great supplications implored the aid of the Christians against their enemy, declaring that they must be sent by the intervention of their great God Ticiviracocha, and that they were his sons; and presently they called them so, giving them the name of Viracocha. They ordered the High Priest and the other ministers of the temple to keep the sacred women there... As these Spaniards were so free from all restraint, and held the honor of the people so lightly, in return for the hospitality and friendliness with which they were received, they corrupted some of the virgins; which was the reason that the Indians, who also saw how little reverence the Spaniards felt for the Sun, and how shamelessly and without the fear of God they violated the mamaconas, which the Indians held to be a great sacrilege, began to say that such people were not sons of God, but that they were worse than Supais, which is their name of Devil. Nevertheless... the name of Viracocha continued from that day.
summary.zh: 說到「維拉科查」這個名字,我要澄清世俗的誤解:人們以為土人因「維拉科查」意為「海之泡沫」(維拉=油脂,科查=海),而西班牙人自海上而來,故以此名稱呼他們。但據我在庫斯科從「耳垂貴胄」處所得的解釋,這是錯誤的。他們說:阿塔瓦爾帕在卡哈馬卡被西班牙人擒獲之前,他與兄弟瓦伊斯卡爾·印加之間已爆發大戰……瓦伊斯卡爾在阿普里馬克河的科塔班巴隘口被查爾庫奇馬生擒,備受凌虐;基斯-基斯在庫斯科大肆屠戮,殺死瓦伊斯卡爾三十位兄弟。正當此際,阿塔瓦爾帕被擒,與皮薩羅約定以一屋黃金贖身。馬丁·布埃諾、薩拉特與莫格雷奉命赴庫斯科收取贖金——大部分藏於名為科里坎查的太陽神廟。受壓迫的印加人聞知阿塔瓦爾帕被擒,大喜過望,苦苦哀求基督徒相助對敵,聲稱他們必是偉大的神提基維拉科查所遣、是他的兒子們——於是便稱他們為「維拉科查」。然而這些西班牙人毫無忌憚,視他人榮譽如糞土:受人殷勤款待,卻姦污了部分守廟的聖女;印第安人又親見他們對太陽何等輕慢,竟恬不知恥、不畏神明地玷污了瑪瑪庫納——在印第安人看來,這是滔天瀆神。於是人們開始說:這些人絕非神之子,而是比「蘇帕伊」——他們稱魔鬼為蘇帕伊——還要壞的東西。但「維拉科查」之名,卻自那日起沿用至今。

title.en: Slings of Gold: Six Ancestors in the House of Production
title.zh: 金彈弓:生產之屋的六位先祖

region.en: Pacarec Tampu (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 帕卡雷克-坦波(象徵性標記)

period: Written by Cieza de León, publ. Markham trans. 1883 (Second Part)

source.work: Pedro de Cieza de León, The Second Part of the Chronicle of Peru, trans. and ed. Sir Clements Markham, Hakluyt Society, 1883

summary.en: When all the races who lived in these regions were in a state of disorder, slaughtering each other and sunk in vice, there appeared three men and three women in a place not far from the city of Cuzco, which is called Pacarec Tampu - the House of Production. The men who came forth from there were, as they relate, the one Ayar Ucho, and the other Ayar Cachi Asauca, and the other they say was named Ayar Manco. Of the women, one had the name of Mama Huaco, the other Mama Cora, the other Mama Rahua. They say that these people came forth dressed in long mantles, and some vestments like a shirt without collar or sleeves, made of very fine wool, with patterns of different kinds, which they called tacapu - 'vestures of kings'. And each of these lords held in the hand a sling of gold with a stone in it. The women came out dressed very richly like the men, and they had much gold. One of the brothers named Ayar Uchu spoke to his brethren that they should make a beginning of the great things that they had to do; for their presumption was such that they thought they were to make themselves sole lords of the land. They were determined to form in that place a new settlement, to which they gave the name of Pacarec Tampu. They say that one of the three, named Ayar Cachi, was so valiant and had such great power, that, with stones hurled from his sling, he split the hills and threw them up to the clouds. When the other brothers saw this they were sorry, thinking that it was an affront to them who could not do such things, and they were enraged by reason of their envy. Then they asked him sweetly and with gentle words, though full of deceit, to return and enter the mouth of a cave where they had their treasure, to bring out a certain vase of gold that they had forgotten. Ayar Cachi, believing that there was no deceit in what his brother said, joyfully went to do what they required of him, but he had scarcely got into the cave when the other two so filled the mouth up with stones that it could not be seen. This done, they relate for a certainty that the earth trembled in such a manner that many hills fell into the valleys. Afterwards, when the Indians exalted them with grand titles, they were called Ancha hatun apu intipchuri! which means 'Oh very great lord, child of the sun.'
summary.zh: 當各地族群陷入混亂、自相殘殺、沉溺於罪惡之際,庫斯科城外不遠處,名為「帕卡雷克-坦普」(意即「生產之屋」)的地方,出現了三男三女。相傳男子三人為:亞亞爾-烏丘、亞亞爾-卡奇-阿薩烏卡、亞亞爾-曼科;女子三人為:瑪瑪·瓦科、瑪瑪·科拉、瑪瑪·拉瓦。相傳他們走出時,身披長氅,內著領口無袖、極細羊毛織就、花紋各異的上衣,名「塔卡普」——意即「王者之衣」。每位主子手中各執一把嵌石的金彈弓。女子們的服飾與男子一樣華貴,且攜帶大量黃金。兄弟之一亞亞爾-烏丘對眾兄弟說:該開創大業了——他們的自負,竟以為自己注定要做天下唯一的主。他們決定就地建一新聚落,名為帕卡雷克-坦普。相傳亞亞爾-卡奇勇猛絕倫、神力蓋世:彈弓擲石,劈山碎嶺,能把石塊擲上雲端。眾兄弟見狀心中不快——自愧弗如,妒火中燒。他們便甜言蜜語、滿懷詭計地請他回到藏寶的洞穴,取出遺忘的金瓶。亞亞爾-卡奇信以為真,欣然前往;他剛一進洞,兩位兄弟便用石頭把洞口塞得嚴嚴實實。相傳此舉之後,大地猛烈震動,許多山頭塌入谷中。後來印第安人以顯赫尊號稱頌他們:「安查·哈通·阿普·因蒂普丘里!」——啊,極偉大的主,太陽之子!

sensitivity.note: Cieza's six-ancestor version with Mama Cora and Mama Rahua; the earth-tremor at the sealing differs from Sarmiento's narrative.

title.en: Ayar Cachi Comes with Wings: 'Your Ears Shall Be Bored as You Behold in Mine'
title.zh: 羽翼的亞亞爾-卡奇:「爾等穿耳,如我所戴」

region.en: Hill of Guanacaure (Huanacauri) (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 瓜納考雷山(瓦納考里)(象徵性標記)

period: Written by Cieza de León, publ. Markham trans. 1883 (Second Part)

source.work: Pedro de Cieza de León, The Second Part of the Chronicle of Peru, trans. and ed. Sir Clements Markham, Hakluyt Society, 1883

summary.en: After the two Incas had settled in Tampu Quiru, careless now about seeing Ayar Cachi again, they beheld him coming in the air with great wings of coloured feathers, and they, by reason of the great fear that this visit caused them, wanted to flee away; but he quickly removed their terror by saying to them: 'Do not fear, neither be afflicted; for I only come that the empire of the Incas may begin to be known. Wherefore leave this settlement that you have made, and advance further down until you see a valley, and there found the Cuzco, which will be of great note. For here are only hamlets, and of little importance; but that will be a great city, where the sumptuous temple must be built that will be so honoured and frequented, and where the sun will be so worshipped. I shall remain in the form and fashion that you will see on a hill not distant from here; and will be for you and your descendants a place of sanctity and worship, and its name shall be Guanacaure. And in return for the good things that you will have received from me, I pray that you will always adore me as God, and set up altars in that place, at which to offer sacrifices. If you do this, you shall receive help from me in war; and as a sign that from henceforward you are to be esteemed, honoured, and feared, your ears shall be bored in the manner that you now behold in mine.' And when he had so spoken they say that he appeared with ear ornaments of gold set round as with a gem. The brothers, astonished at what they saw, were as men struck dumb; when their perturbation had ceased, they replied that they were content to do as he commanded, and presently they went in haste to the hill called the Hill of Guanacaure, which from that time forward was accounted sacred. The Orejones further say that the practice of assuming the fringe and of arming the knights began here.
summary.zh: 兩兄弟定居坦普-基魯之後,已不再掛念亞亞爾-卡奇。忽然,他們望見他憑著絢麗羽翼的大翅膀從空中而來。二人嚇得魂飛魄散,幾欲逃命;他卻迅即為他們除去恐懼,說道:「不要害怕,也不要憂愁;我來,只為使印加帝國自此聞名。離開你們建立的這個聚落,往下走,直到望見一處谷地,在那裡建立庫斯科——它必成大城。此地不過是小村陋巷,微不足道;那裡卻要建起豪華的神廟,受人尊崇,香火鼎盛,太陽將在那裡受萬民敬拜。我將留驻在這不遠處山丘上——你們會看見我的形貌;我與我的子孫將成為你們的聖所與崇拜之地,其名為瓜納考雷。作為你們受我恩惠的回報,我求你們永遠奉我如神,在彼處設壇獻祭。若能如此,戰時我必佑助你們;為記你們從此當受尊崇、敬仰與敬畏,你們要像我這樣穿耳——如你們現在所見。」言畢,相傳他顯出鑲嵌寶石般的金耳飾。兄弟們驚訝得說不出話來;心神稍定,便答應遵命而行,急忙趕往那座自此被奉為聖地的瓜納考雷山。耳垂貴胄們說:戴王纓、封騎士之禮,便自此而始。

sensitivity.note: Cieza's winged-escape variant of Ayar Cachi/Huanacaure; Cieza equates Ayar Cachi with the hill's name and preserves the ear-boring charter.
