title.en: Piran Rescues Farangis and the Dream of a Newborn King
title.zh: 皮蘭救法蘭吉斯與新生王之夢

region.en: Court of Afrasiyab (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 阿弗拉西亞卜王庭（象徵性定位）

period: Composed c. 1010 CE (Warner translation 1905)

source.work: Firdausi, Shahnama, trans. A. G. & E. Warner (1905), vol. II, Siyawush secs. 57-58

summary.en: Afrasiyab would slay his own pregnant daughter Farangis with her husband; Piran, riding day and night with ten remounts, reaches the court as the deathsmen stand about the portal: thou hast slain Siyawush though innocent, and now hast ill-treated thine own child; if the king would make my spirits bright, let him send Farangis to mine abode. The king grants it, and Piran bears her unhurt to Khutan. One dark and moonless night Piran dreams a splendour that outshone the sun itself, with Siyawush enthroned and sword in hand: rest no more, for from to-day new feasts and customs date, because to-night is born Shah Kai Khusrau.
summary.zh: 阿弗拉西亞卜欲殺懷孕的親生女兒法蘭吉斯；皮蘭日夜兼程、換馬十匹趕到——刑吏已列於殿門：「你弑無辜的西亞瓦什，如今又要害己女；若王要寬我心，就把法蘭吉斯交給我吧。」王允之，皮蘭安然將她送往忽檀。一個無月的黑夜，皮蘭夢見勝過太陽的榮光——西亞瓦什按劍高坐：「勿再貪睡！今夜誕生了卡伊霍斯勞王！」

sensitivity.note: Epic literary source; no living community restriction.

passages.text: Piran on hearing this cried out in wrath, descended to the street and from the stable brought forth ten roadsters up to warriors' weight, and with the brave Ruh and Farshidward sent up the dust forthwith. He reached the court in two days and two nights, there found the deathsmen about the portal, Farangis bereft of all her wits dragged roughly by the guard with sword in hand, and all the court in uproar. The populace, men, women, and young children, were talking at the palace-gate and saying: it were a cruel, fearful, shocking deed to cut asunder Farangis! This fury will wreck the reign and none will call him king henceforward.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Firdausi, Shahnama, Siyawush sec. 57 (Warner 1905); not verbatim.

passages.text: When noble Farangis saw him her cheeks were hidden by a flood of tears, and she said: ill hast thou dealt with me! Why hast thou flung me while living into fire? Piran dropped off his steed, rent the raiment that he wore as paladin, and sought Afrasiyab in haste: thou hast slain Siyawush though innocent, and flung his name and kingship to the dust; thou wilt repent of this for many a day. If now the king would make my spirits bright, let him send Farangis to mine abode; have patience only till the child is born.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Firdausi, Shahnama, Siyawush sec. 57 (Warner 1905); not verbatim.

passages.text: He answered: do as thou hast said, for thou hast made me cease to wish to shed her blood. Piran rejoiced, sought the court-gate, rescued Farangis, bestowing many a curse upon the guards, then bore her to the country of Khutan unhurt, amid the applause of camp and court. Time passed by, and the Moon grew near to her delivery.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Firdausi, Shahnama, Siyawush sec. 57 (Warner 1905); not verbatim.

passages.text: One dark and moonless night, while birds, wild beasts, and cattle slept, Piran in dream beheld a splendour that outshone the sun itself, while Siyawush, enthroned and sword in hand, called loudly to him, saying: rest no more! Throw off sweet sleep and think of times to come, for from to-day new feasts and customs date, because to-night is born Shah Kai Khusrau! The chieftain roused him from his sweet repose: Gulshahr the sunny-featured woke, and came hasting to the Moon and saw the prince already born; she went with cries of joy that made the palace ring again back to Piran the chief.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Firdausi, Shahnama, Siyawush sec. 58 (Warner 1905); not verbatim.

title.en: The Shepherd-King Before Afrasiyab
title.zh: 牧羊少年入虎穴

region.en: Mount Kalur pastures (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 卡魯爾山牧場（象徵性定位）

period: Composed c. 1010 CE (Warner translation 1905)

source.work: Firdausi, Shahnama, trans. A. G. & E. Warner (1905), vol. II, Siyawush secs. 59-60

summary.en: Afrasiyab, warned by an adviser that a king of noble birth will lift his head from the seed of Tur and Kai Kubad, has the infant sent to the shepherds of Mount Kalur. At seven his prowess tells the secret of his birth; at ten he fights boars, wolves, lions, and leopards with a rude wooden bow. Afrasiyab swears a royal oath of safety before Piran presents the boy, charging him to appear as an alien and speak insanely; before the king the child answers about leopards only, and love at length prevails within the tyrant's heart.
summary.zh: 謀士告誡：圖爾與卡尤巴德血脈中將出現君王。阿弗拉西亞卜便將嬰兒送往卡魯爾山牧羊人處。七歲時勇武已洩露身世；十歲時憑一支粗木弓獵殺野豬、狼、獅、豹。皮蘭先讓暴君立下安全誓言，再囑少年裝傻充愣、答非所問；王座之前，孩子只談獵豹——最後連暴君心中愛意也佔了上風。

sensitivity.note: Epic literary source; no living community restriction.

passages.text: Piran had shepherds called from Mount Kalur, to whom he spake about the infant prince, then trusted to their care his Heart and Eyes, and said: entreat him like your souls; no wind or dust must see him. They said: we will obey. He furnished them, and sent a nurse to tend the royal babe; they took the young prince with them to the mountains. Now when the brave young prince was seven years old his prowess told the secret of his birth; at ten he was a valiant warrior, who fought with boars and wolves, anon with lions and leopards, armed with that rude weapon only.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Firdausi, Shahnama, Siyawush sec. 59 (Warner 1905); not verbatim.

passages.text: Afrasiyab spake about the past: my heart is vexed by thoughts and grief too hard to put aside; this child of Siyawush hath, so to speak, o'ercast my day; but will high policy allow a shepherd-swain to rear one of the race of Faridun? But while the child suspecteth not the past let him be glad; still, if he showeth any evil bent, he, as his father did, must lose his head.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Firdausi, Shahnama, Siyawush sec. 60 (Warner 1905); not verbatim.

passages.text: Piran replied: this boy is as mad folk are; a child brought up by shepherds on the mountains is like wild animals; what can he know? If at this time the king shall order me, I will present this lauded youth to him, but make me easy by a promise first and swear by such an oath as kings employ. The wits of fierce Afrasiyab were lulled at hearing this, he swore a royal oath by white day and by sombre night, by God the Omnipotent: no harm shall come upon the boy through me.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Firdausi, Shahnama, Siyawush sec. 60 (Warner 1905); not verbatim.

passages.text: Piran equipped him with a royal crown and belt and called for him a pretty palfrey whereon the shrewd, young hero sat and rode toward the palace of Afrasiyab. When he arrived Piran the general took him before the king. The king remembering his pledge and spurning all fell designs gazed in astonishment upon that royal neck. O youthful shepherd, said Afrasiyab, describe to me thy life by day and night. Khusrau thus answered him: there is no game; besides I have not arrow, bow, or string. Where'er there is a leopard the hearts of valiant warriors are rent. There was a pause; the monarch's face relaxed, and love at length prevailed within his heart.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Firdausi, Shahnama, Siyawush sec. 60 (Warner 1905); not verbatim.

title.en: The Gates of Death: Maui Among the Shades of the Pacific
title.zh: 死亡之門：太平洋冥府中的毛伊

region.en: Underworlds of Polynesia (symbolic pin, Savaii)
region.zh: 波利尼西亞冥府（象徵性定位，薩瓦伊）

period: Pan-Polynesian oral traditions; retold 1910 (Westervelt)

source.work: W. D. Westervelt, Legends of Ma-ui, ch. 11, Maui Seeking Immortality (New York 1910)

summary.en: Every island group has its Hades: Samoa's two circular holes at the west end of Savaii; Tonga's shadow island where trees, fruits and birds could not be grasped; the New Zealand saying 'Men make heroes, but death carries them away'. Maui longed for the victory over death - 'Let death be short; as the moon dies and returns with new strength, so let men die and revive again' - but the moon answered: 'Let death be very long, that man may sigh and sorrow.' He transformed his brothers into birds, told them not to laugh until he had passed through Hine-nui-te-po and come out of her mouth; the little bird Pata-tai laughed, the obsidian teeth snapped, and death has ever since been victor over rebellious men.
summary.zh: 各島皆有其冥府：薩瓦伊西端的兩個圓洞；湯加的幻影之島——樹果飛鳥皆不可捉；毛利諺語『人造英雄，死亡帶走』。毛伊欲勝死亡：『讓死亡短暫，如月之死而復生，人亦如是』；月卻答：『讓死亡漫長，使人嘆息哀慟。』他化兄弟為鳥，囑其忍笑至自己穿過海內努伊特波口中而出；小鳥帕塔泰一笑，黑曜石齒合攏——自那人類的叛逆者被腰斬之後，死亡遂永勝於人。

sensitivity.note: Comparative death-of-Maui record; Samoa, Tonga, Hervey Islands and New Zealand hades surveyed.

passages.text: The story of Maui seeking immortality for the human race is one of the finest myths in the world; for pure imagination and pathos it is difficult to find any tale from Grecian or Latin literature to compare with it. The different islands of the Pacific have their Hades, or abode of the dead - with very few exceptions, down in the interior of the earth; sometimes the tunnels left by currents of melted lava are the passages into the home of departed spirits. In Samoa there are two circular holes among the rocks at the west end of the island Savaii: these are the entrances to the under-world for chiefs and people; the spirits of those who die on the other islands leap into the sea and swim around the land from island to island until they reach Savaii, then they plunge down into their heaven or their hades.
passages.note: Paraphrase of W. D. Westervelt, Legends of Ma-ui, ch. 11 (1910); not verbatim.

passages.text: The Tongans had a spirit island for the home of the dead: they said that some natives once sailed far away in a canoe and found this island, covered with all manner of beautiful fruits among which rare birds sported; they landed, but the trees were shadows - they grasped but could not hold them; the fruits and the birds were shadows; the men ate, but swallowed nothing substantial. It was shadow-land. They walked through all the delights their eyes looked upon, but found no substance; they returned home, but ever seemed to listen to spirits calling them back to the island - in a short time all the voyagers were dead. There is no escape from death: the natives of New Zealand say, 'Man may have descendants, but the daughters of the night strangle his offspring', and again, 'Men make heroes, but death carries them away.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of W. D. Westervelt, Legends of Ma-ui, ch. 11 (1910); not verbatim.

passages.text: In Maui's last days he longed for the victory over death; his innate love of life led him to face the possibility of escaping and overcoming the relentless enemy of mankind and thus bestow the boon of deathlessness upon his fellow-men - he had been successful over and over again in his contests with both gods and men. He said to the goddess of the moon: 'Let death be short; as the moon dies and returns with new strength, so let men die and revive again.' But she replied: 'Let death be very long, that man may sigh and sorrow; when man dies, let him go into darkness, become like earth, that those he leaves behind may weep and wail and mourn.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of W. D. Westervelt, Legends of Ma-ui, ch. 11 (1910); not verbatim.

passages.text: Maui did not lay aside his purpose but, according to the New Zealand story, 'did not wish men to die, but to live forever; death appeared degrading and an insult to the dignity of man; man ought to die like the moon, which dips in the life-giving waters of Kane and is renewed again, or like the sun, which daily sinks into the pit of night and with renewed strength rises in the morning.' Maui sought the home of Hine-nui-te-po, the guardian of life; he heard her order her attendants to watch for any one approaching and capture all who came walking upright as a man; he crept past the attendants on hands and feet, found the place of life, stole some of the food of the goddess and returned home; he showed the food to his brothers and persuaded them to go with him into the darkness of the night of death; on the way he changed them into the form of birds.
passages.note: Paraphrase of W. D. Westervelt, Legends of Ma-ui, ch. 11 (1910); not verbatim.

passages.text: Maui warned the birds to refrain from making any noise while he made the supreme effort of his life; he was about to enter upon his struggle for immortality. He said to the birds: 'If I go into the stomach of this woman, do not laugh until I have gone through her and come out again at her mouth; then you can laugh at me.' His friends said, 'You will be killed'; Maui replied, 'If you laugh at me when I have only entered her stomach I shall be killed, but if I have passed through her and come out of her mouth I shall escape and Hine-nui-te-po will die.' His friends called out to him: 'Go then; the decision is with you.' Hine was sleeping soundly; the flashes of lightning had all ceased, the sunlight had almost passed away, and the house lay in quiet gloom. Maui came near to the sleeping goddess; her large fish-like mouth was open wide; he put off his clothing and prepared to pass through the ordeal of going to the hidden source of life, to tear it out of the body of its guardian and carry it back with him to mankind; he stood in all the glory of savage manhood, his body splendidly marked by the tattoo-bones and now well oiled, shining and sparkling in the last rays of the setting sun.
passages.note: Paraphrase of W. D. Westervelt, Legends of Ma-ui, ch. 11 (1910); not verbatim.

passages.text: He leaped through the mouth of the enchanted one and entered her stomach, weapon in hand, to take out her heart, the vital principle which he knew had its home somewhere within her being; he found immortality on the other side of death; he turned to come back again into life when suddenly a little bird, the Pata-tai, laughed in a clear, shrill tone, and Great Hine, through whose mouth Maui was passing, awoke - her sharp obsidian teeth closed with a snap upon Maui, cutting his body in the center. Thus Maui entered the gates of death but was unable to return, and death has ever since been victor over rebellious men. The natives have the saying: 'If Maui had not died, he could have restored to life all who had gone before him, and thus succeeded in destroying death.' Maui's brothers took the dismembered body and buried it in a cave called Te-ana-i-hana, the cave dug out, possibly a prepared burial place. Maui's wife made war upon the spirits, the gods, and killed as many as she could to avenge her husband's death; one of the old native poets of New Zealand, in chanting the story to Mr. White, said: 'But though Maui was killed, his offspring survived; some of these are at Hawa-i-i-ki and some at Aotea-roa, New Zealand, but the greater part of them remained at Hawa-i-ki. This history was handed down by the generations of our ancestors of ancient times, and we continue to rehearse it to our children with our incantations and genealogies and all other matters relating to our race.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of W. D. Westervelt, Legends of Ma-ui, ch. 11 (1910); not verbatim.

title.en: Hina and Kuna, the Eel of the Wailuku
title.zh: 希娜與懷盧庫河之鰻庫納

region.en: Wailuku river and Rainbow Falls, Hilo, Hawaii Island
region.zh: 夏威夷島希洛懷盧庫河與彩虹瀑布

period: Hawaiian oral tradition; retold 1910 (Westervelt)

source.work: W. D. Westervelt, Legends of Ma-ui, ch. 13, Hina and the Wailuku River (New York 1910)

summary.en: Kuna, a monstrous eel-dragon, made the broken pools of the Wailuku his home below the falls, and annoyed Hina with foulness in the very place where she made her tapa. Maui, returning from his travels, hears his mother's complaint, attacks the dragon, and slays him - the boiling pots and the black lava banks of the river marking the struggle; Hina's beaten kapa became the white water of Rainbow Falls.
summary.zh: 巨鰻龍庫納盤踞懷盧庫瀑布下的斷崖水潭，屢屢以穢物侵擾在瀑下捶打卡帕的希娜。毛伊遠行歸來，聽聞母親之苦，遂擊殺此龍——河中沸泉與黑熔岩岸即是搏鬥的痕跡；希娜洗濯的卡帕化作彩虹瀑布的白練。

sensitivity.note: Hilo landmark legend.

passages.text: The Hina of Hilo had her home in the cave under the falls of the Wailuku river, where she pounded her tapa; but Kuna, a monstrous eel-dragon, made the broken pools of the Wailuku his home below the falls, and annoyed her with foulness in the very place where she made her tapa.
passages.note: Paraphrase of W. D. Westervelt, Legends of Ma-ui, ch. 13 (1910); not verbatim.

passages.text: Maui, returning from his travels, hears his mother's complaint, attacks the dragon, and slays him - the boiling pots and the black lava banks of the river marking the struggle, and Hina's beaten kapa becoming the white water of Rainbow Falls; thus the Wailuku river keeps the memory of the battle between the tapa-maker and the eel-dragon.
passages.note: Paraphrase of W. D. Westervelt, Legends of Ma-ui, ch. 13 (1910); not verbatim.

title.en: The Tongan Shadow Island of the Dead
title.zh: 湯加冥界幻影之島

region.en: Spirit island, Tongan waters (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 湯加水域亡靈之島（象徵性定位）

period: Tongan oral tradition; retold 1910 (Westervelt)

source.work: W. D. Westervelt, Legends of Ma-ui, ch. 11 (New York 1910)

summary.en: Tongan sailors who found the spirit island could eat nothing: the trees were shadows, the fruits were shadows, the birds were shadows; they walked through all the delights their eyes looked upon and found no substance, and ever after seemed to hear the spirits calling them back to the island - until in a short time all the voyagers were dead.
summary.zh: 偶然發現亡靈之島的湯加水手什麼也吃不到：樹是影、果是影、鳥是影；眼中所見的樂園，觸手皆空。歸家之後，冥靈的呼喚日夜相隨——不久，全體船員相繼死去。

sensitivity.note: Shadow-land motif parallel to Gill's Motu-tapu.

passages.text: The Tongans had a spirit island for the home of the dead: they said that some natives once sailed far away in a canoe and found this island, covered with all manner of beautiful fruits among which rare birds sported; they landed, but the trees were shadows - they grasped but could not hold them; the fruits and the birds were shadows; the men ate, but swallowed nothing substantial. It was shadow-land. They walked through all the delights their eyes looked upon, but found no substance; they returned home, but ever seemed to listen to spirits calling them back to the island - in a short time all the voyagers were dead.
passages.note: Paraphrase of W. D. Westervelt, Legends of Ma-ui, ch. 11 (1910); not verbatim.

title.en: Rustam Reigns Over Turan for Seven Years
title.zh: 魯斯塔姆君臨圖蘭七年

region.en: Thrones of Chin and Sughd (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 秦地與粟特王座（象徵性定位）

period: Composed c. 1010 CE (Warner translation 1905)

source.work: Firdausi, Shahnama, trans. A. G. & E. Warner (1905), vol. II, Kai Kaus Part V sec. 11

summary.en: Avenging Siyawush, the elephantine hero marches toward Chin, subdues Khata, Khutan, and all the coasts of Chin, and takes the throne of him whose fortune had come to dust. He gives the ivory throne and the government of Chach to Tus: offend not the offenceless, and practise all humanity and justice, for this world is a lodging not a home. To Gudarz, lord of Sughd and Sipanjab: worth is better than high lineage. Then all the folk of Chin bring handsel: we are thy servants and thy slaves; and Rustam occupies himself for many a day with hawk and cheetah.
summary.zh: 為西亞瓦什復仇，英雄進軍秦地，平定赫塔、忽檀與秦地沿海，取其王座。他把象牙寶座與「恰奇」的治權交給圖斯：「勿欺無辜；當行仁義——此世乃客舍，非家園。」對粟特與西帕恩賈布之主古達爾茲說：「德行重於門第。」秦地百姓獻寶歸附：「我們唯您之命是從。」魯斯塔姆則以鷹獵消磨歲月。

sensitivity.note: Epic literary source; Rustam's regency in the conquered east. No living community restriction.

passages.text: The chief, the elephantine hero, marched toward the realm of Chin, and with his sword-arm subdued Khata, Khutan, and all the coasts of Chin, and took the throne of him whose fortune had come to dust. This saw spake Rustam first: the man of worth will seek the enemy; 'tis good to slay him if he countereth thee, and good too if he shun the fight and flee.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Firdausi, Shahnama, Kai Kaus Part V sec. 11 (Warner 1905); not verbatim.

passages.text: He gave torques, armlets, and the ivory throne to Tus, besides the government of Chach, and said: if anybody shall revolt, or even call Afrasiyab to mind, cut off his head; but like a father keep from want and travail the wise and peaceful, shunners of the Faith of Ahriman. Offend not the offenceless, and practise all humanity and justice, for this world is a lodging not a home. None ever had more Grace than had Jamshid, yet still high heaven trod him under foot.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Firdausi, Shahnama, Kai Kaus Part V sec. 11 (Warner 1905); not verbatim.

passages.text: To Gudarz he gave a crown of royal gems, with earrings, torque, and throne, and made him lord of Sughd and Sipanjab: worth is better than high lineage, though lineage assisteth men of worth. The tidings spread through Chin that Rustam sat enthroned as over-lord; then all the folk brought handsel of dinars and royal gems and said: we are thy servants and thy slaves; we only tread the earth to do thy bidding. The chieftain gave them quarter for their lives, perceiving that they had discerning minds, and occupied himself for many a day with hawk and cheetah.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Firdausi, Shahnama, Kai Kaus Part V sec. 11 (Warner 1905); not verbatim.

title.en: Zawara's Oath and the Harrying of Turan
title.zh: 扎瓦拉之誓與圖蘭浩劫

region.en: Hunting-ground of Siyawush (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 西亞瓦什獵場（象徵性定位）

period: Composed c. 1010 CE (Warner translation 1905)

source.work: Firdausi, Shahnama, trans. A. G. & E. Warner (1905), vol. II, Kai Kaus Part V secs. 12-13

summary.en: Zawara rides to hunt, and a careless Turkman guide points out the forest: this was the hunting-ground of Siyawush, where was he wont to be both glad and merry. The hawk falls from his hand; his lashes run tears of blood; his comrades fell the guide to the ground, and Zawara swears: I will not hunt or sleep or cease from vengeance on Afrasiyab. Roused by Zawara's words the matchless Rustam begins to ravage and to massacre till all the land shows signs of misery; over a thousand leagues the reek of burning rose, till all of noble race come with dust upon their heads protesting: we are aweary of Afrasiyab; shed not, provoking God, more guiltless blood.
summary.zh: 扎瓦拉行獵，粗心的突厥嚮導隨口道：「這便是西亞瓦什的獵場。」他手中鷹落、雙目泣血；部下打倒嚮導，扎瓦拉立誓：「不獵不眠，不誅阿弗拉西亞卜誓不休！」魯斯塔姆受激，縱兵屠戮，千里焦土；貴族們頂土求饒：「我們早恨透了阿弗拉西亞卜；請勿再無端流血。」

sensitivity.note: Epic literary source; no living community restriction.

passages.text: Now as it chanced one day Zawara went to hunt the onager. He rode apace conducted by a Turkman. On the open he saw a forest which, thou wouldest say, one cannot pass, it fresheneth the soul, so many were the scents and tints and streams. The Turkman told Zawara thoughtlessly: this was the hunting-ground of Siyawush, this was his favourite spot in all Turan, where was he wont to be both glad and merry, but elsewhere sad.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Firdausi, Shahnama, Kai Kaus Part V sec. 12 (Warner 1905); not verbatim.

passages.text: A hawk was on his hand; he let it go; the lashes of his eyes ran tears of blood. His comrades of the host approached, observed him in grief and tears; then they began to curse the Turkman guide and felled him to the ground. With gall-drops streaming from his eyes Zawara swore a great oath: I will not hunt or sleep, or cease from vengeance on Afrasiyab; I will not give a moment's rest to Rustam: all must prepare for fight.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Firdausi, Shahnama, Kai Kaus Part V sec. 12 (Warner 1905); not verbatim.

passages.text: Roused by Zawara's words the matchless Rustam began to ravage and to massacre till all the land showed signs of misery, and from Turan up to Saklab and Rum folk saw no cultured tract. The Iranians beheaded all the men, both young and old, and made the women and the children slaves. Thus o'er a thousand leagues and more the reek of burning rose. Then all of noble race came with the dust upon their heads protesting: we are aweary of Afrasiyab, and would not see him even in a dream; shed not, provoking God, more guiltless blood.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Firdausi, Shahnama, Kai Kaus Part V sec. 13 (Warner 1905); not verbatim.

title.en: Gudarz's Dream of Kai Khusrau
title.zh: 古達爾茲夢見卡伊霍斯勞

region.en: Hall of Gudarz (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 古達爾茲廳堂（象徵性定位）

period: Composed c. 1010 CE (Warner translation 1905)

source.work: Firdausi, Shahnama, trans. A. G. & E. Warner (1905), vol. II, Kai Kaus Part V sec. 15

summary.en: Gudarz dreams that a watery cloud, emblem of coming prosperity, rises o'er Iran and on it sits Suriish: there is a youthful prince now in Turan, Shah Kai Khusrau, the offspring of the loins of Siyawush, sprung from Tur upon the mother's side; when his glorious feet shall reach Iran heaven will accord to him his full desire, and he will overturn the sovereignty of Tur — among the chiefs of Iran none will discover him excepting Giv. Gudarz awoke and, with his hoary beard upon the ground, gave thanks to God, and told the dream to Giv in many words.
summary.zh: 古達爾茲夢見一朵雲（雨水之兆）升起於伊朗上空，蘇魯什坐於其上：「圖蘭有位年輕王子——卡伊霍斯勞，西亞瓦什之子，母系出自圖爾；當他的榮光之足踏入伊朗，上天必成全其願，他將推翻圖蘭王權。眾將之中，唯吉夫能尋得他。」老人醒來，以斑白之鬚觸地謝神，將夢境細細說與吉夫。

sensitivity.note: Epic literary source; no living community restriction.

passages.text: Gudarz one night dreamed that a watery cloud rose o'er Iran, and on it sat Suriish, who thus addressed him: give to me thine ear as thou wouldst be released from this distress, from this injurious Turkman dragon-fierce. There is a youthful prince now in Turan, Shah Kai Khusrau by name. He is a prince, the offspring of the loins of Siyawush, a man of worship and of noble race, illustrious, of the stock of Kai Kubad, and sprung from Tur upon the mother's side.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Firdausi, Shahnama, Kai Kaus Part V sec. 15 (Warner 1905); not verbatim.

passages.text: Whenas his glorious feet shall reach Iran heaven will accord to him his full desire. Then will he gird him to avenge his father, will overturn the sovereignty of Tur, will make the waters of the Red Sea boil, pause not in vengeance on Afrasiyab, but live in his cuirass the whole year through, and pass his days and nights upon the saddle. Among the chiefs and warriors of Iran none will discover him excepting Giv: such is the outcome destined by the sky. Gudarz awoke and, with his hoary beard upon the ground, gave thanks to God.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Firdausi, Shahnama, Kai Kaus Part V sec. 15 (Warner 1905); not verbatim.

title.en: Tupai, the Priest Whose Look Was Poison
title.zh: 目光即毒的高級祭司圖帕伊

region.en: Temple of the heaven-gods, Samoa (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 薩摩亞天神廟（象徵性定位）

period: Samoan oral tradition; recorded 1884 (Turner)

source.work: George Turner, Samoa A Hundred Years Ago and Long Before, ch. 4 (London 1884)

summary.en: The gods of heaven were supposed to have fallen from the skies at the call of a blind man to protect his son from a cannibal chief. A large temple was erected to one of them with ten seats for the principal chiefs; a large shell was the only visible representation, and in time of war it was carefully consulted - if it stood on end and made an unusual noise they went to battle cheerfully; if it only murmured 'Go back, go back', there was no fighting that day. Tupai was the name of the high priest and prophet: he was greatly dreaded, for his very look was poison - if he looked at a cocoa-nut tree it died, and if he glanced at a bread-fruit tree it also withered away.
summary.zh: 天神本為回應盲人護子之呼而自天而降；眾為其建大廟，設十座以列諸酋；廟中大螺即神之現形——戰時以之占卜：若直立鳴響則勇往開戰；若僅作『回吧回吧』的低吟，則是日罷兵。高級祭司兼先知圖帕伊尤令人畏：其目光即毒——椰樹遭其一瞥便枯死，麵包樹經其一掃便凋零。

sensitivity.note: Deity-descent and priestly-power legend.

passages.text: These gods were supposed to have fallen from the heavens at the call of a blind man to protect his son from a cannibal chief; they were scattered over several villages but did not move about in the bodies of mortals. A large temple was erected to one of them in which there were ten seats on which sat the principal chiefs; a large shell was the only visible representation of the god, and in time of war it was carefully consulted: if it stood on end and made an unusual noise they went to battle cheerfully; if, however, it only murmured what they imagined to be 'Go back, go back', there was no fighting that day.
passages.note: Paraphrase of George Turner, Samoa A Hundred Years Ago and Long Before, ch. 4 (1884); not verbatim.

passages.text: Tupai was the name of the high priest and prophet; he was greatly dreaded, for his very look was poison: if he looked at a cocoa-nut tree it died, and if he glanced at a bread-fruit tree it also withered away.
passages.note: Paraphrase of George Turner, Samoa A Hundred Years Ago and Long Before, ch. 4 (1884); not verbatim.

title.en: Faamalu, the Shade: Conch of the War-god
title.zh: 陰神法阿馬盧：戰神之螺

region.en: Samoan village temple (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 薩摩亞村廟（象徵性定位）

period: Samoan oral tradition; recorded 1884 (Turner)

source.work: George Turner, Samoa A Hundred Years Ago and Long Before, ch. 4 (London 1884)

summary.en: Faamalu, Shade, was the name of a village god represented by a trumpet-shell: on the month for annual worship all the people met in the place of public gatherings with heaps of cooked food; first there were offerings and prayers to the god to avert calamities and give prosperity, then they feasted with and before their god, and after that any strangers present were fed too - the god's conch blown to muster the village to war.
summary.zh: 『陰』法阿馬盧為一村之神，以海螺為象：歲祀之月，全民攜熟食群聚於公共場所；先獻祭祈禱、求神免禍賜福，繼而與神共宴；宴罷，在場的旅人亦得一飽——戰時吹螺，聚眾赴敵。

sensitivity.note: Village feast ritual.

passages.text: Faamalu, Shade, was the name of a village god and represented by a trumpet-shell. On the month for annual worship all the people met in the place of public gatherings with heaps of cooked food; first there were offerings and prayers to the god to avert calamities and give prosperity; then they feasted with and before their god, and after that any strangers present were fed too - the god's conch blown to muster the village to war.
passages.note: Paraphrase of George Turner, Samoa A Hundred Years Ago and Long Before, ch. 4 (1884); not verbatim.

title.en: Sama, the Cannibal God of Savaii
title.zh: 食人神薩瑪

region.en: Village of Savaii (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 薩瓦伊島村莊（象徵性定位）

period: Samoan oral tradition; recorded 1884 (Turner)

source.work: George Turner, Samoa A Hundred Years Ago and Long Before, ch. 4 (London 1884)

summary.en: Sama, Yellow, was the name of the cannibal god of a village in Savaii: he was incarnate as a man, who had human flesh laid before him when he chose to call for it; this man's power extended to several villages, and his descendants are traced to the present day.
summary.zh: 『黃』薩瑪乃薩瓦伊一村之食人神：化身為人，一旦召喚即有人肉奉上；其權勢及於數村，子孫綿延至今。

sensitivity.note: Recorded deity-cult; cannibalism stated in the source.

passages.text: Sama, Yellow, was the name of the cannibal god of a village in Savaii; he was incarnate as a man, who had human flesh laid before him when he chose to call for it; this man's power extended to several villages, and his descendants are traced to the present day.
passages.note: Paraphrase of George Turner, Samoa A Hundred Years Ago and Long Before, ch. 4 (1884); not verbatim.

title.en: Salevao's Feast of Thanksgiving
title.zh: 薩萊瓦奧的感恩盛宴

region.en: Savaii temple (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 薩瓦伊島神廟（象徵性定位）

period: Samoan oral tradition; recorded 1884 (Turner)

source.work: George Turner, Samoa A Hundred Years Ago and Long Before, ch. 4 (London 1884)

summary.en: In some places Salevao was a general village god as well as a war god; a time was fixed for giving thanks for good crops, and prayers were offered for more: each family took it in turn to provide food, and they feasted until it had gone the round of the village - the family who had a great display of good things was praised, but the stingy, stinted offerers were cursed; after all had prayed and partaken for the day nothing was kept for another meal, whatever was over being thrown away or buried.
summary.zh: 薩萊瓦奧於某些村落兼為村神與戰神；豐穫謝恩有定期，並祈來年再豐：各家輪流備辦食物，宴飲巡遍全村——豐盛者獲譽，吝嗇者遭咒；當日祈罷食盡，絕不留宿——所餘盡棄或埋於地。

sensitivity.note: Harvest-feast custom.

passages.text: In some places Salevao was a general village god as well as a war god; a time was fixed for giving thanks for good crops, and prayers were offered for more: each family took it in turn to provide food, and they feasted until it had gone the round of the village - the family who had a great display of good things was praised, but the stingy, stinted offerers were cursed. After all had prayed and partaken for the day nothing was kept for another meal; whatever was over was thrown away or buried. At one place in Savaii Salevao had a temple in which a priest constantly resided: the sick were taken there and laid down with offerings of fine mats; the priest went out and stroked the diseased part, and recovery was supposed to follow - at this place Salevao was declared to be a good god in raising a plentiful supply of food, and also noted for his power in keeping away other gods.
passages.note: Paraphrase of George Turner, Samoa A Hundred Years Ago and Long Before, ch. 4 (1884); not verbatim.

title.en: The Ox's Lament and the Covenant Deferred
title.zh: 原牛之怨與牧者之諾

region.en: Earth of the original creation (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 原初創世之土（象徵性定位）

period: Recorded 9th century CE (Pahlavi; West translation 1880)

source.work: Bundahishn chs. III-IV (Pahlavi), trans. E. W. West, SBE 5 (1880)

summary.en: When the primeval ox passes away, its soul Geush-urvan stands before it and cries to Auharmazd as much as a thousand men at one time: with whom is the guardianship of the creatures left by thee, when ruin has broken into the earth, and vegetation is withered, and water is troubled? Where is the man of whom it was said by thee thus: I will produce him, so that he may preach carefulness? And Auharmazd answers: you are made ill, O Goshurvan; if it were proper to produce that man in this earth at this time, the evil spirit would not have been oppressive in it.
summary.zh: 原牛死去之際，其靈「牛魂」立於牛前，如千人齊呼般向阿胡拉·馬茲達哭訴：「大地已被毀、草木凋零、水已污濁，你曾說要造一人來教人謹守正道——他在哪裡？」答曰：「牛魂啊，你受了苦；若此人該在此世此時降生，惡靈便不會如此肆虐了。」

sensitivity.note: Pahlavi doctrinal text rendered as myth; the ox's protest is Yasna 29's Geush Urvan. Cross-tradition: dismembered-giant cluster (Ymir/Purusha). No living community restriction.

passages.text: This also is said, that when the primeval ox passed away it fell to the right hand, and Gayomart afterwards, when he passed away, to the left hand. Goshurvan, as the soul of the primeval ox came out from the body of the ox, stood up before the ox and cried to Auharmazd, as much as a thousand men when they sustain a cry at one time, thus: with whom is the guardianship of the creatures left by thee, when ruin has broken into the earth, and vegetation is withered, and water is troubled? Where is the man of whom it was said by thee thus: I will produce him, so that he may preach carefulness?
passages.note: Paraphrase of Bundahishn ch. IV, 1-2 (West, SBE 5, 1880); not verbatim.

passages.text: And Auharmazd spoke thus: you are made ill, O Goshurvan; you have the illness which the evil spirit brought on; if it were proper to produce that man in this earth at this time, the evil spirit would not have been oppressive in it. And before his coming to the ox, Auharmazd ground up the healing fruit, small, in water openly before its eyes, so that its damage and discomfort from the calamity might be less; and when it became at the same time lean and ill, as its breath went forth and it passed away, the ox also spoke thus: the cattle are to be created, and their work, labour, and care are to be appointed.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Bundahishn chs. III 18, IV 3 (West, SBE 5, 1880); not verbatim.

title.en: Gayomart, the First Man, Born of Sweat
title.zh: 原人伽堯馬特誕於汗珠

region.en: Centre of the earth, Khvaniras (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 大地中央赫瓦尼拉斯（象徵性定位）

period: Recorded 9th century CE (Pahlavi; West translation 1880)

source.work: Bundahishn ch. III, 19-27 (Pahlavi), trans. E. W. West, SBE 5 (1880)

summary.en: Before the destroyer's coming to Gayomart, Auharmazd brought forth a sweat upon Gayomart, so long as he might recite a prayer of one stanza; moreover he formed that sweat into the youthful body of a man of fifteen years, radiant and tall. When Gayomart issued from the sweat he saw the world dark as night, and the earth as though not a needle's point remained free from noxious creatures; and though Asto-vidad with a thousand demons was let forth on him, his appointed time had not come: after the coming of the adversary he lived thirty years, and spoke: although the destroyer has come, mankind will be all of my race.
summary.zh: 毀滅者來襲之前，阿胡拉·馬茲達使原人伽堯馬特出一身汗——恰夠誦一句禱詞之時——並將汗珠化為十五歲少年之軀，光明而修長。他一出汗便見世界黑如夜、大地遍生毒蟲；死神阿斯托維達特攜千魔來索，然其壽數未至：對頭降臨之後他又活了三十年，並言：「毀滅者雖來，人類皆出自我之族裔。」

sensitivity.note: Pahlavi doctrinal text rendered as myth; Gayomart parallels Purusha/Ymir in the dismembered-primordial cluster. No living community restriction.

passages.text: And before his coming to Gayomart, Auharmazd brought forth a sweat upon Gayomart, so long as he might recite a prayer of one stanza; moreover, Auharmazd formed that sweat into the youthful body of a man of fifteen years, radiant and tall. When Gayomart issued from the sweat he saw the world dark as night, and the earth as though not a needle's point remained free from noxious creatures; the celestial sphere was in revolution, and the sun and moon remained in motion.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Bundahishn ch. III, 19-20 (West, SBE 5, 1880); not verbatim.

passages.text: And the evil spirit thought that the creatures of Auharmazd were all rendered useless except Gayomart, and Asto-vidad with a thousand demons, causers of death, were let forth by him on Gayomart. But his appointed time had not come, and he obtained no means of noosing him; as it is said that, when the opposition of the evil spirit came, the period of the life and rule of Gayomart was appointed for thirty years. After the coming of the adversary he lived thirty years, and Gayomart spoke thus: although the destroyer has come, mankind will be all of my race; and this one thing is good, when they perform duty and good works.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Bundahishn ch. III, 21-23 (West, SBE 5, 1880); not verbatim.

title.en: Mashya and Mashyoi, the First Human Pair
title.zh: 初人夫婦瑪什亞與瑪什雅娜

region.en: Wilderness of Khvaniras (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 赫瓦尼拉斯荒野（象徵性定位）

period: Recorded 9th century CE (Pahlavi; West translation 1880)

source.work: Bundahishn ch. XV (Pahlavi), trans. E. W. West, SBE 5 (1880)

summary.en: From Gayomart's seed, purified in the sun and guarded by the angel Nerioc-sangh, a rhubarb plant grows, joined to form the first human pair. Auharmazd speaks to Mashya and Mashyoi: you are man, you are the ancestry of the world, perform devotedly the duty of the law, think good thoughts, speak good words, do good deeds, and worship no demons. Their first words acknowledge the creation, but antagonism rushes into their minds and they cry that the evil spirit created the water and earth; by that false speech their souls are in hell until the future existence. They milk a white-haired goat, and the taste of the food is taken away by the demons.
summary.zh: 原人之種經日光淨化，生出大黃狀聖草，相合成初人夫婦。阿胡拉·馬茲達告誡：「你們是人類始祖，當守律法、思善言善行，勿拜群魔！」夫婦初念感恩，然魔意乘虛而入，他們竟呼「水土萬物皆惡靈所造」——因此謊言，其魂直待末日方得救贖。他們以口吮山羊之乳，惡魔遂奪去食物的滋味。

sensitivity.note: Pahlavi doctrinal text rendered as myth; first-pair narrative parallels Adam/Manu. No living community restriction.

passages.text: Auharmazd spoke to Mashya and Mashyoi thus: you are man, you are the ancestry of the world, and you are created perfect in devotion by me; perform devotedly the duty of the law, think good thoughts, speak good words, do good deeds, and worship no demons! Both of them first thought this, that one of them should please the other, as he is a man for him; and the first words spoken by them were these, that Auharmazd created the water and earth, plants and animals, the stars, moon, and sun, and all prosperity whose origin and effect are from the manifestation of righteousness.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Bundahishn ch. XV, 6-7 (West, SBE 5, 1880); not verbatim.

passages.text: And, afterwards, antagonism rushed into their minds, and their minds were thoroughly corrupted, and they exclaimed that the evil spirit created the water and earth, plants and animals, and the other things as aforesaid. That false speech was spoken through the will of the demons, and the evil spirit possessed himself of this first enjoyment from them; through that false speech they both became wicked, and their souls are in hell until the future existence.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Bundahishn ch. XV, 8-9 (West, SBE 5, 1880); not verbatim.

passages.text: And they had gone thirty days without food, covered with clothing of herbage; and after the thirty days they went forth into the wilderness, came to a white-haired goat, and milked the milk from the udder with their mouths. When they had devoured the milk Mashya said to Mashyoi thus: my delight was owing to it when I had not devoured the milk, and my delight is more delightful now when it is devoured by my vile body. That second false speech enhanced the power of the demons, and the taste of the food was taken away by them, so that out of a hundred parts one part remained.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Bundahishn ch. XV, 10-12 (West, SBE 5, 1880); not verbatim.

title.en: Tishtrya and Apaosha: The War for the Rain
title.zh: 提什特里亞與阿帕奧沙：爭雨之戰

region.en: Sea Vouru-Kasha (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 烏魯卡沙海（象徵性定位）

period: Recorded in the Avesta, c. 6th-4th century BCE (Darmesteter translation 1883)

source.work: Tir Yasht (Zend-Avesta Part II), trans. J. Darmesteter, SBE 23 (1883), secs. 20-29

summary.en: The bright and glorious Tishtrya goes down to the sea Vouru-Kasha in the shape of a white, beautiful horse with golden ears; there rushes down to meet him the Daeva Apaosha, in the shape of a dark horse, black with black ears, black back, black tail, stamped with brands of terror. They meet hoof against hoof and fight three days and nights, and Apaosha overcomes him, until Ahura Mazda offers up a sacrifice in which Tishtrya is invoked by his own name and brings him the strength of ten horses, ten camels, ten bulls, ten mountains, ten rivers; then Tishtrya proves stronger, overcomes Apaosha, and the waters flow down from the sea Vouru-Kasha, mother-like, friendly, and healing.
summary.zh: 光輝的提什特里亞化作金耳白駿下至烏魯卡沙海；旱魃阿帕奧沙化作黑鬃黑尾、烙滿恐怖印記的黑馬迎戰。二者馬蹄相擊，鏖戰三晝夜，旱魔佔上風——直到阿胡拉·馬茲達以提什特里亞本名獻祭，賜他十馬、十駝、十牛、十山、十河之力；白駿遂勝，烏魯卡沙之水如慈母般奔流而下，潤澤萬邦。

sensitivity.note: Avestan liturgical text read here as the Iranian rain-myth (rain-fight cluster); interpretive tags. No living community restriction.

passages.text: Then, O Spitama Zarathustra! the bright and glorious Tishtrya goes down to the sea Vouru-Kasha in the shape of a white, beautiful horse, with golden ears and a golden caparison. But there rushes down to meet him the Daeva Apaosha, in the shape of a dark horse, black with black ears, black with a black back, black with a black tail, stamped with brands of terror.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Tir Yasht 20-21 (Darmesteter, SBE 23, 1883); not verbatim.

passages.text: They meet together, hoof against hoof, O Spitama Zarathustra! the bright and glorious Tishtrya and the Daeva Apaosha. They fight together for three days and three nights. And then the Daeva Apaosha proves stronger than the bright and glorious Tishtrya, he overcomes him. And Tishtrya flees from the sea Vouru-Kasha, as far as a Hathra's length: Woe is me, O Ahura Mazda! I am in distress, O Waters and Plants! Men do not worship me with a sacrifice in which I am invoked by my own name, as they worship the other Yazatas with sacrifices in which they are invoked by their own names.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Tir Yasht 22-23 (Darmesteter, SBE 23, 1883); not verbatim.

passages.text: If men had worshipped me with a sacrifice in which I had been invoked by my own name, I should have taken to me the strength of ten horses, the strength of ten camels, the strength of ten bulls, the strength of ten mountains, the strength of ten rivers. Then I, Ahura Mazda, offer up to the bright and glorious Tishtrya a sacrifice in which he is invoked by his own name, and bring him the strength of ten horses, ten camels, ten bulls, ten mountains, and ten rivers. Then Tishtrya goes down to the sea Vouru-Kasha in the shape of a white, beautiful horse; they meet hoof against hoof; they fight together till the time of noon. Then the bright and glorious Tishtrya proves stronger than the Daeva Apaosha, he overcomes him; and the waters flow down from the sea Vouru-Kasha, mother-like, friendly, and healing.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Tir Yasht 24-29, 47 (Darmesteter, SBE 23, 1883); not verbatim.

title.en: Verethraghna's Ten Forms
title.zh: 戰神巴赫拉姆十變

region.en: Sky of the Yazatas (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 雅扎塔之天（象徵性定位）

period: Recorded in the Avesta, c. 6th-4th century BCE (Darmesteter translation 1883)

source.work: Bahram Yasht (Zend-Avesta Part II), trans. J. Darmesteter, SBE 23 (1883), secs. 26-31

summary.en: Zarathustra asks Ahura Mazda who is the best-armed of the heavenly gods, and the answer is Verethraghna, made by Ahura — the divine Victory who comes again and again bearing the good Glory made by Mazda: as wind, as bull, as horse, as camel, as boar, as youth, as ram, as deer, as bird — and the tenth time running in the shape of a man, bright and beautiful, holding a sword with a golden blade inlaid with all sorts of ornaments. To the prophet he gives the fountains of manliness, the strength of the arms, and the eye-sight of the Kara fish that can measure a rippling of the water not thicker than a hair in the Rangha whose ends lie afar.
summary.zh: 查拉圖什特拉問阿胡拉·馬茲達：「天神之中誰的甲冑最好？」答曰：阿胡拉所造的戰神韋雷斯拉格納——神之勝利。他一次又一次以馬茲達所造的榮光現身：或為風、為牛、為馬、為駱駝、為野豬、為少年、為公羊、為鹿、為神鳥——第十次化作光明俊美的男子，手執嵌飾珍寶的金柄寶劍。他賜先知臂力與「卡拉魚之目」——能在遠及天涯的朗格哈河中察覺髮絲般細的水紋。

sensitivity.note: Avestan liturgical text; Verethraghna is the yazata of Victory (bahram). Transformation-series tag interpretive. No living community restriction.

passages.text: Zarathustra asked Ahura Mazda: Ahura Mazda, most beneficent Spirit, Maker of the material world, thou Holy One! Who is the best-armed of the heavenly gods? Ahura Mazda answered: It is Verethraghna, made by Ahura, O Spitama Zarathustra! Verethraghna, made by Ahura, came to him the tenth time, running in the shape of a man, bright and beautiful, made by Mazda: he held a sword with a golden blade, inlaid with all sorts of ornaments. Thus did Verethraghna come, bearing the good Glory made by Mazda, the Glory made by Mazda. We sacrifice unto Verethraghna, made by Ahura, who makes virility, who makes death, who makes resurrection, who possesses peace, who has a free way.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Bahram Yasht 26 (Darmesteter, SBE 23, 1883); not verbatim. / Paraphrase of Bahram Yasht 27-28 (Darmesteter, SBE 23, 1883); not verbatim.

passages.text: Unto him did the holy Zarathustra offer up a sacrifice, asking for victorious thinking, victorious speaking, victorious doing, victorious addressing, and victorious answering. Verethraghna, made by Ahura, gave him the fountains of manliness, the strength of the arms, the health of the whole body, the sturdiness of the whole body, and the eye-sight of the Kara fish, that lives beneath the waters and can measure a rippling of the water, not thicker than a hair, in the Rangha whose ends lie afar, whose depth is a thousand times the height of a man.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Bahram Yasht 29 (Darmesteter, SBE 23, 1883); not verbatim.

title.en: The Woman Who Went Down to Panoi in Her Body
title.zh: 身入帕諾伊尋弟之女

region.en: Banks Islands, Vanuatu (symbolic pin: Gaua/Mota)
region.zh: 瓦努阿圖班克斯群島（象徵定位：高阿島／莫塔島）

period: Oral tradition; recorded by R. H. Codrington, The Melanesians, 1891, ch. XV

source.work: R. H. Codrington, The Melanesians: Studies in their Anthropology and Folk-lore (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1891), ch. XV 'Death, Burial, After Death'

summary.en: A woman who much desired to see her lately dead brother perfumed herself with water in which a dead rat had been steeped, pulled up a bird's-nest fern, and descended by the hole she had opened. She found Panoi without difficulty, saw friends who never discovered she was alive, found her brother lying in a house — a recent ghost not strong enough to move about — and he cautioned her to eat nothing there; she returned. In Panoi the dead of violent deaths are fenced apart by the manner of their killing, and life there is eternal, unless as some say there are two Panois, one below the other: from the lower the dead never die, but turn into white ants' nests.
summary.zh: 班克斯群島有一婦人，極想見新亡的弟弟。她以浸過死老鼠的水沐浴，使自己帶上死人之氣；又拔起一叢鳥巢蕨，從挖開的洞口走了下去。她毫不費力便到了帕諾伊，遇見故友，無人識破她是活人；弟弟因是新鬼，尚無力走動，正躺在一間屋裡。他囑咐她什麼都不許吃，她便回來了。帕諾伊之中，橫死之人各按死法分圍而居：中箭者一處、中咒者一處、被棒擊者一處——屋中若聞沙沙聲如箭桿相擊，便說是『撥箭之鬼』。帕諾伊之生永無終期；也有人說上下有兩個帕諾伊：死者自上帕諾伊死入下帕諾伊，如生人死離陽世；自下帕諾伊則永不死，只化作白蟻巢。

sensitivity.note: Missionary-anthropologist record (Codrington 1891); Banks Islands heritage. Descent cluster.

passages.text: Descents to Panoi have been by no means uncommon. There was a woman, who died not many years ago, who once much desired to see her lately dead brother; she perfumed herself with water in which a dead rat had been steeped, to give herself a death-like smell, pulled up a bird's-nest fern, and descended by the hole she had opened. She had no difficulty in finding Panoi, and she saw friends there who were surprised to see her, and never discovered that she was alive. She found her brother lying in a house, because as a recent ghost he was not strong enough yet to move about. He cautioned her to eat nothing there, and she returned. This descent was in the body, as was that of one Molborbor of Valuwa, who went down and saw his wife; but a man in Motlav, more lately dead, used to go down in sleep, his soul descending, and his body remaining as in a trance.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Codrington, The Melanesians, ch. XV (1891); not verbatim.

passages.text: He could do this at will, and received money for doing it, professing to visit the recently dead, about whom their friends were unhappy, and even to be able to bring them back. He never did in fact bring any back; he said he had seen the persons and talked with them, but was prevented from bringing them back. He, too, prepared for his soul's descent by washing his body with water in which a putrid rat, snake or lizard had been steeped.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Codrington, The Melanesians, ch. XV (1891); not verbatim.

passages.text: There are compartments, enclosures fenced apart, in Panoi, in which those who have died violent deaths keep together; those who have been shot are in one place together, those who were charmed to death in a second, those who have been clubbed in a third together. Those who have been shot keep rattling the reeds of the arrows they were shot with; hence if a rat is heard in a house making that kind of noise the saying is that it is a reed-rattling ghost. Life in Panoi is eternal, unless indeed, as some say, there are two Panois, one below the other, and the dead die from the upper to the lower, as living men die from earth; from the lower they never die, but turn into white ants' nests.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Codrington, The Melanesians, ch. XV (1891); not verbatim.

title.en: Vanvanvegirgir and the Widower in Panoi
title.zh: 范氏引魂下冥：斷腕之妻

region.en: Motlav, Banks Islands, Vanuatu (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 瓦努阿圖班克斯群島莫特拉夫島（象徵定位）

period: Oral tradition; recorded by R. H. Codrington, The Melanesians, 1891, ch. XV

source.work: R. H. Codrington, The Melanesians: Studies in their Anthropology and Folk-lore (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1891), ch. XV 'Death, Burial, After Death'

summary.en: Vanvanvegirgir of Motlav once took down with him, soul and body, a widower who had lost his wife: the man washed himself with the liquor of a putrid black gecko, and was given a stick. In Panoi the ghosts detected the living man and cried 'The smell of that world!' — and tested them with dead men's bones, which they rattled rightly, by one, by two, by three. The wife was brought; she said return was impossible and gave him a shell armlet — and when he took her hand and dragged her, the hand came off and the body came to pieces: the ghost in Panoi has a lanpei, a body with form, colour, and consistency, but not in the world.
summary.zh: 莫特拉夫島的范氏能引魂下帕諾伊。一次他帶上一位喪妻的鰥夫：那人以腐臭黑壁虎之汁淨身，攜一根手杖，隨范氏下界。帕諾伊的亡靈一嗅便叫：『陽世的氣味！』二人自辯亦是死人；亡靈便取出死人的骨頭，叫他們像鬼那樣一根、兩根、三根地撥弄——撥對了，方許前行。范氏尋來其妻；夫妻相見，情話綿綿，丈夫求她同返陽世；她說斷不可能，只贈貝釧一枚留念。丈夫執其手拖拽——那隻手竟脫落，全身散架。緣故是：帕諾伊中的亡靈尚有形有色、有質之地；一回到陽世，便只剩個影子般的廓形。

sensitivity.note: Missionary-anthropologist record (Codrington 1891); Motlav heritage.

passages.text: There was a man in former days at Motlav, Vanvanvegirgir by name, who going down to Panoi in his nuieyi, soul, took once another man with him in his body. This man had lately lost his wife, and went to Vanvanvegirgir to enquire about her. He was instructed to give himself the appropriate smell with the liquor of a putrid black gecko, and was given a stick. The two then descended, and reached Panoi; the ghosts detected the living man, and cried out, 'The smell of that world!' The two declared that they were really dead, and to try them the ghosts brought out dead men's bones, to see if they would rattle them as ghosts do, by one, by two, by three; they did this rightly and were allowed to go on.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Codrington, The Melanesians, ch. XV (1891); not verbatim.

passages.text: Vanvanvegirgir went forward to find the man's wife, and brought her to him; they talked together, and the man begged her to go back to the world with him. That she said was impossible, and she gave him a shell armlet by which to remember her. He took her by the hand and began to drag her; her hand came off, and her body came to pieces. For, as the story is explained, ghosts in Panoi have something more of body and substance than they have when they come back into the world; else the man could not have taken hold of his dead wife's hand. When a ghost comes into the world, it is but a tapangiu that is seen, a something circumscribed by an outline like a shadow; but the ghost in Panoi has a lanpei, a body, which has not only form and colour, but a certain consistency.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Codrington, The Melanesians, ch. XV (1891); not verbatim.

title.en: The Journey of the Dead on Maewo
title.zh: 馬埃沃亡者之路

region.en: Maewo (Aurora Island), Vanuatu (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 瓦努阿圖馬埃沃島（奧羅拉島）（象徵定位）

period: Oral tradition; recorded (native account) by R. H. Codrington, The Melanesians, 1891, ch. XV

source.work: R. H. Codrington, The Melanesians: Studies in their Anthropology and Folk-lore (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1891), ch. XV 'New Hebrides. Journey of the Dead'

summary.en: When the soul leaves the body on Maewo it mounts into a bird's-nest fern, sits among the fronds, and laughs at the people crying over him — 'Who is it they are sorry for? Here am I' — then runs his gardens and paths, the stone of thought, the ravine that must be cleared at a leap, and the revenge of those he wronged on the way, to the three leaping-places at the northern point, one for men, one for women, one for ulcerous persons; at Banoi stands Gaviga, the chief of Banoi, and Matamakira with sharp spears, and a huge fierce pig that devours all who never planted the emba, the pandanus of the mats.
summary.zh: 馬埃沃人相信：靈魂一離身體，便爬上鳥巢蕨，坐在葉間對著哭喪的眾人發笑——『哭什麼？可憐誰？我在這裡呢。』肉身不過是脫下的衣裳。此後靈魂走過自家園圃與舊路，至『思之石』處稍歇：若此時想起孩子、妻子或產業，便會跑回去復活。那裡還有兩巖夾一深澗：一躍而過者永死；躍不過者復生。亡者一路奔跑，生前被他殺害冤枉的鬼魂沿途復仇，棒打刀刺，罵道：『你在世上自以為好漢，如今我們報仇了！』北端有斷崖三處跳臺——男子的、女子的、患瘡者的；墮下者摔碎仍跑，至聖山陶烏——下界之洞的入口。洞前，波諾伊之主加維加與脾氣暴躁的馬塔馬基拉持長矛刺戳新鬼；還有一頭巨豬，吞食一切生前不曾種過織席露兜樹的人——種過的方可攀上樹頂避豬。故人人爭種露兜。未穿耳者不得飲水，未文身者不得食美餐；未入蘇蓋會社的亡靈，只能像狐蝠般倒掛樹上。

sensitivity.note: Native Maewo/Tanoriki account translated by Codrington (1891); living after-death belief.

passages.text: In the first place, they think that when the soul, famani, leaves the body in death, it mounts into a tree in which is a bird's-nest fern, and sitting among the fronds, laughs and mocks at the people who are crying and making great lamentations over him. There he sits, wondering at them and ridiculing them. 'What are they crying for?' he says; 'who is it they are sorry for? Here am I.' For they think that the real thing is the soul, and that it has gone away from the body just as a man throws off his clothes and leaves them, and the clothes lie by themselves with nothing in them.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Codrington, The Melanesians, ch. XV (1891), after a native Maewo account; not verbatim.

passages.text: Then the soul goes through his gardens and along his customary paths, and finally leaves the place. He runs along the line of hills till he reaches the end of the island, and there he comes to the place of recollection, the stone of thought; if he remembers there his child or his wife or anything that belongs to him, he will run back and come to life again. In the same place also are two rocks with a deep ravine between them; if the ghost clears this as he leaps across he is for ever dead, but if one fails he returns to life again.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Codrington, The Melanesians, ch. XV (1891), after a native Maewo account; not verbatim.

passages.text: The ghost pursues his course running along the mountain range to the end opposite to Raga, Pentecost, at the land's end, or brink of sea, and when he arrives safely all the ghosts of those who have died before assemble and receive him joyfully. They believe also that as he runs the ghosts of those whom he has wronged in this world, whom he has foully slain by club or arrow, or has killed by charms, take a full revenge upon him, beating him, tearing him, and stabbing him with daggers, such as men stick pigs with; one of them will say to him, 'While you were still in the world you thought yourself a valiant man; but now we will take our revenge upon you.' Another path of the ghosts takes them to the northern point of Maewo, where there is a deep gully and three leaping-places, one for men, one for women, and one for ulcerous persons. It is a curse to wish a man may fall down there; if a ghost falls in leaping he is smashed to pieces, but runs on and comes to the hill Tawu, which is very sacred to ghosts.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Codrington, The Melanesians, ch. XV (1891), after a native Maewo account; not verbatim.

passages.text: Here is Gaviga, a vui, the chief of Banoi, and Matamakira, or Salolo as the Tanoriki people say, a quarrelsome and ill-tempered man on earth; these stand with large and sharp spears and try to stab the new-comers. There is a huge fierce pig also there, which will devour all who have not in their lifetime planted the emba, pandanus, from which mats are made. If one has planted such he can climb up out of the reach of the devouring beast, and for this reason every one likes to plant that tree. Here also, if a man's ears are not pierced, he is not allowed to drink water; if he is not tattooed, he must not eat good food. Here the ghosts of those who have not joined the Suqe hang like flying foxes upon the trees.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Codrington, The Melanesians, ch. XV (1891), after a native Maewo account; not verbatim.

title.en: The Bound Husband of Garat: Pay Your Debts
title.zh: 加臘特山上被縛的亡夫

region.en: Mount Garat, Gaua, Banks Islands (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 瓦努阿圖班克斯群島高阿島加臘特火山（象徵定位）

period: Oral tradition; recorded by R. H. Codrington, The Melanesians, 1891, ch. XV

source.work: R. H. Codrington, The Melanesians: Studies in their Anthropology and Folk-lore (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1891), ch. XV 'Death, Burial, After Death'

summary.en: A woman of Vanua Lava whose Gaua husband died fell very ill and appeared to die; she recovered and told the people she had followed him to the hill Garat and seen him there bound hand and foot. The ghosts told her this was done because he had not paid his debts: 'Go back to the Gaua people and say to them, Pay your debts, don't kill one another; this is how we shall treat such men.'
summary.zh: 瓦努阿瓦島一名婦人，其夫為高阿島人，亡故之後她重病垂危，狀若已死；卻又醒轉，對眾人說：她隨亡夫到了加臘特山，親眼見他在那裡被捆住手腳。亡靈們告訴她，這是因為他生前賴賬未償——『回去對高阿人說：把債還清，不要自相殘殺；我們就是這樣對付這種人的。』

sensitivity.note: Missionary-anthropologist record (Codrington 1891); Vanua Lava heritage.

passages.text: There is still living in Vanua Lava a woman who turned her descent to Panoi to a useful purpose. Her husband, a Gaua man, died, and she herself was very ill and appeared to die. She recovered, however, and told the people that she had followed her husband to the hill Garat, and had seen him there bound hand and foot. The ghosts told her, she declared, that this was done because he had not paid his debts; 'Go back,' they bade her, 'to the Gaua people, and say to them, Pay your debts, don't kill one another; this is how we shall treat such men.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Codrington, The Melanesians, ch. XV (1891); not verbatim.

title.en: Cari and Zapana: The Two Lords of the Collao
title.zh: 卡里與薩帕納:科利亞奧二主之爭

region.en: Hatun-colla and Chucuito, Lake Titicaca (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 的的喀喀湖畔哈通-科利亞與丘庫伊托(象徵性標記)

period: Written by Cieza de León, publ. Markham trans. 1883 (Second Part)

source.work: Pedro de Cieza de León, The Second Part of the Chronicle of Peru, trans. and ed. Sir Clements Markham, Hakluyt Society, 1883

summary.en: In the reign of Inca Viracocha a lord named Zapana ruled over Hatun-colla. In the lake of Titicaca there are islands inhabited by people with large balsas, and another lord named Cari went to the islands, where he fought with the people in great battles out of which the Cari came forth a conqueror - with no other object than to destroy the villagers and carry off plunder. He returned to Chucuito, where he had established himself, and had under his sway the towns of Ylave, Yuli, Zepita, Pomata, and others. With the people he could collect, after having offered up great sacrifices to his gods, he marched against the Canas and defeated them; another victory at Luracachi made him very proud. When Zapana, the lord of Hatun-colla, heard of it he assembled his friends and vassals to despoil Cari, but Cari understood the design and retired in good order to Chucuito by an unfrequented road. Each chief, desiring the friendship of the Incas, sent ambassadors to Cuzco with great presents to secure Viracocha's alliance against the other.
summary.zh: 印加·維拉科查在位時,一位名叫薩帕納的領主統治哈通-科利亞。的的喀喀湖中有島嶼,住著乘大型蘆筏的人民;另一位名為卡里的領主赴島作戰,大戰連連,終為勝者——但其目的不過是屠村掠財。他凱旋回到自己經營的丘庫伊托,治下有伊拉維、尤利、塞皮塔、波馬塔等鎮。祭過神靈之後,他聚眾進攻卡納斯人,大敗之;又在盧拉卡奇獲勝,日益驕橫。哈通-科利亞之主薩帕納聞訊大怒,聚友邦與藩屬欲掠卡里;卡里識破其謀,循僻徑安然退回丘庫伊托。兩雄皆欲結好印加,便各攜重禮遣使庫斯科,求維拉科查聯盟以伐對方。

sensitivity.note: Pre-Inca Collao power politics preserved by Cieza's Orejone informants; the war opened the road to Inca domination of the lake.

passages.text: In the lake of Titicaca there are islands inhabited by people with large balsas, and another lord named Cari went to the islands, where he fought with the people insomuch that there were great battles between them, out of which the Cari came forth a conqueror. But he had no other object than to destroy the villagers and carry off plunder, without troubling himself to take prisoners. He returned to Chucuito, where he had established himself, and he had under his sway the towns of Ylave, Yuli, Zepita, Pomata, and others.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Cieza de León, Second Part of the Chronicle of Peru, ch. 41 (Markham 1883); not verbatim.

passages.text: With the people he could collect, after having offered up great sacrifices to his gods, he determined to march to the province of the Canas. These men, when they heard of his approach, assembled together, came forth to meet him, and fought a battle in which they were defeated with much loss. After this victory Cari determined to continue his advance, and arrived at Luracachi, where it is said that he fought another battle, and was equally fortunate. With these victories Cari became very proud.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Cieza de León, Second Part of the Chronicle of Peru, ch. 41 (Markham 1883); not verbatim.

passages.text: When Zapana, the lord of Hatun-colla, heard of it, he was very sad, and he assembled his friends and vassals to take the field and despoil Cari. But he could not do this so secretly as to prevent Cari from understanding the design of Zapana, and he retired in good order to Chucuito by an unfrequented road... And as the valour of the Incas, and the great power of Viracocha was spread abroad over all that region, each of these chiefs, desiring to obtain his friendship, sent ambassadors to Cuzco to secure his alliance and induce him to take part against the rival chief.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Cieza de León, Second Part of the Chronicle of Peru, ch. 41 (Markham 1883); not verbatim.

canonical_translation: Sir Clements Markham, The Second Part of the Chronicle of Peru (Hakluyt Society, 1883)

title.en: Chin in Breast, Voice Loud: How the Oracles Were Consulted
title.zh: 垂首含胸、高聲傳話:神諭的問法

region.en: Temples of the Andes and the coast (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 安第斯與海岸諸廟(象徵性標記)

period: Written by Cieza de León, publ. Markham trans. 1883 (Second Part)

source.work: Pedro de Cieza de León, The Second Part of the Chronicle of Peru, trans. and ed. Sir Clements Markham, Hakluyt Society, 1883

summary.en: When the Inca determined to seek for an answer from the oracles, he sent for those who were accustomed to manage those things. The reply is sought by the priests in front of the idols: they bow down their shoulders, put their chins into their breasts, and begin to speak in loud voices. Occasionally I myself, with my own ears, have heard the Indians converse with the devil: in the province of Cartagena I heard the devil answer in a clear whistle, so loudly that a Christian more than half a league away heard the same whistle and was dismayed. On another day the Indians made great shoutings, publishing the reply of the devil. In some parts of these lands where they keep the dead in hammocks, the devils occasionally enter into the bodies and give answers: I heard a man named Aranda say that, in the island of Carex, he also saw one of these dead bodies speak, and the lies and nonsense they utter are laughable.
summary.zh: 印加王欲求神諭,便召慣司此事之人。祭司在偶像前求答:垂肩俯首,下巴抵胸,高聲傳話。塞薩自述:「我屢屢親耳聽過印第安人與魔鬼交談。」在卡塔赫納省的海港城巴亞伊雷,他聽見魔鬼以清晰口哨作答,聲聞半萊格之外,令一位在場基督徒惶然失措;另一日,印第安人高聲喧呼,宣告魔鬼的回復。在某些地方,人們把死者安置於吊床之中,魔鬼偶爾附體作答——有人名阿蘭達者說,他在卡雷克斯島親見一具死者屍體開口說話;那些謊言與胡話,聽來簡直可笑。

sensitivity.note: Cieza's rare first-person description of an oracle procedure (posture, voice, possession of hammock-kept dead); 'devil' is his frame, the procedure is the datum.

passages.text: This is done by the priests in front of the idols. They bow down their shoulders, put their chins into their breasts, and begin to speak in loud voices. Occasionally I myself, with my own ears, have heard the Indians converse with the devil.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Cieza de León, Second Part of the Chronicle of Peru, ch. 41 (Markham 1883); not verbatim.

passages.text: In some parts of these lands where they keep the dead in hammocks, the devils occasionally enter into the bodies and give answers. I heard a man named Aranda say that, in the island of Carex, he also saw one of these dead bodies speak, and the lies and nonsense they utter are laughable.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Cieza de León, Second Part of the Chronicle of Peru, ch. 41 (Markham 1883); not verbatim.

passages.text: When the Inca determined to seek for an answer from the oracles, he sent for those who were accustomed to manage those things, and they say that the reply was that he should arrange to go to the Collao and seek the alliance of Cari.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Cieza de León, Second Part of the Chronicle of Peru, ch. 41 (Markham 1883); not verbatim.

canonical_translation: Sir Clements Markham, The Second Part of the Chronicle of Peru (Hakluyt Society, 1883)

title.en: The Dinner of the Sun: Clay Cups Replaced with Gold
title.zh: 日神的晚餐:陶杯換金器

region.en: Coricancha, House of the Sun, Cuzco (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 庫斯科太陽之屋科里坎查(象徵性標記)

period: Inca tradition as given to Sarmiento de Gamboa, 1572; trans. Markham 1907

source.work: Pedro Sarmiento de Gamboa, History of the Incas, ch. 36, trans. Sir Clements Markham, Hakluyt Society, 1907

summary.en: After Pachacuti Inca Yupanqui had conquered the lands mentioned above and had triumphed over them, he came to visit the House of the Sun and the Mama-cunas or nuns who were there. He assisted one day to see how the Mama-cunas served the dinner of the Sun. This was to offer much richly cooked food to the image or idol of the Sun, and then to put it into a great fire on an altar. The same order was taken with the liquor: the chief of the Mama-cunas saluted the Sun with a small vase, and the rest was thrown on the fire; besides this many jars full of that liquor were poured into a trough which had a drain, all being offerings to the Sun. This service was performed with vessels of clay. As Pachacuti considered that the material of the vases was too poor, he presented very complete sets of vases of gold and silver for all the service that was necessary. To adorn the house more richly he caused a plate of fine gold to be made, two palmas broad and the length of the court-yard, and ordered it to be nailed high up on the wall in the manner of a cornice, passing all round the court-yard. This border or cornice of gold remained there down to the time of the Spaniards.
summary.zh: 帕查庫提·印加·尤潘琪征服諸邦、凱旋之後,親臨太陽之屋,查看瑪瑪庫納(貞女)侍奉日神晚餐的情形:眾女將精緻烹調的膳食供奉於太陽神像之前,然後投入祭壇上的烈火之中;酒漿亦然——瑪瑪庫納之首以小杯敬日神,其餘盡焚於火;此外又將滿罐奇恰酒傾入帶排水道的溝槽,盡為日神之祭。這些侍奉原用陶器。帕查庫提嫌器物卑陋,便賜下成套金銀器皿,以供全部所需。為使神屋更加輝煌,他又命人打造一塊兩掌寬、與庭院等長的純金薄板,釘於高牆之上作為簷飾,環繞庭院一周。這道金簷一直留存到西班牙人到來之日。

sensitivity.note: The daily liturgy of the Sun's meal as witnessed by the king; the gold cornice is the Coricancha's famous feature.

passages.text: He assisted one day, to see how the Mama-cunas served the dinner of the Sun. This was to offer much richly cooked food to the image or idol of the Sun, and then to put it into a great fire on an altar. The same order was taken with the liquor. The chief of the Mama-cunas saluted the Sun with a small vase, and the rest was thrown on the fire. Besides this many jars full of that liquor were poured into a trough which had a drain, all being offerings to the Sun.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Sarmiento, History of the Incas, ch. 36 (Markham 1907); not verbatim.

passages.text: As Pachacuti considered that the material of the vases was too poor, he presented very complete sets of vases of gold and silver for all the service that was necessary. To adorn the house more richly he caused a plate of fine gold to be made, two palmas broad and the length of the court-yard. He ordered this to be nailed high up on the wall in the manner of a cornice, passing all round the court-yard. This border or cornice of gold remained there down to the time of the Spaniards.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Sarmiento, History of the Incas, ch. 36 (Markham 1907); not verbatim.

canonical_translation: Sir Clements Markham, History of the Incas (Hakluyt Society, 1907)

title.en: Sixteen Visitors and the Road from Quito to Chile
title.zh: 十六位巡察使與從基多到智利的大道

region.en: Roads of the empire, Quito to Chile (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 帝國大道:基多至智利(象徵性標記)

period: Inca tradition as given to Sarmiento de Gamboa, 1572; trans. Markham 1907

source.work: Pedro Sarmiento de Gamboa, History of the Incas, ch. 45, trans. Sir Clements Markham, Hakluyt Society, 1907

summary.en: Seeing that the people were in greater fear at beholding the valour of Tupac Inca, Pachacuti determined to have a visitation of the land, and nominated 16 visitors, four for each of the four suyus or divisions of the empire: Cunti-suyu from Cuzco south and west as far as the South Sea, Chinchay-suyu from Cuzco to the north and west, Anti-suyu from Cuzco to the east, and Colla-suyu from Cuzco to the south. These visitors inspected, before all things, the work of the tucuyricos and the methods of their government; they caused irrigating channels to be constructed for the crops, broke up land where this had been neglected, built andenes or cultivated terraces, and took up pastures for the Sun, the Inca, and Cuzco; above all they imposed very heavy tribute on all the produce. The visitations occupied two years; when they were completed the visitors returned to Cuzco, bringing with them certain cloths descriptive of the provinces they had visited, and reported fully to the Inca all that they had found and done. The Inca also despatched other orejones as overseers to make roads and hospices on the routes of the Inca: they made roads, now called 'of the Inca', over the mountains and along the sea coast; those on the sea coast are all provided, at the sides, with high walls of adobe, wherever it was possible to build them. These roads go from Quito to Chile, and into the forests of the Andes.
summary.zh: 帕查庫提見民眾愈發畏懼圖帕克·印加之勇武,便決意巡查全境,任命十六位巡察使——四蘇尤各四位:昆蒂蘇尤(自庫斯科向南向西直至南海)、欽查蘇尤(向北向西)、安蒂蘇尤(向東)、科利亞蘇尤(向南)。巡察使首先督察各處「圖庫里科」官長的施政;又主持修築灌溉渠、墾闢荒田、建造安第斯梯田,並為太陽、印加與庫斯科劃定牧場;尤以加征重貢於一切出產為最。巡查歷時兩年;事畢,巡察使攜記述各省的彩布返回庫斯科,向印加王詳細復命。印加王另遣耳垂貴胄為監工,沿王路修築道路與驛館——即今所稱「印加道」——越山嶺、沿海岸;海岸一路,凡可築處皆以土坯砌高牆護道兩側。這些道路自基多直達智利,並深入安第斯森林。

sensitivity.note: The imperial visitation as administrative myth-history; the painted cloth reports echo the Pachacuti annals-library record.

passages.text: Seeing that the people were in greater fear at beholding the valour of Tupac Inca, he determined to have a visitation of the land, and nominated 16 visitors, four for each of the four suyus or divisions of the empire... These visitors each went to the part to which he was appointed, and inspected, before all things, the work of the tucuyricos and the methods of their government. They caused irrigating channels to be constructed for the crops, broke up land where this had been neglected, built andenes or cultivated terraces, and took up pastures for the Sun, the Inca, and Cuzco.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Sarmiento, History of the Incas, ch. 45 (Markham 1907); not verbatim.

passages.text: The visitations occupied two years. When they were completed the visitors returned to Cuzco, bringing with them certain cloths descriptive of the provinces they had visited. They reported fully to the Inca all that they had found and done. Besides these, the Inca also despatched other orejones as overseers to make roads and hospices on the routes of the Inca... These roads go from Quito to Chile, and into the forests of the Andes.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Sarmiento, History of the Incas, ch. 45 (Markham 1907); not verbatim.

canonical_translation: Sir Clements Markham, History of the Incas (Hakluyt Society, 1907)

title.en: 'O Father, Now Take Rest': The Obsequies of Pachacuti
title.zh: 「父王安息吧」:帕查庫提的葬禮

region.en: Cuzco great square (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 庫斯科大廣場(象徵性標記)

period: Inca tradition as given to Sarmiento de Gamboa, 1572; trans. Markham 1907

source.work: Pedro Sarmiento de Gamboa, History of the Incas, ch. 48, trans. Sir Clements Markham, Hakluyt Society, 1907

summary.en: When Pachacuti Inca Yupanqui died, two orejones were deputed to watch the body, and to allow no one to enter or go out to spread the news of his death, until orders had been given. The other Incas and orejones went with Tupac Inca to the House of the Sun and then ordered the twelve captains of the ayllus of the Inca's guard to come. They came with 2200 men of the guard, fully armed, and surrounded the Yupanqui with the fringe, and gave him the other insignia of sovereignty, as he had now inherited and succeeded his father. Taking him in the midst of themselves and of the guards, they escorted him to the great square, where he was seated, in majesty, on a superb throne. All the people of the city were then ordered to come and make obeisance to the Inca on pain of death. Those who had come with the Inca went to their houses to fetch presents to show reverence and do homage to the new Inca; he remained with his guards only until they returned with presents, doing homage and adoring. This having been done, they approached the Inca and said: 'O Sovereign Inca! O Father! now take rest.' At these words Tupac Inca showed much sadness and covered his head with his mantle, which they call llacolla. He next went, with all his company, to the place where the body of his father was laid, and there he put on mourning. All things were then arranged for the obsequies, and Tupac Inca Yupanqui did everything that his father had ordered at the point of death.
summary.zh: 帕查庫提·印加·尤潘琪駕崩後,兩名耳垂貴胄奉命看守遺體:未奉諭旨,任何人不得出入、不得走漏死訊。其餘印加貴胄隨圖帕克·印加前往太陽之屋,召王之衛隊十二世系的隊長;他們率兩千二百名全副武裝的衛士趕到,為戴王纓的尤潘琪呈上其餘王權印信——蓋他已承襲父位。眾人將他簇擁於衛隊中央,護送至大廣場,威嚴地安置在華麗御座之上;旋即傳令全城百姓前來朝拜新王,違者處死。隨王前來之人各自回宅取獻禮,以示尊崇;新王獨留衛隊之中,待眾人攜禮而返,行禮致敬,一一祭拜。禮成之後,眾人趨前說道:「至尊的印加王!父王!如今請安息吧。」聞言,圖帕克·印加面現哀戚,以名為「利亞科利亞」的方氅掩面。繼而,他率全體扈從前往父親遺體安放之所,披麻戴孝。喪儀諸事一一安排;圖帕克·印加·尤潘琪遵照父王臨終遺命,辦理後事,無所遺漏。

sensitivity.note: Accession-by-obsequies: the new king crowned before the death news escapes; the formula 'now take rest' marks the transfer of care.

The other Incas and orejones went with Tupac Inca to the House of the Sun... They came with 2200 men of the guard, under their command, fully armed, and surrounded the Yupanqui with the fringe, and gave him the other insignia of sovereignty, as he had now inherited and succeeded his father.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Sarmiento, History of the Incas, ch. 48 (Markham 1907); not verbatim.

O Father! now take rest.' At these words Tupac Inca showed much sadness and covered his head with his mantle, which they call llacolla, a square cloak. He next went, with all his company, to the place where the body of his father was laid, and there he put on mourning.
