summary.zh: 亡魂在塵世停留三夜：第一夜，善念予其慰、惡念予其苦；第二夜，善言予其樂、惡言予其罰；第三夜，善行使其升揚、惡行使其受刑。第三夜黎明時分，亡魂前往阿爾布茲山上的清算之所，過秤後行至「別傳之橋」——義者拾級而升。此橋如多棱之樑：寬面廣達二十七葦之闊，利面薄如剃刀之刃——橋隨亡魂善惡而自行翻轉。

sensitivity.note: Pahlavi doctrinal Q&A rendered as myth; pairs with arda-viraf-vision and chinvat-bridge (different sources). No living community restriction.

passages.text: The reply is this, that it is thus said that the souls of those passed away and of the dead are three nights on earth; and the first night satisfaction comes to them from their good thoughts and vexation from their evil thoughts, the second night come pleasure from their good words and discomfort and punishment from their evil words, and the third night come exaltation from their good deeds and punishment from their evil deeds. And that third night, in the dawn, they go to the place of account on Alburz; the account being rendered they proceed to the bridge, and he who is righteous passes over the bridge on the ascent.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dadestan-i Denig ch. XX, 2-3 (West, SBE 18, 1882); not verbatim.

passages.text: He who is of the wicked falls from the lower end of the bridge, or from the middle of the bridge; he falls head-foremost to hell, and is precipitated unto that grade which is suitable for his wickedness. As it were that bridge is like a beam of many sides, of whose edges there are some which are broad, and there are some which are thin and sharp; its broad sides are so large that its width is twenty-seven reeds, and its sharp sides are so contracted that in thinness it is just like the edge of a razor.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dadestan-i Denig chs. XX, 4, XXI, 2-3 (West, SBE 18, 1882); not verbatim.

passages.text: And when the souls of the righteous and wicked arrive it turns to that side which is suitable to their necessities, through the great glory of the creator and the command of him who takes the just account. Moreover, the bridge becomes a broad bridge for the righteous, as much as the height of nine spears; and for the wicked, that they may fall from it, it becomes sharp as a needle's point, so that they slip down head-foremost into darkness.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dadestan-i Denig ch. XXI, 4-5 (West, SBE 18, 1882); not verbatim.

title.en: Frashegird: Ohrmazd Answers Zarathushtra About the Resurrection
title.zh: 弗拉肖格爾德：馬茲達答復活之問

region.en: Renovated world of the future (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 未來更新之世（象徵性定位）

period: Recorded 9th century CE (Pahlavi; West translation 1880)

source.work: Bundahishn ch. XXX (Pahlavi), trans. E. W. West, SBE 5 (1880)

summary.en: Zarathust asks of Auharmazd: whence does a body form again, which the wind has carried and the water conveyed? And Auharmazd answers: when through me the sky arose from the substance of the ruby, without columns, on the spiritual support of far-compassed light; when by me corn was created so that, scattered about in the earth, it grew again and returned with increase; when by me a son was created and fashioned in the womb of a mother — each one of them, when created by me, was herein more difficult than causing the resurrection; observe that when that which was not was then produced, why is it not possible to produce again that which was?
summary.zh: 查拉圖什特拉問阿胡拉·馬茲達：「被風吹散、被水帶走的屍身，如何重新聚成形體？復活如何發生？」答曰：「天空由紅寶石之質憑無柱的光支柱起；五穀入土復生且結實增多；嬰兒在母腹中成形——這些創造都比復活更難！既然『無』能生『有』，為何不能讓『已有』者復生？」

sensitivity.note: Pahlavi doctrinal text rendered as myth; the Saoshyant-resurrection parallels the Osiris/Jesus resurrection cluster. No living community restriction.

passages.text: After Soshyans comes they prepare the raising of the dead, as it says, that Zarathust asked of Auharmazd thus: whence does a body form again, which the wind has carried and the water conveyed? and how does the resurrection occur? Ahharmazd answered thus: when through me the sky arose from the substance of the ruby, without columns, on the spiritual support of far-compassed light.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Bundahishn ch. XXX, 4-5 (West, SBE 5, 1880); not verbatim.

passages.text: When by me the sun and moon and stars are conducted in the firmament of luminous bodies; when by me corn was created so that, scattered about in the earth, it grew again and returned with increase; when by me colour of various kinds was created in plants; when by me fire was created in plants and other things without combustion.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Bundahishn ch. XXX, 5 (West, SBE 5, 1880); not verbatim.

passages.text: When by me a son was created and fashioned in the womb of a mother, and the structure severally of the skin, nails, blood, feet, eyes, ears, and other things was produced; when by me legs were created for the water, so that it flows away, and the cloud was created which carries the water of the world and rains there where it has a purpose — each one of them, when created by me, was herein more difficult than causing the resurrection. Observe that when that which was not was then produced, why is it not possible to produce again that which was?
passages.note: Paraphrase of Bundahishn ch. XXX, 5-6 (West, SBE 5, 1880); not verbatim.

title.en: The Song of the Reed
title.zh: 蘆笛之歌

region.en: Rumi's pulpit at Konya (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 科尼亞講經台（象徵性定位）

period: Composed 13th century CE, Books I-II (Whinfield translation 1898)

source.work: Masnavi i Ma'navi, trans. E. H. Whinfield (1898), Book I, Song of the Reed

summary.en: Hearken to the reed-flute, how it discourses, complaining of the pains of separation: ever since they tore me from my osier bed my plaintive notes have moved men and women to tears; he who abides far away from his home is ever longing for the day he shall return. The flute tells the tale of love's bloodstained path; it recounts the story of Majnun's love toils. This plaint of the flute is fire, not mere air: let him who lacks this fire be accounted dead! 'Tis the fire of love that inspires the flute — love signifies the strong attraction that draws all creatures back to reunion with their Creator.
summary.zh: 請聽蘆笛的傾訴——它在低訴離別之苦：「自從被人從蘆葦叢中割下，我的嗚咽曾令多少男女落淚；離家越遠的人，越是日夜盼歸。」笛聲訴說著愛的浴血之路，講述瑪傑農的苦戀。這笛聲是火，不是風——無此火者形同死人！那是「愛」之火在吹動笛管——愛，正是將萬物拉回造物主懷抱的強力。

sensitivity.note: Sufi mystical allegory read as mythic narrative (soul separated from Source); interpretive. No living community restriction.

passages.text: Hearken to the reed-flute, how it discourses, complaining of the pains of separation: ever since they tore me from my osier bed, my plaintive notes have moved men and women to tears. I burst my breast, striving to give vent to sighs, and to express the pangs of my yearning for my home. He who abides far away from his home is ever longing for the day he shall return.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Masnavi Book I, Song of the Reed (Whinfield 1898); not verbatim.

passages.text: My wailing is heard in every throng, in concert with them that rejoice and them that weep; each interprets my notes in harmony with his own feelings, but not one fathoms the secrets of my heart. The flute tells the tale of love's bloodstained path; it recounts the story of Majnun's love toils.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Masnavi Book I, Song of the Reed (Whinfield 1898); not verbatim.

passages.text: This plaint of the flute is fire, not mere air: let him who lacks this fire be accounted dead! 'Tis the fire of love that inspires the flute; 'tis the ferment of love that possesses the wine. The flute is the confidant of all unhappy lovers; yea, its strains lay bare my inmost secrets.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Masnavi Book I, Song of the Reed (Whinfield 1898); not verbatim.

title.en: Four Angels and the Handful of Earth
title.zh: 四天使與一把泥土

region.en: Earth of the creation (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 創世之土（象徵性定位）

period: Composed 13th century CE, Books IV-V (Whinfield translation 1898)

source.work: Masnavi i Ma'navi, trans. E. H. Whinfield (1898), Book V, Story VII

summary.en: When the Almighty determined to create mankind to be proved by good and evil, He deputed the angel Gabriel to bring a handful of earth for the purpose of forming Adam's body. But the Earth remonstrated: the man so created would rebel against God and draw down God's curse upon her; and Gabriel returned without taking the handful. Michael was deputed next, and Israfil, and both were diverted from the execution of it. At last God sent Azrail, the angel of death, who, being of sterner disposition, resolutely shut his ears to the Earth's entreaties and brought back the required handful — and for this Azrail was made the angel of death, operating by disease and sickness, a spear in the hand of the Almighty.
summary.zh: 真主欲造人類以驗其善惡，遣加百列取土造亞當之體。大地卻哀求：「此人將叛神，致我受神咒！」加百列憫而空手而歸；米迦勒與伊斯拉菲爾亦相繼受阻。最後真主遣死神天使阿茲拉伊爾——他性剛如鐵，掩耳不聽大地哀告，毅然取土而返。真主遂命他為死亡天使，借疾病施行；他說：「我不過是全能者手中的一桿長矛。」

sensitivity.note: Sufi retelling of the Qur'anic creation of Adam (from Miskat tradition quoted by Rumi); pairs with clay-humans cluster. No living community restriction.

passages.text: When the Almighty determined to create mankind to be proved by good and evil, He deputed the angel Gabriel to bring a handful of earth for the purpose of forming Adam's body. Gabriel accordingly girded his loins and proceeded to the Earth to execute the divine commands. But the Earth, being apprehensive that the man so created would rebel against God and draw down God's curse upon her, remonstrated with Gabriel, and besought him to forbear.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Masnavi Book V, Story VII (Whinfield 1898); not verbatim.

passages.text: At last Gabriel granted her prayer, and returned to heaven without taking the handful of earth. Then God deputed Michael on the same errand, and the Earth made similar excuses to him, and he also listened to her crying, and returned to heaven without taking a handful. Then God sent the angel Israfil on the same errand, and he also was diverted from the execution of it by a divine intimation.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Masnavi Book V, Story VII (Whinfield 1898); not verbatim.

passages.text: At last God sent Azrail, the angel of death, who, being of sterner disposition than the others, resolutely shut his ears to the Earth's entreaties, and brought back the required handful of earth. The Earth pressed him with the argument that God's command to bear away a handful of her substance against her will did not override the other divine command to take pity on suppliants; but Azrail would not listen to her, remarking that he was to be regarded only as a spear in the hand of the Almighty. The moral is, that when any of God's creatures do us a harm, we ought to regard them only as instruments of God, who is the Only Real Agent.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Masnavi Book V, Story VII (Whinfield 1898); not verbatim.

title.en: Moses and the Shepherd
title.zh: 穆薩與牧羊人

region.en: Desert of Sinai (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 西奈曠野（象徵性定位）

period: Composed 13th century CE, Books I-II (Whinfield translation 1898)

source.work: Masnavi i Ma'navi, trans. E. H. Whinfield (1898), Book II, Story VII

summary.en: Moses once heard a shepherd praying as follows: O God, show me where Thou art, that I may become Thy servant; I will clean Thy shoes and comb Thy hair, and sew Thy clothes, and fetch Thee milk. When Moses heard him praying in this senseless manner he rebuked him; the shepherd was abashed, and tore his clothes and fled away into the desert. Then a voice from heaven was heard: O Moses, wherefore have you driven away my servant? Your office is to reconcile my people with me, not to drive them away from me. I regard not the words that are spoken, but the heart that offers them; I do not require fine words, but a burning heart.
summary.zh: 穆薩聽見牧羊人祈禱：「神啊，祢在哪裡？我願為祢擦鞋、梳髮、補衣、取奶！」穆薩斥其愚妄；牧羊人羞慚裂衣、遁入荒漠。天上忽有聲音：「穆薩！你為何趕走我的僕人？你奉命引人歸我，而非驅人離我。我不看言語，只看奉上言語的心；我不求華美之辭，只求一顆熾熱的心。」

sensitivity.note: Sufi parable on religious forms; read as sacred narrative. No living community restriction.

passages.text: Moses once heard a shepherd praying as follows: O God, show me where Thou art, that I may become Thy servant. I will clean Thy shoes and comb Thy hair, and sew Thy clothes, and fetch Thee milk. When Moses heard him praying in this senseless manner, he rebuked him, saying: O foolish one, God is a Spirit, and needs not such gross ministrations as, in your ignorance, you suppose.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Masnavi Book II, Story VII (Whinfield 1898); not verbatim.

passages.text: The shepherd was abashed at his rebuke, and tore his clothes and fled away into the desert. Then a voice from heaven was heard, saying: O Moses, wherefore have you driven away my servant? Your office is to reconcile my people with me, not to drive them away from me. I have given to each race different usages and forms of praising and adoring me; I regard not the words that are spoken, but the heart that offers them. I do not require fine words, but a burning heart.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Masnavi Book II, Story VII (Whinfield 1898); not verbatim.

passages.text: A voice came from God to Moses: why hast thou sent my servant away? What is praiseworthy in thee is blamable in him; what is poison for thee is honey for him. I regard not the outside and the words, I regard the inside and the state of heart. The sect of lovers is distinct from all others; lovers have a religion and a faith of their own.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Masnavi Book II, Story VII (Whinfield 1898); not verbatim.

title.en: The Elephant in the Dark
title.zh: 暗室摸象

region.en: Dark room of the exhibition (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 展示暗室（象徵性定位）

period: Composed 13th century CE, Books I-III (Whinfield translation 1898)

source.work: Masnavi i Ma'navi, trans. E. H. Whinfield (1898), Book III, Story V

summary.en: Some Hindoos were exhibiting an elephant in a dark room, and many people collected to see it. But as the place was too dark to permit them to see the elephant, they all felt it with their hands: one felt its trunk and declared that the beast resembled a water-pipe; another felt its ear, and said it must be a large fan; another its leg, and thought it must be a pillar; another felt its back, and declared the beast must be like a great throne. According to the part which each felt, he gave a different description of the animal. The eye of outward sense is as the palm of a hand; the whole of the object is not grasped in the palm.
summary.zh: 印度人在暗室中展示大象，眾人湧入觀看；因光線不足，人人用手摸象：摸到鼻者說牠像水管，摸到耳者說是蒲扇，摸到腿者說是石柱，摸到背者說是禦座——各憑所觸，議論紛紜。魯米由此警醒世人：「外感官之眼不過如摸象之手掌，手掌之中豈能容下全象？莫執泡沫而忘大海；我們是海上盲人，雖在大洋卻視而不見。」

sensitivity.note: Sufi parable (blind-men-and-elephant, from the Buddhist Udana lineage); cross-tradition parable cluster. No living community restriction.

passages.text: Some Hindoos were exhibiting an elephant in a dark room, and many people collected to see it. But as the place was too dark to permit them to see the elephant, they all felt it with their hands, to gain an idea of what it was like. One felt its trunk, and declared that the beast resembled a water-pipe; another felt its ear, and said it must be a large fan; another its leg, and thought it must be a pillar; another felt its back, and declared the beast must be like a great throne.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Masnavi Book III, Story V (Whinfield 1898); not verbatim.

passages.text: According to the part which each felt, he gave a different description of the animal. The eye of outward sense is as the palm of a hand; the whole of the object is not grasped in the palm. The sea itself is one thing, the foam another; neglect the foam, and regard the sea with your eyes. Waves of foam rise from the sea night and day; you look at the foam ripples and not the mighty sea.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Masnavi Book III, Story V (Whinfield 1898); not verbatim.

passages.text: We, like boats, are tossed hither and thither; we are blind though we are on the bright ocean. Ah! you who are asleep in the boat of the body, you see the water; behold the Water of waters! Under the water you see there is another Water moving it; within the spirit is a Spirit that calls it.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Masnavi Book III, Story V (Whinfield 1898); not verbatim.

title.en: Astyages' Vine-Dream and the Exposed Infant Cyrus
title.zh: 阿斯杜阿該斯之夢與棄嬰居魯士

region.en: Mountains north of Agbatana (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 阿格巴塔納以北山地（象徵性定位）

period: Written c. 430 BCE (Macaulay translation 1890)

source.work: Herodotus, Histories Book 1, trans. G. C. Macaulay (1890), secs. 107-111

summary.en: Astyages son of Kyaxares saw a vision: it seemed to him that from his daughter a vine grew, and this vine overspread the whole of Asia. The Magian interpreters signified that the offspring of his daughter should be king in his room. So when Cyrus was born he called Harpagos, whom he trusted above all the other Medes, and bade him take the child which Mandane bore, and slay it and bury it. Not even if he shall come to be yet more out of his senses, answers Harpagos, will I agree to his will or serve him in such a murder as this; and he sends the child with a herdsman to the mountains most haunted by wild beasts — where the herdsman's wife, her own child just born, will not suffer the exposure.
summary.zh: 米底王阿斯杜阿該斯夢見女兒身上長出葡萄藤，藤蔓竟遮蔽整個亞洲；瑪術士解夢曰：其外孫將取代其王位。居魯士一降生，王便召親信哈爾帕戈斯：「把曼丹妮所生之子帶走殺掉、埋掉！」哈爾帕戈斯不敢親弑，將嬰兒交給牧人，命他拋於豺狼出沒的山中——恰好牧人之妻剛產下一子，二人便以自己的孩子換下王孫，把居魯士養大。

sensitivity.note: Greek historiography recording the Iranian Cyrus-exposure legend (cf. Oedipus/romulus types); read as legend. No living community restriction.

passages.text: Astyages saw another vision. It seemed to him that from his daughter a vine grew, and this vine overspread the whole of Asia. Having seen this vision and delivered it to the interpreters of dreams, he sent for his daughter, being then with child, to come from the land of the Persians. And when she had come he kept watch over her, desiring to destroy that which should be born of her; for the Magian interpreters of dreams signified to him that the offspring of his daughter should be king in his room.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Herodotus 1.108 (Macaulay 1890); not verbatim.

passages.text: Astyages then desiring to guard against this, when Cyrus was born, called Harpagos, a man who was of kin near him and whom he trusted above all the other Medes, and to him he said: take the child which Mandane bore, and carry it to thy house and slay it; and afterwards bury it in whatsoever manner thou thyself desirest. To this he made answer: if it is indeed thy pleasure that this should so be done, my service at least must be fitly rendered.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Herodotus 1.108 (Macaulay 1890); not verbatim.

passages.text: Not according as Astyages enjoined, Harpagos went weeping and told his wife: for not even if he shall come to be yet more out of his senses and more mad than he now is, will I agree to his will or serve him in such a murder as this. And for many reasons I will not slay the child; first because he is a kin to me, and then because Astyages is old and without male issue, and if after he is dead the power shall come through me, does not the greatest of dangers then await me?
passages.note: Paraphrase of Herodotus 1.109 (Macaulay 1890); not verbatim.

passages.text: He sent a messenger to that one of the herdsmen of Astyages who fed his herds on the pastures most suitable for his purpose, and on the mountains most haunted by wild beasts: Astyages bids thee take this child and place it on the most desolate part of the mountains, so that it may perish as quickly as possible. And it came to pass that the herdsman's wife, being every day on the point of bearing a child, by a providential chance brought her child to birth just at that time.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Herodotus 1.110-111 (Macaulay 1890); not verbatim.

title.en: Dareios Wins the Kingdom by the Neighing of His Horse
title.zh: 大流士以馬嘶得國

region.en: Suburb of the Persian city (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 波斯城郊（象徵性定位）

period: Written c. 430 BCE (Macaulay translation 1890)

source.work: Herodotus, Histories Book 1, trans. G. C. Macaulay (1890), secs. 85-88

summary.en: After the seven conspirators had left their assembly, Dareios spoke to Oibares: we have resolved that the man whose horse first neighs at sunrise, when we are mounted upon our horses, he shall be king. Oibares, the clever horse-keeper, ties up in the suburb the mare that the horse of Dareios prefers, and lets the stallion mount her; at dawn, when the six ride past, the horse runs to the place and neighs — and just when the horse had done this there came lightning and thunder from a clear sky. Dareios made a carving in stone with the figure of a man on horseback, and wrote upon it: Dareios son of Hystaspes by the excellence of his horse, and of his horse-keeper Oibares obtained the kingdom of the Persians.
summary.zh: 七人密謀誅殺偽王者議定：翌日日出時「馬先嘶者為王」。馭手奧伊巴雷斯的詭計是：把大流士坐騎鍾愛的牝馬牽到城郊繫好，縱其交合。破曉六人騎馬路過，那馬直奔牝馬嘶鳴——恰在此刻晴空炸雷掣電！眾人認為天意如此，下馬朝拜。大流士登基後立碑刻像：「大流士憑其駿馬與馭手奧伊巴雷斯之力得波斯王位。」

sensitivity.note: Greek historiography of the Darius accession legend; read as historical legend. No living community restriction.

passages.text: When they had left their assembly, Dareios spoke these words: Oibares, we have resolved to do about the kingdom thus, namely that the man whose horse first neighs at sunrise, when we are mounted upon our horses he shall be king. Now therefore, if thou hast any cleverness, contrive that we may obtain this prize, and not any other man. Oibares replied: if, my master, it depends in truth upon this whether thou be king or no, have confidence, for none other shall be king before thee; such charms have I at my command.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Herodotus 1.85 (Macaulay 1890); not verbatim.

passages.text: Oibares therefore hearing this did as follows: when night was coming on he took one of the mares, namely that one which the horse of Dareios preferred, and this he led into the suburb of the city and tied her up; then he brought to her the horse of Dareios. Now at dawn of day the six came to the place as they had agreed, riding upon their horses; and when they came near the place where the mare had been tied up on the former night, the horse of Dareios ran up to the place and neighed.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Herodotus 1.85-86 (Macaulay 1890); not verbatim.

passages.text: Just when the horse had done this, there came lightning and thunder from a clear sky; and the happening of these things to Dareios consummated his claim, for they seemed to have come to pass by some design, and the others leapt down from their horses and did obeisance to Dareios. He caused to be a carving in stone, and in it the figure of a man on horseback, writing to this effect: Dareios son of Hystaspes by the excellence of his horse, and of his horse-keeper Oibares obtained the kingdom of the Persians.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Herodotus 1.86-88 (Macaulay 1890); not verbatim.

title.en: Tomyris Gives Cyrus His Fill of Blood
title.zh: 托米麗司血祭居魯士

region.en: River Araxes, land of the Massagetai (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 阿拉克塞斯河畔（象徵性定位）

period: Written c. 430 BCE (Macaulay translation 1890)

source.work: Herodotus, Histories Book 1, trans. G. C. Macaulay (1890), secs. 211-214

summary.en: Tomyris, queen of the Massagetai, sends a herald when her son Spargapises is taken by the wine-snare of the Persians: Cyrus, insatiable of blood, restore to me my son and depart from this land without penalty; but if thou shalt not do so, I swear to thee by the Sun, who is lord of the Massagetai, that surely I will give thee thy fill of blood, insatiable as thou art. Cyrus makes no account of her words; her son, when the wine left him, puts himself to death; Tomyris gathers all her power and joins battle, and of the army of Cyrus the greater part is destroyed and Cyrus himself falls, and Tomyris fills a skin with human blood and dips the head of Cyrus in it.
summary.zh: 瑪薩革泰女王托米麗司之子被波斯人的「酒計」所擒。她遣使警告：「嗜血的居魯士啊，還我兒子、退出此土；否則我以瑪薩革泰的主宰太陽起誓——定叫你飲血到足！」居魯士不納其言；王子醒酒後自盡。女王傾全國之兵決戰，波斯大軍盡墨、居魯士陣亡。托米麗司以人血灌滿皮囊，將居魯士之首浸入其中——「讓你飲個夠！」

sensitivity.note: Greek historiography of Cyrus' death legend; Tomyris became a Persian literary figure. No living community restriction.

passages.text: Seeing the feast that was set forth, when the Massagetai had overcome their enemies they lay down and feasted, and being satiated with food and wine they went to sleep. Then the Persians came upon them and slew many of them, and took alive many more even than they slew, and among these the son of the queen Tomyris, who was leading the army of the Massagetai; and his name was Spargapises.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Herodotus 1.211 (Macaulay 1890); not verbatim.

passages.text: She then sent a herald to Cyrus and said: Cyrus, insatiable of blood, be not elated with pride by this which has come to pass, because with that fruit of the vine, with which ye fill yourselves and become so mad, because setting a snare with such a drug as this thou didst overcome my son, and not by valour in fight. Now therefore receive the word which I utter: restore to me my son and depart from this land without penalty; but if thou shalt not do so, I swear to thee by the Sun, who is lord of the Massagetai, that surely I will give thee thy fill of blood, insatiable as thou art.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Herodotus 1.212 (Macaulay 1890); not verbatim.

passages.text: The son of the queen Tomyris, when the wine left him and he learnt in what evil case he was, entreated Cyrus that he might be loosed from his chains and gained his request, and then so soon as he was loosed and had got power over his hands he put himself to death. Tomyris, as Cyrus did not listen to her, gathered together all her power and joined battle, and of the army of Cyrus the greater part was destroyed, and Cyrus himself fell.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Herodotus 1.213-214 (Macaulay 1890); not verbatim.

title.en: The Persians' Sacrifices and the Magian Chant
title.zh: 波斯人的祭祀與瑪術士頌歌

region.en: Mountain heights of sacrifice (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 祭祀山巔（象徵性定位）

period: Written c. 430 BCE (Macaulay translation 1890)

source.work: Herodotus, Histories Book 1, trans. G. C. Macaulay (1890), secs. 131-133

summary.en: Images and temples and altars they do not account it lawful to erect; nay, they even charge with folly those who do these things, because they do not account the gods to be in the likeness of men. But it is their wont to perform sacrifices to Zeus going up to the most lofty of the mountains, and the whole circle of the heavens they call Zeus: and they sacrifice to the Sun and the Moon and the Earth, to Fire and to Water and to the Winds. When a man wishes to sacrifice, he leads the animal to an unpolluted place and calls upon the god, having his tiara wreathed with myrtle; he prays not for himself alone, but that it may be well with all the Persians and with the king; and when he has boiled the flesh, a Magian man stands by and chants over them a theogony, seeing that without a Magian it is not lawful for them to make sacrifices.
summary.zh: 波斯人不許立神像、建廟壇，斥其為愚妄——因神不具人形。他們登高山祭「宙斯」（即蒼穹之環），祭太陽、月亮、大地、火、水與風。獻祭者於潔淨之地呼神名、頭戴桃金娘冠冠冕，只為「全體波斯人與君王」祈福；煮肉陳於青草之上，由瑪術士誦唱神譜頌歌——無瑪術士在場，祭祀即屬非法。

sensitivity.note: Greek ethnographic account of Persian ritual (Zeus = Ahura Mazda, Mitra = Anahita?); read as classical witness. No living community restriction.

passages.text: Images and temples and altars they do not account it lawful to erect, nay they even charge with folly those who do these things; and this, as it seems to me, because they do not account the gods to be in the likeness of men, as do the Hellenes. But it is their wont to perform sacrifices to Zeus going up to the most lofty of the mountains, and the whole circle of the heavens they call Zeus: and they sacrifice to the Sun and the Moon and the Earth, to Fire and to Water and to the Winds.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Herodotus 1.131 (Macaulay 1890); not verbatim.

passages.text: When a man wishes to sacrifice to any one of the gods, he leads the animal for sacrifice to an unpolluted place and calls upon the god, having his tiara wreathed round generally with a branch of myrtle. For himself alone separately the man who sacrifices may not request good things in his prayer, but he prays that it may be well with all the Persians and with the king.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Herodotus 1.132 (Macaulay 1890); not verbatim.

passages.text: And when he has cut up the victim into pieces and boiled the flesh, he spreads a layer of the freshest grass and especially clover, upon which he places forthwith all the pieces of flesh; and when he has placed them in order, a Magian man stands by them and chants over them a theogony, seeing that without a Magian it is not lawful for them to make sacrifices. Of all days their wont is to honour most that on which they were born; and to wine-drinking they are very much given.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Herodotus 1.132-133 (Macaulay 1890); not verbatim.

title.en: The Parsi Flight to Sanjan and the Sixteen Schloks
title.zh: 帕西人渡海至桑詹與十六讚頌

region.en: Sanjan, coast of Gujarat (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 古吉拉特桑詹海岸（象徵性定位）

period: Recorded 15th-17th century CE (Qissa-i Sanjan; Karaka translation 1884)

source.work: Qissa-i Sanjan, in D. F. Karaka, History of the Parsis, vol. I (1884), ch. I

summary.en: Fleeing Persia after the Arab conquest rather than abandon the faith of their fathers, the Parsis make themselves exiles for ever; in a storm at sea they offer up a prayer to the throne of the Most High, and the storm abates and a gentle gale carries them in safety to Sanjan, where they land about the year 716. The dastur explains their sufferings to the liberal chief Jadi Rana, and the most learned among them prepare sixteen schloks or distichs in which they briefly describe the tenets of their religion: we are worshippers of Ahura Mazda and the sun and the five elements; we wear the sacred garment, the sudra or shirt, the kusti or cincture for the loins.
summary.zh: 阿拉伯人征服波斯後，帕西人不肯背棄祖傳信仰，寧為萬世流亡。海上風暴中，他們向至高者禱告，風浪頓息，和風將船隊平安送抵桑詹（約公元716年）。祭司向寬仁的酋長賈迪·拉納陳情；族中賢者遂作十六聯頌詩概括其教義：「我們崇奉阿胡拉·馬茲達、太陽與五行；我們穿聖衣——聖衫與腰間聖帶。」

sensitivity.note: Living-tradition narrative (Parsi community charter myth); recorded respectfully from published 19th-century translation. No restricted content.

passages.text: Rather than abandon the faith they had inherited from their fathers, they had voluntarily made themselves exiles for ever from the land that gave them birth. In their helplessness they called to mind Him who is the author of all good, the Preserver, Supporter, and Cherisher of the poor and the distressed: deliver us, O Merciful Providence, from this trouble, and lead us to the right path, that we may escape from this sea to the shores of India; and we promise, O Lord, to kindle on high the flame sacred to Thee in grateful remembrance of Thy kindness and protection.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Qissa-i Sanjan, in Karaka, History of the Parsis I, ch. 1 (1884); not verbatim.

passages.text: We cannot doubt that this prayer of faith was heard, for the storm abated, and a gentle gale carried them in safety to Sanjan, some twenty-five miles south of Daman, where they landed about the year 716. The territory of Sanjan was then under the rule of a wise and liberal chief named Jadi Rana, to whom a venerable dastur or high priest of the Parsis was sent, with suitable presents, in order to ascertain from him the terms on which they would be permitted to land.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Qissa-i Sanjan, in Karaka, History of the Parsis I, ch. 1 (1884); not verbatim.

passages.text: The most learned among them prepared sixteen schloks or distichs, in which they briefly described the tenets of their religion and their mode of worship: we are worshippers of Ahura Mazda and the sun and the five elements; we observe silence while bathing, praying, making offerings to fire, and eating; we wear the sacred garment, the sudra or shirt, the kusti or cincture for the loins, and the cap of two folds. Consequently, Sanjan became the adopted country of the Parsis.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Qissa-i Sanjan, in Karaka, History of the Parsis I, ch. 1 (1884); not verbatim.

title.en: Kais and Laili in the Schoolroom
title.zh: 凱斯與蕾莉同窗初戀

region.en: School of the Arab shaikhs (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 阿拉伯酋長學塾（象徵性定位）

period: Composed 12th century CE (Atkinson translation 1836)

source.work: Nizami, Laili and Majnun, trans. J. Atkinson (1836), Canto I

summary.en: In the school of the shaikhs of each tribe, Kais assiduously drew attainments and scattered pearls from lips of ruby hue; and there, of different tribe and gentle mien, a lovely maid of tender years was seen: her richly flowing locks were black as night, and Laili she was called. One single glance the nerves to frenzy wrought; and, when o'er Kais affection's blushing rose diffused its sweetness, from him fled repose. Love conquered both; they never dreamt to part; and, while the rest were poring o'er their books, they pensive mused, and read each other's looks: their only taste was love, and writing ghazels to each other's eyes.
summary.zh: 各族酋長的學塾中，凱斯勤學善辯、口吐珠璣；另有一位異族的窈窕少女——秀髮如夜，人稱蕾莉。「一瞥便令心神狂亂」；當愛情的玫瑰在凱斯心中綻放，安寧便棄他而去。二人相愛，從未想過分離；同窗苦讀時，他們只默默相視——「他們唯一的功課，就是為彼此的眼睛寫抒情詩。」

sensitivity.note: Epic literary source; the Arab romance Persianised by Nizami. No living community restriction.

passages.text: Thence his attainments Kais assiduous drew, and scattered pearls from lips of ruby hue; and there, of different tribe and gentle mien, a lovely maid of tender years was seen: her mental powers an early bloom displayed. Her richly flowing locks were black as night, and Laili she was called, that heart's delight: one single glance the nerves to frenzy wrought; one single glance bewildered every thought.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Nizami, Laili and Majnun (Atkinson 1836), Canto I; not verbatim.

passages.text: Soon mutual pleasure warmed each other's heart; love conquered both, they never dreamt to part; and, while the rest were poring o'er their books, they pensive mused, and read each other's looks: while others various climes in books explored, both idly sat, adorer and adored. Science for them had now no charms to boast; their only taste was love, and love's sweet ties, and writing ghazels to each other's eyes.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Nizami, Laili and Majnun (Atkinson 1836), Canto I; not verbatim.

passages.text: Immersed in love so deep, they hoped suspicion would be lulled asleep, and none be conscious of their amorous state; they hoped that none with prying eye, and gossip tongue invidiously, might to the busy world its truth relate. By worldly prudence uncontrolled, their every glance their feelings told; for true love never yet had skill to veil impassioned looks at will.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Nizami, Laili and Majnun (Atkinson 1836), Canto I; not verbatim.

title.en: Majnun in the Cave and His Father's Grave
title.zh: 瑪傑農穴居與亡父之墓

region.en: Rocky cave of Najd (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 納季德岩穴（象徵性定位）

period: Composed 12th century CE (Atkinson translation 1836)

source.work: Nizami, Laili and Majnun, trans. J. Atkinson (1836), Cantos V-VI

summary.en: To me the world is swallowed up: I see nothing but Laili, answers Majnun to his father's counsel in the cave; all is lost to me, save her bright image — father, mother, home, all buried in impenetrable gloom. Syd Omai, with unutterable grief, gazed on his son and parted from that dismal cave, wrapt in deepest anguish — but 'twas, alas, to his expected grave: gently he sank, by age and grief oppressed, from this vain world to that of endless rest. Majnun hears the sad tale, falls upon the earth insensible, and never rested night or day till he had reached the sad spot where lay his father's bones: his arms around the grave he flung, and to the earth delirious clung.
summary.zh: 岩穴中，父親勸子回頭；瑪傑農答：「世界於我已空無一物——除蕾莉倩影，父母家園盡埋於不透光的黑暗！」老父西德·歐邁悲不自勝，踉蹌離穴歸家——竟一臥不起，溘然長逝。噩耗傳來，瑪傑農撲地昏厥，日夜狂奔至亡父墳前，雙臂環抱墓碑、緊抓塵土，以懺悔之淚澆灑聖遺。

sensitivity.note: Epic literary source; the mad lover's withdrawal (majnun = possessed). No living community restriction.

passages.text: Thy counsel, father, is the wisest, best, and I would gladly to thy wish conform: but what am I? a helpless wretch, a worm, without the power to do what I approve, enslaved, the victim of almighty love. To me the world is swallowed up: I see nothing but Laili; all is lost to me, save her bright image: father, mother, home, all buried in impenetrable gloom, beyond my feeling.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Nizami, Laili and Majnun (Atkinson 1836), Canto V; not verbatim.

passages.text: Syd Omai, with unutterable grief, gazed on his son, whose sorrows mocked relief; and, hopeless, wretched, every thought resigned that once was balm and comfort to his mind. Then, showering blessings o'er his offspring's head, groaning, he parted from that dismal cave, and, wrapt in deepest anguish, homeward sped; but 'twas, alas, to his expected grave: gently he sank, by age and grief oppressed, from this vain world, to that of endless rest.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Nizami, Laili and Majnun (Atkinson 1836), Canto V; not verbatim.

passages.text: He fell upon the earth insensible, and, grovelling, with a frantic air, his bosom beat, he tore his hair, and never rested, night or day, till he had, wandering far away, reached the sad spot where peaceful lay his father's bones. His arms around the grave he flung, and to the earth delirious clung; grasping the ashes of the dead, he cast them o'er his prostrate head, and, with repentant tears, bedewed the holy relics round him strewed.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Nizami, Laili and Majnun (Atkinson 1836), Canto VI; not verbatim.

title.en: The Fravashis Hold Up the World
title.zh: 弗拉瓦希守護世界

region.en: Sea Vouru-Kasha (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 烏魯卡沙海（象徵性定位）

period: Recorded in the Avesta, c. 6th-4th century BCE (Darmesteter translation 1883)

source.work: Farvardin Yasht (Zend-Avesta Part II), trans. J. Darmesteter, SBE 23 (1883)

summary.en: Through their brightness and glory, O Zarathustra! I maintain the wide earth made by Ahura, the large and broad earth, that bears so much that is fine, that bears all the bodily world, the live and the dead, and the high mountains rich in pastures and waters. Through their brightness and glory I maintain in the womb the child that has been conceived, so that it does not die from the assaults of Vidotu. Had not the awful Fravashis of the faithful given help unto me, those animals and men of mine would not subsist; strength would belong to the Druj, the dominion would belong to the Druj, the material world would belong to the Druj.
summary.zh: 憑弗拉瓦希（守護靈）之光輝榮耀——阿胡拉所造的寬廣大地、承載生者與亡者的高山草場才得以持立；胎中嬰兒才不致死於死神之手。若無忠信者的守護靈相助，牲畜與人類便不能存立——力量將歸惡魔德魯吉，王權將歸德魯吉，物質世界將歸德魯吉！

sensitivity.note: Avestan liturgical text; the Fravashis are the guardian-souls (Darmesteter compares the Hindu Pitrs). No living community restriction.

passages.text: Through their brightness and glory, O Zarathustra! I maintain the wide earth made by Ahura, the large and broad earth, that bears so much that is fine, that bears all the bodily world, the live and the dead, and the high mountains, rich in pastures and waters; upon which run the many streams and rivers; upon which the many kinds of plants grow up from the ground, to nourish animals and men, and to help the faithful.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Farvardin Yasht 9-10 (Darmesteter, SBE 23, 1883); not verbatim.

passages.text: Through their brightness and glory, O Zarathustra! I maintain in the womb the child that has been conceived, so that it does not die from the assaults of Vidotu, and I develop in it the bones, the hair, the entrails, the feet, and the sexual organs.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Farvardin Yasht 11 (Darmesteter, SBE 23, 1883); not verbatim.

passages.text: Had not the awful Fravashis of the faithful given help unto me, those animals and men of mine, of which there are such excellent kinds, would not subsist; strength would belong to the Druj, the dominion would belong to the Druj, the material world would belong to the Druj. Between the earth and the sky the immaterial creatures would be harassed by the Druj; and never afterwards would Angra-Mainyu give way to the blows of Spenta-Mainyu.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Farvardin Yasht 12-13 (Darmesteter, SBE 23, 1883); not verbatim.

title.en: Nizami's Tale of Sikandar's Birth
title.zh: 尼扎米筆下的亞歷山大誕生

region.en: Roads of Rum (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 羅姆國土（象徵性定位）

period: Composed c. 1200 CE (Clarke translation 1881)

source.work: Nizami, The Sikandar Nama e Bara, trans. H. Wilberforce Clarke (1881), Canto XV

summary.en: In this tale of Sikandar's birth are many disputes, says Nizami; from the sages of Rum thus it came: that of that land and clime, the wife of a devotee became helpless on the day of bringing forth; she deposited her burden in a desolate place and died, saying: I know not who will cherish thee; what wild beast will devour thee. King Faylikus, game-overthrowing, advanced toward that woman; he beheld a woman dead in that pathway, at her feet a child, head uplifted; from want of the mother's milk the child sucked its own finger. He took up the child from the dust of the road — and, by wisdom and judgment, King of the World he became, from Kaf to Kaf territory-conqueror.
summary.zh: 關於亞歷山大的誕生眾說紛紜，尼扎米取羅馬賢者之說：一位苦行僧之妻臨產無助，把嬰孩棄於荒野而亡，臨終悲呼：「誰來撫養你？哪只野獸會吞掉你？」英武的菲萊庫斯王行經此路，見產婦倒斃道上、腳邊嬰孩仰首吮指；他自塵埃抱起嬰兒——這孩子日後憑智慧與英斷，成為「自卡夫山至卡夫山」的征服者、天下之王。

sensitivity.note: Epic literary source; Nizami's Iqbal-nama version of Alexander's birth legend. No living community restriction.

passages.text: In this tale of Sikandar's birth are many disputes: my ear is intent on everyone's speech. From the sages of Rum thus it came, that of that land and clime, the wife of a devotee became helpless on the day of bringing forth; she became a wanderer from her city and husband. When her time of burden-casting came near, the pang of delivery became strong upon her.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Nizami, Sikandar Nama (Clarke 1881), Canto XV; not verbatim.

passages.text: She deposited her burden in a desolate place, and died; she suffered grief for the child and resigned her life to God, saying: I know not who will cherish thee; what wild beast will devour thee. Of this, news none heard, how the Omnipotent would cherish him in His bosom: what treasures He would draw within his load; what fortune He would draw into his bosom. When the woman died, that child remained friendless.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Nizami, Sikandar Nama (Clarke 1881), Canto XV; not verbatim.

passages.text: From the enjoyment of the plain, King Faylikus advanced, game-overthrowing, towards that woman. He beheld a woman dead in that pathway: at her feet a child, head uplifted. From want of the mother's milk, the child sucked its own finger, and bit its own thumb in grief for its mother. He took up the child from the dust of the road — and, by wisdom and judgment, King of the World he became, from Kaf to Kaf territory-conqueror.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Nizami, Sikandar Nama (Clarke 1881), Canto XV; not verbatim.

title.en: Darab's Son and Sikandar's Ambition
title.zh: 大流士與亞歷山大爭鋒

region.en: Field between Iran and Rum (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 伊朗與羅姆之間的戰場（象徵性定位）

period: Composed c. 1010 CE (Warner translation 1905)

source.work: Firdausi, Shahnama, trans. A. G. & E. Warner (1905), vol. VI, Dara secs. 1-6

summary.en: Dara harangued the chiefs and took order for the realm; and when Failakus died and Sikandar acceded to the throne of Rum, Sikandar went as his own ambassador to Dara, demanding tribute and submission. Dara fought with Sikandar and was worsted; the hosts fought a second time; and when Sikandar fought with Dara the third time, Dara fled to Kirman, his fortune sunk, the war-cry rising from both sides and the troops having little rest.
summary.zh: 大流士整軍經武；菲萊庫斯死後亞歷山大繼羅馬王位，竟親作使節赴波斯索貢。三度交鋒，大流士屢戰屢敗，終棄都奔往克爾曼——兩軍吶喊、征塵蔽日，士卒疲於奔命。

sensitivity.note: Epic literary source; the Shahnama's Alexander-as-Persian-prince romance. No living community restriction.

passages.text: Sikandar went as his own ambassador to Dara, demanding tribute and submission; and Dara harangued the chiefs and took order for the realm. The two met in the field, and Dara fought with Sikandar and was worsted. Dara fought with Sikandar the second time; and when Sikandar fought with Dara the third time, and Dara fled to Kirman, the war-cry rose from both sides and the troops had little rest. Sikandar ranged his host, the air grew dark, earth viewless.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Firdausi, Shahnama, Dara secs. 1-4 (Warner 1905); not verbatim. / Paraphrase of Firdausi, Shahnama, Dara secs. 5-6 (Warner 1905); not verbatim.

title.en: Nizami on Dara's Murder and Sikandar's Victory
title.zh: 尼扎米詠大流士之弑

region.en: Night-camp of the two hosts (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 兩軍夜營（象徵性定位）

period: Composed c. 1200 CE (Clarke translation 1881)

source.work: Nizami, The Sikandar Nama e Bara, trans. H. Wilberforce Clarke (1881), Canto XXX

summary.en: The representer of the verse of this history uttered words according to the manner of truthful ones: when the fire of the bright day passed away the vault swiftly revolving became full of the smoke of darkness. Both armies secretly prayer-uttering, saying: would that to-night had been long, perhaps its length would have made delay, the battle-day would have appeared with great delay. Then Dara's own officers abandoned the right due to favours of obligation to the king; they took up the pursuit of slaying the king — and when the thief took the ruby of the sun, the world pressed its foot in ruby-seeking: the murderer of Dara won no glory, and the kingdom passed to Sikandar.
summary.zh: 尼扎米寫道：白日之火熄滅、夜幕如煙籠罩穹廬；兩軍各自密禱：「但願今夜長些，好讓決戰之日遲些來臨！」然而大流士麾下重臣竟背棄君恩、陰謀弑主——「竊賊竊走紅寶石般的落日」——弑君者未得榮耀，江山終歸亞歷山大。

sensitivity.note: Epic literary source; Nizami's moralising version of the regicide. No living community restriction.

passages.text: The representer of the verse of this history uttered words according to the manner of true ones, saying: when the fire of the bright day passed away, the vault swiftly revolving became full of the smoke of the darkness of night. Night established the ornament of the moon; the light of the moon in the dark shade of night was a wonderful thing.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Nizami, Sikandar Nama (Clarke 1881), Canto XXX; not verbatim.

passages.text: Both armies secretly prayer-uttering, saying: would that to-night had been long; perhaps its length would have made delay; the battle-day would have appeared with great delay. By the coming and going of the watchman the night bird rested not; from fear of the raging elephant many a sleeper leaped from sleep.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Nizami, Sikandar Nama (Clarke 1881), Canto XXX; not verbatim.

passages.text: They abandoned the right due to favours of obligation to the king; they took up the pursuit of slaying the king. When the thief took the ruby of the sun, the world pressed its foot in ruby-seeking; with theft of the sun they seized the moon, saying it took away that pure jewel, the setting sun.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Nizami, Sikandar Nama (Clarke 1881), Canto XXX; not verbatim.

title.en: How the World Began: Sky Woman's Fall and the Two Minds
title.zh: 世界之肇始：天女墜落與兩位心智

region.en: Cattaraugus Seneca Reservation, New York (collection pin for Seneca oral tales)
region.zh: 紐約州卡塔勞格斯塞內卡保留地（塞內卡口傳故事的採集定位）

period: Recorded 1900s-1922 from Seneca informants on the Cattaraugus Reservation (Parker 1923)

source.archive: Internet Archive (Buffalo Historical Society Publications, vol. 27)
source.work: A. C. Parker, Seneca Myths and Folk Tales, ch. IV tale 1, 'How the World Began' (1923)

summary.en: In the sky world the Ancient One uproots the great tree at his dream's command and thrusts his pregnant wife through the hole; as she falls, the Fire Beast gives her corn, mortar, pot and pestle, and the water creatures receive her on the great turtle's back, where muskrat brings up earth. Her daughter dies giving birth to twins, and from her grave spring the beans, squash, corn and tobacco; Good Mind finishes the world, releases the animals from the bags of life, and seals his destructive brother Tawiskaron in the cave before molding the first men from clay.
summary.zh: 在天上世界中，遠古者依夢境之命連根拔起大樹，將懷孕的妻子推入洞中；她墜落時，火獸賜她玉米、臼、缽與杵，水中眾獸以巨龜之背承接她，麝鼠潛水取土。其女產下雙生而死，墓上生出豆、南瓜、玉米與菸草；善心者完成世界，自生命之袋釋出百獸，將其破壞之弟塔威斯卡隆封入洞穴，再以黏土捏塑最早的人類。

language: Seneca oral tradition told in English
canonical_translation: Arthur C. Parker's English text (1923)

narrative.en:
Parker's fullest Seneca account of creation opens above the sky. Beyond the dome is another world, a floating land where the great chief and his celestial people live around a central tree of light whose roots run in four directions and whose luminous blossom fills the air with the perfume of burning tobacco. Dreaming, the Ancient One desires a maiden and marries her; she conceives from his potent breath, and his anger at finding her already with child drives the plot. Another dream commands him to uproot the celestial tree; his people try and fail, he uproots it himself, and leads his wife Iagen'tci (the Sky Woman) to peer into the hole. Pushed through it in rage, she snatches as she falls a handful of seeds and the tobacco leaf, and drops through the crust of the sky world.

Below is an unformed sea. As she falls, a fire-emitting beast named Gaa'siohdie't'ha' hands her a small pot, a corn mortar, a pestle, a marrow bone and an ear of corn, with the grim promise that all who eat will one day see him last of all. The water creatures, among them the spirits of Wind, the Defending Face, Thunder and Heavy Night, take council: ducks interlace their wings to receive her, the great turtle rises from below to offer his back, and muskrat alone touches bottom, smearing a little earth on the shell, which grows until it is an island world. The woman shakes out the seeds and sets the root she held, and a new tree of light rises over the turtle island.

Her daughter grows up swinging on a vine, laughs as if embraced, and bears twins, one kind and one warty and savage who tears his way out through his mother's side, killing her. From the daughter's grave, tended by Good Mind, sprout the stringed potato, beans, squash, corn and tobacco: the Three Sisters and the sacred plant grow out of a death. Grandmother Sky Woman then names the animals when Good Mind releases them from the bags of life his father gave him after his four-fold ordeal on the mountain of the east (he casts the cliff, swims the cataract, wrestles Wind and endures flame), and anoints the fat ones in a pool of oil. His jealous brother Tawiskaron (Evil Mind, Flint) follows behind, breeding thorns, poison plants and slimes, and twice attacks Good Mind with cat-tail flags and deer horns. Good Mind wins the final fight and banishes him to the cave with all the enchanted beasts, where he still gives orders. The whirlwind Great Defender is mastered with the mountain-moving test and his bent, twisted face becomes the likeness carved for the False Face Society; Thunder is engaged to slay whatever escapes the cave. At last Good Mind molds men and women of clay in his own image, teaches them hunting, fishing and the incense of tobacco, and departs up the sky road with the first beings.

The story is the anchor record of the Haudenosaunee cosmos: a matrilineal world built downward from a violated marriage and upward from a grave, with the twin polarity (Good Mind / Flint) that the Maya Hero Twins, the Navajo Changing-Bear Twins and countless dual-creator systems share. Its ritual harvest is enormous: corn as milk, tobacco as speech to the Creator, the False Face masks as Defender's contract, the cave as the residence of the Destroyer.

functions: Cosmogony: explains the earth as Turtle Island built by co-operative water beings
Agricultural charter: corn, beans, squash and tobacco grow from the murdered daughter's grave
Ritual charter: tobacco incense, False Face carving and Thunder's pest-control all contracted in the tale
Dualistic ethics: Good Mind finishes and beautifies, Flint spoils; sickness and mischief trace to the cave

variants.name: Parker's footnote variant (Seneca)
variants.text_tradition: A. C. Parker, Seneca Myths and Folk Tales, footnote to tale 1
variants.summary: In another version the sky chief is killed and hidden in the tree's trunk; a rival chief marries his daughter, and it is the bride who demands the tree be uprooted to hunt for her father's body - Parker compares the Osiris motif.

variants.name: Onondaga version (Hewitt, Iroquoian Cosmology)
variants.text_tradition: J. N. B. Hewitt, Iroquoian Cosmology (BAE Ann. Rep. 21, 1904), Simeon Gibson informant
variants.summary: Long Onondaga recension: Sky Woman's fall, the twins (Holder of the Heavens vs. Flint), their contests over animals and the final duel at the great tree.

variants.name: Tuscarora written version (Cusick 1828)
variants.text_tradition: David Cusick, Sketches of the Ancient History of the Six Nations
variants.summary: Early Tuscarora literary rendering of the same cycle: woman descending, turtle island, Good and Bad Minds.
