Testing her, he flourished his hands on high while trampling the wheat with his feet; she answered that as his hands flourished on high, so ought his feet. Praised for her earrings and armlets, she said both had little oxen; asked where her father had gone, she said to make two roads out of one by laying thorn-twigs across the road; her mother, to fetch seeds from the fruits of the field.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Schiefner/Ralston, Mahaushadha and Visakha (1882); not verbatim.

passages.text: She pointed him a crooked road to the Kaksha forest and slipped away to a tank, where she took off her clothes, shut one eye, bowed on one side, and called directions after him - the hand used in eating shows the way. Recognized from afar and greeted in riddling verse, she answered in kind. Driven from the village head-men when he blurted out his proposal - they threatened to have him devoured by fierce dogs - he was coached by the maiden herself in the order of wooing: draw near, gain favor, give hospitality and organize an entertainment, and only then bring forward the desire. So he feasted the head-men and won her.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Schiefner/Ralston, Mahaushadha and Visakha (1882); not verbatim.

passages.text: On the road home a Brahman's wife refused him shelter - and admitted another man. When her husband returned she hid her visitor in a basket; pressed to pour his barley into that same basket, she invented one excuse after another until, terrified, she sent for the lover's father, who bought the 'treasure' basket for five hundred gold pieces and had it carried off by a strong man. Mahaushadha lighted a lamp beside the basket and let them go.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Schiefner/Ralston, Mahaushadha and Visakha (1882); not verbatim.

passages.text: He paid a hundred gold pieces to warn the householder about his wife's character, and sent the remaining four hundred to Visakha with a missive revealing his true name: chief minister of the king of Videha, no Brahman, come only to carry out his quest. When the delivering Brahman handed over three hundred of the pieces, Visakha looked under the bed at once - 'men have come from the court with orders to seize the malefactor' - and caught him by driving a peg into the clay she asked him to test his foot in, holding him for the fourth hundred.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Schiefner/Ralston, Mahaushadha and Visakha (1882); not verbatim.

title.en: The Giant and the Princess Who Loved Him
title.zh: 巨人與愛上巨人的公主

region.en: Banks of the Kanawage (St. Lawrence River), traditional Tuscarora geography
region.zh: 卡納瓦吉河（聖勞倫斯河）沿岸，塔斯卡洛拉傳統地理

period: Written 1825 by David Cusick (Tuscarora), Sketches of the Ancient History of the Six Nations

source.work: David Cusick, Sketches of the Ancient History of the Six Nations, Part II (1825/1848)

summary.en: The northern giants Ronnongwetowanca raid the Eagwehoewe towns while the warriors are away. A family of six princes loses their sister to the raiders; she proves to have fallen in love with the giant. The eldest brother is welcomed, piped and sung to sleep, then murdered on the bed. The stoutest brother, Donhtonha, places faint lights above his eyelids to counterfeit wakeful eyes, exposes the treachery, kills and burns the giant - whose spirit becomes an eastern star - while the despairing sister's spirit becomes a northern star.
summary.zh: 北方巨人羅農威托萬卡趁戰士外出時劫掠伊格威荷威人的城鎮。六位王子之家失其妹；她竟已愛上巨人。長兄受到煙斗與歌聲的款待，卻在床上被殺。最勇壯的兄長頓托哈以微光置於眼瞼之上偽裝清醒之眼，識破詭計，殺巨並焚其屋——巨人精魂化為東方之星；悲傷絕望的公主精魂則化為北方之星。

sensitivity.note: Earliest Native-authored (Tuscarora) prose version of these traditions, 1825; public domain. Cusick's 'ancient history' blends myth and pseudo-chronology.

passages.text: The Eagwehoewe people on the river Kanawage could not enjoy tranquility, as they were invaded by the giants called Ronnongwetowanca, who came from the north; their mode of attack was slily, and they took advantage when the warriors were absent from the town, plundering the houses and making captives. A family of princes lived near the river, with six brothers and a sister; one time while the brothers went out a day's hunt, the giant made vigorous attack and the woman became a prey to the invader.
passages.note: Condensed from Cusick 1825, Part II; not verbatim.

passages.text: The eldest brother pursued the enemy's traces three days to the giant's residence, and saw his sister gathering sticks near the house; but she retired as he approached, proving by her conduct that she had fallen in love with the giant. Entering at dusk he was received with favorable terms; the giant offered his pipe as a tribute of respect, sang songs part of the night, and when the prince slept killed him on the bed and deposited the body in a cave where he stored the carcasses. Seven days later the youngest brother, Donhtonha, the stoutest and most ferocious looking fellow, came seeking his brother; again the singing began - but the prince had procured pieces of wood that made a faint light and put them above his eyelids, so that though asleep his eyes appeared continually awake.
passages.note: Condensed from Cusick 1825, Part II; not verbatim.

passages.text: At daybreak Donhtonha attacked the giant; after a severe conflict the giant was killed and burnt in the ruins of his house, but his spirit fled to heaven and changed into one of the eastern stars. His sister, grieving for her deceased husband, fled to the wilderness and lamented until she died in despair, and her spirit also became one of the northern stars. After the conquest Donhtonha found the remains of his brother, wept over them, and burnt them to ashes.
passages.note: Condensed from Cusick 1825, Part II; not verbatim.

title.en: Yatatonwatea's Flight and the End of the Giants
title.zh: 亞塔托瓦提亞的逃亡與巨人之終結

region.en: Kanawage (St. Lawrence River) country, traditional Tuscarora geography
region.zh: 卡納瓦吉（聖勞倫斯河）流域，塔斯卡洛拉傳統地理

period: Written 1825 by David Cusick (Tuscarora)

source.work: David Cusick, Sketches of the Ancient History of the Six Nations, Part II (1825/1848)

summary.en: While the town is out hunting, a giant falls on the aged chief and his attendant Yatatonwatea, who deserts his master and runs: he drives a flock of pigeons across the path to amuse the pursuer, hides under the river bank, among mountain rocks, and finally meets two warriors on the hunting path. After a terrible combat the Ronnongwetowanea is exterminated, and a convention of chieftains sends a few hundred warriors to subdue the giant tribe, which 'has ever since ceased to exist' - an event Cusick dates 2,500 winters before Columbus.
summary.zh: 鎮民外出狩獵之際，巨人突襲老首領與其侍從亞塔托瓦提亞；侍從拋下主人奔逃：他驅趕鴿群橫越小徑以延宕追者，藏身河岸之下、山岩之間，最後在獵徑上遇見兩位戰士。一番惡戰之後，羅農威托萬人被誅；各酋長會議派出數百戰士征討巨人族，此族「自此絕跡」——庫西克將此事定於哥倫布之前二千五百年。

sensitivity.note: Tuscarora pseudo-chronology, 1825; public domain. The date is Cusick's own mythographic scheme, not history.

passages.text: Another Ronnongwetowanea attacked a small town on the bank of Kanawage in a season when the people were out to hunt; only an old chief and an attendant named Yatatonwatea were in their houses when the giant burst in. Yatatonwatea escaped by the back door and deserted the aged chief to his fate. In vain he endeavored to gain retreat by traversing various creeks and hills; he drove a flock of pigeons in the way to amuse the enemy, hid under the bank of the river, and again among the rocks of the mountain, but the pursuer advanced at every moment.
passages.note: Condensed from Cusick 1825, Part II; not verbatim.

passages.text: Determined not to surrender as long as he could keep out of reach, he took the path to the hunting grounds and met two warriors, who instantly supported him. After a terrible combat the Ronnongwetowanea was exterminated, though one warrior received a severe wound from his club. The people returned to their settlements, and a convention of chieftains resolved on defense; a few hundred warriors were sent, and after decisive contests it was supposed the Ronnongwetowanea tribe had ever since ceased to exist. This fate happened, Cusick reckons, about two thousand five hundred winters before Columbus discovered America.
passages.note: Condensed from Cusick 1825, Part II; not verbatim.

title.en: Shotyerronsgwea, the Greatest Mischief Maker
title.zh: 肖特耶隆格威：最偉大的搗亂者

region.en: St. Lawrence country to south of Lake Ontario (traditional Tuscarora geography)
region.zh: 聖勞倫斯至安大略湖以南之地（塔斯卡洛拉傳統地理）

period: Written 1825 by David Cusick (Tuscarora)

source.work: David Cusick, Sketches of the Ancient History of the Six Nations, Part II (1825/1848)

summary.en: A visitor named Shotyerronsgwea gains the people's confidence and then turns destroyer: he assassinates two warriors secretly, violates six virgins, and breeds dissension until the chiefs banish him. Crossing the St. Lawrence he is received with kindness south of Lake Ontario, murders several warriors at the dancing house, and is driven on - 'the greatest mischievous person that ever existed on the continent, considered an agent from bad spirit.'
summary.zh: 一位名為肖特耶隆格威的訪客先博取人心，繼而行兇：暗中刺殺兩名戰士，強暴六名處女，在族中製造紛爭，終被酋長放逐。他渡過聖勞倫斯河，在安大略湖之南受到善待，卻在舞屋中殺害數名戰士，再被驅逐——「為大陸上從來未有之最大搗亂者，被視為惡靈之使者」。

sensitivity.note: Tuscarora text, 1825; public domain. Sexual violence is reported at story distance as the banishment's cause.

passages.text: A mischievous person named Shotyerronsgwea, visiting the people, at first distinguished himself by a good character and gained the confidence of the people, thereby concealing his real designs. In a short time he began to injure the people: he assassinated two warriors secretly, then violated six virgins, and next ventured to break the harmony of the nation and create dissensions among the people. The chiefs were so offended that Shotyerronsgwea was banished from the village.
passages.note: Condensed from Cusick 1825, Part II; not verbatim.

passages.text: He deemed it proper to desist from returning to any of the towns; he crossed the river St. Lawrence, moved toward the midday sun, and came to a town south of the great lake (Ontario), where he was received with kindness. But his entertainment could not appease his evil designs: one night, while at the dancing house, he killed several warriors, and this offence proving fatal to his person, he was compelled to leave and go elsewhere to do mischief. The Shotyerronsgwea was the greatest mischievous person that ever existed on the continent; he was considered an agent from the bad spirit.
passages.note: Condensed from Cusick 1825, Part II; not verbatim.

title.en: Big Quisquiss and Big Elk: The Monster Beasts
title.zh: 大乳齒象與大麋鹿：怪物之獸

region.en: Settlements south of Lake Ontario (traditional Tuscarora geography)
region.zh: 安大略湖以南的聚落（塔斯卡洛拉傳統地理）

period: Written 1825 by David Cusick (Tuscarora)

source.work: David Cusick, Sketches of the Ancient History of the Six Nations, Part II (1825/1848)

summary.en: Big Quisquiss, perhaps the mammoth, invades the settlements south of Lake Ontario, pushing down houses while the people flee and the warriors fail to stop it, until a chief warrior collects men from several towns and drives the monster off; Big Elk then invades and is killed after a severe contest - the first of Cusick's monstrous-beast episodes that punctuate his chronology.
summary.zh: 大乳齒象（或謂長毛象）入侵安大略湖以南聚落，推倒房屋，居民奔逃，戰士屢戰不勝，直至一位大戰士召集數鎮之眾將怪物驅退；大麋鹿繼而入侵，經一場惡戰後被誅——此為庫西克年代記中怪獸插敘之始。

sensitivity.note: Tuscarora text, 1825; public domain. 'Perhaps the Mammoth' is Cusick's own gloss.

passages.text: About this time Big Quisquiss (perhaps the Mammoth) invaded the settlements south of Ontario lake; the furious animal pushed down the houses and made a great disturbance. The people were compelled to flee from the terrible monster; the warriors made opposition but failed, until a certain chief warrior collected the men from several towns. A severe engagement took place, and at last the monster retired - but the people could not remain long without being disturbed: Big Elk invaded the towns; the animal was furious and destroyed many persons. However, the men were soon collected, a severe contest ensued, and the monster was killed.
passages.note: Condensed from Cusick 1825, Part II; not verbatim.

title.en: The Emperor of the Golden City and the Hundred Years' War
title.zh: 金城皇帝與百年之戰

region.en: South of the Great Lakes (traditional Tuscarora geography, symbolic pin south of Lake Erie)
region.zh: 大湖之南（塔斯卡洛拉傳統地理，象徵性定位於伊利湖以南）

period: Written 1825 by David Cusick (Tuscarora)

source.work: David Cusick, Sketches of the Ancient History of the Six Nations, Part II (1825/1848)

summary.en: A northern prince visits the great Emperor at the Golden City, capital of a vast empire; the emperor builds forts through his dominions until they almost reach Lake Erie. The northern nations, fearing to be deprived of the country south of the Great Lakes, defend it in a bloody hundred-year war won by their skill with bow and arrow and endurance of hardship; every town and fort of the invaders is left in ruins. A great horned serpent then appears on Lake Ontario spreading disease, driven off by thunderbolts, and a blazing star falls into a fort on the St. Lawrence and destroys its people.
summary.zh: 北方王子前往金城——龐大帝國之都——拜謁大皇帝；皇帝在其轄內廣築堡壘，幾近伊利湖。北方諸族恐失大湖南岸之地，遂以弓術與堅忍打贏百年血戰，將入侵者的城鎮與堡壘盡毀為墟。其後大角蛇現於安大略湖，散播疾病，被雷電驅退；一顆熾星墜入聖勞倫斯河上的堡壘，毀滅其眾。

sensitivity.note: Tuscarora pseudo-history, 1825; public domain. The 'Golden City' empire is Cusick's mythic geography, sometimes linked by scholars to mound-builder traditions.

passages.text: Perhaps about two thousand two hundred years before Columbus, the northern nations appointed a prince who repaired to the south and visited the great Emperor who resided at the Golden City, a capital of the vast empire. After a time the Emperor built many forts throughout his dominions and almost penetrated Lake Erie; this produced an excitement, for the people of the north felt they would soon be deprived of the country on the south side of the Great Lakes, and determined to defend their country against any infringement of foreign people. Long bloody wars ensued which perhaps lasted about one hundred years.
passages.note: Condensed from Cusick 1825, Part II; not verbatim.

passages.text: The people of the north were too skillful in the use of bows and arrows and could endure hardships, which proved fatal to the foreign people; at last the northern nations gained the conquest and all the towns and forts were totally destroyed and left in heaps of ruins. About this time a great horned serpent appeared on Lake Ontario; the serpent produced diseases and many of the people died, but by the aid of thunderbolts the monster was compelled to retire. A blazing star fell into a fort situated on the St. Lawrence and destroyed the people; this event was considered a warning of their destruction. After a time a war broke out among the northern nations which continued until they had utterly destroyed each other, and the island again became in possession of fierce animals.
passages.note: Condensed from Cusick 1825, Part II; not verbatim.

title.en: Tarenyawagon Leads the Six Families: Origin of the Long House
title.zh: 塔雷尼亞瓦岡引領六族：長屋之起源

region.en: From Oswego Falls through Mohawk and Hudson country to the Tuscarora south (traditional route)
region.zh: 自奧斯威戈瀑布經莫霍克與哈德遜之地南至塔斯卡洛拉（傳統路線）

period: Written 1825 by David Cusick (Tuscarora)

source.work: David Cusick, Sketches of the Ancient History of the Six Nations, Part III (1825/1848)

summary.en: A people hidden in the mountain at Kuskehsawkich (Oswego Falls) are led out by Tarenyawagon, the Holder of the Heavens, who can change himself into various shapes. He guides them down the Mohawk and Hudson to the sea, then back upriver, stationing six families: Mohawk at the river, Oneida at the Pineries creek, Onondaga on the mountain, Cayuga by the long lake, Seneca south of Canandaigua lake - and a sixth family whose vine breaks over the Mississippi, becoming the Tuscarora far south at Cau-ta-noh in North Carolina. Returning, the Holder forms the confederacy called A Long House and instructs the people in moral rules, corn, beans, squash, potatoes and tobacco.
summary.zh: 藏在庫斯克紹維奇山（奧斯威戈瀑布）中的一族人，由能變化諸形的「天堂之主」塔雷尼亞瓦岡引出。他領眾沿莫霍克河、哈德遜河至大海而返，安置六族：莫霍克居河畔，奧奈達居松林溪，奧農達加居山，卡尤加居長湖，塞內卡居卡南代瓜湖之南；第六族渡密西西比河時藤蔓斷裂，遠徙至北卡羅來納之考塔諾而成塔斯卡洛拉。天堂之主返而締結名為「長屋」之同盟，並教以道德之規與玉米、豆、南瓜、馬鈴薯、菸草之種。

sensitivity.note: Tuscarora ethnogenesis legend, 1825; public domain. The broken-vine episode also explains the Shawnee-derived Stonish Giants (Cusick's footnote).

passages.text: By some inducement a body of people was concealed in the mountain at the falls named Kuskehsawkich, now Oswego. When they were released they were visited by TARENYAWAGON, the Holder of the Heavens, who had power to change himself into various shapes. He ordered the people to proceed toward the sunrise as he guided them, down the river Yenonanatche (Mohawk) and down Shaw-nay-taw-ty (Hudson) to the bank of a great water. Of this company one particular body called themselves one household, six families, who resolved to preserve the chain of alliance which should not be extinguished in any manner.
passages.note: Condensed from Cusick 1825, Part III; not verbatim.

passages.text: The Holder directed the first family to reside near the Hudson (Te-haw-re-ho-geh, a speech divided - Mohawk); the second at the Pineries creek (Ne-haw-re-tah-go, Big Tree - Oneida); the third on the mountain named Onondaga (Seuh-now-kah-tah, carrying the name); the fourth by the long lake Go-yo-goh (Sho-nea-na-we-to-wah, a great pipe - Cayuga); the fifth south of Canandaigua lake (Te-how-nea-nyo-hent, Possessing a Door - Seneca). The sixth family went toward the great lake Erie and on to the river Ouau-we-yo-ka (Mississippi), where a grape vine lay across the river by which a part of the people went over; while they were engaged the vine broke, and those left became enemies of those who crossed.
passages.note: Condensed from Cusick 1825, Part III; not verbatim.

passages.text: The sixth family was directed to reside near Cau-ta-noh, Pine in water, near the mouth of the Neuse river in North Carolina, and was named Kau-ta-noh - now Tuscarora. The Holder of the Heavens returned to the five families and formed the mode of confederacy which was named A Long House. A solemn agent from superior power visited the families and instructed them in matrimony, moral rules and worship, warning that an evil spirit was in the world; he gave the seeds for corn, beans, squashes, potatoes and tobacco, with directions how to cultivate them, and gave them dogs to aid in pursuing the game - and when he ended the interview of consolation, he left.
passages.note: Condensed from Cusick 1825, Part III; not verbatim.

title.en: The Flying Heads and the Woman Who Parched Acorns
title.zh: 飛頭與炒橡實的老婦

region.en: Onondaga, New York
region.zh: 紐約州奧農達加

period: Written 1825 by David Cusick (Tuscarora)

source.work: David Cusick, Sketches of the Ancient History of the Six Nations, Part III (1825/1848)

summary.en: When the Holder of the Heavens is absent, the Ko-nea-rau-neh-neh - Flying Heads - invade by night and devour several people, the towns hiding hut to hut. At Onondaga an old woman left alone sits parching acorns when a monstrous head appears at the door; amazed to see her eat the coals of fire, the monsters are put to flight, and ever since the heads are supposed concealed in the earth.
summary.zh: 天堂之主不在之時，科尼羅內內——飛頭——夜間入侵，吞食人眾，各鎮之民藏身於備好的他屋。奧農達加一位獨居的老婦正炒橡實，忽有巨首現於門前；見她竟吞食火炭，怪物大驚而逃，自此飛頭據信藏於地下。

sensitivity.note: Tuscarora text, 1825; public domain. The flying head is a signature Iroquois horror figure (compare Parker's False Face cycle).

passages.text: The Holder of the Heavens was absent from the country, which was destitute of the visits of the Governor of the Universe; the reason produced the occasion that they were invaded by the monsters called Ko-nea-rau-neh-neh, the Flying Heads, which devoured several people of the country. The Flying Heads made invasions in the night, but the people were attentive to escape by leaving their huts and concealing themselves in other huts prepared for that purpose.
passages.note: Condensed from Cusick 1825, Part III; not verbatim.

passages.text: There was an old woman who resided at Onondaga; she was left alone in the hut at evening, while others deserted. She was sitting near the fire parching some acorns when the monstrous Head made its appearance at the door; while viewing the woman it was amazed that she ate the coals of fire, by which the monsters were put to flight. Ever since the heads disappeared and were supposed concealed in the earth. After a short time the people were invaded by the monster of the deep, the Lake Serpent, which traversed the country and interrupted their intercourse, so the five families were compelled to make fortifications throughout their respective towns.
passages.note: Condensed from Cusick 1825, Part III; not verbatim.

title.en: The Stonish Giants Trapped in the Hollow
title.zh: 石巨人困於凹谷

region.en: Hollow near Onondaga, New York
region.zh: 紐約州奧農達加附近的凹谷

period: Written 1825 by David Cusick (Tuscarora)

source.work: David Cusick, Sketches of the Ancient History of the Six Nations, Part III (1825/1848)

summary.en: The Otne-yar-heh, Stonish Giants - people who had rolled in sand until their bodies grew hard and flinty - overrun the country and devour almost every town. The Holder of the Heavens returns, changes himself into a giant, joins their march on Fort Onondaga, and orders them to lie overnight in a deep hollow; at dawn he ascends the heights and overwhelms them with a mass of rocks. One giant escapes to tell the fate, and the tribe seeks asylum in the north.
summary.zh: 奧特涅亞赫——石巨人——乃因在沙中打滾而身披堅硬石皮之族，蹂躪四方，吞食幾乎每一座城鎮。天堂之主歸來，化身為巨人，混入其進攻奧農達加堡的隊伍，命他們夜宿深谷；黎明時分他登上高處，以巨岩崩落將其淹沒。一巨人逃出報信，其族遂北遁求庇。

sensitivity.note: Tuscarora text, 1825; public domain. Cusick's footnote derives the giants from the vine-breaking migration and a Shawnee tradition.

passages.text: About this time a powerful tribe of the wilderness, called Otne-yar-heh, the Stonish Giants, overran the country; the warriors were collected from several towns, but after severe combat were overpowered, and the country was brought to subjection for many winters. The Stonish Giants were so ravenous that they devoured the people of almost every town in the country. The Shawnee tradition, Cusick notes, derives them from a family separated at the broken vine who forgot the rules of humanity and ate raw flesh, rolling in sand until their bodies were covered with hard skin, and so became giants.
passages.note: Condensed from Cusick 1825, Part III and footnote; not verbatim.

passages.text: Happily the Holder of the Heavens again visited the people and observed their distressed condition. With a stratagem he proceeded to banish their invaders: he changed himself into a giant, combined with the Stonish Giants, and introduced himself to take the lead in destroying the people of the country. A day's march from the fort Onondaga he ordered them to lay in a deep hollow during the night, promising attack on the following morning. At the dawn of day he ascended upon the heights and overwhelmed them by a mass of rocks, and only one escaped to announce the dreadful fate; since that event the Stonish Giants left the country and sought an asylum in the regions of the north.
passages.note: Condensed from Cusick 1825, Part III; not verbatim.

title.en: Kaistowanea, the Two-Headed Serpent Raised as a Pet
title.zh: 凱斯托瓦內亞：被豢養的雙頭蛇

region.en: Jenneatowaka, original seat of the Seneca council fire, near Seneca Lake, New York
region.zh: 傑尼亞托瓦卡——塞內卡議火原址，紐約州塞尼卡湖附近

period: Written 1825 by David Cusick (Tuscarora)

source.work: David Cusick, Sketches of the Ancient History of the Six Nations, Part III (1825/1848)

summary.en: A boy catches a small two-headed serpent, Kaistowanea, and keeps it in a bark box; after ten winters it needs deer and bear for food, and after thirty it is prodigious, broods mischief by night, and at daybreak descends with tremendous noise, uprooting trees and encircling the fort so that none may pass. Warriors are fruitless; the people are devoured but for a young warrior and his sister, who receive dream advice: adorned with his sister's hair, the warrior shoots the serpent's heart, and it vomits what it has eaten and expires in the lake.
summary.zh: 一男孩捕得小雙頭蛇凱斯托瓦內亞，置於樹皮盒中馴養；十冬之後蛇需食鹿熊，三十年後身軀龐大，夜間謀亂，黎明轟然而下，連根拔樹，盤繞堡門，無人得脫。戰士屢攻無效，眾人幾被吞食，僅餘一青年戰士與其妹。戰士得夢示：以妹髮飾臂，射中蛇心；蛇嘔出所吞之物，遁入湖中而亡。

sensitivity.note: Tuscarora text, 1825; public domain. Parker retells a cognate of this tale as 'The Horned Serpent Runs Away with a Girl.'

passages.text: In the days of Atotarho IIII, a woman and son resided near the fort at Jenneatowaka, the original seat of the council fire of the Senecas. The boy, amusing himself in the bush, caught a small serpent called Kaistowanea, with two heads, and brought it to his apartment, where it was first placed in a small bark box to tame and fed with birds' flesh. After ten winters the serpent became considerably large and rested on the beams within the hut, and the warrior was obliged to hunt deer and bears to feed the monster; but after a while the serpent was able to maintain itself on various game, left the hut, and resided on the top of a nole.
passages.note: Condensed from Cusick 1825, Part III; not verbatim.

passages.text: After thirty years it was of prodigious size, and in a short time became inspired with an evil mind against the people: in the night the warrior experienced that the serpent was brooding mischief and about to destroy the people of the fort, and moved to another fort. At daylight the serpent descended from the heights with the most tremendous noise, the trees unrooted by its force, and it immediately surrounded the gate. Some endeavored to pass out and others to climb over the serpent, but were unable; the people remained in this situation for several days, and were devoured, except a young warrior and sister.
passages.note: Condensed from Cusick 1825, Part III; not verbatim.

passages.text: At length the warrior received advice from a dream, and adorned his arms with the hairs of his sister; by this he succeeded in shooting the serpent at the heart, and it was mortally wounded. It hastened to retire from the fort and retreated to the lake to gain relief, dashing on the face of the water furiously in the time of agony; at last it vomited the substance it had eaten, then sunk to the deep and expired. After the fort was demolished the council fire was removed to another fort called Thau-gwe-took, west of Geneva lake.
passages.note: Condensed from Cusick 1825, Part III; not verbatim.

title.en: The Headless Pestilence Creature of Chautauqua
title.zh: 肖托夸的無首瘟疫之獸

region.en: Lake Chautauqua, Seneca country, New York
region.zh: 紐約州肖托夸湖，塞內卡之地

period: Written 1825 by David Cusick (Tuscarora)

source.work: David Cusick, Sketches of the Ancient History of the Six Nations, Part III (1825/1848)

summary.en: A Seneca war party encamped above Lake Chautauqua finds a grey dog-like creature asleep by a den, without any visible head. A joker beats it, seizes it with a tumpline, and cannot hold it as it drags toward its den; a few paces away he dies of the pestilence, a messenger dies running, and the plague sweeps the camp until a few escape. Thus ends the expedition against the Ottawas.
summary.zh: 塞內卡戰隊紮營於肖托夸湖上，發現一頭灰色、似犬而無首的怪獸在巢穴旁酣睡。一名小丑以棒擊之、以背帶拽之，卻拉不住它拖回巢穴；僅行數步便染瘟疫而死，報信者亦死於途中，營中瘟疫橫行，僅少數得脫。對抗奧塔瓦人之遠征就此告終。

sensitivity.note: Tuscarora text, 1825; public domain.

passages.text: The warriors advanced above the lake named Geattahgweah (now Chautauqua) and agreed to hunt two days before proceeding toward the enemy's country. A certain warrior passed a small brook and discovered a strange animal resembling a dog, but without any discoverable head, a greyish creature asleep, exposed to the sun, near a den which was supposed its residence. He reported at evening that it was a very poisonous animal and he was afraid to approach it again - but one of the jokers laughed at him, called him a cowardly fellow, and determined to kill the creature without trouble, wishing spectators of the engagement.
passages.note: Condensed from Cusick 1825, Part III; not verbatim.

passages.text: After beating it a short time with his club, he seized the animal and tied it with a tumline; but while lifting it the creature moved toward the den, and with all his might he could not stop it, and let go. Hastening to retire, when a few paces away he was taken with the pestilence influenced by the creature and suddenly died; another warrior who fled to carry the intelligence also died at a short distance, and the others returned to camp - but the pestilence prevailed among the warriors, and many died in the same manner. A few escaped by leaving the camp before the plague appeared, and thus ended the expedition.
passages.note: Condensed from Cusick 1825, Part III; not verbatim.

title.en: The Furious Lizard in the Hollow Tree
title.zh: 空心樹中的狂怒蜥蜴

region.en: Ohio River encampment (traditional Tuscarora geography)
region.zh: 俄亥俄河畔營地（塔斯卡洛拉傳統地理）

period: Written 1825 by David Cusick (Tuscarora)

source.work: David Cusick, Sketches of the Ancient History of the Six Nations, Part III (1825/1848)

summary.en: Provisioned out on the Ohio, warriors burn a hollow tree to smoke out a bear - but a furious Lizard leaps out, seizes a warrior and carries him into the hollow where its young devour him; the last man remaining is saved by the Holder of the Heavens, who appears in a lion's form, instructs him to burn sticks and hook the lizard's severed flesh into the fire so the body cannot reunite, and the monster is quelled.
summary.zh: 戰士們在俄亥俄河畔糧盡，焚燒空心樹欲燻出黑熊——卻竄出一頭狂怒蜥蜴，抓住一名戰士拖入樹洞，被其幼崽吞食。最後一名戰士得「天堂之主」化身為獅前來救援，教他備火焚枝，以枝勾出蜥蜴被咬斷的肉塊投入火中，使其軀體不能復合，怪物遂被制服。

sensitivity.note: Tuscarora text, 1825; public domain. The fire-hook to prevent the body rejoining is a distinct Iroquoian monster-slaying technique.

passages.text: As the warriors were out of provision, a certain warrior discovered a hollow tree, supposing a bear in it; one of them climbed and put a fire in it to drive out the creature, and the warriors made ready to shoot - but were mistaken. There instantly came out a furious Lizard, and quickly grasped a warrior and leaped into the hollow of the tree, and the young ones devoured him. A grumbling noise ensued; the warriors were terrified and compelled to retire, except one who stayed at the tree while the party was destroyed.
passages.note: Condensed from Cusick 1825, Part III; not verbatim.

passages.text: The last warrior ran on the way and fortunately met the Holder of the Heavens, who offered the aid of making resistance. He instructed the warrior to make fire without delay and to get some sticks with which to prevent the Lizard's flesh from uniting with the body, as being efficacious; the protector changed into a lion and laid in wait. When the monster came up, a severe engagement took place; the warrior hastened with a stick and began to hook the Lizard's flesh, and when it was bit off by his defender he threw it into the fire - by which means the monster was quelled. The warrior gave thanks for his personal preservation; the protector vanished out of his sight.
passages.note: Condensed from Cusick 1825, Part III; not verbatim.

title.en: The Western Expedition: Winged Fish, Tailed Nation, and the Giant at the Mountains
title.zh: 西征記：有翼之魚、有尾之族與山間巨人

region.en: From Sandusky toward the Rocky Mountains (traditional Tuscarora geography)
region.zh: 自桑達斯基向西至落磯山（塔斯卡洛拉傳統地理）

period: Written 1825 by David Cusick (Tuscarora)

source.work: David Cusick, Sketches of the Ancient History of the Six Nations, Part III (1825/1848)

summary.en: King Atotarho VII sends fifteen men of the five nations west to explore. Beyond the Mississippi they are welcomed with dances and drums, meet a hummingbird-quick winged fish, are lodged by the Dog Tail Nation - whose people have short tails like apes with holes through their seats - find a nation that drinks only soup and no meat, and are finally arrested by a giant before the Rocky Mountains and compelled to return home.
summary.zh: 阿托塔霍七世遣五族十五人西行探查。眾人渡密西西比河，受歌舞歡迎，遇動如蜂鳥的有翼之魚；受「犬尾族」款待——其民短尾如猿，座上鑽孔以容其尾——又見只飲肉湯不食肉之族；行至落磯山前為巨人所阻，只得返國覆命。

sensitivity.note: Tuscarora text, 1825; public domain. Cusick's wonder-geography of the far west.

passages.text: King Atotarho VII, authorized by the senate, sent an expedition to explore the countries toward the setting sun: two captains commanded about fifteen men selected from the five nations, with two Ottawa warriors accompanying. They advanced to the Mississippi river, where a duke of Twa-kan-ah collected the people from several towns to meet them; the people danced around them, singing and beating their little drums, and the band was invited into the national house. Crossing the Mississippi they came to an extensive meadow and discovered a curious animal - a winged fish that flew about the trees and moved like a humming bird.
passages.note: Condensed from Cusick 1825, Part III; not verbatim.

passages.text: They came to the village of the Dog Tail Nation and were accommodated and amused with dances; they were astonished that the people had short tails like apes, a hole being made through their seats where they put their tails. Another nation received them kindly, though its people ate no meat but drank only the soup. The band continued, but before they reached the Rocky Mountains they were arrested by a giant and compelled to return; after a long journey they came back and informed the king of all the particulars.
passages.note: Condensed from Cusick 1825, Part III; not verbatim.

title.en: Big Neck, the Giant of the Susquehanna
title.zh: 蘇克漢納的巨人「大頸」

region.en: Susquehanna River, Oneida fort country (traditional Tuscarora geography)
region.zh: 蘇克漢納河，奧奈達堡之地（塔斯卡洛拉傳統地理）

period: Written 1825 by David Cusick (Tuscarora)

source.work: David Cusick, Sketches of the Ancient History of the Six Nations, Part III (1825/1848)

summary.en: A woman on the Susquehanna bears a male child of uncommon size who beats his playmates until his mother corrects him; grown, he becomes a giant hunter named Soh-nou-re-wah, Big Neck, carrying five or six deer and bears strung on his belt, and brings home the scalps of whom he has killed. Diplomacy fails; he builds a fort on the river and ambuses travelers with a plump arrow that breaks a body in two, until three kinsmen bring him his favorite huckleberries and club him from under a cloak; he sinks in the mire and is killed.
summary.zh: 蘇克漢納河畔一婦產下巨嬰，長大後為偉大獵人，名為索努勒瓦「大頸」，腰間常掛五六隻鹿熊，並攜所殺者之髮皮。外交無效；他在河畔築堡，埋伏小徑，以能斷人為二的粗箭射殺行人。三位親族攜其最愛的越橘而來，自斗篷下以棒重擊其頭；巨人陷入泥沼，終被誅殺。

sensitivity.note: Tuscarora text, 1825; public domain. Scalp-taking is reported as the character's own attributed practice.

passages.text: On the Susquehanna a certain woman delivered a male child of uncommon size; when he was twelve years of age he was nearly as large as a grown person, and he beat his playmates, which created disputes, but his mother corrected him, and she prevailed: he promised never to injure his people. When grown up he became a giant and a great hunter, so strong that returning from hunting he would have five or six deers and bears strung round on his belt. The giant was named Soh-nou-re-wah, Big Neck, and brought several suits of dress and the scalps of whom he had killed.
passages.note: Condensed from Cusick 1825, Part III; not verbatim.

passages.text: The Shawnees sent messengers to demonstrate his conduct, and kinsmen persuaded him to reform, but he remained only two winters without disturbance; he went down the river and committed the same outrages on every town, plundering clothes and skins. A chief offered a belt of wampum and terms of peace, which were accepted, but the giant was not disposed to favor the treaty: he built a fort on the Susquehanna, laid in ambush near the path, and shot passersby with a plump arrow so violent it would break the body in two parts.
passages.note: Condensed from Cusick 1825, Part III; not verbatim.

passages.text: Three warriors of his own nation brought him his favorite diet, a mess of huckleberries; while he was eating, one of the warriors, with a club concealed under his cloak, stepped on the bench and gave a fatal blow on the monster's head. So distracted, he ran from the fort intending to cross the river, but sank in the mire near the bank; the warriors prevailed and killed him on the spot. They spoiled his house and obtained a large quantity of skins, and the fort was ruined ever since.
passages.note: Condensed from Cusick 1825, Part III; not verbatim.

title.en: The Great Musqueto of Fort Onondaga
title.zh: 奧農達加堡的大蚊

region.en: Fort Onondaga, New York
region.zh: 紐約州奧農達加堡

period: Written 1825 by David Cusick (Tuscarora)

source.work: David Cusick, Sketches of the Ancient History of the Six Nations, Part III (1825/1848)

summary.en: A great musqueto invades Fort Onondaga, flying about with a long stinger and sucking the blood of many lives; the warriors fail to expel it until the Holder of the Heavens visits the king. He chases the monster for days along the great lakes and round the country, overtakes it, and kills it near the salt lake Onondaga - and its blood becomes the small musquetos.
summary.zh: 大蚊侵擾奧農達加堡，以長針飛繞其間，吸食多人之血；戰士驅之無效，直至天堂之主拜訪國王。他沿大湖追擊怪物數日，繞行大地，終在其附近的鹽湖旁將其誅殺——其血遂化為眾多的小蚊。

sensitivity.note: Tuscarora text, 1825; public domain. A classic etiological chase-monster; compare the Seneca mosquito slayings in Hewitt's cosmology.

passages.text: About this time a great musqueto invaded the fort Onondaga; the musqueto was mischievous to the people: it flew about the fort with a long stinger and sucked the blood of a number of lives. The warriors made several oppositions to expel the monster, but failed, and the country was invaded until the Holder of the Heavens was pleased to visit the people.
passages.note: Condensed from Cusick 1825, Part III; not verbatim.

passages.text: While he was visiting the king at the fort Onondaga the musqueto made its appearance as usual and flew about the fort; the Holder of the Heavens attacked the monster. It flew so rapidly that he could hardly keep in sight of it, but after a few days' chase the monster began to fail: he chased it on the borders of the great lakes toward the sunsetting, and round the great country, until at last he overtook the monster and killed it near the salt lake Onondaga - and the blood became small musquetos.
passages.note: Condensed from Cusick 1825, Part III; not verbatim.

title.en: The Big Bear and the Lion of Skaneateles Lake
title.zh: 斯科尼阿特勒斯湖的大熊與獅

region.en: Skaneateles Lake near Ohiokea, west of Oneida Creek, New York
region.zh: 紐約州奧奈達溪以西斯科尼阿特勒斯湖

period: Written 1825 by David Cusick (Tuscarora)

source.work: David Cusick, Sketches of the Ancient History of the Six Nations, Part III (1825/1848)

summary.en: In Atotarho II's day the Oyalkquoher, Big Bear, invades the hunting grounds of the five nations. Near Skaneateles lake a noise breaks out on the water: a great bear rolls stones and logs on the bank in a rage, until a lion comes out of the lake and falls upon it, beating it so that it leaves the bank. Next day the hunters find the bear; one fore leg is so heavy two men can barely lift it a hand's height, and they keep some of the meat for use in war.
summary.zh: 阿托塔霍二世時，奧雅科赫「大熊」侵擾五族獵場。斯科尼阿特勒斯湖上喧聲大作：巨熊在岸邊憤而滾落石木，直至湖中竄出獅子撲擊，將其擊退。次日獵人尋得熊屍；其前肢沉重，兩人僅能抬離地一手之高；眾人取其肉以備戰時之用。

sensitivity.note: Tuscarora text, 1825; public domain.

passages.text: About this time the Oyalkquoher, or Big Bear, invaded the territory of the five nations, and the hunters were often attacked by these monsters. At the village of Ohiokea, west of Oneida creek, a small party went out to hunt and encamped near the lake Skonyatales. One morning a noise broke out in the lake; a man sent to see the tumult saw a great bear on the bank rolling down stones and logs, the monster in a great rage. A lion came out of the lake and suddenly fell upon the bear; a severe contest ensued, and the bear, beaten, was compelled to leave the bank.
passages.note: Condensed from Cusick 1825, Part III; not verbatim.

passages.text: The next day the men went in search of the bear and found it: one of the fore legs was so heavy that two men could not lift it but a hand's height. They procured some of the meat for useful purposes in the time of war.
passages.note: Condensed from Cusick 1825, Part III; not verbatim.

title.en: The Stonish Giant's Pointer and the Medicine Roots
title.zh: 石巨人的指針與藥根

region.en: Far north beyond the St. Lawrence (traditional Tuscarora geography)
region.zh: 聖勞倫斯河以北的遠方（塔斯卡洛拉傳統地理）

period: Written 1825 by David Cusick (Tuscarora)

source.work: David Cusick, Sketches of the Ancient History of the Six Nations, Part III (1825/1848)

summary.en: Two Onondaga beaver hunters cross the St. Lawrence into the far north; one is taken by a Stonish Giant and forced to race, faints at the giant's whoop, hides by bending a small tree and leaping among the sprouting branches of a basswood stump. The giant's 'pointer' - without which he cannot live - nearly betrays him, but the man leaps out, seizes it by the fingers, and gains the medical roots as ransom; he returns home and cures many diseases, drawing hair and worms blown in by witches.
summary.zh: 兩名奧農達加河狸獵人渡聖勞倫斯河北上；其一被石巨人擄去被迫賽跑，聞巨人呼嘯而昏倒，遂攀小樹折向他樹，藏身於萌出新椏的椴木樹樁之間。巨人賴以為生的「指針」幾乎指破行藏；獵人躍出，攫其手指奪下法器，並以藥根為贖金。他歸鄉行醫，療癒多疾，自被巫者吹入體內之人身上拔出毛髮與蠕蟲。

sensitivity.note: Tuscarora text, 1825; public domain. Bridges the giant cycle and the witchcraft cycle.

passages.text: At the Onondaga, two men went out to hunt beaver, crossed the river St. Lawrence, went far into the north, and discovered a number of beaver dams. One day a man went alone in search of beaver, but he was taken prisoner by the Stonish Giant and compelled to run a race with him. After midday the man gained and almost went out of sight, but the giant whooped, by which the man was so affected that he fainted and fell down; the giant passed him, and the man turned his course and sought to escape, climbing a small tree and bending it to another, and leaping from tree to tree until he reached a large basswood stump which had sprouted several branches, and seated himself in the midst of it.
passages.note: Condensed from Cusick 1825, Part III; not verbatim.

passages.text: The giant came up and examined the stump for some time, then exhibited a curious instrument which he called a pointer, possessed of a power of divination: it directed him where to find game, and the giant could not live without it. The man observed the motion of the hand, and as it was about to point to him he jumped from the stump and seized it by the fingers, instantly possessing the valuable instrument. The defeated giant entreated for the pointer and offered to mention the medical roots as a mark of friendship, which was accepted; the pointer was restored, the giant retired.
passages.note: Condensed from Cusick 1825, Part III; not verbatim.

passages.text: The man came home and began to doctor, and cured many diseases; he was skilled in the business and drew hair and worms from persons whom the witches had blown into their bodies. It was supposed that the Skaunvatohatihawk, the Nanticokes of the south, first founded the witchcraft: great pains were taken to procure the snakes and roots of which the stuff was made to poison the people. The witches formed a secret society, meeting in the night; when discovered they turned into foxes and wolves running swift with flashes of light, or into turkeys and big owls, or stones and rotten logs.
passages.note: Condensed from Cusick 1825, Part III; not verbatim.

title.en: The Origin of Witchcraft and the Witches Burned at Onondaga
title.zh: 巫術之起源與奧農達加焚巫

region.en: Near Fort Onondaga, New York
region.zh: 紐約州奧農達加堡附近

period: Written 1825 by David Cusick (Tuscarora)

source.work: David Cusick, Sketches of the Ancient History of the Six Nations, Part III (1825/1848)

summary.en: The Nanticokes of the south are said to have founded witchcraft: a secret society gathering by night, whose members turn into foxes, wolves, turkeys or great owls to go from town to town blowing hairs and worms into bodies, and into stones or rotten logs when discovered. About fifty persons were indicted as witches and burnt to death near Fort Onondaga by order of the national committee.
summary.zh: 據說南方納提科人首創巫術：一個夜間聚會的秘密社團，其成員化為狐、狼、火雞或巨鴞往來各鎮，向人體吹入毛髮與蠕蟲；被發現時則化為石頭或朽木。約五十人被控行巫，經國族委員會之命，於奧農達加堡附近焚死。

sensitivity.note: Tuscarora text, 1825; public domain. Historicizes the Iroquois witch-belief that Parker's tales treat dramatically.

passages.text: It was supposed that the Skaunvatohatihawk, the Nanticokes in the south, first founded the witchcraft. Great pains were taken to procure the snakes and roots of which the stuff was made to poison the people. The witches formed into a secret society; they met in the night and consulted on various subjects respecting their engagements. When a person becomes a member of their society, he is forbidden to reveal any of their proceedings.
passages.note: Condensed from Cusick 1825, Part III; not verbatim.

passages.text: In the night the witches would turn into foxes and wolves, and run very swift, attended with flashes of light; sometimes they turned into a turkey or big owl, and could fly very fast, going from town to town to blow hairs and worms into a person. If the witches were discovered by some person they turned into a stone or rotten log, entirely concealed in this situation. About fifty persons were indicted for being witches, and were burnt to death near the fort Onondaga, by order of the national committee.
passages.note: Condensed from Cusick 1825, Part III; not verbatim.

title.en: The Night in the Corpse House and the New Burial
title.zh: 屍屋之夜與新葬俗

region.en: Kaunehsuntahkeh, east of Oneida Creek, New York
region.zh: 紐約州奧奈達溪以東考內孫塔赫

period: Written 1825 by David Cusick (Tuscarora)

source.work: David Cusick, Sketches of the Ancient History of the Six Nations, Part III (1825/1848)

summary.en: Returning late from hunting, a man, his wife and another shelter overnight in a house where dead bodies are deposited. When the fire dies the room darkens and something gnaws; kindling the fire, he finds the third person dead, eaten by a ghost. Fleeing with his fainting wife toward the village light, they reach safety; next day the people burn the bodies, and the five nations change their mode of burying - faces set to the east - and later alter it again when still troubled.
summary.zh: 獵罷夜歸，一男攜妻與同伴投宿於停放屍體之屋。火熄屋暗之際，忽聞啃噬之聲；重新點火後，發現同伴已死——被鬼所噬。他攜昏弱的妻子奔向村中燈火而脫險；翌日族人焚屍，五族因而改變葬俗——面朝東而葬——其後仍有擾亂，葬俗再改。

sensitivity.note: Tuscarora text, 1825; public domain. A burial-custom aition told as ghost-story.

passages.text: Near the village of Kaunehsuntahkeh a man and his wife and another person returned from hunting, but the night was getting late before they reached the village; they went into a house where dead bodies were deposited to stay over the night. They kindled a fire and went to sleep, but when the fire was out the room became dark, and the man heard something gnawing. Kindling the fire again, he discovered the person was dead, eaten by a ghost; he trembled with fright, told his wife to quit the room as soon as possible, and followed her out.
passages.note: Condensed from Cusick 1825, Part III; not verbatim.

passages.text: She became faint and could not run fast; they saw a light coming and supposed the ghost was chasing them, but fortunately gained the village. The next day the people went and burnt the dead bodies. This important event was soon made known among the five nations, and afterwards they changed their mode of burying, setting the posture face to the east; but again they were troubled with the dead bodies, and were compelled to make some alterations in burying.
passages.note: Condensed from Cusick 1825, Part III; not verbatim.

title.en: Queen Yagowanea, the Betrayal, and the Fall of the Erians
title.zh: 亞格瓦尼亞女王：背叛與伊利人之傾覆

region.en: Fort Kauhanauka (Tuscarora) and the Genesee country, New York
region.zh: 考哈農卡堡（塔斯卡洛拉）與傑納西之地，紐約州

period: Written 1825 by David Cusick (Tuscarora)

source.work: David Cusick, Sketches of the Ancient History of the Six Nations, Part III (1825/1848)

summary.en: Queen Yagowanea of the Erians, 'mother of the Nations,' keeps a Peace House entertaining both warring parties. When two Canandaigua warriors are smoking with her she admits a party of Messissaugers and advises them to kill her guests. A woman slips away by canoe across Lake Ontario to warn the Governor Shorihowane; his three divisions ambush the Erians behind a bear-skin decoy and slay six hundred. The great war chief Shorihowane is killed at the siege of Fort Kauquatkay, and the Queen sues for peace.
summary.zh: 伊利人的亞格瓦尼亞女王為「諸族之母」，設「和平之屋」款待交戰雙方。兩名卡南代瓜戰士正與她吸和平之菸時，她放入麥西薩格人並唆使其殺害客人。一名女子駕獨木舟渡安大略湖報信給總督肖里豪恩；總督的三個分隊以熊皮誘敵設伏，殺敵六百。大戰士肖里豪恩攻考夸特凱堡時中箭陣亡，女王乞和。

sensitivity.note: Tuscarora text, 1825; public domain. Cusick's Erian (Erie) war traditions.

passages.text: The Kanneastokaroneah or Erians sprung from the Senecas, becoming a numerous and powerful nation. A Queen named Yagowanea resided at the fort Kauhanauka; she had influence among the people and extended her authority over twelve forts. She lived outside the fort in a long house called a Peace House, entertaining the two parties who were at war with each other, and was called the mother of the Nations; each nation sent her a belt of wampum as a mark of respect. Where the Five Nations were engaged in the warfare she admitted two Canandaigua warriors into her house, and just as they began to smoke the pipe of peace, a small party of the Messissaugers came in - she betrayed her visitors, advising the Messissaugers to kill the warriors, which was soon executed.
passages.note: Condensed from Cusick 1825, Part III; not verbatim.

passages.text: During the Queen's absence a woman went privately, took a canoe, and proceeded on Lake Ontario toward Canandaigua as fast as possible, going through the woods to inform the Governor Shorihowane that the Erians were making preparations to destroy the people east of the Genesee river, and directed how to send the spies. Collecting fifteen hundred warriors besides the women and old men, the governor separated the people into three divisions and marched toward the Genesee river. A warrior was dressed in a bear skin and seated on the path; the enemy chased it, which brought them into the midst of the division - at once burst a most hideous yell, followed with a rattling of war clubs. After a severe contest the Erians fled, leaving six hundred warriors slain.
passages.note: Condensed from Cusick 1825, Part III; not verbatim.

passages.text: The King of the Five Nations ordered the great war chief Shorihowane, a Mohawk, to march with five thousand warriors to attack the fort Kauquatkay and extinguish the council fire of the enemy. During the siege, a shower of arrows flew from the fort and the great war chief was killed; his body was conveyed back to Genesee and buried in a solemn manner, but the siege continued for several days. The Queen sued for peace; the army ceased hostilities and left the Erians entire possession of the country.
passages.note: Condensed from Cusick 1825, Part III; not verbatim.

title.en: The Aged Visitor Among the Tuscaroras and the Prophecy of the Whites
title.zh: 塔斯卡洛拉的年邁訪客與白人預言

region.en: Tuscarora settlements, North Carolina (traditional)
region.zh: 塔斯卡洛拉聚落，北卡羅來納（傳統）

period: Written 1825 by David Cusick (Tuscarora)

source.work: David Cusick, Sketches of the Ancient History of the Six Nations, Part III (1825/1848)

summary.en: An aged visitor, abused by the ball-players, throws one into a tree and vanishes; returning he releases the man, teaches the people to respect their dead and love their relations, tells them the whites beyond the great water have killed their Maker but he rose again, and prophesies that the whites will one day take the Big Island and the red children 'melt away like snow before the heat.' He dies, is buried - and some who visit the grave find he has risen, never to be heard of since.
summary.zh: 一位年邁訪客遭打球者欺侮，將一人擲上樹而消失；復返後釋放其人，教眾人敬重亡者、親愛族親，並說大洋彼岸的白人殺了他們的造物主——主卻復活——又預言白人終將佔有大島，紅皮子弟「將如雪遇熱而消融」。他死後下葬；有人往墓探視，發現他已復活，自此杳無音訊。

sensitivity.note: Tuscarora text, 1825; public domain. The Christianized prophecy is a colonial-era accretion Cusick records as tradition.

passages.text: The sixth family, the Tuscaroras, was visited by a person who went to see their amusements, but he was abused by some of the ball-players. He punished the offender by throwing him into a tree, and suddenly disappeared - but the person came again and released the fellow from the tree. The visitor appeared a very old man; he appeared among the people for a while and taught them many things: how to respect their deceased friends and to love their relations.
passages.note: Condensed from Cusick 1825, Part III; not verbatim.

passages.text: He informed the people that the whites beyond the great water had killed their Maker, but he rose again; and he warned them that the whites would in some future day take possession of the Big Island, and it was impossible to prevent it: the red children would melt away like snow before the heat. The aged man, becoming sick, told them to get different kinds of roots to cure diseases, and showed them the manner of mourning. He died among them and was buried; but soon after, some person went to the grave and found he had risen, and he was never heard of since.
passages.note: Condensed from Cusick 1825, Part III; not verbatim.

title.en: The Mantis's Son, the Baboons, and the Child's Eye
title.zh: 螳螂之子、狒狒與孩童之眼

region.en: Strontbergen, Cape Colony (Northern Cape, South Africa)
region.zh: 南非北開普省斯特龍特山（象徵定位）

period: Bushman (|Xam San) oral tradition; recorded 1878 by /Han≠kass'o (Bleek & Lloyd)

source.work: Bleek & Lloyd, Specimens of Bushman Folklore (1911), '||Gaunu-tsaxau (the son of the Mantis), the Baboons, and the Mantis'

summary.en: |Kaggen sends his son ||Gaunu-tsaxau to fetch sticks for bows; the baboons mock the child's errand, break his skull and play ball with his eye. The Mantis dreams the crime, flies down, snatches the eye into his bag, and drops it into the water — and the boy rises from the pool, weak but alive.
summary.zh: 卡根遣子取木，狒狒譏其使命，碎其顱，以眼作球戲之。卡根夢知其事，飛下奪眼入囊，投之於水——孩童自池中復起，體弱而生。

sensitivity.note: |Xam San oral tradition dictated by /Han≠kass'o to Bleek and Lloyd, 1878; presented as an archival record of 19th-century colonial recordings, not as permission to speak for living San communities.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase of Specimens of Bushman Folklore, ||Gaunu-tsaxau (the son of the Mantis), the Baboons, and the Mantis (Bleek & Lloyd 1911); not verbatim. ||Gaunu-tsaxau went to fetch sticks for his father, so that the Mantis might take aim at the people who sit upon their heels. An old baboon questioned him, and as the errand was passed from baboon to baboon with their chant 'First going I listen, to the child yonder,' the last of them cried that it was themselves the child was mocking. 'Ye shall strike the child with your fists.'
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Specimens of Bushman Folklore (Bleek & Lloyd 1911), section I.—5.; not verbatim.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase, same locus; not verbatim. They struck the child with their fists, breaking his head; another struck out his eye, and the eye rolled away. 'My ball! my ball!' they sang, and played at ball with the child's eye while the child lay still and died.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Specimens of Bushman Folklore (Bleek & Lloyd 1911), section I.—5.; not verbatim.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase, same locus; not verbatim. The Mantis lay dreaming that the baboons had killed his son and made a ball of his eye. He shut his tears in, slung his rattling quiver, ran to the game, caught the flying eye as it passed, and whirled it round. He threw the eye toward the baboons; it ascended, played in the sky, and sprang into the little bag tied beside his quiver.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Specimens of Bushman Folklore (Bleek & Lloyd 1911), section I.—5.; not verbatim.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase, same locus; not verbatim. He put the child's eye into the water, saying: 'Thou must grow out, that thou mayest become like that which thou hast been.' The child grew again like its former self; the Mantis caught him as he basked by the water, anointed him with his scent, clothed him with the front kaross, and brought him home — while the young Ichneumon cried that the Mantis must have gone to put the eye into the water.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Specimens of Bushman Folklore (Bleek & Lloyd 1911), section I.—5.; not verbatim.

title.en: The Leopard Tortoise Traps the Hunters' Hands
title.zh: 豹龜困獵者之手

region.en: Katkop Mountains north of Calvinia, Northern Cape (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 南非北開普省卡爾維尼亞北方卡茲科普山（象徵定位）

period: Bushman (|Xam San) oral tradition; recorded 1875 by !Kweiten ta //Ken (Bleek & Lloyd)

source.work: Bleek & Lloyd, Specimens of Bushman Folklore (1911), 'The Story of the Leopard Tortoise'

summary.en: A sick woman of the early race asks passing hunters to rub her neck with fat; each man's hands decay to bare bone inside her neck. The leopard tortoise always seems about to die — she is the deceiver of the early race.
summary.zh: 早期之民病婦請過路獵者以脂膏擦頸；其手入頸即腐為枯骨。豹龜看似將死——實為早期之民的欺詐者。

sensitivity.note: |Xam San oral tradition dictated by !Kweiten ta //Ken to Bleek and Lloyd, 1875; presented as an archival record of 19th-century colonial recordings.

passages.text: The people had gone hunting; she was ill; and she perceived a man who came up to her hut; he had been hunting around. She asked the man to rub her neck a little with fat for her; for, it ached. The man rubbed it with fat for her. And she altogether held the man firmly with it. The man's hands altogether decayed away in it.
passages.note: Quote from Specimens of Bushman Folklore (Bleek & Lloyd 1911), section I.—7.B, p. 37 (public domain).

passages.text: Again, she espied another man, who came hunting. And she also spoke, she said: 'Rub me with fat a little.' He sat, putting his hands behind him, when the other man came, taking them out from the Leopard Tortoise's neck. He showed the other one his hands; and the other one's hands were altogether inside the Leopard Tortoise's neck.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Specimens of Bushman Folklore (Bleek & Lloyd 1911), pp. 37-39; not verbatim.

passages.text: He dashed the Leopard Tortoise upon the ground, while he desired that he should, by dashing it upon the ground, break the Leopard Tortoise. And the Leopard Tortoise held him fast. Then he returned home; and the people said: 'Art thou a fool? Did not thy parents instruct thee? The Leopard Tortoise always seems as if she would die; while she is deceiving us.'
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Specimens of Bushman Folklore (Bleek & Lloyd 1911), pp. 39-41; not verbatim.

title.en: The Moon's Water: Why Game Must Not Be Looked At
title.zh: 月之水：不可注視獵物之故

region.en: Katkop Mountains north of Calvinia, Northern Cape (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 南非北開普省卡茲科普山（象徵定位）

period: Bushman (|Xam San) oral tradition; recorded 1875 by Dia!kwain (Bleek & Lloyd)

source.work: Bleek & Lloyd, Specimens of Bushman Folklore (1911), 'The Moon is not to be looked at when Game has been shot'

summary.en: After shooting game the hunters may not look at the Moon: the beasts of prey will eat the dying animal. For the Moon's water — the honey-like dew — falls on game and makes it rise again; whoever looks at the Moon lets the game 'go along like the Moon,' away to a waterless place.
summary.zh: 射獲後不得仰月：獸將啖其獵物。月之水如蜜露，落於獸身使其復起；觀月者令獵物如月而行，引至無水之地。

sensitivity.note: |Xam San oral tradition dictated by Dia!kwain to Bleek and Lloyd, 1875; presented as an archival record of 19th-century colonial recordings.

passages.text: We may not look at the Moon, when we have shot game; for, we look, lowering our head, while we do not look up, towards the sky; while we are afraid of the Moon's shining. It is that which we fear. For, our mothers used to tell us about it, that the Moon is not a good person, if we look at him. For, if we look at him, when we have shot game, the beasts of prey will eat the game, when the game lies dying, if we look at the Moon.
passages.note: Quote from Specimens of Bushman Folklore (Bleek & Lloyd 1911), section II.—24, p. 67 (public domain).

passages.text: When the game does not die, the Moon's water is that which causes the game to live. For, our mothers used to tell us about it, that, the Moon's water yonder, (that) we see, which is on a bush, it resembles liquid honey. It is that which falls upon the game; the game arises, when it has fallen upon the game. It makes cool the poison with which we shot the game; and the game arises, it goes on... The Moon's water is that which cures it. And it lives, on account of it.
passages.note: Quote from Specimens of Bushman Folklore (Bleek & Lloyd 1911), pp. 67-68 (public domain); minor elisions.

passages.text: Therefore, our mothers did not wish us to be looking about, we should not look at the things which are in the sky... that the game which we had shot, would also go along like the Moon... he was not in the habit of going to a place near at hand, for, the day was used to break, while he was still going along. The game would also do the same, if we had looked at the Moon... we could go to die of thirst, while it, leading us astray, took us away to a place where no water was.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Specimens of Bushman Folklore (Bleek & Lloyd 1911), pp. 68-69; not verbatim.

title.en: The Mantis Throws His Shoe into the Sky: Origin of the Moon
title.zh: 螳螂擲鞋上天：月亮之源起

region.en: Strontbergen, Cape Colony (Northern Cape, South Africa)
region.zh: 南非北開普省斯特龍特山（象徵定位）

period: Bushman (|Xam San) oral tradition; recorded 1871-1875 (Bleek & Lloyd archive)

source.work: W. H. I. Bleek, A Brief Account of Bushman Folk-lore and other Texts (1875), §§ 3 and 16; Bleek & Lloyd, Specimens of Bushman Folklore (1911), footnote to p. 53

summary.en: Piercing the eland's gall, the Mantis creates a darkness into which he springs. Grope-blind among the bushes, he snatches off his shoe — dust and all — and throws it into the sky: 'this my shoe shall verily become the Moon, which shines in the dark.' The Moon is cold because it is leather; it is red because of the dust of Bushmanland; and it dies and lives again like a shoe thrown up and falling away.
summary.zh: 螳螂刺破羚膽，造暗而躍入。摸索林中，急脫其鞋連塵擲天：「吾鞋必為月，暗中照耀。」月冷因皮革；月紅因桑人之塵；月死而復生，如鞋拋落復揚。

sensitivity.note: |Xam San oral tradition from ||kabbo and Dia!kwain lines of the Bleek & Lloyd archive; presented as an archival record of 19th-century colonial recordings.

passages.text: His thinking-strings quickly told him to take off his shoe and throw it up into the sky, for the shoe to light up the earth for him. So he quickly snatched off the shoe from his foot, with the dust on it, he quickly threw it up... Then he saw the Mierkats standing cutting up the Eland in the dark.
passages.note: Quote from D. F. Bleek, The Mantis and His Friends (1924), 'The Mantis makes an Eland' (public domain).

passages.text: The Mantis said to them: 'You must hold a torch to light yourselves in cutting up the Eland, but my shoe stands up there in the sky where I have thrown it, to shine for me...' He said: 'I am the Mantis, and this my shoe shall verily become the moon which shines in the dark.' That is why the moon shines at night. That is why the moon is cold, because it is a shoe, it is leather. It is red, because it has earth on it, the dust in which the Mantis had walked.
passages.note: Quote from D. F. Bleek, The Mantis and His Friends (1924) (public domain).

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase of the long version: he threw the feather up, he said: 'Thou must now lie up in the sky, thou must henceforth be the Moon. Thou shalt shine at night. Thou shalt by thy shining lighten the darkness for men, till the Sun rises to light up all things for men... Thou art the Moon, thou dost give light for men, then thou dost fall away, thou dost return to life, when thou hast fallen away.' That is what the Moon does.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of D. F. Bleek, The Mantis and His Friends (1924), pp. 9-10; not verbatim.

title.en: The Sun's Knife Cuts the Moon Away
title.zh: 日刀割月

region.en: Strontbergen, Cape Colony (Northern Cape, South Africa)
region.zh: 南非北開普省斯特龍特山（象徵定位）

period: Bushman (|Xam San) oral tradition; recorded 1871-1875 (Bleek & Lloyd archive)

source.work: W. H. I. Bleek, A Brief Account of Bushman Folk-lore and other Texts (1875), §§ 15-16; Bleek & Lloyd, Specimens of Bushman Folklore (1911), pp. 50-53

summary.en: In astrological Bushman mythology the Moon is a man whom the Sun, jealous of his night light, stabs and cuts away with his knife of rays until one small piece is left — which the Moon piteously begs the Sun to spare for his children. From that backbone the Moon grows whole again, and the cutting begins again.
summary.zh: 桑人星象神話中，月本為人，因夜光遭日妒，被日以光芒之刀節節割削，僅餘小塊——月哀求日為其孩童留此脊椎。自小塊復長圓盈，割削復始。

sensitivity.note: |Xam San oral tradition from the Bleek & Lloyd archive; presented as an archival record of 19th-century colonial recordings.

passages.text: The Sun comes, the Sun follows the darkness, the Sun takes away the moon, the moon stands, the Sun pierces it, with the Sun's knife, as it stands; therefore, it decays away on account of it. Therefore, it says: 'O Sun! leave for the children the backbone!' Therefore, the Sun leaves the backbone for the children; the Sun does so.
passages.note: Quote from Specimens of Bushman Folklore (Bleek & Lloyd 1911), p. 51 (public domain).

passages.text: The Moon meant mankind to be like himself: dying, and then coming again living back... he again goes to become another moon, which is whole; he again lives... while he feels that he had seemed to die. Therefore, he becomes a new moon; while he feels that he has again put on a stomach; he becomes large; he comes, while he is alive. He goes along at night... while he feels that he is a shoe.
passages.note: Quote from Specimens of Bushman Folklore (Bleek & Lloyd 1911), pp. 52-53 (public domain), in the Sun-and-children narration.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase of W. H. I. Bleek's 1875 summary (§16): the Moon is looked upon as a man who incurs the wrath of the Sun, and is consequently pierced by the knife (rays) of the latter, until almost the whole of the Moon is cut away, and only one little piece left; which the Moon piteously implores the Sun to spare for his children. From this little piece the Moon gradually grows again until it becomes a full moon, when the Sun's stabbing recommences.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of A Brief Account of Bushman Folk-lore (Bleek 1875), §16; not verbatim.

title.en: The Girl of the Early Race Who Made Stars
title.zh: 早期之民造星少女

region.en: Strontbergen, Cape Colony (Northern Cape, South Africa)
region.zh: 南非北開普省斯特龍特山（象徵定位）

period: Bushman (|Xam San) oral tradition; recorded 1871-1873 by ||kabbo (Bleek & Lloyd)

source.work: Bleek & Lloyd, Specimens of Bushman Folklore (1911), 'The Girl of the Early Race, who made Stars'; W. H. I. Bleek, A Brief Account (1875), §23

summary.en: In her seclusion hut a girl of the ancient race, angry that her mother gives her too few |hum roots, throws wood-ashes into the sky — they become the Milky Way — and the roots become the red and white stars, while the peel of her food becomes locusts. She was at last shot by her husband. This is the star-creation story of the |Xam.
summary.zh: 初潮隔離之少女，怨母予根少，擲灰上天成銀河；根化紅白之星；果皮化飛蝗。後為夫所射。此即|Xam造星之神話。

sensitivity.note: |Xam San oral tradition dictated by ||kabbo to Bleek and Lloyd; girlhood seclusion customs are described; presented as an archival record of 19th-century colonial recordings.

narrative.en:
The girl of the early race had reached the age when a Bushman girl is put into a tiny hut with a very small door, which her mother closes upon her. She must not look at the springbok, lest they grow wild; she must not look afar. Her mother brings her food. One day the mother gave her too little of the |hum, the scented root eaten raw, and the girl grew hungry and angry in her hut.

She took up wood-ashes and threw them into the sky, saying: 'The wood ashes which are here, they must altogether become the Milky Way; they must white lie along in the sky, that the stars may stand outside of the Milky Way.' The ashes became the glowing arch of the night, and the stars, she said, should sail along their footprints, standing brightly around, so that the people might find their way home by night, in the middle of the night.

Still angry, she threw up the roots of the |hum she had been given: the red old roots became the red stars and the white young roots the white stars. Then she threw up the peel of the |khissi root she was eating, and the peel became locusts. The Milky Way gently glows, it is said, because it feels that it is wood ashes; it lights a little, so that the people can return home.

But the myth closes darkly. The first girl of the early race acted ill, the narrators say; and she was at last shot by her husband. Girls who transgressed the seclusion rules could fix with their glance the people and things they looked at (§24 of Bleek's Brief Account records men turned into trees by a maiden's glance), and the star-maker's fate warns against the powers of the isolated girl. Her creation stands: every clear night the ashes still lie white along the sky, and the stars sail along behind them. The narrators add the frame: the \xwi-\na-ssho-\k'e, the people of the early race, were said to be stupid and not to have understood things well; their doings are retold so that the Flat Bushmen may know what the first inhabitants of the land did. The girl's ashes were the first light of the night road, and her angry root-throwing peopled the sky; the Milky Way must go round with the stars, lying as it goes, and when the sun turns back the stars also turn back to fetch the daybreak. Bushman children are shown the arch and told that it gently glows because it remembers being wood ashes; and mothers warn their daughters in the seclusion hut with the same story, so that the angry, hungry girl inside the little door is also the maker of the stars she may not stare at too long.

functions: Charter narrative for the Milky Way and the stars of the |Xam sky.
Teaches the girlhood seclusion rules: what a maiden must not eat, see, or do.
Links anger and hunger in the seclusion hut to cosmic creation.

variants.name: Katkop-dialect girl (Dia!kwain's mother's telling)
variants.summary: A variant on the same seclusion girl exists in the Katkop dialect told to Dia!kwain by his mother, with the root-throwing episode elaborated.

variants.name: Maiden who fixed people as trees (Bleek §38)
variants.summary: Another maiden's glance turned people into talking trees; related to the same seclusion powers.

canonical_translation: Bleek & Lloyd translation, printed 1911

primary_sources.work: Bleek & Lloyd, Specimens of Bushman Folklore, 'The Girl of the Early Race, who made Stars'
primary_sources.citation: London: George Allen & Co., 1911, pp. 72-77; manuscript L II.—28. 2505-2520

primary_sources.work: W. H. I. Bleek, A Brief Account of Bushman Folk-lore and other Texts
primary_sources.citation: Cape Town/London 1875, §23

secondary_sources.work: D. F. Bleek, The Mantis and His Friends
secondary_sources.citation: Bleek, D. F. 1924. London: George Allen & Unwin.

secondary_sources.work: David Lewis-Williams, Believing and Seeing: Symbolic Meanings in Southern San Rock Paintings
secondary_sources.citation: Lewis-Williams, J. D. 1981. London: Academic Press.

source_urls.description: Scanned copy of Specimens of Bushman Folklore (1911)
Bleek's Brief Account of Bushman Folk-lore (1875)

sensitivity_guidance: Collected under colonial constraint (some informants were prisoners at the Breakwater); girls' rites appear here through male-colonial transcription — present with archival framing only.

passages.text: My mother was the one who told me that the girl arose; she put her hands into the wood ashes; she threw up the wood ashes into the sky. She said to the wood ashes: 'The wood ashes which are here, they must altogether become the Milky Way. They must white lie along in the sky, that the stars may stand outside of the Milky Way, while the Milky Way is the Milky Way, while it used to be wood ashes.'
passages.note: Quote from Specimens of Bushman Folklore (Bleek & Lloyd 1911), p. 73 (public domain).

passages.text: The Milky Way lying comes to its place... that it may descend nicely... The Stars shall also stand nicely around. They shall sail along upon their footprints, which they, always sailing along, are following... The Stars had been setting; they had, again, been coming out; they had, sailing along, been following their footprints. They become white, when the Sun comes out.
passages.note: Quote from Specimens of Bushman Folklore (Bleek & Lloyd 1911), p. 75 (public domain).

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase, same locus; not verbatim. She first gently threw up wood ashes into the sky, that she might presently throw up |hum roots; while she felt that she was angry with her mother, because her mother had not given her many |hum roots, that she might eat abundantly; for, she was in the hut. The red roots made red stars and the white roots white stars; the peel of the |khissi root she threw up became locusts. And the girl was at last shot by her husband.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Specimens of Bushman Folklore (Bleek & Lloyd 1911), pp. 76-77; not verbatim.

title.en: \gaunu, the Great Star Who Named the Stars
title.zh: 大星加烏奴：命名眾星者

region.en: Katkop Mountains north of Calvinia, Northern Cape (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 南非北開普省卡茲科普山（象徵定位）

period: Bushman (|Xam San) oral tradition; recorded 1875 by Dia!kwain (Bleek & Lloyd)

source.work: Bleek & Lloyd, Specimens of Bushman Folklore (1911), 'The Great Star, \gaunu, which, singing, named the Stars'

summary.en: \gaunu was once a great star; singing, he called out the names of all the stars, which is why the stars possess their names. The smallest, fine stars he made '\whai' — identified by the observatory with Altair and its neighbours — and the porcupine watches for them, for when they turn back it is dawn and he goes home.
summary.zh: 加烏奴昔為大星，唱而呼眾星之名，故眾星有其名。至小至細者，其名為'瓦海——經天文臺證為牛郎星（天鷹座α）。穿山甲候之：星回則天明，遂歸家。

sensitivity.note: |Xam San oral tradition dictated by Dia!kwain to Bleek and Lloyd, 1875; star identifications by Royal Observatory astronomers, 1873.

passages.text: \gaunu, he was formerly a great Star; therefore, his name is \gaunu, while he feels that he was the one who formerly spoke (called) the Stars' names; while he feels that he is a great one. Therefore, he called the Stars' names. Therefore, the Stars possess their names; while they feel that \gaunu was the one who called their names.
passages.note: Quote from Specimens of Bushman Folklore (Bleek & Lloyd 1911), p. 79 (public domain).

passages.text: He formerly sang, while he uttered the Stars' names. He said '\whai' to (some) Stars which are very small; they are those of which he made '\whai'; their small, fine ones are those which are '\whai'. [The stars \whai-gwai and \whai-|pua were identified as Altair and neighbouring stars of Aquila.]
passages.note: Quote from Specimens of Bushman Folklore (Bleek & Lloyd 1911), p. 79 with editor's bracketed note (public domain).

passages.text: Therefore, the porcupine, when these Stars have, sitting, turned back, he will not remain on the hunting ground; for, he knows that it is dawn, when '\whai' has, lying, turned back. He returns home; for, he is used to look at these Stars; they are those which he watches.
passages.note: Quote from Specimens of Bushman Folklore (Bleek & Lloyd 1911), p. 81 (public domain).

title.en: What the Stars Say: 'Tsau!'
title.zh: 星之所言：「呲！」

region.en: Strontbergen, Cape Colony (Northern Cape, South Africa)
region.zh: 南非北開普省斯特龍特山（象徵定位）

period: Bushman (|Xam San) oral tradition; recorded 1879 by /Han≠kass'o (Bleek & Lloyd)

source.work: Bleek & Lloyd, Specimens of Bushman Folklore (1911), 'What the Stars say, and a Prayer to a Star'

summary.en: On summer nights the stars cry 'Tsau! Tsau!' — they are cursing the shining eyes of springbok and the beasts of prey, which also gleam in the dark. The Bushman listens to the stars as a boy sleeping beside his grandfather, and learns their speech.
summary.zh: 夏夜星辰呼「呲！呲！」——詛咒羚羊與猛獸暗中閃耀之目。桑人童子偎祖父而眠，聆聽星語。

sensitivity.note: |Xam San oral tradition dictated by /Han≠kass'o to Bleek and Lloyd, 1879; presented as an archival record of 19th-century colonial recordings.

passages.text: They (the Bushmen) wish, that they may also perceive things. Therefore, they say that the Star shall take their heart, with which they do not a little hunger; the Star shall give them the Star's heart, — the Star's heart, — with which the Star sits in plenty. For the Star is not small; the Star seems as if it had food.
passages.note: Quote from Specimens of Bushman Folklore (Bleek & Lloyd 1911), p. 81 (public domain).

passages.text: The Stars are wont to call, 'Tsau! Tsau!' therefore the Bushmen are wont to say, that the Stars curse for them the springboks' eyes; the Stars say, 'Tsau!' they say, 'Tsau! Tsau!' I am one who was listening to them. I questioned my grandfather, what things it could be that spoke thus. My grandfather said to me that the Stars were those who spoke thus.
passages.note: Quote from Specimens of Bushman Folklore (Bleek & Lloyd 1911), pp. 81-82 (public domain).

passages.text: The Stars said, 'Tsau! Tsau!' Summer is (the time) when they sound. Because I used to sleep with my grandfather, I was the one who sat with my grandfather, when he sat in the coolness outside. Therefore, I questioned him, about the things which spoke thus. He said, the Stars were those who spoke thus; they cursed for the people the springboks' eyes.
passages.note: Quote from Specimens of Bushman Folklore (Bleek & Lloyd 1911), pp. 82-83 (public domain).

title.en: The Prayer to Canopus for a Shooting Arm
title.zh: 向老人星求臂之祈禱

region.en: Strontbergen, Cape Colony (Northern Cape, South Africa)
region.zh: 南非北開普省斯特龍特山（象徵定位）

period: Bushman (|Xam San) oral tradition; recorded 1879 by /Han≠kass'o (Bleek & Lloyd)

source.work: Bleek & Lloyd, Specimens of Bushman Folklore (1911), 'What the Stars say, and a Prayer to a Star'; W. H. I. Bleek, A Brief Account (1875), §60

summary.en: When Canopus rises the old man speaks to the 'Bushman-rice' star: give me thy heart, take mine; give me thy stomach, take mine; give me thy arm, which never misses — for my arm misses its aim. He speaks the prayer sitting in the cool, wishing the arrow might hit the springbok for him.
summary.zh: 老人星升時，老者向「桑人之米」星祈曰：取我之心，予爾飽足之心；取我之臂——常失之臂——予爾百發百中之臂。坐於涼處誦禱，望箭中羚。

sensitivity.note: |Xam San oral tradition dictated by /Han≠kass'o to Bleek and Lloyd, 1879; presented as an archival record of 19th-century colonial recordings.

passages.text: My grandfather used to speak to Canopus, when Canopus had newly come out; he said: 'Thou shalt give me thy heart, with which thou dost sit in plenty, thou shalt take my heart, — my heart, — with which I am desperately hungry. That I might also be full, like thee. For, I hunger. For, thou seemest to be satisfied (with food); hence thou art not small. For, I am hungry.'
passages.note: Quote from Specimens of Bushman Folklore (Bleek & Lloyd 1911), p. 83 (public domain).
