passages.text: 'Thou shalt give me thy stomach, with which thou art satisfied. Thou shalt take my stomach, that thou mayst also hunger. Give thou me also thy arm, thou shalt take my arm, with which I do not kill. For, I miss my aim. Thou shalt give me thy arm. For, my arm which is here, I miss my aim with it.'
passages.note: Quote from Specimens of Bushman Folklore (Bleek & Lloyd 1911), p. 83 (public domain).

passages.text: He desired that the arrow might hit the springbok for him; hence, he wished the Star to give him the Star's arm, while the Star took his arm, with which he missed his aim. He shut his mouth, he moved away, he sat down; while he felt that he wished to sit and sharpen an arrow.
passages.note: Quote from Specimens of Bushman Folklore (Bleek & Lloyd 1911), pp. 83-84 (public domain).

title.en: Dawn's-Heart and the Lynx: The Star Husband's Wife
title.zh: 晨心星與天貓：星夫之妻

region.en: Strontbergen, Cape Colony (Northern Cape, South Africa)
region.zh: 南非北開普省斯特龍特山（象徵定位）

period: Bushman (|Xam San) oral tradition; recorded 1879 by /Han≠kass'o (Bleek & Lloyd)

source.work: Bleek & Lloyd, Specimens of Bushman Folklore (1911), '\ko-g\nuih-tara, wife of the Dawn's-Heart Star, Jupiter'; W. H. I. Bleek, A Brief Account (1875), §25

summary.en: Jupiter, the Dawn's-Heart star, married the Lynx, then a beautiful woman; the hyena, jealous, bewitched her with poisoned 'Bushman rice' so she became a lioness, and by night took her place in the hut. The star's eyes glowed like fires as he came home; he stabbed at the impostor, missed, and his wife, enticed from the reeds and stripped of her lion skin, could never eat Bushman rice again — she became the lynx that eats meat.
summary.zh: 晨心星（木星）娶天貓——其時為美婦；土狼妒之，以毒「桑人之米」巫化其為母獅，夜間代居其位。星目如火歸家；擲矛擊偽者不中；其妻自蘆葦被誘出，剝獅皮復為人——然終不復食桑人之米，遂為食肉之獰貓。

sensitivity.note: |Xam San oral tradition dictated by /Han≠kass'o (from his mother |xabbi-an) to Bleek and Lloyd, 1879; presented as an archival record of 19th-century colonial recordings.

narrative.en:
The Dawn's-Heart (Jupiter) had a beautiful wife of the early race and a younger sister-in-law, \xe-dde-yoe, who carried the digging-stick and minded the child. The Dawn's-Heart buried his child under the leaves of an edible root, hoping his wife would find it; other animals and birds arrived first and each proposed herself as mother, and the child mocked them until it recognized its own mother. Among the insulted animals were the Jackal and the Hyena, who plotted revenge.

They bewitched the Lynx with poisoned 'Bushman rice' — so-called ants' eggs — and she was transformed into a lioness. In the dark the Hyena tried to take her place in the hut when the Dawn's-Heart returned; but he noticed that the woman who sat with her back toward him was not his wife, and his sister-in-law told him of the imposture. He seized his assegai and stabbed at the place where the Hyena had been sitting; she sprang out, trod burning her foot in the fire, and fled, leaving the ornaments she had worn.

The bewitched wife had hidden in the reeds. Her sister called her at morning and again near sunset, and each time she came out to suckle the child, saying that her thinking-strings were falling, that she was forgetting. At last the sister brought goats, and the people hid around; when the wife sprang from the reeds to the goats, the Dawn's-Heart caught her and all the people held her fast. They cut open the goats, took out the contents of the stomachs and anointed her, rubbing off the lion hair; she asked that the hair on the tips of her ears be left, 'for in that manner I shall come to hear.'

She became a fair woman again; but because she had been bewitched by Bushman rice she could no longer eat it. She was changed into the lynx who eats meat, and the Dawn's-Heart, going home from hunting ever after, walked with an arrow on the bow and the assegai stuck in the ground, his eyes large like fires — for the hyenas had poisoned his wife, and his heart would never be quiet again. The discourses attached to this myth are long: the Dawn's-Heart talks to his daughter of their own history, of the lynx-mother, of the sun, moon and stars, and of the habits of lions and Bushmen, running at last into a whole account of the jackals' doings; and the fugitive hyena, her foot burnt in the fire, is followed home through long speeches with her mother and father about suitable marriages. In the second long piece the narrative of about seventy-two columns is followed by the hyena family's talk. The stars keep the story in the sky: Jupiter walks as the only Dawn's-Heart when his heart-daughter is swallowed, and precedes the Dawn's-Heart-child; the identification with Regulus was made at the Cape Observatory in the 1870s, on the narrators' pointing. The myth also fixes Bushman hut etiquette — the wife sits facing her husband, and the stranger who sits with her back to the door is the one to be suspected — and it teaches that poisoned food given in beauty is the most dangerous gift of all, for the Lynx ate what was offered to her and never tasted Bushman-rice again.

functions: Explains the lynx's diet and the tufts on its ears.
Charter for the woman 'sitting with her back' etiquette of the hut.
Links the planet Jupiter and his child-star to a domestic tragedy of the early race.

passages.text: And \kó-g\nuin-tdra exclaimed, she said to her younger sister: 'Thou shalt leave this |haken alone; I will be the one who eats it. For, thou art the one who shalt take care of the child. For, this |haken, its smell is not nice.' Therefore, as \kó-g\nuin-tdra sat, eating the |haken, the ornaments of themselves came off.
passages.note: Quote from Specimens of Bushman Folklore (Bleek & Lloyd 1911), p. 86 (public domain).

passages.text: Then the Dawn's-Heart ran to the hyena; he took aim (with his assegai), he pierced the place where the hyena had been sitting, while the hyena sprang out, she trod, burning herself in the fire, while she sprang away; while the ornaments remained at the place where she had been sitting... And the Dawn's-Heart scolded his younger sister-in-law, why was it that his younger sister-in-law had not quickly told him about it.
passages.note: Quote from Specimens of Bushman Folklore (Bleek & Lloyd 1911), pp. 92-93 (public domain).

passages.text: They cut the goats open, they took out the contents of the stomach, they anointed \kó-g\nuin-tdra with the contents of the stomachs. They, taking hold, rubbed off the hair from her skin. Therefore, when she sat down, she said: 'Ye must, pulling, leave the hair on the tips of my ears; for, in that manner I shall come to hear; for, I do not feel as if I should hear.'
passages.note: Quote from Specimens of Bushman Folklore (Bleek & Lloyd 1911), pp. 95-96 (public domain).

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase of Bleek's 1875 summary (§25): the mother of the Dawn's-Heart-child was the Lynx, who was then a beautiful woman; she was bewitched with poisoned Bushman rice and transformed into a lioness; her brothers pulled off the lion skin so that she became a fair woman again; but, in consequence of having been bewitched by Bushman rice, she could no longer eat that, and was changed into a lynx who ate meat.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of A Brief Account of Bushman Folk-lore (Bleek 1875), §25; not verbatim.

title.en: The Dawn's-Heart Swallows His Child
title.zh: 晨心星吞其女

region.en: Strontbergen, Cape Colony (Northern Cape, South Africa)
region.zh: 南非北開普省斯特龍特山（象徵定位）

period: Bushman (|Xam San) oral tradition; recorded 1875 (Bleek archive)

source.work: W. H. I. Bleek, A Brief Account of Bushman Folk-lore and other Texts (1875), §25; Specimens of Bushman Folklore (1911), p. 96 extract

summary.en: The Dawn's-Heart star has a daughter, his 'heart': he swallows her, walks alone as the only Dawn's-Heart, and when she is grown spits her out again. She becomes another female Dawn's-Heart and spits out another child which follows the pair — the recurring star-child that follows Jupiter across the sky.
summary.zh: 晨心星有一女，是其「心」：吞之，獨行為唯一晨心星；及長復吐出。女遂為另一晨心星，再吐新女隨行——即天上恆隨木星之 repeat 星子。

sensitivity.note: |Xam San star lore from the Bleek & Lloyd archive; presented as an archival record of 19th-century colonial recordings.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase of Bleek's summary (§25): the Dawn's-Heart (the star Jupiter) has a daughter, who is identified with some neighbouring star preceding Jupiter. Her name is the Dawn's-Heart-child, and her relation to her father is somewhat mysterious. He calls her 'my heart', he swallows her, then walks alone as the only Dawn's-Heart Star, and, when she is grown up, he spits her out again.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of A Brief Account of Bushman Folk-lore (Bleek 1875), §25; not verbatim.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase, same locus; not verbatim. She then herself becomes another female Dawn's-Heart, and spits out another Dawn's-Heart-child, which follows the male and female Dawn's-Heart. The Dawn's-Heart hid his first child under the leaves of an edible root, where he thought that his wife would come and find it.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of A Brief Account of Bushman Folk-lore (Bleek 1875), §25; not verbatim.

title.en: The Son of the Wind Rolls the Ball
title.zh: 風之子滾球

region.en: Strontbergen, Cape Colony (Northern Cape, South Africa)
region.zh: 南非北開普省斯特龍特山（象徵定位）

period: Bushman (|Xam San) oral tradition; recorded 1878 by /Han≠kass'o (Bleek & Lloyd)

source.work: Bleek & Lloyd, Specimens of Bushman Folklore (1911), 'The Son of the Wind'

summary.en: The Wind's child rolls a ball to |na-ka-ti, calling his name, but no one knows his; his mother warns |na-ka-ti to utter the name only when the hut is screened, and then run in — for the Wind will blow him away. |na-ka-ti shouts '\erriten-\kuan-\kuan!' and the storm flattens the boy and drives the huts apart; only the Wind's mother can raise him up. The Wind lies when it blows hard, and stands when it is still; and the Wind was once a man who became a bird that dwells in a mountain hole.
summary.zh: 風子滾球喚名，無人知其名；母囑：俟屏帳成方可呼其名，呼畢速入屋，防風捲走。名既出，颶風立至，掀屋倒童；唯風母扶之起。風猛吹時乃「臥」，靜時乃「立」；風本為人，化鳥棲山穴。

sensitivity.note: |Xam San oral tradition dictated by /Han≠kass'o to Bleek and Lloyd, 1878; presented as an archival record of 19th-century colonial recordings.

passages.text:
The (son of the) Wind was formerly still. And he rolled (a ball) to 
a-ka-ti. He exclaimed: 'O 
a-ka-ti! There it goes!' And 
a-ka-ti exclaimed: 'O comrade! There it goes!' because 
a-ka-ti felt that he did not know his (the other one's) name.
passages.note: Quote from Specimens of Bushman Folklore (Bleek & Lloyd 1911), p. 101 (public domain).

passages.text: His mother exclaimed: 'I will not utter to thee comrade's name. For, thou shalt wait; that father may first shelter for us the hut... And thou shalt, when I have uttered for thee comrade's name, thou must scamper away, thou must run home, that thou mayest come into the hut, whilst thou dost feel that the wind would blow thee away.'
passages.note: Quote from Specimens of Bushman Folklore (Bleek & Lloyd 1911), pp. 102-103 (public domain).

passages.text: He beheld that his father had finished sheltering the hut, then he exclaimed: 'There it goes! O \erriten-\kuan-\kuan! There it goes! O \gau-\gaubu-ti! There it goes!' And he scampered away, he ran home; while the other one began to lean over, and the other one fell down. He lay kicking violently upon the vlei. Therefore, the people's huts vanished away, the wind blew, breaking their sheltering bushes, together with the huts.
passages.note: Quote from Specimens of Bushman Folklore (Bleek & Lloyd 1911), pp. 104-105 (public domain).

passages.text: His mother came out of the hut; his mother came, grasping (him), to raise him up... Therefore, the wind became still... Therefore, we who are Bushmen, we are wont to say: 'The wind seems to be lying down, for, it does not gently blow.' The Wind (the Wind's son) was formerly a man. He became a bird. And he was flying... he dwelt in a mountain (that is, in a mountain hole).
passages.note: Quote from Specimens of Bushman Folklore (Bleek & Lloyd 1911), pp. 106-107 (public domain).

title.en: \kagara and \haunu Fight with Lightning
title.zh: 卡加拉與哈烏奴雷電相鬥

region.en: Strontbergen, Cape Colony (Northern Cape, South Africa)
region.zh: 南非北開普省斯特龍特山（象徵定位）

period: Bushman (|Xam San) oral tradition; recorded 1879 by /Han≠kass'o (Bleek & Lloyd)

source.work: Bleek & Lloyd, Specimens of Bushman Folklore (1911), '\kagara and \haunu, who fought each other with Lightning'

summary.en: \kagara the little bird-man rescues his sister from her husband \haunu, a Rain sorcerer. The brother-in-law sneezes blood and lightens at them; \kagara fends off the strokes and at last strikes back with the black lightning that kills, felling \haunu, who lies thundering. The grandmothers said these two fight in the east whenever the clouds stand like a mountain.
summary.zh: 小鳥人卡加拉自其妹夫——雨巫哈烏奴——處奪回妹妹。妹夫噴血閃電擊之；卡加拉揮臂格擋，終以「黑雷」反擊，擊倒哈烏奴，其臥而雷吼。祖母云：雲聚如山時，此二人在東方相鬥。

sensitivity.note: |Xam San oral tradition dictated by /Han≠kass'o (from his grandmother ≠kammi) to Bleek and Lloyd, 1879; presented as an archival record of 19th-century colonial recordings.

passages.text: They formerly, \kagara formerly went to fetch his younger sister, he went to take her away; he went to take her away from \haunu; and he took (her) back to her parents. \haunu gave chase to his brother-in-law, he passed along behind the hill. The clouds came, clouds which were unequalled in beauty; they vanished away.
passages.note: Quote from Specimens of Bushman Folklore (Bleek & Lloyd 1911), p. 113 (public domain).

passages.text: Then \haunu sneezed, on account of it; blood poured out of his nostrils; he stealthily lightened at his brother-in-law. His brother-in-law fended him quickly off, his brother-in-law also stealthily lightened at him. He quickly fended off his brother-in-law. His brother-in-law also lightened at him.
passages.note: Quote from Specimens of Bushman Folklore (Bleek & Lloyd 1911), pp. 115-116 (public domain).

passages.text: Then he stealthily lightened at his younger sister's husband with black lightning, he, lightening, whisked him up (and carried him to a little distance). His younger sister's husband, in this manner, lay dying; he, in this manner, he thundered, while \kagara bound up his head with the net, he, returning, arrived at home... they went along angry with each other.
passages.note: Quote from Specimens of Bushman Folklore (Bleek & Lloyd 1911), p. 117 (public domain).

passages.text: My grandmothers used to say: '\kagara and his companion are those who fight in the East, he and \haunu.' When the clouds were thick, and the clouds resembled a mountain, then, the clouds were lightening, on account of it. And my grandmothers used to say: 'It is \kagara, with \haunu.'
passages.note: Quote from Specimens of Bushman Folklore (Bleek & Lloyd 1911), p. 118 (public domain).

title.en: The Hyena's Revenge on the Grudging Lion
title.zh: 土狼報復吝獅

region.en: Katkop Mountains north of Calvinia, Northern Cape (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 南非北開普省卡茲科普山（象徵定位）

period: Bushman (|Xam San) oral tradition; recorded 1871 and 1875 (Bleek & Lloyd)

source.work: Bleek & Lloyd, Specimens of Bushman Folklore (1911), 'The Hyena's Revenge' (two versions); W. H. I. Bleek, A Brief Account (1875), §27

summary.en: The lion grudges the hyena his meat; the hyena invites him home, ladles boiling soup into his mouth, jams the hot pot over his head, and beats him dead beneath it. In the second version the lion, who also eats people, has carried off an old woman, and the hyena strikes him down while his head is inside the pot.
summary.zh: 獅吝於予土狼肉；土狼邀其至家，以滾湯灌其口，覆熱釜其首，擊殺之。第二版中，食人之獅已擄一老嫗；土狼趁其首入釜時擊斃之。

sensitivity.note: |Xam San fable from the Bleek & Lloyd archive; presented as an archival record of 19th-century colonial recordings.

passages.text: The Hyena was the one who went to the Lion's house, then, he deceived the Lion; while he felt that the Lion had acted grudgingly towards him about the quagga's flesh; therefore, the Lion came to the Hyena's house, when the Hyena was boiling there in the Hyena's pot; the Hyena boiled ostrich flesh in it.
passages.note: Quote from Specimens of Bushman Folklore (Bleek & Lloyd 1911), p. 123 (public domain).

passages.text: The Hyena gave soup to the Lion; therefore, the Lion took hold of the pot, while the pot was hot; the Hyena also grasped the pot with his hands; the Hyena said: 'O Lion! Allow me to pour soup into the inside of thy mouth.' The Hyena poured soup into the Lion's mouth; then, he put the mouth of the pot over the Lion's head, while the pot was hot.
passages.note: Quote from Specimens of Bushman Folklore (Bleek & Lloyd 1911), p. 123 (public domain).

passages.text: The soup was burning the Lion's eyes; the soup also burned the inside of his mouth. Then, he swallowed hot soup with his throat, he swallowed, causing himself to die with hot soup; he died, while his head was inside the pot. The Hyena took up the Hyena's stick, the Hyena was beating him with the stick, while his head was inside the pot; the Hyena was beating him; the Hyena struck, cleaving the pot asunder.
passages.note: Quote from Specimens of Bushman Folklore (Bleek & Lloyd 1911), pp. 123-124 (public domain).

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase of the second version: the Hyena said 'I am accustomed to pour soup into this child's mouth, I also pour soup into my wife's mouth' — and poured soup into the Lion's mouth, put the Lion's head into the pot, while he felt that he altogether put the Lion's head into the pot; that he might altogether kill the Lion with the soup's heat; and he carried off the old woman on account of it, and struck the Lion down while his head was inside the pot.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Specimens of Bushman Folklore (Bleek & Lloyd 1911), pp. 126-127; not verbatim.

title.en: The Lion Jealous of the Ostrich's Voice
title.zh: 獅妒鴕鳥之聲

region.en: Katkop Mountains north of Calvinia, Northern Cape (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 南非北開普省卡茲科普山（象徵定位）

period: Bushman (|Xam San) oral tradition; recorded 1875 by Dia!kwain (Bleek & Lloyd)

source.work: Bleek & Lloyd, Specimens of Bushman Folklore (1911), 'The Lion jealous of the Voice of the Ostrich'

summary.en: The women praise the ostrich's booming; the jealous lion makes them stage a dance, kicks the ostrich's chest as he sings, tears it open, kills him and eats his lungs raw to boom like him. The ostrich's nail decayed from the kick — the scar on its chest is still the lion's nail — and boys must swallow the lungs whole and raw to keep the voice.
summary.zh: 婦人讚鴕鳥鳴聲；獅妒，令婦起舞，趁其鳴時踢其胸膛，撕裂殺之，生吞其肺以效其聲。鴕鳥之爪因踢而朽——胸上疤痕至今乃獅之爪痕。男孩須生吞整肺以存其聲。

sensitivity.note: |Xam San fable dictated by Dia!kwain to Bleek and Lloyd, 1875; presented as an archival record of 19th-century colonial recordings.

passages.text: The Lions conspired together that they might deceive the Ostrich; for, the women were wont, with regard to the Ostrich, they only praised the Ostrich for calling finely; the women did not praise them. And they (the Lions), speaking, said: 'In what manner shall we deceive?'
passages.note: Quote from Specimens of Bushman Folklore (Bleek & Lloyd 1911), p. 128 (public domain).

passages.text: The other Lion answered, he said: 'The ostrich calls with his lungs; therefore, his throat sounds in this manner; his chest's front. Thou dost call with thy mouth; therefore, thou dost not call nicely.' The other Lion answered: 'Ye must make a (game of) \gebbi-ggu, that ye may kill the Ostrich, that ye may take out the Ostrich's lungs... and ye will call, sounding like the Ostrich, when ye have eaten the Ostrich's lungs.'
passages.note: Quote from Specimens of Bushman Folklore (Bleek & Lloyd 1911), pp. 129-130 (public domain).

passages.text: The Ostrich was still yonder at his house; the Lion called; the women did not applaud the Lion, because they felt that the Lion did not call well... And the Ostrich came; and the Ostrich called, sounding afar. And the women exclaimed: 'I do wish that the Lion called in this manner; for, he sounds as if he had put his tail into his mouth, while the Ostrich calls in a resounding manner.'
passages.note: Quote from Specimens of Bushman Folklore (Bleek & Lloyd 1911), pp. 130-131 (public domain).

passages.text: He scratched, tearing it. And he called out: 'Is it a thing which calls sweetly?' while he kicked the Ostrich's chest. And the Ostrich also quickly turned back. And the Ostrich also kicked, tearing his chest... My grandfather also gave us the Ostrich's lungs to eat, that we might also resemble the Ostrich... our grandfather spoke... that we should not cook the Ostrich's lungs... we should not chew them, we should swallow them down, while they were whole.
passages.note: Quote from Specimens of Bushman Folklore (Bleek & Lloyd 1911), pp. 131-134 (public domain), minor elisions.

title.en: The Resurrection of the Ostrich from a Bloody Feather
title.zh: 鴕鳥自血羽復生

region.en: Katkop Mountains north of Calvinia, Northern Cape (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 南非北開普省卡茲科普山（象徵定位）

period: Bushman (|Xam San) oral tradition; recorded c. 1871 by !A!kunta (Bleek & Lloyd)

source.work: Bleek & Lloyd, Specimens of Bushman Folklore (1911), 'The Resurrection of the Ostrich'; W. H. I. Bleek, A Brief Account (1875), §34

summary.en: A hunter kills a male ostrich at its nest; a whirlwind lifts one blood-stained little feather into the sky, drops it into water, and there it becomes ostrich flesh, gains feathers, legs and bone, walks out of the water and returns to his wives as their regained husband. With the Moon and the male ostrich alone of mortal things, he dies and lives again.
summary.zh: 獵者於巢處殺雄鴕；旋風捲血羽上天，落入水中，漸成鴕肉，生羽生足生骨，出水而行，歸其妻為復得之夫。世間凡死不復生者眾，唯月與雄鴕，死而復生。

sensitivity.note: |Xam San oral tradition dictated by !A!kunta to Bleek and Lloyd, c. 1871; presented as an archival record of 19th-century colonial recordings.

narrative.en:
The Bushman kills an ostrich at its eggs and carries the bird home; the wife strips off the bloody short feathers and lays them on the bushes, and the family eats the meat. Then a little whirlwind comes, blows up one small bloodied feather, and lifts it into the sky. It whirls down, falls into the water, becomes wet — and becomes conscious. It lies in the water and becomes ostrich flesh.

In the water it puts on wings and gains its legs; then it walks out of the water and basks on the bank in the sun, for it is still a young ostrich with black quills. It dries its feathers lying on the water's bank, strengthening its feet, hardening its breastbone into bone, eating young bushes, growing. Its little feather it was which became the ostrich, blown up while the wind was a little whirlwind.

It thinks of the place where it scratched its nest; it lets itself grow first, then goes to its old house, to scratch there again, and calls its wives. Because he did die, he will marry three ostrich wives. He roars, hardening his ribs, that his ribs may become bone; he scratches out a house, and roars to call the females, that they may come to him. He meets them, runs round them, examines their feathers, drives them to the house to lay; he lies inside, guards the eggs against the jackal, and drives the jackal away with his feet — for his children are in the nest.

Bleek's summary adds the myth's frame: this idea of revival through a feather is compared to the Moon's revival; and, with the exception of the Moon and the male ostrich, all other mortal things die outright and do not come to life again — the myth is thus a twin to the Moon's monthly rebirth, and its denial is part of the death-decree world. Bleek's summary adds the myth's frame and its dialogue: the revived bird guards the nest against the attacks of the jackals and hyenas, who are thereby driven to seek for the nest of a she-ostrich who will not be fierce, and who runs away; and the flights of the two cowards are followed in a long, still unfinished dialogue between hyena and jackal. The idea of the revival of a dead male ostrich in and through one of its little feathers is also mentioned elsewhere and is compared to the coming to life of the Moon; whilst, with the exception of the Moon and the male ostrich, all other mortal things are said to die outright and not to come to life again. The hunter who told it had watched the whirlwind lift the plume, and the family stood at the water and saw the flesh come upon it; the myth is thus both an observation of the veld and a resurrection doctrine, for it grants to the ostrich the same monthly immortality as the Moon alone possesses among the old people's dead.

functions: Presents the single great exception to the finality of death.
Explains the male ostrich's nesting behaviour and fierceness at the nest.
Links avian resurrection to lunar resurrection in Bushman eschatology.

variants.name: Short 1875 version (B XII.1171-1213)
variants.summary: Brief outline of the feather's revival, ending with the ostrich guarding the nest and driving off jackals and hyenas.

variants.name: Moon's revival parallel (§16, §34)
variants.summary: The ostrich's return is explicitly compared with the Moon's monthly coming to life again.

passages.text: The Bushman kills an Ostrich at the Ostrich's eggs; he carries away the Ostrich to the house... A little whirlwind comes to them; it blows up the Ostrich feathers. A little Ostrich feather that has blood upon it, it blows up the little feather into the sky. The little feather falls down out of the sky, it having whirled round falls down, it goes into the water, it becomes wet in the water, it is conscious, it lies in the water, it becomes Ostrich flesh; it gets feathers, it puts on its wings, it gets its legs, while it lies in the water.
passages.note: Quote from Specimens of Bushman Folklore (Bleek & Lloyd 1911), pp. 137-138 (public domain).

passages.text: It walks out of the water, it basks in the sun upon the water's edge, because it is still a young Ostrich... He dries (his feathers) lying upon the water's bank, that he may afterwards walk away... He swallows young plants which are small... His little feather it was which became the Ostrich, it was that which the wind blew up, while the wind was a little whirlwind.
passages.note: Quote from Specimens of Bushman Folklore (Bleek & Lloyd 1911), pp. 138-140 (public domain).

passages.text: Because his breastbone is bone, he roars, hardening his ribs, that his ribs may become bone. Then he scratches (out a house)... he roaring calls the Ostrich wives, that the Ostrich wives may come to him... he meets them, that he may run round the females; for he had been dead; he dying left his wives.
passages.note: Quote from Specimens of Bushman Folklore (Bleek & Lloyd 1911), pp. 140-141 (public domain).

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase of Bleek's 1875 summary (§34): a male ostrich is killed and carried home by a Bushman; one of its little feathers, stained with blood, is lifted up by a gentle whirlwind and falls into the water, where it gradually becomes an ostrich; it leaves the water as a young ostrich, grows up, and returns to its wives as their regained husband. This idea of revival is compared to the coming to life of the Moon; with the exception of the Moon and the male ostrich, all other mortal things die outright.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of A Brief Account of Bushman Folk-lore (Bleek 1875), §34; not verbatim.

title.en: The Vultures, Their Elder Sister, and Her Husband
title.zh: 兀鷲、其姊與姊夫

region.en: Strontbergen, Cape Colony (Northern Cape, South Africa)
region.zh: 南非北開普省斯特龍特山（象徵定位）

period: Bushman (|Xam San) oral tradition; recorded 1879 by /Han≠kass'o (Bleek & Lloyd)

source.work: Bleek & Lloyd, Specimens of Bushman Folklore (1911), 'The Vultures, their elder Sister, and her Husband'

summary.en: The vultures made a woman of the early race their elder sister and lived by her husband's kills; scolded for devouring the springbok, they fly up into the sky and look down, swooping only when game is sighted — and eating in such haste that they must leave the undercut for their sister.
summary.zh: 兀鷲以早期之民女子為姊，賴其夫所獵而活；因吞盡跳羚遭斥，乃飛上天空俯瞰，見獸方落，倉促啄食——須留「腹條」與其姊。

sensitivity.note: |Xam San oral tradition dictated by /Han≠kass'o to Bleek and Lloyd, 1879; presented as an archival record of 19th-century colonial recordings.

passages.text: The Vultures formerly made their elder sister of a person; they lived with her. They, when their elder sister's husband brought (home) a springbok, they ate up the springbok. And their elder sister's husband cursed them, he scolded at them. And their elder sister took up the skin of the springbok, she singed it.
passages.note: Quote from Specimens of Bushman Folklore (Bleek & Lloyd 1911), p. 155 (public domain).

passages.text: They said, this other one said: 'Thou shalt ascend, and then thou must come to tell us what the place seems to be like.'... a Vulture who was a little Vulture girl, she arose, she ascended... she went, disappearing in the sky, they no longer perceived her... Then, their younger sister descended from above out of the sky, she came and sat in the midst of them.
passages.note: Quote from Specimens of Bushman Folklore (Bleek & Lloyd 1911), pp. 159-160 (public domain).

passages.text: And she said: 'There is nothing the matter with the place; for, the place is clear. The place is very beautiful; for, I do behold the whole place... the place seems as if we should perceive a springbok, if a springbok were lying under a tree; for the place is very beautiful.' Then, they altogether arose, all of them, they ascended into the sky.
passages.note: Quote from Specimens of Bushman Folklore (Bleek & Lloyd 1911), pp. 160-161 (public domain).

passages.text: They said: 'Ye must eat! ye must eat! ye must eat in great haste! for, that accursed man who comes yonder, he could not endure us.' And, they finished the springbok, they flew away, flew heavily away... Their elder sister said: 'Fie! how can ye act in this manner towards me? as if I had been the one who scolded you!'
passages.note: Quote from Specimens of Bushman Folklore (Bleek & Lloyd 1911), pp. 161-162 (public domain).

title.en: Ddi-≠erreten, the Stone-Headed Man and the Lioness's Children
title.zh: 石頭人與母獅之子

region.en: Strontbergen, Cape Colony (Northern Cape, South Africa)
region.zh: 南非北開普省斯特龍特山（象徵定位）

period: Bushman (|Xam San) oral tradition; recorded 1879 by /Han≠kass'o (Bleek & Lloyd)

source.work: Bleek & Lloyd, Specimens of Bushman Folklore (1911), 'Ddi-≠erreten, the Lioness, and the Children'

summary.en: A sick lioness gathers people's children to live with her at the water; Ddi-≠erreten — a man of the early race whose head is stone — sits in her house and sends the children home in batches, telling each that its people's fire burns at the head of this or that ravine. Returning, the lioness finds only the stone head; she bites it, shrieks at her broken teeth, and he goes home, telling her only: 'Our children were not.'
summary.zh: 病母獅聚人童同居水邊；石頭人Ddi-≠erreten入其屋，分批遣童歸家，告以各溝源處其族火所在。母獅歸，唯見石首；咬之，痛呼碎牙。石首唯答：「吾童本非爾有。」

sensitivity.note: |Xam San oral tradition dictated by /Han≠kass'o to Bleek and Lloyd, 1879; presented as an archival record of 19th-century colonial recordings.

passages.text: Ddi-≠erreten, formerly, when the Lioness was at the water, dipping up water there, Ddi-≠erreten felt that the Lioness was the one who had gathered together the people's children, because the Lioness felt that she was an invalid on account of her chest; therefore, she gathered together the people's children, that the children might live with her, that the children might work for her.
passages.note: Quote from Specimens of Bushman Folklore (Bleek & Lloyd 1911), pp. 163-164 (public domain).

passages.text: Ddi-≠erreten said: 'O children sitting here! The fire of your people is that which is at the top of the ravine which comes down from the top (of the hill).' Therefore, two children arose, they went away to their own people. Ddi-≠erreten again said... 'The fire of your people is that which is below the top of the ravine which comes down on this side (of the hill).' And three children thus went.
passages.note: Quote from Specimens of Bushman Folklore (Bleek & Lloyd 1911), pp. 164-166 (public domain).

passages.text: And the Lioness came from the water, she thus returning came. She came along looking (at the house); she did not perceive the children. And she exclaimed: 'Why do the children not do so to me?... It must be this man who sits at the house; his head resembles Ddi-≠erreten.' And she became angry about it, when she perceived Ddi-≠erreten.
passages.note: Quote from Specimens of Bushman Folklore (Bleek & Lloyd 1911), pp. 166-167 (public domain).

passages.text: The Lioness caught hold of his head. She exclaimed 'Growling' to the other one's head. And she exclaimed: 'Oh! Oh dear! my teeth! This must be why this cursed man's big head came to sit in front of my house!' While Ddi-≠erreten said: 'I told thee that our children they were not.'... And he arose, he returned home; while the Lioness sat in anger at her house... she did not a little love the children while she was doing so.
passages.note: Quote from Specimens of Bushman Folklore (Bleek & Lloyd 1911), pp. 168-169 (public domain).

title.en: The Mason Wasp Shoots His Wife
title.zh: 泥蜂射妻

region.en: Strontbergen, Cape Colony (Northern Cape, South Africa)
region.zh: 南非北開普省斯特龍特山（象徵定位）

period: Bushman (|Xam San) oral tradition; recorded 1878 by /Han≠kass'o (Bleek & Lloyd)

source.work: Bleek & Lloyd, Specimens of Bushman Folklore (1911), 'The Mason Wasp and his Wife'

summary.en: A wife mocks her wasp-husband's thin body when he finally lays down his kaross to shoot a hare; enraged, he turns and shoots her through the breastbone — then cries for his wife as if he had not been the shooter.
summary.zh: 妻譏泥蜂夫之瘦軀，夫怒而轉身射穿其胸骨——隨後呼妻痛哭，若非己射者然。

sensitivity.note: |Xam San fable dictated by /Han≠kass'o to Bleek and Lloyd, 1878; contains domestic violence; presented as an archival record.

passages.text: The Mason Wasp formerly did thus as he walked along, while (his) wife walked behind him, the wife said: 'O my husband! Shoot for me that hare!'... And the wife said: 'Put down thy kaross! Why is it that thou art not willing to put down thy kaross?' Therefore, the Mason Wasp, walking along, unloosened the strings of the kaross; he put down the kaross.
passages.note: Quote from Specimens of Bushman Folklore (Bleek & Lloyd 1911), p. 171 (public domain).

passages.text: Therefore the wife said: 'Canst thou be like this? This must have been why thou wert not willing to lay down the kaross.' Therefore, the Mason Wasp walked, turning to one side; he aimed at his wife, he shot, hitting the head of the arrow on his wife's breastbone.
passages.note: Quote from Specimens of Bushman Folklore (Bleek & Lloyd 1911), pp. 171-172 (public domain).

passages.text: And his wife fell down dead on account of it. Then he exclaimed: 'Yi u hihi! O my wife!' (crying) as if he had not been the one to shoot his wife. He cried, that he should have done thus, have shot his wife; his wife died.
passages.note: Quote from Specimens of Bushman Folklore (Bleek & Lloyd 1911), p. 172 (public domain).

title.en: The Young Man Carried Off by the Lion
title.zh: 獅攜之少年

region.en: Katkop Mountains north of Calvinia, Northern Cape (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 南非北開普省卡茲科普山（象徵定位）

period: Bushman (|Xam San) oral tradition; recorded 1875 by Dia!kwain (Bleek & Lloyd)

source.work: Bleek & Lloyd, Specimens of Bushman Folklore (1911), 'The Young Man of the Ancient Race, who was carried off by a Lion, when asleep in the Field'

summary.en: A drowsy young hunter is picked up sleeping by a lion and wedged, alive, head-first into a zwart-storm tree; the lion licks his tears and waits to drink before eating. The man escapes in zigzags, is rolled in hartebeest skins, and the lion — a 'sorcerer' that arrows cannot kill — will take only him; at last his mother gives him up, and lion and man die together.
summary.zh: 獵者午睡，獅啣之，活嵌於樹；獅舐其淚，待飲水後再食。少年逃歸，裹以麋羚皮；獅如巫者，箭不能殺，唯欲其人。母終予之；獅與人偕死。

sensitivity.note: |Xam San legend dictated by Dia!kwain to Bleek and Lloyd, 1875; presented as an archival record of 19th-century colonial recordings.

passages.text: And he lay down on account of it; and he slept, while a lion came; it went to the water, because the noonday heat had killed it; it was thirsty; and it espied the man lying asleep; and it took up the man. And the man awoke startled... And he thought that he would not stir; for the lion would biting kill him, if he stirred... for the lion appeared to think that he was dead.
passages.note: Quote from Specimens of Bushman Folklore (Bleek & Lloyd 1911), p. 176 (public domain).

passages.text: And the lion carried him to a zwart-storm tree; and the lion laid him in it... And it trod, pressing in the man's head between the stems of the zwart-storm tree... And it licked the man's eyes' tears. And the man wept; hence it licked the man's eyes.
passages.note: Quote from Specimens of Bushman Folklore (Bleek & Lloyd 1911), p. 177 (public domain).

passages.text: He did not run straight; but ran first in one direction, then sprang to another place, then ran again... he called out to the people at home about it, that he had just been 'lifted up' while the sun stood high... therefore, they must look out many hartebeest-skins, that they might roll him up in them; for, he had just been 'lifted up'... And the people did so.
passages.note: Quote from Specimens of Bushman Folklore (Bleek & Lloyd 1911), pp. 183-185 (public domain); minor elisions.

passages.text: 'Ye must give a girl to the lion, that we may see whether the lion will not eat her, that it may go away.' The lion did not want the girl; for, the lion only wanted the man whom it had carried off... And the young man's mother spoke, she said: 'Ye may give my child to the lion; ye shall not allow the lion to eat my child; that the lion may go walking about; for, ye shall killing lay it upon my child; that it may die, like my child.'... And the lion bit the young man to death... And it died, while the man also lay dead.
passages.note: Quote from Specimens of Bushman Folklore (Bleek & Lloyd 1911), pp. 190-191 (public domain), minor elisions.

title.en: A Woman of the Early Race and the Rain Bull
title.zh: 早期之民女子與雨公牛

region.en: Strontbergen, Cape Colony (Northern Cape, South Africa)
region.zh: 南非北開普省斯特龍特山（象徵定位）

period: Bushman (|Xam San) oral tradition; recorded 1878 by /Han≠kass'o (Bleek & Lloyd)

source.work: Bleek & Lloyd, Specimens of Bushman Folklore (1911), 'A Woman of the Early Race and the Rain Bull'

summary.en: The Rain bull, breathing mist, courts a woman at her hut; she throws buchu on his forehead, ties her child safe, and mounts him. She anoints him again at a great tree, and while he sleeps she climbs down and slips home, burning buchu to take the rain-scent from herself. He wakes and sinks into his spring — which, the people say, dries whenever the Rain goes out.
summary.zh: 雨公牛呼吸成霧，至屋前求愛；女子以布庫草擲其額，縛幼兒於褥，跨騎而去。至大樹再以布庫擦其頸，趁其睡爬下潛歸，焚草除雨香。牛醒，沉入其泉——凡雨出，泉必涸。

sensitivity.note: |Xam San oral tradition dictated by /Han≠kass'o to Bleek and Lloyd, 1878; presented as an archival record of 19th-century colonial recordings.

passages.text: The Rain formerly courted a young woman, while the young woman was in (her) hut, because she felt that she was still ill. The Rain scented her, and the Rain went forth, on account of it; while the place became misty... He in this manner trotting came; while the young woman was lying down, while she held (her) child on the kaross.
passages.note: Quote from Specimens of Bushman Folklore (Bleek & Lloyd 1911), p. 193 (public domain).

passages.text: The young woman took up buchu in her hand, the young woman threw buchu upon his forehead. And she arose; and she pressed (the buchu) down upon his forehead... she pushed him away; and she took up her kaross; she tied it on. The young woman took up the child, she held the child very nicely... she laid the child down upon a kaross... She mounted the Rain; and the Rain took her away.
passages.note: Quote from Specimens of Bushman Folklore (Bleek & Lloyd 1911), pp. 194-195 (public domain), minor elisions.

passages.text: And the young woman said: 'Thou must go underneath, close to the stem of the tree.' Therefore, he went underneath, close to the stem of the tree... the young woman took out buchu, she rubbed him. Then the Rain went to sleep, on account of it. Therefore, when she saw that the Rain slept, she climbed up, she stole softly away... And she descended at a distance.
passages.note: Quote from Specimens of Bushman Folklore (Bleek & Lloyd 1911), pp. 196-197 (public domain).

passages.text: While the Rain awoke behind her back, when the Rain felt that the place was becoming cool. He arose, he walked away; he went away to the middle of the spring from which he had courting gone out, while he believed that the young woman was still sitting upon his back. He went away to the water. He went into it... she went to burn buchu... taking away the smell of the bush from herself.
passages.note: Quote from Specimens of Bushman Folklore (Bleek & Lloyd 1911), pp. 197-198 (public domain), minor elisions.

title.en: The Girl's Story; the Frogs' Story
title.zh: 少女之故事；蛙之故事

region.en: Katkop Mountains north of Calvinia, Northern Cape (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 南非北開普省卡茲科普山（象徵定位）

period: Bushman (|Xam San) oral tradition; recorded 1874 by !Kweiten ta //Ken (Bleek & Lloyd)

source.work: Bleek & Lloyd, Specimens of Bushman Folklore (1911), 'The Girl's Story; the Frogs' Story'; W. H. I. Bleek, A Brief Account (1875), §41

summary.en: A girl, refusing her mothers' food, kills and eats the Water's beautiful children — striped like a zebra. A whirlwind carries her whole family, mats and all, into the spring; the girl enters first and becomes a frog, and her people become frogs after her. Their arrows and mats still grow out by the springs of the First People's land.
summary.zh: 少女不食母所予之糧，殺食水之美童——其身如斑馬紋。旋風攜其全家連褥入泉；少女先入而化為蛙，其眾亦繼化蛙。其箭與褥至今自泉中長出——此乃早期之民之地。

sensitivity.note: |Xam San oral tradition dictated by !Kweiten ta //Ken to Bleek and Lloyd, 1874; presented as an archival record of 19th-century colonial recordings.

passages.text: A girl formerly lay ill; she was lying down. She did not eat the food which her mothers gave her. She lay ill. She killed the children of the Water; they were what she ate. Her mothers did not know that she did thus... [The Water was as large as a bull, and the Water's children were the size of calves, being the children of great things; beautiful, and striped like a zebra.]
passages.note: Quote from Specimens of Bushman Folklore (Bleek & Lloyd 1911), p. 199 with editor's note (public domain).

passages.text: And when she was seeking about for food, the clouds came up. And she spoke, she said: 'Something is not right at home; for a whirlwind is bringing (things) to the spring. For something is not going on well at home. Therefore, the whirlwind is taking (things) away to the spring.' Because her daughter killed the Water's children, therefore the whirlwind took them away to the spring.
passages.note: Quote from Specimens of Bushman Folklore (Bleek & Lloyd 1911), pp. 200-202 (public domain), minor elisions.

passages.text: The girl was the one who first went into the spring, and then she became a frog. Her mothers afterwards went into the spring; the whirlwind brought them to it... Meanwhile their daughter was in the spring; she was a frog. Her father also came to become a frog; for the whirlwind brought her father — when he was yonder on the hunting ground — to the spring.
passages.note: Quote from Specimens of Bushman Folklore (Bleek & Lloyd 1911), pp. 202-203 (public domain).

passages.text: Her father's arrows altogether grew out by the spring; for the great whirlwind had brought them to the spring. He also altogether became a frog... The mats grew out by the spring, like the arrows; their things grew out by the spring... because they were frogs.
passages.note: Quote from Specimens of Bushman Folklore (Bleek & Lloyd 1911), pp. 203-204 (public domain).

title.en: The Man Who Ordered His Wife to Cut Off His Ears
title.zh: 令妻割耳之男子

region.en: Strontbergen, Cape Colony (Northern Cape, South Africa)
region.zh: 南非北開普省斯特龍特山（象徵定位）

period: Bushman (|Xam San) oral tradition; recorded 1878 by /Han≠kass'o (Bleek & Lloyd)

source.work: Bleek & Lloyd, Specimens of Bushman Folklore (1911), 'The Man who ordered his Wife to cut off his Ears'

summary.en: Thinking his younger brother's head has been skinned — when only shaved — a man of the early race insists his wife cut off his ears. She protests, he screams over his own skin, and the narrators conclude that the early race did foolish things because they were men of a different sort.
summary.zh: 早期之民誤以弟之首皮被剝（實僅剃髮），強令妻割其雙耳。妻拒之不果；己嚎己痛。敘者曰：早期之民行愚事，因其本異類。

sensitivity.note: |Xam San oral tradition dictated by /Han≠kass'o to Bleek and Lloyd, 1878; presented as an archival record of 19th-century colonial recordings.

passages.text: He formerly wished (his) wife to cut off his ears, for his younger brother's head had surely been skinned; whereas his younger brother's wife had only shaved his younger brother's head. Therefore, (his) wife cut away his ears; although (his) wife had said that she would not do so; he was the one who insisted upon it.
passages.note: Quote from Specimens of Bushman Folklore (Bleek & Lloyd 1911), p. 205 (public domain).

passages.text: Therefore, his wife cut off his ears; and he was screaming, on account of his skin, while he himself had been the one who wished the wife to do so; for his younger brother's head had surely been skinned; whereas his younger brother had merely had his head shaved; while his wife shaved, removing the old hair.
passages.note: Quote from Specimens of Bushman Folklore (Bleek & Lloyd 1911), p. 205 (public domain).

title.en: The +nerru and Her Husband
title.zh: 內魯鳥與其夫

region.en: Strontbergen, Cape Colony (Northern Cape, South Africa)
region.zh: 南非北開普省斯特龍特山（象徵定位）

period: Bushman (|Xam San) oral tradition; recorded 1879 by /Han≠kass'o (Bleek & Lloyd)

source.work: Bleek & Lloyd, Specimens of Bushman Folklore (1911), 'The +nerru and her Husband'

summary.en: A man of the early race marries a +nerru (now a bird). She will not put earthy Bushman-rice into the kaross on her back; he snatches it, and her entrails pour out. She rises singing the house-song of the +nerru, her mother binds her up, and the husband is sent back to his own people — for they did not understand.
summary.zh: 早期之民娶內魯（今之鳥）。她不肯將帶土之米置入背之皮衣；夫強奪，其腸盡出。她起而歌內魯家族之歌；母為之縛裹；夫被遣回本族——因彼此不解。

sensitivity.note: |Xam San oral tradition dictated by /Han≠kass'o to Bleek and Lloyd, 1879; contains graphic injury; presented as an archival record.

passages.text: A man of the early race formerly married a +nerru. The +nerru put the dusty (earthy) Bushman rice into a bag, when her husband had dug out Bushman rice... He again dug out other Bushman rice. He put it in above, put in the Bushman rice on the top of the morning's Bushman rice.
passages.note: Quote from Specimens of Bushman Folklore (Bleek & Lloyd 1911), pp. 207-208 (public domain).

passages.text: And he exclaimed: 'Give me thy little kaross, that I may put the Bushman rice upon it.' And the wife said: 'We are not accustomed to put Bushman rice, having earth with it, into our back's kaross, we who are of the house of +nerru.'
passages.note: Quote from Specimens of Bushman Folklore (Bleek & Lloyd 1911), p. 209 (public domain).

passages.text: The wife's entrails, which were upon the little kaross, poured down. And he, crying, exclaimed: 'Oh dear! O my wife! What shall I do?' while the wife arose, the wife said (i.e. sang) — 'We, who are of the house of +nerru, We are not used to put earthy Bushman rice (Into) our back's kaross' — while she walked on replacing her entrails.
passages.note: Quote from Specimens of Bushman Folklore (Bleek & Lloyd 1911), p. 210 (public domain).

passages.text: Then she ran to meet her daughter; she went to put the little kaross upon her daughter; she, holding, put her daughter's entrails upon the little kaross; and she bound up her daughter; and she slowly conducted her daughter home... Therefore, her daughter's husband went back to his own people... for, they did not understand.
passages.note: Quote from Specimens of Bushman Folklore (Bleek & Lloyd 1911), pp. 212-213 (public domain), minor elisions.

title.en: The Death of the Lizard: The Mountains That Bit Him
title.zh: 蜥蜴之死：噬其之山

region.en: Strontbergen, Cape Colony (Northern Cape, South Africa)
region.zh: 南非北開普省斯特龍特山（象徵定位）

period: Bushman (|Xam San) oral tradition; recorded 1878 by /Han≠kass'o (Bleek & Lloyd)

source.work: Bleek & Lloyd, Specimens of Bushman Folklore (1911), 'The Death of the Lizard'

summary.en: The lizard, once a man of the early race, sings a marching song as he goes to live by the red sand-hills; he tries to spring through the mountain pass, and the two mountains close and bite him in two. His forepart becomes \guru-\na, his hinder part \xe-\khwai — two agama lizards — and the passes near !khau-\ka\ka bear his name.
summary.zh: 蜥蜴本為早期之人，歌行赴紅沙丘而居；欲躍過山隘，二山相合咬之為兩段。前段化為古魯那，後段化為舍夸伊——即今兩種鬣蜥。附近山隘仍以其名。

sensitivity.note: |Xam San oral tradition dictated by /Han≠kass'o to Bleek and Lloyd, 1878; presented as an archival record of 19th-century colonial recordings.

passages.text: The Lizard formerly sang — 'For, I therefore intend to go, Passing through, \guru-\na's pass. And, I therefore intend to go, Passing through, \xe-\khwai's pass.' And, when he was passing through, the mountains squeezing broke him, when he had intended to pass through.
passages.note: Quote from Specimens of Bushman Folklore (Bleek & Lloyd 1911), p. 215 (public domain).

passages.text: He seems to have thought that he would spring through the mountain pass... Then, the mountains caught him thus, the mountains bit, breaking him. Therefore, his forepart fell over and stood still, it became \guru-\na; while his hinder part fell over and stood still; it was that which became \xe-\khwai.
passages.note: Quote from Specimens of Bushman Folklore (Bleek & Lloyd 1911), pp. 215-216 (public domain).

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase of the narrator's remarks: he seems to have been going to the red sand hills, to dwell at them; he was going towards the pool \kau-\ka\ka, ascending along the hillside, descending into \na-\kua-rra; the place where he broke in two was where he was going to dwell.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Specimens of Bushman Folklore (Bleek & Lloyd 1911), pp. 216-217; not verbatim.

title.en: The Baboons and ||xabbiten-||xabbiten
title.zh: 狒狒與斑點頭

region.en: Katkop Mountains north of Calvinia, Northern Cape (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 南非北開普省卡茲科普山（象徵定位）

period: Bushman (|Xam San) oral tradition; recorded 1876 by Dia!kwain (Bleek & Lloyd)

source.work: Bleek & Lloyd, Specimens of Bushman Folklore (1911), 'The Baboons and ||xabbiten-||xabbiten'

summary.en: Carrying flour from the white people, ||xabbiten mocks the baboons' 'foreheads like overhanging cliffs'; they plan to beat him, and the children ask for his big head to play with. He climbs a krieboom and bluffs that the white men are coming to drive them off; the baboons flee, and he drops from the tree and runs.
summary.zh: 斑點頭自白人處背麵粉歸，譏狒狒「額如懸崖」；狒狒謀擊之，其子求其大頭為球。他攀克裏布姆樹，詐稱白人將驅之；狒狒奔逃，他自樹落下而遁。

sensitivity.note: |Xam San oral tradition dictated by Dia!kwain (who heard it from ||xabbiten himself) to Bleek and Lloyd, 1876; presented as an archival record.

passages.text: The baboons espied ||xabbiten-||xabbiten, as he was coming away from the white men whom he had been to visit. He was carrying flour, which the white men gave him. And the baboons said: 'Uncle ||xabbiten-||xabbiten seems to be returning yonder; let us cross his path, that we may knock him down.'
passages.note: Quote from Specimens of Bushman Folklore (Bleek & Lloyd 1911), p. 255 (public domain).

passages.text: And ||xabbiten-||xabbiten remarked upon their foreheads' steepness. ['Ye speak to me! ye are ugly! your foreheads resemble overhanging cliffs!'] And the baboons angrily came down to ||xabbiten-||xabbiten; they broke off sticks, with which they intended to come to beat him... The baboons' children also came; going along, they called out: 'O fathers! ye must give us ||xabbiten-||xabbiten's head, that we may play with it.'
passages.note: Quote from Specimens of Bushman Folklore (Bleek & Lloyd 1911), pp. 255-257 (public domain), minor elisions.

passages.text: He thought: 'I will climb a krieboom, that I may sit above in the krieboom; the baboons will have to drag me down...' And ||xabbiten-||xabbiten called out, while he deceived them, he said: 'O white men! the baboons are here, they are with me, ye must drive them away.' And the baboons ran, leaving ||xabbiten-||xabbiten; and he escaped... he quickly descended from the krieboom.
passages.note: Quote from Specimens of Bushman Folklore (Bleek & Lloyd 1911), pp. 258-259 (public domain), minor elisions.

title.en: The Child Who Set the Lion on Fire
title.zh: 縱火退獅之孩童

region.en: Katkop Mountains north of Calvinia, Northern Cape (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 南非北開普省卡茲科普山（象徵定位）

period: Bushman (|Xam San) oral tradition; recorded 1875 by !Kweiten ta //Ken (Bleek & Lloyd)

source.work: Bleek & Lloyd, Specimens of Bushman Folklore (1911), 'A Lion's Story'

summary.en: A crying child, left while her parents sleep, draws out the grass under the lion that has come for her family and sets his hair alight; he bolts and the veld burns behind him. Her mother gives her Bushman-rice, saying: hadst thou not fired the lion, we should have died — and breaks an ostrich eggshell of rice for her.
summary.zh: 啼哭之童趁獅近身，抽其身下之草，燃其鬣毛；獅遁，野火隨之。母贈桑人之米，曰：爾若不縱火，吾等必死——並為之破蛋殼盛米。

sensitivity.note: |Xam San oral tradition dictated by !Kweiten ta //Ken to Bleek and Lloyd, 1875; presented as an archival record of 19th-century colonial recordings.

passages.text: The child cried there for 'Bushman rice'; a lion hearing came to her, while she cried there; her parents lay asleep... And the lion heard, as she cried there. And the lion came to her, on account of it. And she took out (some of) the grass upon which her parents were lying; because she had perceived the lion; the lion intended to kill and carry off her parents; she set the lion on fire with it.
passages.note: Quote from Specimens of Bushman Folklore (Bleek & Lloyd 1911), pp. 259-260 (public domain).

passages.text: The lion ran away; the bushes took fire. Because the child had set the lion on fire. And the child's mother afterwards gave her 'Bushman rice' because she felt that the lion would have killed them, if the child had not set the lion on fire with grass. And the lion went to die on account of the fire. Because the fire had burned, killing it.
passages.note: Quote from Specimens of Bushman Folklore (Bleek & Lloyd 1911), p. 260 (public domain).

passages.text: And the child's mother said: 'Yes, my child, hadst thou not in this manner set the lion on fire we should have died. For thou didst set the lion on fire for us... Therefore it is, that we will break for thee an ostrich eggshell of Bushman rice; for, thou hast made us to live; we should have been dead, we should have died, hadst thou not set the lion on fire for us.'
passages.note: Quote from Specimens of Bushman Folklore (Bleek & Lloyd 1911), pp. 260-261 (public domain).

title.en: The Man Who Found a Lion in a Cave
title.zh: 穴中遇獅之男子

region.en: Katkop Mountains north of Calvinia, Northern Cape (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 南非北開普省卡茲科普山（象徵定位）

period: Bushman (|Xam San) oral tradition; recorded 1875 by Dia!kwain (Bleek & Lloyd)

source.work: Bleek & Lloyd, Specimens of Bushman Folklore (1911), 'The Man who found a Lion in a Cave'

summary.en: A lion makes rain to blind a traveller, then waits asleep in a cave; the man feels the hairy thing, tiptoes out, runs to a distant fire whose flames he first takes for the lion's eyes, and survives. The lion tracks him to the people's huts, asking 'where is the man who came to me?' — and leaves when the sun rises.
summary.zh: 獅降雨蔽途，先眠穴中待之；男子觸其毛茸，踮足而出，誤認獅目為遠火，得至人群。獅循跡至屋，索問「來我處之人何在」；日出乃去。

sensitivity.note: |Xam San oral tradition dictated by Dia!kwain to Bleek and Lloyd, 1875; presented as an archival record of 19th-century colonial recordings.

passages.text: A man long ago did thus: when the rain fell he thought that he would go and sleep in a cave; when a lion had been the one who had made rain for him, so that he should not know the place at which his home seemed to be... The place was not a little dark, for, he continued to go into the bushes; he did not see the place along which he was walking.
passages.note: Quote from Specimens of Bushman Folklore (Bleek & Lloyd 1911), pp. 260-262 (public domain).

passages.text: And the lion had come first to the cave; it came to wait for the man in the cave... it fell fast asleep. And the man came, while it sat asleep. And the man, when he had entered the cave, heard a thing which seemed to breathe... he felt about; and he felt that a thing which seemed to have hair was there... he felt that a lion was the one which slept sitting inside the cave. And he gently stepped backwards and turned round; and he went out on tiptoe.
passages.note: Quote from Specimens of Bushman Folklore (Bleek & Lloyd 1911), pp. 263-264 (public domain), minor elisions.

passages.text: He espied the fire of some other people, which they kindled to warm themselves. And he thought: 'I will run to the fire which stands yonder... Didst thou not think that our fathers also said to me, that the lion's eye can also sometimes resemble a fire by night? I will look whether it be a real fire which burns there.' And he ran nearer to the fire... he saw that people were lying round in front of the fire.
passages.note: Quote from Specimens of Bushman Folklore (Bleek & Lloyd 1911), pp. 267-268 (public domain), minor elisions.

passages.text: Day broke, while the lion was still threatening them... then it was, that the lion went away, leaving the people; because the sun was rising... for the lion is a thing which is not willing to come to us, when the sun stands in the sky.
passages.note: Quote from Specimens of Bushman Folklore (Bleek & Lloyd 1911), p. 269 (public domain).

title.en: The Jackal Sets Lion Cub and Tiger Cub at Variance
title.zh: 豺離間獅崽與虎崽

region.en: Forest of Kalasuta (Kah-gyur narrative India, symbolic pin)
region.zh: 迦臘須多林（迦起律典敘事，象徵定位）

period: Tibetan Kah-gyur (translated c. 9th century), from Indian sources; Schiefner/Ralston translation 1882

source.work: Tibetan Tales Derived from Indian Sources, trans. Schiefner/Ralston (1882), ch. XXXIII B, The Jackal as Calumniator (Kah-gyur vi. 239-243)

summary.en: A lioness adopts a tiger cub and a tigress a lion cub; the mothers charge the two foster-brothers, named Sudanshthra and Subahu, never to listen to calumniators. An old remainder-devouring jackal, finding the tiger the rival of his maw, tells each that the other plans to kill him, warning each to fear the other's stretching, yawning, triple roar. When the two notice for the first time these natural gestures, each draws the wrong conclusion - and then both speak slokas, ask 'who told you?', discover the jackal, and strike him dead.
summary.zh: 母獅收養虎崽，母虎收養獅崽；二獸臨終囑咐兄弟倆勿聽讒言。一隻食殘的老豺見虎為爭食之敵，便向彼此謊稱對方欲害己，並預言對方伸腰、呵欠、三嘯即殺機。兩獸初次注意到這些本性舉止，便誤信讒言——隨後雙方對誦偈語，互問「是誰告訴你的」，揪出豺狼，一掌擊斃。

sensitivity.note: Kah-gyur fable literature; living Buddhist tradition treated respectfully.

passages.text: A tigress, finding a stray lion cub, made it a playfellow for her own and suckled it; the lioness returning cried out 'sister, run not away - let us dwell together, so that when I go out you can take care of my young one, and when you go out, I will take care of yours.' The cubs were named Sudanshthra the lion and Subahu the tiger, and when the mothers lay dying they charged the pair: as ye have both sucked the same dugs, be brothers; the world is full of evil calumniators - take heed not to listen to any of them.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Schiefner/Ralston, The Jackal as Calumniator (1882); not verbatim.

passages.text: An old, remainder-devouring jackal followed the lion, and saw in the tiger the antagonist of his maw. He came with drooping ears and told the lion that the tiger had vowed to kill him, then told the tiger the lion had vowed the same - adding to each the prophecy of the fatal gestures: he will stretch himself, and yawn, and look round on all four sides, and roar three times, and then come into your presence and think, 'he will kill me.' Be sure of that.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Schiefner/Ralston, The Jackal as Calumniator (1882); not verbatim.

passages.text: The day came when lion and tiger each did exactly what the jackal had described - gestures they had made all their lives without once noticing them. Now the seed of discord was sown: each thought the other meant murder. But the lion reflected that he was strong and the tiger not, and investigated; both recited slokas avowing no strife, asked who had spoken, and learned the truth. The lion struck the jackal dead with a slap, and a deity sang that friends must not be abandoned for others' words but the words tested - no reliance on calumniators.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Schiefner/Ralston, The Jackal as Calumniator (1882); not verbatim.

title.en: The Two Otters and the Jackal Mukhara
title.zh: 雙獺與豺摩訶羅

region.en: River bank, Kah-gyur narrative India (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 河岸（迦起律典敘事，象徵定位）

period: Tibetan Kah-gyur (translated c. 9th century), from Indian sources; Schiefner/Ralston translation 1882

source.work: Tibetan Tales Derived from Indian Sources, trans. Schiefner/Ralston (1882), ch. XXXIV, The Two Otters and the Jackal (Kah-gyur ff. 94-95)

summary.en: Two otters agree to fish together, one driving fish ashore, the other killing them; neither dares divide the catch for fear of unrighteous division, so the jackal Mukhara undertakes it. He belittles each otter's share of the work, then divides the heap into heads, tails and middles, assigning tails to the land-otter, heads to the water-otter - and the middle parts to himself, 'he who is conversant with the law.' He carries the choicest middle of a great fish home to his rejoicing mother.
summary.zh: 雙獺合力捕魚，一驅魚上岸，一殺魚；均懼分贓不公而互讓。豺摩訶羅自請主分，先貶低各獺之功，再把魚堆分為頭、尾、中三份——尾歸陸獺，頭歸水獺，中段「歸曉法者」，自己取走大魚最肥的中段，回家向母親炫耀。

sensitivity.note: Kah-gyur fable literature; living Buddhist tradition treated respectfully.

passages.text: Two otters resolved that one should go into the water and frighten the fish ashore while the other killed them, sharing the spoil in common. When the heap of fish was great, each begged the other to divide it, both fearing to make a mistake in a righteous division. The jackal Mukhara, coming up, undertook the task - first questioning each otter's contribution and overawing them both, so that they sat heart-smitten and silent.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Schiefner/Ralston, The Two Otters and the Jackal (1882); not verbatim.

passages.text: Mukhara divided the heap into three parts - heads, tails, and the rest of the bodies - and uttered his verse: 'The goer on land receives the tails, and the goer into the depths the heads; he who is conversant with the law receives the middle parts.' Seizing the middle part of a large fish, he went off to his mother, who joyfully hailed him: 'O Mukhara, fine and fair exceedingly art thou who hast been too much for the otters; they twain are content, and thou hast secured a rich booty.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Schiefner/Ralston, The Two Otters and the Jackal (1882); not verbatim.

title.en: The Jackal Rescues the Lion from the Well
title.zh: 豺救落井之獅

region.en: Hill district with an old well (Kah-gyur narrative India, symbolic pin)
region.zh: 有古井的山地（迦起律典敘事，象徵定位）

period: Tibetan Kah-gyur (translated c. 9th century), from Indian sources; Schiefner/Ralston translation 1882

source.work: Tibetan Tales Derived from Indian Sources, trans. Schiefner/Ralston (1882), ch. XXXV, The Jackal Saves the Lion (Kah-gyur iv. 244)

summary.en: The Bodhisattva, born as a lion, feeds five hundred jackals on his leavings; hunting by night he falls into a well, and all the jackals scatter but one, who studies how to draw him out. Digging a canal from a nearby lake, he fills the well with water until the lion floats free - 'the mighty as well as the rest must make themselves friends.'
summary.zh: 菩薩生為獅王，以獵物殘餘養五百豺；夜獵落井，群豺四散，唯有一豺留而設法——在旁掘渠引湖水灌井，使獅浮起得脫。「強者亦須交友。」

sensitivity.note: Kah-gyur fable literature; living Buddhist tradition treated respectfully.

passages.text: The lion, king of beasts, killed animals and left them lying for the jackals; hunting beasts at night he fell into a well, and all the five hundred jackals dispersed except one, who sat by the edge thinking how he could draw the lion out. Running to and fro, he saw a small lake, dug a canal on one side, and filled the well with water from the lake, so that the lion was able to get out. A deity sang: the mighty as well as the rest must make themselves friends - see how the jackal rescued the lion from an old well.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Schiefner/Ralston, The Jackal Saves the Lion (1882); not verbatim.

title.en: The Blue Jackal, King Sataga
title.zh: 靛色豺王薩多伽

region.en: Dyer's house and forest edge (Kah-gyur narrative India, symbolic pin)
region.zh: 染坊與林緣（迦起律典敘事，象徵定位）

period: Tibetan Kah-gyur (translated c. 9th century), from Indian sources; Schiefner/Ralston translation 1882

source.work: Tibetan Tales Derived from Indian Sources, trans. Schiefner/Ralston (1882), ch. XXXVI, The Blue Jackal (Kah-gyur iv. 255)

summary.en: A greedy jackal falls into an indigo vat, rolls on a dunghill, and comes out a colour never seen before; proclaimed Sataga, king of the fourfooted beasts by Sakra, he rides an elephant with lions in the inner circle and jackals far outside. His mother, invited, notes the wrong ordering and sings that so long as he utters no jackal's cry his prosperity holds - but nature defeats him: hearing his own kind howl, he must howl or lose his hair, and the elephant beneath him, hearing the cry, flings him down and tramples him.
summary.zh: 貪吃的豺跌入靛缸、滾過糞堆、入水曬日，得一身從未見過的顏色；自稱天帝釋所立的四足獸王「薩多伽」，騎象而立，獅虎在內圈，豺群在外圈。其母受邀，嘆息秩序顛倒，唱言「只要他不發豺聲，大象便容他享福」——然而本性難違：不嗥則毛落，他一開口，座下大象知是豺而將他摔落踐斃。

sensitivity.note: Kah-gyur fable literature; living Buddhist tradition treated respectfully.

passages.text: A very greedy jackal fell into an indigo vat in a dyer's house, rolled on a dunghill, jumped into water, and came out with the colour of cyanite. The other jackals stood afar and asked who he was; he answered that he was Sataga, appointed king of the fourfooted beasts by Sakra, and the awed beasts made him their king - the inner circle lions and tigers, the outer jackals.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Schiefner/Ralston, The Blue Jackal (1882); not verbatim.

passages.text: He sent for his mother from her mountain ravine, and the messenger jackal reported that the inner circle was lions and elephants but the outer jackals. 'So much for things not following their proper order,' she said, singing that so long as he utters no jackal's cry the elephant will let him retain his prosperity. But when the jackals howled round him, he knew that if he kept silent his hair would fall off - so, sitting on the elephant, he lifted up his voice; the elephant flung him off and trampled him under foot.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Schiefner/Ralston, The Blue Jackal (1882); not verbatim.

title.en: The Jackal Hanged by the Ox
title.zh: 被牛吊起的豺

region.en: Lotus swamp of a hill-town (Kah-gyur narrative India, symbolic pin)
region.zh: 山鎮蓮塘（迦起律典敘事，象徵定位）

period: Tibetan Kah-gyur (translated c. 9th century), from Indian sources; Schiefner/Ralston translation 1882

source.work: Tibetan Tales Derived from Indian Sources, trans. Schiefner/Ralston (1882), ch. XXXVII, The Jackal Hanged by the Ox (Kah-gyur iv. 293)

summary.en: An ox of signs, stuck in a swamp, asks its owner to throw it a noose and go; if a jackal comes, it will pick up the noose with its horns and throw it over him. The jackal, sure of a feast, refuses warning; the ox invites him to mount its back for food - and slings the noose round his neck, leaving him dancing in the air with verses about dancing-masters and ladders to Brahma's world.
summary.zh: 帶相之牛陷於沼澤，請主人拋繩而去，並言若有豺來，便以角挑繩套之。貪食的豺不聽警告，牛誘其上背覓食，隨即用角甩繩套其頸，令其懸空「起舞」——雙方以「舞師」與「天梯」互相唱和。

sensitivity.note: Kah-gyur fable literature; living Buddhist tradition treated respectfully.

passages.text: The householder flung a noose before the ox and went away; by night up came a jackal asking who tore up the lotus roots and white lotuses. Warned of harm and disgrace, the jackal still prepared to injure the ox, who offered verse-bait: 'No lotus roots do I tear up... if thou wishest for food mount upon my back, there wilt thou find food.' Gluttony carried the jackal onto the ox's back, the ox flung the noose with its horn, caught him round the neck, and let him hang in the air.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Schiefner/Ralston, The Jackal Hanged by the Ox (1882); not verbatim.

passages.text: In mid-air the two traded verses: 'Art thou Jakara the dancing-master?' mocked the ox; 'Sakara has provided a ladder, I betake myself to Brahma's world,' answered the jackal; and the ox closed the contest: 'Sakara has not provided a ladder; as thou hast been laid in the fetters of contrivance, thou wilt never see thyself saved.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Schiefner/Ralston, The Jackal Hanged by the Ox (1882); not verbatim.

title.en: The Jackal in the Elephant's Footprints
title.zh: 踏象跡的豺

region.en: Water-hole in the Himalayan foothills (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 喜馬拉雅山麓水塘（象徵定位）

period: Tibetan Kah-gyur (translated c. 9th century), from Indian sources; Schiefner/Ralston translation 1882

source.work: Tibetan Tales Derived from Indian Sources, trans. Schiefner/Ralston (1882), ch. XXXVIII, The Jackal in the Elephant's Footprints (Kah-gyur iv. 222)

summary.en: Following an elephant to drink, a jackal begins to measure its own stride against the great footprints and claims them for its own; springing forward it sets a foot in one and trips over a broken piece of kandakilaka wood - 'thy footprints and those of the elephant are not alike; give up this useless attempt.'
summary.zh: 豺隨象至水邊，以己步量象跡，妄稱跡為己有；一躍踏跡，絆於斷木而跌——「爾之跡與象跡不同，莫作無益之試。」

sensitivity.note: Kah-gyur fable literature; living Buddhist tradition treated respectfully.

passages.text: An elephant came to the Himalayas to drink, and in its track followed a jackal which began to measure its own stride with the great footprints, saying to itself, 'these footprints are mine.' Springing forward it set its foot in one and tripped over a broken piece of wood. A deity sang: in a word, fool, thy footprints and those of the elephant are not alike; give up this useless attempt - thou wilt only derive weariness therefrom.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Schiefner/Ralston, The Jackal in the Elephant's Footprints (1882); not verbatim.

title.en: The Guilty Dogs and the Hair-Pellet
title.zh: 有罪之犬與毛丸驗吐

region.en: King Brahmadatta's stables, Varanasi (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 波羅奈梵授王馬廄（象徵定位）

period: Tibetan Kah-gyur (translated c. 9th century), from Indian sources; Schiefner/Ralston translation 1882

source.work: Tibetan Tales Derived from Indian Sources, trans. Schiefner/Ralston (1882), ch. XXXIX, The Guilty Dogs (Kah-gyur iv. 212)

summary.en: Two dogs, Ganda and Upaganda, have gnawed the king's horse-gear to pieces; as he takes the field against the Licchavis the sabotage is found, and all the dogs of the court are slaughtered or put to flight. A stranger dog, finding them terrified, offers to implore the king for them, and the whole pack recite a verse of protest from a distance. The king demands a test: the dogs are given a hair-pellet and made to vomit - and only Ganda and Upaganda bring up leather, so all the rest are freed from fear.
summary.zh: 伽達與優波伽達二犬啃壞王的馬具；出征前發覺，犬群或被殺或逃。一外鄉犬替眾犬向王哀求，群犬隔遠合唱抗辯之偈。王令驗證：以毛丸令眾犬嘔吐——唯二犬吐出皮革碎片，於是被處死，其餘免於恐懼。

sensitivity.note: Kah-gyur fable literature; living Buddhist tradition treated respectfully.

passages.text: Some dogs were killed and others ran away; a dog from another country, seeing them in flight, asked what had frightened them, and on hearing the story said: why do you not implore the king? - we who run away have no power to implore, they answered, and the others have been rendered mute. Wait awhile, said the stranger, I will implore the king in your behalf; and after a halt the pack expressed their prayer in a verse: these two dogs full of force and health ought to be put to death; we are not deserving of death - it is not right to let the innocent be put to death.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Schiefner/Ralston, The Guilty Dogs (1882); not verbatim.

passages.text: The ministers, ordered to find out whether the horse-gear was devoured by Ganda and Upaganda or by other dogs, could think of only one way: the dogs must be given a hair-pellet and made to vomit. Given and made to vomit, Ganda and Upaganda brought up fragments of leather; the king delivered them to death and rendered all the others free from fear.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Schiefner/Ralston, The Guilty Dogs (1882); not verbatim.

title.en: The Hypocritical Cat's Penance
title.zh: 偽善之貓的苦行

region.en: Mouse-hole beside a thicket (Kah-gyur narrative India, symbolic pin)
region.zh: 叢邊鼠穴（迦起律典敘事，象徵定位）

period: Tibetan Kah-gyur (translated c. 9th century), from Indian sources; Schiefner/Ralston translation 1882

source.work: Tibetan Tales Derived from Indian Sources, trans. Schiefner/Ralston (1882), ch. XL, The Hypocritical Cat (Kah-gyur iv. 247-248)

summary.en: Aging out of the hunt, the cat Agnija takes to performing fictitious acts of penance beside the mouse-hole, declaring that he atones for the sins of his youth. The five hundred mice, nourished on faith, run their rounds in confidence - and every day the cat devours the one that comes last. The mice-chief, watching his troop dwindle as the cat grows sleek, observes the trick, and pronounces his verse: this is not a genuine penance but one performed only for the sake of gain - because the number of the mice diminished have you, Agnija, thrived.
summary.zh: 老貓阿耆尼惹捕鼠無力，便在鼠穴旁佯作苦行，自稱懺悔青年時代的罪業。五百小鼠滿懷信心出入，而每日末位之鼠總被吞。鼠王見族減而貓肥，窺破其計，隔遠誦偈：「此非真苦行，乃為口腹而修行——鼠數日減，汝阿耆尼惹日肥。」

sensitivity.note: Kah-gyur fable literature; living Buddhist tradition treated respectfully.

passages.text: The cat took to performing fictitious acts of penance at a spot not far from the mouse-hole, and when the mice asked what he was doing he answered that he was making up for many vicious actions of his youth. Confidence grew in the troop; but as they returned to their hole after every round, the cat seized and devoured the mouse which came last.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Schiefner/Ralston, The Hypocritical Cat (1882); not verbatim.

passages.text: Seeing the troop dwindle while the cat thrived fat and well covered with hair, the mice-chief watched from a hiding-place, saw the trick, and pronounced his verse: he who eats roots and berries will not become fat - this is not a genuine penance but one performed only for the sake of gain; because the number of the mice diminished have you, Agnija, thrived.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Schiefner/Ralston, The Hypocritical Cat (1882); not verbatim.

title.en: The Gazelle Prince and the Faithful Doe
title.zh: 羚羊王子與忠貞雌羚

region.en: Netted glade of a hill forest (Kah-gyur narrative India, symbolic pin)
region.zh: 山林網套之地（迦起律典敘事，象徵定位）

period: Tibetan Kah-gyur (translated c. 9th century), from Indian sources; Schiefner/Ralston translation 1882

source.work: Tibetan Tales Derived from Indian Sources, trans. Schiefner/Ralston (1882), ch. XLI, The Gazelle and the Hunter (Kah-gyur iv. 244-245)

summary.en: The Bodhisattva, prince of five hundred gazelles, is caught in a hunter's net while the whole troop flees - one doe alone stays by him. As the hunter nears she offers her own life first: 'kill me and then the gazelle prince - he is my husband.' Astonished, the hunter answers in verse that he will kill neither, that she shall keep company with her beloved spouse - and leads both away at liberty.
summary.zh: 菩薩生為五百羚之首，誤入獵網，群羚盡逃，唯雌羚相守。獵人將至，雌羚請先殺己：「牠是我的丈夫。」獵人驚異，以偈答「二者皆不殺」，遂放兩羚同去。

sensitivity.note: Kah-gyur fable literature; living Buddhist tradition treated respectfully.

passages.text: The gazelle prince struggled against the net in vain, feet sorely wounded; the doe ran to and fro urging him to exert himself, and when the hunter in brown clothes drew near with bow and arrows she approached him with a courageous heart: 'O hunter, draw thy sword and first kill me, and then kill the gazelle prince - he is my husband.' The hunter replied in verse that he would kill neither: thou shalt keep company with thy beloved spouse; and she answered blessing his own household. His astonishment grew greater still, and he went away leaving both gazelles at liberty.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Schiefner/Ralston, The Gazelle and the Hunter (1882); not verbatim.

title.en: The Monkeys Saved from Death by Fire
title.zh: 猴群因火得救

region.en: Tinduka tree by a hill village (Kah-gyur narrative India, symbolic pin)
region.zh: 山村鎮杜迦樹（迦起律典敘事，象徵定位）

period: Tibetan Kah-gyur (translated c. 9th century), from Indian sources; Schiefner/Ralston translation 1882

source.work: Tibetan Tales Derived from Indian Sources, trans. Schiefner/Ralston (1882), ch. XLII, The Monkeys Saved from Death (Kah-gyur ii. 115-116)

summary.en: Tired of crop-raiding monkeys, the villagers cut down every tree but one Tinduka, ringed it with thorns, and set a watchman: when all five hundred monkeys climb the ripe tree they are to be killed. Panic seizes the troop; the chief alone sits calm - 'the busy and the idle are like unto each other.' But a good monkey frees a young captive in the village, who sets the whole place on fire; the villagers rush home to fight the blaze, and the monkeys come down and escape.
summary.zh: 村民厭猴食禾，伐盡周圍之樹，只留一株鎮杜迦，四周設棘篱並派守望者，待猴群盡上樹便聚殲。眾猴驚惶亂竄，猴王靜坐誦偈；而村中一隻被囚幼猴被善猴放脫後縱火焚村，村人奔救，猴群趁機下樹逃脫。

sensitivity.note: Kah-gyur fable literature; living Buddhist tradition treated respectfully.

passages.text: When the Tinduka tree had put forth ripe flowers and fruits, all five hundred monkeys climbed it, the watchman reported, and the villagers came armed with bows, arrows and battle-axes to cut the tree down. Fear came upon the monkeys, who sprang to and fro; the chief sat still, answering their reproach in a verse: the busy and the idle are like unto each other; the ends of the tree are many; let food be taken by him who is intent upon his life.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Schiefner/Ralston, The Monkeys Saved from Death (1882); not verbatim.

passages.text: In the village a young monkey sat captive, absorbed in thought: the whole troop of the villagers had taken the field to put his relatives to death. A good monkey, finding him, freed him from his bonds - and the young monkey at once set the village on fire. Hearing the clamour, the men cried that a great calamity had occurred while they were far away, hastened home to put out the fire, and the monkeys came down from the Tinduka tree and ran away.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Schiefner/Ralston, The Monkeys Saved from Death (1882); not verbatim.

title.en: The Dream of the Caldron: Incredulity Punished
title.zh: 鑊中夢兆：不信者受懲

region.en: Hill-town with elephant stables (Kah-gyur narrative India, symbolic pin)
region.zh: 有象廄的山鎮（迦起律典敘事，象徵定位）

period: Tibetan Kah-gyur (translated c. 9th century), from Indian sources; Schiefner/Ralston translation 1882
