The old man came out of the hollow, bade the youth examine the sky for the smallest speck of cloud, and followed him, looking upward with great anxiety. A cloud appeared and the thunder rumbled; the old man threw down his load and started to run, assuming his proper form of an enormous porcupine, which fled through the bushes discharging its quills like arrows backward as it ran. But the thunder followed, burst upon burst, until a bolt struck the huge animal, which fell lifeless into its den. The Thunderers then gave the young man a cloud-like robe with wings on its shoulders, rose with him into the air, and set him down in his mother's cornfield by night, where the widow, thinking she saw her son's ghost, was overjoyed: 'Do not be alarmed, mother; it is your son come back to take care of you.'
passages.note: Verbatim from Smith 1883, ch. I; public domain.

passages.text: Every spring he put on the cloud-dress and flew with the Thunderers to witness what they did for the good of man. Passing above a mountain he became thirsty, descended to a pool to drink, and when he rejoined his companions his lips shone as if smeared with oil. 'Where have you been drinking?' 'In yonder pool.' 'There is something in that pool which we must destroy. We have sought it for years, and now you have happily found it for us.' They cast a mighty thunderbolt into the pool, which presently became dry; at the bottom, blasted by the thunder, was an immense grub - 'as big as a house,' said the chief - the special patron and representative of all grubs which destroy the corn and beans. Thence originated the honor in which the Thunder is held among the Indians. Many Iroquois still call Hi-nun their grandfather.
passages.note: Verbatim from Smith 1883, ch. I; public domain.

title.en: The Echo God, Mars of the Iroquois
title.zh: 回聲神：易洛魁的戰神

region.en: Hill country of the Six Nations, New York
region.zh: 紐約州六族之地的丘陵

period: Recorded 1878-1881 by Erminnie A. Smith (1883)

source.work: Erminnie A. Smith, 'Myths of the Iroquois' (1883), ch. I: 'Echo God'

summary.en: In war the Echo God repeated only Iroquois war-cries through the hills, insuring victory and carrying home the evening recall; 'Goh-weh!' for each enemy slain, 'Oh-weh!' - our own - for a lost tribesman. If he answered not, a service was held to ask the cause of his anger; after a victorious war a dance was held to him, first mourning the dead. Since wars are over, the feast and dance to the Echo God have ceased.
summary.zh: 戰時，回聲神只在群山中重複易洛魁的戰呼，確保勝利，並於傍晚召回外出征戰者；每殺一敵呼「Goh-weh!」，折損族人則呼「Oh-weh!」——我族之人。若神不應，則行儀式問其怒因；戰勝後為他舉行舞蹈，先悼亡者。戰事既止，回聲神之祭舞遂不復行。

sensitivity.note: Smith 1883; public domain. War-practice deity of record; no operative war-magic is described.

passages.text: When engaged in wars with different nations the voice of the Echo God served for signals, as it would only respond to the calls of Iroquois. At the coming of evening it was used by them to call in those who were out on the war-path. When the warrior would whoop the Echo God would take it up and carry it on through the air, the enemy not being able to hear it, as this was the special god of the Six Nations. When enemies were killed their victors called out as many times as there were persons killed, the cry being 'Goh-weh! Goh-weh!' - 'I'm telling you!' But if one of their own tribe was killed they called out 'Oh-weh! Oh-weh!' meaning 'Our own!'
passages.note: Verbatim from Smith 1883, ch. I; public domain.

passages.text: If no response was made by the Echo God it was an omen that they should not start; they continued calling, and if the god still remained silent, a service was held to ask the cause of his anger. When a warfare was ended victoriously a dance was held to the Echo God and the nations assembled to rejoice - but first to mourn for the dead and decide on the fate of the captives. As the Echo God was never called upon except in emergencies during warfare, now since wars are over the feast and dance to the Echo God have ceased to be a part of the Iroquois ceremonies.
passages.note: Verbatim from Smith 1883, ch. I; public domain.

title.en: Extermination of the Stone Giants in the Great Gulf
title.zh: 石巨人滅於巨壑

region.en: Great gulf in the Seneca country (traditional)
region.zh: 塞內卡之地的巨壑（傳統）

period: Related by O'Beille Beille, grandson of Cornplanter (Smith 1883)

source.work: Erminnie A. Smith, 'Myths of the Iroquois' (1883), ch. I: 'Extermination of the Stone Giants'

summary.en: The stone giants of the far West resolve to come east and exterminate the Indians; a Seneca war party is warned to accept the challenge and appoint a time and place. At the appointed hour, near a great gulf, a mighty wind from the west precipitates the whole race of giants into the abyss, from which they never extricate themselves - and the God of the West Wind is ever after held in reverence by the Senecas.
summary.zh: 遠在西部的石巨人決意東來誅滅印第安人；塞內卡戰隊受警，應下戰書，約定時地。屆時在巨壑之畔，西來的狂風將整個巨人種族吹墮深淵，永不得出——西風之神自此為塞內卡人所尊崇。

sensitivity.note: Smith 1883 (O'Beille Beille informant); public domain.

passages.text: The stone giants, who principally inhabited the far West, resolved to come East and exterminate the Indians. A party of Senecas, just starting out on the war-path, were warned of their impending danger and were bidden to accept the challenge to fight the stone giants and appoint a time and place. This they did. At the appointed time the giants appeared at the place, which was near a great gulf. Then there came a mighty wind from the west which precipitated the whole race of giants down into the abyss, from which they were never able to extricate themselves, and the God of the West Wind was ever after held in reverence by the Senecas.
passages.note: Verbatim from Smith 1883, ch. I; public domain.

title.en: The North Wind, Ka-tash-huaht, the Icy Sacrifice-Demander
title.zh: 北風卡塔修特：索人為祭的冰魔

region.en: The frozen north (symbolic pin on the Canadian Shield, north of Lake Ontario)
region.zh: 冰封的北方（象徵性定位於安大略湖以北的加拿大地盾）

period: Recorded 1878-1881 by Erminnie A. Smith (1883)

source.work: Erminnie A. Smith, 'Myths of the Iroquois' (1883), ch. I: 'The North Wind'

summary.en: While medicine men go their customary rounds demanding gifts, an icy figure appears demanding a man as sacrifice. The Thunder God is appealed to and comes to the rescue with his assistants, chasing the figure far into the north, where the icy demon is doomed to remain: his howling and blustering are heard to this day, and his frosty children punish any venturesome mortal who intrudes too far toward his abode. He is termed Ka-tash-huaht, or North Wind, and ranks as an evil spirit.
summary.zh: 醫人循例向民眾收取獻禮之際，一個冰身之影出現，索一人為祭。眾人求助於雷神，雷神偕其助手追趕冰影遠入北方，將冰魔永逐於彼。至今猶聞其呼嘯怒號；凡人若敢深入其居所，他的霜之子嗣便會懲罰冒犯者。其名為卡塔修特，即北風，位列惡靈。

sensitivity.note: Smith 1883; public domain. Companion piece to Parker's 'Coming of Spring.'

passages.text: It was the custom at a certain season for the medicine men to go about demanding gifts of the people; but an icy figure had also appeared, demanding a man as a sacrifice; whereupon the Thunder God was appealed to, and he came to the rescue with his assistants and chased the figure far into the north, where they doomed the icy demon to remain. To this day his howling and blustering are heard, and when any venturesome mortal dares to intrude too far towards his abode his frosty children soon punish the offender. He is termed Ka-tash-huaht, or North Wind, and ranks as an evil spirit.
passages.note: Verbatim from Smith 1883, ch. I; public domain.

title.en: Great Head: The Witch of the Continual Song and the Nine Brothers Raised
title.zh: 巨首：不停歌詠的巫婦與九兄弟復生

region.en: Rifted promontory in the distant wilderness (symbolic pin in the Adirondacks)
region.zh: 遠方荒野中的裂岩岬（象徵性定位於阿迪朗達克山）

period: Recorded 1878-1881 by Erminnie A. Smith (1883)

source.work: Erminnie A. Smith, 'Myths of the Iroquois' (1883), ch. I: 'Great Head'

summary.en: Great Head, a terrific human head with great eyes and streaming hair, growls 'I see thee, I see thee, thou shalt die' from his rifted rock. Nine brothers vanish one by one hunting; a mould-covered stranger dug from the earth turns out to be Great Head's own brother and entices him home with blocks of maple (his food); sent by the mole's cover, the youngest shoots the Head and mallets him at the door until he laughs, 'Si-h, si-h.' Great Head leads the youth to the witch who sings continually, whose word Schis-t-ki-an turns all to dry bones; they strip and burn her, set her year-old bones in rows, and at the hurricane's call the nine brothers rise shouting for joy.
summary.zh: 巨首——眼大髮長的可怕人首——自裂岩怒吼：「我看見你了，我看見你了，你必死。」九位兄長逐一獵行失蹤；自土中掘出的覆黴怪人原是巨首的親弟，以楓木塊（其食）誘其來家；最幼的兄弟借鼴鼠掩蔽射中巨首，又在門前以槌擊之，直至巨首笑出「Si-h, si-h」。巨首引少年往見不停歌詠的巫婦——其咒語「Schis-t-ki-an」使萬物化為枯骨。二人剝其皮、焚其身，將一年的骸骨排成行列；颶風一喚，九兄弟復生，相見歡呼。

sensitivity.note: Smith 1883; public domain. Links the flying-head cycle to the witch-song motif; compare the quilt-of-eyes resurrection.

passages.text: It was a common belief among Indians that there was a strange, human-like creature, consisting simply of a head made terrific with large eyes and covered with long hair. His home was upon a huge rock, a rifted promontory, over which his long hair streamed in shaggy fierceness. Seen or unseen, if he saw anything that had the breath of life he growled: 'Kunn''-kun, Kunn''-kuin, wa''-h-tci'-ha''-i-h'; that is, 'I see thee, I see thee, thou shalt die,' or 'thou shalt suffer.' In a distant wilderness a man and his wife had ten children, all boys; the father died, and soon the mother, leaving the boys alone with their uncle. One by one the older brothers went hunting and did not return, until only the youngest brother and the aged uncle were left.
passages.note: Verbatim from Smith 1883, ch. I; public domain.

passages.text: Stepping over a log the youngest heard a groan from the earth; digging, they found a man covered with mould, whom they revived with bear's oil. The stranger proved somewhat supernatural, and one night said, 'I cannot sleep; hearken to the great noise - it is my brother, the Great Head, howling through this hurricane. He is an awful being, for he destroys those who go near him... but perhaps I might entice him to come here. You must cut a huge maple tree into blocks, for that is what he eats.' Guided to the haunt and warned of the 'Great Eyes,' the young man called a mole: 'I want you to creep down under the grass where you will not be seen.' Hidden in the mole, he saw the Great Head watching an owl, drew his bow and shot an arrow into the Great Head, crying, 'I came after you.' The arrow became very large as it flew and small again as it returned.
passages.note: Verbatim from Smith 1883, ch. I; public domain.

passages.text: The Great Head came riding on a tempest to the very spot, and the hunter's arrow drove him away; these maneuvers were repeated many times. Meanwhile the uncle had prepared a mallet: as the Great Head came bursting through the door, the two men plied their mallets - at which the Great Head began to laugh, 'Si-h, si-h, si-h,' pleased to see his brother. When the tumult subsided the uncle gave him the maple blocks to eat. Then the Great Head said, 'I know where they have gone; they have gone to a place where lives a woman who is a witch and who sings continually... if he wishes to go to see this witch, I will show him her abode and all the bones of his brothers.'
passages.note: Verbatim from Smith 1883, ch. I; public domain.

passages.text: They came to a place where they heard the witch singing; at length she spoke the word 'Schis-t-ki-an,' at which all turned to dry bones. The Great Head said, 'I will ask the question, How long have you been here? and the hair will fall from my head and you must replace it... then I will bite her flesh and pull it from her, and as it comes off you must take it from my mouth and throw it off, saying, Be a fox, a bird, or anything else, and it will then run off never to return.' When the witch begged for mercy the Great Head said, 'You had no mercy; see the dry bones; you must die,' and they killed her, and her flesh was turned into animals, and birds, and fish. Burning her to ashes, they searched for the year-old bones and laid them in rows, and when the storm and terrific hurricane arose the Great Head out of the wind called to the nine brothers to awake, and they all arose to life, shouting for joy at seeing each other and their youngest brother again.
passages.note: Verbatim from Smith 1883, ch. I; public domain.

title.en: The Stone Giantess Who Nursed the Chief's Child
title.zh: 哺乳酋長之子的石巨人婦

region.en: Hunting wigwam in the olden Seneca country
region.zh: 古時塞內卡之地的獵屋

period: Recorded 1878-1881 by Erminnie A. Smith (1883)

source.work: Erminnie A. Smith, 'Myths of the Iroquois' (1883), ch. I: 'The Stone Giant's wife'

summary.en: A stone giant woman fleeing her murderous husband enters the hunter's lodge while his wife is out, and nurses the chief's child. She warns that her food must be cooked until no blood can be tasted, or she might kill and eat them all; she hauls game a load of four men, then announces her husband is coming and directs the blows - arms, then the back of the neck - that kill him. When the family returns to the settlement she goes home to her people, needing to fear nothing.
summary.zh: 一位逃離殺夫的石巨人婦乘獵人之妻外出時入屋，為酋長的孩子哺乳。她警告她的食物必須煮到嚐不出血味，否則她或將殺而食之；她拖回四人抬不動的獵物，又預告其夫將至，指點擊殺之處——先臂後頸。一家人返村之後，她亦安然歸返族人。

sensitivity.note: Smith 1883; public domain. A rare domesticated Stone Giant; cannibal risk managed by cooking, a food-taboo charter.

passages.text: A great hunter set forth upon a hunting excursion and took his wife with him; he found so much game that he built a wigwam and settled down. When she returned one evening, laden with game, she was surprised at hearing a woman's voice, and as she entered her surprise changed to fear, for she saw a stone giant woman nursing the chief's child. 'Do not be afraid,' said the giantess; 'come in.' She had run away from her cruel husband, who wanted to kill her, and had come from very far, from the land of the Stone Giants. They must be careful what food they gave her: she could not eat raw food, but it must be well cooked, so thoroughly cooked that she could not taste the blood - for if she once tasted blood she might wish to kill them and the child and eat them. She knew where to find the game and would fetch it instead.
passages.note: Verbatim from Smith 1883, ch. I; public domain.

passages.text: After a while she returned bringing in one hand a load which four ordinary men could not have carried. She told her secret: 'My husband is after me. In three days he will be here. We shall have a terrible fight when he comes, and you and your husband must help me to kill him.' When he came in sight she seized him and threw him on the ground: 'Now strike him on the arms, now on the back of the neck' - and so he was finally killed, and she took him out and buried him. She staid quietly with the hunter and his wife until they were ready to leave for the settlement, then said, 'Now I must go home to my people, for I need fear nothing,' and bade them farewell.
passages.note: Verbatim from Smith 1883, ch. I; public domain.

title.en: The Stone Giant's Challenge and the Human Finger Charm
title.zh: 石巨人的挑戰與人指法器

region.en: Rocky race-course in the Seneca country
region.zh: 塞內卡之地的岩石賽道

period: Recorded 1878-1881 by Erminnie A. Smith (1883)

source.work: Erminnie A. Smith, 'Myths of the Iroquois' (1883), ch. I: 'The Stone Giant's challenge'

summary.en: A Stone Giant challenges a Seneca chief to a race. Leading over cornfields, bushes and brooks until his moccasins are nearly worn off, the hunter climbs rocks where the giant - who cannot raise his head - loses him, and takes a human finger from his pocket: placed upright on his hand it points the way. The hunter snatches the charm, and the giant weeps: 'You have taken my charm, and now you can always find game and all you want, for the finger will direct you to it.'
summary.zh: 石巨人向塞內卡首領下了賽跑戰書。獵人穿玉米田、灌木與溪流，鹿皮鞋幾乎磨穿，最後攀上岩石——巨人不能抬頭，迷失了他的蹤影，便自囊中取出一根人指：直豎於掌上，立即指出方向。獵人奪下法器，巨人哭道：「你奪了我的法器，如今你永遠能尋得獵物與所需，因為這手指會指引你。」

sensitivity.note: Smith 1883; public domain. Same finger-charm motif as Parker's 'Animated Finger' tale.

passages.text: A Stone Giant challenged a Seneca chief to a race. The challenge was accepted, and the time for the start appointed two days later. The hunter employed the time in making a pair of moccasins, and in due time the race began. The hunter was in advance; he led the way over cornfields and through bushes, over and around brooks, and went a weary distance until he was very tired and his moccasins were nearly worn off his feet. At last he began to climb rocks. Now, the Stone Giant had no power to raise his head and could not tell where the hunter was when once he was above him, and in this dilemma he had recourse to a charm, and took from his pocket a human finger. He placed it upright upon his hand, and it immediately pointed the way for him to go.
passages.note: Verbatim from Smith 1883, ch. I; public domain.

passages.text: Now, the hunter had turned and seen him do it, so he stooped and snatched the charm from him, whereupon the giant commenced crying and said: 'You have won. You have taken my charm, and now you can always find game and all you want, for the finger will direct you to it.'
passages.note: Verbatim from Smith 1883, ch. I; public domain.

title.en: Hiawatha and the Origin of Iroquois Wampum
title.zh: 海華沙與貝珠之起源

region.en: Lake on the Mohawk mission road, New York (symbolic pin near the Mohawk River)
region.zh: 莫霍克傳道路上的湖（象徵性定位於莫霍克河附近）

period: Recorded 1878-1881 by Erminnie A. Smith (1883)

source.work: Erminnie A. Smith, 'Myths of the Iroquois' (1883), ch. I: 'Hiawatha and the Iroquois wampum'

summary.en: On a mission into Mohawk country Hiawatha comes upon the borders of a lake; the whole sky fills with wild ducks which alight, quench their thirst and soak their plumage, then rise in one great mass - and the lake has become dry, its bed filled with shells. From these the wise chief proceeds to make the wampum which afterwards so firmly cemented the union of the six tribes, forming the great Iroquois Confederacy.
summary.zh: 海華沙行至莫霍克之地的湖畔；滿天野鴨落於水面，飲水解渴、浸潤羽毛，而後一齊沖天而起——湖水已乾，湖底盡是貝殼。這位睿智的酋長與謀士便以之製成貝珠，其後牢牢凝聚六族之盟，成為偉大的易洛魁聯盟。

sensitivity.note: Smith 1883; public domain. Smith notes the wampum-name etymology is the tribe's own interpretation.

passages.text: In one of his missions into the country of the Mohawks, Hiawatha once came upon the borders of a lake. While deliberating in what manner he should cross it, the whole sky became filled with wild ducks, all of which finally alighted upon the surface of the water. After quenching their thirst and soaking their plumage they ascended again into the air in one great mass, and lo! the lake had become dry, while its bed was filled with shells. From these the wise chief and counselor proceeded to make the wampum which afterward so firmly cemented the union of the six tribes, thereby forming the great Iroquois Confederacy.
passages.note: Verbatim from Smith 1883, ch. I; public domain.

title.en: The Warrior Saved by Pigmies
title.zh: 為小人族所救的戰士

region.en: Alleghany Mountains and the salt-lick (traditional raiding route south)
region.zh: 阿利根尼山與鹽沼（南征傳統路線）

period: Recorded 1878-1881 by Erminnie A. Smith (1883)

source.work: Erminnie A. Smith, 'Myths of the Iroquois' (1883), ch. II: 'The warrior saved by pigmies'

summary.en: Falling ill on the homeward raid, a war-chief is abandoned on an Alleghany river bank. In the night three male pigmies land hurriedly and care for him, shooting two buffalo cows that rise from the neighboring salt-lick where strange animals come up out of the earth. Brought home, his story convicts the false warriors, who are punished; a large party then seeks the lick and finds it ringed with the bones of beasts the pigmies have killed.
summary.zh: 南征歸途中，一位大戰士病倒，被同袍棄於阿利根尼河岸。夜裡三位男性小人匆匆登岸照料他，並在鹽沼旁射殺自地中升起的兩頭母水牛。他歸鄉後道出實情，誣報的戰士受罰；族人往尋鹽沼，只見四野盡是小人族所殺巨獸之骨。

sensitivity.note: Smith 1883; public domain. The pigmies (Jogohso'') are a widespread Iroquois little-people race.

passages.text: One of a raiding party away about two years was taken quite ill on the very evening of the journey homeward; after a long consultation the party concluded to leave him, and abandoned him on the shore of one of the rivers of the Alleghany Mountains. At home the warriors were questioned about the missing war-chief and said he must have been lost or killed in the Southern country.
passages.note: Verbatim from Smith 1883, ch. II; public domain.

passages.text: During the night the sick chief lying on the bank heard the soft sounds of a canoe's approach, and saw three male pigmies landing hurriedly. Finding him, they bade him lie there until they returned, as they were going to a neighboring salt-lick where many strange animals watered, and where they were to watch for some of them to come up out of the earth. Hiding themselves, they saw a male buffalo approach and drink, and immediately two buffalo cows arose out of the lick; seeing the animals becoming restless, the pigmies wisely concluded to shoot them, and succeeded in killing the two cows.
passages.note: Verbatim from Smith 1883, ch. II; public domain.

passages.text: They returned to the man and told him they would care for him, brought him to his friends, and from his story they learned that the returned warriors were false, and they were accordingly punished. From a strong desire to see the lick, a large party searched for it and found it surrounded with bones of various large animals killed by the pigmies.
passages.note: Verbatim from Smith 1883, ch. II; public domain.

title.en: Go-Ga-Ah: The Pigmy's Mission
title.zh: 戈加阿：小人族的使命

region.en: Little cave in the Seneca woods
region.zh: 塞內卡林中的小洞穴

period: Recorded 1878-1881 by Erminnie A. Smith (1883)

source.work: Erminnie A. Smith, 'Myths of the Iroquois' (1883), ch. II: 'The pigmy's mission'

summary.en: A pigmy living in a little cave invites a neighboring hunter, shows him the little people in great numbers with corn, huckleberries, games, bows and arrows and even war dances, then detains him until he has told the mission: 'We are to help you, and we have never injured you, but now we are going to move away from here - to where there is more danger from the giant animals, that we may help those who need our aid.'
summary.zh: 居於小洞的小人邀請鄰近的獵人入內，讓他見識成群的小人族、玉米與越橘、遊戲弓箭乃至戰舞，隨後留他聽完使命：「我們是來幫你們的，從未傷害你們；但如今我們要離開這裡——往巨獸為患之處去，幫助那些需要我們的人。」

sensitivity.note: Smith 1883; public domain.

passages.text: There was once a pigmy living in a little cave. Near him dwelt a hunter in a wigwam. The pigmy sent to him and bade him visit him. The hunter went accordingly, and saw many wonderful things; the little people themselves in great numbers, and the corn and huckleberries and other berries which they had in plenty to eat. And the pigmy said: 'This is our home, and all we have is given to us free, and although I am small I am stronger than you.' Then he showed him the games, and the bows and arrows and the dances, even the war dances, and the hunter said when he had seen it all, 'Let me go.'
passages.note: Verbatim from Smith 1883, ch. II; public domain.

passages.text: But the pigmy said, 'Stay! Do you know my name? I am called Go-Ga-Ah (little fellow). I had my choice of name. I will let you out when I have told you our mission. We are to help you, and we have never injured you, but now we are going to move away from here. We are going where there is more danger from the giant animals, that we may help those who need our aid.' Then having finished his speech, he opened the door and let the hunter go on his way.
passages.note: Verbatim from Smith 1883, ch. II; public domain.

title.en: The Origin of Witches and Witch Charms: The Boy and the Snake Water
title.zh: 巫術與巫咒之起源：男孩與蛇水

region.en: Swamps of the Iroquois country
region.zh: 易洛魁之地的沼澤

period: Recorded 1878-1881 by Erminnie A. Smith (1883)

source.work: Erminnie A. Smith, 'Myths of the Iroquois' (1883), ch. III: 'The origin of witches and witch charms'

summary.en: A boy out hunting catches a beautiful snake and keeps it in a bark bowl of water with fibers, down and small feathers - which become living beings. Whatever he puts in the water comes alive; rubbed on his eyes, the snake-water lets him see hidden things; dipped fingers bewitch at a pointing; the draught blown from the mouth gives great light, grants night-vision, snake-shape, invisibility and swiftness; a dipped arrow or feather kills whatever it is aimed at. He then searches out the antidote roots that can undo his own bewitchments - the origin, says the tradition, of witchcraft and witch charms.
summary.zh: 男孩捕得一條美蛇，養於樹皮碗的水中，與纖維、絨毛、細羽同浸——諸物皆化為活物。凡入此水者皆得生命；抹眼可視隱物；沾指一點即令人中巫；口吹生光、夜能視物、化身為蛇、隱身疾行；蘸水之箭羽所指必死。他進而尋得可解自己所施之咒的草根——此即巫術與巫咒之起源。

sensitivity.note: Smith 1883; public domain. Witch-practice is presented as tradition of record, not instruction.

passages.text: A certain boy while out hunting came across a beautiful snake. Taking a great fancy to it, he caught it and cared for it, feeding it on birds, and made a bark bowl in which he kept it. He put fibers, down, and small feathers into the water with the snake, and soon found that these things had become living beings. From this fact he conjectured that the snake was endowed with supernatural powers. He continued his experiments, and discovered that whatever he put into this water became alive; so he went to another swamp and got other snakes, which he put into the bowl.
passages.note: Verbatim from Smith 1883, ch. III; public domain.

passages.text: While experimenting he saw other Indians putting things on their eyes to see sharp, so he rubbed some of this snake-water on his eyes, and climbing a tree found that he could see things even if they were hidden. He learned that by simply putting one of his fingers into the liquid and pointing it at any person that person would immediately become bewitched. By blowing the mixture from his mouth it would give a great light; by placing some in his eyes he could see in the dark and could go through all kinds of impassable places; he could become like a snake; he could even become invisible, and could travel faster than any other mortal. An arrow dipped into this liquid and shot at any living being, even if it did not hit its object, would nevertheless kill it. Having discovered the great power of this snake extract, he diligently searched for roots and herbs having the required qualities, and finally obtained antidotes which would work upon objects which he had bewitched or wounded.
passages.note: Verbatim from Smith 1883, ch. III; public domain.

title.en: The Origin of the Great Medicine of the Senecas
title.zh: 塞內卡大藥之起源

region.en: Night field in the Seneca woods
region.zh: 塞內卡林中的夜間田地

period: Recorded 1878-1881 by Erminnie A. Smith (1883)

source.work: Erminnie A. Smith, 'Myths of the Iroquois' (1883), ch. III: 'Origin of the Seneca medicine'

summary.en: A lone hunter is wakened by singing and a drum; the field holds a hill of corn and a squash vine with three squashes. A watcher warns him he deserves to die for intruding on the sacred, but the gathered dancers pardon him and teach the secret: 'The great medicine for wounds is squash and corn.' They heat a stick and thrust it through his cheek and leg to prove how quickly the medicine heals; singing the medicine song with gourd rattles, they reveal themselves as bears, beavers and foxes flying away. The prescription - dried cob and squash pounded fine, water taken only from up the running spring - is prepared with singing at every deer's coat-change, tobacco burned as prayer.
summary.zh: 孤身獵人夜聞歌聲與鼓聲起身探看；田中有玉米之丘與三瓜之藤。守夜者斥其擅闖聖地、該死，然舞者們赦免了他，並授以秘方：「療傷之大藥，即是南瓜與玉米。」他們以燒熱的木棍穿其面頰與腿，以藥立癒為證；眾人邊搖葫蘆邊唱藥歌，最後現出原形——熊、河狸與狐——翩然而散。藥方以乾玉米心與南瓜搗細、取上游活水調製，每逢鹿換毛時唱製，焚菸草如祈禱。

sensitivity.note: Smith 1883; public domain. The medicine song and formula are narrated historically, not reproduced for use.

passages.text: Nearly two hundred years ago a man went into the woods on a hunting expedition, quite alone. He camped out in a field and was wakened in the night by the sound of singing and a noise like the beating of a drum. To his surprise the place had all the appearance of being inhabited: on the one hand was a hill of corn, on the other a large squash vine with three squashes on it, and three ears of corn grew apart from all the others. In the night, as he slept near by, he again heard a noise, and awakening, saw a man looking at him, who said, 'Beware! I am after you; what you saw was sacred; you deserve to die.' But the people who now gathered around said they would pardon it, and would tell him the secret they possessed: 'The great medicine for wounds,' said the man who had awakened him, 'is squash and corn; come with me and I will teach you.'
passages.note: Verbatim from Smith 1883, ch. III; public domain.

passages.text: He led him to the spot where the people were assembled, and there he saw a fire and a laurel bush which looked like iron. The crowds danced around it singing, and rattling gourd-shells. Then one of them heated a stick and thrust it right through his cheek, and then applied some of the medicine to prove how quickly it could heal the wound; then they did the same to his leg. All the time they sang the 'medicine song,' and taught it to him. Then as he turned to go home he perceived that they were not human beings as he had thought, but animals - bears, beavers, and foxes - which all flew off as he looked. They had given him directions to take one stalk of corn and dry the cob and pound it very fine, and to take one squash, cut it up and pound that; he was to take water from a running spring, always from up the stream, never down. He made up the prescription and used it with very great success, and made enough before he died to last over one hundred years.
passages.note: Verbatim from Smith 1883, ch. III; public domain.

passages.text: This was the origin of the great medicine of the Senecas. The people sing over its preparation every time the deer changes his coat, and when it is administered to a patient they sing the medicine song, while they rattle a gourd-shell as accompaniment, and burn tobacco. Burning tobacco is the same as praying. In times of trouble or fear, after a bad dream, or any event which frightens them, they say, 'My mother went out and burned tobacco.'
passages.note: Verbatim from Smith 1883, ch. III; public domain.

title.en: A True Witch Story: The Beaver Thigh-Bone of Molly Brant's Child
title.zh: 真實巫案：莫莉布蘭特之子的河狸腿骨

region.en: Seneca Reservation, New York
region.zh: 紐約州塞內卡保留地

period: Recorded 1878-1881 by Erminnie A. Smith (1883)

source.work: Erminnie A. Smith, 'Myths of the Iroquois' (1883), ch. III: 'A true witch story'

summary.en: A stingy old Seneca woman suffers great pain in her eye; the conjurer reveals she is bewitched by a poor woman she once refused milk, combing her hair over her face so he could not see her features. The witch - a Chippewa - is brought before the chief, confesses, and demands the hollow thigh-bone of a beaver from a man 'who is the child of Molly Brant, the child of Governor W. Johnson.' Spitting through the bone into scoured brass kettle water, she draws out first a spider, then a feather; the pain leaves the old woman, but the sight is not restored.
summary.zh: 塞內卡一位吝嗇老婦眼疾劇痛；占者卜出：她曾拒絕借乳給一位貧婦，因而被其行巫——那婦人以髮覆面，故他不識其貌。該巫（一名奇普瓦人）被帶至酋長前認罪，並索要「莫莉布蘭特之子、威廉莊臣總督之孫」那人的空心河狸腿骨。她經骨向擦淨的銅鍋清水吐涎，先見鍋中蜘蛛奔走，後化作羽毛；老婦痛止而目不能復明。

sensitivity.note: Smith 1883; public domain. Named historic persons appear as lineage markers in the charm formula.

passages.text: Among the Senecas dwelt an old woman who was very stingy. All at once she began to suffer great pain in her eye. She consulted a conjurer, who went out to a bush and covered it with a tent and then began to sing, keeping time with his hand. After a while he returned to her and said: 'You are bewitched. You refused to give milk to a poor woman who came to beg of you, and she has bewitched you. I have had her house revealed to me, and I saw her, but she was combing her hair over her face, so I could not see her features.'
passages.note: Verbatim from Smith 1883, ch. III; public domain.

passages.text: Next day he tried again; then he said: 'Now I know who she is.' So they sent for a chief and told him all about it, and he brought the woman before them. She was a Chippewa and a witch. The chief had her brought to the old woman's cabin. She owned that she had bewitched her, and said, 'Fetch me the thigh-bone of a beaver from a man who is the child of Molly Brant, the child of Governor W. Johnson.' The bone was brought, and by the time it arrived she had scoured a brass kettle, and had clean water poured into it. As soon as she received the bone, which was hollow, she placed it against the eye that was not painful and spat through it. After a while she ceased spitting, and looked in the water: a spider was running around in the kettle. She covered it over with her handkerchief, then removed it, and a feather lay there instead of the spider. The pain left the old woman but the sight was not restored.
passages.note: Verbatim from Smith 1883, ch. III; public domain.

title.en: An Incantation to Bring Rain: The Sons of Thunder in the Horizon
title.zh: 求雨之儀：地平線上的雷神諸子

region.en: Council-house of the Seneca (symbolic pin at Cattaraugus)
region.zh: 塞內卡議屋（象徵性定位於卡塔勞格斯）

period: Recorded 1878-1881 by Erminnie A. Smith (1883)

source.work: Erminnie A. Smith, 'Myths of the Iroquois' (1883), ch. III: 'An incantation to bring rain'

summary.en: In a dry season, with thunder-heads on the horizon, swift-footed heralds notify the people that the sons of Thunder are near and tobacco must be burned for rain. Each family offers secretly on its private altar, then bears its tithe to the council-house where the gathered tobacco is burned while the athletic dance the rain-dance. Hi-nun, pleased with the incense, calls forth huge dark banks of rain cloud and takes personal charge of the storm to wet the parched earth - for Hi-nun was considered a great lover of tobacco, but always in want of it.
summary.zh: 旱季裡，雷雲現於地平線，捷足的信使奔告眾人：雷神諸子已近，須焚菸草求雨。各家先在私壇密祭，再攜什一之菸至議屋，將聚集的菸草焚於議火之中，壯者則跳雨舞。希農樂聞菸香，召來大片烏雲，親自引導風雨潤澤焦土——人皆言希農極愛菸草，卻永遠欠缺。

sensitivity.note: Smith 1883; public domain. Rain-rite described as custom of record.

passages.text: In a dry season, the horizon being filled with distant thunder-heads, it was customary to burn what is called by the Indians real tobacco as an offering to bring rain. On occasions of this nature the people were notified by swift-footed heralds that the children, or sons, of Thunder were in the horizon, and that tobacco must be burned in order to get some rain. Every family was supposed to have a private altar upon which its offerings were secretly made; after which said family must repair, bearing its tithe, to the council-house, where the gathered tithes of tobacco were burned in the council-fire. While the tobacco was burning, the agile and athletic danced the rain-dance.
passages.note: Verbatim from Smith 1883, ch. III; public domain.

passages.text: When this was done, Hi-nun, pleased with the incense of the burning tobacco, called forth huge dark banks of rain clouds and took personal charge of the gathering storm to guide it to wet the dry and parched earth. Hi-nun was considered a great lover of tobacco, but always in want of it.
passages.note: Verbatim from Smith 1883, ch. III; public domain.

title.en: Witch Transformations: The Fiery Dog, the Hog, and the White Bull
title.zh: 巫者變形：噴火之犬、豬與白牛

region.en: Buffalo Creek and Tonawanda Reservations, New York
region.zh: 紐約州水牛溪與托納萬達保留地

period: Recorded 1878-1881 by Erminnie A. Smith (1883)

source.work: Erminnie A. Smith, 'Myths of the Iroquois' (1883), ch. III: 'A witch in the shape of a dog'; 'A man who assumed the shape of a hog'; 'Witch transformation'

summary.en: Three witch-sighting anecdotes: on the Buffalo Reservation a man shoots a fire-streaming witch-dog and tracks the blood to the Tonawanda Reservation, where a woman lies dead of the shot; three Tonawanda boys chase a big hog to a creek bank and are told by a laughing old man that it was he himself they pursued; and a Canadian Indian follows a huge white bull with fire streaming from its nostrils until, before a house, it becomes a man with a large white blanket, ever afterward known as a witch.
summary.zh: 三則目擊巫者軼事：水牛溪保留地一男子擊中口鼻噴火的巫犬，循血跡追至托納萬達，見一婦人中彈而亡；托納萬達三少年追豬至溪畔，一位大笑的老人說他們追的正是他自己；加拿大一位印第安人追逐鼻噴火焰的巨大白牛，牛行至屋前化作披大白氈的男子——此人此後被稱為巫者。

sensitivity.note: Smith 1883; public domain. Belief narratives of record.

passages.text: On the Buffalo Reservation a man saw a 'witch-woman' coming, with fire streaming from her mouth. Crossing a creek and obtaining his gun, the man returned and saw a dog at no great distance resting its forefeet upon a log, and it had fire streaming from its mouth and nostrils. The man fired at it and saw it fall, but as it was very dark he dared not go near it; on the following morning he went to the spot and saw where it had fallen, by the marks of blood from its wound. Tracking it by this means, he followed its path until it had reached a bridge, where the woman's tracks took the place of the dog's tracks in the path. He followed the bloody trail to the Tonawanda Reservation, where he found the woman. She had died from the effect of the shot.
passages.note: Verbatim from Smith 1883, ch. III; public domain.

passages.text: On the Tonawanda Reservation three boys were coming down a hill when they saw a large hog, which they concluded to follow to find its home. As they pursued it they continually kicked it, and it retaliated by biting at them at times. It retreated toward the bank of a small creek, reaching which it suddenly disappeared. While searching for it they found on one of the banks an old man, who laughed and said, 'What do you seek?' They answered, 'A hog.' After some moments the old man said that it was he, himself, whom they had been chasing, and by this the boys knew that he was a witch.
passages.note: Verbatim from Smith 1883, ch. III; public domain.

passages.text: A Canadian Indian says he saw, one evening, on the road, a white bull with fire streaming from its nostrils, which, after it had passed him, he pursued. He had never seen so large a bull, or in fact any white bull, upon the reservation. As it passed in front of a house it was transformed into a man with a large white blanket, who was ever afterward known as a witch.
passages.note: Verbatim from Smith 1883, ch. III; public domain.

title.en: The Poison Flies and the Black-and-Yellow Bird
title.zh: 毒蠅與黃黑之鳥

region.en: Deer forests of the Iroquois country
region.zh: 易洛魁之地的鹿林

period: Recorded 1878-1881 by Erminnie A. Smith (1883)

source.work: Erminnie A. Smith, 'Myths of the Iroquois' (1883), ch. III: 'A superstition about flies'

summary.en: A species of fly so poisonous that the smell of them can eat the nose from a man's face nests in marked trees and often enters the horns of deer - hence a hunter's first move after shooting a deer is to examine its horns, and if they are infected to run, since the moment the animal dies the fatal insect emerges. Deer congregate around the fly-trees as if bewitched. Only the black-and-yellow woodpecker destroys them; caught with buckskin traps, its feathers fastened to the hunter's arrows make them surely bring down the deer.
summary.zh: 有一種蠅毒烈非常，僅其氣味便能蝕去人鼻。牠們在樹上築巢，蹤跡可循，常入鹿角——故獵人射鹿後必先驗角，若有感染便立即奔逃，因獸一斷氣毒蟲即破角而出。鹿群彷彿被迷住般聚於毒蠅之樹。唯有黃黑相間的啄木鳥能誅之；以鹿皮羅網捕得，其羽繫於獵人之箭，箭矢因而必中鹿身。

sensitivity.note: Smith 1883; public domain.

passages.text: There was once a species of fly so poisonous that sometimes merely the smell of them would eat the nose from a man's face. A certain species of woodpecker was the only thing that could destroy them. Their homes were in trees, on which their poisonous tracks could be traced. They often entered the horns of a deer; hence the Indian hunter's first move after shooting a deer was to examine its horns, and if they were infected, the hunter would run away, since he knew that the moment the animal died the fatal insect would emerge from the horn. Around the trees in which they lived deer ever congregated, seemingly bewitched by these fierce and noxious little flies.
passages.note: Verbatim from Smith 1883, ch. III; public domain.

passages.text: Buckskin and deerskin were used to catch them. The bird that killed them for food was colored black and yellow. In the evening it came forth from its home in a hollow tree and scoured the forests for them. These birds were caught with buckskin traps and their feathers were used as charms, being fastened to the arrows of the hunter. An arrow thus made potent would surely bring down the deer.
passages.note: Verbatim from Smith 1883, ch. III; public domain.

title.en: The Bird of Wampum and the Boy Archer
title.zh: 貝珠之鳥與少年射手

region.en: The 'tree of promise' between two tribes at war
region.zh: 交戰兩族之間的「應許之樹」

period: Recorded 1878-1881 by Erminnie A. Smith (1883)

source.work: Erminnie A. Smith, 'Myths of the Iroquois' (1883), ch. IV: 'Origin of wampum'

summary.en: A man finds in the forest a huge bird coated with clustered wampum; the head chief offers his beautiful daughter to whoever captures it. Each arrow barely draws off some of the coating, which multiplies like the Lernaean hydra's heads. Warriors of the tribe bar a boy of the enemy tribe from shooting; the chief says, 'He is a mere boy; let him shoot on equal terms,' and the boy brings down the bird with unequaled skill. Marrying the chief's daughter, he divides the wampum between the tribes, peace is declared, and he decrees that wampum shall be the price of peace and blood - hence belts of wampum satisfy violated honor.
summary.zh: 有人在林中見一巨鳥，滿身貝珠；大酋長許諾以美麗女兒為賞。眾箭僅能剝落少許，而珠衣如九頭蛇之首，愈剝愈多。敵族前來看熱鬧的男孩被拒射，酋長卻說：「他只是個孩子，讓他與勇士們公平競射。」男孩技驚四座，射落神鳥。他娶酋長之女，將貝珠分贈兩族，締結和平，並立誓貝珠為償血價和平之幣——此後以貝珠帶賠償受辱之名譽。

sensitivity.note: Smith 1883; public domain.

passages.text: A man while walking in a forest saw an unusually large bird covered with a heavily clustered coating of wampum. He immediately informed his people and chiefs, whereupon the head chief offered as a prize his beautiful daughter to one who would capture the bird, dead or alive, which apparently had come from another world. Whereupon the warriors, with bows and arrows, went to the 'tree of promise,' and as each lucky one barely hit the bird it would throw off a large quantity of the coveted coating, which, like the Lernaean hydra's heads, multiplied by being cropped.
passages.note: Verbatim from Smith 1883, ch. IV; public domain.

passages.text: At last, when the warriors were despairing of success, a little boy from a neighboring tribe came to satisfy his curiosity by seeing the wonderful bird of which he had heard, but as his people were at war with this tribe he was not permitted by the warriors to try his skill at archery, and was even threatened with death. But the head chief said, 'He is a mere boy; let him shoot on equal terms with you who are brave and fearless warriors.' His decision being final, the boy, with unequaled skill, brought the coveted bird to the ground. Having received the daughter of the head chief in marriage, he divided the oh-ko-aeh between his own tribe and that into which he had married, and peace was declared between them. Then the boy husband decreed that wampum should be the price of peace and blood, which was adopted by all nations. Hence arose the custom of giving belts of wampum to satisfy violated honor, hospitality, or national privilege.
passages.note: Verbatim from Smith 1883, ch. IV; public domain.

title.en: The Origin of the Human Race: Sky Holder Brings Out the Six Pairs
title.zh: 人類之起源：天主攜六對而出

region.en: State of New York (the six tribal homes), symbolic pin at Onondaga, the council fire
region.zh: 紐約州（六族故地），象徵性定位於擁有議火之奧農達加

period: Recorded 1878-1881 by Erminnie A. Smith (1883)

source.work: Erminnie A. Smith, 'Myths of the Iroquois' (1883), ch. IV: 'Origin of the human race'

summary.en: Deep water covers the earth; ducks in council receive with overlapping pinions a beautiful woman falling from the sky, and the giant tortoise volunteers to hold her, growing into an island. Twin boys are born - one the spirit of good who makes the maize, fruit and tobacco grow, one the spirit of evil who creates the weeds and vermin - and the world still quakes with the tortoise's stretching. Ages later Sky Holder (Ta-rhun-hia-wah-kun) brings six pairs from the bosom of the great island: Mohawk by the great river, Oneida by the big stone, Onondaga on the high hill, the Tuscarora carried up the Roanoke into North Carolina - each tribe claiming it was the favored one, the Onondagas proving it by their council fire.
summary.zh: 深水覆地；群鴨聚議，以層層羽翼承接自天而降的美女，巨龜自願負她於背，身軀漸長成島。婦人誕下雙生——一為善靈，令玉米果實菸草生長；一為惡靈，造出莠草害蟲——大地至今因巨龜伸展而震動。多年之後，天主教主（塔爾洪尼亞瓦岡）自大島懷中攜出六對人：莫霍克居大河之畔，奧奈達居巨石之側，奧農達加居高丘，塔斯卡洛拉被攜往洛亞諾克河上游而至北卡羅來納——各族皆自稱蒙選，而奧農達加以議火為證。

sensitivity.note: Smith's synthesis of Cayuga-Seneca-Tuscarora tellings (1883); public domain. She notes the twins' good/evil wording is likely a modern framing.

passages.text: In the great past, deep water covered all the earth. The air was filled with birds, and great monsters were in possession of the waters, when a beautiful woman was seen by them falling from the sky. Then huge ducks gathered in council and resolved to meet this wonderful creature and break the force of her fall. So they arose, and, with pinion overlapping pinion, unitedly received the dusky burden. Then the monsters of the deep also gathered in council to decide which should hold this celestial being and protect her from the terrors of the water, but none was able except a giant tortoise, who volunteered to endure this lasting weight upon his back. There she was gently placed, while he, constantly increasing in size, soon became a large island.
passages.note: Verbatim from Smith 1883, ch. IV; public domain.

passages.text: Twin boys were after a time brought forth by the woman - one the spirit of good, who made all good things, and caused the maize, fruit, and tobacco to grow; the other the spirit of evil, who created the weeds and all vermin. Ever the world was increasing in size, although occasional quakings were felt, caused by the efforts of the monster tortoise to stretch out, or by the contraction of his muscles. After the lapse of ages from the time of his general creation Ta-rhun-hia-wah-kun, the Sky Holder, resolved upon a special creation of a race which should surpass all others in beauty, strength, and bravery; so from the bosom of the great island, where they had previously subsisted upon moles, Ta-rhun-hia-wah-kun brought out the six pairs, which were destined to become the greatest of all people.
passages.note: Verbatim from Smith 1883, ch. IV; public domain.

passages.text: The first pair were left near a great river, now called the Mohawk; the second by the side of a big stone - the Oneidas; another on a high hill - the Onondagas. Each pair was left with careful instructions in different parts of what is now the State of New York, except the Tuscaroras, who were taken up the Roanoke River into North Carolina, where Ta-rhun-hia-wah-kun also took up his abode, teaching them many useful arts before his departure. Each of the six tribes will tell you that his own was the favored one with whom Sky Holder made his terrestrial home, while the Onondagas claim that their possession of the council fire proves them to have been the chosen people. As the numerous families became scattered over the State, some lived where the bear was the principal game and were called the clan of the Bear; others where the beavers were trapped - the Beaver clan; and for similar reasons the Snipe, Deer, Wolf, Tortoise, and Eel clans received their appellations.
passages.note: Verbatim from Smith 1883, ch. IV; public domain.

title.en: The Fat Turtle Who Became the Progenitor of the Turtle Clan
title.zh: 肥龜化身龜氏族之祖

region.en: Small lake or pool in the early Iroquois country
region.zh: 早期易洛魁之地的小湖

period: Recorded 1878-1881 by Erminnie A. Smith (1883)

source.work: Erminnie A. Smith, 'Myths of the Iroquois' (1883), ch. IV: 'Formation of the Turtle Clan'

summary.en: In a hot summer a pool of mud turtles dries up, and the turtles set out across the country for a new habitation. One particularly fat turtle suffers so from the exercise that his shoulders blister under his shell until, by an extraordinary effort, he throws off his shell altogether; the transformation continues until the fat and lazy turtle becomes a man, the progenitor of the Turtle clan.
summary.zh: 炎夏之季，泥龜所在的小池乾涸，龜群遂跋涉遷居。其中一隻特別肥碩的龜因勞頓而肩胛在殼下起泡，終於奮力掙脫全身甲殼；蛻變之勢不停，這隻肥懶之龜化作人形，即為龜氏族之祖。

sensitivity.note: Smith 1883; public domain.

passages.text: There were in early times many tortoises of the kind familiarly known as mud turtles, inhabiting a small lake or pool. During a very hot summer this pool became dry. The turtles thereupon set out on their travels over the country to look for a new habitation. One of them, who was particularly fat, suffered a good deal from this unaccustomed exercise. After a time his shoulders became blistered under his shell from the effect of his exertions in walking, and he, finally, by an extraordinary effort, threw off his shell altogether. The process of transformation and development, thus commenced, went on, and in a short time this fat and lazy turtle became a man, who was the progenitor of the Turtle clan.
passages.note: Verbatim from Smith 1883, ch. IV; public domain.

title.en: How the Bear Lost His Tail: The Fox, the Fish, and the Duel
title.zh: 熊失尾記：狐狸、魚與決鬥

region.en: Six Nations Reserve, Grand River, Ontario (related by a grandchild of Brant)
region.zh: 加拿大安大略省格蘭德河六族保留地（布蘭特之孫講述）

period: Related by Ka-an-er-wah, grandchild of the Mohawk Brant (Smith 1883)

source.work: Erminnie A. Smith, 'Myths of the Iroquois' (1883), ch. IV: 'How the bear lost his tail'

summary.en: A cunning fox feigns death by a fish-wagon road and is tossed aboard, throwing out fish until he crawls away. He advises a wolf to try the same trick - the fisherman, forewarned, thrashes him. To the bear he teaches the ice-fishing ruse: put your tail in the air-hole; the bear's tail freezes off. Challenged to a duel, the fox chooses a dog and a lame cat as seconds, the bear a hog; a squealing pig puts the whole company to flight, and the bear never avenges the loss of his tail.
summary.zh: 狡狐裝死於運魚車必經之路，被擲上車後丟魚而遁。牠教狼如法炮製——漁夫識破，把狼痛打一頓。又教熊以尾垂入冰洞釣魚；天寒，熊尾凍斷。熊怒而約決鬥；狐以犬與跛貓為助，熊以豬為助；豬受驚尖叫，全場潰逃，熊終未能報失尾之仇。

sensitivity.note: Smith 1883 ('a modern Indian story'); public domain. European trickster-tale elements overlay an Iroquois frame.

passages.text: A cunning fox saw a wagon load of fish and resorted to the following ruse to obtain some of the coveted delicacy: feigning to be dead, he laid himself in the road by which the fisherman must pass, who, thinking the skin of the fox worth preserving, tossed him into his wagon and drove on. After throwing out several fish, the fox slyly crawled out himself. Soon he met a wolf who was informed of his good luck, and advised to try the same experiment; the fisherman had, in the mean time, discovered the trick, and the wolf received a good thrashing instead of a fish dinner.
passages.note: Verbatim from Smith 1883, ch. IV; public domain.

passages.text: The fox next met a bear who was also anxious to procure some fish. 'Well,' replied the fox, 'down at the river you will find an air-hole in the ice; just put your tail down into it as I did and you can draw out the fish as fast as you wish.' The bear followed the directions carefully, but, the weather being cold, instead of securing a fish his tail was frozen off. The bear was very angry and proposed to fight a duel with the fox. The fox chose as his seconds a dog and a cat; the bear chose a hog, and awaited the fox at the appointed hour.
passages.note: Verbatim from Smith 1883, ch. IV; public domain.

passages.text: As the latter was late in appearing the bear clambered into a tree to prospect, and reported that the fox was approaching with two men armed with guns; thereupon the hog, greatly frightened, begged to be covered with leaves. The fox soon made his appearance, but instead of men his companions proved to be a dog and a lame cat; while awaiting their turn, the cat, perceiving the slight motion of one of the uncovered ears of the hog, sprang upon it, whereupon the squeals of the invisible pig put the whole company to flight, and the bear never had the satisfaction of avenging the loss of his tail.
passages.note: Verbatim from Smith 1883, ch. IV; public domain.

title.en: The Sores-Covered Stranger and the Medicine of the Bear Clan
title.zh: 癩瘡怪客與熊族之藥

region.en: Village of clan-marked wigwams in the Iroquois country
region.zh: 易洛魁之地懸有族徽的村寨

period: Related by Chief Mt. Pleasant of the Bear clan (Smith 1883)

source.work: Erminnie A. Smith, 'Myths of the Iroquois' (1883), ch. IV: 'Origin of medicine'

summary.en: A sickly old man covered with sores goes from clan-marked wigwam to wigwam asking food and lodging, and is scorned by the Wolf, the Tortoise and the Heron. At the Bear-skin wigwam a kind-hearted woman feeds him and spreads skins; he directs her to gather and prepare certain herbs that heal him, then, fevered, other herbs, again and again - until he tells his benefactress her mission is accomplished and she is endowed with all the secrets of curing disease. A hemlock tree shall grow above all others before her wigwam, signifying the Bear's precedence, and she and her clan shall increase and multiply.
summary.zh: 一位滿身癩瘡的老人逐一叩乞各氏族之屋，遭狼、龜、鷺之族鄙視驅趕。至熊皮之屋，善心婦人供食鋪皮；老人教她採製諸藥，治癒己身——屢病屢教——直至言明：其使命已畢，婦人已得醫治百病之秘。屋前將生一株高出群木的鐵杉，為熊族居首之徵，婦人及其族人將繁衍興旺。

sensitivity.note: Smith 1883; public domain.

passages.text: Chief Mt. Pleasant, one of the Bear clan, relates that once on a time a sickly old man, covered with sores, entered an Indian village where over each wigwam was placed the sign of the clan of its possessor; for instance, the beaver skin denoting the Beaver clan, the deer skin the Deer clan. At each of these wigwams the old man applied for food and a night's lodging, but his repulsive appearance rendered him an object of scorn, and the Wolf, the Tortoise, and the Heron had bidden the abject old man to pass on. At length, tired and weary, he arrived at a wigwam where a bear skin betokened the clanship of its owner, inhabited by a kind-hearted woman who immediately refreshed him with food and spread out skins for his bed.
passages.note: Verbatim from Smith 1883, ch. IV; public domain.

passages.text: Then she was instructed by the old man to go in search of certain herbs, which she prepared according to his directions, and through their efficacy he was soon healed. Then he commanded that she should treasure up this secret. A few days after, he sickened with a fever and again commanded a search for other herbs and was again healed. This being many times repeated, he at last told his benefactress that his mission was accomplished, and that she was now endowed with all the secrets for curing disease in all its forms, and that before her wigwam should grow a hemlock tree whose branches should reach high into the air above all others, to signify that the Bear should take precedence of all other clans, and that she and her clan should increase and multiply.
passages.note: Verbatim from Smith 1883, ch. IV; public domain.

title.en: The Origin of Tobacco: The Burned Boat of Medicine Men
title.zh: 菸草之起源：焚燒的醫者之舟

region.en: River bank of the Iroquois country
region.zh: 易洛魁之地的河岸

period: Recorded 1878-1881 by Erminnie A. Smith (1883)

source.work: Erminnie A. Smith, 'Myths of the Iroquois' (1883), ch. IV: 'Origin of tobacco'

summary.en: A loud voice proclaims that all must remain indoors as a boat of medicine men passes the river bank; some disobey and die immediately. The boat is found next day with a strange being asleep at each end, and the voice declares that destroying these creatures will be a great blessing to the Indian. They are decoyed into a neighboring council-house, put to death and burned - and from their ashes rises the tobacco plant.
summary.zh: 醫者之舟行經河岸之際，巨聲宣告眾人須閉戶不出；違者立即斃命。翌日尋得該舟，兩端各睡著一位奇異之人；巨聲再言：誅此二物，將大有益於印第安人。眾人誘其入鄰近議屋，殺而焚之——菸草之株自其灰燼中長出。

sensitivity.note: Smith 1883; public domain.

passages.text: A boat filled with medicine men passed near a river bank, where a loud voice had proclaimed to all the inhabitants to remain indoors; but some, disobeying, died immediately. The next day the boat was sought for and found, containing a strange being at each end, both fast asleep. A loud voice was then heard saying that the destroying of these creatures would result in a great blessing to the Indian. So they were decoyed into a neighboring council-house, where they were put to death and burned, and from their ashes rose the tobacco plant.
passages.note: Verbatim from Smith 1883, ch. IV; public domain.

title.en: The Origin of Plumage: The Turkey-Buzzard's Selfish Choice
title.zh: 羽衣之起源：兀鷲的自私擇衣

region.en: The birds' first council ground (symbolic pin in the Genesee valley)
region.zh: 群鳥最初的議事地（象徵性定位於傑納西河谷）

period: Recorded 1878-1881 by Erminnie A. Smith (1883)

source.work: Erminnie A. Smith, 'Myths of the Iroquois' (1883), ch. IV: 'Origin of plumage'

summary.en: Created naked, the birds hide in shame until they petition the gods for covering; the garments lie far off, and each bird has an excuse - until the turkey-buzzard volunteers. On the long journey he is obliged to eat carrion and filth (hence his nature), and finds the coverings, selfishly trying on the most beautifully colored suit - but unable to fly in it - before choosing the least beautiful in which he rides so gracefully through the air. He then returns bearing the feathery garments, from which each bird chooses his present colored suit.
summary.zh: 群鳥初生赤裸，羞而匿藏，終向眾神請求衣裳；衣在遠方，諸鳥各有推辭，直至兀鷲自告奮勇。長途之上，牠（原本潔淨）被迫食腐啖穢，因而成了今日的兀鷲。尋得羽衣後，牠自私地先試最美的一件，卻不能飛；最後選定最樸素者——卻能翩然翔空。牠攜羽衣而歸，眾鳥各自擇得如今的彩衣。

sensitivity.note: Smith 1883; public domain.

passages.text: In the beginning the birds, having been created naked, remained hidden, being ashamed of their nakedness. But at last they assembled in a great council and petitioned the gods to give them some kind of covering. They were told that their coverings were all ready, but were a long way off, and they must either go or send for them. Accordingly, another council was held to induce some bird to go in search of the plumage, but each had some excuse for not going. At last a turkey-buzzard volunteered to go and bring the feathery uniforms.
passages.note: Verbatim from Smith 1883, ch. IV; public domain.

passages.text: It being a long journey to the place whence he must bring them, he (who had been a clean bird heretofore) was obliged to eat carrion and filth of all kinds; hence his present nature. At length, directed by the gods, he found the coverings, and selfishly appropriated to himself the most beautifully colored one, but finding he could not fly in this, he continued trying them on until he selected his present suit, in which, although it is the least beautiful of any, he can so gracefully ride through the air. The good turkey-buzzard then returned, bearing the feathery garments, from which each bird chose his present colored suit.
passages.note: Verbatim from Smith 1883, ch. IV; public domain.

title.en: Why the Chipmunk Has the Black Stripe on His Back
title.zh: 花栗鼠背紋之由來

region.en: The animals' assembly at the hollow-tree holes
region.zh: 群獸聚於空心樹洞之會

period: Recorded 1878-1881 by Erminnie A. Smith (1883)

source.work: Erminnie A. Smith, 'Myths of the Iroquois' (1883), ch. IV: 'Why the chipmunk has the black stripe on his back'

summary.en: The porcupine, appointed leader of all the animals, calls the assembly to decide: shall there be night all the time, or daylight with its sunshine? The chipmunk sings 'The light will come; we must have light' while the bear sings 'Night is best; we must have darkness.' As the day dawns the chipmunk prevails; the enraged bear pursues him, and the huge paw, grazing his back as he enters his hole in a hollow tree, leaves the black imprint the chipmunk has ever since retained. But night and day have ever continued to alternate.
summary.zh: 豪豬奉命為群獸之長，召集眾獸議決：長夜無晝，抑或有日照之光明？花栗鼠唱「光明將至，我們要有光明」，熊則唱「黑夜最好，我們要有黑暗」。天將破曉，花栗鼠漸佔上風；暴怒的熊追之，巨掌在花栗鼠竄入空心樹洞之際擦過其背，留下至今的黑紋。而黑夜與白晝，自此永恆交替。

sensitivity.note: Smith 1883; public domain. A day/night dualism debate, rare in world aitiology.

passages.text: Once upon a time the porcupine was appointed to be the leader of all the animals. Soon after his appointment he called them all together and presented the question, 'Shall we have night all the time and darkness, or daylight with its sunshine?' This was a very important question, and a violent discussion arose, some wishing for daylight and the sun to rule, and others for continual night.
passages.note: Verbatim from Smith 1883, ch. IV; public domain.

passages.text: The chipmunk wished for night and day, weeks and months, and night to be separate from the days, so he began singing, 'The light will come; we must have light,' which he continued to repeat. Meanwhile the bear began singing, 'Night is best; we must have darkness.' While the chipmunk was singing, the day began to dawn. Then the other party saw that the chipmunk was prevailing, and were very angry; and their leader, the bear, pursued the chipmunk, who managed to escape uninjured, the huge paw of the bear simply grazing his back as he entered his hole in a hollow tree, leaving its black imprint, which the chipmunk has ever since retained. But night and day have ever continued to alternate.
passages.note: Verbatim from Smith 1883, ch. IV; public domain.

title.en: The Origin of the Constellations: Pleiades, Bear Chase, Old Man, and Moon Woman
title.zh: 星座之起源：昂宿、逐熊、老人與月娘

region.en: The night sky over the Iroquois country (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 易洛魁之地的夜空（象徵性定位）

period: Recorded 1878-1881 by Erminnie A. Smith (1883)

source.work: Erminnie A. Smith, 'Myths of the Iroquois' (1883), ch. IV: 'Origin of the constellations'

summary.en: Seven little boys denied their feast-dance supplies whirl off into the air around their singer and become the Pleiades, his brightness dimmed by homesickness. Hunters pursuing a bear are attacked by a monster stone giant; three survivors and the bear are carried by invisible spirits into the sky, where the first hunter aims his bow, the second carries the kettle, the third gathers sticks - and only in fall do the arrows pierce the bear, when his dripping blood tinges the autumn foliage. A despised old man sings his death chant up a high mountain and becomes Na-ge-tci, the old man; and a divining old woman, unhappy that she cannot foretell the end of the world, is transported to the moon, where she weaves a forehead-strap forever, her work unravelled monthly by the cat at her side.
summary.zh: 七個被拒絕宴舞食物的小男孩繞著歌者旋轉升空，化為昂宿星——歌者因思鄉而黯淡。獵熊者遭巨石巨人襲擊，三人與熊被無形精靈攜上天空：第一人張弓，第二人攜釜，第三人拾柴——唯有秋天獵箭能刺熊，其滴血染紅秋葉。受鄙夷的老人登高山唱死亡之歌而昇天，是為「老人」星；一位能卜卻算不出世界末日的老婦被移至月中，永遠編織額帶，身旁的貓每月拆散其網——故其工永不能畢。

sensitivity.note: Smith 1883; public domain. Smith assembles four star-aitia in one passage; cut here as one composite record.

passages.text: Iroquois tradition tells us that the sun and moon existed before the creation of the earth, but the stars had all been mortals or favored animals and birds. Seven little Indian boys were once accustomed to bring at eve their corn and beans to a little mound, upon the top of which, after their feast, the sweetest of their singers would sit and sing for his mates who danced around the mound. On one occasion they resolved on a more sumptuous feast, and each was to contribute towards a savory soup; but the parents refused them the needed supplies, and they met for a feastless dance. Their heads and hearts grew lighter as they flew around the mound, until suddenly the whole company whirled off into the air. The inconsolable parents called in vain for them to return; higher and higher they arose, whirling around their singer, until, transformed into bright stars, they took their places in the firmament, where, as the Pleiades, they are dancing still, the brightness of the singer having been dimmed, however, on account of his desire to return to earth.
passages.note: Verbatim from Smith 1883, ch. IV; public domain.

passages.text: A party of hunters were once in pursuit of a bear, when they were attacked by a monster stone giant, and all but three destroyed. The three together, with the bear, were carried by invisible spirits up into the sky, where the bear can still be seen, pursued by the first hunter with his bow, the second with the kettle, and the third, who, farther behind, is gathering sticks. Only in fall do the arrows of the hunters pierce the bear, when his dripping blood tinges the autumn foliage. Then for a time he is invisible, but afterwards reappears.
passages.note: Verbatim from Smith 1883, ch. IV; public domain.

passages.text: An old man, despised and rejected by his people, took his bundle and staff and went up into a high mountain, where he began singing the death chant. Those below, who were watching him, saw him slowly rise into the air, his chant ever growing fainter and fainter, until it finally ceased as he took his place in the heavens, where his stooping figure, staff, and bundle have ever since been visible, and are pointed out as Na-ge-tci (the old man). An old woman, gifted with the power of divination, was unhappy because she could not also foretell when the world would come to an end. For this she was transported to the moon, where to this day she is clearly to be seen weaving a forehead-strap. Once a month she stirs the boiling kettle of hominy before her, during which occupation the cat, ever by her side, unravels her net, and so she must continue until the end of time, for never until then will her work be finished.
passages.note: Verbatim from Smith 1883, ch. IV; public domain.

title.en: The Pole Star: Ti-yn-sou-da-go-err, the Star Which Never Moves
title.zh: 北極星：永不移動之星

region.en: Territory of the pigmies, far north (symbolic pin on the Canadian Shield)
region.zh: 小人族之地，極北（象徵性定位於加拿大地盾）

period: Recorded 1878-1881 by Erminnie A. Smith (1883)

source.work: Erminnie A. Smith, 'Myths of the Iroquois' (1883), ch. IV: 'The Pole Star'

summary.en: A migrating party, lost and famished by an unknown great river, holds council while their ill chief is tended. During the dance and burning tobacco a childlike being comes to guide them; by night she leads with only a small war-club, feasts them at dawn, and pours from a skin jug a draught that makes them feel very strong. Her own chief then arrives with a great number of his race: 'You are in the territory of the pigmies, who will teach you a sign, already in the sky, which will be a sure guide whenever you are lost' - and they point out the pole star, that in the north, where the sun never goes, stands still while other stars move. Following its light, the party reaches home, and the chief names the star ti-yn-sou-da-go-err, the star which never moves.
summary.zh: 遷徙的一族人迷失於無名大河之畔，飢餓瀕死，酋長病重。議會歌舞焚菸之際，一位孩童模樣的小人前來引路；她夜間僅持小杖領行，黎明備宴，並以皮囊倒出令眾人力大之感的神水。其族長率眾小人而至：「你們已入小人族之地。天空中已有一記號，迷路時可為你們的可靠指引。」眾小人指向北極星——在太陽永不到的北方，眾星移動，唯此星靜止。族人循星光歸家，大酋長召集諸族為此星命名「提恩蘇達戈爾」——永不移動之星。

sensitivity.note: Smith 1883; public domain.

passages.text: A large party of Indians, while moving in search of new hunting grounds, wandered on for many moons, finding but little game. At last they arrived at the banks of a great river, entirely unknown to them, where they had to stop, not having the material to build boats. Lost and nearly famished with hunger, the head chief was taken very ill, and it was decided to hold a council to devise means for returning to their old homes. During the dance, and while the tobacco was burning, a little being like a child came up, saying she was sent to be their guide. Accordingly they broke up their camp and started with her that night. Preceding them, with only a gi-wah, or small war-club, she led them on until daylight and then commanded them to rest while she prepared their food; when awakened by her they found a great feast in readiness for them.
passages.note: Verbatim from Smith 1883, ch. IV; public domain.

passages.text: At evening she reappeared, bringing with her a skin jug, from which she poured out some liquid into a horn cup, and bade them each to taste of it; at first they feared to do so, but yielding they began to feel very strong. She then informed them that they had a long journey to make that night, and in the early morn they arrived at a great plain. At night-fall she returned, saying her own chief would soon follow her to explain how they could reach their own homes in safety; in a short time he arrived, with a great number of his race, and immediately all held council together and informed the Indians that they were now in the territory of the pigmies, who would teach them a sign, already in the sky, which would be to them a sure guide whenever they were lost.
passages.note: Verbatim from Smith 1883, ch. IV; public domain.

passages.text: The pigmies pointed out the pole star and told them that in the north, where the sun never goes, while other stars moved about, this particular star should stand still, as the Indian's guide in his wanderings; that they were then but to follow its light and they would soon return to their tribe, where they would find plenty of game. Then they thanked the good pigmies, and traveled every night until they arrived safely in their homes, where, when they had recounted all their adventures, the head chief called a meeting of all the tribes and said they ought to give this star a name. So they called it ti-yn-sou-da-go-err (the star which never moves), by which name it is called unto this day.
passages.note: Verbatim from Smith 1883, ch. IV; public domain.

title.en: Enki Decrees the World Order
title.zh: 恩基頒定世界秩序

region.en: Eridu, Iraq (Abzu shrine)
region.zh: 埃利都（阿卜祖神殿，伊拉克）

period: Old Babylonian manuscript, c. 1700 BCE (ETCSL translation 2003)

source.work: Enki and the world order (ETCSL c.1.1.3)

license: ETCSL translation (Oxford, 2003-2006); quoted in paraphrase with attribution

summary.en: From his shrine in the Abzu, Enki allocates every land, river, tool and craft its role, then blesses Sumer, Urim and Meluhha in turn. When Inanna complains she was passed over, Enki soothes her with speeches of her powers.
summary.zh: 恩基於阿卜祖神殿中，為各邦、河流、器物與技藝一一賦職，繼而依次祝福蘇美、烏爾與美魯哈。伊南娜埋怨遺漏，恩基以頌詞撫慰，盛讚其能。

sensitivity.note: Ancient myth; presented as comparative-mythology material, not religious truth.

passages.text: Enki, lord of the Abzu, comes out of his shrine and decrees the fates. He fills the Tigris and Euphrates with bright waters, appoints the marshes and reeds, fills the sea and its trade, and sends the rains. He gives the plough to the earth, the yoke to the ox, and sets the great crafts — smithery, smithing of metal, weaving and building — in the hands of their lords.
passages.note: Paraphrase of ETCSL c.1.1.3, lines 1-100; not verbatim.

passages.text: He blesses the black-headed people of Sumer, then Urim with its lofty city-walls and cooling shade, then Meluhha with its black mountains and its ships of timber. He gives each its destiny like a shepherd allotting pasture. Nothing is left without its place, its god, or its due of praise.
passages.note: Paraphrase of ETCSL c.1.1.3, middle section; not verbatim.

passages.text: Inanna stands before him complaining: everywhere she looks she finds a lord and a decree, but for herself only a heap of words. Enki answers that she has not been passed over: heaven and earth were her gifts — she turns a woman into a man and a man into a woman, she holds battle, plunder and the plunderer's hand, and where she is, the assembly gathers.
passages.note: Paraphrase of ETCSL c.1.1.3, closing exchange; not verbatim.

functions: Charter text explaining why every land, craft and river has its divine patron
Ritual script for Inanna's claim of the me at the Uruk new year
Panegyric for Urim and the moon god legitimating Ur's primacy
Theological elevation of Inanna from city goddess to universal power

variants.name: Inana and Enki (the theft of the me)
variants.summary: Inanna gets Enki drunk and carries the me to Uruk; a variant plot in which the world order is seized rather than allocated.

variants.name: Enuma Elish, Marduk allocates the cosmos
variants.summary: The Babylonian parallel in which the young champion, having killed chaos, assigns every god his station.

canonical_translation: ETCSL team translation, Oxford, 2003-2006

primary_sources.citation: ETCSL c.1.1.3, trans. ETCSL team (2003-2006), lines 1-304

secondary_sources.work: Sumerian Mythology: A Study of Spiritual and Literary Achievement in the Third Millennium B.C.
secondary_sources.citation: Samuel Noah Kramer, Philadelphia, 1944, ch. on Enki

title.en: Enki and Ninmah: Humans Shaped from Clay
title.zh: 恩基與寧瑪：黏土塑人

region.en: Eridu, Iraq
region.zh: 埃利都（伊拉克）

period: Old Babylonian manuscript, c. 1700 BCE (ETCSL translation 2003)

source.work: Enki and Ninmah (ETCSL c.1.1.2)

license: ETCSL translation (Oxford, 2003-2006); quoted in paraphrase with attribution

summary.en: The lesser gods, weary of digging canals, complain over Enki's beer; Nammu the primeval sea proposes that her womb-creatures shape men from clay, and Ninmah and Enki divide the work of forming bodies and fates. Their contest turns into a drinking game: Ninmah makes six disabled bodies, Enki finds each a livelihood, and her seventh lump he fixes unfinished.
summary.zh: 諸下神倦於掘渠，於恩基的酒宴上抱怨；原初之海娜木提議以黏土塑人，寧瑪塑身，恩基定命。二人化比賽為酒戲：寧瑪造六具殘軀，恩基各予其生路；第七團泥，恩基令其不成而止。

sensitivity.note: Ancient myth; disability is depicted within an ancient theological framing, not endorsed.

passages.text: The junior gods, digging the canals day and night, come drunk with weariness to Enki's gate and refuse the shovel. Enki, lord of the Abzu, sits with Ninhursag and Nammu and drinks; the primeval sea, his mother, tells him to relieve them: her womb-creatures should knead clay and men should be made to carry the gods' baskets.
passages.note: Paraphrase of ETCSL c.1.1.2, opening; not verbatim.

passages.text: Ninmah takes the clay and shapes six bodies in Enki's sight: a weak-armed man, a blind man, one with broken feet, one who cannot urinate, a barren woman, and one without sex. Enki decrees each one's fate so that every shape can live: the weak-armed serves the king, the blind becomes a singer, the lame a worker for hire, and so the imperfect bodies are given perfect fates.
passages.note: Paraphrase of ETCSL c.1.1.2, central contest; not verbatim.

passages.text: Then Enki challenges Ninmah: whatever he shapes, let her decree its fate. He makes a seventh being with neither arms nor legs, neither penis nor vagina, a soft doll that cannot move, and sets it at her feet. Ninmah looks at it and cannot say a word; whatever she decrees, it cannot live. Enki laughs: how do you equal my decrees? — and the contest ends with the two reconciled over beer.
passages.note: Paraphrase of ETCSL c.1.1.2, closing contest; not verbatim.

functions: Explains why humans labor for the gods — creation as relief of divine workers
Etiology of fate-decreeing and the naming of a child's destiny
Template of vocational roles for disabled persons within the temple economy
Drinking-banquet myth performed at Enki's festivals

variants.name: Atrahasis, creation from clay and blood
variants.text_tradition: Akkadian, Old Babylonian (ETCSL parallel c.1.7.x; Rogers 1912)
variants.summary: The Babylonian version in which man is mixed of clay and a slain god's blood after the Igigu revolt.

variants.name: Enuma Elish, mankind from Qingu's blood
variants.summary: Marduk has Ea create lullu-man from the blood of the executed rebel Qingu to serve the gods.

canonical_translation: ETCSL team translation, Oxford, 2003-2006

primary_sources.citation: ETCSL c.1.1.2, trans. ETCSL team (2003-2006), lines 1-166

secondary_sources.work: Myths from Mesopotamia: Creation, the Flood, Gilgamesh, and Others
secondary_sources.citation: Stephanie Dalley, Oxford, 1989, introduction to Atrahasis

title.en: Enki's Journey to Nippur
title.zh: 恩基赴尼普魯之行

region.en: Nippur, Iraq
region.zh: 尼普魯（伊拉克）

period: Old Babylonian manuscript, c. 1700 BCE (ETCSL translation 2003)

source.work: Enki's journey to Nibru (ETCSL c.1.1.4)

license: ETCSL translation (Oxford, 2003-2006); quoted in paraphrase with attribution

summary.en: Enki harnesses his boat of forty and sails from Eridu up the river to Nippur, where Enlil receives him at the Ekur with feasting. Over the banquet Enki officiates as ritual master and blesses the journey, and the poem ends with Enki's praise of the rites.
summary.zh: 恩基套上四十人巨舟，自埃利都溯流而上抵尼普魯；恩利爾於埃庫爾殿設宴相迎。宴中恩基親執禮儀之職，為旅程祝福，詩末恩基頌揚諸儀。

sensitivity.note: Ancient ritual narrative; no living community restrictions.

passages.text: In Eridu, Enki harnesses the great boat of forty and loads it with his gifts; he appoints theAbgal-priest and the masters of the rites to crew it, and the boat glides up the river like a giant among boats, its cabin of white cedar, its prow painted.
passages.note: Paraphrase of ETCSL c.1.1.4, opening voyage; not verbatim.

passages.text: Enki enters Nippur; the city gates open before him. At the Ekur, the temple of Enlil, he is made to sit at the great banquet; he stands and officiates as the master of ceremonies, offering to Enlil and the Anuna gods, and Enlil gives him the Abzu's destiny and the lapis-lazuli house of Eridu as reward.
passages.note: Paraphrase of ETCSL c.1.1.4, arrival and banquet; not verbatim.

passages.text: Over the cups Enki blesses each office and each rite in turn — the libations, the lustrations, the hymns — until the Anuna gods, drunk, bless Enki himself. The poem closes: whoever recites its lines by day shall have no sleepless nights, whoever recites them by night shall have no bad dreams.
passages.note: Paraphrase of ETCSL c.1.1.4, closing blessings; not verbatim.

functions: Script for the liturgical banquet and the etiquette of offering
Myth of reciprocity between Nippur and Eridu, the two senior sanctuaries
Protective incantation: recitation wards off bad dreams
Charter for ritual journeys by barge along the river cult route
