summary.en: Hemlock Bows, who can shake thirty deer small as squirrels and back again, follows his truant wife to a hollow black-ash tree where a fine man in a feathered turban comes out to meet her; his arrow passes between them and she beats him blind, turns the children into the snow and burns the cabin. The dog houses the children; a bear carries off the little girl; the boy survives being swallowed by a great fish, is cut out alive by two fisher women, and later shoots the eagle at his mother's wedding games, rescues father, sister and dog, and burns the cabin where his mother dies - from whose ashes rises a screech owl.
summary.zh: 能將三十隻鹿搖小如松鼠再搖回原大的「鐵杉弓」，跟蹤不貞的妻子至一棵中空的黑梣樹，一位戴羽冠的俊美男子自樹中出迎。他的箭從二人之間穿過，反遭妻子打瞎，孩子被棄雪中，屋亦被焚。犬為孩子搭雪屋；幼女被熊叼走；男孩被大魚吞下卻活著被兩位捕魚婦女剖出。他後來在母親改嫁的射鷹競賽中射中鷹，救出父親、妹妹與犬，焚燒母親所在的屋——母親死後，灰燼中鑽出一隻啼叫的鴞。

sensitivity.note: Smith 1883; public domain. Marital violence is story-register, not endorsement.

passages.text: There was a man whose name was Hemlock Bows; he would kill so many deer that he could not carry them all home - he took them and shook them, and shook, till they were as small as squirrels, and carried them all home, and when he got there he shook, and shook, till they were good-sized deer again. After the birth of her second child the wife seemed to care no more for her husband: when he went hunting she would wash and dress up very fine, take a long strap and an ax, and leave the children alone all day.
passages.note: Verbatim from Smith 1883, ch. V; public domain.

passages.text: The little boy told his father all about his mother going away every day, and he resolved to follow her. He tracked her very closely to a large black-ash tree, which was hollow; a very nice-looking man came out of the tree to meet her, wearing a turban filled with bright feathers. When the man kissed her the hunter drew his bow and shot, and the arrow went between him and the woman. She was very angry, took a club and beat her husband till he could not see; then she went home, put the boy and girl out in the cold and snow, set fire to the cabin, and went off.
passages.note: Verbatim from Smith 1883, ch. V; public domain.

passages.text: The dog fixed the boy and girl in a house in the snow, and the next day they started on a long walk. While the boy was traveling with his little sister on his back she saw a flock of large white turkeys and wanted one; while he was after it a bear came and carried off the little girl, and the dog followed after the bear. The boy cried and cried, wished that he might die; he tried to hang himself, but the strap broke; he jumped down a steep place onto a lot of stones, but still he was unhurt. He plunged into a lake, but it was very shallow, and soon a great fish came towards him with its great mouth wide open. Not far off lived a woman and her daughter who had fences of osier fixed in the lake to catch fish; in the morning they killed and dressed a very large one, and when they cut it up there they found the boy alive.
passages.note: Verbatim from Smith 1883, ch. V; public domain.

passages.text: They heard that the boy's mother was going to be married to another man. Between two cabins was a long stick put up, and on it was an eagle, and the one that shot the eagle was to marry the woman. The boy went among the wigwams and found his sister hanging to a crane in a chimney, and near her the dog; he got his father, sister, and dog away, then went back and set fire to the cabin his mother was in; it burned so fast that she could not get out, and she died. When her head cracked open it shook the ground, and out of the ashes of his mother there rose up a screech owl. His father got well, and they all went to live with the woman and her daughter - the old man married the woman, and the boy the daughter, and so they were happy at last.
passages.note: Verbatim from Smith 1883, ch. V; public domain.

title.en: The Charmed Suit: The Impostor with the Birds That Would Not Light His Pipe
title.zh: 魔法衣：鳥兒不為其點菸的冒名者

region.en: Chief's village to the west of the solitary lodge
region.zh: 孤屋以西的酋長之村

period: Recorded 1878-1881 by Erminnie A. Smith (1883)

source.work: Erminnie A. Smith, 'Myths of the Iroquois' (1883), ch. V: 'The charmed suit'

summary.en: Raised quietly in a solitary lodge, a boy is sent daily to listen until he hears a woman's song naming him: 'I belong to the wolf clan. I am going to marry him.' His uncle dresses him in magic finery - a swan that comes alive on his head, a pipe lit by two little birds, spittle that becomes wampum - but warns of a man at a stream who will beg help killing wild cats. The youth stays the night; the tempter covers him with prickly bark, steals his charmed suit and goes to the chief's daughters, who are deceived except the younger sister. Found in a field asleep, the true youth dreams a dream before a great council: the birds fill his pipe, the swan comes alive, his spittle becomes wampum - and the impostor is left in his own rags.
summary.zh: 孤屋長大的少年日日聽聲，直至聽見女聲唱出：「我屬狼氏族，我將嫁給他。」叔父為他備下魔法行頭——會復活的天鵝冠、由兩隻小鳥點火的菸斗、唾沫化貝珠——並警告途中會有人藉殺野貓求援。少年留宿被騙，被荊皮所蟄，行頭盡失；冒名者前往酋長二女處，只有妹妹識破。真少年在田中被妹妹發現，遂於大議會上「作夢」：鳥兒為他點菸、天鵝復活、唾沫成珠——冒名者被打回原形的破衣。

sensitivity.note: Smith 1883; public domain.

passages.text: An old man brought up his son very quietly in a solitary place, sending him daily into the woods to listen. Morning after morning he heard snow-birds, wolves, owls; at last, as the sun began to rise, he heard quite a new sound, like a voice singing: 'Ha-hum-weh, Ha-hum-weh, Wa-he-dum-nae, Sru-gua he' - 'I belong to the wolf clan. I am going to marry him.' It was a sweet woman's voice. 'The chief of a distant village sends his two daughters to see us,' said the father. He threw ashes all over the boy's bed and put on him his best feathers: 'Do not look at the maidens when they come in; they come to see me, not you; hold your head down while they stay.'
passages.note: Verbatim from Smith 1883, ch. V; public domain.

passages.text: The sisters refused to sit by the old man, cleared up the wigwam, and when the boy went to sleep they lifted him out of his dirty bed strewn with ashes and put him into their clean bed. In the morning the younger one admired him: 'What a beautiful young man!' The old man said, 'Good woman; can clean up, can cook, can make good wife,' and gave his son magic arrows for luck in hunting, and dressed him with a swan stuffed: 'when you take this outside it will be on your head, but it will soon come back to life... many deer and bears will follow your track.' He warned of dangers in the path: 'There stands a man and he will try to kill you. He will call out to you that he has a couple of wild cats... Pay no attention.' And he hung up a curious thing of colored string and deep red elk hair: if it came down almost to the ground, his nephew was in danger.
passages.note: Verbatim from Smith 1883, ch. V; public domain.

passages.text: At the stream the stranger begged for help against the wild cats, then asked him to stop all night. The uncle at home watched the signal go down almost to the ground and cried out in alarm - but the youth agreed to stay. The old man gathered sharp prickly bark, pretending it gave a good light, placed it on the sleeping youth, who writhed in agony; then he took off the young man's handsome clothes, dressed him in his own old rags, and started off to the chief's house with the pipe whose two little birds lighted it, the spotted deer skin, and the handsome bag. The younger sister was disappointed - 'This cannot be the young man' - and observed that the bag did not obey the stranger's command to stand up, and that the birds would not light his pipe 'for a stranger.'
passages.note: Verbatim from Smith 1883, ch. V; public domain.

passages.text: Husking corn in the fields one day, the younger sister found a man asleep near a fire, and recognized the beautiful young man, how greatly changed! She brought him food, and he said, 'I will make a dream. Go and tell the chief, your father, that I have dreamed a dream and all the people must come to hear it.' At the great council he told his story in the form of a dream, and when he spoke of the birds they came and filled his pipe, and the swan skin when placed upon his head also came to life, and his spittle became wampum. So the chief knew he was the rightful owner of the clothes and they were returned to him, and the impostor was obliged to resume his old rags. The young man was then married to the faithful maiden, and became in time a noted chief.
passages.note: Verbatim from Smith 1883, ch. V; public domain.

title.en: The Lad and the Chestnuts: The White Heron's Watch
title.zh: 少年與栗子：白鷺的守望

region.en: Great river and the guarded chestnut tree beyond (traditional)
region.zh: 大河與彼岸受守的栗樹（傳統）

period: Recorded 1878-1881 by Erminnie A. Smith (1883)

source.work: Erminnie A. Smith, 'Myths of the Iroquois' (1883), ch. V: 'The lad and the chestnuts'

summary.en: A younger brother secretly watches his elder cook half a chestnut in a magic kettle that grows with every whip-stroke; the lad's excess fills the house, and the brother, declaring he must die, wastes away singing 'Bring me my pipe and let me die.' Beyond an almost uncrossable river stands the ancestral chestnut tree, watched day and night by a white heron set by half a dozen women who come out with war-clubs at his Thr-hr-hr. The lad crosses on a canoe of three inches drawn large, bribes the heron with the seeds of a plant he dearly likes, fills his bag, cuts five fish-lines thrown by the women, and returns in time to cook the chestnuts and restore his brother.
summary.zh: 弟弟偷看兄長以魔法釜煮半顆栗子——鞭一下釜便大一圈；弟弟學樣，釜大漲滿屋。兄長哀歌「把菸斗拿來，讓我死吧」。在幾不可渡的大河彼岸，立著祖傳的栗樹，由六位婦女所設的白鷺日夜守望，一有聲響便發出Thr-hr-hr的警號，眾婦持棒而出。弟弟以三寸小舟抽大渡河，以鷺所嗜的豆狀草籽引開牠，裝滿栗袋，連斷五根魚線而歸，及時煮熟栗子救回兄長。

sensitivity.note: Smith 1883; public domain. Second version of the chestnut cycle Parker also records.

passages.text: At daylight the elder set off to hunt. Cautiously the boy lifted the trap-door, and there he at once saw the kettle. In it lay half a chestnut. As night drew on he took the kettle, scraped up the chestnut, put in some water, and found the stick. He at once commenced whipping the kettle as he had seen his brother do, saying, 'Now my kettle will grow large' - and it did; but it kept on growing larger and larger, to his surprise, until it filled the whole room, and he had to go up on the roof to stir it from the outside. When the elder brother returned he said, 'What are you doing?' 'I found the kettle,' replied the younger, 'and was getting your supper.' 'Woe is me,' said the elder, 'now I must die.' He struck and struck the kettle, and reduced it by every blow, until at last he could restore it to its place.
passages.note: Verbatim from Smith 1883, ch. V; public domain.

passages.text: Day by day he grew weaker, and after each smoke sang, 'Hah geh-he geh, Non ta ge je o dah!' - 'Bring me my pipe and let me die.' At length the brother said, 'Far, far away is a large river, which it is almost impossible to cross. On the further side stands a house; near it is a tree, a chestnut tree; there my forefathers gathered chestnuts long ago, but now none can reach it, for there stands night and day a white heron watching the tree... He is set there by the women folks; half a dozen of them take care of him, and for them he watches. If he hears a sound he makes his Thr-hr-hr. Then the women come out with war-clubs... Even a mouse is suspected of being a man. There is no chance, no chance at all.' But the brother said, 'I must go and try this for your sake; I cannot have you die.'
passages.note: Verbatim from Smith 1883, ch. V; public domain.

passages.text: He departed after making a little canoe about three inches long; at the river he drew it out and out until it was a good size, and in it he crossed, then made it small again and put it in his pouch. He called a mole out of the ground, which sniffed around a little plant, the seed of which the heron dearly likes - like a bean. Following the mole under the leaves until he neared the heron, he threw the seeds to the bird, and whilst it was occupied and noticed nothing else, the boy filled his bag with chestnuts and set off homewards.
passages.note: Verbatim from Smith 1883, ch. V; public domain.

passages.text: The heron gave his warning Thr-hr-hr, but the lad was already far away. Once more he took out his canoe, and was on the water when the women rushed out: they threw a long fish line and caught his canoe, but he cut it and got loose - and so on till they had no lines left. He reached home and shouted, 'Now, brother, I'm home with the chestnuts, will you have your pipe?' And the brother said, 'You have done me a great favor, now I shall be well, and we will be happy.'
passages.note: Verbatim from Smith 1883, ch. V; public domain.

title.en: The Guilty Hunters: The Face in the Water and the Bitten Thumb
title.zh: 有罪的獵人：水中之臉與被咬的拇指

region.en: Neighboring hunting camps of two clans by a stream
region.zh: 溪畔兩族相鄰的獵營

period: Recorded 1878-1881 by Erminnie A. Smith (1883)

source.work: Erminnie A. Smith, 'Myths of the Iroquois' (1883), ch. V: 'The guilty hunters'

summary.en: Two families camp side by side; one has fine luck, the other none. A mother sees in the stream the reflection of a handsome man with painted cheeks hidden in the branches - a man from the adjoining camp - and reads it as an evil omen. The husband sends her and the child into a hollow log and meets the robbers alone: 'You have bitten me.' She hides in a hemlock over the murderers' camp, hears one say his thumb is painful - 'say a beaver bit you' - and at the general council convicts them: the chief says gravely, 'Go, do your duty,' and the warriors soon put to death the wicked hunters.
summary.zh: 兩族比鄰紮營，一家獵運亨通，一家一無所獲。一位母親在溪水中窺見藏在枝頭、面頰敷彩的俊美男子——正是鄰營之人——她視之為凶兆。丈夫送妻兒藏入空心圓木，隻身赴險：「你咬了我。」她藏身於兇手營上的鐵杉，聽見有人說拇指疼痛——「就說是河狸咬的」——並在大議會上指證兇徒。酋長沉聲道：「去吧，盡你們的職責。」戰士們隨即誅殺了這些惡獵人。

sensitivity.note: Smith 1883; public domain.

passages.text: In one of its hunting excursions two families of different clans happened to pitch their camps quite near each other. One, in which there was an infant, had very fine luck and the other poor luck. While the father of the child was out hunting, the mother went to a neighboring stream to get some water, but before she dipped her vessel she looked into the water and saw, peering up through the sparkling stream, a very handsome young man with painted cheeks. What the woman had seen was but the reflection of some one hidden in the branches overhanging the stream, and she recognized the face as that of a man from the adjoining camp. They rightly judged that this was an evil omen.
passages.note: Verbatim from Smith 1883, ch. V; public domain.

passages.text: When night came the husband said to his wife, 'You and the child must be saved. Go; I shall meet misfortune alone.' She started with the child through the forest until she came to a hollow log, into which she crept; soon she heard a great noise in the camp, and a voice saying, 'You have bitten me.' Torches came searching for her and the child, pushing their sticks into the log, and saying, 'She must be somewhere near here; any way, she cannot live long.' She traveled parallel to the trail and climbed a large hemlock in a clearing, where during the night she heard one of the laden hunters say, 'My thumb is painful; what shall I say bit me?' and the answer: 'Say a beaver bit you.'
passages.note: Verbatim from Smith 1883, ch. V; public domain.

passages.text: Reaching home at twilight, she related what had happened, and the head chief called a general council. None but the hunters were absent, and they came after repeated and persistent requests. 'Now, relate to us all the things that have happened to you,' said the head chief, 'and tell why you have returned without the other party.' They refused to tell anything. When she had finished her narrative she told that one of them had his thumb bitten - by her husband in defending himself against these robbers, who took from her murdered husband the skins and the meats. Hereupon the head chief gravely said to the waiting and impatient warriors, 'Go, do your duty'; and they, with their war-clubs and tomahawks, soon put to death the wicked hunters.
passages.note: Verbatim from Smith 1883, ch. V; public domain.

title.en: Mrs. Logan's Story: The Skeleton's Island and the Pit Under the Bed
title.zh: 羅根夫人所述：骷髏之島與床下之坑

region.en: Swan-propelled island in a great lake, and a cranberry swamp beyond
region.zh: 天鵝舟所達的湖心島，以及更遠的蔓越莓沼澤

period: Recorded 1878-1881 by Erminnie A. Smith (1883)

source.work: Erminnie A. Smith, 'Myths of the Iroquois' (1883), ch. V: 'Mrs. Logan's story'

summary.en: A boy invited to shoot and swim with a stranger is stripped and abandoned on an island. A skeleton near him - mice driven out by pipe smoke - coaches him through the visits of the three-dog man: track the island, jump in and out of the water, sleep in a hollow tree, and lie hidden in a sand pit at the landing until the abductor comes to drink his blood - then steal the swan canoe, 'Come, swans, let's go home,' and never look back. In a rock cave he finds his own clothes; sent east, he rescues the sister the man carried off, hides her brother under her bed-planks, kills the water-drinking abductor with a thrown stone, turns his dogs into wolves, and raises the dead of the skeleton's island to build a long house with six fire-places.
summary.zh: 男孩應陌生人邀約賽射、比泳，被剝衣棄於島上。身旁的骷髏（菸煙驅走滿身鼠群）指導他應付三犬男子：踏遍全島、屢次跳入又躍出水中、夜宿空心樹、藏身沙坑待其登岸吸血——再竊天鵝舟唱「天鵝們，我們回家吧」，永不回頭。岩洞中他尋回己衣；被遣往東方，他救回多年前被擄的姐姐，藏身其床板下的坑中，以擲石誅殺飲水脹身的擄人者，令其犬化為狼，並喚醒骷髏島上的死者，共建六灶長屋。

sensitivity.note: Smith 1883; public domain. Cannibalism is attributed to the villain and reported at story distance.

passages.text: An old man and his little nephew once lived in a dark woods. The boy, tired of playing in one place, went to a large lake, where a man came up and said, 'Let us play together at shooting arrows... Let us go to the island, where you will see many pretty birds.' On either side of the canoe were three swans which propelled it. As soon as they were seated the man began singing, and very soon they arrived at the island; then the man took off all the boy's clothes and, jumping into his canoe, said, 'Come, swans, let us go home.' It began to grow dark, and the boy was greatly frightened when he heard a voice say, 'Hist! keep still' - a skeleton on the ground near him beckoned: 'Poor boy, it was the same thing with me, but I will help you if you will do something for me.'
passages.note: Verbatim from Smith 1883, ch. V; public domain.

passages.text: The skeleton told him to dig on the west side of a tree near by for a tobacco-pouch, a pipe, and a flint, fill and light the pipe and put it in its mouth; then, as the skeleton smoked, the boy saw that its body was full of mice, which went away because of the smoke. 'A man with three dogs is coming to the island that night to kill me... you must run all over the island and jump into the water and out again many times, so that the man will lose the trail; then get into a hollow tree near by, and stay all night.' The dogs ran all over the island, found nothing, and the man killed one of his dogs and ate him all up. 'The man who brought you here will come to-night to drink your blood; dig a long pit at the shore... and when he comes ashore, get into the canoe and say, Come, swans, let's go home - and if the man calls for you to come back you must not turn around or look at him.'
passages.note: Verbatim from Smith 1883, ch. V; public domain.

passages.text: The boy jumped into the canoe, singing as the man had done; the man cried, 'Come back! Oh do come back!' but the boy did not look around. The swans went up into a large rock to a door, and in the cave he found his own clothes and many others, a fire and food all prepared. Returning to the island he found the man killed and nearly eaten up. 'Now you must go and get your sister whom this man carried off many years ago... you will come to some very high rocks where she goes for water.' A bad man kept her there; while he was away at the swamp where women and children were picking cranberries, the sister dug a pit under her bed-planks and covered her brother in it, then cooked a little boy for the man's supper. The dogs barked; 'You surely have visitors,' he said. 'Kill me if you like, but I have none,' she denied - and the saucy answers told him she had seen some one.
passages.note: Verbatim from Smith 1883, ch. V; public domain.

passages.text: In the morning she called her brother, they jumped into the canoe and went off, but the man ran and threw a hook which caught the canoe; the boy broke it with a stone from the bottom. Then the enraged man laid himself down upon the shore and drank the water from the lake, causing the boat to return very fast, until he grew very big with so much water in him; the boy threw a stone and hit the man so it killed him, and the water ran back into the lake. The boy said to the two dogs, 'You bad dogs... You must go into the woods and be wolves,' and they became wolves. At the island the skeleton said, 'Gather up all the bones you see and put them in a pile; then push the largest tree you see and say, All dead folks arise - and they will all arise.' All the dead arose, some having but one arm, some with but one leg, but all had their bows and arrows; the boy and his sister brought them home, and they built a long house with six fire-places, where they lived peacefully many years.
passages.note: Verbatim from Smith 1883, ch. V; public domain.

title.en: The Hunter and His Dead Wife: The Wooden Doll Returned
title.zh: 獵人與亡妻：歸來的木偶

region.en: Forest cabin far from the rest of the tribe
region.zh: 遠離族人的林中木屋

period: Recorded 1878-1881 by Erminnie A. Smith (1883)

source.work: Erminnie A. Smith, 'Myths of the Iroquois' (1883), ch. V: 'The hunter and his dead wife'

summary.en: After his wife dies, a lonely hunter dresses a wooden doll in her clothes and sets it by the fire-place, brushing the fallen ashes from its face. Then fire and wood appear by the door, meat cooks in the kettle - and one early return he finds his wife sitting in the chair, the doll gone. 'The Great Spirit felt sorry for you, so he let me come back to see you, but you must not touch me till we have seen all of our people; if you do, you will kill me.' Within a day's journey of the camp his desire overcomes him; he clasps her - and holds the wooden doll. The tracks in the snow end like a doll's feet, and the man was ever after very unhappy.
summary.zh: 妻死之後，孤獨的獵人以她的衣物裝扮一具木偶置於灶前，日日拂去落於面上的灰燼。隨後門前有火有柴，釜中有肉——一日早歸，他見亡妻端坐椅上，木偶不見。她說：「大神憐你，讓我回來看你；但在見過所有族人之前不可碰我，否則我會死。」距營地一日路程處，他的渴望戰勝了戒律；他擁她入懷——抱著的卻是木偶。雪中的足跡末端恰似偶足。此後他鬱鬱終老。

sensitivity.note: Smith 1883; public domain.

passages.text: The man felt very badly and buried her in the cabin. He was very lonesome; and after a day or two he made a wooden doll about her size and dressed it in the clothes she used to wear. Then he put it down in front of the fire-place and felt better. Then he went hunting; and when he came back he would go up to the doll and brush the ashes off from the face, for as the wood fell down the ashes would rattle onto the face. He had to do his cooking, mending, and making fire, for now there was no one to help him; and so a year passed away.
passages.note: Verbatim from Smith 1883, ch. V; public domain.

passages.text: One day when he came home from hunting there was a fire and wood by the door. The next night there was wood and fire and a piece of meat all cooked in the kettle. He looked all over to see who had done this, but could find no one. The next time he went hunting he did not go far and went back quite early, and when he came in sight of the cabin he saw a woman going into the house with wood on her shoulders; he opened the door quickly, and there was his wife sitting in a chair and the wooden doll was gone.
passages.note: Verbatim from Smith 1883, ch. V; public domain.

passages.text: Then she spoke to him, saying, 'The Great Spirit felt sorry for you, so he let me come back to see you, but you must not touch me till we have seen all of our people; if you do, you will kill me.' So they lived along for some time... When they were within a day's journey of the camp it began to snow, and as they were very weary they lighted fire and partook of food and spread their skins to sleep; but the desire of the man to once more clasp his wife in his arms was too great, and he went up to her and put out his hands; but she motioned him away and said, 'We have seen no one yet.' He would not listen to her, and he caught her in his arms, and, behold, he was holding the wooden doll! His sorrow was very great. Some doubted, and they went back with him and found the doll; they also saw the track of the two people in the snow, and the track just like the foot of the doll. The man was ever after very unhappy.
passages.note: Verbatim from Smith 1883, ch. V; public domain.

title.en: A Sure Revenge: Ga-geh-djo-wa Among the Illinois
title.zh: 必償之仇：伊利諾人中的加格卓瓦

region.en: Seneca settlement on Lake Erie and the Illinois country (traditional)
region.zh: 伊利湖畔的塞內卡聚落與伊利諾之地（傳統）

period: Recorded 1878-1881 by Erminnie A. Smith (1883)

source.work: Erminnie A. Smith, 'Myths of the Iroquois' (1883), ch. V: 'A sure revenge'

summary.en: The Illinois surprise a Seneca settlement and carry off a woman and a boy, who sings his vow of revenge in his own tongue while they think he joins their triumph. The woman is slain after charging him: 'Avenge my blood! Promise me you will never cease to be a Seneca.' Tortured - barefooted on coals, blisters pierced and filled with flint, a race over thorn-briers, the stake, and three drownings - he survives, is adopted as Ga-geh-djo-wa, and fifteen years later leads the Illinois war party against his own people, guides them into an ambush of five hundred Senecas, and stumbles as the signal: three hundred scalps avenge the treachery of the Illinois.
summary.zh: 伊利諾人偷襲伊利湖畔的塞內卡聚落，擄走一名婦人與男孩。男孩以本族語言反覆唱著復仇之誓，敵人以為他同慶。婦人臨刑囑咐：「為我復仇！答應我永不背棄塞內卡。」他歷盡酷刑——赤足踏炭、水泡刺破填入燧石、荊棘叢中賽跑、火刑柱、三次溺水——竟得存活，被收養為加格卓瓦。十五年後他率伊利諾戰隊攻擊族人，將其引入五百塞內卡戰士的埋伏，以跌倒為號——三百枚髮皮為伊利諾人的背信償命。

sensitivity.note: Smith 1883; public domain. Captivity-torture narrative of record; grim but historical register.

passages.text: One eventful winter their enemies, the Illinois, came in great numbers upon the peaceful settlement, surprised the people in their homes, and, in spite of a stout resistance, killed a large number of them and took a middle-aged woman and a boy captive. Around a roaring fire the warriors gloated over the bloody deed, and bid the boy join them in their songs of triumph. The lad pretended that he could not sing their language, but said that he would sing their song in his tongue, knowing that they could not comprehend a word of it. While they shouted out their jubilant delight he repeated, again and again, 'I shall never forget what you have done to my people... If I am spared you will all lose your scalps.' The Illinois warriors understood not a word; they thought he was joining in their triumph.
passages.note: Verbatim from Smith 1883, ch. V; public domain.

passages.text: After they had marched three days the woman became exhausted, and she was too faint to be dragged further. She meanwhile spoke to the Seneca boy in earnest tones: 'Avenge my blood!... and when you return to your own people tell them how the cruel Illinois took my life. Promise me you will never cease to be a Seneca.' As he finished promising all she asked, she was slain and left dead on the ground. At the Illinois settlement the chiefs decided that there was stuff in him, and they would therefore torture him: they held him barefooted on the coals until his feet were one mass of blisters, pierced the blisters with a needle made of fish bone and filled them up with sharp flint stones. 'Now run a race - run twenty rods.' In his dream he had been told that if he could reach the Long House and find a seat on the wild-cat skin, they would vote him worthy of his life. Singing what they thought their war song, he forgot his agony, bounded forward and flew so swiftly that those ready to hit him with thorn-brier branches could not touch him; he rushed into the crowded Long House and managed to seat himself upon the tail of the wild-cat skin.
passages.note: Verbatim from Smith 1883, ch. V; public domain.

passages.text: The majority finally decided that he must die, and in three days should be burned at the stake. When the day arrived they bound the lad to a stake amid a large fire of pine knots, when an old warrior suddenly approached from the forest: 'His eye is bright. I will take him. I will make a warrior of him... and if he survives I will adopt him into the tribe.' He cut the thongs and led him away to a spring: 'Drink!' And as the lad stooped, he pressed him down under the water until he was well nigh strangled; three times he subjected him to this barbarity; then as he was still alive he took him to his wigwam and dressed his feet - and no one guessed that revenge was in his heart.
passages.note: Verbatim from Smith 1883, ch. V; public domain.

passages.text: He had been fifteen years among them when he heard them speak of an expedition against the Senecas. He begged to join, and they elected him chief of the expedition. At the council held that night Ga-geh-djo-wa proposed to go himself with another warrior; when they had gone five or six miles the wily chief said, 'Let us separate... You go over the hills; I will go through the valley.' He found a family he knew: 'The treacherous Illinois are upon you. Warn all the tribe of Senecas: bid them come early and hide along the range above the valley. I will be there with a heron's plume on my crest, and when I stumble it is the signal for the Senecas to attack.' Returning, he reported that he had seen nothing; then he offered to track the Senecas to their hiding-place. Little they dreamed that already five hundred Senecas awaited them in the valley. As they entered it, he, pretending to miss his footing, fell: instantly the war-cry sounded, the Senecas rushed from their ambush, and the slaughter was great. Three hundred scalps revenged the treachery of the Illinois, and Ga-geh-djo-wa lived many years, the most esteemed warrior and chief of the Senecas.
passages.note: Verbatim from Smith 1883, ch. V; public domain.

title.en: Traveler's Jokes: Goh-weh, goh-weh
title.zh: 旅人的玩笑：果威，果威

region.en: Village trail between Iroquois towns
region.zh: 易洛魁各鎮之間的村道

period: Recorded 1878-1881 by Erminnie A. Smith (1883)

source.work: Erminnie A. Smith, 'Myths of the Iroquois' (1883), ch. V: 'Traveler's jokes'

summary.en: Tired of an uneventful journey, a traveler abuses the runners' cry 'Goh-weh, goh-weh' to gather crowds, then invents news: at the last village they danced for joy and kissed him - so the crowd, not wishing to be outdone, sings and kisses him too; at the next town some wept and quarreled, so his audience does the same. Camping with a boastful stranger he asks what log he pillows on - hickory, elm? 'No, it is everlasting sleep' - and in the morning rubs pitchy resin over the sleeper's eyes and leaves, laughing.
summary.zh: 旅途無聊的旅人濫用信使的呼聲「果威，果威」召聚人群，編造新聞：上個村子的人歡舞親吻他——聽者不甘落後，也唱歌親吻；下一鎮則有人哭泣鬥毆——聽者如法炮製。夜宿時他問自誇機智的同伴枕的是什麼木——胡桃？榆木？「不，是長眠之木」；清晨他在睡者眼上抹滿松脂，笑著離去。

sensitivity.note: Smith 1883; public domain.

passages.text: An old Indian custom is for runners, or those carrying important news, to announce the fact and gather the people together by crying, in singing tones, 'Goh-weh, goh-weh.' This the traveler began doing, and when the crowd called upon him to stop and tell his news, he began, 'As I came through the last village the people were so delighted with my news that they all danced for joy, and shouted and kissed me.' This he told so earnestly and sincerely that the people, not wishing to be outdone by any other tribe, also began singing and kissing him and making merry; and while the excitement was at its height, pleased with his success, the facetious traveler escaped and continued his journeyings.
passages.note: Verbatim from Smith 1883, ch. V; public domain.

passages.text: Arrived at the next village he again began calling, 'Goh-weh, goh-weh'; and the people and chiefs gathered around him, crying, 'Let us hear.' And he answered, 'As I passed through the last town some people wept at my news, others began quarreling, kicking, and fighting.' Immediately his contagious news produced its effect, and in the confusion he again escaped, saying to himself, 'What fools people are.' That night, as he was preparing to camp out, a man passed who inquired the distance to the next village; but the traveler said, 'You cannot reach it to-night. Let us camp together.' As the new-comer was boasting of his superior cunning, the traveler inquired, 'What log is that you now use for a pillow?' and he guessed hickory, elm. But the traveler said, 'No, it is everlasting sleep.' In the morning the traveler took some pitchy resin and rubbed over the eyes of his sleeping comrade and left, laughing at the probable chagrin the man would feel when attempting to open his eyes.
passages.note: Verbatim from Smith 1883, ch. V; public domain.

title.en: Kingfisher and His Nephew: The Sticks in the Nose and the Stolen Wings
title.zh: 翠鳥與姪兒：鼻中之枝與被竊的翅膀

region.en: River log and a lovely island, Seneca Reservation (Zachariah Jamieson informant)
region.zh: 河上圓木與可愛的島嶼，塞內卡保留地（扎卡里亞詹姆森講述）

period: Told by Zachariah Jamieson, from Chief Warrior (Smith 1883)

source.work: Erminnie A. Smith, 'Myths of the Iroquois' (1883), ch. V: 'Kingfisher and his nephew'

summary.en: Forbidden to fish west, the nephew spies his uncle To-be-se-ne sticking two sharp sticks up his nose and plunging deep for fish; trying it himself he nearly dies of the ache. Later he joins boys with wings who invite him to swim for distance - and fly away with his clothes and wings, calling 'Uncle, here is game for you to-night.' Hiding tree to tree from the many-faced man's dogs all night, he ambushes the winged boys next morning, seizes every pair, and flies home crying, 'Uncle, now there is plenty of game for you' - 'You had no mercy on me; I only treat you the same.'
summary.zh: 姪兒被禁向西捕魚，卻偷看叔父托貝塞內將兩根尖枝插入鼻孔潛水抓魚；自己一試幾乎痛死。其後他遇上有翼的少年們邀他比賽潛泳——他們卻連衣物帶翅膀全部帶走，喊著「叔叔，今晚有你想要的獵物」飛走。他藏於一樹又一樹，躲過有雙面男人的獵犬整夜；翌晨伏擊有翼少年們，奪走全部翅膀，飛回家中喊道：「叔叔，現在有很多獵物了」——「你們對我沒有憐憫，我也同樣對待你們。」

sensitivity.note: Smith 1883; public domain. The uncle is the kingfisher-bird in human form.

passages.text: The old man said to his nephew, 'When you are a man, remember in hunting never to go west; always go to the east.' The young man reflected: 'Why should this be so? My uncle To-be-se-ne always goes west, and brings home plenty of fish.' He made up his mind at last that he would go. As he passed the marsh land near the river he saw his uncle take from his pocket two sharp sticks and put them in his nose, and then plunge into deep water and come up with a nice fish. Presently the uncle came back bringing some nice fish, but he never guessed that the nephew had seen him. The young man now felt certain that he could fish as well as his uncle; one day he stuck the two sticks into his nose and plunged in - then the sticks went deep into his nose and made it ache dreadfully, and he felt very sick. 'You have done very wrong,' said the uncle; but he took the pincers and drew out the sticks.
passages.note: Verbatim from Smith 1883, ch. V; public domain.

passages.text: After a while, however, he started west again. He heard boys laughing, joined them, and they invited him to swim. 'It is time to go home; you go, too.' Then he saw that they had wings, and they gave him a pair: 'There is an island where all is lovely... come.' They started up in the air, far away above the trees. 'Let us see which can go down and come up the farthest'; and while he was in the water the rest put on their wings and, taking his also, flew up in the air. He plead in vain for them to wait; but they called, as though speaking to some one else, 'Uncle, here is game for you to-night.' He perceived tracks of dogs which had clawed the different trees; to confuse them in their scent he climbed each tree a little way until he reached the last tree on the island. The man had a horrid-looking face, both behind and before; the dogs traced him tree by tree all night long, until the old man said, very angrily, 'There is no game here; my nephews have deceived me.'
passages.note: Verbatim from Smith 1883, ch. V; public domain.

passages.text: After sunrise the poor fellow came down from the tree, saying, 'If those young fellows return I will watch them and contrive to get their wings from them.' He soon heard their voices, saying, 'Now we will have a good time... Let us all dive together.' Then he rushed out, and, taking all the wings, he put on one pair, and flew away, calling out, 'Uncle, now there is plenty of game for you'; and when they entreated him he replied, 'You had no mercy on me; I only treat you the same.' Then he flew on until he came to his old home, where he found his old uncle, to whom he recounted the whole story; and after that time he remained peacefully at home with his good uncle. 'So many times my old grandfather, chief Warrior, told me that story,' said Zachariah Jamieson.
passages.note: Verbatim from Smith 1883, ch. V; public domain.

title.en: The Wild-Cat and the White Rabbit: The Song That Closed the Circle
title.zh: 野貓與白兔：畫圓之歌

region.en: Deep woods near the Seneca Reservation (Zachariah Jamieson informant)
region.zh: 塞內卡保留地附近的深林（扎卡里亞詹姆森講述）

period: Told by Zachariah Jamieson (Smith 1883)

source.work: Erminnie A. Smith, 'Myths of the Iroquois' (1883), ch. V: 'The wild-cat and the white rabbit'

summary.en: Lonely for companionship, the wild-cat sings a plaintive ditty whose meaning is 'When you are frightened, sweet rabbit, you run in a circle.' The white rabbit hears the dangerous voice and scuds away - but, hearing the song again and again, ever nearer, he follows his instinct and runs in a circle, which brings him each time closer to his enemy, until, circling ever nearer, he falls a victim to the wild-cat.
summary.zh: 渴望同伴的野貓唱出一支哀歌，其意為：「受驚的甜兔兒啊，你會繞圈而逃。」白兔聽出那危險的嗓音便狂奔而逃——但歌聲一次次更近，牠只能順從天性繞圈而跑，每次都更接近敵人；圈愈縮愈小，白兔終成野貓的獵物。

sensitivity.note: Smith 1883; public domain.

passages.text: The wild cat, roaming disconsolately in the woods, experienced the sense of utter loneliness which calls for companionship. A friend he must have or die. Cats there were none within speaking distance, but rabbits it might be possible to entice. He commenced a plaintive ditty: 'He gah yah neh, He gah yah! He gah yah, Di ho ni shu gua da-se, He yah gah.' His meaning was simple as his song: 'When you are frightened, sweet rabbit, you run in a circle.'
passages.note: Verbatim from Smith 1883, ch. V; public domain.

passages.text: A short distance off lay a white rabbit in his lair; hearing the melodious ditty he pricked up his ears. 'Heigho!' exclaimed he, 'that dangerous fellow, the wild-cat, is around; I hear his voice; I must scud'; and away he ran, turning from the direction in which the voice came. He had gone but a short distance when he stopped, turned back his ears and listened - there was the song again, and again, nearer each time. Unfortunate rabbit! he could but follow his instinct and run in a circle which brought him each time nearer his enemy. Still the song went on, until, circling ever nearer, white rabbit fell a victim to the wild-cat.
passages.note: Verbatim from Smith 1883, ch. V; public domain.

title.en: The New-Year Festival of the Onondagas: Confession, White Dog, and the Scaring of Witches
title.zh: 奧農達加新年祭：懺悔、白犬與驅巫

region.en: Onondaga council-house, New York
region.zh: 紐約州奧農達加議屋

period: Observed by Smith c. 1878-1881; Handsome Lake's teaching introduced 'nearly a century ago' (1883)

source.work: Erminnie A. Smith, 'Myths of the Iroquois' (1883), ch. VI: 'New-Year festival'

summary.en: At the first new moon of the new year the chiefs assemble a 'holy meeting': four days of speeches introducing the sayings of Handsome Lake, chiefs' and warriors' confession over the wampum ('I have been drunk; I have sinned'), the feather dance, the clan games of Bear-Deer-Eel-Hawk against Wolf-Beaver-Snipe-Turtle, three days of religious gambling - then the scaring of witches, costumed messenger-spirits stirring the ashes, and the roasting of a spotless white dog strangled by five young men of spotless reputation, combed with teasels, decorated with wampum and tobacco, and thrown into the fire while the warriors shoot up at the sun. The festival closes after three weeks with the medicine men chasing diseases from house to house and throwing ashes on the assembled people.
summary.zh: 新年首個新月，酋長們舉行「聖會」：四日講述漢森湖之言，酋長與戰士執貝珠懺悔（「我飲過酒；我犯過罪」），行羽舞，熊鹿鰻鷹對狼狸鷸龜的氏族競賽，三日宗教性賭戲——繼而「驅巫」，化身精靈的使者攪動灰燼；並由五名名聲無瑕的青年絞殺一隻純潔無疵的白犬，以 teasel 梳毛、飾以貝珠與菸草，在戰士們向日射箭之際投入火中。三週後，醫者逐屋驅病、向群眾揚灰，祭典方告終。

sensitivity.note: Smith 1883; public domain. An outside observer's 1880s account of the Midwinter rites; presented as ethnographic description, not ritual instruction. The white-dog sacrifice is described historically.

passages.text: At the first new moon of the new year the chiefs assemble and call what they term a 'holy meeting': a bench is placed in the center of the circle of chiefs, upon which are placed their strings of Indian wampum. One then rises and makes a long speech, in which he introduces the sayings, maxims, and teachings of Handsome Lake, who, nearly a century ago, introduced a new form into the Seneca religion. Speeches of this kind occupy four days. On the fifth day the principal chiefs, taking hold of the wampum, say: 'I put all my words in this wampum'; 'I have been drunk'; or, 'I have sinned.' On the sixth day the warriors go through the same form of confession. At the conclusion of this portion of their ceremonies the U-stu-ae-gu-nae, or feather dance, sometimes called the dance of peace, is performed.
passages.note: Verbatim from Smith 1883, ch. VI; public domain.

passages.text: The clans are divided for the games - Bear, Deer, Eel and Hawk against Wolf, Beaver, Snipe and Turtle - each holding its feasts in separate houses, even although husband and wife be divided. The gambling then commences and continues three more days, and is considered a religious ceremony. The gambling and betting concluded, two Indians, costumed as medicine men, run into all the houses, and raking up the ashes call on all to repair to the Council House. In the evening of this day begins the 'scaring of witches': speeches are made; Indian songs or chants are sung, while an old man or woman enters, appearing to wish or search for something, the assembly guessing at the object desired.
passages.note: Verbatim from Smith 1883, ch. VI; public domain.

passages.text: On the ensuing day, at a given hour, the white dog is roasted. A perfectly pure, unblemished white dog is selected, and five young men of the most spotless reputation are chosen to kill it; around whose neck two ropes are fastened, and the young men pull the ropes till the dog is strangled. When dead it is presented to the victorious gambling party, who comb out its hair carefully with teasels; it is then decorated with wampum, ribbons, Indian tobacco, strips of buckskin, small baskets, silver brooches. While the fire is being lighted the chiefs chant and praise the Great Spirit, after which, while the warriors are shooting up at the sun, the dog is thrown into the fire, which ceremony unites all the clans. The feast follows, of meats garnished with sunflower oil; the third day of dancing is devoted to the war dance, dedicated to the sun, moon, stars, and thunder.
passages.note: Verbatim from Smith 1883, ch. VI; public domain.

passages.text: At the conclusion of the feather dance the Si-ti-ga-ni-ai, or shuffle dance, follows, executed solely by the women, who do not lift their feet from the floor; then succeeds the guide dance, the closing dance of the new year's festival - after which the medicine men reappear and for a day and a night go about in the houses and chase away all diseases. This closes by all repairing to the Council House, where a large kettle of burnt corn, sweetened with maple sugar, is prepared for the medicine men, who eat it from the kettle; from this Council House fire the medicine men throw the ashes upon the assembled people for the purpose of dispelling witches and disease. This concludes the new year's festival ceremonies after a duration of three weeks.
passages.note: Verbatim from Smith 1883, ch. VI; public domain.

title.en: Inanna Steals the Me from Enki
title.zh: 伊南娜竊取恩基之梅

region.en: Eridu to Uruk by river, Iraq
region.zh: 自埃利都溯河至烏魯克（伊拉克）

period: Old Babylonian manuscript, c. 1700 BCE (ETCSL translation 2003)

source.work: Inana and Enki (ETCSL c.1.3.1)

license: ETCSL translation (Oxford, 2003-2006); quoted in paraphrase with attribution

summary.en: Inanna visits Enki at the Abzu, drinks beer with him, and the hospitable god gives her, gift by gift, more than a hundred me — the powers of civilization. When he sobers and sends monsters after her, Ninshubur rescues her, twice, until all the me reach Uruk.
summary.zh: 伊南娜赴阿卜祖造訪恩基，共飲啤酒；恩基乘興相贈，先後授她百餘枚梅——文明之力。恩基酒醒遣怪獸追索，寧舒布爾兩度退敵，梅終至烏魯克。

sensitivity.note: Ancient myth; no living community restrictions.

passages.text: Inanna sails to Eridu to visit her father Enki in the Abzu. He feasts her, and over the beer, the god of wisdom, generous with wine, grants her gift after gift: the exalted crown, the throne of kingship, the priestly offices, the art of the metalworker, the scribe, the smith, the leatherworker, the builder, the weaving, the wisdom of divination and the arts of love and war.
passages.note: Paraphrase of ETCSL c.1.3.1, gifts of the me; not verbatim.

passages.text: Inanna takes the me into the boat of heaven and rows for home. Enki sobers and, one by one, realizes what he has given — the great me, all of them — and sends his servants, then monstrous creatures, to seize the boat. Each time Ninshubur, Inanna's faithful vizier, fights them off.
passages.note: Paraphrase of ETCSL c.1.3.1, pursuit; not verbatim.

passages.text: The boat of heaven arrives at the quay of Kulaba, Uruk's temple precinct, and Inanna displays the me there for her city. Enki sends the flood to stop her; Ninshubur beats it back. Enki finally makes peace: the me shall remain in Uruk, and its powers are Inanna's to govern.
passages.note: Paraphrase of ETCSL c.1.3.1, arrival and peace; not verbatim.

functions: Founding charter of Uruk's primacy among Sumerian cities
Performed at the Uruk new year as Inanna claims the me
Trickster myth of the goddess who wins civilization by charm
Etiology of the crafts, offices and arts as gifts from Eridu to Uruk

variants.name: Enki decrees the world order
variants.summary: A contrasting version where the me are allocated by Enki in counsel rather than seized at a feast.

variants.name: Enuma Elish: gifts of office to Marduk
variants.summary: The Babylonian parallel of powers conferred upon a rising god by the assembly.

canonical_translation: ETCSL team translation, Oxford, 2003-2006

primary_sources.citation: ETCSL c.1.3.1, trans. ETCSL team (2003-2006), lines 1-190

secondary_sources.work: Inanna, Queen of Heaven and Earth
secondary_sources.citation: Diane Wolkstein and Samuel Noah Kramer, New York, 1983

title.en: Inanna Defies the Mountain Ebih
title.zh: 伊南娜怒斥埃比赫山

region.en: Mountain Ebih, northeastern Iraq (symbolic pin at the Zagros foothills)
region.zh: 埃比赫山（象徵性定位於扎格羅斯山麓）

period: Old Babylonian manuscript, c. 1700 BCE (ETCSL translation 2003)

source.work: Inana and Ebih (ETCSL c.1.3.2)

license: ETCSL translation (Oxford, 2003-2006); quoted in paraphrase with attribution

summary.en: Inanna, exulting in the me she carries, passes the towering mountain Ebih; it does not bow, so she vows to destroy it. An warns her the mountain is too powerful and, past warning, will not be moved by his word.
summary.zh: 伊南娜攜梅凱旋，途經巍峨的埃比赫山；山不俯首，她立誓毀之。安神勸誡：此山太過強大，恐難撼動。

sensitivity.note: Ancient myth; no living community restrictions.

passages.text: Inanna, Lady of Heaven, descends from the sky and passes over the mountain Ebih. The mountain rises against her, does not prostrate itself, does not offer her the honor due a goddess; its peaks stand tall and its terraced slopes are full of power.
passages.note: Paraphrase of ETCSL c.1.3.2, opening provocation; not verbatim.

passages.text: Inanna turns to An: the mountain has not bowed to me — I will destroy its terraces, I will make its wheat no wheat. An answers carefully: the mountain is great and heavy, its slopes the dwelling of An's own dread; one cannot reach its rises or overturn it.
passages.note: Paraphrase of ETCSL c.1.3.2, Inanna's vow and An's counsel; not verbatim.

functions: Hymn of Inanna's martial power performed in her temples
Political allegory of Uruk's wars against the eastern highlands
Theology of hubris: even the sky warns, the goddess does not hear

variants.name: Inana and Gudam
variants.summary: Another defier of Inanna, this one a monster of rivers, destroyed by her fury.

title.en: Inanna Destroys the Mountain
title.zh: 伊南娜毀埃比赫山

region.en: Mountain Ebih, northeastern Iraq (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 埃比赫山（象徵性定位）

period: Old Babylonian manuscript, c. 1700 BCE (ETCSL translation 2003)

source.work: Inana and Ebih, second half (ETCSL c.1.3.2)

license: ETCSL translation (Oxford, 2003-2006); quoted in paraphrase with attribution

summary.en: Armed with weapons An gives despite himself, Inanna storms the mountain: she shatters its terraces, pours fire and flood over it, and reduces its wheat to dust. The poem ends with her glory and the mountain's silence.
summary.zh: 安雖不願，仍授予武器；伊南娜突襲群山：毀其梯田，火與洪水傾瀉，麥盡化塵。詩末頌其榮光，山嶽無言。

sensitivity.note: Ancient myth; no living community restrictions.

passages.text: Inanna arms herself with the weapons An gives her: the seventy arrows, the lance, the flood-storm, the storm-whirl. She rises against the mountain like a storm-cloud, opens the house of battle and pours out fury. She shatters Ebih's terraces, cuts down its trees at the root, pours fire upon its slopes and water over its wheat until the grain is dust. The great mountain, full of dread, is made low; its people flee, its springs of water are stopped.
passages.note: Paraphrase of ETCSL c.1.3.2, arming; not verbatim. / Paraphrase of ETCSL c.1.3.2, destruction; not verbatim.

passages.text: Inanna stands on the mountain's stones and proclaims her deed: where the mountain was great and would not bow, now nothing is left. The hymn closes hailing the lady whose word was not refused — Ebih is her conquest and her proof.
passages.note: Paraphrase of ETCSL c.1.3.2, triumph; not verbatim.

functions: Battle hymn performed for Inanna's war cult
Etiology of the smitten highlands and their tribute
Theology of Inanna as the unadvised power

title.en: Shukaletuda's Crime in the Garden
title.zh: 舒卡萊圖達園中罪行

region.en: Gardens of Uruk, Iraq
region.zh: 烏魯克園圃（伊拉克）

period: Old Babylonian manuscript, c. 1700 BCE (ETCSL translation 2003)

source.work: Inana and Sukale-tuda (ETCSL c.1.3.3)

license: ETCSL translation (Oxford, 2003-2006); quoted in paraphrase with attribution

summary.en: Shukaletuda, an ignorant gardener's son, plants a tree in the desert and tends it against all advice; a single leaf gives him shade. When the exhausted Inanna sleeps in the shade, he violates her; she wakes and vows to find him, and hides him no corner of the earth can keep.
summary.zh: 無知園丁之子舒卡萊圖達於荒漠植樹，不聽勸誡而悉心照料，僅得一片葉蔭。疲憊的伊南娜於蔭下沉睡，竟遭其玷污；她醒後立誓搜尋，普天之下無其藏身之處。

sensitivity.note: Ancient myth of sexual violence; presented as literary-historical material without endorsement.

passages.text: Shukaletuda, son of a gardener, plants a tree in the desert where his father says nothing will grow. Against advice he waters it, and one leaf grows. When Inanna, weary from the me's great work, lies down to sleep in the tree's single shade, the fool takes her while she sleeps.
passages.note: Paraphrase of ETCSL c.1.3.3, the crime; not verbatim.

passages.text: Inanna wakes and sees what was done to her in her sleep. Like a flood she pours out her wrath: who has done this to me? She searches the earth for him, and to every animal, every city, every corner she puts the question.
passages.note: Paraphrase of ETCSL c.1.3.3, the wrath; not verbatim.

functions: Morality tale of sacrilege and its inescapable punishment
Warning text about the goddess's honor and vigilance
Etiology of the gardener's low status in temple economy

title.en: The Flight and Death of Shukaletuda
title.zh: 舒卡萊圖達逃亡與伏誅

region.en: Cities of Sumer, Iraq
region.zh: 蘇美諸城（伊拉克）

period: Old Babylonian manuscript, c. 1700 BCE (ETCSL translation 2003)

source.work: Inana and Sukale-tuda, second half (ETCSL c.1.3.3)

license: ETCSL translation (Oxford, 2003-2006); quoted in paraphrase with attribution

summary.en: Shukaletuda flees from city to city; Inanna blights the crops to starve him out, freezes the birds on the wing, and hunts him across Sumer. Found at last, he begs only to see the sun; she grants the sight, then executes him on the spot.
summary.zh: 舒卡萊圖達一城又一城地逃亡；伊南娜摧毀莊稼斷其糧、凍凝飛鳥於半空，追索至蘇美全境。終被擒獲，他只求再看一眼太陽；她允其所請，隨即就地处決。

sensitivity.note: Ancient myth; execution imagery belongs to the mythic register.

passages.text: Shukaletuda runs from city to city, and Inanna follows him with curses on the land: she blights the grain in the fields, stops the cattle in their folds, freezes the birds in the air — all Sumer starves with him in hiding.
passages.note: Paraphrase of ETCSL c.1.3.3, pursuit; not verbatim.

passages.text: At last found, Shukaletuda prays: let me at least see the sun before I die. Inanna answers with terrible justice — she grants the prayer and strikes him down in the sunlight. The poem closes hailing the goddess who leaves no outrage unavenged.
passages.note: Paraphrase of ETCSL c.1.3.3, capture and execution; not verbatim.

functions: Culmination of the sacrilege-warning myth
Hymn to Inanna's justice performed in her cult
Etiology of blight as the goddess's pursuit made visible

title.en: Inanna and the River Monster Gudam
title.zh: 伊南娜與河怪古丹

region.en: Riverways of Sumer, Iraq
region.zh: 蘇美河渠（伊拉克）

period: Old Babylonian manuscript, c. 1700 BCE (ETCSL translation 2003)

source.work: Inana and Gudam (ETCSL c.1.3.4)

license: ETCSL translation (Oxford, 2003-2006); quoted in paraphrase with attribution

summary.en: Gudam, a monstrous horned one who comes down the river devouring everything, defies Inanna; she cuts him down and his blood dyes the water. The short battle poem celebrates her as the slayer of the river's terror.
summary.zh: 河中巨怪古丹吞食萬物、公然挑釁伊南娜；她一刀斬之，其血染紅河水。短小的戰歌頌揚她為河川恐怖的誅除者。

sensitivity.note: Ancient myth; no living community restrictions.

passages.text: Gudam, a horned monster of the river, comes down the waterways eating everything — trees, men, cattle — and defies the Lady of Heaven, challenging her power in her own city. Inanna seizes her weapons, strikes Gudam down, and his blood runs red in the river. The hymn ends with her praise as the terror of terrors, the power that keeps the waterways clean.
passages.note: Paraphrase of ETCSL c.1.3.4, the monster's defiance; not verbatim. / Paraphrase of ETCSL c.1.3.4, the kill and closing hymn; not verbatim.

functions: Battle hymn of the Inanna cult
Etiology of the safe waterway and the slain river-demon

title.en: Inanna Takes Over Heaven
title.zh: 伊南娜接管天庭

region.en: E-ana temple, Uruk, Iraq
region.zh: 烏魯克埃安那神殿（伊拉克）

period: Old Babylonian manuscript, c. 1700 BCE (ETCSL translation 2003)

source.work: Inana and An (ETCSL c.1.3.5)

license: ETCSL translation (Oxford, 2003-2006); quoted in paraphrase with attribution

summary.en: An dwells in Inanna's house at Uruk and grows homesick for heaven; she seizes the chance — when he tries to leave, she demands the E-ana for herself, and heaven grants the ambitious goddess both temple and city in perpetuity.
summary.zh: 安居於烏魯克伊南娜神殿的安神思念上天；欲歸之際，伊南娜趁機索求埃安那神殿——天庭允之，野心之神遂永享殿宇與城池。

sensitivity.note: Ancient myth; no living community restrictions.

passages.text: An comes down from heaven to lodge in the E-ana, Inanna's temple at Uruk, and enjoys its beds and beer; but at night he misses heaven and longs to go back up. When An announces his departure, Inanna's people weep — for with An gone, no blessings remain. Inanna seizes the moment and demands the temple as her own; An, half in affection, half in haste to be gone, gives it to her with its destinies: the E-ana shall be Inanna's house forever. The poem ends with Inanna's glory: she has taken heaven's own residence for her city, and the gods serve her in it. Uruk's temple, the E-ana, becomes the meeting place of heaven and earth.
passages.note: Paraphrase of ETCSL c.1.3.5, An's visit; not verbatim. / Paraphrase of ETCSL c.1.3.5, the transfer; not verbatim. / Paraphrase of ETCSL c.1.3.5, closing hymn; not verbatim.

functions: Founding charter of the E-ana temple at Uruk
Mythic projection of Uruk's cultic primacy
Performed at Inanna's festivals as the temple's legitimation

title.en: Inanna and the Huluppu Tree
title.zh: 伊南娜與胡盧普樹

region.en: Banks of the Euphrates, Uruk, Iraq
region.zh: 幼發拉底河畔烏魯克（伊拉克）

period: Old Babylonian manuscript, c. 1700 BCE (ETCSL translation 2003)

source.work: Gilgamesh, Enkidu and the Nether World, opening (ETCSL c.1.8.1.4)

license: ETCSL translation (Oxford, 2003-2006); quoted in paraphrase with attribution

summary.en: A willow pulled from the Euphrates is planted by Inanna in her garden and grows a crown; a serpent, an Anzu-bird and a ghost-maiden lodge in it. Gilgamesh drives them out, fells the tree, and from its wood makes Inanna's throne and bed — and a drum for himself.
summary.zh: 伊南娜自幼發拉底河拔得一株胡盧普樹植於園中；蛇、安祖鳥與魅女相繼棲於其內。吉爾伽美什逐之、伐之，以其木為伊南娜製御座與寢床，並為自己製鼓。

sensitivity.note: Ancient myth; no living community restrictions.

passages.text: In those days, a single tree grew by the Euphrates; the south wind uprooted it, and Inanna walking by took it and planted it in her garden, watered it with her hand, waiting for it to grow into a throne and a bed.
passages.note: Paraphrase of ETCSL c.1.8.1.4, opening; not verbatim.

passages.text: But at the tree's crown a serpent built its nest, the Anzu-bird set its young in the branches, and in its heart the dark phantom-maiden raised her house. Inanna wept — her tree was taken and she could not cut it down.
passages.note: Paraphrase of ETCSL c.1.8.1.4, the squatters; not verbatim.

passages.text: Gilgamesh her brother came: he slew the serpent at the tree's base, drove out the bird and the maiden to their homes, felled the willow, and from its heartwood made Inanna's throne and bed; of the rest he made the drum for the young men of Uruk.
passages.note: Paraphrase of ETCSL c.1.8.1.4, the rescue and carpentry; not verbatim.

functions: Etiology of Inanna's throne and bed in the E-ana
Etiology of Gilgamesh's ceremonial drum
Miniature cosmogony introducing the netherworld poem

title.en: Enheduanna's Exaltation of Inanna
title.zh: 恩海杜安娜：頌揚伊南娜

region.en: Ur and Nippur, Iraq
region.zh: 烏爾與尼普魯（伊拉克）

period: Sargonic period poem, c. 2300 BCE (ETCSL translation 2003)

source.work: A hymn to Inana: Nin-me-sara (ETCSL c.4.07.2)

license: ETCSL translation (Oxford, 2003-2006); quoted in paraphrase with attribution

summary.en: The world's first signed author, Enheduanna, priestess of Nanna at Ur, praises Inanna as the power who turns An's own lesser gods from her and raises the exiled priestess back to her temple — the hymn ends with her restoration and Inanna's glory.
summary.zh: 世上第一位署名作者——烏爾月神祭司恩海杜安娜——頌揚伊南娜之權能：她能令安神座下諸神背離他人，亦能令被逐的祭司重返聖殿；頌詩以復位與神榮作結。

sensitivity.note: Ancient hymn by a named historical author; no living community restrictions.

passages.text: Lady of all the me, radiant Inanna: you have taken up the great powers and turn the Anuna gods from whoever offends you. Before you, the great rites themselves grow silent; cities and temples obey your word. Enheduanna speaks in the first person: exiled from her temple by Lugalanne, driven from Ur and Nippur, she is made to walk the waste; her gifts rejected, her rites despised, she prays to Inanna — not to the moon god her father — to judge the rebels. Inanna hears and acts: the usurper is brought low, and the priestess returns to her temple. The hymn closes with the first signature in world literature: Enheduanna, en-priestess of Nanna, has composed this exaltation of Inanna.
passages.note: Paraphrase of ETCSL c.4.07.1, opening praise; not verbatim. / Paraphrase of ETCSL c.4.07.1, the exile; not verbatim. / Paraphrase of ETCSL c.4.07.1, restoration and signature; not verbatim.

functions: Political hymn asserting Inanna's supremacy for the Akkadian dynasty
Autobiographical prayer of restoration used in the en-priestess cult
Foundational text of authored literature in world history

title.en: Dumuzi and Enkimdu: Shepherd versus Farmer
title.zh: 杜穆茲與恩金姆杜：牧與農之爭

region.en: Steppe and canals near Uruk, Iraq
region.zh: 烏魯克近郊草原與運河（伊拉克）

period: Old Babylonian manuscript, c. 1700 BCE (ETCSL translation 2003)

source.work: Inana and Dumuzid: Dumuzid and Enkimdu (ETCSL c.1.4.x)

license: ETCSL translation (Oxford, 2003-2006); quoted in paraphrase with attribution

summary.en: Two gods court Inanna: the noisy shepherd Dumuzi and the quiet farmer Enkimdu. Inanna's brother Utu advises her, the rivals trade boasts and insults, and the farmer, yielding, promises the shepherd grain, and the dispute ends in friendship.
summary.zh: 二神同求伊南娜：喧鬧的牧者杜穆茲與沉靜的農神恩金姆杜。兄長烏圖獻策，二神互相誇耀譏諷；農神終讓步許諾贈穀，爭端以友誼收場。

sensitivity.note: Ancient myth; no living community restrictions.

passages.text: Inanna loves a man, and two gods come to court her: Dumuzi the shepherd, loud in his love-songs, and Enkimdu the farmer, lord of canals and plough. Inanna's brother Utu tells her to weigh them both, and the suitors fall to boasting.
passages.note: Paraphrase of ETCSL c.1.4.2, the suitors; not verbatim.

passages.text: Dumuzi taunts the farmer: what is your grain against my cream, your loaves against my milk and cheese? The farmer answers mildly: let him bellow — my gifts will come to his folds in good time. The contest ends in concord: Enkimdu promises Dumuzi his wheat, his flour and his beer, and the shepherd is given the bride. The poem closes with the marriage of Inanna to the shepherd, the farmer reconciled to the household.
passages.note: Paraphrase of ETCSL c.1.4.2, the contest of boasts; not verbatim. / Paraphrase of ETCSL c.1.4.2, reconciliation and wedding; not verbatim.

functions: Charter myth of the shepherd-farmer integration in the Uruk economy
Courtship narrative performed with the Inanna-Dumuzid songs
Etiology of the seasonal alternation of flocks and fields

title.en: Dumuzi's Dream: The Omen of Capture
title.zh: 杜穆茲之夢：被擒之兆

region.en: Alaj ostrich-grove near Uruk, Iraq (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 烏魯克近郊鴕鳥林阿拉吉（象徵性定位）

period: Old Babylonian manuscript, c. 1700 BCE (ETCSL translation 2003)

source.work: Dumuzid's dream (ETCSL c.1.4.3)

license: ETCSL translation (Oxford, 2003-2006); quoted in paraphrase with attribution

summary.en: Dumuzi dreams the reeds rise against him, a stirrup breaks, his sheep scatter — and Geshtinanna, his sister, reads the dream as the netherworld coming for him. He accepts: the dream is fate; only the hiding matters.
summary.zh: 杜穆茲夢見蘆葦崛起、馬鐙斷裂、羊群驚散——妹妹蓋什蒂南娜解夢：冥界將至。他認命：夢即天數，唯藏身之地尚可一搏。

sensitivity.note: Ancient myth; no living community restrictions.

passages.text: Dumuzi, sleeping among the ostrich grove of Alaj, dreams: rushes rise in fire, one reed of the double reed splits, his stirrup shatters, his ewes and lambs scatter, his goats and kids tear at each other. He wakes in terror and tells his dream to Geshtinanna. She reads it: the rushes are the netherworld's henchmen rising to seize you; the broken stirrup and the scattered flocks are the desolation of your sheepfold after you are taken. My brother, the dream is fate.
passages.note: Paraphrase of ETCSL c.1.4.3, the dream; not verbatim. / Paraphrase of ETCSL c.1.4.3, the interpretation; not verbatim.

passages.text: Dumuzi answers calmly: in my youth my mother had me play at the dream's oracle; the dream is not kind, but let us not accept it. Let me hide in the Alaj grove — never tell the galla demons where I am.
passages.note: Paraphrase of ETCSL c.1.4.3, acceptance and resolve; not verbatim.

functions: Model dream-interpretation scene for the oracle craft
Seasonal myth of the vegetation god's approaching death
Performed with the Dumuzid laments in mourning liturgy

variants.summary: The goddess's descent narrative in which Dumuzid's takeover is foretold by his mourning.

title.en: The Hunt for Dumuzi
title.zh: 圍捕杜穆茲

region.en: Alaj grove to the sheepfold, Uruk, Iraq
region.zh: 自鴕鳥林至羊欄，烏魯克（伊拉克）

period: Old Babylonian manuscript, c. 1700 BCE (ETCSL translation 2003)

source.work: Dumuzid's dream, second half (ETCSL c.1.4.3)

license: ETCSL translation (Oxford, 2003-2006); quoted in paraphrase with attribution

summary.en: The galla demons come up from the netherworld as gallows-spirits, enter no clean house, touch no clean man, and hunt Dumuzi. He flees grove to fold; the demons lure his shepherd, who betrays him; he is seized by the arms and dragged down to the great below.
summary.zh: 冥界鬼卒絞刑妖靈自冥土上來，不入潔室、不近潔人，專獵杜穆茲。他自樹林逃至羊欄；眾妖誘其牧人而得线索，遂擒其臂，拖入冥土。

sensitivity.note: Ancient myth; no living community restrictions.

passages.text: The galla come up from the great below — small galla who take one, big galla who take all — spirits that enter no clean house and touch no clean man, that lurk on the roads and hunt one man only: Dumuzi.
passages.note: Paraphrase of ETCSL c.1.4.3, the demons; not verbatim.

passages.text: Dumuzi flees from the Alaj grove to the old woman's house, from the house to the sheepfold, changing hiding places as the demons spread through the city; the demons speak sweetly to the shepherd and get from him the word that shows where the god is.
passages.note: Paraphrase of ETCSL c.1.4.3, pursuit and betrayal; not verbatim.

passages.text: They seize him by the arms, drag him by the hands, and carry him down; Geshtinanna runs through the city mourning her brother, and the shepherd god passes into the netherworld — his song of departure the model of the mourning liturgy.
passages.note: Paraphrase of ETCSL c.1.4.3, the seizure; not verbatim.

functions: Mourning liturgy text for the Dumuzid festival
Theology of the galla demons and their purity rules
Seasonal etiology of the summer decline of flocks

title.en: Dumuzi and Geshtinanna: The Half-Year
title.zh: 杜穆茲與蓋什蒂南娜：半年之約

region.en: Uruk and the great below, Iraq
region.zh: 烏魯克與冥土（伊拉克）

period: Old Babylonian manuscript, c. 1700 BCE (ETCSL translation 2003)

source.work: Dumuzid and Geshtin-ana (ETCSL c.1.4.1.1)

license: ETCSL translation (Oxford, 2003-2006); quoted in paraphrase with attribution

summary.en: The sister refuses to tell the demons where her brother hides and is tortured for it. Dumuzi's shade laments; Inanna weeps for her husband and decrees: for six months the sister serves in his place, for six months the husband — and thus the year turns.
summary.zh: 妹妹拒不出賣兄長藏身處，遭妖拷問。杜穆茲陰魂哀哭；伊南娜為夫垂淚，頒命：半年以妹代之，半年以夫代之——四季由是輪轉。

sensitivity.note: Ancient myth; no living community restrictions.

passages.text: The galla press Geshtinanna for her brother's hiding place; she will not tell, and they torture her as they would a stranger. Dumuzi's shade, hearing of it, laments that his little sister suffered so for love of him. Inanna mourns her husband and goes to Ereshkigal to bargain. The decree is spoken: let the sister serve in the netherworld for the brother half the year, and the husband serve the other half — so the measure of the year is fixed. The poem closes with the ritual: on the day the shepherd returns, the dead man's sister rises, and the people of Uruk offer cream and beer to both. Whoever recites the song shall live long days.
passages.note: Paraphrase of ETCSL c.1.4.1.1, the loyalty test; not verbatim. / Paraphrase of ETCSL c.1.4.1.1, the decree; not verbatim. / Paraphrase of ETCSL c.1.4.1.1, closing rite; not verbatim.

functions: Etiology of the seasonal exchange of Dumuzid and Geshtinanna
Liturgy of the return-day offerings in the Uruk calendar
Model of familial loyalty within the divine house

title.en: Dumuzi in the Netherworld with His Sisters
title.zh: 杜穆茲冥界姊妹吟

region.en: The great below (symbolic pin at Uruk's underworld gate)
region.zh: 冥土（象徵性定位於烏魯克冥門）

period: Old Babylonian manuscript, c. 1700 BCE (ETCSL translation 2003)

source.work: Dumuzid and his sisters (ETCSL c.1.4.1.3)

license: ETCSL translation (Oxford, 2003-2006); quoted in paraphrase with attribution

summary.en: Down in the land of no return, Dumuzi is visited by Geshtinanna, who brings comfort, and by the dark sister Amashilamma; the dialogue of lamentation shows the dead shepherd as a lord among shades, honored but grieving.
summary.zh: 冥土之中，蓋什蒂南娜攝慰藉而至，黑衣姊妹阿瑪什利拉瑪亦來；哀悼對話中，亡故的牧神為幽魂之王——受尊崇而亦哀傷。

sensitivity.note: Ancient funerary literature; no living community restrictions.

passages.text: In the house of the land of no return, Dumuzi the shepherd sits among the dead; his sister Geshtinanna comes to him with comfort in her hands, and speaks to him as the living speak. The dialogue of the two sisters around the dead god teaches the manners of the underworld: the dark sister speaks of the customs of the shades, and Dumuzi answers as one who has learned them — the poem a manual of how the dead are treated and how the living should mourn.
passages.note: Paraphrase of ETCSL c.1.4.1.3, the visit; not verbatim. / Paraphrase of ETCSL c.1.4.1.3, the dialogue; not verbatim.

functions: Mourning manual for the Dumuzid lament festival
Underworld etiquette: how the dead are addressed

title.en: Inanna and Bilulu: The Vengeance at Dugrub
title.zh: 伊南娜與比利魯：杜格魯布復仇

region.en: Dugrub sheepfold, steppe of Sumer, Iraq
region.zh: 杜格魯布羊欄，蘇美草原（伊拉克）

period: Old Babylonian manuscript, c. 1700 BCE (ETCSL translation 2003)

source.work: Inana and Bilulu: an ulila to Inana (ETCSL c.1.4.4)

license: ETCSL translation (Oxford, 2003-2006); quoted in paraphrase with attribution

summary.en: Traveling through the wilderness, Inanna finds the old woman Bilulu who holds her shepherd Dumuzi's herds; discovering in her the death of her husband, the goddess kills Bilulu, turns her son into a guardian spirit, and installs Bilulu as a mourning figure of the fold.
summary.zh: 伊南娜行經荒野，遇看守其夫杜穆茲羊群的老婦比利魯；察知其夫之死與她有關，女神殺之，化其子為守護神靈，令比利魯成為羊欄之哀悼化身。

sensitivity.note: Ancient myth; no living community restrictions.

passages.text: Inanna walks the wilderness roads to find her shepherd; at the Dugrub sheepfold the old woman Bilulu keeps the herds, and in her Inanna recognizes the one who has caused Dumuzi's death. Inanna kills Bilulu and her son, then transfigures them: the old woman is made the mourning figure of the fold, whose laments will open the mourning rites; her son becomes the guardian spirit of the herds, so that the very house of the crime becomes its memorial. The song closes as an ulila, a mourning hymn for Inanna: the goddess who avenges her husband is praised, and the fold remembers both the crime and the mercy of transformation.
passages.note: Paraphrase of ETCSL c.1.4.4, the discovery; not verbatim. / Paraphrase of ETCSL c.1.4.4, vengeance and transformation; not verbatim. / Paraphrase of ETCSL c.1.4.4, closing hymn; not verbatim.

functions: Charter of the mourning figures used in the Dumuzid lament liturgy
Vengeance myth of Inanna performed as ulila hymn
Etiology of the guardian spirits of the sheepfold

title.en: The Wedding of Inanna and Dumuzi
title.zh: 伊南娜與杜穆茲婚禮

region.en: Uruk, Iraq
region.zh: 烏魯克（伊拉克）

period: Ur III cult song, c. 2000 BCE (ETCSL translation 2003)

source.work: A balbale to Inana and Dumuzid (Dumuzid-Inana wedding songs, ETCSL c.4.08.1)

license: ETCSL translation (Oxford, 2003-2006); quoted in paraphrase with attribution

summary.en: The bride's mother, brother and suitor speak in turn as the wedding is prepared; Dumuzi claims his bride with gifts of cream and dates, and the marriage bed of Uruk is blessed — the cult song performed at the hieros gamos rite.
summary.zh: 婚禮將備，母、兄、求婚者輪番陳辭；杜穆茲以乳酪與椰棗為聘迎娶，烏魯克的婚床受祝福——此即聖婚儀式所頌的祭歌。

sensitivity.note: Ancient cult song with sexual imagery in its ritual register; presented as literature, not endorsement.

passages.text: The wedding songs move between speakers: Inanna's mother tells her to bathe and anoint; her brother calls the shepherd's gifts good; Dumuzi offers cream and dates, his sheepfolds full, as bride-price for the lady of Uruk. Inanna consents in love-song: let the shepherd sleep beside me, let me caress the man. The bed is prepared with sweet oil and cedar, and the city rejoices at the union of the lady and the shepherd. The cult song ends with blessings for the city: through the sacred marriage Uruk's year is secured — grain, flocks and kingship renewed by the union performed annually in the temple.
passages.note: Paraphrase of ETCSL c.4.08.1, courtship exchange; not verbatim. / Paraphrase of ETCSL c.4.08.1, wedding night; not verbatim. / Paraphrase of ETCSL c.4.08.1, closing blessing; not verbatim.

functions: Liturgy of the sacred marriage (hieros gamos) at Uruk
Wedding songs performed for royal participation in the rite
Charter of the city's annual renewal of fertility

variants.summary: The courtship narrative that the wedding songs complete.

title.en: Dumuzi's Waking Song
title.zh: 杜穆茲晨歌

region.en: Uruk, Iraq
region.zh: 烏魯克（伊拉克）

period: Ur III cult song, c. 2000 BCE (ETCSL translation 2003)

source.work: A balbale to Inana and Dumuzid (Dumuzid wakens, ETCSL c.4.08.2)

license: ETCSL translation (Oxford, 2003-2006); quoted in paraphrase with attribution

summary.en: Dumuzi wakes beside Inanna and sings the morning of the lovers: the sleeping house, the sheep not yet stirred, the bed not yet cooled — the intimate liturgical morning-song of the sacred marriage cycle.
summary.zh: 杜穆茲在伊南娜身旁醒來，唱戀人的清晨：酣睡的屋宅、未動的羊群、尚溫的床榻——聖婚詩環中最親暱的晨間祭歌。

sensitivity.note: Ancient cult song; no living community restrictions.

passages.text: The morning song opens on the sleeping house: the doors shut, the household asleep, the god rising beside the goddess while the city's fires are not yet lit. Dumuzi sings of the flocks still folded, the meadows unopened, the bed still warm — the shepherd's world paused around the lovers — and the song closes with the couple blessed in their union.
passages.note: Paraphrase of ETCSL c.4.08.2, the sleeping house; not verbatim. / Paraphrase of ETCSL c.4.08.2, the paused world and blessing; not verbatim.

functions: Morning liturgy of the sacred marriage rite
Love-lyric performed in the Inanna-Dumuzid cult
