passages.text: Condensed paraphrase of von Wielligh Deel II No. 31 (1920); not verbatim. There were two old Bushmen of the old race; each had a son. But the son of the one was a good-for-nothing, and the son of the other was clever at hunting, and could dance beautifully and play the ramkie; this made jealousy between the two fathers.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of von Wielligh, Boesman-Stories Deel II (1920), No. 31; not verbatim.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase, same locus; not verbatim. One day the father of the good-for-nothing caught the good son alone in the veld; he took him by treachery, cut off his arms and legs, took his beautiful knitted kaross and gave him a piece of hard old buffalo hide in exchange. The good son, with neither arms nor legs to hunt, dance or make music, crawled about and became the great field tortoise.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of von Wielligh, Boesman-Stories Deel II (1920), No. 31; not verbatim.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase, same locus; not verbatim. The sorcerer father next bewitched his own stout son into a gorgeous bird, waited till the tortoise's young brother crept near, sprang down as an old Bushman, cut off the boy's head and split him from below upwards into two pieces, each with an arm and leg. When the sun went down and the moon came out, the Jackal came to eat the pieces; but the Moon, who comes alive again month after month, poured her dew on the two pieces, the arm and leg of each stretched out, and each piece became a long field snake. The father found the great field snakes but did not know them; and Tortoise knew they were his brothers, so Snake and Tortoise never quarrel to this day.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of von Wielligh, Boesman-Stories Deel II (1920), No. 31; not verbatim.

title.en: Lion, Wolf and Jackal
title.zh: 獅、狼與豺

region.en: Hantam River & Bushmanland, Northern Cape (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 南非北開普省哈坦姆河與布什曼蘭（象徵定位）

period: San oral tradition told in Afrikaans; recorded 1870s-1880s by G. R. von Wielligh, published 1920

source.work: G. R. von Wielligh, Boesman-Stories, Deel II (1920), No. 32

summary.en: At a zebra kill the lioness scatters the pack while cubs bellow; Wolf whimpers 'how-hoo' and Jackal laughs 'ha-ga-ga!' with a dry tongue; when they circle back for scraps the lion slides in beneath them and rakes them both. Wolf learns to eat at the meat, Jackal to beg with one eye on the vulture and one on Wolf — because they too were once Bushmen.
summary.zh: 斑馬獲處，母獅驅散獸群，幼獅怒吼；狼泣「霍霍」，豺乾舌而笑「哈嘎嘎」；二人回頭覓食，獅潛其下抓傷二獸。狼學得就肉而食，豺學得一日視鷲、一日視狼而乞——因彼等本亦是桑人。

sensitivity.note: San oral tradition recorded in Afrikaans by G. R. von Wielligh; presented as an archival record.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase of von Wielligh Deel II No. 32 (1920); not verbatim. Lion also belongs to the old race; therefore he is Lion. His hunting mates walk about little. Wolf can also hunt... but where Lion still stands and says 'Dare to come near!', Wolf has long since thrown down the reins and run till he grew small. Of Jackal there is nothing to say! He is a beggar, bolts at the smallest rustle.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of von Wielligh, Boesman-Stories Deel II (1920), No. 32; not verbatim.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase, same locus; not verbatim. When the sun went down Lion stood up, sniffed against the wind: 'Aha, wife, I smell zebras — they are here near; come with the children behind me as soon as I have the zebra down.' The lioness rounded the zebras, her mate sprang, held the prey with teeth behind the neck... The two eldest cubs tore strips from the skin to make eating-places for the little ones.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of von Wielligh, Boesman-Stories Deel II (1920), No. 32; not verbatim.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase, same locus; not verbatim. Wolf and Jackal drew near at the smell of blood. 'Please, Lion, give me also a piece,' begged Wolf; 'and me too,' begged Jackal. 'Wau! Haau!' was all Lion said, as he tried how deep he could drive his claws into Wolf's hide; Wolf wept and fled... but when they saw the lioness eating again, they came foot for foot nearer — until Lion slid in unawares under the two quarrel-makers: Jackal got a few scratches and Wolf enough to make his hair fly.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of von Wielligh, Boesman-Stories Deel II (1920), No. 32; not verbatim.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase, same locus; not verbatim. Wolf then saw it paid him better to look after his body at the meat and marrowbones than to keep Jackal from it; and Jackal knows it does not become him to eat too near Wolf: he sits, head in the air, tongue out, crying out his heart in sorrow — one eye on the meat, the other on Wolf. That they are so clever is because they too were once Bushmen, who have now become Lion, Wolf and Jackal.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of von Wielligh, Boesman-Stories Deel II (1920), No. 32; not verbatim.

title.en: The Baboons, the Apes and Little Jantjie
title.zh: 狒狒、猿與小揚奇

region.en: Hantam River & Bushmanland, Northern Cape (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 南非北開普省哈坦姆河與布什曼蘭（象徵定位）

period: San oral tradition told in Afrikaans; recorded 1870s-1880s by G. R. von Wielligh, published 1920

source.work: G. R. von Wielligh, Boesman-Stories, Deel II (1920), No. 33

summary.en: Jantjie, a Bushman child taken by white hunters, runs away stuffed with stolen flour and tobacco; the apes — old Korannas — and the baboons — old Bushmen — want his bundle, and the children cry 'kill him and give us the nice grains'. At the river he bangs his tin pail like a thousand-pound cannon and the apes bolt; in the rocks he cannot, so he mocks their flat overhanging foreheads, cries 'Boer, bring your gun!' and escapes over the kranses.
summary.zh: 小揚奇為白獵者所擄之桑童，攜競得之粉與煙逃亡；猿（古科蘭人）與狒狒（古桑人）欲奪其包，幼者呼「殺之予我香粒！」。河邊他敲錫桶如千磅巨炮，猿群奔逃；岩間不能敲，遂譏其平懸之額，呼「布爾人，帶槍來！」，越崖而遁。

sensitivity.note: San oral tradition recorded in Afrikaans by G. R. von Wielligh; colonial-era setting; presented as an archival record.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase of von Wielligh Deel II No. 33 (1920); not verbatim. Hunters from the sunset side (from the sea side) once came and caught a Bushman child and took it home with them; the hunters were white people, and they named the little Bushman Jantjie... He made a plan to run away, and days beforehand packed food quietly in his knapsack: bread, meal, wheat, meat, fish and whatever he could get hold of sneakily — especially tinderboxes and firesteels, knives and tobacco.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of von Wielligh, Boesman-Stories Deel II (1920), No. 33; not verbatim.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase, same locus; not verbatim. The land he had to flee through was inhabited by apes and baboons. The apes lived along a great river and were said to be old Korannas that became apes; and the baboons farmed in the ridge-country and were said to be old Bushmen changed into baboons, now living on veld-food and insects. At the river the apes said: 'Let us go for the man: he carries goods; let us kill him and take the goods.'
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of von Wielligh, Boesman-Stories Deel II (1920), No. 33; not verbatim.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase, same locus; not verbatim. Jantjie got the thought that apes fear a great noise. He mocked them — 'why are your bottoms so black? just above your eyes the skin is still white if you roll your eyes back' — till they stormed him; then he banged on the tin pail and made a thousand-pounder noise; the apes were frightened and flew off, the children wailed, the old ones roared from above and fled into the high trees. At the baboons' rocks the pail was full of water and useless, so he mocked their foreheads — 'like a krans at the front of a ridge' — and cried: 'Boer, boer, bring your gun! Here are the ugly ones you seek!' and while they fled to the cliffs he made off home.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of von Wielligh, Boesman-Stories Deel II (1920), No. 33; not verbatim.

title.en: The Sunbeetles and the Crickets
title.zh: 日甲蟲與蟋蟀

region.en: Hantam River & Bushmanland, Northern Cape (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 南非北開普省哈坦姆河與布什曼蘭（象徵定位）

period: San oral tradition told in Afrikaans; recorded 1870s-1880s by G. R. von Wielligh, published 1920

source.work: G. R. von Wielligh, Boesman-Stories, Deel II (1920), No. 34

summary.en: A father shoots a lion that carried off his baby; later a water-spirit pulls his daughter into a pool and the mother fights her way out with her. Years on, the two children are lost in the veld; the father and sons seek by day, the mother and daughters by night, calling, until worn to skin and bone they become the sunbeetles (doringbesies) that sing and seek by day, and the crickets that sing and seek by night.
summary.zh: 父射殺奪嬰之獅；後水靈曳其女入池，母搏鬥救出。多年後二子失於原野；父與子晝尋、母與女夜尋，呼號不輟，直至形銷骨立——化為晝歌晝尋之日甲蟲，與夜歌夜尋之蟋蟀。

sensitivity.note: San oral tradition recorded in Afrikaans by G. R. von Wielligh; presented as an archival record.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase of von Wielligh Deel II No. 34 (1920); not verbatim. An old Bushman and his wife had one little boy; they went to dig Bushman-rice, and the child fell asleep on the mother's back-kaross under a bush. A lion that had eaten its fill at a hartebeest picked up the kaross with the child and lay down near by to watch what the parents would do. The father climbed a bobbejaan-tou, shot the lion with his last poisoned arrow in the open throat, and brought home meat.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of von Wielligh, Boesman-Stories Deel II (1920), No. 34; not verbatim.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase, same locus; not verbatim. Years passed; a girl child came, and when she could play about, the mother was cutting matjiesgoed by the fountain. The child picked reeds too near the pool; the water-spirit came out and drew the child in; the mother leapt into the water, wrestled with the water-spirit at great risk of her life, saved her child and swam out, exhausted and half dead.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of von Wielligh, Boesman-Stories Deel II (1920), No. 34; not verbatim.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase, same locus; not verbatim. The father played the violin and the mother the ramkie beautifully, and the two children danced before them; they spent many a pleasant evening and night by the veld-fire. One day the two children were sent for veld-food and never came back: the parents sought and called and played violin and ramkie, but no answer came; the father asked the Hammerkop, who sees all in the water, and the mother the Owl, whose dolosse stood still. So father and sons seek by day, mother and daughters by night — and worn out with grief they became the sunbeetles and the crickets, the one singing and seeking by day, the other by night.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of von Wielligh, Boesman-Stories Deel II (1920), No. 34; not verbatim.

title.en: Lion and Wolf Eat Over and Over
title.zh: 獅與狼反覆相食

region.en: Hantam River & Bushmanland, Northern Cape (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 南非北開普省哈坦姆河與布什曼蘭（象徵定位）

period: San oral tradition told in Afrikaans; recorded 1870s-1880s by G. R. von Wielligh, published 1920

source.work: G. R. von Wielligh, Boesman-Stories, Deel II (1920), No. 35

summary.en: The stingy Lion palms off two sucked marrowbones on the begging Wolf; Wolf invites him to ostrich soup, pretends to feed wife and children from a cold pot, then pours the boiling one over the lion's head and claps it tight — and brains him with his kierie. So a mean deed always comes back on a man's own head.
summary.zh: 吝獅以兩根吮盡之髓骨欺乞食之狼；狼邀其飲鴕湯，假作以冷釜飼妻兒，實傾沸釜於獅首而扣緊——復以短杖擊斃之。故刻薄之行，終返其人之首。

sensitivity.note: San oral tradition recorded in Afrikaans by G. R. von Wielligh; graphic violence; presented as an archival record.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase of von Wielligh Deel II No. 35 (1920); not verbatim. Wolf was out the whole night on the hunt without luck; near daybreak he came on Lion's spoor and followed it, for he knows Lion is a lucky fellow who always gets food. Lion had caught a zebra and eaten his fill... 'And there lies more than half a zebra still,' noted Wolf. 'Yes, but that I must keep for my wife and children,' said Lion, and went and fetched a marrowbone whose marrow he had sucked out himself: 'There, eat.'
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of von Wielligh, Boesman-Stories Deel II (1920), No. 35; not verbatim.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase, same locus; not verbatim. Wolf took the bone, gave it a few licks, and asked to be allowed to lick the sops by the zebra; Lion said he himself was so fond of soup he would not give away a drop. Wolf asked for a bone to take home, and got another cleaned-out one: 'There, take it; you beggar. Now go!'... 'Now I ask you, brother Lion, to come and eat at my place to-morrow.' On the way home Wolf caught an ostrich and ate his fill of it.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of von Wielligh, Boesman-Stories Deel II (1920), No. 35; not verbatim.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase, same locus; not verbatim. Next day he cooked the ostrich flesh, poured the cold soup into another pot, and kept the fresh one boiling; when Lion came he pretended to feed his wife and children soup by the mouthful — then set the empty pot down and took up the boiling one: 'Now it is our turn; we have time and can drink at our ease — you first, then I.' He turned the pot of boiling soup over Lion's head and pressed the hot pot fast over it; Lion's eyes, mouth and throat were scalded; he dropped to the ground, and Wolf took his kierie and battered him dead. So a mean deed always comes back on a man's own head.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of von Wielligh, Boesman-Stories Deel II (1920), No. 35; not verbatim.

title.en: The Ostrich Comes Alive Again
title.zh: 鴕鳥復活

region.en: Hantam River & Bushmanland, Northern Cape (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 南非北開普省哈坦姆河與布什曼蘭（象徵定位）

period: San oral tradition told in Afrikaans; recorded 1870s-1880s by G. R. von Wielligh, published 1920

source.work: G. R. von Wielligh, Boesman-Stories, Deel II (1920), No. 36

summary.en: The hunter Raakskiet is trampled senseless by a bewitched ostrich; thirsting for water, he crawls to the pool and drowns. His family find him, lay him in the sun, and kill the boy's pet hare 'for the hare brought death into the world'. As they mourn, Raakskiet revives in the sun. Later a whirlwind carries one bloody plume into the pool where he drowned, and it becomes a little ostrich that grows and returns to his wives.
summary.zh: 獵者直射者遭妖鴕踏暈；渴極爬至池邊而溺斃。家人置屍日下曝之，並殺其子之寵兔「因兔帶死亡入世」。眾方哀哭，直射者日下復甦。後旋風捲一血羽入其溺斃之池，化為小鴕，漸長而歸其妻。

sensitivity.note: San oral tradition recorded in Afrikaans by G. R. von Wielligh; presented as an archival record.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase of von Wielligh Deel II No. 36 (1920); not verbatim. Raakskiet (Straightshot) was known as one of the best hunters of his time... He felt sick and decided to turn back home; an ostrich cock came behind him, blew mightily and wanted only to kick and trample him. He lay flat; the bird sat on him with its sharp breastbone and kneaded him as if it would press him flat like a foot-sole; the string of his bow broke under the kicks.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of von Wielligh, Boesman-Stories Deel II (1920), No. 36; not verbatim.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase, same locus; not verbatim. He bound himself over with twigs so that he looked like a bush and so escaped home, took to his bed, and lay sick. Thirsting for water he crawled to the pool and fell forward into the water and was drowned. The family found him in the water dead, rolled him on the ground, and laid him in the sunshine by the pool to get warm; and the mother killed the boy's pet hare, for the hare is food with which one may not play, and death came into the world through a hare.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of von Wielligh, Boesman-Stories Deel II (1920), No. 36; not verbatim.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase, same locus; not verbatim. But just then his father Raakskiet came alive again; he raised himself, sat in the sunshine, grew better with every breath, and stood up lacking nothing. Later a mighty whirlwind came and whirled all the plumes away; one feather heavy with blood could not whirl so high, came down, and fell into the pool in which Raakskiet had drowned the day before, and swam on the water: while they watched, that bloody feather changed into a little ostrich. The little creature took its down-feathers; they grew; it stepped with weak legs out of the water, sat basking in the sun, grew stronger and stronger — and an adult bird, black and white, trotted off straight to its own home to tell its wives it still lived.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of von Wielligh, Boesman-Stories Deel II (1920), No. 36; not verbatim.

title.en: The Lion Grows Jealous
title.zh: 獅生妒心

region.en: Hantam River & Bushmanland, Northern Cape (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 南非北開普省哈坦姆河與布什曼蘭（象徵定位）

period: San oral tradition told in Afrikaans; recorded 1870s-1880s by G. R. von Wielligh, published 1920

source.work: G. R. von Wielligh, Boesman-Stories, Deel II (1920), No. 37

summary.en: The lionesses praise Ape's springing, Gemsbok's speed and Ostrich's booming; the jealous lions stage a feast, scratch ape's rump, score gemsbok's face, strip ostrich's rump feathers, and stalk off — but hunt ostriches for their lungs till they boom from the chest. The wives learn the value of their providers; and one wife's mockery costs the lionesses their long manes forever.
summary.zh: 母獅讚猿之躍、大羚之疾、鴕鳥之吼；妒獅設宴，抓猿臀、劃羚面、拔鴕臀羽，揚長而去——然轉而獵鴕取肺，直至吼自胸膛。妻等始知供養者之貴；而一妻之譏笑，令母獅自此失其長鬣。

sensitivity.note: San oral tradition recorded in Afrikaans by G. R. von Wielligh; contains domestic violence; presented as an archival record.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase of von Wielligh Deel II No. 37 (1920); not verbatim. The lions often come together in company, and then their wives always praise the apes for their nimbleness, the gemsbok for their speed, and the ostriches for their beautiful booming voice. This did not please the male lions at all, and they grew jealous about it and gave their dissatisfaction to their wives in full company; but the lionesses held that they were right.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of von Wielligh, Boesman-Stories Deel II (1920), No. 37; not verbatim.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase, same locus; not verbatim. The wives made a feast and dance and invited Ape, Gemsbok and Ostrich; the lionesses clapped hands and cheered Ape and Gemsbok and Ostrich, but not their own men. One lion scratched the hair off Ape's seat, another sprang on Gemsbok and scored marks in his face, the third stripped all the feathers off the Ostrich's rump; and the three males walked away and left their wives with the little children.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of von Wielligh, Boesman-Stories Deel II (1920), No. 37; not verbatim.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase, same locus; not verbatim. The lions went and hunted ostriches only to eat their lungs, so that they could boom as beautifully as the ostrich out of the forechest; and after they had eaten many ostrich lungs they no longer boomed as if they had tails in their mouths or bones in their throats. The wives sought their providers out again and promised to do better; and from then on, when Ostrich booms, they clap no more hands; but when their own men boom they feel grand and praise them, for it is harder than any other voice. Yet one wife began again to mock her man's mane; he grew so angry that he dragged her round by the head-hair and plucked her so bald that her head-hair never grew so long again; the other lionesses cut theirs off in fear — that is why their manes are not so long as the males' to this day.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of von Wielligh, Boesman-Stories Deel II (1920), No. 37; not verbatim.

title.en: The Saucy Indians Who Became Rattlesnakes
title.zh: 無禮的印第安人化為響尾蛇

region.en: Passamaquoddy country before the Great Flood
region.zh: 大洪水之前的帕薩馬科迪之地

period: Passamaquoddy tale related by an old woman to Mrs. W. Wallace Brown (Leland 1884)

source.work: Charles G. Leland, The Algonquin Legends of New England (1884), 'How Glooskap changed Certain Saucy Indians into Rattlesnakes'

summary.en: Long time ago the Rattlesnakes were saucy Indians - they had too much face, and could not be put down by much, and they got up for very little. When the great Flood was coming Glooskap told them about it; they said they did not care. 'The Flood will come and drown you all' - then these Indians hurrahed again, got their rattles made of turtle-shells fastened together and filled with pebbles, and had a grand dance. The rain began to fall, but they danced; the thunder roared, and they shook their rattles and yelled at it. Then Glooskap was angry: he did not drown them in the Flood, but changed them into rattlesnakes. Nowadays, when they see a man coming, they lift up their heads and move them about - that's the way snakes dance - and they shake the rattles in their tails just as Indians shake their rattles when they dance.
summary.zh: 很久以前，響尾蛇原是一群無禮的印第安人——架子極大，軟硬不吃，動輒起鬨。大洪水將至，格魯斯卡普勸告他們，他們卻說毫不在乎。「洪水將至，要淹死你們全體！」——這些印第安人再次歡呼，取來龜殼串成、內填碎石的老式響鈴，跳起大舞。大雨落下，他們照舞；雷霆轟鳴，他們搖鈴吼叫以對。格魯斯卡普怒了——他不在洪水中淹死他們，而是把他們化為響尾蛇。如今蛇見人來，便昂首擺動——那是蛇的舞蹈——尾鈴搖動，正如印第安人跳舞時搖鈴一般。

sensitivity.note: Passamaquoddy tale (Leland 1884); public domain. A flood-and-transgression aition in the NE Woodlands register.

passages.text: You know At-o-sis, the Snake? Well, the worst of all is Rattlesnake. Long time ago the Rattlesnakes were saucy Indians. They were very saucy. They had too much face. They could not be put down by much, and they got up for very little. When the great Flood was coming Glooskap told them about it. They said they did not care. He told them the water would come over their heads. They said that would be very wet. He told them to be good and quiet, and pray. Then those Indians hurrahed. He said, 'A great Flood is coming.' Then they gave three cheers for the great Flood. He said, 'The Flood will come and drown you all.' Then these Indians hurrahed again, and got their rattles, made of turtle-shells, in the old fashion, fastened together, filled with pebbles, and rattled them and had a grand dance.
passages.note: Verbatim from Leland 1884, pp. 110-111; not verbatim (OCR modernized).

passages.text: Yes, they had a great dance. The rain began to fall, but they danced. The thunder roared, and they shook their rattles and yelled at it. Then Glooskap was angry. He did not drown them in the Flood, however, but he changed them into rattlesnakes. Nowadays, when they see a man coming, they lift up their heads and move them about. That's the way snakes dance. And they shake the rattles in their tails just as Indians shake their rattles when they dance. How do you like such music?
passages.note: Verbatim from Leland 1884, p. 111; not verbatim (OCR modernized).

title.en: Glooskap Binds Wuchowsen, the Great Wind-Bird
title.zh: 格魯斯卡普縛住風鳥伍喬森

region.en: Great rock at the end of the sky, far to the North
region.zh: 北方天際盡頭的巨岩

period: Passamaquoddy manuscript collection by Louis Mitchell (Leland 1884)

source.work: Charles G. Leland, The Algonquin Legends of New England (1884), 'How Glooskap bound Wuchowsen, the Great Wind-Bird'

summary.en: The Indians believe in a great bird called Wochowsen or Wuchowsen, meaning Wind-Blow, who lives far to the North and sits upon a great rock at the end of the sky; whenever he moves his wings the wind blows. When it blew a tempest so that Glooskap could not go out at all, he sought the Bird-giant: 'You take no compassion on your Koosesek, your grandchildren. You have caused this wind and storm; it is too much. Be easier with your wings!' 'I have been here since ancient times... mine was the first voice, and I will ever move my wings as I will.' Then Glooskap rose in his might to the clouds, took the Great Bird-giant as though he were a duck, tied both his wings, and threw him down into a chasm between deep rocks. The Indians could now go out in their canoes all day long - but with that all the waters became stagnant, so thick that Glooskap could not paddle. Then he raised Wuchowsen, who is immortal, put him on his rock again, and untied one of his wings; since then the winds have never been so terrible as in the old time.
summary.zh: 印第安人信奉大鳥伍喬森——「吹風者」——居極北，坐在天際盡頭的巨岩上；牠一振翅，風便吹起。暴風大到格魯斯卡普無法出舟時，他前去尋這鳥中巨人：「你竟不憐惜你的孫兒們。這風暴皆你所致，太過分了！收斂些翅膀吧！」「自太古我便在此……最初的聲音便出於我翅，我永遠要隨心振翅。」格魯斯卡普躍上雲端，如提鴨般拎起巨鳥，縛其雙翅，擲入深岩之隙。此後印第安人終日泛舟——然而天下之水皆成死水，濃稠得連舟都划不動。主人便再扶起不朽的伍喬森，放回岩上，解其一翼——自那以後，風再沒有上古時那樣狂暴。

sensitivity.note: Passamaquoddy tale (Leland 1884); public domain. Leland compares Wuchowsen to the Norse Hraesvelg and stresses he is a wind-bird, not the western thunder-bird.

passages.text: The Indians believe in a great bird called by them Wochowsen or Wuchowsen, meaning Wind-Blow or the Wind-Blower, who lives far to the North, and sits upon a great rock at the end of the sky. And it is because whenever he moves his wings the wind blows they of old times called him that. When Glooskap was among men he often went out in his canoe with bow and arrows to kill sea-fowl. At one time it was every day very windy; it grew worse; at last it blew a tempest, and he could not go out at all. Then he said, 'Wuchowsen, the Great Bird, has done this!' He went to find him; it was long ere he reached his abode. He found sitting on a high rock a large white Bird.
passages.note: Verbatim from Leland 1884, pp. 111-112; not verbatim (OCR modernized).

passages.text: 'Grandfather,' said Glooskap, 'you take no compassion on your Koosesek, your grandchildren. You have caused this wind and storm; it is too much. Be easier with your wings!' The Giant Bird replied, 'I have been here since ancient times; in the earliest days, ere aught else spoke, I first moved my wings; mine was the first voice - and I will ever move my wings as I will.' Then Glooskap rose in his might; he rose to the clouds; he took the Great Bird-giant Wuchowsen as though he were a duck, and tied both his wings, and threw him down into a chasm between deep rocks, and left him lying there.
passages.note: Verbatim from Leland 1884, pp. 112-113; not verbatim (OCR modernized).

passages.text: The Indians could now go out in their canoes all day long, for there was a dead calm for many weeks and months. And with that all the waters became stagnant. They were so thick that Glooskap could not paddle his canoe. Then he thought of the Great Bird, and went to see him. As he had left him he found him, for Wuchowsen is immortal. So, raising him, he put him on his rock again, and untied one of his wings. Since then the winds have never been so terrible as in the old time.
passages.note: Verbatim from Leland 1884, p. 113; not verbatim (OCR modernized).

title.en: The Great Bull-Frog: The River Made Flesh and the First Water Creatures
title.zh: 巨牛蛙：化為血肉的大河與最初的水族

region.en: Mountain village on a brook, and the up-country dam
region.zh: 溪畔的山村與上游的水壩

period: Told by Tomah Josephs, Passamaquoddy (Leland 1884)

source.work: Charles G. Leland, The Algonquin Legends of New England (1884), 'How Glooskap conquered the Great Bull-Frog'

summary.en: A village by a brook - the only water in all the country round - watches the stream dry to a dead bone. Upstream a monster chief, immense, bloated, with yellow eyes stuck out like pine-knots and a mouth from ear to ear, has dammed the rivulet for nothing, and bellows 'Do as you choose... If you want water, go somewhere else.' Glooskap comes among the honest villagers dressed terribly ferocious - ten feet high, a hundred feathers, clam-shells at each ear - bade them be of good cheer, and at the monster's town demands water: thrusting a spear into his belly, there gushed forth a mighty river, even all the water which should have run on while in the rivulet, for he had made it into himself. Glooskap crumpled his back with a mighty grip - it was the Bull-Frog, whose back bears the prints to this day - and hurled him into the stream. Meanwhile, in the hour when all wishes are granted, the simple villagers had wished themselves into the soft mud, the diving rocks, the rippling waves and the water forever: the first became a Leech, the second a Spotted Frog, the third a Crab, and the fourth a Fish - for ere this there had been in all the world none of the creatures which dwell in the water.
summary.zh: 山村傍溪而居——四野僅此一水——卻眼看溪水枯竭如死骨。上游的怪酋巨大臃腫、黃眼如松節、口裂至耳，平白築壩攔水，咆哮著「隨你們便……要水，另找去」。格魯斯卡普氣勢駭人地來到村中——身高十呎、頂插百羽、耳掛蛤殼——安慰村民，直搗怪酋之城索水；一矛刺入其腹，滔滔大河傾瀉而出——原來整條溪水都被他吞化於己身。主人如握巨松般捏彎其背——正是牛蛙，其背至今留著那可怕的指痕——隨手擲入溪流。同時，在「萬願得償」的那個時辰，純樸的村民許願入軟泥、躍岩潛水、隨波起伏、永居水中：第一人化為水蛭，第二人化為斑蛙，第三人化為螃蟹，第四人化為魚——在此之前，世上從無棲水之物。

sensitivity.note: Passamaquoddy tale (Leland 1884); public domain. Leland notes the bull-frog is the river incarnate - the ice of winter pierced by the spear of the sun.

passages.text: Of old times, there was an Indian village far away among the mountains, little known to other men... The town was by a brook, and except in it there was not a drop of water in all the country round, unless in a few rain-puddles. No one there had ever found even a spring. But after a time they began to observe that the brook was beginning to run low, and that not in the summer time, but in autumn, even after the rains. And day by day it diminished, until its bed was as dry as a dead bone in the ashes of a warm fire. Now it was said that far away up in the land where none had ever been there was on this very stream another Indian village; but what manner of men dwelt therein no one knew.
passages.note: Verbatim from Leland 1884, pp. 114-115; not verbatim (OCR modernized).

passages.text: And after he had traveled three days he came to the place; and there he found that a dam had been raised across the rivulet, so that no water could pass, for it was all kept in a pond. Then asking them why they had made this mischief, since the dam was of no use to them, they bade him go and see their chief, by whose order this had been built. And when he came to him, lo, there lay lazily in the mud a creature who was more of a monster than a man, though he had a human form. For he was immense to measure, like a giant, fat, bloated, and brutal to behold. His great yellow eyes stuck from his head like pine-knots, his mouth went almost from ear to ear, and he had broad, skinny feet with long toes, exceeding marvelous. The messenger complained to this monster, who at first said nothing, and then croaked, and finally replied in a loud bellow: 'Do as you choose... If you want water, go somewhere else.'
passages.note: Verbatim from Leland 1884, pp. 115-116; not verbatim (OCR modernized).

passages.text: Then Glooskap, who was much pleased with all this, for he loved a brave man, came among them looking terribly ferocious; in all the land there was not one who seemed half so horrible. For he appeared ten feet high, with a hundred red and black feathers in his scalp-lock, his face painted like fresh blood with green rings round his eyes, a large clam-shell hanging from each ear, a spread eagle, very awful to behold, flapping its wings from the back of his neck... 'Give me to drink, and that of the best, at once, thou Thing of Mud!' But the chief reviled him, and said, 'Get thee hence, to find water where thou canst.' Then Glooskap thrust a spear into his belly, and lo! there gushed forth a mighty river; even all the water which should have run on while in the rivulet, for he had made it into himself. And Glooskap, rising high as a giant pine, caught the chief in his hand and crumpled in his back with a mighty grip. And lo! it was the Bull-Frog. So he hurled him with contempt into the stream, to follow the current. And ever since that time the Bull-Frog's back has crumpled wrinkles in the lower part, showing the prints of Glooskap's awful squeeze.
passages.note: Verbatim from Leland 1884, pp. 117-118; not verbatim (OCR modernized).

passages.text: Then he returned to the village; but there he found no people - no, not one. For a marvelous thing had come to pass during his absence, which shall be heard in every Indian's speech through all the ages. For the men, being, as I said, simple, honest folk, did as boys do when they are hungry, and say unto one another, 'What would you like to have, and what you?' Even so these villagers had said, 'Suppose you had all the nice cold, fresh, sparkling, delicious water there is in the world, what would you do?' And one said that he would live in the soft mud, and always be wet and cool. And another, that he would plunge from the rocks, and take headers, diving into the deep, cold water, drinking as he dived. And the third, that he would be washed up and down with the rippling waves, living on the land, yet ever in the water. Then the fourth said, 'Verily, you know not how to wish, and I will teach you. I would live in the water all the time, and swim about in it forever.' Now it chanced that these things were said in the hour which, when it passes over the world, all the wishes uttered by men are granted. And so it was with these Indians. For the first became a Leech, the second a Spotted Frog, the third a Crab, which is washed up and down with the tide, and the fourth a Fish. Ere this there had been in all the world none of the creatures which dwell in the water, and now they were there, and of all kinds. And the river came rushing and roaring on, and they all went headlong down to the sea, to be washed into many lands over all the world.
passages.note: Verbatim from Leland 1884, pp. 118-119; not verbatim (OCR modernized).

title.en: Glooskap and the Mighty Wasis: The Invincible Baby
title.zh: 格魯斯卡普與偉大的瓦西斯：不敗的嬰兒

region.en: The sunny lodge floor where Wasis sits
region.zh: 瓦西斯安坐的向陽屋地

period: Told by Maria Saksis, Penobscot (Leland 1884)

source.work: Charles G. Leland, The Algonquin Legends of New England (1884), 'How the Lord of Men and Beasts strove with the Mighty Wasis'

summary.en: When Glooskap had conquered all his enemies - the giants and sorcerers, the magicians, Pamola the evil spirit of the night air, all manner of ghosts, witches, devils, cannibals and goblins - he wondered if his work was at an end. 'Not so fast, Master, for there yet remains One whom no one has ever conquered... It is the mighty Wasis, and there he sits; and I warn you that if you meddle with him you will be in sore trouble.' Now Wasis was the Baby, and he sat on the floor sucking a piece of maple-sugar. The Master smiled sweetly, spoke terribly, and at last had recourse to magic - used his most awful spells, and sang the songs which raise the dead and scare the devils. And Wasis sat and looked on admiringly, and seemed to find it very interesting, but all the same he never moved an inch. So Glooskap gave it up in despair, and Wasis went goo! goo! and crowed. And to this day when you see a babe well contented, going goo! goo! and crowing, and no one can tell why, know that it is because he remembers the time when he overcame the Master who had conquered all the world. For of all the beings that have ever been since the beginning, Baby is alone the only invincible one.
summary.zh: 當格魯斯卡普降服了所有敵手——巨人與巫者、術士、夜氣惡靈帕莫拉，以及一切鬼魅巫妖——他自問功成之業是否已畢。「莫急，主人。尚有一位從未被任何人降服者……那便是偉大的瓦西斯；他就坐在那裡。我警告你，若去招惹他，你必大吃苦頭。」瓦西斯就是嬰兒，正坐在地上含著一塊楓糖。主人先是甜笑柔聲，繼而疾言厲色，最後動用法術——唸起最可畏的咒語，唱起能喚死者、懾鬼魅之歌。瓦西斯只是饒有興味地看著，寸步不動。格魯斯卡普只得絕望作罷；瓦西斯坐在陽光裡「咯咯」而笑。至今嬰兒無故咯咯而笑時，那是他記起了戰勝「征服全世界之主」的那一刻——自開天闢地以來，唯有嬰兒是無敵的。

sensitivity.note: Penobscot tale (Leland 1884); public domain. Leland calls its Indian author 'a genius' and dates the tale ancient because it explains the unaccountable crowing of babies.

passages.text: Now it came to pass when Glooskap had conquered all his enemies, even the Kewahqu, who were giants and sorcerers, and the m'teoulin, who were magicians, and the Pamola, who is the evil spirit of the night air, and all manner of ghosts, witches, devils, cannibals, and goblins, that he thought upon what he had done, and wondered if his work was at an end. And he said this to a certain woman. But she replied, 'Not so fast, Master, for there yet remains One whom no one has ever conquered or got the better of in any way, and who will remain unconquered to the end of time.' 'And who is he?' inquired the Master. 'It is the mighty Wasis,' she replied, 'and there he sits; and I warn you that if you meddle with him you will be in sore trouble.'
passages.note: Verbatim from Leland 1884, pp. 120-121; not verbatim (OCR modernized).

passages.text: Now Wasis was the Baby. And he sat on the floor sucking a piece of maple-sugar, greatly contented, troubling no one. As the Lord of Men and Beasts had never married or had a child, he knew naught of the way of managing children. Therefore he was quite certain, as is the wont of such people, that he knew all about it. So he turned to Baby with a bewitching smile and bade him come to him. Then Baby smiled again, but did not budge. And the Master spake sweetly and made his voice like that of the summer bird, but it was of no avail, for Wasis sat still and sucked his maple-sugar. Then the Master frowned and spoke terribly, and ordered Wasis to come crawling to him immediately. And Baby burst out into crying and yelling, but did not move for all that.
passages.note: Verbatim from Leland 1884, p. 121; not verbatim (OCR modernized).

passages.text: Then, since he could do but one thing more, the Master had recourse to magic. He used his most awful spells, and sang the songs which raise the dead and scare the devils. And Wasis sat and looked on admiringly, and seemed to find it very interesting, but all the same he never moved an inch. So Glooskap gave it up in despair, and Wasis, sitting on the floor in the sunshine, went goo! goo! and crowed. And to this day when you see a babe well contented, going goo! goo! and crowing, and no one can tell why, know that it is because he remembers the time when he overcame the Master who had conquered all the world. For of all the beings that have ever been since the beginning, Baby is alone the only invincible one.
passages.note: Verbatim from Leland 1884, pp. 121-122; not verbatim (OCR modernized).

title.en: The Lament for Ur
title.zh: 烏爾哀歌

region.en: Ur, Iraq
region.zh: 烏爾（伊拉克）

period: Isin-Larsa period composition, c. 2000 BCE (ETCSL translation 2003)

source.work: The lament for Urim (ETCSL c.2.2.2)

license: ETCSL translation (Oxford, 2003-2006); quoted in paraphrase with attribution

summary.en: When the storm god's wind is unleashed against Ur, the moon god's city falls: the temple desecrated, the people scattered as slaves, mothers and children dying of hunger — and at last Nanna mourns to Enlil and the city is promised restoration.
summary.zh: 暴風之神之風襲向烏爾，月神之城傾覆：神殿被瀆，民眾被虜為奴，母與子飢餓而死——南納終向恩利爾哀告，城池蒙許復興。

sensitivity.note: Ancient city lament; no living community restrictions.

passages.text: On the day the storm's order was given, Ur was smitten: its temple looted, its people herded away as captives, its cattle and grain carried off — the city that knew no enemy is stripped bare. The lament's heart is hunger: mothers shut their doors against their children, the river runs with bodies, and Nanna, the moon god, has wrapped his city in silence and gone by boat to another place. Nanna mourns before Enlil; the god of the storm answers that the decree was his, and Ur shall be restored: kingship returns to the city, the temple rebuilt, the people regathered — mourning becomes prophecy of return.
passages.note: Paraphrase of ETCSL c.2.2.2, the destruction; not verbatim. / Paraphrase of ETCSL c.2.2.2, the hunger; not verbatim. / Paraphrase of ETCSL c.2.2.2, the restoration promise; not verbatim.

Prototype of the city-lament genre
Prophecy text of restoration tied to royal ideology

title.en: The Lament for Sumer and Ur
title.zh: 蘇美與烏爾哀歌

region.en: Sumer, southern Iraq
region.zh: 蘇美，南伊拉克

period: Isin-Larsa period composition, c. 2000 BCE (ETCSL translation 2003)

source.work: The lament for Sumer and Urim (ETCSL c.2.2.3)

summary.en: The whole land is visited by the flood-storm: city after city falls — Uruk, Lagash, Umma, Shuruppak — the temples emptied, the land made a wilderness, until the gods restore Sumer and the cities sing again.
summary.zh: 洪水暴風席捲全境：烏魯克、拉加什、烏瑪、舒魯帕克相繼陷落，神殿空虛，大地化為荒野——直至眾神復興蘇美，諸城再啟歡歌。

sensitivity.note: Ancient city lament; no living community restrictions.

passages.text: The flood-storm comes on the land by the gods' decree: city after city is named and smitten — Uruk, Lagash, Umma, Shuruppak — temples emptied, houses burned, the black-headed people scattered like sheep. The lament catalogs each city's ruin, then turns: the gods restore Sumer, kingship returns to Ur, and the land is promised the days of abundance again — the lament closes in blessing.

title.en: The Lament for Nippur
title.zh: 尼普魯哀歌

region.en: Nippur, Iraq
region.zh: 尼普魯（伊拉克）

period: Old Babylonian composition, c. 1700 BCE (ETCSL translation 2003)

source.work: The lament for Nibru (ETCSL c.2.2.4)

license: ETCSL translation (Oxford, 2003-2006); quoted in paraphrase with attribution

summary.en: The storm reaches even Enlil's own city: the Ekur defiled, its rites silenced, the shepherd's flock scattered — and Enlil, whom no city may accuse, must be petitioned to restore his own house.
summary.zh: 暴風竟及恩利爾之城：埃庫爾被瀆、祭儀止息、牧群四散——無人可責之神，須被懇求復興其殿。

sensitivity.note: Ancient city lament; no living community restrictions.

passages.text: The storm visits even Nippur: the Ekur defiled, its hymns silenced, its priests scattered; Enlil's own city learns what ruin is. The petition to Enlil is unique in the genre: no god may be accused, so the lament asks the offended lord himself to remember his house — and the restoration of the Ekur restores the world's axis.

title.en: The Lament for Eridu
title.zh: 埃利都哀歌

region.en: Eridu, Iraq
region.zh: 埃利都（伊拉克）

period: Old Babylonian composition, c. 1700 BCE (ETCSL translation 2003)

source.work: The lament for Eridug (ETCSL c.2.2.6)

license: ETCSL translation (Oxford, 2003-2006); quoted in paraphrase with attribution

summary.en: The oldest city, Enki's own, is smitten: the Abzu defiled, wisdom's house emptied — and the lament mourns the first city as mourning one's own mother.
summary.zh: 最古老的城、恩基之城遭劫：阿卜祖被瀆，智慧之殿空虛——哀歌以悼母之情悼第一城。

sensitivity.note: Ancient city lament; no living community restrictions.

passages.text: Eridu, the first of cities, Enki's own seat, is smitten by the storm: the Abzu defiled, wisdom's house emptied, the rites of the oldest temple silenced. The lament mourns the first city as a mother; its restoration is the renewal of the world's beginning — when Eridu lives again, the order of things is re-founded.
passages.note: Paraphrase of ETCSL c.2.2.6, the ruin; not verbatim. / Paraphrase of ETCSL c.2.2.6, the restoration; not verbatim.

functions: Lament for the first city and its sanctuary
Restoration theology anchored in origins

title.en: The Lament for Unug
title.zh: 烏魯克哀歌

region.en: Uruk, Iraq
region.zh: 烏魯克（伊拉克）

period: Old Babylonian composition, c. 1700 BCE (ETCSL translation 2003)

source.work: The lament for Unug (ETCSL c.2.2.5)

license: ETCSL translation (Oxford, 2003-2006); quoted in paraphrase with attribution

summary.en: The city of Inanna and Gilgamesh falls to the storm; the Eanna is defiled and its people scattered — the lament petitions the goddess herself to restore her own city, and Uruk's renewal is promised.
summary.zh: 伊南娜與吉爾伽美什之城遭暴風之劫：埃安那被瀆，民眾四散——哀歌向女神本身祈求復興其城，烏魯克之新生蒙許。

sensitivity.note: Ancient city lament; no living community restrictions.

passages.text: The storm falls on Unug, city of Inanna and Gilgamesh: the Eanna defiled, its people scattered, the city of the great wall emptied by decree. The lament petitions the lady of the city herself — she who was smitten must smite back the ruin — and Unug's renewal is promised with her restoration of the Eanna.
passages.note: Paraphrase of ETCSL c.2.2.5, the ruin; not verbatim. / Paraphrase of ETCSL c.2.2.5, the petition; not verbatim.

functions: Lament of the Inanna city
Liturgical petition to the city goddess

title.en: The Sumerian King List: Kingship from Heaven
title.zh: 蘇美王表：王權自天而降

region.en: Nippur (compilation site), Iraq
region.zh: 尼普魯（編纂地，伊拉克）

period: Compiled OB, based on older lists, c. 1800 BCE (ETCSL translation 2003)

source.work: The Sumerian king list (ETCSL c.2.1.1)

license: ETCSL translation (Oxford, 2003-2006); quoted in paraphrase with attribution

summary.en: Kingship was lowered from heaven: in the five cities before the flood, eight kings reigned fantastic reigns of tens of thousands of years until the flood swept them; afterwards kingship came again to Kish and passed through the dynasties down to Isin.
summary.zh: 王權自天而降：洪水之前五城八王，在位動輒數萬年；洪水掃盡其後，王權復臨基什，歷經諸朝，傳至伊辛。

sensitivity.note: Ancient historiographical myth; no living community restrictions.

passages.text: When kingship was lowered from heaven, it was in Eridug: Alulim reigned 28,800 years, Alalgar 36,000 — five cities, eight kings, five sars and more, until the flood swept over the land and kingship was taken to heaven. After the flood kingship came again from on high, to Kish first: long reigns shorten through the dynasties — Kish, Uruk, Ur, Akkad, and again Uruk and Ur — each dynasty named, each king given his years, until the list closes with the kings of Isin.
passages.note: Paraphrase of ETCSL c.2.1.1, antediluvian section; not verbatim. / Paraphrase of ETCSL c.2.1.1, postdiluvian dynasties; not verbatim.

functions: Political charter: kingship as heaven-given office
Historiographical frame linking flood, dynasties and legitimacy
Reference text for scribal schools and chronicles

variants.summary: The Babylonian priest's version of the antediluvian reigns.

variants.summary: The longest surviving manuscript of the list.

title.en: The Rulers of Lagash
title.zh: 拉加什諸王

region.en: Lagash, Iraq
region.zh: 拉加什（伊拉克）

period: Old Babylonian compilation of Ur III-Isin records, c. 1800 BCE (ETCSL translation 2003)

source.work: The rulers of Lagas (ETCSL c.2.1.2)

license: ETCSL translation (Oxford, 2003-2006); quoted in paraphrase with attribution

summary.en: A dynastic list in which Lagash's rulers — Ur-Nanshe's line, Gudea's house, the soldier kings of the Gutian interlude — are remembered with their deeds, buildings and wars: city history as sacred memory.
summary.zh: 拉加什王朝記：烏爾南什之系、古蒂亞之家、庫提人插曲中的戰士王——以功業、建築與戰事載入記憶：城邦史即神聖記憶。

sensitivity.note: Ancient chronicle; no living community restrictions.

passages.text: The rulers of Lagash are remembered dynasty by dynasty: Ur-Nanshe who built the temples, Gudea who saw his god in a dream, the kings who warred with Umma over the boundary — each reign measured by deeds and buildings. The list closes with the restoration kings, whose piety returned Lagash's worship to its gods — city history told as a sacred ledger of justice and building.
passages.note: Paraphrase of ETCSL c.2.1.2, the dynasties; not verbatim. / Paraphrase of ETCSL c.2.1.2, the close; not verbatim.

functions: City dynastic chronicle
Charter of Lagash's temple-building legitimacy

variants.summary: The narrative expansion of Gudea's reign.

title.en: The Death of Ur-Namma
title.zh: 烏爾納瑪之死

region.en: Ur, Iraq
region.zh: 烏爾（伊拉克）

period: Ur III composition, c. 2100 BCE (ETCSL translation 2003)

source.work: The death of Ur-Namma (ETCSL c.2.4.1.x)

license: ETCSL translation (Oxford, 2003-2006); quoted in paraphrase with attribution

summary.en: Ur-Namma, the king who built the ziggurat and gave the land its laws, dies in battle; his son mourns him, and the king descends to the netherworld where the dead come out to greet him as their lord — a royal descent poem of consolation.
summary.zh: 建神塔、定律法之王烏爾納瑪戰場殞身；其子哀悼，國王下冥，亡者出迎其主——一首慰藉性的王室冥界詩。

sensitivity.note: Ancient funerary literature; no living community restrictions.

passages.text: Ur-Namma, who built the temple and gave the land its measures and laws, falls in battle; his son Shulgi mourns: the shepherd is taken, the city's father is gone. The king descends to the netherworld, and the dead come out to greet him as their lord: he is given his seat among the shades, and his offerings are appointed — the king in the land of the dead keeps his kingdom's order.
passages.note: Paraphrase of ETCSL c.2.4.1.2, the death; not verbatim. / Paraphrase of ETCSL c.2.4.1.2, the descent; not verbatim.

functions: Royal funerary liturgy of the Ur III founder
Theology of the dead king's netherworld reign
Charter of continuing royal offerings

variants.summary: The heroic prototype of the dead king's enthronement.

title.en: Shulgi's Run from Nippur to Ur
title.zh: 舒爾吉尼普魯烏爾長跑

region.en: Nippur to Ur, Iraq
region.zh: 尼普魯至烏爾（伊拉克）

period: Ur III composition, c. 2100 BCE (ETCSL translation 2003)

source.work: A hymn to Inana (Shulgi cycle, ETCSL c.2.4.2.x)

license: ETCSL translation (Oxford, 2003-2006); quoted in paraphrase with attribution

summary.en: Shulgi boasts that in one day he ran from Nippur to Ur — a hundred miles through the storm — to bring offerings on the New Year; the self-deified king measures his kingship in feats: the run, the writing, the justice.
summary.zh: 舒爾吉自誇一日之間自尼普魯奔至烏爾——穿越風暴的百里之程——為新年奉上祭品；自神化的國王以功業丈量王權：長跑、書寫、正義。

sensitivity.note: Ancient royal hymn; no living community restrictions.

passages.text: Shulgi, king of Ur, boasts: I ran in the storm from Nippur to Ur in a single day, through the teeming rain, and brought the offerings of the New Year with my own hands. The king's litany of feats continues: I learned the scribal art from the tablet-house, I know the songs and the games, I judge the land's cases with justice — the deified king as the complete man.
passages.note: Paraphrase of ETCSL c.2.4.2.2, the run; not verbatim. / Paraphrase of ETCSL c.2.4.2.2, the litany; not verbatim.

functions: Manifesto of royal deification in the Ur III state
Charter of the New Year offering journey
School text of the royal-hymn genre

title.en: Shulgi the Learned King
title.zh: 博學之王舒爾吉

region.en: Ur, Iraq
region.zh: 烏爾（伊拉克）

period: Ur III composition, c. 2100 BCE (ETCSL translation 2003)

source.work: A praise poem of Shulgi (Shulgi cycle, ETCSL c.2.4.2.x)

license: ETCSL translation (Oxford, 2003-2006); quoted in paraphrase with attribution

summary.en: Shulgi praises himself as the son of Ninsun's line: learned in every scribal art, master of music and games, judge of the land — the king as literate demi-god whose praise was copied in schools for centuries.
summary.zh: 舒爾吉自頌為寧蓀後裔：通曉書吏百藝、精於樂藝棋戲、審判全土——身為有學半神之王的讚歌，為校中傳抄數百年。

sensitivity.note: Ancient royal hymn; no living community restrictions.

passages.text: Shulgi, king of Ur, claims the pedigree of heroes: born of the line of Ninsun, nourished by Ninlil, he is the lord whom the great gods raised to shepherding the land. His learning is the boast of a new age: from the tablet-house he learned the scribal art entire — Sumerian and the foreign tongue, the songs and the calculations — and the schools copied his praise for centuries after his death.
passages.note: Paraphrase of ETCSL c.2.4.2.1, pedigree; not verbatim. / Paraphrase of ETCSL c.2.4.2.1, the learning; not verbatim.

functions: Canonization of the deified king in school curricula
Ideology of the literate king

title.en: Iddin-Dagan's Bride of the New Year
title.zh: 伊丁達甘的新娘慶典

region.en: Isin, Iraq
region.zh: 伊辛（伊拉克）

period: Isin dynasty composition, c. 1900 BCE (ETCSL translation 2003)

source.work: A hymn to Inana for Iddin-Dagan (Iddin-Dagan A, ETCSL c.2.5.3.1)

license: ETCSL translation (Oxford, 2003-2006); quoted in paraphrase with attribution

summary.en: The morning of Inanna's festival: the goddess bathed and perfumed takes the hymn's stage — her assembling of the land, the sacred marriage bed prepared, the king blessed — the great liturgy of the goddess as bride of the city.
summary.zh: 伊南娜慶典之晨：沐浴敷香的女神登台——她召集全境、備妥聖婚之床、祝福國王——女神身為城邦新娘的偉大祭儀。

sensitivity.note: Ancient cult hymn with sexual imagery in ritual register; presented as literature.

passages.text: On the morning of the festival, Inanna bathes and perfumes herself and takes her seat; the land assembles to her, the stars bow to the morning star, and the city is dressed for her advent. The bed is prepared with the king: the goddess claims her lord for the night of the sacred marriage, and through the union the year's abundance is secured for Isin — the rite sung as the goddess's bride-gift to the land.
passages.note: Paraphrase of ETCSL c.2.5.3.1, the advent; not verbatim. / Paraphrase of ETCSL c.2.5.3.1, the marriage; not verbatim.

functions: Liturgy of the sacred marriage at Isin
Charter of the year's abundance through the royal union
Masterpiece of cult love-lyric

title.en: Gudea's Dream of Ningirsu
title.zh: 古蒂亞夢見寧吉爾蘇

region.en: Lagash, Iraq
region.zh: 拉加什（伊拉克）

period: Gudea Cylinder A, c. 2100 BCE (ETCSL translation 2003)

source.work: Gudea Cylinder A (ETCSL c.2.3.2.x)

license: ETCSL translation (Oxford, 2003-2006); quoted in paraphrase with attribution

summary.en: In a dream a giant stands by Gudea's bed — a winged storm bird at his feet, a woman with a stylus, a youth with a cornerstone — and the dream is read: Ningirsu orders his temple built, and the ruler obeys to the letter.
summary.zh: 夢中巨神立於古蒂亞榻旁——足下振翅的暴風鳥、執書板的女子、持奠基石的少年——夢解為命：寧吉爾蘇命其建殿，統治者依夢而行。

sensitivity.note: Ancient royal inscription narrative; no living community restrictions.

passages.text: In his dream a giant stands by Gudea's bed, head to heaven; at his feet a winged storm bird, beside him a woman holding a lapis stylus and tablet, and a youth holding a cornerstone slab — the ruler wakes troubled and seeks the dream's meaning.
passages.note: Paraphrase of ETCSL c.2.3.2.1, the dream; not verbatim.

passages.text: Nanshe, lady of divination, reads it: the giant is Ningirsu, who orders his temple built; the storm bird is his weapon; the woman is Nisaba who will draw the plan. Gudea obeys: the temple Eninnu is begun exactly as the dream showed.
passages.note: Paraphrase of ETCSL c.2.3.2.1, the interpretation; not verbatim.

functions: Charter of royal building as obedience to dream revelation
Detailed liturgy of temple construction
Cult myth of Ningirsu's Eninnu at Girsu

variants.summary: The completion and consecration of the temple.

title.en: Gudea's Temple Completed and Consecrated
title.zh: 古蒂亞建殿功成

region.en: Girsu, Iraq
region.zh: 吉爾蘇（伊拉克）

period: Gudea Cylinder B, c. 2100 BCE (ETCSL translation 2003)

source.work: Gudea Cylinder B (ETCSL c.2.3.2.x)

license: ETCSL translation (Oxford, 2003-2006); quoted in paraphrase with attribution

summary.en: The temple Eninnu rises: materials gathered from every land, the foundations laid on the morning of propitious days, the god installed with a seven-day festival — and the land rests in abundance, the year of the temple's dedication blessed.
summary.zh: 埃寧努神殿落成：建材自萬邦匯聚，擇吉晨奠基，七日慶典迎神入殿——國土休養生息，獻殿之年受福。

sensitivity.note: Ancient royal inscription narrative; no living community restrictions.

passages.text: Materials come from every land for the Eninnu: cedar from the mountains, gold and lapis from far countries, and the foundations are laid on the propitious morning the omens chose. Ningirsu is installed with a seven-day festival; the land rests, taxes are remitted, and the temple's year is blessed — Gudea's piety rewarded with abundance for Lagash.
passages.note: Paraphrase of ETCSL c.2.3.2.2, the building; not verbatim. / Paraphrase of ETCSL c.2.3.2.2, the consecration; not verbatim.

functions: Consecration liturgy of the Eninnu temple
World-renewal theology of temple dedication
Charter of the pious builder king

title.en: A Hymn to Inana for Hammurabi
title.zh: 漢謨拉比之伊南娜頌

region.en: Babylon, Iraq
region.zh: 巴比倫（伊拉克）

period: Old Babylonian composition, c. 1750 BCE (ETCSL translation 2003)

source.work: A hymn to Inana for Hammu-rabi (ETCSL c.2.8.2.1)

license: ETCSL translation (Oxford, 2003-2006); quoted in paraphrase with attribution

summary.en: The Babylonian dynasty's king is praised in Sumerian: Inana, lady of battle, is hymned in her thunder and beauty, and Hammurabi named her favorite — the old south's language put to work for a new empire's king.
summary.zh: 巴比倫王朝之王以蘇美語受頌：戰爭女神伊南娜之雷霆與美麗入詩，漢謨拉比列名其寵——舊邦之語，為新帝之王所用。

sensitivity.note: Ancient royal hymn; no living community restrictions.

passages.text: Inana is hymned in her double nature: the terror of battle whose heart is storm, and the beauty whose grace fills the temples — the goddess of both war and desire. The hymn names Hammurabi her chosen: the king of Babylon, beloved of the lady, under whose justice the land finds order — Sumerian sung for a new empire's ruler.
passages.note: Paraphrase of ETCSL c.2.8.2.1, the goddess; not verbatim. / Paraphrase of ETCSL c.2.8.2.1, the king; not verbatim.

functions: Royal legitimacy hymn in the old language
Continuity of the Inanna hymn genre under Babylon

title.en: The Kes Temple Hymn
title.zh: 克什神殿頌

region.en: Kes, Iraq
region.zh: 克什（伊拉克）

period: Old Babylonian manuscript, c. 1700 BCE (ETCSL translation 2003)

source.work: The Kes temple hymn (ETCSL c.4.80.2)

license: ETCSL translation (Oxford, 2003-2006); quoted in paraphrase with attribution

summary.en: The house of Ninhursag at Kes is praised as the mother-temple of the land: the birthplace of kingship's blessings, its rites deep as the Abzu — the hymn copied as a school masterpiece for a thousand years.
summary.zh: 克什的寧鬍爾薩格神殿被頌為國土之母殿：王權祝福的誕生地，其祭儀深如阿卜祖——千年間為校中傳抄之名篇。

sensitivity.note: Ancient temple hymn; no living community restrictions.

passages.text: The house of Kes, great house of Ninhursag, is praised: the mother-temple where the land's blessings are born, whose rites are deep as the Abzu and whose brickwork rises like the hills. The hymn closes with the temple's charter: whoever honors the house of the mother goddess is blessed with kingship's favor — a school masterpiece copied for a millennium.
passages.note: Paraphrase of ETCSL c.4.80.2, the temple's praise; not verbatim. / Paraphrase of ETCSL c.4.80.2, the close; not verbatim.

functions: Classic of the temple-hymn genre
Charter of the mother goddess's sanctuary

title.en: The Temple Hymns of All Sumer
title.zh: 蘇美諸神殿頌

region.en: From Eridu to Nippur and Lagash, Iraq
region.zh: 自埃利都至尼普魯與拉加什（伊拉克）

period: Old Babylonian manuscript of an older cycle, c. 1700 BCE (ETCSL translation 2003)

source.work: The temple hymns (ETCSL c.4.80.1)

license: ETCSL translation (Oxford, 2003-2006); quoted in paraphrase with attribution

summary.en: Forty-two temples from Eridu's Abzu shrine to Nippur's Ekur and Lagash's Eninnu are praised in order: a liturgical map of the land's sanctuaries, city by city, god by god.
summary.zh: 自埃利都阿卜祖神殿至尼普魯埃庫爾、拉加什埃寧努，四十二座神殿依序受頌：一座聖所的禮儀地圖，城以城計、神以神名。

sensitivity.note: Ancient hymn cycle; no living community restrictions.

passages.text: The cycle praises forty-two temples in order: Eridu's house on the Abzu, Nippur's Ekur the navel of the land, Uruk's Eanna, Ur's house of Nanna, Girsu's Eninnu — city by city, god by god. The map's order is theological: the temples are sung as stations of the world's order, each house holding its god's portion of the land's life — a liturgical geography of Sumer.
passages.note: Paraphrase of ETCSL c.4.80.1, the cycle; not verbatim. / Paraphrase of ETCSL c.4.80.1, the geography; not verbatim.

functions: Liturgical map of Sumer's sanctuaries
Charter of each temple's cultic identity

title.en: The Ekur: House of the Mountain
title.zh: 埃庫爾：山之殿

region.en: Nippur, Iraq
region.zh: 尼普魯（伊拉克）

period: Old Babylonian manuscript, c. 1700 BCE (ETCSL translation 2003)

source.work: A hymn to the Ekur (ETCSL c.4.80.4)

license: ETCSL translation (Oxford, 2003-2006); quoted in paraphrase with attribution

summary.en: Enlil's temple is praised as the bond of heaven and earth: its foundations in the underworld, its crown in the sky, the place where the fates are decreed — the world's axis in brick and song.
summary.zh: 恩利爾之殿被頌為天地之紐帶：根基入冥界，頂冠接天穹，命運裁定之所——以磚石與頌歌築成的世界之軸。

sensitivity.note: Ancient temple hymn; no living community restrictions.

passages.text: The Ekur is praised as the bond of heaven and earth: its foundations reach the underworld, its crown touches the sky, and within it the fates of the land are decreed. The hymn names the temple the place of Enlil's speech: what he says in the Ekur stands — the world's axis sung in brick and ritual.

title.en: The Instructions of Shuruppak
title.zh: 舒魯帕克訓言

region.en: Shuruppak, Iraq
region.zh: 舒魯帕克（伊拉克）

period: Old Babylonian manuscript of an older text, c. 1700 BCE (ETCSL translation 2003)

source.work: The instructions of Suruppag (ETCSL c.5.6.1)

summary.en: The antediluvian sage Shuruppak teaches his son Ziudsura the maxims of life — do not buy a wild ass, do not locate a field on the road, do not curse — the oldest instruction text, father to the wisdom books of the whole Near East.
summary.zh: 洪水前的賢者舒魯帕克訓其子祖蘇德拉處世箴言——勿購野驢、勿於路旁置田、勿咒罵——最古老的訓言文獻，近東智慧書之祖。

sensitivity.note: Ancient wisdom literature; no living community restrictions.

passages.text: Shuruppak, son of Ubar-Tutu, speaks to his son Ziudsura: the instructions of the father to the son — a name to be given, a mouth to be held, a heart not to be trusted to strangers. The maxims follow: do not locate a field on the road; do not buy a wild ass; do not swear; do not revile; do not lie in the assembly — the practical wisdom of the antediluvian sage that schools copied for two millennia.
passages.note: Paraphrase of ETCSL c.5.6.1, the frame; not verbatim. / Paraphrase of ETCSL c.5.6.1, the maxims; not verbatim.

functions: Oldest wisdom instruction text
Ancestor of the Near Eastern instruction genre
School curriculum masterpiece

title.zh: 農夫訓言

region.zh: 蘇美田野（伊拉克）

summary.zh: 農耕之神訓誡農夫一年之事：適時犁地、候洪水至、守種防鳥、風暴前收割——以神諭形式寫成的蘇美農學全書。

sensitivity.note: Ancient instruction text; no living community restrictions.

passages.text: The agricultural god instructs the farmer through the year: plough when the land is ready, let the flood-water come, keep the seed from the birds, harvest before the storms of the year's end. The text closes with blessing: the farmer who follows the instructions shall fill the temple's granaries — agronomy taught as divine advice.
passages.note: Paraphrase of ETCSL c.5.6.3, the instruction; not verbatim. / Paraphrase of ETCSL c.5.6.3, the close; not verbatim.

functions: Agronomy in instruction form
School text linking farming and liturgy

sensitivity.note: Ancient humor text; no living community restrictions.

passages.text: Three ox-drivers of Adab each claim the same ox; their dispute is argued in proverbs and precedents, each man proving his right with a saying of the fathers. The case is settled by division rather than victory — the ox shared — and the tale closes laughing at the wit that ends what strength could not: an early literature of dispute settled by cleverness.

title.en: The Elegy for Nannaya
title.zh: 南納雅輓歌

summary.zh: 書屋少年書記南納雅被冥界奪去；輓歌於葬禮哀悼——靈床、哭喪婦、送葬行列——以其學問與情愛之憶為慰。

sensitivity.note: Ancient elegy; no living community restrictions.

passages.text: Nannaya, the young scribe of the tablet-house, is taken by fate; the elegy mourns him at the funeral procession — the bier carried, the mourning women keening, the friends following. The consolation is memory: his learning, his love, his brightness among the students — and the underworld addressed as the household that now receives him.

Liturgical model of funeral mourning

summary.zh: 詩人的心上人娜薇爾圖姆早逝；輓歌以空寂之宅與戛然而止的婚歌哀悼她——書屋之聲裡的愛之慟。

sensitivity.note: Ancient elegy; no living community restrictions.

passages.text: Nawirtum is taken young, and the elegy mourns her in the imagery of the silenced wedding song: the house barren, the bed unslept, the streets she graced now empty. The speaker's grief answers the underworld directly — why was she taken before her time? — and the consolation offered is the memory of love: she is not forgotten while the song is sung.
passages.note: Paraphrase of ETCSL c.5.5.3, the mourning; not verbatim. / Paraphrase of ETCSL c.5.5.3, the grief; not verbatim.

functions: Love-elegy of the scribal world
Liturgical model of mourning a beloved

title.en: An Axe for Nergal
title.zh: 獻內爾伽勒之斧

region.en: Kutha, Iraq
region.zh: 庫薩（伊拉克）

period: Old Babylonian manuscript, c. 1700 BCE (ETCSL translation 2003)

source.work: An axe for Nergal (ETCSL c.5.7.3)

sensitivity.note: Ancient votive text; no living community restrictions.

passages.text: A new axe is presented to Nergal: the smith's work praised in its cutting edge and weight, the god's terror named — lord of the plague wind and the battle's heat. The offering's purpose is spelled: appease the dread lord, turn his face from the city, keep the plague away — gift as negotiation with the god of misfortune.
