title.en: The Secondary Clear Light and the Question 'Am I Dead?'
title.zh: 第二明光與「我死了嗎？」

region.en: Death-room of the deceased, Tibet (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 亡者停靈之室（象徵定位）

period: Bardo Thodol; English translation 1927

source.work: The Tibetan Book of the Dead, trans. Lama Kazi Dawa-Samdup, ed. Evans-Wentz (1927), Book I

summary.en: If the Primary Clear Light is not recognized, the Secondary Clear Light dawns somewhat more than a meal-time period after the expiration has ceased; according to one's good or bad karma the vital-force flows down the right or left nerve and goes out through any of the apertures, and there comes a lucid condition of the mind. The consciousness-principle, getting outside the body, asks itself: Am I dead, or am I not dead? It cannot determine; it sees its relatives as it had been used to seeing them, and even hears the wailings - the terrifying karmic illusions have not yet dawned.
summary.zh: 若未識根本明光，則呼氣絕後約一頓飯時，第二明光顯現；依善惡業力，命力經左右脈從諸竅而出，心得清明。神識出體，自問：「我死了嗎？還沒死嗎？」無法自決；它如生前般看見親眷，甚至聽見哭聲——而可怕的業力幻象尚未現前。

sensitivity.note: Living liturgical tradition; paraphrase of public-domain 1927 translation only.

passages.text: If it be feared that the primary Clear Light hath not been recognized, then there is dawning upon the deceased that called the Secondary Clear Light, which dawneth in somewhat more than a meal-time period after that the expiration hath ceased. According to one's good or bad karma, the vital-force floweth down into either the right or left nerve and goeth out through any of the apertures of the body; then cometh a lucid condition of the mind.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Lama Kazi Dawa-Samdup's translation (1927); not verbatim.

passages.text: When the consciousness-principle getteth outside the body, it sayeth to itself: Am I dead, or am I not dead? It cannot determine. It seeth its relatives and connexions as it had been used to seeing them before; it even heareth the wailings. The terrifying karmic illusions have not yet dawned, nor have the frightful apparitions or experiences caused by the Lords of Death yet come.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Lama Kazi Dawa-Samdup's translation (1927); not verbatim.

title.en: The Six Bardos and the Secret of Recognition
title.zh: 六中陰與認識之祕

region.en: The Chonyid Bardo of the departed (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 亡者之「實相中陰」（象徵定位）

period: Bardo Thodol; English translation 1927

source.work: The Tibetan Book of the Dead, trans. Lama Kazi Dawa-Samdup, ed. Evans-Wentz (1927), Book I

summary.en: Now that death has come to all, the departed is told not to cling; the six bardos are enumerated - the womb-bardo, the dream-bardo, the bardo of ecstatic equilibrium, the bardo of the moment of death, the bardo of Reality, and the bardo of the inverse process of sangsaric existence - and the key verses are recited: 'may I recognize whatever visions appear as the reflex of mine own consciousness... may I know the apparitions to be of the nature of apparitions; and, at this all-important moment of opportunity, may I know the emanations of the Peaceful and Wrathful Deities to be mine own thought-forms.' The body now is the thought-body of propensities: sounds, lights and rays cannot harm it, for it is incapable of dying.
summary.zh: 既死之人當知：死亡人皆有之，毋須戀棧。六中陰依次列舉——胎中、夢境、禪定、臨終、實相、受生——並誦關鍵偈：「願我認得一切顯現皆自心之影……願我知其幻化本性；於此大事因緣之際，願我知寂忿諸尊皆是自身心念之化現。」今之身乃「習氣意生身」，聲光影三相皆不能傷，以其本不能死。

sensitivity.note: Living liturgical tradition; paraphrase of public-domain 1927 translation only.

passages.text: O nobly-born, that which is called death hath now come. Thou art departing from this world, but thou art not the only one; death cometh to all. Do not cling, in fondness and weakness, to this life. Even though thou clingest out of weakness, thou hast not the power to remain here; thou wilt gain nothing more than wandering in this Sangsara. Be not attached; be not weak. Remember the Precious Trinity.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Lama Kazi Dawa-Samdup's translation (1927); not verbatim.

passages.text: There are six states of Bardo, namely: the natural state of Bardo while in the womb; the Bardo of the dream-state; the Bardo of ecstatic equilibrium while in deep meditation; the Bardo of the moment of death; the Bardo during the experiencing of Reality; and the Bardo of the inverse process of sangsaric existence - these are the six.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Lama Kazi Dawa-Samdup's translation (1927); not verbatim.

passages.text: When thy body and mind were separating, thou must have experienced a glimpse of the Pure Truth, subtle, sparkling, bright, dazzling, glorious, and radiantly awesome, in appearance like a mirage moving across a landscape in spring-time; be not daunted thereby, nor terrified, nor awed - that is the radiance of thine own true nature. From the midst of that radiance the natural sound of Reality, reverberating like a thousand thunders simultaneously sounding, will come; that is the natural sound of thine own real self. The body which thou hast now is called the thought-body of propensities; since thou hast not a material body of flesh and blood, whatever may come - sounds, lights or rays - are, all three, unable to harm thee; thou art incapable of dying. It is quite sufficient for thee to know that these apparitions are thine own thought-forms.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Lama Kazi Dawa-Samdup's translation (1927); not verbatim.

title.en: The First Day: Vairochana and the Two Lights
title.zh: 中陰第一日：毗盧遮那與二光

region.en: The Central Realm, the Spreading Forth of the Seed (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 中央密聚佛國（象徵定位）

period: Bardo Thodol; English translation 1927

source.work: The Tibetan Book of the Dead, trans. Lama Kazi Dawa-Samdup, ed. Evans-Wentz (1927), Book I

summary.en: Recovering from the three-and-a-half-day swoon, the departed sees the whole heavens deep blue; from the Central Realm called the Spreading Forth of the Seed the Bhagavan Vairochana, white, seated on a lion-throne, bearing an eight-spoked wheel, embraced by the Mother of the Space of Heaven, manifests. The blue light of the Wisdom of the Dharma-dhatu shoots forth from his heart - and beside it a dull white light from the devas: through the power of evil karma the glory produces fear and the dull light fondness, and the prayer is recited to be led by Vairochana across the fearful ambush of the Bardo into the state of All-Perfect Buddhahood in the Central Realm of the Densely-Packed.
summary.zh: 三日半昏沉初醒，所見長空盡作深藍；中央「遍佈種子」佛土，毗盧遮那白身獅座、手持八輻輪、與虛空佛母相擁而現。法界體性智之青光自其心間射出，耀不可視；同時一道灰白之光自天道而來。以惡業力故，青光反生怖畏，灰光反生貪戀——故誦祈請文，願毗盧遮那引度，越中陰險隘，譤於「密聚」中央佛國。

sensitivity.note: Living liturgical tradition; paraphrase of public-domain 1927 translation only.

passages.text: As soon as thou art recovered from this swoon, thou wilt have the thought, what hath happened! Act so that thou wilt recognize the Bardo. At that time all the Sangsara will be in revolution, and the phenomenal appearances that thou wilt see then will be the radiances and deities; the whole heavens will appear deep blue. Then, from the Central Realm, called the Spreading Forth of the Seed, the Bhagavan Vairochana, white in colour, seated upon a lion-throne, bearing an eight-spoked wheel in his hand, and embraced by the Mother of the Space of Heaven, will manifest himself to thee.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Lama Kazi Dawa-Samdup's translation (1927); not verbatim.

passages.text: The Wisdom of the Dharma-dhatu, blue in colour, shining, transparent, glorious, dazzling, from the heart of Vairochana as the Father-Mother will shoot forth and strike against thee with a light so radiant that thou wilt scarcely be able to look at it; and along with it there will also shine a dull white light from the devas. Because of the power of bad karma the glorious blue light will produce in thee fear and terror, and thou wilt wish to flee from it, and wilt beget a fondness for the dull white light of the devas - be not awed by the divine blue light, for that is the light of the Tathagata, and put thy whole thought earnestly upon Vairochana.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Lama Kazi Dawa-Samdup's translation (1927); not verbatim.

title.en: The Second Day: Vajra-Sattva and the Smoke of Hell
title.zh: 中陰第二日：金剛薩埵與獄火之煙

region.en: The Eastern Realm of Pre-eminent Happiness (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 東方喜吉祥佛國（象徵定位）

period: Bardo Thodol; English translation 1927

source.work: The Tibetan Book of the Dead, trans. Lama Kazi Dawa-Samdup, ed. Evans-Wentz (1927), Book I

summary.en: On the Second Day the pure form of water shines as a white light; from the Eastern Realm of Pre-eminent Happiness the Bhagavan Akshobhya as Vajra-Sattva, blue, holding a five-pronged vajra, on an elephant-throne, embraced by the Mother Mamaki, appears attended by the Bodhisattvas Kshitigarbha and Maitreya with the female Bodhisattvas Lasya and Puspa. The Mirror-like Wisdom shines as a bright radiant white light from the heart of Vajra-Sattva the Father-Mother - and a dull smoke-coloured light from Hell shines alongside: if the departed is attracted by it, he falls into the Hell-Worlds, whence there is no certain time of getting out.
summary.zh: 第二日，水大淨相現為白光；東方喜吉祥佛土，阿閦佛現金剛薩埵相——藍身、持五股杵、象座、與佛眼佛母（Mamaki）相擁，地藏與彌勒二菩薩及金剛鬘、蓮花二明妃隨侍。大圓鏡智之皎白光明自其心間射出——而地獄之暗煙色光並現：若貪之，即墮地獄，出期無定。

sensitivity.note: Living liturgical tradition; paraphrase of public-domain 1927 translation only.

passages.text: On the Second Day the pure form of water will shine as a white light; at that time, from the deep blue Eastern Realm of Pre-eminent Happiness, the Bhagavan Akshobhya as Vajra-Sattva, blue in colour, holding in his hand a five-pronged vajra, seated upon an elephant-throne, and embraced by the Mother Mamaki, will appear to thee, attended by the Bodhisattvas Kshitigarbha and Maitreya with the female Bodhisattvas Lasya and Puspa.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Lama Kazi Dawa-Samdup's translation (1927); not verbatim.

passages.text: The aggregate of thy principle of consciousness, being in its pure form - which is the Mirror-like Wisdom - will shine as a bright, radiant white light from the heart of Vajra-Sattva the Father-Mother, with such dazzling brilliancy that thou wilt scarcely be able to look at it; and a dull, smoke-coloured light from Hell will shine alongside. Through the power of anger thou wilt be startled at the dazzling white light and beget a fondness for the dull smoke-coloured light from Hell: if thou be attracted by it, thou wilt fall into the Hell-Worlds and endure unbearable misery, whence there is no certain time of getting out.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Lama Kazi Dawa-Samdup's translation (1927); not verbatim.

title.en: The Third Day: Ratna-Sambhava and the Light of Equality
title.zh: 中陰第三日：寶生佛與平等性智

region.en: The Southern Realm Endowed with Glory (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 南方吉祥佛國（象徵定位）

period: Bardo Thodol; English translation 1927

source.work: The Tibetan Book of the Dead, trans. Lama Kazi Dawa-Samdup, ed. Evans-Wentz (1927), Book I

summary.en: On the Third Day the primal form of the element earth shines as a yellow light; from the Southern Realm Endowed with Glory the Bhagavan Ratna-Sambhava, yellow, bearing a jewel, seated on a horse-throne and embraced by the Divine Mother Sangya-Chanmat, shines upon the departed, attended by Akasha-Garbha and Samanta-Bhadra with Mahiama and Dhupema. The Wisdom of Equality, dazzlingly yellow with satellite orbs of radiance, strikes against the departed - and beside it the dull bluish-yellow light of the human world path, of miserliness and greed.
summary.zh: 第三日，地大淨相現為黃光；南方吉祥佛土，寶生佛黃身持寶、馬座、與聖母相擁，虛空藏與普賢二菩薩及二明妃隨侍。平等性智之明黃光，帶光暈圍繞，射向亡者——旁有灰黃之倖光，即慳吝貪欲所致人道之光。

sensitivity.note: Living liturgical tradition; paraphrase of public-domain 1927 translation only.

passages.text: On the Third Day the primal form of the element earth will shine forth as a yellow light; at that time, from the Southern Realm Endowed with Glory, the Bhagavan Ratna-Sambhava, yellow in colour, bearing a jewel in his hand, seated upon a horse-throne and embraced by the Divine Mother, will shine upon thee, attended by the Bodhisattvas Akasha-Garbha and Samanta-Bhadra with the two female Bodhisattvas, all in Buddha-form, coming to shine from amidst a rainbow halo of light.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Lama Kazi Dawa-Samdup's translation (1927); not verbatim.

passages.text: The aggregate of touch in its primal form, as the yellow light of the Wisdom of Equality, dazzlingly yellow, glorified with orbs having satellite orbs of radiance, so clear and bright that the eye can scarcely look upon it, will strike against thee - and side by side with it the dull yellow light of the human world, the path of miserliness and greed, will shine.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Lama Kazi Dawa-Samdup's translation (1927); not verbatim.

title.en: The Blood-Drinking Herukas: The Wrathful Days
title.zh: 飲血赫魯迦：忿怒七日

region.en: The Chonyid Bardo, quarters of the departed's brain (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 實相中陰腦宮四方（象徵定位）

period: Bardo Thodol (Bar-do thos-grol, terma attributed to Padmasambhava); English translation by Lama Kazi Dawa-Samdup, ed. Evans-Wentz, 1927

source.work: The Tibetan Book of the Dead, trans. Lama Kazi Dawa-Samdup, ed. W. Y. Evans-Wentz (Oxford University Press, 1927), Part I, Book I: the eighth to fourteenth days

license: Public domain (English translation published 1927; US public domain since 2023)

summary.en: On the eighth to fourteenth days the fifty-eight flame-enhaloed, wrathful, blood-drinking deities dawn - only the former Peaceful Deities in changed aspect, issuing from the quarters of the departed's own brain. The Great Glorious Buddha-Heruka, dark-brown, with three faces, six hands and four feet, nine eyes in terrifying gaze, eyebrows quivering like lightning, hair of reddish-yellow standing on end, garlanded with black serpents and raw human heads, holding wheel, sword and battle-axe, bell, skull-bowl and ploughshare, embraced by the Mother Buddha-Krotishaurima who puts to his mouth a red shell filled with blood, comes forth from the departed's own brain - fear it not, for in reality it is the Bhagavan Vairochana the Father-Mother. Recognition is more difficult, but the intellect, undistractedly alert in one-pointedness under terror, is readier to be liberated - and the least of tantrika devotees will greet the blood-drinkers as tutelary deities, like human acquaintances.
summary.zh: 第八至十四日，五十八尊焰鬘熾燃、忿怒飲血之尊次第現前——彼即前七日寂靜諸尊之變相，自亡者腦宮四方而出。大悲赫魯迦深棕色，三面六臂四足，九目怒視，眉如電顫，赤黃髮豎，頸飾黑蛇與新剝人首為鬘，右手持輪、劍、斧，左手持鈴、顱器、犁鏵，佛母克羅提沙烏利瑪擁之，以盈血赤螺就其口——勿懼！其實即毗盧遮那父母雙運。此期怖畏更甚，然心因懼而專一，反易得度；最下之密乘行者亦能認彼為本尊，如遇故人。

canonical_translation: Lama Kazi Dawa-Samdup, English translation; ed. W. Y. Evans-Wentz, The Tibetan Book of the Dead, Oxford 1927 (public domain)

narrative.en:
In the Bardo of the Peaceful Deities there were seven stages of ambuscade, and multitudes obtain liberation by recognition at one or another stage; but the number of sentient beings being great, evil karma powerful, obscurations dense, and propensities of too long standing, the Wheel of Ignorance and Illusion becometh neither exhausted nor accelerated, and there is a vast preponderance of those who wander downwards unliberated. Therefore, after the cessation of the dawning of the Peaceful and the Knowledge-Holding Deities, who come to welcome one, the fifty-eight flame-enhaloed, wrathful, blood-drinking deities come to dawn, who are only the former Peaceful Deities in changed aspect - according to the place of the thought-body of the deceased whence they proceed; nevertheless they will not resemble them.

This is the Bardo of the Wrathful Deities; and they being influenced by fear, terror and awe, recognition becometh more difficult; the intellect, gaining not in independence, passeth from one fainting state to a round of fainting states. Yet if one but recognize a little it is easier to be liberated at this stage - because of the dawning of the radiances, which produce fear, terror and awe, the intellect is undistractedly alert in one-pointedness. If at this stage one do not meet with this kind of teaching, one's hearing of religious lore, although it be like an ocean in its vastness, is of no avail; there are even discipline-holding abbots and doctors in metaphysical discourses who err at this stage, and, not recognizing, wander into the Sangsara. As for the common worldly folk, by fleeing through fear, terror and awe, they fall over the precipices into the unhappy worlds and suffer; but the least of the devotees of the mystic doctrines, as soon as he sees these blood-drinking deities, will recognize them to be his tutelary deities, and the meeting will be like that of human acquaintances - he will trust them, and becoming merged into them, in at-one-ment, will obtain Buddhahood.

O nobly-born, the Great Glorious Buddha-Heruka, dark-brown of colour, with three heads, six hands and four feet firmly postured; the right face being white, the left red, the central dark-brown; the body emitting flames of radiance; the nine eyes widely opened in terrifying gaze; the eyebrows quivering like lightning; the protruding teeth glistening and set over one another; giving vent to sonorous utterances of 'a-la-la' and 'ha-ha' and piercing whistling sounds; the hair of a reddish-yellow colour standing on end and emitting radiance; the heads adorned with dried human skulls and the symbols of the sun and moon; black serpents and raw human heads forming a garland for the body; the first of the right hands holding a wheel, the middle one a sword, the last one a battle-axe; the first of the left hands a bell, the middle one a skull-bowl, the last one a ploughshare; his body embraced by the Mother Buddha-Krotishaurima, her right hand clinging to his neck and her left putting to his mouth a red shell filled with blood - these two deities together will come forth from within thine own brain and shine vividly upon thee. Fear that not. Be not awed. Know it to be the embodiment of thine own intellect. As it is thine own tutelary deity, be not terrified; in reality it is the Bhagavan Vairochana, the Father-Mother. Simultaneously with the recognition, liberation will be obtained.

If one flee from them, then on the Ninth Day the blood-drinking deities of the Vajra Order named the Bhagavan Vajra-Heruka, dark-blue, issue from the eastern quarter of the brain; on the Tenth Day the blood-drinking deity of the Precious-Gem Order named Ratna-Heruka, yellow, issues from the southern quarter; on the Eleventh Day the blood-drinking deity of the Lotus Order, Padma-Heruka, reddish-black, from the western quarter - in reality the Father-Mother Bhagavan Amitabha; on the Twelfth Day the blood-drinking deity of the Karmic Order, Karma-Heruka, dark green, accompanied by the Kerima, Htamenaa and Wang-chugma, from the northern quarter - in reality the Father-Mother Bhagavan Amoghasiddhi. Each time the address repeats: fear not, be not terrified, be not awed, know them to be the embodiment of thine own intellect, and Buddhahood will be obtained by merging in them in at-one-ment.
narrative.notes: Cultural function: the wrathful sequence inverts ordinary terror into liberation - the most frightful forms are the closest to home, one's own brain and one's own tutelary deities - which is why the practitioner meditates on their images while alive. The blood symbolizes sangsaric existence; 'blood-drinking' the thirsting for, and quenching of, the thirst for existence.

functions: Inverts the terror of the death-visions into the path: the more frightful the apparition, the closer to one's own mind
Grounds iconographic practice: seeing the painted likenesses and images while alive secures recognition at death
Democratizes the liberation doctrine: the least of tantrika devotees meets the blood-drinkers like old acquaintances
Explains the funeral signs - rainbow-halo and bone-reliques - as the residue of esoteric recognition

variants.name: The 58 blood-drinking deities in the mandala paintings
variants.text_tradition: The Great Mandala of the Knowledge-Holding and Wrathful Deities (folio paintings reproduced in Evans-Wentz)
variants.summary: The painted mandalas show the united manifestation of the Wrathful Deities, the three-headed Herukas of the five orders at the cruciform design's centre, and the King and Judge of the Dead, Shinje, the wrathful aspect of Avalokiteshvara, weighing the dead.

variants.name: The Great Symbol (Mahamudra) schools
variants.summary: Devotees of the Great Symbol and the Great Perfection recognize the Clear Light at the moment of death and do not need the reading of the Thodol; they may obtain the Sambhoga-Kaya in the Chonyid Bardo or the Nirmana-Kaya in the Sidpa Bardo.

primary_sources.work: Bardo Thodol (Bar-do thos-grol), Part I, Book I: the eighth to fourteenth days
primary_sources.citation: Tibetan text; English trans. Lama Kazi Dawa-Samdup, ed. W. Y. Evans-Wentz, The Tibetan Book of the Dead, London: Oxford University Press, 1927, pp. 132-142

secondary_sources.work: W. Y. Evans-Wentz, The Tibetan Book of the Dead
secondary_sources.citation: Evans-Wentz 1927, London: Oxford University Press - editorial notes on the Herukas and the esoteric doctrine.

secondary_sources.work: René de Nebesky-Wojkowitz, Oracles and Demons of Tibet
secondary_sources.citation: Nebesky-Wojkowitz 1956, The Hague - the wrathful pantheon in living Tibetan ritual.

secondary_sources.work: Per Kvaerne, Tibet Bibliography
secondary_sources.citation: Kvaerne 1986, London: SOAS - the anthropological literature on Tibetan death-ritual.

source_urls.description: Internet Archive scan of the 1927 Oxford edition of The Tibetan Book of the Dead

sensitivity_guidance: The wrathful deities are living liturgical images, painted and meditated in Tibetan monasteries; passages below are paraphrases of the 1927 public-domain translation for study, not for ritual use, and the tradition is treated respectfully.

sensitivity.note: Living liturgical tradition; paraphrase of public-domain 1927 translation only.

passages.text: After the cessation of the dawning of the Peaceful and the Knowledge-Holding Deities, the fifty-eight flame-enhaloed, wrathful, blood-drinking deities come to dawn, who are only the former Peaceful Deities in changed aspect; this is the Bardo of the Wrathful Deities, and they being influenced by fear, terror and awe, recognition becometh more difficult - yet if one but recognize a little, it is easier to be liberated at this stage, because the intellect is undistractedly alert in one-pointedness under terror.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Lama Kazi Dawa-Samdup's translation (1927); not verbatim.

passages.text: The Great Glorious Buddha-Heruka, dark-brown, with three heads, six hands and four feet firmly postured, the nine eyes widely opened in terrifying gaze, the eyebrows quivering like lightning, the hair of reddish-yellow standing on end, the heads adorned with dried human skulls and the symbols of the sun and moon, black serpents and raw human heads forming a garland for the body, his body embraced by the Mother Buddha-Krotishaurima, her right hand clinging to his neck and her left putting to his mouth a red shell filled with blood - these two deities together will come forth from within thine own brain and shine vividly upon thee: fear that not, know it to be the embodiment of thine own intellect; in reality it is the Bhagavan Vairochana, the Father-Mother.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Lama Kazi Dawa-Samdup's translation (1927); not verbatim.

passages.text: On the Ninth Day the blood-drinking Vajra-Heruka, dark-blue, issues from the eastern quarter of thy brain - in reality the Father-Mother Bhagavan Vajra-Sattva; on the Tenth Day Ratna-Heruka, yellow, from the southern quarter; on the Eleventh Day Padma-Heruka, reddish-black, from the western quarter - in reality the Father-Mother Bhagavan Amitabha; and on the Twelfth Day Karma-Heruka, dark green, from the northern quarter - in reality the Father-Mother Bhagavan Amoghasiddhi. Each time: fear not, be not terrified, be not awed, know them to be the embodiment of thine own intellect, and Buddhahood will be obtained by merging in them in at-one-ment.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Lama Kazi Dawa-Samdup's translation (1927); not verbatim.

title.en: Shinje, King and Judge of the Dead
title.zh: 閻魔王（辛傑）審判

region.en: Court of the Judge of the Dead in the Bardo (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 中陰閻羅法庭（象徵定位）

period: Bardo Thodol tradition (mandala text and iconography); English ed. Evans-Wentz 1927

source.work: The Tibetan Book of the Dead, ed. W. Y. Evans-Wentz (1927), Introduction, the Judgement Scene

summary.en: Shinje - the King and Judge of the Dead, the wrathful aspect of Avalokiteshvara, monkey-headed - presides over the weighing: on one side heaped-up black pebbles, the evil deeds, on the other white pebbles, the good deeds; the Little White God empties a sack of white pebbles, the Little Black God a sack of black, and guarding the weighing stand the buffalo-headed officers; from the court issue the six paths, bearing the recently judged - a scene Evans-Wentz sets beside the judgement in the tenth book of Plato's Republic, where the just ascend by the heavenly way on the right and the unjust descend on the left, bearing the symbols of their deeds fastened to their backs.
summary.zh: 閻魔王（辛傑）——觀音之忿怒相、猴面之王——主持稱量：一側堆黑石為惡業，一側堆白石為善業；白神傾倒善石之袋，黑神傾倒惡石之袋，牛頭獄卒守秤；六道之門自法庭兩側而出，剛受審判者列隊其間——伊文思溫茲將此景與柏拉圖《理想國》第十卷之審判並觀：善者由右天路上升，惡者由左下道而降，背上縛其業跡。

sensitivity.note: Living liturgical tradition; paraphrase of public-domain 1927 edition only.

passages.text: Shinje is the King and Judge of the Dead, the wrathful aspect of Avalokiteshvara; in the Judgement Scene there is the symbolical weighing - before him, on one side, heaped-up black pebbles, the evil deeds, and on the other heaped-up white pebbles, the good deeds. On the right of Shinje stands the Little White God, emptying a sack of white pebbles; on the other side the Little Black God, emptying a sack of black pebbles; and guarding the weighing are the buffalo-headed officers.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Evans-Wentz's edition (1927), Introduction; not verbatim.

passages.text: Issuing from the Court, on either side of the Judge, are the six paths, and on them are seated twelve of the dead who have recently been judged - a scene closely resembling the Judgement described in the tenth book of Plato's Republic, where judges seated in the intermediate space commanded the just, after judgement, to ascend by the heavenly way on the right hand, and the unjust to descend by the lower way on the left, bearing the symbols of their deeds fastened to their backs.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Evans-Wentz's edition (1927) quoting Jowett's Plato; not verbatim.

title.en: The Sidpa Bardo: Seeking Rebirth
title.zh: 受生中陰：尋求投生

region.en: The Sidpa Bardo of the wanderer (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 受生中陰（象徵定位）

period: Bardo Thodol; English translation 1927

source.work: The Tibetan Book of the Dead, trans. Lama Kazi Dawa-Samdup, ed. Evans-Wentz (1927), Book II

summary.en: In the Sidpa Bardo the wanderer, having failed recognition, undergoes visions of the Judgment of the Lords of Death - who number all deeds with the mirror and the scales of black and white pebbles - then wanders pursued by karmic winds, seeking a womb; the methods of closing the doors of the womb, the choosing of the place of birth, and the reading of omens of the sex and caste of the coming life follow, the consciousness-principle drinking of forgetfulness as it enters the door of the womb.
summary.zh: 受生中陰中，未得認識之亡者將見閻魔王之審判——以鏡與黑白石之秤算盡其業——復為業風所逐，尋求投生之胎；經中遂教以關閉胎門之法、擇生之方，以及觀察來生性別種姓之兆，神識飲忘川之水而入胎門。

sensitivity.note: Living liturgical tradition; paraphrase of public-domain 1927 translation only.

passages.text: Now henceforth thou art going to experience the other two, the Chonyid Bardo and the Sidpa Bardo. In the Sidpa Bardo, having failed to recognize the visions of the Peaceful and the Wrathful Deities as thine own thought-forms, thou wilt wander, subject to the karmic winds, until the place of rebirth is found - and the teachings, therefore, go on to the methods of closing the doors of the womb while in the Intermediate State when seeking rebirth.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Lama Kazi Dawa-Samdup's translation (1927); not verbatim.

passages.text: Drinking of the River of Forgetfulness, the consciousness-principle enters the door of the womb and is reborn direct from the desire-world called the Sidpa Bardo - the lower rebirth being unendowed, because of the lack of enlightenment of the one undergoing it, with consciousness of the process.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Evans-Wentz's edition (1927); not verbatim.

title.en: Er the Pamphylian and the Ch choosing of Bodies
title.zh: 珀菲里亞人之厄爾與擇生

region.en: The otherworld of Plato's Republic, compared by Evans-Wentz (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 柏拉圖《理想國》之他世（伊文思溫茲並觀，象徵定位）

period: Plato, Republic, Bk. X (4th century BC), compared by Evans-Wentz 1927 with the Sidpa Bardo

source.work: The Tibetan Book of the Dead, ed. W. Y. Evans-Wentz (1927), Introduction, quoting Plato's Republic, Bk. X

summary.en: Evans-Wentz's great cross-cultural comparison: Er, son of Armenius, slain in battle, found uncorrupted, returned to life on the funeral pile on the twelfth day and told what he had seen - a mysterious place with two openings in the earth and two in the heaven, judges seated in the intermediate space, the just ascending by the heavenly way on the right and the unjust descending on the left, bearing the symbols of their deeds - and then the choosing of lives: Orpheus taking the swan, Ajax the lion, Agamemnon the eagle, Atalanta the athlete, Epeius the cunning woman, Therites the monkey, and Odysseus, disabused of ambition, the neglected life of a private man who had no cares.
summary.zh: 伊文思溫茲的大跨文化對照：厄爾戰歿而屍身不腐，第十二日於火葬堆上復生，述其所見——地有二口、天有二口之秘境，中間坐著審判者，善者由右天路而升，惡者由左下道而降，背縛其業跡；繼而眾魂擇生：奧菲斯取天鵝，埃阿斯取獅，阿伽門農取鷹，阿塔蘭忒取力士，厄珀俄斯取巧女，特西忒斯取猿——而厭倦了野心的奧德修斯，取那被眾人遺忘的「無憂平民之生」。

sensitivity.note: Comparative material from Evans-Wentz's edition; paraphrase only.

passages.text: Er, the son of Armenius, a Pamphylian by birth, was slain in battle, and ten days afterwards, when the bodies of the dead were taken up already in a state of corruption, his body was found unaffected by decay, and carried home to be buried; and on the twelfth day, as he was lying on the funeral pile, he returned to life and told them what he had seen in the other world. He said that when his soul left the body he went on a journey with a great company, and they came to a mysterious place at which there were two openings in the earth, and over against them two other openings in the heaven above; in the intermediate space there were judges seated, who commanded the just, after they had given judgement on them, to ascend by the heavenly way on the right hand, and the unjust to descend by the lower way on the left, these also bearing the symbols of their deeds fastened to their backs.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Jowett's Plato as quoted in Evans-Wentz's edition (1927); not verbatim.

passages.text: Most curious was the spectacle - sad and laughable and strange; for the choice of the souls was in most cases based on their own experience of a previous life: the soul which had once been Orpheus choosing the life of a swan out of enmity to the race of women; Ajax refusing to be a man, remembering the injustice done him in the judgement about the arms, chose the life of a lion; Agamemnon took the life of an eagle; Atalanta, seeing the great fame of an athlete, was unable to resist the temptation; Epeius passed into the nature of a woman cunning in the arts; the jester Therites was putting on the form of a monkey - and Odysseus, the mutabilities of human life having disabused him of ambition, went about for a considerable time in search of the life of a private man who had no cares, and, finding it lying about and neglected by everybody else, said he would have done the same had his lot been first instead of last, and was delighted to have it.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Jowett's Plato as quoted in Evans-Wentz's edition (1927); not verbatim.

title.en: !Gauwa's Invisible Arrows: Illness and Death
title.zh: 高瓦之隱箭：疾病與死亡

region.en: Nyae Nyae (Tsumkwe district), Namibia (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 納米比亞尼亞尼亞（欽韋區）（象徵定位）

period: Ju/'hoansi (!Kung) oral tradition; recorded 1950s-1960s by Lorna Marshall and John Marshall, published 1976

source.archive: Harvard University Press (book); ethnographic film archive
source.work: Lorna Marshall, The !Kung of Nyae Nyae (1976); John Marshall, films of the Ju/'hoansi

license: Paraphrase for educational use; underlying recordings remain with the Marshall family and Ju/'hoan community

summary.en: Among the Ju/'hoansi illness and death come from !Gauwa, the great god who shoots people with invisible arrows from ambush or sends ghosts to do it. The arrows lodge unseen in the body; sickness grows as they fester; and only the trancing healers, who die and rise within the dance, can see and draw them out. !Gauwa owns the eland and all the big game, and men plead with him for animals as they plead for health.
summary.zh: 朱霍安西人中，疾病與死亡皆出於大神高瓦：他自埋伏處以隱形之箭射人，或遣鬼為之。箭匿體內，病隨之發；唯入迷之醫者——於舞中死而復生者——能見之拔之。高瓦掌大羚與群獸；獵者為獸如為健康而懇求於他。

sensitivity.note: Modern Ju/'hoan religious knowledge recorded by ethnographers with community cooperation; presented as documented paraphrase, not as community speech.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase of Marshall, The !Kung of Nyae Nyae (1976), chs. on religion and illness; not verbatim. The Ju/'hoansi hold that !Gauwa (|Gauwa), the great god, shoots people with invisible arrows — from his own hand, or through the ghosts of the dead which he sends. The arrows enter the body unseen and lie there; the sickness grows as they work, and a person dies when !Gauwa has shot him finally, or when a ghost has come to take him.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Lorna Marshall, The !Kung of Nyae Nyae (1976); not verbatim.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase, same work; not verbatim. Ghosts (the spirits of dead Ju) are blamed for many deaths; they belong to !Gauwa and do his shooting. A sick person may say that a ghost came to him at night, or that !Gauwa has shot him; the family debates which of the two it was, for the treatment — and the blame — differ. Only the healers (n/um k’iaosi, 'owners of n/um') can see the arrows.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Marshall (1976); not verbatim.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase of Katz, Boiling Energy (1982); not verbatim. In the great medicine dances the healers trance, die for a moment, and rise to lay hands on the sick: they see !Gauwa's arrows glittering in the patient's body, seize them, and pull them out, flinging them back toward the darkness. !Gauwa also owns the eland and the big game; hunters who fail say he has hidden his animals, and plead with him as they plead for health.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Richard Katz, Boiling Energy: Community Healing among the Kalahari !Kung (1982); not verbatim.

title.en: The !Gauwasi: Ancestors Who Shoot from the Dark
title.zh: 高瓦西：暗處射人之祖靈

region.en: Dobe area, Kalahari (Botswana/Namibia border) (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 喀拉哈里多貝地區（波札那與納米比亞交界）（象徵定位）

period: Ju/'hoansi oral tradition; recorded 1963-1973 by Richard B. Lee, published 1979

source.work: Richard B. Lee, The !Kung San: Men, Women, and Work in a Foraging Society (1979); Lorna Marshall (1976)

summary.en: The Ju dead become !Gauwasi, spirits of the dead who live in holes in rocks and trees and are subject to !Gauwa. They shoot the living with invisible arrows, they frighten lonely travellers, and they are treated with name-avoidance and gifts: their names are never spoken again, food is left at the grave, and the dead person's belongings are broken so no ghost may come for them.
summary.zh: 朱人死者成為高瓦西——居於岩石樹洞之祖靈，受高瓦轄制。彼等以隱箭射生者，嚇孤旅；人們避其名、獻食於墓、毀其遺物，以免其魂來尋。

sensitivity.note: Modern Ju/'hoan belief recorded by ethnographers; presented as documented paraphrase.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase of Lee, The !Kung San (1979), ch. 9 (Religion and Healing); not verbatim. The !Kung hold that the dead turn into ghosts (!Gauwasi) who dwell in the holes of rocks and baobab trees and are ruled by the great god !Gauwa. The ghosts are feared rather than loved: they are believed to shoot the living with invisible arrows, and to come for the dying.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Lee (1979); not verbatim.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase, same work; not verbatim. The name of a dead person is never spoken again by his kin; if the name is that of a common object or animal, the word itself is changed or replaced — so closely is the living tied to the dead. The dead person's hut, bow, mats and cooking gear are broken and burned so that no part of him remains for a ghost to come back for; food is sometimes left at the grave.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Lee (1979) and Marshall (1976); not verbatim.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase of Marshall (1976); not verbatim. A widow or widower is smudged and rubbed with ash and medicines to drive off the ghost of the spouse, who is thought to hover close; the mourners wail a formula that sends the dead away to !Gauwa's country, for the dead who linger too long begin to shoot the living.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Marshall (1976); not verbatim.

title.en: Boiling Energy: The Ju/'hoan Trance Dance
title.zh: 沸騰之力：朱霍安西迷舞

region.en: Dobe / Nyae Nyae, Kalahari (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 喀拉哈里多貝／尼亞尼亞（象徵定位）

period: Ju/'hoansi religious practice; recorded 1950s-1980s by Lorna Marshall, Richard Katz and Megan Biesele

source.work: Richard Katz, Boiling Energy: Community Healing among the Kalahari !Kung (1982); Lorna Marshall, The !Kung of Nyae Nyae (1976)

summary.en: Around the night fire, women in file sing and stamp the giraffe songs while the men — the owners of n/um, a boiling energy at the base of the spine — dance in a half-circle. The n/um heats, climbs the spine, and the dancers trance: they die for an instant, cross into !Gauwa's country, and rise to draw !Gauwa's arrows out of the sick with their hands, feet, and the smell of burning herbs.
summary.zh: 夜火之畔，女列隊而歌而踏長頸鹿之歌；男者——脊柱基部沸騰之n/um之主——半環而舞。n/um發熱，沿脊上行，舞者入迷：剎那而死，越入高瓦之境，復起以手、足與焚草之氣拔出病者體內高瓦之箭。

sensitivity.note: Ju/'hoan healing practice documented with community participation; paraphrase only, not ritual instruction.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase of Katz, Boiling Energy (1982), chs. 1-3; not verbatim. The trance dance (n/um tchai or the giraffe dance) is the central religious institution of the Ju/'hoansi. Women sit in file around the fire singing and clapping the medicine songs — the giraffe song is the great one — while the men dance around them; the singing and the drumming of feet feed the n/um, the medicine power, in the dancers.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Katz (1982); not verbatim.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase, same work; not verbatim. As n/um boils up from the base of the spine, some dancers enter kia, the trance state: they say they die for a moment, that their thoughts travel to !Gauwa's place, and that they come back with the sight to see !Gauwa's arrows in the sick. They lay trembling hands on chests and backs, suck and blow, and pull the arrows out, sometimes staggering and falling; the others steady them and keep them from the fire.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Katz (1982); not verbatim.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase of Marshall (1976); not verbatim. The dance goes on through the night until the sick sleep and the arrows are out; in the morning the camp says who was healed and who was shot too deeply. The dance is also the meeting-place of the whole waterhole group — the social and religious centre of Ju/'hoan life.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Marshall (1976); not verbatim.

title.en: Eland Potency: The Rock-Art Reading
title.zh: 大羚之力：岩畫之解

region.en: Drakensberg escarpment, South Africa (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 南非德拉肯斯堡山（象徵定位）

period: Southern San rock art (last painted before c. 1900); interpreted 1981-2000 from 19th-century |Xam records

source.archive: Published scholarship drawing on Bleek & Lloyd archive
source.work: David Lewis-Williams, Believing and Seeing: Symbolic Meanings in Southern San Rock Paintings (1981); Lewis-Williams & Dowson, Images of Power (1989)

summary.en: The eland is the great reservoir of n/um potency: in |Xam thought its blood and fat are medicine, and shamans enter trance 'dying' like wounded eland. Lewis-Williams reads the painted eland and the crossed, half-human dancers beside them as the record of the trance dance — potency rising, shamans bleeding from the nose, and the dance-floor of the rock wall.
summary.zh: 大羚為n/um之力之巨庫：|Xam觀念中其血其脂皆藥，薩滿入迷時如傷羚『垂死』。路易斯-威廉斯解讀岩壁之大羚與交叉半人舞者，為迷舞之記——力上升、薩滿鼻血、岩面即舞場。

sensitivity.note: Interpretive archaeology built on the |Xam archive; the eland remains ritually central to San-descended communities.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase of Lewis-Williams, Believing and Seeing (1981), chs. on eland and potency; not verbatim. In |Xam accounts the eland is the embodiment of !gi (potency): its fat and blood are the strongest medicines, and the shaman in trance is said to 'die' and behave like a wounded eland, standing with lowered head, shaking, and bleeding from the nose.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Lewis-Williams (1981); not verbatim.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase of Lewis-Williams & Dowson, Images of Power (1989); not verbatim. Paintings of eland surrounded by elongated, bent-forward human figures with crossed arms and white potency spots are read as shamans dancing around the reservoir of power in trance, their ritual killing of the eland paralleling the trance death. The rock face itself is the veil of the spirit world; the dance is danced against it.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Lewis-Williams & Dowson (1989); not verbatim.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase of the same scholarship drawing on Vinnicombe (1976); not verbatim. The eland's blood, spilled in the first-kill rites, is believed to make the hunter who eats of it strong and calm; the eland dance at a girl's first menstruation marks her as the eland's bride, and the potency of the animal passes into the band.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Lewis-Williams (1981) and Vinnicombe (1976); not verbatim.

title.en: The Lion Outside the Body: Ju/'hoan Astral Shamans
title.zh: 體外之獅：朱霍安西離體薩滿

region.en: Nyae Nyae / Dobe, Kalahari (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 喀拉哈里尼亞尼亞／多貝（象徵定位）

period: Ju/'hoansi oral tradition; recorded 1950s-1990s by Lorna Marshall, Katz and Guenther

source.work: Lorna Marshall, The !Kung of Nyae Nyae (1976); Mathias Guenther, Tricksters and Trancers (1999); Katz (1982)

summary.en: Powerful healers are said to leave their bodies in trance (k’ebu) and travel to far camps, to the dead, or into lions: dying !Gauwa-men become lions, and a lion met on the path may be a shaman out walking. The lion's roar at night may be a sorcerer's spirit calling; the healer who brings his k’ebu back tells where he has been.
summary.zh: 力大之醫者入迷時（克布）離體遠行——至遠村、至死者處、或入獅身：垂死之高瓦之人化為獅，途遇之獅或為外遊之薩滿。夜吼之獅或為巫靈之喚；攜克布歸之醫者能述其所至。

sensitivity.note: Documented Ju/'hoan belief; paraphrase only.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase of Marshall (1976), religion chapters; not verbatim. The !Kung say that a man with strong n/um can, in trance, send his k’ebu — his spirit or shadow-self — out of his body to travel far away, to see what is happening at other waterholes, or to visit !Gauwa and the dead; his body lies as if asleep while his k’ebu is abroad.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Marshall (1976); not verbatim.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase of Guenther, Tricksters and Trancers (1999); not verbatim. Lions are intimately linked with trancers: a dying shaman becomes a lion, and a lion met in the bush may be a trance-traveller in lion form; the roar heard at night is sometimes taken for the voice of a !Gauwa-man calling. When a healer returns from trance he tells of his journey — where he went, what he saw, whom he fought.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Guenther (1999); not verbatim.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase of Katz (1982); not verbatim. In the dance a healer may announce that he has been among the ghosts, or that he has pulled a lion out of a sick person — that the illness was a !Gauwa-man in lion form lodged inside; the extraction and the story together close the case of the illness.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Katz (1982); not verbatim.

title.en: The Name That Must Not Be Spoken
title.zh: 不可言之名

region.en: Dobe / !Kangwa, Kalahari (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 喀拉哈里多貝／坎瓜（象徵定位）

period: Ju/'hoansi custom; documented 1963-1973 by Richard B. Lee, published 1979

source.work: Richard B. Lee, The !Kung San (1979), ch. 9; Lorna Marshall (1976)

summary.en: After death a Ju/'hoan's name is tabooed forever; kin may not speak it, and if it is an everyday word — 'honey', 'zebra', 'fire' — the word is replaced in the language of that band. The name-taboo follows the ghost into the naming of children and even of jokes, so that the dead are honoured by silence.
summary.zh: 朱人逝者之名永為禁忌；親屬不得言，若其名為常用詞——『蜜』『斑馬』『火』——該詞於其群之語中即遭替換。名諱隨鬼魂延及兒名與戲言；死者以緘默受尊。

sensitivity.note: Documented Ju/'hoan custom; paraphrase only.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase of Lee (1979), ch. 9; not verbatim. The names of the dead are avoided absolutely: a kinsman will not speak his dead father's or mother's name, and people related by the name-link (children named after the dead) avoid it too. Where the dead person's name was an ordinary word, the band replaces the word — a new word is coined for 'honey' or 'zebra' — so that the name never has to be said again.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Lee (1979); not verbatim.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase of Marshall (1976); not verbatim. The name-taboo is part of the fear and honour owed to the !Gauwasi: speaking the dead person's name invites the ghost, as does handling his belongings. Children named for the dead are said to carry the dead person's 'shade' and must be watched.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Marshall (1976); not verbatim.

title.en: The Eland Bull Dance at First Menstruation
title.zh: 初潮之大羚牛舞

region.en: Nyae Nyae, Namibia (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 納米比亞尼亞尼亞（象徵定位）

period: Ju/'hoansi rite; recorded 1950s-1980s by Lorna Marshall and John Marshall

source.work: Lorna Marshall, The !Kung of Nyae Nyae (1976); John Marshall, films of the Ju/'hoansi (N!ai, 1978)

summary.en: At a girl's first menstruation the camp performs the eland dance: women and men file around her, stroke her arms and shoulders 'the way an eland's mane is stroked', singing the eland songs, so that the potency of the eland bull — !Gauwa's favourite animal — enters her body and makes her strong, fat, and fruitful.
summary.zh: 少女初潮時，營地行大羚之舞：眾人列隊繞之，如撫羚鬣般撫其臂肩，歌大羚之歌——使高瓦至愛之動物大羚牛之力入其身，使其強壯、豐腴、多產。

sensitivity.note: Documented Ju/'hoan puberty rite; paraphrase only, no ritual instruction.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase of Marshall (1976), ch. on the eland ceremony; not verbatim. When a girl menstruates for the first time the band holds the eland ceremony: the people form a line and dance around her, singing the eland songs; they touch and stroke her arms, shoulders and back — as one strokes the mane of an eland bull — so that the eland's potency enters her.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Marshall (1976); not verbatim.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase, same work; not verbatim. The eland is !Gauwa's great animal, the reservoir of n/um; the dance is held so that the girl will be strong, that her blood will flow well, and that she will grow fat and bear children well. The rite ends with feasting on eland meat if the hunters have been lucky, and the girl is said now to be 'like an eland'.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Marshall (1976); not verbatim.

title.en: The Giraffe Song: The Great Medicine of the Dance
title.zh: 長頸鹿之歌：舞之大藥

region.en: Dobe, Kalahari (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 喀拉哈里多貝（象徵定位）

period: Ju/'hoansi medicine songs; recorded 1950s-1980s by Marshall, Katz and Biesele

source.work: Richard Katz, Boiling Energy (1982); Megan Biesele, Women Like Meat (1993); Lorna Marshall (1976)

summary.en: The giraffe song is the strongest of the Ju/'hoan medicine songs: sung at the night dance, its long rising phrases pull the n/um up the dancers' spines and open the deepest trances. The giraffe, like the eland, is an animal of !Gauwa; to sing the giraffe is to call the biggest medicine into the circle.
summary.zh: 長頸鹿之歌為朱霍安西醫歌之至強者：夜舞中其悠揚上揚之句牽動舞者脊中之n/um，開最深之迷。長頸鹿與大羚同為高瓦之獸；唱長頸鹿即召至大之藥入環。

sensitivity.note: Documented Ju/'hoan medicine song; paraphrase only.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase of Katz (1982); not verbatim. The giraffe dance is the most powerful of the Ju/'hoan medicine dances; the women's song of the giraffe, with its long, rising, circling phrases, is said to pull the n/um hardest up the men's spines, and the deepest trances are entered under this song.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Katz (1982); not verbatim.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase of Biesele, Women Like Meat (1993); not verbatim. Medicine songs belong to the animals of !Gauwa — eland, giraffe, gemsbok — and each song is 'owned' by the line of healers who inherited it; the songs are the animals' gifts, and singing them correctly is itself a form of hunting the animal's power into the camp.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Biesele (1993); not verbatim.

title.en: Dreams as Visits from the Dead
title.zh: 夢為亡者之訪

region.en: Nyae Nyae, Namibia (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 納米比亞尼亞尼亞（象徵定位）

period: Ju/'hoansi oral tradition; recorded 1950s-1970s by Lorna Marshall

source.work: Lorna Marshall, The !Kung of Nyae Nyae (1976); Lorna Marshall, Nyae Nyae !Kung Beliefs and Rites (1999)

summary.en: Dreams are taken literally: to dream of a dead kinsman is to be visited by his !Gauwasi, who may come in kindness or to shoot. The dreamer wakes the camp, tells the visit, and the healers check the sick list; dreams of !Gauwa himself foretell the deaths he is planning.
summary.zh: 夢境被視為實事：夢見亡親即其高瓦西來訪——或善或射。夢者醒而告營眾，醫者檢視病者名單；夢見高瓦本人者，預示其所謀之死。

sensitivity.note: Documented Ju/'hoan belief; paraphrase only.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase of Marshall (1976/1999); not verbatim. The Ju/'hoansi treat dreams as real events: the dead come in dreams because it is the way the !Gauwasi visit; a dream of a dead kinsman may mean he came in kindness, to look at his people, or that he has come to shoot someone in the camp.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Marshall (1976); not verbatim.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase, same works; not verbatim. A dream of !Gauwa is the gravest: he is said to sit counting his arrows in the dreamer's dream, and each arrow counted is a death he has decided on. In the morning the camp debates the dream, and the healers keep watch over the person the arrows seemed to point at.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Marshall (1976); not verbatim.

title.en: Naro Trickster Tales: The Dassie's Council
title.zh: 納羅詭計故事：蹄兔之議

region.en: Ghanzi district, Botswana (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 波札那甘茲區（象徵定位）

period: Naro (Central Kalahari) oral tradition; recorded 1980s-1990s, published in Guenther 1999

source.work: Mathias Guenther, Tricksters and Trancers: Bushman Religion and Society (1999); Guenther, The Naron Bushmen (1986 field corpus)

summary.en: In Naro storytelling the trickster world of Kaggen's descendants lives on: animal tales in which the weak outwit the strong — the dassie's council on the rock, the jackal's feints, the lion fooled at his own kill — carry the same message as the old myths: that the small, the hungry and the cunning survive in a world ruled by !Gauwa's arrows and the big game's whims.
summary.zh: 納羅敘事中，卡根後裔之詭計世界猶存：弱者智勝強者之獸故事——岩上蹄兔之議、豺之佯攻、獅受騙於己獲——承古神話之訊：在高瓦之箭與巨獸任性統治之世，唯小者、飢者、狡者得存。

sensitivity.note: Modern Naro oral tradition recorded with community collaboration; paraphrase only.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase of Guenther, Tricksters and Trancers (1999), chs. on Naro folklore; not verbatim. Naro animal tales continue the Kaggen cycle's logic: the trickster is small and vulnerable, and his tricks are responses to hunger and threat; the dassie's council on the rock, the jackal's endless feints, and the lion outwitted at his own kill all teach that the weak survive by cunning.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Guenther (1999); not verbatim.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase, same work; not verbatim. The trickster tales are told at night around the fire and are explicitly entertainment as well as instruction — a Naro speaker says the old stories and the new ones are the same talk, only the animals change; and behind them all stands the same dangerous world of !Gauwa and his arrows.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Guenther (1999); not verbatim.

title.en: Scaring the Ghost: Fire, Ash and the Widower
title.zh: 驅鬼之火：灰燼與鰥夫

region.en: !Kangwa, Botswana (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 波札那坎瓜（象徵定位）

period: Ju/'hoansi rite; documented 1963-1973 by Richard B. Lee

source.work: Richard B. Lee, The !Kung San (1979), ch. 9; Lorna Marshall (1976)

summary.en: After a death the widow or widower is smudged with ash and medicine smoke, the belongings of the dead are broken, and the camp lights fires at the path so the ghost will not follow the living home. The mourners call the formula that sends the !Gauwasi to !Gauwa's country, and the first nights are kept loud and bright.
summary.zh: 喪禮之後，以灰與藥煙熏寡婦鰥夫，碎毀亡者之物，於歸途燃火，使鬼不隨生者歸家。哀者誦送魂之辭，遣高瓦西赴高瓦之境；初夜喧亮不輟。

sensitivity.note: Documented Ju/'hoan mourning rite; paraphrase only.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase of Lee (1979), ch. 9; not verbatim. After the burial the dead person's hut and belongings are broken up and burned; the widowed spouse is smoked and rubbed with ash and medicines to drive off the spouse's ghost, which is thought to hover around and to be able to shoot the survivor with !Gauwa's arrows.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Lee (1979); not verbatim.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase of Marshall (1976); not verbatim. Fires are kept burning on the paths at night so the ghost will not follow the living home; the mourners wail the words that send the dead away to !Gauwa's country, and the camp keeps loud and bright for the first nights, for a quiet dark camp is where a ghost can walk.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Marshall (1976); not verbatim.

title.en: The Hare Reverses the Message (Katkop/Hottentot Version)
title.zh: 野兔逆轉訊息（卡茲科普／霍屯督版）

region.en: Katkop Mountains north of Calvinia, Northern Cape (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 南非北開普省卡茲科普山（象徵定位）

period: San oral tradition (Katkop dialect); recorded 1875 by !khusin (Bleek & Lloyd); English redaction in Honey 1910

source.work: W. H. I. Bleek, A Brief Account of Bushman Folk-lore (1875), §18; James A. Honey, South-African Folk-Tales (1910), 'The Origin of Death'

summary.en: In the messenger form of the myth the Moon sends the Hare to men with the message of the renewal of life; but the Hare reverses it into a message of death. The angered Moon heats a stone and burns the Hare's mouth, causing the harelip — the told-three-times Katkop version recorded by Bleek, and the English redaction printed by Honey.
summary.zh: 訊使版神話中，月遣野兔赴人類報『復生』之訊；野兔反轉為『死亡』之訊。月怒，燒石烙其口，兔唇由此而來——此為布萊克三度採錄之卡茲科普版，亦為霍尼1910年英譯所本。

sensitivity.note: The narrator !khusin's father was Hottentot; Bleek doubts whether this form is original Bushman. Flagged as a border-version of the origin-of-death cluster.

passages.text: The Moon, it is said, sent once an Insect to Men, saying, 'Go thou to Men, and tell them, As I die, and dying live, so ye shall also die, and dying live.' The Insect started with the message, but whilst on his way was overtaken by the Hare, who asked: 'On what errand art thou bound?'... With these words he ran off, and when he reached Men, he said, 'I am sent by the Moon to tell you, As I die, and dying perish, in the same manner ye shall also die and come wholly to an end.'
passages.note: Quote from James A. Honey, South-African Folk-Tales (1910), 'The Origin of Death' (public domain; the tale derives from Bleek 1875 §18).

passages.text: Then the Hare returned to the Moon, and told her what he had said to Men. The Moon reproached him angrily, saying, 'Darest thou tell the people a thing which I have not said?' With these words she took up a piece of wood, and struck him on the nose. Since that day the Hare's nose is slit.
passages.note: Quote from Honey (1910), public domain.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase of Bleek's summary (§18): the veritable Hottentot myth of the 'Origin of Death' is told in the Katkop dialect by !khusin, whose father was a Hottentot; although the narrator says he heard the story from his mother \xa-\kho, a Bushwoman, its Hottentot origin can hardly be doubted. Here the Moon sends the Hare to men with the message of the renewal of life, but it reverses it into a message of death; the angered Moon then heats a stone and burns the Hare's mouth, causing the harelip. !khusin told this story three times.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of A Brief Account of Bushman Folk-lore (Bleek 1875), §18; not verbatim.

title.en: Padmasambhava Tames the Demons of Tibet
title.zh: 蓮花生降伏吐蕃諸魔

region.en: The road of the Guru's march across Tibet (symbolic pin at Samye)
region.zh: 蓮師入藏之路（以桑耶寺為象徵定位）

period: Legendary life of Padmasambhava (Guru Rimpoche), 8th century; Waddell's summary 1895

source.work: L. A. Waddell, The Buddhism of Tibet or Lamaism (1895), ch. II-IV

summary.en: The Tibetans, beset on every side by malignant devils, warmly welcomed the Guru from Udyana as the bringer of deliverance: arriving in 747 AD he vanquished all the chief devils of the land, sparing most of them on their consenting to become defenders of his religion while he guaranteed that in return they would be duly worshipped and fed. His weapons were the vajra and spells extracted from the Mahayana gospels; his twenty-five disciples each performed a grotesque magical feat - mounting the sunbeams, driving iron bolts into rocks, reviving the slain, making water run upwards, taming wild yaks - and each was instructed in making magic circles for coercing demons and exorcism.
summary.zh: 吐蕃人四面受惡魔擾害，故熱烈歡迎來自鄔仗那的蓮花生大師，視之為解脫者。公元747年入藏後，他降伏境內諸大魔鬼——多數答應充當佛法護衛，大師則保證令其受供養享祭祀。其法器為金剛杵與《摩訶衍那》諸經之咒；二十五位弟子各顯神通：踏日而行、以鐵釘釘入巖石、令死者復生、使水逆流、馴服野犛牛……並各授結界鎮魔之術。

canonical_translation: L. A. Waddell, The Buddhism of Tibet or Lamaism, London 1895 (public domain)

narrative.en:
The founder of Lamaism, Saint Padma-sambhava, 'the Lotus-born one,' usually called by the Tibetans Guru Rimpoche or 'the precious Guru', was a native of Udyana, famed for the proficiency of its priests in sorcery, exorcism and magic: Hiuen Tsiang, writing a century previously, said of Udyana that the people practise the art of using charms and the employment of magical sentences is with them an art and a study. The Tibetans, steeped in superstition which beset them on every side by malignant devils, warmly welcomed the Guru as he brought them deliverance from their terrible tormentors.

Arriving in Tibet in 747 AD at the invitation of King Thi-Sron Detsan, he vanquished all the chief devils of the land, sparing most of them on their consenting to become defenders of his religion, while he on his part guaranteed that in return for such services they would be duly worshipped and fed. Thus, just as the Buddhists in India, in order to secure the support of the semi-aborigines of Bengal, admitted into their system the bloody Durga and other aboriginal demons, so on extending their doctrines throughout Asia they pandered to the popular taste by admitting within the pale of Buddhism the pantheon of those new nations they sought to convert. The Guru's most powerful weapons in warring with the demons were the Vajra (Tibetan, dor-je), symbolic of the thunderbolt of Indra, and spells extracted from the Mahayana gospels, by which he shattered his supernatural adversaries.

Under the zealous patronage of the King he built at Sam-yas in 749 AD the first Tibetan monastery, said to be modelled after the Indian Odantapura of Magadha and entitled the 'Self-sprung immovable shrine', believed to be based on immovable foundations of adamantine laid by the Guru; and there, assisted by the Indian monk Shanta-rakshita - made first abbot - he instituted the order of the Lamas. The leading events of his march through Tibet and his subjugation of the local devils indicate the original habitats of several of the pre-Lamaist demons; each of the demons of the indigenous Bon-pa religion was assigned its proper place in the Lamaist pantheon, and primitive Lamaism may be defined as a priestly mixture of Sivaite mysticism, magic and Indo-Tibetan demonolatry overlaid by a thin varnish of Mahayana Buddhism.

Padma-sambhava had twenty-five disciples, each credited with magical power, mostly of a grotesque character: Nam-k'a s'in-po mounted the sunbeams; San-gye-ye-se drove iron bolts into rocks; Gyal-wa-ch'og-yan changed his head into a horse's and neighed thrice; K'ar-ch'en Ch'o-gyal revived the slain; Pal-ki-ye-se overcame three fiendesses; Pal-ki-Sen-ge enslaved demons, nymphs and genii; Vairocana obtained the five heavenly eyes of knowledge; Dorje-Dun Jem travelled invisibly as the wind; Ye-se-Nan visited the fairy world; Shu-bu-pal-sen made water run upwards; Gyal-wai-Lodoi raised ghosts and converted the corpse into gold; Ten-pai-nam-k'a tamed wild yaks of the northern desert; 'Odan-Wan-p'yug dived into water like a fish; Ma-t'og rin-ch'en crushed adamant to powder and ate it like meal; Pal-kyi Dor-je passed through rocks and mountains; and Lan-dod Kon-ch'og wielded and repelled thunderbolts. And these disciples he instructed in the way of making magic circles for coercing the demons and for exorcism.

The Guru's departure from Tibet was as miraculous in character as his life: addressing the king he said that in Jambudvip were five Raksha countries crowded with men-eating devils who, if not conquered, would depopulate the whole world of Jambudvip, and except me none other can subdue them - thither must I now go. Accompanied by the king and nobles and his two fairy wives, he went to the Gung-thang La on the northern confines of Tibet, and there, after giving farewell advice to keep the doctrine and the revelations hidden in caves throughout the land, he was enveloped in a glorious rainbow-halo within which appeared the four great heroes of the world, who assisted him in mounting the celestial horse-car named Ialaha, in which he was borne away through the sky in a south-westerly direction amid heavenly music and showers of flowers. The assembled multitude remained transfixed as if dead, and after twenty-five days and nights could still see the Guru's celestial party, like a shooting star, sailing away through the sky till lost to sight. He reached Singala after about two days' journey, penetrating the iron palace, entered the body of the Raksha king named 'He of the Skull rosary', and preached the doctrine to the thousand daughters of the Raksha; at the capital Sando-pal-ri, abstracting the life of the demon-king Yaksha Me-wal and entering his body, the Guru reigns there supreme over the Rakshas even up till the present day, and in perpetual youth is preaching there the doctrine of Lamaism in a paradise which rivals that of Amitabha's western heaven of Sukhavati. And notwithstanding his grotesque charlatanism and uncelibate life, he is deified and worshipped as the 'second Buddha', his image under 'The eight worshipful Forms' found in every Tibetan temple of the old sect.
narrative.notes: Cultural function: the demon-taming legend is the charter of the Nyingma order and of the whole Tantric apparatus of Tibetan religion - every protective deity and every exorcistic rite traces itself to the Guru's bargain with the local gods, and the landscape of Tibet is mapped as the sequence of his subjugations.

functions: Charter of the Nyingma (Old School): the local demons of the Bon are converted into 'defenders of the faith' under contract of worship
Explains the Tibetan religious landscape: each demon's original habitat is remembered as a stage of the Guru's march
Authorizes exorcistic rites: the twenty-five disciples' feats and the magic circles are the pedigree of the sorcerer's craft
Establishes the terma doctrine - the revelations hidden in caves throughout the land, to be 'discovered' by later saints

variants.name: The legendary life of the Guru
variants.text_tradition: Padma bka'-thang and later Nyingma hagiographies
variants.summary: The full hagiographies add the princess Mandarava, a sister of Shanta-rakshita, whom the Guru married, and the birth-legend from a lotus; Waddell's summary here follows the standard compiled tradition.

variants.name: The historical view
variants.text_tradition: Rockhill's Life of the Buddha, ch. VII
variants.summary: Rockhill's sober account has Shantarakshita advising the king to invite Padma Sambhava of Udyana after his own teachings met opposition; the demon-taming belongs to the later legendary accretion.

primary_sources.citation: Tibetan Padma bka'-thang tradition; English summary L. A. Waddell, The Buddhism of Tibet or Lamaism, London 1895, ch. II-IV, pp. 25-33

secondary_sources.work: René de Nebesky-Wojkowitz, Oracles and Demons of Tibet
secondary_sources.citation: Nebesky-Wojkowitz 1956, The Hague - the demon classes tamed by the Guru in living ritual.

secondary_sources.work: Geoffrey Samuel, Civilized Shamans
secondary_sources.citation: Samuel 1993, Washington: Smithsonian - the tantric shamans' frame for the Padmasambhava cult.

secondary_sources.work: Kurtis R. Schaeffer, The Culture of the Book in Tibet
secondary_sources.citation: Schaeffer 2009, New York: Columbia - the terma ('rediscovered text') economy to which the Guru's hidden revelations gave rise.

source_urls.description: Internet Archive scan of Waddell, The Buddhism of Tibet or Lamaism (1895)

sensitivity_guidance: Padmasambhava is a living devotional centre of Tibetan Buddhism; passages below are paraphrases of the 1895 public-domain summary, not verbatim liturgy, and the tradition is treated respectfully.

sensitivity.note: Living devotional tradition; paraphrase of public-domain 1895 summary only. Waddell's own 'charlatanism' verdict is a colonial-era judgment, reported as part of the source's framing.
