title.en: Marduk Sends the Exorcist: Restoration
title.zh: 馬爾杜克遣驅邪師：復位

region.en: Nippur, Iraq
region.zh: 尼普魯（伊拉克）

period: Kassite period, c. 1400 BCE (Rogers translation 1912)

source.work: Cuneiform Parallels to the Old Testament, 'The So-called Babylonian Job', trans. Robert W. Rogers (1912)

summary.en: In dreams the answer comes: Marduk sends the exorcist who draws out the sickness, the smith who renews the body — and the sufferer is restored, office and household and praise. The lord of wisdom is praised: he turned my captivity.
summary.zh: 夢中得答：馬爾杜克遣驅邪師拔除病根、遣工匠重造軀體——受苦者官職、家室、讚譽盡復。智慧之主受頌讚：「他使我的被擄者歸回。」

sensitivity.note: Ancient wisdom literature; no living community restrictions.

passages.text: In dreams the answer comes: a young exorcist with a signet draws out the sickness root and branch; a smith restores the body as a smith restores a broken vessel — the dream-rite of Marduk's mercy. The restoration follows in fact: office, household and health return, and the closing hymn praises the lord of wisdom who turned the sufferer's captivity — the Babylonian Job ends in praise as it began.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ludlul, Tablets III-IV (Rogers 1912); not verbatim. / Paraphrase of Ludlul, Tablets III-IV; not verbatim.

functions: Dream-rite of divine cure
Arc of the theodicy liturgy: praise-abandonment-restoration-praise

title.en: The Prayer to Every God
title.zh: 告諸神禱文

region.en: Temple of purification, Babylon, Iraq
region.zh: 巴比倫淨化神殿（伊拉克）

period: Old Babylonian penitential psalm (Rogers translation 1912)

source.work: Cuneiform Parallels to the Old Testament, 'A Prayer to Every God', trans. Robert W. Rogers (1912)

summary.en: Has he vexed a god, despised a goddess, offended a father, slighted a mother? The penitent does not know his sin, so the prayer names every possibility to every god — the liturgy of the unknown transgression.
summary.zh: 「他是否觸怒男神？輕慢女神？冒犯父親？輕忽母親？」懺悔者不知己罪，遂向諸神一一歷數諸般可能——無知之罪的禱告儀式。

sensitivity.note: Ancient penitential text; no living community restrictions.

passages.text: Has he vexed a god, despised a goddess? Has he offended a father, slighted a mother? — the prayer names every possible sin because the penitent does not know his own. My god, my sins are seven times seven: forgive my unknown transgression, loose my fetters — the liturgy of the unknown sin, prayed to every god at once, that none be left unappeased.
passages.note: Paraphrase of the Prayer to Every God (Rogers 1912); not verbatim.

functions: Liturgy of the unknown transgression
Formulaic penitence of the purification rite

title.zh: 伊什塔爾頌

region.en: Uruk and Nineveh, Iraq
region.zh: 烏魯克與尼尼微（伊拉克）

source.work: Babylonian and Assyrian Literature, 'Hymn to Ishtar', trans. Muss-Arnolt (1901)

summary.en: The hymn hails the goddess in her double nature — the terror of battle whose heart is storm, the beauty whose grace fills the temples — she who turns men to women and women to men, whom kings and priests alike court.
summary.zh: 頌詩讚美女神的雙重本質——戰陣之怖，其心如暴風；聖殿之美，其恩寵盈殿——她能令男變女、女變男，君王與祭司皆傾慕之。

sensitivity.note: Ancient hymn; no living community restrictions.

passages.text: The hymn hails Ishtar in her double nature: the terror of battle whose heart is storm, and the beauty whose grace fills the temples — she who turns a man to a woman and a woman to a man. Kings and priests alike court her favor: she gives the throne and takes it, she leads the host and blesses the bed — the goddess of sovereignty and desire in one liturgy.
passages.note: Paraphrase of the Hymn to Ishtar (Muss-Arnolt 1901); not verbatim.

functions: Liturgical hymn of the goddess's double nature
Theology of sovereignty as the goddess's gift

title.en: The Accadian Penitential Psalm
title.zh: 阿卡德懺悔詩篇

region.en: Nippur, Iraq
region.zh: 尼普魯（伊拉克）

source.work: Babylonian and Assyrian Literature, 'An Accadian Penitential Psalm', trans. Muss-Arnolt (1901)

summary.en: The oldest bilingual psalm of contrition: the suppliant in the dark temple, his sin unknown, his tears his offering — O my god, my transgressions are great, my sins are seven times seven — the voice of Mesopotamian penitence.
summary.zh: 最古老的雙語懺悔詩篇：懺悔者立於幽暗神殿，己罪不明，以淚為祭——「吾神啊，吾過甚重，吾罪七倍於七」——美索不達米亞懺悔之聲。

sensitivity.note: Ancient penitential text; no living community restrictions.

passages.text: The suppliant in the dark temple has no offering but tears: O my god, my transgressions are great, my sins are seven times seven — the bilingual psalm of contrition, Sumerian and Akkadian together. The psalm's turn is hope: the god who punishes can spare — the merciful turning of the terrible god sought in the oldest prayer formulas of the land.
passages.note: Paraphrase of the Accadian Penitential Psalm (Muss-Arnolt 1901); not verbatim.

passages.text: Ereshkigal, the queen of the great earth, was dragged down as a bride and never came up; her house is described — the rivers of the dead, the walls without sun — and her power praised. The petition asks the queen for mercy for the dead of the household — the underworld given its own liturgy, the land below addressed as a kingdom with its own court.

title.en: Jo-wiis and the Origin of the Bird Dance
title.zh: 喬威斯與鳥舞之起源

region.en: Sky council house of the birds, and the Seneca council house at New Year
region.zh: 天空的群鳥議屋與新年時的塞內卡議屋

period: Converse (1908); Jo-wiis is regarded as the founder of the Eagle Society

source.work: H. M. Converse, Myths and Legends of the New York State Iroquois (1908), 'Ga-do-jih and Sa-go-da-oh, the Golden Eagle and the Hunter'

summary.en: The Ga-do-jih, the Golden Eagle of the far away heavens, is the Head Chief of all the birds; to his subchief Don-yon-do, the Bald Eagle, he has assigned the mountain tops of the earth land. Among the birds of prey is Sa-go-da-oh, the Hunting Vulture, whose obnoxious duty is to plunder in offensive places - but the law of Ga-do-jih is that the earth must be kept clean. One day in the long time ago, Jo-wiis, a young Indian lad, was lost in the woods, and had wept until nearly blinded; hungering and faint he had fallen on the river bank to die, when Don-yon-do discovered him, lifting him on his wings; when no one came for the fast dying boy, Sa-go-da-oh, whose talons were long and strong but whose heart was tender, bore him to Ga-do-jih in the sky, who nourished him and grew to love him. Ga-do-jih took Jo-wiis to the sky council house when the birds were celebrating the New Year, and taught him their dances, the bird songs and all the laws of the birds, especially the sacred law protecting their nests in the spring and sheltering them in the winter; also the corn and the grains, which must be shared with the feathered folk below. Returned under the great vulture's wing while the Seven Star Brothers danced the New Year dance over the council house, Jo-wiis related his experiences to his astonished listeners, and it was decided that he should teach the people the bird dances he had learned in the sky: by this legend the Iroquois know the origin of the Bird dance, the most prominent dance of the Iroquois.
summary.zh: 遠天的金鵰加多吉是百鳥的大首領；副首領白頭鵰當永東多受命鎮守群山之巔。猛禽中還有獵鷲薩戈達奧，乾著最不體面的活——在穢處拾荒；但加多吉的律法是：大地必須潔淨。遠古的一天，少年喬威斯在林中迷途，哭得目將盲，飢渴交加倒在河岸待死。白頭鵰把他托上翅膀；無人來救時，爪利心軟的獵鷲把他抱上天空交給加多吉，鵰王哺育他、寵愛他。群鳥議新年時，鵰王攜他入天上的議屋，教他鳥舞、鳥歌與百鳥律法——尤其是春護鳥巢、冬庇群鳥的聖律，還有必須與下方羽族分享的玉米與五穀。昂宿七兄弟正在議屋上空跳新年舞時，獵鷲馱他回到雪被下的大地；族人驚訝地聽他講述天上的經歷，決議由他把鳥舞教給眾人——易洛魁最盛大的鳥舞，由此傳世。

sensitivity.note: Converse 1908; public domain. The Bird dance (ga-ne-gwa-e) is the public exhibition of the Eagle Society; the sign of membership is a round spot of red paint on either cheek.

passages.text: The Ga-do-jih, the Golden Eagle of the far away heavens, is the Head Chief of all the birds. The Ga-do-jih never visits the earth, but employs many assistants upon whom he imposes various duties. To his subchief, Don-yon-do, the Bald Eagle, he has assigned the mountain tops of the earth land... From his retinue of servitors, Ga-do-jih has chosen many of the vulture family, whose obnoxious duties lead them to plunder in offensive places. But they are faithful in his service, for it is the law of Ga-do-jih that the earth must be kept clean. Yet these proud ravenous birds have tender hearts, and although their scavenger life leads them into base paths, Ga-do-jih does not deny them the pure air of the sky nor the clear waters of the earth.
passages.note: Verbatim from Converse 1908, pp. 69-70; not verbatim (OCR modernized).

passages.text: One day in the long time ago, Jo-wiis, a young Indian lad, was lost in the woods, and had wept until nearly blinded. For many days and nights the rain had flooded the forest, and Jo-wiis could not find his home path. In the black sky there was no sun or moon to guide him, and hungering and faint, he had fallen on the river bank to die, when Don-yon-do, who chanced to be flying across the earth, discovered him, and lifting him on his wings, flew in search of an Indian village... The rain continued to fall, and no one had come for the fast dying boy when Sa-go-da-oh, winging past in search of night prey, espied him and closing in his wings, dropped to the wet earth where the boy was lying. Though Sa-go-da-oh's talons were long and strong, his heart was tender, and gently lifting Jo-wiis, bore him to the village, but failing to find his home, took him to Ga-do-jih in the sky, who nourished him and grew to love him.
passages.note: Verbatim from Converse 1908, p. 70; not verbatim (OCR modernized).

passages.text: Ga-do-jih took Jo-wiis to the sky council house when the birds were celebrating the New Year, and taught him their dances; also to all the feasts throughout the year, teaching him the bird songs and all the laws of the birds, especially the sacred law protecting their nests in the spring and sheltering them in the winter. And he was shown the corn and the grains, which Ga-do-jih told him must be shared with the feathered folk below. All these laws he was enjoined to impart to his people when he should return to the earth... Earth was sleeping beneath her snow blanket when Jo-wiis returned. Her streams were frozen, and her forests silent save for the keen voice of the wind which wandered through their leafless loneliness. Seeing a light in the well remembered council house where the people were holding a feast Jo-wiis entered and related to his astonished listeners his experiences in the sky... it was decided that he should teach the people the bird dances he had learned in the sky, as also the songs the sky birds sing in their councils.
passages.note: Verbatim from Converse 1908, pp. 70-71; not verbatim (OCR modernized).

passages.text: By this legend, the Iroquois know the origin of Je-gi-yah-goh-o-a-noh, the Bird dance, which was brought by Jo-wiis from the land of the sky birds, and is the most prominent dance of the Iroquois. It is celebrated at their New Year feast, and during its performance the dancers imitate the motions of a bird, squatting low and moving their bodies and heads as if picking the grains of corn which have been scattered on the floor. This dance reminds the people of the law of Ga-do-jih, that the Indian must nourish and care for the birds in the winter as well as in the summer time.
passages.note: Verbatim from Converse 1908, p. 72; not verbatim (OCR modernized).

title.en: Ga-nus-quah and the Go-gon-sa: The Stone Giant and the First False Faces
title.zh: 石巨人加努斯誇與第一副假臼

region.en: Cave in the Alleghany mountains, and the basswood forests
region.zh: 阿利根尼山中的石穴與椴樹林

period: Converse (1908)

source.work: H. M. Converse, Myths and Legends of the New York State Iroquois (1908), 'Ga-nus-quah and Go-gon-sa, the Stone Giants and False Faces'

summary.en: Tall, fierce and hostile, they were a powerful tribe, the Stone Giants! Cannibals who would devour men, women and children, they threatened the annihilation of the Confederacy. The Shawnees have a legend of them: once gentle and hospitable, they migrated to the far northwest snow fields where the extreme cold 'froze away their humanity,' and they became 'men of icy hearts'; rolling in the sand to harden their flesh, their bodies became covered with scales which resisted the arrows of an enemy. When Tarenyawagon, Upholder of the Heavens, beheld the Iroquois' distress, he transformed himself to a stone giant, came down to the earth and united with their tribe; made their chief, he brandished his club high in the air - 'Now we will destroy the Iroquois, make a great feast of them' - and led them to hide in a deep hollow near a fort of the Onondagas; before day he scaled a high place above them and overwhelmed them with a great mass of rocks. Only one escaped, who fled to the Alleghany mountains, where he remained and grew in huge strength: Ga-nus-quah, the Depredator, vulnerable only on the bottom of his foot; to look upon his face would be instant death. It was the fate of a young hunter, a chief, blinded and bruised by hail, to seek shelter in the hollow of a great rock during a terrific storm - the cave of Ga-nus-quah. 'No human being has ever looked upon me. I kill with one glance... You came here for shelter; I will not turn you away. I will spare your life, which now is mine, but henceforth you must obey my commands... Whichever of these you meet on your way, do not pass until you have felled a strong tree and carved its image in the wood grain... Go, now, and teach the mankind people kindness, the brother goodness of all dumb things, and so win your way to live forever!' When the young hunter opened his eyes he was standing beside a basswood tree which gradually transformed to a great mask: it could see behind the stars, create storms and summon sunshine, knew the remedy for each disease, and could overpower Death - 'My tree, the basswood, is soft, and will transform for the molder... My tree wood is the life of the Go-gon-sa. Of all in the forest there is none other.' Many years he wandered carving go-gon-sa-so-oh, the false faces, from the basswood, learning the voices of all the forest trees; he who entered the cave a youth had become a bent old man, a giant in stature, when he reached his home and related his story - and became the founder of the False Face Company.
summary.zh: 身量高大、兇暴敵對——石巨人是一支強大的部族！食人的怪物吞噬男女老幼，幾乎滅絕五族同盟。肖尼人的傳說：他們昔日溫和好客，北遷雪原後嚴寒「凍去了人性」，成了「冰心之人」；滾沙硬身，體生鱗甲，箭矢難傷。當「擎天者」塔雷尼亞瓦岡見族人危殆，化身石巨人混入其族；被推為酋長後，他高舉木棒——「現在我們去誅滅易洛魁人，設人肉大宴」——領他們藏於奧農達加堡旁的深谷，黎明前登上高處，以巨岩崩落將其盡滅。僅一人逃入阿利根尼山的洞穴，長成巨力，是為掠奪者加努斯誇——只有腳底可傷，見其面者立死。一位少年酋長在冰雹中瞎眼受傷，誤入其岩穴。巨聲警告：「無人見過我的臉；我一眼殺人……你是來避難的，我不趕你走。我饒你一命，但從今你須聽命於我……路遇何物，須先伐一株強樹、在木紋中刻下它的形象……去教人類以仁慈，教他們待萬物如手足，如此方能永生！」少年睜眼時立在一株椴樹旁——樹漸化作一面巨假臼：能透視星後、興雲召日、知百病之方、能勝死亡。「我的樹是椴，質軟易化，木心多孔，日光可入……椴木就是假臼的生命，林中無出其右。」他成年累月地雕刻假臼、辨識群樹之音；入洞的少年歸鄉時已成偉岸老者——假臼社由此而立。

sensitivity.note: Converse 1908; public domain. Parker notes the proper word for medicine masks is the basswood, and that the mask must first be carved on the living tree with invocation and tobacco.

passages.text: Tall, fierce and hostile, they were a powerful tribe, the Stone Giants! They invaded the country of the Iroquois during the early days of the Confederation of the Five Nations, the Mohawks, Onondagas, Oneidas, Cayugas, and Senecas, who had sent their warriors against them only to be defeated, and they threatened the annihilation of the Confederacy. They were feared, not because of their prodigious size, but they were cannibals as well, and would devour men, women and children. The Shawnees have a legend of these Giants which describes them as at one time living in a peaceful state, and although powerful, were gentle, and hospitable in their intercourse with the neighboring tribes; but from some disturbing cause they became restless, abandoned their home, and migrated to the far northwest snow fields, where the extreme cold of the winters 'froze away their humanity,' and they became 'men of icy hearts.'... In the summer they would roll in the sand to harden their flesh, and their bodies became covered with scales which resisted the arrows of an enemy.
passages.note: Verbatim from Converse 1908, pp. 74-75; not verbatim (OCR modernized).

passages.text: The Iroquois were being rapidly depleted in their numbers when Tarenyawagon, Upholder of the Heavens, who had bestowed upon them their hunting grounds and fisheries, beholding their distress, determined to relieve them of the merciless invaders, and transforming himself to a stone giant, came down to the earth and united with their tribe. Wonderstruck at his marvelous display of power, they made him their chief; and he brandished his club high in the air, saying, 'Now we will destroy the Iroquois, make a great feast of them, and invite all the Stone Giants of the sky.' In pretense of this intention, the Sky Holder led them to a strong fort of the Onondagas where he bade them hide in a deep hollow in the valley and await the sunrise... But before day, he scaled a high place above them and overwhelmed them with a great mass of rocks. Only one escaped, who fled to the Alleghany mountains. There he secreted himself in a cave, where he remained and grew in huge strength, when he was transformed to the myth Giant, Ga-nus-quah.
passages.note: Verbatim from Converse 1908, pp. 75-76; not verbatim (OCR modernized).

passages.text: During a terrific storm, the young hunter, a chief, blinded and bruised by the hail which fell like sharp flints, and having lost the trail, sought shelter within the hollow of a great rock... suddenly the rock began to move, and from a far recess a strange sound approached him... During a pause in the weird harmony, the marveling young hunter heard a voice addressing him in a stentorian strain, saying: 'Young warrior, beware! You are in the cave of the Stone Giant, Ga-nus-quah! Close your eyes. No human being has ever looked upon me. I kill with one glance. Many have wandered into this cave; no one lives to leave it. You did not come to hunt me; you came here for shelter; I will not turn you away. I will spare your life, which now is mine, but henceforth you must obey my commands... Whichever of these you meet on your way, do not pass until you have felled a strong tree and carved its image in the wood grain. When you first strike the tree, if it speaks, it will be my voice urging you and you must go on with your task. When the trees were first set in their earth mold, each was given a voice... Go, now, and teach the mankind people kindness, the brother goodness of all dumb things, and so win your way to live forever!'
passages.note: Verbatim from Converse 1908, pp. 76-77; not verbatim (OCR modernized).

passages.text: When the young hunter opened his eyes, he was standing beside a basswood tree which gradually transformed to a great mask, and related to him its power. It could see behind the stars. It could create storms, and summon the sunshine. It empowered battles or weakened the forces at will. It knew the remedy for each disease, and could overpower Death. It knew all the poison roots and could repel their strong evils... The venomous reptiles knew its threat and crept from its path. It said: 'My tree, the basswood, is soft, and will transform for the molder. My tree wood is porous, and the sunlight can enter its darkness... My tree wood is the life of the Go-gon-sa. Of all in the forest there is none other.' With this knowledge, the young hunter started on his way carving go-gon-sa-so-oh (false faces). From the basswood he hewed them. By the voice of the Stone Giant he was guided to choose; and well he learned the voices of all the forest trees before he completed his task... Many years had passed in the laborious task, and he who entered the cave a youth, had become a bent old man when, burdened with the go-gon-sas he had carved, he set out on his return to his people. Year after year his burden had grown heavier, but his back broadened in strength, and he had become a giant in stature when he reached his home and related his story.
passages.note: Verbatim from Converse 1908, pp. 78-79; not verbatim (OCR modernized).

title.en: De-wan-do and the Flying Head: The Acorns That Were Coals
title.zh: 德萬多與飛首：被誤當橡實的炭火

region.en: Broad river and forest of the early Long House
region.zh: 長屋初立時的大河與森林

period: Converse (1908)

source.work: H. M. Converse, Myths and Legends of the New York State Iroquois (1908), 'Ko-nea-raw-neh, the Flying Heads'

summary.en: The Long House was new and the people were tranquil in its peace when they were terrorized by the visitations of the Flying Heads. These odious Heads were enveloped in long, fire-flaming hair which streamed to the wind in their flying, dazzling and blinding those who dared look at them; and armed with two great bearlike paws, which were ever in motion as if clutching at prey, they shot through the air like meteors. Feasts, invocations and incantations were of no avail; drums, rattles and loud screaming shouts gave forth no sound when the Heads appeared; arrows and spears would glance from their fiery hair, or break like a dead branch. One night at the sundown, De-wan-do, an Iroquois woman with her infant swung across her shoulders, was paddling her canoe across a broad river when a big face lifted from the water, whose flaming hair streaked the waves like serpents of fire. Pressing her infant close she sprang to the shore and fled, throwing it piece after piece of deer meat, her blanket, her doeskin dress, leggings, moccasins - until, despairing, she remembered the charm of an infant's moccasin to avert danger, and hastily removing one from her child's foot, threw it behind her: the Head stopped, and reeling and wandering as if blinded, fell to the ground. When it overtook her lodge, De-wan-do was roasting acorns at the hearth, drawing them away one by one and eating them as they burst their shells; the astonished Head, approaching behind her, wondered, for it thought she was eating the live coals. 'They must be good,' thought the Head, 'and I'll have my share'; and gathering the hot coals with its paws, thrust them into its mouth when, screaming in agony, it fled from the lodge in a great blaze of fire which drifted into the night. And the Head never returned: it is believed that the live coals it had mistaken for acorns burned it to death.
summary.zh: 長屋初成、萬民安泰之時，飛首降臨為禍。這些醜惡的頭顱裹著噴火的長髮，飛掠時灼人雙目；一雙巨熊般的掌爪時時開合，如攫獵物，流星般劃空而過。盛宴、祝禱、咒語都無濟於事；飛首現身時，鼓聲鈴響一齊喑啞，箭矛不是滑過火髮便是折斷如枯枝。一日黃昏，易洛魁婦人德萬多背著嬰兒划舟渡河，一張巨首自水面升起，火髮在波上如群蛇竄燃。她緊摟嬰兒躍上岸奔逃，一路拋下鹿肉、毯子、鹿皮衣、鞋襪——直到窮急之中想起嬰兒鞋能避邪，急忙脫下孩子的一隻小鞋拋在身後：飛首頓時止步，暈頭轉向跌倒在地。等它追到她的屋子，德萬多正在灶前炒橡實——一顆顆爆殼剝出就吃；跟在身後的飛首驚訝不已：它以為她在吃炭火。「這一定好吃，」它想，「我也得來一份」；便用掌爪捧起滾燙的炭塞進嘴裡——慘叫一聲，化成一團沖天的烈焰逃出屋去。飛首從此未再回來：據信它是被誤當橡實的炭火燒死了。

sensitivity.note: Converse 1908; public domain. In some myths the flying heads are false faces; the Mohawks instead of making the Stone Giant the founder credit the Flying Heads with being the original False Faces.

passages.text: The Long House was new and the people were tranquil in its peace when they were terrorized by the visitations of the Flying Heads. These odious Heads were enveloped in long, fire-flaming hair which streamed to the wind in their flying, dazzling and blinding those who dared look at them; and armed with two great bearlike paws, which were ever in motion as if clutching at prey, they shot through the air like meteors. When flying, these Heads were of enormous size, yet, upon the land or among the forest trees, they could become no larger than the head of a bear... but whether in the air or upon the land, there seemed no human power able to combat them, and the people fled in horror whenever they appeared.
passages.note: Verbatim from Converse 1908, p. 79; not verbatim (OCR modernized).

passages.text: Feasts, invocations and incantations were of no avail; drums, rattles and loud screaming shouts gave forth no sound when the Heads appeared, and they heeded them not. Arrows and spears would glance from their fiery hair, or break like a dead branch wind-blown from the tree, and there seemed no succor for the people... One night at the sundown, De-wan-do, an Iroquois woman, with her infant wrapped in a blanket and swung across her shoulders, was paddling her canoe across a broad river. She was hastening before the darkness should set in when, as she neared the shore, a long shadow swept across her canoe and a big face lifted from the water, a face whose flaming hair streaked the waves like serpents of fire and hissed to vapors the smooth-flowing river.
passages.note: Verbatim from Converse 1908, pp. 79-80; not verbatim (OCR modernized).

passages.text: Like all her people, De-wan-do knew the Flying Heads, and pressing her infant close to her breast, she sprang to the shore and ran to the forest... Looking back and seeing the Head following her, she threw it a piece of deer meat, which, as it stopped to devour it, delayed it for a time... through all the night she ran, still pursued by the Head... She threw it her blanket, in rage it tore it to fragments; then her doeskin dress, her leggings, moccasins, piece by piece all the clothes she wore... and the Head had nearly overtaken her when, despairing, she remembered the charm of an infant's moccasin to avert danger, and hastily removing one from her child's foot, threw it behind her. At its sight the Head stopped, and in rage beat the air with its great paws. In vain it tried to avoid the moccasin, and reeling and wandering as if blinded, fell to the ground.
passages.note: Verbatim from Converse 1908, p. 81; not verbatim (OCR modernized).

passages.text: But De-wan-do heard not. Suffering with hunger from her long fasting, she was at the hearth fire roasting acorns, while her infant lay sleeping near the fire. One by one as they burst their shells she drew them away and ate them, and the astonished Head, approaching behind her, wondered, for it thought she was eating the live coals. 'They must be good,' thought the Head, 'and I'll have my share'; and gathering the hot coals with its paws, thrust them into its mouth when, screaming in agony, it fled from the lodge in a great blaze of fire which drifted into the night! And the Head never returned. It is believed that the live coals it had mistaken for acorns burned it to death.
passages.note: Verbatim from Converse 1908, p. 81; not verbatim (OCR modernized).

title.en: The Face in the Water and the Origin of the Death Dance
title.zh: 水中之臉與死亡之舞的起源

region.en: Health-giving spring in the hollow of a rock, and the fires below
region.zh: 岩穴中的治病靈泉與地下之火

period: Converse (1908)

source.work: H. M. Converse, Myths and Legends of the New York State Iroquois (1908), 'The Face in the Water and the Death Dance'

summary.en: In the hollow of a rock in a forest was a health-giving spring known to all red men. This spring, which possessed mysterious power, was protected by two spirits: from sunrise to noon, Oh-swe-da, spirit of the spruce tree, was its guardian, and this was its 'charm time'; but after the noon, when the shadows slanted across it and Och-do-ah, the Bat, had entered the rock, the spring became a baneful poison, sudden or lingering, as Och-do-ah might will. Ah-ne-ah, Rose Flower, went to the spring to weave sweet-smelling grasses into baskets, singing the firefly song, and did not see the noon nearing: as she held her elm bowl to the gurgling water, it seemed never to fill, and she saw there a face more beautiful than any she had ever beheld, smiling and nodding at her - and the threatening shadow entered the spring, and something suddenly seized her and bore her upward far from the forest, plunged down its cataract to a wide water, and led her down below the earth to a place glaring as with flames where numberless people were dancing carelessly - among them some of her own people who had died years before, appealing to her for pity as they moaned 'don-de-gwan-de, don-de-gwan-de' (pity us, pity us). Doomed to the fire dance, she felt herself blind and dying, when she seemed to breathe a new air, life restoring and fragrant of pines of the woodland, and opening her eyes it was sunrise and she stood by the spring! Beside her was a young warrior with an owl wing and an eagle wing, the face that had smiled to her from the spring - Oh-swe-da, who had welcomed her only to warn: Och-do-ah, the Bat, poisons the spring water when the sun turns away, and had sent one of his helpers to take her to the fires below where the witches were dancing the death dance; he had snatched her from the witch fire - but the penalty for lingering too late at the spring must be paid. Soon after a pestilence came to her people, and day by day the beautiful Ah-ne-ah was fading away, until one summer morning at the vanishing of the dew Ah-ne-ah disappeared: by the side of her couch were two fallen feathers, one of the owl, the other an eagle. But the faithful Ah-ne-ah had related to her people the terrible story of the witch fire, and taught them its dance which could no more destroy them: thus originated the Oh-gi-we, the Death dance of the Iroquois, one of the rites of their Death watch which releases a departed spirit from the evil influences of the witches.
summary.zh: 林中岩穴裡有一泓紅人皆知的治病靈泉。泉有二靈守護：自日出至正午，雲杉之靈奧斯維達司泉，是為「靈驗之時」；正午過後，陰影斜罩、蝙蝠奧克多阿入岩，泉水便成了致死的毒——速死或緩死，全憑奧克多阿之意。「玫瑰花」阿內阿去泉邊編織香草籃、唱著流螢之歌，不覺日已近午：她把榆木碗伸向汩汩泉水，水卻總也盛不滿——她看見水中有一張前所未見的美麗面孔，含笑向她點頭。威脅的暗影罩入泉中，微笑隱沒；有物猛然抓住她，凌空帶她遠離森林，俯衝過瀑落入闊水，再引她下行地底——一片火光之地，無數人在那裡漫不經心地起舞，其中竟有她族中死去多年的故人，哀號著「可憐我們，可憐我們」。她被判入火舞，眼將盲、命將絕，忽然吸到一股新氣——松林般復甦的芬芳——睜眼時已日出，她立在泉邊！身旁立著一位獵人裝束的少年戰士，一翼鴞、一翼鵰——正是泉中含笑的那張臉：雲杉之靈奧斯維達，他迎接她只為示警——太陽偏轉時蝙蝠便毒化泉水，且已遣使者要把她送往下界巫火中跳死亡之舞；他把她從巫火中奪回——但遲留泉邊的代價必須償還。不久瘟疫降於其族，美麗的阿內阿日漸枯萎，一個夏晨露散之時悄然消失——榻旁只剩兩根落羽，一根鴞羽、一根鵰羽。但她已把巫火的可怕故事與那支舞教給族人——自那時起，巫火再不能害他們。易洛魁的死亡之舞「奧吉威」由此起源：那是他們「守喪」儀式中的一支，為亡者之靈解除巫者邪力的束縛。

sensitivity.note: Converse 1908; public domain. The Oh-gi-we is a society with regular leaders and fixed rites, sometimes called the 'Talkers with the Dead.'

passages.text: In the hollow of a rock in a forest, was a health-giving spring known to all red men. This spring, which possessed mysterious power, was protected by two spirits. From sunrise to noon, Oh-swe-da, spirit of the spruce tree, was its guardian, and this was its 'charm time'; but after the noon, when 'the shadows slanted across it' and Och-do-ah, the Bat, had entered the rock, the spring became a baneful poison, sudden or lingering, as Och-do-ah might will. No mortal should near it for healing when Och-do-ah was coming all things to drink of its death.
passages.note: Verbatim from Converse 1908, pp. 81-82; not verbatim (OCR modernized).

passages.text: Ah-ne-ah, Rose Flower, who had gone to the spring in quest of its water, was weaving the sweet-smelling grasses into baskets and singing the firefly song as she braided the strands to its tune, and, as happy as she was beautiful, had not seen the noon nearing the spring... As she held her elm bowl to the gurgling water, it seemed never to fill, and she saw there a face more beautiful than any she had ever beheld; and the face was smiling and nodding at her as it floated from side to side of the spring, as if coaxing... As she wondering gazed, the threatening shadow entered the spring, and when the smiling face vanished, something suddenly seized her and bore her upward far from the forest and, as with wings, so swiftly flying, the wind which seemed following lagged far behind them. Then hurrying to the earth below, they crossed a broad river and plunged down its cataract to a wide water, which raged in a fury of confusion.
passages.note: Verbatim from Converse 1908, p. 82; not verbatim (OCR modernized).

passages.text: There again was the face, which led her down below the earth to a place glaring as with flames and where numberless people were dancing, carelessly dancing, and among the vast multitude passing, were some of her own people who had died years before, and who appealed to her for pity as they moaned, 'don-de-gwan-de, don-de-gwan-de' (pity us, pity us). Helpless and dumb in her terror, some monster pushed her into the circle of dancers where, doomed to the fire dance, she felt herself blind and dying, when she seemed to breathe a new air, life restoring and fragrant of pines of the woodland, and as she opened her eyes it was sunrise and she stood by the spring!
passages.note: Verbatim from Converse 1908, pp. 82-83; not verbatim (OCR modernized).

passages.text: By her side was a young warrior robed as the hunter robes for the hunt... on his head were two wings, one of the owl, the other an eagle... as Ah-ne-ah looked into his eyes she beheld the face that had smiled to her from the spring! The owl and eagle-winged warrior took her hand, and as he gently led her to the edge of the forest, related to her the mystery of her strange night journey. He was Oh-swe-da, the Spirit of the Spruce, and guarded the spring from the sunrise to its noon... Och-do-ah, the Bat, was hovering in the shadow which was so near, and Och-do-ah would destroy. He poisoned the spring water when the sun turned away... But Oh-swe-da was freed from the spring, and followed to her rescue. He had snatched her from the witch fire, and now she was here! But the penalty for lingering too late at the spring must be paid - Och-do-ah would have his prey. She had escaped him, but was doomed!... Soon after, there came a pestilence to her people, and a famine was upon them. Hundreds fell victims to an epidemic, and day by day the beautiful Ah-ne-ah was fading away, until one summer morning at the vanishing of the dew Ah-ne-ah disappeared... But by the side of her couch were two fallen feathers, one of the owl, the other an eagle! But the faithful Ah-ne-ah had related to her people the terrible story of the witch fire, and taught them its dance which could no more destroy them. Thus originated the Oh-gi-we, the Death dance of the Iroquois, one of the rites of their Death watch which releases a departed spirit from the evil influences of the witches.
passages.note: Verbatim from Converse 1908, pp. 83-84; not verbatim (OCR modernized).

title.en: Ton-da-yent, the Twelve Warriors and the White Rabbit
title.zh: 通達揚特：十二戰士與白兔

region.en: Burial ground of the war chief, with the young pine planted above him
region.zh: 戰酋墓塚與其上的幼松

period: Converse (1908)

source.work: H. M. Converse, Myths and Legends of the New York State Iroquois (1908), 'Ton-da-yent, the Twelve Warriors and the White Rabbit'

summary.en: In his youth he had been evil, but when grown to manhood, he had conquered his bad and becoming a warrior had won great victories for his people. Now he had passed from his people, the Ton-da-yent, the war chief! The wailers had wept, the death song had been chanted, the war paint lined his strong face, and they had crowned him with the heron feathers, the Iroquois emblem of power; in his hands they laid his stone scalping knife and war club, and robed in deerskin, his dead body waited the sunrise. When the sun neared the east sky, they wrapped the dead warrior in the bark of the elm and lowered it into the earth, and an aged priestess, Mo-non-di-ont, scattered small lumps of clay above him, to propitiate the elements, earth, air and water, through which his spirit must journey to its rest; at twilight they planted above him a young pine. A council of condolence was called at which his successor would be named, when an unknown person appeared, claiming to be the twin brother of the dead chief and demanding that he be given his name by right of twin succession - the people marveled greatly at the wonderful resemblance he bore to the dead chief, and save a glowering fire which lurked in the glance of his eye, it seemed indeed that the Ton-da-yent had returned, and the council did not hesitate to grant his request.
summary.zh: 他年少時曾經為惡，成年後卻戰勝了心魔，成為屢建戰功的戰士。如今他離開了族人——這就是戰爭大酋長通達揚特！哀哭者泣、喪歌已唱，戰紋描上他剛毅的面孔，蒼鷺羽冠——易洛魁權力的徽記——加於其頂；他手中放置石質剝皮刀與戰棒，鹿皮裹身，靜候日出。旭日將升之際，他們以榆樹皮裹屍入土；年邁的女祭司莫農迪昂特在其上撒下小塊黏土，取悅其魂必經的土、氣、水三行；暮色中又在其上植下一株幼松——通達揚特是勇士，過路人該知道他長眠於此。哀悼議會召開、將立繼任人之際，一個陌生人現身，自稱是亡酋的孿生兄弟，要求依「孿生繼承」之權承其名——族人驚異於他與亡者的酷似；除了他眼中潛藏的一團怒火，儼然就是通達揚特歸來。議會毫不遲疑地允其所請。

title.en: Two Feathers and Turkey Brother: The Impostor in the Hollow Tree
title.zh: 雙羽與火雞弟：空心樹裡的冒名者

region.en: Trail to the great chief's village beyond the river, Seneca country

source.archive: Internet Archive (Buffalo Historical Society Publications, vol. 27)

summary.en: Two Feathers receives his dream-protectors - a great spider and a great black snake - and from his uncle's treasure chest the panther-skin costume whose heron feathers watch, whose fisher-skin bag bites, whose pipe-bear growls, and whose medicine root lets him spit wampum. Warned of three enchanted spots, he nonetheless helps a boy at the oak (the sorcerer's wife is knocked into her own fire), drains three monsters from the poisoned spring and burns them - screech-owls fly from their bursting heads - and then, despite every warning, shoots the old man's raccoon, strips off his magic clothes and climbs after it into the hollow tree. The treacherous uncle shoves him down among the bones, dons the magic costume, woos the chief's daughter across the river and marries her. Two Feathers is rescued by spider and snake, appears at the lodge looking like a sick old man in dirty clothes, eats the marriage bread, regains his wampum root when the impostor's bag bites him, and outdoes him bowl for bowl - dark wampum for lizards and toads, white wampum for round worms. When the gluttonous impostor finally sleeps, Two Feathers kills a great herd of deer, dons his magic suit which brightens as it touches him, and grows young; the council sees the costume's powers, the false husband is kicked into the garbage hole, and all the people follow the hero home.
summary.zh: 雙羽得夢中護靈——大蜘蛛與大黑蛇；又自叔父的百寶箱得到豹皮神裝：鴺羽守望、魚貂袋噬敵、熊頭菸斗低吼、藥根吐貝珠。雖被警告三處魔地，他仍助樹下男孩（巫婆被推入自焚）、放盡毒泉的三頭怪物焚之（怪首爆裂飛出啼鴞），卻不聽勸阻射了老翁的浣熊、脫下神衣攀樹入洞。老巫把他推落枯骨之間，披上神裝渡河娶走大酋長之女。蜘蛛與黑蛇救出雙羽；他以襤褸老翁之貌赴宴成婚，趁冒名者被魚貂咬傷之際拾回藥根，一碗吐出烏貝珠勝其蜥蟾蛆蟲，再一碗白貝珠勝其圓蟲。饕餮的冒名者爛醉睡死，雙羽獵鹿成群、披上神衣煥然一新、重返青春。議會上神裝顯靈，假婿被踢入垃圾洞，全族隨英雄凱旋。

sensitivity.note: Seneca tale (Parker 1923); public domain. The spitting-wampum motif is Parker's signature of Seneca magic.

passages.text: On the tenth day of his fast Two Feathers saw a great spider dropping down from the tops of the trees, and it spoke to him saying, 'When you are in great distress I will be your protector.' Again he saw a great black snake rising from the ground and when it had reached the tops of the trees it spoke saying, 'When you are in great distress and need a strong friend, I will be your protector.' His uncle then opened his treasure chest and gave him, after rejecting two costumes, a panther-skin shirt with the head of the panther as a cap and two heron feathers above it. 'The heron feathers on your hood will watch out for you and when you are in danger they will speak. Your fisher skin bag is alive and should anyone seek to harm you when asleep it will bite him... The medicine will give you power to spit wampum. The black end of the root will make dark wampum and the white end will make white wampum. Your pipe has the head of a bear upon it and it will growl when an enemy touches it, while the snakes on the bowl will hiss when you light your tobacco.'
passages.note: Condensed from Parker 1923, pp. 173-175; not verbatim.

passages.text: 'As you journey from here you will find three enchanted spots, and all must be avoided... a certain tree where there will be a boy playing about. He will ask you to lift him from the ground... do not touch the boy for a sorcerer lives in the tree... a deep spring where there is sparkling water... there are monsters living in it who will draw you in and drown you... a grove of very tall trees. Here you will see an old man who will hop around strangely. He will ask you to shoot a raccoon... He will be the cause of your ruin if you heed his pleas.' They traveled very rapidly, until by noon they had traveled a distance that takes ordinary people three years to go. At the oak Two Feathers placed the boy on a stump under the tree, and as he did this there was a great roar and two gigantic arms came down and grabbed the stump, fixing it to the tip of a large arrow; the stump flew through the air into the witch's lodge and knocked her into the fire.
passages.note: Condensed from Parker 1923, pp. 175-177; not verbatim.

passages.text: At the bubbling spring Three monsters leaped from the water and were dragged out and burned, their heads bursting with shrieks as a flock of screech-owls flew away - the clearing had been a prosperous village whose people the sorcerers had poisoned by dragging them into the depths of the water. At the tall trees the old man cried, 'Oh my nephews, there is a raccoon on that branch and I have no bow or arrow.' Two Feathers would not listen to Turkey, who flew about gobbling, and shot the raccoon - which ran down a large hole at the top of the tree. 'Oh my nephew, climb after it for me. Take it off beneath the tree and I will watch it for you.' Up he went like a squirrel, but as he stood looking down into the hole the old man shoved him in, down into a pit beneath the roots where he smelt the flesh of victims and felt their bones beneath his feet.
passages.note: Condensed from Parker 1923, pp. 177-178; not verbatim.

passages.text: The old man went to the clothing Two Feathers had left behind: 'Now I shall be able to cross the river and take the great man's daughter as my wife.' Renewed in body and more handsome with every step, he wooed the elder sister, ate the wedding bread and was married. Two Feathers called his friend Spider, who let down a strand of web that broke and dropped him, then his friend Black Snake, who coiled about him and drew him forth. In the dirty clothing left by the old man he looked like a sick old man, and the girl ferried him across, declaring, 'I am the only girl whom you can marry.' At supper the impostor reached into his bag and cried out, for the fisher bit his wrist; in dropping the bag the magic medicine fell out, and Two Feathers grabbed it and hid it in his bosom. In the morning he filled a bark bowl with dark wampum to the brim, while the impostor's emetic produced lizards, toads and worms; a second bowl of white wampum beat round worms. At last the gluttonous impostor slept, and Two Feathers dragged a great quantity of deer to the lodge and put on his own fine clothing - immediately it became bright and new, and he grew young again. His wife kicked the impostor out of bed, made him put on his old clothes and thrust him into the garbage hole, and nobody ever saw him again.
passages.note: Condensed from Parker 1923, pp. 179-183; not verbatim.

title.en: Two Feathers and Woodchuck Leggings: The Death Charm and the White Eagle
title.zh: 雙羽與土撥鼠綁腿：死亡咒物與白鵰

region.en: Do'ciowe' and the Valley of the Pleasant River (Ganundaseg), Seneca country
region.zh: 塞內卡之地的多喬維與樂河之谷

period: Related by George D. Jimerson (Tahadondeh), 1903 (Parker 1923)

source.archive: Internet Archive (Buffalo Historical Society Publications, vol. 27)
source.work: A. C. Parker, Seneca Myths and Folk Tales, ch. VI tale 22, 'Two Feathers and Woodchuck Leggings' (1923)

summary.en: Two Feathers, kind to the animals he can talk to, receives the powerful arrow of an old man in a bark house, and wins the love of Drooping Flower: 'something went out of his eyes into her eyes, and something went out of her eyes into his.' When famine strikes the valley village he sings a magic song and shoots four arrows into the air - 'Bring me meat from different animals' - and a deer, a moose, an elk and a bear run singing to the lodge and drop dead at his feet; he blows a stream of wampum beads over a tanned skin and the starving village feasts. The jealous uncle Woodchuck Leggings allies with the girl's witch mother, whose dream-demands he must satisfy: the antlers of the two great elk of the cold lake (shot in darkness, the arrow flashing light to reveal them), the shell-coated pelts of the wampum deer, two white beavers of the hot lake - and each gift only increases her rage. Then, camped by the fire, Woodchuck Leggings plunges the death charm of hickory bark between Two Feathers' shoulders, dons his white clothes and fails every test of the costume - his birds bashful, his pouch limp, his breath breathing out loathly worms - and marries instead the pitying sister Wiaso'. The forest animals Two Feathers has befriended nourish him with their blood; a year later the crippled 'Old-Bones-with-a-cough' wins the tournament by bringing down the great white eagle with a single spoken arrow, the stranger who suggests they ask him is his friend the wolf, the arrow clings to his finger, and in the sweat lodge of fat bear skins he pulls the charm from his neck and kills Woodchuck Leggings with it. His ruined suit restores as it touches him; the witch mother, revealed, chews off her own fingers and vanishes down the dog-tracks to a pond with neither inlet nor outlet.
summary.zh: 雙羽善待能與之對話的百獸，得老翁所贈的神箭，贏得「垂花」的愛：『他眼中有光渡入她眼中，她眼中的光也渡入他眼中。』河谷村鬧饑荒時，他唱咒歌、朝天連射四箭——「把不同野獸的肉帶給我」——鹿、駝鹿、麋與熊唱著歌奔至門前倒斃；他朝獸皮吐出貝珠雨，全村得以飽餐。妒忌的叔父土撥鼠綁腿勾結巫婆岳母，其夢索屢屢加碼：寒湖雙巨麋之角（黑暗中箭光閃亮照出）、貝殼鹿之皮、熱湖白河狸——禮物愈貴重，巫婆愈怒。營火之側，土撥鼠綁腿把山核桃皮死亡咒物刺入雙羽肩胛，穿上白衣，卻樣樣失靈——鳥兒害羞、袋子癱軟、吐出的是蠕蟲——轉而娶了憐惜他的姐姐。雙羽受他善待過的群獸以血哺之；一年後，跛咳的「老骨咳」以一支言出法隨的神箭射落白鵰奪魁——提議「去問咳嗽老人」的陌生人正是他救過的狼。箭應指而懸，熊脂汗屋中他拔出頸後咒物，反手擊斃土撥鼠綁腿。破舊的神衣觸體復新；巫婆原形畢露，自噬其指，化犬遁入無出無入的池塘。

sensitivity.note: Seneca tale (Jimerson informant 1903, Parker 1923); public domain. Parker's note: Edward Cornplanter criticized the version's Christian-informant details but approved it for white readers.

passages.text: Two Feathers was a hunter and never feared to hunt any animal, but he was kind to the animals and could talk to them, so they became his friends. He had a pet bear in a small yard and he had a wolf that he had tamed. He said that it was the same as a man... He had fine clothes. They were made of white buckskin and embroidered all over with porcupine quills. He had also a tobacco pouch made of a spotted fawn's skin with the feet and head on and in this he kept a pipe having a bear's head carved on it, and eyes that rolled when the jaws of the bear chewed the tobacco inside. He had a gustoh'we' (feathered hat), with two feathers in front, and on the hat there were two chirping birds. Two Feathers acquired magic and became very strong, but he did not let anyone know that he was Hotci'non'ga', a charm holder. 'I have been looking for you a long time,' said the old man in the bark house. 'You have been merciful to me and I am going to give you my arrow. It does not look like a good arrow, but most truly it has great power.'
passages.note: Condensed from Parker 1923, pp. 184-185; not verbatim.

passages.text: He noticed two girls, one older and one younger, named Drooping Flower. He looked at the younger girl and she looked at him, and something went out of his eyes into her eyes, and something went out of her eyes into his. He said to himself, 'That's the one.' One of the villagers saw this and told Two Feathers that he was now under the spell of a very evil witch, the mother of the girl... A runner came to the village and told them that all the people in the valley across the river were starving: hunters had been unable to secure game and the corn harvest had failed. Two Feathers asked all the women who could to gather about their doorways and play the plum-stone game and to sing: 'Ganio daweeni, the game is coming.' He then went into the woods at the edge of the clearing and sang a magic song, taking out four arrows which had lain close to the arrow the old man had given him. One by one he shot the arrows into the air, each in a different direction, at the same time calling, 'Bring me meat from different animals.'... there was a song in the air: 'The wild animals are coming.' Four animals came running to the doorway where Two Feathers sat waiting. Each animal had an arrow sticking in its heart: a deer, a moose, an elk and a bear.
passages.note: Condensed from Parker 1923, pp. 185-186; not verbatim.

passages.text: The starving village then had food and Drooping Flower recovered... He began to make a noise like 'tsiit, tsut, tsit.' Opening his mouth wide he blew out a great stream of wampum beads. Immediately there was a scramble for the beads and nearly everybody grabbed a handful. As Two Feathers left the house he saw the jealous, blazing eyes of his uncle, Woodchuck Leggings... That night Two Feathers and Woodchuck Leggings slept on one side of the witch's lodge. Midnight came and the old woman began to have a bad dream... 'I have had a dream and must be satisfied. Oh I must have the antlers of two large buck elk that live in a cold lake. I must have them by morning or direful things will happen.'... Long he swam into the darkness, for there was no starlight or moon. Taking his arrow from an oiled skin bag he spoke to it and then shot. There was a great flash of light in the sky and the mysterious lake elk were revealed. The arrow had pierced both of them... 'I am sorry I had to kill you, but the woman desired it in satisfaction of a dream.' The elks spoke again, 'The woman has deceived you.' The gift of the great antlers only increased the old woman's anger: next the pelts of the wampum-coated deer, then two white beavers of the hot lake - 'You may have the meat, but I will keep the skins' - and each gift only made her more angry.
passages.note: Condensed from Parker 1923, pp. 187-190; not verbatim.

passages.text: The crafty old scoundrel watched his opportunity. When Two Feathers was fast asleep, he made his way stealthily to the other side of the fire and drew from his shirt a long sharp point of hickory bark. It was the death charm. Kneeling at his back he lifted the bark high above his head and brought it down with all his strength, plunging it into the back of his victim just between the shoulders. Removing his own dirty garments, Woodchuck Leggings replaced them with the beautiful white clothes of Two Feathers... 'Here comes Two Feathers!'... 'You are not real Two Feathers,' she exclaimed. 'Where is Two Feathers?' 'I am he!' 'Sonohweh! You are a liar!'... he called the council, but his birds were bashful and his commands were in vain; the foul fumes filled the lodge and nearly stifled the people; the pouch clung to his side limper than ever; from his mouth flew a quantity of small white cylinders - clusters of loathly worms... Two Feathers awoke after several days' unconsciousness and found a great herd of forest animals about him. 'Our brother, you have been sick,' said the wolf, the spokesman. 'You were stabbed by Woodchuck Leggings as you were sleeping. But as you were kind, so we are not ungrateful and our blood has kept you nourished while you slept.'... 'Old-Bones-with-a-cough' touched the arrow, it clung to his finger and followed his hand into the air... With a loud cry Two Feathers pulled the bark point from his neck and before the cringing man before him had time to utter a sound, Two Feathers struck him a heavy blow over the neck. The death charm sank into the flesh, passed between the bones in his back and Woodchuck Leggings lay dead... Only tracks of a big dog could be seen leading from the lodge. They were traced to a pond which had neither inlet nor outlet, and there they stopped. It was found out she had been a witch.
passages.note: Condensed from Parker 1923, pp. 190-199; not verbatim.

title.en: Antediluvian Kings and the Flood
title.zh: 洪水前諸王與大洪水

region.en: The five antediluvian cities, Iraq
region.zh: 洪水前五城（伊拉克）

period: Sumerian King List tradition and Berossus, c. 290 BCE as preserved in George Smith 1876

source.work: The Chaldean Account of Genesis, ch. on Berossus and the antediluvian kings, George Smith (1876)

summary.en: Ten kings reigned before the flood, each for tens of sars — 432,000 years in Berossus' sum — the first at Eridu; then the flood swept them, and kingship began again from Kish: history framed between two descents of kingship from heaven.
summary.zh: 洪水前有十王，各在位數以萬年——貝羅蘇斯總計四十三萬二千年——首位建都埃利都；洪水掃盡其後，王權復自基什而始：歷史框於兩次王權天降之間。

sensitivity.note: Ancient chronicle tradition; no living community restrictions.

passages.text: Ten kings reigned before the flood, the first at Eridu, each for reigns counted in sars — 432,000 years in Berossus' sum — until the flood swept them away. After the flood kingship descended again, to Kish, and history ran between two descents of kingship from heaven — the frame that all Mesopotamian chronology kept.

title.zh: 俄安內斯：魚身導師

region.zh: 波斯灣海岸（象徵性定位）

summary.en: In the first year there came out of the Erythraean sea a monster named Oannes, the body of a fish with a man's head beneath — and he taught men letters, arts and the building of temples: the culture-hero of civilization rising from the sea.
summary.zh: 首年，海中出現名為俄安內斯的怪物：魚身而有人首，於魚腹之下——教人文字、技藝與建殿之法：文明源於滄海的文化英雄。

sensitivity.note: Hellenistic retelling; no living community restrictions.

passages.text: In the first year there came out of the Erythraean sea a monster named Oannes: the body of a fish, and beneath the fish's head a man's head, and a man's voice — the composite image of the wisdom from the deep. He taught men letters, arts, laws and the building of temples, and at sunset he returned to the sea and passed the night in the deep — civilization's teacher rising daily from the water that had birthed the world.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Berossus' account of Oannes as given in George Smith (1876); not verbatim. / Paraphrase of Berossus' account (Smith 1876); not verbatim.

summary.zh: 新年之際，國王代神而立、祭司代女神而立：神殿寢室中的結合保障來年豐饒——伊南娜與杜穆茲情歌即此儀式之禮文。

passages.text: On the New Year the king takes the god's place and the priestess the goddess's: the union performed in the temple bedchamber secures the year's abundance. The love songs of Inanna and Dumuzi are the rite's liturgy: the bride-goddess claimed, the bed blessed with cedar oil, the city renewed by the annual performance.

title.en: How Turkey Boy Squeezed the Hearts of a Sorcerer and His Seven Sisters
title.zh: 火雞童捏心記：巫師與其七姊妹之亡

region.en: Lonely lodge of the old grandmother, and the strawberry clearing to the east
region.zh: 老祖母的孤屋與東方草莓林間空地

period: Recorded 1900s-1922, Seneca informants (Parker 1923)

source.archive: Internet Archive (Buffalo Historical Society Publications, vol. 27)
source.work: A. C. Parker, Seneca Myths and Folk Tales, ch. VI tale 23, 'Turkey Boy Squeezed the Hearts of Sorcerers' (1923)

summary.en: An old woman and her grandson Turkey live alone in an old lodge, all their people killed by the monster wizard Deadoehdjadse' who lives to the east near a bed of strawberries as large as hearts. In the forbidden room Turkey finds the drum and the lacrosse ball, and learns the secret from Skin Man, the dried human skin swinging on a pole: he borrows a mole's coat, burrows underground, buys the mysteries with wampum beads stained with berry juice, and learns that the lives of the sorcerer and his seven sisters are secure, their hearts being concealed under the wing of a loon that swims in a pool under a bed in the lodge. Made up to look exactly like Deadoehdjadse' and chewing a strawberry, he eats the human flesh his sisters set before him, then - when Skin Man cries that the deer are in the strawberries - lifts the bed, commands the loon, grabs the eight hearts and runs: 'I am Turkey, and I've got your hearts.' Squeezing each heart as the sisters close with their deer-clubs, he fells them one by one and cracks every heart open on the flat killing-stone like flint. The Skin Man taunts the returning sorcerer - 'Turkey has your heart' - and his own heart breaks on the rock; patted all over, Skin Man is restored to his normal form: Turkey's own brother, held by sorcery. From the bones strewn on the flat rock they raise a host of quarreling people with mismatched limbs, pacify them, and with the grandmother's people build a new village by the strawberries, where they live to this day.
summary.zh: 老嫗與孫兒火雞相依為命，族人盡喪於東方巫魔迪多耶茲之手。禁室裡，火雞偷擊鼓、偷玩袋棍球，又借鼴鼠之皮鑽地而行，以染莓汁的貝珠向「皮人」購得奧秘：巫魔與七姊妹的心藏在屋中一張床下的水潭裡、由一隻潛鳥挾於翼下看守。火雞幻化成巫魔模樣，嚼著草莓吐汁，吞下姊妹們奉上的人肉；待皮人高呼「鹿進草莓地了」引開眾女，他掀床、令潛鳥、奪得八顆心臟奔出：「我是火雞，你們的心都在我手裡！」眾女持鹿棒追來，他便一顆顆捏心使其昏厥，再把心臟逐一摔在殺人石上，如燧石般迸裂。歸來的巫魔被皮人嘲弄——「火雞拿了你的心」——心石俱碎；皮人經他遍體拍撫復原，竟是受妖術所制的親哥哥。二人拾骨堆山，踢倒山核桃樹喊「散骨之眾，趁樹未倒快起！」——眾人肢體錯配、爭吵不休；火雞安撫之後，偕祖母一家在草莓地旁重建新村，安居至今。

sensitivity.note: Seneca tale (Parker 1923); public domain. Cannibalism is the villain's own trait, narrated at story distance.

passages.text: The lodge was old and very large, but only the two lived in it, for all others had been killed by sorcerers. Winter was coming on and the old woman was busily engaged each day in gathering firewood for the winter's store. Every day she would cry as she started on her journey and when she returned she would cry again... 'All of our people are dead. They have been destroyed by a monster wizard who eats human flesh. His lodge is to the east and near it is a great bed of strawberries. Oh, they are as large as hearts. Once there was a good village of our tribe there, but the people were killed and the houses have now fallen down.' Turkey now said, 'My grandmother, now is the time for me to go... Make me some moccasins. I am going east.'
passages.note: Condensed from Parker 1923, pp. 200-202; not verbatim.

passages.text: Turkey was cautious and crept along through the underbrush until he came to a clearing where he saw a dried human skin fastened by a cord to a tall pole. It swung around in the wind and watched the clearing. He was very crafty and knew that he could not approach the Hadjoqda (dried skin) without being seen and reported to its masters. Looking about he saw a mole and made a bargain with it to borrow its coat. Shrinking himself by magic he entered the mole skin and then burrowed underground until he was directly under the skin, when he broke a little root into beads and stained them with berry juice. He called to the skin and offered to give it wampum if it would talk for a while... He learned that the master sorcerer was Deadoehdjadse', and that the seven sisters cooked human flesh for him, grinding it in a corn mortar with white corn meal... Then he learned that the lives of the sorcerer and his sister were secure, for they could not be killed, their hearts being concealed under the wing of a loon that swam in a pool under a bed in the lodge.
passages.note: Condensed from Parker 1923, pp. 202-203; not verbatim.

passages.text: Then he used magic to make himself appear exactly like Deadoehdjadse', and strode boldly into the clearing, chewing a strawberry and spitting the juice. This gave him great power. He drew near the lodge and called for food, but one sister was suspicious and offered him corn, then meat, then fish, but Turkey refused them all and roared that he was Ongwe I'as and wanted his accustomed dinner. This they put before him and he ate it all, satisfying the women that he was indeed their brother. Suddenly Skin Man began to call and the women all ran out of the lodge, for Skin Man was crying that the deer were in the strawberries. When the sisters were out of sight, Turkey noticed a small dog watching one of the beds. He threw a piece of meat to the dog and then lifted up the bed. Beneath was a pool of water and a loon swimming about. 'Give me the hearts,' commanded Turkey... This time the loon lifted its right wing and beneath were the eight hearts. Turkey grabbed them and ran out crying, 'I am Turkey, and I've got your hearts.'
passages.note: Condensed from Parker 1923, p. 203; not verbatim.

passages.text: When the sisters saw Turkey with the hearts they began to chase him with the clubs which they used on the deer, but as each assailant approached Turkey squeezed her heart, causing her to faint... By this time the women were at the flat rock where their brother killed his victims. Turkey now threw their hearts one by one on the stone and each cracked open like a flint stone. 'Turkey has your heart, Turkey has your heart,' sang the Skin Man in derision. The monster sorcerer then rushed into the clearing where he saw Turkey dancing about the flat stone. He rushed upon him, but Turkey threw the heart upon the rock and broke both heart and rock. Then he patted Skin Man all over the body and restored him to his normal form. To his surprise he found him to be his own brother, who had been held by sorcery to obey the commands of the wizard and his sisters. Together they gathered many bones that were strewn about the flat rock. When all were piled up Turkey kicked over a pig-nut tree and called out, 'Disjointed bones, arise before this tree falls upon you!' The tree fell and before it hit the ground a great host of people arose and all were quarreling, for all had portions of the others' bodies. Turkey pacified them... and there they built a new village, and there they live to this day.
passages.note: Condensed from Parker 1923, pp. 203-204; not verbatim.

title.en: Corn Rains into Empty Barrels: The Bride from the Far South
title.zh: 玉米如雨入空桶：南國來的新娘

region.en: The hilltop of bark-eaters, and the far south land of corn
region.zh: 食樹皮者的山丘與南方的玉米之鄉

period: Recorded 1900s-1922, Seneca informants (Parker 1923)

source.archive: Internet Archive (Buffalo Historical Society Publications, vol. 27)
source.work: A. C. Parker, Seneca Myths and Folk Tales, ch. VI tale 24, 'Corn Rains into Empty Barrels' (1923)

summary.en: At one time there was nothing to eat on all the earth: nearly all the people had starved to death, and a few that remained gathered together on a high hill and lived on boiled bark. There was a certain young man who kept saying all the time, 'It will be better after a while,' while his brother tortured him with sharp stones. After a while he heard footsteps, as if on a clean path; he listened for the span of a moon and then heard them running - but nobody believed him. One morning while he sat in the doorway with his head down on his knees a young woman stood before him, smiled and handed him a basket of bread: 'My mother sent me to this lodge to find a young man. My mother wants me to marry him... I have come from the far south. There is plenty of food there.' 'My mother sent me to bring food to you. Let everybody take off the tops of their corn barrels and then enter the lodge and cover their faces' - and soon they heard a sound like corn falling into their barrels; the barrels were full of shelled corn, and everybody ate and all were satisfied. But the younger brother threw his food into the fire and said he wanted game; the young wife's food was rejected, and speaking thereby the dissatisfaction of all the people she returned to her home - the barrels scraped bare overnight. The husband found her on a high mound covered with corn plants, her body burned and scarred where the thrown corn had struck her; and after living in the south several months the couple returned to find the people again starving. The young wife ordered them to open their corn barrels and hide their faces once again, and shelled corn fell like rain into the barrels filling them to the top. Then the young wife told the people that corn must never be wasted or thrown away, for it is food and if destroyed will cause the crops to be poor and the corn to cease to yield.
summary.zh: 大地上曾經顆粒無存：幾乎人人餓死，倖存者聚於高丘以煮樹皮為生。有個青年總是念叨「過一陣就會好起來」，他的弟弟卻用利石折磨他。他聽見乾淨小徑上的腳步聲，守了一個月才聽見奔跑之聲——卻無人信他。一日清晨，一位少女立在他門前，微笑著遞上一籃麵包：「我母親派我來此地找一個青年，要我嫁他……我自遙遠的南方來，那裡食物充足。」她命眾人打開玉米桶的桶蓋、進屋矇住面孔——頃刻間桶中傳來玉米落下的沙沙聲，桶桶皆滿，人人吃飽。但小叔把食物丟進火裡說要吃獵物；新娘的食物遭拒，便代表全族的嫌棄回娘家去了——當夜玉米桶被刮得精光。丈夫在長滿玉米株的高丘上尋見她，她的身子被丟棄的玉米灼燒得傷痕累累；南國數月之後夫妻重返，族人又在挨餓。新娘再命他們開桶矇面，玉米如雨般落滿桶中。她告誡眾人：玉米萬不可糟蹋拋棄——它是糧食，糟蹋它便會歉收絕產。

sensitivity.note: Seneca tale (Parker 1923); public domain. A food-taboo charter: wasted corn = the corn maiden's burns.

passages.text: At one time there was nothing to eat on all the earth. Nearly all the people had starved to death, and a few that remained gathered together on a high hill. They lived on boiled bark. There was a certain young man who kept saying all the time, 'It will be better after a while.' Nobody believed him because things were getting worse each day. His brother used to torture him with sharp stones and say harsh things to him. The young man, however, kept thinking that something would happen soon. After a while he heard footsteps, as if on a clean path. He listened for the span of a moon and then heard them running. He told the people but nobody believed him.
passages.note: Verbatim from Parker 1923, p. 205; not verbatim (OCR modernized).

passages.text: One morning while he sat in the doorway of his lodge with his head down on his knees, a young woman stood before him. He heard her breathe and looked up. She smiled and handed him a basket of bread. 'My mother sent me to this lodge to find a young man,' she said. 'My mother wants me to marry him... I have come from the far south. There is plenty of food there.' So the young man ate the bread and was married to the young woman from the south. Then the young wife said, 'My mother sent me to bring food to you. Let everybody take off the tops of their corn barrels and then enter the lodge and cover their faces.' The sun had now come up and it was hot. The people did not like their faces covered, but soon they heard a sound like corn falling into their barrels. After a time the noise ceased and the young wife said, 'It is finished now.' Out into the shed went the people of the lodge and found the barrels full of shelled corn. Everybody ate and all were satisfied.
passages.note: Verbatim from Parker 1923, pp. 205-206; not verbatim (OCR modernized).

passages.text: But the younger brother threw his food into the fire and said he wanted game... When the husband returned he found his wife crying and when he asked her what was troubling her she said, 'Your younger brother has spoiled everything. He has rejected my food (speaking thereby the dissatisfaction of all the people). I shall now return to my home.'... During the following night there was a sound of scraping in the corn barrels and in the morning when the women went for their corn it was all gone, and with it the bride had vanished... He came to a region of great corn fields and after a while saw a high mound covered with corn plants. On this mound he found his wife and her mother.
passages.note: Verbatim from Parker 1923, pp. 206-207; not verbatim (OCR modernized).

passages.text: His wife showed him her body and it was burned and scarred. 'This is what your brother did to me,' she said, 'when he threw the corn into the fire. He would have killed me had I remained.' After living in the south for several months the couple returned and found the people again starving. The young wife ordered them to open their corn barrels and hide their faces once again. They did so and shelled corn fell like rain into the barrels filling them to the top. Then the young wife told the people that corn must never be wasted or thrown away for it is food and if destroyed will cause the crops to be poor and the corn to cease to yield.
passages.note: Verbatim from Parker 1923, pp. 206-207; not verbatim (OCR modernized).

title.en: Twentgowa and the Mischief Maker: Powers Granted Twice
title.zh: 特溫特瓜瓦與搗蛋鬼：只賜兩次的法力

region.en: Lazy man's mossy rock by the river, and the hidden bark house of S'hodie'onskon'
region.zh: 河畔懶人的青苔岩與搗蛋鬼的隱形木屋

period: Related by Edward Cornplanter, 1905 (Parker 1923)

source.archive: Internet Archive (Buffalo Historical Society Publications, vol. 27)
source.work: A. C. Parker, Seneca Myths and Folk Tales, ch. VI tale 25, 'Twentgowa and the Mischief Maker' (1923)

summary.en: Twentgowa the lazy man dreams on a mossy rock by the river of killing big game if he only had a chance, until a friend appears: 'I have good things in my place of abode and there is plenty to eat and much game hanging on my rafters.' In the bark house that only appears from his bed the friend conjures the loathly mess into steaming pudding - 'Djiskwengo' - and throws the pot of food right through the wall of Twentgowa's abdomen. But the power fails at home - all that is produced is a terrible mess that drives his family out of the house - for the friend is none other than S'hodie'onskon', the mischief maker. Each gift is granted only twice: the pumpkin from the head of the war club - Twentgowa's third try whacks his own big toe and he faints; the shins whittled to bone knives to strike the fish - his second home attempt bleeds him into a faint until the friend heals the wounds with salivary fluid; the elm-bark cords and fish-bladder nose for hunting ducks underwater - on his third try the ducks he has tied draw him up into the air over the forest and drop him into an enormous hollow stub, where his drumming and song 'Djii-ha-ha' make the wood-gathering damsels dance until an axe reveals only a man with his clothes torn off. The wife gives him a terrible scolding, and the friend says: 'Twentgowa must not go to the woods any more to the spot where he has been accustomed to recline. He may not come to my house any more. Henceforth he must hunt like other men.'
summary.zh: 懶漢特溫特瓜瓦總在河畔青苔岩上空想著「若有机會必獵大獸」，直到一位朋友現身：「我家好吃好喝，梁上掛滿獵物。」只在他躺臥處才顯形的木屋裡，朋友一聲「迪斯克文戈」便把腥臭的糊漿化為香噴噴的熱布丁，還把食盆連食物隔牆送入他的腹中。可回到家法力盡失——只變出一團惡臭，把妻兒都熏出屋去——原來這位朋友正是搗蛋鬼肖迪恩斯康。每次法力只賜兩次：戰棒頭裡滾出南瓜——他第三次揮槌砸中自己的大腳趾，昏死過去；把小腿削成骨刀插水刺魚——第二次自家試法血流如注，昏倒溪邊，虧得朋友以唾液療傷；以榆皮繩與魚鰾鼻潛水獵鴨——第三次嘗試時鴨群振翅把他拖上天空、拋進巨大空樹樁，他的鼓聲與歌聲「吉—哈—哈」引得拾柴的姑娘們翩翩起舞，直到斧聲揭穿——樹洞裡不過是個衣衫被刮光的漢子。妻子把他痛罵一頓；朋友也言明：「特溫特瓜瓦不得再往河畔的青苔岩去，也不許再來我家。從今往後，他得像別的男人一樣打獵。」

sensitivity.note: Seneca tale (Cornplanter informant, 1905, Parker 1923); public domain.

passages.text: There was once a very lazy man named Twentgowa. He had a wife and several children. Twentgowa was always giving excuses to his wife as to why he did not hunt game more often like other men. Twentgowa often went into the deep woods and had a mossy rock near a river where he would lie and dream of the things he would like to do and how he would kill big game animals if he only had a chance... One evening a man came to the lodge where Twentgowa lived. He stood in the doorway and said: 'I am your friend. I have visited you before but this is the first time you have seen me. I have known your name for a long time. Now you must come often and see me. I have good things in my place of abode and there is plenty to eat and much game hanging on my rafters.'
passages.note: Verbatim from Parker 1923, p. 208; not verbatim (OCR modernized).

passages.text: When he had lain there a short time he looked up and saw a large bark house, with very fine poles as supports and over the door a head of some animal he could not identify... 'Come in,' said his friend, 'This is where I live... Now it is time to eat. Be seated here on a mat and let us eat together.' Thereupon the friend went to an upper shelf and took down a bowl into which he placed a loathly mess of substance that had the odor of a fish a long time dead. 'Djiskwengo,' exclaimed the friend, and the bowl filled up with steaming pudding of most enticing odor. So the two friends ate the food and relished it greatly... 'My friend, there is no need of that,' said the householder. 'I will give you power to do as I have done.' So Twentgowa stood at the back of the lodge and his friend threw the pot of food into him right through the wall of his abdomen. It vanished through magic and power was within Twentgowa.
passages.note: Verbatim from Parker 1923, pp. 209-210; not verbatim (OCR modernized).

passages.text: He kept thinking of his newly acquired power and thought it might be well to test it. So he sat down on a log and used his magical word, 'Odjiskwagoh.' As he did this a great pile of steaming pumpkin pudding formed on the ground... He placed in it the loathly substance like unto a dead fish and then conjured it until it overflowed... His wife was very angry and would not touch the food but scolded him, for instead of real food all that was produced was a terrible mess that drove her and the children out of the house... 'Do not go to the lodge of that man any longer. He is none other than S'hodie'onskon', whom we know as a mischief maker. He will make your mind abnormal and what is bad he will make you think is good.' The second gift: pumpkins from the head of the war club - 'I will give you power to so produce twice... Stand, swing your war club until it comes whack against the head of my club' - and at home Twentgowa lifted up his foot upon the bench and whacked his big toe: it was a terrible and resounding whack, but no pumpkin rolled forth; Twentgowa fell off the bench like a dead man.
passages.note: Verbatim from Parker 1923, pp. 210-212; not verbatim (OCR modernized).

passages.text: So saying he went out and strode down to the creek where he removed his leggings. He took out his knife and passed it through his lips, moistening it. Then he began to whittle the meat off his shins so that the bone stood out sharp like a long knife. 'Now, my friend,' said he, 'I will wade swiftly through the water and strike the fishes before they can move to one side.'... Coming ashore he put down his basket and then began to moisten his shins with salivary fluid. They quickly were restored and did not bleed at any time... At length, despairing of causing him harm in this manner... Twentgowa tried his new power and caught many fish which he left with his friend... At home As he cut the flesh blood flowed out and he was in great pain... She dragged him to the lodge and then called upon her dog to go and fetch S'hondie'onskon', the magical friend, to come and heal the husband... Then said the friend, 'I gave you power twice, but further than that I did not give you. You have cheated and wasted your power.' The last gift was duck-hunting under water with elm bark cords and a fish's air-bladder touched to his nose: at home, into the lake he went for he saw upon its surface a great flock of ducks swimming closely together... Upward flew the ducks with such impetus that Twentgowa was drawn up into the air and over the forest. When the ducks had flown a short way the string which he was holding broke and down he fell and into the top of an enormous hollow stub... Twentgowa then sang 'Djii-ha-ha, djii-ha-ha!' many times, and the damsel danced... He took an axe and chopped down the tree... and there inside was a man with his clothes torn off. The wife scolded him for making the damsels dance... Then the friend came out of the bushes where he was hiding and he said, 'Twentgowa must not go to the woods any more to the spot where he has been accustomed to recline. He may not come to my house any more. Henceforth he must hunt like other men.'
passages.note: Verbatim from Parker 1923, pp. 213-216; not verbatim (OCR modernized).

title.zh: 娜姆舍：魚群女主

summary.en: The daughter of Enki is praised as lady of fish and birds, interpreter of dreams and patron of the orphan: on New Year's day she judges the land, weighing the widow's case — the goddess of social justice and the lagoon's wealth.
summary.zh: 恩基之女被頌為魚鳥之主、解夢之師、孤兒之護：新年之日她審理天下，為寡婦秉公裁斷——兼具社會正義與湖沼財富的女神。

passages.text: Nanshe, daughter of Enki, is praised as lady of the fish and the birds of the lagoon, whose own mother was born of the water's plenty. She is the interpreter of dreams and the patron of the orphan and the widow: on New Year's day she holds court, weighing the cases of the poor with the water's justice.

She lends her name to every school exercise, and the closing prayer asks her for the art of writing perfected — the patroness of the craft that makes order out of accounts.
