Ali came up from Kufa to meet them; the parleys failed, and the two armies joined in battle under the walls of Basra.
passages.note: Paraphrase of al-Tabari via Muir, The Caliphate (1891), ch. 19; not verbatim.

passages.text: Aisha sat in a litter on her camel, and the fighting gathered around her as around a standard; the battle was called the Battle of the Camel. Talha fell; Zubayr left the field, and was slain in a ravine by a man who came only for the spoils. At last the camel was hamstrung, and the litter sank; Ali won the day, and sent the Prophet's widow home to Medina with every honour — but the companions had fought companions, and the wound did not close.
passages.note: Paraphrase of al-Tabari via Muir, The Caliphate (1891), ch. 19; not verbatim.

title.en: Siffin: Qur'ans on the Spears
title.zh: 綏芬：長矛上的古蘭經

region.en: Siffin, on the Euphrates (literal pin)
region.zh: 幼發拉底河畔的綏芬（實際定位）

period: Event 657 CE; English: W. Muir, The Caliphate (1891), ch. 20

source.work: William Muir, The Caliphate (1891), ch. 20

license: Public domain (English edition 1891; Arabic originals 9th-10th centuries)

summary.en: Ali marches against Mu'awiya, governor of Syria. For days the armies fight; Amr ibn al-As, Mu'awiya's adviser, orders the soldiers to raise copies of the Qur'an on their spear-points and cry 'Let the Book of God decide.' The fight stops; Ali sees the trick — 'I knew them, O people; by night the pages were raised in sight of the Qur'an' — but his army compels him to arbitration. The arbitrators confer; the tide turns against Ali, and the Kharijites break away crying 'Judgment is God's alone.'
summary.zh: 阿里進軍敘利亞總督穆阿維亞。數日大戰；穆阿維亞謀士阿慕爾·本·阿斯令士兵將古蘭經抄本繫於矛端，高呼『讓主之經典裁決』。戰止；阿里識破詭計——『人們啊，我深知他們；夜間他們舉起書頁，卻不見古蘭經』——然其軍迫其行仲裁。仲裁者相商；局勢轉而不利於阿里，哈瓦利吉派高呼『惟主之裁決』而脫離。

sensitivity.note: Early Islamic historiography; presented as received narrative.

passages.text: Ali marched against Mu'awiya, who had withheld his homage from Medina, and the armies met on the plain of Siffin by the Euphrates. For days the lines fought in relays; the spears and swords had decided nothing but the hour.
passages.note: Paraphrase of al-Tabari via Muir, The Caliphate (1891), ch. 20; not verbatim.

passages.text: Then Amr ibn al-As gave counsel to Mu'awiya: let the soldiers lift copies of the Qur'an on the points of their spears, crying, 'Let the Book of God judge between us.' And it was done; the battle stopped of itself. Ali said: 'I knew them — I tell you that these are the men of deception; by night they lifted pages that have nothing of the Qur'an in them.' But his army would not fight on, and compelled him to arbitration. The two arbitrators conferred at Adhruh; and the tide turned against Ali — and the strictest of his own soldiers broke away, crying, 'Judgment is God's alone; there is no arbitration between men.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of al-Tabari via Muir, The Caliphate (1891), ch. 20; not verbatim.

title.en: The Martyrdom of Uthman
title.zh: 奧斯曼之殉難

region.en: Medina, house of Uthman (literal pin)
region.zh: 麥地那奧斯曼宅（實際定位）

period: Event 656 CE; English: W. Muir, The Caliphate (1891), ch. 17

source.work: William Muir, The Caliphate (1891), ch. 17

license: Public domain (English edition 1891; Arabic originals 9th-10th centuries)

summary.en: The besiegers close on the house of Uthman; Ali sends his sons to guard the door. The rebels break in at last, and the old caliph is struck as he recites the Book; his blood runs on the verses — 'and God will suffice thee against them that mock' — read on to the end. Medina has seen its first civil blood; the copy of the Qur'an that he was reading is said to be the one his own commission produced.
summary.zh: 圍困者逼至奧斯曼宅；阿里遣其子守門。叛者終破門而入；年邁哈里發誦經時被擊；其血流於經文之上——『主必使你免受嘲笑者之害』——經誦讀至終。麥地那首見同室操戈之血；相傳其誦讀的抄本，正是他主持委員會所定。

sensitivity.note: Early Islamic historiography; the first caliph slain by Muslims is treated with restraint in all traditions.

passages.text: The malcontents gathered in Egypt and Kufa marched to Medina and besieged the house of Uthman. Ali sent his sons to keep the door, and blood was shed before it. The rebels broke in at last; and the old caliph, seated with the Book before him, was struck, and his blood ran over the page where he had read: 'They will say, art thou the one whom God and His Messenger blessed? — and God will suffice thee against the mockers.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of al-Tabari via Muir, The Caliphate (1891), ch. 17; not verbatim.

passages.text: It was the copy of the Qur'an which his own commission had gathered that lay before him, and the tale is told that he read to the end of the verse. His body was buried at night by his kin; Ali washed his hands, saying, 'God knows that I was innocent of his blood.' The Caliphate of Medina had seen its first civil blood, and the wound of the community was opened.
passages.note: Paraphrase of al-Tabari via Muir, The Caliphate (1891), ch. 17; not verbatim.

title.en: The Martyrdom of Ali in the Mosque of Kufa
title.zh: 阿里殉於庫法清真寺

region.en: Kufa, mosque of Ali (literal pin)
region.zh: 庫法阿里清真寺（實際定位）

period: Event 661 CE; English: W. Muir, The Caliphate (1891), ch. 21

source.work: William Muir, The Caliphate (1891), ch. 21

license: Public domain (English edition 1891; Arabic originals 9th-10th centuries)

summary.en: A Kharijite, Ibn Muljam, waits for Ali at the dawn prayer of Ramadan in the mosque of Kufa. As the caliph is drawn from his couch of sleep and stands at prayer, the poisoned sword falls on the crown of his head. 'By the Lord of the Kaaba, I have succeeded'; the wound is mortal, and the words that follow are of the prayer, the fear of God, and the young man's death. Hasan buries him; the traditions read the murder as the price of arbitration.
summary.zh: 哈瓦利吉派刺客伊本·穆勒加姆於萊麥丹晨禮時候在庫法清真寺等候阿里。哈里發自睡榻起身立於禮拜時，淬毒之劍落於其頭頂。『以天房之主起誓，我已成功。』傷勢致命；臨終之言關乎禮拜、敬畏主、與青年刺客之死。哈桑葬之；諸傳統視此刺殺為仲裁之代價。

sensitivity.note: Early Islamic historiography; Ali's martyrdom is a cardinal event of Shi'i devotion; presented as received narrative without sectarian framing.

passages.text: Ibn Muljam, a Kharijite of the breakaway sect, had bound himself to kill Ali, and waited for him in the mosque of Kufa at the dawn prayer of Ramadan. As Ali came out of his couch of sleep and stood at prayer, the man struck him on the crown of the head with a sword dipped in poison.
passages.note: Paraphrase of al-Tabari via Muir, The Caliphate (1891), ch. 21; not verbatim.

passages.text: Ali cried, 'By the Lord of the Kaaba, I have succeeded.' The wound was mortal. He called his son Hasan, and spoke of the prayer, and of the fear of God, and of the young man who had killed him — 'Kill him gently, if I die of the wound, and do not mutilate him; I heard the Prophet say, do not mutilate even the dog.' And the First of the Muslims to be slain at prayer was buried in Kufa, and the caliphate passed out of the line of the companions.
passages.note: Paraphrase of al-Tabari via Muir, The Caliphate (1891), ch. 21; not verbatim.

title.en: Mu'awiya: 'I Use Cunning Where Thou Usest Chivalry'
title.zh: 穆阿維亞：「你用騎士之勇，我用權謀」

region.en: Damascus, court of Mu'awiya (literal pin)
region.zh: 大馬士革穆阿維亞宮廷（實際定位）

period: Events 650s-660s CE; English: W. Muir, The Caliphate (1891), ch. 22

source.work: William Muir, The Caliphate (1891), ch. 22

license: Public domain (English edition 1891; Arabic originals 9th-10th centuries)

summary.en: Mu'awiya, first of the Umayyads, rules twenty years from Damascus with the tools of the scribe and the soldier. To the last of the companions who reproach him he answers with the famous word: 'By God, I do not use against thee the sword, or the whip, or the market, or the crowding of men; I use cunning where thou usest chivalry.' The anecdote lore of the court gathers around him — the Kharijite who threw his sandal, the man who called out in the mosque, and the letter that ended: 'Do not write to me of women; write to me of power.'
summary.zh: 伍麥葉王朝首主穆阿維亞自大馬士革以文書與士兵之術執政二十年。對最後一位責難他的聖門弟子，他答以名言：『我不用劍，不用鞭，不用市場，不用人潮相逼；你用騎士之勇，我用權謀。』宮廷軼事圍繞他累積——投擲其靴之哈瓦利吉派者、清真寺中高呼者、以及結尾寫道：『勿與我言婦人；與我言權力』的書信。

sensitivity.note: Anecdote lore of the Umayyad court as gathered in Muir from the Arabic historians; Mu'awiya is judged differently in Sunni and Shi'i memory.

passages.text: Mu'awiya ruled from Damascus for twenty years, the first of the Umayyads. To the men of the Prophet's generation who reproached him for his rule by scribes and soldiers, he gave the famous answer: 'By God, I do not use against thee the sword, or the whip, or the market, or the crowding of men; I use cunning where thou usest chivalry.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of the anecdote lore of al-Tabari via Muir, The Caliphate (1891), ch. 22; not verbatim.

passages.text: The court anecdotes gather round him: the Kharijite who flung his sandal at him in the mosque and was told that he would be given his blood-money if he could find his equal; the man who cried out against him and was made to drink honey as a punishment; and the letter to a man who sought a wife: 'Do not write to me of women; write to me of power.' And he was said to be the most patient and the most clement of the caliphs, and the least of them to be provoked.
passages.note: Paraphrase of the anecdote lore via Muir, The Caliphate (1891), ch. 22; not verbatim.

title.en: The Shaman and the Master of the Four Abysses (Zhuangzi)
title.zh: 壺子示相，神巫季咸（莊子）

region.en: The State of Chêng (Zhengzhou, Henan, China)
region.zh: 鄭國（今河南鄭州）

period: Zhuangzi ch. 7, c. 4th-3rd c. BCE (trans. Giles, 1889)

source.work: Chuang Tzu: Mystic, Moralist, and Social Reformer, trans. Herbert A. Giles, ch. 7

summary.en: In Chêng lives the magician Chi Han, who predicts death and life to a day. Lieh Tzŭ, dazzled, thinks his own tutor Hu Tzŭ inferior; but Hu Tzŭ shows the shaman four successive faces — the still earth, the dispassionate heaven, the nine-named abyss of equilibrium, and lastly the TAO before time was, a great blank existing of itself — at which the shaman turns and flees, and Lieh Tzŭ goes home to feed his pigs like human beings for three years.
summary.zh: 鄭有神巫曰季咸，知人之死生存亡。壺子四示其相：地文之靜、天壤之動、太衝莫勝之淵、而未始出吾宗——立未始出吾宗，而巫咸逃；列子三年不出，為其妻爨，食豕如食人。

sensitivity.note: Canonical text of the Taoist canon (Nanhua zhenjing); the shaman-episode is the classic Taoist counter-narrative to divinatory magic. Included as a comparative text.

passages.text: In the State of Chêng there was a wonderful magician, named Chi Han. He knew all about birth and death, gain and loss, misfortune and happiness, long life and short life,--predicting events to a day with supernatural accuracy. The people of Chêng used to flee at his approach; but Lieh Tzŭ went to see him, and became so infatuated that on his return he said to Hu Tzŭ, "I used to look upon your TAO as perfect. Now I know something more perfect still." "So far," replied Hu Tzŭ, "I have only taught you the ornamentals, not the essentials, of TAO; and yet you think you know all about it. Without cocks in your poultry-yard, what sort of eggs do the hens lay? If you go about trying to force TAO down people's throats, you will be simply exposing yourself. Bring your friend with you, and let me show myself to him."

So next day Lieh Tzŭ went with Chi Han to see Hu Tzŭ, and when they came out Chi Han said, "Alas! your teacher is doomed. He cannot live. I hardly give him ten days. I am astonished at him. He is but wet ashes." Lieh Tzŭ went in and wept bitterly, and told Hu Tzŭ; but the latter said, "I showed myself to him just now as the earth shows us its outward form, motionless and still, while production is all the time going on. I merely prevented him from seeing my pent-up energy within. Bring him again." Next day the interview took place as before; but as they were leaving Chi Han said to Lieh Tzŭ, "It is lucky for your teacher that he met me. He is better. He will recover. I saw he had recuperative power."

Next day a third interview took place, and as they were leaving, Chi Han said to Lieh Tzŭ, "Your teacher is never one day like another. I can tell nothing from his physiognomy. Get him to be regular, and I will then examine him again." This being repeated to Hu Tzŭ as before, the latter said, "I showed myself to him just now in a state of harmonious equilibrium. Where the whale disports itself,--is the abyss. Where water is at rest,--is the abyss. Where water is in motion,--is the abyss. The abyss has nine names. These are three of them." Next day the two went once more to see Hu Tzŭ; but Chi Han was unable to stand still, and in his confusion turned and fled.

"I showed myself to him just now," said Hu Tzŭ, "as TAO appeared before time was. I was to him as a great blank, existing of itself. He knew not who I was. His face fell. He became confused. And so he fled." Upon this Lieh Tzŭ stood convinced that he had not yet acquired any real knowledge, and at once set to work in earnest, passing three years without leaving the house. He helped his wife to cook the family dinner, and fed his pigs just like human beings. He discarded the artificial and reverted to the natural. He became merely a shape. Amidst confusion, he was unconfounded. And so he continued to the end.

title.en: The Sage of the Yin Mountain Refuses the Empire (Zhuangzi)
title.zh: 天根問治於蓼水之陽（莊子）

region.en: South of the Yin mountain, by the Liao river (symbolic pin: Liaoyang, Liaoning, China)
region.zh: 殷山之陽、蓼水之上（象徵定位：遼寧遼陽）

period: Zhuangzi ch. 7, c. 4th-3rd c. BCE (trans. Giles, 1889)

source.work: Chuang Tzu: Mystic, Moralist, and Social Reformer, trans. Herbert A. Giles, ch. 7

summary.en: T'ien Kên meets a Sage by the Liao river and begs to ask about governing the empire; the Sage drives him off — borne on light pinions he can soar beyond the cardinal points to the land of nowhere — and on the second asking gives his whole doctrine: resolve your mental energy into abstraction, your physical energy into inaction, fall in with the natural order without admitting the element of self, and the empire will be governed.
summary.zh: 天根遊於殷陽，問為天下於聖人。聖人曰：去！汝鄙人也——予方與造物者為人，厭則又乘夫莽眇之鳥，以出六極之外，而遊無何有之鄉，以處壙垠之野。

sensitivity.note: Canonical text of the Taoist canon (Nanhua zhenjing). Included as a comparative text — a scholarly framing, not a claim about religious truth.

passages.text: "Begone!" cried the Sage. "You are a low fellow, and your question is ill timed. God has just turned me out a man. That is enough for me. Borne on light pinions I can soar beyond the cardinal points, to the land of nowhere, in the domain of nothingness. And you come to worry me with government of the empire!" But T'ien Kên enquired a second time, and the Sage replied, "Resolve your mental energy into abstraction, your physical energy into inaction. Allow yourself to fall in with the natural order of phenomena, without admitting the element of self,--and the empire will be governed."

title.en: Yang Tzŭ Chü Asks Lao Tzŭ What Makes a Wise Ruler (Zhuangzi)
title.zh: 陽子居見老聃問明王（莊子）

region.en: Lao Tzŭ's retreat (symbolic pin: Ku county, Bozhou, Anhui, China)
region.zh: 老聃之居（象徵定位：安徽亳州苦縣）

period: Zhuangzi ch. 7, c. 4th-3rd c. BCE (trans. Giles, 1889)

source.work: Chuang Tzu: Mystic, Moralist, and Social Reformer, trans. Herbert A. Giles, ch. 7

summary.en: Yang Tzŭ Chü asks whether an ardent, courageous, tireless seeker of the Tao would be a wise ruler. Lao Tzŭ answers that he would be a mere handicraftsman wearing out body and mind; the tiger suffers from the beauty of his skin. The wise ruler's goodness covers the empire, yet he himself seems to know it not — it is based upon the baseless, and travels through the realms of Nowhere.
summary.zh: 陽子居見老聃曰：有人於此，嚮疾強梁，物徹疏明，學道不倦——如是者可比明王乎？老聃曰：明王之治，功蓋天下而似不自己，化貸萬物而民弗恃；立乎不測，而遊於無有者也。

sensitivity.note: Canonical text of the Taoist canon (Nanhua zhenjing). Included as a comparative text — a scholarly framing, not a claim about religious truth.

passages.text: Yang Tzŭ Chü went to see Lao Tzŭ, and said, "Suppose a man were ardent and courageous, acquainted with the order and principles of things, and untiring in the pursuit of TAO--would he be accounted a wise ruler?" "From the point of view of a truly wise man," replied Lao Tzŭ, "such a one would be a mere handicraftsman, wearing out body and mind alike. The tiger and the pard suffer from the beauty of their skins. The cleverness of the monkey, the tractability of the ox, bring them both to the tether. It is not on such grounds that a ruler may be accounted wise."

"The goodness of a wise ruler," answered Lao Tzŭ, "covers the whole empire, yet he himself seems to know it not. It influences all creation, yet none is conscious thereof. It appears under countless forms, bringing joy to all things. It is based upon the baseless, and travels through the realms of Nowhere."

title.en: Karbala: The Martyrdom of Husayn
title.zh: 卡爾巴拉：侯賽因之殉難

region.en: Karbala, on the Euphrates, Iraq (literal pin)
region.zh: 伊拉克幼發拉底河畔卡爾巴拉（實際定位）

period: Event 680 CE; English: S. Ockley, History of the Saracens (Bohn ed. 1890); W. Muir, The Caliphate (1891), ch. 25

source.work: Simon Ockley, The History of the Saracens (Bohn ed. 1890); William Muir, The Caliphate (1891), ch. 25

license: Public domain (English editions 1890-91; Arabic originals 9th-10th centuries)

summary.en: Yazid is proclaimed caliph at Damascus; Husayn, grandson of the Prophet, refuses the oath and rides for Kufa. He is met by the army of Ubaydullah ibn Ziyad at Karbala, cut off from the Euphrates, and besieged for days without water. On the day of Ashura the seventy-two are struck down one by one; Husayn falls last, with his infant son in his arms. Zaynab carries the captives to Damascus, and the mourning for the family of the Prophet becomes the rite of Muharram.
summary.zh: 大馬士革擁立耶齊德為哈里發；先知之孫侯賽因拒誓，騎向庫法。於卡爾巴拉遇伊本·齊亞德之軍，被截於幼發拉底河之外，斷水圍困多日。阿舒拉之日，七十二人逐一被殺；侯賽因殿後而歿，懷中抱其幼子。宰乃布攜俘至大馬士革；先知家屬之哀悼成為穆哈蘭月之儀。

sensitivity.note: The martyrdom of Husayn is a cardinal devotion of Shi'ism and a grief-event in Sunni memory alike; recorded as the received narrative of Tabari/Ockley without sectarian framing.

passages.text: On the death of Mu'awiya his son Yazid was proclaimed caliph at Damascus. Husayn, the son of Ali and the grandson of the Prophet, refused the oath and rode from Medina towards Kufa, whose people had written to invite him. The governor Ubaydullah ibn Ziyad sent an army against him; his path was turned aside, and he was met at the plain of Karbala, two days from the Euphrates.
passages.note: Paraphrase of al-Tabari via Ockley (1890) and Muir (1891); not verbatim.

passages.text: Husayn was besieged with his family and companions — seventy-two fighting men, among them his brother Abbas and his young son — and the water of the river was denied them. On the tenth day of Muharram, the day of Ashura, they were struck down one after another; Abbas fell at the water, and the infant of Husayn died in his father's arms, an arrow through its neck. Husayn fell last, faint with thirst, crying the old cry: 'Is there any helper?'
passages.note: Paraphrase of al-Tabari via Ockley (1890); not verbatim.

passages.text: His head was carried to Ibn Ziyad and then to Damascus; his sister Zaynab led the captives, and in the court of Yazid she spoke the protest that the tradition remembers. The mourning for the family of the Prophet — the weeping processions of Muharram, the ta'ziya recitations, the shrines of Karbala and Najaf — grew out of the plain where the seventy-two died; and the Sunni calendar keeps the tenth of Muharram as a fast of grief and of the Ark's resting alike.
passages.note: Paraphrase of the aftermath as told in Ockley (1890) and the Arabic historians; not verbatim.

title.en: Al-Mansur and the Death of Abu Muslim
title.zh: 曼蘇爾與阿布·穆斯林之死

region.en: Kufa and the Khurasan road (symbolic pin at Baghdad)
region.zh: 庫法與呼羅珊道（象徵性定位於巴格達）

period: Event 755 CE; English: W. Muir, The Caliphate (1891), ch. 39

source.work: William Muir, The Caliphate (1891), ch. 39

license: Public domain (English edition 1891; Arabic originals 9th-10th centuries)

summary.en: Abu Muslim, the maker of the Abbasid revolution, has won Persia with the black banners. The caliph al-Mansur summons him to the court; the amir is warned, and comes. The caliph reproaches him with the name of Abu Muslim — 'Art thou Abu Muslim? I will make thee a prey to the dogs of the streets' — and the bodyguard does the rest. The revolution devours its maker; and Persia murmurs for twenty years.
summary.zh: 阿拔斯革命的締造者阿布·穆斯林已以黑旗得波斯。哈里發曼蘇爾召其入廷；封臣受警，仍前來。哈里發以『阿布·穆斯林』之名責之——『你是阿布·穆斯林嗎？我必使你為街犬之食』——衛士續行其事。革命吞其締造者；波斯怨憤二十年。

sensitivity.note: Early Abbasid historiography as received in Muir.

passages.text: Abu Muslim had made the Abbasid revolution in Khurasan and won Persia for the House. The caliph al-Mansur, grown uneasy before so great a man, summoned him to the court. The friends of Abu Muslim warned him; the astrologers warned him; and he came, saying that he had given thirty years to the House and would not refuse its summons.
passages.note: Paraphrase of al-Tabari via Muir, The Caliphate (1891), ch. 39; not verbatim.

passages.text: He entered and saluted; the caliph reproached him, and then spoke the word the historians have kept: 'Art thou Abu Muslim? I will make thee a prey to the dogs of the streets.' The bodyguard closed; and the maker of the dynasty was slain in the caliph's tent. Persia murmured for twenty years after, and the sects that remembered him raised him to a hidden lord.
passages.note: Paraphrase of al-Tabari via Muir, The Caliphate (1891), ch. 39; not verbatim.

title.en: Al-Mansur Founds Baghdad: The Round City
title.zh: 曼蘇爾建巴格達：圓城

region.en: Baghdad, Tigris crossing (literal pin)
region.zh: 底格里斯河渡口的巴格達（實際定位）

period: Founded 762 CE; English: W. Muir, The Caliphate (1891), ch. 38

source.work: William Muir, The Caliphate (1891), ch. 38

license: Public domain (English edition 1891; Arabic originals 9th-10th centuries)

summary.en: The caliph chooses the crossing of the Tigris and Sarat canals near the old Persian villages — 'a market for all the world, and nothing that the river brings can get past it.' Four thousand architects measure a city of concentric walls, Khuld the 'Eternal'; the trench is dug, the foundations laid of burned brick in rows of reed — 'O God, Thou art the Everlasting Lord; build Thou for me.' In four years the Round City stands, and it is called Madinat al-Salam, the City of Peace.
summary.zh: 哈里發擇底格里斯河與薩拉特運河交匯處，近古波斯村落——『天下之市集，河所載者無不經此』。四千名建築師量畫同心圓牆之城，名『永恆』（胡爾德）；掘溝，以蘆葦為行、焙磚為基——『主啊，你是永活之主；為我而建吧』。四年之間圓城立，名『和平之城』（麥地那·薩拉姆）。

sensitivity.note: Early Abbasid historiography; the founding is a landmark of urban and intellectual history.

passages.text: Al-Mansur sought a site for his capital and chose the crossing of the Tigris and the Sarat canals, by the villages of the old Persian name — a market for all the world, he said, with nothing that the river brings able to pass it. He had the ground measured by his engineers: a city of two concentric walls with a ditch between, the mosque and the palace at the centre under a golden dome.
passages.note: Paraphrase of al-Tabari via Muir, The Caliphate (1891), ch. 38; not verbatim.

passages.text: The trench was dug first, the caliph himself striking the first earth and praying: 'O God, Thou art the Everlasting Lord; build Thou for me; the world passes and Thy kingdom abides.' The walls were of burned brick laid in rows of reeds, the gates of iron; and in four years the Round City stood, called Madinat al-Salam, the City of Peace — and under its caliphs it became the seat of the translation of the sciences and of the lore of the world.
passages.note: Paraphrase of al-Tabari via Muir, The Caliphate (1891), ch. 38; not verbatim.

title.en: Harun al-Rashid and the Fall of the Barmecides
title.zh: 哈倫·拉希德與巴爾馬克家族之傾覆

region.en: Baghdad, court of Harun (literal pin)
region.zh: 巴格達哈倫宮廷（實際定位）

period: Event 803 CE; English: W. Muir, The Caliphate (1891), ch. 46

source.work: William Muir, The Caliphate (1891), ch. 46

license: Public domain (English edition 1891; Arabic originals 9th-10th centuries)

summary.en: Ja'far the Barmecide, vizier and playmate of Harun, is suddenly commanded to death; the tale is told that the caliph, feasting, had promised the hand of his sister Abbasa to Ja'far in jest, and that the jest was taken for a marriage. Whatever the cause, the sentence is carried in a night: Ja'far is struck in the hall of justice, his father Yahya cast into prison, the palaces of the family stripped. 'The cup of the Barmecides,' the Persian proverb runs, 'is broken.'
summary.zh: 巴爾馬克家族的賈法爾——哈倫的大臣與少年友伴——忽奉死命；相傳哈里發宴中戲許其妹阿巴西之婚，而戲言成真。無論其因，一夕行刑：賈法爾於議政廳被誅，其父葉海雅下獄，家族宮邸盡抄。波斯諺云：『巴爾馬克之杯已碎。』

sensitivity.note: Abbasid court historiography; the fall of the Barmecides is a locus classicus of the Arabic anecdote tradition.

passages.text: Ja'far the Barmecide had been the vizier of Harun al-Rashid and the companion of his boyhood; the House of Barmak had governed the East for a generation. In the year 803 the caliph commanded his death suddenly, without public cause; the tale is told that he had promised the hand of his sister Abbasa in jest at a feast, and that the jest had been taken for a marriage.
passages.note: Paraphrase of al-Tabari via Muir, The Caliphate (1891), ch. 46; not verbatim.

passages.text: The sentence was carried in a night: Ja'far was struck in the hall of justice, and his head sent to Baghdad; his father Yahya and his brother Fadl were cast into prison; the palaces of the family were stripped of their stuff. The Persian proverb kept the memory: 'The cup of the Barmecides is broken' — and the anecdote lore of the Arabs made the fall of the great House a byword for the turn of the king's favour.
passages.note: Paraphrase of al-Tabari via Muir, The Caliphate (1891), ch. 46; not verbatim.

title.en: The Brothers' War: Amin and Ma'mun
title.zh: 兄弟之戰：阿敏與馬蒙

region.en: Baghdad and Merv (symbolic pin at Baghdad)
region.zh: 巴格達與梅爾夫（象徵性定位於巴格達）

period: Events 809-813 CE; English: W. Muir, The Caliphate (1891), ch. 47

source.work: William Muir, The Caliphate (1891), ch. 47

license: Public domain (English edition 1891; Arabic originals 9th-10th centuries)

summary.en: Harun divides the empire on his deathbed: Amin to reign at Baghdad, Ma'mun to hold Khurasan beyond the passes. The brothers' peace breaks; the Tahirid armies come west, Baghdad is besieged for a year, and Amin is taken in the last sally and slain on a bridge of boats. Ma'mun reigns from Merv, and the House is split between the two capitals for years.
summary.zh: 哈倫臨終分帝國：阿敏都於巴格達，馬蒙轄山外的呼羅珊。兄弟之約破裂；塔希爾軍西來，巴格達被圍一年，阿敏於最後的突圍中被擒，死於船橋之上。馬蒙自梅爾夫執政；王朝於兩都之間分裂数年。

sensitivity.note: Abbasid historiography as received in Muir.

passages.text: Harun al-Rashid on his deathbed divided his empire: Amin to reign at Baghdad, and Ma'mun to hold Khurasan beyond the passes, with his own guard and treasury. The peace of the brothers lasted as long as the guardians appointed; then Amin took the succession to himself, and Ma'mun refused, and the armies of Khurasan came west under Tahir.
passages.note: Paraphrase of al-Tabari via Muir, The Caliphate (1891), ch. 47; not verbatim.

passages.text: Baghdad was besieged for a year, house by house, the palaces burned and the people starved. In the last sally Amin was taken in a boat, and was slain on a bridge of the river by the men of Tahir; his head was sent to Merv. Ma'mun reigned from Khurasan, and did not come to Baghdad for years; and the House that Harun had divided never wholly joined again.
passages.note: Paraphrase of al-Tabari via Muir, The Caliphate (1891), ch. 47; not verbatim.

title.en: Tariq Crosses to the Rock of Gibraltar
title.zh: 塔里克渡至直布羅陀之岩

region.en: Gibraltar and Cadiz coast (literal pin)
region.zh: 直布羅陀與加的斯海岸（實際定位）

period: Event 711 CE; English: W. Muir, The Caliphate (1891), ch. 37 (Spanish conquest); S. Ockley (1890)

source.work: William Muir, The Caliphate (1891), ch. 37; Simon Ockley, History of the Saracens (1890)

license: Public domain (English editions 1890-91; Arabic originals 10th-11th centuries)

summary.en: Tariq ibn Ziyad crosses from Morocco to the rock that bears his name with seven thousand Berbers, and burns the boats: 'Where can you flee? The sea is behind you, the enemy in front.' Roderick the Visigoth comes against him with the hosts of Spain; the battle lasts a week, and the Visigothic kingdom falls. The rock keeps the commander's name; and Spain passes to the Muslims for eight hundred years.
summary.zh: 塔里克·本·齊亞德率七千柏柏爾人自摩洛哥渡至以他為名的岩地，並焚其舟：『你們能逃往何處？海在你身後，敵在你面前。』西哥特王羅德里克率西班牙大軍迎擊；戰事持續一週，西哥特王國傾覆。岩留統帥之名；西班牙歸穆斯林八百年。

sensitivity.note: Andalusi historiography as received in Muir/Ockley from Arabic sources.

passages.text: Tariq ibn Ziyad crossed from Morocco to the great rock of the strait with seven thousand Berbers, and burned the boats behind him. He spoke to them, in the speech the historians have kept: 'Whither can you flee? The sea is behind you, the enemy before you; you have nothing left but truth and courage.' And the rock took his name — Jabal Tariq, Gibraltar.
passages.note: Paraphrase of the Arabic accounts via Muir, The Caliphate (1891), ch. 37; not verbatim.

passages.text: Roderick, the last Visigothic king, came against him with the hosts of Spain. The battle lasted a week on the river of the south; the king fled or was drowned in the Guadalquivir, and his kingdom fell with him. The cities of Spain opened their gates one after another, and for eight hundred years the land of the Visigoths was the land of the Muslims, and its capital became Cordoba.
passages.note: Paraphrase of the Arabic accounts via Muir, The Caliphate (1891), ch. 37; not verbatim.

title.en: Abd al-Rahman and the Palm of Ronda
title.zh: 阿布杜·拉赫曼與隆達的棕櫚

region.en: Ronda, Andalus (literal pin)
region.zh: 安達魯西亞隆達（實際定位）

period: Event c. 756 CE; the poem preserved in Ibn Abd Rabbih's Arabic anthology; retold in later European histories

source.work: The palm-tree anecdote from the Arabic tradition (Ibn Abd Rabbih, al-Iqd al-Farid; retold in European histories of Spain); Muir, The Caliphate (1891), ch. 38

license: Public domain (Arabic originals medieval; English edition 1891)

summary.en: The Umayyad prince Abd al-Rahman, sole survivor of the massacre of his house, lands in Spain and builds his kingdom at Cordoba. Riding in the country of Ronda he finds a palm tree, the first he has seen since Damascus; he lays hold of it and speaks the lines the anthologies have kept: 'A palm like me, in exile far from home, parted from people and children... Turn to me, O palm, and hear me cry: as we are far from our people, so are you from yours.'
summary.zh: 伍麥葉王子阿布杜·拉赫曼——其家被屠之唯一倖存者——登陸西班牙，建都於科爾多瓦。行於隆達之鄉，見一棕櫚，乃其自大馬士革以來所見首株；他執其幹，誦出後世文集所存之句：『如我之棕櫚，離鄉萬里，與族人子女相隔……棕櫚啊，轉向我，聽我呼喊：我們離族人甚遠，你亦離你的族人甚遠。』

sensitivity.note: Anecdote lore of the Umayyad exiles of Spain; the palm poem is among the most quoted texts of Andalusi tradition.

passages.text: Abd al-Rahman ibn Mu'awiya, the sole survivor of the Umayyad house after the Abbasid massacre, fled across half the world to Spain, and built his kingdom at Cordoba. Riding in the country of Ronda, he saw a palm tree — the first since Damascus — and laid hold of it, and spoke:
passages.note: Paraphrase of the anecdote and poem as preserved in the Arabic anthologies; not verbatim.

passages.text: 'A palm like me, in exile far from home, parted from people and children, from kindred and from land: turn to me, O palm, and hear me cry — as we are far from our people, so are you from yours.' And the men of Spain wept to see their prince weep for a tree; and the kingdom of the exiles of Cordoba stood for three hundred years.
passages.note: Paraphrase of the anecdote and poem as preserved in the Arabic anthologies; not verbatim.

title.en: The Assassins' Paradise at Alamut
title.zh: 阿拉穆特：刺客的樂園

region.en: Alamut fortress, Elburz mountains, Persia (literal pin)
region.zh: 波斯厄爾布爾士山阿拉穆特要塞（實際定位）

period: Legend told to Marco Polo c. 1270s; English: The Travels of Marco Polo (Marsden 1818 ed.); Persian sources of the 13th century

source.archive: Google Books (public domain scan of Marsden ed. 1818)
source.work: The Travels of Marco Polo, ch. on the Old Man of the Mountain (English, Marsden 1818 ed.); cf. Juvayni's Arabic-Persian history (13th century)

license: Public domain (English edition 1818; Arabic-Persian originals 13th century)

summary.en: The Venetian traveller tells of the Old Man of the Mountain, Hasan-i Sabbah, who kept at Alamut a secret garden watered with milk and honey, with boys and girls of beauty, to which he brought his young men drugged with wine and hemp; they woke in 'Paradise' and were cast out again, believing their master could return them at will. Hence, the legend says, the obedience of the Assassins to death. Modern historians find the garden only in the Western tellings; the fortress itself was taken by the Mongols in 1256.
summary.zh: 威尼斯旅人所述山中老人哈桑·薩巴赫於阿拉穆特蓄一秘密花園，水以乳與蜜，藏絕色男女；以酒與麻藥之青年入園，醒於『樂園』，復被逐出，信其主可隨意使之復返。相傳刺客由此捨死聽命。現代史家謂此花園僅見於西方敘述；要塞本身於1256年被蒙古人攻陷。

sensitivity.note: A Western legend about a Muslim sect, recorded by Marco Polo and doubted by modern historians of the Nizari Isma'ilis; presented as a story about how the East was told in Europe, not as an established fact.

passages.text: Marco Polo tells of the Old Man of the Mountain, who kept at Alamut a secret garden: he had it watered with milk and honey, and filled it with boys and girls of marvellous beauty, with palaces and music and wine. Thither he brought the young men of his following drugged with wine and a herb, and they woke among the delights and believed they were in Paradise; and after a season he cast them out, saying that Paradise could be theirs again if they did his bidding.
passages.note: Paraphrase of the tale in The Travels of Marco Polo (Marsden ed. 1818); not verbatim.

passages.text: So, the legend says, the young men went to their deaths without fear, obedient to the smallest word of the Old Man — whence the name Assassins, from the hashish of the drug, in the European tellings. The historians of the Mongol conquest of 1256, and the modern students of the Nizari Isma'ilis, find nothing of the garden in the Persian sources; the tale is the West's romance about a fortress it feared, and it is told here as a story about stories.
passages.note: Paraphrase of the tale and of the historiographical caution; not verbatim.

title.en: Al-Hajjaj: The Vizier of the Iron Rod
title.zh: 哈賈季：鐵棒之臣

region.en: Kufa and Wasit, Iraq (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 伊拉克庫法與瓦西特（象徵性定位）

period: Events 694-714 CE; English: W. Muir, The Caliphate (1891), ch. 31

source.work: William Muir, The Caliphate (1891), ch. 31

license: Public domain (English edition 1891; Arabic originals 9th-10th centuries)

summary.en: The caliph Abd al-Malik sends al-Hajjaj to Kufa with no force: he rides into the mosque hooded, unmasks, and speaks the speech the historians have kept — 'I am he who trims the feather and sharpens the point, I am the punishment of God among you.' The city is governed by terror for ten years; the dialect of the mosque is corrected by the rod; and at his death the caliph says the tribute the biographers remember: 'I raised him when he was light, and he made himself heavy.'
summary.zh: 哈里發阿布杜·馬利克不遣一兵而遣哈賈季至庫法：他蒙面入清真寺，揭面而言史家所存之句——『我是削羽磨鋒之人，我是降於你們中間的主之懲罰。』城中以恐怖為治十年；清真寺之語以棒正音；其死時，哈里發言傳記所存之語：『我提拔他時他尚輕，而他自任為重。』

sensitivity.note: Umayyad anecdote lore as gathered in Muir.

passages.text: The caliph Abd al-Malik sent al-Hajjaj ibn Yusuf to Kufa without an army. He rode into the mosque hooded, on a mule, and sat; then he unmasked and spoke: 'I am he who trims the feather and sharpens the point; I am the punishment of God among you.' And he governed the city and then the East by terror for ten years, it is said, and slew more men than the wars of his time had taken.
passages.note: Paraphrase of al-Tabari via Muir, The Caliphate (1891), ch. 31; not verbatim.

passages.text: The anecdote lore keeps his sayings: that he corrected the reading of the mosque by the rod; that he called the men of Kufa 'the dregs of the Arabs'; and that at his death the caliph said of him: 'I raised him when he was light, and he made himself heavy.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of al-Tabari via Muir, The Caliphate (1891), ch. 31; not verbatim.

title.en: Al-Mutawakkil and the Poet's Rebuke
title.zh: 穆塔瓦基勒與詩人的譴責

region.en: Samarra, Abbasid capital (literal pin)
region.zh: 阿拔斯都城薩邁拉（實際定位）

period: Events 847-861 CE; English: W. Muir, The Caliphate (1891), ch. 50

source.work: William Muir, The Caliphate (1891), ch. 50

license: Public domain (English edition 1891; Arabic originals 9th-10th centuries)

summary.en: The caliph al-Mutawakkil builds the great mosque of Samarra with its spiral minaret, keeps poets at his table, and dies of a court plot of his own son — the anecdote lore keeps the word said over him: 'He was the most magnificent of the caliphs and the most prodigal.' The Abbasid court at its height is here: the lute, the verses, the wine, and the sword behind the curtain.
summary.zh: 哈里發穆塔瓦基勒建薩邁拉大清真寺與其螺旋宣禮塔，蓄詩人於席，終死於其子主使之宮廷陰謀——軼事之集存其蓋棺之語：『他是最華麗的哈里發，也是最揮霍者。』阿拔斯宮廷之盛在此：琴、詩、酒，與幕後之劍。

sensitivity.note: Abbasid court anecdote lore as gathered in Muir.

passages.text: Al-Mutawakkil built the great mosque of Samarra, with its minaret wound like a screw into the sky, and kept the poets and singers of the age at his table. The anecdote lore remembers him as the most magnificent and the most prodigal of the caliphs: it was said that he built palaces without number and spent his nights in verse and wine.
passages.note: Paraphrase of al-Tabari via Muir, The Caliphate (1891), ch. 50; not verbatim.

passages.text: He was slain in his sleep by the guard of his own court, at the instance of his son; and the histories write the moral of the Abbasid height: the lute, the verse, the wine — and the sword behind the curtain. And the great mosque of Samarra stood, the largest mosque of the age, its spiral minaret the landmark of the desert capital.
passages.note: Paraphrase of al-Tabari via Muir, The Caliphate (1891), ch. 50; not verbatim.

title.en: Horses' Hoofs: Poh Loh the Horse-Breaker (Zhuangzi)
title.zh: 馬蹄：伯樂治馬（莊子）

region.en: The horse-pastures (symbolic pin: Zhangye, Gansu, China)
region.zh: 馬牧之野（象徵定位：甘肅張掖）

period: Zhuangzi ch. 9, c. 4th-3rd c. BCE (trans. Giles, 1889)

source.work: Chuang Tzu: Mystic, Moralist, and Social Reformer, trans. Herbert A. Giles, ch. 9

summary.en: Horses have hoofs to carry them over frost and snow, and hair against the wind — palatial dwellings are of no use to them. Then Poh Loh appeared saying he understood the management of horses: he branded, clipped, halted, shackled and starved them until more than half died; and bridled and bitted, the horses learn to resist and bite — their natures become depraved, the fault of Poh Loh.
summary.zh: 馬蹄可以踐霜雪，毛可以禦風寒；及至伯樂曰我善治馬，燒之剔之，刻之雒之，饑之渴之，馬之死者已過半矣。

sensitivity.note: Canonical text of the Taoist canon (Nanhua zhenjing). Included as a comparative text — a scholarly framing, not a claim about religious truth.

passages.text: Horses have hoofs to carry them over frost and snow; hair, to protect them from wind and cold. They eat grass and drink water, and fling up their heels over the champaign. Such is the real nature of horses. Palatial dwellings are of no use to them.

One day Poh Loh appeared, saying, "I understand the management of horses." So he branded them, and clipped them, and pared their hoofs, and put halters on them, tying them up by the head and shackling them by the feet, and disposing them in stables, with the result that two or three in every ten died. Then he kept them hungry and thirsty, trotting them and galloping them, and grooming, and trimming, with the misery of the tasselled bridle before and the fear of the knotted whip behind, until more than half of them were dead.

Horses live on dry land, eat grass and drink water. When pleased, they rub their necks together. When angry, they turn around and kick up their heels at each other. Thus far only do their natural dispositions carry them. But bridled and bitted, with a plate of metal on their foreheads, they learn to cast vicious looks, to turn the head to bite, to resist, to get the bit out of the mouth or the bridle into it. And thus their natures become depraved,--the fault of Poh Loh.

title.en: The Strong Thief Carries Off the Till: T'ien Ch'êng Tzŭ Steals Ch'i (Zhuangzi)
title.zh: 胠篋：田成子竊齊（莊子）

region.en: The State of Ch'i (Linzi, Shandong, China)
region.zh: 齊國（今山東臨淄）

period: Zhuangzi ch. 10, c. 4th-3rd c. BCE (trans. Giles, 1889)

source.work: Chuang Tzu: Mystic, Moralist, and Social Reformer, trans. Herbert A. Giles, ch. 10

summary.en: Locks and cords protect trunks from small thieves; a strong thief carries off the till with box and bag, his only fear being that the locks are not strong enough. So T'ien Ch'êng Tzŭ slew the Prince of Ch'i and stole not only his kingdom but the wisdom-tricks of the Sages as well — and for twelve generations his descendants ruled, while the small States did not dare to blame him.
summary.zh: 為之斗斛以量之，則並與斗斛而竊之；為之仁義以矯之，則並與仁義而竊之。田成子一朝殺齊君而盜其國，所盜者豈獨其國邪？並與其聖知之法而盜之。

sensitivity.note: Canonical text of the Taoist canon (Nanhua zhenjing). Included as a comparative text — a scholarly framing, not a claim about religious truth.

passages.text: The precautions taken against thieves who open trunks, search bags, or ransack tills, consist of securing with cords and fastening with bolts and locks. This is what the world calls wit. But a strong thief comes who carries off the till on his shoulders, with box and bag to boot. And his only fear is that the cords and locks should not be strong enough!

And within its four boundaries not a temple or shrine was dedicated, nor a district or hamlet governed, but in accordance with the rules laid down by the Sages. Yet one morning T'ien Ch'êng Tzŭ slew the Prince of Ch'i, and stole his kingdom. And not his kingdom only, but the wisdom-tricks which he had got from the Sages as well; so that although T'ien Ch'êng Tzŭ acquired the reputation of a thief, he lived as comfortably as ever did either Yao or Shun. The small States did not venture to blame, nor the great States to punish him; and so for twelve generations his descendants ruled over Ch'i.

One man steals a purse, and is punished. Another steals a State, and becomes a Prince. But charity and duty to one's neighbour are integral parts of princedom. Does he not then steal charity and duty to one's neighbour together with the wisdom of the Sages?

title.en: Robber Chê and the Tao of Thieving (Zhuangzi)
title.zh: 盜亦有道（莊子）

region.en: Robber Chê's mountain fastness (symbolic pin: Mount T'ai, Shandong, China)
region.zh: 盜跖之山寨（象徵定位：山東泰山）

period: Zhuangzi ch. 10, c. 4th-3rd c. BCE (trans. Giles, 1889)

source.work: Chuang Tzu: Mystic, Moralist, and Social Reformer, trans. Herbert A. Giles, ch. 10

summary.en: An apprentice asks Robber Chê whether there is Tao in thieving. Pray tell me of something in which there is not, he answers — the wisdom to locate booty, the courage to go in first, the heroism to come out last, the shrewdness to calculate success, the justice to divide the spoil equally; there has never yet been a great robber without these five. It was the appearance of Sages that caused the appearance of great robbers.
summary.zh: 跖之徒問於跖曰：盜亦有道乎？跖曰：何適而無有道邪——妄意室中之藏，聖也；入先，勇也；出後，義也；知可否，知也；分均，仁也。聖人不死，大盜不止。

sensitivity.note: Canonical text of the Taoist canon (Nanhua zhenjing); Robber Chê is Zhuangzi's trickster foil to Confucian virtue. Included as a comparative text.

passages.text: An apprentice to Robber Chê asked him saying, "Is there then TAO in thieving?" "Pray tell me of something in which there is not TAO," Chê replied. "There is the wisdom by which booty is located. The courage to go in first, and the heroism of coming out last. There is the shrewdness of calculating success, and justice in the equal division of the spoil. There has never yet been, a great robber who was not possessed of these five."

Drive out the Sages and leave the robbers alone,--then only will the empire be governed. As when the stream ceases the gully dries up, and when the hill is levelled the chasm is filled; so when Sages are extinct, there will be no more robbers, but the empire will rest in peace.

title.en: The Golden Age of Knotted Cords (Zhuangzi)
title.zh: 結繩而用之：至德之世（莊子）

region.en: The age of Yung Ch'êng, Ta T'ing, and Shên Nung (symbolic pin: Song, Henan, China)
region.zh: 容成氏、大庭氏、神農之世（象徵定位：宋，今河南）

period: Zhuangzi ch. 10, c. 4th-3rd c. BCE (trans. Giles, 1889)

source.work: Chuang Tzu: Mystic, Moralist, and Social Reformer, trans. Herbert A. Giles, ch. 10

summary.en: In the Golden Age of the ancient rulers the people used knotted cords, were content with what food and raiment they could get, and lived simple and peaceful lives. Neighbouring districts were within sight, the cocks and dogs of one could be heard in the other — yet the people grew old and died without ever interchanging visits. In those days, government was indeed perfect.
summary.zh: 昔者容成氏、大庭氏、伯皇氏、中央氏、栗陸氏、驪畜氏、軒轅氏、赫胥氏、尊盧氏、祝融氏、伏羲氏、神農氏——當是時也，民結繩而用之，甘其食，美其服，鄰國相望，雞狗之音相聞，民至老死而不相往來。

sensitivity.note: Canonical text of the Taoist canon (Nanhua zhenjing); the Taoist Golden Age (parallel to the mythic first world). Included as a comparative text.

passages.text: Have you never heard of the Golden Age, the days of Yung Ch'êng, Ta T'ing, Poh Huang, Chung Yang, Li Lu, Li Hsü, Hsien Yüan, Hê Hsü, Tsun Lu, Chu Yung, Fu Hsi, and Shên Nung? Then the people used knotted cords.

They were contented with what food and raiment they could get. They lived simple and peaceful lives. Neighbouring districts were within sight, and the cocks and dogs of one could be heard in the other, yet the people grew old and died without ever interchanging visits. In those days, government was indeed perfect.

title.en: The Oilman and His Parrot
title.zh: 油商與其鸚鵡

region.en: Konya, shop of the oil-press (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 科尼亞油坊（象徵性定位）

period: Masnavi I Ma'navi, Book 1 (composed c. 1258-1264); E. H. Whinfield translation, 1887 (abridged), public domain

source.work: Jalaluddin Rumi, Masnavi I Ma'navi, translated and abridged by E. H. Whinfield (1887/1898), Book 1

summary.en: A parrot kept in the shop of an oilman speaks to the customers and drives away trade; the master threatens it, and the bird falls silent and shivers like a dead thing. The oilman carries it out and flings it on the dunghill. The bird rises on the wing, and the master learns that the parrot has taught the other parrots his own trade: silence is the one thing that cannot be talked about.
summary.zh: 油商鋪中一鸚鵡對客高談，趕走生意；主人威脅之，鳥遂默然顫抖如死物。油商攜之擲於糞堆。鳥振翅而起；主人方知鸚鵡已教眾鸚鵡他自己的營生：沉默乃無法言說之事。

sensitivity.note: Sufi parable of a living devotional tradition; paraphrased from the public-domain Whinfield abridgment.

passages.text: An oilman kept a parrot in his shop, a bird that could talk, and it talked the customers into and out of everything; trade went to ruin. The oilman threatened it, and the parrot fell silent and hung its head, and shivered, and made itself like a dead thing. The oilman grieved, and carried the bird out into the court, and flung it on the dunghill with the dead.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Rumi, Masnavi (Whinfield 1887), Book 1, 'The Oilman and his Parrot'; not verbatim.

passages.text: The parrot rose from the dunghill on the wing, and flew to the garden, and sat among the parrots of the garden. And when the master saw it fly, he understood: the bird had made itself dead that it might go free, and it had gone to teach the garden-parrots the one trade it knew — to be silent, and so escape the talker's snare. The moral of the tale is the speechlessness of the lover of God, who must be nothing, that he may be all.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Rumi, Masnavi (Whinfield 1887), Book 1; not verbatim.

title.en: Moses and the Shepherd
title.zh: 穆薩與牧羊人

region.en: Wayside in the wilderness of Sinai (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 西奈曠野路旁（象徵性定位）

period: Masnavi I Ma'navi, Book 2 (composed c. 1264); E. H. Whinfield translation, 1887, public domain

source.work: Jalaluddin Rumi, Masnavi I Ma'navi, translated and abridged by E. H. Whinfield (1887/1898), Book 2

summary.en: A shepherd on the road praises God in shepherd's words: 'I will comb thy hair, I will milk thee, I will kiss thy hand.' Moses rebukes him: 'Thou hast joined to God what does not become Him.' The shepherd tears his garment and departs. A voice comes to Moses: 'Thou hast come to unite, not to sever — I look not at the tongue and the speech; I look at the inward spirit.' Moses runs after the shepherd, who has understood: 'To each his own form of worship.'
summary.zh: 牧羊人以牧人言辭讚主：『我要為你梳髮、擠奶、吻你之手。』穆薩斥之：『你以不當之物配主。』牧人撕裂其衣而去。有聲臨穆薩：『你來是為聯合，非為割裂——我不看言與語，我看內在之靈。』穆薩追上牧人，牧人已悟：『各有各的敬拜形式。』

sensitivity.note: Sufi parable of a living devotional tradition; paraphrased from the public-domain Whinfield abridgment; the tale's theology is the poet's own, not scripture.

passages.text: A shepherd saw Moses on the road and said, 'Where art thou going, beloved of God?' Moses said, 'To pray to God, that He may pardon our sins.' The shepherd said, 'I will pray with thee'; and he prayed in shepherd's words: 'O God, I will comb Thy hair and wash Thy garments and kiss Thy hand and milk Thee, and bring Thee to my tent.' Moses said, 'What babbling is this? Thou hast joined to God what does not become Him: milk, and a comb, and sandals!' The shepherd tore his garment, sighed, and fled into the desert.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Rumi, Masnavi (Whinfield 1887), Book 2, 'Moses and the Shepherd'; not verbatim.

passages.text: Then came a revelation to Moses: 'Thou hast come to unite, and thou hast severed. I look not at the tongue and the speech; I look at the inward spirit and the state. What are courtesy and the canons of speech? The light of the heart is my desire. Thou art gone to the temple and the law; and he has gone to be intoxicated with the Beloved. Thy way is good, his way is good too.' And Moses ran after the shepherd, who understood at last: 'To each his own form of worship; the Sufi has no kite and quarry but God.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Rumi, Masnavi (Whinfield 1887), Book 2; not verbatim.

title.en: The Elephant in the Dark
title.zh: 黑暗中的大象

region.en: Konya, a dark house by night (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 科尼亞夜間暗屋（象徵性定位）

period: Masnavi I Ma'navi, Book 3 (composed c. 1264); E. H. Whinfield translation, 1887, public domain

source.work: Jalaluddin Rumi, Masnavi I Ma'navi, translated and abridged by E. H. Whinfield (1887/1898), Book 3

summary.en: An elephant is brought for show to a dark house; the visitors enter by a lamp each in turn and come out with different reports: a water-pipe, a fan, a pillar, a throne. They quarrel all night with candles in their hands. Had each held a candle, they had been one word short of truth — but each had only one lamp, and the elephant is only a figure of the Real, which each partial seer names after the part his hand has found.
summary.zh: 一象供觀賞置於暗屋；參觀者各持一燈輪流入，出而各異其辭：水管、扇、柱、御座。他們徹夜執燭相爭。若各持全燭，則離真理僅一詞——然每人只有一燈；象只是實在的比喻，各偏見者以手所觸之部分而名之。

sensitivity.note: Sufi parable of a living devotional tradition; paraphrased from the public-domain Whinfield abridgment.

passages.text: Some Hindoos were exhibiting an elephant, and all the people desired to see it; but the house was too dark, and so a lamp was provided, and the beholders went in one by one. In the dark they felt the beast with their hands, and each came out and gave a different report: one had found the trunk and cried 'A water-pipe!' another the ear and cried 'A fan!' another the leg and cried 'A pillar!' another the back and cried 'A throne!'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Rumi, Masnavi (Whinfield 1887), Book 3, 'The Elephant in the Dark'; not verbatim.

passages.text: They quarrelled all night with candles in their hands, each calling the others liars. If each had held a candle, the discrepancy would have gone out of their words — for all would have seen the one elephant. And the tale is told, says Rumi, of the seers and sects, who each see one member of the Real in the dark of this world, and each name it after the part his hand has found.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Rumi, Masnavi (Whinfield 1887), Book 3; not verbatim.

title.en: The Travellers Who Ate the Young Elephant
title.zh: 食幼象的旅人

region.en: Wilderness road of India (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 印度曠野之路（象徵性定位）

period: Masnavi I Ma'navi, Book 3, Story I (composed c. 1264); E. H. Whinfield translation, 1887, public domain

source.work: Jalaluddin Rumi, Masnavi I Ma'navi, translated and abridged by E. H. Whinfield (1887/1898), Book 3, Story I

summary.en: A party lost in the wilderness is starving; a sage shows them young elephants in the wood and warns them that the parents will track and avenge. They kill and eat one, and sleep; in the morning each has hidden in a different quarter, and the great elephants find them out one by one and trample them — every one, as the sage had said, except the man who told him where they were going.
summary.zh: 迷途之眾瀕餓；一智者示林中幼象，並警其父母必追而復仇。眾殺而食之一，睡去；晨間各匿不同方位，巨象逐一尋出踐踏——如智者所言，無一倖免，惟那位曾告訴智者去向者得免。

sensitivity.note: Sufi parable of a living devotional tradition; paraphrased from the public-domain Whinfield abridgment.

passages.text: A party of travellers lost their way in a wilderness and were well-nigh famished. A sage came up and condoled with them, and told them there were many young elephants in the adjacent woods, one of which would furnish an ample meal; but he warned them that if they killed one, its parents would in all probability track them out and be revenged. They saw a plump young elephant, and could not resist killing and eating it.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Rumi, Masnavi (Whinfield 1887), Book 3, Story I; not verbatim.

passages.text: They slept, and each, it is said, hid himself in a different quarter, and one told the sage where they meant to hide. In the morning the great elephants came, and went from hiding-place to hiding-place, and trampled them one by one, every man of them — as the sage had said; and only the man who had told him where they were going came off alive. The moral, says Rumi, is of the men who slay the young of the Lord's creatures and think their hiding from the elephant is hiding from God.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Rumi, Masnavi (Whinfield 1887), Book 3, Story I; not verbatim.

title.en: The Fowler and the Bird
title.zh: 捕鳥者與鳥

region.en: Rooftop snare, Konya (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 科尼亞屋頂羅網（象徵性定位）

period: Masnavi I Ma'navi, Book 1 (composed c. 1258-1264); E. H. Whinfield translation, 1887, public domain

source.work: Jalaluddin Rumi, Masnavi I Ma'navi, translated and abridged by E. H. Whinfield (1887/1898), Book 1

summary.en: A fowler snares a little bird on a roof, and the bird sings three songs to ransom itself: the first from the snare, the second from the hand, the third from the heart of the fowler — 'Three counsels I give in the mouth of thy three gates.' The first: 'Regret not what is past.' The second: 'Do not believe impossibilities.' The third: 'A pearl of great price lies in thy own garden; do not dig beyond it.' And the bird, escaping, mocks him gently: the pearl is its own body, which the fowler held and let go.
summary.zh: 捕鳥者於屋頂網得一鳥；鳥唱三歌贖身：第一歌贖自羅網，第二贖自手中，第三贖自捕者之心——『我以三言付汝三門之口』。其一：『勿悔既往。』其二：『勿信不可能之事。』其三：『至寶之珠在汝園中；勿掘園外。』鳥脫逃後溫言相嘲：珠即其身——捕者曾握而放之。

sensitivity.note: Sufi parable of a living devotional tradition; paraphrased from the public-domain Whinfield abridgment.

passages.text: A fowler caught a little bird in a snare on the roof, and would have killed it; and the bird spoke: 'What wilt thou do with me? I am not a mouthful.' And it said, 'I will give thee three counsels, if thou let me go: the first on thy fingers, the second at the gate, the third in the heart of the field.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Rumi, Masnavi (Whinfield 1887), Book 1, 'The Fowler and the Bird'; not verbatim.

passages.text: The first counsel, given on the fingers: 'Regret not what is past.' The second, given standing free: 'Do not believe impossibilities — believe not that a bird should weigh six ounces and be heavier than an elephant.' And the third, given as it flew from the tree: 'In thy belly are thirty paces of pearl; but beyond thy own garden do not dig.' And the fowler stood repenting of his greed, and the bird called out: 'The pearl is my little body, which thou didst hold and didst let go.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Rumi, Masnavi (Whinfield 1887), Book 1; not verbatim.

title.en: The Sufi and the Qazi
title.zh: 蘇菲與法官

region.en: Court of the qazi, Konya (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 科尼亞法官法庭（象徵性定位）

period: Masnavi I Ma'navi, Book 1 (composed c. 1258-1264); E. H. Whinfield translation, 1887, public domain

source.work: Jalaluddin Rumi, Masnavi I Ma'navi, translated and abridged by E. H. Whinfield (1887/1898), Book 1

summary.en: A qazi of the city judges by the letter; a wandering dervish is brought before him. The dervish tells the story of the jurist who slept with the light burning and demanded of the night why it had robbed him — and the tale turns the court's own grammar against it. The qazi is silent; the dervish goes; and the poem says the judge of the letter has never seen the day of the spirit.
summary.zh: 城中法官依字面而判；一行腳苦行僧被帶至其前。苦行僧講述一法官燃燈而眠、向夜索其被竊之光的故事——此喻反轉法庭自身之語法。法官默然；苦行僧離去；詩云字面之判者未嘗見靈之晝。

sensitivity.note: Sufi anecdote of a living devotional tradition; paraphrased from the public-domain Whinfield abridgment.

passages.text: A qazi judged by the letter of the law, and a wandering dervish was brought before him. The dervish answered him with a tale: of a jurist who slept with his lamp burning, and rose and demanded of the night why it had stolen his light — and of the judge who fined the flood for wetting his shoes.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Rumi, Masnavi (Whinfield 1887), Book 1, 'The Sufi and the Qazi'; not verbatim.

passages.text: The court was silent; the dervish went his way; and the poem's moral is of the jurists who have the letter and not the spirit — 'The fish of the letter is caught in the net of the word, and the man of the sea has gone free.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Rumi, Masnavi (Whinfield 1887), Book 1; not verbatim.

title.en: The King and His Three Sons
title.zh: 國王與其三子

region.en: Royal court and artisan quarter (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 王廷與工匠坊（象徵性定位）

period: Masnavi I Ma'navi, Book 1 (composed c. 1258-1264); E. H. Whinfield translation, 1887, public domain

source.work: Jalaluddin Rumi, Masnavi I Ma'navi, translated and abridged by E. H. Whinfield (1887/1898), Book 1

summary.en: Three princes are set to learn a trade; one learns archery, one the manufacture of arrows, one the cure of men. War comes: the archer can no longer use his art, the arrow-maker's wares are taken, and only the healer is wanted. Rumi's moral: the art of healing souls is the trade that no misfortune dearness makes dearer or cheaper.
summary.zh: 三王子奉命習藝：一習射，一習製箭，一習醫人。戰事起：射者技無所用，製箭者貨物被奪，惟醫者受求。魯米之旨：醫治靈魂之藝乃無論窮通皆受求之業。

sensitivity.note: Sufi parable of a living devotional tradition; paraphrased from the public-domain Whinfield abridgment.

passages.text: A king set his three sons to learn trades. One learned archery, and became the finest bowman of the age; one learned to make arrows, and his wares filled the market; and the third learned to heal the bodies and souls of men. War came, and the archer's art stood idle, and the arrow-maker's stock was seized for the king's men; only the healer was wanted, in war and in peace alike.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Rumi, Masnavi (Whinfield 1887), Book 1, 'The King and his Three Sons'; not verbatim.

passages.text: Rumi's moral is of the science of the saints: the trade that is never dearer for need nor cheaper for peace — the healing of the soul, which every age requires, and which no misfortune can take from the man who has learned it.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Rumi, Masnavi (Whinfield 1887), Book 1; not verbatim.

title.en: The Man Who Was Tattooed
title.zh: 刺青之人

region.en: Konya, shop of the tattooer (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 科尼亞刺青師鋪（象徵性定位）

period: Masnavi I Ma'navi, Book 1 (composed c. 1258-1264); E. H. Whinfield translation, 1887, public domain

source.work: Jalaluddin Rumi, Masnavi I Ma'navi, translated and abridged by E. H. Whinfield (1887/1898), Book 1

summary.en: A man goes to be tattooed with the figures of a lion on his shoulder, an eagle on his breast, a garland about his thigh. The needle touches his shoulder: 'What are you drawing?' — 'A lion.' 'Begin with the tail, for the shoulder is a tender place.' The needle touches his back: 'What now?' — 'An eagle.' 'Begin at the tail, for the back is tender.' — 'Begin at the thigh.' The artist throws down the needle: 'God never made a man with a tailless lion, a wingless eagle and a headless garland.'
summary.zh: 一人往刺青，欲肩繪獅、胸繪鷹、股繞花環。針及肩：『你畫什麼？』——『獅。』『先從尾開始，肩是嫩處。』針及背：『現在呢？』——『鷹。』『先從尾開始，背是嫩處。』——『從股開始。』刺青師擲針：『主造人從未有無尾之獅、無翼之鷹、無頭之花環。』

sensitivity.note: Sufi anecdote of a living devotional tradition; paraphrased from the public-domain Whinfield abridgment.

passages.text: A man went to the tattooer to be marked with a lion on his shoulder, an eagle on his breast and a garland about his thigh. The needle began at the shoulder: 'What art thou drawing?' 'A lion.' 'Begin with the tail, for the shoulder is a tender place.' The needle began at the back: 'What now?' 'An eagle.' 'Begin at the tail, for the back is tender.' 'Then begin at the thigh.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Rumi, Masnavi (Whinfield 1887), Book 1, 'The Man who was Tattooed'; not verbatim.

passages.text: The artist threw down the needle and said: 'God never made a man with a tailless lion and a wingless eagle and a headless garland.' The moral, says Rumi, is of the dervish who would have the delight of the path without its pain — who will be a lion in the spirit if he may be spared the needle.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Rumi, Masnavi (Whinfield 1887), Book 1; not verbatim.

title.en: The Human Heart: Ts'ui Chü Asks Lao Tzŭ (Zhuangzi)
title.zh: 崔瞿問老聃：人心（莊子）

region.en: Lao Tzŭ's retreat (symbolic pin: Ku county, Bozhou, Anhui, China)
region.zh: 老聃之居（象徵定位：安徽亳州苦縣）

period: Zhuangzi ch. 11, c. 4th-3rd c. BCE (trans. Giles, 1889)

source.work: Chuang Tzu: Mystic, Moralist, and Social Reformer, trans. Herbert A. Giles, ch. 11

summary.en: Ts'ui Chü asks how men's hearts can be kept in order if the empire is not governed. Lao Tzŭ answers: no bolt can bar, no bond can bind, such is the human heart — and blames the Yellow Emperor's charity for the chain of coercion that followed, ending with the Confucianists and Mihists preaching amid gyves and fetters. Abandon wisdom and discard knowledge, and the empire will be at peace.
summary.zh: 崔瞿問於老聃曰：不治天下，安藏人心？老聃曰：女慎無攖人心——一宅而寓於無形，不可內於靈臺；其居也淵而靜，其動也縣而天。

sensitivity.note: Canonical text of the Taoist canon (Nanhua zhenjing). Included as a comparative text — a scholarly framing, not a claim about religious truth.

passages.text: "Be careful," replied Lao Tzŭ, "not to interfere with the natural goodness of the heart of man. Man's heart may be forced down or stirred up. In each case the issue is fatal. "By gentleness, the hardest heart may be softened. But try to cut and polish it,--'twill glow like fire or freeze like ice. In the twinkling of an eye it will pass beyond the limits of the Four Seas. In repose, profoundly still; in motion, far away in the sky. No bolt can bar, no bond can bind,--such is the human heart."

"Of old, the Yellow Emperor first caused charity and duty to one's neighbour to interfere with the natural goodness of the heart of man. In consequence of which, Yao and Shun wore the hair off their legs in endeavouring to feed their people. They disturbed their internal economy in order to find room for charity and duty to one's neighbour. They exhausted their energies in framing laws and statutes. Still they did not succeed.

"Until I can say that the wisdom of Sages is not a fastener of cangues, and that charity and duty to one's neighbour are not bolts for gyves, how should I know that Tsêng and Shih are not the forerunners of Chieh and Chê? Therefore I said, 'Abandon wisdom and discard knowledge, and the empire will be at peace.'"

title.en: The Yellow Emperor Visits Kuang Ch'êng Tzŭ on Mount K'ung-t'ung (Zhuangzi)
title.zh: 黃帝問道於空同廣成子（莊子）

region.en: Mount K'ung-t'ung (Kongtongshan, Gansu, China)
region.zh: 空同山（甘肅崆峒山）

period: Zhuangzi ch. 11, c. 4th-3rd c. BCE (trans. Giles, 1889)

source.work: Chuang Tzu: Mystic, Moralist, and Social Reformer, trans. Herbert A. Giles, ch. 11

summary.en: The Yellow Emperor, whose laws ruled the empire, climbs Mount K'ung-t'ung to ask the immortal Kuang Ch'êng Tzŭ for the perfect Tao. Rebuffed once — for under his rule clouds rained before thickening and the sun's brightness paled — he abdicates for three months and kneels in the dust, and the master grants the inner teaching of seeing nothing and hearing nothing, of the gates of Great Light and Profound Mystery, of a self preserved twelve hundred years.
summary.zh: 黃帝立為天子十九年，聞廣成子在空同之上，往見之；再拜稽首而問：治身奈何而可以長久？廣成子曰：至道之精，窈窈冥冥——無視無聽，抱神以靜，形將自正。

sensitivity.note: Canonical text of the Taoist canon (Nanhua zhenjing); the founding scene of the Yellow-Emperor-and-the-Immortal-Master topos in Daoist hagiography. Included as a comparative text.

passages.text: The Yellow Emperor sat on the throne for nineteen years, and his laws obtained all over the empire. Hearing that Kuang Ch'êng Tzŭ was living on Mount K'ung-t'ung, he went thither to see him, and said, "I am told, Sir, that you are in possession of perfect TAO. May I ask in what perfect TAO consists? I desire to avail myself of the good influence of heaven and earth in order to secure harvests and feed my people. I should also like to control the Two Powers of nature in order to the protection of all living things. How can I accomplish this?" "What you desire to avail yourself of," replied Kuang Ch'êng Tzŭ, "is the primordial integrity of matter. What you wish to control are the disintegrators thereof. Ever since the empire has been governed by you, the clouds have rained without waiting to thicken, the foliage of trees has fallen without waiting to grow yellow, the brightness of the sun and moon has paled, and the voice of the flatterer is heard on every side. How then speak of perfect TAO?"

The Yellow Emperor withdrew. He resigned the Throne. He built himself a solitary hut. He lay upon straw. For three months he remained in seclusion, and then went again to see Kuang Ch'êng Tzŭ. The latter was lying down with his face to the south. The Yellow Emperor approached after the manner of an inferior, upon his knees. Prostrating himself upon the ground he said, "I am told, Sir, that you are in possession of perfect TAO. May I ask how my self may be preserved so as to last?" Kuang Ch'êng Tzŭ jumped up with a start. "A good question indeed!" cried he. "Come, and I will speak to you of perfect TAO.

"See nothing; hear nothing; let your soul be wrapped in quiet; and your body will begin to take proper form. Let there be absolute repose and absolute purity; do not weary your body nor disturb your vitality,--and you will live for ever. For if the eye sees nothing, and the ear hears nothing, and the mind thinks nothing, the soul will preserve the body, and the body will live for ever.

"Cherish that which is within you, and shut off that which is without; for much knowledge is a curse. Then I will place you upon that abode of Great Light which is the source of the positive Power, and escort you through the gate of Profound Mystery which is the source of the negative Power. These Powers are the controllers of heaven and earth, and each contains the other. ... I preserve the original ONE, while resting in harmony with externals. It is because I have thus cared for my self now for twelve hundred years that my body has not decayed." The Yellow Emperor prostrated himself and said, "Kuang Ch'êng Tzŭ is surely God...."

title.en: The Spirit of the Clouds Meets the Vital Principle (Zhuangzi)
title.zh: 雲將遇鴻蒙（莊子）

region.en: The expanse of air east of Yu-sung (symbolic pin: Songshan, Henan, China)
region.zh: 過有宋之野而適遭鴻蒙（象徵定位：河南嵩山）

period: Zhuangzi ch. 11, c. 4th-3rd c. BCE (trans. Giles, 1889)

source.work: Chuang Tzu: Mystic, Moralist, and Social Reformer, trans. Herbert A. Giles, ch. 11

summary.en: The Spirit of the Clouds, passing east, falls in with the Vital Principle slapping his ribs and hopping about. He wishes to harmonise the six influences and nourish all living beings; three years later the answer comes: rest in inaction and the world will be good of itself — cast your slough, spit forth intelligence, become one with the infinite, release your mind, free your soul, be vacuous, be nothing.
summary.zh: 雲將東遊，過扶搖之枝而適遭鴻蒙；鴻蒙方將拊脾雀躍而遊。雲將曰：願合六氣之精以育群生——鴻蒙曰：意！心養。汝徒處無為，而物自化。

sensitivity.note: Canonical text of the Taoist canon (Nanhua zhenjing); the cloud-spirit dialogue is a cosmogonic theophany scene. Included as a comparative text.

passages.text: The Spirit of the Clouds when passing eastwards through the expanse of Air happened to fall in with the Vital Principle. The latter was slapping his ribs and hopping about; whereupon the Spirit of the Clouds said, "Who are you, old man, and what are you doing here?" "Strolling!" replied the Vital Principle, without stopping. "I want to know something," continued the Spirit of the Clouds. "Ah!" uttered the Vital Principle, in a tone of disapprobation. "The relationship of heaven and earth is out of harmony," said the Spirit of the Clouds; "the six influences do not combine, and the four seasons are no longer regular. I desire to blend the six influences so as to nourish all living beings. What am I to do?" "I do not know!" cried the Vital Principle, shaking his head, while still slapping his ribs and hopping about; "I do not know!"

"That the scheme of empire is in confusion," said the Vital Principle, "that the conditions of life are violated, that the will of God does not triumph, that the beasts of the field are disorganised, that the birds of the air cry at night, that blight reaches the trees and herbs, that destruction spreads among creeping things,--this, alas! is the fault of government." "True," replied the Spirit of the Clouds, "but what am I to do?" "It is here," cried the Vital Principle, "that the poison lurks! Go back!"

"Feed then your people," said the Vital Principle, "with your heart. Rest in inaction, and the world will be good of itself. Cast your slough. Spit forth intelligence. Ignore all differences. Become one with the infinite. Release your mind. Free your soul. Be vacuous. Be Nothing! Let all things revert to their original constitution. If they do this, without knowledge, the result will be a simple purity which they will never lose; but knowledge will bring with it a divergence therefrom. Seek not the names nor the relations of things, and all things will flourish of themselves."

title.en: Rabia's Fire and Water
title.zh: 拉比雅的火與水

region.en: Basra, streets of the woman-saint (literal pin)
region.zh: 巴士拉女聖徒的街市（實際定位）

period: Anecdotes preserved in Attar, Tadhkirat al-Awliya (Arabic-Persian, 12th c.); English: R. A. Nicholson, The Mystics of Islam (1914), public domain

source.work: R. A. Nicholson, The Mystics of Islam (1914), ch. on the Path; anecdotes of Rabia from Attar's Tadhkirat al-Awliya

license: Public domain (English edition 1914; Arabic-Persian originals medieval)

summary.en: Rabia al-Adawiyya, the freed slave-girl of Basra who became the mother of the Sufi doctrine of love, was seen one day carrying a torch in one hand and a pail of water in the other. 'I will burn the gardens of Paradise and drown the fires of Hell, that men may worship God neither for fear nor for reward — but for Himself alone.'
summary.zh: 巴士拉女奴出身的拉比雅·阿達維亞——蘇菲愛之學說的奠基者——一日手執火把與水桶而行。『我要燒盡樂園的園囿、澆熄火獄之火，使人敬拜主既非因懼亦非因賞——只為主自身。』

sensitivity.note: Sufi hagiography of a living devotional tradition; paraphrased from public-domain sources.

passages.text: Rabia al-Adawiyya of Basra, the freed slave-girl who became the mother of the Sufi doctrine of love, was seen in the streets one day with a torch in one hand and a pail of water in the other. 'Why do you carry fire and water?' she was asked. She said: 'I will burn the gardens of Paradise with the one, and drown the fires of Hell with the other, that men may come to worship God without hope and without fear — for Himself alone.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of the anecdote in Attar's Tadhkirat al-Awliya as given in Nicholson, The Mystics of Islam (1914); not verbatim.

title.en: Ibrahim ibn Adham: The Prince Who Rode Away
title.zh: 易卜拉欣·本·阿丹：騎馬而去的王子

region.en: Balkh, capital of the prince (literal pin)
region.zh: 巴爾赫王子之都（實際定位）

period: Anecdotes preserved in Attar, Tadhkirat al-Awliya (12th c.); English: R. A. Nicholson, The Mystics of Islam (1914), public domain

source.work: R. A. Nicholson, The Mystics of Islam (1914); anecdotes of Ibrahim ibn Adham from the Tadhkirat tradition

license: Public domain (English edition 1914; Arabic-Persian originals medieval)

summary.en: Ibrahim ibn Adham, king of Balkh, was hunting when a voice called after his horse: 'You were not created for this; nor were you created for that.' He looked and saw nothing; the call came again; the third time he rode away from his kingdom with his pilgrim's cloak, and took service as a watchman of orchards — the Prince who renounced, cousin of the Buddha's story told in the Islam of Khurasan.
summary.zh: 巴爾赫王易卜拉欣·本·阿丹狩獵之際，有聲自其馬後呼：『你非為此而受造；亦非為彼。』他環顧無所見；呼聲再至；第三次，他棄其王位，披朝聖者之氅而去，受雇為果園守夜人——放棄王位之王子，呼羅珊伊斯蘭中佛本生故事的親緣。

sensitivity.note: Sufi hagiography of a living devotional tradition; the renunciation tale parallels Buddhist and Christian withdrawal legends; cross-traditional motif tagging is interpretive.

passages.text: Ibrahim ibn Adham was king of Balkh. One day he was hunting, and a voice called after him on his horse: 'You were not created for this; nor were you created for that.' He looked and saw nobody. The call came again from behind him, and again; and the third time he took off his royal cloak and rode away from his kingdom, and became a watchman of the orchards and a waiter at the tables of others.
passages.note: Paraphrase of the anecdote in Attar's Tadhkirat al-Awliya as given in Nicholson, The Mystics of Islam (1914); not verbatim.

passages.text: It is told of him that he served his years in silence, and that when his servants found him and would have brought him back, he said: 'My kingdom is not of Balkh.' The hagiographers make him the pattern of the great renunciation in the Islam of Khurasan; and the tale has travelled as far as the story of the prince who left the palace for the road, in every telling of it, from the Ganges to the Oxus.
passages.note: Paraphrase of the anecdote tradition; not verbatim.

title.en: Hallaj on the Gibbet: 'Ana al-Haqq'
title.zh: 哈拉吉於十字架：「我即真理」

region.en: Baghdad, gibbet of the Mansur gate (literal pin)
region.zh: 巴格達曼蘇爾門十字架（實際定位）

period: Event 922 CE; anecdotes in Attar, Tadhkirat al-Awliya (12th c.); English: R. A. Nicholson, The Mystics of Islam (1914), public domain

source.work: R. A. Nicholson, The Mystics of Islam (1914); the Hallaj tradition

license: Public domain (English edition 1914; Arabic-Persian originals medieval)

summary.en: Al-Husayn ibn Mansur al-Hallaj, the Sufi of Baghdad, cried in the streets the word the jurists could not forgive: 'Ana al-Haqq' — I am the Truth. He was imprisoned for years, scourged, mutilated, and at last gibbeted; and the legend tells that his blood was two words written on the ground, and that passers-by asked him of the love of God as they walked beneath him.
summary.zh: 巴格達蘇菲胡賽因·本·曼蘇爾·哈拉吉於街市喊出法學家不能容之語：『我即真理』（Ana al-Haqq）。他被囚多年，受笞刑、殘肢，最後被釘於十字架；相傳其血於地上寫成兩個字，而行人在其下經過時仍向他問主之愛。

sensitivity.note: Sufi hagiography of a living devotional tradition; the trial and execution are matters of doctrine and history alike; presented as the received narrative.

passages.text: Al-Hallaj, the wool-carder of Baghdad, cried in the streets the word the jurists could not forgive: 'Ana al-Haqq' — I am the Truth. He was cast into prison for years, and scourged, and mutilated; and in the gibbet he was heard to pray: 'Pardon them; for if Thou hadst revealed to them what Thou hast revealed to me, they would not have done what they did.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of the Hallaj tradition as given in Nicholson, The Mystics of Islam (1914), and Attar's Tadhkirat; not verbatim.

passages.text: The legend adds that when they questioned him on the gibbet he asked for his Lord, and that his blood wrote two words on the ground as it fell; and the Sufi poets took him for the martyr of the doctrine that the lover and the Beloved are one — and the jurists made of him a warning. Both readings have carried his name for a thousand years.
passages.note: Paraphrase of the Hallaj tradition; not verbatim.

title.en: Bishr al-Hafi and the Scrap of Paper
title.zh: 比希爾·哈菲與紙片

region.en: Baghdad, street of the taverns (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 巴格達酒肆之街（象徵性定位）

period: Anecdotes in Attar, Tadhkirat al-Awliya (12th c.); English: R. A. Nicholson, The Mystics of Islam (1914), public domain

source.work: R. A. Nicholson, The Mystics of Islam (1914); the Bishr al-Hafi tradition

license: Public domain (English edition 1914; Arabic-Persian originals medieval)

summary.en: Bishr ibn al-Harith, called al-Hafi (the Barefoot), the young rake of Baghdad, found one night in the street a scrap of paper bearing the name of God, trodden in the mud. He bought it, washed it, perfumed it, and buried it; and that night, the story says, he was told in sleep: 'Thou hast honoured My name; I have forgiven thee, and made thee and thy parents of My friends.' He rose barefoot, and was called the Barefoot ever after.
summary.zh: 巴格達的浪蕩青年比希爾·本·哈里斯——後稱『赤足者』（al-Hafi）——一夜於街上拾得一片寫著主名、陷於泥濘被踐踏的紙。他買下它，洗之、熏之、葬之；相傳當夜夢中被告知：『你尊崇了我的名；我已赦你，並使你與你的父母成為我的朋友。』他赤足而起，自是稱為赤足者。

sensitivity.note: Sufi hagiography of a living devotional tradition; paraphrased from public-domain sources.

passages.text: Bishr ibn al-Harith, the young rake of Baghdad, found one night in the street a scrap of paper bearing the name of God, trodden in the mud. He bought it for a dinar from the man who had cast it away, and washed it and perfumed it, and buried it where the ground was clean.
passages.note: Paraphrase of the anecdote in Attar's Tadhkirat al-Awliya as given in Nicholson, The Mystics of Islam (1914); not verbatim.

passages.text: That night, the story says, he was told in sleep: 'Thou hast honoured My name; I have forgiven thee, and made thee and thy parents of My friends.' He rose barefoot, and gave up the tavern, and was called al-Hafi, the Barefoot, ever after; and his teacher Fudayl said of him: 'He was the wickedest of men, and he became one of the best.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of the anecdote tradition; not verbatim.

title.en: Fudayl the Brigand Repents at the Wall
title.zh: 強盜福戴爾在牆下悔悟

region.en: City wall of Merv / Rayy (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 梅爾夫／賴夷城牆（象徵性定位）

period: Anecdotes in Attar, Tadhkirat al-Awliya (12th c.); English: R. A. Nicholson, The Mystics of Islam (1914), public domain

source.work: R. A. Nicholson, The Mystics of Islam (1914); the Fudayl ibn Iyad tradition

license: Public domain (English edition 1914; Arabic-Persian originals medieval)

summary.en: Fudayl ibn Iyad was a highwayman of Khurasan. He lay in wait one night and saw a traveller scaling the city wall, and asked him what he did. 'I am going to a woman I love.' 'And if you are seen?' — 'I fear being seen by men.' 'And do you not fear the sight of God?'
