region.en: First settlement of Adam's children (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 阿丹子女的首處聚居地（象徵性定位）

period: Qisas al-Anbiya tradition (Arabic, c. 8th-11th centuries CE); paraphrase from Arabic

source.archive: Wikisource (Arabic; al-Kisa’i, Qisas al-Anbiya, Leiden ed. 1922)
source.work: Qisas al-Anbiya / tafsir legends (al-Tabari, al-Kisa'i); passages paraphrased from Arabic

license: Arabic original public domain; paraphrase original

summary.en: The legend fills the motive of the first murder: Adam's children were born in twin pairs, boy and girl, and the law of the time was that each brother should marry his own twin-sister from another pair — not his own. Abel's twin was the fairer; Cain refused to take his own and demanded his brother's; Adam bade them offer a sacrifice, and the fire from heaven decided. Cain slew, and the first city was built on the first grave.
summary.zh: 傳說補足首宗謀殺之動機：阿丹子女皆為雙生——一男一女；當時之法，各兄弟當娶另一對的雙生姊妹，而非自己的。亞伯的雙生妹貌美；該隱拒娶己妹而求其弟之妹；阿丹命二人獻祭，天火定奪。該隱殺之；首座城築於首個墳墓之上。

sensitivity.note: Qisas legend of a living tradition; the twin-marriage motif parallels origin-of-death and sibling clusters; paraphrased from the Arabic original; motif tagging is interpretive.

passages.text: Adam's children, the legend says, were born in twin pairs, boy and girl together; and the law of that first age was that each brother should marry his twin-sister from another pair, but not his own. Abel's twin was the fairer of the two; and Cain refused to take his own sister and demanded his brother's.
passages.note: Paraphrase of al-Tabari, Tarikh (Arabic); not verbatim.

passages.text: Adam bade them settle it by an offering: each to bring a sacrifice, and the fire from heaven to take the acceptable one. The fire came down on Abel's lamb and left Cain's sheaf; and Cain said to his brother, 'I will slay thee.' And he slew him — and the legend adds that the first city of the world was built by the line of Cain on the first grave of the world.
passages.note: Paraphrase of al-Tabari, Tarikh (Arabic); not verbatim.

title.en: Muhammad ibn Qasim and the Conquest of Sind
title.zh: 穆罕默德·本·卡西姆與信德征服

region.en: Indus delta, Debal and Daybul (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 印度河三角洲，迪巴勒（象徵性定位）

period: Event 711-713 CE; English: W. Muir, The Caliphate (1891), ch. 37

source.work: William Muir, The Caliphate (1891), ch. 37 (conquest of Sind); from the Arabic Chachnama tradition

license: Public domain (English edition 1891; Arabic-Persian originals medieval)

summary.en: A girl taken by pirates from Sind calls on the caliph from the slave-market of Baghdad — 'I am a daughter of the chiefs of Sind.' Walid sends the young general Muhammad ibn Qasim with six thousand, and the fort of Debal is taken by the stone-thrower that was carried by five hundred men; the pirates' stronghold falls, and the Indus is opened. The young general is recalled, and the tale of his recall is one of the grey anecdotes of the caliphal court.
summary.zh: 一信德女子被海盜擄至巴格達奴市，向哈里發呼救——『我是信德酋長之女。』瓦利德遣青年統帥穆罕默德·本·卡西姆率六千人，以五百人抬運的投石機攻陷迪巴勒要塞；海盜巢穴傾覆，印度河開通。青年統帥被召回；其召回之事成為哈里發宮廷灰色軼事之一。

sensitivity.note: Early Islamic historiography of the eastern conquests; the Ibn Qasim episode opens eight centuries of Muslim presence in the subcontinent; paraphrased from Muir.

passages.text: A girl taken by pirates from the coast of Sind was set in the slave-market of Baghdad, and she called on the caliph in his own hall: 'I am a daughter of the chiefs of Sind; avenge me.' Walid sent the young general Muhammad ibn Qasim with six thousand men, and the fort of Debal, the pirates' stronghold, was taken by the great stone-thrower that was carried by five hundred.
passages.note: Paraphrase of the Chachnama tradition via Muir, The Caliphate (1891), ch. 37; not verbatim.

passages.text: The Indus was opened to the Arabs, and the towns of the river came under tribute; and the young general was recalled in the change of caliphs, and the tale of his recall is told among the grey anecdotes of the court. The conquest of Sind opened eight centuries of Muslim presence in the subcontinent.
passages.note: Paraphrase of the Chachnama tradition via Muir, The Caliphate (1891); not verbatim.

title.en: Stretching Like a Bear, Craning Like a Bird (Zhuangzi)
title.zh: 吹呴呼吸，熊經鳥申（莊子）

region.en: The hygienists' court (symbolic pin: Song, Henan, China)
region.zh: 導引之士（象徵定位：宋，今河南）

period: Zhuangzi ch. 15, c. 4th-3rd c. BCE (trans. Giles, 1889)

source.work: Chuang Tzu: Mystic, Moralist, and Social Reformer, trans. Herbert A. Giles, ch. 15

summary.en: Exhaling and inhaling, getting rid of the old and assimilating the new, stretching like a bear and craning like a bird — this is but valetudinarianism, affected by professors of hygiene and those who try to preserve the body to the age of P'êng Tsu. But in health without hygiene there is oblivion absolute coupled with possession of all things.
summary.zh: 吹呴呼吸，吐故納新，熊經鳥申，為壽而已矣；此導引之士，養形之人，彭祖壽考者之所好也。

sensitivity.note: Canonical text of the Taoist canon (Nanhua zhenjing); the earliest textual mention of daoyin health gymnastics, the aition of the breath-practices. Included as a comparative text.

passages.text: Exhaling and inhaling, getting rid of the old and assimilating the new, stretching like a bear and craning like a bird,--this is but valetudinarianism, affected by professors of hygiene and those who try to preserve the body to the age of P'êng Tsu.

But in self-esteem without self-conceit, in moral culture without charity and duty to one's neighbour, in government without rank and fame, in retirement without solitude, in health without hygiene,--there we have oblivion absolute coupled with possession of all things; an infinite calm which becomes an object to be attained by all. Such is the TAO of the universe, such is the virtue of the Sage.

title.en: When Death Was Unknown: Primeval Man's Perfect Tranquillity (Zhuangzi)
title.zh: 至一之世：莫之為而常自然（莊子）

region.en: The world's infancy (symbolic pin: Song, Henan, China)
region.zh: 世界之幼年（象徵定位：宋，今河南）

period: Zhuangzi ch. 16, c. 4th-3rd c. BCE (trans. Giles, 1889)

source.work: Chuang Tzu: Mystic, Moralist, and Social Reformer, trans. Herbert A. Giles, ch. 16

summary.en: Primeval man enjoyed perfect tranquillity throughout life: the Positive and Negative were peacefully united, spiritual beings gave no trouble, the four seasons followed in due order, nothing suffered any injury — and death was unknown. Then virtue declined through the reigns of Sui Jen and Fu Hsi, Shên Nung and Huang Ti, until Yao and Shun introduced government and scattered man's original integrity.
summary.zh: 至德之世：陰陽和靜，鬼神不擾，四時得節，萬物不傷，群生不夭，人雖有知，無所用之——此之謂至一。

sensitivity.note: Canonical text of the Taoist canon (Nanhua zhenjing); the Taoist myth of the age before death, an origin-of-death cluster analogue. Included as a comparative text.

passages.text: Primeval man enjoyed perfect tranquillity throughout life. In his day, the Positive and Negative principles were peacefully united; spiritual beings gave no trouble; the four seasons followed in due order; nothing suffered any injury; death was unknown; men had knowledge, but no occasion to use it. This may be called perfection of unity.

By and by, virtue declined. Sui Jen and Fu Hsi ruled the empire. There was still natural adaptation, but the unity was gone. A further decline in virtue. Shên Nung and Huang Ti ruled the empire. There was peace, but the natural adaptation was gone. Again virtue declined. Yao and Shun ruled the empire. Systems of government and moral reform were introduced. Man's original integrity was scattered. Goodness led him astray from TAO; his actions imperilled his virtue.

Thus it may be said that the world destroys TAO, and that TAO destroys the world. And the world and TAO thus mutually destroying each other, how can the men of TAO elevate the world, and how can the world elevate TAO? TAO cannot elevate the world; neither can the world elevate TAO.

title.en: The River Spirit and the Spirit of the North Sea (Zhuangzi)
title.zh: 河伯與北海若（莊子）

region.en: The mouth of the Yellow River into the eastern sea (symbolic pin: Dongying, Shandong, China)
region.zh: 黃河入海處（象徵定位：山東東營）

period: Zhuangzi ch. 17, c. 4th-3rd c. BCE (trans. Giles, 1889)

source.work: Chuang Tzu: Mystic, Moralist, and Social Reformer, trans. Herbert A. Giles, ch. 17

summary.en: In the autumn floods every stream pours into the Yellow River, whose spirit laughs for joy that all the beauty of the earth is gathered to himself — until, travelling east to the ocean, he sees no limit to its waves. The Spirit of the Ocean tells him you cannot speak of ocean to a well-frog or of ice to a summer insect, and that the Four Seas are but puddles in the marsh of the universe.
summary.zh: 秋水時至，百川灌河；河伯欣然自喜，以天下之美為盡在己——順流而東行，至於北海，望洋向若而嘆。北海若曰：井蛙不可以語於海，夏蟲不可以語於冰。

sensitivity.note: Canonical text of the Taoist canon (Nanhua zhenjing); the most famous of all Zhuangzi's mythic dialogues, between river-god and sea-god. Included as a comparative text.

passages.text: It was the time of autumn floods. Every stream poured into the river, which swelled in its turbid course. The banks receded so far from one another that it was impossible to tell a cow from a horse. Then the Spirit of the River laughed for joy that all the beauty of the earth was gathered to himself. Down with the stream he journeyed east, until he reached the ocean. There, looking eastwards and seeing no limit to its waves, his countenance changed. And as he gazed over the expanse, he sighed and said to the Spirit of the Ocean, "A vulgar proverb says that he who has heard but part of the truth thinks no one equal to himself. And such a one am I."

To which the Spirit of the Ocean replied, "You cannot speak of ocean to a well-frog,--the creature of a narrower sphere. You cannot speak of ice to a summer insect,--the creature of a season. You cannot speak of TAO to a pedagogue: his scope is too restricted. But now that you have emerged from your narrow sphere and have seen the great ocean, you know your own insignificance, and I can speak to you of great principles.

"There is no body of water beneath the canopy of heaven which is greater than ocean. All streams pour into it without cease, yet it does not overflow. It is constantly being drained off, yet it is never empty. Spring and autumn bring no change; floods and droughts are equally unknown. And thus it is immeasurably superior to mere rivers and brooks,--though I would not venture to boast on this account, for I get my shape from the universe, my vital power from the Yin and Yang. In the universe I am but as a small stone or a small tree on a vast mountain. And conscious thus of my own insignificance, what is there of which I can boast?"

"The Four Seas,--are they not to the universe but like puddles in a marsh? The Middle Kingdom,--is it not to the surrounding ocean like a tare-seed in a granary? Of all the myriad created things, man is but one. And of all those who inhabit the land, live on the fruit of the earth, and move about in cart and boat, an individual man is but one. Is not he, as compared with all creation, but as the tip of a hair upon a horse's skin?"

title.en: The One-Legged Walrus, the Centipede, the Snake, and the Wind (Zhuangzi)
title.zh: 夔憐蚿，蚿憐蛇（莊子）

region.en: The creatures' colloquy (symbolic pin: Song, Henan, China)
region.zh: 群物相語（象徵定位：宋，今河南）

period: Zhuangzi ch. 17, c. 4th-3rd c. BCE (trans. Giles, 1889)

source.work: Chuang Tzu: Mystic, Moralist, and Social Reformer, trans. Herbert A. Giles, ch. 17

summary.en: The walrus envies the centipede; the centipede envies the snake; the snake envies the wind; the wind envies the eye; the eye envies the mind. Each explains its natural mechanism: the centipede works naturally like ejected saliva, the snake's mechanism is not a thing to be changed, and the wind can break huge trees and destroy large buildings though any one who can point at it excels it.
summary.zh: 夔憐蚿，蚿憐蛇，蛇憐風，風憐目，目憐心。夔謂蚿曰：吾以一足趻踔而行；蚿曰：天機之動，不知其然而也。蛇曰：夫天機之所動，何可易邪？

sensitivity.note: Canonical text of the Taoist canon (Nanhua zhenjing). Included as a comparative text — a scholarly framing, not a claim about religious truth.

passages.text: The walrus said to the centipede, "I hop about on one leg, but not very successfully. How do you manage all these legs you have?" "I don't manage them," replied the centipede. "Have you never seen saliva? When it is ejected, the big drops are the size of pearls, the small ones like mist. They fall promiscuously on the ground and cannot be counted. And so it is that my mechanism works naturally, without my being conscious of the fact."

The centipede said to the snake, "With all my legs I do not move as fast as you with none. How is that?" "One's natural mechanism," replied the snake, "is not a thing to be changed. What need have I for legs?" The snake said to the wind, "I can manage to wriggle along, but I have a form. Now you come blustering down from the north sea to bluster away to the south sea, and you seem to be without form. How is that?" "'Tis true," replied the wind, "that I bluster as you say; but any one who can point at me or kick at me, excels me. On the other hand, I can break huge trees and destroy large buildings. That is my strong point. Out of all the small things in which I do not excel I make one great one in which I do excel. And to excel in great things is given only to the Sages."

title.en: Confucius Encircled at K'uang Sings to His Guitar (Zhuangzi)
title.zh: 孔子遊於匡，弦歌不惙（莊子）

region.en: K'uang (Kuangyi, Wei State; symbolic pin: Changyuan, Henan, China)
region.zh: 匡地（衛國匡邑；象徵定位：河南長垣）

period: Zhuangzi ch. 17, c. 4th-3rd c. BCE (trans. Giles, 1889)

source.work: Chuang Tzu: Mystic, Moralist, and Social Reformer, trans. Herbert A. Giles, ch. 17

summary.en: Mistaken for the fugitive Yang Hu, Confucius is closely surrounded by the men of Wei — yet goes on playing and singing to his guitar. To know that failure is fate and that success is opportunity, and to remain fearless in great danger: this is the courage of the Sage. My destiny is cut out for me.
summary.zh: 孔子遊於匡，衛人圍之數匝，而弦歌不惙。子路入見曰：何夫子之娛也？孔子曰：知窮之有命，知通之有時，臨大難而不懼者，聖人之勇也。

sensitivity.note: Canonical text of the Taoist canon (Nanhua zhenjing). Included as a comparative text — a scholarly framing, not a claim about religious truth.

passages.text: When Confucius visited K'uang, the men of Sung surrounded him closely. Yet he went on playing and singing to his guitar without ceasing. "How is it, Sir," enquired Tzŭ Lu, "that you are so cheerful?" "Come here," replied Confucius, "and I will tell you. For a long time I have been struggling against failure, but in vain. Fate is against me. For a long time I have been seeking success, but in vain. The hour has not come.

"To travel by water and not avoid sea-serpents and dragons,--this is the courage of the fisherman. To travel by land and not avoid the rhinoceros and the tiger,--this is the courage of hunters. When bright blades cross, to look on death as on life,--this is the courage of the hero. To know that failure is fate and that success is opportunity, and to remain fearless in great danger,--this is the courage of the Sage. Yu! rest in this. My destiny is cut out for me." Shortly afterwards, the captain of the troops came in and apologised, saying, "We thought you were Yang Hu; consequently we surrounded you. We find we have made a mistake." Whereupon he again apologised and retired.

title.en: The Frog in the Well and the Turtle of the Eastern Sea (Zhuangzi)
title.zh: 埳井之蛙與東海之鱉（莊子）

region.en: The well-frog's domain (symbolic pin: Handan, Hebei, China)
region.zh: 埳井之蛙（象徵定位：河北邯鄲）

period: Zhuangzi ch. 17, c. 4th-3rd c. BCE (trans. Giles, 1889)

source.work: Chuang Tzu: Mystic, Moralist, and Social Reformer, trans. Herbert A. Giles, ch. 17

summary.en: The frog of the broken well invites the turtle of the eastern sea to visit his kingdom of rail, broken brick, mud, and unmatched tadpoles; the turtle's legs stick fast at the rim. A thousand li would not measure the sea's breadth; nine years of flood did not add to its bulk, seven years of drought did not narrow its span. The well-frog was considerably astonished, and knew not what to say next.
summary.zh: 埳井之蛙謂東海之鱉曰：吾樂與！出則跳梁乎井幹之上，入則休乎缺甃之崖；且夫擅一壑之水，而跨跱埳井之樂，此亦至矣。

sensitivity.note: Canonical text of the Taoist canon (Nanhua zhenjing); tagged flood for the Great Yü nine-floods line (interpretive). Included as a comparative text.

passages.text: "Have you never heard of the frog in the old well?--The frog said to the turtle of the eastern sea, 'Happy indeed am I! I hop on to the rail around the well. I rest in the hollow of some broken brick. Swimming, I gather the water under my arms and shut my mouth. I plunge into the mud, burying my feet and toes; and not one of the cockles, crabs, or tadpoles I see around me are my match. Why do you not come, Sir, and pay me a visit?'

Now the turtle of the eastern sea had not got its left leg down ere its right had already stuck fast, so it shrank back and begged to be excused. It then described the sea, saying, 'A thousand li would not measure its breadth, nor a thousand fathoms its depth. In the days of the Great Yü, there were nine years of flood out of ten; but this did not add to its bulk. In the days of T'ang, there were seven years out of eight of drought; but this did not narrow its span. Not to be affected by duration of time, not to be affected by volume of water,--such is the great happiness of the eastern sea.' At this the well-frog was considerably astonished, and knew not what to say next.

title.en: The Sacred Tortoise Dead Three Thousand Years (Zhuangzi)
title.zh: 楚之神龜，曳尾於塗中（莊子）

region.en: The river P'u in Ch'u (symbolic pin: Fuyang, Anhui, China)
region.zh: 濮水之濱（象徵定位：安徽阜陽）

period: Zhuangzi ch. 17, c. 4th-3rd c. BCE (trans. Giles, 1889)

source.work: Chuang Tzu: Mystic, Moralist, and Social Reformer, trans. Herbert A. Giles, ch. 17

summary.en: Fishing in the P'u, Chuang Tzŭ is offered the administration of the Ch'u State by two high officials. Without turning his head he asks whether the sacred tortoise dead three thousand years in its temple chest would rather be dead and venerated, or alive and wagging its tail in the mud — and sends them off: I too will wag my tail in the mud.
summary.zh: 莊子釣於濮水，楚王使大夫二人往先焉。莊子曰：吾聞楚有神龜，死已三千歲矣，王巾笥而藏之廟堂之上——寧其生而曳尾於塗中乎？

sensitivity.note: Canonical text of the Taoist canon (Nanhua zhenjing); tagged oracle-divination for the sacred tortoise-shell cult (interpretive). Included as a comparative text.

passages.text: Chuang Tzŭ was fishing in the P'u when the prince of Ch'u sent two high officials to ask him to take charge of the administration of the Ch'u State. Chuang Tzŭ went on fishing, and without turning his head said, "I have heard that in Ch'u there is a sacred tortoise which has been dead now some three thousand years. And that the prince keeps this tortoise carefully enclosed in a chest on the altar of his ancestral temple. Now would this tortoise rather be dead and have its remains venerated, or be alive and wagging its tail in the mud?" "It would rather be alive," replied the two officials, "and wagging its tail in the mud." "Begone!" cried Chuang Tzŭ. "I too will wag my tail in the mud."

title.en: The Phœnix and the Owl's Rotten Rat (Zhuangzi)
title.zh: 鵷鶵與鴟得腐鼠（莊子）

region.en: The Liang court (Kaifeng, Henan, China)
region.zh: 梁廷（今河南開封）

period: Zhuangzi ch. 17, c. 4th-3rd c. BCE (trans. Giles, 1889)

source.work: Chuang Tzu: Mystic, Moralist, and Social Reformer, trans. Herbert A. Giles, ch. 17

summary.en: Hui Tzŭ, prime minister of Liang, fears that Chuang Tzŭ has come to take his place and hunts the state for three days and nights. Chuang Tzŭ answers with the yüan-ch'u phoenix that flies from the south sea to the north sea, alighting only on the wu-t'ung tree, eating only bamboo fruit, drinking only purest spring water — and the owl with a rotten rat's carcass who screeches at it as it passes. Are you not screeching at me over your kingdom of Liang?
summary.zh: 惠子相梁，莊子往見之；惠子恐，搜於國中三日三夜。莊子往見之曰：南方有鳥，其名為鵷鶵——非梧桐不止，非練實不食，非醴泉不飲。於是鴟得腐鼠，嚇之！

sensitivity.note: Canonical text of the Taoist canon (Nanhua zhenjing). Included as a comparative text — a scholarly framing, not a claim about religious truth.

passages.text: Hui Tzŭ was prime minister in the Liang State. Chuang Tzŭ went thither to visit him. Some one remarked, "Chuang Tzŭ has come. He wants to be minister in your place." Thereupon Hui Tzŭ was afraid, and searched all over the State for three days and three nights to find him.

Then Chuang Tzŭ went to see Hui Tzŭ, and said, "In the south there is a bird. It is a kind of phœnix. Do you know it? It started from the south sea to fly to the north sea. Except on the wu-t'ung tree, it would not alight. It would eat nothing but the fruit of the bamboo, drink nothing but the purest spring water. An owl which had got the rotten carcass of a rat, looked up as the phœnix flew by, and screeched. Are you not screeching at me over your kingdom of Liang?"

title.en: The Pleasure of Fishes on the Hao Bridge (Zhuangzi)
title.zh: 濠梁觀魚（莊子）

region.en: The bridge over the Hao river (Bengbu, Anhui, China)
region.zh: 濠水之梁（今安徽蚌埠）

period: Zhuangzi ch. 17, c. 4th-3rd c. BCE (trans. Giles, 1889)

source.work: Chuang Tzu: Mystic, Moralist, and Social Reformer, trans. Herbert A. Giles, ch. 17

summary.en: Strolling on the bridge over the Hao, Chuang Tzŭ observes how the minnows dart about — that is the pleasure of fishes. Hui Tzŭ objects that he is not a fish; the dialectic goes back and forth until Chuang Tzŭ concludes: your very question shows that you knew I knew — I knew it from my own feelings on this bridge.
summary.zh: 莊子與惠子遊於濠梁之上。莊子曰：儵魚出遊從容，是魚之樂也。惠子曰：子非魚，安知魚之樂？莊子曰：我知之濠上也。

sensitivity.note: Canonical text of the Taoist canon (Nanhua zhenjing). Included as a comparative text — a scholarly framing, not a claim about religious truth.

passages.text: Chuang Tzŭ and Hui Tzŭ had strolled on to the bridge over the Hao, when the former observed, "See how the minnows are darting about! That is the pleasure of fishes." "You not being a fish yourself," said Hui Tzŭ, "how can you possibly know in what consists the pleasure of fishes?" "And you not being I," retorted Chuang Tzŭ, "how can you know that I do not know?"

"If I, not being you, cannot know what you know," urged Hui Tzŭ, "it follows that you, not being a fish, cannot know in what consists the pleasure of fishes." "Let us go back," said Chuang Tzŭ, "to your original question. You asked me how I knew in what consists the pleasure of fishes. Your very question shows that you knew I knew. I knew it from my own feelings on this bridge."

title.en: Drumming on a Bowl at His Wife's Death (Zhuangzi)
title.zh: 莊子妻死，鼓盆而歌（莊子）

region.en: Chuang Tzŭ's home in Sung (Shangqiu, Henan, China)
region.zh: 莊子之居，宋國（今河南商丘）

period: Zhuangzi ch. 18, c. 4th-3rd c. BCE (trans. Giles, 1889)

source.work: Chuang Tzu: Mystic, Moralist, and Social Reformer, trans. Herbert A. Giles, ch. 18

summary.en: When Chuang Tzŭ's wife died, Hui Tzŭ found the widower singing with his legs spread out, beating time on a bowl. Chuang Tzŭ explains that she existed before birth without form or substance, then gained substance, form, and birth; now, passing from one phase to another like spring, summer, autumn, and winter, she lies asleep in Eternity — to go about weeping would be to proclaim myself ignorant of these natural laws.
summary.zh: 莊子妻死，惠子弔之；莊子則方箕踞鼓盆而歌。莊子曰：察其始而本無生；非徒無生也，而本無形——人且偃然寢於巨室，而我噭噭然隨而哭之，自以為不通乎命，故止也。

sensitivity.note: Canonical text of the Taoist canon (Nanhua zhenjing); the most-cited Taoist mourning scene, retold in the drum-on-basin opera tradition. Included as a comparative text.

passages.text: When Chuang Tzŭ's wife died, Hui Tzŭ went to condole. He found the widower sitting on the ground, singing, with his legs spread out at a right angle, and beating time on a bowl. "To live with your wife," exclaimed Hui Tzŭ, "and see your eldest son grow up to be a man, and then not to shed a tear over her corpse,--this would be bad enough. But to drum on a bowl, and sing; surely this is going too far."

"Not at all," replied Chuang Tzŭ. "When she died, I could not help being affected by her death. Soon, however, I remembered that she had already existed in a previous state before birth, without form, or even substance; that while in that unconditioned condition, substance was added to spirit; that this substance then assumed form; and that the next stage was birth. And now, by virtue of a further change, she is dead, passing from one phase to another like the sequence of spring, summer, autumn, and winter. And while she is thus lying asleep in Eternity, for me to go about weeping and wailing would be to proclaim myself ignorant of these natural laws. Therefore I refrain."

title.en: The Skull Under His Head as a Pillow (Zhuangzi)
title.zh: 莊子之楚，見髑髏（莊子）

region.en: En route to Ch'u (symbolic pin: Jingzhou, Hubei, China)
region.zh: 適楚道中（象徵定位：湖北荊州）

period: Zhuangzi ch. 18, c. 4th-3rd c. BCE (trans. Giles, 1889)

source.work: Chuang Tzu: Mystic, Moralist, and Social Reformer, trans. Herbert A. Giles, ch. 18

summary.en: Chuang Tzŭ interrogates a bleached empty skull — ambitious citizen, ruined statesman, shamed wretch, starving beggar, or natural old age? — then sleeps with it as a pillow. In the night the skull explains that in death there is no sovereign above and no subject below, and when offered restoration to life and kin, opens its eyes wide and knits its brows: how should I cast aside happiness greater than that of a king?
summary.zh: 莊子之楚，見空髑髏，髏然有形；撽以馬捶而問之。夜半，髑髏見夢曰：死，無君於上，無臣於下；亦無四時之事，從然以天地為春秋，雖南面王樂，不能過也。

sensitivity.note: Canonical text of the Taoist canon (Nanhua zhenjing); the skull-dream is Zhuangzi's Hamletian counter-meditation on death, tagged dream-vision pending a dedicated motif. Included as a comparative text.

passages.text: Chuang Tzŭ one day saw an empty skull, bleached, but still preserving its shape. Striking it with his riding whip, he said, "Wert thou once some ambitious citizen whose inordinate yearnings brought him to this pass?--some statesman who plunged his country in ruin and perished in the fray?--some wretch who left behind him a legacy of shame?--some beggar who died in the pangs of hunger and cold? Or didst thou reach this state by the natural course of old age?"

When he had finished speaking, he took the skull, and placing it under his head as a pillow, went to sleep. In the night, he dreamt that the skull appeared to him and said, "You speak well, Sir; but all you say has reference to the life of mortals, and to mortal troubles. In death there are none of these. Would you like to hear about death?" Chuang Tzŭ having replied in the affirmative, the skull began:--"In death, there is no sovereign above, and no subject below. The workings of the four seasons are unknown. Our existences are bounded only by eternity. The happiness of a king among men cannot exceed that which we enjoy."

Chuang Tzŭ, however, was not convinced, and said, "Were I to prevail upon God to allow your body to be born again, and your bones and flesh to be renewed, so that you could return to your parents, to your wife, and to the friends of your youth,--would you be willing?" At this, the skull opened its eyes wide and knitted its brows and said, "How should I cast aside happiness greater than that of a king, and mingle once again in the toils and troubles of mortality?"

title.en: Life Is a Loan: The Hunchback and the One-Legged Man at K'un-lun (Zhuangzi)
title.zh: 右師與介者觀於昆侖（莊子）

region.en: The tombs of departed heroes on the K'un-lun mountains (mythic; symbolic pin: Kunlun, Xinjiang, China)
region.zh: 崑崙黃帝之陵（神話之地；象徵定位：新疆崑崙）

period: Zhuangzi ch. 18, c. 4th-3rd c. BCE (trans. Giles, 1889)

source.work: Chuang Tzu: Mystic, Moralist, and Social Reformer, trans. Herbert A. Giles, ch. 18

summary.en: A hunchback and a one-legged man gaze at the tombs of departed heroes on the K'un-lun mountains where the Yellow Emperor rests, when ulcers break out upon their left elbows. Do you loathe this? asks the hunchback. Not I, replies the other — life is a loan with which the borrower does but add more dust and dirt; life and death are as day and night.
summary.zh: 支離叔與滑介叔觀於冥伯之丘，昆侖之虛，黃帝之所休；俄而柳生其左肘。滑介叔曰：亡，予何惡？生者，假借也——死生為晝夜。

sensitivity.note: Canonical text of the Taoist canon (Nanhua zhenjing). Included as a comparative text — a scholarly framing, not a claim about religious truth.

passages.text: A hunchback and a one-legged man were looking at the tombs of departed heroes, on the K'un-lun Mountains, where the Yellow Emperor rests. Suddenly, ulcers broke out upon their left elbows, of a very loathsome description. "Do you loathe this?" asked the hunchback. "Not I," replied the other, "why should I? Life is a loan with which the borrower does but add more dust and dirt to the sum total of existence. Life and death are as day and night; and while you and I stand gazing at the evidences of mortality around us, if the same mortality overtakes me, why should I loathe it?"

title.en: The Sea-Bird in the Temple of Lu (Zhuangzi)
title.zh: 昔者海鳥止於魯郊（莊子）

region.en: The capital of Lu (Qufu, Shandong, China)
region.zh: 魯郊（今山東曲阜）

period: Zhuangzi ch. 18, c. 4th-3rd c. BCE (trans. Giles, 1889)

source.work: Chuang Tzu: Mystic, Moralist, and Social Reformer, trans. Herbert A. Giles, ch. 18

summary.en: When a sea-bird alighted outside the capital of Lu, the prince received it with wine in the temple, the Chiu Shao music, and a slaughtered bullock. The bird, dazed and too timid to eat or drink, died in three days — treated like a man, not as a bird would treat a bird. Water, which is life to fishes, is death to man.
summary.zh: 昔者海鳥止於魯郊，魯侯御而觴之於廟，奏九韶以為樂，具太牢以為膳。鳥乃眩視憂悲，不敢食一膾，不敢飲一杯，三日而死。

sensitivity.note: Canonical text of the Taoist canon (Nanhua zhenjing). Included as a comparative text — a scholarly framing, not a claim about religious truth.

passages.text: "Besides, have you not heard that of old when a sea-bird alighted outside the capital of Lu, the prince went out to receive it, and gave it wine in the temple, and had the Chiu Shao played to amuse it, and a bullock slaughtered to feed it? But the bird was dazed and too timid to eat or drink anything; and in three days it was dead. This was treating the bird like oneself, and not as a bird would treat a bird. Had he treated it as a bird would have treated a bird, he would have put it to roost in a deep forest, to wander over a plain, to swim in a river or lake, to feed upon fish, to fly in order, and to settle leisurely.

"When the bird was already terrified at human voices, fancy adding music! Play the Hsien Ch'ih or the Chiu Shao in the wilds of Tung-t'ing, and birds will fly away, beasts will take themselves off, and fishes will dive down below. But men will collect to hear. "Water, which is life to fishes, is death to man. Being differently constituted, their likes and dislikes are different."

title.en: The Chain of Metamorphoses: From Germ to Man (Zhuangzi)
title.zh: 種有幾：萬化一樞（莊子）

region.en: The roadside (symbolic pin: Song, Henan, China)
region.zh: 道旁（象徵定位：宋，今河南）

period: Zhuangzi ch. 18, c. 4th-3rd c. BCE (trans. Giles, 1889)

source.work: Chuang Tzu: Mystic, Moralist, and Social Reformer, trans. Herbert A. Giles, ch. 18

summary.en: Lieh Tzŭ, eating by the roadside, points a blade of grass at an old skull: only you and I know that there is no such thing as life and no such thing as death. Then follows Zhuangzi's great chain of metamorphoses — germs become duckweed, lichen, the dog-tooth violet, grubs and butterflies, the Kan-yü-ku bird, the wine fly — ending in the leopard that produces the horse, which produces man, who goes back into the great Scheme from which all things come.
summary.zh: 種有幾：得水則為繼，得水土之際則為蛙蠙之衣，生於陵屯則為陵舄——久竹生青寧，青寧生程，程生馬，馬生人。人又反入於機。

sensitivity.note: Canonical text of the Taoist canon (Nanhua zhenjing); the zhong-you-ji passage is Zhuangzi's spontaneous-generation cosmogony. Included as a comparative text.

passages.text: Lieh Tzŭ, being on a journey, was eating by the roadside, when he saw an old skull. Plucking a blade of grass, he pointed at it and said, "Only you and I know that there is no such thing as life and no such thing as death. Are you really at peace? Or am I really happy?

"Certain germs, falling upon water, become duckweed. When they reach the junction of the land and the water, they become lichen. Spreading up the bank, they become the dog-tooth violet. Reaching rich soil, they become wu-tsu, the root of which becomes grubs, while the leaves comes from butterflies, or hsü. These are changed into insects, born in the chimney corner, which look like skeletons. Their name is ch'ü-to. After a thousand days, the ch'ü-to becomes a bird, called Kan-yü-ku, the spittle of which becomes the ssŭ-mi. The ssŭ-mi becomes a wine fly, and that comes from an i-lu. The huang-k'uang produces the chiu-yu and the mou-jui produces the glow-worm. The yang-ch'i grafted to an old bamboo which has for a long time put forth no shoots, produces the ch'ing-ning, which produces the leopard, which produces the horse, which produces man. "Then man goes back into the great Scheme, from which all things come and to which all things return."

title.en: Kuan Yin on the Perfect Man Who Walks Through Walls (Zhuangzi)
title.zh: 列子問關尹：至人潛行不窒（莊子）

region.en: Kuan Yin's retreat at the western pass (symbolic pin: Hangu Pass, Lingbao, Henan, China)
region.zh: 關尹之居（象徵定位：河南靈寶函谷關）

period: Zhuangzi ch. 19, c. 4th-3rd c. BCE (trans. Giles, 1889)

source.work: Chuang Tzu: Mystic, Moralist, and Social Reformer, trans. Herbert A. Giles, ch. 19

summary.en: Lieh Tzŭ asks Kuan Yin how the perfect man can walk through solid bodies unobstructed, pass through fire unburnt, and scale the highest heights without fear. Kuan Yin answers that he is in a condition of absolute purity — man can attain to formlessness and vanquish death — and tells the parable of the drunken man who falls out of a cart and does not die, for his spirit is in a condition of security; and if such security is to be got from wine, how much more from God.
summary.zh: 列子問關尹曰：至人潛行不窒，蹈火不熱，行乎萬物之上而不慄——是純氣之守也，非知巧果敢之列。醉者之墜車，雖疾不死；骨節與人同，而犯害與人異，其神全也。

sensitivity.note: Canonical text of the Taoist canon (Nanhua zhenjing); the invulnerability passage is the charter of later Daoist immortality-arts claims. Included as a comparative text.

passages.text: Lieh Tzŭ asked Kuan Yin, saying, "The perfect man can walk through solid bodies without obstruction. He can pass through fire without being burnt. He can scale the highest heights without fear. How does he bring himself to this?" "It is because he is in a condition of absolute purity," replied Kuan Yin. "It is not cunning which enables him to dare such feats. Be seated, and I will tell you.

"All that has form, sound, and colour, may be classed under the head thing. Man differs so much from the rest, and stands at the head of all things, simply because the latter are but what they appear and nothing more. But man can attain to formlessness and vanquish death. And with that which is in possession of the eternal, how can mere things compare?

"A drunken man who falls out of a cart, though he may suffer, does not die. His bones are the same as other people's; but he meets his accident in a different way. His spirit is in a condition of security. He is not conscious of riding in the cart; neither is he conscious of falling out of it. Ideas of life, death, fear, etc., cannot penetrate his breast; and so he does not suffer from contact with objective existences. And if such security is to be got from wine, how much more is it to be got from God. It is in God that the Sage seeks his refuge, and so he is free from harm."

title.en: The Hunchback Who Caught Cicadas as Though With His Hand (Zhuangzi)
title.zh: 痀僂丈人承蜩（莊子）

region.en: The forest en route to Ch'u (symbolic pin: Jingzhou, Hubei, China)
region.zh: 適楚林中（象徵定位：湖北荊州）

period: Zhuangzi ch. 19, c. 4th-3rd c. BCE (trans. Giles, 1889)

source.work: Chuang Tzu: Mystic, Moralist, and Social Reformer, trans. Herbert A. Giles, ch. 19

summary.en: In a forest on the way to Ch'u, Confucius sees a hunchback catching cicadas as though with his hand. The hunchback explains his training in balancing balls atop his pole, until heaven and earth and all creation may be around him, but he is conscious only of his cicada's wings. Singleness of purpose induces concentration of the faculties, says Confucius.
summary.zh: 仲尼適楚，出於林中，見痀僂者承蜩，猶掇之也。用志不分，乃凝於神——天地之大，萬物之多，而唯蜩翼之知。

sensitivity.note: Canonical text of the Taoist canon (Nanhua zhenjing). Included as a comparative text — a scholarly framing, not a claim about religious truth.

passages.text: When Confucius was on his way to the Ch'u State, he came to a forest where he saw a hunchback catching cicadas as though with his hand. "How clever you are!" cried Confucius. "Have you any way of doing this?" "I have a way," replied the hunchback. "In the fifth and sixth moons I practise balancing two balls one on top of the other. If they do not fall, I do not miss many cicadas. When I can balance three balls, I only miss one in ten; and when five, then it is as though I caught the cicadas with my hand. My body is as motionless as the stump of a tree; my arms like dead branches. Heaven and earth and all creation may be around me, but I am conscious only of my cicada's wings. How should I not succeed?" Confucius looked round at his disciples and said, "Singleness of purpose induces concentration of the faculties. Of such is the success of this hunchback."

title.en: The Boatman of the Shang-shên Rapid and the Gambler's Stake (Zhuangzi)
title.zh: 津人操舟若神，以瓦注者巧（莊子）

region.en: The Shang-shên rapid (symbolic pin: Lüliang gorge of the Yellow River, Shanxi, China)
region.zh: 商深之淵（象徵定位：山西呂梁黃河石門）

period: Zhuangzi ch. 19, c. 4th-3rd c. BCE (trans. Giles, 1889)

source.work: Chuang Tzu: Mystic, Moralist, and Social Reformer, trans. Herbert A. Giles, ch. 19

summary.en: Crossing the Shang-shên rapid, Yen Yüan sees a boatman manage his craft with marvellous skill — they row as if the boat wasn't there. Confucius explains: such a man is oblivious of the water around him, and tells of the gambler who plays well for counters but, staking yellow gold, loses his wits; every one who attaches importance to the external becomes internally without resource.
summary.zh: 顏淵問仲尼：津人操舟若神。仲尼曰：善遊者數能，忘水也；以瓦注者巧，以鉤注者憚，以黃金注者殙——外重者內拙。

sensitivity.note: Canonical text of the Taoist canon (Nanhua zhenjing). Included as a comparative text — a scholarly framing, not a claim about religious truth.

passages.text: Yen Yüan said to Confucius, "When I crossed over the Shang-shên rapid, the boatman managed his craft with marvellous skill. I asked him if handling a boat could be learnt. 'It can,' replied he. 'The way of those who know how to keep you afloat is more like sinking you. They row as if the boat wasn't there.' I enquired what this meant, but he would not tell me. May I ask its signification?" "It means," answered Confucius, "that such a man is oblivious of the water around him. He regards the rapid as though dry land. He looks upon an upset as an ordinary cart accident. And if a man can but be impervious to capsizings and accidents in general, whither should he not be able comfortably to go?"

"A man who plays for counters will play well. If he stakes his girdle, he will be nervous; if yellow gold, he will lose his wits. His skill is the same in each case, but he is distracted by the value of his stake. And every one who attaches importance to the external, becomes internally without resource."

title.en: The Grand Augur Addresses the Pigs (Zhuangzi)
title.zh: 祝宗人玄端以臨牢柙（莊子）

region.en: The shambles beside the temple (symbolic pin: Song, Henan, China)
region.zh: 牢柙之前（象徵定位：宋，今河南）

period: Zhuangzi ch. 19, c. 4th-3rd c. BCE (trans. Giles, 1889)

source.work: Chuang Tzu: Mystic, Moralist, and Social Reformer, trans. Herbert A. Giles, ch. 19

summary.en: The Grand Augur, in ceremonial robes, offers the pigs three months' fattening and a carved sacrificial dish — then, speaking from their point of view, admits it is better perhaps to live on bran and escape the shambles; yet from his own point of view, to enjoy honour when alive one would readily die on a war-shield. So he rejected the pigs' point of view — in what sense then was he different from the pigs?
summary.zh: 祝宗人玄端以臨牢柙，說彘曰：汝奚惡死？吾將三月豢汝，七日戒，三日齋——吾自取之，則異於彘。

sensitivity.note: Canonical text of the Taoist canon (Nanhua zhenjing); the shambles-scene is Zhuangzi's great parable on sacrificial honour. Included as a comparative text.

passages.text: The Grand Augur, in his ceremonial robes, approached the shambles and thus addressed the pigs: "How can you object to die? I shall fatten you for three months. I shall discipline myself for ten days and fast for three. I shall strew fine grass, and place you bodily upon a carved sacrificial dish. Does not this satisfy you?"

Then speaking from the pigs' point of view, he continued, "It is better perhaps after all to live on bran and escape the shambles...." "But then," added he, speaking from his own point of view, "to enjoy honour when alive one would readily die on a war-shield or in the headsman's basket." So he rejected the pigs' point of view and adopted his own point of view. In what sense then was he different from the pigs?

title.en: Duke Huan Sees the Wei-i Bogy by the Marsh (Zhuangzi)
title.zh: 齊桓公見鬼於澤（莊子）

region.en: The marshes of Ch'i (Linzi, Shandong, China)
region.zh: 齊國之澤（今山東臨淄）

period: Zhuangzi ch. 19, c. 4th-3rd c. BCE (trans. Giles, 1889)

source.work: Chuang Tzu: Mystic, Moralist, and Social Reformer, trans. Herbert A. Giles, ch. 19

summary.en: Out hunting with Kuan Chung as charioteer, Duke Huan sees a bogy and falls delirious. The sage Huang Tzŭ Kao Ngao catalogues the spirits — the mud spirit Li, the fire spirit Kao, the K'uei of the mountain, the Wei-i of the marsh, as broad as a cart-wheel, in purple clothes and a red cap, who stands up respectfully when it hears thunder — and those who see it are like to be chieftains among men. Ere the day had closed, without knowing it, the Duke's sickness had left him.
summary.zh: 齊桓公田於澤，見鬼焉。皇子告敖曰：鬼者——水有罔象，丘有宰，山有夔，野有彷徨，澤有委蛇；其大如轂，其長如轅，紫衣而朱冠；惡者殆於霸。

sensitivity.note: Canonical text of the Taoist canon (Nanhua zhenjing); the spirit-catalog is a landmark of early Chinese demonology. Included as a comparative text.

passages.text: When Duke Huan was out hunting, with Kuan Chung as his charioteer, he saw a bogy. Catching hold of Kuan Chung's hand, he asked him, saying, "What do you see?" "I see nothing," replied Kuan Chung. But when the Duke got home he became delirious, and for many days was unable to go out. There came a certain Huang Tzŭ Kao Ngao of the Ch'i State and said, "Your Highness is self-injured. How could a bogy injure you? When the vital strength is dissipated in anger, and is not renewed, there is a deficiency. When its tendency is in one direction upwards, the result is to incline men to wrath. When its tendency is in one direction downwards, the result is loss of memory. When it remains stagnant, in the middle of the body, the result is disease."

"There are," replied Huang, "such things as bogies. There is the mud spirit Li; the fire spirit Kao; Lei T'ing, the spirit of the dust-bin; P'ei O and Wa Lung, sprites of the north-east; Yi Yang of the north-west; Wang Hsiang of the water; the Hsin of the hills; the K'uei of the mountain; the P'ang Huang of the moor; the Wei I of the marsh." "And what may the Wei I be like?" asked the Duke. "The Wei I," replied Huang, "is as broad as a cart-wheel and as long as the shaft. It wears purple clothes and a red cap. It is a sentient being, and whenever it hears the rumble of thunder, it stands up in a respectful attitude. Those who see this bogy are like to be chieftains among men." The Duke laughed exultingly and said, "The very one I saw!" Thereupon he dressed himself and sat up; and ere the day had closed, without knowing it, his sickness had left him.

title.en: Chi Hsing Tzŭ Trains Game-Cocks (Zhuangzi)
title.zh: 紀渻子為王養鬥雞（莊子）

region.en: The prince's cock-pit (symbolic pin: Linzi, Shandong, China)
region.zh: 王之鬥場（象徵定位：山東臨淄）

period: Zhuangzi ch. 19, c. 4th-3rd c. BCE (trans. Giles, 1889)

source.work: Chuang Tzu: Mystic, Moralist, and Social Reformer, trans. Herbert A. Giles, ch. 19

summary.en: Chi Hsing Tzŭ trains fighting cocks for the prince in ten-day stages: still seeking fiercely for a foe; still excited by sounds and shadows; still roused to rage at the sight of an enemy — until they stand as though of wood, virtue complete, at which strange cocks will not dare meet them but will run.
summary.zh: 紀渻子為王養鬥雞。十日而問：雞已乎？曰：未也，方虛驕而恃氣——望之似木雞矣，其德全矣；異雞無敢應者，反走矣。

sensitivity.note: Canonical text of the Taoist canon (Nanhua zhenjing); the 'wooden cock' is a proverbial image of internal concentration. Included as a comparative text.

passages.text: Chi Hsing Tzŭ was training fighting cocks for the prince. At the end of ten days the latter asked if they were ready. "Not yet," replied Chi; "they are in the stage of seeking fiercely for a foe." Again ten days elapsed, and the prince made a further enquiry. "Not yet," replied Chi; "they are still excited by the sounds and shadows of other cocks." Ten days more, and the prince asked again. "Not yet," answered Chi; "the sight of an enemy is still enough to excite them to rage."

But after another ten days, when the prince again enquired, Chi said, "They will do. Other cocks may crow, but they will take no notice. To look at them one might say they were of wood. Their virtue is complete. Strange cocks will not dare meet them, but will run."

title.en: The Old Man Who Swam the Lü-liang Cataract (Zhuangzi)
title.zh: 呂梁丈夫蹈水（莊子）

region.en: The Lü-liang falls of the Yellow River (Shanxi, China)
region.zh: 呂梁瀑布（今山西呂梁）

period: Zhuangzi ch. 19, c. 4th-3rd c. BCE (trans. Giles, 1889)

source.work: Chuang Tzu: Mystic, Moralist, and Social Reformer, trans. Herbert A. Giles, ch. 19

summary.en: At the Lü-liang cataract, whose foam reaches forty li away, Confucius sees an old man plunge in as though to drown himself — and emerge a hundred paces off, carolling along the bank. No way, says the old man: there was my original condition to begin with, then habit growing into nature, and lastly acquiescence in destiny. Plunging in with the whirl, I come out with the swirl.
summary.zh: 孔子觀於呂梁，縣水三十仞，流沫四十里，黿鼉魚鱉之所不能遊也。見一丈夫遊之，數百步而出，被髮行歌而遊於塘下。吾始乎故，長乎性，成乎命。

sensitivity.note: Canonical text of the Taoist canon (Nanhua zhenjing). Included as a comparative text — a scholarly framing, not a claim about religious truth.

passages.text: Confucius was looking at the cataract at Lü-liang. It fell from a height of thirty jen, and its foam reached forty li away. No scaly, finny creature could enter therein. Yet Confucius saw an old man go in, and thinking that he was suffering from some trouble and desirous of ending his life, bade a disciple run along the side to try and save him. The old man emerged about a hundred paces off, and with flowing hair went carolling along the bank. Confucius followed him and said, "I had thought, Sir, you were a spirit, but now I see you are a man. Kindly tell me, is there any way to deal thus with water?"

"No," replied the old man; "I have no way. There was my original condition to begin with; then habit growing into nature; and lastly acquiescence in destiny. Plunging in with the whirl, I come out with the swirl. I accommodate myself to the water, not the water to me. And so I am able to deal with it after this fashion." "What do you mean," enquired Confucius, "by your original condition to begin with, habit growing into nature, and acquiescence in destiny?" "I was born," replied the old man, "upon dry land, and accommodated myself to dry land. That was my original condition. Growing up on the water, I accommodated myself to the water. That was what I meant by nature. And doing as I did without being conscious of any effort so to do, that was what I meant by destiny."

title.en: The Chief Carpenter's Seven Days of Quiescence (Zhuangzi)
title.zh: 梓慶削木為鐻（莊子）

region.en: The workshop of Lu (Qufu, Shandong, China)
region.zh: 魯之梓匠（今山東曲阜）

period: Zhuangzi ch. 19, c. 4th-3rd c. BCE (trans. Giles, 1889)

source.work: Chuang Tzu: Mystic, Moralist, and Social Reformer, trans. Herbert A. Giles, ch. 19

summary.en: The chief carpenter Ch'ing carves a stand for musical instruments so fine that its work seems supernatural. His secret: three days of quiescence until he forgets reward, five days until he forgets fame, seven days until unconscious of his four limbs and physical frame — then into the mountain forest to find the tree that already contains the form required, bringing his own natural capacity into relation with that of the wood.
summary.zh: 梓慶削木為鐻，見者驚猶鬼神。臣將為鐻，未嘗敢以耗氣也——必齊以靜心：齊三日，而不敢懷慶賞爵祿；齊五日，不敢懷非譽巧拙；齊七日，輒然忘吾有四枝形體也。

sensitivity.note: Canonical text of the Taoist canon (Nanhua zhenjing). Included as a comparative text — a scholarly framing, not a claim about religious truth.

passages.text: Ch'ing, the chief carpenter, was carving wood into a stand for hanging musical instruments. When finished, the work appeared to those who saw it as though of supernatural execution. And the prince of Lu asked him, saying, "What mystery is there in your art?" "No mystery, your Highness," replied Ch'ing; "and yet there is something.

"When I am about to make such a stand, I guard against any diminution of my vital power. I first reduce my mind to absolute quiescence. Three days in this condition, and I become oblivious of any reward to be gained. Five days, and I become oblivious of any fame to be acquired. Seven days, and I become unconscious of my four limbs and my physical frame. Then, with no thought of the Court present to my mind, my skill becomes concentrated, and all disturbing elements from without are gone. I enter some mountain forest. I search for a suitable tree. It contains the form required, which is afterwards elaborated. I see the stand in my mind's eye, and then set to work. Otherwise, there is nothing. I bring my own natural capacity into relation with that of the wood."

title.en: Shan Pao the Mountain-Drinker and the Hungry Tiger (Zhuangzi)
title.zh: 單豹張毅：鞭其後者也（莊子）

region.en: The mountains of Lu (Mengshan, Shandong, China)
region.zh: 魯山之阿（象徵定位：山東蒙山）

period: Zhuangzi ch. 19, c. 4th-3rd c. BCE (trans. Giles, 1889)

source.work: Chuang Tzu: Mystic, Moralist, and Social Reformer, trans. Herbert A. Giles, ch. 19

summary.en: Duke Wei asks T'ien K'ai Chih what his master Chu Hsien teaches about the art of life. Keeping life is like keeping a flock of sheep — you look out for the laggards: Shan Pao drank mountain water and at seventy had a child's complexion, until a hungry tiger ate him; Chang I frequented rich and poor alike and died at forty of internal disease. Each failed to whip up the laggards.
summary.zh: 魯有單豹者，巖居而水飲，不與民共利，行年七十而猶有嬰兒之色；不幸遇餓虎，虎殺而食之。有張毅者，高門縣薄，無不趨也；行年四十而有內熱之病以死。豹養其內而虎食其外。

sensitivity.note: Canonical text of the Taoist canon (Nanhua zhenjing). Included as a comparative text — a scholarly framing, not a claim about religious truth.

passages.text: "Well," replied T'ien, "I have heard my master say that keeping life is like keeping a flock of sheep. You look out for the laggards, and whip them up. "In the State of Lu," said T'ien, "there was a man named Shan Pao. He lived on the mountains and drank water. All worldly interests he had put aside. And at the age of seventy, his complexion was like that of a child. Unluckily, he one day fell in with a hungry tiger who killed and ate him.

"There was also a man named Chang I, who frequented the houses of rich and poor alike. At the age of forty he was attacked by some internal disease and died. "Shan Pao took care of his inner self, and a tiger ate his external man. Chang I took care of himself externally, but disease attacked him internally. These two individuals both omitted to whip up the laggards."

title.en: The Tree That Was No Use and the Goose That Didn't Cackle (Zhuangzi)
title.zh: 山木不材，雁以不鳴（莊子）

region.en: The mountain-path and the old friend's house (symbolic pin: Song, Henan, China)
region.zh: 山行與故人之家（象徵定位：宋，今河南）

period: Zhuangzi ch. 20, c. 4th-3rd c. BCE (trans. Giles, 1889)

source.work: Chuang Tzu: Mystic, Moralist, and Social Reformer, trans. Herbert A. Giles, ch. 20

summary.en: On a mountain, the useless tree completes its allotted span; at the old friend's house, the goose that doesn't cackle is killed for dinner. Asked which horn of the dilemma he rests on, Chuang Tzŭ smiles that he rests halfway between — or better, charioted upon TAO, floating far above mortality, changing with the change of time, swaying all things and swayed by none.
summary.zh: 莊子行於山中，見大木枝葉盛茂，伐木者止其旁而不取——此木以不材得終其天年。明日弟子問：昨日山中之木以不材得終其天年；今主人之雁以不材死——先生將何處？

sensitivity.note: Canonical text of the Taoist canon (Nanhua zhenjing). Included as a comparative text — a scholarly framing, not a claim about religious truth.

passages.text: Chuang Tzŭ was travelling over a mountain when he saw a huge tree well covered with foliage. A woodsman had stopped near by, not caring to take it; and on Chuang Tzŭ enquiring the reason, he was told that it was of no use. "This tree," cried Chuang Tzŭ, "by virtue of being good for nothing succeeds in completing its allotted span." When Chuang Tzŭ left the mountain, he put up at the house of an old friend. The latter was delighted, and ordered a servant to kill a goose and cook it. "Which shall I kill?" enquired the servant; "the one that cackles or the one that doesn't?"

His master told him to kill the one which did not cackle. And accordingly, the next day, a disciple asked Chuang Tzŭ, saying, "Yesterday, that tree on the mountain, because good for nothing, was to succeed in completing its allotted span. But now, our host's goose, which is good for nothing, has to die. Upon which horn of the dilemma will you rest?" "I rest," replied Chuang Tzŭ with a smile, "halfway between the two. In that position, appearing to be what I am not, it is impossible to avoid the troubles of mortality; though, if charioted upon TAO and floating far above mortality, this would not be so. No praise, no blame; both great and small; changing with the change of time, but ever without special effort; both above and below; making for harmony with surroundings; reaching creation's First Cause; swaying all things and swayed by none;--how then shall such troubles come? This was the method of Shên Nung and Huang Ti."

title.en: The Fox's Skin, Established-Virtue, and the Empty Boat (Zhuangzi)
title.zh: 魯君之皮，建德之國，虛舟（莊子）

region.en: The prince's court at Lu and Nan-yüeh (symbolic pin: Qufu, Shandong, China)
region.zh: 魯廷與南越建德之國（象徵定位：山東曲阜）

period: Zhuangzi ch. 20, c. 4th-3rd c. BCE (trans. Giles, 1889)

source.work: Chuang Tzu: Mystic, Moralist, and Social Reformer, trans. Herbert A. Giles, ch. 20

summary.en: The philosopher of Shih-nan tells the melancholy prince of Lu that the fox and the leopard die for their skins — is not the State of Lu your skin? — and sends him towards the district of Established-Virtue. And the empty boat: if an empty boat is about to collide with yours, even an irritable man does not lose his temper; but if some one is in it, bad language inevitably follows — if a man could only roam empty through life, who would be able to injure him?
summary.zh: 市南宜僚見魯侯；虎豹以皮為災。南越有邑焉名為建德之國。方舟而濟於河，有虛船來觸舟——人能虛己以遊世，其孰能害之！

sensitivity.note: Canonical text of the Taoist canon (Nanhua zhenjing); the empty-boat parable is a classic of Taoist self-effacement. Included as a comparative text.

passages.text: "Your Highness' method of avoiding misfortune," said the philosopher of Shih-nan, "is but a shallow one. A handsome fox or a striped leopard will live in a mountain forest, hiding beneath some precipitous cliff. This is their repose. They come out at night and keep in by day. This is their caution. Though under the stress of hunger and thirst, they lie hidden, hardly venturing to slink secretly to the river bank in search of food. This is their resoluteness. Nevertheless, they do not escape the misfortune of the net and the trap. But what crime have they committed? 'Tis their skin which is the cause of their trouble; and is not the State of Lu your Highness' skin?

"In Nan-yüeh there is a district, called Established-Virtue. Its people are simple and honest, unselfish, and without passions. They can make, but cannot keep. They give, but look for no return. They are not conscious of fulfilling obligations. They are not conscious of subservience to etiquette. Their actions are altogether uncontrolled, yet they tread in the way of the wise. Life is for enjoyment; death, for burial. And thither I would have your Highness proceed, power discarded and the world left behind, only putting trust in TAO."

"Suppose a boat is crossing a river, and another empty boat is about to collide with it. Even an irritable man would not lose his temper. But supposing there was some one in the second boat. Then the occupant of the first would shout to him to keep clear. And if the other did not hear the first time, nor even when called to three times, bad language would inevitably follow. In the first case there was no anger, in the second there was; because in the first case the boat was empty, and in the second it was occupied. And so it is with man. If he could only roam empty through life, who would be able to injure him?"

title.en: Collecting Subscriptions Without Injury (Zhuangzi)
title.zh: 北宮奢為衛靈公賦斂以為鐘（莊子）

region.en: The city gate of Wei (Puyang, Henan, China)
region.zh: 衛城門外之壇（今河南濮陽）

period: Zhuangzi ch. 20, c. 4th-3rd c. BCE (trans. Giles, 1889)

source.work: Chuang Tzu: Mystic, Moralist, and Social Reformer, trans. Herbert A. Giles, ch. 20

summary.en: Pei Kung Shê levies contributions at an altar outside the Wei city gate for making bells, and in three months the chime is hung. Asked how he managed it, he answers: in the domain of ONE there may not be managing — he made allowances for ignorance and suspicion, forbade not those who came nor detained those who went, showed no resentment to the unwilling nor gratitude to the givers; every one subscribed what he liked.
summary.zh: 北宮奢為衛靈公賦斂以為鐘，為之壇乎郭門之外；三月而成上下之縣。奢曰：一之間，無敢設也——因以為弟子，順其自然而己矣。

sensitivity.note: Canonical text of the Taoist canon (Nanhua zhenjing). Included as a comparative text — a scholarly framing, not a claim about religious truth.

passages.text: Pei Kung Shê, minister to Duke Ling of Wei, levied contributions for making bells. An altar was built outside the city gate; and in three months the bells, upper and lower, were all hung. When Wang Tzŭ Ch'ing Chi saw them, he asked, saying, "How, Sir, did you manage this?" "In the domain of ONE," replied Shê, "there may not be managing. I have heard say that which is carved and polished reverts nevertheless to its natural condition. And so I made allowances for ignorance and for suspicion. I betrayed no feeling when welcomed or dismissed. I forbade not those who came, nor detained those who went away. I showed no resentment towards the unwilling, nor gratitude towards those who gave. Every one subscribed what he liked; and thus in my daily collection of subscriptions, no injury was done.--How much more then those who have the great WAY?"

title.en: The I-êrh Birds of the Eastern Sea (Zhuangzi)
title.zh: 意怠之鳥（莊子）

region.en: Between Ch'ên and Ts'ai, where Confucius starved (Zhoukou, Henan, China)
region.zh: 陳蔡之間（今河南周口一帶）

period: Zhuangzi ch. 20, c. 4th-3rd c. BCE (trans. Giles, 1889)

source.work: Chuang Tzu: Mystic, Moralist, and Social Reformer, trans. Herbert A. Giles, ch. 20

summary.en: Hemmed in between Ch'ên and Ts'ai for seven days without food, Confucius is told by the minister Jen the way not to die: the i-êrh birds of the eastern sea fly simultaneously and roost in a body, none striving to be first, eating only the leavings of others — and so the outside world cannot harm them. Straight trees are the first felled; sweet wells are soonest exhausted.
summary.zh: 孔子圍於陳蔡之間，七日不火食。大公任往弔之——東海有意怠之鳥：其為鳥也，翪翪爾而飛，進不敢為前，退不敢為後；食不敢先嘗，取其餘——是以不入於俗而外乎世也。

sensitivity.note: Canonical text of the Taoist canon (Nanhua zhenjing). Included as a comparative text — a scholarly framing, not a claim about religious truth.

passages.text: When Confucius was hemmed in between Ch'ên and Ts'ai, he passed seven days without food. The minister Jen went to condole with him, and said, "You were near, Sir, to death." "I was indeed," replied Confucius. "Do you fear death, Sir?" enquired Jen. "I do," said Confucius. "Then I will try to teach you," said Jen, "the way not to die.

"In the eastern sea there are certain birds, called the i-êrh. They behave themselves in a modest and unassuming manner, as though unpossessed of ability. They fly simultaneously: they roost in a body. In advancing, none strives to be first; in retreating, none ventures to be last. In eating, none will be the first to begin; it is considered proper to take the leavings of others. Therefore, in their own ranks they are at peace, and the outside world is unable to harm them. And thus they escape trouble. "Straight trees are the first felled. Sweet wells are soonest exhausted. And you, you make a show of your knowledge in order to startle fools. You cultivate yourself in contrast to the degradation of others. And you blaze along as though the sun and moon were under your arms; consequently, you cannot avoid trouble."

"Good indeed!" replied Confucius; and forthwith he took leave of his friends and dismissed his disciples and retired to the wilds, where he dressed himself in skins and serge and fed on acorns and chestnuts. He passed among the beasts and birds and they took no heed of him. And if so, how much more among men?

title.en: Lin Hui Casts Aside the Regalia and Carries Off the Child (Zhuangzi)
title.zh: 林回棄千金之璧，負赤子而趨（莊子）

region.en: The flight from the fall of Kuo (symbolic pin: Sanmenxia, Henan, China)
region.zh: 國亡奔逃之路（象徵定位：河南三門峽）

period: Zhuangzi ch. 20, c. 4th-3rd c. BCE (trans. Giles, 1889)

source.work: Chuang Tzu: Mystic, Moralist, and Social Reformer, trans. Herbert A. Giles, ch. 20

summary.en: When the men of Kuo fled, Lin Hui cast aside most valuable regalia and carried away his child upon his back. The regalia involved a mere question of money, he said; the child was from God. The friendship of the superior man is negative like water; the friendship of the mean man is full-flavoured like wine — the one passes from the negative to the affectionate, the other from the full-flavoured to nothing.
summary.zh: 林回曰：彼以利合，此以天屬也。夫以利合者，迫窮禍患害相棄也；以天屬者，迫窮禍患害相收也——君子之交淡若水，小人之交甘若醴。

sensitivity.note: Canonical text of the Taoist canon (Nanhua zhenjing). Included as a comparative text — a scholarly framing, not a claim about religious truth.

passages.text: Confucius asked Tzŭ Sang Hu, saying, "I have been twice expelled from Lu. My tree was cut down in Sung. I have been tabooed in Wei. I am a failure in Shang and Chou. I was surrounded between Ch'ên and Ts'ai. And in addition to all these troubles, my friends have separated from me and my disciples are gone. How is this?" "Have you not heard," replied Sang Hu, "how when the men of Kuo fled, one of them, named Lin Hui, cast aside most valuable regalia and carried away his child upon his back?

Lin Hui himself said, 'The regalia involved a mere question of money. The child was from God.' "And so it is that in trouble and calamity mere money questions are neglected, while we ever cling nearer to that which is from God. ... "The friendship of the superior man is negative like water. The friendship of the mean man is full-flavoured like wine. That of the superior man passes from the negative to the affectionate. That of the mean man passes from the full-flavoured to nothing." "I hear and obey," replied Confucius; and forthwith he went quietly home, put an end to his studies and cast aside his books. His disciples no longer saluted him as teacher; but his love for them deepened every day.

title.en: The Climbing Ape, the Bramble Bush, and the Prince of Wei (Zhuangzi)
title.zh: 莊子衣大布而補之，猿楠之喻（莊子）

region.en: The Wei court (Anyang region, Henan, China)
region.zh: 魏廷（今河南安陽一帶）

period: Zhuangzi ch. 20, c. 4th-3rd c. BCE (trans. Giles, 1889)

source.work: Chuang Tzu: Mystic, Moralist, and Social Reformer, trans. Herbert A. Giles, ch. 20

summary.en: Chuang Tzŭ, in patched cotton clothes, visits the prince of Wei, who cries that he looks miserable. It is poverty, not misery: give a climbing ape a large tree and it twirls as monarch of all it surveys; put it in a bramble bush and it trembles with fear — living under foolish sovereigns and wicked ministers, how should any one help being miserable? It was under such circumstances that Pi Kan was disembowelled.
summary.zh: 莊子衣大布而補之，正緳繫履而過魏王。王曰：何先生之憊邪？莊子曰：貧也，非憊也——處勢不便，未足以逞其能也。今處昏上亂相之間，而欲無憊，奚可得邪？

sensitivity.note: Canonical text of the Taoist canon (Nanhua zhenjing). Included as a comparative text — a scholarly framing, not a claim about religious truth.

passages.text: Chuang Tzŭ put on cotton clothes with patches in them, and arranging his girdle and tieing on his shoes, went to see the prince of Wei. "How miserable you look, Sir!" cried the prince. "It is poverty, not misery," replied Chuang Tzŭ. "A man who has TAO cannot be miserable. Ragged clothes and old boots make poverty, not misery. Mine is what is called being out of harmony with one's age.

"Has your Highness never seen a climbing ape? Give it some large tree, and it will twist and twirl among the branches as though monarch of all it surveys. Yi and Fêng Mêng can never catch a glimpse of it. But put it in a bramble bush, and it will move cautiously with sidelong glances, trembling all over with fear. Not that its muscles relax in the face of difficulty, but because it is at a disadvantage as regards position, and is unable to make use of its skill. And how should any one, living under foolish sovereigns and wicked ministers, help being miserable, even though he might wish not to be so? It was under such circumstances that Pi Kan was disembowelled."

title.en: The Mantis, the Cicada, and the Strange Bird of Tiao-ling Park (Zhuangzi)
title.zh: 螳螂捕蟬，異鵲在後（莊子）

region.en: The park at Tiao-ling (symbolic pin: Xiangyang, Hubei, China)
region.zh: 彫陵之樊（象徵定位：湖北襄陽）

period: Zhuangzi ch. 20, c. 4th-3rd c. BCE (trans. Giles, 1889)

source.work: Chuang Tzu: Mystic, Moralist, and Social Reformer, trans. Herbert A. Giles, ch. 20

summary.en: In the park at Tiao-ling Chuang Tzŭ sees a strange bird with wings seven feet across fly past his head into a chestnut grove. Stalking it with his cross-bow, he finds a cicada enjoying the shade, a mantis springing upon it — forgetting its own body, which the bird pounces on, forgetting its own nature. Loss follows the pursuit of gain, cries Chuang Tzŭ, and is driven from the park as a thief; for three months he does not leave the house.
summary.zh: 莊周遊於彫陵，睹一異鵲自南方來者；翼廣七尺，目大運寸，感周之顙——見得而忘其形，異鵲從而利之，見利而忘其真。物固相累，二類相召也。

sensitivity.note: Canonical text of the Taoist canon (Nanhua zhenjing); the mantis-stalks-the-cicada scene is one of the most widely popularised images in Chinese art. Included as a comparative text.

passages.text: When Chuang Tzŭ was wandering in the park at Tiao-ling, he saw a strange bird which came from the south. Its wings were seven feet across. Its eyes were an inch in circumference. And it flew close past Chuang Tzŭ's head to alight in a chestnut grove. "What manner of bird is this?" cried Chuang Tzŭ. "With strong wings it does not fly away. With large eyes it does not see." So he picked up his skirts and strode towards it with his cross-bow, anxious to get a shot. Just then he saw a cicada enjoying itself in the shade, forgetful of all else. And he saw a mantis spring and seize it, forgetting in the act its own body, which the strange bird immediately pounced upon and made its prey. And this it was which had caused the bird to forget its own nature.

"Alas!" cried Chuang Tzŭ with a sigh, "how creatures injure one another. Loss follows the pursuit of gain." So he laid aside his bow and went home, driven away by the park-keeper who wanted to know what business he had there. For three months after this, Chuang Tzŭ did not leave the house; and at length Lin Chü asked him, saying, "Master, how is it that you have not been out for so long?" "While keeping my physical frame," replied Chuang Tzŭ, "I lost sight of my real self. Gazing at muddy water, I lost sight of the clear abyss. ... Now when I strolled into the park at Tiao-ling, I forgot my real self. That strange bird which flew close past me to the chestnut grove, forgot its nature. The keeper of the chestnut grove took me for a thief. Consequently I have not been out."

title.en: The Innkeeper's Beautiful and Ugly Concubines (Zhuangzi)
title.zh: 陽子之宋，逆旅人有妾二人（莊子）

region.en: An inn in the Sung State (Shangqiu, Henan, China)
region.zh: 宋國逆旅（今河南商丘）

period: Zhuangzi ch. 20, c. 4th-3rd c. BCE (trans. Giles, 1889)

source.work: Chuang Tzu: Mystic, Moralist, and Social Reformer, trans. Herbert A. Giles, ch. 20

summary.en: Passing a night at a Sung inn, Yang Tzŭ finds the innkeeper loves his ugly concubine and hates the beautiful one. The beautiful one is so conscious of her beauty that one does not think her beautiful; the ugly one so conscious of her ugliness that one does not think her ugly. Note this, my disciples: be virtuous, but without being consciously so, and wherever you go, you will be beloved.
summary.zh: 陽子之宋，宿於逆旅。逆旅人有妾二人，其一人美，其一人惡；惡者貴而美者賤。美者自美，吾不知其美也；惡者自惡，吾不知其惡也。

sensitivity.note: Canonical text of the Taoist canon (Nanhua zhenjing). Included as a comparative text — a scholarly framing, not a claim about religious truth.

passages.text: When Yang Tzŭ went to the Sung State, he passed a night at an inn. The innkeeper had two concubines, one beautiful, the other ugly. The latter he loved; the former, he hated. Yang Tzŭ asked how this was; whereupon one of the inn servants said, "The beautiful one is so conscious of her beauty that one does not think her beautiful. The ugly one is so conscious of her ugliness that one does not think her ugly." "Note this, my disciples!" cried Yang Tzŭ. "Be virtuous, but without being consciously so; and wherever you go, you will be beloved."

title.en: Joachim and Anna: The Childless Offering
title.zh: 約雅敬與亞拿：無子者的奉獻

region.en: Jerusalem temple and shepherd pastures
region.zh: 耶路撒冷聖殿與牧人草場

period: Gospel of the Birth of Mary, c. 150 CE (Wake trans., Hone, 1820)

source.work: The Forbidden Gospels and Epistles: The Gospel of the Birth of Mary, chaps. 1-2 (trans. Wake, in Hone, 1820)

license: Public domain (Wake translation, 18th c., ed. Hone 1820)

summary.en: The pious couple Joachim and Anna, childless for twenty years, vow any child to the Lord; the high priest Issachar publicly rejects Joachim's offerings — 'cursed is every one who shall not beget a male in Israel.' Shamed, Joachim retires to the shepherds, where an angel of the Lord appears 'with a prodigious light', recalling Sarah and Rachel: 'when he shuts the womb of any person, he does it for this reason, that he may in a more wonderful manner again open it' — and promises a daughter to be called Mary.
summary.zh: 敬虔的約雅敬與亞拿無子二十年，起誓將孩子獻與主；大祭司以薩迦當眾拒其奉獻——「凡在以色列中不生男丁的，都是被咒詛的」。約雅敬羞愧退到牧人中間，主的使者帶著大光顯現，引撒拉與拉結為例：「神封閉人的胎，是為要以更奇妙的方式再開啟——使所生的不是情慾之果，而是神的恩賜」——並應許生女取名馬利亞。

sensitivity.note: Apocryphal infancy-cycle text, formative for the Marian traditions (Nativity of Mary feast). Presented as legendary narrative, distinct from canonical scripture.

passages.text: Their lives were plain and right in the sight of the Lord, pious and faultless before men; for they divided all their substance into three parts; one of which they devoted to the temple and officers of the temple; another they distributed among strangers, and persons in poor circumstances; and the third they reserved for themselves and the uses of their own family. In this manner they lived for about twenty years chastely, in the favour of God, and the esteem of men, without any children.

Who, when he saw Joachim along with the rest of his neighbours, bringing his offerings, despised both him and his offerings, and asked him, Why he, who had no children, would presume to appear among those who had? Adding, that his offerings could never be acceptable to God; the Scripture having said, Cursed is every one who shall not beget a male in Israel. But Joachim being much confounded with the shame of such reproach, retired to the shepherds who were with the cattle in their pastures.

On a certain day when he was alone, the angel of the Lord stood by him with a prodigious light. And the angel who had appeared to him, endeavouring to compose him, said: Be not afraid, Joachim, nor troubled at the sight of me, for I am an angel of the Lord sent by him to you, that I might inform you that your prayers are heard, and your alms ascended in the sight of God. For God is the avenger of sin, and not of nature; and so when he shuts the womb of any person, he does it for this reason, that he may in a more wonderful manner again open it, and that which is born appear to be not the product of lust, but the gift of God.

title.en: Mary Danced on the Altar Steps
title.zh: 馬利亞在祭壇臺階上跳躍

region.en: Temple of the Lord, Jerusalem
region.zh: 耶路撒冷，主的聖殿

period: Protevangelion of James, c. 150 CE (Wake trans., Hone, 1820)

source.work: The Forbidden Gospels and Epistles: The Protevangelion, chaps. 7-8 (trans. Wake, in Hone, 1820)

license: Public domain (Wake translation, 18th c., ed. Hone 1820)

summary.en: At three years old Mary is led to the temple by virgins bearing lamps 'that the child may not turn back again', received by the high priest — 'Mary, the Lord God hath magnified thy name to all generations' — placed on the third step of the altar, and there 'the Lord gave unto her grace, and she danced with her feet, and all the house of Israel loved her.' She is kept in the temple 'as a dove educated there', fed by the hand of an angel — the founding legend of the Presentation of Mary.
summary.zh: 三歲的馬利亞由持燈的童女引領入殿——「免得孩子回頭，心裏不願往主的殿去」——大祭司接納她並祝福：「馬利亞，主神已使你的名在萬代中得尊崇。」把她安置在祭壇第三級臺階上，「主賜她恩典，她便以足跳舞，以色列全家都愛她」。她如鴿子般住在殿中，「從天使手中得食」——馬利亞進殿節的傳說本源。

sensitivity.note: Apocryphal; formative for the Presentation of Mary feast. Legendary narrative, distinct from canonical scripture.

passages.text: But the girl grew, and when she was two years old, Joachim said to Anna, Let us lead her to the temple of the Lord, that we may perform our vow. And Anna said, Let us wait the third year, lest she should be at a loss to know her father. And when the child was three years old, Joachim said, Let us invite the daughters of the Hebrews, who are undefiled, and let them take each a lamp, and let them be lighted, that the child may not turn back again, and her mind be set against the temple of the Lord. And they did thus till they ascended into the temple of the Lord.

And the high-priest received her, and blessed her, and said, Mary, the Lord God hath magnified thy name to all generations, and to the very end of time by thee will the Lord shew his redemption to the children of Israel. And he placed her upon the third step of the altar, and the Lord gave unto her grace, and she danced with her feet, and all the house of Israel loved her. And her parents went away filled with wonder, and praising God, because the girl did not return back to them.

But Mary continued in the temple as a dove educated there, and received her food from the hand of an angel. And when she was twelve years of age, the priests met in a council, and said, Behold, Mary is twelve years of age, what shall we do with her, for fear lest the holy place of the Lord our God should be defiled?

title.en: The Rods of the Widowers and Joseph's Dove
title.zh: 鰥夫之杖與約瑟杖上的鴿子

region.en: Temple of the Lord, Jerusalem
region.zh: 耶路撒冷，主的聖殿

period: Protevangelion of James, c. 150 CE (Wake trans., Hone, 1820)

source.work: The Forbidden Gospels and Epistles: The Protevangelion, chap. 8 (trans. Wake, in Hone, 1820)

license: Public domain (Wake translation, 18th c., ed. Hone 1820)

summary.en: To keep the temple undefiled, the angel tells Zacharias to summon all the widowers of Judaea, 'every one of them bring his rod, and he by whom the Lord shall shew a sign shall be the husband of Mary.' The trumpet sounds, all assemble, and as the high priest prays over the rods, a dove comes forth from Joseph's rod and alights on his head. The old carpenter protests he has children and wants no wife; he is compelled, takes Mary home, and returns to his trade.
summary.zh: 為免聖所玷污，天使命撒迦利亞召集猶太全境的鰥夫，「各人拿自己的杖來，主藉誰顯出記號，誰就是馬利亞的丈夫」。吹角聚集後，大祭司拿杖禱告——「約瑟杖中飛出一隻鴿子，落在約瑟頭上」。老木匠連連推辭——「我有兒女，已經年老，再娶妻子豈合宜」——終被勸服，攜馬利亞回家，隨即重操建築舊業。

sensitivity.note: Apocryphal betrothal legend; the sign-by-rod is a divination type noted as such.

passages.text: And behold the angel of the Lord came to him, and said, Zacharias, Zacharias, Go forth and call together all the widowers among the people, and let every one of them bring his rod, and he by whom the Lord shall shew a sign shall be the husband of Mary. And the criers went out through all Judaea, and the trumpet of the Lord sounded, and all the people ran and met together. And Joseph also throwing away his hatchet, went out to meet them; and when they were met, they went to the high-priest; taking every man his rod.

After the high-priest had received their rods, he went into the temple to pray; and when he had finished his prayer, he took the rods, and went forth and distributed them; and there was no miracle attending the last rod which Joseph took. But Joseph took the rod first of all the people... for a dove came out of the rod, and alighted upon his head.

title.en: Joseph's Dream and the Water of Ordeal
title.zh: 約瑟的夢與苦水試驗

region.en: Jerusalem, temple and courts
region.zh: 耶路撒冷，聖殿與院中

period: Protevangelion of James, c. 150 CE (Wake trans., Hone, 1820)

source.work: The Forbidden Gospels and Epistles: The Protevangelion, chaps. 10-11 (trans. Wake, in Hone, 1820)

license: Public domain (Wake translation, 18th c., ed. Hone 1820)

summary.en: Returning from building houses, Joseph finds his espoused wife grown big, and grieves in Adam's words — 'the serpent came and found Eve alone.' Mary answers with tears, 'I am innocent, and have known no man'; an angel settles the matter in a dream. Yet the scribe Annas drags both before the priest, and they drink the water of the Lord's ordeal, like the Sotah of Numbers — 'if any secret sin be in you, it will appear in your eyes' — and both go home unharmed, glorifying God.
summary.zh: 建屋歸來，約瑟見訂婚的妻已懷身孕，便照亞當的話哀哭——「蛇來時，夏娃獨自一人」。馬利亞流淚答「我是清白的，我從未認識男人」；天使在夢中化解此事。文士亞拿斯卻把二人拖到祭司面前，叫他們喝主的水行 ordeal（如民數記疑妻法）——「你們若隱瞞罪惡，必在你們眼中顯明」——二人毫無損傷回家，榮耀歸神。

sensitivity.note: Apocryphal; the ordeal mirrors Numbers 5's Sotah rite; presented as legend.

passages.text: AND when her sixth month was come, Joseph returned from his building houses abroad, which was his trade, and entering into the house, found the Virgin grown big: then smiting upon his face, he said, With what face can I look up to the Lord my God? For I received her a Virgin out of the temple of the Lord my God, and have not preserved her such! Is not the history of Adam exactly accomplished in me? For in the very instant of his glory, the serpent came and found Eve alone, and seduced her. Just after the same manner it has happened to me.

But she, with a flood of tears, replied, I am innocent, and have known no man. Then said Joseph, How comes it to pass you are with child? Mary answered, As the Lord my God liveth, I know not by what means.
